A most accurate edition, easily to be preferred to all others if the following are weighed: the clarity of the type, the quality of the paper, the integrity of the text, the perfection of the correction, both the variety and number of works reprinted, the very convenient format of the volumes and its consistent uniformity throughout the whole course of the work, the low price, and especially this single, methodical, chronological collection of six hundred fragments and short works hitherto scattered here and there, but now for the first time brought together in our library from works belonging to every age, place, language, and form.

**IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1158: PETER THE VENERABLE, NINTH ABBOT OF CLUNY**

[Col. 0009]

## Historical Notice

(*Gallia Christiana nova*, vol. IV, col. 1137)

[Col. 0009A] Peter I, son of Maurice de Montboissier, surnamed the Venerable because of his outstanding knowledge of sacred and secular learning joined to remarkable uprightness of life, deserves to be celebrated with the highest praise among the abbots of Cluny. He was born in Auvergne, of the ancient and noble lineage of Montboissier, the seventh son of Maurice, lord of Montboissier, and Raingard, later a nun at Marcigny. In Letter 17 of Book II, he records that, as he was returning from the Council of Pisa, news was brought to him of her death in 1134.

The devout married pair piously and religiously brought up their children. One of these, Heraclius, became Archbishop of Lyons; Pontius became Abbot of Vézelay, Jordan Abbot of Chaise-Dieu, Armannus Prior of Cluny and thereafter Abbot of Manglieu; and this Peter served his novitiate under Blessed Hugh [Col. 0009B] with great renown for religious life. He was then Prior of Vézelay; finally, after the death of Hugh II on 9 July 1122, he was chosen abbot at nearly thirty years of age, on the octave of the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin Mary, 22 August. He was blessed by the Bishop of Besançon, as is proved by the records of his election from the Celsinian codex, manuscript vol. IV of *Historical Fragments*, fol. 31, inserted there by our Dom Claude Estiennot.

Thereafter Peter never failed to show himself a most worthy minister. In 1125, on the fourth day before the Nones of April, Pope Honorius II, in the first year of his pontificate and the third indiction, granted him an important privilege, published in vol. X of the *Councils*, p. 910. In return, this holy abbot’s loyalty and zeal toward the Holy See were conspicuous in 1130, when Pope Innocent II came to Gaul. Peter sent to meet him sixty caparisoned horses or mules, for the unrestricted use of the pope, cardinals, and those in his company. This was despite the fact that Anacletus, the rival of this pope, had been a monk of Cluny and defended his own election to the chair of St Peter by arguments not wholly to be despised.

The pope then remained at Cluny for eleven days. There, on 25 October, he consecrated the basilica which still survives, under the title of St Peter, on the very day on which Urban II had long before consecrated its high altar. In 1132 he held a general chapter, at which two hundred priors were counted, and with them he promulgated certain decrees to strengthen regular discipline, which had already begun to decline. In the following, twelfth year of his rule, he confirmed an exchange of the church of Montmartre with the church of St Dionysius in Prison. In the same year, on the sixth day before the Nones of March, Pope Innocent II, in the third year of his pontificate and the eleventh indiction, granted him a charter of protection.

Under the same pope he attended the Roman, or Second Lateran, Council in 1138. He was afterwards honoured by that pope with many letters: 28, 29, 31, 33, and others. He was likewise dear to Innocent’s successors: Celestine II, who informed him of his own election; Lucius II, Eugenius III, and Adrian IV, who wrote to him. In 1144, on the Ides of May, he was present at Rome when Lucius II issued a bull [Col. 0010B] concerning the subjection of the Church of Dol to that of Tours.

Two years later he collected into a single body all seventy-six statutes which he had made over twenty-four years and ordered their observance. There is no doubt that he is the Abbot of Cluny indicated by the letter P., who, together with Brocard, Prior of Souvigny, lent five hundred marks of silver to Aymon’s son, who was going to Jerusalem with Louis, King of the Franks. In 1147, Archimbald and his wife Agnes, the countess, swore at the altar of St Maiolus, before many witnesses, that they would repay them, according to the cartulary of Souvigny.

Peter also received no small praise from his disciples: “A wise son is his father’s glory.” I shall name two among many. The first is Alger, canon of Liège, greatly renowned for many writings, especially for his excellent treatise *On the Sacrament of the Body and Blood of the Lord against Berengar*. At approximately the time when Peter was elected abbot, Alger embraced monastic life in the same monastery, and after spending ten years in great innocence and humility of life, died in 1130 or 1131. The other is Peter Abelard, long tossed about, who at last, when received at Cluny as a monk by Abbot Peter, clearly found a harbour of salvation and tranquillity. At that time, say the authors of the *Gallia Christiana*, there were 460 monks in the monastery, though Peter himself declares that there had been only three hundred [Col. 0011A] when he assumed the government. Thus under his leadership the Cluniac order, spread throughout the Christian world, flourished so greatly that it possessed monasteries even in the Valley of Jehoshaphat and on Mount Tabor.

In 1153, in the first indiction, on the third day before the Ides of June, Frederick, king of the Romans, at this abbot’s request granted him a charter confirming both the donation of the monastery of Baume and other possessions made to the Church of Cluny. In the following year Abbot Peter granted an indulgence to the churches of Cluny established in Italy, as testified by the subscription of Arnold, Abbot of Aurillac.

Moreover, he was renowned not only for character and learning, but also for his own writings and those of others, as is clearly shown by so many tributes of learned men. Among them it is appropriate to cite that of Peter of Poitiers, his secretary, who wrote to him:

> “What Plato ever reasoned more subtly? What Aristotle more argumentatively? What Cicero ever discoursed more beautifully or copiously? What grammarian was more learned, what rhetorician more ornate, what dialectician more forceful, what arithmetician more numerate, what geometer more regular, what musician more melodious, what astronomer more penetrating? And, if we dare say anything concerning the holy Fathers, from each of the four rivers of Paradise which, after the holy Evangelists, water the whole world, you have brought back something similar: for you proceed swift with Jerome, copious with Augustine, profound with Ambrose, and clear with Gregory.”

A collected account of Abbot Peter’s life, tributes, and writings may be found in vol. XXII of the Lyons *Library of the Fathers*, p. 812 and following. [Col. 0011C] That he shone among the foremost doctors of his age is attested by his books against the Jews, the Muslims, and the Petrobrusians, written in defence of Christ’s divinity; and by his six books of letters. To these, beyond those commonly published, add three others of great importance, mentioned by the distinguished Dom Fleury in vol. XV of his *Ecclesiastical History*.

Perhaps, however, some will be surprised to find among those works a translation of the Qur’an, which he arranged to have made by several learned men while staying in Spain to inspect and visit the monasteries of his order. Yet he published it for no other purpose than to refute the ravings and dreams of the false prophet Muhammad—and this he did. See Alberic’s *Chronicle*, under the year 1143, p. 301.

Finally, after holding the office of abbot for thirty-five years, four months, and four days, he was transferred to the blessed realms above at Cluny in 1158, on the Kalends of January, according to Robert of Torigni; or rather, according to the Cluniac Chronicle in Miraeus, *Origins of the Order of St Benedict*, p. 93, on the first day of the year. But that the year there began on Christmas Day is evident because on p. 96 of that work he is said to have died on Christmas Day itself, that is, the eighth day before the Kalends of January. On that day he is enrolled among the saints in the Benedictine monastic martyrology.

He was buried there by Henry, Bishop of Winchester, brother of Stephen, king of the English, beside the altar of Saints James and Philip; or, as Miraeus says in the passage cited, at the head of the great new basilica. This Peter, as is noted there on p. 94, relieved the Church of Cluny, which was burdened by a heavy weight of debt, of almost all the burden of its obligations through his prudence and expenditures. Thus, both in paying debts, repairing properties, and acquiring necessary provisions for the household, he spent, as we heard from his own lips, more than seven thousand marks of silver.

His epitaph, as it appears in the *Bibliotheca Cluniacensis*, is as follows:

> This tomb makes clear that life is not lasting.  
> Whatever we are, the earth makes us equal in death.  
> When Peter, the devout abbot, dies, justice is buried;  
> Peace falls, order lies prostrate; it is fitting to weep and die.  
> He was his country’s salvation, the world’s adornment, wisdom’s ark;  
> [Col. 0012C] Knowing no envy, he was a fountain of pardon.  
> On the solemn morning of the day of God’s Nativity,  
> Having died, he attained the many things he deserved.

Besides the monk of Poitiers, Abbot Peter is mentioned by St Bernard of Clairvaux, Suger, Abbot of St Denis, and Peter of Celle, abbots whose many letters to him, and his in return to them, survive; by Robert of Torigni, Matthew Paris, Baronius in the *Annals*, and other ecclesiastical writers on illustrious men. They are set out very fully in the notes to the *Bibliotheca Cluniacensis* edited by André Duchesne.

[Col. 0011]

## Literary Notice

[Col. 0011D] Peter Maurice of Montboissier, surnamed the Venerable, of the Benedictine Order, was ninth Abbot of Cluny from 1122 to 1156. His *Life*, written by the monk Ralph, his disciple, and addressed to Stephen, Abbot of Cluny, appeared in vol. VI of Edmond Martène’s *Monuments*, pp. 1187–1201. In André Duchesne’s *Bibliotheca Cluniacensis*, Paris, 1614, folio, p. 589, there appears a life of him drawn from an old chronicle.

The *Life of Abbot Peter* from the Cluniac Chronicle; [Col. 0012D] and on p. 602 the testimonies of earlier writers concerning him: St Bernard, Letters 277 and 283; Robert of Torigni; Matthew Paris; Henry of Ghent, ch. 29; Nicholas de Clamanges; Johannes Trithemius, ch. 418 of *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, and II.123 of *Illustrious Benedictines*; and others. Then, on p. 607, the monk Peter of Poitiers’ Letter to Peter Mauricius; a panegyric written in elegiac verse upon Abbot Peter’s first arrival in Aquitaine II; and an invective against a slanderer, p. 616 and vol. XXII of the Lyons *Library of the Fathers*, p. 820. Another letter to [Col. 0013A] the same Peter is on p. 618 (Lyons, p. 825), urging him to publish monuments of his genius.

We owe a fuller and more correct edition of Maurice’s works, also furnished with notes, to the editors of the same *Bibliotheca Cluniacensis*. It is found in vol. XXII of the Lyons *Library of the Fathers*, where the first place is occupied, on p. 621 (Lyons, p. 826), by the six books of Letters, long ago published by Pierre de Montmartre, Paris, 1522, folio. To these are appended, on p. 959 (Lyons, p. 967), eight letters by or to Peter which were absent from the old edition. François Duchesne extracted six historical letters from the published collection and reprinted them in *Writers of French Affairs*, vol. IV, pp. 458–491.

[Col. 0013B] Letter to Peter of Saint-Jean against those who say that Christ never openly called himself God in the Gospel, p. 966 (Lyons, p. 970).

*Treatise against the Jews’ inveterate obstinacy*, p. 983 (Lyons, p. 977), from the Ingolstadt edition of 1546.

Letter to St Bernard, Abbot of Clairvaux, concerning his translation—that is, the translation which he caused to be made from Arabic into Latin of [Note: [Col. 0013D] Compare Alberic’s *Chronicle*, p. 301.] the sect or heresy of the Saracens in 1143—together with a brief summary against the heresies and the sect of diabolical deceit of the Saracens, or Ishmaelites, etc., p. 1109 (Lyons, p. 1030); with Robert of Ketton’s preface to the book of the Qur’an translated by him, p. 1116 (Lyons, p. 1033). [Col. 0013C] Add what I have noted in the selection of arguments for the truth of the faith, p. 264 ff., and below under Robert.

Letter or Treatise against the Petrobrusian heretics, p. 1128 (Lyons, p. 1033), from the Ingolstadt edition of 1546, quarto, prepared by Johann Hofmeister together with certain sermons and letters of St Bernard.

Sermon on the Transfiguration of Our Lord Jesus Christ, p. 1231 (Lyons, p. 1080), and in Combefis’s *Concionatory Library*. It begins: “Today, beloved, a day more serene than usual has dawned for us.”

Two books *On the Miracles of His Own Time*, p. 1247 (Lyons, p. 1087), also printed separately many times, for example at Douai, 1595, duodecimo.

[Col. 0013D] Rhythms, prose pieces, verses, and hymns, p. 1338 (Lyons, p. 1125). First among these is an elegiac poem against the detractors of the poems of Peter of Poitiers, in which he praises many men famous in the Latin Church for their writings and poems. The rhythm in praise of the Saviour begins: “He is sent from the Father.” Here you also have both hymns concerning St Benedict and the translation [Col. 0014A] of St Benedict; these are also printed by Arnold Wion, vol. II of *Lignum Vitae*, p. 102, and by Jean de Bosco in the *Bibliotheca Floriacensis*, p. 376. There is likewise Peter Abelard’s epitaph, beginning: “The Socrates of the Gauls.” But I do not find in the *Bibliotheca Cluniacensis* or the Lyons *Library of the Fathers* the other epitaph, beginning, “Peter lies hidden in this rock”; Louis Jacob, however, has it in *On Writers of Chalon*, p. 142.

Statutes of the Cluniac congregation, with seventy-six diplomas and charters and a prefatory satisfaction or apology, etc., p. 1354 (Lyons, p. 1132).

“It would be superfluous,” says André Duchesne, p. 1118, “to append here the entire translation of the Qur’an.” [Note: [Col. 0013D] On this, see below under Robert of Ketton.] [Col. 0014B] Peter the Venerable himself refuted it in five books; since these, though diligently sought, have not yet been found, the reader here must also lack them. Of the four—not five—books which Maurice wrote, Edmond Martène published the first two, against the accursed sect of the Saracens, from a manuscript codex of Anchin written in the author’s own age, in vol. IX of the *Monuments*, p. 1121. He prefixed Peter of Poitiers’ letter, along with the chapter summaries not only of the first and second books but also of the third and fourth, which no one has yet published. Peter of Poitiers declares that he had been the associate of Peter of Toledo and Robert, archdeacon and later of Pamplona, in translating the Qur’an.

We owe to the same Edmond Martène, in vol. V of the *Treasury of Anecdotes*, p. 1419, three sermons: on praise of the Lord’s tomb; on St Marcellus, pope and martyr; and on the veneration of relics. Also five letters in vol. I of the *Anecdotes*, pp. 406 ff. and 416; likewise two other letters to Mabillon, vol. III of the *Analecta*, p. 481 (new edition, p. 159); and the poem *On Virtue*, which begins:

> The world’s adornment, the glory of things, has abandoned the earth—  
> Virtue.

Manuscript in the Pauline Library at Leipzig, according to Joachim Feller, p. 299. The poem on the rites of the Mass, which under the name of Maurice I appended to the first edition of my *Antiquarian Bibliography*, Hamburg, 1713, quarto, I afterwards sufficiently established to have Hildebert of Le Mans as its author, as I acknowledged in the preface to vol. VI of the *Greek Library*. Peter of Cluny’s *Kernel on the Sacrifice of the Mass*, after Hildebert and Rupert of Deutz, was published in the Roman edition of the books *On the Offices and Ministries of the Catholic Church*, 1591, folio, and in vol. X of the Paris *Library of the Fathers*, 1644. [Note: [Col. 0013D] “Nor is it certainly less true that he composed the same treatise *On the Sacrifice of the Mass*, which was added under the name *Kernel* to the latest edition of the *Library of the Fathers*. But when we had carefully considered what he wrote about the Mass against the Petrobrusian heretics, we immediately recognized it to be a section of that letter or book,” says André Duchesne in the prefatory warning to the notes of the *Bibliotheca Cluniacensis*.]

[Col. 0015]

# Life of Peter the Venerable, Ninth Abbot of Cluny, by Ralph, a Monk and His Disciple

(Dom Martène, *Amplissima Collectio*, vol. VI, col. 1187, from a manuscript of the monastery of Souvigny.)

## Preliminary Observation

Since the monastery of Cluny has the privilege that nearly all its earliest abbots were saints, and accounts of their deeds written by serious men circulate widely, all learned persons have hitherto regretted that the great deeds of Peter the Venerable—ninth abbot of that most famous monastery, scarcely second to others in nobility of birth, holiness of life, or abundance of learning—have been lacking down to this day. Yet an ancient codex from the monastery of Souvigny has at last repaired this loss, for in it I was fortunate enough to discover a work by the monk Ralph on this subject.

Ralph had formerly been a disciple of the holy abbot and was at times his companion on journeys and in the visitation of dependent houses, as is evident from chapter 7. He is therefore an eyewitness of the things he relates, and states this expressly in the prologue in these words: “I shall undertake to write of his life, not so much from presumption as from love, relating what I have learned from the accounts of religious men or have myself seen.” If my judgment does not deceive me, I conjecture that Ralph, author of the *Life of Abbot Peter*, is the same Ralph who was made Abbot of Cluny in 1173, voluntarily resigned that dignity three years later, and died in 1176.

Mabillon would have said much more concerning Peter the Venerable, and matters more worthy of so great an abbot, had he been able to complete the seventh Benedictine century, containing the lives of the saints who flourished in our order in the twelfth century. But since death forestalled him and left his undertaking unfinished, we meanwhile present Ralph’s study of Abbot Peter of Cluny.

## Prologue

[Col. 0015A] To the holy father and his lord, **Stephen**, by the grace of God Abbot of Cluny: Brother **Ralph**, the enjoyment of every good thing, now and for ever.

For a long time, Father, I kept silent, and because of modesty did not dare say what I desired to say. But my spirit is troubled within me because the life of our Father, Abbot Peter of blessed memory—a life to be recalled in every age—has been so surrendered to neglect that all of us who loved the man and knew his virtues ought deservedly to be condemned for it. For who, knowing the life and character of so great a father, can remain silent without condemning himself?

Therefore I, the least of all men, shall undertake to write concerning his life, not so much from presumption as from love, relating what I learned from the accounts of religious men or saw myself. I leave greater matters to greater writers, so that God may be honoured thereby, our weakness strengthened by his example, and the Church exalted by the grace bestowed upon her sons; and, finally, that God may always be glorified in his saints, especially in the Church of Cluny.

For this Church filled the world through the offspring of her sons and adorned the children of the West through the grace of religious life, so that there was no region on earth which did not seek from Cluny a father or patron for itself. This is a holy place, [Col. 0016A] and its fathers are always blessed, because, as it excels in the multitude of its religious, so it glories in the Lord through the grace of its virtues. Hence it offers to all a gift of divine grace wonderful to angels and human beings. This is proclaimed in the four quarters of the world; heaven and earth bear witness to it; every sex and every age marvels at it.

It nurtured the blessed fathers Odo, Maiolus, Odilo, and holy Hugh. Like lights in the firmament of heaven, they shone in the world with the light of their splendour, driving away the darkness of humankind. Through their guidance and example they so destroyed people’s wicked deeds that they displayed upon earth the likeness of angels; they shone not only by virtues, but also by miracles. Because they despised themselves, they taught others to despise the world, and by paternal right they left to their adopted sons the discipline of their humility.

The holy election of the aforesaid Father, whose memory is in blessing, follows them. But before we discuss his life, we must speak of his birth and inquire from where he came, who he was, how great, and of what sort. Yet since I see that this surpasses my powers, I must place my confidence in the grace of God, who teaches every person knowledge.

## The Life of Lord Peter the Abbot Begins

[Col. 0017]

[Col. 0017A] **1. His parents. What he was like in the cloister. He is chosen Abbot of Cluny.**—Let us now turn our pen to the history and begin the sacred account of a sacred man. Thus a holy offspring, born from the nobler people of Auvergne, came into the world from his father Maurice and his mother Raingard, parents most honourable by worldly standards.

When his mother had at one time devoutly met Blessed Abbot Hugh, while she was carrying this very child in her womb, the man of God looked at her and said: “Lady, know that the fruit of your womb is dedicated to God and bestowed upon Blessed Peter.” She replied: “Lord, if it is a male, may your will be done.” “Know for certain,” he said, “that it is a male.” When the boy was born, as the man of God had foretold, he was given the distinguished name Peter.

Then, as time passed, the child was entrusted by his parents to learning and was received to be reared in the monastery of Sauxillanges. [Note: [Col. 0017D] In French, *Soucilanges*, which Peter in Book I of *Miracles*, ch. 6, calls a noble monastery. It stands in the diocese of Clermont and is one of the four principal priories of the monastery of Cluny.] The outcome later proved what his childhood was like and how great was his diligence in reading and learning. For through God’s grace he was raised in a short time to such fullness of knowledge that, while still in the early bloom of youth, he was appointed teacher of the elders and guardian of discipline in the monastery of Vézelay. [Note: [Col. 0017D] Vézelay is a distinguished monastery in the diocese of Autun, over which Pontius, brother of Peter the Venerable, later presided. [Col. 0018D]]

After he had vigorously and religiously maintained that office, and had thoroughly watered the new plantation, according to the form of religious life, with the rain of sacred teaching, he was promoted to be prior of Domina. [Note: [Col. 0018D] In French, *Domaine*, a not undistinguished dependent house of Cluny in the diocese of Grenoble.] There he did not forget knowledge and discipline, but advanced more and more toward God. In his youthful years he continually meditated upon that which he would afterwards devoutly fulfil in old age.

[Col. 0017C] He devoted himself to reading and prayer and shone with such splendour of wisdom that he appeared lovable to everyone: gracious in speech, handsome in appearance, admirable in conversation, invincible in eloquence, exceptional in kindness, overflowing with compassionate feeling, sympathetic toward all. Through ineffable charity and inestimable grace, he made his own goodness common to all.

What then? Father Hugh passed from this world to the Father, and Pontius was elected abbot. After governing the Cluniacs for almost fourteen years, and after certain conflicts had arisen, he went to Rome and there voluntarily resigned the abbey, despite the resistance of the supreme pontiff. After him Hugh, Prior of Marcigny, was elected, but he died after a short time. Then the Cluniacs assembled together and poured out prayers to the Lord that God might grant them a shepherd able to benefit them by example and teaching.

When the fast had been completed and the grace of the Holy Spirit invoked, they deliberated over the election, but could not find the one whom God had foreseen. When bishops, abbots, and priors had assembled for the election of the father, Peter too came, according to custom, with the others. Those who had earlier been engaged in a devout contest over the election, when they saw him, all converged upon him with one mind, equal vote, and pious desire. One voice arose from them all, crying together that Peter was worthy of so great an honour, since no grace was lacking to him in any respect.

“This man,” they said, “is noble in birth, adorned in character, devout in faith, pure in religious life, humble and peaceable, brilliant in wisdom, obedient to discipline, and trained in every respect according to the Rule from his earliest age.” Why delay? They rise, rush upon him, seize him, and do everything according to the command of the Rule. They accompany him with the customary acclamations, lead him to the abbatial seat, and he is thus called lord and abbot by all with joy. [Note: [Col. 0018D] This occurred in 1122, indeed on the feast of the Assumption, as he himself relates in Book II of *Miracles*, ch. 12.]

**2. What kind of abbot he was toward his brothers.**—How he conducted himself in the government of the abbey is known to those who adhered to him out of devotion to religious life, and we shall disclose something of it. For we could not attain to all his deeds; but, for edification, we wish briefly to recount certain things worthy of mention.

Thus Abbot Peter, placed over the others, cultivated humility and compunction, judging himself rather than seeking to reprove others. His countenance was serene; he showed kindly care toward the brothers and godly concern for the sick, lest anyone in the house of [Col. 0018C] the Lord be treated negligently. He urged those under him to strive for purity and to purify themselves through confession. In this practice the Father was singular, surpassing all in the sweetness of mercy.

He said that, according to this gift, the good of confession exists in the Church of God, by which every soul is sanctified as if by a sacred baptism. Finally, he had this grace: whoever had confessed to him, he loved with a singular favour, embraced as a counsellor, and cherished. Thus, contrary to the practice of other superiors, all always wished with the greatest desire and love to confess to him, because he knew how to tend and heal both his own wounds and those of others by the medicine of exhortation and consolation—not to expose or publicize them.

He so pursued works of mercy that no one was ever turned away from his assistance. He aided the oppressed, clothed the naked, and fed the hungry. [Col. 0019A] He had particular poor persons to whom he always gave food and clothing. He also built houses for lepers secretly, as though they had been built by someone else, lest the act be credited to himself. Toward the brothers he was so entirely generous that he shared everything of his with those who asked.

For one day, when a monk was shivering from cold and this had been reported to him, he began to grieve because he could find nothing to give. That same night, while in choir, he kept thinking of the unclothed brother and how he might clothe him. Then he summoned him out of choir by a signal, secretly took off his fur garment, and clothed him with it. He did this not only for the brothers but also for pilgrims and the poor, stripping himself so thoroughly that he himself at times lacked clothing.

And because bodily exercise is useful for a little, but godliness for all things, he watched over divine worship so attentively that none like him was found in the office of piety. He was so solemn in divine things, and celebrated the offices with such solemnity, that he became pleasing thereby to angels and human beings, drew everyone’s affection to himself, and drew them with him toward divine things. For above all else in this exile, he thought this a good thing: that God should be glorified in his saints through solemn celebration.

3. He was devoted to sacred reading. He was also attentive to external affairs.—It is not for me to recount in every detail the charity toward the brethren which he preached in affection and deed, and which, by preaching it, he taught still more by action. For he loved the brethren with the inmost fervour of his heart, and cherished and encouraged each one, as if himself, toward [Col. 0019C] divine love. He despised or drove away no one, but with all his heart invited them all, by words and deeds, through divine love to forgiveness. For whoever truly loves is exalted by the favour of his own conscience. He burned with longing, was aflame with love, and despised the world through steadfastness of mind. He said that present things were nothing, and maintained that all would be glorified by the blessings to come. He also taught that one who wished to aspire to heavenly delights could never desire these lowest things in his heart.

Among the people of God he appeared most gentle, and proved a most acute investigator of the divine law, so much so that through zeal for holy reading he became a stranger to his own people and to himself; wholly devoting himself to the sacred books, he drew from the fountains of the Saviour what he would afterwards pour forth freely. He kept teachers about him, from whom he always desired to learn by inquiry, although all regarded him as wonderful in knowledge. He was not lifted up, nor did he make himself great; but, like a little child searching divine things, he continually preferred, with all his desires, to learn. As a kindly father, he taught his own men humility, patience, goodness, gentleness, and to keep their conscience in purity with fear and trembling, preferring in all things the grace of piety, as good sons of the manifold grace of God.

How great was the care that he bestowed even upon external affairs is evident [Col. 0020A] from what accrued to the monastery through his labour. With vigorous diligence he not only built the church, but also adorned it wonderfully with costly ornaments; he enlarged its lands; and he so prudently arranged those things needed by the brethren at different times that, in each month, every man should serve the Fathers from the household entrusted to him, so that by this arrangement the convent might always remain in peace. He did this by providing for the brethren’s quiet, lest they should ever suffer want. Yet while his mind was occupied with these concerns, he cared no less for inward things, but with fervent mind sought the fervour of the order. Hence he removed many superfluities from the cloister and introduced what was fitting for religious life; he prohibited less useful things, always and in every respect seeking the dignity [Col. 0020B] and usefulness of the Church.

4. He meets Innocent II and brings him to Cluny.—Emperors, kings, and princes of the world loved, revered, and honoured him with devout affection, and clung to him as to a father and lord. The Roman Church honoured, embraced, and loved him with special prerogative. For he set himself as a wall against all heresies and schisms of the Church, and manfully assailed the enemies of the faith. This shone forth wonderfully at the time of the schism between Innocent and Peter Leonis.

For when the whole Church was being ruined in such a manner, and different persons held different opinions, while the monk Peter [Note: [Col. 0019D] Hence it is evident that Peter Leonis was a Cluniac monk. Pope Paschal II created him cardinal-deacon of Saints Cosmas and Damian. In 1124 he was acting as legate of the Apostolic See in Gaul together with Gregory, with whom he was then contending for the [Col. 0020D] papacy, as we saw above in the Life of St Stephen of Grandmont.] held his seat at Rome, Peter met Innocent, who was coming by sea, with festive welcome contrary to [Col. 0020C] everyone’s expectation, and, without consulting the Gallican Church, supplied him sufficiently with mounts and brought him with him to Cluny. When the kings of the earth heard this, they wondered how he could leave his own monk established in the see and exalt a stranger. He received Innocent with such solemnity that this reception became known throughout the whole world. For he humbly invited him to consecrate the church which he himself had built, and obtained that he should complete its blessing.

When the Gallican Church learned this, they immediately rushed to meet the pope and revered and honoured him as a father. The king assembled a council, commended the deed of Abbot Peter, and declared it impossible to oppose such great beginnings. The Father brought him to the king’s court; and when the prelates of the Church had been summoned together with the princes, the king received his shepherd with solemn glory and commanded all to receive him and follow the Abbot of Cluny. This report was heard throughout the entire world, and all marvelled at what Abbot Peter had done. Henry, king of the English, the kings of Spain, and Henry, [Note: [Col. 0020D] Rather, Lothair, who had succeeded Henry from the year 1125.] emperor of the Germans, following his lead, made him their guide and on this occasion returned to unity. The Father, moreover, devotedly adhered to the shepherd raised up for the Church and followed him wherever he went, lest anyone on any [Col. 0021A] occasion should fall away from unity. Indeed, he went with him as far as the City and, after the death of the antipope, established him peacefully in the see.

5. His writings.—At this time the heresies of various persons sprang up in the Church and, by their perversity, stained the whole condition of the Church. Seeing this, the blessed Father rose up with all his strength and began to act against them all by speech and writing; and he overcame all by the authority of the Scriptures. His books [Note: [Col. 0021D] Besides the books which he wrote against the Jews and against those who say that Christ never openly called himself God in the Gospel, he wrote against the Petrobrusians.] composed against those afflicted by such error both refute them and furnish us with knowledge of doctrine. He also made a book against the sect of Mahomet, and by remarkable disputation destroyed all its inventions. His letters too, addressed to various persons in the Church, greatly benefit their readers. Let whoever reads the book which he published concerning [Col. 0021B] various revelations or visions understand how great its purity and usefulness are. We also possess other diverse little works from his writings; from all of these the reader may infer how great were the Father’s subtlety and wisdom.

6. He established a monastery of virgins.—Among the other wonderful and marvellous things which the man of God did, this stands out as precious: namely, the monastery of virgins which he established, called Lavenna [Note: [Col. 0021D] It is situated in the diocese of Clermont.]. Today it possesses such religious seriousness and honourableness that all in Auvergne rank it above others for the grace of holiness. For those nuns consecrated to God have nothing in common with the world except that they live in it. They preserve their father’s institution and, removed from every sight [Col. 0021C] of men, maintain a chaste temple for God.

7. His miracles.—Let us now return to describing those things which mortals desire: the signs and miracles which God performed through him. For God did not abandon Cluny, but still magnifies those who adhere to him in truth. At one time, when the man of God was visiting his dependent houses, we came to Ruolium [Note: [Col. 0022D] Ruolium or Ruelium, in French Rueil, a cell immediately subject to the priory of La Charité, lies in Brie, not far from the abbey of Jouarre in the diocese of Meaux.], where he was solemnly received by his sons with humble devotion.

That same night the prior of that house fell mortally ill, and, as he was grievously afflicted, called for the Father and began to disclose to him the wounds of his mind and body. But, as is the habit of a sick soul, he kept silent from shame concerning a certain sin. Nevertheless, on the authority of the Holy Spirit, the Father absolved him from the matters which he had heard and from all the rest. But as his sickness grew grievously worse, at midnight he began to fail exceedingly and was thus brought to the last extremity. The signal for the dying was sounded; all ran together, and the Father with the rest. When by the signs they had pronounced him dead, the Father touched his temples and indicated that life was present.

For he had been snatched away to judgment, and a crowd of demons stood over him, strongly accusing him and saying: “Because he did this and this, he ought deservedly to be reckoned with us.” And when his angel answered for him and said that this was not so—“for he confessed to his abbot”—they prevailed more and more, cruelly alleging that crime [Col. 0022A] which he had kept silent. Then the Mother of the Saviour, our Lady the Virgin Mary, came with a multitude of angels and said: “Why, evil spirits, do you strive to harass my servant? His hour has not yet come. Let him return and confess to his Father, and then come to us.”

Then the troop of evil ones fled, and the sick man, while we watched, returned to himself. He who had previously been thought dead began to seek the Father. Opening his eyes, he cried out loudly, to the amazement of all: “Where is Lord Abbot?” When the latter rose from his chair, the sick man sat up; and, after we withdrew, he related this vision to him. Soon afterwards, when the Father returned to us, he was so overcome with weeping that none of us dared approach him. Having recovered himself somewhat, he said: “Little children, how great is God’s mercy toward us, and none of us knows it! Our brother has been restored not only to us but also to God.”

On the following day, because the church in which this had occurred was dedicated in honour of the Blessed Virgin Mary, the Father ordered an altar prepared for him, that he might give thanks to the Mother and her Son for what had been bestowed upon that man. He prepared himself in his own singular manner and celebrated the divine offices with exceeding solemnity, so that all marvelled. Afterwards he visited the sick man, absolved him, blessed him, and kissed him; and thus commended him to Christ Jesus and his Mother. We departed, and behold, on the third day it was reported that he had died. Then the Father, grieving deeply at his loss, dissolved wholly into tears and, casting himself before the altar, wept bitterly. Then the signals were sounded, and [Col. 0022C] all the offices appropriate for him were performed.

When these had been completed, the elder said: “Let us pray, brothers, and let us do so attentively and earnestly for our brother; for although he is reckoned among the predestined, he nevertheless needs your aid.” We came to Cluny, and there the Brother began again in chapter to speak of the dead brother, in a discourse full of contrition, tears, and devotion. First he said how devoutly he had received him; how he had fallen ill; how he had confessed; how he had kept silent about what caused him shame; how he had been snatched away, accused, excused; how the Mother of Mercy, coming upon them, had delivered him from the hands of the evil ones, restored him to life, and warned him to confess the sin he had concealed.

Again there was mourning; again tears flowed from the fatherly eyes, [Col. 0022D] and invited those who heard them to like feelings. “See, brothers,” he said, “how great is the grace of God, how great the power of confession, which drives demons away and invites the Virgin to bring aid! Through the occasion of confession our brother was saved and gave us an example of confession; by this event he warns us to confess purely. Let us therefore pray more earnestly for him and compassionately share his suffering with the bowels of charity, bestowing upon him the benefits of piety.” After these words, soon afterward the aforesaid brother appeared to the Father and revealed that through the prayers of the brethren he had been absolved from every punishment.

[Col. 0023A] 8. Concerning a tempted novice.—Another event occurred at Cluny which seems worthy of narration to me. There was a brother in the monastery who was agitated by various thoughts, all of which tended to his leaving the monastery. One day, while speaking with himself and being troubled on every side, he saw three monks appear in the novices’ cell. One addressed him thus: “Brother, what is the matter? What are you thinking? Why are you so troubled?” He replied: “Lord, I am grievously afflicted in this monastery and cannot bear the torments of the order; therefore I desire to leave.”

Then the other said: “I am abbot of Grottaferrata, and, if you wish, I shall take you away with me.”

“I wish it, lord; I long for it; I desire it.”

Then he who was thought to be a monk, but was the devil, took him up and bore him over walls and houses. [Col. 0023B] As he passed over the courtyard of a certain townsman, while many people cried out, he dropped him. He was then brought to the man of God and confessed the matter in order. The servant of God gently soothed him and calmed him by spiritual consolation, keeping him with himself and saying: “Thanks be to God, son, because the adverse party was unable to accomplish what it intended; deceived by your own thoughts, you have been restored to soundness.”

Thereafter he was wholly healed, not only from temptation but from the enemy’s prompting. He lived many years, giving thanks to God for the heavenly visitation which divine goodness had bestowed on him. This man, named Stephen, had been a very wealthy citizen in Le Puy, so wealthy that he even made his bed upon coins. But despising everything, he went to Cluny and assumed the religious habit. Yet the tempter, [Col. 0023C] the deceiver of the human race, setting before his eyes the image of the things he had left, brought him into such temptation that he attempted, by his own assault, to carry him away with himself to death.

9. Concerning a brother upon whom three pennies were found at death.—Now, since we are at Cluny, let us again tell what happened at Cluny. There was a consumptive brother who was brought to death by that illness. While he was being washed, those washing him found three obols on his person. Astonished, they reported the matter to the prior. Having summoned everyone, he asked whether the man had confessed this to anyone; and, when he discovered that this had not been done, he was grieved. Taking counsel, they sent to the blessed abbot, who was at Virziliacum [Col. 0023D], to ask what should be done with the monk. He ordered that he be cast out beyond every human habitation and buried without blessing or the office of religion.

They placed him in a cask and cast him outside the town. After a long time, however, he appeared in a vision to the cloistral prior, named Hugh, begging him to have mercy on him and to make known to the lord abbot that he should grant him burial among the servants of God, because in that way he might obtain pardon from the Lord. When Hugh long neglected this, the dead man appeared to two others, persistently repeating the same request. When these three had long been wearied by his continual importunity, they revealed it to the Father and begged him to grant pardon to the dead brother. But, fearing deception, he delayed action.

The dead man [Col. 0024A] pressed them more and more, visibly appearing to them night and day and lamentably complaining that they had no mercy on him. Finally, when the Father could in no way be turned from his resolve because of the strictness of the order, the deceased brought letters of the Lord Jesus to the prior, to show them to the Father and the convent. It was written that the monk ought to obtain pardon, since no other offence rendered him guilty. Then joy and gladness arose in the tents of the righteous; and, at the Father’s command, the three, with others, hurried to the place where he lay. They brought him as he was to the church, and, after breaking the cask, found him intact as they had placed him on the first day. All marvelled at the miracle which had occurred; they placed him in the church and, accompanying him with the customary praises [Col. 0024B], honoured him with burial according to the custom of Cluny.

10. Concerning a monk at Sauxillanges who had concealed a sin in confession.—At a certain time, when the Father was at Sauxillanges, where he had been raised, God granted him an event that must by no means be passed over. A brother in the infirmary was struggling near death and cried out fiercely as though mad: “I am dying, I am dying, I am dying!” The brethren ran to him and asked why he cried thus. He miserably told them that he was being trampled by the hooves of a certain black horse, so that he could in no way hide his face from it.

They immediately ran to the Father and reported the matter. Visiting the sick man, he asked him what was troubling him so [Col. 0024C] grievously. “Lord,” he said, “I am held beneath the feet of a black horse that seeks to devour me.” The Father made the sign of the cross and sprinkled him with holy water, consoling the sick man; but he was no less oppressed by the devil. Then the Father, summoning all his spirit, asked him whether he had made a true confession. The man affirmed that he had. “Certainly not,” said the Father, “for if you had truly confessed, you would in no way be subject to the evil one.”

Then the pious shepherd, compassionately coming to the aid of the sheep wandering under the wolf, diligently sought to have him truly confess the things he had committed. When the man remained silent and did not disclose what was sought, the Father questioned him concerning each crime and came to that which he had concealed. Hearing this, the sick man [Col. 0024D] burst into tears and confessed to the investigating Father everything he had done. As soon as the confession was made, that black horse rushed with the greatest speed toward the latrines and left the sick man, unable to endure the Father’s presence. Seeing this, the sick man, filled with joy, began to cry: “Father, the horse is leaving! The devil is leaving! He is making for the latrines, and I no longer see him!” The Father immediately ordered him fortified with the most holy mysteries; and thus, having received the blessing, he departed in peace.

11. A lamp falling beside him is not broken.—At the time when the Father was staying there, something happened to him which must not be concealed in silence. For one day, after he had celebrated the divine offices according to his blessed custom and, after the celebration, lay prostrate [Col. 0025A] in prayer before the holy altar, the lamp suspended above suddenly fell beside him. Without his knowing it, it neither broke nor spilled its oil. Master Thomas, his chaplain, and Peter of Saint John, who had remained with him, saw this and ran to the others, showing them the miracle that had occurred. The Father perceived neither when it fell nor when the vessel was lifted up: so intent was he upon prayer.

12. Concerning a most poor woman.—As he was leaving that same house, he encountered at the gate a most poor woman asking that alms be given her. When the man of God saw her, he stopped quietly and ordered his servant Bernard, who in such matters was especially and closely attached to him, to be summoned. He privately commanded him to give his very best fur garment to the poor woman [Col. 0025B]. Though he wished this to be done secretly, the charity of the man became publicly known, to the wonder of all. Nor should anyone think it strange that we have included a work of mercy among miracles, since it was said and revealed to him from above: “Mercy shall save you.”

13. He delivers Henry, king of the English, from torments.—How many benefits Henry the elder, king of the English, bestowed upon Cluny is known to many. Having been brought to the final condition of humankind, he entered upon the way of all flesh; and because the mighty suffer mighty torments, he was assigned severer punishments. One day it happened that one of his knights encountered that same king, as though alive, upon a black horse, with a great multitude riding with him [Col. 0025C]. When the knight saw him, he was astonished and began to cry in a loud voice: “Are you not my lord the king?”

“Am I?”

“Are you not dead?”

“Truly,” he replied, “I am dead, and I would have been assigned to eternal death, unless the lord Peter, Abbot of Cluny, and his people had come to my aid. But because I still need his help, I adjure you, by the loyalty which you owed me while I lived in the world, to run as quickly as possible to the brethren who dwell in the monastery of Saint Pancras [Note: [Col. 0025D] A cell once distinguished in the diocese of Chichester, dependent upon Cluny.], and tell them on my behalf what you have seen from me, so that they may indicate these things by letter to their friend, their Father the Abbot of Cluny, and may beg him to remember me and not cease his benefaction until he hears me giving him thanks.”

And so it was done. When the Father [Col. 0025D] heard this, he rose up with all his strength to bring aid. He ordered alms, masses, trentals, and the other good works by which sinners are customarily helped to be increased for the king throughout all his houses in the world, until the king should say, “It is enough.” This was done until that same king appeared to the Father and to many others, giving thanks for his deliverance.

14. He delivers a disciple from quartan fever.—At another time, when the Father was in Rome and remained there for various reasons—one matter concerning the church of Vézelay having especially been completed—he said to his followers: “Who among us will bring to Cluny what we have obtained by right in the court of the lord pope?” Then all cried out that Adhemar the sacristan was worthy to undertake this embassy. Hearing this, he replied: “I can by no means carry out this business, because I continually suffer from quartan fever.”

Then the abbot said: “By the authority of the Holy Trinity and the power of obedience, I command you to go to Cluny without any pain or attack of fever.” The sacristan gladly embraced obedience to the Father, reached Cluny, and showed what the Father had obtained for Vézelay by the authority of the Roman Church. Then, amid the general rejoicing, counsel began to be taken as to who should carry the lord pope’s letters to Vézelay. Since all maintained that the man who had returned sound and unharmed from the City through the power of obedience—and who had seen and heard everything—ought to go, he consented [Col. 0026B] and began his journey in accordance with the elders’ will. Then, in a marvellous manner, the fever which had left him throughout so many intervals of travel seized him as soon as he had gone out through the gate, compelled him to return home, and thus the power of obedience was proved amid the weakness of nature. Let the hearer understand.

15. By revelation he learns that a monk of Charlieu died by poison.—Moreover, while the Father was in the City, a miracle most worthy of narration occurred to him. There was a monk, noble by birth, outstanding in religious life, prior of Charlieu [Note: [Col. 0025D] It is a cell in the territory of Mâcon, founded by Robert [Col. 0026D] bishop of Valence and Edward his brother.], named William of Roanne. Certain men had been inflamed against him by the devil’s envy, so that through their malice they prepared poison for him by means of someone, and ended his life by this plot.

On the very night and hour when he was killed, he appeared [Col. 0026C] to the Father as he sat on his bed after Compline. As was his custom, he greeted the Father reverently and devoutly and recounted in full what had happened. Hearing this, the man of God was greatly distressed. Yet he carefully investigated the cause, asking how and by whom so great a crime had been committed. He also inquired whether the man had confessed, whether he was free from punishment, and whether he had received communion. The dead man replied: “Because I was killed unjustly, I am free from punishment. But I have been sent to you in order that I may receive absolution and communion.”

When the Father heard all this, he absolved him as though dead, and he departed after receiving absolution. The Father then awakened the brethren, told them what he had seen and heard, and immediately sent a messenger to [Col. 0026D] Charlieu, ordering him to inquire concerning the day and hour at which the dead man had appeared to him, and whether he was truly dead. The messenger found that all had happened exactly as had been revealed to the Father and brought him a truthful report. The Father excommunicated the author of this evil deed and separated him forever from the body of the Church of Cluny.

16. Through his merits a peasant vomits up a serpent.—When the blessed man was returning from Spain and was solemnly holding court at Le Puy, where he occupied the foremost place among ecclesiastical persons, a monk named [Col. 0027A] Jordan came to him from the monastery of Saint Faith at Conques. Jordan held a priory at the town of Ebais in the diocese of Le Puy. He sought advice concerning an illness which had befallen one of his peasants. The peasant said that a serpent had entered his body and that he was continually tortured on this account, becoming near to death at every moment.

Hearing this, the man of God was greatly moved with pity. Receiving the Holy Spirit with all his mind, he began to sigh from the inmost affection of his heart. “Brother,” he said, “these things are not ours but belong to the saints of God. Nevertheless, because all things are possible to one who believes, if a man has faith, divine goodness is able to grant help to one in peril. Therefore, at earliest dawn come, you alone with him alone; and where you see us enter to celebrate the divine offices, there follow faithfully.”

Hearing this, Jordan returned to his lodging with great joy. Returning very early in the morning before daylight, he kept watch with the wretched man before the Father’s door until he came out. The Father, mindful of his pious promise, arose before daylight with two monks, Peter of Saint John and Master Thomas, and went to the oratory of Saint Majolus to celebrate the divine offices there. He celebrated the Mass of the Ascension and caused the tormented man to be present. As the Gospel was read and they came to the passage where it says, “They shall take up serpents,” the wretched man opened his mouth and the serpent put forth its head. The Father took it in his hand and drew it from the man’s body; to the amazement of all who were present, he threw it into their midst.

The man fell down and almost breathed out his spirit from the agony. While [Col. 0027C] the Father celebrated the divine offices, he ordered him to be covered. When the solemnity of Mass was completed, he went to the sick man and, raising him from the ground with his own hand, commanded him to confess his sins. After the confession, the man washed his mouth with water and wine and, receiving communion in the most holy mysteries, returned unharmed to his home. The Father then compelled all who were present to swear upon the most holy Gospels that, while he lived, they would tell this occurrence to no one. But after he had heard of the man’s death, Jordan the monk publicly revealed the miracle in the chapter of [Col. 0028A] Saint Faith, as it had happened, and affirmed with certainty that many other such events had occurred.

17. Concerning his parents.—These things have been briefly said concerning the miracles of our Father, not because much more could not be said, but because we do not wish to burden the hearers, as we hasten to other matters. For this man was born of noble and honourable stock, and the antiquity of his family made known how great and what sort of man he was among the people of God. Indeed, his great-grandfather, by divine revelation, built the church of Saint Michael of Clusa; his mother, rejoicing in her numerous offspring, went to Marcigny and there ended her life in holiness. His father was buried in the monastery of Sauxillanges.

He had four brothers in ecclesiastical office and two lay brothers: Jordan, abbot of La Chaise-Dieu; Pons, abbot of Vézelay; [Col. 0028B] Armannus, abbot of Maguelone; Heracleus, provost of the church of Brioude; and two knights, Dissutus and Eustace, whose nobility and honour were known throughout Auvergne. But what is lineage to us? Let us return to the Father.

For thirty years, as he had revealed to me and to many others, he prayed that his end might come to him on the day of the Nativity of the Lord. Therefore he went once each year to the holy men of the Charterhouse, whom he loved with the greatest affection, and earnestly begged them to pray to the Most High for the fulfilment of his desire at the appointed time. When they said, “Father, tell us what your petition is, so that we may more certainly be able to pray to him whom you ask,” he would not disclose it, but only said: “If you are servants of the Most High, pray for your fellow brother, that God may fulfil my desire.”

When [Col. 0028C] the man of God had passed from this world to the Father, the Carthusians sent a letter to the Cluniacs concerning the desire of the man of God and, because that which he had so long desired had been fulfilled, made this clear by evident signs. This lover of peace obtained peace in the glory of God on the day of peace. These things have been briefly said concerning our blessed Father, because we do not wish to cause weariness to our hearers; consequently, we leave very many things to be written by wiser persons.

[Col. 0027]

## SECOND LIFE

(Dom Marrier, *Bibliotheca Cluniacensis*, Paris, 1614, folio, p. 589, from the *Chronicle of Cluny*.)

[Col. 0027D] Peter the First, ninth abbot of Cluny, was elected in the octave of the Assumption of the Blessed Mary, Mother of God, and began to govern in the year of the Lord 1122. This Peter, surnamed Maturitii [otherwise Mauricii, or, as some wish, Mauriaceni], descended from the noblest magnates of Auvergne. From the very cradle of infancy he was offered by his parents to serve God under monastic observance, and was marked with monastic blessing by the holy Father Hugh at the end of Hugh’s life. [Col. 0028D] Later, in the time of Lord Pons, abbot of Cluny, he was made prior of Vézelay and governed the order vigorously. Then, having become prior of Domène, after the death of the venerable man Lord Hugh II, abbot of that place, he was elected abbot by the acclamation, in a general assembly, of the great and renowned monks and religious persons of that place who then flourished; and on the same day he was blessed by the archbishop of Chrysopolis, being about thirty [otherwise twenty-eight] years old.

[Col. 0029A] Having assumed the government of the abbey, he proved a distinguished cultivator of humility and a magnificent and exceptional guardian of holiness. His gait was stately, his speech full of maturity and grace, and his manners well ordered. Wholly adorned with cheerful gravity and grave cheerfulness, he presented to all an example of honourableness and monastic seriousness. Possessing in his time a singular grace in hearing confessions, he was especially skilled in curing the hidden offences of penitents, so that one would believe he alone knew how to heal his own wounds and not reveal or make public those of others. In correcting open faults, he exercised more of a father’s role than a judge’s, more clemency than strictness, more mercy than censure. His bodily stature was so striking that among all persons of his time [Col. 0029B] he was preeminent in the beauty of his face, the carriage of his limbs, and the orderliness of his conduct.

When this same venerable Peter, abbot of Cluny, was returning from Spain and had come to the city of Le Puy, a certain peasant came before him, lamenting with tearful complaint both that a serpent had entered his body and that he was becoming near to death at every moment. The man of God heard this with great compassion and said to him: “O brother, these things are not ours, but belong only to the saints of God, because all things are possible to one who believes. I shall pray to the Lord for you.”

When morning came, the same holy man, mindful of his pious promise, entered the oratory of Saint Majolus to celebrate Mass. While he celebrated the Mass of the Ascension of the Lord, [Col. 0029C] he ordered the tormented man to be present. As the Gospel was read and had reached the passage which says, “They shall take up serpents,” the wretched man opened his mouth and the serpent put forth its head. To the amazement of all present, the Father cast it into their midst. The man fell down and almost breathed out his spirit from the agony. When the solemnity of Mass had ended, he went to the sick man, heard his confession, gave him communion in the most holy mysteries, and sent him home unharmed.

The venerable Peter, abbot of Cluny, flourished in his own time as a man of singular learning, and no one was greater than he. His many writings, which we shall insert individually in the course of this work, show this down to the present day, although in them the order is by no means preserved.

During the time of his administration, our venerable Father Peter, abbot of Cluny, produced many writings. For he wrote various letters with such gravity and in a style so lofty that he seems another Augustine in the composition of books concerning the insane [perhaps: “the saints”].

His book of letters is first divided into six books.

The first book contains thirty-six letters.

The second book contains fifty-one.

The third book contains seven.

The fourth book contains forty-three.

The fifth book contains nine.

The sixth book contains fifty. Among these he inserted a treatise [Col. 0030A] divided into five chapters, setting forth arguments from reason against the inveterate obstinacy of the Jews concerning all that has been said, or can be said.

The first chapter shows that Christ is the Son of God.

The second chapter shows that Christ is proved to be God in a special sense.

The third chapter shows that Christ is not, as the Jews think, a temporal king, but eternal and heavenly.

The fourth chapter shows that Christ is not still to come, as the Jews foolishly suppose, but has already come, at the certain and foreordained time, for the salvation of the world.

[Col. 0030B] The fifth chapter demonstrates and determines matters concerning the ridiculous and utterly foolish fables of the Jews.

The same venerable Peter, abbot of Cluny, also inserted the book which he published and wrote against the Petrobrusian heretics, who said, first, that children are baptized uselessly because they cannot believe.

The second error was that they said basilicas or altars ought not to be built, since, as they affirmed, the Church of God consisted in the unity of the assembled faithful.

The third error was that they said the cross of the Lord was neither to be adored nor venerated, but rather broken and trampled underfoot.

The fourth error was that they said Mass was nothing [Col. 0030C] and ought not to be celebrated.

The fifth error was that they maintained that benefits bestowed by the living were of no use to the dead.

The sixth error was that they said God ought not to be sung to.

This same Peter, our abbot of Cluny, while in Spain with the emperor, translated from Arabic into Latin the *Alchoran*—the Qur’an—of the law of the heretic Mahomet. Yet at Cluny he wrote most vigorously against the aforesaid sect, dividing his work into five books, which books are divided into chapters.

This same Peter, abbot of Cluny, wrote concerning miracles that occurred, or were performed, in his own times. Two books of these survive.

[Col. 0030D] In the first book he treats of twenty-eight miracles, with great Ciceronian elegance—not only in these works of his, but indeed in all of them.

In the second he relates thirty.

The same Peter also wrote four very useful and most elegant sermons, of which:

The first is On the Transfiguration of the Lord.

The second sermon is On the Praise of the Lord’s Sepulchre.

The third sermon is On Saint Marcellus, Pope and Martyr.

The fourth is entitled, On the Veneration of Any Relics Whatever.

Moreover, that eminent Father Peter the Venerable, abbot of Cluny, wrote a letter to Peter [Col. 0031A] of Saint John, an elder member of his community, against those who say that Christ never openly called himself God in the Gospels. This letter is useful and necessary, full of very many instructions.

The same man wrote a rhythmical poem in praise of the Saviour.

A rhythmical poem on Saint Hugh.

A rhythmical poem on Saint Benedict.

Likewise, a rhythmical poem on the Resurrection of the Lord.

He composed a hymn in honour of Saint Mary Magdalene.

Likewise another hymn in honour of the Mother of the Lord.

He also composed a prose sequence concerning that same glorious Virgin Mary.

We must now consider the prudence of our glorious Father Peter [Col. 0031B] the Venerable, abbot of Cluny, in providing for his religious. For in a certain book of statutes of this monastery of Cluny, issued by himself, he states that at the time of his elevation to the abbacy there were more than three hundred religious in the monastery of Cluny itself, as he testifies. For he says:

> Therefore I, Brother Peter, humble abbot of Cluny, make known to all who read this that, when twenty-eight years ago I was elevated to this office, I found a great Church, religious and renowned indeed, but exceedingly poor, burdened with great expenses and, when its revenues were compared with its expenditures, possessing almost no revenues at all. There were three hundred brethren or more, and that house was unable to provide from its own resources even for a hundred. There was a throng of guests, and an endless multitude of poor persons. The grain collected from all the deaneries scarcely lasted four months, sometimes not even three; the wine gathered from every quarter never sufficed for two months, sometimes not even for one. The bread was scanty, [coarse?], and full of bran. The wine was heavily watered, tasteless, and truly vile, apart from the other expenditures incurred and borrowed at heavy interest. In purchasing grain and wine alone, the chamberlain of Cluny spent more than twenty thousand solidi. Seeing these straits, I took counsel with the wise brethren who then lived, and, as seemed reasonable to them and to me, established monthly provisions through the deaneries. I ordained that certain deans should provide for the convent of Cluny, as regards bread, beans, and their fat, some for one month, some for three weeks, some for fifteen days, some for eight days—that is, for the entire year. And so that this ordinance should thereafter be observed annually, I confirmed it by the assent and will of all the brethren, by command in chapter, and in writing. Thus it was decreed, and it was observed for many years afterwards.

In the time of this blessed Father Peter the Venerable, abbot of Cluny, namely in the year 1131, the dedication of the great basilica of Cluny was performed by Pope Innocent II.

In the year of the Lord 1153, because of the excessive and unusually unrestrained malice of the worst plunderers, who raged especially fiercely against the possessions of Cluny, at the request of Lord Peter, abbot of Cluny, and [Col. 0032A] of the friends of Cluny, Lord Odo, cardinal of the Holy Roman Church and legate of the Apostolic See; Lord Heraclius, archbishop-elect of Lyons; together with the suffragans of the Church of Lyons—that is, the bishops of Autun, Mâcon, and Chalon—together with William, count of Burgundy, another William, count of Chalon, Humbert of Beaujeu, Jocerand the Great, Hugh of Berzé, Hugh of Scissé, and no few other nobles of Burgundy, assembled at Mâcon in the Church of Saint Vincent.

There they deliberated for about three days concerning affairs, and especially concerning the restoration of peace for the Church of Cluny. Thus, before the whole clergy and people of the aforesaid city, it was decreed by the lords already mentioned [Col. 0032B] that the aforesaid monks and laymen, and all possessions belonging to Cluny, which lie within the boundaries marked by the rivers Saône, Loire, and Rhône, together with those parts of the lands situated within the city of Autun and the castle of Couches, which lies beyond Chalon, should remain in full and secure peace. And whoever travelled through the aforesaid territory of Cluny, together with them and their goods, should remain and be kept secure and at peace. The aforesaid lords promised, from all their resources, to preserve the aforesaid men of Cluny unharmed in both property and person; indeed, to proceed against those who so injured the monks of Cluny or their possessions, even by taking up arms and besieging the castles or places [Col. 0032C] into which such evildoers had withdrawn. The inhabitants of the city of Cluny also promised there, while these things were being done, that whenever they were summoned to take up arms with the said nobles and lords, they would go, etc. The prelates likewise promised on their part to proceed similarly against such persons, etc.

Further, in the time of the aforesaid Peter the Venerable, abbot of Cluny, in the year of human salvation 1155, the illustrious Henry, bishop of Winchester, at the request of the said Lord Peter the abbot, invited by letters from Pope Adrian IV, and also summoned by Louis the Younger, king of France, and by nearly all the magnates and barons of Burgundy, came to Cluny. By his prudence and at his own expense, he relieved that same Church, oppressed by the weight of heavy debt [*aeris alieni pondere*], of almost its whole burden of liabilities. Thus, both in paying debts and in acquiring properties, as well as procuring necessities for the household, he spent—as was heard from his own mouth and stated by him—more than seven thousand marks of silver. For he fed throughout the year 460 monks then living in the said monastery of Cluny, as is recorded in the chapter-book of the said abbey of Cluny. This Henry, bishop of Winchester, had formerly been a pupil and monk of this monastery of Cluny, and in his time the most outstanding and greatest benefactor of us and of our abbey.

[Col. 0033A] In the year of the Lord 1171, the aforesaid Lord Henry, bishop of Winchester, died on 9 August, the fifth day before the Ides of August.

Concerning distinguished religious and monks in the time of our venerable Father Peter, abbot of Cluny.

The Church of Cluny received—and often, as I have said, received—the treasures of many and diverse persons, who stored up treasures not on earth but in heaven. Therefore Cluny received from the Church of Liège gifts far more precious than gold and topaz, when it joined to its humble community of Cluny eminent men, to be remembered with the highest praise and affection, who came to us. For from the time of our blessed Father Hugh until the days of Peter the Venerable himself, abbot of Cluny, [Col. 0033B] three canons of the Church of Liège came to Cluny: namely Zelon, Tezelin, and Alger—great masters in their own times and disciples of humility.

The first of these, Zelon, laboured for a long time for the Church to which he had come. By singular learning and eloquent speech, he not only formed the conduct of his hearers, but also built the physical fabric of the new church more than all mortals except the kings of Spain and England.

The next, devoting his whole self exclusively to spiritual pursuits, grew old in the holy purpose. First at Cluny under holy Father Hugh, then at Vézelay with Lord Abbot Rainald, his nephew, and finally residing with the archbishop of Lyons, he ended a praiseworthy life with a holy death.

The third, Alger by name, surpassed those who had gone before him in humility, purity, and the sincerity of his entire life. Therefore Peter the Venerable, abbot of Cluny, relates of him in Book I of the *Miracles* that, as is said of blessed Job (Job 1), Alger himself was truly “blameless and upright, fearing God and turning away from evil.” He often and repeatedly complained that demons harassed him greatly to his venerable abbot Peter.

Alger was subtle in intellect and eloquent in speech. In ecclesiastical business he wrote notable letters to various persons and to many churches. Among the other memorials of his talent, he also produced two treatises very useful for ecclesiastical concerns and the Catholic faith.

[Col. 0033D] The first he entitled *On Mercy and Justice*, and divided it into three sections. The first, concerning the tempering of justice by mercy, adequately treats the endurance of evils; the second concerns ecclesiastical sinners and their canonical correction; the third concerns those outside the Church and their sacrilegious communion.

He produced another treatise, as much nobler as it is more exalted, since it concerns a wonderful and necessary matter: namely, *On the Sacrament of the Body and Blood of the Lord*.

This work is divided into three parts. The first, containing twenty-two chapters, treats succinctly of the truth and power of Christ’s body; the second, divided into ten chapters, treats of various questions concerning that sacrament; [Col. 0034A] the third, in fourteen chapters, treats of ecclesiastical ministers and of sinful heretics outside the Church.

In the times of Peter the Venerable, the oft-mentioned abbot of Cluny, Peter of Poitiers flourished, a most illustrious and learned man. He wrote several letters to Peter of Cluny, and many other works, all of which are in our possession.

At the same time Richard, a monk of Cluny by origin from Poitou, flourished. He was a great historian of sacred Scripture, for he wrote chronicles from Adam down to the time of Frederick.

Hugh Catula, a noble knight, promised that he would become a monk. As a sign of this, he had his hair cut by Peter, abbot of Cluny, and kept as testimony. After this had been done, the aforesaid Hugh changed [Col. 0034B] his intention and planned to go to Jerusalem. Peter the Venerable, abbot of Cluny, called him back from the journey, explaining and showing that the greater good must be preferred to the lesser. For it is a greater good to serve God continually in humility and poverty than to make a journey to Jerusalem in pride and luxury. When the aforesaid Hugh had considered these things, he became a monk of the oft-mentioned Peter the Venerable, abbot of Cluny.

Alberic, a monk of Cluny in his time and afterwards bishop of Ostia, was made legate of the Apostolic See in the regions of Jerusalem. Therefore he wrote to Peter of Cluny and to his religious, asking them to keep him commended in their prayers for his pilgrimage.

Lord Natalis, formerly abbot of Tresbace, subsequently became a monk of Cluny, relinquishing nevertheless the abbacy of Tresbace. When many wished to disturb him in this purpose, the aforesaid Peter the Venerable, abbot of Cluny, humbly interceded for Lord Natalis with Pope Innocent in a letter sent to that Innocent, saying thus at its end:

> Since, therefore, he preferred to rest nowhere but in your bosom—that is, at Cluny—let paternal compassion, as I have said, provide for him the repose which, in the proper order, he deserves to have after the labour of Martha.

Hugh, archbishop of Tours, when he was ill, became a monk of Cluny. He was asked by the clergy to return to the place from which he had departed. He was not [Col. 0034D] being sought as a hired hand, who on seeing the wolf abandons the sheep and flees, but as a shepherd, accustomed to set himself against the walls and stand in battle on the day of the Lord for the house of Israel entrusted to him. This Hugh exchanged the common dress of the clergy for the black habit of his Martin.

Abelard, Peter by name, was recalled from errors of faith by Peter the Venerable, our abbot, and Saint Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux. Having previously taught false doctrine concerning the faith, he became a monk of Cluny. Thereafter his mind, his tongue, and his work were always occupied with divine things; he always pondered, taught, and confessed matters philosophical and instructive. And, as is read of the great Gregory, he allowed no moment whatever to pass without [Col. 0035A] praying, reading, writing, or dictating. His reading was continuous, his prayer frequent, his silence unbroken, except when familiar conversation with the brethren or a public address to them in the convent concerning divine matters compelled him to speak. Accordingly, Peter the Venerable, earnestly commending him, wrote this epitaph concerning him:

> Socrates of the Gauls, the greatest Plato of the West, etc.

In those days Matthew came to prominence, a man of noble lineage according to the flesh, born in the province of Reims, distinguished by both parents and their nobility, and wealthy in worldly possessions. In childhood he was committed to study. When he had grown up, he obtained clerical office in the Church of Laon. From his earliest years, however, he began to grow strong in maturity and honourable conduct, shunning and detesting the frivolity and licentiousness of his companions—a corrupt custom of many clerics—and attached himself to clerics notable, though rare in such a class of people, for honour and religion. Among these he selected a cleric of more approved life, then treasurer of the Church of Reims, named Ralph and surnamed Green, and devoted himself to him in a particularly religious friendship. Afterwards, when this Ralph was taken away and elevated to the archbishopric of Reims, Matthew did not abandon the man whom he had chosen, but for some time remained under him, now as a canon of the Church of Reims. Later Matthew, aspiring to the monastic life, relinquished ecclesiastical honours. Because of the celebrated renown of its reputation, he chose Cluny and received the monastic habit at Saint-Martin-des-Champs, and fittingly so.
