For that monastery of Saint Martin was under the monastery of Cluny and was so like its pious parent in its commitment to order, religious observance, and zeal, and so conformed to it, that, like an image impressed in wax, it represented more familiarly than many other monasteries belonging to Cluny the image of the original seal; except for the distances between their places, which prevent their being together, they were not different but wholly one. Therefore, after Lord Matthew had there maintained the rule of the cloister most zealously for seven years in the monastery of Saint Martin, at the abbot’s command he succeeded to the priorship [Col. 0035D] when his prior had died. How and how greatly Matthew, now made prior—indeed, ever submissive to God—conducted himself toward those under him and toward all neighbours, near and distant, could scarcely be explained; nevertheless, let us recount it as briefly as possible.

First, the man of God gave himself to God and cast himself down in true contrition of heart and body, in penitence for past deeds and negligences, in the fullest contempt of the world, and in a devotion toward God almost unique among many thousands of monks. He remained constantly in the cloister with the brethren; and, after his many wanderings in the world, he persevered almost immovably, like the cloister-pillar to which he clung, devoted to the study of sacred reading. The care of the priory entrusted to him could scarcely separate him, even for an hour, from [Col. 0036A] the community of brethren, or draw him away by any bond of worldly occupation from the attention once fixed upon God. And although under his leadership almost three hundred brethren, both within and outside the monastery, served the Lord, and although he was obliged by his office to provide them with bodily support either personally or through others, he could not entirely escape Martha’s importunate demands; yet with the whole desire of his soul he longed for Mary’s repose.

Furthermore, Lord Matthew showed and preserved himself such toward his subjects until the end of his life that he could safely sing to God “mercy and judgment,” not only in relation to God but also in relation to himself. He was merciful toward his subjects, preparing necessities according to his ability and distributing to each, according to the rule of the Apostle and of blessed Benedict, what was needed, acquired through much labour. It was his custom personally to take the chief care of the sick, the poor, and guests, insofar as the office of the priory allowed.

Matthew showed to all a common affection of love in heart and speech. So far as he could without compromising the gravity of his profession, he offered himself cheerful and kindly to all who addressed him. To all, indeed, he bore, in Augustine’s words, the appropriate affection of charity; but toward those whom he could, he showed the corresponding effect of that charity. By the power of charity he had made his monastery, beyond all the monasteries of France, a common home for every guest and, as it were, a general refuge without [Col. 0036C] exception for all. A daily concourse of bishops, abbots, and noble laymen, companies of monks and clerics, and a crowd of poor people that never failed, almost constantly filled all the houses and lodgings. All were received gladly, nor could such a great influx of visitors disturb the cheerful pleasantness of his countenance in receiving them. Hence it came about that, among the other princes stirred by the renown of these and similar virtues to love him and to bestow much of their own upon him, Louis, king of the Franks, and Henry, king of the English, embraced him with singular affection, received him joyfully when he came, honoured him greatly when received, and almost never sent him away empty-handed.

[Col. 0036D] Later, Peter the Venerable, abbot of Cluny, having heard such great fame about Lord Matthew, summoned him to Cluny in the first year of his own calling, to assist the Order, and immediately laid upon him the care of the Order and the cloister. The venerable man Peter, abbot of Cluny, found him, from the moment of his entrance, a great worker and truly a worker for Christ—not sluggish, but outstanding—for assistance in this matter.

Accordingly, when the oft-mentioned Lord Matthew had been drawn to the city in order to bring peace to a schism of Pontius stirred up against the Church of Cluny, once that schism had been settled and entirely swallowed up, Lord Matthew hastened to return home with his companions. But God, who had called him without his knowing it, prevented his return; and, because he had been faithful over a few things, God promoted him, as a steward proven over many things. Pope Honorius II honourably imposed upon him the pastoral care, a burden and honour of greater rank, and, making him a companion in his labour, consecrated him bishop of Albano. Thus Lord Matthew advanced to the lofty rank of the episcopal order and was magnificently exalted upon the lampstand of the Church, to give light to all who were in God’s house. Yet he abandoned none of the marks of the monk, as some do. Rather, as is read of the great Martin, the same humility remained in his heart and the same lowliness in his dress. Under no pretext of any responsibilities did he give up anything of the offices, the chants, or the prolonged psalmody of Cluny. [Col. 0037B] In the palace he observed the institutions of the cloister; and though exposed to the world, by firm and long practice, as though by an inborn religious purpose, he separated himself from secular vanities as with a strong enclosure.

Many more things worthy of remembrance could still be committed to writing about him. Yet this must not be passed over: in his day he had no equal. At length, in the first week of the Advent of the Lord, the blessed Lord Matthew, bishop of Albano, no longer able to bear the utter failure of nature after many labours and struggles, took to his bed. Before his departure from this world, he deserved to see the glory which God had prepared for him. Finally, on the day of the Nativity of the Lord, he ended his last day in Christ Jesus. He was buried in the church of Saint Fridianus [Col. 0037C].

We also read that Gregory, in the time of Peter the Venerable, abbot of Cluny, was a monk of that same house. This Gregory was an illustrious and learned man who, according to Jerome, was always devoted to sacred Scripture. Hence he did not love the vices of the flesh. Peter the Venerable, our abbot of Cluny, commends and praises him in a remarkable manner. Whoever wishes to see this should read Letter 20, Book IV of the Letters of Peter the Venerable, abbot of Cluny.

In the times of the same Peter the Venerable, abbot of Cluny, Raynald, archbishop of Lyons, was a monk of Cluny. He was first [Col. 0037D] a monk of Cluny, then abbot of Vézelay, and finally archbishop of Lyons. Peter the Venerable himself composed his epitaph.

> [Note: [Col. 0037D] You have it below, together with several other epitaphs, among his writings.]

Peter, abbot of Cluny, writes in Book I, chapter 8, of the *Miracles* concerning Gerald, monk of the holy Church of Cluny, describing his holy life and character. While still in clerical dress, Gerald served Saint Hugh, abbot of Cluny, by whom he was eventually made a monk at Cluny. Because of his praiseworthy life, blessed Father Hugh entrusted to him the government and administration of the Church of Saint Saviour at Nevers. Finally, summoned by Peter the Venerable, abbot of Cluny, he was made prior in [Col. 0038A] the monastery of Haut-Jou, where he ended his life. In that priory of Haut-Jou, while he observed the vigils and took diligent care that the brethren should not rise at an improper time, he frequently heard in that church the voices of a certain melody—and deservedly so, since heavenly things belong to the hearing of those whose ears disdain to hear earthly things. He rests in the aforesaid place of Haut-Jou.

The venerable man Peter, abbot of Cluny, also had another disciple named Armannus. While he was a nobleman and a wealthy knight in the world, drawn by the divine Spirit and intending to renounce the world, he first sent to Cluny horses and garments of great value, a great weight of silver, and nearly all his possessions. Then, poor and a pilgrim, he made for Jerusalem. [Col. 0038B] There, after worshipping at the Lord’s sepulchre and being refreshed for some time by the sight of the most holy places, when he saw that the end of life which he ardently desired was delayed, he returned and put on the habit of religion at Cluny. With this he changed his heart so completely from every worldly affection that neither every good thing nor the private gains of various exercises could satisfy the spiritual ardour of his heart. Day did not suffice him for prayer, nor night; scarcely did he give himself to food or sleep.

It happened to this novice Armannus, after the Nativity of the Lord, on the night preceding the day of Saint John the Evangelist, that as he lay, still a novice, in the novices’ cell with the other novices, wearied by his usual prayers, he placed himself in bed and, released from a light sleep, saw a bear so dreadful He saw a bear so dreadful that the horror of the incomparably terrifying vision surpassed every human terror. Therefore he began to cry out terribly, and persisted so that all the brethren were forced to rise from their beds and run to him from every side. They were also obliged to summon Lord Peter the Venerable. Awakened by the sight, terror, and fright, Armannus began to despise the dream he had seen; but, fully awake, he again beheld above himself the very bear that he had seen while asleep, raised in the air only so far that he could have touched it with his hand had he wished. Its gaping [Col. 0038D] mouth was astonishingly and unspeakably horrible beyond all measure, as is written of it: “Terror is round about its teeth” (Job 41); its claws were very long, curved back, and stretched out most eagerly to seize; the whole form of its shaggy body roared most dreadfully as though about to snatch prey at once. Thus the devil so wearied him with terror for a long time that he forced him out of his mind; but he was delivered by God’s mercy. Yet he contracted such weakness from that terror that he could not attend the convent for three days. Peter the Venerable, abbot of Cluny, relates this.

> [Note: [Col. 0038D] Book I of the *Miracles*, ch. 18.]

There was also another man, as is said of the great Benedict, blessed by grace and by name. Before he entered the monastic order, he was a very devout priest; having changed his dress at Cluny, he became a true monk. His emaciated body, thin face, unkempt hair, venerable in its very greyness, downcast countenance, eyes scarcely ever open, mouth unceasingly meditating sacred words, seemed to show a man dwelling not on earth but in heaven. He was always silent, unless a definite and serious reason compelled him to speak. His words were very brief, far removed from trifles, jokes, and every kind of idleness. Whenever there was talk of spiritual matters, it never took place without sighs, never without tears. His psalmody was unceasing; he meditated on holy Scripture night and day. Therefore [Col. 0039B] he always carried about a glossed Psalter, for he sang the psalms not perfunctorily, as some are accustomed to do, but with the utmost attentiveness and devotion. Wherever he encountered something he did not understand, he immediately turned his eyes to the glosses. He spent the whole day chanting psalms and meditating, the night keeping vigil and praying. This same Benedict had as his cell a house of prayer in a very high and very remote tower, consecrated in honour of Saint Michael the Archangel. If I wished to describe his life in every detail, nothing about him ought to be passed over in silence, but the account would take too long.

> [Note: [Col. 0039D] Peter the Venerable himself, Book I of the *Miracles*, ch. 20.]

When this same blessed man, Lord Benedict, lay sick in bed, he looked toward [Col. 0039C] the infirmary and saw an innumerable multitude of white-clad persons enter and gradually fill all the space of that house. Seeing the house filled with those most splendid spirits, he supposed it was the assembly of brethren. He called Otger, the guardian of the sick, a man of good religious character, and said to him: “Brother Otger, is this our custom, that the convent should come to the infirmary dressed in white? Believe me, today I see what I have never heard had happened before.” But when that brother maintained that there were no white-clad persons in the infirmary, still persisting in the same opinion, he added: “I greatly wonder how you can say this, when not merely part of the house but all of it is full of men dressed in white [Col. 0039D], and those same persons surround you on every side where you now speak.” Then at last he understood that the one to whom he was speaking did not see an assembly of men but of blessed angels. After a short interval it came to pass that the servant of God Benedict, summoned by those white-clad and glorious spirits whom he had seen, died; and, entrusting his blessed soul to them, he passed with them, as it is fitting to believe, to the heavenly kingdoms. [lacuna]

Geoffrey was a nobleman, lord of a castle called Sinémur. After living magnificently in the world for a long time, drawn by the divine Spirit, he renounced the world and, together with his son and three daughters, put on the religious habit at Cluny. [Col. 0040A] There, after living long in holiness and without reproach, he was made prior of the sisters of Marcigny, deservedly on account of his religious character and prudence. Having humbly and kindly administered their care for several years, he was overtaken, as mortals are, by bodily illness and died.

In the time of Peter the Venerable himself there was Bernard, monk and prior of Cluny, wholly devout, wholly laborious on behalf of the convent, and always embracing the Church of Cluny with the greatest charity. Commending him, Peter the Venerable, abbot of Cluny, wrote the following epitaph concerning Bernard:

> An eminent elder, to whom nothing youthful clung,  
> Bernard the prior rests buried in this earth.  
>
> [Col. 0040B] Here, entering the heavenly camp after his warfare,  
> he grew old, contending long in this contest.  
>
> For you, Cluny, he never spared himself;  
> no day passed for him without labour.  
>
> Thus, well bearing the burden of the entire day,  
> he rejoices to carry home in the evening his earned penny.  
>
> Brothers, remember this man who lies buried,  
> nor let it fall from your minds that earth covers his bones.

Lord Ralph was a monk and religious of this Peter the Venerable, abbot of Cluny; he later wrote the character and deeds, and the life and death, of Peter, abbot of Cluny himself.

Indeed, it must by no means be omitted how the angel of the Lord marked with Christ’s cross the place where the brethren die. Peter, abbot of Cluny, himself described this miracle in the following [Col. 0040C] manner: “Because of the ancient enemy’s open battles against Christ’s soldiers,” etc. The complete narrative appears in Book I, chapter 19, of the *Miracles*, and it would have been superfluous to repeat it here.

In the time of this Peter the Venerable, abbot of Cluny, the number of monks at Cluny was nearly four hundred. Some of them lived in the woods near that place, among whom Peter the abbot himself sometimes associated with the brethren. Their dwellings in the aforesaid woods—those of holy fathers and monks—were devout chapels: the chapel of Saint Radegund, the chapel of Saint Romanus above Boutavan, the chapel of Saint Vitalis near Cluny, the chapel of Saint John of the Wood, and the church of Costa. In these places they served Christ with [Col. 0040D] great devotion.

From all the aforesaid matters, and because of them, the Order of Cluny and its monastic observance were extended and propagated as far as the Valley of Jehoshaphat, at the tomb of the Mother of our Lord Jesus Christ, where Gelduin, a monk of Cluny, was abbot of the monastery of that valley.

Likewise, the monks of the monastery of Cluny entered into a confraternity with the monks and brethren dwelling on the holy Mount Tabor, where God was transfigured.

Subsequently, the men of Cluny acquired the monastery [Col. 0041A] called Cuntot, which is in the suburb of the city of Constantinople.

Finally, as time went on, these Fathers of Cluny drew into their confraternity and association churches, colleges, and monasteries to the number of nearly 314. Under the subjection of the abbey of Cluny there were abbeys, priories, deaneries, provostships, and offices, immediately as well as mediately subject to it, numbering about two thousand or more.

Now a few words must be said concerning the triumph which Father Lord Peter the Venerable, abbot of Cluny, gained in the schism of Pons, the seventh abbot, by inserting verses of Peter of Poitiers; the latter treats it in an excessively prolix style.

> [Note: [Col. 0041] These verses are found below among the other writings of the same Peter of Poitiers.]

> [Col. 0041B] Now, Peter, your new triumphs are celebrated everywhere;  
> now the hostile party lies beneath your feet, etc.

We must now also speak concerning the glorious end of Peter the Venerable, abbot of Cluny, from the words of Ralph, monk of that blessed Father, who described the life, character, and death of so great a Father.

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1157, on the first day of that year, the reverend and most lovingly remembered Lord Peter the abbot entered upon the way of all flesh; and at that hour his holy soul departed, at which we believe the Word of God was born of the Virgin Mother. He fittingly chose that hour for his ascent, since he had always humbly served Christ descending in birth. Therefore, while Christ Jesus was born of the Virgin Mother on earth, Peter the virgin was received into heaven, so that he who had devoutly celebrated the joy [Col. 0041C] of that singular birth with pilgrims as long as he lived might now, at the hour of Christ’s birth, receive in the seat of eternity the fruit of his devotion.

A great miracle occurred in the separation of the body and soul of this glorious Father, the venerable abbot of Cluny. When the holy man departed from his body, so that there should be no interruption to the divine offices of holy Mother Church, especially on that day, the litany having been said by the bishop and the prayers completed, the holy Father’s body was carried to the place where dead bodies were washed. There, stripped of its garments, the grace of the glorified man appeared to all who saw and marvelled. [Col. 0042A] His dead body was purer than glass, whiter than snow, and a heavenly body, though still on earth, in a certain wonderful beauty. Who would have believed that this holy flesh had ever been covered with haircloth, afflicted by fasts, made thin by holy meditations and contemplations, or worn down by vigils? It was indeed already, as it were, in a certain transformation of future glory: most splendid, without spot or wrinkle, bearing a presage of heavenly endowments. The disciples kissed their master’s head; they drank the water in which it was washed, and each seized whatever he could.

Thus blessed Peter the Venerable, abbot of Cluny, was buried at the head of the greater and newer basilica, with great honour and deep grief among his sons, [Col. 0042B] by the illustrious and most reverend bishop of Winchester.

The glorious man Peter the Venerable ruled this monastery of Cluny for thirty-four years, four months, and three days. Elsewhere, however, I find that he ruled for thirty-five years. He lies beside the altar of Saint James, behind the reliquary cabinet containing the shrine of All Saints, beside the gate through which one goes behind the choir on the right-hand side. His epitaph follows:

> The tomb declares that life is not everlasting;  
> whatever we are, the earth makes equal in death.  
>
> While Peter, the devout abbot, dies, justice itself is buried;  
> peace falls, order lies prostrate, and we are moved to weep and die.  
>
> He was his country’s salvation, the world’s glory, an ark of wisdom;  
> knowing no envy, he was a fountain of forgiveness.  
>
> On the solemn morning of God’s birthday,
[Col. 0042C] Dead, he obtained the many things that he deserved.

ANOTHER EPITAPH.

In the time when Bernard of Clairvaux flourished, there once lived  
Peter the Venerable, an Auvergnat by native land,  
abbot here of Cluny, instructor of Catholics,  
writing treatises against schismatics, Jews, and Mohammedans,  
as well as many volumes,  
various sermons, and compositions in prose and verse.  
He was noble, but loftier than all in character.  
May he, now reigning eternally in the dwelling-places of the Almighty,  
unceasingly intercede for all religious persons,  
and especially obtain for us Cluniacs  
the high joys of heaven, when our allotted time has run its course.  
This Peter lived here, who fixed his eyes upon heaven’s lights.

[Col. 0041]

TESTIMONIES OF THE ANCIENTS CONCERNING PETER THE VENERABLE.

(*Bibliotheca Cluniacensis*, p. 601.)

I. Saint Bernard, Letter 277, to Pope Eugenius on behalf of the Abbot of Cluny.

[Col. 0041D]

It seems foolish to write to you on behalf of the lord of Cluny [Note: namely Peter.], and, as it were, to wish to act as his advocate—he whom everyone desires to have as his own advocate. Yet I write: not because it is necessary for him, but in order to satisfy my own affection, not another’s; for, since I cannot accompany my friend in person, I follow him as he journeys abroad. Who shall separate us? Neither the height of the Alps, nor the cold of the snows, nor the length of the journey. Even now I am present, standing beside him in this letter. Nowhere will he be able to be without me.

I am indebted to his condescension, through which I was deemed worthy to be admitted to that state of grace. Yet grace itself has discharged the debt, because necessity has passed into willing desire. Honour the man, as a truly honourable member in Christ’s body. He is, unless I am mistaken, a vessel unto honour, full of grace and truth, richly supplied with many good things. Send him back with joy, for he will bring joy to very many by his return. Deign to receive him with more abundant favour, as is fitting, so that, when he returns, we may all receive from his fullness.

Indeed, if he should ask anything in the name of the Lord Jesus, he ought not to meet with difficulty from you. For, if you do not know it, this is the man who stretches out his hands to the poor [Col. 0043B] of our order; this is the man who, from the possessions of his Church, as far as he can do so without disturbing his own people, gladly and frequently gives provisions. Hear why I said, “in the name of Jesus.” For if he should ask—as I suspect and fear—that he be released from the governance of the monastery, who that knows him would think that he asks this in the name of Jesus? I am mistaken if he is not more fearful than usual, if he has not become better than himself, since you saw him; although from almost the beginning of his tenure he is known to have improved that order in many respects—for example, in the observance of fasts, silence, and costly and elaborate clothing.

II. The same, Letter 283, to the same person, concerning the monks of Gigny.

At Cluny we met with the men of Gigny in hope of peace; much was laboured for it, but nothing was achieved. [Col. 0043C] For the sole result at last of our entire labour over four days was the collapse of hope, etc. Indeed, to avoid going through each item, one whole abbey was destroyed. Yet, despite such great losses, we were prepared to forgive much, whereas they offered so little that the venerable abbot of Cluny, who was labouring more earnestly than effectively for the restoration of peace, did not judge it worthy of mention. Thus no settlement resulted, because so ridiculous a reparation was offered. They said: “Certain malicious men among our people did all the harm. What is that to us? Let them see to it,” etc. Finally, the lord abbot himself openly refuted and disproved evasions of this kind, affirming that it was justly demanded back by the Church what was clearly known to have been lost through the Church.

III. Pope Innocent II, in a certain manuscript diploma.

[Col. 0043D]

Innocent, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son in Christ, Theobald, prior of the monastery of Saint Martin of the Fields, and to his successors, etc. Therefore, beloved son in the Lord, Prior Theobald, granting your petitions, we fortify by the authority of this present decree the monastery of Saint Martin, over which, by the Lord’s ordering, you preside under the establishment of our venerable brother Peter, abbot of Cluny, etc. Given at the Lateran by the hand of Gerard, priest-cardinal and librarian of the Holy Roman Church, on the tenth day before the Kalends of April, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1142, in the sixth indiction, and in the fourteenth year of the pontificate of Lord Innocent II, pope.

IV. Pope Eugenius III, in another diploma.

[Col. 0044A]

Therefore, beloved son in the Lord, Prior Odo, granting your just petitions, we receive under the protection of blessed Peter and our own, and strengthen by the privilege of this present document, the monastery of Saint Martin, over which, by the Lord’s ordering, you preside under the establishment of our venerable brother Peter, abbot of Cluny, just as the other members of the monastery of Cluny. etc. Given at Paris by the hand of Hugh, priest-cardinal, acting in the place of Lord Guy, cardinal and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church, on the sixth day before the Nones of July, in the tenth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1147, and in the third year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Eugenius III.

V. Peter the Venerable himself, Book II of *Miracles*, chapter 12.

[Col. 0044B]

Brethren, when he also—Hugh II—had thus been removed, they set a day for a new election and summon those nearby and those far away to assemble on the appointed day. A great multitude of monks gathers with certain bishops and abbots; and, on the octave of the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin, alas that they had not provided better for themselves, they assemble before the present writer. They inform the aforesaid pope of this election of theirs and receive from him a rescript confirming what they had done.

VI. An anonymous monk of Cluny, in the treatise *On the Relics of Saint Stephen the Protomartyr*.

[Col. 0044C]

The lord and venerable Peter, abbot, caused these relics of blessed Stephen, as well as the tooth of Saint John the Baptist, with the care and diligence which he displays toward all sacred and divine things, to be most honourably enclosed in separate crystal reliquaries, beautifully decorated with gems and gold; and he ordered one to be suspended on the right and the other on the left above the high altar in silver chains, as may now be seen.

VII. Robert of Torigni, in his Supplement to Sigebert’s Chronicle, in the year of the Lord 1138.

On the Kalends of January, Peter the Venerable, abbot of Cluny, entered upon the way of all flesh.

VIII. Matthew Paris, *English History*, under Henry II, in the year 1155.

[Col. 0044D]

At the same time Henry, bishop of Winchester, having sent his treasure ahead through the abbot of Cluny—namely Peter—secretly departed from England without the king’s permission. Consequently the king caused three of his castles to be razed.

IX. Henry of Ghent, Book *On Illustrious Ecclesiastical Writers*.

Peter, abbot of Cluny, wrote various letters to various persons, useful in their thoughts and pleasing in elegance of language. He also wrote visions and revelations shown to certain persons in his own time.

X. Nicholas of Clamanges, cantor of Bayeux, Letter to Galiot de Petramala.

[Col. 0045A]

Among the more recent writers, Bernard first presents himself, then Hildebert of Le Mans, Ivo of Chartres, Odilo, Hugh, and Peter the Venerable, abbots of Cluny; finally Hugh and Richard, canons who followed the Rule of Saint Augustine.

XI. John Trithemius, Book II of *Illustrious Men of the Order of Saint Benedict*, chapter 123.

Peter, abbot of Cluny, learned in the Holy Scriptures and not ignorant of secular learning, distinguished in intellect and eloquence, no less venerable for religion and integrity of character than for learning, wrote useful and elegant sermons [Col. 0045B] to the brethren, Book I; *On the Solitary Life*, Book I; and Letters to Various Persons, Book I. He also wrote certain marvels and various revelations occurring in his own time, which are held by many. He published some other works also, which I have not yet seen.

XII. The same Trithemius, in the book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*.

Peter, abbot of Cluny, of the Order of Saint Benedict, a man instructed in divine Scriptures by continual study, gentle in mind, sweet and measured in speech, quite capable of persuasion, devout and praiseworthy in conduct, and an eminent zealot for regular observance, made his name known to posterity by writing certain devout [Col. 0045C] little works for the benefit of readers, of which the following are reported:

*Accounts of Many Persons*, Book I.

*On the Eremitic Life*, Book I: “I have received your letter.”

Letters to Various Persons, Book I.

He also published some other works that have not come to my knowledge.

XIII. G. Paradinus, Book II of the *History of Lyons*, chapter 35.

In the year of the Lord 1157, Heraclius was archbishop of Lyons, brother of Peter the Venerable, abbot of Cluny: both men outstanding in holiness of life and learning.

XIV. *Chronicle of Burgundian Affairs*, under the year 1122.

[Col. 0045D]

After Pons, Hugh became abbot of Cluny for three months; and when he died, Peter, surnamed Mauritianus or the Venerable—of whom some writings survive—was placed over the same monastery.

XV. Conrad Gesner, in his *Bibliotheca*.

Peter, abbot of Cluny, of the Order of Saint Benedict, wrote *Accounts of Many Persons*, Book I; *On the Eremitic Life*, Book I; and Letters to Various Persons, Book I. His letter to Lord Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, [Col. 0046A] concerning the translation of the *Alcoran*, or law of the Saracens, from Arabic into Latin, was printed at Basle by Johann Oporinus together with the *Alcoran*.

XVI. Antonio Possevino, in the *Sacred Apparatus*, volume III.

Saint Peter, surnamed the Venerable, a noble Auvergnat, ninth abbot of Cluny and eighth general, was elected on the octave of the Assumption of the Most Blessed Virgin in the year 1123. Having subsequently held the office of general for 35 years, 4 months, and 4 days, he died at Cluny, full of virtues, learning, and years, in 1157, on the eighth day before the Kalends of January; he was buried there between the altar of Saints James and Philip and the altar of Saint Denis. He wrote:

*Accounts of Many Persons*, Book I.

[Col. 0046B] *On the Eremitic Life*, Book I: “I have received the letter of your affection.”

Letters to Various Persons, Book VI.

In these he included a book against the Jews and another against the Petrobrusian heretics. While he was residing in Spain, he translated Mohammed’s *Alcoran* from Arabic into Latin; after returning to Cluny, he refuted it in five most learned books, which were also printed. [Note: [Col. 0045] I have neither seen these nor been able to find them, although I searched most diligently.]

He also wrote:

*On the Miracles of His Own Time*, Book II; *On the Transfiguration of the Lord*; *In Praise of the Tomb*; *On Saint Marcellus, Pope and Martyr*; one sermon *On the Veneration of Various Relics*.

[Col. 0046C] A copious and highly useful letter to Peter of Saint-Jean against those who deny that Christ ever openly called himself God in the Gospels.

*On the Life of Saint Matthew, Cardinal of Albano*, Book I. Epitaphs for various monks. Rhythmic verses in praise of the Saviour. Rhythmic verses *On the Resurrection*. Rhythmic verses on Lord Saint Hugh, abbot. Hymns on the Blessed Virgin Mary. Hymns *On Saint Benedict*. Hymns *On Saint Mary Magdalene*. A prose sequence on the same Most Blessed Virgin Mary.

Some of his works were printed at Paris in 1522 by Damian Hincman, and at Ingolstadt by Alexander Weissenhorn in 1546.

XVII. Benedictine Monastic Martyrology, for the eighth day before the Kalends of January.

[Col. 0046D]

At Cluny, the heavenly birthday of Saint Peter Mauricius, abbot, most renowned for learning and holiness.

XVIII. Calendar of Saint Leonorius of Bellimont.

On the eighth day before the Kalends of January: the death of Lord Peter, abbot of Cluny.

[Col. 0047]

PANEGYRIC BY PETER OF POITIERS, A MONK, ADDRESSED TO PETER THE VENERABLE ON HIS FIRST ARRIVAL IN SECOND AQUITAINE.

(*Bibliotheca Cluniacensis*, p. 607.)

LETTER OF PETER OF POITIERS TO LORD PETER, ABBOT OF CLUNY.

[Col. 0047A]

To the venerable lord and sweetest Father, PETER, abbot of the holy Church of Cluny, PETER of Poitiers, a sinful and weak monk, offers the affection of filial love in Christ.

As you were pleased to command, most loving Father, I have at last issued in corrected form those little verses which, when I was still a young man, at the time when you drew me from the mire of filth and from the pit of misery, I composed in praise of the omnipotent Creator—from whom you have every good thing—and in your praise; and I have copied them in due order at the beginning of your Letters. I have also placed there your verses, by which you most powerfully refuted the coarse barbarity of our rivals. [Note: [Col. 0047] We placed these among the other verses of Peter the Venerable himself.] Although by their golden splendour [Col. 0047B] they cast back the poor brightness of our silver, they nevertheless greatly please my mind, because they stand against our enemies like a sword drawn from its sheath.

But if anyone is indignant with me because I have dared to give something a title bearing my name and attach it to your books, let him know that this was done not through my presumption but by your command—a command which I consider it wicked to oppose. In all things, and in this also, I do not hesitate to obey you, not from a desire for arrogance—may the Lord always keep that far from me!—but from devotion to obedience; especially since I know that many men of proven religious devotion and humility diligently did this same thing long ago with writings of every kind. In this small work of ours I desire rather to imitate them than certain writers of [Col. 0047C] our own time, who, through some caution or ignorance unknown to me, suppress their names everywhere, falling into the folly of apocryphal writers. Those writers, fleeing reproof either for falsehood or for heresy—by which, as is reported, they leavened all their works—nowhere set forth their own names.

Therefore let no one hasten to judge me in this matter before the time, but let him leave me to God and to my conscience; and, if he wishes, let him write Ovid without a title. But may almighty God preserve you, dearest Father, ever mindful here and eternally of your little son, whom you begot for Christ the Lord in a second baptism. Farewell always in the Lord.

THE PANEGYRIC BEGINS.

Applaud, happy Cluniacs; rejoice:

[Col. 0048A] Another Hugh has been restored to you in character.

That man was noble and born of great parents;

the ancestry of his fathers also makes this man illustrious.

The former shines above all those whom

Lyons’ Gaul cultivates and reveres for nobility.

The mighty peoples of Latium, descended from royal stock—the leaders of the Auvergnat people—begot him.

He equals ancient poets in sharpness of mind:

in our age there will be no one his peer.

In prose he is a new Cicero; in verse, Virgil:

he argues like Aristotle or Socrates.

He matches the foremost and surpasses, to his praise, the latter,

who taught us by sacred eloquence.

Hardly does Augustine discern hidden things more subtly:

hardly can Jerome teach him anything.

[Col. 0048B] Gregory contributed nothing to him in lucid and gracious speech;

Ambrose contributed nothing to him in rhetorical power.

Let me briefly say what I think of so great an intellect,

lest, reader, I seem to you uncultivated or excessive.

He is musician, astronomer, arithmetician, and geometer,

grammarian, rhetorician, and dialectician.

But now I fear that I shall succumb to my subject

while I seek to recount his outstanding virtues.

What, I ask, should I relate first? Come to my aid, Muses;

speak verses worthy of so great a man.

Ease of intellect and gravity of character

rarely go together; these two are seldom united.

Therefore I wonder all the more that even in youthful years

Peter, the splendid light of young men, possesses both.

The devoted youth rightly recites his praise,

[Col. 0048C] for our praise properly becomes his honour.

From the eternal Father there was given to the world the one Light,

under whose guidance earthborn men may seek the heavenly kingdoms.

Simplicity and prudence reign together in him,

constant sobriety and chastity.

Chastity, the greatest companion of virtues, always clings to him,

and inwardly and outwardly he always preserves it.

The tongue cannot tell how discerning he is in all things,

and how fitted he is for every duty.

There is no need to fill volumes with many words:

the poet who is brief and good is pleasing.

When anyone has worthily praised your deeds, Peter,

he will be another Virgil, another Homer.

Gentle, peaceable, merciful, fittingly gracious—

no one can tell how good you are.

[Col. 0049A] Let aged old age therefore make room,

and not wish alone to hold sacred rule.

Come, strong young men, strong in courage.

The public care of God’s holy people suits you.

This is the man who calls you to the highest honours,

which his sober life bestowed on him from early youth.

O Cluny, the land of Auvergne sent him to you,

than which our Gaul possesses nothing more fertile.

Happy land, which deserved to bring forth so great a fruit:

it has given fathers to many Churches.

It is ever wont to be mother of illustrious men:

from it magnificent Odilo was given to you.

From it also came the sweet foster-child of Julian,

who ruled the Church of Tours well.

The fields of Auvergne bloom in your writings, Sidonius,

[Col. 0049B] and you were the restorer of the ancient tongue.

When he came again to restore peace among the monasteries.

Tell me, Muse, why does Aquitaine applaud so,

and why can it no longer conceal its joy?

Why too do you, who lately were wont to mourn,

now sing joyful songs with a cheerful countenance?

In time past it was pleasing only to weep

and to add unceasing tears to tears.

For he left us these tears alone,

he in whom, under God the Father, all my hope was placed.

Perhaps report whispers to you that he is coming?

May this be a happy cause for your joy.

But I cannot believe the deceitful monster,

[Col. 0049C] which scarcely ever, or never, speaks the truth.

Yet what it heard is now reported: he is near.

His piety brings him; put on fetters, you guilty men.

Poitiers, rejoice, for now your walls are shining,

and you, noble hall of the suburban place.

Although you have schismatics and seditious men,

if you seek peace, Peter, your peace, is here.

Men of Angers, you draw your swords in vain:

every effort of yours will be futile.

You unhappy men do not know against whom you prepare weapons of war:

this is the man whom no one can conquer in war.

Do you wish to know by what arms our leader is conquered?

Surrender yourselves to him: he will immediately be overcome.

Believe me, I beg you; believe me, companions, I beg you,

[Col. 0049D] and submit your hard necks to the merciful Father.

He comes peaceably: do not reject peace.

He wishes once more to reconcile your guilty men.

Are you thus mindful of the sweetness and mercy

which he showed even to brethren in exile?

Are you thus mindful of the spiritual teaching

which his eloquent tongue so often gave you?

Then the doubled joys of the holy feast shone forth,

when so great an angel was a guest among us.

At that time there was no one among us

upon whom his abundant favour was not bestowed.

Fervent compassion strove in his holy breast,

either in giving good things to the good or pardon to the guilty.

What praises, what vows shall I render you, most high God,

who were pleased to relieve my sorrow?

[Col. 0050A] Let tears now flee; let long sighs cease.

Peter is here: our greatest salvation has returned.

You send him once again to the peoples of Aquitaine, good King,

because you desire to make your Church peaceful.

Aid your servant, most unconquered King,

that he may joyfully bring you back a doubled gain.

Of many, you chose this man to be your standard-bearer

and to give civic laws to your soldiers;

to instruct us, to teach us in the contest

that we are able to conquer Ethiopians by sacred arts.

Therefore preserve him for us through a long life,

that he may draw many peoples to your kingdoms.

O morning star, flashing on earth with heavenly light,

stretch forth, I pray, your gracious hands to my words.

Receive, in your customary kindness, the utterances of your poet,

[Col. 0050B] and read the little verses of Peter, the least of men.

I am that least Peter of yours, O greatest Peter,

who gave you these small writings in your praise.

It was the first time when the Aquitanian people celebrated a triumph,

noble leader, at your arrival.

You were scarcely known to me except insofar as report

had carried to these regions rays of your light.

Nor indeed could so clear a lamp remain hidden,

which God himself had set on high.

The whole world everywhere shone with your light,

and your celebrated fame travelled throughout the world.

My mind was already occupied with your excellence,

and I had the greatest desire to see you,

when suddenly a happy report resounded all around,

[Col. 0050C] and the Father, already present, was announced.

We run at once; we all come forth rejoicing;

both sexes applaud to meet you.

Then the holy hall immediately resounds with new praises,

nor was any layman then without a voice.

We rush competitively to see your consecrated face,

and each wishes to be the first to see you.

O cheerful face, never made severe by any dignity—

how pious, beautiful, radiant, and princely you were!

Your lovely eyes proclaimed royal stock,

as did the modest blush that coloured your cheeks.

Your clothing and bearing, witnesses from a humble heart,

declared that you counted the world as nothing.

Why delay? You enter the walls as a new shepherd,

[Col. 0050D] and, entering, offer holy kisses to the flock.

That day seemed long to me, desirous to hear

how great the grace of your holy eloquence might be.

For your eloquence had been excessively praised among us;

but who could describe it with worthy praise?

I heard it, I confess—but something beyond narration.

I heard the distinguished speech of a prince.

Your speech is mighty; I dare write nothing about you,

lest so weighty a work break my slender pen.

Before you, Cicero, that king of the Latin tongue,

if he should happen to wish to say anything, would be mute.

You conquer Socrates; you make Plato speechless;

you make every rhetorician tremble.

I was astonished, I confess, at such sweetness of speech,

and began to speak thus with myself:

[Col. 0051A] “Fame, you reported nothing worthy of so great a shepherd;
I see something greater than your voice had sung.”

O altogether wondrous power and grace of the King,

who enriches his servants with so great an honour!

For whatever is holy, whatever is regarded as honourable,

and whatever befits a good ruler—

nobility, virtue, wisdom, eloquent speech—

are here; this man lacks no grace.

Then more and more your affection drew me,

and soon I was wholly carried away in love for you.

Your sitting, voice, face, walk, and every action,

O light of humankind, were full of beauty.

If it pleased you to sit in cloistral manner,

your religious appearance terrified the frivolous.

[Col. 0051B] If private conversation wished to be pleasant,

your speech drove every sad thing away.

If words were agreeable when strictness was set aside,

gravity was always mingled with holy jest.

The sweetness of the Father lacked none of a monk’s gravity,

nor was the gravity of the monk without grace.

Who can adequately and worthily recount

how great is your discernment in punishing faults?

When you discern, mercy so moderates anger

that the guilty man himself seeks to be punished by you.

Only rebels are punished with a heavier rod,

if anyone should dare to oppose your authority.

But what am I doing? If I sounded with a thousand tongues,

my pen could not recount everything.

Nor could it then, though it attempted this,

[Col. 0051C] presenting small gifts to so great a man.

For so great was the fervour of pious love in me

that I often spoke to myself in these words:

‘What are you doing, unhappy man, and why is your Muse silent?

Why do you hesitate to commend yourself to the merciful Father?

Believe me: he is merciful; he will disdain no one

who freely devotes himself to his service.

Will such great love lack its own reward?

Or will this labour of yours be in vain?’

Thus encouraged, I presumed upon his kindness;

and from his kindness I received more than I deserved.

His most abundant kindness accepted my little poem;

it accepted the small vows of its servant.

What shall I, light of the world, give you in return for so great a gift,

[Col. 0051D] that our page was in your hands?

The eyes of the blessed man read my poor words:

O what a joyful day that was for me!

That day shall be celebrated by me through all my years,

on which you yourself became my Father and Lord.

But soon—alas!—these joys had an end:

the times of my happiness were brief.

He departed without me—without whom life is death to me;

the merciful Shepherd departed, leaving me behind.

O my great salvation, why have you so abandoned me?

And why did I deserve to lose you so suddenly?

Why did I not make that journey, even on foot?

Why was I not at least a servant or a footman?

Let every burden hang from my neck,

that I might be a little servant to your servants.

[Col. 0052A] Surely no hardship would have delayed my course;

that long road would have conquered my wretched feet.

But, all too unhappy and unworthy of so great an honour,

I was left empty as my hope fled.

Yet when you departed, you gave me these final words,

which I still bear as sure pledges of a father:

‘Peter, I leave you in order to receive you again; cease weeping:

after a short time has passed, you will be ours.’

Behold, I have now spent many sorrowful years,

and do not see the Father’s sweet promises.

Until now I have lived in tears from that time,

nor since then has my mind been without grief.

Although there have been some who revealed what was in their hearts

and told me that you remembered us.

Remember me, then, I pray, O sweetest of all things;

[Col. 0052B] let a father’s care look upon my tears.

Let the compassion in which you always wholly abound keep watch—

that compassion whose aid every shipwrecked man experiences.

If perhaps you ask why I desire this so ardently:

I wish absolutely nothing else than to be yours.

I have vowed to give myself to you as your perpetual servant:

after Christ I wish always to have you as Father.

Give Peter back to Peter—the least to the greatest Peter:

so may that pious Peter, the keeper of the keys, be favourable to you.

So may the wisdom of great Odo increase in you:

so may you be able to restore the way of the Order.

So may the radiant life of Majolus rise again in you:

so may you bring the Lord very great gains from the flock.

So may Odilo and great Hugh flourish anew in you;

[Col. 0052C] may the spirit of both be doubled in you, Peter.

In praise of his triumph at Rome over Pons and the followers of Pons, who were attempting to expel the aforesaid Peter from abbatial office.

Now, Peter, new triumphs are celebrated for you everywhere:

now the hostile people lie beneath your feet.

Now, outstanding Father, because you have returned victorious from the City,

the treacherous tongue of Pons’s followers is silent.

The insolent mouths of dogs have laid aside their rabid barking;

their malicious hearts, bereft of sense, are stunned.

The sacrilegious men did not think this could happen,

when they vomited rigid threats from their swollen mouths,

when, applauding themselves that they had recalled a master like themselves,

they gave loose rein to various crimes.

[Col. 0052D] Truly no human cunning can overturn

the eternal counsel of the supreme Judge.

Hail, bravest victor in great contests;

hail, you for whom Christ was sword and spear.

Beloved of God, you conquered; in vain did profane fury

exert its strength for your harm.

Behold, whether it wishes or not, the impious people, the rebellious crowd,

all Cluny trembles at your commands.

Behold, whether it wishes or not, you shall hold royal sceptres

and be an authoritative conqueror.

What are you doing, impiety? What do you devise in your brutish heart?

What do you say? Surely you can prevent nothing.

Peter is here—Peter, abbot of Cluny,

Peter, death to vices and destruction to your own.

Your lust will feel his arms harsh enough,

[Col. 0053A] and you, criminal people, will not escape his hand.

While he rules, nothing proud can rule;

under his leadership, no path now lies open to crimes.

Though you grieve, though you do not wish it in any way,

the magnificent victor now holds his rightful authority.

People hostile to God, you wished it, but could not achieve it;

but God, as he willed, promptly was able to do it.

With a rejected mind you wished to reject the righteous man;

Christ did not will this and took away your power.

To him alone we deservedly pay thanks

and offerings of praise for the wondrous trophies of our leader,

who, having rescued him from such powerful calamities,

makes him hold high sceptres over peoples.

Therefore we applaud your triumphs, venerable shepherd,

and render due vows to the most high God.

[Col. 0053B] Thus he tests his servants through many perils;

thus, at his command, the enemy rages.

Thus the good Creator has given evil things a place in the order of things,

so that the wicked man may perish through that by which the righteous prospers.

For the unjust man lives for the righteous, and the righteous for the unjust,

as the sacred page of the ancient Fathers teaches.

Our commonwealth indeed seems to have been harmed a little;

but this injury brings us many advantages.

For, in a wondrous manner, the event through which impiety thinks

to harm us brings forth many benefits.

No perfection was lacking to you, holy youth:

already you could equal your Fathers.

Only this remained: that your light should not lie hidden under a cloud,

but should scatter its rays throughout the whole world.

Until now the Ocean had known you, and Gaul alone was aware of your virtues;

[Col. 0053C] and while it rejoiced, made mighty by its distinguished offspring,

that it alone had borne so great a protector,

a new cause of a new triumph arose by God’s will,

through which Roman dominion now favours you.

The sacred court itself, admiring your powers,

calls you to govern the reins of the whole world.

Why should I mention the cities of Latium, the banks of the Rhine,

or the Pannonian people and the neighbouring kingdoms?

Your glory has now penetrated barbarian frontiers,

and the unconquered Getan praises your battles accomplished.

He whom one region of the earth had previously made its leader,

tested by the small fire of conflict,

now, with the enemy put to flight through heavenly aid,

[Col. 0053D] the whole earth desires to see as conqueror.

We make a great gain because, through the cause of this schism,

that treacherous dragon has fallen utterly.

And when the slippery serpent attempts to lift up its head,

it is broken, and in dying spews black poison.

The savage deceptions of the black snake have perished,

nor does Rome suffer the monster to live long;

but Peter quickly protects his Peter from the enemy,

striking down the beast’s neck with a two-edged sword.

No longer beneath the covering of sheep’s wool

will the horrible limbs of the great-hearted wolf be able to lie hidden.

All things which had been covered by the garb of piety lie exposed:

the impious thefts of a sacrilegious mind are evident.

He would have done better to cultivate the fertile shore of the Eridanus,

[Col. 0054A] and it harmed him to leave Italian soil.

Here the first judgment of the sacred senate,

alas, had thrust him into a harmful nearby exile.

The hermit attempted to leave his own woods

and, having once cast aside honour, to enjoy it again.

O how many peoples would unjust frenzy have devastated

had Rome not swiftly brought us aid!

How many ranks would have fallen beneath the devilish weapon,

and how great would have been the ruin of the untaught people!

A report arose in western lands

that one of the great prophets had suddenly arrived.

Already popular error had made a new sect,

while the rustic crowd imagined him to be some god.

One calls him a new Moses, another Daniel, another John;

another calls him Elisha or Solomon.

[Col. 0054B] One declares that he girds his arms with thin iron

and endures a new kind of martyrdom;

another, that he is wholly separated from human food

and can receive no nourishment but heavenly food.

Each praises him for standing barefoot at the altar

and for continuing innumerable prayers.

But one who had been deceived by a greater phantom

cried these words in the middle of the marketplace:

‘Run, you sick; seek out the holy man.

Run: behold, a second Martin is here.

Despising the men of Cluny, he chose

to seek God for himself through the sands beyond the Tyrrhenian Sea.

Now, therefore, returning to reclaim his former rights,

he performs very many signs by angelic direction.

[Col. 0054C] Perhaps that first Martin has come to life again in the world,

he who by a nod alone scatters every evil.’

But who could sufficiently either laugh at or recount

all the empty dreams of the mad populace?

O how often, chosen one of God, did we all tremble,

since true love troubled us,

lest Roman gravity should favour trivial nonsense

and a slippery magician turn sober hearts;

and lest he should attempt to ensnare even learned Bruti and stern Catos

by various deceits.

It is sad to say, but that great Girard himself,

alas, was capable of being taken in by this cunning.

What hope would remain if the sacred senate itself

and the whole Quirinal City favoured him?

[Col. 0054D] But may God avert this far from that noble city,

which holds beneath itself the peoples of the whole world!

There sacred faith has never suffered anything harmful,

where that great sceptre-bearing champion of the faith sits.

Its walls, founded by his purple blood,

fear neither cruel winters nor savage wars.

Paul, no unequal guardian, likewise protects those same walls,

and together the two hold imperial majesty.

No sect of error can harm the city entrusted from heaven

to such great rulers.

Therefore, Fathers and friends of the supreme Thunderer,

it is fitting to offer you the vows of song and praise.

For this triumph concerns you especially,

for the battle was fought on behalf of your soldier.

This is that good soldier whom you desired

[Col. 0055A] to be the first leader of the militant order.

Under your standards he had spent his youthful years

and by virtue had surpassed his own age.

Often he had crushed the fierce enemy with sacred arms;

often formidable Goths had fallen by his sword.

Very often he had ravaged Ethiopians wandering beneath the cold night;
often he had ravaged the Moabites.

Many times, too, he had brought back splendid trophies

from the kings of Assyria by his strong hand.

Finally, no terror of wars could break him,

nor could any barbarism bend him.

Your experience had surely recognized this, Fathers:

nothing in the constitution of things escapes you.

Surely you saw something in that young man

by which he might become a Father to his fathers.

[Col. 0055B] I know not what shone forth in that age,

to which supreme honour fittingly belonged.

Nor is one man chosen in vain from so many legions

to govern public affairs with the Caesars.

O chief senators, to whom the Creator of the world himself

gave the reins of the Roman empire to govern:

I believe that it was not without heavenly counsel

that, when the civil state was now almost wavering,

the venerable assembly, in appointing a ruler,

consulted the hidden counsel of your judgment.

As though especially worthy of royal honour,

this one man alone pleased you out of many thousands.

O you to whom it is permitted to open and close the heavenly gates

and to behold all God’s secrets!

It has been granted to you to know what power of his

[Col. 0055C] was that which earned so great a reward of merit.

Thus Peter, the merciful leader and Father, pleased your eyes,

which no hidden things deceive.

For he is truly happy and worthy of every honour

who can be good in your judgment.

Happy is he whom you judge stronger than all others

and more worthy of supreme rule.

From this, without doubt, it was long clear to me

that this man lacked no endowment of virtue.

Nor, like certain men whom we often see, does he desire

a scanty lineage which his blood denies him.

Thus this man possesses something in which, by perpetual paternal right,

there dwells love of religion and uprightness.

They are shown to have possessed these virtues from their forefathers and ancestors:

[Col. 0055D] Both parents possessed them and always cherished them.

Was not Saint Mauritius once the most illustrious glory of the Arverni, the light and honor of his native land? Our Aquitaine still laments him, snatched away; with him the whole dignity and power of the nation would have been buried, had there not remained a noble offspring in whom, as though transferred into it, there shines an image of his native land’s virtue, in no respect unlike him.

Dry your tears, then, Aquitaine: whatever you lamented as lost in that mortal man by the law of mortality, his sacred progeny repays to you with abundant interest. Nor can one readily tell, when looking at the children born of his fair wife, whether the elder Mauritius made them heirs of character or of wealth; indeed, Otto seems still wholly alive in his brothers.

[Col. 0056A] And although the same piety and virtue, most like that of their father, shine with marvelous splendor in the other seven, yet among them you, our leader and illustrious shepherd, gleaming more brightly—as the morning star surpasses the other stars—outshine, by your radiance, the brilliant luminaries of your lineage.

Hail, blessed mother, to whom the Virgin Mary granted to bear such offspring: in the age of our times you bring forth mighty lights for the western lands. And though you surpass other mothers in your fortunate issue, you too deserved to surpass them in your outstanding Peter. That devout father and serene ruler of men therefore commanded him to ascend to the highest honors, so that, fighting nobly for his ancestral laws, he might break all Antiochus’ forces in the whirlwind of war and renew, in our age, the times of the Maccabee.

[Col. 0056B] But you who hold the realms of highest Olympus—you, I say, Fathers, to whom my Muse has recourse—now that the poem is finished, I ask as helpers of my prayers, in return for what I have accomplished in your praise.

And first of all, gracious gatekeeper of heaven, you who, in order that your soldier might govern the Cluniac realm, cast down the wicked tyrant from the sacred see: by your footsteps once upon the billows of the sea; by the titles of your faith and the rights entrusted to you; by your Latium and Rome, and by those keys which can open heaven and close it to whom you will; and by the holy love through which you so loved him that he alone, out of all peoples, pleased you, so as to become leader and prince of your host—

[Col. 0056C] I beseech, implore, request, demand, entreat, and pray: greatest Peter, make Peter mindful of his own Peter.

You also, holy Paul, whose saving teaching founded Christ’s Church throughout the whole world—you, chosen vessel, heavenly trumpet, greatest herald—we ask: hear the sighs of our prayer. Both together, lords and Fathers, come to our aid, I pray, so that, when the devout, distinguished, most gentle, and gracious man shall deign, while traversing far and wide the lands, cities, camps, towns, and villages of his widespread dominion, accompanied by the senate of noble magnates, to visit our region and the whole people whose lands are bounded on two sides by the farthest Ocean and the banks of the Loire, he may receive great applause worthy of so great a prince.

[Col. 0056D] And when crowds of people converge from every side, and each hastens to be the first to see those features which make despairing minds rejoice and can dispel a person’s sad anxieties, then may he deign, in his customary way, to extend his holy right hand to me, concealed far behind the backs of great men amid the numerous throng of unknown common folk, and say: “My servant, come near and be more cheerful. I shall no longer delay to fulfill what I have promised by my deeds.”

### When he crossed to the island of Aix

While you, devout shepherd, are pleased to visit the brethren of Aix, the very elements render you service. The whole sky was covered with southern rain-clouds; when the frightened rain sees your sails, it departs.

[Col. 0057A] Lest the waves should be swollen by cruel north winds, as soon as you enter upon them, wind and breeze flee away. Many a cloud had covered the sky in black gloom; when you board the vessel, all becomes serene.

O holy and blessed man, to whom all that the supreme power of God creates in the world so gladly obeys!

[Col. 0058A] Now, illustrious man, deign to remember your servant; I beseech you, bring my prayers now to fulfillment. Grant that I may be able to behold your Cluniacs with you! May honor, strength, and long life be yours!

[Col. 0057]

## The Same Peter, to a Slanderer

[Col. 0057A] I know that envy, as long as this age endures, will never wholly die. Although I have nothing for which anyone should envy me—for who envies a poor man?—yet an answer must be provided for those who, judging themselves most holy, may perhaps charge us with vanity and flattery.

[Col. 0057B] To them we answer quite plainly that this little work of ours serves not flattery but the common good. Let this most holy man of ours therefore hear what the usefulness of this matter is. It is in some sense natural and characteristic of noble and freeborn minds that, the more they are raised by greater praises, the more earnestly they strive after virtue.

Indeed, it is clearer than daylight to me that no perfection is lacking in that most reverend man whose praises I have presumed briefly to attempt. But since “every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, descending from the Father of lights” (James 1), whenever we proclaim God’s grace in anyone, all praise is undoubtedly referred back to God himself, its giver.

It is written: “Praise the Lord in his saints” (Psalm 150). If it should be objected that saints ought to be praised only after this life, we reply in return that the Lord Christ himself commended John the Baptist, while he was still living in the flesh, with exceptional praise (Matthew 11), and called Nathanael, when he came to him, a true Israelite without guile (John 1). Likewise, we read that the apostle Paul very often extolled his disciples or fellow apostles with the highest praises. He himself also said: “Outdo one another in showing honor” (Romans 12); and, “to whom honor, honor” (Romans 13).

[Col. 0057C] Sulpicius Severus wrote much about the virtues of the blessed Martin while Martin was still alive. The most celebrated Fathers of the Church—Augustine, Jerome, Ambrose, and Paulinus—honor one another with many praises. Among them the blessed Paulinus, after abandoning worldly rank and becoming priest and monk at Nola in Campania, is read to have composed a most elegant book in praise of the great emperor Theodosius.

Sidonius, a most learned man of most ardent genius, formerly prefect and consul and later bishop of the Arverni, exalts nearly all the illustrious men of his own age with such encomia that his own most elegant letters, both in verse and prose, testify to this for those who understand them. It is also clear with what praises the renowned martyr Cyprian celebrates in his letters Pope Cornelius, the reader Celerinus, and other saints still fighting against the devil and the world.

Fortunatus too, our man of Poitiers, whether priest or bishop, who attained notable distinction in poetry, raised up Gregory of Tours, very many other bishops of his age, and King Sigibert as well, in an applauded panegyric, as we know.

[Col. 0058A] My discourse would fail before my subject if I began to recount individually how many and how great were our Fathers and most religious men who endeavored to honor, commend, and exhort one another with mutual praises—not for the sake of flattery, as certain men of our time, utterly ignorant and wholly unfamiliar with antiquity, dream, but by a most honorable custom of humanity and devotion.

[Col. 0058B] And if we turn to pagan philosophers, who in that period wrote history, or anything belonging to the disciplines of the liberal arts, except in praise of kings or emperors? From their numerous multitude this occurs to me: the most weighty man Cicero wrote in his books *On the Republic* that the leader of a state must be nourished by glory, and that a commonwealth stands only as long as honor is shown to its leader by all.

Let these things suffice for envy; and now let this most holy man of ours blush and allow us reverently to cultivate and honor our lords and Fathers with the due proclamations of praise. For one who is rightly praiseworthy will never be angered by the praises of praiseworthy men.

### Against a Barbarian

Cruel barbarian, man-beast, envious plague,  
you who dare to carp at the praises of Peter the Venerable,  
I am not surprised that you gnash savagely against us.  
For your fierce rage is characteristic of the Suebi;  
according to the custom of your people, this is what you think of our poem.  
What praise is, what poetry is, what sweet solace life possesses,

[Col. 0058D] what peace is, what devotion is, what virtue is, what honor is—you do not know, barbarian; therefore you swell with envy. So be silent, Cimbrian, lest my storm overwhelm you. If you do not desist, I shall proclaim war against the Cimbri not only in these verses but in many books; and your whole race shall pay, together with you, for your impious crimes.

### Epitaph of Pope Gelasius II

John, a man grave and wise in deed and word,  
after having first been, through great merit,  
raised from monk to archdeacon and chancellor of the city,  
when Bishop Paschal had been taken to the stars for his merits,  
at length deserved to ascend the sacred see,  
worthy to be Gelasius the Second after the First.

But because he had been elevated without the king’s command,

[Col. 0059A] the prince raged horribly, and sweet daughter Gaul, in her accustomed way, received the exiled Father. Had it been permitted him—believe it certainly—every virtue, devotion, and honorable quality would have flourished under him; and the peace of the Church would have flowered throughout the whole world.

But black death snatched away the man when the venerable shepherd had scarcely completed his first year of pontificate. Two days remained when he fell asleep at the Cluniac refuge of Roman jurisdiction. Thus laid among his beloved pupils, he rests with the holy Fathers, and awaits the time when the Creator and Judge of the world shall come in power and restore his fallen ashes to their former limbs.

Most blessed Cluny, you will forever remain exceedingly fortunate because the Father of the world, apostolic and supreme priest

[Col. 0060A] of the Church, and a special son of your mother, passed from you to the heavenly realms and rests buried in you. Nor do we believe less fortunate the man to whom gracious Christ granted the great gift that monks might continually behold a monk—their father and beloved pledge—and, watering his tomb with tears, always hold him in special remembrance in their holy prayers.

### Epitaph of Bishop Adefonsus

There is a city in the Spanish land which its inhabitants call Salamanca. Adefonsus governed it in pontifical rank; he lies buried in this tomb. As he was returning from the Council of Reims, here he made an end alike of his life and of his journey.

[Col. 0059]

## Letter of the Same Peter to Lord Peter, Abbot of Cluny

[Col. 0059B] To his most reverend lord and dearest Father, PETER, abbot of the holy Church of Cluny, PETER of Poitiers, sinful and weak monk: whatever a most devoted son owes to the best of fathers.

Dearest Father, I have seen and examined closely the little book which scarcely ever leaves my hand for any interval of time; the more often it is read, the more it draws the reader’s mind, and the more subtly it is examined, the sweeter it tastes. O writing most worthy of every kind of praise, which, as that Flaccus says:

> “Nowhere fears the keen scrutiny of the judge”
>
> (Horace, *Art of Poetry*, line 364),

a fountain of wisdom, a fountain of eloquence, a fountain of learning: with the flashing splendor of your eloquence you have struck all the little lamps of our intellects with sudden brilliance.

[Col. 0059C] I certainly used to think that I knew something. But now, most eloquent man, not only those like myself, but all men of our time who have ability in letters, or think they possess any, what are we in comparison with you? Truly, when I look upon your most lucid, wise, and penetrating utterances and then return to my own foolish, childish, tasteless productions, I blush greatly that I ever thought I knew anything.

I had indeed long known that the keenness of your intellect surpassed that of all the philosophers of our Gaul, especially in these times when all things rush toward decline, including the studies themselves. But since I saw the aforesaid book, I not only prefer your excellence to theirs—for that is too little—but do not hesitate to compare it with the most perfect men of every earlier age.

[Col. 0059D] For we see that you have attained knowledge of all the liberal disciplines in such a way that, unless we knew that your heart was continually illuminated by the secret inspiration of him through whom gifts of knowledge are distributed to each person, we should marvel beyond belief that a man still almost in his prime—and, what is more remarkable, a man of our age, in which we see literary studies completely abandoned and dead—could have grasped so much.

[Col. 0060B] For, to say nothing of sacred letters, both Testaments of which you always have ready to hand through retaining them by memory: who was ever more subtle than Plato, more forceful in argument than Aristotle, more beautiful or copious in discourse than Cicero? What grammarian was better equipped, what rhetorician more ornate, what dialectician more powerful, what arithmetician more skilled in numbers, what geometer more exact in measure, what musician more melodious, what astronomer more clear-sighted?

And if we may dare to say something about the holy Fathers, from each of the four rivers of paradise—which, after the holy Evangelists, water the whole world—you bring back something resembling each: for you proceed swift with Jerome, copious with Augustine, profound with Ambrose, and luminous with Gregory.

[Col. 0060C] Awake, therefore, most eloquent man, and strive to distribute to your faithful fellow servants the food of doctrine, in which you certainly abound more fully than all your predecessors, not only by speaking but also by writing. Thus you will be able to benefit greatly not only us but even the most remote Christians—not merely those now present, but those of future times as well—if, after the manner of your Fathers, as the divine Spirit suggests to you, you leave to the memory of posterity, in sermons, letters, and various treatises, monuments of so brilliant an intellect.

[Col. 0060D] For this end heavenly providence has placed your holiness on the lofty watchtower of its Church: that you may defend those hastening by the way of Zion toward the joys of the eternal Jerusalem from the assaults of hostile Babylonians,

[Col. 0061A] and may restore all wandering travelers to the path of the royal road, without ceasing day or night.

Apply yourself, then, great glory of our age, bright star divinely arisen for the world, lest the treasure entrusted to you lie uselessly concealed; rather, let it be entrusted more and more to the bankers and multiplied a hundredfold through your industry, so that it may obtain for us and for you a lofty degree of immortality.

I know that I am very rash in daring to exhort you thus; but may your most serene kindness, upon which I greatly presume, pardon me. For since, most loving Father, you avoid boasting with every effort, I fear no little that perhaps under this pretext you may wish to hide yourself too much. You must take care, most discerning man, lest, while you flee too greatly the praise of men, you omit those things

[Col. 0061B] for which that faithful evangelical servant will deserve to be greatly praised by the good master of the household (Matthew 25).

Consider, I beseech you, that if our holy Fathers had not found occasions of this kind and written, but had passed even the best life in inactive silence, they would doubtless neither have gained so many peoples for God nor have left among us today so celebrated and sweet a memory. Yet by writing they deserved both to please God through the twofold fruit of holy preaching and to provide all those coming after them an example for devout imitation. Hence they impressed such love for themselves upon the hearts of the faithful, since God speaking in them is heeded and the teaching of the Holy Spirit is honored.

[Col. 0061C] By the wondrous working of divine grace, while they kindle the love of God in the minds of readers or hearers, they themselves also become, among the faithful, lovable and most desired for the sake of God’s love. And, what we may admire with devout delight,

[Col. 0062A] though long dead, they live in their writings; and although they are not seen bodily, they spiritually make their presence available to us daily.

But what am I doing, urging such things upon your majesty and, by superfluity of words, magnifying as though difficult or foreign to the duty of your office a matter which the abbots of Cluny have held from ancient times by special prerogative—the practice of writing? Nor are they compelled to write by authority alone; if they fail to do so, they must blush as degenerate men, greatly unlike the pattern of their native house.

Of their most glorious Fathers, that one alone may suffice us as an example: he who laid the first foundations of our community, and deserved to be the first ruler of so great a commonwealth, the first Father of so great a monastery, the first begetter and nurturer of so many sons in Christ.

[Col. 0062B] I mean the most blessed Odo, outstanding in holiness of life and glorious in learning and miracles. Since he is known to be most celebrated not only among us but throughout almost all the churches of Latin Christendom, especially because of studies of this kind, he seems by hereditary right to have transmitted the grace of this office to all his successors and, as it were, to have consecrated it by his own precedent.

If you object that some of them wrote absolutely nothing, Aymard is excused along with both Hughs, since they lacked that perfection of learning. Maiolus is excused, because perhaps he had no leisure for this. But what excuse do you offer, you who, if compared with these men,

[Col. 0062C] alone among them possess a tongue?

As your blessedness prays for me, may the merciful and omnipotent God preserve you here and for eternity, holy lord, deservedly venerable and most beloved Father.

[Col. 0061]

## Peter the Venerable

> [Note: Col. 0061D]

Peter was an Arvernian by birth, but the family from which he sprang is not clear. Peter of Poitiers, likewise a monk and bearing the name Peter, whose certain short works survive in this library, calls his father Saint Mauritius in the following verses of the panegyric addressed to him:

> Was not Saint Mauritius once  
> the most illustrious glory of the Arverni,  
> the light and honor of his native land?  
> Our Aquitaine still laments him, snatched away;  
> with him the whole dignity and power of the nation  
> would have been buried, had there not remained  
> a noble offspring in whom, as though transferred into it, shines  
> an image of his native land’s virtue, in no respect unlike him.

Nor does the author of the *Chronology of the Abbots of Cluny* depart far from this when he says: “When Hugh II died after three months, the beloved lord Peter, surnamed Mauritius, a man venerable in life, noble by birth, and native of Auvergne, was elected.”

Therefore both the person who calls him “Maturitius” and Papirius Masson, who calls him “Mauriacensis,” as though named from Mauriac, a town of Auvergne, undoubtedly require correction. But whether this surname Mauritius, now for the first time restored to him, ought to be referred to the ancient family of the counts of Saint Mauritius in Auvergne, we may not pronounce. For John Sauro, a most learned man, distinguished for his service to Gallic antiquity, himself a native and ornament of Auvergne, does not hesitate to affirm that Peter sprang from the noble blood of the Montboissiers; and, having even sent us their family pedigrees, he confidently persuaded us to adorn Peter’s portrait accordingly.

[Col. 0063B] This would indeed suit him better—rather, excellently—if it were clear that the first and ancient Montboissier lords, or, as the *Chronicle of Cluny* calls them, young noblemen, had formerly been surnamed Mauritii or had been counts of Saint Mauritius. However the matter stands, it is learned from Letter 27 of Book II that his father, known by his surname alone, was buried after his death at the monastery of Sauxillanges in Auvergne; while his mother, Raingard by name, later received the veil of a nun at Marcigny and commendably spent the remainder of her life there.

[Col. 0063C] Eight children remained from their marriage. Peter of Poitiers calls one of them Otto, saying:

> Nor can one readily tell, when looking at the children born of his fair wife,  
> whether the elder Mauritius made them heirs of character or of wealth;  
> indeed, Otto seems still wholly alive in his brothers.  
> And although the same piety and virtue, most like that of their father,  
> shine with marvelous splendor in the other seven,  
> yet among them you, our leader and illustrious shepherd,
