> gleaming more brightly—as the morning star surpasses the other stars—  
> outshine, by your radiance, the brilliant luminaries of your lineage.

The other seven were: first, Hugh, mentioned in Letter 39 of Book VI, who himself had two daughters, Ponsia and Margaret, nuns at Marcigny with their grandmother Raingard. Second, Pons, mentioned in Letters 16 of Book I and 17 of Book II; he eventually became abbot of Vézelay, as appears from Letter 4 of Book III and Letter 38 of Book VI. Third and fourth, the monks Jordan and Armannus, discussed in Letter 17 of Book II. Fifth and sixth, Eraclius and Eustachius, called brothers of Pons, abbot of Vézelay, in Letter 4 of Book III. The first, Eraclius—whom some also call Heraclius—was first a canon of Lyons, as Letter 5 of Book IV teaches, and later became archbishop of Lyons, as we shall show more fully elsewhere. The second, Eustachius, was Peter’s only brother who remained in the secular world, as is clearly declared in Letter 14 of Book VI.

The seventh, finally, was Peter himself, ninth abbot of Cluny. Besides Peter of Poitiers, his notary and monk; Saint Bernard of Clairvaux; the abbots Suger of Saint-Denis and Peter of Celle, whose many letters to him and from him survive, he is also treated by Innocent II, Roman pontiff, in various charters; by the author of the treatise *On the Relics of Saint Stephen the Protomartyr Brought to Cluny*; by Robert of Monte in his continuation of Sigebert, around the year 1158; by Matthew Paris in the *History of Henry II, King of the English*; Henry of Ghent in the book *On Illustrious Ecclesiastical Writers*; Nicholas of Clamanges, cantor of Bayeux, in a letter to Galiot de la Pierre-Mala; John Trithemius in Book II, chapter 123, of *Illustrious Men of the Order of Saint Benedict* and in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*; Guillaume Paradin in Book II, chapter 35, of the *History of Lyons*; Nicolas Vignier in the *Chronicle of Burgundian Affairs*; Conrad Gesner in the *Library*; Antonio Possevino in volume III of the *Sacred Apparatus*;

[Col. 0064B] Cesare Baronius in the *Ecclesiastical Annals*; Papirius Masson in the *Annals of the Franks*; Arnold Wion in the *Tree of Life* and in his edition of the Benedictine monastic martyrology; René Chopin in the *Monasticus*; and others.

Yet the universal and remarkable encomium of his learning, by which Peter of Poitiers testifies that he exceeded all his predecessors in abundance not only in speaking but also in writing, must by no means be omitted here. The same Peter, writing to him, says:

> Who was ever more subtle than Plato, more forceful in argument than Aristotle, more beautiful or copious in discourse than Cicero? What grammarian was better equipped, what rhetorician more ornate, what dialectician more powerful, what arithmetician more skilled in numbers, what geometer more exact in measure, what musician more melodious, what astronomer more clear-sighted? And if we may dare to say something about the holy Fathers, from each of the four rivers of paradise—which, after the holy Evangelists, water the whole world—you bring back something resembling each: for you proceed swift with Jerome, copious with Augustine, profound with Ambrose, and luminous with Gregory.

The *Chronicle of Cluny* recounts extensively enough his life, devotion, holiness, and other virtues; but only after Radulf, his monk and disciple, who also writes in a certain letter concerning Peter’s death to Pope Adrian IV as follows:

> This holy man departed from the body at the hour when we believe that the Word of God was born from the Virgin Mother; and he rightly chose this hour for his ascent, since he had always humbly served him descending at his birth. Therefore, while Christ is born on earth from the virgin Virgin Mother, Peter the virgin is received into heaven, so that he who, as long as he lived, had devoutly celebrated the joy of each Nativity with pilgrims, might now at the very hour of Christ’s birth receive the fruit of his devotion in the seat of eternity.
>
> A great miracle occurred at this departure. When the saint departed from the body, so that no impediment might be caused to the offices of Mother Church, after the bishop had recited the litany and the prayers had been completed, the body of the saint was carried to the place where the bodies of the dead were washed. There, when it had been washed and clothed, the grace of the glorified man appeared to all who saw and marveled. For he was purer than glass, whiter than snow; by a marvelous beauty his heavenly body, while still earthly, foreshadowed itself. Who would have believed that this flesh had ever been clothed in haircloth, afflicted by fasts, worn down by meditation, and exhausted by vigils? It was already most splendid, as though in a certain transformation into future glory: without spot or wrinkle, bearing an omen of heavenly gifts. The disciples kissed the master’s head, drank up the water in which he had been washed, and each seized whatever he could, etc.

[Col. 0064D] Accordingly, the Benedictine monastic martyrology does not hesitate to place him among the saints and assign him a feast day on 25 December, in these words: “At Cluny, the heavenly birthday of Saint Peter Mauritius, abbot, most distinguished in learning and holiness.”

Frederick the emperor also calls him Venerable in a charter containing these words: “Out of reverence for and at the request of our beloved Peter the Venerable, abbot of Cluny, we also confirm by royal authority the deed of donation bestowed upon the Church of Cluny concerning the monastery of Baume.” This surname, then, seems to have been won for him by an esteem for learning and devotion equal to that accorded the Venerable Bede.

## Six Books of Letters

> [Note: Col. 0061D]

We have restored the sequence and arrangement of these letters to their genuine order, in accordance with the authority and testimony of the *Chronicle of Cluny*. Peter of Poitiers, his notary, divides all the works of Peter the Venerable into letters, sermons, and treatises, saying: “You will be able to benefit greatly not only us but even the most remote Christians—not merely those now present, but those of future times as well—if, after the manner of your Fathers, as the divine Spirit suggests to you, you leave to the memory of posterity, in sermons, letters, and various treatises, monuments of so brilliant an intellect. For this end heavenly providence has placed your holiness on the lofty watchtower of its Church: that you may defend those hastening by the way of Zion toward the joys of the eternal Jerusalem from the assaults of hostile Babylonians, and may restore all wandering travelers to the path of the royal road, without ceasing day and night.”

Peter himself mentions the letters in Letter 35 of Book IV, and his aforementioned amanuensis in Letter 7 of Book VI. But the sole author of the *Chronicle of Cluny* teaches in how many books Peter divided them: he names only six and records how many letters each should contain. Therefore, accepting his authority and testimony, we have attempted—owing to the lack of manuscript copies—to restore to their true and genuine order the sequence and arrangement of all these letters, which Peter of Montmartre, himself a Cluniac monk who first saw to their printing in 1529, had hitherto interpolated. Those who possess manuscripts will be best able to judge whether we have done this correctly; and, should they find anything arranged otherwise, they will not begrudge informing us, if they wish.

(*Bibliotheca Cluniacensis*, p. 621.)

# Book I

## Letter I

To the supreme Shepherd of God’s Church and our special Father, Lord Pope INNOCENT [Note: Innocent II, elected in 1130, to whom he frequently writes elsewhere in Books I, II, III, and IV], Brother PETER, humble abbot of the Cluniacs: the service of most devoted humility.

[Col. 0061D]

The lord archbishop of Bordeaux, Gaufridus [Note: Gaufridus, to whom Letter 12 of Book IV is addressed, where there is more concerning him], among his other virtues—which you yourself also know—recently passed through our region, burning with great love for you,

[Col. 0063A] and gave us no small joy concerning your successful achievements. Since he reported that, for restoring the peace of God’s Church, you devote your whole effort, bring every diligence to bear, and refuse no danger of labor, I was moved to write to you, because I could not cooperate in person.

[Col. 0064A] I grieve indeed, and not a little—before him whom I cannot deceive I am distressed—that you bear such great labors especially at this time without me. But the fragility of my waxen vessel is so great that, as I have often found, it is almost compelled to melt in the Italian sun before it begins to appear. You yourself saw how, for this reason, I was recently both useless to you and burdensome to myself at Pisa, so that, unless I had hastened quickly to depart, I should have ended both my life and my affairs. This is the sole and entire reason that has kept me absent from you for so long. If it could in any manner be removed or mitigated,

[Col. 0065B] nothing thereafter could tear me from the footsteps of your fatherhood; no misfortune could sever a son from his father’s side.

Meanwhile I do what I can, and in these letters, with charitable boldness and filial devotion, urge you to bear manfully the burdens of God’s Church which in our days not human but divine judgment has laid upon your shoulders. Do not be wearied by any length of labor, for he who through his Spirit alone has united the whole Church in you and subjected almost the entire world to your feet will subdue the very few enemies who remain and, as is his custom, exalt the Catholic name above every name of heresies and schisms.

Therefore remain steadfast, as you have hitherto done,

[Col. 0065C] for that prayer by which Christ prayed for Peter that his faith should not fail can never be frustrated; rather, he himself should raise the fallen, strengthen the fearful, and confirm the wavering (Luke 22).

Together with the whole Church entrusted to you by God, you have also me—the least among Christ’s members—and your Cluny; as long as breath remains in our nostrils, we shall be prepared to obey, to cooperate, and perhaps even to die with you. No alteration of changing things will change us, no diversity make us variable; nothing can separate us from the shepherd, from Peter, or from Christ—all of whom we possess in you alone.

[Col. 0066A] Wherever your dwelling may be found, our obedience and devotion will remain with you everywhere. For, according to the poet:

> “While Camillus dwelt at Veii,  
> there was Rome.”
>
> (Lucan, *Pharsalia*, Book V, lines 28–29)

And Peter in prison, Clement in exile, and Marcellus in a stable governed the Church no less than when at the Lateran, and Christ’s sheep obeyed them as true shepherds. Remember that the Church has always grown through labors, been multiplied through sufferings, and overcome every opposition through endurance. May the already elapsed number of years increase your hope of perfect victory: since you have successfully contended for seven years against God’s enemies,

[Col. 0066B] in the eighth, the resurrection, you will sing Alleluia as though hell had been conquered; and the Church, which after her Christ “drank from the torrent on the way,” shall therefore “lift up her head” (Psalm 109).

## Letter II

To his lord and Father, singularly worthy of reverence and special affection, MATTHEW, bishop of Albano [Note: Of the Cluniac family; also addressed by Bernard in Letter 21 and by Peter in Book II, Letter 11; Peter writes of him at considerable length in Book II, chapters 4, 5, 6, and following, of the *Miracles*], F. PETER, humble abbot of the Cluniacs: the salvation promised by God to those who love him.

Hearing your messengers, reading your letters, and recognizing your unfailing love toward us, I blush that I can offer nothing worthy in return for so great affection, and acknowledge that I am unable to make any repayment adequate to so great a charity. Absolutely nothing: for even if I spent all

[Col. 0066C] that I possessed upon you, I still would not make a worthy return. For, as Solomon says in the Song of Songs: “If a man gives all the substance of his house for love, he will despise it as nothing” (Song 8).

Therefore, compared with this, all that I possess is nothing; and so I find nothing commensurate with these merits of yours. Yet there is something which does not seem to be nothing: if one who loves with unfeigned charity is loved in return, this is certainly as great as charity itself is great. I repay this, so far as I can, to your reverence with an undivided heart; hence I trust that I have now repaid something to you.

I have learned that our condition, concerning which I recognized your anxious love, is being graciously and peacefully ordered by the gracious Savior, except that Spain, disturbed by fresh upheavals following the death of the king of Aragon, threatens some of our monasteries with a similar disturbance.

[Col. 0067A] We have made the rest known to the lord pope and to you through our brethren Peter and Beroard. But what we were unable then to communicate to them because they were hastening and we were occupied, we now set forth in this letter. The lord bishop of Troyes, Hato—or Ato, as others write—himself a Cluniac monk and one to whom the same Peter often writes later, is prepared, as he says, to give us one prebend in his church. [Note: [Col. 0067A]

He is ready to grant us a single prebend in his Church. And it is certain that it was indeed granted, from two charters of the same Hato, one of which we have already transcribed on page 1407 of this *Bibliotheca*. The other, taken from the cartulary of the church of Troyes and supplied to us through the kindness of the learned Nicolas Camuzat, reads as follows:

[Col. 0067B] In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Hato, by divine mercy humble minister of the Church of Troyes, to all the children of the Catholic Mother Church, forever.

Upon the friends of the Bridegroom, the vicars of Jesus Christ, this duty especially rests; before all things this is necessary: that, by every means in their power, they should strive to cherish the spotless bride of the Lamb, whom he claimed for himself with his own blood, and to honour the ministry entrusted to their stewardship. Therefore, since in the days of our priesthood the Church of Troyes had been pitiably worn down through the lack and need of its servants, we felt compassionate sorrow—not without much grief, not without great anguish of heart. For the ancient nobility of a once more renowned church had been given over to contempt, its glory to shame; the multitude of sons, in whose constant presence it had been accustomed to rejoice, had become a solitude, since those canons whom it had outwardly possessed sought not the things of God but their own things, and rendered no honour of due service to their mother.

[Col. 0067C] Accordingly, having taken counsel with wise persons, after the many petitions of our canons, prolonged over several years, we decreed—and, with the assent of the religious and venerable man Alberic, bishop of Ostia and legate of the Apostolic See, who confirmed what we did—that henceforth those admitted as canons in our church, unless they presented themselves as resident in service to the church, should receive from the prebendal benefice no more than twenty shillings each year. The Cluniacs alone were excepted: at the request of the aforesaid legate we granted them a prebend in our church.

Moreover, adding this further provision, we prohibited anyone ever thereafter, on any pretext or for the sake of any person, from making a separate prebend out of the common property of the brethren, or granting one to anyone. And so that all this might retain its full force irrevocably, not only among those now present but also before future posterity, by the authority of God, of the lord legate, and of ourselves, speaking in our own voice, with all the brethren consenting in heart and speech, [Col. 0067D] we pronounced sentence of anathema upon those who, at any time or in any manner, should alter what we had decreed in view of piety or—God forbid—annul it, always saving the reverence due to the Apostolic Majesty. Therefore, to secure this present document of our constitution, we have strengthened and confirmed it with the seal of the lord legate, our own seal, and the common seal of the brethren, the names being subscribed of the persons who were present and approved it.

The mark of Lord Alberic, legate. The mark of Hato, bishop. The mark of Theobald, abbot of Saint Columba of Sens. The mark of William of Saint-Martin. The mark of Erard of Saint-Loup and of Hugh of Crésy, abbots. The mark of Baldwin, dean of Noyon. The mark of Odo, provost. The marks of Manasses, another Manasses, Odo, and Fulk, archdeacons; and of Burdin, Warner, and Stephen, priests. [Col. 0068B] The marks of Peter and Drogo, deacons. The marks of Teger, Peter, Gueric, and Hilduin, subdeacons.

Done at Troyes in solemn chapter, in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1145.

Gibuinus, chancellor, wrote and authenticated this.

But afterwards Stephen, abbot of Cluny, restored that prebend to Henry, bishop of Troyes, and to the chapter of the aforesaid Church of Troyes, with the assent of [Col. 0068B] Theobald, prior of Cluny. In compensation Henry, count of Troyes, gave the Church of Cluny twelve pounds of Provins money in annual revenues, as is clear also from the following instruments from the archives of the Church of Troyes.

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. I, Stephen, abbot of Cluny, to the venerable Bishop Henry and the chapter of Troyes, and to their successors forever.

It is fitting and consonant with the duty of equity that transactions and agreements established by the wills of those making them, lest in the passage of time they fall into oblivion, should be committed to the trust of written records. Therefore, the prebend which the Church of Cluny held in your church, with the assent of our chapter [convent], we grant, donate, and restore to you, to be possessed freely and forever without any claim of objection, and assigned to whomsoever you wish.

Moreover, the noble man Henry, count palatine of Troyes, especially devoted to the Church of God, gave the Church of Cluny [Col. 0068C] as alms twelve pounds of Provins currency in annual revenues, generously providing for both churches . . . so that the Church of Troyes recovers its prebend, while the Church of Cluny loses nothing on that account, but indeed receives a better common return from the benefice—one which it cannot doubt is both more productive and more suitable for it. May the Lord God repay him—He who is able to repay, and who is in the cause, indeed is the cause. And lest anything be altered or lost, we have taken care to fortify this with our seal, etc.

This was done in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1164, in the thirty-first year of the reign of Louis, king of the Franks.

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. I, Theobald, prior of Cluny, and the entire convent of the same church, to Henry, by the grace of God venerable bishop of the Church of Troyes, and to its whole chapter, forever.

Since indeed . . . agreements and conventions between contracting parties, lest they be erased by forgetfulness, are glad to be distinguished by writings and seals; and thus that which they contain is believed to be ratified. We approve, grant, and confirm what Stephen, lord abbot of Cluny, did at the request of the pious and glorious Count Henry concerning the prebend which we held in your church—namely, that he restored it to you, to assign to whomever you wish. And although this is contrary to the custom of our church, nevertheless, out of love for the said count, we strengthen it under the protection of our seal. But because the often-mentioned count, in the provident exercise of his discretion, did not wish his requests to appear burdensome to us in any respect, he established at Sainte-Marguerite de Champagne an annual benefice of twelve pounds to be paid to our church, as his charter states, etc.

This was done in the year 1165, in the reign of Louis, most pious king of the Franks.]

just as prebends were granted long ago at Chartres and Orléans [Note: [Col. 0068D]

Just as they were granted long ago at Chartres and Orléans. Concerning the prebend held by the Cluniacs in the Church of Chartres, the following rescript of Pope Alexander IV is found in the Cluniac cartulary; it was most kindly supplied to us from the library of the most celebrated President de Thou.

Concerning the prebend held by the Cluniacs in the Church of Chartres.

Alexander, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons the abbot and convent of Cluny: greeting and apostolic blessing. To the just desires of petitioners, etc. See under Alexander III, for the year 1181.]

so that the need of the Cluniac brethren may be relieved by its revenue—a need of which you are well aware. If this can be done according to God’s will, I ask that it be done through you. But if not, I do not wish to gain even the whole world at any peril to my soul.

Constantine, priest, enemy of Cluny, and author of the old schism, has added a recent perjury to the accumulation of his former evils. Having undertaken a day for litigation with Stephen in our presence, he set out for Pisa without my knowledge, as I have heard, in order to evade the judgment of our court by his customary lies. I ask that you report this to the lord pope, so that our priest may not be permitted to evade the judgment of our church, by which he has suffered no injury. For if it were otherwise, and he permitted so great a church to be dishonoured by so contemptible a person, it would trouble his Cluniacs more than I can presently express—although this is said with all reverence for [Col. 0069B] his majesty.

The abbot of Bonneval [Note: [Col. 0069D] Abbot of Bonneval. Perhaps Hugh, to whom Saint Bernard wrote Letter 351.]—which is near Chartres—intends, he says, to come to Cluny with a great many honourable and learned men, if through the counsel of your wisdom he can obtain the lord pope’s permission to depart. For you know the reasons by which, entangled as he is, he cannot long be kept away from his own people. He therefore asks that letters concerning this matter be sent to him also. Write back to me whatever is the case concerning the state of the lord pope and of yourselves, whose prosperity I most eagerly desire, both for the common good and for your own peace; so that, when I learn what concerns you, I may either rejoice with you or grieve with you.

## LETTER III. To the venerable and most dear lord AIMERIC, cardinal and chancellor of the Apostolic See [Note: [Col. 0069D] Aimeric, cardinal and chancellor of the Apostolic See. To him again in Letter 34 of this book; and Saint Bernard, Letters 15, 20, 48, 51, 53, 54, 157, 160, 162, and 181.], Brother PETER, humble abbot of the Cluniacs, greeting.

[Col. 0069C]

I am sorry, and not a little distressed, that although the needs of ourselves and of certain others would make it expedient for me to stay with you at the curia for a while, I cannot do so, prevented by bodily frailty and the character of the adverse climate. My whole constitution finds both the elements and the food of the Italian region especially harmful, so that it judges going there to be death and returning to be life. Therefore, when matters arise, I more often entrust my place to my letters, [Col. 0070A] so that through them I may accomplish what I cannot accomplish in person.

I therefore ask your friendship towards me, long sincere, that in the present matter—which is mine only by reason of charity—charity itself may be heard rather than I, and that tested truth may be believed rather than myself as writer. In our regions, as I think you partly know, the order of affairs has been so changed and ecclesiastical peace among so many so disturbed that the members of Christ’s body rise against one another. As though a finger threatened to tear out an eye, or a hand attempted to cut off a foot, so they ravage themselves by internal discord, pursuing one another not so much with swords as with hatreds, not so much through assailants as through greed.

And, what is more perverse, superiors are so hostile to inferiors—prelates to their subjects, bishops to monks [Col. 0070B]—that they seem intent with all their strength not, like shepherds, upon feeding the flock, but, like the hirelings truly described in the Gospel (John 10), upon shearing its wool and milking its milk. Though this complaint is one made by many monks against many bishops, we have recently received an intolerable complaint from the monastery of Aniane against the bishop of Béziers [Note: [Col. 0069D] Against the bishop of Béziers. Béziers, a city of Septimania on the river Orb. Usuard, for 22 March: “In Septimania, in the city of Béziers, the deposition of Saint Aphrodisius, bishop and confessor.” William of Newburgh, book II, chapter 11, calls it the city of Beder; Pliny, book III, chapter 4, and Pomponius Mela, book IV, chapter 5, call it *Blyterae* of the Septimani; Hildebert, in the *Life of Saint Hugh*, calls it *Bliterium*; and Rigord, book I, *On the Deeds of Philip Augustus*, calls it the most wealthy city of Biterim. [Col. 0070D] It is subject to the archbishop of Narbonne and is called in the vernacular Béziers.]. If I tried to explain it point by point, I should appear excessively—or perhaps tediously—long-winded. To avoid this, I have resolved to keep silent; and, in place of all the things I could enumerate at greater length, I briefly ask that you kindly hear and heed those brethren who are coming to you, and that, as defender of the spiritual monastic profession, you rescue the noble and, as I myself have seen, devout monastery of Aniane from such great oppressions, both for the salvation of your soul and because it has from ancient times stood under apostolic protection.

## LETTER IV. To the man of every reverence and dignity, truly a priest of God, HUGH, archbishop of Rouen [Note: [Col. 0070D]

Hugh, archbishop of Rouen. Below, book VI, Letter 32. Saint Bernard, Letter 25; and Arnulf, bishop of Lisieux, folio 18, who also composed for him this epitaph:

> Among bishops worthy of special honour,  
> Here Hugh lays down the burden of our flesh.  
> His body, committed, is enclosed in a brief tomb;  
> Yet neither hemisphere confines the man’s deeds.  
> Whatever he dispenses and shares among all,  
> grace had conferred and granted to the man.  
> Thus abundance produced the fruitful harvests of virtues,  
> And the man was magnified beyond what is human.  
> At length, after the happy course of a renowned life,  
> A mournful hour took away the aged man who had earned his rest.  
> Martin, destined to be your equal and companion in the same lot,  
> He obtained by dying the same day as you.

He also wrote one letter to Suger, abbot of Saint-Denis, and left many other monuments of his learning. One of them, not yet printed, on the heretics then swarming in Armorica, he dedicated to Alberic, bishop of Ostia, by a short letter; through the kindness of the learned Lord Martin Marrier, to whom we owe its receipt, it reads as follows:

“To Alberic, bishop of Ostia, son of the holy Roman Church and frequent legate of the Apostolic See, [Col. 0072D] Hugh of Rouen, a sinner and, such as he is, a priest.

Reverend Father, etc.” This is the dedicatory letter to his book *On the Heretics of His Time*. See under Hugh, for the year 1164.], Brother PETER, humble abbot of the Cluniacs, wishes honour and glory among holy priests.

At the end [Col. 0071A] of your letter, your reverend charity directed us to write back concerning the condition of your most dear brother and son William. But we, shrinking from mentioning him last, as though he were a matter of no consequence, place him first, as is fitting: him whom we now hope holds by no means the last place in the heavenly order.

Carried by his holy desire and your praiseworthy concern to the lodging of poor Martin, he rejoiced with a joy beyond words and gave God immense thanks: after such long journeys over the earth, the son had returned to his father’s bosom, the foster-child to his nurturer’s breast, and hoped to breathe out his last spirit in his hands. When we arrived, we found him rejoicing in this joy. His great delight at our arrival increased so much that, almost forgetting all his infirmity, he could scarcely contain himself. Had not the bed to which he was confined revealed his illness, the liveliness of his face and movements would have shown him entirely well. He declared to all who came to him, individually and collectively, that God had visited him and given him beyond what he had asked or understood. [Col. 0071B] He constantly affirmed that nothing now failed him; that he awaited the mercy of the Lord in security; and that he no longer feared but desired his calling.

Visited by us every day, he did not cease to confess his sins, give thanks to God, and commend himself to the prayers of the brethren. Seeing him occupied with such devotions, while his strength gradually ebbed and he became weaker and weaker, we had him anointed by the lord abbot of Vézelay and refreshed with the viaticum of the sacred body. Then, when the Nativity of the Saviour arrived, after hearing Mass and again strengthened by holy communion, he gradually failed in body until the day of Saint John the Evangelist.

On that day, after Vespers, when I had come to visit him with the brethren as usual and saw him very severely weakened, I took the Lord’s body from the church and fed him with the heavenly bread with my own hands. Soon afterward he ceased to speak. Continuing in that silence, which had begun at midnight, throughout the next day, at evening, no longer aware of anything earthly, he began—while we all marvelled—to utter as loudly as he could such words as these: “Lord, have mercy; dear Lord, have mercy; Lord, mercy”; and, as it seemed to us, at times, “Lord Martin, have mercy.” [Col. 0071D] In this prolonged and unbroken invocation of mercy, on the feast of the Holy Innocents, his innocent soul, while we all stood by and prayed, departed from the miseries of the world and, as we may rightly believe, attained the mercy which it had so devoutly and repeatedly sought.

His body was honourably buried by us, as was fitting, in the cloister of the infirmary before the chapel of the blessed Mother of Mercy. There it awaits, by God’s grace, to be raised to the glory of the resurrection; meanwhile, by the representation of himself [Col. 0072A] it invites all passers-by to intercede for the repose of his spirit. Finally, I inform you that the cleric whom you gave to attend this blessed brother of yours performed his assigned office so faithfully and devoutly, and, although serving another, won our favour to such an extent that even if all others fail him, we henceforth cannot possibly fail him. We therefore ask your holiness to ensure that he experiences from the living the fidelity which he strove to maintain toward the dead. That blessed man, while at the point of death, wrote to your fatherhood concerning him; and it is not worthy, I do not say of you, but of any good persons, to refuse anything to his last prayers and quasi-testamentary letter.

## LETTER V. To the venerable lord ATON, bishop of Troyes, to be received in the charity of Christ with all the inward affections of the heart, Brother PETER, humble abbot of the Cluniacs, wishes fullness of salvation and love.

[Col. 0072B]

I do not know where to begin. I am wholly at a loss for an opening. Dark clouds have covered a clear day; the murky vapour of the air has veiled the sun’s bright rays; the noonday splendour has suddenly assumed the appearance of blackest shadows. The order of nature has changed; the east has turned into west; a mighty fire has suddenly been extinguished; the silver cord has been broken; friend has been separated from friend.

O friendship, a thing most precious among mortals—but the dearer it is, the rarer it is—where have you gone? To what place, hating the earth, have you withdrawn? Why have you left wretched human beings, you firm union of souls? Why has your absence made all things desolate? Perhaps, as we read of that ancient dove, finding no place where your foot might rest, you returned to the ark; received by Noah the builder, you escaped the dangers of the flood (Genesis 8). Truly, I say, you, dove and friend of eternal peace, free from gall and knowing nothing but love, recoiled from the waves of tumults and floods of discord which have occupied the whole earth. Finding no resting-place below, you swiftly flew back to the heights. Received by the hand of Noah, builder of the world, you penetrated heaven’s innermost regions; and, by your departure, you threw all outer things into mutual commotion.

Hence I see all earthly things conspiring in their mutual destruction; hence I observe kingdoms rising against themselves; hence I see the whole mass of the worldly body, its joints loosened, everywhere shaken and dissolving. Hence neither neighbour keeps faith with neighbour, nor friend with friend, nor brother with brother, nor son with father; hence the laws of all relationships are violated; hence blood has now stained the surface of all lands. But why do I complain about things outside? Why mourn what is remote? Why lament what belongs to others? When domestic matters are troubled, why care for external ones? If I cannot be at peace with myself, with whom shall I keep peace? [Col. 0073A] If I am evil to myself, to whom shall I be good? (Sirach 14.)

But why this? It concerns you—yes, you—once my friend of one mind, at one time most dear, and, in the words of Flaccus, not indeed now but once, “half of my soul” (*Odes*, book I, ode 3, verse 8). I complain, therefore, that you have wickedly halved me, leaving me not whole; I complain that you have broken the bond of love which I believed indissoluble; I complain that you have violated the pact of fellowship which you swore with me.

Perhaps you will answer that I deal with you more harshly than is just. But I declare that I speak far more leniently than I ought, and than your offenses against me have deserved. If you ask what they are, I have already said, and I repeat again: in one matter you have made yourself guilty of all evils, as the Apostle testifies when he says: “Whoever keeps the whole law but stumbles in one point has become guilty of all” (James 2). No one doubts that this one matter is love. You stumbled in this one matter when you abandoned a friend who had done you no harm, kept faith, and believed that you kept it with him.

But perhaps you will say: “I acknowledge none of the things you charge against me; I keep faith and preserve love.” Very well: you keep faith and preserve love. The proof of love is the performance of a deed. If it is fire, it is warm. If it is warm, it does not long contain its flames. If it contains them long, it will soon cease to be fire. Envoys used often to come to us from your region; messengers would precede messengers; earlier letters would be anticipated by those following; and the public road from Troyes to Cluny [Note: [Col. 0073D] From Troyes to Cluny. Troyes is a city of Champagne on the Seine, called *Augustobona* by Ptolemy, *Tricassae* by Marcellinus, *Tricasses* by Sidonius, and “the city of Tricassina” in Letter 12, book VII. More often, however, it is called *Trecae*, both by Gregory of Tours, Flodoard, and other ancient writers, and by medieval writers; in French, Troyes.] would be continuously travelled by those going and returning. [Col. 0073C] But now all things have become trackless: impassable Riphaean mountains have been interposed; the unnavigable sea of India has been poured out; and the Scythian sea, which freezing cold constricts, prevents access. A new silence of the tongue, idleness of the hands, inability to dictate, and lack of scribes have been proclaimed. There are no reeds with pens anywhere, no birds with feathers, no four-footed animals with skins. Because all these are lacking, that great affection of your love for your friend cannot be expressed.

Therefore, since I “waited, and they did not speak; I listened, and there was none to answer” (Job 32), I am the first to break into speech, since I desire to be faithful even to one who is faithless. Awake, then, at least when roused; return, even when recalled; speak, even when questioned. Write back, speaking not with a heart and a heart, but with a single heart, confessing what is and not what is not. Tell me whether that love, derived from the heavenly love by which we once began together to aspire to the blessed life, still remains. If I learn that it remains in its condition, let us rejoice together; if I find it diminished, let us labour together to restore it.

And if, through some whisperer, you suspect that I have injured the mutual love which ought to exist between us, I am ready either to clear away the stain or to endure with equanimity whatever blows you may inflict upon [Col. 0074A] me. If perhaps I have spoken more boldly than I ought, I ask your pardon, because I have said these things not out of proud presumption but out of love’s confidence. I have written not as an abbot to a bishop, but as a true friend in God, as I believe, to a true friend.

## LETTER VI. To the venerable lord and most dear father ALTON, bishop of Troyes, Brother PETER, humble abbot of the Cluniacs, wishes that he may be crowned with the glory and honour of holy bishops.

The hope of a mutual conversation and expectation of your long-desired fellowship, which I trust I shall soon obtain, restrained the mind that wished to burst into speech after reading your letter. [Col. 0074B] It scattered the mass of arguments already assembled, and, as though a barrier had been placed before it, blocked the vein of a spring just about to flow. For I judged that I was vainly expending labour and time if I preferred to make known by literary work what I could communicate to the sanctuary of your heart through familiar conversation.

If this did not oppose my mental efforts, perhaps I would say, using your own words, that I had not sent more than a hundred pounds of myrrh and aloes in vain. For just as such remedies preserve a beloved body from decay, so I had prepared to aid a languishing love, lest it gradually dissolve. Yet even if incorrupt love had no need of my myrrh and aloes, the service of a devoted heart ought not to have been despised. For although the Psalm says to God concerning the Lord’s body, “You will not give your Holy One to see corruption” (Psalm 15), and no wise person doubts that this occurred by divine power, not by aromatic substances, nevertheless Joseph and Nicodemus, who anointed the Lord with such ointments (John 19), did not lose with him the fruit of their devotion. Thus I too, although I contributed nothing to inviolate love by my ointments, nevertheless displayed my affection’s devotion in offering them.

Nor is it inappropriate that I, who, as your letter testifies, used to send honey and honeycomb of sweet words, have now sent the myrrh and wormwood of harsher words. For I have read that it is said of the Bride in the Song of Songs: “Your lips distil honeycomb; honey and milk are beneath your tongue” (Song 4). And of the Bridegroom: “His lips, distilling choice myrrh” [Col. 0074D] (Song 5). Lips, then, do not always distil honey, but sometimes myrrh as well, because speakers dispense words now sweet, now biting, according to the nature of circumstances.

From there I was proceeding with cheerful mind and unfettered step along the pleasant course of your whole letter, when suddenly I stumbled upon the silver cord. My steps became entangled in it and I nearly fell; and had I not understood that it was stretched out by a friend rather than some deceitful person, I should have wished to cry: “They stretched cords into a snare; they laid a stumbling-block for me beside the way” [Col. 0075A] (Psalm 139). For you thought, when I said “the silver cord has been broken,” that I had money in mind, and that I called the cord broken because your hand had ceased to give. But I cannot sufficiently wonder how such an interpretation could arise in you from my words, how your opinion could so perversely interpret the words of my utterly sincere mind.

I would almost—almost, as would be deserved—say in anger against a friend, if I did not fear to go too far: “Where your treasure is, there is your heart also” (Matthew 6). Not I—not I—though very useless, am not, I say, such a man as to serve Mammon. I am not a friend bought with money; I am not one of those who love only so long as they receive, who honour avarice more than justice, who preserve friendship for money’s sake. Such people are not—are not—to be honoured with the name of friends, but are to be condemned with the disgrace of the greedy. Far—far be their company from me, persons whom not only divine wisdom but worldly prudence also detests! Against such persons the poet ironically inveighs:

> “Citizens, citizens: money must first be sought;  
> Virtue comes after coin.”  
> (*Horace, Epistles*, book I, epistle 1, verses 53–54.)

And elsewhere, no longer mocking but declaring what is true, he says:

> “Silver is less valuable than gold; gold than virtues.”  
> (*Horace, ibid.*, verse 52.)

I have loved your venerable fatherhood freely and [Col. 0075C] shall love it forever, Christ’s love granting it, because, according to the Apostle, “I seek not what is yours, but you” (1 Corinthians 12). I seek you, I say; I desire to rejoice in you, not in perishable money, forever, with that joy which, according to the Lord’s saying, no one may take from us (John 16). While we are in the body, while opportunity remains, while it is the acceptable time, while these are days of salvation (2 Corinthians 6), let us strive to provide for this. Before, as Solomon says, the silver cord is broken, the golden band (*vitta aurea*) is drawn back, the pitcher is shattered over the spring, and the spirit returns to God who made it (Sirach 45).

See what I understood by the silver cord: not some bond or metal, certainly, but the splendid bond of love by which the soul of Jonathan was bound [Col. 0075D] to the soul of David (1 Samuel 18), and of which the Apostle says: “Above all, having continual mutual love among yourselves”; this is “the bond of perfection” (Colossians 3). But because my intended brevity and the approaching conversation, as I have said, command an end to my words, the pen must be restrained, so that what is written less fully here may be discussed more extensively there.

## LETTER VII. To the venerable lord and our friend of one mind, ATON, bishop of Troyes, Brother PETER, humble abbot of the Cluniacs, wishes him what he wishes for himself.

I rejoice and congratulate myself exceedingly that I have not fallen from your mind as completely as I supposed. For I thought that, through that long and monstrous silence of yours, I had been set aside and that, through the easy changeability of your mind, its disposition had altered from the stability of former love. But when I had recently sent your reverence a letter of friendly complaints and was awaiting a reply so that I might judge the uncertainty of your heart by its tenor, love, not altogether asleep, anticipated it and showed that it still breathed—indeed in few words, but with great affection. This, as I said, greatly gladdened me and restored me, as it were, from a certain despair to hope; it encouraged me to reply briefly to what you had written.

You directed me to release our most dear son Peter from the care of the monastery of Gaye [Note: [Col. 0075D] From the care of the monastery of Gaye. Also called the deanery of Blessed Mary of Gaye; it is a member of the Cluniac order in the diocese of Troyes.] and to send him elsewhere [Col. 0076B] to serve God. But because, as the letters themselves show, we recognize that you spoke more from his heart than from your own, and that in writing you satisfied his will rather than yours, we have decided to obey your will rather than your letter. We therefore send him back to your beloved fatherhood, so that you may possess him not as an annual but as a perpetual prior; not merely while alive, but, as you wrote, even after death, forever. So hold him entrusted to you that neither he may regret having returned nor we having sent him back.

When we went to Aquitaine, we intended to travel by way of you; but we were compelled to abandon that plan because of the haste of the journey and lack of time. Yet, with God’s mercy leading the way, we shall take care soon to accomplish what we could not then do. We shall not revisit the walls of home before we rejoice in our mutual presence in the Lord. Expect, then, yet another messenger from us, through whom we shall announce our arrival to you with certainty.

## LETTER VIII. PETER, humble abbot of the Cluniacs, to STEPHEN, priest and jurist: greeting.

You have written a long letter, but, though you are called a jurist, you have not used rhetoric properly in it. If this was through ignorance, it must be pardoned; if knowingly, it must be imputed to obstinacy. The rules of the art direct that a judge is to be appeased, not angered, in a speech. [Col. 0076D] Yet, on the contrary, the letter you sent resounds with reproaches, reeks of insults, and breathes threats. Nothing has ever been obtained from anyone but an unwilling person through such persuasion. What is requested is normally obtained by prayers, not threats; by service, not insults. Therefore do not hope to obtain anything from us by such a remedy. You pleaded foolishly and unlearnedly, when you irritated one whom you ought to have appeased even if he had been angry—one who had been kindly disposed and beneficent beforehand.

Go instead to those who rise up against us and, as you wrote, invite you against us with very substantial rewards. Do not lose the profit promised by others, while from us you will receive only what your letter [Col. 0077A] has earned and justice has dictated in reply.

## LETTER IX. To his beloved son, Master PETER [Note: [Col. 0077D] To his beloved son Master Peter. A monk of Poitiers, whom elsewhere he calls Peter of Saint-Jean, and whom he states below, in Letters 25 and 26 and in book IV, Letter 17, to have been his copyist, or notary and scribe.], Brother PETER, humble abbot of the Cluniacs, wishes a seeing eye and an obedient ear.

To you, most beloved son, who are laboring in the knowledge of secular letters and burdened with the heavy load of human studies, I take pity; and since I see no reward for your labor, no relief for your burden, I lament that you are wasting your time in vain. For if the one sure end of true philosophy is to know where true blessedness consists and, once known, to attain it—so that, having attained it, one may become happy from being miserable—and if blessedness cannot be called such when it lacks any good, while the highest good is blessed eternity: who would dare call him a philosopher who by all his labors tends not toward eternal blessedness but toward eternal misery?

The minds of the ancients sweated in the search for this blessedness, and strove with great effort to dig out, as it were from the hidden bowels of the earth, what lay concealed in deepest secrecy. Hence the inventions of the arts; hence the manifold intricacies of arguments; hence the endless disagreements of mutually warring schools: some placed blessedness in bodily pleasures, others in virtues of the soul; some judged that it must be sought above man, while others, asserting something else, opposed them all. Seeing them err, seek in the depths what was hidden on high, and, through the confusion of falsehood, deceive mortals upon earth, Truth, looking down from heaven and pitying their misery, sprang up from the earth. And, that it might be seen by such persons, assuming the likeness of sinful flesh, it cried out to those afflicted by these and similar evils: “Come to me, all you who labor and are burdened, and I will refresh you. Take my yoke upon you” (Matt. 11).

And because it saw them held fast by a profound ignorance of truth, it took up the voice of a teacher and added: “Learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart, and you shall find rest for your souls” (ibid.). And when it had ascended the mountain, it openly taught not only where true blessedness was to be found, but also how it was to be reached; and it restrained the curiosity of all who seek blessedness, saying: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5). [Col. 0077D] Behold: without Platonic meditations, without Academic disputations, without Aristotelian snares, without the teachings of philosophers, the place and way of blessedness have been found. Let human presumption therefore be silent, having heard the divine teaching. Let falsehood fall silent, because Truth teaches. Let man leave the teacher’s chair, for God-man sits down to teach. “Blessed,” he says, “are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven.”

Why then, dearest one, do you wander through the schools? Why are you both taught and attempting to teach? Why do you seek through thousands of words and many labors what, by a simple saying and with little labor, if you wish, you can attain? Why, in vain study, do you recite with comedians, lament with tragedians, play at metrical games, deceive with poets, and are deceived with philosophers? Why do you now devote so great an effort not to philosophy but—may peace be with you—to folly? To folly, I say. For this too was said by the true philosopher: “Has not God made foolish the wisdom of the world?” (1 Cor. 1).

Run therefore, my son, toward the blessedness of the kingdom of heaven—the sole fruit of all philosophy—set before you by the heavenly Master. You cannot attain it except through true poverty of spirit. For, as I said above, the true Master, presiding over the school of the whole world and overturning the chairs of false teachers, declared the poor in spirit blessed, because the highest blessedness was laid up for him: namely, the kingdom of heaven. Enter upon the way of poverty, by which one goes to the blessedness of the heavenly kingdom: the way, I say, of poverty not merely of the body but of the spirit; not merely of possessions but of humility; not merely of the flesh but of the mind.

Then you will be a true philosopher of Christ, when he himself has made the wisdom of the world foolish in you. For if, according to the same Apostle, you wish to be wise, “become foolish, that you may be wise”; and glory in knowing neither the chatter of logic nor the curiosity of natural philosophy nor anything else, except Jesus Christ, “and him crucified.” For if by his gift you deserve to become this, there will be joy over you among the angels of God, who rejoice over one sinner doing penance (Luke 15); and there will likewise be great joy among holy people, because “if one member rejoices, all the members rejoice together” (1 Cor. 12). And above all there will be delight for me, who shall receive you as though my only son, nourish you with the milk of piety, cherish you in the embrace of love, bring you up among Christ’s little ones, arm you with heavenly weapons among the multitude of recruits, and, so far as I can, encourage you for the spiritual warfare; and together with you I shall fight against the enemy.

Heavenly aid will be present, so that, fighting together in the camps of heaven, we may overcome the enemy; overcoming, may be crowned; and, truly philosophizing, may attain the due end of philosophy—namely, blessed eternity.

## LETTER X. To his heartfelt son, Master PETER, Brother PETER, humble abbot of Cluny, [sends] love for true wisdom.

If I hoped that I could attain what I desire for you by a multitude of words, I would strive to fill sheets with many words. But because the kingdom of God, to which I invite you, “is not in speech but in power” [Col. 0079A] (1 Cor. 4), you must call upon divine power and exercise strength of soul, so that with a resolute effort of mind you may overcome whatever hinders your salvation, and recognize that you must walk not by “the broad and spacious way, which leads to death,” but by the narrow way which leads to life (Matt. 7). Though narrow at the outset, it will gradually widen as you advance, so that, fear yielding to love, you may sing more in spirit than in voice what you perhaps now despair can be done: “I ran the way of your commandments, when you enlarged my heart” (Ps. 118).

Act therefore manfully, and let your heart be strengthened. Let it not grow soft through the delight of things quickly perishing, when every delight of eternal things is promised to it. Meanwhile, my son most dear in Christ, keep this admonition carefully with you, [Col. 0079B] and show without delay, by coming, that I have not advised you thus in vain.

## LETTER XI. To the supreme pontiff and our special father, Lord Pope INNOCENT, Brother PETER, humble abbot of Cluny, [sends] greeting and obedience.

It is indeed superfluous to entreat a father on behalf of his sons, a shepherd on behalf of his sheep, Peter on behalf of the Church. But because the mind often willingly hears from others what it desires to do of itself, and is sometimes stirred more strongly by another’s urging to do what it already delights in doing, I, though a humble yet devoted son of Your Sublimity, appeal to your fatherly compassion for the Church of Orléans.

> [Note: [Col. 0079C] *For the Church of Orléans.* Orléans is a city of the Carnutes on the Loire, which Sidonius was the first to call the city of Orléans, in Epistle 15, Book VIII. It had previously been called Genabum; and those who deny this have opposing traces of the truth in Caesar and many other arguments, as Joseph Scaliger, a man most learned in every branch of knowledge, says in his *Description of Gaul*. Ralph Glaber calls it “Aurelian” in Book XI, chapter 5, where he also gives this etymology and description: “For the aforesaid city was in ancient times, as it is at present, the principal seat of the kings of the Franks: a royal place because of its beauty and populousness, as well as the fertility of its soil and the irrigation of its conspicuous river. For it has received its name also from the fitting river Loire, and is called Aureliana, as though *ore Ligeriana* [at the mouth of the Loire], because its bank is situated at the mouth of that river; not, as some less careful persons suppose, after the Emperor Aurelian, as though he had built it and it were therefore so called, but rather from the river, as we have said—which suits it more correctly and truly.”]

I ask that, for the love of the cross of Christ, in whose name and under whose banner that Church singularly glories, you may deign to relieve its afflictions. Thus, though it shares in Christ’s sufferings through patience, according to the Apostle [Col. 0080A] (1 Cor. 1), and is worn down by harsh and prolonged tribulations, it may at last be relieved by your compassionate provision.

Moreover, the heavenly disposition now seems to will this, for it has united, by an unexpected change, the hearts of clergy and people who, as you know and as we have heard, had hitherto been ruinously divided. Thus among so great a multitude there is found no one who has not wholeheartedly desired, praised, and confirmed the election of Lord Elias, the venerable abbot of Saint-Sulpice—a man indeed religious, prudent, and learned.

> [Note: [Col. 0079D] *They have desired the election of Elias, abbot of Saint-Sulpice.* When Henry I, bishop of Orléans, died, clergy and people, formerly discordant and divided, after a change of hearts unanimously elected this Elias, abbot of Saint-Sulpice. At the request of our Peter, abbot of Cluny, he was confirmed by Pope Innocent II. After his confirmation he also granted certain rights to monks of Cluny serving God at the church of Hienville, a dependency of the priory of Saint-Martin-des-Champs, as is contained in this charter:
>
> [Col. 0080C] “In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. I wish it to be known to all who have the care of God’s holy Church, both future and present, that I, Elias, by the grace of God bishop of the people of Orléans, at the prayers of our most noble lord Louis, king of the Franks, and of Geoffrey, venerable bishop of Chartres and legate of the Apostolic See, and of our archdeacons—namely Henry, brother of the aforesaid king, and Algrin—grant to the monks of Saint-Martin-des-Champs serving God at Hienville, in the church of Hienville itself, which belongs to them, two parts of the offerings made at the chaplain’s altar or received through the hands of that chaplain; all candles and all loaves, without any share for the chaplain; and two parts of all movable legacies [French *legs*]. If land is given or bequeathed, it shall belong to the monks. I also grant two parts of marriage offerings and of oath-fees. And in the church of Neuville, which similarly belongs to the same monks, [Col. 0080D] one half of all offerings; and at the annual feasts, two parts of the loaves and candles, just as they had long ago in the time of my predecessor John of good memory. That this may remain ratified and unshaken, I confirm it by the authority of our seal. Done at Orléans, in the year from the Lord’s Incarnation 1142, in the fifth year of Louis the Younger.”

Since I avoid being lengthy, I advise and entreat alike that you swiftly put an end to so great misfortunes of so great a Church, and that you, God’s vicar, confirm in this matter what appears to have been done by God. Let them perceive, if it please you, that my humble prayers and the place which they suppose me to hold in your favor profit them: demonstrate by the effect of a praiseworthy work whether this is indeed so. [Col. 0080B]

## LETTER XII. To the venerable and beloved Lord WILLIAM, archbishop of Embrun, Brother PETER, humble abbot of Cluny, [sends] greeting.

> [Note: [Col. 0080D] *William, archbishop of Embrun.* To him is also addressed the letter against the Petrobrusian heretics. Embrun is a provincial or archiepiscopal city of the Cottian and Maritime Alps, famous for the council of Riez; the ancient geographers call it *Ebredunum*, commonly Embrun.]

If a complaint could have a place among friends, I could not complain enough of a friend from whom I have been denied—not some great gift, but conversation itself and his very presence. Yet if this is friendship’s reward, it must be borne patiently. Or if perhaps monastic humility has seemed worthless to episcopal sublimity, that is not surprising in view of the differing ranks; but in view of the privilege of friendship it is a great wonder. For old love does not feel the changing of honors; amid every reversal of circumstances it knows how always to preserve unbroken faith toward a friend.

Therefore, if you wish to put an honorable end for yourselves and a useful end for us to this complaint of ours, take care at last to fulfill what you formerly neglected. Come to us, then, with the present messenger, so that through him you may atone for whatever you previously failed in, and show by deed that you are the friend whom you promised in words.

## LETTER XIII. To his dearest brother ODON, Brother PETER, humble abbot of Cluny, [sends] greeting.

> [Note: [Col. 0081D] *To his dearest brother Odo.* He later became prior of Saint-Martin-des-Champs and succeeded Theobald when the latter was elected bishop of Paris, as appears from Letters 40 and 41 of Book IV [Col. 0082D]. He should therefore be added to the catalogue of priors of the House of Saint Martin, printed with the privileges of Saint Martin in 1606.]

Thanks be to God. “The Lord has heard the desire of the poor; his ear has heard the preparation of their heart” (Ps. 9). For a long time, and very earnestly, I had desired, taking whatever occasion offered, to write to your charity, my dearest one, so that my affection—which, hindered by the distance between places, could not make itself known to you by living voice—might at least disclose itself through the dead characters of letters.

But the harsh tyranny of the Egyptians pressed upon me: they taught my hands to serve more in the basket than to be free for the study of writing; they have hitherto compelled them to be defiled by works of clay rather than cleansed by sacrifices to God. Therefore I could not do what I wished, and for that reason have remained silent until now. Thus I was compelled to say nothing for a long time to one to whom, even if I spoke always, I should nevertheless seem mute.

This is why, not as your learning writes, while others received various things, you alone carried away silence from me: I reserved for you an affection dearer than all words and notes. Since it kept silent for a long time, this was not neglect, as I have said, but violence. Yet the force of your spirit blew upon the dead ashes [Col. 0081C] of my breast and made fires long extinguished grow warm again by its breath, when it sent the longed-for letter of my beloved to one who longed for it but did not expect it.

When I read it, my soul was inflamed; suddenly, shaking off torpor, it blazed into invisible flames—flames which I can in some measure conceive, but cannot fully express by any signs. Perhaps at the time I received that letter a hailstorm of affairs had fallen upon me, and my creditors demanded their dues more sharply than usual; so they pressed me with various claims, as if, appropriating my whole self at their own pleasure, they had left me nothing of myself.

Placed amid these circumstances, when I received, as I said, your letter of affection, I hesitated in uncertainty, I confess, and for some time wavered as to whether I ought to answer you or first satisfy my creditors. At last reason prevailed, and immediately advised me that I was indebted in the debt of charity to no one more than to you. The apostolic voice joined reason and showed how we ought to render debts to debtors. Though it commands that tribute be rendered to whom tribute is due, tax to whom tax, honor to whom honor [Col. 0081D] (Rom. 13), yet when it says, “Owe no one anything, except to love one another” (ibid.), it teaches that the debt of charity outweighs every other debt. And if it outweighs them, it declares that it must be paid first.

Therefore I ought first to answer you; first to pay the greater debt; first to comply with the charity of one who had written. But what shall I say? What shall I speak? I desire to answer your letter, and behold, strangely, it both calls me to speech and more strongly enjoins silence upon me. For as often, dearest brother, as I read it, so often I behold the face of your blessed soul as though in the clearest mirror, and more clearly than any light I perceive what disposition you bear toward passing things and what concern toward eternal things.

I see you, as though from Zion’s lofty watchtower, looking down on what is done in the lower Jericho; scorning all worldly things, you have escaped from our thick and smoky air into the free breezes of the ether. I see fulfilled in you—not indeed completely, but soon to be completed—what the Apostle says: “Do you not know that we shall judge angels? How much more secular matters?” (1 Cor. 6); and again: “The saints shall judge concerning this world” (ibid.). For the right to judge the world is deservedly granted only to those who are outside the world, who have withdrawn their foot from its snare, and who can sing rejoicing with the Prophet: “The snare is broken, and we are delivered” (Ps. 123). Of these the Savior says: “They are not of the world, as I also am not of the world” (John 17).

What else indeed do those letters intimate about you? What else do the mockers and those who mock? What else do the worst of the unlettered and the worse learned men? What else does the beast ascending from the abyss? What else does the whole sequence of the letter indicate, except that you set your mind on things above, not on things on earth? [Col. 0082C] (Col. 3). But I still sit and weep beside the rivers of Babylon; I have hung my instruments upon the fruitless willows. How shall I sing the Lord’s song in a foreign land? (Ps. 136).

As I behold, weigh, and consider that condition in you and this in myself, it takes away my words, as I said, and commands silence. Nor do I dare judge others, because I do not sit upon a throne with judges but fear punishment with the accused. Nor do I wish to pronounce against others the sentence which I seek to escape myself, lest I be among those of whom the Apostle says: “In judging another, you condemn yourself” (Rom. 2).

But you, my dearest one—who, unlike those concerning whom you write, are not a perverse deceiver of yourself, but have made a mockery of the world and its prince as of a bird; who have escaped the beast rising from the abyss; who have crushed its teeth as they grind the world, trampled its necks, and broken its horns—you, I say, can speak freely of these matters, dispute safely, investigate subtly, discover what you investigate, and define what you discover.

Therefore I return to you what you have poured into me; I bid you act in my stead. The pen which you urged upon one occupied I return to one at leisure, since streams are more properly expected from most abundant springs than from parched rocks; sound eyes contemplate the splendor of the stars better than bleary ones; and the image of those looking is formed far more clearly in still than in troubled water.

Open your lips, then, that your mouth may be filled with praise; and say what you had proposed for me to say. Thus, because for the present we lose Leah’s fruit in you through your love of quiet and spiritual silence, we may take delight in you through Rachel’s singular beauty. [Col. 0083A] That labor ought to be exceedingly pleasant to you; and your body ought by no means to cease from so fruitful a work, so that while your mind labors in divine meditation, your hands in writing, your eyes in reading, your tongue in speaking, and the whole inner and outer person labors in cooperation, you may offer God a rich whole burnt offering. Since you have withdrawn your whole self from the world, offer your whole self as a sacrifice to God. Remember your friends in these blessed labors, especially in holy prayers, since those joined to you by holy affection ought not to be deprived of devout prayer.

## LETTER XIV. To his beloved brother THEOTARD, Brother PETER, humble abbot of Cluny, [sends] greeting.

> [Note: [Col. 0083C] *Brother Theotard.* He too later became prior of Saint Mary of Charity; below, Letter 30, and Book II, Letters 6 and 7.]

[Col. 0083B]

Why is it—as I use the words of the Jews—“How long do you keep our soul in suspense?” (John 10). How long do you drag one resisting? How long do you draw me round with a tenacious chain? O how grievous is the bond of love, from which neither the guilty is released nor the innocent freed! It is stronger than all bronze, heavier than every weight, because “love is strong as death, jealousy hard as hell” (Song 8). Bound by this shackle, I am held; pressed by this weight, I am burdened; by this chain, wherever I go, I am bound.

A mind never forgetful of you bears this, and though it continually exchanges regions for regions and provinces for provinces, it can never change you alone or cast you from itself. Why is this? Does it expect from you duchies? Kingdoms? The glory of the world? Mountains of gold, as the saying goes? Not this, dearest one, not this; certainly your friend’s mind expects no such thing from you. What, then? You yourself know. Why should I weary myself with speaking? I return you to yourself. Be yourself the discoverer, judge, and knower of these matters.

And, that I may say something: pray for me to him whom, so far as I can, I revere and love in you. Though my mind meditates on him and my tongue speaks of him, my life nevertheless strays far from him. Return the favor, therefore, to your friend, so that one who does not forget you even among the servants of his labor may always be held in constant remembrance in your sweet—and far easier—rest. I have briefly sent these things beforehand in writing; God willing, I shall myself say soon what I have omitted.

## LETTER XV. To our venerable and dearest sister, Lady ADELA, Brother PETER, humble abbot of Cluny, [sends] greeting and every blessing from the Lord.

> [Note: [Col. 0083C] *Our dearest sister, Lady Adela.* Daughter of William the Conqueror, king of England. After the death of her husband Stephen, count of Blois and Chartres, she became a nun at Marcigny. Matthew Paris, speaking in his *William Rufus* of the daughters of William her father, says: “The third, Adela, wife of Stephen count of Blois, a woman of praised power in the world, recently took the religious habit at Marcigny.” The *History of the Lords of Amboise* calls her Ala in these words: “Meanwhile Geoffrey of Calvimont, coming with the king into Normandy, joined the king’s daughter, named Ala, in marriage with Stephen, count of Chartres.” Lord Ivo, bishop of Chartres, wrote to her while she was still living in the world, in Letters 5, 91, 101, 116, 121, 179, and 187. Hildebert of Le Mans congratulates her after her conversion in Letter 63, because, though she had greatly desired until then to venerate and visit the divine places of the Holy Land, when her husband Stephen had at last died, she professed the monastic life in the holy and divine works of the monastery of Marcigny.]

[Col. 0084B]

Since we have not yet informed Your Love of the death of our always beloved lord, the king of the English, the reason was that both the great grief from which we cannot yet free ourselves prevented this, and we rightly shrank from being the first reporters of so great a calamity. Yet, because we desire you to know whatever we know, you should know that we have thus far been able to learn only that he lay sick in a certain village near Rouen for eight days; that the lord archbishop of Rouen remained constantly beside him; and that, fortified by him with all the sacraments of the Church, he departed this world in excellent penitence and faithful confession on the fourth day before the Nones of December [2 December]. [Col. 0084C]

His body, as he had arranged, was brought to Rouen and from there carried toward England by his son Count Robert, to be buried at Reading.

> [Note: [Col. 0083D] *His body was brought to Rouen, etc.* This was according to his testamentary disposition: he wished his heart and brain to be buried in the Norman monastery of Le Pré, but his body at Reading in England. William of Newburgh, *History of English Affairs*, Book I, chapter 3: “His body, with the brain and entrails removed, salted and sewn into hides, was brought from Normandy to England and buried at Reading, in the monastery of which he had been a devout founder and generous benefactor.” Arnulf of Lisieux accordingly drew from this the material for composing such an epitaph:
>
> “Here lie buried in part the limbs of Henry,
>
> Whose name the public voice celebrates.
>
> Neither earth could contain him while living,
>
> Nor could one place bury him when dead.
>
> Divided into three, he assigns his due to each part,
>
> Thus adorning three kingdoms with three portions.
>
> Heaven is appointed to his spirit; Neustria to his heart and brain;
>
> England, which gave him birth, possesses his body.
>
> Hence he drew his fathers and his mind; but perhaps was born among them;
>
> Here he bore the sword; there he wielded the scepters.
>
> When the final night of November had released him in death,
>
> The first of December divided him.”
>
> [Col. 0084D] *By his son Count Robert.* That is, his natural, not legitimate, son. King Henry received only two children by Matilda, his lawful queen and a religious woman: a daughter bearing her mother’s name, already of marriageable age, whom he first betrothed to Henry, Roman emperor, and afterwards to Geoffrey, count of Anjou; and a son called William, heir of England and Normandy, who, while crossing from Normandy to England in the year of salvation 1120, was drowned in a grievous shipwreck. But by various concubines and mistresses he fathered several other children of both sexes. The eldest of all was named Robert; he was made count of Gloucester and by his wife Sibylla himself left many children.
>
> *At Reading.* Reading, or in the singular Reading, was a monastery on the River Thames, which the aforesaid King Henry built in honor of Blessed Mary in 1130 and entrusted to a certain Hugh, summoned from the monastery of Cluny, to govern as abbot.

All Normandy now roars with civil and foreign wars. We have heard nothing certain yet concerning the condition of the kingdom across the sea, for those who told us these things fled Normandy with the greatest speed. Yet we have already sent two couriers, one to the lord of Rouen, the other to the lord of Winchester, [Note: [Col. 0085D] *The lord of Winchester.* Henry, who was himself also a monk of Cluny, as will be noted more fully elsewhere.] [Col. 0085A] that they may swiftly report to us what they learn concerning them and from them.

For the eternal salvation of the deceased king we have established such observances as have never been established at Cluny for anyone else. What you ought to do for him, it seems to us superfluous to direct.

## LETTER XVI. To his dearest brother and kinsman in Christ, PONTIUS, Brother PETER, humble abbot of Cluny, [sends] the greeting which he wishes for himself.

> [Note: [Col. 0086D] *Brother and kinsman Pontius,* who later, from being a monk, became abbot of Vézelay: Book II, Letter 17, and Book III, Letters 4 and 6.]

[Col. 0085B]

You complain that I have forgotten you, been unmindful of our kinship, written nothing to you for a long time, and held your humility in contempt because of my exalted station. But I consider the reasons for my silence so entirely just that I shall scarcely escape blame if I even attempt to speak now. To pass over the tumults of the world, the occupations of affairs, and the entanglements of cases—which you know very well, by which you have often seen me bound in chains and lamented, and which can sufficiently excuse me from writing—let this alone now be in dispute: you, a brother through God, a kinsman through the flesh, an intimate through affection, departed from me like a fugitive, slipped away like a deceiver, fled at dawn like a thief—if I may not say at night—despising me, avoiding me, and without greeting me.

You lived with me for nearly ten years. Throughout that whole time, you yourself know, and I have not wholly forgotten, how much we shared concerning divine things, how fervent was our talk about spiritual matters, how frequent our conversation on contempt for present things, and how earnest our exhortation toward the desire for eternal things. The ardor of charity burned so hotly between us that, though I had begun to love you solely by nature’s impulse, I now knew no way to love you except from God and in God.

In you I found refuge from human affairs and the sea’s waves; in you I rested as in a most secure harbor. I gladly heard of the ruin of the world that continually threatened, as though prophesying the destruction of my enemy. When you lamented both my miseries and those of others, crying, “Spare us, O God,” I listened gladly and rejoiced, and cried the same not in empty vanity but in devout charity. The tower in which you dwelt was for me a tower of strength from the face of the enemy; from it we frequently hurled arrows into the mouths of our enemies and protected ourselves from their arrows by the defense of our rampart.

He who despised, rejected, and trampled upon these and many similar instruments of spiritual life [Col. 0086A]—a deserter of faith, betrayer of friends, and scorner of nature—is he worthy of my letters? Should he be refreshed by my epistle? Should he be visited by my messenger? He is, he is indeed, in my judgment, worthy of severe punishment and undeserving of all pardon. Yet mercy must be mingled with judgment, and then indulgence granted, if he who departed from us in contempt returns ready to make satisfaction.

I praise in you your love for Christ’s precious martyrs, to whose venerable tombs you fled. Though absent in body, I am present in spirit; with my whole affection I honor, receive, and venerate them. But you ought not to have scorned that charity for the preservation of which those great witnesses of God, the shining stars of heaven, gave up their bodies, poured out their blood, and gave their lives to the Creator of all. You ought not, I say, while living to lose what they did not lose even in death.

Therefore write to me no longer, “Love one who loves you”; but write, “Love one who scorns you; love one who deserts you; follow one who flees.” You also wrote to me about sending a tunic. Shall I send a tunic to one who has no need of me, who is sufficient for himself, who, according to the Apostle, “has already become rich and reigns without me”? (1 Cor. 4). Why does he demand my garment who abandoned my roof? Will that injury deserve a reward to which the utmost punishment is due? Here—here indeed—we ought to cry out: “Spare us, O God,” where his justice is most wounded.

But I shall send, I shall send the tunic, lest avarice be imputed to me, provided the law of justice is observed. Yet I wish this law to be imposed: when you have received it, either return home, as I have said, or seek no further tunic or cloak from me. And that you may hear that I speak at the end not in jest but in earnest, I plainly urge you to return; for opposites never suit opposites, but like things always suit like. It is fitting that monk live with monks, cleric with clerics, layperson with laypeople, and that their proper orders not be confused, lest perhaps, in the poet’s words,

> “You may seem to join a horse’s neck to a human head,”  
> (Horace, *Art of Poetry*, verse 1)

and compel a beautiful woman above to end below in a black fish.

I do not say that the sacred orders of the Church, made one by true faith and sincere charity, are opposed to one another; but because of the differences of clothing, food, and customs, I judge that they do not suit one another within the same house. I also hear the Apostle saying: “In the calling in which you were called, remain in it” (1 Cor. 7). I give abundant thanks for the prayers offered for me by your charity to my so great lords, so many holy martyrs; and I implore, more with heart than voice, that this may be done while you remain there and always. [Col. 0087A]

## LETTER XVII. To the supreme pontiff and our special father, Lord Pope INNOCENT, Brother PETER, humble abbot of Cluny, [sends] faithful obedience.

We believe that the abominable deed, punishable outrage, and crime unheard of in our age—the murder of those who resisted unto blood for righteousness—has reached the ears of Your Holiness. We must indeed grieve for the death of those innocents whom the sacrilegious cruelty of murderers destroyed; but we must grieve much more that this more-than-bestial cruelty has not yet met the punishment deserved by its impiety.
