For behold: those who ought long since to have perished from human sight flatter themselves with impunity, their minds bloodstained and their hands still dripping blood; and, as though they had carried off victory from a war, they glory in what ought to shame them. Their impunity supplies others with weapons of fury, so that, just as after the subdean of Orléans the persecutors’ sword turned against Lord Thomas of Paris because the former remained unavenged, so after this man it may pass on against others and involve clerics, canons, and monks in a like condemnation.

Since the royal sword is far too blunt against such people, we ask—and all who zealously love God’s law entreat with us—that the episcopal, indeed the spiritual sword, which according to the Apostle is the word of God, may not be bound [Col. 0087C] (2 Tim. 2), so that, struck by it, they may die to sin but live to God.

For this reason recently in our regions archbishops, bishops, abbots, and many religious and learned persons assembled; and, after consultation, pronounced a sentence of severity against such sacrilegious persons. Let apostolic authority therefore, if it please you, confirm what they have rightly done; let it supplement whatever has been decreed with insufficient severity, so that the wicked may be punished by due vengeance and others deterred from imitating them.

Furthermore, there is no need to inform you how reverent in life and how faithful to your apostolate the lord archbishop of Rouen has been, or how much he has labored for your peace, since we believe that you are fully informed of all these matters. We therefore entreat Your Fatherhood so to provide for his peace and justice that he may render to God what is God’s and to Caesar what is Caesar’s, so that, if possible, he may neither displease divine judgment nor offend royal majesty. [Col. 0087D]

## LETTER XVIII. To the lord and father ALTO, bishop of Troyes, remembered with sweetness and named with honor, Brother PETER, humble abbot of Cluny, [sends] his whole self.

Drawn into the Auvergne regions by the tenacious hook of business, while the Easter holidays were still pressing, I found at Souvigny the messenger of your Blessedness whom you had sent to Cluny, and who had already been waiting for me for many days. [Col. 0088A] When I gladly received your letter from him and hoped to be informed in it concerning your arrival, as we had agreed, suddenly despair arose in place of hope and sorrow in place of joy, when I learned that he whom I was hastening to meet at once, and whom I believed already to be knocking at my doors, had not yet crossed the threshold of his own house. And although, by the excuses which followed, I tried somehow to soothe the distress of my mind, I could not do so despite long effort, because—if I may be permitted to be angry while preserving my love for you—I found them inadequate in every respect. For what of it? Even if, as the letter of your Holiness declares, a general collection was made by order of the lord pope; even if the diligence of the collector could spare no one; even if, because the receipts were exceedingly scanty, recourse was had to the garden; even if the home-grown produce was consumed—that is, what was lacking was supplied from [Col. 0088B] your own treasury—when these matters were completed, was the road then closed? Or was no journey open thereafter? Was there henceforth no possibility of going anywhere? Or, when every road was travelled, did the road to Cluny alone seem hateful and, as though stained with barbarian swords, fit to be avoided? Yes indeed, yes: you seem to me to avoid this journey as though a robber threatened the throat of one approaching, a lion lay in ambush beside the road, and a fire-breathing dragon stood ready, at this very moment, to seize its prey. But be—be, I say—secure: neither robber need be feared, nor lion dreaded, nor dragon, with God and myself accompanying you, need be feared. But what am I trying to persuade you of again? What am I undertaking to urge once more? Why, finally, do I strive to expend my effort in vain? My hope, which has so often deceived me, strongly compels me not to hope for what has been denied so many times. Yet charity, rekindled anew by its fire—which knows no extinction—still does not cease to cry out, and knows no rest until it obtains what it desires. Therefore it resolves to persist with continual cries at the door of its friend, so that, if not because he is his friend, at least because of his importunity, he may rise and give him as many [loaves] as he needs (Luke 11). Accordingly it presses much more strongly than before, and earnestly begs you to designate a definite time for your arrival. For your Cluny awaits you; it will by no means rejoice fully until it is filled by your presence and spiritual blessings. Know that our condition, concerning which I have learned that your friendship is anxious, is prosperous; and that nothing will then be lacking to complete our joys when, by the bounty of God’s grace, you shall happen to be present with us.

## LETTER XIX

To our dearest and now particular friend DULCIANUS, brother PETER, humble abbot of Cluny, greetings.

Would that I were able to match in deed the affection of love which I have conceived in my heart toward you, both formerly and especially of late. Your prudence would certainly recognize what it does not know, and would prove by experience itself that, through its merits, it had purchased for itself such a friend as I am. For whom would such a price of merits not win over? Whom would so many gifts of graces, such a heap of benefits so often bestowed upon us and [Col. 0089A] our people, not win? Whom, I say, would your humble prudence, sublime humility, guarded learning, polished sweetness, outstanding manners, refined speech, and finished life not draw—indeed compel—to love you? These qualities, surely, which ought to draw everyone, have drawn me too as instruments of righteousness, so that I have laid up the memory of you in the innermost chamber of my heart and will not permit it to be torn from my depths by any event whatever. For that reason I desire that you yourself may at some time be joined to me in Christ, so that you may be among those whom, according to the Prophet, God causes to dwell united in one house (Psalm 67). But if perhaps many obstacles have compelled you to defer this for the present, let not a friendly heart refuse me at least this request: that, if not yourself, then one who is yours [Col. 0089B]—that is, one of your sons—you may not so much give as restore into God’s keeping, Him from whom you received him. If through my hand you make this gift to the Church of Cluny, he will be a son to me, and through him you will, as I trust, merit to have God as Father. Inform me by messenger or letter, without leaving me in suspense, what you intend to do in this matter.

## LETTER XX

To his most beloved brother GISLEBERT, especially to be embraced in the depths of Christ.

> [Note: [Col. 0089D] “To brother Gislebert.” To a hermit or recluse, whom he carefully admonishes in this letter—or, as Trithemius seems to call it, book [Col. 0090D]—*On the Praises of the Eremitic Life*.]

Brother PETER, humble abbot of Cluny, wishes him, in exchange for the narrowness of his cell, the breadth of heaven.

I received the letter of your affection, dearest brother, on Holy Saturday, the Sabbath of the Lord’s burial; and, since [Col. 0089C] I could not do so earlier, I read it through while sitting at the altar, after the offices had already begun. Nor did I regret reading it at such a place and time, since I felt that its reading greatly benefited me. For, remembering your enclosure and solitude, I groaned from the depths over myself, exposed to the world; and, rejoicing for you as one dying to it—not to say dead—I understood your state. I rejoiced both that you are not moderately concerned for your salvation and that you have not forgotten me. I exulted in the Lord that a new planting, with its flowers already quickly appearing, gives hope beforehand of the fruit to follow. Though I could not give it growth, I nevertheless bestowed upon it the benefit of watering, however slight, out of the affection of a good heart.

And when, reading through the whole sequence of your letter more than once with careful eye, I found that I was earnestly urged to write to your brotherhood [Col. 0089D], and that you were most eagerly hungering for whatever little exhortation I might offer, I was indeed glad that you were tormented by a delightful hunger for that bread in which alone the spiritual person lives. But, recognizing from whom you sought it, I perceived an error arising from a purpose of piety. For if Scripture speaks truly when it says, “Write wisdom in the time of leisure; and he who is diminished in activity shall attain it” (Ecclus. 38), how can one write anything pertaining to wisdom who has no leisure, whose whole life is one single and burdensome business? How can he attain it who is not merely in no way diminished in activity, but is daily more and more burdened by the most importunate [Col. 0090A] affairs of secular business? How can one fasting from divine delicacies bring forth any savour for his neighbours, when, according to the common proverb, a bitter mouth can never spit out honey? How shall I give what I have not received, when John the Baptist says: “A man can receive nothing unless it has been given him from heaven” (John 3)?

Rather, you—you who are free from every earthly business, abound in heavenly leisure, are refreshed by continual reading, and are nourished by constant prayer, so that your soul is filled as with fatness and richness—you, I say, ought with lips of exultation to refresh me when hungry, give me drink when thirsty, and enrich the dryness of my heart from the overflowing abundance of your spirit. But if, perhaps, persisting more stubbornly as you have begun, you compel even [Col. 0090B] an unwilling man to speak, and make me open my mouth instead of lending you the ears I ought to have lent, I do not know what I can set before you more fittingly than something which no forgetfulness can ever erase from your heart, no change of times abolish, and no instability of mind—by God’s grace—alter. For however great other things may be that are said, once they slip from the embraces of a frail memory, they easily vanish. This will flee your mind all the less because it will always meet the very senses of your body more familiarly.

I therefore set before you your cell: by its presence, though placed in the midst of the world, you are separated from the world; through its aid you seem to have penetrated the inmost recesses of vast solitudes; nor, by its enclosure, do you rival even the remotest Egyptian deserts [Col. 0090C]. This cell, I say, I set before you, so that, according to the saying of a certain ancient Father, it alone may teach you more eloquently by its silence than all masters. Certainly you cannot fail to hear it, when you have it daily as the monitor of your salvation. “Flee men,” says one of the Fathers, “and be silent, and you shall be safe” (Jerome). “Death must be avoided either by shield or by feet.” And Jeremiah says: “He shall sit alone and keep silence, because he shall lift himself above himself” (Lam. 3). And David says: “You have given those who fear you a sign, that they may flee from the face of the bow” (Psalm 59).

This cell, dearest brother, has received you fleeing from the face of divine judgment; this has hidden you, according to Isaiah, like one in a pit in the earth, from the terror of the Lord when He comes to strike the earth (Isa. 2); this, like little Zoar, has preserved you unharmed from the fires of Sodom—that is, of the world [Col. 0090D] (Gen. 19). This furnished Elijah, once fleeing Ahab and Jezebel through the wilderness, a hiding-place; there, while stationed, he heard the voice of God speaking familiarly to him, and learned that God was present to human beings not in wind, not in commotion, not in fire, but in the whisper of a gentle breeze—that is, in the subtle inspiration of His Spirit perceptible only to few (3 Kings 19). This hid that Paul, the chief exemplar of the purpose you have chosen, for sixty years; and after he had long been nourished on heavenly food, it finally sent him, as Antony testifies, to eat forever the bread of life. By its enclosure this cell continually represents you to yourself as not merely dead, but buried, to this [Col. 0091A] mortal life; and it cries out to you, as it were, and to the Colossians with the apostolic voice: “For you are dead, and your life is hidden with Christ in God” (Col. 3). Although this, understood spiritually, is common to you and many others, yet if it is also understood bodily, it becomes at this time almost uniquely yours. For although very many die to carnal actions, no one enters the tomb of the flesh before the death of the flesh. But you, to show yourself truly dead to the world, have entered the tomb itself while still alive.

But you must take heed, dearest brother, and strive in every way that what human opinion believes about you, the divine eye may recognize in you. You have indeed entered [Col. 0091B] the tomb, as I said; therefore whatever of the world formerly lived in you must necessarily be wholly buried with you. For burial is due to no one except one already proved to lack life. As a tomb is due to a dead person, so only a dead person is due to a tomb. Otherwise, just as it is judged inhuman not to bury a dead person, so it is recognized as deadly to bury a living one. Therefore, since you have died with Christ and are buried with Him, you must allow nothing worldly to breathe within you. You have the enclosure of your cave, which prevents people from approaching you; but also provide the wall which alone restrains the assaults of evil spirits. Of it Isaiah says: “A saviour shall be placed in it as wall and bulwark” (Isa. 26). Let the Saviour therefore be for you an impenetrable wall, an unconquerable tower, the cleft [Col. 0091C] of the rock, the hollow of the wall—He who, pierced on the cross by nails and spear, prepared in His wounds the safest refuge for you against every enemy. Established in those wounds and sharing in them through patience, you will both be safe from the attacks of enemies and able to drive them off bravely.

For without this defence neither solitary enclosure, bodily affliction, nor migration to distant places can be of any benefit; rather, it will stir adversaries to battle with sharper stimulus. Therefore the Lord Himself, to show that the enemy of human salvation is not softened but more vehemently provoked by solitude and fasting, and to prepare His own to resist him, did not permit the devil to tempt Him until He had been led by the Spirit into the wilderness and had fasted forty days and nights [Col. 0091D]. The ancient Fathers too bear witness: Antony, Hilarion, Macarius, and the others, worn down by the fiercer assaults of the adversary because of their solitary way of life. For the companionship of those living together in cloisters seems comparable to a multitude of battle-lines arrayed for war, where each person fights against the adversary so much more securely as he expects help more closely at hand from the right hand of a fellow-soldier. In that battle, each fighter relies not only upon his own strength but sometimes has more confidence in the forces of those fighting at his right and left than in his own. There each labours both to destroy those lying in wait for his salvation and to defend his fellow helpers by every means. Nor do they perceive less danger [Col. 0092A] in the death of companions than they experience loss in the life of enemies.

But the solitary combat of the wilderness is waged with so much greater danger as the combatant waits longer for help from another. And what increases the danger is that the struggle is not, as ordinarily in battle, many against many, nor, as in a duel, one against one; but, by an unusual manner of fighting, one person contends under an uncertain lot against very many, superior both in number and in strength. Therefore, to use the words of that blessed and great Father Benedict, this life belongs to those who, having been well trained in the battle-line of the brethren, undertake the single combat of the wilderness with their own hand, or arm, aided only by the support of divine strength.

Therefore, dearest brother, as Scripture says, you must walk attentively with your God [Col. 0092B], prepare strong shoulders for a great burden (Mic. 6), and carry the shield of faith toward those quarters where you understand the enemy to be shooting his fiery darts. For you will protect your right side with it in vain if he hurls his arrows at your left; you will set it before your breast to no purpose if he himself turns toward your back. Consider wisely why I say this. The enemy has familiar weapons against each kind of vocation; he does not use the same missiles against all, but arms himself with varied weapons against different persons. With some snares he attacks laypeople, with others monks; with some subjects, with others prelates; with some the idle, with others the busy. By manifold cunning, but the same wickedness, he rages against everyone.

Thus he persecutes solitaries, and especially recluses, with a warfare peculiarly his own; and, as though challenged to a single combat, he is impelled by singular ferocity to their destruction. From their singularity he instils pride; from leisure, sloth; from silence, talkativeness; from fear of poverty, avarice [Col. 0092C]. The deceitful flatterer whispers to the solitary that it is great and exceptional to have chosen the profession of solitary enclosure; to have taken the narrowest path by fleeing the broad roads of others; to have surpassed their lukewarmness by great fervour of spirit; and to have scarcely any rival in this vocation. Again, because, according to Scripture, “everyone who is idle is given over to desires” (Prov. 21), desires follow upon the arrival of sloth; all the time removed from occupations is spent on [Col. 0092D] vain and harmful thoughts. A headlong troop of manifold temptations rushes in, and, as though running through an empty and unoccupied house, the crowd of vices disturbs everything with confused cries. The whole world is enclosed within the little cell; a narrow enclosure scarcely capable of containing one person embraces the cities and kingdoms of many lands. Most tranquil leisure becomes most turbulent business; and although nothing but solitude meets the bodily senses, the world, with everything belonging to it, presents itself before the eyes of the soul with familiar access.

Now the great hermit claims for himself a judge’s tribunal; now he adorns his head with episcopal mitres; now he presides over many thousands of monks; now he ranges through every other office of ecclesiastical dignity. And lamenting that he lies idle when he might be of use to many at greater profit to his soul, forgetful of his vocation, he labours more laboriously than any labourer in his very repose [Col. 0093A]. I do not recount the countless other things, far worse than these, which pursue the wretched man with sword drawn for his death after he has once turned his back to his enemies, and which often do not desist until cruel murderers carry away hands bloody with his blood. Thus, while the affections of various things rage in the secret places of the mind, and the soul retains nothing of what it thinks except the empty cell, it sleeps from weariness and seeks a remedy for its miserable weariness not in God but in the world, not in itself but outside itself—thereby falling into a greater loss.

For, because he is ashamed to abandon the vocation of hermit once undertaken, an occasion is sought for [Col. 0093B] frequent conversation with others, so that he who suffers many torments in silence concerning himself may at least be relieved by the talk of others. The narrow window of enclosure is opened, and swarms of people flock together as if to a divine oracle. The divine prophet gives answers to all and, as though he must render an account to God for each individual should he remain silent, hears, examines, and decides everyone’s cases. There he fully discharges in speech what he has long pondered in his mind; and as a hungry person, after bitter famine, is refreshed by food, so he is sated with eager bites by the reports of those who flock to him. The door is indeed bolted, perhaps even blocked with stones; but through the narrow opening of the little window he receives whatever he does not admit through the breadth of the door. Certainly the bodies of those who come running do not enter him, but the care of bodies—which alone [Col. 0093C] draws the mind away from its right purpose—penetrates and fills everything. A flood of words pours from his mouth, breaking forth from the cistern of long silence, whose accumulated drops have been scattered. And while individuals among many thousands depart burdened with his discourse, he alone, untiring, promulgates laws to the whole world, if they should all gather together.

Sloth, not cured by such remedies but provoked by them, rises again more strongly after being temporarily lulled. It is like a most acute fever, somewhat soothed by the chill [or “rigour”] of water, but finally rising to burn more fiercely as though the remedy itself had made it worse. Nor can it rest until it returns to the ruinous remedy once tried, and again, under a veil of religion, mingles itself in the tumultuous business of words. For if, perhaps out of reverence for his holiness, people confess their sins to the servant of God, or seek counsel from him because [Col. 0093D] he cannot impose penance, or devoutly commend themselves to his prayers, he judges himself not only worthy of heaven already, but does not refuse to receive the offerings of the devout. In the first of these matters, he is deceived by the spirit of pride, measuring himself by others’ opinion; in the second, by that same pride, which is the beginning of every sin (Ecclus. 10), he is craftily led into the idolatry of avarice. For he who had professed poverty gradually amasses riches and does not stop until he stuffs his own storehouse with the resources of others. In gathering them he pretends that they provide for his own need, or, if anything should exceed his necessity, relief for the needy. He wishes to become the dispenser of others’ [Col. 0094A] goods, though he had renounced possession of his own.

By this occasion the servant of God becomes a servant of mammon, so that while he pretends to provide for the benefit of the poor, he may more freely serve his own greed. For this reason he urges everyone to assist the poor, so that, while he is believed to be a holy ministering Paul, he may by no means be judged a thieving Ananias. By this cunning, the poor man’s hut becomes a royal treasury; the solitary’s poverty is preferred to Solomon’s wealth; and from the cave of want the treasures of India are poured out most lavishly. Afterwards, from care for the poor he is carried over to the lofty works of building. From there he surveys everything beneath with care, lays foundations, stretches out the plumb line, and as an industrious geometer measures the length, height, and breadth of his structure [Col. 0094B]. He builds churches, surrounds cities with walls, bridges rivers, and, destroying himself alone, constructs everything else. Thus the professor of solitude lives in the midst of the age; enclosed in his cell, he moves among throngs of people; as an anxious merchant he wanders through markets and lanes. Rest becomes torment to him, sitting labour, silence punishment, enclosure hell. Thus—thus—blinded in the light of his mind and shut in a dark prison, he returns to the mill of restlessness; and, like Samson, once strong among the Philistines (Judg. 16), the hermit becomes a mockery to demons.

These few matters out of many, dearest brother—yet the things which most often trouble people of a similar vocation most severely—I have briefly recalled before your mind’s eyes, so that you may indeed bare the arm of strength against every temptation of the enemy [Col. 0094C], but may be more watchful against these evils especially familiar to your profession. For after purity and continence of the flesh have been established beforehand—concerning which I judged it superfluous to exhort you even briefly, although Satan is accustomed to leave nothing unattempted—after this, I say, has been established and firmly placed, as it were, in the foundation of virtues, that which the Apostle calls holiness, without which no one shall see God (Heb. 12), there must be built for you the edifice of poverty and true humility, and its loftiest pinnacles, penetrating the inmost regions of heaven, must be raised. For: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5).

These shone forth particularly in your Christ, whose cross you bear, whose tomb you inhabit, and whose resurrection within yourself you await [Col. 0094D]. As God-man walking on earth, He left humankind the footprints of His way; by these the heavenly Teacher showed that His own must walk. He was poor, having nowhere to lay His head (Luke 9). Nor did He through whom the world was made, when entering the world, find a house of His own in which to be born; rather, His mother laid Him in a manger because there was no room for Him in the lodging (Luke 2). He was poor when, consulted about paying tribute to kings, He found nothing in the possession of the person from which He could pay it; He had recourse to the inexhaustible treasures of His divinity, and paid from the mouth of a fish, caught on the hook of the Apostle Peter, what He could not pay from the household coffer (Matt. 17). He was poor, though He was the bread [Col. 0095A] of angels, and was often fed with the bread of tax collectors. He was poor: no field of grain belonging to Him ever fed Him; no vine cultivated by Him ever gave Him drink; no fleece of His own flock ever covered Him; no money, which might have been amassed even from innumerable miracles, ever enriched Him. He did not even have an upper room in which, about to suffer, He might eat the last Passover with His disciples; but borrowed it from the householder, saying: “Where is the lodging in which I may eat the Passover with my disciples?” (Luke 22).

Be both a lover and imitator of this poverty of the Lord. Do not entangle yourself in any sum of money on account of the needs of others, since, in order that you might not be entangled even for your own needs, you have freed yourself from every knot of such concerns. Let those who consult you make friends for themselves, by your counsel—or rather, by the Lord’s counsel—from the mammon of unrighteousness [Col. 0095B]; and let them not have you distribute their money, whom they regard as a despiser of your own. But if they insist, let them give, if they wish, to your prior; let them give to your brothers, so that it may either be retained by them for their own uses or distributed to others through their hands. And even if your brothers themselves command you to be the agent for such things and to conduct business for them out of your poverty, do not consent; set my authority against their compulsion. For in such matters there is no danger of disobedience where reason opposes justice. Let your cell be empty of money, filled with righteousness; lacking in wealth, overflowing with virtues; so that, since there is no agreement between Christ and Belial, it may be emptied of earthly things in order that it may have room for heavenly treasures. Nor let excessive concern for your body trouble you, lest perhaps it force your eye, fixed [Col. 0095C] upon heaven, to look back to earth; and lest, once clinging to a corpse with ravenous desire, it disdain to return to the ark (Gen. 8).

After God, look to your prior for sober food and unexcessive clothing; receiving these from him, be content with them, according to the blessed Apostle (1 Tim. 6). Thus poor, and poor in spirit, follow your poor Lord, so that you may glory in the Lord Himself not so much in the poverty of possessions as in poverty of spirit—that is, humility. Do not walk in great matters or in things too wonderful for you; for if you think yourself wonderful, you will in no way be able to marvel at Him who is wonderful in His saints. For a mind fixed in admiration of a creature can in no way advance [Col. 0095D] to the contemplation of the uncreated reality. The weight by which it is submerged into lower things prevents it from looking upward.

Let not your own solitude flatter you, nor let the multitude of others seem contemptible to you. Rather, pronounce yourself inferior and more worthless than all, not in speech only but also believe it with the inmost affection of your heart. This truly is, according to the Lord’s declaration, to be meek and humble of heart (Matt. 11). Set their life before your own life, their actions before your actions, their labour before your rest, their work before your leisure, so that, while you attend to others’ progress, you may not be exalted over your own deeds. Consider how many exercises of good works are available to them that cannot be available to you; although you may be able to possess the desire for them, you can in no way attain their performance.

You too indeed are a beast of the Lord, but shut within His stable you lie down and chew His fodder [Col. 0096A]. They are strong horses prepared for the day of battle; sitting upon them, the heavenly Rider boldly conquers and kills the prince of this world. They are guided by the bridle of obedience and driven by the spurs of discipline. Breathless and often bloodied in their sides, they race along the way of God’s commandments and do not rest until, having completed their course, they have obtained the prize. They bear the burden and heat of the day, not shut in cells but stationed in the open air; with strong neck they carry the yoke of obedience; with the shield of patience they bravely repel the darts of anger hurled at them by enemies and neighbours. They reserve for themselves nothing of the world, nor even themselves; and, as is written of idols: “They have eyes and shall not see; they have ears and shall not hear; they have hands and shall not [Col. 0096B] touch; they have feet and shall not walk; they shall not cry out with their throat” (Psalm 111). They are needy, distressed, afflicted; sometimes, through the power of obedience, they are not even permitted to do good works, and often suffer penalties for them as if for evil works. Above all these, the world worships you as resting and at leisure, while it gives them, labouring and exhausted, a great cup of contempt and bitterness.

Set these before yourself, and every order of whatever religious profession, so that, when you have placed yourself below all, you may deserve to be placed above all by the Searcher of hearts. For you have been called to a wedding, at which, if you choose the lowest place, you will hear from the host: “Friend, go up higher” (Luke 14). Thus, having trampled down the angel of pride, enriched by the poverty of your Christ, and made higher than the heavens by humility, now arm yourself against the aforesaid spirit of sloth [Col. 0096C] and crush it with the manly right hand by which you have already overthrown the enemies mentioned above. Its subjugation will be easy once you have gained frequent victories over stronger enemies. When it attacks, do not flee to ruinous remedies, nor suppose that in this matter disease can be cured by disease; rather, employ remedies that do not know how to harm and that effectively bring speedy health.

First of all, then, accustom yourself to drive away this evil and all the others by prayer, as by the first and chief good; and in it fix the whole attention of your mind. By prayer, while the body of the one praying rests, the raging aerial powers are conquered; by it the strongest temptations are most powerfully overcome; by it harassing thoughts are driven away like most troublesome flies; by it the dense Egyptian darkness is dispersed; by it invisible light shines upon minds; by it the eye of the heart, still veiled by fleshly grossness, searches out heavenly things; by it the human spirit, insofar as is permitted to a human being, contemplates the uncreated Spirit Himself who creates all things. You have vowed that henceforth you will live for this heavenly contemplation. For its sake, fleeing the world’s expanse, you have confined yourself within the narrowness of a solitary cave; lest the manifold sight of worldly things call you back from this gaze, you have placed firm walls before your bodily eyes. Enclosed between them, and fearing no sight of people, the farther you are removed from them, the nearer be you to God. Separated from others, join yourself to Him, so that, as you are separated in body from bodies, you may be joined in spirit to spirits.

The Prophet exhorts us to this singular grace of prayer: “Come,” he says, “let us worship and fall down before God; let us weep before the Lord who made us” (Psalm 94) [Col. 0097A]. And the Apostle: “Pray without ceasing; in all things give thanks” (1 Thess. 5). And the Lord Himself: “Watch and pray, that you may not enter into temptation” (Matt. 26). Thus, both for avoiding and for repelling temptations, He teaches that the good of prayer is the supreme defence, and that this supercelestial gift cannot be perpetual on earth. For the Apostle John says: “There was silence in heaven for about half an hour” (Rev. 8)—not a month, or day, or hour, not even half an hour itself, but *as it were* half an hour—showing that prayer is indeed a great advancement, but that the time of one praying cannot be long.

Holy meditation must follow prayer, into [Col. 0097B] which prayer, like a mistress returning to her handmaid, may withdraw and rest; from it she may rise stronger, as though after repose. But since meditation too, being wholly spiritual, still needs another and lower support, the aid of divine reading must be applied. Refreshed by it, even after the book is closed, let meditation reconsider what it has read, and, after long reconsideration, minister to prayer as a handmaid. For as fire, when fat is added and the fuel of richness is received, bursts into greater flames, so the fervour of prayer, enriched by the abundance of meditation and reading, rises into the most abundant heat of divine love. These are the delights of the children of the King; this is the table prepared by Mother Wisdom; these are heavenly feasts, to which she cries out in the streets, inviting little ones, not the great, saying: “If anyone is little, let him come to me” (Prov. 9) [Col. 0097C]. And then: “Come, eat my bread and drink the wine which I have mixed for you” (ibid.).

This bread is eaten only by one fasting from every human food; this wine is drunk only by one abstaining from every other drink, because, according to blessed Gregory, one who is fed by carnal pleasures is judged unworthy of the feast of eternal delights. But I know, dearest brother, that these things too are arduous, and that it is not easy for everyone to spend life solely in such pursuits.

When the foregoing three practices have been followed, let manual work follow. Thus, when the mind, wearied by spiritual things and cast down from the heights to the depths by the weight of the flesh, begins to sink, it may turn not to men’s empty talk but to the blessed exercise of the body. Little trees cannot be planted, crops cannot be watered, nor can any rural work be done, since perpetual enclosure prevents it; but—what is more useful—let the hand turn to the pen in place of the plough; instead of furrowing fields, let it furrow pages with divine letters; let the seed-bed of God’s word be sown upon parchment. When its harvests have ripened—that is, when books have been completed—let it, with fruit multiplied, fill hungry readers, and thus let heavenly bread drive away the soul’s deadly hunger.

Thus indeed, thus you may become a silent preacher of the divine word; while your tongue is silent, your hand will resound with clamorous voices in the ears of many peoples. Shut up in the darkness of your cell and among your books, you will traverse lands and seas; in the public assemblies of the Church, from the reader’s mouth you will proclaim the word of God from an elevated place as a watchman; in the remote corners of cloisters and houses you will whisper that same word to silent servants of God. Your profession will make you a hermit; devotion will make you an evangelist, so that what you cannot accomplish in person, you may achieve through your labours.

Let no small reward for labour encourage you in this work: you will obtain it on behalf of all whom you are able to assist through this praiseworthy pursuit. For as many as, through reading your volumes, cast down pride, subdue lust, despise avarice, tame anger, or either refrain from or repent of whatever evils—as sheaves gathered by your sweat, they will fill the granaries of your eternal harvest. And whereas a man’s works ordinarily end with his life and fail when he fails, you will neither die when dead nor, failing from life, cease from good work, when through your works you call the dead back to life. For as long after your death as the life of your books can, so to speak, endure, for that long the gain of your works will be extended before God.

But if, through injury to the eyes, pain in the head, or perhaps wearisome assiduity, you are unable or unwilling to be content with this one kind of manual work, turn in alternating succession also to other exercises of labour: prepare combs for dressing or cleansing the brothers’ heads; with delicate hand and skilled foot turn needle-cases; endeavour to hollow out and fashion wine-vessels, called *justitiae*, or similar objects.

> **[Note: Col. 0097D]** “Wine-vessels, which they call *justitiae*, hollow out.” Peter the Venerable himself distinguishes *justitiae* from drinking-cups in the *Book of the Statutes of Cluny*, when he says: “It is decreed that, at the time when the brothers are accustomed to go for drink after None, each shall drink not from those wine-vessels called *justitiae*, as they were formerly compelled to do, but from his own cup.” I think these *justitiae* are the same as those also called *justae* in charter 28 of the cartulary of the Greater Monastery—that is, of the possessions of Vendôme—[Col. 0098D] in these words: “We shall provide for him a place and a bed with two mattresses, and for one of his men a bed with one mattress; daily, three loaves and four *justae* of wine for the two of them, from bread and wine such as we ourselves use.”

And if marshy places are nearby, make mats, an ancient work of monks, on which you may sleep always or often; soak them with daily or frequent tears; wear them down by frequent bending of the knees before God. Or, as blessed Jerome says, weave a little basket from rushes, or plait a basket with pliant twigs.

> **[Note: Col. 0098D]** “Make mats, an ancient work of monks.” Thus in Letter 50 of Book II he called it a “monastic mat” [Col. 0099D], which was not only made by monks, but upon which monks and all persons of lesser rank were accustomed to sit in conferences, disputations, and public gatherings: “Let it not escape your mind,” he says in the passage already cited, “that the abbot, as was fitting, assigned the bishop a place in his own seat and compelled him, though reluctant, to sit; he himself sat beside him on the monastic mat adjacent to that seat. The conference was held not concerning low things but heavenly things.”

> And before him Saint Ambrose, on the First Epistle to the Corinthians, chapter XIV: “Let those seated dispute: the elders in dignity upon chairs, those following upon benches, and the last upon the floor on mats.” Hence Pope Urban V is said to have provided by rescript that scholars of the University of Paris, while hearing their lectures, should sit on the ground before their masters, not upon benches or seats raised from the earth, in order that an occasion of pride might be excluded from the young. And at that same university the Straw Street still today retains its name from the straw [Col. 0100D] upon which, formerly, scholars intending to dispute and to attain the mastership in arts used to sit. Petrarch also seems to touch upon this in Book IX of his *Letters*, when, speaking of the French, he says: “And what, I ask, do they have to set against so many and such great pursuits, unless perhaps that—as it is a people pleased with itself and given to self-praise—they set against all these things one noisy street of straw?” And in the second letter of Book X: “You know how, in that flowering of rising life, which we spent among the grammarians on straw as though in delights, when once my father and at the same time your uncle, according to custom, had come to the little city of Carpentras of which I was just speaking, my uncle himself, as though a newcomer, was seized with the desire—arising, I think, from nearness and novelty—to see that most famous spring of the Sorgue.”

By occupying the whole span of your blessed life with these and similar labours of holy studies, you will leave no space whatever, either in your heart or in your cell, into which adversaries may plunge themselves, so that, when God has filled all things with His virtues, no place may remain for the devil, for sloth, or for the remaining vices.

Already no small portion of time will be consumed in the nightly and daily offices. Since these must be sung slowly and attentively, as far as solitude permits, you must devote so much greater diligence to them because in them you do not offer God service as though it were gratuitous, but render it to the Lord as a servant renders a due tribute. From there approach the sacred mysteries of our redemption, your heart cleansed by all these good things and your hands purified; and partake, either continually or frequently, of so great a remedy for human salvation, first testing yourself, according to the Apostle (I Cor. II).

The very beauty and suitability of the place, which you lately showed me and which I praised as it deserved, invite you to these things. There, as you stand at the sacred altar and understand whom you attend, dwell then especially in mind among heavenly things; separated from mortals even in body itself, join your whole self to the immortal and blessed spirits.

Concerning fasts and vigils, or any other harsh treatment of the flesh, no law ought, in my judgment, to be prescribed for you by anyone. For neither your individual constitution, nor your previous habit, nor especially the grace for such matters which has been or will be given you by God, is known. Be your own instructor in such things—you who know all that is inward and outward in yourself. Set yourself those limits which need not be exceeded, carefully observing this principle: in these matters and in all your actions follow discretion, the mother of all virtues. It is called the mother of all because, unless that mother nourishes the virtues as her daughters, the whole offspring of virtues immediately perishes.

Therefore you must govern your life with such an even balance that you withdraw from the flesh what might serve its pride, and grant it what can satisfy only the necessity of nature. If you allow it more than is right, insolent through abundance, it will raise itself above itself; but if you deny it what is right, it will most miserably cast itself down beneath itself.

What other rule, moreover, should be appointed for the tongue except that which the Prophet asks of God for himself, saying: “Set a guard, O Lord, upon my mouth, and a door of restraint around my lips” (Ps. 140)? As the holy doctors of the Church say, he asks for a door upon his lips so that, just as a door is opened and closed only when necessity requires, so the door of your mouth may be opened for usefulness and closed against trifling or vanity. Let it be opened to the brothers for edification, closed against the detraction of those who speak ill or murmur. Let it be opened for exhorting religious persons who come to you, closed against the wordiness of the curious. And, briefly, let something useful either be heard or spoken; if neither occurs, let the rule of silence not be broken by the solitary.

And so that you may run in this way of God’s commandments not with a constricted but, in the Psalmist’s words, an enlarged heart (Ps. 118), and attain the virtue of perfection and perseverance, fill the lamp of your mind with the oil of charity, and kindle ever more and more within yourself, by daily increase, the flame of divine love—a flame which many waters cannot quench nor rivers overwhelm (Song 8). When the stiff neck of the heart has been softened by this richness of love, the yoke of God’s commandments, which you formerly thought harsh, will become sweet; the burden which seems heavy to you will become light.

After you have been imbued with this, your cell will be broader to you than the whole world; fasting, refreshment; vigils, sleep; work, leisure; labour, rest. Nothing will be able to weigh you down when hope and love of eternal things raise you heavenward as though on twin wings.

Extend this breadth of charity, derived from above, as far as your neighbours; do not regard yourself as living for yourself alone. For you ought to stand before God on behalf of all, if not by office, at least by that charity of which I have spoken. Be like Moses for the people in matters pertaining to God (Exod. 18). Pour out especially at this time devout prayers principally for the Church of God, for those who preside over it, and, according to the Apostle, for all who are in high station (I Tim. 2). For religious communities, and especially for all your brethren of Cluny, and for each person concerning whom the anointing of the Holy Spirit instructs you, be urgently present at the ears of divine mercy; and, as I would do if I were present, I beg you with bent knee: remember me, the most wretched of all.

Thus, shut within the life-giving tomb of your enclosure, be buried with Jesus Christ, as I wrote above. And as He was anointed with Joseph’s and Nicodemus’ spices, so you too shall be anointed with the fragrances of the virtues already mentioned, so that, buried, you may not decay. Breathing this nectar even up to heaven, you shall exhale before the Most High like a sacrifice offered in an odour of sweetness. While you live in this tomb, your life will be hidden with Christ in God, so that, after the death of the flesh and the ensuing resurrection of flesh and spirit, when Christ—your life—appears, then you too may appear with Him in glory.

## LETTER XXI. To the Supreme Pontiff and our special Father, Lord Pope INNOCENT, Brother PETER, humble abbot of Cluny, offers sincere affection and faithful obedience.

[Col. 0101A]

If I knew that the venerable Lord Archbishop of Lyons, a son of Your Sublimity, required my recommendation or that of anyone else with you, then, in filial confidence in you, I would strive to say much concerning him or on his behalf. But since his integrity is known to your wisdom and his loyalty has been tested by your apostolic office, these, I think, sufficiently commend him to you; and I did not wish superfluously to intercede for one worthy of being heard even on behalf of others. I judged only this to be said: if it please you, give him thanks for your sons of Cluny, whom he kindly cherishes. And since our land, as you know, being without king or prince, lies exposed to every sort of plunderer, remind him to strive more and more earnestly for the establishment of peace, concerning which he is greatly concerned. We too ask, and the manifold need of the region itself demands, that he be sent back soon with your favour and blessing. For the more his presence is necessary to that entire region, the less tolerable his absence proves to be.

## LETTER XXII. To ATON, Bishop of Troyes, venerable and most dear to us, Brother PETER, humble abbot of Cluny, wishes fullness of salvation and affection.

I wonder whether it could have entered the heart of so unanimous a friend that I had so neglected our mutual affection as to see your letters and make no reply to them. Your Sublimity ought not in any degree to think this of my humility, from whom, I think, life might depart sooner than the charity which joins me to you could grow cold in any respect. I heard indeed that those letters had been delivered by someone; but, though I searched into everything carefully, I was unable either to see the letters or to find their bearer. The fault, then, of not replying may more rightly be attributed to the person who sent them negligently. For if they had been sent with suitable care, they would by no means have escaped our notice.

Now, since it is foolish to treat what is sound or mend what is whole, we need not say many words about increasing or preserving the affection between us—an affection which, I judge, cannot grow here, and which, by God’s helping grace, cannot in any way be diminished from its present state. We have directed our chamberlain, Brother Hugh, to reply to the other matters which you subsequently wrote.

> **[Note: Col. 0101C]** Brother Hugh, our chamberlain. He is also mentioned in Letter 38 of Book II, and his death is mourned in Letter 41 of Book IV.

Since we are presently sending him to your region, inquire of him and you will hear.

## LETTER XXIII. To the Supreme Pontiff and our special Father, Lord Pope INNOCENT, Brother PETER, humble abbot of Cluny, offers greeting and obedience.

[Col. 0102B]

The brethren of Luxeuil recently came to us, bringing letters from Your Paternity. In them, with paternal compassion, you lament the destitution of the once great monastery of Luxeuil, and likewise command us to grant to that place an abbot and necessary officials from among our brethren.

> **[Note: Col. 0101C]** The destitution of the once great monastery of Luxeuil. Luxeuil, a monastery of Burgundy which, as the writer of the Chronicle of Bèze says, once flourished before the other monasteries of Gaul and Burgundy in religious observance. But who built it, or at what time it began, does not appear to have been adequately established up to now. For the ancient author of the *Life of Saint Eligius of Noyon* relates in Book I that Dudo, or Audoenus, Archbishop of Rouen, was its first founder. Jonas, however, a contemporary of Saint Columbanus who committed his life to writing, affirms that Columbanus himself founded it in the reign of King Theuderic, in these words:

> “And when blessed Columbanus was now surrounded by a company of many monks, he began to consider seeking a more suitable place in the same wilderness in which to build a monastery. He found a fort, once maintained with a very strong defence, more or less eight miles distant from the aforesaid place, Bellugas, which ancient times called Luxeuil. There were there hot baths constructed with remarkable workmanship. There the neighbouring woods were thick with stone images, which the ancient times of the pagans honoured with miserable worship and profane rite, and to which they offered abominable ceremonies. Wild beasts alone frequented the place: a multitude of bears, buffaloes, and wolves. There the eminent man took up residence and began to build a monastery. At its report people hastened from every side and sought to dedicate themselves to religious observance, so that, when a very great multitude of monks had gathered, they could scarcely be contained within the community of a single monastery. Children of noble families strove to come there from every quarter, so that, despising worldly finery and scorning the pomp of present possessions, they might gain eternal rewards.

> “Blessed Columbanus, therefore, seeing people from every side run to the remedies of penitence, and seeing that the enclosure of one monastery could not without difficulty contain so great a company dwelling together—though they were of one mind and one heart—sought through experience another place suitable to so great a community, adorned by an abundance of waters; and he built another monastery, which he named Fontanas. He appointed superiors and governors whose religious character was beyond doubt. Thus communities of monks were established in these places; he himself in turn attended all of them and, filled with the Holy Spirit, composed the rule which they were to observe. What kind of man the saint was, and how great his discipline, the discerning reader or hearer recognizes in it. And this account is certainly truer and more consonant with reason than the former.”

Through these men, according to the tenor of your letters, almighty God is to be worthily served there; and, by the co-operation of divine mercy, so noble a monastery is to be restored to the distinction of its former standing and its earlier completeness. We received this command with due reverence, but we fear its difficulty not a little. For, as your wisdom knows, in the business of religion it is easier to found new institutions than to restore old ones; because, according to blessed Gregory, for persons otherwise formed it seems very hard to conceive new things in an old mind. He who builds only new things need not labour at the destruction of old ones; but he who strives to restore old things is bound by a twofold concern, since both the destruction of the old and the building of the new fall upon him.

Moreover, we who know the situation are greatly afraid for your Church of Cluny, lest, as often happens, when our brethren are repeatedly transferred to other churches, what brings relief to others bring loss to us. Nevertheless, we set all these considerations aside; and when the aforementioned brethren came to us, we were ready, as had been commanded us, to provide an abbot and the necessary officials. But, requesting things very harmful to us and of little advantage to themselves, they would not acquiesce in our counsel; and saying that they would return to us on an appointed day concerning this affair, they went back to their own home.

We report this to Your Reverence so that, should they persist further in the matter and request an abbot from Cluny, they may not choose what they do not understand, but may place the matter in the hands of us, who know better the countenance of our flock. If they do this, we shall faithfully provide such ministers for the church that almighty God may be worthily served, so far as He grants, in the monastery of Luxeuil; and, by the co-operation of divine mercy, that place, if not restored to its former completeness, may nonetheless be restored to a better condition. If it please you, write back to both us and them to this effect.

## LETTER XXIV. To the venerable Lord and Father GUIGO, prior of the Carthusians, to be singularly embraced in the arms of unfeigned charity, and to the other brethren, Brother PETER, humble abbot of Cluny, wishes the eternal salvation for which they sigh.

[Col. 0103C]

When I attempt to set forth in verbal signs the overflowing and sincere affection of my heart toward you, I confess that I fail in the very attempt. When I treat continually of any other matters, an abundance of words flows forth; but when my entire soul is filled with love and remembrance of you, the mind, seeking to express itself, gives way. It becomes like a vessel filled to the very top with any liquid: if you suddenly remove the stopper placed in it, you will wonder, as though from an empty vessel, that nothing flows out. And though, in the natural order, emptying follows filling, in a wondrous way the very fullness denies emptying an outlet. This is exactly what often happens to me when I wish to write to you: there may be some, even small, matter for speech, but, as the saying goes, abundance makes me poor.

> **[Note: Col. 0103D]** Guigo, prior of the Carthusians. See below, Letter 12 of Book II; and Saint Bernard, Letters 11 and 12. Our Peter himself, in Book II of the *Miracles*; Peter Dorland, in the *Carthusian Chronicle*; Theodore Peter, in the *Carthusian Library*; Peter Sutor, *On the Life of the Carthusians*; and others teach how and by whom the Carthusian order received its beginning. This Guigo, surnamed “of the Castle,” or, as Bunder says, “of the Pine,” incorrectly called Guido by some, was French by nation, from Dauphiné by homeland, and a native of Valence. He was the fifth General Prior of the Grande Chartreuse after Blessed Bruno, and is honourably mentioned in Book III, chapter 1, of the *Life of Saint Bernard*.

> He himself wrote several works: namely, the *Life of Saint Hugh, Bishop of Grenoble*, dedicated to Pope Innocent II and found in Surius, vol. II, under 1 April; various serious meditations, published together with the *Meditations* of Lord William, abbot of Saint-Thierry of the Cluniac order, from Plantin’s press in the year 1189; an as-yet unprinted book *On Contemplation*; treatises *On Truth and Peace*, *On the Four Spiritual Stages*, and *In Praise of the Solitary Life*; and several letters, some of which are found in our Peter the Venerable. Finally, as Sutor says in Book II, chapter 5, of the *Life of the Carthusians*, in the fiftieth year of his age, the thirtieth of his conversion, and approximately the twenty-seventh of his priorship, he rendered up his spirit to the Lord in the year of the Lord 1137, not without a reputation for holiness; the fifty-third year from the beginning of the order.

The difficulty is increased by the pursuit of brevity, in which modern people take pleasure through some inborn sluggishness, I know not what; and I am compelled to bring to a brief conclusion of words thoughts for which a multitude of books would scarcely suffice. For when shall I be able to explain how, though separated from you in body, I am joined to you wholly in mind; how, though remaining elsewhere, I remain always with you; how, though living among others, I dwell spiritually within the number of your sacred community?

When shall I be able to recount how grievous your bodily absence itself is to me—He who cannot be deceived bearing witness? If I could be free of it, I would not hesitate in any way to cast off not only the wretched title of abbot, so far as it concerns me, but even the whole world with all that belongs to it. When, even with the eloquence of anyone most articulate—though the field of speech were left wholly open—could I adequately declare with what fear my unhappy mind, deservedly wavering under the uncertainty of divine judgment, is shaken, when I can neither prudently avoid the danger that especially threatens from my office by remaining, nor lawfully evade it by fleeing?

I am neither so blind that I do not see, nor so foolish that I do not understand, nor so faithless that I do not believe that I must soon stand before Christ’s tribunal, to render account, according to the blessed Apostle, of the things I have done in the body, whether good or evil (I Cor. 5). And since Solomon confirms the same, saying, “God will bring all things into judgment for every error, whether it be good or evil” (Eccl. 12), I am terrified by the uncertainty of my life; and, considering the boundless heap of my miseries, I sigh, driven by deep pain of heart.

I observe the most grievous burden of cares placed upon weak shoulders; and I see a weight for which scarcely the strength of giants could suffice pressing down the neck of a little insignificant man. I, a little ass, am compelled to carry the camps of elephants upon my back; and, armed with Saul’s armour, I, a boy and rustic, must go out from the camp of Israel to battle against Goliath. I see the dragon cast down from heaven, dragging by its tail a third part of the shining stars from the heights to the depths and fighting more fiercely than usual against the seed of the holy woman (Apoc. 12). And while that most skilful craftsman of destruction assails the heavenly camp with manifold snares, he promises himself and boasts of victory over Christ’s soldiers, with me as leader—ignorant, weak, fearful, unable to know, unable to resist, not daring to resist.

Unless Michael is sent quickly against him, the impious accuser of the brethren will prevail. Fearing this beyond what I can express, and knowing that it is dreadful to fall into the hands of the living God (Heb. 10), I am constrained by a double danger as I consider myself and those entrusted to me. For, as blessed Gregory says, in that examination of the dreadful judgment, each person’s testimony will scarcely suffice for that person alone—how much less for himself and his neighbour! How then shall I stand before Christ, the just Judge of the living and the dead, for so many thousands scattered throughout the world, whom I am rarely or never permitted to see, when I shall scarcely be able to stand for myself?

How shall I be able, according to blessed Father Benedict, to render account of the number entrusted to me, when, if questioned concerning the care of my own life, I may perhaps appear speechless? “If the stars are not clean in His sight, how much more man, corruption, and the son of man, a worm?” If this was said by one who lived so that by divine judgment he was called a simple and upright man, fearing God and departing from evil, and who was so concerned for his own that he offered daily sacrifices for them, saying, “Perhaps my sons have sinned” (Job 25), what shall be said by a man asleep, a negligent man, a man who provides neither for himself nor for those under his care?

Great, great is the danger of pastoral office—a danger toward which men of our age run rejoicing, like blind men toward a precipice. They fall more grievously wounded from the highest steps of dignities into the depth of hell; and, in the manner of gladiators of old, they nourish for a brief span of time a fattening of pleasures and pride, which they offer to the devil, in the spectacle of the lost, to be devoured forever.

Happy, and already sharing in eternal blessedness, is the leisure of those released from office, for whom a free and unobstructed way to heaven is prepared. Here, if they are not negligent, they are easily joined to God through invisible charity; and immediately after the funeral of the flesh they are united to Him through the visible reality of vision itself. I acknowledge myself separated from their happy rest and restful happiness; I grieve at the chasm set between them and me, but I cannot cross over to them.

But why, desiring to satisfy my grief, do I fill your ears—occupied with Mary in hearing the Lord’s words—with the importunity of my words? “Who will give me wings like a dove, that I may fly away and be at rest?” (Ps. 54). Yet, so far as the desire of my heart goes, I have fled far away and remained with you in solitude, awaiting Him who may save me from faintness of spirit—which for these reasons unmans me—and from the worldly tempest which surrounds me on every side as though to suffocate me.

Have pity on me, therefore, at least you who are my friends. And as I have poured out my tears to you in dictating these things, so deign to pour out yours for me before the most merciful Redeemer. To keep your minds continually reminded of this, I have sent a second cross bearing the image of the Saviour, that, as you contemplate Him crucified for one crucified in this world, when you pray to Him for your own salvation and that of many others, you may in no way forget me also in your sacred prayers.

Let Him who, according to the prophet, “stands as a sign for the peoples” (Isa. 11) be for you the sign of friends, so that, as remembrance of your Lord is never separated from the sanctuary of your breast, so the misery of your servant may, if possible, at no time be torn from your affections. I have also sent, as you commanded, the *Lives* of the holy men Nazianzen and Chrysostom. I have sent also the little book, or letter, of blessed Ambrose against the petition of Symmachus, pagan prefect of the city of Rome, who, in the Senate’s name, asked the emperors to restore idolatry to the city. Although he seems a most acute orator in his petition, both the venerable Father just mentioned and our distinguished poet Prudentius answered him most powerfully, in prose and verse.

I did not send blessed Hilary’s treatise on the Psalms because I found in our copy the same corruption as in yours. If you wish it even so, send word back and I shall send it. As you know, we do not possess Prosper’s work against Cassian; but in its place we have sent to Saint-Jean-d’Angély in Aquitaine, and, if necessary, shall send again. Please send us the larger volume of the letters of holy Father Augustine, which near its very beginning contains his letters to Saint Jerome and Saint Jerome’s letters to him. For a bear happened to eat a great part of ours at one of our obediences.

Our whole community greets you with devoted heart; and certain brethren, to whom speech is permitted, greet you with heart and voice alike. Among them Brother Peter, our notary, asked to be named in writing. May our almighty God Jesus Christ, who has united us here through the spiritual affection of our hearts, unite us in His kingdom through everlasting cohabitation; and, not entering into judgment with His servants, may He by grace supply what is lacking to our merits.

## LETTER XXV. To the most reverend Lord and Father in Christ, PETER, abbot of Cluny: GUIGO, unprofitable servant of the poor Carthusians, his servant and son by his condescension, wishes him to rejoice in perpetual peace through Christ.

“Crucified, myself also crucified,” etc. See Guigo in volume 153 of the *Patrologia*.

## LETTER XXVI. To Brother and son PETER, most dear to me in special affection, Brother PETER, humble abbot of Cluny, wishes eternal salvation.

[Col. 0106D]

After you departed from us in bodily presence, my dearest friend, and, fleeing the worldly disturbances which often caused you among us and us with you to grow dull in our inmost being, withdrew into whatever repose you could find, I resolved frequently to write to you, to learn of your condition and make mine known to your affection. But because the world—which, if I may so speak, has bound my whole self to itself—would not permit me to relax either mind for dictating or hand for writing, I have not hitherto been able to fulfil this. For this reason, I did not so much delay as was compelled to defer for so long learning how you were and informing you about me.

At last, scarcely withdrawing myself for an hour from the yoke of that most harsh master by slipping away from it, I have furtively written and sent these few words. I rejoice at your quiet; I rejoice with you in your peace—provided, however, that it is such a peace as gives you reason to rejoice in the meantime. And though I toss upon the sea and, my ship shattered by adverse winds and the wild surges of the swelling sea, despair of life, I gladly behold you already holding the harbour and securely laughing at the rage of sea and sky.

The sure indications of this are that, although both the great affection with which I embraced you and the great usefulness for which I needed you continually reminded me that you ought always to remain attached to me, I nevertheless subjected my will to yours, set your welfare above my need, and preferred your repose to my affairs. Yet you, taking no care to return any recompense for this goodwill of mine, appear—if I may say it without violating friendship’s privilege—to live for yourself, to attend to your own concerns, and to despise the concerns of others and, what is worse, of friends.

Having found, like the sparrow, a house, and, like the turtle-dove, a nest, you endure with tranquil mind and dry eyes the miseries of doves groaning and the perils they fear from the claws of eagles and hawks. But far be it from me to think this of your heart, of which I have been accustomed to think nothing other than what I think of my own. I do not think this of your heart; I do not lay upon it that which I do not doubt to be one in mind with mine. Rather, I complain that, although you sympathize with our troubles and distresses, you have shown no signs at all of your sympathy.

For you could, if not rescue us, at least grieve with us; if not assist us, at least advise us; if not lift us up, at least strengthen us. For if inability withheld help, who restrained your words? If the means to aid were lacking, who held back your speech? Who prevented your mind from dictating or your hand from writing? Will you allege that leisure was lacking? Will you prove that you did not know letters? Will you show that something else stood in the way? Certainly nothing.

Negligence, then, will remain. If you meet this charge by repentance alone, you may deserve pardon. But I shall spare your shame, restrain my hand, draw back the reins, suspend my pen, and moderate my speech, lest I attack a friend beyond what reason permits. Grant me pardon. I myself will do what I reproach you for not having done. I wish to know more fully how you are. For if you are well, if you are [Col. 0107D] at peace, if you are free to devote yourself to God—as you have always wished—if the place fully serves that purpose, if you have “given sleep to your eyes and slumber to your eyelids, until you find a place for the Lord, a dwelling for the God of Jacob” (Ps. 131), I shall rejoice. But if otherwise, I shall, so far as concerns a place, provide one suitable, as I think. For I cannot but be concerned for your salvation, which I desire as much as my own, and for whose sake I endure your absence as more burdensome to me than every other trouble.

For I praise what you have desired, extol what you have undertaken, and proclaim what you have begun. For if I cannot yet do what you have been able to do, nevertheless I desire what you have desired. For what is this? Who would not desire it? Who would not long for so great a good? Who would not wish to be rescued from so great an evil—an evil by which life is lost, death acquired, God expelled, and the enemy admitted? For the entanglement in worldly affairs from which you have fled brings either death or a danger close to death; so that scarcely anyone has ever entangled himself in them without incurring one or the other. Nor does it matter much, especially in this age, under what dress, by what profession, or under what pretence of religion one involves oneself in external concerns, since nearly all of us who are occupied in secular affairs on an ecclesiastical pretext seek not the things of Jesus Christ but our own: glory, power, pleasure, money, and whatever else seems advantageous to the flesh but produces many disadvantages for the soul.

We do not even handle earthly things in such a way as to think partly of earth and partly of heaven; or—as would be perverse, but more tolerable—to savour less of heaven and more of earth. Rather, what is wholly most perverse, we utterly put heaven behind us and cling wholly to earth, so that we can truthfully confess: “For our soul has been humbled to the dust; our belly has been glued to the earth” (Ps. 43). On these matters I could go on speaking without end, compelled by the subject itself—or rather, by misery. But because you have often heard me weeping over them, and know most fully what I think of such things, I have judged it best to refrain, lest I appear to drive the chariot beyond its bounds and run outside the road, and lest things which I wished you alone to know somehow become known to any reader. Come to me quickly, therefore, so that I may entrust to the safe ears of a friend [Col. 0108C] what I have generally not dared to commit to untrustworthy pages.

## LETTER XXVII

To the supreme pontiff and our most merciful father, Lord Pope INNOCENT, Brother PETER, humble abbot of Cluny, greetings and obedience.

This is a day of tribulation and distress, because, according to the prophet: “The children have come to the point of birth, and there is no strength to bring forth” (Isa. 37). The messengers of Sennacherib have come, blaspheming the God of heaven (4 Kings 18); Nebuchadnezzar has rushed in and carried the people of God into captivity (4 Kings 24–25); nor was Doeg lacking, to stretch out his hand against the priests of the Lord (1 Kings 22).

I am compelled to unfold again a lamentable history which, my grief of heart interrupting me and tears flowing whether I will or no, I shall scarcely, I think, be able to relate. But because—alas!—it has befallen me to see a crime so unheard-of since the age of the martyrs, I was obliged, though I would rather have been silent, to speak unwillingly.

As we returned from the nourishing breasts of our mother Church which called us, from the council of your Holiness, we, the Lord’s flock walking simply, encountered the bites of wolves; and, scattered by a fury unusual in our age, we were taken captive, wounded, and stripped of nearly all our possessions. There was in our company no mean or insignificant part of God’s Church: a company of archbishops, bishops, and abbots; no small number of monks; and a multitude of noble archdeacons, clerics, and religious persons. It was a terrible sight to see such numerous and necessary persons of God’s Church dragged away, scattered, wounded, and, with swords pursuing them, driven in flight in different directions.

Very many bishops and abbots were violently carried off to nearby camps, and some of them, after beatings and wounds, were imprisoned with barbarous cruelty. Among them the lord Archbishop of Rheims, whom neither age nor rank could protect, is held shut up in a tower after many outrages and wounds. The lord Bishop of Périgueux suffered similar things. But why do I speak of individuals as though they stood alone, when the Archbishop of Bourges and the Archbishop of Sens, having lost nearly all their people, scarcely reached Pont Tremblant trembling and breathless, and there, together with the Archbishop of Embrun; the Bishop of Troyes, struck by a lance and thrown from his horse and thereafter seriously ill; the bishops of Limoges, Arras, Belley, Rennes, and others; and also the abbots of Limoges, Vézelay, Saint-Michel de la Cluse, Saint-Germain of Paris, Corbie, Noyon, Bourgueil, Saint-Sulpice, Saint-Remi, La Crasse, Saint-Jean-de-Pré, the monastery of Hender, [Col. 0111A] Melun, Saumur, and very many others—when they are all held confined in a second prison?

> [Note: [Col. 0109B] “The abbots also of Limoges,” etc.] That is, of Saint Martial. For the monastery of Limoges—whose monks have now been transformed into secular canons—and the monastery of Saint Martial are one and the same. Thus Geoffrey of Vendôme calls Amblard “abbot of Limoges” in Letter 22, Book IV; that is, abbot of Saint Martial, or, as some say, “of Saint Martial.” Ivo, in Letter 206, calls the abbot of Chartres—that is, of Saint Peter—by that designation; and Peter himself below calls certain abbots “of Noyon,” “of Melun,” and “of Saumur,” though others call them abbots of Saint Bartholomew, Saint Peter, and Saint Florentius. The very learned Jacques Sirmond should be consulted in his notes on the aforementioned passage of Geoffrey. I suspect, moreover, that this abbot of Limoges was either Amblard himself, mentioned by Geoffrey, or rather Albert, his successor. For both governed in the time of Peter the Venerable: Amblard until the year 1143, and Albert from 1143 until 1150.]

> [Note: [Col. 0109C] Saint-Germain of Paris.] Or, as it is commonly called, *des Prés*. It is the monastery built by Childebert I, son of the great Clovis, originally in honour of Saint Vincent, but later renamed after Saint Germanus, bishop of Paris, who was buried there. I do not doubt that this abbot of Saint-Germain is Hugh I, formerly, as the continuator of Aimoin says, a monk of Saint-Denis, who departed this present world in the year of the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ 1145, on Palm Sunday.]

> [Note: [Col. 0109C] “Of Noyon.”] That is, of Saint Bartholomew, founded in honour of Saint Bartholomew in 1064 by Baldwin, the fiftieth bishop of Noyon, on the summit of a hill outside the walls of the city of Noyon; he was also buried there after his death.]

> [Note: [Col. 0109C] “Of Bourgueil.”] In the territory of Anjou, where, as Adémar relates, William, Duke of Aquitaine, ordered a great monastery of Bourgueil to be built on his own estate, together with his mother Emma, sister of Odo of Champagne. He placed over it as abbot Theodelin, a man distinguished for learning and wisdom.]

> [Note: [Col. 0109D] “From the monastery of Hender.”] Perhaps [the monastery] of Dervent, also called in French *Monstierender*, an exceedingly ancient monastery in the diocese of Châlons, whose foundation is attributed to Saint Bercharius, abbot, and Childeric, king of the Franks, as is clear from their diplomas published, along with several others from the cartulary of the monastery of Dervent, in the *Promptuary of the Antiquities of Troyes*. But because Nicolas Camuzat, a man of singular kindness and the author of that *Promptuary*, recovered after completing its publication a still-unpublished charter of Emperor Louis concerning the estate of Dodiniaca, which belongs to this monastery, and also an old catalogue of the abbots who governed it from Saint Bercharius onward, and graciously transmitted them to us, we have judged it useful to append them here lest they perish. They are as follows.

> **Charter of Emperor Louis concerning the estate of Dodiniaca belonging to the monastery of Dervent.**
>
> In the name of the Lord God and our Saviour Jesus Christ: Louis, by the ordering of divine providence Emperor Augustus. “If a place,” etc. (See among the letters and privileges of Louis the Pious, *Patrologia*, vol. 104, col. 1204.)
>
> **Catalogue of the Abbots of the Monastery of Blessed Mary of Dervent.**
>
> Saint Bercharius, abbot of the monastery of Dervent, in the year of the Lord 664, received a gift and privilege from Childeric, king of the Franks. Twenty-one years after Saint Bercharius had departed this world, Abbot Synaulius succeeded, in the year of the incarnate Word 685, during the time of Theodoric, brother of Childeric; they were brothers and sons [of the same parents].
>
> In the year of the incarnate Word 693—that is, [lacuna]—immunity and privilege were granted to Abbot Synaulius by Berthoend, bishop of Châlons, at the request of King Childebert, brother of the aforesaid Theodoric. In the year 769 Charlemagne began to reign. In the year 815 Hauto, abbot of Stavelot—that is, [lacuna]
>
> [Col. 0110C] Having restored order in the monastery of Dervent committed to him by Louis the Pious, son of Charlemagne, he obtained for that monastery a privilege from the same king in the year 832. The same Louis gave Abbot Hauto the estate of Dodiniaca—that is, Saint Christopher—and Neuville.
>
> In the year 840 Pardulus was *vicedominus* of Rheims; he later became bishop of Laon. He restored this church and bestowed very many goods upon this monastery. Algarius succeeded him, and after him Abbot Altinarus; Humfredus; Vulfaudus, who was in charge of this place in the year 859 under the name Fulfraudus. After him, until the year 964—a period of 104 years—we do not know who his successors were, apart from the last ones, namely Alard and Benson.
