When Benson was expelled, Lord Albricus was appointed for twenty years; then Berencerus, Hino, Dudo, Milo, Brimo, Dudo, Nocherus, Rogerus, Guillermus, Theobaldus, Gualterus, Jorannus, Ebalus, Raynaudus, Vuiterus, Eurardus, Nicolaus, Raynaudus, Anselmus, Petrus, Hamricus, Raynaudus, and Guillermus, who is now [abbot].
>
> After Guillermus, Ferricus withdrew [read: succeeded] and caused a great part of the cloister to be built. James succeeded Ferricus, during the wars of the Dautiri [reading uncertain], called Dieguo Francio of Saint Martin, and ruled for twelve years. Pons of Mirevaux succeeded James; he caused the stronghold of Sommvecra to be made and ruled for twenty-eight years. After him ruled Brother Simon of Ambonville, a venerable man, likewise for twenty-eight years. After him Brother Peter of Changey ruled for sixteen years. After him Brother Odo of Ficocuria ruled for two and a half years. After him Brother Simon Goix, a notable young man, ruled for thirteen months; he died while the epidemic plague was raging. Brother John of Betiquey succeeded him and ruled during the legal proceedings of the said monastery against the people of [lacuna], ruling almost fifteen years. Brother Simon d’Yeure succeeded him; in his time he laboured manfully in repairing the church buildings and increasing its revenues, obtained in Parliament a judgment concerning the king’s *taille* against the people of the land of the said church, and ruled [lacuna].]

> [Note: [Col. 0111D] “Of Melun.”] Perhaps Jocelin, who in the cartulary of Saint-Victor near Paris is called abbot of Saint Peter of Melun. When Theodoric of Miliac had surrendered into the hands of Henry, Archbishop of Sens, the church of Saint Mary of Floriac in the diocese of Sens—which he had long held freely and peacefully, without objection, as a layman by hereditary right—and Henry had given it to the church of Saint-Victor of Paris and to the canons serving God there, investing Abbot Gilduin with it, Jocelin later began to assert that it belonged to the right of his own church. Judges therefore had to be appointed to settle the controversy; Hato, bishop of Troyes, Manasses, bishop of Meaux, Suger, abbot of Saint-Denis, and Nitalis, abbot of Rebais, attended and subscribed with others. All these were not only contemporaries of our Peter the Venerable, but letters of his to them—except to Manasses—are extant.]

> [Note: [Col. 0111D] “Of Saumur.”] He was also abbot of Saint Florentius on the Loire, as we have noted above, and perhaps successor to that William to whom Geoffrey of Vendôme writes in Letter 7, Book IV.]

That town was filled and crowded with a multitude of holy persons, who, like Jerusalem besieged by the Babylonians, do not dare to set foot beyond it. Entrance is safe for no one; departure is denied to all. Nor is there much hope in anyone except him “who brings the bound man out of the prison-house,” and in you, most holy Father, who perform his office on earth. Therefore that noble portion of God’s Church cries to you as to its singular refuge, and prays that help may most speedily be brought to it, as children pray to their father.

I too, a companion in their dangers, through whom they chose that these matters be written to you, beg that, since they have encountered such dangers for God and for you, your mercy may hasten to aid them quickly in their dangers. [Col. 0111B] I beg, I say, because I must beg, lest I seem to have disregarded the holy companions who had attached themselves to our journey with a certain confidence born of charity.

For I refrain from saying more about my own injuries. When I, together with the lord Abbot of Vézelay, had gone out to meet armed enemies on behalf of the peace of our companions, our mule was at the first onset pierced by a lance-thrust and forced aside. Our brethren were put to flight, our servants captured, and nearly all our possessions carried off. I withdrew to a nearby village and remained hidden until, under the escort of our host, I too reached Pont Tremblant in the evening, where the others had arrived before me.

> [Note: [Col. 0111D] “With the lord Abbot of Vézelay.”] Peter, I suppose, whose letter to Suger, abbot of Saint-Denis, survives; Pons, the brother of Peter the Venerable himself, succeeded him, as may be inferred from Letter 4, Book III.]

From there, therefore, raising with my companions the voice of mournful lamentation, I both beg and advise that you do not consider so great a matter negligible [Col. 0111C] if you judge that regard must at some point be had for the name of Christ, for your honour, and for the welfare of the Church. For if this is neglected, what will be cared for? If the rigour of justice and the severity of the Church sleep amid public injuries, when will they awaken in private ones?

The holy assembly of captives prays and urges with us that the sword of apostolic vengeance may flash forth not only against the perpetrators of this wickedness but throughout the whole bishopric of Luni, so that when it shines out loftily, not only those nearby but even those situated at the furthest bounds of Christendom may be terrified. The Bishop of Luni, who appeared to us briefly, suffered a lunar eclipse far too early: we thought that he would shine upon us for a whole day’s journey, but we could scarcely have him as a companion for one complete league. I have been lengthy, but, to speak boldly, in so great a matter I ought to have been longer. Now, if anything has been said insufficiently, let your wisdom supply and arrange it.

## LETTER XXVIII

To the lord BERNARD, abbot of Clairvaux, venerable for his merits and most dear for his affection toward us, Brother PETER, humble abbot of Cluny, present welfare and eternal salvation.

It has long been, dearest brother, since, drawing in through the inward sense of my heart the spices of your good manner of life, fragrant with spiritual sweetness, and beginning to love you before knowing you, to venerate you before beholding you, I have desired to see you, embrace you, and speak with you about the soul’s progress. Awaiting the fulfilment of that desire until now, I deferred writing to your charity about these matters. For I preferred to disclose the secrets of my heart to you in living speech rather than commit them to this little sheet under the running pen. But the great distance between lands, and the great bitterness of the affairs and tribulations pressing upon us, have hitherto prevented this from happening.

I shall therefore do what is possible and, by such means as I can—for I can only by this means—shall disclose to your brotherhood, dear to me, as I have said, before I knew you, what troubles me in certain respects. For I know you to be alike instructed and adorned by knowledge of secular learning and, what is far more useful, by knowledge of the divine Scriptures; and, having left Egypt, so enriched with the spoils of the Egyptians and the wealth of the Hebrews that, while yourself remaining rich, you can supply the need of others and pronounce a sure judgment in doubtful matters.

Certain persons of yours accordingly object to our brethren:

> [Note: [Col. 0112D] “Certain persons of yours accordingly object to our brethren.”] These objections of the Cistercians, drawn from the Charter of Charity made by Stephen, third abbot of Cîteaux, are thus briefly summarized by John of Paris under the year 1107: “At this time the Charter of Charity was made by Stephen, abbot of Cîteaux, and twenty other abbots, and confirmed by the authority of the apostolic seal. From that time, therefore, they rejected from their order furs and pelisses, woollen cloth, hoods and breeches, combs, bed-coverings and bed-straw, various dishes in the refectory, fat, and everything opposed to the purity of the Rule. They also rejected churches, altars, offerings, tithes, burials, ovens, mills, villages, and peasants, because they did not read either in the Life of Saint Benedict or in his Rule that Saint Benedict had possessed these things; nor that women had entered his monastery; nor that dead women had been buried there, except Saint Scholastica, his sister. They said that tithes ought to be divided into four portions: the first for the bishop, the second for the priest and cleric, the third for guests and pilgrims, and the fourth for repairing the church. And because they did not find in that monastery the person of a monk who possesses his own lands, from which he may live by working both himself and through his animals.” Robert of Torigni should be consulted in the Supplement to Sigebert, as should Caesarius of Heisterbach and the author of the *Cistercian Chronicle*, first printed under this year.]

“You do not,” they say, “follow the Rule whose uprightness you have undertaken to observe, as your deeds themselves show; [Col. 0113A] rather, with crooked steps you pursue unfamiliar paths and every sort of byway. You yourselves devise private laws as you please and call them sacred; you cast aside the commands of the Fathers for your own traditions; in one and the same matter—which seems monstrous—you are both masters and disciples. Moreover, to increase your transgression and divine wrath, you bind yourselves by a vow before God and his saints; by violating it, you undoubtedly show yourselves guilty of a broken vow. For you promise, according to the Rule of blessed Benedict, that you will serve in the camps of heaven and preserve unfailing obedience in accordance with his institutions. Such is your promise. Let us see whether your manner of life corresponds to it.

“And, that we may approach everything in order, how do you observe the Rule in receiving [Col. 0113B] novices, when it commands that they be received only after a year, after their spirits have been tested to see whether they are from God; whereas you receive them at the very moment when they arrive, so to speak, without observing any rule? Consequently, because they are received rashly, they conduct themselves still more rashly once received; and because, when coming, they do not understand what they are coming to, once they have joined the others they do not know what they ought to do. Since, like athletes in a stadium, they are not trained before battle, when they come to the conflict they flee when they ought to fight, and, when they ought to conquer by fighting bravely, being inexperienced in such matters, they are most easily conquered.

“By what authority, moreover, do you defend your use of pelisses and various skins, when nothing of the sort is found in that same Rule?

“Indeed, it orders that those who are sent on a journey receive drawers from the clothing-store and return them there on their return, plainly permitting no one except them to wear them.

“As for bed-straw, see for yourselves whether you follow the master, when you certainly lay beneath and above yourselves more and different things than the Rule commands.

“You read in the often-mentioned Rule that two cooked dishes should suffice for all the brethren, and that, if there are fruits or vegetables from which something may be added, there should be a third. Acknowledge whether you observe this.

“It orders that brethren who transgress and violate their profession—namely, those who cast off the yoke of the Rule, flee from monasteries, and return to the world—be received up to a third time if they wish to return and repent; but if afterward they do this again, that every avenue of return be denied them. Yet you, like the rest, despise this also, and as often as you please receive those who come, contrary to the precept of the Rule.

“[Col. 0114A] What shall we say of the regular fasts, which you have so discarded and altered at will that you have retained scarcely small remnants of them, perhaps more from human shame than divine fear? For whereas monks are commanded to fast from Pentecost until the Ides of September, on Wednesday and Friday until None, unless they have work in the fields or the summer heat is excessive; and whereas from those same Ides until the beginning of Lent they are commanded always to take their meal at None, you, on the contrary, make all weekdays alike throughout the summer and observe the same pattern of fasting by eating twice every day. During the remaining period, fasting when you wish and breaking fasts when you wish, you subject not yourselves to the Rule, but the Rule to yourselves.

“[Col. 0114B] Manual labour—the labour always practised by the holy fathers of the desert and ancient monks, by which the apostles themselves supplied food for themselves and others; concerning which God, punishing the guilt of the first man with this penalty as well, says, ‘In the sweat of your face you shall eat your bread’ (Gen. 3); and concerning which David says, ‘Because you shall eat the labours of your hands, you are blessed, and it shall go well with you’ (Ps. 127)—you have so rejected that neither all these authorities can compel you to work nor the obedience which, according to the Rule, you promised to render to God can draw your delicate hands from idleness in your lap to labour.

“You also know that it is commanded there that, for all guests arriving or departing, the brethren should adore Christ, who is received in them, with bowed [Col. 0114C] head or with their whole bodies prostrate upon the ground. Nor are you ignorant of the other command: ‘Let the abbot give water into the hands of the guests. Let both the abbot and the whole community wash the feet of all guests.’ Yet you do not care to observe even this small matter, though you are despisers of your vow.

“The abbot is commanded to keep an inventory of the tools and goods of the monastery; but he either does not care to keep one through negligence or disdains to keep one through pride.

“Further, although those who cannot come to church for the divine praises which ought to be sung to God are commanded to bend the knee where they are with the fear of God, you, following your usual custom of employing your own laws and despising common ones, neglect even this, though it is not very burdensome; and, inventing certain other practices, you disdain this small command just as you do greater ones.

“It also orders that the abbot’s table always be shared with guests and pilgrims, so that he may deserve always to have Christ, who says that he will declare: ‘I was a stranger, and you received me’ (Matt. 25). You likewise despise this good, so great and yet so easy, as though it were nothing.

“[Col. 0115A] Wherever brethren meet one another, the younger is commanded to seek a blessing from the elder; this is not observed among you.

“An old and wise man is commanded to be placed at the monastery gate; he is not placed there.

“The porter is commanded to answer those who knock or call, ‘Thanks be to God,’ or to give a blessing; this is not observed.

“But that thing—yes, that thing, I say—which is contrary to every rational consideration and every authority: how do you defend it? Those who have once professed stability, conversion of life, and obedience in one place you compel to vow stability again in another place, conversion of life again, and obedience again, thereby making their former pledge void. Thus, in yielding to you, they bind themselves with unavoidable danger, so that whichever way they turn, they cannot fail to be transgressors. For if they keep the first vow, they will be guilty concerning the second; if the second, they will be bound by the fault of the first. Nor will they alone suffer this: the same chain will bind you yourselves, perhaps more harshly. For deceivers ought to suffer greater penalties than the deceived.

“And if you can, offer an adequate excuse also for this: contrary to that same Rule, so often named—your Rule, certainly your Rule, the Rule that either saves or condemns you—you indiscriminately receive monks from another known monastery without permission from their own abbot or letters of recommendation, [Col. 0115C] and do to another what you would not wish done to yourselves. Therefore you lose regard for fraternal charity and do not love your neighbour as yourselves according to the divine command that says: ‘This is my commandment, that you love one another’ (John 15).

“Beyond all these things, you refuse to abandon what is plainly unjust to everyone and contrary to ecclesiastical decrees, and for which you are rightly judged by all: against the custom of the whole world, you refuse to have your own bishop. How absurd this is is clear even to the unlearned. From whom do you receive chrism? From whom holy orders? From whom the consecration of churches and the blessing of cemeteries? Finally, from whom do you receive everything [Col. 0115D] which cannot canonically be done without a bishop or the bishop’s command? Certainly in these things you exceed the Rule not only of monks but of all Christians.

“By what right have you acquired the possessions of parish churches, first-fruits, and tithes, when all these belong by canonical enactment not to monks but to clerics? For they are granted to those whose office it is to baptize, preach, and perform the other things which in general concern the salvation of souls, so that they need not become entangled in worldly business, but may live from the Church because they labour in the Church, as the Lord says: ‘The worker is worthy of his wage’ (Luke 10). But why do you claim these things, when you ought to do none of what we have mentioned? And since [Col. 0116A] you do not bear that labour, why do you take its reward?

“And what will you answer concerning secular possessions held by you in a secular fashion, when in this respect you seem in no way to differ from secular persons themselves? For you indiscriminately acquire and unlawfully hold castles, villages and peasants, male and female slaves, and, what is worse, toll revenues and almost every benefit of this sort; and you defend them by every means against those who attack them. Hence, contrary to the institutions of the monastic order, religious persons conduct secular lawsuits; monks become advocates; they accuse and are accused; they become witnesses; contrary to the Apostle, they appear in courts (2 Tim. 2). Under the pretext of defending their own right, they return in their hearts to Egypt; having already gone out from the Sodomites, they look back at the burning of Sodom; they put their hand to the plough and look back, and therefore cannot be fit for the kingdom of heaven (Luke 9).

“In all these matters we have shown most plainly that you are transgressors of your profession and vow. For if it is established that the Rule commanded these things, and that you vowed to observe it, and if it is established that you have not done this until now, then, as we have said, it is clear that you are violators of a promise not kept. But we observe all these things as they are commanded, and wholly preserve whatever we promised God to observe in the Rule.”

To this our brethren reply: “O, O new race of Pharisees, restored again to the world! You who separate yourselves from others, prefer yourselves to everyone, and say what the prophet foretold that you would say: ‘Do not touch me, for [Col. 0116C] I am clean.’ But, to answer first the things which you have placed last, tell us, true observers of the Rule: how do you boast that you observe it, when, as your own words show, you do not care to observe even that brief chapter which says that a monk ought not merely to declare with his tongue that he is inferior and more worthless than everyone else, but should also believe it in the innermost disposition of his heart?

“Is this to believe and declare oneself inferior: to disparage the deeds of others, extol one’s own, despise others, and appear great to oneself, when Scripture commands: ‘When you have done all that was commanded you, say: We are unprofitable servants’ (Matt. 17)? ‘No living person,’ says the prophet, ‘shall be justified in your sight’ (Ps. 142). And Isaiah: ‘All our justifications are like the cloth of a menstruous woman’ (Isa. 64). Yet you make yourselves holy, singular, the only true monks in the whole world, while all others are false and lost according to the interpretation of the name. Hence you display a habit of unusual colour and, in distinction from almost all the monks of the whole world, exhibit yourselves in white among blacks.

“Certainly this blackness of clothing, devised in ancient times by the Fathers for the sake of humility, when you reject it, means that you judge yourselves better than they by preferring an unusual whiteness. Yet of that great and admirable man, the true monk Martin, we do not read that he went forth in a white and short cloak, but in a black and flowing cloak. In this also you grievously transgress the Rule, whose defenders rather than observers [Col. 0117A] you wish to appear: for under its command you learned that monks ought not to complain about the colour or coarseness of clothing. You are convicted of being its most manifest transgressors, since you reject the colour more fitting for humility and lowliness and adopt white—the colour by which joy and festivity are also signified in Scripture (Acts 1)—contrary to the commands of the Rule just cited. Although those placed in the valley of tears, who are commanded always to attend to mourning and never to joy, ought to wear garments signifying grief and penitence, you, on the contrary, display happiness amid miseries, joy amid sorrow, and gladness amid mourning, through the whiteness of your garments.

“But lest we seem more to avenge verbal injuries with words than to answer rationally the objections brought forward, setting aside for the moment the matters by which we could justly attack you, we answer your objections as follows. And, that we may refute them in the order in which you set them forth, we say that in the observance of the Rule we pursue no byways at all, but follow in every respect the straight course of the guiding Rule. We do not set private laws above the traditions of the Fathers, since those laws themselves were devised by holy Fathers, whom a holy life and many miracles have testified and still testify to have pleased God. They were permitted to command such things, and we are permitted to observe them. Clearly it was permitted, and always will be permitted, that shepherds should command what is right to their sheep, and that sheep should obey their shepherds as God. You strive to show us to be violators of our vow; we show ourselves to be its true observers.

[Col. 0117C] For in receiving novices we observe the Rule in every respect, since we follow Him who said: “Everything that the Father gives me will come to me; and whoever comes to me I will not cast out” (John 6). We should not follow Him if we cast out those who, inspired by Him, come to Him. For, He says, “No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him” (John 3). If, therefore, we expelled one whom the Father draws, the Son receives, and the Spirit—who breathes where He wills—inspires, what else would we appear to do but resist God?

Indeed, He is found not only to receive those who come, but even to invite those who do not come to come, saying: “Come to me, all you who labour and are burdened, and I will refresh you” (Matt. 11). And [Col. 0117D] He adds concerning the bearing of the yoke of our order: “Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am meek and humble of heart. For my yoke is sweet and my burden light” (ibid.).

And lest we seem to invent anything, rather than establish everything by divine authorities, tell us: you who will have a monk only after a year, did He impose upon the man to whom the Saviour said, “If you wish to be perfect, go, sell all that you have and give it to the poor; and come, follow me” (Matt. 19), a year’s delay before conversion? Nor can you deny that the whole substance of our order is contained in these brief words of the Lord. For what else is it to say, “Give all that you have to the poor, and come, follow me,” than “Become a monk”?

But perhaps you will say that the man did not do this. Can you say that the Lord did not [Col. 0118A] give this counsel? And if that man did not fulfil it, the other did: when the Lord said to him, “Follow me,” and he replied by asking permission first to go and bury his father, and the Lord added, “Let the dead bury their own dead; but you, come and proclaim the kingdom of God,” he rose and followed Him (Matt. 8; Luke 9). Did He impose upon him—not a year, but even a day or an hour—before he converted? Rather, did He not compel one who wished to delay even for the cause of filial piety not to delay?

And certainly the Wisdom of God says through Solomon: “My son, do not delay in turning to God, and do not put it off from day to day; for you do not know what the coming day may bring forth” (Ecclus. 6). And, to take up greater examples, we see some of the apostles called from the sea, others from the tax-office, and others from the various occupations of the world; [Col. 0118B] and immediately we see them as apostles.

But lest you call these venerable miracles rather than examples to be imitated, we turn to that life of the primitive Church—which no sane person can deny is the life that ought to be observed among us. For what is the monastic life except that which was then called the apostolic life? That this life and that life are the same, the blessed father himself indicates when, discussing how the brethren should receive necessities, he says: “It was distributed to each according as anyone had need” (Acts 4). Concerning private ownership, too, he decrees the very rule which the apostle Peter established as binding when he condemned Ananias and Sapphira, who wished to retain possessions of their own, to a dreadful death (Acts 5).

Therefore, whoever came to this manner of life—whether I call it monastic or apostolic makes no difference—was received by the apostles, immediately joined to the others, [Col. 0118C] and was not delayed for a year, as among you. Do you not yield to all these authorities, and will you still refuse people approaching God an entrance?

But perhaps you persist still, saying: “You wished to keep the Rule of blessed Benedict.” We answer in turn: Have we excluded the things just mentioned from our profession? Have we vowed to observe the Rule and denied the Gospels? Did blessed Benedict forbid us to imitate the sayings and deeds of the Lord and His apostles? Does not Peter say: “Christ suffered for us, leaving you an example, that you should follow in His footsteps” (1 Pet. 2)? Certainly Christ said to all whom He called that they should follow Him [Col. 0118D]. Recall the Gospels, and you will find this almost everywhere. Our teachers have taught us that “to follow” is used in the sense of “to imitate.”

Above all these things, in these matters and in the rest, we profess that we follow the rule of motherly charity. This claims as its own peculiar prerogative that whatever is done according to it is plainly right rather than warped, equitable rather than inequitable, just rather than unjust. For, as the Lord says, upon it hang the whole Law and the Prophets (Matt. 22). And blessed Gregory says: “Every commandment derives from love alone, and all commandments are one commandment, because whatever is commanded is established in love alone.” And shortly afterwards: “The Lord’s commandments are both many and one: many through diversity of action, one in the root of love.”

Hence blessed Augustine says: “Have [Col. 0119A] charity, and do whatever you wish.” Following this rule of charity, as we have said, we receive novices as soon as they come; indeed, according to the Lord, we even invite them to come, and fulfil what John says in the Apocalypse: “And the Spirit and the Bride say, ‘Come’; and let him who hears say, ‘Come’” (Rev. 22).

Nor are we opposed to the Rule, because we keep the eye of charity open toward our neighbour’s salvation. For we consider that, if we discouraged him so harshly from our order, he would return to the world and turn after Satan; and he who had come for salvation would lapse into destruction. We fear that, at the searching judgment of the strict Judge, we shall be found guilty of that destruction if, by our austerity, we allow to perish someone whom we could save by condescension.

[Col. 0119B] We consider this also: good things are often bestowed even on the unwilling. This is what we see often happening among us. Some, after submitting their necks to this yoke, are after a time oppressed by various temptations or tribulations, and would return to the dregs of the world which they had abandoned, unless they reflected that what they had once done cannot be violated without eternal condemnation. If at any time they venture upon this, yet afterwards, compelled by this fear, they return to their proper sheepfold; and because they know they cannot otherwise be saved, willingly or unwillingly they keep what they vowed.

Blessed Benedict himself, whom you set against us, speaks for us: “Thus,” he says, “let the abbot temper and order all things, so that souls may be saved.” And the Lord also says in the Gospel: [Col. 0119C] “If your eye is single, your whole body will be full of light” (Luke 11). That is, if the intention is good, all works will be right. Relying upon these authorities and this reasoning, we are confident that we act justly and that we observe most fully, in receiving novices, the precept of blessed Benedict, who can in no respect be contrary to the divine Scriptures.

To all these points we add that, with this concern for fraternal charity, it is often lawful for the teachers of God’s Church to depart from the institutions of the Fathers and to moderate the commands of rules for the advantage of souls. For to this end tends the purpose of all divine Scriptures, and this is their final cause: that, whether by arguing, entreating, rebuking, sparing, correcting, or acting in whatever manner, provision may be made for the salvation of souls, [Col. 0120A] and that the human being—for whose instruction whatever has been written has been written—may be reunited to God, from whom he had been separated.

We find much concerning this in the ecclesiastical canons: matters soundly established beforehand by holy Fathers and then, by successors, altered for definite reasons according to the circumstances of times. Thus, for example, those who lapse into heresy or into some damnable and public sin are forbidden by the earlier canons to return to their former rank of clerical office or dignity; but later canons sometimes permit it when necessary causes compel. Likewise, it was decreed that sons of priests should not become priests, and that bishops should not be transferred to another see; yet in many cases these decrees have not been observed for the sake of expediency.

Pope Gregory also permitted the English, newly converted to the faith, [Col. 0120B] to marry in the fifth degree, contrary to the statutes of his predecessors and of many councils.

> [Note: [Col. 0119D] Pope Gregory permitted the English, newly converted to the faith, to marry in the fifth degree. Bede, *Ecclesiastical History of the English People*, book 1, chapter 27: “Meanwhile the man of God Augustine came to Arles and was ordained archbishop for the English people by Etherius, archbishop of that city, as they had received orders from the holy father Gregory. Returning to Britain, he immediately sent to Rome the priest Laurence and the monk Peter, to report to the blessed pontiff Gregory that the English people had received the faith of Christ and that he himself had been made bishop. At the same time he sought his advice concerning questions which seemed necessary. Without delay he received fitting answers to the questions.”
>
> And shortly afterward: “Augustine’s question: To what generation may believers contract marriage with relatives? [Col. 0120D] Gregory answered: A certain secular law in the Roman commonwealth permits the union of brother and sister, or of the son and daughter of two full brothers, or of two sisters. But we have learned by experience that offspring cannot thrive from such a marriage. And sacred law forbids uncovering the nakedness of kinship. It is therefore necessary that now the third or fourth generation of believers may lawfully be joined to one another. But the second generation, of which we have spoken, must in every way abstain from one another.” Yet nothing is said about the fifth degree.]

These and many similar regulations, established by some Fathers and altered by others out of a definite necessity or advantage, are very often found. The Synod of Nicaea, in its second chapter, says: “It frequently happens, either from necessity or in some other way, that men transgress ecclesiastical canons.” And holy Pope Leo says: “Where necessity exists, let him who has authority dispense these matters for the benefit of the Church. For a change of law arises from necessity.” Likewise Pope Felix says: “It is fitting to consider that, where necessity occurs, we often transgress the constitutions of the Fathers.”

We have said these things and surrounded you with these attacking examples and testimonies, so that no avenue of escape [Col. 0120C] remains for you. For when you hear that the Fathers’ commands may be moderated for necessity or usefulness, will you deny that a person who cannot wait a year can be received into monastic life? And what necessity or usefulness greater than the salvation of souls can be found? Because of that necessity and usefulness, lest those delayed should perish, we sometimes receive without delay those who come to us. Since, by acting thus, we procure our neighbour’s salvation through the eye of charity already mentioned, we do not oppose either the Rule, which seeks only human salvation, or any divine Scripture; rather, in fulfilling what they intend, we agree with them in every respect.

After this you ask by what authority we defend our use of furs and of various skins, when nothing of the kind is found in the Rule.

> [Note: [Col. 0120D] By what authority we defend the use of furs and various skins. We have already said that from ancient times this use of skins and fur garments was common in turn to monks and laypeople; we shall now show it by further examples.
>
> Blessed Odo, book 2 of the *Life of Saint Gerald, Count of Aurillac*, chapter 3: “He wore fur garments over linen clothing, because clerics and laypeople alike customarily use this kind of clothing. Yet he never possessed two fur garments at the same time.”
>
> An addition to the chapter of Charlemagne and King Louis, chapter 22, teaches this concerning monks: “If, within the quantity of measures set below, the abbot decrees that something should be increased on account of necessity, let it remain within his authority. Otherwise, let him altogether provide that every monk have two shirts, two tunics, two cowls, two capes, and two fur garments reaching to the ankles,” etc.
>
> And Geoffrey, abbot of Vendôme, book 1, letter 12, to Pope Calixtus: “Let my father recognize these present letters as mine by this token: that I served the monk Armanno well at Rome for his sake; and when at Tours he was stripped by thieves at night, I offered my father—not half a garment as blessed Martin did—but a grey fur garment and variegated skins; for I have always loved him and still love him with surpassing charity.”
>
> William of Chartres likewise bears witness concerning laypeople in the *Life of Saint Louis*, when he says that, “from the first time he undertook the overseas journey, he was never clothed in *squaletum*, green cloth, or brown cloth, nor in variegated skins, but in a garment of black, camel-coloured, or dark-blue cloth.”
>
> Hence Ulpian also says: “A garment may also consist of skins, since some possess fur tunics.”
>
> Indeed, not men only, but women also—both secular women and veiled women—were formerly accustomed to use such skins and fur garments. A notice concerning the mill of La Cappa, situated in the Vendômois: “Let it be known to the descendants of our successors that Hildiardis, wife of Fulcher of Vendôme, bought for the use of Saint Martin of the Greater Monastery one mill, situated on the river Loir at the place called La Cappa, from a certain man named Guismand, with the consent of his wife Emelina. Emelina, who in return first received a fur garment worth forty solidi, and afterwards one hundred solidi.”
>
> And the ancient statutes of the Hôtel-Dieu of Paris: “Each sister shall have three shirts, three ankle-length under-tunics, one new lambskin garment, and her old one, if needed.”]

But we also ask by what authority you attempt to take these things away. Since you will not be able to produce such authority—as indeed you cannot—we shall set forth our reasons and demonstrate from them that we do no wrong in wearing fur garments.

Let us first examine the words of the Rule; and if it has taken skins from us, we shall immediately abandon them. Hear, then, the passage from which you attack us. “Garments,” it says, “are to be given to the brethren according to the character of their localities [Col. 0121A] or the temperature of the air, because more are needed in cold regions and fewer in warm ones. Let this consideration therefore rest with the abbot.”

> [Note: [Col. 0122D] “Garments are to be given to the brethren according to the character [of their localities],” etc. These are the words of chapter 4 of the Rule of Saint Benedict. Interpreting them in their explanatory work, the Cassinese monks add: “Whoever needs a fur garment because of some illness or necessity shall forgo that year the fixed allowance of garments due to him. Such fur garments are to be granted for necessity, not display or luxury. Every ornament must therefore be avoided in them; they may not be used in place of tunics or without tunics, but are to be worn over them, especially when those who use them go to choir or refectory.”]

In saying this, he fixed no definite limit for clothing, withheld nothing necessary, and placed everything at the discretion of the spiritual father. In this matter, as in other like matters, preserving what is necessary, he cut off only what is superfluous. [Col. 0121B] Hence he says elsewhere: “What is superfluous ought to be cut away.” The Apostle confirms the same: “Make not provision for the flesh in its desires” (Rom. 13). Hence blessed Gregory says: “When we are forbidden to make provision for the flesh in desires, we are allowed it in necessities.”

Therefore, according to these apostolic precepts; according to the above-written sayings of blessed Benedict; according to what he cites elsewhere from the Acts of the Apostles, saying, “It was distributed to each according as anyone had need” (Acts 4); and according to all the commands of divine writings: it is lawful for the abbot, after cutting away superfluity, to give fur garments or other clothing to the brethren, and, in the manner of a good shepherd, to provide all necessities for the sheep entrusted to him.

And lest examples seem lacking, we read that God Himself gave garments of this kind to the first human beings after the Fall. “God,” it says, “made Adam and his wife tunics of skins and clothed them” (Gen. 2). Since, therefore, God gave them these garments not for glory but for shame, not for pleasure but for penitence, not for honour but for disgrace, why do you try to deprive monks of skins as though they were luxuries or something grand? Such [Col. 0121C] garments plainly remind those living in exile of their homeland, from which they were expelled, and of the fact that they received them to sustain their frailty.

The Apostle also remembers in praise of the martyrs that holy prophets used skins, saying: “They went about in sheepskins and goatskins” (Heb. 11). The prophet Elijah is described as girded with a leather belt (4 Kings 1). And the Gospel says of John the Baptist: “John was clothed in camel’s hair and had a leather belt around his loins” (Matt. 3; Mark 1). We read that blessed Antony, father of hermits, wore a fur garment. Hence we read also concerning blessed Benedict himself in the *Dialogues*: “At that same time, shepherds found him hiding in a cave. Seeing him clothed in skins amid the bushes, they thought he was some beast.” [Col. 0122B]

If they had believed that the use of skins was sinful, men so great, who are proposed to all for imitation, would never have wished to use them. But because they knew how to distinguish between superfluities and necessities, putting superfluities far away—and though by the merit of greater virtue they abstained in many respects even from necessities—they nevertheless retained for themselves these garments, the use of which is said to make monks cease to be monks; and holy prophets and martyrs continued to wear them.

Consider at last, if you have not yet done so, how discerningly, prudently, and charitably he spoke in what follows concerning the tunic and cowl, and how far his words differ from the inhumanity of your indiscretion. “In moderate localities,” he says, “we believe that a cowl and a tunic suffice for each monk: a shaggy cowl in winter, and in summer a plain or worn one.” [Col. 0122C] What command, I ask, is here? What compulsion? What is said here that we do not observe? He believes that a cowl and tunic suffice for a monk; he does not command it; nor does he say this for every locality, but for moderate localities. Is believing the same as commanding? Are moderate localities all localities? Is this the command that we transgress, the ground on which [Col. 0123A] we are accused of guilt, the ground on which we are called violators of our vow?

But if we violate the Rule by using fur garments, because the Rule says nothing of them, then you also violate it with us: you who refuse to be content with a simple flock garment and cowl, and who, beyond the bounds of the Rule—which says nothing of these things—put on many tunics, as many as you please, and wear them without any discretion. If, however, you answer as some of yours have sometimes answered ours—that you do this because of necessity—we shall answer similarly: that we wear the protection of skins because of necessity, that is, because of the unbearable severity of cold. And if by this reasoning you wish to appear exempt from transgressing the Rule, by the same reasoning we declare that we likewise are not transgressors of the Rule.

Since, then, the Rule orders garments to be given to brethren [Col. 0123B] according to the character of places or the temperature of the air; since it decrees that this consideration belongs to the abbot; since, according to the apostolic statement, it commands that each be given according to his need; since the Apostle forbids provision for the flesh in desires but permits it in necessities: it is plainly lawful for the abbot to supply, as he sees fit, necessary assistance to those whom he judges to need it, whether in garments or in any other things. Indeed, it is not merely lawful: he would be guilty of violating the Rule if he did not charitably supply what the Rule commands to be provided for the needy.

We defend the use of drawers (*femoralia*) on the same grounds of necessity, cleanliness, and decency. Moreover, we recall [Col. 0123C] that God commanded that the high priest should not presume to approach His altar without linen drawers, lest, if he did so, he incur the penalty of death. Although the Church of God applies all those priestly or Levitical garments and ornaments more to conduct than to bodies, and follows not the letter that kills but the Spirit that gives life, there are nevertheless certain things which are still observed in the Church according to that ancient custom for the sake of seemliness: so that things which signified future realities may represent things past. Thus, for example, we see certain features in pontifical vestments imitating the old custom; and we understand that this is done not in observance of superstition but, as we have said, because of the spiritual harmony of the two laws.

For though, according to [Col. 0123D] the Apostle, all things happened to them figuratively (1 Cor. 10), practical decency or usefulness was at times joined to the sacrament. And although chastity was signified to the ministers of God by linen drawers, the decency of covering the indecent parts was not excluded; indeed, it was carefully commanded. Hence the Apostle says: “We surround our unseemly parts with more abundant honour” (1 Cor. 12). The decency of this matter is certainly understood; its necessity would be more openly expounded if we were permitted to speak freely concerning such things. Yet it is decent, useful, and necessary; and therefore, against the Rule—which, as we have often said, forbids no necessities—we do nothing wrong in this matter.

Concerning the bedding of beds, which you have objected to us:

> [Note: [Col. 0123D] Concerning the bedding of beds. Saint Benedict, chapter 55 of the Rule: “Let the bedding of the beds suffice: a mat, a coverlet, a woollen blanket, and a pillow.” The Cassinese monks explain this passage thus: “Prelates shall prohibit decoration of beds, and especially their enclosure all around with linen or woollen cloth of any colour or quality,” etc. Since monks are forbidden to use linen, this should be observed especially in bed furnishings. It is nevertheless permissible to have over the coverlet [Col. 0124D] or mat a woollen cloth, or a coarser linen cloth, which can be removed and washed.]

We wonder how you could have raised this objection. Have you forgotten the words of the Rule, which says: “Let them receive bedding according to the manner of life, by the arrangement of their abbot”? Therefore, whatever, with the abbot’s permission, we place beneath or over ourselves, provided superfluities are absent, we rightly do according to the Rule and without any danger of disobedience. [Col. 0124B] Accordingly, since we cannot be accused of transgression, we who are wrongly reproached may more rightly reproach you for improper reproach.

Let us now turn to the two cooked dishes which you have raised, and see what the Rule says both about them and about the measure of bread and wine.

> [Note: [Col. 0124D] Concerning the measure of bread and wine. We shall explain this elsewhere; Addition 1 to the chapter of kings, chapter 25, also says: “Let abbots be content, in eating and drinking, with the measure which their monks have.” And chapter 77: “Let each brother receive his own separate measure of food and drink, and let him give no one anything from his total ration of food.”]

“The weighed pound of bread,” it says, “shall suffice for a day, whether there is one meal or both dinner and supper. If they are to have supper, let a third part be kept back by the cellarer to be given to those who will eat supper.” Behold: you who fabricate accusations out of one iota or one stroke of the Rule, rise up and rush upon us! You have found what to say and what to object. Here indeed you can condemn us, accuse us of violating the Rule, and call us transgressors of our vow [Col. 0124C] without contradiction.

For if a weighed pound of bread does not suffice a monk for the day; if he takes even a little more than a pound, or something else in place of the pound; if, having eaten twice, he does not return to the cellarer—not another person—the whole third portion to be restored to him for supper; if he eats more or less of the pound at the first meal than leaves a third part to be preserved, that is, so that neither more nor less than a third part remains for the eater—what follows except that we are condemned by God, shut out of paradise, and cast into hell as perjurers and children of perdition?

Yet what will you say of those who travel abroad and, going through various places for the monastery’s necessity, remain away from the monastery for a long time? Will they always be able to weigh their bread? Will they always and everywhere be able to keep with them the monastery’s cellarer, to whom, when they have eaten twice, they may entrust the third part of their pound, to be received for that supper and not eaten from some other bread? [Col. 0124D]

Truly, you strain out the gnat and swallow the camel, tithe mint, dill, and cumin, and leave aside the weightier matters of the Law—judgment, justice, and truth (Matt. 23). In thinking thus, what else do you seek to make God appear to be but a hunter of words rather than a searcher of hearts? Although He is said always to look to the heart, and Himself confirms that the whole body becomes full of light through singleness of eye (Luke 11), you seem, on the contrary, by such statements to think that He observes movements of the tongue and sounds common to all ears.

And although anyone may infer—indeed, plainly know from many places in Scripture—that He most willingly seeks the ground of our salvation because of His boundless mercy, as, for example, when speaking to Abraham He promised, for ten righteous Sodomites, to spare the rest (Gen. 18); when He praised the widow offering only two mites (Matt. 10); [Col. 0125B] when He rewards one who gives a cup of cold water (Luke 15); and when He announces peace to people of good will (Luke 2): you, on the contrary, endeavour to prove that He lies in wait for us.

This you certainly do when you understand and expound these and other words of the Rule not as you ought. You do this when you say that God attends to the words rather than the hearts of those making profession. The saint did not think so—by no means did he think so—he who is said to have been full of the spirit of all the righteous. Hear what he thought. The words that follow show his understanding:

“If perhaps the labour has become greater, it shall lie within the abbot’s judgment and power, if it is expedient to increase anything—above all, gluttony being removed—so that indigestion may never steal upon a monk, [Col. 0125C] since nothing is so contrary to every Christian as gluttony, as our Lord says: ‘See that your hearts are not weighed down by gluttony’” (Luke 21).

In saying this, what else did he do but retain necessity, cut off vice, and judge that all such matters belonged to the abbot’s discretion? And do not all his words, when he treats of the measure of drink, support our interpretation? We would gladly omit them for brevity’s sake, but because they make his intention and discernment especially clear, we must set them down.

“Each one,” he says, “has his own gift from God, one in this way and another in that way” (1 Cor. 7). “Therefore, with some hesitation we set the measure of others’ food. Yet, considering the weakness of the infirm, we believe that a hemina of wine for each person [Col. 0125D] is sufficient for a day. But those to whom God gives the strength to abstain should know that they will have their own reward. If the need of the locality, labour, or the heat of summer demands more, let it rest in the superior’s judgment, taking care in all things lest satiety or drunkenness creep in. Although we read that wine is not at all for monks, because in our times monks cannot be persuaded of this, let us at least agree upon this: that we should not drink to satiety but more sparingly, because wine makes even the wise apostatize” (Ecclus. 19).

Tell us then, you scrutinizers of syllables: do not all these things condemn your indiscretion? Do they not in every way approve our position? He says that diverse gifts are given by God to different persons and therefore [Col. 0126A] sets the measure of others’ food with hesitation; yet in setting it he commands nothing, but believes that the measure he gives can suffice for the brethren. If labour, heat, or any necessity demands more, he places the matter in the superior’s judgment, as usual cutting off only what is superfluous and vicious, and therefore admonishing that satiety and drunkenness be avoided in all things.

Concerning cooked dishes also, affirming nothing, commanding nothing, but putting all under moderation, he writes thus: “We believe that two cooked dishes are sufficient for the daily meal at every table, because of the infirmities of different persons, so that perhaps one who cannot eat of one may be refreshed by the other.” If, therefore, someone because of his own infirmity cannot [Col. 0126B] eat from those two, ought he not to be refreshed from a third? And if not even from a third, should not a fourth be offered him? Thus should not different provisions likewise be charitably distributed to different persons according to the nature of their infirmities—that is, according as each has need—while superfluity is always and everywhere cut off?

This is what that saint understood, this is what he wrote. For this reason he wished to determine and command nothing else in such matters; rather, according to the nature of places, times, customs, illnesses, and different contingencies, he decreed that food, drink, clothing, and, finally, everything necessary both for bodies and souls should be given by Fathers to their subjects. He was concerned only for the salvation of souls, and zealous to procure it whether by giving, withholding, sparing, or correcting.

He shows this in almost every part of his Rule; he states it especially [Col. 0126C] in the chapter mentioned above, in which he treats of whether all ought to receive necessities equally: “As it is written: ‘It was distributed to each according as anyone had need’” (Acts 4). “Here we do not say—God forbid—that there should be respect of persons; rather, there should be consideration of infirmities. Let him who needs less give thanks to God and not be grieved. But let him who needs more humble himself because of his infirmity, not exalt himself because of the mercy shown; and thus all members will be at peace.”

To this reasoning bears witness the rule of charity, which extends to all things and makes all things right by its own rectitude. Blessed Augustine, writing against the Manichaeans in his book *On the Morals of the Catholic Church*, says:

“Those who can do so—though they are countless—abstain both from meat and from wine, for two causes: either because of the weakness of their brethren or because of their own freedom. Above all, charity is preserved. Food is adapted to charity, speech to charity, dress to charity, countenance to charity. They come together and conspire into one charity. They know that it was commended by Christ and the apostles, so that, if this one thing is lacking, all things are empty; if it is present, all things are full. To violate it is considered as wicked as violating God. If anything offends it, it is not allowed to endure for even one day.”

We have answered these and similar points, unless your obstinate will remains determined to defend your own practices by disputation rather than to yield to established reason and authority. Let us proceed to the rest.

You next object that, contrary to the Rule, we receive fugitives more than [Col. 0127A] three times.

> [Note: [Col. 0127D] You next object that, contrary to the Rule, we receive fugitives more than three times. Concerning the reception of fugitives, besides the text of the Rule read in chapter 29, there is also an entire chapter in the book of Cluniac Customs.]

We reply: We wonder—greatly wonder—whence this new Gospel has arisen, which contends against the faith of the whole world and forbids sinners hope of pardon. Let those who close the entrance to persons wishing to return after a threefold violation say why Christ, after Peter had denied Him three times, not only pardoned him but entrusted His sheep to his care a third time, and made him greatest among the great and chief of the apostles.

Let them say whether Scripture lies when it says: “The righteous man falls seven times and rises again” (Prov. 24). Let them say what they think of the Lord’s words by which, when Peter asked how often he ought to forgive a sinning brother—whether up to seven times—the Lord answered: “I do not say up to seven times, but up to seventy times seven” (Matt. 18). Let them show [Col. 0127B] how they understand what the Lord Himself says elsewhere: “If each one of you forgives his brother from your hearts, your heavenly Father will forgive you your sins” (Matt. 6). He did not prescribe a fixed number of remissions, but stated it indefinitely, making it understood that as often as anyone forgives a brother, so often God forgives him.

Hence in the prayer which He left to the Church He adds: “Forgive us our debts, as we forgive our debtors” (Matt. 6; Luke 11). Therefore there is no doubt that, as often as we forgive what is owed to us, so often—as we have said—our debts, that is, our sins, are forgiven us by God.

But why should we linger over examples, when no one of sound faith is unaware that the door [Col. 0127C] of mercy is always open until the final breath to those who wish to turn with all their heart, and that the fountain of the house of David, for washing the sinner and the menstruous woman (Zech. 13), stands open without distinction throughout the whole course of this present life and is denied to no one?

Nor do the words of the Rule—which you have presumed to cite while understanding them wrongly or insufficiently—aid you at all. To make clear the truth of what we say, let us set them forth: “If a brother leaves the monastery through his own fault or is expelled, let him be received in the lowest rank up to three times; but afterwards let him know that every way of return is denied him.” It does not say, “Let it be denied”; it says, “Let him know that it is denied.” Since this statement contains no command, it is evident that the Rule does not establish a barrier against mercy, but threatens the rash with fear.

Therefore [Col. 0127D] cease to speak such things. Do not adapt the Scriptures to your own interpretation; adapt your interpretation to the Scriptures. Receive even a thousand times, without any reservation, those who truly desire conversion. Otherwise, you will be found contrary to God and opponents of the Rule.

In the matter of fasts, we believe that we follow the Rule most faithfully. If you do not believe it, we shall explain. From Pentecost until the Ides of September, as you yourselves object, we are commanded to fast on Wednesday and Friday until None [3 p.m.] [Note: [Col. 0128D] “We are commanded to fast on Wednesday and Friday until None.” Addition 1 to chapter 18: “That those fasting on Wednesday and Friday may perform light work before None, or after None if necessity requires, according to the prior’s judgment.”]; and on other days to dine at Sext [noon]. Yet it says that this Sext-hour meal is to be continued if necessary, and places it in the abbot’s discretion to moderate and arrange everything in such a way that souls may be saved and that the brethren may do what they do without grumbling. And because it says that the hour of refreshment is to be continued on those two weekdays just as on the other days—that is, that from necessity the brethren may eat at Sext—because it places this in the abbot’s discretion, because it commands the abbot so to moderate and arrange everything that souls may be saved, and because provision is made that the brethren do what they do without any grumbling: when, from Pentecost until the Ides of September, we continue to eat every weekday at Sext by the abbot’s command, [Col. 0128B] we believe that we do nothing wrong and do not suppose that we depart from the Rule’s ordinances.

From the Ides of September until the beginning of Lent, according to the Rule, we always take refreshment at None, except on Sundays, on account of the decrees of the universal Church, and on certain feasts having twelve lessons. We have heard that Sundays are observed among you as well. For if we sin by eating twice on the aforesaid feasts, since the Rule does not permit it, then you likewise sin by eating twice on Sundays, since we do not find that Sundays either are excepted in the Rule from the sequence of fasting. But if you act rightly in breaking the fast on Sundays in honor of the Lord, then we too act rightly in eating twice on their solemnities in honor of the Lord and of His servants [Col. 0128C].

Concerning manual labor, which you have added to the preceding chapters, we have reasons more than sufficient—reasons which, showing your objections to be wholly without force, drive them far away and approve and uphold what is done among us. To make this quite plain, let us consider not only what the Rule commands concerning manual labor, but also why it commands it. “Idleness,” it says, “is the enemy of the soul. Therefore at fixed times the brethren ought to be occupied in manual labor, and again at fixed hours in sacred reading.” You have heard that it commands work; observe, as we said, why it commands it. It declares idleness to be the enemy of the soul, and therefore, lest it harm the soul, whose enemy it is known to be, [Col. 0128D] it strives to exclude idleness by both reading and manual labor.

Tell us, then: if the same can be accomplished by other exercises of good works, does it not seem to you that the Rule is well observed? If, I say, monks can occupy the whole span of the day continually with other good works—for many other good works besides manual labor can be found—since they are commanded to work solely in order that they may not be idle, do they not, in doing those works, remain altogether free from violation of the Rule? [Col. 0129A] Certainly so—assuredly so—whether our opponents will it or not. By whatever good exercise idleness is banished, the Rule is observed; none who does these things is rightly called a transgressor, and the accusation brought against him is to be rejected far away.

Unless works other than farming were acceptable to God, the Lord would never have said to the Jews: “Work not for the food that perishes, but for that which endures unto eternal life” (John 6). If indeed bodily works were to be preferred to spiritual exercises, Mary would never have chosen to sit at the Lord’s feet, idle from other occupations, and hear His words unceasingly; she would never have permitted her sister to serve alone; nor would the Lord have said that she had chosen the better part (Luke 10). Therefore, if the mind is occupied in praying, reading, chanting psalms, devoutly fulfilling what is enjoined, or doing any other [Col. 0129B] good works of this kind, the Rule, as we have said, is perfectly observed; for in doing these things the monk is proved not idle, but profitably occupied in all respects.

And, to put forward an example, we read that Saint Maurus, disciple of blessed Benedict himself, who was sent by him into these regions of Gaul to build monasteries according to his teaching, maintained this practice in the monastery which he had built in the diocese of Angers [Note: [Col. 0129D] “In the monastery which he had built in the diocese of Angers”: namely Glanfeuil, where Saint Maurus himself died in A.D. 582 after forty years of government. Thus the monastery is called Saint-Maur of Glanfeuil by the writer of the Cassinese Chronicle, book IV, chapter 67. Odo, monk of Fossatus, reports of it in book I, chapter 3, of *The Miracles of Blessed Maurus*, that “the venerable Count Rorigo, lest in subsequent times, perhaps through the negligence of its inhabitants, it should depart from the straight course of the regular way, obtained by a sacred writing from the most serene Emperor Louis the command of an imperial edict: namely, that the rulers of the monastery of Fossatus, always having charge of that place, should with watchful care apply the diligence of their solicitude in every respect both to the place and to the community, appointing as teachers and superiors for them brethren of their own congregation such that, by their direction and governance, all things to be accomplished there, inward and outward, might be diligently arranged.”

But when the monks of Fossatus themselves did not administer it well, Pope Urban II at last—as the aforesaid Cassinese Chronicle says, book IX, chapter 18—having “entered Gaul on [Col. 0130D] ecclesiastical business,” at the Council of Tours, where “he himself presided, freed the monastery of Saint Maurus at Glanfeuil from the tyranny of the monks of Fossatus, restored it to its former dignity and liberty, to remain forever under the direction only of the Cassinese monastery.” Later Calixtus II, “asked,” says the same Chronicle, chapter 66, “by the cardinals who had come with him into Gaul, and by the monks and Abbot Girard, solemnly dedicated the church of the same confessor of Christ, Maurus. There also he placed with the greatest reverence the bodies of Saints Antony and Constantine, who had gone from the Cassinese monastery to Gaul with blessed Maurus.” Finally, “when the possessions of that monastery were being plundered by certain persons, he wrote to the bishops of Germany, requiring them to see that what had been plundered was restored.” The aforesaid Girard, abbot of Monte Cassino, also “granted to the brothers’ wardrobe the churches of Saint Mary of Casaliplano, Saint Benedict in Petinari, Saint Nicholas in Castro, and Saint Martin, with all appurtenances of those churches.”], namely, that because all necessities were supplied to them without their own labor, they left aside manual work, applied themselves to spiritual exercises, as we have said, and were not idle; and thus, always performing good works, they observed most faithfully the Rule recently handed down to them by the saint.

If blessed Maurus had understood that he was acting contrary to the vow of his profession [Col. 0129C]—and he could in no way have been mistaken about the meaning of this matter—he would never have permitted his monks to live in this way. Moreover, if he had not feared to be a violator of his vow, and had either refused manual work out of laxity or disdained it through pride, God would never have deigned to work such great and manifold miracles through him, nor to restore life to the dead at his prayers.

Let us now proceed to the following chapter, one which ought not to be answered because it ought not to have been objected; and from it let us recognize ourselves, lest the Cistercians be offended, as transgressors above all others. But tell us, you who raise these objections: do you say this in jest or in earnest? For if in jest, a brother ought not to be mocked by a brother. If in earnest, this foolish question ought rather to be despised with silence, unless it were thought impossible to answer it.

It is objected against us that, when any guests arrive or depart, neither the abbot nor the whole congregation prostrates itself upon the ground, nor are all heads bowed before every guest; that the abbot does not give water for guests’ hands; that neither the abbot nor the entire congregation washes the feet of all guests. Those making the objection assert that monks are deprived of salvation unless they choose to observe these matters exactly as the words sound.

And O men, like boys pursuing butterflies, fighting—not against us, but beating the air—putting forward empty objections, [Col. 0130B] not following the path of discretion, the mother of virtues, and therefore straying from the straightness of the way: tell us, we pray you, shall the Cluniac congregation, or any other congregation, be judged a violator of its vow and therefore deprived of eternal salvation unless, with its abbot, it bows to every arriving or departing guest, or lies prostrate before them? Shall it be damned unless it washes the feet and hands of every guest? Then either the convent must remain continually in the guest-house, or guests must be lodged in the cloister and in the brothers’ workrooms. For they cannot otherwise fulfill what is enjoined unless they are together and remain together. The continual arrival of guests will demand continual attendance from those serving them. It will follow that those whom you want to be monks can no longer be monks; living with secular persons, [Col. 0130C] they will lose both the name and the life of monk. And while striving indiscreetly to keep this one command of the Rule, they will abandon the rest and not even attain this one.

Thus indeed—thus it will happen, thus it will come about—that monks will live together with clerics, soldiers, peasants, dependents, actors, and people of every condition, even with women, who are not excluded from the charity of hospitality. Those solitary men, those dead to the world, those to whom not even the common air was freely permitted for breathing, will again mingle with the common society of men which they had abandoned. [Col. 0131A] The multitude of arrivals is almost always so great that, if they must bow to everyone or prostrate themselves before everyone, if they must wash everyone’s hands and feet, all the brethren, as we said, would necessarily have to remain with them from sunrise to sunset and spend the whole day in prostrations (*metanoeae*) and in washing hands and feet [Note: [Col. 0131D] “Spend the whole day in *metanoeae* and in washing hands and feet.” The most distinguished Nicolas Faber, tutor of Louis XIII, the Most Christian King, explained this passage in the following note: “Here he uses *metanoea* for a genuflection, and below on the following page: ‘then, in place of the *metanoea*, we chant the Psalm.’ And in the still unpublished *Correction of the Rule of Cluny*, chapter ‘On Genuflections,’ when it says: ‘But also that genuflection which is customarily made by those who meet someone carrying the Eucharist anywhere, and those *metanoeae* which are performed in chapter in daily practice and are commonly called *veniae* [acts of pardon].’ Anastasius the Librarian also noted that the Greeks use the term μετανοίας (*metanoias*) in this sense in his translation of the Seventh Synod. It is understood in that sense at the beginning of Chrysostom’s liturgy published at Rome.”], though they could not suffice for that task even many times over throughout the entire day.

Let them therefore cease from every divine office; let them cease from keeping the other decrees of the Rule; let them abstain even from bodily refreshment. Let them take no care to celebrate Prime, Terce, Sext, None, Vespers, Compline, or Masses. Let them abandon all these things for the washing of hands and feet, and let either the Church be silent or persons be found to take the brethren’s place [Col. 0131B] in all these matters. Do not these things seem ridiculous? Would not even the senseless themselves detest such things? Would not brute animals themselves cry out that these things ought not to be done?

Nevertheless, we do what we can. Every day throughout the entire year we wash the hands and feet of three pilgrim guests, offering bread and wine, with the abbot doing this in his turn; no one is excepted except the sick, who cannot fulfill these things. Thus we fulfill as much of the Rule as we can, lest we abandon the rest for the sake of these matters. For, as the Lord says, “These things ought to be done, and those not left undone” (Luke 11). And since reason itself, even though we are silent, cries aloud and thrusts your objections far away, we must return to what we set forth above and prove from it that we preserve the Rule in its entirety. Thus, says blessed Benedict, “Let the abbot moderate and arrange everything so that souls may be saved.” He said “everything”; he excepted nothing. If therefore the abbot may moderate and arrange everything for the salvation of souls, then he was permitted so to moderate the things just mentioned that guests lacked no necessity, were received and cared for honorably, charitably, and most diligently, and that the Church of God was not deprived of its proper offices nor regular observance interrupted, even briefly [Col. 0131C].

Because the abbot does not have an inventory of the monastery’s tools and possessions, you call him proud or negligent [Note: [Col. 0131D] “Because the abbot does not have an inventory of the monastery’s tools and possessions.” *Brevis*, or *breve*, which the Greeks call πιττάκιον (*pittakion*) and βρεβίον (*brebion*), is a list or register in which something is recorded. Thus in book III, chapter 82: “That not only the benefices of bishops, [Col. 0132D] abbots, abbesses, counts, and our vassals, but also those of our fisc, be entered in an inventory.” And Saint Benedict himself, who gave the Cistercians occasion for making this objection against the Cluniacs, says in chapter 32 of the Rule: “Let the abbot provide brethren, whose life and character he can trust, for the substance of the monastery in tools, garments, or any other things; and let him assign individual things to them for keeping and collecting, as he judges useful, from which the abbot may retain an inventory.” The Cassinese explain this passage thus: “Within a month from the day of his appointment, each official shall make an inventory of the monastery’s goods belonging to his office. The superior shall retain with himself a universal inventory of all movable and immovable goods of the monastery, lest they be lost.” Hence French *brevet* and *bref*.].

Why then is it read elsewhere: “Let such deans be chosen” [Note: [Col. 0132D] “Let such deans be chosen.” Of them also, Addition 1 to chapter 55: “Let the senior dean be set over the other deans, and, when the abbot or prior is present, let him retain his proper place.”], “in whom the abbot may confidently divide his burdens”? Cannot the abbot, I ask, impose his burdens upon others and accomplish through deputies what, entangled in many and varied affairs, he cannot do by himself? Why is denied to him here what is allowed elsewhere? For, speaking of the signal for the hour of the Work of God, the Rule says: “The abbot shall have care night and day that the hour of the Work of God be signaled, either announcing it himself or entrusting this duty to such a diligent brother as is fit for it.” Why, then, should that which, as we have said, is granted him here and everywhere from necessity be denied in the chapter just cited?

We know, to be sure, that bishops could be without priests and assistants, if alone they could sufficiently provide for all that benefits their dioceses. In the same way, the abbot would have to be cellarer, [Col. 0132B] infirmarian, almoner, keeper of guests, and sole minister for all the other offices, if he were capable of attending to everything. But because it is either impossible or exceedingly difficult for one person to divide himself among all business, it is expedient that several persons do what one cannot accomplish. Thus Jethro, reproving Moses on this matter, said: “Choose for yourself men whom you know to be useful for this, and be yourself for the people in the things which concern God; leave lighter matters to them, but decide yourself the weightier matters which cannot be settled through others” (Exodus 18). Moses trusted the wise man and did so. It is fitting that our Fathers should imitate this also, committing to brethren useful for that purpose the counting or keeping of the monastery’s tools or any other possessions when they themselves have no leisure for it. Thus the Rule, rightly understood, [Col. 0132C] is observed.

Whatever the Rule commands concerning genuflections at the regular hours, we observe in every respect; and before we begin to chant the Hour, wherever we may be, we bend the knee in the fear of God. Excessive rain, deep snow, or muddy ground sometimes prevents this; then, in place of the *metanoea*, we chant the Psalm, “Have mercy upon me, O God” (Psalm 50), and by such a substitution make compensation for the command which we cannot fulfill.

[Col. 0133A] You complain that our abbot’s table is not, according to the Rule, with poor persons and pilgrims [Note: [Col. 0133D] “That our abbot’s table is not, according to the Rule, with poor persons and pilgrims.” Saint Benedict, chapter 56: “Let the abbot’s table always be with guests and pilgrims. But whenever there are fewer guests, it shall be in his power to invite such brethren as he wishes.”]; but you are justly reproved on that account. For it is always with guests and pilgrims. Does not the abbot make all those whom he feeds from the monastery’s resources sharers in his own table? And surely, by God’s grace, among us sufficient charity is shown, according to our means, to every poor person and every guest, and fitting honor is rendered to each.

But if, in your view, the Rule cannot possibly be fulfilled by us in this way, and it is asserted that the command means they must dine with the abbot, this too is sometimes done with persons of honorable rank. For we believe it improper that, in the presence of the convent, the unseemly presence of any persons whatever—not pleasing to all—should indiscreetly be introduced, and that scandal may perhaps thereby arise even among good people [Col. 0133B]. But if you object that guests should be joined to the abbot’s table not in the convent but apart from it, we answer that on this pretext abbots formerly used to separate themselves from the brethren and, under the guise of guests, indulge themselves in richer and more familiar meals, while taking no care for the feeding of their sheep. And, according to the prophet—this we say without prejudice to the mystical meaning—they took what they saw to be fat and cast away what was weak. Having drunk the clearest water, they muddied the rest with their feet, and gave the Lord’s flock turbid and muddy water to drink (Ezekiel 23): that is, they provided very well for themselves and did not care for the rest.

Because they abused a good command badly, a new plaster had to be laid upon a new wound, and the command which had once been wholesome had to be altered by a sounder counsel. Therefore, so that a vice arising from virtue might again be extinguished by virtue, when the rule had passed from the common table to the separate one, the rule of reason and charity brought it back [*reduxit*] from the separate table to the common [Col. 0133C]. Hence our abbots, unless illness prevents, always eat with us; sometimes with guests, when such guests are present, and sometimes without them. Yet they never, or hardly ever, leave the common table, while allowing guests and pilgrims to lack nothing. For these reasons we believe that we do nothing contrary to the ordinances of blessed Benedict, who, as we have often said already, permitted such commands to be adapted by the abbot according to time and persons [Col. 0133D].

The easy and fitting answer to the following chapter which you proposed is evident. Wherever brethren meet one another, the junior asks a blessing from the senior, saying *Benedicite* (“Bless [me]”), if he is outside the regular places, and bowing humbly; but if they meet within the regular workrooms, he says nothing aloud. If you say that this blessing must always be sought by speaking, let discerning persons consider whether useful silence should be imposed upon, or subordinated to, superfluous speech [Col. 0134A]. We call speech superfluous for this reason: the tongue is not necessary for something that can equally well be done in silence, and therefore we judge it superfluous [the text has *superfluam*], especially since the Rule makes no mention of any spoken words to be uttered for this salutation. And even if this were indiscriminately allowed as you wish, perhaps some persons not fully grounded in maturity would utter frivolous things as useful, jesting things as serious, and curses as blessings.
