To prevent this, we prohibit it by the discipline of silence. Thus, observing these principles, we do not depart from the Rule.

You say that the Rule commands a wise old man to be stationed at the monastery gate [Note: [Col. 0134D] “That a wise old man be stationed at the monastery gate.” These are the words of the Rule, chapter 66: “Let a wise old man be stationed at the monastery gate, one who knows how to receive and give an answer, whose maturity does not permit him to wander about. The porter ought to have his cell near the gate,” etc.], and that we do not do this. But we ask: if our porter is wise [Col. 0134B] but not old, shall we be judged guilty of violating the Rule and, for that reason, worthy of hell? What if we cannot find both old age and wisdom in the same person? Must no one be placed at the monastery gate unless he is both old in years and wise in character? And what is the meaning of Scripture’s saying: “The gray hairs of a man are understanding, and the age of old age is an unblemished life” (Wisdom 3)?

Moreover, unless this porter answers those who knock and cry out with “Thanks be to God,” or calls out a blessing, then—even if he performs every other office of humanity for arriving persons—according to you, it will avail nothing. Nor will the whole Rule, however perfectly observed in other matters, suffice for salvation unless the aforesaid doorkeeper gives out “Thanks be to God” in a loud voice [Col. 0134C]. Let reason see this, let truth see it, let lovers of truth see it, and, though we are silent, declare what they think of it.

Why, however, should we station a porter at a gate when we have no gate? Our gates are not shut during the day, but stand continually open and admit arrivals without distinction of persons. No one need knock, no one need cry out, because he finds open not only the entrance through the walls but also the entrance to lodging, and, reclining at once, finds everything prepared. But in order that the brethren may not be compelled to remain outside their own dwellings, we arrange for a wise and honorable servant to remain and sleep nearby, who, at the midday hours or those at which all the monastery doors are customarily shut, may answer those knocking [Col. 0134D] or crying out, not so much by a cry of the voice as by offering service. Certainly, in acting thus, we judge ourselves not violators but, according to our ability, keepers of the Rule.

At last, now let us come to the things you put forward with such great astonishment, declaring them contrary to all reason and authority. Let us examine those things by which, you say, those who comply with us are surrounded by inevitable peril, so that, whichever way they turn, [Col. 0135A] they cannot avoid being transgressors. You say this, surely, of those who, after once promising stability elsewhere, conversion of manners, and obedience, promise stability again in another place, conversion of manners again, and obedience again under another abbot, and so, so far as lies in them, render their former pledge void.

To this we add: since you say that you act for the Rule, why do you show yourselves to be against it? And why do you repel us from following the path of the Rule which you accuse us of not keeping? For we read thus where it treats of how wandering monks are to be received: “But if afterward,” it says, “he wishes to make his stability firm, such a wish is not to be refused.” Behold: one who, as a monk, had certainly made his stability firm elsewhere, is not forbidden, should he wish to establish it again in another place; indeed, it is commanded that such a wish not be refused. If Benedict had known him to be bound by the guilt of abandoning his first profession, it is certain he would not have praised this at all; certain that he would in no way have allowed it; certain that he would have prohibited it completely. Nor could a man so great, so learned, and so filled with the spirit of prophecy that scarcely anything could escape him, have remained unaware of fault in a matter so great and weighty. For to one for whom hidden things were manifest, manifest things could by no means become hidden [Col. 0135B].

Now, if a wandering monk is allowed to make his stability firm, so that he understands himself thereafter always to be stable in the place he has chosen and no longer permitted to wander away from it, it is likewise fitting that he promise obedience to the Father of the monastery, so that he has one to whom he must obey in Christ’s place. What harm is there in promising conversion of manners again, when he ought to promise conversion of manners and amendment of life, with repentance for past evils, not merely twice in profession but daily, countless times in confession, both to God and to men? But if, after his first promise, he may promise stability, conversion of manners, and obedience, he may also make a profession. For what else does a monk promise in profession but stability, conversion of manners, and obedience?

If this is not denied to a wandering monk, why should it not be granted to every person who comes lawfully? Nor need it be feared that by a second profession he will be judged a violator of the first, since he promises not something different but the same thing as before [Col. 0135C]. If he promised God something contrary to his former vow, or something less binding, he would without doubt be guilty. But since, as we have said, he promises the same thing as before, he does not offend in any respect; he need only take care to strive in every way to fulfill what he answers God that he will do.

But perhaps you object: How do you assert that every monk can make a second profession and can promise conversion of manners and obedience a second time, when the Rule says that not the other things but stability alone is to be made firm, and not by all monks but only by wandering monks? To this we reply: that stability can be made firm by wandering monks is proved, as you know, by the authority of the Rule. But that all other monks may make again not only stability but also conversion of manners and obedience—that is, a complete profession—we prove by reasoning drawn from the Rule’s own words. For according to the Rule it is lawful to make stability firm a second time; according to reason it is lawful to promise conversion of manners and obedience a second time. If he who promises conversion of manners and obedience a second time violates his pledge, then he likewise violates it who makes stability firm a second time. For if a subsequent vow overturns a prior one, it overturns it not in part but entirely. If, I say, [Col. 0136A] a monk must not promise conversion of manners and obedience a second time because he has already promised them to another, neither can he make stability firm a second time, because he has already established that he would be stable in another place.

But it is certain that what the Rule commands concerning the establishment of stability is right. It is therefore right that, when persons lawfully come from monastery to monastery, they profess, before the abbots of those monasteries, conversion of manners and obedience together with stability. And if wandering monks are rightly permitted to do this, it should not wrongly be denied to all others who come with permission of their own abbots [Col. 0136B].

You ask why we receive monks of a known monastery without their own abbot’s permission or letters of recommendation [Note: [Col. 0135D] “Why we receive monks of a known monastery without their own abbot’s permission.” Geoffrey, abbot of Vendôme, writing to Pons, abbot of Cluny, complains that Pons had retained a certain monk of his, Peter by name, who had come to him; he says that the Rule of Saint Benedict wholly forbids this. Epistle 2, book IV, which is included in full in this Library. Of similar argument is the first letter of Saint Bernard to his nephew Robert, who had passed from the Cistercians to the Cluniacs.], and you say that in such a matter we act contrary to brotherly charity. Yet, as we defend what we judge right, so we never wish to offer excuses that are not excusable in sins. We know that no one ought to receive another’s monk without that man’s permission, so long as he provides for him—as a true father for his son and as a good shepherd for his own sheep—all things necessary both to soul and body, namely those without which neither the soul can be saved nor the body sustained.

But if any of these things is lacking, a brother may, even against his abbot’s will, leave a place so useless—indeed so harmful and destructive—to him, avoid by every means the destruction of his soul [Col. 0136D], and seek another place in which he can fulfill what he could not fulfill before. For if an eye must be plucked out, if a hand or foot must be cut off (Matthew 18), if father, mother, wife, children, brothers, and sisters must be hated lest Christ be lost (Luke 14), then surely nothing remains to which the salvation of souls should not be preferred.

Nor can a monk be called a transgressor of his vow or profession if, leaving a place which did not allow him to fulfill his vow, he moves to one in which he can discharge that vow, so that he may say with the Prophet: “I will pay Thee my vows, which my lips have uttered” (Psalm 65) [Col. 0137A]. Rather, he would deserve blame and be judged worthy of death if, treating the loss of so great a matter as insignificant, he endured his death through foolish patience.

The Church of Cluny retains from the Apostolic See permission to receive those who come to it in such a manner [Note: [Col. 0137B] “The Church of Cluny retains from the Apostolic See permission to receive those who come to it in such a manner.” Pope Alexander II, in a diploma addressed to Saint Hugh, abbot of Cluny, says: “We also decree, and by the authority of Him whose office we discharge, though unworthy, establish, that this same place shall be to all who flee to it for salvation a bosom of mercy, a harbor of all piety and salvation. Let the righteous obtain a place there, and let no wicked person who wishes to repent be driven away. Let the innocent be shown the charity of mutual brotherhood, [Col. 0137C] and let hope of salvation and the mercy of forgiveness not be denied to offenders. If anyone seeks that same place for the sake of his humility and salvation, let him by no means be excluded from pardon and the mercy he desires, but let him be gathered in kindly and cherished with the oil of saving medicine. For it is just that in the house of piety the righteous should be shown the love of holy brotherhood, and that the medicine of forgiveness and salvation should not be denied to a sinner fleeing for pardon. Let it be for all who come there a cause of salvation, now and forever a refuge of divine compassion and piety, and a protection of apostolic blessing and absolution.”

And Urban II: “We also grant you this prerogative: that whoever, being a monk of another monastery, comes over to you for the improvement of his life, may be received freely, complaints from his former place being set aside, so that, by the Lord’s gift, he may obtain among you the result of the salvation which he appears to seek. We also grant permission to receive regular clerics, whom they call canons, who either cannot be saved in their own places or flee to your places out of necessity, and to admit them to your way of life.”]. It possesses this, however, not as a private or singular privilege, but as something common and lawful for all. Thus not only that Church but all monasteries of Christ ought to receive, retain, and cherish those who come in this manner.

You add to these points, and magnify with much invective, the assertion that we refuse to have our own bishop. We answer that this objection stands in direct opposition to the truth, since it is evident that we do have our own bishop [Col. 0137B]. For what bishop can be found more right, more true, or more worthy than the Bishop of Rome? Is he not the one whom divine, not human, authority has ordained to preside over the rest? Is he not the one to whom it was said: “When thou art converted, strengthen thy brethren” (Luke 22)? Is he not the one to whom it was said: “I will give unto thee the keys of the kingdom of heaven; and whatsoever thou shalt bind upon earth shall be bound also in heaven, and whatsoever thou shalt loose upon earth shall be loosed also in heaven” (Matthew 16)?

We glory in having this one, sole, and greatest bishop; to him alone we owe special obedience; from him alone, if cause required it—God forbid—we could be interdicted, suspended, and excommunicated. The irrefragable authority of that holy See itself has decreed this; and the decrees are preserved in our mother Church not of one pope only but of many. They established these things not in order to remove the Church of Cluny of which we speak from another bishop who had previously possessed it, but, being asked by its founders, who had built it upon their own allodial estate [Col. 0138B] [Note: [Col. 0137D] “By its founders, who had built it upon their own allodial estate”: namely William, duke of the Aquitanians, and his wife Ingelberga, concerning whom we have already dealt with the charters of the foundation itself.], they retained it as their own and decreed that it should be subject forever to the Roman pontiff alone, confirming this by many privileges [Note: [Col. 0137D]

“And decreeing that it should be subject forever to the Roman pontiff alone, they confirmed this by many privileges.” We have also treated this at length elsewhere, and the following rescript of Pope Gregory VII demonstrates it still more clearly and plainly.

**The exemption of the monastery of Cluny, decreed by Pope Gregory VII at Rome in the year 1077.**]

“Lord and most blessed Pope Gregory VII, in the seventh year of his pontificate, was holding a general council in the Lateran basilica, also called the Constantinian basilica, in honour of the Saviour and of blessed John the Baptist. Having imposed silence on all, he rose and said:

[Col. 0138B] ‘Know, brothers and our fellow priests—indeed, let this whole holy synod recognize and understand—that beyond the mountains there are many monasteries nobly and religiously founded in honour of Almighty God and of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul. Yet among them all there is one in those regions which is regarded as adhering, by a special right, almost as the peculiar and proper possession of blessed Peter and of this Church: namely Cluny. From its very beginnings it was principally assigned to the honour and protection of this holy and apostolic see; and, by the favour of divine mercy, [Col. 0138C] under religious and holy abbots it has attained such a height of dignity and religious devotion that, so far as I know, it surpasses other monasteries—even many of greater antiquity—in God’s service and spiritual fervour, and there is none in that land, so far as I know, which can in any respect be compared with it.

‘For there has never been an abbot there who was not holy. Moreover, the abbots and monks of this Church have always proved in no way degenerate sons; they have not bent their knees before Baal or the Baals. Rather, imitating the liberty and dignity of this holy Roman see, which they derived from the beginning, they have nobly preserved for themselves its authority through the succession of generations. They have never submitted their necks to any foreign or earthly power, but have remained in subjection to and under the protection of blessed Peter and this Church alone.

‘Therefore we will, and by apostolic authority confirm and prohibit, that no person whatsoever, small or great, nor any power—not archbishop, not bishop, no king, duke, margrave, prince, count, nor [Col. 0138D] even any legate of mine—shall ever open his mouth over that place and monastery, or exercise any authority over it. Rather, according to the tenor of our privilege, the authority of our predecessors, and the immunity of liberty granted it by this see, let it possess that liberty wholly and perpetually; and let it breathe, under apostolic wings alone, free from every heat and storm of attack, and rest most sweetly for ever in the bosom of this holy mother Church, to the honour of Almighty God and of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul.’

“And then the lord pope, turning to the right-hand side of the synodal assembly, questioned them, saying: ‘Does this please you? Do you approve it?’ They answered: ‘It pleases us; we approve it.’ Turning again to the left, he asked in the same manner. The holy assembly made the same reply: ‘It pleases us; we approve it.’ After these words, having spoken while standing upon the pontifical throne, the lord pope sat down.”

By his command, moreover—because, being so very far from him, [Col. 0139A] we cannot receive these things from him—we receive chrism from any Catholic bishop [Note: [Col. 0139C] “Chrism from any Catholic bishop.” Paschal II, in a letter written to Pontius, abbot of Cluny, says: “If necessity requires it, have chrism consecrated in your monastery, or receive it from whichever bishops you wish.”], oil, holy orders [Note: [Col. 0139C] “Holy orders.” Urban II to Hugh: “We decree that no bishop, nor any priests whatsoever, may presume to come to act in that venerable monastery, or indeed in any place subject to it, for an ordination or consecration of priests or deacons, or for the celebration of Mass, unless he has been invited by the abbot of that monastery or by priors subject to that monastery. But let your monks, wherever they are placed, be permitted to receive whatever grade of ordination they wish, wherever it shall please you, them, and your successors.” Paschal II likewise: “We also decree that this liberty shall be firmly maintained for the monastery of Cluny: that monks of your monastery who are to be [Col. 0139D] promoted to holy orders may be promoted by whichever bishops you prefer.”

Indeed, an even greater prerogative was granted by Pope Urban himself, the fifth of that name, to Simon, abbot of Cluny, and his successors: the privilege of conferring the first clerical tonsure. This was in the fifth year of his pontificate, namely A.D. 1366, by this diploma:

“Urban, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Simon, abbot of the monastery of Cluny, which belongs to the Roman Church without intermediary, in the diocese of Mâcon: greetings and apostolic blessing. The sincerity of manifest devotion and the honourableness of religion deserve that we favourably [grant] your petitions, especially those concerning the prerogative and honours of your own estate and of the monastery of Cluny, belonging to the Roman Church without intermediary, in the diocese of Mâcon. [Col. 0140C] Therefore, inclining to your supplications in this matter, we grant by apostolic authority and by the tenor of these present letters to you and to your successors, the abbots of the said monastery for the time being, that both in that monastery and in the priories, churches, and places immediately subject to you and to the same monastery, provided that they lie within the bounds of the exemption of that monastery, you may confer the first clerical tonsure upon each and every scholar born in such places who wishes to be marked with the clerical character—any apostolic constitutions or other contrary provisions whatsoever notwithstanding. Therefore let no person at all be permitted to infringe this page of our concession or rashly oppose it. Should anyone presume to attempt this, let him know that he will incur the indignation of Almighty God and of his blessed apostles Peter and Paul. Given at Avignon, on the Kalends of April, in the fifth year of our pontificate.”], consecrations of churches and cemeteries [Note: [Col. 0140D] “Consecrations of churches and cemeteries.” Calixtus II to Pontius: “If the diocesan bishops refuse freely to perform the consecrations of your churches, you shall receive them from any Catholic bishop.” Honorius II likewise, to Peter the Venerable himself: “Let the brethren of your places receive consecrations of churches or altars from the bishops in whose dioceses those places lie, provided that they are willing to perform them freely and without improper exaction. Otherwise, let them receive the sacraments of those consecrations from whichever Catholic bishop they prefer.”], and other such things. We obey the apostolic see, to which it would be wicked not to obey, both in these matters and in all others; and therefore we do not violate the rule either of monks or of Christians, as you say that we do.

But if you still persist and maintain that we act wrongly, attack him whom we invoke, and, leaving us aside, deal with him about these matters. Since we ought not to oppose him, we choose to obey; nor shall we ever presume to judge his judgment—a thing permitted to no mortal person. This is not a privilege of Cluny alone: we see that it has been granted to very many others, and that, long before Cluny was founded, the same apostolic see had conferred it upon many other monasteries. The bishops of that see were men of great wisdom and religious devotion, and the merits of some of them shone solemnly throughout the world also in the radiance of miracles. It is incredible either that they could have been deceived in such matters or that they should have wished to act thus against their consciences.

For with the same mind and intention with which the popes of our own times, providing for the peace of monks, bestowed the things we have mentioned upon very many monasteries, the more ancient bishops of the Roman Church likewise decreed, for the same reason, that many monasteries should be free from the yoke of bishops. Thus blessed Gregory says in a letter to Castorius, bishop of Rimini:

“Luminosus the abbot reports that in very many monasteries monks have suffered many injuries and burdens from bishops. Therefore the foresight of your brotherhood must provide by a salutary ordinance for their future peace, so that those dwelling in them may persevere with free minds in God’s service, through the assistance of his grace. [Col. 0139C] We also altogether forbid public Masses to be held in the monastery, lest any occasion for a popular gathering be afforded in the retreats and dwelling places of God’s servants, because this is not beneficial to their souls. Nor may a bishop dare to place his chair there, exercise any authority of command, or perform any ordination, however slight, unless requested by the abbot, so that the monks may always remain under the authority of their abbots and, all vexations and burdens being removed, may carry out the divine office with the fullest devotion of mind.”

Again, elsewhere he says: “Let the bishop of the city visit the monastery whenever he pleases, for the sake of visitation and exhortation. But let the bishop fulfil there the office of charity in such a way that the monastery suffers no burden.” And elsewhere:

“How necessary it is to provide for the peace of monasteries and to take thought for their perpetual security is taught us by the former office which we exercised in the government of a monastery. And because we know that monks in very many monasteries have suffered many injuries and burdens from bishops, the foresight of our brotherhood must provide by a salutary ordinance for their future peace, so that those dwelling in them may persevere with free minds in God’s service, through the assistance of his grace. But lest, under the custom which ought rather to be corrected, anyone should presume to inflict any trouble upon the monks, it is necessary that the matters which we have taken care to enumerate below be observed with such diligence by our brother bishops that no occasion may thereafter be found for [Col. 0140C] inflicting disturbance. Therefore, in the name of our Lord Jesus Christ, and by the authority of blessed Peter, prince of the apostles, [Col. 0141A] in whose stead we preside over this Roman Church, we forbid any bishop or secular person henceforth to presume, in any manner or upon any pretext, to diminish the revenues, property, or charters of monasteries, or their dependent houses or villages, or to employ any fraud or make any encroachment against them.”

Therefore, if they were permitted, on this account, to enact what was not found decreed in the earlier canons, then plainly these men too were permitted, for the same reason, to decree and establish the matters for which you attack us: namely, that, as the former freed monks from episcopal oppression in part, so the latter should free them wholly, because they judged this expedient. For all the authority possessed by the most ancient and earliest men they transmitted in its entirety to the most recent and latest. Who, then, would dare judge that what the Church of God is known to have held valid through so many ages [Col. 0141B] under so many and such great Fathers ought to be made void, unless he judges himself, in the swelling spirit of pride, better than the holy Fathers? So much on this point.

Then you add this question: by what reason or authority have the possessions of parish churches, first-fruits, and tithes been conferred upon us, [Note: [Col. 0141D] “By what reason or authority have the possessions of parish churches, first-fruits, and tithes been conferred upon us?” Agapetus II, Roman pontiff, writing to Aymard III, abbot of Cluny, says: “We restore to you in full the tithes which formerly belonged to your chapels and have been taken away by some bishop under a kind of modern authority or licence. We permit any chapels already built there, or yet to be built, to remain in such a manner that nothing is diminished from the tithes of your churches.” The same was granted—or rather confirmed—by Urban II, Paschal II, Calixtus II, Honorius II, Innocent II, Eugenius III, and others, whose diplomas we have already transcribed in full in various places in this Library. Indeed, certain kings of France did so as well, such as Louis IV “from Overseas.” His decree concerning Salustriac and other places belonging to the monastery of Cluny contains these words: “Let them have their demesne tithes for the Hospital. Let them hold and possess their churches with all tithes, as they acquired them by Roman privilege and by the writings of bishops.”], since these belong by canonical enactment not to monks but to clerics.

Yet, as in the matters stated above, so also in these, we invoke the authority of the Catholic Church; and by its enactments we affirm that we lawfully possess parish churches and consequently their first-fruits and tithes. For if no inheritance was given to the tribe of Levi among its brothers, in order that its members might be freer for the worship of God and the divine mysteries [Col. 0141C] and might not be recalled from them by secular hindrances, and if for that reason they were supported by the first-fruits, tithes, and offerings of others, then these same things are rightly granted to monks, who, like that tribe, have been deprived of an inheritance of temporal things and devote themselves day and night to divine services.

For who more justly receives the offerings of the faithful: monks, who constantly intercede for the sins of those who offer them, or clerics, who, as we now see, zealously seek temporal things and wholly set aside spiritual concerns and all that pertains to the salvation of souls? And how shall those who do not care for their own souls strive to save the souls of others? He who cannot relieve his own sickness will certainly treat another badly. And, as the Lord says: “If a blind man leads a blind man, both will fall into a pit” (Matt. 15). We say this while preserving the understanding by which we know that the Church is indeed saved in its divine mysteries through the ministry of clerics, but is little aided by the prayers of certain such persons.

Since, therefore, monks are for the most part watchful for the salvation of the faithful, though they do not themselves administer the sacraments, we judge that they may worthily receive first-fruits, tithes, offerings, and whatever benefices, since they arrange for the remaining things necessary to the Christian people to be supplied by priests and clerics. In saying this, we do not at all wish to exclude clerics from the possession of churches and ecclesiastical property; rather, by these reasons and authorities, we establish that monks too may lawfully possess all these things. For if clerics wish to live from ecclesiastical revenues on account of the office of baptism, penance, preaching, and the other sacraments provided to the people, why should monks not use ecclesiastical property and the offerings of the devout on account of prayers, [Col. 0142B] psalms, tears, almsgiving, and manifold good works offered to God for the salvation of the people?

And lest these things appear to be imagined by our own reasoning rather than strengthened by the authority of the canons, let us bring forward the words of those same canons. They say: “If a bishop wishes to dedicate one of his parish churches as a monastery, so that a regular congregation of monks may live in it, he has permission to do this with the consent of his council” (can. XII, q. 2, *Si ep.*). Again: “Since it is clearly established by earlier enactments what portion of the goods of parish churches is to be assigned to the bishop, we have nevertheless judged it fitting to decree that if a bishop determines to confer the third part which he knows is due to him by enactment from those same goods either upon the church whose goods they are shown to be or upon another church of his choosing, his decision shall remain lawful and shall have irrevocable force.”

In this final chapter, although it says that a bishop may give his own portion to any church, it does not deny that he may do the same with the whole. The authority written above fully demonstrates this. Therefore, according to these and similar authorities—which we decline to set down here because of their length—we freely, justly, and canonically possess churches and all their goods, conferred upon us by bishops without purchase.

After this, you advance certain strange and unheard-of charges against us, so that we are compelled first to be astonished rather than to answer. For you blame us and say that we differ in no respect from secular people because we possess castles, villages, peasants, male and female slaves [Note: [Col. 0142D] “We possess castles, villages, peasants, male and female slaves.” The same Louis, in the aforementioned royal decree: [Col. 0143D] “Let no one coerce their free persons or slaves without their consent. Let them hold and possess inviolate the estates which they acquired through the decrees of our predecessors or of other kings.” [Col. 0144D] And Agapetus: “Furthermore, we strengthen by apostolic authority all the villages belonging to the same monastery of Cluny,” etc.], and—what is worse—receive indiscriminately the profits of tolls and nearly all emoluments of this kind; we hold them unlawfully and defend them by every means against those who attack us.

You add that, for this reason, setting religious purpose aside, we take up the office of legal advocates: we are accused and accuse others; we produce witnesses from among ourselves; we take part in judgments contrary to the Apostle; and therefore we cannot be fit for the kingdom of heaven. It would have been appropriate, however, for you who have advanced these claims to establish their truth not merely by bare words, which move us little, but by the authority of Scripture, to which we are compelled to yield. For the law rightly requires that one who attacks another prove what he alleges, since proof always lies upon the plaintiff.

Yet here we shall act contrary to this judicial custom, and, sparing you—whom we know cannot prove your own assertions—we shall establish ours as follows. We know that “the earth is the Lord’s and its fullness, the world and all who dwell in it” (Ps. 23). But elsewhere in the same Psalms we read: “The heaven of heavens belongs to the Lord, but he gave the earth to the children of men” (Ps. 113). It is therefore clear that heaven and earth belong to the Lord, but that he gave the earth to human beings for a time, so that, if they made good use of it, they might deserve heaven after earth, and that things which were his by power might become humanity’s by his kindness.

By this most merciful kindness and most gracious compassion, although he measures the mass of the earth with three fingers and weighs the mountains in scales and the hills in a balance (Isa. 11), he nevertheless receives back that same earth and earthly gifts from the very people to whom he gave them; and, so to speak, he permits the heavenly kingdom to be bought at his own expense. He seeks in this no gain for himself but the salvation of human beings, and embraces it as his own profit. Thus, when he commands that food be given to the hungry and drink to the [thirsty], he first creates bread in the fields, wine on the vines, fruit upon trees, and offspring in animals. The very water with which, when it fills a cup and is given to one in need, he declares a reward to be laid up (Matt. 10), he causes to rise from springs and flow through rivers everywhere. Finally, he himself first gives to the givers all the things for which he rewards their good will.

Accordingly, the Church of God, by authority drawn from both the Old and the New Testament, receives all things offered not to itself but to God, in his stead; and from them it charitably supports those of its own who need such things and possess nothing of their own in the world—namely clerics and monks, poor persons, or whomever it knows to suffer need of these resources. Hence monks—for we are now speaking only of them—receive all offerings of the faithful, whether movable or immovable, and repay their benefactors by the devotion of prayers, fasts, and other good works.

[Col. 0144A] But since we are at present accused concerning the reception of immovable property, let us answer concerning that matter now. First we invoke the Rule. For, treating of the reception of novices, it says: “If he has any property, let him first distribute it to the poor, or, having made a solemn donation, let him confer it upon the monastery.” By saying, “if he has any property,” it excludes no kind of property. If it excludes no property, it excludes neither an estate, village, peasants, male slaves, female slaves, nor anything of that kind. But it is clear that nothing is excluded. It is therefore evident that the things we have mentioned are not excluded.

The statements of blessed Gregory set out above accord with this ordinance of the Rule. In them he forbids any bishop or secular person to presume, by whatever method or pretext, to diminish the revenues, property, or charters of monasteries, or their dependent houses or villages, or to employ fraud or make any encroachment against them. For by forbidding anyone to diminish these things or make frauds or encroachments in them, he shows most clearly that monks may lawfully possess revenues, property, dependent houses, and villages. He would by no means forbid them to be troubled regarding such things if he knew that they held them unjustly.

Since the land has many kinds of revenue, since the diversity of different things is shown to be varied, and since villages cannot exist without inhabitants—men and women of differing legal condition—and since no specification of an exception is found in these statements of blessed Gregory, it is plainly shown, without any exception, that monks may rightly possess every kind of revenue, every kind of property, every kind of village, and inhabitants of differing condition alike—that is, free or servile.

But perhaps you object that, without the aid of all these possessions, monks ought to provide their necessities from their own labour and farming. We believe no one can fail to see how improper and impossible this is. To show first that it is impossible: how can a weak people, nourished on vegetables and legumes, which give almost no bodily strength—indeed, scarcely sustain life itself—and thereby greatly enfeebled, endure the harsh labour of agriculture, which is severe even for peasants and ox-drivers, and suffer such hard breaking and turning of the soil, accompanied sometimes by burning heat and sometimes by the violence of rain, snow, and cold? And how can those who, for the sake of abstinence, often deny even cheap and meagre food to themselves endure the harshness and constancy of so great a labour? Even if they could bear all this by bodily strength, when, without the help of others, could they sufficiently provide for themselves the necessities of food and clothing?

After demonstrating its impossibility, let us show also its impropriety. Does it not seem improper—indeed, most improper—that brothers commanded constantly to remain in the cloister and to devote their most earnest efforts to silence, prayer, reading, meditation, the other precepts of the Rule, and the services of the Church should abandon all these and apply themselves to rural and common labours? They ought, like the fine linen of the tabernacle, to adorn their inner selves with preciousness and fineness—that is, by subtle contemplation of heavenly things; instead, like the coarse haircloth placed outside, they would endure the force of winds, flooding rains, and every disturbance of the air—that is, the excessive occupations of worldly work, dragging them outward from their inner life.

Since this is proved, as we have said, both improper and impossible, you must necessarily permit monks other resources by which they can devote themselves to their order without great want. If you do not choose to permit them, we shall hold them by permission of the authority of the saints. You have indeed heard above that blessed Gregory granted these things to monks; hear now that he also gave them. For thus we read in his Life: “When Gregory acquired free authority to dispose of his property, he built six monasteries in Sicily and endowed them with a sufficient number of brethren. He gave them so much landed property as could provide, without want, for the daily sustenance of those serving God there.”

Likewise we read of blessed Maurus: “On the following day, blessed Maurus went out to inspect and receive the estate which that king had bestowed upon the monastery itself.” And elsewhere: “At the same time Clothar, coming from Angers, sent word to the man of God that he wished to go to the monastery. When the man of God sent back word that he should come, he set out, taking a few men with him. When he arrived, he granted to that place the royal estate called Blazon. He also assigned there by royal authority the village called Longuscampanus.”

We find that blessed Columbanus possessed almost all the things which you disapprove of monks possessing; so did many other holy monks, whose merits God demonstrated by many and great miracles and whose memory the Church solemnly observes.

And, to add some further reasoning to what we have set out: who would not judge it more right, better, and more beneficial that all the matters individually listed above should be possessed by those whom their assumed order and religious profession compel lawfully to possess them, rather than by those who, through negligence and the security of a less exacting purpose, not only disdain to govern them beneficially, but even destroy themselves by an unsuitable attachment to such things and heedless management of them? For as long as they are held by secular people—as we see in almost every case—they are administered in a secular fashion. But once ownership of them (eorum [earum]) passes to religious persons, if those persons are religious not merely in name but in actual effect, then they are certainly dealt with religiously by religious persons.

To give particular examples: if a castle is given to monks, it ceases to be a castle and begins to be an oratory. No one thereafter fights from it in bodily battle against bodily enemies, but men are accustomed to repel spiritual enemies with spiritual weapons. Thus what had formerly served the devil begins to serve Christ, and what had formerly been a den of robbers becomes a house of prayer.

We can offer the same reasoning regarding peasants, male slaves, and female slaves, by which we most fully establish that monks can lawfully possess these as well. For all know how secular lords rule over peasants, male slaves, and female slaves. They are not satisfied with their customary and due service; they mercilessly claim for themselves both their goods with their persons and their persons with their goods. Hence, besides customary dues, three or four times a year—or whenever they wish—they plunder their property, oppress them with countless services, and impose heavy and unbearable burdens. They often compel them to abandon even their own land and flee to foreign places; and, what is worse, they do not fear to sell for so cheap a price—that is, money—the very persons whom Christ redeemed at so dear a price, that is, with his own blood.

Monks, however, though they have such persons, do not have them in the same way but in a very different way. They use only the lawful and due services of peasants for the support of life; they harass them with no exactions and impose nothing unbearable. If they see them in want, they support them even from their own resources. They regard male and female slaves not as slaves but as brothers and sisters; accepting from them such distinct services as circumstances permit, they suffer them to incur no burden. Thus, according to the apostolic precept, they are “as having nothing, yet possessing all things” (1 Cor. 6).

Therefore, by the authorities and reasons set out above, it is now clear, we believe, even to the blind, that monks may possess the things mentioned above not only justly, but more justly than laymen. Why, however, are we forbidden to possess toll revenues, when the rulers of the world are found to hold them lawfully? Do they not appear lawfully to hold what the Apostle commands their subjects to render them, saying: “To whom tribute, tribute; to whom tax, tax” (Rom. 13)? What is done throughout the world and is not reproved by the Church of God, which permits nothing unjust, seems to us unquestionably lawful. No one is excommunicated for it, nor is anyone summoned to account on that ground.

Since rulers themselves hold these things without anyone’s objection, just as they hold their other rightful possessions, why should they not similarly bestow them upon God’s churches and monasteries? Why should monks not rightly receive these, as they do other things, from them? If, however, you cite blessed Matthew, called by the Lord from the toll-house, and say that he did not return afterward to it, as to an unjust occupation: Peter and the other apostles, skilled fishermen and likewise called by the Lord, are nevertheless found afterward to have fished; and by this they proved fishing to be lawful. We answer that this gives no support at all to your side and weakens ours in no respect, because we defend not the violent exactions which Matthew abandoned, but the just customary dues which the Church receives.

To all this you add that monks are legal advocates. You have thus advanced three objections, and have forbidden them to become accusers, witnesses, and judges. Let us examine each of these three separately and investigate carefully whether the matter stands as you say.

What law or reason forbids monks to be accusers, or plaintiffs, in their own cases? For if you grant monks the matters stated above, you must necessarily grant this as well. If possession of worldly goods comes first, an action against those who attack the possessors must follow. Otherwise, if they choose to abandon their property to slanderers and invaders, they will immediately cease to be possessors. And if they do this, they will immediately incur the offence of God the giver, because, by leaving in silence and failing to resist invaders, they do not fear to take from him those things which belonged by right to him.

To prevent this from happening—to prevent the Church of God, which possesses justly, from losing its property to wicked plunderers; to prevent God’s servants, after losing their own possessions, from falling into want and thereby becoming unable to serve God—it is permissible for monks honourably, simply, and religiously, without litigation, to lay before the avenging authority the wrongs they suffer in their own cases; and to seek, as befits monks, not vengeance upon their adversary, but recovery of what their adversary has taken from them.

If you say that, according to canonical institutions, monks ought to conduct their cases through advocates, we do not oppose that authority, provided that advocates can always be available through whom their cases may be well defended, so far as justice permits. But if, because of certain hindering circumstances—for these often occur—they cannot obtain advocates, it seems that monks ought first to act in the matter themselves rather than that we should allow ecclesiastical property to be lost.

And who could forbid monks to be witnesses of truth, when we see countless saints of God so steadfastly bear witness to truth that neither death nor any bodily torture could impose silence upon them? Hence they deserved the name of martyrs, that is, witnesses. We read that John the Baptist came “to bear witness to the light” (John 1); we hear the Lord himself say in the Gospel: “If I bear witness concerning myself, the Father who sent me also bears witness concerning me” (John 5); and of the Holy Spirit: “When the Paraclete comes, he will bear witness concerning me” (John 15); and of the apostles: “You also shall bear witness” (ibid.). We have cited these passages to show that monks ought not to conceal truth but, according to what circumstances and times require, ought to testify to it, because, as one of the wise men long ago said, it is not right to lie and conceal the truth.

Why also should they be excluded from judgments, when the Apostle says: “Do you not know that we shall judge angels? How much more, then, worldly things?” (1 Cor. 6). And as he says elsewhere: “The spiritual person judges all things, and is judged by no one” (1 Cor. 2). By all these authorities and reasons, therefore, we annul the objections you have made; we establish what we hold; [Col. 0148A] but we do not wish to condemn what you hold, although in certain respects we could do so.

Yet your charity ought to recall that the divine commandments are in part changeable and in part unchangeable. By divine commandments we mean not only those which the Godhead itself, appearing to human beings in the flesh, delivered, or those which it established to be observed through the apostles, or those which before assuming flesh it commanded through the patriarchs or prophets; but also those which, after the apostles, apostolic men following in the apostles’ footsteps commanded to be observed by the unanimous consent of many Catholics. For the same divine Spirit, which, pouring itself into the hearts of the earlier Fathers, gave through them commandments suited to human salvation, has not ceased, through these men also who seem more recent, to work for human salvation by enjoining what is salutary. Therefore we venerate the Lord’s words published through diverse heralds; in diverse instruments we recognize the breath of the same Spirit. Of these commandments, then, as we have said, some are changed according to the circumstances of causes and times; others permit themselves to be changed for no reason whatever.

And, so that we may begin with what we placed last in making the division, since it is more worthy, we say that among the unchangeable commandments are—since it would take too long to gather them all—that greatest and first commandment of the love of God, and the second, like it, concerning love of neighbour; likewise the precepts of humility, chastity, and truth. Although there are many others like these, we believe that these suffice to make clear what we intend. For these are found never to have been changed for any reason or by any dispensation. What Catholic Father ever commanded that God should not be loved with the whole heart, the whole soul, and the whole mind, or took away anything, however small, from this commandment? Who denied that one’s neighbour ought to be loved by oneself as oneself? Who ever allowed anyone to be proud even in the slightest degree? Who ever permitted fornication, lying, theft, or coveting one’s neighbour’s property? It is evident, therefore, that these and many such things are altogether unchangeable.

Among those things, however, which may be changed by dispensation, following the authority of the Fathers, we place those of which we find most in the ecclesiastical canons: things which, just as they were devised when they did not exist for the common benefit of the whole Church or the particular benefit of some one Church, so in turn have been altered, charity taking precedence in all things, for the common salvation of the whole Church or the particular salvation of some people, nation, or Church. And since not even these can all easily be enumerated, let those suffice which we set out in the earlier part of this little work. Since we have already written them, we decline to write them again. Whoever wishes to know them will find them written there.

Let readers understand that we state this in order to show that those decrees of the Rule which you say we transgress must be placed among the things we call changeable, and therefore, when charity commands it—to which obedience is due in all things—they may be altered without fear of transgressing them. For what compelled the alteration of the Rule concerning bishops not being transferred, handed down by the earlier Fathers, except charity, providing more wisely for the Churches? What set heretics and criminals over the Churches of God, after a fitting penitence for their crimes, though the first Fathers had forbidden it, except charity, having regard for the salvation of many? What at times ordered the sons of priests to be made bishops, contrary to the ancient decrees of the holy apostles, except charity, judging that the usefulness of those very persons was useful to the Church? What permitted marriages to the English while forbidding them to others, except charity fearing for their newly embraced faith? What altered many ancient precepts in this manner, instituted new ones, and commanded now these things and now those, except charity, diligently serving human salvation according to manners, times, and places—sometimes generally, sometimes specially?

Since, therefore, all canonical commands, indeed the entire Law and the Prophets according to the Lord’s declaration, are contained under the rule of charity, who among you would dare to say that the Rule of blessed Benedict is not subject to the dominion of charity? How is the Rule not subject to charity, when it was composed through that holy man by charity? For if it was composed without charity, it was composed without God. The apostle John says that God is charity: “God is charity” (1 John 4). And if it was made without God, it follows that it is now nothing; for God, Christ, says: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15). If it is error to believe this, it follows that the Rule must yield to charity as to its teacher and allow itself to be governed according to the will of its ruler. For if it claims anything for itself apart from charity, it will no longer benefit those who follow it.

But perhaps you still return to your earlier point and say: “Because you vowed to observe the Rule of blessed Benedict, you ought to fulfil your vows.” To this we reply: if you repeat this a thousand times, you will receive from us the same answer a thousand times. We vowed the Rule; we did not exclude charity from the vow. If we excluded charity, what we vowed cannot be called a Rule. For if the rectitude of the Rule is lacking, the Rule can no longer stand. But charity is the rectitude of the Rule. Therefore, if charity is excluded, rectitude is excluded; if rectitude is excluded, crookedness follows; and if crookedness follows, the Rule must necessarily be destroyed. Straightness and distortion cannot exist together. Once the Rule is destroyed, judge what you profess to follow. You must follow either the Rule with rectitude, or crookedness without rectitude: that is, you must retain either the Rule with charity or the Rule without charity. But as it is impossible to hold a cloud, so it is plain that no one can observe the Rule without charity. Hence it is clear that when, not with the feigned charity condemned by the Apostle but with the true charity which he famously praises (1 Corinthians 13), we bestow something upon our neighbour, we follow the Rule of blessed Benedict without any error; for to think otherwise about it is nothing other than error. Thus we neither vow the Rule without charity nor, as this reasoning proves, hold it without charity. We do hold the Rule; indeed, we hold it on this very ground, even in all those matters on account of which, throughout your invective, you said that we transgress it.

Although above we answered each point of that invective separately, we now answer generally: in receiving novices before a year has elapsed, we observe the Rule very well, because we provide through charity lest Satan be allowed to draw back to the world—or rather to destruction—those who come to God with fervour of spirit. Therefore we do not wish to give his temptations a long time, nor do we allow the struggle to be prolonged, because it is dangerous for the weak to grapple with the strong, the unwary with the deceitful: for a man standing on earth to grapple with him who is said to draw a third part of the stars of heaven down to earth; for an earthen vessel to contend with him who tried to resist the unconquered Godhead itself, first in heaven and afterwards on earth, and who will swiftly crush it unless God helps. Therefore we seek to snatch food from his mouth and, according to Job, to “break the jaws of the wicked and tear the prey from his teeth” (Job 29).

And because, as we have said, we do this through charity, we are in no respect opposed to the Rule composed through charity and seeking the salvation of souls alone, in whatever way—not in one way only, as you maintain. For we too, when we see it expedient, gladly use your one method: that is, we wait a full year before receiving a novice. At other times, after half a year, we join him to the other brothers. Very often we wait not merely a month or a week, but not even two days. Yet we never delay doing what we judge more beneficial for souls. Thus, following charity, we follow the Rule and obey God.

The same Rule of charity clothes us in furs so that the body may be protected from cold and the soul from murmuring. Nevertheless, the command concerning clothing given in this chapter of the Rule itself, received simply as it stands, suffices for us to possess garments of this sort. Since we believe that we have already fully shown this above, we decline to repeat it now. Charity—often to be mentioned—taking thought for necessity and decency, which forbids nothing necessary and embraces all that is decent, has also permitted us to have drawers. Hence we know that we possess them according to the Rule. If, from necessity, anything has been added beneath or placed upon the bedding of our beds, it is certainly from charity; and therefore it cannot truthfully be called non-regular. For, as we have always said above, we utterly detest superfluities of every kind, declare them contrary to the Rule, and profess that they must be completely cut away. Far be it from anyone to suspect that we wish to draw the mire of vices from charity, the purest source of all virtues; for, according to the Apostle, charity “does not think evil, does not rejoice over iniquity, but rejoices together with the truth” (1 Corinthians 13). And because it “bears all things and endures all things” (ibid.), let those consider whether they possess it who cannot bear not only the malice of evil people, but not even the need of their brothers, and who, though able, refuse to relieve it by supplying necessities.

[Col. 0151A] With this same shield of charity we fortify ourselves against the blows of our assailants in all the following chapters—a shield surely of such solidity and strength that it cannot be pierced by any assault of attackers, however powerful. We hold it up also against the objection concerning cooked dishes; and with it we defend ourselves well if a moderate and necessary addition is made in view of infirmities and differing conditions. We use it in the repeated reception of fugitives, lest, if they are not received, they return to the husks of swine and, consumed by hunger, perish miserably from that which the Gospel’s fugitive escaped when he found his father merciful. Protected by it, we rest from manual labour, placing better works before it; for, to say nothing of the manifold exercise of spiritual works, no one except a madman would deny that it is better to pray than to cut down a tree. The Apostle bears witness when he says: “Bodily exercise is useful for a little, but godliness is useful for all things” (1 Timothy 4).

Hence we do not wash the feet of every guest who arrives, nor do we prostrate ourselves before everyone, because we do not wish to burden with an unsuitable washing of feet those whom charity commands us to gladden in all things. Nor would the number of brothers generally suffice for the multitude of guests, if they had to wash the feet and hands of all without detriment to the remaining commandments. Since this is altered through charity, it is sometimes done among us and sometimes not done; it is not therefore irregular. But why, by going through everything said above, should we perhaps create tedium for the reader? So too concerning fasts, the abbot’s table with guests and travellers, tools or the possessions of the monastery—in short, concerning all the matters objected to above, to which we answered more fully then—charity has made provision through our Fathers as it saw fit for times, customs, and places; and in these things it strove to serve not human wills or pleasures, but their eternal salvation.

You can show that the things which we defend as just are unjust on this one ground alone; on this one ground you will compel us, defeated, to yield to you as victors: if by certain arguments you demonstrate that what we defend for ourselves by the law of charity does not belong to charity. For in all these things, as we have often said, protected by charity alone, we remain secure and invincible against all enemies. For since, according to the Lord, this is that “on which all the Law and the Prophets hang” (Matthew 22), and, according to the Apostle, it is “the fulfilment of the law and the end of the commandment” (Romans 13), who would dare, with a Catholic understanding, to deny that, under its governance, every law exists fulfilled and every commandment completed—that is, perfected?

But perhaps you reply: “You say that you have altered the Rule through charity, as though you meant to affirm that it was composed by that saint without charity. If you think this, it is certain that you err. How could one who was filled with the spirit of all the righteous lack charity when composing the Rule? But if you refuse to think and say this, why do you strive to alter what had been instituted through charity by so great a man? Or perhaps you judge your charity to be preferable to his? Do you think that you can surpass in keenness of sight and foresight that eye which, in a single moment, could behold the whole world gathered together? Therefore, if, as we have said, the saint could by no means compose the Rule without charity, it is plain that it ought not to have been altered by anyone. Accordingly, either you will wrong the saint by changing and overruling his writings, or, in reverencing him, you will obey in all things the precepts which he gave.”

Moreover, we do not know how the very name “Rule” can stand if we do not follow it as a Rule and guide, but bend and change it at pleasure; if, so to speak, we become the rule of the Rule, and do not follow it, as we have said, but compel it to follow us.

But we reply, on the contrary: You certainly show yourselves excellent defenders of blessed Benedict, to whom, in defending him, you inflict greater injuries. You inflict injuries when you attempt to praise him in such a way that you seem to detract from the praise of other saints. Saints do not wish to increase through the diminution of others, so that others’ loss may seem their gain. Such a thing is accustomed to occur among those whom charity unites.

To make our meaning clearer, we ask: was it lawful or not lawful for those saints, whom we said above had altered the statutes of the earlier Fathers, to alter them? If you say, “It was not lawful,” we reply: then all who changed earlier decrees acted wrongly; Saint Gregory acted wrongly in allowing the English marriages that were unlawful; a Catholic synod acted wrongly in altering a Catholic synod; very many Roman bishops, famous and renowned for holiness, acted wrongly in altering the commands of other holy Roman pontiffs; Paul himself acted wrongly and was contrary to himself when, after having earlier circumcised his disciple Timothy, he later wrote to the Galatians and sternly forbade it, saying: “I, Paul, say to you that if you are circumcised, Christ will profit you nothing” (Galatians 5).

If this is granted, what was judged just is found to be unjust; those who until now were saints will cease to be saints; the Church, having followed error for so long, will be judged to have erred; and only now, through your preaching, brought back to the path of righteousness, it will begin to follow the truth. If you judge it proud and blasphemous to say this, you will say that by wise counsel they could alter the earlier statutes; or perhaps—which alone remains—you will be silent. But if you are silent, you will show that you have adopted the counsel of the Pharisees, who, unwilling either to confess the truth or able to attack it, when questioned by the Lord about John’s baptism, whether it was from heaven or from men, chose silence (Matthew 21).

But if, refusing silence, you give the answer which we just set forth—namely, that it was lawful for those men but not for these—we ask the reason. You will answer that the Roman pontiffs could do this both because of their distinguished and acknowledged holiness and because of the authority of the governance of the whole Church entrusted to them; Catholic councils likewise deserved the same privilege because of the authority and holiness of those gathered; but our Fathers, since they did not possess comparable holiness and authority, could not do comparable things. If holiness and authority are the issue, and these gave those saints leave to modify the statutes of their predecessors, they will give it also to our Fathers, whom holiness—and perhaps equal holiness—made saints; nor did they lack equal authority in respect of the offices entrusted to them by God.

As witnesses to their holiness we have their upright conduct and God himself, who declared that they were pleasing to him both while they lived and even after their death by the display of many miracles. The Church too is witness, recounting their memory among the holy Fathers and solemnly celebrating their feasts. We said that they had equal authority in respect of the offices entrusted to them by God because, although the Roman pontiffs have greater authority than other Fathers of the Church—that is, although they have Peter’s authority throughout the whole Church—yet, in this respect, those whom we defend have equal authority: as Roman bishops preside over the whole Church and other bishops over individual Churches, so these men rule their own monks with equal power and authority in every respect. For although the Roman bishop may correct the errors of others by a special power, these men nevertheless have full power over their own subjects, and, where faults are absent, equal authority in commanding, as we have said.

And if this is so—and it plainly is—then, unless some other objection is raised, it is clear that our Fathers had full authority to alter certain observances of the Rule, given for a particular time, for the salvation of those entrusted to them, although no necessity compelled us to invoke their holiness in order to prove this. For what? Would they cease to be teachers even if they were not saints? Or can no one now preside over a Church unless he is holy? Must we always consult miracles in order to recognize who ought to be placed over others? And what is the meaning of the Lord’s saying: “The scribes and Pharisees have sat in Moses’ seat. Therefore observe all things whatsoever they tell you; but do not act according to their works” (Matthew 23)? For in saying, “Do not act according to their works,” he shows that they were not holy but wicked; he would in no way have forbidden the imitation of their works if he had known them to be good. Since he forbade their imitation, it is certain that he judged them evil. It is clear, therefore, that all obedience must be rendered by subjects even to bad rulers.

[Col. 0153D] From this it follows that, even if holiness were lacking to the Fathers mentioned above, the authority of their office alone would suffice to require obedience to them. Therefore it was lawful for them, even apart from holiness, to command their subjects the things mentioned; and it was lawful for the subjects to observe what was commanded. Yet we still demand your answer. You said that, because of distinguished and acknowledged holiness and the authority of governance entrusted by God, later saints were allowed to alter the statutes of earlier saints. This reasoning seems insufficient to us. For how could the holiness and authority of later persons prejudice the holiness and authority of earlier ones? How, indeed, could holiness take anything away from holiness, or authority from authority, without injury to the holiness and authority of one or the other? We say “take away” when a later authority changes what an earlier one established.

What the authority of later persons altered from earlier decrees either made better than before or worse. If better, the earlier institution was not wholly good; it follows that it was inferior. If it was inferior, it had inferior founders. But if later men altered for the worse the institutions of earlier men, it is clear that they themselves were inferior. Thus it appears that either the earlier or later Fathers, unless defended, suffer loss of praise. Either the earlier Fathers established what was best, and what is best ought not to have been changed by later men; or, if those changing it acted justly in changing it, it is plain that the former things were not best. Now the error of the institutions rebounds upon the heads of the founders. For Scripture says: “By your words you shall be justified, and by your words you shall be condemned” (Matthew 12).

If, otherwise, you wish to defend the saints from blame by the shield of charity, then, God’s grace helping us, you will be unable even to defend yourselves. But how long are we to listen before you answer what we can answer? To fight without an enemy is nothing other than to beat the air. Charity, therefore, remains. If you wish to untie this knot by charity, you can do so most swiftly, most easily, and most rightly. For this is, as we have often said, that on which all the Law and the Prophets hang. This is the fulfilment of the law and the end of the commandment. This is that which, as the Apostle says, has been poured into the hearts of the saints through the Holy Spirit given to them (Romans 5): speaking different things through different saints at different times, it itself has remained not various, not divided, not manifold, but simple, steadfast, immovable, and always the same.

For as a mistress of a household, intent upon the advantage of the whole household, sends some servants to till the ground with oxen, others to dig the vineyard, others into the wood to cut timber; orders some to kindle a fire and others to bring water; sends this one to market for trade; rebukes that one for being idle; and, praising another for diligence, exhorts him to better things—yet she herself, although the things which she commands are diverse, does not become diverse; nor does diversity of command make diversity of advantage. For that whole variety of offices is directed toward one single and simple thing, namely the benefit of the household, and innumerable services accomplish that one thing. Nor is she to be blamed if she commands this to one and something else to another, because she commands those many things for the accomplishment of the one end mentioned above; nor should she be judged contrary to herself because her commands differ.

So charity, because it commands all things solely for the benefit of the house of God, must not be said to be contrary to itself; rather, whatever it commands, through whomever and whenever, must be followed without reservation. For even if diverse commands have been given by it through diverse messengers at diverse times, they are nevertheless not contrary in their commands, messengers, and times. There appears indeed a certain diversity; but because all serve the divine will and human salvation, there can be no opposition among things which charity, incapable of being deceived, orders wholly toward this one end.

And just as a stubborn and condemnable servant would be judged if, when his mistress commanded water to be brought, he answered: “Because yesterday you commanded me to cut wood in the forest and bring it home, I shall henceforth bring neither water nor perform any other work, but shall always go to the forest and, cutting wood there, carry it home”; and, when she said, “That was necessary yesterday, and therefore I commanded it; since it is no longer necessary, do what is now necessary,” he, despising both the reverence due to the one commanding and the benefit of the household, refused obedience in every way and even, to increase his contumacy, forbade his fellow servants who wished to carry water—so must he be judged who refuses obedience to charity as teacher, which commands all things, though diverse and at diverse times through diverse persons, nevertheless all for the benefit of the Church.

So indeed are those to be judged who answer charity when it commands, and seeks by every means only the salvation of human beings: that they receive novices within a year when they see it expedient; that they give brothers necessary clothing; that they devote themselves more to spiritual than bodily exercise; that, concerned only for the salvation of souls, they do many similar things. They answer: “Because long ago you delivered these commands through Saint Benedict, we shall not allow them to be altered, nor shall we ever obey you in these matters.” Charity says: “At that time human nature was stronger for enduring labours, as the age itself was stronger; but now, as the world grows old and is already near death, everything in the world has grown weak, and therefore many things then necessary have now become contrary. Do what is now necessary. For it is not mine, nor is it characteristic of this time, to frighten novices in such a way that, while I wish to test them for a year, rejection follows. It is not mine, I say, not to supply the need for food, drink, clothing, and other things according to the differing infirmities, regions, and times, lest, while I do not render to a human being what is his due, he himself be unable to render to God what is God’s.”

With proud superstition they disdain to obey salutary counsels; and not content merely to withdraw themselves from the law of charity, they attempt, with all the force they can, to join to their transgression others who desire to obey it. Thus you Cistercians act; thus you resist charity; thus you are shown not to keep even the Rule for which you had contended.

But let us return to the solution of your question. So that we may solve it more clearly, let us again place the question itself before the solution, but in briefer terms.

You said: “Blessed Benedict composed the Rule either without charity or with charity. But none of you dares affirm that he composed it without charity. Therefore you do not deny that it was composed with charity. Now, because it is evident that it was composed through charity, it ought not to have been changed. If it ought not to have been changed, it ought to have been kept. Therefore either by changing it you inflict an injury upon the saint, or by keeping it you obey him in all things.”

And we reply: From the fact that the Rule was composed through charity, it does not follow that it ought not to have been changed. Rather, from the fact that it was composed through charity, it follows that it ought to have been changed. To make this plain, let the office of charity be considered. And what is charity’s office? The one and only office of charity is to seek human salvation by every means. The Lord himself, the apostles, and all his saints proclaim this to be its office. All the divine books testify, as we have often said, that whatever it commands is just. And what greater argument is there? The Lord says that the whole Law and the Prophets hang upon it. The Apostle testifies that it is the fulfilment of the law and the end of the commandment (Romans 13).

Blessed Augustine says of it: “If this one thing is absent, all things are empty; if this alone is present, all things are full.” Elsewhere he says: “The whole fruit is charity, without which a human being is nothing, whatever else that person may possess.” And in another place: “Have charity, and do whatever you will.” Therefore, in order to provide for human salvation, it does whatever it wills. If it may do whatever it wills, it was permitted to make the Rule and permitted also to alter it. Nor should an injury to the saint be alleged, since the Rule was altered not by another, but by that charity which, poured into his heart through the Holy Spirit given to him, used him as its instrument when he composed the Rule.

And because charity “does not envy” and “is not puffed up”; because it “is not ambitious” and “does not seek its own” (1 Corinthians 13), those who are filled with it know none of these things. Since they lack envy, pride, and ambition, they do not know how to take offence. Therefore no injury was done to the saint, because charity made its Rule according to what suited that time; and, after it saw that what it had made ought profitably to be altered, it altered it, while preserving from the same Rule what ought to be kept.

Just as it would not follow that an injury had been done to a scribe if the dictator, for a definite reason—perhaps known to himself alone—caused what the scribe had earlier written to be altered either by that scribe or by another, so it does not follow that an injury was done to blessed Benedict if charity, for reasons already given, altered through him, had it so wished, or through another because it so wished, either all or some of those things which it had written through him. Nor is it unworthy of a saint to be called charity’s scribe. For John in his Epistle calls God charity (1 John 4), and Saint Gregory says in his Homilies: “The Holy Spirit is love.” But love is charity. Therefore the Holy Spirit is charity. It is not unworthy of Benedict, then, to be a scribe of the Holy Spirit. Indeed all the prophets were that Spirit’s scribes. It does not dishonour him to be like the prophets.

Therefore, if the alteration of the Rule inflicted injury on that saint by those altering it, injury was also inflicted on the saints mentioned above by later persons who altered their decrees. And, to say something greater, injury was done to the Law by the Gospel and to Moses by Christ. But if no injury was done for this reason either to Moses, to the Law, to canonical statutes, to any divine command, or to those through whom those commands themselves were promulgated—because the Holy Spirit, which we have proved to be charity, provided what suited human salvation at different times; and although certain things in the commands were changed and the commands themselves were given through persons who changed, yet that Spirit itself was not changed, because it is unchangeable—then it is clear that the Rule of Saint Benedict, in certain of its chapters, has been altered without injury to him, even though you grant this unwillingly.

For it was altered through charity, through which the Word was made flesh; as the Apostle says: “Because of his exceeding charity with which God loved us, he sent his Son in the likeness of sinful flesh” (Romans 8).

Therefore, because certain things in the Rule have been changed, charity did it; and because they were changed without injury to the saint, charity did it. Let no one think that we say this because we wish to justify ourselves. We do not say these things because we wish to seem righteous; rather, by both reason and divine authorities we demonstrate that the institutions of our Fathers do not depart from truth, and that those who observe them as they were commanded by those Fathers do not err. Thus, now that we have cleared ourselves of the stain of transgression which you cast upon us, act on your own behalf and show, if you can, that you are free from transgression of the Rule itself.

For we say that you transgress the Rule when, failing to preserve its rectitude—that is, neglecting charity, which the Apostle calls the fulfilment of the law (Romans 13)—you compel it in many matters to serve your own will instead. Therefore, in matters in which you observe the Rule without charity, as follows from what has gone before, you are no longer observing the Rule but, rectitude having been removed, observing crookedness.

To these things perhaps you answer in words or in thought: “Where do you say that we exclude charity from the commands of the Rule? Where do we neglect to provide for the salvation of souls?” We answer by offering some examples. Do you not neglect the salvation of souls, and thus charity, when you deny brothers necessities; when you afflict them with cold, deprived of the use of furs; when by this compulsion—for many among you endure it unwillingly—you force them either into murmuring or into flight? Even if there are some who somehow endure this, as time goes on their bodies are damaged by illnesses; they lose their health from the cold and, frequently rendered permanently sick, cannot serve God. Thus, certainly, having abandoned discriminating charity, you neglect to provide for the salvation of souls in those who murmur, flee, and become sick.

The words of the Rule itself make us wonder even more at this position of yours; for even negligent readers can see from them that monks are not forbidden to use furs. As we said above when dealing with this chapter, no prohibition and no command concerning this matter is read there; rather, it commands that monks should have furs.
