For when the Rule says, “Let garments be given to the brothers according to the character of the places or the temperature of the climate, because more are needed in cold regions and fewer in warm ones; and let this consideration lie with the abbot,” does it not thereby grant the brothers furs and other necessary clothing? If, according to the Rule, the condition of the air—that is, the coldness of the region—requires them, we say that they ought to be given by command of the Rule. For what the coldness of the region requires, necessity requires; and what necessity requires, charity plainly requires. Now if anyone says that charity must not be yielded to, that person judges that God must be opposed. Therefore whoever says that monks ought not to use furs contradicts the command of God and of the Rule.

Yet perhaps the objection is still raised: “Although the Rule does not command this, it nevertheless advises that the monk should proceed to better things.” Certainly you have spoken well: it advises. For plainly it advises; it does not command. But if it only advises, it does not compel. For one who advises that what he wishes be done, recommends it. But one who commands compels, by commanding, the performance of what he commands. The Rule therefore recommends better things; it does not forcibly compel anyone to them. Why then do you compel what the Rule does not wish to compel? Or are you perhaps holier than he who composed it? Whence, I ask, comes such authority to you? The Apostle says: “I would that all men were even as I myself” (1 Cor. 7). And the Lord says in the Gospel: “Not all receive this saying. He who is able to receive it, let him receive it” (Matt. 19). And elsewhere to a certain man: “If you wish to be perfect, sell all that you have and give to the poor; and come, follow me” (ibid.). Certainly he says none of these things by commanding, but by exhorting.

And whereas it is the practice of all divine Scripture sometimes to command those things which must be commanded, and sometimes to advise those things which it sees to be more arduous, you, scorning, that is, this Rule of his, do not fear to force men to that to which they ought only to be invited by exhortations. Indeed, it seems to me that monks should not only not be compelled, but should not even be advised, not to wear furs—at least in these regions. For how ought I to advise someone concerning that through which I know, or fear, that he will fall into worse things? If I love my neighbour as myself, I ought in every respect to provide for his welfare as for my own. Otherwise I do not love him as myself. And this is the surest rule of charity: that I should not prohibit what I see to be necessary for my brother, nor violently impel him to bear unsuitable and harmful labour; but, if I can, should endeavour to furnish him with all that he needs; and, if I cannot, should know how, by compassion for his need, to condescend in a spirit of mercy.

What benefit there is in wearing out the body with labours without charity, the Apostle teaches when he says: “If I deliver my body so that I burn, but have not charity, it profits me nothing” (1 Cor. 13). And lest we should seem to forbid those who, not compelled but voluntarily, strive to subdue their flesh for God by whatever austerities, let readers understand that in saying these things we do not intend this, nor do we wish to call anyone back from voluntary good; rather, relying on the preceding authorities, we oppose the forcing of unwilling persons to practices which do not belong to their vocation or which are harmful. For just as we know that those who flee the pleasures of the world and, for greater merit, prudently embrace its hardships are altogether to be praised, so we say that those who wish violently to force others to what they have not undertaken and what is not expedient are by no means to be heeded.

Dearest brother, necessity of the matter has carried me beyond the brevity proper to letters in writing this to you; and in these pages I have expressed my own understanding in the words of others. For apart from the harshness of expression which I used to indicate the concealed hostility of parties, I understood all the rest as it was published. It will henceforth be your task, if you think otherwise, to disclose this also fully to me, so that, after the matter has been carefully examined and chiefly determined by you, both the uncertainty of those who suffer scandal over this issue may be removed, and charity—which is truly wounded daily in the hearts and on the tongues of many—may be established, with every rust of envy far removed.

## LETTER XXIX. Brother PETER, humble abbot of Cluny, to his venerable and intimate lord BERNARD, abbot of Clairvaux: the affection of sincere charity.

When I was recently returning from the district of Poitou, the canons of Langres met me

[Note: [Col. 0159D] The canons of Langres. Langres, or Lingones, is a city in Lyonnaise I, which ancient geographers call Andomatunum of the Lingones, the Chronicle of Saint Benignus of Dijon calls the city of the Lingones, and Frodoard calls the city of the Lingones.]

and and, when I suspected nothing of the kind, told me that they had unanimously and canonically elected one of our brethren bishop, together with the whole clergy and people of their Church, with the advice and confirmation of the metropolitan of Lyons. They pressed me with all their strength, both through their own prayers and through the commands and letters of the lord of Lyons, that, since he was our monk, I too should confirm what they had done concerning him. For some time I hesitated, unwilling to lose the benefit of the man; at last I consented, yielding to the importunity of those who asked.

Having thus obtained from me what they sought, after the recent feast of the blessed Mother of God they approached the royal court at Anicium, at which I myself was present from necessity, not from choice; and they asked and obtained from the lord king of the Franks confirmation, so far as lay in him, of their elect. For when the king heard of the election and saw the man, who had perhaps then come to me, he approved what the Church of Langres had done concerning him and solemnly invested him with royal rights by his own hand, as is customary.

And since the wishes of clergy, people, metropolitan, and, as I have said, of the prince himself had thus converged upon this one decision and this one elect, I learned a few days ago that certain men of Lyons had, by I know not what rumours, turned your will aside from the common purpose of all and had nullified what had been done. When I discovered this, I would have preferred to confer face to face about these matters rather than commit my thoughts to a letter. Since both your distance and my uninterrupted business prevent this, I do what I can, because I cannot do what I wish.

I do not indeed wonder, nor is it wonderful, that evil reports displeased a good man; but it ought to have been considered that, as they could be true, so they could be false. Therefore, before the matter was known, it ought not to have been brought either before the tribunals of judges or before the seats of bishops. It ought to have been considered—though I lay this down as a familiar complaint in the ears of a like-minded friend—that the man in question is a monk of your Church of Cluny and a son of an abbot dear to you. It ought to have been noted that those persons from whom your affection received what moved you had for some time undertaken sworn warfare against Cluny with such violence that they have been unable to restrain either their tongues from insults or their hands from sacrileges. It should have been seen whether the slanderous words of men “whose mouth has spoken vanity” (Ps. 153 [Vulgate numbering]), shamelessly lying, and whose right hand is a right hand of iniquity, irreverently beating innocent monks, ought to have won the confidence of your prudence.

For this reason, to believe such great and manifest enemies, to place trust in such great and manifest foes, belongs neither to you nor to any good person. Believe household members rather than strangers, those known rather than those unknown, truthful friends rather than slanderous enemies. Believe me, who glory before you in the name of household member, acquaintance, and friend. Although I cannot be free from the common falsehood by which every human being is a liar, nevertheless far be it from me not to guard against lying where I can guard against it.

When I heard the rumour mentioned above, I myself met with the man; I set before him what was being said and, lest he deny the truth, begged, admonished, and adjured him fatherly. I told him that I wished to approach his conscience not as the faithless director of a secret, but as the faithful guardian of things entrusted to me; that I did not wish to mock at wounds of souls once laid bare, but to heal them. I added whatever could occur as useful for eliciting the truth, and I did not conceal that I was searching the inner recesses of the wall with the digging-tool of sharp questioning. After all this I received the answer that he had never veiled his heart before me in the garment of falsehood, nor had ever proposed to veil it; that he was certain that, if he lied to me, he would lie also to God; that he had no doubt as to the fidelity of what had been entrusted to him; and that he was so free from the matters alleged that, if I wished, he would most securely clear himself of every allegation by oath.

I myself know by whom, why, and how those words which produced scandal for you arose, grew, and were disseminated. If I had been allowed to speak freely with you in person, I would have explained them exactly; and I would have shown clearly how a murky cloud of falsehood had tried to strike the clear countenance of your mind from a shadowy abyss. I shall do so when I can. Meanwhile I ask that I may always retain your affection, and I beseech you by that which made us of one mind in the house of God: do not, I say not merely wish, but do not even permit, the body of the Cluniac congregation to be disfigured by the blemish of falsehood. For shame at the imputed disgrace itself would compel us to regard it not as charged against that one man alone, but as imputed to us—to each and all. “When one member suffers, all the members suffer with it; and when one member is afflicted, all the members share its affliction” (1 Cor. 12).

Nor should Your Holiness suppose that I say this in order to defend for our monk the rank of bishop. For it is neither new nor remarkable to us that our monks should be bishops, since so many stars from that Church—as you yourself know—have shone and still shine illustriously among the Churches. Rather, it is because neither a true Israelite can spread an evil name concerning a daughter of Israel, nor can a true Israelite endure it. And if many secular clerics of the Church of Langres, distinguished neither for great religious devotion nor for great learning, formerly governed there under the episcopal title, with the Church not only tolerating but even approving it, what is unbecoming if a religious, wise, learned monk of a religious Church has been elected bishop of Langres from that source from which episcopal, archiepiscopal, patriarchal Fathers, and even the Apostolic and Roman See itself—the summit of all Churches—have customarily taken their Fathers?

And if, perhaps, to state all that I think, monks fear monks, religious men religious men, Cistercians Cluniacs, and place too little trust in those in whom they ought greatly to trust, let this suspicion be cleared away. Let them learn, nature herself teaching them, that every creature loves what is like itself and clings to it more closely. If nature has such force among animals alone, will not the Author of nature have at least as much force among men—and men who are monks? Therefore, if he is a monk, the bishop of Langres will love the Cistercians and the other monks, because by loving he will find greater gain for himself, and by not loving greater loss. Nor will our monk dare to do otherwise than what he sees us do in loving.

## LETTER XXX. Brother PETER, humble abbot of Cluny, to my honoured and often-named THEOTARD: all that he is.

Whenever the memory of you, as you know, comes sweetly and gratefully to me—which happens almost without ceasing—it soothes and revives my heart, torn by the thorns of cares and exasperated by the briars of anxieties, as draughts of spices and fragrant ointments do; so that I feel that I am no longer myself, and, forgetting the man I was, rejoice that I have been changed into another man.

What then will happen, dearest friend—what will happen in that reality which we await in happy hope, I mean in immortal and blessed life—when, in this mortal and miserable life, full of vomit and filth, such an affection can still arise in human minds and remain in the feelings of those still unhappy? What will happen when the soul of the saints, by the unknown nourishment of that heavenly sweetness, will be filled as with marrow and fatness, when, still fasting and wasted with leanness—indeed, according to the Gospel, miserably perishing with hunger (Luke 15)—it rejoices so greatly in so small a taste? What will happen when those supremely happy persons “shall be made drunk with the abundance of the house of God, and shall drink of the torrent of his delight, because with him is the fountain of life” (Ps. 35 [Vulgate numbering]), if one little drop of that abundance, falling down here, accomplishes this?

Yet this, dearest friend, is the affection by which, as you know, I have always loved you, always honoured you, and always clung to you even while absent. This is what has never allowed you, though separated from me by great distances and many times, to be torn away from my mind; by presenting you frequently—indeed almost continuously—to the sight of my soul, it never permits you to be absent. This is what throughout this whole year has continually spurred my heart and, impatient of your long absence, daily invites me to write to your charity; and, unless it had often been repelled by the obstacle of cares, it would have fulfilled its intention before many days had passed.

Therefore, even now scarcely permitted, it does what it can. Seeking its absent beloved, awakening one who sleeps, inviting one who delays to come, it advises and exhorts; and because it has endured your delay until now, it even commands with authority that you hasten to come at once, either before I begin my journey to Montpellier or immediately after you learn of my return.

[Note: Before I set out for Montpellier. Mons Pessulus, or Pessulanus—also called by some the Mount of Maidens—is the renowned city of the Volcae, to which, in 1536, the bishopric was transferred from the nearby island of Maguelone, with the assent of Francis I, king of the Franks.]

And because I have heard of the recent deaths among the brethren of Luparciac, I wish you to hasten your journey earlier—indeed, as quickly as you can—and not fail to present yourself to us at Cluny by the next Sunday of Septuagesima.

[Note: And because I have heard of the new calamity among the brethren of Luparciac. Luparciac, or, as some write more correctly, Luperciac, is a borough in the diocese of Nevers, where there was a Cluniac priory, built in honour of Saints Gervasius and Protasius. Dom Gelduin, descended from the noble line of the magnates of Poitiers, after voluntarily embracing poverty in the monastery of Cluny, was at one time made its prior, as appears from the acts concerning the translation of the relics of Saint Stephen the Protomartyr to Cluny in the time of Abbot Pons. It is commonly called Leurcy-le-Bourg.]

Not because I now fear more than usual for you, or fear your death more than I am accustomed to do—especially since, being mortal, you cannot avoid death anywhere, and it is far more to be awaited and desired by you than fled—but in order that I may see my Aaron standing between the dead and the living (Num. 17), devoting his care to the one and burial-service to the other. Come, therefore, come; and lest you think yourself lightly invited, I say again: Come.

## LETTER XXXI. Brother PETER, humble abbot of Cluny, to his venerable and most beloved lord, the bishop of Bethlehem: greetings.

A certain brother, a monk of Mount Tabor as he said, recently came to us in the dress of a pilgrim. He reported to us very many good things concerning your blessedness and, presenting you as the singular friend of the monastery of Cluny among all ecclesiastical persons of the East, magnificently stirred the minds of all of us to love and embrace your reverence.

For whom would the affection, stirred by his Spirit, of not just any bishop but of the bishop of Bethlehem toward humble and remote poor of Christ not inspire? Whom would it not move from the depths of his heart? Of the bishop of Bethlehem, I say: guardian of the Lord’s manger; that manger to guard which scarcely righteous Joseph and the Virgin Mary were admitted; that manger which eternal Majesty, clothed in mortal flesh and appearing to human eyes, first chose, and in which, beyond all places on earth, the King of heaven first wished to rest, as it is written: “His mother laid him in a manger” (Luke 2).

Thanks, therefore, to him at whose birth in Bethlehem the angels sang, “Glory to God in the highest”; who, reckoning you among people of good will, inspired your heart with the gift of that peace which surpasses all understanding (Phil. 4), and encouraged you to extend very widely, even to those far away, the broad commandment of charity across the immeasurable spaces of land and sea. We have experienced this, placed as we are in the western and almost uttermost world—that is, at Cluny. We have perceived the fragrance of Eastern spices and, in the odour of your ointments—that is, your precious virtues—have begun to run like young women, that is, the weaker persons.

We shall therefore run, and shall not fail in running until we have attained our goal: until by the affection through which we run, we reach the house not passing away but eternal in heaven. There, rejoicing not merely in charity begun, but in charity already completed and in perpetual dwelling together in Christ, may we cleave to him with you for ever. Let then the exalted mother Bethlehem be joined for ever to her daughter Cluny, so that what they cannot fulfil by bodily sight, they may fulfil by spiritual and sincere love.

## LETTER XXXII. Brother PETER, humble abbot of Cluny, to the supreme shepherd of God’s Church and our special Father, lord Pope INNOCENT: filial love in Christ.

My humility, often writing and often writing back to Your Apostolic Majesty, fears that it may be presumptuous or excessive toward ears occupied with hearing the voices of the whole world. Yet paternal mercy is accustomed to bear not only with a talkative son but sometimes even with an offending one. Though it sometimes chastises him for his faults, it cannot fail to love him even amid the blows. Hence, taking courage, filial confidence asks paternal kindness on behalf of the lord archdeacon of Lyons—although, so far as he is concerned, this seems no rash presumption in petitioning, but a just prayer.

To speak in secular terms, his personal integrity merits this; his obedience and service toward Your Sublimity merit this; his diligence and devotion toward those who belong to you merit this. His personal integrity merits it because, situated among the men of Lyons, he has raised the standard of prudence and honour higher among his fellow canons, not indeed as Job in the land of Uz, but according to his measure—if it is permissible to compare small things with great—even as Stephen the deacon did among his fellow deacons. At a time when nearly everything is corrupted among people of this kind, this archdeacon of the same name has preserved inviolate the distinction of the clerical order.

Who has ever stained his life with any infamous designation? Who has assailed his integrity with any dishonourable suspicion, not to say accusation? Who has disturbed his conduct from boyhood onward, which is exceedingly rare, by any whisper, not to say reproach? As I have said, his obedience and service merit this, because—to leave other matters aside and speak of the present situation—he almost alone, indeed alone, kept the obedience to the apostolic command imposed upon the Church of Lyons through your legates, and, as I say now without accusation, alone among all avoided contumacy.

His diligence and devotion toward those who belong to you merit this, since he embraces, assists, and defends all those who are yours, and especially the Cluniacs, whom he regards as especially yours. Nor does he do this only for them. All whom he supposes to be religious by any mark of religion, he receives, supports, and serves; and by his almost constant reception and provision for them he shows that his house—or houses—are not merely lodging, but their refuge. I know that all this renders a good son pleasing to the most holy Father even without my commendation; but would that my testimony, which I bear from seeing and hearing, made him still more pleasing to paternal mercy. He has a case before the Father against certain persons; since you know him as well, there is no need to instruct your wisdom about it, especially because you know yourselves to be the vicar of him “who will render to each according to his works.”

## LETTER XXXIII. Brother PETER, humble abbot of Cluny, to the supreme pontiff and our special Father, lord Pope INNOCENT: greetings and obedience.

A great subject would compel me to speak at length, but I fear to be troublesome or excessive to the ears of Your Majesty. Therefore I humbly submit to your beloved and belovedly to be loved fatherhood that letters recently sent to me by you have gravely wounded me, your son, and the whole assembly always subject and devoted to you, because they contained unprecedented and harmful measures.

I say unprecedented and harmful because they took away tithes which, until these times, for two hundred years and more, your Church of Cluny has received indiscriminately from all and rendered indiscriminately to all. I say unprecedented and harmful because, after forty days, they interdicted divine offices in the great monastery of Gigny on account of the tithes of its parish that had been reclaimed.

[Note: In the great monastery of Gigny. Gigny is a member of the monastery of Cluny. Saint Bernard also speaks of it in Letter 283 to Pope Eugene: “At Cluny,” he says, “we met the men of Gigny in hope of peace, for which much labour was undertaken, but nothing was achieved. For at last the only result of our entire four days’ labour was the collapse of hope. Indeed, to avoid ranging through individual cases, a whole abbey was destroyed.” Peter the Venerable himself says below, in Letter 35: “What am I to say concerning the sentence pronounced against the men of Gigny without summons and without hearing? I find no words. For now, for the first time, a sentence of excommunication or interdict against Cluniac monks has been promulgated by the Apostolic See.”]

And although it has been confirmed by many privileges of your holy predecessors that the brethren of Cluny should receive, without anyone’s opposition, not only the tithes of all their parishes but also retain those which they cultivated at their own expense, they have nevertheless not wished to use this power, knowing that it is written: “Woe to him through whom scandal comes” (Matt. 23 [as printed]).

[Note: That the brethren of Cluny should receive the tithes of their parishes. Above, Letter 28.]

Therefore they humbly and modestly pay the tithes of both their peasants and their serfs not only to monks and canons but also to any clerics, priests, knights, and even robbers. And since they themselves peacefully render to everyone tithes both owed and not owed, and any other dues whatever, why should they not in turn receive from others in peace?

I myself have given tithes in certain places to the Cistercian brethren, as the lord abbot of Clairvaux can testify. But now, by God’s grace, the number of them and of other religious everywhere around us is so great that, if we grant tithes to all, we shall lose nearly a tenth part of our own number. For if brevity permitted, we would show very many of our monasteries so surrounded by diverse religious houses that, within two or one league, a single old monastery is hemmed in by five or seven new monasteries. These, built in our parishes, both with and without our consent and contrary to canon law, already possess the greater part of our parishes. If tithes are granted to all of them, our own people will have to diminish their number, as I have said, or perhaps in certain places yield both site and buildings.

Therefore your faithful congregation, venerable Father, always subject to Apostolic Majesty, begs that new sons should not expel old ones from paternal love. For although new sons ought to be loved, old ones ought not, on account of new ones, to be cast aside unless they have deserved it. Remember how much honour was shown among God’s ancient people to firstborn sons: unless Esau had sold his birthright, Jacob, though holier, would never have been, I do not say preferred to him, but not even compared with him in the dignity of the firstborn. If therefore we are firstborn, it is fitting that we should not lose for younger sons what we have not sold.

If the matter proceeds otherwise, I say this without prejudice to the Father’s favour: either his Church will retain it with me, or it will lack me in the possessions it has justly held until now. You know my heart—would that, by this or by any occasion, its desire, not sudden but long-standing, might be fulfilled. Therefore, with repeated prayers, the whole body of your sons entreats, and I too, though unworthy, yet yours, beg: if another course does not now please you, at least defer the sentence of interdict until Easter of the Lord, so that within this period I may send prudent brethren to you and through them negotiate with you both concerning these matters and others.

## LETTER XXXIV. Brother PETER, humble abbot of Cluny, to his venerable brother and most beloved friend, lord AIMERIC, cardinal and chancellor of the Apostolic Sublimity: greetings.

When shipwreck threatens, there is nowhere safer to flee than to harbour; when dangers are feared, there is nowhere more salutary to flee than to a friend. Therefore, because our ship fears shipwreck as contrary winds drive against it, it has especially chosen you, to whom it may make its dangers known and through whom it may avoid every adversity.

If the abundance of the matter should compel me to multiply words, I ask you to bear it patiently, because no one can say briefly what a multitude of words can scarcely explain. Many things can indeed sometimes be said briefly, but only where brevity does not diminish the weight of the meanings, not where it deprives understanding of many things that must necessarily be understood. The indolence of modern people has prevailed also: it immediately calls superfluous whatever does not accord with its sloth. It was not so among the ancients; if your wisdom wishes to remember them, it will judge even our very long words extremely short.

I received letters sent from the Majesty of the Father to my humility. If, as they were sent to me alone, they harmed me alone, consolation would easily come to the injury of one man. But now letters are working toward the common destruction of our monastery; and they seem all the more bitter because they are shown to have appeared contrary to custom. For those which formerly poured milk and honey upon sons from paternal breasts now, in my time—I say it with a humble heart, but not without deep pain—offer myrrh and wormwood.

But if, because of my sins—which I do not discern—this storm has risen against Christ’s little ship, which the skilled hand of that very one guides, he having entrusted it to him, then, to use the prophet’s words: “Take me and cast me into the sea, provided that the sea cease from those who are shipwrecked” (Jonah 1). For what? Is not the Church of Cluny, of which we now speak, called and believed to be, among all the Churches subject throughout the world, the singular daughter of him who presides over it by God’s authorship? Is it not that Church which, though perhaps another is higher in ecclesiastical rank, has never been found earlier in the Father’s favour? Is it not that Church which the supreme shepherds of God’s Church, his holy predecessors, cherished, loved, increased, and advanced from the first stone of its foundation, as though in their own bosom?

[Note: Is not that the Church of Cluny which the supreme shepherds of the Church cherished in their own bosom from the first stone of its foundation? William, duke of Aquitaine, in his testament concerning the foundation of Cluny; Louis “Transmarinus,” king of the Franks, in his charter concerning Salustriac and other places belonging to Cluny; Urban II in *The Liberty of the Monastery of Cluny*; and other Roman pontiffs, whose diplomas have already been transcribed elsewhere.]

Is it not that Church which he undertook from them as a duty to cherish, love, increase, and advance; which he promised in words, and confirmed in a general chapter? But now, in a new order of things, darkness has arisen from light; day has been changed into night; the serene face of heaven has been transformed into a dreadful storm. And lest you perhaps suppose that I wish to exaggerate this in words, know that I speak to a friend in truth: I say nothing merely to magnify matters, and can scarcely express the very accumulation of my troubled thoughts. I know my own heart, and I know the mind of the sacred community to be more saddened than I can say, because at this time they have heard things which, having never heard them before, they could in no way have expected.

For when has any Church—I say not Cluny, I say not even a Church, but at least some lowly little woman—been deprived of its right by Apostolic justice through mere will, without judgment? When has another person’s property been granted to others without the assent or will of the person to whom it belongs? When has an offering pleasing to God been made from goods violently extorted from others? The Apostolic letters command us not to receive tithes from monks or regular canons, although we pay them to monks, clerics, regular canons, and—if it could be said—to secular persons, nuns, knights, and even robbers.

And I do not speak of those tithes which peasants or cultivators render from their farming, but of those which our brethren cultivate by their own hands or at their own expense. The Cluniacs possess numerous and ancient privileges in this respect; the Cistercians say that they possess special and new privileges from the same source. Yet, knowing the Lord’s sentence, “Woe to him through whom scandal comes” (Matt. 18), they do not wish to use the granted power, lest, being the origin and cause of scandals, they be judged worthy to have a millstone hung about their neck and be drowned in the depth of the sea.

But some men are generous with what belongs to others: “These are poor; those are rich. Therefore the rich ought to assist the poorer.” And rightly so. But let them consider what Solomon says: “Where there are great riches, there are many also who consume them” (Eccles. 5). And because at times a poor man in a hut is richer than a king upon a throne: for if the former is satisfied, he needs no one; whereas the latter, when he cannot provide for many thousands, begs. The world knows upon what uses Cluny spends the revenues of its lands, its money, its tithes, and its possessions. Let the more inquisitive investigator first carefully examine and compare the revenues and expenditures of Cluniacs and Cistercians [Col. 0167D], and only then pronounce judgment on their wealth or poverty. But let it be so: they are poor, these are rich. Let the matter be tried in court. “You shall not,” says the eternal Law, “show partiality to the poor, nor honor the countenance of the powerful” [Col. 0168A] (Lev. 19). Likewise in Exodus: “Neither shall you show pity to the poor in judgment” (Exod. 33). If mercy is to be shown to the poor, is injury then to be inflicted by the poor? If alms are to be given to him, is robbery to be practiced by him? It is a monstrous kind of plunder if holy poor men labor to extort from the rich what the worst rich men used to take from the poor.

Nor should those brothers of ours flatter themselves if they do not do these things with their own hands; for it is not merely he who is innocent in hands who “ascends the mountain of the Lord” and “stands in his holy place,” but he who is pure in heart (Ps. 14). Therefore, one who by words proceeding from his heart sets the hands of others in motion cannot excuse himself from their deed by any dissimulation. When in charity they asked me, I granted them certain tithes; but one thing is what is freely offered to God, another what is violently taken away. It might in some fashion have been tolerable to grant this in certain and few places; but through God’s grace the multiplication of the new harvest is so great that, if—as they demand—the old are compelled to yield to the new, the ancient labors must perish. I have loved, and always wish to love, those brothers, as both our congregation and theirs bears witness for me; but they must take heed, if they are servants of God, lest through their occasion—or, what is worse, through their deliberate pursuit—charity, the perfection and end of all virtues, be harmed.

For, to say what I truly think, such scandal is being prepared from this that it may indeed begin in our time, but can never [Col. 0168C] be ended within our lifetime. It is not a matter from which obedience may be withdrawn, but one from which, what is greater, charity may be destroyed. I say destroyed, not harmed; for truly, not only among our own people but among all against whom this decree has been issued, it is not merely injured but even extinguished. Your prudence knows that the Church of God needs ointment, not cautery; that it must be supported by a staff, not driven headlong by a thrust—especially at this time, when, its strength exhausted, a great part of it totters with trembling limbs; and when the field of scandals now lies widely open, and the days seem near of which the Lord says in the Gospel that, if possible, even the elect will be led into error (Matt. 24).

What I should say about the sentence issued against the men of Gigny without summons and without a hearing, I cannot discover. [Col. 0168D] For, apart from the storm stirred up by Lord Pons, this is the first time that a sentence of excommunication or interdict against Cluniac monks has been promulgated by the Apostolic See.

> **[Note: Col. 0167D]** “For the first time a sentence of excommunication or interdict against Cluniac monks has been promulgated.” Among the chief privileges once obtained by the Cluniacs from the Apostolic See is found the provision that no bishop or priest may pronounce in their places, or against them, a sentence of excommunication or interdict. Pope Alexander II, in a rescript to Hugh, abbot of Cluny, says:
>
> “Under the same proclamation of anathema, moreover, we forbid that the said place be subjected to a title of interdict, or to the bond of excommunication or anathema, by any bishop or priest whatsoever. For the authority of the holy Apostolic See does not permit the freely granted liberty conceded by it to anyone to be cut off by the bond of any person whatsoever; nor may the brothers of that place, wherever they are situated, be held bound by the curse or bond of excommunication of any bishop whatsoever. For it seems dishonorable to us that a son of the holy Apostolic See should be anathematized by anyone without our judgment, as though he were the disciple of some subject church.” [Col. 0168D]
>
> Pope Urban II likewise, writing to the same Hugh, says:
>
> “Furthermore, as was established by Pope Gregory of blessed memory in the Roman synod, and recently by ourselves at Piacenza, by the authority of this present privilege we decree that no archbishop, no bishop, and no legate of the Apostolic See may, without a specific command of the Roman pontiff, pronounce against you or your monastery a sentence of excommunication or interdict.” [Col. 0169D]
>
> Indeed, even the abbots of Cluny themselves were at one time granted the power to excommunicate, with candles lighted, wrongdoers and despoilers of their property, especially in the province of Lyons, if they could not be compelled to make satisfaction. Thus Pope Innocent says:
>
> “Wishing to fortify your monastery against undue vexations by a special privilege of liberty, following the example of our predecessor Pope E. of happy memory, we establish by the authority of these presents and graciously grant to you that, if the bishops and prelates of the churches of the province of Lyons, having been requested by you three times, do not see fit to compel all wrongdoers against you and your men who belong to that province to render you fitting satisfaction, it shall be lawful for you and your successors, by apostolic authority and with candles lighted, to subject them to the sentence of excommunication and interdict. You shall declare them bound by the bond of excommunication and interdict until they have made adequate satisfaction for their offenses; and, if the gravity of the offense requires it, they shall come to the Apostolic See, with the testimony of your letters, to be absolved.” [Col. 0170D]

But that statement also, contained in the same letter of our lord, that certain letters had been fraudulently extorted from him, filled me and those who heard it with no small astonishment. [Col. 0169A]

For when we long sought among ourselves who had committed this fraud, who had extorted them, who had been the author of so great a crime, we could not discover it. I remember only that I sent from Saint-Ambrose a messenger to the lord pope and to you, and through him transmitted a written chapter of the following kind, as I afterwards gathered from the very sheet which I had sent, in these words: “Let the monks of Miratoire be written to, who take tithes from our brothers of Gigny and make them appeal to powerful men [or, perhaps, *depraedari*, ‘be plundered’], that they may restore the tithes.”

> **[Note: Col. 0170D]** “To the monks of Miratoire.” In the last letter of Book VI he calls their abbot his kinsman in these words: “What shall I say of my kinsman, the abbot of Miratoire—wonderful and admirable? I cannot find words.”

Whose fraud, I ask, could this have been? [Col. 0169B] If it was the messenger’s, it is astonishing that such a tiny little man could deceive such great judges of the world. If it was the chapter itself, this is no less astonishing. For fraud is said to occur when falsehood is put forward with an intention to deceive and truth is concealed. How, then, were letters fraudulently extorted which concealed nothing true with intent to deceive and advanced nothing false? But if anyone whispered this into the ears of our Father, it was proper to believe him when, in the presence of the man who wrote it, he could prove that he had written something false. To pass judgment before matters have been examined is nothing else than to condemn an absent person by mere will.

Our men did not think that they had laid up such merit with their lord, for whose obedience and service they are said to have spent themselves and nearly all that was theirs. [Col. 0169C] But lest I seem to boast of our own merits, I leave these matters meanwhile to his own conscience, praying, in return for all the things that I could enumerate, that the Church entrusted to him by God may suffer, if not increase, at least no losses that it has not deserved. Let him remember that he consecrated that Church with his own hands—a thing which it is quite certain some of his predecessors had greatly desired. If he diminishes it, he will seem to have destroyed [Col. 0170A] what he had appeared to build.

Its enemies, who have already begun in part to do so, will insult us. Their multitude is everywhere; and although it does not openly oppose us, it openly hates us. Nor will they cease to repeat what they habitually say: “Look, Cluniacs, have your pope, whom you chose for yourselves in contempt of your monk. Such a hope is worthily followed by such a reward.” But because, dearest brother, confidence in the great love which I have always had for you compelled me perhaps to speak more fully than I ought, I ask that you not wonder; for both the great murmuring in our Church over this affair and the tongue which was lacking to the mediator’s messenger compelled me to impress such weighty words upon paper.

Therefore now, by that hope in which the whole Church of God, and Cluny in particular, relies upon you after the lord pope, I beg you to labor [Col. 0170B] to have the sentence changed for the better. Wise men should not find it strange if someone seeking his own advantage was able to mislead a man distracted in many directions by the cares of the whole world; but it will seem very strange if, after recognizing its harmfulness, so great a shepherd does not provide for his sheep. But if an immediate change does not please him, let him, as I asked in my own letter, defer the severity of that new interdict until the coming Easter; for even before I heard these things I had intended to send him suitable messengers by that time. But the appointed period is so short that, unless a messenger is quickly sent back with a remission, the monastery of Gigny will, at the very Nativity of the Lord—which I can scarcely say without tears—be deprived of the divine [Col. 0170C] offices, and an indelible pain of savage bitterness will burn itself into the hearts of our brothers.

After you, I ask that only those see this familiar letter who will not impede our business but will endeavor, according to their strength, to assist it.

## LETTER XXXV

To our dearest and venerable brothers gathered in Christ’s name: the lord abbot of Cîteaux,

> **[Note: Col. 0170D]** “To the lord abbot of Cîteaux.” No one has described the earliest beginnings of the Cistercian order better than Caesarius of Heisterbach, *Book I of Miracles*, chapter 1:
>
> “In the diocese of Langres there was a monastery called Molesme, most renowned in reputation, conspicuous for religion, ennobled by distinguished men, abundant in possessions, and famous for virtues. Since riches and virtues cannot long remain in partnership, certain wise men, lovers of virtue, understanding more deeply that, although they lived honorably in the aforesaid monastery, they nevertheless observed less fully the Rule which they had professed, took common counsel together. Twenty-one monks, together with their father Robert, came with one accord and in one spirit to a place of horror and vast solitude called Cîteaux, wishing there to live by the work of their own hands according to the precept of the Rule. Therefore, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1099, strengthened by the counsel and authority of the venerable Hugh, bishop of the Church of Langres [Col. 0171C] and then legate of the Apostolic See, of the religious man Walter, bishop of Chalon, and also of the most illustrious prince Odo, duke of Burgundy, they began to build an abbey in the aforesaid place. And because the monastery from which they had departed had been constructed in honor of the blessed Mary, Mother of God, both they and their successors descended from that new monastery decreed that all their churches should be dedicated in honor of that same glorious Virgin.”
>
> Robert, then, abbot of Molesme, was the first renewer of the Cistercian order. Although not long afterward, when the monks of Molesme urgently demanded their abbot back, he was restored by command of Urban II and with the consent of Walter, bishop of Chalon; nevertheless, because he was of such holiness that even after death he deserved to be numbered among the saints, and because the bull of his canonization, which Honorius III decreed, is not found in the recently published Cistercian Chronicle, we have judged it highly suitable to insert here the document supplied to us through the kindness of Sir Nicolas Camuzat, canon of Troyes. It is as follows:
>
> “Honorius, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons the abbot and convent of Molesme: greeting and apostolic blessing. Since formerly, through your letters and messengers, aided by the testimonies and intercessions of many persons, you urgently petitioned us to enroll in the catalogue of saints blessed Robert of holy memory, whose body rested in your church and shone forth through many great miracles, we commanded our venerable brothers, the bishops of Langres and Valence, to inquire both into his life and into his miracles, lest we seem to employ any levity in so great a matter. For, in order that someone may be regarded as a saint in the Church Militant, it is necessary that sound merits of true faith—which works through love—together with final perseverance, should precede, and clear miracles should follow; nor are either fully sufficient without the others as evidence of holiness. For some perform their works in order to be seen by men, and at times the angel of Satan, transforming himself into an angel of light, often deceives men, as is written of Pharaoh’s magicians. Since the aforesaid investigators fully reported the truth to us concerning these matters, although they informed us of certain miracles which he performed after death, they did not furnish complete proof regarding those which he is said to have performed in life. Yet, lest we seem wholly to deny your prayers, we grant you permission to venerate him as a saint in your church and confidently to implore his intercessions with God. Given at the Lateran, on the sixth day before the Ides of January, in the sixth year.” [Col. 0171D–0172C]

to the abbots of Clairvaux, Pontigny, and the others,

> **[Note: Col. 0172C]** “Of Clairvaux, Pontigny, and the others.” “The first offshoots of Cîteaux,” says the aforesaid Caesarius, “were La Ferté, Pontigny, Clairvaux, and Morimond. The abbots of these four houses are of such authority that they visit the abbot of Cîteaux jointly, and he in turn visits them individually.” [Col. 0172D]
>
> We have already spoken above about Clairvaux. It will now suffice to add a few things about Pontigny from Robert, monk of Saint-Marien, who speaks in his *Chronology* concerning its foundation and first abbot as follows:
>
> “In the year 914, the monastery of Pontigny was founded on the freehold of Hildebert, canon of the mother church of Auxerre, at the request of that same Hildebert, under the venerable bishop Umbald, then presiding at Auxerre. The first abbot of this monastery was Lord Hugh, a man of exceptional religious devotion and outstanding integrity.”
>
> Nor would it perhaps be far from the truth to suppose that this Hugh is precisely the abbot of Pontigny to whom our Peter writes here, as Saint Bernard also does in Letter 33. Indeed, Bernard himself, abbot of Clairvaux, to whom Peter’s present letter is also directed, writes together with the said Hugh both to Pope Honorius, in Letters 46 and 49, and to Odo, abbot of Marmoutier, at the end of the letters of Ivo, bishop of Chartres.

and to all others gathered in Christ’s name: Brother PETER, humble abbot of the Cluniacs, greeting and true love in the Lord.

[Col. 0171A]

Dearest brothers, with what affection I have always loved your whole community above all who profess the religious life; with what honor I have revered it; with what benefits—this I say not as a reproach—I have assisted some of you according to my ability and opportunity: my Witness and Knower on high knows; the entire congregation of our Church, established throughout the world, knows; and many of you know, if not all—those whom I was able either to know personally or in whatever way to learn of through the mediation of others.

The reason for this love of mine toward you was neither repayment for something received nor hope of receiving any temporal advantage [Col. 0171B], but he who was the origin and substance of the whole matter, whom, because I could not worship him in himself, I worshiped in you through such offices. I revered in you the ardor of a new institution, the constancy of labor, the frugality of food, the plainness of clothing, and countless other things expressive of the humility of the monastic purpose. With all the arms of my soul I embraced your exercises of holy works; eagerly I drank in the sweet fragrance of your good name; nor could I calmly listen to anyone who interpreted you maliciously.

I was not content to hold these opinions of you alone. Having become your herald, I proclaimed to our own people and to outsiders the praises of your manner of life; and, exalting what was yours in many praises, privately and publicly, I turned many minds, even minds once hostile, toward love of you. Because, through the grace of God, I had no path open to me amid withering envy, he himself gave effectiveness to my words; and he “who makes both one” (Eph. 2) united the hearts of our brothers to you by the unity of his Spirit, so that, as in faith, so also in charity, we might now be believed to be not two congregations but one. [Col. 0172A]

I pressed on in increasing and strengthening this love, so that salvation, which cannot be preserved without charity, might remain unharmed, and that the mark of Christ’s discipleship might appear among us—that mark by which he taught that his disciples were to be distinguished from strangers, saying: “By this all shall know that you are my disciples, if you have love for one another” (John 15). I believe that the heavenly order rejoiced in our concord, and that the evangelists of peace, the Spirit of peace, rejoiced together among men of good will (Matt. 13). But the envious enemy could not endure long to be tormented by the happiness of others; and the enemy man sowed tares by night over the divine seed (Luke 2). [Col. 0172B]

He cast an apple of discord between us, so that, once the one and only charity had departed, he might more easily drive away every kind of virtue, and, when the head of all goods had been cut off, all the members might be compelled to perish together. This is precisely what he did when he persuaded some among you—not all, for that I know—that tithes should not be rendered from your people to Cluniac brothers or to others, and that this should be confirmed by an apostolic privilege. Who could believe that this had been persuaded upon all of you? [Col. 0173A] Who, I say, could believe that those once dead to the world would wish to live for it again? Who could believe that your holy company had despised luxury and worldly delights for Christ, yet now litigates for the sake of want, filth, and misery?

“But,” some among you say, “outsiders ought not to receive tithes from our labors.” I spare the very long replies gathered from divine authorities, which cannot easily be contained in the brevity of a letter [perhaps *possent*, “could be contained”]. I advance only this: that, in the order of justice, modern sons ought to be subject to the ancient fathers; and that it is dangerous for what the Church has hitherto maintained with faith and charity unimpaired to be changed. In the time of the Fathers, not only laypeople but churches pay tithes to churches, monasteries to monasteries, both from the work of peasants and from their own [Col. 0173B] labors.

If, therefore, you exceed these boundaries, what do you do except give detractors occasion for slander? But the matter concerns gain. Yet what gain is that which is considered gain when reputation is injured and charity endangered? For, to confess the truth to brothers and friends, by this one word, as by a single dart, you have pierced alike the hearts of friends and rivals, and stirred bishops, clerics, abbots, monks, and even laypeople themselves, so far as it could reach them, unanimously against you. Nor could Satan find a more useful scheme for his wickedness than to brand with the mark of avarice those whom the world admired, lest, while admiring, it should imitate them; and to draw others away from love of them, spurred by the pain of their injury. [Col. 0173C]

“But poverty,” some among you say, “distresses us.” And where is what the Lord says: “Woe to him through whom scandal comes” (Matt. 18)? And again: “It is better that a millstone be hung about his neck and that he be drowned in the depth of the sea” (ibid.)? Where is what the Apostle says: “I will never eat flesh, lest I cause my brother to stumble” (1 Cor. 8)? Should not this too be your saying: “I will never eat from these tithes, lest I cause my brother to stumble”? The Apostle said this lest he be thought to have eaten food sacrificed to idols. But what will you say, when, to speak without prejudice to brotherly love, no doubtful opinion but the certainty of judgment maintains that you eat what is unlawful?

But perhaps you say that this teaching concerning scandals condemns our people more, [Col. 0173D] because they refuse to distribute to the poorer what is superfluous to them. I concede that the abundance of the richer ought to relieve the need of others. But whether any of us or of you is richer or poorer is neither the time to investigate nor within our capacity to discuss. I ask only this: if the richer man will not give what is his own to the poorer, should the poorer take away what is the richer man’s? Who appears more unjust: the miserly rich man or the violent poor man? Who deserves the greater punishment: one who keeps what is his own, or one who robs what belongs to another?

But, dearest brothers, I say these things not in bitterness of spirit, but as I admonish my most beloved brothers. Nor was I compelled to write these things so much by the gains from tithes as by the losses of souls. For what hope, either for you or for ours, can remain in labors, fasts, vigils, chastity, almsgiving, and the other exercises of sacred works, if charity—as I said above—is removed? [Col. 0174A] Why should I recall the apostolic words which you always keep in mind? Why repeat what you continually ponder? You know what the Apostle says concerning the tongues of men and angels, concerning possessions distributed to the poor, and concerning giving up the body so that it may burn (1 Cor. 13); you know what the Lord himself says concerning a gift offered at the altar (Matt. 5). I touch on these matters only most briefly, so that, when those things which are more worthy are shown to be nothing without charity, all remaining things, which are inferior, may be shown to have absolutely no value without it.

And lest I hold the ears of your holiness too long with lengthier letters, performing an embassy for my flock I both ask and advise: I ask as a suppliant and advise as a friend [Col. 0174B] that in this present question of tithes you provide alike for yourselves and for us—so that you inflict no disgrace upon yourselves, no violence upon us, and do not take away at once from us and from yourselves charity, the sole remedy of Christian souls. Your sacred assembly can find nothing more prudent than not to allow charity, which is God, to perish between us.

## LETTER XXXVI

To the dearest and venerable brothers gathered in Christ’s name at Cîteaux: Brother PETER, humble abbot of the Cluniacs, greeting in that eternal salvation for which they have assembled.

[Col. 0174C]

Several persons have reported to me that the letters which my humility sent to your charity last year injured some among you and somewhat disturbed their minds from the steadfastness of a love no longer new but ancient. When I learned this, I could not bear that the sweetness of so great a charity, maintained so long between us, should be embittered, even slightly, by any occasion whatsoever. Therefore I send this present letter once more, so that, if what I heard is true, the later letter may heal the injury which the first inflicted, and so that, as the bond of the Holy Spirit joins what is separate, however great the rupture of our minds may be, it may be made one.

Let the readers of that first letter consider in what spirit they read it and in what sense they interpreted it. I know that, in composing it—I ask you to accept this statement without any arrogance—I had a spirit not of pride but of [Col. 0174D] humility, not of discord but of peace; and, with him whom I cannot deceive as witness, that I wished in this way to provide for the charity which I saw endangered in our hearts by the occasion of those tithes. And because it is said, “Woe to the sinner who enters the land by two ways” (Ezek. 2), I did not wish, according to the Prophet, to speak “in heart and heart” (Ps. 11), nor, among friends before whom all things ought to be naked, to cover my heart with the veil of duplicity. Rather, I wished your wisdom to see the knot uncovered, so that by the common counsel of those assembled it might labor more effectively to untie it.

This was the entire reason for writing. If it could then scandalize some because it was unknown, now at least, with me revealing it and laying it open, I hope and pray that it may be able fully to satisfy my dearest brothers. [Col. 0175A] For I rest and shall rest in you; I delight and shall delight in you; even when injured, I shall not depart from you. [Col. 0176A] Yet what I so earnestly desire to preserve for you, preserve likewise for our people and for us.

# BOOK TWO

[Col. 0175]

## LETTER ONE

PETER, humble abbot of the Cluniacs, to the dregs of heresies not even to be named.

[Col. 0175A]

Although your brutish folly, profound stupidity, and utter lack of learning persuade me to despise your wandering opinions as unworthy even of a cheap reply, there are nevertheless two considerations which urge my mind, though it recoils from you, to answer you. [Col. 0175B] One is that I am commanded to heal the weak of my flock, strengthen the broken, seek the lost, and fortify the feeble. The other is my fear that simple little sheep joined to you in long cohabitation have been infected by your corruption. Not that you are the kind of person to whom anyone either can or ought to give credence, but because, just as I trust that no one could have been attracted by that foolish and ridiculous speech of yours, so I do not deny that perhaps you have given some incautious people matter for unlawful thoughts through such silly tales.

Thus this short writing, if you are willing to read and able to understand, may either call you back to the salvation from which you have fallen, or perhaps cut away the material of scandal conceived by others. This heresy of yours is extremely ancient, having long ago been devised by a certain erroneous Apollinaris. As soon as it seemed to breathe, it was suffocated by the powerful arguments and innumerable authorities of the Fathers. Since you could neither have these at hand nor perhaps understand them with your brutish mind, I have composed for you this short treatise, sufficiently clear, as I judge, for anyone: so that either, if possible, you may come to your senses from so wicked an opinion by my labor, or, if you have been given over to a reprobate mind, you may perish without danger to me.

And, not to delay the matter further: like a beetle generated from ancient rottenness, you mutter and rasp the ears of the brothers with discordant screeching, saying that our Savior did not possess a human soul, although you do not deny that he possessed the nature of human flesh. It is indeed monstrous to dispute about the faith at this time, when the prince of this world has already been cast out of the world; [Col. 0175D] when Christ already rules from sea to sea; when all have already been made teachable by God, after, according to Isaiah, “the earth has been filled with the knowledge of the Lord, as the waters of the sea cover [the earth]” (Isa. 11); after Satan, persecuting Christ’s faith for a long time through heathen attacks and heretical disputations, has so exhausted the quiver of his wickedness that no arrow remains to him with which he may wound it.

Thus all his fraud has been exposed; thus the deceit of the malignant spirit has, by the disclosure of the Holy Spirit, been brought into the light. Even simple people mock that most deceitful bird as it were; and he who was strongest, now unworthy even to be overcome by men, bound and made subject to God’s handmaids, groans, according to the words of blessed Job (Job 40). If, when you suggested such things, he had found you either a male servant of God or a handmaid, he would have withdrawn easily, defeated by labor as from others, so from you. But because he found you neither, that is, neither man nor woman, the night-thief, breaking down the unguarded doors of your mind, drove you like the vilest beast of burden from the Samaritan’s stable and violently compelled you to run through hollow valleys and over rough mountains. [Col. 0176A]

For this reason, while I endeavor to bring you back to the flock from which you have strayed, I perhaps become presumptuous [Col. 0176B] in seeking to strengthen by my own, as it were, rudimentary arguments that faith which is founded upon Christ, the Son of the living God; foretold by the voices of the prophets; delivered through the ministry of the apostles; consecrated by the blood of martyrs; and celebrated by the fullness of the nations and the rejoicing of angels. But charity, I believe, will excuse my rashness—charity which, if it proceeds from a pure heart, a good conscience, and sincere faith, no iniquity can violate.

Listen, then; and if you are a human being, at least put on human dispositions, so that, if you cannot attend to the things of God, you may at least attend to those things which are yours—that is, the things of a human being.

You recognize, I think, that you are a human being; you understand of what substances you consist. You do not deny that the Son of God descended from heaven to earth and assumed humanity. [Col. 0176C] You say, as do we, that he became man in order to save man. Since these things are so, I challenge you on the ground of your own belief: when the Son of God assumed humanity, did he assume the whole man or half of him? You answer: half. I ask again: when the Son of God saved man, did he save the whole man or half of him? You answer: the whole.

Now at least look, even with bovine eyes, into what abyss your abominable profession has thrown you. You say that the Son of God clothed himself with half a man—that is, flesh alone, without a rational soul—yet saved the whole man, that is, soul and flesh together. What reasoning, then—to say nothing for the moment of the authorities of Scripture—O most foolish of men, what reasoning, I say, permits the Savior to have saved what he did not [Col. 0176D] assume, when the entire rationale of salvation consists in the truth of the assumption? For divinity assumed nothing of humanity except what it purposed to save; nor, conversely, did it purpose to save anything except what it assumed. These two are correlative and cannot be separated from one another: a nature is saved only if it is taken up, and conversely it is taken up only if it is saved.

Thus I cannot sufficiently marvel at your madness and at a mind buried in the deepest stupidity: although you confess that Christ saved the human body and soul, you maintain that he assumed flesh alone. Choose whichever of these alternatives you wish, for whatever you choose, you will be caught by the same noose at my hands. For whatever of man was assumed by God must necessarily have been wholly saved; or whatever was saved must necessarily [Col. 0177A] have been wholly assumed. But I know that you choose the latter: you say that not everything belonging to man was assumed, yet that everything was saved. Therefore, if according to you everything was saved, according to me everything was assumed. For if nothing was saved, nothing was assumed; if something was saved, something was assumed; if the whole was saved, the whole was assumed. Yet, as I said, you concede that the whole was saved. Therefore, whether you wish it or not, compelled by irrefutable reasoning, the whole was assumed.

And if the whole was assumed, the soul, the more worthy part of man, was not excluded. The soul, I say, is more worthy than the flesh. Without it, what else is flesh but a useless trunk? And, that you may understand better how perversely you are foolish, examine what the Creator of both implanted in flesh and what in soul; [Col. 0177B] then perhaps what I wish to suggest will become clear. For the Author of nature, distinguishing the parts of visible and invisible things, confined the manifold infinity of created things within only four kinds, so that he bestowed existence upon some, life upon others, sensation upon those more excellent, and reason upon the best. The latter three and higher qualities he granted to the soul; the first alone, and the basest, he granted to human flesh.

He made the soul living, sentient, and rational, while he bestowed upon the flesh nothing beyond its earthy origin and the fitting harmony of bodily members. And when in the beginning he had thus formed man, taking the matter of his flesh from the earth, and human flesh retained nothing but inactive existence, he breathed into his face [Col. 0177C] the breath of life, “and man became a living soul” (Gen. 2). By this act, flesh received from another what it did not possess from its own substance: the ability to live, feel, and use reason in every respect. Without the soul it would be unable not only to possess these things, but even to preserve long intact that lowly matter which was its own.

For what flesh can do when spiritual substance is removed is demonstrated by human flesh itself when the spirit is absent. If you will not believe this on my reasoning, you will, I suppose, at least believe it on the evidence of your own eyes. How then can it be that, when God assumed man in order to save the whole man, he assumed the part that is the least of man and abandoned that which is incomparably greater? By what order could the highest things be despised and the lowest taken up? By what reasoning [Col. 0177D] could a nature which by itself can neither understand by reason, feel by sensation, nor live any kind of life, be capable of that supreme majesty, when it is evident that no creature can receive the Creator unless it can acknowledge him by intellect, love him by affection, and worship him by voluntary obedience?

And since according to Scripture not the body but the soul of the righteous is called the seat of wisdom; and since God is said, through grace as mediator, to sit, walk, and dwell in holy men only through his image—which is not in the body but in the human soul—what must be thought of that man whom grace alone did not fill, as it fills other saints, but into whom, according to Jerome, “the whole flood of divinity poured itself,” and in whom, according to the Apostle, “all [Col. 0178A] the fullness of divinity dwells” (Col. 2), and whom God himself, personally and wholly, fills wholly—the whole man assumed from the mass of humankind?

Has reason in a rational creature become so dormant that it believes God’s grace is poured into human beings only through the mediation of a rational soul, yet confesses that God himself is personally united forever, with the soul removed, to brute flesh? But why do I labor to explain matters which perhaps you do not understand? Consider the very “man” whom you confess, and you will recognize that you are condemned by your own words. You certainly confess that the Savior is man. But if you confess him to be man, why do you deny man? Why do you not perceive that in the same word you contradict yourself? As I said, you confess man and deny man. You plainly deny man when you deny the soul. For when, foolishly speaking so as to say something in your terms, [Col. 0178B] have you seen a man without a soul? Either show me a man without a soul, or, if you call Christ man, confess that he is man of flesh and soul. Unless “man” is used equivocally, where the name alone is common—as when one speaks of a painted or sculpted man—or synecdochically, as in “a lifeless man,” you cannot by any reasoning call him man whom, by removing the soul, you make a half-man.

See, then, to what extent you have hitherto offered yourself to be deceived by the apostate spirit, and into how many snares of diabolical impiety you have unknowingly entangled yourself: you deny in Christ that substance whose removal does not merely take away a part of the faith, but at once destroys the whole truth of human restoration. For if Christ did not have a human soul, then he either had a beastly soul, or divinity itself—as I have perceived that you think—performed the offices of a living and sentient spirit. Each alternative is so abhorrent in its equal absurdity that whoever thinks either of Christ can no longer be a Christian.

For if I say that he had a beastly soul, I shall confess that, in respect of soul, he was a beast. But who, even among unbelievers, could bear to hear Christ called a beast? Once this is granted, Christ will be a beast and, like a beast, will lack human reason. But if he lacked human reason, who will defend the truth of our faith, the hope of human salvation, or the authority of the heavenly writings? For the Gospel says: “Jesus advanced in wisdom, [Col. 0178D] age, and grace before God and men” (Luke 2). It also says: “Jesus, full of the Holy Spirit, returned from the Jordan” (Luke 4). And the prophet says: “The Spirit of the Lord shall rest upon him: the spirit of wisdom and understanding, the spirit of counsel and strength, the spirit of knowledge and piety; and the spirit of the fear of the Lord shall fill him” (Isa. 11). And another says: “God, your God, has anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Ps. 44). Likewise the apostle Peter: “God,” he says, “anointed him with the Holy Spirit and power” (Acts 10).

The increase in age, according to the order of nature, by which an animate and sentient body gradually grows, is also granted by a brute soul—which is living and sentient—to the bodies of dumb animals. If such a soul were also in Christ, it could bestow the same upon his flesh. But could it advance in wisdom and grace before God and men? Could it return from the Jordan full of the Holy Spirit? Shall we confess that the spirit of wisdom, understanding, counsel, strength, knowledge, piety, and fear of the Lord rested upon a beastly soul [Col. 0179A] and filled it with such great gifts of grace? Shall we say that, according to the Prophet, it was anointed with the oil of gladness—that is, according to the Apostle, with the Holy Spirit and power—above its companions, that is, above all chosen human beings?

Certainly the things I have mentioned, and countless others I have passed over, must be attributed either to the flesh, to the soul, or to the Savior’s divinity. For no heretic has dared, or could devise, that anything else existed in Christ besides these three. But who can give these things to flesh alone, which is incapable, as said above, of receiving in itself not merely the Holy [Col. 0179B] Spirit, but even an aerial spirit? And who will attribute to divinity an advance in wisdom and grace, or an increase of other virtues? Divinity can neither be diminished by losses nor increased by any gains—unless he is one who “sets his mouth against heaven” and is impiously blasphemous against God.

With these two substances excluded, there remains the beastly soul of which I was speaking. Who does not see that it could not receive these gifts, since it is certainly altogether devoid of reason? For that which cannot discern the causes of temporal things is shown to be still more powerless and incapable concerning eternal and divine things. But if neither flesh alone, nor a beastly soul, nor the substance of divinity could, because nature forbids it, receive in itself those gifts of the Spirit, it follows necessarily that a rational soul joined to flesh received them.

Now that the beastly soul has been excluded from the Savior, it remains for me to pursue the remaining part of the division set out above. Lest it escape notice, I repeat the division which secular learning calls disjunctive: I said, “If Christ did not have a human soul, he either had a beastly soul, or divinity itself performed the offices of a living and sentient spirit.” But since it has, I think, been proved that he did not have a beastly soul, it must now be proved that divinity did not perform the offices of a soul.

For if divinity performed the offices of a soul in Christ’s body, it made the body living and sentient; that is, Christ’s flesh received from divinity the power to live and feel. For every soul, as has often [Col. 0179C] been said, gives the body the power to live and feel. Divinity, therefore, in place of a soul gave Christ’s body the power to live and feel. If this is so, since the soul feels and suffers through the body, and the body from the soul, then whatever Christ’s flesh suffered, divinity too must have suffered along with it.

How wide the field of blasphemy thereby opens, anyone may perceive, even if I say nothing. For, as has been said, whatever the flesh feels or suffers, the soul feels or suffers through it; therefore divinity, which is said to hold the place of the soul, must feel and suffer through the flesh. Divinity, then, will suffer the sorrows of infancy and the toils of childhood; Bread will hunger, the Fountain thirst, Strength grow weary, Rest labor, Joy become sad; and at last the impassible will be tortured with most cruel torments, the eternal will fail, [Col. 0180A] Life will die.

All these things, indeed, Catholics confess that God suffered through man. But it is one thing, because of the union in one person, to say that God suffered human things in man; it is another to say that anything of pain or injury could be suffered in the impassible nature itself. The latter is maintained by one who says that God existed in a human body in place of a soul. Since there is no need to dwell upon what is obvious, the matter must be concluded briefly. Either God was in the flesh of the assumed man in place of a soul, and therefore succumbed to human sufferings; or, if it is impious and detestable to think this, Christ’s flesh must be believed to have possessed a soul which suffered human things without injury to divinity. And since it has been proved that he did not possess a beastly soul, it must be confessed that he possessed none but a rational soul.

Having set forth these arguments concerning the Savior’s [Col. 0180B] rational soul—arguments able, I believe, either to satisfy rational minds or to expose beastly minds to the ridicule of others—let the authority of Scripture now be brought forward, which holds the chief place in divine doctrines. Thus by the twofold remedy of reason and authority, if one is unbelieving he may necessarily yield to reason, or, if believing, he may acquiesce in the sacred authorities.

It is indeed astonishing how a deaf heresy could ever arise, since prophetic, evangelical, and apostolic speech speaks of the Savior’s soul as plainly as of his flesh, with such equal and almost unceasing cry that one who does not hear it seems either to have no ears or to have stopped them like a venomous asp. Does not David, [Col. 0180C] speaking in Christ’s own person, say: “You will not abandon my soul to hell” (Ps. 15)? And: “Deliver, O God, my soul from the sword, and my only one from the hand of flesh” (Ps. 21)—words concerning his Passion; and: “My soul shall live for him” (ibid.)—concerning the resurrection; and: “Into your hands I commend my spirit” (Ps. 30)—a spirit which in man is nothing other than the soul. Isaiah too says: “Because he delivered his soul to death” (Isa. 43); and Jeremiah: “They dug a pit for my soul” (Jer. 18).

Does not the Lord in the Gospel make almost continual mention of his soul, saying: “I have power to lay down my soul and to take it again” (John 10); and: “No one takes my soul from me, but [Col. 0180D] I lay it down and take it again” (ibid.); and: “Now my soul is troubled” (John 12); and: “My soul is sorrowful unto death” (Matt. 26); and: “No one has greater love than this: that someone lay down his soul for his friends” (John 15); and: “I lay down my soul for my sheep” (John 10)? And whose recollection could enumerate all such passages? These suffice, and more than suffice, to demonstrate, even to blind persons feeling their way, both that Christ had a soul and that it was rational.

To take up rather the principal—that is, the evangelical—points: when the Savior says that his soul is troubled and sorrowful, he denies that divinity, to which the accidents of disturbance or sorrow cannot apply, stood in place of a soul; when he says that he has power to lay down [Col. 0181A] his soul and take it again, he declares that it could in no way have been irrational. Brute animals can indeed lay down an irrational soul by dying; but they cannot take it up again, because after the body there is no continuing substance of such a soul. For the spirit that fails after the flesh has no return to the flesh, because in dying it underwent a common extinction with the flesh.

It is characteristic of irrational spirits never to subsist apart from their own body, whereas rational spirits never fail even after the body. For the Creator has implanted in rational substance a certain image or likeness of divinity, which, whether blessed or miserable, must nevertheless always be eternal. Since this is not present in a beastly spirit, it must perish together with its body. Thus the soul laid down in death by the good Shepherd for the sheep could not be resumed if it had not existed after death; nor could it have subsisted after death unless it had been rational, as a human soul is.

What else, moreover, does that utterance of the crucified Lord—which I cited above from the Psalm—indicate when he says, “Father, into your hands I commend my spirit” (Luke 23)? Does it not, in few words, hurl down at one blow every opinion of such errors and, with one stroke of the sword, cut off the upraised neck that brings common ruin? For he did not commend to the Father a spirit which would have no existence after death, nor did he entrust divinity, which receives neither less nor more, is equal to the Father in all respects, and needs no commendation. With these theories of the two spirits—[Col. 0181C] the beastly and the divine—set aside, it remains that he commended to the Father the spirit, namely the rational soul, and, as the Gospel says, “bowing his head, gave it up” (John 19).

And if the argument turns to the Apostles’ Creed, every Christian tongue confesses that the Lord Jesus Christ died, was buried, and descended to the lower regions. Since he did not descend in the flesh, [Col. 0182A] this is indicated by the body’s three-day burial. Nor did he descend in the nature of divinity alone, as invincible reason makes plain.
