For it is written that he struck the proud one by wisdom, not by power; he would have struck him by power alone if, intending to strike the condemned archangel, he had descended into hell in divinity alone. But it was fitting—and the eternal counsel required it—that the proud prince of this world should be conquered by the nature which he had conquered, and, being often defeated, lose the boasting of his deceitful victory; and that, just as human flesh had triumphed over him through Christ on earth, so human soul might triumph over him through Christ in the lower regions.

## LETTER II

To the venerable lord PETER, archbishop of the holy Church of Lyons, most eminent in the members of Christ’s body:

[Note: [Col. 0181D] “To the lord Peter, archbishop of the holy Church of Lyons.” He writes to him also below, in Letter 18, where he calls Peter patriarch of the Church of Lyons. He had been transferred from the Church of Viviers to Lyons in 1131 and, dying shortly afterwards during an overseas pilgrimage, had Falcon as his successor in the archbishopric, as William of Tyre, himself an archbishop, states. Saint Bernard of Clairvaux confirms this: writing back to Pope Innocent II in Letter 172, he says: “The Lord looked down from heaven upon our mother Church of Lyons; upon the death of Peter, archbishop of pious memory, he peacefully appointed as his successor the excellent man Falcon, the dean.”]

Brother PETER, humble abbot of Cluny, wishes him the spirit of counsel and strength.

[Col. 0182B]

From the time when my humility was granted to recognize, venerable one most dear to me, the exalted eminence of your high station, my soul has clung to you with the most tenacious bond of affection, as I believe you do not fail to know. As the conscience which deceives no one bears witness to me, I loved in you neither the dignity of a prelate, nor the riches of a rich man, nor the power of a powerful man; nor any abundance of temporal goods whatever which might surround you. I did not love, I say, all those things which seemed to be about you, but only those things which I had recognized in you and which alone deserved to be loved in you. I loved in you purity of mind toward divine things, [Col. 0182C] integrity of conduct toward human things, love of true wisdom, and, amid the height of episcopal rank, the sincere moderation of your life. Drawn by these and many other great virtues of your soul, even when you were far away I was with you, nor could I be torn from you even for the smallest span of time.

But after divine providence transferred you from the hill of Viviers [Note: [Col. 0181D] “After you were transferred from the hill of the Vivarii.” Vivarium of the Albenses—or Eluenses, who are also called Helvii—is a city on the Rhône: Viviers. It is mentioned in the *Notitia provinciarum Galliae* under First Viennese Province in these words: “City of the Albenses, now Vivarium.” This is how the manuscripts read, not, as in the printed editions, the corrupt reading: “City of the Albenses, that is, Belisio.”

Nor should one pass over something hitherto noted by few: the episcopal seat of Viviers was first at Alba Helviorum, today called Aubenas, in the diocese of Viviers. In Ptolemy it is Ἀλβαύγουστα Ἑλικωκίων, “Albaugusta of the Helicocians,” that is, of the Helvii; in Sidonius, *Letter* 12, Book VI, it is *the city of Alba*. But when that city was eventually destroyed by the Vandals, the episcopal see was transferred to Vivarion, or Vivarium. Hence Pope Paschal II confuses the two insofar as the bishopric is concerned, when he writes to Guy, archbishop of Vienne: “Alba, which is also called Vivarium.”

Viviers is also mentioned by Gregory of Tours, Book X, chapter 24, who reports that the cities of Viviers and Avignon were severely devastated by an outbreak of bubonic plague; and by Usuard under the Kalends of May, where he testifies that in Gaul, in the territory of Viviers, the blessed subdeacon Andeolus is commemorated, whom Saint Polycarp had sent from the East to preach the word of God.] to the hill of Lyons [Note: [Col. 0182D] “To the hill of Lyons.” Lyons in Gaul is a city situated on a hill or mountain. Gregory of Tours, in Book I of his *History of the Franks*, chapter 18, testifies that he most clearly found it “founded in the nineteenth year of Augustus’ reign by Lucius Plancus, later made illustrious by the blood of martyrs, and called most noble.”

Yet Plutarch, in his book *On the Names of Rivers and Mountains*, teaches both that it was founded long before Lucius Plancus and that it was first named *Lugdolon* from another and more probable cause. He writes: [Col. 0183D] “Beside the Arar is Mount Lugdulus, so called because when Momorus and Atepomarus, deprived of authority by Seseron, wished in obedience to an oracle to found a city upon it, ravens suddenly appeared as the foundations were being excavated and, spreading their wings, occupied the trees round about. Hence Momorus, skilled in augury, named the city Lugdolon. For *lougon* in their native language means ‘raven,’ and *doulon* means ‘eminent,’ according to Clitophon, Book XIII of *Foundations*.”

And indeed I wonder whether *Lugdunum* may not be derived still more aptly from *lougon*, “raven,” and *dunum*, which in the ancient language of the Gauls signifies a mountain or elevated place. For Diodorus Siculus, who suggests that Lucius Plancus restored rather than founded it, declares in Book XVI that *Lougoudunum* had formerly, in the old Gallic language, been called “Mount Raven,” when he says:

> Ἵνα τε μηδὲν ὑποτυπήσωσι κᾀκ τούτου τ` κακουργήσωσιν, ἐκέλευσαν αὐτοῖς τοὺς ἐκ Οὐϊέννης τῆς Ναρβωνησίας, ὑπὸ τῶν Ἀλλοβρόγων ποτὲ ἐκπεσόντας, καὶ ἐζ τὸ μεταξὺ τοῦτε Ῥοδανοῦ καὶ τοῦ Ἀράρίδος, ᾗ συμμίγνυνται ἀλλήλοις, ἱδρυθέντας συνοικίσαι, καὶ οὕτως ἐκεῖνοι ὑπομείναντες, τὸ Λουγούδουνον μὲν ὀνομασθὲν [Col. 0184D] νῦν δὲ λούγδουνον καλούμενον, ἔκτισαν.

That is: “So that they should not suspect any hostile intent—namely Lepidus and Lucius Plancus—and commit some misdeed, the senators ordered those who had once been expelled by the Allobroges from Vienne, a town in Narbonensian Province, and had settled where the Rhône and Arar meet, to found a city. So they remained there and built Lyons, which formerly had been called *Lougoudunum* [or *Lugudunum*].”

Although Eric, a monk of Saint-Germain of Auxerre, gives yet another etymology for this name in Book IV of *The Life of the Already Mentioned Saint Germanus*, maintaining that Lucdunum was called by the Gauls, as it were, “bright mountain,” in these verses:

> The Saône, in its even course, bore itself to the citadels of Lyons,  
> hiding itself beneath the walls in the Rhône.  
> The Gauls recount that the name Lucdunum  
> was once given in their speech, because it is likewise a bright mountain.

But however the matter may stand, it is clear from these observations both that the city of Lyons is older than Lucius Plancus and that our Peter very appropriately used “the hill of the people of Lyons” for the city of Lyons itself.]

and made you more exalted from exalted, you began indeed to be nearer in place; but would that you had in no way become more distant in spirit! Let not the wisdom which I venerate in you be surprised that I have said this. For I spoke not from the feeling of one complaining, but from the precaution of one offering warning. Although I know that your prudence is not easily moved by every whisper and that you are not carried about with the mobility of a reed, yet because it is written, “Evil conversations corrupt good morals” (1 Cor. 15), and because the verse which has now become proverbial says:

> Water hollows a stone, not by force, but by falling often,

I think you must guard against heedlessly lending—not the ear of the body, which [Col. 0183B] you sometimes cannot help doing, but the ear of the heart, which you always can control—to wicked lips and the whisperings of a deceitful tongue, by which you are frequently disturbed.

For by a fraudulent show of service such persons often ensnare the hearts of their masters through anxious importunity; under the appearance of advisers, while serving enemies, they act more harmfully as enemies. Indeed, they are worse than enemies because, as your wisdom well knows, an external enemy is much more easily avoided than an internal one, a distant enemy than one close at hand, and a fierce enemy much more readily than a flattering one. The cruelty of the former can harm so much the less because less credence is given to him. But the concealed cruelty of the latter harms so much the more because it is granted greater liberty to rage beneath the covering of love.

I wished to say this so that the care taken to preserve mutual love between us, my dearest friend, might become more watchful, [Col. 0183C] and that the envy of any detractor might not be able to turn it from its purpose. For if what the Apostle says is true, “Love never fails” (1 Cor. 13), and if what is read in the Song of Songs is true, “Many waters cannot quench love, neither can floods overwhelm it” (Song 8), and if it is evident that this love has existed between us until now, then it is certain that it can neither fall by failing nor have its flame extinguished by a multitude of waters—that is, of people muttering evil things—nor be overwhelmed by the pressure of any persons, like the violence of a mighty flood.

No reason compels me to state more openly what I intended in cautiously prefacing these remarks. The subtlety of your intelligence can easily perceive it, and I ought to spare the shame or anger of those who might be offended by being identified in this matter. It is enough to know that in all these things I aim at this one end: that through the love which joins things unlike, we may remain united in what we have already begun to be, so that neither difference of places, nor division of hearts, nor diversity of tongues, nor the changing outcomes of events can divide our unity, by which we are truly united in God; nor may the instability of the shifting and passing world tear it from its own stability and firmness.

For this one and only end I particularly and especially desire that this unity of love between us be strengthened: [Col. 0184B] that we may seek to direct its usefulness not only to our own salvation but also to that of many others. For if this virtue, which I call love, is truly what it is said to be, it ought to watch not so much for its own salvation as for that of others, and labor for it in every way; because, as everyone knows, the Apostle says of it: “Love does not seek its own things” (1 Cor. 13).

Although this obligation rests upon all, as debtors under the command that enjoins them, “You shall love your neighbor as yourself” (Lev. 19; Matt. 22), and they should all provide for others equally as for themselves, it rests most especially upon those to whom the care of others has particularly been entrusted, to whom, as guardians of sheep, children, or citizens, the names of shepherd, father, and watchman have been given. Among these your holy fatherhood holds, by God’s appointment, no small place, indeed a great and preeminent one: among all the spiritual rulers of the Christian people you have no superior whatsoever except the bishop of the holy and supreme Apostolic See.

Great, I say, truly lofty, and wholly heavenly is the dignity of the episcopal office; and no less great, truly fearful, and wholly terrible is the dread of episcopal peril. For, as your pastoral vigilance well recalls, the Lord says to you through Ezekiel: “Son of man, I have made you a watchman for the house of Israel” (Ezek. 3). And again: [Col. 0185A] “If you do not announce his iniquity to the wicked man, I will require his blood from your hand” (ibid.). And again: “If the watchman sees the sword coming and does not cry out, and the sword comes and takes someone away, I will require his blood from the watchman’s hand” (Ezek. 33). And through Jeremiah: “Behold, today I have appointed you over nations and kingdoms, to uproot and destroy, to ruin and scatter, to build and plant” (Jer. 1). I could weave together an endless work from similar testimonies; but since I speak to one who is wise and knows all such things, it was fitting to offer a few out of many.

But to what end are all these things? That your pastoral vigilance may be stirred to assist the Church of God suffering under your care, especially at this time, [Col. 0185B] when the dangerous times foretold by the Apostle are at hand (2 Tim. 3); when all seek their own things, not those of Jesus Christ (Phil. 2); when among many hirelings scarcely a shepherd is found; when, scorning the salvation of the flock and without pastoral labor, they hanker after pastoral wages. God reproaches them through the prophet: “You ate the milk and clothed yourselves with the wool, but you did not feed my flock” (Ezek. 34); and again: “Woe to the shepherds who fed themselves” (ibid.); and again: “Behold, I am against the shepherds, and I will deliver my flock so that it may not be a prey for them, and the shepherds shall no longer feed themselves” (ibid.).

Truly they are hirelings, not shepherds: fattened and adorned by the flock’s wages, walking about in splendor, appearing glorious and exalted, delighting to be greeted, honored, and called Rabbi by men; loving, according to the Lord’s saying, the chief places at banquets and the first seats in synagogues (Matt. 12); seeing the wolf come to destroy the sheep and fleeing; seeing sheep perish infected by the corruption of pestilential air and giving no aid; seeing them consumed by mutual contagion and keeping silent; seeing them die by diverse kinds of death and laughing.

But since it is not the purpose of the present work, nor my office, to deal now with such persons, this discourse must be checked, and I must instead continue with you what I began. For I believe that God has established you at such a time upon the lofty watchtower of the Church so that, while others are silent, you may almost alone proclaim to the world the things of God; [Col. 0185D] that, placed among the leaders of the spiritual battle, while others flee you may with a few defeat the enemy; that, distinguished by the title not only of bishop but of primate or patriarch [Note: [Col. 0185D] “Not only with the title of bishop, but of primate or patriarch.” The title *primate* arose from the chief provinces, whose metropolitans were primates over the remaining provinces of the same designation. Thus, after various disputes with Sens, the archbishop of Lyons was finally declared and pronounced by Gregory VII to be primate of the four provinces of Lyons—that is, Lyons, Rouen, Tours, and Sens—as is evident from Gregory’s Letters 35 and 36, Book VI. We have already said something elsewhere on this matter.]—you may recognize yourself as not only greater than the people but also the leader of the rulers themselves, and may strive rather to benefit all than to rule over them.

“Gird your sword upon your thigh, O most mighty one” (Ps. 44). Let your zeal be kindled like fire. Remember Phinehas, Elijah, and Jesus Christ: the first killed the sexually wanton with the sword (Num. 25); the second burned the proud with heavenly fire (3 Kings 18); the third drove the avaricious from the Temple with a whip (Matt. 21). These are surely the three things which the apostle John mentions in his Epistle: “All that is in the world,” he says, “is the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the ambition of the world” (1 John 2). Though, according to this apostolic saying, these have infected the whole world with a common plague, in your patriarchate—but especially in the province, or, what ought to be more alarming to you, in your own diocese—they seem to have established a special seat for themselves and seized countless persons with their deadly disease.

But why should I speak of soldiers or laypeople, [Col. 0186B] when I see clerics—and, what grieves me more, men of our own, that is, monastic, order—forgetful of their profession, greedily seeking, even more than laypeople, what they seemed to have left behind; returning from the tent of God and Moses their leader to Pharaoh and Egypt; eagerly swallowing back what they had vomited, like the most unclean dogs; and those who should have shone like gold in the house of God casting themselves down like vile mud, to be trampled beneath everyone’s feet in every street?

Is Jeremiah not compelled to lament such people and say: “How the gold has grown dim; how its finest color has changed! The stones of the sanctuary are scattered at the head of every street” (Lam. 4). And again: “How have the glorious sons of Zion, clothed in finest gold, been accounted as earthen vessels, the work of a potter’s hands?” (ibid.)

Indeed, I speak thus of almost all the monks and monasteries of the province entrusted to you by God—with due allowance for the good men who live among them. They say that they are monks, but they are not; rather, they are the synagogue of Satan (Rev. II). For what do they claim for themselves from the monk except the name and habit? Where in them either exists or appears a monk’s humility? Where is charity? Where is that poverty which makes men blessed? I say “which makes men blessed” because, while they greatly desire to become rich, they suffer greatly from that poverty which makes men wretched. And rightly so. For as those who seek the Lord lack no good thing (Ps. XXXIII), so those who forsake him [Col. 0186D] must necessarily abound in every evil.

Such men call themselves monks—that is, solitary and unique in the world—although in heart and deed they mingle with crowds and human tumult. They assert that they live the apostolic, that is, the common life, although, apart from food and clothing, all else is held by them in common. Yet it is a great thing, among such people, if they use a church, refectory, and dormitory in common: so that it is not the hearts of those chanting but the church that is one; not the food of those eating but the refectory [Col. 0187A] that is common; not the garments in the dormitory but the dormitory itself that is shared. I grant that even this is a great thing among such men. But would that even this were preserved! Would that they all at least lived in the same houses and did not choose, for feasting or dwelling, the houses of others who are strangers both to themselves and to their order!

I pass over what follows, sparing them less than I spare my own shame; for I blush to utter such things, and I seek to protect the holy name of our order. Although that name is stained by no contagion of the unclean, yet through the ill repute of such persons, those less instructed are scandalized and the Lord’s name is blasphemed. Thus Scripture speaks also of them: “Woe to those through whom the name of the Lord is blasphemed” (Isa. XLII). For through whom, if not through these, is the Lord’s name [Col. 0187B] blasphemed? In hypocrisy they wish to feign every kind of holiness, but can no longer do so because they cannot remain hidden; they become public apostates. Following the image of the prostitute, they spread their legs to every passer-by, and in perverse obedience bend their backs to malignant spirits commanding, “Bend down, that we may pass over” [cf. Isa. LI].

Fickle, unstable, headlong, proud, desirous, avaricious: their profession is transgression; their stability, wandering about; their conversion of manners, turning away from God; their obedience, stubbornness; their cloister, the whole world; their god, the belly; their abbot, their own will; their yoke, none at all; their mortification, every kind of fleshly delight. By evil living they profane places consecrated to God; they make the house of prayer a den [Col. 0187C] of robbers (Matt. XXI). There, by ruinous deeds, they sacrifice to the devil not calves or rams but their own souls, professing that they know God but denying him by their deeds. These are unfruitful trees, uselessly occupying the ground, worthy to be cut down, worthy to be burned; most wicked tenants of the vineyard, scorning to render its fruit in due season and unjustly holding the Son’s inheritance.

It must be done to them as the Gospel says that the householder did to evil husbandmen: “He will miserably destroy those wicked men and will lease his vineyard to other husbandmen, who will render him the fruit in its seasons” (Matt. XXI). Thus you, who hold the place of this householder, must deal with such men: if they refuse to render to the Lord the fruits of righteousness from the Lord’s vineyard, you must by no means permit them to occupy his [Col. 0187D] inheritance. For these evils have become so inveterate and hardened, to the full measure of their destruction, by an overgrown callus that they can now neither hear words of correction nor feel even the harshest blows of discipline. They are the scales on Leviathan’s body, concerning which it is said: “One is joined to another, and not even a breath passes through them” (Job LI). One will cling to another, and those that hold together will by no means be separated.

Yet the harder sword of God’s word can divide this most wicked unity and hardness of the devilish body, and the sharper arrow of the spiritual quiver can pierce it. The Apostle speaks of this sword: “The sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (Eph. VI). And the prophet says of the arrow: “He made me like a chosen arrow [Col. 0188A]; he hid me in his quiver” (Isa. LIX). This arrow—namely, you, venerable and most beloved Father—God has from eternity hidden in the quiver of his counsel until these times; and now, we believe, he has sent you forth from the bow of his strength to crush his enemies. He has placed in your mouth the sword, that is, his word, which, according to the Apostle, is not bound (II Tim. II), and concerning which it is said: “Cursed be he who withholds his sword from blood” (Jer. XLVIII). With this sword, according to the Psalmist, the tongues of the wicked, and iniquities and contradictions in the city, are divided (Ps. LIV).

Therefore consecrate again to the Lord your hands, once consecrated in the priesthood. For, according to blessed Gregory, no sacrifice is offered to God more pleasing than zeal against [Col. 0188B] sin. Let the nobility of your holy soul be ashamed that the province entrusted to you, superior in ecclesiastical dignity to all the Gallican Churches, should be inferior in religious life. For, as may be seen, throughout the whole western region—and especially within our Gaul—religious houses arise in great number, even where none had ever existed, and those which had grown old are renewed. In the province of Lyons, by contrast, scarcely any new houses have arisen, and hardly any of the old remain.

May this have been reserved by God for your time and energy: if you lack the means to found new houses, let there at least be every effort and will to renew the old. For this work you will have all the assistance that my ability can possibly provide, and God, who suffices for you in [Col. 0188C] all things. Let it be yours, having received his grace, to begin; it will be his work to bring to completion what has been begun by you. Although I do not fail to recognize that this undertaking is exceedingly arduous, nevertheless, trusting in God’s grace and your proven character, I exhort, beseech, admonish, and entreat you through the mercy of almighty Jesus Christ that no cares may drive from your heart so good, so pleasing to God, so saving an undertaking. Rather, let the root of holy purpose remain in your mind until it comes forth into the desired fruit of glorious action.

For I too lack no countless temporal anxieties, on account of which, as is customary, I might necessarily trouble your Blessedness. But I now have no question concerning gold and silver; no customary appeal reaches the ears of your Majesty concerning injuries, plundering, burnings, and the various and manifold [Col. 0188D] losses of our property. This one matter—this singular and chief matter, which must be spoken of often and requested often—I beg, ask, and entreat: subordinate everything to this divine cause, to which nothing human ought, I do not say to be preferred, but not even compared. Spend even yourself, if necessary, like a good shepherd, for the salvation of so many and such great sheep.

I too am ready—though this concerns me not from duty but from charity—to spare neither my possessions nor myself for God’s cause; hoping for no present reward, I am prepared to expend not only what is mine but myself. This, certainly, was the whole and sole reason for writing to you. It remains for you to see that it is not in vain. Therefore, at the end of my letter, I beg your love, most sweet to me and to be embraced with all my inmost affection [Col. 0189A], to set aside your occupations somewhat and make room also for the letter of a friend solicitous for you, providing even an hour to read it attentively. Repay, I say, this return to my labor: what I could scarcely write amid the immoderate distractions of my cares, strive to read amid your daily tumults. Let not its length deter you from reading, for it has been produced by a necessity which, as you yourself recognize, is just.

## LETTER III

To the supreme shepherd of God’s Church and our special Father, lord Pope INNOCENT, Brother PETER, humble abbot of Cluny, faithful obedience.

I cannot adequately express in words how anxiously, because of the love for your fatherhood implanted in me, I anxiously seek news [Col. 0189B] of your condition, and how I long to hear from your regions something that will gladden my heart. What could gladden it more than to hear that you live prosperously, peacefully, and triumphantly? To state what I feel: this desire rules over every other desire that can exist in the human heart, so that, excepting only the longing by which heavenly things are desired, it holds first place among all desires.

Nor is it surprising that I so ardently long for the end of your labors, since for this one purpose, from the beginning of your apostolate, I have refused no labor within my capacity; I have spared neither myself nor what had been entrusted to me whenever it was expedient; and—what may perhaps be greater than all this—I have never failed to be, as I [Col. 0189C] myself know best, as faithful a son as I could truly be to a Father. For amid party conflicts, divisions of heart, and schisms among both our own people and outsiders, whether near or far away, I have always stood with sword drawn, so far as the character of my person or office permitted; nor, when necessary, did I ever withhold it from the blood even of those dearest to me.

Whomever I knew to be bound to me and to the Church of Cluny by any friendship—kings and princes, noble and lowly, great and small—I did not delay, by myself or through others, through speech, writing, messages, threats, and persuasion, to bring them beneath the feet of your Majesty as far as I could. But since I did not begin in order to boast of any works of mine that have been upright toward you, my pen [Col. 0189D] must be restrained. This alone must be said: I have touched on these matters so that your wisdom may recognize that I rightly desire your peace, for which I have had occasion to labor greatly.

There is also this, which should move not only me but everyone to desire it: the peace of all and of the whole Church depends upon your peace. Just as the Church, generally speaking, with the exception of a few schismatics, has received you as supreme shepherd, so it can never rest without your repose. You owe no small gratitude to her for the labors she endures for Christ and for you—if I may say this without prejudice to the reverence due to your Sublimity—for as she offers you filial love, so it is fitting that you show her paternal love.

And, as it seems to me, all indeed [Col. 0190A] are to be loved by the Lord’s command; but according as their life or deeds require, some are to be preferred to others in the discernment of love. Let your fatherhood, dearer to us than gold and topaz, consider for a moment why I say this. Among those to whom your charity is more especially indebted for every affection and favor, we have until now counted Lord Alban, bishop. I forbear to recount what he has done, endured, and lost for you; how faithfully, in coming and going throughout the kingdom of the Church over which you preside, he has acted at your command. Your wisdom knows this well; and his long illness—indeed, death itself, from whose gates he was scarcely at last brought back—can sufficiently indicate it. It is evident to all, unless I am mistaken, that he suffered all this because of immense labors and continual journeys and expeditions through almost the whole [Col. 0190B] world in your service.

Since, therefore, he has expended himself wholly for you; since his religious character, learning, and physical strength have been known to all; since from the beginning of your pontificate they have served only you, and have almost failed in serving you: I, who am wholly yours—I say, wholly yours—and those who know this with me, cannot sufficiently wonder that he has deserved to receive not, I will not say a great favor for such great services, but not even a small reply when he especially requested one. Then certainly—this we say in a wholly submissive and humble, and therefore bold, spirit—the bowels of your mercy and response were entirely closed to him precisely when he opened to you as Father all the innermost matters of his conscience. Then [Col. 0190C] the abundance of the spring was truly dried up when the dryness of the land most required watering.

In my view, a conscience laid bare ought to have earned more love; former favor ought not to have been diminished because the veil over the heart was removed. To cite what has now become proverbial: if among friends all things are naked, between such a Father and such a son no secrets ought to have remained veiled. If he had disclosed these matters to others and not to you alone, a Father’s displeasure might perhaps have been justified. But since he bared his heart only to the one from whom he ought to have concealed nothing of this kind, he ought, it seems, to have earned not anger but greater favor.

Dearest Father, filial and therefore faithful affection compelled me to write this briefly, lest those who deserve more from you seem to obtain less [Col. 0190D], and lest very many thereby be deterred from serving you. I advise you, then—if you judge my counsel worthy to be admitted among the counsels of wiser, though perhaps not more faithful, men—to strive without delay, by sending a letter, to soothe your bishop, your associate, your most faithful servant, whom by this matter you could have greatly embittered, had not wisdom restrained his indignation.

Remember that no one can ever be loved too much; remember that no one has ever had too many friends; remember Solomon’s words: “Let your friends be many” (Ecclus. VI). Therefore never think that you have enough of such men—especially in this time when, as you experience every day, iniquity has abounded and the charity of many has grown cold. After recovering his health, he had [Col. 0191A] prepared, in obedience to your command, to return to you. But after receiving that silence from you, not knowing what it portended, he too resolved to remain silent.

Let, then, that fruitless silence—which ought never to have existed—be broken. Either have him return to you with the honor fitting for both you and him; or have him remain with us—that is, within Gaul—by your authority, until it pleases you to recall him, in order to overthrow the schismatics and support your cause, which is also God’s cause. This is more expedient for you and the Roman Church at present than we can say because of the urgency of the matter. Would that leisure were granted to your ears! Since they do not now have it, we are compelled to impose silence on our mouths even concerning matters that are most necessary.

Therefore reply concerning this [Col. 0191B] matter and concerning your peace, which I desire in every way and await with longing, telling me how things stand, so that, if it exists, I may rejoice; or, if it does not yet fully exist, I may expend whatever I can—even myself—to bring it to completion. I ask also that, for our sake, you break the Roman custom of retaining messengers for a long time, and send our courier back to us as soon as possible with certainty concerning the matter requested.

## LETTER IV

PETER, humble abbot of Cluny, to GILO, formerly bishop of Tusculum. [Col. 0191D]

> [Note: “To Gilo, formerly bishop of Tusculum.” He is also addressed below in Letter 30 of this book. He was first a monk of Cluny, then became cardinal bishop of Tusculum. He schismatically supported the party of Peter Leonis against Innocent II; and, having been sent by him to Girard, bishop of Angoulême, he stirred up numerous disturbances in Aquitaine, as Abbot William teaches in Book II, chapter 6, of the *Life of St Bernard*. Hence John of Paris, in his historical memorial for the year 1136: “At that time the whole province of Bordeaux labored under the oppression of the schismatics, and there was no one in all Aquitaine able to resist the prince, whose heart God had hardened. Persuaded by Girard, bishop of Angoulême, who dripped seeds of dissension into his heart, he had become the defender and author of schism. This Girard sent to Peter Leonis, asking him to grant him a legation, and promising that he himself would obey him under sworn fidelity. Moreover, he promised that he would bring the prince of the land, and whomever else he could, under his authority. The utterly ruined man rejoiced that he had found a place in which to spread his malice; he quickly and gladly agreed, and sent to him Gilo, cardinal bishop of Tusculum, who alone among the Romans, with Peter of Porto, adhered to him. By these two William, bishop of Poitiers, an honorable and Catholic man, was violently driven from his see; and another man, noble in birth but degenerate in faith, was intruded in his place. Likewise, in the Church of Limoges they intruded a certain Radulf of Dorat, who not long afterward fell backward from his horse on a level road, and, when a single avenging stone struck his head and his brain was shattered, expired.”]
>

The enormity of the subject indeed commands me [Col. 0191C] to say much to your affection; but the measure of letters, and especially of modern letters, constrains the pen as it seeks to expand, lest it overflow even in necessary matters. If it were not held back from what I have proposed and necessarily conceived, not a letter but a book would result. For who does not see how great is the matter for speech—or rather, for lamentation? A most dear brother, and, so to speak, a brother from the same womb, torn from the entrails of a single mother not without her great pain, remains so stony that he seems neither to remember his separation, nor to sympathize with his mother’s sufferings, nor to be recalled by the love of his brethren, nor to be moved to repentance by any incantations whatever.

Does the love of a foreign woman have such power that harlotry’s pleasures are preferred to the chaste embraces of the bride? Are citizens of Babylonian confusion to be valued so highly that they are preferred to the citizens [Col. 0192A] of peaceful Jerusalem? Or has Babylon’s golden cup, from which the kings of the earth drink, seemed sweeter to swallow than Christ’s cup, concerning which he himself says: “My cup that makes drunk—how glorious it is!” (Ps. XXII).

Why do I say these things? With your permission, because we grieve that so illustrious a member of God’s Church is at present separated from her; because we mourn that so beloved a brother is separated from his brethren; because we see a bishop apostatize from the Roman and Catholic Church, and a monk of Cluny apostatize from that Church of Cluny. But perhaps you will cry out in response that we are mistaken, astray, deceived. And what shall we say? Let lengthy disputation cease; let the objection of innumerable arguments fall silent; let ambition, avarice, sacrilege, simony, perjury, [Col. 0192B] armed force, and murders—which support not your side but your pope’s—let all these, I say, and whatever things may be still worse, be set aside. Consider, examine, and reflect on this one thing: where is the Church to be thought to exist? In all the nations of the world, where it must be believed to exist; or in a corner of the city of Rome? In the whole world, or in a small part of Aquitaine? Among the very few, almost no people at all, or among all nations under heaven?

Either the Church is with us, along with the fold containing the sheep of the true shepherd, of whom he says: “My sheep hear my voice” (John X), while your fold contains not sheep but goats to be placed at the left. Of these the Church reproaches you, saying: “Feed your goats beside the shepherds’ tents [Col. 0192C]” (Cant. I). Or, if the Church is with you, alas, Christ’s kingdom has been greatly narrowed. If, I say, the Church is with you, false is the Father’s voice promising the Son: “I will give you the nations as your inheritance and the ends of the earth as your possession” (Ps. II). False is the prophet’s voice: “He shall rule from sea to sea, and from the river to the ends of the earth” (Ps. LXXI). False also is what he says: “All nations whom you have made shall come and worship before you, Lord, and shall glorify your name” (Ps. LXXXV).

Certainly all these things are false if his inheritance and possession have become so small that they possess only the towers of Peter Leonis and a few little fortifications of the count of Poitiers [William, also duke of Aquitaine and father of Eleanor].

If this is true, let Christ now lay aside what he [Col. 0193A] assumed; and, since he has already become inferior in possessions to any petty ruler, let him also lose the royal name. Let no one dare call him King of kings or Lord of lords. If this is true, Christ died in vain, since by his death he gained so very few. I thought it necessary to say this so that your learning may recognize how dangerously you set your opinion before the judgment of the whole world and acquiesce more in the proud obstinacy of a few than in the devout unanimity of many. Since even the canonical decrees prescribe that in every matter one must yield to the greater and sounder party, one who does not yield to men so numerous, so learned, and so holy must be thought to be governed not by wisdom but by madness.

More could be said on this point, but a wise man—to be sure, one whom we know to have been wise and trust will be wise again—needs little. Therefore the common mother, the Church [Col. 0193B], recalls you. The Church of Cluny, which bore you again to Christ, recalls you in a manner more affectionate still: ready to receive you again in pious arms; ready to cherish you more sweetly than it did before; ready to bear every burden for you; ready to restore you again to Christ, to the Church, and to the lord pope.

## LETTER V

To our sweetest and most pious Father, lord P., abbot: Brother THEOTARD, unworthy prior of Charity, and the whole convent, all that most devoted sons can offer.

If we could render thanks equal to your fatherhood for the immense benefits which you deign to bestow on us, your unworthy servants, it would certainly be fitting [Col. 0193C] that we devote every effort to doing so. But since we cannot do this fully and effectively, at least we acknowledge ourselves debtors to such great favor. How indeed can we respond to your benefits, when you have done for us, your insignificant servants, as much as you would scarcely—or not at all—do for great lords? Yet, so that your kindness may know that we remember your benefits and acknowledge ourselves bound in debt, we recall some of them, although we cannot repay them.

You received our cellarer, and in him all of us, with the highest honor; you showed him affection and gave him an excellent mule, a proof of your love. You sent us Lord Peter, an image of your heart, to bring your heart to our hearts and, by his presence, to gladden us as much as pleased you. Finally, to crown such great kindness, you gave us great relics of a great martyr: a great treasure, great riches, more precious to us than gold and many precious stones. For all these things we give thanks, as best we can, to him from whom comes every good, to blessed Mary, and to you, sweetest [Col. 0193D] Father.

Let your fatherhood know that both we and our townsmen have great consolation from these things and great assurance of your holy affection. May the blessing of the Lord and yours be upon us and upon all your sons. What we ought to have placed at the beginning we place at the end: again we thank you for promising us that you will honor, by your presence among us, the feast of blessed Mary [Col. 0194A]. Therefore, concerning these matters and all else, send us word of your wishes and intentions, especially whether we may find you at Cluny until the feast of St Peter; for, if we can prepare the novices, we shall send them for blessing.

## LETTER VI

To the venerable lord Theotard, our intimate friend and prior, and to the convent of Charity, most beloved to us: Brother Peter, humble abbot of Cluny, fullness of every salvation, grace, and blessing.

We read and reread your letter attentively. It filled our heart with as much joy as it declared that you had been made glad. For why should your joy not gladden us, when we owe you all [Col. 0194B] that we are able to give? And when, concerning even those to whom we owe far less than to you, we are commanded to “rejoice with those who rejoice, weep with those who weep” (Rom. XII)? For, to use the Apostle’s words: “What is my joy and my crown—is it not you before the Lord?” (Phil. IV). Although this is not due to my labors for you as it was due to his labors for them, nevertheless the affection of good will may perhaps hope for what the outcome of good work does not give.

And although we do not confer much, still, if there can be much love in us, we love greatly. Your charity greatly assists and kindles the fire of this love, when—as is proper to good sons, and as I say without prejudice to the reverence due to the pledges of saints—you regard even a father’s small gifts as great; when you consider not the [Col. 0194C] gift but the giver’s affection; when from a little spark you show yourselves to blaze greatly.

May God, true Charity, preserve and increase in you this affection of charity, so that by hope you may cling to him here and in eternal life be united to him by sight. Hold as entrusted to you our most dear brother Peter, whom we have sent to you from our side as a part of our heart; and love him whom you formerly loved, as it were, simply for your own sake, now doubly, if that can be done, for ours. We shall celebrate at Cluny the feast of the chief Apostles Peter and Paul; and, because we have learned that you wish it, we trust through God’s mercy that we shall celebrate the Assumption of the blessed Mother of God among you.

## LETTER VI

To Brother THEOTARD, prior of Charity, cherishing him with the inmost affection of sincere charity: Brother PETER, humble abbot of Cluny, the attainment in the Holy Spirit of discernment of spirits.

[Col. 0194D]

You write to me often, dearest brother, and frequent messengers succeed one another, whom you send to me with petitions that I release you from the charge I imposed upon you and permit you, as you say, to serve God without the burden of office. You allege weakness of constitution, the severity of summer weather, and the discomfort of illnesses. You report that the house entrusted to you suffers many losses because you suffer such things and are unequal to its affairs. You demand that I require from you what is impossible, and you assert that I compel your shoulders to bear things which they cannot [Col. 0195A] bear.

I recognize these complaints as proceeding not from a raven’s but from a dove’s heart. Therefore I am neither angered by them nor, as some who do not relish the things of God are accustomed to do, stirred by the accusations to respond insultingly. I ask only that you attend to what I am about to say. You cannot possibly do so unless you break the appetite of an obstinate will. For the mind cannot be capable of true counsel unless it has subjected its own will, by reason, to its own advantage. Certainly, for the wise person, bitter things that bring health are far more to be sought than sweet things that bring death. A useful sorrow must be preferred; a harmful will must be subjected. Attend to why I say this.

I hear you complaining about the difficulty of the pastoral office, but I see you yourself bringing upon yourself the causes of that difficulty. I see you, I say [Col. 0195B], acting against the office imposed upon you, against the virtue of obedience, against charity, the mother of virtues, and therefore against your own salvation. For while you do not spare your age, while you wear yourself out with continual work, while through indiscriminate living you grind down still further a body shattered by innumerable illnesses, you bring upon yourself all the charges [Col. 0195B] that I have laid against you.

By treating yourself thus, you are proved to act against the office imposed upon you. For, as is seen daily, beasts of burden collapse under a load if they are not given the food necessary for their work. Even the strongest animals fail if labor is prolonged too long and no relief from it follows. Our holy teachers cry out that the enemy must be killed and the citizen nourished. But you, contrariwise, cannot kill the enemy while you try to destroy enemy and [Col. 0195C] citizen alike. For there will be no one to oppress the enemy if the citizen collapses.

The Law commands that the head of the bird offered in sacrifice not be entirely torn off, but twisted back toward its wings (Lev. V). But you, despising God’s law, strive with all your might to sever the head from the entire body. Yet God does not accept a burnt offering which he sees offered contrary to the decrees of his law. The devil suggested to Christ that he kill himself, saying, “If you are the Son of God, throw yourself down” (Matt. IV). But he who had come to lay down his life for the salvation of the world refused to die by voluntary precipice, in order to teach that the flesh should indeed be mortified in a beneficial way, but not cruelly destroyed in the manner of murderers.

“No one,” says the Apostle, “has hated his own [Col. 0195D] flesh, but nourishes and cherishes it, as Christ also does the Church” (Eph. V). “As Christ does the Church,” he says. For Christ nourishes and cherishes the Church—the Church, not wickedness; righteousness, not impiety; nature, not iniquity. The Apostle showed, in following Christ, that he too cherished the Church when, after saying among other things to the disciple, “Be an example to the faithful in speech, conduct, charity, faith, and chastity” (I Tim. IV), he later said, because his stomach hurt: “Do not continue to drink water only, but use a little wine because of your stomach and your frequent infirmities” (I Tim. V). Thus, after Christ, the chief teacher of the Church admonished his disciple to provide prudently even for his body; he did not compel him violently toward destruction. And that disciple obeyed him, fulfilling the laborious office of preaching and ecclesiastical administration not by fleeing or protesting, but by remaining and persevering [Col. 0196A].

You too, who plead impossibility, could fulfill the office laid upon you if, as a disciple of truth, you consented to obey. If, I say, you wished to obey the command of your father, to comply with the charity of your brothers, and to avoid the sin of disobedience, you would be able to bear the burden of governance laid upon you, however heavy it may be. Nor should you wonder that I have called disobedience a sin, since the prophet prefers it to many sins, saying: “For rebellion is as the sin of divination, and unwillingness to submit is as the crime of idolatry” (I Kings XV).

I repeatedly commanded you, because of the excessive discomfort of illnesses which you yourself acknowledge, to withdraw a little from the convent [Col. 0196B] and rest, as other sick men do; but you did not do so. I ordered you to use somewhat less restrictive food; but you did not obey. I directed you to comply, insofar as it concerned relief for your illness, with the arrangements of the brothers, whose abundant charity toward you delighted me; but you did not heed this. If you consider it rightly, you will recognize that in despising brotherly charity you have sinned not a little. For even apart from the authority of a father’s command, what charity commands from the hearts of faithful and piously living subjects, even toward their prelates, must by no means be despised. If this is done, it is not the person who seems to utter charity’s words but Charity itself, which utters those same words, that is despised. Whoever despises it is proved in no way to possess it.

Now [Col. 0196C] hear from the Apostle what fasting, or any bodily austerity, profits one who does not have charity: “If I give my body so that I may burn, but do not have charity, it profits me nothing” (I Cor. XIV [probably XIII]). Abstain, therefore, from meat; abstain from fish; abstain, if you will, from everything. Afflict, whip, and crush your beast of burden; give no sleep to your eyes; let not your eyelids slumber; spend your nights in vigils and your days in labors. Whether you wish it or not, you will hear the Apostle: even if you give your body to be burned, it profits you nothing (I Cor. XIII).

This is no longer inability for a servant to serve the Lord, but unwillingness. Indeed, to make the insult greater: it is preferring to die rather than obey, to perish rather than serve, to hide by fleeing from [Col. 0196D] his face rather than bear the burdens of servitude. But since I hasten to end my words, recall your mind, I beg you, dearest brother, from this purpose. Strive, sweating in a very brief contest for everlasting rest. Do not, like the slothful servant, bury your talent in the earth. Let the very small labor of this present life be sufficient for so great a reward, if you persevere. And so that you may be able to endure through labor, alternate your labors at times with rest, that you may strive to attain—not, as you have done until now, by working obstinately to the failure of your labor, but by acting with discernment to the success of your labor—which perhaps will not be long delayed.

## LETTER VII

To SIGIVARD, king of Norway, the most noble of kings and friend of our fellowship: Brother PETER, humble abbot of Cluny, to reign happily in the present life and most happily with Christ in the life to come.

[Col. 0197A] We give thanks with all the affection of our heart to the almighty and eternal King, who has deigned to inspire your mind with His fear and love, and has shown in you that love of heavenly things has prevailed over earthly affections. For although the disposer of the ages has placed you at the farthest ends of the world and beneath the frozen pole, yet by the southern warmth of His Spirit He has so tempered your northern cold that, the ice of unbelief and of the flesh being melted, it may also be sung of you: “Arise, north wind, and come, south wind; breathe upon my garden, and its spices shall flow forth” (Song of Songs 4). And again: “I shall say to the north: Give; and to the south: Do not withhold” (Isa. 43).

Truly, all of us—and especially we who [Col. 0197B] love you more affectionately than others—hear with rejoicing the report of your devotion to God’s service: how you reverence and love the things of God; how you have most devotedly subjected royal magnificence to the sweet yoke of Christ; how you have made yourselves protectors of God’s Church; how you have formerly driven back, by force of arms on land and sea, the enemies of Christ’s cross from dominion over the faithful, not only within your own territories but also in the remotest regions of the south and east; and how you now hasten to repel them again with a very great fleet. Above all, because such fervour of the Holy Spirit has blazed up in your soul that it has inspired in you the desire to despise so great an eminence of royal power and such abundance of possessions, and to take up the way of perfection for the sake of the eternal kingdom [Col. 0197C], we render such thanks as we can to Him who bestows every good; and with all our prayers we entreat you to strive to bring this purpose to fulfilment.

## LETTER VIII

To our beloved sons and brothers at Norantona, brother PETER, humble abbot of Cluny, greeting, grace, and blessing.

[Note: [Col. 0197D] To our brothers at Norantona. Norantona was a Cluniac priory in England, perhaps also called the Priory of Arenthona in the Catalogue of Benefices [Col. 0198D] dependent on the monastery of Cluny; it was subject to the priory of Blessed Mary of Charity.]

Although we love all who belong to the body of the Cluniac congregation by the common obligation of charity, we embrace you among the rest with a certain special affection. And though we have never seen your house with bodily eyes, yet by the gaze of true love we behold you not merely daily, but continually. This is brought about by the report of your good manner of life, but [Col. 0197D] especially by that Thomas who is yours—indeed, ours—whom, though you lack him in person, nevertheless through him you possess us and all that is ours. For he is close to us and exceedingly dear in Christ; so that, although your England has often sent Cluny countless gifts, it has never offered anything more welcome or dearer than he.

Therefore, do not be distressed at his absence, because, when the time comes, his presence with us can confer much upon you. If you conduct your business wisely, you ought to display your wares there whence you may in due season carry back greater profits. Patiently, therefore, endure for the present the loss of so great [Col. 0198A] an advantage, because what, as we have said, you now feel to be harmful, by the Lord’s helping grace you will one day find profitable.

## LETTER IX

To the supreme shepherd of God’s Church and our special father, Lord Pope INNOCENT, brother PETER, humble abbot of Cluny, humble obedience and devoted service.

The great distance of intervening lands, which separates us from your fatherhood by a wide expanse, compels us sometimes to send longer letters than your ears are accustomed to endure. For if we had you nearby, the frequent unrest of our affairs, hoping that it could have recourse to you, would be briefer in its words. But because it almost despairs of being able to penetrate to you again, both through the distances of many lands and, what it fears still more, through the barriers of very many swords, it becomes more importunate in its report, thinking more of what paternal care ought to provide for it than of what may weary you to hear in its account. Therefore pardon must be granted to prolixity if necessity is not denied what belongs to it.

I heard, and read in letters sent to the lord Bishop of Albano, that Your Sublimity had directed him to hasten his return to you and present himself before you. This has also reached the ears of many who are greatly concerned for your peace and safety. All of them, bound to you by the devotion of love, greatly wonder that such a decree should have issued from Your Majesty—a decree which, if you weigh it well, brings nothing to your advantage and much to your harm.

And, leaving aside that there is no road to you except through the hands of enemies prepared, on your account, to capture or kill him—what if he could arrive unharmed? What would an unarmed man do amid wars and armed men, he who is no warrior? Rather, because he is a priest of God, he is accustomed, with Moses, by the raising of hands to God rather than by the shedding of another’s blood, both to turn away the Lord’s wrath and to overcome Amalek (Exod. 14). If Moses was far better able, when the mountain afforded the secrecy of prayer, to overcome the enemies of God’s people than in the field exposed to war, then your bishop also, whatever your enemy may whisper against him, would truly be much more able to assist both you, his father, and the whole Church of Christ [Col. 0198D] by prayers and counsels with us than by tumults and battles with you.

This seems so not only to my folly, but to the wisdom of many wise and religious men, among them the Lord Abbot of Clairvaux, who, as you know, devotes his whole self to your affairs. Before the abbots of Vézelay and Pontigny, he told the same Lord Bishop of Albano that he was deeply grieved to be summoned by you to those regions. On this matter both I and several persons of our country had proposed to write to Your Wisdom; but, being forbidden by the Lord Bishop of Albano himself, we abandoned the plan. For he hastens, so far as he can, to fulfil your command with all his strength. Accordingly, though still very weak from that long illness, he has resolved to undertake the various hardships of so great a journey and to penetrate Italy, rendered harsher by the tumults of wars than by the crags of its mountains.

Calm, therefore, I beseech you, whatever cloud of displeasure may have passed, even lightly, over your mind toward so great a man, so useful and faithful to you; and show yourself toward him such as we certainly know him to be toward you. And just as I admonished you in another letter with faithful boldness, so I still advise you: if the letters which he often sends happen to sound somewhat harsh in your ears, receive them with equanimity, and attend more to the sweet affection of the writer than to the words [Col. 0199B] represented by the letters he has written. For, as you know better than I, “the wounds of one who loves are better than the deceitful kisses” of another (Prov. 27); and compassion that bites is more salutary than wickedness that soothes.

Nor is it unworthy of your greatness to say what that greatest king and Prophet said of these two kinds of people: “May the oil of the sinner not anoint my head; but let the righteous man correct me in mercy and rebuke me” (Ps. 140). This indeed he does not do; rather, being accustomed not to speak with one thing in his heart and another in his heart, he preserves a kindly affection for you in his mind, but expresses what he thinks in more severe language. I myself have often experienced this manner of speech from him much more harshly in person and face to face than you have at a distance through letters; but, considering the heart from which those words proceeded, I endured everything patiently.

For who would not bear—indeed, who would not give thanks for—charity that admonishes or corrects, not publicly, but secretly, as if in the chamber of the heart? Yet in writing or speaking he commands nothing as a lord, but humbly suggests, as one subject, what ought to be said. Receive, therefore, your bishop when he comes to you, or near you, with the honour which, as you know, he deserves before God and men—if it please you, with honour, and especially with that love which he has earned from you—so that you may render to him what is just, and by this example kindle others more and more toward your service.

But lest he remain idle in the regions of Italy at this time, when the harvest of Christ has few labourers [Col. 0199D], we pray that, if it please you, you send him back to our Gaul, where, the better known he is, the more useful he can be to us and to you. There, in proportion to the authority he possesses on your behalf, he will be able to accomplish benefit on your behalf.

## LETTER XI

To his singularly venerable and especially beloved lord and father, MATTHEW, Bishop of Albano, brother PETER, humble abbot of Cluny, greeting which God has promised to those who love Him.

Jerome, the noblest spokesman among Christians, says in one of his letters: “Many monsters have been born in the world. In Isaiah we read of Centaurs and Sirens, of owls (*ululae*, printed *viulae*) and onocrotali; Job describes Leviathan and Behemoth in mystical speech; the poets’ tales recount Cerberus, the Stymphalian birds [Col. 0200A], and the Erymanthian boar; Spain has produced the three-bodied Geryon. Gaul alone has had no monsters, but has always abounded in men most brave and eloquent.”

Yet although our Gaul, by the testimony of so great a man, had always from ancient times lacked such prodigies, alas! in our own day she has brought forth a monster far more misshapen than all those named above. Happy were the former ages, which remained barren for so long lest they should be disfigured by so evil an offspring! But pitiable are our times, which in unspeakable fertility have produced a detestable brood. That former age had, if only in fable, Evander, slayer of Cacus; Hercules, binder of Cerberus; and that same Hercules, cutter down of the Hydra’s many heads. But the portent newly arisen among us has no one to bind it, and likewise no one to destroy it. Thus all who ought to have suffocated the hateful prodigy as soon as it appeared have become so enfeebled that by their silence they seem to confess either that no evil has been done or that no novelty has arisen.

Almost the sole final hope remains in your customary zeal for justice and in the strength at your disposal; and these ought to be applied to this matter all the more vigorously because the expectation of all of us rests, shamefully, upon your help. Since by this kind of preface, I think, I have sufficiently made you attentive (*intentum* [*attentum*]), I shall not keep you in suspense long. I complain; all our brothers complain to whom this matter could come; the entire monastic order complains and laments a common injury with one and the same complaint: that the monks of Verdun have been expelled from their dwellings; that clerics have been intruded in their place; that these men have abandoned their own places, occupied those of others by force alone and without any judgment, put the sickle into their neighbours’ harvest, and greedily devoured its fruits while its rightful cultivators go hungry.

And what greater marvel? What more detestable monster? What more monstrous portent? Clerics of various orders, canons of various professions—and why should I speak of lesser persons?—even the Church’s very highest ranks, I mean bishops, were accustomed to exchange episcopal dignity for the lowly estate of monks, and to lower themselves from the highest steps of ecclesiastical honours to the humble rank of this vocation. You yourself know the honour in which this order stood among the ancient Fathers; you are not ignorant how zealously the Apostolic See cultivated it above other ecclesiastical institutions; nor is it hidden from you how abundantly it has borne fruits for God more richly than other fields of Christ.

But now, having suffered I know not what adverse judgment, it can no longer even retain what is its own, although it was accustomed to make what belonged to others its own by transforming it for the better. It is despised, expelled, trampled underfoot, and now deemed unworthy even of association with the laity. Worse still—what is not done even to thieves—it is condemned before it is heard; proscribed before its alleged fault is tried before a judge; and, before the charge is known, declared guilty as a criminal.

But, say its adversaries, the monks were expelled, or deserved to be expelled, for their misdeeds; let common report, agreeing with this, arrogate judicial authority to itself. Yet what sin did the holy order commit, even if individual persons sinned? What justice deserved this because others had transgressed? Why has innocence been condemned together with the guilty? Why, if bad monks were expelled, as some say, has the monastic institution itself been expelled? Why at least did good monks not replace those bad ones? Was it because such men could nowhere be found? Oh, what an innumerable host of monks, multiplied especially in our own days by heavenly grace, has covered almost all the countryside of Gaul, filled its cities, castles, and towns! What a varied army of the Lord of Hosts, diverse in clothing and observances, has sworn under one faith and charity to the sacraments of the same monastic name! Either, then, all these were lacking to the expellers for the replacement of those expelled, or abundance, as the saying goes, made them poor after it had become nauseating to them.

And lest I detain too long the ears of Your Blessedness, occupied with ecclesiastical affairs, we earnestly ask—and with us the Lord Bishop of Châlons [Note: [Col. 0201] The lord Bishop of Châlons: Geoffrey, to whom Letter 43 below is addressed.] and many other persons of our order entreat—that you labour to wipe from our order the disgrace of so great an ignominy, lest the reverence always preserved for this profession by the Apostolic See should perish while you sit beside the lord pope, and lest so great an injury, if it remains unavenged, furnish mockery to the enemies of the monastic order. Do not wonder that I am more strongly troubled concerning this than concerning my own affairs, since I have always preferred common goods to private ones.

## LETTER XII

To the most blessed, singularly honoured and renowned lords and fathers, the Carthusians—to Lord GUIGO, prior, and the other brothers—brother PETER, humble abbot of Cluny: may you receive eternal salvation from the most merciful Saviour Jesus Christ, and fullest consolation from the consoling Spirit.

[Col. 0201C]

Beloved brothers, having heard—and scarcely believed—of the sudden and unforeseen diminution of your apostolic number and heavenly fellowship, I confess that I stood long amazed, as though carried away in ecstasy. On one side the novelty of the event, on the other the abyss of God’s counsels, came before me and, as it were, forcibly plunged themselves into my heart; on one side, “precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of His saints,” and on the other, grief at that same death from human affection—a grief which, although not owed to the funerals of saints, is nevertheless forced from loving hearts by the very power of love.

But after reflecting on these things for several days, and after sitting sorrowful and silent upon the ground, like the friends of blessed Job, I resolved to write to your love, dearer to me than gold and topaz, and to learn, so far as I could, the condition of your minds. For I would not have allowed my letter to precede me if any opportunity had been given me to visit your holiness. But when everyone agreed that, because of an immensely great obstructing mass, no horseman could reach you, I despaired of being able to go on foot. Indeed, had even that been possible, I would not have refused to attempt it despite great labour.

Therefore, although I trust that I shall do this as soon as I can, meanwhile I send you this message as the forerunner of one who will follow. And although, according to the common proverb, it seems most foolish to carry wood on one’s shoulders to the forest, or to pour water brought in a pitcher into the sea, nevertheless the charity poured into your hearts through the Holy Spirit who has been given to you cannot despise anything that seems to flow from the fountain of that same charity.

I therefore exhort and entreat you; and with me the whole brotherhood which serves the Lord Christ at Cluny and sympathizes with you from the heart prays: do not lay this blow to heart; do not grieve over it beyond measure; do not afflict yourselves, exhausted as you already are by many other labours, over the death of righteous men—a death at which you ought rather to rejoice. For, if the matter is rightly weighed [Col. 0202B], it is not something that ought to bring you sorrow, but plainly something that supplies immense joy. What sorrow is owed to those who have escaped sorrow? What tears to those who have cast off every cause of tears, who have reached that life of which a voice from heaven said to John in the Apocalypse: “God shall wipe every tear from the eyes of the saints, and death shall be no more, nor mourning, nor sorrow” (Rev. 21)?

What, I ask, should be mourned for those who have at last deserved to attain what they long desired? What indeed did they desire while living, if not what the Apostle says of himself: “I desire to be dissolved and to be with Christ” (Phil. 1)? What traveller, laboriously making a long journey and advancing by the same road toward his desired rest, is so foolish that he would wish never to reach his rest, never to end the most arduous toil of the way? What farmer is so hard that, when winter presses, rains fall, and heat burns, he wishes only to plough the earth and sow seed, and never to receive its fruits? What merchant, frequently suffering robbers on land and sea, always fearful, always suspicious, repeatedly enduring many blows or wounds, would not desire with all the affection of his soul to be free from such evils and to return to his homeland and parents with great profit? What heir appointed by his father does not strive with all his mind to reach the inheritance granted him?

Thus indeed, beloved brothers—thus truly and without doubt—must we think, believe, and say concerning these dead of yours, indeed these dead of ours: that, according to the Gospel, having ended the narrow way which leads to life (Matt. 7), they have been led to the Life who says, “I am the resurrection and the life” (John 11 [the printed citation reads II]); that, the labour of farming having ceased, they who “sowed in tears,” according to the Psalmist, now “reap in joy” (Ps. 125); that, like the merchant seeking good pearls (Matt. 13), they gained much from their trade even by dying, since they sold all things and bought the one precious pearl; for to them to live was Christ and to die gain (Phil. 1); and that, as good sons, they reached the inheritance of their gracious Father by dying. Of this inheritance the Prophet says: “When He gives sleep to His beloved, behold, the inheritance of the Lord” (Ps. 121).

Therefore, as the Apostle says, you ought not to grieve for those who sleep as those grieve who have no hope (1 Thess. 4), nor lament for them as though they were unhappy; rather, because they are, in truth, now eternally blessed, you ought to rejoice with all your heart. For it seems very incongruous that, while your companions rejoice above, you should mourn below for them.

Yet if any place can be given to grief, it seems to lie only here: that while they rest, you still labour; that, their course already finished, you run breathlessly on; that, while they already hold the palm of victory, you still toil in the contest. But an easy consolation meets this thought: what has already bestowed glory upon them advances you toward a crown. For in the furnace [Col. 0203B] in which they were made radiant after every rust had been boiled away, you too are purified no less, since it is not gentler upon you but perhaps harsher, because more prolonged. For although you did not die with them, when the sword of their death passed through your souls, you endured death without dying; and you felt it more harshly because you could not fail along with those who were failing.

The Lord did this to test you: to show you, even in this conflict, whether you were strong or weak; and, by displaying your strength to the world, to strengthen the weak. For those whom the world formerly knew to be strong in peace, it now recognizes, by God’s grace, as steadfast in war. The longing of my affection for you would gladly pour itself forth in words; but the importunity of affairs compels it, lest it overflow too much, to shorten many things.

Therefore, since it has pleased the heavenly Judge to assail you partly by the way of temptation in which righteous Job was tested, and since the heavenly judgment held you worthy enough to endure the scourges of so great a man, may it please you, amid the destruction of your cells and the oppression of your brothers, to cry with complete tranquillity of heart what he cried in worship when the desert wind had overthrown his house and the collapse had destroyed his sons and daughters: “The Lord gave, the Lord has taken away; as it pleased the Lord, so it has been done; blessed be the name of the Lord” (Job 1).

The Lord, who does not permit anyone to be tempted beyond what he can bear (1 Cor. 10), will be present, so that, at His own time, when other things have been restored twofold, just as Job’s sons and daughters returned to him unharmed, so the brothers now destroyed may return to you and be joined with you forever, never again to be separated. Rejoice us, then, who have been made greatly sorrowful together with you. This will happen at once if we learn as soon as possible that you have laid aside your sorrow.

## LETTER XIII

To the venerable and most beloved lord, Lord HENRY, Bishop of Winchester, worthy to be praised in the seat of the elders, brother PETER, humble abbot of Cluny: after the honour of the pontifical stole, may you be clothed in the glory of the robe.

[Note: [Col. 0203D] To Lord Henry, Bishop of Winchester. This Henry, to whom Peter often writes below, was the fourth son of Stephen, the elder count of Blois, and Adela, eldest daughter of William the Conqueror. “Lest,” says William of Newburgh, *History of English Affairs*, book 1, chapter 4, “she should seem to have borne children only for the world, his mother had him tonsured at Cluny.” Later, when Henry I, king of England, had joined the only daughter of the count of Boulogne, to whom the whole inheritance belonged, to his nephew Stephen, who was brother of the Henry already mentioned, and had bestowed many possessions in England upon him, he also “gave Glastonbury Abbey to his brother Henry, a monk of Cluny, and afterwards added the bishopric of Winchester.” But after several years had passed, Henry II, king of the English, being hostile to him, gave him cause, after he had sent ahead his treasure, as Matthew Paris relates, secretly to leave England without the king’s permission through Peter, abbot of Cluny, in 1155. Consequently the king caused three of his castles to be levelled. Saint Bernard also writes to him in Letter 93, and John of Salisbury in Letter 247; he is mentioned also by John Paris in the *Memorial of History*, the Necrology of Saint Martin-des-Champs at Paris, and the Cluniac Chronicle.]

The broad stretches of land and sea, burdensome to those who love deeply, which have divided your Britain from our Celtic Gaul [Note: [Col. 0204D] Which have divided your Britain from our Celtic Gaul—indeed, from the rest of the world as well. Hence Virgil: “The Britons, divided utterly from the whole world.” Why that island of the Ocean, now called England and Scotland, is named Britain is explained at length by the most learned William Camden in his *Description of Britain*; and we, following him, have recently made many observations on the subject in our *History of England, Scotland, and Ireland*.], have until now separated us not only from mutual sight but from familiar conversation. I therefore, fearing lest long separation of bodies might also produce separation of minds, have resolved to communicate to you by letter the secrets of my mind which I could not communicate in speech.

For, remembering our former love, and fearing that it might perish precisely at the time when this mutual affection of your charity might be of greatest benefit to many—when, after God, the salvation of many depends upon the governance of us both—I strive to stir with whatever fan I can the fire long dormant beneath ashes, lest it fail altogether. I did indeed wait, and long remained in suspense, to see whether I might deserve to hear something pleasant from your region. But, if I may say something in jest, I vainly hoped that the sun would rise for me from your west; fruitlessly I thought that ocean storms might clear the darkness of our day; superfluously I imagined that our cold might be warmed by southern breezes from the quarters of the north.

But perhaps Your Dignity will not receive even this jest of ours with equanimity. What then shall I do? If I speak seriously, I shall not be welcome. If I jest, I shall not please even then. If I complain, I shall seem harsh. If I come as a praiser, I shall be branded a flatterer. What counsel, then, can there be for pleasing you? What, unless that which you yourself give? Give counsel—give it, I say—and obedience will immediately follow the commands of the one who orders.

Yet I suppose, and even trust that I know, what your wisdom will command me in these matters. Why? Because, just as it is impossible for light to produce darkness, so it is not lawful for a wise person to command anything contrary to wisdom. Therefore I am certain that you will judge me not to be jesting, complaining, or flattering—such as I represented myself above—but will command me to preserve toward you the fidelity of a true friend. I confess: I now receive this as a word uttered, as it were, from your mouth; and if this same answer is given me, I promise by every means to keep it. I am now bound by my promise and have willingly laid upon myself bonds which I shall never shake off. I have promised to keep the faith of a true friend toward you. If so, it is fitting that I detest the treachery of a false friend.

Now I should be a false friend if, speaking with one thing in my heart and another in my heart, I concealed one thing in my mind and uttered another with my mouth. Therefore, since among friends all things are naked, I have resolved to conceal nothing further from him to whom I have proposed to reveal everything, even my inmost thoughts. With the confidence of intimacy, then, I complain that Your Excellency was some time ago moved against me more quickly than justice allowed, and that over a very slight matter you disturbed the steadfast weight of friendship with fickle readiness. You yourself know what this was; I am silent about it for that very reason, because I judge it unworthy even of remembrance. I do not call it low or slight; rather, I would show that it was altogether nothing, if I were not avoiding the length of a letter because of the reader’s weariness.

What ought not to have been done even if there had been a serious cause was done without any preceding ground; and the heart of that great and singular friend was turned against me. Thus I, who had deserved nothing of the kind, suffered much; and the man whom I believed my closest friend I unexpectedly found to be an enemy. By “enemy,” however, I mean not one who inflicts evils, but one who withholds good; not one who manifests hostility in deeds, but one who withdraws the affection of friendship.

Nor do I recount the frequent complaints with which you used to fill the ears of our envoys crossing the sea into England; nor do I mention those monstrous acts committed against us at Charity, of which you ought to have been the nurturer, not the defender—or at least the mediator. I am silent about these things, and about any others there may be, lest I seem perhaps to provoke the person whom I am labouring to appease.
