The whole point of my complaint comes down to this alone: when I was staying in England last year for a long time and was almost continually in your company, you said nothing whatever about having any ill feeling toward me, and yet you continued to harbour it in your heart. We discussed many matters together; this was covered over by profound silence. Your familiar conversation concealed from me none of your other concerns; but your mind, pondering I know not what, hid this away in its innermost recesses with utmost care. Your generosity bestowed innumerable benefits upon me and mine; but your retentive conscience concealed this one thing, which we would have counted as a gift.

Why say more? Brief speech must constrain a fertile subject for words. Let this, if you please, be the end of our mutual complaints. I forgive first, without imposing any penalty, the many things unjustly committed against me. I ask forgiveness for myself also, though I have not sinned. Yet I leave it to your authority to exact the punishment of sins according to your will. I know that the mind of royal blood, when it recognizes that it has conquered itself, is then all the more conquered.

Henceforth possess me and all Cluny even more fully than you possess Winchester [Note: [Col. 0205D] Possess Cluny more fully than Winchester. Winchester, the city of the British Belgae, is called *Venta Belgarum* by Ptolemy and Antoninus; *Guintonia* by Necham and certain others; still *Caer Gwent* by the Britons; *Wintancester* by the ancient Saxons; and [Col. 0206D] Winchester by the English today.]; and from now on be father of our country, ruler, abbot, and bishop.

## LETTER XIV

To his intimate friend, Lord STEPHEN [Note: [Col. 0206D] To his friend Lord Stephen: a cleric of Lyons.], brother PETER, humble abbot of Cluny, greeting as to himself.

My soul, concerned now for yours as for itself, cannot rest from considering, speaking, and writing concerning its salvation. You have begun, dearest friend; you have begun to run—do not cease. “All run, but one receives the prize” [Col. 0206B]. “So run that you may obtain it” (1 Cor. 9). Take care that the malicious thief does not obstruct your way. For you have begun not to descend from Jerusalem to Jericho, but to ascend from Jericho to Jerusalem.

But, as someone says:

> . . . . . Easy is the descent to Avernus;
>
> But to recall one’s steps and escape to the upper air—
>
> This is the labour, this the groaning [*opus*, “work”] . . . . .
>
> (Virgil, *Aeneid*, book 6, lines 126 ff.)

To what end is this said? So that you may wisely observe that human nature is prone to plunge into vices which lead to destruction, while human sluggishness raises itself only with difficulty toward virtues that lift it to heaven. For, fleeing labour and seeking rest, it prefers everlasting pains to a brief and slight labour [Col. 0206C]; it prefers an hour’s pleasure to eternal delights. But the lover of eternal things is not so, nor is the hearer of the Apostle who says: “The world passes away, and its desire” (1 John 2).

But because I have discussed much of this with you, and hope shortly to discuss more, I do not wish now to make the letter long—especially because I have already perceived God’s Spirit speaking to you and know that He has fully touched your heart. Only take care not to receive His grace in vain, nor extinguish the same Spirit given to you by God. Come to me quickly, therefore, as I agreed with you and afterwards sent word again, so that whatever remains to be said on these matters may be said, and whatever must be fulfilled may be fulfilled. During this first week of Lent and the following week, your beloved self will find me at Cluny.

## LETTER XV

To our most dear friend, Lord HUGH CATULA [Note: [Col. 0206D] Hugh Catula: a knight, also mentioned by the Cluniac Chronicle under Peter I.], brother PETER, humble abbot of Cluny, greeting and much love.

[Col. 0206D]

Compelled by the great affection of love by which I am bound toward you, I cannot fail to rejoice at your welfare and grieve at your danger. You know by what chain you are bound—not to me, but to God, or rather, what is truer, to me for God’s sake. For, with no one compelling you but God’s Spirit inspiring you, you placed body and soul before witnesses into my hand consecrated by the heavenly mysteries; you gave yourself over to be made a monk at my discretion; as a sign of your surrender you wished your hair to be cut off by me and preserved; and you swore that you would receive the religious habit at Cluny on the appointed day.

And now, as I hear, against the divine pronouncement which says, “You shall not swear falsely, but shall render your oaths to the Lord” (Matt. 5), and against the Prophet who says, “I shall fulfil for You the vows which my lips have uttered” (Ps. 65), you intend to go to Jerusalem. But who could believe that a wise man could be so utterly foolish? Let whoever wishes believe it; I wholly refuse to believe it. It is unworthy that I should believe of so great, serious, and truthful a friend things which scarcely anyone could believe of any buffoon.

But since, though I speak to a wise man, I speak nevertheless to a layman and a knight, I ought to answer the considerations which may reasonably be turning in your mind. Perhaps you say to yourself: “What life, what work, what conversion can be compared with the Lord’s tomb? If anyone goes there, what similar thing can he do?” To this I reply: lesser goods may be relinquished for greater goods, but greater goods must never be exchanged for lesser or equal goods. It is greater to serve God perpetually in humility and poverty than to undertake the journey to Jerusalem amid pride and luxury. Thus, if it is good to visit Jerusalem, where the Lord’s feet stood, it is far better to long for heaven, where He is seen face to face.

Therefore, one who promises what is better cannot compensate for it by offering what is worse as though it were better. If you have promised someone a hundred solidi, you may, without violating your promise, pay two hundred; but you can in no way discharge it by paying only fifty without breach of faith. Consider these matters wisely, and take care lest you begin gravely to displease God in the very matter by which you hasten to please Him. I ask you, therefore, to hasten to come with the bearer of this letter, who is your true friend, so that I may communicate to you in living speech what I do not wish to commit to this letter.

## LETTER XVI

To our most beloved and honoured brothers, priors, obedientiaries, and others dispersed through various regions of the earth, brother PETER, humble abbot of Cluny, greeting and the Lord’s eternal blessing.

[Col. 0207D]

If the feelings of your charity, the depths of your compassion, the breasts of your mercy toward me—your servant and minister, such as I am—still flourish, I pray that I may now experience them. Therefore, though absent in body, present in spirit, I prostrate myself with all the devotion of my heart at the feet of your holiness [Col. 0208A], and implore with all the prayers I can offer that I may deserve to be heard by you. Raingarda, a handmaid of God—my mother according to the flesh, your sister according to the spirit, a nun of Marcigny [Note: [Col. 0207D] “Raingarda, a nun of Marcigny.” Peter himself also discusses her at length in the following letter and likewise in Letter 20, where Raingard is called a nun of Marcigny by profession and cellarer by office.]—after a long and excellent manner of life with the holy sisters, according to the Lord’s will paid the common debt of death in holy confession on 25 June, the seventh day before the Kalends of July. Since, having left all things behind, she fled especially to you from the shipwreck of the world and placed in you her whole hope of salvation, you owe it not only to my prayers but also to her own devotion to assist her soul as it has passed to the eternal judgment. Therefore both mother through son and son for mother pray that a trental of Masses be performed for her, wherever possible [Note: [Col. 0207D] “That a trental of Masses be performed for her.” Thus also the aforesaid Letter 20: “And that in the abbeys and other communities of your diocese, through you a trental of Masses be performed for her, and that certain poor persons be fed.” And Heloise, Letter 21, Book VI: “You also granted me a certain special privilege, as it were, of love and sincerity: namely, that after my death the community of Cluny should perform a trental for me” [Col. 0208D]. Likewise the Necrology of Saint-Martin-des-Champs: “Let the present inhabitants of this place and those who shall come after them know that Lord Matthew, prior of this church, sitting in the common chapter with the assent of Lord Pons, abbot of Cluny, established that in succeeding times, every year, a trental of Masses should be celebrated for his two predecessors, the priors of this place: namely Lord Theobald and Lord Ursus.”], and that twelve poor persons be fed. [Col. 0208B] Let the remaining priests chant two Masses for her repose, without the Office and without the general Mass which is celebrated according to custom; and let there be added whatever the charity of God, through the Holy Spirit given to you, has poured forth in your hearts.

## LETTER XVII

To his dearest brothers and sons, JORDAN, PONS, and ARMAND: Brother PETER, humble and unworthy abbot of the brethren of Cluny, offers brotherly affection to brothers and paternal affection to sons.

For a long time I searched, and anxiously turned my eyes this way and that, seeking with whom I might share the secrets of my heart, or before whom I might set forth—and, if possible, lay down—the grief lately conceived in my spirit. No one appeared more fittingly than you [Col. 0208C], who share with me both the same cause for sorrow and the common means of comforting that sorrow. Give your minds attention, and gather together the feelings that are scattered wherever they may be; do not think that the matter ought to be read carelessly, since not only your studies but you yourselves are owed to it. No part of your hearts ought, through any obstacles whatever, to be absent from the matter now in question—a matter at which the providence of God has brought you to be present.

When I had lately returned from the Council of Pisa, after the many inconveniences encountered on that journey, there came to meet me news sadder than every sorrow; and by its sudden arrival it disturbed the alternating conversations which, according to custom, were joyfully exchanged about escape from dangers, the safety of companions, and other fortunate events. For while we were speaking, a man stood by in silence; amid rejoicing people he displayed a clouded face as the sign of grief; he approached me more closely and thrust funeral letters upon me, who suspected nothing of the sort. I recognized him as a household messenger and knew whence he came; and, presuming that no misfortune could be reported to me from those [Col. 0209A] parts, I confidently received the letter sent by familiar people, and, as though it brought excellent news, began to run through it rapidly with my eyes.

But when, after the greeting placed at the beginning, I hurried on to what followed, I suddenly stopped as though repelled by the mass of a beam; I was stunned as if my head had been struck by a stone; I groaned as if pierced by a sharp wound from a weapon, when I learned from the silently speaking letter of the swift and, as it were, stealthy departure of my blessed mother from the world. Then, as the excessive force of grief pressed upon my breast, and the letters, before I had read them through, were soaked by the abundance of my tears, I quickly rose from the place, which I had already come to hate, and sought a more private place. There I satisfied, for a while, my impatient heart somewhat more freely with groaning and tears.

Thereafter grief advanced beyond measure; and, despising now all self-command, I refused even the consolation of the great persons present. Then night came, and by its rest quieted, to whatever small extent, the magnitude of my sorrow—something others could not do. On the following day, intending to commend the beloved soul to the merciful Redeemer, I approached the altar. Joining the sacrifice of a contrite spirit to the saving victim, I implored the divine clemency to be propitiated for her failings. Present in our company were venerable men of the highest rank—archbishops, bishops, abbots, learned clerics, devout monks—from Rheims, Rouen, Troyes, Coutances, Sées, and very many others assembled from diverse regions. They had remained inseparable companions on our journey because of the aforesaid council, and were returning with me from the same [Col. 0209C] synod. Compelled by their kindly consolation, and especially by the reverence due to their company, lest the cloud of my grief should darken the serene joy of so many great men, I finally forced myself against myself; suppressing my true grief in my heart, and knowing it to be deceptive, I suddenly presented to my holy companions a cheerful face. Changed by this change in me, those who had formerly grieved with one who grieved, thinking me consoled, began likewise to rejoice with one who rejoiced.

After the remaining distance of the road had been traversed in this feigned joyfulness, and after they had been solemnly received at Cluny as was fitting, I bade them farewell and quickly set out for Marcigny. For this also increased my goads and, as though the wound inflicted upon me had been made more savage, made my conscience bleed: that my light had been extinguished without my having seen her, while I was absent and had not bid her farewell. Therefore, what I had not deserved to see, alas, while she still breathed—at least in her last moments—I now sought to moisten with tears when it had been withdrawn from my sight and shut within the tomb.

I came, then, and found that great and sacred flock of the handmaids of God almost buried with her in grief at her death. For nearly twenty years she had so lived with that heavenly company of holy sisters that, as their sobs, groans, and lamentations testified, they would almost have preferred to die with her rather than live when she was taken away. The church of the Blessed Virgin Mother, to which I first turned aside according to custom for prayer, resounded with mourning. It resounded, I say, and, as though destruction threatened all, answered their sighs and sobs. I thought that I alone loved so great a mother with filial affection; but, when I observed them, I was compelled to judge them all her daughters. By their mourning they increased my sorrow, and while they wept for her freely, solely from the affection of compassion, they taught me what I owed to nature and what to God.

At last, when the sorrowful prayer was finished, I began the office for the dead; and, as though she had then died—because I had been unable to do so earlier—I then completed everything according to custom. But when we came to converse together, I cannot describe such a great repeated outpouring of pious complaints. For, to pass over the innumerable things which I can neither recount nor recall, one testified that she had lost a mother, another a daughter, another a sister, another a mistress. They said [Col. 0210B] that she had been the comfort of the sorrowful, the strength of the sick, the staff of the weak, the help of the needy, and finally the support in every kind of necessity. The various business of affairs fell silent, nor was there discussion even of daily needs. The whole monastery, with one voice, spoke of the dead handmaid of God. Nor did these things occur only in the inner precincts of the holy place: all the outer and adjoining parts likewise murmured with a similar lament.

The poor, to whom she had always been generous according to her means, groaned that the supports of life had perished for them. The very poor establishments of nuns surrounding the place, to which she had often been accustomed to give what she used to deny herself, bewailed her as their own mother of the household. Even the knights and laymen to whom she was obliged to answer and render service said that they no longer knew Marcigny. But why say more? Everything had put on the face of grief, and the whole appearance of the monastery was dreadful with a certain dark pallor. Yet the holy community did not cease from prayer: each sister, and all together, commended the beloved soul to God.

The next day, when I entered chapter, before I had scarcely opened my mouth to speak, they immediately filled everything again with groaning; and whatever I said in any manner, they drenched entirely with abundant tears. At last I absolved, as my duty required, the soul of my mother; and they, by answering a tearful “Amen,” undoubtedly brought her to eternal life. Then, entering the church with them all, I again offered the saving sacraments for her. Afterwards, approaching her tomb, I gave solemn absolution with prayer over her venerable body. When I had implored rest for her soul and resurrection to life for her body, I, an unhappy son, bade farewell to my blessed mother; and thus I departed from her—not in spirit, but only in body.

When, therefore, three days of mourning and burial at Marcigny had been completed, on the third day, as if rising from death, I recovered my spirit. Leaving that place, I resolved to write for you, my dearest ones, this lamentable epitaph for our common mother. I chose you from among thousands, with whom the same affection of weeping with me might exist, and whose condition is shown to be not unlike mine. I want the children of one mother to weep together over her funeral, lest anyone unwilling to weep reveal that he was not her son [Col. 0211A].

I do not want—do not want—any troublesome comforter to intrude into our mourning and put forward as though for his own purpose the apostolic testimony: “We do not wish you, brethren, to be ignorant concerning those who sleep, lest you grieve” (1 Thess. 4). If he should say this, I shall answer that the Apostle took this sense away from such people, and expressed what he said with a qualification. For after saying, “lest you grieve,” he added: “as do the others who have no hope” (ibid.). Thus he spoke of unbelievers, not believers: those who thought that the soul perished with the body; who said that after death no rewards remained for merits; who were accustomed to deny the resurrection of the flesh. They wept for the dead in despair of their resurrection; they wept for their beloved, believing that they would never see them again for eternity. For that reason, such weeping—opposed to Christian hope—had to be dried up by the apostolic command; unbelieving sorrow had to be expelled from the hearts of believers; and faith in the resurrection had to be more strongly commended.

But ours is not such weeping: we shed it not in despair of things to come, but in compassion for nature. Ours is not such pain: it is produced not by a failure of faith, but by the affection of mutual kinship, which no law forbids. By this weeping the righteous men of old wept for their dead relatives in the flesh; in this grief the great patriarchs attended the funerals of their beloved. Thus Scripture says of Isaac: “He brought Rebekah into the tent of Sarah his mother, and loved her so greatly that she moderated the sorrow which had come upon him through his mother’s death” (Gen. 24). Who, then [Col. 0211C], dearest ones, can forbid us to grieve at the devout death of a holy mother, when he hears that so great a father grieved at his own mother’s passing?

What if we bring forth also Joseph, the most dutiful son of a devout father, of whom we read that, when Jacob had died, “he fell upon his father’s face, weeping and kissing him” (Gen. 50)? When he had borne his body from Egypt and buried it in the land of Canaan, he celebrated the funeral rites for seven days with great and vehement lamentation, accompanied by his brothers and Egyptians; and the Canaanites said, “This is a great lamentation for the Egyptians,” and gave the place the name “Lamentation of Egypt” (ibid.). Nor will David, that singular king and prophet among the early fathers, fail us. Knowing what he owed to nature, after first mourning his slain enemies with remarkable charity, he mourned with covered head for his son, a fratricide and moreover a patricide, saying: “Absalom, my son, my son Absalom! Who would grant that I might die for you?” (2 Kings 18).

But why do I repeat these as though they stood alone, when it was the custom of all the ancients, descending from nature’s kindness, to mourn any relatives or elders who had died [departed], and to celebrate their funerals with public mourning? In this a certain venerable harmony of human fellowship was commended: it was a consolation of desolation for devout minds and, from the loss of present things, a great inducement to seek eternal things. The Book of Wisdom also affirms this, where it says: “My son, shed tears over the dead; and, as though you had suffered dreadful things, begin to weep” (Sirach 38).

Therefore it is neither contrary to faith nor discordant with the customs of the Church if devout people are moved with devout intention at the funerals of the devout, and, as by a certain prelude, speak of the place to which they themselves will depart. For when they mourn other dead persons, they mourn also that they themselves have been made mortal. By such prayer they ask that, through Christ’s grace, they may be rescued from this miserable mortality and brought to blessed immortality.

If the pen is turned to the Gospel, it will appear that it was not said without reason to the Blessed Virgin Mother: “And a sword shall pierce your own soul also” (Luke 2). It would not have pierced her soul unless she had grieved, with an ineffable affection of humanity, at the death [Col. 0212B] of God and of her Son. Although she did not doubt that the death of her Son was the life of the world, nevertheless she grievously mourned him dying, whom she wonderfully knew to rescue humankind from death.

Therefore let the inward feeling of our mourning remain among us, my beloved ones; and with these examples let us weep for the blessed ashes of our mother. Let what was lamentable become delightful, so that she who, while living, bore us with pain into present misery may now, with her flesh dead, bear us with joy into everlasting glory. She will bear souls by her prayers, she who, as I said, bore our flesh with pains; and let this be a singular refreshment for her, when she has brought with her into heaven those whom she brought forth from herself into the world.

I dare say this also of her, lest anyone judge that I affirm it rashly: for her conversion differs in no respect from my understanding of it, and her manner of life agrees with me in every respect. For she was such a woman as, so far as a human being can know, was sufficient for herself and ought to assist others. Let, then, the admirable manner of life of so great a woman be set forth, so that, once you know it, you may recognize that I speak truth, and may soothe minds embittered by grief through a pleasant reading and mutual discussion. This will be a certain living presence of an absent and departed mother, and the image that rivals realities will not leave the inner chambers of our hearts—an image that cannot die for you after her setting, nor perish after her tomb.

The usefulness of the subject itself compels me not to be silent, lest, if I keep silent about what should be said, I seem to begrudge you such abundant material [Col. 0212D]. Nothing should become peculiar to any one of us, for not only charity but nature has willed everything to be common to us. I have not undertaken to praise the distinction of her estate, or whatever glory of the flesh might be commended in it—though in those things she was superior to many and inferior to few—but rather her mind devoted to God, her contempt of the world, and her desire for heavenly things.

To pass briefly to these matters: while she still reclined in the flower of grass, joined to a husband and bound to the world, she sighed for them as a captive sighs for freedom, one bound for release, an exile for a homeland. She mourned with the anguish of a heart unknown to men but known to God that she was hindered by the marital bond. For this reason, whenever citizens of that city for which she longed or toward which she sighed happened to come, she reverenced them, received them, honored them, and, casting aside every domestic and worldly care, poured her whole self into affection and service toward them. Monks were received, hermits drawn in; and all adorned by the habit or repute of religion were everywhere compelled to lodge with her, even when they resisted. No person of this kind now dared to travel through land subject to her jurisdiction without turning aside to her, and, staying with her for one or more days, satisfying her devout disposition toward divine things. Before men of known holiness, after observers had been dismissed, she wept and poured forth deep groans because, not yet released from the law of her husband, she was forced to serve the world: to care for others while neglecting herself; to be entangled outwardly in tumults and hindered inwardly by occupations; to embrace present things, despise future things [Col. 0214A], and store up against herself countless evils as wrath on the day of wrath.

Saying these things, she cast herself at the knees of holy men and, as with Mary the sinner, washed their feet with tears. She prayed them to knock earnestly for her at the gates of eternal mercy, so that she who did not deserve to be heard through herself might be heard through the mediation of their prayers. Such resolve was carried so far, nor could she be wearied from the course she had begun, until, stirred by a violent surge of mind, she gave herself as a nun—without her husband’s knowledge—to the famous Robert of Bruzelle [Note: [Col. 0213B] “To the famous Robert of Bruzelle.” Authors vary in the surname of this Robert. William of Newburgh calls him Robert of Arbusculus; the Tables of the Abbey of Saint Mary of the Wood, commonly called de la Rota, in the diocese of Angers, of which he was also the first abbot, call him de Arbricel; the Chronicle of Saint-Albin, de Arbrissellis; the Le Mans manuscript of the Letters of Geoffrey of Vendôme—which also writes to him in Letter 47, Book IV—de Arbrussello; finally, Geoffrey the monk, in the Life of Saint Bernard of Pontivy, calls him de Arbrissello and Arbressellensis.

He was present at the Council of Poitiers, held in 1100; when the other prelates fled from the fury of Duke William, he alone, together with the aforesaid Bernard, remained steadfast and immovable, as the already mentioned Geoffrey aptly teaches in these words: “At the same time two cardinals, John and Benedict, acting as legates of the Apostolic See, summoned a council at the city of Poitiers. One hundred and forty fathers were present, and they struck Philip, king of the Franks, with the punishment of anathema because he kept in adultery the wife of Fulk, count of Anjou. When this excommunication became known, Duke William of Aquitaine, who was present and was an enemy of all chastity and holiness, fearing that he might suffer a similar punishment for like offences, was inflamed with excessive fury and ordered them all to be plundered, whipped, and killed. When his servants began to do this, all the bishops and abbots fled in every direction and sought safe hiding places in order to preserve their temporal lives. But Bernard and Robert of Arbrissel, who were present at the council—most valiant champions of justice and destroyers of all wickedness and injustice—remained so firm and steadfast while the others fled shamefully that they did not desist from the excommunication they had begun, but judged it most glorious to suffer death or insult for Christ. And although the persecutors did not inflict death on them, they nevertheless endured martyrdom so far as it lay in their power” [Col. 0213D].

The title of the Abbey of La Rota, no. 15, also commends his eloquence and effectiveness in preaching: “Let posterity and those now living know how the church of Arbrissel, with all its appurtenances, was given to the church of Saint Mary of La Rota, etc. While Robert of Arbrissel, a man of great authority and boundless religious devotion, was sowing the word of God in diverse places, many gathered to receive the grains of so great a seed,” etc.], when he came to her and stayed with her for some time, so that, when he died or gave permission, she might immediately depart for Fontevraud [the Fountain of Évraud; *fons Ebraudi*] [Note: [Col. 0213D] “Immediately to the Fountain of Évraud.” A very famous monastery of nuns in the district of Poitou, which Suger calls the Fountain of Ebrald; Hildebert and Saint Bernard, the Fountain of Everard; and John of Paris, the Fountain of Evrard. It was founded shortly after 1100, as the author of the Chronicle of Tours notes in these words: [Col. 0214B] “In the year of the Lord 1100, the forty-fourth of Emperor Henry and the fortieth of King Philip, a council was held at Poitiers; and not long afterward the abbey of the Fountain of Ebrald was built in the diocese of Poitiers.”

Its first founder was the aforesaid Robert of Arbrissel, who also prescribed to the nuns the rules of religious life, now divided into two books. Thus William of Newburgh, *History of English Affairs*, Book I, chapter 15: “Robert, called de Arbusculo, built that most famous monastery of Fontevraud and formed it by regular disciplines.” And the other William of Malmesbury, Book IV, *On the Deeds of the English*: “Robert Arbreisel and Bernard, abbot of Tiron, were contemporaries and companions in religion of Peter, bishop of Poitiers [ [Col. 0213] ‘Turonensis’ is corruptly printed in the editions, and in William of Newburgh ‘tyrocinium’ is even more corruptly printed for ‘Tyronio,’ French *Tyron*]. The former, the most famous and most copious preacher of all the orators of his time, flourished with an eloquence almost foaming, yet honeyed; and, as people competed in piling up wealth for him, he founded that outstanding monastery of nuns [Col. 0214C] near the Fountain of Ebrald, in which, stripped of every pleasure of the world, a multitude of women dedicated to God—such as exists nowhere else—burns with zeal in the service of God. For, besides the renunciation of other allurements, how slight a thing is it that they speak nowhere except in chapter, a rule of perpetual silence having been proposed by their master, since, once silence has been relaxed, women are prone to whisper foolish things.”

The Chronicle of Saint-Albin also touches on this institution when it says: “In the year 1116 Robert of Arbrissel died, on 25 February, the fifth day before the Kalends of March. He was the founder of the monastery of Fontevraud.” It calls him founder, while others call him its institutor; the aforementioned William of Malmesbury calls him Master, and the Le Mans manuscript of Geoffrey of Vendôme calls him the administrator of the nuns of Fontevraud. This institution or foundation was made by the will and authority of Peter, bishop of Poitiers, “who afterwards,” as Geoffrey relates in the *Life of Saint Bernard of Pontivy*, “suffered exile for justice until death; and the holiness of his life was remarkable, as was shown even after his death by the testimony of miracles.”

Moreover, from the beginning that place was of such religious distinction that it deserved to be consecrated by Pope Callixtus II himself in 1119. In the time of Abbot Suger of Saint-Denis—who wrote to Pope Eugenius on behalf of its nuns, and testified that, when he was studying in those parts, they had grown by God’s will from their recent beginning to nearly four or five thousand—the place had likewise flourished. Honorable mention of it is also made by Hildebert, Letter 79; Saint Bernard, Letter 200; James of Vitry, chapter 20 of the *Western History*; and William of Tyre, Book XIV, chapter 1.], if she survived him, she might withdraw thither.

She did this; and, as it were, adding a lesser weight to the greater weight of the fear of God which she had conceived [Col. 0215A], she awaited the Lord’s mercy in blessed hope. Yet lest she should seem to defraud her husband, to whom she owed the same as herself, of so great a grace, she approached him, uncovered what was hidden, revealed her secrets, set before him the dreadful evils of eternal death, commended the desirable joys of eternal life, preached contempt for the deceptive world, and begged him to depart quickly from it. Finally, that woman, leader of so great a deed, moved her husband to promise that, if God granted him life, he would at a fitting time renounce the world with her. If either of them should first die, the survivor would immediately fulfil the vow of both.

For he too had not lived wholly devoid of the fear of God: he was strong in singular faith, frequent in prayers, searched out the tombs of saints each year, persisted in almsgiving, and rejoiced beyond what can be said in receiving guests without distinction. Once this compact had been confirmed between the spouses, its fulfilment was delayed by countless obstacles, especially wars, opposing the devotion of them both. Then came the day of grief: when her husband was taken from life, she remained widowed, like a turtledove bereft of its mate. If I begin to tell how she conducted herself in that crisis, with what manly spirit she bore such misfortune, and how faithful a wife she showed herself to her husband—a very rare thing even after death—I fail; if I undertake it, I am overcome; if I attempt it, I am cast down.

Believe me, dearest ones: I fear my own words, and, considering what must be said and how it must be said, I almost abandon the undertaking I have accepted. But what shall I do? Ignorance restrains me; love impels me; the subject frightens me; charity urges me; its weight presses me; nature spurs me. Yet in my judgment useless silence is more to be feared here than any unpolished speech. Therefore let be said, however inadequately, what it would be almost wicked to leave unsaid.

While he lay dying, she sat immovably beside his bed. Forgetting herself, she considered nothing except his salvation. Her whole mind burned to procure it. So that the attention of the sick man might not be diverted from this even in the least, she first freed his mind from every bodily concern: in his presence she drew up his will, settled disputes, appointed heirs, divided castles, and completed everything exactly. When these matters had been arranged, so that, freed now from bodily concerns, he might care for his soul, she instructed him—while I listened—as though from a teacher’s chair [Col. 0215D]: to examine his conscience, confess his sins, bestow his possessions upon the poor and monasteries; that God’s judgment is fearful and his mercy great; and to provide, while he still lived, absolution for his spirit and burial for his body.

Everything rang with cries; all things were mingled with mourning and tears; the confused voices of the people shook the heights of heaven [Col. 0216A]; the circle of sons, the multitude of the household, the sorrowing company of nobles groaned. She alone, surpassing womanhood, endured with dry eyes and manly steadfastness. She judged it better to occupy her mind with what would benefit the dying man than, having cast aside reason to no purpose, to join in the people’s tears. Therefore, after she had sent him on his way, strengthened by confession, refreshed with Christ’s body, and clothed in a monk’s cowl, rejoicing and grieving at once, she conveyed his body to Sauxillanges [Celsinaniae] [Note: [Col. 0215D] “She conveyed his body to Celsinaniae.” Celsinaniae—also called Celsiniae and Celsanicae, commonly Saucillanges—was one of the principal priories of the Cluniac order in Auvergne. Pope Agapetus II shows to whom the Cluniacs owed it, writing thus to Aimar, abbot of Cluny: “Likewise we decree concerning Celsanicae, the freehold formerly of Count Hecfred, which our son Stephen, examining the case with a just balance, assigned to the aforesaid place [Cluny] for the salvation of all Christians” [Col. 0216D]. Hence Peter the Venerable himself, *Book I of Miracles*, chapter 6, calls it “the noble Cluniac monastery of Celsinaniae”; and on p. 1411 of this *Bibliotheca* there appears in full the privilege of William, count of Auvergne, “On the agreement between himself and the aforesaid Lord Peter, abbot of Cluny, concerning the monasteries of Mozac and Celsinac.”], and delivered him to monks to be buried among monks as a monk.

Thus, commending earth to earth and entrusting it as a deposit to be restored in its own time, she turned all her effort toward securing repose for his spirit. Driven by the goads of love, she searched everywhere [Col. 0216B], ranged through provinces, visited churches, went round monasteries, emptied her treasury upon the poor, made friends for herself from the mammon of iniquity, and considered it a crime if she left anyone without a gift. She prayed for the dead man, and prayed also for herself: that remission of sins might be granted to him, and conversion from sins to her.

Meanwhile she arranged her flight; and, while the world sought once more to hinder her steps with new nets, she deceived it by giving hope that she would remain. For when important friends urged her finally to remarry, saying that she could enter a union of great wealth and power and that still greater worldly success lay ready at hand, she answered: “Indeed, I shall do what you advise, and, as soon as I can, having married again I shall enter new bridal chambers.” By this reply, as though attending to another matter [Col. 0216C], she deceived the devil, and with fitting retaliation deceived the prince of deception. The prey which he believed he already held in his jaws she strove to steal and snatch away by whatever art she could.

She therefore hid the secret of her salvation deep within her breast, and concealed it like a treasure from robbers, so that what remained hidden from all might be safe from all. But because her undertaking required the help of some persons, she revealed the mystery only to two, whose proven fidelity and constancy persuaded her that all things could be entrusted to them. To one, living with lay freedom, she committed every energetic preparation for the escape; to the other, a monk of proven religious life, she disclosed her spiritual secrets.

The day was fixed on which she was to go out from Egypt, on which, long weighed down by a grievous burden, she was to withdraw her neck from Pharaoh’s yoke. In the hope of freedom, the burdens of the Egyptians now seemed lighter, and the muddy labors that would shortly be changed were endured. A new Passover was awaited, in which, casting away the leaven of malice and wickedness, she might feast on the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth (1 Cor. 5). And, oh, with what skill in dissimulation she veiled her mind with her countenance! How much she promised the world concerning herself! How cheerful she showed herself to everyone, even more than usual! [Col. 0217A] She seemed to have devoted herself entirely to the world, and now to long more than before for secular advantages. But secretly she sang to God: “Lord, all my desire is before you, and my groaning is not hidden from you” (Ps. 37).

The desired day drew near, and her spirit, fervent in zeal, could not rest. On the night preceding the last day of her worldly life, imitating Nicodemus, she came by night and—oh unheard-of devotion!—went to her husband’s tomb. Unknown to everyone, with only the aforementioned monk present, she threw herself before it and, opening the fountain of her tears, flooded it with copious showers. Before the presence of the merciful Creator, she first lamented the death of the deceased man and mourned her own offences with boundless grief. Then, after a long part of the night had passed and she had satisfied her heart with sorrowful lamentation [Col. 0217B], she turned to confession. She began at the beginning to recount all her husband’s sins and then her own sins and crimes; and in confessing she continued almost until the middle of the night. She spoke as though with the mouth of the dead man; and, as though their persons had been exchanged, the husband did penance in his wife.

With these matters thus completed, and the old dregs of sins wholly emptied out, she begged that the priest and vicar of Christ, to whom she had laid bare the wounds of her soul, would subject her—guilty as she was of every crime—to the harsh rules of the remedy, and shut her up at Marcigny in the perpetual prison of penitence. For she had preferred this place to the above-mentioned monastery of Fontevraud, because the venerable Robert, to whom she had devoted herself, had already passed from mortal life; and because, after her first entrance into a cloister, she considered it unlawful, according to the custom [Col. 0217C] of those nuns, to set foot outside it. She recoiled even from seeing what now seemed to her fouler than mud; and, not through pride but through a heavenly disdain of spirit, she began to despise all earthly things as utterly worthless. Therefore, above other holy places, she chose Marcigny, where, like a column fitted for a heavenly building, she might remain perpetually immovable, and, always keeping her own tomb before her eyes, might mourn herself as dead in continual lamentation. Nor did she fear the reproach of having altered her vow, when the occasion of changing places had produced an increase of devotion. For she was permitted to choose a place where she could cling more steadfastly to Christ.

Then, having received from the monk the yoke of severe penitence which she herself had prepared for herself, she rose from the ground in mind and [Col. 0217D] body; and, concealing her deeds under the very darkness of night, and bidding a final farewell to her buried husband, she withdrew from his tomb, herself now soon to be buried. [Col. 0218A] Then, choosing an escort of certain wise and noble persons so that, in accordance with her accustomed manner, she might seem still to relish worldly things, she left her native soil. As though she were going to Cluny and intending to ask the holy brothers to pray for her husband, she entered foreign lands as a traveller and hastened, as she had said, to Cluny. Arriving there devoutly, she distributed of her own goods as much as she judged fitting for herself and for the place; and, having completed all that she had intended, she swiftly returned. Her vows outrunning her journey, she at last entered Marcigny, from which she was to enter Paradise.

She was received with immense joy by the brothers and sisters, who, unaware of what she bore in her heart, honoured her greatly as a new guest. That house was then very poorly supplied with necessities, since it contained nearly a hundred sisters and provided, without distinction, for every visitor [Col. 0218B] at its own expense. The estate was small, and the revenues of its fields scarcely sufficed for even a small number. Then, under Lord Geoffrey of Semur,

> [Note: [Col. 0217D] “Then also under Lord Geoffrey of Semur.” He was the brother, namely, of Saint Hugh, abbot of Cluny. Peter himself speaks of him in *Book I of the Miracles*, ch. 26: “Geoffrey,” he says, “a nobleman, lord of the castle called Semur, after living magnificently in the world for a long time, was touched by the divine Spirit, renounced the world, and with his son and three daughters took on the religious habit at Cluny. There, having long lived holily and without reproach, he was, by reason of his religious life and prudence, made prior of the sisters of Marcigny. After humbly and kindly administering their care for some years, he was afflicted, as mortals are, by bodily sickness and died.”]

Gerard was the diligent steward of the place, concerning whose devout and sincere manner of life I have spoken more fully in the first book of the *Miracles*. Since he was wholly and continually occupied with divine works and with the celebration of sacred heavenly rites, he had joined to himself certain men of virtue whom he knew, and had filled the ears of the merciful Lord with prayers that He might visit His house and provide necessities for those who served Him.

One day, while he stood at the altar and celebrated Mass as usual, he heard—as he himself affirmed, calling Christ, the Word, as witness—a voice descend to him in these words: [Col. 0218C] “Know that you have obtained what you asked.” Then, when at night he had gone to bed as usual, he saw, as he related, in a dream: behold, a dove beautiful in snowy whiteness came to him. Flying above and around him, it invited him, as it were by a tame flight, to catch it. He caught it in his hand and joyfully offered it to Hugh, prior of the sisters.

> [Note: [Col. 0218D] “To Hugh, prior of the sisters.” He had succeeded the aforesaid Geoffrey and was later elected abbot of Cluny after Pontius also. Our aforementioned Peter reports this in *Book II of the Miracles*, ch. 12, in words wonderfully commending his holiness: “After receiving the command and taking counsel, the brothers of Cluny unanimously elect as their abbot the venerable Hugh, prior of the sisters of Marcigny, a man of complete religious devotion and religious repute. That holy man accepted, though very unwillingly, what was imposed upon him; but scarcely five months later he departed from this life and, as his long life in holy conduct had deserved, passed, as is worthily believed, to better things.”]

But Hugh gladly received it, broke the pinions of its wings so that it could not fly away, and enclosed it in a wooden cage. Those who heard this vision as Gerard reported it interpreted it as concerning her; and the event itself showed that their interpretation was true. For, when day came, she entered the inner precincts of the sacred place; summoned the prior of the monastery, called together the sisters, and brought in also her companions for the unexpected spectacle. [Col. 0218D] She began thus:

“Dearest friends, mortal life has long made us companions under the common law of living, and has brought us from the cradles of infancy to [Col. 0219A] an age now almost old. We have gone through everything, surveyed all things with our eyes, tested whatever could promise greater pleasure; and inquisitive keenness has left untried nothing among the things visible before us. Abundance of riches, a throng of relatives, a multitude of friends, the distinction of high birth, ample power, pleasure of the flesh, and pride of life persuaded us to seek nothing beyond themselves on earth. Therefore nothing further remains for us to seek in the depths below. We have found whatever earth can promise, whatever it can give. But see whether these things can suffice us.

“We have lived long, but it is as if we had not lived even for a moment. We have possessed much, but what we possessed has already passed away, and we can by no means call it ours now. We have gratified the flesh, but we retain not even the smallest remnant of delight. [Col. 0219B] Therefore these things never satisfy us: the more greedily we feed upon them, the more they leave us hungry amid their very abundance. Other remedies must be sought elsewhere—remedies able to relieve hunger, quench thirst, and drive away want. The treacherous friendship of the world urges us toward this, for it deceives only those whom it knows have placed their hope in it.

“And, to take examples close at hand: what have you, who had so much cause to be grateful to our husband—who gave you arms, horses, money, and lands; you his faithful, intimate, and dearest friends—rendered him after his death, even without bodily expense? Whom did you ask to pray for his eternal rest? Which saints did you approach? Which monks did you ask? What alms, however small, did you give?”

When they answered that they had truly done none of these things, [Col. 0219C] she added: “You have become my teachers and have taught me what I ought to do and what I ought to avoid. Henceforth I cannot expect from you what I see that you refused to so great a lord and friend. It would be foolish to place further hope in a human being, since no one can find hope even in the closest friends. I must act for myself, and I must not place the hope of my own salvation in another, lest, while idly awaiting another’s aid, I lose divine aid through my own fault. Let the body labour while it lives, and let the soul pray to God for itself, lest, if it fails first, there be no one to intercede for it when dead.

“And, to conclude many things briefly and disclose to you what I have hitherto concealed: I shall never cross the threshold of the enclosure which you see; the world shall never see me under the open sky; I shall never again leave this tomb which I have chosen for myself.”

At this they rose against her and, as though suddenly driven mad by grief, cried that the house would be ruined if she were kept there. Then, turning to tears, she said again: “After a storm comes calm; after rain, fair weather returns; and after your weeping laughter will follow, as we all know. Meanwhile, return to the world; before your eyes I now go to God.”

Having said this, accompanied by the sisters she entered the cloister. Her hair was cut, her clothing changed, and her heart rejoiced. The dove now made white was shut into its cage by Lord Hugh the prior, in accordance with the vision; and the woman, now blessed, was joined to the holy women. Rejoicing that she had been snatched from Babylon’s furnace and brought from fire into refreshment, she was glad that she had entered the courts of the Lord. [Col. 0220A] Now she ran joyfully through the grass of Paradise and, placed in a pasture, was led beside waters of refreshment. Like the Lord’s sheep, she eagerly plucked lovely flowers in greedy bites; wandering through rich meadows, she made up for her former hunger by plentiful pasture. In a short time she amassed the wealth of many virtues and did not allow herself to be found slower than others on the way of God’s commandments. Rather, matching those before her with new swiftness, she hastened with rapid steps to outstrip the older sisters.

First she subjected herself to everyone in humility. She called herself a handmaid and showed herself a servant, because, in accordance with the Lord, she had come not to be served but to serve (Matt. XX). In this virtue she pleased everyone so much that, withholding nothing of their affection, they embraced her with all their heart. What can I say of her contrition of heart, [Col. 0220B] her daily confession, and continual lamentation, when she seemed inferior neither to the Ninevites in contrition, nor to David in confession, nor to Mary in lamentation? Nor did she do these things only at the beginning of her conversion, as some are accustomed to do; throughout her life she devoted her body to labour, her heart to penitence, and her eyes to tears.

Her tears were her bread by day and by night, so that she often said spiritually to her own soul: “Why are you sad, O my soul, and why do you trouble me?” (Ps. XLVI). And, consoling it, she added: “Hope in God, for I shall yet confess to him: the salvation of my countenance and my God” (*ibid.*). The sisters testified that she was so often overcome by weeping that she seemed almost to faint away. This humble handmaid of the most merciful Redeemer cast herself bodily down before Him; and sometimes, while praying on bent knees, the violent heat of her spirit threw her to the ground even against her will. Such was the force of the spirit within her that, her mind being carried up to heavenly things, she sometimes seemed no longer mistress of her own body.

Yet she concealed herself as far as she could; but because she was continually present in church, she could not always be alone. Moreover, she imposed upon her body an immense persecution through vigils and fasts; and so exhausted her strength and flesh by these and other labours that, her flesh wasted away and her skin clinging to her bones, she said secretly to me when, some years later, I came to Marcigny—playfully addressing me as a mother addresses a son: “Thanks be to God, because I have lost the world’s excess; I have shed the old flesh by which I served the world. [Col. 0220D] Now I shall put on new flesh, with which I shall render new services to God.”

She continually chanted the psalms which she had learned even while in the world. As she gave every attention to spiritual contemplation and raised her mind heavenward by daily growth in every virtue, they transferred her to the ministry of Martha and ordered her, on account of her exceptional ability, to be cellarer of the monastery. For she was not “a deceived dove, without heart” (Hos. VII), but “a dove by streams of water” (Cant. V), washed in the milk of evangelical simplicity and endowed not with the serpent’s malice but with its prudence. She had brought back from Egypt the spoils of the Egyptians, to expend them upon her Hebrew brethren and to serve God with them in the desert of this pilgrimage.

Therefore, compelled by obedience, she was unwillingly led out of the cloister [Col. 0221A] and forced to undertake the care of the sisters. How she performed that office I can scarcely explain. She attended to everyone with such zeal that she was called the mother of all by love and the handmaid of all by service. The ardour of charity long conceived was exercised; the fire long concealed in her breast eagerly burst forth into flame. It was fitting that she who had learned to love God with her whole heart in silence should also prove, according to the Lord’s commandment, that she loved her neighbours by serving them.

She kept the name of each sister firmly in memory and, whenever need required any one of them to be named, produced it as though from a book. She had written in her mind the bodily ailments from which each suffered and had carefully noted their diseases and conditions, so that she might assist each [Col. 0221B] without error, since nothing of this kind escaped her knowledge. She knew that, as noble and delicate women, frail and infirm on account of sex, place, and habit, they required many things; and therefore she troubled her mind with great anxiety lest anything be lacking to them. She took upon herself the care of every menial duty and, rejoicing to be the servant of God’s handmaids, performed every humble service. In her mind she devised different preparations of food; though inexperienced in such matters, she was obliged to learn the discipline of the kitchen. She diligently strove to provide roast food for one, boiled food for another; salted food for this one, unsalted for that. She herself prepared it, cooked it, and served it; and, lest anything be lost to her reward, she allowed nothing to be diminished from her labour.

She had gathered the hearts of each individual into her own [Col. 0221C] heart; recognizing what each desired most, she met the desires of all through the effective work of service. When poverty could not answer the wealth of her charity, she was saddened and grieved; and because she could not satisfy all as she wished, she was tormented by a great anguish of suffering. When much was demanded of one who did not possess much, she kept patience in her heart according to the Rule and answered with gentleness in speech. No one could leave her empty-handed, for she filled them with cheerfulness of mind and pleasant words.

In this virtue she so excelled that, after her death, all the sisters testified that during the nearly twenty years in which she lived among them they had never heard even a slight harsh word from her mouth. Always cheerful, always pleasant, [Col. 0221D] she not only showed no cloudiness herself but, if she ever encountered clouds of sorrow in troubled minds, drove them away with the bright light of her words. Holy minds have this characteristic: they always dwell in spiritual joy, exulting not in the world but in God, and fulfilling what the Apostle says: “Rejoice always in the Lord; again I say, rejoice” (Phil. IV). Anyone who considers it understands that the Apostle did not repeat this without reason. For just as wicked people, evil at heart, display darkness in their faces and foretell the place to which they are going by the horror of their frenzied words, so holy souls, brightened by the glory of a blessed conscience and rejoicing in the hope of future goods, know how to think only what is joyful and speak only what is pleasant.

Thus the handmaid of God, learning from Christ to be meek and humble of heart, hearing from Him, “Blessed are the meek” (Matt. V), and from the Prophet, “The Lord loves the meek” (Ps. CXLVI), cultivated humility of heart and gentleness of speech. Like the blessed Cecilia, of whom it is written, she served the handmaids of her Lord “as an industrious sheep.” Although she pleased all so greatly in everything she said, she uttered nothing frivolous or idle; rather, she imposed on her tongue a manner of speech which neither exceeded the Rule nor failed to satisfy everyone.

But when she came, of her own will or when summoned, to a gathering concerning any matter whatever, one could then truly perceive what she bore within or turned over in diligent meditation. For, to confess what I think, she surpassed all whom I remember having seen in both gravity and [Col. 0222B] holiness of speech, so that, had you heard her, you would have thought not that a woman but that a bishop was speaking. Her whole discourse was seasoned with sacred salt and contained nothing tasteless; it all hung upon heaven, it all expressed contempt for present things and love for invisible things. When private conversation turned to such matters, speech could not long remain dry; rather, the abundant tears that flowed forth soon revealed by what spirit she spoke.

For I remember how often, when I came to Marcigny, she wept upon my knees as upon those of a father, though I was as a son; calling herself guilty, asking absolution, weeping over the evils of the world, and panting for desire of Christ. Then, when she threw herself upon the ground and I tried to raise her with due reverence, she did not consent, but remained motionless. As though she had never repented before, she repented again in fresh [Col. 0222C] lamentations. She groaned that her exile was prolonged and entreated in vows, prayers, and groans that it might soon be ended. Amid such words, calling me at once son and father, she asked the father to absolve her as his office required, while she instructed the son with maternal affection and singular wisdom.

And when the time for my departure pressed, this was always her final farewell: “Son, I commend you to the Holy Spirit and the Blessed Virgin Mother.” Indeed, she had always used these words even in the world, and had so accustomed her mouth to them that, above other sacred words, she frequently named the Holy Spirit and the Blessed Virgin. Rightly did she join these two names in speech, teaching by her very manner of speaking that those who were joined had never been divided. But to return to what came before: [Col. 0222D] while she devoted whatever strength, knowledge, and zeal she possessed to God and to the sisters of her household, she by no means forgot guests and poor people. She received the former honourably and carefully provided for the latter, so that the former lacked nothing suitable and the latter nothing necessary.

Yet her concern was more intense for the poor, whose need weighed more heavily upon the heart of the holy woman: the greater their want, the greater the care shown them above others. Therefore, whatever could remain over from the obedience entrusted to her, she devoutly spent for their use. Frequent alms were distributed; clothing was prepared as resources allowed; either new garments were bought, or old ones set aside by the sisters were given away. To all who asked, according to the Gospel (Luke VI), [Col. 0223A] she gave without question whatever food or clothing she could scrape together from anywhere. Some, whom she playfully called her sons, she sustained with daily food and expense.

Her mind, devoted to God, found rest in them and rested, as it were, from the ancient labours of the world, believing that she had at last found “a place for the Lord, a dwelling for the God of Jacob” (Ps. CXXXI). For whatever she scattered among the poor, she rejoiced to have gathered wholly for herself, knowing that what others considered loss of property was her own gain. But why say more? She cared for all matters as a great mistress of a household, so that in serving the sisters she seemed Martha, in serving guests Sarah, and in piously providing for the poor Tabitha. Thus this woman of virtue, denying herself, taking up her cross, and following Christ, atoned by living for others for all that she had formerly lived for herself in the world. [Col. 0223B] She lived, I say, for God and for her neighbours: for God, in obedience; for her neighbours, in service—so that, according to her measure, she could say with the Apostle’s voice: “I live, yet no longer I; but Christ lives in me” (Gal. II).

Since it is difficult for a mind scattered among diverse occupations readily to gather itself again, and since the dust contracted through earthly business is not lightly wiped from the eyes of the mind, this was remarkable in her: when returning from outward things to inward, she never seemed to have departed from what was most inward. Deep silence immediately succeeded her words; the sociability of cheerfulness was changed into heavenly gravity; after public business, abundant tears flowed forth. The sisters who told me these things marvelled that her mind could be so suddenly changed among different matters and yet could not be diverted from its purpose by so many occupations. They declared that Martha’s business took nothing from Mary’s leisure, nor did Mary’s repose hinder Martha’s labours.

By these pursuits she had so united to herself the hearts of all, so established affection for herself in every heart, that they loved her with extraordinary [Latin *miro*, printed *mero*] love and called her the mother of the monastery. But how long, O soul, do you linger over words? How long do you delay what must at last be said? I know what you shrink from; I know what you doubt; I perceive what you fear. You fear to hear that she is dead, whose life, if it were fitting, you would have wished eternal even here. You dread the extinction of your lamp, lest hated darkness follow when its light has fled. You recoil from honey being changed into [Col. 0223D] wormwood; you fear day being changed into night—the sweetness of which used to refresh you, the brightness of which used to illumine you.

If she deserved so much from others, how much do you think she deserved from you? What did she cultivate on earth so greatly? What did she love so much? To whom among human affections did she grant—not, I say, merely grant, but even equal—the love she gave you? She certainly had other sons, but compared with you they seemed strangers in her maternal love. She had been your mother not once only: she repeatedly gave birth to you amid great anguish of heart. Frequent births pressed upon her, and every day, in fear over all that might happen to you, she gave birth to you again in renewed pains. She was troubled by constant care; devoting all her thought to you, she often forgot herself. She feared everything for you and thought nothing safe enough.

She kept her mind in suspense over every turn of events and feared even the best reports. [Col. 0224A] Wherever she heard that you had turned your course, she followed you in imagination even into distant regions. If you crossed to Britain, entered Italy, or went to Rome, she sailed the seas with you, surmounted the dreadful summits of the Alps and the depths of the Apennines, underwent every danger, and remained your companion in remote places through every hard circumstance. You felt the burdens of office, but she bore them. You carried them, but she supported you. You put your shoulders beneath them, but she supplied strength through prayers. She ran about, laboured, and prayed to each sister and to all alike, that they might labour for you and implore for you the mercy of the merciful Lord. They owed it, she said, to charity [Col. 0224B] by commandment, to you by obligation, and to herself by service. She said this tirelessly to sisters, brothers, and visitors; and without distinction she prayed for you far more than for herself.

Beyond all this effort, she herself devoted herself to prayer; exhausting before God every power of her soul, she poured out her inmost heart in tears before the Lord for you. She had prescribed for herself a fixed rule of prayers, so that, even if other things were omitted, that prayer for your salvation might daily be offered to the Lord. The sisters often urged you, if you remember well, to restrain her lamentations and prevent her excessive concern for you. You did so, but achieved nothing by forbidding it. How, then, will you see her dying? How will you tell of her failure? With what spirit will you behold her drawing her last breath; with what words will you bid her farewell; with what tears will you be able adequately to mourn so great a funeral? [Col. 0224C]

Yet we must come to the matter and patiently receive the common lot, until creation itself is freed from slavery to corruption into the freedom of the glory of God’s children (Rom. VIII). The handmaid of God, exhausted from her daily labour, rested during the night hours on her bed and refreshed with sleep limbs loosened by labour, in order to resume work more vigorously. And behold, she saw a woman of lovely face standing by her and calling her, by a nod and gesture of the hand, to follow. Waking, she thought that it was one of the sisters who had roused her for the night praises; she rose and, angry as though at her own sluggishness, prepared to hurry with quick readiness to church. But, looking this way and that, and seeing everyone lying around her, [Col. 0224D] she realized that she had been mistaken and laid her head down again to sleep.

As soon as sleep again touched her, she saw the same figure as before, calling her in the same manner. Therefore she awoke again and began to think the same thoughts as at first. But when she came to herself a third time, returned to sleep a third time, and was called a third time by the beautiful visitor to follow, she was also told to come quickly and delay no longer in coming. At last, when she awoke the third time, she recognized in herself the sign of the summons. Immediately seized by illness, she told the sisters that she was about to die. At once they all gathered round her, surrounding her on every side with mournful groaning. Like daughters running to their [Col. 0225A] mother, and as if they were to die with her, they lamented what they called an irreparable loss. No one could console the afflicted women, and their boundless sorrow seemed incapable of ending.

She lay unmoving in the midst of those who mourned, and although dying retained the full use of her mind. She spoke with the sisters, confessed her sins, asked to be absolved, was absolved by all, and waited in firm hope for her Lord when He should return from the wedding. She omitted none of the sacred means of salvation. The burning fervour of faith remained strong in her, so that, as the Lord says, it might almost have been compared to a grain of mustard seed (Matt. XVII; Luke XVII); it could neither grow old through a long course of life nor be chilled by the onset of cold death. At her own request she was anointed with holy oil and strengthened for eternity by Christ’s body. [Col. 0225B] Armed with humility and made secure by confession, she asked that a cross bearing the Lord’s image be brought to her. When it was brought, she stirred the monastery to renewed groans. She placed the Lord’s likeness to her mouth; licking His feet with her tongue, she pressed it against her face with all the strength of her body. She adored the Passion of the Saviour and invoked His death and wounds as conferring salvation. Before all who heard, she professed that no glory and no hope of salvation remained for her except in the cross of her Lord.

When her prayer was completed and those standing round tried to remove the Lord’s image from her face, she said, aflame with the heat of faith: “Why do you wish to take away my Lord? Leave Him with me while I live, for I am soon to pass to Him in death.” Thus, believing that she saw not an image but Christ Himself in that cross, she could not be torn from its embrace. [Col. 0225C] At last, exhausted both by illness and prayer, her bodily powers gradually failing, she came to her end on the third day after she had fallen ill.

The Nativity of the Lord’s Forerunner was then being celebrated according to solemn custom; and though it came amid mourning, it brought the promise of joys. For since he himself had been the supreme herald of eternal joy, it was fitting that she should pass on that day from mourning to joy—she of whom it had been said by the angelic voice: “Many will rejoice at his birth” (Luke I). She died on his Nativity, so that she might be believed to be among the number of those to whom the angel promised joy at his birth. Therefore, on that day which was truly her day, on which she passed to the everlasting [Col. 0225D] Day, Christ’s handmaid lay almost lifeless and deprived of all bodily strength, while her spirit alone knew no loss. Though her body had failed, her mind alone remained strong; her mind hung upon heavenly things, awaiting the hour when the Lord of the house would come.

As His approach drew near, the sisters decided to lift her from the bed and lay her in ashes and sackcloth. When they put their hands to this task, she said: “Wait, and support me a little.” When they had released her, she turned to the Lord and said: “I know, most merciful Redeemer, where this body is to be taken; but where the soul is to be transferred I do not know. The body, Lord, has for the present its lodging in the earth; but where, O gracious Jesus, O eternal Saviour, will the soul lodge this night? Who will receive it? Who will meet it? [Col. 0226A] Who will console it? Who will free it from death, pains, and sorrows? Who will provide a place, life, and rest after so many labours of the world? No one,” she said, “except You, merciful Jesus, my Saviour. All my neighbours will be far from me, and I can find no refuge except with You, my God. Therefore I entrust to You what You created; to You I confess myself guilty of every evil; from You I now ask the mercy for which I have long waited; and into Your hands I commend my body and my soul.”

“Now,” she said to the sisters, “take me and carry me where you intended.” Then all were stirred afresh to tears and weeping. She was lifted up and laid in ashes and sackcloth, an exile, poor, and humble handmaid of Christ. Shortly afterward, at the hour—at that hour when the merciful Redeemer, dying for the life of the dead, bowed His head and gave up His spirit—His gentle handmaid passed peacefully to the Lord. [Col. 0226B] Those present testified to us that, though her body was already lifeless, they saw the glory of a glorified human being. Her face shone brighter than light; death, which destroys beauty in others, increased in her a living beauty.

But perhaps someone will wonder why I have applied to a woman, so greatly unequal to him, things said of the great Martin. Whoever thinks this should observe how many things in the canonical Scriptures, spoken principally of Christ, are applied to the body of the saints, of which He is the head. Since these are innumerable, I do not wish to recount them one by one, but refer such a person to the breadth of the Scriptures. Let him recall how many things from the prophets, [Col. 0226C] the psalms, and the Gospel are recited on the birth-feasts of martyrs and the festivals of confessors—things which suit the servants in such a way as to diminish nothing from the Lord.

Let him know that the Lord does not take offence at an indiscriminate sharing with His servants of words by which He has bestowed upon them nearly all His own names, and has made known to them whatever He heard from the Father. And lest he be scandalized that sinners are equated with the righteous, let him know that I offer an equal judgment not concerning merits, which are uncertain to everyone, but concerning miracles, which are known to all. For what then? If Christ raised the dead, healed lepers, gave sight to the blind, and drove out demons; and if others too are believed to have raised the dead, healed lepers, given sight to the blind, and driven out demons, [Col. 0227A] they are said to be compared with Christ because of similar works. It is not an injury but praise of God’s name when God is said to be wonderful in His saints, not in one alone but in many. [Col. 0226D]

And lest the righteous Martin alone be thought to have had this miracle of the face, let the sinner Theophilus also be brought forward. As the now widely used account relates, after forty days of penitence and after receiving Christ’s body, his face shone like the sun. Why, then, should it be wondered at that, after many years of penitence and a praiseworthy life, the blessed woman’s face glowed with unusual brightness, when after a few days of contrition the face of one disfigured by such great crimes prevailed in splendour like the sun? Christ could do in a woman of our time what He chose to show in the sinner Theophilus and the righteous Martin of that earlier time. If the events themselves are similar, why should I shrink from using similar words of the events? Therefore let it be said similarly what is proved to have happened not dissimilarly. Nor will they consequently seem to be judged equal, because likeness of miracles does not make equality; equality of merits does.

Thus the visible face of her dead body shone with the visible splendour of the spirit; and her flesh, made luminous, showed that the daughter of light had passed to the region of light. Who could sufficiently describe the offices of the holy congregation around the blessed woman’s burial? In them there truly appeared a great example of eternal love, and the condition of the heavenly Jerusalem was foreshadowed in that service of God’s handmaids. The ardour conceived through the inspiration of God’s Spirit burned, and a stream of charity, flowing from the abundance of God’s house, poured forth from breasts of compassion. They could not satisfy [Col. 0227B] their hearts with psalm-singing, weeping, and prayer. Though they remained here in body, with their whole affection they accompanied her as she went away to a foreign country. They begged the Lord that she might not be disappointed of her hope, and prayed in continual supplication that the merciful Redeemer might console her long groans.

Continuing the night next to that day in these sacred observances, they joined to it also the following daylight. On that day, after frequent sacred offerings for her eternal rest, when the holy sisters, exhausted by vigils, psalmody, prayers, and tears, could scarcely remain standing, she was carried to the tomb. Pleasing to God, dear to human beings, living to Christ and dead to the world, she was buried according to Christian custom. The grieving sisters departed, carrying her away from the tomb in their hearts. Though they left her lifeless in the grave, they continually confess that she lives with them as long as they themselves live.

Now what return can I, O most holy sisters, worthily make for so great a kindness bestowed upon me? What can I repay for so great a gift, what recompense for such benefits? For you preserved my soul for me; you rescued it from death, my eyes from tears, my feet from stumbling. You freed me from the snare of hunters and from the harsh word. You became the house of the sparrow, a rock of refuge for the hedgehogs. All this, I say, you were to me, when you received that light of mine fleeing from darkness; when you cherished the flame of your sacred breast for so long lest it be extinguished; when, kindling it ever more through the fuel of eternal love, you have now at last joined that light, now indivisible, to the eternal Light. [Col. 0227D]

The reward for this blessed work of yours remains laid up for you in heaven; nor will the gracious Savior forget your saving attentions toward the saved sinner. For he who declares that a cup of cold water ministered to bodily salvation cannot lose its reward (Matt. 10), will far more certainly not permit so great a labor, bestowed by you upon a soul to be saved for eternity, to be lost. The angels of God rejoice over one sinner doing penance (Luke 15), though that sinner, not yet released from this body of death, still fights with the flesh of sin, the wickedness of the world, and apostate angels, uncertain of the outcome of the battle. Rejoice also, most beloved sisters: in the repentance of your sinner you are given the surest ground for rejoicing, [Col. 0228A] since by grace going before you brought her repentance to such an end that she now has no cause for fear, but every reason for you to rejoice with secure gladness.

May he increase your joy, because you hope in yourselves for what you possess in her; for you may be certain that a like contest of labors will also bring likeness of rewards. Behold, before the eyes of your compassion lies buried the humble handmaid of God and of yourselves. Though lifeless and silent, she nevertheless exhorts you with a living cry—indeed, with a loud cry, if you attend. She continually offers herself to you, sets her ashes before your eyes, and, as a sister crying out to sisters, as one dead crying out to mortals, urges you to remember her and not to forget yourselves. She shows what she now is and what you will shortly be; she points out where your bodies are to be buried and whither the spirit will migrate. [Col. 0228B]

By daily sight you behold your graves and always look upon the lodgings of mortal nature: there you are to rest while death holds dominion, and from there you hope to rise when death has been swallowed up. Let this shared contemplation, then, be a continual sermon to you; and let the decay of temporal things, which you see, itself inflame you to seek eternal things with all your effort. Meanwhile, just as seeds of trees are sown in a garden, so your bodies are sown in the holy cemetery. According to the Apostle, they cannot be made alive unless they first die; they cannot rise unless they are slain; nor grow green again unless they decay (1 Cor. 15). They must indeed decay in order to grow green again; wither in order to flower; be slain in order to rise; die in order to live. [Col. 0228C]

The winter of this present life must be endured, and the harshness of snow and rain borne with courage, so long as the fruitful beauty of the trees is hidden, so long as what you shall be has not yet appeared, so long as your life is hidden with Christ in God (Col. 3).
