The time will come when, the air having cleared, eternal spring will follow the cold storms; when the Sun that shall never set rises, driving all darkness away by its splendor and all cold by its heat, flooding the world with a light unknown to the earth, while nature stands astonished, banishing the old night and bringing a new and unending day. Then the earth, made fruitful at that wondrous time, will compel the seeds of your bodies to burst forth into new flowers and fruits, when this corruptible thing has put on incorruption and this mortal thing immortality.

Then in feeling and in reality you will sing [Col. 0228D] what you now sing by voice and faith: “Flowers have appeared in our land” (Song 2), when, going out to meet the Bridegroom with burning lamps, you enter the wedding feast that will never end. Then you too will say with the Prophet in rejoicing: “And my flesh has flowered again, and willingly I will confess him” (Ps. 27). For then confession will be voluntary, not compelled, when, according to another psalm: “You will sacrifice willingly to the Lord, and confess his name, because it is good” (Ps. 53). “Wherever the body is, there the eagles also will be gathered” (Matt. 24), because when Christ, your life, appears, then you too will appear with him in glory (Col. 3).

And you, my brothers, sons of so great a mother, to whom I have written this letter, blush to appear degenerate. From her from whom you received the origin of this life, derive into yourselves the heavenly love to which she devoted you from childhood. Let her who was mother of your bodies become again the begetter of your souls, lest you who resemble her in body be found—God forbid—unlike her in character. May she bring you to birth by her example and prayers until Christ be formed in you, so that through her you may deserve to have as Father him through whom you deserved to have her also as mother. [Col. 0229A]

## LETTER XVIII

To the venerable lord and bishop worthy of God, PETER, patriarch of the Church of Lyons: Brother PETER, humble abbot of the Cluniacs, wishes that he may deservedly be exalted to the heavenly seat of the episcopate.

Would that it were as open to the intellectual eyes of your mind how sweetly the memory of you is impressed upon my mind, and as though shaped by the image of a careful sculpture, [Col. 0229B] as it lies hidden in the recesses of my mind. But since “no one knows the things of a man except the spirit of the man that is in him” (1 Cor. 2), and the secret of the human mind remains incommunicable to others, neither can you clearly know the hidden places of my heart, nor can I fully explain them by any effort.

Yet that Spirit who, according to the Apostle, “searches all things, even the deep things of God” (1 Cor. 2), knows that I am joined to you by such love that, even while you are established at Lyons, I carry you with me everywhere; nor can you be absent through any intervening region of the earth, since the unbroken recollection of a singular affection always makes you present to me. [Col. 0229C] Thus from far away I become near, from distant adjacent, from separated joined, from sundered clinging close; so that the hateful remoteness of regions can no longer in any way separate us from one another, whom the inseparable closeness of our souls binds with firm knots.

By this remedy, though far away, I refuse to console my sorrow at your absence. For I have long been absent, and by now am accustomed to be consoled; but now, being nearby, I hunger greatly to see you in that manner, and have resolved during these days of fasting to break this fast of mine. Therefore I beseech your Blessedness, in this present Lent, to appoint for me a day and place for conversation, so that I may satisfy my longing and confer with you, so far as lies in me, concerning some matter of common advantage.

For I rejoiced at the reports [Col. 0229D] brought to me that your pastoral concern, not wholly lulled to sleep, had prudently considered the peace of the flock entrusted to you, and had thought, insofar as it was lawful for a bishop, of repelling wolves from assault upon the sheep—not only by divine but also by human strength. How praiseworthy this is, and how pleasing to God, no one is ignorant; and the prophet proclaims: “How beautiful,” he says, “upon the mountains are the feet of one announcing and preaching peace, announcing good, preaching salvation!” [Col. 0230A] (Isa. 52; Nah. 1).

Although these words may concern eternal peace, it nevertheless makes no difference if they are understood also of this present peace, which is a certain trace and image of eternal peace. In this wretched region of ours one must labor especially for it: so bereft of good rulers, exposed to plunderers, and filled with sons of Belial—that is, “without a yoke”—is it, that one might say of it what Scripture records of the land of the Israelites: “In those days there was no king in Israel, but every man did what seemed right to himself” (Judg. 17). Yet our people do not do what seems right to them, but what seems worst to them, with their whole eagerness.

Therefore, unless you first fail, I pledge to this glorious undertaking and blessed burden of yours my whole strength, and, if necessary, will undergo every labor for it. To this end I send with this letter a gold ring as a token of love, containing a precious stone of an unknown kind, and possessing in itself something more precious than the stone itself. For it is said to dry up every flow of blood. Receive, then, these gifts as dear for the sender’s sake, and understand that your friendship is more desirable to me than much gold and precious stone, and sweeter than honey and the honeycomb. Let the ring not depart from your episcopal right hand, [Note: [Col. 0229D] “Let the ring not depart from your episcopal right hand.” The ring is one of the principal insignia of bishops. *Chronicon Cluniacense*: “Gregory VI, when appointing Odilo bishop of Lyons, sent him the pallium and ring. But the saint of God, devoted to humility, utterly refused this; nevertheless, retaining the pallium and ring, he reserved them for a bishop who should be worthy.” [Col. 0230D] The same is reported by Rodulfus Glaber, *History of the Franks*, book V, chapter 4.] so that by its continual presentation it may compel the remembrance of me to remain always in your heart.

## LETTER XIX

To the lord HENRY, bishop of Winchester, to be loved with single-hearted affection and honored with singular honor: Brother PETER, humble abbot of the brethren of Cluny, wishes prosperity in this present life and the blessedness of eternal salvation.

[Col. 0230C]

Having experienced the harms of prolonged silence, I now flee from the like; and I, who had chosen silence lest I exceed in words, now fear silence itself. Therefore I again send back to your sincere affection, with a letter, the messenger who has scarcely yet returned from you. And although a long journey—and above all the intervening sea—may begrudge us mutual conversation, yet the Ocean, with its threatening aspect, will not at least be able to hinder bearers of friendly letters, nor to delay the forerunners of peace by the savage terror of its waves.

Thus I have resolved to overcome the whole nature of things, so that frequent letters may fear neither winter’s [Col. 0230D] harshness, nor summer’s heat, nor the depths of waters; and, with whatever resists our friendship conquered, the elements themselves may also speak. Indeed, by a mound of letters and a whirlwind of messengers, I have determined to overwhelm whatever hardness may still remain in you, so that, once buried beneath an immense heap, it may never again emerge anywhere to disturb the harmony of our peaceful concord.

And what Solomon says of a friend—“Let your foot wear away the threshold of his doors” [Col. 0231A] (Ecclus. 6)—since I cannot accomplish it in person, I shall take care, God granting, to fulfill through my own people. I recognize in myself—if it is so also in others—the nature of friendship: the more frequently a friend visits me, the more the fervor of his friendship grows in my heart. It is also a certain trace of eternal love: whoever is more inflamed by it is more satisfied, and whoever is more satisfied is inflamed far more abundantly.

Let, then, the firm bond of love, an indissoluble chain, unite us though far removed from one another; and let no windy talkativeness break it, like the childish frivolity of people tearing down spiders’ webs. Let your wisdom remember and beware the proverb of Wisdom: “A ruler who willingly listens to lying words has all his servants wicked” (Prov. 19). Far be it from me to believe that you willingly listen to lying words! I do not, I say, believe this; rather, I desire that your singular prudence be watchfully attentive against the many-shaped words of flatterers or compliant attendants. For the tongue, as Scripture says, is “an unquiet evil, full of deadly poison” (Jas. 3). Of it the Prophet says: “The poison of asps is under their lips” (Ps. 13): it is hostile to all, but especially to those in high station. The duty of guarding against it ought to be the more urgent because such persons have the greater power to do harm if they yield to such words. If it is not safe to be disturbed by true reports, how dangerous it is to be troubled by believing false ones!

Therefore I wished to consult you concerning Robert, a corrupter of peace and most wicked sower of enmities, who has sown sorrows but has not yet reaped them; out of reverence and love for you, I have thus far withheld my sword from his blood. As I have learned, he sowed tares not among just anyone, but between you and me; yet he has not deserved to be judged an enemy. Send me your will concerning him.

I would have sent you a monk rather than a courier, had I not been careful not to trouble the sacristan again so soon. Since you have now twice received our courier, send back to us also, at least once, your messenger. For they are accustomed to come to Marcigny, go to Lyons, penetrate the province, and travel everywhere beyond and on this side; yet they avoid Cluny alone as though it were Scyllaean dogs or rugged rocks. But I no longer charge this against you, since I trust that it has been erased from both my memory and yours. And, to comprise much in few words: think of us and ours in such a way that I may feel no trace of distrust concerning them remains. [Col. 0231D]

## LETTER XX

To his most beloved lord and intimate friend, the venerable lord HENRY, bishop: Brother PETER, humble abbot of the Cluniacs, wishes present and eternal salvation.

Just as it is necessary to apply medicinal remedies to a sick body, so it is superfluous—indeed, sometimes harmful—to administer them to one already completely healed. Therefore, when I thought that the mutual love which we had held toward one another had been injured even slightly, I could not refrain from administering abundant verbal antidotes for its healing. But now that the settled purpose of firm love remains steadfast in us, and the indissoluble bond of charity is firmly tied on both sides, it seems fitting to spare words, so that those words which, through God’s grace, can cure nothing in your heart resembling the past may not be allowed, by their multitude, to burden a mind occupied with many useful matters. [Col. 0232A]

For what could I say to increase or strengthen love, when your actions rather than words bear witness to your feeling toward us? What honor, favor, and benefit you bestowed upon our brother recently coming to you, upon daily messengers, and upon the couriers themselves—neither can they fully recount it, nor can I in any way offer you worthy thanks. And why should I proclaim that lofty summit of your works: that, like Cyrus by royal generosity [Col. 0232B] and like Ezra by priestly care, you recalled to the Temple the vessels of the house of the Lord plundered by Babylon (1 Esdras 1, 7, and 8); and that you have clothed again in the same covering Christ, whom the Jews of your time had stripped of his garments as though to crucify him anew?

He himself, I believe, beholds the intention of your mercy with the kindly eyes of his compassion; and although he has no need to be covered by any garment, yet he delights in the devotion of holy service. For he who, though he had no need of it, received the costly ointment of holy women when about to die (John 12), now dead and raised again upon his cross will not refuse your gold, which is more precious than that ointment. Yet, as regards you, we can repay nothing worthy of so great a love, nothing proportionate to such benefits, except this: whatever we are is yours; whatever we know is yours; whatever we can do is yours.

This is shown in all assemblies of our Church by the mention of you, second among all our friends and benefactors after the lord king of England; by the singular remembrance of you in the prayers of all the brethren; and by the special and almost daily commendation of you before God and men. And because, lest I become prolix to you, I have for the present restrained myself, I say briefly: let not the great distances of land and sea gain anything from your remoteness, but let charity unite and strengthen within us the love which the distance of lands strives to steal away from us, and against which no bodily spaces can prevail. [Col. 0232C]

After this, let the friendly and concerned mind know that both we and our commonwealth are well, indeed flourishing exceedingly; that, although not in myself, yet in our brethren, through God’s mercy, the former brilliance of religious observance, charity, and reputation shines; that I set out for Pisa, suffered much, went quickly and returned more quickly; that, having fallen ill there, I was healed sooner than I had hoped; that I endured much and brought back little, yet in all things abound with the Lord’s favor. All these matters we shall entrust more fully and safely, if God grants life. For the unfaithfulness of letters has often harmed their own masters more than a treacherous tongue.

Finally, that it may dwell the more deeply in your heart, I commend the holy funeral of my blessed mother to my dearest and exalted friend. I humbly ask that through you a thirty-day cycle of Masses be performed for her in the abbeys and other religious communities of your diocese, and that some poor persons be fed. She died on the eighth day before the Kalends of July, that is, on the feast day of Saint John the Baptist. Her name was Raingardis; her profession, a nun of Marcigny; her office, cellarer. [Col. 0233A]

## LETTER XXI

To our venerable and most loving lord, the lord HENRY, by God’s grace bishop of Winchester: Brother PETER, humble abbot of the Cluniacs, greeting and himself.

I have no subject for writing, but you yourself are for me a great subject for writing always. Therefore, if perhaps I trouble you beyond due measure with frequent letters, it should not seem strange, since love that is full of speech cannot be silent, and an inexhaustible subject of discourse knows no failure whatsoever. By this device I satisfy my desire as best I can: to the person with whom, if the opportunity were given, I would wish to converse in person every day, I make up through messengers either deliberately sought or encountered by chance what I cannot accomplish.

For this reason I wished to write something through this brother of ours, your monk, although, as I said, I had no subject for writing. Henceforth it will be for you not to be silent in necessary matters, since you see that I, driven by such great love for you, cannot keep silent in superfluous ones. [Col. 0233B]

## LETTER XXII

To his dearest son PETER: Brother PETER, humble abbot of the brethren of Cluny, wishes that through the service of a good son he may receive the inheritance of a kindly father.

After my conversation with the prince of Aquitaine [Note: [Col. 0233D] “After my conversation with the prince of Aquitaine”: William, who defended the cause of Peter Leon against Innocent II. On this matter see further Saint Bernard, Letter 126 to the bishops of Aquitaine, and Abbot William, book II of the *Life of Saint Bernard*, chapter 6.], whom [Col. 0233C] we could not make drink from Christ’s cup when he was drunk with Babylon’s cup, nor drain away by a Catholic antidote the schismatic taste with which he was excessively imbued, I judged a return more useful than an advance for many reasons and resolved to turn back.

Yet I did not return by the route on which I had come. Rather, making my journey through the furthest districts of the Angevins, the people of Le Mans, and the Normans, and having traversed nearly the entire shore of the western Ocean, I withdrew with my companions into France and spent at Paris the adorable feast of the Savior’s Nativity. While there, remembering you—or rather, never forgetting you even for the briefest space of time—I embrace your presence more joyfully when it is at hand, and bear your absence more painfully in proportion. To alleviate this pain somewhat, as the season allows, I wished to write to you from the flat country, as you stand upon the summit of a high mountain; so that by at least such a remedy, while you read, you may make yourself more present to me in mind, and may attentively consider how great is the difference between the lowliness of my plains and the height of your mountains. [Col. 0233D]

For you, placed upon a mountain, behold heaven with an unobstructed eye; I, set in the lowlands, and now nearly among the number of those who, according to the Prophet, “shall enter into the lower parts of the earth” (Ps. 62), look only upon broad plains and fields spread over the widest spaces. [Col. 0234A] You, by the very position of your place, seem to tread the world subjected beneath your feet; I, laid beneath the feet of all, lament with the Psalmist, saying: “My enemies have trampled me all the day” (Ps. 55). You, surrounded by the thickness of woods, are hidden on high as though in a most profound valley; I, exposed to winds blowing from every side, am seized and swept along as though headlong wherever the violent variety of gusts drives me. You, scarcely touching the ground with your steps, are raised aloft by your mind’s striving toward heavenly things; I, cleaving to earth with fixed foot—alas!—continually foul my tracks with filthy dust.

O that I fouled my steps only with light dust that could quickly be wiped away, and did not plunge my whole self, through necessity or at times even through choice, into the mud of worldly affairs! Whenever I am plunged in it, would that I emerged at once, [Col. 0234B] and sang to God with the Prophet: “Deliver me from the mud, that I may not be stuck fast!” (Ps. 68). Yet because I lament my miseries, I do not therefore envy your happiness. I do not envy it, I say, but rejoice with you; for although I cannot imitate the life of the good in action, I have always resolved to honor it with devout affection.

Therefore, amid your mountains, remember our valleys. Moses too, ascending the mountain of God, did not forget the people stationed in the plains, but earnestly begged the Lord’s mercy for them (Exod. 32). And though in the mountains he always had more familiar conversation with God, nevertheless prayer was more frequently poured out for those who remained below. God indeed threatened the people through the lawgiver, saying: “Whoever touches the mountain shall die” (Exod. 19). Yet, so that the people might not die, matters were chiefly conducted on the mountain. Whatever Moses did alone upon the mountain profited the salvation of all who were in the valleys. For their sake he ascended; for their sake he fasted forty days; for their sake he received the Law written by God’s finger upon tablets; for their sake he scarcely obtained pardon for sacrilege by many prayers; for their sake he devoted not only the mountain’s solitude but also, so far as lay in him, his own life.

So too the Lord and Savior, after saving preaching, after healing human bodies, after working many miracles, went up into the mountains, as the Gospel says: “And having dismissed the crowd, he went up alone into the mountain to pray” (Matt. 14). [Col. 0234D] And again: “Jesus therefore went up into the mountain, and remained there with his disciples” (John 6). And as is read elsewhere: “At night indeed he remained on the Mount of Olives, but at dawn, coming into the Temple, he taught” (Luke 21). The evangelist Luke also indicates that he did this habitually, saying: “Having gone out, he went according to his custom to the Mount of Olives” (Luke 22).

Another evangelist confirms that in the very solitude of the mountain he prayed not with others but apart from them. He records that Jesus said to his disciples: “Sit here while I go there and pray” [Col. 0235A] (Matt. 26). Luke continues: “And he was withdrawn from them about a stone’s throw, and being in agony prayed more earnestly” (Luke 22). Although he sought so earnestly the secrecy of prayer, he prayed not for himself but for the people persecuting him, saying: “Father, if it be possible, let this cup pass from me” (ibid.). For he did not pray not to suffer, who had come in order to suffer, as he himself had said a little earlier: “For this reason I came to this hour” (John 12); rather, he prayed that the faithless Jewish people might not be condemned through his passion, by which the world was saved. Whoever understands that he is the Savior and the Lamb of God who takes away the sins of the world cannot possibly be ignorant that he always prayed not for his own salvation but for that of the world.

Therefore, dearest son, since in ascending the mountain and living in solitude you imitate the Lord and his servant according to the grace given to you, imitate them also in other things as you can. As I have provided for your good will the quiet of solitude, so provide by prayer some relief for my labors. For through the affection with which, as you know, I embrace you in Christ’s charity with all the effort of my soul, you owe me not merely your prayers but, as Paul says to Philemon, “your very self” (Philem. 1). [Col. 0235B]

For what do you not owe me, when in loving you I have scarcely counted anyone your equal? What do you not owe me, when I have never wished to owe even myself more than I owe you? Nor is it surprising if you have been able to earn so much from me, since a recompense proportionate to your character and manner of life can scarcely be found. [Col. 0235C] At what price, or for how much, to say nothing of your other virtues, could I ever buy someone resembling or conforming to me or my habits?

If I wished to explore the hidden things of Holy Scripture, I always found you most ready. If it pleased me to discuss, by divine grace, anything from the learning of secular literature, I found you quick and perceptive. If the conversation concerned contempt for the world and love of heavenly things—matters which occurred more frequently and familiarly between us than the rest—your words were so far removed from earthly things and sounded nothing mortal that you seemed already to say to me: “Let not my mouth speak the works of men” (Ps. 16).

When I returned from human occupations, frozen with northern cold, these words relaxed me as if in the season of southern breezes and melted me by the warmth of the spirit into divine love, so that here too the Psalmist’s words might be spoken: “Send forth your word, and it will melt them; his spirit blew, and the waters shall flow” (Ps. 147). [Col. 0235D] And I could sing with the Bride in the Song of Songs: “My soul melted when my beloved spoke” (Song 5).

All things were wearisome to me; I felt everything burdensome, groaning as though crushed beneath the heavy load of punishment. I was joined to those of whom Job says: “Behold, the giants groan beneath the waters” (Job 26). There was nowhere any rest, no relief from anyone, until necessity itself directed me to return to you. But once I could obtain some little privacy with you and exchange even brief conversations, I rose more vigorously to work, as though strengthened by abundant food and renewed in strength. You fulfilled that divine command: “If you see your neighbor’s ass fallen down on the way, you shall not pass by, but shall lift it up with him” [Col. 0236A] (Exod. 23).

Certainly, through your zeal, according to blessed Gregory, I was drawn back as though by an anchor-rope, lest adverse winds carry me away into the deep sea; and, close to shore, though still tossed much even there, I held fast. Has that frequent and fervent discussion of the world’s manifold miseries slipped from your mind? Has that tearful lamentation over our own dangers, as the saying goes, been entrusted to memory? Has the repeatedly revived purpose of fleeing all earthly things and devoting oneself to God alone been removed from your memory?

O how often, with the doors shut and no mortal admitted with us, there was held—with him alone as witness, who is never absent from those who think or confer concerning him—a fearful conversation about the blindness and hardness of the human heart; about the diverse snares of sins; the varied envies of demons; the abyss of God’s judgments, how terrible he is in his counsels over the children of men; that he has mercy on whom he wills and hardens whom he wills; that a man does not know whether he is worthy of love or hatred; our uncertain and fearful calling; the ordering of human salvation accomplished through the incarnation and passion of the Son of God; the dreadful day of the last judgment; the incomprehensible severity of the divine tribunal by which he punishes the wicked forever; and the ineffable mercy by which he renders eternal rewards to the good. [Col. 0236B]

Discussion of these and like matters, removed from worldly noise, somehow made a desert for me amid people and presented the tabernacle of the Lord: to it I fled from the tumults of the world, as Moses fled from the stones of the Jews (Exod. 17; Num. 20). Weary from human quarrels and the forensic debate of cases, here I rested. Anxious over the modest care of household affairs, and worn out by many conflicts, here I was restored. Troubled by the incursions of robbers, the killing of our people, and the various devastation of places, here I changed my sorrowful mind. Here I washed away the blemishes acquired from the filth of the age, and here I cleansed out the leaven contrary to the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth. [Col. 0236C]

And why say more? Truly, according to Isaiah, this tabernacle was to me “a shade by day from the heat, and a security and hiding place from whirlwind and rain” (Isa. 4). Nor was this only at home: [Col. 0236D] wherever I turned my step, I had you accompanying my footsteps. As we traveled together through different regions of the earth, neither the heat of the sun, nor the icy North Wind, nor blasts of wind, nor stormy day, nor muddy ground, nor the ruggedness of mountains, nor the slopes of valleys took this refuge from us. Everywhere, whenever the waves of the great sea grew calm a little, this secrecy remained for us.

Thus I had you of one mind with me in all things; thus I recognized in you what I perceived in myself; so that in you alone, or almost alone, I experienced that definition of true friendship: namely, to will the same thing and to refuse the same thing. Nothing could ever please me that displeased you, nor displease me that pleased you; and, according to what is recorded as said by someone, not two souls in two bodies, but one soul seemed to dwell in each of our bodies. [Col. 0237A]

If such an affection of love could exist among those who did not know God—so that, not by confusing substances but by uniting wills, they could say this—what wonder if the charity of God, which is poured into human hearts through the Holy Spirit, united us in him “who makes both one” (Eph. 3), and who said to the Father concerning his disciples: “That they may be one, as we are” (John 17)?

But now it is time for complaints, that what I have long carried in my womb I may at last bring to birth. For you—yes, you, I say—have sinned against this charity; you divided the divine unity; you tore apart the heavenly covenant, when as friend you left a friend, as intimate companion an intimate companion, and, to speak now in terms of authority, as subordinate you left your superior, as disciple your teacher, as monk your abbot—not to say, as servant your lord. But if I called you servant, in what would I be going too far? For the Rule commands that a monk submit himself in every obedience to his superior. If in every obedience, then in servile obedience also; but it commands every obedience, therefore servile obedience. You are therefore my servant.

Accordingly I complain of my servant, who avoids his lord, seeks hiding places, refuses to follow, and is unwilling to serve. In imitation of your Lord and God, you certainly promised obedience unto death; yet you did not preserve it even unto a slight labor. He descended obediently from heaven to earth; you flee from going from one part of the earth to another. “His going forth is from the height of heaven, and his course unto its height” (Ps. 18); yours, having neither gone forth from Mount Algidus for Christ’s sake nor completed a short journey, cannot have returned to it. I did not indeed think you so oppressed by the great snows of the mountains that you would allow the fire of charity to be extinguished in you. [Col. 0237C]

[Col. 0237B] But you say: “I did not exceed the limit of obedience, because I remained with my father’s permission.” Yet you did not receive that permission spontaneously; you snatched it by extorting it with importunate prayers. This plainly was not obedience. What, then, is obedience? As the law of monks declares: to abandon one’s own will and fulfill the will of one’s teacher. Therefore it is written in the same Rule: “The second degree of humility is this: that a person, not loving his own will, should take no pleasure in fulfilling his desires, but should imitate in deeds that saying of the Lord: ‘I came not to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me’” (John 6).

The will of the one commanding, therefore, rather than his word, the intention rather than the voice, the understanding rather than the sound, are what a true monk must observe. But you said: “I shall indeed remain, but I shall pray to God for your safety.” So too Saul, perversely choosing to sacrifice to God rather than to obey, and preferring his own desire to God’s will, heard from the prophet: “Does God desire burnt-offerings and sacrifices, rather than that his will be obeyed?” (1 Sam. 15).

It is clear, therefore, that one must obey the will of superiors; and the disciple’s obedience is then at last true and salutary when, setting aside his own will, he follows not so much the master’s voice as his will. For when, through obstinacy or faint-heartedness, a disciple wrests from his master an order contrary to the master’s will, it is not the disciple who is said to have obeyed the master, but the master who has obeyed him. Thus I, obeying your will, when I saw that you did not wish to continue the journey, permitted you to remain. You, then, overturned the proper order; you turned the head into the tail; by an inverted rank you placed me last and yourself first, when, as son, you scorned to follow your father; as disciple, your master; as monk, your abbot.

Behold: while I labor, you rest; while I keep watch, you sleep; while I call out, you are silent; while I fight, you are idle; while I range through the world, you remain seated upon your mountain. Not so the good woman Ruth. When her mother-in-law Naomi, to whom she had long clung, urgently pressed her to return to her own people, she answered: “Do not oppose me, that I should leave you and depart. Wherever you go, I shall go; where you remain, I too shall remain. In whatever land you die, there I shall die, and there I shall receive a place of burial. May God do these things to me, and add these things, if death alone does not separate me from you” (Ruth 1).

But perhaps you will think her a Gentile woman, not admissible as a witness. Yet she is the one whom both the Old Scripture and the Gospel honorably mention, and from whose stock they write that the Son of God took human flesh. Let there come, however, that foreigner indeed by nation but a man who by the praise of his virtue deserves to be reckoned among men of worth—Ittai the Gittite—who, leaving behind the errors of his native land, had attached himself to the great king David and was his inseparable companion. When he was going before the king, who was fleeing before his parricidal son with a large company of companions, and was prepared to fight for his safety, the king himself said to him: “Return, and dwell with the king, for you are a foreigner and have departed from your own place. You came yesterday, and today are you compelled to go out with us? Return, and take your brethren back with you. You have shown kindness and faithfulness” (2 Sam. 15). And Ittai answered the king, saying: “As the Lord lives, and as my lord the king lives, in whatever place you shall be, my lord king, whether in death or in life, there your servant shall be” (ibid.). And David said to Ittai: “Come and cross over” (ibid.).

But why have I called that woman and this man foreigners, as though this supported your case rather than served my argument? For the weaker her sex in the one, and the more remote each of them had formerly been from the worship of God, the more praiseworthy was the faith and charity of each. Yet their praise diminishes your praise; their faith marks your unbelief; their fervor condemns your lukewarmness. For what daughter-in-law did for her mother-in-law, what a soldier did for his king, a monk does not do for his abbot. They were compelled by their own lords to return, yet they would not leave them even amid great dangers; but you, deserter and despiser alike, do not heed your master, who begs not to be abandoned.

I see Elijah, now about to be taken up and borne into heaven through the heights of the air by fiery horses and chariots, travelling with Elisha; and I hear him say: “Stay here, for the Lord has sent me as far as Bethel” (2 Kings); and a second time: “Stay here, for the Lord has sent me to Jericho” (ibid.); and a third time: “Stay here, for the Lord has sent me as far as the Jordan” (ibid.). To him, for the third time, I hear the prophet reply: “As the Lord lives, and as your soul lives, I shall not leave you” (ibid.). Because, as a disciple truly loving his master, he would not abandon him, he both saw him taken up to heaven and obtained that his spirit might become twofold in himself. Elisha, I say, said to Elijah: “As the Lord lives, and as your soul lives, I shall not leave you” (ibid.). But what do you say to me? “As the Lord lives, and as your soul lives, I shall not follow you.”

But perhaps you scorn to follow because you despair that I can, like Elijah, be caught up into heaven. If this is the reason, I beg you not to despair. I beg you, I say, and admonish you not to despair, because this is the whole and sole reason for our travelling together: that I may not, like Elijah, be caught up alone into heaven, but together with you. Behold, I dare promise you more than Elijah promised Elisha, if you are willing. He was caught up alone while his disciple marvelled and cried out; you shall be caught up with me before all the people who behold it. Perhaps you wonder at what I say and suppose that I speak as one mad. But I am not mad, because I confirm what I say by apostolic testimony. “We shall be caught up,” he says, “in the clouds to meet Christ in the air, and so we shall always be with the Lord” (1 Thess. 4). The Lord himself confirms this: “The Son of Man,” he says, “will send his angels with trumpet and loud voice, and they will gather his elect from the four winds, from the farthest bounds of heaven to their ends” (Matt. 24).

If, therefore, we strive to be among the number of the elect, we shall be gathered by the elect angels, and, to meet Christ in the air in the clouds, we shall be caught up—not separately but, as the Apostle says, together; nor shall we return as Elijah did, but we shall always be with the Lord. Therefore, as I said above, this is our whole reason for remaining together, whether at home or abroad, on the road or wherever we may be: that here we may serve the Lord together and there, caught up together, may dwell with him eternally. But I know what you will say in reply to this: “My native country, to which I never intended to return, prevents me from following you.”

To this I grant that Abraham, at God’s command, left his native country (Gen. 12), and did not afterward return to it. Yet I do not fail to know that Job, in the land of Uz, which was his native land, was a blameless and upright man, fearing God and departing from evil (Job 1). I hear from the Apostle Peter that Lot in Sodom—though not a native there, but a resident alien—was righteous in sight and hearing (2 Pet. 2). I read that the Magi, coming from the East to the cradle of the child Jesus and worshipping him with offerings of gifts as king, God, and man, returned, though by another way, to their own country (Matt. 2).

But if you cite Abraham, whom I mentioned above, I say that, as a perfect man, he feared nothing for himself in leaving an unbelieving country, but wisely provided for a weaker posterity. For he feared that his offspring, chosen by God, might dwell among idolaters and people corrupt in morals, and might gradually be drawn away from divine worship by the example of evil people. Accordingly, showing his own descendants what they ought to follow in his conduct, he neither wished himself to return to the country he had left nor permitted his son to be taken back there. In this he showed what he wished to be done concerning those who would follow him, commanding his servant: “Take heed that you never bring my son back there” (Gen. 24). It is clear, therefore, that he was providing not for himself but for his descendants, since he so earnestly forbade his son to be brought back there.

But for what sons are you providing, you who so dread returning to your native country? If one’s native land were necessarily to be shunned by good people, Job, as I have said, would not have remained in his own; the devotion of the Magi would not have returned to it; nor would the Lord himself have made it illustrious by his miracles. It is not one’s country, therefore, but the customs of one’s country, if they are evil, that good people must flee. And if, without abandoning a purpose of holiness, one may remain in one’s native country, how much more may one pass through it? But perhaps you will still maintain that this belongs to the perfect. You, then, who have been called to a purpose of perfection, will you deliberate about imperfection? You, who according to the Apostle ought to stretch yourself forward, will you go backward? (Phil. 3). You, who ought by daily progress to become greater than yourself, will you become lesser? “Be perfect,” says the Lord, “as your heavenly Father is perfect” (Matt. 5).

I certainly commend it—because it is commendable—if the sight of parents, friends, and kinsfolk causes you fear; if their grave words and their continued presence are suspect to you, lest through carnal affection they move you, however slightly, from your upright purpose by their looks, bend you by their words, or weaken you by their lingering. I truly commend vigilant caution against evils; but I do not commend obstinate resolve even with respect to good things.

But if these things terrify you, if you dread household members who cling to you as though they were hostile assailants—for “a man’s enemies are those of his own household” (Mic. 7)—raise the tower of Zion against Damascus; take up the armor of God, by which you may extinguish all the fiery darts of the enemy (Eph. 6). If the thought of perishable things murmurs in your mind, let delight in eternal things restrain it. If the serpent should dare to hiss anything through the mouths of your parents, not only should he not be heard, but his wicked head should immediately be crushed by manly strength. If you see those whom, if one may call them so, are your friends or parents still infected by the pestilence of the inhabitant by which they wished to infect you, do not cease until, cleansed by salutary admonition, you restore them to salvation; so that, having despoiled the vessels of the worst enemy, you may win from that very enemy a noble triumph before God. For it is fitting that you should make them strong, not they you weak; that you should make them spiritual, not they you carnal; that you should make them heavenly, not they you earthly. You must strive, therefore, not to place an imperfect confidence in flight, but, as a son of perfection, to offer examples of virtue to imperfect members of your household. For the laurel of victory is given not to one who flees but to one who remains; not to one who trusts, but to one who resists; not to one who yields, but to one who conquers.

I too would wish it, if the possibility were granted; nor would I wish it deceitfully, with yourself as witness. I would certainly wish, according to Isaiah, to hide myself in a pit of earth from the face of the terror of the Lord (Isa. 2), who is soon coming to strike the earth, and to seek for myself a place, not only spiritual but bodily also, in a cleft of the rock, in a hollow of the wall. But if this is not granted, or until it is granted, let us emulate him who, amid crowds of peoples, royal banquets, and gilded walls, said: “Behold, I have fled far away and remained in solitude” (Ps. 56). And, as though within the enclosures of mountains, let us build solitudes for ourselves within the hidden places of our hearts, where the true wilderness is found only by those who truly despise the world; where no outsider is admitted; where the whirl and crash of worldly tumults are stilled; where, without any sound of a bodily voice, the voice of God speaking is heard in the whisper of a gentle breeze.

To this solitude, most beloved son, while we are in this body and are away from the Lord in a foreign land, even though placed amid crowds, let us constantly have recourse; and let us find within ourselves—for “the kingdom of God is within us” (Luke 7)—what we would seek at the farthest ends of the earth. There, having attained solitary silence, let us worship and fall down before God; let us weep before the Lord who made us; let us pour out our hearts before him; and, as blessed Jerome says, let us mourn alike our own miseries and those of the world.

For there is much matter for mourning, to say nothing of what is personal: that the world lies in evil; that dangerous times are at hand; that iniquity has abounded and charity has grown cold; that truly now the holy person fails; that truths have been diminished among the children of men; that all have turned aside and together become worthless; that there is none who does good, not even one; that daily lost men crucify the Son of God again for themselves with Jewish frenzy and hold him up to contempt; that, unceasingly storing up wrath for themselves on the day of wrath, they continually furnish themselves as fuel for eternal fire. And who could enumerate everything? Gazing with more intent attention upon these things and others like them, and lamenting them before the Lord within the wilderness of the mind, let us, as coal kindles coal, kindle one another; let us beseech that ever-open fountain of mercy not to withhold itself from us. Let us choose to be in the house of mourning with those who mourn wisely, not in the house of feasting with fools who banquet, so that the Lord may say also to us: “And you indeed now have sorrow; but I shall see you again, and your heart shall rejoice, and no one shall take your joy from you” (John 16).

But behold, while I write these things, a sorrowful report, fitting our sorrow, has arrived; and it reported with abundant tears that memorable man—our Gerard, truly ours, ours—had departed from us and, to speak what I truly feel, had not fallen from life into death but had exchanged death for life. When I learned this through the sudden report, I hesitated for a time, as commonly happens in an unexpected event. Then, giving him absolution before the brethren with a voice scarcely sufficient for the purpose, I rose as an inward fire urged me, went to the church, and immediately began the office that was to be performed. There, pursuing with many tears, as was fitting, his sweet funeral—though he was absent and the news had come late—and on the vigil of the Epiphany of the Lord myself offering for him the sacrifice of the sacred body and blood, I commended that devout soul to the most devout Redeemer, to whom he had always clung.

For, to pass over his other good qualities, which would require a separate and lengthy treatment: in whom is the Lord’s promise more rightly fulfilled, when he says, “He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me, and I in him” (John 6); and again, “I am the bread of life that came down from heaven; if anyone eats of this bread, he shall live forever” (ibid.)—in whom, I ask, more rightly than in this our dead brother, who, as long as he lived, received this bread of life, that is, the body of his Lord, almost every day, always unto life? He lives, I say, he lives forever, who with the testimony of a good conscience always ate the bread that gives life forever.

## LETTER XXIII

To the venerable lord and father most intimate to us, Henry, bishop of Winchester, Brother Peter, humble abbot of Cluny, greeting.

The many and great benefits which your magnificence has bestowed upon us and upon your Cluniac brethren rightly demand many and great expressions of thanks. But the one benefit lately conferred, by the greatness of its own magnitude, justly surpasses the others, though splendid, and more excellently commends to us the affection of your benevolent heart. For who, even if dull-witted, would fail to see how great a force of love dwelt in your noble heart—a love which, breaking through biting cares, setting aside royal business, and interrupting so many entanglements of your commonwealth, drew your highness to Cluny to visit your humble and devoted sons?

I rejoiced beyond measure upon hearing this, but I was grieved beyond measure upon learning that I could not go out to meet so great a guest. No business of ours, however great it might be, could possibly have held me back from the journey. For what business could compare with this? But ignorance alone detained me—ignorance which I could not forestall. For the certain news of your arrival reached me so late that, according to the days reported to me by the messenger, I could by no means have overtaken your traces even in the county of Nevers. For that reason, though I was already willing, after breaking every provincial tie, not so much to go as to run all the way to you, compelled by impossibility I remained behind more sorrowful than I can say. Therefore, since I could not accompany you in person, I follow the beloved one through those whom I can send; and through Brother Drogo, our wise companion, known to you, I think, I convey to my singular lord and friend what it was not possible to write.

## LETTER XXIV

To the venerable lord and dearest father Henry, bishop of Winchester, Brother Peter, humble abbot of Cluny, greeting and his whole self.

Often, when wishing to write to you and to communicate my heart to a friend by at least this remedy, I reflect that nowhere else is this done. For my impatient mind, eager to reveal itself in words, burns to speak and yet fears: it burns to disclose itself, it fears lest it displease. It fears that, if it is too silent, it may seem estranged; if it speaks too much, importunate. Thus it happens that I fear both speaking and keeping silent alike. Yet I prefer sometimes to exceed in words rather than to leave unsaid what ought to be said. I have said this in order to make a way for the frequent letters that I send, and to open your eye, my friend, even if sluggish, to read them often. I choose rather to remain a talkative friend than, silent, gradually to languish away from love.

And, lest I keep either myself writing or you reading in suspense any longer: this one thing, this thing uniquely, this thing before and above all things, I ask and beseech of you on this occasion, by that hope of your salvation which you have in your Cluny: do not deny your body also to that Church of yours to which, after God, you have entrusted your soul. This will be a gift of your generosity dearer to us than every other gift; we shall receive it as more precious than all English treasures, if we find you generous in this matter. It is fitting that Cluny possess your body at least after your spirit, so that you may render yourself, after completing your priestly office, to the place to which you vowed yourself in monastic life. It is fitting that the place which most devoutly in all the world will provide for your soul’s rest through perpetual prayers should provide burial for your flesh also. On these matters we urgently request a joint written reply, and ask that it be sent to us and to the chapter. Moreover, we commend Brother Durannus and all his affairs to your magnificence. Since we have heard that he has found favor with you, we are now sending him to England.

We ask you especially concerning the manor of one hundred marks: that, as Cluny possesses it indeed by the king’s gift but especially through your goodwill and exertion, you may provide that it may always possess it in peace.

> **Note: “It is fitting that Cluny possess your body.”** In 1155 this Henry, bishop of Winchester, invited both by these and other letters of our Peter, abbot of Cluny, and of Pope Adrian, and at the same time summoned by King Louis the Younger of France and by nearly all the leading men of Burgundy, came to Cluny from England without the king’s permission, having first sent his treasure through the said Peter, abbot of Cluny. With this treasure—which was immense—he wholly relieved and cleared the debt-burden of that Church, which had been so overwhelmed that it could scarcely breathe any longer; and he supported and fully provided for the convent, then numbering more than three hundred brethren, for a year and a day. He also gave the Church forty notable chalices for the daily celebration of Masses, as well as a very costly and most beautiful silken cloth. He constructed many new buildings and repaired not a few others. All these benefits which he bestowed were then assessed, in their own outlays and expenses, at a total of forty thousand pounds, or, as others write, seven thousand marks of silver.
>
> In perpetual memorial and remembrance of these things, Ralph, abbot of Cluny and his nephew, with the counsel and consent of the fathers of the monastery, decreed that henceforth, on 8 August, an anniversary for the said Henry should be proclaimed there by the Armarius at the hour of chapter; that the customary observance should begin on that day; that on the following day every priest should celebrate one Mass, the novices should say seven psalms, and the lay brothers should be bound to say one hundred *Paternosters*; that his benefits should be recounted in the aforesaid chapter; and that a Mass for him should be celebrated daily at the altar of St Thomas by the cross.

> **Note: “We ask you especially concerning the manor of one hundred marks.”** Henry I, king of the English, residing at Rouen in 1131, in the presence of Pope Innocent II, with eight cardinals, eleven archbishops, four bishops, three abbots—especially St Bernard of Clairvaux—two English counts, and very many other noblemen standing by, gave to the monastery of Cluny one hundred marks of English silver coin annually. He assigned them as follows: sixty marks from the exchequer or toll of London, and forty from the toll of Lincoln. Documents of this donation are also found in the Cartulary of Cluny.
>
> **Concerning the hundred marks in England**
>
> “Henry, king of the English, to the archbishops, bishops, abbots, counts, sheriffs, and all his faithful subjects established throughout England, greeting. Know that I have given and granted to God and to the church of St Peter of Cluny one hundred marks to be paid every year in England: namely, sixty marks from my revenues at London, from the farm of the city, and forty marks from the city of Lincoln. Thus the officers of those cities who hold my farms shall bring this money with them to my Exchequer at the feast of St Michael and there deliver it to the messenger of St Peter. But if the officers fail to do so, the same justice shall be done for St Peter from the aforesaid money as would be done concerning my own farm.
>
> “I therefore grant this donation of mine, strengthen it for perpetual possession by that church, and confirm it by royal authority, together with those whose signs are subscribed in their own hands. I shall pay them these hundred marks every year from my treasury, and after my death they shall receive them from my successors, as is noted above. I also confirm and strengthen this donation of mine; Pope Innocent has confirmed it at my request and has bound with the bond of anathema whoever should presume to diminish or violate it.
>
> “The mark of King Henry.
>
> “The mark of Matilda, his daughter, the Empress.”
>
> The marks of the rest are lacking.
>
> Later Stephen, king, Henry’s successor and nephew, bound by duty to follow and devotedly imitate his good deeds, assigned in perpetuity to that same church, in settled revenues of land, what the aforesaid Henry his uncle had conferred upon the Church of Cluny in money from his treasury. He gave and granted to that Church forever, in exchange for those hundred silver marks, his manor of Ledecombe, which was from his own demesne, in 1136, as is clear also from his documents transcribed on p. 1398 of this *Bibliotheca*. This is the “Manor of One Hundred Marks,” concerning which our Peter, abbot of Cluny, asks Henry, bishop of Winchester “that, as Cluny possessed it indeed by the king’s gift but especially through his own goodwill and exertion, he might deign to provide how it could always possess it in peace.”

## LETTER XXV

To the dearest lord and venerable father Henry, bishop of Winchester, Brother Peter, humble abbot of Cluny, greeting.

“I rejoiced in the things that were said to me.” Formerly I used to complain of your silence, because letters from your graciousness, sent to all manner of surrounding persons, passed over me alone. Now I give whatever thanks I can, because both your letters often cheer me and your messengers delight me. For lately both a certain cleric of Auxerre, unknown to me, and the prior of Montacute of Cluny reported, in the presence of the convent, matters so friendly and magnificent that they much more kindled minds already long fervent in love for you, and more strongly set blazing those already warm. They raised the hearts of their hearers on high, and all offered a heartfelt sacrifice to the giver of so great a gift, who inclined your heart by his merciful hand to love their lowliness and raised up a strong column upon which, more especially, his whole house of Cluny might rest.

And, not to be long-winded, I ask again, through the bearers of this letter, that I not suffer refusal in the matters which I requested through Brother Durannus: choose in that place a resting-place for your body—the place to which, more devotedly than to the rest, you have dedicated your soul.

> **Note: “And the prior of Montacute.”** There were two priories of this name in the Cluniac family: one in France, subject to the priory of Celsiniarum; the other in England, which formerly belonged directly, without intermediary, to the Church of Cluny. Hence it might be doubtful which prior is meant here by our Peter, were it not that the remembrance of Henry, bishop of Winchester in England, and the subject and matter of the letter itself readily persuade us that English affairs are being discussed.

## LETTER XXVI

Innocent, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Peter, abbot of the Cluniacs: greeting and apostolic blessing.

“Concerning the care and diligence,” etc. See among the letters of Innocent II, *Patrologia*, vol. 179, no. 280.

## LETTER XXVII

To the supreme and our special father, Lord Pope Innocent, Brother Peter, humble abbot of Cluny: greeting and obedience.

I give such thanks as I can because, in paternal compassion, you spared your son and provided for my frail constitution, lest I fail on the journey. I ought not to appear ungrateful for such condescension, since he justly disinherits the heir who is not generous toward the giver of the inheritance. I had resolved to send, through the bearers of this letter, things worthy of the Father and to assist the Church in its distress, even in temporal matters. But because I intended to do this in person, I delayed. Therefore, if it please you, instruct us where, suitably, either I myself, if I can, or at least other messengers of ours may find you before Easter. Through them I may in turn visit you and assist the needs of the Church. Meanwhile, send word through these men of where you are and of the state of peace, matters which I and our brethren greatly desire to know.

## LETTER XXVIII

To the supreme pontiff and our special father, Lord Pope Innocent, Brother Peter, humble abbot of Cluny: obedience and love.

A report has reached us that certain persons are importuning the ears of your fatherhood in order that the lord abbot of Vézelay may be transferred from the monastery of Vézelay to the Church of Langres, from abbot to bishop. We ask you not to listen to them, and reason itself implores it. Nor does it merely implore; rather, to speak boldly and truthfully, it commands and compels. It plainly commands and compels, because, while apostolic majesty rightly rules over all, it glories in being subject only to reason.

What condition the man whom your authority placed there from among us found in that place, and what condition he has now restored it to—I shall not be long: you have heard it, but we have known it; perhaps you know it, but we know it better. Raised as a sign upon a dry and misty mountain, he has rendered it so rich in religion and so luminous in good reputation that, in our regions, Vézelay—apart from Cluny—allows none to take precedence over it in the pursuits of our Order; and it may truly be said of it: “A curdled mountain, a rich mountain; a mountain in which it pleased God to dwell” (Ps. 67).

What is especially difficult and therefore wonderful is that, by this man’s labor, the crowd there cannot take away its seclusion, noise its silence, clamor its order, or the world its peacefulness from the monks. Your wisdom must therefore take care lest goods acquired through long time and much labor perish in a moment: for a house built by prolonged sweat may be destroyed in one day; a tree which has scarcely been brought to fruit after many years may suddenly be uprooted; and a child, reared at length to manhood by the great care of nurses, may be killed by a single blow. We fear that this will happen if the abbot of Vézelay is removed.

But if authority cannot aid reason, remember that you ought first to care for your own, and hear the Apostle saying: “Let us do good to all, but especially to those of the household of faith” (Gal. 6). And he who neglects the care of his own, especially of his household—there is no need for me to add what follows, nor to bring before an apostolic Father some harsher words even from the Apostle. You yourself know what follows. I say this because, although the Church of Langres is yours, Vézelay is much more yours, and Cluny much more yours still. Therefore, what is more yours must be loved and preserved by you more zealously, in both authority and reason. This will happen if, with the lord abbot restored to his own place, you listen to none who counsels the contrary.

> **Note: “Vézelay, apart from Cluny, allows none to take precedence over it in the pursuits of our Order.”** Henry, duke of Burgundy, as the Chronicle of Dijon relates, “having heard the report of the religious life of the outstanding Father William,” a disciple of St Mayeul, abbot of Cluny, and then abbot of St Benignus at Dijon, “entrusted to him the abbey of Vézelay, nearly reduced to nothing, that it might be restored by him to its former condition. And he did so with God’s help.”
>
> Later St Hugh, likewise abbot of Cluny, reformed it again, as the words of the anonymous author who also wrote his Life testify: “Who,” he says, “restored the church of Blessed Mary Magdalene at Vézelay to its former condition of regular order, if not this blessed man?” Hence Roman pontiffs entrusted it to the abbots of Cluny and ordered it to remain, though older, under their discipline, as is clear from the letter of Paschal II written in 1103 to Altardus, abbot of Vézelay. Though rather lengthy, it deserves to be read here in full both for its substance and for the purpose of this work. Thus it stands in the Cartulary of Cluny:
>
> “Paschal, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved brother Altardus, abbot of the monastery of Vézelay, and to his lawful successors in perpetuity. Because by apostolic documents, etc. See among the letters and privileges of Paschal II, *Patrologia*, vol. 163, no. 83.”

## LETTER XXIX

To the venerable and most beloved to me Lord Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, Brother Peter, humble abbot of Cluny: may you always prosper in the Lord.

He whom I revere and embrace in you knows how much reverence and how much love my soul keeps for you in its inner chambers. I did this even while your absence, begrudging me the sight of your bodily face, concealed it; for fame, swifter than the body, was already presenting the countenance of your blessed soul to the eyes of my mind in whatever way it could. But when I finally attained what had long been denied, and the phantoms of dreams vanished as truth succeeded them, my soul clung to you and could no longer be torn away from your love.

Thus your charity henceforth claimed me wholly for itself; thus your virtues and the character that I came to know carried me away, so that they left me nothing of myself that was not yours, and allowed you nothing of yourself that was not mine. From that time mutual charity, begun for Christ’s sake, has remained steadfastly in me; and would that it so remain in you. This charity alone, because it knows how never to fail, has most excellently preserved its own character in me, so far as depends on you. And although I have laid it up in my bosom, hidden it among treasures, as dearer than all gold and brighter than every gem, I wonder that for so long I have received from you no such signs as I might wish of this charity which you have preserved for me.

I do indeed give thanks that, often sending greetings through various people, you have shown that you have not wholly forgotten your friend. But I complain that you have not hitherto given more certain tokens by letters. I say “more certain,” because paper does not know how to alter the words impressed upon it, while the tongues of speakers, adding or subtracting, often alter the truth entrusted to them. Therefore, since, as a chosen warrior prepared for the day of battle, you use right hand and left alike for the dangers of God’s Church, and through the arms of righteousness on the right and on the left you hold dangers in contempt, I confidently entrust to your friendship the messengers whom I send to the lord pope. For one who assists the causes of strangers cannot fail in the concerns of his own. Through them, that my complaint may be allayed, communicate by your letters not only to my envoys but also to me where you are, your return, and the condition of the lord pope. Would that, you freed from the laborious curia and I from hazardous care, one unchanging place might hold us, as I have always wished; one charity unite us; one Christ receive us.

## LETTER XXX

Brother Peter, humble abbot of Cluny, to Gilo—would that he were a brother: the spirit of counsel and of the fear of the Lord!

I would keep silent rather than speak, be still rather than write, if charity when despised could despise, if wounded could feel pain. But since, according to Scripture—and again according to that same Scripture—it “bears all things,” I have been unable either, when scorned, to scorn, or, when wounded, to take revenge. Not [Col. 0248A] because I either boast or suppose that a virtue of so lofty a kind belongs to my humility, but because I am conscious that, although I have not kept it toward you, I have at least wished to keep it until now.

The very character of the time itself bears witness to this affection of mine toward you: at a time when charity itself scarcely dared show its face, the semblance of charity could in no way falsely claim to be charity. So too does that saying of Solomon: “A friend is not recognized in prosperity, nor is an enemy hidden in adversity” (Ecclus. 12). On the contrary, if you recall it, you acknowledge that I was never absent from your good fortunes and never failed you in misfortunes. This indeed—this, in my judgment, and perhaps also in the judgment of the wise—is the complete measure of true friendship: that a friend shares the fortunes of his friend not more in prosperity than in adversity; [Col. 0248B] that he feels the other’s evils no less than his own.

Although I have not possessed such friendship toward you, I have nevertheless, as I said, endeavoured to possess it; and I possessed it insofar as I strove to possess it. You wounded it when you separated yourself from us. You despised it when, invited, entreated, and adjured, you disdained to return. Did you not wound it when you cut off from the body of the Christian world a most useful member—namely, yourself—with the sword of an unspeakable schism? Did you not wound it when, as a Christian, you withdrew from the universal Church; as a bishop, from the Roman Church; and as a monk, from Cluny? Did you not at once wound and despise it when, though I and your other brothers, pierced by the pain of your severance and therefore protesting, recalling, and drawing you back, you have until now neither heard us, nor regarded us, nor accepted us?

“I have laboured crying out; my throat has grown hoarse” (Ps. 67). My voice failed from crying; my pen was blunted; my joints worn out by writing; manifold dangers were attempted; prayers were poured forth; an irresistible argument was set before you. Yet neither threats could frighten, nor prayers soften, nor reason persuade you to return. You know what was said at Poitiers, what was promised by you to me and the brothers who had come with me at Grenoble in the last year. The ring is a witness, and the pledged faith more closely bound to its ring by its stone than the ring itself: that faith you delivered to me as a pledge that you would, as it were, follow, sealing it again with the ring I have mentioned. But the ring is kept by me; the faith pledged is preserved by God; and it is still awaited, so that the pledge may prove faithful.

Yet the Pentecost which had been fixed, before witnesses, [Col. 0248D] as the deadline for your return has passed; and the same feast of the following year is now close at hand. Perhaps, however, you delayed the matter in the hope—as you then indicated—that you expected either Peter of Leo to be preferred to Pope Innocent by the Emperor Lothair, or, both being removed, another to be raised to the Apostolic See. But now what further revolution can you either contrive or await, when Lothair is dead, Peter is extinguished, Innocent has been raised as pope and supreme pontiff—first by one part of the City, then by the whole world, and finally by the entire City—and every hope of vanity has been cut down on every side by the sword of the divine mouth?

“Return, return, Shulamite; return, return” (Song 6). Nor should you wonder that I have called you a Shulamite, because I am carried away both by zeal against your long-standing obstinate will and by love for your salvation. For—may this be said with your leave—you have indeed hitherto been a Shulamite: having departed from your brothers and household, you have lived among strangers as a captive, an exile for almost ten years. Do not allow your heart, as is written of Behemoth (Job 41), to be hardened like stone or compressed like a smith’s anvil, which, the more frequently it is struck, the more densely it is hardened into itself by the blows.

Let the brotherly admonition, so often repeated, move your heart at least at last. Let a happy migration move your body—not toward enemies, but away from enemies to fellow citizens and kinsmen. We shall rejoice more in you restored than we formerly rejoiced in you possessed; and, if you do not wish to misuse this expression, you will be the more welcome because you have been the slower to return. If this counsel of mine, now no longer new but old, pleases you, reply by letter or certain messenger, so that, since few friends and many enemies surround you, I may be able to supply not only counsel for coming but, if necessary, assistance for coming. But if perhaps you have resolved on something else—which may God avert from you!—make that known as well. For, to add something of biting truth at the end of my letter: if you despise these things too, we cannot love you more than you love yourself, nor can we now call you back if you have resolved so obstinately to perish.

## LETTER XXXI

To the venerable and beloved WILLIAM, bishop of Orange, Brother PETER, humble abbot of Cluny, greetings.

> [Note: [Col. 0249D] “William, bishop of Orange.” Better, “bishop of Arausio,” from Arausio, a city of Viennensis Secunda, which Usuard also calls Arausica at 6 Kalends of June, in these words: “In Gaul, in the city of Arausica, Saint Eutropius, bishop, whose Life Bishop Verus wrote.” In French, Orange.]

Since I know that you have been wise and devout, [Col. 0249C] and do not doubt that you are so still, I cannot sufficiently wonder that you have devoted the first fruits of your episcopate—receive this, I pray, in the spirit in which it is said—to the persecution of monks with such zeal. Those whom a greater profession of religion ought to have commended more strongly to a devout bishop have, for some cause I do not know whence arising, found in you, as the saying goes, a harsher enemy than the rest, though beyond others they should have experienced you as a father.

And when Scripture says, “The righteous Lord will cut off the necks of sinners” (Ps. 128), it would have been fitting, in my view, for the sword of your judgment first to shine upon the necks of ungodly resisters, rather than to be whetted or drawn against the throats of obedient monks. Nor, alas, could victims for your sword have been lacking, when the unhappy fertility of your land has produced sacrilegious persons, schismatics, and heretics of various ranks, as concealed as they are public; so that, had your sword resolved not to spare them, it could have grown dull before it had destroyed them all. And if perhaps its edge had remained unimpaired in dealing with them, only then would it have been just to turn against the lesser offences of monks after the graver offences of laypeople had been cut away.

But what is more unseemly—not to say shameful—is that the dispute between a holy bishop and devout monks concerns not grave or slight sins, but financial affairs. Yet the Apostle says—not to bishops or monks, but to laypeople themselves—“It is altogether a fault that there are lawsuits among you” (1 Cor. 6). But since I know you to be learned in both divine and human laws, having once discussed these matters with you publicly and privately, remember the divine law which says: “Whatever you have vowed, you shall render to the Lord for your salvation” (Deut. 23); and: “Do not transgress the ancient boundaries which your fathers established” (Prov. 22).

Recall also that principle of Roman law: “Nothing is so consonant with natural law as that the will of an owner wishing to transfer his property to another should be held valid.” I say this because it is established among our brothers—and perhaps yours, not to say among you—that [Col. 0250B] the brothers of Podiolenum possess the church of Saint Martin, through the gift of your predecessor, bishop of Orange, and the grant of Pope Urban, not only by legal title but also by bodily possession, for the lawful period which you yourselves know. Yet they have until now been wearied by excessive—let me not say unjust and damaging, let me not say vexatious—harassment from you.

> [Note: [Col. 0250D] “The brothers of Podiolenum.” Podiolenum, or Podiolanum, commonly Piolenc, is a Cluniac priory in the diocese of Orange; its church is consecrated in honour of Saint John the Baptist.]

Although they have produced both the instruments of the donation made and of the subsequent settlement—as they say, and as we have seen—which, if they are trustworthy, take the place of witnesses, they have been unable to obtain from a father, as sons, and from a bishop, as monks, either the peace they pursue or the rest especially necessary in such circumstances. Moreover—what it would be very hard to believe about so great a man unless the event itself taught it—apostolic documents which have customarily assisted others have, contrary to custom, harmed those brothers. For though they instructed your charity, as I have heard, that in the sentence of interdict promulgated by you in those churches the final decision should be reserved to them, you obeyed for only eight days, repaying that obedience with a year’s disobedience when, contrary to apostolic commands, you caused those churches to be deprived of divine services.

But why say more? Spare, if you please, your friends, brothers, and sons; do not choose to bring a stain upon your glory, to take pride in the disgrace of lowly men, or to grow rich on the spoils of the poor. But if this does not please you, name a day on which, although we gain nothing from a friend, you may learn, through apostolic judgment—though too late—that you may retain what is yours, but that what belongs to another is not yours. Yet we shall enter into litigation unwillingly. Unless we were dragged to it by the hook of compulsion, it would be both pleasing to our will and fitting to our profession to avoid lawsuits, especially episcopal lawsuits.

## LETTER XXXII

To the most noble prince and our dearest friend, Lord AMADEUS, count and marquis, Brother PETER, humble abbot of Cluny, greetings and a share in the eternal principate.

[Col. 0251A]

The glorious Louis, king of the Franks, has previously sent us his messengers and has now sent them again. He has asked that they be directed to you and that, through our hand, what they request of you may be granted. Although by his own person—as the distinguished flower and radiant star of your lineage—he ought to obtain from you whatever he wishes, yet because he has chosen me as mediator of his requests, I ask that, as he is confident that by making this request through me he will obtain it more effectively, so you may show by granting it that he has not hoped for this in vain.

Since by heavenly grace he is the supreme glory of your family, almost doubling the boundaries of the kingdom and adorning youthful years with virtues, he ought not to suffer refusal in any request, for both royal greatness and kinship of blood persuade him to hope for everything from you. And since, deriving your name from his father, you are called the king’s paternal uncle, it is fitting both that you should provide for his kingdom and that you should care for him in all things as for a son. You will fulfil both things at once if you heed him in the present affair.

But I have not inserted the matter into this letter which I send, because you will be able to receive it more fully from the mouth of the messenger than from the hand of a writer. When you have learned it—which indeed you have already heard—I ask that the sins of forefathers may not harm an innocent boy, nor perhaps the old faults of the queen or royal courtiers harm a new king. For according to the divine saying of the prophet: “The son shall not bear the iniquity of the father, nor the father the iniquity of the son” (Ezek. 18). Apply yourselves to his advancement and honour—as nature itself compels you to do for all mortals—because in his advancement you will advance yourselves, and because, I believe, you will find that his honour brings glory to you.

## LETTER XXXIII

To the venerable lord and intimate friend, ATTO, bishop of Troyes, Brother PETER, humble abbot of Cluny, the same greeting he wishes for himself.

Because your messenger was hastening to return, and because of the timely inconvenience of the season of Lent, I was unable recently to reply to your letter. I could indeed have dictated a message to any person whatsoever, but I preferred to pour what was to be entrusted from my heart into yours from my own heart rather than from another’s mouth. The reason for this preference is as follows. Wines have this characteristic: when they are frequently transferred from vessel to vessel, they grow weak in their natural strength; but, if they are drawn fresh, they are found to have kept the flavour of wine intact. So words to be entrusted to other hearts through the ears of others are sometimes made to enlarge, alter, or diminish truth by the ignorance, carelessness, or contrivance of their bearers—whether the truth has not been understood, has been neglected, or has been distorted.

Therefore, since each person knows his own heart more certainly than another can know it, and explains himself more truthfully than another can explain him, I have always resolved, when opportunity permits, to entrust myself to a friend to whom I owe my whole self—not through someone else, but by setting myself before him myself—[Col. 0252B] so that suspicion of falsehood may be removed and the mind may converse in person with one loved above others, the others being set aside.

You asked what you should answer concerning the ordinations performed at La Charité to a new man speaking new words. To this I reply: an old and experienced man ought not to fear the novel words of the inexperienced. A horse at first impatient of the bridle gradually slackens after prolonged running and finally does not obey even spurs steeped in its own blood. A boxer unbearable in fresh strength often yields to a weaker opponent. A sword newly sharpened grows dull, whether it strikes or lies unused. So it is with every immoderate movement of novelty: admirable to itself and to others because of its very newness, it burns fiercely at first and cools more quickly than one expects. It dazzles the eyes like the flash of lightning; just as it appears suddenly, so it departs scarcely seen. Thus it lights up the night only to leave thicker darkness behind as it recedes.

Therefore one must endure, and the fickleness of novelty must be borne steadfastly.
