For the man who, still burning with fresh spirit, thinks that everything is permitted him will learn, when his breast is exhausted and he can accomplish nothing, that one who is talkative now must someday be silent. At the proper time, privileges both new and old will be brought forth from the treasure-house of Rome to the one speaking novelties: privileges by which it is decreed by apostolic authority that Cluniac monks may receive sacred orders from whatever Catholic bishop they choose, [Col. 0252C] and every opponent, unless warned and brought to repentance, is bound by the bond of anathema.

> [Note: [Col. 0251D] “That Cluniac monks may receive orders from whatever Catholic bishop they choose.” We have already touched upon something above concerning this privilege of the Cluniacs from various diplomas of Roman pontiffs. But because another document, older than all those, has now for the first time come into our hands—and it contains both the same privilege and several others—it will not be entirely inappropriate to set it out here in full. It reads as follows:
>
> **Diploma of Pope John XIX concerning the election of the lord abbot of Cluny, addressed to Odilo.**
>
> “John, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his most beloved son Odilo, abbot of the monastery called Cluny, consecrated in honour of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, situated in the county of Mâcon, and, through you, to all your successors as abbots for ever.
>
> “Since the grace of apostolic charity ought to assist the requests and needs of all the faithful, the mercy of its benefaction ought much more to be bestowed upon those whom the holy Roman mother Church rejoices to have as peculiarly her own and specially as sons—both by reason of their usefulness and through the distinguished authority of the preceding Fathers. The loftiness of apostolic authority ought to comply all the more fully with their desires and prayers because it is certain that they desire and seek only those things which promote the honour of holy piety and the usefulness of true religion.
>
> “Whenever, in matters advantageous to their need, they have humbly sought our assent and the protection customary to apostolic authority, it is fitting that we should of our own accord, with an eye to kindness, duly strengthen matters for their complete security, so that from this especially a reward may also be granted to us by God, the Creator of all, in the heavenly heights. Therefore you have requested us to protect the aforesaid monastery by a decree of apostolic authority, to confirm in perpetual right all its appurtenances, remaining there inviolably, and by the document of our privilege to endeavour to establish it free from every yoke or jurisdiction of any person whatsoever.
>
> “Accordingly, moved by your prayers, through the intervention of the lord Henry, most unconquered and pious emperor Augustus, [lacuna] and for the remedy of his soul, we establish and decree by this privilege of our authority that you may securely and peacefully possess, without contradiction from anyone, all places and monasteries belonging to the aforesaid monastery of Cluny which have been granted to that place by most faithful Christians, bishops, dukes, or princes, and which have been acquired by your predecessor abbots—namely Berno, Odo, Aymard, and your predecessor Saint Maiolus of blessed memory—or whatever else appears to belong to that same place; and that all your successors may possess them through you for ever.
>
> “Moreover, under proclamation and confirmation of divine judgment and the prohibition of anathema, we decree that no bishop or priest of any kind may presume to come to act in that venerable monastery for any ordination, consecration of a church, ordination of priests or deacons, or celebration of Masses, unless invited by the abbot of that place. But let the monks of that place be free to receive whatever grade of ordination they wish, wherever it may please you and your successors. Under a like proclamation of anathema, we forbid that the same place be burdened by any bishop’s or priest’s sentence of interdict, excommunication, or anathema.
>
> “For the authority of the holy Apostolic See does not permit the freely bestowed liberty granted by it to anyone to be impaired by the binding act of any person whatever; nor may the brothers of that place, wherever they are situated, be held bound by the curse or excommunication of any bishop. For it seems dishonourable to us that, without our judgment, a son of the holy Apostolic See should be anathematized by anyone as though he were a disciple of any subject church. But if some legitimate reason should move anyone against them, and the matter cannot otherwise be determined or decided, apostolic judgment—which allows no one to claim prejudice—must be patiently awaited and humbly sought.
>
> “We also decree, and sanction by the authority of him in whose place we act, though unworthy, that the same place shall be a bosom of mercy and a harbour of every piety and salvation to all who flee to it for salvation. Let the righteous find a place there, and let the wicked person who wishes to repent not be rejected. Let mutual brotherly charity be provided for the innocent; let hope of salvation and the pardon of mercy not be denied to offenders. And if anyone bound by anathema of any sort should seek that place, whether for bodily burial or for some other benefit and salvation of his own, let him not in the least be excluded from pardon and the mercy he seeks, but let him be kindly received and cherished with the oil of saving medicine. For it is just that, in the house of piety, the love of holy brotherhood should be offered to the righteous and the medicine of pardon and salvation should not be denied to the sinner fleeing for forgiveness. Let it be for all who come there a refuge of divine compassion and piety, a cause of salvation here and for ever, and a support of apostolic blessing and absolution.
>
> “Furthermore, we decree and altogether establish that, upon the death of the abbot of the aforesaid place, no other person may be appointed there for ordination through the violence of any person; rather, according to the fear of God and the rule of the lawgiver Benedict, the congregation of the place itself shall elect the father who ought to preside over it, and whichever bishop they choose shall be called to ordain him. Whatever lands you now hold, and whatever lands you and your successors may acquire, we grant to you for perpetual possession.
>
> “If anyone, in rash boldness—which we do not believe will happen—should attempt to act or proceed contrary to the tenor of this our apostolic confirmation, let him know that he is to be bound by the bond of anathema of our Lord and Peter, prince of the apostles, and that he will be burned in eternal fire with the devil and his most dreadful pomp, and with Judas, betrayer of our Lord and Saviour Jesus Christ; and that, plunged together with the ungodly into the abyss and Tartarean chaos, he will perish. But whoever shall be guardian and observer of this our privilege, let him receive from the Lord the grace of blessing and eternal life,” etc.]

I would have sent copies of these documents to your holiness; but because the man in question has until now either presented or called himself our friend, affection must not be wounded. If it exists, it will become apparent; if it does not, it will not remain hidden. Therefore I have resolved to write to him and make a second trial in this matter. If he is a lover, he will set aside his complaint for the sake of his friend; if not, he will deal with us, not with you, concerning these matters. It is not just that you should suffer any trouble without us in an affair which you did neither for yourselves nor on your own behalf, but for us and on our behalf. I shall be your shield: protected by it, you will either not feel missiles sent by the enemy, or you will be unable to feel them unless I have first been pierced.

But behold, while I was preparing these things, a messenger intervened like one who ends a future dispute and reported that the affair of which I was treating had been removed from judicial proceedings by a peaceful settlement. He said that the bishop of Troyes had reached agreement for peace with the bishop of Auxerre and, after discussion of the matter already mentioned, that, all hostility having been calmed, they had peacefully departed from one another. Write back whether this is so, so that, if it is true, I may rejoice; if false, I may more quickly proceed to the matters I have set out above.

Concerning the following point which you inserted in your letter, receive this answer. A messenger was sent to Rome at the feast of Saint Martin—one of the priors living around us, whom I do not name because you do not know him, but who is suitable for the task. He returned in the week immediately preceding Mid-Lent. He said that, while visiting the Cluniac cells and our monasteries situated on this side of the Apennines, he had remained in Italy; and that, after travelling through everything as far as the Venetian Sea, he had wished to press on with all diligence to Rome concerning the business entrusted to him, but had been unable to do so. Monks were being captured, bishops despoiled, clergy killed; neither the former’s religious state nor the latter’s rank could avail them even a little. The roads were blocked by robbers, the fields filled with plunderers, the woods with swordsmen; and Latium itself, once the singular seat of Roman glory, groaned that it was subjected not to citizens but to barbarians and savage enemies.

When he saw that every route was closed to him, he adopted a better plan. In his own place he sent a certain brother, formerly chaplain to Lord Matthew, bishop of Albano—a man whom I too know to be vigorous, and who is very well known to the lord pope, the cardinals, and all the others who survive, since he remained many years at the curia and travelled through their course in various places. He entrusted everything committed to him to this man and sent him with our letters and yours. Before the Lord’s Easter [Col. 0255A] I expect him, by the Lord’s help, to return and report to your reverence everything he has learned. If, contrary to my expectation, anything necessary to the completion of the affair has been lacking to him, I shall then carry it out myself.

Concerning the clerk Guarin: the lord pope, our monk having gone before, laid upon you a sufficiently moderate instruction: if a free prebend were available, it was to be given to him; if not, the first one to become available was to be provided. But the prebend given earlier at Cluny, at the prayers and command of the pope himself, is not open; nor is that given to the son of Odo. And since, as I think, no other remains at present apart from these two, none is to be given. When another later becomes available, you will either fulfil the instruction or ask the author of the instruction to alter his decision. Meanwhile, if he has returned to Rome, as I have heard, make that known as well.

## LETTER XXXIV

To the venerable lord and almost his only friend, ATTO, bishop of Troyes, Brother PETER, humble abbot of Cluny, greetings, etc.

Your archdeacon, Master Gebuin, came to Cluny on the Sunday of the coming Mid-Lent.

> [Note: [Col. 0255D] “Your archdeacon, Master Gebuin.” Hildebert, bishop of Le Mans, also mentions this Gebuin in Letter 53 in these words: “Moreover, Jebuin, archdeacon of Troyes, has contributed greatly to this desire of ours, a man distinguished in conduct and learning.” Atto himself, bishop of Troyes, also records in his charter concerning the exchange and gift of Bussi for two churches that he was not merely archdeacon but also cantor, when he says: “Our son Gibuinus, cantor and archdeacon, to whose care the same churches belonged, was a collaborator in this affair.”]

When I asked him where he was going and what was the reason for his journey, he replied that he was going to Rome and that the reason for the journey was an embassy from the people of Langres. But as I observed both the clouded expression on his face and his brother Garin with him, I understood that tricks were concealed in the fox. Thinking concealment improper, I approached the man and, with the bare hand of speech, uncovered his veiled heart. I said that he was striving in vain against the current of a river, wasting strength to no purpose: he could be overwhelmed by the mass of waters, but could not force the untamed violence of the waves backward.

He must yield either to reason as a religious man or to stronger necessity: a subject to his prelate, a cleric to his bishop. He could not extort a prebend or anything similar by prayers turned into threats, by obstinacy instead of humility, by a threatening voice instead of a suppliant face; he could obtain it by entreaty. If he preferred to persist in his undertaking rather than comply with counsel, he should know that I would add whatever slight strength I had to your strength, and that I would sooner allow both of us to fail than permit persistent injustice to prevail against steadfast justice.

Hearing this, as though pierced by a dart, he rushed away from me; and after no great delay finally returned. He said that he was returning sounder than he had departed; that severe words, which had no sweetness of sound, had benefited him; that he had truly brought from you a bitter heart, but had now changed bitterness into sweetness; that henceforth he wished to submit to your command and my counsel; and that he prayed me, acting as mediator, to restore to the lord a now peaceful and obedient servant, to the father a son, and to the bishop an archdeacon, and to take care that I might return him to you as such as I had, through friendly zeal, made him for you.

He said that, because of the office of the embassy which he had undertaken, he had to go where he had begun to go; but that he had now become truly—not feignedly—faithful to you, would go not against you but for you, and would faithfully keep faith henceforth at home and abroad. Since he perceived that he had not yet persuaded me of this, he took my hand and, after requesting a kiss, as is customary in such matters, gave his pledge. He then asked me to send a letter making known to you what had been said and done. Thus he departed on the very day on which he had come.

But because, as it is almost said,

> “Nowhere is faith secure. . . . . .”  
> (Virgil, *Aeneid*, IV.373),

and because I had already sent a messenger to the City concerning the business of that prebend, before the first man returned I dispatched a second, who might either overtake or follow his journey, so that, if the pledged faith perhaps wavered, he might convict the faithless man; but, if it endured, bear testimony to it.

Besides this, I ask and advise that, in accordance with the lord pope’s command, you reserve for Guarin the first prebend that becomes available, and take care henceforth not to promise what you do not yet possess. For it is safer to deliberate long about what is to be said than to regret it after it has been said. And lest you wonder that two letters are sent to you at once, know that circumstances followed one another so closely that, scarcely had the first left my hands than the occasion for the next presented itself; and just as they had almost to be written together, so they also had to be sent together.

## LETTER XXXV

To the reverend Father and exalted in the word of glory, PETER, by God’s grace abbot of Cluny, ATTO, humble minister of the Church of Troyes, his other self, and whatever lies beyond that.

[Col. 0256C]

Holy Father, in your letter I have found the desirable treasure of heavenly consolation. Sweeter than honey and the honeycomb, it has gladdened my spirit: in teaching, it displays a spiritual physician; in action, a heavenly philosopher. In it overflow the affection of charity, natural eloquence, and the discipline of grace. For you, not ignorant, I believe, of divine counsel, being made Israel out of Jacob, both think faithfully, speak profitably, and accomplish effectively.

For this reason, like one panting for shade and thirsting for a fountain, I desire to see your blessed presence. My countenance rejoices to be refreshed by your cheerfulness and sweet speech; my soul rejoices to be formed by your example; and the condition of both inner and outer person desires to behold this great vision. It is enough for me to see you, to be with you before I die.

Indeed, to confess it with your leave, you seem another John of our age, one who has drawn streams of doctrine from the very fountain of the Lord’s breast. Thus you are able to pour forth, to those both near and far, the hidden mysteries of heaven, the teachings of Scripture, and refutations of heretics, so that all who hear may say: “Glory to God in the highest, because a great prophet has arisen among us.”

Therefore I rejoice with joy in the Lord because, by the Lord’s generosity, I have merited not only to behold with my eyes but, to speak more plainly, to touch with my hands the spices of your religious life, which, though I am absent, breathe forth to me sweetly and wonderfully; your name is oil poured out. Your name is honey in my mouth, melody in my ear, jubilation in my heart. Your name is better than great riches. Therefore I embrace with pious longing the solemn reverence due to your beloved person, in whom God has greatly been pleased; indeed, because of the indissoluble bond of love, I have bound it to my own inmost being with a pen, as it were, of adamant.

You are a golden vessel, a vessel of election in the house of the Lord, a mirror and pattern of life: your conscience is pure before God; your reputation good before human beings; your deeds upright; your words useful. All this redounds to God’s glory, to your crown, and to the shared joy of us and all good people. To your service and devotion I offer, and have offered, myself beyond what can be believed. Yet we refrain from praising certain things in you, lest our speech seem to smell of flattery.

But the integrity of your religious life, the glory of your wisdom, and the dignity of your conduct—the threefold cord which is not easily broken—compel us, so that in your religion we admire discernment, in your wisdom humility, and in your conduct sweetness. There remains what is worthier of praise: your removal of vain glory. You have emptied yourself of it so completely that the saying is fulfilled in you: “The wise man places the fruit of virtue in his conscience; the less perfect man places it in glory.” God has called your name “a luxuriant and beautiful olive tree.” Yet at the sound of a great utterance, fire has not blazed within it, nor have all its thickets been burned; for you so conceal your virtues in the secret place of your mind that you flee the scent of vain glory. I pass over lesser goods overshadowed by greater: virtues common to you and singular in others.

In all these things—indeed, in each one of them—you have wounded my heart; nor can many waters quench this love. For although the wave of the worldly stream stirs my heart all around, yet the fire of your charity, burning continually and memorably, absorbs the flooding waves [Col. 0257D]. But I am foolish, presuming to teach Minerva, wholly blind though I would enlighten one who sees. Yet this is what charity does—charity that knows no cosmetic of pretence: it commands me to lay myself wholly open to you. I wish to restrain my tongue, but it does not permit it; I wish to lay down my pen, but it forbids me. I fear a discourse that is lengthy and unpolished. But it says: “Do as you wish, for you are writing in a singular manner to a singular friend.”

You instructed me to write back to you [Col. 0258A] concerning the abbot of Pontigny or the bishop of Auxerre: what he thought concerning the ordinations performed under your charity’s auspices, or whether he had subdued the harsh language of some counsel with the hammer of counsel. You said that you were my shield: protected by it, I should either not feel the missiles hurled by the enemy, or, if I were pierced without you, could not feel them. I wish to give thanks, but the gift exceeds thanksgiving, and so my tongue is silent in giving thanks.

Yet that man, as you heard, laid down his arms before the battle; and he who had made himself a lion against himself sent himself to us as the gentlest lamb; and, before the storm could sink the ship, he set aside in peace whatever grievance there was. He recognized that it is contrary to reason that novices should be preferred to veterans, untrained men to experienced masters. You made it clear by explicit assertions that no prebend was vacant [Col. 0258B]. In accordance with your counsel, the prebend shall be kept for Master Guarin, unless the author of the judgment changes his judgment. I shall promise a prebend to no one further, because although promising does no harm, fulfilling a promise is sometimes burdensome.

That you approached Gebuin so ardently, and then, by sending a messenger after him, forestalled cunning with cunning, was divine counsel and the clearest proof of your wisdom. Therefore thanksgiving and a voice of praise resound in our mouth. We praise you concerning our messenger and yours, who has now come and has entrusted to another what had been entrusted to him, because we recognize that it could not have been done otherwise. Indeed, he is awaited by us as rain upon the fleece: that he may blunt the wrath of the raging clerics [Col. 0258C], rebuke the disobedient with the sword-point of apostolic vengeance, and make those unable to understand realize how grave a matter it is to despise apostolic commands and disparage the Cluniac name.

For they are those who neither fear God nor respect man: alien children, wise to do evil but unable to do good (Jer. 4); dead flies, which have spoiled all the sweetness of the ointment (Ecclus. 10); Egyptian flies (Exod. 8), by whom we are troubled, who drink blood made from water, and whose firstborn all die: a whirlwind wind coming from the north, a blinding cloud, an enveloping fire—evil in disposition, worse in speech, worst in life. But you, who ascend to Jerusalem with the Lord, cry out [Col. 0258D] to the Lord with the deepest cry of the heart, that he may protect us beneath the shadow of his wings until iniquity has passed, and bring to nothing those who afflict us—he who alone considers toil and pain.

Manasses of Rumilly, our reverend son and your singular friend, greets you. Odo the archdeacon, my nephew, greets you, as specially yours as he is singularly ours.

> [Note: [Col. 0257D] “Odo the archdeacon, my nephew.” The same Hato, bishop of Troyes, his maternal uncle, also mentions him in the aforesaid *Signum*, as follows: “We have made the sign in the name of the witnesses who were present: Lord Geoffrey, bishop of Chartres, a man of great authority and blessed memory; Manasses; Falco; Odo the archdeacon. [Col. 0258D] Done at Troyes in the year 1140 from the Incarnation of the Lord.” And in the subscription to the donation of a prebend which he assigned to the Cluniacs in the church of Troyes: “The sign of Odo the archdeacon; the sign of Manasses the archdeacon,” etc.]

Nicholas, your servant, greets you. He sets no measure to his love for you, but above all others continually keeps your memory especially present [Col. 0259A]. He is our helper, and especially for your sake loves us; and, by loving us, protects us. We ask your fatherhood concerning Ascelin, that you send him back to us, because he is, above all, both necessary and special to the church of Saint Margaret.

> [Note: [Col. 0259D] “The church of Saint Margaret.” This is a cell belonging to Cluny in Champagne, in the diocese of Troyes, popularly called de Mergerie. Theobald, count of Champagne, in the charter concerning Merkelicourt—which Pope Innocent III also calls “the court of Mercury,” p. 1491 [Col. 0260D] of this Library—says: “I gave to the church of Cluny the chapel situated within the enclosure of the grange called Merkelicourt, that it might belong perpetually to the church of Saint Margaret, which is a cell of the church of Cluny.”]

Lord Manasses joins me in making this request with special affection, for he loves you greatly in truth.

## LETTER XXXVI. To the Supreme Pontiff and our special Father, Lord Pope INNOCENT, brother PETER, humble abbot of the Cluniacs: obedience and love.

Asked, we ask that your fatherly mercy hear the prayers of a noble daughter, and command that the liberty of election which bishoprics, abbeys, of lesser name and lower dignity, possess by canonical and common law, be preserved to the noble, great, famous Church of Langres [Col. 0259B], so that they themselves may lose occasions of discord and give thanks to God and to you for the peace secured for them through you.

We earnestly commend to you the son of the duke of Burgundy, now for the first time approaching the clemency of your majesty, that he may be received by you with such love and honour that, as a son of good promise, he may rejoice that he has approached a good father, and may thereafter become much more bound to your service.

## LETTER XXXVII. To the lord BERNARD, abbot of Clairvaux, to be cherished with singular reverence and affection, brother PETER, humble abbot of the Cluniacs: greeting and himself.

[Col. 0259C]

I recently wrote a longer letter; now I send a shorter one. It is inarticulate for this reason: it relies on the bearer’s tongue. Its only purpose was to send its reader to the bearer and urge the reader to demand from him what it itself kept silent. Therefore, while you read this letter, ask its carrier to report what it does not say; and hear from him what you cannot hear either from me or from it. This is Gebuin, of whom we speak, well known to me and to you, and, I believe, very dear to us both.

## LETTER XXXVIII. To Lord and most reverend Father PETER, abbot of the Cluniacs, his BERNARD—his indeed.

May the Dayspring from on high visit you, good man, because you visited me [Col. 0259D] in a foreign land and comforted me in the place of my pilgrimage. You dealt kindly, understanding the needy and poor man. I was absent, and absent now for a long time; yet you remembered my name, great man though you are, occupied with great matters. Blessed be your holy angel, who suggested this to your pious heart. Blessed be our God, who persuaded you. And I have something in which to glory among strangers: your letter—indeed, those letters in which you poured out your soul to me. I glory that you hold me not only in memory [Col. 0260A], but also in favour. I glory in the privilege of your love. I have been refreshed from the abundance of sweetness in your heart.

Not only so, but I also glory in tribulations, should I have been judged worthy to suffer any for the Church. This, assuredly, is my glory, and the Church’s triumph that lifts up my head. For if we have been companions in labour, we shall also be companions in consolation. We had to labour with and suffer with our mother, lest she complain of us, saying: “Those who were near me stood far off, and those who sought my life used violence” (Ps. 37). But thanks be to God, who gave her victory, honoured her in her labours, and completed her labours (Wis. 10). Our sorrow has become joy, and our mourning has been turned into a harp. Winter has passed; the rain has gone and departed. Flowers have appeared in our land; the time of pruning has come [Col. 0260B] (Song 2).

The useless branch, the rotten limb, has been cut off. That wicked man—he, he who made Israel sin—has been swallowed by death and conveyed into the belly of hell. For, according to the prophet, he had made a covenant with death and entered into an agreement with hell (Isa. 28). Therefore, according to Ezekiel, he has become destruction and shall not stand forever. Another enemy too, as greatest of all, so also worst, has likewise been cut off. And he was one of the Church’s friends—but of those concerning whom she is accustomed to complain and say: “My friends and my neighbours drew near against me and stood” (Ps. 37). If any remain, we hope soon for the same judgment upon men of the same kind.

I am close to returning to my brethren, if life accompanies me, intending to pass by way of you. Meanwhile I commend myself [Col. 0260C] to your holy prayers. We greet Brother Hugh the chamberlain, and all who are with you, together with the rest of that holy multitude.

## LETTER XXXIX. To the glorious prince and magnificent emperor of the city of Constantinople, JOHN CALO, brother PETER, humble abbot of the Cluniacs: greeting from him who gives salvation to kings.

We give thanks to the almighty King of kings, whose kingdom is the kingdom of all ages, who has exalted your imperial majesty above all princes of the Christian name and placed it, as though in the midst of East, West, and North, to protect his Church throughout the world. Thus, when in former times northern barbarians—and also the Arabs, the final and worst enemies of the Christian name—broke into the western and southern regions, he permitted the territories of your empire to be attacked [Col. 0260D], but never conquered; rather, he transferred to you the glory and name of that great Roman Empire.

He willed that, just as authority, so also the title should pass to you; and that, with religion changed and empire transferred, your city should be called Constantinople after Constantine, its Christian restorer, just as Rome had been named after the pagan Romulus. This city, as I have said, [Col. 0261A] the all-providing heavenly Eye placed before pagan kings and barbarian peoples as an impassable goal, an unconquered barrier, a fixed boundary which they must never be permitted to cross: so that the East may be terrified, the North subdued, and the West defended.

Repelled by this barrier of your empire, the surviving pagans of the ancient error and the Turks, the new enemies of the Christian name, are restrained within themselves, content with their own territories, so that they do not dare invade those of others; and, as the power of the divine arm strengthens the hand of your might, they often lose even what is theirs. For this we, though humble, give thanks to your royal greatness; and we do not doubt in the least that God will adorn you with an eternal crown if you remain faithful in these things.

Besides this, we appeal to your faithfulness and nobility on behalf of the king of Jerusalem, the prince of Antioch, and indeed all our Franks [Col. 0261B]. For they have left great cities, estates, parents, and a wealthy homeland for love of the Lord Christ; they have purchased the places of human redemption at no price other than their own blood and continually defend them at their own peril. Sustain, cherish, and help them for love of that same Christ who is yours, lest what has been gained by such zeal of faith and such labours should perish—God forbid. This will be not only a reward for your faith but also no small protection for your empire: for just as you blunt the assaults of the North, so they will blunt those of the East.

Your father Alexius, worthy to be numbered among outstanding princes, did this. As you succeeded him happily in the kingdom, so it is fitting that you should succeed him still more happily in so good a work. Among the many praiseworthy deeds he performed, he did not permit his Greece to contain all his benefits within itself; he extended the hand of his generosity to the most distant places and enriched not only lands beyond the sea but also those beyond the Alps with abundant gifts and precious ornaments. Among these gifts, he gave to the monastery of Cluny, renowned among all Latin kings and peoples, and to the great and religious place subject to it called Charity, the monastery beside the imperial city itself called Civitot, and subjected it forever to the obedience of the abbot of Cluny and the prior of Charity [Col. 0261C].

Foreign monks seized it when our own had died, departed, or been expelled; and now, as we have heard, they have held it for almost three years. Therefore I ask—and with me the whole congregation of Cluny beseeches your royal majesty and mercy—that through the bearers of this letter you cause the monastery taken from us to be restored to us and to the house of Charity; and, for the everlasting salvation of your soul, defend from injuries and preserve in peace the servants of God who are to dwell there.

And that we may make some spiritual return to you for doing this: just as our predecessors and we ourselves have made the kings of France, England, Spain, and Germany, the Roman emperors themselves, and the kings of Hungary neighbouring upon you, brothers and sharers in all the benefits of the Cluniac congregation, so we receive your highness, on behalf of almighty God, the most blessed Mary ever-virgin Mother of God, the holy apostles [Col. 0262A], and all the saints, fully and perfectly, insofar as we may, into those same spiritual benefits. May the almighty Saviour increase and preserve your temporal empire here, and in the world to come bring you with the holy kings to everlasting life. Amen.

## LETTER XL. To the venerable and great pontiff of God, the patriarch of Constantinople, brother PETER, humble abbot of the Cluniacs: may you be clothed with the stole of the eternal priesthood and crowned with glory and honour.

Although both the remoteness of lands and the division of languages deny us one another’s faces and deprive us of speech, yet one Lord, one faith, one baptism [Col. 0262B], one charity ought at times to join what has been divided, unite affections, and establish communication of words. We ought to be united on earth by that bond through which we expect to cleave together in heaven, never to be separated, so that in our miseries may be our consolation what will be our perfect reward in blessedness.

Would that the body could do in me what the spirit desires: that I might see the city founded in Christ by Jesus Christ, king of heaven, and Constantine, prince of earth; and that I might see and venerate there, not buildings or adornments, but the faith of the God-subject princes and prophets, apostles, evangelists, and many martyrs translated there from diverse regions of the world—as though a common cemetery. I would pour out whatever prayers I could to those holy fathers of our faith and hope; and great hope of attaining salvation would be born in me if I might deserve to have as intercessors for it those whom I have had as its preachers [Col. 0262C].

I would see your desired face; I would venerate in you the blessed bishops of your city; and, from their blessedness, mourn my manifold misery as was fitting. I would enter into a covenant never to be dissolved, and, unless perhaps you rejected it, swear to mutual and spiritual love. Present, I would ask what I also ask while absent: that you receive me and the flock of Cluniac brethren, in the spiritual gift of your charity and of your people’s prayers; and that, insofar as concerns us or ours, you may obtain the same from us with equal affection.

After this I would ask what I now ask: that you command the place belonging to the church of Cluny and the monastery of Charity, called Civitot and situated near Constantinople, to be restored; and that, if necessary, you ask the lord emperor to restore it [Col. 0262D]. Alexius, his father—an emperor of great name and glory even among us—gave it to Cluny and the monastery of Charity. As he succeeded him in the empire, so it is much more fitting that he should succeed him in justice and piety. We therefore commend the humility of our monks and brethren to your pontifical excellence, so that through you you may cause what is ours to be restored to us, and so that justice may obtain what is its own and sons may deserve to be heard by their Father.

## LETTER XLI. To the most dear and now truly venerable brother, Lord ROBERT, brother PETER, humble abbot of the Cluniacs: greeting.

[Col. 0263A]

I give thanks to God and rejoice with you, most dear brother, that I now behold, as report has it, the happy fruits of holy works in the heavenly purpose you have embraced. Long ago I had seen in you the flowers of divine seed in devotion and its foliage in devout speech. I cannot say how gladly I hear how you have subjected beneath the feet of your mind, by contempt, the glory of worldly pomp—whose exaltation I used to see, not in you, but you within it; how you have exchanged luxuries flattering you from every side and the overflowing Babylonian rivers of pleasures for the delights of God’s paradise and the torrent of his delight; and how you, once the eloquent tongue of the court and almost the sole interpreter of the royal hall [Col. 0263B], have now chosen busy leisure and religious silence, like one who does not hear and a mute person who does not open his mouth.

This admonishes me too—and would that it did so unto imitation!—that by a blessed exchange you have exchanged king for King, kingdom for kingdom, life for life, glory for glory: the deceptive for the true, the mortal for the living, the fleeting for the eternal. Having laid aside the wretched hope you had in the world, you await the blessed hope and appearing of the glory of the great God and our Saviour Jesus Christ, never to be deceived by him. I congratulate you upon casting off the yoke of a harsh taskmaster, submitting your neck to Christ’s sweet yoke and light burden, and passing from the muddy works of the Egyptians to the pure sacrifices of the Israelites.

But, to add some admonition, you must walk carefully with your God in this divine work you have begun [Col. 0263C], lest, beginning in fervour, you turn to lukewarmness; lest your lamp be extinguished in the midst of darkness; lest day be changed into night. For “many are called, but few are chosen” (Matt. 21, 22); for “all indeed run, but one receives the prize” (1 Cor. 9); for the daily denarius is rendered not in the morning or at the sixth hour, but in the evening (Matt. 20); and because, as you have often heard, that well-known and most-desired reward of eternity is promised to beginners but given to those who persevere. Therefore walk so that you may arrive; run so that you may grasp; fight so that you may conquer. If you persist, the heavenly watcher will assist your contest: crushing Satan swiftly beneath your feet, he will make you fight happily, conquer more happily, and be crowned most happily.

The news that you wish to come to Cluny and visit that place to which so many benefits have been bestowed through you so enlarged the joy already begun in my heart that, if charity could have achieved what it wished, I would have transported you from England to Burgundy, from Reading to Cluny, across so great a stretch of land and sea, at the very moment when this was reported to me [Col. 0263D]. Since this could not happen, I pray that the good spirit once conceived in your heart may not be extinguished by any occasions, and that your mind may not be turned away from a purpose so beneficial to you and to us, until a fitting resolve follows through with the good result which I both desire and hope will shortly come about.

Would that the day might shine upon me when I could see you in that church, just as formerly clothed in the old man, so then adorned in the new. That company of saints, which you then saw only in part, will rejoice with you and, seeing you made like them not only in spirit as formerly but then also in outward habit, will rejoice together with you. I too shall embrace with new joy the new soldier of God and rejoice that you have been transferred from the court of a good but mortal—indeed, now dead—king to the palaces of the best and immortal King.

Concerning your sister, whom you instructed us through our beloved son Thomas that you wished to join to the handmaids of God at Marcigny: I praise this praiseworthy intention and advise that the prepared salvation not be delayed. I shall make ready Marcigny for the sister as I make ready Cluny for the brother [Col. 0264B], so that, with joy doubled, you may rejoice not only in your own advancement but exult also in her salvation.

## LETTER XLII. To the reverend Father and his lord PETER, venerable abbot of the holy church of Cluny, GEOFFREY, by God’s grace humble minister of the church of Châlons: a son’s love, a subject’s willing obedience in all things, and devout prayers without ceasing.

> [Note: [Col. 0263D] Geoffrey, bishop of Châlons. He is the first bishop of this name, and Peter himself replies to him in the following letter. Châlons is a city of Belgica Secunda on the Marne, concerning which Fulbert, bishop of Chartres, writes: “Lest you deny its due honour to the city or church of the Châlonnais [Col. 0264D], you should remember that in ancient descriptions of Belgica Secunda that city held third place after Rheims; in French, Châlons-sur-Marne . . .”]

Because you received my son—indeed, my Ethiopian—with such sweet affection that at the very outset of your favour you advanced him to a priorship, I form a conjecture concerning myself. For if the servant is received with such honour and such affection [Col. 0264C], with how much greater glory, should the opportunity present itself, would his master be received? Yet I perceive, I perceive the useful ingenuity of your holiness. You placed him, as it were, at the exit of my house, so that in all his necessities he might find a familiar resting-place. This is how you are accustomed to make your friends blessed. Lest we should be idle, you always bind burdens upon us to carry. And God knows: our will is ready, according to our knowledge and ability.

But let your holiness write back to my humility whether I shall find you at Cluny in the third week after Easter. For on the Sunday, “I am the good shepherd,” I shall be at Étampes, and from there I desire to set out to you, unless severe illness or the lord king detains me. May God, our God, bless us. Write back what you please; but do not interrupt your great affairs [Col. 0264D], if any there are.

## LETTER XLIII. To his singular and intimate lord and friend, the illustrious bishop of the church of Châlons by God’s grace, Lord GEOFFREY, brother PETER, humble abbot of the Cluniacs: greeting.

True, true is what Truth says: “They do not gather grapes from thorns, nor figs from thistles” (Matt. 8). But conversely this too is true, true: they do not gather thorns from a vine, nor thistles from fig-trees. I have experienced in your letter what I say [Col. 0265A]: from an olive, nothing but oil; from a honeycomb, nothing but honey; from a full udder, I could draw nothing but milk. Your words might have been doubted, had your deeds not preceded them.

My friendly heart has acquired friends not with bare affection. You are accustomed to show greater generosity in heart than in mouth, more in deeds than in words. I remember—and it has not slipped from my mind—the cleric who, commending himself solely by my name, was kept in your household for so many years by your blessedness, loved so singularly, cared for so diligently, instructed so carefully. I remember—and it has not slipped from my mind—again, that another succeeded the former when he departed, and thus that a familiar hearth was always occupied by members of the household. I remember—and it has not slipped from my mind—what you resolved concerning the cell of Verdun, concerning that one which I wish to name but cannot; what you said [Col. 0265B], and what, so far as depended on you, you did.

I remember you as the foremost disseminator, founder, and promoter throughout all France of the Cluniac—indeed, divine—order; you, I say, as the expeller of the ancient dragon from the lairs of so many monasteries; you as the awakener from long sleep and prolonged monastic torpor. While I recall, ponder, and retain these things and a thousand like them, I blaze wholly and entirely with sacred love for you. This is why I chose you as one of two men whom, at the summit of unfeigned charity, I not only considered but publicly proclaimed to be set above all the friends of your whole Belgic Gaul.

And what of this too: although it is necessary that you be not merely bishop but prince of so great a city, the bishop claims nothing from the monk, the prince usurps nothing from religion, and the world steals nothing from the ancient order [Col. 0265C]? Since this is so, what favour have I done you if I received your son, whom you also call your Ethiopian, as was fitting; kept him with me for you for some time; and sent him back to you in the manner in which you wrote? But I truly sent back a son; I did not send back an Ethiopian. For he is not that Ethiopian “who does not change his skin”; even if perhaps he once had it black, he nevertheless brought it back from us, I believe, white.

And if it still needs to be made whiter, take pains, as a skilled fuller or craftsman, since you are accustomed not only to adorn the head with a pontifical mitre but also to tame the backs of the unruly with an abbot’s rod. If he conducts himself equally well here, the merit is yours; if otherwise, I shall demand punishment from you. As for what you have indicated concerning your coming: happy will be that day [Col. 0265D], a day unequalled by any others, which deserves to see you and your Cluny together. But far be it that it should see you without me and begrudge me the sight of you! I shall be there; setting aside everything except perhaps the unavoidable, I shall meet my festive friend—an uncommon title—as a solemn friend.

This indeed at any time; but if your arrival is hastened for the time you indicated, my presence, I trust through God’s grace, will not be lacking. Finally, because, in accordance with your words, I do not wish you to languish in idleness, I commend to you the brother of our most dear subprior Lord Garnerius. When, through your labour, he has become worthy, wise, and learned, send him back to us as you did the other, so that we may always gather what you scatter [Col. 0266A], reap what you sow, and eat what you grind.

## LETTER XLIV. To the honourable brethren, to be received venerably in the charity of Christ, serving God at Mount Tabor, brother PETER, humble abbot of the Cluniacs: eternal salvation.

A brother of your congregation, as he said, recently came in the dress of a pilgrim to the regions of Gaul and Spain for the sake of prayer, as he asserted. Passing through our parts, he greatly gladdened us, as was fitting, by telling us of your condition, formerly unknown to us; of your order; and of your zeal for religious life. He much increased—indeed, entirely united to your holiness—the affections of our hearts [Col. 0266B], by reporting that you are united to our body in the present age not only by the common faith and monastic profession, but moreover by the careful observance of the Cluniac order.

We therefore rejoiced in the Lord that we had sent back something of good endeavour, though not through ourselves yet through our own people, to that holy land from which we received the salvation of faith and faith in salvation. You too should rejoice if you have been able to receive some harvest from the seed you sowed, some fruits, however modest, from the shoot you planted. For, as the great Apostle says, “he who ploughs ought to plough in hope, and he who threshes, in hope of receiving fruit” (1 Cor. 9).

This grace was also bestowed in our and your days upon our and your Gaul by the heavenly Giver: before other parts of the world, before all the world’s peoples and nations, it was chosen to free the sacred sites of human redemption from the yoke of the ungodly, restore them to liberty, and open them to the faithful peoples of the whole world. Previously these places had for nearly five hundred years been made inaccessible by the resistance of the faithless; now they have been made passable [Col. 0266C].

Therefore you inhabitants of the holy region, dwellers on that holy mountain where, when the Lord was transfigured, the prince of the apostles Peter desired to remain—though he did not know what he was saying—when he said, “Lord, it is good for us to be here” (Matt. 17; Mark 9); the mountain whose holiness Peter, now of soundest mind, extols when he says, “We heard this voice with him on the holy mountain” (2 Pet. 1): you, most beloved, labour to be holy upon the holy mountain. For the Holy of holies enjoins this and repeatedly reiterates and impresses it, saying: “Be holy, for I am holy” (Lev. 19, 20).

Although this is said generally to all Christians and especially to all monks, it is in some manner said still more especially to you. Not only Christian profession, not only monastic devotion, but also, as I have said, habitation in the holy place itself ought to make you readier for every good work, more devout, and more blessed as you persevere steadfastly in such works. Therefore you should devote all your effort to chastity, humility, and charity, lest your deeds oppose your salvation and hinder your Saviour, who wishes to save you. For, as you yourselves know very well, holy places do not save; holy deeds save.

And because [Col. 0267A] all or many of you migrated from the lands on this side of the sea to those beyond the sea, let them consider their souls and examine the intention they had in passing from here to there. Let them also attend to the intention they have now. For, in the saying of a pagan but wise man:

> They change their sky, not their spirit, who hasten across the sea.  
> —Horace, *Epistles*, book 1, epistle 11, line 27.

I introduce this saying in order that, if you recognize that your former dispositions must be changed, you may change them for the better. For according to the Lord: “If the eye is single, the whole body will be full of light; but if it is evil, the whole body will be full of darkness” (Luke 11). Purify, then, the eye of the heart both by right intention and by sacred virtues, so that, transformed by spiritual transformation, you may deserve to contemplate Christ, transfigured upon his mountain—not now, as of old, in bodily but in spiritual glory—now through hope and love, but in the future face to face [Col. 0267B].

“We are transformed from glory to glory, as by the Spirit of the Lord” (2 Cor. 3): that is, from the glory of faith to the glory of sight; from the glory of virtues to the glory of joys; from the glory of merits to the glory of rewards. “As by the Spirit of the Lord,” because, comparing spiritual things with spiritual, he teaches that through the Spirit of God manifold graces are bestowed here and the immensity of glory granted there.

Works of darkness cannot in any way accord with this mountain, illustrious in mind and luminous even in name—for *Thabor* rendered into our language means “light coming”—a mountain so splendid; for “there is no fellowship of light with darkness” (2 Cor. 6) [Col. 0267C]. “For you are all children of light and children of the day; you are not of night or of darkness” (1 Thess. 5). Let the heavenly and celebrated splendour of your sacred place not slip from your hearts: almighty Father, Son in his glorified body, and Holy Spirit in a shining cloud willed to consecrate it. The whole fullness of the Godhead, consecrating that place, foresaw, beyond the universal salvation which it provided thence for all, your own days also and these last times.

By such great miracles and holy revelations it warned the inhabitants of so great a place that they must always be most vigilant concerning sacred things, and must not bring deaf ears to the commands of the heavenly Master, to whom the world has been subject from ancient times. Of him it was commanded on your mountain to the whole human race: “Hear him” (Matt. 17). And since this sound has gone out into all the earth and penetrated even the remotest ends and furthest corners of the world, it ought to resound more clearly where it first sounded, and be heard more promptly and continuously where it was first heard [Col. 0267D].

But I know that you do this and, with the help of the grace of the Saviour of all, will do so much more. Therefore, as soon as I heard of you, I drew you into my heart and welcomed you there with the fullest love, asking that you repay to me and to the brethren serving the same Lord who is ours and yours what I, first and uninvited by anyone, bestow upon you: namely, that you pray for us as we pray for you, so that the faith and charity which unite us here with you, though unseen and most distant, may unite us by the grace of Christ the Lord and gift of his Spirit [Col. 0268A] to live together and rejoice together forever.

Henceforth, though we have come to know you late, we shall bestow upon all of you, as brethren now most dear, such affection as we can fully give, and upon all your concerns such practical aid as we are able. May the grace of the Holy Spirit be with you all. Amen.

## LETTER XLV. To the priest of God, Lord ATON, bishop of Troyes, to be named with honour and remembered with love, brother PETER, humble abbot of the brethren of Cluny: greeting and blessed life.

You wrote; I did not write back. You sent; I sent nothing in return. You spoke; I did not answer. Why this? That I may use apostolic words in speaking to an apostolic man: “Is it because I do not love you? God knows” (2 Cor. 11). But what use is it to me [Col. 0268B] that God knows this, while my friend does not know it? And—oh, what have I said!—does my friend not know it? For how does one remain a friend who does not know that he is loved? Or how will that ancient definition of friendship stand, according to which friendship is said to be nothing other than agreement, with goodwill and affection, concerning things divine and human? Such agreement—or, as one of the learned calls it, such affection—cannot exist between fewer than two. Yet neither according to Tully nor according to Gregory can two or more agree in one goodwill or affection while they do not know the reciprocal feelings of their hearts, while they do not communicate their sentiments to one another, while they are ignorant whether they love or hate each other.

Why say this? Because I heard—and, what is more, saw in your letters [Col. 0268C], for seeing is more certain than hearing—that your Beatitude had been informed by some person, as I might say, an ex-monk, that the ardour of my friendship toward you, a friendship not new but long-standing, had either grown altogether cold or become very lukewarm. If this was only heard and not believed, I give thanks; if heard and believed, I raise a complaint. But since neither is certain to me, I neither give thanks nor raise complaint.

First, I say this: I am not so inconstant in friendship, so fickle, so unstable, as to cast away what I know to be sweeter, nobler, and more useful in this life which we possess and in that which we hope for, and so abandon such sweetness of life while keeping bitterness for myself alone. For, as Ennius says, [Col. 0268D] “what life can be life indeed which does not consist in the mutual goodwill of a friend?” What is sweeter than to have someone with whom you dare speak of everything as with yourself? Therefore the friendship between us has not been cast aside; it has not grown cold; it has not grown lukewarm—so far as I am concerned.

Yet, while mutual affection remains safe, I may complain: although it has not grown lukewarm, that same friendship seemed to have grown lukewarm on your side, since, even if the words of that false-speaking man were not believed, they were nevertheless considered important enough for you to write to me about them in doubt. But enough of this.

The reason why, when you wrote once, twice, and three times, I wrote nothing in reply was this: first, a harmful bodily illness; second, the haste of the messenger; third, the pressure of busy times, which then required my whole attention, compelled me by a forcible command to be silent. For unless the most urgent necessity pressed, my speech could not remain mute so long toward one to whom my heart is always attached and with whom it always speaks [Col. 0269A].

I had intended to write much about many matters; but because these are rather necessary matters and should be discussed with you more privately than published in letters, I restrain the spirit that wishes to overflow into words, and reserve for a meeting in person things that ought not rashly to be pressed upon one who is absent. Therefore I ask—indeed, I entreat, and, if that is not yet enough, I even beg—that neither any distance of lands nor the burdens of episcopal business deprive me or your Cluniac house any longer of your presence. Rather, at least by the feast of the Apostles, may your Cluniacs see their bishop, whom they have long hungered to see.

> [Note: [Col. 0269D] “Your Cluniacs see their bishop.” Aptly, “your Cluniacs.” For Hato, bishop of Troyes, to whom this letter is written, was a monk of Cluny, as is also evident from these words of the necrology of Arremanes, a monastery: [Col. 0270D] “On the fourth day before the Kalends of September died Hato, bishop of Troyes and monk of Cluny, who gave the churches of Clareyo, Follis, and Anglodura, and conferred other benefices upon this monastery.”]

May they see him, I say, and rejoice [Col. 0269B], since nothing could make them happier than if they should be granted, even for a little while, the presence of so intimate a friend and so desirable a father. The rest, which I did not wish to commit to a letter, I have entrusted to the bearer, that, since he is known—and, I believe, beloved—both to me and to you, he may convey my matters to you and report yours to me.

## LETTER XLVI

To the glorious and magnificent king of the holy city Jerusalem, Brother PETER, humble abbot of Cluny, salvation from Him who gives salvation to kings.

We give thanks to the almighty King of kings, who has raised your Highness to the royal throne of His royal city Jerusalem and crowned you with a glorious diadem [Col. 0269C]; who has appointed you ruler over His people, defender of His Church, enemy to His enemies, in a city so great, so holy, so noble, so renowned; and who, greater than all these things, has distinguished you by His own exalted name.

For since He Himself was called by the Fathers, prophets, angels, Jews themselves, and Gentiles, King of Israel and King of Jerusalem, He has willed that you should be king after Him and for Him of that same Jerusalem, of true Israel itself: so that, concerning your person and the kingdom entrusted to you by Him, “the sceptre of equity may be the sceptre of your kingdom,” that you may love justice and hate iniquity; while you rule with an iron rod the enemies of Christ’s cross and of the Christian name—I mean Turks and Saracens, Persians and Arabs, or whatever barbarians oppose human salvation, indeed His own salvation—and break them with a mighty right hand like a potter’s vessel [Col. 0269D].

Since we cannot further this undertaking by arms, we support it in spirit; since we have no power by the sword, we strive, as we can, to aid your martial labours by prayers. Give glory, then, to Him who has glorified you, so that, as Christ daily triumphs through His priests over the devil and his angels, He may likewise win frequent trophies over the nations through Christian kings. Thus, while you fight and refuse no dangers for His people, He will continually supply victory, add glory to glory [Col. 0270A], and, when your transitory kingdom has passed, provide for you an everlasting kingdom with the holy kings.

We commend to your generosity the venerable bearer of this letter, Lord Drogo, precentor of the Church of Nevers, so that, should need arise, he may find you so munificent that he will give thanks both to God and to you.

## LETTER XLVII

To the venerable lord Patriarch of Jerusalem, most dear to us, Brother PETER, humble abbot of Cluny, greeting and prayers.

Since the grace of the Lord Jesus Christ has made you priest of that Church from which the priesthood of the old Law and of the new grace began, and in which the Saviour Himself, reconciling the world to God by a unique sacrifice, willed to be both priest and victim, I desire, seek, and long—as I honour the Church itself—to cherish its prelate with special affection, honour him with special reverence, and, if the means were granted, serve him with special devotion.

Nor do I alone do so; the entire humble congregation of Cluny, spread throughout however many lands, likewise desires, seeks, and longs for this, as is fitting. For since the eternal Sun, far more brightly than the morning sun, illuminated the darkness of our West from your East, and willed that the Gospel of the eternal kingdom be preached from Jerusalem among all nations, we are bound by the debt of so great a benefit that we ought, wherever we can, to serve not only your Highness, who presides over places of such holiness [Col. 0270C], but even the least person who serves them; and to cherish with singular affection, as is just, those to whom we cannot render such service.

For, since monastic order forbids us bodily to visit those—those, I say—heavenly places of our redemption, to kiss them, to bedew them with tears, or to worship where the Lord’s feet stood, we do what alone remains: we pour out our hearts before Him, beseeching you, His vicar, to stand before Him for us all and to fulfil our part, as common charity commands. And whenever devotion or duty leads or summons you to visit the saving places of His birth, burial, resurrection, and ascension, carry us everywhere with you in spiritual affection [Col. 0270D], and pray to the most merciful Saviour for your Cluniacs.

This I beg, each of us begs, all of us together beg; and, though absent in body, present by letter, we ask that you hold our memory unfailingly and forever. We add this to our prayers and beseech with all the effort we can: that you may visit, enrich, and honour your Church of Cluny with relics of the Lord’s tomb, of blessed Mary, and with such others as may seem good to you.

I should gladly speak with you longer, at least in this manner; but because the bearer was hastening on his journey, the longer discourse had to be cut short [Col. 0271A]. At his own request, we commend him especially to your affection. He is worthy of much recommendation and, as we believe, known well either to you or to many of yours: namely Lord Drogo, precentor of the Church of Nevers. Now undertaking the journey to Jerusalem for the third time, he has by many labours, with happy hope, gained for himself, as we believe, much rest.

## LETTER XLVIII

To the venerable Lord ALBERIC, bishop of Ostia, to be treasured in the innermost recesses of the soul, and legate of the Apostolic See, Brother PETER, humble abbot of Cluny, greeting and immortal life.

> [Note: [Col. 0271D] “To Alberic, bishop of Ostia.” Hugh, archbishop of Rouen, also dedicated to him a book against the heretics of Armorica, as we have already noted elsewhere. The Chronicle of Cluny says of him: “Alberic of Cluny [Col. 0272D] was a monk in the time of his own abbot—that is, Peter; afterwards, having become bishop of Ostia, he was apostolic legate in the regions of Jerusalem.”]

We sympathize with anxious heart in your pilgrimage, so long and so prolonged; and, with Him who alone knows the secrets of hearts as witness, we journey with you almost in affection and longing. For although obedience and your apostolic legation have sent you to those eastern regions, and the welfare of the Christian people has made you, as it were, an exile from your native soil and from your brethren, yet we grieve that we have almost lost the man whom, after Matthew the bishop of great and pious memory, we had as the sole consolation of our order and heart in the Roman palace. With so many lands lying between us and so great a sea threatening, we scarcely dare hope for your return.

And whereas it might have been enough that the West, keeping you within its borders—that is, at Rome [Col. 0271C]—had made you very remote from us, now at last the East, as if violently snatching you away, makes you most remote. Nor has it permitted even a report, much less a message, concerning so intimate a brother and friend to fly to us, however faintly, through the air.

Yet I received, read, and reread the letter which you sent us from the City at your departure; and, when all the brethren had been called together in chapter, I recited it myself. Although I have learned nothing certain from it concerning your condition, both when your letter was received from you and repeatedly afterwards I commended your sweet and praiseworthy memory to that same assembly. They always receive this kindly and, with such words and prayers as they can, most devoutly accompany your journey; and they continually beg that Christ the Lord may restore you to them as their beloved one, their father, their lord [Col. 0271D]. And, as the disciples rejoiced when they saw the Lord rising from the tomb, your brethren and sons earnestly pray that they may rejoice when you return from that same tomb.

## LETTER XLIX

To his singular father and friend, Lord PETER, by the grace of God abbot of Cluny, ATO, bishop of Troyes, sends the same greeting that he sends to himself.

To use the words of a philosopher: spaces of place cannot divide the sovereignty of love; the inconveniences of time cannot separate it [Col. 0272A]. Affection, holding and ruling its dominion, always loves, even when it cannot see the one it loves. True friendship knows no forgetfulness and suffers no interruption. It takes no comfort from impossibility, nor remedy from difficulty. Though troops of business press upon it, though it is oppressed by the tumultuous voices of clamouring people, yet it remains in thought with the one it loves, thinking of him and rejoicing in him.

I am governed by these laws of friendship, so that I rejoice in you, think of you continually, and do not forget your holiness, in which I rejoice that I have many times found both counsel and help. Blessed am I, because I trust that the same return of love exists in you; but more blessed if it may be certain. Yet there is something that I can no longer conceal, which friendship compels me to bring forth. O God! Where are the frequent letters, the repeated consolation, the accustomed eloquence by which you used to comfort an elderly friend [Col. 0272B]? But perhaps pens cannot be found, ink is lacking, messengers are absent, the road is mountainous, and dangers accompany it. But enough has been said to the wise.

Lord Theobald, archdeacon of Sens, has this one longing: to come to you. Our affairs, which Master Nicholas, your friend, carried to Rome, have been handled better than we hoped. Write back the good pleasure of your graciousness, that I may know what I ought to answer the archdeacon.

## LETTER L

To Lord ATO, bishop of Troyes, beloved and always to be remembered by me with affection, Brother PETER, humble abbot of Cluny, the greeting that he wishes for himself.

[Col. 0272C]

Dearest friend, you have the manner of a bellows, which by the breath with which it is full compels an almost dead spark to kindle and sometimes burst forth into immense flames. Thus your spirit—not like that airy breath, but, as I believe, divine—by writing often strives to awaken, not the dead fire of my heart’s affection for you, but the vapour of my speech, long covered by silence; and, like a bellows continually blowing, it endeavours to recall it to its customary words.

But I do not want—I say, I do not want—a friendly heart to judge this as indifference, or to take slowness of words for failure of feeling. For even if speech is interrupted, that fiery vigour and heavenly origin of the seed conceived long ago is neither extinguished nor put to sleep. For, according to our Scripture, “many waters cannot quench love, neither can floods overwhelm it” (Song 8). Yet, as is seen almost everywhere, beneath the hollow spaces or overhanging vaults of furnaces a blazing fire lies hidden; nevertheless, though shut out by stone barriers, it displays outside no sign of any heat [Col. 0272D].

So the force of my affection, by which I always keep you hidden in the depths of my heart, continually repressed by the obstacles of cares—as you yourself once saw—can indeed always remain within, loving as it does; but it can scarcely ever reveal by words how great it lies hidden inside [Col. 0273A].

There is another reason that has counselled silence to me for some time and has made my spirit grow cool, not, as I said, in love but in speech: I see that the hope which I profess concerning your salvation—a hope which I had received from your own lips, when and where you know—is deferred more than I once believed it would be; and therefore I fear that it has not vanished, but has languished. Either, then, you will take care that I may recover the hope I had presumed of you, or else I shall not loose the bonds of the silence once conceived, the one thing I can do. For I prefer fruitfully to keep myself enclosed within myself than idly to pour myself out beyond myself. For one who has experienced it knows what a task the leisure of silence is, especially since the tree of works comes forth and flourishes from the root of meditations.

Why, then, should I be fruitlessly talkative to you, when I might rather be judged an importunate man persistently raising shouts at one who is deaf? For, to speak boldly to a friend of one mind, who would not despair of your progress in matters about which I have often warned you, when I see your daily failure concerning those same matters [Col. 0273B]? Who would now presume that he could uproot an aged oak, already supported by deep roots, when no force of the most diligent farmer could break from its native soil a soft twig, still tender in its recent growth?

But now, that I may no longer spare you and may at last entrust to faithful letters secrets known to us two: where is that devotion? Where is that affection approaching heaven—indeed, as it then seemed, surpassing heaven itself—by which you vowed yourself to me, to me, I say, indeed rather, as must be said, to God Himself, not merely as a brother but, that I may rebuke you familiarly in your own words, as a son and a monk [Col. 0273C]? Where is the pledge given, where the appointed time, where the named day, when you vowed that you would abandon the world, seize the kingdom of God, cast off worldly grandeur, follow the humble and poor Jesus, though still a lofty and wealthy bishop?

Was that ever-watchful eye, seeing all things whole and together, closed when these things were done? Was that ear, hearing all things together and whole, deaf when these pledges were reciprocally exchanged, so that they cannot be heard as the testimony of two witnesses of the Gospel or of the world, “in whose testimony every word is said to stand” (Matt. 18)? Or perhaps, when the troops of episcopal business rushed in, these things were driven from your mind and, as other thoughts occupied the place, were thrust out and yielded it [Col. 0273D]?

But behold: let fleeting memory return—return surely to your mind, if indeed it had already been driven away. Let it remember the festive day of Palms; let it not forget the public sermon to the people by which you solemnly adorned that day. Let it remember that chapel of Cluny—

> [Note: [Col. 0273D] “Let it remember that chapel of Cluny.” This means the chapel of the Blessed Virgin Mary, commonly called the Abbot’s Chapel, dedicated in 1118 by Lord Guy, archbishop of Vienne, as is clear from the acts of that dedication printed on p. 564 of this *Bibliotheca*.]

—which, more beautiful than the churches of our Burgundy, adorned with fitting paintings and marked by more illustrious miracles of Christ’s deeds, afforded us a most suitable place for secret conversation [Col. 0274A]. Let it not escape your mind that the abbot assigned the bishop, as was fitting, the place in his own seat and compelled him to sit despite his reluctance; he himself sat beside him on the monk’s mat adjoining that seat.

The conversation was held not about low things but about things above. It was prolonged for some time because the matter required it. Finally it came to this: that a day should be appointed by you for your return to us, accepted by us, awaited when accepted, and deferred when awaited. And although, at your request and with my consent, it was postponed from one time to another, it is nevertheless still awaited, urged, and invited by me.

But, alas, what am I to do? Am I trying to separate a priest from the altar, a bishop from his people, a shepherd from his sheep? Am I labouring to draw down from heaven and join to mud that brow gleaming with a golden plate and bearing the ineffable name of God; that head adorned with a mitre; that breast with a breastplate; those shoulders with an ephod; that body shining in sacred, jewelled raiment; and the feet themselves, last in the construction of the whole body, shod with sandals [Col. 0274B]? Am I, I say, striving to bring down all these things, and still more that sound of heaven, and the man arrayed in them—no longer earthly but altogether heavenly—and join them to mud, while I seek to unite such exaltation and such eminence to monastic humility, and desire him to become equal with men who have become the refuse of all?

I know, I know the dignity of the priestly order; I recognize its exaltation. But I judge humility to be higher and safer than these. I hear Christ saying: “The scribes and Pharisees sit upon Moses’ seat” (Matt. 23). But I recall Him adding: “All things whatsoever they tell you, observe and do; but do not do according to their works” (ibid.). I remember too that, reproaching the scribes and experts in the Law, He said: “Woe to you who have taken away the key of knowledge. You yourselves did not enter, and you hindered those who wished to enter” (ibid.). Again, to the same: “Truly I say to you that tax collectors and prostitutes will go before you into the kingdom of God” (Matt. 21). Again, to them: “Woe to you, blind guides, who say: Whoever swears by the temple, it is nothing; but whoever swears by the gold of the temple is bound” (Matt. 23). Again: “Woe to you, scribes and Pharisees, hypocrites, who devour the houses of widows while making long prayers. For this you will receive a greater judgment” (ibid.). Again, through the ancient prophet: “Woe to the shepherds of Israel who were feeding themselves” [Col. 0274D] (Ezek. 34). And shortly afterwards: “Behold, I myself am against the shepherds; I will require my flock from their hand. I will make them cease from feeding the flock any longer; nor shall the shepherds feed themselves any more. I will deliver my flock from their mouth, and it shall no longer be food for them” (ibid.).

Why these things? So that, dearest friend, as you consider the eminence of the episcopal order, you may consider its danger also; as you recognize its honour, you may recognize its labour also; and, perhaps loving a higher rank, you may fear, as the ancients said, a more grievous fall. If certain pleasures entice you, far more things that sting, bite, and embitter should deter you from loving them—not only those expected after death, but those felt here and now [Col. 0275A]. Let these and those deter you; let these and those invite you, so that you flee holy but dangerous things and take refuge in things holy and safer.

For, to speak more openly: as a higher place on high is prepared for holy bishops, so, if I may put it thus, a lower hell in the depths is reserved for bishops by reason of their life and conduct. And lest anyone think that I rashly presume to offer such counsel to a bishop, let not he alone but the whole world with him receive examples clearer than the sun, by which not only royal but even pontifical dignity—that is, not merely secular but ecclesiastical exaltation also—is shown sometimes to be contemptible.

Concerning royal or secular dignity, the Gospel says: “Jesus, when He knew that they would come to seize Him and make Him king, fled to the mountain” (John 6). Concerning pontifical or ecclesiastical dignity: “The child grew and was strengthened in spirit, and was in the deserts until the day of his manifestation to Israel” (Luke 1) [Col. 0275B]. In saying this of John the Baptist, son of the priest Zechariah, it shows that in the order of his course, according to ancestral custom, he could have held the priesthood; yet he exchanged it, with its pomp, luxury, and delights, for lowliness, fasts, and solitude.

But if it is objected that John the Baptist fled an episcopate not yet acquired but to be acquired, innumerable examples of great bishops and holy abbots come to hand. Fleeing honours not merely to be acquired but already acquired, they taught later generations that one must indeed stand firm and faithful in an office entrusted to one, but that every office, every rank, every dignity must nevertheless be renounced when inward danger presses.

But lest it be burdensome to bring forward, from nearby examples, Saint Justus, bishop of Lyons, with many holy fellow-bishops, or Saint Hilarion, the Syrian abbot, with many holy fellow-abbots, I refer the reader to the ancient deeds of the saints, so that he may either learn what I say if ignorant, or, if he knows it, recognize that I speak truly [Col. 0275C].

I do not say this because I fear so greatly for you, or despair of your salvation in your present ministry. Rather, because I see that in these most evil times of ours the wickedness of the world has grown in strength, human sloth has fallen away from virtues, an abundance of wickedness has issued forth as though from fat, and justice and piety have been left as though bloodless [Col. 0275D], I desire for you not what is stronger, but what is quieter; not what is more glorious, but what is safer. For, as Father Augustine says, a small good with a small evil is better than a great good with a great evil.

But grant that, as concerns the soul, there is no danger and all things are safe and secure; grant that abundant reward in heaven remains for a shepherd on behalf of his sheep: what of the barking of dogs? What of the snares, deceptions, and frauds of those around you, attached to you, and serving you? Did not he feel these things and grieve over them who said: “Lord, deliver my soul from wicked lips and from a deceitful tongue” (Ps. 119)? Again, when he said: “Lord, divide their tongues, for I have seen iniquity and contradiction in the city” (Ps. 54), did he not desire to flee these things, especially when he had said above: “Behold, I fled far away and remained in solitude” (ibid.)?

Does not Wisdom say through the wise man: “It is better to go to vegetables with love than to a fatted calf with hatred” (Prov. 15)? Does not the same Wisdom again say: “It is better to sit in a corner of the roof than with a contentious woman” (Prov. 21, 25)? Do you not daily—indeed, continually—experience this contentious woman, I mean the Church entrusted to you, in one part of herself [Col. 0276B]? Have you not become deafened by her lawsuits and perpetual contentions? Or do those things not shake you alone which, even when merely heard, wear out your friends?
