Hence annual journeys and returns to the city of Rome; hence frequent envoys from Gaul to Italy and from Italy to Gaul, ranging over everything from sunrise to sunset, and again from sunset to sunrise; they disturb one who is peaceful and do not cease to assail without cause one who wishes to live peaceably with those who hate peace. These things, then, are to be fled, as it seems to me, dearest friend, not embraced. Blessed rest is to be preferred to labour, security to fear, safety to dangers. One must come away from enemies to friends, from strangers to brothers—indeed, to sons and servants [Col. 0276C]—who long for you and desire to refresh their long hunger upon you.

Your paradise of affection at Cluny awaits you before the paradise of delight:

> [Note: [Col. 0275D] “Your paradise of affection at Cluny awaits you.” Geoffrey, abbot of Vendôme, also calls it paradise, in Letter 1, Book IV, to Hugh, abbot of Cluny: “May he not give them an occasion for crying out against the place of Cluny, which I dare to call a second paradise.” Peter of Celle, in Letter 1, Book II, to our Peter the Venerable, calls it the Lord’s garden in these words: “Count the stars of heaven; count the sand of the sea; and you will be able to count the fruit of the Lord’s garden, namely, the Church of Cluny.”]

There are the tree of life, delightful beauty, and beds of aromatic plants set out by perfumers: by their sight you will be gladdened, by their fragrance delighted, by their taste satisfied. You too will repay your sons in return, by your holy virtues, when, humbling episcopal majesty, you teach monastic humility not to become proud.

Until this happens by God’s granting grace and the inspiration of God’s Spirit, the ever-devoted unity of our multitude continually begs you by its prayers: at last, after long ages, to present yourself to them; to celebrate with them, as a priest of God, the most sacred days of the Lord’s Passion and Resurrection [Col. 0276D]; and to increase the light of those radiant days by the splendour of your arrival.

The remaining matters about which your fatherhood wrote, especially concerning Lord Theobald the archdeacon, I have placed in the mouth of the trustworthy envoy. Because he is mine by profession and yours by devotion, I have taken special care to send him diligently to your affection, dearer to me almost than all these mortal things.

## LETTER LI

To the distinguished son NICHOLAS, Brother PETER, humble abbot of Cluny, everlasting salvation in the Lord.

[Col. 0277A]

Since from the time I came to know you I have always reserved a good and secluded lodging for you in my heart, it is fitting that you should sometime repay my affection in return and compensate it with whatever diligence you can. I grieve that the lord bishop of Troyes, whom, as you know, I placed long ago in the supreme citadel of my heart, has somehow become invisible. I invite him to appear again by letters and prayers sent to him.

For he has kept himself absent for so long that, when through the grace of God and his own he presents himself—as we hope in the near future—I greatly fear that I shall not recognize him without an identifier, and that, though affection itself has not been erased from my heart, the image of the beloved has been erased; when he comes before those standing by, I shall blush. Therefore, lest this happen, make every effort that he may come sooner, and that in the week of the Lord’s Passion and Resurrection—of mourning and joy, sadness and consolation—the disciple and bishop may visit by his presence Christ’s servants and Christ’s monks, stir them up by exhortation, and celebrate days so great for human salvation not with raging crowds but with those who are quiet and humble [Col. 0278A].

## BOOK THREE

[Col. 0277]

## LETTER I

To the venerable Lord HENRY, bishop of Winchester, remembered with the pleasant memory of the heart, Brother PETER, humble abbot of Cluny, greeting prepared by God for those who love Him.

[Col. 0277B]

Since your reverence, so worthy to be embraced, recently departed from Cluny, my tongue has remained mute toward you, but my conscience has not been silent concerning you. My speech has been silent, but my devotion has not been silent; my talkativeness has grown cool, but my affection has not grown cold. Nor is this surprising. For since almost all the friends of the Cluniac fold, all its protectors, and all its benefactors have converged in you alone, it is no wonder if our love, formerly divided among many, has gathered itself to you alone.

But since we have certain assurance that this is established with you, [Col. 0277C] there is no need to multiply words about it, nor tediously repeat what you know very well. Yet I ask, and most earnestly request that you write back to me, the matter that has now given me cause to write: what is the condition of the kingdom of England, and especially what is your condition and that of your people? What is the state of your health and prosperity? How are our own places faring—do they rejoice in peace, or still labour under an uncertain lot? What is the conduct of our people, and what report is there of them?

I ask all this of you because all our affairs chiefly depend on you and look to you, as you know, for singular help after God. Our brethren, your sons, continually imploring Almighty mercy for you in affection and prayer, reverently greet your reverence and ask that you remember them also before the Lord [Col. 0277D].

## LETTER II

To the eminent and most highly venerable ALBERO, great bishop of the great Church of Liège, and to the noble community of that same Church, Brother PETER, humble abbot of Cluny, and the humble flock of the Cluniac fold, greeting.

> [Note: [Col. 0277D] “To Albero, bishop of the great Church of Liège.” This Albero, or Adalbero, second of the name but fifty-ninth in order among the bishops of Liège, was made bishop in the year of Christ 1136, having been primicerius of the Church of Metz. “A young man indeed [Col. 0278D] in age,” as Aegidius, religious of the Golden Valley, writes, “but gray-haired as a sign of a mature mind, and born of the Namur lineage”; his sister’s son Godfrey was duke of Leuven.]

Would that such ability were granted to my humility as the will has long since been granted: that I might embrace in person, for ourselves and for all good men, your person; that I might see the sacred and venerable body of the Church entrusted to you by God; and that, as I have long desired, I might communicate not by writings but face to face the most ardent affection of charity which I bear toward you. For although we owe both honour and love, united by the bond of charity, to all the Churches of Christ which by their multitude make up the body of the one Catholic Church, yet among all the Churches of Germany we owe this to you by a certain special and familiar prerogative: not only because we have been moved by your love, but because by frequent benefits and very great gifts we have been magnificently invited to return a reciprocal kindness.

Indeed, the monastery of Cluny has often received many gifts and many benefits from teachers of God’s Church and from innumerable leaders of the Christian people. But when these are compared with your gifts, your benefits, and your presents, although they are great and precious, they become insignificant. Truly the Church of Cluny has received, and often, as I have said, receives the treasures of many and various persons who lay up treasure not on earth but in heaven; yet your gifts surpass those of others as greatly as man surpasses beasts, and wisdom surpasses all riches. Cluny therefore received from the Church of Liège gifts far dearer than gold and topaz, when it joined to the humble fellowship of its own members the distinguished men who came from you—men to be remembered with the highest praise and affection.

For, to say nothing of others who came before our time and were unknown to us in appearance, when can the memory of the Church of Liège perish at Cluny—a Church which made Hezelo, Tezelin, and Alger, canons and great teachers in their own day, disciples of humility and, as we ourselves who saw them testify, true monks?

> [Note: Hezelo, Tezelin, Alger, canons. We have already discussed Hezelo in connection with the *Life of St Hugh*. Tezelin is also commended by the author of the *Chronicle of Cluny* which we published. Finally, Alger is praised thus by our Peter in the *Treatise against the Petrobrusian Heretics*: “The third, namely Alger, formerly canon and teacher at Liège, afterwards in our own time a monk and priest in the monastery of Cluny, where his book *On the Sacrament of the Altar* is also kept, was a man of pure and devout conduct.” Another author of the *Chronicle of Cluny* likewise reports that “for ecclesiastical business he composed letters to various persons and many eminent Churches, which are carefully preserved and read with the greatest zeal by many. For he was subtle in intellect, eloquent in speech, steadfast in purpose, and—what is more precious than all these things—was deemed, and was, Catholic both in faith and doctrine. When already an old man, he was also ordained priest; and, having lived religiously for nearly ten years, he ended by a happy death the good life which he had led also while a cleric.”]

The first of these, labouring long for the Church to which he had come, with exceptional learning and an eloquence worthy of proclamation, not only trained the characters of his hearers but also built the material fabric of the new church—which some among you have seen—more than any mortal after the kings of Spain and England. The next, giving his whole person to spiritual studies alone, grew old in his holy purpose and, having lived first at Cluny under holy Father Hugh, then at Vézelay with Lord Abbot Rainald, his nephew, and finally under the archbishop of Lyons, ended a praiseworthy life with a holy death.

> [Note: With Lord Abbot Rainald. Our abbot celebrated his memory in an honorific epitaph, found among his other verses and rhythms.]

The third, whose memory I can scarcely mention without tears, surpassing the preceding men in my judgment by humility, purity, and the integrity of his whole life, lived among us in my time and conducted himself so kindly and holily that, although he has departed from us in the flesh, he cannot fail to remain always with us in spirit and singular remembrance while we live. He left us his book *On the Sacrament of the Altar*, invincibly fortified by the authorities of the holy Fathers: both a distinguished testimony to his faith and a singular defence against the ignorance or error of certain modern persons.

May the almighty Spirit, who breathes where He wills, inspire your hearts, so that you may imitate the life and examples of those holy men whom I have recalled before the eyes of your minds. Coming from you, as I have said, and departing, after the manner of the great patriarch, from country, kindred, and their own house, they recovered through holy pilgrimage the fatherland they had lost; and, exchanging the pride of the world for humility, luxury for frugality, and riches for poverty, they have now by God’s grace attained it. Therefore, beloved brethren, clinging to you by this remembrance as by a kind of glue of charity, and asking you in return to cling to us, we pray that this memory may be continuous among you, as it is perpetual among us.

With this confidence we also earnestly ask you concerning the Cluniac places situated in your diocese, hoping that we shall not be repelled by you but heard. In particular we commend to your friendship Lord Gerard, prior of Bertreis, and the house committed to him. He deserves this, we believe, not only through the nobility of his birth, by which he is well known to you, but also through the honourable conduct of his life, for which he is to be commended by us.

> [Note: Concerning Lord Gerard, prior of Bertreis. This priory, also called St Mary of Bertreia, is in the diocese of Liège. By whose gift it came into the right and subjection of the Cluniacs is shown by the letters of Adalbero, bishop of Liège, to whom this letter is addressed; those letters too are printed in full on p. 1387 of this *Bibliotheca Cluniacensis*.]

## LETTER III. To the illustrious and glorious king of Sicily, Lord and friend ROGER, Brother PETER, humble abbot of the Cluniacs, greeting from Him who gives salvation to kings.

> [Note: To Roger, king of Sicily. Roger the Norman, surnamed Borsa, son of the count of Sicily and duke of Apulia, was the first, as Thomas Fazellus says in book VII of the latter *Decade of Sicilian Affairs*, “who no longer allowed himself to be called duke of Apulia and count of Sicily, but took care that the royal name should be fitted to the provinces over which he ruled, and that the enduring remembrance of himself should be commended by a royal stock and this splendid beginning.” Therefore, “being hailed king by his people both of Italy and Sicily, he was anointed and crowned king of Sicily at Palermo, in the year of salvation 1129, on the Ides of May.” Not long afterwards Pope Innocent II also granted him, besides the royal title, “the city of Naples, which until then had obeyed the emperor of the Greeks, together with the rest of Terra di Lavoro, Apulia, and Calabria, as far as the Sicilian strait.”]

[Col. 0280B]

“Through me,” says the Wisdom of God, “kings reign, and lawgivers decree what is just” (Prov. VIII). Since the heavenly judgment has judged you to belong to their number, we render such thanks as we can to that supreme governance: not only because it has set your highness over great peoples, but especially because in setting you over those peoples it has provided for them. For this reason we rejoice; for this reason we glory in the Lord; for this reason, though unknown to us in face, we embrace your exalted person in the arms of true affection; and we humbly and frequently pray that the almighty Saviour may magnify and preserve your royal power for the honour of His name and the salvation of His people.

For who would not rejoice? Who would not, with all his strength if need be, work together that, after so many storms of wars and evils, the blessing of such profound peace bestowed by God through you upon Sicilians, Apulians, Calabrians, and many other peoples may be preserved, increased, and extended? Who, acknowledging himself a member of God’s Church, would not exult in the Lord at the peace of so many Churches, so unshaken and stable, restored and preserved through you, as I have said? Who, hearing that clerics, monks, knights, peasants, merchants laden with money and various goods, and every class of persons dwelling in or passing through your land hold all that is theirs peacefully, all fear of tyrants, plunderers, and even robbers themselves removed—who, I say, hearing that such great benefits are bestowed through one good ruler upon so many and such great classes of men, would not render such thanks as he can to the King of kings and pray that the kingdom may be preserved and enlarged for such a king by Him?

These things, as I have said, first moved me to love you; these compelled me to admit you also among the greatest friends and benefactors of the Church of Cluny, among the great kings—I mean the Romans, Franks, English, and Spaniards. For that reason, for a long time now, I have made myself both an intercessor before God and a herald among men for your peace, honour, and welfare; and I have drawn to the same task, as many as I could, both from among our own people and from others. My conscience bears witness to this; the Roman chancellor bears witness; and the Lord Pope himself bears witness. Whether he was at Pisa, Rome, or within Gaul, I repeatedly approached him—present in speech and absent by letters—about your peace, beseeching and urging him not to trust your enemies, who disturbed your peace and right.

Although long delayed, this has now at last been brought to fulfilment. It rejoices us and all lovers of peace who could hear of it, and invites us to render thanksgiving to God. Therefore I beg and, so far as I can, admonish you as my dearest and exalted friend: embrace with all your heart this peace offered by your shepherd and the supreme teacher of God’s Church, and strive with all your effort to retain it, so that he may rejoice in you as in an excellent and special son, and you in him as in a kindly and singular father, alike in spiritual and temporal things.

We send back to you with this letter our son Geoffrey, who came to us with your letter redolent of every goodwill; and we commend both him and the small monastery entrusted to him—which is thus far the only possession Cluny has in your kingdom of Sicily—to royal clemency. Since he reported that both he and that place are especially loved by you, we give thanks. I said that we have as yet only that one place in the kingdom of Sicily because, from the exceptional friendship of so great a friend, I fully expect that this will not remain so long. For if God were to inspire this in the royal heart and, through you, multiply that small beginning in your kingdom from seed already sown into an abundant harvest, the desire to multiply monastic religion in that land would also grow in our heart. As your wisdom well knows, the hope of greater gain becomes a greater incentive to labour.

By greater gain I mean the increase of religion when it has been multiplied—an increase which a larger number of monks can preserve better than a small one. For, as Holy Scripture says: “Woe to him who is alone! For when he falls, he has no one to lift him up” (Eccles. IV); and again: “A brother helping a brother is like a strong and fortified city” (Prov. XVIII). Therefore a greater number, if it could be achieved, of brethren or places would kindle in us a greater desire to spread religion, because in their multiplication we perceive greater progress. Nor could a more useful treasure be added to royal treasuries than that which, transferred from earth to heaven, no booty carries off, no robber steals, and which, according to the holy Gospel, moth does not corrupt and thieves do not dig up or steal (Matt. VI).

May not only the fear of God—the greatest strength of all kingdoms, and the chief thing—but also the reputation for integrity which I have mentioned, spread throughout regions here and there, encourage you and kindle you more and more toward good works. For it is glorious for a magnificent king to submit his neck to the justice of the fear of God; and to desire to enlarge an excellent reputation is at once useful and honourable.

## LETTER IV. To the venerable and most beloved brother PONTIUS, abbot of Vézelay, Brother PETER, humble abbot of the Cluniacs, greeting.

I had expected that the strength of fraternal youth would take upon itself not indeed fraternal old age, but the long exhaustion of toil that outweighs old age; and that it would support the strength worn down by continual sweat, not with a reed staff but an ivory one. But matters have turned out otherwise—otherwise than I had thought. Fraternal affection has not found in a brother the rest it hoped for.

I go about, bustle, am anxious, am distressed, pulled this way and that by business of my own and of others, anxiously concerned amid great agitations of mind. The elder labours; the younger rests. Neither yielding to affection nor to age, the shadow of the labourer hides himself from the heat of labour. But thanks be to God: the one who labours wins a noble triumph from his own labours; and, not envying glory to another, he alone gains the palm of victory which he has earned.

Therefore I announce to my sleeping brother, unwilling to wake from long sleep either for his brother or for the brethren, that by my own—my own, I say—effort, care, and unrest, with God’s grace going before and assisting, so great and so long a war among brethren has been put to sleep; and that the brothers Heraclius and Eustace have sworn, by inviolable oaths, a perpetual covenant and friendship. By reporting this, and as if reproaching me, he directed that you should rejoice with me at the peace of brethren presently secured through my labours; and henceforth enable us to rejoice with you at the repose gained for us through your efforts. But, to speak something serious, send me word through my most beloved son William when you can come to Cluny or its neighbourhood and speak with us.

## LETTER V. To the supreme pontiff and our special Father, Lord Pope INNOCENT, Brother PETER, humble abbot of the Cluniacs, obedience with love.

Our venerable brother Lord Natalis, abbot of Rebais, lately returning from your fatherhood, came to Cluny.

> [Note: Lord Natalis, abbot of Rebais. He subscribed the letters of Henry, archbishop of Sens, by which he invested Gilduin, abbot of Saint-Victor of Paris, with the church of St Mary of Floriac in the diocese of Sens. He is also mentioned in the records of the dispute of Hatton, bishop of Troyes, with Goslenus, bishop of Soissons, concerning the delimiting and separation of boundaries, where, however, he is corruptly called Datalis, abbot of Rebais. The monastery of Rebais is in Brie, commonly Rebais-en-Brie. St Ouen, chancellor of King Dagobert and archbishop of Rouen, founded it under the Rule of St Benedict, as is clear from chapter 7 of his *Life*, read in Surius under 24 April.]

Received honourably by us, as was fitting, after two or three days he disclosed his unexpected intention, first to a few persons and then before all our brethren: namely, that he wished, having laid aside pastoral care, to serve God more quietly with us. Although we were greatly pleased at the prospect of living with so great a man, knowing that his most useful prudence and religious devotion would benefit the Church of Cluny, we nevertheless advised him not to abandon the Church to which he had been called, lest perhaps the many good things which, as I myself knew, had been planted and multiplied through him in that house should perish through his absence.

Though I advised and repeated this often, both alone and with his companions, I could not recall his mind from the desire for the repose he had purposed. And because I clearly learned that, in hope and love of eternal things, he was altogether unwilling to turn the eye of his mind back toward transient things, not even under the pretext of ecclesiastical administration, I beg, with our brethren, the servants and sons of your mercy, that you now assent with fatherly kindness to his good intention and no longer permit his spiritual and blessed leisure to be disturbed either by his own monks or by any other persons.

Nor should your wisdom listen to anyone who, under colour of the usefulness of his person, seeks to disturb him. For though he has been very useful to your Church of Rebais, as you yourself do not fail to know, he may nevertheless be not useless to the Church of Cluny, which is more especially yours. Since, therefore, he chose to rest nowhere other than in your bosom—that is, at Cluny—let your fatherly mercy, as I have said, provide him the rest which he deserves in just order after Martha’s labour.

## LETTER VI. To brother PONTIUS, Brother PETER, humble abbot, greeting.

Paul says to the knocking Anthony: “No one asks in such a way as to threaten. No one adds injury to prayers. Do you threaten, if you are not received when you arrive at death?”

That is my voice. What Paul says to Anthony, I say to Pontius: You ask and threaten, and you join injury to prayers. You draw a honeyed sword, yet a sword nevertheless. Unless I provide for you, you threaten vengeance from heaven. But because I do not wish to contend with God, nor is it safe for me to confront so mighty a torrent, I must yield to the stronger. Trusting in His power, you who are powerless do not fear the powerful; weak, you do not fear the strong; poor, you do not fear the rich. I beseech you, spare your threats. May God Himself spare, not only me but also you, so that, when you have spared us, your own “spare” may more easily deserve to be heard.

## LETTER VII. To the venerable and most beloved brother GREGORY, Brother PETER, humble abbot of the Cluniacs: to contemplate the wonders of the law of God.

[Col. 0284A]

I rejoice, and, as is fitting, exult greatly, because among the innumerable wretches of our time I find almost you alone blessed. I am not a new herald of this blessedness of yours, nor do I speak of something first discovered by myself; rather, I suitably apply to you, who are a member of Him, the voice of Christ your Lord, speaking in the Psalms: “At the head of the book it is written of me” (Ps. XXXIX). The Head speaks what is true of Himself: “At the head of the book it is written of me.” And I too say—and do not think myself mistaken—“At the head of the book it is written of you.”

For if he is called blessed at the head of the Psalms whose will is in the law of the Lord, whose meditation is in the law of the Lord day and night (Ps. I), why should I not consider, call, and proclaim you blessed, whose will is in the law of the Lord; whose meditation is in the law of the Lord; whose eyes persist in reading the law of the Lord; whose mouth persists in sounding the law of the Lord; and whose not only fingers but all limbs persist—indeed, sweat—in writing the law of the Lord night and day? Another Psalm says: “Blessed are they who search out His testimonies, who seek Him with their whole heart” (Ps. CXVIII). Therefore, in accordance with these sayings, not mine but those of the Holy Spirit, not of man but of God, do I not rightly proclaim you blessed?

Wherever business draws me, whatever houses I must enter, whatever inner chambers or secluded places of houses I am compelled to penetrate, I find Gregory with sermons, Gregory with letters, Gregory with various treatises, with an infinite heap of sheets or books. On every side and always I see these surrounding your sides, filling your breast, weighing down your lap; and I marvel at a monk philosophizing at Cluny far better than any philosopher philosophizing in the Academy.

I see the sickly, feeble, and wretched filling the world, occupied not with God but themselves, neglecting study, burying the talent in the earth according to the great Gregory, and, according to another writer, living their lives in useless silence like cattle when they might profit greatly by speaking or writing. But why did I say “by speaking or writing,” when they scarcely even strive to encourage themselves to divine studies by reading? But you are not so. Following Jerome’s saying, “Love the study of the Scriptures, and you will not love the vices of the flesh,” you have not merely banished the vices of the flesh from yourself through this holy study; you have also caused the fruits of spiritual graces and virtues to rise from the seed already sown into an abundant harvest.

Would indeed that my affairs were moderated in this way; would that such leisure offered itself, so that I might frequently meditate and discuss such matters with you, and communicate to you by some spoken or written means the things meditated and discussed. Meanwhile, let what presses be done. You have proposed three topics and woven three knots of questions from those very topics, choosing me as if a suitable solver to untie them. I am not such a person, even in other matters. Nevertheless, I neither ought nor can fail, to the best of my ability, your will and the charity by which I am bound to you.

Your first proposition, by which you say that you and many others together with you are troubled, is whether anything of grace was added to the blessed Virgin Mother, to whom it was said, “Hail, full of grace” (Luke I), and added, “The Holy Spirit shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you” (ibid.); and into whom, according to Jerome, the whole flood of divinity poured itself—whether, certainly, at the coming of the Holy Spirit upon the apostles on the day of Pentecost, any increase of graces came to her.

For you state it thus: “If she received any grace beyond what she had previously possessed, she received what she did not have. But if she had it, she did not receive it.” And you add: “Yet we do not believe that this opinion is derived from any source of divine Scripture.” And immediately: “For if we review the entire history of the Acts of the Apostles, we shall find in it nothing from which anyone could draw even the slightest conjecture—still less a proof—of this matter, as I think. For since, on evangelical authority, the fullness of all graces was in Mary, into whose flesh the whole flood of divinity poured itself; and since, saluted by the angel with singular and unprecedented veneration as ‘full of grace,’ the Spirit came upon her above every creature and she was overshadowed by the power of the Most High—it seems astonishing and incredible to me that she should have needed some additional grace, she who conceived the Son of God in her virginal womb by the Holy Spirit.

“Certainly the apostles, still weak and carnal, and less capable of the divine mysteries which they were to pour into the minds of believers throughout the world, needed to be confirmed and strengthened when the Holy Spirit came. And because ‘their sound was to go out into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world’ (Ps. XVIII), it was fitting that they should know the languages of all peoples, lest, sent among the nations of the Gentiles, they should be in any degree ignorant of the diversity of languages. Must it be said that Mary, who went with Joseph and the Child into Egypt when the angel appeared in a dream, did not know the Egyptian language before this solemn coming of the Holy Spirit?”

These, certainly, are your words, which I have excerpted from the letter sent to me by you. In part they appear to ask whether, as has just been said, that holy Virgin and Mother received some additional grace on that day of Pentecost; in part, they appear to maintain that she received nothing more than she had before.

To speak without prejudice to a perhaps sounder judgment: whether it is so or otherwise will be seen more clearly if graces are separated from graces, and the greater charisms of the Holy Spirit distinguished from the lesser. By the greater charisms of the Holy Spirit I mean those which pertain to perfecting human righteousness, such as those of which the Apostle writes: “But now faith, hope, charity, these three remain; and the greatest of these is charity” (I Cor. XIII). Elsewhere he speaks more plainly of it: “Charity,” he says, “comes from a pure heart, a good conscience, and unfeigned faith” (I Tim. I).

This is that charity which not only produces but wholly perfects righteousness. The other virtues, cooperating in righteousness, look to it as daughters to their mother; they arise from its root, and from its trunk, as from a most fruitful tree, an innumerable beauty of branches hangs down. There are chastity, humility, truth, sincerity, obedience, and every righteousness. Read the Apostle, and you will find the rest set forth individually. Read the Gospel, and you will hear Christ: “On this hang the whole law and the prophets” (Matt. XXII).

This is the charism greater than all charisms; this is the grace, if I may say so, greater than all graces. This, I say, is that greatest and surpassingly excellent grace of which Gabriel said to the blessed Virgin: “Hail, full of grace.” I understand that from the time the angelic salutation was uttered this singular Virgin was so full or filled with this grace that it would be impious to prefer any creature—whether earthly or heavenly—to her, and utterly absurd even to compare one with her.

It was fitting that this spiritual and bodily dwelling-place of the almighty Creator, excelling all creatures in the grace of every virtue, should be filled and adorned with that grace: so that the Wisdom of God, who confesses through the Wise Man that He delights Himself day by day, plays in the world, and has His delights with the children of men (Prov. VIII)—and who cannot delight Himself, play, or take delight except in holy virtues and holy affections—might delight, play, and take pleasure more greatly in this holy and superheavenly Virgin, His Mother, full of the grace of virtues above all men and angels.

Clearly, above all creatures it was fitting that she should be adorned with the grace of virtues on earth and glorified with sublime glory in heaven—she who alone among all creatures deserved to be adorned with the name Mother of God. For though many are called martyrs of God, many apostles of God, many prophets of God, many angels of God, and many saints of God of different orders, she alone is called Mother of God. Therefore it was right that, as the Apostle says to the Hebrews, just as Moses was a faithful servant in the house (Heb. III), and Christ the only Son ruling in the house (ibid.), so she, His Mother, should preside after Him in that same house over the whole household by virtues and glory.

Therefore, just as in her the name Mother of God is singular and above all things after God, so too the grace and glory of that Mother of God are singular and above all things after God, on earth and in heaven. Accordingly, in respect to that grace through which it was fitting that she, as conceiver, bearer, and nurse of the almighty Son of God, should be purified, sanctified, and glorified by the Holy Spirit and the power of the Most High, I believe that nothing was added to her on the day of Pentecost; indeed, I affirm this without any hesitation.

For who in his right mind could ever so much as suspect that any portion of grace, with respect to any part of righteousness, was added to her after the conception of the Son of God within her and His birth from her, when before these things the angel had called her full of grace? Does not anyone, even one very dull, see that it would be absurd—indeed impious—that she should have been imperfect while conceiving or bearing God, but should have reached after the divine conception or birth a perfection she did not possess before? Who would not merely reject but recoil from this?

For until the final limit of her mortal life, no perfecting grace came to her which she did not possess while conceiving and bearing God; because, from the time she was called full of grace, she must be believed always to have remained full of that same grace without any increase. If, then, nothing of the aforesaid grace was added to her at any time of her life after the often-mentioned conception or birth, nothing of that kind was added to her on the day of Pentecost either. Since what is full is understood to be empty in no respect, nothing could be added to her who is proclaimed full of grace.

What spiritual virtue pertaining to the justification or sanctification of the soul could she have received on that day of Pentecost, when among other things she received in the fullness of grace announced by the Gospel that which none of the apostles deserved to receive, either on that day or at any time in life? For although the apostles received great and immeasurable gifts from the Spirit of God, the giver of graces, especially on that day, none of them merited the gift of being wholly without sin in mortal flesh until the death of the flesh. Hence those words of the Apostle James: “In many things we all offend” (James III). Hence also those of John: “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us” (I John I). Hence also those of the great Apostle: “I am conscious of nothing against myself, but I am not thereby justified” (I Cor. IV).

What, then, the apostles did not deserve to receive even on the day of Pentecost, the Virgin Mother in question received long before Pentecost. Hence Augustine, against the Pelagian Caelestius, in his book *On the Perfection of Human Righteousness*: “When sins are being discussed, I wish no question at all to be raised concerning the Mother of the Lord. For how do we know what more grace was conferred upon her for overcoming sin in every respect, she who merited to conceive and bear Him whom it is certain had no sin? Therefore, with this holy Virgin excepted, if we could gather all holy men and women while they lived here and ask whether they were without sin, they would undoubtedly answer what John the Apostle also says of himself: ‘If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us’” (I John I). Thus far Augustine.

By no means could it be—or ought it to be—the very reason itself crying this out—that any, even a small, cloud of sin should afterwards have entered the sanctuary of the Holy Spirit, the resting-place of the Son of God, the throne of the whole Godhead; or that some fleeting flight, even slight, of dark thought should have shadowed that heart shining with the light of the Godhead conceived within it.

Therefore, according to what has been set forth, nothing was added to the blessed Virgin Mother, neither on the day of Pentecost nor on any day after the conception of the Son of God, insofar as the greater gifts of grace mentioned above are concerned. But just as I affirm that nothing was added to her in the greater gifts, so I do not deny that perhaps something was increased for her in the lesser gifts. What those lesser gifts are, the Apostle so often mentioned teaches: “To one,” he says, “is given through the Spirit a word of wisdom; to another, a word of knowledge; to another, gifts of healings; to another, prophecy; to another, discernment of spirits; to another, kinds of tongues; to another, interpretation of words” (I Cor. XII), and the like.

They are called lesser in comparison with the greater gifts written above, because the greater can save without these lesser gifts. For without a word of wisdom or knowledge—I do not say without wisdom and knowledge themselves—without gifts of healings, without prophecy, without discernment of spirits, without kinds of tongues, and without interpretation of words, I can be saved; but without charity and the holy virtues connected with it, I cannot. The greater gifts, therefore, are those without which salvation does not exist; the lesser are called those without which salvation can remain whole.

Accordingly, in regard to those greater gifts, as I have said, the blessed Virgin was increased on the day of Pentecost. But with regard to these lesser gifts, all were given to the apostles, though I do not know whether they were also given to the blessed Virgin. For it was fitting that to those whose sound, as you yourself wrote, was to go out into the world, and whose words were to reach the ends of the world, there should be given a word of wisdom, a word of knowledge, gifts of healings, kinds of tongues, and whatever other gifts the Holy Spirit, distributor of those gifts, judged necessary for the office of so great a preaching.

The same Spirit of God also added courage of heart to them, without which their knowledge of all languages would have profited them nothing. For what would skill in speaking have profited if the power to dare had not been present? What would manifold knowledge of words have profited unless timidity of mind were driven out? Therefore, so that they might be strong and invincible in spirit, they were clothed, as Christ had promised them, with power from on high; lest they seem mute before barbarian peoples, and so that they might be capable of preaching what they were sent to preach, the mouths of them all were filled with the word of all nations under heaven.

But what shall be said of the Mother of the Lord? What shall be said also of the other holy women, whom no one can deny were with the apostles at the time of that great coming of the Holy Spirit? Who, I say, can deny that they were with the apostles at that time, when Scripture says that, after the Lord’s ascension, the apostles returned from the Mount of Olives to Jerusalem and went up to where Peter, John, and the others were staying (Acts I), and immediately adds: “All these were persevering unanimously in prayer with the women, and Mary the mother of Jesus, and His brethren” (ibid.)?

For it cannot be said that this unanimity in prayer of the disciples and the holy women was dissolved before that day on which the divine Spirit descended, through visible signs, [Col. 0289A] upon the apostles and the other believers. And if that unanimity and perseverance in prayer, and in the place itself, continued until that day, then certainly the Mother of the Lord and those women disciples of the Saviour remained with the apostles and the other believers, and did not leave them before that sacred day made notable by heavenly gifts. There indeed was the aforesaid holy Mother of the Lord; there were Mary Magdalene, Mary the mother of James, and Salome, and the others who, as the Gospel says, had followed him from Galilee, ministering to him (Matt. 27).

[Col. 0289B] What then? Did that holy Virgin and Mother of the Lord, and did the other blessed women who were present, receive the same grace or gifts of the Holy Spirit as the apostles? Did they receive a greater sanctification? Did they receive a greater steadfastness of heart than they had possessed? Did they receive the same grace of languages as the apostles? Concerning the blessed Virgin, indeed, it has been said above, and it is altogether certain, that nothing was added to her in purity, sanctification, or in any respect whatever to the perfection of all spiritual virtues. For through that coming of the Holy Spirit no increase could accrue to her fullness of righteousness or holiness: before the conception, and at the conception, of the Son of God, the same Spirit had filled her with the sanctification and perfection of every virtue.

But neither is there doubt concerning the other good women that before that coming of the Holy Spirit they lacked much of a similar grace of virtues; their imperfection was perfected by that same Spirit, who breathes where [Col. 0289C] he wills and as he wills, according to measures of his gift known only to himself. For since the apostles themselves lacked very much of perfection before that day, it is no wonder that much remained to be perfected in those women. They therefore received grace which they had not previously possessed; and just as they were found in the same place with Christ’s disciples when the sudden sound came from heaven, so they were not excluded from the grace bestowed upon the apostles, insofar as particular virtues of the soul are concerned.

But what of miracles? What of the various languages? Did the blessed Virgin and the women just mentioned receive these also with the apostles? Christ’s disciples had indeed received the power of other miracles even before his Passion, when he commanded [Col. 0289D] them: “Heal the sick, raise the dead, cleanse lepers, cast out demons” (Matt. 10); and, moreover, after the Resurrection, when it was said both of them and of those who would believe: “These signs shall follow those who believe” (Mark 16), and the rest. Yet they received the grace of all languages not on another day or in another place, but on the day of Pentecost, when the apostles, the Mother of the Lord, and the repeatedly mentioned women were persevering unanimously in prayer in the upper room. Thus the apostles and the other disciples who were present received that grace of languages on that day.

Did the blessed Virgin, then, receive it? Did the holy women also receive it? Yet the reason why this grace was given to the disciples is certain: they were to preach the Gospel, as was said above, to the whole world. But was the blessed Virgin, [Col. 0290A] or were the other holy women, sent or to be sent throughout the whole world to preach that same Gospel? Certainly not. For the Mother of the Lord had been chosen not to preach the Word of God but to bear the Word of God, and she was not to be sent to any nation for that purpose. Nor do we read that the remaining women were appointed anywhere to a similar office. What befitted the male sex did not befit the female: namely, to be sent abroad to preach in various places, since women ought rather to prepare their ears to hear than to open their mouths to preach—especially as the Apostle says: “I do not permit a woman to speak in the church” (1 Tim. 2). And again, concerning these same women: “If they wish to learn anything, let them ask their husbands at home” (1 Cor. 14).

[Col. 0290B] But someone will say: did not certain holy women compose divine hymns or canticles? Yet singing is one thing and preaching another; chanting psalms is one thing and proclaiming the Gospel another. For just as sound doctrine befits a man, so religious songs befit a woman. Hence Mary, Aaron’s sister, after Pharaoh was drowned (Exod. 15); Deborah, after Sisera was killed (Judg. 5); Hannah, after Samuel’s birth (1 Sam. 2); and this Virgin herself and Mother of the Lord, upon conceiving the Saviour, are recorded to have rejoiced and sung (Luke 1). Yet no one of these women, nor any other woman, is related in any divine text to have been sent to preach. Mary Magdalene alone is recorded, not indeed to have preached, but to have announced to the disciples: “I have seen the Lord, and he said these things to me” (John 20).

The Mother [Col. 0290C] of the Lord, therefore, and the other holy women devoted to her, who were not being sent to any nations, what need had they to receive from the Holy Spirit on the day of Pentecost the languages of every nation? As for what I read in your letter—that when she fled into Egypt with her Son, she was not ignorant of the Egyptian language—if this can be proved from the Scriptures, it must be maintained; if it cannot be proved, it should not be pressed too hard. For what necessity was there for her to know the Egyptian language, when Jews, whose language it was, were not absent from Egypt, though already scattered throughout the world, and when interpreters could not have been lacking?

Therefore, to state briefly what I think: I neither affirm nor deny that on the day of Pentecost she received that grace of all languages. I do not affirm it because I find no necessary or probable [Col. 0290D] reason why she ought to have received that grace. I do not deny it because perhaps someone else may discover a reason which I am not yet capable of finding. I only firmly maintain what I have already said above: that after conceiving the Son of God, nothing of those excellent gifts of the Holy Spirit was increased in the blessed Virgin at any time while she lived as a mortal. Of lesser gifts, however, nothing superfluous or unbecoming was added; but if it befitted the Mother of the almighty Son of God to possess anything among such gifts, it was added without counting it as an accession. Yet whether all or part of such charisms as were given to the apostles on Pentecost was given to her and added to the greater gifts already mentioned, or was not given, she is not for that reason to be judged inferior to the apostles; nor is any apostle, on account of gifts of this sort or of any others, to be considered greater than or equal to her.

For Elisha is not preferred [Col. 0291A] to Elijah because a double spirit appeared in him—not of spiritual virtues but of outwardly manifest miracles. Nor, I think, would Judas the traitor compare himself with the apostle Peter because he was seen to be equal to him in miracles; nor would he exalt himself above John the Baptist by the pride of such signs, concerning whom the Gospel reads: “John the Baptist performed no sign” (John 10). These, as regards the first question proposed, are my present views, without prejudice, as I said above, to a better judgment.

The substance of your second proposition is this: How, after she had conceived the Son of God and he had been personally united to human nature in the virginal womb, could that glorious [Col. 0291B] Mary have been ignorant of anything among created things? How could anything among created things have been hidden from her in whom “all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” were hidden “even bodily” (Col. 2)? For it is written of a certain saint—Gregory, *On St Benedict*: “To the soul that sees the Creator, every creature is narrow.” And shortly afterward you add: “Therefore, by the grace superadded and by the prerogative of merit through which she deserved to be both Virgin and Mother of God, even while in the flesh she seems to have surpassed by her wisdom the knowledge of the angels, just as we believe that she was exalted above every angelic nature. But if according to the knowledge of the Godhead one person becomes more blessed than another, and one wiser than another, this Virgin seems to me, even while in the flesh, to have been far wiser than all the orders of angels: she to whom [Col. 0291C] it was granted not only to live in the flesh beyond the flesh, but also to bear God’s very Word made flesh.”

You wrote these things, indeed; but, as I trust in your learning, you put them forward not so much as your own as another’s. For who, to speak briefly, among even moderately educated people does not know that the glorious Mary of whom you write—and truly write—after conceiving the Son of God, was ignorant not merely of one thing or some things, but even of many things among created things? Did she not know many things among created things—many things which she did not know even in domestic affairs? Did she not know many things elsewhere, she for whom it was necessary that Joseph her betrothed should be warned by an angel and told: “Arise, take the child, flee into Egypt, and remain there until [Col. 0291D] I tell you” (Matt. 2)? Could she not have been ignorant of many things among created things, she for whom it was again necessary that an angel should appear again to Joseph in Egypt and say: “Arise, take the child and his mother, and go into the land of Israel, for those who sought the child’s life are dead” (ibid.)?

For if she herself had known this and that beforehand—namely, that Herod was seeking the child to destroy him, and then, after her flight into Egypt, had foreknown that he had died—the angel needlessly urged Joseph to flee at that time, and afterward needlessly reminded him to return. Why should an angel trouble himself, or trouble anyone, to save the child, whose mother knew everything, knew all his persecutors, discerned their intentions, counsels, deceptions, and stratagems by the subtle knowledge of the Spirit, and could in no way be ignorant either of their lives or of their deaths? [Col. 0292A] Let these matters be doubtful for those to whom, after the manner of certain philosophers, it is permitted to doubt everything. Yet let an example follow after which even those who place everything under a question can no longer hesitate.

“The child Jesus remained in Jerusalem, and his parents did not know it. Thinking that he was in the company, they travelled a day’s journey and sought him among their relatives and acquaintances. And not finding him, they returned to Jerusalem, seeking him” (Luke 2). How, certainly, how could a sound mind suppose that nothing among created things was hidden from the blessed Virgin, when it was hidden from her that her Son had remained in Jerusalem; when she thought he was in the company; when, not finding him among relatives and acquaintances, she returned to Jerusalem; [Col. 0292B] and when she found him only after nearly two days of searching? But let the Virgin herself be heard, and let her own testimony about herself be believed rather than any heedless opinion: “Son,” she says, “why have you done this to us? Your father and I were seeking you in sorrow” (ibid.). And she surely would not have sought him sorrowfully in various places had she known by subtle spiritual investigation where he was. How then could she who did not know where so great a Son was know everything that could happen among created things?

But, as you propose, it is remarkable how anything among created things could have been hidden from her in whom “all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge” were hidden “even bodily” (Col. 2). Yet this statement, which you advance on the authority of I know not whom, is, as you know, apostolic; and it was spoken not of that blessed and ever-to-be-named Virgin, but of her Son. [Col. 0292C] For in him—that is, in God and in her Son—are truly hidden all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge. Hence it is impossible for anything among created things to be hidden from him as God, or for him to be ignorant of anything done in heaven, on earth, or indeed in the lower regions. For he alone is the Creator of all things; he alone is ruler and knower of the universe.

Therefore, although he in whom all these treasures were hidden was concealed even bodily, as you say, in this Virgin’s womb, yet this holy Virgin did not receive, from those treasures of wisdom and knowledge hidden in him, knowledge of all things while she lived here as a mortal. This belongs to God alone and has been granted to no mortal in this life. What belongs to God alone [Col. 0292D] cannot have a participant. Hence he himself speaks through the prophet: “I will not give my glory to another” (Isa. 52 [apparently Isa. 42:8]). And through a certain wise man it is said to him: “You alone know the hearts of the children of men” (2 Chron. 5 [apparently 1 Kings 8:39]).

If, however, anyone wishes to adapt this apostolic statement about Christ to the glory of the blessed Virgin, let him at least do so in this manner; let him show himself dutiful and devout toward the holy Virgin without exceeding the rule of faith. Let him observe and see how cautiously Jerome proceeds when he transfers to her such things concerning Christ. For in a similar matter he says: “Into Mary came the fullness of all the grace that is in Christ.” And immediately he adds: “Although in another way.” For the fullness of all the grace that is in Christ came into Mary because Christ, full of grace and truth, was conceived in [Col. 0293A] Mary and came forth from Mary to humankind. Yet it was in another way, because she herself did not receive that fullness of grace which is in Christ insofar as it pertains to her own person. For it is one thing to possess in one’s own person that fullness of grace; it is another to have borne the person in whom that fullness of grace was.

Thus perhaps—indeed, thus plainly, as it seems to me—it may be said that the treasures of wisdom and knowledge were hidden in Mary, not because those treasures were hidden in her personally, that is, insofar as her own person is concerned, but because her sacred womb bore Christ the Lord, in whom they were truly hidden personally.

Now [Col. 0293B] let your prudence consider the force of the following statement, which was put forward as though to strengthen the false opinion. For it is easy to see—not only for you, who very swiftly perceive far more difficult matters, but also for anyone who attends even lightly—that this statement gives no support whatever to the opinion already mentioned. First, because it is not taken from such a canon that we are compelled to grant it absolute faith. For although this saying was uttered by St Gregory in the *Dialogues*, we ought not to give to every writing of learned doctors the faith which we know is owed to the supreme canon of the holy Scriptures. After the books of the Old and New Testaments, we are not compelled to defer to the writing of any person, however learned and Catholic, as much as to that divine canon.

Hence Augustine [Col. 0293C] says to Jerome: “Far be it from your holiness and wisdom to wish such authority to be given to your writings as is reserved for the dignity of the holy Scriptures alone! For any person’s writing may be examined, but no one whatever is permitted to doubt those writings.” You will find this statement in Augustine’s letter, and although not in precisely these words, it contains exactly the same meaning.

Moreover, even if it were taken from that divine canon, it would still be of no use in proving the claims set forth above. This will at once be clear to anyone who considers more carefully. For because that saint says, “Every creature is narrow to one who sees the Creator,” it does not follow that nothing in creation could have been hidden from such a person. He attached this statement to his words in which he had already said that the whole world had appeared to the holy Father Benedict as though gathered beneath a single [Col. 0293D] ray of the sun. Yet that saint could both see the whole world gathered together and still remain ignorant of many things happening in the world. There is no necessity to concede that because he saw the whole world gathered together, he also simultaneously knew what was occurring in it.

Our ordinary sight itself offers this analogy: from a tower, a mountain, or some high place, we see many stretches of country at once, though we can scarcely discern a few of the things done in those areas. And although that saint’s sight, enlarged by God, was much stronger than ours—so much so that, as has been said, he could see the whole world at once—yet where we read that he saw the whole world gathered together, we do not read [Col. 0294A] that he learned in any manner all the things then taking place among created beings. Therefore there is no analogy, whether from like to like or from a lesser case, by which it ought to be believed that because he is written to have seen the whole world gathered together, the holy Virgin Mother of the Lord knew all things that took place among created things while she lived in the body.

There remains something else to say concerning this statement, which perhaps has offered itself for examination. What he says—“Every creature is narrow to one who sees the Creator”—is true, but in the future life. For that the Creator cannot here be seen by a mortal as he is, is testified by the familiar saying known throughout the world: “No man shall see me and live” (Exod. 33). Yet I do not for that reason call this statement [Col. 0294B] false, nor do I deny that during that interval in which he surpassed the customary vision of human beings, that saint saw the Creator insofar as it was granted to him.

For I know that there were or are other modes—or a mode—of seeing God: the mode by which Jacob confesses that he saw him when he says, “I saw the Lord face to face” (Gen. 32); by which it is written of Moses, “The Lord spoke to Moses face to face, as a man is accustomed to speak to his friend” (Exod. 33); by which he appeared to the seventy elders of Israel, as it is written: “They saw God, and ate and drank” (Exod. 34 [apparently Exod. 24:11]); by which Isaiah said, “I saw the Lord sitting upon a high and exalted throne” (Isa. 6); by which Micaiah said, “I saw the Lord sitting, and all the host of heaven standing by him at his right and left” (3 Kings 22); and many similar passages. Hence also the Apostle’s words: “Now we see through a mirror, in an enigma; but then face to face” (1 Cor. 13). Hence also John’s words: “It has not yet appeared what we shall be; but when he appears, we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3).

[Col. 0294C] Although, then, all these saw God not in the mode of the future life but in a mode suited to each, under none of their visions do we read that every creature was compressed into narrowness. It might have happened in the case of this one who saw God what did not happen in the cases of the others who saw God. But however those saints, or this saint, saw God, the matter comes down to this: neither they nor he knew, at the time of those visions, everything that was occurring among created things. And if, as has been said, many things among created things were hidden from them in their visions, then what was brought forward to prove that nothing was hidden from the holy Mother of the Lord among created things, and that she could have been ignorant of none of the things occurring among created beings in her own time, has no force.

[Col. 0294D] Even if it had been granted to any saint in the present life for an hour—which, nevertheless, is nowhere recorded—we would not therefore be compelled to believe that this too had been granted to the blessed Virgin. For this would be a kind of miracle, belonging not to the highest and greater gifts of the Holy Spirit, which, as was stated above, the blessed Virgin possessed beyond every creature, but to those intermediate gifts among which miracles are counted. So far as I think, no one remembers having read anywhere in the whole divine canon that the blessed Virgin, while placed in mortal flesh, received such gifts. Yet no sound-minded person could [Col. 0295A] for that reason consider her inferior to those who performed miracles: having received what is highest and greater, she did not need such gifts, although they are gifts of the Holy Spirit.

And if anyone, persistently insisting, should say that she either was or appeared to be without miracles or inferior to miracle-workers, let him also say that Christ is or appears inferior to that Christian who performed greater miracles than Christ. Of this Christ himself says in the Gospel: “He who believes in me will also do the works that I do, and will do greater than these” (John 14). We often read that many Christians performed miracles greater than Christ’s. Yet it is not to be argued that they are greater than he, since it is certain that they are immeasurably inferior to him. Since, then, I think sufficient has been said about the words of the *Dialogues*, to show that they cannot support the claims proposed, let the pen proceed to what follows.

There we [Col. 0295B] read that some hold the view that the often-mentioned Virgin Mother of the Lord, even while placed in the flesh, surpassed by her wisdom the knowledge of the angels, just as she is believed to have been exalted above every angelic nature. The author then continues: “For if, according to the knowledge of the Godhead, one person becomes more blessed than another and one wiser than another, this Virgin seems to me, even while in the flesh, to have been far wiser than every order of angels: she to whom it was granted not only to live in the flesh beyond the flesh, but also to bear God himself made flesh.”

To confess what is true: these words, presented to me by your venerable and most dear affection not from yourself indeed but through you, and setting forward not your own opinion but that of certain people, seem to me [Col. 0295C] so absurd, and to proceed from a crude and utterly unreflective mind, that I can scarcely be sufficiently amazed. For who could be sufficiently astonished that one to whom these things seem right has failed to distinguish what was very easy to distinguish: grace from grace, labour from reward, merit from blessedness?

But why did I say grace from grace, labour from reward, merit from blessedness? These words are not now uttered by me for the first time, but are read in John’s Gospel: “We all received from his fullness, and grace for grace” (John 1). What does “grace for grace” mean? His saints receive a twofold grace from him, so that another grace follows upon the preceding grace. First, here they receive the grace of action, and [Col. 0295D] for it elsewhere the grace of reward., and for it elsewhere the grace of reward. First, here they receive the grace of sanctification, and for it elsewhere the grace of glorification. For they do not at the same time do a good work and receive the reward of that good work; nor are they at the same time perfected in holiness and virtues and attain the glory of virtues and holiness. Here they work; there they are rewarded. Here they are sanctified; there they are glorified.

Therefore, insofar as purity of character, perfection of life, and the sanctification of every virtue are concerned, the blessed Virgin, even while in the flesh, supremely surpassed every created being, human or angelic. But insofar as the wisdom [Col. 0296A] is concerned by which some think that, even while in the flesh, she surpassed angelic knowledge, it seems to me entirely otherwise. For if I grant this, I shall join reward to labour and blessedness to merit; I shall concede that she received before death that recompense, glory, and magnificence by which she was set above all creatures after the death of the flesh. If I grant this, stripped of every authority and reason, I shall be a spectacle to angels and human beings.

For if I say that, while placed in mortal flesh, I do not say that she surpassed but that she even merely equalled the wisdom of the angels, it will necessarily follow that while still on earth I must strip her of every misery of mortality and clothe her with every incorruption, immortality, and blessedness. For if, while in the flesh, she attained angelic wisdom, she also attained blessedness. Angelic wisdom cannot exist without blessedness, and it is true wisdom precisely because it is blessed. But what is blessed is blessed only by blessedness. Blessedness, to define or describe it, is a sufficiency of every good without any distress.

[Col. 0296B] Who does not know that the glorious Mother of the Lord did not attain this blessedness in this mortal life? For if she had attained it, while still on earth she would have lacked every bodily affliction and would have rejoiced in the delight of possessing every good. She would certainly have lacked want, fear, pain, and finally every inconvenience of corruption or mortality. But that this was not so is very easy to see, whether one believes evangelical authority or considers reason itself. For although after the conception of the Son of God she was without every sin, yet while [Col. 0296C] she lived in the flesh she was not without the punishment of sin. Punishment is contrary to blessedness.

For if it is not blessedness to be in want, if it is not blessedness to fear, if it is not blessedness to suffer pain, and finally if it is not blessedness to die, then she was not blessed while in the flesh, she who endured all these things in it. Was she not in want when, after giving birth to her Son and God’s Son, she laid him in a manger because there was no room for her in the inn? (Luke 2.) Was she not in want, she who, when offering sacrifices to God for her Son, offered a pair of turtledoves or two young pigeons because she could not offer a lamb? (ibid.) Did she not fear, she who fled into Egypt [Col. 0296D] from Herod? (Matt. 2.) Did she not suffer pain, she whose soul, when the Saviour her Son died, was pierced by the sword of excessive sorrow, according to the words of the righteous Simeon? (Luke 2.) Did she not experience every misery of the human condition except sin? And finally, did she not die?

All these things are certainly contrary to angelic blessedness, which one must say that she attained even in mortal flesh if one says that she either surpassed or equalled angelic wisdom. For angelic wisdom and angelic blessedness are so indivisible—indeed, so completely one—that neither can angelic wisdom exist without blessedness nor blessedness without wisdom. Otherwise, which is altogether foolish and brutish to think, their wisdom would be miserable or their blessedness unwise. Since it is impossible that wisdom, insofar as it is wisdom, should be miserable, or that blessedness should be unwise, one must confess [Col. 0297A] that angelic wisdom is always blessed and that blessedness is always inseparably wise.

Therefore, since no one can in any way separate blessedness from angelic wisdom, if angelic wisdom is granted to the blessed Virgin in mortal flesh, angelic blessedness must consequently also be granted. If that is granted to her in that mortal flesh, it will be said that she neither suffered want nor fear nor pain nor, finally, death; indeed, that she was not even human. Let there therefore be granted to her in mortal flesh much and great wisdom, but not so much as either surpasses or equals the wisdom of the angels.

For although that sublime and [Col. 0297B] super-celestial Virgin bore in her womb, gave birth to, suckled, cherished, and nourished the Wisdom of God—who “reaches mightily from end to end and orders all things sweetly” (Wis. 8)—clothed in human flesh, nevertheless, while she lived as a mortal, she did not know him as the angels did, nor did she comprehend him as they did, with face unveiled and the veil removed. For what was written above remains: “No man shall see me and live” (Exod. 33). The angels saw him as he is; the Virgin Mother saw him more than any living mortal could see him. She, full of grace, full of God, full of virtues, full of the Holy Spirit and the power of the Most High, and full of faith and of an incomparable fullness of divine love, saw him. Those blessed spirits saw him not by faith but in reality; not as a human being sees through a mirror and in an enigma, but face to face.

They saw him [Col. 0297C] more clearly in the very womb of the Virgin Mother than the blessed Virgin Mother could see him. For she joyfully marvelled with ineffable exultation of spirit at God hidden in flesh; they, unhindered by any obstacle of flesh, beheld, adored, contemplated, and were nourished by him in flesh just as before the flesh. Thus, satisfied by the nourishment not of veiled but of unveiled divine vision, and made wholly wise by the clearest contemplation of the supreme Wisdom, they could not fail to be blessed, for in him whom they beheld they possessed complete blessedness.

Therefore, were not those who, while the blessed Virgin lived as a mortal, saw Christ, the power of God and the wisdom of God, far more clearly, subtly, and perfectly than she did, far wiser than the blessed Virgin [Col. 0297D] by that eternal and supreme Wisdom which they beheld? They were plainly wiser, for they saw it unveiled, as it is with the Father, rather than veiled, as it was with the Mother. They certainly saw it as it is, and in that vision they possessed a singular wisdom and blessedness granted to no one in mortal flesh. The blessed Virgin already possessed, beyond all saints, that wisdom and blessedness through faith, hope, and the most sublime charity, whereas they, as has been said, enjoyed it face to face.

Therefore the blessed Virgin did not possess, while she lived in the flesh, the wisdom possessed by the angels, because she could not yet, as they were, be blessed—a state that came later. For to grant her fully [Col. 0298A] angelic wisdom without blessedness is, just as it is contrary to every authority and reason, also no small folly. For what would angelic wisdom without blessedness be but, so to speak, a kind of demonic knowledge? Demons are called knowing or knowledgeable because they know very many things; but because they possess blessedness neither in reality nor in hope, they are utterly miserable and detestable. I cannot call them wise, though they grasp many things in the nature of things beyond what human beings grasp, because that cannot be called wisdom which does not serve divine or eternal things, nor can one be called wise who does not seek divine or eternal things for himself through fitting duties or affections.

Hence the wisdom of the world is called folly, and those who serve the world rather than God, though called wise, are called fools. Therefore, while she lived liable to death, the blessed Virgin had neither a wisdom greater than or equal to that of the holy angels—because she could not possess the blessedness without which their wisdom can never exist—nor the wisdom of demons or wicked human beings, which cannot truly be called wisdom at all. She did not have wisdom greater than or equal to that of the holy angels because, as has been said, she could not possess the blessedness which they possess in reality. She did not have the wisdom of evil angels or demons because that is not wisdom which they do not refer to blessedness, either in reality or in hope.

But she plainly possessed [Col. 0298B] an immense wisdom, greatly to be preferred to the wisdom of all saints living mortally: not the wisdom which, in philosophical fashion, curiously disputes about creatures, but that which devoutly [Col. 0298C] and diligently seeks knowledge of the Creator. However greatly understanding advances in investigating merely the truth of created things, it is called knowledge rather than wisdom. But that understanding which through creatures, or without creatures, extends itself to the knowledge and love of the Creator alone is truly called wisdom. This wisdom, which, setting aside other affections, pours itself wholly, aided by the grace of its Creator, into the knowledge and purest love of the Creator alone and the author of all good things, the blessed Virgin and Mother of God possessed beyond every mortal living in the flesh. By that wisdom, supremely wise, she knew, worshipped, and loved her Creator and the Creator of all more excellently than any mortal creature; and, insofar as the incomprehensible one could here be seen or comprehended by a living person, she comprehended him.

[Col. 0298D] This is my understanding of these matters, dearest friend: I speak, as I think, as a Catholic, without prejudice to a truer opinion. But the statements of St Jerome which I read in your letter as though they confirmed the opinion just discussed do nothing whatever to support it. Rather, they were written either to demonstrate the privileges of virtue which she received while still mortal, or to show her sublime glory surpassing every creature, which she received after the death of the flesh. They must, however, be distinguished by the diligent reader, because Jerome sometimes appears to set together indiscriminately both the grace of sanctification by which, while on earth, she was blessed and sanctified and made fit to bear, give birth to, and rear God in the flesh, and the glory of exaltation by which, perhaps after the death of the flesh and the resurrection, she was adorned, glorified, and exalted above all choirs of human beings and angels.

Sometimes, [Col. 0299A] in two or more adjacent verses, and sometimes in a single verse, he sets down both almost together, so that he may sometimes seem to assign earthly things to heaven or heavenly things to earth—that is, things which the blessed Virgin received on earth before, or in heaven afterward, either wholly to earth or wholly to heaven. If, therefore, wherever these distinct things are set together, they are assigned to their proper meanings, there will be no error or uncertainty, nor can one thing being taken for another generate any confusion for the reader.

Thus, for example, [Col. 0299B] I read in your letter the following from the words of that saint: “It must be believed that the blessed Virgin merited privileges of virtues greater than those of the angels, and received a grace praised even by angels.” And this: “If their virtue and the firmness of their perpetuity are wonderful, yet more wonderful is this in Mary, whom the power of the Most High overshadowed, so that what was done in her is beyond every angelic power and a mystery wonderful to all ages.” These things were fulfilled partly in her and concerning her in this life, and partly in the future life.

But the two verses [Col. 0299C] that follow, the first of which begins, “And through this even greater grace is bestowed upon the angels,” down to the end of the second, where it reads, “It resounds all the more brightly in glory,” are to be understood not of this life but of the future. And, lest I become lengthy by examining every individual point, the remaining similar passages must be read, understood, and distinguished in the same way.

The third question, arising from the words of the same Doctor in the same sermon on the Blessed Virgin, is prompted by his statement: “Time did not prejudice the sacrament of the united man and God, so that he who was not yet born of the Virgin Mary was already in Him, through the unity of person, from the beginning of the world.” Your shrewd and circumspect learning acknowledges itself disturbed by these words because he affirms that this man—that is, the man assumed by God—who was not yet born of the Virgin Mary, was already, from the beginning of the world, in Him—that is, in God, by whom he was assumed—through unity of person. You knock, therefore, and by your singular vigilance in our time awaken me, who in studies of such matters often seems to be drowsing—or rather, asleep—and urge me not merely to read, but also to understand what I read. Truly, this is how it has now happened to me at this point in the treatise.

For I had often, indeed almost continually, heard this read in the nocturnal offices of our Lady, yet had not noticed it as I now do. But after the breath of your studious heart had blown upon the little spark of my understanding, almost dead so far as this matter was concerned, a little light suddenly forced from it drove away, in some measure, the preceding darkness. For I saw, as it seems to me, that those words of that holy man, whatever other holy men may have written on such a subject, convey something novel, yet agree in every respect with Catholic understanding. And since the Church of our time and language has nowhere doubted, even slightly, the faith and sound understanding of so great a man—one whom she counts among the chief defenders of her faith after the Apostles and martyrs—we ought to make every effort we can to defend his Catholic meaning, expressed perhaps in words less customary.

Nor are you alone in being troubled by words of this kind. I remember that two or three years ago I dealt not merely once but frequently with a learned man, reputedly religious, who was interpreting these same words wrongly. Taking occasion from them, he seemed rather to conjecture than to establish certain strange and almost heretical notions, nearly agreeing with those ancient heretics who both suspected and professed that the Savior had brought human flesh from heaven before the Virgin. It is impious to suppose that the holy man held such a view, since his exceptional learning, his most proven faith, and above all his own words—unambiguous, not obscure, but certain and utterly clear—joined to the words under discussion, wholly defend him from this suspicion.

For in that sermon, from which the words already cited were taken, he says: “Not that Jesus or Christ was already from Mary, but because in that one Son of God the unity of person was already being set forth, though hidden in mystery.” What could be clearer? Clearly, as you see, he denies that Jesus or Christ, so far as the flesh assumed from the Virgin is concerned, existed before the Virgin. Who, then, will admit that he thought what he so openly denies?

But you object: “It is true that he denies this. Yet he firmly asserts and proclaims that time did not prejudice the sacrament of the united man and God. Immediately afterward he says more plainly: ‘Thus, he who was not yet born of the Virgin Mary was already in Him from the beginning of the world through unity of person.’ And shortly afterward: ‘Therefore Jesus was already in the Son who led forth the people, and Christ in him who was tempted, because it is not doubted that he was in God through the unity of the sacrament.’ And, after an intervening line: ‘The Scriptures in which the unity of person in Christ is set forth must be searched, a unity to which time does not prejudice, lest he always be called one.’” [Col. 0300D]
