What is to be said to this? He says that the one who was not yet born of the Virgin Mary—that is, the man—was already in Him, that is, in God, through unity of person. He says that Jesus was already in the Son, and Christ in him who was tempted; he says that time does not prejudice the unity of Christ’s person, lest he always be called one. How will time not prejudice this union of different natures, when the divine nature has always existed from eternity, while the human began to exist from the Virgin? How will time not prejudice it, lest he always be called one, when this union of different natures—that is, human and divine—had no past duration, but, from the time when the Virgin’s flesh was assumed from her and united to the Son of God, made one God and man both to exist and to be called such?

Not in reality, I say, but in sacrament or mystery. For he himself uses these words when it is said that time did not prejudice the sacrament, and when he acknowledges that the unity of person was hidden in mystery. Yet you ask again what this sacrament is, or what sort of mystery is understood here. And indeed, as it seems to me, the whole difficulty of this question, however great, lies in or revolves around these words.

For in every sacrament two things are ordinarily sought: that which conceals and that which is concealed; that which signifies and that which is signified. This is indicated by its definition or description: a sacrament is called a sign of some sacred thing. Thus one may ask concerning this sacrament now under discussion what in it is hidden, what is manifest, what signifies, and what is understood as signified. If the name “mystery” is asked about, it is certain that it differs here from “sacrament” in this: sacrament is said always to conceal something, while mystery is proclaimed to be concealed, not to conceal, though sometimes one is used for the other.

This, then, is the whole cause that casts this cloud of obscurity over the reader’s understanding: in the innumerable sacraments both of the Old Testament and of the Gospel, one immediately sees what is open and what is hidden; but in this sacrament of which we are speaking, it is not apparent what ought to be taken as sign and what as signified. For the question is whether, just as in the ancient sacraments, for example, these two distinct things appear—the Red Sea which was seen, and Christ’s baptism prefigured by that sea; the Passover lamb which the Jew ate, and Christ whom the same Jew was to slay and the Christian was to eat; the tabernacle built by Moses, or the temple built by Solomon, and the Church of our own time prefigured by both structures—so likewise these two things may be distinguished in this sacrament. [Col. 0301C]

The word “mystery,” likewise used here, becomes clearer especially because the Apostle uses the same word of a similar matter in the Epistle, saying, “the mystery kept silent through eternal ages” (Col. 1). But lest, by long seeking what cannot otherwise be discovered, I impose fruitless labor on myself and tedious prolixity on the reader, I judge that by the name sacrament or mystery he understood, distinguished, and established nothing other than the eternal and hidden counsel of the Godhead itself: eternally present with Him, but manifested to human beings in time. His own words, inserted into the extended discussion, indicate this: “If it seems new to you that he assumed man for you, know that it was always with Him and in His counsel that it should be done thus; and now, when the fullness of time came, that was done which had always been in Christ.”

This certainly is all, so far as I can see, that he asserts; this is all by which he teaches that the unity of Christ’s person from God and man was made even before the Virgin. This is all that he calls mystery or sacrament: not that, as he himself admits, Jesus or Christ existed in reality before the Virgin, but that it was already established eternally in the unchangeable counsel of the Godhead. For just as God the Word was always with God, so in the unchangeable and eternal counsel already mentioned—although it did not yet subsist in reality—the Word had become flesh.

What wonder, then, if he himself thought this concerning Christ and we think it too, since we think it concerning every human being, indeed even concerning lower creatures? For concerning the elect, the Apostle says—and this holy man adduces the passage to confirm what he intended to prove—“He chose us in Him,” that is, in Christ, “before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and without blemish” (Eph. 1). He who chose human beings before they were human beings, and chose them to be holy and without blemish before they could be holy and without blemish—what wonder, then, if Jerome, indeed the Apostle himself, says that Christ existed at a time when that from which he was called Christ did not yet exist?

Indeed, what wonder if this is said of a rational creature, when we read that something similar was said by the same Apostle concerning an irrational, indeed even an insensible, creature? For, speaking in the Epistle to the Romans about Abraham’s faith and highly commending it, he introduces God as saying to him: “I have made you the father of many nations before God, in whom you believed, who gives life to the dead and calls those things which are not as though they were” (Rom. 4). Thus, according to this statement, God gives life to the dead and calls things that are not as though they were.

But if God gives life to the dead—or rather, what is more, if according to another saying of the Gospel all the dead, though still dead, live to Him (Luke 20)—this is not because they truly live in the flesh, but because they already in a manner live in the unchangeable counsel of Him through whom they shall live. And if He calls not only the dead but even any other things not yet existing as though they already existed, because their future existence already exists in His fixed counsel, what is either very remarkable or worth prolonged discussion if God, who was to be united to a man in the same person, is said already from the beginning of the world to have been united, when, as has been said, not in reality itself but in the firm and constant counsel of the Godhead, that union is believed to have been made from eternity?

For it is said of Him: “Who made the things that shall be.” This is confirmed also by that sublime saying of the Gospel, long familiar throughout the world: “What was made, in Him was life” (John 1). For angels and human beings, sun and moon, heaven and stars, sea and earth, and the things contained beneath them, did not live substantially in the Word of God. For if they had so lived in Him, they would have been coeternal with Him. But “what was made, in Him was life,” because in His unchangeable will or counsel whatever was to be created existed; indeed, to use the Gospel’s expression, in that unchangeable will or counsel it already lived, being without doubt destined to receive its own existence.

If all these things lived in that Word of God in this manner, why should not that union of human flesh with the Word of God—which was to come about in its own time—also be called, written, and proclaimed as already made from eternity in this manner? Especially since the Apostle says: “Who was predestined Son of God in power, according to the Spirit of sanctification” (Rom. 1). For that man, assumed by the Son of God and personally united to Him at the fitting time, was made the Son of God by eternal predestination before every age, before all time, before every creature. And He who, according to the Spirit of sanctification coming upon and overshadowing the Virgin, after, according to the Apostle, the fullness of time had come, was essentially conceived in that Virgin and born from her (Gal. 4), was already, according to the Psalm, “before the morning star” (Ps. 109), eternally united to Him by the predestination just mentioned and by everlasting counsel. [Cols. 0303A, 0304A]

Therefore, unless a clearer or truer interpretation of the words proposed should appear, let this for the present be maintained; and if it seems so to you, dearest one to whom I have written this letter, let the reading, often read, be read without anxiety.

## BOOK FOUR

[Col. 0303]

### LETTER I. Brother PETER, humble, to his bishop of Troyes, the customary greeting.

[Col. 0303B]

Behold, the king has returned; the commanders, girded for Mars, now revisit their domestic homes; military preparations have ceased; no one compels a bishop to serve in war; the feared heat of summer has fled; the mildness of autumn smiles upon travel; the harvest has been stored in granaries; the new wine is already fermenting in the vats; no household necessity, no concern of public affairs, prevents a friend’s journey to a friend. All the excuses customarily offered as reasons for not coming have been excluded; only willingness or unwillingness, bare and uncovered, without the entanglements of business or the coverings of excuses, will now be revealed.

Moreover, Lord Hugh, the sole companion expected for the journey, will go either to Vézelay, or Auxerre, or even Troyes, if you command it; and if the messenger sent beforehand into your region reports this, he will set out to come to you on the day following the Nativity of the Blessed Virgin, and will not leave until he has returned you to your Cluniacs. And because, I believe, other letters sufficiently express the desire—indeed hunger—to see you, let this letter be silent, lest a mission repeated so often, while it achieves nothing, appear to close observers either superfluous or disregarded.

### LETTER II. His bishop of Troyes to his abbot of Cluny: the same as to himself.

[Col. 0303D]

I was preparing to answer your letter from the poor vein of my own ability. Yet I restrained myself, lest your eloquence bury the poverty of my words. The abbot of Clairvaux was present. The bishop of Chartres had besieged my house. My Nicholas—indeed yours also—was returning from Rome. Count Theobald was urgently and continually pressing me about his affairs.

> [Note: Col. 0303D. Count Theobald: the Count Palatine of Champagne, who receives very fine praise in the *Chronicle of Limoges*. In it, around the year 1136, he is called: “Theobald, Count of Champagne, father of orphans and judge of widows, eye of the blind, foot of the lame, exceptionally generous in sustaining the poor, and incomparable in liberality in building monasteries and toward all religious persons.”]

And behold, the letter of a friend, the hand of a friend, enters. A passion takes possession of me away from all things—indeed from myself—and joyful eyes feast upon the longed-for page. I confess I was astonished both by the sweetness of the letter and by your uprooting of the business concerns which you have so effectively suppressed with your golden speech. The king has truly returned; the clash of arms has fallen silent; the mildness of the air has breathed forth. But the harvest has not been stored in granaries, because it found no reapers. There was hope before our eyes, but behold mourning in our hands, because a storm sent by the Lord has stripped the face of our land. There is no new wine in the vats, because our vines have scarcely yet begun to ripen. The frequent needs of our bishopric and the care of household affairs prevent us from leaving.

But if we trust business affairs, when will business ever end? I shall tear myself from this body of death and go to Him whom my soul loves, that I may behold the will of the Lord and visit His temple. On the fifth day before the feast of Saint Remigius, we wish Lord Hugh to be at Troyes, so that with him and through him we may at last be able to see those whom we desire to see.

### LETTER III. Brother PETER, humble abbot of Cluny, to the Supreme Pontiff and our special Father, Lord Pope INNOCENT: obedience and love.

If I say anything insufficiently wisely, I ask that paternal kindness bear with it. For perhaps it may be inept, but it cannot be lacking in devotion toward you. I implore apostolic kindness on behalf of the lord king of France,

> [Note: Col. 0303D. “On behalf of the lord king of France”: Louis VII, called the Younger, son of Louis VI, surnamed the Fat.]

your great, noble, and special son, [Col. 0304D] because he is not only a king, not only a magnificent ruler of the Christian people, but also the work of your hands: you advanced him to the kingdom,

> [Note: Col. 0304D. “You advanced him to the kingdom”: John of Paris, under the year 1131: “In this year Pope Innocent held a synod at Rheims, at which Saint Bernard was present; and, after many arrangements had been made for God’s honor, he crowned Louis, son of Louis, king in his father’s presence.”]

you anointed him with your sacred hands, and you designated him king, more powerful for our Gauls than his forefathers. If perhaps, still young in years, he has acted inconsiderately, bear with him, and perhaps cover his error with the veil of your wisdom. For it is a father’s duty both to correct a son’s error—especially that of so great a son—and to preserve his honor.

I say this because of the dispute between him and the lord Archbishop of Bourges.

> [Note: Col. 0305D. “Because of the dispute between him and the lord Archbishop of Bourges”: undoubtedly Peter of La Châtre, born of the noble family of the Châtres in the territory of Bourges. Innocent II had sent him to Bourges as archbishop-elect; when King Louis opposed him, the said Innocent consecrated him, as William of Nangis wrote.]

As I understand it, this is no slight matter; and great caution is needed lest a grave beginning end in something graver. May the Spirit of counsel, who blows where He wills and through you continually provides for His Church spread throughout the world, now also through you provide for the kingdom of France, no small part of His Church; and may His anointing teach your heart both concerning these matters and all others. For it is not mine to proceed further or to instruct your wisdom—upon which, by God’s grace, useful counsel will not be lacking—what ought to be done in this affair.

Furthermore, I inform you that the monastery of Luxeuil, for which you wished, through our Cluniac brethren, to provide last year—and did indeed provide, though for only a short time—has fallen back into a worse condition than before. It has been deprived of nearly all monastic religion and observance and differs little from secular institutions, so that what in ancient times surpassed all the monasteries of Gaul now seems scarcely able to follow almost all of them even at a distance. To this evil is added the dullness—lest I say the stupidity—of its pastor, who presides over his own flock in such a way that scarcely anything remains to him of an abbot except the name. Why say more? “The whole head is sick, and the whole heart sorrowful. From the sole of the foot even to the crown of the head there is no soundness in it” (Isa. 1). Let the Father provide for His children.

### LETTER IV. Brother PETER, humble abbot of Cluny, to the Supreme Pontiff and our special Father, Lord Pope INNOCENT: obedience and love.

[Col. 0305C]

Master Peter, as I believe, very well known to your wisdom, recently coming from France, passed through Cluny. We asked where he was going. He replied that, weighed down by the persecutions of certain persons who were charging him with the name of heretic—a charge he greatly abhorred—he had appealed to the Apostolic Majesty and wished to take refuge with it. We praised his purpose and urged him to flee to a refuge known and common to all. We said that apostolic justice, which has never failed anyone, not even a stranger or traveler, would not fail him. We promised that mercy itself would come to meet him wherever reason required.

Meanwhile the lord Abbot of Cîteaux arrived and, concerning peace between him and the Lord of Clairvaux, because of whom he had appealed, discussed the matter jointly with us and with him. We too labored for his peace and urged him to go with the Abbot of Cîteaux to that man. We added to our admonitions that, if he had written or said anything offensive to Catholic ears, he should, at the urging of the Abbot of Cîteaux and other good and wise men, both withdraw it from his words and erase it from his books. And this was done. He went and returned, reporting that through the mediation of the Abbot of Cîteaux he had reached a peaceful settlement with the lord of Clairvaux and that the previous complaints had been silenced.

Meanwhile, admonished by us—or rather, inspired by God, as we believe—he set aside the tumults of schools and studies and chose Cluny, which is yours, as his permanent dwelling. We judged this suitable to his old age, his infirmity, and his religious profession; and, believing that his learning, which is by no means wholly unknown to you, could benefit our great multitude of brethren, we assented to his wish. If this should likewise be pleasing to your kindness, we kindly and joyfully permitted him to remain with us, yours in every respect as you know.

Therefore I, however unworthy still yours, ask; the Cluniac community most devoted to you asks; he himself asks through himself, through us, through your sons who bear this letter, and through this letter which he asked me to write: command that he spend at Cluny the remaining days of his life and old age, perhaps not many; and, lest by the pressure of certain persons he be either expelled or moved from the house which, like a sparrow, and the nest which, like a turtledove, he rejoices to have found, protect him with the shield of apostolic defense, in the manner in which you cherish all good men and have also loved this one.

### LETTER V. Brother PETER, humble abbot of the brethren of Cluny, to the Supreme Pontiff and our special Father, Lord Pope INNOCENT: obedience and love.

Trusting in paternal kindness, I am accustomed, with filial confidence, to commend even persons remote and unknown to the Apostolic Majesty. Since I have often found myself heard by you in their cases, I have hoped to be heard even more readily in those of persons known and close to me. Therefore I commend to apostolic kindness, with my whole heart, Lord Heraclius, canon of Lyons, my brother by blood.

> [Note: Cols. 0305D–0308D. Heraclius, canon of Lyons, our brother by blood: This Heraclius was brother of Peter the Venerable; others also call him Eraclius. From a canonry he was afterward raised to the archbishopric of Lyons. In that dignity he was enriched and exalted with many privileges, honors, and benefits by Frederick, Emperor of the Romans, as this decree of Frederick, issued at Arbois in 1157, most clearly shows:
>
> “In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Frederick, by the favor of divine clemency Emperor of the Romans and ever Augustus. In the judgment of God, who foresees all things, we believe that the giver and the confirmer have nearly equal merit. We also believe that it belongs to our imperial majesty to consider the welfare of all God’s holy churches, especially those which stand particularly under the right and lordship of the Roman Empire, to grant them the assistance of our confirmation, enduring forever; and to remove whatever inconvenience there may be, so that amid the storms of this raging sea they may serve God securely and without fear, and by unwearied prayers may obtain divine mercy for the stability of our Empire.
>
> “Therefore let all faithful of Christ and of our Empire, both the present age and succeeding posterity, know with what honors our forefathers and divine emperors exalted the Church of Lyons, with what ample benefits they enriched it, and how worthily they handed it down to us, their successors, to be raised henceforth to the imperial heights of dignity. Accordingly, we received with due honor the Archbishop and Primate Eraclius, who came to our court from the see of Lyons—which in ancient times excelled other cities in the life of the pagans through its chief flamines, or first teachers of the law, but now holds wider precedence through divine religion and imperial magnificence, is first among all the churches of Gaul, and shines with the dignity of primacy. Having treated him with our customary favor, as the pious and venerable authority of our predecessors ordained and as their sacred records instructed us, we fully invest him with the whole body of the city of Lyons and with all royal rights, established either within or outside the city throughout the archbishopric, which the Church of Lyons appears to have held in either ancient or modern times.
>
> “We therefore grant to the aforesaid Archbishop and Primate Eraclius, and through him to all his successors forever, the whole body of the city of Lyons and all royal rights throughout his entire archbishopric on this side of the Saône (Arar): within or outside the city; in abbeys and their possessions; monasteries; churches and their appurtenances, wherever situated; counties; markets; judicial duels; fairs; coinage; ferries; tolls; transit dues; castles; villages; hamlets; building-sites; male and female serfs; tributaries; tithes; forests; woods; hunting rights; mills; millworks; waters and watercourses; fields; meadows; pastures; cultivated and uncultivated lands; and all other things in the bishopric of Lyons which belong to the Empire.
>
> “We also grant the estates of the Count of Savoy, together with all other things belonging by ancient or new right to the Church of Lyons, and general jurisdiction in all the aforesaid matters, whether they lie within or outside the bishopric. Therefore let no attack of tyrants rage in any of the aforesaid matters; let no authority violently intrude there; let no count or judge presume to make law in them except the Archbishop and Primate of Lyons. Let every possession of the Church be held under immunity. Let the city of Lyons and the whole bishopric be free from every foreign authority, imperial justice being wholly preserved, so that those serving God there may worthily celebrate the memory of their first founder and may be able and willing to commend us, their patrons and confirmers, to God by diligent prayers.
>
> “Moreover, so that the Church of Lyons may always rejoice and exult that it has acknowledged the Emperor of the Romans as its lord, let its archbishop be endowed with a greater and more eminent prerogative of dignity, namely that he shall always be the most glorious exarch of our sacred palace of Burgundy, the highest prince of our council, and foremost in all our undertakings and affairs. And so that this our grant and confirmation may obtain the strength of perpetual validity, we have ordered this charter to be drawn up and sealed with a golden bull, marked with the character of our sign and supplied with suitable witnesses, whose names are these: Humbert, Archbishop of Besançon; Ado, Abbot of Saint-Oyend; Henry, protonotary of the court; Eberhard, Archdeacon of Besançon; Matthew, Duke of Lorraine; Berthold, Duke of Cenuga; Leopold, brother of the Duke of Bohemia; Ulrich, Count of Luxembourg; Hugh, Count of Thurgau; Stephen, Count.
>
> “Sign of the invincible lord Frederick, Emperor of the Romans.
>
> “I, Rainald, chancellor, acting in place of Stephen, Archbishop of Vienne and archchancellor, have authenticated this.
>
> “Given at Arbois, the fourteenth day before the Kalends of December, in the fifth indiction, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1157; in the sixth year of the reign of the most glorious lord Frederick, Emperor of the Romans, and the third of his Empire.”
>
> He was also finally Abbot of Saint-Just at Lyons and legate of the Apostolic See throughout Gaul, as he himself attests in this other charter:
>
> “Heraclius, by the grace of God Archbishop of Lyons and legate of the Apostolic See, to all, forever. Let present and future persons know that we and the Church of Saint-Just, over which, by God’s will, we preside with the title of abbot, have granted in perpetuity to the house of Chasiriac, through the intervention of our venerable brother the Archbishop of Tarentaise, the tithes of the lands which they have acquired or shall acquire in the parish of Villars, when they cultivate them in the manner of farmers. We retain for ourselves and our Church of Saint-Just an annual rent of two sextarii of rye, according to the measure of Calamont, for each plow. The witnesses were William of Marsiac, Gaudemar Brun, Artaud, Girinus Scotus, Master Berno, and Aymo Colomb. And so that this may remain firm hereafter, we and our community have wished it confirmed by the authority of our seals.”
>
> These matters have been noted in commendation of our abbot’s brother, though perhaps at greater length than the elucidation of the passage required.]

His sole reason for coming to the city was to see his Father and to bind more closely to himself your heart, occupied with the many interests of your children. I ask on his behalf, nor am I ashamed to ask, because the testimony of his former youth, especially among what are called secular clergy, neither puts him to shame in his petitions nor turns your ears away from hearing them. Let your former diligence inquire, if it please you, from the Church of Lyons, in which he was educated and spent most of his life; inquire also from Lord Stephen the archdeacon, whose credibility I leave you yourself to judge. Receive him therefore, I beseech you, into your affection; cherish him in your bosom, so that, when he perceives that he has not been excluded from your favor, he may strive more diligently to do those things by which he may acquire more abundantly for himself both God’s favor and yours.

### LETTER VI. Brother PETER, humble abbot of Cluny, to the honorable and beloved brethren, Lord LEO the abbot, Lord STEPHEN the archdeacon, and the whole chapter of the holy Church of Lyons: greeting.

[Cols. 0307B, 0308A]

The Apostle’s command is: “Pursue peace with all people, and holiness, without which no one shall see God” (Heb. 12). Again, his command is: “If it be possible, so far as it depends on you, live at peace with all people” (Rom. 12). Giving heed to these and similar commands of the sacred law, I have resolved, as my conscience testifies, from long ago to devote every effort to brotherly love and peace. Nor do I think that this is entirely unknown to your affection. Except for last year’s dispute, during almost twenty years no lawsuit, no contention, no even slight injury to friendship has arisen between the Churches of Lyons and Cluny, Christ uniting our hearts to one another.

I strove devotedly to preserve this unity in the times of the archbishops of revered memory, Hubald, Rainald, and Peter; and I always did what I could to ensure that it was kept intact by our people. I have therefore maintained, and, as I have said, have always intended to maintain, the good of peace and concord between ours and yours. Nor have I followed certain predecessors in their frequent stirring up of your minds; rather, I have continually endeavored that the bond of this love might remain indissoluble.

I am therefore surprised, and lay before you a still friendly complaint, that the pact of peace which, less than a year ago, we concluded through the hands of wise and religious persons has been broken—not indeed by all, but, as has been reported to me, by some among you. They even publicly forbade the lord Archbishop of Lyons to dedicate the cemetery at Villefranche according to the terms of the agreement. Whether this ought to have been done, see for yourselves.

Yet, that whatever concerns us may be fulfilled in word and deed, I admonish your reverence—and, lest you think that I omit this through any pride, I also ask—that you do not allow the illness of discord, recently healed, to creep back again; and that you in turn keep sincerely with us the peace which we intend to keep with you without pretense. And lest the foot of mutual peace between us stumble over any obstacle, however small: if perhaps anything remains to be fulfilled from the terms of the agreement—though we do not know that it does—we are ready to fulfill it and to cut away, so far as lies in us, every cause of dissension or scandal. For we wish always, if possible, to be peaceable not only with you, whom we believe, as befits ecclesiastical men, to love peace, but even with those who hate peace.

### LETTER VII. Brother PETER, humble abbot of Cluny, to the Supreme Pontiff and our special Father, Lord Pope INNOCENT: obedience and love.

Often I am verbose with you and, as I fear, burdensome. My fear is comforted by a fatherly kindness which scarcely knows how to be angry with sons; and, if it is angry, is soon appeased. The clergy and people of Lisieux [Lexovium], and, as I have heard, the whole Church together, left bereft by the death of their bishop [Note: [Col. 0309D] “The Church of Lisieux, bereft by the death of its bishop.” John, who died in 1140.], chose Lord Arnulf, archdeacon of Sées, as bishop and pastor, and caused him to be consecrated according to ecclesiastical custom by the lord archbishop of Rouen, to whom the consecration belonged by canon law [Col. 0309D]. [Note: [Col. 0309D] “Arnulf, archdeacon of Sées.” Nephew of the aforesaid John. He also wrote many distinguished letters, which we possess from the library of Odo of Tournebus, son of Adrian; and, after governing for forty years, he finally resigned the episcopate and, in the monastery of St Victor at Paris, professed the order of the Regular Canons of St Augustine. To these he had earlier—namely in 1170—granted as alms the church of Blessed Peter of Gacé in the diocese of Lisieux, as is clear from his letters concerning that grant.]

I say that they chose him and had him consecrated, not only because he is a person of the best and singular reputation among his own people; not only because he possesses distinguished learning [Col. 0310A]; not only because, I believe, his prudence and energy are not unknown to you; but because he is your special son and, from his very youth, a familiar foster-child of the Roman Church. For who, having heard him, has not recognized him as a foster-child of the Roman Church? Who, observing him speak of her, has not thought him reared from boyhood in the bosom of the Roman Church? Who, so far as the Spirit is concerned, has not judged him truly your son—anyone who has been able not merely to hear his words but also, what is exceedingly rare in our time, to read his writings?

As Solomon says, “A friend is not known in prosperity, nor an enemy concealed in adversity” (Ecclus. 12); so the time of schism revealed him as a friend, that it is almost superfluous for us to commend to you his fidelity and friendship [Col. 0310B], since the tumults of so many storms and tempests are known to have proved him a most faithful and devoted foster-child. May it therefore benefit the Church which chose him and, with this confidence, set him over itself as pastor, that it desired in him integrity, learning, maturity of character despite his youth, and finally your favour in his promotion. May it benefit it that his election and consecration be confirmed by the Apostolic See, and that no hearing be granted against him to the enemy not only of himself but of the whole Church of God in those regions—the count of Anjou. [Note: [Col. 0309D] “The count of Anjou.” Geoffrey, surnamed Plantagenet, son of Fulk, king of Jerusalem, and father of Henry II, king of England.]

For whatever he may say, whatever he may claim under the name of an appeal made by himself, it is certain that he appealed not as one aggrieved, but wishing to aggrieve; not as one oppressed, but desiring to oppress; not with the intention that justice should act for him, but devising that iniquity might overcome equity and falsehood truth [Col. 0310C]. To prevent there being a bishop for the Church of Lisieux, he wished to gain time for his malice, so that, with the pastor absent, there might be no one to resist the wolf, nor anyone to oppose, even slightly, its beastly bites from destroying the flock of God. Let your wisdom consider all these things; let your compassion provide for them all; and let your prudence not permit the tyrant, as is said, to abuse an apostolic appeal, due not to tyrants but to those in need.

## LETTER VIII. To the venerable lord, Lord MILO, bishop of the Morini, Brother PETER, humble abbot of Cluny, greetings.

[Note: [Col. 0310D] “To Milo, bishop of the Morini.” The first of this name: consecrated in the year of Christ 1131, he held the see until 1149. He is highly praised also by Robert of Torigni in these words: “In the year 1139 the Gallican Church flourished through men illustrious in religion and wisdom: Milo, bishop of Thérouanne, outstanding in the virtue of humility; Alvisus of Arras, renowned for generosity, counsel, and eloquence; Geoffrey of Langres; Hugh of Auxerre; Joscelin of Soissons; Geoffrey of Chartres; and Alberic, archbishop of Bourges, most distinguished for learning and prudent counsel” [Col. 0311D]. The Morini, says an ancient poet, are the remotest people of Gaul; so called in the old Celtic language as though “people of the sea” or “dwellers by the sea.” For *mor* means “sea,” and the maritime people are still called *morinwyr* by the Britons of England, who retain the ancient language of Gaul. Their city, Thérouanne, not long ago but now utterly destroyed, had its bishops’ seat transferred to Boulogne, a city on the Ocean known to Ammianus Marcellinus.]

Because an offence against charity is held of such weight before God that, as your learning knows, not even an offering brought to the altar is accepted with it [Col. 0311A], nor do alms avail, nor martyrdom profit, nor sins receive forgiveness; indeed, sins already forgiven return upon the one who committed them—I ought not to conceal it, nor stir my mind against a brother, and especially a bishop, unless perhaps there is just cause for such stirring through zeal for justice. For to be moved for justice is not an offence against charity, but an act of equity. I should wish, if God granted grace, to have this disposition toward all; I should wish to preserve it wholly toward you also.

That I may do so more fully, I have resolved not to conceal my mind from you, nor to speak with a double heart; but, as to a friend, to lay bare without any veil of deceit what incites me to indignation. We have been told—if indeed it is so—not by a few nor by insignificant persons, but by many and eminent persons [Col. 0311B], that you, to say it without prejudice to brotherly peace, disparage the monastic order; that, upon any occasion, even a slight one, you frequently tear it to pieces; that you declaim against it in public assemblies; diminish even its greatest merits; and magnify with rhetorical speeches minor faults, which still sometimes steal upon men, not angels.

It has also been said that in your synod, before a multitude of clergy and people, you uttered the imprecation that God might destroy the pride of the Cluniacs, and laid upon the people the charge to entreat the Lord for this. Would that the merciful Saviour might destroy in us and ours, and in all his own, not merely the walls of pride but every wall of Satan down to the ground; might build in them the walls of the spiritual Jerusalem [Col. 0311C]; and from there hear the prayers of all good people. But if this was to be said, it was not to be mocked; if admonition was needed, it was not to be preached abroad; if prayer was needed, it was not to be declaimed. Let it be so: we are proud, guilty, sinners. Yet the sins of brothers were not to be preached in the Church, nor monks’ offences displayed to the people as examples; lest the people, hearing of proud monks, and especially Cluniacs, be drawn to imitation, and be taught to think pride less blameworthy in themselves because they heard it was conspicuous in monks.

The presentation of an example of pride is not a sufficiently fitting persuasion to avoid pride; for the disease of pride [Col. 0311D] and other evils are more commonly purged from human hearts by contrary examples of humility and other virtues. Your wisdom ought to have preached this not among the people of Thérouanne but in the chapter of Cluny [Col. 0312A], and, as befits a bishop, recalled the pride of our brothers to the way of humility by sacred persuasion. This was to be pressed upon their ears without the people, not upon the people’s ears without them, so that exhortation might correct them, not disparagement defame them.

For the Cluniac brothers, from such diverse and remote regions of the earth, could not hear—much less heed—the bishop at Thérouanne disputing about their pride; whereas perhaps they would have obeyed had they heard him admonishing them about such matters in their own chapter, which he attended twice or three times. I mean that chapter which, as I said, he attended twice or three times, and where he gave those proud men no small encouragement by his promise of friendship, benefits, and support. Bishop Augustine did not thus preach to the people the true or alleged evils of brothers, or order them preached in his writings, when he said: “Where sin arises, there let it die; nor let its correction extend to more persons than its knowledge.” Neither did the earlier Fathers and teachers of God’s Churches do so; nor, to speak of singular men in our own time, did Lord Guigo, prior of the Carthusians, who had drawn this from the fountain of true, not feigned, charity: that he made each person’s faults known only to their author, while he publicized each person’s merits not to the person himself but to all when that person was absent.

But whence, after all, this pride? Which bishop do the Cluniac brothers resist? Whom do they not obey? Whom do they not serve? To whom do they not render rightful obedience, service to the extent of their ability, and reverence beyond almost all monks of other congregations [Col. 0312C]? I do not know, I do not know: God knows. If I knew, I would not tolerate it; if I recognized it, I would correct it. I see the resources of Cluny as though they were the treasury of the entire Christian commonwealth: all draw from it, almost exhaust it; few put little into it; many receive much from it. Yet because, by God’s grace, we have almost all priests of the Latin Church as friends, we ask that we may have you also favourable among the rest. Our few possessions located with you are at your disposal, and our many other possessions scattered through different parts of the world stand ready to serve your reverence, if that is your pleasure.

A domestic grievance is added to this complaint: the college of secular canons at Abbeville, which the count of Ponthieu gave to the monastery of Cluny insofar as secular right is concerned [Col. 0312D]—[Note: [Col. 0311D] “The count of Ponthieu.” Among Cluny’s benefactors the counts of Ponthieu occurred at no great interval. One of them is the man here mentioned, who gave to the monastery of Cluny, as regards secular right, the college at Abbeville, a celebrated city of the district of Ponthieu. Another was William, count of Ponthieu and Montreuil, who, as is found in the Cartulary of Cluny, charter 224, in the year 1035, “as alms for his soul and those of his heirs, granted and conveyed in perpetuity to the community of St Peter of Cluny ten thousand herrings, to be distributed for the community’s own use, and to be received annually before the feast of the blessed apostle Andrew from his viscounty of Abbeville by whomever, whether himself or another, held it from him in farm.”]—would also have been granted by the bishop of Amiens, to whom it belongs through ecclesiastical oversight, had he not been dissuaded by you and a few others [Col. 0313A].

But why do I complain here about others? I can indeed complain of them with justice, but I have more right to complain of you. Since both common charity and special friendship urged that nothing be done against a friend, you exceeded the limits of friendship and harmed a friend who harmed you in nothing. And whereas, under your jurisdiction and according to the hope you gave us, we expected manifold benefits, that hope turned to the contrary: not only did your generosity grant us nothing within the bounds of your bishopric, but it also opposed the gifts and benefactions of others.

This is proved, as I have heard, by the recent gathering of bishops at Reims. There, when the lord archbishop of Reims, the bishops of Soissons, Châlons, Arras, and other bishops—certainly great, wise, and religious men—gave their assent in the matter already mentioned, you alone appeared to dissent from all. Why was this? If for a just cause, well. If not, see to it yourself. Yet I think that St Bertin [Note: [Col. 0313C] “I think, however, that in your regions St Bertin,” etc. That is, the abbey of St Bertin the Confessor in the town of Saint-Omer. St Hugh, abbot of Cluny, made it, with several other monasteries of Flanders, illustrious by religious observance, according to the anonymous writer of his Life, whom we have appended to the monk Hugh. Letters of Count Robert of Flanders, issued in 1106 concerning that same matter, are also read; we have already copied them on p. 558 of this Library.]—Abbeville, Gast, Rumilly, and other places adjoining your city [Note: [Col. 0313D] “Rumilly, and other places adjoining the city.” Rumilly, or, as others pronounce it, Rumilliac, is also a dependency of Cluny, commonly called the priory of St Peter of Rumilly-le-Comte, in the diocese of Thérouanne in earlier times, now in that of Boulogne. But who subjected it to the monastery of Cluny has not yet been discovered. Yet it may in some degree be inferred that it was under Cluny’s obedience even before the time of Abbot Peter, from these words of Pope Lucius III’s letters, by which he especially protected this monastery with its appurtenances: “Let the place itself,” he says, “namely the aforesaid monastery of Rumilly with all its appurtenances, as it is known to have been hitherto, remain forever under the obedience and subjection of the monastery of Cluny” [Col. 0314C].]—should judge that episcopal authority ought not so readily and severely to condemn the brothers of Cluny.

I spare words, lest I seem to provoke a friend whom I am striving to appease. Therefore, at the close of my letter, I pray—I pray, and our brethren also entreat—that your truth may keep what your kindness promised us in friendship, as I said above. Far be it that, by acting otherwise than by promising, there should be “yes” and “no” in your holy mouth; rather, by fulfilling the same things that you say, may there always be “yes” in it [Col. 0313C].

## LETTER IX. To the universal and our special father, Lord Pope INNOCENT, Brother PETER, humble abbot of Cluny, obedience and love.

The emperor of Spain [Note: [Col. 0314C] “The emperor of Spain, a benefactor of the Church of Cluny.” Alfonso, who, besides the many gifts by which he enriched the monastery of Cluny, gave our Peter the church of St Vincent at Salamanca through the hand of Guy, cardinal of the Church and legate, in order that he might convert the canonical habit then maintained there into the monastic habit; as appears from his ordinance concerning that gift, inserted in full at the end of this volume.]—the great prince of the Christian people, a son devoted to your majesty—although he can and ought to have great influence with your compassion, nevertheless chose me at this time as his mediator and intercessor with you, because he is the foremost modern friend and benefactor of the Church of Cluny [Col. 0314A].

That I may deserve to be heard for him, I do now in absence what I would do if present: with all my brothers, your sons, who have been able to hear this, I cast myself at the feet of your compassion, not merely in heart but in my very body. I ask that you not, on this occasion at least, reject from your customary kindness the prayers of those whose petitions your favour has received so fatherly and graciously, again and again. For the bounty of your fatherly grace, by which you have almost always been accustomed to hear us, spread everywhere and known to all, draws many to us and compels us, through repeated petitions, to trouble you.

Yet I would not offer prayers for the king of Spain, the emperor of the Romans, or any mortal whatever [Col. 0314B], if I knew this to conflict with justice. Therefore, though I cannot be a witness of matters at which I was not present, I am compelled to trust the testimony of many wise, eminent, and proven men no less than my own eyes and ears. By the attestation of all these—many clerics, some monks, and several bishops—the aforesaid emperor presents through my lowliness to the Apostolic Majesty the election of the lord bishop of Salamanca as archbishop of St James: an election made canonically, peacefully, and unanimously by all the clergy and all the people.

And because that Church to which he was elected—glorious through the body of so great an apostle [Note: [Col. 0314D] “And because that Church is glorious through the body of so great an apostle.” Namely Compostela, which is also called that of St James the Apostle in Galicia. Alfonso, another king of Spain, testifies that it had long gloried greatly in the presence there of the apostle’s body. Writing in 906 to the guardians of the tomb of St Martin of Tours, he says: “Moreover, concerning your question as to whose apostle’s tomb we have here among us, know most certainly that we possess in marble chests, in the province of Galicia, the tomb of James, the apostle of Zebedee, Boanerges (“Son of Thunder”), who was beheaded by Herod.””]—had been raised high by so many privileges of the Apostolic See and lifted its head as chief among all the Spanish Churches, it required a noble, prudent, honourable, and tested person, preferable to those of the other Churches of that land [Col. 0314C]. Rejoicing that it had at last found such a man in him, it elected him unanimously, as stated, as its pastor.

Therefore, if anyone, after that common and solemn election, has withdrawn from it in order to serve some private advantage, let fatherly solicitude provide that he not be allowed, for private gain, to hinder public goods or on that account disturb the peace of so great a Church. Thus the emperor of Spain, and the clergy and people of St James, stand at the doors of your mercy and knock with our hand [Col. 0315A], asking that you receive their elect, who comes to you not loftily or proudly but humbly and gently; loosen the bond of apostolic severity which he has borne with moderation; and grant, which is yours alone to grant, his translation from Salamanca to the city of the apostle St James.

And so that the embassy may be aided with a gracious Father by consideration for the envoy himself, we have sent to your fatherhood our venerable and beloved brother Natalis, lately abbot of Rebais, whom you know and love. Since we could not, by our own strength, induce him—though unwilling and protesting—to leave the repose of Mary which he had chosen among us, we compelled him by the force of obedience to undertake this business, which he could not resist. Therefore, if it please you, make glad by granting his petitions him whom we have distressed by sending him [Col. 0315B].

## LETTER X. To the supreme pontiff and our special father, Lord Pope INNOCENT, Brother PETER, humble abbot of Cluny, obedience and his whole self for all purposes.

Lord Hugh, archbishop of Tours [Note: [Col. 0315D] “Lord Hugh, archbishop of Tours.” The second of this name, successor of Hildebert, and, as this letter also testifies, a great friend of the Cluniacs. He is found to have subscribed a charter of R., duke of the Normans and count of Anjou, confirming one hundred marks’ worth of land in England. Although mutilated, that charter seems to be addressed to our Peter, abbot of Cluny, and may appropriately be inserted here. It is as follows: “To the most reverend father, by God’s grace abbot P. of Cluny, and to the most holy community of Cluny, R., by the same grace duke of the Normans and count of Anjou, eternal greeting in the Lord. Our predecessor of blessed memory, Henry king of England, gave yearly to the brothers of Cluny one hundred marks of silver as alms. Upon his death, land was assigned to the aforesaid brothers for the said one hundred marks,” etc., as in the letters of King Stephen found on p. 1398. “Therefore we grant that land to the Church of Cluny and to the brothers serving God there, to possess by perpetual right. We approve and confirm also the grant of the said land made by the empress. Witnesses: Hugh, archbishop of Tours; Pagan of Clairvaux; Guy of Sablé.” How these items may agree with one another chronologically will be for others to judge. This Hugh, archbishop of Tours, is also mentioned in the Old History of the Lords of Amboise: “Geoffrey, count of Anjou, to whom nothing great was great enough, came with his army to Luché; and there, through the mediation of Archbishop Hugh, peace was made on both sides”—that is, with Sulpicius, lord of Amboise.]—while hastening to approach your majesty’s presence, was struck by illness at La Charité on that very journey of devotion. As it worsened, when he was compelled already to despair of life, he received the monastic clothing there; and, receiving the habit of religion from the hand of our prior of La Charité, he became a monk of Cluny.

When the Church of Tours heard this [Col. 0315C], and feared that on this occasion he might wish to abandon the pastoral care, it sent to him Lord P., archdeacon, and Lord Hugh, abbot of Noyers, with others, and took every care, with all diligence and most urgent prayers, to ask that the pastor return to his flock. He refused, and did not yield to the entreaties of many great men urging his return. While they persisted and were unwilling in any way to desist from the prayers they had begun, he answered only this: that he would do none of these things before the matter had been made known to you and he had heard from your fatherhood what he ought to do.

Therefore that noble and great Church of Tours supplicates as earnestly as it can; we too supplicate. Justice itself—which is far more weighty—also asks, as it seems to us, that your sublimity, to whom the care of all Churches has been entrusted by God, persuade the father to return to his sons, the shepherd to his sheep, the prelate to his subjects [Col. 0315D–0316A], and, if he will not do so willingly, compel him even unwillingly. For, as public report testifies, he is not a hireling who, seeing the wolf, leaves the sheep and flees; but a shepherd who has been accustomed, for the house of Israel entrusted to him, to set himself as a wall and stand in battle on the day of the Lord.

But why, I ask, why do I entreat? I entreat as though for an accused man who ought to receive some indulgence, as though some grave offence committed by him ought to be forgiven. Yet if I have ever known you, if I have observed your sweet affection toward the professors of religious life and especially toward its defenders, then one who has become better from good, a monk from a cleric, who has been converted from the common dress of the clergy to the black habit of his Martin, will not be judged unworthy of it, especially after having first attained an episcopal see [Col. 0316B].

Indeed, if he had wished to heed great and wise men, he would have returned to his own see not worse but now better; but with wise humility he preferred to await from there the Apostolic judgment. Therefore let it not harm him or his Church—which indeed I say superfluously—that he submitted himself wholly to apostolic disposal by his own counsel, not another’s; that he put on, as stated, Martin’s habit; and that he finally became your monk of Cluny—your monk in a more proper sense, so to speak. Your Holiness approved in certain other bishops, whom I could name, their passing from the common garb of clerics to the canonical habit. May it approve—and I believe it will approve—that the great archbishop of Tours turned himself to the humble habit of monks and, thus changing habit and life for the better, diminished nothing of his pontifical dignity by becoming better [Col. 0316C].

## LETTER XI. To the venerable A., priest of God and archbishop of Narbonne, Brother PETER, humble abbot of Cluny, greetings.

Hearing from several persons that your graciousness, because of the slight service rendered you by our people at the time of the Council of Reims, was more favourable to us than we deserved, I had resolved, on my return from Spain, first to come back by way of you in order to offer thanks for your goodwill. But because the manifold distraction of cares changed my plan, I was unable to return by way of you as I had intended [Col. 0316D]. Therefore, since I cannot present my person to one dear to me, I send my letter [Col. 0317A], so that in it you may feel me present and hear from it what you would hear from me.

Our common friends have told me that your reverence, already worn down toward old age by episcopal affairs, is more and more worn away daily and, oppressed by the troubles of pressing cares, is wearied more severely than usual. And since it is written in the Life of the great Martin, “After labour, the old man desired release,” I grieve that one who has earned release by righteous sweat must labour after earning his discharge, and who, as I have been told, desires to pass from Martha’s labours to the rest and leisure of Mary.

Yet if—speaking without prejudice to the right of friendship—you had a spirit victorious over years and refusing to yield to old age, I should hesitate to draw your pontifical sublimity down from the heights to the lowly place [Col. 0317B] and to invite you to pass from the episcopate into the monastic order. But since a lower place is commonly safer, while a higher always fears a fall, the mountain exposed to every whirlwind must, in my judgment, be fled; the valley, subject to no gusts of air, must be embraced. This valley may be Cluny for you, signified as such not only by humility but by its very situation. It has received many men humbled for Christ, not only from a lower order but also from your own, and in its time has advanced them to heavenly exaltation.

Let not, therefore, a soul to be exalted by God above the heavens fear to be humbled on earth; nor let him be ashamed to submit himself to men who does not doubt that by such humiliation he will be joined to blessed spirits.

## LETTER XII. To the venerable and deeply cherished friend, Lord GEOFFREY, archbishop of Bordeaux, Brother PETER, humble abbot of Cluny, greetings and sincere affection.

[Note: [Col. 0317D] “To Geoffrey, archbishop of Bordeaux.” Two archbishops of Bordeaux of this name were renowned in the time of Peter the Venerable. One obtained from Louis the Fat, king of the Franks, a privilege in 1137 both for himself and for his suffragans; the other presided at the Council of Beaugency in 1150 for the dissolution of the marriage of Louis the Younger and Eleanor. It is not altogether certain to which of these he writes, though perhaps the following letters to Popes Lucius and Eugenius, who sat before 1150, indicate in some degree that it concerns the first.] 

[Col. 0317C]

Among the various cares of my heart, there has sometimes intruded a thought concerning friendship, anxiously inquiring whom I ought to rank above or below whom as a friend. Searching all the recesses of my soul, and penetrating every hidden place after all clouds had been dispersed, it found that in friendship I ought to rank beneath no one and above almost everyone, so far as it concerned myself, that man—certainly my archbishop of Bordeaux—whom neither pontifical dignity nor temporal eminence associated with me as a spiritual and true friend [Col. 0317D], but whom a mind despising earthly things and longing for heavenly ones, refined manners, singular prudence, constant friendship, and truly Christ himself, presenting himself as the mediator at every beginning of mutual love, joined to me indivisibly.

This has always clung most firmly to my heart, has clung and, by God’s grace, will cling forever, from the time when the journey to Chartreuse made your holiness known to me. Since these things had to be prefaced, I have prefaced them [Col. 0318A]; now I add what ought to follow in order. I render whatever thanks I can because I found you not unequal in constancy of mutual affection—the man whom, as a friend departing for the remote regions of Spain and, as it were, foreign lands, I had as a devoted guardian of the trusts committed to him by my prayers. I entrusted to you our monasteries, abbeys, priories, and cells; and behold, on the testimony not only of his voice but of all of us, I found you most faithful also in this entrusted charge.

I had indeed intended first to return through your province; but a chance turn of events—or rather, what is truer, God’s ordering—changed this. Therefore I was not permitted to enjoy your presence, which, as you know, is most dear to me, nor had I the opportunity to speak or confer with you concerning the plans for the Church of Angély and other affairs [Col. 0318B]. Yet I wrote about this to the lord pope and, informing him of everything through my own messengers, sent him also letters from your Holiness. But, as your wisdom knows, and as was then agreed between us, the affair must remain secret, lest, while we seek to destroy the body of sin in the Church of St John, its disclosure before the right time should, God forbid, increase it.

Know that our condition, concerning which your sincere, humble, and exalted kindness and dignity wishes to be assured, is as follows. That past journey of ours brought more honour than befits my person—though not, I say, than befits the Church; for while it did not befit the person, it did befit the Church. Its temporal profit was not as great as desire wished, but nevertheless greater than merit demanded. As regards my person, would that soundness of spirit rivalled bodily health! As regards the Church, it enjoys peace above all things, both mutual and general, and humbly and devoutly serves Christ its Lord, as it seems, better than ever; and, having often been admonished by us as is fitting, it entreats the mercy of its gentle Lord for its lord and father, the archbishop of Bordeaux [Col. 0318C].

If you judge this useful, recall Constantine, concerning whom you wrote, to the fourth league; and confidently make dispositions in all Cluniac affairs not merely as legate, but as though you were the abbot of Cluny himself. For I do not think myself absent where you are, nor can you be absent where I am. Finally, I ask you to pray diligently to God not only for me and your Church of Cluny [Col. 0318D], but I implore you, more with my heart than with words, to urge those good men of your regions, whom you always equip and encourage for Christ’s warfare and service, to do the same.

## LETTER XIII. To our bishop of Winchester, Brother PETER, his abbot of Cluny, greetings and the whole affection of his heart.

[Col. 0319A] I am accustomed to ask for Cluny; now I ask for Marcigny. As you know, there is abundant cause for asking: a singular house, an outstanding religious community, not merely the death but the perpetual burial-place of holy sisters, who die before death and are buried before the grave for the sake of their Christ. Besides this, the religious life, blessed departure, and holy tombs there of many parents—and especially of my mother, and further, of your heavenly mother—compel me to ask, and you to grant, that you may always keep that place before your eyes, always venerate it, always cherish it.

In this hope, I ask you to receive, hear, and favour in your usual gracious manner the brother bearing this letter, sent from those handmaids of God to you and to your regions [Col. 0319B]. May our almighty and merciful Saviour, whom we continually attend for you as far as we can, turn your storm into a gentle breeze, and let its waves be still.

## LETTER XIV. To the venerable and deeply cherished friend, Lord GUERIN, bishop of Amiens, Brother PETER, humble abbot of Cluny, the greeting which he wishes for himself.

[Note: [Col. 0319C] “To Lord Guerin, bishop of Amiens.” He too was among the foremost, and not the least, benefactors of the Cluniac brothers. This may be gathered both from his letters concerning the grant of the church of St Peter with its altars in the diocese of Amiens, copied already on p. 1403 [Col. 0319D], and from many other documents in the Cartulary of St Martin of the Fields, a noble dependency of the monastery of Cluny. Among them is one concerning Vany, in which he calls himself “Galrin, most humble minister of the Church of Amiens,” and says that “at the request of the most reverend Gauslen, bishop of Soissons, and the prior of St Martin of the Fields, I confirm to St Martin the church situated in the territory of Vany, in honour of the outstanding confessor and most precious bishop of Christ, Martin, the altar of Bonnay, and the altar of Courcelles.” In 1127. There are also several documents in which he is styled sometimes Guarinus and sometimes Warinus; and finally several in which he is designated Gaurinus, bishop of Amiens, such as this one concerning the church of St Gervais at Encre: “In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Since in the body of Christ, which is the Church, the prelates, like eyes, are charged with greater vigilant care over the faithful, especially religious persons, it is fitting that we confer our benefits upon those by whose prayers peace and security are granted to us. Therefore I, Gaurinus, by God’s grace bishop of Amiens, freely and absolutely give as alms to the monks of St Martin of the Fields the church of St Gervais of Encre, which for a long time, contrary to apostolic decrees, had been in lay hands with the plague of simony, together with all its appurtenances, in the presence of Lord Alberic, bishop of Ostia and legate of the Apostolic See; Lord Gauslen, bishop of Soissons; and Lord Geoffrey, bishop of Châlons; with Lord Guerin, treasurer of the Church of Amiens, and Master Rainer, archdeacon of Châlons, as witnesses. Done in the year of the Incarnate Word 1138” [Col. 0320C–0320D].]

What can I say? What can I speak? What thanks can I render to so sincere a friend? Your wise affection has distinguished—truly distinguished—between friends and friends, between true and false, between those who give words and those who perform deeds. Others promise great things in return for their friends’ great merits, and pay nothing. You promised nothing, and, despite no merits of ours toward you, have paid much and greatly. This is the cause, this the principal matter, this the indissoluble bond by which we are bound and joined to you, by which, though absent, we pour out to you the whole inward substance of all our love and affection. Nor is this surprising. For who would not be powerfully drawn, who would not be attracted, by such benefits bestowed on your part and—so it has been said—by no benefits returned on ours? But if you intend to offer God a full sacrifice, a whole burnt offering; if you have resolved to sacrifice head and tail together, come—come, I say—to us, so that we may see him whom for so long we have wished to see, and enjoy here also in Christ him whom we desire to enjoy perpetually elsewhere. Through him who loved us and inspired you to love us, we not only ask but entreat that, before the coming summer ends, Cluny may behold you, and may be gladdened and rejoice at your long-desired presence.

## LETTER XV. To our beloved, altogether beloved and venerable friend, Lord SUGER, Abbot of Saint-Denis, brother PETER, humble abbot of Cluny, sends greetings.

> **Note:** [Col. 0320D] “To Lord Suger, Abbot of Saint-Denis.” Peter also writes to him below, Book VI, Letter 20; and Suger himself writes to Peter in return in the preceding letter. The manuscript codex of his letters has now for the first time made it possible to add several others besides these. The most learned Charles Labaeus is shortly to publish them from the library of the never sufficiently praised president J. A. Thou, to the great benefit, it is hoped, of all.

O unhappy lot of humankind, and—if it may be said—lamentable fortune! I often see, against my wishes, those whom I would not wish to see. Yet I cannot see, even once in many ages, those whom I should desire to behold continually. What is this? Worldly and harsh exactors of worldly affairs often press upon and stand before me—men whom, if I could, as I said, I would avoid with the greatest care. But my beloved—yes, that beloved one of mine—the Abbot of Saint-Denis, dear to me even before either of us became an abbot, and made from dear into dearest after that, I cannot see even after long intervals. France keeps him and is ever envious of him toward our Burgundy, so that I have never been able to see him at Cluny except once.

I therefore make this familiar complaint of him, giving such thanks as I can because, though he has withdrawn himself from us, he nevertheless does not cease to bestow manifold benefits. Our brethren dwelling in your regions bear witness to this, saying that in their affairs and needs they have found in you not merely the father of the monastery of Saint-Denis, but their own abbot as Cluniacs. Yet I grieve at this: not because you, always welcome to us without payment, are welcome, but because we, finding nothing that we can offer in return, always seem ungrateful for your benefits. Meanwhile, I ask and beseech, as earnestly as I can, that, whether by occasion of God, friendship, or your realm, in whose remotest parts we are situated, we may see you at Cluny before the winter now approaching. And I believe that, if you come, then, according to the prophecy, you shall see joy and gladness, not only in the life to come, of which this was said, but also in the present; you shall rejoice, and your heart shall be glad (Isa. 60).

## LETTER XVI. To the reverend Father and Lord PETER, by God’s grace Abbot of Cluny, brother BERNARD, called Abbot of Clairvaux, sends himself, such as he is.

“Is it your pleasure to jest thus? Truly, graciously and in a friendly manner,” etc. See among the letters of St Bernard, *Patrologia*, vol. CLXXXII, col. 396.

## LETTER XVII. To the man to be honored with singular reverence, embraced with all the arms of charity, the inseparable guest of my heart, Lord BERNARD, Abbot of Clairvaux, brother PETER, humble Abbot of Cluny, sends the salvation for which he sighs eternally.

[Col. 0321B]

Because I come late with my reply to the letters of so sweet and delightful a friend—letters which I myself ought to have met with a glad and swift response—your alert holiness may perhaps wonder, and, as I fear, attribute it to sloth or contempt. But far be both; indeed, not only far be they, but both are altogether absent, since, so far as letters are concerned, I have hardly ever received anything more willingly or read anything more eagerly. The cause of the delay lay partly with their bearer. On coming to Cluny and not finding me there, although I was not very far away, namely at Marcigny, he neither brought nor sent me the letters he carried, but left them at Cluny. And lest I seem to accuse a good man, I believe that he was either detained by some business or deterred, by the severity of the bitter winter then upon us, from attempting to visit me.

I too remained there for a month, detained both by snow and by business, and only at the beginning of Lent did I manage, with difficulty, to return home. At last I received from the subprior, to whom they had been entrusted, those letters of yours. My heart was immediately drawn; and, since it had long been warm with affection for you, it was kindled far more by those same letters, by the breath of your breast, and allowed nothing further of coldness or lukewarmness to remain within it. Drawn, I say—and so drawn that, as I do not remember ever having done except out of reverence for sacred books, I kissed the letter as soon as I had read it through. And so that I might, according to my custom, stir up toward the affection of your charity those whom I could—for I could not then stir up all—I gathered round whoever was present, reread to them what I had read alone, and to the best of my ability moved them to greater affection toward you.

I immediately put the letters away and added them to the silver or gold coins which, according to a custom left me by the Fathers, I usually carry with me for almsgiving. Nor was this unfitting. For your favor is good to me above all gold and silver; your charity is precious. I wished to write back at once, on the following day, what had settled in my mind; but I was prevented by a daily—indeed, nearly continual—exactor demanding other things, and kept silent. A most harsh ruler, whom I could not resist, imposed silence upon me: the manifold care of countless affairs compelled me to be silent, not for one day only but for many. Sometimes fifteen days passed, sometimes a whole month, sometimes successive months, during which I always endeavored to write but was not permitted by the ruler already mentioned. At last I broke the troublesome bond and, though with difficulty, by writing in secret overcame the yoke of the burden and the sceptre of the exacter.

And lest I seem excessive in so earnestly excusing my delay in replying, you yourselves compelled me to make my defense when you said: “It is not long since, writing to you, I greeted your crown with due reverence, and you did not answer me a word. Nor long before that had I written to you again from the city of Rome, and even then I received not a single iota. Do you now wonder that, on my recent return from Spain, I did not presume again to thrust my trifles upon you? For if it is a fault, for whatever reason, not to have written, it surely cannot be without fault not to have wished—not to say to have disdained—to reply.” So you say. But what do I say? Precisely this: I could in no way deny the fault you lay upon me, if I had scorned to reply to so great a friend writing first. For I admit that I ought to have replied to one who wrote first. But, as I can recall, while you were staying in Rome, I wrote first and you replied afterward. Therefore it was not for me to reply, since I had written first; rather, it was for you to reply, because I had written first.

I could indeed have replied even to your reply; but your answer, complete and satisfying my letter to the last detail, imposed silence upon me in answering. If this is so, then the fault imputed to me leaves me and begins to look toward you, since you wished to blame one who was blameless and to burden the shoulders of an innocent brother with another’s burden—not to say your own. As to your statement that I did the same on another occasion, because the matter is not present in my memory, an answer is absent. If one can perhaps be supplied, either a plausible excuse or a humble satisfaction will not be lacking.

But you added: “See in what way justice would rule in my favor.” And I say: “Meanwhile, in view of the reasons stated above, justice rules in my favor, because no fault is found in me.” If I were unwilling to spare you, I could now call you, as you called yourself, an injured friend and could justly exact the penalty for injury or wrongs. But I spare you, as is my custom; I forgive everything, even without being asked. I remember none of the wrongs of which you spoke. For this too pertains to what follows: since I strive, not playfully but seriously, to remove marked enmities from the hearts of many and intend to urge you to remove them, I ought myself to forgive everyone first and to do beforehand what I labor for others to do.

But perhaps you will say again: “Is it your pleasure to jest thus?” It is indeed my pleasure—but with you. Certainly with you, though not in the same way with others. For with certain others I would fear, in passing beyond seriousness, to fall into frivolity. With you, however, I do not fear frivolity; I pursue charity, lest it fail. Hence it is always sweet to speak with you and to preserve between us, by pleasant conversation, the honeyed sweetness of charity. For I take care, as far as I can, not to be numbered among those brethren who hated Joseph in their heart and could not speak peaceably to him (Gen. 21).

Would that all our brethren and yours did likewise—and I say this not boastfully—and did not degenerate from the line of charity, by which alone, after faith and the sacrament of baptism, they are called brothers and are joined to one another in a special kinship. Let them fear what the Apostle calls “danger among false brethren” (2 Cor. 11). Would that all did this, indeed, and guarded their heart from deceitful thought and their tongue, according to the psalm they frequently recite, from harsh speech (Ps. 90).

These things which I have said seem to promise something great and, as it were, to prepare for the accomplishment of the greatest things. But lest the familiar saying be spoken of them:

> What worthy matter will this promiser bring forth with so wide a gape?  
> (Horace, *Ars Poetica*, v. 138.)

I confess that I have no very great cause—indeed, no great, moderate, or even small cause—for writing to you, among those matters which secular people deem great or very great, and from which the children of this age hope to become great or very great.

Yet there is a great cause, surpassing all causes so greatly that the Apostle calls it greater than all (1 Cor. 13). And if its name is sought, he calls it charity. This was my whole and only reason for writing: charity, which I trust I preserve entire toward your person, and which, through your especial effort, I do not despair that our men and yours will preserve toward one another better than usual. For, so far as concerns the charity which from long ago I have held in reserve for you in the hidden place of my heart, it seems to me that “many waters cannot quench it, nor can rivers overwhelm it” (Song 8). In some circumstances I seem often to have experienced that many waters cannot quench it nor rivers overwhelm it. For when can the sincere and ardent affection of my breast toward you be quenched or overwhelmed by any little streams of hostile rumor, when not even the many waters of tithes could quench it, nor the rush of the rivers of Langres overwhelm it? You know what I mean; and I say it for no other reason than that, recalling these marks of my heart’s steadfast purpose of love toward you, your prudence may presume that I can henceforth remain firm. I presume the same of you and trust that no assault of any kind can exclude me from the inner chambers of your heart.

But since each of us is called a shepherd, since our sheepfolds are filled with no small multitude of Christ’s sheep, and since both of us are commanded, “Know diligently the countenance of your flock” (Prov. 27), we must see whether our flock is known to us: whether it is healthy or sick, weak or strong, certainly whether dead or alive. For since that beloved disciple says, “He who does not love remains in death” (1 John 3), why should I be concerned about the sickness of my flock when I know it to be already dead? If he who does not love remains in death, in what death does he remain who hates? If he who does not love remains in death, in what death does he remain who maligns another?

Why do I say this? I see certain men, from both our sheepfolds and yours, who have undertaken sworn wars against one another; those who ought to dwell united in the Lord have revolted from charity, which they have maimed. I see them to be of the household of the same Lord, soldiers in the army of the same King, called Christians by the same name and likewise called monks. I observe that they are subject not only to the bond of a common faith but also to the yoke of the same monastic Rule, cultivating the Lord’s field with many but differing labors. And although, as I have said, the Christian name joins them and monastic profession unites them, some hidden and abominable diversity of minds alone separates them and disunites them from that sincere unity of hearts into which they seem to have been gathered.

And—O thing full of lamentation, not to be mourned worthily by any fountains of tears!—the proud archangel, cast down from heaven, has again occupied heavenly places; and he who could not establish his throne in the north has fixed it in the southern part—that is, the brighter part—of heaven. Truly, yes, he boasts that he has done so, whenever, after expelling him who dwells in heaven, whose place is constituted not in mutual rancor but in brotherly peace, he tyrannically rules the minds of men who shine by the profession and example of heavenly things. And since one stronger than that strong man, who had guarded his court in long-standing peace, has conquered him; since he has cast out the prince of this world; since he has overthrown the throne of him who is king over the children of pride even among lay Christians—how great must our lamentation be if Satan erects in monks’ hearts the throne of his wickedness which has been overthrown elsewhere?

Far be it—far be it—that he who, the Savior says, has been so weakened that he is bound even by His handmaids and mocked by His servants as though he were an old man, should so mock His servants and handmaids and rule over them as worthless slaves. But why do they oppose one another? Why do they speak evil of one another? Why are they consumed by one another? Let the ground of the dispute, I beg, be brought forward; and if they can advance any just complaint against each other, let it be settled by impartial arbitrators. What, I ask, does brother demand from brother? And, so that in two named parties the whole diversity of the disputants may be comprehended: what do you demand, I say, Cluniac brother, from Cistercian brother, or conversely? If it is cities, fortresses, villages, an estate, any landed possession great or small; finally, if it is gold, silver, or any amount or kind of money, speak—come, set it forth. Judges are at hand, not of injustice but of equity, prepared immediately to settle all disputes of this kind. Peace will easily be restored and wounded charity healed once it is known that so great a division of hearts arose from such or similar matters.

But I see that both of you have cast away all these things, leaving nothing for yourselves on earth, and have resolved, enriched by blessed poverty, to follow poor Christ. This, then, is not the ground I sought. Yet I shall not desist, grow weary, or rest until I reach the bottom of the truth for which I inquire.

Perhaps the cause of this dispute between you is differing custom, varied observance of monastic order. But if this, beloved brethren, is the cause of so great an evil, it is most unreasonable and—speaking without prejudice to either of you—most childish and foolish. Does not that appear unreasonable, childish, and foolish which all reason abandons and which everyone of sound judgment rejects? For if diversity of custom, if the manifold variety of innumerable matters, ought to tear Christ’s servants away from mutual charity, what peace, concord, unity, or indeed anything of Christ’s law will remain for monks—not only monks, but all Christians?
