Of that law the great Apostle said: “Bear one another’s burdens, and so fulfil the law of Christ” (Gal. 6). If, I say, the law of Christ—that is, charity—must be abandoned by all who follow differing practices, it is nowhere thereafter to be sought. For it could be found nowhere once it had been excluded from all who follow a different custom.

Is not the whole world, beloved brethren, now from ancient times filled with Christ’s churches? And though the multitude of churches serving God under one faith and the same charity exceeds almost every number, among them there is found nearly as much diversity of practice as there is an infinity of places: in chants, readings, and every ecclesiastical office; in varied dress; in fasts, apart from the authoritative fasts that cannot be changed; and in the varying observances of the fasts themselves. The same is true of all similar matters instituted, according to differences of times, places, peoples, and regions, by the prelates of churches—who, as the Apostle says, may each abound in his own judgment in matters of this sort (Rom. 14). Shall all these churches, then, abandon charity because they have changed custom? Shall they cease to be Christians because they differ in varied practices? Shall the supreme good of peace perish from them all because each works good in a different manner?

Ambrose, teacher of the Church in life and word, did not think so. Speaking of the Saturday fast, which he had seen observed at Rome but did not find observed after becoming bishop at Milan, he said: “When I am at Rome, I keep the fast observed by the Roman Church. When at Milan, following the custom of that Church, I do not fast.” From this also Father Augustine, describing the devotion of his good mother, recounts that she wished at Milan to offer her offerings according to the custom she had seen maintained in the African churches, contrary to the observance of the churches of Italy, but was forbidden by Ambrose.

But why do I labor over these things? I would vainly surround an evident matter with many testimonies or examples, especially since neither among the ancients the divergence concerning the very time of Easter, nor among the moderns the well-known difference between Greeks and Latins concerning the Christian sacrifice itself, could injure charity or produce any schism of unity. The holy Fathers and the approved books they have left to the churches witness to the former point: the East celebrated the Lord’s Easter at one time, the West at another, and in the same island of Britain the English at one time and the Christian Scots—that is, the more ancient Scots—at another.

> **Note:** [Col. 0325D] “The English celebrated the Lord’s Easter at one time, the Scots at another.” Bede, *Ecclesiastical History of the English*, Book II, chapter 19: “Pope Honorius, he says, sent letters to the nation of the Scots, whom he had learned to be in error in their observance of holy Easter, earnestly exhorting them not to regard their small number, situated at the farthest ends of the earth, as wiser than the ancient or modern Churches of Christ throughout the world, nor, contrary to the paschal computations and decrees of the bishops in synods of the whole world, to celebrate a different Easter.” And Book III, chapter 25: “In these times there arose a frequent and serious question concerning the observance of Easter, those who had come from Kent or Gaul maintaining that the Scots celebrated the Lord’s day of Easter contrary to the custom of the universal Church.” Who these Scots and English were, and whence they were first brought into the island of Britain, we have already explained after William Camden in our *History of England and Scotland*.

We ourselves are witnesses in our own time: we see the Roman Church and the whole Latin world offering God the saving sacrifice of unleavened bread, while the Greek Church, the greater part of the East, and barbarian yet Christian peoples are said to offer sacrifice with leavened bread. Since this is so, neither ancients nor moderns have fallen away from mutual charity because of such celebrated and famous divergences of practice, because they have found in all this nothing that injured faith or charity. Why do I say this? So that if, brethren, your minds have become divided because of differing practices, if they have been made diverse by differences of custom, if they have grown sick in the charity of peace or unity because of one custom and another handed down to you by the founders of churches, they may return into one by the most venerable examples of so many Fathers and, in the manner of the saints who “were made strong out of weakness” and “became valiant in battle,” may recover from the alarming sickness of charity, a sickness worse than every disease.

But you will say: diversity of practices must be understood differently in different churches and differently among men of the same order. It is no wonder if the practices of many churches vary while faith and charity remain intact; but if persons of the same purpose and profession do not observe the same rule of institutions, that is surprising. Is this, I ask, the whole thing that separates you, beloved brethren, from one another? Is this the whole thing that wounds charity among you? Is this the whole thing that prevents sons of peace from being peaceable among themselves? If a layman was peaceable with those who hated peace, shall a monk fight a monk in an accursed duel? The son of light loves the sons of darkness lest the good of peace be disturbed; shall a son of light attack a son of light?—I refer this to their purpose, not to their monastic status.

If this truly is the whole of your indignation of mind, the whole wound to charity, it will be easily healed, provided obstinacy is absent. Take care, therefore, lest love of your own opinion darken the light of your understanding, because no one deserves to attain unity who defends not unity itself, but what he himself wishes. I therefore ask you, without party spirit and without concern to defend your own opinion, to examine whether this is a just cause of division; and when you recognize it as unjust, to unite your divided minds. For behold, you both serve under the same Rule, by whose special warfare each of you hopes to attain eternal salvation. If neither of you is disappointed in his hope, I do not know what room can now remain for discord, division, or reproach.

For you said it was surprising if persons of the same purpose and profession did not preserve the same rule of institutions. To this I reply: if persons of the same purpose and profession do not preserve the same rule of institutions, yet by different observances arrive at the same salvation and eternal life, what does it matter? What, indeed, does it matter or harm, if one comes by different paths to the same country, by many roads to the same life, by many journeys to the same Jerusalem above, which is our mother? For if you, Cluniac, knew that the Cistercian—or you, Cistercian, that the Cluniac—was in error in the profession he had undertaken, and perceived that he was tending, according to Scripture, by a way that seems right to men toward destruction, then, I confess, you would have just cause to correct, recall, or, if he refused to listen, rebuke and condemn your brother. Then indeed, if you spoke against him, contradicted him, even hated him, I would acknowledge that you judged justly and acted rightly; especially since I hear the great Prophet saying to God: “Do I not hate those who hate you, O Lord, and waste away because of your enemies? I hated them with perfect hatred; they became enemies to me” (Ps. 138).

Moreover, I would rejoice that you were not a deaf hearer of Scripture, which says: “Run, hasten, rouse your friend; give no sleep to your eyes, nor let your eyelids slumber” (Prov. 6); and: “Cursed is he who withholds his sword from blood” (Jer. 48). Then I would certainly admit that you had just grounds for hatred, and, girded myself with the sword of zeal, I would accompany you as an inseparable companion in your steps against the enemies of God and those who, according to the Apostle, “speak lies in hypocrisy” (1 Tim. 4). But now, when I see both of you, under the same [Rule], tending from earth to heaven through different yet holy institutions, and running by diverse paths toward the same prize in such a way that you may attain it, no cause remains for you, as it seems to me, for indignation, hatred, or reproach.

But you still require me to prove what I have said and to show how, under the same Rule or profession of the same Rule, a monk may safely proceed by different paths. To this my answer is very easy; and authority joined with reason is not lacking to establish that you, Cluniac, in your practice, and you, Cistercian, in your custom, can both run happily in the way of God’s commandments and arrive still more happily at the end due to your course. And since I have set first the authority which must always be put first in such matters, let it also come first in this discussion; nor let reason be separated from it by even a small interval.

But what do you object, brother? You say that those professing the same Rule do not observe the commandments of the same Rule alike. What you say is true: in certain chapters, those professing the same Rule observe the commandments of that Rule differently. But lest you think monks of this sort guilty on that account, lest you dare accuse them of transgression for this reason, hear the heavenly authority—indeed, the authority of the King of heaven: “If your eye is single, your whole body shall be full of light” (Luke 11). Hear also the Apostle: “Let all your things be done in charity” (1 Cor. 16). Hear Father Augustine: “Have charity, and do whatever you wish.” Hear the very writer of the Rule—indeed, the Holy Spirit, dictator of the Rule itself: “Let the abbot,” he says, “so temper and arrange all things that souls may be saved, and let what the brethren do be done without murmuring.”

What could be clearer, plainer, or more luminous? Does not the very serenity of the words show itself to be altogether without cloud and, with the veil of every cloud removed, reveal to mortals the brightest light of truth? Behold: the heavenly teacher instructs you, brother, that your whole body—that is, all your works—be bright through singleness of eye, the purity of your intention. Behold: after him the supreme teacher of the Church commands that everything of yours be done in charity. Behold: the greatest instructor of churches after the Apostles grants you power to do whatever you wish, provided charity remains. Behold: Benedict the Father himself, upon whom you rely, commands the abbot so to temper all things that souls are saved and murmuring is absent. And do you fear for the salvation of those who follow differing practices under the same Rule? Do you not see them as entirely secure from every danger, when, what is greater, the intention of saving souls in accordance with the Rule itself excuses their observances from every instability or fault arising from diversity?

But now, so that reason itself may be understood in every respect to serve the authorities set forth above and to adhere inseparably to them, let some chapters of the question at hand be added, in which certain changes may be shown to have been made with singleness of eye, sincere charity, and an intention to save souls. For once these have been shown, I think I shall leave you nothing further to seek in respect of the present matter.

For you employ a single eye when you do not open the entrance of the cloister to a novice until after a year, because, according to the Apostle and the words of the Rule, you investigate throughout a whole year whether the spirit of one newly arrived is from God. And you too employ a single eye when you receive one who arrives before the end of that year, because you fear that, delayed so long, he may return to his former dregs and the detestable evils of his previous life.

You employ a single eye when you are content with two tunics and two cowls, or with a few additional garments of the same kind, because, though not following a command, you preferred to follow the counsel or judgment of the writer of the Rule rather than add or adopt garments of another kind. And you too employ a single eye when you have admitted the use of moderate furs, because you have provided for the weak, the sick, the delicate—and, as concerns the colder regions of the earth, for everyone—lest they murmur, grow ill, or, when reasonable necessity is withheld, some should depart from their profession.

You employ a single eye when you receive returning fugitives only up to the third time, because you endeavor both to preserve the very words of the Rule and to deter foolish or unstable monks from frequent flight by finally denying them re-entry. And you too employ a single eye when you receive a monk returning more than three times, because you fear that, if pardon is denied, he may perish, exposed to enemies, and that the wolf—who is accustomed to seize and scatter even enclosed sheep—may destroy the wandering sheep.

You employ a single eye when you observe the regular fasts of both summer and winter without any exception, because you wish both to preserve them as they were handed down and to receive the more abundant fruit of a longer abstinence. But, speaking with a pure heart of charity, I do not altogether approve that fasts should be observed by anyone during the eight days of the Lord’s Nativity, on Epiphany, and on the Purification—days that are truly in every respect days of the Lord.

And you too employ a single eye when you exempt both the days I have named and every solemnity of twelve lessons from this practice of regular fasts, because you endeavor thus to honor the Lord himself, the Apostles, and certain other saints, and propose to imitate the practice of nearly all religious persons who fast in this manner.

You employ a single eye when you observe manual labor according to the Rule’s command, because you wish both to obey the Rule and, according to the sayings of that same Rule, to avoid idleness, the enemy of the soul, through such occupations—institutions not merely sacred and monastic but apostolic—and, insofar as resources permit, to provide necessities of life in accordance with the ancient Fathers. And you too employ a single eye when you have in part set aside this manual labor, because you are established not in forests or deserts but amid cities and fortified places, surrounded everywhere by people. You cannot go and return again and again for the sake of such work through a mixed multitude of both sexes without some—or great—danger; moreover, you generally do not possess suitable places in which you can undertake such labor.

But lest idleness, hostile to religious persons, find an opportunity to harm you when you are unoccupied, you either work with your hands where and when you can, or, where you cannot, make up for this manual labor by alternately varying it with the divine offices. Thus, lest an evil spirit claim for itself the house of your heart when vacant, you fill the whole time of your life with such sacred pursuits as you can.

You employ a single eye when, before all guests arriving or departing, you adore Christ with bowed head or with your whole body prostrate on the ground, and wash the feet of them all, because, as is fitting, you labor with the greatest care to cultivate the supreme good of hospitality according to the decrees of the Gospel and the Rule, and strive to secure for yourself a worthy reward by the performance of such holy kindness. And you too employ a single eye when you do not prostrate yourself before every guest and do not wash everyone’s feet, because it would be wholly impossible for you, before so great a multitude of constantly arriving guests, always to prostrate yourself on the ground and wash everyone’s feet—so impossible that, if you wished to attend to these things continually, even after neglecting all the other exercises of your order, you could not accomplish this alone. Since you omit what you see to be impossible for you, provide according to your ability what is necessary for receiving guests, and honor them as far as you can, you are excused by singleness of eye from the things already mentioned which you cannot perform.

You employ a single eye when you wish the abbot’s table always to be with guests and pilgrims, because you seem both to obey the Rule and to minister more humanely to guests. And you too employ a single eye when you decree that the abbot’s table shall not always be with guests but always with the brethren, because you remedy the extravagance, to speak mildly, of many abbots who, indulgent to themselves on the pretext of guests, were accustomed to be cruel toward their own men, by bringing him back to the common table.

You employ a single eye when, as Ezra restored the Law and as the Maccabees restored the ruins of God’s Temple, you labor to repair the many damages of monastic order and the many ruins, in many monasteries, of the conduct of many people; and, driving out concessions made for refinement rather than necessity, strive to recall the lukewarmness of our times to the practice of ancient and original fervor. And you too employ a single eye when you moderate both the commands of the Rule and those of the order in such a way that, in the words of the same Rule, “the strong may desire more and the weak not draw back”; that one who cannot subsist on bread may at least be nourished with milk lest he lose his life; and that one who cannot reach the proposed prize by breathless running may be taught at least to attain it by a slow step—for the man who returns to his homeland after a year is called no less its inhabitant than the one who returns after a month.

Yet I say this while preserving the difference in the labours of those who travel, because, in the Apostle’s words, “Each shall receive his own reward according to his own labour” (1 Cor. 3). You have Benedict as the author of this your undertaking; although, where charity commands, you are by his own testimony in no way compelled to follow his writings, you nevertheless take praiseworthy delight in following them out of devotion, because they seemed fitting to so great a man [Col. 0330D]. You also have the same Benedict as the author of your institutions, who directs that all his writings be brought to the end of charity and serve the salvation of souls in whatever way, by this order or that. You have also Maurus, the chief disciple among his disciples, who, sent by him into Gaul, is said to have altered some—or many—points of his Rule with the intention mentioned above. You have, after him, many Fathers of monasteries, whom both their outstanding lives and the innumerable miracles wrought by God through them, both during their lives and after their deaths, make clearer than light to have been moved by the Spirit of God, according to times, places, and persons, to adapt the prescriptions of the aforesaid Rule. And what more need I say? Following the same principle through all the remaining chapters which appear different [Col. 0331A], you will everywhere find the single eye which one calls charity and another the intention of saving souls; and thus you will find nothing different, nothing discordant, since all things are made one by charity in matters that appear to be observed in varying ways.

To these points I add—for it is evident to everyone—that scarcely anything of this sort is prescribed in the Rule without some qualifying condition and without being expressed subject to the abbot’s discretion. Even if it had been stated imperatively, it could in no way prejudice the single eye, that is, evangelical charity. For such matters, as you know, belong to the class of changeable precepts, and, when charity commands, they must be changed without any fear of transgression. Nor should a departure from the Rule be suspect in this respect to those professed under the Rule [Col. 0331B], because the Rule of that holy Father depends upon that lofty and universal Rule of charity, from which and in which, according to the words of Truth, “the whole law and the prophets hang” (Matt. 22). And if the whole Law hangs there, then so does the law of his Rule. Therefore the monk who professes the Rule of Father Benedict truly keeps it when, whether he retains or changes any of its chapters, he everywhere preserves the law of charity.

What then? If this was indeed, brothers, the entire cause of your mutual disagreement, does it not now seem wholly removed? Should not the hearts of monks now be united in fraternal peace, when simple charity has made one those diverse practices for which they had been torn apart? Does it not make many things one, bringing those who pursue diverse but good things under the one purpose of monastic order or of a single Rule to the one appointed end of the highest good or eternal life? “Let peace be in your strength, O Jerusalem, that abundance may follow in your towers” (Ps. 121). But lest perhaps we be found among those who say, “Peace, peace,” when there is no peace (Jer. 6), let us examine whether some cause of separation still remains, lest, while we sleep secure, a serpent suddenly leap from its den and bite one among ours or yours who is resting incautiously.

Perhaps these garments of different colours furnish an incentive to discord, and the manifold variety of garments likewise produces variety of minds. For, as I see almost continually, and as all who look even carelessly can very easily observe [Col. 0331D], a black monk, if he happens to meet a white one, looks at him with a sidelong, hostile eye; a white monk barely looks at a black one with half his eye, and only when the latter forces himself upon his notice. I have seen many among the black-clad—nor can I remember how often—laughing at a white-clad man they met as though he were a monster, and signalling in voice or bodily gesture that they were amazed, as if a chimera, a centaur, or some strange prodigy had presented itself to their eyes. Conversely, I have seen white monks who had first been talkative and exchanging many observations with one another fall suddenly silent at the arrival of any black-clad monk, protecting themselves by the remedy of silence as though enemies were probing the secrets of enemies.

I have watched the tongues of both kinds of men silent, while their eyes, hands, and feet spoke; and what they did not wish to indicate by voice lest they betray themselves [Col. 0332A], they proclaimed more clearly through the support of gestures: a mute voice, eloquent limbs; and, in a perverse reversal of nature’s order, stones crying out while men were silent toward men. Often, on seeing such things, I recalled that saying of Solomon, in which he describes a similar kind of person: “He winks with his eyes, scrapes with his foot, speaks with his finger, devises evil with a perverse heart, and at every time stirs up quarrels” (Prov. 4).

O evil and obstinate counsel of the wicked angel cast down from God, who, unwilling to perish alone from eternal peace, acquires companions in his destruction from every quarter; and who, that he may rejoice in a more glorious trophy, strives by the violent impulse of his wickedness to overthrow the cedars or fir trees of the paradise of God, of which he himself was once an inhabitant! He grieves that the palm of heresies has perished to him, by which in former times [Col. 0332B] he used to divide the Church of God; and, seeing that he can no longer injure the faith in any way, because the Spirit of God has filled the whole world with that faith, he directs all his effort toward injuring mutual charity. For because he can no longer persuade Christian people to become unbelievers, he works with all his might to prevent them from loving one another. The sects of Arius, Sabellius, Novatus, Donatus, Pelagius, and of the more ancient, execrable Manichaeus have now perished; the mists of innumerable heretics, which overshadowed the light of faith, have vanished at the breath of God’s Spirit and have left us a clear day with every darkness removed.

But the African whirlwind which succeeded them strives suddenly to throw everything into confusion; and because it recognizes that faith has prevailed [Col. 0332C], it seeks to compensate for its former losses by injuring charity. But, leaving aside lamentation, let me return my pen to the matter with which I began. Why does the blackness of your brother, O white monk—not of his mind, but of his clothing—seem detestable to you? Why does the whiteness of your brother, O black monk—not of his mind, but of his clothing—seem astonishing to you? Are not both of you among the sheep of that Shepherd who says: “My sheep hear my voice, and I, the Lord, know them, and they follow me; and I give them eternal life, and they shall not perish for ever, and no one shall snatch them from my hand” (John 10)? And what shepherd—let alone God, even a man—has ever disputed about the differently coloured fleeces of his sheep? Who has ever complained? Who has ever judged his white sheep to be more his own than his black sheep, or his black sheep more his own than his white? Who has ever attended not to whether they were black or white, but to whether, black or white, they belonged to his same flock?

O human malice! O innocence of cattle! O substance created in brute animals, steadfast in its original nature! O nature perverted in the rational animal! When did a white ram ever disdain a black one? What black ewe ever detested a white one? Do they not fill the shepherds’ folds together, peaceably, and altogether quietly, without any question about their many colours and without any disturbance? Certainly, a ram sometimes attacks another ram with its horns, and a ewe strikes another ewe with repeated blows; but it is not variety of colour that incites the rams or ewes to battle: rather, anger innate in all animals and stirred up in whatever way provokes them [Col. 0333A]. Yet now, as I see, man—more foolish than cattle—“being in honour, does not understand”; and, what is more grievous, the monk, diversified by diverse colour, separates himself from the unity of charity.

Do not, I beg you, brother—do not, if you wish to be a sheep of Christ—complain about a varied fleece. That Shepherd casts no one from his fold except the person whom not difference of colour, but injury to faith or charity separates from the flock of his sheep. He does not, I say, separate anyone from his fold on account of colour: he who gathered together in the one fold of Christian faith both Jew and Gentile, from regions so remote and religions so diverse. Perhaps this was also taught by the patience of that holy patriarch Jacob, who bore with equanimity the wage changed ten times by Laban, and showed, while feeding a multicoloured flock with the same spirit and care of a good shepherd, that white, black, and variegated cattle were no different.

And since the Apostle says, “In Christ Jesus neither circumcision avails anything nor uncircumcision, but a new creation” (Gal. 5), and elsewhere, “Where there is neither Gentile nor Jew, circumcision nor uncircumcision, barbarian nor Scythian, slave nor free, but Christ is all and in all” (Col. 3) [Col. 0333B], what childish mind could be so foolish as to suppose that, if the new creation in Christ is preserved, either the colour of different garments or a differing customary practice makes any difference with respect to salvation? And if it makes no difference with respect to salvation, why does varied colour of dress separate monks? Why does it generate schism, divide minds, injure charity? There is no cause, no reason whatever—not, I do not say, for hating; not, I do not say, for dividing; but not even for grumbling—about these things.

You have an adequate defender of your whiteness: the single eye of your conscience, as I said above. So that, after black had long been established through custom, people might not suppose that a monk could exist only under that dark colour, you put on a white cowl and tunic; and because under the black habit you saw innumerable members of this order grown lukewarm toward their purpose, you laudably wished by this hitherto unusual whiteness of clothing to stir them to a greater and new fervour of monastic religion. You too have an equally credible author for your blackness: the long-established custom handed down from the Fathers [Col. 0333C], by following ancient things rather than devising new ones you believe yourself safer.

Each of you has an invincible defender of your respective colour in the voice of the common Rule itself, which commands monks not to dispute over the colour or coarseness of their garments, but to use garments of such colour or quality as can either be found more readily or acquired more cheaply in the province where they live. Therefore the reason mentioned above, or perhaps some greater reason still unknown to me, protects your whiteness. Paternal authority protects your blackness, an authority equal in weight to every argument and one which no person of sound judgement ought to consider inferior.

What example of a Father can I adduce for this purpose? Whom could I find greater than the great Martin? That great Martin, I say—the monk and bishop Martin—consecrated the colour of black garments by wearing them himself. Concerning this, his Life says: “When the animals close by him saw him wrapped in a black and flowing cloak, they were frightened and withdrew a little to the other side.” That he was a monk is attested by the monastery which he built not far from Poitiers, the monastery at Milan, and the monastery which he built for himself at Tours. Behold Martin the monk; behold Martin clothed in black garments. But what does Jerome write of such matters in his letter to Nepotian? “Avoid,” he says, “dark garments as much as white ones” [Col. 0334A]. That is, he warned him to avoid pride or self-display, not only in white clothes, which secular people used more at that time, but also in dark ones, which religious professed persons of that age customarily wore.

On this subject the admirable Paulinus, bishop of Nola, contemporary and friend of the already mentioned Martin, Ambrose, Augustine, and Jerome, and often praised by them as well as by the great pope Gregory, describes the journey of a most noble woman recently converted to the purpose of monastic religion. In a letter addressed to Sulpicius Severus he writes:

> We saw the glory of the Lord in that journey of mother and sons—indeed in it, but in a manner of dress far different. She sat upon a lean donkey of poorer sort, while all the pomp of this world attended her, with senators, honoured and wealthy, able to surround her in splendour: the Appian Way groaned and shone with swaying carriages, harnessed horses, gilded litters, and many wagons. But before the splendours of vanity shone the grace of Christian humility. The rich marvelled at holy poverty, while our poverty laughed at them. We saw a confusion of this world worthy of God: purple, silk, and gilded furnishings serving old and black garments. We blessed the Lord, who makes the humble exalted, fills the hungry with good things, and sends the rich away empty.

Behold: not only men of ancient religious profession, but also women who undertook a purpose of holiness are recorded as having worn black garments [Col. 0334C]. For, to confess what I think, it seemed to those great Fathers, as it seems to me, that this black colour in question was more suited to humility, repentance, and mourning. Since a monk ought especially to devote his whole life to these pursuits, they decreed that colour might be joined, insofar as possible, in kinship with morals and garments with virtues.

For white garments were of old a sign rather of glory than lowliness, of joy rather than sorrow—as the Church itself interprets them, as all know—and both the angel of the risen Christ and the angels who announced the Lord’s ascension showed this. The Saviour himself likewise appeared radiant in snowy clothing in the glory of his Transfiguration. Thus the good and learned Sidonius, bishop of Auvergne, sharply ridiculing the faults of certain persons, says among other attacks upon them: “They go white-clad to an abbot’s funeral, and dark-clad to weddings,” showing that they were so confused in conduct and practice that they perversely exchanged funeral dress for wedding dress and wedding dress for funeral dress [Col. 0335A]. For those who observed the common custom of that time went not white-clad to funerals and dark-clad to weddings, but white-clad to weddings and dark-clad to funerals, so that the white attire matched nuptial joy and the dark attire funeral mourning.

I myself, while recently in Spain, saw and marvelled that this ancient custom is still observed by all Spaniards. When a wife dies, her husband; when a husband dies, his wife; when children die, their parents; when parents die, their children; when any relatives die, their relatives; when friends perish by any mischance, their friends—at once lay aside their ornaments, throw off silken clothing and coverings of exotic furs, wholly renounce every variegated and costly dress, and cover themselves only in black and humble garments. Cutting short their own hair and the tails of their beasts of burden, they render both themselves and the animals entirely black. With such emblems of mourning and grief they lament those dear ones taken from them, and by public law spend at least a full year in this mourning.

With such great authority and argument I satisfy you and your colour, black monk; yet I do not therefore condemn the white man’s whiteness [Col. 0335B]. You are praised because you do not wish to depart from the holy custom of your Fathers; he too is praised because, through the unfamiliar whiteness of his garments, he thereby increasingly stirs the fervour of his own mind in its holy purpose. By such colour he distinguishes himself in a way, not from common charity—which would be wicked—but from the universally known lukewarmness of many in this order.

Therefore, since you live under one Shepherd, Jesus Christ; since you dwell in the one fold of the Church; since you live by one faith and hope of eternal things—why, white monk and black monk alike, do you, to speak somewhat sharply, quarrel like the most foolish sheep over your differing fleeces? Why do you provoke one another for so empty—indeed, so foolish—a reason? Why, on so childish an occasion, do you tear the first robe of charity? Why do you separate your very dwellings? Why do you bite one another, no longer with a sheep’s tooth but a wolf’s? Why do you slander? Why do you rend?

See to it; beware lest the name of innocence by which you are called sheep should place you not among those whom the supreme Shepherd will set at his right hand, and of whom he says: “My sheep hear my voice, and I, the Lord, know them, and they follow me, and I give them eternal life, and they shall not perish for ever” (John 10) [Col. 0335D], but—far be it!—among those of whom it is written and sung: “They are set as sheep in hell; death shall feed upon them” (Ps. 48). Do you still see that it is foolish to dispute about colour; damnable to hate a brother because of colour; utterly evil to slander a brother because of colour? If this was the whole cause of your mutual division, the only material of so great a separation—if, I say, it was the sole and whole occasion of monastic schism—then, now that it has been refuted by so many arguments, will not the old rupture of your hearts be healed? Will not injured charity be cured? Will not evangelical peace return to the children of peace?

Make satisfaction, therefore, to peace, children of peace, and enter with it into an everlasting covenant, lest, if it should be otherwise, that most dreadful sentence of the prophet may one day be pronounced even against you: “There is no peace, says my God, for the wicked” (Isa. 48) [Col. 0336A]. And now, thanks be to God, I thought that I had penetrated the ancient causes and hiding places of hatred among certain men of our order, and that no further object of anxious thought remained for me to seek. If the matter stands thus, then you, white monk, will not assail the black-clad; nor you, black monk, the white-clad, if you are willing to observe what has been said above; nor will you be moved from the state of highest charity against a brother because of a differing customary practice or the so often mentioned variety of colour.

But what have I said? How have I gone out of my mind? Where is my mind’s understanding? Whence comes this darkened power of sight? I thought I had found every source of scandal; I supposed that I had uncovered every hiding place of hatred. As I said, I suspected that diversity of customs alone, variety in colours, the quality or quantity of garments or foods, had wounded charity among monks, and that this alone was the cause of so great an evil. I saw the speck in my brother’s eye, but could not see the enormous beam and mighty oak in my own eye or in his [Col. 0336B]. But now that my eye has been made clear, the day serene, and the noonday sun permits nothing to remain hidden, I see—I see, I say—what I may say with everyone’s permission, indeed what I am certain I may say with the approval of all good people. For whoever is angered will confess that it has been said of himself, as Jerome says. The sound part of the body does not reject the physician’s hand; but that part which tremblingly withdraws itself from the probing fingers shows beyond doubt that a disease lies hidden within.

What, then, had escaped me? Speak—speak, I say—you, that I may first address the person involved in my purpose. Speak, black monk; give glory to God, and reveal what still lies hidden in the depths of your heart against your brother. “Who,” you ask, “can endure that new men should be preferred to old, their pursuits put above our deeds, ourselves considered of less account and them more dear? Who can look with an impartial eye upon the world turning away in its greater part from our ancient order toward their new undertaking, abandoning paths worn by centuries and crowding to trails hitherto unknown? Who can endure new men preferred to old, younger to elder, white monks to black monks?” This, I say, is what you, black monk, say.

But what do you, white monk, advance? “Happy are we,” you say, “whom a far more commendable institution recommends; whom the world proclaims more blessed than other monks; whose reputation obscures the esteem of others, whose day their lamp, whose sun their star. We are restorers of a ruined religious life, revivers of a dead order, most just condemnors of languishing, lukewarm, foully negligent monks. We, set apart from the rest in morals, deeds, practices, and garments, have exposed the lukewarmness of the old and demonstrate the surpassing excellence of our new fervour” [Col. 0336D].

Behold, behold the true cause—more hidden, yet far more hostile to charity than the others—which tore apart the unity of your minds, separated your very houses from one another, and, as the Prophet says, so often sharpened your tongues like a sword for slanderous or abusive words [Col. 0337A]. Let the deadly sword be blunted by the sword of the divine word. And if you are wise, take care lest the fruits gathered by so great exertions be scattered by the light wind of empty glory.

O loss most wretched and most to be lamented! What if one wicked hiss of the serpent should scatter the spotless continence of your very long life, your invincible obedience, unbroken fasts, continual vigils, such a heavy yoke of discipline, so many palms of patience—in short, to gather many things into few words, labours so great and countless, no longer for earthly but for heavenly life—which by God’s grace you have accumulated through so many years as provision for eternity? What if the ancient dragon, by emptying you with a single breath, should render you empty before the sight of the supreme Judge?

And where is what the Saviour said to disciples still suffering from this disease: “I saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven” (Luke 10)? Where is what he says elsewhere, when a similar dispute had arisen among them concerning which of them seemed to be greatest: “But you are not so; rather, let the greater among you become as the younger, and the leader as the servant” (Luke 22)? Where, hidden from the eyes of memory, is that saying of him who is lofty and great, “whose greatness has no end,” according to the Psalm (Ps. 144), and who, according to the Apostle, is “God over all, blessed for ever” (Rom. 9): not setting himself above or comparing himself with his servants, but humbling himself, he goes on to say, “But I am in the midst of you as one who serves” (Luke 22) [Col. 0337B].

An apostle is rebuked lest he prefer himself to an apostle, and will a monk not be rebuked lest he prefer himself to monks? By Christ the Teacher, the greater is placed below the lesser disciple, the superior below the inferior—and shall I, a Cluniac, attempt to raise myself above a Cistercian? Christ himself submits to his disciples, and shall a Christian and monk raise a neck swollen with pride above a brother perhaps far better than himself? Majesty lowers itself, and weakness boasts? Loftiness humbles itself, and rottenness exalts itself? God serves, and clay strives to rule? And how, brother, have you fallen from the degree of your Rule to which you boasted you had ascended: that a monk should declare himself inferior and more contemptible than all, not only with his tongue but also believe it in his innermost heartfelt disposition?

Why labour further? There is no need to press the point more sharply upon religious, wise, learned people, nor, as the saying goes, to teach Minerva, or carry wood to the forest, or water to rivers or the sea. The wisdom of you both understands and acknowledges that, just as it is impossible to please God without faith, so it is impossible without charity; and that no one who has cast humility aside can retain that same charity by any effort whatever. For where humility withdraws, pride necessarily succeeds; where pride succeeds, envy immediately arrives; where envy arises, charity at once dies. The envious person cannot love the person he envies, nor can charity in any way remain in one who does not love [Col. 0338A]. Accordingly, where charity is absent, humility is absent; and where humility is absent, charity too is absent. The Apostle teaches this clearly when he says: “Charity does not envy, does not behave improperly, is not ambitious” (1 Cor. 13). And because it is not even covetous of another’s possessions, he adds: “It does not seek its own things” (ibid.).

Charity therefore excludes every swelling of pride, every ambition, every desire, every greed; indeed, through charity, according to what follows in the Apostle, all iniquity is expelled together. Now, if you, brother of Cluny, brother of Cîteaux, wish to preserve whole this charity which the same Apostle calls the law of Christ; if through it you wish to lay up for yourself the greatest treasures in heaven, and to preserve those that have been laid up [Col. 0338B], devote all the effort you can. Drive away from yourself causes which, I do not say, put charity to flight, nor, I do not say, kill it, but even slightly injure it. If, when expelled, they desire to return, shut the door of your steadfast breast against their return, and hold fast with the whole embrace of your holy soul this everlasting fellow-dweller.

Charity, firmly retained, will raise you to the kingdom of heaven; it was charity’s overwhelming and sweet power that bent the King of heaven down to earth. The Apostle is a faithful witness to this, saying that because of his exceeding charity God sent his Son “in the likeness of sinful flesh” (Rom. 8). You will rejoice eternally before God through charity, and your joy, as he himself promised, “no one shall take from you” (John 16), when God is all in all (1 Cor. 15). When shall you be satisfied from your long hunger? When his glory has been revealed. When you appear, you shall be like him, and through this charity, eternally united to him, you shall see him as he is (1 John 3) [Col. 0338C].

At last, my dearest one, let my pen return to you, to whom this present letter is sent, so that it may perhaps end in you its unwelcome lengthiness, as it took its beginning from you. As I declared above, with conscience as witness, my sole cause for writing has truly been charity: that, so far as concerns both of us, I might compel it to grow warm again through the breath of our conversation and to burst forth in its accustomed—or greater—flames of mutual affection. It remains for you, whom supreme providence has prepared as a milky and strong pillar upon which the edifice of the monastic order rests, and who, like a radiant star, have in our time conspicuously bestowed light by example and word not merely upon monks but upon the whole Latin Church [Col. 0338D]—it remains, I say, that you devote all the effort you can to this divine work, and no longer permit the great congregations of one name and order to disagree.

I have always endeavoured to commend those holy monks of your congregation to our brethren and, if possible, to unite them to the latter even in the deepest inward bond of perfect charity. I have not neglected to do this publicly, privately, and in the great assemblies of our people; and I have laboured, by means available to me, to eradicate that rust of envy and hostile zeal which ordinarily gnaws secretly at the inner organs. You too, by the great grace granted you by God [Col. 0339A], attend to the common field: just as no one after you has been found in our age to have planted more useful things in it, so, by praiseworthy zeal and industry, let everything contrary to what is sufficiently useful be uprooted. With that lofty eloquence aflame from the Spirit of God, expel from their hearts—if I may speak mildly—that childish rivalry; expel whispering from their tongue; and in place of these, whether they will or no, implant brotherly love.

Let difference in practices and variety of colours no longer separate your flocks from ours. Rather, let charity, derived from the highest unity, repair what has collapsed, restore what has been torn apart, make one what has been divided, and unite all things. Yes, this is fitting: that those who have one Lord, one faith, one baptism; whom one Church contains; whom one eternal and blessed life awaits—should likewise, according to Scripture, have “one heart and one soul” (Acts 4) [Col. 0339B].

I have sent to my gem-like friend a jewel of salt, whose bodily use I once heard was beneficial to you, and whose special meaning I thought necessary to the matters written above. For however many and precious the arrangements of their virtues which they bring to the table of the eternal King, if they bring them without the salt of brotherly love, they will be rejected as tasteless; if they season them with this salt, the now pleasing dishes will be accepted along with those who offer them. For he who accepts no sacrifice without salt in his Law shows that no offering of virtue is pleasing to him without such seasoning.

I have also sent our new translation disputing against the utterly wicked heresy of Mahomet.

> **Note:** [Col. 0339D] “I have sent our new translation against the utterly wicked heresy of Mahomet.” He also mentions this translation in the *Brief Summary of the Saracen Sect*, which we have now for the first time appended to this edition from the *Koran*. There he gives the reason why he undertook to translate that sect from Arabic into Latin, and promises, God helping, to refute it in writing as well, should his great occupations permit. The author of the *Chronicle of Cluny* testifies that he did so in five books. [Col. 0340D] Yet because, despite our diligence, we have not so far been able to obtain these books, it seems most opportune here to provide at least their summaries, arranged by chapters, which came to our knowledge a few days ago, from another Chronicle of Cluny. Lord Martène published the first two little books of the work *Against the Sect of the Saracens*, prefacing them with the chapter-headings of four books. See below.

This translation, while I was lately staying in Spain, was rendered from the Arabic language into Latin through my efforts. I had it translated by a man skilled in both languages, Master Peter of Toledo. But because Latin was not as familiar or known to him as Arabic, I gave him as an assistant a learned man, my beloved son and brother Peter, our notary, well known, I think, to Your Reverence. Polishing and arranging the Latin words which the former had for the most part expressed inelegantly or confusedly, he completed this letter—or rather little book—which, I believe, will be very useful to many because of its information about unfamiliar matters [Col. 0339C].

My purpose in having it translated was to follow the custom of the Fathers, who never passed over in silence any heresy of their own times, however slight, so to speak, but resisted it with all the forces of faith and showed by writings and disputations that it was to be detested and condemned [Col. 0339D]. I wished to do this concerning this chief error of errors, this dregs of all heresies, into which have flowed the remnants of every diabolical sect that has arisen since the coming of the Saviour [Col. 0340A], so that, just as nearly half the world is known to be infected by its deadly plague, so those who do not know may recognize, once its folly and turpitude have been exposed, how execrable and deserving of contempt it is.

By reading, you yourselves will recognize—and, as I suppose, rightly lament—that through such impious and most abject filth so great a part of humankind has been deceived and, even after the grace of the Redeemer, so lightly turned away from its Creator through the sect of a most foul man. I do not indeed fail to know that this writing, which could not benefit those lost people in their own language, will benefit them less when translated into Latin. But perhaps it will benefit some Latins: it will instruct them about things unknown to them, and by attacking and overcoming it will show how condemnable is the heresy which has reached their ears.

And so that nothing of this condemnable sect might remain hidden from our people, I had their entire law, which in their own language they call *Alcoram* or *Alcyren*, translated in full and in order [Col. 0340B]. If a word-for-word translation is made, *Alcoran* or *Alcyren* means “a collection of precepts,” which that wicked man falsely claimed had been sent down to him piecemeal from heaven. I further had translated certain of his tales involving a Jew named Abdias and other Jews; by unheard-of ravings and phantasms like dreams, these make the sect, beyond all his other impious writings, an object of ridicule even to cattle. But because the matter is extensive and, owing to the barbarity of the language, for the most part difficult to understand, I shall briefly say who this man was and what he taught [Col. 0340C].

For some think that he was that Nicholas who was one of the first seven deacons, and that the sect called after him the Nicolaitans, also named in the Apocalypse, is the law of these modern Saracens. Others dream other things; and, being careless in reading and ignorant of events, as in other instances, they imagine every sort of falsehood.

He lived in the time of the emperor Heraclius, shortly after the time of the great and first Gregory, bishop of Rome, nearly five hundred and fifty years ago: an Arab by nationality, low-born, a worshipper of the ancient idolatry, uneducated and almost wholly without letters; energetic in secular affairs and possessed of great cunning, he rose from obscurity and poverty to wealth and fame. As he gradually increased in power, repeatedly harassing all his neighbors, and especially his nearest blood-relations, by treachery, plunder, and raids—killing secretly those whom he could kill secretly, and openly those whom he could kill openly—he magnified the terror inspired by himself; and, often victorious in encounters, he began to aspire to kingship over his people. But when he saw that all alike resisted him and despised his low birth, and that he could not attain by this route what he hoped for, he attempted to become king, since he could not do so by force of the sword, under the veil of religion and in the name of a divine prophet. And because he lived a barbarian among barbarians, an idolater among idolaters, and among people whom he knew to be, above all nations, destitute of and ignorant of both divine and human law, and therefore easy to lead whither he wished, he began to pursue the iniquity he had conceived. And because he had heard that the prophets of God had been great men, he began publicly to proclaim everywhere that he was God’s prophet.

Meanwhile, by the judgment of Him who is called terrible in His counsels over the children of men, who has mercy on whom He wills and hardens whom He wills, Satan gave success to the error and sent Sergius, a monk and follower of the heretic Nestorius, expelled from the Church, into those regions of Arabia; and he joined the heretical monk to the false prophet. Thus Sergius, joined to Mahomet, supplied what he lacked; and he expounded the sacred Scriptures, both Old Testament and New, partly as he saw fit, according to the interpretation of his master Nestorius, who denied that our Saviour was God. Turning him away from idolatry, he made him a Nestorian Christian. And, so that the full measure of iniquity might flow together in Mahomet and nothing might be lacking to destroy himself and others, Jews were joined to the heretic. Cunningly taking care that he should not become a true Christian, the Jews whispered into the ears of this man greedy for novelties not the truth of the holy Scriptures but their own fables, in which they abound even now.

Thus Mahomet, instructed by these excellent teachers, Jews and heretics, composed his Alcoran, weaving together in his barbarous manner an impious writing made up alike of Jewish tales and the foolish ditties of heretics. He falsely claimed that it had been brought to him gradually, in volumes, by Gabriel, whose name he had by then learned from holy Scripture; and he infected a people ignorant of God with a deadly draught. Like such men, he smeared honey on the rim of the cup, while deadly poison followed; and he destroyed, alas, both the souls and bodies of the wretched people. This thoroughly impious man acted thus when, praising both the Jewish and Christian law yet asserting that neither ought to be kept, he rejected them by approving them—reprobate that he was.

Hence he affirms that Moses was an excellent prophet, that Christ the Lord was greater than all; he proclaims that Christ was born of a Virgin and acknowledges Him as God’s messenger, God’s Word, and God’s Spirit—yet he neither understands nor confesses messenger, Word, and Spirit as we do. That He should be called or believed the Son of God, he utterly ridicules. Measuring the eternal birth of the Son of God by the analogy of human generation, like a bovine-minded man, he denies and mocks with all his might that God could either beget or be begotten. Repeatedly he maintains the resurrection of the flesh and does not deny that the common judgment at the end of the age will be carried out not by Christ but by God. Yet he madly asserts that Christ, as Lord of all, and he himself, for the protection of his own people, will be present at that judgment. He describes the torments of hell as he pleased and as befitted a great false prophet to devise. Paradise he portrays not as the fellowship of angels, the vision of God, or that supreme good which eye has not seen, ear has not heard, nor has entered into the human heart (1 Cor. 2), but truly as the sort of place flesh and blood—indeed, the dregs of flesh and blood—desired, and as he wished to have prepared for himself. There he promises his followers the eating of meat and fruits of every kind; streams of milk, honey, and glittering waters; and embraces and sensual pleasures with most beautiful women and virgins—things in which his entire paradise comes to its end. Amid these matters, vomiting up the dregs of almost all ancient heresies that he had swallowed at the devil’s instigation, he denies the Trinity with Sabellius, rejects Christ’s divinity with his master Nestorius, and denies the Lord’s death with Manichaeus, though he does not deny His return to heaven.

Teaching his people such things and similar doctrines—not unto salvation but unto ruin—he turned them utterly away from God. And so that the evangelical word might have no further place among them, as though they knew all that belongs to the Gospel and to Christ, he blocked the entrance of their hearts with an iron bar of impiety. Moreover, he decreed that circumcision, supposedly derived from Ishmael, the father of that people, must be observed. Above all, so as more easily to attract the carnal minds of men to himself, he loosened the reins of gluttony and lust. Having eighteen wives at once, and committing adultery with the wives of many others as though by divine answer, he attached to himself, as though by prophetic example, a greater number of the damned. Yet, lest he be exposed as wholly dishonorable, he commends almsgiving and certain works of mercy, praises prayers, and so is monstrous from every side: as the poet says, he joins a horse’s neck and birds’ feathers to a human head (Horace, *The Art of Poetry*). Since, at the urging of the monk already mentioned and of the aforesaid Jews, he both abandoned idolatry and persuaded whomsoever he could to abandon it; since he preached that one God, the multiplicity of gods having been discarded, must be worshipped—he seemed to say unheard-of things to rustic and ignorant people. And because this preaching agreed with their reasoning, they first believed him to be a prophet of God; then, as time and error advanced, they elevated him to the kingship he had desired.

Thus mixing good with evil and confusing truth with falsehood, he sowed seeds of error; and in part during his own time, but in part—and especially—after his time, he produced a wicked harvest to be burned in eternal fire. For when the Roman Empire was at once languishing, indeed almost failing, and He by whom kings reign permitted it, the dominion of Arabs or Saracens infected with this pest arose. Gradually occupying by armed force the greatest parts of Asia, together with all Africa and part of Spain, it transmitted both its empire and its error to those subjected to it. Although I call these people heretics because they believe some things in common with us while differing from us in more matters, perhaps I should more correctly call them pagans or heathens—which is worse—because, though they say some true things about the Lord, they preach more false things, and share in neither baptism, sacrifice, penance, nor any Christian sacrament—a thing which no heretic except these has ever done.

I have set down as briefly as I could the life of the man and the outline of his impious law. I did this in order both to make the matter known to you and to encourage you to write against so destructive an error. For although, as I said above, a response may, I think, be unable to benefit those lost people, nevertheless the Christian arsenal ought to possess an answer worthy of the matter, against this heresy as against others. If anyone should call such a work superfluous because those against whom they ought to resist are not present, armed with such weapons, let him know that in the commonwealth of a great king some things are done for defense, some for adornment, and some for both.

Thus Solomon the Peaceful made weapons for defense, though they were less necessary in his own time; David prepared resources and ornaments designated for the construction and adornment of the divine Temple. Yet these did not benefit anyone in his time, but passed after his time into divine uses. They therefore remained unused for some time; but when necessity pressed, things long idle became useful. Nor, in my view, ought this work even now be called idle, because, according to the Apostle, it belongs to you and to all learned men to oppose, destroy, and trample down, with every diligence, in speech and writing, every form of knowledge that exalts itself against the height of God (2 Cor. 10). Even if those who err cannot be converted by this means, a learned man—or teacher—if he has zeal for righteousness, ought at least not neglect to provide and take thought for the weak members of the Church, who are accustomed to be scandalized or secretly disturbed even by slight causes.

I set before you all the Fathers, and especially Father Augustine. Although he could not convert Julian the Pelagian or Faustus the Manichaean to the true faith by either his words or his labor, he nevertheless did not fail to compose great volumes against their error. Acting similarly against the other heretics of his own time and of times not his own, against Jews, and against pagans, he not only armed the people of his own age against them, but also transmitted to us and to all posterity a gift of the greatest edification and instruction. Therefore, if your Reverence has the will to labor in these matters, God inspiring it—for the ability cannot be lacking through His grace—write back, and we shall send the book that we have not yet sent, so that through your mouth, filled with His praise, the gracious Spirit may answer the spirit of wickedness and may enrich the treasures of His Church with the storehouses of your wisdom.

Please send, through the bearer of this letter or another, that letter of yours, as I think addressed to certain monks of Chartres, responding concerning the precepts of the Rule and the various observances of the monastic order. I read it once at Cluny but have never afterward been able to obtain it for rereading. I too would have sent to your learned charity the work of ours which I wrote four or five years ago against certain articles of the provincial heretics, had I had it at hand, so that you might read it and, should anything require addition, supply it in some treatise or letter of your own. But it was recently carried by one of our brothers into Auvergne, and a year ago I sent it to Provence in another volume against those same heretics; thus it could not be sent to you. It will be sent after I have recopied it from some exemplar. Write back concerning what seems good to you in all these matters. And although I, hindered by many impediments, have delayed, you, if you have the opportunity, do not delay long.

## Letter XVIII. To the universal pontiff and particular Father of the Church of Cluny, Lord Pope Celestine

[Note: To Lord Pope Celestine. The second of that name, elected in the year 1144.]

Brother Peter, humble abbot of the Cluniacs, sends sincere love and complete obedience.

[Col. 0344B]

Blessed be the Lord our God, who, mindful of His word in which He gave us hope, has shown even in this time, according to His custom, that He has in no way forgotten the words by which, departing from His own, He deigned to console them: “Behold, I am with you always, even unto the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28). This appears in the innumerable gifts of His grace; it appears now especially in you, whom divine goodness favorable to mortals has granted in these days as supreme pontiff, guardian of our souls, and bishop of His whole Church still wandering on earth—that is, of the one dove groaning among ravens.

This was not brought about, as has already been reported to us, by human pride, by human greed looking out for itself, or by the Roman tumult so often heard of and accustomed to shake the whole world by its impulse. Rather, that Spirit who blows where He wills gently accomplished it—as in the whisper of a gentle breeze, according to the word of the Lord spoken to Elijah (3 Kings 19)—reconciling opposites, joining what is divided, and restoring what is torn apart. We rejoiced upon hearing these things, and our heart was filled with boundless gladness, recognizing that God’s cause is defended not by arms, towers, or threatening hosts, but by the merciful Lord’s hand alone and His gentle protection, which have established peace. We recognized truly what ought to be recognized: that Christ commanded the winds and the sea and that an unaccustomed calm came about; that He turned the storm of the sea into a breeze and its waves were silent.

And who would not marvel at this? Who, I ask, would not marvel that from the time of Pope Alexander II, through Gregory, Urban, Paschal, Gelasius, Calixtus, Honorius, and Innocent—the supreme and illustrious pontiffs of God’s Church—ecclesiastical peace, as concerns their elevation, had passed on, yet had rested in none of them except you? We are not so stony as not to feel, nor so brutish as not to understand, that He without whose command—as Scripture says—not even a sparrow falls to the ground nor a leaf falls from a tree, did not without cause, nor without a definite counsel of inexhaustible wisdom, withhold this peace from their beginnings and grant it to yours. I think that it is that peace, and I trust that it shall always endure with you, of which the Prophet says to God in the Psalms: “According to the multitude of my sorrows in my heart, Your consolations have gladdened my soul” (Ps. 93). For I believe and hope in God my savior that He who granted your beginnings such lovely peace will also grant your end, in its due time, praiseworthy renown.

The world, henceforth subject to you, shall rejoice beneath the shadow of His wings, and shall glory that in you alone it possesses such great fathers of its faith: apostolic men, confessors, and—what is greater—martyrs; or, what is more excellent still, the chief apostles Peter and Paul themselves—indeed Christ Himself. Your little flock of Cluny, little not in number but in virtues, shall rejoice, and already rejoices beyond expression. Since it cannot do so in person, it offers you through my mouth and these letters its obedience, submission, and—what is greater—its love; and, though absent, it subjects itself wholly to the feet of your Holiness.

I learned late of the certainty of your election and of the apostolate bestowed by God, and for that reason I wrote late. For, as rumor varied for a long time, I scarcely received your letter sent to me and the community on the vigil of Saint Andrew; and on that same day I read it publicly in chapter and explained it both to the learned and to the unlearned, whom we call converts. It was truly heard and received by all with filial affection. I shall soon, by God’s grace, make this known to you more fully in person or through messengers. For I have every wish to come to you and to visit with fitting love and honor a new father indeed, but an old friend. I shall do this if I can suitably do so. Otherwise, with Christ’s grace assisting, I shall visit you through our brethren as soon as possible.

Meanwhile, I commend to your fatherhood the business of the brother bearing this letter, so that you may kindly hear and decide it, insofar as justice permits, for the benefit of his church. Finally, I give such thanks as I can because, as I have been told and have read in your letters, you kindly received certain other cases referred to your predecessor of blessed memory, and decided them in such a way that, in the judgment of the successor, we need not mourn the holy death of the predecessor.

## Letter XIX. To the universal pope and our own particular Father, Lord Pope Lucius

[Note: To Lord Pope Lucius, successor to Celestine, likewise the second of his name, who ascended the Chair of Saint Peter in the same year.]

Brother Peter, humble abbot of the Cluniacs, with due obedience sends the most sincere affection of love in the Lord.

[Col. 0345D]

After I departed from your fatherhood, so dear to me, I, as a devoted son, diligently and zealously fulfilled everything which had been enjoined by the Father, commanded to your sons and servants, the Cluniacs, and otherwise prescribed to me by you. I imposed frequent sacrifices, almost continual prayers, and many kinds of almsgiving upon our brethren, both at Cluny and elsewhere, both through myself and through messengers. On hearing your letters and learning from them, as well as from my report and that of my companions, of your great affection toward them, they most willingly accepted these obligations and perform them with the utmost devotion.

Therefore they stand, and shall always stand, before God on your behalf; nor shall they cease henceforward, to the extent of their power, to commend so great a Father, so kind, so merciful toward them, to God, the Father of all. For I also impressed this upon their hearts as much as I could, since I could not forget the kindness I had experienced from a Father even while absent, nor the honor bestowed upon me beyond my station or deserts. For, to speak before two witnesses whom no one can deceive—namely, God and my own conscience—the affection of sincere love which I hold for you in the innermost recesses of my soul truly surpasses, and far surpasses, the affections I bore toward all your predecessors. This, as I said, was caused by your kindness and benefits bestowed upon us; but even more by the abundant devotion toward divine religion which I perceived to lie hidden in your holy breast.

But lest I appear to flatter, I shall leave these things and proceed to what follows. I have sent the bearer of this letter with these letters, both to make known to your Reverence what I have said and to deserve to be assured by your letters concerning the condition of your Highness, especially concerning peace with the king of Sicily. Believe me: I am not a little concerned for your peace, since I desire it greatly. For the peace of all of us depends upon your peace; in your rest we, your Cluniacs in particular, rest; and in your suffering we suffer with you, not falsely but truly, because members which do not suffer with the pain of the head are judged not merely diseased but dead.

Write to us, therefore, if it please you, concerning this matter, so that, if it exists, we may rejoice with you as is fitting; if it does not yet exist, we may cooperate with you, according to our knowledge and ability, both with God and among men. Furthermore, because Cluniac affairs are so extensive that we must almost continually write to your fatherhood on diverse matters, I pray that you do not take this ill but, as befits a special and kindly Father, hear and grant them when they are entrusted to you. I further ask that you command us whether, as was enjoined upon me at Rome by your Majesty, I ought to send twelve brothers to Rome by the feast of Saint Andrew, together with a thirteenth who is to be appointed their abbot. Once I have received this command from you again, I shall immediately prepare them for the journey.

## Letter XX. Lucius, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Peter, abbot of Cluny: greeting and apostolic blessing

“The letters of your Love,” etc. See among the letters and privileges of Pope Lucius II.

## Letter XXI. To the venerable and greatly beloved sister in Christ, Heloise, abbess

[Note: Beloved sister Heloise. Who this Heloise was, and what manner of woman she was—called by others Heloyssa—is explained by Peter Abelard in the book of his *Calamities*, in these words: “In the city of Paris there was a young woman named Heloyssa, niece of a canon there called Fulbert. The more dearly he loved her, the more diligently he endeavored to advance her in every branch of literary learning within his power. Though not lacking in beauty of face, she was preeminent in abundance of letters.” Abelard himself, though a cleric and canon, fell passionately in love with her, seduced her, and even married her. But afterward, touched by grief for his guilt, he sent her “to a certain abbey of nuns near Paris called Argenteuil, where she had formerly been brought up and educated as a girl; and he had religious garments fitted for her, appropriate to monastic life.” He likewise received the sacred habit in the abbey of Saint-Denis.

Some time later, “it happened that Suger, abbot of Saint-Denis, acquired in whatever way the aforesaid abbey of Argenteuil, as belonging from ancient times to the right of his monastery, and violently expelled the community of nuns, where his former companion Heloyssa—now in Christ a sister rather than a wife—held the priorship. When they were scattered as exiles in various places, Abelard recognized an opportunity to provide for his own oratory, which he had shortly before built in the territory of Troyes and wished to call by the name of the Paraclete, to whom it had been consecrated. He invited her there with certain others of the same community who adhered to her; and, having brought them there, granted and donated to her the oratory itself with all that belonged to it. Pope Innocent II afterward confirmed this donation forever by a privilege to them and their followers, with the consent and intervention of Hato, bishop of that land.”

Heloise was therefore abbess of that oratory—or, as Innocent himself calls her in his privilege, which holds a place among the precious monuments of the *Antiquities of Troyes*, prioress—when our Peter wrote to her. She was also buried there after her death and honored with the following epitaph:

> In this tomb lies the wise abbess Heloise;  
> She established the Paraclete and rests with the Paraclete.  
> Her joys are in the lofty heights of heaven among the saints;  
> By her merits and prayers may she raise us from the depths.

She died on 16 May, as appears from the obituary book of the monastery of the Paraclete, which contains on that day this eulogy concerning her: “Heloise, the mother of our religious order, its first abbess, most distinguished in learning and religious devotion, happily passed to the Lord, her life having given us good hope.”]

Brother Peter, humble abbot of the Cluniacs, sends the salvation promised by God to those who love Him.

[Col. 0347A]

Having received the letter of your charity, which you recently sent me through my son Theobald, I rejoiced and affectionately embraced it for the sake of its sender. I wished immediately to write back what had arisen in my mind; but the importunate demands of my duties, to which I am often—indeed, almost always—compelled to yield, prevented me. Yet, when at last a day had scarcely been snatched from these tumults, I attempted what I had conceived. It seemed right that I should hasten at least to return words in answer to your affection toward me, which I had learned then from your letter and earlier from gifts sent to me, and show you how much place in my heart I reserved for love of you in the Lord.

For in truth, I do not begin to love you now for the first time, whom I remember to have loved me for a long time. I had not yet fully passed the bounds of adolescence, nor yet entered upon youth, when fame made known to me the name—not yet, indeed, of your religious life, but of your honorable and praiseworthy studies. At that time I heard of a woman who, though not yet freed from the bonds of the world, devoted the utmost effort to literary learning—which is very rare—and to the pursuit, though secular, of wisdom, and who could not be drawn away from this useful purpose of learning the arts by the world’s pleasures, trifles, or delights.

Since almost the whole world lies numb in detestable idleness concerning these pursuits, and since wisdom can scarcely find a place for its foot to stand—not, I say, among the female sex, from which it has been entirely driven out, but scarcely even among male minds—you, through the excellence of your study, surpassed all women and outstripped almost all men. But soon afterward, according to the Apostle’s words, “when it pleased Him who separated you from your mother’s womb to call you through His grace” (Gal. 1), you changed your studies of learning for something far better: in place of logic, the Gospel; in place of natural philosophy, the Apostle; in place of Plato, Christ; in place of the Academy, the cloister. Now wholly and truly a philosophical woman, you chose these things.

You stripped the spoils from conquered enemies and, passing through the desert of this pilgrimage with the treasures of Egypt, built in your heart a precious tabernacle for God. With Pharaoh submerged, you sang a song of praise with Mary (Exod. 15); and, bearing in your hands the timbrel of blessed mortification as she once did, you, a skilful female musician, sent the melody of a new song up to the very ears of the Godhead. Already at your beginning you trampled down the head of the ancient serpent, ever lying in wait for women; by persevering well through the grace of the Almighty, you shall crush it so that it will never again dare to hiss against you.

You make, and shall make, the proud prince of this world a spectacle; and you shall compel him whom the divine voice calls “king over all the children of pride” (Job 41), bound to you and to the handmaids of God dwelling with you—as God Himself said to blessed Job (Job 40)—to groan. And it is indeed a singular miracle, to be exalted above all wondrous works: that he beside whom, according to the prophet, the cedars were not taller in the paradise of God and whose leafy height the fir trees did not equal (Ezek. 31), should be conquered by the frail sex, and that the strongest archangel should be overcome by a most weak woman. By such a contest the Creator gains the greatest glory; conversely, the deceiver suffers supreme shame. In this struggle he is reproached as having been not merely foolish but supremely ridiculous in aspiring to equality with the most exalted Majesty, when he cannot endure even a short conflict with feminine weakness. The head of every woman who conquers him receives, by the merit of so great a victory, a jeweled crown from the King of heaven, so that the weaker she was in the flesh during the struggle now past, the more glorious she may appear in eternal reward.

These things, dearest sister in the Lord, I say not truly in flattery but in exhortation: seeing the great good in which you have remained for some time, you may become more resolute in carefully preserving it, and may kindle by words and examples alike the holy women who serve the Lord with you, according to the grace bestowed upon you by God, to strive diligently in the same contest. For you are one of those living creatures seen by the prophet Ezekiel (Ezek. 1); though a woman, you ought not only to burn like a coal, but to burn and shine like a lamp. You are indeed a disciple of truth; but by your office, so far as those entrusted to you are concerned, you are also a teacher of humility. The teaching office of humility, indeed of all heavenly discipline, has been laid upon you by God. Therefore you must have care not only for yourself but also for the flock entrusted to you, and for all of them you must receive a reward greater than that of them all.
