Certainly the palm of victory awaits you for them all, because, as you know very well, all who under your leadership conquer the world and the prince of the world will prepare for you as many triumphs and glorious trophies before the eternal King and Judge. Yet it is not altogether unheard-of among mortals for women to command women, nor entirely unprecedented for them even to fight and to accompany men into battle. For if the saying is true, “It is right to learn even from an enemy,” then among the pagans Penthesilea, queen of the Amazons, is said to have fought often with her Amazons—not men but women—during the Trojan War; and among the people of God the prophetess Deborah is read to have encouraged Barak, judge of Israel, against the heathen (Judg. 4).

Why then should women of virtue, advancing to battle against the strong man armed, not be permitted to become leaders of the Lord’s army, when that woman—though it seemed unbecoming—nevertheless fought the enemies with her own hand, and our Deborah stirred up, armed, and inflamed men themselves for divine wars? After King Jabin had been conquered, Sisera the commander killed, and the profane army destroyed, that woman immediately sang a song and devoted it in piety to the praises of God. By God’s grace, after victory has been granted to you and yours over enemies far stronger than you, your song will be far more glorious; you shall sing it with such joy that thereafter you will never cease to rejoice and never cease to sing. Meanwhile, you will be to the handmaids of God—that is, to the heavenly army—what Deborah was to her Jewish people; nor shall you cease from so profitable a contest at any time or by any circumstance, except through victory.

And because the name Deborah, as your learning knows, signifies a bee in the Hebrew language, you too shall be Deborah in this respect: that is, a bee. You shall make honey, but not for yourself alone, because whatever good you have gathered through diverse persons and from diverse sources, you shall pour it all back, by example, word, and every means you can, upon the sisters of your household and upon any others. During this brief span of mortal life, you shall satisfy both yourself with the secret sweetness of sacred letters and the blessed sisters with open preaching, until, according to the prophetic voice, “on that day which is permitted, the mountains shall distill eternal sweetness and the hills shall flow with milk and honey” (Joel 3). Although this is said of the time of grace, nothing prevents—indeed, it is sweeter—to understand it of the time of glory.

It would be sweet to me to prolong a conversation with you on such matters, because I delight in your renowned learning and am drawn still more strongly by your religious devotion, praised to me by many. Would that our Cluny had possessed you! Would that the pleasant prison of Marcigny had enclosed you with the other handmaids of Christ, awaiting there heavenly freedom! I would have preferred the riches of religious life and learning to the greatest treasures of any kings whatsoever, and I would have rejoiced that the distinguished company of those sisters shone more brightly through your presence. You too would have gained from them no small profit and would have marveled at the highest nobility and pride of the world laid beneath your feet. You would have seen every kind of worldly luxury transformed through wondrous frugality, and vessels of the devil once filthy converted into the purest temples of the Holy Spirit. You would have seen girls of God, as though stolen away from Satan or the world, raise high walls of virtues upon the foundation of innocence and carry the summit of their blessed structure up to the very heights of heaven. You would have rejoiced to see those flourishing in angelic virginity joined with most chaste widows, all alike awaiting the glory of that blessed and great resurrection, enclosed even bodily within the narrow bounds of their houses, as though already laid in the tomb of blessed hope.

Although you possess all these things, and perhaps still greater ones, together with the colleagues given you by God; although perhaps nothing pertaining to the study of sacred things can [or: could] be added to you, yet our commonwealth would be enriched by the increase of your graces, to no small advantage, I think. But although this has been denied us concerning you by the providence of God, the dispenser of all things, it has nevertheless been granted us concerning that servant of yours—him, I say, who must often and always be named with honor—Master Peter, a true philosopher of Christ, whom the same divine ordering brought to Cluny in the last years of his life [Note: [Col. 0349D] “Master Peter, whom divine ordering brought to Cluny in the last years of his life.” Above, Epistle 4: “Master Peter,” he says, “writing to Pope Innocent, who I believe was very well known to your wisdom, made his passage through Cluny.” And a little later: “Having left behind the tumults of schools and studies, he chose at Cluny a permanent dwelling for himself.” These words both elucidate this passage and, together with it, testify that the Master Peter called Abaelard [Col. 0350D]—who had been accused before King Louis at Sens by St Bernard, Suger, and other prelates of the Gallican Church of a profane novelty in wording or thought—finally performed severe penance at Cluny for his errors. Some also say that Berengar, deacon of the Church of Angers, came there at almost the same time, in order, having become a monk there, to repent likewise of his heresy.]; and he enriched it in him and through him with a gift more precious than all gold and topaz.

What, or how great, a testimony Cluny bears to his holy, humble, and devout manner of life among us cannot be explained in a brief discourse. Unless I am mistaken, I do not recall having seen anyone like him in humility of dress and bearing: so much so that not even Germanus appeared more lowly, nor Martin himself poorer, to one who judged rightly. And although, at my bidding, he held a higher rank in that great company of our brethren, he seemed the last of all in his exceedingly plain clothing. I often marvelled; and when in processions he went before me with the rest, according to custom, I was almost astonished that a man of so great and renowned a name could despise and abase himself so completely.

There are some professed religious who desire the religious habit which they wear to be excessively costly. He, on the contrary, was altogether sparing in such matters: content with plain clothing of any sort, he sought nothing beyond it. He observed the same rule in food, drink, and every care of his body; and he condemned, in word as well as life, not only superfluities but everything, both in himself and in others, unless it was very necessary. His reading was continual, his prayer frequent, his silence unbroken—except when familiar conversation with the brethren or a public discourse to them in chapter on divine matters compelled him to speak. He frequented, as far as he was able, the heavenly sacraments, offering to God the sacrifice of the immortal Lamb; indeed, after he was restored to apostolic favor through my letters and exertion, he almost did so continually. And why say more? His mind, his tongue, his work were always occupied with, taught, and confessed things divine, philosophical, and instructive.

Such a man—simple and upright among us, fearing God and turning away from evil—consecrated the last days of his life to God in such a manner of life for some time. Then, because he was more heavily burdened than usual by scabies and certain bodily ailments, I sent him to Chalon for rest [Note: [Col. 0351C] “I sent him to Chalon.” That is, to the monastery of St Marcellus, itself under Cluniac jurisdiction, where shortly afterwards he ended his days with a most excellent death. Hence the *Chronicle of the Archbishops of Sens*: “In the year of the Lord 1140, at Sens, in the presence of King Louis, an assembly of bishops and religious abbots was held [Col. 0351D] against Peter Abaelard, who was scandalizing the Church by a certain profane novelty of words or meanings. When summoned by them to answer, fearing the judgment, he appealed to a hearing before the Apostolic See; and so escaping, not long afterwards he died at Chalon, at Saint-Marcellus.” After his death Peter, abbot of Cluny, wrote an epitaph for him, which survives among other verses composed by him. Yet his body was buried neither at Chalon nor at Cluny, but was carried to the convent of the Paraclete at Heloise’s care, in accordance with what he himself had long before prescribed to her in these words:

> “If the Lord should deliver me into the hands of enemies, so that they prevail and kill me, or if by any chance, while you are absent, I enter upon the way of all flesh, I beg you to have my body, wherever it may lie buried or exposed, carried to your cemetery, where our daughters—indeed, sisters in Christ—often seeing our tomb may be more often invited to pour out prayers for me. For I think no place safer or more healthful for a grieving soul, desolate because of the error of its sins, [Col. 0352C] than that which is truly consecrated in a special sense to the Paraclete, that is, the Comforter, and fittingly distinguished by his name.”

That this instruction or command was fulfilled by Heloise is also shown by the writer of the *Chronicle of Saint-Pierre-le-Vif*, when he says: “In the year 1142 Master Peter Abailard, formerly a canon [Col. 0352D] of the greater Church of Sens, died. He founded monasteries of nuns, especially the abbey of the Paraclete, in which he is buried with his wife. He was a canon, and afterwards married.” Therefore another epitaph was also placed for him there, in these verses:

> Peter lies hidden in this tomb, whom the world  
> Called Homer; but now the stars possess their star.  
>   
> He was a sun to the Gauls, but fate has now borne him away;  
> Therefore the land of Gaul lacks its own sun.  
>   
> Knowing whatever was knowable by anyone, he surpassed  
> Masters, teaching the arts without a teacher.  
>   
> The eleventh day before the Kalends of May carried Peter off,  
> Depriving the halls of logic of their king.  
>   
> Enough of the tomb: here lies Peter Abaelard,  
> To whom alone all that can be known lay open.

And these words concerning him are also read in the necrology of the Paraclete: “21 April: the anniversary of Master Peter Abelard, founder of this place and institutor of our religious order.”].

For the pleasantness of that place alone, which surpasses almost all parts of our Burgundy, I had provided for him a suitable site near the city, but with the Saône flowing between. There, insofar as his illness allowed, renewing his former studies, he was always intent upon books; nor, as is read of the great Gregory, did he allow a single moment to pass without always praying, reading, writing, or dictating. In these exercises of sacred works, the coming of that evangelical visitor found him; it found him not sleeping, as it finds many, but awake. It found him truly watchful and summoned him to the marriage-feast of eternity, not as a foolish but as a wise virgin. For he brought with him a lamp full of oil—that is, a conscience filled with the testimony of a holy life.

Having been seized by illness in order to pay the common debt of mortals, and the sickness growing worse, he was brought to his end in a short time. Then how holily, devoutly, and catholicly he made first confession of faith and afterwards confession of sins; with what longing of heart he received the provision for his journey and the pledge of eternal life, namely the body of the Lord Redeemer; how faithfully he commended to him his body and soul here and for eternity—the religious brethren and the entire community of that monastery, where the body of St Marcellus the martyr lies, are witnesses. Thus Master Peter ended his days; and he who, through his singular mastery of learning, was known and famous almost throughout the whole world, persevering gentle and humble in the discipleship of him who said, “Learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart” (Matt. 11), passed to him, as it is fitting to believe.

Therefore, venerable and dearest sister in the Lord, remember in the Lord this man, to whom, after your carnal union, you clung by the bond of divine love, so much stronger as it is better, and with whom and under whom you served the Lord for a long time. This man, I say, whom He cherishes in his bosom in your place, or as another you, and keeps in reserve to be restored to you through his grace at the coming of the Lord, amid the voice of the archangel and the trumpet of God descending from heaven. Remember me also, if you please; and earnestly commend to the holy sisters serving the Lord with you the brethren of our congregation and the sisters who, throughout the world, according to their ability, serve the same Lord whom you serve.

## EPISTLE XXII  
To the universal pontiff and our own father, Lord Pope Lucius, Brother Peter, humble abbot of Cluny, faithful obedience with sincere love.

I have often begged, and still beg, that my very frequent letters may not seem burdensome to your reverence, occupied as it is with so many things. For many matters often arise which compel me, even unwilling and trying to avoid it, to be importunate. Sometimes these are my own affairs, which are many; sometimes the affairs of great friends, which must not be neglected: these are the cause of this importunity.

The unrest of certain clerics of Orléans, which has almost destroyed their church, has not yet learned to rest. For these canons who are no canons, pretending to seek the things of God but—as is plain to all—under that pretext seeking their own things, have almost mortally wounded their mother the Church, and have raised their heel against their father and bishop. Your wisdom knows what God himself thinks of such people: “Whoever curses his father or mother shall surely die” (Exod. 21; Lev. 20). If this is said of cursing, how much more of despoiling? If it is said of cursing, how much more of injuring? If it is said of those who curse, how much more of those who, so far as lies in them, kill?

Such, I say, are some in that church—such indeed they truly are, insofar as report bears witness—not religious persons but irreligious; not men of the higher ranks, but inferiors; not many, but few. Seeking to make profit from persecuting their father and imagining that they can obtain some gain thereby, while he is peaceable with those who hate peace, they attack him without cause, whether he speaks or is silent (Ps. 119). They are not ashamed to appear as a very small number among many, and as only seven or eight against thousands of clergy and people preaching the contrary to them, as liars and babblers.

The testimony of many great and religious persons moves me to write thus; some of these are ours, but far more are outsiders. Therefore, if you please, let the testimony of so many prevail and weigh more with you; and let your wise justice defend your bishop against these few men of ill repute, who, as it seems to me, deserve rather to be tossed on horns than heard by ears. Let the long-standing companionship of a good, religious man, exceptional among his own, support him: at the command of Pope Celestine, though not named specifically, we chose this man because of his outstanding religious life and gave him to the bishop as a companion. Let that man, then, if this seems just to your wisdom, be questioned concerning him; let him be consulted. Since I testify that he wishes by no means to lie, let him be believed rather than those rogues. May your holiness always flourish in Christ.

## EPISTLE XXIII  
To Raymond, monk of Toulouse, Brother Peter, humble abbot of Cluny, greetings.

Though your head grows white, your Muse knows no old age;  
Nor, because you are grey, does she sing the less.

You are white and you sing: you imitate the white swans,  
In whom voice and brightness, joined, are more pleasing.

Here their pale color, there their sound, delights the ears:  
Thus nothing in that bird of the whole river fails to please.

The Garonne had not known how to nurture garlanded birds;  
Now the swan fills her banks with song.

Toulouse had wept, bereft of poets of old;  
See, let her pursuit of learning rejoice that it restores you.

You write that you wish to see the ruins of Rome,  
If it pleased me to attempt such a journey.

When by chance I read the astonishing boldness of your heart,  
I was amazed, I confess, and was silent for a long time.

Just as if a man, weakened by fever in his bed,  
Promised the strength and shoulders of Typhon;

Or as if a tortoise born in Spanish soil  
Matched itself in races against a horse.

For who could be silent concerning such wonders of your praise:  
That, old man, you undertake the brave deeds of youths?

Your unconquered old age has not been able to yield  
To the dreadful Alps, or to turn back the step already begun.

The lofty cliffs, which were accustomed harshly to conquer  
Hearts, have yielded to your courage.

As a veteran soldier, a well-earned discharge  
And lofty rest after your former deeds befitted you.

But strength of spirit knows not how to spare grey hair,  
And bloody wars please you more than rest.

Come then to Rome: I shall not delay; I do not wish you to linger.  
The Latin realms summon fighting spirits.

Rome was born of wars, smeared with blood, glorious in triumphs;  
She is accustomed through such men to subject all things to herself,

If she girds you, strong as you are, with a shining sword  
And makes you leader of warriors.

Soon the public enemy will perish by the victorious sword,  
And the whole world will still be subject to her.

We have played, and led forth measured songs with you,  
Lest the swan laugh at all the birds of the world.

Now it is fitting that serious matter kindle our play,  
And that a monk’s jest be adorned with gravity.

If nature supplies you with strength and ability,  
Nothing will hinder my journey while you accompany me.

You will not be unwelcome, for widespread fame, learning, life,  
And your aged head know how to make you dear.

You will adorn the whole company by your known goodness  
And be the sole standard-bearer among men of virtue.

Nowhere in the woods does a fairer olive flourish,  
While by its brightness it makes every green thing seem dull.

May devout youth deserve to have you as its companion,  
So that younger and elder alike may praise the Lord.

Recently Robert drew me into these verses,  
Through whom you sent me many poems.

Saying that you wished to go with me to Rome,  
He urged me to answer in verse.

I have answered him; yet I add this to what came before:  
I have proposed for myself no settled route.

Yet if, as I have said, chance brings about what I think it will,  
You shall become my constant companion in foreign lands.

But do not blame me if fortune brings anything adverse—  
Fortune, which makes all people equal.

That power commands what it wishes to kings and slaves alike;  
Rich and poor alike are subject to her.

I have sung at another’s urging; if you wish, you too will sing—  
A dark and a white swan, contrary to the nature of birds.

## EPISTLE XXIV  
To the universal pontiff and our own father, Lord Pope Lucius, Brother Peter, humble abbot of Cluny, faithful obedience.

In accordance with the will and command of your sublimity, we send from the bosom of the cloister of Cluny these beloved brethren and sons of ours to their common father—indeed, to ours and theirs in a special sense. We commend them to apostolic mercy; we commend them, I say, for they are highly commendable. For the cause of God, by the power of obedience, they forcefully subdue themselves; they leave their native soil, go to foreign parts, and do not shrink even from death itself, which Roman air is accustomed quickly to bring upon our countrymen. Thus, as far as this fear of our Gauls is concerned, they go like lambs to the sacrifice.

Therefore let a fatherly eye look upon them with kindly regard, and let it console its exiles through frequent benevolent admonitions and suitable assistance. Let them, if you please, be established in one of the two monasteries at Rome which you named to me, and let the former inhabitants be expelled in order to be settled elsewhere. For, in the Apostle’s words, “A little leaven corrupts the whole lump” (1 Cor. 5); and, as your wisdom knows, persons differing in customs, practices, and dispositions

> Do not agree well, nor remain in one dwelling.

And because, according to Gregory the Great, it seems hard for an old heart to entertain new thoughts, and it is almost a hopeless matter to convert a monk from a corrupt custom to better observances, care must be taken lest those who cannot be corrected corrupt others. If anyone should perhaps attempt to separate some of those whom I have sent from one another and transfer them to other places, I beg you not to allow it. Divided into portions, they would make no progress and would lose the fruit which, placed together, they can bear.

For if all were to be sent two or three at a time to different places, I would have selected others and in a different way. But because you have so ordered that I should send thirteen suitable brethren for the organization of one cloister only, I selected the greater part of them as useful simply for maintaining the cloister; I assigned some who are more shrewd in secular matters to provide for the others; and to the said thirteen I added, as a supplement, two who are Romans by birth. For this reason, it seems to me harmful for them to depart from one another and profitable for them to remain together.

To these matters I add this request: both in my own name and on behalf of all our brethren, I beg that our labor, which for God’s cause and at your command we have undertaken for the organization of the said monastery, may never at any time be turned to the detriment of your Church of Cluny. Your prudence can guard against and provide for this, if the gift publicly made by you is confirmed, according to Cluniac custom, by an apostolic privilege.

## EPISTLE XXV  
To the supreme ruler of God’s Church, Lord Pope Eugenius [Note: [Col. 0355D] “Lord Pope Eugenius”: Eugenius III, who was elected in the year 1145.], our father, Brother Peter, humble abbot of Cluny, diligent obedience with love.

Because of the great confidence of affection which we have always been accustomed to place in the Apostolic See, many of our friends are accustomed to have recourse to us and, through our mediation, to offer their petitions to apostolic gentleness. Therefore, relying both upon this very ancient practice and upon the pastoral love and care which you have already shown us in the expulsion of our brethren from St Sabas [Note: [Col. 0355D] “Our brethren from St Sabas.” The monastery of St Sabas, founded from the time of the most holy Pope Gregory in religious observance and integrity and enriched with great and extensive possessions, had later fallen away from religious life, as sins demanded and the wickedness of evil men abounded. In 1144 Pope Lucius II entrusted it, with all its appurtenances, to our Peter, abbot of Cluny, and his successors forever, to reform, improve, and govern, as appears from the charter of Lucius himself.]—you received those who had been cast out, fed the desolate, and cherished the beaten—we confidently approach your fatherly reverence and pray your greatness on behalf of the lord archbishop of Besançon, a good friend of the Church of Cluny.

For, as has been reported to us, he is accused by a few mean persons of his church; he is excused and commended by many trustworthy men, especially by professors of stricter religious observance and order. As we reasonably believe, they would offer no prayers and make no petitions for him if they perceived justice to be opposed in any respect to their petitions or commendation. Therefore, if you please, let your careful discernment hear them, and hear us who petition for him with them, lest wicked men be given easy and irreverent access against good men, base persons against the best, and men of ill fame against one supported by many and great testimonies of good people.

Finally, we ask you to preserve for us in your heart a place of favor for him, which we possessed, as though by hereditary right, with your holy predecessors; so that you, who by the ordering of almighty God have succeeded them in the office of apostolic dignity, may also succeed them in love and benefaction toward us and toward your Cluny.

## EPISTLE XXVI  
To the venerable Lord Rainard, abbot of Cîteaux, most warmly embraced in Christ, Brother Peter, humble abbot of Cluny, greetings and the full affection of charity.

The flock of the Lord, the sheep of his pasture, bereft of their shepherd, lately came to us at Cluny on the solemn feast-day of the Holy Spirit. They had sought their shepherd through mountain heights, valley descents, and rough roads, with much sweat. We sympathized, as was right, with their religious pilgrimage; and, weary from so long a journey, we compelled them to lodge with us for three days.

Consider that they—something rare among men of the monastic order—were carried neither on horses nor mules nor even asses, but proceeded on foot as pilgrims, with the utmost devotion of heart, toward you, in order to secure—or, if possible, restore to themselves—the shepherd whom they had lost; and for that reason they shrink from no labor and avoid no danger. It did not suffice them to send one or two of their number to your reverence with this purpose. Displaying a number worthy of the apostles, they believe that nothing will be refused them, especially because they ask only what is just.

They ought therefore, if you please, to be kindly received by you; and in my judgment they ought to be heard and granted their request. For, according to the Lord’s words, “They do not follow a stranger’s shepherd, but flee from him, because they do not know the voice of strangers” (John 10). I act and intercede for them, drawn by their holy zeal; but I am particularly compelled to this by the singular love I have for them and for the place where they dwell. My brothers, nephews, and almost the whole line of my kindred have cherished that place with great affection from the first foundation-stone; some of their possessions—indeed, not a few—they bestowed for the sake of your order and religious observance. I support their devotion, if not with material benefits, at least with the affection of sincere love.

Let your sentence in removing their abbot have been severe, and such as instils fear in others; but let there be, if it is no burden, prudent provision in restoring him. For the accusation against him was neither capital nor final; nor are there so many things in him—whose good qualities I partly know well—that deserve condemnation, as I suggest in friendship. Therefore, if you please, restore the good shepherd to his good sheep; and since justice has been satisfied, let mercy also be satisfied, so that those who come to you with much labor and humility may return with great joy and full consolation to their own fold during the solemn days of the Paraclete.

## EPISTLE XXVII  
To the intimate and now long-standing inhabitant of my heart, the venerable Lord Aton, by God’s grace bishop of Troyes, Brother Peter, humble abbot of Cluny, the greeting he wishes for himself.

It is read in Solomon: “New wine, a new friend: let it grow old, and you will drink it with sweetness” (Ecclus. 9). What does this mean? Attend, dearest friend. It says what may be seen. For when wine is new, having cast off the now useless sweetness of must, it indeed attracts the drinker by its novelty; yet, like the unripe violence of youth, it pricks the taste of the one drinking. It delights and irritates; wholesome and biting at once, it refreshes the inward parts in its draught, but gives less pleasure while it is drunk.

But when, as though its youthful heat had been calmed, it begins to grow old and to season itself with a gentle taste, as with the sweetness of mild old age, it becomes not only good but pleasant. It is taken not only as wholesome but also as delightful, and nothing which may prick or bite is then feared in it. According even to the literal sense of Scripture, it makes glad the heart of man (Ps. 103), and consoles the laborious course of mortal life with the sweetness placed in it by the Creator of things.

Thus indeed, dearest friend, I recognize this Solomonic saying to be fulfilled in you. While you were a new friend, you often benefited me; but you never delighted me as you do now that you are old. Friendship has grown old with you—not through decay, not through age, but solely through the antiquity, as it were, of time—so that, according to the foregoing comparison, you may be received more fittingly, drunk more sweetly, and imbibed more joyfully.

For a long time, through the austerity either of your new friendship or your age, you greatly resisted, recoiled, and fled, lest I might drink you or pour you into the body of Cluny. But I hope, and trust in the grace of that Spirit who “breathes where he wills,” that what the youth of friendship did not grant, old age will at least confer. I know what was said to the apostle Peter: “Rise, Peter; kill and eat” (Acts 10). Even if I am not an apostle, I am nevertheless Peter. Therefore, in accordance with this divine saying, I have desired not only to drink you but also to kill and eat you.

Come then, come. Do not any longer fear my sword, though you must be killed; nor dread my teeth, though you must be attended to [or, perhaps, ground down] and chewed by them. But lest, perhaps, afraid and hearing such great threats, you do not dare come, know that I wish to kill not you but the world within you; to raise up the monk; to consume what will perish; to restore what will endure. And lest anyone judge me presumptuous because I, a humble man, write and suggest such things to one exalted, an inferior to a superior, an abbot to a bishop: you yourself gave me, where you know and as you know, matter for speaking and supplied the boldness. Therefore I do not fear to discuss with you matters which you first discussed, nor to confer with you about things to which you first urged me.

Now, since I long ago filled many pages with frequent letters to a friend, let words cease at last and deeds succeed, lest I appear—or be—always like sounding bronze or a clanging cymbal.

## EPISTLE XXVIII  
To the universal yet special father, Lord Pope Eugenius, Brother Peter, humble abbot of Cluny, due obedience and faithful service.

Just as Jacob the patriarch of old loved, honored, and cherished Joseph among all his sons with a singular and almost exclusive love, so your blessed predecessors of happy memory loved, honored, and cherished your Church of Cluny more affectionately, more familiarly, and more tenderly than almost all churches subject and entrusted to them, as I think is not unknown to your blessedness. Since by the ordering of almighty God you have succeeded them in the Apostolic See, we pray—and although absent in body, we entreat you—that, having succeeded them in office, you may also succeed them, if you please, in love and benefaction.

For, to use the words once spoken by Israel, the people of God: “As we obeyed Moses, so we shall obey you; only may the Lord be with you, as he was with Moses” (Josh. 1). For we, though unworthy, have deserved this increase of favor from our said fathers—men truly apostolic in life and office: that we were heard not only in our own affairs but in those of others also, even in matters concerning persons very far removed; and that we were almost always heard most kindly. We ask this with filial confidence from our father, whom we have wished to obey, love, and serve according to that custom of ours so ancient and known throughout the world.

The venerable man and priest of God, the lord bishop of Orléans [Note: [Col. 0359] “The lord bishop of Orléans”: perhaps Elias, mentioned above, who held office until the year 1146.], a devoted son of your fatherhood, has suffered much from sons of Belial. Though, like a most gentle sheep, he is always peaceable with those who hate peace, he has lately fled—and again has recourse—to you as to a peaceful harbor and secure refuge of mercy, that apostolic strength and gentleness may be for him a tower of strength against the enemy. Almost the whole Gallican Church writes and entreats for him, humbly imploring that pontifical sublimity, assailed with lying insults by infamous and utterly base persons, may not be allowed to suffer dishonor.

We too add our prayers to the prayers of others, if our prayers can have any weight. Since he is distinguished not only by episcopal rank but also by monastic integrity and habit, may the Father hear both orders on his behalf, gladden both with oil, honor both, and send him back to his own people and place with the fullness of apostolic blessing and favor—he whose innocence has long been harassed by wicked men amid so many and such great troubles.

## EPISTLE XXIX  
To his sweetest lord and father, Peter, his little and unworthy servant.

Since the day of the glorious first martyr among the apostles, through God’s mercy and your prayers, I have felt myself somewhat relieved; and I cannot be so near you without saying anything to you. With Christ’s help I am ready to begin your *Prudentius*, if you command the lord prior of the cloister to provide parchment and Bonitus to make preparations. I rejoice greatly that you unexpectedly commanded me to do something which, with the Lord’s aid, I both can do and desire to do out of obedience, so that henceforth I may be able to boast before you that I have done something for obedience’s sake.

Nor should I be silent at all about this: from the very hour when, on the feast of the most gracious apostle James, while the solemnities of the principal Mass were being celebrated, our brother Theobald conveyed to me, unworthy as I am, your greeting, my foot began to improve. Thus I trust that, through the grace of that apostle and through your prayer as well, being greeted by you will mean the same to me as being saved. May we soon see you safe and well, pious and most longed-for lord and father. May your fellow-hermits and all my lord’s companions, who dwell with you in the woods, flourish.

## EPISTLE XXX  
To Peter, honored and son in Christ, Brother Peter, humble abbot of Cluny, greetings.

I ought not to be altogether mute in answer to one who writes. We dwell in woods, weary of cities; we love the countryside. And, to add something poetic:

> No longer does turbulent royal Rome please me,  
> But empty Tibur and unwarlike Tarentum.  
> —Horace, *Epistles* I.7.44–45

We are already veterans, and have left warfare to young men—to you and those like you. Arm yourself, therefore; and since, as you wrote, your foot has recovered through God’s grace, go forth to battle, fight manfully, subdue your enemies by strength. Since the whole world now conspires in arms, join yourself too to the number of the armed. For that reason you were unwilling to become our fellow-hermit.

Yet I did not wish that leisure which you impute to me to be wholly idle. And, again using the words of the poet quoted above:

> The ivy, reward of learned brows, mingles me with the gods above.  
> The cool grove—be silent about the rest—  
> Sets me apart from the crowd.  
> —Horace, *Odes* I.1.29–32

You know how much false songs in the Church of God grieve me, and how hateful to me are tuneful trifles. Among these—for they are very many—when recently, on the feast of the great father Benedict, I heard sung—and was compelled to sing—a hymn excellent in all respects except sense, metrical rule, and sequence of words: I was deeply troubled, though not for the first time, and was ashamed that the true praises of so great a man should be falsely uttered. For, besides its total lack of suitability in meaning, I found in that song, as I ran through it quickly in my mind, no fewer than twenty-four falsehoods.

Therefore, not as a presumptuous man, but as one zealous for the things of God, even in this small matter, I composed, taking my subject from the words of Gregory the Great, a hymn in the same metre in praise of almighty God and of the aforesaid father; and I sent it to you, to whom I frequently press my productions, whatever their quality. Receive it, then, and, if it seems worthy, add it to the other works which you are accustomed to copy. For I do not wish to leave this unsaid: while that old hymn scarcely touches upon one of the many and great miracles of the holy man, this one briefly sets forth twelve of his miracles in addition to his spiritual virtues. And because, once I had begun upon his translation and burial, I issued a second hymn in another metre, shorter than the first because of the weariness of singers. I send that also. Farewell forever.

## EPISTLE XXXI  
To Peter of Poitiers, beloved elder and prior of our fellowship, Brother Arnulahus, a novice hermit, least of his fellow-hermits, greeting of mind and body.

Your greeting, which you sent to be conveyed to the Father of the new inhabitants of the wilderness, our lord abbot, became known to me almost last of all among the brethren; and, like ointment descending from the head to the hem of the garment, it descended graciously. I thank you because, drawn by affection for us, you think such exalted things of us as to deem us worthy of the name of hermits; and because you attribute to religion that which, out of fearful concern to preserve some measure of safety, we undertook. For we, like inexperienced hermits, still think about tomorrow, and consider ourselves not a little religious if we escape alive from the danger of the present time. But you I would call the more philosophical hermit: fearless of death, you live securely beside the dying, and, separated from the turbulent onset of those arriving, stationed alone in your upper room, you dwell with yourselves.

Yet I had attempted somehow to write how much envy your wilderness—or rather your solitude—arouses in us; but the letter of the lord—

[Note: “But the letter of the lord”: that is, of the abbot or provost. St Benedict, Rule, chapter 63: “But because the abbot is believed to hold the place of Christ, he is to be called lord and abbot.” And blessed Odilo, in the Life of St Majolus: “and he is honoured by all as lord and abba.” Likewise later: “namely, Lord and Abba William.” He was also called *senior*, as is evident throughout the Life of Odilo himself written by Jotsald. Priors, however, were called *nonni*, as St Benedict teaches in the cited place when he says: “Priors shall call their younger brethren brothers; but younger brethren shall call their priors *nonni*, which signifies paternal reverence.” And the Synod of Aachen, in the year 816: “Those who are set over others are to be called *nonni*, that is, with paternal reverence.” Yet later the brethren of Cluny themselves began to be called *domni*, commonly *dom*. Thus the Cassinese monks say in their declaration: “By our ancient custom, to distinguish our monks from mendicants, we call them *domni*, but in affection, brothers.” Nuns too were called *nonnae*, in French *nonnains*. St Jerome, to Eustochium: “And because, having experienced the domination of husbands, they prefer the freedom of widowhood, they are called chaste women and *nonnae*.” And Capitularies, book V, chapter 11: “Likewise veiled nuns shall be subject to the same penance.” Hence Xiphilinus, in Domitian, called virgins νόννας, *nonnas*, distinguishing them from other women in these words: “He often held contests by night, and sometimes even matched nuns and women against one another.”]

—who, while I was writing, suddenly came upon me and, according to his custom, thundered forth in loftier tones with philosophical words, overwhelmed me, making me mute and tongueless, and slower than if I limped with you. I therefore fell silent. Yet one thing which I had conceived in my mind I could not suppress, like another Elihu; and, though overwhelmed, I set it down in a rude and unpolished style. What was it? If you would deign to come to us with your Augustine from the Academics, [Col. 0361C] all leisure would flee away and we should establish a new Academy. What end is there to these trifles? To confess the truth, meanwhile we desire your arrival among us more than our own return to you. This feeling is so common to all that even our old ox does not kick against it: captivated by the pleasant delightfulness of the wilderness, hungry as much as full, he ruminates unweariedly.

## LETTER XXXII. Brother ROBERT to the venerable brother and dearest companion PETER: what follows.

At the evening twilight of the past Sunday, when, after those who were deemed worthy first to see what is sent and first to hear what is spoken into the ear, it first happened to me to read your letter, which I had not previously heard, I rejoiced. For there was in it—as some of ours [Col. 0362A] observed with a more penetrating gaze of mind—something which not only caressed the ears of its hearers, but also moved their mouths and soothed the minds of us all. And what was this, or what could it have been? That, I say, for which the benches in a theatre sing or shout. I speak of the conclusion of your little letters, which you addressed to the lord. Although their beginning and middle had been full of much praise, you nevertheless brought them to a close with more delightful artistry and more elegant maturity. For you said: “May the lord, his companions, and his fellow-hermits, who inhabit the woods with him, flourish.” Thus you implied that the lord was a hermit. You designated his companions as fellow-hermits. You did not conceal that, instead of the dry habitation of a wilderness, the master delights with his flock in damp and cold woods.

And whence came this to you, O [Col. 0362B] venerable old man? Whence came this to you, O minister of Christ, O angel of God—unless it be that an angel does not know how to grow old, turn grey, or limp? And whence, I say, came this to you: that with so lofty a breast, or perhaps with a new spirit of prophecy, you should foretell what is not yet known, sing beforehand what has not yet begun, and show in advance what none of those whom you have bestowed upon the wilderness considers possible to do or love without you? Therefore, when you come to us, you will find neither a wilderness nor hermits. For our Parnassus is three-peaked, no longer two-peaked, as the ancient poets once spoke of it. Having horned Fauns on one side, dancing Satyrs on another, everywhere the noises of beasts and the sweet chirping of birds, it suggests no such thing.

Seek here above all hooded poets; admire black-clad monks; [Col. 0362C] desire brothers who love religion, prayer, and reading. Suppose nothing painted or counterfeit among these men; fear no admixture of vice. For justice, the guardian of virtues, permits nothing to waver upon our mountain, where charity is mistress. This is said of those who dwell upon the middle mountain. But those who occupy the other two peaks of Parnassus are reckoned among that household which condemns the first beginnings of articulated speech to perpetual silence, and which remains religious to such an extent that it never answers unless called or awakened. If you are religious, approve the resemblance; if you are one who has believed,* approve the solitude; if you are a grammarian and a lover of reading, approve the condition of their common life. These things are found among us, dearest brother.

## LETTER XXXIII. Brother GISLEBERT to the venerable and dearest Father, lord PETER of Saint John: greeting.

[Col. 0362D]

After the most splendid letters, radiant with the brilliance of shining eloquence, which were sent to your reverence by my lords—whom, if it may be said, [Col. 0363A] I have deserved to have as brothers and companions—we too send this poor little page of our most impoverished tongue, rich only as the bearer of your greeting. I hope that you will readily pardon the presumptuous rusticity of a poorly fashioned and insufficiently polished style. What I especially fear, I ask you to make safe: namely, lest this delay in writing be thought to have arisen from slowness or lukewarmness in a love less fervent in me, rather than from the reason set out below.

You yourself know that, since I am younger in age than all my companions, inferior in learning, and unequal in merit, I ought rather to follow them than to go before them. Therefore I yielded to my elders, gave honour to the older men, and presumed to write nothing [Col. 0363B] until I knew that all had written. Moreover, there is another reason: for, to confess the truth, not so much prudently as naturally, it has always clung to me that, although I may not be very quick to hear, I am nevertheless very slow to speak. See: it is not because I love less, but because of the reasons I have stated, that I write more slowly. Let my companions go before me in speaking; let them go before me in writing; but I shall never allow them to go before me in loving.

I judged it necessary to set this down beforehand, so that both the delay of the page sent might be excused and what follows might be heard with greater goodwill. Therefore, after the matters which you conveyed in particular to the common Father in your letter, you greeted the Father’s sons—namely, your brothers and companions—and honoured them sublimely with that great name of hermits. [Col. 0363C] I recognize myself as the son of the aforesaid Father; I recognize myself also as the son of a brother, though older, and as the brother of a youth of whom I seem more properly to be the son; hence I do not deny that I am a companion. Therefore I recognize that, among those greeted, I too have certainly been greeted. But can I likewise say that I know myself to be a hermit?

Indeed, as you write, we inhabit woods, and the leafy roofs of trees are often more familiar to us than the stone or brick roofs of houses. Yet we have not become hermits in that manner in which the sparrow is solitary upon the housetop. For it is not merely the surrounding thick shade of groves, but rather the society of mortals itself, far removed, that makes him solitary. But how are we solitary, when, after entering [Col. 0363D] the vast solitude of this wilderness, we have drawn such a multitude of people after us that we seem to have built a city rather than a wilderness? For, to say nothing of that tumultuous crowd which streams in bands from the entire surrounding region concerning its lawsuits, whether to settle them by mutual agreement or delimit them by judicial sentence: both the overseas East and the transalpine West send us such an abundance of envoys that scarcely would the vastest administrative care of any great king suffice to give them answers.

Why then is the name of hermits imposed on us? Or perhaps, when your foot began to walk more correctly, your tongue incurred a more serious limp, so that, straying from the truth, it said what it ought not to have said? For he who slips with his tongue limps more seriously than one who, with a swollen foot, treads the ground cautiously. Yet let it be granted that we truly are hermits and are truthfully called by the name of hermits. Then you, most valiant warrior, keenest soldier, victorious fighter, who for so long a time have learned to fight bravely in the battle-line of the brethren against the savagery of the roaring enemy, and who are marked with the glory of as many palms as wars you undertake against him—why do you not leave the camp? Why do you not gird yourself with that spiritual sword of yours? Why, finally, do you not join us solitaries, so as to enter with us into single combat against the public enemy? Behold, we all look for you; we all desire your arrival; and, if you come, you will prove that we new [Col. 0364B] hermits have you as companions.

## LETTER XXXIV. To the most serene Father and lord, PETER, though useless, nevertheless his devoted servant and son.

Since, as I see, your woods abound not only, as I had said, in hermits, but also in philosophers and poets, and since I once desired, although I did not attain, to pursue studies of that sort, I am now powerfully drawn—even though I cannot yet do so in a body weakened by illness—to inhabit those same woods with you in mind and through such conversation as I can manage. I had therefore intended to send something in verse, a thing formerly familiar both to woods and mountains and to me; but since that divine philosopher says, “Music in mourning is an untimely tale” (Ecclus. XXII), and we deal almost daily with the funerals of those dearest to us, I have ceased singing, for amid judgments of God so inscrutable I scarcely dare to speak.

For this reason above all I remained silent so long and made no timely reply to your sweet and most delightful letters and those of your venerable companions, which never cease to gladden my soul. For, to say nothing of the most learned and prettily playful letters of others, who could reply to your letter alone with a dignity equal to its elegance? Truly it is a sweet and piously playful letter, in which you so defend yourselves against the reproach of the woodland or hermit name that I am greatly pleased to have sinned in this way, since I receive praise instead of blows.

But what shall I say about the hymn of the greatest Father of the wilderness, [Col. 0364D] who until now had had no hymn and had not deigned to have one fitting his merits, until one was composed for him in the Cluniac wilderness by the chief master of his own order? It seems quite plain to me—although perhaps you did not think of this—that these hymns should be sent to those brothers who keep his body. For I believe that they will gladly sing of the miracles of their own place so splendidly described, lest, by continually singing of Maurus running upon the waters in that foolish and false song of which they may by now be weary, they torture him further.

You know how sweet it always is to me to speak with you about such matters. Hence it is that both now, and whenever you are absent, I am alone. Even if many are present and the whole world makes a din, without you I feel myself truly to be alone. Know also that your most famous city of Cluny, with one accord, daily longs for your imperial and most gracious countenance; and that we all greatly envy that mountain and wood, because, though we see them continually, their intervention prevents us from seeing the object of our desire. Yet when we consider more closely the reason for which you are there, we endure your absence, though painfully, with equanimity.

May we see you sound and safe soon, and possess you for ever, holy lord Father. May your dearest companions and fellow-philosophers also flourish again and ever thrive with you—if indeed they deserve to be reckoned under even this name. They rejected so vehemently the title of hermits, by which I had sought to honour them, that I did not get off unpunished for not calling them Fauns and Satyrs instead. For I have so many pages, and am overwhelmed by so many urbane sayings most remote from hermit simplicity, that they could not have been more eager to clear themselves of the charge of being hermits than these strong young men were to find so many well-prepared skins and assail one poor, lame old man with such great encomia.

May all who are with you flourish in the Lord. After these playful things by which we somehow relieve an anxious life, let us also, in earnest, remember one another in holy prayers. Forgive the poor page and worthless writing, because, owing both to your absence and frequent funerals, [Col. 0365C] and to the continuing weakness of my foot, I scarcely feel inclined to do anything. I ask also that this little page of mine, and another smaller one which gave us material for so great a consolation, be kept for me. For I too embrace and preserve your letters most diligently.

## LETTER XXXV. Brother PETER, humble abbot of the Cluniac monks, to the venerable and dearest brother and son PETER: greeting, grace, and blessing.

Wherever my journey leads me, you nevertheless are always with me. This is a miracle: a man confined in one place accompanies those who travel everywhere and is not absent from them for even a moment of time. This happens by the mind, not the body; by affection, not effect; by charity, not companionship. You are indeed [Col. 0365D] at leisure, and we are occupied; but we do not wish your leisure to be wholly idle. Whatever we do not sow with us concerning our dearest matters, we customarily leave to you. Books, and especially Augustinian books, as you know, are more precious among us than gold. Yet those which I have produced as humble works may perhaps be no less dear.

Accordingly, we interrupt your leisure and do not wish it to be entirely holiday, so that you may send us some comforter from the Augustinians for our laborious journey, together with our letters and the Life of Lord Matthew the bishop—

[Note: “The Life of Lord Matthew the bishop”: bishop of Albano; it is found in its entirety in Book II of the *Miracles*.]

—since the book written against the heretics—

[Note: “The book against the heretics”: namely, the Petrobrusians and Henricians, concerning whom see below.]

—is lacking, as though they were conceptions and offspring of your own heart.

## LETTER XXXVI. Brother PETER, humble abbot of Cluny, to the illustrious and magnificent prince, lord LOUIS, glorious king of the Franks: may he happily reign here and behold the King of kings in his kingdom and splendour.

[Col. 0366A]

Although I cannot accompany, as it goes to foreign lands, the army of the eternal King which through you, an earthly king, he has resolved to arm against the enemies of his cross, nevertheless I desire to support it with devotion, prayer, counsel, and assistance, of whatever kind and degree I am able. Nor is this surprising. For who, even the least marked with the Christian name, would not be stirred at so great and astonishing a movement of the army of the Lord of Hosts? Who would not gird himself with all the powers of his soul to assist, according to his measure, this heavenly expedition?

In our time ancient ages are now renewed, and in the days of new grace the miracles of the ancient people are restored. Moses went forth from Egypt and destroyed the kings of the Amorites with their subject peoples. Joshua succeeded him and, by God’s command, overthrew the kings of the Canaanites with countless nations; having exterminated the ungodly, he divided that land by lot among what was then God’s people (Num. XXI, etc.; Josh. VI, etc.). Going forth from the furthest bounds of the western region—indeed, from the very setting of the sun—the Christian king threatens the East and, armed with Christ’s cross, attacks the impious people of Arabs or Persians who are attempting again to subject the Holy Land to themselves.

Those Jewish leaders shone greatly and surpassed modern princes in holiness of life; yet they do not now seem in some manner superior—indeed, perhaps they are inferior—to this king of Christians. By God’s command they destroy profane peoples through military force and claim their lands for God and themselves. This king too, by the will and command of that same God, will destroy the Saracen enemies of the true faith and will strive to subject their lands to God, not to himself. They fulfilled divine commands and laboured in military affairs partly in hope of an earthly reward. This king exposes and offers up to God his kingdom, wealth, and life itself, not so that he, a great king, may gain anything earthly in the world, but so that after the end of his mortal kingdom he may be crowned with honour and glory by the King of kings.

Therefore certain and exalted victory will not fail a king armed more with heavenly than earthly weapons; nor, however great it may be, will eastern barbarism be able to resist the army of the living God. For who could resist those who, wholly leaving behind honours, riches, pleasures, and even their homeland with their parents, have chosen to follow their Christ, to labour for him, to fight for him, to die for him, and to live for him? Who, I say, can oppose on earth the army of him who said of himself: “All power has been given to me in heaven and on earth” (Matt. XXVIII)? Although he received this power from God in the humanity which he assumed for humankind’s sake, he nevertheless possessed it from eternity as true God.

But [Col. 0367A] what will it profit to pursue and persecute the enemies of Christian hope in foreign or remote regions if wicked, blasphemous Jews, far worse than Saracens, not far from us but in our midst, freely and boldly blaspheme, trample underfoot, and defile Christ and all Christian sacraments with impunity? How shall zeal for God consume the children of God if the Jews, the supreme enemies of Christ and Christians, escape altogether untouched in this way? Has the king of Christians forgotten what was once said by a holy king of the Jews? “Do I not hate those who hate you, Lord,” he says, “and waste away because of your enemies? I hated them with perfect hatred” (Ps. CXXXVIII).

If Saracens are to be detested because, although they confess with us that Christ was born from a Virgin and agree with us in much concerning him, they nevertheless deny that he is God and Son of God—which is the greater matter—and deny his death and resurrection, in which the whole sum of our salvation lies, how much more are Jews to be execrated and hated, who hold absolutely nothing concerning Christ or the Christian faith, and reject, blaspheme, and mock his virgin birth and all the sacraments of human redemption? I do not say this in order to sharpen the royal or Christian sword for the killing of those impious persons, because I recall what is written concerning them in the divine Psalm, where the Prophet speaks thus in God’s Spirit: “God has shown me concerning my enemies: do not kill them” (Ps. LVIII).

For God does not wish them to be utterly killed or wholly extinguished, but, for greater torment and greater disgrace, preserved in a life worse than death, like Cain the fratricide. For when Cain, after shedding his brother’s blood, said to God, “Everyone who finds me will kill me” (Gen. IV), it was said to him: “No,” says God, “you will not die by death as you suppose, but you shall be groaning and a fugitive upon the earth which opened its mouth and received your brother’s blood from your hand” (ibid.).

Thus the most just severity of God acts, and will continue to act until the end of the world itself, concerning condemned and condemnable Jews from the very time of Christ’s passion and death. Since they shed Christ’s blood—indeed, the blood of their brother according to the flesh—they are servants, miserable, fearful, groaning, and fugitives upon [Col. 0367D] the earth, until, according to the prophet, the remnant of the wretched nation (Isa. X), once the fullness of the Gentiles has been called, is converted to God; and thus, according to the Apostle, “all Israel may be saved” (Rom. XI).

I urge not that they be killed, but that they be punished in a manner fitting their wickedness. And what method of punishing those impious persons is more fitting than one by which iniquity is condemned and charity assisted? What is more just than that they should be deprived of the goods they fraudulently acquired, and that what they wickedly stole should be taken away from thieves—and, worse still, from thieves hitherto bold and unpunished? What I say is known to all. For they fill their granaries with grain, their cellars with wine, their purses with coins, and their chests with gold or silver, not so much from simple farming, lawful military service, or any honest and useful occupation, [Col. 0368A] as from what, as I have said, they deceitfully take from Christians, and from things secretly bought from thieves, purchasing objects of the greatest value at a low price.

If a nocturnal thief has broken into Christ’s Church, and with sacrilegious audacity has carried away candlesticks, ewers, censers, even sacred crosses or consecrated chalices, he flees Christians and takes refuge with Jews; and there, secure in culpable security, he not only finds hiding-places but sells to the synagogues of Satan what he has stolen from holy churches. He disposes of the vessels of Christ’s body and blood to the killers of his body and shedders of his blood—those who then inflicted upon him, while he dwelt among mortals, every insult and injury within their power, and who now, while he sits in the majesty of eternal divinity, do not cease to assail him with every blasphemy of speech they dare.

Nor are those sacred vessels, which are held captive among them, as once among the Chaldeans, in the manner I have described, free from injury although they are insensible. Christ certainly feels in these vessels consecrated to himself, which themselves feel nothing, the continuing Jewish insults; for, as I have often heard from truthful men, those impious persons apply these heavenly vessels to such uses to the dishonour of Christ himself and of us—something horrible to think and detestable to say. Moreover, that such heinous theft and Jewish trading might be safer, an old but truly diabolical law has been enacted by Christian princes themselves: if an ecclesiastical object, or, worse, a sacred vessel, is found in the possession of a Jew, the Jew is not compelled either to restore the thing held through sacrilegious theft or to identify the wicked thief. A very great and detestable crime remains unpunished in a Jew, which in a Christian is punished by the horrific death of hanging. The Jew grows fat and abounds in luxuries from the very cause for which the Christian is hanged by the noose.

Let the ill-gotten abundance of Jewish wealth therefore be removed, or at least greatly reduced; and let the Christian army, which in order to conquer Saracens spares neither its own money nor lands out of love for Christ its Lord, not spare treasures most wickedly acquired by Jews. Let life be reserved to them, but money taken away, so that through the hands of Christians, aided by the money of blaspheming Jews, the audacity of the unbelieving Saracens may be conquered. Even unwillingly, let Jewish wealth serve Christian peoples, just as formerly, when their fathers pleased God, the wealth of the Egyptians was, by God’s command, given to them for service (Exod. II). I have written these things to you, gracious king, out of love for Christ, for you, and for the Christian army; for it would be foolish and, I think, not free from divine offence if the wealth of the profane did not serve far more abundantly a holy expedition to which, in an appropriate measure, the resources of Christians ought to be devoted.

## LETTER XXXVII. Brother PETER, humble abbot of Cluny, to the glorious and magnificent prince ROGER, king of Sicily: may he possess the dignity and glory of good kings.

[Col. 0369A]

Thanks be to the omnipotent King of kings, who has distinguished your Highness among all the kings and princes of the Christian world with a certain special magnificence of glory, and singularly exalted you with the renown of a glorious name, so that, though you have many partners in the royal title, you are found to have none or almost none equal to you in greatness of spirit, prudence, and virtue. Sicily, Calabria, Apulia, and Italy subject to you in no small part in certain other regions demonstrate this. Before your time they were either refuges of Saracens, [Col. 0369B] dens of marauders, or caves of robbers; now, by the grace of the merciful God inspiring your efforts and aiding your labours, they have become a dwelling-place of peace, a home of tranquillity, and the peaceful and most delightful realm, as it were, of another peaceful Solomon.

Would that—the God who knows all secrets bearing witness, I say this not as flattery—would that the regions of wretched and unfortunate Tuscany, together with the adjoining provinces, were joined to your prosperous dominion, and that affairs in the most ruined condition were united to the peaceful body of your realm! Truly then divine and human affairs would not, as now, be thrown into confusion with no order preserved; cities, castles, boroughs, villages, public roads, and even churches consecrated to God would not be exposed to murderers, sacrilegious persons, and plunderers. Penitents, pilgrims, clerics, monks, abbots, priests, and even priests of the highest rank—bishops, archbishops, primates, and patriarchs—would not be handed over to such men, robbed, sold off; and what shall I say? Beaten and killed.

All these things, indeed, and many similar acts, so impious and so execrable, would cease once cut down by the sword of royal justice; the rapacious claws of bears, leopards, and wolves would grow weak; and, as was said of blessed and great Job, “All the beasts of the field, which now rage for prey, would be at peace with you” (Job V). But the unhappy land still pays the penalty of its crimes and groans beneath the divine scourge, because in all these things [Col. 0369D] God’s anger has not yet turned away, but his hand is still stretched out (Isa. V, IX, X).

Yet I cherish the greatest hope and trust in Jesus, my salvation and that of all his people: that the Lord will hear the desire of many poor persons who desire this, and his ear will hear the preparation of their heart. But lest the corrupt hearts of certain men, who measure others by themselves, suspect that I speak with one heart and another, or that I am a seller of oil, my speech must be restrained, lest, if by chance this letter sent to you reaches any such person, they meditate vain things and suspect falsehoods. For my witness and the one conscious of my thoughts in the heights knows that I speak only as I think; and for no other reason than that you may know that I think what I think, and that your royal nobility may be more and more encouraged toward better things, recognizing that I think these things, along with many others.

For, as I have often told your Majesty, and it is true, for these reasons I have sincerely loved you, for twenty years, above all the kings and princes of our time—with one exception, who is dead—as a lover of peace and avenger of crimes; and I have resolved to preserve this affection toward you until my last day. For this reason, in the presence of Roman pontiffs, kings, princes, persons great and small, I have always extolled these and similar virtues of yours; and I have most earnestly commended your person and kingdom to almighty God and to religious communities, both ours and others. But enough concerning these matters.

Now I wish your greatness to know [Col. 0370B] that I came to Rome, stayed there for several weeks, and, after settling almost countless affairs of the Church of Cluny, resolved to make my way as far as you. But just as in past years I attempted this in vain, so I wished it now to no effect, because recalled by the manifold concerns of the said Church, I could not do so. I had a twofold reason for coming to you: both that I might see your person, dearer to me than that of other kings, as I have said, as I had wished a thousand times; and that I might make known to you in particular, as a king whom we believe loves us, the needs of your monastery of Cluny, which are unknown to you.

Since I could not accomplish this myself, as has been said, I have sent in my place to your most noble generosity an honourable and wise man, our venerable brother A., sacristan of Cluny, so that he may say what I would say and, if it does not displease you, hear also what I would hear. Your Church of Cluny cries to you and knocks at the door of a friend, that, just as it has moved your kindness to love it, so it may move your generosity to do it good. Necessity itself presses this request, as do the boundless expenses of that great and famous monastery, known to all, which from the first stone of its foundation customarily collects from everyone so that it may pour out to all.

From its beginning it was made not merely a lodging-place for outsiders, nor only an asylum for refugees, but, if I may so speak, a public treasury of the Christian commonwealth. It acts more sparingly toward its own people and more lavishly toward outsiders; it considers not what it can do but what the visitor wishes. For this reason neither its own resources nor those of others suffice, because the quantity of its expenditures is far greater than the generosity of its donors. Necessity is increased because the customary income from benefactions has failed along with good kings and princes: for the powerful men of the neighbouring lands today, even if they have the will to benefit us, lack the means.

Thus Cluny has many debtors and few benefactors. The German king loves Cluny; the Spanish king loves it; the English king loves it; and another king nearer to us, the king of the Franks, loves it too—and, although these and similar persons bear us great love, the effect of that love is almost nothing. They equal their predecessors in loving but differ from them in giving. In the words of the Apostle John—spoken not as a reproach—they love “in word or tongue,” not “in deed or truth” (1 John III). And why say more? To speak to you in the words of the Psalmist speaking to God: “To you the poor man is left; you will be a helper to the orphan” (Ps. IX).

For the kings just mentioned have left the Church of Cluny to you, as though deprived of its former helpers, so that, because they wish to be generous to us but, as they say, cannot, we ask that you, who through the grace of the supreme King can do so, may also be willing. Therefore lay up for yourselves, according to the Lord’s words, treasures in heaven, where neither rust nor moth destroys and where thieves do not break in or steal (Matt. VI). If it please you, supply in deed the bare affection of others, so that, as you surpass almost all kings and princes of our age in many virtues, as stated above, you may also excel in this work so divine and fruitful. Whatever has been said insufficiently, you may ask and hear from the aforesaid bearer of this letter, a prudent man.

## LETTER XXXVIII. Brother PETER, humble abbot of Cluny, to our venerable and dearest lord, the prior of the Charterhouse, and the other brothers: the same salvation as to himself.

[Note: “The lord prior of the Charterhouse”: Basil, Guigo’s successor, to whom he also writes below, Book VI, Letter 40.]

I acknowledge what I owe you; I acknowledge that, above all mortals devoted to religion but not bound by the vow of profession to our Church, I have always loved, cherished, and venerated you more dearly in the Lord. I have done so until now, still do so, and shall do so as long as breath remains in my nostrils. Christ is the cause of this love of mine toward you: since I cannot personally love, embrace, and honour him in himself, I do so in his vessels—that is, in you, in whom he dwells.

Your reverend charity wrote to me asking that I send you certain books of Ambrose. Your request was welcome to a man who often expects to be visited by your letters or messengers. He always desires this, but rarely obtains what he desires. I do what you wrote; I send what you request. But to whom? The letter you sent spoke only of books, but said nothing about the persons to whom they were to be sent. Not so—not, to make a familiar complaint among friends—[Col. 0371D] did Lord Guigo, of pious and holy memory, the prior, write; rather, in epistolary fashion, after a greeting first given, he appropriately showed the affection of his kindly heart in the words that followed.

But perhaps you feared being verbose among us, or, lest we ourselves be verbose, instructed us by such brevity. Perhaps you thought, though you did not say it, what holy Job said to his friends: “My friends are talkative; my eye distils tears to God” (Job XVI). But to speak either figuratively or literally, I answer both points: as far as the affection of my heart is concerned, if you spoke always, you would seem silent to me; if I spoke always to you, I would seem mute to myself.

Send through the bearer of this letter, or through any other trustworthy person, pledges for the books I have sent—not because this gives greater assurance of preserving them, but so that the command of our holy Father Hugh concerning such matters may be observed. Farewell; always remember us in the Lord.

## LETTER XXXIX. Brother PETER, humble not so much abbot as servant of the venerable and most beloved lords and brothers serving almighty God at Cluny: the fullness of all salvation and blessing from the Lord.

I have heard, dearest brothers, and before I recently departed from you had partly seen, that the hand of the Lord has touched you; that the overflowing scourge has passed through you; that the sword of divine judgment, our sins having deserved this, has cut off many and precious members of our body. Like ripe and unripe fruits shaken from a great tree by a violent wind, they fall together; and now, by their continual fall, they have almost covered the whole ground beneath. The living fall upon the dead, and the very burier collapses over the one he has buried. At no age of life is there any security: young men fall mingled with old men, adolescents with the decrepit, and almost children themselves, by dying, go before centenarians. Truly the day of the Lord, as He Himself says, comes as a thief in the night (Matt. XXIV; 1 Thess. V; 2 Pet. III), stealing away both the vigilant and the unwary alike; and scarcely does one who dies perceive that he is dying, since each is carried off by death before the mind of the dying person can fully turn back upon itself.

That great and celebrated, indeed heavenly, number of Christ’s sheep is daily diminished, and, as it is fitting to believe, is gathered to its supreme Shepherd in pastures ever green. We who live suffer—and though we do not know for how long, we still remain. We suffer, I say, losses to be mourned and wept for with every fountain of tears: that we are presently deprived of the bodily fellowship and customary assistance of so many brethren, so useful and so holy, dying among us and in various places. All ought indeed to grieve for these, but above all I. For how could I not grieve more than all others, I to whom grief belongs more by office, more by obligation? For, to speak first of office: what father has ever been so hard as iron, so stony, that he could see—not so many, not such choice sons, but even one lowly son—dying without bitter grief and many tears?

And, to add what belongs to obligation: what father was ever so indebted to his sons as I am to you? What father ever found in carnal sons such obedience, such sincere love, such great and ready services toward himself, as I have found in you? Who, taught by repeated experience itself, could ever feel such sweetness toward any beloved persons as I feel toward you? If I crossed the Italian or Spanish Alps, you crossed with me in affection and mind. If I went to Rome—as often happened—you clung to me as inseparable companions. If I crossed seas, you sailed with me in spirit, devotion, and prayers. If I began even slightly to fall ill, you too were sick with me through compassion and great distress of heart. I could never labour without you; I had no strength to undergo any dangers without you. How then shall I be able, without the greatest and deepest grief of heart, to see so many and such dear ones torn from my side by death so frequent and almost sudden? How shall I see my own bowels torn away from my innermost parts without groaning? How shall I bear with an even mind losses so great—not of gold or silver, but of what is far dearer and more precious than every treasure: of so many brethren?

Former ages have returned: we no longer read of them, but experience them. It seems that the angel of the Lord has stretched out his hand over our Jerusalem; yet I trust in the mercy of almighty God, that he has done so not to destroy it but to correct it. Would that, in this calamity—or rather in God’s eternal ordinance—I were David, that I might in some respect meet so great a disaster, so that, when the wrath of the Lord had been turned into mercy, it might be said to the smiting angel: “It is enough; now restrain your hand!” (2 Kings XXIV.) Yet I can say with David, without the charge of falsehood: “I am he who sinned; I am he who acted wickedly” (ibid.). Perhaps I may say this also: “But these sheep, what have they done? I beg you, let your fury be turned away from your people” (ibid.).

But what am I doing? I who had purposed to console you seem to make you desolate; I who ought to have lessened your sorrow perhaps increase it by such words. We must plainly not linger longer in these lamentations, lest I be accused of adding sorrow to your sorrow and tears to your tears. This is forbidden by the apostolic saying known throughout the world, which admonishes those grieving over a similar death of loved ones: “Do not grieve as the rest do, who have no hope” (1 Thess. IV). And although, as the Book of Wisdom commands, “tears are to be shed over the dead” (Ecclus. XXXVIII), yet they must be moderated by the mean of reason, lest they exceed what is fitting.

I indeed restrain you from tears, though while writing these words I could not restrain them myself. Yet let us moderate sorrow that exceeds its proper bounds, and in this respect let such misfortunes be borne with manly courage; while in secret, before God, let us pour out our souls in prayers and tears, both for ourselves and for these brethren. Let us weep for the repose of the departed; let us weep also for our own salvation, we who shall at some time—and perhaps even soon—follow them. None of us can say: “What is my soul amid so great a creation? The Most High does not care for us; he pays heed neither when we live nor when we die.” The Apostle openly confronts this detestable opinion, without veils, saying: “Whether we live, we live to the Lord; whether we die, we die to the Lord. Therefore, whether we live or die, we are the Lord’s” (Rom. XIV). And elsewhere: “For this reason Christ died and rose again, that he might be Lord both of the living and of the dead” (ibid.). And the Lord himself says: “God is not God of the dead but of the living; for all live to him” (Luke XX).

Certainly, as your reverence knows, nothing in human affairs occurs by chance; no Fortune confuses the deaths or lives of human beings. All things are weighed in a just balance; and although the abyss of God’s judgments is hidden from us, we nevertheless do not doubt that it is wholly just. Not one sparrow falls to earth without the heavenly Father (Luke XII), and shall any servant of God end mortal life without that same heavenly Father? All the hairs of our head are numbered (Matt. X), and are those whose hairs they are without number before eternal Wisdom? She numbers our steps (Job XXI), and does she not also order our life and death?
