Since these things stand established among you, dearest brothers, your minds must not be afflicted with sorrow beyond measure; rather, your whole mind, whole purpose, and whole devotion must be lifted up to God.

He indeed kills and makes alive, brings down to hell and brings back. But far be it from you to suppose that he who, having himself become man, came by his death to make the dead alive, intends to put you to death when converted to him, who is true life, through the fruit of repentance. In my faith, he does not do this for that reason; rather, by terrifying the living through the deaths of their departed brethren, he more vehemently kindles them to repentance, while gathering the dead as the radiant lilies of his garden—lilies white with chastity, fragrant with examples and sweetness of virtues. By deaths of this kind he does not wish to cut you off from himself, but, like a diligent husbandman tending a vineyard, to prune you; for, as we read in the Song of Songs, “the time of pruning has come” (Cant. II).

The time has come when, to the servant saying, “Lord, what you commanded has been done, and there is still room,” he will answer: “Go out into the roads and hedges, and compel them to enter, that my house may be filled” (Luke XIV). Oh, how many have been compelled to enter unwillingly, that his house might be filled! For who ever wished to die? Not even Peter himself, to whom it was said: “When you are old, you will stretch out your hands, and another will gird you and lead you where you do not wish to go” (John XXI). If Peter did not wish to die, held back by a certain human fear, what wonder if Peter’s disciple too does not wish to die through the same fear? If Paul, who said, “We do not wish to be unclothed, but to be clothed upon, so that what is mortal may be swallowed up by life” (2 Cor. V), did not wish to die, what wonder if, drawn by nature and habit, you fear to depart from this present life?

Yet, although carnal affection protested, Peter gladly embraced death on the cross for his Lord; and Paul, who had said, “For me to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (Phil. I), most joyfully suffered his head to be cut off by the sword. Thus Peter and Paul were, in one respect, willing and yet compelled to die; and our brethren are compelled to the same end by the same Master of the household, that God’s house may be filled.

Therefore the gracious call of the Father must be received with joy. Though the road of death by which one passes seems hard, the life to which one arrives is most joyful and everlasting. And you, Jesus Christ, creator of all and redeemer of your own, who said: “He who believes in me, even though he die, shall live” (John XI); and again: “I did not come to judge the world, but to save the world” (John III); and again: “My sheep hear my voice, and I the Lord know them, and they follow me; and I give them eternal life, and they shall never perish, nor shall anyone snatch them from my hand” (John X)—you, I say, Jesus Christ, author of our temporal and eternal life, grant that these sheep of your flock, believing in you, whether dead or dying, may live for ever.

Receive them, most gracious Shepherd; do not permit them to be devoured by wolves, nor deliver to beasts the souls that confess you. Be present also, most blessed Virgin, Mother of that same Saviour and Redeemer of ours; do not in any way permit those who place their most special confidence in you, beyond all others after him, to be confounded in their hope. And you, supreme apostles of God, chief princes of the world, universal fathers indeed of all Christians but our own special fathers, to whom they rendered almost continual service and to whom they were specially entrusted by God: will you not aid them as they fail? Will you not be present to them as they die? Will you not defend them from the assaults of wicked enemies? Remember your principality, and do not suffer any of those entrusted to you to be snatched away from the prince of darkness. Let them experience now the time they have always hoped for from you; and since the keys of the kingdom of heaven are in your hands, we humbly and devoutly entreat you with them: after others have been admitted, do not permit these in any way to be excluded from that same kingdom.

Therefore, dearest brothers to whom I write this letter, kindle the censers of your minds with divine fire, as Aaron or the sons of Levi; send forth to heaven the smoke of holy prayers as of spices; and, standing between the dead and the living, appease the merciful majesty of almighty God with the whole effort of your souls, yourselves made for him a sacrifice of contrite and humbled heart. I would have returned to you myself and preferred to say in person what I write; and, as the holy man says, “I would comfort you with words and shake my head over you” (Job XVI), had not the journey I have begun toward the lord pope, to whom for certain reasons I am hastening greatly, prevented me. If by God’s favour I return safely from there, I shall not pass by until I see those whom my soul loves.

Meanwhile, what I cannot do in person I do while absent; and, by virtue of our office, on behalf of almighty God, author and creator of all things; and of the most blessed Mary ever Virgin, mother of God and of our Lord Jesus Christ; and of the supreme apostles Peter and Paul, of all the apostles, of Saint Benedict our father and master, and of all the saints: insofar as we can and know how, with heart and voice we absolve all of you, and your holy community, whether remaining at Cluny or elsewhere, from all sins whatsoever. We trust in the abundance of his grace, he who said also to us in his disciples: “Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven” (Matt. XVIII). Farewell, my own bowels; and when you remember yourselves before God, I ask you, if you please, do not forget us also.

## LETTER XL

To the venerable and most dear brother and our friend, Lord Theobald, by God’s grace bishop of Paris, brother Peter, humble abbot of Cluny: greetings and the sincere affection of love in the Lord.

[Note: Theobald, bishop of Paris. This Theobald had been prior of Saint-Martin-des-Champs, of the Cluniac order. From being prior he became bishop of Paris in 1140; he governed the Church until 1151, and after his death wished at last to be buried in his own monastery.]

Your reverence, most dear to me, was pleased to console us in our desolation—so great and manifold because of the deaths of our brethren—and, as Job says, by sharing our suffering “to shake your head over us” (Job XVI). When your letter was brought to me, I would then have written the same thing I write now, and would have offered such thanks as I could for your friendly consolation. But because then I was not able, I did not do so; and because even now I am scarcely able, I scarcely do so now. Nevertheless, as I am able, I earnestly give thanks to your graciousness for your concern for us: neither manifold business, nor the pomp of honour, nor the height of episcopal office has alienated you from the Cluniac body. Rather, in accordance with the Apostle, keeping “the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace” (Eph. IV), I see you rejoice with those who rejoice and weep with those who weep (Rom. XII).

And rightly so. A common loss demands common mourning, so that we may mourn the deaths of loved ones for at least a few days, as the ancients mourned them for many months. They mourned their dead, and faithful persons could not be recalled from weeping for a long time—faithful toward their living friends and affectionate toward the departed. Those who were devout sometimes did this for the devout; even the impious sometimes suffered this from attachment of love toward the impious; and, although for differing reasons, all alike were held by the same affection toward their dead. Since, therefore, we have both the devout and the impious as examples of mourning, is it not inhuman or bestial if we do not mourn our own dead—so many, so great, so useful, so necessary?

This should indeed be done before human beings, but with moderation; before God, however, with perseverance. Unfruitful grief must be turned into fruitful tears, so that tears which can no longer restore the bodies of loved ones to us may endeavour, insofar as they can, to commend their souls to God. We do this sometimes, and our people do it more often; do the same yourselves, if you please, for those dead men were your true friends: they sincerely loved you and honoured you with all their affection. Do this not only as a monk, but, what is far greater, as a bishop: that is, not only assist them with your own prayers, but moreover commend them to the mercy of the Almighty through the prayers of your subjects.

What remains for me to say except what Job said when he had lost his possessions, sons, and daughters? “The Lord gave; the Lord has taken away. As it pleased the Lord, so it has been done; blessed be the name of the Lord” (Job I).

## LETTER XLI

To our venerable and most dear brother and sons, Lord Odo, prior, and the rest serving almighty God at Saint-Martin-des-Champs, brother Peter, humble abbot of Cluny: greetings, and from the author of all good things the fullness of all grace and blessing.

[Note: Odo, prior—namely, of Saint Martin, after Theobald.]

What shall I say? What shall I speak? In harsh circumstances, and especially at the death of our most dear brother and son Hugh, I thought I could forestall you by writing, forestall you by lamenting, forestall you by weeping. But, as I see, you have forestalled me in letters and anticipated me in complaints; yet you have not anticipated me in tears. You mourned his funeral after his death; but I, while he was still alive, because I did not doubt that he would die, mourned his death before he died. You have surpassed me in writing, but not in lamenting. I wept first because I saw him first failing; but I could not write first, because I was not allowed to do so by unceasing business—those importunate torturers of my life.

At last, now that I am at some point permitted, I write and mourn together with you, though absent, the loss of our common brother, son, and friend. I have matter for mourning that scarcely could a camel bear on its high and strong shoulders if it were written down; you have as much as you yourselves know, and as I perhaps do not wholly fail to know. To speak first of matters belonging to myself: among all people under heaven, who for twenty years and more has so faithfully, steadfastly, and perseveringly borne and endured the burdens imposed upon him by me—undertaken devoutly for the cause of God and of myself—spending all the strength he possessed in enduring them and working with me?

And, to add matters belonging to you: who loved your commonwealth more than he did, or so cultivated it? Who so encouraged both me and all our brethren to love, protect, cherish, and defend it? These matters, briefly stated—which, if stated more fully, would require another time and leisure—admonish and urge us not to forget, even after death, a brother, son, and friend so beloved, dear, and unique; but, if we were or are true friends, to show this more now that he is dead than if he were alive. Let us mourn his funeral with devout compassion; let us accompany his soul rather with hidden tears and prayers, so that, since we can no longer show him our affection by speaking with him or rejoicing with him, we may show it by praying, offering sacrifice, and weeping devoutly before God for his soul.

Let this be done among you especially for him; let it also be done for our prior; and, if you please, for the many holy, religious, and great men before God who have lately died among us. Their memory, as I well know, is in blessing; their remembrance will not be blotted out before God, but they shall be in everlasting remembrance and, by God’s grace, shall not fear evil tidings. Let vain tears, then, extracted by unconsidered grief before men, now cease; and let groans poured out before God for the salvation of these men succeed them, together with prayers. May your holy community flourish, acceptable to God, a joy to us, and, by God’s favour, always advancing from good to better.

## LETTER XLII

To my venerable and most dear lord of Rupes, brother Peter, humble abbot of Cluny: greetings, which are in Christ Jesus.

Although I seem to be a late writer of an event that followed, and accuse myself of slowness, I am nevertheless largely excused by the flood of manifold affairs which sometimes rush fiercely upon us like waves of the sea. More pressed and fatigued by them than usual during this Easter season, I am now at last breathing somewhat from my cares and say what should not be passed over, write what should be made known to your charity. Had I found this opportunity earlier, I would have allowed no one to precede me in this report to you.

Our brother and son John, a good young man worthy of love and remembrance, whom your kindly affection had entrusted to me, and whom I was not permitted to keep as long as I wished, was lately—namely, on the Ides of May—removed from human affairs, and exchanged this present life, as I trust in the Lord, for a better one. I know that you grieve; I know that you bear this heavily. Nor is it strange. You wished him to have a longer life, so that you might later rejoice in its greater usefulness to himself and to many others. But if you grieve and take it heavily, be consoled: in these matters you are not alone.

You are plainly not alone in this; for, to confess the truth to a friend, I scarcely recall anyone among our brethren, for a long time now, whose companionship was dearer through manner of life and character than John’s, or whose death was more bitter to everyone. The grief of all bears witness to this, as do the tears of almost everyone: tears shed while he was ill, and poured out much more profusely as he died. I could scarcely have believed, unless I had seen it with my own eyes, that within the course of a few days he could imprint upon the hearts of so many such affection for himself as he did imprint and deserve over the succession of many years.

They hoped to gather from him, as from a good tree, the best fruits in their proper season; he held out the fairest promise of such fruits in the blossoms of his kindly conduct and sweet character, surpassing almost all the young men of our cloister. But alas! “The grass has withered and the flower has fallen, because the Spirit of the Lord breathed upon it” (Isa. XL). He was taken away, I think, lest perhaps with the passage of time wickedness should change the understanding he had begun so well, or lest deceit—which sometimes corrupts even those deeply devoted to religion—should deceive his soul (Wisdom IV).

Our young man did not forget his salvation because of the infirmity of the flesh, nor could bodily suffering turn him away from care for his soul. For as soon as he felt himself burdened by the illness he had contracted more than he had hoped, he turned his whole heart and effort to those things which follow death. Although he had not yet despaired of life, while his senses still remained sound and the reason of his mind was not diminished in any way, he confessed with complete sincerity to our aged men, tried and proven in religion, as he afterward told me himself, everything that he could recall concerning his past life.

Not content with this, though that confession might have sufficed for him, he sent messengers to me, asked me to come, and begged that I would absolve him as my office required. At that time I too was ill and, according to our custom, could not easily visit the sick. At last he compelled me myself; and although ill, though not so ill as he, I came to one who was ill. He was oppressed by a more severe than usual suffering of illness, yet his mind continued sound. Why say more? At last he repeated everything as though from the beginning, omitting not even his daily and childish faults. He wept over trivial sins as though they were most grave, and, as fully as he could, with a most sincere and sorrowful confession most affectionately commended his soul and body to the gracious Saviour.

And what must by no means be passed over: when, in the course of that confession, the memory of the glorious Mother of the Lord arose on some occasion, sobs were added to sobs and tears to tears; and the continuation of his confession was interrupted at the name of her by whose aid he especially hoped to be saved, through an increase of tearful devotion. Again, when the pressure of illness sometimes bore more heavily upon him as he confessed, he said: “Holy Spirit, help me; and if I have forgotten anything in my confession, bring it back to my memory.” Saying this not once or twice only, but often, he taught me how carefully one ought to confess greater sins, since he himself confessed even lesser ones with such zeal.

Then, absolved by me and assigned penance, after he had recited at my command the confession of faith and the Lord’s Prayer, he survived two days. Throughout those two days, casting aside all concern for the body, he devoted his whole mind and whatever strength he could possess solely to invoking divine mercy; and in this intention of mind he closed the last day of his life.

I therefore urge you, as a friend exhorts an intimate friend, not to attribute the common failing of human nature to yourselves alone as though it were something strange and solitary; nor, since you yourself must someday die, to afflict yourselves beyond measure, like those who have no hope, concerning your brother’s good and truly Christian departure (1 Thess. IV). It does not become a religious person to be displeased by what pleases God. For he without whose will not one sparrow falls to earth could not be mistaken, so that brother John should die and fall to the ground, and be hidden in the earth by the service of burial, without his command or permission.

Direct all your zeal and love toward the departed to this end: as we and almost all our brethren, insofar as we can, assist him who has passed to eternal things through such spiritual aids as we can provide, so you too—indeed more than we, because you can do more—should help him as much as you are able. I had wished to return to you better the good man whom you entrusted to me; but, as I believe, what happened was better for me, for you, and for him: for him whom I could not restore to you, I returned into the keeping of God, from whom I had chiefly received him.

## LETTER XLIII

To the honourable and great priest of God, and most dear to us, Lord Geoffrey, renowned bishop of the holy Church of Chartres, brother Peter, humble abbot of Cluny: greetings and the affection of all love in the Lord.

[Note: Geoffrey, bishop of the Church of Chartres. He was the second of that name, to whom Saint Bernard also writes in Letters 55, 56, and 57. William, abbot, in Book II of the Life of that same Saint Bernard, chapter 6, and others, state that he was legate of the Apostolic See in Aquitaine.]

Before offering thanks, I shall preface complaints. I complain as a friend that so great, so dear, and so long-standing a friend has abandoned, disregarded, and cast me off as though I were a friend unknown to him, unseen, and untried. You seem to have done this not for a few days but for many years now. For since the Council of Pisa, held in Pope Innocent’s time, at which you were present and I too was not absent, I have read neither letters from you nor seen messengers from you, nor received anything that a friend usually hopes for from the side of a friend. I did indeed see letters and hear certain messengers, but they brought common business, not anything expressing the true affection of a friend. Therefore I say that I have seen nothing from your side and profess that I have heard nothing. Do I not therefore complain with reason? Do I not rightly become angry?

My soul loved you and still loves you. And why? Because I have always revered God in you, always honoured him in you, and loved the dwelling for the sake of the one dwelling within it. Although I am held in some degree of connection, for one reason or another, with nearly all Latin bishops, with you nevertheless—though perhaps you do not know it—I long ago prepared among the many chambers of my heart a singular dwelling place, and still preserve it. This is, as I said, because I venerate God in you, because I have always experienced you as a true and sincere worshipper of divine things.

For when shall I be able to enumerate your labours, your journeys and return journeys on behalf of the Church of God, Christ’s bride? When shall I be able to recount your love of religion and its carefully pursued increase everywhere? When shall I have strength to describe your frequent visitations of holy places themselves? Yet, my dearest friend, these things should be passed over; in these matters especially, the pen ought not to overflow beyond measure. For I believe—and indeed know—that you do not await human favour for your devout works, but eternal reward. Nevertheless, I have briefly touched upon these things so that you may know and remember both that I love you, why I have loved you, and why I love you still.

I am now unequal to giving thanks to your religious reverence, because I know that its benefits have surpassed my merits. For what return worthy of the things I learned through the prior of Nogent could I make? He wrote to me how much love you had shown toward the Church of Cluny, and especially toward himself and his own people, and how much you had demonstrated this not by affection alone but by deeds. For he said that you had recovered the church at Châteaudun—said formerly to have belonged to Cluny—from the canons of that church, from the viscount, advocate of the church, and finally from all who claimed to have some right in it, both by entreaties and by the force of justice; and that you restored it to your Church of Cluny, to which it had belonged by right.

[Note: The church at Châteaudun. That is, the Church of the Holy Sepulchre, which Geoffrey, viscount of Châteaudun, its first founder, ordered by testament to serve the monks of the basilica of Saint-Denis at Nogent, with all its appurtenances. We have said elsewhere that he himself had laid its first foundations. Accordingly Geoffrey, bishop of Chartres, wrested it away, both by prayers and by the force of justice, from the canons, the viscount—the advocate of that Church—and all others who claimed to have some right in it, and restored it to the Church of Cluny, to which it belonged by right, as our Peter shows here.

Yet because of this, all dispute between the monks and the viscount did not cease. For in the time of Stephen I, abbot of Cluny, it broke out again between Ivo, prior of Nogent, and Hugh, viscount of Châteaudun. Nevertheless, it too was soon settled by William, bishop of Chartres, fourth after the aforesaid Geoffrey, as appears from these words of the record of settlement: “William, by the grace of God elected bishop of the Church of Chartres, etc. Lest in the course of time the dispute between the Church of the Holy Sepulchre and the viscount—reformed by the zeal of our diligence into the peace of unity and the concord of tranquillity—should be disturbed in future times by the craftiness of wicked men, we have taken care to commit it to writing by decree of this present document. Therefore let all know that the dispute which was being conducted between Ivo, prior of Nogent, and Hugh, viscount of Châteaudun, concerning the customary dues of the borough of the Holy Sepulchre, in which borough the latter claimed certain customary dues for himself, was settled in our presence as follows, at the prayers of Stephen, venerable abbot of Cluny, and at the request of the aforesaid viscount, who granted that they would hold ratified whatever we should determine in this matter,” etc.]

For these things I give thanks indeed, but far greater thanks because in this action I recognize how greatly you love your Church of Cluny—to say it once more. You would formerly have recognized, and would still recognize, if you wished to experience it, how I love you and how truly I preserve this love in my heart. Why should I say more? Perhaps I ought to seem wordy, if I had not been silent for so long a time. But beside silence of so long duration, what speech can seem prolix?

Therefore, good, long-lived, and proven old man and bishop of God, remember—though I believe that it is always in your heart—that neither your remaining time nor mine can now be long in this miserable life. You indeed are older, but neither am I now young. What then remains for us except that all our speech should return to Jesus, the supreme priest and bishop of our souls; that our whole soul should sigh toward him; that our whole inner and outer person should pant after him? Already, almost according to his own words, the thief by night hastens to break into the house of our body. Already the master of the house hastens to come; already the cry made at midnight wakes those lying in their beds and says: “Behold, the bridegroom comes; go out to meet him” (Matt. XXV).

What use, then, will there now be in being a bishop? What use, if I may speak so, in being an abbot? What use in loving earthly things under the pretext of heavenly things? What use in loving perishable—indeed, already perishing—things beneath the shadow of eternal things? But I have become foolish. I seem, as the saying is, to teach Minerva; I seem to carry timber to the forest; I seem to pour a bottle of water into a mighty river. Yet truly I do not say this to teach, but, taking this small occasion, I lament my own misery; and because I do not know whither I am to be carried after death—which perhaps is not far away—I tremble.

Farewell in Jesus our salvation, lord bishop and most dear friend. Since I believe that by God’s grace you suffice for yourself, remember before the Lord me, who suffice for myself in nothing. Whatever spiritual or temporal good there is in our Church is yours.

## BOOK FIVE

[Col. 0381]

## LETTER I

To his beloved and venerable brother PETER, abbot of Saint Augustine at Limoges [Note: To Peter, abbot of Saint Augustine at Limoges. This Peter later became abbot of Saint Martial, succeeding Peter, prior of Cluny, in 1154, as is learned from the chronology of the abbots of Saint Martial. Roricius I, bishop of Limoges, founded the monastery of Saint Augustine, as the *Deeds of the Bishops of Limoges* attest in these words: “That Roricius is said first to have founded at Limoges the monastery of Blessed Augustine in honour of that same saint, and to have established regular canons there. But after King Pippin had utterly destroyed the city of Limoges and all the churches existing there, Turpio, or Turpin, likewise bishop of Limoges, eventually rebuilt the aforesaid monastery and decreed that monks rather than canons should be there. He endowed them with very extensive possessions and revenues, as is evident even from this testament concerning that endowment, which I gladly wish to be ascribed to the kindness of the eminent man, both for piety and learning, John Cordes: ‘In the name of the holy Trinity and undivided Unity, in whom we are commanded to do all things.

“Since the world is now growing old, religious devotion has fallen into decay; and irreligion or injustice so abounds that we ourselves, who more than others ought to have cleaved to the Lord, in whose inheritance we are known to stand, have become, as the prophet says, a snare of ruin to others (Hos. IX); and we who ought to have been shepherds have become evening wolves. The prophecy of Malachi is daily fulfilled in us when he says: You have departed from the way and caused many to stumble (Mal. II). And a little later: Therefore I have made you contemptible (ibid.). And Job, speaking in the voice of the sorrowing Church: All my limbs have been reduced to nothing (Job XVI). Jeremiah too laments, saying: How darkened is the gold! How changed is its finest colour! The stones of the sanctuary are scattered at the head of every street (Lam. IV). Whoever does not now grieve is proved to have lost the light of his heart. For the Lord is unchangeable, as he himself speaks through the aforesaid prophet, saying: I am the Lord, and I do not change (Mal. III).

“[Col. 0383D] Whoever he may be is proved to have lost the light of his heart if, hearing that the unchangeable God spared neither the sinning angel nor the first man, who was still new and unformed, he nevertheless believes that he himself will be spared if he chooses to persist in sins and refuses to rise through repentance. Therefore I, Turpio, the lowliest of all the bishops of Limoges, seeing religion removed from the see which the Lord deigned, though I was unworthy, to commit to my governance and protection, became greatly afraid. Returning to myself, I long implored the Lord in prayer for help: that, with his assistance, holy religion, which had come down to our time undefiled, might not perish in our days, but might pass on inviolate to our successors.

“Then, with God’s help, a good counsel occurred to me, as I believe and confess: namely, that I should build a cloister and gather there brethren of good repute, who, living in common without any private property, might devote themselves to the service of God without any worldly tumult. What we, being mixed up in worldly crowds, cannot accomplish, they at least who dwell within the cloister should perform earnestly and without carnal hindrance. For it is written—and the Apostle says this—If the firstfruits are holy, so also is the whole lump (Rom. XI).

“[Col. 0384C] This I did, with the consent of our kinsmen and nobles dwelling in the district of Limoges: namely Lord Aimeric the abbot, Aymon the abbot, Peter the provost, Boso the archiclavus, Arnulf the archdeacon, and Aymon the porter; and, among the laity, Hildegarius the viscount, Rainald the viscount, Arcambald, and Ademar. I wish—and earnestly desire—that they may strive to serve God without poverty and without any disturbance. That this may be done more fittingly, I give them the estate called Baccalaria, which is known to contain ten holdings, and one holding at Curte Wlteziaco, in the estate called Parciacus. Beside that holding, I grant them another vineyard containing six arpents, formerly belonging to Frotarius. From my demesne vineyard I grant them a tenth, namely from the vineyard situated in view of the church of Wlteziacum. All the aforesaid movable and immovable things, mentioned above, I transfer from my right into their power.

“[Col. 0384D] Moreover, I entrust to them the oratory in which they serve God, so that they themselves may provide for the signalling of the Hours of God’s work, and that no one may trouble them in God’s house. We likewise entrust to them the ministry of singers and readers, books, and all things belonging to the sacred mystery or offered there to God. They themselves are to oversee and govern the cloister and all that is within it. In what I give or entrust to them, or shall hereafter give or entrust, no one shall have authority or licence to rule except the one whom the humbler party among them, for God’s sake and according to merit of life, shall have requested to preside over them—after, however, their own bishop.

“I beseech you, my successors, in God and for God’s sake: let none of you presume to violate this testament of my lowliness, which I commanded to be written for the salvation of my soul and of my predecessors and successors. But if anyone should act otherwise—which God forbid—let him not appear before the sight of divine majesty with the good shepherds, but burn without end in hell with the ravening wolf, that is, the devil. So may it be done to him. For it is written: Do not transgress the ancient boundaries which your fathers established (Prov. XXII).”], in the suburb, brother PETER, humble abbot of the Cluniacs, sends greeting and the fullness of sincere love.

[Col. 0381C]

I have seen your letter, and in it I perceived the great affection of your heart toward us. I observed—easily enough—that the common proverb which says that honours change character is partly false. For the honour you have assumed has not in any respect changed you from the love for us once long ago conceived, nor diverted you into anything other than what you previously were.

[Col. 0383A] You have not followed certain men of our time who, raised from our congregation either to abbacies or adorned with bishoprics, flee from us in mind as well as body, withdraw from the affection of their own community, and rejoice as though they had cast off, so far as they are concerned, the burdensome yoke of the monastic order. They show with what disposition they served God while they seemed humble: once offered the opportunity of ecclesiastical rule, they withdraw themselves from God as fully as they dare, devote themselves to the world, and, not as servants of God but as though using liberty as a cloak for wickedness, run everywhere unbridled and headlong, as if they had now attained what they had long desired. They put their own people aside and pursue strangers; nor do they now remember where they first came, where they lived, or whence they departed.

But you, dearest brother, do not act thus, as I hear. [Col. 0383B] Certainly you do not: you who always put our affairs before your own; who travel here and there to bring Cluniac causes to a conclusion; and who, at our command or that of our brethren, boldly oppose everywhere those who attack our commonwealth. Therefore, giving you many thanks, know for certain that we return to you the full measure of affection and reserve for you an excellent place in the inner recesses of our heart. May you always prosper in the Lord, and so exercise the office laid upon you through God’s grace that you may be a burning coal in life and a shining lamp by example.

## LETTER II

To the reverend and dearest friend, Lord STEPHEN, brother PETER, humble abbot of the Cluniacs, sends greeting and sincere affection of love in the Lord.

Know that the fact that, from the time of your departure from the city and the see of Vienne, I have sent your affection no message and written nothing, nor consoled you in or after that misfortune of yours, arose not from forgetfulness of the mutual love which I have always borne toward you, but from your removal to regions which I did not sufficiently know. For frequent and conflicting reports concerning your situation, brought to us from different persons, said at one time that you were at Saint-Ruf, at another that you were staying in certain churches subject to it, and at another that you were in places unknown to me.

[Col. 0384B] In addition, the daily—indeed continual—pressing concerns of the Cluniacs, which sometimes force me even to forget myself, obstructed my remembrance of you; they did not indeed remove, but delayed, my consolation of a friend in his tribulation. At last, though perhaps late, returning to myself I write to my friend and ask that, for these reasons, he may excuse my tardiness.

[Col. 0385A] For I do not wish to belong to the number of those friends who love only while they receive, who care only while they hope. I do not wish to belong to the number of those called companions of the table, because, in the words of the wise man who said it: A friend loves at all times (Prov. XVII); and likewise: A friend is not known in prosperity, nor an enemy concealed in adversity (Ecclus. XII). Therefore I exhort, desire, and urge that, since what grieves us has happened to you, you should come to us and to your Cluniac Church and discover, not through a messenger but in your own person, whether what I say is true.

I ask, however, that you come in such a manner that your stay with us may not be for an hour but permanent. It is fitting for your position that henceforth you should by no means move from place to place, nor go to any other churches, but come to that Church which is both great and yours, which is prepared with great affection to serve you and provide for you in every way according to its ability; and that you entrust your whole self to her who offers her whole self to you. If this please you and proves possible, accomplish it by Quinquagesima Sunday. For thereafter I must set out on the road toward the council.

## LETTER III

To the noble man and our friend, Lord STEPHEN OF CASTELLO, brother PETER, humble abbot of the Cluniacs, sends greeting and affection.

Since all things flee with swift flight, and the world hastens without ceasing toward destruction with great strides, I cannot sufficiently wonder that a man so wise and hitherto so provident in perishable matters seems to have no concern for eternal things. And since, if I may say so without offence to you, age itself now forbids you the hope of a long life, you are, on the contrary, thought to have fixed the root of your heart in this wretched and deceptive life, as if you would never die.

[Col. 0385C] Therefore I exhort you as a most beloved friend; and what I would do in person if I could, I urge upon you from afar as far as I can: do not allow the salvation of your soul any longer to hang in uncertainty. Rather, before it departs never to return, seize it now with every effort of your heart and without delay. Let not only the ancient examples of men of old, but also the present examples of modern men—which are usually more persuasive—invite you to this: men who, fleeing when almost swallowed up by the very jaws of Satan, either by the journey to Jerusalem or by diverse and sudden conversion to God, force their way into the kingdom of heaven and, as it were, snatch it by violence.

[Col. 0385D] Seize it yourself as well, and do not, as you have done until now, defer from day to day; for, according to divine Scripture, you do not know what the coming day will bring forth (Prov. XXVII). Leave earthly things before they leave you; and if you have been unwilling to offer God the first part of the victim—that is, your life—then at least devoutly offer him its tail, that is, the end of your days.

[Col. 0386A] If you do this promptly, the master of the household will be at hand. To his labourer who has been idle for so long—that is, to you, coming at the eleventh hour—he will grant in the evening the equal coin of eternal life, though not the same recompense as to the first labourers. You know what you promised Saint Hugh and what you promised us, and how often, both personally and through your messengers, you gave me hope concerning your salvation and conversion. Nor do you fail to know what your fathers did and to what they turned after laying aside the secular habit.

[Col. 0386B] We have always been ready suitably to serve you; we are now much more ready for this, which we see is more beneficial to you and which, if you delay, we fear will be dangerous to your old age. May the anointing of the Holy Spirit teach your heart. We have done what belongs to us and have acted as a friend should. But take care that it is not in vain.

## LETTER IV

To the supreme pontiff and our special father, Lord Pope EUGENIUS, brother PETER, humble abbot of the Cluniacs, sends due obedience with sincere love.

Whenever I write to Your Fatherhood, knowing that your ears are open to the whole world, I am accustomed, as the matter in hand permits, to avoid prolixity. [Col. 0386C] If I cannot do so now, I pray that paternal kindness may not take it ill.

Your Sublimity wrote to the archbishop of Arles and the bishop of Viviers that they should diligently hear, at a suitable place and on a day to which both parties had been summoned, the dispute which had arisen concerning the monastery of Saint Baudilus [Note: Concerning the monastery of Saint Baudilus. Baudilus was a subdeacon and martyr who suffered at Nîmes under the Goths. His body was buried by the faithful in that city itself, and a church was built over it which retained his name afterward. Hence Gregory of Tours, *Miracles*, book I, ch. 78: “In the town of the city of Nîmes, there is the glorious tomb of the blessed martyr Baudilus, from which many miracles are often made manifest.”], between the bishop of Nîmes [Note: Between the bishop of Nîmes. Nîmes, a city of the Arecomici in Gaul according to Mela and other ancient writers, is commonly called Nîmes; it lies in Viennensis Secunda, though by some in Narbonensis Prima.] and the abbot of La Chaise-Dieu [Note: And the abbot of La Chaise-Dieu. La Chaise-Dieu was a most celebrated monastery in Auvergne, built about the year 1050 by Saint Robert of Auvergne, himself a native of that region, who was its first abbot, as his biographer recounts more fully. Geoffrey the monk also testifies in the *Life of Saint Bernard of Pontis*, when speaking of Renaud, abbot of Saint Cyprian at Poitiers: “He had been a disciple of Saint Robert, founder of that monastery which is called La Chaise-Dieu.”]. Apart from the definitive sentence, which you ordered to be reserved for yourselves, they were to examine all matters carefully and report their findings to you by messenger or letter.

But because, Father, you cannot possibly ascertain everything, particularly distant matters, unless from persons familiar with them, I make known that I have learned for certain from many religious, wise, and trustworthy clerics and monks that these investigators are so suspect to one party that assigning the matter to the archbishop of Arles is almost the same as assigning it to the bishop of Nîmes himself. So that Your Wisdom may know that either I or they speak truly, know that the archbishop of Arles was born [Col. 0387A] in the diocese of Nîmes, was offered by his father as a boy to the Church of Nîmes, was brought up in that Church from childhood to youth, and became a canon of the Church of Nîmes. After becoming bishop of Agde [Note: Bishop of Agde. Gregory of Tours mentions Agde in the *History of the Franks* and in *Miracles*, book I, ch. 79. Like Nîmes, it was a city of Viennensis Secunda and was made illustrious by the council held there in the time of Alaric, king of the Visigoths. In French: Agde.], and after being promoted to the archbishopric of Arles, he always defended the interests of the Church of Nîmes and always fought against its opponents.

What shall I say of the bishop of Viviers? Although, with regard to his religious profession, he is a Cluniac monk and ought not, in a cause concerning God and us, to fail in justice toward La Chaise-Dieu, nevertheless it seems to me—and to all who know and consider the matter—that, as regards this case, carnal affection has more weight with him [Col. 0387B] than the spiritual affection which ought to have bound him more closely to us and ours. For he has long been, both formerly and now, a close neighbour to the people of Nîmes; and even now he remains joined to them by familiarity, affinity, and kinship with the bishop of Nîmes himself.

To this is added that they recently bore witness to this very opinion concerning themselves—that they are suspect as judges or investigators in this case—not by verbal confession, but, what is more significant, by their conduct. For although the discernment of your justice prudently ordered them to summon both parties before them at a suitable place and time, they have transgressed not partially but completely the bounds of the apostolic mandate. For your Roman law and the *Authentic* say, not only concerning your mandate, which is supreme, but concerning any reasonable mandate, that an agent must not exceed the limits of his commission.

[Col. 0387C] They have entirely transgressed the apostolic mandate. They appointed for the abbot and monks neither a suitable time with an unsuitable place, nor a suitable place with an unsuitable time, but both together—that is, both place and time—not merely unsuitable, but, if it could be said, most unsuitable. The place: because they decreed that the cause should be heard in the city, church, and very house of their adversary, under the authority, arms, threats, and terrors of his friends, relations, and kinsmen. The time: because it was the busiest period of the whole year, when every head of household, especially poorer men, is occupied in reaping, gathering, and storing the new crops.

[Col. 0387D] Although famous, the abbot of La Chaise-Dieu cannot, for the most part, be excepted from that number. Such a time, I say, did these most just investigators or judges choose for examining an affair of such importance. Yet in obedience to your mandate—as he has always been ready to do in all things—the abbot came, not as he wished but as he could, at so unsuitable a time to so unsuitable a place.

[Col. 0388A] Unable, through fear, entreaty, or payment, to secure in those parts of the province any lawyer or advocate except one almost wholly useless because of the aforesaid enemies, he attended on the appointed day with a few advocates begged from Burgundy. Though acting among enemies, he obeyed your mandate in everything. He complained before the aforesaid men about the place; he complained about the time; he stated his reason for complaint, but gained nothing by complaining. Another day, no less unjust, was assigned for proceedings, and the same place of which he had so often complained was prescribed.

Since he sees himself burdened not secretly now but openly, he has recourse to the seat of justice; he flees from his enemies to his father; before you, who hold on earth the place of Peter—indeed, of him who renders judgment for those suffering injury—he lays down so great a complaint. He prays, he entreats, and with him the whole community of La Chaise-Dieu, which, as you know, is not to be despised. I too pray, trusting in the grace of Your Majesty, which I have often experienced: remove from this case these investigators or judges who are so manifestly and unmistakably suspect, and, if it please you, take the examination and determination of it upon yourselves.

[Col. 0388B] Although the journey from our regions to you is longer, more arduous, and deadly because of Italian diseases, nevertheless nothing can burden those brethren if they may learn with certainty whether they have retained or lost in law the matter at issue. Yet they hope and confidently presume that the monastery which, as they say, they have possessed for so long and so peacefully, and which, through much labour and expense, they raised from a poor, mean, and irreligious little church into a rich, noble, and religious church—indeed, what is greater, into a monastery—compared with its former poverty, will, once the calumnies of their adversaries have been dismissed by the judgment of your justice, be granted to them for perpetual possession.

## LETTER V

To the supreme pontiff and our special father, Lord Pope EUGENIUS, brother PETER, humble abbot of the Cluniacs, sends filial affection with due obedience.

Certain worthy men, canons of the Church of Angoulême [Note: Canons of the Church of Angoulême. Angoulême, called *Ingulisma* by Ausonius and *Eccolisma* by Gregory of Tours, is a city of Aquitania Secunda, situated on a hill, whose base is washed by the river Charente.], recently approached me and asked me to intercede for them with [Col. 0388D] Your Majesty and commend to your clemency the matter which they will lay before you. I at first declined for a while, fearing that I might be a burden to your great occupations; but at last I yielded to their urgent requests.

They say—and, I suppose, Your Dignity will hear it from them—that, after their bishop’s death [Note: After the death of their bishop. Lambert, who died in 1148 and wished to be buried in the church of the monastery of Couronne, which he himself had founded.], with no cleric of the Church at all excluded from [Col. 0389A] the unanimous election, and with the assent, as the canons command, of the leading men and the entire people, they elected a person entirely suitable for the episcopal office: the precentor of that Church [Note: They elected the precentor of that Church: Hugh II, who governed the Church of Angoulême from 1149 to 1158.].

They state that they canonically presented this election, so universal and unanimous, to the metropolitan of Bordeaux [Note: The metropolitan of Bordeaux. Perhaps Bertrand, succeeded by Geoffrey in 1150.], who canonically confirmed it; that he set a day for consecration; that they came on the appointed day with their elect, to be consecrated, as the metropolitan had promised; but that they did not find the consecrator. Why he withdrew his presence and why he did not fulfil his promise, they have not learned from him and told me that they still do not know.

Let, then, if it please you, your apostolic sublimity provide—what it would do even without my letter—for this Church distressed by this occurrence. As you hold the place of him who was made by God apostle of the nations and upon whom the care of all the Churches was imposed, let your care not be absent from this Church. Thus, if the election was properly conducted, let it be confirmed by you; and may that Church, which is among the members of the one dove, that is, the universal Church, of which it is said, My dove is one; my perfect one is one (Song VI), rejoice in the peace given to it by God and by you.

[Col. 0389B] I have stated this conditionally because I could not be a witness either of the elect or of the election. Yet I state one thing with almost no qualification: the metropolitan of Bordeaux does not appear to me to be taking straight steps or to have a single eye in this election of Angoulême; rather, in it he seems to seek the things of a hired man rather than of a shepherd, his own things rather than those of Jesus Christ.

And, to speak with filial boldness and make known to you as Father what is said by almost everyone in those regions and ours: they say that the metropolitan of Bordeaux wishes to subject Angoulême to himself as he subjected Saintes [Note: As he subjected Saintes. Caesar calls them *Santones*; commonly Saintes, likewise a city of Aquitania Secunda, situated on the Charente.], so that in those churches he may have not so much bishops as servants, not so much prelates as men obedient to him in everything. This, they say, is his aim, this his intention, this his religious principle in these matters: to spare his own expenses and, using his suffragan bishops as chaplains, exhaust not his provisions but theirs.

[Col. 0389C] Father, I have briefly conveyed these things to you, lest minds concealed beneath a fox’s guise deceive you in this respect. For the false prophet deceived even the man of God who had come from Judah (III Kings XIII), and Ziba, servant of Mephibosheth son of Jonathan, insinuated himself by lying even to the great prophet and king David (II Kings XVI). And though, as you know, I do not sufficiently love that man, far be it—far be it, I say—that before God and you I should accuse or slander any person contrary to the truth of my conscience.

## LETTER VI

To our venerable and beloved Lord HUMBERT, archdeacon of Autun, brother PETER, humble abbot of the Cluniacs, sends greeting from him who commands the deliverance of Jacob.

[Col. 0390A] I rejoiced at the things said to me (Ps. CXXI), because, inspired by him who breathes where he wills, you now begin to sing with some others: We shall go into the house of the Lord. My mouth was filled with joy and my tongue with exultation (ibid.), because, although you seem to flourish while surrounded on every side by worldly advantages, you now begin to despise the world, dry even while it is in flower.

For this I give thanks to God; give thanks also yourself, without whom you can accomplish neither this nor anything good. For every good gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights (Jas. I), and, as John the Baptist says: A man can receive nothing unless it has been given him from heaven (John III); and as the Lord himself says: No one can come to me unless the Father who sent me draws him (John VI).

[Col. 0390B] Blessed, then, are you—if only you persevere—whom the Father draws, whom the Son receives, and into whom the Spirit of God breathes this will over which I rejoice. Therefore hasten, dearest brother: come to your Saviour who invites you. Hear his saving voice, with which he speaks to you and to all: Come to me, all you who labour and are burdened (Matt. I). Hear also what follows: Take my yoke upon you (ibid.). Remember, too, mother Wisdom admonishing her son in a mother’s voice: My son, do not delay in turning to the Lord, and do not put it off from day to day (Ecclus. V). Fear also what follows: You do not know what the coming day will bring forth (Prov. XXVII).

[Col. 0390C] Steal from the devil the treasure of your holy desire, lest perhaps—God forbid—there happen to you what Truth says of certain people: Then the devil comes and takes the word from their heart, lest they should believe and be saved (Luke VIII). For nothing pleases God so much, and nothing displeases the devil so much, as a good will; indeed, more truly, nothing pleases God and nothing displeases the devil except a good will. From it, among the other goods which flow from it, arise contempt for temporal things and love for eternal things.

For this reason delay is unsafe for you, lest, if you procrastinate too long, envious Satan place some obstacle in the way of your holy journey to God and retard your steps, so that you may not accomplish the good you have begun. He has done this to many whom I could name, if the brevity of a letter allowed.

[Col. 0390D] Let that venerable man, worthy to be named with honour, Lord Stephen, bishop of Autun—your uncle, as I hear—add incentives for you to come. Despising parents, nobility, pomp, wealth, and even casting aside the episcopal mitre itself, he followed poor Christ in poverty. Persevering with all the affection of his heart in holy devotion, he gave up his final breath to God in my hands; and he was buried at Cluny, by both me and the brethren, with veneration fitting so great a priest.

[Col. 0391A] Follow, therefore, his footsteps. Since, as you know, he was a man commendable for wisdom, he would never have chosen Cluny above other monasteries for himself and his salvation unless he had judged it more expedient for himself. Come and fill the place of the dead man, for I am ready to receive you with no less affection than I received him, and no less to provide in every respect for you and your salvation. And not only you: I am ready besides to receive, love, embrace, and cherish as many as you wish to bring with you, drawn by the Spirit of God.

It is fitting that you strive toward this with your utmost effort, so that, if you can, you may come to God not alone but bringing profit to others, and may not appear empty before the face of the Lord your God. Thus you may be crowned more abundantly also for those whom you bring, because, as John says in his Apocalypse, the one who hears must say: Come (Rev. XXII).

## LETTER VII

To THEOBALD, abbot of the monastery of Saint Columba [Note: To Theobald, abbot of the monastery of Saint Columba. He subscribed the letters of Hatto, bishop of Troyes, which we have already quoted in full above when discussing the prebend of the Cluniacs in the church of Saint Peter at Troyes. The monastery of Saint Columba is in the city of Sens. Gerard, likewise abbot of that place and perhaps the immediate successor of this Theobald, afterward rebuilt its church from the foundations and procured its solemn dedication by Pope Alexander III in 1163, as the author of the *Chronicle of Saint-Pierre-le-Vif of Sens* reports.], in the suburb of Sens, honourable and beloved in Christ the Lord, brother PETER, humble abbot of the Cluniacs, sends greeting and sincere affection of love.

I recently read your letter, dearest brother, and perceived in it that a great gulf has been fixed between you and nearly all others of your order; you appear far removed from their pursuits. For whereas, as has been said, the hearts, words, and writings of nearly all of them savour of worldly things, your heart, tongue, and letter seem to savour and think far otherwise.

[Col. 0391C] The letter which, as I said above, you formerly sent me shows this. To confess what is true, it sounded nothing mortal and displayed none of those concerns which I am accustomed to read in the very frequent letters of others. There was in it no question about gain, no mention of lawsuits, no lament for losses, no rejoicing over profits. Whatever I could read in it from the first point to the last spoke entirely either of fatherly care for those entrusted to you, questions concerning the Scriptures, or a desire, bestowed on you by the grace of the divine Spirit, to advance from good things to better.

[Col. 0392A] For I recognized in that letter the following distinct requests. First, you asked that I permit the brethren from La Charité who were with you—and who had handed down to your sons true philosophy, that is, Cluniac discipline, for you had interpreted “philosophy” in that sense—to remain in your monastery and exercise your office there.

Second, you asked why the anointing of the sick alone, and only at Cluny, is repeated; and how Joseph’s dream, in which he dreamed that he was worshipped by the sun, moon, and eleven stars (Gen. XXXVII)—that is, by his father, mother, and eleven brothers—can have been true, since his mother had died before his rise to power and did not worship him with his brothers.

Third, you requested that I add or insert consoling words in the letter I was to send you: words which, amid the imminent dangers of the journey to Jerusalem which you have now vowed to God, might perhaps afford support, and amid bitter events bring sweet comfort by land and sea.

[Col. 0392B] I am certainly not such a person as to believe that I am adequate to such matters or able to give you a fitting answer concerning things so great. Yet because I have long taken great pleasure—not only now for the first time—in your praiseworthy and devout zeal, and especially in your religious life and reputation, I do what I can, because I cannot do what you have asked.

And to the first point of your requests I have already replied more by deeds than words, since I granted everything you requested concerning the monks mentioned above. It would therefore be superfluous to linger longer in words over a matter already granted.

Accordingly, let the discussion proceed to the question raised concerning anointing [Col. 0392C], and show why at Cluny the sick are anointed with the sacred oil more than once.

[Note: [Col. 0391D] Why at Cluny the sick are anointed with the sacred oil more than once. Geoffrey, abbot of Vendôme, and Ivo, bishop of Chartres, held that not only the anointing of the sick but no sacrament of the Church could be repeated. Geoffrey’s words are in Letter 19, Book II: “And, to say nothing of the rest, in this, as it seems to us, they err not slightly: they think that the anointing of the sick ought to be repeated, although it is called a sacrament by the holy catholic and apostolic see, and although no sacrament ought to be repeated.” Ivo, moreover, says in the following letter: “I do not judge that the anointing of the sick should be repeated, because, as you yourself asserted, according to the institution of the Apostolic See it is a kind of sacrament. But whoever repeats the sacraments of Christ and the Church commits an injury against those sacraments.” Yet, since, according to the principles of theology—as the most learned Jacques Sirmond observes there—only those sacraments that imprint a character cannot be repeated, namely baptism, confirmation, and orders, it follows that extreme unction, since it is not among that number, may be repeated not only at Cluny, as this Peter of ours here defends, but everywhere: both in different illnesses and also in one and the same illness, whenever, after an interval, the illness flares up so as to threaten a fresh danger to life.]

I think that anyone who either thinks or says that the anointing of the sick ought not to be repeated raises this objection against himself: since baptismal anointing, confirmational anointing, priestly anointing, episcopal anointing, the anointing of churches, and the anointing of ecclesiastical vessels are each single and are never repeated afterwards, why is the anointing of the sick alone not merely doubled among some, but also given without any fixed number, at various times, to certain sick persons who relapse into illness? [Col. 0393A]

Whoever thinks this, or raises this objection, should consider not only the singularity of those anointings, but also—and this is more important—should investigate and understand the reason for that singularity. Why, then, is one who has already been baptized anointed, except that the remission of sins already bestowed—not to be bestowed—upon the baptized person through the Spirit of God may be shown? Since this done once suffices, since the single anointing with sacred chrism shows sins remitted once, no reasoning persuades us that it should be repeated.

But why is that anointing of confirmation performed by bishops not repeated? It is plainly not repeated for this reason: because it shows that once a Christian, after baptism, has been fortified by that anointing with the arms of the Spirit of God, the Advocate, against the wars of Satan and the world, he cannot again be equipped by that single anointing with another spirit or other weapons. Certainly, through his own negligence, after laying aside these weapons, he may be overcome by the enemy; and, having taken up the same weapons again, he may again overcome the enemy. Yet for that reason the one anointing is not to be repeated, because whenever he overcomes the enemy, the sacred anointing by its singularity signifies that this is done not through one spirit and then another, but through the same Holy Spirit. [Col. 0393B]

But why is the anointing not repeated by which the hands of a priest, about to consecrate and handle heavenly sacrifices, are anointed; or that by which the head of a bishop, when he is ordained, is drenched with a more abundant outpouring of chrism? There is no cause for doing this again, no reason for anointing a priest’s hands or a bishop’s head anew. For the sacrament which they receive once from the Spirit of God they can by no means lose or forfeit, even when, by the judgment of the Church, they are suspended or deposed from office. This is indicated by the Church’s common and public practice: it neither consecrates afresh priests restored to office after however prolonged a period of degradation, nor repeats the sacraments of anointing in bishops who are at times transferred from their original sees to others. [Col. 0393C]

Nearly the same reason is given for the anointing of inanimate things themselves: neither the material fabric of churches nor the preparation of sacred vessels needs a double or triple anointing. The blessing of the Spirit of God, suitably imparted once through the episcopal office, fills them and will remain so long as they themselves remain. For these reasons, in God’s Church, none of the anointings just mentioned is repeated.

[Col. 0393D] But concerning the sick, another law and another reason are shown for their frequent anointing. In my judgment, the anointing of the sick must be repeated, because the remission of sins—for the sake of which that anointing is performed—must be repeated. The very words of the Apostle who commands this indicate it: “Is any among you sick?” he says. “Let him call for the priests of the Church, and let them pray over him, anointing him with oil in the name of the Lord” (James 5). And he continues: “And the prayer of faith will save the sick person, and the Lord will raise him up; and if he is in sins, they shall be forgiven [remitted] him” (ibid.).

Since, then, it is certain that the purpose of anointing is this: that the prayer of faith may save the sick person, that the Lord may raise him up, that, if he is in sins, they may be forgiven him—why should the anointing not be repeated when the reason for anointing recurs? [Col. 0394A] For if, after health had once been restored, a sick person never afterwards fell into illness, and if after the first anointing he never fell into sins, I grant that it would never thereafter be lawful to repeat the anointing just mentioned. But if he is sick again, if he sins again, what reason will forbid his being anointed anew, so that he may again be raised up and again have his sins forgiven?

Does not the Apostle himself show that this is what he intends: that as often as anyone falls sick, so often he should be anointed? For what else do his words mean: “Is any among you sick? Let him call for the priests of the Church”? He does not say, “Is any among you sick once,” or, “If anyone among you falls sick once, let him call for the priests of the Church once.” Rather, without mentioning a single, double, or triple anointing, he commands that, with no number prescribed, the priests of the Church be called to the sick person, the prayer of faith be made, and the sick person be anointed with sacred oil for his restoration and the remission of sins. [Col. 0394B]

Therefore, it does not seem to me that we ought to say what the Apostle did not say, add what he did not write, or think what, as his words indicate, he did not think. It is plainly not apparent from those words that the Apostle either considered or commanded a single anointing, since he knew that people not only fall once into various illnesses, but frequently relapse into the same or different illnesses after recovering health; and since he knew that, when their former sins had been forgiven, wretched mortals sin again and again, and many times. For the words are those of the same Apostle of whom I speak—that is, James: “We all stumble in many things” (James 3).

He, therefore, who provided medicinal anointing for prior illnesses and sins—did he deny it for later illnesses and sins? This is surely not apostolic faith; this is not apostolic preaching: that fitting mercy should be denied to the sick, or forgiveness of sins to the penitent. [Col. 0394C] Although this forgiveness is very often bestowed through ecclesiastical ministry without the sacrament of any anointing, both on sick persons and on the healthy, sacred anointing should nevertheless not be withheld from the sick together with absolution; for, according to the explanation given above, the Apostle just cited commands it to be administered to them whenever they are sick.

For this alone is found in the entire canon of the New Testament: not borrowed, like the other anointings, from the Old Testament, but instituted in the age of grace itself by apostolic exhortation and command. Therefore, because this institution was made not in the shadow of the old law but in the truth of the new Gospel, it is not to be interpreted in one way and then another, but must be understood and observed by believers as it was handed down: covered by no wrappings, veiled by no allegorical signs. [Col. 0394D]

Now let my pen turn to Joseph’s dream, which you raised. You say that you wonder why it was not fulfilled literally as his father interpreted it. For when Joseph saw in a dream that he was worshipped by the sun, moon, and eleven stars, and when his father rebuked him as he told it, saying that he himself was signified by the sun, the mother by the moon, and the eleven brothers by the eleven stars, Joseph was indeed worshipped by his eleven brothers, but not also by his mother, since she had already died before his advancement. To this I answer at once: neither was he worshipped by his father. For this is nowhere read.

Nor would it have befitted that kind man, praised in the sacred Scriptures, to permit himself to be worshipped by so great a father, always so dear to him, when the father rather ought, by divine and human right, to have been honoured by the son. Yet it cannot therefore be said either that the dream was false or that Jacob interpreted it falsely. Although his father did not worship him, prevented by paternal dignity; although his mother did not worship him, death intervening; although, I say, they did not personally worship him, nevertheless they worshipped him, as the Fathers have said, in their whole household or lineage, which altogether and universally worshipped him. [Col. 0395A]

And lest the resolution of the question proposed seem to do violence to the letter, let there be brought forth from the same book of Genesis, in which these things are written, a very clear example, without any cloud of obscurity. Are these not the words of the patriarch Isaac, speaking to his son Jacob? “Be lord of your brothers, and let the sons of your mother bow down before you. I have made him your lord, and I have subjected all his brothers to his service” (Genesis 27).

Did Jacob ever personally rule Esau? Did Esau ever personally submit to his brother Jacob? Did he ever personally bow down before him? Read again that sacred volume, and you will find that this never happened, that Jacob was nowhere personally worshipped by Esau. On the contrary, you will encounter, as you read, that Esau met Jacob as he returned from Mesopotamia with wives, sons, and flocks, and that Jacob himself worshipped Esau in supplication. [Col. 0395B] For it is thus written: “And he”—that is, Jacob—“going forward, bowed down to the ground seven times, until his brother came near” (Genesis 33).

How, then, shall the prophecy just cited stand: “I have made him your lord”? How shall this stand: “I have subjected all his brothers to his service”? How shall this stand: “Let the sons of your mother bow down before you”? For, as I said before, Jacob never ruled his brother Esau, nor did Esau ever bow down before him. Rather, the reverse occurred: when Jacob himself bowed down to the ground seven times, he certainly bowed before his brother. For unless he had bowed down, he could not have prostrated himself seven times upon the ground; and plainly, unless he had bowed down, he could not have worshipped his brother.

What then? Shall the prophecy of so great a patriarch be believed false? [Col. 0395D] Do you see how cautiously one must proceed through so many narrow paths of God’s utterances? Things similar to this obscurity often occur, and unless the reader is wisely on guard, he will often stumble, his foot striking against a stone. Thus also, there will be no way out of the narrow place of the question proposed unless you turn not to Esau himself but to his descendants. For he did not personally serve his brother Jacob, nor did he personally bow before him; but in his descendants—that is, in the nation of the Edomites—he was truly subject for some time to the descendants of Jacob, that is, the Jews.

That the Edomites were indeed at some time subject to the Jews is taught by their casting off of servitude itself. Isaac, whom we have just mentioned, had also foretold this casting off to the weeping Esau: “The time will come,” he said, “when you will shake off and loosen his yoke from your neck” (Genesis 27). [Col. 0396A] The book of Kings indicates that this was then fulfilled when it says: “In those days Edom revolted, so that it might no longer be under Judah” (4 Kings 8).

Therefore, just as Esau served his brother Jacob not in his own person but in the succession of his race, and bowed down not his own person but his own people—not before Jacob but before the Jews, Jacob’s descendants—so Jacob the father and Rachel the mother worshipped their son Joseph not in their own persons but in their descendants. I could offer other examples similar to this one, if I did not think that this single example could suffice. But because, I believe, this one fully establishes the point for whose confirmation it was introduced, let the discussion proceed to what remains.

Since, therefore, you wanted something inserted or added to the letter [Col. 0396B], by which you might be stronger and more ready to endure, by land and sea, the hardships of the Jerusalem journey, I do not know what more fitting thing I can set before you, nor what more powerful thing I can suggest for restoring your strength of spirit, than the testimony of your own conscience. For this always consoles the saints in all their tribulation; it makes them steadfast in all their labours; it makes them victorious in all their struggles.

For they recall that their Christ spoke and laid down the surest rule for human deeds when he said through his Gospel: “If your eye is single, your whole body will be full of light” (Luke 2). Therefore, if your eye, dearest brother, is single in this undertaking, if your intention in this journey is pure and sincere, then, as you have heard Truth itself affirm, your whole body—that is, all your works, all your labours, all your sweats on this journey—will be bright, not dark. [Col. 0396C]

I believe, moreover, and infer from the excellent reputation of your former life, that you have undertaken this so arduous a journey with this eye: so that, since in this present bodily life you lack the presence of your Saviour, you may at least contemplate him with holy affections of the mind in those sacred places where he was born, lived, suffered, died, and was buried; from which he rose, and from which he ascended into heaven. I judge that for this reason you boldly make your way from the furthest regions of our West to the lands of the East still unknown to you, exposing your body to hardships and your life to every danger: so that in Nazareth you may behold Christ’s conception, in Bethlehem his birth, in the tomb his three-day burial, and in every place of human redemption the Redeemer himself, with the blessed eyes of faith, as has been said. [Col. 0396D]

You will worship in the place where, even bodily, according to the prophecy, his feet stood (Psalm 131); and, with no dissimilar affection—indeed, with surer faith—you will devoutly seek in his tomb the Saviour who sits in heaven at the eternal majesty of the Father, as did the Gospel women, lovers of the Lord. In my judgment, your pilgrimage to such remote parts of the world will be of no lesser value before the gracious inspector of hearts and just judge of holy affections than was the visitation at Christ’s tomb by the women and disciples just mentioned, who came from nearby.

They ran from the neighbouring hiding places to which they had fled to the saving cave of the Lord, recently buried; you run through the perils of land and sea to the same cave to which they came. [Col. 0397A] I think that a longer course, a more laborious journey, and an affection no less fervent will earn—not a greater reward, in deference to the apostolic privilege, but at least an equal one.

That this may happen, that eye of which I have spoken before, by which all the works of mortals are either bright or dark, must be purified with the utmost care, lest frivolity, instability, or curiosity—which often immerse themselves in such wanderings—should by any effort prevail to darken or cloud it. Care must be taken lest hope of profit enter from the spoils of enemies perhaps to be conquered, and compel a servant of God, setting aside care for the souls entrusted to him, to roam here and there, no longer from devotion but from avarice. [Col. 0397B] It must be seen to that love of empty praise does not touch the heart, and that a monk and abbot does not display himself as military and warlike, contrary to his purpose and order.

The eye of the mind must be purified from these and similar things, lest perhaps, while we neglect carefully to examine why we do what we do, our eye bring us darkness in place of light and our whole body become dark. We must fear lest our lamp, thought to be full of oil, prove empty when the Bridegroom comes, and we be excluded from the blessed and eternal wedding feast. He is foolish, and truly a foolish virgin, who destroys what he builds, scatters the fruits he has gathered, and exposes to raging winds rushing in from every side the grain already collected in the barn, by which eternal life is nourished so that it may not fail.

This is what the followers of pride, vain glory, and avarice do: [Col. 0397C] nothing thereafter can remain to them of the necessities of life that they have gathered, while either the wind of vainglory scatters them through the air, or avarice hides them with hooked hand in the deepest bowels of the earth, so that they can benefit neither themselves nor anyone else. But far be it from me, my dearest brother, to suspect this of your holiness. I trust that neither profit nor glory nor frivolity, but God alone, has led you to undertake this most holy journey. [Col. 0398A]

For it would be utterly absurd even to suspect that you, who for a long time have tormented yourself with holy fasts, many vigils, and various mortifications of the flesh, and can say to God with the Prophet, “For your sake we are put to death all day long” (Psalm 44), would most foolishly allow labours so great and so long acquired to perish in the most worthless commerce of vanity. But because you yourself wished this, because you yourself asked it, I have set before the mind of my dearest friend those things which could help or harm such a fruitful journey.

Let this, then, be the end of the letter: that you may wisely preserve your labours for yourself, and that you may diligently help me—who have no small need of the aid of good men—with your good deeds, your toil, and above all your holy prayers at the Lord’s tomb, as I earnestly pray and ask. [Col. 0398B]

## LETTER VIII

To the venerable brother in the Lord Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, whom I recall and name with honour: Brother Peter, humble abbot of the Cluniacs, greeting and the affection of sincere charity.

Your Holiness was pleased to ask my humble self what I thought concerning the election of Brother Henry, your son.

[Note: [Col. 0397C] What I thought concerning the election of Brother Henry, your son. He speaks of Henry, brother of Louis VII, king of the French. While living as a monk of Clairvaux under Saint Bernard, Henry was nominated pastor and bishop of the Church of Beauvais, as is more clearly apparent from his letter to our Peter which follows. That he had first been a cleric is taught by the charter of Louis the Fat, his father, by which he gave the monastery of Saint Guinald at Corbeil to the church of Saint Victor near the city of Paris in 1134.
