That he had also been a subdeacon is clear from the charter of Stephen, bishop of Paris, concerning the gift of one prebend to the same church of Saint Victor in the greater Church of Blessed Mary; likewise that he had been archdeacon of Orléans, from the charter of Bishop Elias concerning the church of the monks of Saint Martin of the Fields at Hienville; that he had been abbot of the church of Blessed Mary at Étampes, from the charter of Odo, prior of Saint Martin of the Fields; abbot of Saint Denis of the Prison, from the charter of Louis the Younger by which he granted that church of Saint Denis to be possessed by the monks of Saint Martin of the Fields; abbot of Saint Exuperius at Corbeil, from another charter of the same king, by which he confirmed his gift of a prebend in the church of Saint Exuperius to the canons of Saint Victor; and finally abbot of Saint Mary of Meudon, Saint Mary of Poissy, Saint Mellon of Pontoise, and, to put it in a word, abbot of all the royal abbeys.

John of Paris explains the nature of this dignity under the year 1149: “At this time,” he says, “Pope Eugenius set Henry, brother of King Louis, a monk of Clairvaux, over all the abbeys of France; and he was also general abbot over the particular abbots, etc. Later, at the end of this year, he was made bishop of Beauvais.” Finally, he passed from the bishopric of Beauvais to the archbishopric of Reims in 1166. His brother Philip succeeded him both in the archdeaconry of the Church of Orléans and in the administration of certain royal abbeys, as appeared to us from several charters in the cartulary of Saint Victor.

For in one charter, that of Manasses, bishop of Orléans, concerning the vineyards of the canons of Saint Victor in the diocese of Orléans, Philip, archdeacon and brother of the king, subscribes. In another, concerning the annual revenues assigned by Louis the Fat, his father, to the community of Saint Victor, he is called: “Philip, brother of the illustrious Louis, by God’s grace king of the French and duke of Aquitaine, and by God’s grace abbot of certain royal churches, namely Saint Mary of Étampes, Saint Mary of Corbeil, Saint Mary of Meudon, Saint Mary of Poissy, Saint Mellon of Pontoise, etc.”]

Whether you ought to give your assent to his election or not: yet you, full of the spirit of counsel and fear of God, have no need of my counsel on this matter, nor do you need to borrow from anyone such as I am what, from the grace bestowed upon you by God, you are accustomed abundantly to supply to others and to us. Nevertheless, because you wish to hear what I think, I shall speak briefly.

If merit of life is sought, it is great. For how could it not be great, when from so great a person he has made himself so little; when he has trampled underfoot, with the foot of such robust humility, the pride of royal blood, so to speak; when he has exchanged luxury and the worldly delights flowing in full flood for countless torments and a thousand deaths; when he has scorned a world smiling upon him from every side; when, denying himself and taking up his cross, he has followed Christ in death? [Col. 0398C]

If unanimous election is sought, not one person among the clergy or people of Beauvais is said to dissent. If the assent of the metropolitan and fellow bishops is sought, as I have learned, all of them have frequently offered you their entreaties for confirmation of so holy a work. If, in addition, the will of the lord pope is sought, how pleasing this was [is] to him is attested, I hear, by his letter sent to the lord of Reims. What then remains, venerable man, except that you submit your will to the will of God, which seems to declare itself through so many signs, and no longer allow that Church to toil or to squander its resources in vain, either in coming or returning? [Col. 0399A]

If you distrust his learning as though he were less experienced in such matters, God, who has already given him great things, is able also to bestow greater ones. Therefore, so far as can be discerned, there must be no further delay, no further postponement. Rather, when the leading persons from your region, who, as I have been told, will soon come for this purpose, have arrived, receive them gladly, hear them graciously, and swiftly fulfil—because this is just—their long-standing desire and their repeated petition, for the sake of him who fulfils in good things the desire of his own.

## LETTER IX

To the most reverend Father and dearest friend, Peter, by God’s grace abbot of Cluny: Brother Henry, by God’s command or permission elected bishop of Beauvais, offers himself and whatever more he can offer.

[Col. 0399C]

May almighty God forgive you! What have you done? You have recalled a buried man to men, [Col. 0400A] and by your counsel, which has been trusted far too much, I have been exposed and cast back into the dreadful sea of cares, so that the height of office may swallow me again. “I did not know; my soul troubled me because of the chariots of Amminadab,” which I have undertaken to govern, though I have need to be governed, not to govern.

“They have set my hands to mighty things”: I have need of strength. I have been made a watchman for the house of Israel: I have need of prudence. I have been made debtor to the wise and the foolish: I have need of justice. I have been set to preach to the people of God: I have need of temperance, lest perhaps, when I have preached to others, I myself be found reprobate—which God forbid. But what are these things, and who am I? Or where are these things, and where am I?

Lord Father and God of my life, your eyes have seen my imperfection. Lord, I suffer violence; answer for me [Col. 0400B], because obedience alone compelled me—without which, according to the holy man Gregory, anyone is proved faithless even if he seems to be faithful. And because no one acts with greater confidence than one who loves from affection, I now appeal to you as to a portion of my soul, laying before you a familiar and sorrowful complaint.

What seemed good to you, that, after sending your letters to the lord abbot, you should cause my folly to be lifted onto a lampstand? You “believed, Lord, and therefore spoke”; you wished neither to deceive nor to be deceived, but you did not escape the second consequence. Nevertheless, however this has happened, and whatever outcome the Lord our God directs the matter toward, I am yours, and, if you deem me worthy, prepared for your service. Receive me as a servant, a friend, and a son; and bind me by an everlasting covenant to that holy multitude over which, by God’s authority, you preside, as a monk specially and intimately their brother—not to say as their bishop. [Col. 0400C]

# BOOK SIX

[Col. 0399]

## LETTER I

To the venerable lord Ademar, beloved and worthy of love, abbot of Figeac: Brother Peter, humble abbot of the Cluniacs, greeting, and love sincere though wounded.

[Note: [Col. 0399D] To Lord Ademar, abbot of Figeac. Figeac, or Fiac, is a monastery in the district of Cahors, built from its foundations by Pepin, king of Aquitaine, and wonderfully consecrated in the presence of Pope Stephen. Thus Pepin himself says in the foundation records: “We wish all worshippers of Christ, present and future alike, to know how we transferred the place formerly established by our predecessors in the valley of the Lunant, in the district of Cahors, and now almost destroyed by rushing waters, to a neighbouring forest in the same district, a more suitable site to which we gave the name Fiac. There we built the monastery and the other buildings from their foundations. In the presence of Lord Pope Stephen we beheld it wonderfully consecrated by God; there, by divine merciful clemency, we gathered a company of monks under the observance of religion, and, by God’s authority, appointed the venerable man Anastasius abbot over it.”

Hence Bernard Gui says in the Chronicles: “The abbey of Figeac, then called Fiac, was built by Pepin in the territory of Cahors; its oratory was consecrated in the presence of Pope Stephen and the king themselves, as is more fully contained in the ancient records of that monastery.”]

[Col. 0399C]

[Col. 0399D] I wrote once; I wrote a second time—to one who wrote once, but did not write a second time. I wondered that you had written nothing in reply to my first letter, nothing to my second. As I considered the reason, none but one could occur to me. If you ask what I think it is, I answer: that you found no reply to the charges made. If that is so, one thing remained: namely, to confess your guilt. At least from that there would be material for writing back; from that your letter could speak to me. “I confess my fault; I ask forgiveness.”

And, to undertake something serious now, it is good that you delay no longer in coming to us, who are gladly prepared to see you. Nor let my complaint hinder your journey, because, as Solomon says, “there is a return to a friend.” I shall await your arrival, either at Cluny or nearby, at Christmas or at its Epiphany, and shall do whatever you tell me according to your desire. [Col. 0401A]

## LETTER II

To the most reverend Father and dearest friend, Peter, by God’s grace abbot of Cluny: Brother Bernard, called abbot of Clairvaux, greeting in the true Saviour.

Would that, just as I can send you this present letter, so I could send you my heart! Without doubt you would then read most clearly what the finger of God has written in my heart concerning love for you, what he has impressed upon my inmost marrow. What then? Am I beginning to commend myself to you again? Far be it! My soul has long been joined fast to your soul, and equality of charity has made equal minds out of unequal persons.

For what has my lowliness to do with your exaltation, unless condescension had inclined dignity? From that time it has come about that my lowliness and your exaltation are mingled each with the other, so that I could not be lowly without you, nor you exalted without me. [Col. 0401B]

I say this because my Nicholas—indeed yours also—deeply stirred in spirit, stirred me by asserting that he had seen our letter sent to you, in which expressions of bitterness were contained. Believe one who loves you: nothing arose in my heart, nor was anything forced from my lips, that could offend the ears of your blessedness. The multitude of affairs is to blame, because, while our scribes faithfully retain our meaning, they sharpen their pens beyond measure and cannot see what I ordered to be written.

Forgive this once; for, whatever may be the case with others, I shall see your letters myself and believe only my own eyes and ears. This common son will report the rest more plainly and fully to you in person. Hear him as you would hear me: he loves you not in word or tongue, but in deed and truth. Greet for us that holy multitude of yours, and pray that they may pray for their boy.

## LETTER III

To the venerable and distinguished man among the members of Christ, Lord Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux: Brother Peter, humble abbot of the Cluniacs, wishes him, after God and in God, that which is.

What shall I say? I am accustomed to speak, but now I have become mute. Why is this? Because your letter, which should have made me eloquent, has made me silent. Why? Because I read so much in it, though it is brief, that if I attempted to pour myself out in reply, I would appear more silent than talkative. Yet I speak to a serious man, to a religious man. Therefore, we must proceed as seriousness requires, as religion—if not mine, at least yours—demands. [Col. 0401D]

What? Is what I say not true? The letter is short, but it supplies much matter for reply. Bear with me, I ask, if I say anything less suitably than I should. For it belongs to true friendship not only to accept a friend’s errors, but also either to season or to endure what is tasteless. I have received from you, as I said, a letter—an exceptional letter—displaying the sweetest love and an honour greater than is due to me. You call me most reverend, name me Father, and address me as dearest friend.

I rejoice at this, but while preserving the truth which has flowed into you from Christ, I do not know the first two titles; I acknowledge the third. For, leaving aside the titles “most reverend” and “dearest friend”—one of which, as I said, I do not know, while the other I acknowledge—I write this to you meanwhile concerning the title “Father,” reverend brother: the singular man and most eminent flower of religious life in his time, Lord Guigo, prior of the Carthusians, once wrote to me. [Col. 0402A]

I wrote to him frequently and often took pleasure in conversing with him, either by exchanging words in person or by familiar letters; and in my letters I called him Father. At first he tolerated this, thinking that I would cease writing. But after he saw that I persisted and repeated the title Father in frequent letters, that holy man finally broke out in these words. For he wrote me a letter in which, among other things, he inserted this:

“Therefore, through that love by which your heart preserves compassion for us unworthy persons, we ask that, whenever your serenity deigns to write to our smallness, you should so consider your own edification that you do not inflate our weakness with dangerous pride.”

And immediately: “Above all and beyond all that we are, we ask and beseech you on bended knees, that you should no longer judge our usefulness worthy of the name of Father. It is enough and more than enough if he who is not deemed worthy even of the name of servant is called brother, friend, or son.”

He wrote this to me; I write the same to you. It is enough, and more than enough, if I may glory in being called by you or before you brother, friend, dear, or dearest, or if anything of that kind is fitting for you to give or for me to receive. [Col. 0402C]

This concerning the salutation that came before. But what of what follows? “Would that, just as I can send you this present letter, so I could send you my heart.” And immediately: “Without doubt you would then read most clearly what the finger of God has written in my heart concerning love for you, what he has impressed upon my inmost marrow.” Truly these words, while preserving the sacrament of a greater mystery, are “like the ointment upon the head, which runs down upon Aaron’s beard, unto the hem of his garment” (Psalm 132). Truly they are like “the dew of Hermon, which descends upon Mount Zion” (ibid.). Truly also “the mountains drip sweetness, and the hills flow with milk and honey” (Joel 3). [Col. 0402D]

Do not wonder that I attend to and retain your words so carefully. For I know that they were not uttered by just any mouth, but by one who does not know how to speak except from a pure heart, a good conscience, and unfeigned love. I know this, I say; and the world knows with me that you are not among those who, according to the Psalm, “speak vanity to their neighbour” (Psalm 11), nor among those “whose deceitful lips speak with heart and heart” [that is, with a double heart] (ibid.). Therefore, whenever it pleases your Holiness to write to me, I receive, read, and embrace your writings not negligently or in passing, but earnestly and affectionately.

For who would not read attentively and embrace with great affection both the things I have cited and those which follow? You have already said: “My soul has long been joined fast to your soul” (1 Kings 18), “and equality of charity has made equal minds out of unequal persons. For what has my lowliness to do with your exaltation, unless condescension had inclined dignity? From that time it has come about that my lowliness and your exaltation are mingled each with the other, so that I could not be lowly without you, nor you exalted without me.” [Col. 0403A]

Are words of this kind, then, to be read carelessly? Ought they not to hold the reader’s eyes fixed, carry away the heart, unite souls? Consider, my dearest friend, you who wrote them, what you think of this. I can think nothing else of them than what the letter says, than what I take to have been said by so great, so truthful, so holy a man. Nor, as you yourself said, am I beginning again to commend myself to you. While still young we began to love one another in Christ [Col. 0403B], and now, old men—or nearly so—shall we doubt a love so sacred and so long-lasting? Far be it! Believe one who loves you, to use your own words: neither has it arisen in my heart nor been forced from my lips that I have ever doubted your words in any way, provided, that is, they were spoken seriously. Therefore what you wrote in the letters at issue I embrace, preserve, and guard. A thousand talents of gold could more easily be stolen from me than these things be torn from my heart by any chance. But enough on this.

What moved your prudence, as it supposed, concerning me in the rest of the letter was this: your letters dealt with the affair, well known to you, of a certain English abbot. They seem to say that judgment has been overthrown, justice has perished from the earth, and there is no one to rescue the helpless from the hand of those stronger than they, the needy and poor from those despoiling them (Ps. 34). But, if you believe me, know that I was moved by this precisely as the Prophet says of himself—though I am no prophet: “But I was like a deaf man and did not hear, and like a mute man who does not open his mouth” (Ps. 38). And again: “I became like a man who does not hear and has no rebukes in his mouth” (ibid.).

I was not offended in these matters. But even if I had been offended, ample satisfaction was made when you said: “The multitude of business is at fault, because, while our scribes do not faithfully retain our meaning, they sharpen their style beyond measure; nor am I able to see what I have directed them to write. Forgive us this once, for whatever may be true of others, I shall see your letters myself and shall believe nothing except my own eyes [Col. 0403D] and ears.” I therefore forgive, and readily grant pardon. For me—it is humbly said—even in grave offenses, it is no hard task to forgive one who asks, or grant pardon to one who seeks it. If it is no labor to forgive grave matters, how much less is it so in light matters, or in none at all?

Concerning the testament of Lord Baro, the Roman subdeacon, which he is said, on dying, to have made in favor of your churches of Clairvaux and Cîteaux from goods he had deposited with us: the matter was carried out as certain persons wrote to me who said that he had imposed this duty upon them. Yet I want you to know that, as certain witnesses whom I consider trustworthy maintain, the favor of the abbot of Cluny bestowed more upon you in these things than Baro’s testament did. I know indeed—and am not so ignorant of divine or human laws [Col. 0404A] as not to know—that a testament, legacy, and trust made in contemplation of death are valid by a later testament. Yet elsewhere I read: “Nothing accords so closely with natural law as that the will of an owner who wishes to transfer his property to another should be held valid.” I say this because, as the aforementioned witnesses admit, he had given to Cluny everything that he had deposited at Cluny, unless perhaps it happened that he recovered it before ending this present life. I did not, however, wish to avail myself of that right; rather, what, according to their testimony, I believed to be mine, I granted to you and yours.

What I think concerning the election at Grenoble, against which our Carthusians are proceeding, I have carefully reserved to be disclosed to you by the mouth of my dearest friend and your faithful Nicholas. Hear him, and believe without the slightest hesitation that whatever he reports to you from my mouth is true. If anything that ought to have been conveyed has slipped my mind, when I remember it I shall entrust it to one who is most dear to me in Christ.

In conclusion, I ask and beseech you as earnestly as I can—as I have already sent word through certain persons of your order—that, in this great gathering of holy men assembled at Cîteaux, you remember me, who am indeed yours, and earnestly commend me and the whole body of the Cluniac congregation to their prayers.

## LETTER IV

To the lord Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, our dearest friend, to be remembered with singular honor: Brother Peter, humble abbot of the Cluniacs, wishes the salvation promised by God to those who love him.

[Col. 0404C]

The days of man are short. They flee and do not return. They leave no footprints behind them. Wretched man slips away with them, like flowing water, and in a headlong course runs toward an end he does not know. Therefore there must be no delay but haste; dangerous procrastination must not be endured; no period of leisure is granted us, because man does not know, as Scripture cries, what the coming day will bring forth (Prov. 27). We must obey the saying found elsewhere: “Whatever your hand is able to do, do it at once” (Eccl. 9).

Why do I say this? I do not say it, venerable and dearest brother, in order to urge you to work as though you were idle—your manifold holy works are known to me and to the world—or to charge you with any slowness when you hasten toward heavenly and eternal things with many labors [Col. 0404D]. For it is foolish to say to those running in the stadium, “Run.” But it is not foolish to say, “So run that you may obtain” (1 Cor. 9). Thus far you have run greatly, the Lord assisting your steps; but you must not cease until you can safely dare to say, “I have finished the course; I have kept the faith” (2 Tim. 4).

I seem, as the saying goes, to be teaching Minerva. Yet I do not teach Minerva; rather, I strive to urge you with all my strength to devote every effort you can to accomplishing what has taken root in your mind. And, not to prolong the matter or hold you in suspense too long, hear what I intend.

I grieve—indeed, I have long grieved—and I have sympathized with certain unhappy men (I say this without prejudice to the good) [Col. 0405A], because those who have become a spectacle to the world, to angels, and to men; who are fools for Christ, weak, and lowly; who until this present hour hunger, thirst, are naked, and labor with their hands; who follow almost wholly the great Paul: these men do the things that are burdensome, but refuse to do the things that are light. “We have heard,” says he whom Jesus loved, “his commandments. And his commandments are not burdensome” (1 John 5). Whoever you are, such a servant, you keep Christ’s burdensome commandments when you fast, watch, grow weary, and labor; yet you do not wish to keep the light commandment, namely, to love. On account of the words of his lips you keep hard paths, walking strongly upon them; and on account of the words of those same lips you refuse to keep the easy path, walking gently and peacefully upon it. You chastise [Col. 0405B] your body and reduce it to slavery lest perhaps you be found reprobate; yet, by refusing to nourish yourself with the sweet milk or honey of charity, do you not fear becoming reprobate? What good is it to consume yourself with torments and, with charity absent, make progress toward no profit from those torments?

You, dearest brother, can come to the aid of so great a peril among the brethren; you can heal so harmful a disease of souls, if you unite by a praiseworthy art the flock of your community—or rather, the sheep of Christ’s pasture, who after Christ esteem you above all mortals and chiefly rely on you—to the body of our fellowship. Perhaps you will wonder that I said “art.” But do not wonder. I cite the familiar saying: “The governance of souls is the art of arts” (Gregory). An art, I say, is necessary to you if you wish to accomplish this work so praiseworthy, so salutary, so pleasing to God.

But you ask: what art? Your wisdom knows that the number of fools is infinite, while that of the wise is limited and small. Nor are you ignorant that the eye of spiritual persons differs from that of carnal persons. You remember what is written: “The natural man does not receive the things of the Spirit of God” (1 Cor. 2). Why do I say this? Diversity of color, different dwellings, and dissimilar usages oppose love and run contrary to unity. One in white sees one in black and marvels as at a monster. One in black looks upon one in white and marvels as at a shapeless prodigy. New observances offend a mind accustomed to other usages, nor can that which it is unaccustomed to seeing readily please it [Col. 0405D].

This, however, is true among those who see only the face and do not attend to what is at work in the mind. Rational eyes do not look upon these things thus; spiritual eyes do not contemplate them thus. They see, understand, and recognize that among God’s servants diversity of color, diversity of observance, and divided dwellings make no difference, since, according to the Apostle, “neither circumcision counts for anything nor uncircumcision, but a new creation” (Gal. 6); and again, according to the same Apostle: “There is neither Jew nor Greek, neither male nor female, neither barbarian nor Scythian, neither slave nor free, but Christ is all things and in all” (Col. 3).

Such persons plainly see, understand, and recognize this. But since not all are such, and those to whom it is granted to perceive this are rarely found, allowance must, in my view, be made for the weaker; and, in accordance with him who said, “I became all things to all men, that I might gain all” (1 Cor. 9) [Col. 0406A], observance must be administered according to their custom. I do not say that color should be made one—that is, that black should be made white or white black. I do not say that old usages should be changed into new ones, or new ones transferred into old. I say none of these things, although in part I might rightly say them. I fear that, if I stated what I think about this, I might perhaps offend one side, utter words in vain, and irritate by unwelcome language those whom I desire to reconcile to one another.

Let each use the color he has chosen; let each retain the observances to which, with faith and charity preserved, he has committed himself. Let their dwellings at least be united; let those of different colors and observances dwell together without distinction. Let charity be nourished [Col. 0406B] and advanced among God’s servants by this art, and let the iniquity opposed to charity be disturbed and expelled.

This will happen, wholly or for the most part, I think, if, whenever monks of the old order come to the monasteries or residences of the new brethren, they are not excluded from church, cloister, dormitory, refectory, or the other workshops. The scandal will be removed from the heart of the visiting brother; his mouth will be silenced, lest he speak ill, when those received and those receiving share a common dwelling or lodging. The old words which he was accustomed to utter and repeat will depart from his mouth: “Am I a Jew? I thought myself a Christian, and I am treated as a pagan. I believed myself a monk, and I am cast out as a publican. I considered myself a fellow citizen [Col. 0406C], and I am expelled as a Samaritan. Now indeed I have learned that Jews have no dealings with Samaritans.” And who could recount all the similar malicious words uttered for this reason?

Let the mouth of those uttering such things—indeed, I will not say wicked things—therefore be stopped by such a barrier of charity. Let provision be made for the weak, whose physician Christ called himself (Matt. 9). Let scandal to the little ones be guarded against; let the millstone be feared which plunges the unwary into the depths of the sea (Matt. 18).

Let not that be feared which I recently heard at Clairvaux from certain brethren who were discussing this with me: they feared that, if visiting monk-guests were received inside their cloisters, the austerity of the observances and the unusual harshness of the food would deter them; they would dread such unfamiliar lodging and thereafter prefer not to enter such cloisters rather than endure so severe a rule [Col. 0406D]. To this I still reply as I replied then. Remove only the scandal of not being allowed to enter; let lodging according to your established custom be available among your people. Let the dwelling be common to both parties, and let the service customarily provided among you to others be provided. Let those who choose to enter be content with the custom of the place which they find. In this let them follow apostolic practice; let them follow the practice of Christ’s disciples, whom he himself commands to eat and drink what is set before them (Luke 10). If they refuse to endure this, they will have nothing further to object and nothing left to say. They will no longer be able to complain that monks are shut out from monks’ cloisters [Col. 0407A], nor mourn injured charity or bewail a schism among brethren when the cloisters are open and lodgings ready to receive them.

And though I say this, though I maintain that those entering your cloisters ought, according to the Rule, to be content with the custom of the place, I am not forgetful—and I believe that you, venerable man, are not forgetful—that the Rule says this concerning such persons in the chapter on receiving guests. For, after adoration, prayer, and reading, it adds concerning guests who have been received: “After these things, let every kindness be shown to him.” I believe that these words command that more kindness be shown to a guest than to a fellow citizen, to a newcomer than to a native, to a traveler than to a resident. Yet the Rule does not say what I say, “Let some kindness be shown him” [Col. 0407B], but “Let every kindness be shown him.” By “every” I understand not superfluous kindness but necessary kindness; not that which is customarily bestowed daily upon one’s own people, but that which, beyond the ordinary custom, is rightly bestowed upon strangers by the law of hospitality.

It seems to me, therefore, that such full kindness, in the sense I have explained, must be shown not only to clerics and laymen who remain outside, but also to monks themselves who enter the cloisters. But what did I say—“not only to clerics and laymen, but also to monks”? Rather, with the monk’s profession preserved, more should be shown to monks than to clerics or laymen. For if it is commanded by right, “Let us do good to all, but especially to those of the household of faith” (Gal. 6), good must be done to all clerics and laymen, but especially [Col. 0407C] to members of the household of the same monastic order. In those words the Apostle then preferred the household of faith—that is, Christians—to Jews and pagans; by a certain similar reasoning, I prefer monks even to other Christians.

Accordingly, monks ought not to provide less fitting hospitality, in keeping with their profession, for a monk who is their guest in the cloister than for a cleric or layman who is a guest in the outer guesthouse. But I shall not linger over this. Let monks, while they are guests, simply have monks’ cloisters in common; let them, if this pleases your brethren, be content with your ordinary food, order, and observances. Let them endure, as has been said, the things which are among you and done among you, if they wish to enter among you; for if they do not wish to enter, they will cease murmuring. If they do not cease, reason will fail them, and charity will plead for you.

I have anticipated my words with deeds—I say this without exalting myself—and began to do before I taught. Fifteen years ago I admitted and ordered the reception of all the brethren of your order into every one of our cloisters except the Cluniac cloister; nor did I care that white and black colors were mingled together in our places, nor did I listen to those who objected, though many pressed me not to allow it [Col. 0407D]. I therefore confidently urge you to do what I have already done: as all our places except the one mentioned above stand open to yours, so let all yours without distinction stand open to ours. If this is done, I shall add to the others that greater cloister which had been excepted, and order that it too be opened to all your brethren [Col. 0408A].

Let both kinds of brethren be taught—if not by speech, at least gradually through frequent cohabitation—that no distinction is to be made on account of differing color, no division on account of different observances, between these monks and those whom the same faith and charity ought truly to make brothers. I have written this to you, my dearest friend, in haste, so that I might send it more hastily, before certain abbots of your order assemble with you on the appointed day, which, as I hear, is to occur on the feast of All Saints. Discuss this point of mine with them among other matters, bring them to this opinion—which, as I judge, is not only mine but yours also—and proclaim it, that henceforth it may be observed by all the brethren of your order, everywhere observed, everywhere promulgated.

Set before them [Col. 0408B] the words of the Lord: “Whatever you wish men to do to you, do likewise to them” (Matt. 7). If they wish to enter our cloisters, do not forbid it. If they demand from others the duty of service at charity’s command, let them render its return after the example of him who says, “I came not to be served, but to serve” (Matt. 10). If they wish to be served, let them also serve the brethren—that is, Christ’s members—that they may fulfill what is said: “Through charity serve one another” (Gal. 5). Let all things be common to all, not only property but the very dwellings themselves. By this remedy divided hearts will gradually be united, and, seeing nothing differentiated among themselves, they will learn, though different—indeed, I would not say opposed—to be one, through the inspiration of him who blows where he wills [Col. 0408C].

## LETTER V

To Nicholas, dearest brother and son: Brother Humble—*you know whose surname this is*—wishes salvation and sincere love.

Because I love you with unfeigned charity, I cannot be forgetful of you for long. I loved you while you were ours in color; but even now, though your color has changed, I think, not your heart, I love you no less so far as I am concerned. I would rather you had been mine than another’s; but because you belong to God everywhere, I count you mine everywhere as well. Return this love, then: love one who truly loves you. For neither the whole world, with all its strength, can draw me away from this resolve, nor let anything draw you away from a like resolve.

You know that I expect no temporal advantage from you [Col. 0408D]; you know that no other cause moved me to love you except that one thing in you which alone was worthy of love. But you ask: what is it? Because I have known or judged you to be learned, energetic, and—what is greater—religious, although so only in time and not from eternity. But enough of this. Let the rest follow.

I am writing a letter to the lord of Clairvaux, which I wish you to present to him. Read it to him attentively and carefully, and, as far as you can, urge him to bring into effect what I wrote solely for charity’s sake. Press him, because the shortness of time requires urgency, that at this approaching feast of All Saints what I desire may be done; and, if he perhaps finds any opponents, let him compel them to come over to my opinion—which, I think, is also his [Col. 0409A].

Affectionately greet on our behalf the king’s brother [Note: [Col. 0409D] The king’s brother: Henry, mentioned above.], Philip of Liège [Note: [Col. 0409D] Philip of Liège: who later became prior of Clairvaux, as is written below in Letter 37.], Galcherius the cellarer [Note: [Col. 0409D] Galcherius the cellarer: to whom Letter 38 below is also addressed.], our Garnerius, Fromundus the keeper of guests, and the remaining brethren whom you know better than I do.

## LETTER VI

To his dearest father and lord Peter, by God’s grace abbot of the Cluniacs: Brother Bernard, called abbot of Clairvaux, wishes salvation and prayers.

“I have seen the letters,” etc. See among the letters of St Bernard, *Patrologia*, vol. CLXXXII, col. 00.

## LETTER VII

To his father, the lord abbot of Cluny: Brother Nicholas.

[Col. 0409B]

Since, as I think, I shall shortly see your face, I send you your letters. I also send the book of the lord abbot of Clairvaux to the lord Pope, as well as the two letters which you sent this year to that same lord abbot and to me. Let not your eminence be unaware that your letters greatly advanced the promotion of Brother Henry; they were heard most willingly by the archbishops and bishops of France, and many thanks were returned to your serenity, as I shall report better and more faithfully in person.

## LETTER VIII

Eugenius, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother Hugh, archbishop of Vienne [Note: [Col. 0410D] Hugh, archbishop of Vienne: he succeeded Humbert I and obtained in 1153 from Frederick, emperor of the Romans, a privilege for the Church of Vienne, which is preserved in the Library of Fleury.], greetings and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 0409C]

“As much as your person,” etc. See Eugenius III, pope, under the year 1153.

## LETTER IX

To the venerable lord Peter, beloved in Christ, by God’s grace abbot of the Cluniacs: Hugh, called archbishop of Vienne, wishes greeting and love.

The more earnestly we love you and yours, and the more we trust in your affection, the more we wonder—indeed, cannot wonder enough—that frequent complaints against us from you or your people should have reached the ears of the lord Pope, as his letter indicates, before they reached us. For if we had perceived that we had offended your majesty in anything [Col. 0409D], the Lord knows that both before and after any complaint we were prepared to make satisfaction. But if, as we believe and hope, such reports were communicated to the lord Pope not by you but from elsewhere through false insinuation, we beseech your love with all the urgency of which we are capable not to delay in informing him that they are false, and that we are well-disposed and favorable toward you, not hostile.

## LETTER X

To the supreme pontiff and our special father, Lord Pope Eugenius: Brother Peter, humble abbot of the brethren of Cluny, offers sincere goodwill together with devoted obedience.

[Col. 0410A]

I cannot give thanks as much as I wish because you do not cease to show, not only through messengers frequently sent by me to your reverence, but also through others approaching the apostolic majesty on their own business, what disposition you bear toward me and your Cluniac church. I have many examples of this, which I forbear to bring forward now. Yet I shall give one, for which, as I owe you much love, so I hope that, on its account—though I speak with filial presumption—you will take care against this or similar matters [Col. 0410B].

Your wisdom knows, and often recites from Holy Scripture, of men who speak with heart and heart: “They have sharpened their tongues like a sword” (Ps. 63); and, as the same man who uttered these words says again: “They have sharpened their tongues like a serpent; the poison of asps is under their lips” (Ps. 139). Such men, precisely such men, often contrive to steal in upon great persons occupied with great affairs and frequently administer falsehood for truth and poison for an antidote. Of their number were those who, not fearing to lie, poured into the ears of your holiness so monstrous a falsehood as to say, and to bring frequent complaints to you, that the lord archbishop of Vienne did not protect the Cluniac monks at all but attacked them, and that he nevertheless disturbed those whom, by your memorable and most welcome word, we far away beg him especially to love.

What shall I say of those who suggested these things to you? What shall I say but what the Psalm whose expressions I have touched on above says: “They have spoken vanity, each one to his neighbor; with deceitful lips they have spoken with heart and heart” (Ps. 11) [Col. 0410C]. What shall I say except also what the same author of these assertions says elsewhere: “Iniquity has lied to itself” (Ps. 26)? The father, I believe, knows the heart of his son. If he remembers what I privately represented to him at Auxerre or at Bar, he knows that, so far as I could read in the book of my conscience, to lie to you and to die were nearly the same thing.

Therefore know that I speak truth and speak to you in Christ as before God: the hands of the lord of Vienne, as far as I can remember, are clean from the blood of all the Cluniacs; and, as I judge—unless perhaps, as I do not think, I am mistaken—since he became metropolitan of Vienne, he has been innocent of every injury to any Cluniac, not only in deed but also in word [Col. 0410D]. Therefore, if anyone wishes to disparage him and diminish in any respect the favor of apostolic love toward him, let that person seek others than us, others than your Cluniacs, as a pretext or occasion for doing so; and let him not strive to cloak his iniquity with the covering of falsehood.

But to leave these matters, concerning which I have, I believe, done enough: I pray, Father, that you show due regard, as you do to all good men, for so great a man, so tested, of such a life and purpose, who has offered to God nearly all his days from boyhood to old age; and that you hear no accusation against him except concerning a matter fully discovered and most thoroughly proved [Col. 0411A].

## LETTER XI

To the supreme pontiff and our special father, Lord Pope Eugenius: Brother Peter, humble abbot of the brethren of Cluny, offers the obedience due with filial love.

Trusting in paternal kindness, I often, Father, make requests to you for others; but now I beseech the apostolic majesty for one who lies nearest my heart above all others, as though for another self. This is Lord Jordan, abbot of Chaise-Dieu. I would commend him to you with greater confidence, because he is commendable, were I not afraid of being blamed because he is a brother. Yet I say briefly and truthfully that he has no need of my recommendation to you if your wisdom knew his character, his learning, and his reputation as we know them.

He approaches your presence, as I have learned from himself, driven by no business except the sole desire to see and visit you. If it please you, let your kindness—which I have experienced more than once—receive him graciously; and let it receive me in him, if I hold, as I do not doubt, any place of favor with you [Col. 0411C]. Let anything that may ever have been clouded in your mind against him be erased, if it please you; and let your favor return to him, for which alone he has journeyed as a pilgrim all the way to you. Because I plead briefly for him, I believe you do not wonder: for he is our kinsman and brother.

## LETTER XII

To the supreme pontiff and our special father, Lord Pope Eugenius: Brother Peter, humble abbot of the brethren of Cluny, offers devoted obedience with sincere affection.

I am indeed importunate in writing to you often, but I fear that, by frequently excusing that very importunity, I become still more importunate. What then shall I do [Col. 0411D]? If I keep silent, I shall harm myself and many others. If I speak, I shall appear tiresome, as I have said. But of the two I choose one. With your paternal kindness preserved, I prefer to appear talkative or excessive before you rather than keep silent about many things which ought not to be concealed from you.

What I am about to say does not concern my own affair. Yet how is that foreign to you which in any way belongs to you? And it belongs to you to hear the cases of the whole Church of God, journeying in this vale of tears; to examine them when heard; and, when examined, to determine them by apostolic judgment. And although your person has been set over nations and kingdoms, “to root up and destroy, to waste and overthrow, to build and to plant,” yet, since you are neither God nor Jeremiah the prophet, to whom this was said, you can be deceived; you can be misled by those [Col. 0412A] who seek not the things of Jesus Christ but their own.

To prevent this, a faithful son, if there is one, ought faithfully to disclose to his Father what is known to himself but perhaps unknown to you, and, lest those of whom it is written, “The poison of asps is under their lips” (Ps. 13), should be able to infect your sincerity with their toxin, ought to forearm you as he can. For it is no small gift of God to be delivered from such men, especially since the familiar Psalm says: “Lord, deliver my soul from wicked lips and from a deceitful tongue” (Ps. 119).

But what is this? Perhaps I am again speaking too diffusely, falling into the very fault I had excused. I therefore restrain my pen and briefly say, of matters on which I wished—and, I think, ought—to say much, why I have prefaced these remarks. There is one cause, though not the only one. I shall state this one now and reserve the others for their proper time.

Many know how greatly I have loved, love, revered, and embrace the institutions of the Carthusian order and profession; I myself know it better, and God best of all [Col. 0412B].

For if my mind does not deceive me, if my conscience bears witness to what is true, if finally the divine saying is true which declares, “No one knows the things of a man except the spirit of the man which is in him” (1 Cor. 2), I acknowledge that for almost thirty years now, that is, even before I began to hold office, I have loved the Carthusians’ religious life above that of nearly all mortals, honored their sincerity, and embraced their truth. I understood, and did not think myself mistaken, that their profession ought to be preferred to the institutions of all Latins, and that they are not among those who strain out a gnat and swallow a camel (Matt. 23): that is, who make void God’s commandment for human traditions, tithe mint, dill, and cumin (ibid.), and, according to one Evangelist, every vegetable (Luke 11), yet neglect the weightier matters of the law—judgment, mercy, and faith.

For they do not think that God’s kingdom consists chiefly in foods, drink, clothing, labors, or similar things—although such practices, when performed with discretion, serve that same kingdom of God greatly—but in that godliness of which the Apostle says: “Bodily exercise is of little profit, but godliness is profitable for all things, holding promise of the life that now is and of that which is to come” (1 Tim. 4). Those holy men truly feast [Col. 0412D] at the table of wisdom and delight in the fare of the true Solomon, not in superstitions, hypocrisy, vanities, or the leaven of malice and wickedness, but in the unleavened bread of sincerity and truth (1 Cor. 5). They are therefore great, worthy of love, worthy of embrace.

And what shall I say? Reluctantly I bring forth what I think; compelled by reason, I say what I do not wish to say. I seem to touch the ark of God and presumptuously raise it with my hand, as Uzzah once did when the oxen were frisking (2 Sam. 6). But I am no presumptuous man; I am not, so far as this case is concerned, worthy of death like him, because the words of him who said, “If your eye is single, your whole body will be full of light” (Luke 11), make me confident. I shall speak, then, and delay no longer. Let the Father hear his son’s words with an even mind and not suppose that anything crafty or deceitful lies hidden in them [Col. 0413A]. For, as I remember having lately written to your eminence in another letter, to lie to you would be the same to me as to die.

In the matter still at issue, the election at Grenoble, it seems to me that an unforeseen storm has darkened the clear day of the Carthusian order, and that a little cloud arisen from I know not where has obscured its hitherto crystalline brightness. The holy community, divided against itself, which until these times had been more especially one in Christ than others, is fighting against itself over this affair. On one side stand the Charterhouse [Note: [Col. 0413C] The Charterhouse: namely the Grande Chartreuse, situated in the mountains of Dauphiné near Grenoble. Saint Bruno began to live there with his companions in the year of Christ 1084, with the gift of the place from Saint Hugh, bishop of Grenoble, as is related in the history of his life in Surius under 6 October. The prior of this house is the head of the entire Carthusian order, and general assemblies of the order are customarily held there every year.], Les Écouges, Durbon [Note: [Col. 0413C] Durbon: the house of Durbon, or, as others write, d’Urbon, is in the province of the county of Provence, in the district of Marseille.]; on the other, Portes [Note: [Col. 0413C] Portes: the house of Portes was founded in the province of Burgundy in the time of Saint Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, as is clear from Peter Sutor, book II of *On the Life of the Carthusians*, treatise III, chapter 5, and from the Carthusian Chronicle of Dorland, book IV, chapter 9.], Meyriat [Note: [Col. 0413C] Meyriat: the monastery of Meyriat still exists in the same province and is one of the most ancient Carthusian monasteries [Col. 0413D].], Sylva [Note: [Col. 0413D] Sylva: likewise a house in the same province, commonly called *Sylva Benedicta* (“Blessed Forest”).], Arvières [Note: [Col. 0413D] Alverium: also called *Arveriae* in the plural, likewise in that province of Burgundy.], and whatever other places belong to that sacred order. They set themselves up like opposing walls; and both groups profess, according to the Prophet, to “go up to stand in the battle on the day of the Lord” for the house of Israel (Ezek. 13) [Col. 0413B].

The former say that the man elected ought not to be made bishop, and they allege certain reasons which it is not mine to state now. The others, conversely, say: “What have these matters to do with you? The institution of the Carthusian order is to make known to those concerned whatever evils they may know, but not to litigate. Their role is simply to say what they think, not to enter palaces in order to argue cases. It is not for our wilderness to stand at courts of judgment; it is not for those who appear dead to the world to act as prosecutors or defenders in public affairs. Our simplicity has nothing to do with worldly cunning; nor is it fitting that we who chose the wilderness while in the world should now return from the wilderness to the world [Col. 0414A]. And if it is unfitting that we should return there even when dragged thither, is it fitting that we should thrust ourselves voluntarily, while all are unwilling and objecting, before the tribunals of judges?”

This is the cause, not indeed of open litigation but of hidden hostility, among holy men. It would become more fully known to the Father if I were permitted to speak to your majesty not only in writing but also in person. For there are certain things which I do not wish to commit to letters; but because I did not think it advisable to write them, I have reserved them to be communicated to you by the mouth of our beloved brother and your son Arnald.

## LETTER XIII

To our venerable and beloved brethren at Limoges, serving God and Saint Martial, His and their apostle: Brother PETER, humble abbot of the Cluniac brethren, fullness of salvation, grace, and blessing from God.

[Note: **[Col. 0413D] “To our brethren,” etc.** Whether blessed Martial, the first bishop of Limoges, ought to be declared an apostle was extensively debated at the Council of Limoges under Aymon, Archbishop of Bourges, in the time of Robert, king of the Franks. Yet John Cordesius, a man of exceptional learning, promises to investigate the question still more fully and carefully. We shall therefore not linger longer now over that controversy. We add only that the monastery of this Saint Martial at Limoges was at that time also reckoned among those governed by the abbots of Cluny, and was accustomed to pay them annually one hundred Tours pounds as tribute. Thus Peter, priest-cardinal of the title of Saint Marcellus, delegated by Innocent IV to settle the dispute between the abbot of Cluny and the abbot and convent of Saint Martial, ruled in 1246:

“For the abbot and convent of Cluny alleged”—as appears in the letters of Cardinal Peter himself—“that the monastery of Saint Martial and the churches subject to it belonged to their order and pertained directly to their monastery; and [they alleged rights] concerning the appointment and removal of the prior to be made in that monastery of Saint Martial at Limoges by the abbot of Cluny himself; and concerning one hundred and fifty Tours pounds, which the said abbot and convent of Cluny claimed in perpetuity as an annual payment from the aforesaid abbot and convent of Saint Martial at Limoges and from their monasteries. The abbot and convent of Saint Martial, on the contrary, maintained that they were not bound to this, etc.

“But we,” says Peter, “desiring the good of peace and wishing to remove the material of contention, so that the parties may wholly withdraw from litigation and disputes, pronounce as follows: judging, arbitrating, defining, establishing, and amicably settling between the parties, we assign to the monastery of Cluny an annual perpetual payment of one hundred Tours pounds from the monastery of Saint Martial at Limoges; condemning it by this judgment to render and pay the said one hundred Tours pounds each year in perpetuity at Paris, in the monastery of Saint-Martin-des-Champs of the Cluniac order, on the day after the Purification of the Blessed Virgin Mary, to the prior of Saint-Martin-des-Champs at Paris in the name of the abbot of Cluny, or to another who presents a special mandate from the abbot of Cluny concerning this matter. He shall give letters certifying payment once the said money has been paid in full, etc. Done in the year of the Lord 1246, the fifth indiction, 12 Kalends of December, in the fourth year of the pontificate of Pope Innocent IV.”]

[Col. 0414B]

My heart has rejoiced in the Lord—not because I now see, but because I hear—at your manner of life and the renown of your order, illustrious before God and men. I have heard this not merely once but often, from persons whom it would be wrong not to believe, since they are truthful, and whom your actions, whether good or bad, could not escape, since they are near you. I rejoice indeed over all those of whom I hear similar reports; but over you in a fuller measure, because I owe you more.

But someone among you will say: “Why do you rejoice more over us than over others?” For this reason, most dear brethren: I rejoice more over you than over certain others because, according to the words of the Apostle Peter, “set in the midst of a crooked and perverse nation” [Col. 0415A] (Phil. 2), you shine by your good example as lights in the world. You inhabit the land of Hus, yet do not follow that land’s vices. For, as I understand it, from our Cluny as far as those Pyrenees which divide the Gauls from the Iberians, I know of no monastery of the Cluniac or any other ancient order in which the order handed down by the Fathers has flourished until now so firmly, so steadfastly, so unshakenly, and has tirelessly preserved its observances amid the roaring beasts and savage jaws of the Limousin territory. For that reason, as I said, I rejoice more in your good reputation than in that of certain others.

For, as that teacher of the Church whom you know says: “It is a great thing to be good among the good; but far greater to be good among the bad.” Moreover, as those who experience it often report to us, you show in deeds, not words only; in results, not intentions merely, that you have not forgotten the milk of Cluny by which you were reared in the fear and service of God. You receive our brethren, who are also yours and who come to you almost continually, with such devotion; and you serve them with such affection.

We have heard these things from many; but now especially from our beloved son Rannulf, your prior. He has reported to us and to your brethren more good concerning you than we now wish to express, and has affirmed that he is greatly loved by you for God’s sake and ours. If those who love in God are worthy of love, do not regret having loved him; for, whenever he is with us, he does not cease to show in every way he can his love toward you.

Furthermore, most dear brethren, with sincere affection I ask and exhort you in [Col. 0415C] the Lord to take care to enlarge the good things said of you by still better advances. God’s servants must never lack the desire to progress; the fear of falling away should always make them diligent in God’s work. For, as the great Pope Leo says, the human mind, just as it can always have something toward which it may decline, can also always have something toward which it may grow.

Let both you and all of your order be ashamed to seem inferior to any newcomers in the observance of monastic religion, lest—contrary to the Lord’s words, God forbid—the disciple be above the master (Matt. 10); lest, while others draw water from your spring, you thirst; lest, while others are filled from your table, you remain hungry. For you know that almost whatever the new religious men of our age seem to possess took its beginning from you and received from you its material and form.

Run therefore, no more sluggishly than any others, in the way of God’s commandments. Let no one outrun you as you run; let no one steal from you the prize set before those who run well. Do this with such urgency as the Apostle says: “So run that you may obtain” (1 Cor. 9). Devote yourselves especially to works of peace and obedience, so that, as you labor in these and in the other exercises of holy virtues, secular people may see your works and glorify the Father who is in heaven (Matt. 5).

May the almighty Savior hear your charity as it prays for me and for the whole Church or congregation of Cluny, and may He order your deeds, conduct, and life according to His good pleasure, which is everlasting salvation.

## LETTER XIV

To his beloved brother—indeed, son—EUSTACE: Brother PETER, humble abbot of Cluny, present and eternal salvation, which I desire for myself.

[Col. 0416A]

I rejoice, nor can I express with my mouth my joy that, although you are my only brother in the flesh so far as this world is concerned, I know that you fear God, revere God, and love God. And what greater joy could there be for my soul?

I see the world raging on every side. I see Satan, prince of the world, playing with mortals as with birds. I see him daily—indeed, unceasingly—dragging down to hell most miserable souls, given as eternal food to avenging flames. I see him, both near you and far from you, claiming for himself by sword, plague, sudden death, or any deceit of the devil’s snare, so many thousands of human souls that Christ, our Savior and God, may say of them: “Many are called, but few are chosen” (Matt. 22); and, in a similar case: “Amen, I tell you: none of those men who were invited shall taste my supper” (Luke 14).

Since I hear these things from my Lord, and know you to be beset on every side by so many and such great evils, ought I not to rejoice when the fear of God and concern for saving your soul separate you from men who are lost and being lost, and join you to the camp of His soldiers who are saved or to be saved?

If poverty, the advance of enemies fighting against you, or the reckless violence of fortune—if I may so speak—envying your prosperity compelled you to this, I should indeed rejoice that you were among those of whom the Savior already mentioned says figuratively: “Go out into the roads and hedges, and compel them to come in, that my house may be filled” [Col. 0416C] (ibid.). But now, when I see you abounding in worldly goods and in all that a horn of plenty is accustomed to pour upon most mortals, with scarcely anything lacking of what is desired, I exult far more and rejoice much more greatly: your mind is drawn to divine things, not by want of temporal things, but by a God-given longing for eternal things.

You once were, but by the aid of God’s mercy you are no longer, “in the labor of men,” nor are you scourged with the wicked; yet pride has not therefore taken hold of you, nor are you covered with your iniquity and ungodliness. Hence, as I have said, I rejoice exceedingly and again exceedingly that the snare of prosperity—which often entangles even minds strong and steadfast in their resolve for salvation—has in part untied its knots so as not to capture you; and that it has given me and yours a most certain hope that this may at some time happen, not partly but wholly, if God helps.

But to come to the matter for which I began to write: I am pleased—and very much so—that you did not disdain the dream about which the cleric wrote to you, and that, through this opportunity, however slight, you have sharpened yourself to the fear of God. For although dreams are often empty, so that Christian Scripture says of them, “You shall not practice divination or observe dreams” (Lev. 19); and elsewhere, “Dreams follow many cares” (Eccl. 5); and likewise that saying of the Wise Man, “Do not heed dreams” (Jer. 29), nevertheless not all dreams are to be despised, because they have often been proved true by the effects which fulfilled their meaning.

[Col. 0417A]

The Church of God has in the divine books Pharaoh’s seven fat cows and seven lean cows, seven full ears and seven barren ears, foreshadowing seven years of Egyptian fertility and seven years of sterility (Gen. 16). It has also the loaf of barley seen in Gideon’s dream—that is, Gideon himself—rolling into the great camp of Midian and, by God’s power, capturing it with only three hundred soldiers and destroying it to its furthest reaches (Judg. 7). It has also, long before, in that same Heptateuch, Joseph appearing in dreams as though, at harvest time, the sheaves of his brothers were worshipping his sheaf, and then the sun, moon, and eleven stars worshipping himself (Gen. 37). In Daniel it shows, both concerning Daniel’s own dreams and those of King Nebuchadnezzar, that they foretold the future (Dan. 2 and 7).

The magnificent and heavenly Scripture also testifies in the Gospel concerning righteous Joseph, spouse of the holy Virgin, the Lord’s mother: the angel of the Lord appeared to him in a dream when he was considering dismissing the Lord’s mother, and forbade him to dismiss her (Matt. 1); and in dreams commanded that she be taken into Egypt with her Son and brought back again (Matt. 2).

Why, dearest brother, do I say these things? So that you may understand that dreams are neither always to be followed nor always to be despised. Hence my brief advice is this: whether the things reported by the author of the dream are true or false, whether they portend something or do not, make prudent use of either the reporter’s truth or falsehood. That is, make worthy satisfaction to God, as far as you can, for past offenses; and take every care that no evil whatever, especially no crimes, impede your satisfaction.

I say this not because I place any nobleman of your party before you in good pursuits—so far as one still held in the bonds of the world can be concerned—although I have heard this of many; but because I know that the more cautious you are, the better you will be.

For if the vision about which you wrote to your elder brother is true and meaningful, or perhaps true but signifying nothing, you will not be found before God a despiser of truths, as King Zedekiah was found. A book was sent to him by the prophet Jeremiah containing many threats against him. Not only was he not frightened, nor did he obey God’s commands sent to him through the prophet, but he tore the very book with a scribe’s knife which happened to be at hand and threw it into a brazier full of coals, where it was burned (Jer. 36). For this reason, shortly afterward he was captured by enemies, had his eyes torn out, was carried to Babylon, and at last died in bitter captivity.

[Col. 0417D]

But if the reporter of the dream just mentioned lied from any motive—for, as Scripture says, “the heart of man is wicked and inscrutable” (Jer. 17)—if, I say, he lied and, like the false prophets of old, whom God mockingly represents as saying, “I have dreamed, I have dreamed” (Jer. 23), invented falsehoods, you will profit even from the falsehood itself, when on this occasion, as I have said, you become more cautious in all your actions.

For many such false prophets, or lying reporters of dreams, really did lie in old times. Against them God says: “Woe to those who prophesy from their own heart!” (Ezek. 13). And again elsewhere: “If anyone does not put something into their hands, they sanctify war against him” (Mic. 3). If you use their reports in the manner I have described, they can greatly benefit you and can harm you in no way.

Act, then, sole and almost only hope of our family, so that, as you are called energetic and prudent in the world, you may at last be called no less energetic and no less powerful in God. I would speak more fully and pour many things which I keep in my heart’s inmost chamber into your ears, if I did not hope to speak with you face to face shortly—that is, before the Lord’s Pascha. Since I hope this, I now end my speech. The Lord be with you.

## LETTER XV

To our venerable and beloved brethren, both Priors and Guardians of the Order, wherever established: Brother PETER, humble abbot of Cluny, greeting, and grace and blessing from the author of graces.

[Col. 0418B]

Shall I speak or be silent? Shall I open my lips or close them? If I wish to belong to those of whom it is said, “My people, those who call you blessed deceive you and ruin the way of your steps” (Isa. 3), and to those of whom Holy Scripture speaks mockingly in the voice of a foolish people, “Speak pleasant things to us; see visions for us” (Isa. 30); or to those of whom it says again, “Many dogs, unable to bark” (Isa. 56), then I must either flatter you or keep silent.

If I flatter, I shall incur that prophetic woe which is read in Isaiah: “Woe to those who call evil good and good evil, who call darkness light and light darkness, who turn bitter into sweet and sweet into bitter!” (Isa. 5). If I keep silent, I fear also this: “If you do not announce his iniquity to the wicked man, he indeed shall die in his iniquity, but I shall require his blood from your hand” (Ezek. 3). And this: “Woe is me because I have been silent!” (Isa. 6).

Therefore I have resolved neither to flatter you nor to be silent. Both are equally dangerous in relation to what I intend to say. Of the two alternatives I proposed, then, one remains: not silence, but speech. And why do I say that speech remains? Rather, I must speak and cry aloud: “Cry,” He says, “do not cease; raise your voice like a trumpet” [Col. 0418D] (Isa. 58), and the rest which you know.

Therefore I speak and cry out, and I exhort you, who preside over others, to speak and cry out these things yourselves. For if you keep silence, you have no less to fear than I—not even by a little—since you know that you have been called, if not to the fullness of power, yet to a share in pastoral concern.

And, lest I delay longer in saying what must be said, I have been told—nor by insignificant or frivolous persons, which I say with deep sorrow of heart—that, as regards eating meat, there is now no difference between our brethren and laymen, between secular persons and religious—indeed, to speak more plainly, between buffoons and monks. I said there is no difference between these and those; but alas, there is much difference in a perverse direction.

Mimes or camp-followers abstain from meat every Saturday for God’s sake; moreover, most laymen abstain every Wednesday, and some even every Monday. Yet our brethren—monks of a holy order and heavenly calling, Cluniac monks at that—despising God and casting away shame, continue, as is said, to consume meat throughout the whole year, with no day except Friday excluded. They do this not even secretly but openly and publicly, proclaiming their sin, according to the prophet, like Sodom (Isa. 3).

[Col. 0419A]

They run from place to place and, like kites or vultures, wherever they see the smoke of kitchens or smell the odor of roasted or boiled flesh, swiftly fly there. Because the sacred order is blasphemed by those who observe this evil example, they themselves blaspheme the Lord’s name through their mouths. “Woe,” says Holy Scripture, “to those through whom the name of the Lord is blasphemed!” (Isa. 52).

If anyone, led by fear of God, wishes to abstain from such food, he is now mocked by such men and called a hypocrite, pretender, and profane person. They regard him as a heathen and a publican and proclaim that he must be avoided like a public enemy. Beans, cheese, eggs, even fish themselves, have now become nauseating. Only the pots of Egypt please them. Roast or boiled pork, a fat heifer, a cirogrillus [animal name uncertain], and a hare, a goose chosen from the flock of geese, hens, and indeed every domestic quadruped or bird cover the tables of holy monks.

But even these things have now become cheapened. Their constant use has produced disgust. A transition has been made to royal and foreign delicacies: the monk, already full, can now eat only roe deer, stag, wild boar, or bear. Forests must be scoured; hunters are needed. By the skill of fowlers, pheasants, partridges, and turtledoves must be caught, lest God’s servant perish from hunger. Care must be taken that, since he cannot live otherwise, all his desires are satisfied.

[Col. 0419C]

What remains, then? Since throughout the entire week only Friday is excepted from these banquets, let Friday itself be added, and let not the Christian fast of Lent interrupt their uninterrupted feasting. Away with the fasts of spring, summer, autumn, and winter. Let the whole, entire year be continued in feasts and merriment, lest perhaps the god of such men be offended—of whom and of whose god the Apostle says: “Their god is their belly, and their glory is in their shame” (Phil. 3).

For why are monks of this kind fruitlessly wearied? Why, without hope of reward, do they abstain from meat on Friday, in Lent, or on the other days already named? What hope of reward can remain to men who appear to abstain from meat on those holy days not willingly but unwillingly, not voluntarily but under compulsion? No one—no one, I say—will persuade me that, were it permitted them without punishment, such people would wish to abstain from meat on those days.

Therefore let them abandon what they do unwillingly. And, as strangers to that bread of which the Gospel says, “Blessed is he who shall eat bread in the kingdom of God” (Luke 14), and exiles from that table of which Christ says, “That you may eat and drink at my table in my kingdom” (Luke 22), let them meanwhile not lose their pork, beef, or any other meats, even on Friday or during Lent. Let the whole and entire year, as I have said, be continued in merriment and feasting, so that sorrow and torments may be perpetuated for these feasting men through the ages.

[Col. 0420A]

The Cluniac estates, as I have learned from some of our trustworthy brethren, are now insufficient for the tables and feasts of our spendthrifts—to such an extent that, if a devoted servant wishes to satisfy their appetite for meat and their desires, the very lands and estates must be sold.

And whoever you are, butcher for such banquets: is this what you vowed to God when you professed yourself a monk? Is this what you promised before your abbot and brethren? Is this the Rule according to which you pledged yourself to live? Let us see; let us see: let the Rule itself be brought forward, and let it be recognized whether one who professes what it commands concerning meat keeps his profession.

“The eating of the flesh of quadrupeds,” it says, “is to be wholly abstained from by all, except only the very weak and the sick.” And elsewhere: “Whenever it is beneficial, eating meat may be offered to the sick. But when they have recovered, let all abstain from meat in the customary manner.”

What do you say? “I am a monk.” Oh, would that you were! If, then, you are a monk, where is what you professed? You certainly professed obedience according to the Rule of Saint Benedict. These are the words of the Rule on this chapter that you have heard. Why then do you transgress? Why do you lie to God? Why do you deceive yourself? Your own words condemn you; from your own mouth they judge you as a wicked servant (Luke 19).

[Col. 0420C]

Men keep the written bond which you made; angels preserve it. It shall be set before you on the day of God’s great judgment, before the tribunal of the highest and true Judge, Jesus Christ. It shall be set before you and read, whether unto life or unto death.

And lest you resort to your usual answer—that this chapter, like some others, was altered by certain holy Fathers for sound reason—I reply: it is otherwise. For if, after Saint Benedict, good Fathers altered provisions concerning the reception of novices, manual labor, clothing, and certain similar matters, this was done for a certain, reasonable cause, not a doubtful one. That cause or rationale I carefully described twice in two letters formerly addressed to the Lord Abbot of Clairvaux; I judge it superfluous to repeat it here. If you are so studious, you will find it there in full.

But by what argument can transgression of this chapter be excused? By what cause can a monk who is sound and whole in strength, yet eats meat, be shown not guilty? Say what you have, and if there is any true or plausible reason, defend meat for yourself if you can. You have nothing—you have nothing, I say, as I judge—to say. You have absolutely no ground on which to cleanse the stain, not to say the guilt, of perjury. The Rule confronts you; justice contradicts you. And why do I speak? Let the Rule be silent for the moment.

After great Benedict and his disciple Maurus, let Odo come forward: the supreme restorer of monastic order among the Gauls and foremost reformer of the Rule. Odo, I say, first Father of the Cluniac order, who undertook with utmost effort to revive the fervor of monastic purpose, then dead and almost everywhere buried.

[Col. 0421A]

In his time the holy man had failed; truths had been diminished among the children of men. In almost every region of our Europe, there was nothing of the monk except tonsure and habit. He applied himself almost alone at that time to the divine work. Laying the first foundations at Cluny, he did not cease, as long as he lived, to sow seeds of religion now here, now there.

What then, brother, did this first Father of yours think, say, and write about the chapter concerning meat? Consult his book; reread his words. You will find, among other matters, that to frighten persons of this kind he wrote of a monk in that corrupt age who came one morning to his parents’ house and asked that a meal be prepared for him. When his parents answered that they had fish ready, he grew angry at the word “fish,” struck with the stick he happened to hold a hen standing nearby, and said: “Why do you say you have fish? This, plainly, will be fish for me today.”

Ashamed by the words of the shameless man, they hastily prepare the hen which the monk had struck for food, put it to the fire, and begin to roast it. As it roasted for some time, the man, made impatient by gluttony and as though driven by madness, attacks the hen, tears out a morsel, and puts it into his mouth. When he had immediately chewed it and tried to swallow, he could not; nor was he able to spit it out.

Everyone runs up; cries arise from every side; repeated blows are struck upon the sufferer’s neck. With all effort and exertion he struggles to expel the food of death. But in vain. Thus, with the passage of his throat blocked and the breath of life cut off, that monk, unable either to confess his sins or, impeded by deadly food, to receive the saving food—that is, Christ’s body—died in an instant.

[Col. 0421C]

Thus overtaken by so terrible a death, he taught both those present and those to come how fearful it is to fall into the hands of the living God, and clearly showed that eating meat does not belong to monks who are strong and healthy.

This certainly, Cluniac brother, is the judgment and teaching of your first and holy Father Odo concerning monks’ meat-eating. But lest you perhaps say that he condemns this vice in one monk only, recall the account of his life and remember with what diligence he restrained from eating meat the monks of Saint Benedict’s monastery on the Loire committed to him. For there it is written thus:

“Moreover, in those days he began to persuade them to withdraw from eating meat, to live sparingly, and to possess nothing as their own.” And after some intervening material: “But those brethren were trying, by eating, to consume precisely the thing which they had renounced, together with the other things which our Father had brought with him, so that, once everything had been consumed, he might at least unwillingly permit them to eat meat. For this reason they continually demanded fish. Conversely, the pious Father supplied them with all suitable things in order to restrain them from one thing.” From what one thing? Surely from eating meat.

This, I say, as I have said, if you are Cluniac, is the teaching of your Father; this is his example; this is his command.

Either, then, deny that he is your Father and eat your meats, or acknowledge him and abstain from meats that are not yours. I call them not yours if you are a monk and healthy.

[Col. 0422A]

And why do I say, if you are a monk and healthy? I shall say something stronger: see how greatly the eating of meat by monks ought to be condemned, when it was condemned by God with the utmost severity even among the Jews. They said: “Who will give us meat to eat? Our soul is dry; our eyes look upon nothing except manna” (Num. 11). And what followed? “The anger of the Lord,” says Holy Scripture, “was greatly inflamed.” The matter also seemed intolerable to Moses (ibid.).

If God was angry, if the matter seemed intolerable to Moses because a Jew desired meat, can it please God, can it be a tolerable matter, when a monk eats meat against his own vow? But hear God’s fearful judgment. Although God was angry for that reason, and although that murmuring appeared intolerable to Moses, Jewish desire was nevertheless satisfied, that they might be punished after obtaining what they desired wickedly, and that the torments might be fulfilled in them according to the judgment which says: “I let them go according to the desires of their heart; they shall go in their own devices” (Ps. 80).

Indeed, so it happened: “They desired a desire in the wilderness, and tested God in the waterless land. And He gave them their request, and sent satiety into their souls” (Ps. 105). For this was said to them: “Sanctify yourselves; tomorrow you shall eat meat. For I,” says God, “heard you say: ‘Who will give us food of meat? It was well with us in Egypt.’ Therefore the Lord shall give you meat, and you shall eat—not for one day, nor two, nor five or ten, nor even twenty, but for a whole month, until it comes out through your nostrils and becomes nauseating to you—because you have rejected the Lord who is in your midst” (Num. 11).

[Col. 0422C]

Behold: what they desired was fulfilled. They ate and perished.
