Hear Moses: “The meat was still in their teeth, and food of this kind had not yet failed, when behold, the anger of the Lord was stirred up against the people and struck them with a very great plague. That place was called the Graves of Craving, because there they buried the people who had desired meat” (ibid.).

Hear David also: “Their food was still in their mouths, and the wrath of God came up against them. He killed their fat ones and hindered the chosen men of Israel” (Ps. 77).

What could be clearer? What more terrible? Hear, raven monk; and do not be angry because I call you so. For how do you differ from a raven, how from a vulture, how from a bear, how from a wolf? Those birds and beasts gape after bloody fare; they distinguish neither day from day nor hour from hour in eating. So, as I see, do you, who, as I wrote above, allow no season and no day to be free from such eating unless you are compelled by force.

Hear, observe, understand: the Jews, whose desire for meat God avenged so terribly, had never previously vowed to God abstinence from meat. Though they had vowed and promised God nothing of that kind, nevertheless because they desired, murmured, and ate, God’s anger rose against them; Israel’s chosen men were hindered; countless persons were killed; they were buried in the Graves of Craving because they had desired meat (Ps. 77).

But you, who vowed to God, for the sake of a greater merit to be laid up in heaven, that you would not eat meat while healthy—you whose voice almost unceasingly echoes before God in the Prophet and boldly promises Him, “I will pay you my vows, which my lips have uttered” (Ps. 65)—will you escape unpunished when almost daily you render void the compact made with God?

[Col. 0423A]

You wish—indeed, demand—that what your neighbor promises you be paid to you, and do you think that what is promised to God will not be demanded by God? He is silent now indeed; but, as He Himself says, “Will He be silent forever?” Certainly at some time He will speak like a woman in labor; certainly, in His own words, He will cry aloud and shout, and will prevail against His enemies (Isa. 42). He will demand payment because you have transgressed; He will demand it because you have lied; and He will remit nothing, down to the last farthing.

Let all these things, then, frighten you; and if you have not yet been cast from the face of God, fear what you hear. Do not regard these things as empty or trifling, for the judgment of God, which no mortal ever could escape, nor you, I believe, can escape (Rom. 2). These words are not mine but the Apostle’s—indeed, Christ’s, who speaks in the Apostle.

“Set,” as Solomon says, when you come to the table, “set a knife to your throat” (Prov. 23). Pierce your flesh with the fear of God; compel it to abstain from meats that are not yours. By a fruit—which is less—not by flesh, the progenitor of humankind perished and destroyed the world. Anyone who attends even a little recognizes how great that fault was. For unless the first guilt had been in that eating, the Son of God would not, in assumed flesh, have endured so much to expiate it.

But why do I linger over examples? Holy Scripture contains countless testimonies condemning gluttonous excess, showing how great are the evils which follow from it, and proclaiming that all Christians—not to say monks—must wholly avoid it. Thus the Apostle mentioned above says: “Not in revelries and drunkenness” (Rom. 13). And showing what follows, he adds: “Not in beds and indecencies” (ibid.).

[Col. 0423C]

But perhaps you will object to Isaac’s kids, with which he was filled and blessed his son (Gen. 27). Perhaps you will also raise the case of Elijah’s ravens, of whom it is written that they brought him bread and meat in the morning, and bread and meat in the evening (3 Kings 17). Yet I, although you are no patriarch, willingly grant you the patriarch’s kids—if only, once filled, you give me also the blessings which he gave his son. Nor will I deny you Elijah’s meat if either you are a prophet or you receive meat brought by ravens.

But lest I seem excessive in speaking, I now end my words. Why should I prolong them further? If these things do not frighten you, more, I think, would not frighten you either. If these things do not correct you, greater things, as I judge, would not correct you either. May God therefore grant that what has been said may benefit you. But if it does not benefit you, it will at least benefit me. For I shall say to God what Father Benedict declares that teachers despised by their subjects will say: “I have not hidden Your justice in my heart; I have declared Your truth and Your salvation. But they, despising, have rejected me.”

## LETTER XVI

To the magnificent prince, Lord ROGER, king of Sicily: Brother PETER, humble abbot of Cluny, present salvation and an everlasting kingdom.

[Col. 0424A]

How deeply we love Your Highness, and how greatly we desire your deeds to prosper both in the Lord and in the world, is known to Him who knows all things. On hearing of the death of your sons, we grieved deeply; and, both for your welfare and for their souls, we directed that Masses be celebrated, prayers poured out to God, and alms given in our community. Nor only now: often on feast days and at our major chapters we commemorate you among our other kings, friends, and benefactors. Henceforth we make known to your royal greatness [Col. 0424B] that we grieve greatly over the hostilities being conducted between you and the lord king of the Germans, or emperor of the Romans. For I, as well as many others, strongly feel that this discord damages the Latin realms and the spread of the Christian faith. Since, as we have often heard, many advances for the Church of God result from your military strength in lands belonging to God’s enemies—that is, the Saracens—far greater advances, we believe, would result if a firm peace and concord united you with the aforesaid king.

There is another consideration which much more strongly inflames our hearts, and the hearts of nearly all our Frenchmen, to love and seek your peace: namely, that most wicked, unheard-of, and lamentable treachery committed by the Greeks and their evil king [Col. 0424C] against our pilgrims—that is, the army of the living God. For, to speak according to what I perceive in my heart, if it were necessary, I would not refuse, so far as it may belong to a monk, to die, if the justice of God should deign through one of His servants to avenge the death of so many, so noble men—indeed, the flower of almost all France and Germany—destroyed by miserable treachery. Yet among Christian princes under heaven I see none through whom this work, so holy and so desired by heaven and earth, could be accomplished as well, suitably, and effectively as through you. For, by God’s grace—and I do not say this in flattery—as I infer from your past deeds and the words of many, you are, for accomplishing so great a good, [Col. 0424D] keener in judgment, richer in resources, more practised in valor, and moreover nearer to the place itself, than other princes.

Rise up, therefore, good prince. Though it is my voice that speaks, I speak both my own desire and that of all. Rise to the aid of God’s people; be zealous for God’s law as the Maccabees were; avenge so many reproaches, so many injuries, so many deaths, and the blood of God’s army so impiously shed. For the cause of the peace just mentioned, I am ready, as soon as an opportunity presents itself, to approach the aforesaid emperor and, bringing with me whomsoever I can, to employ all my strength and every effort in negotiating the restoration and confirmation between you and him of a peace so beloved by God. God willing, immediately after obtaining an interview, I shall write to you and set everything out in a letter.

## LETTER XVII. Brother BERNARD of Clairvaux to his most beloved Father, PETER, by God’s grace venerable abbot of Cluny: greeting, and such prayers in the Lord as he is able to offer.

[Col. 0425A]

“The exceedingly grievous and pitiable lament of the Eastern Church,” etc. See among the letters of St Bernard, *Patrologia*, vol. CLXXXII.

## LETTER XVIII. To the venerable and illustrious lamp of God’s Church, to be embraced with all the arms of charity, Lord BERNARD, abbot of Clairvaux: Brother PETER, humble abbot of Cluny, greeting and his whole self.

The letter which your Holiness sent me, although I had not previously been wholly unaware of its subject, moved me—and moved me greatly, as was fitting. [Col. 0425B] What Christian, having any hope in his Christ, would not be moved by so lamentable a report? From the letter of the lord abbot of Saint-Denis I have learned that it has now been spread almost everywhere: the brethren of the Temple, the king of Jerusalem, and even the Lord’s saving Cross itself are besieged in the city of Antioch with many others; and unless the hand of the Lord, stretched out in might, swiftly comes to their help, all will shortly be taken captive. Who would not be moved lest that Holy Land, rescued not long ago from the yoke of the impious by the labors of so many Fathers and by so much blood of Christ’s worshippers, should again be subjected to the impious and blasphemous? Who would not be moved if the most salutary path of penitent sinners—which, as we ought to believe, has for fifty [Col. 0425C] years now removed countless thousands of pilgrims from hell and restored them to heaven—should be closed by the obstructing barrier of wicked Saracens?

Far be it—far be it, I say—that heavenly wrath should rage so fiercely against its Christians, the people acquired for itself, that to a wound newly inflicted and still burning it should again add a wound so grievous that, by its magnitude, it would now seem not purgative but destructive. He could not truly be reckoned among the members of Christ’s body who were not moved from the inward depths of his heart by so great a peril—indeed, so great a calamity—of the Christian people. I do not speak merely of being moved to share in suffering, which is easy for everyone, but of being moved to help according to one’s strength and even to undertake whatever is burdensome. For if, in the human body, hand does not fail to assist hand, foot foot, or any member any other member when injured, and regards that injury not as another’s but as its own, how much more in Christ’s sacred body, which is His Church, must brother come to meet and help brother, and neighbor neighbor, with all effort and all strength—especially in the greater dangers? [Col. 0425D]

In human flesh this is done by the one spirit that gives life to all the members; in the body of the Church it is done likewise by the one Holy Spirit, who gives life to all its members. Therefore, one who does not feel the wounds of Christ’s body is not animated by Christ’s Spirit. It is consequently made plain that both you and certain other men of your regions belong to the chief members of His body, since its injury moves and afflicts you so deeply. This especially shows [Col. 0426A] the truth of what I say: although you are situated in the farthest West—indeed, almost on the shore of the western ocean—you hasten, across such intervening expanses of land, to help the Christian name suffering in the East with the utmost zeal in your power.

For this reason you have resolved to assemble at Chartres, on the appointed day, with the lord king, other Fathers of the Church, and the leading men of the realm; and you have asked me to be present at that sacred gathering. I confess what is true: I am ashamed to excuse my absence, yet I cannot possibly come. Among other obstacles is the nearly uninterrupted infirmity of my body from the Nativity of the Lord onward. Moreover, before I knew anything of these matters, I had, for an unavoidable reason, at almost the beginning of Lent, ordered many [Col. 0426B] of our priors by messenger and letter to come to Cluny on the very day appointed for the gathering at Chartres. I disclosed part of the reason for their coming in confidence to the venerable man, the lord abbot of Fontenelle, who brought me your letter; if you wish, you may hear it from him.

I beg you, then—and beg you again and again—not to take this ill, or to think that I speak with one thing in my heart and another on my lips. I guard against this not only when speaking with you, but have always been accustomed to guard against it. For I would not merely come as far as Chartres for so great a cause: if the needs of the Church entrusted to me allowed it, I would not hesitate in any way even to go to Jerusalem itself, which is the subject under discussion. Yet if at another time another assembly should be held, whether in your regions or ours, unless an unavoidable cause again prevented me, [Col. 0426C] let Your Reverence know that I would most gladly go and, with an assembly or without one, furnish according to my strength assistance for so great a matter.

## LETTER XIX. To his most beloved lord and venerable Father, PETER, by God’s grace abbot of Cluny: SUGER, abbot of Blessed Saint-Denis, offers devoted prayers in Christ and the fullness of love and service.

“The calamity of the Eastern Church,” etc. See Suger, *Patrologia*, vol. CLXXXVI.

## LETTER XX. To the venerable man and our heartfelt friend, Lord SUGER, abbot of Saint-Denis: Brother PETER, humble abbot of Cluny, the fullness of both present and eternal salvation.

[Col. 0426D]

I grieve, and grieve beyond what I can express, because I cannot attend your sacred assembly, which the lord king, on the counsel of your wisdom and that of other wise men, has convened at Chartres. Believe your intimate friend; believe one who speaks truthfully: I truly wish to come, but cannot; and because I cannot, I grieve. For who would not grieve at being absent from so holy a council, where no one will seek personal gain, where no one will seek what is his own, but what belongs to Jesus Christ? For no ordinary matter is in question; the matter under discussion is one than which none is greater—indeed, it is the greatest of all.

Is it not the greatest of all matters to make provision and exert ourselves lest what is holy be given to dogs; lest the places where stood the feet of Him who wrought salvation in the midst of the earth be again trampled under the feet of the wicked; [Col. 0427A] lest royal Jerusalem, consecrated by prophets, apostles, and the Savior of all, and that noble metropolis of all Syria, Antioch, again be subjected to blasphemous and abominable men; lest the saving Cross itself, now, as is said, besieged by the impious, be captured as once by Chosroes [Cosdroe]; lest the Lord’s very sepulchre, which until now, according to the prophet, has been glorious throughout the world (Isa. 11), perhaps—as they are accustomed to threaten—be torn up by the roots?

I would therefore most gladly, as I have said, have attended this discussion, so holy and necessary, to which you, venerable sir, wished to invite my humility, had I possibly been able. The obstacles to this journey are many. But among them two are particular: first, the manifold infirmity of my body, which I have suffered almost continually from the Nativity of the Lord to this time; second, a great gathering of priors whom, before I knew anything of what you communicated, I had ordered to come to Cluny, almost at the beginning of Lent, for consultation on an unavoidable matter, on the day when your assembly at Chartres was appointed. [Col. 0427B] Let Your Reverence, then—unanimous and most dear to me—if you please, receive my excuse with equanimity, not as feigned but true; and hold my absence excused, both in your own judgment and before others.

## LETTER XXI. To PETER, most reverend lord and Father, and venerable abbot of Cluny: HELOISE, humble servant of God and His handmaid, wishes the spirit of saving grace.

Through God’s mercy visiting us, the favor of your condescension [Col. 0427C] visited us. We rejoice, most kindly Father, and glory that your greatness has descended to our lowliness. Your visit, indeed, is a great glorying for any who are great. Others know how much benefit the presence of your exalted person has brought them. I certainly cannot, I do not say describe it in words, but cannot even comprehend in thought how beneficial and delightful your coming was to me.

> **Note [Col. 0427D].** “How beneficial and delightful your coming was to me.” The coming of holy Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, had earlier also been beneficial and delightful. Peter Abelard, writing to him, says: “When lately I had come to the Paraclete, compelled by certain business to carry out there, your daughter in Christ and our sister, who is called abbess of that place, reported to me with the greatest exultation that you had come there, long desired, for the purpose of a holy visitation, and that you had strengthened both her and her sisters by sacred exhortations, not as a man but as though an angel.”

Our abbot, our lord, last year, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of December [16 November], you celebrated Mass among us, in which you commended us to the Holy Spirit. In chapter you fed us with the blessing of the divine word. You gave us the body of the Master and granted the Cluniac benefit. You also bestowed upon me—whom your exalted humility did not disdain, both in writing and in speech, to call sister, though I am not worthy even of the name [Col. 0427D] of handmaid—a certain singular privilege, as it were, of love and sincerity: namely, that after my death the Cluniac community should perform for me a *tricenarium* [a thirty-day series of Masses]. You also promised to confirm that gift with sealed letters. Therefore fulfill, brother—or rather lord—what you granted to your sister—or rather handmaid. Be pleased also to send me another sealed document, containing in an open letter the Master’s absolution,

> **Note [Cols. 0427D, 0428D].** “Be pleased to send another sealed document containing the Master’s absolution.” This seal, containing the absolution of Master Peter of Chalon, deceased—and which the following letter testifies was sent from our Peter, abbot of Cluny, to the Paraclete at Heloise’s request—is found in the obituary-book of the aforesaid Paraclete expressed in these words: “I, Peter of Cluny, who received Peter Abelard as a monk of Cluny and granted his body, secretly conveyed, to Abbess Heloise and the nuns of the Paraclete, by the authority of almighty God and of all the saints absolve him, as regards the office, from all his sins.”

so that it may be hung on his tomb. Remember, too, for the love of our God, Astralabe,

> **Note [Col. 0428D].** “Remember also, for the love of our God, Astralabe.” He was the son of the aforesaid Peter and Heloise, as is clearly evident from the letter, or book, of the same Peter in which he describes his calamities and miseries, and as the most distinguished Nicolaus Faber noted before us.

and for your own sake, to procure for him a prebend from either the bishop of Paris or any other bishop. Farewell. May the Lord keep you and at some time grant us your presence.

## LETTER XXII. To our venerable and most dear sister, and God’s handmaid, HELOISE, leader and teacher of God’s handmaids: Brother PETER, humble abbot of Cluny, fullness of salvation from God and of love from us in Christ.

[Col. 0428B]

I rejoiced—and not a little—on reading Your Holiness’s letter, in which I learned that my visit to you had not been passing; from it I perceived that I had not only been among you, but had never afterward departed from you. As I see, that lodging of mine was not like the memory of a guest passing through for one night; nor did I become among you a stranger and pilgrim, but a fellow citizen of the saints and a member of the household—would that it were God’s household! Thus everything I said and did in that fleeting, or winged, visit of mine clung to your holy mind; thus everything was impressed on your kindly spirit, so that—not to mention things then deliberately said by me—perhaps not even a word carelessly uttered [Col. 0428C] fell to the ground. You marked everything so closely and, out of the affection born of sincerity, committed it to a tenacious memory, as though it were great, heavenly, most sacred, or the very words and deeds of Jesus Christ.

Perhaps the words of our common rule—yours as well as ours—moved you to retain these things thus: it commands that Christ, who is received in them, be adored in guests. Perhaps also those words concerning superiors, although I am not your superior: “Whoever hears you hears me” (Luke 10). Would that I might always be granted this favor among you: that you may deign to remember me and, with the sacred company of the flock entrusted to you, pray for me to the mercy of the Almighty! I in turn repay you as I can in this respect, since both [Col. 0428D] long before I saw you and especially from the time I came to know of you, I have reserved for you in the innermost recesses of my mind a singular place of true, not feigned, charity.

The gift concerning the *tricenarium* which I gave you in person, I now send in writing and sealed, as you requested, while absent. I also send, as you instructed, the absolution of Master Peter, likewise written and sealed on parchment. As soon as means are available, I shall gladly endeavor, for your Astralabe’s sake—and, for your sake, ours—to obtain a prebend in one of the noble churches. Yet the matter is difficult, because, as I have often found, bishops usually make themselves very reluctant to grant prebends in their churches, alleging various obstacles. Nevertheless, for your sake I shall do what I can, as soon as I can.

## LETTER XXIII. Brother PETER, called humble prior of the poor of Majorevum, to PETER, venerable and honored by God’s grace, abbot of Cluny: with those same poor persons, eternal salvation from the Lord.

[Col. 0429B]

Let the sweetness of Your Paternity know that Lord Peter Vivian possesses two of our books: namely, the Continuous Glosses on Matthew and the Glossed Gospel of Blessed John. Since he has kept them long enough—about twenty years, that is—we humbly beseech your charity to deign to command him to arrange their return to us without delay. May divine grace keep Your Paternity mindful of us and safe for a long time. Know finally that, if you were merely some other abbot and not so celebrated and famous, we would openly demand satisfaction for the broken pledge and unfulfilled promise which your condescension has repeatedly made concerning a visitation of us.

## LETTER XXIV. To God’s most beloved and magnificently honored servants, serving Christ in the wilderness at Majorevum: Brother PETER, humble abbot of Cluny, eternal salvation in Him to whom they have wholly devoted themselves.

The Prophet sings to God in the Psalms: “How sweet are your words to my palate, sweeter than honey to my mouth!” (Psalm 118 [119]). I too can write to you truthfully that your words or letters are far sweeter to me than honey. For I have always reserved the highest summit of my heart for you and the men of your order; I have preferred the Carthusian institutions to the institutions of all religious orders; from almost the earliest years of my youth [Col. 0429D] I have cultivated with sincere affection the sacred purpose of your religious life. Therefore, whenever I could find leisure, I did not shrink from frequently visiting certain older places of your order. I did not recoil from crags almost inaccessible through snow and exceedingly high with ice. I found it sweet to see and visit the brethren serving almighty God amid those narrow places of mountains and cliffs, and to rejoice with them in the Lord.

This taste, with which I was imbued while I was still an unformed vessel, I have long preserved and, through God’s grace, retain even until now—not by seeing you, which hitherto I have been unable to do as I wished, but by loving, honoring, and reverencing you and all that is yours with unfeigned charity. Yet I am accused concerning the broken pledge and unfulfilled promise by which, as you say, I repeatedly promised to visit you; and I am sharply challenged by such great friends. [Col. 0430A] I hear that, if I were merely some other abbot and not so celebrated and famous, satisfaction worthy of open demand would be sought for these matters.

But I thank God that I am not merely any abbot, but so celebrated and famous that none of you dares attack me or openly demand satisfaction for the broken pledge and unfulfilled promise. For if I were not so great, but merely some other abbot, certainly I would not have escaped unpunished. Who could believe otherwise? For from men so truthful, the deed would not differ from the word. Nevertheless, to satisfy friends—and such intimate friends—I willingly lay aside the pomp of a greater name and rank myself with abbots, though inferior ones, if indeed they are inferior. Choose from the whole world whichever you wish as the least, and exact from me, as from him if he were guilty, the penalties for breaking a pledge.

Yet the penalty should be more sparing, that I may plead at least a little in my own defense, because the pledge was not broken in bad faith. Many things prevented the pledge undertaken and the promise of visitation from being kept: innumerable affairs, a winter harsher than usual, and manifold bodily infirmity, under which nature has labored for more than half a year and still cannot wholly overcome the enemy that has so long assailed it. [Col. 0430B] For this reason, as it seems to me, one who cannot fulfill what he says, promises, and most desires ought to be punished more gently.

In a similar matter I have the great Apostle acting with me and for me. He wished to come to the Corinthians, that they might have a second favor; he wished to pass through them into Macedonia; he wished also to come again to them from Macedonia and to be sent by them into Judea. He wished this, but could not do as he wished. He excuses himself; and by excusing himself he excuses not only himself, but also me together with himself against you. “Did I then act lightly,” he says, “or do I plan according to the flesh, so that with me there should be ‘yes and no’?” Who is speaking? A great Apostle. If you ask, “Which great one?” I answer: there is no need to ask. Where “great” is added to “Apostle,” Paul is understood.

This Apostle, then—and a great one—maintains that he did not act lightly if at one time he said “yes” and at another time “no.” For he understood that truthfulness in speech must indeed always be preserved, but that words are not thereby any less truthful if the manifold variety of differing circumstances compels them to be altered. [Col. 0430C] The following words also show this: “But God is faithful, because our word which is made to you is not in Him ‘yes and no,’ but in Him is ‘yes’” (2 Corinthians 1). He could in no way have said this while preserving truth, if he held that words straightforwardly uttered from the heart, without the stain of falsehood, could not be changed when necessity of circumstances required it.

Therefore what I said was true: “I will come to you.” But a certain and reasonable cause prevented me from coming to you. For this reason, then, there was not in my mouth “yes and no,” but in it was “yes.” Thus I consider myself excused and, unless you wish to be excessively harsh exactors, I judge that I have made satisfaction.

Concerning the books retained for a long time, and contrary to your wishes, by Brother Peter Vivian, as we read in your letter, [Col. 0431A] I reply that, if God permits, I shall meet with the man and, as the nature of my office requires, shall see that what is just is done and that they are restored to you. For the rest, I commend you to God whom you serve, and myself and ours to Him and to you. Do not ascribe my late writing to you to negligence on my part—for in this instance there is none—but to the endless importunity of affairs, which is almost always burdensome to me. Had this allowed me even for a short space of time—not to say for a moment—to attend to myself, your eye would have seen my letter two or three months ago.

## LETTER XXV. To the supreme pontiff and our special Father, Lord Pope EUGENIUS: Brother PETER, humble abbot of Cluny, devoted obedience with filial love.

[Col. 0431B]

Because I consider it almost a crime to receive or carry out apostolic commands negligently, I have undertaken in this letter to excuse myself before my Father concerning certain matters written and enjoined upon me by Your Paternity now for a second year, as it were, and which I have not yet performed. Nor should your wisdom wonder that I have delayed so long to write to you concerning them, for I received knowledge of the matter and set pen to write almost at the same time. Had it been possible to know it earlier, my hand would not have delayed to perform what it has now begun to do.

A year ago Your Reverence wrote to the lord bishop of Limoges and to me, as I read in a copy of apostolic letters brought to me by certain clerics of Brioude,

> **Note [Cols. 0431D, 0432D].** “By certain clerics of Brioude.” That is, clerics serving God at Saint Julian’s in the Auvergnat town of Brioude. There is also another Brive, surnamed Corrèze, in Limousin; likewise Brive-sur-Isère, also called Brive-Isère and Pontisara, now commonly Pontoise. All these names derive from the ancient Gallic word *briva*, which according to some means a crossing or ford, but according to others—and perhaps more correctly—a bridge. Hence also Briva Odera, where they formerly crossed the Oder, and Samarobriva, where they crossed the river Somme, whether at a ford or, more likely, by a bridge. And in Great Britain, whose inhabitants first spoke the old language of Gaul from which they sprang, Durobriva, that is, “river-crossing by bridge,” and Durocobriva, that is, “red-water crossing,” are now called by the English Dornford near Casterton and Hertford [Col. 0432D].

that I should meet the bishop of Clermont,

> **Note [Col. 0432D].** “That I should meet the bishop of Clermont.” In the margin of the old edition this bishop was formerly called Nicholas. But since no bishop of that name is found in either the ancient or the recent catalogues of the bishops of Clermont in the time of Pope Eugenius III, to whom our Peter writes here, I consider most true what the most learned Joannes Savaro, president of the Auvergnats, noted in his *Origins of the City of Clermont*: namely, that the matter concerns Stephen, surnamed Mercolius or de Mercolio; and that this very surname Mercolius, written in the margin of the manuscript, gave occasion to a copyist—perhaps not understanding it—to substitute “Bishop Nicholas” for “Bishop Mercolius.”

summoned, with the associate already mentioned, to a suitable day and place; that I should command him to restore a certain knight whom he had held captive for almost two years; and that, strengthened by your authority, I should settle a dispute concerning the castle of Alson between certain nobles. Certain other matters concerning the bishop were added, which were entrusted to us for hearing, not for deciding. The clerics brought those letters from the city, but delivered them not to me, rather to that same bishop of Clermont. As they themselves testified to me, they did so because they could not otherwise recover from the bishop their captive, who was the brother of one of them. As soon as he had the letters, he made them invisible to us up to this day. This is why the apostolic commands were not performed by me. For I did not neglect to carry out commands received; rather, I could not carry out commands not received. [Col. 0431D; 0432A]

I do not indeed know this same thing concerning the bishop of Limoges, but I think that I know it. It is not for me, then, to say upon whom this evident fault falls. Yet I shall say what follows, because it should not be kept silent: it is harmful not to one, two, or three, but to many peoples. That Auvergne was once, both in extent of territory and multitude of peoples, as Caesar and certain other historians testify, a kingdom by the measure of ancient kingdoms, is known to many, though not to all. When its kings and counts failed, being more harmful to the Christian people than their defenders, almost its entire care long ago passed over to the just and gentle governance of the Church. Leaning upon that Church alone, while its princes either failed, as I have said, or oppressed it, Auvergne has remained safe and secure under it and rejoiced to do so.

For the bishops who ruled that land before this man by ecclesiastical right both fulfilled what belonged to them according to the grace granted them, and, so far as was possible, supplied what belonged to kings or princes in defending the Church. But now for almost twenty years that great and numerous people of God has remained, in the words once spoken in Holy Scripture of the Jews, “without king, without prince, and”—what alone remained to it—“without law,” and, what is worse, “without priest.” [Col. 0432B] For how can he be called a priest who, apart from the episcopal sacraments, has performed almost nothing of a bishop’s office since he began to be bishop? Where is his watchful guardianship over the flock entrusted to him? Where is his pastoral care? Where his compassion for those who perish and daily descend into hell before his eyes?

One attacks another without ceasing; almost all sharpen swords for mutual slaughter; brother conspires for brother’s destruction. The lower-ranking soldiers of the Lord’s camp, townsmen, country people, every sort of layman, cry out concerning him what the prophet of God once said to the wicked king of Israel: “I saw all Israel scattered upon the mountains like sheep without a shepherd.” If ecclesiastical justice against wrongdoers is demanded of him, it is either refused or sold. But that was in the first period. Now it is no longer refused, because it is no longer sought. Such despair has arisen among his subjects that the man can ever change for the better that, though all suffer innumerable miseries and his whole diocese abounds in endless evils, [Col. 0432D; 0433A] scarcely anyone now among so great a population approaches his court, lays his complaints before him, seeks counsel, or demands judgment or justice; for no one doubts that none of these things can be found with him.

He remains idle amid infinite affairs and, seeing not merely one wolf but countless wolves rushing upon the sheep entrusted to him, flees—as great Gregory says—not by changing his place, but by withdrawing assistance. He flees; and as he flees, the wolves seize and scatter the sheep. But perhaps he neglects the laity and despises them as more remote from his order or profession. Perhaps, content with them, he has assumed the care of monks and clerics, who are nearer to him by profession. But—would that, so far as he is concerned, clerics and monks were equal to laypeople! Yet they are not at all equal. Although he denies effective assistance equally to all, he nevertheless shows, so far as can be seen in him or heard from him, a far greater inclination toward laypeople than toward clerics or monks. [Col. 0433B]

They return from him content to their own affairs, and, because they see the sword of the Spirit, which is God’s word, bound up in him, they turn to their own swords. What he could pacify by speech, they cannot pacify despite much shed blood. Yet they have some resource in counsel when, as I have said, abandoned by their bishop, they themselves protect themselves with armed force. But what counsel have clerics? What remedy have monks? Under such a bishop they truly lack not only divine but human assistance: divine, because they are not defended by the spiritual sword; human, because the secular sword, which they themselves may not use, cannot defend them, nor does any prince take it up to defend them.

The apostolic saying which Paul declares concerning a king or prince—“For he does not bear the sword without cause” (Romans 13)—has long been changed in part, but now in our own days entirely. What then shall the clerical or monastic order do, especially in that land, miserable in this respect, where it is protected neither by ecclesiastical censure nor defended by the secular sword? [Col. 0433C]

I pass over graver, destructive matters, which for many years I have heard from many persons who seem to me trustworthy, and which I continue frequently to hear from those reporting them. Since I cannot be their witness, I do not wish to be their reporter. Your Exaltedness will, I believe, hear them in due time from those who report them to us and can testify concerning them before you. Moreover, if it please you, we commend to Your Excellency the bearer of this letter, a noble cleric and, insofar as we can know, an honorable one. He has a case against this same bishop. If it is just, although our intercession is not necessary, we nevertheless ask that your clemency assist him.

## LETTER XXVI. To the venerable man and my most dear lord, EBRARD, Master of the Temple of God which is at Jerusalem: Brother PETER, humble abbot of Cluny, whatever salvation and affection he can offer.

> **Note [Cols. 0433D, 0434D].** “Lord Ebrard, Master of the Temple.” The military brotherhood of the Templars, or Order of the Knights of the Temple, began at the Temple of Jerusalem in 1119, or thereabouts, under the venerable and high-minded Hugh, first master of that order. It was soon marvellously extended throughout Christendom in houses and possessions, and its institution and rule were approved by Pope Honorius II and Stephen, patriarch of Jerusalem. But later, for other reasons moving the Apostolic See, the order was eventually suppressed and condemned at the Council of Vienne, and its possessions and houses were assigned to the Hospitallers of St John.

[Col. 0434A]

That I have always loved your person and the sacred soldiery of the holy Temple entrusted to you by God, among all who profess the religious life, with a certain special and singular affection; that I have always venerated it—I know, my witness and confidant on high knows, many of your own know; you know, I believe, and I do not doubt that you yourself know it. I have done so from the very beginning of your foundation, which, having arisen in my own time, shone upon the world like the radiant light of a new star, and I both marvelled and rejoiced. Nor is this surprising. For who does not rejoice at any hope of eternal salvation? Who does not exult with all the inmost feelings of the soul in God his Saviour, when he sees the knighthood of the eternal King, the army of the Lord of Hosts, assembled from diverse regions of the world to overthrow the prince of this world and to storm the enemies of Christ’s cross, advancing to new battles as though from heavenly camps? Who does not rejoice, who does not exult, that you have gone forth not to a single but to a twofold conflict, in which you fight both against spiritual wickedness, according to the Apostle, with the virtues of the soul, and against bodily enemies with the strength of the body?

In the one conflict you have undertaken all that belongs to holy monks and hermits; in the other you have surpassed the purpose of all religious persons. They indeed serve as soldiers of God; and although they labour to chastise their body and reduce it to servitude, yet in body they rest from the storms of the world, and especially from the tumults of war. But you, as has been said, both overcome the strong man armed by those same arts of theirs, and do not cease continually to fight against those infernal camps which he openly brings forth against Christ—I mean the companies of Saracens. You are monks in your virtues, soldiers in your deeds: fulfilling the former spiritually, exercising the latter bodily. For your brethren you have exposed your souls to life and your bodies to death; you have already shed blood not formerly shed, blood which every day in wars you offer to God to be shed. You are truly sharers in that highest and chief charity of which the Saviour says: “No one has greater love than this, that someone lay down his life for his friends” (John 15).

This is the reason why, as I wrote above, I have always loved you in a special manner, honoured you, and venerated you. I have done this hitherto, and by God’s grace I shall do it as long as breath remains in my nostrils. In this confidence—that one who loves always hopes to be loved by him whom he loves—I too hope that I am loved by you and that, if I make any suggestion, I shall be heard kindly.

The noble man Lord Humbert of Beaujeu [Note: [Col. 0435] “The noble man, Lord Humbert of Beaujeu.” Father of Guichard, concerning whom see also the following letter and Book I of the *Miracles*, chapter 28.], recently returning from the lands beyond the sea, came back to our regions and was received throughout that whole country with immeasurable rejoicing. I was absent at the time, drawn elsewhere by business; but on returning I found such jubilation everywhere at his arrival that, had I not seen it, I could scarcely ever have imagined its extent. Clerics rejoiced, monks congratulated one another, peasants applauded, and the whole choir of churches neighbouring ours sounded as though with a new song.

Conversely, robbers grieved; invaders of churches; plunderers—or rather oppressors—of monks, the poor, widows, orphans, and the low-born populace unable to defend itself by its own strength, groaned and, though not openly in words, nevertheless with most abominable hearts murmured against the barrier set in the way of their wickedness. For your land adjoining Cluny is such, as we believe you know, that, because it has neither king, duke, nor prince, it greatly rejoices whenever it hopes that it has found some means of peace. Because it trusts that in this man and through him it has found that means in very large measure, it rejoices, as I have said, and cannot conceal the joy of its hope.

Since his return, the said Humbert has shown that this hope placed in him is not vain. For he so subdued the viscount of Mâcon—the morning, evening, and nightly wolf of our country—that in this respect he may rightly say with just Job: “I broke the jaws of the wicked man, and plucked the prey out of his teeth” (Job 29). In the very short time since his return, he has done the same to many others situated both on this side of the Loire and beyond it. Your Cluny hopes the same from him, for it needs his counsel and aid more than all the monasteries or churches of our regions.

I therefore entreat you, and, as your intimate friend—as you know—advise you, that if you have any complaint against him because of his return to us, you set it aside for the present; and, since he is a wise and discerning man, leave him to himself and to the judgment of his own conscience. For I believe that you will gain more with him by tolerating him than by provoking him with complaints. I know, I think, his disposition; and from familiar conversation with him I have perceived that he fears God and would set the whole world, if he could gain it, below the salvation of his soul.

Leave him for a time to this unhappy land, and allow it at least for some while to enjoy his help and protection, which it needs beyond anything I can say. This is proper to your military office, and for this you took up arms: to defend God’s Church from its assailants and, according to the prophet, even literally to stand against those coming up from the opposite side, setting yourselves as a wall for the house of Israel (Ezek. 13).

But perhaps you say: “We took up arms against pagans, not against Christians.” Yet which ought more to be attacked by you or yours: the pagan who does not know God, or the Christian who confesses him in words and fights against him in deeds? Which ought more to be pursued: one who is ignorant and blasphemes, or one who acknowledges him and attacks him? Do not those attack God, do they not persecute him, who plunder, kill, beat, and sometimes—as frequently happens—actually murder his Church and the people purchased by his blood, without exception of persons, ranks, or dignities wherever they are able or dare? The Christian who unjustly suffers violence from a Christian is certainly no less to be defended by your counsels—indeed, by your swords—than he would be if he suffered the same violence from a pagan.

Therefore, if you please, yield to my counsels and prayers, and for the present leave to us, in the manner I have stated, the man in whom almost the entire hope of our peace rests. Test whether my counsel is useful both to him and to you; for I would by no means say this if I understood it to be in any way contrary to God. I further believe, and earnestly desire, that I may speak with you before you depart from the regions of Gaul, and then shall supply by word of mouth, better than now by writing, whatever needs to be said on this matter.

## LETTER XXVII

To the supreme pontiff and our special father, Lord Pope EUGENIUS, Brother PETER, humble abbot of Cluny: filial love with devoted obedience.

At the outset I beg that a fatherly ear may receive my words calmly; and that, if through ignorance I should perhaps say anything otherwise than I ought, your kindness—which is debtor both to the wise and to the foolish—may bear it with an even mind.

The noble man Lord Humbert of Beaujeu, recently returning from the lands beyond the sea, was received with such rejoicing by the whole country adjoining us that I could scarcely have believed it had I not, upon my own return from a journey—for I happened then to be absent—seen it myself. Clerics rejoiced, monks were glad, burgesses exulted; and even those who had customarily been the prey of robbers—indeed, food for wolves—peasants, cultivators, poor people, widows, orphans, and every sort of common person congratulated one another so greatly that they could scarcely contain themselves. Conversely, despoilers of the poor, destroyers of churches, oppressors of clerics and monks, though not openly, because they did not dare, groaned among themselves and grieved beyond expression that so strong a barrier had been opposed to their wickedness.

For that unhappy land of ours, as your wisdom knows, is in this respect almost more miserable than all other lands: having neither king, duke, prince, nor defender, it lies exposed to the teeth of wild beasts; and, as it is written—which I now take literally—“all the beasts of the field play there” (Job 40). For if any there bear the names of dukes, counts, or princes, they conduct themselves as though they ruled not in order to defend but to devour God’s people. The greater they are, the worse; the stronger they are, the more savage in oppressing the powerless and the poor.

Therefore a people eager for peace and yearning for it with all the desires of their soul welcomed the coming of the said Humbert as though God had sent him to them for this very purpose. And lest they seem to have hoped in vain, they have already experienced this in very large measure. For—to confess to my lord and father what I know to be true—he appeared so changed at his arrival, and so altered from the man I had known, that, so far as his words and deeds are concerned (for I am not a searcher of hearts), he could truly say with that ancient man: “I am not what I was”; and we may say of him those divine words: “It is the change wrought by the right hand of the Most High” (Ps. 76).

Thus in a short time he checked whatever wars were raging around us; thus, by his word alone, he quieted the disputes of military men, so that chiefly through fear of him peace was restored among them, and security was restored to churches and poor people, who had feared their tyranny. Merchants no longer feared enemies on the public roads, nor cultivators in their fields; almost the entire land lying between the Saône and the Loire, suffused with a new light of peace, rejoiced. Encouraged by these very good beginnings, it hoped for far greater and better things.

While all rejoiced at this, and especially your Cluny, which he had wholly devoted himself to defend and which exulted greatly both over what it saw and what it hoped for, suddenly a sad report disturbed our joy, declaring that he had not departed from you with your full favour and had changed the religious habit for a secular one without your permission. For we had been persuaded by the reports of many that this had been done both with your assent and by the judgment of the Apostolic See. Once we learned that this was not so, we did not wish to impede the good of peace, and we maintained toward him the course which we ought.

But consider, Father—consider and see whether, with justice preserved, a man so useful and, in respect of deeds worthy of a prince, almost alone in our regions, may be restored to us and to the common peace. For, to say what many of ours think: if he had abandoned a canonical, monastic, eremitical, or any other order established in ancient times, ecclesiastical censure would rightly compel him to return to what he had unlawfully forsaken. But since he has only passed from one knighthood to another; since he has turned the sword which he had taken up against Saracens against false Christians worse than Saracens; since, moreover, as I have received from many trustworthy persons, he has not lawfully separated from his wife—let your wisdom see whether he should be compelled or tolerated, until the truth of the matter is clearly established and so great a question concerning so important a man is determined by apostolic judgment.

Let your prudence and discernment, set over the whole Church of God, certainly consider again whether persons who, according to Scripture—leaving aside its higher sacramental meaning—have even literally become one flesh from two, can or ought to be so separated from one another that one appears to serve God in a religious habit while the other serves the world in secular dress; indeed, to speak more plainly, that one lives chastely while the other lives unchastely; one is joined to no one except the one and only God, while the other, through innumerable fornications and adulteries, prostitutes herself wholly and completely to the one and only devil.

Hence it is that the woman formerly joined to him has not, as I have heard, even been heard by anyone to vow chastity in bare words; and even if she had vowed it in words alone, what would such a vow amount to? If vows of this kind—made from hatred, frivolity, or an intention to sin more freely—are commonly permitted to Christian men and their wives, let the Father of the Church consider how widely the field of destruction will lie open, and how many thousands of men and women hell will swallow with greedy jaws on this occasion.

Therefore, though I speak as one less wise, giving counsel to him from whom I ought to receive it, it would seem to me just and canonical that either, if after diligent examination of the truth of the case the vows of these spouses ought to be judged invalid, they should be compelled to return to one another; or, if the vows are to stand, that each should be compelled to serve God under a definite religious profession. Otherwise, if this one is saved and that one lost—or rather, what is truer, if one is condemned because of the other, the latter perishing in the world while the former cannot save himself even in his religious profession—what advantage is the conversion of one where the certain ruin of both follows?

For when can marriage be preserved honourable and the marriage-bed undefiled, according to the Apostle (Heb. 13), where one gives himself to chastity and the other to lust; one to holiness and the other to impurity; one to cleanliness and the other to wickedness? When, too, will that be observed which the same Apostle says: “To those joined in marriage I give command—not I, but the Lord—that the wife should not depart from her husband. But if she departs, let her remain unmarried or be reconciled to her husband; and let the husband not put away his wife” (1 Cor. 7)?

What do you say, Apostle? What do you say: “I give command—not I, but the Lord”? Does not the Lord command what you command? Did you not yourself say: “Do you seek proof of Christ who speaks in me?” (2 Cor. 13). Since, therefore, Christ speaks in you, does not Christ also command what you command?

“It is true,” he says, “it is true. What Christ says, I say also; and what I say, Christ says. But lest my words should seem of less value than Christ’s to the people of my time, still unformed in faith, I set before them his own words, so that, as good though new hearers, they might be more compelled to obey by the authority of the greater name. There is another reason why I wished to give this counsel, not indeed to the unlearned but to all: that they might understand that the matter in question was not to be dispensed according to my pleasure, but preserved as it was handed down by the Lord.

“For there are matters which, according to reason, we can dispense at will; and others which we neither can nor ought to alter by dispensation from what has been established. Among the matters which we can alter are those which I added: ‘To the rest I say, not the Lord: if any brother has an unbelieving wife, and she consents to live with him, let him not put her away. And if any woman has an unbelieving husband, and he consents to live with her, let her not put away her husband’” (ibid.). And after a few intervening words: “‘But if the unbeliever departs, let him depart; for a brother or sister is not subject to bondage in such cases’” (1 Cor. 7).

If, in such cases, brother or sister is not subject to bondage, it is permissible for a Christian man to put away a pagan wife, or for a Christian wife to put away a pagan husband. Indeed, they are free both to live together, if they wish, and to separate from one another, if they wish. Therefore, because these matters can be dispensed, “I say, not the Lord.” But where both are faithful—that is, Christian—the Lord, not I, commands that the wife not depart from her husband and that the husband not put away his wife. Here, certainly here, the Apostle says, dispensation is not to be admitted.

I have presumed too much, speaking more copiously than I ought and seeming to teach a father and master. But a son does not teach his father; a disciple does not teach his master. Far be such presumption from me! I do not teach a teacher or instruct a master; rather I ask, entreat, and beseech that your apostolic solicitude, which watches over all, may provide for the salvation of the noble man, whom for the reasons stated above I greatly fear to be in danger; and, if it can be done with justice preserved, may kindly leave him to our land, where he is far more necessary than in the lands beyond the sea. There he will be reckoned as one alone; among us, as ten thousand.

## LETTER XXVIII

To the supreme pontiff and our special father, Lord Pope EUGENIUS, Brother PETER, humble abbot of Cluny: due obedience with filial love.

Your apostolic solicitude, set over the world, often hears many things from many people: sometimes good, sometimes bad, sometimes excellent, sometimes most evil. But now in our regions something has happened of which we may truly say that word of Scripture: “Such a thing has never been seen in Israel” (Judg. 19).

The Church of Brioude, subject to apostolic jurisdiction without the intervention of any other bishop, long remained great and noble according to the custom of its own foundation; but for some time, degenerating from its ancient and good purpose, it acknowledges that the prophet’s saying applies to it: “Your silver has become dross; your wine is mixed with water” (Isa. 1). Many things would show that what I say is true, if I did not fear being much too lengthy for you. Yet I say briefly that the wicked deed which recently occurred in that church could scarcely have happened except as the deserved consequence of preceding evils, so that, according to the revelation of the Apostle John, “let him who is filthy become filthy still” (Rev. 22).

A thief, no one knows who, recently stole the golden *phylactery* of the church. [Note: [Col. 0439C] “The golden *phylactery* of the church.” Jerome, on Matthew, chapter 23: “Those little labels of the Decalogue,” he says, “they called *phylacteries*, because whoever possessed them had them as if for his own protection and defence.” And *Capitularies*, book VI, chapter 72: “Let neither a cleric nor any Christian make phylacteries.” *Phylacteries*, that is, belts or bands, as St Augustine explains in his sermon *On Martyrs and Phylacteries*; and this also seems to be their sense in *Additions* II, chapter 18.]

The clerics heard of it. Whereas that city, once full of justice, ought to have investigated and examined the matter by judicial and canonical procedure and settled it by ecclesiastical censure, they set God aside, cast away faith, and despised not merely canonical religion—of which the name alone remains to them—but Christian religion as well. As though there were no God in Israel, they sent to consult Beelzebub, god of Ekron (4 Kings 1). You will hear more fully from the bearer of this letter or from his companions how he was consulted by them and how he answered them. For, from what I have heard, consulting that magician, from whom they said they had learned these things, was no less an act than sacrificing to Moloch, the demon of the Moabites.

Having received his answer, they charged the bearer of this letter with the sacrilege. He denied it and steadfastly—and, I believe, truthfully—declared that he had neither committed the crime nor been in any way privy to it. He added that he was prepared, on a day appointed by them, to undergo ecclesiastical judgment [Note: [Col. 0439D] “Ecclesiastical judgment”: that is, an ordeal or customary proof, which was not one but various. It was performed either by oath, by hot or cold water, by red-hot iron or glowing ploughshares, by a pyre or kindled fire, or finally by combat or duel. He declared himself ready to undergo any of these and to prove his innocence of the charge by every lawful mode of proof, as appears from these terms of the plea between Hilgod and Dado in the Cartulary of the Greater Monastery, which contains the affairs of Vendôme: “Thus Hilgod himself, our lord Severtus the monk, and the aforesaid accuser, namely Dado, met at Rainald’s castle before many barons; and there Hilgod was prepared to prove by every lawful mode that he had given or sold that land neither to Dado nor to anyone else, except to St Martin and his monks.”

On oaths, the same cartulary, in the notice of Count Fulk of Vendôme’s guarantee concerning the land of Mont-Hidulf: “Count Geoffrey of Anjou, having heard the case, immediately replied to Fulk that he himself would prove by oath, if he wished, that he had restored that land to us in its entire integrity.” And in the notice of the claim against the serf Hildrad and his sons: “When William, son of Hildrad, contended that his father had been a free co-holder, Lord Ascelin, monk of the Greater Monastery, pledged himself to swear to him that he had been a serf, not a free co-holder. He had this oath made to him by a man of the same household, named Alcherius of the village of Reblais at Roches-l’Évêque.”

On hot or cold water, Hincmar, *Against Hincmar of Laon*: “Because the aforesaid men are not of free condition, they should go forth to God’s judgment either by cold water or by hot water.” Likewise Ivo of Chartres, letter 74, where the learned Juretus writes much on this subject, and also Pithoeus, another man in every respect most learned, in his *Glossary*. On red-hot or heated iron, Hildebert of Le Mans, letter 17, and the aforesaid Ivo, letter 205. To their testimonies may be added this passage from the cartulary mentioned above, charter 122: “This fief of Regniac possesses the following privilege: if any of its inhabitants should commit an offence for which either combat must be undertaken or the customary ordeal of red-hot iron borne, or should offend in any other punishable way, the judgment belongs to no other person but to the lord and possessor of the fief itself, who by reason of it is also enforcer and judge of the offence, whatever its kind; he exacts the legal amends, so that, even if that judgment is borne at the church of St Amand, no right in it belongs to anyone else but him.”

And charter 37, concerning the fishery of the Water of Glandesse: “You ought to know that Rainald of Château-Gontier, at the time when he held Château-Rainald in Touraine, brought a claim against us concerning the fishery of the Water of Glandesse. After the ordeal of hot iron had been undergone by our man Haimon of Boëlet, it was proved against him that all who lived in that land possessed the ancient custom of fishing in that water whenever they wished.”

We shall speak of combat or duel in Book I of the *Miracles*. Of the pyre or kindled fire, later. Let us add only here that from all the foregoing authorities one may in some measure infer that scarcely any but persons of servile condition were customarily offered for such proofs; these themselves were eventually forbidden by the supreme pontiffs Stephen V, Innocent III, Honorius III, and others, as exceedingly dangerous to souls and very harmful.] and to carry out whatever they should decide from it.

So that they could not doubt even slightly concerning what he promised to do, he gave himself to them as a hostage until he had completed all things; he bound his money and all his goods to them by oath, and added to the foregoing the pledges of his relatives and many friends. The twentieth day for conducting the case was appointed. He was ordered to come on that day so prepared that, by the prejudice—not judgment—of fire, he might, if possible, clear himself of the imputed crime. They further declared that they knew well enough that what they commanded was not canonical, but that the community of canons would believe him in no other manner.

The day arrived. A very great pyre was built [Note: [Col. 0441D] “A very great pyre was built, through the middle of which he was to pass on foot.” Purification by fire was threefold: by a pyre, by coals, or by red-hot iron, ploughshares, or something similar. Iron has already been discussed in the preceding note. An example involving coals occurs in Gregory of Tours, who reports that Bricius, successor of St Martin in the see of Tours, underwent their ordeal to remove an accusation of fornication. A nearly similar example is found in the *Life of St William the Abbot*, commonly called “of Denmark”: against certain accusers, he asserted that the true head of the holy virgin Geneviève was enclosed in his reliquary, and publicly declared that he would prove this by the ordeal of a burning furnace.

Finally, many are found to have entered a pyre of the kind here described to prove their innocence: Peter of Marseilles, suspected of heresy, in Paulus Aemilius, book IV of the *History of France*; Poppo, a Danish priest, as proof of the Christian faith, in Crantzius, book III of the *Metropolis*, chapter 43, and Saxo, book X of the *History of the Danes*; and others discussed by Martin Delrio, book IV of the *Magical Investigations*, chapter 4, question 4, section 3. But what Blasius Melanesius relates in the *Life of John Gualbert* about Peter, archbishop of Florence, should not be passed over, because it splendidly illustrates this passage of our Peter: “A place and a day are fixed,” he says, “on which this was to be done, so that those wishing to do so might witness it publicly. The appointed place was the monastery of Septimo. The day was Wednesday in the first week of Lent. The method of proof was this: in a public place two piles of wood were made beside one another, each ten feet long, five wide, and four and a half high; between the two piles ran a path one cubit long, strewn with burning coals, through which one of the monks was to pass.”], through the middle of which he was to pass on foot, proving his innocence of the imputed crime if he emerged unharmed.

Compelled by the overwhelming violence of perverse men—indeed, I should say impious men—he yielded what they demanded and, recovering his courage, promised that he would pass through the fire. He asked only that the power and justice of almighty God might be invoked over that flaming pyre in the manner of an exorcism [Note: [Col. 0442D] “The justice of God [was to be invoked] over the pyre in the manner of an exorcism.” Blasius, in the passage cited above, seems to describe this exorcism when he says: “Accordingly litanies and other prayers are said by the monks; the sacrifice is solemnly celebrated by the abbot of that order, with clerics and monks assisting. When the *Agnus Dei* is reached, one monk brings holy water for sprinkling, another a censer for burning incense, a third torches for setting the wood alight, and a fourth an image of the Crucified. The Lord Jesus Christ and his most holy Mother are invoked aloud by all, that the truth may be revealed.” Juretus, Pithoeus, and Delrio, in the passages already cited, also give formulas for exorcising hot water.] and, as he had heard had sometimes been done, that it might be blessed in his name.

The excellent and pious judges utterly refused. He still persisted and undertook to pass even through unblessed fire, trusting, as I suppose, in the testimony of his conscience. But they, fearing that he might perhaps accomplish what he said, sent servants to destroy the fire already prepared and, with unheard-of wickedness, did not permit him to be cleared even by the procedure which they themselves had proposed. They immediately seized all his property and, as though the case had been judged with the utmost justice and the accused clearly convicted, left him absolutely nothing of the goods which, as stated above, he had pledged to them.

What could a man oppressed by so many, so great, and so unheard-of acts of violence do? Nothing at all remained to him. He did the one thing he had, the one thing he could do. He fled to that one chief and singular defence of the oppressed; he chose that one and final refuge of the miserable: I mean apostolic aid, the tabernacle “which is a shade from the heat by day, and a security and shelter from storm and rain” (Isa. 4).

Hoping for these things in you and from you, Father, when he perceived the false—indeed, no—judges gaping to seize his goods, he interposed the barrier of an apostolic appeal, which, as he supposed, they were not permitted to overstep. He hoped they would not dare what they dared, say what they said, or do what they did. But he hoped in vain, for his hope disappointed him. Those whom he had hoped would become gentler he found far more savage. For after his appeal, they carried out the entire plundering of his property which I have recorded above.

Moreover, verbal insult was added—insult which at the courts of secular emperors would make men guilty of treason against majesty and punish them by at least a capital penalty. Yet although the Church does not possess the emperor’s sword, she nevertheless has authority over all lesser persons and even over emperors themselves. Therefore she is told under the figure of a prophetic name: “I have set you over nations and kingdoms, to pluck up and to destroy, to ruin and to scatter, to build and to plant” (Jer. 1). Hence, if she cannot kill, she can pluck up; if she cannot kill, she can destroy.

As I have heard, the abbot of Brioude said outright to the appealing cleric: “Why do you appeal? Why do you set the pope against us? The pope is entangled and occupied in such great affairs beyond the Rhône that we shall never be compelled to answer him on this side of the Rhône.” Father, I have received all these things as I have written them, yet from persons whose religious character, maturity, and truthfulness compelled me to believe them. Perhaps you also, if you heard and knew them, would believe what I believed and say what I have said.

Therefore, to spare both my words and your ears, as is fitting, I ask, entreat, and beseech you to take up the cause of this poor but prudent cleric—whom, as I think I have come to know, is useful in many respects—and defend him against powerful and violent adversaries. For you know that your see is the see of him to whom it is said: “Righteousness and judgment are the foundation of your throne” (Ps. 88); and again: “Your right hand is full of righteousness” (Ps. 47); and again, concerning whom it is said: “He executes judgment for those suffering wrong” (Ps. 145).

If I were speaking to anyone other than you, I would add that saying of Isaiah: “Seek judgment, help the oppressed, judge for the orphan, defend the widow; and come, and argue with me, says the Lord” (Isa. 1). Your religion and wisdom will bring all this to fitting effect if your authority commands the provost, who is of the greatest consequence in that church; the abbot; Odilo of Magone; John of Cornon; and finally those who participated in so great a sacrilege—indeed, idolatry—to restore in full everything taken from the cleric. After this restoration, let them present themselves before you on an appointed day, prepared to do and carry out what is just concerning the enormities charged against them.

For this above all both the cleric asks and we pray: that you entrust the determination of this cause to no judge other than yourselves. When this has been done and the matter has come before the judgment of your majesty, remember what Elijah said to the profane king who consulted a demon and was sick: “Because you have done this, you shall not come down from the bed upon which you have gone up, but shall surely die” (4 Kings 1). Your wisdom understands why I have added this final point.

## LETTER XXIX

To the strong and splendid pillar of the monastic order—indeed, of the whole Church of God—Lord BERNARD, abbot of Clairvaux, Brother PETER, humble abbot of Cluny: that salvation which God has promised to those who love him.

If it were permitted, if God’s ordinance did not stand in the way, if a man’s path lay within his own power, dearest brother, I would rather cling to your blessedness in an indissoluble bond than rule anywhere among mortals or reign. For why? Ought not your companionship—pleasing not only to men but even to the angels themselves—to be preferred by me to all earthly kingdoms? If I call you their fellow citizen, I shall not lie, though hope has not yet become reality, through the grace of the merciful God.

Indeed, if it had been granted to me to be with you here until my last breath, perhaps afterwards it would also have been granted to me to be where you are, and to remain there for ever. For where would I run except after you, drawn by you through the fragrance of your ointments? Since this cannot always be granted, would that it were granted at least often! And since not even that is possible, would that I might at least frequently see those sent by you! And since this too happens rarely, I desire that at least in the near future your holiness may visit one who loves you through your Nicholas, who will stay with me until the octave of the Lord’s Nativity; in him, as it seems to me, your spirit rests in part and mine wholly.

In him I shall see you, holy brother; through him I shall hear you; and through him I shall entrust certain matters, which I wish to make known secretly to your wisdom. To your holy soul, and to those holy persons serving almighty God under your rule, I commend myself and my people with all the strength and devotion I can command.

## LETTER XXX

To his own NICHOLAS, Brother PETER, humble abbot of Cluny: greeting, and himself.

If you are mine, as I say, if my opinion does not deceive me, although you are a man under authority, I nevertheless command—and absolutely wish—that you come. I have delayed ordering this, although I had resolved upon it in my mind, not because I disregarded it but because I was awaiting a suitable time. For, as you know, I am always unsettled even in my residence, not knowing how long I shall remain in any place or when, or where, I shall depart from it.

Therefore, since at least now an infirmity of body compels me to remain at Cluny until Christmas, come and do not delay; for perhaps, if you postponed it, you might not find me there until some unknown time. When you arrive, I shall explain why I press the matter so urgently. In other letters I have requested nothing of your lord abbot, but as though by command have ordered him to send you to me. Bring with you the History of Alexander the Great and our Augustine’s Against Julian, provided that your copy has now been corrected from his; and bring whatever other good books you have.

## LETTER XXXI

To his sweetest lord and father PETER, by God’s grace abbot of Cluny, Brother BERNARD, called abbot of Clairvaux: greeting from him who ordains deliverances for Jacob.

What are you doing, good sir, etc.? See among the letters of St Bernard [Col. 0444D], *Patrologia*, vol. CLXXXII.

## LETTER XXXII. To the great priest of God, the distinguished archbishop HUGH of the Church of Rouen, brother PETER, humble abbot of Cluny: may you be clothed in the robe of gladness and adorned with the crown of beauty.

I am often accustomed to admire very many things that seem wonderful, and frequently to commit them to writing, as appears fitting. But now I admire not any other thing, but myself—which is more wonderful. I marvel, indeed, that I have remained silent toward you for so long, when, apart from you, almost all others have not hitherto found me silent toward them. I have written and write often to others, to whom neither am I attached in mind as I am to you, nor do I reserve for them that place of true love—so sweet, so sincere, so exalted—which I keep for you in the inmost recesses of my soul [Col. 0445A]. Certainly I ought, and I greatly regret having neglected it, to have filled whatever books I have with letters sent to you, and adorned them with replies from you as with jewelled flowers. Rich material for writing overflowed; nor did any lack of real subjects compel the invention of false or flattering ones.

For what could more draw my heart to love, or move my hand to write, than your perseverance—so holy, so gracious, so long enduring in a holy purpose—from almost your earliest youth to an old age broken more by divine labour than by the number of years? What could move me more, what ought to move me more, than that now ancient recollection of Cluniac affairs, known, I think, to you and me and to a few others, of which I believe you are not unmindful [Col. 0445B]? It has not fallen from my memory how, in the first season of your youth, I saw you distinguished among those ancient senators of our commonwealth. It has not fallen from my memory how greatly your learning and piety adorned that sacred and great flock of Cluniac sheep; how splendidly, before almost all others, you shone in guarding the order entrusted to you.

I pass over—and while I live shall not be able to forget—that, from the purpose of holy religion which you had undertaken, through the various ranks of ecclesiastical honours, your countenance was not changed in different directions; but both among us and when separated from us, as prior, abbot, and finally supreme bishop of God, you were always, by the merit of virtue and knowledge, according to the Apostle, a sweet savour of Christ in every place [Col. 0445C] (2 Cor. 2). You did not fear powerful tyrants in God’s cause, nor kings themselves, great and famous though they were; but, so far as lay in you, you never calmly endured that the Church of God, established by Him over nations and kingdoms, should be shamefully enslaved to any mortal.

Besides this, I remember also that no concern, no distraction, however great, of important affairs could ever tear from your heart the memory of us or love for your Cluniac Church. For these reasons, if it were possible and divine providence allowed it, I would rather enjoy your presence than that of any mortal—not merely often, but continually: that I might speak with you, rejoice with you in the Lord [Col. 0445D], and, what I should desire above all, and what the profession of us both requires, take continual delight in the table of wisdom, not unknown to you, by thinking of Him, speaking of Him, and disputing about Him.

Since this cannot always, or even often, be granted, would that it might at least be granted rarely! And since I despair of the first two, I earnestly request that at least the last may be fulfilled by you. I request, I say, that your desired presence may shortly satisfy my longing and that of your Cluniac sons; for it is right that you should in this respect satisfy, as I have said, the desire of your sons, through the grace of Him who fulfils the desire of His own with good things. And lest anyone perhaps say or think that it is more fitting for the abbot of an inferior order to go to the archbishop of a superior order [Col. 0446A] than the reverse, I answer: it is right; it is fitting. But the whole flock of the one whose cause has chiefly occasioned these words could not follow its abbot; whereas a bishop, alone and without his flock, can far more easily visit an abbot from afar.

May your holy and now wholly heavenly blessedness fare well, dearest brother. On my behalf urge the clerk Airald—our countryman by birth, yours by benefice—to render without further delay what he promised me. What he promised was the chant of a prose composed by me last year in praise of the Mother of the Lord, and the chant of a responsory likewise composed by me on the same subject, which begins:

> Christ, splendour of God, who created all splendid things.

When he was at Cluny, he promised to send these chants shortly, but has not yet sent them. Urge him, or compel him [Col. 0446B], to fulfil his promise, lest perhaps the falsehood of a man of Auvergne be imputed to innocent Auvergnats—among whom I cannot deny that I am one.

## LETTER XXXIII. To his lord and father of Cluny, brother NICHOLAS.

Tell me, you whom my soul loves. When shall I come and appear before your face? When shall I see you? When will you console me? You will console me, I say, because consolation is hidden from my eyes until I see your presence—both desired and still to be desired—and my soul is sorrowful unto you. Certainly your most sweet memory does not leave me wherever I go; but the sweeter the memory, the more burdensome is the absence.

Far be it that I should be consoled by that plausible but untrue saying: “Those who behold one another in their minds are more present than those who behold one another with their eyes; and to be joined in heart is more than to be joined in body” [Col. 0446C]. As though sight and conversation did not possess some living delight which cannot come to those who are absent. But, I think, that splendour of Roman eloquence—eloquence itself having been born and brought into the light with him—spoke this from reason, not affection. This is Tully, of whom it was also said that what he had formed by study he pressed into practice, carried out by art, transferring his heart into speech with the greatest ease.

What am I doing? I have wandered from my business; what I have done is not a digression but a transgression.
