Who will compensate me for not seeing together those two great lights in the firmament of heaven—namely, in that place which the Lord chose out of all places on earth, that His name might be there [Col. 0446D]? I am angry at my occupations, which brought it about not that I did not wish to come, but that I could not—and even that I did not know. The affair of your brother, my lord the abbot of Vézelay, was the cause; by your command I had to fight beasts for it, lest man prevail. According to the prophet, “year has been added to year; the feasts have run their course” (Isa. 1); and a day has been given me for a year, since I have seen—not, I say, my lord—but my beloved.

For formality yields when affection approaches, and personal reverence disappears when familiar friendship begins to speak freely. Let him honour who is awestruck, who is astonished, who fears, who marvels; all these things have no place with a lover [Col. 0447A]. But concerning you I have long been persuaded of this: your loftiness has been matched, your singularity has been accompanied, so that you may serve as an example even to those who had been examples.

But whose fault is it that I have been so long deprived of my desire? It is not mine, both because of weakness and because of the occupation imposed upon me by you. Is it yours? Far from it! For in a double letter you both urged and summoned me, writing to my Father in these words: “Send me your Nicholas, in whom your spirit, as it seems to me, rests in part, and mine wholly.” O voice of love, a voice for which I cannot render a return throughout all the days of my life.

If I have found favour in your eyes, if any remembrance of your Nicholas touches you, write to my Father through your messenger, and to our prior [Col. 0447B] and to your Gaucher—for I am entangled and involved in the business of all these—that they may send me to you at holy Easter. Then I shall know that power proceeded from the pen—or rather, that the pen proceeded from power—for “with desire I have desired to eat this Passover with you,” most loving Father. Let it be so, moreover, that I may be permitted to remain with you for some days; and, if not to be satisfied, at least to be refreshed by your presence. For I confess—and, if necessary, profess—that almost nothing else pleases me while that which pleases me greatly is not present.

Send me secretly a reply to the letters which you will send; and then, if I can, I shall bring you Alexander the Great, return your Augustine, and whatever good things my hand can find [Col. 0447C]. Now let all that favour which I possess in your eyes appear. I commend myself to your most holy soul, because I was yours, am yours, and shall be yours as long as I am, in the heart of Jesus Christ. Through the bearer of this letter share with me some of those heavenly and sweet words, that meanwhile I may see in a mirror, until I see face to face.

If what I command cannot happen at Easter, then at least after Easter. I know that the lord abbot told you not to command my presence without necessity, as he told me also; but it is a necessity, indeed the greatest necessity, to see you, though I am occupied with many things. Why say more? Command that I come.

## LETTER XXXIV. To his dearest NICHOLAS, brother PETER, humble abbot of Cluny, greetings.

[Col. 0447D] I read the honey-sweet letter sent to me by you, dearest friend; and I judged it impious and hostile to mutual love to answer it hastily or negligently. I feared that a messenger unknown to us and hurrying home would not fully perform my commands, or perform them as I wished. Therefore, almost as soon as I received that letter, I sent this man back with this brief note. I shall immediately send one of my own men, who will dare neglect none of his instructions and will follow you and the lord of Clairvaux wherever your foot goes. I shall take care that you have not written in vain, nor that I myself need again write vainly to the lord abbot, as happened recently, concerning your long-desired coming to us.

## LETTER XXXV. To the venerable lord BERNARD, abbot of Clairvaux, to be named with due honour, brother PETER, humble abbot of the brothers of Cluny: the salvation which God has promised to those who love Him.

[Col. 0448A] If it is permitted to complain of a friend, and such a friend, I complain, and say to him what certain persons said to someone: “Father, even if your friend had told you to do a great thing, you certainly ought to have done it. How much more when now in writing, now by word, he has said, requested, and with familiar boldness commanded: ‘Send your Nicholas to Cluny’?” Yet I do not deny that it is a great matter; but the journey is not great.

What if you had written to me only once: “Send me this man or that, or several”? What would I—what would I, I say—do except what I am accustomed to do? I am accustomed not only to yield to one who requests, but also to obey one who commands. But you ask the reason. Is not this reason enough: to see one beloved [Col. 0448B]? He is yours indeed, but he is beloved by me. Does it not please you if I love what is yours? Does it not please you that I should love more affectionately one whom you, I think, love more tenderly than many of your own people? And what greater proof of true friendship is there than to love what one’s friend loves?

I love him for your sake; I love him also for his own sake: for your sake, because he serves you; for his own sake, because since the time of Lord Bishop Trecentius he has deserved this through many merits. Until now I have repaid him for all those things in no way except by always loving him sincerely in the Lord. And whereas others are accustomed to repay services with services and benefits with benefits, would I not seem ungrateful beyond all measure if, without cost or expense, I denied at least affection to one who loves me [Col. 0448C]?

That I may prove, if only by the signs of words, that this affection toward him has not altogether vanished, is it strange if I seek, at least once a year, to see him, speak with him, and delight with him in the Lord concerning Scripture, the saints, or philosophy, with which he is filled to the utmost? If it is idleness to speak and converse about God, about divine things, about matters supremely useful to the soul, then Nicholas’s coming to us is idle. If it is idleness to implant love for your person in our hearts, commend to all the things belonging to your order, and finally unite your whole community to the body of our congregation with the glue of charity, then Nicholas’s coming to us is idle. His heart always pours forth to us a good word concerning you and yours; he seeks good things for his people, and asks for what belongs to the peace of Jerusalem [Col. 0448D]. These are Nicholas’s idle or frivolous amusements among us.

Why then, my dearest friend, is he not granted to me, at least for one month, when I have granted you Peter, Robert—your kinsmen by blood—Garnerius, and certain others drawn by love for you, not for one month but forever? How many abbots, how many monks, have I granted to other churches—not to say foreign ones—overcome by your letters or counsels? Nor do I regret having yielded to a friend, to whom I am still ready to yield in many matters. But it is right that he too should make a return; right that he too should sometime yield to one who always yields to him.

This is more profitable to yours than to us, because after you, venerable man—after you, I say—they will be able to plead more effectively among us in persuasion, and fish more abundantly with some hook in the Cluniac sea or river [Col. 0449A]. But I recall what your Holiness, when you were staying at Cluny recently, said to me: “What do you want Nicholas for?” I replied: “It is no such thing; it is nothing great.” But I confess, dearest friend—forgive me if I exceeded proper bounds—those were the words of one more indignant than, as is true, of one confessing. Truly I was then double-minded in speech, by some chance, though I am not often so; plainly, I was then double in word. One thing was kept in my heart; another was uttered by my tongue.

For thus, certainly, my silent mind suggested: “Why did you wish to make such a profession so many times? Perhaps, as you have already twice, you would now a third time be disappointed in what you asked. You requested and were not heard. Why pour out prayers again?” I wished to answer as the man blind from birth answered the Pharisees: “I told you, and you heard. Why do you wish to hear again?” (John 9) [Col. 0449B]. I wished to answer this, but I did not. See, I confess it. May my confession do good: good, because I did not conceal truth beneath a covering of falsehood; good, because, as they say, all things are naked between friends, I uncovered before my friend a heart concealed by the cloud of deceit. I say: may it do good.

But to what end? That you may take something from your barns for my sake? That you may withdraw something from your cellars? That you may diminish anything from treasuries of silver and gold, even if they were present? What then? That you send Nicholas—not only now, but also whenever I ask hereafter. For I shall take care, if I can, to ask for nothing which may rightly be refused or which may harm you—or, not to say me—in any respect. Let it then be granted me; let what I desire be done: that Nicholas may spend this coming Easter among us, and that, returning from us in his customary way, he may pour out your heart to us and ours to you [Col. 0449C].

## LETTER XXXVI. To his dearest NICHOLAS, brother PETER, humble abbot of Cluny: the greeting he wishes for himself.

What shall I say? My soul is weary of my life. Why? Because I do not do what I wish, but do the very thing I hate. This has been given me—and I do not know whether from above—and, like an almost inseparable accident, has clung to me nearly from childhood: that I am almost always driven toward what I do not wish and repelled from what I wish. Yet, though I say these things, I am not among those who are dissatisfied with their lot, who despise their own possessions and covet those of others. I am not among those of whom a well-known writer says:

> “O happy [fortunate] merchants!” says the soldier, burdened with years . . .  
> (Horace, *Satires*, book I, satire 1, verses 4–5.)

And again:

> “The merchant, when the winds toss his ship, says: ‘Military service is better.’”  
> (*Ibid.*, verses 6–7.)

No, I say, I am not among such men or their like, who, always anxious or uncertain in mind, complain that everyone else lives in ease while they alone are labouring. If, indeed, my mind were longing after harmful things, I would give thanks to Him who wisely blocks my ways with a thorny hedge. But if good and useful things are desired, why are they not granted? If I wished to be silent, I had to speak. If I wished to be free, I had to work [Col. 0450A]. If I ever desired to fix my gaze on heaven, concern for temporal matters immediately drew it down to earth.

Why say this? Because thus, thus, I say, dearest friend, it has happened to me concerning you until now. I wished—indeed, desired with all my heart—that you might always be with me, and it was not granted. I wished at least that you might often be with me, and this was not allowed. Fortune still remains obstinate in this hateful condition; and she who never ceases to vary her turns persists, contrary to her custom, unchangeable. Yet I trust God that this ill-established stability will be broken, and that, though I cannot satisfy my hunger for you, I shall at least shortly relieve it by your pleasant and sweet conversation.

Truly pleasant, truly sweet. For if your style is such, what is your mind? If your letter is such, what is your speech? You are not—you are not—like certain people who are eloquent in writing but mute in speech, or conversely lavish in speech but mute in writing. And, if it is permitted to compare lesser persons with greater, you, a follower of Tully, have not merely followed your Tully, who wrote with the greatest ease in transferring his heart into speech; but, what is worthier, you, an apostolic man, imitate the Apostle [Col. 0450B].

He said that it was said of him: “His letters are weighty and strong, but his bodily presence is weak and his speech contemptible” (2 Cor. 10). He said this, but promised that he would act otherwise: “As we are absent,” he said, “such shall we be also when present” (*ibid.*). Thus both were present in the Apostle: a living spirit in his letter and life-giving speech on his tongue. Nature has fashioned both in you with equal balance; grace added besides has seasoned both, so that, apart from a certain power innate in your living speech, even the sharp and jealous examiner finds nothing beyond or short of the mark, nothing more or less [Col. 0450C].

Why this also? Because, I confess, your letter drew my heart—drew it greatly, indeed seized it. That letter, plainly, spoke from the abundance of the heart and proceeded from much richness and fatness of love. When you wrote it, as was said of one known to you, you dipped not a reed-pen but a little quill in your mind. As it was read to me, it dripped sweetness and poured milk and honey into my heart through every word. I reflected, by that comparison, how true was what David said to God: “How sweet are your words to my palate, sweeter than honey and the honeycomb to my mouth!” (Ps. 118). If human speech is so sweet, how much more divine speech? If an earthly drop is so sweet, how much sweeter the heavenly shower? If the dew of human discourse soothes the mind, how much more does the torrent of delight soothe it [Col. 0450D]?

I inferred many similar things from this and referred all that you wrote to divine and eternal things. But enough of this. Let letters be silent for the present; instead of a letter, come yourself at once. I believe that you will no longer be detained, nor will the decision of your Father, my dearest friend, further delay your journey to us. I wrote to him about you, as you yourself will see. I wrote to the prior; I wrote to Gaucher: “I await you before Easter, that I may have you at Easter.” We have a great, furnished upper room, where Jesus, as He has already commanded, will eat the Passover with His disciples; to it I invite you.

## LETTER XXXVII. To the honoured and beloved brother, Lord PHILIP, prior of Clairvaux, brother PETER, humble abbot of Cluny: greeting and love.

[Col. 0451A]

Solomon says: “New wine, a new friend; let him grow old, and you will drink it with sweetness” (Ecclus. 9). Thus, brother, you seem to me to be. I give thanks to God that you are a new friend. I hope in Him that you will grow old in friendship; and that, though you please me while still new, you will please me much more as you grow old. For the longer sincere love lasts, the sweeter it is usually.

From the time I first saw you, it has always pleased me to be yours; and your gentle and kindly manners have persuaded me to love you greatly. Command whatever you wish from now on: I am ready to obey. But you too, by the law of friendship, obey one who commands. Ask the lord abbot to send me his Nicholas, who is also yours, before the feast. Secure from him the fulfilment of what I ask.

## LETTER XXXVIII. To his dearest brother and son GAUCHER, brother PETER, humble abbot of Cluny: full salvation from the Saviour.

[Col. 0451B]

Because you are now a friend not merely of recent date but of many years, I do not labour over many words with you, nor do I use a long introduction for what I intend. For a friend does not wait for requests, but for the will of his friend; once he recognizes it, he immediately works to fulfil it. My wish is that Brother Nicholas may spend Easter with us. You now recognize what I desire. It is henceforth your task that I may not desire, or write, in vain. I have asked the lord abbot about it; if need be, ask him too.

## LETTER XXXIX. To his dearest nieces and sweetest daughters, MARGARET and PONTIA, brother PETER, humble abbot of Cluny: whatever there is of salvation and grace.

[Col. 0451C]

I have read the letter which you wrote to me, in which you sympathize with my illness and attempt to cure me not only by spiritual support but also by medical art. I thank your pious concern and embrace your filial affection with the kindly and sweet disposition proper to it. But I wonder how pupils of Jesus Christ smell of the schools of Hippocrates; how daughters of Jerusalem have purchased Babylonian wares.

I do not indeed despise medicinal aids, which often heal corrupted nature, especially since I read that medicine was created by the Most High (Ecclus. 38), and hear Christ say: “Those who are healthy have no need of a physician, but those who are ill” (Luke 5) [Col. 0451D]. Yet I rebuke enemies of nature, killers of their own flesh, crucified with the Crucified One, for thinking again of life, again of remedies for life, again of the condition of their bodies. Has the familiar saying of the virgin Agatha slipped your minds: “I have never administered bodily medicine to my body”? Was she alone a handmaid of Christ? Was she alone a bride of Christ? Are you not also handmaids? Are you not also brides? She, indeed, was martyr and virgin, far more excellent and far more exalted than you. Yet your purpose is not alien to hers, since you serve God by a martyrdom proper to your state and adorn the appearance of the heavenly fields with the flower of virginity.

I am plainly glad—and believe me, daughters, I shall rejoice greatly—if those lofty virgins, famous throughout the whole world, Agatha, Agnes, Faith, and the rest, and even, which is far more worthy, the Virgin of virgins herself, should one day have you as attendants, sprung from my stock and blood [Col. 0452A]. If, as I said, they deign to have you as servants—not to say companions—I shall rejoice and exult in the Lord and in Jesus my Saviour.

But you, O my virgins, if I may speak thus; O handmaids—indeed brides of the eternal King—provided that you are not among the foolish but among the prudent virgins: when it falls to your lot to be companions of such women, with what joy will you dance, with what gladness will you exult! What will be that delight, unknown to wretched mortals, when, drunk from the torrent of His delight with an insatiable satiety, after these so thick and hateful Egyptian darknesses, you see light in His light, with Him in whom is the fountain of life?

What then will there be, what will happen among you, when you escape from the prison of Marcigny into the free radiance of pure ether, and, in that Jerusalem above which, according to the Apostle, is our mother (Gal. 4), with your flesh and heart rejoicing in the living God, say and sing: “As we have heard, so have we seen in the city of the Lord of hosts, in the city of our God” (Ps. 98) [Col. 0452B]? What will happen when Jesus, King of heaven, for your brief continence and holiness, plays gently with His little girls, His handmaids, His virgins, with His gracious right hand?

How great and unimaginable will be the happiness that you, together with the virgin choir of both sexes, shall follow the Lamb—the son of a Virgin—with virgin confidence wherever He goes, while even the highest apostles, in that life promised by the God who does not lie, do not follow Christ [Col. 0452C] everywhere. They indeed will shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father and like stars shining for everlasting eternity; for the merits proper to their state, they will obtain a glory far greater and loftier. Yet in this respect they cannot be equal to you, nor can they possess that privilege which blessed virginity alone deserves, although the countless and immeasurably resplendent host of saints possesses it.

Hence our Augustine (*On Virginity*, book I, chapters 27–30):

> Therefore go on, holy children of God—boys and girls, males and females, celibate men and unmarried women—go on perseveringly to the end. Praise the Lord more sweetly, whom you contemplate more richly. Hope more happily in Him whom you serve more earnestly. Love more ardently Him whom you please more attentively [Col. 0452D]. With loins girded and lamps burning, await the Lord when He comes from the wedding. You bring to the marriage of the Lamb a new song, which you will sing upon your harps. It is certainly not such a song as the whole earth sings, to which it is said: “Sing to the Lord a new song; sing to the Lord, all the earth” (Ps. 95). Rather, it is a song that no one except you can utter.
>
> For one beloved above the rest by the Lamb saw you thus in the Apocalypse—the one accustomed to recline upon His breast, who drank in and poured forth marvellous things concerning the heavenly Word, God. He saw you as one hundred and forty-four thousand holy harpists, possessing unstained virginity in body and inviolate truth in heart. And because you follow the Lamb wherever He goes, he wrote this concerning you (Rev. 14).
>
> Where do we suppose this Lamb goes, where none except you either dares or can follow Him [Col. 0453A]? Where do we suppose He goes? Into what groves and meadows? There, I think, are grassy joys—not the vain joys and deceptive madness of this age, nor even joys such as are granted in the very kingdom of God to those who are not virgins, but joys distinguished from the lot of all other joys. The joys proper to Christ’s virgins are not the same as those of Christians who are not virgins. For others have joys of one sort or another, but none have joys like these: the proper joys of Christ’s virgins, from Christ, in Christ, with Christ, after Christ, through Christ, and for Christ.
>
> Go; follow the Lamb into these things, because the flesh of the Lamb is surely virgin. For in His birth He retained what conception and birth did not take from His mother. Rightly you follow Him in virginity of heart and body wherever He goes. For what is following except imitating? “Because Christ suffered for us, leaving you an example,” as the apostle Peter says, “that you may follow in His footsteps” (1 Pet. 2) [Col. 0453B].
>
> Each person follows Him in that in which he imitates Him—not insofar as He is the Son of God, the One through whom all things were made, but insofar as He presented in Himself for imitation what was fitting for the children of men. Many things in Him are set before all for imitation; bodily virginity, however, is not set before all. For those in whom it has already come to pass that they are not virgins have nothing they can do in order to be virgins.
>
> Therefore let the other faithful who have lost bodily virginity follow the Lamb—not wherever He goes, but as far as they are able. They can follow Him everywhere except when He walks in the beauty of virginity. But behold, that Lamb proceeds along a virgin path. How shall those who have lost what they can in no way recover go after Him [Col. 0453C]?
>
> Therefore you—yes, you—His virgins, go after Him. Go there after Him, you who for this one reason follow Him wherever He goes. We can exhort married persons to every other form of holiness in which they may follow Him, except that which they have irreparably lost. You, then, follow Him by holding fast with perseverance to what you ardently vowed. Do what you can, lest the good of virginity perish from you; for you can do nothing to make it return.
>
> The rest of the multitude of the faithful, unable to follow the Lamb in this way, will see you. They will see and not envy; and by rejoicing with you, they will possess in you what they do not have in themselves. For they will not be able to utter that new song which is properly yours. Yet they will be able to hear it [Col. 0453D] and delight in so excellent a good. But you will both utter it and hear it, because you will hear from yourselves what you utter. You will exult more happily and reign more joyfully.
>
> Yet no sorrow will arise from your greater joy. For that Lamb, whom you follow wherever He goes, does not abandon those who cannot follow Him where you can. He will go before you, and He will not depart from them, when God is all in all. Those who have less will not shrink from you. For where there is no envy, difference is harmonious. Therefore presume, trust, be strengthened, remain steadfast: you who vow and render vows of perpetual continence to the Lord your God (Ps. 75), not for this present age but for the kingdom of heaven.

How great, daughters, how great is the praise of virginity! My Margaret, if she persists, will deserve [Col. 0454A] what Mary Magdalene does not deserve. Why is this? Because not patience, not humility, not even charity, nor any other virtue, is called the sister of angels, but virginity. Hence blessed Jerome:

> “It is fitting that an angel is sent to a Virgin, because virginity is always akin to angels. Certainly, to live in the flesh beyond the flesh is not an earthly but a heavenly life. Therefore, to acquire angelic glory in the flesh is a greater merit than merely to possess it. For to be an angel belongs to happiness; but to be a virgin belongs to virtue, since she strives by her powers together with grace to obtain what the angel possesses by nature.”

Hence again Augustine (*On Virginity*, book I, chapters 53, 54, 56):

> Behold, you are already such women, because you ought to be such. These things added to virginity display the angelic life among human beings [Col. 0454B] and the manners of heaven upon earth. Therefore, since you have despised marriage with the sons of men, love with all your heart Him who is beautiful in form beyond the sons of men. Your heart is free; it is released from marital bonds.
>
> Consider the beauty of your Beloved: think of Him as equal to the Father and yet subject also to His mother; ruling in heaven and serving on earth; creating all things and created among all things. What the proud mock in Him, see how beautiful it is: see with inward lights the wounds of Him hanging, the scars of Him risen, the blood of Him dying—the price of the believer, the exchange of the redeemed.
>
> Consider what these things are worth; weigh them in the scales of love; and whatever devotion you would have bestowed upon your marriage, bestow it upon Him. It is good that He seeks your inward beauty, where He gave you power to become daughters of God. He does not seek a beautiful body from you [Col. 0454C]. No one can lie about you and make a jealous lover rage. Husband and wife love one another because they see one another; and in one another they fear what they do not see. Nor do they rejoice securely in what is manifest, while they often suspect, in secret, what is not.
>
> But in Him whom you do not see with your eyes and behold by faith, you have nothing to reprove; nor do you fear lest you perhaps offend Him through a false accusation. Therefore, if you owed great love to husbands, how greatly ought you to love Him for whose sake you were unwilling to have husbands? May He who was fixed upon the cross for your sake be fixed in your heart by your vow. May He wholly occupy in your minds whatever you refused to have occupied by marriage [Col. 0454D]. You may not love too little Him for whose sake you did not love even what it was lawful to love. Since you love Him who is gentle and humble of heart, I fear no pride in you.

Likewise St Ambrose (*On Virgins*, book I, chapter 8):

> But for you, holy virgins, there is a special protection, because by unstained chastity you preserve the sacred bedchamber of the Lord. Nor is it surprising that angels fight on your behalf, since you fight by the manner of angels. Virginal chastity deserves the protection of those whose life it imitates.
>
> Why should I pursue the praise of chastity at greater length? Chastity even made an angel. Whoever preserved it is an angel; whoever lost it is a devil. From it he even received his name. A virgin is one who marries the Lord; a prostitute is one who makes gods [Col. 0455A].
>
> And what shall I say of the resurrection, whose rewards you already possess? “For in the resurrection they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are as angels of God in heaven” (Matt. 22). What is promised to us is present for you; the practice of our vows is yours. You are from this world, yet you are not in this world. The age was worthy to have you, but could not hold you.
>
> How glorious it is that angels, through their lack of self-restraint, fell from heaven into the world, while virgins, through chastity, pass from the world into heaven! Blessed virgins, whom no enticement of bodies troubles and no flood of pleasures casts down. The food of moderation and the drink of abstinence teach them not to know vices, because they teach them not to know the causes of vices.

Again the same Ambrose (*On Virgins*, book I, chapter 8):

> “A garden enclosed is my sister, my bride; a garden enclosed, a fountain sealed” (Song 4), because in gardens of this kind, impressed with seals bearing the image of God, the water of a pure fountain shines forth, lest, muddied by the wallowing places of spiritual beasts, it be disturbed. Hence modesty, enclosed by that wall-like spirit, is shut in lest it lie open to plunder [Col. 0455B].
>
> Therefore, just as a garden inaccessible to thieves breathes the fragrance of the vine, is fragrant with the olive, and gleams with the rose, so may religion flourish in the vine, peace in the oil, and the modesty of consecrated virginity in the rose. This is the fragrance which the patriarch Jacob breathed in when he deserved to hear: “Behold, the smell of my son is as the smell of a field full of fruit” (Gen. 27).
>
> For although the field of that holy patriarch was full of nearly every kind of fruit, he caused crops to spring up through the greater labour of virtue; this garden, flowers. Therefore, virgin, gird yourself, and if the privilege of being such a garden breathes upon you, enclose it with prophetic commands: “Set a guard over your mouth, and a door around your lips” (Ps. 140) [Col. 0455C], so that you too may say: “As an apple tree among the trees of the forest, so is my beloved among the sons. Under his shadow, which I desired, I sat; and his fruit was sweet to my throat” (Song 2).—“I found him whom my soul loves; I held him and will not let him go” (Song 3).

After those lofty and sweet words of the saints, hear, my dearest ones, Hilary, eminent in name and reputation, inviting and exhorting his own biological daughter by every effort to preserve virginity of both body and soul, holding out to her, as it were, a divine garment and a heavenly pearl:

“In the first year,” says Saint Hilary (*Letter to His Daughter*), “[Col. 0455D] I saw a garment. I saw, daughter, I saw what I cannot express. Was not silk, compared with its fineness, like coarse rope? Did not snows, compared with its whiteness, become black? Did not gold, beside its brilliance, grow dull? For its many colors themselves surpassed all delightful things, and absolutely nothing could be made equal to it by comparison. Afterwards I saw a pearl. At the sight of it I immediately collapsed; for my eyes could not endure so great a color. No appearance of heaven, light, sea, or earth could be compared with its beauty.”

So much Hilary to his daughter. But let the great Cyprian of Carthage come at last after all the others: equal to all his predecessors in office, their peer in teaching, greater in martyrdom. For he says (*On the Dress of Virgins*):

“Now our discourse is addressed to virgins: the more exalted their glory, the greater also is their care. That is the flower of the Church’s growth; the beauty and adornment of spiritual grace; a joyful disposition of praise and honor; God’s work, whole and uncorrupted; an image answering to the Lord’s holiness; the more illustrious portion of Christ’s flock. Through them and in them the glorious fruitfulness of Mother Church, flowering abundantly, rejoices; and in proportion as plentiful virginity adds to its number, the mother’s joy increases. We speak to these, we exhort these, [Col. 0456A] more by affection than by authority. For they are equal to God’s angels, since they are daughters of the resurrection. You have already begun to be what we shall be. Already in this age you possess the glory of the resurrection. You pass through the world without the world’s contamination, when you persevere chaste and virginal; you are equal to God’s angels.

“Only let virginity remain solid and inviolate, and endure; and, as it began bravely, let it persevere continually. As we have borne the image of him who is from the dust, let us also bear the image of him who is from heaven. Virginity bears this image; integrity bears it; holiness and truth bear it. Those who bear it remember God’s commands, holding fast to righteousness with devotion, steadfast in faith and humble in fear; strong for every endurance, gentle in bearing injury, ready in showing mercy, united and harmonious in brotherly peace. Each of these things, O good virgins, you ought to observe, love, and fulfill—you who, free for God and Christ, go before toward the Lord to whom you have dedicated yourselves by the greater and better portion [of yourselves]. Those advanced in years, [Col. 0456B] teach the younger; those younger in age, offer encouragement to your equals. Stir one another by mutual exhortations; by examples that rival one another in virtue, call one another onward to glory. Endure bravely; go forward spiritually; arrive happily. Only remember us then, when virginity begins to be honored in you.”

These men, my dearest ones—from whose books, as from most flourishing meadows, I have gathered these delightful flowers—are among God’s highest priests, teachers of the Latin Church; indeed, were it not for the manifold barbarity of differing languages, they would be teachers of the whole Christian world. I have shown you their pearls; from them I have poured out before you, in some measure, treasures more precious and desirable than gold and topaz. It remains [Col. 0456D] for you to receive with eager hearts what is freely offered, to guard it with utmost care and diligence, and to enable me—more concerned for your salvation than all other mortals—to rejoice with you when, through angelic virginity, deepest humility, and most exalted charity, you have become beloved handmaids—indeed, beloved brides—of Jesus Christ.

Remember my blessed mother, your holy grandmother. Remember, I say, with what faith and with what fervor of charity, conceived from above though unknown [in its source], she stole you away from the world while you were still little girls, unable to distinguish right from left; withdrew you from the devil; offered you to God; and joined you to holy sisters. As I often heard from her own mouth at Marcigny, she feared lest she perhaps be snatched from this wretched vale of tears, by the will of the Lord who calls, [Col. 0457A] before she saw you rescued from the hunters’ snare; before she left you alive, added to the number of holy women in the school of virtues. The kindly Savior looked down from on high upon the humility and prayers of his handmaid; and he who satisfies the desire of his servants with good things, and fulfills the will of those who fear him, at last fulfilled her desire. He joined you bodily to the choir of virgins. See to it, see to it, that he also joins you to it in mind.

Not all who live with you are virgins in the flesh; yet, as Father Augustine says, they are virgins in faith. On the solemn day of the Lord’s Nativity he solemnly declares concerning them: “Where bodily integrity can no longer exist through sexual intercourse, let the conscience be a virgin in faith, according to which the whole Church is virgin.” In the same sense the apostolic trumpet frequently proclaims, concerning both virgins and those living continently and holily: “I have betrothed you to one husband, to present you as a chaste virgin to Christ” (2 Cor. 11). Established in this virginal choir by the happier lot—that is, unblemished not only in spirit but also in body—[Col. 0457B] order your lives and compose your conduct according to the admonitions of the saints whom I have set before you. Fight the good fight; by earnest running bring happily to completion the course begun from your tender years. Imitate your sisters and mothers with whom you serve God; especially that blessed grandmother of yours whom I have mentioned, who has gone before you to God and who invites you to follow her, not only while she lived but now also in death.

Grant me, I beg, the voice of the great Apostle, so that I may safely say to each one of you [Col. 0457C] what he wrote to his disciple Timothy: “I am filled with joy as I recall the unfeigned faith that is in you, which first dwelt—not, as he says, in your grandmother Lois and your mother Eunice, but in your grandmother Raingard and your father Hugh—and I am certain that it is in you also” (2 Tim. 1).

## LETTER XL

To my dearest and uniquely cherished lord Basil, prior of the servants of God at Chartreuse, Brother Peter, humble abbot of Cluny, sends the eternal salvation to which he has devoted himself.

Recently, when I was preparing for the journey to Rome, I wrote to you and the brothers from our little monastery of Herbens, [Col. 0457D] a letter which I believe has now reached you. In it I informed you both of my intention to visit you and of the reason which compelled us to remain. I wrote then in general terms; now I write personally. I write from the very approaches of the Alps, and I apologize that in that letter I did not, as usual, mention either your name or your office. Forgetfulness alone was the cause. I think the haste of the journey brought it upon me, together with the ship standing ready to carry us across the river Isère.

Yet I want you, dearest friend, to know that the affection which had led me to decide to visit your mountain region arose more from the desire to see you than to see the place, however holy. For I had already often seen that place and the other brothers over many years; but from the time when you embraced that arduous and heavenly calling, I had never visited you. I was not, nor am I, forgetful of the affection with which you have always honored me; of how, from your very early years, you have yearned after divine things with a devoted and sincere heart; how often, in that spirit, you visited your Cluny—truly your own; and, further, how long you served God in that cloister, joined to our brothers and yours.

Thereafter it pleased that Spirit who breathes where he wills to advance you from virtue to virtue; and, disposing ascents in your heart, to transfer you from good things to better, from high things to higher. He has set, and by his grace will steadfastly set, your feet upon the rock; and he will direct your steps in the way of his commandments. He has placed you in that rank of life above which scarcely anyone, or perhaps no one anywhere, appears. For this reason I had intended to visit you [Col. 0458A] and rejoice in your progress, by which you strive violently to seize the kingdom of God.

I had resolved to renew with you those ancient and holy conversations, often held between myself and your predecessor of blessed memory, Lord Guy. They kindled me as though by sparks issuing from his mouth and compelled me to forget almost all human affairs. I would also have discussed with you certain matters necessary at this time, which I wished neither to entrust to writing nor to confide to the ears of many. Since these things cannot presently be done, dearest friend, pray earnestly to the mercy of the Almighty that they may at least be granted in the future.

I commend to you, as to a special and intimate friend, my journey and my companions on it. It needs the greater assistance because, in this winter season, it is made the more fearsome by greater dangers. I ask you affectionately to greet on my behalf Brother Peter of Waping, whom I saw long ago as a recruit in Christ’s service and who is now a veteran; and Brother Geoffrey, who has fought the good fight for so long and has now almost completed his course. Earnestly commend me and ours to their holy life and prayers. For I do not know whether any other soldier from that first period of my life still survives. Likewise greet that noble man in flesh and spirit, Otmar, convert of Valbonne, and all the others together whenever they assemble.

## LETTER XLI

To the venerable lord and father Peter, most kindly abbot of the holy Church of Cluny, reverenced also with sincere affection: Brother Basil and the brothers with him at Chartreuse send everlasting salvation and peace from the Lord.

[Col. 0458D]

This truly is the mark of your ancient and firmly rooted love. For although, because of the obstacle of snow, you can scarcely make your way to us more readily, neither the dignity of your person nor the burdensome length of the journey restrains your affectionate devotion toward us. For the labor you undertook we give thanks; for the journey you did not make we pour forth prayers. We know the result; we know the effort. Let the love that is accustomed to endure remain, since we are deprived of the most welcome joy of your visit. Though we do not have it now, by God’s grace we do not despair of it in the future. At the fitting time God, who took it away, will grant it.

Although my lord and my brothers greatly desire you, I hunger for you more eagerly by reason of obligation. For am I not the one whom, though poor and needy, you did not despise, but loved, cherished, and trained with pious care for the sweet work of religious life? The Cluniac order, Cluniac discipline, the lovable and honorable Cluniac community—truly I confess it—has always urged me toward better and stricter things, and certainly still urges me. What then? Can the discipline of the choir, cloister, dormitory, refectory, [Col. 0459A] and the other noble workshops of Cluny, worthy of every person’s emulation, be torn away from one whose soul is subject to God? But not everyone sees what I saw; not everyone knows what was made known to me. Thanks be to God.

Why say more? I am yours, I was yours, and I shall be yours forever, because you too are truly Christ the Lord’s. Preserve by your prayers what you have built by your holy examples. Most kindly Father, we commend the house of Chartreuse and our whole undertaking, whatever it may be, to your holy intercessions.

## LETTER XLII

To the supreme pontiff and our special Father, Lord Pope Eugenius: Brother Peter, humble abbot of Cluny, offers devoted obedience with filial love.

Father, it has been reported to me that certain monks of Bremen are approaching Your Majesty in order to accuse their abbot before you. What they will say, I do not know. But I am confident that I know one thing: they will be unable to allege anything reasonable for which he deserves to incur paternal displeasure. You yourself saw the man recently; but I think he is more fully known to me, since I received him when he was almost a boy, reared him, and for many years have tested his good conduct and unimpaired reputation both at Cluny and outside it. For these reasons, and deservedly, I placed him over several great priories; and you, as I have learned, when a similar reputation commended him to you, placed him over a great abbey.

I call it great in possessions, but small, wretched, and ruined by the errors—if I may speak more mildly—of its inhabitants. I saw this myself in part as I was preparing to come to you, when, invited by the same abbot, [Col. 0459D] I celebrated the Nativity of the Lord in that abbey this year. I saw a monastery almost a hovel; I saw a place little removed from wilderness; I saw everything needing to be not merely renewed as from the beginning, but founded from the first stone. I saw monks devoted to us indeed, yet requiring instruction anew as though novices. It was easy for me to know the tree from its fruit and judge the inhabitants from their dwellings.

Not yet stripped of the old man nor clothed with the new, because your abbot compels them, though old in heart, to contemplate new things, they prefer to be sheep without a shepherd and to rest in their own dregs rather than oppose their customary pleasures or wills. This is why they have undertaken what I said: so that, once the shepherd is struck, the sheep of the flock may be scattered. Let Your Holiness know, however, that—with the exception of a very few, more ex-monks than monks—all whom I could hear in those regions offer him commendable testimony, saying that he is devout in spiritual matters and prudent in temporal ones. Therefore, if it please you, provide for him as your son and your abbot, lest the enemy man uproot what your hand has planted; lest the impious party boast and say, “I have prevailed against him” (Ps. 12).

## LETTER XLIII

To the supreme pontiff and our special Father, Lord Pope Eugenius: Brother Peter, humble abbot of Cluny, filial love and due obedience.

[Col. 0460B] I have often excused the importunity by which I weary my father with frequent letters. I have indeed excused it; yet, pressed by urgent causes, I do not cease to be importunate. Indulge me, Father, if it please you. You see that in these matters, as in almost all others, I do not do what I will, but do what I hate.

I believe that Your Paternity remembers that at Segni I spoke to you about the nobleman, Lord Guy of Domna, and asked that the case for which he lamented that he had been subjected to a sentence of interdict might be justly examined and decided in our regions by a suitable person appointed at your command. Your kindness replied to me that the metropolitan of Vienne, who had been the author of that proceeding, would shortly receive a mandate from you; that he would be summoned by you concerning these matters; and that, when you had heard him, you would impose an appropriate end upon that dispute.

Accordingly, when I was returning from you and traveling through Italy, now near the Alps, I heard that he was hastening toward you and might already be near the city. Therefore I promptly sent a messenger after him to you with this letter, asking that, if possible, before he departs from you, your wisdom may decide, as is its custom, the case of the nobleman just mentioned; or else, as I requested when present, may commit it for decision in the province of Vienne or Lyons, as you please.

And lest Your shrewd prudence wonder that I have needlessly taken on a matter apparently foreign to myself, know that this is not foreign but my own, because the man to whom it belongs is not a stranger but ours. He is ours by affection, ours by kinship, ours by benefaction: by affection with respect to himself, by kinship with respect to his family, and by benefaction with respect to both. With respect to himself, because he loves us and ours above all monasteries in the world; with respect to his family, because his fathers, grandfathers, and great-grandfathers did the same; with respect to both, because both he and they enriched with many great properties and revenues monasteries founded by them and given to Cluny. For these reasons I regard his affairs not as foreign but domestic, not as another’s but my own.

Since the man about whom I am concerned for you and for whom I pour out prayers to the Apostolic Majesty is absent, and as a man engaged in military life and bound to the world by innumerable chains of cares cannot readily come to you, please hear briefly, through this letter, his words as conveyed by me. [Col. 0461A] He says that he believes he contracted his marriage with the wife of whom he is accused lawfully and justly. Another woman is indeed alive, to whom he is said first to have been bound by a marital bond; but he maintains that she was never his wife. He offers the following reason—or rather, reasons—why she neither was, nor is, nor can be his wife.

First, because he took her against the opposition of his bishop of Grenoble; second, because he joined himself to her when she was below marriageable age and unable to give canonical consent; third, because he is closely related to her by a line of consanguinity; fourth, because at no time or moment was he able in any way to consummate the marriage with her, however much he wished to do so; fifth, because, just as he took that first woman wholly against the opposition, as stated, of his bishop, so he took this woman with the same bishop willing, permitting, commanding, and indeed almost compelling him; sixth, because when you returned from Gaul to Italy, in the Jura mountains between the bridge of Arle and Villa Junia, you commanded him to obey in all things the oft-mentioned Lord Archbishop of Vienne, and thence to hope for salvation not doubtful but certain; seventh, because before all these matters were examined, after he had more than once—both personally and through other religious or secular men—said and sent word to his bishop that he was prepared to undergo the judgment of justice, he was subjected by him to the sentence of interdict.

The man already sufficiently mentioned judges that any one of these grounds, even if the others were set aside, could alone fully suffice to effect a divorce between himself and that first woman, who was not his wife. How much more all of them together? Let the universal Father see and examine all these things; and let him who owes paternal care to all the Church’s children provide for the soul entrusted to him, not one of the lower or more insignificant souls. Let him either decide the matter before himself, as I have said, if possible; or entrust it for decision to worthy men of our regions, if he pleases.

For the man grieves greatly, and—something which scarcely or never befell any of his predecessors—he weeps, truly as a Christian beyond what would be thought believable of a layman, that he has incurred a sentence of ecclesiastical interdict. [Col. 0461D] I myself saw it and bear truthful witness before the Father: one day, as he was traveling with me between the castle of Vizille and the castle of Domna and speaking of these matters, he suddenly burst into such bitter weeping and sobbing that he moved us also, and several who were riding nearby with us, to tears and weeping. Therefore let a noble son’s tears, though absent, move paternal compassion: he both grieves, as a faithful Christian, that the grace of ecclesiastical communion is withdrawn from him, and, when the matter of dismissing or retaining his wife comes to examination, is prepared to obey apostolic and ecclesiastical command.

## LETTER XLIV

To the supreme pontiff and our special Father, Lord Pope Eugenius: Brother Peter, humble abbot of Cluny, whatever filial love and obedience can offer.

[Col. 0462A]

The clergy, consuls, and people of Piacenza, deeply and profoundly grieved because they are presently displeasing to your kindly fatherhood, and wishing above all earthly things to please you, have chosen me as their advocate. They hope that through me their prayers may be more readily received by the Father and perhaps even heard. They do this because of the favor which they believe I retain with you, judging that their wishes will not wholly fail if my intercession is joined to their prayers. Whether this is so, may I experience it now in the cause I have undertaken as I have often experienced your favor in both my own affairs and those of others.

I am their debtor, both by common charity and by particular affection. Your wisdom knows this, I think, and it has, I suppose, reached the ears of Your Majesty that five years ago, when I was going to Rome in order to see and visit you, they acted concerning the injury inflicted upon me—and indeed upon you—by Marquis Opizo. They showed how greatly they were grieved; with what force they dragged the fleeing beast, seeking hiding places, from his den into public view; how they compelled him to vomit up, down to the last penny, everything he had swallowed; and how they compelled both him and his accomplices in crime, willing or unwilling, to make satisfaction at my discretion. They did this, as I said, not for me alone, because what is done to the son is done also to the Father.

For this reason I would deservedly be condemned for ingratitude if, where a reasonable cause requires it, I were afraid to set my prayers, of whatever value, against paternal displeasure on their behalf. These men whose cause I have undertaken say—and, as I learned from them, they are prepared to prove it by oath—that they have done nothing of the things of which they are accused to the injury of Your Majesty, nor ever intended to do anything of the kind. But they are told: “A bishop was consecrated by your metropolitan of Ravenna, moreover by order of the lord pope; yet you refused to receive him, and, what is worse, you bound yourselves by oath never to receive him at any time.”

To this they reply: “Our metropolitan is not the archbishop of Ravenna, not that of Aquileia, nor any other, but the Roman pontiff. We prove this by innumerable witnesses; we prove that, for many centuries past, the bishop-elect of Piacenza has been consecrated by the supreme and universal bishop, not by another. We produce as examples, apart from the more ancient cases, Urban II and Calixtus II, who laid the hand of consecration upon our elect and clearly showed by their example what ought to be observed by posterity. Let the dignity granted to our city by so many pontiffs be preserved; and we are prepared to do or undergo whatever the Apostolic Majesty may command, should we have erred in these matters.”

These are their words, Father. To them I add: Have mercy, Father, have mercy on so great a city, scarcely second to any in Italy. Have mercy on so great a people, who, if they acted otherwise than they should, are prepared to obey what has been stated above and observe every command. Consider—consider, I say, in your discerning manner—that even if they have sinned, what a multitude commits is ordinarily left unpunished. Reflect, though I speak as one less wise, as if teaching a teacher, that that good Shepherd whose place you hold on earth was wounded for our infirmities and, offering himself to his vicars as an example to imitate, said: “Those who are well do not need a physician, but those who are ill” (Luke 5).

See that they are near danger—danger of eternal death—if you do not accommodate yourself to them, if you insist upon maintaining your rigor, if you say: “I shall not be reconciled unless they receive the bishop consecrated by the bishop of Ravenna; I shall not rest unless they invalidate their oaths.” I fear, my lord, I fear that by this severity the Church may suffer loss rather than gain; that this rigor may prove more ruinous than fruitful. I am afraid that of the city of Piacenza in this Christian commonwealth of ours it may be said what was once said among the Jews in the time of the Judges concerning the tribe of Benjamin: “One tribe has been taken away from Israel” (Judg. 21).

If Your Wisdom reviews the matter, it will recall how many and how great dispensations have been made by the Apostolic See in the cases of pagans, heretics, and even Catholics; and for no other reason than that great and discerning Fathers, enlightened by the spirit of counsel and fear of God, saw that, with faith and charity preserved, they could benefit God’s Church more usefully by accommodation than harmfully by observing stricter measures. The letter would extend to infinity if I wished to offer the examples which occur. But because such matters are unnecessary for one who knows them all, I refer him to himself and beg him to reread these things in the book of his singular memory.

Yet I call back to mind, if perhaps it has slipped away, the memorable saying—not the exact words in sequence—of the great Father Augustine, the highest teacher of God’s Church after the apostles. “Grafting,” he says, “is such that a branch brought from elsewhere cannot be grafted into a tree unless some small wound is made in the tree. Thus the Church is sometimes wounded, whether in its own members or in others, by accommodating itself in charity, in order that one who had been estranged or was a stranger may be grafted in.” But perhaps I have gone too far. Confidence conceived from paternal kindness has made me do so.

Therefore, to conclude at last: I pray, entreat, and supplicate with my heart—indeed, with my very body I prostrate myself, though absent, before the feet of Your Holiness—that you accommodate yourself to your people of Piacenza, who seek with all their power to please you; and correct their error in whatever manner seems good, provided that you preserve them, their Church, and their bishop for yourselves, [Col. 0464A] not for another; for the Roman Church, not for Ravenna or any other.

## LETTER XLV

To the supreme pontiff and our special Father, Lord Pope Eugenius: Brother Peter, humble abbot of Cluny, devoted obedience with filial love.

If God’s providence had made me geographically close to Your Paternity, I would have wished both to report to you everything done by me and to take counsel with you concerning what was to be done. Now, being far away, I often wish to do what I cannot always do. Therefore I make known to Your Kindness what happened after my return from you concerning the castle which Hugh the Barefoot was building above, so to speak, Cluny’s very head.

> **[Note: [Col. 0463D]**
>
> **What was done concerning the castle Hugh the Barefoot was building.** The *Chronicon Cluniacense* assigns the settlement of this dispute to the year 1153, where it also calls this Hugh “of Scalcieu.” A rescript of Pope Alexander concerning this dispute, or a similar one, is also found in the Cluniac cartulary. It too calls him Hugh of Scalceo, commonly “de la Chaux.”
>
> **Pope Alexander’s confirmation of the peace sworn between the Church of Cluny, the Count of Forez, and the barons [Col. 0464D] of the region; and remission of one year’s penance for those who keep that peace.**
>
> “Alexander, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the noblemen Hugh of Beaujeu and his sons, the Count of Forez, the Viscount of Mâcon, John Grossus, Hugh of Berzé, Hugh of Scalceo, and the rest who preserve the sworn peace of the Church of Cluny: greeting and apostolic blessing.”
>
> “And the benefit of this present life,” etc. See Alexander III under the year 1181.]

I had complained about it to you, as you know, and your providence had subjected it to a severe anathema. On my return, therefore, I found it not merely begun but already enclosed with strong walls; and, except for the stone tower, for which the aforementioned Hugh had already gathered nearly all the material, a wooden tower had in the meantime been erected and the work was almost entirely complete. [Col. 0464B] I also found that our people had surrounded with ditches and fortifications a village belonging to us, called Clarummane, very close to that castle. So far as the shortness of time allowed, they had fortified it and set it against Hugh’s castle as a counter-castle.

I found all our neighboring knights and castellans, and even the counts and dukes of our Burgundy, greedy—as the saying is—for a golden fortune; and, drawn by the scent of silver smoke, urging our men on every side to take up arms. They said many things under the appearance of friends sympathizing or advising. Hearing them, I perceived the direction in which they tended; yet I gave them a peaceful hearing, as though they were offering good counsel. Many of our own people also insisted—though with what spirit, let them see—maintaining that prudent men should be believed, since, being friends and practiced in warfare, they would neither exhort us to useless acts nor recommend what ought to be rejected.

Conversely, far more of them declared that Cluny had never gained anything by military arms; that anyone who advises monks to fight or girds a hooded monk with a sword is either mad or an enemy; that if such a monster were to proceed to war, it should be regarded as an astonishing prodigy. Such soldiers or champions, they said, ought to be laughed at and mocked by the whole world; secular people would no longer wish to come there to receive the religious habit, when they saw that habit already laid aside by religious men themselves. They added that innumerable losses could arise from this, since in a short time the devastation of war could absorb revenues even much greater than those possessed by that Church, and by consuming them gradually cause it to fail within itself. Finally, men trained in other pursuits and wholly ignorant of the arts of war would be nothing but prey or food for crafty enemies reared in such things from the breast.

Since these counsels proved the sounder, a settlement of this kind was made through the mediation of Hugh of Berzé and certain other knights, while on our side Brother Enguizo especially and several others pressed for it. The builder of the castle himself pulls down and demolishes the castle from its very foundations, with his own hands or those of his men; and he confirms by oath that he will never thereafter build anything there. Moreover, he gives the very hill to the Church. He adds by oath [Col. 0465B] that from the castle of Buxeria as far as Cluny he will never again establish any fortification whatsoever in any place. He also forbids this to all his heirs and promises that he will execute this instrument containing these terms, with the authority and testimony of the Archbishop of Lyons and his fellow bishops, Count William, and the other nobles of that land.

For these reasons we gave him two hundred and twenty pounds. Let Your Sublimity know that these things were done especially for this reason: mindful of the counsel you gave us, we preferred to spend much under terms of peace rather than perhaps consume limitless sums in the uncertainty of war.

## LETTER XLVI

To the distinguished and exceptional man of our age, Lord Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux: Brother Peter, humble abbot of Cluny, sends eternal salvation.

[Col. 0465C]

Since I delayed for so many days in replying to your Holiness, who wrote to me so sweetly and kindly, do not be surprised. At that time such a storm of business had rushed upon me, and so great a mass of cases was choking me on every side, that I scarcely had leave even to live, much less, as I shall not say, to write. An immense mass of waters overflowed after the barrier had been broken: waters which the Roman journey, gradually gathering them while I was absent and holding them back for some time like a pond, now poured out upon me in fullest measure. Then I could rightly have cried: “Save me, O God, for the waters have come in even unto [Col. 0465D] my soul” (Ps. 68). This was the reason why I withheld, though only for a few days, the reply owed to him to whom I owe my whole self.

Now at last drawing breath, I respond, as I can in words, to the affection of so great a friend; and shortly, by God’s grace, I shall respond in person as well. The Lord has indeed magnified his dealings with us; and, as your words, almost surpassing human speech, declare, he made our journey prosperous and, by his grace, through your zeal and your people’s prayers, led us out and brought us back safe and sound. He granted us according to our heart and fulfilled our petitions. Even literally, crooked things became straight for us and rough places smooth paths. The icy Alps themselves, and the crags condemned to perpetual snows, almost forgot their ancient terror. The very air, which, as I learned after our return, showed itself harsher than usual to our Gaul during the winter months through excessive rains—apart from five days only—throughout the whole time I remained in Italy, both on the land journey and on the river journey (for during several days and nights the Po detained us as we sailed), always showed itself pleasant and serene. We found almost stony from dryness the muddy roads by which we chiefly feared to be distressed—indeed, as everyone threatened us, to be stuck fast.

We recovered alive certain brethren who were companions on the journey, men of pure and simple life, when they had been overwhelmed by waves and were already on the point of perishing, from the very jaws of death, so to speak. I myself, bolder than usual, while I tried to mount on horseback a certain bridge because I disliked going on foot, was almost thrown into a chasm beneath that bridge when the hind feet of my mule were dragged back by very tenacious mud. But when God’s power gave strength to the mule, I suddenly found myself with her upon the bridge; and so, contrary to expectation, having suffered nothing grievous, I escaped.

Why say more? Such grace—not fortune—accompanied me continuously both on the outward and the return journey, that nothing happened to me or to ours contrary to our wish, except the exhaustion or death of beasts, for which God has no care. I found everything cheerful on the road, but I found things still more cheerful with the Father. I found him good at the beginning, better as matters proceeded, best at the end—indeed, to confess what I draw more truly from my heart, always best. And although that countenance of his, in which apostolic vigor and bearing truly shine, changed according to the variety of cases, persons, and events, showing itself with most discriminating judgment now cheerful, now clouded to different people, it was never changed toward me in another direction. As I found him when I came, so I left him when I departed. I observed him often putting on a sterner or sadder expression than he was compelled to assume for other reasons; yet whenever he addressed me, privately or publicly, he changed from the appearance of a judge to a father’s graciousness.

I was preferred even before all those of higher rank; not even patriarchal dignity, when the Archbishop of Ravenna was also present, was allowed to precede me, he himself often urging me to go first. I was not merely joined to the senate of Romans, bishops, or cardinals, but was sometimes compelled to join it. All non-Romans were excluded from Roman deliberations; I alone, or almost alone, was summoned to the sworn secrets. This was in public. Who could explain the more private conversations, removed from others? I say—I say what is true. Let no one think that I speak otherwise than I feel. To say anything too arrogantly is not permitted me in this matter. Never have I experienced in such conversations a more faithful friend, a more sincere brother, or a purer father. His ear was patient in hearing; his tongue ready and effective in answering—not as a greater person to a lesser, but as either an equal to an equal, or sometimes an inferior to a superior. There was no pride, no lordship, no majesty; rather equity claimed the whole man for itself, humility the whole man, reason the whole man. Whatever I asked there or elsewhere was either granted, or reasonably denied in such a way that I could not complain.

In saying this I do not boast, but declare that your prayers for me were fulfilled through him. It is not new for the monastery of Cluny to be honored by the supreme pontiff in whatever pastor it has; but it is new that nothing unfavorable could be observed in his conduct, his words, or his very bearing toward it. I had seen him at Rome in the first year of his pontificate; afterward I had seen him at Cluny, at Auxerre, at Châlons, at Rheims, and elsewhere. But he now appeared such as though I had never seen him. I shall briefly report what I found concerning the disposition of the whole Roman curia toward me and our condition: that of faithful friends, sweetest brothers, and household companions, so far as could be perceived, from a pure and sincere heart.

All your people, especially that singular man the lord Bishop of Ostia, stood by me no less, no more faintly, than he would have stood by you had you been present. Because a brief discourse is insufficient to explain his conduct, I defer it to letters; but when I am present, by God’s grace, I shall not spare words. Next, the text of your sweet and holy letter exhorts me that it is time and my duty not to repay evil to those who repay me evil; it urges that those who wished, but could not, act otherwise should now experience our clemency, and that a father’s affection should receive back departing sons into his own bosom. It presses that they should perceive that we have found in the lap of the apostolic see more of a father than of a judge, and that the sword already drawn to strike has been returned to the scabbard of mercy, [Col. 0467C] and so forth in this manner.

To this I reply: This task is neither difficult nor unfamiliar to me. Nature itself sufficiently inclines me to pardon; the very habit of pardoning urges me on. I am accustomed to suffer, and accustomed also to forgive. The schism of Pontius demonstrates this, though I do not boast of it proudly: when innumerable persons fell into it and committed abominable acts unheard of in the monastic order, they never experienced my sword, my blade, or my spear; scarcely ever did they hear a harsh word from my mouth. I did this then and have often done so afterward—not indeed in matters so grave, yet in grave offences, and offences perhaps justly punishable severely if forbearance had not intervened. I still do it frequently, nor, so to speak, do I cease constantly to do so.

But what then? Is it always so? Shall I always sing to God of mercy and never of judgment? Are all the ways of the Lord mercy only? Is there not truth also? Shall every soldier of God always keep his sword from blood? If so, not only the king but also his soldier bears the sword in vain. In vain also are read those words known to the Christian world: “Do you wish not to fear authority? Do good, and you shall have praise from it” (Rom. 13). “But if you do evil, fear.”

But someone will say: “The Church has no sword; Christ took it away when he said to Peter: ‘Put your sword into its sheath. Everyone who takes up the sword shall perish by the sword’” (John 18). It is true, I say, it is true. The Church does not have the king’s sword, but it has the shepherd’s rod. Of this the Apostle says: “What do you wish? Shall I come to you with a rod, or in a spirit of gentleness?” (1 Cor. 4). And why do I say it has a rod? Indeed, it also has a sword, according to the same Apostle: “Take the helmet of salvation and the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (Eph. 6). If this sword remains inactive, if it is always hidden, if it is never drawn and never inspires terror in anyone, what will happen? Perhaps, according to Solomon, beasts of the field will multiply against a slack hand, nor, in the words of a certain friend of Job, will they be at peace with him. And what will the perversity of the wicked do, when impunity makes them worse in their evils?

I pass over Phinehas, pass over Elijah, and say nothing of the Maccabees, whom the Church reads and sings as fierce avengers of crimes. I set before you that man, gentlest above all men who dwelt upon the earth. Who does not know his name? Although he was so great in the virtue of meekness, he did not fear to avenge God’s injuries and his own by a terrible example of death. A matter so well known need not be prolonged. Why should I speak of Samuel praying for his enemies? Why of David, again and again sparing most wicked foes? Yet the former, not by another’s hand but by his own, cut the very fat king of the Amalekites into pieces; and the latter did not say only mystically: “I shall pursue my enemies and overtake them, and I shall not turn back until they fail” (Ps. 17). For he pursued enemies, often in actual fact as well, and overtook them, nor did he turn back until they were destroyed.

What did the Savior himself—what did Jesus himself, plainly the merciful one—do? He indeed endured scourges, but he also inflicted scourges. He drove from God’s temple, not through servants but by his own action and with blows, merchants unlawfully trading in a place unsuited to commerce, when the disciples remembered the saying of the Psalm concerning him: “Zeal for your house has consumed me” (Ps. 68).

Why all this? I seem, as the saying goes, to teach Minerva, pour drops into the Rhône, carry wood to a forest. Yet I do none of these things. What then? One thing is my intention, one thing that I suggest to my most special and most holy friend. Your Blessedness perhaps believes or supposes, while reading this, that I rage against such men and wish to be glutted by their torments or punishments. I was not, I am not, nor can I be the torturer of those who, although they have sinned greatly by maliciously disparaging, whispering against, and speaking against their brethren—although they have torn their flesh with canine teeth, ripped apart their own entrails with their own claws, and wickedly, as I know, mangled the body of their Church in certain of its members—may they have forgiveness, if this seems useful to you, so that they may not deserve a reward. If they refuse to misuse one benefit, they may be drawn thereby toward what is better; by the other, they may be deterred from falling into something worse.

But it will be said: “Charity will not be complete if it does not harm, but it will be whole if it benefits.” Come then. Willing or unwilling, I am compelled to be perfect. I shall be—what I had not thought—perfect as my heavenly Father is perfect. I shall not take vengeance on enemies; indeed, I shall do good to enemies. Let them be preferred, preside, and rule—but without me.

How “without me”? Let them have dignities. Let them have honors from me—monastic honors, if that expression must be used—but not around me. Let them, placed outside, have both my possessions and, if they deserve it, even my heart; let them not seek my side. No plague, as you know, and as that man whom you know says, is more effective for harm than a familiar enemy. There is also a common proverb: “To be deceived the first time is unfortunate, the second time foolish, the third time disgraceful.” And, to add something divine: “Let your friends,” says Solomon, “be many; one counselor out of a thousand” (Ecclus. 6).

I seem in part to speak as a son of this world, although, God being witness, I have little concern for the world. Indeed, it might perhaps be little or none if the sons of this world allowed it. But because they are wiser in their generation than the sons of light, would that I were given the simplicity of the dove for avoiding their wickedness, and the prudence of the serpent for guarding against their malice. So much for the present concerning these matters.

What can I say concerning the remaining points that follow this subject, expressed in the words of your sacred mouth? I find nothing; I am not equal to it. Yet I am equal, not indeed to answering, but to returning to so great a love the whole and undivided affection of my mind and heart. I shall come—certainly I shall come—wherever seems good to you or yours. I shall come, I say, to my servant, as I have it from you, either at Dijon or at Clairvaux itself. For I recognize, and truly recognize, what you said: that insofar as I spare you, I shall spare myself also.

I grant you the gift which you wrote that you would regard as great, until I deserve to enjoy our desired conversation. Concerning Germanus, what you suggested rather than said, I am doing as much as I can. I reserve the rest for the awaited day. Regarding the subprior, what you added astonished me not a little when I read it. I immediately met the man, and from him I heard that almost everything which had been reported to you about him was utterly false. I feared the hissing of the serpents among my own people, lest they had hissed into your ears things like those which they poured out this year. And indeed the greater part of the material contained in your letter seems to have been supplied by them. Although they are very few and, as they think, very secret, they hate what I love and love what I hate. But this is gratuitous, as the Psalm says (Ps. 68), and as the Savior recalls.

I love that man because he is far more prudent than he appears, useful, necessary, and faithful. Perhaps this last quality, and this alone, is what they hate in him. He himself will write to you, excusing what he did not do and not denying what he did do; he will make satisfaction in every respect if he offended you even in something small. Believe a man who, as I know, is worthy of belief. Farewell.

## LETTER XLVII. Brother PETER the humble, to Brother NICHOLAS, his customary greeting.

To speak without preface: what indeed—what is this? Are you the one to whom it may be said, “O you of little faith, why did you doubt?” (Matt. 14). Yet I am not Christ, nor are you Peter. Or, good man, to speak with some indignation, did you think that I had become another person? Had your opinion of my love for you, which I had believed had grown into a very strong oak, struck such firm roots that I now discover it has scarcely grown together into the tenderest twig? Or perhaps you thought that, when I changed regions, I changed my mind as well; and that, infected by the touch of foreign air, I had—if I may insert something fabulous—through Circe’s drugs been changed from a man into a beast and broken out into some monster, though the man whom you know says:

> “Those who hasten across the sea change their sky, not their mind.”  
> (Horace, *Epistles*, I.11.27)

The Roman or Campanian shore has not so prevailed over me as to compel me to forget what I was and change, not for the better but for the worse. That would be strange if it could have done so over a long time; but stranger still if it could have done so in so short a time. But it is not so. I am indeed not what I was, but through alteration of the body, which takes place in all things at every moment, not through change of mind. If perhaps I am thought changed because I was silent, then let the same be thought when I speak, because I do not always speak; let it be thought also when I sleep, because I do not always sleep; and so with the other things that happen to body or mind.

But diminution of love was not the cause of my silence. My silence—my failure to write to you, dearest one, if you do not still doubt that you are this, during so long a journey about so long a journey—occurred not because I did not wish to, but because I could not. What could I write while placed upon a journey, when I could scarcely live? I say “live,” not because, thanks be to God, through friends, brethren, and sons both praying and striving, anything happened to me against my wish; but because, riding for nearly the whole day, eating at midnight, rising very early, and sweating in continual exertion, what mind could prepare itself for reflection, what tongue for dictation, what hand for writing? These obstacles, besides many others too long to recall, imposed silence upon me both beyond and on this side of the Alps.

There was also this: I reserved, as was fitting, the first information concerning my actions or experiences for the lord abbot before all others. And if I was silent for a while after my return, it is not surprising; rather, that I could speak at all was very surprising. How so? I found everything glad, pleasant, and smiling; and, besides the devout welcome of clergy and laity, I found among the brethren—what was more dear to my heart—not only a song of voices but a jubilation of hearts.
