I rejoiced in them, not in myself, but gloried in the Lord, because the sheep—not mine, but Christ’s—showed by tears as well as songs their pious affection, which powerfully guided their hearts, toward me, their whatever-sort-of shepherd. I wondered that my absence of scarcely five months had suddenly emerged from hidden places into so great a flame of love that it might have seemed remarkable had a delay of five years produced so much.

While I was in this situation, and had scarcely passed the limit of four days, I entered at once, after the lilies of joys, the thorns of business. Waters flooded over my head, and I almost said, “I have perished.” I immediately invoked the Lord’s name, and by it I have not yet been submerged; henceforth it will be my task, yours, and my people’s, that I not be submerged. These waters were peoples and nations, flowing to Cluny from Italy, [Note: [Col. 0471B] “Nations from Italy,” etc. Thus also the anonymous writer who composed the life of St. Morand, monk of Cluny: “At that time, as to a common refuge of piety, almost the entire world fled to Cluny for the spiritual renewal of its places. Hence the whole house of the world was filled with the nard of spiritual virtues poured out from the fragrance of the ointment, while the fervor of monastic religion, which at that time had almost grown cold, was rekindled by the example and zeal of those men. Gaul, Germany, and Britain beyond the sea bear witness to this. Spain, Italy, and all Europe confess it, [Col. 0472B] full of monasteries either newly founded by them or restored from ancient decay,” etc.], Germany, Spain, England, and our own Gaul, and gathered there during the whole of my absence into immense heaps of cases. As soon as they sensed my presence, as though they had conspired against my head, they poured out everything they had long held back. I did what I could and escaped as I could. What did one deserve who did not notice, reflect upon, or consider this? But I shall pardon him, grant forgiveness, and follow my custom. I do not wish to lose in the case of one accused person that gentleness which I commonly preserve toward many thousands.

Now, concerning my journey, about which you asked to be informed—what I did, said, and found—I send you to the letter which I am writing to the lord of Clairvaux, so that through it you may be informed of all these matters. There you will read everything; there you will find everything. I wrote to him to show it to you.

Concerning my kinsman, the astonishing and admirable abbot of Miratoury, I do not find what to say. I might perhaps find it, were not concern for brevity compelling me to finish the letter. Besides this short time, approaching Pentecost and the haste of the messenger hinder the course of my words and restrain a mind eager to express its great disturbances. Nor would a short letter contain that matter of Miratoury, even if it were wholly devoted to it; scarcely a whole book could suffice.

Please make every effort that a day for a meeting between me and the lord of Clairvaux may be arranged, if possible, at Dijon on the third Sunday after Pentecost. I have asked the lord abbot to send you to us as quickly as possible. Do not, however, find it burdensome to come sooner by any means. You are very necessary to me, both for these matters and for certain others. Do not blame the messenger for having delayed so long, but blame me; and excuse him to the others. Farewell.

[Note: [Col. 0472B] To complete the number of letters in this sixth book, which are reckoned as fifty in the *Chronicle of Cluny*, three still appear to be missing here—unless perhaps someone judges that the three writings addressed to Peter of St. John and against the Petrobrusians, which most regard as treatises rather than letters, and which the same *Chronicle* teaches us are to be joined to them, should be counted among them.]

[Col. 0471]

# SUPPLEMENT TO THE SIX BOOKS OF LETTERS OF PETER THE VENERABLE. LETTERS OF PETER THE VENERABLE AND VARIOUS PERSONS TO HIM, NOW COLLECTED TOGETHER FOR THE FIRST TIME.

## I. Letter of R., Abbot of Vézelay, to PETER, Abbot of Cluny.—He begs mercy from him for a certain irreligious monk, Philip. (About 1125.)

[MARTENE, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, I, 366, from an autograph in the archives of St. Mansuetus.]

[Col. 0471C]

To the most reverend lord P., Abbot of Cluny, Brother [Note: [Col. 0471] This is Raynald, brother of Peter the Venerable, who later became Archbishop of Lyons after having been Abbot of Vézelay.] R., Abbot of Vézelay, greeting and blessing.

When we had lodged at Luperciacum, on that very night a certain young Philip, whom you recently sent there from Château-Canin, driven to desperation by a certain penance imposed upon him through your letter, climbed the church tower and tried to crush with stones the brethren who were seeking him. At last we went to the church and summoned him under a pledge of safety—for otherwise he would not come down—and asked why he had done this. He said that Lord Ildinus, prior of Château-Canin, had disclosed his confession; and he complained that Ildinus had taken his clothes, which Philip’s uncle, Ildinus’s predecessor, had left him at his death. His clothes, however, were brought before us and were quite thin and worn. We therefore implore your mercy both to relieve Brother Philip of a burden which he does not know how to bear in so small a community—namely, custody and abstinence both from wine and in general—and to restore to him the clothes left him.

## II. Peter the Venerable, Abbot of Cluny, directs that masses and prayers be celebrated, both at Cluny and throughout the Order, for Rudolf of Péronne, a benefactor. (About 1140.)

[*Spicilegium*, quarto edition, vol. XI, p. 332.]

[Col. 0473B]

I, Brother PETER, humble Abbot of Cluny, make known to readers what follows. Count Rudolf of Péronne, son of Hugh the Great, brother of Philip, King of the French, was a great friend and benefactor of this holy Church of Cluny, in which we desire to serve almighty God. After his other good works, by which, while he lived in health, he strove to make God favorable to himself, he added something greater when already sick and near death. For he endowed the monastery of Crépy, which had been built long ago in the same castle of Crépy and was subject to the Church of Cluny, so richly in lands and income from lands that the annual revenues of those lands exceeded one thousand solidi.

Besides this and many other gifts which he assigned to different monasteries belonging to Cluny, he also gave to the monastery of Cluny itself, by testamentary right, five hundred marks of silver. A few days after he had departed this life, these were brought to Cluny and publicly presented to the Cluniac community in chapter.

Therefore, unwilling—indeed, seeking to avoid appearing wholly ungrateful for such great benefits—we direct by common counsel and prayers that two thirty-day observances be performed for him; that each priest sing three masses; and that all the others who are not priests recite three times the seven penitential psalms. In all monasteries belonging to Cluny where the observance is maintained, thirty-day observances are to be celebrated; priests other than those performing the thirty-day observances are to celebrate two masses without any exception.

Beyond all this, what is rarely granted to anyone has also been granted him: a solemn anniversary, like that given to one of our greatest friends and benefactors after emperors and kings. So that the nature of this anniversary may be known: on the day when it is to be celebrated, the general office shall be held for him in the community, likewise with a public mass. All brethren of priestly rank residing at Cluny shall on that day celebrate mass for his salvation; the others shall say the psalm *Miserere mei Deus* (“Have mercy upon me, O God”); and thirteen poor persons shall be fed. In addition, there shall be an annual cycle of masses: that is, for a whole year a mass shall be celebrated daily for him. These things were done so that almighty God, the merciful one, through his immeasurable mercy may have mercy on him, rescue him from the lot of the wicked, associate him with the number of his own, and deign to make him a sharer in blessed and everlasting life. Amen, amen.

## III. Letter of Peter, Abbot of Cluny, to Diethelm, priest.—He incorporates the monastery of Thierbach, in the diocese of Basel, into the Cluniac Order. (1142.)

[MARTENE, *Thesaurus Anecdotorum*, I, 395.]

To the venerable priest Lord DIETHELM, and to all dwelling in the parish of Sulz, Brother PETER, Abbot of Cluny, greeting.

When you first began the new foundation at Thierbach and intended that it should be subject to Cluny, you incorporated yourselves into the prayers of all the brethren of Cluny. Therefore, by the said privilege we establish that the same place shall remain henceforth under the lordship of Cluny and be subject to no other church; and we decree that nothing contrary to the privilege shall have force. Thus we make all who do good in that place participants in all the good works of all the brethren of Cluny, make them our confrères, and decree that in death and in life we shall pray for them, that God may absolve them from all sins. Amen.

Given at Cluny, in the year 1142, on the third day before the Nones of March.

## IV. Letter of Peter the Venerable to Odo, Bishop of Beauvais.—Peter, monk of Cluny, becomes Abbot of St. Lucian. (1147.)

[*Gallia Christiana*, new edition, vol. X, col. 256.]

[Col. 0474C]

To O[DO], by God’s grace venerable Bishop of the Church of Beauvais, to the canons of the same church, and to the community of Blessed Lucian: Brother P[ETER], Abbot of Cluny, greeting and affection.

Although it is burdensome to us to grant our brethren to other monasteries, nevertheless, in view of charity, we have not refused assent to your request. We grant Brother Peter free and released, for as long as he shall be abbot of the church of Blessed Lucian. Farewell.

## XIII. Letter of Peter the Venerable to Hugh, Abbot of Trois-Fontaines.—At St. Bernard’s request he makes a grant to the monastery of Trois-Fontaines. (1150.)

[MARTENE, *Anecdota*, vol. I, col. 407, from the Cluny cartulary.]

[Col. 0475A]

To his beloved and venerable brother HUGH, Abbot of Trois-Fontaines, and to his successors regularly appointed: Brother P., humble Abbot of Cluny, in perpetuity.

Nothing is more fitting for both our person and our Church than to seek the things that make for peace and, under the concord of charity, gently to cherish the other orders joined to us and ours throughout the world. Above all, we wish in every way to preserve those who have come forth from the Cistercian Order, especially the house of Clairvaux, most particularly our dearest abbot of that place, and all that pertains to him.

Accordingly, we secure by the page of this present privilege the church of Trois-Fontaines, firstborn daughter of the monastery of Clairvaux, against our sons, the monks of St. Margaret’s and those of Baud-Villars, so that no further dispute may arise among them concerning neighboring lands. At the request of our dearest Abbot of Clairvaux, we give and confirm to the aforesaid monastery of Trois-Fontaines everything that we possessed from the side of Trois-Fontaines to the spring called Berar Sarcus: so that from the said spring the boundary and line shall run by the road of Robert of Spain as far as the Caladia of Rocheriis, which is the road beyond the old chapel and beyond the Salmaria road; and from there as far as the territory of Clanseniacum. Thus everything within these boundaries shall belong to the aforesaid monastery of Trois-Fontaines, free from every customary due, for an annual rent of ten solidi in Provins currency, to be paid each year on the feast of the Ascension of the Lord to the house of Baud-Villars.

In this land the monks of Trois-Fontaines held a third part in many places, and they also gave us a certain part which they held outside the spring of Berar Sarcus, namely, whatever they held there. This was nevertheless arranged so that our monks of Baud-Villars might cultivate there the land which they had customarily cultivated: the valley lying between the old chapel and the meadow, and lengthwise as far as the Caladia road mentioned above, and nothing more. If the monks abandon that land, they may not give it to anyone except the monastery of Trois-Fontaines. They shall also have there rights of use in the wood in all respects for the benefit of their own house, and common pasture throughout all the boundaries of Trois-Fontaines for all their livestock; and the monks of Trois-Fontaines likewise throughout all their boundaries and for all their livestock. So that this might not through the passing of time or the perversity of any person either be changed or lost, we have confirmed it with the impression of our seal.

[Col. 0476A] Done in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1150.

## XIV. Letter of Peter the Venerable to R., Prior of St. Benedict’s.—He permits the election of an abbot. (About 1150.)

[MARTENE, same work, col. 408.]

To our venerable and beloved brethren, R., prior, and the others serving God at St. [Note: [Col. 0476D] That is, at the monastery of St. Benedict on the Po, whose subjection to Cluny Pope Honorius II confirmed in a letter to the Cluniacs.] Benedict’s: Brother P., humble Abbot of Cluny, greeting and blessing from the Lord.

We have seen the letters of your affection and heard the messengers announcing to us the death of your lord Abbot William. In them we also read that you request from us permission, favor, and blessing to elect an abbot able to govern your monastery in honor and religious observance and, with the Lord’s help, advance it to better things in temporal as well as spiritual matters.

To this we reply that those who came with Lord Abbot Honestus and his companion, whom you sent to us, showed us the privileges of certain Roman pontiffs; and we read them in part in their presence: namely, those of Pope Gregory VII, Urban II, Paschal II, Gelasius II, Calixtus II, Honorius II, and Lucius II. In them is clearly contained the manner in which, on the death of your abbot, you ought to proceed to the election of another abbot. If you observe this manner in your election, as is fitting, we willingly grant it to you, as is just. And we not only wish but earnestly urge you to proceed in the Lord’s name to make such an election.

But if perhaps, as we learned from your aforesaid delegates, you possess a command of our venerable father, Lord Pope Eugenius, or another decree containing something which we have never seen or received, we in no respect oppose his will, command, or decree, nor do we hinder you in any respect from fulfilling his precept or order. May the Spirit of counsel and fear of the Lord be with you now and always. Amen.

## XV. Letter of Peter, Abbot of Cluny, to R., Abbot of Moissac.—He commands the brethren of Blessed Mary of the Golden Church to render justice to the canons of St. Stephen of Toulouse. (About 1150.)

[MARTENE, same work, col. 409, from the cartulary of St. Stephen of Toulouse.]

[Col. 0476D]

To the venerable and beloved brother Lord R., Abbot of Moissac: Brother P., Abbot of Cluny, greeting and affection.

The provost of St. Stephen’s, the see of Toulouse, would have made complaint in council against the brethren of St. Mary of the Golden Church, had we not restrained him by promising him justice concerning the brethren of the aforesaid place. We therefore command you to cause those brethren to submit with the canons to a judgment of justice, and to ensure that what the equity of judgment shall dictate is observed and carried out, so that there may be no grounds on which they can rightly make complaint. For we promised them this, and we wish and command it to be done thus.

## XVI. Letter of Peter, Abbot of Cluny, concerning the fellowship established between the monks of Cluny and Reichenbach. (Year uncertain.)

[MARTENE, cited above, from a Reichenbach manuscript.]

To all brethren of the holy Church of Cluny established throughout the world: Brother PETER, Abbot of Cluny, greeting, grace, and blessing.

The devout and well-known reputation for proven religious observance of Lord Natalis, Abbot of Reichenbach, persuaded us to incorporate him and his community into our community—that is, the Cluniac community—and ours into the Reichenbach community, by a certain bond of familiar prayers within the bowels of Christ. Know therefore that we have granted him and his brethren a chapter in all our houses; and when the notice of the death of any of the Reichenbach brethren comes to us, he shall receive a general mass and office in the community. Lord Natalis himself, and his successors, shall hold chapter in our houses, sit at the bell in the refectory, and after his death shall receive a thirty-day observance at Cluny. We have decreed that this shall be observed.

## XVII. Letter of Peter, Abbot of Cluny, to the Venetian senators.—For entering into a fellowship of intercessions. (Year uncertain.)

[MABILLON, *Analecta*, folio edition, p. 159.]

[Col. 0477C]

To the most beloved lords, most devoted to us: L. V. D. B. PETER L. and the brothers Basil, brothers by blood; from Brother P. C. F. S., unworthy, with the whole congregation of Cluny: the fullness of every salvation, every goodness, and every blessing.

To God, the inspirer of all good things and the almighty giver of all things, who has inspired in your hearts so devout and most ardent a fervour of charity toward us and our congregation, we render boundless thanks. For when we were at Venice for prayer at blessed Mark’s shrine and to visit the brethren, we are unable to express the generosity of your devotion and service. But since it is altogether inhuman to be unmindful of so great a benefit, to omit other matters, we wish to state and commit to memory how it has pleased your charity to decree and confirm that each year you shall give one hundred pounds of white incense to God and to His blessed Peter and Paul, and to their Church at Cluny, for the remission of your sins.

Accordingly, for the forgiveness of the sins of your deceased relatives, both men and women, we decree that every year, on the day after the feast of the passing of Saint Benedict, a general office with Mass shall be held; Mass shall be sung by all priests, and the remaining brethren shall say psalms according to the custom of our order. Henceforth may almighty God bless you [Col. 0478A] and bring you to eternal life.

## XVIII. Letter of the Same Peter, Abbot of Cluny, to the Carthusians.—On the Same Subject. (Year uncertain.)

[MABILL., *Analect.*, ibid.]

I, Brother PETER, humble abbot of the Cluniac brethren, make known to all who read this what follows.

How marked and renowned the religion of the Carthusian brethren has always been is clear from countless miracles spread abroad throughout the world. For this reason, from the first years of my elevation to this office, and even before, my soul has clung to them; and above all congregations of religious profession, excepting those entrusted to us, I have always loved and revered them. Nor have they returned to us less affection, now already for thirty years, and, wherever it was possible for them, the corresponding service in deed.

Therefore, with the consent of the brethren, it has been decreed by us in the chapter at Cluny that, when a brother of the Carthusian Order dies, an office and Mass for him shall be held at Cluny in the convent. Each priest shall say one Mass; the others shall say seven psalms, or seven times, “Have mercy upon me, O God”; while in the other priories of the Cluniac congregation a public office with Mass shall be performed. It has also been decreed that, after their deaths, their names shall be written after the names of our deceased brethren in the memorial of the dead, both at Cluny and in our other [Col. 0478C] places.

## XIX. Letter of the Carthusians to the Cluniacs. (Year uncertain.)

[MABILL., *Analect.*, ibid.]

We, the unworthy and humble poor of Christ who dwell in the wilderness of Chartreuse for love of the name of Jesus, together with our other provosts and priors and their brethren, make known to posterity what follows.

How greatly Lord Peter, abbot of the Church of Cluny, has loved us from the first years of his elevation, and with what charity he has been bound to us, we ourselves have experienced, and it is manifest to many. The brethren also of that holy congregation, both earlier and later members, have always loved us from the beginning of the house of Chartreuse, have held us in great reverence in Christ Jesus, and have sustained our poverty with many benefits.

Therefore, lest we prove ungrateful for so great affection, in accordance with our measure—for we are few in number—yet so as to offer something according to our ability and custom, after assembling all our provosts and priors and reading the letters which the aforesaid abbot had recently brought, it was decreed and confirmed, by their will, mind, and judgment in the general chapter, as follows. For Lord Peter, abbot of Cluny, when it happens that he dies, in all houses [Col. 0479A] of our order, apart from the anniversary entered in our martyrology, the same and equal office shall be performed as is customarily done for a prior or professed monk. For all the other deceased members of the whole Cluniac Order, besides private prayers, once a year a general office shall be celebrated in convent, both of Mass and of the office for the dead. Each priest shall perform one Mass for those deceased; non-priests shall perform one psalter; lay brothers shall perform three hundred Lord’s Prayers.

> **[Note: Col. 0479B]**
>
> **1.** I have brought together here various formulas of spiritual association, both because most are from distinguished men and in order that, taking occasion from them, I might illuminate the origin, development, and rites of associations of this kind. Although some authors have touched on the matter, they seem to me to have passed over certain points not unworthy of notice; I have therefore judged it worthwhile to discuss them here.
>
> This custom arose from the belief in ecclesiastical communion and from the use of diptychs, which formerly prevailed in sacred rites as a symbol of that communion. They had a twofold order, of the living and the dead, whose names were recited during the sacred rites. On the model of the diptychs, monks devised the necrology, or book concerning the dead, in which were entered the names of brethren, benefactors, [Col. 0479C] and those admitted to the association by agreement. These were recited by name on the day of each month on which they had died, after the reading of the Martyrology and the Rule at Prime. They were said to be enrolled in the Rule, or in the Martyrology, or in the book of life. Hence at Saint Gall they were called “enrolled brethren” (*Fratres conscripti*).
>
> **2.** This rite had already become established among our people from the beginning of the sixth century. Witness the letter of the matron Theodilana, or Theodetrudis, who, because of gifts made to the monastery of Saint-Denis, requested that her name be enrolled in the book of life, in the forty-third year of King Chlothar. Bertchramnus, bishop of Le Mans, asked the same thing in his testament at the same period.
>
> A notable passage on this matter from the same age occurs in Bede’s letter to Bishop Eadfrid and to the community of Lindisfarne monks, prefixed to the prose *Life of Saint Cuthbert*. In place of a small reward, he asks for prayers for himself while living, and further adds:
>
> > “And when I have died, deign, for the redemption of my soul, to pray and offer Masses for me as for one of your household and servants, and to write my name among your own. For you also, most holy bishop, now remember that you promised me this; and, as testimony to the future enrolment, you commanded our religious brother Gudfrid, the steward, to enter my name even now in the roll of your holy congregation.”
>
> Thus, at Charlemagne’s request, Alcuin was admitted by the bishops of the Synod of Frankfurt into communion of intercessory prayers.
>
> **3.** These were associations of individual persons. But when congregations or monasteries first entered into enduring associations of this kind with other bodies is not so clear. I have found nothing earlier on the matter than Letter 24 of Saint Boniface to Abbot Aldherius, in which he asks for prayers for the souls of departed brethren, “whose names,” he says, “the bearer of this letter will show.”
>
> There are two further letters on the same subject among the Bonifacian letters. One is no. 74, from Bishop Cineheard to Lull; the other, no. 84, is from Abbot Dodo of Hornbach to the same Lull, or Lul, archbishop of Mainz. In it Dodo speaks with his congregation of monks of Saint Peter as follows:
>
> > “Accordingly, with the offices of greeting we humbly ask that you always hold this household of Christ and Saint Peter in your remembrance; and that you likewise cause your intercessors in this congregation of Saint Peter to commemorate, to your merit, all your friends—bishops and their clergy, abbots and their monks, abbesses and women dedicated to God—whether living or dead, in their sacred prayers, so that through their intercessions we may one day deserve [Col. 0480C] to enter the desired country of paradise. Likewise we beg you to cause the names of all your friends, both men and the dead, to be sent to us in a brief written list through our brother Saganald, so that, as we do for our other brethren, we may remember them in our unceasing prayers.”
>
> By these letters a spiritual association of prayers was established with the Church of Mainz and with all whom it had admitted into its communion—not merely for the benefit of the dead, but also of the living.
>
> **4.** The *brevia* or *breves* mentioned in the letter were rolls on which the names of associates were sent back and forth by bearers. Haeftenus supplies examples of such *brevia* in volume II of his *Monastic Disquisitions*, p. 793. “General” briefs covered one year—that is, they contained those who had died within a year; but when the difficulty of travel did not prevent it, individual notices were sent for each person. It was customary for monasteries to which such slips [Col. 0480D] were sent to return mournful verses on the death of especially eminent persons; these verses were called *tituli*, as “the *Titulus* of Saint Remigius,” and so forth.
>
> **5.** Thus, from about the eighth century, a communion of prayers of this kind became widespread in churches and monasteries. Such is the agreement, found in volume IV of the *Spicilegium*, made in the twenty-fifth year of Louis the Pious between the monks of Saint-Denis and of Saint-Remi: the agreement provided that such fervour of charity and such strength of affection should remain between them as though they dwelt, if possible, in one place.
>
> It then ordained that, whenever one of them had been freed from the bonds of the body and departed from the world, each of them should complete the whole psalter within thirty days; priests should endeavour to celebrate Masses corresponding to that psalter for him; and they should jointly perform three vigils—on the first, seventh, and thirtieth days—for him. “But if,” they say, “one of them is afflicted with some bodily infirmity, as soon as this is reported to us [Col. 0481B], each of us shall carefully complete five psalms every day until he recovers or departs this life.” Finally, the names of their dead were to be inserted [Col. 0481C] among the names of our dead, so that, as for our own, sacrifice might likewise be offered daily to God for them.
>
> In addition, letters of association made between the monks of Saint Gall and Reichenau in Charlemagne’s time add an annual commemoration of all the dead in place of each individual annual observance—namely on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of December [14 November]. That day is still observed by us, apart from the solemn commemoration of all the dead, which traces its origin to Saint Odilo.
>
> **6.** In the foregoing formulas, roughly the following are performed for each dead person: Masses; vigils or offices for the dead; the recitation of a certain number of psalms for stated days, or of the Lord’s Prayer; and the distribution of rations or provisions to the poor, either daily throughout the whole year or for thirty consecutive days. There is no mention of the Angelic Prayer or greeting—that is, the *Ave Maria*—nor of sacramental communion. For the use of the Angelic Greeting was not yet so widespread, nor was communion on behalf of many persons, which in these times [Col. 0481D] is everywhere accepted.
>
> Why indeed should this not be possible, when the merits of works can be transferred to another? Thus Gregory Nazianzen made a written agreement with Eulalius: Eulalius was to share with him the merit of fasting, and Gregory with Eulalius the merit of silence. Nor should anyone deny that a more abundant share of merit flows back to one who has obtained, by agreement, a communion of intercessory prayers than to another who shares in the same things by the general principle of ecclesiastical communion. In the same way, a person who has obtained another’s prayer merits its efficacy more particularly than one who becomes a participant in that prayer through the unity of the mystical body.
>
> **7.** Such associations were also in use in cathedral churches. We have given above the example of the Church of Mainz. Fulbert, bishop of Chartres, adds another concerning his own Church in Letter 110 to the bishop of Lisieux. In it he urges him to remit the *circadae* in these words:
>
> > “For we desire rather, moved by no small love for your own advantage, that you be numbered in the roll of the blessed order of our benefactors; so that, while offering to the Lord an unceasing sacrifice both for them and for you, and rehearsing your acts of kindness before Him, we may declare you worthy also of enrolment in the book of heavenly life.”
>
> But a particularly striking example occurs in the acts of Aldric, bishop of Le Mans. At the synod of the year 840 he established prayers for himself; and following his example, those attending the synod promised individually to sing twelve Masses with offerings and the other prayers for their fellow brethren within the year. “And whenever,” they say, “any one of us has died, the dean shall bring to our synod at each appointed time a list of the names of his juniors; and each of us shall complete twelve Masses for them, with offerings and the other prayers, and shall faithfully perform for the deceased brethren a vigil with nine psalms and an equal number of lessons and responsories, together with the morning synaxis [what we call Lauds].”
>
> This is in volume III of Baluz’s *Miscellanea*, p. 148. There follow Masses for both the living and the dead, in whose secret [Col. 0482D] prayers mention is made of the diptychs of the living and the dead.
>
> **8.** Finally, one must not omit what I remember reading in letters of association concluded in 927 between the canons of the Church of Laon and the monks of Saint-Remi: namely, that whenever anyone of either congregation, by divine calling, puts off the human person, all, when they hear of it, should at once go to church at the sounding of the bells and together sing the office for the departed; and, as if a brother present there had died, commend his soul to God in prayers. Afterwards they should sing four vigils and the same number of Masses—on the first, third, seventh, and thirtieth days—and all together sing the entire psalter. The brother’s name should also be entered in the catalogue of the dead, to be placed upon the holy altar at the time of sacrifice. These were the diptychs placed before the priest’s eyes during the sacrifice for remembrance.]

.

## XX. Ordinance or Constitution of Peter the Venerable concerning the Monastery of Baume. (Year 1151.)

[MABILL., *Annals of the Benedictines*, vol. VI, p. 500.]

[Col. 0479B]

I, Brother PETER, humble abbot of the brethren of Cluny [Col. 0480A], make known to the same brethren and to all readers the following matters.

The monastery of Baume, founded, as report has it, by Saint Columbanus, persevered for a long time—not only under him, but for a still longer time after him—in the purpose of holy religion undertaken by its holy founder. It displayed such steadfast perseverance in these sacred pursuits that, when monastic observance had previously grown weak at the principal monasteries of Luxeuil and Lérins and indeed throughout almost all Gaul, its fleeting remnants seemed, long afterwards, to have settled in the church of Baume alone, as though driven from their proper seats.

A witness to these things which I say is our holy father Odo, to be named with much love and honour. Having set out from almost the furthest bounds of the West to investigate religious life, he visited many monasteries [Col. 0481A] established in various regions, yet found nowhere for his foot to rest except at Baume. Finding there a place suited to his vows and holy desires, he put off there the old man with his deeds and put on the new man, created according to God.

Subsequently, when William, the great and noble duke of the Aquitanians, selected a valley called Cluny in the diocese of Mâcon to establish a new monastery and assigned its care to Berno, abbot of Baume, the aforesaid Father Odo was advanced from monk to abbot of Cluny. Transferred from Baume to Cluny, he laid the first foundations of the Cluniac Order. Establishing them not on sand but on rock, he himself and the holy fathers of our order who succeeded him raised the building of holiness then begun, as may now be seen, through the grace of almighty God almost to the very heights of heaven.

But so that innumerable examples of this sort might show proud mortals that not merely a human being, but nothing human in the world can be lasting, and that what truthful Scripture says of man is true—“he never remains in the same state”—and that “even the highest are denied long continuance,” the aforesaid monastery of Baume, after a long-established and carefully preserved course of religious life, gradually collapsed by some misfortune unknown to me and fell from the heights to the depths.

I pass over the fall, too well known to persons of our time and too shameful to be transmitted in writing to posterity. To come quickly to the matter for which we have briefly prefaced these things: in my own time, Father Lord Pope Eugenius III unexpectedly entrusted to me the often-named monastery of Baume, a place almost wholly bereft of monastic fervour; and by his letters he both asked and commanded me to devote whatever care I could to reforming it for the better.

He also commanded and further decreed by apostolic privilege that the place of Baume should always be subject to the monastery of Cluny, not under the title of an abbey but of a priory [Col. 0482B]. He did this so that our labour or care bestowed upon that place might more surely [variant: more quickly] and more freely produce the desired fruit, and, with every obstacle removed, might more readily attain its fitting end. Humbert, archbishop of Chrysopolis, who is also called by another name archbishop of Besançon, in whose diocese the place lies, confirmed the same; his entire chapter approved and confirmed it in my presence. This is also attested by a charter preserved at Cluny and sealed with his seal.

Nor was the will and assent lacking of William, count of Burgundy, advocate of that monastery; indeed all was done not merely with his assent but at his instigation. This is shown by a charter preserved in the Cluniac archive and marked with the impression of his seal. I, Brother Peter, humble abbot of the brethren of Cluny, undertaking the governance of this monastery at the command of the aforesaid Lord Pope Eugenius III, with the assent of the archbishop of the Church of Besançon and at the request of Lord Count William, as I have said, laboured much in it; I expended much so that it might advance both spiritually and temporally; and at last, in a short time, by the grace of the Holy Spirit, I transformed an aged mother into a young and beautiful daughter of Cluny, to be adorned increasingly day by day.

Therefore, since, according to one evangelist, the Lord says that “the labourer is worthy of his food,” and according to another, that “the labourer is worthy of his reward,” I would wish, if it pleased almighty God, to receive some fruit of this labour of mine not here but elsewhere, and to have the labour of my hours recompensed with an everlasting reward. I therefore command and decree that on the day when it pleases the Lord for me to enter upon the way of all flesh and to summon me, as I pay the common debt of death, wherever He commands: the prior of Baume, whoever he may be, shall provide a meal for the brethren, both in the convent and in the infirmary, according to the custom of the elders and of solemn entertainments, consisting of good bread and beans, good wine, and the finest and largest fish; or, if the season is suitable, he shall provide meat generously and magnificently for the sick [Col. 0483C].

In addition, I decree that on the same day one hundred poor persons shall be fully fed with bread, wine, and meat; or, on days of public abstinence, with foods appropriate to the season. By God’s grace this is always to be done annually after my death. While I live, however, the aforesaid meal shall be provided without any diminution for brethren and poor persons on the ninth day before the Kalends of November [24 October], that is, on the vigil of the dedication of the greater and new church, which Pope Innocent II, of blessed memory, dedicated in our time at our request and through our efforts.

What shall be done for my soul, whether I am living or dead, on that day is not for me to command, and I establish nothing concerning it, because I leave this to the care and charity of our brethren.

Done in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1151, on the day of the Circumcision of the Lord [1 January], and read in the chapter at Cluny before all the brethren; it was confirmed with their approval.

> **[Note: Col. 0483D]** Frederick the emperor confirmed this constitution of Peter the Venerable by his letters two years later (see below), and after him Pope Adrian IV [Col. 0484D]. Their letters specify the monasteries and churches dependent upon the monastery of Baume.

## XXI. Exemption Granted to the Cluniac Churches of Italy by Peter, Abbot of Cluny. (Year 1154.)

[BALUZ., *Miscellanea*, folio ed., vol. IV, p. 18.]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. In the year from the Incarnation of our Lord Jesus Christ 1154, on the third day [Col. 0484A] of May, in the second indiction.

Since one who presides over any see ought diligently to provide for himself and his subjects—for when the members are weak, the head does not recover—we, Peter, by the grace of God of the holy Church of Cluny, after consultation, remit and, by pardoning, decree for all churches established throughout Italy subject to our jurisdiction that, from now until twelve years have elapsed, neither we nor any successor of ours nor any person of our congregation may exact wax or any exaction from the aforesaid churches, except for the maintenance due to ourselves and our messengers and the annual rent which the prior of Pontida and the prior of Cremona are bound to collect for us.

We also make this arrangement because the aforesaid churches have paid three hundred pounds of old Milanese denarii, less fourteen pounds and five solidi, which we owed in the regions of Lombardy. But if anyone of our congregation should presume to rise against or violate the command of this our decree, the above-named churches shall by no means receive him or spend anything upon him. So that this may be more truly believed, diligently observed by all, and in God’s name obtain fuller force, we have ratified it below with our own hand and ordered it to be distinguished with the impression of our seal and subscribed by certain of our senior fellow brethren.

Done happily in the city of Pavia, in the name of God. Amen.

[Col. 0484C] I, Peter, abbot of Cluny, have subscribed. I, Arnald, abbot of Aurillac, have subscribed. I, Peter, formerly prior of Souvigny, have subscribed. I, Eravizus, chamberlain of Lord Abbot, have subscribed. I, Balchius, prior of Gaïa, have subscribed. There were present as witnesses Simeon of Sagonne, Rufinus son of Georgius Sartor, Laprandus of Rubonibus, William of Genoa, Jacob Castaneus, and Frasso. I, Mignonus, notary of the sacred palace, was present and, at the request of the aforesaid Lord Peter, abbot, wrote this decree.

## XXII. Letter of the Prior of Argon to Peter, Abbot of Cluny. (The Same Year.)

[BALUZ., *Miscellanea*, ibid.]

[Col. 0484D]

To the most holy father Lord P., venerable abbot of C., the prior of the monastery of Argon, together with all his brethren, offers most humble obedience in Christ.

Since, illustrious Father, by the help of divine mercy you are nourished by the promptings of holy thoughts, we beg to be fed daily, not only spiritually but also bodily, from the overflowing bosom of your mercy and compassion. We have therefore thought it not inappropriate briefly, though truthfully, to inform your graciousness concerning the house of the monastery of Quintian.

At the beginning, in obedience to your charitable instruction, we sent you our brother Gisilbert. With God’s favour, though with much sweat, he laboured as if from nothing to such an extent that an honourable service might be had at Cluny. While there obeying God and you, he was much accused by a certain layman before Lord Roland, charges in which we have thus far discovered no truth whatsoever. Lord Roland ordered him to remain at the monastery of Saint Paul.

But that brother, on the pretext of taking counsel on this matter with the prior of Saint Gabriel, went without permission to Cremona [Col. 0486A]. Soon returning from there, he was received according to the Rule. Yet by your command the prior of Pontida placed him under strict custody, to carry a lantern. Therefore, most merciful Father, I and all our brethren, since he renounced the world and received the monastic habit among us, prostrate at your feet, humbly beg your mercy to release him and cause him to return to our cloister. In this the prior of Pontida will not be at all burdened. Farewell.

[Col. 0485]

# DIPLOMAS OF PETER THE VENERABLE.

(*Bibliotheca Cluniacensis*, p. 1395 ff.)

## I. Charter of Ambronay.

[Col. 0485B]

I, Brother PETER, humble abbot of Cluny, wish to make known to all who read this the exchange made between us and the lord abbot and brethren of Ambronay. It has pleased both parties, and has been decreed, for what we believe to be their benefit and ours, that henceforth the men of Ambronay shall possess in perpetuity what we used to hold in the chapel of Chalamont—namely, one-third share—and one vineyard at Ambérieux, two others at Saisiriac, and certain other parcels of land situated there.

They, for their part, grant us in the same way whatever rights they used to have in the chapel of the Father: namely, the entire parochial right, burials, offerings, [Col. 0485C] tithes, and seven sextaries of grain which they used to receive from our threshing-floor. Everything known to belong to rightful exchanges, by reciprocal undertaking, we shall preserve for them and they for us, free from every claim or contradiction. So that this may remain perpetually valid, we have decreed that it be confirmed by both our seal and that of the lord abbot of Ambronay, and that copies be preserved both with us and with them.

## II. Charter of Peter Called the Venerable, Abbot of Cluny, Concerning the Church of Saint Dionysius de Carcere. (Year 1133.)

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. The careful foresight of preceding Fathers, and likewise the diligent sagacity of their prudent care—nurse of peace, friend of concord, providing for the benefit of present and future alike—has instituted, foreseen, and, by God’s inspiration, decreed this: whenever some important action is performed, or a benefit worthy of remembrance is conferred upon those serving God, it should be strengthened by the testimony of letters [Col. 0486B] and the privilege of written documents, so that it may be more firmly committed to memory.

Following the teaching of this divinely promulgated ordinance, I, Brother PETER, abbot of Cluny, approve and grant the salutary transaction solemnly concluded between the most pious king of the Franks Louis, his wife Queen Adelaide, and their sons, and Lord Theobald, prior of Saint-Martin-des-Champs, with the convent: concerning, that is, the Church of Montmartre and the Church of Saint Dionysius de Carcere. So that it may be held more firmly in our own time and in the future, kept inviolate, and preserved valid, I confirm it by this present indissoluble written instrument.

The things which I and the convent grant are these: the church, free, but only in the manner in which our monks had held it; the tithe belonging to that church; vineyards and arable land, with one tenant at Darentiac; and the other appurtenances which those serving God had possessed there. In addition, we grant the church of Saint-Martyr, together with Adam’s vineyards and Morel’s cultivated field, and also the cultivated field which Lord Matthew the prior bought from Warnerius of Port.

Done at Paris, at Saint-Martin-des-Champs, in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1133, in the fourteenth indiction, while Pope Innocent sat in the apostolic see, Louis was king of the Franks, and in the twelfth year of Lord Peter, abbot of Cluny.

## III. Charter of Peter, Abbot of Cluny, concerning the Church at Morsalines.

[Col. 0486D]

To the venerable lord and most dear RICHARD, bishop of Coutances, Brother PETER, humble abbot of Cluny, sends greetings and prayers.

Be it known to your brotherhood that we have confirmed the agreement made between the abbey and monks of Montbourg, and our sons W., prior, and the monks of Saint Cosmas, concerning the church of Morsalines: namely, that the monks of Montbourg shall have and hold two-thirds of the grain tithe from all the land held by the monks of Saint Cosmas at Morsalines; and in acknowledgement they shall annually pay ten Angevin or Rouen solidi to the prior and monks of Saint Cosmas.

The church itself, however, the appointment of the priest, and everything pertaining to the altar and cemetery shall remain freely and peacefully with the prior and monks of Saint Cosmas. In order that this agreement may remain valid and unshaken between them forever, we ask your highness to make them your charter concerning it and confirm their agreement by your authority. [Col. 0487B] May your fatherhood prosper.

## IV. Another Charter of the Same Peter, Abbot, concerning the Same Church.

To the venerable and beloved Lord WILLIAM, abbot [Col. 0488A] of Montbourg, and to the entire convent: Brother P., humble abbot of Cluny, greetings and prayers.

We have seen and heard the letters of our beloved son William, prior of Saint Cosmas. Be it known to your brotherhood that we have confirmed the agreement made between your abbey and the church of Saint Cosmas concerning the church at Morsalines: namely, that you shall have and hold forever two-thirds of the grain tithe from all the land held by the monks of Saint Cosmas at Morsalines, and that in acknowledgement you shall pay ten Angevin or Rouen solidi to the prior of that place.

The church itself, the appointment of the priest, and everything belonging to the altar and cemetery shall remain freely and peacefully with the prior and monks of Saint Cosmas. So that this agreement may remain valid and unshaken forever, we have taken care to send you these present letters fortified by the authority of our seal. Farewell.

[Col. 0487]

# THE NINTH LETTER OF PETER THE VENERABLE, ABBOT OF CLUNY, TO PETER DE JOANNE, AGAINST THOSE WHO SAY THAT CHRIST NEVER OPENLY SAID IN THE GOSPELS THAT HE WAS GOD.

[Col. 0487C]

To the good and peaceable old man, Brother and son PETER: Brother PETER, humble abbot of the Cluniac brethren, sends greetings.

Only a very few days had passed when, as was my custom, I was conversing with you about certain matters not wholly superfluous. By some chance—I know not whence—the discussion turned to the divinity of the Saviour. Since I intended quickly to conclude it, being occupied with other matters, themselves useful, I heard from you, as if in passing, something which I did not receive in passing. You said that you had heard from certain brothers—and, as then seemed to me, from companions themselves attached to my side—that the Saviour nowhere in the Gospels had openly, that is, without veils, called himself God. You added that they had examined, not carelessly but attentively and diligently, the whole course of the Gospel text for this reason, and had nowhere been able to read this.

[Col. 0487D] Although you did not name to me the brothers from whom you had heard these things, nor did I persist in asking who they were, nevertheless, though I am a useless shepherd, I do not wholly fail to know the countenance of my flock. I believe that those who say this are prompted not by weakness of faith, but by love and eagerness to know what they have hitherto not known. For all whom I recall among us as able to treat, examine, or resolve something concerning these or similar matters, I know to be learned; I see them to be practiced; I recognize them to be religious. [Col. 0488C] Far be it from me, therefore, to suspect anything unsound of them, especially in such matters: their learning makes them learned, and the grace which, as I have often experienced, has hitherto not been idle in them, both in faith and in life, is accustomed always to make them cautious.

But since this discussion has arisen concerning a matter more necessary than all others to our salvation, it is right, as it seems to me, to set forth what I think about it, lest perhaps, if what has been heard is neglected, some doubt should arise in certain hearts, as often happens in such matters. It would have been more useful to suppress the matter in silence than, once brought forward publicly, to leave it undiscussed. It is known, nor is it hidden from anyone practiced in such matters, that Satan, the common and public enemy, has always laboured with the utmost exertion and every effort lest the true divinity might be either known or worshipped by mortals; [Col. 0488D] and he has pressed most fiercely, not only in the time of grace, not only in the time of the Mosaic law, but from the very origin of the first human beings, to uproot from human hearts the sincerity of faith.

Hence it came about that before the famous Flood—apart from him who first began to call upon the name of the Lord (Gen. IV), together with a few followers from the same stock—and afterwards down to the times of Moses, except for certain great and renowned patriarchs, knowledge of the highest and true God had already been extinguished among wretched mortals; and the whole world, wrapped in the grim darkness of manifold errors, was dreadful. [Col. 0489A] Then, in the ensuing time, the supreme Majesty, taking pity on its perishing creature, displayed a fuller kindness than usual in giving the Law to the Jews. Yet, having called that people alone to worship of the true Deity, it left all the other nations in the dregs of their already ancient error. At last, no longer restraining its mercies in its anger (Ps. LXXVI), it sent forth its Son, poured out its Spirit, and with most abundant compassion called not merely some nations in part, but whatever peoples exist anywhere, to acknowledge the one God, author and governor of all.

Since that wicked one could not wholly obscure this splendour of truth, either in the first, middle, or last age, he did not cease, as far as he was permitted by the Deity governing all things, to attack it. [Col. 0489B] This is clear before the Saviour’s coming in the persecutions of the prophets, whom the great Apostle himself says endured mockings, beatings, chains, and prisons; were stoned, sawn asunder, tempted, needy, afflicted, and distressed; and died by the sword (Heb. XI). It appears especially from this also: in the days of Christian grace, though strong, he was conquered by One stronger, for he saw his weapons being taken away and his spoils distributed by the victor; yet he roused almost the entire world against those who acknowledged the true Deity.

Thus that most wicked and persistent persecutor sprinkled the surface of the whole earth with the sacred blood not merely of many thousands but of innumerable legions of Christians. [Col. 0489C] Since he did not prevail even thus—or rather, since recognition of the true faith grew much more through so many deaths—he attempted to accomplish by fraternal schism what he could not accomplish by hostile force. For this reason errors of various names and sects, raised up by him, increased, striving to take away the one hope of human salvation. They indeed proceeded by varied and wandering paths, but almost all, turned toward the same end, tended to it: whether with a phantom body, as the Manicheans, or with a real one, as the Arians, they denied the true divinity of Christ.

Satan did not care what people might think about God at any time, provided only that the one true and sole saving Deity should be denied. He showed more clearly than light that this alone was what he sought, and toward this alone he strove, because both before Christ and after him he fought so fiercely and constantly, on behalf of the worship of many false gods and goddesses, against the worshippers of the one true God. [Col. 0489D] In the former he embraced human destruction; in the latter he persecuted human salvation.

He still employs the same cunning. Having occupied almost half the world through the Saracens, he teaches them to proclaim Christ as altogether the best and greatest, while nevertheless utterly denying that he is God. This false plurality of gods, opposed to the true unity of God, which he introduced from Paradise itself by saying to the first human beings, “You shall be as gods” (Gen. III), he seeks to bring to completion at the end, when through that vessel of perdition which he will possess in a singular manner—that is, Antichrist—he “will oppose and exalt himself above everything called God or worshipped, so that he sits in the temple of God, showing himself as though he were God” (II Thess. II).

[Col. 0490A] Truly wretched, and eternally cast away from the face of God, he will through the merit of his long-standing wickedness be hardened like a stone and constricted like a smith’s anvil (Job XLI): so mad and blind that he who, immediately upon being made, said, “I shall be like the Most High” (Isa. XIV), being shortly to be plunged into the immense chaos of the infernal pit, says, “I shall be greater than the Most High.”

To what end is this? That the reader may recognize and retain the true divinity of Christ in Christ all the more certainly and firmly, the more the enemy fears it, persecutes it, and always strives to take it away from Christ’s faithful and servants. For he plainly knows that humanity’s salvation subsists nowhere except in Christ: [Col. 0490B] in his divinity, by which humanity is saved, and in his humanity, through which it is saved. Therefore, as stated, he does not care how exaltedly people may think of Christ, provided that they do not believe him to be the true Son of God and God. For, if divinity is removed from him, what greater salvation could the Son of Man confer upon a human being than any other son of man? Beyond doubt, it would then be not religious but sacrilegious for anyone to place hope of salvation in him who, divinity having been removed, could neither be called Saviour nor have power to save anyone. For, as Scripture says, “Cursed is the man who trusts in man and makes flesh his arm” (Jer. XVII).

With this poison the corrupter of human nature both imbued and infected those modern Saracens of whom I spoke above. He taught them, according to their own understanding, to proclaim Christ as born of a Virgin, sent by God, the Word of God, and the Spirit of God; but he persuaded them that Christ is neither God nor that he died. [Col. 0490C] For the impious one perceived that all other things are believed and preached in vain if faith in Christ’s divinity and death is extinguished in human hearts, and that no salvation then remains to mortals whom neither Christ’s divinity would save nor the mediation of his assumed flesh redeem.

Now, to return to the point for which I prefaced these matters: let authority answer either the doubter or the inquirer whether Christ calls himself God without veils or covering, and where this may be read as written in the Gospels. For it seems to me that those who ask this are chiefly moved by the fact that they do not read in the Gospels Christ calling himself God, speaking either to the disciples or to the Jews, so plainly and solemnly as they frequently hear in the Heptateuch: for example, in Genesis, God speaking to the patriarch Jacob: “I am the Lord God of Abraham your father and the God of Isaac. The land on which you sleep I will give to you and to your seed” (Gen. XXVIII). [Col. 0490D] And again elsewhere: “I am the most mighty God of your father; do not fear, and go down into Egypt, because there I shall make you into a great nation” (Gen. XLVI). And in Exodus: “God spoke,” it says, “all these words: I am the Lord your God, who brought you out of the land of Egypt, from the house of slavery” (Exod. XX). And a little later: “I am the Lord your God, strong and jealous, visiting the iniquity of the fathers upon the children to the third and fourth generation” (Exod. XX); and many similar passages in those books.

Indeed, I judge it superfluous to produce examples and testimonies with which the books of both the Old and New Testament are strewn concerning the true divinity of Christ, because I speak to one who is faithful, learned, and accustomed to these things. [Col. 0491A] Very many such passages are read in prophetic and apostolic writings; moreover, innumerable volumes of Greeks, Latins, and other peoples are found bearing truthful witness to the true divinity of Christ. But the proposed subject prevents their being brought forward, because the present question is not whether Christ is God, but whether he himself said that he is God. If that were the question under debate, as it once was, an immense field of many answers and an ocean of Scriptures overflowing with testimonies to Christ’s true divinity could not, by God’s grace, be lacking to us with little difficulty.

Nor would much labour in these matters be incumbent upon me, even if I were equal to it, since I would not invite the reader to read my own writings on them, but would immediately send him to the great volumes once composed by the Fathers on these subjects. Since this does not at all pertain to the matter at issue, let the discussion return to why the Saviour, as it seems to those whom I mentioned, does not call himself God in the Gospels in the manner in which, as stated above, he calls himself so in the ancient writings. [Col. 0491B] Lest I keep the reader long in suspense, I say this, without prejudice to a truer and clearer judgment.

The prophetic voices very frequently foretold that the Son of God, God, would take flesh from Jewish stock and be born from the holy Virgin at a time ordained before the ages; and they left to posterity in writing what they had foretold. Yet the Jewish mind could not be capable of so great a mystery, of so singular a reality; nor did they perceive that the supreme Majesty either would or could at some time be humbled to these lowly and mortal things. They measured [the text reads *metiti*; read *mensi*] the height of that immeasurable Majesty by the pride of their own hearts, and the fountain of inexhaustible goodness by the hardness implanted in human breasts—not so much by nature as by corrupted nature. [Col. 0491C]

This indeed, this was common both to the Jews and to all proud persons; this obstructed belief in the dispensation whereby God assumed flesh, because they never supposed that God could humble himself so far as to assume human things into himself. Rather, they recoiled from confessing or even thinking this as the greatest impiety. They understood the Christ foretold by the prophets not as God, but as a great king, one who would be far greater, more powerful, wiser, and more just than the other kings of the Jewish nation; who would rule more extensively than all preceding kings; and who, in a manner not divine but human, would reign only on earth, not in heaven and earth, as Lord of all.

The Wisdom of God, already clothed in flesh and not ignorant of this understanding—this opinion of almost that entire nation—condescended to their weak minds. As with the milk of assumed flesh before the solid food of divinity, so it willed gradually, not suddenly or as if unexpectedly, to pour into them knowledge of its true divinity hidden in a human being. [Col. 0491D] And because he was the Sun and that true Light “which enlightens every human being coming into this world” (John I), he did not wish, appearing suddenly in the blaze of immeasurable light, to blind the diseased eyes of mortals. Rather, by interposing the cloud of flesh and setting before them the moderation of his words, he fostered their spiritual sight, so that they might contemplate and in due time clearly see the light of divinity hitherto unknown to mortals.

For that reason, he did not, as he had done in the first age, call himself God at once in that solemn manner when he began to preach. Instead, the physician adapting himself to the sick according to the time, and employing as it were gradual introductions and hints, advanced them step by step from lesser things to greater. [Col. 0492A] He fashioned his words so as both to temper the scandals of unbelievers, as was fitting not only for one truthful but for Truth itself, and to proclaim himself God no less than in the time of the Mosaic law to believers and those capable of understanding.

Thus, according to Matthew, when the Pharisees were assembled, he asked them what they thought concerning Christ, whose son he was. When they answered, “David’s,” he immediately added: “How then does David in the Spirit call him Lord, saying, ‘The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand’? If then David in the Spirit calls him Lord, how is he his son?” (Matt. XXII). But what answer had they to this? The Evangelist does not pass it over: “No one,” he says, “was able to answer him a word” (ibid.).

Do you see, reader, why they could not answer him a word? Here indeed, here what I prefaced shines more clearly than the sun. [Col. 0492B] Do you not plainly see that that nation—apart from a few great persons—never perceived, understood, or believed the Messiah, that is, the Christ promised to it, to be God? The Pharisees just mentioned, though teachers of the Law, could not answer the questions with a word because they had neither perceived nor understood Christ to be God. For in this respect alone, certainly in no other, could Christ, David’s son, be David’s Lord: not because he was human as David was, but because he was God, which David was not.

Human custom yielded before this prerogative, and paternal dignity failed in this one and only Son of God, because he was not only David’s son according to the flesh, but also God’s Son according to divinity—indeed, himself God. The Pharisees, though they often read this in the Law, did not understand it; they could not untie the knot of the proposed question or give any rational answer. For that reason they chose silence; for that reason they could not answer.

[Col. 0492C] Does it not therefore seem to you that Christ confessed himself God in this passage without covering, without veils, as you had proposed? He plainly confessed himself God, yet in such a way that, as stated, he both avoided scandalizing the weak, who were not yet capable of receiving things so exalted, and did not conceal from those able to understand that he was God. For among human beings it was unheard of and still wholly alien to common understanding for anyone mortal to think or believe himself God. This is shown also by the public error under which almost the whole world was for a very long time buried and oppressed.

For although the error mentioned above, once understanding and worship of the one true God had been lost among humans, deified certain human beings after death and wished them both to believe and to be believed to have been gods, it nevertheless believed none of them to be God while he lived, nor wished anyone to believe him so. For Saturn, Jupiter, Mercury, Mars, Juno, Venus, Minerva, and countless other gods and goddesses were not considered gods or goddesses while they lived. [Col. 0492D] After they had been removed from life by various fates, divine honour was offered to them by people far cast away from the face of God.

The reasons why rational human minds could be deceived—or could deceive themselves—by so irrational a folly as to believe so lightly and absurdly that gods were made out of human beings are readily available to diligent readers. Since this does not concern the matter proposed, I pass it over. For it is agreed that while the persons just mentioned lived—not gods, but plagues of humanity—no worship of divinity was paid them by human beings.

Alexander alone is reported, after he had subdued Persians, Medes, and Indians themselves, together with the farthest East, to have rushed into such empty and insane pride that he partly persuaded and partly compelled divine honours to be paid him; and that he put to death certain persons who did not comply but mocked him—such as the philosopher Calisthenes, along with some others—after first torturing them. [Col. 0493A] For, as I have said, the human mind recoiled from this, and has always recoiled: it could not endure persons whom it saw to be human beings being called gods, nor did it judge divine height capable of fitting with human lowliness.

Although, as stated, they believed divinity to be in those persons after their death, they nevertheless could in no way think or believe this while they lived and associated with them. Perhaps this is because the human mind is commonly more inclined, even though mistakenly, to admire or honour absent persons rather than present ones, and dead persons rather than living ones. Present things commonly become cheap among such minds, while absent things are more desired and loved. This disposition existed among the pagans, who lacked the divine Law; nor was it absent from the Jews instructed in that same holy Law.

The Saviour, aware of this, so moderated words commending his Deity to human understandings that, as I have said, in the manner of a wise teacher he made provision for minds of no faith or of little faith, [Col. 0493B] avoiding scandal as was fitting, while withholding nothing concerning the truth of his divinity from clear understandings. This is also plainly indicated by his words at the feast of the Encaenia, that is, the Dedication of the Temple, when, walking in Solomon’s portico, he addressed the Jews.

For then they surrounded him and said: “If you are the Christ, tell us plainly” (John X). He did not immediately answer, “I am the Christ,” but said: “I speak to you, and you do not believe. The works which I do bear witness concerning me” (ibid.). What witness? Witness that he was Christ; witness that he was the Son of God; witness that he was God. For none of these could be separated from another. If he was Christ, necessarily he was also the Son of God; if the Son of God, necessarily God. For Christ, not in the Jewish sense as a mere human being, but in the true and Christian understanding, was at once human being, Son of God, and God. [Col. 0493C] Such had been foretold by the prophets; such had been proclaimed by the apostles. Such he showed himself in the words set forth, and such he undoubtedly declared himself.

It is apparent and clearly proved that he confessed himself Christ when, in answer to the Jews just mentioned saying, “If you are the Christ, tell us plainly,” he replied, “I speak to you, and you do not believe.” Then indeed, although he did not utter the name “Christ,” he gave it to be understood that he was Christ when, as I said, he answered those questioning him, “I speak to you, and you do not believe.” For what else is “I speak to you, and you do not believe,” than “I tell you that I am Christ, and you do not believe”?

The words which follow prove that he was also the Son of God: “The works which I do,” he says, “in the name of my Father” (ibid.). For he would not call God his Father unless he himself were also the Son of God. [Col. 0493D] And the works concerning which he testified, “The works which I do bear witness concerning me,” indicate that he proved himself also to be God. For those works were not human but divine. Or, to put it more clearly, they were not, nor could they be, works of a human being alone, but of God and human being together; and because they were God’s works, they were therefore also the works of the human being.

Christ himself was not one of those concerning whom it is written, “Do not touch my christs [anointed ones]” (Ps. CIV); rather, he was Christ—anointed according to his humanity by God “with the oil of gladness above his fellows” (Ps. XLIV). He was not a son of God as were those of whom it is written, “I have begotten and exalted sons” (Ps. I), nor as those of whom the apostle John says: “Beloved, we are children of God, and it has not yet appeared what we shall be” (I John III). [Col. 0494A] He was not, I say, Son of God as they were by grace, but was Son of God by nature, as the Father himself testified when he cried from heaven: “This is my beloved Son” (Matt. XVII).

And because he was Son of God by nature, he was also God, as certain reasoning compels. For nothing could be begotten or proceed from the Father’s essence unless it was what the Father himself was. Therefore, being begotten from God, he was also God, as undeniable truth compels. The works he performed bore truthful witness to this his divinity. For his works were not like human works; his miracles were not equal to prophetic miracles. They were certainly not equal, because they were far more excellent and greater.

The prophets themselves had indeed performed wonderful works and very many miracles, but as human beings they dispensed what had been granted; doing nothing from themselves, they obtained from God by prayers the things they did. [Col. 0494B] Christ’s works, however, proceeded not from another’s power but from his own power. As one who did nothing by prayer, as though needing another’s help, he bestowed by the power of his majesty everything which he gave mortals as remedies, whether spiritual or bodily.

In this way he distinguished his works or miracles from the works or miracles of other human beings: he not only himself did, as God, what he willed, but also granted to others the power to do the same, as he willed. Thus his works bore witness concerning him that he was Christ, Son of God, and God; and, even while he himself was silent, they proclaimed this no less clearly than if he spoke—to Jews, Gentiles, heaven, and earth alike.

By these and similar words, as stated above, he both most clearly commended the truth of his divinity to those able to understand and moderated those same words in fitting ways, lest a sudden brilliance should darken rather than enlighten the intellectual eyes of the still weak people of that time. [Col. 0494C] The entire following passage indicates the same:

“But you,” he says, “do not believe, because you are not of my sheep. My sheep hear my voice, and I know them, and they follow me; and I give them eternal life, and they shall never perish, and no one shall snatch them from my hand” (John X).

Whose words can these be but God’s? Whose, but his who said through the ancient prophet: “Behold, I myself shall seek my sheep and visit them as a shepherd visits his flock” (Ezek. XXXIV)? Whose voice could say, “I give them eternal life,” but God’s? Whose voice could say, “They shall never perish,” but God’s? Whose voice could say, “No one shall snatch them from my hand,” but God’s? For who can give eternal life to his own except God? Who can save them from perishing eternally except God? Who is so strong that no one can take them from his hand except God?

You see, reader, how clearly under the name of sheep he confesses himself to be that God who gives eternal life to his own, saves them from eternal destruction, and affirms that none of his own can be snatched from his hand—that is, from his power—and that none outside can snatch them away. [Col. 0494D] But continue, and read what remains: “What my Father gave me is greater than all; and no one can snatch anyone from my Father’s hand” (John X). And immediately: “I and the Father are one” (ibid.).

What could he have said more clearly to prove himself true God? If what the Father gave him is greater than all—which he gave, certainly, not by granting it but by begetting—what could have been said more sublime? If no one can snatch it from the Father’s hand, and therefore not from his own either, because he and the Father are one—that is, of one and equal divinity—how or in what manner could he have confessed himself God more openly?

The Jews understood this and professed what they had understood in his words. At first, as if against a blasphemer, they took up stones to stone him. When Jesus answered, “I have shown you many good works from my Father; for which of those works do you stone me?” (ibid.), [Col. 0495A] they answered: “We do not stone you for a good work, but for blasphemy, because you, being a human being, make yourself God” (ibid.).

Then shall a faithful Christian fail to understand what a blaspheming Jew could understand? “We stone you,” they say, “because you, being a human being, make yourself God.” They did not indeed believe—rather, they recoiled from believing—that he was God; nevertheless, they observed and understood that he called himself God. Although he had so clearly confessed himself God that those unbelievers, provoked by those words, took up stones to stone him, he nevertheless provided for the salvation of those among them whom he foreknew would be saved. Discreetly healing their scandal, he reserved himself for one time according to what he had foreseen from eternity, and for another time according to the manner of his Passion, adding these words to what he had said:

“Is it not written in your Law, ‘I said, you are gods’? If he called them gods to whom the word of God came—and Scripture cannot be broken—do you say to him whom the Father sanctified and sent into the world, ‘You blaspheme,’ because I said, ‘I am the Son of God’?” (ibid.).

[Col. 0495B] What are you doing, reader? Do you not see what I have already said often? He set a cloud before those unable to bear so great a splendour. For the time being he restrained them and calmed their mad swelling pride, putting forward what they recognized: that many persons in Holy Scripture are called sons of God by grace. With this covering for the time, he concealed what in its own time he disclosed both to them and to the world: that he was not an adoptive but the natural Son of God.

And lest he appear through fear to have denied what he had above confessed concerning the truth of his own Deity, he repeats and confirms what he had said. For it follows: “If I do not do the works of my Father, do not believe me. But if I do them, even if you are unwilling to believe me, believe the works, so that you may know and believe that the Father is in me and I in the Father” (ibid.). Behold again, he commends both the Father’s works and his own. Behold again, he directs them to attend to their power. He earnestly warns them to recognize the author from the works, and to observe that, since such works could belong to no one but God, he who works such things is God.

[Col. 0495C] But you who read this ought not to forget this purpose; rather, you must firmly retain that I have undertaken, from the words of the Saviour himself, to show his divinity, because of those who said, or might say, that nowhere in the Gospels had he called himself God without covering, without veils. I do not deny that he sometimes veiled his words bearing witness to his true divinity with a rational covering, for the reasons I have set forth. But I say that the covering with which he sometimes seems to veil those words was placed before the eyes not of Christians, if they attend rightly, but of Jews; not of believers, but of unbelievers.

Thus in both ways—whether he prudently conceals these things or presents them without covering—we must believe and understand that he has provided for the salvation of all. In the former case, as stated, he provided lest they should become more darkened by untimely light; in the latter, he openly showed what they ought to think of him. [Col. 0495D] So too, when he came into the region of Caesarea Philippi, he questioned his disciples, saying: “Whom do people say that the Son of Man is?” (Matt. XVI). To this question, the disciples gave various answers concerning what people thought of him. But when he pressed them, requiring not others’ opinion but their confession, Peter gave the answer known to the whole world: according to one Evangelist, “We say that you are the Christ of God” (Luke IX); according to another, “You are Christ, Son of the living God” (Matt. XVI).

Who does not know what he answered such a profession, and with what great praise he commended that faith and its words? Yet he did not say: “What you believe is true; what you confess is true, because I truly am, as you say, the Son of the living God.” Did he therefore say something less, or employ here any covering of words, when he added: “Blessed are you, Simon Barjona, because flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven” (ibid.)? [Col. 0496A] What dull or obtuse-minded person can say that Christ said something less when he declared that confessor blessed because of that confession, and affirmed that he had received this not from flesh and blood but from the heavenly Father, than if he had said, “I am Christ, Son of the living God”?

And what of the words that follow? Did he not likewise bear witness to the truth of his divinity when he added, “You are Peter, and upon this rock I will build my Church, and the gates of hell shall not prevail against it” (ibid.)? When he exalted that profession with such praise, when he foretold that he would build his Church upon it, did he not bear the same testimony to his true divinity as he would have borne had he said, “I truly am Christ, Son of the living God”?

Therefore, let not what is clear even to the slowest minds without veils or covering be called obscure. For here also he openly confessed himself Son of God; and, because Son of God, also God, by the authority and reasoning already set forth.
