For he who was Son of God not by grace but, as I have said, from the very substance of divinity, could be nothing other than God.

[Col. 0496B] Now, that there may be a swift passage to other similar instances, let the Samaritan woman come forward; and let us set out what he professed concerning himself amid the many and very mystical words which, weary from the journey and seated by the well, he exchanged with her. For here every misty darkness departs; here he states without covering what he thinks of himself, or teaches us to think.

For when the woman said: “I know that Messiah is coming, who is called Christ, and when he comes, he will announce all things” (John IV), he added: “I am, the one speaking with you” (ibid.). What more, I ask, could be sought? She had said, “Messiah is coming, who is called Christ”; immediately he said, “I am, the one speaking with you.” Therefore Christ confessed himself to be Christ. And because he was Christ, plainly, according to what has been stated, he was also Son of God and God.

Let also that famous blind man, blind from birth, come forward. Christ restored—indeed, rather gave—him eyes which nature had denied, in the manner known to all. [Col. 0496C] After bodily light had been given him, he was also made a confessor through increased grace and, as the sacred history relates, was cast out. The Gospel continues: “Jesus heard that they had cast him out; and when he found him, he said to him: ‘Do you believe in the Son of God?’” (John IX).

But he, cautious in his own way and wisely provident, did not foolishly answer the eternal Wisdom with which he was speaking: “Who is he, Lord, that I may believe in him?” (ibid.). He immediately deserved to hear: “You have both seen him, and he who speaks with you is he” (ibid.). Behold, plainly, an answer without a veil. Whoever thinks this veiled, what will he judge direct speech to be? “He who speaks with you,” he says, “is he” (ibid.). Who is he? Surely the Son of God, concerning whom he had asked him when he said, “Do you believe in the Son of God?” Behold, again Christ professed himself Son of God openly, clearly, without veils, without covering.

[Col. 0496D] The man formerly blind, then seeing, recognized this; and after the light of the body, with light of mind added, he answered: “I believe, Lord.” And falling down, he worshipped him (ibid.). Who then does not see what the blind man, now seeing, saw? Who does not recognize what he recognized? He recognized the Son of God, and he recognized God also. For he would not otherwise have believed in him unless he understood him to be God; nor would he have worshipped him by falling down, an act belonging only to divine worship.

Nor should this escape the mind: when Christ himself elsewhere said, “My Father works until now, and I work” (John V), the Evangelist adds: “For this reason,” he says, “the Jews sought all the more to kill him, because he not only broke the Sabbath but also called God his Father, making himself equal to God” (ibid.). Hence Father Augustine (*Tractate* 16 on John, ch. 5) says: “Behold, the Jews understand what the Arians do not understand. For the Arians call the Son unequal to the Father, and on that account heresy has been driven from the Church. Behold, those blind men, those killers of Christ, nevertheless understood Christ’s words. They did not understand him to be Christ, nor did they understand him to be the Son of God; yet they understood from those words that such a Son of God was being presented as equal to God.”

[Col. 0497A] Behold, according to the words of the Gospel; behold, according to Augustine’s words: even the Jews noticed this, and for this reason sought to kill him—Christ called God his Father, making himself equal to God. Another did not say this about him; he himself affirmed it about himself. What did he affirm? That God was his Father, and that he was equal to God.

Something similar occurs elsewhere. For when he himself said to the Jews, “Unless you believe that I am, you shall die in your sins” (John VIII), and they answered, “Who are you?” (ibid.), he said: “The Beginning, who also speaks to you” (ibid.), followed by certain further words. To these words the Evangelist adds his own: “They did not know,” he says, “that he was calling the Father God to them” (ibid.). Consequently, he likewise presented himself as Son of God and, according to the reasons written above, also as God.

To these let others equally great, or perhaps greater, be added. In one place, disputing with the Jews, he says: “If I glorify myself, my glory is nothing. It is my Father who glorifies me, whom you say, ‘He is our God’; and you have not known him. But I know him” [Col. 0498D] (John 8). See: here he not only says that his Father is God, but also shows which God he is. For there are, as the great Apostle says—whether he means the false gods of the nations, or great and holy human beings, or expresses both together—“many gods and many lords” (1 Cor. 8); concerning whom the Psalm also says: “The God of gods, the Lord, has spoken” (Ps. 49 [50]); and, “God stood in the assembly of gods” (Ps. 81 [82]); and, “For the Lord, the Most High, is terrible, a great king over all gods” (Ps. 46 [47]); and many similar things in the Scriptures.

From the number of these gods he excludes that God whom he calls his Father, when he says to the Jews concerning him: “Whom you say, ‘He is our God.’” For the God of the Jews is distinguished from all the gods of the nations or lands that then existed or may still exist somewhere [Col. 0499A]. For, says the Jewish Prophet, “All the gods of the nations are demons; but the Lord made the heavens” (Ps. 95 [96]). And in another psalm: “Our God is the God of salvation; and to the Lord, the Lord, belong the issues from death” (Ps. 67 [68]). And: “And now, O Lord, you are our maker; we indeed are clay, and you are our potter, and we are all the works of your hands” (Isa. 64). And, with a verse intervening: “Behold, look: we are all your people” (ibid.). And Elijah says: “O Lord, God of Abraham, Isaac, and Israel. I am your servant, and according to your command I have done all these things” (3 Kings [1 Kings] 18). And he says to the idolatrous king: “Because you sent messengers to consult Beelzebub, the god of Accaron [Ekron], as though there were no God in Israel from whom you might inquire for an oracle, therefore from the bed upon which you have gone up you shall not descend, [Col. 0499B] but you shall surely die” (4 Kings [2 Kings] 1). And when the Lord says to Jeremiah, “I have appointed you a prophet among the nations,” he replies: “Ah, ah, ah, Lord God! Behold, I do not know how to speak, for I am a child” (Jer. 1).

By these and innumerable other testimonies of Scripture it is shown that the God of the Jews alone is the true God and the only God—the one of whom Christ, as has been said, speaks to the Jews: “Whom you say, ‘He is our God.’” Clearly, Christ here calls his Father the one who was then called the God of the Jews, who both then and now is called, and is, the God of all; and by speaking thus he declares himself to be his Son.

But hold firmly in constant memory, reader, what I have often already stated: whenever the Savior calls himself Christ in the Gospels, or praises the declarations of those who confess him, he thereby declares himself the Son of God and God. Likewise, whenever he calls himself the Son of God, he teaches us that he is Christ and God. For Christ is necessarily the Son of God, because human flesh was assumed by that Son of God; and again, the Son of God is God, because, as I have said, he was born from the Father, who was God. By this bond of truth I wish you to understand that, as often as he professed himself either Christ or the Son of God, he professed himself God. Understand, then, that in this manner and for this reason he called himself God when, as was stated above, he said to the Jews: “It is my Father who glorifies me, whom you say, ‘He is our God.’”

For I am on guard against those who say or think that Christ indeed is God, but nowhere in the Gospels plainly professed himself [Col. 0499D] to be God. What he adds a little later, since it is not dissimilar, must now be considered. For I do not know whether Christ anywhere more plainly commended the truth of his divinity than when, after the things set forth above, inserting a few intervening words while the Jews disputed against him, he added: “Your father Abraham rejoiced that he might see my day; and he saw it and was glad” (John 8). But when the Jews were stirred up by this and said, “You are not yet fifty years old, and have you seen Abraham?” (ibid.), he immediately added: “Amen, amen, I say to you: before Abraham came to be, I am” (ibid.).

What could be truer, clearer, or more open for proving his true divinity? He did not yet have fifty years—indeed, not even forty—and he said that he existed before Abraham. But which of all human beings born after Abraham could have existed before Abraham? Surely none. For neither human bodies born after Abraham existed before Abraham, nor could souls joined to bodies, created after Abraham, by any reasoning have existed before Abraham. Nor could Christ’s own flesh, nor the soul joined to that flesh, have existed before Abraham. Therefore, if neither the body or soul of any person arising after Abraham, nor the flesh or soul of Christ himself born after Abraham, could have existed before Abraham, how can that be judged true which Truth affirms with so forceful a mode of declaration: “Amen, amen, I say to you: before Abraham came to be, I am”?

Since I speak now not to Jews, as he did then, but to Christians, it is clearer than light that Christ existed before Abraham not in flesh nor in soul, but in divinity—the divinity by which alone he truly exists not only before Abraham but before every creature [Col. 0500B]. For this is that Wisdom of God which says: “I was established from eternity, and from ancient times, before the earth was made” (Prov. 8).

Yet I say this while preserving that understanding according to which, as Jerome holds, time did not prejudice the mystery of the united man and God: so that, by unity of person, he who had not yet been born of the Virgin Mary was already in him from the beginning of the age. Nevertheless, before he was born of the Virgin Mary or conceived in the Virgin Mary, the Son of God was not substantially human; but by a certain ineffable unity of the mystery, [Col. 0500C] even from eternity he was at once God and man. The same doctor affirms this, after inserting certain words concerning the same matter:

> “Not that Jesus, or Christ, was already born of Mary,” he says, “but because in that one Son of God the unity of person, which was hidden in mystery, was already being set forth. Therefore, according to what precedes, does it not seem to you that Christ said the same thing when he said, ‘Before Abraham came to be, I am,’ as he would have said had he said, ‘I am God’?”

Certainly nothing else—absolutely nothing else. For if, as I stated long before, he had said this so bare and unqualifiedly, just as of old, before assuming man, he said to Moses and certain others: “I am the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob” (Exod. 3)—if, I say, he had said this without any moderation of expression, who among those people could have endured it? For they could then have borne far more patiently an invisible voice wonderfully thundering forth from heaven, or from any other place: “I am God,” whether “the God of your fathers,” “the God of heaven and earth,” or something similar, than a visible man dwelling humbly among proud human beings, if he had called himself God in that manner—if he had disclosed his divinity without a fitting veil of words to people unable to receive it, or rather, to say it more fittingly, had forced upon those who rejected it the food of life.

And if, therefore, he suitably moderated his words, did he for that reason call himself God any less, he who asserted that he existed before Abraham? Let those who doubt these things, then, search—search, I say, the Scriptures more carefully; and both in the passages I have cited and in the many I have passed over in silence, [Col. 0501A] they will find that the Savior frequently called himself Christ, declared himself the Son of God, and, whence all these things arise, plainly proclaimed himself God in the ways I have described.

Did he not plainly declare himself God when, about to raise Lazarus, he said to Martha, who was discouraging the removal of the stone from the tomb: “Did I not tell you that, if you believed, you would see the glory of God?” (John 2 [OCR error for John 11]). Did he not earlier plainly declare himself God when the sisters of Lazarus said through messengers, “Lord, behold, he whom you love is ill,” and he answered: “This illness is not unto death, but for the glory of God, so that the Son of God may be glorified through it” (ibid.)? Did he not plainly declare himself God when, lifting his eyes to heaven, he said: “Father, just as you gave him”—speaking of [Col. 0501B] himself—“power over all flesh, that he may give eternal life to all whom you have given him” (John 17)? For power over all flesh belongs to no one but God, nor does giving eternal life to anyone belong to anyone but God.

Whether this power was given to him by the Father through begetting according to divinity, or conferred upon him according to the humanity he had assumed, he who possesses this power cannot be other than God; he who bestows eternal life upon those given to him cannot be other than God. And what shall I say about the words that follow? “This,” he says, “is eternal life: that they may know you, the only true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent.” He says, “That they may know you and Jesus Christ whom you have sent, the only true God” (ibid.). What more plainly does John his apostle write of him in his Epistle [Col. 0501C] than he himself here says of himself? “We know,” he says, “that the Son of God has come and has given us understanding, that we may know the true God and may be in his true Son. This is the true God and eternal life” (1 John 5).

What further need be sought? Why should there still be disputation after these words have been heard? He calls himself and the Father the only true God; he affirms that himself and the Father are the only true God; he proclaims that himself and the Father are the only true God—not silently, not in someone’s ear, but before all who were present at that sacred and final supper during his mortal life. And what shall be said of the verse placed close by: “And now glorify me, Father, with yourself, with the glory which I had with you before the world existed” [Col. 0501D] (John 17)? As man, he could not have had glory with the Father before the world existed. For before the world existed, man did not exist; therefore, according to the manhood which did not exist, he could not have had glory with the Father. It remains, then, that he had that glory according to the divinity by which he was God, because, as has been said, he could not have had it according to manhood. What, then, do these words indicate him to have been before the world existed? Surely they proclaim him God. Recognize, therefore, from this also that he is God—he of whom it is established that before the world existed he was with God.

Nor should you try to recoil from this sense by invoking that other interpretation according to which the Son is said to have been glorified by the Father before the world existed; that is, foreordained and predestined to be glorified and exalted in his own time—namely, [Col. 0502A] after assuming manhood—by that glorification of which the Apostle speaks: “God gave him the name which is above every name, that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth” (Phil. 2). Although this happened in time, nevertheless, because of the predestination by which what had been predestined necessarily had to occur, he is said and written to have possessed before the world was made that glory which did not yet exist but was to exist. Yet because of this interpretation the former sense is not excluded: Christ both was with the Father before the world existed and was God.

Are not these things that have been said sufficient? Does he not plainly and frequently declare himself God? Does he not plainly and frequently, as befitted one who was human and still mortal among mortals, confess the truth of his own divinity to individuals, to many, to all—to disciples, crowds, and especially to the envious Pharisees who were always slandering him [Col. 0502B]? All these things are said, declared, and affirmed of himself not by a prophet, not by an apostle, not by any other person, but by himself—that is, by the very Word of God, Christ himself, the Son of God himself, God himself.

Let those, therefore, awake and fix their eyes more sharply than usual upon the invisible light, who perhaps, paying insufficient attention and searching the Gospel mysteries too little, said that Christ nowhere openly and without veils declared himself God. For proving that this is not so, perhaps what has been said is sufficient. But let them still hear him himself speaking, and saying at the supper to the disciples what has already been mentioned: “Let not your heart be troubled. You believe in God; believe also in me” (John 14). Let them hear here not my own opinion, but the thought—indeed, the words—of the blessed Father Augustine himself (*Tractate 68 on John*, ch. 14):

> “Lest they fear death as human beings and therefore be troubled,” he says, “he comforts them, declaring himself to be God: ‘You believe in God; believe also in me.’ For it follows that, if you believe in God, you ought also to believe in me. This would not follow if Christ were not God. Believe in God, and believe in him whose nature it is—not robbery—to be equal with God” (Phil. 2).

That is, whether he was God and equal with God, he himself again teaches while already in his Passion: “I adjure you,” says the chief priest, “by the living God, tell us whether you are the Christ, the Son of God.” According to Matthew he answered: “You have said it” (Matt. 2 [OCR error for Matt. 26]); according to Luke: “If I tell you, you will not believe me; and if I question you, you will not answer me, nor let me go” (Luke 22). But according to Mark—whom I have put last for this reason, that he expresses the answer more clearly—he answered: “I am” (Mark 15 [OCR error for Mark 14]).

And according to Matthew it follows: “Nevertheless I say to you: henceforth you will see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of Power and coming on the clouds of heaven”; according to Mark, without even a word changed: “You will see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of the power of God and coming on the clouds of heaven”; but according to Luke thus: [Col. 0503A] “From now on the Son of Man will be seated at the right hand of the power of God.”

When, therefore, you hear that, being adjured by the high priest through God to say whether he himself was Christ, the Son of God, he did not deny it according to two Evangelists, and according to the third openly answered that he was Christ and the Son of God, saying, “I am,” what will you say? Even if all the other testimonies and examples that I have set forth—by which he professed himself Christ, the Son of God, and God—were lacking, would not this, I say, suffice? Would it not fully satisfy both you and anyone else who perhaps doubts about it? For this, as you know, was what you were asking and demanding: where in the Gospels he called himself Christ, where he called himself the Son of God, and especially God. See: you hear him answer the chief priest, who asks whether he himself is Christ, the Son of God, not through veils but openly and without concealment: “I am.” He who answered that he was Christ and the Son of God thereby at the same time professed himself God. For, as I have said often above—and repeat so often lest it escape the mind amid a long discussion—he could not confess himself Christ or the Son of God without confessing himself God. The reason for this has been stated above.

Now attend to the words by which, immediately after saying, “I am,” he confirms himself to be God: “You will see,” he says, “the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of Power and coming on the clouds of heaven.”

What more plainly do the greatest apostles, Peter and Paul, preaching his divinity, write concerning him in their Epistles than he here says of himself [Col. 0503C]? The former says: “Through the resurrection of Jesus Christ, who is at the right hand of God” (1 Pet. 1); and the latter: “Christ Jesus, who died—indeed, who rose again—who is at the right hand of God” (Rom. 8). Mark says likewise: “And the Lord Jesus, after he had spoken to them, was taken up into heaven and sits at the right hand of God” (Mark 16). Did they not say in these words the same thing that he himself said when he declared: “You will see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of Power, and you will see [him] on the clouds of heaven”?

See: what, as I said, he had often avoided earlier for definite reasons, he now does not avoid—the scandal of the Jews. Rather, so that they might fulfill concerning his Passion what they had already conceived, he in some sense provokes them by bearing truthful testimony to his true divinity. For the hour had already come of which, before he was seized and bound, he had said: “This is your hour and the power of darkness” (Luke 22) [Col. 0503D]. Therefore he judged that nothing should now be concealed, nothing of the truth hidden, since on the day after that night he was to be crucified and die, urgently striving to accomplish the thing for which he had come into the world. Standing before the judge Pilate on that same day, he said: “For this I was born, and for this I came into the world, that I might bear testimony to truth” (John 18; *ceritati* in the text, evidently for *veritati*).

He therefore bore testimony to truth when he said what has been stated: “You will see the Son of Man sitting at the right hand of Power and coming on the clouds of heaven.” But to sit at the right hand of Power belongs to whom but God? To come on the clouds of heaven—and this at the end of the world, as elsewhere it is read, “with great power [Col. 0504A] and majesty” (Matt. 24)—belongs to whom but God? Therefore, he who sits at the right hand of Power is God; he who is to come on the clouds of heaven with great power and majesty is God.

Concerning that power and majesty in which he will come to judge the living and the dead, he himself says elsewhere: “For the Father judges no one, but has given all judgment to the Son” (John 5). To these words he adds the reason why judgment was given to him: “That all,” he says, “may honor the Son as they honor the Father” (ibid.). For the Son of God is to be honored as the Father is honored, because, apart from the human substance by which he is man, he is the same as God is. For the Father is God; therefore the Son of God is God—the same as the Father is. Therefore let all honor the Son as they honor the Father: that is, let them believe, understand, and confess him to be God just as they do the Father. All these things, by which he professed himself to be the true God, Christ says of himself, not anyone else of him.

After all these things which, while still mortal, he uttered about himself and by which he taught himself truly to be God, let other things follow, by which, death now conquered and he made immortal, he commends that same divinity which was his before and as it was before, and confirms himself to be the true God. For, entering among the disciples on the very day of his resurrection while the doors were shut, after the double announcement of peace, by which he twice said to them, “Peace be with you” (John 20), he breathed upon them and said: “Receive the Holy Spirit” (ibid.). They could not receive the Holy Spirit unless it were given to them by him. He gave it when he said, “Receive.” But he could not give it unless he were God. For the Holy Spirit is God and can be given only by God. It follows, therefore, that he by whom it could be given is God. He thus taught himself to be God when, as was said, he told the disciples: “Receive the Holy Spirit” [Col. 0504C].

As he gave it while still among them on the day of his resurrection itself, so on the day of Pentecost—that is, the fiftieth day after the resurrection—now established upon the highest throne of divinity, he sent it, as he had promised, far more solemnly and abundantly. He had promised when, in the discourse at the sacred supper, from which I have excerpted certain things above, he said to the same disciples: “When the Paraclete comes, whom I will send to you from the Father, the Spirit of truth” (John 15), and what follows.

[Col. 0504D] Therefore, when he promised that he would send him, because Truth could promise nothing falsely, he professed himself to be God—the one who declared that he would send God. And when he gave him on earth, and when he sent him from heaven as he had said, he testified that he was God. But when he also added: “Whose sins you forgive, they shall be forgiven them” (John 20), how could he more openly profess himself God? For that forgiving sins, or granting to anyone power to forgive sins, belongs to God alone is confessed not only by the Christian but was testified long ago by the unbelieving Jew.

For when Christ said to the sinful woman, “Your sins are forgiven you” (Luke 7), certain of those reclining with him began, as the Evangelist testifies, to say among themselves: “Who is this, who even forgives sins?” [Col. 0505A] (Luke 7). And elsewhere, when he said to the paralytic, “Son, your sins are forgiven you” (Mark 2), certain persons said: “He blasphemes. Who can forgive sins but God alone?” (ibid.). For sins are truly forgiven by him alone against whom alone sins are committed. For however I transgress, I sin against him who forbade sin; I offend against him who commanded me not to offend. Thus come those words of a man who was indeed a great righteous man, but at times also a great sinner. After committing certain grave sins, he speaks repentantly to God: “Against you alone have I sinned and done evil before you” (Ps. 50 [51]).

Therefore, just as it belongs to God alone to punish the sins he has forbidden, so it belongs to him alone to remit both sins and the punishment of sins. When, then, he said to the sinful woman or to the paralytic, “Your sins are forgiven,” he declared himself truly to be God. When, moreover—which is greater—he conferred that same power of forgiving sins upon human beings, he taught himself to be God much more fully. On that same day of Easter, on which he rose, after the things mentioned above, he said to the same disciples according to Luke’s Gospel: “Thus it is written, and thus it was necessary for Christ to suffer and rise from the dead on the third day, and that repentance and remission of sins should be preached in his name among all nations, beginning from Jerusalem” (Luke 24) [Col. 0505B]. For repentance and remission of sins could not truly be preached in his name unless he in whose name it was preached were God, because remission of sins could be bestowed upon sinners only in the name of God.

What shall I say also about those words, so solemn and so splendidly commending his divinity, with which Matthew ends his Gospel and with which I have proposed to end this discourse? “The eleven disciples,” he says, “went into Galilee, to the mountain where Jesus had appointed them; and when they saw him, they worshiped him. But some doubted” (Matt. 16 [OCR error for Matt. 28]). This revelation of himself after the resurrection shines with a certain singular glory more brightly among the others, because none of the others is read to have been predicted by him as this one was. While still about to suffer, he had indeed said to the disciples: “I go, and I come to you” (John 14); and again: “I will see you again” (John 16). But he had not singly foretold any of those visions other than [Col. 0505D] this one; he had not specifically designated any other.

But concerning this one, while already almost in the midst of his Passion, using the testimony of the prophet Zechariah (Zech. 13), he said: “I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep of the flock will be scattered. But after I rise, I will go before you into Galilee” (Mark 14). The angel descending from heaven amid a great earthquake said the same thing to the women who had come to the tomb: “Go quickly and tell his disciples that he has risen; and behold, he goes before you into Galilee. There you will see him, as he told you” (Matt. 28).

Therefore, appearing to those eleven disciples on the mountain in this singular vision, he spoke thus: “All power in heaven and on earth has been given to me” (ibid.). Do you hear? What could he say more plainly to me, to you, or to the world, by which he might bear testimony to his true [Col. 0506A] divinity and prove himself God? “All power in heaven and on earth,” he says, “has been given to me.” Whose voice can this be except his of whom it is written: “The Lord has done whatever he willed in heaven and on earth” (Ps. 134 [135])? For who can have power in heaven and on earth except God? Who can do whatever he has willed in heaven and on earth except God?

But if perhaps you are troubled because he says that this power was given to him, I ask you not to be troubled, for there is a sure reason why this ought not trouble you. If you wish to understand this according to what he is as God, this power was given to him when he was eternally begotten by God the Father. But if you prefer to take it here according to what he is as man—which perhaps ought more readily to be understood here—understand that this power was given to the man because of that ineffable union by which, divinity and humanity coming together into the one person of Christ, just as rational soul and flesh are one human being, so God and man are one Christ [Col. 0506B].

Concerning the power given to that man, you have the words of the Father in the psalm speaking to the Son: “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and the ends of the earth as your possession” (Ps. 2). According to this gift given by God to the man, Christ could say: “All power in heaven and on earth has been given to me.” Choose, then, whichever you prefer. For you can choose nothing that does not mean the same thing. For all power in heaven and on earth was given to Christ either eternally according to divinity or temporally according to humanity. Therefore, in whichever of these ways he says that power in heaven and on earth was given to him, he confesses himself God; he proclaims himself God.

And what follows? “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28). What is clearer than this splendor?

I am astonished, and have often been greatly astonished, that the ancient Arian heretics did not perceive this and could not behold so clear a splendor of truth. For if, aided by the Spirit of God, they had been able to see this alone, they would utterly have driven all the darkness of such a dreadful error from their minds. Nor could those grades which those blind people established within the unity of the Trinity have had place in their hearts, if they had wisely considered these words. For when they said that the Father alone is the true and supreme God, that the Son is less than the Father, that the Holy Spirit is less than the Son—indeed, that the Son and Holy Spirit are creatures—they would neither have believed nor said this if they had recognized that the sum of human salvation cannot consist in the name of any creature [Col. 0506D].

For when does a creature save a creature? When does it snatch one away from death? When does it restore one to life, especially eternal life? “In God,” says David, “we shall do might” (Ps. 59 [60]); and, “Shall not my soul be subject to God?” (Ps. 61 [62]); and, “Our God is the God of salvation” (Ps. 67 [68]). The wretches did not realize that they had become idolaters when, in their view, they joined the names of creatures to the divine name and baptized people after God’s name in the names of created things. They did this by wrongly understanding [Col. 0507A] the saying: “Teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit.” But because it is sacrilege to baptize in a creature’s name, it remains that the Son, like the Father, must be understood as God; it remains that the Holy Spirit also, like the Father and the Son, must without doubt be recognized as God.

Therefore Christ, or the Son of God, confessed himself truly to be God when he commanded all nations to be baptized in the name of the Father and likewise of the Son—that is, of himself—and of the Holy Spirit, saying: “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit.” What is added at the end, “Behold, I am with you unto the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28), no less than the preceding statements declares him himself to be God. For how could he be with his own until the consummation of the age after he ascended into heaven, after he had raised human substance as far as the Father’s throne, unless he were God? For since he ascended he has not been bodily with the disciples, because that substance of flesh could not by its nature exist at the same time in different places.

What else remains, then, if the words of Truth are to be proved true, except that, since he could not be with his disciples according to what he is as man, he has been with them until the consummation of the age according to what he is as God [Col. 0508A]? Therefore, as before, while still about to suffer, so now, no longer to die, he proclaimed himself to be the true God when he said to the disciples: “Behold, I am with you until the consummation of the age.”

Now, dearest brother, of one mind with me and one to whom I have long been joined, publish at the appropriate time to the brothers whom you had heard doubting the matters stated above this letter which I have sent to you indeed, but for the sake of others. Persuade them that Christ not only is the true God—which is clear to them—but also that he has more than once professed himself to be the true God. For this alone was my reason for writing this: not to instruct them that Christ is the true God, since they have no need of that, [Col. 0508B] but to show them that in the Gospel he frequently professed himself to be truly God, in many ways and at different places and times. For I had heard them say that they could nowhere read this without veils and covering. Let them therefore read and understand, search and see that the Lord Jesus in the ways I have set forth frequently called himself Christ, frequently called himself the Son of God, and frequently declared himself God.

[Col. 0507]

# Ninth Treatise of Peter the Venerable, Abbot of Cluny, Against the Jews’ Inveterate Hardness

## Prologue

[Col. 0507C]

I address you—yes, you, I say—O Jews, who to this day deny the Son of God. How long, wretched people, will you refuse to believe the truth? How long will you resist God? How long will you fail to soften hearts of iron? Behold: while nearly the whole world has long acknowledged Christ, you alone do not acknowledge him; while all nations obey him, you alone do not hear him; while every tongue confesses him, you alone deny him; while others see, hear, and understand him, you alone remain blind, deaf, and stony—blind indeed in your eyes, deaf in your ears, stony in your hearts.

Nor is this new in your case. The world reads this everywhere and recites it in frequent reading: God saying to Moses concerning you: “I see that this people is stiff-necked. Leave me, that my wrath may grow hot against them, and that I may destroy them” (Exod. 32). And again to you: “You are a stiff-necked people. Once I shall come down in your midst, and I shall destroy you” (Exod. 33). It reads again your Moses—indeed, ours—rebuking you thus: “I know,” he says to you, “your contentiousness and your exceedingly stubborn neck. While I am still alive and going about with you, you have always acted contentiously against the Lord. How much more when I am dead!” (Deut. 31). It reads also Isaiah, the prophet of singular excellence, to whom God says concerning you: “Make the heart of this people blind, make their ears heavy, and shut their eyes, lest perhaps they see with their eyes, hear with their ears, understand with their heart, turn back, and I heal them” (Isa. 6).

It reads and hears his Stephen, whom your stones, O stony race, first made after Christ a witness of Christ (Acts 7). It certainly reads and hears him, full of the Holy Spirit, reproving in you the spirit of most wicked obstinacy: “You uncircumcised in hearts and ears, you betrayers and murderers, you have always resisted the Holy Spirit, as your fathers also did” (ibid.). But will this be forever? Will you forever, by the deserved penalty of such great hardness, make yourselves a spectacle for the whole world? Come to your senses; come to your senses now; at last return, as another prophet says to you, O transgressors, “to the heart” (Isa. 46).

Return to your heart, at least now, when by the just judgment of the Most High you have fallen not only from heavenly glory but even from that earthly glory which alone you always loved [Col. 0509A]. See fulfilled in your own circumstances what Christ, whom you deny, said to your fathers and foretold concerning you, unless you repent: “The kingdom of God shall be taken from you and given to a nation producing its fruits” (Matt. 21). Therefore, since the heavenly kingdom has been taken away, and since for a long time now the earthly kingdom itself has been taken away, acknowledge by what guilt of impiety this has befallen you.

Acknowledge that the cause of so dreadful a condemnation is this: the Christ whose coming you sang, read of, and proclaimed so long beforehand, you did not recognize when he came; you did not receive him; you did not worship him. Rather, in your detestable manner, you despised him, mocked him, and killed him. But what then? If you resolve to turn back, do not be afraid because you killed him. He is not eager to avenge his death if the correction of your conversion follows [Col. 0509B]. Once, hanging upon the cross according to the humanity he assumed, he prayed for those very people who crucified him (Luke 23); and he not only prayed while he suffered, but after he rose from death he forgave those same people when they had repented and been converted.

He did not forget that he had endured death for the life of humankind; and those whom he had as mockers and killers, once converted he received with ready, truly most abundant divine compassion—compassion surpassing every human being. That same boundless generosity will not fail you; nor will that grace which gathered almost the whole world exclude your small number from the number of those to be saved, if you do not reject it. Believe your own Law, not one foreign to you; believe the prophets, not foreign prophets but yours; believe the Scriptures, not foreign Scriptures but your own.

Why does at least this not move you? Why does this not move you: that the whole strength of Christian faith, that the entire hope of human salvation, takes its origin from your writings? Why does it not move you that we have received the patriarchs, the prophets who foretold, the apostles who preached, the most exalted and superheavenly Virgin, mother of Christ, and Christ himself, the author of our salvation—who was also called by your prophet “the expectation of the nations” (Gen. 49)—not from barbarian peoples, nor from just any nations, but as descending from your race, from the stock of great Abraham? [Col. 0509C]

I therefore refer you back to men of your own race; I refer you back to the Scriptures which you received from God; and from these I offer testimonies to which any Jewish contention, however great, is compelled to yield. Yet I do not deny that in one respect you agree with us, while in most respects you obstinately disagree. You agree with us in affirming that Christ was foretold in many ways and by many means by the prophets. You disagree in that you do not believe him to be the Son of God, deny that he is God, assert that he will reign temporally after the manner of other kings, and affirm not that he has already come but that he is yet to come. Therefore, in the order in which they have been proposed by us against you, the chapters already stated must now be pursued.

## Chapter One. That Christ Is the Son of God

Hear, then, O Jews, and from your own Scriptures acknowledge that Christ—or, in your terminology, the Messiah—is the Son of God. Come first, Isaiah, most eminent of prophets, and again set forth your words to a people which believed the truth neither in your time nor in ours [Col. 0510A]. Tell what God said concerning the eternal generation of his Son: “Shall I, who cause others to bear, not myself bear?” says the Lord. “Shall I, who grant generation to others, be barren?” says the Lord (Isa. 66).

What could be clearer, O Jews, for proving the generation of the Son of God? For if God begot, then, with respect to the one whom he begot, he is necessarily Father; and the Son of God, with respect to the one who begot him, is necessarily Son. Yet I neither wish nor believe that you are so foolish and senseless as to attempt to compare the eternal generation of the Godhead with fleshly generation by any, even slight, resemblance. Far be such an asinine conception from you; far from every understanding be the thought of comparing in any manner the eternal, ineffable, inconceivable generation of the omnipotent Father—the birth of the omnipotent Son—with any earthly or customary generation or birth!

Nevertheless, if anything resembling bodily generations may be drawn from such an ineffable matter, the Son of God is said to be begotten of God as light from light, a ray from the sun, brightness from fire. I have said this briefly, O Jews, lest you should understand—or suppose that we understand—the birth of the Son of God absurdly or brutishly. Hence this prophetic testimony compels you to understand and confess Christ as the Son of God, not according to what he is as man, but according to what he is as God. For it belongs to no human being, no angel, indeed to no creature whatever, that he should be understood as begotten by God or as Son of God in respect to the nature of deity. And if this belongs to no creature insofar as it is a creature, it belongs only to Christ, who, insofar as he is God, was born of God [Col. 0510C].

But let clearer examples follow this testimony which has been brought forward, so that it may be shown more plainly than the sun that Christ is the Son of God. Speak, David, prophet of God, king of what was then God’s people, father according to the flesh of the Son of God. Say whether you understand Christ to be the Son of God: “I,” he says, “have been appointed king by him over Zion, his holy mountain” (Ps. 2). Say also what follows: “The Lord said to me: You are my Son; today I have begotten you” (ibid.).

What do you say to this, O Jews? Behold, speaking in Christ’s person, when he says that Christ himself was appointed king by God, he confesses Christ, proclaims him anointed, and affirms him to be human [Col. 0510D]. When he adds that God said to him, “You are my Son; today I have begotten you,” he indicates his divinity, by which he is naturally the Son of God. But you deny it; you mock it. You say that these words apply not to Christ nor to anyone else, but only to David himself, who was formerly appointed king by God over your Zion, over the Jerusalemite mountain, formerly holy.

You say that the same David is called son by God, and called begotten, not because he truly was the Son of God or begotten by God, but because, pleasing him by holy conduct and many virtues, he deserved to be honored with this name. Yet this sense and interpretation do not escape us, O Jews: although not here, we often read elsewhere that people are called sons by God. We know that this was said to Pharaoh concerning your fathers: “Israel is my firstborn son. Let my son go, that he may sacrifice to me” (Exod. 1). And according to one of the prophets: “Israel is a child, and I loved him; and from Egypt I called my son” (Hos. 10).

Although this was said more particularly in the prophetic voice concerning our Lord, who as man fled from Herod into Egypt and in due time was called thence by God the Father, it is nevertheless understood also of the people from whom you derive your fleshly descent. That people, once increased in Egypt from a few fathers into a great people, long resident there and grievously oppressed, cried to God, was heard, was called out from there, and was honored by God with the name of son. And, suitably concerning you, according to Isaiah: “I have begotten and exalted sons, but they have despised me” (Isa. 1).

Nor does that interpretation escape us: not only are human beings called sons of God or begotten by God through some grace or merit, but even insensible things are designated by such names. Thus: “Who is the father of rain, or who begot the drops of dew?” (Job 38). Again: “From whose womb came ice, and who begot the frost from heaven?” (ibid.) [Col. 0511B]

Do not, then, do not suppose, O Jews, that the Church of God could not have seen matters so clear as these. It sees them; it distinguishes them. It distinguishes that similar names in unlike things must be understood differently, and that terms having the same sound need not always be understood in one and the same manner. You have this in innumerable examples from your Scriptures: the same names do not always signify the same thing. And when could these be brought forward individually? But let some be presented by way of illustration, so that many more may easily be inferred from these few.

Certainly “head,” “eye,” “ear,” “hand,” “arm,” and “foot” are names properly signifying certain bodily parts; yet these same terms are often transferred to signify other and different things. “To stand,” “to sit,” “to lie,” “to sleep,” “to wake,” “to walk,” and “to fly” are verbs properly designating some accident or state; yet these too are transferred to signify other different things. Since these matters are clear even to the moderately educated, they need no examples.

In this way, therefore, when the name “generation” is understood of God, it does not always signify the same thing, but sometimes denotes things far different. The prophetic testimonies I have set forward clearly show this, teaching that “generation” signifies very different things [Col. 0511D]. Does not the generation of which it is written, “I have begotten and exalted sons, but they have despised me,” seem different to you, O Jew, from that of which it is said, “Who is the father of rain, or who begot the drops of dew?”—or from that of which we read, “From whose womb came ice, and who begot the frost from heaven?”

I suppose you have not become so deaf, nor so senseless, that what is clear to all should be obscure to you alone, that what is light to all should be darkness to you alone. For it is plain to everyone that there is a great, not slight; certain, not ambiguous difference in the meaning of the term “generation” in these sayings. God is said to beget people by loving, cherishing, advancing, and saving them; he is said to beget rain, drops of dew, ice, and frost by willing, creating, bringing forth, and establishing them.

Therefore, just as you now see, I think, that in this one word “generation” such varied and distinct things are signified, so, once the old darkness has been wiped away from your eyes, behold in the same word something else, far more sublime [Col. 0512A]. Behold, I say, and consider what you can see only if God reveals it; and in those words which you read, “The Lord said to me: You are my Son; today I have begotten you,” understand neither this generation nor the other already mentioned, but the natural birth of the Son of God from the essence of the Father.

For just as the omnipotent Creator is called father of rain and is said to have begotten drops, ice, and frost by bringing them forth; just as he is called father of Israel and is said to have begotten sons by cherishing them: so he is written to be Father of his only-begotten Son, and is proclaimed to have begotten him—not from elsewhere, not from nothing, but by bringing him forth from his own substance. To believe this, O Jews, although only the Spirit of that same Father and Son can draw you to it, yet if you accord sacred Scriptures the deference due to them, and do not obstinately resist them in your Jewish manner, you will at least yield to the following reasoning.

For what follows? “Ask of me, and I will give you the nations as your inheritance, and the ends of the earth as your possession” (Ps. 2). Behold: if you can, apply this to that David who once reigned over the Jews. He was commanded to ask that the nations be given him as an inheritance and the ends of the earth as a possession. And because he was commanded, we must not suppose that he disobeyed. Therefore he asked, and, as had been stated, nations were given to him as an inheritance and the ends of the earth as a possession.

But what nations? Perhaps, according to you, the Philistines, of whom it is written: “David took the bridle of tribute from the hand of the Philistines” (2 Kings 8). Perhaps your opinion may also include Syria adjoining Damascus, of which we read: “The Syria of Damascus was serving David under tribute” (ibid.). Perhaps, according to your tortuous interpretation, the sons of Ammon, or certain surrounding nations whom he is recorded to have subdued in war (2 Kings 10). But reread and diligently search your *Malachim* [Books of Kings], and you will find that David indeed checked the Philistines but did not subjugate them; that Syrian Damascus served him for a time (2 Kings 21 and 23), but after not much time had elapsed rebelled, and at once proud and very powerful kings succeeded there in Damascus itself; and that the sons of Ammon, or the other peoples whom he had separated, soon recovered their breath (3 Kings 20), and throughout the period during which the Jewish people had kings possessed their own kings down to the Babylonian exile of your fathers (4 Kings 3) [Col. 0512D].

Therefore those words of God were not spoken to that David, because neither these nor any other nations besides the Jews were given him as an inheritance. But what will you say to the final words of this divine verse? For after saying, “I will give you the nations as your inheritance,” he immediately added, “and the ends of the earth as your possession.” “The ends,” he says, “of the earth.” What are the ends of the earth? Are they not where the earth ends and human habitation ceases? These ends of the earth, therefore, were given to that David as a possession. If these ends of the earth were given to David as a possession, then the whole world was given to him as a possession. If this is so, Indians, Persians, Gauls, Germans, Scythians, Africans—and finally whatever peoples the world contains—were given to him as a possession.

Do you still see this thing, so obvious and absurd, unsuitable even to beasts themselves? Why do you not perceive, wretched people, according to the words of our Apostle, that the letter is killing you? (2 Cor. 3). Why do you almost alone in the world not follow the life-giving Spirit? (ibid.) Did that David rule the world, whose kingdom was confined within the rather narrow region of Syria? Seek, therefore, seek another to whom these words of God were spoken and to whom the nations were given for an inheritance, the ends of the earth for a possession. And whom else can you find except Christ? Whom else than the Son of God whom you have hitherto denied?

Him indeed: that Christ, that Son of God, that Jesus, at whose name—whether you wish it or not—every knee bends, in heaven, on earth, and under the earth (Phil. 2); him who says, “All power has been given to me in heaven and on earth” (Matt. 28); him to whom the Father’s voice was addressed: “You are my Son; today I have begotten you” (Ps. 2) [Col. 0513B].

But let the discourse proceed to matters clearer still than these, and let us hear what David himself further understands concerning that Son of God. For he introduces the Lord speaking to a certain lord of his, and saying among other things: “In the splendors of the saints, from the womb, before the morning star, I have begotten you” (Ps. 109). Who is this lord whom another Lord begot before the morning star? Run, O Jews; think, toil, sweat, gnaw your nails; twist and distort this statement also, if you can, and in your manner turn so divine and wondrous a saying into this or that other meaning.

Here indeed you must plant your foot; here you must join battle with us; here you must either answer something reasonable or, as your fathers of old fell silent when Christ put before them the beginning of this psalm, fall silent yourselves. They, as I said, kept quiet when the first verse of the psalm was presented to them; you, perhaps wiser than your fathers, answer this verse of ours if you can: “From the womb, before the morning star, I have begotten you.” Who is this lord of David, begotten before the morning star by another lord of his?

Show me, show me David’s lord, begotten by another lord as has been said, and this before the morning star [Col. 0513D]. Show, at the time these words were uttered, some king, prophet, or great person besides God who was lord of so great a king; and, to include many in brief terms, show someone among Adam’s children from the first Adam down to the last who will be born at the end of the age. Search also, if you wish, the heavenly realm itself; and from the various orders of holy spirits, customarily called angels, find for me a lord of David.

For although certain fathers of earlier times, when angels appeared to them, called them “lords,” angels are not lords of human beings, nor are human beings subject to their dominion in the dignity of their nature, since they were created equal to angels. If, then, no angel rules any human being in this manner, it is clear that no angel is called David’s lord. Nor did God beget angels from a womb; rather, as with other creatures, he created them by his omnipotent will. But concerning this one to whom he speaks, he declares that he did not create him but begot him from the womb.

Since, therefore, this lord of David cannot be found apart from God, either among angelic spirits or in human descent, deny that your psalm is divine, or produce someone whom reason compels us to believe is David’s lord. “Before the morning star,” he says, “I have begotten you.” Behold again your distress; behold again the snare; behold again the pit prepared for your mad blindness to fall into. No way out is open to you here unless you are led out by him “who brings the captive out of the prison-house, who opens and no one shuts, shuts and no one opens” (Rev. 1).

“Before the morning star I have begotten you.” Who is this morning star? If you say that it is the star which, because it shines more brightly than other stars apart from the principal luminaries, and therefore seems to bear a greater light, is called the light-bringer or morning star (*lucifer*), I answer: no human being was created before that morning star. For you know from Moses’ account that on the fourth day it was created with the other stars (Gen. 1); humanity was made afterward, that is, on the sixth day. Thus to no human being did God say, “Before the morning star I have begotten you.”

Nor was this said to any angel, because the reasoning already given compels us to see that it was said only to David’s lord. And no angel, by the same reasoning, is David’s lord. It is established, therefore, that to no angel was it said, “Before the morning star I have begotten you” [Col. 0514B]. But if you say that *Lucifer* is the apostate archangel, concerning whom the prophet Isaiah, taking a comparison from this star, speaks under the name of the Babylonian king—“How have you fallen from heaven, Lucifer, you who rose in the morning?” (Isa. 14)—I answer: before that Lucifer not only was no human being made, but no angel was created either.

For the divine words concerning him in Job are as follows: “He is the beginning of the ways of God” (Job 40). But if he is the beginning of God’s ways—that is, of God’s works—then no work of God was created before him. And if none of God’s works was before him, then to no human being and to no angel did God say, “Before Lucifer I have begotten you.” For I do not think you are so mad as to suppose that God said this concerning the Babylonian king himself, designated by the name Lucifer. The divine utterance would say nothing great if it merely related what everyone knew: that David was begotten before the Babylonian king.

Therefore, O most wretched race of human beings, do you not perceive matters so evident, do you not see things so clear? At last open your eyes, unseal your ears, and be ashamed to appear alone blind in the world, alone deaf among mortals. Do not continue so long to be a spectacle for the world; do not for such prolonged ages make yourselves a byword. Observe that David’s lord could have been none but God; acknowledge that David called his own lord none but God.

And because he first said “Lord” and immediately named another “Lord,” understand that they cannot be one and another except Father and Son [Col. 0515A]. Thus at the beginning of the psalm already mentioned he introduces this Lord, the Father, as speaking to the Lord, the Son, when he says: “The Lord said to my Lord.” For, according to what has preceded, since no lord of David is found among creatures, his Lord must be called none but his Creator. And since the name Creator and the name God signify the same thing, David’s Lord is David’s Creator; David’s Lord is David’s God. Therefore another Lord—certainly himself Creator, certainly God—speaks to this Lord of David, this Creator, this God.

What does he say? “Sit at my right hand.” And to whom could this be said by God except to God? To whom, I say, could God say, “Sit at my right hand,” except to one of such dignity that God could say to him, “Sit at my right hand”? And where could such dignity be found as could be worthy of sitting with Deity? What nature could have such dignity as to merit the throne of deity? Certainly none, O Jews, except the divine nature; and, in Christ alone, the human nature which merited this because of its union with the divine.

If your choice can place anyone other than God in God’s seat—whether from heavenly or earthly creatures—let it name, produce, and show him. But it cannot and will not prevail, for deity admits no equal but God; the throne of deity receives no one but God; none is equal to God the Father except the Son of God, who is himself God with him. Indeed, the Spirit of both is equal to Father and Son; but this voice of the Father is not addressed to him, because he was not begotten by the Father.

But to this one, to whom it was said, “Sit at my right hand,” was also added: “From the womb, before the morning star, I have begotten you” [Col. 0515C]. “From the womb,” he says, so that you may acknowledge him as born not from another’s essence but from God’s own essence. “Before the morning star,” so that you may perceive that his birth preceded every creature. “I have begotten you,” so that you may understand him not as made from some matter, not as created from nothing, but as eternally begotten by the Father.

Behold: whereas in the first part of my fourfold division I had proposed to prove no more of Christ than that he is the Son of God, now, O Jews, by the force of this divine psalm I have proved him God as well. But you will say: “The psalm you have adduced against us and introduced to prove the divinity of your Lord does nothing for your side, and does not help your proposition. For it was written by David not in David’s person, but in the person of Eliezer, Abraham’s servant.”

The sense of the psalm, you say, is this: “The Lord,” that is, God, “said to my lord Abraham: Sit at my right hand.” Abraham’s merit with God was great, O Jews, as we ourselves acknowledge, and his privilege with God was great and manifold. His merit was great because Abraham believed God (Gen. 15); his grace was great because this “was reckoned to him as righteousness” (ibid.). His merit was great because, at God’s command, he stretched out his hand and grasped the sword in order to sacrifice his son; his grace was great when, having been forbidden to kill his son, he heard: “By myself I have sworn, says the Lord, because you have done this thing and have not spared your only-begotten son for my sake, I shall bless you and multiply you as the stars of heaven and as the sand on the shore of the sea” (Gen. 22) [Col. 0516A].

Truly Abraham’s merit with God was great—not merely simple, but manifold; and great indeed, greater than all the gifts bestowed on him by God, was that singular excellence of grace by which he was promised: “In your seed all nations shall be blessed” (ibid.). But was it so great that God commanded him, “Sit at my right hand”? Was it so great that what is peculiar to God, as was said not long ago, became common to God and to a human being? I mean a human being only, such as we know Abraham was—not a human being who is also God, such as we know Christ to be. Was it then to this one, who was nothing more than a human being, that God said, “Sit at my right hand”?

Where is that contemplation of human lowliness—unworthy, as you say, of fellowship with divine majesty—which alone restrains the Jewish heart from believing in Christ? [Col. 0516B] Where is that zeal for God, as our Apostle says, yet not according to knowledge? (Rom. 10). Was it not on account of these words which you ascribe to Abraham that you stoned Stephen, our first martyr—stopping your ears as though at blasphemy, gnashing your teeth as though for vengeance, ever greedy for sacred blood?

What did Stephen say concerning Christ? “I see the heavens opened, and Jesus standing at the right hand of God” (Acts 7). What does the Jew say concerning Abraham? “The Lord,” that is, God, “said to my lord Abraham: Sit at my right hand.” Why was it that you could not endure even once to hear Jesus standing at the right hand of God’s power, yet can now calmly endure to hear every day that Abraham sits at the right hand of God?

Do not, do not, I beg you, make anyone God’s partner except God; do not establish anyone in the divine seat except God. If you grant this—which up to now you have by no means been accustomed to deny—the words allegedly uttered in Eliezer’s person are false: “The Lord,” that is, God, “said to my lord Abraham: Sit at my right hand.” And not only do they show that what has been said is false, but all the following lines of the psalm clearly declare the same thing.

Among them is the verse immediately following: “Until I make your enemies the footstool of your feet” (Ps. 109). “Sit,” God says according to you, “O Abraham, at my right hand, until I make your enemies the footstool of your feet”—that is, until your enemies are subjected to you. What enemies did Abraham have while he lived? Search, O Jew, the whole text of your sacred canon, and, unless I am mistaken, you will be able to find not many enemies of Abraham, but not even one [Col. 0516D].

For although he lived in the land of Gentiles, a righteous man was by his religion, sobriety, and wisdom so good among the wicked, and so peaceable among those who hated peace (Ps. 119), that neither Christian nor Jew has been or will be able to read in the Hebrew canon that he had any enemy. But if you say that with three hundred and eighteen retainers he fought against the kings who had defeated the Sodomites and taken captive Lot, his brother’s son; that he defeated the plunderers, freed Lot, and carried away much spoil from his enemies (Gen. 14), I answer: neither did the kings go to battle because of Abraham, nor did they seize Lot, the son of Abraham’s brother, because of Abraham.

Scripture relates the reason why the kings were roused against kings—namely, four against five—to war: the five kings had served the four for some time, but then, judging the law of slavery shameful, refused to serve. This was the reason why Lot was found among the defeated and taken by the victors; and Lot himself was the reason why Abraham encountered those plunderers. It is clear, therefore, that not even in this way can the Jew find enemies of Abraham, concerning whom he might pretend that God said to him: “Until I make your enemies the footstool of your feet” [Col. 0517A].

And if he cannot find Abraham’s enemies, neither can he expound the third verse of the psalm concerning him: “The Lord will send forth from Zion the rod of your strength” (Ps. 109), and the words allegedly said to him by God: “Rule in the midst of your enemies” (ibid.). But because I am speaking to Jews, I am prevented from touching the marrow of the sacred psalm—which they disdain—and compelled to linger around the useless husk of the letter, which alone they are accustomed to gnaw like beasts.

Tell me, according to your brutish understanding, by what reasoning God said to a kindly and peaceable man, one who is almost always described as unarmed: “The Lord will send forth from Zion the rod of your strength.” How was the rod of Abraham’s strength sent forth by the Lord, when he had no need of it for fighting? How was it said to him by the Lord, “Rule in the midst of your enemies,” when he had none? But I pass on even to the fourth verse: “With you is the beginning.” What is this beginning with Abraham? Is the beginning of heaven and earth with Abraham? Is the beginning of any creatures with Abraham? “In the day of your strength.” What is this day of Abraham’s strength? What is this day in which the beginning is joined to Abraham’s strength?

“In the splendors of the saints, from the womb, before the morning star, I have begotten you.” Who are these splendors of the saints, O Jew, among whom Abraham was begotten before the morning star? But I do not dwell on these nearly ineffable matters, because they are to be expounded, if possible, not by a Christian concerning Christ but by a Jew concerning Abraham. And what follows? “The Lord has sworn and will not repent of it” (ibid.). What has the Lord sworn? What is it that he will not repent of having sworn? “You are,” he says, “a priest forever according to the order of Melchizedek” (ibid.).

Was Abraham a priest? Was Abraham a priest—and forever? Was he priest, forever, and according to the order of Melchizedek? For if Abraham was a priest according to the order of Melchizedek, why, since both were of equal office, equal order, and equal dignity, did he allow himself to be blessed by Melchizedek? Why did Melchizedek offer bread and wine? Why did Abraham give him tithes from everything he had taken? (Gen. 14.) Explain all this concerning Abraham, O Jew, if you can.

But I believe—indeed I know, indeed I affirm—that neither you nor the whole synagogue of Satan gathered together can expound these words, so sacred, so divine, so surpassing every human being, either concerning the human Abraham or concerning any merely human person. Therefore the Jewish interpretation, falsely asserting that these words were spoken by God to Abraham, is false; and the Christian interpretation, affirming that they were spoken by God to a person who is both God and human being, Jesus Christ, is true [Col. 0518A]. To God, I say, and to a human being.

And so that I may stir the Jew more and more, if not to belief, at least to anger, by often saying what he refuses to hear: not merely to a human being and to God, but, as has often been said, to a human being and to God, and at the same time to the Son of God. Why does the Jew flee so greatly from the name “Son of God,” when the pagan confesses it freely and steadfastly? Was not Nebuchadnezzar a pagan? And what does he say as he approaches the door of his furnace? “Did we not cast three bound men into the midst of the fire? Behold,” he says, “the appearance of the fourth is like a Son of God” (Dan. 3).

Behold, a Gentile king proclaims the Son of God, while the Jew denies him. A king without God’s law confesses the Son of God; a man brought up and educated in God’s law disavows and rejects the Son of God. But that Son of God who saved the confessing youths from that Babylonian furnace will without doubt torture his Jewish deniers without end in the infernal furnace [Col. 0518B]. Therefore, whether the Jew denies or confesses, by the authorities already set forth Christ is God; Christ is the Son of God.

But hear now, after what has already been set forth, one further testimony of your Solomon concerning the Son of God. For he says in Proverbs: “Who has ascended into heaven and come down? Who has held the spirit in his hands? Who has bound up the waters as in a garment? Who has raised up all the ends of the earth?” (Prov. 30). Of whom, O Jews, can these words be understood, if not of God? To ascend into heaven and to descend may indeed seem capable of applying either to holy angels or to certain blessed spirits of the saints [Col. 0518C]. But the following words prove that these words are spoken neither of angels nor of spirits of saints. They prove, I say, that this is not said of any spirit whatsoever, nor of any creature, but of God himself, the Creator of all spirits—indeed, of all things—when it is added: “Who has held the spirit in his hands?” For who holds the spirit in his hands—that is, in his power—except he of whom Job says: “Whom did you intend to teach? Was it not him who made breath?” (Job 26). To him surely may be applied: “Who has bound up the waters as in a garment?”—unless it is he of whom, in the same book of Job, we read: “At God’s breath ice is formed, and again the broad waters are poured forth” (Job 37). Of whom could it be said: “Who has raised up all the ends of the earth,” except of him of whom the psalm sings: “You made all the ends of the earth; summer and spring—you formed them” (Ps. 73).

Therefore your Solomon did not conceive or utter these things of just anyone, but only of God. Hear then what follows: “What is his name, or what is the name of his Son, if you know?” (Prov. 30). What are you doing, O Jews? Behold, Solomon seeks the name of God; he seeks, as though ineffable, the name of the Son of God. That wise man would certainly not seek the name of God who has a Son, unless he believed him to be the Father. He would certainly not investigate the name of his Son unless he perceived that there was some Son of God. Thus Solomon perceived what you have not yet perceived; he confessed what you have hitherto denied: both that he is God the Father, whom he testifies to have a Son [Col. 0519A], and that he is his Son, whom, by his inquiry into the name, he confesses to be the Son of God.

What could be clearer than these words? What more splendid than this light? Is it not necessary, O Jews, even from this testimony of Solomon alone, apart from the other testimonies of Scripture pressing upon you, that you confess the Son of God? For no opening for laying snares is open anywhere to you, by which you might attempt to distort this singular title, “Son of God,” into a plural designation, “sons of God.” For the inquiry which Scripture appears to make concerning the name of God and the inquiry concerning the name of the Son of God exclude a plurality of sons of God. For neither the holy angels nor righteous human beings—whom, as stated above, Holy Scripture calls sons of God by a certain outstanding grace—were without proper names where necessary [Col. 0519B], nor were their already bestowed names so concealed that Solomon should marvel at them so greatly and be believed, in his wonder, to investigate them with such diligence as to say: “What is his name, or what is the name of his Son, if you know?”

Nor does any reasoning permit that, after what he so solemnly uttered concerning him when he said, “What is his name?” what follows should be understood of some human being or angel: “Or what is the name of his Son, if you know?” For then an angelic or human name would seem to be made equal to the divine name; then the name of a creature would be said to be made equal to the Creator. But the name of God is above every name, as you know, no less ineffable and no less incomprehensible than God himself. For God is not one thing and his name another; rather, both he himself and his name—that is, the same simple and supreme God—are exalted above all his works [Col. 0519C]. Hence this Scripture, which says, “What is the name of his Son, if you know?” not only proclaims the Son of God, but also demonstrates that he is God. For there is no reason why the name of the Son of God should be sought with equal diligence as the name of God, unless the Son of God himself were also shown to be God. Therefore the name of the Father and the name of the Son, sought with equal sublimity, are taught to possess equal deity as well.

Either then produce for me some other person, O Jews, whom I am compelled by certain authority or reasoning to believe and confess to be—not one among a plurality of sons of God, but—the one Son of God; or receive our Christ, who has been demonstrated by so many authorities and so many arguments to be both God and the Son of God.

## Chapter II. That Christ Is God in a Special Sense

But now that Christ, O Jews, has been proved by the authority of your writings to be the Son of God and God, perhaps you will still persist with your customary perversity and demand that his divinity be shown to you more clearly by other examples. And what, I ask, can be shown more clearly? What in worldly things is clearer than light? What more radiant than the shining sun? Yet to the blind, light itself is night and the sun is darkness. Thus, indeed thus, the brightness of the sacred Scriptures shines upon you in such a way that what illuminates others cannot give light to you, and what shines for others is darkened for you.

For whom, except you, would that most luminous testimony of the divine psalm already set forth—“The Lord said to my Lord, Sit at my right hand,” and the rest—not suffice to establish Christ’s deity? For whom, except you, would Solomon’s splendid statement not suffice to establish Christ’s deity, when, by seeking the name of the Son of God as he seeks that of God himself, he shows that Christ is not only the Son of God but also God? For whom, except you, would reason itself alone not suffice: that because Christ has been shown by sacred authorities to be the Son of God, he has thereby also been proved to be God? And how is this so? Listen.

For if he is the Son of God, he is the Son of God either naturally or merely by designation. But, as I stated above, certain angels and certain human beings were called sons of God merely by designation, not naturally, through some grace or merit: certain angels, as in the book of Job: “One day, when the sons of God came to stand before the Lord” (Job 1); certain human beings, as God speaks through Ezekiel: “I had them, and they bore sons and daughters to me” (Ezek. 24) [Col. 0520B]. But Christ, because it has been proved above that he was begotten before every creature from the very essence of the Father, is naturally the Son of God. And if he is naturally the Son of God, he is certainly nothing other than what the Father is. But the Father is God. Therefore the Son cannot be anything other than God.

For, to draw some example from bodily generation, though it is far from equal: just as one begotten from a human being is human; just as one born from a bird is nothing but a bird; just as light kindled from light is nothing but light; so one born from God is God and nothing but God. Does this reasoning alone not suffice for you? Let, then, other examples from your Scriptures follow the argument; and let plain testimony concerning Christ’s true deity be produced from Moses himself, your lawgiver.

Come forward then, holy Moses—you, I say, the singular friend of God; you whom God himself says that he knows by name; you who were given to the Jews under a veil but are unveiled to us. Come forward, no longer to the people of God but against the enemies of God, and expound to us as well as to them the deity of the Son of God. “The Lord,” he says, “rained upon Sodom and Gomorrah sulphur and fire from the Lord out of heaven” (Gen. 19). Who is this Lord, O Jews, who rains sulphur [Col. 0520D] and fire from heaven from another Lord? You have already heard David say, “The Lord said to my Lord”; hear Moses also say, “The Lord rained from the Lord.”

Do not take refuge in the angels who had gone before, who came to Sodom in the evening, and who in the morning led Lot with his wife and daughters out of Sodom. They had already gone; they had already departed; they had already completed the task for which they were sent. Neither of them can be called Lord, because each is called an angel, each a messenger; each is called not lord but servant. They were sent for ministry: to lead out righteous Lot, to separate him from the ungodly—not to take upon themselves, which did not belong to them, the name of deity or dominion.

Nor are we moved because Lot calls them lords, worships them, and prays to them. It is a human custom that sometimes equals are called “lords” by equals, and superiors by inferiors, as a mark of honour. It was an ancient and remains a modern custom that, apart from that unique worship by which Deity is honoured, people reverence one another in a certain fashion, either with partial supplication or by prostrating the whole body. It is a common custom, hidden from no one, by which people often make mutual prayers for whatever causes and mutually grant one another what is requested. We often read that holy people did this and honoured either appearing angels or one another with such acts of respect. It was in this manner, not in that by which Divinity is worshipped—in this customary human observance of reverence—that Lot worshipped those angels, called them lords [Col. 0521B], and entreated them.

For that they were angels—not God, not lords, but servants—their own words to Lot declare: “We shall destroy this place, because their outcry has grown great before the Lord, who sent us to destroy them” (Gen. 19). Therefore, those sent to destroy the place are certainly not lords but servants of the Lord who sends them. Nevertheless, it is recorded that various injuries or plagues are inflicted on people not only through good angels but also through evil angels. This is proved in the case of Job; it is also proved by those of whom it is written: “He sent upon them the wrath of his indignation: indignation and wrath and tribulation, dispatches through evil angels” (Ps. 77).

Nor does it move us that one of those angels who appeared said: “Behold, I have granted your request even in this matter, not to overthrow the city concerning which you have spoken” (ibid.) [Col. 0521C].
