For here the angel seems, as it were, to exceed the bounds of an angel and assume the person of God, as does the one whom the same Scripture of Genesis introduces as speaking to Abraham: “Behold, the angel of the Lord called from heaven: ‘Abraham, Abraham’” (Gen. 22). And after an intervening verse: “Now I know that you fear God and have not withheld your only son for my sake” (ibid.). Yet Abraham had not withheld his son for the angel’s sake, but for God’s sake. Thus in these words the angel seems either to have assumed the person of God, or God to have spoken in the angel. Perhaps it is the same here. But whether this is so or not, the angels appearing to Lot were, as has been said, angels, not God; servants, not lords; obeying, not commanding; rendering service, not exercising dominion.

From this it is evident that the words “The Lord rained from the Lord” were said of none of them. For angels are not called lords; ministering spirits are not called lords. Rather, he alone, truly and supremely, is called Lord who spoke through Moses to your fathers, O Jews: “Hear, Israel: the Lord your God is one God” (Deut. 6). He is certainly the one God, he the one Lord, of whom our Apostle—though you do not believe him—speaks: “One God, the Father, from whom are all things; and one Lord, Jesus Christ, through whom are all things” (1 Cor. 8).

Your Scripture speaks of this Lord Father and this Lord Son when it says: “The Lord rained from the Lord.” Clearly, the Lord rained from the Lord: the Son from the Father, God from God. As he has it from God that he is God, and as he has it from the Lord that he is Lord, so he has it essentially from him to reward the righteous, punish sinners, glorify the good, and condemn the profane [Col. 0522A]. And this he did then, when he rained sulphur and fire from the Lord out of heaven upon Sodom and Gomorrah.

For such expressions as “to rain,” “to snow,” “to thunder,” and the like do not apply to any creature; they belong to the Creator of creation alone, who makes and brings them forth when he wills and as he wills. The words of the Book of Kings say the same: “The Lord gave voices and rains on that day” (1 Sam. 12). In the Psalms it is likewise read literally: “The Lord thundered from heaven, and the Most High gave his voice” (Ps. 17). And in Exodus: “All the people heard the voices and saw the lamps, and the sound of the trumpet and the smoking mountain” (Exod. 20).

Therefore observe, O Jews, that Christ is called Lord and God in your Scriptures. Do not deny him to be Lord; do not deny him also to be God, lest perhaps, as upon those ungodly men, so upon you blasphemers he rain sulphur and fire from the Lord out of heaven, and what is read in the psalm be fulfilled in you: “He shall rain snares upon sinners: fire and sulphur, and a storm-wind shall be the portion of their cup” (Ps. 10).

But perhaps you will say: “You maintain from the Scriptures that Christ is indeed called Lord, as it seems to you; and you wish to compel us thereby also to confess him as God. But leave aside for a while this title ‘Lord,’ and show from those same Scriptures that he is openly called God as well.” And I shall certainly do so, if I have you as hearers—or rather, if I have you as understanders, which is everything.

[Col. 0522C] Hear then again your David, often named and yet often to be named—indeed, much more ours than yours. He says: “Your throne, O God, is for ever and ever; the sceptre of uprightness is the sceptre of your kingdom. You loved righteousness and hated iniquity; therefore God, your God, anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions” (Ps. 44). Who speaks? According to us, God the Father; according to you, David himself. To whom does he speak? According to us, God the Father to his Son; according to you, David himself to his royal son. But setting aside our interpretation for the present, let the psalm be expounded in accordance with yours. Let it be seen whether these words can apply to King Solomon, to any of his descendants, or to anyone other than Christ.

According to you, then, as has been said, David speaks to his son Solomon or to one of those who follow him: “Your throne, O God, is for ever and ever.” And certainly you may perhaps distort the preceding or following words of the psalm and, in your customary way, twist them toward one or another interpretation. But what will you do with these words? By what sense, what ingenuity, what exceedingly laboured interpretation can you manage to apply these sacred words to any mortal other than Christ? “Your throne,” he says, “O God.” By what reasoning or with what audacity is a human being called God by the prophet?

But you will say: God spoke to Moses, “I have made you a god to Pharaoh” (Exod. 7). And you will add: It is written in the Psalms, “God stood in the assembly of gods; in the midst he judges gods” (Ps. 81). Nor will you omit: “I said, ‘You are gods’” (ibid.). We too, O Jews, know these passages [Col. 0523A]. They are clear and open; they could not have escaped us. Those persons are called gods, not because there was any deity in them, but because by some rulership, dignity, or holiness they had been set by God over certain others. You yourselves know this: they were not called gods by God because they were gods, but because by outstanding grace they had been set above others by God.

But he to whom David speaks is not called God by him in this sense. What follows shows this: “For ever and ever.” “Your throne, O God,” he says, “is for ever and ever.” For the throne of no king and no earthly ruler remains for ever and ever. Contradict this, if you can, and show that the throne of any mortal can remain for ever and ever. But you cannot: nature resists, the world protests, every human being denies it. You must therefore confess that this throne cannot belong to just any king, but only to God himself; and that this God is none other than Christ himself, of whom the discussion is concerned.

For the following words of this verse also make this clear. Without any change of speaker, he addresses the same God: “The sceptre of uprightness is the sceptre of your kingdom.” And immediately: “You loved righteousness and hated iniquity; therefore God, your God, anointed you with the oil of gladness.” If, then, this anointed one is God, Christ is certainly God. For the one whom we call “the anointed one,” whom you call “Messiah,” both we and you plainly call and proclaim Christ. Only the languages differ; the sense of the languages is the same. The sound is twofold; the understanding is one. Therefore this anointed God is Christ, and the anointed one—that is, Christ—is God.

“God,” he says, “your God anointed you.” Take heed, O Jews. He does not call him God once only. He had first called him God when he said, “Your throne, O God.” Now he calls him God again when he says, “God anointed you.” For what follows, “your God,” is now a different grammatical case. The first “God” is vocative; the second is nominative. It is as though he said: “O God, God anointed you.” Do you see that Christ is called God by so great a prophet, not merely once, but twice in two consecutive verses, so clearly and splendidly? Confess, then—though late—Christ as God, whom the greatest of your prophets so radiantly proclaims to be God. And not just any kind of God, but one whose throne, according to that same prophet [Col. 0523D], remains for ever and ever.

But who is that God by whom this God was anointed? For thus I read it: “O God, your God anointed you.” You have acknowledged the anointed God; acknowledge also the anointing God. See, if it may be granted you, what until now you have been unable to see. Observe now at last that one must necessarily be the one who anoints and another the one who is anointed. Yet this one and that one are called God by your prophet. For the one anointed is called God, and the one who anoints is called God. Why do you struggle? No escape is open anywhere. It is your Scripture that is being recited; it is your prophet who speaks—indeed, it is God’s words that he speaks. Therefore be silent, and, hemmed in on every side by divine force, understand at last that the two called God can be no other than Father and Son.

The Father, who, as has been proved, speaks to the Son elsewhere in Scripture: “Today I have begotten you.” The Son, who invokes that same Father, as the Father himself elsewhere says of that Son: “He called upon me: ‘You are my Father’” (Ps. 88) [Col. 0524A]. God the Son was anointed by God the Father; Christ was anointed, not insofar as he is God, but insofar as he is human. For, as concerns the nature of God, nothing can be added to God the Son by God the Father. With regard to the same divine essence, God the Father could confer nothing by giving, since in eternally and ineffably begetting him he bestowed all things at once.

Yet he truly bestowed much, truly gave much, to the human nature assumed by his Son; through that nature, the human being cast away from the face of God, expelled from God’s paradise, and made from a servant into God’s worst enemy, was restored and joined to God. Therefore God Christ was anointed by God the Father insofar as he is human: with oil, not that oil with which kings among you were once anointed, but with the oil of gladness, the oil of grace. By that grace the human being assumed by God was, by that same assumption, made divine; and the whole world was reconciled to God, glorified, and saved. Thus, then—thus, not in Jewish error but in the Christian manner—read, understand, and expound: “Your throne, O God, is for ever and ever,” and, “God, your God, anointed you with the oil of gladness.”

And although these things suffice to prove Christ’s deity even to brutish minds, let there nonetheless come forward either a prophet or a prophetic man: Baruch, the secretary or colleague of the prophet Jeremiah. Let him come, and, though drawing the Spirit from the prophetic heart of Jeremiah rather than from his own, let him, as the prophet’s fellow-priest, declare without veils but openly and clearly what he thinks of Christ’s deity. After many things previously said about God, he certainly adds: “This is our God, and no other shall be reckoned in comparison with him. He discovered every way of instruction and gave it to Jacob his servant, and to Israel his beloved. After these things he was seen upon earth and conversed with human beings” (Bar. 3) [Col. 0524C].

What could be clearer? What more open? He calls God—whom? Him who discovered every way of instruction. What way? Clearly that which he gave to Jacob his servant and Israel beloved by him. And what way of instruction did God give Jacob or Israel, except the commandments which he handed down to your first fathers, except the law which he gave through Moses? This God, indeed, who discovered every way of instruction, who gave it to Israel through the Fathers and especially through Moses, “was seen upon earth and conversed with human beings.” Resolve this; explain it otherwise, if you can: explain how God, who gave the law to Israel through Moses, was seen upon earth; explain how he conversed with human beings.

But perhaps you will reply: God was seen by Jacob and conversed with Jacob when, as Scripture says, a certain man wrestled with him until morning, and Jacob himself said of him: “I saw the Lord face to face, and my soul was saved” (Gen. 32). Perhaps you will say that in this manner God was seen upon earth by many. You will add, I suppose, that God was then seen by people and conversed with them when Moses went up the mountain and was with God forty days, and when God from Mount Sinai sounded forth with a bodily or audible voice to the people stationed below (Exod. 20 and 24).

But, to refute these objections briefly: neither Jacob nor Moses nor the people nor anyone, God himself testifying, could see God. Recall God speaking thus to Moses: “No human being shall see me and live” (Exod. 33). Therefore, if those people lived in the flesh, they could not see God. But I believe that you concede that those of whom we speak lived in the flesh. You must therefore concede that none of them could see God.

They did, however, see certain appearances bearing the person of God; they heard certain voices and bodily sounds, uttered not from the divine essence but by God’s command. For that they did not see God himself, and did not hear the voice of that divine and uncircumscribed essence, is proved not only by what I have already cited—“No human being shall see me and live”—but also by what is read in Exodus concerning the people of Israel: “Go down,” he says to Moses, “and warn the people, lest perhaps they desire to cross the boundaries to see the Lord, and a very great multitude of them perish” (Exod. 19) [Col. 0525B]. And after some words: “But let not the priests and the people cross the boundaries or go up to the Lord, lest perhaps he kill them” (ibid.).

How then can you say, O Jew, that God was then seen upon earth and conversed with human beings, when he so forbade the boundaries to be crossed in order to see him; when he threatened destruction to transgressors; when he said not only concerning the people but also concerning the priests themselves: “Let them not cross the boundaries or go up to the Lord, lest perhaps he kill them”? Therefore he was not then seen upon earth and did not converse with human beings. At what time, then? At what time, except when, according to our Gospel, “the Word was made flesh and dwelt among us” (John 1), and, according to the words of Wisdom written by your Solomon, who says, “My delights are to be with the children of human beings” (Prov. 8)—when the Wisdom of God, clothed in flesh, conversed with the children of human beings?

Then, therefore, truly then—not before and not afterward—that God of yours who discovered every way of instruction, who had given it to Jacob his servant and through Moses to Israel his beloved, was seen upon earth and conversed with human beings [Col. 0525D]. Yet the previously cited statement remains: “No human being shall see me and live.” For the invisible God was not seen upon earth by mortals, he who, according to our Apostle, “was in Christ reconciling the world to himself” (2 Cor. 5); rather, he was truly and without doubt seen upon earth and conversed with human beings according to the human nature which he had put on, by which he had veiled his immeasurable majesty.

This prophetic man therefore calls God the one seen by human beings and conversing among human beings—not an alien God, but his own, yours, and that of all Jews—when he says: “This is our God, and no other shall be reckoned in comparison with him” (Bar. 3).

What more is needed? Do not so many divine testimonies now fully satisfy you that Christ, whom we worship and proclaim, is our God, your God, the God of all? Or do you still wish other testimonies to be produced? They are indeed innumerable and could not be unfolded in a brief work; they would require many volumes. But insofar as the intended brevity allows, after those whom you have heard, hear not only a prophetic man but Isaiah, the greatest of the prophets.

Return to us, great Isaiah, and you who had revealed that Christ is from eternity the Son of God, declare also to the Jews that he is God, born of a virgin upon earth. The Jews indeed are Jews and stony-hearted; and, as you yourself experienced, they are not hearers of the prophets but betrayers and murderers. Yet speak, declare, do what belongs to you, so that the Jews may either believe you and be converted, or, if they refuse to believe, may, according to their psalm, be turned backward and put to shame (Ps. 31) [Col. 0526B]. Your discourse, opening divine mysteries, cannot fail of the best result: if the Jew rejects it, the Christian will hear it; if the small number of unbelievers cast it aside, the countless multitude of the whole world will receive and venerate it.

“For a little child is born to us, a son is given to us” (Isa. 9). What follows? This is common: many little children are born to people, and many sons are given to people by God. “And dominion has been placed upon his shoulder.” This too can belong to many, for many have held and do hold dominion upon earth. “And his name shall be called Wonderful.” Here the little child whom you spoke of, the son whom you named, is separated from the common dominion of others. “Counsellor.” Here too something great and singular is indicated. But continue: “God.” Have you heard, O Jews? This little child who is born, this Son who is given, upon whose shoulder dominion is said to have been placed, who is written to be Wonderful and named Counsellor, is also called God by the prophet.

What more do you seek? What can you even mutter? Be ashamed, wretches, be ashamed; and yield at least to truth so clear and so splendid, since you see that you cannot resist it. Great Isaiah, a great man, a great prophet, filled with God, a friend of God, known to you and known to the world, says this: “The name of the little child shall be called Wonderful, Counsellor, God.” But note what follows: “Mighty.” It is now clear to everyone that he who is God is mighty, the author of strength and the Lord of hosts. But what follows? “Father of the age to come.” Who speaks? The prophet. Where does he speak? Certainly in this life, certainly in this age [Col. 0526D]. What, then, does he mean by saying, “Father of the age to come”? Clearly, not of this age in which he lived and spoke, for that age was present. Therefore he speaks of another age, not the present one: “Father of the age to come.” And what kind of age is that? Certainly one invisible to mortals, certainly eternal. And who can be Father of that age except God?

For since no one can rightly be called Father even of this visible and passing age except God, much less can anyone be called Father of that invisible and eternal age except God alone. It must therefore be believed that he who is called Father of the age to come is also God. But perhaps, by Jewish subtlety, you will say that the little child was called Father of that age in which he was to reign, because he was its king. Since it did not yet exist, it was of course future. Yet even so the Jewish interpretation cannot prevail or stand, for what precedes utterly destroys this understanding. How so? Because he is called God. But you yourselves confess that no earthly king and no temporal ruler either could have been or can be God.

Thus even according to your interpretation it follows that he who is called God is not called by the prophet a temporal king or ruler of this age. If this is true, then “Father of the age to come” is not spoken of this present age. “Prince of peace.” This also can be understood only of God. For any human being may be called a lover of peace, friend of peace, pursuer of peace, son of peace, and the like. But Prince of peace, Father of peace, Author of peace—these can be understood only of God [Col. 0527B]. Turn over the sacred pages, and, unless I am mistaken, you will see that these titles are applied only to God. Since this is true, no one but God is called Prince of peace by the prophet.

He is plainly and certainly called Prince of peace who so ruled over peace that he called it his own and, as something belonging to himself, gave it to his disciples when he was about to suffer and die, saying: “I give you my peace; I leave you my peace” (John 14). He, I say, is truly Prince of peace, who, even after he rose from the dead, appearing to his disciples, solemnly used this same title of peace in his very first utterance, saying: “Peace be with you” (John 20).

Nor are we unaware—though perhaps you are ignorant of it—that the seventy translators, whom your Josephus reports were sent by the high priest Eleazar to King Ptolemy of Egypt to translate the sacred Scriptures from Hebrew into Greek, omitted these six most sublime names of the little child who was born and translated instead, “Angel of great counsel.” But they did this, as authorities both yours and ours relate, lest they cause offence to the king, who already worshipped one God, and lest, by setting before him the deity of the man Christ when he was newly abandoning idolatrous worship and could not penetrate the depth of so great a mystery, they should disturb him rather than instruct him [Col. 0527C].

But whether they did this with that intention or another, what is it to you? If the Greek books do not have those names, the Hebrew books have them. If the Greek does not have them, the Hebrew does. Read Isaiah again, examine these words, and believe not my words but your own writings; yield not to foreign books but to your own.

With these preliminaries, proceed to what follows: “His dominion shall be multiplied” (Isa. IX). Whose dominion? That of the aforesaid little child. What follows? “And there shall be no end of peace.” Here, Jews, plant your feet. What is this dominion, written as destined to be so multiplied that its peace shall have no end? Who is this little child, who is this son, whose dominion is declared not merely extensive, not merely enduring, but moreover eternal? Untie this knot if you can; disentangle the bond of this question. “His dominion shall be multiplied, and there shall be no end of peace.” And what is, or whose is, the throne of so great a dominion? “Upon the throne,” he says, “of David, and upon his kingdom” (ibid.).

Run through and count all the kings from David’s line, from David himself or Solomon his son down to the last kings of Davidic descent—I mean Jehoiachin or Zedekiah. The former, after laying aside his kingdom, voluntarily surrendered himself to the Babylonians (IV Kings XXIV). The latter was captured by military force, had his eyes put out, and was taken captive to Babylon (IV Kings XXV). See whether this Scripture fits any one of them. Certainly, as you see, as is plain, it agrees with none of them. Nor does it fit even the good king Josiah, to whom, as I once heard, some among you dreamingly strive to apply these sacred words already cited. But was Josiah God? Was he the Prince of Peace? Did not the swiftest end follow upon the peace of his kingdom? Did he not himself, reigning for a very short time, perish in the field of Megiddo, slain by Necho, king of Egypt? (IV Kings XXIII.) Did not, upon his death, both his life and the peace of his kingdom come to an end? For after a few years came the devastation of your city, the burning of God’s temple, the captivity of the Jews, and their removal to Babylon.

It is therefore utterly false and foolish to interpret these prophetic words of Josiah. It is altogether ridiculous, intolerable to human ears, to understand of Josiah, or of any king of the Jews or of any nations, things that can be applied only to God and to God Christ. “Upon the throne,” he says, “of David, and upon his kingdom.” What is said finally? “That he may establish it and strengthen it in judgment and justice from henceforth and for ever.” And to whom do these things belong, if not to God? To whom, I say, if not to God, are they fitting? Who indeed can establish the throne of any kingdom, who can strengthen it in judgment and justice for ever? Can a human being? But can one who is not eternal establish the throne of his kingdom for ever? Is it not clear, is it not plain even to the blind, that nothing can be established for ever by anyone except one who is everlasting?

Therefore, since these things cannot be gainsaid, since neither Jew nor gentile nor any Satan can prevail against so luminous a truth, it is certain that the little child marked out by so many divine utterances is God—none other than our Christ. Hence it is established that Christ is true and eternal God. Either give me another little child, another son, of whom all these things can be understood; or, if you cannot—as truly you cannot—you are necessarily compelled to understand this little child, this son, concerning whom so many divine things are written, as none other than Christ our Lord. In accordance with human age he is a little child; in accordance with birth he is a son; yet in this wonderful and unique way: the Son of a Virgin, according to the nature of deity perpetually united to the assumed humanity, he is Wonderful, Counsellor, God, Mighty, Prince of Peace, Father of the age to come. His dominion is continually multiplied by the countless number of all nations; the peace of his kingdom never ends; his throne is established and strengthened, not for many years only, as are those of mortal kings, but for ever, as befits the eternal King.

But I know, Jew, that though pressed by so many and such great authorities, you may be defeated, you may be overwhelmed, yet perhaps still cannot believe. Why is this? Because you are ashamed to believe a man to be God; you blush to confess a man to be God. The condition of human nature seems contemptible in your heart; you judge it unworthy of the name or honor of divine majesty. You contemplate the humility of the one and behold the sublimity of the other. Things so lofty seem to you unable to agree with things so lowly; things so sublime with things so abject—that is, human things with divine. This certainly is the whole reason why you remain unbelieving, why you resist God, why you do not believe even your own Scriptures, which again and again declare Christ to be God.

And do you suppose, foolish man, that the thought of divine sublimity and human humility has escaped Christian wisdom? Truly, I say, before so sublime and ineffable a work of God the Christian stands astonished, nor does he suffice to admire so singular a miracle of deity. But it is one thing to marvel and believe; another to marvel and despise. The Christian marvels and is enlightened; the Jew marvels and is blinded. The Christian marvels and, because of the unique miracle, praises God in a unique manner; the Jew marvels and blasphemes. In his astonishment at so great a thing he does not follow the caution of his prophets, who, knowing and foretelling future things, did not despise them; rather, in marveling and prophesying, they even trembled at them.

These are the words of one of them: “Lord, I heard thy report, and was afraid; I considered thy works, and was terrified” (Hab. III). What did he fear? At what was he terrified? Hear: “Lord, thy work” (ibid.). What work? Perhaps the fabric of the world. But the following words contradict this opinion: “In the midst of the years,” he says, “make it live” (ibid.). And certainly the work of heaven and earth, and of what lies beneath them, had long since been made; it had long since been brought to life according to the fitting distinction of its parts.

There is therefore another work which he here fears and before which he trembles, which he asks to be made alive in the midst of the years. Nor does he merely ask that it be made alive: he also predicts that it will be made known, adding, “In the midst of the years thou shalt make it known” (ibid.). Seek, Jew, what this work can be which the prophet Habakkuk marvels at and so earnestly prays may be fulfilled. Certainly all the miracles and wonderful works formerly done among the Jews had preceded this prophet. None of those which, reading in your Canon, you are accustomed to admire remained still to be done. Either show another work, so wonderful that the prophet ought to have been so concerned for it, whether fulfilled or yet to be fulfilled; or, if you cannot, acknowledge that this work, so fearful and so desirable, was accomplished in the Son of God when, for the salvation of human beings, he assumed human nature.

Because he saw this work to surpass all God’s works, he both marveled and feared. And lest he be thought to have feared through unwillingness or refusal, he also prayed that it might be fulfilled. This plainly is the work which Isaiah, that frequent revealer of God’s secrets, does not fail to call both alien to God and yet a work which God himself would perform: “That he may do his work, his work is alien; that he may perform his work, it is a work strange from him” (Isa. XVIII). For what work of God was so alien to God as that by which man was personally joined to God? That heaven, earth, sea, and all that they contain were created by him was not an alien work to God. That lesser or greater miracles were performed by him at any time was not an alien work from him. But when lowly man was joined to the highest God, then truly, then alone, that work was alien to him.

This also is the work of which Jeremiah says: “How long wilt thou be dissolved in delights, wandering daughter? The Lord shall make a new thing upon the earth” (Jer. XXXI). What new thing? For what is new upon the earth? Solomon says: “There is nothing new upon the earth, nor can anyone say: Behold, this is new” (Eccles. I). What then is this new thing? “A woman,” he says, “shall encompass a man” (Jer. XXXI). If you can, Jew, explain this in a Jewish manner. How can a woman encompass a man so that it is new? If by her hands or arms, this is not new. If a mother is said to encompass with her bodily womb the infant whom she carries, neither is this new. In whatever way a woman may be said to encompass a man, it is plainly not new. Yet, as you see, if the prophetic words are to stand, some woman must so encompass a man that it can be new. Because you cannot find this in human usage, you must have recourse to divine things. You must, I say, have recourse to divine things, and together with me confess him whom the Virgin, conceiving from the Spirit of God alone, carried encompassed in her virginal womb: Emmanuel, whom the Latin calls *Nobiscum Deus*—“God with us”—that is, God made man.

Why say these things? So that, seeing Christians—seeing God’s prophets themselves—fear, marvel at, and venerate this singular work of God, by which God deigned for human beings’ sake to become human, you may cease to be unbelieving and cease to be blasphemous. Let not the fact that the matter is great, beyond you, ineffable and inconceivable, draw you back from faith or recall you from hope of salvation. For, as you hear from your own prophets, that God should become human was indeed an alien work to God, in so far as the difference of natures is concerned; but it was not alien to him to show mercy. For the prophet just cited adds that God, in assuming humanity into himself, ought to have mercy upon humankind. Having said, “In the midst of the years thou shalt make it known” (Hab. III), he adds: “When thou shalt be angry, thou shalt remember mercy” (ibid.).

Why then does it seem to you astonishing even to unbelief that God had mercy on humankind through the human being whom he assumed? See and consider that this work of God, so alien and so strange, did not draw those great men of God away from faith or force them into blasphemy; rather, it raised them in wonder and moved them to devotion. They judged that because of a greater grace God should be loved more and glorified more. They knew that human beings ought not to be scandalized by what makes them more indebted; that they ought not to break forth into insults over what makes them greater debtors.

For what was lacking to divine praise except the assumption of human lowliness? That he was exalted, greatest, omnipotent, was certain; but that he would deign to become humble man, no one except those great men believed. For who could think or suspect that one so great would assume so small a thing, the greatest one a little thing, the eternal one a mortal thing, immeasurable Majesty a human worm, so to speak, into himself, and raise it into God? Since this work surpasses all his works, it ought, above all his works, not to provoke you to anger or blasphemy, but to draw you to more exalted wonder, praise, and glorification of him. This very work of his, as was said, Jew, though it is excellent and foremost among all his works, strangely has moved you to such obstinate unbelief.

Why is a human being moved to scandal because God willed to speak to human beings through a human being? Read Exodus again, and you will find that God spoke with Moses from the bush, or from the flame of the bush (Exod. III). Turn also to the books that follow, and you will find that he often gave answers to those consulting him from the golden mercy-seat which stood between the two cherubim. Nor should it escape your mind that God frequently appeared to the fathers, and frequently spoke, through aerial bodies of angels. Yet neither the bush, nor its flame, nor that golden plate of the mercy-seat, nor an aerial body temporarily assumed by angels, is equal to a human being. As you know, man excels these and all earthly creatures; nor can he for whose sake those things were made, and to whom all things were subjected by God, possibly be inferior or equal to them. If he is neither lesser nor equal, he is certainly greater.

You believe, then, that God could speak to human beings from or through an inferior creature, and do not believe that he willed to speak to those same human beings through a greater one? If he is believed to have given answers to mortals from the bush, the mercy-seat, or senseless air, why is it denied that he spoke to mortals through an assumed rational soul and sentient flesh? And although those bodies from which or through which he spoke were not assumed by him in the way he assumed man—not united to himself as he united human nature eternally, nor deified as he deified the assumed human being—nevertheless, he who was heard from the bush or mercy-seat, he who spoke through an aerial body, himself appeared to human beings through an earthly, sentient, and animate body, and sounded to them with a bodily and audible voice. Be therefore now, Jew, a Jew not by faithless obstinacy but by true confession: since you confess that God spoke to your fathers from or through inferior creatures, confess that the same God both appeared and spoke to human beings through the greater creature which he assumed—that is, human nature.

But perhaps you still suffer scandal and refuse to confess God incarnate, or born of a virgin, lest you be compelled to think him involved in or polluted by the defilements of the human body. You fear that, if you confess him incarnate, you will also be compelled to confess him polluted in the flesh he assumed, whether by bodily defilements, as stated, or by the spiritual defilements of sin. Moreover, you fear appearing blasphemous if you judge, believe, or profess that God labored, hungered, thirsted, wept, finally suffered, died, and was buried. But this fear of yours is foolish; this dread or suspicion is altogether empty.

Not so, not so, Jew: the Christian eye is not so blind, nor does Christian wisdom so lose its understanding, as to believe that the one who cannot be contaminated is defiled by the impurities of human flesh or the crimes of the human soul; that the impassible suffers; that the immortal dies; or that he who is the resurrection of all the dead is buried, as you suppose, according to the common manner of all. It knows, and with the common voice of all Christians confesses, that God, as regards divine majesty, can neither be defiled by the filth of flesh nor polluted by human sins, nor can he be afflicted by the punishments or miseries of condemned nature.

And to show you this more clearly by a comparison drawn from visible things: can the light of the stars themselves, or the daylight of the sun, or the nightly light of the moon, whether shadowed by opposing clouds or made clear by free rays, be defiled when it illuminates any places, however filthy or foul? If a thousand times it should seem to be struck or cut by swords or axes violently swung through empty air, can it be harmed or wounded? Can it be soiled by the touch of something unclean, or feel pain from any cutting of iron? In such a manner the Christian both believes in his heart unto righteousness and confesses with his mouth unto salvation (Rom. X) that the essence of deity can never anywhere be defiled, never anywhere be wounded, never anywhere suffer any torment or pain.

Hence, when the Son of God assumes human flesh with a soul from a virginal womb and thereafter lives among human beings in that human substance, the Christian declares not only that he could not be polluted by any defilements of flesh or spirit, but also affirms that he cleansed both the nature which he assumed and the Virgin from whom he assumed it from every stain of sin. Hence the Christian understands and confesses that God did not hunger with the hungry flesh, nor thirst with the thirsty, nor weep with the weeping, nor suffer with the suffering, nor die with the dying, nor be buried with the buried—not with respect to the unity of one person from diverse substances, but with respect to the property belonging to each substance.

Remove, then, Jew, the stumbling-block of folly from your heart; separate brutish understanding from your mind. The true assumption of human flesh does not obstruct Christ’s true deity; God is not defiled, does not suffer, is not humbled because of the human being assumed; rather, the human being is cleansed, glorified, and exalted because of the God who assumes him—indeed, deifies him. And certainly the matters stated above can suffice to prove to every person except one of stone that Christ is true God.

Nevertheless, so that the impious serpent’s head may not merely be crushed but also buried beneath a great heap of arguments, let Micah also come forward and say what he thinks concerning Christ’s deity. He did not fear the wicked king Ahab, nor through fear or favor toward him did he suppress the truth. Let him now do the same against wicked Jews, and not fear those stones by which stony human beings are accustomed to overwhelm God’s prophets. “And thou,” he says, “Bethlehem Ephratha, art thou small among the thousands of Judah? From thee shall come forth for me one who shall be ruler in Israel” (Mic. V).

Behold, holy prophet: you say that the ruler of Israel will come forth from Bethlehem, that is, will be born in Bethlehem and go forth from there. But there have been many rulers of Israel, and many may still be. Explain this more plainly and distinguish this ruler of Israel from the other rulers of Israel. “And his goings forth,” he says, “are from the beginning, from the days of eternity” (ibid.). What are you doing, Jews? Which of all your kings, which of all Israel’s rulers, can you find whose going forth could be from the beginning, from the days of eternity? For whose going forth can be said to be from the beginning except God’s? Whose days can be called days of eternity except God’s? Without doubt, that one’s going forth is from the beginning, that one’s proceeding is from the days of eternity, whose birth in Bethlehem from a Virgin Mother was temporal, while his origin from God the Father before every creature was eternal.

Indeed, the going forth from the days of eternity belongs to him who speaks under the name of Wisdom in the Book of Wisdom: “From eternity I was ordained, and from of old, before the earth was made. The abysses were not yet, and I was already conceived. The springs of waters had not yet burst forth; the mountains had not yet stood with their heavy mass; before the hills I was brought forth. He had not yet made the earth, and the rivers, and the pivots of the earth’s circle” (Prov. VIII). Therefore the going forth of this Wisdom, this Son of God, who according to the flesh was born in Bethlehem, is according to deity from the Father, from the beginning, from the days of eternity.

But if you Jews have anyone else of whom these things can be said, bring him forth. Yet you have none. Therefore, if you believe your prophet, you must receive this one. After him let David, strong of hand, who for a time seemed to have withdrawn, return; and let him, whom no enemy could ever withstand, now conquer the Jews who have made themselves his enemies. The Philistine yielded and perished when struck by his stone; let the Jew, an enemy worse than the Philistine, yield and perish under the cast of his sacred words.

“God,” he says, “give thy judgment to the king, and thy justice to the king’s son” (Ps. LXXI). Who speaks, Jews? You answer: David. To whom does he speak? To God. Of whom does he speak? Of a king and a king’s son. And who is this one who is both king and king’s son? You answer: Solomon. And you add: “The title of the psalm which you cite indicates this; it reads: ‘A Psalm of David concerning Solomon.’” Therefore, according to you, David in this psalm speaks of Solomon his son.

Let us see, then, whether all things in this psalm agree with Solomon. And, to pass over certain matters that might in some fashion seem capable of being fitted to Solomon by Jewish interpretation, answer this: “And he shall endure with the sun, and before the moon, through generations of generations” (ibid.). In what sense will you apply this to Solomon? How could he endure with the sun when he reigned only forty years? Do you not daily see the sun in the heavens? Do you not acknowledge that Solomon passed away two thousand years ago? Open, open your eyes; and, as I said, look upon the sun in heaven and remember Solomon laid in his tomb. How then did Solomon endure, or how could he endure, with the sun?

Consider also, “and before the moon.” Is not this even more absurd? Was not the moon created not merely before Solomon, but before every human being? Was not Solomon, son of David, born not only after his father but after many generations of mortals? How then did he endure, or does he endure, with the sun; how did he endure, or does he endure, before the moon, through generations of generations? As was said, while the sun still endures, he died long ago; and though the moon already existed, he was born many ages later.

But we need not linger long on matters so clear. Run through the psalm and read, after an intervening verse: “In his days justice shall arise, and abundance of peace” (ibid.). Yet this, in some way, may stand according to you. But how will what follows stand: “until the moon is taken away”? (ibid.) Does not the moon still remain? And did not the abundance that had existed in Solomon’s time in that great kingdom of the Jews perish with him when he died? To learn whether this is true, listen—listen to your own Scripture speaking in the Book of Kings: “In the fifth year of King Rehoboam, Shishak king of Egypt went up against Jerusalem and took the treasures of the house of the Lord and the royal treasures, and carried off everything. He also took the golden shields which Solomon had made, in place of which King Rehoboam made bronze shields” (III Kings XIV).

And lest I seem to have brought forward only one witness from your Canon on this subject, read again your *Dabrehiamim* [Chronicles], and if your hostile eye finds in it anything different from what I have set forth, accuse me of lying. Both books just named report that in the fifth year of Rehoboam’s reign the abundance of Solomonic peace was extinguished. Extinguished, I say, when Shishak king of Egypt invaded Judaea with twelve hundred chariots, sixty thousand horsemen, and an innumerable multitude; extinguished when, with his Libyan, Troglodyte, and Ethiopian army, he captured the fortified cities of Judah; extinguished—or, to speak more mildly, interrupted—when he took away the treasures of the house of the Lord and of the king’s house, and departed with all the things mentioned above as rich spoil into his own kingdom (II Chron. XII).

If these things occurred in the fifth year of Rehoboam, Solomon’s son, then what you wished to apply to Solomon from the truthful psalm is false: “In his days justice shall arise, and abundance of peace, until the moon is taken away.” For justice arose in part before him and especially after him; and the abundance of peace which had gently delighted the Jews in his days was extinguished in the fifth year of Rehoboam his son (III Kings XII). I pass over the secession of the ten tribes from Rehoboam; I pass over the nearly continuous wars between the two kingdoms, which, because Jewish sins had deserved it, had been made twofold from one—namely Judah and Israel. These were continuous, or nearly continuous, from Rehoboam himself, king of Judah, down to Shalmaneser king of the Assyrians, who, lest the strife be prolonged so very long, took captive ten of the twelve tribes of the Hebrew stock.

If these things are true—and no Jewish perversity, however great, can deny that they are true—it is clear to those who see, plain even to the blind, that the prophetic Spirit did not say of that Solomon of yours, “In his days justice shall arise, and abundance of peace.” And since it is plain that this cannot fit that Solomon, read the following verse: “And he shall rule from sea to sea, and from the river to the ends of the earth” (Ps. LXXI). Who cannot see that this cannot apply to Solomon? From what sea to what sea did he rule, whose kingdom was confined within the narrow bounds of Syria?

If you should say that he ruled from the Asphaltic Lake, which in the idiom of your language is called a sea, to that which, with respect to the location of Palestine, is called the western sea and which we call the Tyrrhenian or Mediterranean, you would confine his kingdom within a narrower space than it actually had. For that place lies in the middle of Galilee; and Solomon himself is said to have ruled from the brook of Egypt, which flows beyond that lake at a distance of some days’ journey, as far as the nearer regions of the Mediterranean Sea. Therefore the limit of his kingdom was not from sea to sea. Nor was it from the river to the ends of the earth. For the “ends of the earth” are called the places where the world ends. Yet it is known to all nations that Solomon not only did not rule to the ends of the earth, but reigned over a far more limited tract of land than many kings of the world.

For in ancient times there were countless kings who, though they did not rule over the whole world, exceeded the narrowness of Solomon’s kingdom by the great extent of their own realms. It is therefore clear to all that that Solomon did not rule from sea to sea, nor from the river to the ends of the earth. Proceed from here, and, leaving out only two verses, read the third: “And all kings shall adore him; all nations shall serve him” (ibid.). That Solomon? No, no, no—the world cries out. For I do not say merely that few kings are recorded as having adored Solomon; nowhere are any recorded. That all nations served him need not even be disputed, for it is clearer than the sun that they did not serve him.

Run through the psalm and read, or hear, what follows a few verses later: “May his name be blessed for ever” (ibid.). Whose name? According to you, Solomon’s. Read again the whole sequence of the sacred Scriptures, and you will scarcely, or nowhere, find this or anything similar said of the name of any human being: “May his name be blessed for ever” (ibid.). Scripture is accustomed to say this only of God, only of the name of God, as in: “Blessed be the name of his majesty for ever” (ibid.); “We who live bless the Lord” (ibid.); and “Blessed be the Lord God of Israel, who alone does wonders” (ibid.); along with many similar sayings.

Therefore the words, “May his name be blessed for ever,” must be understood not of that Solomon, a mere human being, but of someone more than human. The following clearly indicates this: “His name endures before the sun.” That is, “May his name be blessed for ever” means, “His name endures before the sun.” Did Solomon’s name endure before the sun? Did Solomon precede the sun? Was he created before it? Was he named before it? Do you see that it is not only impious but blasphemous for anyone to understand these things of Solomon?

Nor let the following little verse escape you: “And in him all tribes of the earth shall be blessed” (ibid.). In whom? In Solomon? We ought not to dwell upon what is so manifest; while I and every disputant remain silent, it is easiest to prove it utterly false. What follows? “All nations shall magnify him” (ibid.). Whom? Solomon? Nor should time be spent here on what is universally known neither to be nor to have been.

Seek therefore, Jews, seek another of whom all these things can be understood, of whom it can plainly be proved that the divine psalm was written. And whom will you find? Certainly none—absolutely none, none even if you could fly with wings to the stars—except Christ our Lord, our God, whether you will or no, also your Lord and your God. Of him these things are written, understood, and proclaimed. How is this so? Because they can be fitted to none except the God-man: not to man alone, nor to God alone, but, as has been said, not separately but jointly to God-man. Yet no one except Christ can be found who is at once God and man.

But the words of the psalm written above can fit no one except the God-man. Therefore they were uttered of none other than Christ. And this must be demonstrated: “God,” he says, “give thy judgment to the king, and thy justice to the king’s son” (ibid.). Therefore he who is the king’s son, as you too confess, is certainly human. Our people indeed understand by the king and the king’s son our Christ: insofar as he is called Son, he is the only Son of God the Father; insofar as he received judgment and justice from God, he is the Son of Man. But for the moment I yield to your interpretation and grant that this was written concerning David’s son. For if it was said of David’s son, it was certainly said of a human being.

Yet it has already been proved that the subsequent matters in the psalm, cited above, cannot be understood of Solomon or of any of David’s sons who succeeded him temporally in the kingdom. Therefore someone must be found who, according to your interpretation by which you expound the first verse of this psalm, is David’s son and of whom not merely part of the psalm but the entire psalm can be expounded. But do not labor; do not vainly torment your heart by seeking false byways. Our Christ exists—our Christ alone, I say—who according to the flesh is David’s son, that is, of David’s stock. For you too call “sons” not only those begotten by their fathers but also those who spring from their lineage after many generations.

In this manner, then, Christ is David’s son, or a human being’s son, and the verse just cited was written of him according to his humanity. There are also certain other things written in the sequence of the same psalm according to the fact that he is human. Since, as I said above, you try to apply them to Solomon, the testimonies already produced exclude and repel you from that interpretation. Because they cannot be understood of any merely human being, they compel you to understand them of Christ, human and God. For truly, insofar as he is God, he endures with the sun, because he has no end; he endures before the moon, because he precedes every creature and nothing is prior to him. In his days justice arose, which justifies all who believe in him; and abundance of peace, which joins the children of peace to the peace that is to come. And this lasts “until the moon is taken away”—that is, until human mutability comes to an end and the eternity of blessed peace succeeds.

He rules from sea to sea because, within the circuit of Ocean which surrounds the whole earth, he rules among all languages and nations, wholly or in part, not only by the power of deity but also through the Christian faith. You yourselves see this; you confirm it with your own eyes and ears. And he rules from the river—certainly none other than the Jordan, from which, beginning his baptism and spreading it among all nations, he has advanced in dominion—to the uttermost ends of the earth. “All kings of the earth adore him” (ibid.), either because “all” is understood synecdochically for the greater part, or because even the kings of the gentiles themselves revere him as, after God, greatest of all. “All nations serve him” (ibid.), because, apart from you—who have been excluded by the Prophet from this name of “nations”—all nations, universally or in part, believe in him, serve him, and obey him.

And his name is blessed for ever—as God’s, as Redeemer’s, as Savior’s—which you yourselves hear daily spoken by every tongue, continually blessed, incessantly celebrated. “His name endures before the sun,” because the name of his deity and majesty precedes every created thing without any beginning. “In him all tribes of the earth shall be blessed,” because those who until Christ were subject to the curse of the first parent deserved through him to be blessed and saved. All nations magnify him—indeed all, certainly all, altogether all, except the Jew. Since the Jew is not among the number of these nations, is excluded from the blessing of all tribes of the earth, and is rejected so as not to deserve to magnify him with all nations.

[Col. 0537D] Since, therefore, these things cannot be understood otherwise, since truthful Scripture can stand only in this sense, it is necessary for you, O Jews, to change your blasphemous speech; necessary, pressed by authorities so numerous and so great, henceforth to confess that Christ is not merely man, but also true God. Are so many and such great proofs not enough for you to confess that our Christ is the Son of God, and to confess him God as well? It might now seem superfluous to adduce the many remaining examples from the Law or the Prophets. But if your own testimonies have become cheap in your eyes, or if foreign testimony pleases you more, hear also the Sibyl prophesying from among the Gentiles, so that even through the mouth of a Gentile woman the Spirit of God may crush the enemies of God. This same Spirit of God is accustomed sometimes to do this, and to utter prophetic or divine things through a Gentile tongue. [Col. 0538A] He did so through righteous Job, not a Jew but an Idumaean. He did so also through the wicked Balaam, who, among other future events which he foretold, uttered the celebrated and well-known prophecy concerning Christ: “I shall see him, but not now; I shall behold him, but not near. A star shall arise from Jacob, and a rod shall rise from Israel” (Num. XXIV). And after some intervening words: “Alas! Who shall live when God does these things?” (ibid.).

What then did the Sibyl say about Christ? What testimony did she offer to Christ’s divinity? Hear, and believe the woman who execrates the names of false gods and so firmly and openly confesses Christ’s divinity. For, speaking among the many things which she had prophetically said about Christ’s passion, she says this:

“Afterwards he shall come into the hands of unbelievers. But with unclean hands they shall give slaps to God, and with defiled mouth they shall spit poisonous spittle. Yet he shall simply give his holy back to blows, and, receiving buffetings, shall be silent, lest anyone recognize that he is the Word, or whence he came, to speak to those in the underworld; and he shall be crowned with a crown of thorns. For food they gave gall, and vinegar for thirst. This table of inhospitality they shall display. For you, foolish one, did not understand your God, who plays upon the minds of mortals; but you crowned him with thorns and mixed bitter gall. The veil of the temple shall be torn, and at midday there shall be exceedingly dark night for three hours; and he shall die by death. Having received sleep for three days, and then returning from those below, he shall come first into the light, having shown the beginning of resurrection to those recalled.”

The Sibyl said these things concerning Christ a long [Col. 0538C] time before Christ. You will not be able to say that her words ought not to be received, because, although she did not derive her bodily lineage from the people of God, she nevertheless thought and confessed the same things that the law of God contains and confesses. Will you then dare henceforth, miserable people, to deny that Christ is God, when you hear him called God through both your prophets and the mouths of Gentiles who worship not idols but the one God—so openly, so clearly, so splendidly, and not merely once but a thousand times? Will you deny that he is God, now that he has been born and rules heaven and earth, when, before he was yet born, so many truthful witnesses confessed him God again and again many ages beforehand? Will you deny that he is God whom, both in the Gospel of Christians and in the profane temples of pagans, even the demons themselves—whom you have now become worse than—by divine compulsion [Col. 0538D] confessed to be God?

## CHAPTER III. That Christ is not, as the Jews suppose, a temporal king, but eternal and heavenly.

But since enough may now have been said on these matters, let the discourse of divine wisdom proceed, in the third place of the division mentioned above, against another spirit of your most foolish error, and show how senseless you are in this respect. For because you hear Christ called king by the prophets, and read of his kingdom in the Scriptures, you suppose that he will be a temporal king and will reign temporally in Jerusalem, Judaea, or Galilee, after the manner of David, Solomon, or other kings. You dream that he will sit upon David’s earthly throne, [Col. 0539A] rule all nations or nearly all of them, free the Jews from so great and so long a captivity, summon them back from every place or nation, and restore them, gathered from every side, to that land of ancient promise for which you alone, always brutish people, long. You set before yourselves countless scriptural examples, and whatever is said in them concerning such things in a very different sense, you twist, with your understanding perverted and sunk in love of earthly things, bestially toward that which alone you are accustomed to desire. Unhappy people, you feed your souls on empty hope; and while you stubbornly crave earthly and perishing goods, you reject the heavenly things which Christ unceasingly both promises and grants continually to all nations except yourselves. Others daily seize [Col. 0539B] the kingdom of heaven; you, ever taught to love merely carnal dregs, vainly await a kingdom on earth.

This is why you try to adapt to your empty hope those things which were foretold in prophetic utterances concerning Christ’s eternal kingdom, such as this of Jeremiah: “Behold, days are coming, says the Lord, and I shall raise up for David a righteous branch; and a king shall reign, and shall be wise, and shall execute judgment and justice on earth” (Jer. XXIII). And, concerning the restoration of your captivity, shortly afterwards: “They shall no longer say, ‘As the Lord lives, who brought the children of Israel out of the land of Egypt’; but, ‘As the Lord lives, who brought out and led back the seed of the house of Israel from the land of the north, and from all the places where they had been scattered’; and they shall dwell in their own land” (ibid.). These, indeed, are the passages you bring forward from Jeremiah. But you can also produce something similar from [Col. 0539C] Ezekiel: “Behold, says the Lord, I shall take the children of Israel from among the nations to which they have gone; and I shall gather them from every side and bring them to their own soil. And I shall make them one nation in the land, on the mountains of Israel; and one king shall rule them all” (Ezek. XXXVII). And below: “I shall save them from all their defilements in which they have sinned, and I shall cleanse them. And they shall be my people, and I shall be their God; and my servant David shall be king over them, and there shall be one shepherd of them all” (ibid.). There are many other passages similar to these, which, just as they could have enlightened you by their radiance, have instead—because your sins have deserved it—blinded your carnal eyes, unable to bear spiritual light.

[Col. 0539D] So long, therefore, O Jews, as this bovine understanding has settled in your hearts, you will not by any effort be able either to see God’s Scriptures, recognize Christ, turn away from falsehood, or be converted to truth. Cast away, then, if you believe me, the mentality by which you will always appear not sensible but senseless; and take up the understanding by which you may deserve to recognize truth, receive Christ, and attain the king and kingdom—not as you conceive them, but as the Scriptures conceive them. But if you do not wish this, and resolve to remain in your customary madness, and choose rather to apply the Scriptures to your own understanding than to bend your understanding to the Scriptures, hear them resisting you and setting before you things contrary to your perverse understanding.

And first, whoever you are among these profane people, most eager [Col. 0540A] disputant, come forward, exert your strength, and, if you can, oppose God speaking. You certainly want Christ to be a carnal king; you await an earthly kingdom for Christ. Answer then God speaking through the prophet: “Say to the daughter of Zion: Behold, your king comes to you, gentle” (Zech. IX). Who is this king? Perhaps David, perhaps Solomon, perhaps some other king of Judah or Israel from the past. But you cannot say this, O Jew. Why? Because the date of the prophet forbids it. And who is this prophet? Zechariah. At what time did this Zechariah live? After all the kings of Judah, after all the kings of Israel from the preceding period. For the word of the Lord came to him in the time of Darius, as the sequence of his own prophecy relates. This Darius was, with Cyrus, the overthrower of the Chaldaean kingdom, and became the releaser of the Jewish captivity that had been brought about through Nebuchadnezzar. But all the kings of Israel or Judah reigned before that Babylonian captivity. It is therefore certain that the words, “Behold, your king comes to you, gentle,” were said of none of those who had already both preceded and passed away.

But if you set before me a certain Aristobulus, who long after the prophet Zechariah placed the diadem of the Jewish kingdom upon himself, I answer that the prophet did not mean him, for, against right and God’s command, he usurped kingship together with the priesthood. Since he was unworthy of it, he held it scarcely one year. For he could not rule long, having deserved rejection by God for so unlawful an act. If you propose Herod, it is likewise plain that this was not said of him. For the prophet speaks thus: “Behold, your king comes to you [Col. 0540C] gentle.” But it is certain, as Josephus, their own Jewish historian, writes, that Herod was not a Jew but a foreigner; not gentle but harsh, fierce, cruel, and moreover the killer of his wife and sons. If you object to his other sons—Archelaus, Herod, or the remaining tetrarchs of their father’s kingdom—it is well known, on the report of the historian already mentioned, that Archelaus, a foolish king, was expelled from the kingdom by Augustus and grew old at Vienne; while Herod, condemned to exile with his Herodias by Gaius, Augustus’ third successor, ended an unhappy life in the regions of Spain by a miserable death. It is also known that the rest, who ruled not the whole kingdom of the Jews but particular parts of it, scarcely endured until the destruction of Jerusalem [Col. 0540D] and of the whole Jerusalemite kingdom, and finally, when Vespasian and Titus ravaged that whole land, perished by various ends.

But perhaps, so that you may furnish the whole world with a new laugh at your expense, you will say this prophecy was fulfilled in that ass-riding king of our own time, who rose up in parts of Africa against the king of the new name, namely of Merroch. For the sake of a detestable sect—that is, the Muhammadan sect—he joined to himself an immense multitude of that ruined people; and though formerly a commoner, he gradually advanced in evil progress to greater things, and, fighting often with the king just mentioned, was frequently victorious in battle. And because in the first days of his advancement, in order more easily to win over the foolish people by feigned humility, he used to ride on an ass, he was commonly called the king of asses. When the Jews had received report of such a man, they immediately raised their hopes, and many of them declared that their king had come—the king whom the prophet already mentioned had foretold would ride upon an ass. What are you doing, O Jew? Are you not ashamed? Are you not confounded by these sayings of your own people? Such is the hope of your people: such the vain, foolish, ridiculous expectation of the Jews. Who could fittingly mock such great madness in ruined men? The Jews interpreted as a gentle king, a mild king, a kindly king, a man of execrable error, deceitful and cruel, a murderer not merely of some people but of many peoples. Why did they not at least notice that he had sprung neither from the land nor from the kingdom that had once belonged to the Jews, nor even from the final [Col. 0541B] remnant of the Jewish stock itself? You surely see how far such people are cast away from the face of God: with no effort whatever do they pursue what is true, while they so lightly follow what is false. And since I inserted this only in order to display prodigious people as a spectacle, let what follows now succeed.

For, all these having been excluded, it is certain that of none of them did God say through the prophet to the daughter of Zion—that is, to the Jews—“Behold, your king comes to you, gentle, seated upon an ass.” But what king promised here do you understand, or can you understand, except Christ? For now that the kings named have been excluded, no other king remains of whom it can be proved that the prophet said these things, except Christ. You must therefore yield to invincible truth and acknowledge that it was said to the daughter of Zion not of any other king whatever, but of Christ: “Behold, your king comes to you, gentle.”

Yet, as stated above, you want Christ to be a carnal, temporal king, sitting in a lofty throne after the manner of great kings, gleaming with purple, jewels, and gold, abounding in riches, subduing his enemies by arms and force, ruling widely over all the peoples of the Jews or the Gentile nations. But Christ is not such a king, nor is such a kingdom of Christ described by the prophet. How is this? Listen. For immediately after the prophet said, “Behold, your king comes to you, gentle,” he added: “He himself is poor, and riding upon an ass, and upon a colt, the foal of an ass” (Zech. IX). Attend, O Jew; awaken; understand your prophet. What does he say? “He himself is poor, and riding upon an ass, and upon [Col. 0541D] a colt, the foal of an ass.” Who is this man who is both king and poor? Who is this man who is both king and rides upon an ass? Who is this man who is both king and rides upon an ass’s colt? What have kingship and poverty to do with each other? What have kingship and an ass to do with each other? Explain how a king who, in your view, is supremely rich is called poor by the prophet; how he is written as one who will ride not upon a proud, foaming horse, but upon an ass and upon a colt, the foal of an ass. For to ride horses, or at least mules or hinnies, belongs to kings and powerful people; to ride asses or she-asses belongs to the poor and needy. Speak, then; say something; join together according to your interpretation king and poverty, abundance and want, exaltedness and lowliness. But you cannot.

Proceed, then, and read what follows: “I shall destroy the chariot from Ephraim and the horse from [Col. 0542A] Jerusalem, and the bow of war shall be shattered” (ibid.). Who is this king so poor that extreme poverty compels him to ride upon an ass and an ass’s colt? So peaceable that at his coming he destroys the chariot from Ephraim and the horse from Jerusalem, and shatters the bow of war? What king flourishing and secure in his own kingdom could you find so secure in abundant peace that he would cast away chariots and horses and disdain the bow of war—that is, all implements of warfare? This is not, this is not the peace of any earthly king or kingdom. Read again the times of Solomon himself, and you will find that he not only did not cast away from Jerusalem or Israel the chariots, horses, and weapons of war that he found, but rather increased them beyond measure. Should one believe that what was not done by so peaceable a king in so peaceful a time of his reign could ever be done by some earthly king?

But continue: “And he shall speak peace to the nations, and his power shall be from sea to sea, and from the rivers unto the ends of the earth” (ibid.). What will you say here too? Compare once more the poverty of the king just mentioned with the power you read of him. “This poor man,” it says, “shall rule from sea to sea, and from the rivers unto the ends of the earth.” What sort of monstrous poverty is this, that he is called poor who rules from sea to sea? What sort of prodigious power is this, that one ruling from sea to sea is so poor that he is compelled to ride upon an ass and a colt, the foal of an ass? But why do I repeat so often what is most clear? It is not surprising: I speak to a Jew; I speak to one deaf; I speak to one stony-hearted.

Either, then, O Jew, find me a poor king; find me one ruling from sea to sea and, through extreme need, riding upon an ass and a colt, the foal of an ass—which you cannot do—or receive our Christ as king and ruler from sea to sea, because he is almighty God; poor and riding upon an ass and an ass’s colt, because he is true man. This alone you can do. Though he was God, he became not merely man for human beings, but poor man for those same human beings. Read our Gospel, [Col. 0542D] and through it you will be able, without veils, to prove that your prophet spoke truthfully concerning how he mounted the ass, how, seated upon it or its colt, he came to the daughter of Zion—that is, to your Jerusalem at that time—shortly before he was to suffer.

But perhaps, in your manner, fleeing light and seeking darkness, unwilling that truth be disentangled from error, choosing by the demonic impulse that drives you to be entangled in falsehood, you will say: “Why do you press me about a king and an ass? Why do you confront me with a king and an ass’s colt? Do we not read that many powerful and wealthy people rode upon asses or she-asses, upon colts of asses or she-asses? Does not the Book of Judges relate that Jair the Gileadite, who judged Israel for twenty-two years, had thirty sons riding upon thirty colts of she-asses?” (Judith X). “Do we not read, among those same Judges, that Abdon son of Hillel the Pirathonite had forty sons and thirty grandsons among them, riding [Col. 0543A] upon seventy colts of she-asses? Nor can you deny that the sons or grandsons of such great judges, who judged the entire people of Israel and ruled it before the kings in the place of kings, were wealthy; nor can you deny that they used the colts of she-asses for travel, not because poverty forced them to do so. If this is true, your objection against us has no force: namely, that from the prophetic words one cannot understand any earthly king who also rides upon an ass’s colt.”

To this I say: I do not wish, I say, to complain that you are pressed by me on these points. I press you—indeed, I plainly press you, nay, I press you hard—so that you may perceive that your understanding, by which you seek a temporal king and do not deny that he rides upon an ass or its colt, is far from the prophetic meaning. Nor will the hundred sons or grandsons of Israel’s judges whom you have enumerated assist you. You adduced them in order to show both that they were rich and that, because they rode wherever they pleased upon colts of she-asses, what we seek to prove of our king is untrue.

I know, certainly, and am not so forgetful of sacred Scripture or human practice, that many powerful and wealthy people did ride, or could have ridden, upon she-asses or their colts. I recall, indeed, your great father Abraham, of whom we read both that he was wealthy and that he saddled his ass. We have as witness to his wealth Damascus, his servant, whose byname was Eliezer. These are his words, speaking to Laban and to the other kinsmen of Abraham’s family: “I am Abraham’s servant, and the Lord has greatly blessed my master. He has become great, and he has given him sheep and oxen, silver and gold, male and female servants, camels and asses” (Gen. XXIV). These words, I say, which have been brought forward show that he was wealthy. But to hear that he saddled his ass, listen to the same book of Genesis, concerning the same man of whom these things are said. For when his faith was tested by God through the sacrifice of his son, we read: “Therefore Abraham, rising in the night, saddled his ass, taking with him two young men and Isaac his son” (Gen. XXII). I knew these things before I argued with you, O Jew, about them. I knew also that Achsah, the daughter of Caleb, a wealthy man, sighed while seated upon an ass and said to her father: “You have given me southern and dry land; add also watered land” (Judith I).

But neither the things you have objected nor those which I have added [Col. 0543D] to your objection assist you in any respect, even slightly. You object that the sons of judges were wealthy and nevertheless sat upon she-asses. I too, as though arguing on your side, add that wealthy Abraham saddled an ass for himself, and that the son of a wealthy man sat upon an ass; yet from the cases you have put forward you have established nothing consonant with your interpretation. For of none of these is it read or written that he was a king, that he was poor, or that he was compelled by great poverty to ride upon an ass or its colt in order to travel. It is one thing—indeed, plainly another thing—if any wealthy person of old, either by the custom of the age or by a chance impulse of mind, such as commonly attends the wealthy as if proceeding from the fatness of riches, chose to ride upon an ass sometimes or often. It is another question whether any king, ancient or modern, can be understood to be at once poor and, as stated, forced by poverty to use such conveyances.

Wherever, therefore, you turn, no way out lies open. For either you will admit a king and remove the poor man, or, if you call him poor, you will be unable to call him king. In order that you may confess both truthfully and agree with the meaning of heavenly Scripture, cast away the Jewish mind, close your blasphemous mouth, and, taking up Christian understanding, believe in your heart unto righteousness and confess with your mouth unto salvation Christ as eternal king by divinity and poor man by humanity assumed for humankind (Rom. X).

But let us now pass again to Isaiah. Hear what similar thing he too says: “Behold,” he says, “my servant shall understand, and shall be exalted and lifted up, and shall be exceedingly high” (Isa. LII). Who speaks through the prophet? Surely God. “Behold,” he says, “my servant shall understand.” But he has many servants. Yet he distinguishes this one from them when he says: “He shall be exalted and lifted up, and shall be exceedingly high.” But many have been exalted and lifted up by God and made high; how then shall this servant of God be distinguished from those many? Continue: “As many were astonished at you, so shall his appearance be inglorious among men, and his form among the children of men” (ibid.). What will you answer so great a prophet, O Jew? You do not dare even to think him a liar. What he says is therefore true. You answer: “Entirely true.” Who, then, is this servant of God, exalted, lifted [Col. 0544C] up, and exceedingly high, whose appearance, conversely, is inglorious among men, whose form is without glory among the children of men? Seek; labor; say something if you can. But read further: “He shall sprinkle many nations; kings shall shut their mouths over him” (ibid.). Who again is this man who is said to sprinkle many nations, and over whom kings are said to shut their mouths? Certainly the same one who was said to be exalted, lifted up, and made high. And who is this one, so great, so powerful, so mighty, that he sprinkles many nations and kings shut their mouths over him? Clearly, he is not only great but greatest; not merely powerful but most powerful. Fearing his greatness and marveling at his power, kings hold their peace: they do not dare to speak; they wait as it were for the nod of one greater, they endure as it were the command of one ruling.

Yet this is the man whose appearance among men is called inglorious, whose form among the children of men is proclaimed contemptible. Perhaps you seek what to answer and labor to discover how you can lie and twist the heavenly oracle into a perverse sense. But no avenue lies open for you to escape these straits, nor can heavenly light be obscured or darkened by Egyptian darkness. Of which king or ruler can you interpret such diverse and contrary things? Who among all those you can invent is exalted and inglorious, lifted up and inglorious, exceedingly high and inglorious? Who is this man, so great and so dreadful, that kings dare not speak before him, while the children of men despise his form? And because I know you will find nothing in [Col. 0545A] these sacred words by which you can reasonably pervert this meaning, you are forced by the power of reason to return to us and inquire who this is of whom such contrary things are written.

Rightly, as is also written among these prophetic words, many were astonished at him of whom such varied things are said; but not all, like you, remained unbelieving. They were indeed astonished at the unique miracle, but by their very astonishment—not all, certainly, but many—were converted to Christ, their God and salvation. For they understood this one, and no other—precisely this Christ of ours, and no other—to have been exalted, lifted up, and made exceedingly high; and again, his appearance among men to have been inglorious and his form contemptible among the children of men. He was exalted, lifted up, and made exceedingly high because, as our Apostle says, God, in the man whom he had assumed, exalted him and gave him the name above every name, “that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth” (Phil. II). His appearance was inglorious and his form contemptible among the children of men because, as the same Apostle had previously said, “he became obedient unto death, even the death of the cross” (ibid.). Kings shut their mouths over him because the highest kings and rulers of the world, closing their mouths for silence and opening their ears to hear, listen to him as the Prince of princes, obey him as King of kings, and serve him as Lord of lords.

Therefore, because these things cannot be said of any mortal, because in no human being can such contrary things be found, you must understand, recognize, and receive our Christ in these words. Nor could we pass over what perhaps you might object: that many kings or rulers were first great and exalted, and later fell from the power of rulership or the glory of a kingdom through various misfortunes. But remember that the discussion concerns Christ, whom you contend will never be miserable but happy, never subject but ruling, never inglorious but glorious. These things were proposed in order to exclude that claim: in order that an eternal rather than temporal kingdom may be understood in Christ, and divine rather than human glory perceived in him.
