For I do not believe you are so mad as to try to explain these prophetic words, from the prophet’s own time onward, of some king of Judah or king of any nation. But perhaps Jewish cunning will attempt to apply them either to King Manasseh, son of Hezekiah, who was taken captive and later restored to the kingdom; or to Josiah, slain by the Egyptians; or to Jehoiachin or Zedekiah, who were carried into Babylon. These alone among the kings of Judah, after the time of the prophet uttering these prophecies, seem to have fallen from royal glory. But you will try this in vain. Is the wicked king Manasseh called God’s servant? For this was stated first: “Behold, my servant shall understand.” Is an idolater, is a profane man, is the one who, as we read, filled Jerusalem beyond measure, even to overflowing, with innocent blood (IV Kings XXI), called God’s servant? Nebuchadnezzar, a most wicked king, is indeed elsewhere called God’s [Col. 0546A] servant, not because he was good but because, fighting against wicked nations according to God’s will—though not with a praiseworthy will—he served God’s purpose. But although Manasseh repented, God’s Scripture does not call him God’s servant, nor does it relate that he performed any military service for God. Manasseh, therefore, was not called God’s servant. It follows that this Scripture was not uttered concerning him.

Nor do words so exalted, so solemnly spoken, and so often repeated suit either him, Josiah, or the rest: that they should be called exalted, lifted up, and exceedingly high. Though they were kings, the prophetic words surpass their greatness and their exaltation. Nor does what follows suit any of them: “As many were astonished at you” (Isa. LII). For who would be astonished if any king were exalted and then humbled, lifted up and cast down, raised high and removed from that height? This is commonplace; this is usual in kings and powerful people. But people are not accustomed to be astonished at an ordinary matter. Therefore the matter at which many are said by the prophet to have been astonished must necessarily be singular, wonderful, and unprecedented. If this is true, these words were not spoken of captive kings, slain kings, kings struck by any misfortune, or persons of any rank whatever.

And who does not see that these words also suit neither these nor any kings of the Jews: “He shall sprinkle many nations, and kings shall shut their mouths over him”? (ibid.). And lest frequent repetition obscure what is clear, I say briefly: if this Scripture can be understood of no king of Israel or Judah, indeed of no Jew at all who has existed down to our own times, then it can be understood of no one other than the Christ proclaimed by the prophets.

It remains, therefore, that these prophetic utterances be understood only of Christ. Yet not of the Christ falsely expounded by you, but of the Christ truthfully understood by us: not of Christ ruling temporally, but of Christ ruling eternally; not of Christ reigning on earth after the manner of kings, but of Christ presiding, after the manner of God, over all things on earth and in heaven. He is called God’s servant by the prophet because “he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Phil. II); [Col. 0546D] he is exceedingly high, presiding over every creature; and he is inglorious, freely submitting himself to the shameful passion. He sprinkles many nations, whom he commands everywhere to be baptized with the sacred water of baptism. Kings shut their mouths over him because everywhere the pride not only of other people but also of kings themselves obeys him.

Attend, then, O Jew, to what is said; understand the Scripture that speaks; believe in the Christ who is proclaimed; be ashamed of your unbelief; imitate the faith of the nations, concerning whom the same prophet immediately adds: “Those to whom no report of him was made shall see, and those who have not heard shall contemplate” (Isa. LII). Hasten from here to what follows, and although the preceding things have fully shown that Christ’s kingdom neither was nor will be carnal or temporal, recognize this again from what follows. And, so far as the subject undertaken permits, to avoid the weariness of prolixity, I set before you the whole of what is read in Isaiah from the verse beginning “Who has believed our report?” (Isa. LIII) to the verse beginning “Rejoice, barren woman, you who do not bear” (Isa. LIV).

I believe that you understand those many utterances to concern no one other than Christ. For to whom can the prophet’s words, “To whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?” apply except Christ? To whom can the words, “Who shall declare his generation?” apply except Christ? To whom can it apply that “he committed no iniquity, nor was deceit found in his mouth,” except Christ? To whom can the words, “He himself, being righteous, shall justify many of my servants, and he himself shall bear their iniquities,” be adapted except [Col. 0547B] Christ? Of whom can it be believed, “He was offered because he himself willed it, and did not open his mouth,” except Christ? Who does not see that this one alone, of whom such great things are said, is not among the ordinary multitude of human beings but is above every human being?

Give me, if you can, anyone besides Christ who should be called the arm of the Lord—that is, the power of the Lord. Give anyone whose generation cannot be declared. Give me a human being who committed no iniquity and had no deceit in his mouth. Give me someone who, himself righteous, justifies many others and bears their iniquity. Give me, if you have one, someone who was offered because he willed it and did not open his mouth. For although you understand your Christ as merely man, nevertheless, in this respect, the things said are above humanity. Look, then, and judge not Jewishly but justly, whether the arm of the Lord—that is, the power of the Lord—can be understood as a human being and merely a human being. For God is called the power of man; man is not called the power of God. This is plainly the voice of a human being addressed to God: “Lord, in your power the king shall rejoice” (Ps. XX). If the king who surpasses others in power and rank is not the power of God, but rather rejoices in hope in the power of the Lord, it is clear that the one called the arm of the Lord rules not only those below him but kings themselves.

When, moreover, you hear, “Who shall declare his generation?” do you not understand that his generation is distinguished from human and common generation? It belongs indeed to God alone to know how a human body is formed from received matter in the womb of its mother; yet the manner in which bodily generation proceeds is evident to everyone. What is therefore known to all, what cannot escape anyone, the prophet makes singular and, as it were, unutterable. Does it not seem to you, then, that he whose generation is so distinguished from human generation that it is even called unutterable is not merely man but also above man? But if the prophetic word is understood also of that higher and eternal generation from God the Father, then Christ is proved much more thereby to be not merely man but above man. For that generation from the Father is far more wonderful and much more unutterable than that from the Virgin.

What do you infer, what do you judge, when you hear the prophet say of the same one [Col. 0548A] that “he committed no iniquity, nor was deceit in his mouth”? Do you remember those words: “No one on earth is free from sin, not even an infant of one day”? Does not he, therefore, who committed no iniquity and in whose mouth was no deceit seem to you to have surpassed humanity, to be above humanity? Consider also this: “He himself, my servant, shall justify many, and shall himself bear their iniquities.” He who is called righteous, who is written to justify many, who is proclaimed to bear their iniquities—an act belonging to God alone—consider whether he can rightly be understood, believed, or received as merely a human being and not more than human. Whoever finds this obscure is, without contradiction from any wise person, not a human being but a beast.

Likewise, when you read, “He was offered because he himself willed it,” do you not go beyond the common number of human beings? For what human being dies voluntarily? Who is killed willingly? I have said these things beforehand so that whatever the prophet says in the sequence already mentioned may be believed capable of referring only to Christ. For it is certain that these things are said of a man. But from what has already been said, it follows that this man must be above man. Now no human being other than Christ is found above humanity. And because you, O Jew, maintain that none can be greater than Christ, your prophet compels you to confess that one human being is greater than others; and you must consequently understand this one, who is called greater than all, to be none other than Christ. Therefore all these things are said of Christ. And since all these things [Col. 0548C] are said of Christ, it remains to prove the point proposed: whether Christ’s kingdom should be judged earthly and temporal, as you, O Jew, suppose.

Trace, then, the prophet: “He has no form or comeliness; and we saw him, and there was no appearance; and we desired him, despised and the last of men, a man of sorrows and acquainted with infirmity. And his face was as though hidden, and despised; whence we did not esteem him” (Isa. LII). What here sounds royal? What here appears kingly? Where is the gold? Where the purple? Where the jeweled crown? Where the silver throne? Where the power and pomp of one who rules? He has no form, no comeliness, no appearance. Yet he is desired though despised; he is the last [Col. 0548D] of men; he is a man of sorrows; his face is hidden, nor is he himself restored.

Proceed, and, for brevity’s sake, select not everything but certain passages: “And we thought him as it were leprous, and struck by God, and humbled. But he was wounded for our iniquities; he was bruised for our crimes.” And after some words: “Like a sheep he shall be led to slaughter.” And, after a few intervening words: “He was cut off from the land of the living.” And finally: “He delivered his soul unto death and was reckoned among criminals.” What do you say, Jew? Do you not stand amazed? You are now compelled by the force of reason to understand these things of Christ. Where, then, in all these passages do you find his temporal kingdom? Where do you perceive the glory of one reigning? Is bearing infirmities, carrying sorrows [Col. 0549A], reigning? Is being thought leprous, thought struck by God, thought humbled, reigning? Is being wounded, killed, delivered to death, reckoned among criminals, reigning? I pass over the rest. What are you doing? Do you not yet recognize that Christ’s kingdom cannot be earthly or temporal? You surely recognize it, if you are a human being. And since this is clear, there is no need to dwell long upon what is clear.

Hear, then, this same one, placed amid these reproaches, led to these wounds and to this killing, delivering himself to death: “My kingdom,” he says, “is not of this world. If my kingdom were of this world, my servants would certainly fight, that I should not be delivered to the Jews” (John XVIII). Therefore cease now to think Christ a temporal king and his kingdom earthly. [Col. 0549B] For loftiness and abasement, glory and disgrace, power and weakness, kingdom and destruction, do not accord and cannot coexist. Understand that Christ does not reign in this customary manner of kings, but rules heaven and earth and the whole creation, not merely as king, but as God and Lord. Acknowledge that his kingdom enjoys, not the measure of a few years, but the blessed infinity of all ages; from it the denying Jew is always excluded, and to it the Christian confessing Christ is always admitted.

Nor indeed am I ignorant what the ancient serpent whispers in the synagogues of Satan into the ears of the lost; nor is it hidden from me what poisons wicked teachers, hemmed in by the straits of so clear a truth, pour into their hearers. For, as I have heard from some persons, they say [Col. 0549C] that their Christ was born about the time of Vespasian and was conveyed to Rome by some art unknown to me. There, torn and gnawed by dogs, he lies hidden in underground crypts or caverns, enduring the pains and wounds of that gnawing for Jewish sins or iniquities; and from this comes the saying: “He was wounded for our iniquities; he was bruised for our crimes.” They assert that he will live and endure these pains in the bowels of the earth until, at the time appointed by God, he comes forth; gathering Jews from all nations, he will bring them back to the original place of their promised land. Then, they say, all things foretold by the prophets concerning the future happiness of the Jews will be fulfilled; [Col. 0549D] then their Christ will rule many nations; then peace will exist without fear of any disturbance; then they will live amid the highest delights and glory.

They testify that long ago he appeared to one of their number, a great teacher among his own people, in the guise of a beggar and a wretch. And when the man to whom he appeared recoiled from the great baseness and deformity of the apparition, he was suddenly changed into the form of a handsome man, and his very cheap garments were transformed into precious clothing. They further boast that he at once held out a sapphire stone in one hand and a jasper in the other, and said to the one to whom he appeared: “Why are you astonished? Behold, I—behold, I—am that Christ of yours, so long awaited by you. It is near for me to come; it is near [Col. 0550A] for me to appear. For I shall bring you back from all nations, gather you from every land, and lead you into your land. Then there shall be fulfilled in your Jerusalem what Isaiah wrote: ‘Poor little one, shaken by tempest, without any consolation: behold, I shall lay your stones in order and found you upon sapphires; and I shall make your battlements of jasper’” (Isa. LIV). “Behold the sapphire upon which Jerusalem is to be founded; behold the jasper from which the defenses of your city are to be built.”

O consolation! O hope to be embraced! O happiness to be awaited without hesitation! O dregs of humankind! Do such things soothe you, charm you, persuade you to await Antichrist in place of Christ? Truly Satan plays with you as men do with apes; truly, like the basest beast of burden, he draws you wherever he wishes by the bridle of folly; truly, as the father of lies, he promises you many things in order to take everything away; he gives dreams in order to rob you of realities; he feeds with fables those whom he deprives of Christ, the bread of angels and human beings. [Col. 0550B] And what shall I say? Words fail before such profound folly in foolish people. Behold, you offer us a canine Christ; and, ashamed that he was killed by Jews, you lay this upon dogs. Yet we do not deny it. Truly Christ was gnawed by dogs—by the unclean, by those who barked against him—as you say; and, as we confess, he was killed. Let Christ himself be heard in the Psalm: “Many dogs surrounded me; the assembly of the wicked besieged me. They pierced my hands and my feet” (Ps. XXI). Were you not dogs when, after the manner of dogs, [Col. 0550C] you thirsted for blood and, in excessive madness, nearly licked it, saying: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Ps. XXVII)? Were you not barking when, while the judge denounced and repeatedly sought to avoid your crime, you cried again and again, “Crucify him, crucify him!” (John XIX)?

But, to speak of these dogs from which the comparison with your madness has been drawn: can anyone be led to death by dogs? For Isaiah speaks of Christ: “Like a sheep he shall be led to slaughter.” To lead belongs to human beings, not dogs; to lead belongs to human beings, not beasts; to rational beings, not irrational creatures. It is therefore clear that Christ was foretold by the prophet as to be led to slaughter, not by dogs of this kind, but by Jews far worse than these. [Col. 0550D] And since it is almost the same thing either to expend oneself in argument against utterly trifling fables, contemptible at first hearing, or to weary one’s strength by repeatedly and vigorously striking empty air, let what has been said suffice. Let the discourse return to the point for which this material concerning Jewish fables—of which they abound more than all other erring people—was introduced. That point which the argument intended to prove, indeed which it has already proved by both authority and reason, is that Christ must not be understood as a temporal king, nor Christ’s kingdom as earthly and destined to end.

What has been set forth could indeed suffice to give any person certainty on this matter. But because I am speaking with a Jew, whom I do not know whether he is a human being, [Col. 0551A] some further points must be added. I truly do not know whether a Jew is human, who yields neither to human reason nor acquiesces in divine and his own authorities. I do not know, I say, whether he is human, from whose flesh the heart of stone has not yet been taken away, to whom a heart of flesh has not been given, and in whose midst the divine Spirit has not yet been placed—without whom a Jew can never be converted to Christ.

Return, then, Jew, to the contest, and consider from your own authorities, not foreign ones, that Christ cannot be a temporal king and Christ’s kingdom cannot be earthly or transitory. Daniel says: “His power is an eternal power, which shall not be taken away; and his kingdom, which shall not be destroyed” (Dan. VII). Whose “his”? Is it not Christ’s? If you doubt, attend to what precedes: “I watched until thrones were set, and the Ancient of Days sat. His garment was white as snow, and the hair of his head like clean wool. His throne was flames of fire; its wheels, burning fire. A swift river of fire issued from before him. Thousands of thousands ministered to him” (ibid.). [Col. 0551B] And after a few intervening words: “I watched in the vision of the night, and behold, with the clouds of heaven one like a Son of Man came. And he came even to the Ancient of Days, and they presented him before him. And he gave him power and honor and a kingdom; and all peoples, tribes, and tongues shall serve him” (ibid.). And immediately the passage I have cited is added: “His power is an eternal power,” and the rest.

Who is this Ancient of Days? Who is this one who came with the clouds of heaven as though a Son of Man? Who is he who came to the Ancient of Days and was presented before him, and to whom all the things just mentioned were given? Speak, Jew, if you have anything to say. Can you imagine anyone as the Ancient of Days except God? Can you name anyone to whom thousands of thousands minister and ten thousand times one hundred thousand stand attendant, except God? Again, whom will you understand as one like a Son of Man, coming with the clouds of heaven, except Christ? Whom as having come to the Ancient of Days and been presented before him, except Christ? To whom was power, honor, kingdom, and all that follows given, except Christ? Search through the infinite mass of the human race person by person, and see which among all the children of men can be understood as so great, so exalted, a Son of Man. And since this must be understood of some [Col. 0551D] son of man, consider whether anyone besides Christ can be called such and so great a Son of Man. Remember at the same time those things which you conceded above: that none of the children of men can be greater than Christ. Consider also this: if you understand these prophetic words of someone other than Christ, you will thereby confess someone greater than Christ. For the man upon whom God confers so great an honor must be believed greater than every human being. If you wish to avoid this absurdity, you are compelled to confess, all others excluded, that these things are said of Christ alone.

It has therefore been proved, as it seems to me, that this Son of Man ought to be understood by anyone as no other than Christ. By Christ we mean our Redeemer and Savior Jesus; by you, that one whom, as has already been said, your fathers vainly dreamed of and whom you and your people’s ridiculous expectation await in vain. Of this Christ, then, it was said: “His power is an eternal power, which shall not be taken away; and his kingdom, which shall not be destroyed.” But eternal power and an incorruptible kingdom cannot exist on earth. Hear your Psalm speaking to God: “In the beginning, O Lord, you founded the earth, and the heavens are the works of your hands. They themselves shall perish” (Ps. CI). [Col. 0552A] If heaven perishes, if earth perishes, where will Christ, a temporal and earthly king, reign? If earth fails, how can the power of an earthly king be eternal? If the earth in which, according to your understanding, he is to reign comes to an end, how will his kingdom not be destroyed? Either, then, ensure that the earth does not perish, so that the kingdom of your Christ [Col. 0552B] may always remain in it; or, if his kingdom perishes along with the perishing earth, know that you are far from the prophet’s meaning, when he says of Christ: “His power is an eternal power, which shall not be taken away; and his kingdom, which shall not be destroyed.”

Hear Ezekiel likewise, saying something similar: “They shall dwell,” he says, “upon the land which I gave to my servant Jacob, in which your fathers dwelt. And they themselves and their children shall dwell upon it forever, and David my servant shall be their prince forever. And I shall make with them a covenant of peace; it shall be an everlasting covenant for them” (Ezek. XXXVII). What will you say to these things also? Explain David to me, and explain David’s everlasting rule. Do you not read that David died almost five hundred years before these things were said? [Col. 0552C] How, then, is he whose kingdom had already passed, who had ended it by death, said to be about to rule and reign? For in the same sequence of words, by the same prophet, he who is now called prince is also called king a little earlier: “They shall be my people, and I shall be their God; and David my servant shall be king over them, and there shall be one shepherd for them all.” Who, who is this David, who is said by this prophet—born many years after David’s death—to be both prince and king and the one shepherd of the Jewish kingdom? But I know that no degree of Jewish perversity can interpret this of anyone except Christ. For because Christ was to be born from David’s stock—indeed, from his very house and family—and because he was to reign over his people, whom he saves from sins and every enemy, in judgment, justice, and all equity, in David’s manner, though more than David and differently from David, he is called David and is written to rule over his people. Hence Jeremiah: “Strangers shall no longer rule over him, but they shall serve the Lord their God and David their king, whom I shall raise up for them” (Jer. XXX). [Col. 0552D]

How can this be “forever”? How “unto eternity”? For this, as I said, is what is written there: “David my servant shall be their prince forever.” And immediately thereafter: “I shall make with them a covenant of peace, an everlasting covenant.” If you understand a carnal kingdom, if you expect an earthly dominion, say how this David can reign on an earth that is not eternal, in a world destined to end.

That these present things are destined to end and cannot be eternal, hear also another prophet: “Former things,” he says, “shall not be remembered, nor shall they come up upon the heart” (Isa. LXV). [Col. 0553A] But if former things shall not be remembered, if they shall not come up upon the heart, surely earthly kingdoms and the dominions of mortals will not merely fail to remain, will not merely fail to endure, but will not even be remembered or come up upon the heart. Since this is incontestable, since it cannot be contradicted when the invincible reasoning of truth stands in the way, I wonder whether from now on the thought of a temporal kingdom, or henceforth the expectation of an earthly dominion with regard to Christ, will enter your heart, or whether it can impede you from understanding Christ’s true and eternal kingdom.

[Col. 0553B] And, so that the Jewish heart, conquered by manifold reasoning, may now cease to be foolish and begin to be wise, say whether you believe and confess the resurrection of human flesh. But I know that you believe; I know that you confess it. For you have this from your teachers, both ancient and modern, and the manifest and manifold authority of divine Scripture compels you to believe it. Hence you have in the Psalms: “My flesh shall rest in hope” (Ps. XV). If in hope, certainly it rests either in some other hope or in the hope of resurrection. But in what other hope can flesh rest except resurrection? What else can dead flesh hope for but restoration to life? What can that which is lifeless hope for but reanimation? What can that which has already fallen hope for but resurrection? Human flesh, therefore, rests in the hope of resurrection.

You also have in Isaiah: “All flesh shall come to worship before my face, says the Lord” (Isa. LXVI). Read the section of prophecy in which this is written, [Col. 0553C] and you will find that the prophet there understood also the resurrection of the flesh. Hence, a few words later, he adds concerning the impious: “And they shall be unto satiety of vision to all flesh.” Those impious cannot be an object of vision unto satiety for all flesh unless all flesh then lives, unless all flesh is animate, unless it has the capacity, even through bodily eyes, to behold the torments of the wicked.

You have also in Ezekiel: “Behold, I shall open your tombs and bring you out of your graves, my people, and bring you into the land of Israel” (Ezek. XXXVII). And in Job: “On the last day,” he says, “I shall rise from the earth; and in my flesh I shall see God” (Job XIX). From this I know that you cannot contradict the resurrection of the flesh. But that resurrection is preceded by a fall; that restoration to life is preceded by death; that animation of bodies is preceded by lifelessness. Since you cannot deny this, especially as you behold it daily, say over whom Christ, your carnal king, will rule when all are already dead; say how he himself, also dead, will rule over the dead. Say over whom he will reign, when he and all have been extinguished at the end of the world; say, I ask, over whom he will then be prince. [Col. 0553D] For his kingdom and dominion, as you heard from the prophet, must be eternal.

Escape these straits if you can; draw your foot from this snare if you are able. Either you will show uninterrupted eternity in the earthly kingdom of your Christ, or, if you cannot deny the end of the world and the passing away of bodily things together with human beings, [Col. 0554A] you will understand with us that Christ’s eternal kingdom is not on earth but elsewhere. Nor will I allow you to take refuge in those things which follow the resurrection of the flesh, so as to dare imagine that your Christ’s kingdom will exist even in them. For as long as you understand his kingdom carnally, so long you are equally excluded by the authority of Holy Scripture from a kingdom both present and future. For what beast so foolish, apart from a Jew, could be found to suppose after the resurrection of the flesh a carnal life, a carnal king, and a carnal kingdom? In saying this, I do not exclude the true substance of human flesh, but demonstrate that the condition of the flesh will be far different. If you, reared in the dregs of flesh and blood, who have made flesh your arm, cannot grasp this, [Col. 0554B] what is that to me? Hear Scripture, and follow not my judgment but its judgment.

Hear, and so that even after that universal restoration of human flesh you may not imagine Christ’s kingdom to be such as other kings’ kingdoms usually are, observe: “The sun shall not be for you a light by day, nor shall the brightness of the moon enlighten you. But the Lord your God shall be for you an everlasting light” (Isa. LX); and elsewhere: “Eye has not seen, O God, apart from you, what you have prepared for those who love you” (Isa. LXIV). And Zechariah: “The Lord my God shall come, and all the saints with him; and on that day there shall be no light, but cold and frost. And there shall be one day, known to the Lord—not day and not night” (Zech. XIV).

What will you say to these things? Invent something, if you can. Show an earthly Jerusalem’s kingdom, the carnal empire of your Christ, without sun or moon, without day or night. Say whether you can understand of that kingdom thus conceived what was said: “Eye has not seen, O God, apart from you, what you have prepared for those who love you” [“those who love you”]. [Col. 0554C] If no eye except the divine could see what has been prepared for those who love God, could yours? Could anyone’s? You see, then, how briefly and clearly this condemns every thought of a carnal king, earthly dominion, and worldly glory. For in these very few words not only earthly Jerusalem, not only Judaea or Galilee, not only—what is more—the whole of Syria, in part of which the Jewish kingdom once flourished, but the entire world itself is excluded; and it is declared that Christ’s kingdom or the glorification of his saints cannot be understood as existing even in that whole world. [Col. 0554D]

But if you cannot find Christ’s kingdom, as you are accustomed to conceive it, either in this life which is destined to end or in that eternal life which follows it, soften your inveterate hardness; cast away the heart of stone; take up a heart of flesh; and acknowledge that our Christ reigns in this world through the invisible power of deity, through faith and grace, and in the life to come through manifest glory. Certainly, if I am speaking with a human being and not with a beast, examine carefully; and, if God’s grace helps you, you will perceive that the final purpose of the Law, the Prophets, and your whole Canon is no other than the blessed eternity promised to the saints.

For what? Do you suppose that so many and such great works—so unusual, so marvelous, so worthy of proclamation—were performed by God merely for a brief, miserable life subject to innumerable deaths? [Col. 0555A] Was Egypt struck with ten famous plagues, Pharaoh with his people drowned, manna rained daily for forty years, a pillar of cloud given by day and fire by night, a rain of quail flesh, water from rocks, the Jordan divided and turned back, the sun made obedient, the dead raised, such solemn miracles joined to prophetic oracles, and many like things—were all these, I ask, done for so slight, indeed so nonexistent, a carnal and miserable life? Were they done merely so that you, Jew, might stuff your belly with various foods and meats? Were they done merely so that you might become drunk and snore in drunkenness? Were they done merely so that you might devote yourself to pleasures and dissolve into lusts? Were they done merely so that you might [Col. 0555B] abound in riches, fill your chests with gold, silver, and many treasures, and exalt yourself above those subject to you in the proud pomp of a ruler? Far, far be this from human minds! Let it be far from souls capable of reason! Let it depart far from all who know God!

Reason does not admit this; justice itself opposes it: that a human being, whom the Creator set above all irrational creatures, should, though this may happen in certain respects, be likened to beasts in every aspect of his kind and made like them. For if it were so, if God bestowed only these carnal goods upon humanity, what more would the most miserable human possess than an ox, an ass, or any most worthless worm? [Col. 0555C] Created from eternity unto eternity, though through the desert of his sin he lost it for a time, he nevertheless did not lose the hope of recovering it. Hence God, nursing you like a child, gradually nourishing you by carnal benefits toward spiritual things and by temporal things toward eternal things, bestowed transitory goods upon you in the first stage, so that led by them you might learn to keep God’s law and, advancing from there, pass to hoping for and loving heavenly and eternal things.

This eternity was the purpose of those so exalted miracles: that a rude people, drawn on the one hand by benefits and stirred on the other by wondrous works, might grow accustomed to obeying their Creator and, by obedience, return to the blessed eternity from which their disobedience had cast them. And because it was not fitting that everything be poured out at once to people [Col. 0555D] newly arisen in the newness of the world and wholly ignorant of divine matters, this eternity is read of more rarely in the Pentateuch or Heptateuch; it is commended more frequently by the prophets, and is proclaimed most frequently—indeed continually—through Christ’s Gospel. But until you assent to the Gospel, it is not reasonable to advance an argument from the Gospel against you. Hear, however, your own authorities, whom you cannot refuse to hear.

Hear Jacob himself, the great father and your patriarch; hear him blessing his son Joseph: “The blessings of your father are strengthened by the blessings of his fathers, until the desire of the eternal hills should come” (Gen. XLIX). Hear Moses himself likewise, blessing Joseph’s tribe: “Of the blessing of the Lord is his land” (Deut. [Col. 0556A] XXXIII). And after a few intervening words: “From the summit of the ancient mountains, from the fruits of the eternal hills” (ibid.). Who are these eternal hills? This earth of ours has no eternal hills or eternal mountains. For if it itself, as the reasoning set out above establishes, is destined to perish, how can its hills be eternal? If the whole earth perishes, how can a part of it remain? Therefore the hills too will perish when the earth perishes. Hence its hills cannot be called eternal. Who then are the eternal hills? As long as you are earthly, as long as you seek eternal hills upon the earth, you will not find them. Raise your minds; seek above the heavens. There you will find not only eternal hills but everlasting mountains. Of these the Psalm says: “You shine forth wondrously from the eternal mountains” (Ps. XXV).

Who these are is not for me to teach. I am contending against an enemy, not instructing a pupil. If you believe, you will understand. If not, you will know neither these nor the other mysteries of God. Recall likewise what David says of this eternity: “I considered the ancient days, and I kept eternal years in mind” (Ps. CLXXVI). But, as I said concerning the hills, you will not find eternal years in time that is destined to end. For he himself indicates elsewhere, speaking to God, that time is to end and human years fail: “But you are the same, and your years shall not fail” (Ps. CI). [Col. 0556B] He would not say this, would not present it as something distinctive, if he knew that human years did not fail. The preceding words also show this: by them he had demonstrated that human things are destined to perish, and then added that divine things remain forever. [Col. 0556C]

Hear Isaiah also concerning this eternity, which is to exist not beneath this heaven and this earth: “As the new heavens and the new earth, which I make to stand before me, says the Lord, so shall your seed and your name stand” (Isa. LXXVI). These words teach that both this heaven and this earth are to pass away, and by the name of new heavens and a new earth indicate the new condition of the age to come, which God makes to stand before him: because all things will receive after the world’s end a condition which they will no longer lose as before, but will retain steadfastly and without end. Trace all the prophets, and you will find this eternity frequently proclaimed and solemnly commended.

Turn your mind, therefore, from passing things; separate your heart from perishable things; and labor to believe Christ our Lord to be the author and king of this blessed eternity and to be enrolled in his eternal kingdom through Christian faith and works of faith. [Col. 0556D] For Christians understand Christ to be such a king; in such a king we believe; such a one we worship; and to attain such a kingdom of his, according to grace and our strength, we hasten.

We indeed invite Jews into this kingdom on such terms. But they, insofar as they can, repel both us and all who are born from the nations. For they say that God spoke only to them, that the Law was given to them, that prophets were sent to them, and, further, that Christ is to be sent after them all and that his kingdom pertains only to Jews. But just as it was foolish to think that God performed so many and such marvelous works merely for present and perishable things, [Col. 0557A] so it is no less foolish and beastlike to suppose that the Author of the universe, setting aside the nations, cared only for Jews and gave none but them hope of breathing unto life. God, who has care for all, did not think so; nor did he confine his mercy within such narrow limits that, choosing a tiny portion of a tumultuous and ungrateful people, he should reject the infinity of nations and allow them, as though unrelated to himself, to slip perpetually by the paths of error into the depths of destruction. It befitted him who created every race of mortals to have mercy upon all at the fitting time and, when Jews were rejected under the pressure of their own wickedness, to call the fullness of the nations to salvation in generous kindness.

But if, in your usual manner, Jew, you dare to chatter even against these things and boast that you alone are called God’s special people, hear again your Scripture and recognize that not you alone are chosen or called by God. [Col. 0557B] Read again the verse of your Psalm speaking to God: “All nations whom you have made shall come and worship before you, O Lord” (Ps. LXXXV). Will you henceforth boast that God cares only for you? It foretells that the nations will worship God—not merely this, but all nations. And so that no nation might be excepted from this meaning, although “all nations” would have sufficed, it adds: “whom you have made.” Now it is certain that all nations were made by God, and none can be found that was not made by him. Therefore, with no nation excepted, all nations are written as coming and all nations as worshiping God.

[Col. 0557C] Hence you have also in the Psalm: “All the ends of the earth shall remember and turn to the Lord, and all the families of the nations shall worship in his sight” (Ps. XXI). Does not this testimony of the Psalm alone, even without others, suffice to demonstrate the calling of the nations? Hear God through Isaiah also, among many similar statements: “Those who did not formerly ask for me sought me; those who did not seek me found me; and I said: ‘Behold me, behold me,’ to a nation that did not call upon my name” (Isa. LXIV). What will you say? Do you see God hastening to go over to a nation that did not call upon him? For “Behold me, behold me” are the words of one hastening and greatly eager. And truly it has now happened thus; truly it has now been fulfilled thus. The Jew, calling upon God only with his voice, was rejected; the people of the nations, who did not know God, was chosen.

Observe both things, [Col. 0557D] observe, I say, both things; and hear through Malachi most plainly both that Jews are rejected and nations chosen: “I have no pleasure in you, says the Lord of hosts, and I shall not receive an offering from your hand. For from the rising of the sun even to its setting my name is great among the nations, and in every place a clean offering is sacrificed and offered to my name” (Mal. I). But this was not so in Malachi’s time. For then the whole world, except for a few Jews, served not the Creator but the creature; it sacrificed not to God but to idols. Therefore, what was not accomplished at that time had to be fulfilled at some time. The present tense is indeed used in the prophecy, but the future is meant. Even if you are little learned, you will recognize this to be the custom of your Scriptures. Therefore what is shown not to have existed in the time when the prophet preached is recognized as fulfilled in these days of the Christian faith.

Truly, God’s name and that of his Christ are now great among the nations, and from the rising of the sun to its setting every tongue confesses that “the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father” (Phil. II). [Col. 0558A] But what shall I say also about what follows: “In every place a clean offering is sacrificed and offered to my name”? What shall I say concerning, “I shall not receive an offering from your hands”? Has not your temple long since been overthrown? Has not the altar been dug up? Have not sacrifices been withdrawn? Have not burnt offerings been taken away? Here Jewish controversy certainly fails; here hardened obstinacy wholly yields.

You see, Jew, what you cannot deny; you see what you are unable, in your usual manner, to interpret this way and that. See, therefore, also how in every place a clean offering is offered to God. See Christ’s churches built throughout the whole world; altars consecrated everywhere; the Lamb of God, whom you killed upon the cross, continually offered in those same churches upon those same altars to the almighty Father for the salvation of the world. You behold in all these things the fulfillment of those prophetic words: “I shall not receive an offering from your hands,” and, “In every place a clean offering is offered to my name.” [Col. 0558B] Therefore cease henceforth to be so absurdly foolish as to say that you alone are chosen while others are despised, or suppose that you alone are received while others are rejected, when on the contrary you hear that he has chosen others after rejecting you, called others after repulsing you, and received others after casting you aside.

[Col. 0558C] Therefore, to conclude this chapter with its proper ending: either reject the Scriptures that deny Christ’s temporal kingdom, or, if you do not dare, accept the everlasting kingdom of our Christ.

## Chapter IV. That Christ is not, as the Jews foolishly suppose, still to come; but has already come, at the certain and preordained time, for the salvation of the world.

A fourth and almost final battle against you, Jew, now remains for me; and He who granted me victory in the earlier ones will, I think, easily grant me the palm in this one. I trust that, if you refuse to live, the sword of Goliath will not fail me for your destruction: after you have been cast down by it, I shall employ it for your utter ruin, cutting off with the blade your blasphemous head—the head with which you had marched armed against God. [Col. 0558D] For when this combat, which alone almost remains, has been ended, you will cease to draw breath any further; when this battle is complete, you will never dare anywhere to mutter again.

The issue for which this present conflict must be undertaken is this. I say that Christ, foretold by the prophets, has already come; you deny it and say: “No, but he is to come.” I say: “He came”; you say: “He will come.” Therefore it is incumbent on me to prove what I have proposed. And, lest I delay long or keep you in suspense long, listen: listen, I say, not to just any prophet, but to the very great father of the prophets, a great prophet—indeed, a great patriarch—Jacob. Listen to him in whose lineage and name you glory, from whom you are called Israel, and from whom—would that you might be called, not only in name but in fact, a man seeing God. If, then, you are a seeing man, see, understand, attend to [Col. 0559A] what he says:

> “The sceptre shall not be taken away from Judah, nor a ruler from his loins, until he comes who is to be sent; and he himself shall be the expectation of the nations” (Gen. XLIX).

Come now: what evasions can still be sought? What subterfuges? There is no way by which you can escape. For if this was spoken of Christ, you must either show me a royal sceptre from Judah, or a ruler from Judah’s loins, or concede that Christ has already come. But that it was spoken of Christ, I think, no Jew disputes. I once discussed this saying with certain Jews, who declared that they understood it to have been uttered of none other than Christ, and that all Jews agreed in this interpretation.

But if someone from that number of the faithless, despairing that he can resist such evident prophetic language, should wish to interpret this of some other person whatsoever, he will fail, defeated in his futile effort to deceive. Of whom besides Christ can words so singular and so solemn be understood? Of which prophet besides Christ, or of which king besides Christ, can this be understood: “until he comes who is to be sent”? Of whom besides Christ can it be understood: “He himself shall be the expectation of the nations”? Since all prophets are sent by God, who is this one of whom it is said uniquely, “until he comes who is to be sent,” if not Christ? Certainly the holy patriarch knew that this name of being sent was common to all prophets.

What, therefore, he knew to be common, he uttered specially of one person. Unless that person’s mission were greater than the missions of the prophets, he would not have described it as singular in this singular manner. Since he did so describe it, he showed that the one whom he said was to be sent was greater than all who had been sent or were to be sent. And that Christ is greater than all mortals, you too, Jew, confess. It is therefore established that what was said of him who is greater than all must be understood only of Christ, whom you yourself also profess to be greater.

Moreover, who besides Christ could be called “the expectation of the nations”? What is asserted is no small thing, nor is he small of whom so great a thing is asserted. He whom the nations are said to await, who is proclaimed as destined to be the expectation of the nations, must necessarily be great and greater than all. He is certainly not one of the common crowd, not among the ordinary number of men, [Col. 0559D] in whom both the failure of Jewish rule and the expectation of the nations to be saved take their beginning.

See, Jew, whether perhaps he whom the patriarch calls “the expectation of the nations” is the same one whom the prophet writes as standing “as a sign for the peoples.” For these are the words of Isaiah:

> “On that day the root of David, who stands as a sign for the peoples—the nations themselves shall entreat him” (Isa. XI).

Thus the one whom Jacob said would be awaited by the nations, Isaiah said would be worshipped by those same nations. Search the whole text of divine Scripture and show that such or similar words were spoken of any king of Jews or Gentiles, of any ruler of Jews or Gentiles. But I know that you will fail; I know that apart from Christ you will find no one to whom these things can apply.

And since this is evident, return [Col. 0560A] to the matter proposed. You who maintain that Christ has not yet come—according to the judgment of your patriarch, show a sceptre from Judah or a ruler from his loins. The prophetic voice compels you to this. Either, as has been said, you will confess with us that Christ has come; or, if you deny that he has come, you are compelled to show a king or ruler from the tribe of Judah. For, as you know, by the sceptre, with which only a king’s right hand is customarily distinguished, a king is signified; by the title “ruler,” a prince of lower rank; and by Judah’s thigh, his posterity is signified.

Bring me, then, a king from Judah’s offspring; or, if you cannot do this, at least show a ruler. But I shall not, in order to provide something laughable, accept as king that man whom some of your people admit they possess at Narbonne, a city of Gaul, and others at Rouen. I shall not, I say, accept as king of the Jews any Jew dwelling in Gaul, Germany, Italy, or the remote regions of the East, Africa, or the North—or anywhere else. I shall not accept a Jew as king of the Jews unless he dwells and reigns in the kingdom of the Jews.

You do not fail to know that the ancient kingdom of the Jews is that in which David, Solomon, and the other Jewish kings once reigned: the kingdom for which you now sigh with inveterate lamentation, and from which you bewail yourself, in never-ending mourning, as an exile. I do not want you to put before me the empty title of king; nor do I want you, even if he sprang from the tribe of Judah itself, to object to me any one of your people. I do not want a king in name alone; nor do I want a king of that very stock who lacks royal power. And, O souls deceived by Satan’s various phantasms! Because they cannot glory in realities, they glory in the empty names of things. They pursue the shadows of bodies, holding nothing solid in their hands; and while, like dogs, they try to snatch images reflected in a stream, they lose through the thoughtless gaping of their mouths the food which they could already have been chewing, grasped in their teeth.

Should I accept a wretch as fortunate, a captive as a native citizen, a slave as a king? For I do not say a king, I do not say a ruler: show me, at least, even one Jew in the whole world who is free from the disgrace of servitude. What nations do not rule Jews? To what peoples are Jews not subject? What race of men does not trample them as the most worthless slaves? Truly, as God once threatened them in [Col. 0560D] Deuteronomy, although in respect of religion they had been the head of all peoples, they have now been turned into the tail of all nations (Deut. XXVIII). Thinking nothing anywhere secure for themselves, fearing even what need not be feared, and anxiously awaiting every turn of events, they are, like the fratricide Cain, wanderers and fugitives upon the earth. Their life, as is written in the book just mentioned, hangs continually before their eyes; shaken by the great force of fear, they do not believe in their own life (ibid.).

Will you then give me, Jew, a king from the number of such people? Will you offer an exile as a king? Will you produce a slave as a king? Will you put forward a bondsman as a ruler? Will you say that the prophecy still remains in such persons: “The sceptre shall not be taken away from Judah, nor a ruler from his loins”? And since it is [Col. 0561A] clear that, without royal dignity, to glory in the empty title of king is childish and foolish, if you will not confess that Christ has already come, show a king who has royal power as well as the royal name. If you cannot, at least produce a ruler of the Jews.

But since, upon Christ’s coming, both the glory of kingship and the power of rulership utterly perished among the Jews, understand that Christ has come—the one whom Jacob said was to be sent, whom we believe and declare was sent by God a very long time ago. I have indeed already shown that he was sent; but I have not yet proved at what time. Yet the prophecy just cited clearly demonstrates this. For it says that Christ was to be sent at the time when, kings or rulers having been removed, Jewish sovereignty was to be taken away.

Examine with me, therefore, the sequence of Judah’s line; and when you have learned that kingship or rulership in the tribe of Judah ceased, then acknowledge that Christ came, then worship him, then receive him. Although Scripture does not conceal that Judah himself, while he lived, was more worthy than his brothers, and that his tribe enjoyed certain privileges distinguishing it from the others, nevertheless his kingdom or rule began principally with David and endured until Christ’s times. Begin, then, with David, the first king, in counting the tribe of Judah; and recognize that from then on the sceptre did not fail from Judah, nor a ruler from his thigh.

Pass through each ruler, and, having counted Solomon, Rehoboam, Abijah, Asa, and the successors, proceed as far as Jehoiakim or Zedekiah, the last king of the tribe of Judah before the Babylonian captivity. Then continue through Shealtiel and his son Zerubbabel, the restorer of God’s temple and the first ruler from the tribe of Judah after the royal dignity, [Col. 0561C] and through those whom Josephus, the Jewish narrator of Jewish antiquity, himself describes, down to Herod. When you have learned that all those rulers who governed the Jewish people throughout that period derived their lineage from the tribe of Judah, observe that in the aforesaid Herod not only kingship but also rulership failed from that tribe.

If you have read, recall; if you have not read, read and learn: throughout the period lying between Zerubbabel and Herod, those descending from the aforesaid tribe of Judah held Jewish sovereignty—sometimes under the title of rulers, sometimes kings, but more frequently high priests.

[Col. 0561D] But if you say that the origin from the tribe of Judah of those who ruled from Zerubbabel to Herod cannot be established clearly from the histories, I answer: although this cannot be gathered openly from the histories, it is nevertheless clearly established from the prophecy already cited, which surpasses all such histories. For although the histories of Josephus or others did not expressly state by name from which Jewish tribe the aforesaid leaders derived their descent, still they in no way deny what they do not affirm. The prophecy, therefore, fully supplies what the histories lack, since the Spirit of God speaking in prophecy is far more worthy of trust than any writer who, in the human manner, describes what seems fit to him. What the historical writer left unspoken, the Spirit declared; what was lacking to him, God supplied.

Therefore, as stated, from Zerubbabel to Herod leaders deriving their line from the tribe of Judah presided over the Jews, sometimes under the name of rulers, sometimes kings, sometimes high priests. Though they unlawfully and ambitiously seized the high priesthood—which by the Law was due to the sons of Levi—they nevertheless governed the Jews throughout that period under one title of dignity or another. For when the Persians or Macedonians, under whose authority they were subject, prevented them from using the royal title or splendour, they presided over the Jews either through simple rulership or by the dignity of the priesthood.

If you wish also to know their names, listen. Zerubbabel, ruler of Judah, was succeeded in the honour of the high priesthood by Joachim, son of Jesus the high priest, who is mentioned in the prophet Haggai. Eliasu succeeded him; Eliasu, Joiada; Joiada, John; John, Judas; Judas, Onias; [Col. 0562B] Onias, Eleazar; Eleazar, another Onias; Onias, Simon; Simon, a third Onias; Onias, in sovereignty without priesthood, Judas Maccabaeus; Judas, both in rulership and priesthood, his brother Jonathan; Jonathan, in both offices, Simon, brother of them both; Simon, John; John, Aristobulus.

This man, the first after Zedekiah to assume the royal diadem while retaining for himself the high-priestly dignity, governed the people for only one year, as stated above. Aristobulus was succeeded by Alexander, who, like him, was both king and priest. After him his wife Alexandra also ruled. Thereafter the two sons of the said Alexander and Alexandra succeeded: Hyrcanus in the high priesthood, Aristobulus in the kingdom. When Aristobulus had been defeated, bound, and sent to Rome by Pompey, the Roman consul, Herod—wholly alien from the lineage of Judah or of the Jews—obtained the kingdom of the Jews by order of the Roman senate, after Hyrcanus, the already-mentioned brother of Aristobulus, had been killed.

Trust your Josephus, who writes that Herod himself was born of an Idumaean father named Antipater and an Arabian mother named Cypris. While this Herod held the Jewish kingdom, not only does the voice of the Gospel proclaim that Christ was born, but the history of the aforesaid Josephus and the reliable report of many Christians and pagans declare it. From Herod’s time, then, until this present time in which I have written these things—the one thousand one hundred and forty-fourth year—exert all your effort and show, if you can, even one ruler, not to say king, from Judah or from any tribe of the Jews. [Col. 0562D]

Does not this same Josephus of yours report that, when Herod the First died, his son Archelaus succeeded, by command of the Roman Caesar, to the rule of the entire Jewish kingdom? When he was removed, did not other sons of Herod himself, or near relatives by blood, succeed in the same kingdom through tetrarchies or numerous divisions? And did not all these rule scarcely sixty years, from Christ’s birth until the vast and final destruction of the city of Jerusalem and of the entire Jewish kingdom? Thereafter that land, once given by God to the Jews, spat out all Jews as though they were worthless bodily filth; scattering them through the whole world, it exposed them to be trampled under the feet of all nations. You know that they have not been able not only to aspire to any kingdom or sovereignty, but [Col. 0563A] not even to breathe free in any way from shameful servitude.

What, therefore, remains? Plainly this: either you will show that a royal sceptre or the office of ruler from Judah’s descendants still remains; or, since the sceptre has now been removed from Judah and a ruler from his thigh, you will confess that Christ has already come. Nor is that all. You must either rationally disprove everything I have produced from the divine books or reliable histories, or, if you cannot do this, confess that Christ was born under King Herod.

But truly, as is clear even to bleary and blind eyes, no Jewish perversity, no madness of any error, can withstand so firm a truth. Let the stiff neck therefore bow down; let the blasphemous tongue be silenced; and let it worship Christ, the Saviour of the world—not awaiting him as one who has not yet come and will come, but worshipping him as one who has already inundated the world with the bright radiance of his advent.

What do you think of all these matters, Jew? Has not your Jewish heart yet been buried beneath so great a heap of divine judgments? Does anything of condemnable unbelief still remain? Perhaps I am excessive in the eyes of others, because, suspecting your hardness, I seem perhaps to have been more prolix in speaking than is just. Let the discourse, therefore, draw toward its end, and let it bring this long-protracted matter to a conclusion in the last of the prophets.

Come, then, Daniel: after the others, you too, inferior to none of the preceding prophets, declare what concerning Christ’s coming God revealed to you through Gabriel. Unfold every covering, make clear the obscure things, unlock what is closed. Compel the Jews to confess what they deny, [Col. 0563C] and declare to them not only that Christ would come but also the very time at which he was to come. And lest any escape should lie open to their stubborn evasiveness, or any place remain for excuse, count out for them the years from the time of the vision shown to you up to Christ. Hear, then, Jews, the prophet of God; and calculate, with little stones or even with the fingers of your own hands, the prophetic years from Daniel to Christ. Seek Christ no longer either before or after; hold fast the utterly certain year of his coming.

Hear, then, Gabriel speaking to Daniel:

> “Daniel, attend to the word and understand the vision. Seventy weeks are determined concerning your people [Col. 0563D] and concerning your holy city, that transgression may be consummated, sin may come to its end, iniquity may be wiped away, everlasting righteousness may be brought in, vision and prophecy may be fulfilled, and the Holy of Holies may be anointed. Know therefore and attend: from the issuing of the word that Jerusalem should be rebuilt until Christ the ruler there shall be seven weeks and sixty-two weeks. Street and walls shall again be built, in the straitness of times. And after sixty-two weeks Christ shall be killed, and the people who would deny him shall not be his. A people with a coming leader shall destroy the city and the sanctuary, and its end shall be desolation. And after the end of the war, desolation is decreed. He shall confirm the covenant with many for one week; and in the middle of the week sacrifice and offering shall fail, [Col. 0564A] and in the temple shall be the abomination of desolation. Desolation shall endure until consummation and the end” (Dan. IX).

What are you doing, Jews? Behold, your prophet describes not only the year of Christ’s coming, but also the time of his passion and death. Nor does he describe only this: he has not omitted to foretell or describe everything that befell you from that time—the fate of your city, your sanctuary, and the entire Jewish stock up to the present day. Return, therefore, to the calculation of years, and from this vision of Daniel to Christ derive not only the elapsed time but the very year in which he was born.

But lest the words of a modern narrator seem contemptible to you, receive this same calculation not from a modern writer but from Tertullian, an ancient and most learned man. Though he was one of ours, you cannot refuse to believe him when, from the dates of rulers and the authority of reliable histories, you are forced by him to yield to truth. Hear him, then:

> “Whence,” he says (*Against the Jews*, book I, ch. 8), “have we shown that Christ came within seventy-two weeks? Count from the first year of Darius, because at that time the vision itself was shown to Daniel. For he says to him: ‘Understand and infer from the prophecy of the word that I answer you these things.’ Therefore we must calculate from the first year of Darius, when Daniel saw this vision. Let us see how the years are completed up to Christ’s coming. Darius reigned nineteen years; Artaxerxes, forty-one; Ochus, also Cyrus, twenty-four years; Argus, one year; another Darius, also called the Mede, twenty-two years; Alexander the Macedonian, twelve years.

> Then, after Alexander, who had ruled both Medes and Persians after defeating them and had established his kingdom at Alexandria—then also calling it by his own name—there ruled there, after him, Soter among the Alexanders, thirty-five years; he was succeeded by Philadelphus, who reigned thirty-eight years. After him Euergetes reigned twenty-five years; then Philopator, seventeen years; after him Epiphanes, twenty-four years; likewise another Euergetes, twenty-seven years; Soter, thirty-eight years; Ptolemy, thirty-eight years; Cleopatra, twenty years and five months. Then Cleopatra reigned jointly with Augustus for thirteen years. After Cleopatra Augustus ruled another thirteen years. For all the years of Augustus numbered fifty-six.

> We see, however, that Christ was born in the forty-first year of the reign of Augustus, [Col. 0564D] who ruled after Cleopatra’s death. Moreover, Augustus himself lived fifteen years after Christ’s birth. Thus the remaining periods of years, on the day of Christ’s birth, amount to the forty-first year of Augustus after Cleopatra’s death: four hundred and thirty-seven years and five months. Hence sixty-two weeks and a half are completed, amounting to four hundred and thirty-seven years and six months on the day of Christ’s birth. Everlasting righteousness was manifested; the Holy of Holies, that is, Christ, was anointed; vision and prophecy were sealed; and sins were remitted, which are granted through faith in Christ’s name to all who believe in him.

> What does it mean for vision and prophecy to be sealed? All the prophets announced concerning him that he would come and would suffer. Therefore, because prophecy was fulfilled by his coming, he said that vision and prophecy were sealed, because he is the seal of all prophets, fulfilling all that the prophets previously announced. For after his coming and passion there is no longer vision or prophet announcing that Christ is to come.”

And a little later he says (*ibid.*):

> “Let us see in what event the other seven and a half weeks, which are divided in the cutting-off of the former weeks, were fulfilled. For Augustus survived Christ’s birth by fifteen years. Tiberius Caesar succeeded him and held the empire twenty-two years, seven months, and twenty-eight days. In the nineteenth year of his reign Christ suffered, being about thirty-three years old when he suffered. Likewise, Gaius Caesar, also Caligula, [Col. 0565B] three years, seven months, and thirteen days; Tiberius Claudius, thirteen years, seven months, and twenty days; Nero, eight years, nine months, and thirteen days; Galba, seven months and twenty-eight days; Otho, three months and five days; Vitellius, eight months and eighteen days. In the first year of his reign Vespasian subdued the Jews; and the total comes to fifty-two years and six months. For he ruled ten years. Thus, to the day of their conquest, the Jews completed the seventy weeks foretold by Daniel.”

What now remains for your error, O Jews; what remains for your wicked obstinacy—indeed, what for your condemnable madness? Behold: while a truthful and learned man expounds and distinguishes the number of years, you see that from the year in which this vision was revealed to the prophet to the final [Col. 0565C] overthrow of your city and kingdom, within seventy weeks—that is, 490 years—transgression was consummated, sin came to its end, iniquity was wiped away, everlasting righteousness was brought in, vision and prophecy were fulfilled, and the Holy of Holies was anointed.

How was this done? Produce whatever you have and show when, how, or through whom these great, wondrous, and most worthy things were completed within this prescribed period. Say in what way transgression was consummated; how sin came to its end; how everlasting righteousness was brought in within the same term; how vision and prophecy were fulfilled; and finally who he was who, at that time, is proclaimed as the anointed Holy of Holies.

Indeed, in the days mentioned above for the sake of another argument, there were some who, together with the diadem that they assumed, perhaps also employed royal anointing for themselves: first Aristobulus, then his successor Alexander; again another Aristobulus, and afterwards Herod or Archelaus. But was Aristobulus the Holy of Holies? Was Alexander the Holy of Holies? Was Archelaus the Holy of Holies? Did not the oft-mentioned Josephus report that all of these were followed by wicked beginnings, worse courses, and most evil ends? None of these, therefore, was the Holy of Holies. Of none of them, therefore, did the angel say to the prophet that the Holy of Holies was to be anointed.

You must therefore seek another within these seventy weeks, of whom the words “the Holy of Holies shall be anointed” can be understood. You must further either show how, in the same period, sin came to its end, everlasting righteousness was brought in, and vision and prophecy were fulfilled—or, if you cannot, ask others how it happened. Nothing therefore remains except that you understand the anointed Holy of Holies to be Christ our Lord, who, in respect of his humanity, was anointed by the almighty Father with the oil of gladness, and who is the Holy of Holies because he is above his companions. For the Spirit was not given to him in measure, as to other saints (John I), and thus he was the Holy of Holies. Nor was he Holy of Holies only for this reason, but also in order that he might sanctify all who were to be sanctified by that same Spirit with which he was filled. [Col. 0566B]

And when can you understand sin to have come to its end, and iniquity to have been wiped away within the aforesaid weeks, except either when, through his baptism, the sins of all who were baptized or were to be baptized were forgiven by him, or when he said to his disciples: “Receive the Holy Spirit; whose sins you forgive, they shall be forgiven them” (John XX)? What will you say also of the exceedingly clear prediction of Christ’s passion and death? In what does the evangelist reporting Christ’s death appear more plainly than the prophet foretelling it? “After sixty-two weeks,” he says, “Christ shall be killed.”

O pitiable deafness of the faithless! O detestable blindness of the ungodly! Why do you not awaken at so great a thunderclap of the prophetic voice? Why do you not open your eyes at so great a brightness of the angelic sun? You hear the angel speaking; you see the prophet writing: “After sixty-two weeks Christ shall be killed.” What are you doing? What are you saying? Behold, the angel says and the prophet writes that, over seventy weeks of years—that is, over 490 years—a period of free wandering was granted you, and that after sixty-two weeks Christ was to be killed.

What, then, remains of the seventy weeks after sixty-two have been set down? Eight, certainly. Therefore the prophetic utterance presses you to confess that Christ suffered, that Christ was killed, within those eight weeks. But of those eight, half a week, according to the calculation of the author just named, was completed on the very day of Christ’s birth. Seven and a half therefore remain. In their calculation, beginning from that same birth of Christ, four weeks are completed; then, with five and a half years of the fifth week added—that is, thirty-three and a half years, Christ’s age up to his passion—there remains of that fifth week one year and a half after Christ’s passion. With that year and a half joined to the two weeks remaining of the seven aforesaid weeks, there result fifteen and a half years. To those fifteen and a half years, adding that half-week which remained after the seven, containing three and a half years, produces nineteen years. It is therefore evident that the number of these seven and a half weeks is thus completed, and that Christ suffered within those same weeks, nineteen years after his passion. [Col. 0567A]

If, therefore, these seven and a half weeks—within which we have proved that Christ suffered, and which, we have said, begin from the very day of Christ’s birth—are added to the other sixty-two and a half which preceded Christ’s birth, then the sum of the seventy weeks foretold by the angel Gabriel or the prophet Daniel will be completed. Within these, according to the foregoing division of times, transgression was consummated, sin came to its end, iniquity was wiped away, everlasting righteousness was brought in, vision and prophecy were fulfilled, and the Holy of Holies was anointed. Within these, moreover, that Holy of Holies who is called the Anointed—that is, Christ—was killed; and the Jewish people, [Col. 0567B] who denied him with a blasphemous mouth, were rejected by him.

If this seems obscure to you, hear the same matter more plainly. Once, as has been said, sixty-two and a half weeks had been completed from the year of this prophetic vision up to Christ’s birth, do not seven and a half weeks remain of the total of seventy weeks? You cannot deny it. And how many years are counted in seven and a half weeks? Certainly fifty-two and a half. For it is certain that, just as weeks of days are always reckoned by the number seven, so in this prophetic vision weeks of years are reckoned by the sevenfold number.

The total, therefore, of seven and a half weeks makes [Col. 0567C] fifty-two and a half years. These fifty-two and a half years remain from Christ’s birthday until the complete fulfilment of the seventy weeks. Count, then, Jew, as precisely as you can, and you will find that Christ suffered within these fifty-two and a half years, after thirty-three years and a half had already elapsed—indeed, as your prophet says, that he was killed. When thirty-three and a half years are subtracted from fifty-two and a half, nineteen years remain. When these nineteen years after Christ’s passion or death are completed, the full number of the seventy weeks foretold by Daniel is found; and within these the Holy of Holies was anointed; within these the same Anointed—that is, Christ—was killed; within these iniquity was wiped away, everlasting righteousness was manifested, and vision and prophecy were made clearer than the shining sun.

But if you are so expert in histories as to object that Tertullian entirely omitted the years of Claudius Caesar and differs from certain other historians in his count of the years of that period, I answer: this has nothing to do with the matter proposed. Let historians differ as much as they wish in their calculation of years from the Lord’s passion, since it is clearly established, according to the oft-cited prophecy of Daniel, that within seventy weeks Christ was born, Christ suffered, iniquity was wiped away, and everlasting righteousness appeared; and that absolutely all the mysteries of human salvation were completed in him and through him.

Yet, although I say this, although some faulty copy excerpted from Tertullian’s principal book, [Col. 0568A] as I once read, omits the years of Claudius Caesar among the years of the Caesars, the author’s own book itself—where no Caesar from Augustus to Vespasian and Titus is omitted, and where, as it excludes none while counting them in their succession, it carefully records the entire number of years during which they held power—states this. Since water from the spring is always purer than water from a stream, greater trust must be given to an author diligently investigating the truth than to any excerptor carelessly copying another’s work.

Therefore, O Jews, that I may come more quickly to the due conclusion of the arguments set forth: you must, you are required either to show another anointed one, another Holy of Holies, plainly another Christ, killed in the time of the weeks just mentioned, [Col. 0568B] in the very year of those weeks; or to receive with us our Anointed, our Holy of Holies, our Christ—the redeemer and saviour of his own—not as crucified by any persons whatsoever, but as crucified in those days by your own fathers and killed by the very torment of the cross.

And because it has been proved that Christ was killed after sixty-two weeks and within the seventieth; because the very week in which he is written to have been killed has been shown, and the very year in which he was killed has been made clear: do not, do not, if you are of sound mind, seek another Christ any longer; do not await another.

Attend also to what follows in the prophecy, [Col. 0568C] and read what was indeed foretold therein but has been fulfilled more clearly in you: “The people who will deny him shall not be his” (Dan. IX). Truly, you are no longer his; truly, so long as inveterate madness remains in you, you will not be his. You will not be his, you will not be, as of old, his own people; but you are and will be strangers, as God speaks of you in the Psalm: “Strange children have lied to me; strange children have grown old and have limped from their paths” (Ps. XVII). And there has been fulfilled in you what he himself threatens such persons with also in our Gospel: “Whoever denies me before men, I will deny him before the angels of God” (Matt. X). You denied him when you killed him; you denied him when you rejected the stone which has now been made the head of the corner (Ps. CXVII); you denied him when, to the judge who said, “Shall I crucify your king?” [Col. 0568D] (John XIX), you answered, “We have no king but Caesar” (ibid.). From this recognize what was foretold of you by the angel and spoken by the prophet: “The people who will deny him shall not be his.”

Nor should what immediately follows escape you: “The people with the coming leader shall destroy the city and the sanctuary, and its end shall be desolation. And after the end of the war, desolation is decreed.” Did not your fathers experience all these things? Did they not behold them all with their own eyes? Did not, immediately after these seventy weeks had ended, the Roman people, coming with their leader Vespasian and his son Titus, destroy the Jewish kingdom? Did they not overthrow all its cities? Did they not destroy, burn, and raze to the ground Jerusalem itself, the capital of your kingdom, and its sanctuary? [Col. 0569A] Did they not condemn the entire Jewish people to varied outcomes of diverse miseries? Did they not, besides countless others, kill or take captive three hundred thousand persons found in Jerusalem itself, your chief city, during the siege? This desolation was the end of your city, the end of your sanctuary. In accordance with the prophetic utterances, decreed desolation followed that end.

“But perhaps the desolation was brief, a desolation of a few years.” No, no. And why do I say merely no? Hear the prophet himself; hear the angel speaking to the prophet: “Desolation shall endure until consummation and the end.” It will not, he says, be brief; it will not be of short duration; it will not resemble other desolations. It will not resemble Egyptian oppression; it will not resemble Babylonian captivity; [Col. 0569B] it will not resemble subjection to the Assyrians, Macedonians, or any other peoples. For relief followed all those after no great length of time. But this last desolation has for one thousand one hundred years now been followed by no consolation, not even a slight one. And why do I say that none has followed? I say something greater: indeed, none will ever follow thereafter. Hear the prophet attentively: “Desolation shall endure until consummation and the end.” Until what consummation? Until what end? Surely until the consummation of all things, until the end of the world.

Why then do you still dream of an imaginary Christ? Why do you still hope for a false Christ—indeed, for no Christ at all? Why do you suppose that earthly freedom is still to be restored to you? Why do you await a return to the ancient land of the old promise? [Col. 0569C] Hear, receive, heed Gabriel speaking and Daniel writing: “Desolation shall endure until consummation and the end.”

It has therefore been proved, O Jews, as I think, by a fourfold division, that the Christ repeatedly foretold or proclaimed by the prophets must be understood as the Son of God—not a son of God in the manner of certain human beings who, because of some grace bestowed on them by God, have been called sons of God, but the Son of God by his very natural generation from the essence of the Father. It has been proved that this Son of God is also God. Not one of the number of those gods of whom it is written, “The God of gods, the Lord, has spoken” (Ps. XLIX); but [Col. 0569D] truly, as light from light, true God from true God. It has been proved that this same Christ must in no way be regarded as an earthly or fleshly king, nor his kingdom believed to be temporal. For it has been shown that earthly rule does not befit God, and perishable things do not suit the eternal one. It has been proved that Christ has already come, and that he who has come is not to be awaited by Jews or anyone else as though he had not come.

Since all these things, O Jews, have been proved by sacred authorities and invincible arguments, what are you holding out for? If you give credence to your Scriptures, yield to their authorities.
