If you are rational or reasonable, assent to reason. But if you are also inquisitive—because, according to our Apostle, “Jews seek signs” (1 Cor. I)—believe these things, confirmed by miracles. [Col. 0570A] Do not now exalt your horn on high; do not speak iniquity against God (Ps. LXXIV). Do not boast of the miracles wrought in the time of your law, nor prefer them, for any reason, to Christ’s Gospel. The miracles of the Jewish law were indeed great and many; but the wondrous works of Christian faith are far greater and incomparably more numerous. For, leaving aside the miracles themselves, which cannot be numbered, who could recount the workers of miracles from the beginning of Christian grace to our own time? Who could recount so many and such great persons, spread throughout the whole world from the very days of the Lord Christ, who by divine and astonishing deeds crushed the proud neck of the world and subjected it to the humility of Christian faith?

[Col. 0570B] Compare your Moses, O Jew, not, I say, with Christ, but at least, if you dare, with his apostle Peter, and you will see which ought to be preferred to which in such matters, which surpasses which by mighty miracles. Let Moses, at God’s command, have divided the Red Sea; let manna have rained from the clouds; let him have brought water from the rock; and let him have done certain similar things—great indeed, but few. But what are these beside Peter? I pass over his commanding demons, raising the dead, often curing every kind of disease not only by command but even by the shadow of his body alone, and doing all the wonders he wished, in whatever manner he wished. What memory could recall, what tongue could utter, only those works which he performed through countless disciples sent to different parts of the world in order to carry the faith there?

For I do not say a few, I do not say many, but whole peoples rescued from various plagues, cured of diverse diseases; the dead, not merely three or four days dead but forty years dead, raised by the power of Peter’s disciples; the sun held still, mountains moved, seas divided, waves trodden underfoot, the elements conquered—when could I suffice to recount them? [Col. 0570C] But perhaps you think Peter alone among the apostles shone with such signs. This was not said to Peter alone; it was enjoined by Christ upon all twelve of his fellow apostles: “Heal the sick,” he says, “raise the dead, cleanse lepers, cast out demons” (Matt. X). And again: “Behold, I have given you authority to tread upon serpents and scorpions, and over all the power of the enemy” (Luke X). And above: “Do not rejoice because the spirits are subject to you” (ibid.). And elsewhere: “If you have faith like a grain of mustard seed, and say to the mountain, ‘Move into the sea,’ it will move” (Matt. XVII).

Nor was this lofty and great power of miracles given only to the twelve apostles or to those who adhered to him bodily during his mortal life. Hear what is said by Christ, now having suffered, died, and risen, concerning all who truly believe: “These signs shall follow those who believe: in my name they shall cast out demons; they shall speak in new tongues; they shall take up serpents; [Col. 0570D] and if they drink anything deadly, it shall not harm them. They shall lay their hands upon the sick, and they shall be well” (Mark XVI). There is no number, O Jew, to Christian signs; there is no number to the wondrous works of Christian faith. Truly infinite is the number of works, infinite the number of workers. Apart from Moses, Joshua, Gideon, Samson, Samuel, Isaiah, Elijah, Elisha, and Jonah, distinguished by wondrous works, your law has few; Christian faith has had and has innumerable performers of miracles.

Why then do you still whisper? Why do you mutter? Yield at last, yield your hands to Christ, whom by so many sacred authorities, so many unquestionable arguments, and so many and such great miraculous signs you have proved to be the Son of God, God, the eternal king, and one who came already at the certain time foretold long beforehand. Do not complain further that the Mosaic law was changed by Christ; for as God is he who gave that law, so God is he who commanded that this Gospel law be observed. It is not one God and another—one giving that law and another this one—but the very same God, Christ, [Col. 0571B] who gave the former law to the Jews before he appeared to humankind in flesh; he himself, now made man, commanded all alike, both Jews and Gentiles, to observe this second, new, and final law. And if he is God, what he commands must certainly be observed. But he has been proved to be God by authorities, arguments, and miracles. It follows, therefore, that what he has said must be held valid, and what he has commanded must be kept as God’s commandment.

If, therefore, you shrink from opposing God, you must accept the commands of Christ God; you must submit your neck, long and greatly proud of old, to his sweet yoke, as he himself calls it (Matt. XI). If you acknowledge Christ as God, you will no longer have with us the inveterate [Col. 0571C] dispute, nor the old complaint—as though your law had been scorned—that Christians reject circumcision, disregard the Sabbath, and do not serve legal sacrifices. You will see and understand that God was permitted to dispense what was fitting to each time: now these things, now those; to different persons in different ways; now to individuals, now to many, now to all, according to his reason, fully known to himself alone, concerning persons, causes, and times.

If you look carefully, you will observe that God did not issue new commands only in the era of Christian grace, once you recognize that, from the very beginning of the human creation, as your Scriptures attest, he often did similar things. Did he not say new things, things he had not said before, when, punishing guilty humanity in its sin, he said: “Cursed is the earth in your work; in labours [Col. 0571D] you shall eat of it all the days of your life” (Gen. III), and the rest? Did he not grant new things, things which he is not recorded as having permitted before, when, after the world had been destroyed by the flood, he spoke to Noah: “All the fish of the sea are delivered into your hand, and everything that moves and lives shall be food for you” (Gen. IX)? And immediately: “As green plants I have given you all things, except that you shall not eat flesh with blood” (ibid.). He also, promulgating a new law concerning which he had until that time been silent, added: “For I will require the blood of your lives from the hand of every beast, and from the hand of man. From the hand of a man and his brother I will require the life of a man. Whoever sheds human blood, his blood shall be shed; for man was made in the image of God” (ibid.).

[Col. 0572A] Did he not command new things, things concerning which he had previously been altogether silent, when he enjoined our father Abraham according to faith, saying: “This is the covenant which shall be kept between me and you and your seed after you. Every male among you shall be circumcised, and you shall circumcise the flesh of your foreskin, that it may be a sign of the covenant between me and you” (Gen. XVII), and the rest that follows? Did he not command new things, things which he had concealed through so many ages, when through Moses he gave your fathers the Sabbath, the beginnings of months, manifold festivals, varied sacrifices, and, to gather much into a brief statement, the entire body of the law—of which you are more accustomed to be proud than edified—by word and writing? And who could easily enumerate all that the Godhead, providing for human salvation, commanded to be observed not all at once but gradually, whether universally or particularly, through many persons, not at the same but at different times?

If, then, before Christ became man God so often gave new and different commands to humankind, what wonder is it if the same Christ, in the same person both man and God, commanded what he saw to be more fitting for mortals in these days? But perhaps you will say: “You have proved that God often commanded new things. Yet you have neither proved, nor can prove, that the law given last through Moses was to be changed and ended.” I prove it, I say; and first I set forward Isaiah: “What use to me is the multitude of your victims? says the Lord. I am full. The burnt offerings of rams, the fat of fatlings, [Col. 0572C] and the blood of calves, lambs, and goats I have not desired” (Isa. I). And below: “Incense is an abomination to me. I will not endure the new moon, Sabbath, and other festivals. Your assemblies are iniquitous. My soul has hated your new moons and your solemnities” (ibid.).

But perhaps you will say that these are the words of an angry and indignant God, and contend that he rejects all these things only because of the sinfulness of the people at that time. But hear him speaking in the Psalm, with no prior cause of anger stated: “I will not take calves from your house, nor goats from your flocks” (Ps. XLIX). And after some words: “Shall I eat the flesh of bulls, or drink the blood of goats?” (ibid.). Having rejected such sacrifices, he adds what he prefers to them: “Offer to God a sacrifice of praise” (ibid.), and what follows. Hear also Malachi’s testimony, which above I cited for another reason: “I have no pleasure in you, says the Lord of hosts, and I will not receive an offering from your hand” (Mal. I).

Hear also that against which you will not be able to contend and which, once established, will compel you to silence. Hear God plainly promising that he will give new commands and change the old covenant, the Mosaic covenant, into Christ’s new and eternal covenant: “Behold, days are coming, says the Lord, and I will establish a covenant with the house of Judah, not according to the covenant which I gave their fathers when I took their hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt; but I will establish a new covenant for them, giving my laws in their minds and writing them in their hearts” (Jer. XXXI). He also speaks through Ezekiel, humbling and confounding your pride which boasts of such matters: [Col. 0573A] “I gave them statutes that were not good and judgments by which they would not live; and I defiled them in my gifts, when they offered everything that opens the womb, because of their sins” (Ezek. XX).

What then? Has it not been proved with ever greater clarity that God frequently gave new commands to the world and foretold that Moses’ law itself would be changed? Recognize, O Jew, that this was done through Christian faith, fulfilled through Gospel law, and that the old, transitory covenant remained in force only until the new and eternal covenant was reached.

But that the Jewish quiver may be emptied of the sharper arrow which you think it contains, bring it forth now and, with all the strength you can, shoot it toward our destruction, as you most earnestly desire. “And what,” you ask, “is the meaning of what God so frequently repeats in the law given to us, so often reiterates: that the law itself is never to end; that he commands sacrifices, diverse forms of worship, and every rite there described to be perpetuated by us? What, indeed, are the words read in Exodus, where God commands the immolation of the lamb: ‘You shall have this day as a memorial, and shall celebrate it as a solemn feast to the Lord throughout your generations, with everlasting worship’?” (Exod. XII). “And what of the passage written shortly afterward on the same matter in the same book: ‘Keep this ordinance for yourself and your children for ever’?” (ibid.).

Does not Leviticus assert the same? For, recounting and setting forth distinctly God’s many commands concerning the various kinds of sacrifice, it inserts these words: “The priest shall take a handful of flour mingled with oil, and all the frankincense placed upon the flour, and shall burn it upon the altar as a memorial of sweetest odour to the Lord” (Lev. VI). And after some intervening matters it adds: “It is an everlasting ordinance throughout your generations, concerning the sacrifices of the Lord” (ibid.). Again, a little later: “You and your sons shall not drink wine or anything that can intoxicate when you enter the tabernacle of testimony, lest you die, because it is an everlasting commandment throughout your generations” (Lev. X).

Likewise, when the same book of Leviticus treats of the first fruits of the harvest to be offered to God, it adds: “On the same day on which the sheaf is consecrated, [Col. 0573D] an unblemished lamb of one year shall be slain as a burnt offering to the Lord. Libations shall be offered with it: two tenths of flour mingled with oil, as an offering made by fire to the Lord, a most sweet fragrance; likewise a quarter-hin of wine” (Lev. XXIII). And after one verse: “It is,” he says, “an everlasting commandment throughout your generations and in all your dwellings” (ibid.). And shortly afterward: “You shall also offer a goat for sin, and two year-old lambs as peace offerings. When the priest has lifted them up with the loaves of first fruits before the Lord, they shall fall to his use” (ibid.). And immediately: “You shall call this day a most celebrated and most holy day. You shall do no servile work on it. It shall be an everlasting ordinance in all your dwellings and throughout your generations” (ibid.).

The following book, Numbers, adds something similar concerning the eternity of our law: “On the Sabbath day you shall offer two unblemished year-old lambs, and two tenths of flour mingled with oil as a sacrifice, and the libations duly poured out on each Sabbath, as an everlasting burnt offering” (Num. XXVIII). And not many words later, discussing the sacrifices on the first day of the seventh month, it says: [Col. 0574A] “You shall also offer a goat for sin, offered for the people’s expiation, besides the burnt offering of the new moons with its sacrifices. And you shall offer the everlasting burnt offering with the customary libations and the same ceremonies, as an offering of sweet fragrance made by fire to the Lord” (Num. XXIX).

Since, then, the eternity of our law is so repeatedly commended, why do you assert that it has been changed? Why do you affirm that it was foretold that it would be changed? But hear still more explicit testimony from Deuteronomy, and learn at least from it that it neither ought to have been nor should be changed at any time. For Moses, speaking in the aforesaid book to our fathers, says: “Lay up these words of mine in your hearts and souls; bind them as a sign upon your hands, and place them between your eyes. Teach your children to meditate upon them” (Deut. XI). And after some intervening words: “That your days and the days of your children,” he says, “may be multiplied in the land which the Lord swore to your fathers to give them, as long as heaven hangs over the earth” (ibid.). What could be said more clearly to demonstrate the perpetuity of our law?

Hear also the commands of our lawgiver from the same book of Deuteronomy, and consider from them whether our law is to be changed even in any point: “You shall not add to the word which I speak to you, nor take away from it” (Deut. IV). And elsewhere in the same book, after the many preceding curses, as though in the conclusion of those same curses, it is added: “Cursed is he who does not remain in the words of this law and fulfil them by deed.” And all the people say, “Amen” (Deut. XXVII).

It is true, O Jew—entirely true, as I see—that what our Apostle says concerning you and yours is true: “So long as Moses is read, a veil lies upon their heart” (2 Cor. III). True also is what Christ—not yours but ours—said after giving sight to the man born blind: “For judgment I have come into this world, that those who do not see may see and those who see may become blind” (John IX). For behold, your eyes, which once saw God, [Col. 0574D] have been blinded; the eyes of the Gentiles, shut until Christ’s time, have been opened by him. “All who hold the law,” he says, “have not known me” (Jer. II). The Jew indeed holds the law and does not know God; the Christian reads that same law and, recognizing God from it, worships him.

But return to the matters proposed, O Jew. You have objected everything you could object most forcefully in order to show that the Mosaic law ought to be perpetual, and to overthrow, as though by an invincible argument, what had been said about its change. But I ask: were the statements which you cited from the Pentateuch in order to prove the eternity of your law uttered by God through Moses? You answer, certainly, “By God.” I continue: were the statements which I advanced from the prophets to demonstrate the changing of your law uttered by God through them? This too, I think—indeed, as I know very well—you do not deny. If this is so, how great a discord in the divine words appears according to your interpretation is evident.

And, that what I say may appear more clearly, I shall take, from the sacred-scriptural testimonies which you cited, one in place of all—the representative of them all: God says, speaking of the immolation of the Paschal lamb, “You shall have this day as a memorial, and shall celebrate it as a solemn feast to the Lord throughout your generations, with everlasting worship” (Exod. XIII). From those texts which I have set forward in reply, I take one likewise as representative of all: Jeremiah’s testimony: “Behold, days are coming, says the Lord, and I will establish a covenant with the house of Judah, not according to the covenant which I gave their fathers [Col. 0575B] when I took their hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt. But I will establish a new covenant for them, giving my laws in their minds and writing them in their hearts” (Jer. XXXI).

You have heard, O Jew. Look, attend, turn every net toward the task, and draw together all that you can by mind or skill. You cannot deny—indeed, you confess, as I do—that the former was uttered by God through Moses and the latter by the same God through Jeremiah. Therefore make it so, make it so, I say, if you can, that he whom you read to be “faithful in his words” (Ps. CXLIV), and of whom you frequently read and sing that “he destroys all who speak falsehood” (Ps. V), may not himself appear plainly false in his words, and may not be joined to the liars whom he is written to destroy. For you seem, though perhaps you do not notice it, to hold such a wicked and blasphemous opinion about him. And why do I say, “You seem to hold it”? Rather, you openly profess it when you admit that God gave a perpetual law here, yet there foretold that it would end.

Choose, then—choose whichever of the two you wish. For if what he said through Moses concerning the law’s eternity, according to the Jewish understanding, is true, then what he foretold through Jeremiah about its change is false. If what Jeremiah says, that it was to be changed, is true, then what God commanded through Moses, that it should be perpetual, is false. Since, as you know, it is impious and detestable to think this of God, either untie, if you can, the knot thus put before you by a Jewish interpretation; or, if you cannot—which truly you cannot—assent to the sound and truthful [Col. 0575D] Christian understanding.

Hear, then, and do not be ashamed to be taught; for above all things it is foolish to prefer error to learning, to prefer being enveloped in one’s own darkness to being poured into light, even another’s light. Observe that God could not utter words contrary to himself or opposed to one another, saying in one place, according to your interpretation, that the law he gave was eternal, and in another foretelling that it would end. He gave the law to you and yours not as eternal in the strict sense, but expressly as one that would end. For how could he give a law not destined to end in a world which, together with all Jews and Gentiles in it, is destined to end at the time known and appointed by God? How, I ask, was a law given without end in a world that does not lack an end? How was an eternal law given to non-eternal beings? [Col. 0576A] How was it given to beings not merely dying gradually but at some time to fail altogether? For if, as I stated much above for a similar reason, heaven and earth will perish according to the words of your Psalm (Ps. CI), who does not see that neither Jewish sacrifices nor the various rites nor, finally, all that was commanded or described in that law can remain?

But perhaps you will quibble over the word; perhaps, according to your custom, you will cling to the sound of the letter. You will obstinately contend that Scripture calls that law perpetual, calls it eternal. But remember, if you have heard it; learn, if you have not learned it: “eternal” is not always understood as without limit, nor is “perpetual” always taken as without end. You have this in the Second Book of Kings: “And it came to pass in that night, and behold, the word of the Lord came to Nathan, saying: Go and speak to my servant David: Thus says the Lord: Shall you build me a house for my dwelling?” (2 Kings VII). And after some verses: “I will raise up your seed after you, who shall come forth from your womb, and I will establish his kingdom. He shall build a house for my name, and I will establish the throne of his kingdom for ever” (ibid.). And after some further matters: “Your house and your kingdom shall be faithful for ever before my face, and your throne shall be established continually” (ibid.).

What do you say to this? Have you not now found “for ever” with a limit? Have you not found “eternal” with an end? “I will establish the throne of his kingdom for ever.” Whose kingdom? Plainly, according to your Jewish—that is, fleshly—interpretation: Solomon’s, or that of kings succeeding him in the Jewish kingdom. Do you see that this “for ever” ended many ages ago? It truly ended with the coming of Christ our Lord, from and through whom the temporal throne of David’s sons was overthrown and shall no longer be restored for ever. What, too, will you say of the following testimony that was cited—namely: “Your house and your kingdom shall be faithful for ever”? Did David’s house—that is, David’s power—remain faithful to God after him, and this for ever? Even while the kingdom of David’s line remained in Judah, was not the unfaithfulness or perversity of certain kings so marked that truthful Scripture testifies of some of them: “So-and-so reigned so many years and did what was evil [Col. 0576D] in the sight of the Lord”? Was Joram faithful to God? Was Achar? Was Zedekiah? In Manasseh, Hezekiah’s son—an idolatrous, profane, and detestable man—did David’s house or kingdom remain faithful to God?

And where now is that “eternal” which I am contesting? For if it was eternal, how did it end, not merely at some point, but so soon? What more do you now demand? You hear that David’s throne was to be established for ever, though it ceased a thousand years ago. You hear that his house would be faithful for eternity, though, leaving aside those already mentioned, in Solomon himself, his son, worshipping idols, that faithfulness called eternal failed. And to prove, by manifold authority from books not foreign but yours, that “eternity” is often used for a finite time, hear what David himself sings to God concerning the same matter: “I will establish his seed for age upon age, and his throne like the days of heaven” (Ps. LXXXVIII). And below, after several verses: “Once have I sworn by my holiness: I will not lie to David; his seed shall remain for ever” (ibid.). And immediately: “And his throne shall be as the sun before me, and as the perfect moon for ever” (ibid.).

Why need these also be noted one by one? It is certain, plain, and cannot be denied that in the words, “I will establish his seed for age upon age,” or “His seed shall remain for ever,” or “His throne shall be as the sun before me, and as the perfect moon for ever,” eternity is by no means signified as infinite—an eternity which we see partly [Col. 0577B] ended and know will wholly end. We see it partly ended because we observe that the kingdom and temporal throne of David’s sons were overthrown long ago, as has already been said; and no one can doubt that David’s seed—that is, David’s succession—will at least end with the end of the world.

These examples, which I have cited from the Book of Kings and the Psalms concerning David’s seed and the kingdom of David’s seed in order to prove a finite eternity, we Christians understand of Christ in the Christian sense. In that interpretation, as we deny that his throne, that is, his kingdom, is earthly, so we affirm in every respect that it is eternal, not temporal, and without any end. But because I am dealing with you, who are far from this interpretation, I meet you upon your own ground and show that infinite eternity cannot be understood in those words. For a kingdom which has already perished cannot be called eternal, that is, infinite; David’s seed, that is, the succession of rulers after David, which no longer exists, cannot be called perpetual.

Do you still wish, O Jew, for more testimonies than these, in which eternity is not, so to speak, always shown to be eternal? Hear, after those you have heard, what your Moses—or rather, more truly, ours—commands concerning a Hebrew sold as a slave. After some preceding matters which I omit because they do not concern the point at issue, he adds: “But if he says, ‘I do not wish to go out, because he loves you and your household and finds himself well with you,’ you shall take an awl and pierce his ear at the door of your house, and he shall serve [Col. 0577D] you for ever” (Deut. XV). Hear also another passage from the same book of Deuteronomy, from which the preceding one was also taken. For Moses, writing of the priests’ due from the people and from those who offer sacrifices, adds: “For the Lord your God has chosen him from all your tribes, that he and his sons may stand and minister in the Lord’s name for ever” (Deut. XVIII). You will find something similar in First Chronicles: “Aaron,” it says, “was set apart to minister in the holy of holies, he and his sons for ever, to burn incense to the Lord according to his rite and to bless in his name perpetually” (1 Chron. XXIII).

But will it always be necessary for me so repeatedly to unlock what is open or illuminate what is clear? [Col. 0578A] What have I said? It seems strange indeed, but it is true. For what is open to everyone else is closed to you alone; what is clear to everyone else is obscure to you alone. It is clear to everyone and known to all that neither a Hebrew slave, whether his ear be pierced or unpierced, could serve his master for ever, nor a priest chosen by God, nor his sons, could minister to God for ever. For when the slave died, his service necessarily died also, so to speak; and when the priest or his sons failed, their ministry necessarily had to fail.

From all these things infer, observe, understand that the words “eternal,” “perpetual,” and “everlasting” are not always used to denote something infinite, but are sometimes used to indicate something temporal and finite. Thus also comes the passage which, if you can either resist or perversely twist to the opposite meaning, you may truly be able to interpret all things sound in a mad manner. Hear, then, the song of Moses himself, Aaron, Mary, and your whole people called Israel. It is a song known not only to you and yours but to the whole world. For, after the Red Sea had been crossed, Pharaoh drowned, and the Egyptians destroyed, the singers added this to the divine praises: “The Lord,” they say, “shall reign for ever and beyond” (Exod. XV).

Is this “for ever” taken as infinite? If it is taken as infinite, why is “and beyond” added to it? What can be added to infinite eternity? What, indeed, lies beyond it? Either remove this “beyond” and understand eternity here as infinite, or, if you will not remove that “beyond,” understand the “eternal” written there as signifying, though a very long duration, nevertheless a finite one. Since, therefore, you cannot otherwise escape from this point or draw your foot out of this snare, acknowledge that the “eternal” in question is written for an immense, though finite, extent of time; but when “beyond” is added to it, it must be understood as everlasting without any end or limit.

In addition to these sacred authorities cited above, this is also a divine, human, and common mode of speaking, by which not infinity but some greater or lesser duration of time is denoted. If you lend even an inattentive ear to speakers, you will notice that almost everyone uses this manner continually: “I have always loved you; I shall always love you; I have always heard him; I shall always hear him; this man will always be poor; this man always rich; that man always lies; this one always speaks; this one is always silent,” and a thousand similar expressions. Yet although, taken in its proper meaning, the term of which I speak signifies nothing less than infinite eternity, those who use it understand no infinity in it, but, as I said above, a long, greater or lesser, yet finite duration of time.

Hence comes this saying of our Latin poet:

> “He will be a slave for ever who does not know how to use a little.”  
> (HORACE, *Epistles*, book I, epistle X, v. 41.)

[Col. 0579A] And this of another:

> “. . . . . Unhappy Theseus sits,  
> and shall sit for ever.”  
> (VERGIL, *Aeneid*, book VI, vv. 618–19.)

Although the utterer of the end of this verse and the beginning of the next understood certain of Theseus’ sufferings as eternal—that is, without end—he did not at all mean that Theseus would sit without end, that is, eternally.

Hence too that great Latin poet:

> “Scarcely out of sight of the Sicilian land,  
> joyfully they spread their sails to the deep, and with bronze they churned the foaming salt,  
> when Juno, keeping an eternal wound in her breast,  
> said these things to herself: ‘Am I, defeated, to abandon my undertaking?’”  
> (VERGIL, *Aeneid*, book I, vv. 34–37.)

Likewise, the same poet:

> “[Col. 0579B] . . . . . Could such great indignation compel—”

Jupiter: that the nations would be destined to dwell in eternal peace? (Ibid., book XII, vv. 503–504.) But the utterer of these verses understood neither that the wound in the breast of Juno, enraged against the Trojans, was eternal without end, nor that the nations would remain in eternal—that is, infinite—peace, which could not be. There are still more examples of this kind, but these, I think, are sufficient.

By all these things, O Jew, it has been proved that, in seeking to prove the infinity of your law, you have produced so many names for eternity to no purpose, since it is established both by sacred authorities and by examples of ordinary human usage that the term “eternity” does not always denote infinite things, but sometimes finite ones as well. But perhaps you reply to this: “From what precedes, you prove indeed that the name of eternity is sometimes taken for a finite time; but you do not deny that it is sometimes taken also for infinity.” I do not deny it, I say; rather, I wholly affirm it. “Therefore,” you say, “you concede both: that the name of eternity is sometimes taken for finite time, and sometimes also for infinity.” It is true, I say. “If, therefore,” you say, “it is true that the name of eternity is often used for either meaning, finite or infinite, whence do you compel or prove that the testimonies I have adduced to demonstrate the infinity of the Jewish law must be finite rather than infinite?” I prove it, I say, and by a necessary argument compel you to concede this.

That this may be shorter and clearer, let those two passages set forth above return again to the centre: one from me, the other from you—the words of Jeremiah from me, the words of Moses from you. Jeremiah’s passage is this: “Behold, days are coming, says the Lord, and I shall establish a covenant with the house of Judah, not according to the covenant which I gave to their fathers, when I took their hand to lead them out of the land of Egypt. But I shall establish a new covenant for them, giving my laws in their minds, and I shall write them in their hearts” (Jer. XXXI). Moses’ passage is this: God says, speaking of the sacrifice of the Paschal lamb, “You shall have this day as a memorial, and you shall celebrate it as a solemn feast to the Lord throughout your generations, with an everlasting observance” (Exod. XIII). These two, as I said above, are set in opposition to one another and, according to your understanding, are altogether contrary. For what one of the two statements affirms, the other denies. Moses affirms an eternal law—that is, in your view, one never to end. Jeremiah affirms that it is to be changed—that is, that another is to be given, not according to the manner or rite of the former one.

[Col. 0580A] Do you see that one of these two cannot stand? Do you see that, unless you think otherwise, either Moses or Jeremiah must be false? Therefore, lest such solemn and famous ministers of truth appear to be liars, it is necessary either to explain Jeremiah so that the infinity of the law may be shown according to your opinion, or to take Moses’ words in such a way that what Jeremiah declared concerning the change of the law may be proved true. But in Jeremiah’s words, what Jewish eye, or even a Christian eye most keen and lynx-eyed, as the saying goes, can investigate anything other than what has been stated? What else can it understand than what they disclose without cloud, without covering, without the wrappings of figures? They disclose this indeed; they openly announce this: that God would establish another covenant, not according to the covenant given to the fathers. He plainly calls it new because an old one had preceded it. What else, then—what certainly else—can you understand by the Old Covenant but the Jewish law which preceded, and by the New Covenant but the Christian one which was to follow?

Since this is so, since in these words of Jeremiah nothing can be understood except what has been said, nor can they by any Jewish ingenuity be twisted in any other direction, you are compelled, O Jew, to turn to the statements of Moses and to agree with me that the terms eternity or perpetuity set forth above were used not for infinity but for finite time. Understand in this way the saying you advanced concerning the Paschal lamb; in this way concerning the manifold variety of sacrifices; in this way concerning the observance of the Sabbath; in this way concerning circumcision itself, which, as our Lord says, is not from Moses but from the fathers. Understand it in this way, I say; explain it in this way wherever, in similar passages of your law, you find the name of eternity written. And when there you understand “eternal” as finite time, you will find neither Moses contrary to Jeremiah nor Jeremiah contrary to Moses, and you will acknowledge as ended the law which Jeremiah foretold would end.

I say ended, as one great man among us says, [Col. 0580D] not with regard to the manner of living, but with regard to the manner of signifying life. For with regard to the manner of living, what the old law commands the Jews, the Gospel also commands Christians, and each of us strives to observe it according to grace and ability. For: “You shall love the Lord your God with all your heart, and your neighbour as yourself” (Lev. XIX); and: “You shall have no strange gods before me”; and: “Honour your father and your mother”; and: “You shall not kill; you shall not commit adultery; you shall not steal; you shall not bear false witness against your neighbour”; and: “You shall not covet your neighbour’s house, nor desire his wife, nor his male servant, nor his female servant, nor his ox, nor his ass, nor anything that is his” (Exod. XX)—and similar things suitable to right faith, honourable conduct, and holy life—are commanded to the Christian just as they were commanded to the Jew. Hence, with respect to this manner of living, the law in question has not ended.

But with respect to the manner of signifying life, it has wholly ended. For carnal circumcision, which prefigured a spiritual circumcision; the Sabbath rest, which intimated something else; sacrifices of four-footed animals, birds, fine flour, wine, oil, and the like, which foreshadowed the one supreme sacrifice of Christians—all these have given way, as shadow to body, as signifier to thing signified. Therefore, with respect, as has been said, to all those things which pressed upon the neck of a stiff-necked people, liberty was granted by him who said, “My yoke is sweet, and my burden light” (Matt. XI); and so that they might no longer be burdened by a useless yoke, they were altogether ended.

[Col. 0581B] But if you delight so greatly in this word “eternity,” of which we are speaking, and by it still try to prove your law to be without end, change your understanding, and you will find your eternity without end. Change your understanding, I say, and what I confess concerning the New Covenant, confess also concerning the Old. I say that the covenant given by Christ is both new and eternal. New, because yours is older. But eternal—how? Is baptism established by Christ eternal? Is the sacrifice handed down by him to his followers eternal? Are the other sacraments given to Christians eternal? Can many other commands of the Gospel be eternal? They are not eternal, because, as I have said of yours, they are to end with the world; and yet they are eternal because they prepare for eternal things. Those things end, but the eternal life to which they lead does not end.

Say, then—but say it in faith; believe unto righteousness; confess unto your salvation—that the law can be understood to be eternal in this way: because it existed as a precursor and foreshadowing of this Christian grace, which alone truly leads through Christ to blessed and eternal life. In this sense alone, the eternity of your law, of which you have spoken, can be understood as without end; in no other sense, unless it has an end.

But lest any of your objections remain unexamined or undecided, receive our answer also to those last objections of yours. Among other things, you opposed to us Moses speaking to your fathers: “That your days and the days of your children may be multiplied in the land which he swore to your fathers that he would give them, as long as heaven hangs over the earth” (Deut. XI). To this I reply: for as long as heaven hangs over the earth, possession of that land—which was distributed partly through Moses and partly through Joshua to those first Jews—was promised, according to your understanding, to the Jewish stock. Yet heaven still hangs over the earth, and that land has long since been taken from the Jews. But you will say: “This happened because they neglected the commandments entrusted to them by God.” And what, I ask, is that to me? I truly confess that because they neglected God’s commandments—indeed, because they were always rebellious and opposed to God, because they were idolaters, because they were profane, because they were killers of the prophets, because, to fill up the measure of their fathers, they were the most wicked crucifiers of Christ himself, the Saviour of the world and their own judge—they were cast away by God and excluded both from that land and from all worldly prosperity and eternal blessedness.

[Col. 0582A] As for the addition you made, that Moses commanded, “You shall not add to the word which I speak to you, nor take away from it” (Deut. IV): is it not strange—very strange—that you make this objection as though you yourself observed it? For which of us has ever added anything to the word of your law? Who has taken anything away? On the contrary, we preserve the books untouched; we preserve them uncorrupted; and just as they were written through Moses and, through faithful interpreters, translated from Hebrew into the languages of all nations, so they are preserved, as has been said. Nothing is added to them; nothing is diminished. Thus the Latin, the Greek, and the barbarian have from those books whatever you, O Jew, have. We write what you write; we read what you read. But we do not altogether understand what is written or read as you understand it; we do not altogether receive it as you receive it. At times you follow in them the letter that kills; I always follow in them the spirit that gives life. You gnaw the rind; I eat the marrow. I do not cast aside the covering of the letter where it exists, nor do I despise the mystery of salvation hidden under the letter. Receiving the letter in this way, while following more closely the Spirit, author of the letter, I add nothing, as I said, to the word of your law and take nothing away; rather, I accuse and correct the Jew who follows neither the letter of his own law nor recognizes the divine Spirit in that letter, and who will not rest in truth; I condemn him.

After these two matters have thus been settled, you threaten us concerning the third and last of your three points, and unless we become Jews you attempt to show that we are subject to the divine curse. “Cursed,” you say, “is everyone who does not remain in the words of this law and put them into practice; and all the people shall say, Amen” (Deut. XXVII). This curse, O Jews, is not upon Christians but upon you and your children. For we Christians from the nations were not drawn from the Jews, nor was the yoke of the Jewish law laid upon us. The necks of the stiff-necked people, which could not otherwise be tamed to serve God, were subjected to the commandments of the Mosaic law; the neck of Christian faith was raised into liberty suited to its time through our Christ.

[Col. 0582D] For this reason the Christian understands that the Jewish curse does not concern him, since, as times have changed, so too he knows that commandments have changed. But because, in the manner stated above—either in regard to the conduct of life or to the signification of life—we believe your law to be ours and call it ours, it is necessary for us to avoid its curses and desire its blessings. We avoid—indeed, wholly escape—its curses if we live according to its decrees: that is, by not coveting, not killing, not committing theft, not bearing false witness, and observing the other like things, which both the old Scripture commanded to be observed and the Gospel of new grace ordered to be kept much more fully. We escape its curses if we observe not the signifier but the thing signified: that is, if we observe not carnal circumcision, not a carnal Sabbath, not carnal sacrifices, but the spiritual virtues signified by those carnal sacraments.

[Col. 0583A] Therefore, in both these ways—either by doing what is openly commanded or by fulfilling what lies beneath the veil of the sacraments—the Christian is not subject to the curse of the law, and shows that he has been falsely assailed by the Jew, since in these ways he declares that he remains in the words of the law. Thus the curse you have adduced, O Jew, does not touch him in the least; rather, it concerns you and thrusts itself wholly upon you, who remain neither in the words of your law by the spirit of liberty, as Christians do, nor, for the most part, fulfil them in deed according to the servile and carnal condition of the first Jews. Observe, therefore, that not the Christian, as has now been said, but you are subject to the curse which you threw at him, concerning which Moses says: “Cursed is everyone who does not remain in the words of this law and put them into practice; and all the people shall say, Amen.”

By all these points the matter has come to this: that you should no longer dare to believe the law given through Moses to be perpetual according to the understanding which you have held up to now, nor dare to profess it eternal. Acknowledge, I say, that this was accomplished through Christ, author of the New and Eternal Covenant, who in it added, diminished, and changed many things beyond what ancient usage had possessed. He added when he said: “Unless your righteousness exceeds that of the Scribes and Pharisees, you shall not enter into the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. V). And he added: “You have heard that it was said to those of old: ‘You shall not kill; and whoever kills shall be liable to judgment.’ But I say to you that everyone who is angry with his brother shall be liable to judgment” (ibid.), and what follows. Again: “You have heard that it was said to those of old: ‘You shall not commit adultery.’ But I say to you that everyone who looks upon a woman to desire her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (ibid.). And then: “You have heard that it was said to those of old: ‘You shall not swear falsely.’ But I say to you, do not swear at all” (ibid.). And afterwards: “You have heard that it was said: ‘An eye for an eye and a tooth for a tooth.’ But I say to you, do not resist evil. But if anyone strikes you on your right cheek, offer him the other also” (ibid.), and the remaining things which the reading of our Gospel records: “You have heard that it was said: ‘You shall love your neighbour and hate your enemy.’ But I say to you: Love your enemies, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who persecute and slander you” (ibid.), and the rest recounted by that heavenly Scripture. When Christ commanded these things, he plainly added many commands above those of the old law.

[Col. 0583D] He diminished them, however, when through his apostles, in whom he spoke, he established the following. For their Epistle reads thus: “The apostles and elder brethren, to the brethren from among the Gentiles who are in Antioch, Syria, and Cilicia, greeting” (Acts XV). And after an intervening verse: “It has seemed good,” they say, “to the Holy Spirit and to us to lay upon you no further burden than these necessary things: that you abstain from things sacrificed to idols, from blood, from what is strangled, and from fornication. If you keep yourselves from these, you shall do well” (ibid.). When he commanded these few things to be observed, he greatly reduced the multitude of legal precepts.

He changed them when, in place of circumcision, he established baptism; in place of Sabbath rest, rest from sins; and in place of the countless sacrifices of bread, fine flour, wine, four-footed animals, and birds, he established that the one pure, innocent, spotless Lamb of God—that is, himself—should be offered daily to the almighty Father for the salvation of all. He commanded these things; and because he was proved to be God, he imposed by divine authority whatever he wished and cut off the objections of unbelievers who doubted his commands. For when Jews wondered and complained most foolishly that, by healing with a word, he worked cures for many afflictions on Sabbaths, [Col. 0584B] he answered: “The Son of Man is Lord even of the Sabbath” (Luke VI). But he who is Lord of the Sabbath is surely God; for no one except God can be Lord of the Sabbath. Hence it is clear that he who is Lord and God of the Sabbath is Lord and God of circumcision, Lord and God of sacrifices—indeed, of all things.

Therefore, just as it was lawful for the Lord and God of all things, when he willed, to create things not existing, and, when he willed, to change things already created into one kind and another, so it was lawful for him, for reasons of justice hidden and known to himself alone, to set before humankind laws not yet given, for whom he willed and at the time he willed; and again, for whom he willed and when he willed, to increase, diminish, or change the same laws.

[Col. 0584C] Cease, therefore, O Jew, to take offence at the laws of Moses changed through Christ, because the same God who appeared to humankind through the man Christ, when he willed, promulgated legal precepts that had not previously existed, and, when he willed, changed those already given. Nor should you henceforth maintain that anyone could be justified only through that old law, now ended, since you find that many were called righteous both before it, during its time apart from it, and even after it.

Did not Abel, returning to the earlier ages, please God by innocence of heart and purity of a simple sacrifice, without circumcision, without observance of the Sabbath, and without any rite of your law imposed upon him? (Gen. IV.) Did not Enoch walk with God, without circumcision, without observance of the Sabbath, and without the manifold burden of our law; and “he was not seen, because God took him”? (Gen. V.) Is it not written of the great man Noah, without circumcision, without observance of the Sabbath, and without the manifold burden of the Jewish law: “Noah was a righteous and perfect man in his generation, and walked with God”? (Gen. VI.) Does not God himself say to him: “I have seen you righteous before me in this generation”? (Gen. VII.)

What shall I say also of the very one in whom you especially customarily glory, father Abraham? Was it not said of him, without all those things mentioned before, without Sabbath or legal commandments, even before circumcision itself: “Abraham believed God, and it was reckoned to him as righteousness”? (Gen. XV.) And what of his descendants Isaac and Jacob, and the rest down to Moses? Did not they also please God by observance of circumcision alone, but especially of righteousness, without all the other decrees of the law later given; and did not these two, together with Abraham who preceded them, merit the singular and glorious name of patriarchs?

[Col. 0585A] This was before the law. But now, when the law had been given or was about to be given, I see Job—not a Jew but almost foreign to the Jewish race—without circumcision, without Sabbath observance, and without every legal institution, called by the divine voice simple, upright, fearing God, and departing from evil. I see Balaam also, without circumcision and without the manifold precepts of Moses, conversing with God, obeying God, and by God’s inspiration foretelling many things that would serve human salvation (Num. XXIV). Although he fell, and although he both foresaw and foretold his fall, yet by the very fact that he speaks of his fall, he declares that before that fall he had stood. Therefore, though he did not remain in righteousness, he nevertheless merited to be a hearer of the Lord’s words only through some merit of righteousness.

I observe also very many kings, and I behold not a few men of foreign nations, who, in the very time of the law, without circumcision, without Sabbath observance, and without Mosaic institutions, worshipped God, pursued righteousness, and were justified without preserving that same righteousness. Though they are not read of in the Jewish canon, they are proved by truthful histories to have been such. But to what purpose are these things? That, seeing that many pleased God before the law and under the law without the works of the law, you may cease to boast as though of the singularity of your law and lay aside the antiquated arrogance you have derived from it. And not for this reason alone, but also that you may observe that, just as before the law and under the law you see very many honoured with the title of righteousness without legal observances, so after the law you may understand that not merely many but all can be justified by the grace of the Christian Gospel alone.

[Col. 0585C] For this is that New Covenant concerning which you have already heard God and the prophet speak: “Behold, days are coming, says the Lord, and I shall establish a covenant with the house of Judah, not according to the covenant which I gave to their fathers when I led them out of the land of Egypt” (Jer. XXXI). Either, then, show another covenant given by God that is not according to your covenant which he gave, or receive this covenant of our Gospel, which was truly given by him. It is not according to that one because it is more than that one; it is not according to that one because that one is earthly, while this is heavenly; it is not according to that one because that one is temporal, while this is beyond doubt everlasting. Not because the Gospel Scripture given by Christ, or the things commanded in it, ought to remain eternally, but because the glory promised by Christ to those who keep the Gospel remains eternally, with no reasonable obstacle to prevent it.

By a similar argument I conclude also all that has been said more fully above concerning Christ. For either you must produce another person of whom all those things can truly be understood, or you must agree with us that they are all said of our Christ.

But perhaps you object: “Even if I cannot produce anyone to whom the aforementioned prophetic utterances may apply, by what reasoning do you compel me to understand your Christ in those prophetic utterances rather than anyone else?” By a great reasoning indeed—a great reasoning, I say—I compel you to think this. But before that reasoning is set forth, let authority come first. You ask why I understand all the aforesaid things of our Christ rather than of anyone else, and why I compel you to receive them. I understand our Christ, not another, in all those prophetic utterances and urge that he be understood, precisely because I recognize that those words were uttered of him and not another. Or, to select by way of example some of the innumerable things pertaining to him: of no one else but him can the saying of your prophet, often repeated by our Church, be understood: “Behold, a virgin shall conceive and bear a son, and his name shall be called Emmanuel” (Isa. II). For no virgin has conceived, will conceive, has borne, or will bear a son, except the heavenly and perpetual Virgin Mary, who bore Jesus Christ our Lord.

[Col. 0586B] Of no one else but him can this be understood: “A star shall arise from Jacob, and a sceptre shall rise from Israel” (Num. XXIV). For not a comet, said to change kingdoms, nor any brightly shining heavenly body, arose when our Christ arose from Israel according to the flesh; rather, a star more splendid than all stars and rivaling the sun’s very brilliance shone forth, foretelling the birth not of anyone whatsoever but of him alone.

Of no one else among humankind can this be understood: “I shall pour upon you clean water, and you shall be cleansed from all your defilements” (Ezek. XXXVI). For he, and no other, poured clean water that cleanses from every defilement of sins upon all, when he commanded his disciples: “Teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. XXVIII). Of no other time but his can this be understood: “Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened, and the ears of the deaf shall be unsealed; then the lame shall leap like a stag, and the tongue of the mute shall be opened” (Isa. XXXV). For in his time, by his power, at his command, both through himself and through countless others receiving that same gift from him, sight was restored to the blind, hearing to the deaf, walking to the lame, speech to the mute; and countless miracles of every kind or species were performed.

[Col. 0586D] Of no one else but him can this be understood: “He was wounded because of our iniquities, and by his bruise we were healed” (Isa. LIII). For no one but him is found to have been wounded because of human iniquities; by no one’s bruise but his was health restored to humankind. No one but him was offered because he willed it; no one but him was led like a sheep to slaughter because he willed it. Of no one else but him can this be understood: “You will not give your Holy One to see corruption” (Ps. XV). For, as our apostle Peter says, speaking—as I too do—to the Jews (Acts II), neither David, who speaks here, nor any human being or saint who was buried, except this same Christ of ours, could escape the corruption of the flesh.

Of no one else but him can this be understood: “After two days he will revive us; on the third day he will raise us up” (Hos. VI). For no dead person other than him, resting in a three-day burial, on that very third day rose in the resurrection of his own flesh; and then he raised many saints, and at the end of the age will raise all alike, both good and evil, either to eternal life or to eternal death. Nor did the same prophet add this of anyone else: “His going forth is prepared as the dawn” (ibid.). For his coming forth from the tomb into immortal life was like dawn, because before the sun, at the first beginning of light, he rose, just as both our Gospel and he himself say in the Psalm: “I shall rise at dawn” (Ps. LVI). Nor is this all: he joined to the light of his passing resurrection an everlasting light and illuminated by it the ancient darkness of mortals.

[Col. 0587B] Of no one else but him can this be understood: “Ascending on high, he led captivity captive; he gave gifts to men” (Ps. LXVII). For divinity alone cannot properly be said to ascend on high, since it is always both on high and below, and everywhere. But it was said also of him, according to the words of our Apostle: “He ascended,” because he first descended into the lower parts of the earth; and from there, having assumed human flesh, “he who descended is the same who ascended above all the heavens, that he might fill all things” (Eph. IV).

Of no one else but him was it said: “There shall be a root of Jesse, and one who shall rise to rule the nations; in him the nations shall hope” (Isa. XI). You can observe this more by seeing with your own eyes than by lending your ears to prophetic writings. For in our Christ, who sprang from the stock of Jesse, the nations hope—as the whole world tells you; him they entreat, him they worship. Of no one else but him was it said: “I know that my Redeemer lives, and on the last day I shall rise from the earth, and in my flesh I shall see God” (Job XIX). For none can be called Redeemer except one who redeems. But Job had not been redeemed, nor was anyone going to redeem him, except this Son of God, this Christ of whom we speak. Foreknowing that he would give, as the price of Job’s redemption and that of the world, his body and blood, Job calls him his Redeemer, names him God, and declares that in his own flesh, already raised, he shall see him on the last day.

All these things, and many like them, [Col. 0587D] because they can be understood of no one else but Christ, we believe were spoken of him; and we know that they were fulfilled in him and through him, except for this one last thing, which remains to be fulfilled at the end of the world. We urge unbelieving Jews to believe and think the same. You have heard, O Jew, on what authority—indeed, on what authorities—the Christian believes and understands all the foregoing things to have been said of no one but Christ. Hear also by what reasoning the Jew is compelled, willingly or unwillingly, to yield.

And by what greater reasoning can this be persuaded to you than by those immense and infinite divine miracles? For who possessing human understanding does not see that so many and such great miracles wrought by Christ and through Christians could in no way have been done except by divine power? And he indeed confessed himself to be the Son of God, God, the eternal king, and the Christ foretold by the prophets. If these things were false, not only would no signs follow him and no efficacy of miracles accompany him, but rather—though it is criminal even to think it—he would be condemned as a liar, blasphemer, and impious man. And since he preached all these things concerning himself, since he made those who believed these things concerning him into workers of miracles as though omnipotent—for, as he himself says, “All things are possible to the believer” (Mark IX)—it is clear, it is evident, that whatever he taught should be believed concerning himself must be believed without even the least doubt, and whatever he commanded to be done must be observed without any opposition.

[Col. 0588A] But, so that I may myself raise whatever objection you could make, perhaps you will say that those miracles either did not occur or were magical. If you say that they did not occur, if you say they were invented by our people, I answer quickly and meet you with your own argument: if, because you did not see them, you claim that the miracles said to have been wrought by Christ or through Christians did not occur or were invented, we likewise claim that those read of as wrought through Moses, Joshua, or the other Jews, because you did not see them, did not occur or were invented. For you can adduce no greater certainty for Jewish miracles than we can for Christian ones. For just as you have Jewish books in which those are written, so we have Christian books in which these are reported. By this reasoning, then, either deny Christian miracles and we shall deny Jewish ones, or confess Christian miracles and we shall acknowledge Jewish ones.

But because, although you have not seen those signs, you give them faith solely upon reading books handed down by your fathers, you are compelled to grant that we too give faith to books handed down to us by our elders; and, further, because we assent to yours, that you also assent to ours. We believe your prophets; believe our apostles too. Believe for this reason: that whatever they said would happen concerning Christ and matters pertaining to Christ, these others have shown to have been fulfilled in the world in their entirety, without any diminution. Therefore you will not be able in this manner to prove Christ’s miracles nonexistent or invented by our people. But by what other means will you be able to prove that they did not occur or were invented, when you see not merely certain parts of the world but almost the whole world itself subjected to Christian laws?

[Col. 0588D] The pride of the world now lies cast down beneath Christ, and the whole arrogance of worldly glory serves the ignominy of one condemned by men and crucified. It worships his cross, which it formerly shuddered to behold; and what it once judged foolish it now does not doubt to be far wiser than all its own wisdom. It recognizes as weak the power by which it was accustomed to subdue all earthly things, once Christ, who is the power of God, has been recognized; and measuring its own wisdom by him who is the wisdom of God, it despises that wisdom as foolish. How, then, would it voluntarily have subjected its wisdom to Christian, so to speak, folly; its strength to weakness; its nobility to ignobility; its glory to ignominy, unless this had been persuaded to it by wondrous, astounding, and previously unheard-of works? It is therefore established as false that Christian miracles did not occur or were invented.

But perhaps, still seeking Jewish evasions, you will object: “Why do you wish to compel the conclusion that the world could have believed in Christ only through miracles, when before Christ almost the whole world—indeed, at some time the whole world—served idolatry, and turned to that idolatry not through any signs but through its own error?” I grant, I say, that without signs—apart from certain vain and demonic ones by which, though rarely, an error once conceived was fostered in the hearts of foolish people—the world at one time succumbed; but it began to give its hands to that detestable worship at the time when, newly expelled by God from Paradise in its first parents, it was cast forth as an exile from the face of God into this valley of error and blindness.

[Col. 0589B] There, deservedly because of its iniquity, gradually forgetting its Creator, yet not uncertain by the force of innate reason that divinity existed somewhere, but ignorant where it should be sought, it sought divinity either in men celebrated for praise, or in their images, or in beautiful creatures suited to its uses; and so, instead of the Creator, it became accustomed to worship with divine devotion the things he had created. “For when he was in honour, he did not understand, but in divine knowledge as well as in his own conduct he was compared with senseless beasts and made like them” (Ps. XLVIII). You yourself know—if indeed you have been a diligent student of your Scriptures—that what I say is true, and that there was no other cause of so great an error than this: with reason asleep in humankind, and with no law yet given that could awaken its reason, the fool said in his heart, “There is no God” (Ps. XIII). Hence it was no wonder if a part of the world, or the whole world, could easily be deceived at that time.

But conversely, in the already educated times of Christ and the Christians, when the Jewish law had been given almost two thousand years before, when philosophical schools and studies of divine and human matters flourished everywhere, and when both natural law and written laws, through the vigor of human intellect and knowledge, were again in bloom, it was impossible for people to be deceived and thus universally to submit themselves to Christian faith, changing their faith, morals, and life at the command of one man into something other and contrary, without immense prodigies and signs. Therefore the objection you proposed has no force.

[Col. 0589D] But I fear that the hardness of a brazen brow, notorious to all, may again come forward with its customary shamelessness and say: “If Christian times, now enlightened, could neither be deceived nor believe without miracles, how is it that, five hundred years after Christ had passed, the Mohammedan heresy arose, and that utterly wicked sect, won by no miracles, infected such vast regions of the world? Did not those times, notwithstanding their learning, yield to so great an error?”

To this I first reply that it is one thing for regions of the world, another for the whole world, to yield to any error; and therefore one must judge differently concerning a particular error and a universal one. For, apart from the beginnings of the human race that I touched upon above, there never was, nor will there be, a time in which darkness is not mingled with light, error with truth. And although, according to our Gospel, light [Col. 0590A] shines in darkness and the darkness does not comprehend it (John 1), though they are not uniform, they are nevertheless contiguous. Therefore, as has been said, some regions of the world can be infected by an error; the whole world cannot. Thus that error, like many others, could infect certain regions of the world; it could not occupy the whole.

But the Christian faith, not after the manner of errors, subjected to itself mere fragments or parts of the world, but, as truth derived from the highest Truth, who is Christ, subjected the whole world to itself. I say “the whole world,” because, although Gentiles or Saracens exercise dominion over certain parts of it, although Jews lie concealed among Christians and heathens, yet there is no part of the earth, however small, no part of the Tyrrhenian Sea, nor even the remotest islands of the Ocean, which is not inhabited by Christians, whether as rulers [Col. 0590B] or subjects; so that what Scripture says of Christ appears true: “He shall rule from sea unto sea, and from the river unto the ends of the earth” (Psalm 72). Or this saying of our Apostle: “At the name of Jesus every knee should bend” (Philippians 2).

If, therefore, the Mohammedan error corrupted some part of the earth after the law given by Christ, what does that have to do with the matter at hand? Many heresies arose among the Jewish people after the law of Moses; many arose in the world of Christians after Christ’s Gospel. Therefore, although the times in which this heresy arose were learned, that pestilence nevertheless prevailed not throughout the whole world but in some part of it, and, as I have already said, infected the sea of other heresies as some member of a great body is infected by corrupt [Col. 0590C] humours. Hence there is no comparison between this diabolical falsehood and the divine truth of the Gospel: the former gained possession of some, though many; the latter, in the manner stated, of all.

But you object that in these Christian times those people, deceived by a wicked deceiver, believed without miracles, and you bring this forward to invalidate our miracles. You argue by analogy that Christians could be deceived in these learned times without miracles, just as Saracens in the same learned times happened to be most miserably deceived without miracles. But the inference is invalid; this analogy is wholly without force. For I prove that in the same learned times Saracens yielded to error without miracles, while Christians did not believe in Christ without the necessary miracles.

For it was impossible that either those of whom we are speaking, or any others, in those learned times, could be turned away from an established or inborn custom and converted to strange and new things without some definite cause either attracting or compelling them. And the cause attracting or compelling them to those novelties, unless I am mistaken, was none other than authority, reason, miracles, force, or pleasure—or all of these together, or some of them. But let no one wonder that, whereas above I set miracles in place of reason, I now distinguish reason from miracles. There I said that miracles have the force of reason because, as reason draws a rational mind to believe something, so miracles compel it toward that which they intend to persuade. Here, however, I separate them from one another, rendering to each what belongs to it: by the name “reason” let rational understanding be meant, whether silently present in the mind or expressed in words; and by the term “miracles” let the remarkable power of wondrous works be expressed.

[Col. 0591A] Thus these two, understood in this way and joined with the three already mentioned, make, as was stated, five: authority, reason, miracles, force, and pleasure. Examine these causes which could either attract or compel those ruined people to embrace a new error. First remove those which, by their own witnesses, were not the cause of their error. For that no reason attracted them is attested by themselves and by the master of the error itself. For in his book, which ought not even to be named, he says, introducing God as speaking to him: “If anyone wishes to dispute with you, tell him that you have turned your face, and those who follow you, toward God; by doing this, both those skilled in laws and the illiterate will follow the good law. But if not, your task is merely to make my commands known to the nations.” Again: “If anyone wishes to enter into a contest with you concerning the law, pronounce anathema upon him, and threaten such persons only with the wrath of God.” Or again: “Do not dispute with those who possess the law. For slaughter is better than contention”; and much else of this kind.

That he did not summon them by any miracles is likewise put into his mouth, as though by the voice of God: “You certainly will not come to them with manifest miracles of God, because they reject them as hateful and opposed to themselves.” Again: “Unless we knew that they would not believe you, just as they did not believe others, we would give you signs and wonders”; or he often [Col. 0591C] repeats the same thing. These two must therefore necessarily be excluded, because, as was said, both they themselves and the author of their heresy confess this very point.

There remain the causes by which they are shown to have been deceived: authority, force, and pleasure. By authority I mean not any that could have been divine, but that which its lying and deceiving author feigned to be divine, and which the foolish people deceived by him accepted as divine from a lying and deceiving author. By force I mean that of which the same presumptuous man speaks in the book just mentioned: “I was sent only with the power of the sword.” Again, to his followers: “Until you become stronger than all others, be plunderers and conquerors.” And: “Unless you confess that I am a prophet sent by God, I shall despoil you of all your property, subject your wife and your sons and daughters to captivity, and kill you yourself.” And much in this manner.

For both he while he lived, and the successors to his rule, are reported to have done this; and, as though observing it as imposed upon them by divine command, they violently subjected by arms and force to that wicked sect those whom they could. By pleasure I mean that to which the wicked deceiver most especially gave free rein, and to which, as everyone knows, that miserable people are particularly enslaved. Many things written by him are read on this subject, including these: “God,” he says, “deals gently with you, because in the faith of the Saracens there is nothing but tranquillity and rest; and God does not want from you what is difficult, but what is easy.” Again: “Then you shall eat, drink, and have intercourse throughout the whole night, until [Col. 0592A] the white thread can be distinguished from the black.” Again: “Let there be for you at least four wives. As for concubines, as many as you can, even a thousand such.”

Thus, by the testimony of their own books and deeds, they were either attracted or compelled, by authority, force, and pleasure, to embrace a sect of an accursed name; they were not so by reason or miracles. Do you see, Jew, that in an educated age that people was seduced by other causes, not by miracles? Do you see that the point for whose sake you advanced this supposed analogy establishes that the Christian world was not converted to Christ without immense signs? This I shall demonstrate by an argument not merely probable but necessary.

I therefore set before you the same causes which I have already set forth, and from them necessarily prove Christian miracles. Let authority, reason, miracles, force, and pleasure then return [Col. 0592B] to the discussion. All or some of these either attracted or compelled the world to embrace the Christian faith. But, as was done above, let those be removed by which the world was neither attracted nor compelled to embrace the Christian name.

It was not attracted by authority. For although it now venerates Mosaic and prophetic authority as truly divine, it did not venerate it before it believed in Christ. Indeed, after it was converted to the Christian faith, it recognized by the authority of those Scriptures that all which it sees fulfilled in Christ or his Church had been foretold; but before its conversion it did not know that these things had been predicted by a prophetic spirit. It did not assent to those Scriptures, as being foreign to it, nor think that the law of the Jews had anything to do with it. Therefore it was not first brought to believe in Christ by the authority of those writings; rather, because it first believed in Christ, it accepted the authority of those same Scriptures.

Nor could it have been converted to this faith by ancestral traditions or by the authority of its forebears, since ancient error always, with all its strength, by books, threats, and punishments, so long as it was permitted, drew it back from this faith. Hence it is evident that the world was converted to the faith of Christ by no authority whatever.

Nor by reason, because, as Christian doctrine itself declares, since in it the merit of faith is great, that faith has no merit to which human [Col. 0592D] reason provides proof. Certainly some things in it seem to follow human reason, as its Apostle says: “Be ready to give an answer to everyone who asks you for a reason for the hope that is in you” (1 Peter 3). But there are far more things which can be comprehended by no insight of the mind and penetrated by no keenness of human intellect.

Certain great masters of secular philosophy investigated, through the things that have been made, the invisible things of God; and the inquisitive philosopher investigates almost all that the Christian proclaims about the divine majesty. Hence, as one of ours says, “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God” (John 1), and certain following matters, the philosopher as well as the evangelist [Col. 0593A] writes. [Note: [Col. 0593] Plato, namely, as Augustine says, *Confessions*, book VII.] But “the Word was made flesh” (ibid.) he comprehends by no acuteness of mind. For the proud mind cannot comprehend the most profound humility by which the Word of God deigned to become flesh. Only the devotion of the humble understands it, when the Spirit, by God’s grace, leads it. Hence also are the words of our Saviour speaking to God the Father: “You have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones” (Matthew 11).

There are also those words of our great Apostle, who, seeing the Jews rejected and the Gentiles chosen by Christ, and wishing but failing to understand the reason, cries out: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are his judgments, and unsearchable his ways!” (Romans 11).

[Col. 0593B] It is therefore clear, Jew, by the confession of Christ himself and his apostles, that the world was not converted to the Christian faith by human reason. But was it compelled by force to embrace the same faith of Christ? Here plainly one must dwell for a long time. I say that one need not dwell here, in order to show that no one compelled people to embrace the Christian law. For those who are proved to have been coerced in a thousand ways not to accept it were in no way compelled to accept it. Hence they suffered terrors, tortures, prisons, fires, and swords; yet, though enduring every kind of death, they could not be frightened away from it or drawn back. The unbelieving world is witness, having long spent all the strength of its malice against them in vain; and the earth itself, everywhere stained with Christian [Col. 0593C] blood and covered with the sacred bodies of Christ’s martyrs, is witness. Therefore the world was not compelled to faith in Christ by any force.

But was it attracted by pleasure? And what is pleasurable, Jew, in Christ’s law? Did he not himself say to his followers, “In the world you shall have tribulation” (John 16)? Did not his Apostle say, “All who wish to live piously in Christ Jesus shall suffer persecution” (2 Timothy 3)? Does not the Christian sword cut off whatever pleasure can exist anywhere? Very many examples from the Gospel law occur here; but lest I burden readers with tedium, I pass them over and select only a few from that multitude, for the sake of brevity.

The carnal person wishes to feast luxuriously and excessively, to drink luxuriously and excessively, and to become drunk. Christ opposes him and says, “Take heed lest your hearts be weighed down in gluttony and drunkenness” (Luke 21); and his Apostle: “Not in revellings and drunkenness” (Romans 12). The carnal person wishes to live pleasurably and lustfully. Christ opposes not only the act but even the pleasurable thought, saying: “Whoever looks upon a woman to lust after her has already committed adultery with her in his heart” (Matthew 5); and elsewhere: “There are eunuchs who have made themselves eunuchs for the kingdom of heaven” (Matthew 19). Elsewhere he admonishes: “Let your loins be girded” (Luke 12). And the Apostle: “Not in beds and indecencies” (Romans 13); and again the same Apostle: “Let fornication and every uncleanness not even be named among you” (Ephesians 5).
