[Col. 0594A] In the spiritual pleasure of taking vengeance upon an enemy the carnal person wishes to indulge himself; Christ resists and says: “But I say to you, do not resist evil” (Matthew 5). With the pleasure of possession the carnal person wishes greedily to amass money; Christ warns him and says: “You cannot serve God and mammon” (Matthew 6), and again: “Do not lay up for yourselves treasures on earth” (ibid.); and elsewhere: “Whoever does not renounce all that he possesses cannot be my disciple” (Luke 14). From the pleasure of boasting the carnal person wishes proudly to set himself above others; Christ warns and says: “He who is greatest among you, let him be as the least, and he who goes before, as one who serves” (Luke 22); and again, threateningly: “Everyone who exalts himself shall be humbled” (Luke 14); and: “I saw Satan fall like lightning from heaven” (Luke 10).

From the desire to live, or an unconsidered fear of punishments, the carnal person wishes, by injuring justice, to flee death and avoid torments. Christ exhorts and says: “Blessed are you when they revile you and persecute you and, lying, say every evil thing against you” (Matthew 5); and, concerning a similar matter: “Do not fear those who kill the body and after this have nothing more that they can do” (Matthew 10).

[Col. 0594B] It is therefore plain that the world was not attracted to believe in Christ by any pleasure of mortal life or possessions. Thus there remain miracles, placed in the middle among the aforementioned causes. For if it is true that no nation can be attracted or compelled to embrace things new and unfamiliar except by authority, reason, miracles, force, or pleasure, it is certain that the Christian world could not be attracted or compelled to embrace Christ’s law, new and unfamiliar to it, without some one of these causes. But it is true that no nation could be attracted or compelled to embrace novelties without some one of these. It is therefore established that the Christian world was neither attracted nor compelled to believe in Christ without one of them. But it has again been proved that it was converted to Christ neither by authority, reason, force, nor pleasure. It is therefore plain that it was summoned to embrace Christ’s faith by miracles alone and by the grace of the Spirit alone.

But lest my replies should seem not to meet your objections in their proper order, I briefly restate what you objected. You said: “The miracles by which you say the world was converted to Christ’s faith either did not occur at all or are magical.” But that it is false that none occurred—indeed, that it is true that many and great ones occurred—has now, I think, been fully proved. That they were not magical, however, still remains to be proved; for the miracles of Christ or his disciples, as will be apparent from what follows, could in no way have been magical.

You press me, Jew, to show this also. I show, I say, that they could not have been magical but were divine. For no one is accustomed to learn or transmit magic unless he is literate and learned. But the apostles and first disciples of Christ were wholly illiterate and unlearned in respect of liberal or magical arts and disciplines. For thus it is read among you concerning the chief disciples: “When the Jews saw the constancy of Peter and John, and discovered that they were unlettered and ordinary men, they recognized that they had been with Jesus” (Acts 4).

[Col. 0595A] This is also demonstrated by their occupations, through which they earned a poor livelihood. Four of the apostles—namely, the two just mentioned, together with Andrew and James—were fishermen; another was a tax collector; the rest were taken from other lowly occupations, Christ choosing the ignoble things of the world in order to destroy the proud. It is therefore clear that magic, which without letters can either not be learned or transmitted at all, or scarcely be so, was neither received by them from Christ nor transmitted by them to others.

But lest you perhaps oppose to me the illiterate actors or mimes of our own time, who are accustomed to deceive the eyes of onlookers by certain tricks, I add that magic, whether handed down with learning or without learning, requires not a brief but a long time to learn. Clearly it requires not only days or months but often many years, owing to its difficulty, during which the raw disciple can gradually be imbued with Satan’s teachings and at length emerge learned through this most evil progress. When, Jew, will you be able to find this lengthy period, necessary for that wicked art, among Christ’s disciples? For it was not necessary that they be instructed by Christ in performing wondrous works over many years, months, or even days, since the power of the eternal Word—which he himself was—suddenly, as if in a moment, equipped them to perform them at will.

Hence in our Gospel, though you do not assent to it, it is written: “Jesus, having called together his twelve disciples, gave them power over unclean spirits, that they might cast them out and heal every sickness and infirmity” (Matthew 10). And he says to the same: “Heal the sick, raise the dead, cleanse lepers, cast out demons” (ibid.). What commands could be shorter than these? What interval, in which so few words were uttered, could be briefer? Does this not occupy, as has been said, not merely years, not merely months, but not even a week, a day, or a whole hour itself? It is therefore certain that the magical art, so laborious, demanding such study and such protracted effort, could not in so very short a time either have been transmitted by Christ or learned by the disciples.

[Col. 0595D] But if you perhaps contend that this too, because it is read in the Gospel, is not true but fabricated, see, infer, consider: if magical art had been transmitted by Christ to Christians through written or spoken instructions, it could in no way have remained hidden from the multitude of Christians throughout the world. An evil art could not have been concealed for so long with so great a consensus of all; nor would great, learned, devout, God-fearing Christian people of such different nations and languages have allowed themselves to be deceived for so long by a diabolical art, execrable even to the heathen.

To what precedes I add two further points, by which I show that Christian miracles were not merely probably, but necessarily, not magical. First I propose this: magical wonders are always false and deceptive. They display nothing real, produce nothing substantial; they deceive human senses and, by demonic agency, feign that what is not exists, that what is not seen is seen, and that what is not heard is heard. They imitate their author, so that, as he is a liar and its father (John 8), so magic, his offspring, may present nothing true but put forward everything false.

[Col. 0596A] Thus it displays not human beings but false images of human beings; not four-footed animals or birds but false images of four-footed animals or birds; not creeping things but false images of creeping things, deceiving human senses by hidden tricks. Thus magical power presents to human sight phantasms of springs, rivers, trees, and every kind of thing. Satan, in his customary proud envy, rivals in these things the author of nature: just as the latter both creates new things as he wills and changes things already created into other substances or forms as he wills, so this artificer of deception, because he cannot create truly, at least invents false likenesses of created things in order to deceive foolish people.

The instability of fabricated phantasms exposes the emptiness of such tricks: as soon as they appear, they immediately vanish in swift departure, like mist or smoke, and, being suddenly withdrawn from the eyes, show how completely nothing they were even while they seemed to exist. By contrast, Christ’s miracles, wholly ignorant of this diabolical falsehood, show themselves divine not by fabricating empty and false things but by displaying things substantial and real. Christ walked with his feet upon a real, not phantom, sea without the aid of any vessel (Matthew 14); he changed water into real and good wine, not phantom wine (John 2); he either restored or gave real, not phantom, eyes to the blind; natural hearing, not simulated hearing, to the deaf; real, not simulated, speech to many. He healed lepers not deceptively but truly; he expelled demons from human bodies not deceptively but truly; he healed every sickness of humankind not deceptively but truly, and raised any dead person. And finally, not as any prophet, not as any magician, but as God and Lord of all creation, he did all that he willed in heaven and earth, in the sea and in all the deeps (Psalm 135).

[Col. 0596D] Nor only did he do these things, but moreover granted the same power of miracles to all who truly believed in him—something only God can do. For all who are read of, believed, or affirmed to have done any wondrous things either before him or after him employed not their own but another’s power in doing them; they acted not by human but divine power. Hence, when they were about to perform them, they always first offered prayers to God, and, having obtained them by those prayers, performed the miracles by which they became renowned.

Thus you read that Moses, though the passage is silent about it, before he divided the Red Sea and drowned Pharaoh, was told by God: “Why do you cry to me?” (Exodus 14). You read also that Elijah, before he either raised the dead, consumed with heavenly fire the sacrifices offered to God, or watered a three-year drought with rains, prayed, bent his knee, [Col. 0597A] and did none of these things without first praying (3 Kings 17 and 18). So too with the rest. For none of them could do any such works by himself; but when he did them, he obtained from God that they be done. And if he could do nothing of himself, certainly he could not grant this power to others.

But if you object that Elisha said to Elijah, “I beg that your spirit may be doubled in me” (4 Kings 2), recall what Elijah answered him and you will recognize that he could grant nothing of himself. For when he said, “If you see me when I am taken from you, what you have asked shall be; but if you do not see, it shall not be” (ibid.), he showed that both the working of miracles and granting to anyone the power of such works belonged to another—not to himself, but to God.

But Christ did not work miracles, like Moses, Elijah, or any of the prophets, by a power not his own and after first offering prayers; rather, as God, though also man, he performed them, whenever he wished, by the proper power of his divinity; and in divine liberality he granted to whom he wished the ability to do the same.

[Col. 0597B] From all this, Jew, it is clear that the miracles of Christ by which the world was converted to the Christian faith were not magical, phantom-like, false, or empty, but divine, true, substantial, and beneficial. Attend again carefully to what I said, “beneficial.” This is the last of the two points which I proposed above, from which I promised to prove, by an argument not merely probable but necessary, that Christ’s miracles were not magical or false but divine and true. For the genuine benefit of Christ’s miracles alone, even if all the foregoing were absent, would suffice to prove the same thing. The clear, certain, unquestionable proof of wondrous works is their very usefulness, which reveals, even to inattentive observers, whether they come from God or not.

For whatever of this kind is done by God on earth serves human salvation; whatever of a similar kind is done by Satan serves vain curiosity. Human benefit wholly distinguishes and separates divine miracles from diabolical fabrications: the devil’s wonders are always devoid of it, whereas Christ’s miracles always serve it alone. What benefit is there, for mortals—not, I say, in eternal goods, but even in present advantages—in the aerial flight of magicians, a phantom river-course, the laughter of images, fabricated changes of age, battles of shadows, walls constructed in a moment, lofty towers erected, enormous cities built as in the fantasies of dreams, and all such things: all Satan’s deceits and deceptive inventions?

[Col. 0597D] I intend what I said—that magical fabrications do not benefit even people’s present interests—to be understood as I understand it. For I know that magicians, or any most empty followers of demonic wonders, sometimes gain much when they either tell curious or covetous people hidden matters known to demons through their subtle knowledge of nature or through very long experience, or feed their sight with empty and smoky images; and they often procure many advantages either for themselves or for those by whom they are urged to do these things. I am not speaking of these advantages, nor do I count profits of this kind among even the present benefits of human well-being. For these things are more harmful than profitable, more destructive than saving.

I am speaking, rather, not of advantages acquired by the shameful and wicked empty arts of magicians, mimes, or their adherents, but of those miracles which either serve the eternal salvation of souls or at least heal human bodies by their remedies. For what sick person was ever healed by these deceptive deceits and lying inventions of Satan? What afflicted person was ever helped by such remedies? For whom are such things fit except the vulgar’s laughter? What do they feed except the eyes of fools?

But you will bring forward the Egyptian magicians and propose that they performed before Pharaoh signs like Moses’ signs. [Col. 0598B] But remember that Moses’ miracles were true, not phantom-like as those of the magicians; remember that they served the benefit of God’s people, a benefit entirely lacking in magical fabrications. Moses performed signs and, by God’s command, brought plagues upon the Egyptians, so that the people rebellious against God, together with their faithless king, might be justly punished and the nation then chosen by God might be mercifully saved.

But the magicians’ wonders had neither the same nor a similar purpose, no intention of human benefit; for they were done not for salvation or any useful end but were fabricated in emulation of sacred signs and to display skill in an accursed art. Magical tricks lacked the usefulness of divine signs; divine miracles are wholly removed from the damnable vanity of curious people.

[Col. 0598C] Do you still see, Jew, the difference between signs and signs, miracles and miracles, wonders and wonders? Henceforth distinguish them—something you perhaps did not know until now—and understand as false those which you recognize to be devoid of human salvation; recognize as divine those which you learn serve it. Do you not observe that no blind, deaf, mute, or sick person was ever healed by any magician, however skilled—not to mention that no dead person was raised? Demonic power and will alike wholly failed in such matters: it never had the will to help mortals, nor any power to repair what is broken or heal what is corrupted.

But Christ, and the Christian faith delivered through him to the world, aimed at absolutely nothing else and expended its whole effort upon nothing else through these and innumerable other wondrous [Col. 0598D] works, except that bodies might be healed here, souls justified, and, after the time appointed by him before every creature, the whole and complete human being might be delivered from every death, corruption, and misery, and joined forever to angelic blessedness. Since, constrained on every side by the truth, you cannot deny this, Jew—since Christian miracles have plainly been proved to serve human salvation alone—it is established that they are not deceptive but true, not magical but divine.

Recognize, therefore, that your twofold objection set forth above has been fully answered. For your assertion that Christ’s miracles did not occur or were fabricated is shown false, since many have been proved to have occurred. Your assertion that they were magical is shown untrue, since they have been proved wholly divine.

[Col. 0599A] But why should I convince you from Christ’s past miracles that our Redeemer is truly Christ and God, when I can more easily either convince one who denies it or strengthen one who confesses it by the wondrous works of my own time? I pass over, over the course of a thousand years, the innumerable and most exalted miracles—first those of Christ, then those of the apostles and other disciples who adhered to him while he still lived in mortal flesh. I set aside the innumerable legions of Christ’s martyrs throughout the world, the companies of confessors, the priests of both orders, the flocks of monks, and the phalanxes of hermits, no small part of whom shone with heavenly signs while they lived. I pass over all these, I say, and omit whatever wondrous works they performed while living mortally.

I come to their tombs or graves, and from their sacred ashes show what blessedness or glory their spirits meanwhile possess with their almighty and gracious Creator. Review, Jew, and read attentively again all the books of the ancient and sacred Canon handed down to you of old; and, apart from the bones of Elisha and of a certain other prophet, show that any wonders were performed through any dead person under the Jewish law, however holy, up to the passion and death of our Christ. Since you cannot do this, turn your eyes from the dead of the Law, so to speak, to the dead of the Gospel, and observe how great are the works Christ has performed through the corpses—or now almost the mere ashes—of his Christians.

[Col. 0599C] Look upon the peoples of the world running to the grave of any Christian once despised, and often seeking from those who had once been put to death by cruel torments aid in dangers and remedies for every adversity. Observe them frequently heard by the dead sooner than anyone could be heard from youth onward, and returning from Christ’s churches and their shrines with the benefits they desired. I do not want you to labour much: merely open your eyes and see those who entered sacred places blind go out seeing; the deaf return with hearing, the lame with the ability to walk, the mute with speech restored; and finally all sick people rejoice, having laid aside there their grievous illness.

Behold the ever-virgin mother of Christ herself—whom you have always hated with a special hatred—as heavenly and more radiant than the sun; look, though with an envious eye, upon Christ’s saving cross, which you have hitherto especially abhorred. Recognize that these things, or greater things, occur more often and more solemnly at places dedicated more especially to their memory or honour, so that you may be most confounded by that at which you take greatest offence, and so that those things which are most despised by you in greater ignominy may be adorned above the rest with greater glory.

[Col. 0599D] Among innumerable people afflicted by diverse miseries, those scorched by a dreadful and grim fire run to those same places; filling those churches by their multitude, not merely two or four but often fifty or a hundred are healed within a short time. I myself saw a certain woman rejoice when, after her nose had been consumed by that pestilential fire down to the innermost roots of her face, it was restored whole through a nocturnal vision. I also saw others who, according to the testimony of many truthful persons, had long been—or always had been—blind, and who, their sight restored by divine power, saw.

I saw other things as well. But what are these compared with those which I received from truthful and trustworthy men, whether from those who saw them or from those who received the reports from eyewitnesses? Among them: a pilgrim of the Apostle James, killed by himself through demonic deception, was raised by that same Apostle some days after death; and he recounted what he had seen when freed from the body, and that through the merits of that saint he had returned to the body. The many miracles of Christ done in the present age escape my mind—so great that, even if the ancient ones were lacking, they could suffice fully to establish the strength of the Christian faith.

But perhaps you will say that you are unwilling to accept Christians’ testimony concerning Christ. I ask the reason. You answer that every sect favors itself, and that in such matters, or in similar ones, it may be deceived or may deceive. To this I add: if anyone is so wicked as to deceive others, can he be so depraved as to wish to deceive himself? Yet those persons would deceive themselves who, concerning Christ’s miracles, while saying that they had seen what they had not seen and heard what they had not heard, should strive either thereby to confirm themselves in the Christian faith or to induce others to the same by a prodigious lie. This kind of deception—everyone agreeing with me in declaring it so—never could have existed and never can exist.

I think [Col. 0600C], moreover, that not even Satan wishes to deceive himself, although he is the author and father of falsehood (John VIII). But if the father of falsehood and lies, although he always desires to deceive, does not wish to be deceived, much less do his offspring wish to be deceived, either by anyone else or by themselves. Besides, whoever lies or deceives does so either through fear of losing what he possesses and loves, or through hope of gaining what he does not possess and loves. But those who said that they had seen or heard of Christ’s miracles performed in our own time neither feared that they would lose anything if they did not say so, nor hoped to gain any profit because they did say so. It is therefore clear that they said nothing but what was true.

But why do I labor to explain individually to a Jew the admirable works of Christ performed in various parts of the world, when, though innumerable, far fewer are known to me than are unknown? Certainly, miracles unknown exceed those known by far. Yet what book’s extent, what volume’s bulk, could contain those which I know with undoubted certainty? Let these, then, be set aside and reserved for their own time or volume. At the end of this work I set before you, Jew, one heavenly and public work of Christ: one which you cannot deny; one which, with the whole world proclaiming it, you will be compelled to confess, lest your silence condemn you.

You have heard of Christ’s disciples’ miracles; you have heard of Christ’s mother’s miracles; you have heard of Christ’s cross’s miracles; hear also the sublime miracle of Christ’s tomb. You cannot say that Christians invented this, since it has as witnesses [Col. 0601A] both pagans and Saracens themselves. For there is scarcely any Christian anywhere in the whole world, no heathen, no pagan, who does not know it, or who can remain ignorant of it, however remote his location may be.

Christ visits his tomb with a light sent down annually from heaven, and illuminates it with heavenly radiance not on any other day, but on that day on which he lay in it. From his death he displays life; from the darkness of his cave he shows that eternal light has shone upon the world: so that the faithless Jew, despising his death, may be confounded, and the faithful Christian saved, placing all his hope in that same death.

Fifty years ago, Christ’s enemies occupied, together with the divine and royal Jerusalem itself, Christ’s temple and tomb, and exercised an impious lordship over it. [Col. 0601B] A few Christians of eastern peoples, together with occasional westerners, kept watch at that same tomb of the Lord; out of love for the Savior, patiently bearing the most grievous yoke of the impious, they served the saving cave. The violent guard of those Saracens pressed upon that most sacred place; and the savagery of the faithless extorted, by torments and blows, whatever it could from not only those who served there but also visiting pilgrims, who had come with great labor and fervent longing for their Redeemer’s tomb.

Yet even then the heavenly light did not cease to shine amid the darkness of the impious; and on Holy Saturday, preceding the Paschal Sunday of the Lord’s resurrection, it shone from above and with visible fire upon the Savior’s tomb on earth. Egyptians held Persian bows, [Col. 0601C] and Ethiopians, whether in jest or earnest, threatened to pierce with their arrows the angel, as they called him, who bore the divine fire. So greatly did the manifestness of so sublime a miracle overcome the minds of unbelievers that, though by impious acts, they confirmed what they could not deny.

If, therefore, Jew, you deny what Christians confess concerning this great miracle, can you deny what the pagans and Saracens of the whole East and South confirm concerning it? Formerly God kindled fire upon the offerings of righteous Abel, but did not kindle it upon the sacrifice of impious Cain (Gen. IV). He sent fire from heaven upon the burnt offering of the great Elijah; he did not send it upon sacrifices prepared for Baal the demon (4 Kings XVIII). Thus indeed, thus, O Jew, in our own time that same God distinguishes between Jewish vows and Christian sacrifices. He rejects your offerings, which for a very long time he has not even permitted to exist; he receives the Christian burnt offering, when by an annual recurrence he honors with such great miracles of divine fire that place in which once lay dead the Lamb who offered himself immaculate to God.

Therefore, to gather briefly, O Jew, what has been said more fully: recognize, by the manifold authority of the Scriptures and the manifest argument of miracles, that it has been proved; hold it certain that Christ our Lord is not the adopted but the essential Son of God; not God by title, but true God; not a temporal but an eternal king; not one to be awaited as though he had not yet come, [Col. 0602A] but received and worshipped as one who already came at the appointed time.

## CHAPTER V. On the Ridiculous and Utterly Foolish Fables of the Jews

It seems to me, Jew, that by so many authorities and such great arguments I have, as I think, satisfied every person concerning those matters proposed in the question. If every person, then you also—provided that you are a human being. For I do not dare to profess that you are a human being, lest perhaps I lie; because in you I recognize reason—the quality separating a human being from other animals or beasts—as extinguished, indeed buried.

Your own psalm testifies to me in this matter, where it laments a human being transformed into a brute animal: “Man, when he was in honor, did not understand; he was compared to senseless beasts and became like them” (Ps. XLVIII). Although this may, according to one interpretation, be understood of the universal human being—that is, the human race—yet you cannot deny that it is said especially and uniquely of you, in whom all reason lies buried.

For why should you not be called a brute animal? Why not a beast? Why not a beast of burden? Bring beside yourself an ox—or, if you prefer, an ass, than which nothing among cattle is more foolish—and listen together with it to whatever may be said. What difference, what distinction, will there be between your hearing and the ass’s? The ass will hear and not understand; the Jew will hear and not understand. Am I the first to say this? Was it not said long ages ago? Does not your exalted prophet himself testify to the same? “You shall hear with the ear and shall not understand; and seeing you shall see and shall not perceive [receive]” (Isa. VI).

Therefore, although it has been fully proved by these sacred authorities that you are a beast of burden or a beast; although this has been sufficiently shown by me in the preceding four chapters, even if you have not been moved by them, let a fifth chapter nevertheless be added, so that when it is brought to light it may become evident not only to Christians but to the whole world that you are truly a beast of burden, and that, in affirming this, I have nowhere exceeded the bounds of truth. I therefore bring forth the monstrous beast from its lair and exhibit it for ridicule in the theater of the whole world, before the sight of every people. Before all men I produce for you, O Jew—beast—your book, that book of yours, [Col. 0602D] that Talmud of yours, that excellent doctrine which is to be preferred to prophetic books and all authoritative judgments.

But you are astonished, since I am not a Jew, at how this name became known to me, how it sounded in my ears. Who revealed Jewish secrets to me? Who uncovered your innermost and most hidden things? He—I say, he, he—Christ whom you deny, that Truth, uncovered your falsehood and disclosed your shame; he who says: “Nothing is covered that shall not be revealed, and nothing hidden that shall not be known” (Matt. X).

Certainly, by that book of yours it will be shown, by it it will be clearly demonstrated, by what just judgment of God you have been given over to a reprobate mind: since by no effort of human study are you willing to assent to the clearest truth, while you have so readily yielded to the darkest falsehood. [Col. 0603A] The words of our Apostle have been fulfilled in you and those like you, who says: “God will send them the working of error, that they may believe a lie, that all may be judged who did not believe the truth but consented to iniquity” (2 Thess. II).

It is indeed marvelous, and almost unbelievably marvelous, that men should not believe, as has been said, a credible and most evident truth, and should believe an unbelievable falsehood. Yet conversely it is not surprising that, when every trace of light has utterly departed, the dense darkness once driven out of Egypt should occupy Jewish hearts; because, according to true Scripture, there is no agreement between Christ and Belial, nor any fellowship between light and darkness (2 Cor. VI).

But now the darkness itself must be laid bare, and your chosen Scripture, the Talmud, must be brought forth publicly. According to you and those like you, it is of such greatness and such lofty dignity that God does nothing else in heaven except continually read that Scripture and discuss it with the wise Jews who composed it. But what am I to do? If I begin to answer this madness, or other things like it, I myself will almost seem mad. Would not a man be judged mad who answered someone suffering madness, or frenzied under demonic impulse, when that person speaks alien or utterly absurd things? Would he not seem deranged who tried to dispute as though rationally with such a person, in whom all reason is buried and who utters nothing but empty and foolish things?

Thus indeed, people might think this of me, unless a certain reason excused me from this folly: that certain reason by which, though I may not benefit all Jews by this disputation of mine, I may perhaps help some. For although at present they have deservedly been cast off by God because of their iniquity and are not to be recalled until, according to prophecy, after the multitude of the Gentiles has preceded, the remnant of Israel shall be saved (Isa. X), heavenly mercy nevertheless sometimes gathers some in the meantime and separates them, though few, from the mass of perdition. My reply or disputation may perhaps not lack useful effect among them. Having long been defiled among the Jews by the dregs just mentioned, when they pass over to Christ’s Church they may be more fully cleansed by such an antidote and purged by this reading from the pestilence with which they had been imbued.

Hear, then, Jew, the madness of yourself and your people—and, what is worse, your blasphemy. [Col. 0603D] For the madness of lunatics which I mentioned above is the punishment of sin, but is not itself sin. Blasphemy, however, is not only an intolerable sin but, so far as yours is concerned, also a punishment for preceding sins. You would not have become so wretchedly foolish unless you had deserved it by the preceding sins or crimes of yourself and your fathers.

“You say, God does nothing else in heaven except continually read the Scripture of the Talmud and discuss it with the wise Jews who composed it.” First I ask: why does God read in heaven? In order to become more learned, to learn what he previously did not know, or to recall things he had forgotten? For every reader reads for these reasons: either to learn what he did not previously know, or to recall things he had forgotten, or to instruct, delight, or rebuke someone by reading, and for whatever other purposes belong to the nature of reading.

But to take up the first possibility which I proposed: does God read in order to learn? Does he lack any knowledge or wisdom? Do we not read not only of his greatness but also of his wisdom: “Great is our Lord, and great is his power, and there is no number to his wisdom” (Ps. CXLVI)? Do not the same psalms say to him through the Prophet: “You have made all things in wisdom” (Ps. CVIII)? Does not the same prophet again say to that same God: “Behold, Lord, you have known all things, the last and the ancient” (Ps. CXXXVIII)? If he knows all things last and ancient—that is, all things final and first—then surely he does not fail to know what lies between. [Col. 0604B] For it follows concerning these matters: “Your eyes saw my imperfection, and all shall be written in your book” (ibid.).

But do not suppose that this book of God is your Talmud. Say, if you can, whether all human beings—those who have been, who are, or who shall be—are written in that book of yours. For these are the psalm’s words: “All shall be written in your book.” But it is certain that by no art or effort can you show that all are written in that book of yours of which we are speaking. Therefore that book of which it is said, “All shall be written in your book,” cannot be the Jewish Talmud.

Hear also the good woman Susanna, who, though she is not in your canon, was nevertheless of your people. Hear her profess in her own prayer whether God can be ignorant of anything: “Lord,” she says, “you know all things before they happen” (Dan. XIII). If he knows all things before they happen, then surely he does not fail to know them after they have happened. God, therefore, does not read the Talmud in order to learn anything.

Nor does he read the Talmud in order to remember anything. Hear your prophet: “Can a woman forget the child of her womb? And even if she should forget, yet I will not forget you” (Isa. XLIX). Recall also that verse which you seem to have forgotten: “If I forget you, Jerusalem, let my right hand be given to forgetfulness” (Ps. CXXXVI). But perhaps you will object: “God said this because of the great affection which he felt toward our fathers.” Nor, Jew, do I deny this. But even if love for the ancient Jews caused him to say it, it did not cause him—even as you concede—to say it falsely. It is true, therefore, that he could not forget your fathers; it is true that he could not forget your city Jerusalem.

But could he forget anyone besides Jews? Does not Job, who belongs to your canon, speak to God and say: “Although you hide these things in your heart, nevertheless I know that you remember all things” (Job X)? He who hides remembrance of all things in his heart surely forgets none; surely he remembers all continually. For if the memory of all things should perish in him for any moment of time, he would not hide it in his heart during that interval in which it had perished. For no one is said to hide what does not exist, but what does exist. It is therefore clear that God can in no way be forgetful of any human beings or of any things whatever. [Col. 0605A]

But you object that it is written in Genesis: “God remembered Noah, and all who were with him in the ark; and he brought a wind upon the earth, and the waters diminished” (Gen. VIII). You also object: “He remembered that they are flesh, a spirit that goes and does not return” (Ps. LXXVII), and add: What then does it mean when it says, “God remembered Noah,” and “He remembered that they are flesh,” if God forgets nothing and remembers nothing?

I too ask: Had God forgotten Noah and all who were with him in the ark before he sent the wind and the waters diminished upon the earth? Had he forgotten the man whose ark, amid every storm, amid the blasts of raging winds, amid elements released from the law of nature and most violently battling one another, under rains pouring down without order, over the immeasurable sea of the abyss—amid all these things, I say—he steered for almost an entire year without a helmsman, sails, rudders, or any aid whatsoever of human skill?

It seems to me, Jew—indeed, what is greater, it is altogether established for me, and established also for all who are not Jews—that God could in no way have forgotten those of whom he showed, by such manifest proofs, that he had not forgotten them. See for yourself, see and judge—yet justly—whether, amid so many and such great obstacles to navigation, Noah’s ark could float across the one sea of the whole world without the divine hand and without human skill, when even a small boat cannot navigate or cross a narrow stream without much labor from sailors. If this is clear to you—which is obscure to no one except you—you are compelled to confess that Scripture did not say that God remembered Noah because he had forgotten him even for an instant, but because sacred Scripture, observing the human manner of speaking, after adding certain matters concerning the nature of the Flood and naming Noah beforehand, fittingly recalls how he was rescued by God from such great dangers.

Therefore confess, compelled by reason, that at no time did God forget Noah or those who were with him in the ark. Confess also that when it says, “He remembered that they are flesh, a spirit that goes and does not return,” God’s forgetfulness is not being indicated, but his mercy commended. [Col. 0605D] For how can it be believed that he had forgotten that people, whom he distinguished not only by sublime and frequent miracles but also by continual signs and benefits? I pass over his dividing the Red Sea for them, producing water from a rock, and glorifying them by certain other signs done only once. Did he not, from Israel’s departure from Egypt—“the house of Jacob from a barbarous people”—until the division of the Jordan, for forty years feed them daily, except on the Sabbath, with heavenly manna flowing down from above? Did not a pillar of cloud by day and of fire by night continually show them, without error, through trackless wastes and deserts, the measure and extent of their whole journey: when they should pitch their tents and when they should strike them?

He cannot therefore be said to have forgotten even briefly those for whom he showed himself continually mindful, not by intermittent signs but by continual signs—which is greater. Thus God in heaven, O Jew, neither read nor reads your Talmud in order to restore to memory anything he had forgotten concerning them. It is therefore clear that God needs the reading of neither that book nor any other in order either to learn or to remember. Nor does he read in order to instruct as a master instructs pupils, or to delight as tragedians and comedians delight the populace, or to rebuke as satirical censors rebuke the profane. But why speak of these things? They are ridiculous and intolerable even to hear, unless your profound stupidity, O Jew, forced me unwillingly to speak of what I shudder even to think. Let the remaining matters follow. [Col. 0606B]

“You say, God reads the book of the Talmud in heaven.” But what sort of book? If it is such a book as those we use daily for reading, then surely it is made from the skins of rams, goats, or calves; or from papyrus or reeds of eastern marshes; or from scrapings of old rags; or perhaps from some other still cheaper material; and written with birds’ feathers or marsh-reeds, stained with whatever dye. And, miserable man, have you subjected almighty Wisdom to such necessity that, in order to learn or remember anything, he must consult the meanest sheets and beg understanding from skins or papyri?

How could he learn anything from Jewish books, he who gave the Jews the law written by his finger—that is, by his Spirit—upon tablets of stone? What could he learn from any Jewish book, when he himself is their author and lawgiver? But again I am reluctant to answer such utterly abject trifles; yet because you, so wise, believe them, I cannot keep silence.

“You say, God does nothing else in heaven except read the Scripture of the Talmud.” This has already been examined. And what follows? “And discuss it with the wise Jews who composed it.” Great indeed is Jewish dignity, great their excellence: God deigns in heaven to read a Scripture composed by them and to discuss it with wise Jews. But why does God discuss that Scripture with wise Jews? In order to teach or to learn? For the custom of human discussion is that one who confers with another about some matter either teaches, is taught, or becomes more practiced, more ready, or more hesitant to do something.

Does God, then, by discussing the said book with Jews, become more learned, more practiced, readier, or more sluggish? Answer as you please. If through this discussion he becomes more learned, more practiced, or readier, you contradict your prophet, who says: “Who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counselor?” (Isa. XL). You also contradict him who said: “Whom did you wish to teach? Was it not him who made the breath of life?” (Job XXVII). See, then; consider; observe that such discussion in heaven between God and Jews happens in vain—indeed, it never happens—because God cannot have a counselor or a teacher. [Col. 0607A]

For when it was said, “Who has been his counselor?” the question was not asked in order to show who he was, but to show that there was no such person. Likewise, when it was said, “Whom did you wish to teach? Was it not him who made the breath of life?” it was shown in astonishment that God cannot in any way receive instruction from another, since he created the breath of all living beings. For how can anyone teach God, without whom he cannot even breathe? How can wisdom teach God, without whom it could not itself have life? But if it could not have life without God, how can it impart wisdom to God?

It is therefore false, with the whole world judging, that God continually reads the Scripture of the Talmud in heaven and discusses it with wise Jews. But now let that wonderful Scripture, composed by wise Jews, be brought forth publicly, and let it be seen how greatly all men, and God himself, ought truly to admire its wisdom.

“At one time,” says the Talmud, “while Jews were discussing this same Scripture with God, a question arose concerning the different kinds of leprosy contained in the book of Moses, baldness, and certain other illnesses. When God said that baldness was leprosy, but they on the contrary denied it and strongly contradicted him in argument, and could not in any way agree, after long disputes and most serious quarrels they agreed that whatever Rabbi Nehemiah should say about it should be held true.”

Rabbi Nehemiah was still alive in the world; the Jews assert, namely, that he was great and holiest above all their masters. Therefore God commanded the striking angel to bring his soul forth quickly and carry it to heaven. Coming, the angel found him reading the Talmud—the aforesaid Scripture, which Jews call so holy that no one can die while reading it. As soon as Rabbi Nehemiah saw the angel of death, he asked why he had come. The angel said that he had come for his soul. Nehemiah, horrified and afraid to die, solemnly adjured him by God himself and by the holy Scripture of the Talmud which he was reading not to lay hands upon him, because he did not wish to die at all yet.

When the angel said that it was better for him to be with God in heaven and with the holy Jews, delighting in heavenly things, and urged him to permit his soul [Col. 0607D] to be taken out, he would by no means consent, continually reading the Talmud so that he could not be killed. The angel therefore returned and reported this to God, saying that Rabbi Nehemiah was in no way willing to die and continually read the Talmud, so that he could do nothing.

“I,” said God, “will give you counsel. Return quickly to him, and make above his head in the air a great whirlwind and something like a commotion of hail and stones, so that, when terrified, he turns his eyes away from reading the Talmud, you may seize his soul and bring it here.” The angel returned and did as God commanded. But as soon as Rabbi Nehemiah’s soul had been carried up to heaven and saw God seated on a throne and disputing with Jews about the aforesaid question, it began to cry out in a loud voice: “It is clean! It is clean!” That is: “You have been defeated, O God, by the Jews in this question, because baldness is not leprosy as you said, but a clean ailment.” Then God, blushing somewhat and not daring to say anything against the testimony of so great a man, answered the Jews who were arguing with him in playful acknowledgment: “NAZA HUNI BENAI”—that is, “My sons have defeated me.” [Col. 0608A]

Now, Jew, I no longer argue with you. I am insufficient; I am unable; I find no words suited to refute such madness. Let your prophet—indeed, no longer yours but ours—Isaiah take my place. What do you say against the Jews, greatest of prophets? “Hear, O heaven, and give ear, O earth, for the Lord has spoken: I have begotten and exalted sons, but they have despised me. The ox has known its owner, and the ass its master’s manger; but Israel has not known me, and my people have not understood. Woe to the sinful nation, a people heavy with iniquity, an evil seed, criminal sons! They have forsaken the Lord, blasphemed the Holy One of Israel, and turned backward in estrangement” (Isa. I).

When you say such things in God’s person against the Jews of your own time, O prophet; when you attack them so sharply and declaim so sublimely against the impious—when Jews still partly believed in God with right faith, confessed him, and continually offered sacrifices—what would you say of these men if you heard these things? What would you say if you heard Jews asserting that God disputes in heaven with dead Jews as though with equals? What would you say if you heard that, concerning kinds of leprosy, God held one opinion and Jews another; that God asserted baldness to be leprosy, while Jews denied it and vigorously contradicted God in argument? [Col. 0608C]

What would you say if you heard that for this reason, after long contentions and most serious quarrels between Jews and God in heaven, Rabbi Nehemiah had been chosen by agreement of both sides to settle the dispute and pronounce the decisive judgment on this question between God and Jews? What would you say if you heard that God commanded the angel to bring him the soul of Nehemiah, still living in the flesh, in order to render this judgment, and that Nehemiah defended himself from being compelled by the angel to die by continually reading the Talmud? What would you say if you heard that at last his soul was wrenched from him by divine deceit and carried to heaven; and that, upon finding God seated upon a throne and still disputing with Jews about the question already mentioned, he immediately began to cry out that God had lied in his proposition and had been defeated by Jews?

What would you say if you heard that God, defeated by Nehemiah’s judgment, blushed; if you heard that he had dared say nothing against the judgment of so great a judge; if you heard that he had even confessed the Jewish victory in his own words, saying, “My sons have defeated me”? I believe that you could not patiently hear God called foolish, called a liar, taught by human beings, subjected to human judgments, deceitfully tearing human souls from their bodies, and that so many things unfit and unworthy not only of God but of any wise or good person were being said about God.

For you hear him called foolish by Jews when they say that he lacked the knowledge to distinguish the varieties of human illnesses; and they deny to almighty God what they grant to any physician. They plainly call him foolish in the respect in which they deny him knowledge. What, then, do you say about this? I certainly hear you, in your own manner, resisting this Jewish opinion in a free voice, when you say: “God, the everlasting Lord, who created the ends of the earth, shall not fail nor grow weary; and there is no searching out of his wisdom” (Isa. XL). I hear also Job: “Hell is naked before him, and there is no covering to destruction” (Job XXVII).

For if God’s wisdom is so great, as you say, that there is no searching of it—that is, that no one can investigate it—it is certain that nothing is hidden from him. If nothing is hidden from him, no species of any illness is hidden from him. But according to your judgment, which it would be impious not to believe, [Col. 0609B] nothing is hidden from him. Therefore the Jew lies who says that the kind of illness mentioned above—whether it was leprosy or not—was hidden from God.

Again, if hell is naked before God, if there is no covering before him for destruction, then that which the Jew says was hidden from him cannot have been hidden from him. For if hell—that is, all things that are or occur in hell—is naked in his sight, can any things that are or occur on earth be covered from his eyes? Does he see demonic spirits and human souls held in hell, and what is done concerning them, but remain ignorant of human beings still placed on earth and living in the flesh, and of what is done in them or concerning them?

Since this cannot be, since it plainly cannot be that anything in creatures should be hidden from the Creator, since the maker cannot be ignorant of what he has made, I say again—and you likewise affirm the same with me: the Jew lies who dared say that God was ignorant of anything.

And what shall I say? Formerly I was dealing with the Jew; now I turn my words to you, holy prophet. Why? Because I am ashamed to speak to a deaf man, to a madman, to a beast of burden. But I am glad, if you do not disdain it, to deal with these matters with you, whom I know always dealt with similar matters while you lived, though not with persons so mad. Full of God’s Spirit, you detested their madness. Following far behind with some zeal for God, I execrate in such words as I can their faithlessness, more detestable than it was in your time.

Is not what I have set forth execrable beyond all measure? Nor do they add things less execrable, though worthy of every curse. Simple blasphemy does not suffice them: they have filled immense volumes with innumerable blasphemies against God. Over several thousand years they have amassed, in condemned sinners, a vast sea of impieties; and gathering for so long the abominable poisons from the mouth of the venomous serpent, they pour them daily upon God, as much as they can and as much as they dare. They said that God is foolish; they also say that he is a liar. Do they not call him a liar when they confess that he said concerning the illness written above what is not so, and denied what is so?

But reason destroys this; authority destroys it; wisdom also destroys it, speaking through Solomon: “My throat shall meditate truth, and my lips shall detest the impious. [Col. 0610A] All my words are just; there is nothing crooked or perverse in them. They are right to those who understand, and equitable to those who find wisdom” (Prov. VIII). And what is this wisdom that speaks through Solomon? Is it not God himself? Indeed, it is God himself.

For Solomon and his wisdom were distinct: Solomon could exist even if he lacked wisdom. But God cannot exist without wisdom, because he and his wisdom are not different things; rather, what God is, that his wisdom is also. Thus whether God is named or his wisdom is named, the same is meant; for God is wisdom and wisdom is God. Therefore God speaks: “My throat shall meditate truth, and my lips shall detest the impious.” God’s throat, therefore, shall meditate truth, not falsehood; God’s lips detest the impious, not the just. Yet there are none more impious than you, lying Jews, who endeavor to declare God’s wisdom a liar.

And because even a just and truthful human being is often deceived, if not through injustice then through ignorance, and sometimes moreover lies through creeping injustice, Scripture adds: “All my words are just; there is nothing crooked or perverse in them” (ibid.). If, therefore, not some but all God’s words are just; if there is nothing crooked in them; if there is nothing perverse in them, then what the Jew said, O prophet, when he called God a liar, is false. [Col. 0610C] And it follows: “They are right to those who understand, and equitable to those who find knowledge” (ibid.).

It is not surprising, then, that all God’s words are not right to Jews, since they are not right to those who do not understand; nor is it surprising that they are not equitable to those same Jews, since they are not equitable to those who do not find knowledge. Therefore, because Jews do not understand and do not find knowledge, all God’s words cannot appear right to them. “You will destroy all who speak lies,” says the Psalm to God (Ps. V).

See, wretches, that I am compelled to return from conversing with the prophet to you. See, I say, wretches, into what an abyss you have cast yourselves when, through the abominable Scripture in which you believe, you have called God a liar. For if God destroys all who speak lies, and God himself speaks lies, then God surely destroys even himself. Who can endure this? Who can tolerate it? Who can bear it?

And since, if I linger long over matters so manifest, I shall seem to be beating the air in vain, I shall proceed to what follows. Does not this fable of yours, O Jew, after branding God with foolishness and falsehood, also subject him to human discipleship? Does it not subject him to human discipleship when it says that he learned from Nehemiah what he did not previously know? These things are monstrous, more astonishing than every ghostly apparition. I marvel; amazed, I stand still; I cannot marvel enough at how a human mind could invent this, how a human hand could write it, how a human mouth could—or dared to—utter it. I myself fear to say such things even in contradiction, and do you not fear to say them even in affirmation? I hesitate to utter them even for instruction, while you do not hesitate to consider, write, and say them, unto the destruction of yourself and your people?

Let the discourse nevertheless carry out what it began. You say, as I have said, that God is taught by human beings—that the eternal borrows wisdom from mortals, the heavenly from the earthly, supreme wisdom from the foolish. Hear whether all your Scriptures, not profane but sacred, resist or yield to so perverse an opinion. For against profane things I argue from sacred things; with divine writings I resist impious letters. Above you heard, on a similar matter, the testimony of the righteous man Job, by which he defends God against this wicked assertion of yours, when he says: “Whom have you wished to teach? Is it not him who made breath?” (Job [Col. 0611B] XXVI.) Hear also a similar example from the Psalms, by which the Spirit of God assails you and yours, and detests this unheard-of opinion concerning God: “Understand, you foolish among the people; and you fools, at last become wise” (Ps. XCIII). By what words could he more forcefully indicate the feeling of one stirred and indignant? “You foolish,” he says, “understand; you fools, at last become wise.” What follows? “He who planted the ear, shall he not hear? Or he who formed the eye, shall he not see?” (ibid.) What then? “He who rebukes the nations, shall he not reprove? Or he who teaches man knowledge?” (ibid.) That is: “He who rebukes the nations, shall he not reprove? Or he who teaches man knowledge, shall he not reprove?” (ibid.) Have you heard that final point, Jews? According to your Psalm, God teaches knowledge to man; man does not teach knowledge to God. I too will use divine words against you: “You foolish, understand; you fools, at last become wise.”

What do I wish you to understand? What do I wish you to be wise about? Again I say that man does not teach knowledge to God, but God teaches knowledge to man. If this is true, your Nehemiah—whom you admit to be a man—did not teach knowledge to God. Does not this single prophetic utterance, Jew, even putting aside innumerable other testimonies saying the same thing, suffice to prove that God cannot be taught by a human being? I know that it suffices. But hear further: “All wisdom,” says one of your Scriptures, “is from the Lord God, and has always been with him, and is before the age” (Ecclus. I). If all wisdom is from the Lord God, then the wisdom or knowledge by which the Jews knew that alopecia was not leprosy [Col. 0611D] was from him. If it was from him, it was certainly his. If it was his, he could not be ignorant of what they knew. But this is so; you cannot deny it. Therefore what you thought is false, and what you believed is fabulous.

And lest perhaps you object—if indeed you know how to object—that the sentence just cited is not from the highest canon of Jewish letters, return to the Psalms and see what they say elsewhere on a similar matter. “Your knowledge has become wonderful from me,” says that Prophet (Ps. CXXXVIII). “From me,” he says, according to Hebrew idiom; “above me,” according to the Latin sense: that is, your knowledge has become wonderful—beyond what I can understand, beyond what I can grasp. And what more? He explains what he had said and adds what he had not said: “It has been strengthened, and I shall not be able to attain it” [Col. 0612A] (ibid.). See, Jew: when so great a man, so great a king, so great a prophet says that God’s knowledge is wonderful above him, affirms that it is strengthened, and declares that he cannot attain it, will the knowledge of your Nehemiah not merely surpass David’s knowledge but even exceed God’s own knowledge? I think you will not dare to compare that Nehemiah with King David, much less place him above him. But if you do not dare compare him with your king, how will you set him above your God? Cease, then, to be foolish, and cast this laughable madness from your heart.

Are you not ashamed that you are accused of impieties? Are you not ashamed that you have made the Nehemiah already mentioned a judge over God? Are you not ashamed that you have subjected to human judgments him who is called by the Prophet “a righteous Judge” (Ps. VII), who, according to the same Prophet, “judges [Col. 0612B] the world in equity and peoples in his truth” (Ps. LXVI)? If you have human eyes—not those of the body, but of the mind—look, behold, observe: if the prophetic declaration is true, by which he said that God will judge the world and its peoples in equity and truth, then it is false that he appealed to a human judgment; false that he subjected himself to it.

But perhaps you will object: “The Prophet said, ‘He will judge,’ not ‘He judges’: he used a future tense, not a present one.” Therefore, since that judgment was still future when the Prophet spoke, God could meanwhile be judged by a human being. But if you say this, if you seek by the name of the future tense to free yourself from this difficulty, hear God as Judge also in the present time; hear him in the past; hear him at once [Col. 0612C] in the future.

When God came down to destroy the Sodomites and Gomorrhaeans, Abraham met him and said: “Will you destroy the righteous with the wicked? Far be it from you to do this thing, to kill the righteous with the wicked, so that the righteous should become like the wicked! This is not yours. You who judge all the earth, will you by no means render judgment?” (Gen. XVIII). Do you recognize, Jew, the name of Abraham? I know that you recognize it and, I suppose, retain it in your mind more tenaciously than the names of all other human beings. Will you then prefer your Talmud to Abraham’s words? What did Abraham say? “You who judge all the earth, will you by no means render judgment?” Behold, Abraham uses the present tense when he says, “You who judge all the earth.” Yet this present includes in meaning both the past and [Col. 0612D] the future. For Abraham meant, when he said “You who judge all the earth,” that God judges all the earth at every time.

The sense is the same in the Psalms: “You who sit above the cherubim” (Ps. LXXIX); “You who make your angels spirits” (Ps. CIII); “You who rule Israel, give heed” (Ps. LXXIX); “The Lord rules me” (Ps. XXII); and many similar passages. For God did not sit above the cherubim, make his spirits angels, rule Israel, or rule David only at the moment when this was said, and not before or afterward; rather, he did so then, before, and afterward. David understood this when he uttered these things; Abraham understood it when he said, “You who judge all the earth.” Therefore, in this passage, the verb at issue is present in sound, but in meaning past, present, and [Col. 0613A] future.

If, therefore, what Abraham said is true—that God judges all the earth at every time—then it is false that a fable invented that he was at some time subject to the judgment of an earthly man. But I think you will fear to call Abraham a liar. If you fear this, if you do not wish to call him a liar, you will certainly deny that God is subject to human judgments.

Do you wish something more to be added to what precedes? Let it be done, if you wish, though it is superfluous. Let us suppose that this Nehemiah of yours was great, wise, learned—indeed, as you maintain, a teacher of the law. Was he greater than the one of whom another Scripture of your Canon says: “Behold, God is exalted in his strength, and no one is like him among lawgivers” (Job XXVI)? A few intervening verses later it adds: “Behold, God is great, surpassing our knowledge; the number of his years is beyond estimation” [Col. 0613B] (ibid.). See, then, that although Nehemiah was, in your view, a great teacher of the law, he was nevertheless neither greater than God nor equal to him, because no one is like him among lawgivers. You see also that, however wise Nehemiah may have been as you maintain, he was neither greater than God in knowledge nor his equal, because, as the truthful Scripture says, God surpasses our knowledge—that is, all human wisdom.

Who can endure the further thing which the wicked writing dared to devise: that, because otherwise he could not do so, God by deceit wrested Nehemiah’s soul away, Talmudic reading opposing him, and thus carried him by an angel to heaven in order to make him judge between himself and the Jews? First, who but Satan could teach, who but a Jew could hear—much less believe—such absurdities: that the reading of the Talmud [Col. 0613C] could prejudice God’s power, that the fabulous recitation of an infernal book could resist God’s will or command? Is that book of yours holier, Jew, than the five books of Moses? Holier than the books of the prophets? Better? More worthy? Yet Moses, both lawgiver and reader, died; and the prophets, writers and readers of their books, died. The reading of such holy books could protect none of them from death, and the reading of the Talmud could oppose God’s judgment so that Nehemiah might not die? Truly, such is the immense power of that book that it is able to exempt from the common lot of all, declared in the one man for every human being: “You are earth, and into earth you shall go” (Gen. III), anyone who reads it. But [Col. 0613D] since this is plainly the emptiest nonsense, I turn to divine deceits.

When the angel returned to God and said that Nehemiah in no way wished to die and for that reason continually read the Talmud, so that he could do nothing to him, God said: “I will give you counsel. Return swiftly to him, and make above his head in the air a great whirlwind, like a disturbance of hail and stones, so that, when frightened, he turns his eyes away from reading the Talmud, you may thus seize his soul and bring it here.” The angel returned and did as God had commanded. O divine counsel! O counsel, than which a Deity in need of counsel could find none better! To add something ludicrous, and to advise God better than he advised himself: would it not surely have been more fitting [Col. 0614A] to wait for the unavoidable necessities of the human body, which would compel Nehemiah to be drawn away from reading the Talmud, than to resort to ridiculous trickery? For however resolutely he intended to continue reading, if nothing else, the need to eat—or at least to sleep—would, after two or three days, turn even an utterly mute person away from reading. In that span of time, an angel sent to kill him could not merely seize his one soul and carry it where he pleased, but could also draw a thousand or more human souls from their bodies.

An angel of God did this of old when he struck the Egyptians and killed countless thousands of firstborn within almost a single hour of the night (Exod. XI). He did something similar under the Assyrian king, when in that king’s camp he destroyed one hundred and eighty-five thousand, asleep or awake, in the brief instant of nighttime [Col. 0614B] (IV Kings XIX). He could have done the same when Nehemiah, in order not to die, was fighting against God by the reading already mentioned. It would plainly have been more suitable to take his soul while he was eating or sleeping than to frighten this most obstinate reader away from so holy and most sacred a reading by a whirlwind of hail or stones.

But perhaps God could not endure delay and hastened to settle the most weighty dispute of the question proposed by citing the judgment of a wise man. A great necessity indeed: to pacify heavenly quarrels, lest, perhaps, if prolonged, they should grow greater over time and raise public enemies against God in heaven itself. To prevent this, provision was made that Nehemiah should be summoned quickly by whatever artifice, and that through him peace, lost between God and the Jews, should be restored. Yet I do not think that God would have summoned such a judge from earth to heaven if he had foreknown that he would be inferior to that judge and that the Jews would prevail in the protracted dispute. For Nehemiah did not spare him and did not flatter him. As soon as he was snatched from his body, ascended to heaven, and beheld God sitting on the throne, he immediately, as one steadfast and a lover of truth who accepted no person in judgment, delivered a sentence condemning God, saying concerning the kind of disease which God had thought, pronounced, and contended was leprosy: “It is clean; it is clean.” The repetition of this expression means: “It is certain, it is fixed: God, in your proposition you have been defeated by the Jews, because they have spoken truth and you have been found to have lied” [Col. 0614D].

What remains, then, Jew? Since you have found a man wiser than God, since you have given a judge to the Judge of all: let God descend from his seat; let him yield to one better, yield to one wiser. This, I say, is necessary. For if anyone has been found wiser than God, then he who was thought to be God neither was nor is God.

But it is not enough that God be condemned by Nehemiah’s judgment unless he is also condemned by his own confession. “When the judgment had been pronounced,” he says, “God blushed; and, not daring to say anything against the testimony of so great a man, he replied in jest: ‘NAZA HUNI BENAI,’ that is, ‘My sons have defeated me.’” What remains? Defeated by a man’s judgment, defeated as blushing reveals, defeated by his own declaration—why does God linger [Col. 0615A] upon the throne of omnipotence? God has been deposed by the Jews, cast down by the Jews; he is shown by the elders, and therefore wiser, Jews neither to be almighty nor to know all things.

I know indeed that words so more-than-mad, even demonic, ought not to be refuted by authority or reasoning, but—if it could be done—spat upon with fitting mockery and execration. But since these things are believed, spoken, and written by you, O people lost and destined for destruction, who could keep silence? Who could restrain his hands, much less his words? For since now for eleven hundred years you have groaned beneath the feet of the Christians whom you hate above all others, having become the mockery not only of them but also of the Saracens themselves, and of all nations and demons alike, what restrains our hands from your blood except [Col. 0615B] the command of that God who rejected you and chose us, saying through your Prophet: “Do not kill them” (Ps. LVIII)?

For he wills you to be preserved, not for honor but for reproach; not for your advantage but as a spectacle to the world. He wills you to be preserved as Cain the fratricide was preserved, who, when God rebuked him after he had shed his brother’s blood, said: “Everyone who finds me will kill me” (Gen. IV), and heard: “It shall by no means happen so. But you shall be cursed upon the earth, and you shall be wandering and a fugitive upon it” (ibid.). Thus you are cursed, thus wandering, thus unstable upon the earth, after shedding Christ’s blood—your brother according to the flesh, your Lord according to divinity—so that, what is worse than death, you may in the present be an object of prolonged reproach to human beings, and in the future an everlasting [Col. 0615C] mockery to demons.

Certainly your wicked heart deserves all this; your blasphemous mouth deserves it, pouring out not only continual curses upon human beings but also impious and wicked utterances against God himself. For what is so impious, what so wicked, as what you say: “God is a liar; God has been defeated; God blushed; God declared that he was defeated”? But it has been proved above that he is not a liar. And to whom, except yourselves, is it obscure that he cannot blush? For anyone who blushes seems to acknowledge some guilt, error, or transgression. Unless these or similar causes have preceded, it is impossible for anyone to blush.

Do you still see, my champion, what you have said—how proudly, [Col. 0615D] how wickedly, how foolishly you have set your mouth against heaven? To ascribe guilt, transgression, or error to God—what else is this but madness? “You thought wickedly,” says God, “that I should be like you. I will rebuke you and set you before your face” (Ps. XLIX). And lest he seem to speak to one Jew only, he rebukes all the rejected Jews together when he adds: “Understand these things, you who forget God, lest at any time he seize you and there be none to deliver” (ibid.).

In this verse he strikes at, indeed—what is greater—destroys, the fable already mentioned about your Nehemiah. For you said that God wished to seize Nehemiah’s soul through angelic ministry, but that Nehemiah himself, by reading the Talmud, resisted him so that he could not seize it. Therefore he rebukes you thus and demonstrates that your fable is utterly false: “Understand,” [Col. 0616A] he says, “these things, you who forget God.” What could be truer? Did you not forget God when you thought such unworthy things of God? Therefore it is said to you: “Understand these things, you who forget God.” But what does he urge you to understand? “Lest at any time he seize you and there be none to deliver.” Do not, he says, be deceived; do not be led astray; do not suppose that, when he intends to seize souls, Nehemiah or anyone else can resist him.

He confirms this with another verse of another Psalm. After saying, “Make vows and pay offerings to the Lord your God” (Ps. LVII), he adds—to what God?—“To the terrible one,” he says (ibid.). And immediately: “To him who takes away the spirit of princes” (ibid.). But perhaps he takes away only the spirits of princes, not those of others. Hear Job speaking to God, not only about princes but about all: “You know that I have done nothing impious, since there is no one who can deliver from your hand” (Job X) [Col. 0616B]. It is not this person or that who can deliver from your hand, but absolutely no one can deliver from your hand.

It is therefore clear that your teacher, so often mentioned, could never by any device have delivered his own soul from God’s hand. But, as I stated above, Jew, when you say that God blushed, you admit that he incurred either guilt, error, or transgression. If I should wish to defend him from these by authorities or arguments, I might perhaps appear superfluous or excessive. For who would think that God can incur guilt, error, or transgression, except perhaps the fool who said in his heart, “There is no God” (Ps. LII)? I fear also that I may be told what Job replied to his friend: “Whose helper are you? Is it one [Col. 0616C] who is weak? And do you support the arm of one who is not strong?” (Job XXVI). For it is almost the same to labor over matters so clear as to point with one’s finger to the sun illuminating the world with bright rays on a clear day, to clear and wakeful eyes.

Therefore things wholly evident, even if a Jew objects them, should be passed over with a brief answer or none. Of this sort are also the statements contained at the end of the fable, when it asserts that God was defeated and invents that he confessed himself defeated with his own mouth, lying that he said: “My sons have defeated me.” Who but a Jew could fail to know that this needs no contradiction at all? Certainly no contradiction is needed for what is known to all by manifest truth to be false. For to whom can it be obscure that God cannot be defeated by anyone in power or wisdom, when the whole world has from ancient times heard him say: “To whom have you likened me, made me equal, compared me, and made me like?” (Isa. XLVI.) And shortly afterward: “Remember the former age, for I am God, and there is no other God; none is like me, declaring the last things from the beginning, and from the outset things not yet done, saying: ‘My counsel shall stand, and all my will shall be done’” (ibid.) [Col. 0616D].

And although, as has been said, it seems superfluous to defend God from these mocking absurdities, nevertheless, lest anyone think that the Jews erred or blasphemed only once—which would be more tolerable—there is reason for this discourse to bring forward publicly other errors of theirs on a similar matter. For amid these so numerous blasphemies the reader can readily observe how far from the face of God those have been cast who could think or believe so many things so unworthy and absurd concerning the most high and incomprehensible majesty of God.

For besides what has been set out above, they say and teach in their synagogues—indeed, synagogues of Satan—that when God made this firmament visible to our eyes, he did not complete it wholly, but left unmade the space of a great hole in its northern part. They provide a very fitting and reasonable reason why he did this: they assert that he did it by this providence so that, if at some future time someone should arise and declare himself to be God and equal to God, God might put before him the aforesaid imperfection of the firmament, [Col. 0617B] saying: “If you are God like me, make at least in part what I too have made. I made the greater parts of the firmament; you too, if you can, make this portion which I left incomplete.”

Why do I further complain, O Jews, that you do not recognize spiritual things with the spiritual eye, when you do not even recognize bodily things with the bodily eye? The firmament is certainly bodily, and the eyes of your flesh are bodily as well. What reason, then, is there that this should be hidden from Jewish eyes alone, when it is open to the eyes of the whole world besides you? Every eye except yours plainly sees the firmament, not imperfect in its northern part, nor in its southern, nor in any other part, but whole in all its parts. The northern pole itself, always gleaming above the earth, refutes your great fabrication [Col. 0617C] of falsehood. Set opposite to the southern pole, which never appears to human sight, it shows to the eyes of all—as has been said, except Jewish eyes—that nothing in that region of heaven is imperfect. Since this is most well known, the world itself being judge, let us pass to far worse mockeries of blasphemy.

For you maintain that God becomes angry once every day, and you try to establish this by the strong, as you think, testimony of a Psalm: “God is a righteous judge, strong and patient; will he be angry on every day?” (Ps. VII.) And, O beasts, you now fail even to understand the letter of your Scriptures, which alone you seemed to follow. Was this said affirmatively or declaratively, and not rather put in an interrogative form so as to deny it? For it says: “Will he [Col. 0617D] be angry on every day?” as though it had said, “He will not be angry on every day.” Read again your Hebrew idiom, and you will recognize that this is the sense of that text, if Jewish blindness does not prevent you. Although we are Latins, nothing in your truthful Scriptures could remain unknown to us, whom the ample instruction of many persons skilled in both languages has taught.

I pass over the fact that you most foolishly imagine God to become angry in a human manner. If you think this, you certainly assert that he is changeable. For if, in the usual human manner, he is now angry, now appeased, now joyful, now sorrowful, now forgetful, now mindful, and either does or suffers the other like things in our manner, then your Prophet lies, who, discussing the changeability of heaven and earth and God’s constancy, says to God: “They”—that is, heaven and earth—“shall perish, but you remain” (Ps. CI). And a few words later: “You shall change them, and they shall be changed; but you are the same” (ibid.) [Col. 0618A]. If, therefore, God remains, if he is not changed, he is changed neither in essence nor in affection. For perhaps you could object that God is not changed in essence but is changed in affection; not changed naturally, but changed accidentally. Scripture removes and excludes both claims, even if you deny it a thousand times, when it says, “But you remain,” and when it says, “But you are the same.” Therefore God is not now angry and now appeased in our manner.

To the matters already stated above you add that he becomes angry in the first hour of the day; and you give this reason for his anger: in that hour—the first—kings of wickedness arise, put diadems upon themselves, and worship the sun. You add that no one has ever known the precise moment of that hour at which he becomes angry except Balaam son of Beor. And you add, giving him a suitable companion in this knowledge, namely a rooster, which you assert alone with Balaam knows the precise moment of the hour already mentioned.

What can I say? As I confessed above, I do not know whether it is more fitting to answer such utterly foolish trifles or to remain silent. To answer seems superfluous; to remain silent seems unsuitable. It is superfluous because the matter proposed displays its folly without a covering; unsuitable because, when it has been proposed for an answer, silence is unhelpful.
