And, to meet first with the first points presented: what authority taught, what reason persuaded you to believe that God becomes angry, becomes angry daily, and becomes angry in the first hour of the day? [Col. 0618C] What authoritative lawgiver said this? What prophet wrote it? Which of those read in your entire divine Canon taught it? Produce anyone from that whole multitude of ancient saints who wrote, taught, or even thought this, and I concede the point. But if authority fails you and you cannot fortify your statements by its strength, defend so monstrous a fable by some reasoning. If you have not even that, what remains? What remains, I say, except that you, most foolish people, together with your mocking fables, should become a spectacle to heaven and earth, angels and human beings?

For who does not see that, when the cause is removed, the effect cannot stand? But I must say what I call the cause and what I call the effect. For if I can remove the cause, I shall remove the effect also. I call the cause, O Jews, the thing you yourselves allege: that, in the first hour of the day, kings of wickedness rise, put diadems upon themselves, and worship the sun; the effect being that God, seeing this take place in the first hour of the day, becomes angry in that same first hour, and because he sees it happen daily at the same hour, becomes angry daily [Col. 0618D].

Who are these kings of wickedness who never, in the third hour of the day, never in the fourth, fifth, sixth, or any other hour, but always in the first hour of the day, put diadems on themselves and worship the sun? Truly they are most zealous and distinguished worshippers of wickedness, whom no business of their kingdoms and no hindrances can draw away, so that daily and at the same hour [Col. 0619A] they put on diadems and worship the sun. Entirely peaceful kings and most tranquil kingdoms, fearing no adversity, troubled by no domestic, civil, or foreign disturbances, enjoying the calmest leisure and tirelessly devoting themselves to profane worship. Clearly these are, as was said of old, golden ages, affording their kings so desirable and prolonged a leisure that, laying aside arms and putting away cares, they serve their own religion with such devotedness that over such long spans of time they miss neither a single day nor the same hour of the day.

I have indeed heard that certain eastern kings once worshipped the sun; but that they did so daily, always in the first hour of the day, I do not know. More accurately I could say that I know that they did not do so daily or always in the first hour of the day. For they were warlike and almost always under arms; hence reason itself teaches that they could neither serve execrable rites daily nor always keep the same hour of the day. But why do I speak of ancient errors and cults of kings, when this Jewish fable says this not merely of past time, but rather of the present and continuing time? For the fable does not speak of ages gone by, but of the present time, saying that every day in the first hour of the day kings of wickedness arise, put diadems upon themselves, and worship the sun. Anyone paying slight attention will perceive how unconsidered it is to think this of our own days, how false to say it.

For now there is no king in the East, none in the West, none in the South, none in the North—those four regions by which the whole world is described—who, I do not say in the first or sixth hour, but at any hour of day or night, worships the sun; there is none who renders to the creature the worship due to the Creator [Col. 0619C]. For concerning the kings of Christians and the kings of Saracens, who, whether Christian or Saracen, rule almost the whole world, it is certain that they do not worship the sun. And concerning certain others, though very few, who still rule some pagan peoples, it has never been heard. Hence it is now sufficiently established that no king of our time worships the sun. Since this is true, the Jewish fable lies when it says that the sun is worshipped daily in the first hour of the day by certain kings of wickedness. For if now no king worships the sun at any time, certainly none worships it daily or in the first hour of the day.

And if no king worships the sun on any day or at any hour, that too is false which the Jew had added: that Balaam or the rooster knows the precise moment of the first hour at which God was accustomed to become angry. For neither Balaam nor the rooster can know the precise moment of an hour which does not exist; nor can it be called an hour of a day which occurs in no course of time [Col. 0619D].

The cause having thus been excluded, the effect too is excluded: God no longer has anything for which to be angry, since no king anywhere in the world is found to worship the sun. Therefore everything proposed by the opposing side was false: both that God was angry every day, and that kings of wickedness placed diadems upon themselves and worshipped the sun. Why Balaam and the cock have deserved from you Jews so great a distinction above all other human beings and birds of God, I now wonder and ask. I ask, I say, why they deserved so much from you that you wished to attribute knowledge of divine wrath—and knowledge of the very hour at which you say God is angry—to these two alone and to no others besides them. A great prerogative indeed, a supreme privilege, for Balaam and the cock: by it the former surpasses all men, and the latter all birds. It is certainly astonishing to us, and to all besides yourselves. Since you declare everything astonishing, you are now unable to be astonished at anything: at Balaam’s being preferred to Moses, to David, to Solomon, to Isaiah, to all the prophets, and finally to all wise and divine men, in knowing the aforesaid hour.

Is it not astonishing if Balaam is preferred to him concerning whom God says to Aaron and Miriam: “If there be among you a prophet of the Lord, I shall appear to him in a vision, or speak to him in a dream; but not such is my servant Moses, for I speak to him mouth to mouth, and openly; not through riddles and figures does he see the Lord?” (Num. XII.) Is it not astonishing if he is also preferred to him who says to God: “You have made known to me the uncertain and hidden things of your wisdom”? (Ps. L.) Is it not astonishing if he is preferred to him to whom God says: “I have given you a wise and understanding heart, so that none like you has existed before you, nor shall arise after you”? (III Kings III.) Is it not astonishing if Balaam is preferred, in knowing the secrets of God, to him who could behold the Lord sitting upon a throne high and exalted, the seraphim standing above the temple and covering God’s face and feet with their wings, and hear them cry, “Holy, holy, holy”? (Isa. VI.)

But perhaps he seems to you worthy of preference above them all because he foretold some true things and conversed with his she-ass (Num. XXII). But did he foretell things loftier, more divine, or more numerous than the prophets? Because a she-ass once spoke to a man in human words, is he preferred to such great and astonishing signs as Moses performed? Yet, to satisfy you in some respect, lest perhaps you accuse me of always being your enemy, I grant that Balaam—whether prophet, divine man, or diviner, even though of inferior merit—received some singular grace above men of greater merit. He therefore had this grace: that he knew the hour or instant of divine wrath. He had that grace—but only as long as God pleased. Did he have it after he displeased God? Did he have this grace after God had said to him through the angel: “Your way is perverse and contrary to me”? (Num. XXI.) Did he have it after, on returning to his people, he gave wicked counsel against God’s people; after he was killed by your fathers, O Jews, not as a prophet of God honored, but as one impious toward God and as a public enemy? I do not think you are so utterly senseless, so devoid of human reason, as to believe that impious men, especially after death, share in God’s secrets or counsels. If this is so, then it is false that Balaam can daily recognize the hour or instant of divine wrath.

[Col. 0621A] Now, as to your associating the cock with divine counsels and calling it privy to God’s secrets: let the world see; let the whole earth judge. Let it see and judge whether a cock ought to be admitted to know divine secrets or acts—secrets to which scarcely any human being has ever been admitted. But since it is Jewish custom always to misuse the Scriptures, just as you misused the previously cited verse of the Psalm to prove God’s daily anger—“God is a just judge, strong and patient: is he angry every day?” (Ps. VII)—perhaps you also misuse, to display the singular wisdom of your cock, that verse of Job: “Who put wisdom in the inward parts of man, or who gave understanding to the cock?” (Job XXXVIII.) Perhaps here you have established your strength; this you presume to be the impregnable tower of Jewish understanding; from this you prefer the cock’s outstanding intelligence to the understanding of all human beings.

But if the cock is to be preferred to all understanding of birds, cattle, and men because it is written of it, “Who gave understanding to the cock?”, what then will be thought of the perception of the ox, or the intelligence of the ass, concerning whom the prophet writes: “The ox knew its owner, and the ass its master’s manger” (Isa. I)? What will be said of the remarkable skill of certain birds, of whom another prophet says: “The turtle-dove, the swallow, and the stork observed the time of their coming” (Jer. VIII)? Not to speak of the varied and wonderful intelligence of larger animals, what, I ask, will you think or say of the bee, producing honey by such shrewd labor and industry? What will you think or say of the ant itself, almost without bodily form, which your Solomon praises so highly that he even sends men to it to learn wisdom? For what does he write of it? “Go to the ant, O sluggard; consider her ways and learn wisdom” (Prov. VI), and the rest.

But what is this understanding of your cock? I pass over the spiritual understanding, which does not belong to you, to whom it has not been given to know the mystery of the kingdom of God. The understanding of the cock of which Scripture speaks is plainly what we all observe and continually see: by songs long interrupted or more frequently repeated amid the deep darkness of night, it declares that it perceives the approaching advent of light by a certain natural and innate quickness of understanding. Because it can do this, because it understands this, will you immediately admit it to know God’s counsels, immediately to know the hour of divine wrath unknown to all mortals? Will you immediately prefer the cock’s intelligence to the wisdom of all—not only human beings, but even the angels themselves?

Let, then, the birds mentioned above by way of example—the turtle-dove, swallow, and stork—likewise be preferred above all these. Let the ox and ass be preferred; let bees and ants be preferred; and whatever animals seem to possess, above others, anything pertaining to any kind of intelligence, spiritually implanted in their own nature. Let them immediately be admitted even to the third heaven, to which our Apostle, though you do not believe it, was caught up (II Cor. XII). Let them be caught up, and let no mystery of God remain hidden from bird or quadruped after it has been able to claim for itself, by natural right, some characteristic of whatever sort of intelligence above others. But I believe there is no rational creature—not only in heaven, not only on earth, but not even in the underworld—that would not spit out, ridicule, and abominate this Jewish interpretation. Let these remarks about these matters therefore suffice; and, as your prophet says, let a swift passage be made to behold abominations and blasphemies far greater than these (Ezek. VIII), for it is wearisome to linger long over so many abominations.

You say—and read in that heavenly and most truthful scripture of yours, the Talmud—that God weeps once every day, and that two tears issuing from his eyes fall into the great sea; you assert that these are the brightness which at night seems to fall from the stars. You say also that the cause of the weeping which you attribute to God is the captivity of the Jews. Indeed, because of grief, you assert that three times a day he roars like a lion and for that reason strikes heaven with his feet, as men tread a winepress. Moreover, in the manner of a dove, he makes a certain murmuring sound, moves his head each time, and says in the voice of one in pain: “Woe is me! Woe is me! Why have I reduced my house to a desert, burned my temple, and transferred my children among the nations? Woe to the father who transferred his children, and woe to the children who were transferred from their father’s table!” You also say that certain of your teachers heard this voice in a ruined place, because he strikes his feet together as though they itched, claps his hands like one in pain, and daily prays that his mercy may be above his wrath and that he may deal mercifully with his people.

[Col. 0622C] What are you expecting, reader? What are you waiting for? Do you suppose that I shall argue against the Jews about these things? Far be it from me to argue against them concerning these things! Far be it from me to answer dogs of the utmost shamelessness and swine of the utmost filth as though they were capable of reason, and to show them worthy of any reply whatever on these subjects. Are those worthy of my answer, or of anyone’s, who seem born only to blaspheme God and assigned as fodder to eternal fire? Even if I called them dogs or swine, I have not exceeded in any respect. For though these animals commonly signify carnal impurity in the sacred Scriptures, such impurity nevertheless goes no further than bodily evils; but how great and how often-repeated is this blasphemy!

I do not wish to despise the words of my Lord by exposing divine pearls to be trampled by such beasts (Matt. VII). Although in the foregoing I may seem to have done so, there was nevertheless a reason, which I myself stated: that this writing of mine might benefit, if not all or many, at least a few Jews whom we see sometimes converted to God and who either have been infected by this pestilence or might be infected by it. But since intolerable things follow unheard-of things, it is not fitting to deal with those who say such things as though they were human beings using reason. Their tales and traditions wholly foreign to God’s law are indeed innumerable; concerning them the Lord says to the Pharisees in the Gospel: “You have abandoned the commandments of God because of your traditions” (Matt. VII, 15). Yet those traditions are far more tolerable which, although they say many absurd things about people or human affairs, do not touch divine things, preserving them inviolate. But utterly accursed and wholly intolerable are those which burst into such madness that they boldly proclaim of God things which human ears can scarcely endure. Among such traditions is the thing just recounted.

Who, then, ought—or would deign—to answer those who say these things? Who would deign to answer this blasphemous, foolish, impious voice, which says that God weeps once every day; that two of his tears fall into the great sea; that three times a day he roars like a lion; that, angry—indeed almost raging—he strikes heaven with his feet in repeated blows; that he groans like a dove; that he moves his head like one indignant; that, acutely distressed, he strikes hands and feet together; and that, in miserable grief, he says: “Woe is me! Woe is me!”

[Col. 0623B] Nevertheless, I would reply, as I did above, if in all these things they possessed even a little sound understanding; if they interpreted, according to the sense of sacred Scripture, weeping, roaring, groaning, and pain—which, according to the sound of the letter, they attribute to God in horrifying blasphemy. For although I do not recall ever having read in the Old Scripture of divine weeping or, as regards God, dove-like groaning, I nevertheless read that he roars, suffers pain, cries out—and, what would be still more astonishing if sound understanding were absent, that he whistles and creaks.

He roars, as in Amos: “The Lord will roar from Zion, and from Jerusalem he will utter his voice” (Amos I). He suffers pain, as in the book of Judges: “The children of Israel cried to the Lord, who was grieved over their miseries” (Judg. X). He cries out, as in Isaiah: “He will cry aloud and shout, and will prevail against his enemies” (Isa. XLII). He whistles, as in the same prophet: “The Lord will whistle for the fly that is at the end of the rivers of Egypt, and for the bee that is in the land of Assyria” (Isa. VII). He creaks, as in Amos: “Behold, I will creak beneath you, as a wagon loaded with hay creaks” (Amos II). If in any of these or similar expressions—for many similar things are found said of God in the sacred writings—Jewish interpretation agreed with Christian, or, if they recoil from this, with rational interpretation, I would still reply to the Jews, as I did before, and would not disdain to speak with them of such matters.

But since the Jews refuse to admit metaphor, allegory, or any of the customary and manifold modes of speech by which all these things are fittingly applied to God, and understand in them only the killing letter, what could I say? Why should I vainly defend God against the foolish weeping, mad roaring, miserable groaning, and other monstrous and frenzied habits alleged against him? For who that is wise and sound—or at least not wholly foolish—does not know that weeping, roaring, groaning, and the other most prodigious things just mentioned cannot belong to God, and that the divine nature is altogether alien to all of them?

[Col. 0624A] Who does not know that the incorporeal, simple, uncircumscribed nature, far removed from every compound or composition of bodily elements, to which no likeness or differentiation of head, body, or any human limbs belongs, is free from all the things which detestable Jewish error imputes to it? For who weeps without eyes? Who roars without a voice? Who strikes hands and feet together if he does not have them? Finally, who performs the functions of limbs without instruments of any limbs? I pass over the rage of one angry, the sadness of one grieving, the misery of one crying, “Woe is me! Woe is me!” I pass over the fact that Jewish wisdom has made the omnipotent powerless: that, wishing to end the Jews’ long captivity, he cannot; that for this reason he weeps, roars, bellows, groans, suffers pain, and strikes hands and feet together. For who, apart from a Jew, has ever devised or dared to assert that God says, “Woe is me!”?

I do indeed read him saying through the prophet: “Woe! I shall be comforted concerning my enemies, and shall be avenged upon my foes” (Isa. I). But that “woe,” though uttered by God, is not God’s but human beings’; it is not God’s but that of his enemies.

Let God’s enemies therefore see what absurdities they impute to God’s majesty. For to say “Woe is me” belongs only to one who is miserable; to say “Woe is me” belongs only to one lamenting his own misery. Therefore, when the Jew says that God says “Woe is me,” he plainly says that God is miserable. But who, apart from a Jew, would not shudder even to think of calling God miserable? Truly miserable is that race of people; truly a nation turned from the head into the tail of all nations: they fashion God, with respect to the essence of divinity, as though he were human; divide him according to human limbs; assign human functions to these supposed human limbs; and attribute to God not only human but even bestial movements, roars, and groans.

[Col. 0624C] Their Moses did not think this about God; he does not say it; he did not leave it written in the final book of his Pentateuch. “You did not see,” he says to the Jews, “any likeness on the day when God spoke to you at Horeb from the midst of the fire, lest, deceived, you make for yourselves a carved likeness of all cattle upon the earth, or birds flying under heaven, or creeping things moving on the earth, or fish moving beneath the earth in the waters; lest, raising your eyes to heaven, you see the sun and moon and all the stars of heaven, and, deceived by error, worship and serve them, which the Lord your God created for the service of all nations under heaven” (Deut. IV).

What could he have said more plainly to a foolish people, always ready to think and believe every wickedness? How could he have warned those people more plainly not to become idolaters, not to believe that in God’s nature there was any image or likeness of male or female, cattle or birds, creeping things or fish, sun, moon, or stars? Plainly, in these words he denied and did not permit it to be understood that God is male or female, cattle or bird, creeping thing or fish, sun, moon, or stars. Moses would not, however, have forbidden the Jews to make carved likenesses or images of these things if he had known such to be the truth of the divine nature. Since he forbade it, he understood God’s nature not to resemble the natures of any of these animals or living beings, nor those of sun, moon, or stars.

What authority or reason, then, does the Jew possess for fashioning God—as has already been said, with regard to God’s nature—as a human being, attributing human limbs to him, assigning him human or bestial gestures or affections, and saying that he roars like a lion and groans like a dove? Let these wretches remember that for this reason God commanded that the craftsmen of the tabernacle under Moses, and the craftsmen of the temple under Solomon, should not weave in the tabernacle or carve, cast, paint, or fashion in the temple or tabernacle any likeness of any animal—except the two seraphim, which were indeed made in part in a human likeness, but for the remembrance and reverence of angels. Thus, at least when reminded by this sight, the hard Jews might understand that God must be preferred not only to earthly human beings but even to heavenly powers.

[Col. 0625B] Let them also recall the bronze serpent, made by Moses at God’s command (Exod. XXI), preserved for a long time afterward, and broken by the good king Hezekiah (IV Kings XVIII), lest the Jews—who believed scarcely anything true and thought nearly everything false to be true—should at some time believe that God was a serpent. For they had for some time already regarded it as a god and sacrificed offerings to it as to a god. Since every body and every likeness of bodily things has thus been excluded from God, I believe that the proposed Jewish tale has now wholly perished. A nature which has nothing in common with bodily things, to which powerlessness, pain, and misery cannot be attributed, is likewise free from all the other affections of bodily things. Therefore whatever the blasphemous Jews above proposed concerning such matters is false.

But now I return from conversation with the reader to the Jew. Since I refused to argue with him concerning the blasphemies alleged against God, because it seemed unworthy, I shall deal with him in my customary manner concerning great errors which nevertheless do not concern God’s nature. Tell me then, Jew: do you think true what your Talmud relates about Og king of Bashan? I know that you not only think it true, but believe it to be true even more than the words of the Law or prophets. Let it therefore, whatever it may be, be brought forward and be seen in the full brightness of manifest truth.

“Og king of Bashan,” says the Talmud, “when he saw the immense army of Israel—namely six hundred and four thousand five hundred men, from thirty years old and upward, excluding women and little children, who could not be counted—placed upon his head a mass of unheard-of size and wished to crush the entire expedition with it. While he was devising this, the hoopoe, a very small bird, alighted upon the mass and battered it with its beak until, having made a great hole corresponding to the size of that king’s head, the mass passed over his head and settled upon the king’s shoulders. When this had occurred, the same mass resting upon his shoulders and the king’s head rising above the mass, suddenly lengthened teeth prevented him from setting it down again.

“Seeing this, Moses—whose body was ten cubits high and whose staff had the same length—rose in the manner of one leaping, ten cubits above the ground, in order to strike him with the staff in some part of his body. Although he was raised so high from the ground by the leap, the tip of the staff with which he intended to strike Og could not reach farther than the joint where the leg is joined to the foot, commonly called the ankle. When Moses struck King Og there, he immediately fell and died.”

[Col. 0626A] This is certainly your noble tale. But see how much more foolish—or wiser—you are than all nations. Many ancient pagans indeed invented many diverse tales about different things, as Aesop among the Greeks and Naso [Ovid] among the Latins. They invented many laughable things; yet the authors of the tales themselves did not understand them according to what they wrote, but wished them to be applied either to physical realities or to human morals. Hence they said that Atlas supported heaven; that Typhoeus, a giant with a hundred hands—that is, possessing one hundred hands—heaped mountains upon mountains and fought from their summit against heaven and Jupiter; and that after his long struggle against the heavenly gods, Jupiter cast Cyclopean thunderbolts and threw him down. They said he was not killed, but that the great island of Sicily was placed upon him so that he might not rise again to wage war against the gods; and that frequent earthquakes of the island result from his striving again to rise and fight against the gods.

So they wrote that Orpheus, by wondrous songs and unprecedented melody of the lyre, caused moving woods to run after him and rivers to stand still; that Hercules fought the many-headed hydra, but that when he cut off one head, a hundred heads suddenly arose, and that at last, Greek fire having been applied, he burned that monster together with the Lernaean marsh in which it dwelt. They handed down in writing that Phaethon, son of the Sun, badly driving his father’s chariot, nearly set the world on fire; that Circe, daughter of that same Sun, changed Ulysses’ companions into wolves, lions, tigers, and beasts of various kinds by herbs and spells; that a sleepless dragon guarded the golden fleece of a ram; that human beings became gods, women stars, foxes cocks, hares geese, and other beasts or birds; that these spoke to one another in human words; and many other laughable things of this sort.

[Col. 0626D] Yet though they said and wrote these things, they nevertheless understood them quite differently, as has been said, and wished others likewise to understand them. For they were human beings and rational; though remote from divine worship, they were wise concerning matters which the world could not yet comprehend. I would clearly expound their meaning in these several tales, were I not to see that this would prolong this work beyond measure and did not pertain to the matter proposed. Therefore it would not be very surprising if you Jews also possessed tales and turned their meaning toward some true and useful matter. For that true and holy page itself has this quality: it sometimes recounts things whose wording is false according to the letter, but whose meaning is true and necessary.

Thus, in your book called Judges, you read that the trees went to anoint a king over themselves, and that they spoke to the olive tree, the fig tree, the vine, and the bramble (Judg. IX). Whoever knows that trees cannot speak recognizes that this is not literally true. Yet whoever does not doubt that such a mode of expression is common throughout Scripture understands its truth in the reality conveyed through a comparison drawn from insensible plants. One instructed in these matters understands the vine, olive, and fig tree as signifying fruitful shrubs, namely the sons of Gideon; and the unfruitful, harsh bramble as signifying Abimelech the fratricide. This sense is frequently found in other parables of your divine Canon, such as that which the prophet Nathan set before David after David had committed adultery with Uriah’s wife.

[Col. 0627B] It was not literally true what Nathan told him about the rich man and his hundred sheep, the poor man and his single sheep, or the rich man’s sparing his hundred sheep and violently taking the poor man’s one sheep to prepare a meal for his guest (II Kings XII). Yet what the prophet meant in those words was true: David was the rich man; Uriah, poor in comparison with the king; the one sheep, his wife; the traveler and guest, the king’s desire; and the sheep made into a meal for the guest, the woman surrendered to unlawful desire. There are many similar examples of this kind.

If you Jews interpreted your tales in this way, understood them wisely in this way, and expounded them usefully in this way, I would not praise you, yet neither would I be surprised. I would not praise you because I do not approve your having accepted, or accepting, anything outside your sacred Canon as authoritative. But I would not be surprised if I saw you approve things beyond the Law, the Prophets, or the other divine books transmitted to you from antiquity, when they were covered with a fabulous veil yet directed to some useful instruction. But since your tales lack all these things, since nothing whatever useful lies hidden in them, but everything appears foolish, impious, and blasphemous, there is no reason why my pen should spare you—because God himself does not spare you.

[Col. 0627D] Jewish tales surpass all the tales of the ages, because what had not been heard from the beginning of time is recounted by the sacred text of the Talmud’s Jewish tales. O astounding turning-away of the Jewish people from God! Under the guise of divine worship, which they believe themselves to serve, they think concerning the Creator and his nature things which even idolaters themselves could never have believed or invented. Concerning you and in you, O ruined people, has been fulfilled what the Apostle—your countryman by birth, ours by teaching—says of such people: “There will be a time when they will not endure sound doctrine, but according to their desires will heap up teachers for themselves, with itching ears. They will turn their hearing away from the truth and turn instead to tales” (II Tim. III).

[Col. 0628A] Behold truly that time in which we see the Apostle’s saying fulfilled. Behold the time in which we see that you do not endure sound doctrine. Or will you say that you endure sound doctrine, you who, rejecting God’s Law and the prophets, prefer foreign trifles to heavenly words? But this is the result of your itching ears: weary of familiar things, you love unheard-of things, and, tired of the ancients, you have heaped up new teachers for yourselves. Truly you have heaped them up; truly you have made a great heap of teachers, so that the number of the old teachers is scarcely visible in comparison with the new. But teachers of what? Certainly not of salvation, but of perdition; not of truth, but of falsehood. Therefore the Apostle continues: “They will turn their hearing away from the truth and turn instead to tales.” Is it not so? It truly is. With the whole world as witness, you have turned your hearing away from truth and, as I said, turned to tales. Among them is the tale of Og king of Bashan, which I had introduced for discussion.

For what could be called more fabulous, false, and ridiculous than your reading and believing that the height of his foot alone was thirty cubits? How so? Because you assert that Moses’ body was ten cubits long, his staff also ten cubits long, and Moses himself, when he struck the giant at the joint of leg and foot with the tip of his staff, rose by a leap ten cubits above the ground. For that reason, ten cubits of Moses’ body, ten cubits of Moses’ staff, and ten cubits of Moses’ leap, joined together, make thirty cubits—apart from the length of his outstretched arm, which may be reckoned between his head and the lower end of the staff that he held in his hand.

[Col. 0628C] If this is true, then, according to the usual proportion of the human body, his leg alone, from foot to the beginning of the calf, was, to say the least, one hundred and fifty cubits. Hence there is no doubt that the same calf, longer than the leg, from knee to the joint of the thigh, was, according to the natural bodily proportion I have mentioned, at least two hundred cubits. Then, if the proper proportion extends to the summit of the spine adjoining the neck, you will find more than two hundred and thirty cubits; and this apart from the size of the neck and head, in which you will find no fewer than eighty. Added together, these make seven hundred cubits, less ten.

You see, therefore, Jews, that according to this measurement—not ours, but yours—the stature of Og king of Bashan extended to six hundred and ninety cubits in height, and his breadth likewise reached one hundred and twenty. Who but you could ever have devised such a monster? Who, I say, but you could have imagined a man six hundred and ninety cubits long and one hundred and twenty cubits broad? Since there is no need to argue at length against such madness of yours, but rather to laugh at it—for it is so plain that not even the blind could miss it—I offer only this one point. Do you believe Moses? I know that you do. Since, therefore, you believe Moses, how could you believe so [Col. 0629A] absurd a thing contrary to Moses’ words? For he himself writes in the book of Deuteronomy, a book which, if you are Jews, you cannot fail to know: “Only Og king of Bashan remained of the stock of the giants. His iron bed is shown at Rabbath of the children of Ammon; it is nine cubits long and four broad, by the measure of a man’s cubit” (Deut. 3). A bed is always greater in length and breadth than the person lying in it. He who said, therefore, that that giant’s bed was nine cubits long and four cubits broad plainly showed that its occupant was somewhat less than the bed in length and breadth. It is clear, then, that that king was neither a full nine cubits long nor a full four cubits broad. But I grant that he lacked nothing of the nine cubits in length [Col. 0629B] nor of the four in breadth. Was he longer or broader than his own bed? I think the Jewish dispute comes to rest here.

It is false, then, that you have said that man was of such huge stature. And it is no less false that you have said Moses himself was ten cubits tall. For Moses would not have written, as though it were an unprecedented marvel, that the giant Og’s bed was nine cubits long. If he himself was ten cubits tall, on what grounds does he seem to marvel at a man’s bed of nine cubits? With better reason he ought to seem to marvel at himself, a man of ten cubits, than at another man’s bed of nine cubits. But lest I prolong this more than is proper, I conclude thus. If you believe Moses when he says that Og king of Bashan’s bed was only nine cubits [Col. 0629C] long, I think you will not say that Og could have been larger than his bed. Yet, as I have already said, I know that on this point you believe Moses. Henceforth, therefore, you ought to be certain that the often-mentioned giant’s stature was not six hundred and eighty cubits, but at most nine.

And, to link on the next part of the tale: how could a man—even if his body were larger than ours—place upon his head a mass of such unprecedented and unimaginable magnitude that by throwing it he thought he could overthrow six hundred and four thousand armed men and five hundred men of the Jewish army, besides innumerable women and little children? To accomplish this, to say something myself resembling your fables, either Olympus would have had to be raised into the air for him, [Col. 0629D] or our Mount Jupiter—although overseas in relation to him—would have had to be placed upon his head; or Taurus in Cilicia, or some mountain of Armenia, which was closer to him, would undoubtedly have had to be torn up from its roots. And if he placed his hope of victory in that mass, he had brought forth such a great army in vain to fight against Moses and God’s people. Of that army Moses himself says: “Og king of Bashan came out against them with all his people to fight at Edrei” (Num. 21).

But behold so great a mass; behold so vast a region placed upon his head. What follows? What does the excellent Scripture say next? “The hoopoe,” it says, “a very small bird, perched upon the mass itself and kept striking it with its beak until, when a large hole had been made proportionate to that king’s head, the mass passed over his head and settled upon the king’s shoulders” [Col. 0630A]. Among matters beyond expression in their wonder, I do not know what I should marvel at more. Should I marvel more or less that the tiny hoopoe, with a smaller beak, undertook to bore through so great a mass and kept hammering at it until it made in it a hole capable of receiving a giant’s head; or at the endurance or strength of that man, who supported so great a mass resting upon his head until a small bird, with its short beak, gradually penetrated the dense hardness of so enormous a body with feeble blows? And this continued until, once a hole proportionate to the royal head had been made, the mass, no longer able to remain upon the head, slipped down by its natural weight and was caught upon the poor man’s broader shoulders; because it could not pass through the narrower hole, in comparison with the width of those shoulders, and fall lower [Col. 0630B].

And what follows? When this had happened, with that same mass resting on his shoulders and the king’s head protruding above it, suddenly his teeth grew to an enormous length and prevented him from removing it any further. I do indeed read not a Jewish but a pagan fable which invented that dragon’s teeth were sown and that from them sprang the Theban peoples—not unarmed, but armed, equipped with helmets, cuirasses, shields, swords, and every kind of military gear. But, as I said above, in such matters and similar ones the pagans did not doubt that they had written fables, not historical events; and they believed and taught alike that the tales were not true but signified certain things already accomplished. For when they said that the people just mentioned arose from a dragon’s teeth, they intended, by the likeness of a poisonous and raging creature, to signify a people stubborn [Col. 0630C] and unyielding in wickedness. By saying that it came armed from the earth, they indicated that it was warlike and would always be engaged in arms.

If the teeth of your giant, Jews, after the mass had fallen upon his shoulders, signified something of this sort, as I stated above, it might somehow be tolerable. But since this fable, like your other fables, contains nothing mystical in divine matters and nothing signifying anything in human matters, whether in its outer shell or its inner core, what am I to say? What am I to say when I see a man whom you have truly dreamed of as buried in the sleep of profound folly, carrying a mass—or rather, a vast region—upon his shoulders, with his head projecting above it and teeth of immense size thrusting out, more than a boar’s fashion, and yet able to remove it, hindered neither below by his shoulders nor above by his opposing teeth [Col. 0630D]?

But why, according to you, did Moses pass over such great miracles in silence? Why did he omit such things—he who, although he wrote much that was great, nevertheless wrote many lesser things? Why did he omit that a little hoopoe, with its fragile beak, penetrated the frequently mentioned mass, so dense and so hard? Why did he omit the giant’s lengthened teeth? Why did he omit that Moses attacked him alone, was lifted from the ground by a stupendous leap, and with a light touch of his staff threw him to the earth, struck him down, and killed him? It is astonishing that he who, before Pharaoh, by divine power changed this same staff into a dragon (Exod. 7), who by it changed the Egyptian waters into blood (Exod. 14), divided the sea, and brought water from the rock (Exod. 17), passed over in silence this most remarkable [Col. 0631A] miracle. He did not, certainly, omit it because he did not wish to write what happened; he omitted it as one unwilling to write what never happened. He did not refrain from writing it to avoid recording what was true, but because he would not write what was false. And why do I say “would not”? Rather, he was unable to write what had never been, what was unheard of. Since no tongue suffices adequately to execrate this point by point, let the discourse hasten to similar things. Let our people hear, Jews, your mysteries; let them penetrate your deep secrets, so that your wisdom may be revealed to all. Let them hear the following passage from the precious book of the *Talmuth*:

> Among the Jews there was a certain man, called among them Jozah Ben Levi, whom we call Joshua son of Levi, a man, as they say, devout and fearing God, who devoted himself to this book [Col. 0631B] from his infancy until decrepit old age, so that in this way he might escape death. When the Lord saw this, wishing to take away his soul so that he might rejoice with the Jews, friends of the Lord, who had spent their whole lives studying the *Talmuth*, he commanded the smiting angel to go there and take that man’s soul.
>
> Immediately the angel, rejoicing, obeyed the Lord’s command. He came and stood upon the roof of that man’s house, not far from him. When Joshua lifted his eyes and saw him, he immediately recognized that he had come for his soul. And he said: “What do you seek?” “The Lord has sent me,” he said, “for your soul.” But Joshua said: “The Lord has sent you in vain, since I am turning over and reading the *Talmuth*. But I adjure you by this book that you have no power to take my soul” [Col. 0631C].
>
> The angel returned and reported this to the Lord. “Return,” the Lord said to him, “and tell him to come, rejoice, and feast with us; and let him learn that it will be better for him here than there.” The angel returned and announced what the Lord commanded. Joshua answered the messenger that he would by no means obey the Lord’s command unless He were willing, under a covenant, to grant him the request that he should ask of Him. When the angel had reported to the Lord what Joshua requested, He granted it, though unwillingly. The angel quickly announced what the Lord had granted. Hearing this, Joshua said that during his lifetime he wished to see the gates of hell and paradise. “Climb upon me,” said the angel, “and I shall take you wherever you wish.” “I shall not climb up,” Joshua said, “nor go with you unless you give me your sword; for I fear that you will kill me on the way.” The angel immediately [Col. 0631D] gave him the sword. When Joshua had climbed up, the angel said: “Where do you wish me to take you?” He replied: “To the gates of hell, that afterwards I may delight in the sight of paradise.”
>
> Having been led there, he saw many peoples from every nation under heaven: Christians, Amorites, Jebusites, Hivites, Hittites, Perizzites, Moabites, Ammonites, Arabs, and Philistines. He also saw kings: Pharaoh, Sihon, Og, and all the others killed by Joshua; Jabin and his commander Sisera; Eglon, who was killed by Ehud; Nebuchadnezzar; and Holofernes, his commander. When he asked one by one the cause of their condemnation, Joshua said: “Why are Christians condemned?” The angel said: “Do you not know?” He answered: “I know, but I desire to hear it from you.” The angel said: “Because they believe in Mary’s son, do not observe Moses’ law, and especially because they do not believe [Col. 0632A] in the *Talmuth*.” It would take a long time to recount the cause of the condemnation of the other peoples and kings; but this alone is the cause: they do not believe in the *Talmuth*, or they had attacked the children of Israel.
>
> Pharaoh lay cast down in hell, his head held beneath [or: supporting] the threshold of hell’s gate; his eye served as the hinge of that gate. The gate through which souls entered turned around on every side upon his eye. Joshua asked why he suffered so great a punishment. The angel replied: “Because he afflicted the children of Israel in the land of Egypt and, after afflicting them, pursued them as far as the sea.” Having seen all the torments that occurred in hell, Joshua said: “Lead me to paradise.” Paradise, it is said, is enclosed on every side by a wall. When the angel had brought him to it, he placed him in such a position that he could scarcely see paradise. “Lead [Col. 0632B] me higher,” Joshua said, “for my eyes are blinded and my senses dulled by hell’s smoke.” The angel led him a little higher. Joshua said to him: “Unless you place me upon the wall, so that I may see the delightful places and holy souls, know that you have not fulfilled my request.” So he placed him upon the wall. Looking within, he saw very many holy souls: patriarchs, prophets, and others whose deeds in their lifetime had pleased God. Among the rest he saw Pharaoh’s daughter sitting upon a most excellent throne. Joshua asked, therefore, by what work or service she had deserved so great a reward. The angel said: “Because she saved Moses from death, nourished him, and taught him the wisdom of the Egyptians” (Exod. 2).
>
> Afterwards [Col. 0632C], when he had seen many others who were honored above the rest, he asked why they had deserved such glory. The angel replied that these were the men who had discovered and composed the *Talmuth* from their own hearts, and their successors, who had studied the *Talmuth*. The angel told him to come down from the wall. He answered: “I still wish to see more.” Having said this, he threw himself down from the wall with the sword. The angel cried out to him: “You have deceived me.” He replied: “Whether you are deceived or not, I do not care.” The angel told him to leave as quickly as possible. But he swore that henceforth he would not leave that place. When those who inhabited paradise saw him, they marveled that a living man, clothed and bearing a sword, had entered paradise in this manner [Col. 0632D].
>
> Since he could find no seat there, he stood and went to Pharaoh’s daughter. “Rise,” he said, “go: behold, your father is at the gate.” She rose quickly and hurried to the gate. Joshua at once seized her seat. When she did not find her father, she returned and said to Joshua: “Why did you lie to me?” “I did not lie,” he said, “for your father is at the gate of hell.” “Why,” she said, “have you stolen my place?” He said: “Because the Lord granted it to me, and from now on it will be mine.”
>
> Meanwhile the angel returned to God and reported what had happened. The Lord ordered that Joshua should leave quickly. When the angel had imposed this command of God upon him, Joshua said: “By God Himself and by the holy *Talmuth*, I shall not leave this place any further.” When the angel reported this oath, God said: “Let the whole library be searched; and if he is found ever to have sworn falsely, he must leave. But if not, he must be allowed [Col. 0633A] to remain, either because of his piety or because he always studied the *Talmuth*.” The library was searched [Col. 0638D], and he was not found to have lied or broken an oath. Therefore the Lord allowed him never thereafter to depart. The angel approached Joshua and asked for the sword with which he was accustomed to kill people wherever he found them. Joshua replied that he would not return the sword unless the angel swore that from then on he would not kill people in that way. The angel returned to the Lord and reported Joshua’s words. The Lord, though unwillingly, decreed that his request should be granted. Joshua then returned the sword to the angel on that condition.

A long tale has been read, one capable of filling the mouths of readers with laughter and the hearts of hearers with scorn. Who [Col. 0633B] can contain laughter, who can restrain derision, on hearing from men things which they could not even hear from demons themselves? To what mortal has anyone ever persuaded, or attempted to persuade, that in this life he could avoid dying? To whom has anyone said: “Read something, say something, do something, and you will not die”? These are the things, Jews, that you endeavor to persuade people of, and the above-mentioned abominable writing has already persuaded your own people of them. For you affirm that no one can be subject to death who meditates upon or reads a letter of the book *Talmuth*. You believe the subject of this tale—Joshua son of Levi—to have been among that number. But why should I pursue the whole tale point by point and perhaps weary the reader by needless length? I shall not, therefore, pursue everything [Col. 0633C], but shall pluck a few things from this thorny heap and cast them into the eternal flame, where they deserve to be burned together with their authors.

I judge that the beginning of this fable should be passed over, because what is here read concerning this Joshua son of Levi is almost the same as the first tale in the fifth chapter of this work against you, Jews, concerning Rabbi Nehemiah. The answer, therefore, need not be repeated, since perhaps it has already been set out above to the letter against similar trifles. For the tale is alike insofar as each man resisted God and His angel, by reading the *Talmuth*, in order not to die. It differs, however, in this: God overcame by fraud in killing the former, but could not deceive the latter, as though he were shrewder, despite many carefully devised stratagems. The former, as written above [Col. 0633D], was driven away from reading the *Talmuth* by the terror of an aerial whirlwind, and thus, in that interval, God seized his soul. The latter, obstinate in his reading and watchful against divine and angelic snares, when God could do nothing to him as he continually read the *Talmuth*, was unwillingly permitted to live.

Thus he, as though secure, answered the smiting angel who said, “The Lord has sent me to take your soul”: “The Lord has sent you in vain, since I turn over and read the *Talmuth*. Therefore I adjure you by this book that you have no power to take my soul.” Although God sent word again through the same angel that Joshua should come, rejoice, and feast with Him because it would be better for him with God than in the world, the wise man nevertheless could not be deceived and yielded in nothing to divine tricks. Knowing [Col. 0634A] that God eagerly desired his death, and fearing that God might at some time deceive him also by some device, as He had deceived Nehemiah, Joshua very shrewdly secured for himself a dwelling in paradise against God’s will, God not guarding against his tricks. For, after making with God this condition—that he would by no means obey Him in dying unless God granted the request he should wish to ask—he said that before dying he wished to see the gates of hell and paradise. Let readers consider what sort of thing this is, and how he could overcome God’s infinite wisdom by human tricks. I shall say nothing about it. For I should seem to be acting uselessly and superfluously, I think, if I labored to show that God was more powerful, wiser, or better than Joshua. I do not judge readers to be so dull and foolish that they would demand my argument on these matters [Col. 0634B], or say that I ought to answer such inanities. But I come to what follows:

> “Climb upon me,” the angel said, “and I shall take you wherever you wish.” Joshua said: “I shall not climb up nor go with you unless you give me the sword you carry; for I fear that you will kill me on the way.” The angel immediately gave him the sword. And when Joshua had climbed upon the angel, the angel said: “Where do you wish me to take you?” He answered: “To the gates of hell, that afterwards I may delight in the sight of paradise.”

And what am I to say of these things? Where are the shoulders, the back, the angelic body upon which that man climbed, by which he was carried—as upon a beast of burden—to behold hell’s horrors and paradise’s delights? Where, too, are the angels’ wings? Because you never see them depicted without wings, do you therefore think that they never lack them [Col. 0634C]? Are those who, as regards their proper essence, are separated from every nature of the elements, who lack every bodily composition and form, to be believed to possess bodies like the bodies of earthly animals, or parts of bodies? Certainly people will not believe this, even if beasts have thought it. But even if an angel, ready to obey God, wished to adopt such a body as you Jews imagine him to possess in order to carry Joshua, Joshua was nevertheless not so incautious as to climb upon him. He plainly refused to climb upon the angel unless the angel surrendered the sword he bore, lest perhaps he kill him on the way.

Exceedingly cautious, as I said, and exceedingly shrewd in avoiding angelic tricks, he feared that perhaps, contrary to the agreement God had made with him, God through His angel might plot some snare against him. Therefore he would not entrust himself to the angel until he had received the sword from him [Col. 0634D]. Once he had received it, as though secure that the angel could no longer kill him, he climbed upon that noble beast of burden, more than befits a human being. Whether these things can be so, let readers say, let hearers judge. But I proceed. Carried in an angelic vehicle, he was led to hell; he was led to behold the delights of paradise. And what follows?

Having first been led to hell, he saw many peoples from every nation under heaven: Christians, Amorites, Jebusites, Hivites, Hittites, Perizzites, Moabites, Ammonites, Arabs, and Philistines; and kings: Pharaoh, Sihon, Og, and [Col. 0635A] all the others killed by Joshua; Jabin and his commander Sisera; Eglon, who was killed by Ehud; Nebuchadnezzar; and Holofernes, his commander. But I ask you here, Jews: he saw in hell these kings and peoples, formerly enemies of and neighboring peoples to your land; why did he omit Gauls, Iberians, Africans, Germans, Dacians, Noricans, Scythians, and, not to pass over eastern peoples, Persians, Indians, and the remaining peoples of the world? Did he not behold their enormous multitude in hell? Did not your prophet Ezekiel say of such peoples: “There is Elam, there Assyria, and all its multitude; its graves all around it” (Ezek. 32), and much else of the same sort? Perhaps he did not have an eye as keen as the prophet’s, so as to see with bodily eyes all that the prophet saw [Col. 0635B] by spiritual understanding. I do not dissent from this view.

But one who could see many outsiders there, why could he not recognize there also many of his own people? He saw Christians, whom he names first; why did that supreme investigator of paradise and hell not recognize in hell Dathan and Abiram, rebellious Korah and all his congregation, the two hundred men whom heavenly fire burned up in the wilderness, and the innumerable thousands of Jews whom divine wrath consumed at various times, whether for idolatry or for various crimes? I say: why did he not recognize all these men of his own people, or at least some of them? And surely they were in hell beyond any question, concerning whom Holy Scripture speaks in the book of Numbers: “They went down alive into hell, covered by the earth” (Num. 16) [Col. 0635C]. What, plainly, was the reason that he could not see his own native people there but recognized alien Christians so clearly? Why it was invented by your teachers, Jews, needs no interpreter.

But the alleged cause of so great a condemnation must not be passed over: “Why,” Joshua asks the angel, “are Christians condemned?” The angel says: “Because they believe in Mary’s son, do not observe Moses’ law, and especially because they do not believe in the *Talmuth*.” If asked by someone why all Jews, from the time of our Christ onward, except those who have believed in Him, are in hell, I too could answer more truthfully: “Because they do not believe in Mary’s son, do not keep His Gospel [Col. 0635D], and especially because they constantly blaspheme Him.” Nor would it cost me much effort to speak truth when speaking; nor, Jew, does it cost you much effort to fabricate falsehoods. Thus I state this easily, and you state that easily. But I do not discuss here which of our judgments is truer, because I have discussed it above. I treated it in the preceding four chapters, in which by countless authorities and arguments I proved that our Christ is the Son of God, God, and a king not temporal but eternal; and that He is not, as you think, still to come, but has already come. If those things are true as I have set them forth—indeed, because they are true—it is false what you have said: that your Joshua saw Christians in hell because they believe in Mary’s son, do not observe Moses’ law, and do not believe in the *Talmuth*.

I proceed to the next part of the vision: “Pharaoh lay cast down in hell, his head beneath the threshold of hell’s gate, his eye serving as the hinge of the gate. The gates for souls’ entrance turned around on every side upon his eye” [Col. 0636A]. O miserable people! Since I continually hear astonishing things, I am often compelled to cry out or declaim: miserable people, I say, will you never think anything except what is beastly? Will you never believe that anything can exist among the heavenly or infernal regions except what you have learned on earth? Why do you not understand that, as the nature of spirits is far removed from bodies, so spiritual things also differ greatly in their condition from bodily things? For the light there is not such as it is here; the darkness there is not such as it is here; the rest there is not such as it is here; the punishments there are not such as they are here; the houses there and gates there are not such as they are here [Col. 0636B]. Indeed, all things there, except for the reality of their substances, are of another kind and quality from those here.

And, to pass over the rest not relevant to the present matter: as that infernal prison is other than this one, so it is far other indeed. A human prison is built of stones, wood, or some other earthly material. In it very strong gates are made, so that an entrance may be open for entering while those shut within have no opportunity to leave. Does God fear this in the infernal prison, perhaps that someone of those confined may leave without His will, so that He has blocked its entrance with gates as this precaution? Or are souls, or angels whether good or evil, of such a nature that they cannot pass through bodies unless bodies are removed? Or, unless that infernal gate of which you speak is opened, can souls or demons not freely enter or leave those places? Truly you are most impoverished in understanding, unable, when reason is consulted, to observe that incorporeal things are of a very different quality from corporeal things, and that no bodily thing can obstruct spirits. Even when we lie in a house with every door shut, through the bodies of doors, windows, and walls themselves, spirits have an open route to us as through the air itself [Col. 0636C].

Since this is true; since no bodily thing can obstruct spirits; since it is said of God, “There is none who can deliver from His hand” (Job 10), let your unnecessary gate be removed from hell’s entrance. Let Pharaoh rise from beneath its threshold; and let him who for so many ages has borne, with his eye alone, the heavy hinge of that gate under such horrible torment be freed by our mercy. But let us hear the reason for so great a torment:

> “Because,” says the angel, “he afflicted the children of Israel in the land of Egypt and, after afflicting them, pursued them as far as the sea.”

From this it seems that you have examined that Scripture very little. For not only the Pharaoh who perished in the sea afflicted the children of Israel in Egypt; another Pharaoh had afflicted them before him, of whom that truthful Scripture says: “After a long time the king of Egypt died; and the children of Israel groaned because of their labors and cried out” (Exod. 2). But perhaps you distinguish this Pharaoh from the other because the angel said: “and he pursued them as far as the sea.” But now at last let us leave your hell and come [Col. 0637A] to our paradise.

“The *Talmuth* says that paradise is enclosed on every side by a wall.” And indeed paradise’s inhabitants must take care lest, as nation often rises against nation and kingdom against kingdom, some people perhaps rise against it. If this occurs, they must first be repelled from afar by weapons, and then, should they become so strong as to approach paradise itself, by the wall. Let the cherub and flaming sword which God set to guard paradise after Adam had been cast out be removed (Gen. 3). For what would it do there, if that wall is sufficient to fortify paradise? If it is perhaps necessary even with the wall, let it remain, and at least with the wall’s assistance free the holy inhabitants of paradise from fear of enemies. We indeed believe that Christ’s death [Col. 0637B] removed it and that the flaming sword has now been extinguished by His blood. But what follows from this? Let it return to guard paradise, so that by its circuit the saints resting there may be made safer.

Now comes the fraud that must be exalted, so that the whole world may marvel at a man inhabiting paradise against God’s will. The angel, the man’s bearer, compelled by the agreement he had made with God, led him to paradise; first farther away, then nearer, and finally placed him upon paradise’s very wall, not knowing how to guard against the crafty man’s tricks. While, standing on the wall, he asked the angel many questions about those who inhabited paradise, whom he now saw nearby, and while the angel suitably answered him concerning each person, Joshua deceived the angel, whose mind had been distracted from itself by their exchange of words [Col. 0637C]. While the angel neglected to guard him, he suddenly threw himself from paradise’s wall into paradise itself, carrying the sword of death which the angel had entrusted to him.

O foolish angel! O wise man! Angels were accustomed to surpass human beings in wisdom; now men surpass angels. Why did the angel again trust a man whom he had once and twice experienced to be deceitful? Why did this most foolish of all angels not take precautions against being deceived and becoming a laughingstock to the people? Behold the angel deceived so often; behold the man so often deceiving the angel. At last, scarcely returning to himself, the angel grieved that he had been tricked; and, not in a low voice but shouting as one greatly agitated usually does, he said to the man who now possessed paradise against his will: “You have deceived me.” He received the fitting answer: “Whether you are deceived or not, [Col. 0637D] I do not care.” The angel then commanded him to leave as quickly as possible. He swore and answered that by that same oath he would henceforth not leave that place.

When those who inhabited paradise saw him, they marveled that a clothed, living man had entered paradise in this way with a sword. And what can I say? Let each say what he can. I now profess that I can say nothing worthy of these matters. I read indeed in the Christian Gospel, which you miserable people do not believe, that “the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it” (Matt. 11). But does it suffer violence by weapons? By fraud? By lies? No. How, then? By repentance, humility, self-restraint, and truth. Though this man was far removed from those virtues, he nevertheless slipped into paradise, possessed paradise, and retained paradise. How? With God willing? Rather, with God unwilling; indeed, opposing it. Perhaps with the angel consenting? Rather, grieving, protesting, and with every cry he could make forbidding it to happen [Col. 0638A]. Thus such a man possesses paradise against God’s will, against angels’ will, and against human beings’ will. Let others say what sort of thing this is. I hasten to the rest. Yet I say this one thing: it is no wonder that paradise’s inhabitants were astonished that a clothed, living man carrying a sword entered paradise. For since Adam was cast out, they had learned that no one living in flesh, no one—even Adam before his expulsion—clothed in human garments, and no one carrying a sword could be its inhabitant. But let the rest follow.

The man thus occupying paradise, says the *Talmuth*, when he found no seat there [Col. 0638B], stood and approached Pharaoh’s daughter. She had earned an exalted seat in paradise because she had saved Moses from death, nourished him, and had him instructed in all the wisdom of the Egyptians. He approached her and said: “Rise, go; behold, your father is at the gate.” She quickly rose and hurried to the gate. Joshua immediately seized her seat. When she did not find her father, she returned and said to Joshua: “Why did you lie to me?” “I did not lie,” he said, “because your father is at the gate of hell.” “Why,” she said, “have you stolen my place?” He answered: “Because the Lord granted it to me, and from now on it will be mine.”

Who will grieve at this trick? Certainly I shall not grieve. Let Pharaoh’s daughter grieve, if she wishes. Let her grieve that she was so foolish and improvident that, though she had Moses instructed in all the wisdom of Egypt, she nevertheless allowed herself to be so easily deceived by a man of lower wisdom than Moses—if indeed you Jews grant even this—and lost, through so slight a persuasion, her seat that had been given to her in paradise [Col. 0638C]. I pursue what follows:

> Meanwhile the angel returned to the Lord and reported what had happened. The Lord commanded that he leave quickly. The angel said to him: “He has sworn by You Yourself and by the *Talmuth* that he will not leave that place.” The Lord said: “Let the library of his life be searched. If he has incurred either perjury or falsehood, he must leave. But if not, he must be allowed to remain, either because of his piety or because he always studied the *Talmuth*.” The library was searched, and he was not found to have lied or broken an oath. Therefore the Lord allowed him never afterwards to leave.

Perhaps some readers learned in such matters will wonder that I so frequently repeat the manner of ironic speech. Perhaps they will also wonder why I do not answer every one of these trifles point by point, as though by rational argument. But what else can I do? What else ought I to do? I answered certain earlier fables and refuted them partly by authority and partly by reason. I did this so that, if I always used the method I now frequently employ, some simple reader might think that I had nothing else to say against the Jews. For unless this reason had compelled me, I would never have introduced any authority against them in this disputation. I would merely have shown, by answering them as I have said, that they do not deserve a rational reply, but only—beyond all fabulizing people—the sole and highest derision [Col. 0639A]. This is why, more frequently than is customary, I answer them ironically: not as though by rational argument, but because they have deserved this above all mortals.

Of that kind of fables to which it seems fitting to reply in this manner is also the one now before us. For what other response than laughter and derision befits a tale which says that a foolish angel, deceived by a clever man, after he saw that he had been tricked, returned to God—when that man was already possessing paradise against God’s will—and reported what had happened? God, plainly ignorant of events, did not know what had happened [Col. 0639B]. It was therefore necessary for the angel, sent by Him, to return to Him in order to report what had occurred. For perhaps at that time God had forgotten His wisdom, by which He knows all things even before they happen. But if before they happen, then surely also when they happen? That wisdom too had perished, of which it is written: “You have made all things in wisdom” (Ps. 103 [104]). And that wisdom had perished of which it is said: “Who shall search out the wisdom of God, which comprehends all things? Who can number the sand of the sea, the drops of rain, and the days of the age?” (Ecclus. 1). Could He have been ignorant of the tricks of the man who had deceitfully stolen His paradise? Why, then, did the angel report to Him what had already occurred?

But since we have heard how the wisdom of God becomes foolish, let us see also how His power [Col. 0639C] becomes feeble. “The Lord,” it says, “commanded that he should depart at once. ‘Everywhere,’ He said, ‘he has deceived you by fraud. By fraud he has said everything he has spoken; by fraud he has forced himself into My paradise. But let what he has done profit him nothing; let him gain nothing among us by deceit. Let him go out, let him depart, let this deceitful man leave our paradise to us.’”

To this the angel replied: “He has sworn by Yourself and by the Talmud that he will not depart from there.”

That is to say: What are You saying, Lord? You command that this man depart from paradise. But this is impossible. It is impossible that Your word should prevail over his word, that his decision should be changed by Your command. The man is of such power that You must yield to him; he is of such truthfulness that his truth rightly prevails over Yours. For he has sworn by Yourself and by the Talmud that he will not depart from there [Col. 0639D]. Therefore, since he has sworn by Yourself, You must act against Yourself and place his word above Your own utterance.

And more still: he has also sworn by the Talmud. If You despise Yourself, You must preserve the Talmud for Yourself. If You disregard what he swore by Yourself, You cannot disregard what he swore by the Talmud. For the Talmud is greater than You. Indeed, the Talmud is so much greater than You that, even if You command men to die, the Talmud resists; if You send Your angels to seize human souls, the Talmud resists; if anyone is summoned by You through whatever messengers, the Talmud resists and does not permit him to come. For these reasons the Talmud is greater than You. Hence You command this man in vain to leave paradise, when the Talmud commands him not to depart.

“It is true,” says the Lord to the angel [Col. 0640A], “what you say. That man cannot leave paradise, even at My command, unless the Talmud permits it and, after My command, grants him permission to depart.

“But, since there is no other plan, let the library of that man’s life be reviewed. If it is found in it that he has ever perjured himself or lied, he must leave paradise. But if not, it must be granted him to remain, either because of his own religion or because he has always studied the Talmud.”

I shall answer this. Is the Jew, as I said above—the most evil enemy of God and of myself—worthy of my reply? First he said that God’s wisdom had been made foolish; now he says that God’s power has been weakened. What then is meant by what Holy Scripture says: “He shall rule from sea to sea, and from the river unto the ends of the earth” (Ps. 71 [72])? Perhaps His power rules from sea to sea—that is, in this earth of ours—but does not reach as far as His paradise, which is unknown to us. Yet, if the question arises from this point, it may be resolved from it, if paradise is shown to be on earth. It is shown to be on earth, for Scripture says: “The Lord God planted a paradise of delight from the beginning” (Gen. 2). And afterwards it says more plainly that it was on earth—indeed, that it was earth: “God brought forth from the ground,” it says, “every tree beautiful to behold and pleasant for food, and also the tree of life in the midst of paradise” (ibid.). If He brought those trees forth from the ground, He certainly brought them forth from earth. For *humus*, though it has another name, is nothing but earth. But the earth from which those trees were brought forth [Col. 0640C] is paradise. Therefore paradise is earth, and is on earth.

Now the Psalm says of earth: “The Lord has done whatsoever He willed in heaven and on earth” (Ps. 134 [135]). If, then, paradise is earth, and God does all that He wills in heaven and on earth, surely He also does His will in paradise, because it is earth. Therefore what the Jew says is false: that this man did not obey God’s will and command when God willed and commanded him to leave paradise. It is false that he defended himself against being compelled to leave by invoking the divine name and adding the book of the Talmud.

But perhaps what follows is true: that God commanded the library of his life to be reviewed, so that a diligent reader might examine whether he had ever incurred perjury or falsehood in it. If he were convicted from that writing of having perjured himself or lied [Col. 0640D], he was to be expelled from paradise. But if not, he was to remain, and was no longer to fear that anyone could expel him from paradise. The library was reviewed, and it acquitted him of perjury and lying. By that merit, with God’s permission, he remained an inhabitant of paradise.

Could God not remember deeds done without a book? Could His fleeting memory not be restored without the assistance of books or parchments? This is why an edict went forth that the library of that man’s life should be reviewed. But if God’s memory failed in remembering the deeds of one man, how could it remain vigorous in retaining the deeds of all mortals? What parchments would suffice? What ages would not be exhausted? And indeed I know—I have this also from a Jewish book—that Solomon said: “God shall bring into judgment all things that are done, for every error, whether it be good or evil” [Col. 0641A] (Eccles. 11 [12:14]). But will He do so from books? Will He reread all those human deeds in books, or produce them from books? Has God’s memory thus perished, or will it perish? And who is it who speaks in one of your books through a certain wise man: “My memory is unto generations of ages” (Ecclus. 24)? Is it not God? Certainly it is God.

I do not rehearse innumerable similar statements bearing witness to the eternal memory of God, because this one point, though not enough for a Jew—whom nothing satisfies—is nevertheless enough for every person other than a Jew.

What of the remaining matters that follow? The library was reviewed; and, because it was read that he had neither perjured himself nor lied, it was granted to a man still living in mortal flesh that he should not die any longer [Col. 0641B], and it was conceded that he should never thereafter be compelled to depart from paradise. Great indeed is the merit of this man, who must beyond doubt be preferred to all your patriarchs and prophets; for he received what David could not merit, of whom it is written in your *Melachim* [Kings]: “David slept with his fathers” (3 Kings [1 Kings] 2); what Moses could not merit, of whom it is said in Deuteronomy: “Moses, servant of the Lord, died, and the Lord buried him” (Deut. 34); and what Abraham himself could not merit, of whom Genesis says: “Abraham died, old and full of days” (Gen. 35 [probably 25:8]).

The ancient Jews did not understand it this way, nor did those very sowers beforehand of your impiety. For when our Savior said to the Jews, your fathers: “Amen, amen, I say to you, if anyone keeps My word, he shall not see death forever” [Col. 0641C] (John 8), they answered in a sense far different from theirs or yours: “Now we know that You have a demon. Abraham died, and the prophets; and You say: ‘If anyone keeps My word, he shall not see death forever’? Are You greater than our father Abraham, who died? And the prophets died” (ibid.).

Those men, impious though they were, certainly rejected to the utmost this interpretation of yours: that you say that the man extorted from God by fraud the privilege of not dying, and extorted by fraud the grant of an everlasting dwelling in paradise while he was still living in mortal flesh, even against God’s will. Repent, therefore—though I say it in vain—of having believed and said this, when you hear and see that your fathers answered God and our Redeemer so harshly in a matter which He Himself nevertheless understood otherwise.

Though these exceedingly astonishing matters have been set forth, matters still more astonishing follow. That man, already possessing paradise against God’s will by such deceit as has been described, because great things had succeeded for him, devises greater things. It was not enough for him to have been conveyed into paradise in a nobler vehicle than that in which Elijah was carried up to heaven [Col. 0641D]: Elijah was carried into heaven in a fiery chariot, while this man was borne into paradise by a heavenly angel. It was not enough that, having conquered God, he dwelt as victor in God’s paradise. It was not enough that he had earned the privilege of being the only mortal able to escape death [Col. 0642A]. Enticed by the excellent outcome of his exploits, he attempts to make all others immortal as well.

For when the angel demanded back the sword entrusted to him, with which, as that urbane writing says, he was accustomed to kill men wherever he found them, whether on the road or in the marketplace, he replied—what? Joshua plainly replied that he would not return the sword to him unless he swore that he would no longer kill men with it. Truly a pious man, continually pitying mortals who died, and kindly providing that they should no longer be able to die. For this reason he refused to return the sword, the instrument of death, and did not yield to the death-angel, greedy for human death, when he unlawfully reclaimed it. The angel, so often deceived, returned to God and reported Joshua’s answer.

[Col. 0642B] But the Lord granted Joshua’s petition, though unwillingly. Joshua returned the sword to the angel on that condition. Among the many points requiring inquiry here, I ask this one: since the angel was so foolish that he could not guard against the trick of a man who cunningly extorted the sword of death from him, why did he demand it back thereafter? Could he not make another sword when this one had thus been lost? Is divine power so needy that, if something has been lost through the stupidity of a foolish messenger, nothing similar can ever again be obtained? What necessity compelled Him to beg for the sword, fraudulently taken away by a deceitful man, when He could, I suppose, have made many swords? Have good or evil angels, slayers of men by divine command, always been accustomed to use one and the same iron sword?

[Col. 0642C] I read that an angel struck the firstborn of so many Egyptians in one night, so that in all great Egypt there was no house in which there was not a dead person (Exod. 11 [probably 12:30]). I read also that one hundred and eighty thousand of the army of the Assyrian king were destroyed by divine command in a short interval, or a moment (4 Kings [2 Kings] 19).
