And I read certain other things like these. Were all these killed by one only and single sword of God? What would those angels who then destroyed such thousands of men have done if they had already lost the killing sword? With what instrument could they have killed so many peoples when the sword was gone? It was very well provided for them that Joshua, the snatcher of the divine sword, should not be born before all those previously mentioned had been slain by the same sword [Col. 0642D]. For, had it been snatched away earlier, the angel, minister of death, could not have fulfilled God’s command once the sword was taken away.

Yet with what sword were the innumerable multitudes of people subsequently slain at God’s command from Joshua’s time onward? With what sword, I ask, were they struck down when the earlier one had been lost? Answer here, Jews. Here difficulties constrain you—though not for the first time—and you can never be extricated from them. Either return to God the sword that your Joshua wickedly stole, so that He may kill men as He is customarily able, according to His will; or, if you do not do this, make mortals immortal and warn all men never again to fear death.

But lest it perhaps seem to us astonishing or false that a man made immortal in the manner described should inhabit paradise [Col. 0643A], you wish to console us and induce belief by a noble and truthful example. You say that Joshua’s possession of paradise in this way should be believed, since Eliezer also, Abraham’s servant, was similarly removed from death and possesses even heaven, which is greater. You relate how this occurred, as follows, on the teaching of the frequently named book:

In the afternoon Isaac went out into the field to meditate and met the servant Eliezer returning from Mesopotamia, whither Abraham had sent him, together with Rebecca. When Rebecca asked the servant who the man was whom they had met, he said, “This is my lord Isaac.” On hearing this, Rebecca, according to our truthful Scripture, covered herself with a veil and descended very quickly from the camel (Gen. 24); but according to your false one [Col. 0643B], in that descent she lost the signs of her virginity. They came to intercourse. When the husband did not recognize the signs of virginity in his wife, he began to accuse the servant of having corrupted his wife like a traitor. When Eliezer denied this on oath, Isaac said: “May you enjoy the vision of heaven in the same measure as what you confess is true!” As soon as Isaac said this, Eliezer was immediately taken up into heaven.

Who then will dare to deny that what you say of Joshua is true, when you put forward such a thing regarding Abraham’s servant? Since it is unquestionably certain that the immortal Eliezer possesses heaven, who, O Jews, would dare oppose you concerning your Joshua’s dwelling in paradise? Let it henceforth be believed without any question at all, since it is proved by so weighty and indissoluble an example.

Let that too be believed which you believe: that, when Jews have been gathered from every region of the world and assembled by your Messiah in the land of your promise, what God once promised Abraham will be fulfilled: “I will multiply your seed as the stars of heaven and as the sand which is on the shore of the sea” [Col. 0643C] (Gen. 22). This will occur in such a manner that every woman bears one son every day, and thus gives birth to three hundred and sixty-six children during the course of only one year. Great fertility and rapid multiplication of Abraham’s seed! Yet it is not so great, even if every woman from the first Eve to the last who shall be at the world’s end bore one child every day of this age, as the number either of the stars of heaven or of the sand of the sea.

Truly unhappy women, who, if the divine curse pronounced upon women remains in force, will, just as they give birth daily, be tormented daily by that most severe pain of women in labor. I think they would prefer never to conceive than to bring forth or bear children amid such sharp and frequent pains. But what will become of that chapter of the Law which commands that a woman giving birth to a male abstain from intercourse with a man for forty days, and one giving birth to a female for eighty days? (Lev. 12.) But I pass on, for one must not always linger over such things.

Yet I have not determined wholly to pass over that point in which you have been given the ability to interpret the Holy Scriptures wisely and cautiously. For I wish to hear from you how you expound the verse of your Psalm that says: “You ascended on high, you took captivity captive, you gave gifts to men” (Ps. 67 [68]) [Col. 0643D].

[Col. 0644A] “You ascended on high.” Who ascended? Moses, as you say. He ascended into heaven by God’s command. When the angels saw him, they wished to kill him. Moses, terrified, cried out to the Lord. Hearing this, the Lord threatened the angels. “Why,” said the Lord, “do you wish to kill My servant? You are raising a rebellion against Me.” The angels were ashamed and said: “We are not raising a rebellion, but we grieve because an earthly and defiled man has ascended to heaven.” “No,” said the Lord, “he is neither unclean nor defiled, for before he ascended to heaven we sanctified him from uncleanness.”

The holy angels complain further, not only about this, but also because God gave the holy and immaculate Law first to defiled human beings rather than to themselves, to whom it ought first to have been given. But the Lord says: “You act foolishly against My commands. For here no vices are committed, no crimes. Therefore the Law is not necessary here, but for human beings, who commit murders, adulteries, and other evils.” Then the angels made peace with Moses and gave him, as an increase, half of their wisdom. “‘You took captivity captive’: that is, you stripped the angels and heaven of wisdom; ‘you gave gifts to men’: that is, when descending to earth, you gave that wisdom to the children of Israel. For they do not believe that the Lord God dwells” (ibid.): that is, Gentiles and Christians do not believe that the Lord dwells in Moses.

Why should I ridicule these things? Why should I condemn them? Why should I trample them underfoot? At once—indeed, most fully—they themselves declare how ridiculous, how detestable, and how contemptible they are [Col. 0644B]. They also declare what faith should be put in teachers of this sort, who expound the sacred Scriptures so subtly and so truthfully.

What shall I say about Korah’s keys? You say they were so numerous that he had three hundred camels, loaded with those keys and scarcely bearing their immense weight, in the wilderness where Moses was leader of the Hebrews. To make them easier to carry, the keys were made not from iron, wood, or any other material, but from dried hides of cows. These keys alone guarded the treasures of the aforesaid Korah, stored in various caves or caverns. A man richer than all other men, whose wealth could suffice for the entire human race through endless ages! [Col. 0644C] But the loss of such treasures is lamentable: for Korah himself, with his sons and daughters, his tents, and all his possessions, was swallowed up by divine will along with Dathan, Abiram, and the other rebels.

What shall I say also about the matter from which the preceding fable is drawn? Namely, that when the sons of Jacob were carrying their dead father to the tomb, the sons of Esau, likewise carrying their dead father to that same tomb, met them with a great company; and on both sides they waged enormous disputes in order to claim the tomb for themselves. What shall I say of Dan, Jacob’s son, ascending a mountain, cutting from it a stone as large as Esau’s entire army, and placing it upon his head [Col. 0645A] so as to cast that one stone and strike down the whole army? Or of his return, when he found both armies already reconciled, and throwing that immense mass into the sea? The sea, driven back by its size, overflowed its limits and destroyed two cities by its overflow, Pithom and Rameses. Nearly four hundred years after their destruction, Pharaoh, as you say—so that you may seem to say something resembling truth—rebuilt them, and in rebuilding them afflicted your fathers with harsh labors in clay and brick (Exod. 1).

These things are endless and could not be set forth even in the longest time, if I wished to pursue similar Jewish trifles and report everything precisely. For who could reply to such vast volumes of nonsense, with which lost men have filled their bookcases for almost two thousand years now, and refute every item as though by reason? As far as reason is concerned, even a very stupid person could answer these things, and scarcely any labor would be needed to devise the answer. But time would scarcely suffice, and it would not be rational at all. What reason permits discussion of such matters to be extended beyond measure, when every human mind, even if every disputant is silent, understands them to be false, recognizes them as laughable, and acknowledges them as detestable? Let the pen therefore hasten to an end and delay no longer.

Accordingly, from the immense heap of similar fables, as though from a great pile of dust given over to the winds, I shall recount only one story concerning Jeremiah’s daughter and her son, and so, through Christ’s grace, shall complete this Jewish work—or rather Christian work against the Jews [Col. 0645C]. But how shall I speak? What words shall I use? Shame commands silence, and it fears that, in uttering indecent things, the language itself may seem less decent. It is embarrassed to force shameful things upon the ears of the chaste, and dreads to pour such abominations into ears accustomed to hear holy and heavenly matters.

But what then? Let Christian and sober speech lay aside its unconsidered blush and, rebuking the impious and indecent, compel them at least to blush over these things. God often does this in the first Law, and in the second He does not keep silence about the same matters. Because He wishes to correct people of evils scarcely fit to name, He sets out even more shameful things in order to forbid them. Our Apostle does this as well, as is known throughout the world, and he left scarcely anything untouched, however shameful, among those things he saw needing correction in mortals [Col. 0645D]. Nor therefore shall I leave this unattempted, so that the enemies of the Christian name may be increasingly put to shame, and it may be clearer than sunlight, even after what has gone before, how detestable are those who believe such detestable things.

“At one time,” they say, “when young men, as often happens, were bathing together, they lustfully touched themselves and discharged male semen into the water. When the prophet Jeremiah, compelled by the necessities of travel, came there and saw them doing such things, he was grieved and rebuked them, crying out that they were committing an abominable crime. When they heard this, they both urged him in words and compelled him by force to do the same thing. At first he refused and said that he preferred to die rather than do such things; at last, compelled by them, he consented and discharged semen into the water, as they had done.

“After it had remained in the water for a long time, Jeremiah’s daughter came, who happened to be present at those baths; encountering the semen by chance, she received it into the female receptacle and immediately became pregnant. The time for giving birth came; she gave birth and called his name Bencera. As soon as he was born, he began to speak and asked for hot bread, the richest meat, butter, and honey. When his mother wondered at this, she said, ‘Why do you ask for such things, when you ought to take milk?’ He replied, ‘Such foods please me more than your milk.’ When his mother showed this to very wise men and invited many men, engaged in conflicts of disputation among themselves, to see the child, the child defeated them all in argument.” [Col. 0646A]

His mother, more astonished still, said: “What is this that you do, my son? Whence comes such wisdom to you? Whence come so many modes of disputation, when you have learned no letters?” “I am Jeremiah’s son,” he replied, and related how this had happened.

What shall I say, reader? Must I speak or open my mouth concerning or against these things? I hear from a Jew what I could not hear even from the devil. By his lies, he surpasses the prince of lies and makes him—who is not merely a liar but also the father and teacher of lies—almost into his son and disciple. The devil, indeed, as our Apocalypse says, is “the accuser of our brethren, accusing them before the presence of our God day and night” (Rev. 12). Sometimes he accuses them truthfully; sometimes falsely. But is Satan so deceitful in accusing the brethren that he would accuse Jeremiah of fornication before God’s presence, that he would dare to charge him before the supreme Judge as though he were a fornicator? [Col. 0646B] Or would he do so before men? I do not think so either. For how could he dare? How indeed could he dare call him a fornicator and pronounce him unclean, when he hears the Lord speaking to him concerning his purity and holiness: “Before I formed you in the womb, I knew you; and before you came out of the womb, I sanctified you” (Jer. 1)?

The devil surely hears this, although the Jew does not hear it. He knows with certainty, though he does not lack the will to deceive, that if he wished to lie about such things, no one would believe him against the divine oracles. Therefore, so that he might not appear shamelessly deceitful and be less able to deceive people by this means, he provides for his malice—not wisely, indeed, but deceitfully. But the Jew is not like this: in order that no one should trust him in anything, he has devoted himself wholly to lies more than diabolical. He has left himself absolutely nothing such that anyone might believe him, apart from authentic words, even if he should at some time utter something true [Col. 0646C].

Nor is this surprising in so great a liar. For even a person who alleges falsehood once in court, or is found a false witness once, is both excluded from legal actions and barred from testimony. Should not what is done to one who lies once be done to one who always lies and deceives? For the Jew lies when he asserts what is false; he deceives when he misleads others by his lies—though this happens rarely. Yet I believe that in the matter under discussion no Jew can deceive anyone except a Jew, not even Machumeth, once his disciple, whom he has imbued with dreams of similar fables. But he will be able to deceive no one into believing, or even faintly suspecting, that so great a man, so great a prophet of God, who strove unto blood and unto death for truth and justice against liars and impious men—none other than Jews—could have committed so monstrous a crime or could have been compelled to commit it by any terror or violence.

He would sooner have endured Egyptian stones cast by Jewish hands, and would not have postponed suffering what he later suffered for truth, rather than join unclean youths by any consent. He had not become so senseless that he who, from childhood, appeared worthy of converse with God would, as a youth or a mature man [Col. 0647A], neglect so great a grace and deprive himself, through the defilement of any crime, of the prerogative of divine intimacy.

He did not stain innocence, clean from every crime through whatever differences of age, with any such blemish—he to whom, when saying, “Behold, I do not know how to speak, for I am a child,” God answered: “Do not say, ‘I am a child,’ for you shall go to all to whom I send you, and you shall speak all that I command you” (ibid.). And then: “Behold, I have set you today over nations and kingdoms, to root out, to destroy, to scatter, and to overthrow, to build and to plant” (ibid.). Would this man, still a child, have been sent by God? Would it have been announced that he would speak everything commanded him? Would he have been placed over nations and kingdoms, to root out and destroy, and again to plant and build [Col. 0647B], if God foresaw that he would become such as you, O Jews, make him?

But where do you read that he had a daughter? Either produce—not from your customary trifles, but from Holy Scripture—that he had a daughter, or I shall produce from those same divine writings that he had neither daughter nor son. But, I suppose, you will fail. I shall not fail. For the Lord says to Jeremiah: “You shall not take a wife, nor beget sons and daughters” (Jer. 16). Read again the book of the prophet himself. When you have read this, either learn it if you did not know it, or remember it if you had forgotten: Jeremiah the prophet had no wife and begot neither sons nor daughters. For so great a man, so zealous an observer of the divine commands [Col. 0647C], could not neglect a divine command and after this prohibition either take a wife or beget sons and daughters.

Who would dare assert that he begot a son or daughter by a woman other than a wife, unless he wished to prove him incontinent and shameful? And I think no one except a Jew would dare. But if Jeremiah was never joined to either a wife or any woman at any time, he plainly begot neither a son nor a daughter. Let this daughter, then, whom you, O Jews, have assigned to Jeremiah, withdraw from the scene and seek another father for herself. But perhaps he did not need union of the sexes for begetting, since, according to you, his semen possessed such power that, even though it was far removed, it could—as you say happened here—both impregnate and generate [Col. 0647D]. To your most shameful miracle—namely, that semen discharged into water could neither be dissolved by the liquid nature of the element nor lose its generative power—I reply not by disputing but by spitting.

Now, leaving aside the remaining miracles of the prophet’s child—that immediately upon being born he began to speak, asked for hot bread, the richest meat, butter, and honey, ate them, and defeated wise men in disputation—or rather, that he did none of these things: it would now be foolish, without excuse, to wish to prove it. For how could anyone prove that he neither said nor did these things when it is certain that he never existed? To make this certain, I add this one further detail pertaining to the same fable: when Nebuchadnezzar heard the great fame of this aforementioned child [Col. 0648A], he sent to him a thousand armed men, each of whom carried one soldier upon the nail of his finger. Wishing to discover whether what was said of him was true, he commanded him to come. The child refused to come, but sent him a hare, writing on the hare’s forehead everything Nebuchadnezzar wished to ask or inquire of him. When Nebuchadnezzar saw this, he recognized that the child was wiser than all others.

Although this fable is not extracted from the Talmud, it is extracted from a book that has no less authority among Jews than the Talmud.

These are your mysteries, O Jews; these your innermost sacraments; this your wisdom, to be preferred even to every divine wisdom. Now truly it appears fulfilled in you what Isaiah—often named above, now no longer your prophet but ours—said among many similar things concerning you: “They have broken the eggs of asps and woven spiders’ webs. He who eats of their eggs shall die, and that which is hatched shall break forth into a basilisk. Their webs shall not become garments, neither shall they cover themselves with their works” [Col. 0648B] (Isa. 59).

The eggs you brood are not like hens’ eggs, so as either to be useful as food in themselves or to produce some bird suitable for human use. Rather, they are eggs of asps: broken by you, they infect you with the deadly venom of impiety and at last produce, near the end of the age, Antichrist, king of all impious persons, like a basilisk, prince of all venomous creatures, long and wickedly hatched by you. You have for a long time hatched a deadly egg, at the worst time, for such a most evil fruit of such teachings: so that, once broken, it may kill you, and at last, as was said, the supreme offspring of malice may burst forth from it, harmful to the whole world.

Your webs, over which you have labored for a long time, are not like the webs of female weavers or weavers, so that some garment or covering might be made from them. They are not, plainly, according to the prophet, for clothing; nor shall you be clothed from them. Why? Because in all your works, in all your labors, in every weaving of impious doctrines, you have produced nothing useful for mortals, because you have woven spiders’ webs [Col. 0648C]. Truly vain, truly futile, is the labor of so many ages in which, since the time of the prophets—that is, since a prophet has not appeared in Israel—you have woven nothing else, done nothing else, and filled Jewish books with no other doctrine than blasphemous, sacrilegious, ridiculous, and false matter.

For so long you have fought against divine books with diabolical books and labored to cover and obscure heavenly teaching with the smoke of the infernal pit. Unless you are caught in the nets of your own webs, you have attempted to ensnare foolish animals and heedless birds with deceitful traps. But your invention is not of such a kind, not of such artistry or power, nor is the Jewish fabric of such a character, as to be able to ensnare even the lowliest quadruped or bird. You have woven no man’s or woman’s web; you have completed no man’s or woman’s work. Rather, according to the truthful prophet, in the fables and similar trifles already mentioned, you have woven spiders’ webs alone. Though compacted with much long labor, by their excessive fragility they could deceive or catch no one except a Jew [Col. 0648D], like a most worthless fly.

Therefore, so that a fitting end may at last be imposed upon this fifth chapter against you, I briefly recapitulate what preceded [Col. 0649A; 0650A]. You have done nothing against us except by divine books, and afterwards by fabulous ones. By divine books we have conquered you. We have shown that the fabulous books are of no value. What then remains? Namely, that, casting aside fables, you understand the divine books in such a way that in them and from them you believe, worship, and glorify Christ—that is, in your terminology, the Messiah—not as a deceiver but as truthful; not as one still to come except for judgment, but as Him who has already come, who through His birth from a Virgin, His life in the world without any sin, His heavenly preaching, His divine miracles, His death—not cheap, as you suppose, but precious—His resurrection, and His ascension, redeemed, saved, and glorified the world destined for eternal life. For I believe that, overwhelmed and refuted by truth itself through such great witnesses and reasons, you ought neither to resist further nor seek anything further [Col. 0650B].

## Of Peter the Venerable, Abbot of Cluny: Ninth

[Col. 0649]

## Letter concerning his translation, by which he caused the sect or heresy of the Saracens to be translated from Arabic into Latin, in the year 1143

[Col. 0649C] To the lord Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, worthy of singular veneration, to be embraced with all the arms of charity, the inseparable guest of our heart: Brother Peter, humble abbot of Cluny, sends you eternal salvation, for which you long.

[Note: [Col. 0649] This is almost identical with part of Epistle 17, Book IV.] I am sending you, dearest friend, our new translation, which argues against the utterly wretched and worthless heresy of Mahomet. While I was recently staying in Spain, it was rendered from Arabic into Latin through my efforts. I had it translated by Master Peter of Toledo, a man skilled in both languages. But since Latin was not as familiar or well known to him as Arabic, I gave him as collaborator a learned man, my beloved son and brother Peter, our notary, whom, I think, Your Reverence knows well. Polishing and arranging the Latin words which he had for the most part expressed crudely or confusedly, he completed this letter—or rather, little book—which, I believe, will be very useful to many because of its account of unfamiliar matters.

Moreover, I also brought into Latin the entire impious sect, the life of the wicked man, and the law which he called the *Alcoran*, that is, “collection of precepts,” claiming that it had been delivered to him from heaven by the angel Gabriel and persuading most miserable people of this. The translators were men skilled in both languages: Robert of Ketton from England, now archdeacon of the Church of Pamplona, and Herman of Dalmatia, a scholar of exceptionally keen and learned intellect. I found them in Spain, studying the astronomical art near the Ebro, and hired them for this work at considerable expense.

My purpose in this work was to follow the custom of the Fathers, who never passed over in silence any heresy of their own times, however slight, but resisted it with all the powers of faith and showed in writings and disputations that it was to be detested and condemned. I wished to do this concerning this principal error among errors, this dregs of all heresies—in which, I say, have converged the remnants of all diabolical sects that have arisen since the coming of the Savior—so that, just as nearly half the world is known to be infected by its deadly plague, so those who do not know may recognize, once its folly and foulness are exposed, how execrable and to be trampled underfoot it is.

You yourselves will recognize this by reading, and, as I think fitting, will lament that so great a portion of humankind has been deceived by such wicked and utterly base filth, and, even after the grace of the Redeemer, so lightly turned away from its Creator through the impious sect of a most filthy man. I have made all this known to you especially so that I might share my studies with so great a friend and encourage that magnificence of learning which God has uniquely bestowed on you in our time to write against so destructive an error.

For although this could not, in my judgment, benefit those who are lost, nevertheless the Christian arsenal ought to possess a worthy response against this plague, as it does against other heresies. If some should consider this superfluous because those against whom such weapons ought to be used are not present, it is recognized that in the commonwealth of a great king some things are made for defense, some for ornament, and some for both. The arms made by peaceful Solomon were intended for defense, although in his time they were less necessary. David prepared resources, and the furnishings ready for the construction and adornment of the divine temple were assigned for its building and decoration. Yet these did not serve any use in his time, but passed into sacred uses after his time. Thus they remained idle for a while; but when necessity arose, things long unused appeared useful.

Nor, as it seems to me, ought this work even now to be called idle, because, according to the Apostle, it is the duty of you and all learned men to attack, overthrow, and trample down with every effort, word, and writing every form of knowledge that exalts itself against the height of God (2 Cor. 10). And if those who err cannot be converted by this means, at least a learned—or more learned—man, if he has zeal for justice, ought not neglect to provide and take thought for the weak members of the Church, who are accustomed to be scandalized and secretly unsettled even by slight causes.

I set before you all the Fathers, and especially Father Augustine. Although he could not, by his words and labor, convert Julian the Pelagian or Faustus the Manichaean to right faith, he nevertheless did not fail to compose great volumes against them concerning their error. Acting similarly against the other heretics of his own time and of other times, against Jews, and against pagans, he not only armed the people of his own day against them, but also transmitted to us and to all posterity a gift of the greatest edification and instruction.

Therefore, if by God’s inspiration Your Reverence should have the will to labor in these matters—for through His grace the ability cannot be lacking—write back, and we shall send the book, as we have sent . . . . . so that through your mouth, filled with His praise, the gracious Spirit may answer the spirit of wickedness, and may supply the treasures of His Church from the riches of your wisdom.

## A Certain Brief Summary Against the Heresies and the Sect of the Diabolical Deceit of the Saracens, or Ishmaelites

[Col. 0651]

[Col. 0651C] This is the sum of the entire heresy and diabolically deceptive sect of the Saracens, or Ishmaelites. First, their first and greatest execrable error is that they deny the Trinity in the unity of the Godhead. Thus, while they do not believe in the number of three persons in the one divine essence, avoiding number in unity—while, I say, they do not admit the number three, the beginning and end of all forms, and therefore the cause, origin, and limit of formed things—they confess God with their mouths but are wholly ignorant of Him.

Yet they, being themselves wayward and changeable, confess in unity only the principle of diversity and of every otherness, namely the number two: the divine essence itself and its soul. Hence their Alcoran—by which name they designate their law—introduces God speaking in the plural. *Alcoran* is interpreted from Arabic as “Collection of Precepts.” But these blind people deny that God the Creator is Father, because according to them no one becomes a father without sexual intercourse. Therefore, though they say that Christ was conceived by the divine Spirit, they do not believe that He is the Son of God, nor even God, but a good and most truthful prophet, free from every lie and sin; the son of Mary, born without a father, and never dead because He was not worthy of death.

Rather, when the Jews wished to kill Him, they say that He escaped from their hands and ascended to the stars; and that He now lives there in the flesh in the presence of the Creator until the coming of Antichrist. When Antichrist comes, that same Christ will kill him with the sword of His power and will convert the remaining Jews to His law. Christians, however, who long ago lost His law and Gospel, both through His departure and through the death of the apostles and disciples, He will then teach His law perfectly. In that law all Christians, like those first disciples, will be saved.

Together with them and all creatures, Christ Himself will die when Seraphim—whom they call a single archangel—sounds the trumpet; afterward He will rise with the rest and lead His own to judgment, helping them but by no means judging them. For God alone will judge; each prophet and messenger will be present as intercessor and helper with and for his own people. Thus taught them that most miserable and utterly impious Mahomet, who, denying all the sacraments of Christian piety through which human beings are especially saved, has already handed over nearly a third of humankind—by what judgment of God we do not know—to the devil and eternal death through unheard-of ravings of fables.

Who he was and what he taught ought, it seems, to be stated for those who will read this book, so that they may understand better what they read and know how detestable both his life and his teaching were.

[Col. 0653A] Some also think that this man was that Nicolas, one of the first seven deacons, and that the sect of the Nicolaitans, named after him and reproved in the Apocalypse of John (Rev. 2), is the law of the modern Saracens. Others dream other things; and, like persons careless in reading and ignorant of events, they hold every sort of false opinion here as in other cases.

But he was, as the *Chronicles* translated from Greek into Latin by Anastasius, librarian of the Roman Church, narrates most plainly, in the time of Emperor Heraclius, a little after the times of Gregory the Great, the first Roman pontiff of that name, nearly five hundred and fifty years ago: an Arab by nation, lowborn, at first a worshipper of ancient idolatry, as the other Arabs still then were; almost entirely uneducated and without letters. Bold in particular undertakings and possessed of much cunning, he rose from obscurity and poverty to wealth and fame.

As he gradually advanced, he increased fear of himself by continually pursuing his neighbors, and especially blood relatives, with plots, robberies, and raids, killing secretly those whom he could kill secretly and openly those whom he could kill openly. Often victorious in encounters, he began to aspire to kingship over his people. But when he saw that, because all alike resisted him and despised his low birth, he could not obtain by this route what he hoped for, he attempted to become king under the cover of religion and in the name of a divine prophet, since he could not do so by force of the sword.

And because he lived as a barbarian among barbarians, an idolater among idolaters, among people whom he knew to be easily deceived because, beyond all nations, they lacked and were ignorant of both divine and human law, he began to devote himself to his conceived wickedness. Having heard that God’s prophets had been great men (Rom. 2), he called himself God’s prophet; and, to make some show of good, he tried partly to lead them away from idolatry, though not to the one God, but to the deception of his heresy, which he had already begun to bring forth.

Meanwhile, by the judgment of Him who is said to be terrible in His counsels over the children of men, who has mercy on whom He wills and hardens whom He wills, Satan gave success to error. He sent into those parts of Arabia the monk Sergius, a follower of the heretic Nestorius, expelled from the Church, and joined the heretical monk to the false prophet. Thus Sergius, joined to Mahomet, supplied what he lacked. Expounding to him, as he saw fit, the sacred Scriptures of both Old and New Testament according to the understanding of his master Nestorius, who denied that our Savior was God, and fully steeping him at the same time in apocryphal fables, he made him a Nestorian Christian.

And so that the whole fullness of iniquity might converge in Mahomet and nothing might be lacking to him for his own destruction or that of others, Jews were joined to the heretic. To prevent him from becoming a true Christian, they deceitfully took precautions for a man eager for novelties, whispering into him not the truth of Scripture but their own fables, with which Mahomet still abounds. Thus instructed by the excellent teachers, Jews and heretics, Mahomet composed his Alcoran and fashioned, in his barbarous manner, an impious scripture made up alike from Jewish fables and heretical trifles.

He falsely claimed that it had been brought to him piecemeal in books by Gabriel, whose name he had already learned from sacred Scripture, and infected a people ignorant of God with this deadly draught. Like persons of that sort, smearing the rim of the cup with honey while fatal poison followed, he destroyed, alas, the souls and bodies of the miserable people. That impious man plainly did this when, praising both Christian and Jewish law but declaring that neither was to be observed, he appropriated [perhaps “approved”] and rejected [perhaps “the reprobate rejected”] them.

Hence he declares Moses to have been an excellent prophet, affirms that Christ God was greater than all others, proclaims that He was born of a Virgin, and acknowledges Him as God’s messenger, God’s Word, and God’s Spirit; yet he neither understands nor acknowledges “messenger,” “Word,” or “Spirit” as we do. He utterly ridicules the claim or belief that Christ is called the Son of God. Measuring the eternal generation of the Son of God by the analogy of human generation, like a bovine man, he denies and mocks, with all his force, that God could either beget or be begotten.

He repeatedly affirms the resurrection of the flesh. He does not deny that judgment at the end of the world is to be carried out by God, not Christ. Yet he raves that Christ will be present at that judgment as the greatest of all after God and as a protection for himself and his people. He describes the torments of hell as he pleased and as befitted a great false prophet to devise. Paradise he depicts not as the fellowship of angels, nor as the divine vision, nor as that supreme good which eye has not seen, ear has not heard, nor has entered into the human heart (1 Cor. 2), but truly such as flesh and blood—or rather, the dregs of flesh and blood—desired, and such as he wished prepared for himself.

There he promises his followers eating of meats and fruits of every kind; streams of milk, honey, and shining waters; embraces and sensual pleasures with most beautiful virgins and women—the pleasures in which his entire paradise ends. Amid these things he vomits up almost all the dregs of ancient heresies that he had swallowed through the devil’s instigation: with Sabellius he denies the Trinity; with his Nestorius he rejects Christ’s divinity; with Manichaeus he denies the Lord’s death, although he does not deny His return to heaven.

By instructing a people in these and similar doctrines not of gain but destruction, he turned them wholly away from God. And, so that evangelical speech might have no further place among them, as if they knew everything belonging to the Gospel and Christ, he stopped up the entrance to their hearts with an iron barrier of impiety. He also taught that circumcision, as received from Ishmael, the first ancestor of that people, must be retained. Beyond all this, so that he might more readily attract the carnal minds of men, he loosened the reins of gluttony and lust; having eighteen wives at once and committing adultery with the wives of many others as if by divine answer, he joined to himself a greater number of the lost, as though by prophetic example.

And so that he might not appear altogether dishonorable, he commends zeal for almsgiving and certain works of mercy; he praises prayers. Thus monstrous in every direction, he joins, as the poet says (Horace, *Art of Poetry*), a horse’s neck and birds’ feathers to a human head. Since, at the urging of the monk just mentioned and of the aforementioned Jews, he both entirely abandoned idolatry and persuaded those whom he could to abandon it, and preached that one God, after rejection of the plurality of gods, should be worshipped, he seemed to rustic and uneducated persons to say unprecedented things. And because this preaching suited their reasoning, they first believed him to be a prophet of God. Then, in the course of time and error, they raised him to the kingship he desired.

Thus mixing good with evil and confusing truth with falsehood, he sowed the seeds of error and produced, partly in his own time and partly—indeed especially—after it, an impious harvest to be burned in eternal fire. For immediately when the Roman Empire was weakening, indeed almost failing, by the permission of Him through whom kings reign, the dominion of Arabs or Saracens infected by this plague arose. Gradually occupying by armed force the greatest parts of Asia, all Africa, and part of Spain, it transferred both dominion and error to its subjects.

Although I call them heretics because they believe certain things with us, they disagree with us in more things; perhaps I should more correctly call them pagans or heathens, because that designation is more fitting. For although they say some true things about the Lord, they preach more false things, and they partake neither in baptism, the sacrifice of penance, nor any Christian sacrament—something no one except these heretics has ever done. The chief purpose of this heresy is that Christ the Lord should be believed to be neither God nor the Son of God, but, although great and beloved of God, nevertheless a mere human being, indeed a wise man and the greatest prophet.

This doctrine, conceived long ago by the devil’s machination, was first sown through Arius; afterward it was advanced through this Satan, namely Mahomet; and through Antichrist it will be completed entirely according to the diabolical intention. For blessed Hilary also says that the origin of Antichrist was in Arius: what Arius began—by denying that Christ was the one [true, or “Word”] Son of God and calling Him a creature—Antichrist will finally consummate by asserting that He was in no way God or God’s Son, indeed not even a good human being.

Most rightly, then, the utterly impious Mahomet, placed between the two, appears to have been provided and prepared by the devil, so that he might become in some way Arius’s supplement and the greatest nourishment, in the minds of unbelievers, for Antichrist who would speak worse things. For nothing is so contrary to the enemy of humankind as faith in the incarnate God. Through this faith we are especially stirred to piety, renewed by heavenly sacraments; through the working grace of the Holy Spirit, we hope to return again to that from which he boasted that he had cast us down: namely, to the vision of our king and our homeland, since God Himself—our king and creator—descended into our exile and calls us back to Himself by merit.

The devil has labored from the beginning simply to extinguish both the end and love of this piety and divine dispensation from human hearts. At the beginning of the still nascent Church, if he had then been permitted, he also attempted with most cunning subtlety to uproot it, almost by the very means through which he was afterward permitted to deceive this most unhappy people.

Blessed Augustine also says that Porphyry the philosopher, after miserably apostatizing from Christianity, reported in the books he published against Christians that he consulted the oracles of the gods and asked what Christ was. The demons replied that Christ had indeed been a good man, but that His disciples had grievously sinned by attributing divinity to Him and inventing something that He had not said of Himself. This opinion is found very frequently, almost in the same words, in these fables.

How great was this subtlety of the devil: that he should say something good about Christ! For if he had spoken altogether badly of Him, he knew that he would in no way be believed. He did not care what Christ was thought to be, provided that His divinity—which most of all saves human beings—was not believed. Whoever wishes to understand this more fully should read Book XVIII and Book XIX of the same Father Augustine’s *City of God*, and Book I of *On the Harmony of the Evangelists*. There, if one has a good and diligent mind, one will certainly infer both what the devil then schemed to do, but was not permitted, and what at last, when permitted by a hidden judgment, he accomplished among this one most miserable people.

For no mortal could possibly have invented such fables as those written below unless the devil had been personally cooperating. Through them, after many ridiculous and utterly insane ravings, Satan especially strives by every means to bring it about that Christ the Lord, the Son of God and true God, should not be believed to be the Creator and Redeemer of humankind. This is truly what he wished then to persuade through Porphyry, but was driven from the Church by God’s mercy while the Holy Spirit was still fervent in its first beginnings. At last, alas, using this most miserable man Mahomet—said by many to have been possessed and subject to falling—as an instrument and organ most suitable to himself, he plunged with himself into eternal destruction a vast people, now reckoned almost half the world.

Why this was permitted, He alone knows, to whom no one can say, “Why do You act thus?” and who said that of many called, few are chosen. Therefore I would rather tremble than dispute. I have noted these things briefly so that the reader may understand. And if such a person exists as both wishes and is able to write against this whole heresy, let him recognize with what enemy he will have to fight.

Perhaps there will yet be someone whose spirit the Lord will awaken, to free the Church of God from the great disgrace it suffers from this source. For although it has refuted by responses all ancient and modern heresies down to our own times, it has not only answered nothing to this one—which, above all others, has caused infinite ruin to humankind in body and soul—but has not even undertaken, however slightly, to investigate what so great a plague was or from where it arose.

This, indeed, was the whole reason why I, Peter, least abbot of the holy Church of Cluny, while staying in Spain to visit our establishments there, caused the whole impious sect and the execrable life of its most wicked inventor to be translated from Arabic into Latin at great effort and expense, and, once exposed, brought to the knowledge of our people: so that it might be known how suspect and frivolous the heresy was, and that some servant of God, inflamed by the Holy Spirit, might be moved to refute it in writing.

But because, alas, now that the ardor of studies of this kind has grown cold almost everywhere in the Church, there is no one to do it—for I waited a long time, and there was no one to open his mouth, move his pen through zeal for holy Christianity, and cry out—I myself have resolved, if my great occupations permit, sometime to undertake it with the Lord’s help. Yet I should simply be glad for this to be done better by anyone else than worse by me.

[Col. 0657]

## Robert of Ketton’s Preface to the Book of the Law of the Saracens, Which They Call the Alcoran, Translated by Himself

To Lord Peter, Abbot of Cluny.

[Col. 0657C] To his lord PETER, abbot of Cluny by divine prompting, ROBERT OF KETTON, least of his servants: perfect joy in God.

When I had frequently and seriously [perhaps “late”] perceived how and how greatly your mind, devoted to the sole and whole good, thirsted to make fruitful the barren marsh of the unseen Saracen sect, to drain its well, and to overthrow its defenses altogether, I, having performed only the office of a foot-soldier going ahead, opened the ways and entrances with the utmost care. For who will lengthen his stride? Who will not run most swiftly, so that he may recognize everywhere the enemy’s error—and the enemy himself—as defeated, while he himself holds an opinion firm and victorious?

Yet all Latin Christendom until now, oppressed—though I will not say by harmful disadvantages—by ignorance or neglect, has allowed the cause of its enemies both to remain unknown and not to be driven back. But your wakeful foresight, always looking to the holiest and most chosen doctors of the Church, in no way wished this. Therefore, since you imitate as disciple and son that Father and doctor whose entire inheritance is set up for sale, each according to his ability, I hoped, turning nowhere else, that I, though the least of all your people, might be able to earn your favor if, setting aside the vow of worldly dream and military service, I diligently attended to your commands.

Therefore, although a throng of wise men surrounds you like a pupil and heir of wisdom, graciously offering their hands to your commands—men whose company I feel myself by no means yet worthy to join—still I beg that your penetrating gaze may deign to look, at least once and directly, upon your small gift, opening the well indicated above.

Although many hindrances have beset me, supported as I am by a frail little talent—poverty of expression on one side, slenderness of learning on the other, and, most effectual of all in producing inaction, despair, the mother of sloth and negligence, manifold because of the base, loose, and unconnected material of our translation, which must, according to its character, be presented to Your Majesty merely with the Arabic veil removed—nevertheless I undertook your service no less earnestly, trusting that no undertaking can be shaken in its result toward which your divinely inflamed desire aspires.

Therefore I have brought stones and wood, selecting nothing and changing nothing perceptibly except for understanding alone, so that afterward your most beautiful, useful, joined, and indissoluble building may rise. I have exposed Mahomet’s smoke, to be extinguished by your bellows; his well, to be drained by your vessel; fuel and heat for your fire, by your fan; and the course of our stream, by your channeling of its source.

Justice therefore demands that, by destroying the enemy’s fortress—or rather, cage—and drying up his well, you, who are the best right hand of the world, the sharpest whetstone of religion, the open-handed hand of charity, should strengthen the defense of your people, carefully sharpen their weapons, and cause its spring to flow more strongly and the rampart of its charity to extend farther and more capaciously.

If anyone reproves me for the uselessness and incoherence of matters and words, perhaps justly, I nevertheless beg him to desist, knowing that my purpose here was never to cover poison with flowers or to gild a base and rejectable thing. The admirable light of your mind, powerful in marvelous fecundity and vigorous in most valiant action, has repeatedly and carefully made this clear to me when I reflected upon it and wished to speak briefly. Yet this law, although deadly in many places, offers those who see and are chosen the strongest testimony and argument for the holiness and excellence of our law. This did not escape your wisdom, which compelled me for the time being to leave aside my principal study of astronomy and geometry.

But lest the preface produce weariness, I now set an end to it and promise you a heavenly gift that penetrates the whole heaven and embraces in itself the completeness of knowledge: namely, that which opens most diligently to diligent students, according to number, proportion, and measure, all the heavenly circles and their sizes, orders, and relations; finally all the movements of the stars, their effects and natures, and other such matters, relying now on probable, and sometimes on necessary, arguments.

[Col. 0659] It is superfluous to append here the entire translation of the Alcoran itself. Peter the Venerable refuted it in the following books.

[Col. 0659]

## Two Books of Peter the Venerable, Ninth Abbot of Cluny, Against the Wicked Sect of the Saracens

(Edited by D. Martene, *Amplissima Collectio*, vol. IX, col. 1119, from the manuscript codex of Anchin, written in the author’s lifetime.)

## Preliminary Observation

The privilege of the most celebrated monastery of Cluny is that all its first abbots were distinguished alike for learning and holiness. By their example no less than by their industry and zeal, the observance of regular discipline flourished there intact and undefiled for about two hundred years. The first to depart from it was Abbot Pons, successor of St. Hugh. But Peter Maurice, commonly called the Venerable, who was appointed in his place and was scarcely inferior to the others in nobility of birth, learning, and piety, immediately took care to repair the ruin Pons had inflicted.

Concerned to erase not only the stains of the monastic order but those of the Church herself, he vigorously attacked her chief enemies in learned writings. He refuted the Jews in a separate book, and overthrew the heretics of his age in an excellent treatise against the Petrobrusians. Nor did he leave untouched the most hostile opponents of the Christian name, called Mahometans.

Accordingly, when he traveled to Spain in 1141, he used every effort to have their law—commonly called the *Alchoran*—translated into Latin. For this undertaking he called upon three men highly skilled in Arabic: Robert of Ketton, Herman of Dalmatia, and Peter of Toledo. So that the translation might be fully complete in every respect, he added a fourth, a Saracen named Mahomet, as being more knowledgeable in his native language, sparing no expense whatever.

Since Latin was less familiar to them, he also gave them a learned assistant, his beloved son and brother Peter, his notary, whom I believe to be the same Peter of Poitiers whose chapters for the four books are given here at the beginning.

After the venerable abbot’s return to France, his chief concern was to send the translation he had procured to his closest friend, St. Bernard, so as to encourage him to write against so destructive an error, using the magnificence of learning divinely bestowed upon him. Peter’s letter, dated 1143, may be found in the *Bibliotheca Cluniacensis*, p. 1109; Bernard’s response to it has hitherto been sought in vain. Nor does it appear that he ever wrote anything on that subject; this province was left to the abbot of Cluny.

Therefore, following the custom of the Fathers, who never passed in silence over any heresy of their own age, however slight, without resisting it with all the powers of faith and demonstrating through writings and disputations that it was to be detested and condemned, Peter undertook an outstanding work. Peter of Poitiers had prepared for it the chapters of four books, although Peter did not allow himself to be strictly bound by them. Andrew du Chesne asserts that Peter the Venerable’s entire work was divided into five books and laments that, although he sought them diligently, they could not be found. We, somewhat more fortunate, have discovered the first two books of that much-desired work in a very ancient codex of Anchin, elegantly written in the author’s own age, where they occur at the end of his letters. While the remaining books may be found, we present these two here to learned readers.

## Chapters by Peter of Poitiers to Lord Peter the Abbot

[Col. 0661]

[Col. 0661A] To his one and singular father and lord, Lord PETER, abbot of Cluny, PETER, the least of his sons: may you always rejoice in Christ.

Since you always do everything philosophically, after your manner, you have sent me, suitably enough, a passion to read—I who am patient and worthy of many sufferings. Thanks be to your sweetness that, at least on this occasion, I have your letter and the grace of your paternal greeting; by these I bear much more lightly, meanwhile, the distress of your absence, which is always most grievous to me.

Nevertheless, after I learned that you intended, with the Lord’s guidance, to cross over to England [Note: [Col. 0661D] Peter the Venerable mentions two journeys to England in Book II, chapter 32, of *Miracles*, and testifies that he remained for a long time on at least one of them in the [Col. 0662D] letter to Henry, bishop of Winchester, formerly a monk of Cluny: Book II, Epistle 13.], I became very much more anxious for you, your companions, your entire journey, and your prosperous return to us. I offered prayers and vows of supplication to almighty God, insofar as He grants it [Col. 0661B]; and I endeavor, and shall strive more and more as Christ grants, to ask those whom I know to be more devout and more diligent in holy prayers to do the same.

May the Holy Spirit direct your journey and your counsel, and make our joy complete in your return to us. I send you the chapter headings which you ordered John to have lost, and I believe that they are arranged much more distinctly than before. For they are now set down beforehand in accordance with what you have begun to do—or what, if it seems right to you, you will henceforth do—against those who are truly enemies of the cross of Christ.

From the great confidence with which I know your ability, if I have ventured to add or change anything and it so pleases you, let it remain; but if not, it is yours to correct whatever we have erred in. Nor should the chapter there concerning the shameful misuse of wives scandalize you in any way, because it is truly so in the Alcoran. As I learned with certainty in Spain, both from Peter of Toledo, whose partner I was in translating, and from Robert of Pamplona, now archdeacon, all Saracens do this freely, as though by Mahomet’s command.

I desire that you should confound these people as you have confounded the Jews and the provincial heretics. For you alone in our time have struck down with the sword of the divine word the three greatest enemies of holy Christianity—the Jews, the heretics, and the Saracens—and shown that Mother Church is not so bereft or desolate of good sons that, by Christ’s favor, she does not still possess those who can give an account to everyone who asks of the hope and faith within us, and humble every arrogance and pride of the devil [Col. 0661D] exalting itself against the height of God [Col. 0662A].

Health, prosperity, and every good to you first of all; also to your companions and ours: Lord Hugh the Englishman; John, who lost the chapter headings; our Bartholomew; Lord Constable; Godfrey; Gerard; Alemannus, if indeed he is with you; and all the rest. Forgive, I pray, my delay and weakness, because the Lord knows that, although I greatly wished it, I could not send this to you sooner, being confined by a severe weakness of my whole body, especially the habitual weakness of my feet. For I have written all this also in a larger book, fearing that these things too might be lost on the way, as the chapter headings were lost; and that was very laborious.

The letter ends.

## Chapters of the First Book of Lord Peter, Abbot of Cluny, Against the Wicked Sect of the Saracens

[Col. 0662B]

I. A preliminary address to the Saracens, warning and urging them to listen patiently and understand rationally what follows.

II. How foolishly and ridiculously they say that the Jews have lost their law and now possess only a falsified and corrupt version.

III. By what reasoning their opinion is proved foolish and vain.

IV. Since they likewise assert that Christians have lost the Gospel and the apostolic writings, how this assertion may most easily be refuted.

V. That the falsity of the Gospels could not have escaped Christians, especially since they are spread throughout the whole world and divided by great diversity of languages, yet all possess exactly the same Gospel, and at this time no Christians differ from the truth of that one and the same Gospel. [Col. 0662C]

VI. That, if the Gospel had been falsified, this could not have escaped so many men of languages and nations, so studious and learned; nor would they themselves have allowed themselves to be deceived by an uncovered falsehood, nor, abandoning truth, have held false things for true and uncertain things for certain.

VII. That from the part in which they accept the Gospel, it is proved that they must necessarily accept it wholly.

## Chapters of the Second Book

I. That Muhammad ought neither to be called nor believed a prophet, for the following reasons.

II. That he was a robber, and that this is demonstrated by what follows.

III. That he also became the murderer and parricide of many.

IV. That he was a traitor, often slaughtering the unsuspecting and sleeping.

V. That he was a heinous adulterer, saying in his Alchoran that God had granted him leave to commit adulteries. [Col. 0662D]

VI. That he also taught the most shameful Sodomitical practice, commanding in his Alchoran and speaking, as it were, in the person of God: “O men, take for yourselves women subject to you from whatever quarter pleases you.” [Col. 0663A]

VII. That he is very often inconsistent with himself in his Alchoran, now denying and now affirming the very thing which he previously denied.

VIII. That no miracles commended his legislation, whereas Moses, giver of the ancient Law, and Christ, founder of the New Testament, established by many great miracles that the laws they gave were divine and holy.

## Chapters of the Third Book

I. That Muhammad could not have performed miracles is proved from his above-mentioned wicked life.

II. That he himself confesses in his Alchoran that no signs were given him by God.

III. How frivolous—indeed, how nonexistent—is the reason which he there puts forward for not performing miracles, introducing God as speaking to him thus: “If we did not know that they would not believe you, we would give you signs and wonders.” [Col. 0663B]

IV. That in this too he is inconsistent with himself, when he calls himself a prophet and yet declares that no signs were given him, although prophecy is the greatest sign.

V. That he must be lying in one of these two claims: for if he was a prophet, he received prophetic signs; if he received no signs, he was not a prophet.

VI. That the light which, according to the tale of his birth and upbringing, was enclosed in Adam’s ribs, then in Noah’s ribs, and thus by succession reached him, never existed at all, but is most worthy of everyone’s laughter.

VII. That the assertion that he predicted those who would succeed him in rule—first Abubachar, second Aomar, third Odmen, fourth Hali—and certain other matters, is shown false by the account of the historian himself who reports it. [Col. 0663C]

VIII. That again he could not have been a prophet, as is demonstrated from the Gospel of Christ, which they believe in to some extent.

## Chapters of the Fourth Book

I. That the words of the Lord in the Gospel, “The Law and the prophets were until John” (Luke 16), were not spoken of all prophets, but only of those who, before Christ, foretold the universal salvation of the world accomplished through Christ. [Col. 0664A]

II. That after John or Christ there were, or perhaps will be, other prophets who foretold, or perhaps will foretell by the prophetic spirit, not those great things uniquely effecting human salvation, but matters concerning particular peoples, lands, or persons; and of these we possess many examples.

III. That Muhammad was neither among these nor among those: he did not foretell the salvation accomplished through Christ, since he came long after Christ; nor did he say anything, however slight, pertaining to prophecy.

IV. That this is shown from his Alchoran, in which he wrote absolutely nothing prophetic, since there is no basis whatever for saying that he ever spoke prophetically. And he was silent on this point in that writing which, in his own judgment, was sublime and unique: although he calls himself a prophet, he recounts nothing prophetic. [Col. 0664B]

V. That Muhammad’s entire writing is nothing but horrible dregs and foul remnants of heresies condemned and buried by the universal, most holy Church of the whole world five hundred years before he was born—especially the heresies of the Manichaeans, apocryphal writings, and above all the accursed book of the Jews, the Talmud. The Saracens, because they neither read nor know how to read truthful histories and ecclesiastical records, have never heard that those times or those heresies once existed; and therefore, brutish and miserable, they received this Satan, speaking as though of marvellous and novel things.

VI. An exhortation and admonition that, at least in this last age, when the end of the world is now near, they should come to true and holy Christianity, rejecting the devil’s fables and ravings, and believing in the cross and death of Christ—in which alone lies the true and complete salvation of humankind—through the washing of sacred baptism. [Col. 0664C]

Here end the chapters of the fourth book.

# Here Begins the Prologue of Lord Peter, Abbot of Cluny, to the Book against the Sect or Heresy of the Saracens

[Col. 0663]

1. Being about to act against the impious sect of the impious Muhammad, I first invoke the almighty Spirit of God, that he who has never failed anyone acting against his own enemies and those of his Church may not fail me either, as I undertake to act against the worst enemies of both. He spoke through the prophets, inflamed the apostles, and flooded the world with overflowing chrism; and, as ointment upon the head flowed down to the very hem of the garment, may such abundance of his grace, I pray, be present to me, the least of his servants. May he “who has knowledge of speech, encompassing all things” (Wisdom 1), fill my heart with knowledge and my mouth with fitting speech and expression, so that I may profitably carry out the work I undertake.

I hope that he will be present when invoked, because he is gracious. For “the Spirit of wisdom is gracious” [Col. 0664D] (ibid.); indeed—and I do not doubt that this is greater—because I belong to that Church to which the Saviour promised: “I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete, that he may remain with you for ever” (John 14). But perhaps the reason for writing is sought; lest I seem a superfluous writer, it must be set forth.

2. **The reason for writing this work.—Ancient writers against heretics.—**This, plainly, was my reason for writing: the same reason that moved many great Fathers. They could not endure any loss, however small, to the Christian faith; nor did they tolerate the madness of heretics in their many forms, raging against sound doctrine. They took care not to be silent when speech was required, perceiving—indeed, knowing most fully—that at the strict judgment of God they would be held no less accountable for unfruitful, or, what is worse, harmful silence than for an idle or injurious word. Therefore by letters, by books, by diverse and powerful treatises, they “stopped the mouths of those who speak iniquity” (Psalm 62); and, with the Spirit of God speaking through them, they overthrew, trampled down, and destroyed every height of Satan “that exalts itself against the knowledge of God” (2 Corinthians 10).

I pass over heretics less famous because of their very antiquity: Basilides, Apelles, Marcion, Hermogenes, the Cataphrygians, Eucratites, Montanus with the mad women Prisca and Maximilla, Novatian, Eunomius, and many other monsters bearing the Christian name. The great and learned men of those times opposed and withstood their madness: Agrippa, Justin the philosopher and martyr, Theophilus bishop of Antioch, Apollinaris bishop of Hierapolis, Philip bishop of Crete, Musanus, Modestus, Irenaeus—the famous bishop and martyr of our Gallic Lyons—Rhodon of Asia, Miltiades, Apollonius, Serapion, Hippolytus, Victorinus, Rheticius bishop of Autun, and many others unknown to us. These too I pass over.

I come to the chief plagues of diabolical perversity, by which Satan especially attempted to infect the Church of God and overthrow it as though by more powerful engines: namely, the Manichaeans, Arians, Macedonians, Sabellians, Donatists, Pelagians, and, last of all, Nestorians and Eutychians. [Col. 0665B]

The first of these, the Manichaeans, rejected all the books of the Old Testament, repudiated the prophets, accepted the Gospel in part and scorned it in part, and established two principles, one of good and one of evil. These monstrous men, wandering amid utterly empty fables, raved that God had fought the race of darkness; that, lest he be overcome, he had mingled a part of himself with crops, meats, herbs, trees, and all such things; that this part was gradually to be liberated, after people ate these things, through human belchings; that the Lord’s death was phantasmal, his resurrection false; and many other things better left unsaid than spoken. [Col. 0665C]

3. **On the Arians.—**The Arians, a more fertile crop of the devil than the others, “set their mouth against heaven, and their tongue passes through the earth” (Psalm 72). Abusing at will the divinity of the one true and highest God—Father, Son, and Holy Spirit—they ascribed deity to the Father alone and numbered the Son and Spirit among creatures. They said that the Son was the greatest of creatures, and that the Holy Spirit was inferior to the Son but greater than the other creatures. [Col. 0665D]

4. **On the Macedonians.—**The Macedonians, likewise mad, shared their heresy with the Arians, confessing the Son to be true God and consubstantial with the Father, but separating the Holy Spirit from the deity of both.

5. **On the Sabellians.—**The Sabellians, stripping themselves of the question of the Trinity as though it were excessively burdensome, thought that only one person was to be understood in the Godhead under three names.

6. **On the Donatists.—**The Donatists, taking occasion from sacred books handed over to persecutors during persecution, maintained that, with the entire world excluded from salvation, the Church could exist only in Africa—contrary to Christ, who said: “It was necessary for Christ to suffer and rise from the dead on the third day, and that repentance and remission of sins should be preached in his name to all nations, beginning from Jerusalem” (Luke 24). [Col. 0666A]

7. **On the Pelagians.—**The Pelagians, proud and most wicked enemies of the grace of God by which alone we are saved, sharpened their tongues more subtly than other heresies “like serpents” (Psalm 139), “the poison of asps being hidden beneath their lips” (Psalm 13). Among their manifold blasphemies on this matter, they said that human substance came from God, but that human goods came from human beings themselves through free choice.

8. **On the Nestorians.—**The Nestorians, next to last of these, removed deity from Christ, God and man, denying that he was God and professing him to be merely human. [Col. 0666B]

9. **On the Eutychians.—**The Eutychians, last among those named above, though opposed to the Nestorians, were no less impious: differing in their doctrine, equal in their faithlessness. As the Nestorians denied that Christ was true God, so the Eutychians denied that he was true man. Nestorius says: “Christ is man only.” Eutyches says: “Christ is God only.”

10. **Which authors wrote against these heretics.—**And so that, in the order in which the heresies have been set out, their destroyers too may be set out: against the Manichaeans, first or almost first, Archelaus, bishop of Mesopotamia, acted by publishing a book of disputation. After him Serapion, also a bishop, composed and published an excellent book. Younger than these in time, but far greater in thought and eloquence, great Augustine followed; by powerful books published both against Faustus and against Fortunatus, leaders of the Manichaeans, he defeated that impious heresy. [Col. 0666C]

Against the Arians, so far as writings are concerned, I read that Eustathius, bishop of Antioch, was the first to go armed into battle with faith and eloquence. After composing many works against the Arian doctrine, he was exiled from his see and country by order of Emperor Constantius, and in death adorned his own exile by glorious and steadfast confession. After him I read that Marcellus, bishop of Ancyra, wrote many volumes against the same people. I read also that Athanasius of Alexandria pressed the Arians not only by labours and words but also by writings, and wrote an entire book against Valens and Ursacius, defenders of the Arians. Who does not know that Hilary, bishop of Aquitaine—a truly holy man, learned in every branch of knowledge—produced twelve books against the Arians? Who is unaware of his one little book addressed to the Arian emperor Constantius, which he presented to him during his life, and another against the same emperor, which he wrote after Constantius’s death? There is also another which he issued against the aforesaid Valens and Ursacius.

The famous rhetor Victorinus likewise wrote books in dialectical form against Arius, teacher of the Arians. Didymus of Alexandria also treated the same subject against the same opponents in two books. Maximus, philosopher and bishop, presented at Milan to Emperor Gratian a notable book on the faith against the Arians. [Col. 0666D]

Against the Macedonians, the aforementioned books published against the Arians are indeed sufficient, for they affirm the deity of the Holy Spirit, in substance as well as majesty, just as they do that of the Father and Son—a deity which the Macedonians denied. But so that they might also be refuted by books specifically devoted to their error, the aforementioned Didymus wrote one book *On the Holy Spirit*. Basil, bishop of Caesarea in Cappadocia, composed a volume on the same Holy Spirit. Gregory of Nazianzus issued another book on the same subject. Ephrem, deacon of the Church of Edessa, also published in the Syriac language a volume on that same Holy Spirit. [Col. 0667A]

Although I have not found particular works against Sabellius, all who resist the Arians and all who oppose the Macedonians alike contradict the Sabellians. Indeed, I say something more: not only do Catholics act against them, but heretics too resist the Sabellians. Sabellius says that the Trinity has one person; the Catholic denies this, Arius denies it, and Macedonius denies it. Thus, the agreement of Catholics and heretics is sufficient for the condemnation of the Sabellians.

Against the Donatists the whole world, whose enemies they are, cries out; but Optatus, African bishop of Milevis, wrote six books specifically against them. In the final contest, our own—and truly our own—Augustine of Hippo defeated them by words and writings. Against the Pelagians and their founders Pelagius, Coelestius, and Julian of Campania, that same Augustine, the greatest and highest teacher of the Latin-speaking world, devoted almost the last years of his life to writing notable books. [Col. 0667C]

Against the Nestorians and their founder Nestorius, the second council of Ephesus was assembled. In it the Nestorian heresy was condemned, Nestorius was judged a heretical author, and he was expelled from the bishopric of Constantinople. Against Eutyches and the Eutychian heresy named after him, Saint Leo, first pope of this name, a man great in faith, learning, and eloquence, wrote notable letters worthy of remembrance both in thought and in style. By his pastoral zeal nearly six hundred bishops gathered at Chalcedon cut off Nestorius and his followers, Eutyches and his followers, from the body of Christ—that is, his Church—and consigned them to perpetual anathema unless those who remained repented. [Col. 0667D]

Against Jovinian, who made marriage equal to virginity; against Helvidius, who denied the perpetual virginity of the Lord’s mother; and against Vigilantius, who despised the bodies or relics of departed saints, Jerome, a priest of consummate learning, issued notable volumes in his customary brilliant style and showed how detestable they were. These men preceded Nestorius in time, but could not establish any sect bearing their names.

11. **That there is no error against which writings ought not to be composed.—**This the Church of God has always done and does: by the diligent hand of its husbandmen, it roots out brambles and thorns sufficiently hostile to the Lord’s crops. The tireless strength of the saints never yielded at any time to hostile missiles; overcoming force by courage and cunning by wisdom, it both protected its own by the shield of faith from the enemies’ fury and hurled back their thunderbolts with powerful force to their destruction. It could not endure the hissing of the venomous serpent prevailing against the heavenly oracles, nor the path of right faith, which leads to blessed eternity, being twisted by the crooked tracks of error toward hell. [Col. 0668A]

This, I say—this alone and wholly—was the reason those saints wrote: for it they attacked the enemies of Christian salvation not merely in speech and books, but spared neither their possessions nor themselves, nor finally even their own lives. The same reason is mine. Nor ought I, though far inferior and unequal to them, to be less zealous for the Church of God, Christ’s bride, than they were, since both they and I have—or had—the one faith, one baptism, one God, and one eternal life, which they now possess and for which we sigh.

But perhaps some errors are to be opposed and others passed over in silence. Such was not the opinion of the Fathers. Hippolytus showed this, among his many other works, by writing *On Easter against All Heresies*. Barthesanes too, once famous among his people in Mesopotamia for diverse writings, showed it: ardent in intellect and vigorous in disputation, he wrote countless works against almost all the heretics who flourished in his age. Among these, Jerome testifies, was that most famous and powerful book which he presented to Marcus Antoninus. [Col. 0668B]

Victorinus likewise affirms it—not the man previously mentioned, but the bishop and martyr of Pettau—who, trained in Greek and Latin, wrote against all heresies of earlier times or his own and showed, by writing against them all, that none ought to be neglected. Whether later writers ought to imitate him in writing, let the reader consider—not only because of his doctrine, but also because of the martyrdom which at last he underwent for the faith he had defended. Saint and famous Epiphanius, bishop of Salamis on the island of Cyprus, likewise maintained this point, writing books against all heresies and giving them to the Churches of the whole world to be read.

Therefore, as these examples of saints teach, no heresy is to be neglected; instructed by such great teachers, none is to be passed over in silence. Every error must be refuted; every evil understanding opposed to faith must be rebuked and, if possible, corrected. The Church, entrusted to its guardians by Christ himself, must be presented to Christ “without spot or wrinkle,” so that it may hear him say: “You are wholly beautiful, my beloved, and there is no blemish in you” (Song of Songs 4). [Col. 0668D]

12. **But especially against the Muhammadan error, which has spread very widely.—**If, then, no heresy arising at any time could be free from “the sword of the Spirit, which is the word of God” (Ephesians 6), will the Muhammadan error be safe from it? Or will it be passed over by the Christian tongue because it is nonexistent or insignificant? Or will it be spared as harmless or less harmful? And what heresy, reader, ever harmed the Church of God so greatly? What error ever so afflicted the Christian commonwealth? What one so drastically cut back its borders? What one increased the infernal number by so vast a mass of the lost?

The Arian plague, the greatest of the heresies mentioned, occupied for a time certain regions and infected them with the deadly draught offered by Satan. It added certain kings of the Goths to its wickedness and corrupted two Roman emperors—what is more serious—Constantius and Valens. It crossed from barbarian territory into Pannonia, then migrated to Italy; driven out from there, it invaded the southern part of Gaul, namely Aquitaine. But, at last driven out by Clovis king of the Franks, it settled in Spain after conquering it by military force. There, scarcely a hundred years having passed, it failed when the king of the Goths, who ruled that heretical people, was converted to the Catholic faith by the working of the Spirit of God. [Col. 0669A]

But Muhammadan fury, taking its beginning from the Ishmaelite Arabs, corrupted Persians, Medes, Syrians, Armenians, Ethiopians, Indians, and the remaining kingdoms of the East, and almost all of Asia itself, the greatest of the three regions of the world. Turning them either away from Christianity or from whatever ancient errors they had held, it converted them to the sect of a lost man; it withdrew them from Christ and placed them beneath the devil. Then, not by gentle persuasion but by violent assault, after subduing almost all the East by arms, as has been said, it subjected Egypt, Libya, and all Africa to its profane religion.
