Thus, having occupied two parts of the world, it did not leave Christ—or his Christians—even the third, called Europe, whole, after overrunning Spain. [Col. 0669B]

And what more can I say? Even if you were to count all the heresies raised up by the diabolical spirit from Christ’s time through eleven hundred years, and weigh them together as if in a balance, they could not equal this one; nor would you find that all together had supplied so much material for eternal fires.

13. **Whether Muhammad’s errors should be called heresies.—**Will the Christian tongue, which has passed over no heresy, however small, now pass sluggishly or silently over this greatest of all errors? But perhaps someone will say or think: “The Church answered those earlier heresies which, as the apostle John says, ‘went out from us, but were not of us’” (1 John 2); “but this error neither went out from us nor was of us.” The Fathers mentioned above answered Christians drawn away or departing from the Church—that is, Christ’s body—into any error; they contemptuously disregarded by silence errors foreign to the Church and wandering outside it. This error too may be numbered among the latter, since, as was said, it did not go out from the Church; and that it did not go out from the Church is sufficiently shown by calling it an error rather than a heresy, as the other heresies are called. For a heresy is not so called unless it goes out from the Church and acts against the Church. [Col. 0669D]

To this I confess—yes, I myself say—that Christians who persistently act contrary to any part of right faith are called heretics by an ancient and customary name, because they think or confess wrongly; and their error is called heresy. But whether the Muhammadan error ought to be called a heresy, and its adherents heretics or pagans, I do not clearly discern. For I see that, in the manner of heretics, they accept certain things from the Christian faith and reject others; yet in pagan fashion they both do and teach what no heresy is ever recorded to have done.

For, along with certain heretics, the impious Muhammad writing thus in his Alchoran, they proclaim that Christ was born from a Virgin, call him greater than every human being and than Muhammad himself, affirm that he lived without sin, preached true things, and did wonderful deeds. They confess that he was the Spirit and Word of God, but neither understand nor explain “Spirit of God” or “Word” as we do. They madly maintain that Christ’s passion or death was not merely phantasmal, as the Manichaeans held, but did not exist at all. These and similar things they think with heretics; but with pagans they reject baptism, repudiate the Christian sacrifice, mock repentance, and ridicule all the other sacraments of the Church. [Col. 0670B]

14. **Whether they are heresies or pagan ravings, they must be opposed.—**Choose, then, what you prefer: either call them heretics because of their heretical opinion, by which they partly agree and partly disagree with the Church; or call them pagans because of their excessive impiety, by which they surpass every heresy in their profession of impious error. If you call them heretics, it has been proved above that every heretic or heresy must be opposed. If you call them pagans, I demonstrate—and show by the authority of the Fathers—that they too must be resisted no less.

For confirmation, let Justin the philosopher and martyr, named above, return to the discussion. He laboured greatly in defence of Christ’s religion, so much so that he gave to Emperor Antoninus, his sons, and the senate a book written against the Gentiles, without being ashamed of the disgrace of the cross; and another book to Antoninus’s successors, Marcus Antoninus Verus and Lucius Aurelius Commodus. He also wrote another volume *Against the Gentiles*, in which he discusses the nature of demons; likewise a fourth work against the Gentiles, to which he prefixed the title *Elegeos* [uncertain reading]. There is also his dialogue against the Jews, which he conducted against Trypho, leader of the Jews. [Col. 0670C]

Let Apollinaris, bishop of Hierapolis, a city in Asia, follow him in establishing this point. He not only gave Emperor Marcus Antoninus Verus a notable volume in defence of the Christian faith, but also wrote five books against the Gentiles. Irenaeus of Lyons likewise issued a volume against the Gentiles. Miltiades wrote other books against Gentiles and Jews. Apollonius, a senator of Rome under the emperors Commodus and Severus, composed a notable volume against pagans. Giving an account of his faith, he read it in the senate; after its reading, he was beheaded for Christ by sentence of that same senate. [Col. 0670D]

Arnobius the rhetorician followed under Emperor Diocletian and wrote *Against the Gentiles*, works publicly read in those times. Methodius, bishop of Tyre, composed books against the pagan philosopher Porphyry. Apollinaris, bishop of Laodicea, also sharpened his pen against the same man and produced thirty books. Nor was Athanasius, bishop of Alexandria, whom I have mentioned above and must mention often, lacking in support of this position: he wrote not only against the Arians, his particular enemies, but also published two books against the Gentiles. Let Eusebius, bishop of Emesa, a man of elegant and rhetorical talent, follow: he composed, as is read, innumerable books, the chief of which were against Jews and Gentiles. [Col. 0671A]

After all these let Augustine follow, inferior in learning to none of those named—indeed perhaps superior—and by his twenty-two most celebrated books *On the City of God* teach that it is fitting, in due season, to act in speech and writing not only against heretics who leave the Church, but also against pagans and Jews who were never in the Church, and against every error whatsoever.

15. **So that a work could be written against the Muhammadan law, Abbot Peter had the Alchoran translated from Arabic into Latin.—**Therefore, whether the Muhammadan error is disgraced by the name of heresy or branded as Gentile or pagan, it must be opposed in writing. But since Latins, especially modern Latins, the ancient pursuit having perished, know—as the Jews said of the apostles once marvelling at their various languages—only the language in which they were born, they could neither recognize the nature of so great an error nor, still less, oppose it. Therefore “my heart grew hot within me, and in my meditation the fire was kindled.” I was indignant that Latins should be ignorant of the cause of so great a perdition, and that this very ignorance should prevent anyone from being stirred to resist it; “for there was none to answer, because there was none to know.” [Col. 0671C]

I therefore approached persons skilled in Arabic, the language from which the deadly poison issued to infect more than half the world. By both entreaty and payment I persuaded them to translate from Arabic into Latin the origin, life, doctrine, and law itself—called the Alchoran—of the lost man. So that the translation might lack no fullest credibility and nothing be withheld from our knowledge by any deceit, I joined a Saracen to the Christian interpreters. The Christian interpreters were Robert of Ketton, Herman the Dalmatian, and Peter of Toledo; the Saracen was named Muhammad. Searching the innermost arsenals of that barbarous people, they produced for Latin readers a substantial volume from the aforesaid material. This was done in the year in which I went to Spain and conferred with Lord Alfonso, the victorious emperor of the Spains: the year 1141 from the Incarnation of the Lord. [Col. 0671D]

16. **What benefit the undertaking may have.—**But perhaps someone still asks: “What good is it to offer food to people who loathe it? What does it profit to sound a lengthy disputation in the ears of a deaf asp that stops its ears? For the people against whom you propose to act are foreigners and barbarians, alien not only in customs but in language itself; they acknowledge nothing in common between themselves and the Latins. How, then, will an Arab hear—much less heed—a Latin, a Persian a Roman, an Ethiopian or Egyptian a Gaul? We must see to it that labour is not expended in vain; we must beware, lest useful work be abandoned and time spent on what is superfluous.”

To this I reply: what is written can be translated into their language; Christian truth can be rendered in Arabic letters or any others, just as impious error, through my efforts, was able to pass into the knowledge of the Latins. Thus a Latin work translated into a foreign language may perhaps benefit some whom grace, the guide to life, may wish to gain for God. Thus the Old Testament was transferred from Hebrew writings, and, except for Matthew’s Gospel, the New Testament from Greek into all the languages of the entire world; it subjected the world to God and, recalling it from hell through Christian faith, restored it to heaven. [Col. 0672A]

Thus many other works of the Fathers were borrowed by Latin from Greek and received by Greek from Latin. Nor was this exchange of languages lacking among the many other languages of the world unknown to us, of which one may almost say, as of the apostles: “There are no speeches or languages in which their voices are not heard” (Psalm 18).

But even if this Scripture under discussion should have no translators, or should not benefit people once translated, the Christian armoury will at least possess weapons against these enemies, by which it may either defend itself or, should battle perhaps arise, pierce its foes. Perhaps this published volume will meet the hidden thoughts of our people, by which they may be scandalized, imagining that some piety exists among those impious people and believing that some truth exists among the ministers of falsehood. To this reason is joined no small authority; and though authority ought rightly to lead in such matters, there is no obstacle to its following reason in the present case. [Col. 0672C]

17. All those whom I have mentioned, and many more whom I have left unmentioned, wrote great, diverse, and wonderful works against heretics, Jews, or Gentiles; yet, while writing, they neither chose nor foresaw whom they might benefit. And although they neither chose nor foresaw for whose salvation their own labours should serve, they nevertheless did not for that reason permit their minds to lie idle from study, their tongues from dictation, or their hands from writing. The Greek writer did not consider that Greek learning could not benefit a Latin; the Latin did not think that Latin writing was read in vain by a Greek; nor did any person, however barbarous but Catholic, acting against any errors, consider that he was undertaking the labour of writing in vain because his work could not benefit people of a foreign tongue unless translated into various languages. [Col. 0672D]

They knew and were certain that “the Holy Spirit breathes where he wills” (John 3), but they could not know whom, when, or how much he inspires. They knew that “neither the one who plants nor the one who waters is anything, but God who gives the increase” (1 Corinthians 3). Therefore, in watering and planting, like good servants they fulfilled what was theirs; what was God’s they left to the Lord. Whoever wishes to follow them, I think—indeed, I affirm—will not err. And if I do the same, I am certain that I shall not err. I certainly shall not err if, with a single eye, I do what is mine and reserve for God, as I have said, what is his.

Surely—surely indeed—labour undertaken for God’s cause cannot escape without fruit: whether it benefits converts, opposes enemies, fortifies members of the household, or at least does not fail to win for its writer the peace promised to people of good will. Therefore let the beginning of the extended work follow in the name of the Lord Jesus. At the end I add that I know and am certain that, by an unusual prolixity in such matters, I have exceeded somewhat the customary limits of a prologue; but, so that the reader may hold me excused, let him know that this happened because of the importunate objections of disputants. Lest I seem too brief, perhaps I became more prolix than was right for others. [Col. 0673A; 0674A]

# Here Begins the First Book of Lord Peter, Abbot of Cluny, against the Impious Heresy or Sect of the Saracens

[Col. 0673]

[Col. 0673B] **Peter the Venerable undertakes this book out of love for the Muhammadans.—**In the name of the Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, the one almighty and true God: Peter, a man of Gallic birth, Christian in faith, abbot by office of those called monks, to the Arabs, sons of Ishmael, who observe the law of him called Muhammad.

1. It seems remarkable, and perhaps it truly is, that a man most remote from you in place, different in language, separated in religious profession, alien in customs and manner of life, should write from the furthest West to people situated in the regions of the East or South, and should address in speech persons whom I have never seen and whom perhaps I shall never see. Yet I address you—not, as our people often do, with arms, but with words; not by force, but by reason; not with hatred, but with love. Yet it is such love as ought to exist between Christians and those turned away from Christ; such as existed between our apostles and the pagans of that time whom they invited to Christ’s law; such as existed between God himself, the Creator and ruler of all, and those whom, while they still served the creature rather than the Creator, he turned away through his own servants from the worship of images or demons.

Indeed, he loved them before they loved him; he acknowledged them before they acknowledged him; he called them while they still despised him. He bestowed good things upon those doing evil; by grace alone he had mercy on those perishing, and thus rescued them from everlasting misery. The Church of Christians receives this from him: that, just as he—according to the saying of our Christ—“makes his sun rise upon the good and the evil, and rains upon the just and the unjust” (Matt. 5), so she also loves friends in him and enemies for his sake.

To this Christian authority there succeeds an evident argument from reason: every animal, as someone has said, loves what is like itself. This is proved by the fact that, since under the genus *animal* are contained all the species of quadrupeds, birds, and whatever creatures are of that kind, each animal is more closely related to those of its own species than to those of the universal genus. This is apparent among domestic animals and evident even among wild beasts, which either always or often shrink from those whom nature has distinguished from themselves, and pursue those whom they perceive to be like or akin to themselves. If, as often happens, stirred by anger for some cause they contend against one another, yet, when the agitation has subsided, they quickly return to peace, nor can they for long forget what they were made to be.

And since among the innumerable species which, as has been said, are contained under the category of animal, man too is included—and since he is endowed also with reason, something possessed by no other animal—he is compelled far more strongly to love one like himself, reason persuading him, than the other animal is drawn by nature.

2. The author invites the Mohammedans to salvation.—These are the reasons by which a Christian ought to love you and ought to desire salvation for you. One of them is divine; the other human. In the former he obeys a divine command; in the latter he satisfies his own nature. In this way I, the least among innumerable servants of Christ and among innumerable people, love you; loving you, I write; writing, I invite you to salvation.

I do not invite you to the salvation of the sons of men, in whom, according to David’s word, “there is no salvation” (Ps. 145), because, according to the same man, “the salvation of man is vain” (Ps. 59); but to that salvation of which he also says: “But the salvation of the righteous is from the Lord, and he is their protector in the time of tribulation” (Ps. 36). I set these words of the Psalms before you because I hear from your Mohammed that the Psalms were given to David by God. For, speaking to the Jew Abdias, he says:

> “God indeed is one; Adam and Eve are two; Gabriel, Michael, and Seraphiel are three; the Law of Moses, the Psalms of David, the Gospel, and the *Alfurchan* [the Furqān] are four.”

Likewise:

> “For the word of God did not descend upon me all at once, as the Law of Moses, the Psalms of David, and the Gospel were given all at once to Christ.”

I invite you to a salvation that does not pass away, but endures; not one that ends with this brief life, but one that remains unto eternal life. It is granted to mortals to attain this salvation and, at the time appointed by God, to enjoy it; but only to those who think concerning God what is true, not what is false; who worship him not according to the fantasies of their own hearts, but as he himself both wills and commands that he be worshipped.

3. They are unwilling to hear those who wish to challenge their law.—It is innate in man not to wish to be deceived and to seek truth.—To this you say: “Far be it that our understanding should think otherwise! Far be it that our profession should be otherwise! We have imagined nothing about him; we have invented absolutely nothing. What we think and confess concerning him is not according to the inventions of our own minds, but according to what our prophet, sent by him, handed down to us. Since he is last in the order of prophets, as it were the seal of all prophets, and is not the author but the bearer of the divine law, not God but a messenger, he received heavenly commands sent to him from God through Gabriel, containing neither more nor less than was required; and he handed over what he received for our fathers and us to observe. These things we observe; these things we keep; to these we have devoted our souls, our bodies, our life and our death.”

And, O men—men, I say, not merely rational by nature, but capable of reasoning also by intelligence and skill—would that you might here lend me the intellectual ears of your hearts! Would that, setting aside the obstinacy of superstition, you might hear what I am preparing to set forth.

I say “hear” because, though it is astonishing, if true, I have heard that you are unwilling to hear anyone who wishes to act against the custom to which you are accustomed, anyone who wishes to oppose your ancestral laws, anyone who seeks to dispute against the rites handed down to you by your prophet whom I named above. And I have learned not only that you are unwilling to hear this from anyone, but that you are commanded by law—so widespread report, from your East to our West, declares—to stop even the very beginnings of such speech with stones, swords, or any other form of death.

Therefore consider, men prudent according to worldly knowledge; consider, I say, and, removing the obstacle of obstinate will, examine carefully whether this custom is defensible, whether it can rest upon any reason. No person who is not only rational by nature but capable of reasoning through the lively sharpness of mind wishes to be deceived in temporal matters. He certainly does not wish to accept uncertainty in place of certainty, so that, deceived by another’s craft or ignorance, he should judge what is true to be false and suppose what is false to be true. In this matter he yields to no relationship and assents to no one, however dear, concerning such things: not friends, not persons joined to him by blood, nor even spouses united to him by the closest bond of love, can he calmly endure knowingly to deceive him.

Although friends often patiently endure many and very great burdensome things in body and spirit for the sake of friends, nevertheless nature has implanted this in man: that he should not, on any terms, permit himself to be deceived by anyone, however close or friendly. Examine all mortal occupations and the liberal arts themselves; consider also those called servile arts. Does any devotee of secular learning wish to be deceived concerning them or within them, rather than to receive from learned persons or teachers a true and certain knowledge of them?

This is shown especially by the study of earthly wisdom itself. Those called *philosophi* [“lovers of wisdom”] in Greek, and “lovers of wisdom” in Latin, strove with the utmost effort to acquire it; and, according to the diversity of their talents, thinking differently about it, they gave free rein to speech. According to the greater or lesser sharpness of their reasoning, they brought forward publicly what they thought and laboured, through innumerable forms of disputation, to reach the truth of the matters at issue in the questions proposed. They did not stop the mouths of those whom they believed diligent in seeking truth; rather, disputing over opposing views, they eagerly encouraged themselves and others, by every kind of speech, toward this praiseworthy study.

This was always the purpose and practice of the wise among Greeks, Latins, Persians, Indians, and other nations: both to persist always in investigating the truth of things and to encourage students, through frequent conferences, to inquire into, examine, and determine the same. Who could now enumerate their vast multitude—the men who, above all others, flourished in investigating the truth of things? Famous and well established among us is the knowledge of those who brought to light the truth and power of created things, not by silence nor by shutting human mouths so that they might be silent, but by speech and disputation concerning the hidden things of nature; and who handed down to the people of their own age and to posterity what they had found to be certainly true.

4. Therefore the inquiry into truth must not be neglected, especially concerning divine things. Falsehood alone seeks darkness; therefore the law of Mohammed is false.—Since, then, every rational mind desires to know the truth of created things and wishes to turn knowledge of that truth to its own advantage, and since it wishes to obtain by inquiry and disputation what it cannot attain by silence, the true knowledge of the uncreated reality must never be neglected.

Surely, until he who does not grasp it understands it, ought he not to inquire, dispute, and examine? Ought not the human mind to be urged by far sharper incentives to know the uncreated essence than to investigate created nature? Let it be considered which of these two outweighs the other, which serves human benefit more. Let this, I say, be considered; then it will be recognized to whose knowledge the human mind ought to devote itself more earnestly.

I certainly wish to know the force or power of things presently visible, so that, while I live here as a mortal, they may bring some assistance or benefit to this my passing pilgrimage. But why do I seek to know the uncreated reality, which creates all things and rules all created things, except that it may grant me appropriate support for this life while I live here, and, after this death, grant that I may live eternally and happily? What is this nature, this substance or essence? Is it not that which, according to the common custom of all nations and in the proper language of each, is believed and called God? Therefore that nature is God; and he alone is uncreated who alone is Creator, who alone is ruler of all, who alone is the author and giver of present and eternal goods.

Therefore consider—you, I say, to whom I write—and, according to the Psalm of David, whom, I believe, you do not disbelieve: “Judge justly, sons of men” (Ps. 57). Is the creature to be debated while the Creator is to be kept silent about? Is free power of speech to be granted to one inquiring about lowly and passing goods, while the mouth of one inquiring and arguing concerning the highest and eternal good is to be closed?

May I have free range everywhere in speaking of all created things, and then, as soon as I wish to speak of their Creator, will Mohammed’s law stop my mouth—or, if I say anything against it, will it cut off my head when scarcely the first words have escaped? Does any law besides yours do this? Truly, none; absolutely none. Turn your eyes in every direction, from sunrise to sunset, from south to north; examine the laws, rites, and customs of all nations, and if you can find anything similar established or handed down anywhere, produce it publicly.

Not so—not so, to say nothing for the moment of others—does the Christian law act; not so does a certain great apostle of Christ command: “Be ready,” he says, “to give an answer to everyone who asks you concerning the faith and hope that are in you” (1 Pet. 3). What, then, does such a custom surely indicate? What does such a law mean, which forbids one disputing against you to be heard, which cannot endure anyone proceeding by prior reasoning against what are believed to be your errors? Does this not seem to you full of every shame? Do you not see that it is wholly filled with disgrace?

Virtue always has an open brow. It does not seek corners, disdains to be veiled, flees obscurity, and seeks what is clear and open to all. Falsehood alone fears to be known, dreads examination, delights in hiding places, and fears being brought into public as it fears death. Why is this? Why, I say, does truth seek light and falsehood darkness? There is plainly this reason, and absolutely no other: the reason which our Christ sets forth in his Gospel—which your Mohammed both said and wrote had been given to him—concerning those who do good and those who do evil: “Everyone who does evil hates the light and does not come to the light, lest his works be reproved. But he who does truth comes to the light, that his works may be made manifest, because they have been done in God” (John 3).

Certainly these are words of truth, plainly the words of him whom your Mohammed—of whom I wrote a little earlier—extols with boundless praises, whom in various places of his *Alchoran* he acknowledges as messenger of God, Word of God, and Spirit of God, whom he does not deny to have lived without sin, and to be greater than every human being, even than himself. If, according to him, this man lived without sin on earth, he certainly was not a liar; for if he had not avoided the mark of falsehood, he would have been not a small but a great sinner.

His are the words I set forth above: “Everyone who does evil hates the light, and he who does truth comes to the light.” To what purpose are they? They stand against a wicked custom, against an unheard-of law, which declares unlawful what is lawful for everyone, and closes hearing and access against those wishing to proceed against it by reason. For if that custom, if that law, is of truth, what does it fear in coming to the light, so that it may be made manifest that its works are done in God or from God? But why should I make long detours about a matter known to all? That custom, that law so often named, plainly and without doubt hates the light, loves darkness, does not tolerate one who rebukes it, and does not endure a contradictor, lest its falsehood be reproved and its wickedness, hidden by deceitful silence, become known to the world.

5. Therefore Mohammed’s law is ridiculous.—Now attend to these things also, and recall the words of that whom you consider your prophet: how frivolous they are, how weak, how devoid of every strength of truth and reason:

> “If anyone, making God speak for himself, wishes to dispute with you, say that you have turned your face and the faces of those who follow you to God. By doing this, both those learned in laws and the illiterate will follow the good law; but if not, it is yours merely to make my commands known to the nations.”

Likewise:

> “If anyone wishes to enter into a contest with you concerning the law, say ‘anathema’ to him, and threaten such persons only with God’s wrath.”

And again:

> “Do not dispute with those who possess a law; for slaughter is better than contention.”

What, I ask, are words of this kind? Is a rational mind buried in such asinine stupidity that, after the manner of that brute animal, it patiently bears whatever or however great burdens are laid upon it, does not dare to debate them, and does not presume to ask whether they are good or evil, beneficial or harmful? If I grant this, I must henceforth be carried about by every wind of doctrine and, like a reed shaken by any breeze, bent this way and that; I must yield to every error, assent to every falsehood, hold nothing certain, and indiscriminately confuse good things with bad, true things with false.

Once this is granted, what difference will there be between a human being and cattle? What between the human mind and a beastly spirit? Plainly none, as regards foolish obedience—though there remains much difference in their distinct natures. For then man will not merely be compared with beasts of burden, but will rightly be judged more stupid than a sheep. A beast does not resist any command because it lacks a rational mind; but the rational mind assents while reason’s judgment objects. Judgment is not given to cattle: it yields without discrimination to every commander. Yet man, for whom it is natural to distinguish good from evil and true from false, obeys even things which he judges worthy of condemnation, having become more worthless than cattle.

I marvel—and cannot marvel enough—how any person’s craft could have extorted this from knowledgeable and learned men: that they should believe that the words I have set forth were spoken by God, when neither an inattentive nor a diligent reader can find in them anything whatever except folly, cruelty, and madness.

6. For what is this: “If anyone wishes to dispute with you, say that you have turned your face and the faces of those who follow you to God”? Therefore, to address you yourself, O Mohammed: if I wish to debate with you concerning your law, whether it is just or unjust, and you answer me nothing but that you have turned your face and the faces of those who follow you toward God, shall I believe that you have spoken truth? Shall I believe that you were a true prophet of God? Shall I believe that the law which you handed down to your people was handed down to you by God? Truly, I should be more than an ass if I agreed; truly, more than a beast if I assented.

For how do you give me grounds to believe, even in a small matter, that you have said anything truthfully, if you assert that you have turned your face toward God or away from God? And moreover, what a monstrosity, I beg you, is the saying which you add that God told you: “By doing this, both those learned in laws and the illiterate will follow the good law”? By doing what? If you say that you have turned your face toward God, then on that account both those learned in laws and the illiterate will follow your law, which you call good.

But why do I pursue a matter that is openly ridiculous? Let another verse follow this preceding one. For you write that God added: “But if not, it is yours merely to make my commands known to the nations.” What is this? You had said that God said that, if you spoke the foregoing things, both those learned in laws and the illiterate would follow the good law. Why, then, did you add: “But if not, it is yours merely to make my commands known to the nations”? First you make God speak in the indicative mode, and now you introduce words of doubt. He spoke in the indicative mode when he said that those learned in law and the illiterate would follow the good law; but in a doubtful mode when he said, “But if not.” If he spoke declaratively, why do not all, learned and illiterate alike, follow your law? But if he doubted that they would believe you, why did he say that all would follow your law?

7. But another passage which I set forth follows:

> “If anyone wishes to enter into a contest with you concerning the law, say ‘anathema’ to him, and threaten such persons only with God’s wrath.”

And to whom would this not be permitted? To whom among men would this plainly not be very easy? What you are commanded to say to me, I too am not forbidden to say to you. Just as it is easy for you, when I wish to enter into a contest with you over your law, to say “anathema” to me, so it is very easy for me, when you argue with me about my law, if you refuse to assent, to say “anathema” to you. If it is easy for you to threaten me with God’s wrath unless I believe you, it is likewise easy for me or anyone else equally to threaten and invoke that same wrath of God against you unless you assent to me.

Is it therefore just, is it reasonable, that, when no authority has been set before me and no reason previously shown, I should believe you and assent to your law merely because you say nothing else to me but “anathema,” merely because you threaten nothing other than God’s wrath? But because even brutish minds can see the weight of these words of yours, I proceed.

8. Only Jews and Christians properly received a law from God. Why Mohammed did not wish his followers to dispute with those possessing a law.—“Do not,” he says, “dispute with those who possess a law; for slaughter is better than contention.” Who does not see that this is an infernal counsel? “Do not,” he says, “dispute with those who possess a law.” Who are those possessing a law? As far as we can understand that man’s obscure language, those possessing a law are none other than Jews or Christians.

For, looking in every direction, I see that when these things were said by him, no others in the world then possessed—or still possess—a law except those whom I have named: namely, Jews and Christians. They, and no others, had previously received a law and kept what they had received according to their respective observances or understandings: the Jews, the law given through Moses; the Christians, the law given through Christ.

For pagans, or Saracens of your own stock who preceded your Mohammed, cannot be said previously to have received a law. No law had been given to pagans by anyone; error alone had infected them with false opinions of men—not opinions now even worth mentioning. Nor had a law been given to Saracens, since the bearer—lest I say author—of your law, mentioned above, had not yet come. If someone perhaps objects that certain legal ordinances had been handed down to Greeks, Latins, or other peoples—for example, Solon’s laws to the Greeks of old, or the laws of certain Latin sages to the Romans—I answer that those laws neither established nor handed down what they should believe concerning God, nor by what rite or manner they ought to worship him. They merely provided, not by divine command but by human counsel, how each nation should govern its commonwealth and in what order it should conduct life in peace or war, lest, if they attempted to live in a beastly manner without the boundary of some definite law, indiscriminately mixing evils with goods and just things with unjust, they themselves or their commonwealth might not long endure amid such great disorder.

But among them there was no discourse concerning divine matters, except such as, deprived of every authority and reason, derived its origin either from ridiculous fables, foolish human ravings, or deceitful oracles of demons. Such discourse did not lead people to true knowledge or worship of deity, but turned them away from it most completely and utterly miserably, by proposing for worship idols or any created things in place of the Creator.

For this reason, persons of this kind cannot be said to possess a law: they did not receive one from God, but themselves invented a manner of life or of worshipping God according to their pleasure. Therefore only Jews or Christians before Mohammed, or in his time, can be said to possess a law, since they received it not as invented by themselves, but as handed down by God. It seems to me, then, that his saying, “Do not dispute with those who possess a law,” was spoken of these persons.

Why did this man say this? Why did he command that they should not dispute with those who possess a law? If he was confident in the truth of his law, why did he forbid his followers to debate? If he distrusted it, why did he write what his followers could not defend? But he himself—or, with your permission be it said, Satan who spoke through him—knew that the Jewish or Christian law possessed such strength and so firm a foundation that it could not be overturned, not merely by human words or arguments, but not even by military force, the clash of arms, the most dreadful tortures, or deaths of any kind, nor even slightly altered by any assault.

He had experienced, in the time of the first law, the constancy of the Jews in the Maccabees; and in the days of evangelical grace, the endurance of the martyrs. He knew that human arguments could not prevail against eternal wisdom, nor the feeble and weak efforts of mortals resist unconquered power. Therefore, seeing worldly wisdom and human strength already withdrawn from divine laws, how could he flatter himself with the prospect of victory for his own side when a dispute was proposed, or even endure the first blows of debate? Deprived, then, of every means of resistance, he resorted to flight; and, unable to offer or object anything reasonable, he chose silence.

9. He wished matters to be settled not by reason but by the sword.—Yet, lest he seem to yield entirely to the opposing side, he took up arms in place of reason; and, after the manner of madmen, giving no answer to anyone who questioned him, he turned to stones, clubs, and swords. Armed with these, he attacks one who proceeds against him; indeed, before the man proceeds, almost before he begins to proceed, like a cruel beast rushing unexpectedly upon him, he destroys him.

Such a just and rational conclusion to disputations does your prophet Mohammed, O Hagarites, impose; with such an equitable decision does he decide between parties opposed to one another; such a judgment, unheard of through all ages until his or your time, does this praiseworthy arbiter pronounce. For, as I have set forth, these are his words: after saying, “Do not dispute with those who possess a law,” he adds, “For slaughter is better than contention.”

And what can I say? Words fail to refute such absurdity, such beastly cruelty, such unspeakable wickedness. Truly Satan, a beast avid for human blood, devised this; through this man, as through an instrument suited to himself, he breathed it forth. Using his tongue as a pen or reed, he both spoke and wrote so inhuman and monstrous a crime. He knew that this fabulous and utterly trivial sect, as will be proved in its place, could not otherwise stand for long. He was not ignorant that its erroneous doctrine, like a spider’s web, would be easily dissolved if a free path were open to those wishing to proceed against it, if preachers of the divine word were permitted, according to ancient custom, to debate against it.

He had not forgotten that formerly “their sound had gone out into all the earth, and their words unto the ends of the world”: those sent by Christ had sown the word of eternal life everywhere and brought almost the whole world to knowledge of truth. He understood that none of those who believed through them could have believed unless he first heard what he ought to believe; nor could he hear this if he lacked a preacher. For, as one great apostle of ours says: “Faith is from hearing, and hearing through the word of Christ” (Rom. 10). Christian faith could not have arisen in human minds without a heard preaching; nor could preaching have been heard without a preacher.

And because the fallen angel, subtle in deception and destruction, knew that he would be deprived of a very great gain—as he had grieved that he was deprived of it in former times—if access were given to hearing the word of God, and did not doubt that he would be expelled from the hearts of those he had deceived if that word were admitted, he placed in the way an iron barrier, drawn from the abyss of wicked counsel, which no one could cross. He did this so that, guarding his court—alas! now a great one—in peace, he might possess it more securely, and so that one who could be saved by hearing the word of salvation, being deprived of hearing by such an artifice, might perish eternally.

10. The Church condemns disputes and killings, but killings more strongly.—For all these reasons that so notoriously detestable saying was uttered by this one of yours so often named: “For slaughter is better than contention.” Christian law also disapproves of contentions, according to the teaching of the aforementioned apostle of ours: “The servant of God,” he says, “must not quarrel” (2 Tim. 2). For it condemns the spirited wranglings of such disputes, which occur not in order to discover truth but through a shameless eagerness to defend one’s own opinion.

Christian sobriety, as I have said, certainly disapproves proud and furious quarrels, teaching the disciple wisely and modestly either to propose what ought to be proposed or to raise what ought to be objected. Yet it does not approve slaughter, as your prophet does, nor does it say, “Slaughter is better than contention.” For it teaches that both are evil, and does not conceal that both are condemnable. But although both are condemned by its judgment, it nevertheless condemns one of them more strongly.

It does not say, “Slaughter is better than contention,” or “Contention is better than slaughter,” because something wholly evil cannot be compared with something wholly good, nor conversely. Comparison can be made between two goods or between two evils, not between one good and one evil, or one evil and one good. Therefore our apostle does not say, as your Mohammed asserts, that slaughter is better than contention, or contention than slaughter; rather, that slaughter is far worse.

And what mind even a little—much less greatly—rational would fail to see this to be true? Examine the judgments of all nations and investigate everything upon earth that the sun sees, whether human laws, though diverse in many other matters, do not agree in this single point: that the guilt of unjust killing is punished with a far greater penalty than the offence of abusive contention. It would be remarkable if even your laws, which we know are prudent according to the flesh, did not agree in this most just matter—something which nature itself proclaims even when words are silent: that a greater injury should be punished by a greater penalty, and a greater loss condemned by a greater retribution.

If this is so, then “slaughter is better than contention” is false; but “contention is evil, slaughter far worse” is true. If, however, his meaning in saying, “Do not dispute with those who possess a law,” did not except even the ancient pagans, inventors of whatever things, then he wrote this all the more disgracefully and distrustfully, since he did not dare to dispute even with those whose laws appeared before the public supported by no divine authority and no power of truth.

What, then, remains? Lay aside such disgrace, and no longer allow yourselves to be branded with so shameful a mark: the impression that you so greatly distrust your own sect, and that it is so completely devoid of every strength of reason, that you dare not come forward publicly—let alone voluntarily, even when challenged—or join battle in disputation with any, even the least, opponent.

11. Speaking from charity, he urges them at least to listen.—And how will the justice or truth of your party, if it can exist, become known to us or to the world? How will the light of Christian faith shine upon you and yours if neither you present your own doctrines, whatever they may be, nor hear ours from our people? Although we do not fail to know that your own doctrines appear sufficient to you, that you believe yourselves to possess a full knowledge of deity, and that you judge both us and all other followers of other or foreign laws to be in error except yourselves, nevertheless hear what is to be set forth peacefully. Do not alone dissent in this from the custom of all nations or laws, especially since, when all disputations and arguments are complete, you are free either to approve or disapprove, accept or reject, whatever has been said.

And because concern for your salvation impelled me to write these things, and because the charity which I have for you—not as toward Christians, but as toward pagans—did not permit me to be silent, though you were utterly unknown and far removed, you ought at least to return this service to my charity: if you are unwilling to assent to what is to be said, at least do not refuse to hear it.

Let the tenacious memory of you who read or hear these things retain this also: because in doubtful matters what is true cannot be known unless what is false is first destroyed, I must necessarily proceed, in language appropriate to the subject, both against your lawgiver and against his legislation. For truth would suffer no small injury if one recounting matters of judgment or argument spared falsehood.

12. The example of Christians, who hear even Jews preaching contrary doctrines. By this method kings and princes adhered to Christian truth.—Therefore do not immediately become agitated; do not immediately, if I may speak thus, become mad and rush to stones or swords, as I said above. At least imitate our people in this respect. Although they regularly engage in conversation with Jews—of whom a very large multitude dwells subject among them—and hear from them many, indeed nearly all, things contrary to the Christian faith, they are not stirred to fury and do not rise up to kill them as blasphemers. Rather, they listen patiently and answer wisely; they do not immediately destroy them as enemies of their salvation, but wait patiently, in case perhaps they may someday be converted.

They maintain this practice also toward innumerable captives of your own people and law, whom they frequently capture in battle; and, except for withholding the possibility of returning to their native land, they do not take away freedom of speech. And, that we may ourselves raise something against us, as though from your side—something which, perhaps because you do not know it, you could not raise yourselves—we read in the law of the Jews, which is also that of Christians but is understood by us as it ought to be understood, that God commanded blasphemers to be killed: those who dared impiously to violate by word or deed anything pertaining to God.

But this does not help your side even slightly, because no one now in the world doubts, except a few pagans, that the author of that law is the true God; whereas every people among all the nations under heaven except yourselves maintains that your sect is not from God. Therefore it is just that you postpone killing those whom you consider blasphemers until, by an unquestionable examination of truth, it is known that your prophet was sent by God and your law was given by God—as he who commands blasphemers to be killed is proved to be the true God.

By such a method and such consideration—careful rather than furious, modest rather than precipitate—all the nations of the whole world received Christ’s messengers and heard those whom they received. Although they strove long and greatly to resist, at last they yielded to reason, at last to manifest truth—indeed, to the illuminating Spirit of God. Among them, lest I become excessive, setting aside countless others, I offer you an example: a certain kingdom situated in the farthest parts of the West and almost outside the world, together with its king, named Ethelbert, who was almost a contemporary of your Mohammed.

13. How the English received the faith. — Britain was formerly the name of that kingdom from the ancient Britons; but now, with its name derived from the people of the Angles, it is called England. About five hundred years previously that people had left the regions of Saxony and, through warfare, occupied great parts of that island—for it is an island surrounded by the great Ocean sea—and established a kingdom there. This people was still entangled in the ancient error of idolatry, bestowing upon the creature the worship due to the Creator, and thus far removed from Him. At last the gracious Creator had pity on the erring people and, through the supreme teacher of Christians—I mean the Roman pontiff, called Gregory—delivered it from death and joined it to eternal life. For, moved by the divine Spirit, he sent chosen disciples to proclaim Christ’s Gospel to that people; foremost among them was a certain holy man named Augustine. By their words and conspicuous deeds, the king, with the whole people, was converted to Christ’s faith and faithfully added to the number of Christians.

But hear how he received the messengers sent to him; what answer he gave after they had stated the reason for their arrival; what he did; and how he conducted himself toward them. This bears greatly—indeed wholly—upon the matter at issue. The following are the very words excerpted from the ancient history of the English:

At that time King Ethelbert was exceedingly powerful in Kent, and had extended his dominion as far as the boundary of the river Humber, by which the territories of the southern and northern peoples of the English are divided. On the eastern side of Kent there is the substantial island of Thanet, namely six hundred hides in extent according to the English manner of reckoning. It is separated from the mainland by the river Wantsum, about three stadia broad, passable only in two places, for both its mouths extend into the sea. Upon this island the servant of the Lord Augustine landed with his companions, about forty men, as is reported. By Pope Gregory’s command they had obtained interpreters of the Frankish people; and they sent word to the king that they had come from Rome, bearing very good news, which without any doubt promised eternal joys in heaven and a kingdom without end with the living and true God to those who obeyed it. [Col. 0685A]

Upon hearing this, he ordered them to remain on the island where they had arrived and to be supplied with necessities until he should see what to do with them. After some days the king came to the island; sitting in the open air, he ordered Augustine and his companions to come there for a conference with him. For, following an ancient augury, he had taken care that they should not enter any house in his presence, lest, if they possessed some magical art, they might overcome him through deception upon their arrival.

But they came endowed not with demonic but with divine power, carrying a silver cross as their banner and an image of the Lord and Saviour painted on a board; and, chanting litanies, they implored the eternal Lord for both their own salvation and that of those for whom they had come. [Col. 0685B] When, at the king’s command, they sat down and preached to him and to all his attendants who were present the word of life, he replied:

“The words and promises which you bring are indeed fair. But because they are new and uncertain, I cannot give assent to them while abandoning those things which I and the whole people of the English have observed for so long. Yet since you have come here as travellers from far away and, as it seems to me that I have perceived, have wished to share with us also those things which you believed true and best, we do not wish to trouble you. Rather, we shall receive you kindly as guests and take care to provide what is necessary for your sustenance. Nor do we forbid you, by preaching your religion, to join to the fellowship of your faith all whom you can.”

Accordingly, he gave them a dwelling in the city of Dorobernia [Canterbury], which was the metropolis of all his realm; [Col. 0685C] and, as he had promised, while providing for their temporal maintenance, he did not take from them the liberty to preach whatsoever they wished.

Thus this king, and thus countless other kings of other peoples, received Christ’s messengers; and, having received them, treated them with every humanity and honour. It befits you to do likewise; or, if you do not intend to imitate them wholly, at least hear and test whether they bring you any benefit or salvation.

14. Since Mahomet took much from Jewish and Christian writings, it is wondered why he did not take everything. — Since the Jewish and evangelical law is from God, it is wholly holy and must be kept. — Let the discourse now hasten to the propositions, and let it first, aided by God’s Spirit, gird itself for battle against the most wicked enemy of God. But before the customary method of fighting advises that we join battle at close quarters, I shall preface what must be prefaced and ask what must be asked.

Ever since, some years ago, I translated by my own labour the Mahometan law from the Arabic language into my native tongue—that is, Latin—I have not ceased to wonder, nor can I wonder sufficiently, on what ground your prophet mingled into his Alchoran certain extracts from the Hebrew law and others besides from the Christian law, and, while presenting himself as a great enemy to each people to the extent of his power, nevertheless, like a Jew or Christian, confirms very many of his written statements by the authority of their law. For if he believes what is ours, then, insofar as he believes it, he agrees with us, with no reasonable objection possible. If he agrees with us in part, why does he not assent to all that is ours? [Col. 0686A] If he accepts Jewish or Christian writings in part, why does he not accept them wholly? Why does he make himself monstrous by receiving from our Scriptures what he wishes and rejecting what he does not wish?

For I read that in his book he introduces the names or deeds of those whom Hebrew writings recount; I see him naming those whom Christian Scriptures mention. From the former I see him as though excerpting Noah, Abraham, Lot, Jacob, Joseph, Moses, Pharaoh, David, and certain others; from the latter, Zacharias, Elizabeth, John the son of Zacharias, Mary, Jesus or Christ the son of Mary, Gabriel speaking to Zacharias or Mary, John’s birth, Christ’s birth from a Virgin, and certain other things. Therefore, since, as I have said, he has excerpted certain things from the Scriptures just mentioned, why did he not become either a Jew, by receiving all Jewish things, or a Christian, by approving Christian books in their entirety? [Col. 0686B] Why has he called the Jewish law good, though he does not follow it? Why does he proclaim the Christian Gospel which he criticizes?

For either these Scriptures are corrupt and ought to be rejected, or they are true and ought to be proclaimed. Divine words are governed by a law altogether different from that governing human words; the principle of divine law is altogether different from that of human tradition. In the laws of any peoples, even if certain things have been justly decreed, it nevertheless often happens that some things, perhaps even many things, are enacted contrary to the rule of equity. But this is absolutely not so in the heavenly law, nor in the heavenly oracles, at any time or under any circumstances whatsoever. Even if human intellects, reasonably using reason, utter certain truths, because they are human they may sometimes err, seldom or often. Hence, in the Psalms which your aforementioned prophet David declares to have been delivered to him, it is read: “Every human being is a liar” (Ps. CXV [116]). But that eternal Majesty which is God, from whom comes every truth—indeed, who is truth essentially—cannot be changed into falsehood, just as light cannot be changed into darkness; and when speaking to rational creatures, whether by audible sound or intelligible inspiration, He does not know how to lie. [Col. 0686C]

It therefore follows that all things delivered by Him to mortals and committed by them to writing are true, certain, and beyond doubt. From this it follows that if Hebrew or Christian writings—or rather, more truly, their meaning—proceeded from God to human beings and was delivered by Him to them, they must, as true and as a stream derived from the fountain of truth, be received and honoured not in part, as your prophet does, but wholly. [Col. 0686D] Why, then, does your lawgiver partly approve these Scriptures and partly disapprove them, partly receive them and partly reject them? For, as has been said, if they are divine, they must be received not in part but wholly; if they are not divine, they must be rejected not in part but wholly. Let him therefore either receive these Scriptures as divine, or keep his Alchoran; or, if he denies that they are divine, let him remove from his Alchoran the things which he drew from them. Indeed, having adopted a more just course, by removing the false things which he had taken from false Scriptures, let him at the same time render his whole Alchoran false and remove it on their account.

[Col. 0687A] 15. Mahomet’s followers maintain that the Old and New Scriptures were corrupted. — In reply, one of you says: “I do not deny that Jewish or Christian books were divine, but only as they were written by their first authors. But I maintain that, in the course of time, through various events, those original volumes perished; and that later certain Jews restored Jewish books and certain Christians Christian books. Ignorant of the original truth, as it were, of the first books, they composed the books now possessed by Jews and Christians as they pleased, partly from various reports of predecessors and partly from conjecture of their own hearts. By mingling true things with false and false with true, they deprived them of all constancy of truth. For this reason I give no credence to books of this kind, which both peoples now use; for this reason I call them falsified or corrupted. Yet those things which were known to be true were selected by God and delivered to our prophet, and were mingled by him into the writing of our law. Through our lawgiver God distinguished truth from falsehood, sending to him in sections those things from the Scriptures which He knew to be true, and not sending those which He knew to be false.” [Col. 0687B]

16. They are refuted. — O men prudent according to the flesh, from where is this proved? By what, I ask, do you prove your assertion? How do you show that books formerly true were corrupted by later Jews or Christians? And indeed I thank God that you assert that they were once true, for in this respect you agree with us and in this respect you agree with the Jews. But, to prove, as stated, that they were falsified, what authority or what reasoning do you bring which compels us to yield?

Certainly, under divine law and under that Roman law, I mean, which surpasses the written laws or legal systems of all peoples, the burden of proof always rests upon the party acting. You believe and assert that, in the course of time and through various accidents, divine Jewish books were corrupted by Jews and Christian books by Christians. But since you cannot answer an absent writer, I shall put the matter to myself and, no less diligently than you, investigate the volumes upon which you rely. With none of you opposing, I suppose, your aforementioned Alchoran is proclaimed by you to stand above all your writings, as the summit, as it were, of them all. [Col. 0687C–D] For you assert that it was sent from heaven by God and delivered—not all at once but gradually and in parts, in the month called Ramazan among you—to your prophet by Gabriel.

Therefore, from the very beginning of that book—“In the name of the merciful and compassionate Lord”—sanctifying You, the Lord of all nations, King of all, and God of all, I continually and humbly entreat You: turn over in its entirety that book of your supreme law; and, if you can extract from it anything said either by God or by your prophet about Jewish or Christian books being falsified, bring it forward publicly. Search also the other books, though of far inferior authority, which are read or possessed among you, and present to us some brief word—or at least one iota—indicating that the Scriptures just mentioned were corrupted by anyone at any time. [Col. 0688A]

But we are not so ignorant or unacquainted with your literature, nor has the Arabic language been so inaccessible to Latin learning, that anything relevant to the issue undertaken could have remained unknown to us, or that we could have been unaware whether your writings contain anywhere the claim that ours were falsified. Our people have many persons skilled in both languages who have carefully extracted from your writings not only those things relevant to your religion or observance, but have also penetrated the innermost recesses of your libraries in matters concerning liberal or natural studies. Therefore, both from writings translated and now Latin, and from the Arabic texts themselves, we know that neither your Alchoran, nor the book of the Jew Abdias, nor Mahomet’s genealogy, nor any other volumes treating of your law or lawgiver, makes even the slightest mention of Hebrew or Christian Scriptures having been falsified by any event at any time. [Col. 0688B]

Since this is so, since your books nowhere state that our writings or those of the Jews were ever falsified, as has often been said, whence comes this opinion among you? Whence this report? On what authority did so false—or rather, so utterly nonexistent—a tradition arise? It is marvellous, and more marvellous than I can say, that men, as I have already written above, prudent in temporal and human matters, should be so dull in eternal and divine matters that they cannot see that no tradition should be believed without examination and that common report should not be accepted without a certain and trustworthy authority. It is plainly foolish to yield to an uncertain authority; but above all it is brutish to maintain a report spread merely by the empty gossip of foolish common people, without even the name of an authority. [Col. 0688C] For this now appears to be the only basis remaining upon which you quite foolishly—indeed imprudently—suppose that divine books first perished by accident and afterwards were restored, truth having been mingled with falsehood, according as new writers pleased.

17. But now let this famed tradition come forward and demonstrate by undoubted truth the events through which the books so often named perished. And first, preserving proper order, let it explain how the Jews lost the law given them by God, along with the prophetic and other connected books. For it is known to the world that Jewish volumes long preceded Christian ones, while evangelical and apostolic writings were written much later by evangelists and apostles. It is therefore right that their alleged loss be proved in the order in which they allegedly perished, and their alleged falsification in the order in which they are said to have been falsified. [Col. 0688D]

18. By what absurdities the Mahometans seek to prove that the Jewish law was corrupted. — They say: the Jews, released from Babylonian captivity by the favour of the Persian king and permitted to return to their Palestine, loaded the divine books which they had possessed while held captive onto an ass, and thus set out with the mixed multitude. Since, as happens with a travelling multitude, some advanced more quickly and others more slowly, and since they were distracted by many different necessities of the journey, occupied now with one thing, now with another, they watched the ass carrying the divine law too carelessly. As those in front proceeded negligently, separated from those behind by a long stretch of road, the brute animal, now without a guide and frolicking as animals of that kind do, left the road and followed byways. Wandering gradually onward, now running over level ground and now climbing mountains, separated from its own people and pursued by no one, it disappeared; and by such an accident it perished with the law of God which it bore. [Col. 0689A]

19. They are refuted. — Is this, O men, the report? Is this the tradition by which it is established among you that the Jewish law was lost and the prophetic books misplaced? How, how, I ask, could prudent people be persuaded that Jews returning from the captivity just mentioned could have been so careless, so slothful, so undevoted toward their sacred things, which alone remained to them after they had lost all else? For seventy years earlier, when they were taken captive, their city had been destroyed, their temple burned, the ark of God lost, and the gold, silver, and heavy bronze vessels consecrated to God carried with the captive people to Babylon. When they returned, nothing of their sacred possessions remained to them except the law and the vessels restored to them by royal gift. [Col. 0689B]

How, then, can it appear either true or probable that persons hurrying home with the most ardent hearts, burning with all their strength for the religion delivered to them, should so neglect the law of God, on which all their hope depended and in which alone they gloried among all peoples of the world, near and distant alike; should load it upon a most worthless animal in such a manner; and should leave it unguarded, with not even one follower from among so many thousands? Where were the ministers? Where the Levites? Where were the priests who had returned from captivity? And if the crowd of nobles and commoners, travelling together or scattered about, to whom no duty of preserving the law had been entrusted, either followed or went ahead of the law-bearing ass without noticing where it turned, is it not consequent that all those selected for this task should likewise have turned elsewhere together, and that they should not have left even one person from the great number of guardians to preserve the law—indeed, as I may say, their whole hope? For who readily neglects his own horse or any beast of burden in this way, without all concern for its safekeeping? [Col. 0689C–D]

20. There were many copies of the law among the Jews. — But grant it—though it was not so—that the ass wandered off and, travelling along the road, disappeared; that a stupid and inert people lost the law through an ass’s wandering and lost by such an accident—indeed, such a disaster—the sacred volumes which the animal mentioned had then carried. Did no other copy of the same law remain anywhere in the entire world, whether among Jews or among any others? Among so many thousands of Jews—whether those returning from Chaldaea to Syria or those who had been carried captive or driven into flight through many different parts of the world—was there no one who possessed the same law transcribed in another volume?

And indeed, if you do not refuse to believe either divine or other truthful histories, before that captivity of the Jews carried out by the Chaldaean king called Nebuchadnezzar, the kings of the Assyrians had transferred ten tribes of the Jewish stock into Media, Persia, and other eastern peoples. Did so great a nation—indeed, so many peoples, to whom that law of God was common—take with them no books of their celebrated law when they were deported? [Col. 0690A] And what people living under any written law is content with one and only one volume? How could one single copy of their law suffice for innumerable peoples dwelling throughout many cities, villages, camps, and country estates, spread across and occupying a large part of the earth?

Do not all peoples everywhere retain, not merely in each city but almost in every small village, one or perhaps several copies of the law to which they have devoted themselves? Do not the Jews themselves, whose law is in question, living under Christians throughout Europe and other regions of the world, show, lend, and offer to us and ours in their synagogues the entire law, all the prophets, and other books in the Hebrew language—not merely where a thousand or a hundred, but even where sixty or fifty live together in one place? Among us, Jews living together in a group of twenty are scarcely ever found without books of this kind. Is it not likewise among you? Search in those regions where you have subjected them to your dominion, and, I think, you will recognize that I do not speak falsely. [Col. 0690B]

21. Sacred volumes were preserved in all cities. — This too was their custom while, before they were taken captive by kings of different peoples, they still inhabited certain parts of Syria granted them by God, along with their metropolis Jerusalem: they preserved copies not only of the law but also of other books, not only in that city, in which alone they were permitted to sacrifice to God, but in all their other cities and almost throughout all the fortresses and towns of their dominion. For otherwise, as prudent reason declares, they could not learn or commit to memory the teaching of so extensive a law, especially among a people so numerous, unless there were both a multitude of books in many diverse places where they lived and the skill of many teachers.

For it was not possible that the whole people, assembling only three times a year by God’s command in the principal city to pray and sacrifice, could be instructed in God’s law during the very few days of their stay there, or, despite whatever effort the teachers might make, could be fully taught when the narrowness of time prevented it. [Col. 0690C–D] Thus they possessed many places, and many people living in diverse places possessed the complete body of the divine law and other volumes; accordingly, the law of God, preserved by innumerable persons both in those regions of Syria and in other lands scattered through the world, could not perish.

22. The Saracens themselves also possess many copies of their Alchoran. The law-book is proved not to have been lost from Ezra. — But why do I speak of Hebrews? Why do I speak of other peoples, who do not keep the laws by which they live—whether delivered by God or devised by themselves—in one place only, but distribute them throughout the places they rule or inhabit? I address you—yes, you. Is your Alchoran, which you say was delivered by God to your Mahomet, kept only in Mecca, where he lies? Does no other city of Arabia, Egypt, Africa, or the eastern cities subject to you, no fortress or village among them apart from Mecca, possess that Alchoran?

Unless you wish to be monstrously obstinate and oppose a truth known to all, you will, I believe, concede, from the example both of yourselves and of all peoples, that the Jews at no time were content with a single copy of their Scriptures, and that the law of God could not have perished on that return of the Jews from Babylon because of the fabulous, lying—or rather nonexistent—wandering of a brute animal. [Col. 0691A] For copies flowed in abundance from different regions of the world: there was no lack of means by which it could be recovered or copied again from innumerable exemplars.

Since this cannot reasonably be denied, let the discussion proceed to what follows and demonstrate that after their return from Babylon the Jews lacked the books of divine law. For the following is read in the book of Ezra, which belongs to the number of Jewish volumes:

“The entire people assembled as one man in the square before the Water Gate, and they told Ezra the scribe to bring the book of the law of Moses, which the Lord had commanded Israel. Therefore Ezra the priest brought the law before the entire assembly of men and women and all who could understand, on the first day of the seventh month. And he read from it in the square before the Water Gate, from morning until midday, in the presence of men, women, and those able to understand; and the ears of all the people were attentive to the book” (2 Ezra 8).

And after an intervening verse: “Ezra opened the book before all the people, and Ezra blessed the Lord God with a loud voice. And all the people answered: Amen” (ibid.). [Col. 0691B–C]

Did Ezra, one of the number of those captives through whose negligence, according to your opinion, the law of God had perished, so quickly compose a false law? Since he himself is proclaimed in the same volume to have been a righteous and wise man, and since neither he nor the people then had any hope except in the Lord, who of sound mind would dare even suspect that he had corrupted God’s law and brought it forth to be read before the eyes of the entire people? But because one ought not linger long over what is so manifestly false, let definite evidence be produced in act, by which the book of divine law may be proved to have been falsified either by Ezra or by anyone else; otherwise let this ridiculous and senseless opinion, proceeding from the father of lies, be rejected. [Col. 0691D]

23. If the law had been falsified, it would have been impossible for all people always to receive it without anyone noticing. — Again and again I am moved to wonder, and I cannot wonder sufficiently at such prodigies: by what cunning of Satan could rational human beings have been persuaded either to believe or to suppose that books, true by the testimony of so many and such great ages, and everywhere distributed through the world for more than two thousand years, could have been corrupted by the skill of any falsifier? What then? Even if, according to your suspicion, it were established that they had been falsified by certain falsifiers, would it be established that the world received them without examination of their truth? Was human understanding ever so overwhelmed, was reason so buried, that it could not discern what it received? Or rather—what is far more astonishing—would every language and people, except yourselves, assent to so great a falsehood?

How, for nearly a thousand years while that law of God, as you believe, still remained uncorrupted, was it received and falsified by no one except Jews, then disseminated among every people to the furthest ends of the world? [Col. 0692A] But what falsehood could be identified in those volumes? In what parts of them? In what verses does the first book of that law, called Genesis, appear corrupted, truth changed and falsehood mingled in? In what verses of Exodus? Leviticus? Numbers? Deuteronomy? For in these five books the chief substance of the Jewish law consists. In what passages do the books of Joshua, Judges, and Ruth—which are joined to the preceding five and called the Heptateuch in Greek—appear falsified? Is it perhaps in historical narrative? Or in legislation?

If the question concerns history—that is, deeds done from the creation of heaven and earth to the end of those books—does not Mahomet, pretending in his Alchoran that God speaks to him, acknowledge nearly all of them as you read them there? This applies to the creation of heaven and earth; to Adam and Eve; to paradise; to the grove of paradise; to the forbidden tree and the serpent; to Adam and Eve’s expulsion from paradise; to Cain and Abel; to Noah and the ark; to the Flood; to Abraham and Jacob; to Joseph; to Moses and Aaron; to Pharaoh and the Egyptians; to Israel and the crossing of the Red Sea; to that people’s long wandering through deserts; to the land of Canaan promised and given to Israel; and, as stated, to nearly everything those books recount. [Col. 0692B–C]

Although he omits much, changes much, and adds besides a great accumulation of lies, in his barbarous and prodigious manner of speaking he recounts very many such matters. If the question concerns legislation through Moses, he likewise mentions certain things from it while omitting much. Since he bears witness to the truth of the greater part of the Hebrew volumes and, as I have said above, does not call them falsified even in the slightest respect, from where could you have derived this opinion, which you did not receive from your master? You could have thought, and ought to have said, something much more correct and much more reasonable:

“Although Hebrew and Christian Scriptures are known to us, we infer from this that they are true: our prophet approves in the law delivered to us very many things precisely as they are written there, while he condemns none, whether in those Scriptures or elsewhere, of all the things I have written above. Nor do I conclude, by either necessary or probable argument, that Hebrew books have been lost or falsified. If Mahomet inserts into his law and yours certain matters written among the Jews, as though in response to a divine answer made to him, yet does not assert that the rest were either lost or falsified; and if none of you can prove what you suspect or assert concerning the loss or falsification of those same Scriptures, it follows that, without any stain even of the least falsehood, they retain, as divine truths, the most firm and supreme authority which they had when first issued by their authors.” [Col. 0692D–0693A]

But neither in your Alchoran nor in any other writings of your sect is anything read about these matters; nor do you bring forward anything from elsewhere by which Jewish books could be proved either lost or falsified.

24. If the law is false, the Alchoran, containing much drawn from it, must be rejected. — It is therefore clear, once false objections and suspicions have been put far aside, that the Scriptures so often mentioned are true not partly but wholly. It is certain, now that none can successfully resist, that they are divine. This being so, I add what I touched upon above: you must necessarily either receive the Hebrew Scriptures entire or reject the Alchoran. For since, as I have already said, many things in that volume occur just as they do in the Jewish books, if those books are said to be falsified, then the things either taken from them or set down as they stand there are shown to be wholly false or doubtful. [Col. 0693B]

But if false or doubtful things are written in your law, then absolutely everything contained in that book is false or doubtful; for nothing except what is false and doubtful could have been taken from falsified books, nor could anything have been placed there as in those books except what is false or doubtful. Yet it is established, as has often been said, that many things either taken from there or corresponding to what is read there in meaning have been placed in the Alchoran. By this reasoning, therefore, it is established that that law—yes, that law of yours, which you boast was sent from heaven—is not merely partly but wholly, in its entirety, false or doubtful.

But if you refuse either to say or believe that your Alchoran is false or doubtful, then truth, certain and incapable either of deceiving or being deceived, pressing you on every side, will compel you to acknowledge that the books from which your Mahomet either took many things or inserted many things into your law in accordance with their meaning are true not partly but wholly, divine not partly but wholly. [Col. 0693C]

25. Christian books must also be admitted. — Having conceded this, you will receive not only Jewish volumes, without any mark of falsehood, as divine; by precisely the same reasoning in every respect you will also admit Christian books. For, as I have mentioned above, many things from them were likewise mingled into your law by your aforementioned lawgiver and inserted into almost the whole body of that volume.
