If they must be rejected as drawn from falsified books, then, in the manner described above, all the things to which they were joined must also be condemned. If you avoid this conclusion, then by the same—indeed identical—connection of reasoning as before, you grant Christian books the same authority as Jewish ones.

And although this cannot be denied, although it has become clear by a brief argument that Christian books are true and divine, let the opinion now come forward and be set forth by which your people, whether all or some of them, maintain that these books too were lost or falsified. [Col. 0693D]

26. Mahometans’ absurdities concerning Christian books alleged to have been lost and falsified. — They say: “During the time of Roman emperors, who fiercely persecuted Christians for a very long time by exile, confiscation, and diverse kinds of death, and who also ordered their books themselves to be burned everywhere by public edicts, the Gospels and the Acts or Epistles of the Apostles perished. Afterwards they were copied again and restored as Christians pleased—Christians succeeding them after a long succession of years, who had certainly received nothing from the first authors of the books and had not seen the books composed by them, since those books had previously, as stated, been burned.” [Col. 0694A]

27. They are refuted; and first it is shown that the books were not lost. — Is this all? Is this, I ask, all that you allege? Is this all and the only ground on which you assert that the Gospel writings or apostolic writings have perished, or have been falsified? If this is all, I proceed against you by the same course as above, and by the same manner of reply show that the arguments you advance have no force—indeed, that they are altogether [Col. 0694B] powerless.

I admit, certainly, that the Roman emperors, who ruled all Europe, all Africa, and the greater part of Asia together with the islands adjoining it, whether in the Ocean or in the Tyrrhenian Sea, persecuted Christians, already spread everywhere, for nearly three hundred years almost continuously—now more harshly, now more mildly. I admit that one of the last persecutors, named Diocletian, who attacked them more fiercely and for longer than the others, decreed by public edict that, on the most sacred day of the Christian Pascha itself, Christian churches should throughout all regions subject to him be destroyed and their books burned. This, certainly, as I have said, I admit as though it were a point favouring your side.

But how does this serve you? Even if this edict was promulgated by that emperor throughout the extent of the Roman Empire; even if, in part or perhaps wholly, so far as the destruction of churches was concerned, it was carried out; even if the books that were found were burned—did all the writings of Christians perish through that single occurrence? Was there no one among so many and such great peoples scattered throughout that vast empire who, upon hearing the imperial edict, hid some of the innumerable books? No one who rescued them from the fire? No one who preserved them?

Indeed, as can be proved from truthful histories, scarcely in that famous and widespread empire was there a city, scarcely a town, scarcely any village, that did not contain a multitude of Christians mixed among the pagans. In every city bishops, presbyters, deacons, and no small number of clergy presided over Christian communities, and with the utmost and exceptional care preserved the sacred books of the Christian law together with the other heavenly holy things and sacraments entrusted to them. Did, then, the whole purpose of the Christian religion perish in them? Did their love for divine holy things fail so entirely that, while they exposed their own bodies to fires, swords, and deaths of every kind in order to preserve God’s law, they should thus universally neglect the very law of God for which they did not hesitate to die?

And what of the Persians and Medes? What of the Ethiopians and Indians? What of your own Arabia? What of the other kingdoms which, you say, the Roman [commonwealth] could not subdue? For when, as Christ’s disciples proclaimed everywhere, the sound of Gospel preaching had gone out into the whole earth, and scarcely any corner of the world lay hidden from Christians spread through every language of the nations—did the Christian books perish, or were they lost, among these peoples also? Did the Gospel perish? Did the apostolic writings perish? Did no people, no language, no Christian region preserve the Christian books, as it had received them from its first preachers, so that they could not perish?

But they were preserved—plainly preserved by innumerable Christian nations: the Gospel as it had been handed down by the Evangelists, and the apostolic writings through most certain successions, transmitted down to our own times. And, not to speak of the more remote parts of the world less known to us, the Latin Church possesses the Gospels handed down from Peter; the Greek Church possesses those handed down from Paul; all Europe possesses the Gospels committed to it by both, and the apostolic writings entrusted to it.

[Col. 0695B] Since these were the chief and foremost among Christ’s disciples—the one taught bodily by Him, the other invisibly—they began from Jerusalem and went as far as the furthest boundaries of the West. Sometimes together, sometimes separately; now in person, now through their followers, they preached Christ’s Gospel by word and handed it down in writing to posterity. Peter handed down Mark’s Gospel, which he himself had approved; Paul, Luke’s Gospel, which Luke had written in the regions of Greece. Nor was John absent, another of Christ’s disciples, chosen and taught by Him while He still dwelt among human beings, who gave the Christian peoples of Asia Minor the Gospel which he had written.

Nor could Matthew’s Gospel, which he had written first, perish after it had been handed down to the peoples and regions on this side of the sea by the apostles already mentioned; for, having been speedily copied and circulated everywhere, it was preserved by the diligence of many peoples. The Roman Church, head of all the Churches of the world, besides innumerable others, preserved these writings, handed down to it by the apostles just named immediately and as they had been written, through successive apostolic pontiffs known to us from writings, beginning with Peter and continuing to our own times. It thus shows to be wholly false and empty what your people either believe or say—that these books have perished.

The same is true of the apostolic writings: Acts of the Apostles from the already mentioned Luke; two Epistles from Peter; three from John together with his Apocalypse; and fourteen Epistles from Paul, writing partly from Italy and partly from Greece and sending them to Churches in various cities. These were handed down to the first believers in Christ and, both in Rome and in the other cities, preserved with the utmost diligence, as stated, through succeeding generations of the faithful down to us.

There remain in the new Christian canon the two Epistles of the apostles James and Jude—that is, one of James and another of Jude. Although written in Greater Asia, they reached both your East and our West at nearly the same time, and, immediately joined to the others, were preserved with the same care by those whom I have named. From there they have come into the hands of us and of all faithful persons now living, to be preserved by us and our descendants as long as heaven hangs over the earth.

28. But neither were they corrupted. — These points having been established, [Col. 0696A] what remains? What remains, plainly, except this? Those among you who believe or suppose that Christian books have perished must either demonstrate by certain reasoning that they were lost, or yield to the preceding, so probable arguments and confess that they were preserved by Christians.

Now, if it is established that they did not perish, it is established that neither were they falsified. For, as we experience in frequent daily use, even the secret of any mystery agreed upon by a few cannot long remain hidden when human inconstancy presses upon it; and the proverb of our Gauls is true: “What two know, all know.” By what art, in what manner, could books scattered throughout the world and preserved by the diligence of so many and such great numbers, as has been said, have been falsified? Did the whole Christian world simultaneously consent to so profane a falsification? Did Christian learning everywhere permit its books to be corrupted so universally? Did no one among so many peoples devoted to Christ resist the first corrupters of their books?

For if they were corrupted, they were first corrupted by one person, or by a few, or perhaps by many agreeing with one another. How else could this happen, unless the corruption had begun from a few? Therefore this corruption began from a few, because, as I said, it could not otherwise have crept in; or perhaps from more persons—but from the peoples of the entire world? Did all everywhere at once either corrupt the books they had received or yield to the first corrupters? Did they all, either falsifying them themselves or suddenly or gradually submitting to falsifiers, betray their eternal salvation, which those books alone proclaim?

Could a report of so general [Col. 0696C] a falsification be concealed, when, as was stated above, scarcely any secrets even among a few people can be hidden, though the very sacraments of fidelity be interposed? Or perhaps did the whole world then consent to the falsification, and does the whole world now possess not even the faintest report of so universal a falsification? That the world should have corrupted its books and not known that they were corrupted surpasses every monster and every portent.

But perhaps this came to the Saracens alone and could not come to Christians alone. Perhaps the loss or corruption of other people’s books became known to them, though it lay hidden from Christians for so long a time. Things belonging to others are known to Saracens; things belonging to Christians themselves are unknown to Christians. But what further? What further answer ought one make to utterly empty trifles or frivolous persons? Why should the pen pursue at such length what is plainly seen, without any covering, to be frivolous and false? Let the reasoning already set forth now close the matter, and let it not longer attack as if strong what is powerless.

Whoever you are that maintains or supposes this, prove by certain arguments that Christian books have been falsified; or, if you have nothing to offer in reply, believe them true, believe them divine. For they could not have been universally falsified without any Christian protesting; nor, if they had been falsified, could what had been done by the world, so far as the countless peoples bearing the Christian name were concerned, have remained hidden from all Christians throughout the world.

29. Saracens cannot falsify the Gospel without falsifying the Qur’an also. — To what I have already said concerning the Hebrew books I add this: you cannot falsify [Col. 0697A] our Gospel unless you also falsify your Qur’an. For if the Gospel is false, then those things which are read as being in the Gospel, if they occur in the Qur’an, are false or doubtful. But if those things are false or doubtful, the entire book in which they are mingled is false or doubtful. For it is clear that nothing can be drawn from a falsified book except what is false or doubtful.

But if you consider it impious to believe or say that your law is false or doubtful, then, compelled by reason, willingly or unwillingly, you affirm that the Gospel or evangelical Scriptures are true and divine. You do affirm this if you say that the Gospel statements intermingled with your Qur’an are true. For, as has often already been said, either you reject those statements, and the book in which they are inserted is rejected; or you approve them, and the book is approved with them.

By this reasoning we are compelled to believe and confess that the Hebrew books, as has been stated, together with ours—that is, the Christian books—are alike true and divine: true, because it is now evident that they have been purged of the blemish of falsehood; divine, because, according to the testimony of your lawgiver, both the Hebrew law was given to Moses and the Gospel was delivered to Christ by God. By this consequence, so far as the divine canon is concerned, you must altogether receive the Hebrew books as Hebrews do and approve the Gospel and apostolic volumes as Christians do.

For this reason I declare that you have been forewarned and fortified: when, in the course of the proposed work and discourse, the occasion is suitable, I shall attack you from those writings which you now necessarily hold to be divine; and, as the method of disputation from conceded premises directs, I shall, as far as I can, attack the falsehood in which, except for the Jews, you are ensnared and overwhelmed beyond all other mortals, and, protected by the shield of truth, with God’s help I shall overthrow it to the extent of my strength.

But because I called the evangelical and apostolic writings ours, whereas I did not write that the Jewish volumes are ours, let none of you suppose that the Hebrew books are not Christian books. For a Christian receives the law of Moses and the prophets no less than the Gospel or the Acts and Epistles of the Apostles. From the same God, the Creator of all visible and invisible things, the Christian both believes in the heart unto righteousness and confesses with the mouth unto salvation the canonical Scriptures of both peoples, delivered at different times to the two peoples. And although these peoples differ greatly from one another, Christian universality nevertheless receives the Jewish writings with the understanding proper to them, and honours them as the chief support and foundation of our faith.

Let these remarks suffice for the present to prove, O Saracens, from your own law in which you believe, that the Hebrew or Christian Scriptures are true and divine, and that human inventions cannot stand against their truth—Scriptures which not only invincible truth commends, but which even your own lawgiver, whatever kind of man he was, confirms to be sacred in the manner I have stated. The following matters will show that your oft-mentioned law is wholly devoid of all truth, and that he himself—yes, precisely he—was neither prophet nor messenger of God, but a deceiver and a profane man.

## THE SECOND BOOK BEGINS

[Col. 0697]

1. He urges the Ishmaelites to hear what he is about to say. — Now because, O Ishmaelites, after setting forth what had to be set forth, I must proceed against the chief strength of your religion, restrain, as I warned you, your swords; put aside your stones; open your ears; and, if there is in you even a little merely human prudence, lay aside the stubborn and childish eagerness to prevail, and listen with attentive minds to what follows.

This may be useful to you and, if the grace of God wills to have mercy on you, supremely necessary: that you should examine earnestly, investigate carefully, and through investigating recognize to whom you have entrusted yourselves, to whom you have entrusted your salvation—not merely this fleeting and transitory salvation, but that eternal salvation which succeeds it; to whom, I say, you have committed your bodies and souls. Unless perhaps, according to the famous prophet [Col. 0697D] Isaiah, there is a lie in your hand; unless perhaps you hold falsehood in place of truth, iniquity in place of righteousness, and diabolical sacrilege in place of divine worship.

Speaking of idolaters, he says:

> “They have not known, neither have they understood; for their eyes are shut, lest they see, and their hearts, lest they understand. They do not reflect in their mind; neither do they know nor perceive, so as to say: ‘Half of it—that is, of the tree—I burned in the fire; upon its coals I baked [Col. 0698C] bread; I cooked meat and ate it; and shall I make an idol from the rest of it? Shall I fall down before a block of wood?’ Part of it is ashes. A deceived heart has worshipped it, and it has not delivered its soul, nor said: ‘Perhaps there is a lie in my right hand.’ Remember these things, Jacob and Israel, for you are my servant” (Isa. 44).

The same thing may have happened to you. You are not, indeed, as I have heard, idolaters, nor do you worship wood, stones, or things of that sort. But what then? What, I ask, what? What benefit is it to you not to receive the creature in place of the Creator, if you are not granted to worship God as He wishes and commands Himself to be worshipped?

Therefore examine; and, though you have now been imbued with error for a long time, do not disdain to examine whether what you have hitherto believed is false and what you have hitherto considered false is true. It is the part of wise people, even if they are ashamed, to correct their errors. It is the part of fools, through foolish shame, not to correct even what the world condemns. And, if it is granted, drive from your hearts that shame, stubborn and destructive to you, at least by considering the erring multitude, lest you suppose that you alone have erred. I shall offer examples both foreign and our own: people who, though driven by the enemy through many monstrous errors so as to depart from the way of truth, did not yield; rather, while countless persons wandered and perished by devious paths, they alone did not depart from the path of right faith previously shown to them.

2. By many examples he shows that they could have been deceived. — Look and carefully investigate the past ages; and, if you are wise, consider how many, how great, and how manifold snares of error have entangled the human race from the apostate angel, called Satan, who instigated the very first parent of mortals, down to your own times.

God took vengeance upon the wicked who lived in the time of the patriarch Noah, as even your Qur’an admits, and destroyed by avenging waters that entire generation which had departed from divine worship and filled the whole earth with intolerable wickedness. Afterwards, when the lands had dried and security had been restored by God’s gift, there succeeded offspring no less wicked than their predecessors. Having cast off divine worship—or rather, to speak more truly, having not even known it—they bestowed the Creator’s honour on the creature. Then, advancing to idolatry, they covered the whole surface of the earth with heaps of iniquity, both by profane religion and by wicked life.

Only a very few righteous persons were excepted, distinguished from the universal mass of the lost solely by God’s grace. Thus, while a rare light shone amid the dense and everywhere-spread darkness of the impious, the prince of darkness possessed the whole world, according to the Gospel which your Mahomet wrote as given to our Christ—alas!—as his courtyard in long-lasting and deadly peace, down to the time of Moses.

Thereafter one nation alone, chosen by God out of all nations, was illuminated by the divine law through the prophet Moses already mentioned. All the others were left in the darkness of their now ancient error; but this one nation, subjected to commands given and proclaimed by God through Moses, was separated from the common destruction of the impious.

Yet the profane and stubborn enemy did not cease, even after the law was given, to turn that nation away from divine worship and, by deceitful arts—tempting, alluring, and seducing—to join it again to the condemned and abandoned idolatry, its wickednesses, and the abominable practices of the Gentiles. At length the gracious Deity had mercy on perishing humanity, and Truth arose from the earth to aid the wretched—that is, Christ, born of a Virgin. Gradually dispersing the darkness with His heavenly light, He filled the world and everywhere spread the Gospel [Col. 0699D] of the eternal kingdom, of which He Himself, as will be proved in its place, was king.

You see His Gospel spread among all nations, and the faith of Christ flourishing in the hearts of all, excepting the Jews wholly and you in part. Yet multiple errors also arose under the Christian name in the hearts of Christians; these the truthful Church of God, a follower of truth, rejected as soon as it detected them and condemned as soon as it recognized them.

Why say this at the beginning of this book? So that, as I began to say, you may consider and reconsider that not only the pagans whom I mentioned, not only the Jews, not only Christian heretics, but you also could have erred, could have been deceived, could have received darkness for light, falsehood for truth, a deceiver for a prophet, and—as the Jews will do near [Col. 0700A] the end of the world—the Antichrist for Christ. And lest the matter be delayed further, weapons must now be cast not from afar but hands joined in close combat—yet with peace, as I said above, not fury; with reason, not madness; with fairness, not injustice—lest we seem not to investigate what is true from love of truth, but to defend what is false from partisan zeal.

3. Their fantasies concerning the manner in which they received their law from God. — In the preceding and immediately prior book I said: “I invite you to a salvation which does not pass away but remains; which does not end with short life but endures unto eternal life.” Mortals are indeed granted to attain this salvation and to enjoy it at the time appointed by God, but only if they think of God what is true, not what is false; if they worship Him not according to the fantasies of their own hearts, but as He Himself wishes and commands to be worshipped.

To this you replied: “Far be it that our understanding should think otherwise! Far be it that our profession should be otherwise! We have imagined nothing about God; we have fabricated absolutely nothing. What we think and confess concerning Him is not according to inventions of our own heart, but according to what our prophet, sent by God Himself, handed down to us. Since he is last in the order of prophets and, as it were, the seal of all prophets; since he is not the author of the divine law but its bearer, not its Lord but its messenger, he received heavenly commands sent to him from God through Gabriel, containing nothing more or less. He handed down what he received to our fathers and to us for observance. These we observe, these we keep; to these we have devoted our souls, bodies, life, and death.”

4. Mahomet cannot be called a prophet. What prophecy is. Moses truly was a prophet. — Hear, then, for now it is time, to whom you have devoted your souls, bodies, and death. Consider whether you have established your hope in a safe place, whether you have believed a sound doctrine, a true prophet of God, and His messenger. You call him a prophet and describe him as God’s messenger. We grant that a true prophet of God must be believed, and that a true messenger of God must be obeyed. But, as I said, let it be considered whether he was truly God’s prophet, whether he truly is His messenger.

To understand this, consider what prophecy is and what is called prophecy. The first and chief apostle among Christ’s apostles, the apostle Peter—whose name, being known to the whole world, we do not believe that you ignore; and whose life in part, death, and tomb at the head of the world, in the city called Rome, you presumably do not ignore—says: “Prophecy was not at any time brought by human will; but holy men of God spoke, inspired by the Holy Spirit” (2 Pet. 1).

From these words of that apostle we may rightly describe or define prophecy thus: prophecy is a declaration of unknown things, whether past, present, or future, made not by human invention but by divine inspiration. The etymology of the name looks more toward future matters than past or present ones; yet because past and present things also sometimes become known by the same divine power by which future things are revealed, the revelation of these two times too is called prophecy.

From the definition of prophecy we can also define a prophet: a prophet is one who, taught not by human knowledge but inspired by the Spirit of God, makes known to mortals unknown matters of past, present, or future time.

Moses unfolded prophecy concerning past time when he said that in the beginning God created heaven and earth; created light; made heaven a firmament and placed it in the middle between the upper and lower waters; brought forth from the earth green grass bearing seed and fruit-bearing trees producing fruit; made the sun, moon, and the remaining stars; produced from the waters fish and birds, and from the earth four-footed creatures and creeping things; and finally created man in His own image and likeness and gave him a like companion.

These were prophetic words, not concerning present or future time, and they prove themselves prophetic especially because, as one of our great men said: “A man spoke of that time when man did not exist.” Moses is likewise proved a prophet by prophecy concerning present time, as is read in one of his five books, called Numbers. For when Korah, Dathan, and Abiram, rebels against Moses, were swallowed up by divine vengeance through the earth’s immense opening, with their tents and all their property, and when for that reason the Jews murmured against Moses and intended to kill him, he fled to the tabernacle of the Lord.

As he lay prostrate upon the ground before God, he said to Aaron his brother, then God’s chief priest: “Take the censer, and, having taken fire from the altar, put incense upon it; go quickly to the people and pray for them. For wrath has already gone forth from the Lord and the plague is raging” (Num. 16). Thus his spirit was enlightened by prophecy concerning present time when, lying prostrate in God’s tabernacle, he knew what was happening among the distant and widespread multitude.

The same Scripture immediately continues: “When Aaron had done this and run into the midst of the multitude, which the burning was already devastating, he offered incense; and, standing between the dead and the living, prayed for the people, [Col. 0701D] and the plague ceased. Those struck down were fourteen thousand seven hundred persons, besides those who had perished in the rebellion of Korah” (ibid.). This too, as I said, is prophecy concerning present time.

But who could readily enumerate Moses’ prophetic words concerning future time? God informing him, he foresaw and foretold that Egypt would be struck by ten famous plagues—not together but separately, not on one day but on many different days: now waters changed into blood; now frogs filling everything; now gnats; now flies of various kinds; now a most grievous pestilence among animals; now dust covering Egypt; now hail mixed with fire; now locusts covering the face of the earth; now dreadful, palpable darkness; now the deaths of the firstborn, when in the whole land of Egypt there was no house in which there was not a dead person.

There followed the greatest and last plague, bringing all the preceding plagues to an end: namely, Pharaoh’s own drowning in the sea and the destruction of his entire army, with no one escaping. Moses foresaw and foretold the terrible destruction of the rebels already mentioned. He foresaw and foretold that a prophet would be raised up by God in Israel, and that whoever did not listen to him would be cut off from his people. He foresaw and foretold very many other things, arranged in their respective places throughout his Pentateuch—that is, throughout the five books mentioned above.

The Moses already mentioned, filled with the prophetic Spirit, foretold all these things individually before they occurred, and by the very fulfilment of his words showed himself truly to be a prophet of God. The same was true before him of certain men, such as Enoch, Noah, Jacob, and Joseph; and after him of very many: Samuel, David, Isaiah, Elijah, Elisha, Jeremiah, and many others well known to the world.

5. Mahomet cannot be called a prophet. — But your Mahomet, O Hagarites, by what evidence can he be proved by you to be a prophet? Was it because he revealed unknown things of the past to mortals? Or because he disclosed present things hidden from others? Or because he foresaw and foretold future things, however slight and trivial? On what basis, I ask, is he called a prophet? Because he often calls himself a prophet in his Qur’an?

If he calls himself a prophet, let him show what prophetic thing he said, what prophetic thing he did. And you yourselves, who believe him to be a prophet and call him a prophet, show me from what it appears that he was a prophet of past things, of present things, or of future things. Turn over your oft-mentioned Qur’an; examine the whole text of that scripture which you regard as heavenly. Read again and review, beginning with the first *Azoara*—that is, “oracle”—of that book, entitled “Of the Cow,” containing eighty-five words; pass through the *Azoara* “Of the People of Joachim,” containing two hundred words; and continue your swift course through the others dispersed throughout the body of that impious work, as far as the one hundred and twenty-third *Azoara*, placed in the last book and bringing it to an end. Prove, from that exalted scripture of yours already mentioned, that he uttered even one single prophetic word.

And where, if he was a prophet, was it more fitting that he should show himself a prophet than in a book brought down from heaven in volumes, as he writes, and transmitted to him by God through Gabriel? Where ought he more to have shown himself a prophet than in the book to which you cling above all else, to which you have entrusted the entire sum of your faith, your salvation, and, as I wrote above, your bodies and souls? What reason can there be for God to call him a prophet, and for one called a prophet by God, as he says, to proclaim no prophecies? Which of the earlier prophets was ever called a prophet by God and nevertheless spoke no prophecy? Not so our Moses, as I said above; not so Isaiah, whose almost entire book resounds with nothing but prophecy, announcing nothing but things to come, whether soon or far off.

6. Isaiah was truly a prophet. — Of things near at hand, as when he said to Hezekiah, king of the Jews, who was sick and already despairing of life: “Thus says the Lord: Behold, I shall add fifteen years to your days, and I shall deliver you and this city from the hand of the king of the Assyrians, and I shall protect it” (Isa. 38).

This was fulfilled. Restored to health, he lived another fifteen years; he was delivered from the hand of the king of the Assyrians, both he and his royal city Jerusalem. In less than the span of one night God killed one hundred and eighty-five thousand men of the blaspheming king’s army; God protected him, and throughout his entire lifetime no king and no nation prevailed against him. Likewise, by certain other things foretold by him and soon fulfilled, he was proved to have been God’s prophet.

Of things far off, as the devastation of Babylon by the Persians and Medes, which was both accomplished and foretold by him; as the release by a king of the captives taken seventy years earlier by the Chaldean king. With the subtle eye of prophecy, he both foresaw and foretold Cyrus’s name nearly three hundred years beforehand. He also foretold, after much time, the complete destruction of the Babylon already mentioned, as now seen; nor did he leave unmentioned that it would be reduced to solitude and become a habitation not of human beings but of monstrous animals and venomous serpents.

Again, he foretold from afar Christ’s birth when he said: “Behold, a Virgin shall conceive [Col. 0703C] and bear a son” (Isa. 7), which you yourselves also affirm to be true; the saving baptism handed down by Christ to Jews and Gentiles, when, introducing God as speaking, he says: “I shall pour clean water upon you, and you shall be cleansed from all your defilements; and from all your idols I shall cleanse you” (Ezek. 36); Christ’s miracles, when he says: “Then the eyes of the blind shall be opened, and the ears of the deaf shall be opened; then the lame man shall leap like a servant [the printed reading is *servus*, perhaps for ‘deer’], and the tongue of the mute shall be opened” (Isa. 35); and Christ’s passion, when he says: “Like a sheep He was led to slaughter, and He gave up His soul to death; and He was reckoned with criminals” (Isa. 53).

What more should I say of so great a prophet? Whatever is seen to have come to pass concerning Christ, concerning Christian sacraments, concerning the rejection of the Jews and the calling of the Gentiles, concerning the present condition of the Church after Him and the faith of things to come—all this Isaiah, illuminated by God’s Spirit, foretold so clearly that, in the words once spoken by a certain wise man, he seems rather to recount past events than to predict future ones.

7. On Jeremiah. — Thus after Isaiah came Jeremiah. After God said to him, “I have made you a prophet among the nations” (Jer. 1), he demonstrated by many signs that he was truly God’s prophet—not only after his death, but also while still alive.

After his death, this was shown by the number of seventy years during which, as has already been said, the Jews were held in Babylonian captivity. The release from that captivity was foretold by Isaiah, as I wrote above; but Isaiah did not specify the number of years. Since this number was specified by Jeremiah alone, and was fulfilled after his death, as we both read and know, it is clear that he foretold it by the prophetic Spirit and was therefore truly God’s prophet.

So too, when he himself foretold the Babylonian desolation predicted by Isaiah; when he spoke beforehand concerning Christ and His mother: “The Lord shall make a new thing upon the earth: a woman shall encompass a man” (Jer. 31); and in many other such cases. Before his death, when he proclaimed that the king of the Chaldeans would come into Syria, besiege Jerusalem through his commanders, capture it after a very few years, and take captive the Jewish people who despised the divine law, he lived to see fulfilled what he had foretold.

Among these prophetic words was the following; for I decline to gather everything and bring it forward, lest I seem excessively prolix to those who will read this. One such utterance, I say, was what he said to King Zedekiah, when the king summoned him to a private conversation and asked him, “Is there a word from the Lord?” He answered: “There is: you shall be delivered into the hand of the king of Babylon” (Jer. 37).

When the king added, “The Jews who have defected to the Chaldeans—lest perhaps I be handed over into their hands and they mock me,” Jeremiah, summoned a second time in a similar matter, replied: “They will not hand you over. I beg you, listen to the voice of the Lord which I speak to you, and it shall go well with you, and your soul shall live. But if you refuse, this is the word which the Lord has shown me: behold, all the women remaining in the house of the king of Judah [Col. 0704C] shall be brought out to the commanders of the king of Babylon; and all your wives and your sons shall be led out to the Chaldeans. You shall not escape from their hands, but you shall be seized by the hand of the king of Babylon, and he shall burn this city with fire” (Jer. 38).

The king would not, or feared to, follow the prophet’s counsel, and he experienced everything that the prophet had foretold to him.

8. On Ezekiel. — Thus Ezekiel—to pass over many people and many events—concerning that same captivity of Zedekiah, although far away in Chaldea, foretold what would happen in Judaea and what was already almost happening: absent in body, present in spirit. He said: “Shall one who breaks the covenant escape? As I live, says the Lord God, in the place of the king who made him king, whose oath he made void and whose covenant with him he broke, he shall die in the midst of Babylon” (Ezek. 17).

And in the following course of prophecy: “And all his fugitives,” he says, “with all their army, shall fall by the sword; but those who remain shall be scattered to every wind, and you shall know that I, the Lord, have spoken” (ibid.). All these things happened exactly as that prophet foretold: King Zedekiah was seized by enemies and taken captive, then died in Babylon; all his fugitives with their entire army fell by the sword; and the survivors were scattered to every wind.

9. On Daniel.—Thus Daniel too, throughout the whole text of his book, foretelling things to come both near at hand and far off, plainly shows himself to be a prophet of God. From his lengthy volume I have selected these few passages. He said [Col. 0705A] to a certain Chaldean king called Nebuchadnezzar, under whose rule he himself lived, when the king presented his dream and requested its interpretation:

“My lord, may the dream be for those who hate you, and its interpretation for your enemies. The tree which you saw, lofty and strong, whose height reached to heaven and whose appearance extended over the whole earth, whose branches were most beautiful, whose fruit was abundant, and in which was food for all—beneath it the beasts of the field dwelt, and in its branches the birds of heaven made their home—you are that king, who have been magnified and grown strong; your greatness has increased and reached even to heaven, and your power to the bounds of the whole earth. But whereas the king saw a watcher and a holy one descending from heaven and saying, ‘Cut down the tree and scatter it abroad; nevertheless leave the stump of its roots [Col. 0705B] in the earth, and let it be bound with iron and bronze among the grass outside; let it be drenched with the dew of heaven, and let its pasture be with the wild beasts, until seven times pass over him’: this is the interpretation of the decree of the Most High which has come upon my lord the king. They shall drive you from among men, and your dwelling shall be with beasts and wild animals; you shall eat grass like an ox and be drenched with the dew of heaven. Seven times also shall pass over you, until you know that the Most High rules over the kingdom of men and gives it to whomever he wills. But whereas he commanded that the stump of its roots—that is, of the tree—be left, your kingdom shall remain yours after you have recognized that power belongs to heaven. Therefore, O king, let my counsel please you: redeem your sins by alms [Col. 0705C] and your iniquities by acts of mercy toward the poor; perhaps he will pardon your offenses” (Dan. IV).

After he had foretold all these things, enlightened by the prophetic Spirit, he does not fail to say that they were fulfilled after the interval of only one year:

“All these things,” he says, “came upon King Nebuchadnezzar. At the end of twelve months the king was walking in the palace of the king of Babylon, and he said: ‘Is not this great Babylon which I have built as the house of my kingdom, by the strength of my power and for the glory of my majesty?’ While the word was still in the king’s mouth, a voice fell from heaven: ‘To you it is spoken, King Nebuchadnezzar: the kingdom has passed from you, and they shall drive you from among men, and your dwelling shall be with beasts and wild animals. You shall eat grass like an ox, and seven times shall pass over you, until you know that the Most High rules in the kingdom of men [Col. 0705D] and gives it to whomever he wills.’ In that same hour the word was fulfilled upon Nebuchadnezzar. He was cast out from among men; he ate grass like an ox; his body was drenched with the dew of heaven, until his hair grew like eagles’ feathers and his nails like birds’ claws. Therefore, after the end of the days, I, Nebuchadnezzar, lifted my eyes to heaven, and my understanding was restored to me; and I blessed the Most High and praised and glorified him who lives for ever, because his power is everlasting power and his kingdom endures from generation to generation. All the inhabitants of the earth are accounted as nothing before him. He acts according to his will both among the powers of heaven and among the inhabitants of earth; and none can resist his hand or say to him, ‘Why have you done this?’ At that time [Col. 0706A] my understanding returned to me, and I returned to the honour and splendour of my kingdom; my appearance returned to me; my nobles and magistrates sought me out; I was restored to my kingdom, and still greater magnificence was added to me. Now therefore I, Nebuchadnezzar, praise, magnify, and glorify the King of heaven, because all his works are true and his ways are judgments, and he is able to humble those who walk in pride” (ibid.).

Likewise, when King Belshazzar, successor of the king just mentioned, consulted him concerning the writing on the wall, Daniel answered what was to occur immediately—that is, on the very night on which he was speaking. Thus, foretelling many great and wondrous things, both in the near and, as I have said, in the distant future, that prophet showed by the fulfilment of the things foretold that he was truly God’s messenger and truly God’s prophet.

[Col. 0706B] 10. Likewise, in the time when Rehoboam son of Solomon reigned over two tribes of the Jewish people, a certain man, truly a prophet, whose name is suppressed, came to another king, an idolater ruling over ten tribes of the same nation. Finding him sacrificing to idols upon the altar, he said:

“Altar, altar, thus says the Lord: Behold, a son shall be born to the house of David, named Josiah, and he shall sacrifice upon you the priests of the high places who now burn incense upon you, and he shall burn men’s bones upon you.” And on that day he gave a sign, saying: “This shall be the sign that the Lord has spoken: behold, the altar shall be split apart, and the ashes that are in it shall be poured out.”

When the king heard the word of the man of God, who had cried out against the altar at Bethel, he stretched out his hand from the altar, saying: [Col. 0706C] “Seize him.” And the hand which he had stretched out against him withered, and the king could not draw it back to himself. The altar too was split apart, and the ashes were poured out from the altar, according to the sign which the man of God had foretold in the word of the Lord. The king said to the man of God: “Entreat the face of the Lord your God and pray for me, that my hand may be restored to me.” The man of God entreated the face of the Lord, and the king’s hand returned to him and became as it had been before (III Kings XIII).

See how great were the things this prophet foretold, both concerning a time far in the future and concerning what was immediate. He foretold a time far in the future when he named even the king who was to be born at least two hundred years later, saying: “Behold, a son shall be born to the house of David, named Josiah” (ibid.). He foretold what was immediate when he said: “This shall be the sign [Col. 0706D] that the Lord has spoken: behold, the altar shall be split apart, and the ashes that are in it shall be poured out” (ibid.); for as soon as he ceased speaking, the altar was split and its ashes were poured out.

11. On Elijah and Elisha.—Thus Elijah, thus Elisha, and innumerable others, whom it is tiresome to recount because of their multitude, foretold many great things. Events showed their prophecy to be true in every respect, by fulfilling without diminution what had been foretold. To offer some prophetic instances also from those whom I have named: what Elijah foretold in threatening the idolatrous people was fulfilled: “As the Lord lives, there shall be”—that is, there shall not be—“dew or rain, except according to the word of my mouth.” For during three years and six months all dew and rain were withheld; then at his prayers heaven gave [Col. 0707A] rain and the earth gave its fruit.

That too was fulfilled which he prophetically foretold to a certain king of the Jews: “Because,” he said, “you sent to consult Beelzebub, the god of Ekron, as though there were no God in Israel from whom you could inquire for an oracle, therefore you shall not come down from the bed upon which you have gone up, but you shall surely die” (IV Kings I).

There was also fulfilled another saying—not by Elijah himself, indeed, but by the sons of the prophets concerning him, not merely once but twice, to his disciple Elisha: “Do you know that today the Lord will take your master from you?” (IV Kings II). When asked twice, Elisha answered twice: “I also know; be silent” (ibid.). That this was fulfilled was shown by the fiery chariot and fiery horses separating master and disciple, and by Elijah himself being caught up to heaven [Col. 0707B] in a whirlwind.

And what of Elisha? He had asked that a double portion of Elijah’s spirit might come upon him; and although, as the same prophet testified, this was difficult to obtain, he obtained what he had asked for. But when could his prophetic spirit and mind—an eager investigator and most truthful announcer of matters both present and future—be fully set forth? He promised cleansing from leprosy to the leprous commander of the king of Syria. When he ordered him to immerse himself in the waters of the Jordan in order to be cured, the man obeyed; though at first indignant at the command, he accepted the counsel of his servants, rendered obedience to the prophet’s command, and obtained the health he desired.

Gehazi, his servant, was touched by the pestilent and all-too-familiar greed of wretched mortals. What had been given freely by God through the prophet, he seemed to sell for a great price of silver [Col. 0707C] and garments. Therefore, he himself was suddenly made leprous, and claimed for himself at once both the leprosy of the commander now cured and the wealth unlawfully coveted. This did not escape the prophet, although absent; and he showed that it had not escaped him when the servant returned. For he said to him: “Where have you come from, Gehazi?” He answered: “Your servant went nowhere.” And Elisha said: “Was not my heart present when the man turned back from his chariot to meet you? So now you have received silver, and you have received garments, so that you may buy olive groves, vineyards, sheep, oxen, male servants, and maidservants. But Naaman’s leprosy shall cling to you and to your seed for ever” (IV Kings V). And Scripture adds: “He went out from him leprous as [Col. 0707D] snow” (ibid.).

See: a prophet not deceitful but truthful, not false but a true messenger of God. He both knew beforehand and foretold that the leper would be healed, and it happened; he both knew beforehand and foretold that the greedy servant would be infected with the leprosy of the healed man, and it happened.

12. How utterly unlike these was Muhammad.—What, O Hagarenes, did that man of yours—yes, that very prophet of yours—either know beforehand or foretell, even concerning some mean and trifling matter, comparable to so many, such great, and such exceedingly great prophets? Let his book be produced; let his Qur’an (*Alchoran*) be examined; let that lofty and heavenly scripture, according to you, as I have said, be run through word by word, without excepting a single *Azora* [sura]. Let him come publicly before the peoples of so many prophets, and show from the book which he left to his followers that he foretold prophetically, as has been said, anything mean or trifling [Col. 0708A].

But let us return again to Elisha. “The king of Syria,” says a certain Hebrew and Christian Scripture, “was making war against Israel; and he took counsel with his servants, saying: ‘Let us lay an ambush in that place.’ Therefore Elisha, the man of God, sent to the king of Israel, saying: ‘Beware of passing through that place, because the Syrians are there in ambush.’ Therefore the king of Israel sent to the place which the man of God had told him, and forestalled him and kept watch there, not once or twice. The heart of the king of Syria was disturbed by this matter; and summoning his servants, he said: ‘Why do you not tell me who among you is betraying me to the king of Israel?’ One of his servants said: ‘Not at all, my lord king; rather, Elisha the prophet who is in Israel reports to the king of Israel all the words [Col. 0708B] which you have spoken in your chamber’” (IV Kings VI).

Have you heard? Filled with the prophetic Spirit, the prophet knew beforehand and foretold to the king of Israel the ambushes of the Syrians; nor could the invisible eye of that prophet anywhere escape through any stratagem of the enemies’ battle-lines. The subtle and penetrating perception of the prophet entered distant lands, the depths of valleys, and the hidden places of forests; his prophetic hearing was present at secret deliberations. It could not be shut out by barriers or by the bolts of gates; it was not absent from royal chambers. By messengers continually going back and forth, the prophet informed his king of everything which his hostile and cunning adversaries, though far away, were plotting.

13. He never foretold anything.—Why then did your prophet, so famous in your estimation, fail to provide either for himself—let alone another—some slight spark of prophecy in his so frequent expeditions [Col. 0708C] against enemies? Why, when he often fled defeated from battles, did he not know beforehand that he would be defeated by enemies? Why did he not foresee and guard against the fact that, in one campaign in which he was personally present, one of his lower teeth would be knocked out, his lip cut, and wounds inflicted upon his brow and face by enemies?

But why do I expect, O Ishmaelites, that either you or he will produce from the Qur’an just mentioned—that is, from your law—anything that your prophet foretold prophetically, still less that any of the things foretold came to pass as he had foretold them? For what of his predictions could come to pass, when it is clear that he foretold nothing? Yet perhaps one among you will object and bring forward [Col. 0708D], as though it were something great, another writing containing his genealogy, certain acts of his, and battles. In it one reads that he foretold that twelve men from his own tribe or family, called Quraysh (*Chorais*), would succeed one another individually in rule after his death; and it is written that he named the first three: Abu Bakr (*Eubecaras*), Umar (*Aornar*), and Uthman (*Odmen*). Yet not even so, nor in any way, can diabolical deceit assist its own cause, nor can it introduce darkness in place of brilliance, or sooty Satan in place of an angel of light.

And who, O Hagarenes, whom the necessity of my subject compels me to name so often, could be found more suited to prove that the man in question was not a prophet of God than the very man whom you call God’s prophet? If he himself plainly denies [Col. 0709A] that he is a prophet, will you call him a prophet despite his opposition? How is this so? Listen. And if any rational understanding remains in you, attend carefully. That I may not keep you in suspense too long and beyond measure, hear him himself speaking in your Qur’an, a scripture which you consider it unlawful for anyone to contradict:

“Whatever you find written concerning me, compare it with the Qur’an; and if it does not agree with it, know that I am innocent of that writing, and it is not mine.”

Let the writing just mentioned, therefore, be compared with this Qur’an, and let it be seen whether it agrees with it or differs from it. The former writing says, as was just stated, that he foretold that twelve men from his stock or tribe, called Quraysh, would successively rule after him, and, as previously noted, it names the first [Col. 0709B] three. That writing, indeed, was issued by someone other than himself; but he himself, and none other, says in reply: “Whatever you find written concerning me, compare it with the Qur’an; and if it does not agree with it, know that I am innocent of that writing, and it is not mine.”

Now it does not agree with the Qur’an, because the entire text of his book gives no indication that he spoke anything prophetically and records no prediction by him concerning future things. Therefore, as both ecclesiastical and Roman judgments—indeed, divine and human alike—acknowledge, and as reason itself teaches, no one’s testimony is to be believed more than that of one confessing about himself. Let writings encountered from whatever source be set aside from a book of such authority in your eyes; for, according to the testimony of your Muhammad, if any writing, to use his words, [Col. 0709C] “does not agree with his Qur’an,” he is innocent of it, and it is not his.

Are these things not enough, men, to prove that he is not a prophet? But let other matters follow them and show that this impious—indeed utterly lost—man was far excluded from every prophetic grace, even by his own admission. For that wicked and deceitful man, presenting God as speaking to him as though in a poetic fiction, says in the Qur’an:

14. The Qur’an contains falsehoods.—“You certainly will not come to them with manifest miracles of God, because they reject them as hateful and contrary, and they have contradicted the truth coming to them.” And again: “Unless we knew that they would not believe you, we would give you [Col. 0709D] signs and wonders.”

What can I say? Who can adequately marvel? Who can express—or with fitting words mock—such stupidity, indeed madness, in a man? To turn to the words of the very man in question: Is this, Muhammad, the great reason why you came to men sent by God without miracles: because they would reject them as hateful and contrary, and would contradict the truth coming to them? Is this, I say, the reason why signs and wonders were not given to you: because God foresaw that they would not believe you, just as they did not believe others?

If this, as you say, was told you by God, God’s foreknowledge is plainly and beyond doubt false. For how, on the terms you advance, is God’s foreknowledge not false, if he foresaw that men would not believe you even when sent with signs and wonders, [Col. 0710A] whereas, without miracles, signs, or wonders, many peoples believed your utterly frivolous tales, accepted the wicked sect, and without hesitation submitted themselves to your infernal teaching? And to whom is this invention of yours not plainly weak, brittle, and made of clay?

Choose, certainly choose, which of the two you prefer. Either say that God erred in his foreknowledge, say that he lied when he said that men would not believe you even with signs and wonders, although Arabs, Persians, Syrians, Egyptians, and a great part of the Africans believed you even without miracles; or, if you are afraid to admit that God erred or lied, remove the false and blasphemous statements from your book—or rather, which is the sounder course, condemn your entire Qur’an as steeped in errors, lies, and blasphemies.

[Col. 0710B] 15. Men inspired by God believed on account of signs and miracles.—But what is that other statement which, after you introduce God as speaking to you in the words I quoted above, “Unless we knew that they would not believe you,” you add: “just as they did not believe others”? Who are these persons in whom people did not believe? Moses, perhaps? Christ himself, perhaps? No others occur to me—indeed no others at all—from whom I could infer that you meant this or said it: just as these are the supreme and sole lawgivers in the world, Moses for the Jews and Christ for all nations.

Moses came with signs and wonders; Christ came much more with signs and wonders. The Jewish people believed Moses when they saw the signs and wonders. The world believed Christ and his apostles when it saw the greatest and innumerable miracles. Who, then, are those [Col. 0710C] of whom you said, “just as they did not believe others”? For men inspired by God believed these men when they performed miracles; men deceived by you believed you, who spoke vain and false things without signs. Therefore your oracle which you pretended was spoken to you by God is false: namely, that people did not believe them and would not believe you.

16. By Muhammad’s testimony he proves that Muhammad was not a prophet.—But I return to what I proposed to prove: that by your own testimony you are not a prophet. For when you affirm that signs were not given you by God, you surely deny that you are a prophet. What, indeed, is more notable than prophecy? What sign is greater than prophecy? What is more properly called a sign, a wonder, or a miracle [Col. 0710D] than to report things past but unknown to men, to disclose things present, or to foretell things future? Since prophecy is among the splendid signs given by God, when you declare that signs were not given you by God, you surely deny that you are a prophet.

Either, then, profess that signs were given you by God and remain a prophet; or, if signs were not given you, cease to be a prophet. Reason presses and constrains you on every side: if, as has been said, you deny that signs were given to you, you must equally renounce being a prophet; if you say that they were given to you, you must accuse God of lying, and must correct what you falsely wrote.

And because your monstrous and hitherto almost unheard-of words compel me to astonishment, tell me: who, O wretch, among the whole company of prophets [Col. 0711A] called himself a prophet as you do? Who wished to be believed a prophet as you do? As true and humble servants of God, they avoided the glory of a great name; and, though truly prophets of God, they declined, so far as truth allowed, to call themselves prophets. Thus one of them, called Amos, when told, “Do not prophesy at Bethel, nor pour forth words against the house of the idol” (Amos VIII), answered: “I am not a prophet, nor am I a prophet’s son; but I am a herdsman, plucking sycamore figs” (ibid.).

And John—whom your prophet avoids calling the Baptist, but calls the son of Zechariah, while relating much in his Qur’an that exalts both him and his parents in praise—when envious Jewish priests and Levites said to him, “Are you a prophet?” answered: [Col. 0711B] “I am not” (John I). Yet these men were truly prophets of God; but they said that they were not prophets in another sense, which does not concern you now while you remain unbelievers, while preserving the profession of their truth.

They nevertheless left in their books prophetic signs which could not be doubted: they showed that what they foretold was either fulfilled in their own time, or was to be fulfilled, as later became clear among posterity. But that man of yours—and I cannot cease often enough to repeat this in amazement—calls himself a prophet; in his writings he introduces God calling him a prophet; and although he calls, affirms, and repeatedly declares himself God’s prophet almost to nausea, he says nothing about future things, speaks nothing prophetic, and shows not only nothing foretold or fulfilled by himself, but does not even predict anything to be fulfilled [Col. 0711C].

I pass over his promises of a sensual paradise and a fantastical hell, in which he cannot be shown to be a prophet before those who have been in paradise or hell prove that those promises have been fulfilled. It would not have been difficult for him, nor would it be difficult for me if I wished, to call myself a prophet; it would not be difficult to write, and to introduce in writing God calling me a prophet; it would not be difficult to proclaim myself God’s prophet to men. I could invent whatever I wished about matters which, after the end of the world and the passing away of things, either will or will not occur; nor could I be accused of lying in this life for predicting matters which will or will not occur after this life.

17. Let that diabolical invention be silent—fragile, weak, and made of clay, as [Col. 0711D] I said above—for no one can be believed a prophet by predicting what will happen after the end of this world, unless he proves himself a prophet by matters which occur before the world’s end. If he wishes to be believed a prophet, let him produce witnesses of his prophecy not from the dead but from the living; not from things which he promises will be fulfilled after death, but from things which he shows to have been fulfilled before death.

By this means, by such a clear and evident proof, the Christian people believe their prophets: not because they merely called themselves prophets, but because they proved themselves prophets beyond every trace of doubt by evident signs, clear miracles, and the actual fulfilments of things foretold by them. Therefore show yourself a prophet by such proofs, Muhammad; [Col. 0712A] or, if you cannot do this, cease, O condemned and condemnable man, to call yourself a prophet. And although what I have stated may suffice to show that you are far from prophetic grace, I shall nevertheless begin, as it were, afresh to show readers that you are not a prophet.

18. Some prophets are called good, others evil. Who are good.—Of prophets, whether those who existed or those who are called such, some are good and some evil. Among the good, some foretell universal matters, others particular matters. Among the evil, some are false and some truthful. Besides these are persons who are not prophets but are called by the common name *divini*, such as augurs, diviners, haruspices, magicians, and soothsayers. Let the discourse therefore pursue the distinctions of each in the order in which they have been set forth.

Good prophets are those whose life is commendable and whose prophecy or preaching is true. Among their number are those whom I mentioned above: Moses, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Ezekiel, Daniel, and many others. Among them is Christ himself, who, although he is the Lord of all prophets insofar as he is God, was nevertheless called a prophet because he spoke many prophetic things. The Gospel, which, O Saracens, you admit was given to him, bears witness to this; for there it is written that the crowds said of him: “A great prophet has arisen among us” (Luke VII); and he himself said of himself: “It cannot be that a prophet should perish outside the city.”

Bearing testimony, as was fitting, to the truth both of his life and of his preaching, he said in the same Gospel, while disputing with the Jews: “Which of you will convict me of sin?” (John VIII). For no one could convict of sin one who was without sin [Col. 0712C]. This concerns his life; but what of his preaching? “If I speak truth, why do you not believe me?” (ibid.). For Truth could utter nothing except what was true. Therefore he is among the other good prophets, and indeed a good prophet above the others.

19. Who are evil prophets.—But who are evil prophets? Those whose life is reprehensible and whose prophecy or preaching is false. Such in Elijah’s time were those four hundred and fifty prophets of Baal, and likewise four hundred prophets of the groves, whom one reads of in the book of the Kings of Israel and Judah. After the sacrifice offered to God had been consumed by heavenly fire, Elijah, inflamed with a great fervour of divine zeal, caused them, when by his command the people had seized them, to be dragged to the torrent of Kishon, where he killed them as the worst idolaters. [Col. 0712D]

20. Some good prophets foretell universal matters.—Among good prophets, as I said, those who foretold universal matters—that is, things pertaining to all—are, in part, those whom I named above, together with almost all the others called good prophets, whose life, as I said, is commendable [Col. 0712B] and whose preaching true. For what they foretold concerning Christ pertains to all, Christ who, as a certain great righteous man says in the Gospel, “is set for the fall and resurrection of many” (Luke II). His life, his preaching, his death, his resurrection, his departure from heaven, and his return thither have become life for believers and death for unbelievers.

Finally, at the end of the age, his universal and final judgment will assign everlasting abodes according to the merits of each person to the whole mass of mortals, divinely gathered before his dread [Col. 0713A] majesty: delivering each either to everlasting fire or restoring him to everlasting life with himself. In this manner all the remaining things which are read in those prophetic words or books, pertaining to all rather than to some, whether received for good or for evil, concern those whom I call universal prophets.

21. Others foretell particular matters.—I call particular those who did not foretell things pertaining to all, but spoke beforehand by the prophetic Spirit about matters pertaining to certain peoples or to certain expressly named persons. Among them is Jonah, who was sent by God only to the Gentile people of Nineveh—although that mission of his prefigured the calling [Col. 0713B] of all nations; although, by being cast into the sea, swallowed by the fish, remaining unharmed in its belly, and emerging safe from both beast and sea, he prophetically represented in action, not in word, Christ’s saving death and the resurrection which would carry its miracles to all from death.

Among them also is Samuel, who foretold not universal matters but certain things particularly concerning certain persons: to Eli the priest, things relating to the descendants of his house; to Saul, the first king of the Hebrews, first concerning the lost and found asses of his father Kish, and afterwards concerning his kingdom’s transfer to a neighbour and rival; and other matters concerning either the Jewish nation alone or certain specified persons.

Among them too is the prophet of the same [Col. 0713C] time whom Holy Scripture calls “the Man of God,” without recording his personal name. After foretelling many things that were to happen to the Eli just mentioned, he also added: “This,” he said, “shall be a sign to you of what shall happen to your two sons, Hophni and Phinehas: both shall die on one day” (I Kings II). And this happened.

Among them is also the prophet whom the same Scripture names without naming him personally, and whom it represents as speaking to a certain king of Israel after victory over the king of Syria: “Go, strengthen yourself, and know and consider what you must do; for in the following year the king of Syria will come up against you” (III Kings XX). Again another unnamed prophet said to the same king: “Thus says the Lord: Because the Syrians have said, ‘The Lord is a God of the mountains and not a God of the valleys,’ I will give this whole great [Col. 0713D] multitude into your hand, and you shall know that I am the Lord” (ibid.). This was fulfilled immediately on the seventh day, exactly as foretold. For when the Hebrews had engaged the Syrians in battle, they struck down one hundred thousand infantrymen in a single day. Those who remained fled into the city, and a wall fell upon twenty-five thousand of the men who remained.

These things foretold by the prophets already mentioned were not universal matters, but were predictions concerning individual nations or particular persons and their own outcomes. Among them is the great Elijah; among them Elisha, not inferior to Elijah with respect to miracles. One of them, as I said above, threatened King Ahaziah with death, and he died as had been foretold; the other foretold to another king, called Joash, frequent triumphs over the king of Syria, and this too came to pass, along with certain similar things foretold by them to certain persons and fulfilled as had been said. [Col. 0714A]

22. After Christ there were no universal prophets; there were many particular prophets.—Therefore those whom I have mentioned, and many whom I have passed over, belong to the number of those whom I call particular prophets because they foretold by the prophetic Spirit not things concerning all, but things concerning some. Yet a distinction must be made between these and the others, and it must be carefully and diligently observed that, from Christ’s time onward, prophets foretelling universal matters—that is, matters concerning all—could neither have existed nor can exist until the end of the world.

For everything relating to the common condition or destruction of mortals, or of the world [Col. 0714B] itself; everything relating to true or false religion; everything relating to the due and universal ends of the good or evil—all this was foretold by the prophets already mentioned who are called universal, and was committed by them to writing for the instruction and remembrance of later generations. The greater part of it has already been fulfilled; the whole is reserved to be fulfilled at the end of the age.

Accordingly, when prophets ceased—and, in John, whom we call the Baptist and whom you call the son of Zechariah, though we do not deny that he is Zechariah’s son—when prophets, I say, entirely failed among the Jewish nation, which alone until Christ had been the worshipper of the divine law, only that kind of prophecy which pertained to the universal condition ceased, because all matters belonging to it had already been fully set forth [Col. 0714C] and it was no longer necessary.

Your Muhammad, therefore, was not, as you say, the seal of the prophets—that is, the last among prophets—but John the Baptist, of whom Christ says in the Gospel, which according to you was given to him: “The law and the prophets were until John” (Luke XVI). These were plainly the prophets who foretold matters concerning all, not those who prophesied certain personal matters.

For the Church of Christ has often possessed and experienced, at different times and in different parts of the world, persons who after John the Baptist foretold by the prophetic Spirit various events affecting individuals or particular periods: for example, the apostle Paul, who foretold many future matters, some fulfilled and others still to be fulfilled. Fulfilled matters, as in ourselves and the Jews, when [Col. 0714D] he said: “There will be a time when they will not endure sound doctrine” (II Tim. IV); and in the same verse: “They will turn their hearing away from the truth and turn aside to fables” (ibid.). For it is plain to the world, apart from yourselves and them, that both you and they, as will be proved in its proper place, have turned your hearing away from the truth and turned it to fables: you from Christian truth to Muhammad’s fables, and the Jews to the fables of the Talmud (*Talmulth*).

He foretold matters still to be fulfilled when he wrote that the man of sin would be revealed: “the son of perdition, who opposes and exalts himself above everything that is called God or worshipped” (II Thess. II), and that he would sit in God’s temple; this man we call Antichrist. Likewise, there were other apostles, and very many of their other disciples, who were called prophets and showed by the fulfilments [Col. 0715A] of what they foretold that they were prophets.

Among such was the man called Agabus, who, binding his own feet with the belt of Paul as he was going to Jerusalem, said: “The man whose belt this is, they will bind thus in Jerusalem” (Acts XXI). A short time later, when Paul had reached that city, he was seized by the Jews, bound by a tribune, and scourged by the Romans, thus showing that prophet to have spoken truthfully. And who could recount the number of prophets of this kind who, after Christ, shone among Christians in both life and prophecy?

### 23. Some prophets were universal, others particular.

If I were speaking to the faithful and to believers in Christ, an immeasurable field would lie open before me. For when could so great a multitude of prophets be fully set forth, whether by me or by anyone else—prophets who, from Christ down to our own times, proclaimed not universal matters, as I said before, but particular ones, as I have said? If I wished to recount individually the names or the number, gathered from trustworthy records, of those who shone in some measure with this prophetic grace, you would, I think, refuse to give credence to what I said. For how could you believe God’s prophets, when you do not yet believe God himself?

Yet I know this to be your understanding, this to be your profession: that you believe in God, and in the true God. But whether this is true, the argument which follows, and which by God’s Spirit convicts you, will show. Meanwhile, let the discourse, serving the argument, continue the subject proposed. That discourse, that argument, concerned the mode of universal prophecy, after the distinction had first been made, and then the following mode—that is, singular or personal prophecy—according to the proposed division. I mean plainly that mode of prophecy by which particular matters, as I have said, are foretold, not that by which universal matters are prophesied.

For that mode which, if I may so speak, is universal prophecy arose almost from the very creation of the first human being; but, as I have said, it was completed in John. Particular or personal prophecy, however, was given to many both before John and after him, and perhaps will still be given to more. Having described this twofold distinction of prophetic grace, let the discussion return to prophets at once universal and particular, and declare from the writings who they are.

### 24. Isaiah, for example.

From their number I again bring forward Isaiah. Just as he has been shown to have foretold universal matters, so it must be proved that he also foretold particular matters concerning certain peoples, or personal matters concerning certain persons: concerning certain peoples, such as what he prophesied against Babylon, against Moab, against Damascus, against Egypt, against the Idumaeans, against Arabia, and against Tyre, as the reading of his book indicates; concerning certain persons, such as what he prophesied about Sennacherib, king of the Assyrians, about Hezekiah, king of the Jews, and about certain others, as is more fully read there.

### 25. Jeremiah.

Jeremiah, named above, follows him. In the same way as he foretold many things pertaining to all people, so he did not pass over very many particular or personal matters: particular matters concerning certain nations, such as those which, filled with the prophetic Spirit, he prophesied against the Philistines, against Moab, against the children of Ammon, against the kingdoms of Hazor, against Elam, and against Babylon; and personal matters, as when he foretold that King Zedekiah would be captured and carried captive by the Chaldeans; and when he threatened a certain false prophet Hananiah in these words:

> “The Lord has not sent you, and you have caused this people to trust in a lie. Therefore thus says the Lord: Behold, I shall remove you from the face of the earth; this year you shall die, because you have spoken against the Lord.”  
> (Jer. 28)

Likewise, when he said to two men:

> “Thus says the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel, concerning Ahab son of Kolaiah and Zedekiah son of Maaseiah, who prophesy lies to you in my name: Behold, I shall deliver them into the hand of Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, and he will strike them down before your eyes.”  
> (Jer. 27)

### 26. Daniel.

Daniel belongs among these prophets both universal and personal. As I stated much earlier, full of both gifts, he often foretold things pertaining to all people and things pertaining only to some. He spoke to all, for example, when, recounting the dream of the Chaldean king—a dream which the king himself had forgotten—he foretold what it signified. The king had seen a statue whose head was of gold; its breast and arms of silver; its belly and thighs of bronze; its legs of iron; and its feet partly of iron and partly of clay. These signified the greatest kingdoms of the world, succeeding one another, having diverse courses and outcomes, and indicating by their successive changes such continuance of themselves, until, when the world should fail, they too would be brought to an end after being struck by a stone cut from a mountain without hands.

Again, he foretold matters concerning all, as the final part of his prophecy indicates, which anyone among you who reads it will find. And he foretold matters concerning certain persons, such as those which he predicted to King Nebuchadnezzar and those to King Belshazzar. Daniel, therefore, like the two prophets mentioned above, is not merely a universal or a personal prophet, but at once a universal and a personal prophet.

### 27. Ishmaelites ought to listen to the prophets of the Hebrews.

But because I set Hebrew prophets before you, just as I do before the Jews, perhaps some among you will be astonished. Yet, that he may cease to wonder, let him hear what follows. The prophets already mentioned are indeed Hebrews; but, though Hebrews, they are also yours.

“But how are they ours?” you will say. “What has an Arab to do with a Hebrew? What has an Ishmaelite to do with a Jew?” Very much indeed. First, because Ishmael and Isaac were brothers, although the former was born of Hagar the slave-woman and the latter of Sarah the free woman. Second, because, besides your line of blood relationship and a language almost shared both in the forms of its letters and in speech, you have also distinguished yourselves from the natural practices or inherited laws of all other peoples by the distinctive and ancient sign of circumcision, as though derived from Abram, the father of both nations. Third, because it has been shown by evident and invincible arguments in the book mentioned above that the Hebrew or Christian prophets under discussion, as inspired by the divine Spirit and filled with prophetic grace, ought to be accepted by you. It is superfluous to set these arguments down again in full, as though newly committing them to writing, if you have given attentive hearing to what preceded.

But if perhaps you heard carelessly, as persons contemptuous of the urgent matters under discussion, or if through the common indolence which occupies almost everyone except the diligent, you consigned what was read or heard to a lethargic forgetfulness, I briefly repeat what was said more fully above, so that, if you have so great a concern for your salvation, you may recall it. From these arguments, clear and unquestionable reason will show that the Jewish or Christian prophets, concerning whom a long discussion has already preceded, are yours also, and that you ought to believe them as your own—provided that obstinacy resisting manifest truth, as I wrote above, has been removed and every darkness of clouds driven away.

And why do I say, “will show”? Rather, it has already shown this. Were I not speaking to unbelievers, to persons wholly alienated from God, I would refuse to repeat what has so often been said. Yet let my pen patiently endure everything and accommodate itself to heretical or pagan persons, while preserving the firmness of faith and truth.

### 28. Or else they ought to insert nothing from them into their Alcoran.

What do you demand of me, Ishmaelite? From what source am I to prove that my prophets are yours? From what source am I to fight against you by their words, as though conceded by you? Certainly I have much—very much. What? Listen.
