Why do you accept anything from my books, which are far older than yours, when I am a Christian and you are, as I have said, a heretic or a pagan? What have you and I to do with one another? I take nothing from your books; why then do you steal something from mine? Do you envy what is mine? Or perhaps do you wish to become a Christian? Oh, would that you did! Yes, would that you did indeed! Would that, abandoning an error foolish, deadly, devoid of all reason, bereft of all truth, vanishing amid empty phantoms and unheard-of trifles, you might turn to the true God; acknowledge Christ as the power and wisdom of God; and, freed from the snares of a wicked and most shameful man, be able to sing with David, king and prophet, whose divinely given psalms that evil man wrote down:

> “The snare has been broken, and we have been delivered.”  
> (Ps. 123)

If you conceal this intention, leave what is mine alone and keep what is yours for yourself. I insert nothing from your Alcoran into my books; do not mix anything from my Gospel into your writings. Leave me my Moses; leave me my prophets. Do not create a monstrous mixture, intolerable to any rational mind, by inserting words of a heavenly oracle into infernal writings, or by defiling them with an admixture of wicked fables and with a mound of lies heaped around them on every side.

By what reasoning—rather, by what madness—have you mixed certain things from Hebrew or Christian books, which you believe and proclaim false, into that Alcoran of yours, which you suppose to have been sent from heaven? With what mind have you inserted Jewish or, as you think, Christian lies into your truthful scripture? For if our books are false, then the things excerpted from them are false; and if the excerpts are false, then the writings into which they have been inserted are false. But it is true that they have been inserted into your Alcoran. It is therefore certain that, since falsehood has been mixed into it, your Alcoran itself is false—not only in part, but wholly false. For even if some things in it are perhaps true, they have been corrupted by the admixture of falsehoods and are no longer worthy of belief.

Is this not how the judgments of all nations stand? Everywhere in the world this rule prevails: if I am found a false witness even in one word, I shall not be heard even in matters that are true, nor shall I deserve belief even in true matters. By this justice I reject your Alcoran; by this judgment of equity I condemn, not certain parts of it, but your entire Alcoran without exception.

Choose one of the two alternatives I set forth far above. Either reject the Alcoran because of the false things taken from books which, as you say, are false and inserted into your book; or, if you refuse, confess that the Hebrew and Christian books from which those things were taken are true. Since no path anywhere lies open by which you can otherwise escape these straits, I believe that you will prefer to confess that our books are true, lest all that you have hitherto kept according to your ancestral law perish together with the very author of that law.

If you choose this alternative, you will give faith to the books so often named—that is, the Hebrew and Christian books—as to Scriptures that are your own. For these reasons I have set Hebrew prophets before you and shall continue to set them before you, just as I set before a Hebrew Christ, and Christ’s disciples before a Christian. Therefore, when I intend to prove something, I bring forward examples from what is conceded, from the things to which you already assent, as reason teaches.

### 29. Muhammad was neither a universal nor a personal prophet.

And since the books mentioned above have now become common to us and to you, O Hagarites, let the discussion return to its undertaking and state for what reason it has brought forward so many examples of prophets.

That Muhammad, your lawgiver, was not a prophet or messenger of God has indeed been fully proved from what has gone before. Yet, for greater clarity for those who read this, it must still be proved according to the divisions already set out. For, as I wrote above, among prophets—whether those who truly were prophets or those who were called such—some are good and others bad. Of the good, some proclaim universal matters, others particular matters; others proclaim at once universal and particular or personal matters. I have named these latter explicitly and have stated individually which share of the threefold distribution of prophetic grace befell each.

I have done this so that you—whoever you are who call Muhammad a prophet, whoever affirm that he is a prophet—may show, and prove either by authority or reason, that he was a prophet: whether among universal prophets, by predicting something universal; among particular prophets, by predicting something particular; or among personal prophets, by predicting something personal.

But why should I expend labor in vain? Why should I contend to no purpose? I have invited and still invite you; I have challenged and still challenge you, to answer by what power, by what reasoning, by what device—truthful or deceptive—you, O Arab, believe and declare this man to be a prophet. Did he predict anything by which he could be called a particular prophet, proclaiming matters pertaining to some and not to all? Did he predict anything by which he might be proved a prophet, foretelling some true thing before it came to pass, not about some persons collectively but about certain persons individually?

But why, serving your error so stubbornly and opposing your salvation, do you flee what belongs to salvation and pursue what is destructive? Speak, speak: if you have anything, show that your Muhammad belongs to one of the stated divisions—either a universal or a particular prophet, or both at once, or a personal prophet; that is, one prophesying matters that concern not everyone or many people, but certain persons.

But what are you doing? Why do you keep me in suspense? Speak, if you have anything, that you may be justified. These are indeed words of God, but after him, and with him, they are mine as well. If from your Alcoran, so often named and named even to weariness, you can produce and relate anything great—or even something lowly or small—spoken or written by prophetic spirit, produce it and relate it.

Do you find, as has already been said above, in that whole book of yours, sacred in your judgment and accursed in ours, anything prophetically stated by your prophet about past events, anything about present events, anything about future events? For the whole substance of prophetic grace consists in this threefold distinction, as was stated above. Whatever is prophetically foretold concerns either past things, present things, or future things—whether the matters said be universal, particular, or personal, and whether they are foretold for the present time, for the near future, or for a distant future.

In which, then, of these divisions of prophetic grace, so subtly and carefully examined, will you be able to find your prophet, O Arab, against whom I write? But I refrain from raising again the objections I have already raised. For I have proved that he was neither a universal, nor a particular, nor a personal prophet; and I have shown that he revealed nothing about the past, made known nothing about the present, and prophesied nothing about the future. If this is so, then this man of yours is not a prophet of anyone’s, as you said; rather, as follows from what has been stated, he is read to have said or written nothing at all prophetic. Therefore, he is not a prophet.

*(Two books are missing, which I have been unable to find.)*

[Col. 0719]

# Ninth Letter, or Treatise, of Peter the Venerable, Abbot of Cluny, Against the Petrobrusian Heretics

[Note: This treatise Peter the Venerable himself calls a letter in Letter 17 of Book IV; but he also calls it a book and indicates in Letter 35, to Peter his notary, that it was published separately from the other books of letters, in these words: “Send our letters and the Life of Bishop St Matthew, because the book issued against the heretics is lacking.” As far as I know, this book was printed only twice before the present edition: once at Paris in 1525 together with the other letters, and once separately at Ingolstadt in 1546.]

## Preface

To the lords and fathers, teachers of God’s Church—the archbishops of Arles and Embrun, and the bishops of Die and Gap—Brother Peter, humble abbot of Cluny, greetings and service.

I recently wrote a letter to Your Reverences against the heresies of Peter of Bruis; but innumerable and important affairs, delaying my mind from dictation and my pen from writing, have until now postponed my sending it. At last I now send it to your prudence, so that through you it may become known to the heretics against whom it was written and also to Catholics to whom it may perhaps be useful.

[Note: *Against the heresies of Peter of Bruis.* No mention of this Peter, who gave his name to the Petrobrusian heretics, is found either among historians of that time or even among those who then, or shortly afterward, composed accounts judging heresies and heresiarchs. Alfonso de Castro, I think, is the first after our author to mention him, in Book III, under “V, Baptism, Heresy V”; and he writes that he was a Gaul from the province of Narbonne. Bernard Gui likewise states that Pope Calixtus II held a council at Toulouse on 6 June 1120, the eighth day before the Ides of June, with cardinals, archbishops, bishops, and abbots of the provinces of Gothia, Gascony, Spain, and Lesser Brittany. At that council, among other proceedings, heretics were condemned and expelled from the Church: all who, while feigning a religious appearance, condemned the sacrament of the Lord’s body and blood, infant baptism, the priesthood and all ecclesiastical orders, and the bonds of lawful marriage. In this treatise our Peter attacks all these heresies as invented and disseminated by Peter of Bruis and propagated by Henry, his successor.]

I send it to you because in your regions, or near them, that foolish and impious heresy has, like a powerful pestilence, killed many and infected more. But, stirred and aided by the grace of God, your efforts have caused it to withdraw somewhat from your territories. Yet, as I have heard, it has migrated to places quite near you; and, driven out of your Septimania while you pursued it, it has prepared hiding places for itself in the province of Novempopulana, commonly called Gascony, and in the regions adjoining it.

[Note: “From your Septimania”: that is, Gothia or Languedoc, as we have explained elsewhere.]

[Note: “In the province of Novempopulana”: this is also called by Isidore “Third Aquitaine,” so named from the nine peoples or cities subject to the archbishop of Auch. It is now commonly called Vasconia, or, as Peter himself calls it, Gasconia—Gascony.]

There it now hides itself in fear; now, taking courage from those same hiding places, it comes forth. It deceives whom it can, corrupts whom it can, and administers deadly poisons now to these persons, now to those. It therefore belongs to you, to whom the care of God’s Church in those regions chiefly pertains both by office and by exceptional knowledge, and upon whom it especially rests as upon strong pillars—it belongs to you, I say—to drive it from those places in which it rejoices to have found concealment, both by preaching and, if necessary, by armed force through laymen.

But because Christian charity ought to devote greater effort to converting them than to destroying them, authority should be brought forward and reason also applied, so that, if they wish to remain Christians, they may be compelled to yield to authority; if they wish to remain human beings, to reason. Perhaps the letter which I wrote for you against their errors will help them in this matter, if they are willing to attend to it. If they do not wish to be contentious and obstinate, then perhaps, after studying it carefully, although they have been exceedingly foolish, they may recover from the folly of so great an error.

But if they have been given over to a reprobate mind and choose rather to be foolish than wise, to perish rather than be saved, to die rather than live, the letter, once read, may perhaps satisfy the hidden thoughts of certain Catholics and either heal their minds from an infirmity of faith unknown to people, or fortify them against those whose tongue is called by the Prophet a sharp sword (Ps. 56). This final purpose was the greater reason why I wrote: so that, even if the writing could not benefit heretics, it might nevertheless serve some useful purpose for God’s Church.

For this is what the Church has always been accustomed to do throughout the centuries past: among the many and great varieties of heresies which have frequently attempted to ferment its purity, it has never passed any over in silence, but, for its own protection and the perpetual instruction of all, has purged away the blasphemies of every heretic by sacred authorities and also by reasoning. Though among the least members of Christ’s body, that is, of his Church, I have attempted to do this in writing these things: that what I have written might benefit heretics, if possible, and might render more cautious against this wicked doctrine or similar doctrines those Catholics into whose hands it should fall.

And because the first seeds of this erroneous doctrine, sown and cultivated by Peter of Bruis for almost twenty years, produced five especially poisonous shoots, I dealt principally, as far as I could, with these five, so that my mind and words might be directed more attentively to the matters in which they showed the greater injury to faith and the greater danger. Therefore, since the work itself is rather extensive, and since you are occupied with the Church’s many concerns and may perhaps have little leisure for a long reading, I briefly recapitulate those articles and show against what errors the lengthy series of that letter is directed.

The first article of the heretics denies that children below the age of understanding can be saved by Christ’s baptism, and denies that another’s faith can benefit those who cannot use their own; because, according to them, it is not another’s faith but one’s own faith together with baptism that saves, the Lord saying:

> “He who believes and is baptized shall be saved; but he who does not believe shall be condemned.”  
> (Mark 16)

The second article says that the construction of temples or churches ought not to take place; that those already built ought moreover to be demolished; and that Christians do not need sacred places for prayer, because God, when invoked, hears equally in a tavern and in a church, in a marketplace and in a temple, before an altar or before a stable, and hears those who deserve to be heard.

The third article commands that sacred crosses be broken and burned, because that form or instrument by which Christ was so terribly tortured and so cruelly killed is worthy neither of adoration nor veneration nor any supplication. Rather, in revenge for his torments and death, it ought to be dishonoured by every degradation, cut to pieces by swords, and set alight.

The fourth article not only denies the reality of the Lord’s body and blood, daily and continually offered in the Church through the sacrament, but decrees that it is wholly nothing and ought not to be offered to God.

The fifth article mocks sacrifices, prayers, alms, and the other good works done by living believers for deceased believers, and maintains that they cannot benefit any of the dead even in the slightest degree. To these five articles, as God granted, I answered in the letter sent by me to your Holiness; and I endeavoured, however inadequately, to bring about both the conversion or confounding of the impiety of the faithless and the strengthening of the belief of the devout.

But after the pyre of Peter of Bruis at Saint-Gilles—when the zeal of the faithful avenged upon him, by burning him, the flames which he had kindled against the Lord’s cross—that wholly impious man made his passage from fire to fire, from a passing fire to an eternal one. Henry, heir of his wickedness, together with I know not what others, did not amend but altered his diabolical teaching; and, as I recently saw written in a volume said to have been taken down from his lips, he set forth not merely five but more articles.

[Note: “Henry, heir of his wickedness.” St Bernard also speaks of him in Letter 240 to Ildefonsus, count of Saint-Gilles; and Matthew Paris, the English historian, under the year of Christ 1051, writes as follows: “About these days, when the perverse teaching of a certain heretic Henry was spreading, especially in Gascony, the Lord stirred up the spirit of a young girl in that province to refute the heresy which he preached against the articles of faith. For every week the girl lay for three days without voice, sensation, or breath; afterward, when she returned to herself, she said that Blessed Mary prayed for the Christian people and that Blessed Peter had taught her the orthodox faith. Thus she disputed wisely concerning the Catholic faith and, especially by refuting Henry’s heresy, brought back to the bosom of holy mother Church many who had been led astray by him.”]

My mind is stirred to address these doctrines again and to oppose demonic words with divine speech. But because I have not yet been fully convinced that he thinks or preaches this way, I postpone my answer until I have unquestionable certainty regarding what is reported. If perhaps I deserved to be assured of this through the wisdom of your careful investigation, I would make whatever effort I could so that the cup of death, which these most miserable people offer to others like themselves—a cup already partly drained—might, through renewed answers, be entirely emptied even of its remaining dregs.

Meanwhile, if it please you, make known, as time and place offer occasion, the letter published for the benefit of readers and to be conveyed through you to those who need it; so that, as I have said, it may either correct some of the heretics against whom it was written, or make Catholics, for whom it was written, more cautious in these and similar matters. If anyone should wish to copy it, let him not omit to place this shorter letter before it as a preface, because in it both the purpose and the subject matter of that entire great work are briefly indicated.

# The Letter Begins

To the distinguished priests of God, most worthy of honour in Christ’s body—William of Embrun, Ulrich of Die, and William of Gap—Brother Peter, humble abbot of Cluny, greetings.

Because among all the bishops of the whole province of Septimania, or of the Maritime Alps, divine providence has especially adorned the summit of the episcopal office through you with religious devotion, knowledge, learning, and pastoral care, I have resolved to honour Your Reverences always with a special affection beyond the others and to disclose to you more familiarly the movements of my mind.

Do not suppose that I am moved by any advantage of temporal affairs or by any present inconvenience. Rather, know that the whole cause of this concern is that which has often moved you also, and for which your pastoral care has hitherto laboured not a little. Therefore, thanks be to God, who has not rendered your labour wholly futile, but, as experience itself teaches, has almost wiped out through your exertions the enemies of the Christian faith, and consequently the enemies of human salvation.

I say “almost wiped out,” because, while recently travelling through your dioceses, I found that the erroneous doctrine with its authors had for the most part been expelled from those provinces; yet I also found some remnants of it among many persons—not open defenders so much as secret whisperers. I found the serpent’s head crushed, again lying in wait for the victorious heel; and its wicked throat, with poisons renewed for the killing of people, giving warning through repeated hissing.

This must by no means be despised by minds such as yours, trained in such matters. Growth comes much more quickly to evil things than to good, and the devil’s tares spread themselves through his field far more easily and fruitfully than God’s wheat. Nor should the persistent enemy, because he is believed once to have been defeated, be despised as though he would dare nothing further. For, according to the poet:

> “We often see the victor overcome by the conquered.”

We have frequently experienced that a fever driven from the very marrow by the long labor of physicians has crept back more fiercely and often torn away the soul through a slight negligence of either the sick person or the healer.

It is indeed necessary—though I say this not as one teaching, but as one advising—that the pastoral eye remain watchful against the manifold snares of wolves and labour with unceasing zeal lest the Lord’s flock be harmed in any respect. But that bite must be driven away from Christ’s sheepfold far more diligently, and that bestial tooth crushed with far greater force by the pastoral staff, when it seeks not to tear his sheep apart but to slaughter them, not to break a leg but to strangle them.

This is not some ordinary injury, but the loss of salvation itself in its entirety. It is suffered above all by those who, wandering from the path of right faith, rush through the byways of error into the abyss of profound destruction. If a dispute arises concerning adultery, theft, perjury, fraud, murder, or indeed any other crime whatever, so long as faith remains whole, through it an entrance to life will stand open. For if, according to Scripture, “the righteous lives by faith” (Hab. 2; Rom. 1), the sinner will return to life through faith. However great the wounds he has incurred, they cannot harm one for whom the life of faith—which works through love—has been preserved.

The man wounded by robbers could therefore be healed (Luke 10), because he was not entirely dead, but after the wounds of sins remained alive through the life of faith. Had he lost faith together with works, no hope of healing would thereafter have remained. I know, certainly, that even an unbeliever often resumes faith after apostasy; but while he remains an unbeliever, he has nowhere to return after dangers have come upon him.

Thus the children of Edom, persecuting Jerusalem, say:

> “Lay it bare, lay it bare, even to its foundation.”  
> (Ps. 136)

Any vessel is emptied of its liquid, but not down to the bottom, when any sinner, although diminished in his former good qualities by the arrival of evils, is nevertheless not emptied down to the foundation of faith. But if even that foundation is drained away, when the hostile wishes have been fulfilled, Jerusalem, wholly emptied of God, is filled with unclean spirits.

I would gladly linger longer in praise of faith, so that both its great usefulness and the grievous impiety of those who detract from it might shine more clearly, and so that the more praiseworthy it appears, the more condemnable might appear the heretic who contradicts it. But because the fields of Scripture are everywhere strewn with flowers, the pen must be restrained, lest, delayed over superfluous matters, it arrive too late at necessary ones.

I call a discussion of faith’s praise superfluous because what is known to nearly all believers ought not to be treated at length as though it were unknown. For who is so deaf that he has not heard? Who is so lethargic that he does not remember Christ in the Gospel exalting faith with repeated praises and saying almost continually to the sick, sinners, and individuals:

> “Your faith has saved you.”  
> (Luke 8)

And to the disciples:

> “If you have faith, you will say to the mountain, ‘Move,’ and it will move.”  
> (Matt. 17)

And again:

> “Have faith.”  
> (Mark 11)

And Peter is told:

> “O you of little faith, why did you doubt?”  
> (Matt. 14)

And:

> “He who does not believe has already been judged.”  
> (John 3)

And:

> “He who believes in me will also do the works that I do; and he will do greater than these.”  
> (John 14)

What literate person has not heard from childhood the Apostle crying out:

> “Without faith it is impossible to please God”?  
> (Heb. 11)

And the Psalmist:

> “All his works are in faith.”  
> (Ps. 32)

And Isaiah:

> “Unless you believe, you shall not remain.”  
> (Isa. 1)

Who could pass by with stopped ears the thunderings of the Apostle to the Hebrews, in which he recounts most abundantly that the elders obtained testimony through faith; that the ages were framed by God’s word through faith; that Abel through faith offered a more abundant sacrifice than Cain; that Enoch through faith was translated so as not to see death; that Noah, through faith, having received an answer concerning things not yet seen, built an ark for the salvation of his household; that Abraham through faith obeyed and, when tested, offered Isaac; and that all the saints, whoever they were from the beginning of the world until the time of grace, through faith conquered kingdoms, worked righteousness, and obtained promises? (Heb. 11)

He further tells how some of them through faith stopped the mouths of lions, quenched the force of fire, escaped the edge of the sword, recovered strength from weakness, and became mighty in war; while others endured mockery and scourging, chains and imprisonment, were stoned, sawn apart, tested, and died by the sword; others wandered in sheepskins and goatskins, needy, distressed, afflicted, and so forth (ibid.). After all these things he concludes the praise of faith thus:

> “And all these, approved by the testimony of faith, did not receive the promises, God having provided something better for us, that they should not be made complete without us.”  
> (ibid.)

And shortly afterwards he says:

> “Let us run the race set before us, looking to Jesus, the author and finisher of faith.”  
> (Heb. 12)

These things, venerable Fathers and priests of the Lord, concerning the praise and efficacy of holy faith, I have not so much explained as recalled briefly, so that from these few things many more may occur to your learned minds and that you may recognize how great an evil follows upon neglect of so great a good.

That you have already experienced this far too greatly is hidden from scarcely any corner of the western world: in your regions, to the injury of the Godhead and contempt of the sacred law, by a new crime unheard of among Christians, people were rebaptized, churches profaned, altars dug up, crosses burned, meat publicly eaten on the very day of the Lord’s Passion, priests scourged, monks imprisoned, and men compelled through terror and tortures to take wives.

You have expelled the leaders of these plagues from your regions, by divine aid as well as by the help of Catholic rulers. But, as I have said, their members remain, still infected by deadly poison, as I myself recently discovered. For their healing, God’s mercy must be invoked and your medicinal diligence applied. This may perhaps be accomplished if, in addition to the other counsels of your wisdom, religious authority and, so far as possible, reasoning are not lacking for those who inquire. For every question concerning divine as well as human matters is resolved by these two, so that whoever yields neither to authority nor to reason may now be called not a human being but a beast.

Therefore, since by the apostolic voice disciples of the truth are commanded to be ready to give an account to everyone who asks concerning the hope and faith that are within us [Col. 0726D] (1 Pet. 3), it has seemed right to me to answer heretical calumnies by reason, and especially by authority, upon which faith chiefly rests, lest, if no one should answer, misguided people should boast or suppose that Catholics have kept silence, not from judgment, but from inability to reply. Indeed, to persons learned and instructed in the Christian faith in our own time, this abominable heresy would seem more deserving of contempt than of a response, were it not that public dangers, the ruin of souls, and the stubborn persistence of this very error now for twenty years, warn us that it must not be ignored, but rebuked, refuted, and detested.

A report recently brought also urges me more strongly to this task and, as though spurs had been added to my back, incites me more sharply: namely, that the slippery serpent [Col. 0727A], having escaped from your regions—or rather, having been expelled by you as you pursued it—has made its way into the province of Narbonne; and that what among you hissed fearfully in wildernesses and little villages now preaches boldly in great assemblies and populous cities. I had thought that the icy Alps and crags covered with perpetual snow had introduced barbarism among your inhabitants, and had made a land unlike every other land, and a people unlike every other people; and that thus a foreign doctrine had more readily crept in among the rustic and unlearned habits of men. But the farthest banks of the swift Rhône, the plain surrounding Toulouse, and the city itself, more populous than its neighbours, disprove this opinion of mine.

> [Note: “The plain of Toulouse disproves this opinion of mine.” That Toulouse was purged of this Henrician heresy is also shown at length by Saint Bernard, Epistle 241, [Col. 0728D].]

For it ought to have been the more cautious against false teaching in proportion as it could be more learned through [Col. 0727B] the continual resort of peoples and experience of many doctrines. Yet it received—this I say not in reproach but in grief, not to disparage the good but desiring to draw the wicked away from their evils—it received, I say, a city noble in itself but made ignoble by error, the forerunners of Antichrist against Christ. Forgetting the divine milk by which it had been imbued, nourished, and brought to the strength of maturity, it judged stolen waters sweeter and hidden bread more pleasant. It did not remember, according to the prophet, the days of its youth (Lam. 1); nor did it rest content with the Christian faith, attested by the blood poured out by so many witnesses of Christ. Instead, it became like a woman who, enhancing her price through disdain, brings strangers over [Col. 0727C] her husband.

And, O sheep of Christ, is this what your Shepherd deserved from you—he who laid down his life for you? Is this what he deserved from you—he who, leaving the ninety-nine sheep in the wilderness, came to seek and save that which was lost? (Luke 15.) Is this what he gained from you by his blood: that, abandoning the good Shepherd, you should cling to wolves as they ravenously scatter you? But why do I call you sheep, unless perhaps that you may be like those of whom it is said: “Like sheep they are laid in hell; death shall feed upon them” (Ps. 48). For if the simplicity and obedience of Christ’s sheep had truly remained in you, you would flee from wolves and take refuge with the Shepherd; and the voice of the Shepherd himself would be fulfilled in you when he says: “My sheep hear my voice, and I [Col. 0727D] the Lord know them, and they follow me; and I give them eternal life, and they shall never perish, and no one shall snatch them out of my hand” (John 10). And concerning wolves or hirelings he says: “They do not follow a stranger, but flee from him, for they do not know the voice of strangers” (ibid.).

And, O wretched men, whoever you are, emptied of all truth and seriousness, surpassing every chaff and stalk in vanity and frivolity, carried about by every wind of doctrine (Eph. 4), and swept away through the emptiness of errors at every new breath of breeze—having nothing solid or stable, like the wandering stars [Col. 0728A] spoken of by the apostle Jude (Jude 13)—what would you do if the peril of death and final necessity pressed upon you? If a bloody persecutor, as of old, assailed you with fires, swords, and devised tortures? If he whose coming is “in all power, and signs, and lying wonders” (2 Thess. 2)—who will persecute poverty with golden heaps, frugality with the luxuries of the age, constancy with tortures, faith with miracles, and do all this far more fiercely than others—pressed upon you, what then? What, I say, what would you then do in the face of such things? You who are stirred with reed-like fragility by the breath of a light breeze—how would you remain unmoved when you had to endure such tempests as tear up even age-old oaks and fir trees lifted high toward heaven? When would you resist, for your Christ, wise [Col. 0728B] Greeks, powerful Romans, cruel Persians, or the wonder-working times of Antichrist—you who so easily yielded not to many nations, but to only two insignificant men, Peter of Bruys and Henry, his pseudo-apostle? No wisdom of theirs refuted you, no power subdued you, no tortures terrified you, nor did any magical tortures deceive you. Yet you have become “like a deluded dove without understanding” (Hos. 7), and like an ox led to the sacrifice (Prov. 7), which, about to be slaughtered at any moment, runs in brutish ignorance toward death as though toward rich pasture.

But because zeal for the house of God, and Christ so lightly deserted by Christians, have compelled me to digress a little and drive my chariot somewhat beyond the course, let my pen return to its purpose and at last bring forth what it has long been labouring to bear. Therefore you—yes, you whom I named above—teachers of errors, blind guides of the blind, dregs of heresies, remnants of schismatics: you, I say, deceivers of deceivers, I summon and invite to come out from your hiding places into our public view. Truth, as the common saying goes, has no corners; nor does light wish to lie hidden under a bushel. Nor does that which is called Catholic delight in becoming exclusive, because that which has been spread throughout the whole world by Christ’s command is not content with portions of the world. Come from the maritime districts of Septimania at the call of the Church which summons you; and if you bring anything, as you yourselves say, on behalf of it—or, as we believe, against it—declare it. I too shall proceed in reply, not as wiser than others, but perhaps [Col. 0728D] as more unrestrained, ready according to my measure to yield to truth once it is made known, and to oppose falsehood.

### First proposition of the new heretics

“Christ,” they say, “when sending his disciples to preach, said in the Gospel: ‘Go into all the world; preach the Gospel to every creature. He who believes and is baptized shall be saved; but he who does not believe shall be condemned’” (Mark 16). From these words of the Lord it is plainly shown that no one can be saved unless he has believed and been baptized—that is, unless he possesses the Christian faith and has received baptism [Col. 0729A]. For it is not one of these, but both alike, that save. Therefore infants, although baptized by you, cannot be saved at all, because their age prevents them from believing. It is thus idle and vain when you sprinkle people with water at a time when you can indeed wash their flesh of bodily dirt according to human custom, but cannot in the least cleanse their soul from sins. We, however, await the suitable time for faith; and once a person is prepared to acknowledge his God and believe in him, we do not, as you charge us, rebaptize him, but baptize him. For one who has not been washed by that baptism which washes away sins must be said never to have been baptized.

### Reply to the assertion of the heretics that little children cannot be baptized

[Col. 0729B] And O you aforesaid men, who at last explain to the foolish and unlearned what they had hitherto been unable to understand: have past ages become so senseless that for more than a thousand years they bestowed an illusory baptism upon so many thousands of little children, and from Christ’s time until yours produced not real Christians, but phantoms? Has the world been so blinded and so enveloped in darkness until now that, to open its eyes and illumine so long a night, after so many Fathers, martyrs, pontiffs, and leaders of all the Churches, it waited so long for you, choosing Peter of Bruys and Henry his follower as its latest apostles to correct its long error? Did the world perish until the appearance of these new restorers of the age [Col. 0729C], and were all things done among the children of light and truth in darkness and falsehood, so that—although nearly all those of our own age or memory were baptized in infancy, assumed the Christian name, and at a suitable time were appointed to various ranks in the Church—no bishop was a bishop, no presbyter a presbyter, no deacon a deacon, no cleric a cleric, no monk a monk—nor, so to speak, was even one Christian to be found among that innumerable multitude?

For anyone not baptized with Christ’s baptism was not a Christian. If he was not a Christian, he could belong neither to clergy, people, nor Church. And if this is so, the absurdity which follows is evident. Since all Gaul, Spain, Germany, Italy, and the whole of Europe [Col. 0729D] for nearly three hundred or five hundred years have had no one baptized except in infancy, they have had no Christians. If they have had no Christians, they have had no Church. If they have had no Church, they have had no Christ. If they have had no Christ, it is certain that they have perished. Therefore our fathers perished, because they could not be baptized with Christ’s baptism in infancy. And we who live, who remain, shall perish unless, after Christ’s baptism, we are also baptized with Henry’s baptism.

Countless saints, whom baptism in infancy, holiness of life, the testimony of the world, and divine miracles had commended, will be dragged down from the heights of heaven to the depths of hell. Those who were companions of angels will become companions of demons; and those who had already received eternal [Col. 0730A] life for their devout labours will suddenly fall into everlasting death. Our feast days will be turned into mourning, Sabbaths into reproach, honours into nothingness. Who can endure this? Who can hear it? Who would not either stop his ears or rise up against the new heresiarchs along with the whole world which they labour to condemn?

But come, come, I say, to me, you with whom I am speaking. Come to your senses after such a monstrous claim, and choose rather to learn truth from the Church of God than to teach falsehood through the spirit of error. Learn that our little children are in no way lacking the faith by which they are saved, because they cannot be called children of unbelievers, since the faith of Mother Church intercedes for them. But I know that you ridicule this, and amid much mockery among rustic and unlearned crowds [Col. 0730B] deny that one person can be saved through another’s faith.

For refuting this brutish and impious heresy of yours, innumerable testimonies of ecclesiastical doctors support me; but your authority and wisdom are so great that I do not dare bring them before you—especially since I have learned that Hilary, Ambrose, Augustine, Jerome, Leo, Gregory, and the rest have been condemned by the judgment of your majesty. And since you have excluded all Latins both from the chair of teachers and from the kingdom of heaven, I do not know whether you have spared Greeks or men of another language. But if perhaps they too have been able, through the sobriety of your examination, to escape your peremptory sentence, what is that to me? So far as the present matter is concerned, it profits little or nothing, since I am only a Latin, and cannot make use of testimonies in a foreign language, which I do not know, in order either to convert or convict you [Col. 0730C].

Let Catholic readers of this work consider what you deserve for this one point alone, which I have now mentioned—you who have resolved to strip the Church of God of its weapons and set it unarmed among its enemies; or rather, so far as lies in you, have already exposed it to hostile darts and swords. But since I have undertaken at present not the task of invective but of disputation against your errors, my discourse must be restrained, and I must deal with you alike by authority and by reason. Therefore, because you disdain to put faith in the holy doctors of the Church, I must return to the purest fountain of all the streams and produce testimonies from Gospel, apostolic, and prophetic utterances—if indeed you receive even these [Col. 0730D]. We must see whether those who yield to none of the great teachers of the world at least submit to Christ, the prophets, or the apostles.

I say this because common report has spread that you yourselves do not wholly believe even Christ, the prophets, and the apostles, and has indicated, if it is true, that you disparage the very majesty of the Old and New Testament, which from ancient times has subjected the whole world. Yet because I ought not readily give assent to the monstrous falsehood of rumour—especially when some assert that you have rejected the whole divine Canon, while others maintain that you have received certain portions of it—I do not wish to accuse you on uncertainties. Instead, I shall prove by certain authorities that you ought necessarily to receive the entire Canon accepted by the Church.

### Proof of the entire New Testament from the Gospel

[Col. 0731A]

For if, as everyone affirms, you receive even the Gospel alone, then necessarily, as has been said, you will receive all the rest as well. You cannot believe the Gospel and doubt those things which the Gospel itself accepts. And since the entire text of the heavenly oracle, by which God has spoken to humankind either himself or through others, consists in the Old and New Testaments, let the New Testament first be brought forward—not because it is earlier, but because it is worthier. It is called a Testament because, as the Old was dedicated by the death and blood of a calf, so the New was consecrated by the death and sprinkling of the blood of Jesus Christ.

Its holy beginning is the Gospel, to which, as the consistent report [Col. 0731B] shows, you as well as Catholics render full faith and due reverence. Therefore, since it remains among you as among us in its divine and stable dignity, let the discourse pass to the evangelical and apostolic books, and prove from the Gospel itself that they are, as I have said, evangelical and authentic.

The first of these books is the Acts of the Apostles. That it is wholly evangelical and of chief authority after the Gospel is demonstrated, among many converging considerations, first and most especially by the proof that its writer was not just anyone but the evangelist himself. For Luke, the more diligent narrator than the others of Christ’s humanity, wrote it. He himself acknowledges this at the beginning of the book when, writing to Theophilus—to whom he had earlier written the Gospel also—he says: “The first account I made, O Theophilus, concerned all that Jesus began to do and teach, until the day on which, having given commands through the Holy Spirit to the apostles whom he chose, he was taken up” (Acts 1).

The beginning of that first account, that is, of the Gospel, is as follows: “Since many have undertaken to set in order a narrative of the things fulfilled among us, just as those who from the beginning were themselves eyewitnesses and ministers of the word delivered them to us, it seemed good to me also, having carefully traced all things from the beginning, to write them to you in order, most excellent Theophilus, that you may know the truth of the words concerning which you have been instructed” (Luke 1). This, as I have said, is the beginning of his first account. Its conclusion is such as he said in his second account that he had made: [Col. 0731D] “Until the day,” he says, “on which, having given commands through the Holy Spirit to the apostles whom he chose, he was taken up.” “He led them out,” it says, “as far as Bethany, and lifting up his hands he blessed them. And it came to pass, while he was blessing them, that he departed from them and was carried up into heaven; and they, worshipping him, returned to Jerusalem with great joy, and were continually in the temple praising and blessing God” (Luke 24).

Behold: the same style with which he writes both books; the same person to whom he writes both books; and the same subject concerning which he writes both books, demonstrate more clearly than light that the same person composed both. I have said that the subject is the same because, just as he narrates Christ’s Ascension at the end of his Gospel, so in this second and final account he most fully supplies what he omitted concerning that same Ascension [Col. 0732A] in the Gospel. For, going back a little and beginning with Christ’s resurrection, he repeats what he had said and adds what he had not said.

But I cannot sufficiently wonder how this doubt could arise in any Christian minds, even moderately educated ones, when this book, as is clear to everyone who reads it, contains nothing but evangelical matter, although it is not called a Gospel. For after setting forth in the Gospel the acts and words of Jesus Christ and his many promises, here it shows those promises fulfilled, and then passes on to narrate the acts and words of the apostles. If anyone is so foolish, unbelieving, or obstinate as to refuse to place in its words not merely any sort of faith but complete and robust faith [Col. 0732B], let him show us, to speak first of the opening sequence of the book itself, where or when the coming of the Holy Spirit upon the apostles, promised by Christ, was fulfilled; where he has read that the Spirit descended in fire; where that he bestowed upon them the gift of every language; where that Pentecost, a day so solemnly celebrated not only by the whole Church throughout the world but by the apostles themselves, ought to be celebrated. For unless authority is assigned to this book, not merely the Jewish Pentecost of the old law, but the Christian Pentecost of the new law, is lost.

And where are the words of truth so often preached and promised to the disciples: “When the Paraclete comes, whom I shall send to you from the Father, the Spirit of truth who proceeds from the Father, he shall bear witness concerning me” (John [Col. 0732C] 15)? Where is what he says in the same Gospel about the same Spirit: “But the Paraclete, the Holy Spirit, whom the Father will send in my name, shall teach you all things” (John 14)? Where is what he says in consoling them: “If I do not go away, the Paraclete will not come to you; but if I go away, I shall send him to you” (John 16)? Where is what he likewise says: “I shall ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete, that he may remain with you for ever, the Spirit of truth” (John 14)? Where is what he urges upon the same disciples through another evangelist: “But remain in the city until you are clothed with power from on high” (Luke 24)?

If, I say, as I have said, this book is rejected, all these promises of Christ will appear void. It will therefore be necessary either to confess Truth to be a deceiver—which it is impious even [Col. 0732D] to think, much less say—or to show where or when so great, so solemn, and so frequently repeated a promise was fulfilled. It will also be necessary to prove how the apostles and Christ’s other disciples could fulfil that final and universal command of his by which they were ordered: “Go into all the world, preaching the Gospel to every creature” (Mark 16). It will be necessary, I say, to prove how simple, unlearned men, speaking only one language—Hebrew—and almost speechless even in it, could preach in so many, so diverse, and so barbarous languages of the whole world the Gospel of the eternal kingdom enjoined by Christ.

By what signs could they communicate their thoughts to the minds of foreigners if the gift of languages bestowed on them by [Col. 0733A] the Holy Spirit is denied, if that noble miracle of the New Testament is despised, if the book in which these things are recorded is not believed? Certainly this grace bestowed upon the apostles is denied when the Scripture that alone contains the account is rejected. For one who says that he does not believe that book without exception contradicts everything that it contains.

This being so, let the deniers of the Scriptures say whether the world was converted to the faith in silence. For by taking from them the languages of nations, they undoubtedly impose silence upon them so that they cannot preach to the nations. Christ therefore sent his disciples in vain to preach the Gospel to diverse languages and peoples, if, as has been asserted, he dispatched them speechless. And what means the Psalm’s saying: “Their sound has gone forth into all the earth, and their words to the ends of the world” (Ps. 18)? What means Christ’s own saying: “What I say to you in darkness, say in the light” (Matt. 10)? What means his other saying: “The Gospel must be preached throughout the whole world, and then the end shall come” (Matt. 24)?

Either deny the Pentecost of Christians, deny that the Holy Spirit was poured out upon the apostles on that day, deny that the gift of languages was bestowed upon them by that same Spirit on that same day; or, if you shrink from this, receive the Scripture which reports these things and henceforth be reconciled with the Church of God, from which you have until now departed.

And although what has been said is sufficient to convert you, even if only by shaming you, let the pen nevertheless turn back a little and show from the same book that Matthias filled the place of the traitor by apostolic election [Col. 0733C], and completed the number of twelve instituted by Christ. Say, if you can, where else this is recorded, where this twelfth apostle is found to have been numbered by divine lot among the eleven apostles, apart from this book. If you cannot, believe what we believe. For neither authority nor reason permits the apostolic number chosen by Christ, as I have said, to remain maimed or diminished—especially since he himself said to the apostles: “You shall sit upon twelve seats” (Matt. 19). Since he foresaw that the sacrilegious Judas would not sit upon the twelfth seat, he was surely predicting that Matthias would succeed him and preparing an apostolic throne for him.

But if perhaps you object that the twelfth throne, to which Judas the chosen traitor had been appointed, was conferred upon the apostle Paul, lest so great an apostle appear to lack an apostolic throne, answer this: if Paul has been placed in the twelfth seat, and only twelve seats appear to have been promised by Christ, who will be able to construct seats for Barnabas, Timothy, Silas, and the many other apostles of the early Church [Col. 0733D]? The omnipotent Craftsman has not forgotten his skill so completely that, besides those twelve seats, he cannot prepare a thousand more if necessary. For it is not those alone who are called apostles who will judge the world with Christ; rather, whoever has truly despised the world will come to judge, with Christ and the apostles, that world which he despised.

It follows, and is proved by unassailable reasoning, that when Matthias, the apostle under discussion, has been placed upon the promised twelfth seat, a seat no lower than his has been prepared for Paul, the greatest of the apostles, upon which he may sit at Christ’s judgment and, inferior to none, judge the world with Christ [Col. 0734A]. For if more than twelve judges are to come to judgment, more than twelve seats must likewise be prepared for the multiplied judges. You must therefore either deny that Matthias was an apostle or receive the book in which alone he is recorded as having gained the apostolate.

Let Stephen also come forward, the first martyr of the New Testament, whom Christ’s Church from the very age of Christ has placed, after the apostles, upon the lofty summit of authority as Christ’s outstanding witness. Since no history other than this Scripture recounts his life, teaching, examples, miracles, and passion [Col. 0734B], either deny that he existed at all, or receive this Scripture as divine. But with what audacity will you deny him, when you see that the martyr’s name and fame are spread over land and sea, and that no corner of the whole world remains—not even among unbelievers—where the name of Stephen the protomartyr does not resound, whether with veneration among Christians or admiration among pagans? Greek, Latin, barbarian, East, and West confess this.

By “West” I mean that region in whose principal Churches, for the most part, the modern dedications in the martyr’s name—as well as those dating almost from the apostles’ own time, indeed, as is reported, from the apostles themselves—indicate sufficiently, and more than sufficiently, that this Scripture is neither contemptible, false, nor apocryphal. By its report alone the martyr himself attained so high an eminence of dignity among all peoples. If it is denied, the honour, fame, and name alike of so great and famous a martyr are annulled [Col. 0734C].

It is therefore necessary, as I said before, either to contradict the whole world which receives the martyr, or to receive the Scripture by which alone the martyr’s name and merit became known to that world. After these, to strengthen still more the evangelical dignity of the book, let Paul come forward: the last of the apostles, yet after Peter the greatest of them all. Let him show that those who contradict so divine a history deserve to be displayed rather than even heard. His name and fame have filled heaven and earth alike; through his labours and teaching above all, that great Roman empire which ruled the whole world was subjected to Christ; through the more excellent, clearer, and loftier trumpet of his preaching, he converted the whole world to the Lord of the world from whom it had turned away; and his name is no less feared among demons than famous among men, as that one testified who said to the exorcists: “Jesus I know, and Paul I know; but who are you?” (Acts 19).

Say, you deniers of the volume which I have so often named—say, I ask—whence you have this apostle, so great and so exalted, when you deny the book from which the world derives almost all its knowledge of him [Col. 0734D]. In what other book have you read, or can you read, the account of his conversion, persecution, and preaching? Where have you read that he was blinded, enlightened, baptized, appointed apostle of the whole world, and sent as an envoy to kings, regions, and Jews, when the Lord said to Ananias: “This man is for me a chosen vessel, to bear my name before kings and nations and the children of Israel” (Acts 9)? Where, plainly, have you read, heard, or found all these things except in this book?

Where have you found, unless in this book or heard them from others concerning it, his imprisonments, beatings, shipwrecks, journeys, hardships, dangers, and the greatest fruits of his dangers—the innumerable peoples converted to Christ through him? And what of that final conflict of his with Jews and Gentiles at Jerusalem, so far as this book is concerned? There he was seized in the Temple, beaten, bound, and, in those very chains, sent from tribune to governor and from governor to Caesar, to the city that was the head of the world and of which he was apostle [Col. 0735A].

For it was fitting that the greatest apostle be sent to the greatest city: there, in Rome itself, no small number of Romans having been converted through his miracles and teaching, his preaching fulfilled and his passion completed, his body would be preserved permanently by that City, as though at the summit of the world; and heretical unbelief would be convicted by so eminent a testimony of the apostle—or of those who refuse to believe the apostle. Behold: all these things compel and forcibly constrain even your most obstinate unbelief either to reject so great an apostle in opposition to such great divine and human testimonies, or to confess both that he is an apostle and that his history is true.

Nor should this point be passed over altogether or carelessly neglected: Peter, James, John, and the other apostles are recorded here as having uniquely experienced the persecutions promised by Christ in the Gospel, when that Scripture says of them: “They departed rejoicing from the presence of the council, because they were counted worthy to suffer dishonour for the name of Jesus” (Acts 5) [Col. 0735C]. Here too, and nowhere else, they imposed an end, by the authority of the Holy Spirit, upon the obligation to preserve circumcision, observe the Sabbath, and maintain sacrifices and the old observances. “It has seemed good,” they say, “to the Holy Spirit and to us to lay upon you no greater burden than these necessary things: that you abstain from things sacrificed to idols, from blood, from what is strangled, and from fornication; if you keep yourselves from these, you will do well” (Acts 15).

Behold, they release not only Gentiles but even Jews converted to the Christian faith from the fleshly observance of legal precepts, and show by what authority the Church does not circumcise Jews if they have been converted to Christ. Since this authority is found nowhere except here, apart from the Apostle’s Epistles, in which perhaps you do not believe, you must now either subject converted Jews to circumcision and the other decrees of the Law, or grant canonical authority to the book whose reading forbids this [Col. 0735D].

By all these authorities and arguments we have shown—indeed, compelled—you henceforth to accord authentic dignity to the often-mentioned book of the Acts of the Apostles, and no longer to oppose, even in the slightest degree, the Church of God by refusing to receive it.

[Col. 0736A] From this point let the discourse proceed to the Epistles or books of the apostles Paul, James, Peter, John, and Jude, in which the Scripture of the New Testament is concluded, and prove by suitable authorities or arguments that they possess evangelical and canonical dignity. Since Paul’s Epistles are not only of greater volume but also of loftier doctrine, let this discussion place them before the others, though they are not so ordered in the Canon. Let this first be proved from the preceding book, so that, because it has itself already been made canonical, it may make them canonical too and confer upon them not an inferior but precisely the same authority which it possesses.

This may perhaps be shown more clearly if the words of this book and of those Epistles—similar and mutually attesting one another—are brought forward. For what Luke reports concerning Paul in his book, Paul confirms in his Epistles written to diverse Churches and peoples. Luke records, as I said above, Paul’s persecutions, conversion, preaching, miracles, and sufferings. Paul acknowledges the same concerning himself, and almost everything that the evangelist’s volume recounts concerning him, apostolic Scripture likewise narrates in full.

To offer some testimonies that make the remaining matters plain: what Luke says concerning the persecution carried out by him—“Saul, still breathing threats and slaughter against the disciples of the Lord” (Acts 9), and the rest—Paul says thus: “I was formerly a blasphemer, a persecutor, and a man of violence” (1 Tim. 1); and likewise, “I am not worthy to be called an apostle, because I persecuted the Church of God” (1 Cor. 15). What Luke reports of his conversion—“Lord, [Col. 0736C] what do you wish me to do?” (Acts 9), and the Lord’s reply to him, “Rise and enter the city, and you will be told what you must do”—Paul states thus: “But when it pleased him who set me apart from my mother’s womb and called me through his grace to reveal his Son in me among the Gentiles” (Gal. 1), and the rest.

What Luke says of his preaching—“Paul, entering the synagogues, preached Jesus” (Acts 9); and likewise, “He also spoke to the Gentiles and disputed with the Greeks” (ibid.), and a thousand similar matters—Paul says thus: “From Jerusalem as far as Illyricum I have filled all places with the Gospel of Christ” (Rom. 15). What Luke says of his miracles—“The whole multitude fell silent and listened to Barnabas and Paul recounting how many signs and wonders God had performed among the Gentiles through them” (Acts 15)—Paul says thus: “I do not dare speak of anything except what Christ has accomplished through me, in bringing the Gentiles to obedience by word and deed, by the power of signs and wonders, by the power of the Holy Spirit” (Rom. 15) [Col. 0736D]. Again, in another Epistle: “Although I am nothing, nevertheless the signs of my apostleship were performed among you in all patience, in signs and wonders and mighty deeds” (2 Cor. 12).

What Luke says concerning his labours, imprisonments, stonings, blows, shipwrecks, chains, ambushes, and manifold kinds of death, Paul says thus: “I have laboured more abundantly, been in prisons more frequently, endured blows beyond measure, and faced death often” (2 Cor. 11), together with the rest which the sequence of the Epistle enumerates. I too would enumerate them, were I not persuaded that through the Church’s frequent reading they are known to almost [Col. 0737A] everyone. These few examples are drawn from many.

Since, therefore, the words of the evangelist and of the apostle agree with such manifest clarity that the former reports in historical style, and the latter in epistolary style, the same event as having occurred, and each bears such harmonious testimony to the other's truth, what further do you seek? Does not the Gospel book appear to confer sufficient authority upon the apostolic writings? But what shall be said of the exceptional renown and celebrated authority of these same Epistles? Has not their heavenly doctrine, surpassing human measure, raised the scriptural work of these Epistles to such a summit of dignity that, after the Gospel, it resounds more clearly throughout the whole world, is believed more firmly, recited more solemnly, and heard more devoutly than the other Scriptures, Old and New? Was it not held in such esteem even among your own predecessors—I mean the ancient heretics—that, among the many heresies of past centuries, no heresy ever dared to assail it? Neither Apelles, Cerinthus, and Montanus of earlier times, nor Arius, Novatus, and Sabellius of later times, nor even Manichaeus himself, more detestable than the rest, did this. Though he gave himself up to the emptiest fables, became vain in his reasonings, and rejected not only the entire Old Testament but even, for the most part, the Gospel itself, he did not deny that he believed the apostle Paul and his writings, and he received Paul's Epistles with honor. But why do I speak of heretics? Did not the reading of these apostolic Epistles, as we read, strike even the pagans, indeed even those philosophers among them who seemed to devote themselves more earnestly to wisdom? Did not that famous philosopher Seneca himself tell Paul that he thought no ages would suffice to comprehend the profundity of those writings? Did not that cruel beast Nero, when he heard them read aloud by this same philosopher, say that he wondered how such knowledge could reside in a man whom he called unlearned? Certainly this, this alone, subjects your lies to truth and enervates all the strength of the heretical body: in a matter in which the whole Church throughout the world, and even a portion of those outside the Church, agrees, the rashness of a few men—indeed, of almost no men—does not dare to dissent.

But if you seek for what is fortified by such great authorities also to be strengthened by reason, listen. As I said above, common report agrees that you accept the Gospel; it is certain that you either reject the other Scriptures of the divine canon or call them doubtful. But I ask you: why do you not accept the Epistles of the apostle Paul and of the other apostles—to say nothing for the moment of the other divine books? You answer: “Because their authority is not sufficiently certain to us for us to be willing to give them credence.” Does their authority not seem certain to you when they are called apostolic and believed to have been written by the apostles? Here you say: “If it were established by certain authority or reason that they are apostolic, we would have to accept them. But if they are said or believed to be apostolic and are not, they are not to be accepted by us.” But if they are called and believed to be apostolic by persons to whom one ought to give credence as to the apostles themselves—what then? What, I say? Once this is proved, must they not be accepted by you? They certainly must be accepted.

But where will one find a person to whom we must give credence as to the apostles themselves? One will certainly be found. And, not to keep you in suspense, I mean the Church, to which, as to the apostles themselves, I affirm that you are absolutely bound to give credence. Perhaps you say again: “And what is this Church of which you speak?” Why, I ask, do you say that you do not know this name, when formerly it was only too, too well known to you, when you were destroying its material fabric? For then you used to say that you destroyed the buildings of churches because the name Church signifies not a structure of walls but an assembly of the faithful. If you have either forgotten this or pretend not to know it, I shall explain it briefly. Church, as you yourselves said, means an assembly—not of birds, not of cattle, but of human beings; nor of all human beings, but of the faithful, the good, the righteous. If some wicked persons are hidden or evident among those good people, or unrighteous persons among those righteous people, it is nonetheless called the Church. This is the Church which, spread through the whole world in an innumerable multitude by the command of Christ its Lord, has reached down to us and, as you see, fills no less the whole world now than it did formerly. To it, as I said, you must truly give credence as to the apostles themselves; for Christ himself, in this respect, bestowed upon it no lesser authority. I do not say that the Church, planted and increased by apostolic labor, is equal to the apostles; but I say that its testimonies must be accepted, just as apostolic ones are, without any contradiction.

And if you want evangelical authority for this too, hear Christ saying: “Behold, I am with you all days, even to the consummation of the age” (Matt. 28). But the apostles did not remain in the world until the consummation of the age. Therefore this must be understood of the Church, which is to be in the world until the consummation of the age. Likewise: “I will ask the Father, and he will give you another Paraclete, that he may remain with you forever” (John 14)—certainly not with the apostles alone, but with the Church that was to come, to which, at the request of the Son of God, the Spirit of God was given by God the Father, to remain with it forever: consoling it in this life and glorifying it in the life to come. But lest you perhaps say that this exposition of mine is not Christ's meaning, hear him in another evangelist: “I pray not for these only,” he says, “but also for those who are to believe in me through their word, that all may be one, as you, Father, are in me and I in you; that they too may be one in us, and that the world may believe that you sent me. And the glory which you gave me I have given them, that they may be one, as we also are one” (John 17). Do you see that the Son of God prays to the Father not only for the apostles, but also for those who, when he spoke these words, were still to believe in him through the apostles' word? And who are they? Is it not this Church of which we speak? For who else believe and will believe in Christ except that which is called the Church, that is, the assembly of those believing in Christ? He does not divide all these because of different times or separate them because of different places; rather, he wills all of them—those preceding and those following—to be one, and not in any other manner, but as solemnly as the Father is in him and he in the Father. He shows them to be not few but innumerable when he adds: “That the world may believe that you sent me.”

Then should the testimonies of the Church not be believed, when Christ dwells with it indivisibly until the consummation of the age? Should the testimonies of the Church not be believed, when the Holy Spirit remains with it inseparably, not only here but forever? Should the testimonies of the Church not be believed, when it is one with the Father and the Son, as the Father is in the Son and the Son in the Father, and when the Son of God gave it the glory which he received from the Father? Should the testimonies of the Church not be believed, concerning which—that is, concerning the elect and predestined—it is said: “Father, those whom you gave me, I will that where I am, they also may be with me, that they may see my glory which you gave me, because you loved me before the foundation of the world” (John 17)? How then could the Church follow so great an error for so great a time—I do not say for such a great period, but even for a short time? How, I say, could it both be deceived and deceive for more than a thousand years, when the truthful Father, Truth the Son, and the Spirit of Truth continually remained with it? But since this is altogether impossible, it follows that all its traditions, like the apostolic traditions, must be granted complete faith by all the faithful. For if the Church's doctrine or tradition was received from the apostles, and if that same doctrine was transmitted from Christ to the apostles, it is clear that it is true and must be accepted by the children of truth. That the apostles received it from Christ is doubted by no one; and that the Church received it from the apostles has been proved both by authority and by reason.

It follows, therefore, that the doctrine or tradition of the Church must be accepted by all. You must therefore believe the testimonies of the Church if you do not wish to remain enemies of Christ and of the Church.

This Church bears witness that the Epistles in question are apostolic, and that it firmly and immovably retains this as something handed down to it by preceding Fathers and by those very apostolic men.

But you reply: “We cannot resist evangelical testimonies, but this makes us doubtful: nowhere, not even in the whole Church of which we are speaking, can we find testimony in the manner of witnesses who give evidence. For the law of the world itself commands that one should believe witnesses, not testimonies. The duty of witnesses is to testify to what they have heard or seen, not to what has been told them by others; whereas it is the custom of testimonies to report what has been told them by others.

“The Church on which you rely, and whose eminent dignity you attempt to establish by bringing forward so many and such great testimonies, acts not in the place of witnesses but of testimonies, because it recounts not what it has seen or heard but what has been handed down to it by others; and it grants canonical authority to the books in question not because it knows them, but because it believes them.”

Behold, behold: at last you have dug a pit for yourselves, into which you are immediately to be thrown. You have forged bonds with which you are to be bound. You have stretched out a snare in which you yourselves are to be caught first.

For if what you have brought forward is true, you have lost not only the books we defend but also the Gospel itself, which you accept. For if assent is to be given only to what has been seen and heard, one must not believe not only the other books but even the Gospel itself.

Tell us first whether you have seen with your eyes or heard with your ears any of the things you read in the Gospel or believe concerning the Gospel. To omit countless matters and briefly mention those on which the whole substance of the Gospel rests: have you heard or seen the archangel Gabriel announce to the Virgin Mother the conception of the Son of God and the coming of the Holy Spirit?

Have you seen or heard Christ born, the shepherds visiting him, and the Magi worshiping him? Have you seen or heard Christ baptized, preaching, performing those solemn miracles, imposing the same preaching upon his disciples, and conferring upon them the same power to perform wondrous works?

And what need is there to say more? Have you seen or heard him suffer, be crucified, die, be buried, rise again, and ascend? Have you seen or heard what has not yet happened but is to happen—although you read it in the Gospel you believe, though I do not know whether you believe it—all the dead of the world rising, Christ judging, hell gaping open, heaven unsealed, the wicked entering eternal fire, and the godly entering eternal life?

Where, then, is what you were holding? You had the Gospel, but once it was lost, you lost Christ. For if you do not have the Gospel, you do not have Christ. If you do not have Christ, you are not Christians.

Behold the pit, behold the bonds, behold the snare which, as I said, you have already prepared for your own destruction. In this way, once the Gospel has been taken away together with Christ, all the prophets and all the apostles have also been removed, and all their works and all Scripture have likewise been destroyed with them.

It will therefore now be necessary for you either, after rejecting the books we propose, to reject the Gospel, Christ, the Christian faith, the hope of salvation, and eternal life; or, after accepting our books, to preserve the Gospel and Christ together with everything I have enumerated.

For since the world believes, hopes, and loves all these things not from what it has seen or heard but from the tradition of the Church and the Fathers, and since you too hold the Gospel not from what you have seen or heard but from the tradition of that same Church and those same Fathers—which you cannot deny—you will either, compelled by an invincible argument, accept what has been handed down equally to us and to you by that same Church, and retain the Gospel together with the Epistles of the apostles and all the books that you denied; or, after rejecting our books, you will likewise lose the Gospel, which alone remained to you.

Once you have lost it, you will no longer be Christian heretics in relation to us, but will be like pagans and publicans.

By this reasoning, Paul, James, Peter, John, and Jude, together with the Apocalypse of that same John, have been accepted into the canon of the New Testament; indeed, by the same reasoning the New and Old Scriptures alike have been most firmly established. Let us now proceed to examine the books of the Old Testament individually and to confirm them by evangelical and apostolic authority.

## Proof of the Whole Old Testament from the Gospel

For the Gospel bears witness to the whole Old Testament, and, by the authority of the Old Testament as well, confirms the very things it proclaims.

Did Christ not strengthen the authority of the Old Testament by his own authority when, appearing after his resurrection to all the disciples, he said: “It was necessary that all things written in the law of Moses, and in the Prophets, and in the Psalms concerning me should be fulfilled” (Luke 24)?

Did he not confirm it by an unbreakable bond when he opened the minds of those same disciples so that they might understand the Scriptures?

Did he not confirm it when he said to the two disciples traveling to Emmaus: “O foolish men, and slow of heart to believe in all that the prophets have spoken!” (ibid.)?

What more will you demand? Is such great and clear authority not enough for you—the authority by which Christ bore witness distinctly, not confusedly, to the law of Moses, to the Prophets, and to the Psalms, teaching first that the writings of the Law, then those of the Prophets, and finally those of the Psalms concerning him had to be fulfilled in him?

Although what I have already said fully suffices to confirm the authority of the Old Scripture, I shall nevertheless produce from the same Gospel, which you believe, testimonies—abundantly and individually—bearing witness to the divine books, so that, once you have heard them, you may not only believe those books to be divine but may also be ashamed that you ever doubted any part of them.

And, to begin at the head of those sacred books, recall, if you do not remember, how Christ bears witness to the book of Genesis and brings forward many testimonies from it to confirm his own words.

“As it was,” he says, “in the days of Noah, so will be the coming of the Son of Man. They were eating and drinking, marrying and being given in marriage, until the day on which Noah entered the ark; and the flood came and destroyed them all” (Luke 17).

Again: “As it happened in the days of Lot, they were buying and selling, planting and building. But on the day when Lot went out from Sodom, fire and sulfur rained from heaven and destroyed them all” (ibid.).

The beginning of the Gospel according to Matthew also affirms this and bears witness to the same book when, in a fitting narrative, it joins together the book of the generation of Jesus Christ through Abraham, Isaac, Jacob, Judah, and Phares—all of whom are taken from the same book of Genesis.

Proceed from there to Exodus and hear Christ appealing to that book as a witness against the Sadducees: “That the dead rise, Moses showed beside the bush when he says that the Lord is the God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob” (Luke 20).

Again, from the same book: “Your fathers ate manna in the wilderness, and they died” (John 6). For that book, before all the others, relates that God rained manna upon the Hebrews for forty years (Exod. 16).

Again, in that book: “You shall not break a bone of it” (Exod. 12; John 19).

And again the Apostle says: “Nor become idolaters, as some of them did, as it is written: The people sat down to eat and drink, and rose up to play” (Exod. 32; 1 Cor. 10).

Come next to Leviticus, and you will hear Christ say to the leper whom he had commanded: “Go, show yourself to the priest, and offer the gift which Moses commanded, for a testimony to them” (Lev. 14; Luke 5).

From there extend your step to the book of Numbers, and you will hear Christ drawing from it a testimony and likeness of his Passion: “As Moses,” he says, “lifted up the serpent in the wilderness, so must the Son of Man be lifted up” (Num. 21; John 3).

And the Apostle says: “Nor let us tempt Christ, as some of them tempted him and perished by serpents. Nor murmur, as some of them murmured and perished by the destroyer” (Num. 21; 1 Cor. 10).

Come also to the final book of the Pentateuch—that is, of the Mosaic Law—which is called Deuteronomy, meaning “the second law”—and you will hear Christ producing many testimonies from it in the Gospel.

Among these are the words he answered to the devil when he was being tempted: “It is written: Man does not live by bread alone, but by every word of God” (Deut. 8; Matt. 4).

And again: “It is written: You shall not tempt the Lord your God.”

Then: “Go away, Satan; for it is written: You shall worship the Lord your God, and him alone shall you serve” (ibid.).
