And this saying: “My house shall be called a house of prayer” (Matt. 21; Luke 19).

Do you still see that the books which Christ so approves must not be rejected; that they are not false or apocryphal, since Truth bears witness to them; that they must not be cast aside, since the very Word eternal, the very Wisdom of God, strengthens his own words by them?

After these, let the other divine and prophetic books follow. The first of them is the one called Joshua, to which authority is given by Deuteronomy itself, the immediately preceding book that earned authority from the Gospel.

For in it is written: “The Lord commanded Joshua son of Nun and said: Be strong and courageous. For you shall bring the children of Israel into the land that I promised, and I shall be with you” (Josh. 1).

The Psalms also give it authority—those Psalms which, as I said above, were written concerning Christ, with Christ himself as witness, and bear prophetic testimony to him in truth.

For in them it is written: “And he drove out the nations before them, and divided their land among them by lot, by the measuring line of distribution” (Ps. 77).

Again, in those same Psalms: “The sea saw and fled; the Jordan turned back” (Ps. 113).

And, with a verse intervening: “What is the matter with you, O sea, that you fled? And you, Jordan, that you turned back?” (ibid.)

The sea fled through the power of God exercised through Moses (Exod. 13); the Jordan turned back through the operation of the same God through Joshua (Josh. 3). This is nowhere read except in the very book of Joshua, which is under discussion.

But elsewhere too, in the Psalms already mentioned, it is written figuratively: “I will remember Rahab and Babylon, those who know me” (Ps. 86).

The Gospel itself confirms this not figuratively but historically: “Naasson,” it says, “begot Salmon; and Salmon begot Boaz by Rahab” (Matt. 1).

Rahab is recorded only in this book as having hidden the messengers of Joshua—namely, the spies of the land of Canaan—and by her skill or counsel sent them safely back to the one who had dispatched them; and on this account she deserved salvation together with her entire household and association with the people of Israel (Josh. 2).

Next follows the book of Judges. The book immediately preceding it, which we have discussed and which has already been proved by the testimonies written above to belong to the canon, makes this book canonical as well.

For it is written in it: “Israel served the Lord throughout all the days of Joshua and of the elders who lived a long time after him, and who knew all the works of the Lord that he had done in Israel” (Judg. 2).

This clearly designates the leaders and judges who governed Israel after him.

The frequently mentioned Psalms also bear witness to the authority of the book of Judges, when they enumerate in part the foreigners and oppressors of the people of God during the period of the judges.

For thus it is read in them: “They conspired together with one accord against you; the tents of Edom and the Ishmaelites, Moab and the Hagarenes, Gebal, Ammon, and Amalek; foreigners together with the inhabitants of Tyre. Assur also came with them; they became an aid to the sons of Lot. Do to them as to Midian and Sisera, as to Jabin at the torrent of Kishon. They perished at Endor; they became like dung for the earth. Set their princes like Oreb and Zeeb, and Zebah and Zalmunna” (Ps. 82).

And if the Apostle is consulted—whose every word, as has been proved above, necessity itself compels you to trust completely—you will hear him in the Epistle to the Hebrews proclaiming the faith of these judges among the other Fathers and granting canonical authority to the same book, when he says: “And what more shall I say? For time will fail me if I tell of Gideon, Barak, Samson, Jephthah” (Heb. 11). These men certainly governed the same Jews before kings ruled over them, not under the name of kings but of judges.

Next comes the small book of Ruth, confirmed by the Gospel itself, as appears in the genealogy of the Savior: “Boaz,” it says, “begot Obed by Ruth” (Matt. 1).

Since she was a foreign woman, only that book explains how she was joined to a Jewish man; and that book, as has been said, earned canonical authority from the Gospel.

From here let our discourse hasten to the books of Samuel and Kings, and demonstrate equally to believers and unbelievers that they are most firmly supported not only by prophetic but also by evangelical authority.

Is not the very beginning of the Gospel enough to overthrow any machine of hostile resistance, however strongly fortified, when throughout the whole world it is read in an evangelical and heavenly voice: “The book of the generation of Jesus Christ, son of David” (ibid.)?

For when the Son of God is proclaimed to be the son of David, what could more exalt either David himself or the history written about him?

Although it is a great thing, for the commendation of David’s person and of the history written about him, that the evangelist relates Jesus Christ to be David’s son, it is greater—indeed greatest—that the same Son of God confirms himself to be David’s son.

For when he asked the Pharisees whose son they said Christ was, and they answered, “David’s,” he set before them a riddle concerning Christ’s divinity. Since they could not understand and solve it, as the Gospel says, “No one was able to answer him a word” (Matt. 22).

Is it not sufficient for the fullest authority of those books that almost their entire sequence is filled with accounts of so great a man, so exalted a king, so divine a prophet, or that the whole genealogy of the Savior, beginning with David, is recorded in them as in the Gospel down to the migration to Babylon?

Will it be necessary to bring forward the Savior’s own words and establish their authority from them? But why should shameless or foolish rashness weary us?

Let the words of saving Truth come, then—come, I say—to confuse and refute it more and more, and to bring testimony from truthful books against liars, unless they repent.

When the children in the temple were crying, “Hosanna to the Son of David” (Matt. 21), and the Pharisees were saying to Christ, “Do you hear what these are saying?” (ibid.), and he answered them, “Have you never read: From the mouth of infants and nursing children you have perfected praise?” (Ps. 8; Matt. 21), did he not both confirm the children’s words, teach that he was the son of David, exalt David, and confer canonical authority upon the books that contain David’s deeds?

Hear him, nevertheless, also producing testimonies from those same books and thereby commending their authority more and more.

When his disciples were going through the grainfields on the Sabbath, plucking ears of grain and eating them, and the Pharisees said, “Behold, your disciples are doing what is not lawful for them to do on the Sabbaths” (Mark 2; Luke 6), he answered: “Have you not read what David did when he was hungry, he and those who were with him—how he entered the house of God and ate the bread of the Presence, which it was not lawful to eat except for the priests alone?” (ibid.)

Again, in another place, he said to the same Pharisees: “I tell you, there were many widows in Israel in the days of Elijah, when a great famine occurred in the land, when the heaven was shut up for three years and six months; and Elijah was sent to none of them except to a widow at Zarephath of Sidon” (Luke 4).

“And there were many lepers in Israel under Elisha the prophet, and none of them was cleansed except Naaman the Syrian” (2 Kings 4; Luke 4).

Behold, Truth produced all these things from the books of Kings and thereby showed that they are truthful.

From there let the discourse proceed to the prophets, and first let the Gospel itself bear witness to the evangelical prophet Isaiah.

“Jesus,” it says, “came to Nazareth, where he had been brought up, and entered the synagogue according to his custom on the Sabbath day. And he rose to read, and the book of Isaiah the prophet was handed to him. And when he had unrolled the book, he found the place where it was written:

‘The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because he has anointed me; he has sent me to proclaim the Gospel to the poor, to heal the brokenhearted, to proclaim release to captives and sight to the blind, to set the oppressed free, to proclaim the acceptable year of the Lord and the day of recompense.’

“And when he had folded the book, he returned it to the attendant and sat down. And the eyes of all in the synagogue were fixed on him. Then he began to say to them: ‘Today this Scripture has been fulfilled in your hearing’” (Isa. 61; Luke 4).

Likewise, another evangelist says concerning the same book: “Jesus, knowing this, withdrew from there, and many followed him, and he healed them all. And he charged them not to make him known, so that what had been spoken through Isaiah the prophet might be fulfilled:

‘Behold, my servant whom I have chosen,  
in whom my soul is well pleased.  
I will put my Spirit upon him,  
and he will proclaim judgment to the nations.  
He will not contend or cry aloud,  
nor will anyone hear his voice in the streets.  
A bruised reed he will not break,  
and a smoking wick he will not extinguish,  
until he brings judgment forth to victory;  
and in his name the nations will hope’” (Isa. 42; Matt. 12).

Likewise another evangelist says: “Although he had performed so many signs before them, they did not believe in him, so that the word of Isaiah the prophet might be fulfilled, which he spoke:

‘Lord, who has believed our report, and to whom has the arm of the Lord been revealed?’” (Isa. 53; John 12).

And again: “Therefore they could not believe, because Isaiah said again:

‘He blinded their eyes and hardened their heart, so that they should not see with their eyes, understand with their heart, turn, and I should heal them.’

Isaiah said these things when he saw his glory and spoke concerning him” (Isa. 6; John 12).

Do you not think that this prophet ought to be accepted—one whom Christ accepts in this way, whose book he reads, whose prophetic words he shows to have been fulfilled in himself, whom the evangelists use in such frequent and manifold testimonies, and whose prophetic words they employ so greatly to establish their own evangelical words?

Jeremiah follows. The Gospel does not fail to state that he is truly a prophet and that his words are to be received as prophetic. For when the Lord asked his disciples whom people said the Son of Man was, they answered: “Some say John the Baptist, others Elijah, others Jeremiah, or one of the prophets” (Matt. 16).

Again, concerning the silver thrown down by the traitor Judas, and the field of the potter purchased by the priests with it as a burial place for strangers, the evangelist says: “Then was fulfilled what was spoken through Jeremiah the prophet:

‘And they took the thirty pieces of silver, the price of him who was valued, whom they valued from the children of Israel, and gave them for the potter’s field, as the Lord directed me’” (Zech. 11; Matt. 27).

A similar testimony is also found in Zechariah.

And concerning the slaughter of the innocent children the same evangelist says: “Then was fulfilled what was spoken through Jeremiah the prophet:

‘A voice was heard in Ramah, weeping and great wailing: Rachel weeping for her children, and she would not be comforted, because they are not’” (Jer. 31; Matt. 2).

The apostolic words of Paul also make Ezekiel canonical. In the Second Epistle to the Corinthians he introduces God speaking from that prophet: “For I will dwell in them and walk among them; I will be their God, and they shall be my people” (Ezek. 11; 2 Cor. 6).

And in the Epistle to the Romans, using the words of the same prophet as though they were his own, the Apostle says: “The name of God is blasphemed among the nations because of you, as it is written” (Rom. 2)—understand, in that same prophet (Ezek. 36).

The same evangelical authority, so often mentioned, compels you to receive Daniel among the prophets and not to deny that his writings are prophetic. For Christ says in the Gospel: “When you see the abomination of desolation, spoken of by Daniel the prophet, standing in the holy place—let the reader understand” (Dan. 9; Matt. 24).

After these great and, as it were, principal prophets, let us proceed also to the Twelve who are called Minor—not because their authority is inferior, but because of the smaller size of their books—and let us prove that all of them are canonical, not collectively or confusedly, but individually and distinctly.

And so that they may be brought forward one by one in the order in which they were arranged by the Fathers and in which they are recited by the Church, let the merciful Savior bring forward in the Gospel, against the harsh Pharisees, a testimony concerning mercy from the prophet Hosea.

“Go,” he says, “and learn what this means: ‘I desire mercy and not sacrifice’” (Matt. 9, 12).

That prophet expressed it thus: “For I desired mercy and not sacrifice, and knowledge of God more than burnt offerings” (Hos. 6; Matt. 9).

And the Apostle says concerning the same prophet: “I will call ‘not my people’ ‘my people,’ and her who had not obtained mercy, ‘having obtained mercy.’ And it shall be, in the place where it was said to them, ‘You are not my people,’ there they shall be called sons of God” (Hos. 2; Rom. 9).

And concerning Joel, who follows Hosea, after the outpouring of the Holy Spirit promised by Christ in the Gospel to the disciples and bestowed on the day of Pentecost, the Apostle Peter says to the Jews in the Acts of the Apostles:

“This is what was spoken through the prophet Joel:

‘And it shall be in the last days, says the Lord: I will pour out from my Spirit upon all flesh, and your sons and your daughters shall prophesy. Your young men shall see visions, and your old men shall dream dreams’” (Joel 2; Acts 2), together with the rest, which I do not write because of its length.

The often-mentioned book of Kings, established by evangelical authority, bears witness to the prophet Amos, who follows Joel. For what is recorded as having happened is foretold in this prophet.

Thus he says: “For three crimes of Damascus, and for four, I will not turn it back, because he threshed Gilead with iron threshing-sledges. And I will send fire upon the house of Hazael, and it shall devour the houses of Ben-hadad, and I will break the bar of Damascus” (Amos 1).

Concerning these things the prophet Elisha says to Hazael himself in the book of Kings: “I know the evils that you will do to the children of Israel. You will burn their fortified cities with fire, kill their young men with the sword, dash their little ones to pieces, and rip open their pregnant women” (2 Kings 8).

There too the account of Ben-hadad and Damascus and of Hazael’s evils, by which he nearly crushed Israel, is fully recorded.

Concerning Obadiah the same Apostle says in the First Epistle to the Corinthians: “I will destroy the wisdom of the wise, and reject the understanding of the prudent” (Obad. 1; 1 Cor. 1).

And who has not heard—indeed, who has not stored deep in his heart—what the Savior says in the Gospel concerning Jonah? Comparing his death and resurrection with Jonah’s shipwreck and escape, he says to the Jews:

“No sign will be given to you except the sign of Jonah the prophet. For as Jonah was in the belly of the sea-monster for three days and three nights, so will the Son of Man be in the heart of the earth for three days and three nights” (Jonah 2; Matt. 12).

And again: “The men of Nineveh will rise in judgment with this generation and condemn it, because they repented at the preaching of Jonah; and behold, something greater than Jonah is here” (Jonah 3; Matt. 12).

Among all the prophecies concerning Christ, what prophecy resounds more clearly in the Gospel than that of the prophet Micah? When Christ was born in Bethlehem, the chief priests and scribes of the people, questioned by Herod, brought it forward:

“And you, Bethlehem, land of Judah, are by no means least among the rulers of Judah; for from you shall come forth for me one who is to rule Israel, whose going forth is from the beginning, from the days of eternity” (Mic. 5; Matt. 2).

After these let the prophet Nahum come, whose testimony the Apostle uses in the Epistle to the Romans: “How beautiful,” he says, “are the feet of those who proclaim peace, who proclaim good things!” (Rom. 10.)

Although with a few words altered, Nahum says: “Behold, upon the mountains, the feet of one announcing and proclaiming peace” (Nah. 1).

Isaiah produced this testimony in almost the same words, though in one and the same verse (Isa. 52), because it is not a multiple or different Spirit, but one and the same Spirit, who spoke through Isaiah, Nahum, and all the prophets.

Therefore, because both spoke the same thing through the same Spirit, the Apostle’s testimony has been taken from both.

To whom throughout the whole world has the authority of the prophet Habakkuk not become known, since the account is both frequently read and gladly heard of his being carried by an angel by the lock of his hair from Judaea to Babylon, and there providing Daniel, shut up in the lions’ den, with the meal he had prepared for the reapers? But if this seems insufficient according to blessed Jerome, because it is not found in the Hebrew books, [Col. 0747C] let the Apostle come forward in his customary manner and, by a testimony drawn from him, prove that he is a divine and truthful prophet, not a false one. Thus in the Epistle to the Romans and in that to the Hebrews he says: “As it is written”—that is, of course, in this prophet—“the righteous person lives by faith” (Hab. 1; Rom. 1; Heb. 10).

Moreover, concerning both Zephaniah, who came after him, and Isaiah, the Apostle says in the Epistle to the Romans: “The remnant of the children of Israel shall be saved” (Rom. 9). Zephaniah, explaining the same thought in his own words, says: “The remnant of Israel shall hope in the name of the Lord.” Isaiah says: “In truth a remnant shall return” (Zeph. 3)—the remnant, I say, of Jacob—to the mighty God (Isa. 10). [Col. 0747D]

Further, the very evangelical truth bears witness to the prophet Haggai when it says: “After the deportation to Babylon, Jeconiah begot Shealtiel; and Shealtiel begot Zerubbabel” (Matt. 1). Sent by God to this Zerubbabel, the prophet says: “Take courage, Zerubbabel, says the Lord; and take courage, Joshua son of Jehozadak, great priest; and take courage, all people of the land, says the Lord of hosts, and act, because I am with you, says the Lord of hosts” (Hag. 2). For the prophet of the Lord was sent to strengthen the ruler and the people for rebuilding the house of God which the Chaldaeans had destroyed.

The Apostle likewise, in the Epistle to the Hebrews, brings forward a distinguished testimony from Haggai’s text in confirmation of certain great matters which he was discussing: “Yet once more, and in a little while, [Col. 0748A] I will shake heaven and earth, sea and dry land; and I will shake all nations, and the Desired One of all nations shall come” (Hag. 2; Heb. 12).

Let the order of the books and of time join to him his companion Zechariah, whose testimony the Gospel solemnly quotes: “Rejoice exceedingly, daughter of Zion; shout aloud, daughter of Jerusalem. Behold, your king comes to you, righteous and a Saviour: he is humble and riding upon an ass, and upon a colt, the foal of an ass” (Zech. 9; Matt. 21; John 12). The Lord himself, near his Passion in the same Gospel, adopting the words of the same prophet, says to his disciples: “It is written: I will strike the shepherd, and the sheep shall be scattered” (Zech. 13; Matt. 26). Again, the Gospel says of the same prophet: “They shall look on him whom they pierced” (Zech. 12; John 19). [Col. 0748B]

Last in the order of the twelve prophets, but not inferior in authority, comes Malachi. The Apostle pleasingly recalls almost the prophet’s first words in the Epistle to the Romans: “Jacob I loved, but Esau I hated” (Mal. 1; Rom. 9). And the Saviour himself, speaking in the Gospel about John the Baptist, says to the crowds and disciples: “This is he of whom it is written: Behold, I send my messenger, who shall prepare the way before my face” (Mal. 3; Matt. 11). By employing this testimony, the Saviour shows that one whom he judged worthy to receive, not secretly but publicly, must not be rejected.

From this point let the discourse proceed to the remarkable Job. Though not a Jew but a Gentile, he was nevertheless pre-eminently praised by the mouth of God; and after the prophets let the apostolic voice bear testimony to this prophetic man. For the Apostle, saying, “The wisdom of this world is foolishness with God” (1 Cor. 3), adds: “For it is written: I will catch the wise in their craftiness” (Job 5; ibid.). Certainly he adduces this from no Scripture other than the Book of Job.

Ezekiel also, whom we have already proved authentic, bears witness to Job’s book when, mentioning Job’s righteousness, he speaks in the person of the Lord: “If I send pestilence upon the land and pour out my indignation upon it in blood, so as to remove man and beast from it; and Noah, Daniel, and Job are in its midst, as I live, says the Lord God, they shall not deliver son or daughter, but they themselves shall deliver their souls by their righteousness” (Ezek. 14).

Now, although I have fully demonstrated above the authority of the Psalms, yet because the sequence of the divine books has brought them forward here, let further testimonies from the Gospel be added, bearing ever stronger witness to their majesty. The Saviour often uses them; and although he needs no one’s testimony in order to establish the credibility of his words, he nevertheless often confirms those words by the Psalms, as was said above. Hence is that passage which, as I previously said, he put before the Pharisees: “The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand until I make your enemies the footstool of your feet” (Ps. 109; Matt. 22). [Col. 0748D]

And hence also is the passage where, after the parable of the vineyard and the murdered heir, and the destruction of the murderers, when the same Pharisees said, “He will miserably destroy the wicked men” (Matt. 21), he replied: “Have you never read: The stone which the builders rejected has become the head of the corner. This was done by the Lord, and it is marvellous in our eyes?” (Ps. 117; ibid.). The Evangelist too, drawing a testimony from them, confirms their dignity when he says: “Jesus spoke all these things to the crowds in parables, and without parables he did not speak to them, so that what was spoken through the Prophet might be fulfilled: I shall open my mouth in parables; I shall utter things hidden from the foundation of the world” (Ps. 77; Matt. 13). [Col. 0749A]

Since the authority of the Psalms shines, as it were, from the very summit of heaven’s firmament through these and countless other witnesses and testimonies, let the pen hasten after David and his Psalms to Solomon and his books, and show Christ himself in the Gospel bearing witness to his wisdom: “The queen of the south shall rise in judgment [Col. 0749B] with this generation and condemn it, because she came from the ends of the earth to hear Solomon’s wisdom; and behold, one greater than Solomon is here” (3 Kgs. 10; Luke 17).

The same Saviour also bore testimony to Solomon’s books when, standing in the temple on the great day of the feast, he cried out: “If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink” (John 7). And, in a testimony drawn from Solomon’s books: “He who believes in me,” he says, “as the Scripture says, rivers of living water shall flow from his belly” (ibid.). The Apostle too, taking certain things from Proverbs in the Epistle to the Hebrews, says: “My son, do not neglect your father’s discipline, nor grow weary when you are rebuked by him. For God chastens the one whom he loves; indeed, he scourges every son whom he receives” (Prov. 3; Heb. 11). Likewise, from the same books of Solomon, he says in the Epistle to the Romans: “Vengeance is mine, and I will repay” (Ecclus. 28; Rom. 12).

But the Book of Kings, which, as I showed above, Christ placed in the citadel of the canon, bears witness to Solomon’s extraordinary wisdom and to his often-mentioned books in these words: “God gave Solomon wisdom and understanding exceedingly great, and breadth of heart like the sand which is on the seashore. And Solomon’s wisdom surpassed the wisdom of all the Eastern peoples and of the Egyptians; and he was wiser than all men—wiser than Ethan the Ezrahite, and Heman, and Chalcol, and Darda, the sons of Mahol” (3 Kgs. 4).

It gives this testimony to his books—namely Proverbs, Ecclesiastes, the Songs, that is, the Song of Songs, and the rest: “Solomon spoke three thousand parables, and his songs were five thousand; and he discoursed about trees, from the cedar that is in Lebanon to the hyssop that grows out of the wall. He also discoursed about beasts, reptiles, birds, and fish” (ibid.). [Col. 0749C]

The Book which is called in Hebrew *Dabrehaiamin*, in Greek *Paralipomenon*, and in Latin “Words of the Days,” is also attested by the often-mentioned Book of Kings, which assigns it authority equal to its own by frequently referring its readers to it. For, in treating and recounting the deeds of the kings of Judah and Israel, it adds of almost all of them: “Now the rest of the acts of this or that king, are they not written in the Book of the Words of the Days of the Kings of Judah, or in the Book of the Words of the Days of Israel?” (2 Chron. 25).

The greatest of the prophets, Isaiah, also establishes the canonical standing of Ezra’s volume, by showing that things which he himself foretold many centuries beforehand came to pass there. For Isaiah says, introducing God as speaking: “I who say to Cyrus: You are my shepherd, and you shall fulfil all my will; who say to Jerusalem: You shall be built; and to the temple: You shall be founded” (Isa. 44). And immediately afterward: “Thus says the Lord to Cyrus, my anointed” (Isa. 45). After inserting some words concerning Cyrus, God turns his speech to Cyrus himself and says to him: “I will go before you and humble the glorious ones of the earth. I will break bronze gates and shatter iron bars; and I will give you hidden treasures and secret mysteries” (ibid.). He adds the reason why he confers such power upon him: “That you may know,” he says, “that I am the Lord, the God of Israel, who calls you by name, for the sake of my servant Jacob and Israel my chosen one” (ibid.). [Col. 0750A]

That is, Cyrus is to bring the seventy-year Babylonian captivity to its end and, after sending the people of Israel back from it to their homeland, cause Jerusalem and the temple destroyed by the Chaldaeans to be rebuilt and founded again, as the testimony already cited confirms, where God says: “I who say to Jerusalem: You shall be built; and to the temple: You shall be founded.” Ezra’s book sets out in order how all these things were fulfilled and weaves from them the entire fabric of its history. Jeremiah too had foretold this rebuilding of the city and temple after the seventy years of captivity, as is clear to readers.

Ezra therefore recounts in his own time the fulfilment of Isaiah’s and Jeremiah’s prophecy, as appears sufficiently from the very beginning of his book: “In the first year of Cyrus king of the Persians, that the word of the Lord from the mouth of Jeremiah might be fulfilled, God stirred up the spirit of Cyrus king of the Persians, and he proclaimed throughout his entire kingdom, even in writing: Thus says Cyrus king of the Persians: The Lord God of heaven has given me all the kingdoms of the earth, and he himself has commanded me to build him a house in Jerusalem, which is in Judaea. Who is there among you from all his people? May his God be with him. Let him go up to Jerusalem, which is in Judaea, and build the house of the Lord God of Israel. For he is the God who is in Jerusalem. And in every place where any of the rest live, let the men of that place help him with silver, gold, goods, and livestock, besides what they voluntarily offer to the temple of God which is in Jerusalem” (1 Ezra 1). [Col. 0750B]

Last among the Hagiographa—that is, the books of Holy Scripture—comes the Book of Esther. The authority of the other Hagiographa confers authority upon it. For if those books, deriving their origin from the Hebrew truth, had this book as their companion and of equal authority in the same Hebrew canon, it follows that all should equally be received, with none of those books excepted. Moreover, not only Christian but Jewish writings themselves bear witness that, in the order written above, all the books from Job through the Book of Esther now under discussion—Esther not excluded but included—are of equal authority. [Col. 0750C]

Therefore all ought to have been received equally, without any distinction. And since this is so, when Christ, the apostles, and the prophets gave authority by their testimonies to the preceding books and to books equal in standing to this one, compelling reason leaves no doubt that they conferred a similar dignity upon this book also.

After these authentic books of Holy Scripture remain six books that must not be passed over: Wisdom, Jesus son of Sirach, Tobit, Judith, and the two books of Maccabees. Although these could not attain the lofty rank of the foregoing books, they deserved reception by the Church because of their praiseworthy and highly necessary teaching. There is no need for me to labour to commend them to you. For if the Church has any value in your eyes, something—at least a little—must be accepted by you on its authority. But if, as Christ said of the Jews concerning Moses, you do not believe that Church, how will you believe my words? (John 5.) [Col. 0751A]

Behold, you who said that you believed only the Gospel: I now ask you to believe only the Gospel. For, as I said at the outset, if you believe the Gospel alone, you will necessarily believe this entire Old Testament which you hear. For the Gospel bears witness to all those whom I have named above and gives them canonical authority when it confirms its own sayings by their sayings. But perhaps you will say that the Gospel has not drawn testimonies from every one of the preceding books. Yet are not testimonies drawn from the Gospel when they are drawn from those books from which the Gospel itself adduces testimonies? Will not a book be judged truthful and canonical when it receives the praise of truth from one to which Truth bears witness? If, I say, prophets and Psalms obtain canonical authority not only from themselves [Col. 0751B] but also from the Gospel, why cannot they confer that same authority upon the books to which they bear witness? Or does the Gospel not err when it bears witness to prophets or Psalms, while prophets or Psalms lie when they bear witness to others?

Do not even secular testimonies recognize this principle: that someone shown to be praiseworthy may by his testimony prove others to be praiseworthy as well? By this reasoning we prove books from books: the earlier from the later and the later from the earlier; divine, canonical, and authentic. And by their authority, in accordance with the Apostle, we cast down, destroy, and trample underfoot every knowledge exalting itself against the height of God (1 Cor. 10). [Col. 0751C]

Thus, when you have believed all these books of which we have spoken, you will believe, as you said, the Gospel alone. Therefore, since authentic authority has been assigned to the remaining books of the New Testament by the Gospel alone, in which alone you believed, and to all the books of the Old Testament by the New Testament itself, we must now, with God’s Spirit going before, pursue the matter with which I began in addressing you.

The proof of the first chapter set forth above follows in order.

And because, among the five propositions put forward, the first was that which argues concerning the baptism of little children, let the discourse return to that point, so that, now that evangelical, apostolic, and prophetic authority has confirmed both this point and the others—and you can no longer resist these authorities—the heretical error may cease. We must surely consider whether one person has been saved by another’s faith, as you deny. [Col. 0752A]

The royal official in the Gospel, requesting his son’s health, heard from the Lord: “Go; your son lives.” “The man believed the word which Jesus spoke to him, and went” (John 4). And what follows? “As he was now going down, his servants met him and brought word, saying: Yesterday at the seventh hour the fever left him” (ibid.). What then? “The man therefore knew that it was at that hour at which Jesus said to him: Your son lives” (ibid.).

To the centurion pleading for his paralysed servant, after highly praising his faith, the same Saviour says: “Go, and as you have believed, let it be done to you” (Matt. 8). And it is immediately added: “And the servant was healed in that hour.” To the ruler of the synagogue pleading for his daughter near death, he says: “Only believe, and she shall be saved.” Shortly afterward, when he had entered and taken the hand of the girl, now dead, he said: “Girl, arise.” And she arose, and he ordered that food be given her (Mark 5; Luke 8).

To another who pleaded for his demon-possessed son, he said: “If you can believe, all things are possible to one who believes” (Mark 9). And he said: “I believe, Lord; help my unbelief” (ibid.). To Martha, who said concerning Lazarus dead four days, “Lord, he already stinks, for it is now the fourth day” (John 11; the citation’s “John II” appears erroneous), he says: “Did I not tell you that, if you believed, you would see the glory of God?” (ibid.). To the Canaanite woman pleading for her daughter, he says: “O woman, great is your faith; let it be done to you as you wish” (Matt. 15). And the Gospel continues: “And her daughter was healed from that hour” (ibid.). [Col. 0752B]

“But perhaps you will say: Since the question is about the souls of baptized little children—whether they are cleansed from sins through baptism—why do you set before us bodily healings?” Rightly, I say; for when I show that the bodies of some persons are cured through the faith of others by the same Creator of souls and bodies, I show that the souls of some are cleansed through the faith of others. For it is impious to believe that the Saviour healed bodies while leaving souls aside, since he is especially called the Saviour of souls, and every healing of bodies performed among humankind by him was a grace bestowed upon souls.

Yet, God granting it, I shall not lack proof that, as flesh, so also the human spirit was saved by him. I would demonstrate this by the words of holy teachers, had they not withdrawn from the discussion after you presented me with your bill of repudiation. Christ was once teaching the crowds in a house, and the Word of God himself was preaching the word of God to mortals. [Col. 0752C] Some men came bringing a paralysed man lying on a bed. Since, as the Gospel says, they could not bring him in because of the crowd, they went up upon the roof and lowered him through the tiles into the midst before Jesus. “When he saw their faith, he said: Your sins are forgiven you” (Matt. 9; Mark 2; Luke 5). When some took offence at this saying, he said: “That you may know that the Son of Man has authority on earth to forgive sins,” he said to the paralytic: “Rise, take up your bed, and go to your house.” And he rose and went to his house (ibid.). [Col. 0752D]

What have you to say to these things? Behold, I have brought this forward not from Augustine but from the Gospel. Since you claim especially to believe it, either finally concede that some may be saved through the faith of others, or, if you can, deny that what I have presented comes from the Gospel. Behold, the royal official’s faith, pleading not for himself but for his son, is heard. The centurion’s faith, humbly interceding not for himself but for his servant, is not merely heard but extolled with singular praise. The synagogue ruler’s daughter rises not through her own faith but through her father’s. The demon-possessed person is healed not through his own faith but through his father’s. Because Martha believes, she sees God’s glory in Lazarus’s resurrection. The Canaanite woman, praying not for herself but for her daughter grievously tormented by a demon, hears: “Let it be done to you as you wish.”

Through the faith of those who carried him, Christ not only heals the paralytic but also forgives his sins; and the Saviour, full of mercy, saves not half but the whole person. Christ, I say, grants such great things to others through the faith of one believer, and will the faith of the whole Church avail nothing for baptized little children? What then is the meaning of the Lord’s saying which I wrote above: “All things are possible to one who believes”? What also is the meaning of his saying elsewhere: “If anyone does not waver in his heart, whatever he says shall come to pass, it shall be done for him” (Matt. 11)? [Col. 0753A] What of this: “Amen I say to you: whatever you ask in prayer, believe that you receive it, and it shall be done for you” (Matt. 17)? And what of that well-known saying: “If you have faith as a grain of mustard seed, you will say to the mountain, ‘Move into the sea,’ and it shall move” (ibid.)?

If all things are certainly possible to one believer, they cannot be impossible to the whole world believing and praying for baptized little children. The royal official believes, and his son is saved. Martha believes, and Lazarus is raised. The world believes, and a little child is saved. A father believes, and his daughter rises. A Canaanite woman believes, and her daughter is cleansed of a demon. The Church believes, and a soul is cleansed of sins. The centurion believes, and not only is his servant healed, but his faith is set above that of Israel. Those who brought the paralytic believe that Christ can heal his body, and both his soul and body are healed. Each day those who bring little children believe on their behalf; and while the body is washed with visible baptism, their souls are cleansed from sins by the invisible power of the Spirit. [Col. 0753B]

And who can gather from the Gospel every example like these? The faith of those standing by prays to the Lord for Peter’s mother-in-law, sick with fever; standing over her, he commands the fever and dismisses it. And what follows? “When the sun had set, all who had sick persons with various diseases brought them to him, and they were healed” (Mark 1). Here, amid so great a multitude of sick persons, the individual faith of some is not plainly shown; rather, the faith of the people who brought them to the giver of salvation is openly commended. You see, therefore, that Christ healed by another’s faith not only the few sick persons whom I mentioned above at different times, but also many at one moment [*sanatos*, “healed”; *salvatos*, “saved”].

If I turn after the Gospels to the narrative of the Acts of the Apostles, Peter, first of the Apostles, comes before us. At the disciples’ request, through the faith and prayers of the widows, he raised the dead Tabitha (Acts 11), and he himself later came out of Herod’s custody and chains through the Church’s faith and prayer (Acts 12). How greatly another person’s faith can benefit others is shown by the streets of Jerusalem, into which, as that Scripture says, “a multitude of believing men and women cast out the sick and laid them on beds and pallets, so that, as Peter came, at least his shadow might overshadow some one of them, and they might be freed from their infirmities” (Acts 5). [Col. 0753C]

It adds: “A multitude also gathered from the cities around Jerusalem, bringing sick persons and those troubled by unclean spirits, and all were healed” (ibid.)—surely not so much by their own faith as by the faith of the peoples who brought them. “The unbelieving husband,” says the Apostle, “is saved through the believing wife, and the unbelieving wife is saved through the believing husband” (1 Cor. 7). If an unbelieving wife is saved by her husband’s faith and an unbelieving husband by his wife’s faith, why shall not the child of both be saved through the faith of husband and wife together? If those two, bound by a double chain, are freed by mutual faith, why is a little child—bound only by the original bond and, as regards himself, innocent—not freed by the faith of both parents and, as I have said, of the whole Church? Otherwise, according to this interpretation too, “their children would be unclean” (1 Cor. 7). But now they are holy. They would indeed be unclean if they had no parent, or person standing in a parent’s place, through whose mediation they could be imbued with the sacraments of faith and cleansed from the uncleanness of sins. [Col. 0754A]

But if I turn to the Old Testament, I shall show that by the faith of Abraham alone a great nation was chosen, taken up, and saved by God; that by the faith and prayers of Moses alone the same nation was often rescued from death; that by David’s faith and devotion his tribe and lineage were preferred above the other tribes and above the whole nation; that Samuel, Isaiah, Jeremiah, Daniel, and the rest bore the unbelief and perversity of an unbelieving people by their faith and conduct; that holy Job pleaded with God for his children by faith and daily sacrifices; that the Maccabees faithfully fought for God’s people; and that absolutely all the Fathers of both Testaments strove to perfect the imperfections of the imperfect through the perfection of their own faith and charity, supplying in themselves what others lacked. [Col. 0754B]

Let reason now examine your very proposition. You said: “Neither baptism without personal faith, nor personal faith without baptism, could avail anything. For neither saves without the other.” To this I reply: I think it has been made clear to intelligent persons that baptism can sometimes save without personal faith. But I consider that it must be established by authority or reason that personal faith can sometimes save without baptism.

We read that many martyrs, forestalled by the onset of suffering, could not reach baptism and, before the saving washing, gave up their souls to death for Christ in fervent faith. What then, eminent teachers and venerators of evangelical words, will you say to this? In all your rashness, will you dare even to condemn the holy martyrs? Will you force the illustrious inhabitants of heaven to descend from on high and rejoice among the dead? Spare them, I say; spare at least these. Do not wish to mingle Christ with Belial, light with darkness, or saints with the ungodly.

If this does not please you, hear Christ saying: “Whoever has confessed me before people, I also shall confess him before my Father” (Mark 8; Luke 12); and: “Whoever hates his soul in this world shall keep it unto eternal life” (John 12); and: “Blessed are you when people hate you and persecute you” (Matt. 5); and: “Rejoice in that day and exult, for behold, your reward is great in heaven” (Luke 6). Hear also one of the elders speaking in the Apocalypse of John the Apostle: “These are those who have come from great tribulation, and have washed their robes and made them white in the blood of the Lamb. Therefore they are before the throne of God and serve him day and night in his temple” (Rev. 7), and the rest. [Col. 0754C]

Since in all these declarations Christ says nothing about baptism, those who did not indeed despise baptism but did not have the opportunity for it must be saved by faithful suffering alone. For, I think, you will not venture by any audacity to exclude from the kingdom of heaven those whom Christ confesses before his Father as confessing him here; or those who, hating their soul—that is, despising mortal life—keep it unto eternal life, that is, live eternally; or those who are blessed because people hate and persecute them; or those whose reward is said to be great in heaven; or those who are before God’s throne and serve him day and night in his temple.

But if perhaps, because we are compelled to suspect every blasphemy from you, you break out with your customary rashness even upon this point, then, as deniers of Christ and his Gospel, you will no longer be heretics to us, but, as was said above, heathens and tax collectors. If, however, you avoid this, you must believe Christ and his Gospel and acknowledge that martyrs can be saved without bodily baptism, by faith and martyrdom alone, in the manner I have described. For those who washed their robes in the Lamb’s blood, washing them from uncleanness and whitening them from the blackness of sins, could not have had unclean robes. [Col. 0755A]

If you grant this, you will say that some can be saved by personal faith without baptism. But if you say that some can be saved by personal faith without baptism, why will you not believe that some can be saved by baptism without personal faith? If martyrs are saved by their own faith without baptism, why shall little children not be saved by baptism without their own, as I have said, faith? Either, according to your new heresy, no one shall be saved without personal faith and baptism; or, if someone is saved by personal faith without baptism, then, consequently, someone shall be saved by baptism without personal faith. For they are equal and cannot outweigh one another: united, they accomplish the same things; separated, they are proclaimed in a like manner. Therefore, if, according to what has been set forth, one saves without the other, your proposition is shaken, in which you said: “Neither saves without the other.” [Col. 0755B]

But if, after the Jewish manner, you have resolved to cling altogether to the letter—which, unless it is understood carefully, kills even in the Gospel—explain at least what precedes in the chapter you have proposed. For the wording runs thus: “Go into the whole world; preach the Gospel to every creature” (Mark 16). Come then: according to the sound of the letter, it must be preached to every creature, rational and irrational, sentient and insentient. [Col. 0755C] It must be preached to heaven and earth, sun and moon, sea and air, birds and cattle, herbs and trees, timber and stones. It must without any distinction be preached to absolutely every creature in the world, lest Christ, who commanded the Gospel to be preached to every creature, be disobeyed.

What could be more insane? For I do not suppose that you have so lost your senses as to believe that Christ either preached or wished the Gospel to be preached to beings other than human beings. If this is so, then the bare sound of the letter must not be followed; it must be received and expounded soundly and catholicly. Either, according to the teachers of the Church whom, as I said, you have cast aside with impious boldness, man is denoted by the name “every creature” because he possesses something of every creature; or, by that well-known and customary form of speech in which the whole is taken for a part—one used almost continually by ordinary people—the whole mass of creation denotes only the human being, who alone was to be saved by the Gospel. [Col. 0756A]

For who does not use this manner of speech daily—indeed, continually? “You have lost everything; you have thrown everything into confusion; you have restored everything; you have saved everything; you do every good thing; you have done every good thing; everyone seeks you; everyone loves you.” Yet both the speaker and the person addressed understand these words to be said not universally but particularly. The speaker and hearer plainly know that not everything that exists was lost, thrown into confusion, restored, or saved by one person; that not every good thing was done by that one person; and that he is neither sought nor loved by everyone. But under the name of universality they understand a certain excellence of a part. [Col. 0756B]

Hence worldly sages also—poets and philosophers—as well as divine writers, prophets and apostles, retained similar forms of speech drawn from human custom. Christ used this form when he said: “Preach the Gospel to every creature.” If you grant this—and you cannot refuse it without denying the Gospel—you will necessarily grant that the Gospel is to be preached to human beings alone. Once this is granted, you will pass from the killing letter to the life-giving Spirit, and recognize that one must follow not always the sound of the letter but sometimes rather its meaning. [Col. 0756C]

Why say these things? Because, if you had attended to this; if you had preferred to bend your understanding to the Scriptures rather than bend the Scriptures to your understanding; if you had chosen to approach their interpretation with fear rather than arrogance—for understanding them is no small or commonplace task, since Christ, risen from the dead, opened the mind to understand the Scriptures not to just anyone, but to the Apostles (Luke 24)—if, I say, you had not scorned this, you would not have taken any pleasure in founding a new heresy or making yourselves notorious heresiarchs.

Nor would you have forced that saying of the Gospel, which I have often repeated and from which this heresy of yours arose, to serve your error and human destruction. For just as the Lord’s body brings eternal death to those who receive it unworthily, so the Lord’s word brings eternal death to those who understand it perversely. [Col. 0756D] You deceivers and those deceived by you have alike incurred it, unless you repent, when you rebaptized most wretched human beings in opposition to the Church’s one baptism.

For what other thing drove you to so monstrous a crime except the Gospel saying perversely understood: “Whoever does not believe shall be condemned” (Mark 16)? You thought that little children were bound by this chain: because they could not believe, baptism could not avail them. But it is not so. The sacred words themselves show it: they show it to those who see, not to the blind; to the humble, not to the proud. The Lord says: “Go into the whole world; preach the Gospel to every creature. Whoever believes and is baptized shall be saved; but whoever does not believe shall be condemned” (ibid.). [Col. 0757A]

These words terrify the obstinate; they do not condemn the innocent. They strike wrongdoing; they do not accuse an age without speech. They destroy despisers of grace; they do not condemn the simplicity of nature. The word “preach” shows this. For how is the Gospel to be preached to little children, who do not understand it; announced to those who do not grasp it; made known to those who do not perceive it? How, as the Apostle says concerning people of greater age, “shall they call upon him in whom they have not believed? Or how shall they believe him whom they have not heard?” (Rom. 10.) If those who have no preacher cannot believe, neither can those who lack the age for believing. [Col. 0757B]

If the former are excused from the fault of unbelief because a preacher is absent, the latter too are excused because infancy is less fitted to preaching. For if “faith comes by hearing, and hearing through the word of God” (ibid.), faith could not exist where there was no hearing, nor could hearing exist where Christ’s word did not sound forth. Original sin indeed keeps unbaptized little children from salvation; actual sin added to it drives them still further from it. But the guilt of faith despised cannot prevail to condemn either group, since, because they did not hear it, neither could they despise it. [Col. 0757C]

For the Lord is righteous and loves righteousness (Ps. 10). He never requires from anyone what that person has not committed, nor compels anyone to pay what is not owed—he who often pardons even the greatest debts.

Moderate, therefore, the excessive severity you have assumed; do not wish to seem more just than he whose “all ways are mercy and truth” [Col. 0757D] (Ps. 24); nor exclude from the kingdom of heaven the little children of whom he himself says: “For of such is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 19). For it is utterly unseemly and impious that we should deny to the children of Christians what we grant to the children of Jews. It is plainly wicked not to grant to the time of grace what was granted even to children of wrath; it is perverse to give such privileges to a people of slavery as are denied to the children of freedom. For the Law could not outweigh the Gospel, nor Moses Christ, since the former was a faithful servant, while the latter, according to the Apostle, was the only Son in the house (Heb. 3). Jewish children were circumcised on the eighth day by divine command (Lev. 12), and were cleansed from original sin. What faith had those children? What understanding did they have concerning the sacraments they received [Col. 0758A]? What knowledge of God? What profession of the mouth? Where are you who condemn Christian little children? The children of Jews are saved by the sacrament of circumcision, and shall the children of Christians not be saved by the sacrament of baptism? A Jew believes, and his son is cleansed from sin; a Christian believes, and his son shall not be freed from a like guilt? There is no faith in the children of Christians; but neither is there any faith in the children of Jews. Yet they are saved through another’s faith when they receive circumcision; these too are saved through another’s faith when they receive baptism. What voice, then, can remain for you? Will it dare ever again to mutter after being crushed beneath so great a weight of authority? If you are human, yield to reason; if Christians, submit to authority; [Col. 0758B] if seeing, acknowledge the light; if blind, at least grope in the darkness. Indeed, the truth convicting you is so plain that it can not only be proved but, if you wish, even touched.

It is known to all that circumcision held the place of baptism. What baptism confers in the Gospel, circumcision conferred in the Old Testament—except that it did not at once open the kingdom of heaven to those circumcised. This was reserved for him “who brings the bound one out of the prison-house,” who “opens and no one shuts, shuts and no one opens” (Rev. 3); who alone was the “Expectation of the nations,” and the king of the kingdom of heaven (Gen. 49). With Christ’s coming, sacrament was changed for sacrament, and by the author of grace the yoke of the Law was lightened, [Col. 0758C] so that, as the punishment of the flesh expiated the fault of the flesh, so without a wound of the flesh a light sprinkling of water might cleanse sins. The benefit bestowed by heavenly generosity was enlarged: as the whole Jewish people was saved by circumcision, so the whole world is saved by Christ’s baptism. Therefore, since a shadow cannot in any way appear superior to the body, nor a figure to the truth, you must necessarily confess that Christian children are saved by baptism, since you admit that Jewish children are saved by circumcision. And since, according to the Apostle, without faith it is impossible to please God, whether in circumcision or baptism (Heb. 11), and since, according to Psalm 31, all his works are in faith: because a Jewish child could not be saved by his own faith, he was saved [Col. 0758D] by another’s; and because a Christian child cannot be saved by his own faith, he is daily saved by another’s. Thus the Jew was saved through the sacrament of circumcision and another’s faith; the Christian is saved through the sacrament of baptism and another’s faith, by Christ’s grace. Therefore the proposition you advanced is false: “Neither baptism without one’s own faith, nor one’s own faith without baptism, saves.”

And so that this wicked opinion may be overwhelmed beneath a great heap of judgments, hear also the apostolic trumpet, crying out with such a sound that, since its voice has gone forth into all the earth, it is very strange if it could have passed your ears by. For, discussing the guilt of the first Adam which condemns the world, and the righteousness of the second Adam which saves the world, he says among other things in the Epistle to the Romans: “For if by one man’s offence death [Col. 0759A] reigned through one, much more those receiving abundance of grace and of the gift of righteousness shall reign in life through one, Jesus Christ” (Rom. 5). “Therefore, as by the offence of one [judgment came] upon all men unto condemnation, so also by the righteousness of one [the gift came] upon all men unto justification of life.” And in the First Epistle to the Corinthians: “By man came death, and by man the resurrection of the dead” (1 Cor. 15); and: “As in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive” (ibid.). What now? Is not the mouth of those speaking iniquity already stopped? Or, when this one and only apostolic weapon has pierced its canine throat, will it dare ever again to bark? He says that death reigned through one, but that those receiving abundance of grace shall reign in life through one Jesus Christ; [Col. 0759B] that through the offence of one man all human beings were condemned; through the righteousness of one, all human beings justified; that in Adam all are dead, and in Christ all are made alive.

Take heed, and lay aside the obstinacy that destroys you. He says “all”; he excludes no one. He speaks universally, not particularly. This is not the figure of which I spoke above, where the whole is taken for a part. To exclude that interpretation here, he supplied a comparison: “As,” he says, “unto all men unto condemnation, so unto all men unto justification of life.” And, “As all die, so all shall be made alive” (Rom. 5). Therefore, according to the Apostle’s wording and meaning, as all are condemned, so all are justified; and as all die, so all must be made alive. For the comparison requires that what is understood of the condemned be understood of the justified; and that what is believed concerning the dead likewise be believed concerning those made alive. Yet you do not deny the preceding clause: namely, that all human beings without any exception die in Adam, that all are condemned. If, then, both according to you and according to the Apostle, all are condemned in Adam and all die, then according to that same Apostle all are justified in Christ and all are made alive. For true is what he said: “As by the offence of one [judgment came] upon all men unto condemnation, so also by the righteousness of one [the gift came] upon all men unto justification of life”; and true is what he said: “As in Adam all die, so also in Christ shall all be made alive.”

[Col. 0759D] If this is so, then as all human beings were condemned through the offence of one, so little children too were condemned. And as all human beings were justified through the righteousness of one, so little children too were justified. And as all die in Adam, so little children all die. And as all are made alive in Christ, so little children all are made alive. Therefore it is heretical and impious to exclude baptized little children from the number of those who are saved: heretical, because it is contrary to right faith; impious, because it is contrary to piety. And lest even a small corner be left for your snares, it has been said that all little children indeed die in Adam, but none are made alive except in Christ. For the children of Jews, of pagans, or of those who despise the faith or sacraments of the Christian dispensation are not saved, because they remain [Col. 0760A] in their condemnation, Christ’s righteousness not coming to their aid; and in death, Christ’s life not raising them. This is plainly shown when he says that all are justified through the righteousness of one, and more plainly when he says that all are made alive in Christ. Since all children are condemned in Adam, unless they are justified in Christ, they perish. And since they die in Adam, unless they are made alive in Christ, they in no way rise from death. Therefore children have no righteousness unless they are justified in Christ, nor life unless they are made alive in Christ. But if they are aided by sacraments instituted by Christ, they do not remain unrighteous, because according to the authorities cited above all human beings are justified through the one Christ; nor do they remain dead, because all are made alive in Christ. [Col. 0760B] Either, then, deny that this condemnation and justification, death and resurrection, belong to all human beings, and you will exclude little children; or, if you grant that they belong to all, you will necessarily admit little children among all. You will admit, I say, those little children whom the blessed Apostle himself first placed among the condemned in order to admit them among those who are saved.

For it was fitting that a future heresy, even after so many ages, should not escape the notice of the prophetic Apostle, and that he should pierce it not only with common missiles but with a special dart. For he says: “Death reigned from Adam unto Moses, even over those who did not sin after the likeness of Adam’s transgression” (Rom. 5). Who are those who did not sin? Does not the divine utterance say of these very little children: “There is none upon earth without sin, not even an infant of one day” (Job 14:4, according to the Septuagint)? And has not this also passed from the mouth of that great man into the mouths of all Christians: “Behold, I was conceived in iniquities, and in sins my mother conceived me” (Ps. 50)?

And what need is there to surround a manifest matter with many testimonies? Certainly no one is without sin, if not even an infant of one day is without sin, nor an infant conceived in its mother’s womb without sin. For when he says, “I was conceived in iniquities,” he marks not merely the iniquity of the parents who conceived him, but penitently recalls also the sin of the one conceived, derived from the parents. For he would not ask God to have mercy on him for that in which he did not recognize the misery of sin. [Col. 0760D] Therefore, since no one can be without sin, while actual sin cannot be found in little children—because everyone who sins sins either originally or actually—little children, who could not sin actually, surely sinned originally. It is therefore concerning them that it was said: “Death reigned from Adam unto Moses, even over those who did not sin,” that is, who did not sin by actual sin but sinned by original sin. He teaches that this origin was drawn from the first human being and transmitted to all human beings when he adds: “after the likeness of Adam’s transgression.” For it is not their own transgression that makes little children guilty, as it made Adam himself guilty, but the likeness of Adam’s transgression.

Since, then, death reigns even over little children who have not [Col. 0761A] sinned, tell us, holy Apostle: are these little children to remain forever in the kingdom of death, or are they to be rescued from it through the aid of someone? For when you spoke of the condemnation of all human beings, you did not without cause add the condemnation of little children also. “I,” says the Apostle, “show both great and small human beings to be ungodly in Adam, in order that I may show them justified in Christ” (Rom. 5). I show them condemned in Adam, in order that I may show them saved in Christ. I show them dead in Adam, in order that I may show them made alive in Christ. I show that the former losses have through Christ not only been repaired but that, through superabounding grace, benefits have even been increased. “For the gift is not as the offence. For if many died through the offence of one, much more the grace and gift of God in the grace of one man, Jesus Christ, [Col. 0761B] abounded unto many. And the gift is not as through one sin. For judgment was from one unto condemnation, but grace from many offences unto justification” (ibid.).

And lest I seem too prolix to readers by examining these apostolic words one by one, I say briefly that this is the sum of the Apostle’s words: namely, that Christ’s grace has abounded more for salvation than Adam’s sin abounded for condemnation. Adam’s fault corrupted the whole offspring of his stock in its very root, and struck down at once the entire mass of the human race with the wound of original sin alone. But Christ’s righteousness, gift, and grace saved it not only from that plague called original, with which Adam had infected the world, but also from [Col. 0761C] all the actual sins which the world had added.

For this reason the Apostle mentions little children who did not sin and mingles them with the sinful mass, so that those numbered among the condemned through Adam may likewise be reckoned among those saved through Christ. And since superabounding, saving grace has remitted not only the world’s original evils but has forgiven actual ones also, whoever reads the Apostle should understand that little children, bound by a single chain, do not remain unloosed, since the chain of a double guilt could not hold the rest. Let the world learn this, let the heretic understand it, let the Catholic recognize it: reason itself compels that sinful little children cannot be excluded from the people of the Saviour, who “saves his people from [Col. 0761D] their sins” (Matt. 1), when even great sinners have deserved admission within the most ample bosom of his mercy.

And, oh, what a difference there is between kindness and malice, between piety and impiety, between Christ kindly receiving little children and heretics impiously repelling them. Long ago Christ’s disciples did something not indeed identical, but similar, in repelling little children from Christ; but they were rebuked by their master so that they should not do it. “Certain persons,” says the Gospel, “offered to him,” that is, to Christ, “little children, that he might touch them. But the disciples threatened those who offered them” (Matt. 19; Mark 10). Now, Lord Jesus, good master, teach us by your word—or rather, that I may venture still further, show us [Col. 0762A] by your example—whether little children who do not come to you by their own faith but are offered to you by another’s are to be received by you, as your Church teaches, or repelled, as the rashness of novel people commands. Your disciples indeed, as your Gospel says, threatened those who offered them; but how did you receive these threatening disciples? “When Jesus saw it,” it says, “he was indignant” (ibid.). Since, therefore, your disciples threatened those who offered little children, you were indignant; but what did you say to those who threatened them? “Allow the little children to come to me, and do not forbid them. For of such is the kingdom of heaven” (ibid.). You said this indeed; but what did you do? “Embracing them,” says the Gospel—that is, the little children—“and laying hands upon them, he blessed them” (ibid.).

What will you say to these things, cruel expellers of little children [Col. 0762B]? Behold: because little children were being repelled from him, Jesus was indignant; Jesus commanded that little children be allowed to come to him and not forbidden; Jesus said that the kingdom of heaven belongs to such; Jesus embraced them; Jesus laid his hands on them; Jesus blessed them. Will you dare any longer to repel childish innocence from Christ—not with manly steadfastness, but with obstinate malice? Will you tear little children away, against Christ’s own will, from Christ who embraces them, from Christ who lays hands upon them, from Christ who blesses them? Let the Church see; let the whole world judge to whom the kingdom of heaven ought rather to be shut: to you, who oppose the words of the king of heaven, or to little children, of whom the king himself says: [Col. 0762C] “For of such is the kingdom of heaven.”

## Against the Remaining Articles of the Petrobrusians

If enough has been said on these matters, let us now proceed to the subsequent points of the wicked Gospel according to you, and let us see how the most excellent Christians strive to build the Church of their Christ. For you do not merely refuse to permit the Church’s faith to remain unharmed, but you also labour to undermine its very buildings. And whereas Christ says, “Upon the rock I will build my Church” (Matt. 16); Peter, “You also, as living stones, are built up” (1 Pet. 2); Paul, “As a wise architect I laid the foundation” (1 Cor. 3); David, “Its foundations are upon the holy mountains” (Ps. 86); and [Col. 0762D] says a thousand such things—you attempt, by an equal ruin and with one impulse of your own strength, at once to overthrow both the spiritual works of so great builders and the walls wrought by the toil of stonecutters themselves. For, as I have said, you cannot long endure either the Church’s faith unharmed or its walls intact.

You preach that churches are built superfluously, because the Church of God does not consist in a multitude of stones joined together, but in the unity of gathered believers. You say that the Lord’s cross ought neither to be honoured nor adored, because the object which was the instrument of the Lord’s sufferings and death ought to be cast away rather than venerated; that an insensible object ought to be burnt with fire rather than invoked by foolish supplications. You assert that the Church does not possess the Lord’s body in the sacrament of the altar, and that whatever [Col. 0763A] priests do therein is wholly empty and has no effect of truth, because Christ gave it once only, not to future Christians forever, but solely to the disciples then present. You affirm that it is vain to pray or do anything good for the dead, because the good deeds of the living cannot assist those who, when they departed from here, carried away their whole merit, to which nothing can be added. You add that God is mocked by ecclesiastical songs, because he who delights only in holy affections can neither be summoned by loud voices nor charmed by musical measures. Let the pen, therefore, run through each point with God’s assistance, and examine everything individually in the order in which it was proposed. When the authorities have been displayed, you will recognize—if indeed you can recover your senses—that you have been either too blind to see so great [Col. 0763B] a light, too foolish to understand matters so plain, or too obstinate to believe such great witnesses.

## Against Their Saying That Churches or Altars Ought Not To Be Made

You too say, as I hear, that the Church of God consists in the unity of gathered believers; and this is clear to everyone. But you affirm that buildings for sacred places ought not to be made, and that those already made ought to be overthrown; we, joined by the whole world, contradict you. And lest you think that I am trying to use the terror of a great name to force truth—if any truth is on your side—hear the authority to which Christian necks above all ought to submit. Therefore, that the testimonies may be set forth in the sequence in which Sacred Scripture published them: Genesis, at the beginning of the divine writings, recounts that Noah after the Flood built an altar to the Lord, offered sacrifice upon it, and that God smelled an odour of sweetness (Gen. 8); that Abraham, when he wished at God’s command to sacrifice his son Isaac, first built an altar and laid wood upon it (Gen. 22); that Jacob set up a stone as a monument, poured oil over it, and said: “Truly the Lord is in this place, and this is none other than the house of God and the gate of heaven” (Gen. 28). Exodus likewise, lest God’s army should lack a sacred place for prayer or sacrifice—a portable tabernacle being the only thing appropriate to those stationed on campaign—records that Moses constructed by divine command a portable tabernacle from many kinds of materials, [Col. 0763D] and that it was visibly consecrated by God also (Exod. 40).

After the land of Canaan had been possessed by the Hebrews, its enemies and those of other nations having been destroyed, although they abounded in innumerable cities and towns, they could gather by God’s command for prayer or sacrifice only first at Shiloh and finally at Jerusalem. Scripture testifies that in those places alone the tabernacle of skins and curtains remained, until the stone temple succeeded it. When King David intended to build it, God, disputing ages beforehand against this error of yours arisen in our own days, said: “Because you have thought this, you have done well in pondering it in your mind. But you shall not build me a house, because you are a man of blood; but the son who shall come forth [Col. 0764A] from your womb, he shall build me a house” (3 Kings 8). “You have done well,” he says, “in pondering it in your mind.” What thing? Namely, building a temple for God. If David did well merely in thinking of building a temple for God, you did ill even in thinking of destroying God’s temple. If, I say, he did well in desiring the construction of God’s temple, you do ill in turning over in your hearts the overthrow of sacred temples. If it is evil merely to think this, how much more to preach it? If it is evil to think it, how much more to carry out what has been thought? If it is evil to deliberate in the mind about the ruin of churches, how much more to destroy them? If the thought of destruction is evil, how much worse is destruction itself?

What the Jews charged Christ with as a crime, Christians worse than Jews have committed by a new sacrilege. They falsely accused the Lord of saying, “I will destroy this temple made with hands” (Mark 14); we truthfully accuse you not only of having said it, but of having destroyed the Lord’s churches with wicked hands. It was no small matter, even among the unrighteous, for anyone to threaten the ruin of God’s temple; yet people of our time and name have not feared to inflict it upon his churches. See, see, destroyers of the Lord’s temple, what you have committed in destroying it, when you see that the great king and prophet David was forbidden to build it. He—he indeed was forbidden, of whom the divine voice said: “I have found David, a man after my own heart” (Acts 13); and who could say: “I have kept my feet from every evil way; I hated every way of iniquity; and I loved your commandments above gold and topaz” [Col. 0764C] (Ps. 118). If the hands of so great a man were not considered worthy to undertake the building of God’s temple, could your hands prepare themselves with impunity for its destruction? Uzzah wished to lift up the ark of the God of Israel when it was leaning, and died (2 Kings 6); and do you seek with all your effort to overthrow the Church of the God of Israel and yet be safe? If he who supported it was killed, will he who casts it down live? Consider, zealous overthrowers of temples, how contrary a spirit drives you against God: you strive to overthrow his work, to destroy the structure raised by his command. That the structure of the former temple was raised by his command you have heard above; hear it again: “You shall not build me [Col. 0764D] a house,” God says to David, “but your son, whom I shall give in your place upon your throne, he shall build a house for my name.”

And lest you think God was the author only of its construction, behold him as its sanctifier. For when Solomon had completed the temple with its many kinds of ornament, and the priests had brought the ark of God into its place, the same truthful Scripture says: “When the priests came forth from the sanctuary, a cloud filled the house of the Lord. And the priests could not stand and minister because of the cloud; for the glory of the Lord had filled the house of the Lord. Then Solomon said: ‘The Lord said that he would dwell in the cloud’” (3 Kings 13). And that you may have God himself as witness to the temple’s consecration, hear him appearing to Solomon and saying: “I have heard your prayer and supplication, which you made before me. [Col. 0765A] I have sanctified this house which you built, that I might put my name there forever; and my eyes and my heart shall be there all days” (3 Kings 9). Judge, then, whom one ought rather to believe: God, who commands the construction of his temple, or you, who urge its destruction; God, who consecrates, or you, who profane; God, who assigns a fitting place for prayers and sacrifices, or you, who command Christians to exist without churches and sacrifices.

Truly you are new restorers of an ancient error: you command that God be worshipped not in his temple but, like Baal, on every high hill and beneath every leafy tree, when you sanctify fields and groves and prefer them to his places. Showing how contrary this was to him, God was willing that sacrifices should be offered only in the place that he said he had chosen for this purpose. [Col. 0765B] There he commanded the whole nation to assemble three times a year, to worship God, discharge vows, and hear what was to be declared from the Law. And although, according to Solomon’s prayer, God does not need a house, whom heaven and the heaven of heavens cannot contain (3 Kings 8), and although, according to the psalm of David saying, “Bless the Lord, O my soul, in every place of his dominion” (Ps. 102), he is to be worshipped everywhere, he nevertheless chose to give a distinctive privilege to the house especially dedicated to him: there he would pour out greater grace upon peoples praying, and hear their prayers more effectually.

Therefore, in order to commend the grace and dignity of the new sacrifice of Christians—which, while you remain fleshly and proud, you will not comprehend—he permitted sacrifices only in that place chosen for this purpose, as I have said; so much so that Scripture reckons it as a grave offence even in good and praiseworthy kings of Judah that, though they utterly abolished idols and their worship in their own kingdom, they nevertheless permitted the people subject to them to sacrifice in high places—that is, in places other than the temple—not indeed to idols, but to God himself. Rebuking each of them, Scripture says: “Nevertheless he did not remove the high places. The people still sacrificed and burned incense in the high places” [Col. 0765C] (4 Kings 12). Thus, by condemning not the worship but the place of worship, Scripture shows that God did not will the sacred rites of that time to be celebrated indiscriminately everywhere; for them he wished both to appoint particular ministers and dedicate a particular place.

All the Jews and many Gentiles came to this place; great kings and prophets came there to offer either commanded sacrifices or vows specifically belonging to God. As a sign that King Hezekiah would ascend there after his illness, he received from God through the prophet Isaiah the sun’s backward movement, a thing unknown to all ages (4 Kings 20; Isa. 38). This temple, destroyed by the king of the Chaldeans, was restored by the princes Zerubbabel and Salathiel, the priests Ezra and Jesus, and the prophets Haggai and Zechariah (1 Esdras 1); and when it was again profaned by Antiochus, the Maccabees sanctified it (2 Macc. 10). In it Christ, the end of the Law and beginning of the Gospel, while still a child offered by his parents, fulfilled every rite; and what reverence is owed to sacred places, he proclaimed first silently by example before teaching it aloud in words (Luke 2).
