And lest you should wish, with the obstinacy you have begun, to interpret this too in another direction, read the Gospel and see how often, at Passover, at the Feast of Tabernacles, and at the feast of Dedication, he came to Jerusalem and went up into the temple; how there he openly preached to the people the word of life which he himself was; how, seated beside the treasury, he praised most highly those who offered gifts to God, especially the widow (Mark 12; Luke 21); how he commanded the leper whom he had healed to offer the gift Moses prescribed (Matt. 8); and how he healed those blind and lame persons who approached him in the temple, thereby honouring the place with divine miracles.

Recall also that deed by which, as by a battering ram alone, the entire machinery of your insane doctrine is overthrown. Recall, I say, what he did when, near his Passion, he made a whip of cords, drove sellers and buyers out of the temple, overturned the seats of those selling doves, and, rebuking them with a testimony taken from Deuteronomy, said: “It is written: My house is a house of prayer. But you have made it a den of thieves” [Col. 0766B] (Matt. 21; Mark 2; Luke 19).

To what end are all these things said? That you may at last be ashamed of a most foolish error, which neither Jew nor pagan nor any other Christian besides you could have devised. Every religion desires a place where it may venerate its sacred things and more familiarly serve its established observances. Thus Jews offered sacrifices only in God’s temple; pagans in their shrines, though profane ones. Thus Christians, until your time, possessed the churches instituted by God, which you seek to overthrow. Therefore, so long as you remain in these opinions, you will deservedly [Col. 0766C] be outside the number of all people, since you oppose the laws of all, and, expelled by believers, will find no hiding place even among unbelievers. “Return to your heart, transgressors” (Isa. 46); and you who have long been foolish, at last begin to be wise. See God raising the fabric of his temple and sanctifying it when raised; prophets restoring what had been destroyed and consecrating what they had restored; Christ himself, the Lord of the temple, honouring the temple with heavenly speech and exalted miracles, expelling merchants from it by words and blows, and calling God’s house the house of his Father and a house of prayer. No longer destroy what you see God build; do not profane [Col. 0766D] what you see him dedicate; do not despise what you behold him honour.

Understand that the God of Christians was the God of the Jews: as he then did not will to be without a temple, so now he does not will to be without churches. If you ask why he then wished only one temple to be built for him by the Jews, but now many by Christians, the reason is plain: one temple nearby was sufficient for a single nation and the people around it; and God was providing that a people prone to idolatry might not gradually be enticed into joining the sacrifices to demons which were performed everywhere. There is also a higher reason, provided that you do not reject figures as Judaizing: by that one temple the one Church was signified; by the sacrifices of that one temple, the one sacrifice of the Church. Since this is so, once the former multiplicity has been removed, the one sacrifice can be offered only in the one Church of Christ [Col. 0767A], because the place of the true sacrifice is not outside the Catholic Church: “one Lord, one faith, one baptism” (Eph. 4), one Church, one victim.

These are the reasons that have occurred to me for the present why God was worshipped by the Jews in one temple only, whereas Christians now honour him, as regards buildings, in innumerable churches. If they suffice, well. If not, may he open your understanding to comprehend the Scriptures, so that you may recognize, according to the Apostle, that “all these things happened to them in a figure and were written for our correction” (1 Cor. 10). As they have corrected many from their errors, would that they might correct you also from yours! Why, after that unity of the Jewish temple, this multiplicity of Christian churches has arisen is clearly demonstrated by what has been said above. One temple, sufficient for one people, can no longer suffice for the whole world. For what was spoken to the Church through Isaiah has been fulfilled: “Spare not; make your cords long, and strengthen your stakes. Enlarge the place of your tent” (Isa. 54). “You shall spread abroad to the east and west, to the north and south.” Hence also Malachi: “I have no pleasure in you, says the Lord, nor will I accept a sacrifice from your hands. For from the rising of the sun to its setting my name is great among the nations, and in every place a clean offering is offered to my name” [Col. 0767B] (Mal. 1).

The Lord, following out the prophet’s utterance exactly, says to the Samaritan woman in the Gospel: “Woman, the hour comes when you shall worship the Father neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem” (John 4). And after some words: “The hour comes when the true worshippers shall worship the Father in spirit and truth” (ibid.). What could you seek clearer, plainer, or more manifest? Behold: in the Jews’ rejection and the Gentiles’ election, the question of the sacred places under discussion is settled; and it is plainly shown that many places of offering must succeed the one temple of sacrifices. Oh, the prophecy of the prophet and Christ’s foreknowledge, marvellously harmonious in different times! For what the former says—“I will not accept a sacrifice from your hands”—the latter says in these words: “The hour comes when you shall worship the Father neither on this mountain nor in Jerusalem.” And what the former says—“In every place a clean offering is offered to my name”—the latter says in these words: “The true worshippers shall worship the Father in spirit and truth.”

Behold the hour of which the Lord said, “The hour comes,” when, as we see with our eyes, neither Jews in Jerusalem nor Samaritans on their mountain—which they regarded as the only sacred places—worship according to the ancient rite. For God does not accept the shadowy sacrifice now that truth has succeeded it; nor is a lamb, ram, or calf necessary when the one sacrificed Christ is sufficient for all. This is indeed the time when true worshippers worship the Father in spirit and truth, when a clean offering is offered to his name not in one place only but in every place [Col. 0767D]. Since it is clean, the places in which it is offered must also be cleansed. This occurs when places are sanctified by the Spirit of sanctification through human ministry, and are made divine from being common; when, the Lord’s name having been invoked, a dwelling is prepared there for him alone, whose singular essence does not permit a partner.

Thus the places are first cleansed, and then in the cleansed places a pure offering is made to his name. So, in this time of Christian grace, according to this prophetic utterance, a pure offering is made to his name in every place; and that offering is made only in places that are definite and sanctified. For when the Apostle, speaking of the sacrifice of each Testament, says, “It was necessary that the copies of the true things should be cleansed with these, but the heavenly things themselves with better sacrifices than these” (Heb. XI), who of sound mind could even suppose that the inner sacrifices, by which the copies of the true things are cleansed, may be offered only in sacred places, whereas the better sacrifices, by which the heavenly things themselves are cleansed, may everywhere be lawfully offered in places not sacred? There an ox is slaughtered only in the sacred temple, while here the Lamb of God will be sacrificed in a grove or field, house or marketplace, stable or tavern? There, for the shedding of beasts’ blood, the tabernacle or temple is built, adorned, and consecrated with such care by God’s command; and will the blood of Jesus Christ—who, as the apostle John says, “loved us and washed us from our sins in his blood” (Rev. I)—not deserve a place even among those redeemed? The Jew prepares a temple with immense care for servile sacrifices; and will the Christian not prepare a church for the liberating sacrifice? There the man who offers sacrifice, even to God, outside the appointed place is condemned; and can he go unpunished [Col. 0768C] who has sacrificed Christ, the end of all sacrifices, in an alien place? But I know, as I said above, that you despise even this sacrifice of ours and altogether deny that it now exists in the Church. I promised above to argue against that heresy, and, God helping, I shall fulfill my promise in its place.

Meanwhile, even if not for sacrifice, you cannot deny that temples or churches ought to be made for prayer, since in both the Pentateuch and the Gospel—that is, in the Old and New Testament—you hear the Lord saying: “My house is a house of prayer” (Isa. LVI; Matt. XXI; Luke XIX). In that house, while he was there, he answered his mother, who was seeking and reproaching him: “Did you not know that I must be in the things of my Father?” [Col. 0768D] (Luke II). He also tells of two men who went up into the temple to pray, one heard and the other rejected (Luke XVIII). And Luke the Evangelist records that Anna, a widow until the age of eighty-four, served in the temple with fastings and prayers night and day (Luke II). Therefore acknowledge at least a house of prayers, so that afterward you may also acknowledge a house of sacrifices.

But if you seek apostolic testimony concerning these matters too, hear John writing to the seven Churches which are in Asia (Rev. I); and Luke, in the Acts of the Apostles, celebrating both the growth of the Church and the very name “Church.” In the Gospel he also testifies that, after the Lord’s ascension, the apostles were continually in the temple, praising and blessing [Col. 0769A] God (Luke XXIV); and in Acts, that Peter and John, at the ninth hour of prayer, did not make for the marketplace but went up into the temple (Acts III). Recall also the apostolic epistles, including those of Paul himself, sent to different Churches. But if you say that by the designation “Churches” the spiritual congregation of believers is signified more than a physical structure, see what Paul, reproving the Corinthians, says: “When you come together in church, I hear that there are divisions among you, and I partly believe it” (I Cor. XI). And shortly afterward: “Do you not have houses in which to eat and drink, or do you despise the Church of God?” (ibid.).

For some of the Corinthians brought to the Church food which they could have eaten at home, and ate private food where they ought to have eaten only the Lord’s Supper; and the wealthier, who could provide for themselves, shamed the poor, who could not. Again the Apostle says: “When you come together in one place, it is no longer to eat the Lord’s Supper. For each one takes his own supper beforehand to eat; and one is hungry while another is drunk” (ibid.). Behold: not only the assembly of the Church, but also the church building itself is plainly indicated by these words. A definite and consecrated place for assembly is clearly shown, in which, the Apostle says, it is lawful to eat only the Lord’s Supper; and from it he repels the Corinthians’ suppers or banquets with stern rebukes. From this he charges them with schism; from this he calls them despisers of God’s Church; from this he calls them presumptuous persons. [Col. 0769C] For this reason he sends those feasters back to their own houses when he says, “Do you not have houses in which to eat and drink?”—that is, so that they may use in their own houses those foods which they could not use without guilt in the house of God.

The Church’s supreme teacher after Christ teaches the distinction between houses and houses, and in his customary clarity shows what is fitting for the divine house and what for the human. He does not allow sins of the flesh to be practiced in the house of the Spirit, but wishes Christians to eat ordinary food in their own homes and only the Lord’s Supper in the house of the Lord. He instructs them to learn to seek in the former nourishment for the body, and in the latter nourishment for the soul; to provide for themselves in the former mortal life, and in the latter [Col. 0769D] eternal life. The disciple, in whom Christ spoke, imitated his teacher Christ. And as Christ did not wish God’s temple to be a house of commerce, so the Apostle did not allow God’s church to become a house of eating. Thus, Christ expelling merchants and the Apostle expelling eaters teach that those were sacred places in which it was not lawful even to perform necessities of human life; and that Christians must always provide such places, in which only the business of prayer may be conducted and in which only the Lord’s Supper may be eaten.

Now, if I am speaking with Christians, you must believe Christ and his Apostle; and their invincible authority will compel you to seek not now the ruin, but the building up, of sacred buildings—not their loss, but their increase. I cannot sufficiently wonder from what source this tasteless and brutish heresy could have arisen. For it is so utterly devoid of every authority and reason that, unless the danger to simple souls compelled me, my mind would recoil from even opening my mouth against such base trifles. For what? During the twenty-five years in which the apostle Peter resided at Rome, was he without [Col. 0770B] a temple or church—that is, a house of prayer—or at least a small oratory? Does not the sequence of truthful deeds recount—if, indeed, you grant some assent to historical acts besides the divine Canon—that Peter himself, chief of the apostles, first built a temple for Christ in the city that is head of the world, amid innumerable temples of the Gentiles, and, as the blessed and great Pope Leo declares in an eloquent sermon, brought the trophy of Christ’s cross into the Roman strongholds? Have not we ourselves, while at Rome, frequently seen in the most ancient crypts oratories and altars such as could then have been made, which are shown to believers as monuments of so great a holiness—built and consecrated by that Apostle, as the unanimous and most famous tradition transmitted by succession attests—and which those same believers kiss most sweetly and devoutly?

At Arles, which your filthy error has not yet, through God’s grace, infected, did Trophimus, Paul the Apostle’s disciple—at whose fountain, as Pope Zosimus writes, all the streams of faith in Gaul received their waters—always preach, baptize, and pray in field or marketplace, and never himself possess a house of prayer or establish that others should possess one? And from where did so many holy successors of his dare to assume what he did not teach, he from whom they received the streams of faith? But in order to say something more fully about the first apostles of our Gaul, whom your impious foolishness and foolish impiety have hitherto failed to know, the histories handed down to us by holy men, as antiquity itself testifies, relate: not only we, but all Christian peoples—little and great, old and young—holding your madness up to ridicule, most certainly maintain that Irenaeus at Lyons, Crescens at Vienne, Ursinus at Bourges, Paul at Narbonne, Saturninus at Toulouse [Note: [Col. 0769D] “Saturninus at Toulouse, Dionysius at Paris,” etc. At what time these bishops were sent into Gaul with Gratian, Martial, Stremonius, Paul, and Trophimus is still disputed by many. Yet Gregory, himself bishop of Tours and the most ancient writer of Frankish history, states most explicitly that they were sent under the consuls Decius and Gratus—that is, in the sixth year of the emperor Philip—from these words in the Life of Saint Saturninus: “Under the consuls Decius and Gratus, as faithful recollection preserves, the city of Toulouse first began to have as its chief and first priest Saint Saturninus. These therefore,” he says, “were sent: Gratian, bishop to Tours; Trophimus, bishop to Arles; Saturninus, bishop to Toulouse; Stremonius, bishop to the Arverni; Martial was appointed bishop to the Lemovices.”

And concerning Saturninus, an old author who wrote the first book of the Life of Saint Genulphus holds a similar view. For in chapter 9 of that book he says: “In these times of Decius, others also are handed down as having been sent into Gaul from the Apostolic See. Among these the most eminent and most holy Saturninus was the first bishop of the city of Toulouse.” As for Saint Dionysius, Hilduin, abbot of Saint-Denis, much later—namely, during the reign of Louis the Pious, emperor and king of the Franks—was the first to endeavor to prove by many reasons and arguments that he was that Areopagite, the disciple of Saint Paul, as Peter Abelard relates in the History of My Calamities. Hugo, abbot of Saint-Martial at Limoges, imitating him, also wished to maintain that Saint Martial had been one of the disciples of the apostles; and, as Ademar says in the Commemoration of the Abbots of Limoges, he held in France a conference concerning Martial’s apostolic status with King Robert, Gauslenus archbishop of Bourges, and many bishops and learned men of France.

But, to pause at Saint Dionysius, the old Roman Martyrology, recently published by Heribert Rosweyde, a man exceptionally skilled in antiquities, settles the entire matter in a few words. It reports that the Areopagite suffered at Athens and the Parisian at Lutetia, at different times and on different days. Yet because we hope that the most learned Sauron will investigate the matter still more fully and extensively, we refrain from saying more now.], Austremonius among the Arverni, Martial among the Lemovices, [Col. 0771A] at Bordeaux and Poitiers, Fronto at Périgueux, Eutropius among the Saintes, Garianus at Tours, Julianus at Le Mans, Dionysius at Paris, Potentianus and Savinianus at Sens, Lucianus at Beauvais, Andochius among the Aedui, Benignus at Langres—and who could suffice to enumerate all the most glorious fathers and apostles of our faith?

These men, certainly these, wherever they proclaimed the name of the Lord, immediately overthrew the shrines of idols as far as was lawful, or founded new churches or converted the temples themselves into churches. Thus even today, in very many places, as we ourselves have inspected with our own eyes, churches or basilicas constructed by them and altars founded and consecrated by their hands are preserved and shown by the faithful people in remembrance of their antiquity and holiness; and they speak, as though in a living voice, of how laughable and detestable you are to all people. And, to pass to the East and the other parts of the world: who filled Illyricum, Greece, and Scythia except Paul and Andrew? Who filled the greater part of Asia except John and Philip? Who filled the Persian kingdoms and neighboring peoples except Simon and Jude? Who filled India and lands adjoining the sunrise except Thomas and Bartholomew? Who filled all Ethiopia except Matthew—by destroying the temples of ancient superstition and filling them with churches of new grace—the first and last apostles of Christ? Thus all the authors of the old and new law oppose you with unanimous zeal, so that you must either yield to such great witnesses or falsely continue to be Christians without Christ, prophets, and apostles.

## Against those who say that the Lord’s cross is neither to be adored nor venerated, but rather broken and trampled underfoot

[Col. 0771C]

From here my discourse must hasten to defend the Lord’s cross against your axes and swords, although it can now arrive only too late. By wicked deeds you outran the swiftness of words, and, driven by profound hatred of religion, you dared to remove the emblem of our faith—an act which it was criminal even to contemplate. This occurred when, in an unheard-of insult to divinity, you built a great pile of crosses, set fire to it, made a pyre, cooked flesh, and, on the very day of the Lord’s Passion, which precedes Easter Sunday—publicly invited the people to such a meal and [Col. 0771D] ate it. Thus, feeding sacrilegious fires with sacred wood, you said, I suppose, with idolaters according to the prophet Isaiah: “Ah! I am warmed; I have seen the fire” (Isa. XLIV). Warmed by flames and fattened by flesh, you offered yourselves, swollen with marrow, as a sacrifice not to God but to the devil; and, as Moses says of the transgressing people: “The beloved grew fat and kicked; he grew fat, became stout, grew broad; he forsook God his maker and departed from God his savior” (Deut. XXXII).

You too have plainly departed, if you refuse to submit, by denying the cross, from God your Savior. No one whatsoever can obtain salvation from him if he despises the cross in which salvation is supremely established. I believe you discovered this scheme by heretical cunning; or rather, that the prince of wickedness has admirably provided for his deception through his own lackeys: if with this single dart he could wound the unwary, he could easily take away not only safety but life. For once the name of the cross is removed from the midst, [Col. 0772B] where will any mention of the Crucified remain? Once the title “Crucified” is taken away, where will remembrance of death or Passion endure? Once memory of death and Passion is abolished, what hope of salvation remains for the redeemed when the price of redemption has been emptied of effect?

But I know that you grieve over the wrongs suffered by your companions, and that, being heretical people, you desire to avenge demons’ injuries. Apostate spirits are driven away when the sign of the cross appears; and the proud angels, who dared raise their heads against that invincible Majesty, vanish like a cloud scattered by the rays of the morning sun at this mark of abasement which you so despise. Moved by this injury, you have undertaken sworn wars against the Lord’s cross, and, more wicked than demons, cannot bear the indignities that they suffer. Certainly you cannot love what they hate, since your conduct in this life and the fires awaiting you in the next show that nothing is contrary or different between you. Accordingly, the likeness which makes you alike in present conduct and in eternal flames leaves us unsurprised that you will what they will and reject what they reject. But perhaps the fires with which we threaten you do not frighten you, since, according to Isaiah, “you have made a covenant with death and entered into an agreement with hell” (Isa. XXVIII). Yet, according to the same prophet, your covenant with death shall be annulled and your agreement with hell shall not stand. For, as that poet says:

> No faith is due to partners in a kingdom.

And as Christ says in the Gospel: “Every kingdom divided against itself shall be laid waste” (Matt. XII; Luke II). Therefore, because you have chosen a kingdom in common with demons, your ill-gotten agreement will soon be dissolved, and the peace of the ungodly cannot endure; for “there is no peace,” says my God, “for the ungodly” (Isa. XLVIII). Thus the wood of life will become for you a wood of death, so that the fires which you once kindled from fragments of that sacred wood [Col. 0773A] may remain perpetual for you; and as you will remain immortal for them, so they will remain unquenchable for you.

But, lest I delay, let the serpent now breathe forth its hissing and pour out the poison with which it has long been swollen. “It is foolish,” it says, “and profane to adore or venerate the cross, because the wood that stretched Christ’s limbs should be shattered or burned rather than venerated or adored.” O splendid wisdom! O reasoning drawn from the depths of philosophy! You do not avenge the Lord’s sufferings with a punishment worthy of them, nor condemn so great a crime with fitting retribution. The Lord’s death cannot be expiated by an hour’s torture; an injury to the Creator must be punished by nothing less than an everlasting penalty. There is no need for your axes to be blunted by repeated blows, nor for your limbs to be wearied by striking. Extinguish the fires you have kindled; scatter the piled heap of crosses: there is one who will avenge his own wrongs. The Creator himself, who suffered, will torture the impious cross that tortured him; and with Herod and Pilate, Judas and Caiaphas, he will thrust it into Gehenna. Their punishment will be common, whose guilt was equal; and because together they inflicted torments upon God, together they will burn in hell. Yes, indeed: it is just that one accused of causing the death of the God of heaven should be punished by a penalty no less than hell’s.

By this standard of justice, whatever was an instrument of insult or indignity to the God-man must be condemned. Therefore the very places of the Passion must be execrated, the city destroyed, the tomb dug up—in which, although he rested, it was nevertheless an injury for God to be buried. Moreover, his death must be detested, his Passion trampled underfoot, and, to say much in brief, the whole dispensation of saving humility must be despised. Why do I speak thus? So that, confronted with such absurdity, you may blush and recognize that nothing deserves punishment or insult when guilt cannot attach to it. For guilt cannot exist where there is no reason. Reason exists only in a living creature. But a cross is not a living creature; therefore reason is not in it. And because reason is not in it, neither, as I said, is guilt. If it bears no guilt, the charge for Christ’s death cannot be imputed to it. If this is true, no insult should have been inflicted upon it as though in punishment for guilt; it should not have been hewn with axes or burned with fire.

For in the torments or death of the Savior only the perverse will [Col. 0773D] of wicked people is condemned, because only the disposition of a rational creature—assisted or abandoned by the Creator’s grace—is always either rewarded or condemned. Thus the cross is cleared of responsibility for the sufferings on this twofold ground: where there was no consciousness, there could have been no assent to the crime; and no one, I think, whether you yourselves or anyone else, judges the other locations of the Passion to be accursed because of a guilt which they could not incur through the saving punishments. Therefore it was wickedly done when the innocent wood, as though liable for an abominable crime, was broken by your presumptuous hands; wickedly done when it was burned in unjust fires. But you still say:

“If someone, men, brought you the noose by which your father’s throat had been broken, or the sword by which your friend or brother had been killed, and urged you to honor or adore those things, would you not rise against the adviser, if the means were available, with every movement of your soul? Would you not either consume the objects in flames or destroy them by whatever means you could?”

When you are accustomed to put such things before gatherings of senators, the sort you are wont to assemble on the Capitoline, from a consular or royal tribunal, with declamatory voice and terrifying gesture, that gathering of your exceedingly learned men is immediately drawn to your opinion; they suddenly applaud the invincible speech, all rejoice aloud at the truth at last made known by you, immense hatred is forged against the cross, and all arm themselves with swords and fires against the cross to avenge the Crucified’s torments. And who ever, except you—O asinine stupidity!—demanded vengeance for a father’s murder or a brother’s blood from nooses or swords [Col. 0774B] rather than from the hangers or killers [murderers]? Who ever, except you, burned nooses or broke swords to avenge blood? Who ever, except you, was angry with the instruments of killing rather than the wicked killers? Who ever, except you, armed himself against weapons rather than against those who bore weapons? O the times! O the customs, which can even hear such things!

When an army has been routed, I shall rage against the enemies’ missiles; when my father has been killed, I shall undertake war against swords. I shall be angry, when my brother has been slain, with the missile that killed him; and when my friend has been hanged, I shall stir up wrath against the noose. Innocent things shall pay for enemies’ deeds, and an innocent creature shall be condemned for the crimes of the ungodly. Punishment shall be inflicted on what cannot feel, and insult shall be offered to a brute thing. [Col. 0774C] It shall be cut apart [or: cut off] by swords and shall not suffer; it shall be burned by fires and shall not care; it shall be disfigured by mockeries and shall not blush. The hostile mind will feed upon these torments and, satisfied by its magnificent vengeance, will gradually subside from its conceived rage. Our hatred will blaze against our enemies’ swords; and, victory gained, as the enemies must be killed, so these swords must necessarily be broken.

Not so—not so, if I may add an example of authority—did that famous warrior David act. He did not, I say, curse or break the sword of the Philistine Goliath, which Goliath had drawn against him, vaunting himself by it, reproaching the ranks of Israel, and blaspheming the battle lines of the living God. Rather, armed with it, David then cut off the enemy’s head (I Sam. XVII), and afterward received that same sword from the priest out of the sanctuary (I Sam. XXI). It would not have been kept among sacred things or taken by the prophet for use in warfare if, according to your wisdom, it had been judged fit to be cursed or broken; nor would it have been said of it: “Give it to me; for there is none here like it” (ibid.).

Moreover, truthful Scripture records of Judas Maccabaeus, the excellent leader of the Hebrews, that, after annihilating the pagan army, he took the sword of the general Apollonius, whom he had killed, and fought with it all his days (I Macc. III). Thus certainly, O heretics, thus indeed Christ used his cross against the prince of this world. Advancing to single combat against Christ, he brought forth Christ’s cross in order to kill him by it; but divine wisdom reversed the devil’s cunning: by the cross with which he attacked Christ, he was himself tortured; and by the death with which he extinguished Christ, he was himself killed. Then was fulfilled what you once often sang in the psalm of the presbyter: “His pain shall return upon his own head, and his iniquity shall come down upon his own crown” (Ps. VII).

But allow me too to enter that assembly of yours and to put a few matters before the common people deceived by you, in the deceptive idiom of your own speech. “If someone, men, holding a noose or sword before you were to say: ‘Behold the noose by which the hanger of your father was hanged; behold the sword by which the murderer of your brother or dearest friend was killed: break them, burn them, destroy them’—what would you do? Would you believe one giving such advice? Would you not judge such a person either mad or moved by hostile intent, since he exhorted you both to torture insensible things and to burn with avenging wrath against objects [Col. 0775B] whose piety had been violated?” This is what those teachers do—not teachers of your truth but of your error; not of your salvation but of your destruction—who persuade you to break, burn, and destroy the Lord’s cross, by which he who, according to the Gospel in which they say they believe, “was a murderer from the beginning” (John VIII), was destroyed.

This is indeed what they do: they desire to avenge the devil, murderer of your fathers, of yourselves, and of Christ himself according to the flesh. They confess it themselves when they so greatly desire the destruction of the cross by which he was chiefly destroyed, while they endeavor to eradicate the instrument which the Savior used for your salvation—an instrument which reason itself compels them to receive rather than break, venerate rather than burn. And, O justice, to condemn a thing, as I said, that bears no guilt! O vengeance, to subject a senseless thing to tortures, pour rage upon a dry log, and exhaust abominable hatreds upon wood that feels nothing!

By this reasoning, Christians excessively faithful to Christ will gird themselves with the sword of zeal against the crosses of Peter and Andrew; Lawrence’s gridiron, though it is iron, will be burned in its own fires; Stephen’s stones will be reduced to lime; the racks, metal plates, claws, scourges, chains, fetters, prisons, and stocks of martyrs will swiftly disappear in flight, lest they suffer from Christians what they inflicted upon them. By this law, whatever causes distress to the human body will be worthy of human hatred; wherever they are found, the hostile hands of enemies [Col. 0775D] will not escape. In this manner our indignation will be kindled against fire that burns, air that corrupts, water that suffocates, and earth that crushes; it will abhor the sun blazing in summer and frost tormenting in winter. And because there is nothing bodily which does not, in some way, become a punishment to wretched human beings because of their guilt, the whole human race will rise with all its effort against the whole world, and, wherever it has the power, the inhabitant himself will destroy his dwelling-place with all his strength.

But perhaps, emulating the spirited arrogance of King Cyrus, you have resolved to imitate him. Wishing to avenge a beloved horseman swallowed up by the great river called the Ganges, he raged against the river and threatened to make it passable on foot; and he fulfilled his promise. For, dividing the swelling mass of waters into three hundred and more channels, he arrogantly reduced the river’s arrogance and, diverting its single magnitude through many courses, made the river traversable with dry feet, scarcely worthy of a naval procession, as he had said. Yet he, though with insane zeal, desired to avenge his soldier’s death, but still took care that others should not die in a similar accident. You, by contrast—since you hold it certain that in Christ’s death, accomplished through the cross, the life of all depends—when you wish to remove the cross from the midst, you begrudge life to all.

Do you still see the incongruity, so obvious even to beasts? Do you see that a thing without guilt does not deserve punishment, and that torments ought not to be inflicted upon insensible things? Do you see that punishment is unjustly imposed on the innocent and that torments are foolishly inflicted on what cannot feel them?

[Col. 0776B]

Since this is so, if you are so eager to avenge the Redeemer’s torments, seek one who is guilty and can deserve punishment, and one who is capable of feeling the punishment inflicted. Since, in the whole visible creation, only the human being will be found to be both guilty and sentient, you will at last recognize that you have acted with brutish stupidity and, like a boar or bear, after the hunter escaped, have vainly savaged the hunting spear with bites and claws. You will surely recognize that innocent creatures have been unjustly and ridiculously harassed by your beastly tooth, since only what is sentient can feel punishment, and only what is guilty should be condemned. As I have said, the human being alone will appear liable to guilt and therefore rightly subject to torments—the one being whom you can justly charge for deeds committed and from whom alone you can properly demand the vengeance due.

When this has been done, neither the whole of insensible or irrational creation will incur your indignation for any troubles of human beings, [Col. 0776C] nor will the Lord’s cross, which trembled beneath your fires and swords, fail to escape through the compelling force of this reasoning. It will escape, I say: as innocent, from guilt; as insensible, from punishment. It will no longer be condemned as guilty of Christ’s death, nor punished as sentient. Rather, once justice has returned to its proper lines, the one who could commit the offence will be sought out, and only the one who committed it will be condemned. By that equity, since, as I have stated, among earthly creatures only the human being will be found capable of wrongdoing, only the human being found guilty of so great a crime will be condemned. Yes, indeed: the file of truth requires that, as justice saves everyone not guilty, so injustice condemns everyone unjust.

Then, since guilt for the Lord’s sufferings or death will show not every person but certain persons guilty, they themselves will be condemned while others are left uncondemned; those alone whom a perverse will has rendered culpable will be punished while others are unpunished. Nor indeed will even all of those be punished, because, having changed their dispositions and turned to Christ, cleansed from guilt by his justice, they have been rescued from death by the death which they themselves inflicted. Why say this? So that, seeing the truly guilty perpetrators of the Lord’s sufferings escape deserved punishment through the remedy of repentance—seeing, I say, that even guilty people are at times saved—you may never blush to condemn the Lord’s cross as guilty.

Since this is so, your comparison, which you are accustomed to offer to the most rustic and ignorant rabble in order to condemn [Col. 0777A] the Lord’s cross, has no force. For, on the grounds already set forth, neither the noose should have been burned because a father’s throat was broken, nor the sword broken because a brother or friend had been slain. Hence, if these objects ought not to have been destroyed to avenge a father, friend, or brother, neither should the Savior’s cross have been broken or burned as though to avenge his blood and death. For, as has already often been said, they could not commit an offence because they were irrational, nor again could they offend or feel because they were insensible.

Therefore it was done most foolishly and wickedly when the Lord’s cross, which had committed no offence and felt nothing, was subjected to torment. This invincible argument shows that the insult you inflicted upon the saving wood was unjust; but it has not yet proved it worthy of the honor in which we hold it. Let authority therefore come forward, and reason follow it, and let the wood of the cross be declared glorious rather than contemptible to Catholics and heretics alike. Let Moses, first in the Canon and first in our discourse, come forward: let him mark the Hebrews’ doorposts and the lintel of the house with the lamb’s blood in the form of a cross and, after both posts have been anointed, prevent the angel who strikes from entering (Exod. XII). Then, in the wilderness, let him cast into the water wood prefiguring this wood, and make it sweet from bitter and drinkable from useless (Exod. XV). Again, let him strike the rock twice with the rod (Exod. XVII), while the Jew twice cries, “Crucify!” (John XIX), and let most abundant waters come forth from the struck rock—that is, from the crucified Redeemer [Col. 0777C]—to wash the whole world in baptism and doctrine, and to refresh both people and beasts: that is, both the shrewd and the foolish, who are failing through a long thirst for the saving word.

Let also the widow of Sarepta gather two pieces of wood and arrange them as a cross, upon which she may bake the bread of life through the fire of the Passion; and let her add the oil of the Holy Spirit, by which she may be sustained until eternal abundance succeeds the famine-stricken season of this present life (III Kings XVII). Then in the prophet Ezekiel let the letter Tau be imprinted upon the foreheads of the men who groan and grieve over iniquities (Ezek. IX), so that, distinguished from others by that sign, they may escape death. Let this letter be understood as not chosen among all the Hebrew letters without purpose for marking the foreheads, since by such a mark the cross is no longer merely prefigured but displayed; and whoever is marked with it alone is rescued from the world’s destruction. The common destruction cannot harm those whom both iniquity condemned by tears and God’s mercy coming to their aid through the cross separate from the death of others.

If, passing from heresy to Judaism, you wish to twist these matters into other interpretations with your distorted minds, answer what necessity compelled the doorposts of houses to be marked with lamb’s blood and human foreheads with the sign just named. Could the former not otherwise escape the striking angel, or the latter the avenging sword? Might heavenly vengeance perhaps err and be unable to distinguish Hebrews from Egyptians, righteous from sinners, unless it read upon the doorposts that the former [Col. 0778A] were not Egyptians, and unless a marked forehead taught it that the latter were to be separated from condemned ungodly people? And why is the tint of blood preferred there to all the colors of the Egyptians, when a smear of blood can scarcely preserve its color even for a moment or show what it has stained? Why are not merely the lintel or merely the doorposts, but both lintel and doorposts marked? Why, as I said, are they marked with blood, and with no blood but a lamb’s blood? Neither Christian nor Jew dares say that these were commanded or done superfluously; and, I suppose, neither Christian nor Jew will deny that they foreshadow something beyond what then appeared.

And because I am now speaking with Christians, though evil ones, and with those who say that they especially believe the Gospel, I believe they can offer nothing more fitting to solve this riddle than that this is the lamb of whom John the Baptist says in the Gospel, “Behold the Lamb of God” (John I); and of whom the prophet says, “Like a lamb before its shearer he shall be silent and shall not open his mouth” (Isa. LIII). The lamb was sacrificed at evening; Christ was killed at the end of the age. Hence the Apostle says, “Christ our Passover has been sacrificed” (I Cor. V), and David says, “The lifting up of my hands is an evening sacrifice” (Ps. CXL). The lamb’s blood is that of which the Apostle says: “If the blood of goats and bulls sanctifies the defiled, how much more the blood of Christ?” (Heb. IX). Since it was shed upon wood, the wooden doorposts were anointed with it. And because on the cross the right, the left, and the upper part were stained.

[Col. 0778C] But neither would the lower part have been lacking to express the complete shape of the cross, had not the Spirit of God, who spoke this, indicated by silence that the blood of the eternal covenant was not to be trampled underfoot. Why also was that letter, before all the other letters or symbols of all nations, chosen for marking the foreheads of those who mourn and grieve? Let the Jew say; let the heretic say, if he can. And when both have either kept silent or failed in their inventions, let the Catholic say that the prophet, wishing to foretell that Christians who were to be saved from the common destruction would be marked with the sign of the cross, could not have expressed this more openly than by the very sign of the cross. He depicted this not on any arbitrary part of the body, but upon the forehead itself, so that we may neither be ashamed with the Jews of the reproach of Christ [Col. 0778D] nor judge with the heretics that his cross, now an emblem not of disgrace but of honour, should be cast away or burned.

For this letter, called Thau, possessing the form of a cross, retains both its name and its figure not only among the Hebrews but also among the Greeks. Among the Hebrews, indeed, it changed neither the name nor the figure which it had from the beginning. Among the Greeks, however, although it changed its shape, it has preserved its name down to the present. If the reason for the altered character is sought, it will be found in ecclesiastical and Hebrew books. “Ezra,” Scripture says, “went up from Babylon, and he himself was a swift scribe in the law of Moses” (1 Ezra 7). He was swift, not in changing the meaning or the names of Hebrew letters, but in discovering characters more suitable and more convenient for writing.

[Col. 0779A] The form of this letter was still preserved among the Samaritans in the time of blessed Jerome, that most learned man in these languages; and perhaps it is still preserved either among them or among some others. For when the Jews changed their letters, that people did not wish to change the characters which it had received from the Jews; but, just as they had first been handed down to it, it preserved unimpaired both the signs and the names of the letters. The words of St Jerome, if indeed you deign to accept them, are as follows in his commentary on the prophet Ezekiel: “In the ancient Hebrew letters, which the Samaritans use even to this day, the final letter Thau has the likeness of a cross, which is marked upon Christians’ foreheads and signed by the frequent impression of the hand.” Thus blessed Jerome.

Therefore this prophetic character supports our faith, and not a little exalts [Col. 0779B] the glory of the cross: it was devised and handed down not by Ezra, though he was a great man, nor by any other, but by Moses himself, the greatest lawgiver and writer. For Moses wrote concerning Christ, as Christ himself testifies (John 5). Hence, since, according to the blessed Apostle, “all these things happened to them in figure” (1 Cor. 10), just as the whole body of the law spoke of Christ, so this element of the law proclaimed Christ’s cross. Nor did it merely proclaim it: by its visible form it presented it to the eyes of those reading. This letter, I say, by its shape presented Christ’s cross to the readers’ eyes, and by its name proclaimed Christ’s passion on the cross. For since *Thau* is called “consummation” in Latin, did it not already sound forth by this very name Christ’s final utterance on the cross, when [Col. 0779C] he said, “It is finished”? (John 19). Did it not testify by this name that everything foretold beforehand concerning Christ was to be fulfilled and brought to completion through Christ’s cross? Did it not demonstrate most plainly by this name that the things in heaven and on earth were to be reconciled through the blood of the Son of God (Col. 1), shed upon the cross?

This also serves this interpretation: this letter is written neither first nor in the middle, nor inserted in any other position, but last in the order of Hebrew letters, so that the letter having the form of a cross, while setting an end to the preceding letters, may declare that Christ, through the mystery of his death which he suffered on the cross, imposed through the cross an end completing the former sacraments. Thus this prophetic letter, serving Christ’s cross and passion, having occupied Hebrews, Greeks, and Latins alike by either its form or its name, signified nothing other than that Christ would rule through the cross over all languages and nations by means of the three principal languages. It plainly signified that Christ would rule the world through the cross, as the Apostle himself confirms, saying: “Christ became obedient for us unto death, even death on a cross. Therefore God also exalted him and gave him the name which is above every name, that at the name of Jesus every knee should bend, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth, and every tongue confess that the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father” (Phil. 2).

Since these things are so, who does not [Col. 0780A] see that the Lord’s cross is not merely not to be despised, but is rather to be held in the highest honour, since the Spirit of the Lord himself, who spoke through the prophets, judged it worthy of such great honour? He indeed judged it worthy of great honour when, so long before the time of the cross, he saved neither the Hebrews from the destroying angel nor righteous mourners from the destruction of the impious without its sign. He judged it worthy of great honour when he placed its sign not in concealment or obscurity but openly and in the light, when he marked with it both, as I have said, the doors of houses and the foreheads of men, which more readily present themselves to the gaze of those looking upon them. By the crosses upon the doors he judged that the whole house of the world would yield to him through the cross. By the crosses upon the foreheads he showed that he would claim the whole human being for himself [Col. 0780B] through the cross.

Great as these things are for the glory of the cross, let still greater things be added, and let examples or testimonies from the body of the New Testament serve the glory of the cross. Let the Apostle come, according to his custom, to establish it beyond objection, and by the terror of his coming alone impose silence upon chattering fools. At least hear him, you who disdain to hear us; and, if you dare, mutter against the heavenly trumpet in your hoarse whisper. Hear the friend of the cross, enemies of the cross, and attend carefully to what he thinks of you: “Many,” he says, “walk, of whom I often told you, but now tell you even weeping, that they are enemies of the cross of Christ, whose end is destruction, whose god is their belly, and whose glory is in their shame” (Phil. 3).

[Col. 0780C] What do you say to this, most wretched of men? The Apostle weeps beforehand, so many centuries ago, for your destruction. He weeps for enemies of Christ’s cross not yet born. He weeps for your glory turned into shame. He weeps, and you laugh; he weeps aloud, and you rejoice; he grieves, and you are glad. Why is this? Because, according to the word of the weeping Lord, “in this your day, the things that make for your peace … are now hidden from your eyes” (Luke 19). But they are open to apostolic eyes, and he declares what end awaits the enemies of Christ’s cross: “Whose end,” he says, “is destruction.” Unhappy is your lot. Others, according to the same Apostle, “have their fruit unto sanctification, and the end, eternal life” (Rom. 6). You have glory unto shame, and the end, everlasting destruction.

But if those deserve so much who were not, as [Col. 0780D] you are, hostile to Christ’s cross, but are called enemies of the cross because they both did and said certain things contrary to the cross—that is, to spiritual mortification—what can you deserve, who oppose not only the sacred virtues signified by the cross but even try to take away the very name of the cross from the worshippers of the Crucified? For if the cross is removed, as I said above, where will the Crucified be? If the Crucified is withdrawn, who will be your god? Surely the one of whom he continues: “Whose god is their belly.” I believe the Apostle foresaw in the Spirit your bellies distended with flesh roasted by the fire of crosses, and therefore appointed the belly as your best god, so that you who denied the Crucified by burning the cross might now have the belly, once filled, as god in his place.

Let him who began the praises of the cross complete them, and, after lamenting its injury, let the supreme teacher of the Church reveal [Col. 0781A] its glory. “Far be it from me,” he says, “to glory except in the cross of my Lord Jesus Christ” (Gal. 6). I think he does not judge that worthy of insults or burning which he proclaims so glorious that he considers it wicked to glory anywhere but in it, or to establish his glory anywhere but in it. “Far be it!” he says: let it not happen; let it never be; far from me be such meditation, such desire, such thought—that I should wish to place the goal of my purpose, the rest of my labours, the reward of my sufferings, all that glory for which I wait, anywhere but in the cross of the Lord, or receive it from any source but the Lord’s cross. Not that I understand the cross, insofar as it is a cross, to contain anything but torment; but because I acknowledge that through the cross’s torment salvation, through its disgrace glory, and through its death life have been given to me by Christ. Hence I also glory in my infirmities, not for the infirmities themselves, but “that the power of Christ may dwell in me” (2 Cor. 12).

[Col. 0781B] The evangelical beatitudes also confirm this apostolic understanding, when “blessed” are called the poor, those who mourn, those who hunger, the peacemakers, and those who endure persecution (Matt. 5): not because poverty, mourning, hunger, or endurance makes them blessed, but because the kingdom of heaven is given to the poor, consolation to mourners, satisfaction to those who hunger, and adoption as God’s children to peacemakers. So likewise with the rest. Therefore, just as these virtues, which, though they cause suffering, nevertheless confer glory, are not contemptible but glorious, so the Lord’s cross, though it tormented him, deserved to be glorious because in tormenting him it brought forth glory.

Accordingly, the Apostle glories in the cross and rebukes those who do not glory in it—among whom you are—by attacking them. He glories, I say, in the cross and proclaims it worthy of glory when again, in the Epistle to the Ephesians, he declares that Christ reconciled both—that is, Jew and Gentile—in his one body to God through the cross, and slew enmities in himself (Eph. 2). He glories in the cross and proclaims it worthy of glory when, in what follows, he says that he bends his knees to God the Father, asking, among other things which he seeks for them, that he grant them to comprehend with all the saints what is the breadth, length, height, and depth of that same cross (Eph. 3).

[Col. 0781C] Do you see that the Apostle, after Christ the supreme teacher of Christians, thinks in every respect and altogether contrary to your opinion, and teaches things discordant with your preaching? Do you perceive that he applies not only the Crucified One but also his cross so emphatically to the greatest mysteries of human salvation? Do you observe how great an honour that investigator of heavenly secrets judged, declared, and wrote to be due to its form, which appeared to you so contemptible that you judged it worthy of flames? He enumerates not merely some part of it, nor the whole collectively, but individually and carefully all the parts of the cross; and he indicates that it is laden with mystical sacraments no less than with the body of Christ crucified itself, like a tree heavy with the manifold fruit of life.

He calls breadth the timber set crosswise, [Col. 0782A] upon which the Lord’s hands were nailed; length that which extends from it down to the ground, upon which his feet were nailed; height that portion of the timber rising above his head, upon which was inscribed the title containing the statement of his charge; and depth that which was hidden below and could not be penetrated by the eyes. These are the parts of the cross which he describes. He affirms that the Lord’s cross, consisting of these, is enriched [or: filled] with great mysteries. For this reason he bends his knees; for this reason he prays that they may be able to comprehend these things; for this reason, as I said, he declares that the breadth, length, height, and depth of the cross should be not hateful to men but precious.

But if the parts of the cross are praiseworthy by apostolic testimony, I believe that the whole cross itself, composed [Col. 0782B] of those parts, is not to be despised but praised and honoured. If this is so, it is shown not only that the Lord’s cross ought to be free from your insults, but also proved worthy of praise and glory. But if perhaps you ask what mystery the breadth proposed by the Apostle, the length, the height, and the depth contain, it is not for this place to expound it, because I have undertaken the office not of teaching above you but of disputing against you. Yet if, changing your pursuits for the better, you wish to turn from impiety to piety, you too will be able to comprehend this with all the saints: so that, not by blaspheming but by humbly and modestly asking, you may receive; by seeking, find; and by knocking, have opened to you.

[Col. 0782C] After the Apostle, let the Lord of the apostles come and disclose to us as we await him what attitude he bears toward his cross. I do not think anyone ought to be more angry at the torments of the cross than he was, since no one else was tortured by them so greatly, and since the power to dispense punishments or rewards belongs properly not to another but to him. Hear, therefore, after the others, the judgment about the cross even of the Crucified One; and at least by his judgment, decide whether it is worthy of honour or of insult. Announcing in the Gospel that he would come at the end of the age to examine and judge the deeds of mortals, he says: “The powers of heaven will be shaken, and then the sign of the Son of Man will appear in heaven” (Matt. 24). What, I ask, do you think the sign of the Son of Man here means? The Son of Man himself? But a sign is not the very thing of which it is the sign. For the sign is one thing, and the thing of which it is a sign another. Thus that which is the Son of Man himself could not be the sign of the Son of Man. What, then, will it be? Consider, seek, investigate. What sign will be of such worth, such glory, such exaltation that it appears in heaven when the Son of Man himself descends from heaven with great power and majesty?

[Col. 0782D] But why do you labour? Do not pursue the fickleness of winds, the vanity of shadows, the phantoms of dreams, the twisted paths of error. Cast away lies, in which nothing is stable; embrace truth, in which nothing is changeable. That, that is the sign of the Son of Man which most clearly declares him to be the Son of Man. And what declared him so clearly to be the Son of Man as death, which no son of man ever escapes? Since Christ chose to suffer death upon this cross of which we speak, although he was the Son of God, he signified by dying on the cross that he was the Son of Man. Because it signifies the true Son of Man, the cross is rightly called the sign of the Son of Man.

The evangelical prophet Isaiah agrees with this Gospel saying when he says: “The Lord will raise a sign among the nations” (Isa. 5). And likewise what the same prophet adds: “He will gather the outcasts of Israel and collect the scattered of Judah from the four winds” (Isa. 11). See how aptly this agrees with the Gospel passage. For after the Lord said, “Then the sign of the Son of Man will appear in heaven,” after one intervening verse he says: “The Son of Man will send his angels with trumpet [Col. 0783A] and great voice, and they will gather his elect from the four winds, from the ends of heaven to their boundaries” (Matt. 24). Thus surely, thus do prophet and evangelist agree not only in sense but also in words. What the one says, “The Lord will raise a sign among the nations,” the other says, “The sign of the Son of Man will appear in heaven.” What the one says, “He will gather the outcasts of Israel and collect the scattered of Judah from the four winds,” the other says, “He will send his angels with trumpet and great voice and gather his elect from the four winds.” Except that the prophet seems to speak more of Christ’s first advent, while the Evangelist most plainly speaks of his second.

But whether at the first advent or the second, the sign raised among the nations is the cross, and the sign of the Son of Man appearing in heaven is the cross. Since Christ raised it here as a sign and it gathers the nations of the world from the four winds to faith in eternal salvation, and since at Christ’s final judgment, appearing in heaven, it summons the elect from the four winds—that is, from the whole world—to that same eternal salvation and glory, it is believed, declared, and preached to be worthy of the highest honour from them. Is it fitting that earth should reject what heaven displays to commend the cause of human salvation? Is it fitting that men should cast away what angels honour? And do they not honour it, when, with the powers of heaven stirred for judgment, they present it together with themselves to the world being judged? For he who said, “The powers of heaven will be shaken,” immediately added, “and then the sign of the Son of Man will appear in heaven.”

[Col. 0783D] And since, as has been said, this sign is Christ’s cross, when the powers of heaven—that is, the whole order of heavenly spirits—appear coming from above, then it too will shine in heaven with them. It will shine in heaven so that those born of earth may learn that they cannot ascend to heaven except through it, and the sons of men may recognize that only through it can they become companions of angels. Is that not therefore to be honoured by men which prepares angelic honour for them? Is that not to be glorified by mortals which bestows immortal glory upon them? Is that not to be adored as life-giving and salvation-bringing which will give blessed life to the dead and eternal salvation to the lost? And indeed, whether heretics wish it or not, it is life-giving because it gives life; salvation-bringing because it gives salvation; honourable because it gives honour; lovable because it gives love; admirable because it gives [Col. 0784A] wonder; happy because it gives happiness; noble because it gives nobility; blessed because it gives blessedness; glorious because it gives eternal glory.

Therefore those who hate the cross because it tormented the Lord should love it because it brought glory not only to us but also to him. It brought him the glory of which the Apostle says: “We see Jesus, because of the suffering of death, crowned with glory and honour” (Heb. 2). The cross, I say, brought glory to the Crucified One, as the same Apostle says elsewhere: “He became obedient unto death, even death on a cross. Therefore God also exalted him” (Phil. 2), and the remainder, as we have placed it above elsewhere. Because it brought him such glory, who was assumed by God, and moreover bestowed life and eternal glory upon us, it deserved to be glorious.

[Col. 0784B] Therefore, since it is proved by unanswerable authority and invincible reason that Christ’s cross ought to be honoured, praised, and glorified by Christians, it is denied by some heretics that it ought also to be adored, while some Catholics inquire whether this should be done. This must be considered and examined according to the understanding which the Lord deigns to grant us and the capacity which he himself bestows.

There is an honour rendered to a creature, and there is an honour due only to the Creator. Of the honour which a rational creature ought to show to another, it is written: “Honour your father and your mother” (Exod. 20; Matt. 5); “Outdo one another in showing honour” (Rom. 12); “Honour the king” (1 Pet. 2); “Presbyters, especially those who labour in the word, are worthy of double [Col. 0784C] honour” (1 Tim. 3); “Marriage is honourable in all” (Heb. 13); and a thousand such sayings, which command observance more or less according to the different persons, ranks, and offices. Of the honour to be rendered to God alone, Scripture says: “You shall adore the Lord your God, and serve him alone”; “You shall have no strange [other] gods before me”; “You shall not make for yourselves a graven image or a molten image, nor put them into the fire so as to adore them” (Exod. 20; Deut. 6); “Honour the Lord from your substance” (Prov. 3); “I will not give my glory to another, nor my praise to graven images” (Isa. 42); and six hundred other passages in which, as is said in the Book of Wisdom, the incommunicable name and service belonging exclusively to the solitary Godhead are plainly shown to be due uniquely to it. According to the blessed Father Augustine, this service, to be expressed more distinctly, is called *latria* in Greek and “the worship of God” in Latin.

[Col. 0784D] To this divine service, to this worship of God, belong the sacrifices offered by the patriarchs before the Law, instituted by Moses under the Law, and commanded by Christ in the time of grace and ordered by him to be observed by Christians until the end of the age. To this worship of God also belongs the word “adoration” now under discussion, but properly only when the worshipper understands God to be his sole author and ruler; when, acknowledging him as God, he glorifies him as God and gives thanks; when, placing all his hope in him, he believes that he receives from him alone every necessity; when, removing all ambiguity, he confidently knows that his help comes not from any mountains—that is, from saints or any others whatsoever—but from the Lord who made heaven and earth.

The Creator has granted this service, this worship due to himself, this incommunicable name, neither to heavenly spirits, nor earthly human beings, nor any creature, nor even to his own most blessed mother and virgin, the mother of all creatures. For just as, by the very order of creation, the Creator is deservedly and rightly set above the creature which he created, so it was fitting that this pre-eminence itself should be marked by some suitable sign. The Godhead set above creatures is therefore marked by the sign of sacrifices; it is marked by this sign; it is marked by the manifold sacrament now celebrated among the Christian people. Whoever desired to arrogate this to himself lost even what he possessed.

[Col. 0785A] Hence the first archangel, because he attempted to be like God, fell like lightning from heaven. Hence the Godhead, rejecting Adam as its companion because, through the one who condemned his offspring, he consented to his deceived wife, cast him out of paradise. Hence too Christian Scripture calls those who rendered *latria*, which we have called worship, to idols “idolaters,” and condemns them as perverters of divine honour and order.

Not even the man assumed by God would have possessed honour of this divine kind, unless he were one and the same person with him. But because he himself says, “Heaven is my throne, and earth is the footstool of my feet” (Isa. 66), and the Psalm commands, “Adore his footstool, because it is holy” (Ps. 98), we adore the earth of our body in the Son of God—not as something remote from him, [Col. 0785C] but as so united to him that, while the distinct properties of the natures are preserved, we venerate it as the very same as himself with the honour due to God.

Therefore with this adoration we adore Christ, Son not only of God but also of man; and we adore the cross—indeed, in the cross, the Crucified One himself, who is God and man. Nor, as far as lies in the cross itself, do we worship or adore wood, because the pronouncement remains: “You shall adore the Lord your God, and serve him alone” (Matt. 4). But when I say that I adore the cross, I profess that the crucified one is my Lord God and that I ought to serve him alone. This understanding is also confirmed by the fact that the Catholic Church declares, with praiseworthy devotion, that she adores not only the Lord’s cross but also his passion, death, resurrection, [Col. 0785D] and similar things.

Yet it is certain to everyone that the Lord’s death, passion, resurrection, and ascension are past events and no longer exist. For these were temporal accidents of this kind affecting God: as they came to belong to him in time when they had not belonged to him before, so they departed with time. For by dying within a definite and finite span of time, rising within a definite and finite span, and ascending within a definite and finite span, he taught that these things had passed, while he himself remains forever. Hence, as things no longer existing, they cannot, as has been said, be adored. Therefore, just as a certain rational principle, based on their having no substance or subsistence, prohibits these things from being adored, though a reasonable devotional usage requires it; so a wholly submissive and devoted affection of Christ-worshippers finds, preserves, and establishes that the Lord’s cross—which authority commands is not to be adored in itself—is to be venerated and adored from Christ and in Christ, or rather Christ in it.

[Col. 0786A] For when I say, “I adore the Lord’s death, the Lord’s resurrection, the Lord’s ascension,” I profess that I adore nothing other than the Lord dead, the Lord rising, the Lord ascending—indeed, the Lord who died, the Lord who rose, the Lord who ascended. With a like understanding, when I bow down humbly before the cross, I adore as God and Lord, to whom alone this is due, him who was once tortured upon it for our rest and died for our life. This privilege was given to the Lord’s cross: that among creatures it alone, after the Son of Man, who is also the Son of God, should be believed worthy of adoration. This is so that we may know that in the Lord’s death, which he suffered upon the cross, the end and summit of human salvation were established, and that we may show by sure and chief signs of humility that we are in no way ashamed, after the manner of unbelievers, of his cross and death.

For, as a good man says, “Our being born would have profited us nothing unless our redemption had profited us”; and we adore neither confessors who confess, nor martyrs who bear witness, nor apostles who proclaim, nor prophets who foretell, nor angels who minister, nor even his mother and virgin, the resting-place of the supreme King and sanctuary of the supreme God. For although the salvation just mentioned was administered in its respective ways through all those persons, it was nevertheless brought to completion through none of them except the cross.

[Col. 0786C] It was therefore completed in the cross and through the cross, upon which Christ, bowing his head in death, said: “It is finished” (John 19). We accordingly adore it above other things because of the salvation for which it was chosen above other things. We adore it, as I have said, as a chief sign of humility, lest we appear to think with the Jews, to whom it is a stumbling-block (1 Cor. 1); with the Gentiles, to whom it is foolishness (ibid.); or with the heretics, to whom it appears madness. By this chief sign of humility we commend Christ’s humility, the world’s chief saving power, which none of the rulers of this age knew (1 Cor. 2), and which was hidden from the wise and prudent and revealed only to little ones (Matt. 11). We commend it especially when we submit our necks to indignity, cruel torment, and public disgrace, and proclaim, by adoring the cross of the humbled one, that the world condemned by the pride of exalted man was saved by the humility of humbled God.

But there is another manner of adoration which, although it is called by the same name as that which denotes divine worship, nevertheless signifies only human reverence—the reverence, as said above, which ought to be rendered to human beings. With this, the great patriarch Abraham adored the people of the land, namely the sons of Heth (Gen. 23). With this Lot, righteous according to the testimony also of the Apostle Peter, adored the angels who overthrew Sodom (Gen. 19; 1 Pet. 2). With this Joseph’s brothers, prostrate upon the earth, adored him (Gen. 50). With this Joshua adored the angel, captain of the Lord’s host (Josh. 5). With this the prophet Nathan adored King David [Col. 0787A] (3 Kings 1). With this perhaps even the wicked Nebuchadnezzar adored the prophet Daniel (Dan. 2). For it must not be believed that holy men or holy angels either rendered to human beings the worship due to God alone or patiently endured its being offered to themselves.

It is therefore clear that this manner is not divine adoration but human veneration; nor is it that singular mark of Godhead, but a dutiful and common rendering of honour. But the special kind excludes every creature, while the general kind belongs to both the Creator and rational creatures. For authority forbids, and reason dissuades, offering even a small honour to an irrational thing. Yet when honour is rendered to relics of saints, sacred places, vestments, vessels, or any such things, it is not believed to be done because they are insensible, beautiful, pleasant, precious, or physically useful to people in any way; but because suitable honour is rendered in them to God or to his saints who will live with him forever.

[Col. 0787B] Therefore, if the Lord’s cross is received as worthy of adoration—that is, honour—in this manner also, this is neither impious nor erroneous, but pious and salutary: pious, because it does not depart from the path of right faith; salutary, because it procures salvation for its pious adorers, or venerators. It is therefore permissible to adore the Lord’s cross in either manner: in the former, God rather than the cross itself is adored; in the latter, God rather than the cross itself is honoured. In the former, the Crucified One is worshipped in the cross; in the latter, his author is venerated in the wood. In the former, divine worship is rendered to God himself through the cross; in the latter, the common honour rendered by many is paid through that same cross to the same God, to whom all honour and glory are due.

Against what they say: that the Mass is nothing and ought not to be celebrated.

After baptism has been denied, crosses burned, and churches destroyed, so that your criminal rashness may leave nothing sacred unharmed, it now stretches itself forth in the fourth place against the Crucified One himself, both Lord of churches and giver of baptism, and attempts to take from his Church not only what belongs to him but him himself. It denies that the body of Christ and blood of the divine Word are made by divine power or through the ministry of priests; and it affirms that everything which the ministers of the altar appear to do in [Col. 0787D] the sacrament of the altar is empty and superfluous.

But because I do not wish to report your words, set forth your own words yourselves, and disclose to our readers and hearers what you are accustomed to preach about these matters to the people whom you have deceived. Your words which were able to reach us are these:

> “Do not, O peoples, believe bishops, presbyters, or the clergy who deceive you. As in many matters, so also in the office of the altar they deceive you, where they lie that they make the body of Christ and give it to you for the salvation of your souls. They plainly lie. For the body of Christ was made only once, by Christ himself, at supper before his passion; and it was given to the disciples only once—that is, then only. Since then it has neither been made by anyone nor given to anyone.”

[Col. 0788A] Hear, all who have ears to hear; hear a doctrine supported by invincible reasoning. I had heard the pronouncement of these new apostles and, because it is so novel that they are its first preachers, I expected it to be fortified with great authorities and strengthened by powerful arguments. But behold: this monstrous utterance, penetrating—or rather boring through—human ears, has so boldly, stripped of every argument and bereft of every power, forced itself upon us not secretly but publicly, that either the Delphic Apollo seems to give answers to pagans, or Moses to Jews, or Christ to Christians. Their words, because they have been believed or are believed divine among their worshippers, need no reasoning, since they possess the fullest authority. Where divinity is believed, reason is not sought. It is sufficient in itself and is not compelled to give an account of its deeds or words, since it is held certain that it does nothing unjustly and can command nothing without reason.

[Col. 0788B] Thus these teachers—thus, I say, these most audacious enemies of Christ—offer their poisonous doctrine to the Christian world; and, without a structure of authorities, without the sinews of reasons, these foolish men have poured their follies into your minds, O hearers, as though you were compelled to give them faith as sacred oracles. But if, conscious of no divinity, they uttered these things in this manner, it is plain that those uttering them thus were not without a demonic spirit. But let words now be turned against them; and let the kindly Spirit of wisdom answer those warned not by a divine spirit but driven by a demonic one—indeed, answer the malign spirit itself speaking through them—and not spare the accursed thing from his lips.

Come then, come, my champions, with whom I share the field; and after the blows you have struck, return such a blow as you can. Those who stand around the fighters will be witnesses of our contest; and the heavenly observer will be present, who, examining not the strength but the causes of the combatants, will according to his custom award the palm only to justice.

[Col. 0788C] If this heresy of yours were confined within Berengarian limits—which denied indeed the reality of Christ’s body, but not the sacrament, species, or figure—I could easily discharge the labour of this chapter. I would send you not, I say, to Ambrose, Augustine, Gregory, the ancient and holy doctors of the Church whom you have rejected, but to learned and Catholic men of recent times: Lanfranc, Guitmund, and Alger. If only you would deign to read them, or allow them to be heard, not indeed for greater authority but for the nearness of their time and their familiar knowledge. The first was Archbishop of Canterbury; the second, Bishop of Aversa; the third, formerly canon and master at Liège and afterward, in our own time, monk and priest at the monastery of Cluny, where his book is also kept. He was a man of pure and devout life.

The first of these discussed well, fully, and perfectly the truth of Christ’s body and blood, which is concealed beneath the veil of the sacraments; the second better, more fully, and more perfectly; the last best, most fully, and most perfectly—so that he left nothing for even the most scrupulous reader to seek.

[Col. 0789A] If you read these books and understood what you read, they would truly compel you to recover from foolish obstinacy; for they have recalled many who were in error, instructed many who doubted, and confirmed many believers as well in the rule of right faith. These books, I say, could both correct you and compel you to come to your senses, if, as said above, you held no doctrine worse than that of the Berengarian heretics. But because, as I have said, you have surpassed error by error, heresy by heresy, wickedness by wickedness, you deny not only the reality of Christ’s flesh and blood but also the sacrament, species, and figure; and thus you judge his people to exist without the sacrifice of the supreme and true God.

Therefore, just as a new disease must be cured by a new remedy, so a new error must be refuted by a new work, [Col. 0789B] lest what had been passed over by great men, because it had not been heard of—for it has only now first arisen—should remain wholly undiscussed. The Church of God therefore answers you, enemies of God, that she is neither without a sacrifice nor offers in that her sacrifice anything other than the body and blood of her Redeemer.

She does indeed offer to the Lord her God the sacrifice of a contrite spirit, of which the Prophet says: “A contrite spirit is a sacrifice to God” (Ps. 50). She offers the sacrifice of righteousness, of which the same man says: “Then you will accept the sacrifice of righteousness” (ibid.). She also offers the sacrifice of praise, of which the one mentioned above says: “Sacrifice a sacrifice of praise to God” (Ps. 49).
