But she offers a sacrifice far more acceptable: namely, him who, according to the Apostle, “through the Holy Spirit offered himself without blemish to God,” in order that [Col. 0789C] he might “cleanse our conscience from dead works to serve the living God” (Heb. 9). She offers the Lamb of God who takes away the sins of the world (John 1), who neither dies when sacrificed, nor is diminished when divided, nor consumed when eaten. She offers him for herself, who offered himself for her; and what he did once by dying, she does continually by offering.

But because these things should rather be said to faithful persons who venerate them than to unbelievers who mock them, let the pearls meanwhile be put away, lest they be trampled by swine (Matt. 7); and demonstrate, with whatever effort you can, why you forbid earthly people to sacrifice to the God of heaven. Since this is the chief sign of divine worship and of a mind subject to God, and an ordinance established by God himself, produce, if you have any arguments on your side—which, I believe, you do not—why you refuse that servants should serve their Lord, human beings their God, created things their Creator, redeemed things their Redeemer; and why, with all the powers of wickedness available to you, you do not allow the kind of veneration owed to him alone and to be rendered by these beings to be rendered to him. [Col. 0789D]

Or perhaps, because your priesthood brought you too little profit while you ministered as priests, you decided to profane, overthrow, and sell off every ecclesiastical mystery and ministry? So that, because you were unwilling to baptize children, you denied their baptism; because it was laborious to carve crosses and paint or sculpt crucifixes, you burned them; because it was expensive to build churches, you destroyed them; because your parishioners did not, as you wished, fill your hands and purses with money or wax candles, [Col. 0790A] you annulled the sacrifice of the altar? Or because one of you was expelled from the church he held—he himself knows why—and the other, abandoning monastic life, became an apostate, you wished to avenge the injuries inflicted upon you, and, like the philosopher Porphyry, beaten by Christians, resolved to become blasphemers against Christ, seducers and impious enemies of Christians? Or because the darkness of obscurity covered you, did you choose, like that ancient burner of Diana’s temple, to become illustrious from obscure, known from unknown, famous from contemptible—by cunning rather than understanding, audacity rather than virtue, wickedness rather than probity? But let the impulse of an indignant mind be restrained, lest, in overflowing too much, it delay the matters proposed.

Tell me, I beg you, why Christian sacrifices do not please you Christians—if indeed you are such—when [Col. 0790B] God has always distinguished his own from outsiders by the sign of sacrifice; when by this sign he has distinguished divine service from human acts of obedience; when, above all, he has distinguished by this sign the honor uniquely owed to the Creator from the honor by which rational creatures ought, according to the Apostle, to show preference to one another (Rom. 12). Recall the ancient ages; examine the generation of saints from Adam to Christ. You will find that either none or very few worshipped God without the rite of sacrifices, because all who pleased God by righteousness immediately worshipped him with the veneration of sacrifices.

You will certainly see that first righteous man Abel offering gifts to God, and God kindling fire over his gifts (Gen. 4); Noah, after the Flood, dedicating the beginnings of a new age by sacrifices (Gen. [Col. 0790C] 8); Abraham, after offering to God a three-year-old heifer, a three-year-old she-goat, and a three-year-old ram, together with a turtledove and a pigeon (Gen. 15), also placing his bound son upon the altar, over the pile of wood, in order to sacrifice him, but being forbidden by the very one who had commanded this, lest he fulfill his vow (Gen. 22). After Abraham offering and Isaac offered, you will see Jacob, moved by the vision of God and angels, raise a stone in honor of the divinity he had seen, pour oil upon it, and say: “Truly the Lord is in this place, and this is the house of God and the gate of heaven” (Gen. 28). You will also learn that in the land of Uz—that is, among the Gentiles—Job, upright and blameless, whom none in his time resembled upon earth, [Col. 0790D] rose early in the morning and offered burnt offerings for each of his children, saying: “Perhaps my children have sinned” (Job 1).

You will proceed thence to the times of great Moses and find that the whole stock of the Hebrews, from whom the Savior whom you oppose was to be born according to the flesh, was subjected by God through Moses to diverse and innumerable sacrificial rites: continually, almost without interruption, offering victims of oxen, calves, lambs, sheep, rams, goats, he-goats, turtledoves, pigeons, various four-footed animals and birds—for sin, for a beloved person, for purification, for cleansing—so that, as the Apostle says, without sacrifices and the shedding of blood there was no remission of sins (Heb. 9). Read Leviticus, if even its name is known to you; [Col. 0791A] indeed, read the whole Pentateuch, properly called the Law, and review the entire sequence of the Old Testament. It will teach you what you do not know: that God gave frequent answers through sacrifices to holy kings, leaders, prophets, and priests; and that he made clear that their offerings were pleasing and acceptable to him, either by the smoke with which he overshadowed them, or the cloud with which he covered them, or the fire with which he consumed them, and by other signs.

Thus, at Solomon’s dedication and sacrifice, when one hundred thousand sheep and twenty thousand oxen were offered, the glory of the Lord filled the house of the Lord through a cloud (1 Kgs. 8; 2 Chron. 5, 7). Thus heavenly flame descended upon Elijah’s burnt offering and consumed not only the offered ox, but also the altar’s wood and stones, down to ashes; and by such a sign showed Elijah’s sacrifice accepted by [Col. 0791B] God (1 Kgs. 18). Thus, at the consecration of the wilderness tabernacle, it is written: “After all things were completed, a cloud covered the tabernacle of testimony, and the glory of the Lord filled it; nor could Moses enter the tent of the covenant, because the cloud covered everything and the majesty of the Lord shone forth, for the cloud had covered all things” (Exod. 40). That tabernacle, certainly, had been constructed, set up, and sanctified by God himself through Moses for no purpose except the worship of God and sacrifice to him. Thus Isaiah, in his vision—though a spiritual vision—of the high and exalted throne, after the winged seraphim and their cry, “Holy, holy, holy,” says: “The thresholds of the hinges were shaken at the voice of the one crying, and the house was filled with smoke” (Isa. 6).

[Col. 0791C] You have, if you attend, evidence that the sacrifices of the ancients pleased God so greatly that he not only caused the places in which the sacrifices were performed to be built, but also blessed and consecrated both the sacrifices and those places; and he glorified what had been established, blessed, and consecrated by smoke, cloud, fire, and the other signs I have mentioned. For sacrifices are not celebrated for the sake of a temple or altar; rather, temples and altars are built, consecrated, adorned, and glorified for the sake of sacrifices. Sacrifices themselves are directed solely to him to whom they are rendered alone, with no co-participant.

For this is the service of sacrifice; this is the honor to be rendered to deity alone; this is worship to be offered only to the divine name. It rejects every creature as a substitute for the Creator, because, just as the majesty to which it is offered is incommunicable, so too what is offered rejects all sharing. By this distinctive service, a human being is marked as subject to God alone, so that, in accordance with the condition of his origin, he recognizes nothing above himself except God, knowing that he has his beginning from God alone and his unfailing end in him, and therefore submits and obeys him as author, ruler, and rewarder. [Col. 0791D]

By this outward observance the inward disposition of the mind is marked, a disposition that could never be known unless shown by external signs. By this service both substances of the human being are marked as subject to God: as the one embraces God in devotion, the other serves God in action, so that the whole human being may be shown to be subject to him and may truly say: “Will not my soul be subject to God?” (Ps. 61), and: “My heart and my flesh have rejoiced in the living God” [Col. 0792A] (Ps. 83).

For this reason no creature—not merely one inanimate, not merely one without sense, not merely one irrational, but not even a rational and blessed creature—has been permitted to receive honor by sacrifices. This has been granted neither to an angel nor to a human being, nor even to the highest order of seraphim, because the sign that distinguishes the Creator from created beings among mortals has rightly always remained unshared. The blessed apostles Barnabas and Paul knew this: when the Lycaonians wished to sacrifice to them, they prohibited it with abhorrence; and, because victims had already been prepared, they tore their garments (Acts 14). They knew that this had been granted to no one; they also knew that it was sternly forbidden by God himself, who says in Scripture both concerning those who sacrifice otherwise than to God and those to whom they sacrifice: “Whoever sacrifices to gods shall be utterly destroyed, except to the Lord alone”; and: [Col. 0792B] “I will execute judgment upon the gods of Egypt.” And concerning both parties: “Let those who make them, and all who trust in them, become like them” (Ps. 113).

For proud spirits, apostates from God, envying God’s divinity and appropriating it to themselves, persuaded blind people—made forgetful of God by the long duration of their exile—to render to creatures what, as has been said, belonged to the Creator alone, so that they might turn them completely away from God. They established public sacrifices both for themselves and for dead human beings. And, so that they might subject the image of God to greater indignities by mocking it to God’s dishonor, they even compelled miserable people to serve irrational creatures. Thus they put reason to sleep in a rational animal, so that, serving dogs, birds, creeping beasts, and those over whom they had been set, voluntarily subjecting themselves to them, they would not even remember that they were human. [Col. 0792C] Hence the Apostle says: “They changed the glory of the incorruptible God into the likeness of corruptible man, and of birds, and four-footed animals, and serpents” (Rom. 1).

Not content with these things, they dragged them down to still baser things and made them servants even of insensible objects. Hence the Book of Wisdom says: “For they wandered long in the way of error, esteeming as gods those superfluous things found among animals, living in the manner of foolish children. Therefore, as though they were senseless children, you gave them a judgment for mockery” (Wis. 12). And again: “From the good things that are seen they could not understand him who is, nor, by attending to his works, did they recognize who the craftsman was; but they thought either fire, or spirit, or swift-moving air, or the circuit of the stars, [Col. 0792D] or vast water, or the sun or moon, to be gods governing the world” (Wis. 13).

Deceived by all these things, people attributed God’s glory to them and honored them with divine worship and sacrifices, against him who said: “I will not give my glory to another, nor my praise to carved images” (Isa. 42). To what end is this said? So that, seeing that the ancient fathers and all the righteous of earlier times pleased God through righteousness and sacrifices; observing that God commanded such things to be done for himself alone; hearing that he destroyed those who sacrificed to foreign gods; recognizing, I say, that through sacrifices especially the honor of deity has been rendered to God by all the saints in every age, you may grant what you have hitherto forbidden and permit people of our age to offer God the sacrificial gift owed to him.

[Col. 0793A] For why are children forbidden to follow their fathers? Why are those whom they imitate in faith not allowed to imitate them in the chief sign of faith? Or perhaps God approves Jewish sacrifices and rejects Christian ones? Does he not rather express disgust with their sacred rites, saying through Isaiah: “I am full of burnt offerings of rams, and I have not desired the fat of fatlings or the blood of calves, lambs, and goats” (Isa. 1)? Does he not also say through another prophet: “I will not take calves from your house, nor he-goats from your flocks” (Ps. 49)? Does he not say through Malachi: “I have no pleasure in you, and I will not accept an offering from your hand” (Mal. 1)? In saying this, he does not reject the sacrifices appointed for that time, but reproves the evil life of those offering them. Thus he adds through Isaiah: “For your hands [Col. 0793B] are full of blood” (Isa. 1).

It is very strange if the principal worship of deity, as has already been said, is not rendered to God in our time, though in every age before ours it was practiced with the greatest zeal and anxious devotion. It is strange if Christians are kept from sacrifices offered to the one God, when patriarchs, prophets, Jews, Gentiles, and believers are compelled by God himself to sacrifice to God himself. It is strange that divine sacrifices should now for the first time be removed from the world, although in its past generations the world has never been without sacrificial rites. For even in the deep darkness of its ignorance and wickedness it did not so perish from God as to lack some persons, though few, who both worshipped God through righteousness and showed by sacrifices that they worshipped him.

But now, if the world listens to your new doctrine, [Col. 0793C] it will do what it has never done, and, like that captive people, will sit without law, without king, without priesthood, without ephod and *teraphim*. When it has ceased to sacrifice to God, it will itself cease to belong to God. In these times of grace there will be what never existed even in the time of wrath: when Christians cease sacrificing to God, the worship that has always existed in the world will utterly perish from the world; and one who is shown to be subject to God by worshipping God according to his rite, on abandoning his worship, will appear to have no God at all.

For in our day there are four principal divisions of sects in the world: Christians, Jews, Saracens, and pagans. If Christians do not sacrifice, then no one in the world sacrifices. Jews, looking at everything in their own fashion with bovine eyes and bearing the burdens of God’s law in asinine fashion, without receiving its fruit, sacrifice nowhere, because they say that Jerusalem alone is the place where God ought to be honored and worshipped by sacrifices. Since they have been forbidden to inhabit it, contrariwise, for eleven hundred years, they have ceased to sacrifice. [Col. 0793D]

The Saracens, deceived by the most exalted deceiver of all deceivers, and wavering as though submerged between Jewish and Christian law, accept circumcision, make frequent use of washings, devote themselves to prayer at fixed hours by day and at fixed hours by night, especially, it is said, after food and drink, and wholly loosen the reins for sensual indulgence.

And although almost the whole eastern and African region has been deceived by that wicked Muhammad and has served these and innumerable superstitions [Col. 0794A] for nearly five hundred and fifty years; although they confess that Christ God, born from the Virgin by, as they say, a divine breath, lived holily, taught true things, and performed miracles—among them we have neither any precepts concerning sacrifices nor even any small offering made by them as a sacrifice. They nonetheless say that they worship almighty God, creator of all things, to whom, as I have said, they render no sacrificial rites.

The pagans, though few and unknown to the inhabited world, hide away at the farthest limits of the north beneath the icy pole and inhabit places said to be near the Maeotian marshes. Since they are ignorant even of the errors of idols and know neither their names, rites, nor sacrifices, they worship as a god for the whole day whatever meets them when they rise from bed in the morning—horses, donkeys, pigs, cocks, or anything else. [Col. 0794B] Thus they worship gods not lasting or even annual, but, so to speak, daily or hourly gods. Although these pitiable people are mocked by the devil more disgracefully than others in these and many ways unknown to us, they nevertheless render sacrifices neither to Creator nor creature, but preserve, without any knowledge of sacrifices, what innate error has taught them.

Since, therefore, sacrifices are observed neither among Jews nor Saracens nor pagans, if they are not permitted to Christians either, that unique sign of deity—by which, as I have said, divine service is distinguished from human service from the beginning—has perished, since it can now be found in no nation or part of the world. [Col. 0794C] But perhaps modern times are less indebted to God than earlier ones, so that these people rightly despise to pay the honor which ancient ages rendered to God. And rightly so! Yes, rightly, rightly: those who have received greater things ought to render lesser; those bound by a more numerous sum of debt ought to be compelled to pay the smallest amount; and, contrary to the voice of Jesus Christ, who says, “He to whom less is forgiven loves less” (Luke 7), and contrary to the opinion of Simon the Pharisee, who says that the person to whom more is forgiven loves the creditor more—whereupon it was said: “You have judged rightly” (ibid.)—contrary to these judgments of the Lord and the Pharisee, the Christian owes God less than the Jew, apostolic times less than prophetic times, and the entire world subjected to the Gospel’s voice less than one people subject to Mosaic law.

And where is the Savior of the nations, promised to them and presented to us; offered to them and born to us; taken from them and given to us? Where is the blood of the eternal covenant, which flowed down from them to us, ran down to us through their conduit, and, leaving behind the muddy channel through which it ran, cleansed us—made from mud and placed beneath the channel—from all mud and filth? Where is, according to the Apostle, “the mystery hidden from ages and generations, but now made manifest to his saints, to whom God willed to make known the riches of the glory of this mystery among the Gentiles, which is Christ, the hope of glory” (Col. 1)? [Col. 0794D] Where is, according to the same Apostle, the power of God’s mystery kept silent through eternal ages? (Eph. 3). Where is the veil of the temple torn, and what had long been veiled revealed? Where is the kingdom of heaven, of which the King of heaven says: “Repent, for the kingdom of heaven has drawn near” (Matt. 3)?

[Col. 0795A] Do these times, so blessed—and, to use a poetic expression, these golden ages—in which the Father has had mercy on the world, the Son has been offered for the world, the Spirit of the Most High has been poured into the world, death has been destroyed, life restored, righteousness repaired, and resurrection prepared, owe God less than earlier ages? Not at all. No: though the whole world cry out otherwise, they owe no less to him to whom they owe not only themselves and all that they can rightfully possess by creation, but, what is dearer, also by redemption. And if all things, then sacrifices also.

Therefore, compelled by necessary reason, you heretics will necessarily restore the sacrifices that you wished to take away from Catholics. [Col. 0795B] You will restore them by reason; you will restore them by what among us has greater strength, authority—not fabricated but true; not earthly but heavenly; not human but divine.

God, angered by the long-standing evils of the Jewish people—who were impious toward God and unjust toward human beings—and no longer enduring that spiritual and heavenly promises should be trampled by earthly and carnal persons, chose successors for them: persons who would receive what they rejected, will what they refused, and render the vineyard’s fruit in its seasons. In place of one people he chose all nations; in place of a part of Syria, the whole world. Through his Son, the Angel of this great counsel, he delivered to it his law, [Col. 0795C] his worship, and his sacrifices; and through him, rescuing the world from death, restored it to immortal life. So that these things might be believed without any doubt to be true and received in their time, he foretold them through his messengers in many ways and by many means. And who could enumerate everything?

But with regard to the worship in question, hear David speaking in the Spirit of God: “All nations whom you have made shall come and worship before you, O Lord” (Ps. 85); “All kings shall worship him; all nations shall serve him” (Ps. 71); “All nations, clap your hands” (Ps. 46); “God shall reign over the nations” (ibid.); “Say among the nations: The Lord has reigned” (Ps. 95); and a hundred similar statements. But these concern worshipping God. Likewise, concerning sacrifice: “Bring to the Lord, O families of the nations; bring to the Lord glory and honor; bring to the Lord glory to his name. Take victims and enter into his courts” (Ps. 28); and Isaiah: “All flesh shall come to worship before my face, says the Lord” (Isa. 66); and Malachi: “From the rising of the sun even to its setting, my name is great among the nations; and in every place a clean offering is offered to my name, because my name is great among the nations, says the Lord of hosts” (Mal. 1).

[Col. 0795D] And what more remains for you, brutish people, to seek? Do you not see that, just as the law, so sacred rites, sacrifices, and all divine worship have been transferred from the Jews to the Gentiles? Even if sacred rites are not celebrated among us in the same manner, they are nevertheless sacred rites; if priesthoods are not constituted in the same order, they are nevertheless priesthoods; if sacrifices are not made from the same things, they are nevertheless sacrifices. For sacrifices are celebrated, priesthoods ordained, and offerings rendered in another manner indeed, but not to another God.

Therefore cease—cease now from madness—for no authority and no reason permits Christian times to render less honor to God than Jewish times, since those who have received more gifts ought to show not less but greater obedience to the giver of those same gifts. Hence it is truly fitting and just that those who serve him in this time of grace by different but not inferior rites should venerate him more devoutly by this supreme and divine worship of sacrifices. Since, by God’s grace, it is now established that Christian sacrifices are not to be abolished, it must nevertheless be considered whether they ought to be such as those that are offered. [Col. 0796A]

The sacrifice of the Christian world [Col. 0796B] is not manifold but single; not many, but one. For just as throughout the whole world there is only one Christian people offering it, one God to whom it is offered, and one faith by which it is offered, so too what is offered is itself one. The plurality of Jewish victims has given place to the unity of the Christian victim, because by its multiplicity it could not make perfect the worshipper; God therefore provided a victim which by its singleness would cleanse, sanctify, and perfect those who offer it. Ox, calf, ram, lamb, she-goat, and he-goat fill Jewish altars with flesh and blood; the Lamb of God alone, who takes away the sins of the world, is laid upon Christian altars.

[Col. 0796C] Hear not me but the Apostle of God: “Christ our Passover has been sacrificed” (1 Cor. 5). That is: the Passover of the Jews is a sacrificed lamb; but our Passover—that is, that of Christians—is Christ sacrificed. Therefore Christ is this one sacrifice of Christians. This sacrifice was reserved for the Christian age. It was reserved, I say, for the time of grace, since it was not fitting that it should be given in the time of wrath. The Jew had an ox; the Christian has Christ, whose sacrifice excels Jewish victims as much as Christ exceeds an ox. A servile victim was then fitting for servants; in our days the liberating victim has been reserved for sons and friends, to whom it is said in the Gospel: “Little children, I am still with you a little while” (John 13), and: “I will no longer call you servants, but friends” (John 15).

The text of divine law is sprinkled with innumerable testimonies that the multiplicity of ancient victims signified this one victim of the Gospel. And because it was impossible for sins to be taken away by the blood of lambs and goats (Heb. 10), the Law itself, which had commanded those many sacrifices, directed everyone toward this one victim. Of this David says: “The lifting up of my hands is the evening sacrifice” (Ps. 140); Isaiah: “He was offered because he himself willed it” (Isa. 53); Peter: “You were redeemed not with gold or silver, but with the precious blood, as of an unblemished and spotless lamb, of Jesus Christ” (1 Pet. 1); and Paul: “The Lord Jesus Christ did this once by offering himself” (Heb. 7).

But I know that by the names offering, sacrifice, victim, burnt offering, and the like, the Lord’s passion and death are signified, and I have never heard you deny this. [Col. 0796D] [Col. 0797A] His death is denoted by these names because, just as sins were said to be cleansed by the death of the animals offered, so the sins of the whole world are taken away by his death. And because the Apostle says, “He offered himself without blemish to God” (Heb. 9), he is said to offer himself because he surrendered his life to death not under compulsion but willingly. He offered himself to God in this way because eternal death for humankind could be dissolved only by the temporal death of one who was God and human.

[Col. 0797B] For the gracious God, whose every way is mercy and truth (Ps. 24), being so just that he does not cease to be merciful, and so merciful that he always remains just, did not permit even the evils which he had not created to remain disordered among the things he had created. Therefore, justly ordering human sin, which had unjustly forced itself, as it were from elsewhere, into his kingdom, he condemned the sinner and consigned the exile from everlasting blessedness to misery and eternal death. For the offender had become guilty to such an extent that his guilt would remain utterly disordered in God’s most ordered kingdom if God’s justice punished the sinner with a penalty less than eternal. Nor could that justice any longer be called justice if it did not render what was proportionate to deserts. For this reason the offspring of the human race, corrupted in its root, drew from its origin both the defect and its condemnation, and all alike lay subject for long ages, by the law of justice, to eternal death.

[Col. 0797C] At last God, in his essential goodness, took pity on ruined humankind and wished to save it; yet he neither wished nor was able to do so except justly. While in his eternal counsel he sought how, with justice preserved, he might show mercy to the wretched, this above all presented itself: a means by which justice would be preserved, humanity freed, grace increased, and God glorified.

He therefore sent God the Son to the children of humankind, so that, putting on human nature and healing human defects, he might in assumed flesh take on not sin but the penalty of sin, namely bodily death; and so by his single death might exclude their double death, and by his death lasting an hour, their eternal death. In this dispensation mercy showed mercy, and nothing was taken from justice, since in place of humankind’s eternal punishment the temporal punishment of God-and-human, and in place of humankind’s eternal death the temporal death of God-and-human, was offered. [Col. 0797D] This is known to carry such weight upon the very scales of justice that, for justly ordering the sins of the world, the transitory death of the Son of God outweighs by far the eternal death of the children of humankind. Clearly more was rendered to justice when Christ died than is repaid when humanity is condemned.

Justice therefore has all that belongs to it, because the Son of God died for human sins. Thus justice, which had long stood in the way of human salvation, at last yielded to mercy; and mercy and truth, which had proceeded for several thousand years by different paths, met one another in the way—which is Christ. And justice and peace, which had seemed opposed to each other when humanity was condemned, kissed one another when humanity was now saved [Col. 0798A] (Ps. 84).

Thus, according to John the Baptist, “the Lamb of God took away the sins of the world” (John 1). Thus, according to the Apostle Peter: “He himself bore our sins in his body upon the tree, so that, dead to sins, we might live to righteousness”; and, according to the prophet Isaiah, “by whose bruise we have been healed” (1 Pet. 2; Isa. 53). This is our sacrifice: this is the burnt offering of the evangelical law, of the New Testament, of the new people. It was then offered once on the cross to God by the Son who is God and human; and it has been commanded and instituted by him to be continually offered upon the altar by his own people. For what was offered then is not something different from what is now offered; rather, what it is said that Christ offered once (Heb. 7, 9), he left to his Church to offer continually.

[Col. 0798B] And because a more direct way has now opened, through which freer speech may proceed to expose and refute this most foolish error, hear not me but the Lord; not a Christian but Christ; not merely a human being but God. Hear him: whoever does not hear him shall be cut off from his people. Speak, Lord Jesus, our God, our Savior, our Priest, our Victim. Speak; answer the adversaries of your covenant, who wish to annul what you have established, uproot what you have planted, and destroy what you have founded. Speak: perhaps those who resist your Church will yield to you; those who irreverently oppose you will fear your face; and, if they are your sheep, they will hear your voice (John 10). [Col. 0798C] Forgive me for questioning presumptuously, yet with zeal for your Church—your dove, your bride—whom these men seek to violate. Certainly they deny that you are Redeemer, since they strive to take from the redeemed the price of human redemption that you gave us—your body, I mean. They wish again to bind the knot of captivity that you long ago loosed, while rejecting the giver of freedom.

Speak, therefore, Lord, testator of the new and eternal covenant: did you wish this covenant, as these men say, to be of one day’s duration, or did you instead decree that it should be eternal? Let them hear not me but you, so that they may turn not to me but to you. What then? At the Last Supper, which you celebrated with your disciples, exchanging the old Passover for the new, you took bread, gave thanks, broke it, and gave it to your disciples. But what did you say? “Take: this is my body, which shall be delivered for [Col. 0798D] you” (Luke 22). And what did you add? “Do this in remembrance of me” (ibid.). Likewise, after supper, you took the cup, saying: “This is my blood of the New Testament, which shall be shed for you and for many for the remission of sins” (ibid.).

Have you heard? Do not become idols that have eyes and do not see, ears and do not hear (Ps. 113; 134). You hear this not from any teacher, but from him of whom the Father, crying out, commands: “Hear him” (Matt. 17; Mark 9; Luke 9). You heard him giving a body. But what body? For there are heavenly bodies and earthly bodies, and whatever here lies under sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch is a body. Therefore, lest anyone should suppose this to be the body of some animal or of any human being, in order to exclude every other sensible or insensible body, after he said, “Take: this is [the] body,” he added, “my.” Therefore he gave his own body, not another’s, to his disciples.

[Col. 0799A] Again, lest perhaps some hidden thought should creep in [“subriperet”: steal in] that he could have created in his hands a body that was indeed his own but nevertheless was not what he himself was, he added, “which shall be delivered for you.” As though he said: Do not doubt; do not imagine this thing or that; do not think one thing and then another. For this is the body—not another body, nor another person’s, but mine; not transformed or newly created, but that which shall be delivered for you, crucified for you, and die for you. So likewise concerning the cup: “This,” he says, “is [my] blood.” It is not the blood of an ox or ram, of a lamb or any human being, but mine—not another’s, nor brought forth by a new creation, but that which shall be shed for you, drawn out by scourges, forced forth by nails, poured out by the spear.

[Col. 0799B] What could be said more clearly, lucidly, or openly to demonstrate the reality of the Lord’s body and blood? Did he not, long before his passion, commending the magnificent and saving sacrament, repeatedly say to his disciples and the Jews: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves” (John 6); “The bread which I shall give is my flesh” (ibid.); and “My flesh is truly food, and my blood is truly drink” (ibid.)? Why this? So that if, under the name “body,” you wander in thought among various bodies, on hearing the name “flesh” you may be called back from the innumerable multiplicity of bodies. Again, on hearing the name “Son of Man,” you may suppose it to be the flesh of no other than him who, though he was the Son of God, by unique grace and a singular operation became the Son of Man.

Because this work of such great mercy must be remembered most steadfastly and embraced uniquely, he often uses, while leaving unspoken the name “Son of God,” which he is in himself, the name “Son of Man,” which he is for us. He calls it flesh so that it may not be thought to be just any body; he calls it the flesh of the Son of Man so that it may not be judged another’s rather than his own. But perhaps it is thought impossible either that bread should be changed into flesh or wine into blood. Perhaps it is also thought that the finite and quite limited quantity of Christ’s one body cannot suffice for the bites of the whole world through so many ages.

This, indeed, is what I once heard Berengar say. For when he was perhaps at Angers and was discussing this sacrament of Christ’s body with some people, he said: “If Christ’s body had been as large as this tower, which rises before our eyes in a massive bulk, it would already have failed many years ago, having been eaten by so many peoples throughout the whole world.” As perverse as he was, so perverse were his words.

But what answer is to be made to those who are unwilling to allow God any power except what they themselves possess, any knowledge except what they themselves know, any action except what they themselves perform? What answer shall be made to those who strive to confine the height of eternal wisdom and the omnipotence of divine power in such a way that, if assent be granted them, with God’s wisdom and omnipotence gone, God can no longer be God [Col. 0800A]? What shall be said to the deaf, unwilling to hear the prophet crying: “Who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counsellor?” (Isa. 40); and elsewhere: “What is the way of wisdom, or what is the place of understanding? It is hidden from the eyes of all living beings” (Job 28). And another says: “Who has crossed the sea and brought her, and carried her above choice gold?” (Baruch 3). Does not the whole world resound, from sea to sea and from the rising of the sun to its setting: “Whatever the Lord willed, he has done in heaven and on earth, in the sea and in all the depths” (Ps. 134)? And who could enumerate everything?

But look to yourself, whoever you are that do not believe in heavenly miracles, O man. First attend to your own wisdom and power, and then begin to weigh those of God. Certainly, God, establishing ranks [Col. 0800B] among his creatures, preferring some to others and subjecting others to some, has subjected every bodily creature to you, and has distinguished you with reason, which he granted to no bodily substance. Hence you surpass very many creatures in power and all of them in wisdom. You recognize how greatly you excel in strength over creeping things, birds, and four-footed animals. You do not doubt that in knowledge you surpass all earthly things. You have therefore been set over the world; but the Maker of the world has been set over you. Wisdom has been set over you; power has been set over you: wisdom, because yours is confined within the narrowest limits, while his “reaches mightily from end to end and orders all things sweetly” (Wis. 9); power, because yours daily yields in many ways, whereas his, as has been said, does whatever he wills.

Therefore be to your God what your beast of burden is to you [Col. 0800C]. It does not strive to investigate your secrets; do not strive rashly to violate the mysteries of your God. It does not know how you arrange a journey, how you order a battle, whom you place first, in the middle, or last in the contest; by what counsel, after much bloodshed, you accept peace; or how you provide that your estate, household, wife, children, and servants do not lack necessities. And, to undertake greater matters, as the subject requires, it does not know at what time seeds ought to be sown, crops planted and grown harvested, vines planted, pruned, and cleansed; or what spring, summer, autumn, and winter hold in common with one another and what belongs properly to each. It does not perceive how, by the liveliness of your mind, you comprehend not merely earthly but heavenly matters; how you distinguish the courses, positions, and times of the Moon, Sun, Mercury, Venus, Mars, Jupiter, Saturn—names belonging to ancient superstition—and of the other stars; how you determine the measures and intervals of years, months, days, hours, divisions, and instants; or how, by the subtlety of reason, you discern how heat, cold, moisture, and dryness either expand, contract, moisten, or dry human things [Col. 0800D]. It does not dispute concerning your thoughts, words, or works. It judges, not by understanding but by nature, that something has been granted you which it may not penetrate. Therefore, although it understands none of these things, it does not complain, rebel, or demand that the rationale of everything be revealed to it; but, obedient to you its commanding master, it complies without question with what it is ordered.

Your ass teaches you, to speak of the meaner animals, what the Lord your God wills you to do; if you wish to penetrate his secrets, you will be unable to be his beast of burden, of whom the psalm says, “I became as a beast of burden before you” (Ps. 72) [Col. 0801A]. Preserve, therefore, for your God what you wish preserved for yourself by your ass. Do not seek things higher than yourself or investigate things too strong for you; but always think upon what God commands, and do not be curious about his many works (Ecclus. 3). And as Solomon likewise says: “Eat honey that is sufficient, lest perhaps, when filled, you vomit it” (Prov. 25); for, according to the same author, “He who searches out majesty shall be overwhelmed by glory” (ibid.). Likewise: “Turn your eyes away from me, because they have made me fly away” (Song 5); and, according to David: “Man shall approach to the lofty heart, and God shall be exalted” (Ps. 63). All these things, as is fitting, subject your pride to God’s majesty, your folly to God’s wisdom, and your weakness to God’s power; nor do they permit you to speak foolishly against him or to dare what ought not be dared [Col. 0801B].

Yet although the mouths of those speaking iniquity ought already to have been stopped by authorities and reason, lest they dare compare the foolishness or weakness of the creature with the wisdom or power of the Creator, let examples nevertheless be supplied, so that, unless they are wholly beasts or ungodly persons, not only their ears but their eyes may be satisfied. Look, then, whoever you are who either do not believe, or doubt, that in the sacrament of the Church bread is changed into Christ’s flesh and wine into his blood, because you distrust either his will, his power, or both [Col. 0801C]. For nothing else impels you either to disbelief or doubt. Either he willed it and could not accomplish it; or he could accomplish it and did not will it; or he neither willed nor could accomplish it. But if you believe the Gospel, you cannot doubt that he willed it. For he would not have commanded this to be done in memory of himself if he had not willed it to be done. And if you believe the prophet, you will hold it certain that he could accomplish it. For if he did whatever he willed, then assuredly he also did this, because he willed it. Therefore he willed and was able that bread be changed into his flesh and wine into his blood. And because he willed and was able, he therefore did it.

For if God is almighty and Christ is God, it follows that he is wholly able to change bread into his body and wine into his blood, just as he is able to do all things [Col. 0801D]. And although God’s omnipotence destroys every hostile fortification, let examples nevertheless follow, as has been said, by which even brute cattle may be compelled to assent. What, I ask, do you say, you who contradict so clear a truth? “I do not believe,” says one; “I doubt,” says another, “that the bread of the altar is changed into flesh and wine into Christ’s blood, because for a substance of one kind to be converted into a substance of another kind seems to me novel and unprecedented: novel, because it has never happened; unprecedented, because it has never been seen.” If you are willing to recall former times, I say, you will find that what you called novel is old, and you will recognize that what you called unprecedented is customary.

Read again, as Ambrose says, of Moses’ rod changed into a serpent; recall the Egyptian waters changed into blood [Col. 0802A]. If you acknowledge the differing substances of rod and serpent, water and blood, recover from your wrongly conceived opinion. Nor can you say that these were magical illusions, since God was not like Satan, the teacher of magical arts, nor Moses like Jannes and Mambres. Although they made dragons, changed waters, and produced larger flies, when they failed at the smaller flies—that is, gnats—they said: “This is the finger of God” (Exod. 8). For what they did was not real but phantasmal: by magical power they set before human eyes not real things but images of them, thereby deceiving unlearned and unbelieving people. But what was done by God through Moses was not false but true, not imaginary but real [Col. 0802B], since truthful signs had to be wrought by the Author of truth and lying signs by the father of lies. Thus the magicians’ serpent was false, whereas the serpent and blood truly produced by Moses from the rod and river were real.

Recall also that first, unique, and universally famous miracle of the Savior, by which he changed water into wine—not imaginary wine, but true and good wine—as the steward testified when he said to the bridegroom: “You have kept the good wine until now” (John 2).

The providence of the Almighty distinguished the beginnings of the Old and New Testaments with miracles of this kind so that anyone who denied that things may by divine power be changed into things—that is, substances into substances—might recognize that he was acting against the majesty of both laws [Col. 0802C]. After Moses’ and Christ’s miracles, so solemn and well known, let the world itself bear witness to the truth, and for this purpose bring forward snow and hail, clouds and the elements. Let it convict unbelievers and compel them no longer merely to believe with their ears, but to see with their eyes what they have doubted. Let it show that one thing after another is continuously produced in many and varied ways from one thing after another—or rather, that created things are changed into other and other creatures. Let it teach that the purity of the air is daily condensed into the thickness of clouds; that the clouds themselves almost continually descend into rain, soften into snow, harden into hail, and blaze into fire; and that in all these cases diverse substances are produced from substances, varied species from species—not only for the seeing to behold, but even for the blind to touch.

Let the inquisitive eye descend from heaven to earth [Col. 0802D] and marvel at the daily miracles which it does not marvel at. Let it see how foolish is the unbelief, how blind the doubt, which either does not believe or doubts that bread is changed into Christ’s flesh and wine into his blood by divine power, when by that same power many things are often changed into something else in the natural order. Does not coral become stone through fire, although the substance of fire and stone differs? Does not copper become gold through the powder of *reguli* [uncertain term, perhaps “regulus”], although these two, while agreeing in the name of metal, are greatly unlike in nature? Does not the phoenix, a bird said to be five hundred years old, dying when burned among aromatic substances, revive from ashes alone, although the substance of ash and that of the bird are now different? And lest he excuse himself on the ground that these things are unfamiliar or unknown, let him attend to the most customary and daily matters [Col. 0803A]; then, even if he attends carelessly, he will cease to doubt.

And so that he may assent more readily to works of his own hands than to those of others, let him make, by the well-known art, glass of a wholly different nature from hay or flint; and thus, so to speak, let him marvel at miracles not divine but his own. Let him observe the most limpid and fluid element of water, in winter among us, but at every season among the Noricans and Scythians, freeze most firmly into an icy shell; and in the Alps and many regions of the earth grow so hard that a stone is made from water and is called crystal—that is, ice hardened over many years. Let him consider how, from this same crystal, or from a transparent glass vessel filled with water, when it is set against a sunbeam, fire emerges contrary to the natures of the elements, although crystal is shown to be cold and dry, water—more remarkably—to be cold and moist, and fire hot and dry [Col. 0803B].

Let him examine likewise the globe of the earth itself: how, at the Creator’s command, from this shapeless and weak element of earth there are continually produced things so diverse in substances, varied in qualities, manifold in colors, and multiple in powers. If these were considered one by one, the investigator, overcome by the infinity of things, would fail before the things to be investigated.

But why do I linger over examples to establish the truth that bread is changed into Christ’s flesh and wine into Christ’s blood, when every day I see that very bread of which we speak changed into human flesh and wine changed into human blood, so manifestly that, in order to affirm it, one need not consult faith but open one’s eyes [Col. 0803C]? The world is a witness; every human being is a witness, especially since not one human being can survive without this change of bread into flesh and wine into blood. There are indeed many who pass their mortal life without bread, and likewise more who pass it without wine; but they are far fewer than those who always use bread and sometimes wine. Therefore, because of the greater number, I intended the whole when I said that no one can survive without the conversion of bread into flesh and wine into blood.

In truth, the greater part of humankind lives chiefly on bread and uses wine more solemnly; and all humans would do so, had the barrenness of the land not deprived certain colder regions of vines, and colder regions still of grain [Col. 0803D]. Yet this is certain: all human beings, unless they are under age or held by illness, either use bread and wine or are able to use them. Those under age or prevented by an adverse condition cannot indeed do so because of weakness, but can by nature. Thus, in one way or another, every person uses bread and wine. Hence nature works in every person what sceptics doubt, or unbelievers do not believe, concerning Christ alone as man. In every human being, by fitting digestion, nature works what is doubted to take place in Christ alone as man through divine consecration.

Nature indeed works through digestion in the human body, so that bread is changed into flesh and wine into blood, while—as those know who have acquired even slight knowledge of human affairs [Col. 0804A]—separating the cleaner and purer part of the food or drink received from the dregs, it distributes it to the individual limbs of the body for nourishing, sustaining, and increasing the substance of flesh and blood, and expels through orderly evacuation the baser portion, unnecessary to the body. In this well-known way, then, flesh is made from bread and blood from wine, not in one person but in every person, and not at one time but at every time.

Why, then, is it not believed? Why is it doubted that God can accomplish by power what nature can accomplish by digestion? Could God grant that to human origin and not be able to grant it to restoration? Could he establish that in creating man, and not be able to do this in redeeming man? Ought that to occur when man was fashioned by God, but ought it not to occur when man was assumed by God [Col. 0804B]? Let unbelief, then, cease and doubt be healed, because the almighty Word of God, through whom all things were made, just as he daily causes bread, through human eating and digestion, to be changed into flesh and wine into the blood of many sons of men, so daily causes, through consecration and divine power, bread and wine to be changed into his own flesh and blood—that is, into those of the one Son of God and man, not of many sons of men.

For he who “spoke, and they were made; commanded, and they were created” (Ps. 32), by the same power by which he brings this about universally in others brings it about uniquely in himself, so that the change of substances which formerly bestowed mortal life upon human beings now bestows everlasting life upon those same human beings—but upon believers [Col. 0804C]. But why do people marvel that God makes something from something, when in the beginning he created all things from nothing? For, as the holy Fathers of the Church say, it is far greater to create things that do not exist than to form different things from things that exist.

But perhaps someone will object: “It cannot indeed be denied that things are changed into things in many ways; but in these cases, when substances are changed into substances, their forms likewise are changed. In this sacrament, however, even if the substance changes, the form does not change.” I could indeed say that these questions are exceedingly tiresome, since the utterly powerless human being wishes to claim all omnipotence for himself, and the utterly foolish human being all wisdom for himself—especially since there is a certain rationale, plain to almost everyone, why, when the substance changes, the form does not likewise change [Col. 0804D]. But because one must endure all such things in order to satisfy people probing the mysteries of the third heaven, examples of this too shall be supplied: just as it has been shown that, in the natural order, species change with substance, so it shall also be shown that substances sometimes change while their former form does not change.

And so that it may not be necessary to strain the powers of the mind in seeking out whatever foreign examples, let examples be drawn from some of those written above and adduced to prove the preceding points. By them, the truth, as it is believed, of invisible things may be demonstrated to the bodily senses through examples of visible things. Consult, therefore, your own carnal eyes, whoever you are who marvel that Christ’s flesh lies hidden under the sacrament of bread and Christ’s blood under the sacrament of wine, and are astonished that the nature of the things themselves is changed into something else while the appearance of bread and wine remains unaltered [Col. 0805A]. Consult, I say, your eyes; and, though it is unworthy, accept through their judgment, in respect of visible things themselves, the truth of invisible things.

Look at water changed into ice, ice altered into crystal, and in these you will plainly see substances changed while the forms, or appearances, of the substances are preserved. Do you not see ice hardened by the coldness of water, and that ice itself, by the same cold continuing for a longer time, changed into crystalline stone, preserving its former appearance while its substance is transferred into something other than it was? Do you not perceive that, apart from its icy hardness and stony firmness, nothing at all has been taken away, insofar as regards the appearance or transparency of the element just mentioned [Col. 0805B]? Do you not see here the former substance changed into a shell or stone, there the brightness of the former form or appearance preserved?

If you wish to ascertain more exactly what I say, bring your hands near and sharpen your eyes, with water, ice, and crystal placed before you together—provided, however, that they have been formed not from a muddy or turbid, but from a clear and purified drop of water. When you see that all are equally transparent, you will recognize by touch that the substance has been changed; you will recognize by sight that the former form has been retained. But if these three, set separately before you, do not wholly satisfy you as proof of what I say, do not now set them separately; instead mix the ice or crystal itself, whole or broken, with the fluid purity of water [Col. 0805C]. When you perceive the same clearness in the shining stone as in the fluid element, understand that the substance has changed and recognize that the original form remains.

Hence our Jerome—whom you heretics rejected lest he should be yours—in Book XV on Isaiah, chapter 54, says: “But the gates of that city are of crystal stone, which is carved in various ways; no stone is purer than it. Finally, it is said that waters congeal into crystal amid the most severe cold of the Alps and in caves inaccessible to the sun, being stone to the touch but water to the sight.”

Nature presents a somewhat similar example in the eastern regions of Spain—indeed, as far as it lies beyond ordinary human knowledge, it presents a miracle. At first, hearing of it, I scarcely believed it; but afterward, seeing what I had heard, I could not doubt [Col. 0805D]. In those regions there are, so to speak, salty or salt-bearing mountains, which contain stony salt in place of stones or cliffs, so transparent that, since it rivals the gemlike brilliance of precious stones, it is called a gem of salt. Superior to sea salt, well salt, and every other salt both in transparency and usefulness, it is extracted with much labor by the inhabitants from those mountains and given as a great gift, or sold for great profit, to people in distant places.

When the prolonged labor of country people, greedy for gain, has extracted a large quantity of that shining stone from these mountains and left many pits empty of this salt through the excavation, in the course of time rainfall fills the emptiness of those pits; and, shortly after they have been filled, it is changed into the nature of the stone with which it is mixed [Col. 0806A]. By such recompense the excavated mountain almost yearly repairs the losses inflicted upon it, and whatever it lost in stone is made good by water changed into stone. Thus heavenly water becomes earthly stone. Although it passes into an alien substance, changing its natural softness into stony hardness, it nevertheless preserves its former form and appearance, as I said above concerning crystal.

But as I did not say this of every kind of ice or every kind of crystal, so I do not say it of every stone of that mountain, but only of that which has formed not from muddy water but from the clearest water, and which, even changed into something else, does not lose the clarity of its origin.

[Col. 0806B] Let another example, not contemptible but indeed quite suitable to the matter under discussion, be added concerning vinegar, so that what was not lacking in the sacrament of Christ’s passion, as necessary for some purpose, may not be lacking also, for some useful purpose, in the sacrament of Christ’s body of which we speak. For in it there is a certain change—not substantial indeed, but accidental—because, when natural or sweet wine turns sour by acquiring an unnatural sharpness, it changes, as I have said, not its substance but its quality; it changes only its accidents while preserving its former appearance. For what was formerly hot and dry, when one quality is changed, becomes cold and dry. Thus, if one accepts the judgment of sight, it will be believed to be nothing but natural wine. If taste is brought in, it will be proved to be unnatural vinegar [Col. 0806C].

What reason, then, remains for you either not to believe or to doubt, O investigator of heavenly mysteries, when external sense, through undoubted examples, compels you not now merely to believe but to see the things doubted concerning the sacrament of the altar, which inward faith commanded you to believe? Water becomes ice; ice becomes stone; likewise, as said above, water becomes a salt-bearing or salty stone: in all these instances the substance is changed while the appearance is retained. Wine becomes vinegar, its quality, as stated, changed while its appearance is retained, by the command of divine will thus operating. And shall flesh be unable to be made from bread and Christ’s blood from wine, their substance, as in those cases, changed while their appearance remains, by the will and command of the almighty Word of God, through whom all things were made [Col. 0806D]?

Is the Almighty believed capable of those things but judged powerless for these? Shall nature be considered stronger than the Author of nature in changing the substance of those things while preserving their appearance, and shall the Creator of nature itself be judged weaker in changing the substance of bread and wine into something other than it was and preserving the appearance they had? And because this sacred and saving sacrament appears to be one thing and is another, its substance being changed through the power of the divine Word, as has often been said, while its appearance is preserved, let the examples offered concerning change suffice.

But let some further examples be offered of things which appear to be one thing and are another. When you are sprinkled with wine or draw it in by tasting it, do not touch and taste respectively report and affirm that it is cold and moist, though in its composition or nature—without contradiction from anyone who has tested it—it is hot and dry [Col. 0807A]? When you put an oar, rod, stick, or anything similar into water, does not sight report that the portion beneath the water is broken, while nature preserves intact and unbroken what appears broken? When you set your own face or another’s, the sun or moon, heaven or stars, a picture or some body before a shining mirror or still water, do you not seem to see all the things set before it in them, although, so far as the truth of things is concerned, you see nothing in them except the bodies of the mirror or element?

And if it is permissible to bring forward certain matters from forbidden arts in proof of sacred heavenly things, does not mechanical or magical art, by a power granted by God, dazzle human eyes and falsely assert that what is not exists, while declaring that what exists does not exist [Col. 0807B]? Do not dreams themselves, when the external senses are asleep, continually deceive human souls, almost without ceasing presenting them with countless images and phantasmal illusions, concealing from sleepers what exists and displaying what does not exist?

Since, then, wine appears to be one thing and is another—for when touched or tasted it seems cold and moist, which it is not, while its true hot and dry nature is not sensed; since an oar immersed in water appears broken, which it is not, and does not appear intact, which it is; since a body set before a mirror or water appears to be a body that it is not, and does not appear as what it is [Col. 0807C]; since magical power, through a hidden art, presents to the eyes a phantasmal infinity of diverse images which does not exist and conceals beneath such coverings the reality of things which does exist; since the vision of dreams presents every bodily thing to the mind itself, not to the senses of the body, through manifold vision, things which do not exist, and veils beneath such coverings what does exist—what wonder if the mercy of almighty God, arranging also in this way to have mercy on wretched man, preserves the appearance of bread and wine for human senses in the sacrament of the altar, so that in that sacrament bread and wine, which are not present, may appear, while flesh and blood, which are present, may be hidden from the eyes of the flesh?

Countless other examples of these matters could be given; but because I avoid excessive length, and this does not pertain to the purpose undertaken [Col. 0807D], let what has been said suffice. Whoever is not satisfied with these should consult and read the authors of great volumes concerning this sacrament. And if perhaps even they do not satisfy an inquisitive mind, I do not know what more useful counsel I can offer than that, if one is a Christian, one should submit one’s neck to Christian faith and, if one cannot understand, should, according to the command of Holy Scripture, believe in order that one may understand (Isa. 7). For in these thick darknesses of human ignorance, faith is not the fruit of understanding; rather, understanding is the fruit of faith. Let God’s power, of which I spoke above, untie every knot of doubt for him. For nothing can remain for unbelief where the Almighty, providing for mortals, so willed, so was able, so commanded, and so did—he whose will is reason, whose omnipotence is unfailing [Col. 0808A], whose command is compassion, and whose work is mercy.

But since enough may now have been said on these matters, let us return to those for whose sake we touched on them.

Come then, companions in the contest: do what you began, and repeat what has been said, lest it slip from your minds. And since, I believe, sufficient has been said concerning the truth of the Christian sacrifice, explain why, begrudging this same sacrifice—that is, as I have said, the body and blood of the Redeemer—to others, you concede that it was given only to the disciples who were present at that famous and final supper of the Lord before his passion, and never afterward except then. But if you delay, as you have delayed until now, I shall prove that this was given neither only to them nor only now, but was prepared as a generous gift from the giver of all gifts for all believers until the consummation of the age [Col. 0808B].

Yet I marvel beyond expression, and in marveling am astonished, how this opinion could arise among people who, as they say, believe the Gospel of God, when Christ’s words contrary to this new heresy are set down there in such a manner that, if they are considered doubtful or obscure, none of his sayings or commands can seem certain or plain. For what could be said more certainly or clearly against those who maintain that Christ’s body and blood are made sacramentally only then and given only then, than what Christ himself commanded his disciples, saying: “Do this in remembrance of me” (Luke 22)? For after saying, “Take and eat; this is my body”; and, “Take and drink; this is my blood” [Col. 0808C] (ibid.), he immediately added what I have said: “Do this in remembrance of me.”

How, then, can a sacrament be said to have been made only once and given once to those present, when Christ, excluding no apostle and excepting no time, said: “Do this in remembrance of me”? How then does the heretic dare to say, “Do not do this,” when Christ commands, saying, “Do this”? This plainly means nothing other than the very thing which you receive to eat and take to drink—namely, my body and blood. “Do this,” I say, “in remembrance of me.” What more? What further point, certainly, will you seek? Behold: this single and very brief word destroys many most lengthy words of error, so that, unless superabundantly, it is no longer necessary to seek the means by which the wicked enemy should perish.

For he did not merely say, “Take and eat,” or, “Take and drink,” but added: “What you receive and eat, what you receive and drink, do this.” If this is so, then what you heretics have said is false: that this sacrament was given by Christ only then and received by the Apostles only then. For what he did, he commanded them to do; what he distributed to them, he willed them to distribute to others [Col. 0808D]. But perhaps this authority to consecrate and administer this sacrament was given only to those who were present then and heard these things from Christ, not to others.

If that is true, then the command, “Go into all the world; preach the Gospel to every creature” (Mark 16), was given only to the apostles and those who heard it from the Savior, and after the apostles no one was permitted either to teach all nations or to baptize. For just as it was said, “Go, teach, baptize, preach,” so it was said, “Do this.” Hence whoever preached, taught, or baptized after the apostles acted wrongly, since Christ had commanded it to no one other than those then present; for neither was that person’s teaching Christ’s teaching nor that person’s baptism Christ’s baptism. For what Christ neither commanded nor urged is plainly not Christ’s. For as the Apostle says: “How shall they preach unless they are sent?” (Rom. 10), so also: how shall they baptize unless it is enjoined?

Since, therefore, Christ made no distinction in these commands or in similar ones, either grant all these things only to those then present [Col. 0809B], and take away from later generations, together with baptism and the sacrament of the altar, the whole Gospel; or, if you grant baptism and the Gospel to later generations, you must necessarily grant them the sacrament of the altar as well. For if, as has been said, no distinction was made in these commands, then either all were commanded together only to those present and subsequent persons were excluded, or, if any one of these things was commanded to later generations, it is evident that the whole was enjoined upon them. Therefore, either you will give the sacrament of the altar only to those persons and take away baptism; or, if you give baptism to these persons, whether you wish it or not, you will give them the sacrament of the altar also.

But why do I devote effort to a laborious dispute, when such great and ready authority supports the case that, once it appears, impiety speaking vainly immediately falls silent? For what of this? Did the apostle Paul take part in that Lord’s Supper of which we speak? Was he present when it was said to the disciples, “Take and eat; this is my body”; and, “Take and drink; this is my blood”; and, “Do this in remembrance of me”? Yet what does he say in the First Epistle to the Corinthians? Listen: “The cup,” he says, “of blessing which we bless, is it not a sharing in the blood of Christ? And the bread which we break, is it not a participation in the body of the Lord?” (1 Cor. II). Did the Corinthians themselves take part in that already-mentioned supper? Yet the Apostle himself says to them: “You cannot drink the cup of the Lord and the cup of demons. You cannot partake of the table of the Lord and of the table of demons” (1 Cor. X). Do you see [Col. 0809C–D] the Apostle, converted to the faith after the Lord’s ascension, blessing the cup of blessing and calling that same cup a sharing in Christ’s blood? Do you see him break that same bread and call the bread itself a participation in Christ’s body? Do you hear that the Corinthians could indeed drink the Lord’s cup, but not together with the cup of demons; could partake of the Lord’s table, but not together with the table of demons? Yet the apostle Paul, while consecrating the Lord’s body and blood, had not taken part in the Lord’s Supper; nor had the Corinthians, while receiving that same body and blood from the Lord’s table, taken part in that same supper.

But it is too little merely to hear him speak of the breaking of heavenly bread, unless you also see him breaking it. “On one day,” says blessed Luke in the Acts of the Apostles, “when we had assembled to break bread, and Paul was discoursing with them because he was to depart on the next day” (Acts XX). And, after some intervening matters: “Paul,” he says, “having gone up, and broken bread and tasted it, and having spoken at length until daybreak, departed on the next day” (ibid.). But whether this last passage which I have cited refers to heavenly bread or common bread, behold, as I said, the Apostle; behold the Corinthians, who had not taken part in the supper of which we speak and yet received the Lord’s body and blood.

And if you wish to hear apostolic authority convicting you not only from the Apostle and the Corinthians but from all persons, listen: “Whoever,” he says, “shall eat the bread or drink the cup of the Lord unworthily shall be guilty of the body and blood of the Lord” (1 Cor. X). And consequently [Col. 0810A–B]: “But let a man prove himself, and so let him eat of that bread and drink of that cup” (ibid.). What will you say to this? “Whoever,” he says, “eats; whoever drinks.” Not this man or that man, but whoever. “Let a man prove himself”: not merely a Corinthian man, not a Roman man, not a Greek man, not a Latin man, but a human being. And what else does this mean but every human being? For when he used an indefinite expression, what else did he indicate but an unlimited person? He thus indicates not one person but every person, because in the singular number “man” he intended the plurality of all human beings to be understood. If this is so—indeed, because it is so—the impious error is not only dead but buried. For if it is evident that the Apostle said this not of any particular person but of every person [Col. 0810C], then what you have said, that this was said only of those who were present at the Lord’s Supper, is false. Rather, apostolic authority teaches the truth: not only those persons, as you concede, but whoever—that is, every person—may eat the bread of the Lord and drink the cup of the Lord, that is, according to the same Apostle, the Lord’s body and blood. Therefore what you said is false: that only those who were present at the Paschal supper could receive the Lord’s body and blood.

And although what has been proved concerning every person has also been proved concerning every time, nevertheless hear whether the authority to make and receive this sacrament was given only to that time when that supper was celebrated. For the same Apostle, speaking of this sacrament and thereby instructing both faith and morals, introduces Christ as saying to the disciples: “Do this, as often as you receive it, in remembrance of me” (ibid.). Then the Apostle adds his own words and says to those to whom he was speaking: “For as often as you eat this bread and drink the cup, you shall proclaim the death of the Lord until he comes” (ibid.).

What will you say to these words, you who say that this sacrament was made and given only once? You say “only once”; Christ and his Apostle say not once, not twice, not three or four times, not merely a hundred or a thousand times, but “as often as.” There is a great difference between “once” and “as often as.” Here is the beginning of a number; there is a number surpassing every number. Here is singularity; there is manifold infinity. Yet, as I have said, you say “once” [Col. 0810D–0811A], while Christ and his Apostle say “as often as.” It must therefore be considered—and no great effort is needed—to whom one ought more rightly to give credence: to you or to Christ, to human beings or to God, to truth or to falsehood.

But why say more? You have heard that this sacrament of Christ’s body and blood was given to every faithful person; you have heard that it was given without limit of number. Hear also that it was given for every present time. “As often as,” says the Apostle, “you eat this bread and drink the cup, you shall proclaim the death of the Lord until he comes.” Apostle of God, it would have been enough for confounding and destroying the new heresy that you said Christ had said: “Do this, as often as you receive it, in remembrance of me.” It would have been enough that, following your Lord’s words, you had added by way of explanation: “As often as you eat this bread and drink the cup, you shall proclaim the death of the Lord.” But what did you add? “Until he comes.”

Who is to come? Perhaps the Lord’s death? No; for you yourself most plainly deny this when you say: “Christ, rising from the dead, dies no more” (Rom. VI). Who then is to come? Certainly the Lord himself, whom you named when you said, “You shall proclaim the death of the Lord.” But when will he come? When else but when he is to come to judge the living and the dead, as he himself foretold and his Church believes? And when is that? When, according as he himself says, he comes at the end of the age in his majesty, with all the angels with him (Matt. XXV). Therefore until he comes at the end of the age, he gave this sacrament of his body and blood to the faithful throughout the whole time of this age—that is, until the consummation of the age. Let the heresy, then, which said that this was given only at the Lord’s Supper, fall silent [Col. 0811B–C]. For if it was given until the consummation of the age, it was given not merely at the Lord’s Supper but, compelled by the authorities already cited, until the consummation of the age. Therefore, not only at the Lord’s Supper.

Now we must consider the question which is raised not only by unbelievers but also by believers: why is this sacrifice repeated so often, when Christ, offered once upon the cross to take away the sins of the whole world, is sufficient—especially since there is not one sacrifice here and another there, but here and there precisely the same sacrifice, that is, the same Christ, is offered? For if that sacrifice on the cross was sufficient, this sacrifice on the altar appears superfluous. But it is not superfluous [Col. 0811D], because it was performed and handed down for a certain reason by the Son of God, who, according to the Apostle, is the wisdom of God (1 Cor. I). Since that Wisdom is supremely rational—indeed, the source and perfection of all reason—it could neither do nor command anything irrationally. Hence, when he spoke thus and handed this sacrament down to his own, he certainly did so for a definite reason. That reason alone satisfies all who believe Christ, the author of this sacrament, to be God and the wisdom of God.

Yet the giver of so great a gift was pleased to state the cause of so great a bestowal. He disclosed that cause in giving the sacrament itself. For after saying, “Do this,” he immediately added, “in remembrance of me.” This, then, is the cause of the sacrament: the remembrance of Christ. The Savior knew what he had done and what he was about to do for humankind; he knew the singular work he had accomplished by assuming humanity; he knew the astounding work he would accomplish by dying for humankind. He knew that by this work he would save humankind, but that no one could be saved without love for this work. He knew that the work of his humanity and death, just as it was to be celebrated above all his works, was especially to be commended to mortals for whom it was done [Col. 0812A]. It had to be commended, since his flesh was tortured for them, his soul grieved for them, and finally his death was made the means of their life. This surely had to be solemnly commended, so that Christ might be loved, might be held in love, and, once possessed, might never be lost.

But this love of him could not be preserved by human beings if memory perished; nor could fleeting memory remain long unless a fitting sign were set before it. Therefore, lest what most ought to dwell in the heart should flee from the heart, memory was bound to the heart by a sign appropriate to the thing, as though by an indissoluble rope. Bound firmly by it, the redeemed person would always think upon the price of redemption and, giving thanks to the Redeemer, would not, through faith working by love, show himself ungrateful for so great a grace. It would indeed have been possible for the memory of this matter somehow to dwell in human minds without a visible sign, as the remembrance of many divine and human things is either produced or preserved in them by report, reading, and instruction. But because, in the words of a certain writer,

> Things received through the ear stir minds more slowly  
> Than things set before the trustworthy eyes.

[Col. 0812B–C] (HORACE, *On the Art of Poetry*, verses 180–181),

and because the matter was so great that human minds had to be stirred toward considering, loving, and embracing it not sluggishly but extraordinarily, it was fitting and just that the remembrance of Christ’s humanity and death should not be heard through the ears alone, but should also be aided by sight through the eyes.

For this reason Christ set forth this sign: it is such a sign that it is nevertheless the very thing which it signifies. This is unlike the multiplicity of the old sacrifice, which was not in any respect the same as what it signified—except that the former was a sacrifice and this is a sacrifice, and the former was offered to God and this is offered to the same God. The former signified this sacrifice of ours in the present time [Col. 0812C–D], but was not the same as this sacrifice, because that was shadow and this body; that was figure and this truth; that consisted of animal carcasses and blood, this of the body and blood of the Son of God. For that reason it was not the same as what it signified. But this sign of our sacrifice is not something other than, but is itself, what it signifies.

It is indeed the same as what it signifies insofar as the body is concerned—that is, insofar as the reality of Christ’s flesh and blood is concerned.
