For Christ does not there, as formerly, suffer pains or death, although he is said to be sacrificed. He is said to be sacrificed because, though remaining inviolate, he is broken, divided, and eaten on the altar; and by these and certain other signs, as far as is possible, the Lord’s death is most fully represented. Therefore, as I have said, insofar as the reality of Christ’s body and blood is concerned, it is the same as what it signifies, although it signifies it in the fullest manner.

I say “in the fullest manner,” because the Apostle states this most plainly in the verse that I mentioned above: “As often as you eat this bread and drink the cup,” he says, “you shall proclaim the death of the Lord.” Why this? Why, Apostle of God, did you not likewise say “the Lord’s incarnation,” “the Lord’s birth,” “the Lord’s circumcision,” “the Lord’s baptism,” or, what might appear greater, “the Lord’s resurrection” or “the Lord’s ascension,” when you said “the Lord’s death”? Why did you leave aside those things that seem glorious and choose what was more shameful? “So that,” he says, “I might show that the salvation of the world is uniquely contained in the Lord’s death; so that I might show that this work of his outweighs all his works; so that I might show that by that torment rest was given, by that shame glory, and by that death life was restored to the dead.”

Thus indeed, according to the Apostle, when the Lord’s bread—that is, the Lord’s body—is eaten, and when the Lord’s cup—that is, the Lord’s blood—is drunk, the Lord’s death which his body suffered on the cross is proclaimed—that is, represented: not another body, but the same Lord’s flesh which is present; not another blood, but the same Lord’s blood which was shed and is received [Col. 0813A–B]. And when this occurs, it occurs so that the mind, stirred much more powerfully by receiving the Lord’s body than it could be by the reminder of the Lord’s word, may blaze with love for him whom it not only hears but also sees and receives. Seeing the Word made flesh so that he might dwell in us, and dwelling bodily also in itself, it can no longer forget him whom it believes by faith, embraces in love, touches by hand, and receives by mouth. Recalling by that reception him who once died for it, and recognizing that life was prepared for it by that death, it may refrain from the works of death and so live forever with Christ, its Lord, now immortal and living eternally.

Therefore this sacrament of the Church, because through its continual representation it renews memory, increases faith, strengthens hope, and confirms charity, is not superfluous but very [variant: supremely] necessary. For this reason, as has been said, the Lord commanded it to be done in remembrance of himself. For this reason the Apostle taught that the Lord’s death is proclaimed in this sacrament [Col. 0813C–D], so that the remembrance of Christ and his death could not be torn from human hearts by any agitation of the world or any length of time. This memory, awakening love, drives every evil from the recesses of the soul and fills all things with virtues; and thus, daily renewing redemption through this sacrament, it brings forth daily forgiveness of sins for penitents.

The Lamb of God, sacrificed on the cross, indeed loosens and wholly takes away the sins of the world; nevertheless, as I have said, his offering on the altar is not therefore superfluous. To see this in yourself, whoever reads these things, observe and question yourself: if you firmly believe what you profess, when are you more moved—when it is said, “Christ once appeared among human beings,” or when it is said, “Christ now dwells among human beings”; when it is said, “He once hung upon the cross,” or when it is said, “He is now offered on the altar”? I ask whether his proclaimed absence or his manifested presence moves you more and inflames you toward wonder and love.

But I know that you do not deny what is true: human hearts are moved more by things present than absent, because absent things are often not believed, whereas the mind is not permitted even slight doubt about present things. Therefore it is moved more by Christ present than by Christ absent, more by Christ seen than by Christ heard; it is moved toward wonder and toward love. By this love forgiveness of sins is generated for the one who loves. The measure of a person’s love toward Christ is the measure of pardon, as the Lord himself attests when he says concerning the sinful Mary: “Her many sins have been forgiven, because she loved much” (Luke VII). And since it is elsewhere written, “Charity covers a multitude of sins” (Prov. X; 1 Pet. IV), how great a multitude of sins does charity toward Christ cover, if charity toward one’s neighbor covers so great a multitude?

Therefore, as has been said, the sacrament of Christ’s body and blood is not superfluous, by which memory is awakened more vividly, love is aroused more fervently, and a fuller forgiveness of sins is obtained. It is not superfluous because he is with us until the consummation of the age not only in that whereby he is God, but also in that whereby he is human. It is not superfluous because he who redeemed us through his body also refreshes us through that same body [Col. 0814A–C], so that, redeemed through his body and refreshed by his body, we may be nourished and fed by his humanity until we are satisfied by his divinity and glory.

This is why he instituted this sacrament in forms especially suited to human food and life: so that those who observe might recognize that, under the appearance indeed of earthly bread but through the reality of heavenly bread, human beings receive not the mortal life which earthly bread ordinarily gives, but immortal life. Thus, by a solitary and astounding miracle, what is in that sacrament lies hidden, while what is not in it is visible, lest a human being recoil, against custom and nature, from feeding on raw, living, and especially human flesh. Some even among the disciples of old, execrating this and failing to understand what the Lord had said, declared: “This saying is hard; and who can hear it?” (John VI).

But this is not a hard saying; rather, it is gentle and sweet. For although the flesh of Christ the man is eaten, it is not the flesh of one injured or cut apart, diminished or mutilated, unwilling or suffering; rather, flesh is eaten and blood drunk of one who wills and provides for it. According to the words of the blessed apostle Andrew, he remains in his kingdom whole, untouched, inviolate, immortal, incorruptible—indeed beautiful, glorious, and worthy of worship—and through his now immortal body leads mortals to that same immortality [Col. 0814D–0815A]. Therefore it is not hard or cruel, but pious and lovable, because he gave his flesh to human beings for eating and his blood for drinking not unwillingly or under compulsion, but willingly and of his own accord. Nor is it irrational, because from that from which pardon comes to sinners, glory is owed to the giver of so great a grace.

Nevertheless, the reality of both flesh and blood remains veiled beneath the fitting appearance of bread and wine, so that human usage may be accommodated, faith exercised, and merit increased. Hence it is called sacrament, mystery, appearance, and figure, because within what the outward form declares, divine power hides the true body and blood of the Redeemer.

But the still carnal mind, not yet wholly purified from human habit, objects and says: “I know that the faithful receive the true body and blood of the Redeemer under the appearance of bread and wine in the sacrament of the altar; but, if it is permitted to ask, I ask why they are given for eating and drinking. If they were given only for honoring or worshiping, there would be no question. But because they are also given for eating, this troubles a mind that does not yet perfectly understand lofty things. For whom would it not trouble—as it once troubled Christ’s disciples—that, contrary to human custom and to piety, Christ’s flesh or blood—indeed, God and man—should be broken by human hands, ground by teeth, and devoured as though in the manner of ordinary foods: the teacher by disciples, the master by servants, Christ by Christians?”

You who raise these objections, I say, admit yourself that they were raised against Christ by Christ’s first disciples when they said: “This saying is hard; and who can hear it?” These things were said by unbelieving Jews disputing over this matter: “How can this man give us his flesh to eat?” (ibid.). This question is certainly not new but ancient; not recent but most ancient. As it arose in the very foundations of Christian faith, so it was extinguished not by some ordinary teacher but by the Savior himself, as the holy Gospel relates [Col. 0815B–D]. Since it had both its birth and its death at virtually the same moment, a Christian who is still disturbed by questions buried a thousand years ago seems exceedingly unlearned.

Yet because nothing should be despised that can either injure faith or stir hearts to anyone’s scandal, let charity—which bears all things—also bear this patiently, so that the weakness of Christ’s members may be healed through its patience. For the Savior himself, the heavenly physician, taught that this is how such weak persons must be treated. When his disciples were still unlearned and scandalized by sayings of this kind, he did not rebuke them harshly but admonished them kindly, saying: “Does this scandalize you? What if, then, you see the Son of Man ascending where he was before? It is the spirit that gives life; the flesh profits nothing” (John VI).

In these brief words, if you attend closely, the wisdom of God resolves this whole riddle more brightly than the sun, because with spiritual light it drove away the mists of carnal thoughts. “If,” he says, “you see the Son of Man ascending where he was before: it is the spirit that gives life; the flesh profits nothing.” That is: because you see me as a human being among human beings, you cannot yet conceive anything concerning me, insofar as this sacrament is concerned, beyond what you conceive concerning another human being. And therefore, thinking carnally, you believe that I wish to give you my flesh as though cut into pieces. But after I have ascended into heaven, after I have glorified in God this flesh of which we speak, still mortal at present, then you will understand that it is the spirit which gives life—that is, my words give life when received spiritually; but flesh profits nothing because, when understood carnally, it kills.

For I shall give my flesh to human beings, not to be cut apart, diminished, or consumed in the manner of corpses, because my flesh so received would profit nothing. Rather, I shall give it to be divided without pain, apportioned without diminution, and eaten without consumption, because it is the spirit that gives life; and because, understood and received in this way, my flesh gives its recipients not mortal but eternal life [Col. 0816A–B].

But you still press the question and say: “Even if Christ’s flesh is given to human beings immortally and inviolably for honoring and worshiping, why is it given for eating? That it ought to be honored and worshiped is certain to all the faithful; but that it is also eaten—since no rationale for eating is apparent—is surely marvelous and astonishing above all things.” Certainly I too confess, and every sound-minded person confesses, that this is astonishing and marvelous above all miracles. But do you, who demand the reason for so great a sacrament, comprehend all God’s other sacraments by reason? Is not the will of God alone more rational than all human reason? Or do you not understand that what surpasses reason is the will of God, since every will of God is reason and every reason is his will? For just as his will cannot be irrational, so reason cannot fail to belong to his will.

Since these things are so, his will satisfies every reason and rational mind, even when the reason for his will is not explained. Therefore, in this sacrament as in the others, his will and command are sufficient, since it is certain that supreme wisdom cannot err and supreme reason cannot do anything irrationally. Thus, as a reason, it is sufficient—indeed wholly and abundantly sufficient—that Christ the Lord gave his flesh to human beings for eating and his blood for drinking. Yet although, as has been said, once God’s known will is established, it is contrary to reason to seek its reason, nevertheless, lest Catholics here be thought to lack or be unaware of what God, the institutor, reveals concerning the rationale of so great a sacrament, let it be disclosed [Col. 0816C–D].

Christ indeed gives his flesh and his blood to human beings not only for honoring and worshiping, but also for eating and drinking, so that just as no mortal is seen able to pass through mortal and miserable life without bodily food and drink, so no one may be believed able to attain immortal and blessed life without this spiritual food and drink. For how could he better or more clearly commend himself to the world as the life of human beings than by the example of those things in which human life consists? For in food and drink lies the life of all human beings; and among the diverse foods and drinks by which human life is sustained, bread and wine hold the chief place. By these, human life is most wholesomely and solemnly refreshed and renewed each day.

Therefore the wisdom of God, who “orders all things strongly and sweetly” (Wis. VIII), willed to take up these customary substances, chief among those preserving human temporal life, in order to restore human beings to everlasting life. For this reason he decreed to give his flesh to human beings for eating under their appearance, and his blood for drinking [Col. 0817A]. In them he showed—and taught this sacrament far more clearly than by words—that he himself is the only eternal life of human beings, since, in likeness to their bodily food, he willed to give them for spiritual food and drink nothing other than himself.

For when he says, “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John XIV), and likewise, “This is eternal life: that they may know you, the true God, and Jesus Christ whom you have sent” (John XVII), people learn by hearing that he is eternal life. But when he says, “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves” (John VI), and likewise, “The bread which I shall give is my flesh for the life of the world” (ibid.), people learn by eating that he is their everlasting life. Therefore, by eating rather than by hearing, people learn better that he is their immortal life, just as by bodily foods they nourish their mortal life [Col. 0817B–C].

Therefore, so that human beings might learn not only by words but also perceive more familiarly in deeds that, separated from Christ, they die forever, and that they cannot live forever unless joined and united to Christ, they receive Christ’s body and drink Christ’s blood in the likeness of bodily food and life. They receive and drink not what is given by another, nor what is received from another, but from Christ himself, who after this life will be their food—that is, their eternal life and blessedness.

To show this, and to signify that for this reason he wishes to give his flesh to all for eating and his blood for drinking, he drew an analogy from desert manna. In the Gospel he says to the Jews, who boasted of their manna: “Moses did not give you bread from heaven; but my Father gives you the true bread from heaven. For the bread of God is that which descends from heaven and gives life to the world” (ibid.). That bread was not heavenly but aerial—that is, it descended from the air, God creating it there—although air is improperly called heaven and manna, descending thence, is on that account called heavenly bread. Yet that manna was not heavenly bread; rather, the Son of God descending from heaven, as he himself attests, is heavenly bread. Before he descended from heaven he was bread—that is, the life—of angels; and after he descended from heaven he became bread—that is, life—for human beings. Therefore he calls himself not dead bread, as manna was, but living bread: manna refreshed the mortal bodies of Jews destined to die, but this living bread refreshes the souls of Christians destined to live eternally [Col. 0817D–0818A].

The effect itself of life, which the living bread grants, is not bestowed in the present but deferred to the future, because the sacrament is bodily, being the true body and true blood of Christ, whereas the thing of the sacrament—that is, the effect of salvation which follows—is spiritual. Therefore the sacrament itself, namely the food of Christ’s body and drink of Christ’s blood, although bodily—that is, truly bodies—is nevertheless called spiritual, that is, producing the effect of salvation spiritually. Thus the Apostle teaches, speaking of the Fathers: “All ate the same spiritual food, and all drank the same spiritual drink” (1 Cor. X).

That he understood and wrote this not of Jewish manna or of water brought forth from the rock, but of Christ—that is, of his body and blood, of which Moses also wrote—is most clearly shown when he adds: “They drank from the spiritual rock which followed them; and the rock was Christ” (ibid.). He therefore said this of the rock which would follow them—that is, of Christ who was to come after them. He gave in the often-mentioned sacrament spiritual food and spiritual drink—that is, his body and blood, which spiritually bestow eternal life on human beings. Its power was such that not only the faithful who follow Christ, but also those faithful persons who, from the beginning of the world, preceded him, all ate the same spiritual food and drank the same spiritual drink: not bodily as all did after him, but spiritually as all did; that is, from Christ’s body and blood all of those as well received the same effect of salvation as Christians after Christ [Col. 0818B–C].

Therefore, as has now been said, all—both first and last—who belong to Christ’s body and to the mystery of eternal salvation, all without exception, ate the same spiritual food and drank the same spiritual drink. So that eternal life, spiritually and invisibly conferred upon the world in the present, might be signified as to be bestowed bodily and visibly in the future, Christ’s flesh was given under the appearance of bread for eating and Christ’s blood under the form of wine for human beings to drink. Thus, just as people chiefly use bread and wine for mortal life, so for immortal life, which is Christ himself, they may be fed by Christ’s body and blood here spiritually, and thereafter both spiritually and bodily forever [Col. 0818D].

The reason is therefore clear not only in the future, when one must enter the sanctuary of God and understand their latter end (Ps. LXXII), but also in the present, while all things are still done under cloud. Clear, I say, is the reason why Christ wished to give Christians his flesh for eating and his blood for drinking, not only for honoring, not only for worshiping, but also for eating: the Lord to servants, God to human beings. Let no one, therefore, object that there is impiety, as though the Lord were injured or eaten; let no one object cruelty, as though the body were cut apart or suffering; let no one object folly, as though human beings ate human flesh without reason. For there is no impiety where all piety is; no cruelty where there is no suffering; no irrationality where supreme Wisdom is, which suffers no pain from its own division, no diminution from participation in itself, and no consumption from being eaten. Rather, it provides and prepares eternal restoration for those who eat, so that in this age and in the age to come it may be bread and life for human beings—he who is always the bread of the blessed and the refreshment of angels [Col. 0819A].

## Against the claim that the benefits of the living are of no advantage to the dead
Fifth and final chapter. The missile of the adversaries, twisted upon a heretical thong and now flying toward the destruction of the Church, must be repelled by setting the shield of truth against falsehood. Of this the Prophet says: “His truth shall surround you as a shield; you shall not fear the terror of the night, nor the arrow that flies” (Ps. 72). For the malice of the faithless has grown, and their iniquity has issued forth as though from fatness, since they envy not only the salvation of the living but also the hope of the dead; and, having become the common and public enemies of all, they strive not only to kill the living but even, if it were possible, to annihilate the dead anew. They press mortals to die quickly; and they bar the dead from any daring to breathe again unto life. They spare not the pitiable lot of humankind; and toward human beings who, after a life of misery, are again suffering under divine judgment, they know not how to show mercy—as though they themselves would never die. Truly impious, they hear as deaf men Christ, who graciously commends mercy, saying: “Blessed are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” (Matt. 5). Since they neither retain this mercy in affection toward others nor show it in deed, they shall never obtain it as blessed persons, but as wretched ones.

Certainly they are to be judged generous men, and most munificent from their own resources—men who cannot look with an impartial eye upon, or endure in any degree, liberality exercised from another’s goods; who, ignorant of the riches of God’s goodness and patience, prescribe laws for divine generosity. Yet, according to the Apostle, God “is rich toward all who call upon him” (Rom. 10); and, according to another, “gives abundantly to all and does not reproach” (Jas. 1). They prohibit even the free one among the dead from showing mercy to the dead, setting themselves up as judges over heavenly judgment. They do this when they maintain that altar-sacrifices, offerings, prayers, alms, and the other good works of good living persons cannot benefit the good dead; and when, despite the protest of the whole world, they despise so celebrated and ancient a custom of Christ’s Church, observed from Christ himself—indeed, before Christ by his worshippers. Hence even those who consider the matter negligently can perceive how far this error is from being contemptible, and with what diligence it ought to be refuted.

For who, O Catholic readers, does not perceive that Satan—whose devices, according to the Apostle cited above, “we are not ignorant of” (2 Cor. 2)—has devised this in order, by this stratagem, to divert so many good things continually performed throughout the world by so many good people for the dead, and by infernal counsel to remove constant alms, continual sacrifices, unceasing prayers, and such things, which procure merit for the living and rest for the departed? But the Spirit will uncover the deceits of his counsel, strip bare the face of falsehood veiled by cloud, and show that this temptation has proved more profitable than harmful to his Church. For what the great Apostle said many centuries ago—“There must be heresies, so that those who are approved may become manifest” (1 Cor. 10)—we experience not only in the times of the Fathers but also in our own days: as the Church is always enlarged by persecutions of enemies from without, so by the trials of false brethren within it is purified more and more. Therefore, by the help of the divine Spirit, the Church will be enlarged, not narrowed; purified, not corrupted, when that which is advanced by the opposing party is more diligently examined, more subtly investigated, more perfectly discovered, and more vigorously defended.

And, not to delay long: what is it, O heretic, that you propose? “The good works of the living,” he says, “cannot benefit the dead, because, once they have passed from life, merits can neither be increased nor diminished. For beyond this life there can no longer be a place for merits, but only for recompenses; nor can the dead hope to obtain from anyone what they did not obtain while alive in the world. Therefore I say that whatever is done by the living for the dead is vain, because when mortals pass through death, the way of all flesh, into the state of the age to come, they carry with them their entire merit, to which nothing can be added.”

The whole Church of God knows, I say, and I, however humble a pupil of hers, do not fail to know, that the wisdom of God said through Solomon: “God will bring into judgment all that is done, for every error, whether it be good or evil” (Eccles. 12); and the Apostle: “Each shall bear his own burden” (Gal. 6); and: “We must stand before the judgment-seat of Christ, so that each may receive according to what he has done in the body, whether good or evil” (2 Cor. 5); and David: “These two things I have heard: that power belongs to God, and mercy to you, O Lord; for you will render to each according to his works” (Ps. 61); and Christ the Lord: “The Son of Man will come in the glory of his Father with his angels, and then he will render to each according to his work” (Matt. 16). I surely know these things, and many more besides. Nor could testimonies so numerous and so clear deceive the Church of which I have spoken; nor could the entire world be so blind that it could not see what some isolated heretic could see: namely, that each person is either justified or condemned by his own works.

The Church saw these things, certainly, and no great effort was required to see them. It saw whatever you could see; but, heretic, you did not see whatever it saw. It saw that the ends of everlasting blessedness and misery depend upon mortal life; and from this it recognized that, according to the condition of each, the mercy of the Almighty aids the dead even after death through the pious works of others. For although the works of the living appear to be another’s, nevertheless, in order that they might benefit the dead, they have been obtained by the merits of those dead persons while they lived. Therefore they are not to be judged foreign possessions, since by the preceding merits of the dead they have become their own.

For this reason the Church prays for the rest or glory of her members who have passed into the condition of another life; and those whom she knows, through faith and charity, to belong to the members of her Lord, she does not exclude from the fruit of her good works. She does not exclude them; rather, as is fitting, she receives them most fully. Thus, just as the concordant justice of God casts away from its memory those rejected from the face of God, and just as, concerning those perfect before God’s face, she knows with certainty from God’s mercy that they do not need her aid, so she strives by every means in her power to assist those laboring under God’s judgment, trusting in the riches of God’s goodness.

She has authority for this from the words of the Lord her God, from whom she hears through the Gospel that sins are forgiven not only in this age but also in the age to come. For when, speaking of blasphemy against the Spirit, he says: “Whoever speaks a word against the Holy Spirit shall not be forgiven, neither in this age nor in the age to come” (Matt. 12; Luke 12), he shows that forgiveness of sins is always granted in this age to those worthy of it; yet remission of the penalties exacted by sins is sometimes deferred to the future age. According to the hidden dispensations of God’s justice and mercy, these penalties are either shortened in duration or mitigated in severity through the pious works of good living persons, for the relief of the good but imperfect dead. I call them good because they do not fall away from salvation; imperfect because they need purification. This purification, which separates them from eternal condemnation, is either imposed upon those guilty persons by God’s hidden judgment according to the character of their guilt, or is compensated through his inexhaustible goodness by the Church’s sacrifices, prayers, alms, and similar things. For the true utterance of Truth remains: sins—that is, the penalty of sins—are sometimes forgiven in this age, sometimes in the age to come.

But now let us employ the very ample examples of Scripture, by which it may shine forth more clearly than the sun that the heretical proposition has been not harmful but profitable to us: proving that not only the good works of the living may benefit the dead, but also the good works of the dead the living; and that the good works of the living may benefit the living, and those of the dead the dead, and that they both benefited in former times and can benefit or be effective daily. To establish this, let Jesus the Lord himself come first: author and savior of humankind. While he was still living among people, it is neither doubtful nor obscure, but certain and evident, that the good works of the living benefited the living, of the dead the dead, of the living the dead, and of the dead the living.

For when can his good works be counted, which, while he still lived as a mortal among mortals, benefited those same mortals not only spiritually but also bodily? Spiritually, I mean, when he said to the sinful woman: “Your faith has saved you; go in peace” (Luke 7); to the paralytic: “Son, your sins are forgiven you” (Matt. 9); concerning Zacchaeus: “Today salvation has come to this house” (Luke 19); when he turned and looked upon Peter (Luke 22); when he said to the thief: “Today you shall be with me in paradise” (Luke 23); and in five hundred other instances. Bodily, when he said to the leper: “I will; be cleansed,” and immediately his leprosy was cleansed (Matt. 8); when he commanded ten other lepers meeting him together: “Go, show yourselves to the priests,” and, as they went, they were cleansed (Luke 17); when he commanded the man born blind: “Go to the pool of Siloam and wash,” and he went, washed, and saw (John 9); when he said to another blind man: “Look up; your faith has made you well,” and immediately he saw (Luke 18); when many blind and lame people came to him in the Temple and he healed them all (Matt. 21); when, at sunset, all who had sick persons afflicted with various diseases brought them to him and they were healed (Mark 1; Luke 4); when, at his command, demons came out of many, crying and saying, “You are the Son of God” (Luke 4); and in a thousand similar acts, performed both by himself and through his disciples. Thus I have shown that the good works of the living Lord benefited the living.

But who doubts that the good works of the dead Lord benefited the dead, whoever believes and confesses in the Christian creed that he suffered under Pontius Pilate, was crucified, died, was buried, and descended to hell? Rescuing innumerable souls of the saints from there and restoring them to eternal blessedness, he fulfilled what solemn prophecy had foretold: “From the hand of death I shall free them; from death I shall redeem them. I shall be your death, O death; I shall be your bite, O hell” (Hos. 13); and what another says: “God of vengeances, the Lord God of vengeances has acted freely” (Ps. 93); and what the Apostle says: “He has been appointed by God judge of the living and the dead” (Acts 10).

But what is remarkable if the dead Lord assisted the faithful dead by his death, when by that same death he daily assists—more wonderfully—all Christians who have died or are about to die, preordained to life, until the consummation of the age? Thus I have shown how the good works of the dead Lord have benefited and continue to benefit dead human beings. But from what is it proved more clearly that the good works of the living Lord benefited the dead than from the resurrection of the dead itself? Does not the threefold and well-known resurrection of the dead testify to this: the girl in the house (Matt. 9), the young man at the gate (Luke 7), and Lazarus from the tomb (John 11)? Does not that extraordinary, noble, and famous miracle, occurring while he who had died was now alive because risen from death, likewise confirm it: when, as he rose, and was now living immortally, many bodies of saints who had fallen asleep arose? (Matt. 27.)

Nor is it surprising that, by the power of the living One, bodies of the dead rose, when all the words and deeds of that same living One contributed to the resurrection not only of bodies but also—what comes first—of the souls of all faithful people. Therefore it has been shown that the good works of the living Lord benefited the dead. But, to complete the whole argument, let it also be shown that the good works of the dead could benefit the living. Here the whole earth cries out, without waiting for my answer, proclaiming that through the benefit of the Lord’s death it has been rescued from eternal death, restored to salvation, and returned to everlasting life. This is testified by the twelve apostles, the seventy-two disciples, the five hundred brethren to whom he appeared at once after rising, and the innumerable multitude of believers and unbelievers who, while he was temporarily dead in the flesh, were themselves also temporarily living in the flesh.

All these, I say, testify to this: while, as I have said, they were living in a mortal body, he who was dead in a mortal body at the same time saved them, and showed that the benefits of his death availed those living persons. Since this is so, with no sound-minded person, I suppose, objecting, it has been proved that the good works of the living Lord benefited the living, those of the dead Lord the dead, those of the living Lord the dead, and those of the dead Lord the living.

But since this has fittingly been shown in the Lord and Savior—as in the head of his body, which is the Church—it must next, insofar as he grants, be shown in that same body, that is, in his faithful people. No believer is permitted to doubt regarding the Savior himself, to whom it uniquely belonged that his life or death should be expended for the salvation of the living and the dead. But concerning the rest—namely, that the good works of the living can benefit the dead—these heretics deny it, and even some Catholics seem to doubt it. It must chiefly be demonstrated for their sake, so that the heretic, if possible, may recover the faith which he has cast away, and the Catholic may not grow weak any longer in the faith which he confesses.

And so that these things may be shown below concerning faithful servants in the same order in which those matters concerning the Lord were shown above, it must be proved that the good works of the living have benefited the living, those of the dead the dead, those of the living the dead, and those of the dead the living in past ages, and can benefit them even in ages to come, until the consummation of the age. But what day could suffice if I wished to pour forth the examples which meet us everywhere and press themselves forward in competition, showing that the good works of the living benefited the living, and that all good persons aided one another by reciprocal benefits before the Law, under the Law, under grace, in the Heptateuch, in the prophets, in the psalms, in the Gospels, in the Acts and Epistles of the apostles, and finally in every divine law, both that called old and that called new?

But since it is unnecessary to gather into one place all such material drawn from Scripture, let examples sufficient for the purpose be advanced, by which the propositions set forth may be most vigorously defended. The proposition is that the good works of the living may benefit the living. I might, indeed, turning to more remote examples, speak of Abraham for Ishmael (Gen. 17), Isaac for Rebekah’s barrenness (Gen. 25), Jacob for his grandsons (Gen. 48), Moses for the Jews (Exod. 5), the same Moses against Amalek (Exod. 17), against Dathan and Abiram, and against many rebels and seditionaries (Num. 16): I might say that these great patriarchs prayed either for others or against others and were heard; that David by his prayers turned away the angel from slaying the people (3 Kings 24); that Samuel, a little earlier, said to that same Jewish people: “Far be it from me that I should sin by ceasing to pray for you” (1 Kings 12); that the prophets Isaiah and Jeremiah, and the kings Hezekiah and Josiah, often turned away from that same people, by prayers as well as merits, the wrath of the angered Lord. Besides these I could produce innumerable others, whom I omit for brevity’s sake: persons who by their strength sustained weakness, by their righteousness iniquity, and by their good deeds the evils of former times; who, as it were using force, held back with prayers God when he was preparing to punish human iniquities.

Leaving these aside, then, we must come to our evangelical times, in which the discourse should bring forward Paul—greatest among the apostles, as has often been said—and especially show from him that the good works of the living benefit the living. For he says in his Epistle to the Romans: “God, whom I serve in my spirit in the Gospel of his Son, is my witness that without ceasing I always make mention of you in my prayers” (Rom. 10). Again, to the Ephesians: “I bend my knees to the Father of my Lord Jesus Christ, from whom all fatherhood in heaven and on earth is named, that he may grant you, according to the riches of his grace, strength to be strengthened through his Spirit” (Eph. 3), and the rest. Again, to the Colossians: “Persist in prayer, watching in it with thanksgiving; praying also at the same time for us, that God may open for us a door of speech, to speak the mystery of Christ, that I may make it manifest as I ought to speak” (Col. 3). Again, in the already mentioned Epistle to the Romans: “I beseech you, brethren, through our Lord Jesus Christ and through the charity of the Holy Spirit, that you assist me in prayers to God, that I may be delivered from the unbelievers who are in Judaea, and that the offering of my service may be acceptable in Jerusalem to the saints” (Rom. 15).

Again, to Timothy: “I exhort first of all that supplications, prayers, petitions, and thanksgivings be made for all people, for kings and all who are in high position, so that we may lead a quiet and peaceful life in all piety and chastity. For this is good and acceptable before God our Savior” (1 Tim. 2). Hence James, after saying, “Confess your sins to one another” (Jas. 5), adds: “And pray for one another, that you may be saved” (ibid.). He proves that this should be done by prophetic testimony, when he introduces Elijah as having prayed that it should not rain upon the earth, and it did not rain for three years and six months; and as having prayed again, and heaven gave rain and the earth gave its fruit (3 Kings 17).

What more? What more, indeed, should I tire myself by speaking, or you, O reader, by reading? Behold, by these few and brief examples it has been shown most fully and abundantly that the good works of the living have benefited the living in former times and, as said, can always benefit them while life here endures, according as divine grace dispenses and the merit of each party requires. For while Paul remembers the Romans in his prayers; while he bends his knees to God for the Ephesians; while again he beseeches the Romans through Jesus Christ and through the charity of the Holy Spirit to assist him in prayers to God; while he urges the Colossians to persist in prayer and to pray also with him for himself; while he tells Timothy that supplications, prayers, petitions, and thanksgivings are to be made for kings and all in high position—and not only for these, but, as he first states, for all people; while James exhorts the twelve tribes in the Dispersion, and in them the faithful throughout the world, to pray for one another, adding the reason, that they may be saved; while he recalls that Elijah even prayed for the impious and was heard—what else, I say, is taught in all these great and solemn testimonies of the sacred law than that all Christ’s members should bring every sort of aid to one another, pray for one another, and, so that Christ’s law, which is charity, may be fulfilled, bear one another’s burdens (Gal. 6), whether spiritual or bodily, by spiritual or bodily assistance?

The proof of the next section is best proved from the proof of the preceding one. For by sacred authorities it has been repeatedly demonstrated that the good works of the living can benefit the living, if they are worthy. It therefore follows that the good works of dead persons can contribute to the salvation or relief from evils of dead persons also, if they too are worthy. For if the prayer of good living persons has benefited the living, why cannot the intercession of the same or similar persons, now dead, benefit the dead? Do righteous people living on earth have more power before the most merciful Majesty, and righteous people dead less? Are the prayers of good people while living of greater value before God than the supplications of good people who have died? Do saints still dwelling in the body possess greater merit before their Lord, and those stripped of mortality lesser? Are those still placed in flesh of a higher rank or grace, and those now united to God of a lower? Reason and justice do not permit this—do not permit it, I say—that when they ought to be stronger they become weaker; when more powerful, powerless; when more perfect, more imperfect; when glory ordinarily increases for such persons, grace diminishes; when the gifts of heavenly generosity toward such persons are ordinarily accumulated beyond speech, those gathered before should appear to be taken away.

Paul could certainly pray for the Romans and bend his knees for the Ephesians while he lived in wretched flesh; and, as is fitting to believe, he was heard. And now, stripped of every misery and joined to everlasting blessedness, will he pray for the same persons or for any others worthily, and not be heard? Elijah, as was said, prayed that rain might be withheld and prayed that it might be restored while remaining in the body; he was not disappointed even in the smallest degree of the effect of his prayers. When he has been stripped of the body—for he still lives in the body—will he pray for any worthy persons and not obtain what he has prayed for? The apostles ask the Lord for the Canaanite woman, saying: “Send her away, Lord, because she cries after us,” and they are heard (Matt. 6). Martha and Mary pray that their brother Lazarus may rise, and, when Christ hears them, he rises (John 11). These holy women and holy disciples, still wretched, obtained this; if they ask anything worthy, will they not obtain it once blessed? Prayer was made by the Church, still a pilgrim, to God for Peter, that he might be delivered from prison; and, when an angel was sent, he was delivered (Acts 12). Will the Church now united to God pray to be heard concerning benefits to be obtained for certain persons, and not be heard?

Indeed, by her own authority the same Church bears witness to this reasoning: that the good works of dead persons can benefit the dead. For every day throughout the world she commends her dead—those departing from the body under the sign of faith and sleeping the sleep of peace—to more perfect dead persons, namely holy martyrs and other supremely righteous persons. She would not commend persons now dead to other dead persons unless she considered that the good works of perfect dead persons can benefit dead persons who are good but imperfect. No Catholic has ever doubted this ecclesiastical custom, nor has any heretic ever been found who opposed it. The reading of the books of Maccabees also supports this: as will be more clearly explained in its proper place below, it presents the high priest Onias and the great prophet Jeremiah, already dead, as praying and being heard for the living (2 Macc. 15). Therefore, since the living are commanded to pray for the living, and the dead are read to have been heard for the living, why should it be doubted that the dead can benefit the dead by holy supplications?

But if someone perhaps objects that the good works of the dead cannot benefit the dead because, in that state of the age to come, there is no place for merits, good or evil, but for good or evil recompenses, I answer that here indeed is the place of merits and there the place of recompenses; but, just as one must distinguish varieties among evils and evils, so one must discern distinctions among goods and goods. For just as, from different points of view, I call evil both that which is sin and that which is the punishment of sin—the Prophet says of the first evil: “My sin is always before me. Against you alone have I sinned and done evil before you” (Ps. 50); but God himself says of the latter: “I am the Lord making peace and creating evil” (Isa. 45), and again: “Is there evil in a city which the Lord has not done?” (Amos 3)—so from a different viewpoint I call both his work good and its reward good. Of the first good sacred Scripture commands humankind: “Do good” (Ps. 36); of the latter it says: “I believe that I shall see the good things of the Lord” (Ps. 26).

The first good, therefore, is merit; the second good is the reward of merit. The first good is laborious; the following good delightful. The first good belongs to bitterness; the following good to sweetness. The first good exists with temporal misery; the following good with eternal happiness. Therefore the first good is practiced only in the present life; the following good is possessed perpetually in the future. I entirely exclude from saints, or those already blessed, that good which obtains merit, which I called a matter of labor, bitterness, and misery. But I affirm that they enjoy only that good which I called delightful, belonging to sweetness and eternal happiness. For those blessed persons will no longer need to be poor, to hunger or thirst bodily, to weep or groan, or to suffer persecution for righteousness; nor will they need other such things that obtain the good of merit. But that more excellent good, which I called the reward of preceding good works, cannot be absent from them—the good which every blessed inhabitant of heaven will possess eternally.

This is that good called blessedness, whose chief, or entire, cause is contemplation, love, and delight in the Creator. This contemplation, joined, as I said, to love of the Creator, will fill the whole rational and blessed creation; claiming it entirely for itself, it will animate it eternally to unwearied praise of the Creator. Among its own goods it will also have this good, so long as it is necessary: graciously to aid fellow servants still laboring in temporal misery, and, not by miserable lamentations but by blessed merits, to draw them into fellowship in its blessedness. Therefore the affection with which the dead supplicate God for the dead arises not from misery but from blessedness; not from the laborious supplications of this life, but from the stream of charity and everlasting blessedness flowing into them.

Thus the more perfect dead pray for the more imperfect: they implore God for those who are worthy, not with the miserable groanings of this life but, as becomes that life, with holy affections. They need not labor in prayer, since eternal Wisdom, which bestowed those holy merits or affections, cannot fail to know them, and supreme Goodness cannot fail to hear them. The Lord himself would not bestow such affections upon them if he were not going to hear them. Thus both authority teaches and reason persuades that the good works of the dead can benefit the dead. These good works of the saints, I say, will not diminish blessedness, but will assist, as stated, the imperfection of others. They will not be called a good that increases merit, but a good that rewards merit.

If Scripture’s authority is sought here by either believers or doubters, it will not be lacking, with the help of him who is “a helper in times of need” (Ps. 9). It certainly will not be lacking, so that our assertion, fortified on every side not only by the reasoning written above and not only by ecclesiastical institution, but also by divine authority, may stand unmoved, fearing no overthrow. Let the authoritative book called Kings, strengthened by evangelical testimonies, be brought forward, and by a wonderful and delightful example confirm, as has often been said, that the good works of the dead can benefit the dead. Let the great and renowned prophet Elisha, performer of great and marvelous works, come forward to establish this point: upon him rested Elijah’s spirit, and when that great prophet was carried to the heights in a chariot and horses of fire, Elisha deserved to receive a double portion of that same spirit (4 Kings 2).

The bones of this Elisha—not living, but already dead and buried—demonstrated, as soon as they touched another dead person, whether the good works of the dead can benefit the dead. “Certain persons,” says that Scripture, “while burying a man, saw robbers and cast the corpse into Elisha’s tomb. When it touched Elisha’s bones, the man came to life and stood upon his feet” (4 Kings 13). What could the Deity, foreknowing all things, have displayed more wonderful or more plainly suited to affirming the matter under discussion? By what clearer means could eternal Wisdom, which provides all things, have shown that the good works of the dead can benefit the dead? Who, considering this noble miracle, could not merely contradict or mutter against it, but even in the slightest degree doubt that the good works of the dead can benefit the dead?

God showed these open miracles to people of another age so that people of every age might be instructed, and might be admonished not only by divine words but also by marvelous deeds what they ought to believe and do. This bodily benefit, conferred by a dead prophet upon a dead man, teaches that God not only assists other dead persons through bodily benefits of dead people which he himself has granted, but also gives spiritual aid to other dead persons through the spiritual goods of those same dead persons, as the mercy joined to justice requires. Since these matters rest so firmly upon such great authorities and so many arguments, all doubt being utterly cast out, it is demonstrated more clearly than light that the good works of the dead can benefit the dead.

From here we must proceed, with the Spirit of God defending his own cause, to defend the third part of our division—the only part attacked by our heretics, the sole subject from which this fifth chapter has arisen. It is this: the Church of God teaches by words, and confirms by her daily works of mercy performed for the dead, that the good works of the living can benefit the dead. You heretics, with whom my discourse is chiefly concerned in this matter, cannot rashly assail this custom of the Church and this practice handed down to us by that same Church, because you are unable to resist the reasoning stated at length above and the invincible argument. Lest it slip from memory, I shall briefly repeat what that reasoning and argument are.

Above you said that you receive from the Church no books and no traditions besides the Gospel, but maintain your firmest faith only in it—that is, the Gospel. To this I answered: if you have received from the Church the Gospel and the other books which we call canonical, together with other authoritative traditions, without distinction, then you ought without distinction either to accept everything or reject everything. For what has been handed down without distinction by the Church to both us and you must without distinction either be wholly received or wholly rejected. But you do not concede that the Gospel ought to be rejected. Therefore, since you do not concede that the Gospel ought to be rejected, invincible reasoning compels you to receive whatever has been handed down together with the Gospel by that same Church which handed down the Gospel.

And you have found handed down by that Church, in the Church, that faithful persons living in the flesh should strive, by divine sacrifices, sacred prayers, and other works of piety, to assist others who have departed from the flesh with the sign of faith and Christian hope; and that, devoutly presuming upon the overflowing mercy of the Creator, they should strive to supply what was lacking to those departed persons’ lives—lives good indeed, but imperfect. Since this has been handed down to you by the Church already mentioned in the same way as the Gospel, it must altogether be received by you, as by all persons, in the same way as the Gospel.

Let, however, the authority of the sacred books succeed, and let the clear-voiced testimony both of the divine canon and of the other volumes connected with it and handed down by the Church scatter the darkness of error by its light and open the ears hitherto stopped in deaf people. First of all, let the Second Book of Maccabees be brought forward, from which the heretical opponent may hear the most famous reading, daily recited in the divine sacrifices continually offered throughout the whole world for the dead; and, hearing words of piety that resound piously everywhere throughout the world, may he be ashamed to be almost alone impious among innumerable devout persons who pray to divine mercy for the dead.

Let him hear that the most valiant Judas made a collection of twelve thousand drachmas and sent it to Jerusalem so that offerings might be made there for the sins of certain persons who had died shortly before in battle—a sin described as so grave that it is scarcely found worthy of pardon. “On the following day,” says that Scripture, “Judas came with his men to take up the bodies of the fallen and place them with their relatives in the ancestral tombs. But they found beneath the tunics of the slain offerings dedicated to the idols which were at Jamnia, from which the Law forbids the Jews. Thus it became manifest to all that they had fallen for this reason. Therefore all blessed the just judgment of the Lord, who had made hidden things manifest; and so they turned to prayers and begged that the sin which had been committed might be consigned to oblivion” (2 Macc. 12).

So grave, I say, was the sin that offerings dedicated to idols were found beneath the tunics of the slain. Concerning so grave a sin, faithful Jews turned to prayers and indeed begged God that the sin which had been committed might be consigned to oblivion. Therefore faithful Jews pray to God for the grave sins of the dead, that what they had done might be forgotten; and will faithful Christians not pray to the same God for departed believers of good hope, that sins not yet fully forgiven may be remitted to them? Those Jews prayed for this even in the time of wrath, and will these Christians not pray for it in the time of grace? Judas offered—because he sent twelve thousand drachmas of silver to be offered—for the sins of dead Jews; and will our Judas, that is, the Christian who holds and confesses piety, not offer for the sins of dead Christians the body and blood of Christ, incomparably more precious than gold and silver?

That Judas rightly and religiously reflected upon the resurrection; he rightly and religiously considered that those Jews who had fallen asleep in piety had a most excellent grace laid up for them. Do those think wrongly and irreligiously who consider that those Christians who sleep in piety have the same grace, and a better, laid up for them? Certainly not, because, as that good Scripture continues, “it is a holy and wholesome thought to pray for the dead, that they may be freed from sins” (ibid.).

Let the whole divine and evangelical prophet Isaiah be added to this example from the Maccabees. It is superfluous to extol either his truthfulness or his dignity, since the apostles, the evangelists, and the Saviour himself are found very frequently to read and proclaim him and to strengthen their own words by his utterances. For, speaking to the Jewish people to whom he had been sent, rebuking and instructing them, he says: “When they say to you, [Col. 0830B] ‘Seek out necromancers and diviners who chirp in their incantations,’ is not a people to inquire of its God for the living and the dead?” (Isa. VIII). It is as if he said: When deceivers tell you that things which ought to be sought only from God should, contrary to God, be sought from necromancers and diviners, who, in the manner of such persons, chirp and hiss in their incantations, answer: “Is not a people?” That is: Is it not the custom of all peoples to seek from the God whom each worships those things which ought to be sought, whether for the living or for the dead? Therefore we shall not, as you say, seek these things from necromancers and diviners; rather, following the custom of all peoples, who seek from their God what should be sought both for the living and for the dead, we too shall do likewise, seeking from our God whatever is to be sought for the living, or whatever is to be sought for the dead.

Do you not see, whoever reads this, that the prophet Isaiah most plainly proclaims that God is to be sought—that is, consulted—by his people both for the living and for the dead? And if God is to be consulted and prayed to for the living as well as for the dead, what answer do those give who say that prayer ought not to be offered for the dead? Was this granted to the Jewish people alone and now denied to the Christian world? That people is taught to answer deceivers that God must be sought or entreated for the living and the dead; and shall the Christian people not be taught that heretics who deny [Col. 0830D] that God should be prayed to for the dead are to be trampled underfoot?

But if they say that some copies do not contain, “Is not a people to inquire of its God for the living and the dead?” but rather “for the living from the dead”—that is, for living human beings from dead images—I answer that this too was said, if indeed the reading is so, in reproach of idolaters. For they sought from false and innumerable gods, as they themselves held them to be, what ought to have been sought only from the one true God for the welfare of the living or the dead. Thus it is said to King Ahaziah: “As though there were no God in Israel, you sent to consult Baalzebub, god of Ekron; therefore you shall not come down from the bed upon which you have gone up, but you shall surely die” (IV Kings I). I say, then, that this was said in ridicule of idolaters; but the prophet’s meaning was that God’s people ought to seek from the true God the welfare of the living and the dead. Whoever reads this attentively will understand it and will oppose those erring persons who deny these things. For what follows—“To the law rather and to the testimony”—shows that, concerning these and similar matters, the divine law and its testimonies must be consulted, and believed more than necromancers or diviners. And the additional words, “If they do not speak according to this word, there shall be no morning light for them” (Isa. VIII), threaten heretics who deny or contradict this: if they do not say in accordance with this word, namely, that God must be consulted or prayed to for the salvation of the living and the dead, they shall have no morning light—that is, they shall never attain that eternal morning of which, after saying, “Weeping shall linger at evening,” [Col. 0831B] the Prophet added, “and joy in the morning” (Ps. XXIX).

But let the argument pass from the Prophet to the Apostle, so that the supreme teacher of the Church after Christ may, in his customary fashion, disclose what he thinks of these matters not only to disciples but also to these troublesome people. Treating in the First Epistle to the Corinthians of the resurrection of the dead and establishing it in many ways, he says: “Otherwise, what do those do who are baptized for the dead? If the dead do not rise at all, why are they baptized for them?” (I Cor. XV).

For at that time certain persons, with a good but unsound intention, were baptized for unbaptized dead persons, supposing that baptism which they had not received while alive could benefit them after death if living persons were baptized on their behalf. In speaking thus of their practice, the Apostle so qualifies his words that he does not approve such baptism, while he commends the intention of those baptized. He certainly does not approve the notion that one person’s baptism can benefit another, living or dead, insofar as baptism is concerned; but he plainly approves and confirms the intention of those baptized persons, who seemed to hold that the dead could be helped by the good works of the living, as in this practice—that is, in such baptism. Therefore the Apostle rejects what ought to be rejected and accepts what he recognizes ought to be accepted, so that he may teach that the dead can be helped by the living not by baptism, which is one alone, but by every other good work, which is manifold. Hence [Col. 0831D] he declares the proposition which I set forth above so firmly in his proof of the resurrection, and repeats it for stronger emphasis: “Otherwise, what do those do who are baptized for the dead?” and immediately, “If the dead do not rise at all, why are they baptized for them?” It is as though he said: If there is no resurrection, what benefit is a good work, or the good intention of the living for the dead? What benefit is the goodwill of the living for the dead if the death of the flesh is not followed by the resurrection of the dead? What benefit is a good work of the living for the dead if, after the common fall, the human body is not believed able to rise to everlasting life?

But since it is evident that the dead rise, it is likewise not hidden that the good things of the living can benefit the dead. Since it is clear that the blessing of resurrection is reserved for human flesh, it is equally plain that the blessing of prayer, by which the living supplicate God for the dead, is reserved for the human soul. Since it is established that bodily substance will be restored either from a corpse, from dust, or from nothing, it is certain that meanwhile spiritual substance will be aided by the good works of the living. For if human nature were utterly to perish without hope of restoration, then, just as there would be nothing from which it could be restored, so there would be nothing from which it could be helped. But since it is established that through resurrection it will be remade for the better, it is certain that it can be helped—not indeed through baptism, but through other good works of the living, if these are done for it. This, plainly, is the apostolic sense and understanding: [Col. 0832B] whoever agrees with it is a Catholic; whoever disagrees with it is proved to be a heretic. Hence he continues: “Why too are we in danger every hour? I die daily, by your glory, brethren” (ibid.).

You see, reader, that the Apostle made the baptisms of those who were baptized for the dead—that is, the good things done by the living for the dead—parallel to his own dangers and daily dying. He did not make his works equal to theirs in dignity, for his works incomparably surpassed theirs; but he equated his deeds with theirs insofar as they furnished an argument proving the resurrection of the dead. For he said that the living are baptized for the dead in vain if the dead do not rise; he said that he is in danger every hour in vain if the dead do not rise; that he dies daily in vain if the dead do not rise; that he fought with beasts at Ephesus in vain if the dead do not rise; and that all these acts, and similar ones, were or are done in vain if the dead do not rise.

But if the dead rise, neither does he suffer or do all these things in vain, nor—so far as concerns the intention mentioned above—are the living who were baptized for the dead baptized for them in vain. For his works benefited not only the living but also the dead, and the good deeds of other living persons which were piously done for the dead unquestionably advanced the salvation of the dead. Let the argument now pass, from this silver column—that is, this bright and strong apostolic proposition—upon which the structure of this work firmly rests, and from the proof that the good things of the living can benefit the dead if they are worthy, to the Acts of this Apostle and of the other apostles. With the help of him whose cause is at issue, let it show from that book, not itself a Gospel but evangelical, that what it establishes from others is true.

Certainly two great and supreme apostles, Peter and Paul, lived in the flesh. The former, to speak briefly, raised the dead Tabitha in response to the prayers and lamentations of widows (Acts IX); the latter raised Eutychus, who had fallen from a window (Acts XX), moved by the fall of a young man devoted to the word of God. Peter, I say, lived in the flesh; Tabitha was dead as to the flesh. Lest anyone doubt this, Holy Scripture testifies: “It happened in those days that Tabitha fell sick and died. When they had washed her, they laid her in an upper room.” What is said of Peter? “Peter,” it says, “knelt down and prayed.” And a little later: “Having called the saints and widows, he presented her alive” (Acts IX). What of Paul? “A certain young man named Eutychus, overcome with sleep, fell down from the third storey and was taken up dead. Paul went down to him, lay upon him, and embracing him said: ‘Do not be troubled, for his soul is in him.’” And, after an intervening verse: “They brought the young man alive, and were not a little comforted” (Acts XX).

Behold Peter alive; behold the woman unquestionably dead. Behold Paul alive; behold the young man unquestionably dead. Yet because Peter knelt and prayed, the dead woman rose; [Col. 0833B] and because Paul lay upon this young man and embraced him, the dead young man rose. What further proof is sought? Why is it denied or doubted that the good things of the living can benefit the departed, when such sublime examples teach that the aforesaid dead rose through the prayers of such great apostles? Who would now dare even to whisper that the Church prays for the dead in vain, when he sees its greatest teachers both invisibly call back the souls of the dead from the hidden seats of God’s judgments and visibly raise their very bodies? It is sufficient—plainly sufficient—for heretics who deny it and Catholics who doubt it: even if there were no other example, this proves that the Church rightly prays for the dead, and that, if the prior life of the dead requires it, her devout prayers or works can benefit the dead.

But lest this grace appear to have been bestowed only upon those great apostles, let those of lesser rank also come forward; and let the Gospel itself now declare that Christ granted them power to perform like works. Let not only the twelve apostles come forward, but also the seventy-two disciples; and, among the other commands, let them hear Christ say: “Raise the dead” (Matt. X). And lest even to these alone the power of such wondrous works seem to have been given, let those with whom I am speaking attend to the Lord’s declaration concerning these things, a declaration not special to some but general to all: “He who believes in me will himself also do the works which I do, and he will do greater than these” (John XIV).

For what purpose is this said? To show that the power of raising the dead was granted not only to the twelve apostles, not only to the seventy-two disciples, not only to other believers who saw Christ in the flesh, but to all who truly believe, whenever a definite cause concerning human salvation required it. And why this further point? So that, from the grace granted by God to the living in the resurrection of the dead, and from the dead rising throughout the world through the prayers of the living, the living may no longer doubt that the good things of the living can benefit the dead. Since you hear that the apostles, the ancient prophets, and innumerable saints under the dispensation of grace raised the dead so often; since you recognize that they did this not by their evils but by their good deeds, not by their wrongs but by God’s gifts, you heretics will by no means deny, nor will you Catholics any longer doubt, that the good things of the living can benefit the dead.

But if you object that in the Old Scripture only Elijah and Elisha, and in the books of the new grace only Peter and Paul, are found to have raised the dead, I answer that more such examples may indeed not be read in the Canon, but that the words and commands of the Lord which I have set forth ought most amply to be treated as examples. For what? When we read that Christ commanded the disciples, “Raise the dead,” and that he said of all believers, “He who believes in me will himself do the works which I do,” are we not to believe that he foretold the resurrection of many dead persons through the disciples? For if the dead were not raised by them, then either the disciples neglected Christ’s command, [Col. 0834B] or they did not fulfil what he commanded.

But, to pursue those who evade the issue to the last detail, I grant that they did not raise the dead; yet I affirm what you heretics cannot deny: they received the fullest power to raise the dead. If they received it, then truly they could either use it or not use it. If they used it, they raised the dead. If they did not use it, they did not in fact raise them, but they were able to raise the dead. Whichever you grant, you cannot deny what we affirm. For if they raised the dead, they certainly raised them by the Lord’s command and by their good prayers. If they did not raise them, they were able to raise the dead by the same command of that same Lord and by the same good prayers. Since this is established, just as their good deeds would have benefited the dead if they had raised them, so even if they did not raise them, their good deeds could nevertheless, if they wished, have benefited the dead.

All this comes to the point that, in the power received to raise the dead—whether they raised them or did not raise them—the foremost testimonies of the holy Gospel show that every kind of good work of the living can benefit the dead. Yet it is false that Christ both commanded and foretold such resurrection of the dead, and that what he commanded and foretold was not fulfilled. For many—indeed innumerable—disciples of Christ arose who throughout the whole world, amid their other countless and stupendous works, observed what Christ commanded concerning the raising of the dead and fulfilled what had been foretold. By these heavenly and wonderful works, making the wisdom of the world foolish and subjecting the world’s power to God, they rescued human beings from eternal death and restored them to the everlasting life which they had lost. And who can count them? “I shall number them,” says he, “and they shall be multiplied beyond the sand” (Ps. CXXXVIII), because no mortal can number them.

Christ says: “He who believes in me will do the works which I do,” so that, among other wonders, because I raise the dead, he too may raise them. “And he will do greater than these.” O surpassing grace! O overflowing kindness! The Christian will do greater things than Christ; the saved person will perform greater things than the Saviour; a human being will accomplish greater things than God. Why is this? “Because I go to the Father” (John XIV): because I withdraw bodily from the world, because I remove my presence from mortal eyes, lest the world suppose that, when my presence is withdrawn, my grace too is withdrawn from it; lest it think that I have forgotten it because it sees itself bodily abandoned; lest it judge that I have entirely departed from here because it sees human form withdraw into heaven. Therefore I pour a greater grace upon the earth; therefore I send another Paraclete to my own, “who may remain with them for ever” (ibid.), who “will teach them all truth” (John XVI). Therefore I grant them a greater fullness of spiritual gifts and a greater efficacy of wondrous works, both that they may be consoled for my visible absence and that they may be stirred in many ways to ardently desire my eternal presence. Therefore, he who believes in me “will not only do the works which I do, [Col. 0835B] but will do greater than these.”

For, to say nothing of other admirable men and their wondrous works, did not Eucharius, sent by the apostle Peter to preach in Germany, raise a dead man by a greater miracle than Christ did? Christ raised Lazarus after four days; Eucharius, sent by Peter, raised a man dead for forty days. Lazarus lay lifeless in the tomb for four days; this man too had lain dead in burial for forty days. Therefore Eucharius did greater things than Christ, because Christ himself had willed and said that this should be so. I could say the same of many others—for example, of Saint Fronton, bishop of Périgueux, and Maurilius, bishop of Angers. The former, when he too was being sent by the same, often-mentioned apostle Peter into Aquitaine, restored to life by that apostle’s staff his companion George, who had been dead on the road for more than ten days. The latter, long after the time of the apostles, raised by an outstanding miracle a boy who had already been in the tomb for seven full years and whom, for this reason, he later called Renatus, “the Reborn.”

What has this to do with the matter proposed? It shows that Christ commanded that the dead should rise through the living, and hence teaches that the good things of the living can undoubtedly help the dead. Let what has been said from the sacred Canon, apart from what I have included concerning Eucharius, Fronton, and Maurilius because of the celebrated renown of those saints, suffice especially against heretics, who say that they believe only the Canon. But for Catholics, who receive the holy Fathers and teachers of God’s Church with due reverence, I think examples and testimonies should be set forth from their sayings and deeds. Those who may perhaps until now have read them less diligently may henceforth read them more diligently and recognize that they kept watch against this heresy many centuries ago.

I say “for Catholics” because in certain regions, although not many, some are said to exist who, though they do not openly contradict the aforementioned truth as heretics do, nevertheless show by what they discuss with others that they doubt it. Their doubt is said to have progressed so far that, when consulted on these matters by others, they give lukewarm answers; [Col. 0836A] and either fail or grow slack both in offering sacrifices to God for the dead, in giving alms, and in performing other works of piety according to ecclesiastical custom. I ought not to call them heretics, because in these matters they do not resist the Church publicly or obstinately. Obstinacy alone, resisting the Church’s teaching, makes a heretic. Yet I do not dare confidently call them believers, because I see them grow slack or lukewarm regarding ecclesiastical ordinances.

There are indeed innumerable and very diverse customs among the various Churches which belong to the one Catholic Church, so that the variety of practices is almost as great as the multiplicity of Churches. But a differing institution does not condemn anyone when it serves true faith and does not dissolve the bond of charity. But wherever faith is harmed or the unity of charity endangered, if it happens secretly it is condemnable; if publicly, it is both condemnable and heretical. I have introduced this point so that anyone who denies that the good things of the living can benefit the worthy dead may understand that he belongs not to the variety of good practices mentioned above, but to an injury of the common faith. And because this pertains to an injury of faith, it must, when public, be expelled as a heretical plague; while the hidden sickness of those who languish must, if possible, be treated with medicinal remedies.

By medicinal remedies I mean the examples and admonitions of the Catholic Fathers: what cannot benefit heretics, because they do not listen to it, may benefit these persons, by whom it is received. For teachers of God’s Church hold no small place either in the kingdom of heaven or in God’s Church, since God himself says concerning the kingdom of heaven or the Church of God: “He who does and teaches shall be called great in the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. V). And the Apostle, in his Epistle to the Corinthians, places them in a lofty rank—the third after apostles and prophets—when he says: “God has set some in the Church: first apostles, second prophets, third teachers; then miracles; then gifts of healing, assistances, governments, kinds of tongues, interpretations of speech” (I Cor. XII).

Therefore hear, all you who turn any such thoughts over in your minds; hear the great saints and chief teachers of the Church after the apostles and prophets. If you are their children, submit to your fathers; if disciples, to your teachers. Do not in perverse order wish to prefer your own intellects, however acute or subtle, to their judgments; for, as Truth says, “Everyone will be perfect if he is like his teacher” (Luke VI). Yet, since the matter itself requires us to aim at brevity, we have by no means set forth examples from all those who bear the celebrated name of teacher in the Church and whom we could have as Greek or Latin witnesses. We have judged it sufficient to produce the testimonies only of those who, in the stronghold of Latin learning—whose language we speak—excel the rest in authority and knowledge.

Thus blessed Ambrose, bishop of Milan, whom, as is recorded to have been said of him long ago, not even an enemy ever dared to criticize, said in the discourse which he delivered to the people “On the Death of the Great Emperor Theodosius”:

> “I loved the man who, in his final moments, sought me with his last breath. I loved him, and I trust in the Lord that he will receive the voice of my prayer, by which I accompany a devout soul.”

And after some intervening words:

> “I am broken in heart because a man has been taken away whom we can scarcely find. Yet you alone, Lord, must be invoked, that you may represent him again in his sons. Grant, Lord, perfect rest to your servant Theodosius, that rest which you have prepared for your saints. May his soul return to that place whence it descended, where it cannot feel death’s sting, where it may know that this death is not the end of nature but of guilt.”

Again, shortly afterward:

> “I loved him, and therefore I accompany him as far as the region of the living; nor will I abandon him until, through weeping and prayers, I bring the man—where his merits call him—unto the holy mountain of the Lord.”

In the work which he wrote *On the Consolation of the Emperors Valentinian and Gratian*, praying for Valentinian, who had died in the true faith, he says:

> “Do not, I beseech you, Lord, separate him from his brother, nor break this bond of devout brotherhood. Grant a son to his father, his own brother to his brother; for he imitated them both—the one in faith, the other alike in devotion and piety.”

And after some intervening words:

> “And am I still to seek intercession for him whose reward I confidently expect? Give the holy mysteries into our hands; let us ask rest for him with devout affection. Give the heavenly sacraments.
