Let us accompany the devout soul by our offerings. Lift up your hands with me, peoples, unto holy things, that by this at least gift we may repay him according to his merits. I shall not scatter flowers upon his tomb (Cant. II), but shall bathe his spirit in Christ’s fragrance. Let others scatter lilies from full baskets; for us Christ is the lily. With this I shall consecrate his remains; with this I commend his grace. Never shall I separate the names of the devout brothers or distinguish their merits. I know that this remembrance wins the Lord’s favour and that this union delights him.”

Then, after much else:

> “Blessed are you both, if my prayers have any power. No day shall pass you over in silence; no prayer of mine shall pass you by without honour. No night shall run its course without being adorned by some weaving together of my prayers. I shall commemorate you in all offerings.”

In the first book *On the Death of His Brother Satyrus*, he says: “The poor wept, and, what is far more precious and abundant, washed away his sins by their tears. Those are redeeming tears, those groans which hide the grief of death—the grief which, by the everlasting abundance of joy, covers over the sense of former sorrow.” Again, at the end of the same book: “To you now, almighty God, I commend an innocent soul; to you I offer my sacrifice. Receive graciously and serenely a brother’s gift, a priest’s sacrifice.” In the second book: “We too forget the birthdays of the departed and renew in solemn celebration the day on which they died.” And, later in the same work, exhorting parents to give alms for departed children, he says: “You have not lost the heir whom you help as a co-heir. You have one who represents your heir to you. Give the poor what is owed to the heir, so that he may survive not only the old age of his mother or father, but even his own life. You will leave more to your dead successor [Col. 0838A] if his portion does not promote the luxury of the present, but purchases the things to come.”

Behold Ambrose, great and renowned throughout the Christian world: he teaches not only prayer and almsgiving for departed believers, but himself prays, offers sacrifices, sheds tears, and—as he himself here confesses—keeps anniversaries, so that heretical impiety, rebuked by so great a trumpet of God’s priest, may no longer dare to murmur.

The glorious Augustine, the Church’s unique teacher after the apostle Paul, replied to Paulinus’s questions concerning the care to be taken for the dead. Among many things which he wrote there most cogently, eloquently, and forcefully to establish this matter, he says:

> “The kind of life which each person has led in the body determines whether or not whatever is piously done for him after he has left the body benefits him. Thus it comes about that neither the Church nor the care of his own people vainly bestows upon the departed whatever religious service it can; and yet each bears according to what he has done in the body.”

Then, shortly afterward:

> “When the mind recalls where the body of one dearly loved lies buried, and there comes to mind a place venerable for the name of a martyr, the affection of one remembering and praying commends that beloved soul to the same martyr. And when this affection is shown to the dead by their dearest faithful friends, it is undoubtedly beneficial to those who, while living in the body, deserved that such things should benefit them after this life. Nor are the supplications for the spirits of the dead to be omitted, which the Church has undertaken to offer for all who have died in the Christian and Catholic fellowship, even when their names are not mentioned, so that those who lack parents, children, relatives, or friends to provide these things may receive them from the one common devout mother. And even if a devout mind cannot bury one whom it loves where it chooses, it must nevertheless by no means cease from the necessary supplications in commending him. Nor should we suppose that anything reaches the dead for whom we care except what we solemnly ask for them through sacrifices of the altar, prayers, or alms. Yet these things do not benefit all for whom they are done, but only those who, while alive, acquired the means by which they may benefit them. But because we do not distinguish who these are, we ought to do them for all the regenerate, so that none may be omitted to whom these benefits can or ought to reach.”

Also in the *Enchiridion*, which he wrote to Laurentius:

> “Nor must it be denied that the souls of the dead are relieved by the piety of their living friends, when the sacrifice of the Mediator is offered for them, or when alms are given in the Church. But these things benefit those who, while living, deserved that they might later benefit them. For there is a manner of life neither so good that it does not require these things after death, nor so bad that these things cannot benefit it after death. There is also a kind of life so good that it does not require them; and again one so evil that it cannot be helped even by them. Therefore every merit is acquired here, by which someone may after this life be relieved or burdened [lacuna].”

“Therefore the things which the Church frequently does in commending the dead are not contrary to that apostolic declaration: ‘For we must all stand before the tribunal of Christ, that each may receive according to what he has done in the body, whether good or evil’ (Rom. XIV; II Cor. V). For each person acquired even this merit while alive, namely, that these things might be able to benefit him. Therefore, when sacrifices—whether of the altar or of any alms whatsoever—are offered for all baptized persons who have died: for the very good they are thanksgivings; for those not very bad, propitiations; for the very bad, even if they are no assistance to the dead, they are nevertheless consolations of some kind to the living. But for those whom they benefit, they benefit either by producing full remission or at least by making condemnation itself more tolerable.”

In the books of the *Confessions*, this great man of God also made most clear what he thought on this matter when recounting the life and death of his blessed mother. Among other things he says: “When, behold, the body was carried out, we went and returned without tears. For even in those prayers which we poured out when the sacrifice of our price was offered for her, with the corpse placed beside the grave, I did not weep.” Then, at the end of the prayer which he pours out most affectionately in the same book for his departed mother:

> “Inspire, O my Lord, my God, inspire your servants, my brothers, your sons, my masters—whom I serve with voice, heart, and writings—that all who read this may remember at your altar your servant Monica, together with Patricius, once her husband, through whose flesh you brought me into this life. May they remember with devout affection my parents in this transient light, and my brothers under you, our Father, in the Catholic mother, and my fellow citizens in the eternal Jerusalem, for which the pilgrimage of your people sighs from departure until return; so that what she asked of me as her final request may be granted to her more abundantly through the prayers of many, through both my *Confessions* and my prayers.”

What the blessed and great Pope Gregory either wrote or said on this matter, or himself did in his monastery at Rome, need not, in our judgment, be narrated point by point, since his *Life*, *Homilies*, and *Dialogues* are recited and heard, read and understood daily and almost without interruption by countless brethren, including those less educated and simple. Nevertheless, I shall by no means pass over the most blessed Paulinus, bishop of Nola, whom the great Gregory himself calls “an ancient Father” and concerning whom he relates a wondrous and singular event in his *Dialogues*. Paulinus was also a contemporary, acquaintance, and friend of the aforesaid Fathers Ambrose and Augustine. I shall set out his own words to explain what he thought in his letters—written to various persons by a man learned, as Pope Gregory’s foregoing testimony attests, even in secular studies—concerning the benefits done in the Church for departed believers. Thus, by the testimony of these four great saints and bishops—Ambrose, Augustine, Gregory, and Paulinus—serving in place of the four Evangelists, the ancient judgment which the universal Church holds, or ought to hold, concerning the matter under discussion may shine forth with the clearest authority for Christians both present and future.

Thus says the ancient and noble Paulinus, in his letter to Delphinus, bishop of Bordeaux—namely, his spiritual father in baptism—asking him to pray for a certain blood-brother of his who had died, having made insufficient provision, so far as his soul was concerned, in disposing of his affairs at death:

> “We have received with all the heart for which we longed your brief letter of holy affection, abundant to us through its great affection. But since there is a time for every matter, now, in a time of sorrow, it has seemed also to be a time for shortening our speech. We confess, moreover, that we are deeply grieved—not so much by the bodily death of our brother as by his spiritual negligence: mindful rather of the cares to be left here than of remedies to be provided there [Col. 0840B], he put before what ought to have been put aside, and put aside what ought to have been put before. He ought both to have attended to those more important matters for himself and not to have neglected these temporal matters for his children. Therefore we ask that, compassionating this sorrow of ours with paternal affection, you may deign to remember that he was once spiritually begotten to you as a son by the grace of God, and that for this reason this matter belongs especially to your care; lest we, your children in whom your loving-kindness took pride, be put to shame by the dissipation of our inherited portion. Rather, may it be granted him through your prayers, so that a drop of refreshment, distilled even from the least finger of your holiness, may sprinkle his soul; and so that, while there is time, when we return to you, divine mercy may come to our aid through your intercession.”

The same writer, in a letter [Col. 0840C] to Bishop Amandus, on the same matter and for the same person, says:

> “Your discourse possesses at once the sweetness and the strength of the heavenly word, and ministers them to us, so that we too may be seasoned with the salt of your wisdom. Therefore we too shall imitate in this letter the economy of your speech; and, if we cannot imitate its fullness of meaning, we answer only this: that while we wrote these things, our chief concern arose from the fresh pain of our brother’s separation. Although we know that he has been taken from this world in temporal terms, we yet mourn that he died for a truer reason: because, from those things which he did or arranged toward the end, we perceived that he had acted in a manner more fitting to our sins than to yours, in that he preferred to pass to the Lord as a debtor rather than free. For this reason [Col. 0840D] we earnestly ask that, as a brother—as you deign to be to us in the Lord—you may help your brethren in one mind, and may increase for yourself this reward of your faithful merits: that you may have compassion on him in our weakness and join us in the labour of prayer; so that the compassionate and merciful Lord, who does all that he wills in heaven, on earth, in the sea, and in the depths (Ps. 134), may refresh his soul with drops of his mercy through your prayers. For, just as a fire kindled by him shall burn down to the depths below (Deut. 32), so undoubtedly also the dew of his forgiveness shall penetrate the lower regions, so that those who burn in fiery darkness may be refreshed by the dewy light of his mercy. Pray also for us, lest we die in our sins.”

In the letter which he wrote to Pammachius, senator of the city of Rome, consoling him over his wife’s death, [Col. 0841A] he praises and exalts in the highest terms the almsgiving which that senator had zealously distributed among the poor for the repose of his deceased wife:

> “I shall come to the praise of your works, and shall pass from the holiness [or ‘dryness,’ *siccitate*] of tears to pious actions. For you have rendered to each part what was due: pouring out tears for the body and bestowing almsgiving upon the soul. Truly conscious of the truth, and a son of light: where you knew death to be, you wept; where you believe life to be, you acted—paying what is empty to the empty, and what is living to the living.”

Then, after many similar statements, concluding his letter in praise of this devout act, he says:

> “You now have in Christ a great pledge of yourself and an influential advocate: namely, your wife, who prepares for you as much favour in heaven as you supply her with wealth on earth [Col. 0841B]. You honour her, as I have said, not with fruitless grief but by heaping up living gifts, in which she now rejoices. Already she has the benefit of your work in its fruit, while for you the gift still exists in its seed. Already she is honoured by your merits; already she is fed by your bread and abounds in your wealth. She does not need to be refreshed by the finger of another’s hand, being herself suffused with the dews of her own fingers—that is, with the works of your right hand. You had not enriched her when she married you with a dowry equally as ample as that with which you now enrich her in her rest. How great a part of your gifts did she receive then, when she enjoyed only what she could wear? Now, however much you bestow, her rich soul shall possess it all at once with the delight of every sense. Blessed is she who has so many advocates with Christ, and whose head is encircled by so manifold [Col. 0841C] a crown of splendid jewels—not woven from another’s flowers, but radiant with lights from her own household!”

Nor indeed shall we allow the holy presbyter Jerome to be absent from our side in any way, so that with the dart of his singular eloquence he may pierce the poisoned breasts of the heretics of our own age, as formerly he pierced those of the ancients. Writing a consolatory letter to the same above-named senator Pammachius, at the same time and on the same subject, and lavishly extolling in his customary splendour of speech the almsgiving made for his deceased wife, he says among other things:

> “Other husbands scatter violets, roses, lilies, and purple flowers upon their wives’ tombs, and console their grief-stricken hearts by such observances. Our Pammachius [Col. 0841D] moistens the holy ashes and venerable bones with the balsams of almsgiving. With these spices and fragrances he cherishes the resting ashes, knowing what is written: ‘As water extinguishes fire, so almsgiving extinguishes sin’ (Sirach 3).”

Therefore, when the holy doctors of the Church say these and similar things, what else do they show more clearly than daylight except that the good deeds of the living benefit the dead? And, while slaughtering impious heresy with the sword of the divine word, do they not also rebuke the slumbering indifference concerning devotion of certain of our own people whom we mentioned above? Let anyone therefore beware lest, being excessively righteous in his own eyes, he dare further to think or dispute against this teaching of devotion and mercy—received unanimously, not without the authority of the Holy Spirit, through so many centuries before our time by the whole Church, and strengthened by devout custom [Col. 0842A]—lest he impede, by his overly narrow justice, the mercy which others show toward their departed brethren, and, when he himself perhaps needs it, be estranged from the mercy which he forbade to others. For “blessed,” as we recalled the Lord saying far above, “are the merciful, for they shall obtain mercy” (Matt. 5).

Here let the pen hasten to the final division of our classification; and, as it has shown that the good deeds of the living can benefit the dead, so let it demonstrate that the good deeds of the dead can benefit the living. The aforementioned Second Book of Maccabees relates that Judas Maccabaeus, that warlike and God-faithful man, when he was about to fight Nicanor, a pagan commander, encouraged his companions to battle by divine and steadfast exhortation; [Col. 0842B] and, among other things, made them much more confident of victory through a dream seen on the day before the battle. The vision, as Scripture tells it, was of this kind:

> “He saw Onias, who had been high priest, a good and kindly man, modest in appearance, restrained in character, graceful in speech, and one who had been trained in virtues from childhood, stretching out his hands and praying for all the people of the Jews. After this there appeared another man, remarkable in age and glory, possessing great and splendid dignity about him. Onias answered and said: ‘This is the lover of the brethren and of the people of Israel. This is he who prays much for the people and for the whole holy city: Jeremiah, prophet of God.’ Then Jeremiah stretched out his right hand and gave Judas a golden sword, saying: ‘Receive this holy sword [Col. 0842C], a gift from God, by which you shall cast down the adversaries of my people Israel’” (2 Macc. 15).

By what example, then, could it more clearly shine forth that the good deeds of the dead are able to benefit the living? Does it not seem to you, whoever read these things, that this vision was shown to that good man Judas Maccabaeus precisely so that the Christian age might be taught by the customary pattern of the Jewish age? Do you not perceive that the citadel of divine wisdom, wisely providing for its own people in every age, by that vision both granted victory over enemies to its Jews in that time and provided triumph over opponents for its Christians in our time? Behold, the righteous man Onias, a priest already killed at Jerusalem for righteousness, prays; behold, the holy prophet Jeremiah, stoned in Egypt for truth, prays [Col. 0842D]. These righteous men, certainly, now dead, pray to God for Jews still living—and is it not to be believed that the prayers of holy dead persons can benefit the living? It is therefore necessary either to yield to the book which is believed to be divine and accept these things in it, or, if this book is rejected on the authority of the Church, to reject these things in it as well. But if deference is given to the Church’s authority in accepting this book, it must necessarily be accepted by the faithful. And if it is admitted, the vision described in it must also be admitted.

But perhaps someone will allege that this was a dream and therefore ought to be despised as vain dreaming. I certainly do not deny that, just as dreams are often vain, so they are often to be disregarded. Nor have I forgotten the saying of Wisdom: “Dreams follow many cares” (Sirach 5). [Col. 0843A] Nor has the precept of Deuteronomy escaped my mind, which says: “You shall not practise divination, nor observe dreams” (Lev. 19). Yet I maintain that dreams are not always true, but neither are they always false; not always to be approved, but neither always to be rejected. Certainly no sound-minded person will deny this who remembers the dreams of Pharaoh (Gen. 41) and King Nebuchadnezzar (Dan. 2, 4), or Joseph in Genesis (Gen. 37) and Joseph in the Gospel (Matt. 1). Let him moreover search the entire history of the Old and New Law; and if he finds even one dream in it to be vain, let him judge all dreams without exception to be vain. But perhaps the result of victory did not follow, and therefore the vision is to be despised. It was not so. For on the next day the pagan army was defeated by the people of God; and, as the golden sword marked the glorious triumph of victory, the commander himself was struck down, his head cut off, his proud right hand severed, his blaspheming tongue torn out, and given piecemeal to the birds as food [Col. 0843B].

And although the proposed example fully suffices to show that the good deeds of the dead can benefit the living, let there nevertheless be added the more worthy testimony of apostolic revelation, which in Greek is called the *Apocalypse*, and let it demonstrate by a truthful report that complaints were made by the dead against the living and heard by God, who lives for ever:

> “When the Lamb had opened the fifth seal, I saw under the altar of God the souls of those slain because of the word of God and because of the testimony which they held; and they cried with a loud voice, saying: ‘How long, Lord, holy and true, will you not judge and avenge our blood upon those who dwell upon the earth?’” (Rev. 6).

And what follows? “White robes were given to each of them” (ibid.). But what answer was given? They were told to rest yet a little while, until their fellow-servants and brethren who were to be killed as they had been should be completed (ibid.). Do you see, reader, the complaints of the holy martyrs delayed indeed, but heard by God? Yet those who complained were dead; those concerning whom they complained were living. Thus, in order that the former might be shown to be dead, the souls of the slain are said to have cried out. And in order that the latter might be proved living, they are called those dwelling on earth. Therefore, could the dead who were able to complain concerning the living not pray for the living if they wished? Shall they be permitted to complain, but not permitted to make intercession? Shall they be able to demand vengeance for their blood, yet be unable to entreat for the mitigation of the punishment of sins? Or shall the saints in heaven lose that freedom to pray for what is just which even the lost rich man did not lose in hell? He burned in the infernal flames and prayed for his relatives who were still living in the world; and although he was not worthy to be heard, he was nevertheless able to entreat Abraham for their salvation. Abraham’s answer to him shows that, although it was not just that he should be heard, it nevertheless would not be contrary to justice for any righteous person to pray for the living. For he did not say to him: “Be silent; you must not pray; you will not be heard, nor even listened to.” Rather, giving a reason to the petitioner who asked that [Col. 0844A] Lazarus be sent to his father’s house to testify to his brothers, lest they too should come into that place of torments, he added: “They have Moses and the prophets; let them hear them” (Luke 16). It was as though he said: “If they hear Moses and the prophets, they will not come into this place of torments.” And when the man repeated, “No, father, but if someone goes to them from the dead, they will repent” (ibid.), Abraham again repelled him with a reason, saying: “If they do not hear Moses and the prophets, neither will they believe if someone rises from the dead” (ibid.).

Therefore Abraham did not hear the rich man who prayed because he was not to be heard; but because he repelled him by reason rather than command, he indicated that the dead might on some occasion be heard when praying for the living. I know indeed—and I am not so stupid as not to see such plain things or understand such clear things—that saints situated here pray to God for others in one manner, and saints transferred from here pray in another: for in saints here who pray for the salvation of others, compassion is joined to misery; there, mercy diminishes glory in no respect. Here the righteous person in some sense shares in the miseries of others when he mercifully prays for the miserable; but after misery has been changed into glory, a pitiable prayer, which is accompanied by unchangeable blessedness, cannot be poured forth. It is therefore unnecessary for those to bend their knees, shed tears, or labour by pouring out many words, who, in that city which, because of its singular preciousness, is compared with pure gold and, because of its light-bearing transparency, with clear glass (Rev. 21), [Col. 0844C] as their devout affections are known to God, so, with God hearing them, assist all who are worthy merely by presenting themselves. Since they can now will nothing that conflicts with God’s justice, their mercy for others is immediately heard. Thus the saints there pray for others not in a miserable but in a blessed manner, where their prayer is a holy desire and the hearing of their prayers is a granted benefit.

From this came that heavenly and blessed custom, transmitted by the Spirit of God into the Church: while she still toils in the present struggle, the Church calls upon those whom she judges truly holy and joined to God, asking them to assist her. Hence the unceasing prayers; hence the frequent litanies; hence the continual supplication. By all these, she not only beseeches God to be reconciled to her [Col. 0844D], but also entreats the saints, that she may be able to obtain this through their mediation. By this authority and holy custom of hers, to which from ancient times the whole world has yielded without contradiction, she admonishes this, does not command it, and urges this belief: namely, that the good deeds of the dead can benefit the living, since she never ceases continually to commend herself and her own, living in the flesh, to the blessed dead. Taught by Christ her teacher, she understands that those dead persons to whom she prays live to God, when she hears him say in the Gospel, taking testimony from Exodus: “God is not the God of the dead but of the living; for all live to him” (Exod. 3; Luke 22). She remembers also that the ancient saints asked God to be reconciled to the living on account of the merits of the dead, as Moses, praying to God in the same passage for the idolatrous people, says: [Col. 0845A] “Let your anger, Lord, cease, and be appeased concerning the wickedness of your people. Remember Abraham, Isaac, and Israel, your servants” (Exod. 32). Behold, Moses strives for and obtains God’s reconciliation to the people through the good merits of the dead Abraham, Isaac, and Israel; and he teaches that the good deeds of the dead can sometimes benefit the living.

Let the voice of the Lord himself also come forward and say to Solomon in sin: “Because you have done this, and have not kept my covenant and my commandments which I commanded you, I shall tear your kingdom apart and give it to your servant. Nevertheless, I shall not do it in your days, for the sake of David your father. I shall tear it from the hand of your son. Yet I shall not take away the whole kingdom, but shall give one tribe to your son, for the sake of David my servant and Jerusalem which [Col. 0845B] I chose” (3 Kings 2). And again through Ahijah the Shilonite, the prophet: “I shall not take the kingdom from his hand, but shall make him ruler all the days of his life, for the sake of David my servant whom I chose, who kept my commandments and my precepts” (ibid.). And, after a verse omitted: “But to his son I shall give one tribe, that a lamp may remain for David my servant before me all the days in Jerusalem, the city which I chose, that my name might be there” (ibid.). And who would dare resist such lucid truth? Behold: for Solomon, who sinned—indeed, who was an idolater, which is worse than all sins—the righteousness of his dead father preserves the kingdom and excuses him, so that it is not even diminished during all the days of his life. It also protects his son and his whole progeny for ever from falling completely from the kingdom, and, by most exalted merits, preserves for one who has committed sin royal and enduring power. And what are those merits? “For the sake of David,” God says, “my servant whom I chose, who kept my commandments and my precepts.” Behold: because David kept God’s commandments and precepts, he benefited not only himself, but, though dead, also secured from God for his sons and heirs, even when sinning, the royal power of which I have spoken. Therefore doubt is excluded and every unbelief driven away by the sacred oracles, so that, if trust is placed in patriarchs, prophets, and God himself, no one may any longer doubt that the good deeds of the dead can benefit the living [Col. 0845C].

Yet let Azariah, the middle one of those three named Hebrew youths, come forward and testify what he thought concerning these matters when set in the Babylonian furnace and overcoming it by mighty power:

> “We beseech you, Lord, do not hand us over for ever for your name’s sake; do not destroy your covenant, nor take your mercy away from us, for the sake of Abraham your beloved, Isaac your servant, and Israel your holy one” (Dan. 3).

Behold, these men, placed in such great danger, surrounded by balls of fire and masses of flame, not awaiting their dreadful death as something near at hand but beholding it present, believe that no refuge is safer for them than the merits of holy dead persons. By these merits they implore not only their own rescue from the fires but deliverance for themselves and their entire people from impending captivity and miseries. And, to show that the merits of good dead persons [Col. 0846A] can mitigate the dangers of the living, God both delivered them uninjured from the fire, with their garments untouched—through both their own faith and the merits of the holy dead whom they had invoked—and showed what the living ought to think concerning the merits of the dead.

The good Jews who at that time were in Judaea likewise send this message, at the beginning of the above-mentioned book of Maccabees, to their brethren dwelling throughout Egypt: “May God do you good and remember his covenant which he spoke to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, his faithful servants” (2 Macc. 1). It is as though they said: “That God may do good to you who are living, may he remember those good dead persons, Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob; and, by both the covenant he made and their merits, may he give you a heart to worship him and to do his will with a great heart [Col. 0846B] and willing spirit. May he open your heart to his law and his commandments, and make peace. May he hear your prayers and be reconciled to you, and not abandon you in time of evil.” May he certainly grant all these good things to you who are living through the good merits of those dead persons, and thereby show that the good deeds of the dead can often benefit the living.

There are many similar examples in sacred Scripture alongside those which I have given; but because I considered these able fully to suffice for readers, I declined to set forth more, lest excessive multiplication produce weariness. Therefore I judge it sufficiently proved, by authority—which holds chief place especially in divine matters—and by reason—which in both divine and human matters distinguishes good from evil, just from unjust, true from false—and [Col. 0846C] sufficiently established for heretics and Catholics alike: that, as the divisions set out above require, the good deeds of the living may sometimes benefit the living, the good deeds of the dead the dead, the good deeds of the living the dead, and the good deeds of the dead the living; nor can anyone justly or reasonably deny this.

Since these things are so, and since I too, my conscience bearing witness, have resolved to write this for the benefit of the Church of God—to which I owe what I am able to give, being one who knows himself to have been brought up from the womb in her bosom, and who trusts that beneath the wings of her faith and charity he shall be saved and one day raised up to those things for which he hopes—I ask the reader and admonish the hearer to read profitably and hear wholesomely what, as I have said, I wished to write for the Church’s benefit. Why have I said this? Because, as I myself have experienced, just as some are excessively distrustful, so others are excessively confident; so that the former by their despair, and the latter by their excessive, so to speak, hope, seem either to be endangered or utterly to fall away from salvation [Col. 0846D]. For just as the heretics against whom I have written maintain that the good deeds of the living cannot in any way benefit the dead, so those whom I criticize—Catholics, if the expression may be used, to an excessive degree—have disordered presumption concerning the good things done by the Church of the living for the dead.

Indeed, some such persons presume so disorderly upon these things that, relying on devout prayers or good works performed by the living for the dead, they themselves grow lukewarm in zeal for prayer and good works; and, deceived, turn to their own destruction what was instituted for the salvation of all. These clearly purchase poison from an antidote, destruction from salvation, death from life, by a foolish exchange; and whereas the Apostle says, “Awaiting the blessed hope” (Titus 2), and, “By hope we were saved” (Rom. 8), when they ought to be saved by hope, they perish against hope through hope, because they do not consider how hope ought to be used. They do not consider, indeed, that eternal life is acquired principally not by the good works of others but by one’s own works, grace preceding and accompanying. I have said “principally,” however, because the living person’s own merits must at least be such that the merits of others may benefit him when he is dead. But they cannot benefit him unless the living person’s good deeds have been such that eternal life is owed to him both justly and mercifully. For if he has been predestined to eternal life by God’s grace and by merits that follow grace, then he is certainly inscribed in the book of life [Col. 0847B]. And if he is inscribed in the book of life, then, according to the words of the Saviour, he is a son of God and a son of the resurrection (Luke 20).

Whoever attains this attains it through “faith working through love” (Gal. 5). Therefore, while living, he must act in faith and love so as to belong to the children of God and heirs of eternal life. Once he has attained this, if he departs this light in that state, the manifold good deeds of the living will be able to perfect any other imperfection in him, cleanse what remains to be purified, and assist in expiating or alleviating the penalties of a more severe purification and in eradicating all the rust of remaining sins. For the prayers of the living cannot restore the substance of the dead that has been wholly lost [Col. 0847C]; but they can restore beauty of form when the substance remains whole. By “the substance of the dead that has been lost” I mean persons lost through their crimes; by “beauty of form deformed,” persons imperfect through lighter sins. I have said that lost substance cannot be restored—that is, that condemned persons cannot be saved by any good deed of the living. I have said that deformed beauty of form can be restored—that is, that those who have died guilty not of mortal crimes but of venial sins can more swiftly be restored to salvation through the good deeds of the living.

Therefore let the dead person know that the good deeds of the living can benefit him only if, through his former life, he has deserved to share in eternal life. For then whatever still hinders him from attaining it can be removed, through the prayers and devout works [Col. 0847D] of the living, by the abundant mercy of God. But if, when he departed this life, he did not deserve to belong among those who “receive the inheritance of salvation,” he will no longer be able to flatter himself with the good deeds of the living, since while he lived he did not strive to be counted among the number of the predestined. Therefore, lest he wrongly despair or, further, hope still more wrongly, while he lives and is able let him labour to obtain this: that if he departs from here imperfect, he may deserve to be helped by the works of others; or rather—which is better—let him strive while living to do such deeds that, when dead, he will not need the good deeds of the living.

Against their assertion that God ought not to be sung to.

But now, as to the further claim added by the heretics—namely, that God is mocked by ecclesiastical chants, because He who delights only in devout affections can neither be summoned by loud voices nor soothed by musical melodies—my mind recoils from answering such drivel. For what it is brutish and stupid not to perceive even when brutish men deny it, it is almost equally foolish to wish to refute as though by reason. Therefore, since Wisdom commands, “Do not answer a fool according to his folly, lest you become like him” (Prov. 26), let the tongue be silent in part; and since it again commands, “Answer a fool according to his folly, lest he seem wise to himself” (ibid.), let it briefly speak what ought not to be left unsaid.

But do you not blush, O most foolish of men who say these things, that from the beginning of our extensive disputation to its present conclusion, whatever has issued from your mouths has appeared both empty of authority and wholly devoid of reason? Thus you pour out words in vain; thus you cast words into winds and clouds, so that, in the manner of madmen, the entire usefulness is to open the mouth for words, the entire reasoning to strike the air. O utterly obtuse men, when you began to think or say this, did no divine authority out of the innumerable available authorities occur to your minds? Why did not at least the psalms occur to you, which are regularly used by all the clergy of the Church of God—and especially by priests, as you yourselves once were—when you thought, said, and preached this?

Do you not often, or almost continually, read in those very psalms—and, setting aside the majesty of their higher mystery, observe even their literal sense, if you are wise, if you have understanding:

> “Sing to the Lord a new song; sing to the Lord, all the earth. Sing to the Lord, and bless his name” (Ps. 95).

And again:

> “Sing to the Lord a new song, because he has done wondrous things” (Ps. 97).

And again:

> “All nations, clap your hands; cry aloud to God with a voice of exultation” (Ps. 46).

And in the same psalm:

> “Sing psalms to our God, sing psalms; sing psalms to our King, sing psalms, for God is King of all the earth. Sing psalms wisely, and sing well to him with loud acclaim” (Ps. 32).

And a thousand such passages? This concerns the singing of the human voice. What of the various instruments and their diverse modes of melody? Why could things so familiar to the whole world not occur to you alone? For in the same psalms the divine voice says concerning musical and bodily instruments:

> “Sing to the Lord with the harp, with harp and voice of psalm; with drawn trumpets and the sound of the horn trumpet” (Ps. 97).

And again:

> “Praise him with the sound of the trumpet; praise him with psaltery and harp. Praise him with drum and dance; praise him with strings and organ. Praise him with well-sounding cymbals; praise him with cymbals of jubilation” (Ps. 150).

And a thousand similar passages. Did he who said these things, who wrote them, who especially composed these instruments, who played, who sang—did he intend, by speaking, writing, playing, and singing, to mock God? Did not Moses himself, the first lawgiver, command that silver trumpets be made for battle, for rest, for striking and pitching camp, for sounding before the ark of the Lord in the wilderness, in the tabernacle, and at the jubilee? (Num. 10.) Did not he, and the priest Aaron; did not the already-mentioned king and prophet David; did not Solomon, Ezra, and many holy kings and prophets make musical instruments, establish thousands of singers, and themselves play, sing, and dance? Did they do all these things in order to mock, despise, or ridicule God? No, I say, fools: not for these ends, but to praise, adore, honor, and glorify him.

If you seek also the evident usefulness among men of those who sing, chant psalms, and play instruments in such a manner, hear what, I think, you do not know: in Holy Scripture demons are driven away, illnesses relieved, and God summoned by such modes; and through them he answers those who consult him and grants what they request. For the above-mentioned Book of Kings says:

> “Whenever the evil spirit of God seized Saul, David took the harp and struck it with his hand; Saul was refreshed and felt easier, for the evil spirit departed from him” (1 Sam. 16).

You have heard David chanting psalms with the harp; hear the minstrel singing before Elisha. Elisha says:

> “Now bring me a minstrel.”

And when the minstrel played, the hand of the Lord came upon him, and he said:

> “Thus says the Lord: Make this torrent-bed ditch upon ditch. For thus says the Lord: You shall see neither wind nor rain, and yet this channel shall be filled with waters; and you, your households, and your beasts shall drink. And this is a small thing in the sight of the Lord; moreover, he will also deliver Moab into your hand. You shall strike every fortified city and every chosen city; you shall cut down every fruitful tree, stop up every spring of water, and cover every excellent field with stones” (2 Kings 3).

Therefore, while David played the harp before Saul, the evil spirit departed from him. While the minstrel sings before Elisha, the Holy Spirit is summoned. For it was he who then gave answers through Elisha, as he was accustomed to speak through all the prophets. Thus by musical singing the evil spirit is driven away; by musical singing the Holy Spirit is summoned. God could indeed, without singing of this sort and without the sound of a musical instrument, both heal the king’s illness and give answers to the prophet. Yet he wished by the lofty examples of so many prophets to show that he graciously receives the voices of those who sing devoutly and the sounds of those who play instruments reverently, and approves these things too when they are offered devoutly among the other services of God.

And in order to show that the service of such religious singing pleased him not only under the former Law but also in the subsequent Gospel, when boys in the Temple sang, “Hosanna to the Son of David” (Matt. 21), and the Pharisees were indignant and said to him, “Do you hear what these are saying?” (ibid.), he rebuked the indignation of the jealous Pharisees and praised the devotion of the singing boys, answering even from Scripture:

> “Have you never read: ‘Out of the mouth of infants and nursing children you have perfected praise’?” (Matt. 21; Ps. 8.)

Since, therefore, the final and senseless objection of the heretics has, as I judge, been answered both briefly and fully, and since, as I believe, the whole engine of the error described above has been overthrown by the invincible power of God, I turn my words to you, O holy bishops and priests of the Lord, to whom I wrote this letter; and I entreat you diligently to make it known both to the heretics and to the Catholics for whose sake I wrote it. Truly, truly, zeal for the house of God and the destruction of so many souls impelled me to write these things, so that, as I stated at the beginning of the letter, following the practice of the Church of God—which has always chiefly suppressed heretical calumnies in this way—authority might not be lacking for the devout, nor reason for curious inquirers.

The reason why, after the heretics, I requested that this writing also be made known through you to the Catholics of your land is this: recently, while travelling through those regions and your dioceses, I learned that the public heretics, whom you especially had expelled, had indeed migrated to other, though neighboring, districts; but that they had nevertheless left behind no small seeds in your own regions. If these are neglected, they may spring up into a hostile crop and, as they did before, grievously injure the Lord’s harvest after the manner of tares. There is also this: by this remedy the secret thoughts even of good Catholics should, if possible, be cleansed; for although they do not assent to heretical calumnies, they can nevertheless be scandalized by unheard-of questions.

Therefore, lest the mouths of heretics be open to blasphemies or the hearts of Catholics be easily exposed to such scandals, so that the former may be shut by such a barrier and the latter, if possible, healed by such a remedy, I have offered this writing to Jesus Christ my Lord as a small gift of my faith for the faith, and sent it through you to be communicated to his Church. For I thought that this could not more rightly or justly be done through any others than through the stewards of the wheat—that is, of the divine word—which you are: that this measure, whatever it may be, of sacred word might be distributed to the household entrusted to you by the supreme Master of the household, and be imparted in due season to individuals or to all alike.

For it becomes apostolic men to uphold apostolic teaching above all else, so that you who, through the dispensation of heavenly grace, have succeeded the apostles in office may defend the apostolic faith with especial zeal. For that same Christ who, through the apostles while they lived, provided for his pilgrim Church, prepared you in their place to provide for it in your own time. Therefore, since not only by the common charity owed to all, but also by the particular office belonging to bishops alone, the Church of God entrusted to you must be healed if it languishes, recalled if it errs, kindled if it grows lukewarm, strengthened if it wavers, raised if it falls, instructed if it doubts, and taught by you if it is ignorant of anything necessary: for this reason I have chosen you particularly to commend this writing to the Church of God. I know that you have been appointed to this work by office, made fit for it by wisdom, and trained for it by labor, so that you may defend with the utmost zeal the land which, by God’s Spirit and your own exertions, you have cleansed of most wicked heresy, lest its putrid [*putidae*] remnants be able to come to life again against it. This shall be a distinction of your episcopacy before the gracious rewarder of all good things: the fury of wolves shall not prevail, through your vigilance, against the sheep of the good Shepherd entrusted to you by himself.

[Col. 0851]

# Peter the Venerable, Abbot of Cluny: Ninth Work—Two Books Concerning Miracles

## Book One Begins

## Prologue

[Col. 0851A]

Since among the gifts of the Holy Spirit the grace of miracles holds no small dignity, inasmuch as it contains such great usefulness within itself that chiefly through it the world was delivered from the darkness of unbelief and endowed with the eternal light of truth; and since even now, through it, faith is increased, hope grows, and truth is confirmed in the hearts of many believers to whom it is sometimes granted to see such things—I am often indignant that those events which occur in our own times should perish, hidden under unproductive silence, because no one applies his mind to writing down what, if made known, could benefit readers.

Therefore, since I could compel no one but myself to undertake this, I preferred to approach it in whatever style I could, not fearing to be judged presumptuous in so great a matter; and, as someone said before me, I preferred that for the exposition of so useful a matter I should exist rather than no one. And, lest I keep the reader long in suspense, beginning with the worthier subject, I shall begin to recount such miracles concerning the body of the Lord as could reach me in modern times.

## Chapter I. On the Miracle Which Occurred in the Territory of Auvergne

There was in the territory of Auvergne a certain peasant who had beehives, in which swarms of bees customarily produce the honeyed sweetness of combs. Fearing that his bees might fly away, die, or perish through some mishap, this peasant, using the evil counsel of sorcerers—who by diabolical operation are accustomed to turn even God’s benefits into evils and, intolerable as it is to say, abuse even the divine sacraments through magical arts—went to church. Having received from the priest, as is the custom of Christians, the Lord’s body, he kept it in his mouth and, unwilling to swallow it, as he had already been instructed, approached one of the aforesaid hives containing bees. Placing his mouth to the opening in it, he began to blow.

[Col. 0852A]

For he had been told that if, keeping the Lord’s body in his mouth, he blew upon the bees contained in the vessel, none thereafter would die, depart, or perish; but, with all entirely preserved, he would rejoice in a yield far greater than before. He therefore did as he had been told and, placing his mouth to it, sent his breath with all his force into the interior. While, eagerly panting for gain, he blew violently, the Lord’s body was cast out by the movement of his tongue and breath and fell to the ground beside the hive. And behold: the entire multitude of bees came forth from within and reverently hastened to the body of their Lord. They lifted it from the ground and, in the manner of rational creatures, brought it with great veneration into their dwellings, while the man watched.

Seeing this, the man, either heedless of or attaching little importance to what had happened, turned his steps to other tasks to which household care summoned him. But as he went on his way, suddenly disturbed by an intolerable terror—as he himself afterwards recounted—he began, in a sounder state of mind, to think that he had acted wickedly. Therefore, struck with compunction—or rather compelled by an inward force—he immediately turned back and, in punishment of his crime, drowned with a great deluge of water the bees whose life he had wished to preserve by a wicked deed. When they were dead, he searched the interior of the combs which he wished to store and preserve for himself. And behold—marvellous to relate—he saw the Lord’s body which had fallen from his mouth lying among the combs and honey, transformed into the form of a most beautiful boy, as though newly born.

[Col. 0852B]

[Col. 0852C]

At this miracle he trembled with astonishment, as was fitting. But, hesitating for a time as to what he ought to do, he came upon this plan: to take him in his hands, carry him to the church, and, because he seemed lifeless to him, bury the little boy alone, without anyone knowing. When he set about this and, taking him in his hands, was carrying him to church as if to bury him secretly, he suddenly disappeared, invisibly snatched from the hands of the man who was bearing him unworthily.

These events, recently performed, I have taken care to make known in order by writing: the man himself reported them to his own priest; the priest to his bishop of Clermont; that bishop to me; and I to all who read this. Nor was punishment for so great a sacrilege wholly deferred to the future; rather, within a short time, the place, once populous, was reduced to solitude as its inhabitants perished through various misfortunes.

## Chapter II. On a Certain Priest Who Handled the Divine Mysteries Unworthily

Likewise, in the German regions, there was a certain priest who appeared to lead a religious life and celebrated the sacred solemnities of Mass almost daily. But, failing to guard himself sufficiently carefully, he fell into the snares of the ancient enemy and descended into a shameful but secret pit of sin, the pleasure of the flesh. For at first he visited a certain nun under the pretext of visitation; but finally, enticed by frequent conversation and imprudent familiarity, he fell into sin with her.

[Col. 0853A]

[Col. 0853B]

After his fall, he should have returned to himself and risen again quickly. Instead, delighting in his own filth, he long delayed conversion; adding sin to sin, he made a habit of sinning and thus, by continuous sin, wove the long rope by which he would be bound all the more tightly. And although he wallowed in the mire of crimes, he was not ashamed to approach the altar of the Lord irreverently and to profane the sacraments of our redemption by celebrating Mass repeatedly.

Since for a long time he did not fear to act thus, having cast off the fear of God, he experienced in a wonderful manner both the anger and the mercy of the Lord toward himself, as what follows makes clear. For while he neither abandoned his crime nor ceased, as has often been said, to touch the holy divine things with impure hands, it happened one day that, after he had performed the whole Mass as usual as far as the reception of the sacred body of Christ and was preparing to receive the sacraments themselves, the flesh and blood of Christ, no longer tolerating so unclean a dwelling, suddenly vanished from the hands that were almost holding them. Amazed and astounded, he very quickly left the altar after finishing the Mass.

[Col. 0853C]

Recognizing that the Lord’s indignation had been aroused against him by so manifest a sign, he nevertheless wished to test this more certainly and undertook Mass a second time. When he had performed everything as before and the moment came to receive the sacraments, all was withdrawn as before. Now, appropriately overcome by no small fear and trembling, and wishing to be made entirely certain beyond all hesitation about the miracle that had happened twice, he did not fear to attempt for a third time what had already occurred twice.

But after all had been performed as before, he watched more anxiously with his eyes what had been set before him, touched it with his hands, and prepared his mouth to receive it. Suddenly, for the third time, it disappeared, invisibly removed from his eyes, hands, and mouth. At last, shaken by so evident a miracle, the priest recognized beyond doubt that he had acted most wickedly and incurred the terrible anger of the Lord. He changed his heart and began anxiously to consider how he might escape so great a danger.

[Col. 0853D]

[Col. 0854A]

Knowing that the final remedy for sinners is repentance, he fled to it with his whole heart. He went to his bishop and disclosed to him with many tears everything that he had done and everything that had occurred. He devotedly and steadfastly performed with all the effort of his soul the penance imposed upon him. By fasts and vigils, by scourging and diverse torments, he chastised, according to the Apostle, the lustful beast—that is, his own body. Having become reprobate by following its desires, he labored to be joined to the number of the elect by condemning those desires in himself.

After much time had elapsed in this contrition of body and heart, when a more secure conscience encouraged his mind to hope for pardon, he went to the bishop. Reporting what he had done, he asked whether he might dare to approach the sacred things as he had previously been accustomed to do. The bishop, fearing that he was not yet fully reconciled to God, urged him still to persevere in penance, so that, after offering God the fitting fruits of repentance, he might at the appropriate time, more cleansed and secure, receive the sacraments of the altar not unto judgment but unto eternal salvation.

[Col. 0854B]

He accepted the salutary admonition. Returning to his purpose of repentance, with all the strength of flesh and spirit he knocked at the doors of divine mercy and, by a contrite spirit and unceasing tears, compelled the Lord’s anger to turn into mercy. In short, after another long period had passed in this penitence, he returned to the bishop and, privately disclosing everything to him as to a father, humbly begged that he might be judged worthy to share in the sacraments. The bishop, confident that his conversion was now acceptable to God, both from what he had heard from him and from what he saw in him, consented that he should undertake the priestly office.

Trusting in the Lord’s goodness and in the testimony of his conscience, the priest took care to fulfil this not now in presumption but in devotion. He approached the altar, wholly sacrificing himself to God in tears and contrition of heart, and, performing all things rightly, came to the reception of the sacraments.

[Col. 0854C]

[Col. 0854D]

And behold, in a new miracle unheard of, at least in our age: the breads of the three previously mentioned Masses, which had been taken away from him while he wished to receive them unworthily, were brought from heaven. Now that he had been made worthy by divine judgment to receive these things, they appeared placed before him upon the altar. When he also looked into the chalice, he saw it filled with blood almost to the brim, and saw that the deficiencies of those Masses had become an increase in this one.

Amazed, and giving thanks to God with all the joy of his inward self, he recognized that his repentance had been accepted and the Lord’s majesty appeased. Made certain of the Lord’s mercy, he received with great rejoicing, as was fitting, the four breads set before him instead of one—or rather, one body and blood of Christ. This too the aforesaid bishop of Clermont related to me in the presence of very many people.

## Chapter III. On Him Who Could Not Retain the Lord’s Body Unless He First Made Confession

> **Note:** [Col. 0855D] In manuscript S. V.: “On a certain sick man who could not swallow the body of the Lord.”

[Col. 0855A]

Nor should that similar event which occurred at the same place, Karumlocum, be passed over in silence. There was there a young man given over to worldly vanity and, as men commonly do at that age, loosening the reins for pleasure. While he had long been devoted to it, it happened that he was branded with the stain of infamy concerning a certain married woman. For some time he was held under this suspicion by all his neighbors. Then he fell into so serious an illness that people were compelled to despair for his life.

As he lay in bed, already very near death, a priest was summoned to him according to ecclesiastical custom, so that he might hear his confession and provide the dying man with the viaticum of human salvation. When the priest arrived, he began earnestly to exhort and admonish him not to be ashamed to confess his sins and to disclose through salutary confession the crime for which he had been especially defamed.

[Col. 0855B]

The young man agreed and earnestly began to confess his crimes. When he had done so, and the priest again questioned him concerning the crime mentioned above, he lied, saying that he was in no way guilty of it. As the priest, moved by the man’s long-standing infamy and the suspicion, did not desist from questioning him, he said: “May I be worthy to receive for salvation this body of the Lord which you have brought, just as I have never incurred any guilt in the matter alleged against me.”

The priest, made credulous by this reply, confidently gave him the Lord’s communion. But once he had received it in his mouth, the sick man immediately lost the power of swallowing. For although only a little earlier even coarser foods had easily gone down into his stomach, this very tiny fragment of Christ’s body could not reach—not to say his stomach—but not even his throat by the slightest amount. Realizing this, he began to struggle with all his strength to swallow it. Although he tried repeatedly and always saw his efforts frustrated, the very inability to swallow compelled him to spit it out beside the bed on which he lay.

[Col. 0855C]

Greatly terrified by the outcome, he asked that the priest who had departed be summoned back to him. The priest returned and, visiting the sick man, asked why he had called him back. But the sick man, struck with compunction by the working of the Spirit of God, confessed that he had acted wickedly, had lied to God, and that what he had previously denied was true. Seeing him repent and make satisfaction with much groaning, the priest who had come, moved with compassion for one worn out and consumed by grief, absolved him according to custom and again refreshed him with the Lord’s body. Once he received it, he swallowed it with such freedom that it was then plainly evident that he had been prevented, not by chance but by divine power, from receiving it earlier.

[Col. 0855D]

[Col. 0856A]

Thus, after confession of his guilt and reception of Christ’s body, he survived only a little while and rested in peace. I learned this not merely from two or three witnesses, but from the prior of the aforementioned place, an honorable and trustworthy man, from the brothers of the same monastery, and from many others. Some testified that they had seen it; others, that they had heard it from the priest. And since the subject of confession has arisen, I shall endeavor to show by another example how great is its usefulness for souls.

## Chapter IV. On the Death of a Certain Brother and His Final Confession

> **Note:** [Col. 0856D] Alternatively: “On a certain brother who diligently concealed his sins.”

A certain priest named Gilbert [Gerbert] came to conversion at the monastery of Saint John of Angély, situated in the district of Saintonge, and lived there devoutly for some time, until his death. It happened, not much time later, that the illness he had contracted brought him to his end. According to the custom of Christians, and especially of monks, the brothers laid him upon haircloth and ashes, and he awaited the hour of his calling. The brothers of the monastery came to commend his departure in prayers and stood around him on every side, singing psalms.

[Col. 0856B]

As they waited for him to die, behold, he suddenly recovered his breath, opened his eyes, and began to recite aloud the profession of faith that is sung daily: “Whoever wishes to be saved,” and the rest. Although all knew that he had previously been uneducated and ignorant of letters, he pronounced each item so distinctly and clearly that persons unfamiliar with him, had any been present, would have believed him most highly trained in such matters. All those standing by were astonished and wondered at the event.

[Col. 0856C]

After they had long remained in wonder and uncertainty, the prior, named Gregory, a man of good religious character—upon whom this responsibility rested above the others—understood that the man had seen something in secret. He bent down toward him and asked the cause of his outcry, and whether he had seen anything hidden from them. The man answered:

“I saw a person of venerable appearance, clothed in white and of venerable gray hair, bring a vessel of water shortly before and say to me: ‘Know that the reason for my coming to you is this: I am to wash your feet, which are defiled, and, once they are washed, make you wholly clean.’ When he saw me marveling at what he said, he added: ‘Do you not know that this water is necessary for your cleansing—you who committed the crime which you yourself know and which, deliberately concealing it, you have until now been unwilling to reveal to anyone? Know, therefore, that you cannot possibly be saved unless you endeavor through confession healthfully to disclose what you have ruinously concealed. Yet God, in his great mercy, not permitting you to perish even for so great a guilt, permits you to return to bodily consciousness, so that by confessing you may repent of so great a crime and, by repenting, merit to attain salvation. For this reason, then, I was absent from you and have been permitted to return to you.’”

[Col. 0856D]

[Col. 0857A]

Having said this, he sent the others away, summoned the prior, and confessed that sin to him. After receiving from him absolution for this and all his sins, he rested on the following day, at the first hour of the day, while the brothers stood by and prayed, with a joyful expression and a good end. I learned this not from another person but from a monk of that monastery named Lecto, who had seen and heard all these things. Later he came to Cluny out of devotion and became our scribe and a most beloved son in Christ.

## Chapter V. On Another Man’s False Confession

> **Note:** [Col. 0857D] Alternatively: “At nearly the same time there was in the monastery near the tower above the Materna a certain brother to whom the care of that same monastery had been entrusted by the abbot of Cluny, to whose jurisdiction it is subject.”

At nearly the same time there was a certain brother in a monastery in France near the Tower above the Materna, under our jurisdiction, to whom the care of that place had been entrusted.

> **Note:** [Col. 0857D] “Near the tower above the Materna.” That is, a monastery under Cluniac jurisdiction, consecrated in honor of Saint Genesius. The charters of the archbishopric of Rheims, pp. 1389 and 1390 of this Bibliotheca, already transcribed, show to whom the Cluniacs are bound to attribute its foundation.

[Col. 0857B]

Compelled by the necessity of a prolonged illness, he asked Radulf, then abbot of the monastery of Châlons, to come to him for the healing both of his soul and his body, matters in which Radulf was well experienced. Moved by charity, Radulf did not delay in coming, and upon arriving immediately attended to visiting the sick man. Seeing that he was seriously afflicted by illness, he began to exhort him to confession.

The sick man professed himself willing to do this and began to confess his sins, though not in simplicity of spirit. For, through foolish shame, he kept silent about the graver and deadly sins, while, laying aside the fear of God, he confessed only daily matters and things that seemed slight. When this disguised confession had been completed, he asked that the body of the Lord be brought to him.

[Col. 0857C]

When it was brought and received with a presumptuous mouth, he tried long and hard to pass it down, but could not. He was compelled to crumble the entire body of Christ, together with the wine he had received, and to pour it back into the vessel placed beneath his mouth—all in vain. Moved by this occurrence, or rather by divine judgment, the abbot who had come, thinking that the sick man had not been fully cleansed by confession, again began to admonish him not to be ashamed, if he had concealed any crime, to disclose it in a true confession.

Struck with compunction both by the abbot’s exhortation and by divine prompting, the man returned to himself. Vomiting forth whatever pestilence lay hidden within, he disclosed by life-giving and true confession the crimes which he had earlier hidden through deadly shame—not falsely now, but truthfully, with a contrite and humbled heart.

[Col. 0857D]

Once every filth of iniquity had been cleansed away by the antidote of repentance, and once he had merited absolution through the aforesaid abbot by true confession, he devoutly received the Eucharist which he had earlier been compelled to reject; and he swallowed it without any difficulty, as would some most holy man. And, so that every doubt about the miracle might be removed: having previously been forced to reject in fragments the portion of Christ’s body which he could not swallow, after his confession he received not only the body of the Lord but also other foods without any impediment.

[Col. 0858A]

Thus strengthened in the Lord by confession, absolution, and reception of the sacrament, the brother lived only three more days, and then died. Learning this from Abbot Radulf himself, I have taken care to communicate it to all readers and hearers.

## Chapter VI. On Him Who Was Delivered from the Devil through True Confession

It now seems fitting to add that not-to-be-despised miracle which I myself, along with many others, saw, as what follows will show. The occasion was well known to all people of that time: I went to Rome with several of our brethren. Returning from there, I brought back with me rather severe Roman fevers. For their cure, it was decided that I should return to my native soil and air. For that reason I went to Celsinanias [place-name uncertain], a noble Cluniac monastery, and there spent the entire Lent, much more troubled by the burning of fever than by the labor of fasting.

[Col. 0858B]

Meanwhile, while I lay in a secluded room throughout that period, I was assailed by the almost continual cries of a sick brother lying in a lower and neighboring room, and from day to day was more and more disturbed. At first he shouted whatever might confusedly occur to a mind troubled by illness. But in the end he always and solely cried out one thing, without any interruption, with all his strength:

> “O brothers, why do you not help? Why do you not have pity? Why do you not remove from me that enormous and terrible horse—*runcinus*, to use his own word—which, turned toward me with its hind feet, batters my head with its hooves, tears apart my face, and crushes my teeth? Remove him, lords, remove him! I beg you through the Lord, remove him!”

Then, turning his voice toward the demon whom he saw in the form of a horse, he spoke before all who heard:

> “By my Lady Saint Mary, Mother of the Lord, and by the holy apostles, I adjure you: do not torment me, but leave me in peace.”

This brother had been, before his conversion, a vigorous secular knight. For a long time in the monastic order he had been well known to me as a man of sound faith and, insofar as a man can be known by men, of honorable conduct.

[Col. 0858C]

[Col. 0858D]

I endured these cries as best I could through almost the whole of Lent. Throughout that time he did not cease his shouting, nor did my own infirmity allow me to go to him. During the continuation of this outcry, the feast of Easter arrived. When it had passed and I had somewhat recovered, though still sick, I went to the sick man and asked what he meant by such prolonged shouting. He answered:

> “That horse—yes, that very one—is intolerably troublesome to me. He crushes my face with continual blows.”

And as he said this, he pointed, as it were, with his finger to a place—the wall, namely, against which he himself was lying. Meanwhile, as very many standing with me watched, he began to turn his head now here, now there, and, as if withdrawing it from the blows of one striking him, tried to hide it in or beneath the pillow. We pitied the man in his distress, being unable to provide any other assistance.

I therefore ordered blessed water to be brought, and sprinkled with it both the sick man himself and the place which he indicated. After the sprinkling I asked whether he still saw that demon. He declared that he both saw it and suffered from it as usual. But lest anyone wonder [Col. 0859B] that the demon was not driven away by the sprinkling of blessed water, let him recognize that, when a hidden corruption lies within, remedies applied externally can achieve nothing. By “corruption” I mean a deadly sin which, so long as it lies concealed within anyone, no outward reception of a sacrament can benefit him. This is plainly shown in the chief sacraments of the Church, namely baptism and the body of the Lord. For if these could save while inward wickedness remained, Judas would not, after receiving with the other disciples the sacrament of Christ’s body, have hanged himself with a noose; nor would Peter have said to Simon Magus, though already baptized: “You have neither part nor lot in this matter; for I see that you are in the gall of bitterness and in the bond of sin” (Acts 8). For just as Christ commanded the sacraments of faith to be observed, so also he commanded the works of faith [Col. 0859C] to be observed, as may be understood in this same sacrament of baptism from the declaration of its institutor. For he who said, “Go, teach all nations, baptizing them in the name of the Father and of the Son and of the Holy Spirit” (Matt. 28), himself added, “Teaching them to observe all things whatsoever I have commanded you” (ibid.). Therefore he commanded both; he wished both to be observed; he showed that neither can suffice for salvation without the other.

Thus this sick man could be sprinkled with saving water and yet, because of the hidden stain of sin, as later became apparent, could not be freed from the demon. As soon as I perceived this, I urged him carefully to examine his past life and, if he recognized in it anything harmful—especially among the graver matters—to confess it. After he agreed, the others having withdrawn and only two remaining with me, I sat down before him and held in my hand a small wooden cross bearing the image of the Lord, so that he might be the more encouraged to confess, until everything was concluded. He therefore began to confess, and for some time continued his confession. Since his great weakness occasionally disturbed the order of his words, I sometimes helped him, bringing back to his mind whatever might occur to him. With my slight assistance, however, he immediately recovered the sequence and carried out what he had begun.

When he had explained very many things and was proceeding to explain others, behold, he again turned away his face, moved it this way and that, and, as I have said, sometimes tried to hide it beneath the pillow. When [Col. 0860A] I asked what this disordered behavior meant, “Behold, lord,” he said, “that horse which is always with me presses more fiercely than usual, and with all its force crushes my teeth and my whole head with its hooves.” But I said: “Press on, then, brother. It is the evil spirit, hastening to impede your salvation; if you persist, you will conquer it.”

At once he returned to the purpose of his confession and confessed more devoutly than he had begun, omitting nothing that could occur to him, whether from his secular or monastic life. But suddenly, in the very course of his account, a new complaint arose, and the sick man’s voice, which had been speaking with me, was directed toward some other person unknown to me. “Why,” he said, “do you hinder me? Why do you interrupt my words? Either say what I wish to say, or allow me to speak.” When I asked to whom or why he was saying this, [Col. 0860B] he replied: “An entirely unknown man stands at my head, and from him I hear all the evil things I have done being recounted. Yet he recalls them in such a way that he will not allow me to utter them: what he says is true, indeed, but he prevents me from speaking them though I wish to do so.”

I said that this too was a demon and urged him not to abandon his purpose. He, returning again to what had gone before, tried to bring his undertaking to its end. Yet it was a remarkable sight to see how often he was compelled to change his speech: now he spoke to me, confessing his sins; now he complained that demons were laboring to shut his mouth, at times by words and at times by blows. Sometimes he declared with much groaning and sighing that the horse was battering his mouth with its hooves; sometimes that the demon seated at his head was cutting off his words [Col. 0860C]. Indeed, unless I am mistaken, this interruption of the confession was caused by the demons nearly forty times. So persistent was the enemy, and, according to his customary manner, so avid for human ruin, that he struggled both with me and with the sick man.

This battle of ours continued from the first hour of the day until the third hour. Then, precisely at that hour when the Spirit of God is especially wont to pour himself into human beings, we conquered with the aid of that same Spirit. We conquered, I say; but more rightly he is said to have conquered, without whom the evil spirit is never overcome. Divine mercy certainly conquered the wicked enemy; and, granting to the brother now at the point of death an outstanding memory of his past life and courage to disclose it, it bestowed upon him perfect cleansing [Col. 0860D] through the full satisfaction of confession. Wonderful indeed—but far more to be revered and loved—is that overflowing heavenly mercy toward the wretched, which did not permit this brother to depart the world until it had granted him, through the remedies of penance and confession, release from what could truly hinder his eternal salvation.

I also proved at that time, on the spot, how remarkable his memory was in confession. He said that many years before he had entrusted a consecrated altar to a certain brother. Wishing on this occasion to ascertain whether his memory was sound, I had that altar sought from the brother whom he had named. After inquiry, it was brought to me by the very man to whom it had been entrusted. When the confession was complete, I summoned the brothers and absolved the sick man in the customary manner, [Col. 0861A] imposing upon the brothers a penance on his behalf should he die. Receiving this absolution with great devotion, the brother humbly adored the cross offered him by me and most earnestly commended both soul and body to the saving Passion of the Lord.

When all this had been done, before all the monks and laymen standing by, I asked what he would say about that often-mentioned horse of which he had complained so frequently, and whether he still saw it as before. He raised his head as though in great fear and, directing his eyes as if he were about to be struck toward the place now left clear, then moving them about the neighboring places, suddenly said with tears of joy: “By the soul of my father, it does not appear.” When I asked also about that most wicked counselor who had clung to his head for so long, [Col. 0861B] he turned his gaze again toward the place where he had formerly seen him and said: “This one too has gone away.” We all gave thanks with our whole hearts to God, who saves those who hope in him.

Thereafter I ordered that he be watched more carefully, assigning particular guards. No one afterward heard him crying out even a little, whereas before, the brothers lying in that house, exhausted by his cries, had been unable to rest. Frequently questioned by brothers and even by servants whether he saw any of those things which he had seen before, he maintained that he saw nothing sad and suffered no distress at all. When I myself later questioned him about these things, he replied that all was joyful and according to his wish. He survived through that entire day and the following night; on the next day, about the sixth hour, he ended his life in peace, [Col. 0861C] leaving us good hope for his salvation and an example of true repentance.

## CHAPTER VII. How demons were driven away by blessed water

Since indeed [variant: “and since”], in the course of this miracle, I have said that demons were by no means put to flight (*effugatos*; variant *fugatos*) by sprinkling water blessed according to the Church’s custom because of a hidden sin, it seems pertinent to set forth what happened concerning the same matter in the same monastery of Celles. A certain layman had come to that place, compelled by bodily illness, and, clothed by the brothers in monastic garb as is customary, had renounced the world. Many do this even when at the point of death. Although they may seem not to attain the praise of those whom no bodily affliction drives to this, nevertheless, if they are converted from the heart, they are by no means excluded before the eyes of the eternal Judge from the number of monks. And although a greater reward is due to greater merits, those who came at the eleventh hour also received the coin earned by those laboring in the Lord’s vineyard from the first hour of the day. For the manner of conversion does not prejudice the devotion of the heart; nor does God inquire for what reason a person has converted, but how he has lived after conversion.
