Nor is the extent of a long or short period considered where the end of one’s deeds alone is rewarded.

The man just mentioned, having been received in this manner and brought to the infirmary, struggled for several days upon the boundary between life and death. On the night preceding the day of his death he lay in bed, already, as it were, near death, watched in turns by two servants. Since the following account requires their names to be mentioned, one of them was called Stephen and the other Olive. During that watch of the night when he was being attended by Stephen, the sick man called to the servant who was keeping vigil beside him. When the latter stood by him and asked what he wanted, he said: “Who are these ugly, beaked peasants whom I see flowing in here and gradually filling this entire house?” The servant answered that no one was in that house, that only he and his companion were keeping watch over him. Astonished, the sick man added: “Do you not see,” he said, “the gloomy [Col. 0862B] men who now fill every space in this house, whose dreadful appearance and faces sharpened into exceedingly long beaks bring me no small terror?”

Then at last the servant understood—as he himself afterward often told me—that this was not a crowd of human beings but of evil spirits. Therefore, calling loudly for his companion Olive to rise, he seized in faith a vessel, which happened to be hanging nearby and contained blessed water, and confidently sprinkled the consecrated element here and there, dousing every part of that dwelling. As he did so, the sick man began to cry out loudly: “Come, come! Do what you are doing; persist, press hard upon the enemies. For behold, they are trying to escape with the utmost speed, as though fleeing before a sword; and because they cannot endure delay, crashing into one another, those behind violently force forward those in front.” On hearing this, Stephen pressed on vigorously and strove with the water of blessing to drive the children of cursing from the house.

When they had been entirely expelled, as the sick man—who alone saw this—testified, he was freed from the demons’ assault; and it was demonstrated how powerful the sprinkling of saving water with faith is in such matters. On the following day, while the brothers rejoiced at the report of this vision, the new monk died after a good confession; and by that flight of the demons he persuaded everyone that God had received the devotion of his conversion.

## CHAPTER VIII. On Gerard, a monk of pure and simple life

[Col. 0862D] Having inserted these matters incidentally but necessarily, the subject originally undertaken now compels me to return to my purpose. Accordingly, the miracles still to be related concerning the magnificent and super-celestial sacrament of Christ’s body must no longer be deferred.

A brother worthy to be named with honor and remembered with affection, Gerard by name, was a monk of that great monastery of Cluny, himself great by merit of life. From childhood, in clerical dress, he had been brought up at the feet of the blessed and memorable Father Hugh, and he showed in himself an image, in many respects, of Hugh’s virtues. For—what is no slight difficulty—though set amid the world and in the fire, he was not burned; he passed through his youthful years without shipwreck of chastity [variant: *exegit*, “he spent/passed”]. Abhorring the wantonness of his contemporaries through an innate modesty, [Col. 0863A] he attached himself to mature clerics and monks. Through living with them he was formed toward a higher love of uprightness and was gradually trained also to frequent and love the services of the Church. Thus, as sound practice gradually grew stronger with age, he conceived such love for divine things that, beyond all other virtues, this more strictly possessed his mind always.

After almost all his adolescence had passed in these and similar pursuits, he was received as a monk by the already mentioned blessed Father Hugh. Clothed with the habit of religion, he showed by good and almost perfect deeds that he had put off the world. A monk of pure and simple life, truly, according to the Lord’s saying, “an Israelite in whom there is no guile” (John 1), he maintained a forgetfulness of injuries and patience. If it happened that he became angry, shortly afterward he was deeply sorry that he had been angry. He knew nothing of pretense; rather, as he was inwardly, so he showed himself outwardly. If you approached his mouth, you would immediately prove what I say to be true.

He preserved so tenaciously the savor of divine things that he had imbibed from childhood that nearly all his words and deeds, to those who considered them carefully, breathed nothing but a heavenly fragrance. He devoted himself so earnestly to the services of the Church that neither labor by day nor rest by night could ever make him slack in them. He would have considered himself guilty of a grave offense if, compelled by sleep or summoned away by thoughts, he omitted even a single verse of the lengthy Cluniac psalmody [Col. 0863C]. And since no psalm and none of the remaining offices passed his lips without attention, he also applied to the words such understanding as he could; continually offering to God the sacrifice of praise, he sang psalms, in accordance with the Apostle, with spirit and mind (1 Cor. 14).

He also possessed a graceful and vigorous religious effectiveness in outward affairs. For this reason, in administering many priories, he was useful to his subjects and beloved by all to whom he could become known. An exceptional guardian of obedience, he cherished it with such affection that he judged it a crime to exceed even in a small matter the command of one who ordered him.

I myself experienced his great steadfastness in this virtue. When I often imposed upon him difficult tasks—such as I would scarcely have dared to impose on others—he accepted what was enjoined cheerfully [Col. 0863D] and performed it more cheerfully still. Once, when I was traveling to Rome and he and others were accompanying me, I turned aside to lodge at Siena, one of the principal cities of Tuscany. Wishing to obtain lodging earlier on the following day, I set out before dawn. When I had already completed almost two miles of the road from the city, I suddenly heard behind us the voice of a rider hurrying from some distance, and, hearing it, I stopped. When he reached us as we waited, he reported that, at the instigation of certain persons, Duke Conrad was preparing an ambush for us on the road, and for that reason he urged our return.

Having accepted this advice, I returned with my companions; but Gerard—since no one more ready to obey was at hand—I sent to the lord pope because necessity demanded it. Departing from us, after he had gone, I think, not quite six miles along the road, [Col. 0864A] he encountered those lying in ambush. They seized him, stripped him of all his possessions, and violently carried him away to deserted and precipitous mountain places. There, shut up in a very high tower and suffering many hardships, after he escaped the perils of imprisonment, he rejoiced that he had suffered something for obedience.

Above all, he had placed the love of the saving sacraments of the altar as a kind of summit upon the body of his virtues. Raised aloft by the vigorous striving of his heart, through this summit he penetrated even the innermost places of heaven. For who could easily recount with what clear eye of faith he beheld the Lord Jesus beneath the veil of the sacraments—not veiled, but revealed? No outward appearance cast darkness upon his understanding; rather, he perceived by spiritual sight Christ walking on earth with the apostles, hanging on the cross with the blessed Virgin, and rising from the dead with Mary Magdalene [Col. 0864B].

Upon the mystery of Christ’s sacred body and blood he had placed all his hope; and by almost daily offering he sacrificed the Son to the Father for his own sins and those of the whole world, while he also offered himself together with him in great devotion of heart and an outpouring of tears. You could see him standing at the altar, often shaken throughout by deep weeping; you could see his words broken by sobs and his breast pressed by heavy sighs. It was thereby made clear that he was utterly removed from human things and lifted up to divine ones—not only in mind, but almost in body itself—dwelling so in heavenly places that the Lord’s words might seem to have been spoken even of him: “He who eats my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me, and I in him. And he who eats me, he too shall live because of me” (John 6). And elsewhere: “The bread that I shall give is my flesh for the life of the world” (ibid.) [Col. 0864C]. Lest anyone suppose that life to be temporal, he again says: “If anyone eats of this bread, he shall live for ever” (ibid.).

Certain through these promises of our Lord that in them he received eternal life, our Gerard hungered, with an insatiable appetite, so to speak, for the bread of heaven, and refreshed the blessed hunger of his soul with daily nourishment. Having pursued these exercises of good works from early youth almost to extreme old age [Col. 0864D], he was at last deemed worthy for the Lord to reveal to him something of his secrets. He chose to act singularly in these mysteries of his body and blood in order both to show the truth of those sacraments and to demonstrate that the man of whom we speak had not placed his hope in them in vain. Thus he showed that Gerard’s heart’s devotion was acceptable to him when, by a miracle suited to that devotion, he adorned him so magnificently.

Gerard himself is the witness of this most wonderful miracle; whether he deserves belief is shown by his preceding life and subsequent end. Yet he was not its voluntary narrator. Rather, when I privately adjured him, he indicated that what he had previously told, as if under another’s name, had been revealed to himself. And lest any scruple remain in my heart—even though I did not doubt at all the words simply spoken by him—he confirmed, with an attestation invoking the name of God and Christian hope, what he disclosed concerning the vision. First, however, he exacted from me a pledge of secrecy: that while he lived I should preserve it in profound silence. But now that death of the flesh has removed him from this present life, what he wished concealed during his lifetime for his own protection ought to be made public for the glory of God.

[Note: [Col. 0865D] In manuscript S. V. another chapter begins here, with this title: “Account of the first miracle shown to the same man.”]

In the diocese of Chalon there is an estate called Bellemont, belonging to the jurisdiction of the monastery of Cluny. There is there a church in honor of the blessed Mother of God and Virgin, which, because of the latter’s singular remembrance, grants, as I have learned from many, a singular grace of prayer. There are also small dwellings there, adequate for a few monks to live in [Col. 0865B]. Around the feast of the Lord’s Nativity, the venerable Gerard mentioned above was there and was tirelessly pursuing the practices described above. The sacred day of the Lord’s Circumcision arrived; having devoutly completed the night vigils, he prepared himself to perform the daytime offices still more devoutly.

The Mass was reached, and, prepared outwardly in the sacred vestments as was his custom, inwardly filled with spirit and faith, he approached the altar. When, after completing the other rites, he had reached the Canon and had pronounced the divine words which change the substance of bread and wine into Christ’s flesh and blood, he happened shortly before the Lord’s Prayer to turn his eyes toward the sacred elements themselves. Behold—he related this in astonishment—he did not see the form of the bread which he had placed upon the altar; instead he saw in its place a little child, moving hands and arms with infantile gestures [Col. 0865C].

Gazing upon this, he stopped, troubled by fitting fear and not knowing what to do; trembling, he marveled at the unprecedented and heavenly spectacle. Long ago I read something similar to what I relate, but divine condescension wished to add something to our miracle by which no equal to it could be found. For no past age deserved to see what in our days God, the author of these sacraments, granted our Gerard to behold. For while he stood amazed at this sight, he turned his eyes toward the side of the altar and saw a woman of most honorable appearance—indeed, as he understood, the blessed ever-Virgin, mother of that divine little child—watching over him diligently and, as it were, with maternal care, in great reverence [Col. 0865D]. Beside her he saw a man of angelic beauty, or rather, as he truly was, an angel sent by God, standing together with her beside the heavenly sacraments.

How greatly joyful fear then grew in the heart of him who saw these things; how multiplied was his joy; how his heart and flesh rejoiced in the living God—I cannot write it, nor could he recount it to me. An angelic testimony was added to the unheard-of miracle: he heard the angel standing at the altar say to him. I shall report the very words, often recounted to me by Gerard, containing neither more nor less: “Why,” said the angel, “do you marvel? This child whom you behold governs heaven and earth.” With these words the heavenly vision departed.

Afterward, when he turned his eyes again to the saving sacraments, he could no longer see the child; but he saw the form of bread placed upon the altar as it had been before. Judged worthy of so great a miracle and nourished by that same body of Christ which he had seen, this priest of God completed the Mass, endowed with gifts of heavenly grace [Col. 0866B].

[Note: [Col. 0865D] Likewise another chapter begins here in manuscript S. V., under this title: “Another miracle concerning the same monk.”]

At one time he governed the monastery of Saint Saviour at Nevers, which we possess, having been entrusted with it by the holy Father Hugh. A dispute arose between him and one of his provosts. On the day appointed for the proceeding, each came to the hearing. A crowd of nobles was present, together with no small number of clerics and monks, while a packed mass of common people filled the entire place. Prior Gerard sat in the midst; the rest surrounded him on every side. The provost came with his followers, intending to prosecute his case against Gerard [Col. 0866C]. Chosen judges were present to settle the dispute in judicial order after hearing each party’s claim.

There is no need to name the matter in dispute; it was, however, an ecclesiastical matter and one greatly necessary to the monastery’s interests. The provost of whom I have spoken sought with the utmost effort to claim it for himself because it seemed highly profitable. Gerard, on the other hand, did not acquiesce, because he knew that it belonged by right to the monastery entrusted to him. Gerard was given leave to speak and, before all who were present, set out his case as befitted a religious man. When he had finished speaking, his adversary cried out that what Gerard had said was false. Ordered afterward by the judges to come forward and prove what he had said, the adversary approached and, repeating his allegations, persisted in asserting, with the rashness he had begun, that they were true.

As he continued, the judges again commanded him, according to the custom of the region, to place in the hand of Prior Gerard himself the thing which they call *gadium* [variant: *vadium*], namely a pledge by which he was to prove the matter [Col. 0867A]. As though emboldened by a good conscience, he put the *gadium* in Gerard’s hand and said: “I am witness, as I have said, to this matter, and I shall prove it by other witnesses or by judicial combat.”

[Note: [Col. 0865D] “That which they call *guadium*.” Here our excellent author himself interprets the term when he adds: “namely, a proof of the matter to be established by him, to be placed by his own hand in the hand of Prior Gerard himself.” For *guadium* or *wadium*—from which we still commonly say *gage*—was an earnest or pledge, either of a grant [Col. 0866D] or also of a future duel. The account of the translation of the body of St German, on the day when King Pippin gave the estate of Palatiolum, with all its appurtenances, to the abbey of St Vincent at Paris, says: “And placing his *wadium* upon the tomb, he said: ‘Receive, most blessed German, our estate of Palatiolum with all its appurtenances, hitherto hostile to you and your household, but henceforth and forever to be beneficial.’”

From this also came the verb *guadiare*, that is, to give a *guadium* or *wadium*, as is evident from these words concerning the claim against the serf Hildrad in the cartulary of Marmoutier [Col. 0867B]: “And when he showed that the man had been a half-free person, Lord Ascelin pledged to him an oath that he was a serf, not half-free.”

[Note: [Col. 0867B] “I shall prove it by judicial combat.” Various examples of the duel—which was also called *bellum*, “war”—are found among ancient writers; and Jacques Sirmond, a man of exceptional learning, has also published certain newer examples in his notes [Col. 0867C] on Geoffrey, abbot of Vendôme. But since the subject here is a duel between monks and laymen, we shall nevertheless bring forward some further examples, perhaps themselves new, from ancient treasures in order to clarify the passage.

First, King Robert, in his ordinance concerning the vicariate of Anthoniacum, says: “That Pipinellus, vicar of the knight Guarin, having come to judgment, was in no way able to resist because of the lawful objection of the servants of St Vincent and St German, who were prepared to resist by the legal conflict of a duel.”

Likewise Louis VII, in a privilege granted to the canons of St Geneviève concerning the servile status of the people of Rodoniacum: “According to the custom of the kingdom of the Franks, we judged that, since the people acknowledged the Church’s right of hospitality and tenancy, but, calling themselves free, denied their servitude, they should go to the court of the abbot whose tenants they were; and there, if the Church wished to retain them, it should prove by duel that they were its serfs.”

Prepared to repel a claim or defend some right by this conflict of duel [Col. 0867D], they gave the opposing party a *guadium*, which act was called both *guadiare* and *arrhamire bellum sive duellum*: that is, to give an earnest or pledge, to promise or give security before a judge or in court concerning the day of battle or combat. Thus the monks of St Martin, Charter IX, say: “In order to settle these matters, confident in our cause and having been challenged to it, we pledged battle in the court of Vendôme. But when the appointed day for engaging in the fight arrived, our friends who were then present advised us to put an end to so great a dispute by peace instead.”

And Charter CLIX: “Stephen Cambacanis of Ferraria denied that he was a serf of St Martin, and concerning this he pledged battle against us. But within the period in which the battle was to occur, he acknowledged that he had acted wrongly; he came into the chapter-house of Marmoutier and made his acknowledgment, namely, according to custom, he placed four denarii upon his head and by them surrendered himself to St Martin.”

Once the day had been set and the duel awarded by judge or by the lord’s court, the combatants assembled in the field, where leading men of the region were also accustomed often to be present. Hervey Malset describes this in a charter concerning the church of Verrières, which belonged to the monks of St Denis of Nogent-le-Retrou, as follows: “After arguments had been heard from both sides, Lancelin was adjudged to restore the horse to the monks with its legal appurtenances. Yet, although the count and nobles testified to the truth which they had heard, he always denied it as he had denied it before. Therefore a duel was awarded between the monks and Lancelin. A certain servant of the monks, named Ingelric, son of Ragenaud the Jongleur, challenged Hugh son of Ausgerius on Lancelin’s side, declaring that he had heard what Lancelin denied, and that Hugh himself denied it. But because he was weak in body, as those who knew him said, a certain nephew of his named Guitcelin gave the judicial pledge of duel on his behalf, and they came to the field to fight the duel. When they had come as far as the oath, the nobles who were present—namely Robert, the count’s steward, and his kinsman, and Robert of Beaumont, and Aymeric of Villerey, nephew of Lord Hugh, and the other nobles who were there—although they knew the monks’ cause to be true, urged the prior and monks who were present not to consent to the battle,” etc.

Hence it is evident that those who were to fight customarily gave an oath before the engagement. The same monks of St Martin explain the arms ordinarily used by those called *campiones*, from *campus*, “field,” and commonly *champions*, in their Notice concerning Fulbert’s Mill: “Fulbert of Lavarzin, who for many years while in the world had paid that mill-toll rent, and had now become our monk, caused it to be defended against him—namely against Constantius of Radenac—by one of our men, fighting with shield and staff against Constantius’s champion: [he maintained] that he had never paid a rent for that stake and that none was due by right. This Constantius, willing or unwilling, eventually acknowledged; and, his champion having been overcome in that combat, he renounced forever every claim concerning that palisade and promised that he would lawfully make amends for the battle unjustly undertaken, as Alberic of Monteaureo, under whose judgment these events occurred, should determine.”]

But because, as it is written, “a false witness shall not go unpunished,” after he uttered these words, before the eyes of all who had gathered to hear that case, he fell backward and immediately expired. All rose in terror; seeing that the matter had been judged by God, they presumed to judge no further. For some of them had previously known for certain that the wretched man was lying, many suspected it; but all alike came to know that he had lied when, by God’s judgment, he happened to die so suddenly after speaking the lie [Col. 0867B]. In this miracle, although divine truth, avenger of falsehood, shone magnificently, it nevertheless showed what Gerard’s merit might be by avenging the wrong done to him.

[Note: [Col. 0868D] Likewise concerning the same monk, the same manuscript.]

At another time he lived in a place near Cluny called Altumjugum, “the High Ridge.” The place took its name from the height by which it surpasses all the surrounding [Col. 0868A] land. For it is a very high mountain rising above the summits of mountains; it often sees below itself the masses of clouds which, weighed down by moisture, cannot climb higher; from it the Alps of Italy can be seen, as can the greater part of the low-lying lands of Gaul. Thus the mountain rises far into the air, surrounded by dense forests, continually exposed to harsher winds, subject to long-lasting snows, and difficult both to ascend and descend. It has driven ordinary habitation far from itself and persuaded those seeking more remote places to seek nothing beyond its solitude. Therefore it received only monks as residents, and by its barrenness did not permit even many of them to remain.

Gerard, wearied for a long time by obedience across various parts of the world, accepted this place near the end of his life, having obtained from me what was, as it were, an honorable discharge from service [Col. 0868B]. There, with a few brothers who likewise feared God, he was occupied more diligently than usual in divine works: he persisted in prayer, devoted himself to reading, and by frequent discussion of sacred words kindled himself more ardently toward divine love. Content with sober fare, he expiated by present austerity anything in which he might perhaps at any time have sinned [Col. 0869A]. Having put off every concern of this world, he drew nearer to God in spiritual desires in proportion as he had withdrawn from human affairs.

He had always, as I said above, been devoted to the services of the Church; but then he attended to them with the utmost devotion, with all the affections of his mind and powers of his body. Almost continually standing at the sacred altar, he revered above all else, with inexpressible devotion of mind and daily celebration of Mass, that singular safeguard of the whole world: namely, the body and blood of the Redeemer. When he had thus completed the day, he kept the night vigils as well, carefully ensuring that the brothers did not rise at an unsuitable time. Always, or often, anticipating them himself, he spent much of the night [Col. 0869B] in tears and prayers.

At that time he reported to me, and related also to some others who later told me of it, that he frequently heard in that same church the sounds of a certain heavenly melody. Nor is this surprising. It belongs to those to hear heavenly things whose ears disdain to hear earthly things. For human senses perceive things above themselves all the more as they are less given over to things below. Fighting with such a contest and tirelessly pursuing such a course of life, Gerard at last obtained the palm due to victors and the prize promised to those who run with perseverance, and rested in that place with a blessed end.

Removed from this present life, he openly showed, not long after his death, that he was now a participant in eternal life; and in himself he proved true the Apostle’s saying: “Whatever a man sows, that he shall also reap” (Gal. 6) [Col. 0869C]. For because, as I have often said, he had placed all his hope in the sacrament of Christ’s body and blood, with the testimony of a good conscience, another miracle concerning that frequently named sacrament was shown through him after his death, so that both his hope might be proved not futile and the faith of those hearing it might be strengthened.

[Note: [Col. 0869D] How the same monk appeared to someone after his death, same manuscript.]

Not yet half a year had passed after his death when a memorable vision appeared to a certain brother, whom, since he is still alive, I do not wish to name. He saw, and behold, a demon stood by his bed, having assumed the form of a small, utterly black Ethiopian. Threatening terror to the beholder with his monstrous ugliness, he thrust the shapes of hands out through the openings of his ears; he stretched out without limit a fiery tongue, projected from the abyss of his foul mouth, and said that, by licking the whole body of that brother with it, he would utterly consume his flesh. Trembling at the demon’s appearance, the man expected nothing but death, being on the point of being devoured.

And when, shaken by the unbearable terror of that dreadful vision, he hoped that no remedy remained for him, behold Gerard stood beside him, resolute in spirit and, as the brother declared, splendid in countenance. [Col. 0870A] He seized that Ethiopian in his hands, dashed him to the ground, and courageously crushed the abominable throat beneath his foot. As he pressed his captive enemy hard, the latter, as though from violent compression, puffed up his unspeakable head like a great cauldron; and with his flame-bearing tongue, as though ploughing the earth, burned the things around him.

Gerard addressed the brother, who was now nearly beside himself from the horror of this sight: “Do you wish,” he said, “to be freed from this demon?” When the brother answered that he wished it by every means, Gerard added: “If you wish to be freed, go to the abbot. Tell him, on my behalf, that he should summon to himself a certain brother whose occupation is a craft, and diligently inquire of him whether he ever doubted the truth of the Lord’s body and blood [Col. 0870B]; what was shown to him to remove that doubt; and how his faith was confirmed by that revelation. Once he has learned these things, let him take care to commit them to writing. For just as it benefited that brother to see this, so it will benefit many to hear it. The manner of life of that brother is pleasing to God, and He did not wish the labours he had endured in such temptation to perish. If you promise that you will tell the abbot these things, you will immediately be freed from this demon.”

When he again pledged this, Gerard drove the demon into flight and rescued the brother from its assault. Rising from sleep, and recovering his senses, he eventually testified with joy that he had truly escaped death.

A few days after this, the brother to whom this had been shown came to me and recounted everything I have related above. But I, [Col. 0870C] still giving no credence to the dream, rested entirely upon the account of the brother who had been indicated. I summoned him to myself, identifying him not by name but by the description of his craft and manner of life, and secretly asked whether he had seen anything memorable concerning the Lord’s body. After he had remained silent for some time, as though stunned by travel—

[Note: [Col. 0870D] Otherwise, “by questioning.” N. Faber: “by an unfamiliar form of address.”]

—when I commanded him, by virtue of obedience, not to conceal what had been shown him, he finally disclosed everything.

“For a long time,” he said, “the ancient enemy violently assailed my faith by tempting me concerning this matter, and, unless God’s grace had helped me, nearly shook it from its position. As I long endured that temptation—which was grievous to me beyond what I can say—and because of it thought that I had lost all the labour I had undertaken in religious life [Col. 0870D], and as faint-heartedness was already driving me to sink into despair, I turned to the blessed Mother of God as my last hope. With all the strength of my soul I began to entreat her to rescue my wretched soul from so great an evil.

“Before fifteen days had elapsed from the beginning of my prayers, I seemed to myself to be standing before the high altar of the greater church. Upon it a little child, as though one year old, was sitting and commanded me to approach him. When I came near, he instructed me to receive in my mouth the holy bread which he held out in his hand. After I had done so, he added: ‘Receive me,’ [Col. 0871A] he said, ‘and carry me in your arms through the length of this church.’

“Although I undertook this with great fear, I received him in my hands and carried him with much reverence from that altar to the far end of the choir. From that day my heart was so emptied of every temptation by which it had been troubled that not even a trace of the former disturbance remained in it; and it retained faith in the saving sacrament with unshaken firmness.”

After hearing this from that brother, I could no longer doubt the vision, since I found the reporters of the two revelations in agreement in every respect. For everything that the former had heard from Gerard concerning the other brother, the latter confirmed in full by his own testimony. And since the first knew nothing of the second’s thoughts, while the second was wholly ignorant of the first’s visions, each gave complete credibility to the other’s revelation: the one disclosed this man’s temptations, and the other, by his confession, made known to all that the former had seen true things. [Col. 0871B]

## CHAPTER IX. On events which occurred at Cluny and in its vicinity

Having first touched on those matters which concern reverence for the divine sacraments and the sincerity of true confession, let us proceed, with the Lord’s help, to other matters no less useful for the edification of conduct. First, then, I shall explain as best I can visions or revelations of the dead which I have been able to learn from various persons. For these are said to occur frequently especially in our times. Indeed, very many trustworthy men affirm that figures of the departed appear to the living and very often announce to them many things that are true and verified. I think that accounts of such matters will not be unwelcome to readers, especially those who, out of love for the life to come, disdain the present life and strive to attain the former by right faith and pious works.

For these things are a great refreshment to them and, amid the miseries in which they groan daily, a very great consolation, when they hear something about the homeland from which they live in exile during this pilgrimage and for which they yearningly sigh—something that kindles their faith and hope more and more. I have heard many such things from many people. In recounting them I observe no chronological order, because I could not plainly gather one from the narrators’ words; nor, even if I could have done so, did I care to preserve it. What advantage is there in such a matter in knowing what happened first and what later, provided that it is certain that it happened? For it is far more appropriate to investigate the deeds of times than the times of deeds. [Col. 0871D]

It seems fitting to me, however, that we begin with what is near and move on to what is more remote. Therefore, [Col. 0872A] let us first bring forward the matters which we have heard occurred in the monastery of Cluny or in its vicinity.

The monastery of Cluny is renowned almost throughout the whole world for its religious life, discipline, strictness, number of brethren, and every observance of the monastic order.

[Note: [Col. 0871D] “The monastery of Cluny, renowned almost throughout the whole world for its religious life, discipline, and strictness.” The praises bestowed upon the abbey of Cluny by popes and kings in charters, and also by ancient writers in their books, are many. Paschal II calls it, in his own time, “a mirror and model of monastic religion in Gaul”; Louis VII, “the noblest member of his kingdom”; Riquin, bishop of Toul, “the universal house of the supreme Householder, and a court in which sacred praises resound to God”; [Col. 0872D] the author of the Life of St Majolus, “noble, a friend of salvation, and a friend of monastic religion”; Geoffrey of Vendôme, “a second paradise”; Peter of Celle, “the garden of God”; Hildebert, in the Life of St Hugh, “a bath for souls”; Peter Damian, in his letter to the same Hugh and the monks of Cluny, “a spiritual field where heaven and earth meet, and as it were an arena of contest, in which frail flesh, as in a spiritual wrestling-school, struggles against the powers of the air”; and finally Trithemius, “a monastery famous throughout the world.”]

It is the singular and common refuge of sinners; through it many losses have been inflicted upon hell and very many gains bestowed upon the heavenly kingdoms. There innumerable multitudes of people, casting off from their shoulders the heavy burdens of the world, have submitted their necks to Christ’s sweet yoke. There persons of every profession, rank, and order have exchanged worldly pride and luxury for the humble and poor life of monks. There venerable fathers of the churches themselves, fleeing even the burdens of ecclesiastical business, chose to live more safely and quietly, preferring to be subject rather than to rule. There an unwearied and implacable struggle against spiritual wickedness affords Christ’s soldiers daily palms of victory.

For the inhabitants of that place, who by continual combat subject the flesh to the spirit, truly, according to the Apostle, “to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (Phil. 1). From there the perfume of spiritual virtues has been poured forth, and the whole house of the world has been filled with the fragrance of the ointment (John 12), while the fervour of monastic religion—which at that time had almost grown cold—was rekindled by the example and zeal of those men. Gaul, Germany, Britain beyond the sea, [Col. 0872C] Spain, Italy, and all Europe attest this, filled with monasteries either newly founded by them or restored from ancient decay.

There communities of monks, standing before God in their ranks after the manner of heavenly hosts, together with other exercises of holy virtues apply themselves so steadfastly to divine praises by day and night that the prophet’s words may also be understood of them: “Blessed are those who dwell in thy house, O Lord; for ever and ever they shall praise thee” (Ps. 83). But why should I enumerate particular regions of the world, when this renown has reached from our farthest West to the East itself and has escaped no corner of the Christian world?

For this is the vineyard; these are the branches which, cleaving to Christ the true vine and cleansed by the Father, the husbandman, bear much fruit according to the Gospel saying [Col. 0872D] (John 15). Of this vineyard we read in the Psalms: “He stretched out his branches unto the sea, and his shoots unto the river” (Ps. 79). Although this was said of the synagogue of the Jews transplanted from Egypt, and especially of the present Church, nothing prevents its also being understood of this church of Cluny, which is no lesser member of that universal Church. [Col. 0873A]

It would please me to linger longer here; but since this does not pertain to the work now proposed, and so great a subject cannot be explained in brief discourse by one hastening to other matters, we must for the present leave these things aside and proceed, as we promised, to the accounts of revelations of the dead.

## CHAPTER X. On the remarkable apparition of Stephen, called Blancus

[Note: [Col. 0873D] Otherwise: How Stephen, once abbot of Saint-Gilles, appeared after death to a certain brother.]

What I am now about to relate first was told to me by persons whose testimony I was compelled to believe no less than my own eyes. For their life and conduct required that I should give credence, without any doubt, no less to their account than to my own sight. They told me, then, that there was at Cluny a certain brother called Bernard Savinellus. They related of him that, although he sometimes behaved lightly in certain matters, when corrected, as is customary under regular discipline, and subjected to many reproaches both in words and blows, he endured them most patiently and, after the stripes, showed himself meek by cheerfulness of face and activity in work.

One night, while the brethren were chanting the nocturnal praises of God in church, he left the choir where he was singing psalms with the others and made for the dormitory. As he was climbing its steps, he suddenly encountered Stephen, commonly called Blancus, [Col. 0873C] formerly abbot of the monastery of Saint-Gilles—

[Note: [Col. 0873D] Abbot of the monastery of Saint-Gilles. This monastery was one of the many which St Hugh, abbot of Cluny, reformed and also admitted into the Cluniac family. Thus says the anonymous author who wrote his Life: “Who,” he says, “restored in religious observance the churches of the blessed confessors Martial and Giles, if not this blessed man?” [Col. 0874D]]

—who had died a few days before. At first sight, not recognizing him and thinking him someone else, he hastened on to where he was going. But the image of the dead man which had appeared spoke first: “Where are you going?” he said. “Stop, and hear what I have to say.” The brother, astonished and indignant because a monk seemed to be speaking such things contrary to the Rule, at an unsuitable hour and in an unsuitable place, tried by such gestures as he could to silence him.

But since that dead abbot had come not to be silent but to speak, and pressed him more and more, the brother, compelled by his importunity, stopped and asked who he was and what he wanted of him. He replied: “I am Stephen, called abbot of Saint-Gilles, who sinned much both before receiving the abbacy and afterward. For these sins I now suffer bitter punishments, from which, through the ineffable mercy of God, I shall be delivered all the sooner if help is given me. I therefore beg you to entreat Lord Abbot and all the brothers, acting as my messenger, to pour forth prayers to almighty God for my deliverance and [Col. 0874A] to make every effort to rescue me from so great evils by whatever means they can.

“When the brother answered that he would indeed do what he asked, but that no one would believe his report, the dead man who was speaking added: ‘So that no one may be able to entertain any doubt concerning what you must report, know that within these eight days you shall depart from this life. When you have foretold this to them, the outcome of the subsequent event will demonstrate that you spoke the truth.’”

He said this and immediately vanished from his sight. The brother returned from the dormitory to the church and, not unnaturally much troubled by the announcement of his death, spent the night meditating upon these matters. When morning came, he first disclosed what had been enjoined upon him to the prior, then to the venerable and holy Father Hugh, and finally to the great and reverend assembly of brothers. [Col. 0874B]

When this reached everyone’s ears, as human minds commonly hold differing opinions on the same matter, some believed it, while very many declared it false. Yet all waited for the sign of that death which the brother had announced, by which they would clear the matter of every doubt. And behold, the next day the narrator of the vision was seized by illness and, gradually failing, came to his end. Affirming steadfastly until his last breath what he had said, he rested in a good end within the days specified, and thus proved by his death that he had been a messenger of truth.

The community of brothers, therefore, assured after the death of the vision’s narrator, offered manifold sacrifices of supplication to the ineffable mercy of God both for the dead abbot and for his messenger. With all their strength they devoted themselves to sacred prayers, almsgiving, and especially to offerings of the saving sacrifice for eternal rest. [Col. 0874C]

## CHAPTER XI. On the similar apparition of Bernard, called Grossus

[Note: [Col. 0874D] Otherwise: On the remarkable posthumous apparition of Bernard surnamed Grossus.]

I received from the same narrators whom I mentioned above a similar—indeed, almost identical—miracle concerning Bernard surnamed Grossus (“the Fat”).

[Note: [Col. 0874D] On Bernard surnamed Grossus. Many references are found in the charters of Cluny to the Grossi, who were also lords of Brancion; some of these charters we have already transcribed in this Library.]

Distinguished by secular nobility and power, he possessed certain fortified places near the monastery of Cluny and inflicted many evils upon that place and the other churches around it. At last, changing his disposition and resolving to put an end to his evils, [Col. 0874D] he came to the venerable Father Hugh mentioned above and declared that he wished to go to Rome for prayer on account of his sins. If he were permitted to return, he promised to renounce the world and become a monk at Cluny.

Accordingly he went to Rome, and everywhere, at the glorious bodies of the chief apostles and of many martyrs, he gave himself to prayers and alms, expiating as best he could the crimes of his former life by penance. Having thus spent in the city a period of forty days—the period properly prescribed for sinners to do penance—he left Rome and, returning to his homeland, reached Sutri. While staying in that city, which is quite near Rome, he met the end of his life as an illness long contracted grew worse. There, as was possible in a foreign land, his companions tended and buried him honourably.

Not many years later, the provost of a village subject to the jurisdiction of Cluny was travelling at midday through a wood near the castle of Uselle. Bernard himself had recently built this castle, [Col. 0875B] from which robbers frequently emerged and plundered whatever they could from every direction. As the provost travelled, as has been said, he suddenly encountered Bernard himself. Seeing him mounted on a mule and dressed in new foxskins, he remembered that he was dead and was afraid; nevertheless, overcoming his fear, he asked whether he was indeed the person he appeared to be, and why he had come.

He received this reply: “Know me to be Bernard, once lord of this region. Certainly, as all who remain here know, while I was in the world I committed many evils, for which I now suffer much. But above all, the building of that nearby castle torments me, which, as you yourself know, was recently built by me. Yet because at the end of my life I repented of my evils, I escaped eternal damnation; but I still need much help for complete deliverance. For that reason I have been permitted to come to the abbot of Cluny to implore mercy.

“I followed his company for a long time. Since he lodged at Anse in the preceding week, I remained by night among his attendants and servants. I therefore beg you to go to him and earnestly entreat him to have mercy on me.”

When the man to whom he spoke asked why he was clothed in a foxskin garment, Bernard replied: “Long ago I bought this garment new, and on the very day on which I first wore it I gave it to a certain poor man. As it was given new, so it remains always new, and amid punishments it affords me unspeakable refreshment.” [Col. 0875D]

After these words, he who had appeared vanished; the other hastened to fulfil what had been enjoined upon him. Coming to the blessed man to whom he had been sent, he recounted everything to him in order. Receiving the dead man’s message kindly, and filled with the spirit of charity, he bestowed upon the soul suffering under eternal judgment many aids of almsgiving and many of divine sacrifices. By these means, as is fitting to believe, Bernard was freed from punishments and joined, according to the measure of the heavenly dispensation, to the rest of the faithful.

For reason does not permit us to suppose that that spirit, hidden in the most secret recesses of God’s judgments, was permitted to return to human beings for the sake of its liberation and that no benefit followed from its return. For it would then seem to have been sent in vain. Nor would he have asked to be aided by sacraments and the performance of sacred works if he had not known that they were of benefit to him. Since he asked that help be given him by such aids, he showed both that they were effective for assistance and that he was worthy of their help. [Col. 0876A]

The holy abbot mentioned above foretold imminent death to the man to whom this vision appeared. For when manifestations of this kind from the dead have often occurred in our times, scarcely anyone who has spoken with a dead person is reported to have delayed death for long. Thus this man, prompted both by the horror of the vision and by the saint’s warning, immediately renounced the world; having become a monk, he reached the end of his life within a few days.

## CHAPTER XII. How greatly the devil has always raged in envy against Cluny

[Col. 0876B]

Although I promised in the preceding chapter to speak of revelations of the dead that occurred in Cluny or its vicinity, yet because many other things no less worthy of memory are said to have happened in our age in that famous monastery, I judge it not inappropriate to bring them forward also in this account for the benefit of readers.

For, as I touched on above, the ancient enemy has always greatly begrudged the discipline and zeal for divine works of that abbey, and by many indications has shown his envy toward the inhabitants of that place to burn fiercely. If I attempted to recount each of these things as they have come to me, I might perhaps weary readers or hearers with a large volume, [Col. 0876C] and myself wander far from my purpose. For who could explain with how great a malignity he has always—or often—assaulted that heavenly camp; how hostile he has always been to Christ’s soldiers who resist him; how frequent were the attacks he launched in his violent attempts to break in?

For, in his customary manner, seeking to destroy the inner citizen—that is, the spirit—he brought against it externally whatever engines of temptation he could; and grieving that he had been repulsed from within, he stirred up as many battles outside as he was able. Thus, blinded by his own fury, while he always attacked all invisibly, he sometimes also appeared visibly to certain persons. And, not knowing what good God had decided to bring from his evil, he often unwillingly built up the Lord’s flock precisely where he sought to destroy it. [Col. 0876D]

## CHAPTER XIII. On the brother whom he wished to deceive under the appearance of an abbot

This gave rise to the following event. A certain brother named John, an Italian by nationality, had grown weary of the strictness of regular discipline and was even thinking of fleeing the monastery. The devil himself appeared to him in the guise of an abbot. Accompanied by two demons in the guise of monks, he appeared to the brother as he sat alone in a secluded place in the monastery, turning many things over in his mind, and thought that he had found a suitable time to deceive him.

Sitting beside him, he said: “Brother, I have just turned aside here to lodge; but, happening to see you, I recognized that you are burdened by much anxiety and are entertaining many turbulent thoughts in your heart. Although the cause of these thoughts is partly known to me through certain informants, nevertheless, if you disclose it more fully, perhaps I can give you useful advice. Tell a friend who asks who you are and why you are sad.”

The brother feared to disclose the secrets of his heart to a man whom he supposed to be unknown, and replied only that he was Italian by birth. The demon who appeared as a monk added: “I too am abbot of that same region and can help you well in every way. For, although you are silent, I know that the abbot of this monastery and the others treat you badly; they do not honour you as is fitting, and frequently harass you with many injuries and insults besides. I therefore advise you to look to your own interests and leave this place, which is altogether ruinous, and depart with me. [Col. 0877B] I am prepared to rescue you from these evils and, once you have been brought to my abbey, which is called Grottaferrata, to raise you there to every honour.”

To this the brother replied: “I cannot leave here in any way, because the enclosure of the monastery forbids it and a multitude of brothers surrounds me.”

Then the devil said: “Nor can I help you in any way while you remain here. But contrive by whatever means to cross the monastery’s bounds. Once you have done that, I shall immediately be present and take you, as I said, to my place.”

But merciful God, who does not permit us to be tempted beyond what we can bear (1 Cor. 10), did not allow the enemy to proceed further. Rather, as Scripture says, “he who made him has applied his sword to him.” For while this was happening, the community of brethren was seated in the refectory at the customary hour for supper. When it was finished, the prior, according to custom, struck the bell once. At the sound, the demon who pretended to be the abbot, driven by divine power, immediately tore himself away from the brother to whom he was speaking. Running headlong with great force toward the nearby latrines, he plunged himself into their depths before the eyes of the brother already mentioned. Thus indeed God’s mercy both rescued the brother from the temptation of the most wicked enemy and expelled the unclean spirit from His house through a place fitting for its uncleanness. [Col. 0877C]

## CHAPTER XIV. On the man who heard demons boasting of their crimes

At another time, another brother, a worker in wood, lay at night in a place somewhat apart from the others. [Col. 0877D] As is customary in monastic dormitories, the place was lit by a burning lamp. While he lay awake in bed, he saw a monstrous vulture, scarcely able to support the weight of its immense body on wings and feet, come forward panting as though from exertion and stand opposite his bed.

As the brother looked at it in wonder, behold two other demons in human form arrived and addressed that vulture—or rather, demon—as follows: “What are you doing here? Can you accomplish anything here?”

“Nothing,” it replied, “because I am repelled on every side by the protection of the cross, the sprinkling of water, and the murmuring of psalms. I have laboured here the whole night and expended my strength in vain. Therefore, being unable to achieve anything, I have come here exhausted. But tell me of your journey, and let me know if anything has succeeded well for you.”

They said: “We have come from Chalon, where we compelled a certain knight of Geoffrey of Donzy to fall into adultery with his host’s wife. Likewise, passing through a certain monastery, we caused the schoolmaster to fornicate with one of the boys. But what are you doing, you idler? Rise, and at least cut off the foot of this monk who is looking at us, which he has carelessly stretched out beyond his bed.”

When they had said this, the demon seized the brother’s axe, which lay hidden under the bed, [Col. 0878B] and rose with all his strength to strike. But when the brother saw the axe raised over him, he drew back his foot in fear. Thus the demon’s blow was deprived of its effect and fell upon the far end of the bed. The evil spirits immediately disappeared.

The brother who had seen these things hurried in the morning to the oft-mentioned Father Hugh and told him everything. To investigate the certainty of the matter, Hugh sent to Chalon and Tournus.

[Note: [Col. 0877D] “He sent to Tournus.” A town on the Saône, which was formerly divided into three parts: namely, the castle of Trinorchium, the town of Tornutium, and the cell of St Valerian. In French, Tournus. It is, I believe, the same as Tinurtium, mentioned by Spartianus in his *Severus* in these words: “After many varied achievements in Gaul, Severus first fought most successfully against Albinus at Tinurtium [Trinurtium].” [Col. 0878D]]

Carefully investigating what the demons had said, he found the servants of falsehood to have spoken truly. But someone may ask: Since evil spirits surpass human cunning in the subtlety of their malice, being made swift for all things by the lightness of their nature, unburdened by any weight of body, and rendered more shrewd by long experience of affairs, [Col. 0878C] how do they disclose the counsels and deeds of their wickedness to human hearers? Do they not consider how many of their snares people are often delivered from when their plots are revealed, and how often they themselves are frustrated in the result of those same plots? Why, then, did they disclose, in the hearing of the aforesaid brother, both the evils that they had done and their inability to do other things which they desired?

The answer is that, although they possess great capacity for harming and a ready will to deceive, yet by the hidden dispensation of God they are often deceived in their very falsehood by means so wondrous and incomprehensible that they are sometimes compelled, invincible though they are, to serve the salvation of humankind, against which they are always willingly hostile. For, as it is written, true Wisdom “takes the false-wise in their own craftiness” [Col. 0878D] (Job 5): so that they are deceived in the very means by which they wish to deceive, and are themselves rather destroyed by the means through which they desire to destroy. God uses them, indeed, as a prudent householder uses evil servants, who are moved by no love of service but obey their master’s commands only through servile fear.

Accordingly, sometimes knowingly and sometimes unknowingly, but always unwillingly, they accomplish things that pertain to human salvation. That they always act unwillingly is certain to everyone. But that they sometimes do so knowingly, the Gospel declares, where it says: “Demons came out from many, crying out and saying, ‘For thou art the Son of God’” (Luke 4). The demons who cried out these words did not fail to know that believing Christ to be the Son of God pertains to humanity’s salvation. But that this confession was not uttered by the devotion of faith, but forced out by the severity of torments, they themselves show when they add: “Hast thou come before the time to torment us?” (Matt. 8). Thus, unwillingly yet knowingly, they became heralds of human salvation.

Likewise in the Acts of the Apostles, when a demon cried through a demoniac, “Jesus I know, and Paul I know” (Acts 19), it surely bore witness to the truth unwillingly and confessed what could benefit its hearers. Again, in the Gospel, when the legion of demons begged the Lord and said, “If thou castest us out, send us into the herd of swine” (Mark 5), they both testified to their own powerlessness, since they could not rule even swine without permission, and, unwillingly and knowingly, warned people by such words to flee from themselves—those most evil enemies of human salvation—and take refuge with their Saviour. [Col. 0879B]

That they sometimes accomplish things helpful to people unknowingly is shown by innumerable examples in Holy Scripture, but especially by the temptation of blessed Job and the Lord’s Passion. Satan would not have tempted Job had he foreseen that he would be overcome by Job’s patience; nor would he have incited the Jews to crucify the Lord had he foreseen that by His death he himself would be condemned much more severely and the world saved. [Col. 0879C] For the Apostle calls the mystery of the divine Incarnation and Passion a mystery hidden from ages, “which none of the rulers of this world knew” (1 Cor. 2).

Therefore, as was said, sometimes knowingly and sometimes unknowingly, but always unwillingly, evil spirits, driven by the dispositions of supreme Wisdom, serve human benefit—whether they speak or act, whether hidden from human eyes or visibly appearing before them. Thus when, by God’s ordering, they appear to some persons or do or say certain things, their greedy will to harm indeed remains in them; but the power that governs all things restrains it, subjected to its laws.

For whatever the aerial powers may rage to overthrow, Wisdom nevertheless conquers malice, “reaching mightily from end to end and ordering all things sweetly” (Wisdom 8). Wisdom is said to reach mightily from end to end because eternal Wisdom wisely catches the wiles of enemies, and invincible Power subdues their strength. It is certain, then, that when the demons appeared to the aforesaid brother and related the matters already mentioned, they either knew what good would result from them or did not know it. Nevertheless, unwillingly, they served the divine will and the salvation of some persons.

I have inserted this discussion concerning the disclosure made by demons—whether already related or perhaps yet to be related—so that no one may wonder that they disclose their counsels or deeds as though voluntarily. For this is not their own work but the counsel of divine dispensation, which, for the greater glory of its name, uses even evil things well and brings about great kindness toward its own people from the malice of those very beings. [Col. 0880A] For how could human weakness resist so mighty an enemy, of whom it is said, “There is no power on earth that can be compared with him” (Job 41), unless He who is called the Power of God opposed Himself for us against so strong an adversary? How could the dulled understanding of the human mind, pressed down in lowliness, guard against so many subtle deceptions of his, unless He who is called the Wisdom of God disclosed them to us?

Since the devil’s deceits and attempts, by which he has often been shown restlessly to have attacked the holy abbey of Cluny, have been made known by several revelations, it seems fitting to carry out the account which I began.

## CHAPTER XV. What blessed Hugh related in chapter on the vigil of the Lord’s Nativity

[Col. 0880B]

It is the custom of this monastery to celebrate the Nativity of the Saviour with a devotion more singular than that shown for other solemnities: with the melodies of chants, the length of readings, the lighting of many candles, and—what is far more excellent—with special devotion and an abundant outpouring of tears, it joyfully keeps the feast together with the angelic spirits. When the cycle of that season returned, the brethren, according to custom, prepared themselves and all that was theirs; adorning the churches and suitably arranging the other places of the monastery, they strove to appear festive both within and without. The blessed and venerable Father Hugh still survived, in extreme old age, near indeed to bodily death, but also near to eternal life after death [Col. 0880C].

When the solemnity itself was now at hand, he entered the chapter-house where the brethren had assembled and spoke these words to all:

“Know, brethren, that Jesus, our gracious Saviour, has resolved to be present at the solemnities of his Nativity and of your deliverance, and to await with great joy the service of your devotion. Yet know, on the other hand, that the wicked enemy, envying your happiness, labours to mingle, if he can, some clouds of his own darkness with so great a splendour, and to diminish, if only ever so slightly, the glory of so great a festival.

“For a certain brother,” he said—plainly indicating himself—“saw on this very night the Mother of Mercy herself, the perpetual [another reading: ever-] Virgin, holding in her most sweet lap the Son whom she bore on this present night, while a multitude of holy angels stood beside her in immeasurable light. And the same God-child rejoiced and exulted with boundless joy, showing the gladness of his heart by the movement of his glorious body and by clapping his hands. Turning to his mother, he said to her: ‘Do you see, Mother, the night now at hand, which is to be made bright with the joys of my Nativity? In it the utterances of the prophets and the proclamations of the angels will be renewed, and at my rising from you all things in heaven and on earth alike will rejoice. Where now is the treachery of the condemned enemy? Where is his power, by which before this singular joy he ruled the world?’

“When he heard this, that shameless one came out of his hiding-place and appeared from afar, shamefully disfigured; with much weeping and wailing he begged to be admitted. His purpose in saying this was that he might, in his usual manner, be able somehow to darken the joys of that great brightness which he envied. ‘And if I am admitted into no part of the church,’ he said, ‘let me at least be received in some place among the remaining workshops.’

“The Son of the Virgin said: ‘Go, gallows-bird, and do not complain that you have been prejudged by my power; attempt what you can.’

“Set free, he made for the archway of the chapter-house, but though he tried to enter, he could not. For he found himself so swollen with pride, and the entrance to the chapter-house so narrow, that he could not enter at all. Truly, puffed up with the ancient plague of pride, he could not pass through a humble entrance; for the same entrance does not contain both the proud man standing erect and the humble man bent low.

“From there he turned his steps toward the brethren’s dormitory, and, trusting that he could disturb them with his customary phantoms, he tried to enter. But, driven back from the door by that same bulk of his own, he departed.

“At last [another reading: as his final hope] he transferred his hope of doing harm to the refectory, supposing that there, because of some concern for the body, there would be greater negligence of mind. Yet there too he encountered so many barriers from the reading of divine words, so many beams from the devotions of the hearers, so many bolts from the charity of those serving one another, that, being wholly unable to go further, he was forced to turn back. Thus rejected from all the offices of the monastery, that pestilent being departed from the sight of the most merciful Redeemer and his glorious Virgin Mother with the confusion he deserved.

“Therefore be watchful, and give immense thanks to the almighty and most merciful Saviour, who has both driven the most wicked enemy away from you and himself remained to celebrate his feast with us [another reading: with you].”

[Col. 0881C] These things spoken to the brethren by the holy man show both the wickedness of the malignant spirits raging against that very place and the mercy of the Lord who protected it. Although those wicked enemies lay snares generally for all, they nevertheless pressed much more fiercely upon those newly converted. They indeed grieved, in envy, at the progress of the veterans; but at the added conversion of recruits they were more violently enraged, as though they had received a fresh wound. As if in despair after a long time, setting aside the spoils of their former prey, they burned far more fiercely against those who were being snatched from before their eyes. Hence they stirred up strong wars against the novices; hence, armed with the various weapons of temptations, they assailed them with all their efforts.

## CHAPTER XVI. Concerning the brother who saw demons walking as though religious men.

[Col. 0881D]

And, to say something of occurrences in our own time, I myself saw very many people recounting to me the various snares which demons had laid for them. Nor do I speak of the spiritual warfare waged through suggestions of vices, but of things done, as it were, in an open field of battle, with no small exertion on either side. For the enemy’s overflowing abundance of malice, when he could gain nothing by tempting inwardly, burned all the more fiercely in anger. Grieving that he had been invisibly defeated, he attempted to see whether, by visibly engaging with Christ’s soldiers, he might at least prevail in some respect.

This is why a certain brother told me that he had seen an innumerable troop of demons passing through the house called the Cell of the Novices [Col. 0882A]. One night before Matins [another reading: at Matins], he was lying in bed and meditating to himself, I know not what, from the Psalms. Then, while all were asleep, he saw that accursed company, transformed into the likeness of monks, coming out from the door above his head. Clad in hoods [another reading: cowls], imitating the appearance of religion, they marched in order and with apparent great gravity. Understanding what they were, and being, as commonly happens in such circumstances, greatly frightened—for terror always accompanies a vision of malignant spirits—he hid his head as best he could beneath the covering that covered him. Yet, in order to observe the outcome, he left a small space for his eyes [Col. 0882B]. Carefully watching to see what they would do, he saw that entire army of Satan pass through the house of the resting brethren, unable to accomplish anything of its own there, and thus make its exit through the latrine-house, which was nearby and quite suitable to it.

## CHAPTER XVII. Concerning Algerus, a devout elder.

Another brother also, named Algerus—truly, as is said of blessed Job, “blameless and upright, fearing God and departing from evil” (Job 1)—often and repeatedly complained to me that demons attacked him fiercely. To pass over very many [another reading: several] of the things he told me, he related that he was once asleep in the aforesaid house of the novices, with many others lying around him [Col. 0882C]. It seemed to him that the signal in the church, customarily summoning the brethren to the night praises, was being rung. He therefore rose and, hearing the bell as it seemed ring loudly, hurried toward the church.

As he passed through the same house in which he had been lying, he looked round at the beds of the brethren and saw some already risen and others preparing themselves to rise. But when he had passed through the house and reached the adjoining cloister, the sound of the signal—which ought to have been heard much more clearly from so near—seemed to have utterly ceased. Supposing that the signal had stopped sounding because of his tardiness and that everyone had gone before him to the church, he walked more quickly. But when he came to the larger cloister, instead of the brightness of lamps which, by custom, illuminates everything at the hour of rising, he encountered darkness [Col. 0882D]. And when he approached the church, he found shut the doors which he was accustomed to find open. There too, putting his ear to them in case he might hear the voices of those chanting psalms, he perceived everywhere the deepest silence.

Astonished, therefore, and unable to enter the church, he returned to his dormitory, where he found all those whom he had earlier seen risen lying down and asleep. Coming to himself, then, he recognized that it had been a demonic illusion. Since they cannot endure that any time should be free from their malice, when by divine ordering they are restrained from a greater possibility of harm, they busy themselves with whatever lesser harms they can. For, being enemies of human nature with their whole might, when they cannot injure souls, they are at least troublesome to the bodies themselves, insofar as they can be [Col. 0883A]. Thus they often disturb monks in dreams so that, having lost the hours suitable for sleep, they sleep when they ought to be awake and so lose the gain of holy vigils.

I have many times received the complaints of many concerning such disturbances. Some said that while they slept their coverings had been stolen from them by demons during the night and thrown some distance away; others said that when demons tried to steal those same coverings, they had violently torn them away; some affirmed that, while relieving nature in more secluded places, demons had stood beside them in mockery. Moreover, at night they sometimes assailed with many terrors certain men who, while others rested, sought the holy thefts of prayer and for that purpose walked through the cloister and churches; so that they visibly rushed upon some of them and, beating them, threw them to the ground [Col. 0883B].

## CHAPTER XVIII. Concerning the novice Armannus, whom the devil terrified in the form of a bear.

I myself saw a certain brother named Armannus. While he was a noble and wealthy knight in the world, touched by the divine Spirit and intending to renounce the world, he first sent to Cluny horses and garments of great value, a great weight of silver, and almost all that he possessed; then, poor and as a pilgrim, he set out for Jerusalem. There, after worshipping at the Lord’s tomb and refreshing himself for some time by the sight of the holiest places, he saw that the end of life—which, as he later told me, he greatly desired to attain there—was being deferred [Col. 0883C; another reading: conveyed]. He returned and put on the religious habit at Cluny.

With this change, he so altered his mind from every worldly attachment that neither the common goods nor the private gains of various ascetic exercises could satisfy the spiritual ardour of his heart. Neither day for prayer nor night sufficed for him; he scarcely yielded to food or sleep, so great was his zeal. Though I often admonished him to be more sparing in such matters, since he seemed to exceed due measure, he would not yield because of his excessive fervour of spirit.

It happened, then [another reading: therefore], after the Lord’s Nativity, on the night preceding the day of blessed John the Evangelist, that he, still a novice, lay in the above-mentioned cell of the novices with the other novices. And behold, he began to cry out terribly [Col. 0883D], and so persistently that all were compelled to rise from their beds and run to him from every side. They came and found him speaking incoherently. Then a great number came to me where I was lying. Since, because of the prescribed silence of the night, they could not speak, they indicated by gestures that something strange had occurred. I rose and reached the suffering brother with them. I found him distraught and shouting, raging as though mad.

I remained with the brethren beside him until daybreak. During that time some prayed to the Lord for him, while all grieved deeply over his suffering. As dawn approached, he gradually ceased crying out and at last fell asleep while the brethren stood by. A little later he awoke and began to speak calmly with me [Col. 0884A]. When I asked him whether he knew what he had suffered, or what had been the cause of such loud and disorderly shouting, he answered:

“Wearied by my customary prayers, when I had lain down in bed and was overcome by a light sleep, I felt a bear lying upon me so terrible that the horror of that incomparably dreadful vision surpassed every human terror. Yet, awakened from sleep by that same fright, I began as though to despise the dream I had seen. But again, wholly awake, I saw above me the bear whom I had seen while sleeping, raised so far in the air that I could have touched him with my hand if I wished.

“But who could adequately describe the appearance that was before me? The gaping jaws of that accursed mouth were horrible beyond all measure, as it is written of him: ‘Round about his teeth is terror’ (Job 41) [printed: Job 14]. His claws were very long, curved back, and stretched out with the keenest eagerness to seize; the whole form of his shaggy body growled fiercely, as though already about to snatch its prey. What else could I suppose but that I was immediately to be torn to pieces and devoured? The devil, having long wearied me with this terror, compelled me to lose my mind, as you saw. Now, delivered by the Lord’s mercy, I know what I suffered and from whom, and I give such thanks as I can to my deliverer.”

The brother related these things, as stated, to me and to all who were present. Because he had contracted great weakness from that terror, he could not attend the community for three days; but when those days had passed, strengthened by his weakness, he rose again for his former combats against malignant spirits.

## CHAPTER XIX. That an angel of the Lord marked with the cross of Christ the place where the brethren die.

[Col. 0884C]

Since I have narrated the open battles of the ancient enemy against Christ’s soldiers, fought and overcome in that memorable place, it is fitting to show also certain palms of those victories openly bestowed, so that, as I have shown the envy of malignant spirits toward blessed men, I may likewise show the watchful protection of holy angels over them. For those whom the former were known often to have tempted were often, by God’s command, glorified by the latter.

Therefore, just as I have recounted one instance among innumerable encounters with enemies, so I shall tell a few among the many miracles of heavenly visions [Col. 0884D]. A German named Eppo, received as a monk by the often-mentioned blessed Father Hugh, lived religiously throughout the rest of his life. When the hour of his calling drew near, he was seized by illness and, according to custom, carried to the infirmary. Other brethren were there as well, suffering from various illnesses; some of them, nearer to death than the rest, were drawing almost their last breath as nature gave way.

Meanwhile the brother already mentioned, as his sickness worsened, was himself brought to extremity and struggled in the crisis between life and death. Yet still sound in mind and speech, he saw an unspeakable troop of demons rushing in with firebrands smoking with flame and raging everywhere through that infirmary in furious violence [Col. 0885A]. While they raved and turned this way and that, behold, the blessed Apostles came from heaven, gently encouraged the frightened brethren not to be afraid, and immediately put those brigands to flight by the glorious presence of their coming. The words of the speaking saints were heard by those standing by, but their persons were not seen.

Thus, when the house of God had been cleansed of unclean spirits by the apostolic presence, the glory of the heavenly vision increased, and holy angels joined the blessed Apostles. In the middle of the house there is a place large enough for one body, fitted out for this purpose: that brethren, laid there in ashes and haircloth, may render their last breath to God. The brother who beheld this vision shrank from that place with such an unthinking fear that he could not endure to approach it at all [Col. 0885B].

While he was contemplating the things just described, he looked and saw an angel of the Lord stretch his hand aloft and mark that same place with the sign of the holy cross. When this was done, the vision was taken from his eyes. With every foolish fear now removed from his heart, after a little while he had himself placed in that same spot, and there gladly entrusted his soul to the saints who had appeared.

## CHAPTER XX. Concerning Brother Benedict, who while dying saw a multitude in white.

There was another man also, like the great Benedict described in Scripture, blessed both by grace and by name—Benedict—whose equal in sacred studies I do not know whether I ever saw. Before he entered the monastic order he had been a very devout priest [Col. 0885C], so much so that before becoming a monk he lacked scarcely anything belonging to a monk. But, as it is the custom of holy men always to regard the good they do as nothing and with their whole desire to strive to ascend to greater things, he changed his habit at Cluny and became a true monk.

If I attempted to describe his life point by point, he would not deserve passing mention but lengthy treatment. A short chapter could not set forth the man whose holy manner of life could scarcely be adequately treated by an entire book. But since the necessity of the work I have undertaken forbids this, let this at least be a slight memorial of the blessed man, lest the example of so true and perfect a monk in our times should seem to have been wholly buried with him [Col. 0885D].

For who in these worst of times—when, as the Psalmist says, “the holy man has failed, and truths have been diminished among the children of men” (Psalm 12 [printed: Psalm 2])—was so intent upon heavenly pursuits? Who trampled the world and all worldly things so completely? Who, uprooting from himself in so general a way every offspring of vice, sowed the field of his mind with the sweet and fragrant plants of every virtue?

For, as the Apostle says, “we speak before God in Christ” (2 Corinthians 12), I call as witness the very one before whom we speak that I speak no otherwise than I believe: namely, that scarcely the perfection of any virtue was lacking to this man. When could one adequately describe his humility, by which he submitted himself to everyone and, in accordance with the precept of the Rule, considered himself inferior and more worthless than all? [Col. 0886A] When could any discourse declare his charity, by which he embraced all the brethren in such a way that he seemed to live not for himself but for everyone, according to the measure of his office? When could his patience be set forth, with which he seemed singularly endowed?
