For because of his outstanding zeal for justice, which together with his other virtues made him burn against the faults of negligent brethren, he was among those whom blessed Benedict ordered to be circuitors of the monastery, for the greater safeguarding of discipline. Since in that ministry he spared no one, and treated superiors and inferiors alike in respect of rebuking vices, without any distinction of persons, he endured many verbal insults from some who did not dare strike him.

I remember that he was often attacked by such persons in the common assembly of the brethren with false or almost groundless accusations; countless times, as though he were guilty, he lay prostrate on the ground, although he had committed absolutely no fault, and answered only that he was guilty [Col. 0886B]. This was his practice: whenever he was accused, he almost never denied the accusation. He was continually silent unless a certain and serious cause compelled him to speak. His words were very few, remote from trifles, jokes, and every kind of idleness.

If conversation turned to spiritual matters, it never occurred without sighs or without tears. His psalmody was unceasing, and he meditated upon the Holy Scriptures night and day. For this reason he always carried a glossed psalter about with him, since he did not chant the Psalms carelessly, as some do, but with the utmost attention and devotion. If he came upon anything he did not understand, he immediately turned his eyes to the glosses [Col. 0886C]. He spent the whole day chanting psalms and meditating, and the night in watching and prayer. Even during the long winter nights he scarcely rested in bed for the briefest time.

Whenever he could secretly withdraw to the altars, the need for rest scarcely ever kept him in bed. But when, for the observance of the common order, he dared not be absent from bed, he used it more for sitting than lying down. Yet even that sitting was not idle: his eyes rarely ceased from tears, and his tongue never from psalmody. He had made it his practice to afflict a body worn out by countless torments with extremely harsh haircloths throughout almost his entire life [Col. 0886D].

The same blessed man had as his cell an oratory in a very high and remote tower, consecrated in honour of Saint Michael the Archangel; this place served his devotion more especially than all other places in the monastery. There, wholly intent night and day upon divine contemplation, he transcended in mind all mortal things and almost continually attended, with the most blessed angels, upon the inward vision of the Creator. This place alone was indeed then witness to these unceasing prayers, these constantly overflowing tears, these harshest scourgings, and these daily sacrifices; yet it could not altogether conceal them from us. For holy men always labour to conceal their works in hidden retreats; but if men are silent, the stones cry out [Col. 0887A].

If my pen now turns to the appearance of his body, it will be judged sufficient merely to speak of him. His emaciated body, thin face, untrimmed hair venerable in its very greyness, downcast countenance, eyes scarcely ever open, and mouth without rest chewing over sacred words showed a man dwelling not on earth but in heaven. To this listener, certainly not deaf, the Apostle spoke: “Seek the things which are above, where Christ is seated at the right hand of God; set your mind on things above, not on things upon the earth” (Colossians 3). He too could have said with the Apostle: “But our citizenship is in heaven” (Philippians 3 [printed: Philippians 2]).

But because, as I said above, my purpose was to tell not everything—an impossible task for me—but certain things about his holy manner of life, lest the memory of the blessed man should utterly fall asleep, having briefly set these matters forth, my account now turns to his glorious end [Col. 0887B].

Having thus completed the course of his life in every exercise of virtue, he was brought swiftly to his end by bodily infirmity. It was the Paschal season, when, after the forty days of fasting had passed, Christ found his flock purer and like a more mature harvest; he took many from this light and stored them, like chosen grains, in the heavenly granaries. For at that time many, struck by a slight illness, immediately followed, as it were, the beckoning of the Lord who called them.

Among these the man of God, as stated, lay ill. After he had been made fit to ascend upon the heavenly journey by the anointing with holy oil, the saving reception of Christ’s body, and the common absolution of the brethren, there came the last day of labour, the first of reward [Col. 0887C]. He lay in bed, awaiting the Bridegroom with a lamp full of oil—that is, a conscience full of testimonies of virtues—and, I suppose, saying with the Apostle: “This is our glory: the testimony of our conscience” (2 Corinthians 1).

Looking, therefore, he saw an infinite multitude clothed in white approaching and gradually filling the entire space of the house. When he saw the house filled with those most splendid spirits, he thought it was the assembly of the brethren. He called the keeper of the sick, a man of good religious character named Otgerius, and said to him: “Brother Otgerius, is this our custom, that the community should come to the infirmary clothed in white? Believe me, today I see what I have never heard to have happened before.”

Truly, although the blessed man’s body had lost its strength, the vigour of his mind and his zeal for the house of God still flourished in him, as they always had. But when the brother affirmed that no men in white were in that infirmary, Benedict persisted in the same opinion and added: “I greatly wonder how you can say this, when not one part of the house but the whole is full of these men in white, and those same persons surround you on every side where you now speak” [Col. 0887D].

Then at last he understood that the assembly of which he was speaking was not one of men but of blessed angels. Without doubt they had descended from heaven for their fellow citizen, who had always in mind lived with them upon earth, so that through the very presence of his spirit he might dwell with them eternally in heaven. And he who here, “through a mirror and in an enigma,” according to the Apostle, had hungered intensely for the desirable vision of God, might, filled with the revelation of God’s glory, see him face to face (1 Corinthians 13).

A short interval followed, and the servant of God, summoned by the white-robed and glorious spirits whom he had seen, died. Entrusting his blessed soul to them, he reached, as it is worthy to believe, the heavenly kingdoms in their company. But lest anyone suppose that I rashly affirm this when I say that his soul was lifted to heaven as though without purgatorial punishments, let him understand that those in whom nothing remains requiring purification need no purification [Col. 0888A].

Since no one can deny this, he may perhaps hasten to ask whether this man had been so purified. I, however, insofar as it is granted to human beings to know, say that this man so cleansed his soul in this life by God’s grace through various exercises of holy works that I believe nothing remained in him to be cleansed. If this is granted to many even without martyrdom, why should it not be granted to him? A man whose crimes were none, whose even venial faults could scarcely ever be detected—could he not be cleansed, lest he be tortured by the fires of the age to come, through so many tortures of his body and so great persistence in sacred studies? Indeed, he could [Col. 0888B].

He ought by no means to experience the flames that avenge sins, since within himself he had subdued the heat of every desire. Nor did penal fire find anything in him to refine away, for divine fire had purified him wholly.

## CHAPTER XXI. Concerning Turquillus, prior of the sisters of Marcigny.

> [Note: Col. 0887. In MS S. V.: “Concerning a certain man who, caught up out of the body, saw the glory of God.”]

Another brother also, named Turquillus, a man likewise proved in every sincerity and truth of virtue, who from youth to extreme old age bore the yoke of the monastic order with the utmost gentleness, and who in the very mild and humble appearance of his body and face displayed something heavenly, carried out, by my appointment, the care of the sisters of Marcigny. Having administered it most religiously for some time, he began, when bodily sickness came upon him, to draw near to paying the common debt of death [Col. 0888D].

While brethren stood around him on every side as he lay in ashes and haircloth, he was suddenly caught away in spirit from them and became silent. For this reason a certain brother among those standing by, named Unfredus, a man of honourable religious life, who because of the familiarity by which he had always been especially attached to him, bent toward him and asked whether he had seen anything of spiritual things. He replied in these words: “I have seen the Lord,” he said, “and his sweet company” (Latin: *Vidi Dominum, et dulce consortium ejus*).

After saying this not in ordinary words but in the Latin words just set forth, he died after a short interval. And since I have mentioned Marcigny, a miracle which once occurred there through divine power must by no means be passed over in silence [Col. 0889A].

## CHAPTER XXII. The miracle that occurred in the same monastery of Marcigny.

> [Note: Col. 0889D. In the same manuscript: “How fire was extinguished in the monastery of Marcigny by divine power.”]

This place holds a singular grace among other holy places of nuns and shines forth, as it were, with a brightness peculiarly its own among the shining stars of heaven. There a multitude of noble women, including women descended from the loftiness of royal blood itself, despise riches, scorn honours, trample pride underfoot, subdue luxury, and, following Christ’s poverty, conquer the world together with its prince by their own renunciation. Of their number, very many, bereft by the death of their husbands, refused to enter second marriages; others, though their husbands were still alive, left them; some, untouched by every corruption of the flesh, preferred the angelic honour of virginity to carnal pleasures [Col. 0889B].

Yet all alike, surpassing feminine weakness with masculine constancy, subject not only all worldly things but even themselves to themselves. By manual labour, psalmody, constant prayer, and unceasing weeping, they either wash away the stains of their former life or strive to increase their heaps of merits. Despising altogether every visible thing, they spur one another on to kindle themselves in the love of invisible things.

Among all these good practices, by a grace almost singular and previously unheard of, they condemn themselves to perpetual enclosure. Thus, after they have once made profession according to the Rule and been joined to the body of the monastery, they never, for any necessity whatever, pass beyond—not merely, I do not say, the boundary of the walls, but even the very regular houses in which they dwell [Col. 0889C]. They themselves have forbidden themselves, by the command of their abbot, the customary liberty allowed to other nuns of riding or walking abroad, lest on any occasion either the world should see in them anything it might desire, or something harmful should compel them, even during an outing, to see or hear it. For him whom they have wholly driven from the gaze of their minds, they disdain also to see with their bodily eyes.

> [Note: Col. 0889D. We have added this entire clause from the manuscript.]

For, according to the Apostle, the world is dead to them and they to the world (Galatians 6), because on no occasion can they be seen by anyone. From the very entrance at which they are received into religion, their eyes are veiled and their faces covered with the veil customarily placed upon them; they wear the veil itself, as though it were a burial-cloth, until the day of death, in remembrance and preparation for their departure [Col. 0889D].

Therefore, enclosed in a saving cloister and, if I may so speak, buried in a life-giving tomb, they await everlasting spaciousness in exchange for their present confinement, and a blessed resurrection in exchange for their grave. Hence they chose to die rather than go out, to perish before crossing the threshold of the appointed door.

This became evident when, at a certain time, fire accidentally broke out in the houses of the village surrounding them. Balls of flame were carried upward, and, after all the surrounding houses had been burned, the fire drew near to the dwellings of those holy women [Col. 0890A]. The people raised a cry to heaven, more anxious lest the sacred houses should be burned than about their own losses. Everyone ran to the defensive works of the surrounding wall; climbing on the roofs of the houses, they prepared with all their strength to oppose the flames. They threw far away whatever dry material they found lying above; they eagerly poured collected water onto the fire; they left nothing untried that might avail to repel the force of the blaze.

But in vain. For the air, stirred by the wind, gave increased strength to the flames and, driving smoke mingled with fiery vapour into the faces and eyes of the defenders, prevented them from defending [Col. 0890B]. After resisting for some time, at last defeated by the violent conflict of the elements, they abandoned the roofs. Throwing themselves down here and there to the ground, they now strove to save not the houses but their own bodies.

With the obstacle removed, the fire ranged freely everywhere. Attacking the nearer part of the buildings, it consumed great masses of timber with a terrifying roar. Then [another reading: when] the sorrowful voice of all filled everything with a confused clamour, and, ignorant of any plan of deliverance, they expected nothing but the final destruction of the handmaids of God.

At that time there happened to be in the place the venerable Hugh, archbishop of the Church of Lyons [Note: Col. 0890D. Hugh, archbishop of the Church of Lyons. He is also mentioned by Ivo, Letter 18, and by Saint Anselm, Letter 11, Book II, and Letters 24 and 123, Book III.], a man of great moral excellence and religious life, whom Pope Urban had appointed legate over almost all the Gauls. Everyone fled to him as to a father and, as often happens in troubled circumstances, anxiously sought counsel from him [Col. 0890C]. Above all, they begged him to persuade the enclosed holy women to leave, and not, as their shepherd, allow so great a flock of Christ’s sheep to perish in the fire.

Moved by this, the archbishop hurried into the cloister, assembled them all swiftly, and urgently exhorted them to yield to the danger. When they wholly refused and steadfastly declared that they could die before they could violate their purpose, the bishop said: “By the authority of blessed Peter and of the lord pope, in whose stead I act, and by obedience to our [another reading: your] abbot, I command you to leave this place at once and not allow yourselves to be burned here with your dwellings in the fire.”

To this a sister of very great [another reading: great] nobility and singular manner of life, named Gisla, whom I myself also saw many times, aflame with spirit and faith, answered: “Father, the fear of God and the command of our abbot enclosed us within these bounds which you see, to remain there until death, so that we might escape eternal fire [Col. 0890D]. Therefore, under no circumstances can we cross the limits of penance set for us, even by a step of the foot, for any necessity whatsoever, unless we are released by him who enclosed us in this place in the name of the Lord.

“Therefore, lord, if it please you, do not command what it is not lawful for us to do. But as you command us to flee the fire, so rather command the fire, armed with the power of Christ our Lord, to flee from us.”

Astonished at the woman’s faith, and suddenly himself filled with faith, the archbishop went outside. Gazing upon the flames before all present, with his face wet with tears, he said: “In the name of the Lord, and through the power of faith of the woman who has now spoken, withdraw, pestilent fire, from the dwellings of the handmaids of God; do not dare to inflict any further harm.”

When these words had been uttered by the bishop, as those who saw it testified to me, the vast mass of flame was suddenly checked by an invisible power; as though barred by an iron wall, it could proceed no further. Without any human assistance, without a single drop of rain, it extinguished itself with incredible speed [Col. 0891B].

Thus, by a magnificent and unexpected miracle, divine mercy showed that the purpose of the holy women was pleasing to it; and, by the merit of true faith, it demonstrated that all things are possible to one who believes, as it had promised in the Gospel.

## CHAPTER XXIII. Concerning a dead knight who appeared three times to a certain priest.

I remember that I promised above that I would first bring forward into the middle of my work the visions or revelations of the dead which I had heard had occurred at Cluny or nearby; and thus, having first set down those which I had learned of at close hand, I would gradually carry my pen onward to more distant matters. I did indeed begin to do as I had intended; but, drawn aside by other miracles to be related from the same place, I wished to insert some things of, I believe, no lesser usefulness. Now that these have been completed, let my pen return in orderly fashion to the matters it had proposed.

There still lives in the district of Vienne a priest named Stephen, a man pre-eminent among many men of his order for his reputation for uprightness and religion. Before many brethren who were with me, he assured me on his faith that the things I am about to relate were true. Since he said that he had seen them himself, I introduce him as the speaker, so that the account may be heard not from me but, as it were, from the very man who first related it to me.

“A certain knight,” he said, “from the castle of Moras, named Guy, having been wounded in battle and carried home from there, came to his last moments. As he lay in bed, his own bishop—the archbishop of Vienne, namely Guy, who afterwards presided over the Roman see [Note: That is, under the name Calixtus II, in the year 1118.]—came to visit him and, with pastoral concern, urged him to confess his sins. I too was present, since the care of him after the archbishop belonged to me, and the archbishop had kept me with him to hear that confession.

“The sick man faithfully confessed his sins, insofar as his memory could assist him in confessing, and deserved to receive solemn absolution from the lord archbishop. A few days later he died and was buried beside a church belonging to Cluny, called Mantula [Note: In the diocese of Vienne; the Catalogue of the benefices of the Cluniac order also calls it the priory of St Peter of Menthula, commonly Menthe.].

“Not long afterward, I was travelling at midday beside the wood adjoining the aforementioned castle of Moras, when suddenly I heard behind me a noise like that of an immense army. Terrified by it, I entered the nearby wood to hide myself. Plunging into its thick growth, I sat down in what I thought was such a place that I could see those passing by without being seen by them. Then, as a great host of armed men passed by, the knight whom I mentioned above as dead suddenly stood before me, mounted on horseback, his shield held before his breast and leaning upon a military lance. At first sight of him I shuddered. But, seeing that I was terrified, he said:

“‘Do not be afraid. I have come here not to strike fear into you, but to ask for mercy. I suffer dreadful torments for my sins, especially for two which I forgot while I was confessing the rest. One was this: long ago, with certain other knights, I broke into a cemetery to which very many common people had fled with their possessions for greater safety, and violently took one ox from a certain peasant. Likewise, I imposed unjust exactions upon land which was not mine by right, and compelled its inhabitants to pay them to me for a long time. I therefore ask you to go to my brother Anselm and entreat him on my behalf to restore what was taken in my stead, and to make satisfaction for me to those whom I injured. If he does so, I shall without doubt be freed from the punishments that I suffer.

“‘But I know my brother’s hardness, and that he will by no means comply when you report these things to him. Therefore, let what I am about to say be a sign to both you and him, so that neither of you may be permitted to doubt the certainty of the matter. You know the money which you had stored in a chest and with which you intended to go to Saint James: when you return home, you will find that it has been stolen. Moreover, before coming to you I appeared in his own house to William, a knight of the castle of Moras known to you. When you ask him, you will hear from him all that I have now told you.’

“He said this and immediately vanished from my sight. Overwhelmed with fear, and despairing of my life because I had conversed with a dead man, I departed from there as quickly as I could. When I came home, I found my chest broken open and the money of which he had spoken gone. I went to the knight to whom he had said that he had spoken, and learned from him that all these things had indeed been said. But I had no opportunity to approach the dead man’s brother, because he was absent for several days.

“Meanwhile, one day when private business compelled me to travel, I turned aside into a pleasant place by the road, where a great multitude of willows imitated the seclusion of a small wood. Wishing to rest there a little, I sat down. Without delay I saw the knight already mentioned, wearing his usual arms, standing before me. And as I, troubled by doubled fear, attempted to break into speech, he spoke first:

“‘Ah, Lord Stephen! What a fine messenger I chose to send to my brother concerning my salvation! I thought indeed that you pitied me; but, as I see, however I may fare, you do not care for me.’

“But I, with my fear greatly increased, replied as best I could: ‘It was not through neglect that I delayed what you had requested, but because I did not find the brother to whom you had sent me. Yet as soon as you depart, I shall go to him without delay and tell him what you first requested. Only I beg you to leave quickly, for my heart is greatly disturbed by the sight of you and does not permit me to converse with you longer.’

“‘You have nothing to fear,’ he said, ‘for, as I have already said, I have been permitted to come to you not so that I may harm you, but so that you may have mercy on me.’

“With these words he vanished. But I, driven by great fear and no longer daring to delay the commission laid upon me, went with the knight to whom he had revealed himself to the often-mentioned brother of the dead man, and recounted to him in order all that his brother had commanded.

“But he, being a man wholly devoted to the world, either not believing or making light of what he heard from me, answered: ‘What is my brother’s soul to me? He had his own possessions while he lived. Why did he not make satisfaction for himself to those whom he injured? Let him look to himself. I do not wish to do penance for his sins.’

“Having received this answer from him, we departed. A few days passed, and, while I sat alone in my house reflecting upon what I had seen, suddenly the often-mentioned dead man appeared to stand before me—not now on horseback but on foot, not armed but unarmed. Nearly driven mad by excessive terror, I burst out in these words:

“‘By the power of almighty God and all His saints, I adjure you, whatever spirit you are, depart and cease to harass me with such terrors.’

“And he said: ‘Since you are thus disturbed by my coming, know that you will see me no more in this world. Yet God has willed that I appear to you a third time, so that I may deserve to obtain through you what I cannot obtain through my brother. If you consider it rightly, you too ought to pity me more than my brother does. He was my brother according to the flesh; you were my spiritual father in God.’

“And I said: ‘I too will do for you what I can; only, I beg you, depart quickly.’

“After these words he was immediately withdrawn from my sight. I then went at once to the peasant from whom he had said that he had taken the ox and paid him the price of the ox. For he had told me who the man was and where he lived. But regarding the other matter, since it exceeded my resources, I was unable to do anything. Nevertheless, gathering a number of priests, I caused the solemn sacrifices of God to be offered on the appointed day; I distributed alms to the poor according to my ability; and I asked many men of both clerical and monastic orders to pray to the Lord for him.”

## CHAPTER XXIV. Concerning Guy [Wido], bishop of Geneva.

[Note: The manuscript adds: “how he appeared after his death.”]

After the vision which I have related, let Guy, bishop of Geneva, be brought forward, and let it be explained what similar thing happened concerning him. He was of great nobility according to the world and, for that reason, lived more dissolutely than befitted a bishop. For, being the brother of Aimon, count of that same city, relying both upon secular rank and ecclesiastical dignity, and overflowing on every side with power and riches, he served the world more than God, and carnal rather than spiritual pursuits.

Although he neglected many things that ought to have been done and did things that ought not to have been done, nevertheless he earnestly devoted himself to works of mercy: he generously distributed alms to the needy, fed the hungry, clothed the naked, patiently listened to the complaints of the afflicted, and kindly aided many according to his ability. He honoured ecclesiastical persons magnificently, especially those whom he heard to be more religious; above all he devoted the full affection of his heart to monks. He gave them not only the service of reverence but many gifts from his own property. Among them he embraced the brethren of Cluny with singular love and bestowed very much upon them in hope of eternal reward. For, to pass over the other things which that nobleman generously gave them, he granted in perpetuity to various monasteries belonging to Cluny the revenues of sixty churches and more.

When the course of his temporal life had thus ended, he departed from this light in a good confession, with repentance for his sins and contrition of heart, as those who were present testified to me. Some report that after his death he appeared in various ways to very many people. Since I was unable to find a certain author for these visions, I declined to write matters that were doubtful. From all of them I selected only one, which, because the fact had been verified, I judged worthy to insert here.

His successor as bishop was holding a synod at Geneva, scarcely a year after his death. Priests were coming to the synod in the customary ecclesiastical manner, among them a priest of good reputation. On the journey, by chance—or rather by the divine will—having become separated from his companions by some distance, he encountered the dead bishop already mentioned. Disturbed by this unusual meeting, he hesitated for a while; at last he asked him whether he was indeed the dead bishop whom he appeared to be. When the bishop replied that he truly was, the priest added:

“And what is it, my lord, or what cause has made you visible to me, though you are dead?”

The bishop answered: “Divine clemency has permitted me to appear to you so that you may assist my need. For I know that you are hastening to the synod. I ask you, therefore, to attend the holy assembly and earnestly commend me to their prayers. For I have laboured and endured many torments since the time of my death. I may soon be delivered from them if I deserve to be helped by their prayers.

“Tell the bishop and those assembled with him that, on every day of the council, they should all chant together for me the psalm, ‘Have mercy upon me, O God,’ and that they should all commend my soul to God in a common absolution. Moreover, let them endeavour to propitiate the divine majesty for my repose by saving sacrifices and alms. Let them know that I shall go to Cluny to do penance, and thence shall proceed to Jerusalem to complete it. When you have told them all these things, reserve my name to be spoken only on the final day of the synod.”

Having said this, he vanished from the eyes of the man with whom he had been speaking. The priest entrusted with these matters hastened his steps, came to the synod, and faithfully set everything before the bishop in the presence of all. Seeing that many believed while some doubted, he asked for the book of the Gospels to be brought, and, intending to confirm by oath what he had said so that he might convince all, firmly stretched out his hand over the sacred volume. When all saw that he was unquestionably prepared to prove these matters, they restrained him from swearing; and those who had previously doubted cast every scruple of doubt from their hearts.

Then another unexpected witness arose, who, to the amazement of all, confirmed that these same things had been told to him by the dead bishop. Accordingly the good sheep graciously received the commands of their former shepherd, devoutly fulfilled all that he had ordered, and, from the overflowing charity of their hearts, voluntarily added many things besides. This was told to me by persons entirely worthy of belief who had attended the aforementioned synod and heard these things from those same reporters.

## CHAPTER XXV. Concerning a priest who died terribly.

[Note: Alternatively in the manuscript: “who, concealing his sins, died terribly.”]

Now there must be added a terrible and widely known vision, not of a man already dead but of a priest dying, which may shake the minds of hearers with fitting fear and, as with a fierce fire of concern, kindle them to avoid the evils of eternal death.

Near the castle of Liziniac, situated in the district of Poitiers, there was recently a certain priest who disfigured the heavenly dignity of the priestly order by the conduct of a most wretched life. He used his sacred ministry not to care for the souls over which he presided, but to satisfy the pleasure of his flesh. According to the prophet, feeding upon the milk of his flock and clothing himself with its wool (Ezekiel 34), without any hope of eternal things he greedily nourished himself upon the wages of a hireling. He frequently received the most pure flesh and blood of Christ, which cleanse all things, in the sacrament of the altar as an official act rather than from devotion; yet he did not restrain himself from the unclean works of the flesh.

While, like an unclean sow, he had long wallowed in the mire of lust and delighted in his own stench, he was frightened by the evil of his conscience. As even wicked persons are sometimes pricked for an hour, he sought the friendship of certain good men and joined himself, in outward appearance only, to the abbot of Bonneval and the brethren of that monastery. For a long time they admonished him concerning amendment of life and continually urged him to renounce the world, but could obtain from him nothing except at times an empty hope. Pretending that he gladly heard what they said, and always keeping them in suspense regarding his conversion, he boasted of his association with those holy men, yet was not drawn back from evil by their admonitions or example.

Persisting thus in these and other deeds of his ruined and ruinous life, and by impious obstinacy storing up wrath for himself on the day of wrath, he fell ill. When the illness grew worse after several days, he came to his last moments. The prior of the aforementioned monastery went to visit him and, at the sick man’s own request, remained with him for some part of the day.

Then, when night came and everyone else departed, the prior sat alone by his bed. The sick man began to cry out terribly to him: “Help! Help! Behold, two lions, more dreadful than all savagery, are rushing upon me. With gaping mouths and savage jaws, they want to tear me to pieces and consume me utterly. Pray quickly to the Lord that I may be delivered from them before I am consumed by their bites.”

As he spoke, he trembled and, as though fleeing those about to devour him, drew backward; fear, overcoming him, gave strength to his body. The prior too was disturbed by terror at the cry and gesture, and was not without great fear himself. Yet, driven by the necessity of the moment, he turned to prayer and interceded with the Lord for the wretched man as best he could.

As he prayed, the sick man changed his tone: “Good, good! The cruel beasts have departed, and through your prayers they no longer appear anywhere.” Since he remained in possession of his faculties until his final breath and did not suffer even the slightest impairment of sense, as some dying people do, he turned to the prior and began, as though entirely well, to speak with him about various matters.

While they exchanged many words about these and other things, after almost an hour had passed he again began to cry out, far more terribly than before: “Behold, behold! Fire descends from heaven like a flooding torrent. It is coming upon this bed of mine and will immediately burn me to ashes. Hurry, help, pray, if perhaps I may be delivered from this death also.”

As he said this, he lifted the bedclothes with his hands and arms and, disturbed by invisible fires, held them up as though they could offer some protection. But in vain. For bodily coverings could not shield from spiritual fires one whose impious works exposed him to heavenly vengeance.

The prior, with increased fear, again turned to prayer and, as far as was possible in such a case, implored the Lord’s mercy. While he continued in prayer as before, the sufferer, after a little while, interrupted his petitions with cries of joy:

“Rest now; I am safe from the fire. For when, as I said, it descended violently upon me, a linen cloth was interposed. The fire reached as far as it, but could not pass through it. Now delivered from this danger also, I beg you not to leave me until you learn what end awaits me in these matters.”

Then the prior, who wished to depart both from fear and from the obligation of hospitality, remained. Rising from prayer, he sat beside him again. As he comforted the man distressed by such terrors, and the two conversed with one another as before, the sick man suddenly became silent, carried away to invisible things. Understanding that he had been taken away from human affairs, the prior awaited the outcome.

After a long part of the night, the man returned to himself and, groaning miserably, said: “Ah! Ah! I have been taken to eternal judgment, and alas, wretched man that I am, I have been condemned to eternal death. I have been handed over to horrible tormentors, to be tortured forever in unquenchable fire with the devil and his angels. Behold, behold, a fiery frying-pan full of boiling fat, which the ministers of torments have brought before me and kindled all around in order to fry me in it.”

When the prior bent again to prayer, as he had already done twice, the man said: “Stop, stop praying for me, and do not labour any longer for one for whom you will by no means be heard.”

But when the prior said, “Brother, return to your senses, and while you are still alive seek mercy from God,” he added: “Do you think that I speak as a madman? I am not mad, but in a sound mind I affirm what I have said.”

Taking the prior’s cowl in his hand, he asked him: “Is not this which I hold in my hand your cowl?”

When the prior answered, “It is,” he added: “Just as this garment is a cowl, and just as that which lies beneath me is straw, so also that which I see before me is a fiery frying-pan.”

And while he spoke, a drop of invisible fire came from the frying-pan which he described and fell upon his hand as the prior watched; and—marvellous to relate—it consumed skin and flesh down to the very depths of the bone. Then, with a piercing groan, he said: “Behold an undeniable proof of the matter. For as this drop, which you see has fallen from the frying-pan, has consumed part of my flesh, so immediately the fiery abyss will consume me altogether.”

As the prior stood amazed at these things, he said again: “Behold, the infernal ministers themselves are bringing the frying-pan nearer, and are now, now stretching out their hands to throw me into it.” And shortly afterward: “Behold, they come rushing from every side to take the linen cloth on which I lie and cast me into the fiery frying-pan, into eternal frying.”

This was, as it were, his final farewell. As soon as he had spoken it to the prior and to those who had gathered for this dreadful spectacle, his voice failed, his neck bent back, and he handed over his spirit to be punished to the condemned spirits. Such terror seized them all that they immediately fled, and none dared remain in the house where the corpse of the dead man remained. When morning came, the wretched body was committed to burial.

A few days later, when this most terrible report had reached all those living round about, they wished to test the truth of the matter. They opened the tomb and found in the dead man’s corpse the hollow which, in the hand of the still-living priest, the drop foretelling damnation had made. According to what blessed Gregory says, the unhappy priest by no means saw all this for his own benefit, since the vision itself did him no good; rather, through him the heavenly dispensation showed how cautiously the priestly office must be administered and how reverently the divine mysteries must be handled.

Who would not be astonished at these things? Who would not tremble at so fearful a sentence of divine judgment? Who would not now recognize, in these events, not merely that faith in invisible things has arisen, but that the invisible things themselves have in large measure been made subject to bodily senses?

This is done by the merciful compassion of the Creator. Seeing that the inward eye of the human mind is blinded by the sight of bodily things, He grants that certain spiritual things may become known to some even through the flesh, so that by at least this remedy He may warn or compel them to love or fear invisible things. For what could more plainly instruct the faith of believers than that a man living in the flesh should here converse with human beings in sound mind, and there behold spiritual things with spirits?

What, indeed, did the dreadful lions, the fiery torrent, and the fiery frying-pan teach those wickedly secure persons, except that they must in no way doubt the reality of invisible things and that it is dreadful to fall into the hands of the living God? We must not believe that varieties of beasts dwell anywhere except in the present world, or that iron frying-pans are manufactured where there is no material of metals. But because the terror of future punishment can be shown to people still living in the flesh only through familiar words or images of things they have experienced, God chose by such bodily likenesses to show what souls stripped of their bodies are compelled to endure as their evil merits require.

Although these things were displayed in the times of the Fathers by more ancient miracles, divine mercy has nevertheless willed even now to confirm former things for us by revelations and to awaken by recent urgings those who despise old things, as though numbed by the sleep of negligence. Those who despise this heavenly warning cover themselves with a correspondingly greater accumulation of condemnation in God’s judgment, inasmuch as with a graver guilt they despise not only ancient things but things set before their very eyes. And because it has become my purpose to write, for the building up of faith and morals, various miracles of our own times especially, heard from different persons and verified, I have not wished to neglect any that seemed to me capable of benefiting hearers.

## CHAPTER XXVI. Concerning Geoffrey, lord of Sinemur.

[Note: Alternatively: “Concerning the apparition of the nobleman Geoffrey of Sinemur.” And in manuscript S. V.: “Concerning the prior of the sisters of Marcigny, who appeared to a certain sister after his death.”]

Geoffrey, a nobleman and lord of the castle called Sinemur, after living magnificently in the world for a long time, was touched by the divine Spirit, renounced the world, and assumed the religious habit at Cluny together with his son and three daughters. There, living for a long time in holiness and without reproach, he became prior of the sisters of Marcigny, whom I mentioned above, on account of his religious merit and prudence.

After he had humbly and kindly administered their care for several years, he was visited by bodily illness, as mortals are, and died. The sisters, retaining the sweet memory of his simple and blessed way of life, followed his funeral with many tears; and, burying him in the church, they laid him away far better in the secret places of their hearts.

Not many days after his death he appeared in a dream to one of the sisters, a woman of great mortification named Alberea, and said to her: “Do you recognize me?”

When she answered in a trembling voice, as she herself afterward reported, that he seemed to her to be Lord Geoffrey, her prior, he added: “I am indeed the man you name, and I have been sent to you in order to make known to you what concerns me.

“At the hour of my departure, malignant spirits rushed upon me with a horrible noise and surrounded me from every side as though in battle formation. Terrified at the sight of them, and thinking that I was about to be carried off by them, I suddenly saw blessed Peter appear. Driving away that assembly of demons by his presence, he said: ‘Wicked spirits, why have you come here to this man?’

“‘He is ours,’ they said, ‘and while he lived in the world he performed our works.’

“‘But,’ Peter said, ‘he repented from his heart for all those things; and, what is greater, he renounced the world.’

“While the enemy raised many objections and the apostle cleared away everything said by sound reasoning, the defeated enemy at last burst out: ‘One thing remains which can be annulled by no argument. He imposed new exactions upon garments and weapons brought from every direction to be washed at the castle of Sinemur, and neither he nor anyone after him removed them. Therefore, since the sin remains, the punishment for the sin must remain also.’

“To this the apostle replied: ‘Making no exception, he became a monk for all his sins, and therefore must beyond doubt be called to a share in salvation.’

“When he had said this, he drove the enemies into flight and delivered me from their terrors. It remains for you to make these things known to my son Geoffrey, who succeeded me in my secular inheritance, and to tell him from me to restore that evil exaction to the former custom.”

Having said this, he departed. The aforementioned sister then went to Lady Adela, sister of the king of England, formerly countess of Blois and now the humble handmaid of Christ, and told her everything. Lady Adela summoned the Geoffrey already mentioned and asked him whether his father had imposed any new custom upon the weapons and garments washed beneath the castle. When she learned from him that it was true, as the dead man had said, she recognized that the vision which she had heard from a truthful reporter who had not previously known the matter was not deceptive but real; and the testimony of the son, who knew the matter, confirmed it.

This was also my reason for writing it: although I have proposed to write among miracles only revelations experienced by waking persons, this pen should not reject those visions of sleepers alone which the certain evidence of surrounding circumstances confirms. Lady Adela certainly asked and, at the command of the dead father, warned the son to remove the harmful practice of exaction and to take careful thought that it should not likewise be imputed to him as sin. Whether he did so was not sufficiently known to me.

What answer should be made to those who despise the visions of sleepers requires no great effort. For it readily occurs to one how the laughter of mockers may be checked and how it may be made clear even to slow minds that revelations of this sort are not to be wholly despised.

## CHAPTER XXVII. Concerning a dead knight who appeared to Humbert of Beliocus.

[Note: Alternatively: “Concerning Geoffrey, a knight slain, who visibly appeared after death, not sleeping but awake, to the nobleman Humbert of Belloloco.”]

Let there be joined to the visions described above a more recent revelation, occurring almost before our own eyes. If anyone doubts it, I do not know what miracle he can thereafter believe. For it took place in such clear fashion and was proclaimed so solemnly by most trustworthy witnesses that whoever judges this obscure will be unable to find anything clear in similar accounts.

The event occurred in the year when I travelled to Spain. My pen followed it with such speed that, although it took place in the diocese of Lyons after the Nativity of the Lord, I committed it to writing in Spain during that same year, before Pentecost. I have stated this for the same reason: lest the report of the event be thought corrupted by antiquity of time. Having received certainty concerning it at Cluny, and because I could not do so earlier, I committed it to writing in Spain, as I have said.

In the bishopric of Mâcon is a castle called Beliocus. By its own nobility and by the prudent prowess of its lords, it surpasses almost all the neighbouring castles. Guichard received its lordship by hereditary right and surpassed in secular power and renown the fathers whom he succeeded, though they too were vigorous men. Using this more for worldly magnificence than divine service, as we often see in such people, he spent most of the days of his life on vanity and worldly pride, labouring greatly as though weaving spiders’ webs.

At last, corrected by God through a long illness and, through its length, despairing of life, he became a monk at Cluny in my time. There, humbling his heart and making satisfaction to God, insofar as it was granted him, by Christian repentance and confession, commending himself to the prayers of the holy brethren, he lived only a few days more. Having received the provision for his final pilgrimage—that is, the sacred body of Christ—he closed the last day of his life.

His son Humbert succeeded him in the paternal inheritance. Bound to the world by adolescence and wealth as though by strong chains, he for a time roamed without restraint along the broad paths of the world in ruinous freedom. Wishing to correct him and lead him back to the straight way of salvation, divine goodness showed him how he himself might be saved and others might be deterred from similar acts.

For on one occasion, when he had raised an army and marched against certain men who opposed him in the district of Forez—

[Note: In the district of Forez. The people of Forez were formerly Segusiavi; some prefer to call them Forinates, namely from the town of Forum Segusianorum, whose ancient inscription, placed on the wall of a temple beside the public road, mentions it as follows:

“To the divine spirit of Augustus, to the god Silvanus: the guild of carpenters established at Forum Segusianorum, at their own expense, dedicated [this].”  
*NUMINI AUG. DEO SILVANO. FABRI TIGNUAR. QUI FORO SEGUS. CONSISTUNT D. S. P. P.*]

—he lost in the battle one of his valiant knights, Geoffrey of Iden, pierced by a lance-thrust. When the battle was broken off, each man departed to his own place, either fleeing or pursuing.

Not yet two full months had passed when the knight whom I have said was killed appeared to another knight of Ansa, named Milo, as he rode without a companion through a wood adjoining that same castle. At the sudden sight of him, the knight was astonished and disturbed by no small fear, considering whether it would be better to flee or to remain. The dead man who had appeared spoke first:

“Do not be afraid,” he said, “nor think of fleeing. I have been permitted to come to you not so that I may harm you, but so that you may endeavour to help me. For above all others I have received permission to come to you, because, bound to me in the world until recently both by affection and by fidelity, you seem likely to carry out more faithfully than others the matters entrusted to you by me.

“I ask you, therefore, to carry my message to Humbert of Beliocus and, in my stead, to announce to him what I shall tell you. Attracted by his recklessness, I lost my mortal life by the sword, as you know; and even now, by his continuing fault, I am delayed from deserving to pass into the blessed life. For I had come with him to the battle in which I ended my life for a cause not sufficiently just, and I receive no relief from spiritual benefits against the dreadful torments which I suffer for that sin and countless other evils of mine.

“But what wonder if he appears ungrateful for my services and for the death I expended on his behalf, when he does not show that he cares even once, or in the least degree, for the repose of his father, who in some manner neglected his own eternal salvation for [Humbert’s] temporal welfare? For while his father suffers cruel torments for many things which he unjustly acquired for him, for countless evils which he inflicted upon various churches and especially upon Cluny, and especially for the castle and land of Aia, Humbert rejoices without any thought of his punishments and feasts splendidly every day upon those very things for which his father now groans most wretchedly.

“Let him therefore have mercy on me and on his father, lest perhaps, if he refuses now to have mercy on us wretches, he himself be added all the sooner to the number of the wretched. For if he endeavours to help us by the celebration of Masses, the bestowal of alms, and the intercession before God of good men, he will both procure our salvation more swiftly and free himself from the debt by which he is bound to us.

“But if he either does not believe you or does not obey, I shall now have to go to him in person and urge him to fulfil these things. Know also that the public absolution recently performed at Lyons in the synodal assembly has already greatly benefited me; therefore I earnestly entreat assistance of this kind and similar assistance.”

He said this, and immediately vanished from his sight. The knight, troubled by the injunctions laid upon him and afraid that, if he ignored them, some misfortune might overtake him, went to Humbert; recounting everything he had heard, he concealed none of the commands. Humbert, on hearing the message of so great and manifest a vision, was terrified with fitting fear; he trembled at what he had heard, yet did not apply suitable diligence to it. Like people of this sort, he feared more the promised coming of the dead man [Col. 0902B] than he cherished concern for his salvation. Therefore, afraid to lie alone at night, he warned his household not to leave him alone on any occasion.

And behold, after a short time had passed, the aforesaid dead man—whom invisible torments compelled, by divine permission, to communicate words to mortals—appeared visibly to him in the morning, when broad daylight had already come, as he lay awake in bed. Sitting beside his bed and displaying the form he had possessed, the clothing he had worn, and the mortal wound received on the day of his death, still apparently fresh upon breast and back, he addressed the astonished and frightened Humbert thus:

“Because you refused to hear the messenger whom I sent to you, I have myself come to you by the mercy of God, who has permitted it. For although my life spent on you made you my very great debtor, and mercy ought to have made you a kindly helper in my extreme sufferings, you neither help me nor even strive, by the small assistance of some spiritual benefit, to lessen the cruel torments I endure. Moreover, you have cast behind your back your father also, subjected to pitiable punishments and unspeakable misery; and although he is tortured chiefly on your account, do you show him no compassion? He groans amid cruel torments, and you do not care; he is tortured, and you rejoice; he suffers, and you are glad. These things displease the gracious God, who has almost already pronounced the sentence of your destruction: because you pretend to have no pity on those to whom you are most greatly indebted, you will learn by suffering like things how you ought to have shown pity.

“But in His customary goodness He has deferred justice, and has permitted me to warn you lest you take part in Count Amadeus’s expedition, which you are hastening to join. For if you go there, you will lose both your possessions and your life. Take counsel, therefore, for yourself; have pity also on us; and delay no longer to bestow upon us the relief of spiritual goods, so that, through the clemency of the Creator, you may provide both salvation for yourself and rest for us.”

While the dead knight was thus speaking to Humbert, and Humbert, made somewhat more confident by their long conversation, was preparing words to answer or to ask questions, his counsellor Wichard of Marziac—a valiant knight in secular affairs—arrived, returning from church at the early morning office. As soon as he reached the threshold of the house where the dead man was conversing with the living, the dead man who had appeared immediately vanished. Humbert, struck with fitting fear, made partial satisfaction to the dead knight’s request by giving him some assistance; and he professed that, for the sake of penance, he would set out for Jerusalem and visit the Lord’s sepulchre.

In writing these things for the edification of faith and morals, I have wished to persuade certain heretics or erring persons of our time—who either deny or doubt that ecclesiastical benefits can profit the faithful departed—to return [Col. 0903B] to the way of truth and to the teaching of the Church. Yet I have also resolved, by examples so great and clear, to warn that mortal life is not to be passed in negligence in reliance upon such aids. For behold: the heavenly mercy which refused to hear the poor man buried in hell when he begged for his brothers—“if one should go to them from the dead, they will repent”—but, foreknowing the hardness of their hearts, answered: “If they do not hear Moses and the prophets, neither will they believe if one should rise from the dead” (Luke 16)—that same divine goodness, I say, in our days did not raise a dead body, but permitted the spirit or image of a dead body to appear to the living, and to admonish and entreat them to repent and to assist it.

Let the harmful error, then, now cease, which does not believe that the spirits of the faithful are aided by prayers and by the good works of the Church. Let slothful negligence likewise be roused, which, while sleeping, trusts to be saved after death through the good works of others; and let it know certainly that, unless works worthy of salvation have preceded a person, the subsequent good works of others cannot save him after his departure. But if his works have been such that, with God’s grace accompanying him, he ought deservedly to escape eternal condemnation, then whatever imperfection remains may be expiated both by the merits of holy dead persons and by the benefits of living believers.

## CHAPTER XXVIII. Likewise, concerning another apparition in Spain

> [Note: Col. 0903D. Alternative heading: “On the apparition of a certain deceased person in Spain.”]

And since we have once entered Spain, what we heard had occurred in those same regions while we were staying there, concerning a similar matter, must not be passed over. In the regions of Spain there is a noble and famous castle, which, because of its suitable location, the fertility of the adjoining lands, and the multitude of inhabitants dwelling there—by which advantages it surpasses the neighbouring castles—is, I think, not inappropriately called Stella. In this castle there was a townsman named Peter Engelbert. Famous for his courage and abounding in worldly possessions, he led almost his whole life in the world until old age. At last, touched by Him “who breathes where He wills,” he renounced the world and received the habit of monastic profession in a monastery constructed near Nazara under the jurisdiction and Rule of Cluny.

> [Note: Col. 0903D. At Nazara, under Cluniac jurisdiction. Alfonso, king of the Spains, who himself confirmed the donation in 1177, clearly indicates in the following words who gave this monastery to the Church of Cluny: “I, Alfonso, by the grace of God king of Spain, for eternal recompense and the salvation of my soul, and also for the repose of our parent, the most illustrious King Sancho, and of my mother Queen Blanche, and of all my relatives, grant and confirm to God, to the blessed apostles Peter and Paul, and to the Church of Cluny, and to all abbots and monks serving God there for ever under the Rule of blessed Benedict, the church of Blessed Mary of Nazara, which my royal predecessors—namely King Alfonso of blessed memory, my grandfather Emperor Alfonso of good memory, and my father King Sancho—gave to you, and granted and confirmed in perpetuity, by legal right and royal sanction, solely to the Church of Cluny.”]

When I came there two years after his conversion, I heard that he had recounted a memorable vision. Its report had reached us earlier, but had not stated who its narrator was. On learning this, I anxiously asked where the narrator of so great a vision was; and I heard that he was living in a certain cell dependent upon, and quite near, the monastery of Nazara [Col. 0904B]. When the necessity of travel brought me to that place, I saw a man whose maturity of age, gravity of character, testimony of all, and very white hair strongly recommended him as wholly trustworthy.

Nevertheless, wishing to remove every scruple of doubt from my heart and from the hearts of all, before the venerable bishops of Oloron and Osma, before our companions—persons of much religious devotion and learning—and before certain others, I confronted him. Setting before him that “Truth destroys all who speak falsehood” (Psalm 5), and adding many similar warnings to deter him from lying, I not only urged him to recount what he knew for certain about that vision, but also commanded him, by virtue of the obedience which, as a monk subject to his abbot, he owed to me.

To this he added something that had until then been wholly unknown to us all: “What you ask of me,” he said, “I did not receive from another; I myself saw everything with my own eyes.” On hearing this, we rejoiced much more, since we now had not a reporter of another’s words but the most certain eyewitness of the event itself. Therefore, increasingly eager to inquire and intent on hearing, we could bear no further delay, but all began to press him to relate what he had seen. I wish now to introduce him speaking, so that whoever reads or hears this may think that he hears not only the meaning of his words, but the very words from his mouth:

> [Col. 0904D] “At the time when Alfonso, king of Aragon, held the kingdom of the greater Alfonso, the now-dead king of the Spains, it happened that he raised an army against certain men who resisted him in the region called Castile; and he decreed that from every household of his kingdom one foot-soldier or horseman should be sent there. Compelled by that command, I sent to the army one of the hired men serving me for wages, named Sancho. A few days later, when all who had taken part in that expedition were returning home, he too returned home.

> “Not long afterwards, seized by an ordinary human sickness and not struggling long with the illness, he died. Then, about four months after he had departed this life, while at Stella, in wintertime, I was lying awake in bed beside the fire in my house, the aforesaid Sancho suddenly appeared to me about midnight. Sitting by the fire and turning the coals this way and that, as though to warm himself or make them brighter, he made himself all the more recognizable to me. He was naked and without any clothing except a small and worthless covering, with which he concealed, as it were, the more shameful parts of his body.

> “When I saw him, I said, ‘Who are you?’ In a humble voice he replied, ‘I am Sancho, your servant.’

> “‘What are you doing here?’ I asked.

> “‘I am going to Castile,’ he said, ‘and a great army accompanies my journey, so that where we sinned, there too we may pay the penalties due for our sins.’

> “‘And why have you turned aside here?’ I asked.

> “‘There is hope of pardon for me,’ he said, ‘and if you are willing to have pity, you can obtain swifter rest for me.’

> “‘For what?’ I asked.

> “‘When I recently took part in the expedition which you know,’ he said, ‘drawn by hostile licence, I attacked a church with certain companions; I plundered what was found inside, and, returning, carried off priestly vestments with me. For this I am especially afflicted, subjected to dreadful punishments; and I implore a remedy from you as from my lord, with all the prayers I can. For you can help me if you strive to assist me with spiritual benefits. I further beg that, acting in my stead, you entreat my mistress, your wife, on my behalf, and that she delay no longer to pay the eight solidi which she still owed me for my service under the law governing hired labour. Let her distribute them to the poor, bestowing upon my soul—which needs them far more—what she would have supplied for the necessities of my body had I remained alive.’

> “Greatly encouraged by this conversation, I asked, ‘What has become of Peter of Jaca, our fellow citizen, who recently died? I beg you, if you know anything about him, reveal it.’

> “‘Works of mercy bestowed upon the poor,’ he replied, ‘frequently indeed, but especially during the recent famine, have joined him to the rest of the blessed and made him a participant in eternal life.’

> “And when I heard him answer me so readily and easily, I added, ‘And do you know anything about Bernerius, another fellow citizen of ours, who, as you know, also died a short while ago?’

> “‘Hell possesses him,’ he said, ‘because, when he was appointed over this town to settle disputes and conclude them by judgment, he often judged unjustly, enticed by gifts or favour; and because on one occasion he did not fear cruelly to take from a poor widow a single piece of bacon—whatever support it was for her life.’

> “Then, inflamed with still greater eagerness to ask weightier things, I added, ‘Could anything be known to you concerning our King Alfonso, who died some years ago?’

> “At this, another man, seated in the window immediately above the head of my bed, said: ‘Do not ask this man what he does not know, since his recent arrival in our regions has not yet allowed this to become known to him. But to me, who since the day of my death have spent five years among spirits of this kind, more things than are newly known to this man could not be unknown; and what you ask about the king could not be unknown to me.’

> “Startled again at hearing a new voice and wishing to see its author, I turned my eyes toward the window; aided by the brilliance of the moon, which at that time brightly illumined the whole space of the house with its light, I saw a man sitting upon the lower ledge of the window. Seeing him in the same dress in which I had seen the other, I said, ‘And who are you?’

> “‘I am the companion of the man you see,’ he said, ‘and I am travelling to Castile with him and many others.’

> “‘And do you know something about King Alfonso, as you said?’ I asked.

> “‘I know where he was,’ he replied, ‘but I do not know where he is now. For after he had for some time been tortured by severe torments among the guilty, the monks of Cluny removed him from there. But what has happened to him since then, I know absolutely nothing.’

> “Having said this, he turned to his companion sitting by the fire and said: ‘Rise, and let us begin to complete the journey we have already undertaken. For behold, the army of companions following us has now filled all the roads within and outside the castle; and because many have already passed us with the greatest speed, we are pressed to follow them quickly where we must.’

> “At these words Sancho rose, and, repeating in a mournful voice what he had previously requested, said: ‘I beg you, lord, do not forget me; and earnestly exhort my mistress, your wife, to restore to my wretched soul what she owed to my body.’”

> [Col. 0906C] Having said these things, both immediately vanished. I at once woke my wife, who was sleeping beside me in bed, calling loudly; and before I told her what I had seen or heard, I asked whether she owed anything in wages to Sancho, our common hired man. She answered something which I had until then heard from no one but the dead man: namely, that she still owed that very Sancho eight solidi. I could no longer doubt, since both the account of the dead man and the confirmation of the woman gave me complete assurance.

> When morning came, I received those eight solidi from my wife and added from my own resources whatever seemed suitable. For the salvation of him who had appeared, I distributed the money to the poor; and I increased, through my prayer and diligence, the aid of holy masses offered for him by priests, for the fuller remission of his sins. I have transmitted this vision, so clear and commendable, to both present and future generations in a faithful written account, expressing it almost word for word, for the edification of faith and morals; and I have shown, by the testimony of the dead themselves, how great is the caution necessary for mortals.

Nor does a little, but rather very much, testify to the truth of this vision: the dead man said that King Alfonso had been removed by the monks of Cluny and rescued from the torments of similarly guilty persons. For, as is known to almost all the peoples of Spain and Gaul, this same king was a great friend and benefactor of the Church of Cluny. Not to mention his innumerable other works of piety bestowed upon that monastery [Col. 0907A], that most magnificent and famous king had made himself and his kingdom tributary to Christ’s poor for the love of Christ; and each year he paid to the Church of Cluny the tribute established by himself and his father Fredelannus, namely 240 ounces of wine—alternatively *ivri*, but more correctly, gold.

> [Note: Col. 0907A. “By his father Fredelannus, namely 240 ounces of gold.” Hildebert sheds light on this passage in the *Life of Saint Hugh*, where he says: “Ildefonsus, king of the Spains, was held captive in chains by his brother Sancho. When this was learned, the abbot ordered that prayer be urgently made for the king, mindful of the love of his father Fredeleidus, who had bound himself to the monastery of Cluny by a benefaction which it had not sought.” And a little later: “Thus Ildefonsus, restored to his kingdom, lest he should ever seem ungrateful to his intercessors, arranged that, doubling his father’s tribute, two hundred ounces of gold should be assigned every year to the monastery of Cluny.”]

Moreover, he constructed at his own expense two monasteries in Spain.

> [Note: Col. 0907A. He constructed at his own expense two monasteries in Spain, in which he placed monks of Cluny. One of these monasteries was Saint Agatha; in the Cartulary of Cluny the following charter is found concerning it: “Fredelannus, by the grace of God king of the Spaniards, sends greeting and abundant affection to the beloved council of the city of Rodrigo. Let your affection know that I have given and grant the church of Saint Agatha to the monastery of Cluny and to this monk of the same monastery, named Ato, so that he may hold it from and for the monastery of Cluny, and so that it may obey and render obedience to that monastery and to no other. I will and command, moreover, that it pay annually, as tribute, eight morabitinos to the monastery of Cluny; and that the aforesaid church of Saint Agatha possess in peace, and without any opposition, all its territory together with the village of Saint Felix and all its territory. Farewell.”]

He permitted others to be built by other persons and assisted in determining where they should be built. In them he placed monks of Cluny, liberally and abundantly granting from royal generosity the means by which they might serve almighty God according to the Rule. He restored in part, in Spain, the fervour of monastic religion, which was almost dead; and by this endeavour, after his temporal kingdom, he obtained for himself also an everlasting kingdom, as it is right to believe.

He obeyed the command of the gracious eternal King, making for himself friends from the mammon of unrighteousness; and, when the stewardship of his kingdom was ended, according to the tenor of the vision just related, he was both delivered from punishments by those friends and received into eternal dwellings (Luke 16). For what could be more fitting to that merciful justice which renders to each according to his works, than that he should appear to be delivered by those whom he had aided; that mercy should be bestowed upon him by those upon whom he had had mercy; and that he should be restored to the blessed life by those whose lives, amid their present misery, he had sustained with generous support? Truly the voice heard by John from heaven is not deceptive: “Their works follow them” (Revelation 14). This was shown in that king, whom works of mercy—as though by those upon whom they had been bestowed—rescued from torments and joined to the rest of blessed spirits.

# BOOK II

> [Col. 0907]

## PROLOGUE

> [Col. 0907B]

Since I have proposed to write, for strengthening faith and instructing morals, miracles performed in our own time and known with certainty, after the matters already set forth I must add others which, I believe, are no less useful to readers or hearers. In these, as I have already said above, I observe no chronological order and avoid no kind of miracle; but as I have either learned them long ago or can learn them daily from different trustworthy persons, I commit them to writing.

For I grieve, and am angry—more than perhaps many would find credible—at the apathy of many people. Although they abound in learning, letters, and eloquence, they are too indolent to preserve in writing for the memory of posterity the wondrous works of almighty God, which are often performed in different parts of the earth for the instruction of the Church. [Col. 0907C] Although it was an ancient practice not only among the earliest Fathers of the Christian faith but also among the pagans to commit to writing whatever was worthy of remembrance, these men, imitating neither Christian nor pagan pursuits, languidly allow to perish everything that happens in their own times which might be of no small use to those who come after.

And since the divine Psalm says to God, “Let all your works give thanks to you, O Lord” (Psalm 144)—that is, let them praise you for all your works—how will God be praised for works that are unknown? How will they be known by those who did not see them, unless they are reported? How can they remain in the memory of past and future ages unless they are written down? And since all things, whether good or evil, done in the world either by God’s will or by His permission, ought to serve His glorification and the edification of the Church, how, if these things remain hidden from people, will God be glorified through them or the Church edified by them?

The unfruitful apathy of this silence has now reached such a point that nearly all things done in the Church of God or in Christian kingdoms during the last four or five hundred years are unknown to us and to everyone. So great is the apparent distance between our times and earlier times that things done five hundred or a thousand years ago are very well known to us, whereas things done since then, even in our own days, are wholly unknown. Thus we abound in ancient histories, ecclesiastical deeds, and books of the Fathers containing teachings and examples of manifold doctrine; but of events which happened in times close to our own, I do not know whether we possess even one account.

Those earlier men, most diligent investigators of useful matters, searched even among distant peoples and unfamiliar languages, to discover whether they could draw forth anything worthy and useful for humankind. Thus Egyptians carefully investigated Greek learning and language; Greeks, Latin; and Latins, Greek and Hebrew and the languages and learning of other peoples. They communicated to one another, through various writings and diverse translations, what they judged necessary. By contrast, our Latins not only investigate no foreign matters, but do not even deign to learn what is close at hand or to commend it to others in writing or speech. But let the discussion return to its purpose, and, according to the powers granted by God, let it make known to present and future readers anything worthy or useful it can discover, for God’s praise and their benefit.

## CHAPTER I. On an oppressor of churches, visibly seized by the devil and carried through the air, to the astonishment of all who were present

First, then, for the terror and correction of wicked rulers, let us relate what occurred at Mâcon. For an extraordinary event, unheard of in all earlier ages, as I think, occurred there and is reported by the celebrated and public testimony of nearly all the inhabitants. Mâcon lies within the borders of the kingdom of the Franks, which the river Saône—rising in Lorraine—and the Rhône—flowing into the Mediterranean Sea—separate from the empire of the Germans or Romans. Called a town by some and honoured with the name of city by others, Mâcon occupies fifth place among the sees of the primacy of Lyons. In ecclesiastical jurisdiction it is subject to the primate of Lyons; in secular jurisdiction, to the king of the Franks.

At one time a certain man held the lordship of this city under the title of count [Col. 0909C], exercising an abominable tyranny over ecclesiastical persons and property.

> [Note: Col. 0909D. A certain man holding the lordship of this city under the title of count. That is, William, count of Mâcon, surnamed by some Alamandus. Peter the Venerable here relates the tragedy that he was carried up into the air by a demon and never afterwards appeared, because he was hostile to the possessions of ecclesiastical persons, and especially of the Cluniacs. Bugnonius and Paradinus judged this to be a story staged and invented by the Cluniac monks in the time of Louis the Fat; nevertheless, Adémar, in the *Chronicle of the Aquitanians*, reports that something not unlike it happened earlier to William—or to another, or to the same—count of Mâcon, in these words: “William, count of Mâcon, surnamed *Buccauncta*, because he harassed the monks of the monastery of Cluny, was struck by censure from the abbot and, when he wished to walk, could not move a step.”]

Far surpassing the wickedness of other robbers, he not only plundered portions of church property, but subjected all its revenues and possessions to himself by tyrannical violence. Expelling canons from churches and monks themselves from their monasteries, he mercilessly took all the lands, all the revenues, and everything given by ancestors for their support in this life, and made them his own property. The inhabitants still point out the ruins of ancient churches from which he expelled the servants of sacred religion and reduced venerable places, filled with multitudes devoutly serving almighty God, to the solitude of a wilderness.

He so entirely withdrew himself from God and devoted himself to the world, forgetting hell and the fearful judgments of God, that, like the judge in the Gospel, he neither feared God nor respected man (Luke 18). Having abused for a long time the power granted him, becoming worse every day, and with no remaining hope of his correction, he stirred against himself the now irrevocable wrath of almighty God. He experienced in himself, most dreadfully, the sentence of Holy Scripture: “It is fearful to fall into the hands of the living God” (Hebrews 10).

Because his wickedness had provoked God not secretly but publicly, not fearfully but boldly, he was made a terror and an example to tyrannical rulers not secretly but publicly, not only invisibly but visibly. For, on a solemn day, while he sat in his own palace at Mâcon, surrounded by a crowd of knights and persons of various rank, an unknown man on horseback suddenly entered through the palace door. Before the eyes of all, who watched and wondered, he rode up to the count himself. Standing beside him, he said that he wished to speak with him and ordered—not merely advised—him to rise and follow.

The count, constrained by an invisible power and no longer able to resist, rose and went to the door of the house. There he found a horse ready; ordered by the stranger to mount it, he mounted. The stranger at once seized its reins, and immediately began, at the swiftest pace, to carry him through the air before the eyes of all. The whole city, stirred by his immense shouting and piteous wailing, rushed together to this hateful spectacle. Stupefied, they watched him speeding through the air as long as their natural sight could follow him. Hearing him cry for a long time, “Help, citizens, help!” and unable to aid him, they at last lost sight of him; and he became, as he had deserved, an eternal companion of demons.

All returned home from this horrendous sight and learned, by an unheard-of and pitiable example, as I have said above, that it is fearful to fall into the hands of the living God. That this happened as the common report of all affirms is attested by something occurring in our own days—not indeed so marvellous, but still remarkable. For the count delivered to the devil, of whom I wrote above, when he left the palace with his evil companion as described, passed through a doorway behind the palace, in a wall adjacent to it. Because of horror at the event and to preserve its memory for posterity, the citizens blocked that doorway with stones.

Otgerius, provost of Count William, recently wished to restore it and make it passable for certain matters thought necessary for public or private use. One day, having hired workmen, he was removing the barrier of stones from the doorway. He too was, to the extent of his power, a fierce persecutor of churches and, whenever a slight opportunity arose, harassed their property by various efforts. As he pressed on with this work, behold, he was invisibly seized by the devil and, before the eyes of those present, raised high into the air for a considerable distance; but he was immediately let fall. His body was severely battered in the fall, and his arm too was broken by that sudden collapse.
