Seeing this, his companions again blocked with stones the opening of the doorway which they had begun to open, and condemned it to perpetual closure in everlasting remembrance of both prodigies.

## CHAPTER II. On the man buried beneath the earth who was fed by an angel through the sacrifices and prayers of the Church

> [Col. 0911B]

The following event, which gives no small testimony in our own time to the saving sacrifice—that is, the sacrament of the most holy body and blood of Christ—must be added to the preceding accounts. In the diocese of Grenoble there is a place whose underground veins contain a great abundance of iron. It is continually extracted with much labour by inhabitants and peasants, then smelted and purified in furnaces, and sold for profit to ironworkers and others throughout the surrounding lands. Therefore the village inhabited by these people is called Ferraria.

Such people, while searching out the hidden places of the earth by digging, commonly proceed farther in hope of greater gain and persistently search the underground caverns for a larger supply of iron ore. Once, while a certain indefatigable peasant was hard at this work and keenly investigating the innermost parts of the earth by digging, a vast mass of earth suddenly fell and blocked the entrance through which he had entered. Yet because he had advanced far in digging and had left behind him a great empty space where earth had been removed, he escaped death. Like a man confined in a closed house and surrounded on every side by strong defences, he could not get out, but remained unharmed.

But enclosed in the darkness of so dark a prison, with every hope of escape removed, and as though buried in a spacious tomb, he thought that he saw death itself while still living. His wife, believing him dead when he had not appeared for several days, turned to helping his soul through spiritual benefits. For an entire year she had priests celebrate one mass for him every week, offering bread and a candle for him; and according to the custom of the Church, she diligently sought to aid, by the saving sacrament, the soul of her husband whom she believed dead. There was, however, one week in the year when the woman, occupied with other affairs, neglected to provide the mass for her husband as she had intended.

Behold, when almost a whole year had elapsed, miners tirelessly continuing their customary work gradually dug their way to the place in which the aforesaid peasant still lay hidden alive. When the imprisoned peasant heard their voices and the sound of their hammers drawing near, he began to cry out as loudly as he could. Hearing his voice, and recognizing—as men skilled in that craft—that it was the voice of a man beneath the earth, they encouraged one another and at last reached him after much labour of digging. Lighting lamps and carefully looking around, they recognized him as the man whom they knew had been buried there in the preceding year.

Astonished and almost, as was fitting, stupefied by the novelty of so great an event, they urgently asked how he could have remained alive there for so long. He replied:

> “When the mass of earth which you have not removed had blocked the opening by which I entered, and I was kept within this prison which you see, after I had remained for several days without food or light, a certain man suddenly stood beside me as I was almost failing. He brought bread and light. Strengthening me and urging me to take food, he brightly illuminated those foul shadows with the candle he carried. Refreshed by that bread for, as it seemed to me, seven or eight days, and illuminated for the same number of days by that candle, I escaped the danger of hunger and avoided the darkness of this pit.

> “After seven or eight days, he who had first come returned, bringing fresh bread and renewed light; leaving them with me, he departed immediately. Throughout the course of what seemed to me a year, he never failed to do this at almost equal intervals of time, except during one week, when, for some reason unknown to me, he withdrew both his presence and his customary gift. During that time I was greatly tormented by hunger and darkness, until that kindly preserver of my life returned and restored my life, now close to death, by similar assistance.”

When they heard this from him and recalled what his wife had done for him throughout that entire year, they immediately explained everything to him. Then they led the man out of those underground caverns and restored him unharmed to his own wife, to all his neighbours, and to the people rushing from every side to so great a spectacle—marvellous to relate!—after his year-long burial. When they assembled and examined more closely the account he told of himself, they discovered that, on the very days when the woman had a Mass celebrated for his repose and offered bread and a candle to the priest celebrating it, the bread by which he was refreshed and the candle by which he was illuminated had been offered to him in that cave.

Therefore, glorifying the Lord and giving thanks, as was truly fitting, no less than for a dead man raised to life, they recognized more clearly than light how greatly right faith pleases God, how much the offerings of believers profit either themselves or others, and, above all, how great a salvation the saving sacrifice offered to God works for those worthy of it.

## CHAPTER III. An explanation of why the writer of these accounts could not observe chronology and order in narrating events
I have often acknowledged above that, in recounting these miracles, I preserve no chronological order and avoid no kind of miracle; and I wish this to remain fixed and settled in the readers’ memory. For then they will not be disturbed by any apparent confusion or intermingling of times, once they understand that I have observed not the sequence of times but the truth of things done at whatever time. I would nevertheless have preserved the times themselves together with the deeds, if I had received both at once from my informants in that order. But because I sometimes learned last what had happened first, and received first what had been done later, I was compelled to write them not at the time when the deeds occurred, but at the time when they were related to me.

This is why, when above I described the good acts of certain good monks, I passed over the deeds of one monk of good and magnificent life. For, after I had undertaken that work and several years had already passed, I heard these matters concerning him from trustworthy persons; and what I had learned about him myself, I delayed writing down while awaiting that end of his—for he was still living in the flesh—in which all praise may safely be sung. But now that he has happily been removed from human affairs and joined, as it is fitting to believe, to God to whom he had always devotedly clung, it is time to write something about him and to commend to posterity the holy memory of this blessed man.

## CHAPTER IV. On the birth and virtuous youth of Lord Matthew, bishop of Albano.

[Note: Col. 0913D. The manuscript adds: “a monk of Cluny.”]

He was of no obscure family according to the flesh, born in the province of Rheims, with both parents distinguished, as has been said, by nobility and rich in worldly possessions. In boyhood he was given to letters; and after he had grown up, he obtained clerical office in the Church of Laon. From his earliest years, contrary to the corrupt custom of many clerics, he began to increase both in age and in honourable conduct; fleeing and detesting the frivolity and wantonness of his companions, he attached himself—something very rare among persons of this class—to clerics distinguished for integrity and religion.

## CHAPTER V. How he attached himself to the venerable Ralph, later archbishop of Rheims.

Among them he chose a cleric of more approved life, then treasurer of the Church of Rheims, named Ralph, surnamed the Green, and devoted himself especially to him in a religious intimacy. Thereafter, when that same Ralph had been taken up and appointed archbishop of Rheims—

[Note: Col. 0913D. “Ralph appointed archbishop of Rheims.” Robert of Torigni, *Chronicle*, under the year 1114: “In the metropolitan see of Rheims, after the illustrious Manasses, Gerursius having been expelled, Ralph succeeded, who bore the surname the Green.” And Ivo, Letter 190, to Pope Paschal II: “We wish Your Excellency to know that I and Lord Theobald, prior of the monastery of Blessed Martin at Paris, having heard of the pitiable and astonishing desolation of the Church of Rheims, pressed the king of the Franks, opportunely and importunately, by the freedom of personal acquaintance, that, the invader Gervasius being expelled, he should restore peace to the aforesaid Church and permit Lord Ralph, metropolitan of that Church, restored to his favour, to preside over that same Church.” Suger, in the *Life of Louis the Fat*, and the continuator of Aimoin, Book V, chapter 50, call him Rodolph, and add that he incurred very serious enmity with King Louis because he had been elected and enthroned in the see of Rheims without the king’s consent. Lisiard also, chapter 36 of the *Life of Saint Arnulf*, mentions him under the same name of Ralph the Green; and under this name he is still recorded by Nicholas the monk in Book III, chapter 24 of the *Life of Geoffrey, Bishop of Soissons*.]

—he did not abandon the man whom he had chosen. Rather, the religious and prudent young man followed for some time this man proven in life and prudence, remaining under him as a canon of the Church of Rheims, now under his authority. The devout bishop rejoiced in his company and returned him no lesser measure of affection. He saw in him what he recognized in himself, and embraced in him, as it were, an image of his own virtues. For, as a certain wise man says, “Similarity of character produces harmony of minds.” And indeed, things unlike one another can never be united, nor can different things remain in one abode. For what is separated by dissimilarity, if anyone tries to join it without some likeness, he labours in vain. They immediately spring apart from one another and can be joined only through something similar and intermediate, as has been said. This is evident in the elements, in bodies, in character, and indeed in all things; it is clearer than light.

Thus the good canon, joined to the good bishop by congruity of good character and honourable life, advanced little by little, through daily growth, toward a greater love of religion and holy conduct.

## CHAPTER VI. How, aspiring to the monastic life, he abandoned ecclesiastical honours.

From this it came about that the divine fire, springing from a spark in his breast, longed to burst into flame; and he resolved to serve God not now beneath that canonical—indeed almost secular and deceptive—covering, but under the true and sincere order of monks. He saw that those clerical institutions possessed scarcely anything of religion; that much was feigned there and little genuinely done; that all things were thrown into confusion by ambition, greed, and rivalry; and that under tonsure or clerical dress they could more properly be called hirelings than canons.

Detesting these and similar kinds of death in them, and seeking to flee, as from the midst of Babylon, according to the prophet’s voice (Isaiah 48), he approached the bishop and asked that a private conversation be granted him. When this was obtained, he uncovered part of the secrets of his heart, but kept the larger part hidden under silence. For he feared that, if he disclosed everything to the bishop who loved him, that same bishop, bound to him by affection, would oppose his efforts. He knew indeed that the bishop desired in every way the progress of his virtues; but he feared his departure from himself as the tearing of some limb from a body.

For this reason, concealing whatever he had resolved concerning renunciation of the world, he disclosed the rest and declared that he had received canonical revenues in a manner less than canonical. He feared that ecclesiastical revenues, which ought to be given and received freely, had been provided for him by a rich and secular father, using an inducement of price or request; and that, together with bodily support, eternal destruction had been acquired. He said that he had not known of such transactions, nor had he been summoned to dealings of that sort. Nevertheless, he said that he feared, on the basis of report alone brought to him, that he might be called a Christian only in name and be proved in the reality of things to be a disciple of Simon.

“The Father,” he said, “ought to provide for the salvation of his son and to take care lest by some mischance a sheep from the number of the flock entrusted to him should perish. And, to make an end of speaking and reveal what has hitherto lain hidden in my heart, I surrender into your hand all prebends and all ecclesiastical revenues given me in whatever manner, and I renounce altogether all ecclesiastical benefices—those bestowed upon me not spiritually but bodily—up to this point.”

Hearing this from the young man, and rejoicing that he had surpassed countless old and decrepit men in devotion of soul, the bishop dissolved into tears and urged him not to do it, nor to renounce ecclesiastical benefices because of an uncertain fault. But he did not yield. Persisting steadfastly in the purpose he had begun, he completed what he had undertaken. Thus, renouncing ecclesiastical affairs on this ground—indeed all secular business—he departed, taking leave of the bishop, who sent him on to his other affairs. He did not delay long, but hastened swiftly to fulfil what he had conceived concerning his eternal salvation.

## CHAPTER VII. How, choosing Cluny because of its celebrated reputation for religion, he received the monastic habit at Saint-Martin-des-Champs.

[Col. 0915C]

Considering where he should turn or where he should fulfil the resolution he had conceived of living religiously, he chose Cluny. For he had heard that monastery praised by his archbishop of Rheims, both before and after the latter held episcopal office. He had heard him extolling with many praises the rule and practice of the Cluniac order; he had observed him preferring Cluniac observances to many different observances of religious persons. He judged that a man learned in divine things and experienced in human affairs could not lightly be mistaken in this: a man who by long practice and subtle meditation could be ignorant of almost nothing in divine matters, and who had left almost nothing in secular learning—indeed, one might say wisdom—unattempted.

Trusting therefore in his words, he resolved to join the religious order which he had heard him approve most highly. But what, I ask, was that fervent and devout soul to do, so inflamed with divine fire that it considered it death to defer long the thing it had conceived? The spirit pressed him to fulfil his vows quickly; but Cluny was far away, far away: a long journey lay between. He feared that, if so much time were allowed to the tempter, he might be overcome by the wicked enemy and the spirit he had conceived might by some chance be extinguished. Therefore, whether because he feared this, or because, as someone has said, nothing is hurried enough for a desiring mind, he did not then go to Cluny, the mother house, because it was more distant; but he turned his steps to its nearer Cluniac daughter, Saint-Martin-des-Champs.

[Note: Col. 0915D. “To the Cluniac daughter … Saint-Martin-des-Champs.” This monastery, founded by Henry I, king of the Franks, was granted by his son Philip I to Hugh, abbot of the Cluniacs, for reform. Hugh did so, replacing the canons with monks of Cluniac observance and order, as the continuator of Aimoin notes, after the royal charters already transcribed in this Library, Book V of the *History*, chapter 48, in these words: “At that time King Philip, admonished by divine inspiration, removed from the church of Saint Martin-des-Champs the clerics who served God and the altar there less honourably; and, assigning that place to the jurisdiction of the monastery of Saint Peter of Cluny, he established monks there, while Saint Hugh governed the aforesaid monastery, namely Cluny.” Hence also John of Paris, under the year 1507: “About this time,” he says, “the priory of Saint-Martin-des-Champs was founded at Paris by Hugh, abbot of Cluny; King Philip, and after him his son Louis the Fat, and other princes of France, enriched it with many great possessions.” And another anonymous historian, who lived under Philip, king and son of Louis the Pious: “This King Philip removed the clerics from the church of Saint-Martin-des-Champs and established Cluniac monks there to serve God.”]

And fittingly so: for the monastery of Saint Martin is, in its commitment to Cluniac order, religion, and fervour, so like and entirely conformed to its mother monastery of Cluny, according to its capacity, that, like an image impressed in wax, it represents more familiarly than many other monasteries belonging to Cluny the image of the original seal. Except for the distances between places, which cannot be together, they are not different but altogether one.

To this Cluniac monastery Matthew came, called by Christ not indeed from the tax-office but from the rank—indeed, the circumstance—of a canon, and asked Lord Theobald, the prior, to receive him as a monk.

[Note: Col. 0916D. “From Lord Theobald the prior.” This is the first prior of that name, concerning whom Ivo, Letter 190.]

The prior rejoiced, yet, as often happens in desperate matters, he could scarcely believe for joy that Matthew was speaking seriously. At last Matthew persuaded him that he had come for this purpose and began urgently to insist that he be received quickly. The hour, according to the Cluniac order, was unsuitable, and it was not permissible at that hour to receive anyone coming to become a monk. Prior Theobald advised Matthew to wait and await the suitable hour at which this could customarily be done on the following day.

Matthew replied that he could not bear delay: he had companions, and if the matter became known to them in any way, he would thereafter be unable to bring what he wished to completion. The prior, overcome by the argument, overcome by the young man’s devotion, and above all overcome by the loss of so great a gain should he not yield, gladly granted what was requested. He entered the chapter house, summoned all the brethren, and disclosed the reason. All rejoiced and begged that it be done quickly. Matthew was brought in haste and presented before the sight of all. At his own wish and request, he was stripped of the old man, clothed with the new, subjected to the monastic rule, and joined, so far as could or ought then to be done, to the body of the monastery.

After a short time had elapsed, he came to Cluny. Whatever had been lacking there for him concerning a written profession or the customary blessing of a monk was supplied by blessing from the Cluniac abbot; and now a monk whole in heart, speech, habit, and life, he rejoiced in the Lord that scarcely anything of monastic profession was still lacking to him.

## CHAPTER VIII. What manner of man he showed himself toward the Lord [God] in his priorate.

Sent back by his abbot’s command to the monastery of Saint Martin, after he had most fervently maintained the discipline of the cloister for seven years, he succeeded to the priorate by command of that same abbot, his prior having now died and, as certain hope concerning a good man leads one to believe, having passed to the state of blessed life.

What and how great a man he showed himself there to God, to his subjects, and to all persons near and far can scarcely be explained by me. Yet, so that I may set out in order those three matters which I have proposed: he showed and humbled himself before God by true contrition of heart and body, by repentance for former deeds or negligences, by contempt for the world, and by a most complete and almost singular fervour of devotion to God among many thousands of monks. He remained constantly in the cloister with the brethren, and after his many wanderings through the world, he persisted almost immovably—like the cloister pillar to which he clung—in diligent study of sacred reading.

Even the care of the priorate entrusted to him could scarcely separate him, even for an hour, from the fellowship of the brethren, or draw him away by any hook of worldly occupation from the attention once fixed upon God. And although nearly three hundred brethren, both within and outside the monastery, served the Lord under his leadership, and though the duty of his office compelled him to provide them bodily support, either himself or through others, he could not wholly escape Martha’s importunate demands; yet with all the desire of his soul he longed for Mary’s repose (Luke 10). Thus he chose, as has been said, the common cloister, the common oratory, and the common dwellings of the brethren, in which he might remain safer from the tumults of the world, as Moses in the tabernacle was safe from the stones of the Jews (Exodus 33).

And because with the Prophet he had asked this one thing from the Lord—that he might dwell not only in heaven but also on earth in the house of the Lord all the days of his life (Psalm 26)—and because he had preferred to be lowly in that same house of God rather than dwell in the tents of sinners (Psalm 83), he gladly remained there. There, by frequent reading, constant meditation, and most fervent prayer, commending and uniting himself to God, he cleansed away, if there were any, the blemishes of his former life—perhaps not many—and daily laid up in heaven treasures of pious endeavour through daily increases of virtues.

He left no part of contemplation untouched. Taming his body by fasts, vigils, and harsh hair-shirts, and through silence, psalmody, and the pursuits already mentioned, he strove to be wholly changed from the old into the new man, and so to make an almost complete passage from the oldness of the world into the newness of Christ. Above all he was wholly intent upon divine sacrifices and holy heavenly rites. Offering these to God not merely frequently but daily, he commended to divine mercy every worthy person, but especially the brethren of his own congregation, and most especially those entrusted to him, through that saving and ineffable sacrament.

As in certain other matters, so in this daily offering of divine sacrifice he imitated righteous Job. Of Job, after it has been said, “Rising early in the morning, he offered burnt offerings for each one” (Job 1)—that is, it is understood, for his children—it is added shortly afterward: “Job did this all his days” (ibid.). So Matthew offered the heavenly sacrifice, at the same hour as Job, that is, in the morning when he could, and daily like Job, for himself, for his subjects, and for all who belong to Christ’s body and need this remedy.

Who could now describe that good soul, forgetful of every earthly affection, almost transcending the flesh itself, caught up in vision many times into heaven? Who could describe his sighs, his groans, not tears but torrents of tears descending indeed to the depths of earth yet ascending to the highest summit of the Godhead? Who could fail plainly to judge blessed that soul whose sins, from the first day of his monastic life to his last departure from life, were none; whose good works were many and unceasing; and whose offering of the spotless Lamb who takes away the sins of the world was daily for almost twenty years? Such was the man he showed himself to God. But what was he like toward his subjects?

## CHAPTER IX. What he was like toward his subjects.

[Col. 0918C]

Certainly he showed himself such toward his subjects, and preserved himself such until life’s end, that he could safely sing to God not only “mercy and judgment” with regard to the Lord, but also with regard to himself. For, as good and truthful brethren who lived with him for a long time testified to me, and as I myself experienced for the greater part, he was merciful to his subjects and more just than almost all priors of the Cluniac congregation in his time; and he left many examples, both in his own days and afterward, of this mercy and justice.

He was merciful to them, providing necessities according to his means and giving to each, according to the apostolic rule and the Rule of Father Benedict, what was needed, acquired with much labour. The house entrusted to him was poor in material things, though truly rich in many virtues. Because this need often pressed grievously and constantly wearied his heart with distress and his body with much labour, he sometimes went to nearby, sometimes to distant kings and princes, and often relieved the need of God’s servants by their gifts and donations.

While he remained at home, it was his practice—indeed by command of the Rule, but especially through a gift derived from God—to take personally the chief care, as far as the duties of the priorate allowed, of the sick, the poor, and guests. Whenever urgent business compelled him to depart, he assembled the brethren, whether in chapter or elsewhere, and, after much exhortation on the matter, most carefully entrusted to them this care as though it were their own particular office.

Nor was his merciful spirit occupied only with these three classes of people. The healthy brethren themselves, especially those who devotedly applied themselves to the labour of the community, often experienced the care of their merciful shepherd. They lacked almost nothing for food, nothing for rest when weary, nothing for consolation when overcome by faintheartedness. He was a father to all, without exception and with fitting discernment.

Moreover, many others—and we among them who saw these things—bear true witness to the discriminating severity of his justice. For he was so angry with the negligent, and especially with those committing most damnable sins, that, his heart, words, and countenance all inflamed under the pressure of the inward flame of God’s zeal, he might have seemed ready to rise for their utter destruction, if one did not know him. Had you observed him, neither Phinehas striking the lustful with an unprecedented wound nor Elijah consuming idolaters with heavenly fire would have appeared more angry with those sinning irreverently.

Accordingly, following Cluniac custom, he punished offenders with bloody lashes according to what appeared just; he restrained them with iron, fetters, and bonds of different kinds; he consigned many to a dark prison; he broke the pride of flesh and spirit by severe hunger and thirst. Sometimes too—only once, it is said, because circumstances required it—he confined someone in perpetual burial.

This happened when he prepared for a certain man spiritually dead an underground cell like a tomb. Confining him there, he achieved by that art of his—by which he had buried a living brother as though dead in the hope of immortal life—that he who could not live above ground learned to live once buried. This was done when that brother, as if buried, returned to life, terrified by the very image of his bodily tomb; through repentance he returned to spiritual and eternal life, from which he had been estranged by sin. For although he had previously been very obstinate, nevertheless, through the frequent admonition of the father and brethren, and at the same time the exhortation of his own tomb, as has been said, he renounced from his heart every evil, and especially those for which he had deserved confinement; and persevering in humility and contrition of spirit, he ended his last day.

Such a tomb of a brother spiritually dead and restored to life perhaps—indeed, certainly—does not differ from the tomb of Lazarus, bodily raised from the dead. For Lazarus, prefiguring the man of whom the discourse speaks, when called from his tomb, received a life that would die again; but this man, raised from his own tomb by that Lord through Matthew, merited everlasting life.

Burning with this zeal for justice and wholly, so to speak, aflame, he spread everywhere the reputation of this fervour of his; by Matthew’s name alone he terrified not only negligent or lax subjects but also any others, near or distant. Like the cherub of old (Genesis 3), he always held forth a drawn flaming sword for the destruction of crimes, and never withheld it from the blood of wrongdoers. In this virtue he excelled so greatly that he brought the house entrusted to him to a much higher state of customary religious observance, and, aided by the assistance of certain good men, reformed many surrounding monasteries or abbeys—which had grown weak in all monastic fervour—into an excellent commitment to religious life.

Such, as has been said, was Matthew toward those subject to him. But what manner of man did he show himself toward others, near or far?

## CHAPTER X. What he was like toward all persons, near or far.

He showed all people a common affection of love both in heart and word, and, so far as he could without compromising the seriousness of his purpose, he presented himself as pleasant and cheerful to everyone who addressed him. Toward all, indeed, he had, in accordance with the words of Father Augustine, the appropriate affection of charity; but toward those whom he could assist, its effect.

By that virtue of charity he had made his monastery, beyond all monasteries in the whole of France, a common lodging for all and, as it were, a general refuge for everyone without exception of persons. The daily concourse of bishops, abbots, and noble laymen; troops of monks and clerics; and the crowd of poor people, which could never be absent, almost constantly filled every house and all lodgings. They were received gladly, nor could the importunity of so many arrivals disturb the cheerful kindness of the receiver’s countenance, for his heart was wholly possessed by that virtue which does not know how to seek its own interests but those of others.

He spent on these charitable expenses not merely all that was his own, but often, at heavy interest, even what he could borrow from others. For in order to serve all who flocked to the monastery, provide for all, and satisfy all, he stretched himself beyond himself; paying no attention to his own strength or the extent of his resources, he almost compelled himself to do impossible things.

Whereas many abbots or bishops—some of whom I know—with full purses, indeed, to put it so, overflowing treasuries, can scarcely offer even a morsel to a poor person or rarely open their door to a guest, this man, on the contrary, according to the Apostle, as having nothing and yet possessing all things (2 Corinthians 6), did not know how to refuse anyone even things that were lacking. Thus, when the household was diminished and everything exhausted, he was often distressed with great anxiety of mind even while the monks went hungry, so that guests might be satisfied.

But recalling again the prophetic saying, “Those who seek the Lord shall lack no good thing” (Psalm 33), understood also of bodily provisions, and the Lord’s saying, “Do not be anxious, saying, ‘What shall we eat?’ or ‘What shall we drink?’” (Matthew 6), and another saying, “All these things shall be added to you” (ibid.), he restored his mind to hope; casting all his care upon the Lord, he rejoiced as though his granaries and cellars were full.

Nor was he long disappointed of his hope; nor did He who provides for the birds of heaven, which neither sow nor reap (ibid.), forget His servants. The invisible Provider often supplied them through kings and princes, His ministers—not masters but temporary dispensers of their own possessions. He often provided them necessities and frequently sent much. When they were hard pressed by severe poverty and burdened with much debt, He often arrived unexpectedly, emerging with a horn full of abundance, and suddenly turned sorrow into joy and need into plenty.

Thus, thus does the magnificent Rewarder customarily act: what is spent in such services, as though entrusted to Him, He restores—more than faithful in what has been entrusted—not merely doubled, but sometimes a hundredfold. For this reason, among the other princes who loved Matthew when stirred by the fame of these and similar virtues and who gave him much from their own resources, Louis, king of the Franks, and Henry, king of the English, embraced him with singular affection. They gladly received him when he came to them, honoured him greatly when received, and almost never sent him away empty-handed.

This was especially done by the great King Henry just named, who, as is known to almost the whole world, surpassed all Christian princes of his time in prudence, exceeded them in deeds, and outdid them in generosity. Matthew had won his favour through the favour of his virtues. For he often visited Henry, was honoured by him with acts of service, and laden with royal gifts returned joyfully to the brethren, consoling their endurance of want with remedies of this sort.

Thus this good man, pleasing first to God and then, for God’s sake, to all, welcome to all, had bound all persons to himself by such pursuits of life and virtue; and, according to the Apostle, becoming all things to all people according to his capacity (1 Corinthians 9), he pleased all. Therefore, as I set out in the foregoing division, Matthew showed himself thus first to God, then to his subjects, and afterward to all others near and far, leaving such an example of himself to the monks of his own time and to all monks of the future.

## CHAPTER XI. How, summoned to Cluny by Lord Peter the abbot, he maintained the rule with the utmost strictness.

At that time it happened, by I know not what will or permission of God, that I, most unworthy, was called to the governance of the Cluniac congregation—this I say simply, not in any double sense—and that I, a wholly useless and improvident shepherd, undertook the care of Christ’s sheep, so great in number and so great in worth.

Because I had heard the reputation of the man of whom I speak before entering this office, and for that reason already knew him and was acquainted with him to some extent, I summoned him to Cluny in the very first year of my calling, as an aid to the order and to help bear the burden of the care imposed upon me. I bound him to myself by a stronger bond of love, never to be dissolved, and immediately laid upon him the care of the rule and cloister, of which, as has been said, he was a most fervent lover.

A little earlier, in that great and noble field of the monastic order, things hostile enough to what was useful, requiring to be cut back—or rather torn out—had sprung up in abundance, through the fault or negligence of certain persons whom I do not wish to name, since for the greater part they have now departed this life. Calling this great man, then, and no idle labourer in Christ’s vineyard, to help in this matter, as I have said, I found him a truly distinguished helper.

For, pursuing vigorously every harmful or superfluous thing in food, drink, and conduct, although on that account he endured many things which must now remain unspoken, he nevertheless brought them to a fitting conclusion—not immediately, indeed, but with God especially helping, and with myself and certain others assisting as far as we could.

Yet he did not therefore lay aside his care of the monastery already mentioned, because, since circumstances required it, he could not refuse to obey me when compelled both to maintain discipline at Cluny and to provide for the aforesaid house. For he was such a man as knew how to use not only the virtue of one right hand, but even the left hand itself as a right hand, as Sacred Scripture reports of certain men (Judges 20). And rightly so: it is the mark of a just man never to have a left hand, but always to turn things of the left—that is, of the adverse side—into the right, that is, the straight side.

Having tested the man’s virtue as sufficient to bear not merely one but a double burden, I placed both upon his shoulders and arranged that, as was fitting to the grace I recognized in him, he should benefit his brethren by his labour while being somewhat separated from them. After some time had passed in this condition, once a certain useful reason required it, I appointed for him a successor in discipline at Cluny and sent him back to govern, as before, the monastery of Saint Martin.

## CHAPTER XII. On the Cluniac schism stirred up by Pons, who had been abbot.

[Col. 0922C] Thereafter, when not quite two full years had passed, that well-known dreadful storm rose against Christ’s little ship—that is, the Church of Cluny—and something like civil war blazed throughout all the lands of our commonwealth. Lest I seem to dwell too long on earlier events, I shall describe it briefly insofar as it concerns the present matter.

Lord Pontius of Cluny, successor in the final period of the same holy Father Hugh, with no abbot intervening, came to Cluny from the monastery of Saint-Pons. Having made a new profession, according to the custom for such persons coming from other, or from outside, monasteries, he became a monk of Cluny. While still very young, he was elected abbot [Col. 0922D] by the Cluniac brethren, who were prompted by hope in his good disposition; and he succeeded that great and renowned man, the aforesaid Father Hugh.

During the first years of his appointment he conducted himself quite modestly and soberly. But as time went on he changed his character, and, by many and various misfortunes or causes, embittering the minds of nearly all the brethren, he gradually stirred them up against himself. They disagreed with him and murmured among themselves—at first a few, then many, and finally nearly all—because, as they said, through great instability or levity of mind, acquiescing in no sound counsel, he was ruining the monastery’s affairs. Yet the matter remained concealed among them for some time and did not reach secular ears for almost ten years. At last the dispute, so long hidden, burst forth so far that not only did the evil of this dissension reach those nearby, but it also spread to the most distant places and filled even the ears of the supreme pontiff and the Roman curia. [Col. 0923A]

Provoked by these reports, Lord Pontius turned against himself the force of indignation which perhaps he ought to have directed against others. Hastening to Rome as if in headlong flight, he urgently begged the lord pope to release him from the burden of pastoral responsibility. At that time the Roman Church was governed by Pope Calixtus II, distinguished by the nobility of royal blood, but far more distinguished by character, integrity, and the magnificence of his generous spirit. He had previously presided over the Church of Vienne. At first, with every effort of exhortation, he resisted Abbot Pontius’s wish and request. But when he saw that Pontius could not be turned from his purpose, he released him, as requested, from every care of the Church of Cluny.

Released, with permission from that same pope, he went to Apulia; thence, crossing the sea, he arrived at Jerusalem, intending, as he had proposed, to remain there always. The pope informed the brethren of Cluny what had been done and commanded them, by apostolic authority, to choose a father for themselves. After this command, having taken the counsel of the whole religious community and of men of religious repute, they unanimously elected as their abbot the venerable Hugh, prior of the sisters at Marcigny. That holy man accepted, though very reluctantly, the burden imposed upon him; but scarcely five months having elapsed, he departed this life and—so his long life in holy observance had deserved, as is rightly believed—passed on to better things.

When this man too had thus been taken away, the brethren set a day for a new election, summoning both those nearby and those far away to assemble on the appointed day. A great multitude of monks gathered, together with certain bishops and abbots; and on the octave of the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin—would that they had provided better for themselves!—they assembled in the presence of the present writer. [Col. 0923C] They notified the aforesaid pope of their election and received from him a rescript confirming what they had done. Thereafter the affairs of Cluny remained at peace for some years; and, as though its former evils had been buried, it flourished with the best outcome of tranquillity and growing prosperity.

At last the aforesaid Pontius, weary of his dwelling overseas, returned from the East and, contrary to custom, brought darkness into the West. On reaching Italy, unwilling to turn aside to Rome, he established a residence for himself in the territory of Ravenna—that is, in the diocese of Treviso. [Col. 0923D] There he built a small monastery; after staying there for a short time, he returned to Gaul. Once he had learned of my absence—for I happened then to be occupied with Cluniac affairs in the regions of Aquitaine II—he pretended not to wish to come to Cluny, but nevertheless gradually drew near.

[Col. 0924A] Then, having joined certain fugitives to himself and armed with the weapons of common men whom he had enlisted, he unexpectedly arrived at the gates of Cluny. Having broken them down, and having scattered here and there the venerable old man Bernard, the prior, and the other brethren, he entered the cloister with that mixed crowd of armed men, women themselves also rushing in.

> [Note: [Col. 0923D] “The venerable old man Bernard, the prior.” This Bernard was a native of Poitou, refined in character, energetic in action, and prudent in providing for the house entrusted to him, as our Peter the Venerable himself says below in chapter 32. He also wrote Bernard’s epitaph after his death.]

Once inside, he immediately occupied everything, compelling those whom he found, by threats, terror, and tortures, to swear oaths of allegiance to him. Those unwilling he either expelled or consigned to harsh imprisonment. At once he laid hands upon sacred things, seizing golden crosses, golden panels, golden candlesticks, golden censers, and many other vessels of great weight. He even carried off the most sacred chalices, sparing neither golden nor [Col. 0924B] silver cases or caskets containing the bones of many martyrs and saints. From these and similar objects he melted down an immense weight of gold, and with it invited the neighbouring soldiery, and any others greedy for gold, to predatory warfare.

Protected by these men, he attacked the villages and strongholds surrounding the monastery; and, attempting in barbaric fashion to bring religious places under his control, he destroyed all that he could with fire and sword. He abstained from no kind of warfare: through soldiers hired with sacred gold, he raged everywhere in plundering goods and slaughtering men. The whole summer, from the beginning of Lent until the Kalends of October, was consumed in battles of this sort; not even for a few days was there respite from so great a calamity of evils.

The aforesaid Prior Bernard, together with noble religious men and men of high standing, remained outside Cluny wherever they could, and in the safer places defended themselves as best they could against the attack of such great enemies. Thus, in that holy and most famous house of Cluny, by God’s hidden but just judgment, Satan, loosed for a time, raged. But, according to the book of blessed Job, “He who made him has brought his sword near him” (Job 40); and He swiftly imposed an appropriate end upon evils so great.

## Chapter XIII. On the end of the Cluniac scandal, and the wisdom of Lord Matthew

The venerable Pope Calixtus, mentioned above, had already departed this life, and Pope Honorius had succeeded him, not inferior to him. Hearing of such great tumults in so great a Church, he sent a legate from his side—namely Lord Peter the cardinal—and, joined by Hubald, primate of Lyons, [Col. 0924D] he condemned Pontius and all the followers of Pontius, as they were then called, by a terrible anathema.

> [Note: [Col. 0923D] “Hubald, primate of Lyons.” He was the successor of Gozeran; some call him Humbald, others Humbert or Umbert. He is that same H., archbishop of Lyons, to whom Pope Innocent II, writing concerning the nuns of Marcigny, testifies that they were cherished and loved by him. The beginning of the letter is: “Innocent, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable H., archbishop of Lyons, greeting and apostolic affection. The letters sent by us to your brotherhood concerning the nuns of Marcigny,” etc. And immediately afterward follows: “As for the fact that, as we have learned, you cherish and love the aforesaid sisters, we are grateful; and we ourselves wish their rights to remain inviolate for them.”]

Nevertheless, a day was afterward appointed, and by apostolic letters he summoned both parties to undergo judgment concerning so great a dispute in his presence. [Col. 0925A] All our party promptly obeyed; and among the innumerable priors of monasteries came the aforesaid venerable Matthew, for whose sake these matters have been inserted. Pontius too was present, though unwillingly, with his followers, and on the appointed day was summoned to submit to judgment.

He was ordered, however, first to make satisfaction, since an excommunicated person can neither litigate nor canonically undergo judgment; by making satisfaction he was to release himself from the bond by which he had lawfully been bound. Messengers were sent by the pope and ordered him, on the pope’s behalf, to make satisfaction for such great evils. He refused, asserting that he could not be bound by an anathema pronounced by any living person. Peter alone, he said, was in heaven; apart from him, he admitted that no one had this authority.

The lord pope was all the more disturbed by such an answer, and the whole city was likewise thrown into commotion; all proclaimed him not merely excommunicated but schismatic. Since, as stated, he could not be admitted to judgment unless released, the lord pope sought an answer through the messengers from those who had come with him: whether, if Pontius himself would not do what was required, they at least wished to make satisfaction. [Col. 0925B] They immediately answered that they were ready to do so at his command. All therefore entered the palace barefoot, acknowledged themselves guilty in the sight of all, and were at once absolved.

Once absolved, they entered upon the case, leaving untouched nothing that could support either themselves or the man for whom they pleaded. On the other side, the venerable Matthew assumed the voice of them all and spoke wisely on the whole case. As soon as both parties had been heard, the pope rose, accompanied by the entire Roman curia, and withdrew apart to examine the matter. He remained away for a long time, then after some hours returned with all of them to his seat and ordered the bishop of Porto to pronounce the judgment they had reached in counsel.

The bishop, at the pope’s order, pronounced the sentence; and, to give his very words:

> “Pontius, an invader, a sacrilegious man, a schismatic, and an excommunicated man, the holy Roman and Apostolic Church deposes forever from every ecclesiastical rank or office; and it restores Cluny, the monks, and all things belonging to that monastery to the abbot who is at present in office, from whom they had been unjustly taken.”

Once sentence had been pronounced, those who had been divided were united; and, as if in a moment, the body of Cluny was restored and so great and long-enduring a storm of evils was calmed. A deadly Roman epidemic descended a few days later upon the defeated and the victors alike, [Col. 0925D] and in a short time struck down nearly all, monks as well as servants. It attacked Lord Pontius when scarcely a month had passed, and after a few days extinguished him.

I append a letter concerning his end, addressed to me by the aforesaid Pope Honorius of blessed memory, in case knowledge of it may be judged useful:

> Honorius, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son Peter, abbot of Cluny, greeting and apostolic blessing. In the past month of December Pontius entered upon the way of all flesh. Although he had often been admonished to do penance for the evils inflicted on Cluny and had refused, nevertheless, out of reverence for that monastery of which he had been a monk, we had him honourably buried. Given at the Lateran.

He died thus, having been afflicted for some time by the Roman disease. The same illness did not spare me either, but for more than half a year it burned me with a scarcely tolerable fever. I would not, I think, have escaped the fate of my companions, had not both the prayers of the brethren and the care of medicine, bestowed upon me with much devotion by a certain wise cleric, helped me. At last, by God’s favour, I escaped; and through His grace that greatest seat of religious life recovered with remarkable speed from the worst disease of its own kind—disturbance and schism—and returned to its former, [Col. 0926B] and perhaps in some measure improved, condition of religious observance, reputation, and resources.

I seem to have departed from my purpose. Yet because I feared that a matter which seemed to me not to be suppressed, and exceedingly useful as a warning for the future, would perish from the memory of later generations, I feared to pass over in silence, having found occasion in Lord Matthew—by whose effort above all others so great an evil was subdued—what needed to be said. Let my pen therefore return to him and carry out, as it began, the remaining things concerning him.

## Chapter XIV. How he was appointed bishop of Albano, and how holily he conducted himself in that office

Having been drawn to the City on the matter already described, and once it had been settled, he was hastening to return with his companions to his own place.

> [Note: [Col. 0925D] The beginning of this chapter is much fuller in the manuscript as follows: “Thereafter it happened that, when certain causes had arisen against Christ’s little ship—that is, the Church of Cluny—the aforesaid venerable Matthew was drawn to the City among the innumerable priors of Cluniac monasteries; and at last, through God’s grace and Matthew’s effort, greater than that of the rest, when the causes had been settled to the honour of God and of the Church of Cluny, he was hastening to return with his companions to his own place.”]

[Col. 0926C] But God, who had called him while he was unaware, prevented his return; and because he had been faithful over a few things, He promoted him, as a proven steward, over many things (Matthew 25). Pope Honorius, worthy of honourable mention, imposed on him the pastoral care of a greater honour and burden; and, taking him as a companion in his own labour, consecrated him bishop of Albano.

Thus advanced to the lofty rank of the episcopal order, and magnificently raised upon the Church’s lampstand to give light to all who were in God’s house, he abandoned nothing of the monk, as some do. Rather, as is read of the great Martin, the same humility remained in his heart and the same lowliness in his clothing. Under the pretext of no responsibilities did he abandon any part of the offices, the chants, or the lengthy Cluniac psalmody. He kept the observances of the cloister in his palace and, though exposed to the world, by firm and long practice, as if by an inborn purpose of religious life, separated himself from secular vanities as though by a very strong enclosure. [Col. 0926D]

He restrained himself within himself, never more occupied than when alone. Above all his works and every holy pursuit, he preferred his daily practice of offering sacrifice to God. Neither care for worldly goods, nor manifold occupation, nor even the unceasing solicitude for all the Churches laid upon him after the supreme pontiff could draw him away from it. The pope often complained of this and, when others customarily assembled at court in the morning but Matthew himself scarcely appeared by the third hour, reproached him, as it were, for being too much of a monk.

He observed this attentively not only in Rome but everywhere. On summer days he would often remain occupied in these sacred pursuits through the more intense heat of the Italian sun, so that he could scarcely be drawn out of church even about the sixth hour. Since he possessed not only simple religious innocence but also prudent and singular wisdom, he was often sent by his master to various parts of the world; called to share the apostolic burden of responsibility, he prudently administered apostolic functions in the pope’s stead. [Col. 0927B] Nor, in proportion to the grace granted him by God, was he inferior in this respect to David, of whom Holy Scripture says that, going in and out at the king’s command, he was faithful throughout that kingdom. For David was faithful in that Jewish kingdom, while Matthew was faithful in the far loftier kingdom of the Christian commonwealth, expending all the powers of body and mind.

## Chapter XV. How, while still prior, he forbade borrowing money from Jews

Since the Jewish kingdom has been mentioned in order to extol his faithfulness or faith, let there be related something relevant to proving this which had slipped my mind. For it happened to be demonstrated among, and concerning, the Jews themselves.

As stated above, he had recently undertaken the administration of the priory of Saint-Martin [Col. 0927C]; and among other business the brethren presented to him the monastery’s debts. Inquiring after the creditors, he learned that some of them were Jews. At once he turned to the brethren who were reporting these matters:

> “How came you, Christians and monks, to wish to borrow money from Jews and impious men? ‘For what agreement has Christ with Belial? Or what partnership has light with darkness? Or a believer with an unbeliever?’ (2 Corinthians 6.) Go, go,” he said, “and by paying that money quickly break the bond of this reprehensible association. Henceforth do not wish—or take care not—to have dealings with Jews in matters of money given or received, loans or deposits, or any kind of commerce.”

When they answered that the monastery’s poverty compelled them and that they could not refrain from borrowing Jewish money, [Col. 0927D] he said:

> “Far be it, far be it! Let this speech never again proceed from your mouths. With what face, with what conscience, shall I attempt to approach the altar of Christ the Saviour, or with what brow to come into converse with His holy Mother, if I have sought favour with His blaspheming enemies? How, having become a friend of their most wicked enemies, shall I be able to please them? How shall I dare to invoke or entreat them with that mouth with which I have sought favour with their enemies for the sake of money or of any other thing? See, therefore, that there be no further question about this. Pay quickly whatever you owe them, and henceforth abstain from all their transactions as though this had been fixed by an eternal law.”

Thus the devout man, filled with zeal for faith, both prohibited those contracts and showed [Col. 0928A] how much love he cherished in the depths of his heart for Christ his Lord.

## Chapter XVI. On the schism of the Roman Church, and how courageously he defended the Catholic party

He showed this faith of his toward Christ and His Church especially at the time when schismatic fury set up a profane altar against the unity of the one dove—that is, of that same Church. The Roman Church, and afterward the whole Latin Church, was divided—indeed, torn apart—and at first, for a great part of itself, followed the son of Leo, intruded by force and money. He resisted firmly with certain companions and strove with all his strength to uproot that which the heavenly Father had not planted.

For this reason, expelled from the City with his pontiff—indeed, with Pope Innocent, the pope shared by all—he endured much for the sake of justice. Then, entering the sea by the Tiber, he came to Gaul. There Pope Innocent first consecrated the new and larger church of Cluny; and after holding two councils, one at Clermont and the other at Reims, he united to himself—or rather, to Christ—all Gaul except part of Aquitaine, Spain, England, and Germany, chiefly through the exertions of the aforesaid Matthew. [Col. 0928B]

Matthew remained with him in those regions for a long time, then returned with him across the Alps into Italy, as far as Pisa, where he too had earlier remained for a time. Peter, the son of Leo, still occupied the apostolic see, and Leo’s cubs raged against the Catholic party. Christ permitted this; He who would permit Antichrist, the head of all schismatics, to sit in God’s temple, allowed His own followers to live in exile and Peter’s see to be occupied by those who were not His own. Therefore Matthew remained with Pope Innocent at Pisa for the remainder of his life, and no opportunity was given him to see either his home or his own see again. Throughout that whole time, never drawing back in anything, he continually became better through growth in virtue; always occupied with sacred studies, the nearer he came to his end, the more exercised in virtues he appeared.

## Chapter XVII. On his glorious end, distinguished by wonders

Since the sequence and progress of the narrative now admonishes me, I ought not longer postpone adding something concerning his end. [Col. 0928D] Certainly, many more things worthy of remembrance could still be committed to writing about him; but because occupation prevents this, at least that in which he had no equal in his own days or ours must not be passed over in silence. I do not deny that in those days of his and ours an excellent end followed the good life of many good men. But so far as information could reach my ears, no one’s passing in that period was marked by such wonders.

The blessed man had been sent by the lord pope to Milan to restore peace, and he was hastening to restore to the unity of the Church that greatest Italian city after Rome, which had fallen away through the schismatic Anselm. God quickly granted the best outcome to his labour; and with remarkable speed He restored to Mother Church many peoples of Liguria who had turned away from Catholic peace. Then, as once Martin had done, when he had completed the business of ecclesiastical peace, he at once perceived in himself the summons of Him who called him. His inward parts were weakened by diarrhoea, and his bodily strength gradually failed.

He had previously suffered such an affliction at Cluny for a year; consumed by severe dysentery, he had scarcely escaped death despite the many prayers offered to God for him by the brethren. He was therefore seized, as I have said, by the same illness; and as it worsened through the toil of travel and the heat of the sun—for it was then summer—it began to press him toward the failure of nature. At last he returned to Pisa and for several months, a man of courage, struggled with this infirmity. [Col. 0929A]

Though greatly constrained by sickness, he would not lie down in bed; he would not abandon any part of his customary work; he would not spare his body even a little. He steadfastly endured the labours of the apostolic curia, was never absent from ecclesiastical cases, and did not know how to withdraw himself from the benefits of the brethren. He tirelessly attended the divine services to which, as stated above, he had wholly devoted himself from childhood. In his customary manner he spent himself entirely on them, so that, as far as these were concerned, one would not know that he was ill but would think him sound and vigorous.

Unceasing prayers, eyes constantly flowing with tears, and psalmody in the Cluniac fashion, occupying nearly all the time of day and night—these showed that he had devoted to them his heart, his tongue, his works, and finally his whole self. But that singular refuge of his—that is, I mean, the sacrifice of the altar—which he had continued through almost his entire life with insatiable longing, no force of illness and no weakness could compel him to omit even for one day. [Col. 0929C] With remarkable devotion he fought obstinately against illness and, as is read concerning his aforementioned Martin, according to his measure and strength did not relax his spirit, unconquered in prayer.

This health-giving contest was prolonged from the Ides of July until the Kalends of December. Throughout that entire time, he compelled limbs weakened by sickness to serve the spirit by force, nor could he be recalled from these divine or similar sacred works by anyone’s persuasion. At last, in the first week of the Advent of the Lord, unable any longer to bear the complete failure of nature, he lay down in bed.

When he sensed that the end of his mortal life was now not far off, [Col. 0929D] he summoned the brethren attending him and also his servants. Addressing and consoling them kindly, he added:

> “I ask you, brothers and sons, since I understand that I shall soon depart from human affairs, to bid farewell on my behalf and affectionately greet, first, my lord and father the abbot of Cluny; the prior and subprior; Hugh the chamberlain; Arbert the sacristan; and the whole community together of our brethren of Cluny; Abbot Alberic of Vézelay; and the prior of La Charité. But especially greet my intimate and beloved sons serving God at Saint-Martin-des-Champs, whom, as best I could, I have raised in God’s service.”

In saying this, the blessed man showed not only how great was his affection for God [Col. 0930A] but also how great was his affection for his brethren and sons.

## Chapter XVIII. On the vision concerning him seen by the prior of Saint Zeno

Not many days before, the prior of the monastery of Saint Zeno, which is situated at Pisa, had seen in a dream the man of whom this account speaks, dressed in a monk’s habit, with a boy of handsome appearance standing beside him, who was also said to be the son of a king. The boy held in his hands a book written in golden letters. Opening it, he offered it to the venerable Matthew and urged him to read it. When Matthew replied by asking what benefit would come to him from reading it, the boy added:

> “By reading this book, you will gain knowledge of all languages.”

[Col. 0930B] After he had read, when the boy addressed him in the Hebrew language, he replied in Hebrew. When questioned in Greek, he answered in that language as well. Then the boy said:

> “Just as you have proved yourself learned in these two languages, so know that you have acquired the diversity of every language.”

Having said this, he immediately showed him a royal palace, remarkable for a wondrous and most beautiful structure, and commanded him to enter. When Matthew answered that, because he was unprepared, he could not enter, the boy added:

> “Go, and hasten quickly to prepare yourself so that you may enter.”

Matthew withdrew aside; quickly arraying and adorning himself with every priestly and pontifical vestment, he at once returned to the boy. With him he found also innumerable boys of angelic beauty. He approached the palace indicated, [Col. 0930C] and, while all sang in joyful and exalted voice, “Alleluia! Let us bless the Father and the Son with the Holy Spirit,” he entered it.

## Chapter XIX. On the vision of another brother

The next-to-last week of the Advent of the Lord had come. Another brother, from another monastery of Saint Michael likewise at Pisa, saw in a dream John, a man of venerable life, who had first been prior of Camaldoli and afterward bishop of Ostia, as though coming toward him. When he asked him, “Where are you going, lord?” John replied:

> “I am coming to Pisa to take up my brother, the bishop of Albano, and add him to our number. Know, moreover, that on the eighth day before the Kalends of January he will come to us and remain with us forever.”

Those who saw these visions—or rather, revelations declaring the man’s merit—reported them before his death to certain persons; and, furthermore, to the good and trustworthy man who reported these things to me.

## Chapter XX. How he drove demons away from himself by the sign of the cross, and on his tireless attention to God

The night before the Sunday immediately preceding the Nativity of the Lord had arrived. The blessed man, exhausted by prolonged sickness, lay in bed while his companions rested. Suddenly, breaking out as though into a cry of distress, he called those lying around him. When they stood by, he told them that a horrible multitude of evil spirits [Col. 0931A] had appeared to him and greatly terrified him.

> “They were so visible to me,” he said, “that I wonder whether they could have escaped your notice. When I made the sign of the cross, they were terrified and immediately vanished; yet as they withdrew, they left behind the foul remains of an unbearable stench. Quickly summon the lord pope’s chancellor, therefore, and ask him to hasten to come to me.”

This was done. When the chancellor, a religious and wise man, came shortly afterward, Matthew again told what he had seen. The chancellor wisely urged him not to fear, saying that this was the common passage of all who leave the world, even very good men. Adding what was appropriate to the situation, he kindly strengthened the good man in the Lord and encouraged him by religious speech to await his end in good hope.

[Col. 0931B] He was increasingly pressed toward the end by the severity of his illness; yet, as has already been said, with his heart wholly raised to heaven, he could not be drawn away from divine offices or works. In accordance with the Psalm, his mouth no longer knew how to speak the works of men (Psalm 16), nor could his ears endure to hear human matters. If anyone spoke to him of transitory affairs, he gave no answer whatsoever and was thought not to have heard. But if anyone uttered spiritual discourse before him, he immediately turned his hearing to it and answered most readily, as though he suffered nothing.

Whenever bishops, monks, religious clerics, or his own companions came to him, he recited each time, to each person, his *Confiteor Deo* (“I confess to God”), which according to monastic custom he had learned. Thus he confessed to all, asked absolution from all, and commended himself to all. And so, although a holy soul, in accordance with what is written, “Let the holy person be made holy still” (Revelation 21), he strove to be made holier through confession, prayer, and the brethren’s absolution. [Col. 0931C] He continued these things until the final breath of life; nor could that excellent, long-practised habit of devout spirit fail even while he still breathed, however slightly.

## Chapter XXI. On the revelations shown to him before his death, and on the glory which he saw prepared for himself
The kindly Savior showed him, before he wholly failed, that these works and these endeavors of his had pleased Him; and He revealed in part to what place he would depart after death. He lay in bed on the night before Monday, while his companions, a little before the customary time because he himself had ordered it, were chanting the nocturnal praises. And behold, as psalmody sounded on every side, he was suddenly caught up and, estranged from human senses, was recognized as such by the very change in his face. The brothers pressed on more earnestly with the divine offices and waited, as though he were then about to die.

Brother Pontius, long bound to him by familiarity on account of his honorable character, took up the Gospel; he took it up, I say, and, sitting beside him, devoutly recited the Passion of the Lord according to Matthew, Mark, and Luke. When these had been read through and he had finished reading, the blessed man said: “And where is the Passion of the Lord according to John? If it pleases you, son, read that also.” Truly a blessed man, wholly intent, as I said above, in spirit and mind upon divine things: even when caught up to invisible realities and with his bodily senses nearly dead, he could not forget sacred things.

Accordingly, when that fourth reading of the Passion of the Lord according to John had also been read through, he said: “May almighty God repay you, son, in eternal recompense for all the benefits you have always bestowed upon me, but especially for this service. Know for certain, moreover, that I was dead and was caught up to invisible and heavenly things. Therefore be assured that I shall by no means die tonight. Go now meanwhile and rest. But return to me when morning has come, and then I shall tell you the wonderful things I saw.”

At the appointed time the aforesaid brother returned to him with his companions. When the psalms of the first hour of the day had been chanted and it was now time for speaking, he said to his companions—and I shall report his words as he uttered them in Latin, adding, changing, or diminishing nothing:

“Go,” he said, “to the lord chancellor, and tell him to tell the lord pope to come here and remove me from this tomb in which I lie. And indeed he would gladly do so, if he knew the little bed prepared for me. For no bed has ever had such beauty or such marvelous sweetness as the one prepared for me. For I was dead this night, and I was before my Lord Jesus Christ; and I saw blessed Mary His mother, and Him who granted me a place at His feet, where I shall sit.”

When the brothers to whom he related these things asked him to describe the condition, manner, or blessedness of the things he had seen, he said: “And who, brothers, could do this? Who indeed could describe that good, that happiness, those ineffable goods unknown to mortals? There is—there is plainly no mortal who could do this. Among the innumerable things I beheld there, a singular reverence for discipline is maintained; and everything there stands arranged to the smallest detail.”

After this he was silent for a little while. Then he said: “I regret not having asked the Lord what He has decreed to do concerning His house at Cluny, or what its condition is with Him.” The aforesaid brother replied that he need not concern himself if this had then slipped his mind, since, standing before God, he would pray to Him for that house. He added: “And truly I shall gladly do this, and shall beseech Him for it with every affection of my soul.”

Behold the mind of a man always, indeed, but now especially devoted to God: even after that supreme and chief longing for the Godhead, love and care for his brethren could not fall away from it even in the least matters.

That same day toward evening, William, bishop of Palestrina, a man of great and proven religious devotion, came to visit him. Sympathizing with his illness in the manner of good men, he consoled him. Among other things the venerable Matthew told him:

“This night a man of venerable countenance came to me, adorned with much handsome whiteness both of head and garments. He seemed to me to be one of the inhabitants of the desert. Leading me out of this house, he brought me across a splendid meadow, and thence led me before the Lord. That meadow through which I was brought forth bloomed with singular loveliness, and nothing seemed lacking to its delightfulness. There were trees laden with fruits of every kind; fields patterned with greenest grasses and flowers beautiful beyond all beauty; everything delightful to sight, fragrant to smell, and pleasing to every sense. If anyone deserved to obtain even one flower from it, throughout all the days of his life he would be healthier, more cheerful, and happier.”

After the aforesaid bishop departed, John, a monk of Cluny and then chaplain to the lord pope, later bishop of Perugia, likewise came to visit and began to speak with him. When John said that it seemed to him Matthew would die soon, Matthew replied: “Certainly I shall not die this night—no, not this night. For it has been granted me by the Lord that, on the day on which He came forth from the Virgin to humankind, I too, departing from humankind, may go to Him, His mercy going before me.”

Truly the Lord is merciful; truly He is the most kindly comforter of His servants; truly, according to the song of Moses, He has compassion on His servants (Deut. 32). He does not forget to console their long labors, nor does He despise the services they have devoutly rendered Him. Truly, as He Himself says, “As a mother comforts her children,” so He not only comforts, soothes, and gladdens His servants in the life to come, but sometimes also in this one: so that, tasting beforehand the joys that follow, they may be drawn by ineffable sweetness and, while still placed in the body, be carried thither by the whole desire of their souls.

For He did not wish wholly to conceal from Matthew, not yet entirely released from the body of death, that great abundance of His sweetness which He is accustomed to hide for those who fear Him (Ps. 30); nor did He wish to defer altogether until after death the things He was to give. Rather, even before death He sent certain signs beforehand, so that Matthew might be encouraged much more to hope for and love them, and so that those ignorant of it might learn what merit he possessed with God. Thus the blessed man, refreshed by such splendid revelations, remained more cheerful to the end and, strengthened in the Lord, awaited his final hour.

## Chapter XXII. How [how greatly] holy and glorious was his passage from this world, at the first dawning of Christmas Day

[Col. 0933D]

Now on the very vigil of the Nativity of the Lord, after he had devoutly completed, as was his custom, both the nocturnal and daytime offices, and as the evening hour approached, he asked for the Lord’s body to be brought to him. When it had been brought, he said to the brothers: “Hear my confession, and be witnesses here and for eternity of my faith. I confess that this sacred body of my Savior is truly and essentially that which He took from the holy Virgin, which hung upon the cross for the salvation of the world, which was laid in the tomb, which rose from the dead on the third day, which ascended into heaven, and which shall come to judge the living and the dead and the world by fire. Through it I believe that I am incorporated into Him, made one with Him, and possess eternal life.”

Having said this, he was refreshed before the brothers with that same saving body of Christ; through that flesh which gives life eternally, he was made ready for the eternity to come.

When the first watch of the holy night had arrived and he heard the bells of the whole city being rung for the nocturnal praises, he immediately burst forth with all his mind and voice into a cry of exultation. With such voice and gesture of joy as he could, he called aloud to his companions and everyone: “Christ is born to us! Glory to God in the highest!” When the angelic hymn, as it is sung at Mass, had been chanted in full, he left the remaining parts to those standing around, for he lacked strength for them.

Yet, with his mind fixed upon those sacred praises of the Lord’s Nativity, whenever in the chants or readings he noticed the name of the blessed Virgin, Mother of the Lord, being read or sung, he raised his eyes upward and stretched his hands toward heaven, showing where his mind dwelt and whither that holy soul was carried.

When the nocturnal praises had been completed and the priest standing at the sacred altar was chanting the Mass called the Mass of the Night, he raised himself with all the effort he could and, assisted by a brother because he lacked strength to stand, sat up in bed. Turning toward the Lord’s cross before him, as though he saw in it the Savior crucified as of old, he said: “Now, O merciful Savior, it is time for You to fulfill what You promised and, as Your Nativity approaches, grant me leave to depart from mortal life and pass over to You, who are eternal life.”

With this final utterance he ended all his speech. Reclining upon the bed, shortly afterward he was carried by the brothers onto haircloth sprinkled with ashes. He had often previously asked these same brothers not to allow him, under any circumstance, to die otherwise than in ashes and haircloth, according to Christian custom. He feared that, moved by some compassion for his illness, they might omit or neglect this. In this, as in other matters, he strove to follow the examples and words of his Martin, who, as everyone knows, when dying taught his disciples that a Christian ought to die only in ashes.

Thus Matthew, placed there by his brethren or disciples, awaited the final hour of his calling. When it arrived, as the darkness of night turned into light and the community of monks established in that church sang at the second Mass, “Light shall shine upon us today,” Matthew, truly a monk and bishop of God, left behind the thick Egyptian darkness—that is, the darkness of this world—and, through the death of the flesh, attained everlasting light and life.

## Chapter XXIII. Of his most celebrated funeral rites and his honorable burial in the basilica of Saint Fragdian [Frigdian]

The body of the righteous man was immediately borne by devout men into the monks’ cloister, while psalmody according to the custom of Cluny was chanted on every side. It was washed, as the common custom requires, and, as he himself had ordered, first clothed in the haircloth from which he had never been without as a monk, then in the monastic cowl. The brothers added priestly and pontifical vestments, and thus, as priest and bishop of God, he was adorned fittingly [the transmitted reading is *dignus*, “worthy,” for *dignum*, “fittingly”].

On receiving the news, Pope Innocent himself hastened there, with the entire company of bishops and cardinals and the whole body of the Roman Church or curia. Nearly the whole city of Pisa assembled; and they regarded seeing him and paying him homage as more important than all their business. Very many kissed the hands or feet of the body lying there, confidently hoping, with faith not without effect, to be sanctified by such touch or kisses.

That city had been accustomed, through much sought-after labor, to pursue maritime commerce and to bring back every kind of precious thing from distant regions of Africa and the East. It had filled its bosom with merchandise of many peoples amassed from every quarter, and rejoiced to have become richer than nearly all the cities of Italy. At last it received from the furthest bounds of Gaul a pearl sent to it, to be preferred above all the riches of Egypt, and rejoiced that it was far wealthier than before. In this dead man it showed how greatly heavenly treasures outweigh earthly riches, and how the riches of Christ, even after death, surpass the riches of the living.

He lay dead and possessed or perceived nothing in the world. Yet the living venerated him, the powerful reverenced him, and the wealthy extolled him with praises. Even lovers of the world discern—and judge by the very honors they bestow upon saints—how much earthly things are subject to heavenly, human to divine, and fleeting to everlasting things.

The body of the venerable man was kept throughout that day of the Lord’s Nativity, attended with psalms and prayers poured out to God.
