On the following day, that is, on the feast of the great martyr Stephen, the aforesaid Pope Innocent offered to God the solemn sacrifice for his eternal rest and devoutly implored the mercy above for the repose of this bishop, his companion in labors. The bishops who happened to be present did likewise; and all together, pouring out prayers to God, escorted their fellow bishop, setting out for foreign lands.

At last, about the sixth hour of the day, after all the rites of Christian burial had been performed, and with nearly the entire clergy and people of the city also in attendance, the man venerable in life, death, and renown was carried to burial and interred in the church of Saint Frigdian, formerly bishop of Lucca, which is in Pisa.

Then, seven years having passed, when I was traveling to Rome to restore peace between the Pisans and Lucchese, but especially drawn by devout remembrance of him, I visited Pisa. On the second day after my arrival in that city, I went with my companions to the tomb of my dearest friend, visited and honored the sacred ashes as was fitting, and offered the saving sacrifice for him. Although I trusted that I could be helped much more by his merits, nevertheless I commended to almighty Creator and most kindly Redeemer, with such prayers and tears as were then granted me, the man who had been one heart with me while living.

May that faithful, devoted, and God-accepted soul, therefore, rest through the immeasurable mercy of the Almighty Himself in perpetual peace; may it enjoy forever the fruit of its good works; and may it not forget before God the brethren and sons who love it. Amen.

## Chapter XXIV. Of a certain wicked monk who died a most evil death

After the wonderful works or signs set forth above for the spiritual edification of readers or hearers, let this also follow, which I happened to learn after all those things. Nor did I merely happen to learn this after them: it also occurred after all of them.

There was in the monastery of Lihons, subject to the Church of Cluny:

> **[Note: Col. 0935D: “In the monastery of Lihons, subject to the Church of Cluny.” This monastery, in the diocese of Amiens, is one of the thirteen deaneries of the Cluniac Order held in benefice. It is commonly called the deanery of Saint Peter of Lihons in the purified blood; in French, *Lihons-en-Santerre*.]**

There was a certain brother, a monk in name and habit, but in life and character not a little opposed to monastic observance and holiness. He was energetic and perceptive in human matters, but dull and blinded in nearly everything divine and pertaining to the monastic vocation. He was often rebuked by his prior and by the religious brethren living with him in the aforesaid monastery, and on account of his offenses he frequently endured many reproaches and injuries, both verbal and physical, willingly or unwillingly.

At times the care of spiritual physicians seemed to make progress in him, and he was thought, in outward appearance, to have turned from his depraved pursuits. But after a short time he appeared not merely no better in any respect, but even worse than before, having rejected every remedy of heavenly medicine. This obstinacy persisted for a long time and could not be ended by anyone’s effort, until, with him hardened, He “who reaches mightily from end to end” (Wis. 8) imposed a fitting end upon evils so prolonged.

Because of his crimes he had been removed from external administration and, unwilling and complaining, was kept within the regular enclosure of the cloister. At last he could not endure this confinement, hateful to him, and, goaded by a devilish grief, he desired somehow to repay upon the prior or his brethren the wrongs of what he considered his prison.

Near the church itself were barns prepared to store the monastery’s grain. The prior and brethren had shut up in them almost the whole year’s provisions and had prepared from those crops what they needed both for food and drink. For that land produces little wine; therefore they were accustomed to make not only bread to eat but also beer to drink from the juice of these grains.

Against these provisions of the brothers that wicked man burned with rage. Thinking that the losses he would inflict upon them would be the best repayment for the evils he had suffered from the brothers on account of his crimes, he prepared to set fire to the aforesaid barns. Stealing the keys of the cloister like a thief in the night, he left the cloister and, after ascertaining that everyone was absent, secretly set fire to the barns, returning to the cloister without anyone knowing.

The brothers had now, after completing the morning praises as customary, returned to their own beds; and behold, the fire set by the monk, gradually growing, suddenly burst into visible flames. That sacrilegious man was the first to cry out and, as if innocent and ignorant of the deed, ran with the others as though to put it out. Yet while all labored and busied themselves as best they could to extinguish the flames, he watched without helping and stood by as an idle spectator, as though rejoicing in vengeance.

Divine judgment did not endure this for long, nor, as it is wont in similar cases, did it defer punishment of so great a crime to the future. For immediately, delivering him to the smiting angel, it killed him with an invisible sword and, in the sight of all present, struck him down with both present and eternal death. Terrified by his sudden and dreadful death, the brothers took up the man, cast down upon the earth and already lifeless, and carried him away to wash him according to custom. When he had been stripped for washing, they found him still clutching in his wicked hand the key he had stolen shortly before.

It pleased God thus to act, and He so ordained it to correct persons obstinate in evil. For although, as the life-breath departs, it is customary for every limb of the body to relax, He made this dead man’s hand retain its grip upon the key which it had stolen to commit so great a crime. He did this lest vengeance for so great a crime be attributed to chance; He did it so that his poison might become known, so that by a greater miracle the wicked man, dead, might reveal what he had refused to reveal while alive, and so that all to whom the report of so terrible a crime came might be deterred from a like deed.

The brothers, therefore, made certain of the author of so great an evil by the evidence of the aforesaid key and other things that I now pass over. They expelled that corpse—whose soul hell already possessed—from the company of holy bodies, as that of a thief, sacrilegious person, arsonist, and excommunicate; and they cast it far outside the Christian cemetery.

## Chapter XXV. Of a vision that I saw while in Rome

Although my purpose is, in recounting miracles of this kind, either never or rarely to admit dreams, because they are often false or doubtful, I have nevertheless admitted among the miracles I relate a certain dream, because it appears worthy of belief. For, as our holy Father Odo wrote in the *Life of the holy man Gerald*, visions in dreams are not always empty. The Gospel itself proves it, as is well known to all: “Hear, therefore, the dream which I saw” (Gen. 37).

At the beginning of the pontificate of Pope Eugene, I went to Rome to visit both him and our common mother, the Roman Church. On arriving there, I took lodging at the cardinalate of Saint Mary the New, which is built beside the ancient temple of Romulus. There, as I rested one night, behold, the lord William, a man of venerable life who had recently departed this life, appeared to me in a dream while I slept.

Because this is necessary to the narrative that follows, I must briefly state who he was, what manner of life he had lived, and by what event he had departed this life. By birth he was noble, but far nobler in spirit; from the first years of youth he was a lover of the religious life, in which, for as long as he lived—that is, almost into old age—he progressed, always adding better things to good. He was a monk of angelic purity, possessed of singular mercy toward the poor and desolate. He burned wholly with zeal for God against the negligent, and especially against grievous offenders; apart from his night vigils and private watches, he occupied nearly half of every day almost continually with prayers and tears.

Although I write these things chiefly about him because in them he shone especially, I do not praise these alone either of him or in him. For, insofar as capacity and learning were present in him, according to the custom and practice of the Cluniac Order and vocation, he constantly applied himself to sacred exercises of other virtues as well. For this reason, and because besides these qualities he possessed much grace granted by God in managing external affairs, I set him over many great monasteries at different times, as necessity required. Thus, when I had placed him as prior at Ambert, Charlieu, Sauxillanges, Souvigny, and finally at Cluny itself, he was then made abbot of Moissac.

> **[Note: Col. 0937D: “Made abbot of Moissac.” Moissac, a monastery in the district of Cahors, likewise subject to the monastery of Cluny, was formerly founded by King Clovis, restored by Louis the Pious, son of Charlemagne, and finally dedicated in 1180 in the presence of the bishops of the province of Auch, as is shown by these verses of an ancient stone placed in the church:**
>
> *On the eighth Ides of November this house was dedicated;*  
> *It rejoices that these famous bishops assembled:*  
> *Auch gave Ostindus; Lectoure, Raymond;*  
> *Comminges, William; Agen sent William;*  
> *Béarn ordered that kindly Heraclius be not absent;*  
> *Oloron granted Stephen, and Aire Peter;*  
> *You, Duran, its own man and our patron of Toulouse;*  
> *Fulk, establishing Simon’s laws for Cahors, is rejected.*  
> *Adding thirty times twelve five-year cycles,*  
> *Then shall the world receive the Virgin’s venerable offspring.*  
> *For you, Christ God, King Clovis founded this;*  
> *Thereafter the generous Lord Louis enlarged it.*
>
> **There is also a privilege of Pope Innocent in the Cartulary of Cluny, which records that he granted the abbot of this monastery of Moissac, of the Cluniac Order in the diocese of Cahors, the use of pontifical insignia, the hands of his beneficence having been enlarged in favor of the Order. But, lest a favor bestowed upon subjects should prove burdensome or injurious to their superiors, or lest sons grow proud against their mother because of the honor shown them, yielding to the prayers of the abbot and convent of Cluny, he also forbade abbots thereafter presiding over Moissac and other monasteries of the Cluniac Order to use pontifical insignia before rendering obedience to the abbot of Cluny.]**

Everywhere he left evident marks of the aforesaid virtues. Then, because of an occurrence which there is no need to name, he gave place to wrath, left that office, and returned to Cluny. There, for some time, he performed the office of chamberlain—that is, the office of provider for the brethren—and at last was sent back to administer a priory in their place.

There, wholly devoted to the customary pursuits of religion and discipline, sparing no one at all in the cause of God and, as I have said, wholly inflamed with zeal for justice, he was ensnared by a most wicked man who feared that what he saw William doing to other offenders might happen to himself. He was put to death through poisonous treachery. Having received such an end to his life, the good man was made worthy of the kingdom of heaven and, as it is right to believe, joined to those of whom Christ, the Truth, says: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5). Therefore, because he not only suffered persecution for righteousness’ sake, but also—and this is greater—died for righteousness’ sake, he is rightly judged worthy of the kingdom of heaven.

Before I undertook the journey to Rome, the treachery by which so great a man had been removed from life had been reported to me through certain indications and was under investigation. But the haste of the journey impeded the inquiry and did not allow the matter to be brought to a conclusion. Thus, meanwhile anxious and uncertain about so abominable a deed, I began the journey I had planned and reached Rome, as I have written above.

There, in the place, time, and manner already described, I saw the venerable William standing before me. Seeing him, I rose with great joy and began to embrace and kiss him with deep affection. Although deep sleep occupied the functions of my outward senses, memory remained active as in one awake, and while sleeping I was not unaware that I slept. Nor had it escaped my mind that he who appeared to be seen in a dream had died not long before and had been killed by the treachery described above.

What is more remarkable, by some hidden force of nature it immediately occurred to my mind that a dead man could not remain long with a living one or engage in lengthy speech. Therefore, before he was compelled by an invisible power to depart, I decided quickly to question him about certain matters. Yet, so that the vision that appeared might seem not imaginary but true, I had by no means previously thought these matters out; rather, while asleep I then began to think them, as I suppose, by God’s prompting, newly arising in my mind.

I therefore put four questions to him, which came to me in sleep from I know not where. “How is it with you, lord prior?” I said, calling him not by his proper name but by his office. He answered briefly, as he had always been sparing of speech, repeating his words twice or three times in his customary manner: “It is very well with me, very well with me.”

To this first question I joined a second: “Have you yet seen the Lord?” He answered: “I see Him continually, I see Him continually.”

To these two I added a third: “Is what we believe concerning God certain? Is the faith we hold true beyond doubt?” “Nothing,” he said, “is so true; nothing so certain.”

And fourth: “Is it true,” I said, “what report declares, what many suppose—that certain persons, whom you know well, killed you by their treachery and poison?” “It is true,” he said, “it is true.”

Having said these things, he vanished, and I awoke and began to recall and marvel at what I had seen. While I was doing this and committing the vision to memory, I was again overcome by sleep and, as happens in the length of winter nights—for the days of the Lord’s Advent were then approaching—I again laid down my head to sleep.

Without delay the same man appeared and showed himself in the same manner as before. I went to meet him no less eagerly than earlier; wholly forgetful of the preceding vision, I began as before to embrace and kiss him. In short: in this second vision there was nothing more or less in my mind, and nothing more or less on my lips, than there had been in the first. I asked the same questions as above and heard the same answers as above. Asked in the order already given about his state, the vision of God, the certainty of Christian faith, and his death, he made the same answers, neither fewer nor different.

Yet something was added at the end of this second vision. As soon as he said that he had truly been killed by the treachery of false brethren, I burst, as it seemed to me in the dream, into bitterest weeping. Since I now doubted no longer about the deed, I bewailed so great a crime with insatiable tears. Awakening amid that weeping, I found my eyes wet and my cheeks warm with fresh tears.

To confirm the undoubted truth of this vision or dream, I returned from the city and, coming back to our Gaul and reaching Cluny, proved true by the public confession of the very wicked parricide what I had suspected concerning the death of the holy man. Since ecclesiastical mercy forbade me to punish that man, most worthy of Gehenna, by sword, noose, fire, or the extremest tortures of the wicked, I condemned the infernal traitor to perpetual exile—the only penalty that was almost available to me.

For, having brought forth the most holy Gospels, I compelled him in the public chapter of Cluny, in my presence, to swear that, after three months set for him by me had elapsed, he would never thereafter remain within the boundaries enclosing all Gaul, but would seek outside them a place suitable for his salvation and, having found a place, would duly make satisfaction to God for his sins.

Although the vision written above appeared in sleep, it seems to me worthy of belief because the sleeping man’s memory remained so whole in matters so great, as I have said; because the second vision was repeated and in every respect like the first, except for the addition at the end; and because the public confession of that detestable man altogether demonstrates, in my judgment, that it was not false but true.

## Chapter XXV. Of the vision of Brother Enguizo

Let another vision be added to this one. Although it appeared in sleep like the former, the outcome itself proved it true.

In my time a nobleman named Enguizo came to Cluny for conversion; and, that he might become accustomed from the outset to devote himself more earnestly to divine things, he took up residence in the church in order to serve the Church. While he was sleeping one night there, he saw a former fellow soldier, called Peter of the Rock, from a castle situated in the diocese of Geneva. This knight had died not long before on the journey to Jerusalem, but the aforesaid brother knew nothing whatever of his death. Not even a faint rumor of it had yet reached him.

Thus, as I said, Peter appeared to him while he slept in the form in which he had been accustomed to see him in the secular world. The brother rejoiced and began to address him familiarly, as someone very well known and intimate.

“What is it? How are you?” he asked.

The other replied: “I died on the overseas journey which, as you know, I undertook with your knowledge.”

“And what,” said the brother, “of the companions who set out on that journey with you?”

“Such-and-such persons,” he said, “have also died; but such-and-such others still survive.”

“How is it with you in the state of that life to which you have passed?”

To this he replied: “It is well with me, because I have now obtained the mercy for which I had hoped from God. But it still greatly harms me and hinders the fullness of my salvation that, shortly before setting out for Jerusalem, I drove through a vineyard a priest of the church of Seconiac, who was demanding a tithe from me, and irreverently struck him at the vineyard’s exit.”

After hearing this, the brother said: “And what do you think of me? Shall I be able to attain the salvation for which I hope?”

“You shall be saved,” he said, “but before salvation you will suffer many grave things.”

Having said these things, the knight who had appeared vanished. The brother woke from sleep and at once related to me in the morning everything he had seen and heard. He also asked permission to visit the region from which the knight came and in which these events involving the priest had occurred, and to determine whether the aforesaid vision was true or false. For, just as no one had told him of the knight’s death before the knight himself did, so neither had he previously heard anything, even in the slightest degree, of the death or survival of his companions, of the priest’s flight, or of the knight’s assault.

Having therefore received permission according to the Rule, he went to the region of Geneva. There, from persons known to him and trustworthy, he learned that everything he had heard from the dead man was true. He learned from the priest himself and from others what had been done to the priest; and, a few days later, he heard of the knight’s death and of the deaths of those whom the knight had said were dead.

When these matters became known to the deceased man’s relatives, they acted upon good counsel: by making due satisfaction to the priest for the wrong he had suffered, they atoned on the dead man’s behalf. Since the aforesaid vision was proved true by such certain evidence, I have recorded it among the other miracles not as doubtful but as certain.

## Chapter XXV. Of the marvelous vision of a certain waking boy
And although many things have been said above concerning open manifestations of the dead, I still wish to add one more, which, having recently come to my knowledge, does not seem fit to be passed over in silence. For it happened in the year in which I wrote these things. On the vigil of the Nativity of the Lord—that is, on the night on which *Sanctificamini hodie* (“Be sanctified today”) is sung—a certain boy-monk lay [Col. 0942A] at Carumlocum, before the sacred matins, in the brothers’ dormitory; and, reflecting upon I know not what, he could not sleep. And behold, when a considerable part of the night had passed, he looked and saw a brother of venerable life, named Achard, who had been prior of that same monastery and had departed this life a few years before, approaching him as he ascended the steps of the dormitory. Now the aforesaid boy was this brother’s nephew. He came, therefore, and sat down upon a bench set before the boy’s bed. With him was also that venerable Lord Prior William, likewise deceased, who, as I related above, appeared to me in a dream at Rome. Yet the boy had seen neither of them while they lived; nevertheless, from what he heard them say, he recognized them without any doubt, as though he had seen them before [Col. 0942B].

They remained and conversed together for some time, with the boy listening, until Lord William departed, and Brother Achard alone remained seated before him, as has been said. Turning to the boy, he urged him to rise and go with him as far as the brothers’ cemetery, to see certain marvelous things. The boy replied that this could not be done, since, although the fear that had seized him had now been partly calmed by the familiar conversation of his uncle, he was under a guardian; he feared that, if anyone saw him going out contrary to rule, he would suffer severe flogging, and that his uncle would be unable to assist him amid the many blows. To this his uncle replied that he had nothing to fear; he should trust his uncle, who would take every possible care that no harm came to him, and would lead him out and bring him back safe and sound [Col. 0942C]. The boy was persuaded; rising and clothing himself according to the rule, he followed his guide.

He led him through the greater cloister into the infirmary cloister, and thence to the cemetery gate. When this was opened, they immediately went farther in. And behold, the boy saw the entire enclosure of the cemetery filled with countless seats, and men clad in monastic dress sitting upon those seats. His uncle had told him that a seat was reserved for him among the others, upon which he was immediately to sit when he arrived, after the manner of the rest. He had also told him that a complaint would be raised against him in that assembly, on account of which he would have to rise and hasten to the judgment of the one summoning him. Moreover, he had warned him that, during this interval of examination, the boy should occupy that same seat [Col. 0942D], fear nothing, and keep it for him until he returned. And so it happened.

For Brother Achard entered that assembly with the boy and immediately took the seat prepared for him. At once a cry arose, and a complaint was made by someone seated nearby: namely, that this brother had come late to his assembly. He immediately rose and stepped into the middle to make satisfaction according to monastic custom. When this had been done, the boy, as he had been instructed, rose and firmly seated himself in the same chair.

In the middle of the cemetery stood a certain stone structure, whose top was large enough to hold one lamp. Out of reverence for the faithful resting there, this lamp illuminates that sacred place with its brightness throughout the nights. There were also steps by which one ascended to it, and above was a space sufficient for two or three persons to stand or sit. As the boy looked there at the seat of a certain great and venerable judge, and at the judge seated upon it, he saw the aforesaid Brother Achard prostrate before him, as if making satisfaction. Though he tried hard, he could not understand what was said or what answer was given him. Yet he could see everything clearly, because a very great radiance, without the aid of human lights, illumined the whole space of that cemetery [Col. 0943A].

After a short interval, the often-mentioned brother returned to his own place and, as the boy yielded it to him and sat at his feet, resumed his seat. A little time passed, and behold, the boy saw that whole assembly rise from their seats and hurry toward an exit—not toward the gate by which he had entered, but toward another. Before they went out, however, he saw a great fire kindled immediately before that gate. Through it, as many in that procession reported while passing through, some remained for a long time, while others passed quickly. He saw these things until all had gone through that gate. After so great a spectacle, the boy alone remained with his uncle. As he had promised, his uncle led him back by the way he had come, ascended with him to the brothers’ dormitory, accompanied him to his own bed, and immediately disappeared.

Since I first heard this vision from others and afterward from the boy himself, who did not know how to deceive, I judged it worthy of belief and wished to write it down, as I have the preceding accounts, for the benefit or warning of readers, lest it escape their memory [Col. 0943C].

## CHAPTER XXVIII. Concerning the observances of the Carthusian monks.

> **[Note: Col. 0943D. Concerning the observances of the Carthusians.]** The following notes have been copied from the printed copy belonging to the distinguished Nicholas Fabri, at whose death all learned men will declare that they have suffered an irreparable loss for all time.

And since my purpose in narrating miracles, concerning which I have already frequently instructed the reader, is such that, without prejudice from chronology, I attend not to when something was done, but to when it was reported to me, and record for the glory of God and the edification of readers those things which I have ascertained to be certainly true, I now place before readers what I learned a few days ago. But before beginning to write it, I shall set forth certain matters relevant to it.

In Burgundy there is preserved, among all the professions of the monastic order in our Europe [Col. 0943D], a profession holier and more guarded than many others of the same monastic purpose. It was instituted in our time by certain great, learned, and holy Fathers: Master Bruno of Cologne, Master Landuin, an Italian, and certain other truly great and God-fearing men. Taught by the lukewarmness, negligence, and sloth of certain earlier monks, these men desired to renounce the world and made more careful provision for themselves [Col. 0944A] and for their followers on God’s way. With watchful eyes they established an order guarded against almost all the snares of Satan.

Thus, so that the order founded by them might be armed, so far as was humanly possible according to their understanding, against pride—which, according to Scripture, is the beginning of every sin (Ecclus. 10)—and against its wicked offspring, namely envy, ambition, vainglory, and whatever else there may be, they adopted clothing of the cheapest kind.

> **[Note: Col. 0943D. Clothing of the cheapest kind.]** But now the Carthusians’ garments are ample [Col. 0944D] and very clean.

Their garments were short and narrow in size; in quality, so rough and dirty that they could scarcely be looked upon. They showed that no fault of self-glorification could find admission in them. I know indeed that even in a filthy habit the devil seeks what belongs to him, and sometimes interweaves the fabric of pride with garments of humility. Yet these righteous men who sought God took the greatest care, so far as they could, that the prince of this world might find no place in themselves or in their followers through pride or pride’s household.

Moreover, they uprooted covetousness, which is called the root of all evils (1 Tim. 6), or avarice, which is called the service of idols (Eph. 5), lest [exceedingly] poisonous shoots should at any time spring forth [the text alternatively has “be produced”] from it. They fixed definite boundaries [Col. 0944B], larger or smaller according to the fertility or barrenness of their sites, around their cells; beyond these boundaries, even if the whole world were offered to them, they would not accept so much land as a human foot occupies.

> **[Note: Col. 0944D. “They fixed definite boundaries.”]** Very many possessions, spread far and wide.

For the same reason, they established a fixed limit, which it was not lawful to cross, for their animals and livestock—oxen, asses, sheep, goats, and he-goats. And so that it should never be necessary for them either to add more land than has been stated to their property or to increase the number of their beasts of burden or livestock, they decreed that there should perpetually be in monasteries of their order only twelve monks [Col. 0944C], with a thirteenth as prior, eighteen lay brothers, and a few hired workers, with absolutely no one added beyond these.

> **[Note: Col. 0944D. “Only twelve monks.”]** And now there is a numerous multitude of brothers and a vast household.

Besides this, in order to tame the beast of their body and, in the Apostle’s words, to subdue the law in their members which resists the law of their mind (Rom. 7), they continually mortify their flesh with harsh haircloth; by nearly uninterrupted severe fasts they afflict, wear down, and dry out their bodies [Col. 0944D]. Hence they always use coarse bran bread, and wine so watered down that it may rightly be called more water than wine. They abstain forever from all eating of meat, whether healthy or sick. They never buy fish, but accept it if it happens to be given in charity. Only on Sunday and Thursday do they allow themselves cheese or eggs for food. On Tuesday and Saturday they eat either legumes or cooked vegetables. Every Monday, Wednesday, and Friday [Col. 0945A], they are content with bread and water alone.

They always eat once a day, except during the eight days of the Nativity of the Lord, the eight days of Easter, and the eight days of Pentecost; on the Epiphany of the Lord; his Presentation—that is, the Purification of Saint Mary; the Annunciation of the Lord when it falls in Eastertide; the Ascension of the Lord; the Assumption and Nativity of the aforesaid holy Virgin, his mother; and on the feasts of the twelve apostles, Saint John the Baptist, Saint Michael, Saint Martin, and the feast celebrated in the Kalends of November, the feast of All Saints.

In addition to all this, following the ancient custom of Egyptian monks, they dwell continually in individual cells. There they labor without rest in silence, reading, prayer, and manual work, especially in copying books [Col. 0945B]. In these same cells, when summoned by the church bell, they pay to God the due service of the canonical Hours: Prime, Terce, Sext, None, and Compline. At Vespers and Matins they all assemble in church. There, not perfunctorily as some do, but most intently—with eyes cast down to the ground and hearts fixed in heaven—they offer prayers to God and thanksgivings to God. By their bearing, voice, expression, and all visible things, they show their whole person, inward as well as outward, intent upon—indeed fixed upon—God, transcending visible things and despising all else.

They except from this practice the feast days written above. On those days they eat twice; and, in the manner of monks living together rather than dispersed through cells, they not only chant all the canonical Hours together in church [Col. 0945C], but also eat together in the refectory, after both Sext and Vespers, with no healthy person excepted.

> **[Note: Col. 0945D. “On those days alone, in emulation of the ancient hermits.”]** But now every day they both offer the sacrifice and chant the Canonical Hours [lacuna]es suitably together in common.

On those days alone, in emulation of the ancient hermits, lest they be hindered by other sacred duties, though inferior in dignity, they offer to almighty God the saving sacrifice for their own salvation and that of the world—the sacrifice called, by an old customary name, *Missa* (“Mass”), because it is sent to God. They celebrate Mass on those holy days called Sundays by the Lord’s special privilege and by his Resurrection, and on the often-mentioned solemnities of himself or his saints. On days when they are permitted legumes, they receive them in a measured amount and prepare and cook them for themselves. This is when the eremitic institution commands them to eat alone in their cells, rather than together in the refectory [Col. 0945D]. At no time do they take wine before or after the meal; but if anyone is thirsty then, he may use water, not wine.

Having briefly set forth these matters, so that we might not seem to have passed over so holy an institution in complete silence, we must proceed to miracles performed in our own time through certain members of their order. For this, as I have often said, was the principal reason for writing this whole work: to transmit to the memory of present and future generations miracles performed anywhere and at any time.

## CHAPTER XXIX. Concerning a Carthusian brother who, while awake, saw marvels.

[Col. 0946A]

I have learned from many that many miracles occurred in this sacred order. But because, by the power of that humility through which servants of God always conceal their marvelous works with all the effort they can, they scarcely wished to reveal any of them to anyone, only rare—indeed very rare—miracles, to which complete trust could be given, reached me. Yet those which I found certainly true beyond doubt, I neither wish nor intend to keep silent.

There was among them a certain lay brother—not indeed one of the monks, but one of the converts—humble in birth and young in age, but noble in character and advanced in holiness of life. Applying all the diligence he could to obedience, humility, and mortification [Col. 0946B], he had not only crucified the world to himself and himself to the world, but had also buried himself. He had devoted himself entirely to divine love and especially to remembrance of the Mother of the Lord. Thus, good men who knew him and his life judged that he knew nothing except Christ Jesus and him crucified (1 Cor. 2), and Mary, the holy mother of the Crucified One, perpetual Virgin, and, after the Lord, the singular lover of human salvation.

Having begun these pursuits at the outset of his conversion, he applied himself to them more and more. In this valley of tears, as the Psalm says, advancing from strength to strength (Ps. 83), and arranging ascents in his heart (ibid.), he stirred up against himself the envy of the ancient and common enemy as if it were newly and especially directed against him. That enemy then showed openly, rather than secretly [Col. 0946C], how eager he is for human ruin.

One night this man lay in the cell assigned to him, as is the custom of such men, for relief from labor and for secret prayer. And behold, deep into the night, while he was still awake and meditating on heavenly things, a troop of demons appeared to him in the form of savage swine. They raged everywhere throughout the cell and surrounded the terrified, trembling man with frantic rushing, horrible gaping mouths, and exceedingly long teeth, sharpened, as it seemed, for his death. As I was told, he sweated from fear and, as though he were about to be torn apart by beasts, expected nothing but imminent death.

While he suffered these things, his terror was increased, and he saw a man of enormous size enter the cell in which this was occurring—a man whom, by the judgment of his heart, he took to be the prince of demons [Col. 0946D]. At his first entrance, the latter turned toward the swine and said: “Why are you idle? Why have you not carried him off already? Why have you not torn him to pieces?”

The swine replied: “We have striven with all our might to do what you say; but though we have tried everything, we have been able to do nothing.”

“I,” he said, “will now do what you sluggards could not do.”

Having said this, he stretched out with threatening hand a terrifying iron hook with long, curved claws, and prepared it to seize—indeed, to tear apart—the man of God. By this immense terror he almost forced him [Col. 0947A] out of his mind. But God, to whom that good man often prayed, saying, “Lead us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil,” did not allow so harsh a temptation to proceed further. In the great mercy by which he always cares for his own, he brought him out of temptation and delivered him from evil.

For as soon as that wicked one stretched forth his hand to seize him, as has been said, and the hook, which seemed to be iron, to tear him apart, the Mother of the almighty Son of God immediately appeared visibly: truly, as we call her, the Mother of Mercy, in whom he had placed all his hope after God. Extending a rod in her gentle hand, she said: “How have you dared, you detestable beings, to come here? He is not—he is not—yours; nor will you now be able to prevail against him in anything.”

[Col. 0947B]

She spoke; and faster than speech, that whole unspeakable company vanished like smoke. After the demons fled, she remained with the still-trembling man and comforted him with these words: “What you are doing pleases me; know that your heart’s devotion is pleasing to God and to me. Therefore do what you are doing, and strive to advance steadfastly from these things to better things. And, that I may give you something particular as a command: pursue humble food, embrace lowly clothing, and devote yourself diligently to manual work.”

Having encouraged the man thus, the Virgin left him and returned to heaven.

Another miracle follows concerning this good man, not inferior to the preceding one. A certain peasant was poor, but his poverty did not impede the devotion of his faith. He had joined himself in friendship to those good men of whom [Col. 0947C] the preceding account spoke, and he was no little familiar with them. For they loved in him not merely poverty of possessions—which profits nothing with respect to the salvation of the soul—but the blessed poverty of spirit of which the Lord says: “Blessed are the poor in spirit, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5). Therefore, in proportion to the devotion toward God that they perceived in him, they made him more intimate a companion.

It happened accordingly that they received his two little sons and brought them up in holy religion, chiefly for the father’s sake after God. Not long afterward, one of them died, leaving the other alive. Wishing to bring up and instruct this survivor religiously, they entrusted his care to the aforesaid good man, to whom the marvels described above had been revealed [Col. 0947D]. He, no negligent executor of commands, received the boy entrusted to him, nourished him, and, imbued him with the sacred milk of religion by which he himself had been reared to manhood, quickly taught him to relish none of the things of earth and to love none of the things that are on earth.

The good teacher taught the youth entrusted to him to behold heaven with the mind, long for heavenly things, yearn with all the powers of the soul toward Christ, the God and Lord of heaven and earth, and seek the things above, not those upon earth, where Christ sits at the right hand of God (Col. 3). The boy showed, once instructed by him, that his teacher had not labored in vain, as certain undisciplined persons do. Rather, as someone well known has said, a freshly made vessel, once imbued with a heavenly flavor, preserved the fragrance it had absorbed not merely for a long time, as that writer says, but throughout his life [Col. 0948A].

But it pleased God that a boy so well reared and so holy taught should not long remain a participant in mortal life, lest he acquire some stain from prolonged association with mortals. He was therefore taken away, lest wickedness change his understanding or deceit—which sometimes tends to be familiar even to certain religious persons—deceive his soul (Wis. 4).

Thus the disciple, dying before his master, left him a good hope for his salvation, but along with that hope a great and almost intolerable grief at his death. For, as has been said, he had received him from his prior to bring him up; but seeing, admiring, and embracing his good character and holy purpose, he loved him not merely as one entrusted to him but uniquely as a son [Col. 0948B]. And therefore he mourned almost continually, grieving over his so swift—indeed almost stealthy—departure from the world.

Moved by this affection, he prayed continually for him, poured forth to God daily whatever psalms he knew, and could not have his fill of praying, chanting psalms, and grieving for the boy’s soul. Since he scarcely ever interrupted these pious labors of his most devout heart, nor desisted from them insofar as he was able, God wished either to relieve his servant from so hard a labor or to show the merit of the man himself or of his boy. He therefore made him worthy of a heavenly vision, by which he might himself be comforted and readers or hearers might learn what should be thought concerning him and the boy.

The good man was once keeping watch outdoors throughout the night, as he often did [Col. 0948C], and did not relax his spirit, intent upon heaven, from the labor and concentration of prayer, as is recorded of the great Martin. As, with the eyes not only of his mind but also of his body fixed upon heaven, he contemplated God, so far as a human being could, beyond the ether that obstructed bodily sight, behold, suddenly a light, far brighter than all bodily light, shone upon him from above through the middle, as though through the middle of a cleft in the air. It flooded him and the places around him with immense splendor.

And so that he who fulfills the desire of those who fear him might satisfy his servant’s prayers, he saw his beloved boy—indeed, his son in God—come down from heaven with that same light, joyful and radiant, and approach him. Troubled in that unfamiliar vision by joy and fear together, he stood transfixed. The boy who had appeared said to him: “Why are you troubled? Do you not recognize your son? Recover yourself, and speak with me as you used to. But, that I may disclose to you what is happening concerning me, know that it has greatly benefited me that you loved me so tenderly for God’s sake, that you compassionately grieved at my death, and that you poured out to God such anxious and continual prayers for me. Henceforth, by God’s grace, know that I have reached such a state that, just as you have helped me until now, so I may henceforth be able to help you before him.”

He said this and immediately began gradually to return whence he had come, while the man watched. The observer of this vision related that, as the boy departed from him and ascended into heaven, he did not go away with face turned aside, nor turning it here and there, as people do when taking leave [Col. 0949A]. Rather, just as he had spoken with him face to face, so he continued, with his countenance always turned toward him, to make his way upward, until, as is recorded of the aforesaid Martin, he was received into the opened heaven and could no longer be seen.

This vision perhaps outweighs that vision in this respect: Severus Sulpicius, as he himself attests, saw the other while lightly asleep in the morning hours—yet asleep; whereas this man saw the present vision not asleep, but awake, standing under the open sky and attending to prayer with his whole heart.

## CHAPTER XXX. Concerning the miracle of Roman candles in the church of the Mother of the Lord.

I shall no longer delay in committing to the memory of future generations that noble and delightful miracle [Col. 0949B] which I learned many years ago and which had now almost slipped from my mind with time. At Rome there is a patriarchal church consecrated in honor of the perpetual Virgin, mother of the Lord, called in common speech Saint Mary Major. It is called “Major” because, after the Lateran church of the Holy Savior, it is greater in dignity not only than the churches of Rome, but than those of the whole world.

On the chief and most solemn feast days—the Nativity of the Lord, Easter, and the Assumption of the aforesaid glorious Virgin—the apostolic pontiff goes there, crowned according to Roman custom and accompanied by a splendid procession. There he holds a station; there, with the clergy and people of the whole city present, he offers the solemn sacrifice to God and observes the holy days with all the honor he can [Col. 0949C]. Apart from himself, his seven assistant bishops, and the cardinal priests, no one may celebrate Mass there.

It must be related what unheard-of miracle has occurred there not merely once, but for a long time now takes place every year on the aforementioned feast of the Assumption. It is the custom of the Romans to observe that feast of the Assumption of the Mother of the Lord with special honor above all the festivals of the year, and to venerate it with special devotion. Therefore, among the many signs of their devout disposition toward the most exalted Virgin, they make very large candles and bring them, ready prepared, to the named church on the vigil of the feast; in the evening, or about that time, they light them. Yet they retain at home the candles’ weight, carefully measured on an equal balance [Col. 0949D], so that, after the solemn Mass on the following day, they may weigh them again and discover by the scale how much of their quantity the fire has consumed.

Thus the Romans’ candles remain lighted in the church of the Mother of the Lord, in honor of both mother and son, from the evening hours, as I have said, until the sixth or ninth hour of the following day. When the ceremonies of the festal Mass have been completed, each is carried back from the church by its owner. Each person bringing back his candle, as soon as he arrives home, prepares the two pans of a balance, places the candle on one and the previous day’s weight on the other. The careful examiner observes how much could be lacking from the candle’s previously measured quantity; counting the evening, night-time, and daytime hours during which the candle burned continuously, he awaits what the balance will report to him about the diminution of its first weight. And behold—marvelous to relate—the anxious weigher and observer finds nothing less in weight after so prolonged a burning of his candle [Col. 0950A]. Rather, as though nothing had been consumed, he marvels that he has recovered intact all that he had devoutly burned for God and his Virgin Mother.

This noble miracle, unheard of elsewhere until then, divine mercy and power works to commend to mortals the glory of the Mother of the Lord—not in some unknown or lowly place, not in just any city, however great, but in the very city that is the head of the world; not once only, as I have said, but continually, in annual recurrence. God does this so that the frequency of the miracle may increase wonder, build faith, and kindle love, and so that such a celebrated place may allow no one to remain ignorant of what heavenly providence has wished to make known to many—indeed, perhaps to all—through the occasion of so famous a site [Col. 0950B].

Great indeed in prophetic times was the fact that, when God sent Elijah to the widow, the jar of flour did not fail and the flask of oil was not diminished, according to the word of the Lord which he had spoken through Elijah. Great was the fact that Elijah, the great prophet of God, was fed with God’s food: ravens, at God’s command, bringing him bread and meat in the morning and bread and meat in the evening. Those things were great in the time of wrath; these are no less great in the time of grace. Those were great in the time of the Mosaic law; these are no less great in the time of the Christian and evangelical law. The bread and meat supplied by ravens in the morning and evening did not fail the prophet; the little flour and oil did not fail him for only three and a half years [Col. 0950C]; and, on the great feast of the Mother of the Lord, the quantity of candles offered to God has not failed, nor does it fail, after such prolonged consumption by day and night, as has been said—not merely for three and a half years, but already for a hundred years and more, down to our own time, and for as long thereafter as it shall please God.

## CHAPTER XXXI. At Souvigny, through Saint Maiolus, a dead boy is restored to the nourishment of life.

Let there be added also the resurrection at the aforesaid place, by the power of Christ through Saint Maiolus, of a certain boy of Souvigny from death. This miracle is commonly held to surpass almost all miracles. For this saint, as is known to almost all the peoples of Gaul, was great in life and distinguished in miracles both while he lived as a mortal and especially after death. By this grace of miracles he has now shone for a hundred and forty-two years—that is, from the time of his death—so brightly that, after the holy Mother of God, no saint in all Europe has his equal in works of this kind [Col. 0950D].

This is attested by countless people afflicted with various kinds of illness, who, praying at his tomb that divine mercy might have pity on them through his merits, have been heard. Among them, within the last seven years, a woman who had a little son experienced a similar—indeed, a greater—mercy of God through him. For when this boy, already more than three years old, was seized by illness, he died [Col. 0951A].

The woman grieved bitterly, touched by maternal affection; but, driven by the sharp stings of overwhelming grief, she directed all the strength of her spirit not toward womanly weeping but steadfast faith. Stirred by the marvelous works which she had not only frequently heard had occurred at the tomb of this most holy confessor, but had often herself seen, she raised her heart in hope and, with faith that was not vain, presumed that her son could be restored to her by him. She immediately arose and hurried not to prepare a burial for the funeral, but, taking the dead child in her arms, hastened to the church. As she went with quick steps, impatient of delay, many asked what she was carrying and what she intended. To all she gave this one answer: “It is my son,” she said, “whom I am bringing dead to Saint Maiolus, that he may restore him to me” [Col. 0951B].

Those who heard marveled at the woman’s so resolute answer concerning so unprecedented a matter and waited anxiously for the outcome. At last the woman came to the saint’s tomb with the child and, full of faith, laid him before the altar. Great was the expectation of those standing by. They knew, as has been said, and had sometimes seen, that many people had been healed there by the saint’s power; but they had neither seen anyone restored alive from death nor received such an account from their fathers. Thus monks and laypeople alike watched attentively at so great a spectacle, awaiting the will and good pleasure of the Almighty.

The boy remained lifeless from the first hour of the day—for it was then the summer season—until the ninth hour. At last he opened his eyes and, in a weak child’s voice, called his mother, who was sitting near him and watching over him with maternal care [Col. 0951C]. His astonished mother rose and was not alone in approaching him. Seeing, along with many present, him alive and speaking whom she had laid down dead, she knew that the saint’s mercy had not disappointed her hope. At once joyful cries arose among the people, and voices raised on high resounded in praise of God and proclamation of Saint Maiolus.

The brothers, according to the rule, were resting in their beds at the midday hour; they ran together. All Souvigny likewise, although scarcely any town in Gaul is inferior to a city in the number of its inhabitants, flew in a moment to the place when it heard the happy news. The church was filled with the noisy yet devout voices of rejoicing people, and those who saw alive the boy whom they had left dead could scarcely contain themselves for joy [Col. 0951D].

Thereupon the devout woman offered the boy to the saint. Since he had received, so to speak, his first life from both parents, and through so extraordinary a miracle had received back a second from Saint Maiolus, she decreed by maternal authority that he should forever be called the son of Saint Maiolus. Moreover, lest any doubt concerning so great a miracle remain for reader or hearer, let them know that before writing these things I visited Souvigny twice, and, upon careful inquiry, received this account both from the mother and from many trustworthy witnesses.

## CHAPTER XXXII. Concerning the confession finally made by a certain Cluniac brother to the lord abbot, truthful and devout.

Already another vision concerning the benefit of confession, besides those which I related much earlier [Col. 0952A], I shall not pass over, because it occurred much later. For in the year when I returned from England for the second time, it happened that I heard the following account, which, lest it escape my memory, I committed to writing in that same year. On returning from the parts of England already mentioned, as I was journeying through France toward Cluny, I turned aside for lodging at a certain monastery of the Cluniac order called Radolium, which belongs to La Charité. At that time a certain brother, Bernard by name, a native of Poitou, presided over the place in the manner of a prior: young in age, refined in character, energetic in action, and prudently providing for the house committed to him. He was then held by a severe fever, so grave that he was obliged to lie continually in bed. I came, therefore, and found him afflicted with this illness.

Having at once made the customary prayer, I approached him [Col. 0952B] and anxiously asked how he was. He replied—as was plain and could not be concealed from anyone seeing him—that he was greatly oppressed by the illness mentioned above. In accordance with my office, I urged him, while he remained in possession of himself, to examine his conscience, confess his sins, and omit nothing pertaining to the salvation of his soul; rather, by confession, devotion, and prayer, to prepare himself with all the effort he could for safely completing the pilgrimage-journey. He willingly accepted the advice; and, after the others had withdrawn and I alone sat before him, he began devoutly to make his confession. When the confession, as far as was then granted, had been completed, I did what belonged to me and absolved the sick man who had confessed, according to Christian custom. Having imposed upon him a suitable penance, according to what I had heard from him and what seemed right to me, I departed, intending to return to him on the following day.

When morning came, I returned as I had proposed, and, after those standing by had withdrawn, privately exhorted him on similar matters, as I had done before. But he, turning wholly toward me in mind, though only as much as his body allowed, said: “I have sinned, lord, and sinned greatly, in that I deliberately withheld certain things from yesterday’s confession, which I ought to have made sincerely. On that account I was summoned to judgment this night and compelled to see marvelous and terrible things. In a certain place stood a multitude of men of dark color and dreadful form, whose ugliness human sight could scarcely endure. They brought forth two scales: in one I saw my soul, in the other my deeds. They accused me on every side, putting forward many charges, sometimes true and sometimes false, according to their custom [Col. 0952D]. I burned with distress, hemmed in as I was, and could not answer for fear while, as it seemed, so many thousands of men hurled innumerable accusations against me.

“And when for a long time they had tormented me with lawsuits and accusations of this kind, keeping me in suspense and trembling over everything, at last there came a man beautiful in appearance. Standing in the midst, he said to the raging crowds—or rather, to the demons, as I understood them in my mind—‘What do you seek? This man plainly is not, this man is not one of yours. The confession which he made yesterday to his abbot has surely snatched him from your hands.’

“‘It is not so,’ they said; ‘it is not so as you say. For we know, and are fully aware, what he said and what he kept back. Certainly he was silent about some things of which he himself is conscious—not led by forgetfulness, but misled by deliberation.’ Therefore, when that good defender of mine could not deny the truth brought forward, even though by liars, and yet did not wish to abandon me, I spent this whole night in immeasurable toil and terror. When it had passed, and dawn, as I think, began the day, I awoke and returned to myself. Now, because I fully understand that in this vision God has bestowed much mercy upon me, wishing me to confess what I had resolved to conceal, I shall disclose everything wholly to God and to you, Father; nor shall I further deprive my soul of the salvation prepared for it.”

Having said this, he turned again to confession and, by God’s grace, completely emptied out everything that he had left unexhausted [Col. 0954A]. When his sincere and devout confession had been completed, I absolved the brother in fulfillment of my office; and, after he had been anointed with holy oil and refreshed with the body of Christ for the gaining of eternal life, I earnestly commended him to God and to the prayers of the brethren. Thus, taking leave of him, I departed with my companions. Afterwards, when I came to Cluny, I heard of his death after a few intervening days; and I requested that the benefits due to him for his soul should be diligently rendered by the brethren, and I added many things beyond what was due.

[Col. 0953]

# NINE SERMONS OF PETER THE VENERABLE, ABBOT OF CLUNY

## SERMON ONE. ON THE TRANSFIGURATION OF THE LORD

*(Bibliotheca Cluniacensis, p. 1231.)*

[Col. 0953B]

Today, most beloved, a day more serene than usual has dawned upon us: the day when heavenly light shone forth upon earth, when the true light illumined the darkness of mortals, when the divine radiance manifested itself visibly, even bodily, to human ages. Today the eternal Sun, having for a little while removed the darkness of bodily weakness, shone brilliantly through his still mortal body by a new and stupendous miracle. Today the Word made flesh displayed, by the glorification of his face and garments, the deification of the flesh united to him. Today “we saw his glory, glory as of the Only-begotten from the Father” (John 1), when from the magnificent glory there descended to him this voice [Col. 0953C]: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I have been well pleased; hear him” (2 Pet. 1).

This is the glory of the Only-begotten from the Father: when the Father acknowledged the Only-begotten, revealed him to those who did not know him, showed by divine works that he was his Son, glorified him uniquely today, and, distinguishing him from adopted sons, cried from heaven that he was his Son properly and truly, saying: “This is my beloved Son” (Matt. 3). “This,” he says, “is my Son. I indeed have many other sons by grace, but this Son is mine by nature. The others exist in time; he is before time. Others have been made; he has been begotten. He has been begotten in such a manner that he is also the Only-begotten. And he is Only-begotten because he alone, and not several, has been begotten from my substance.”

John saw this glory as of the Only-begotten from the Father when he recognized God from God, when he saw him himself transformed in glory and heard the Father instructing humankind concerning the Son. Therefore he says: “We saw his glory, glory as of the Only-begotten from the Father.” He saw it, and others saw it also. He heard it, and others heard it also. For Peter too said: “We heard this voice when we were with him on the holy mountain” (2 Pet. 1). That they saw and heard these things is likewise testified by the holy Evangelists Matthew, Mark, and Luke: “Jesus,” they say, “took Peter, James, and John, and led them apart up a high mountain; and he was transfigured before them” (Matt. 17; Mark 9; Luke 9).

James is added as a third witness to so great a vision because, according to the judgment of the same Lord, “every word shall stand on the testimony of two or three witnesses” (Matt. 18). So great a word, so great a vision, so exalted a matter required confirmation by the witness of three chief apostles. Thus the Savior rightly takes three disciples, so that the Trinity of the Godhead which appeared might be signified by the threefold number of the disciples. For there appeared there the Father in the voice, the Son in glorified flesh, and the Holy Spirit in the bright cloud: “Behold,” he says, “a bright cloud overshadowed them” (Matt. 17). Truly, the cloud is the Holy Spirit: a cloud, because he cools the minds which he overshadows from the heat of fleshly pleasures, and makes fruitful with heavenly rain those whom he finds dry; bright, because by his radiance he illumines the darkness of obscurity. Of this cloud’s overshadowing it is said also to the Virgin Mother: “The Holy Spirit shall come upon you, and the power of the Most High shall overshadow you” (Luke 2).

See, brethren, the glory of the feast; see the work of the Trinity; see the mystery of the resurrection. And why did I say, “of the resurrection”? The Father cries out, the Son shines, the Holy Spirit overshadows. The apostles see this, but only after nearly [Col. 0954D] eight days. For Luke the Evangelist says: “About eight days after these words, Jesus took Peter, James, and John” (Luke 9). You who have applied your minds to the sacred Scriptures know that the number six signifies the suffering of present evils, seven the rest of souls, and eight the resurrection of the body. For on the sixth day man was created and born for labor; Christ suffers insults, scourges, the cross, and death; on the seventh God commanded rest from labors, and he himself, in assumed flesh and free from suffering, rests in the tomb; and on the eighth, rising again, he gave us hope of resurrection and immortal life.

Therefore he reveals the heavenly vision of the Master to the disciples not fully after eight days, but “about eight days”—that is, before the eighth day had passed, while it was still present. He forms them for hope of eternal resurrection and more effectively urges them by examples than by words to hope for themselves what they see in him. For this reason his face shone as the sun and his garments became white as snow. Matthew and Mark wrote: “After six days Jesus took Peter, James, and John” (Matt. 17; Mark 9). Why, then, did Luke say that the Lord was transfigured after nearly eight days, while they said after six days?

As has already been said, six days were assigned at the beginning to the creation of the world; hence they signify all the time of this present life as suited to work. For as in those six days alone God performed all things and then rested from all of them, so during these six ages extending from the beginning of the world to its end—that is, throughout all the time one lives here, as though in one day—we must devote ourselves to works by which eternal rest is acquired. Of this day the Lord himself says: “I must work the works of him who sent me while it is day. Night comes, when no one can work” (John 9).

Therefore after six days the disciples contemplate the Lord’s glory, because only those shall be worthy of the eternal vision of God who have not neglected the Sabbath preceded by these six days, who have applied themselves to divine works, who have not allowed this day given them for working to be darkened by its passing into night. They must therefore pass through those six entire days by laboring, and see the God of gods in Zion and the King in his beauty. Thus the two Evangelists rightly said, “after six days.” But Luke said, “about eight days,” because, as stated above, after the labor of the six days in this life, followed by the rest of holy souls on the Sabbath, and with the resurrection of the body coming on the eighth, the saints “shall be caught up in the clouds to meet Christ in the air, and thus shall always be with the Lord” (1 Thess. 4).

Therefore he does not say “after eight,” but “about eight.” He who says “about eight days” says that the eighth day was not yet ended. Thus while the eighth was not yet finished, but was still present, the Lord showed himself glorified to the disciples. From the day of the promise—for he said, “There are some standing here who shall not taste death until they see the Son of Man coming in his kingdom” (Luke 9)—to the day on which what had been promised was fulfilled, if both the first day of promise and the last day of fulfillment are counted, eight days are found. But if these two are removed, only six are shown to have intervened. The Evangelists therefore said nothing discordant, but everything harmonious and consistent, both in the history and the significance of these days: “He took them,” it says, “and led them apart up a mountain” (Matt. 17).

[Col. 0956A] If the Lord’s transfiguration is the future resurrection of the saints, what is the high mountain except the heavenly dwelling? What does it mean that they are led apart, except that they shall ascend to it? Of this mountain and this ascent the Prophet says in the Psalms: “Lord, who shall dwell in your tabernacle, or who shall rest upon your holy mountain?” (Ps. 14). And elsewhere: “Who shall ascend the mountain of the Lord, or who shall stand in his holy place?” (Ps. 23). The disciples are therefore rightly led by Christ onto the mountain, because, after they have received again immortal bodies, the saints are raised by him from low things to high, from humble to exalted, from earthly to heavenly things; and they are joined to him forever, never thereafter to be separated from him.

Then truly they shall be led apart, because the tares, hitherto mingled with the wheat, shall no longer remain hidden but shall be bound by the reaping angels into bundles to be burned; the wheat, however, shall at the Lord’s command be gathered apart into his barn. Then truly they shall be led apart, when, according to the likeness of the net cast into the sea and gathering fish of every kind, at the end of the age the good fish shall be selected into vessels and the bad cast out. Then truly they shall be led apart, when, in that resurrection and final separation, the Son of Man—to whom the Father has given all judgment—shall separate the good from the evil, as a shepherd separates sheep from goats.

But who, brethren, are those said to be led apart onto the high mountain—Peter, James, and John? No one, then, is led unless he is Peter, James, and John. Why? Examine the names themselves, and the reason will immediately appear. Peter means “one who recognizes”; James, “supplanter”; John, “the grace of God.” The names suit their bearers. For who recognized Christ better than Peter? When Christ himself asked whom his disciples said that he was, Peter replied: “You are Christ, the Son of the living God” (Matt. 16). And elsewhere: “Lord, to whom shall we go? You have the words of eternal life; and we have believed and known that you are Christ, the Son of God” (John 6). Peter therefore recognized the Lord; hence he is rightly called “one who recognizes.”

Who more wisely supplanted the world than James? Though he had been occupied with his father and brother in fishing for worldly gain, as soon as Christ called him from the boat, he exchanged bodily gain for spiritual, transitory gain for eternal, worldly gain for divine; and he deserved to become, from a fisher of fish, a fisher of human beings. James is therefore not undeservedly called the world’s supplanter. And who could more rightly be called “the grace of God” than John? He was endowed so abundantly with that grace that, among the other marks of it, he deserved by Christ’s commendation to become the son and servant of the Virgin Mother; to recline upon his breast; to reveal to the world, so far as was permitted to a human being, the mysteries of the Godhead; to be loved by the Master above the others; and, as by a special proper title, to be called “the disciple whom Jesus loved.” It is evident, therefore, that he who attained the grace of God so outstandingly was accordingly called “the grace of God.”

[Col. 0957A] Thus, because these gifts shone uniquely in them, they deserved to be taken apart up the mountain to see God’s glory; and they taught that no others but those of such a character shall be taken up in the future resurrection to contemplate such glory. For no one shall be taken up unless he is Peter, James, and John—that is, one who recognizes, a supplanter, and the grace of God. Whoever wishes then to be taken up must become Peter: he must recognize his Lord and recognize himself; recognize him as Creator and himself as creature; him as maker and himself as work; him as Lord and himself as servant; him as righteous and himself as unrighteous; him as sanctifier and himself as sinner; him as Redeemer and himself as redeemed. Let him not say with Pharaoh: “I do not know the Lord” (Exod. 5), lest perhaps at the end he too should hear with the others: “Amen, I say to you, I do not know you” (Matt. 25).

Rather, let him strive with all his strength to recognize all these things by faith, because “without faith it is impossible to please God” (Heb. 11), and because “the righteous lives by faith” (Heb. 10), so that he may be among the sheep of the good shepherd, of whom he himself says: “My sheep hear my voice, and I, the Lord, know them” (John 10); and elsewhere: “I know mine, and mine know me” (ibid.); and of whom the Apostle says: “Knowing God—or rather, being known by God” (Gal. 4).

And because faith of recognition without the work of love is not sufficient—for faith is idle unless it is the sort of faith “which works through love” (Gal. 5)—let him be James, that he may supplant the one who wishes to supplant, deceive the one who desires to deceive: the devil, the world, and sin. For the devil tempts, the world entices, and sin kills. Therefore, since the devil wishes to deceive by delighting and to kill by deceiving, let us cautiously learn to avoid the deceiver, so that, prudently recognizing the wickedness of the flattering enemy, we may say with the Apostle: “For we are not ignorant of his devices” (2 Cor. 2). When these have been recognized and conquered by God’s power, the soldier of God shall gloriously triumph, supplanting that worst enemy; and he shall sing with the Prophet: “Through you we shall push down our enemies with the horn; in your name we shall trample those who rise up against us” (Ps. 43).

To these two the third, John, must also be joined, so that the investigator of heavenly visions may understand that he has been able, or can be able, to do nothing; to believe nothing worthily or perform nothing worthily, apart from God’s grace—as God himself declares in the Gospel, speaking to the disciples: “Without me you can do nothing” (John 15). The Apostle Paul confirms this: “By the grace of God I am what I am, and his grace in me has not been empty” (1 Cor. 15). And the Psalmist: “My God, his mercy shall go before me; and your mercy shall follow me” (Ps. 58). But if God’s mercy goes before and follows after every human good, it is known that no human good can exist apart from his grace.

Thus Peter, recognizing God by faith; thus James, glorifying him by holy works after the world has been deceived; thus John, recognizing and giving thanks that what he possesses in faith and works he has received not from himself or another, but from the grace of him from whom comes “every good gift and every perfect gift” (Jas. 1)—these, with no others admitted, deserve to contemplate the mysteries of divine grace. These alone shall be able to attain the glory of eternal resurrection, ascend the high mountain, and see Christ transfigured in majesty, because “he shall transform the body of our lowliness, making it like the body of his glory” (Phil. 3), when “we all come to the unity of faith and of the knowledge of the Son of God, to a perfect man, to the measure of the age of the fullness of Christ” (Eph. 4).

Then Peter shall have a knowledge of truth much better and more perfect than before, because, as God says through the prophet: “No man shall teach his brother or his neighbor, saying, ‘Know the Lord’; for all shall know me, from the least to the greatest” (Jer. 31). Then James, supplanter and conqueror of vices, shall appear more glorious, because the earth of our body shall no longer bring forth thorns and thistles of carnal pleasures. It shall be possessed by the saints forever, without any danger of war, as it is said: “Blessed are the meek, for they shall possess the earth” (Matt. 5). Then the saying written shall come to pass: “Death has been swallowed up in victory. Where, O death, is your victory? Where, O death, is your sting?” (1 Cor. 15). Then John shall obtain the grace of God far more excellently, because, as he himself wrote: “From his fullness we have all received, and grace for grace” (John 1): grace of recompense for grace of action; grace of glorification for grace of work.

Nor does the following differ from this understanding: Peter, prince of the apostles, singular shepherd of Christ’s sheep, and supreme teacher of the Church after Christ; and James and John, Boanerges—that is, “sons of thunder”—were chosen to see these things, so that Peter’s authority might seem more worthy of faith in testifying to this; so that the whole Church might be signified in its chief Shepherd as destined to be raised to see God; and so that James and John, hearing the Father thundering from heaven, might fittingly be called sons of thunder.

For all these reasons Jesus took only Peter, James, and John, led them apart up a high mountain, and was transfigured before them. “And his face shone like the sun, and his garments became white as snow” (Matt. 17). What are these things to you, O human being? Do you hear them with deaf ears [Col. 0958D]? Do you ungratefully behold such great benefits from your Creator? Do you not marvel in astonishment at the Divinity’s concern for you? When you did not exist, he created you by free goodness, that by clinging to him forever you might be blessed. For you he made and subjected heaven, earth, sea, everything in them, and the entire mass of the world. For you—far surpassing all these things—when you had been subjected to eternal death and were failing amid the innumerable evils of the world, he was born in your flesh, suffered, and died.

And lest you delay in believing the saving admonitions of your Lord and God, he compelled you to give him faith through wonderful works. Hence he gave sight to the blind, cleansed lepers, healed every sickness of humankind, and even raised the dead; hence he walked with unhindered step upon the swelling mass of the sea’s waves, commanded the elements, and granted this same power of miracles to all who truly believe in him. Hence today, as I have said, transfigured in corruptible flesh, he showed that your corruptible body too can put on incorruption, your mortal body immortality. For as his own face shone like the sun, so he showed that you too can shine, when he said: “Then the righteous shall shine like the sun in the kingdom of their Father” (Matt. 13). If, therefore, you are righteous, you too shall be able to shine as he does.

His face became like the sun. What wonder that his face became like the sun, since he is himself the Sun? What wonder if the face of the Sun became as the sun? He was the Sun, but hidden beneath a cloud, and then, with the cloud removed, shining forth for a little while. What does “the cloud removed” mean? Not the flesh, but the weakness of the flesh, taken away for a moment. This is the cloud of which the Prophet says: “Behold, the Lord shall ascend upon a light cloud” (Isa. 19). The cloud is flesh, veiling divinity; it is light because it bears no iniquity. It is a cloud because it conceals the divine radiance; light because it too shall be raised in everlasting splendor. It is a cloud because, as is read in the Song of Songs: “I sat under the shadow of him whom I desired” (Song 2); light because it is the flesh of the Lamb who takes away the sins of the world. When these are taken away, the world is lifted to the heights of heaven, now burdened by no weight of sins.

The Sun, veiled by this cloud of flesh, is not the sun which rises upon good and evil, but the Sun of righteousness, which rises only upon those who fear God. This light, certainly veiled by the cloud of flesh—the light which enlightens every human being—shone forth today [Col. 0959C]; today, glorifying that very flesh and showing it deified to the apostles, he revealed it to the world through himself and through the apostles. And you too, blessed City, shall enjoy forever the contemplation of this Sun, when, descending from heaven, prepared by God, you shall be adorned like a bride for her husband. This Sun shall never again set for you; remaining always the same, it makes the everlasting morning serene. This Sun is now covered by no cloud, but, shining tirelessly, delights you with continual light. This Sun no longer strikes your eyes painfully, but strengthens you to behold it and delights you with divine radiance. This Sun suffers no eclipse, because its brightness is interrupted by none of your sorrow. For there shall be no more death, mourning, pain, or crying to darken the splendor given you by God, because, as was said to John from heaven: “These former things have passed away” (Rev. 21).

This is the Sun of which it is said through the prophet: “You shall no longer have the sun for light by day, nor shall the brightness of the moon give you light; but the Lord your God shall be your everlasting light” (Isa. 60). This is your everlasting light, shining from the Lord’s face. You hear the Lord’s voice; you hear the Lord’s face shining as the sun. In the face, by which each person is known, understand his recognition; in its brightness, the illumination of those who recognize him. Here he is believed by you through faith; there he shall be known in himself. Here he is apprehended by understanding; there he shall be comprehended. “Here you see through a mirror and in an enigma; but there you shall see face to face” (1 Cor. 13). Then, truly knowing him as he is, you shall be illuminated forever by the eternal splendor of this Sun; you shall be happily enlightened and most excellently illumined. Then, with the Lord’s face truly shining upon you, that which the Prophet long ago desired shall be fulfilled: “May he make his face shine upon us” (Ps. 66).
