But how shall his face be illumined, when it has never lacked light, when it is itself the light that enlightens every human being? God’s face, I say, shall not be illumined in itself; it shall be illumined over you—over you it shall be illumined, because it shall give you light, shine for you, and gleam for you. Therefore the Prophet expressed this distinctly, saying: “May he shine upon us.” Of this light he says elsewhere: “Lord, they shall walk in the light of your face” (Ps. 88).

This face, then, is the face of the Lord which shone like the sun upon the mountain, and which shall shine like the sun in heaven [Col. 0960B]. In the light of its true knowledge you shall rejoice forever, as has been said. In its light you shall walk without weariness. In its light you shall see everlasting light. Therefore the Gospel says: “His face became like the sun, and his garments became white as snow” (Matt. 3). Who are signified by Christ’s garments except those who cling most closely to him in faith and manner of life? Though they are not what he is, they are nevertheless where he is. Hence elsewhere he says to the Father: “Father, I desire that where I am, they also may be with me” (John 17).

Those garments themselves are white as snow. For such brilliance of face admits nothing dark around it. The face shines; the garments gleam. With what gleam? With one fitting for so great a radiance. And what gleam is fitting for such radiance? What but snowy whiteness? For what is brighter than the shining sun, or whiter than snow? The garments must gleam with this whiteness; but such whiteness is acquired for garments through much labor and effort. Garments plainly cannot attain fitting whiteness unless they are boiled by fire, washed with water, and dyed with the juice of herbs. As these three things are necessary to a garment for the body, so they must be applied to Christ’s garment.

I have said that Christ’s garment is Christ’s faithful people. What, then, is the fire necessary for this garment? What is the water? What are the herbs? The fire is that which burns harmful things and illumines dark things. What fire is this? That of which John says: “I baptize you with water, but he shall baptize you with the Holy Spirit and fire” (John 1). The Lord, ascending into heaven, tells his disciples what this fire is, saying: “For John indeed baptized with water, but you shall be baptized with the Holy Spirit” (Acts 1). This fire, therefore, is the Holy Spirit.

What is the water? The water of baptism and of tears. Of the water of baptism the Lord says in the Gospel: “Unless a person is born again of water and the Holy Spirit,” etc. (John 3). Of the water of tears the Psalmist says: “Every night I shall wash my bed; with my tears I shall water my couch” (Ps. 6). Of both, another prophet says: “I shall pour clean water upon you, and you shall be cleansed from all your defilements” (Ezek. 36). Therefore hearts are kindled by the fire of the Spirit, desires for God grow hot, one first runs to baptism, and water grows warm for cleansing the garment through the fire’s burning; this water too is sanctified by the Spirit’s power for cleansing the soul [Col. 0961A]. That water washes away whatever filth had clung to the soul. The human being is made new and clothed in white, new garments, so that, as one made white and renewed in spirit, he may appear fitting within the garment of Christ’s body.

If this garment, cleansed in this way, is afterwards defiled, it must be purified not by baptismal water, which knows how to cleanse only once, but a second time by the fountain of tears. By it Peter washed away the stains of his denial; Mary, watering the Lord’s feet, extinguished the flames of vice; and the Lord himself raised Lazarus, their dead brother, through his sisters’ tears. But just as the first fountain can do nothing without the Spirit, so the second can obtain nothing without him. That baptismal water is nothing without the Spirit is indicated by the Lord, who, after saying, “Unless one is born again of water and Spirit” (John 3), later made no mention of water but added: “What is born of the Spirit is spirit” (ibid.), showing that the Spirit is the author of this rebirth and that, without the Spirit, water is nothing but a cold and moist element. The Apostle shows that tears of repentance can be poured out only from the same Spirit when he says: “The Spirit himself intercedes for us with inexpressible groanings” (Rom. 8).

We have recognized the fire and the water that purify Christ’s garment and cleanse it when it has again been defiled. Let us seek also the herb necessary for this work [Col. 0961C]. What, then, can it be except that of which the Prophet says: “You shall sprinkle me with hyssop, and I shall be cleansed” (Ps. 50)? And why did he choose it above the rest? Because it is a lowly herb: it does not seek heights, shuns exaltation, and embraces humiliation. What it possesses by nature, therefore, the person to be cleansed must possess by grace. For just as the Spirit cleanses no one by water unless that person repents, so no one repents unless he humbles himself. Humility, therefore, is the herb by which every iniquity is wiped away through water and Spirit.

By these means Christ’s garment must be cleansed; by these means the Lord’s clothing should be purified. By these means that vestment must be made white, with which the Son of God, transfigured into the majesty of divine glory, is to be adorned. You therefore, who desire to be joined to Christ, labor and exercise yourself; chastise your body and subject it to servitude. Wash away whatever is foul, whatever is unclean, whatever is unworthy of the covering of Christ’s body; and, removing every deformity of vice, add to yourself the snowy whiteness of virtues, saying to God with the Prophet: “You shall wash me, and I shall be made whiter than snow” (ibid.).

Nor should you wonder if the glory of this blessed whiteness is not yet revealed in you. For “we walk by faith, not by sight,” etc. (2 Cor. 5). “We know that it has not yet appeared what we shall be; but when he appears, we shall be like him, because we shall see him as he is” (1 John 3); and, “When Christ, our life, appears, then we too shall appear with him in glory” (Col. 3). Mark indicates this when he says: “His garments became white, such as no fuller on earth can make white” (Mark 9) [Col. 0962A]. This glory is indeed gained upon earth, but it is not bestowed upon earth. Therefore these things must be awaited in heaven, not on earth; they must be received in the resurrection, not in mortality, when those who have deserved it shall be like the angels of God in heaven; when Christ shall fit his own to himself, as a garment, for glory and beauty; when what was spoken through the Prophet shall be fulfilled: “You shall clothe yourself with all these as with an ornament” (Isa. 49).

But see whence whiteness comes to this garment of Christ: “Such as,” he says, “no fuller can make.” You know that garments acquire whiteness through the fuller’s frequent beating and continual treading. The fuller’s treading, therefore, is the contempt with which the proud despise the saints, of which the Prophet says in the Psalm: “Our soul has been greatly filled with the reproach of the prosperous and the contempt of the proud” (Ps. 122). The fuller’s continual beating is the persecution by the wicked, by which they wear the saints down daily. Yet through this compression and persecution, although the saints are much afflicted in the present, they are made white as they advance toward the Lord’s adornment; and they are fitted, so that in the manifestation of the kingdom they may cling to their King as royal linen. Hence it is said of them: “Blessed are those who suffer persecution for righteousness’ sake, for theirs is the kingdom of heaven” (Matt. 5).

“And behold, Moses and Elijah appeared with him, speaking” (Matt. 3). Moses and Elijah appear with Christ: the Law and the Prophets are joined to the Gospel. They address the one present whom they had earlier foretold as absent. “And,” says the Evangelist, “they spoke of his departure which he was to accomplish at Jerusalem” (Luke 9). Understand that they did not recount his departure to the Lord in order to teach one who could be ignorant of nothing; rather, it was so that you might recognize them as those of whom the Lord himself, after his departure and resurrection, said to his disciples: “It was necessary that all things written concerning me in the Law and the Prophets should be fulfilled” (Luke 24).

That Moses wrote concerning him is testified by Christ himself when speaking to the Jews: “If you believed Moses, perhaps you would believe me also; for he wrote of me” (John 5). It is certain that Elijah, by lofty prophecy, went beforehand to announce Christ’s first coming. But that he shall go before the second coming in a still more exalted way is indicated by the voice of God speaking through the prophet: “Behold, I shall send you Elijah the prophet before the great and terrible day of the Lord comes” (Mal. 4). And the Lord says to the disciples: “Elijah is to come, and he himself shall restore all things” (Matt. 17).

“**Moses and Elijah appeared with him**,” he says. Attend, brothers, to a great mystery. Attend, and marvel at a new miracle. See why, before all the other Fathers and prophets, these two in particular are joined to the Lord in this heavenly vision. It is written of Moses: “Moses was a man most meek above all who dwelt upon the earth” (Num. 12). Who could better attest this remarkable meekness than that Jewish people? When, at God’s command, he had led them out of Egypt through fearful signs and had brought them on foot across the sea; when on the seashore he had shown them their enemies destroyed by divine power; when for so long a time he had fed them in the wilderness with heavenly manna, had often given them water drawn from the rock, had fattened them with flesh brought by the service of the wind, and had exposed himself to countless deaths for their sake—after all these things, I say, you have heard what gratitude he received from them. Gathering together, they rushed upon him, heaped many insults upon him, attacked him with stones, and compelled him to flee to the tabernacle of the Lord. Had he not been powerfully rescued by God, he would undoubtedly have perished, slain by the impious. And although he frequently suffered such things from them, and God threatened the destruction of that perverse nation because of these and their countless evils, he opposed himself to vengeance on their behalf and strove, so far as he could, that those who sought to destroy him should not perish.

For when God said, “Let me alone, that my wrath may be kindled against them and I may destroy them, and make thee into a great nation” (Exod. 32), he answered: “If thou forgivest them their sin, forgive it; but if not, blot me out of the book which thou hast written” (ibid.). You have heard Moses’ meekness; hear also Elijah’s severity. Provoked by the excessive impieties of an idolatrous king and people, he shut up the waters of heaven; and lest the reprobate earth should bear fruit, for three years and six months he withheld rain by his word, saying: “As the Lord lives, there shall be neither dew nor rain except according to the word of my mouth” (3 Kings 17). He put to death four hundred prophets of Baal, together with three hundred others, having led them down to the river. He consumed two captains of fifty, with their fifties, by heavenly fire, saying to each: “If I am a man of God, let fire come down from heaven and devour thee and thy fifty” (4 Kings 1). Thus the one was exceedingly meek, the other exceedingly severe.

Therefore these Fathers, the one most gentle and the other most unyielding, appear with the Lord, because “the Lord is merciful and compassionate” (Ps. 102); because “the Lord is righteous, and he hath loved righteousness” (Ps. 10); because “all the ways of the Lord are mercy and truth” (Ps. 24); because the Prophet sings to the Lord “mercy and judgment” (Ps. 100); because “mercy,” which is Christ [Col. 0963D], “and truth have met together; righteousness and peace have kissed” (Ps. 84). Thus the merciful one signifies the merciful Lord, and the righteous one the righteous Lord. Hence Scripture fittingly places not Elijah first and Moses afterward, but Moses first and Elijah afterward, considering not so much the order of time in which one preceded the other in birth, as the order of meaning by which the former goes before the latter in signification. Moses signifies the Lord’s first coming, Elijah his second.

For at his first coming he came with mercy; he came with gentleness, because he came as Savior, Redeemer, and Liberator, as he himself says to Nicodemus: “For God sent not his Son into the world to judge the world, but that the world might be saved through him” (John 3). Hence, when his disciples elsewhere were angered because certain persons would not receive him as a guest and said to him, “Wilt thou that we command fire to come down from heaven and consume them, as Elijah did?” he answered: “You know not of what spirit you are. The Son of Man came not to destroy souls, but to save them” (Luke 9). And to Zacchaeus, among other things: “For the Son of Man came to seek and to save that which was lost” (Luke 19).

When he showed himself the author of this salvation by divine deeds—healing every sickness, raising the dead, and bestowing many other temporal goods even upon an unbelieving people—and when, what Moses had never been able to do, he promised eternal goods and gave them to those who believed in him, he was called by the ungrateful and lost, in wicked insolence, “a foreigner,” “one having a devil,” “a gluttonous man,” “a drinker of wine,” “a friend of publicans and sinners.” [Col. 0964B] He was often attacked with stones, like Moses; and finally, crucified, he prayed to the Father for those who crucified him: “Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do” (Luke 23). Behold our Moses: meek, gentle, merciful, and indulgent toward all.

Now see Elijah; behold the righteous one; consider the terrible one, bringing torments upon sinners. Fear the fire that will consume not merely a hundred men, as then, but the whole world. This fire the man of God Elijah—that is, the Son of Man, Jesus—will bring down upon the impious when he comes from heaven in his majesty to judge: when “God shall come manifestly, our God, and shall not keep silence” (Ps. 49); when “a fire shall burn in his sight, and a mighty tempest round about him” (ibid.); when “he shall call heaven from above, and the earth, to judge his people” (ibid.); when he shall come “in strength, and his arm shall rule” (Isa. 40); when “he shall cry out and shout, and shall prevail against his enemies” (Isa. 42).

Of this coming he himself says in the Gospel: “Then if any man shall say to you, Behold, here is Christ, or behold, there, do not believe it. For as lightning cometh out of the east and shineth even unto the west, so shall be the coming of the Son of Man” (Matt. 24). And shortly afterward: “Then shall the sign of the Son of Man appear in heaven; and then all the tribes of the earth shall mourn, and they shall see the Son of Man coming in the clouds of heaven with great power and majesty” (ibid.). And John says in the Apocalypse: “Every eye shall see him, and they also who pierced him; and all the tribes of the earth shall mourn over him” (Rev. 1).

He therefore who, as was said, was meek in the first coming, shall appear as Elijah in the second; humble in the first, exalted in the second; despised in the first, dreadful in the second; hidden in the first, manifest in the second; gentle in the first, severe in the second; judged in the first, judge in the second; Savior in the first, and in the second not only Savior but also condemner.

What had long before been promised to Moses is now rendered to him. When he burned in spirit, saying, “If I have found grace in thy sight, show me thy face,” he heard: “Thou hast found grace in my sight, and I know thee by name; but thou canst not see my face. For man shall not see me and live; but when I shall pass by, thou shalt see my back parts” (Exod. 33).

What, brothers, are God’s “back parts”? See what are his “foreparts,” and then you will see what his “back parts” are. For what is before God except that before which everything else is subsequent? What is prior to God himself? What is not subsequent to that substance of which it is said, “From the womb, before the morning star, I begot thee” (Ps. 109); and which says, “Before the hills I was brought forth. He had not yet made the earth, nor the rivers, nor the foundations of the world” (Prov. 8); and which was in the beginning with God, so that all things were made through him, and without him nothing was made? Since all these things were made by him, he is necessarily prior to them, and they subsequent to him. The Creator is prior to the creature; the creature is always subsequent to the Creator. Therefore the creative substance is prior; created nature is subsequent.

Was Moses, when he sought to see the Creator, promised—by way of a great gift—to behold indiscriminately the whole mass of creation instead of the Creator? Far be it! Not every creature, but a certain creature was promised to him as a great sight. This, I say, is that unique creature. This is that unique humanity which, received by God himself in the Virgin’s womb without any corruption of sin and united to the Word of God, is called no longer a creature but Creator because of the union of one person with him. Since, according to the manner of the Creator and according to the order of time in which, as the Apostle says, it appeared at the consummation of the ages for the destruction of sin, it is subsequent to God, God’s “back parts,” previously promised to Moses, were shown to him today. For, as is clearly established, God’s foreparts are his divinity, existing before all things; God’s back parts are the humanity afterward assumed.

Moses, beholding today this glorification of that humanity, rejoiced that what had been promised him was rendered. Nor without cause: for he recognized what he had foretold before, and rejoiced in the humility of that humanity by which both he and the world were to be saved. Thus he recalled what had formerly been said to him: “When I shall pass by, thou shalt see my back parts.” “When I shall pass by,” he says. For what else was Christ then doing in the world but making a passage? He had come not to remain here, but to pass hence. He was passing from death to life, from corruption to incorruption, from humility to glorification, from the world to the Father, as the Evangelist says: “Jesus, knowing that his hour was come that he should pass from this world to the Father, having loved his own who were in the world, loved them unto the end” (John 13). And shortly afterward: “I came forth from the Father and came into the world; again I leave the world and go to the Father” (John 16). And in the Psalms: “I am solitary until I pass by” (Ps. 140).

In this passage Moses saw Jesus, because he appeared with him on the mountain, still according to the flesh mortal and corruptible, though then for a time glorified. And why do you marvel that Moses saw Jesus’ deified flesh, when Abraham, before Moses, “rejoiced that he might see his day; he saw it and was glad” (John 8)?

“Moses and Elijah,” says Luke, “were seen in majesty” (Luke 9). They were seen in the majesty both of Christ and of themselves, because they too were glorified with the glorified one: he as God, they as men; he as Lord, they as servants; he as the only-begotten, they as adopted sons. But see further what Moses and Elijah signify when they appear with Christ. Scripture says of Moses, as of others, that he died: “Moses, the servant of the Lord, died; the Lord buried him” (Deut. 34). But concerning Elijah it testifies that he did not die, but was taken up by fiery horses (4 Kings 2), that he still lives, and that in his own time he is to die (Mal. 4). Whom, then, do the dead Moses signify except the dead; and whom does the living Elijah signify except the living? Thus these two are seen with the Lord as a figure of the resurrection, to show that living and dead alike shall be judged by God in that resurrection.

The Apostle confirms this in his Epistle: “The Lord himself shall descend with a command, and with the voice of the archangel, and with the trumpet of God; and the dead who are in Christ shall rise first. Then we who are alive, who remain, shall be caught up together with them in the clouds to meet Christ in the air; and so shall we be always with the Lord” (1 Thess. 4). Although he appears to speak there only of the elect living and the elect dead, elsewhere he plainly declares this concerning both elect and reprobate, living and dead: “For to this end Christ died and rose again, that he might be Lord both of the living and of the dead” (Rom. 14). He rightly judges the living and the dead, because “he died for our sins and rose again for our justification” (Rom. 4).

Then Peter answered and said to Jesus: “Lord, it is good for us to be here. If thou wilt, let us make here three tabernacles: one for thee, one for Moses, and one for Elijah” (Matt. 17).

Peter, what are you saying? Why do you seek an earthly dwelling? Why do you desire him to remain here, when he came in order to depart? Why do you provide a temporary habitation for him who dwells in heaven? He did not come to acquire a house on earth, since he chose to have nowhere to lay his head. He did not come that you might build him a dwelling on earth, but that he might prepare a place for you in heaven. He did not come to inhabit here a house built by you, but to raise you after himself to that prepared dwelling above. Concerning it he himself said to his disciples: “And if I shall go and prepare a place for you, I will come again and take you to myself, that where I am, you also may be” (John 14). You ought to be where he is; it is not fitting that he should remain where you wish.

“It is good for us to be here.” Where, I ask, then are death, the Passion, the redemption of the world, the resurrection, and the ascension into heaven? Where is that which the Prophet says: “His going forth is from the height of heaven, and his circuit unto the height thereof” (Ps. 18)? For if he remains with you as you desire, he will neither accomplish all those things for which he came, nor return whence he came.

“It is good for us to be here.” If, Peter, it is good to be here, as you say, far better is that which you will enjoy in your homeland. If momentary delight is good, eternal blessedness is much better. If the humanity of Christ glorified for a time delights you, his divinity, eternally beheld, will delight you beyond comparison. I mean that divinity into which angels desire to look (1 Pet. 1), from which they never suffer their gaze to turn away, which is promised to the pure in heart and will someday be granted them in the end. You too shall enjoy it; but as Christ suffered for you, so you must first suffer for Christ. You must first become a companion of his Passion, that afterward you may also share his consolation.

There he will receive you and his own into eternal tabernacles. There, truly, you will prepare yourself as not, as here, three tabernacles for Christ, Moses, and Elijah, but one tabernacle for Father, Son, and Holy Spirit, when “God shall be all in all” (1 Cor. 15); when, according to the Apocalypse, “the tabernacle of God shall be with men, and he shall dwell with them” (Rev. 21); when they shall be his people, and he himself, God with them, shall be their God (ibid.).

“While he was yet speaking, behold, a bright cloud overshadowed them; and behold, a voice from the cloud saying: This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased; hear ye him” (Matt. 17). Come here, nations; hasten here, peoples; draw near, all of you. Make haste here, unbelievers, and be converted; be present here, believers, and be instructed. You wished to be assured concerning the Son of God: now, having received so great a testimony, doubt no longer. Patriarchs were sent beforehand to bear this witness; prophets were subjected to this task, who saw through the Spirit that he was to come and announced him to the world before he was born. The Apostles also saw him—not, like those men, by the Spirit alone, but in the flesh. In that flesh they saw not one yet to be born, but one born; not one who would preach, but one preaching; not one who would perform divine works, but one performing them, fulfilling all that had been said of him and all for which he had come. As was said, Peter and James were led by him up the mountain to see this. So too was John, who confesses that he not only saw but also handled with his hands the Word which was from the beginning, saying: “That which was from the beginning, which we have heard, which we have seen with our eyes, and which our hands have handled, concerning the Word of life” (1 John 1).

Moses was present from the lower regions, and Elijah came from the heights, so that you might know that to Christ, the Son of God, heavenly things in Elijah, earthly things in the Apostles, and infernal things in Moses bear testimony; and that he is the one whom God exalted in assumed flesh and to whom he gave “a name which is above every name, that at the name of Jesus every knee should bow, of things in heaven, on earth, and under the earth” (Phil. 2); nor is there “any other name under heaven given” in which we must be saved (Acts 4).

You have heard their testimony; hear also that testimony greater than which none can be found among created things. No human testimony can be greater than his, because among all men none can be found greater than John—I mean John, who “was sent from God” to bear witness, “to bear witness of the light, that all men might believe through him” (John 1). His testimony indeed is: “He that hath the bride is the bridegroom” (John 3); and, “There hath stood one in the midst of you whom you know not, whose shoe-latchet I am not worthy to loose” (John 1); and, “He that believeth not the Son shall not have life, but the wrath of God abideth on him” (John 3); and, “Behold the Lamb of God, who taketh away the sins of the world” (John 1); and, “I saw, and bore witness” (ibid.). This, I say, is the testimony of the great John, than which, as has been said, none greater can be found among men.

Yet Christ, as Christ himself says, has a testimony greater than John’s (John 5). Because it is greater than John’s, it is no longer human but divine; not from man but from God; not from earth but from heaven. This is what sounded forth today from the cloud: “This is my beloved Son.” And what more do you demand? Behold the patriarchs; behold the prophets; behold the Apostles; behold the living; behold the departed; behold the world and the lower regions; behold he who is above all—God himself, the author of light, the fountain of divinity, the Father from heaven of the glorified Son—crying: “This is my Son.”

You have heard the testimony of prophets concerning him; you have heard the testimony of Apostles concerning him; you have heard John’s testimony concerning him. Hear also my testimony concerning him: “This is my Son.” If you have believed men, you should much more believe God saying: “This is my Son.” If you believed others concerning my Son, much more ought you to believe me, his Father, from whom you have heard: “This is my Son.” For I know whom I have begotten, because “no one knoweth the Son but the Father” (Matt. 11). I know whom I have begotten; I know whom I have brought forth from myself; I know whom I have produced not from nothing and not from elsewhere, but from my own substance: God from God, Creator from Creator, almighty from almighty, invisible from invisible, incomprehensible from incomprehensible, immortal from immortal, eternal from eternal, knowing all things from one knowing all things, containing all things from one containing all things. For he who was begotten from me could be none other than I am, from whom he was begotten; and therefore, “This is my Son.”

The flesh assumed does not deceive me, as it deceives those who see only the outward appearance. The humanity which you behold does not deceive me; my divinity, which creates all things, created it; the obedient humility of this my Son assumed it; through it eternity, long lost to mortals, is restored. I made this humanity; I did not beget it. Yet because it is eternally united to him whom I begot—dividing and distinguishing nothing, but showing that the man assumed by God is deified by the very assumption—I say without distinction: “This is my Son.” Moses is not my Son; Elijah is not my Son; Peter, James, and John are not my Son; but this is my Son. And that you may know that not they but he is my Son: when Peter, James, and John hear this voice, they fall down; Moses and Elijah depart, because they know that the voice does not concern them. Jesus alone neither falls nor departs, because he shows himself alone to be my true Son.

Do not, I say, in any respect doubt the testimony of those who went before him and declared him to be my Son, for behold, I bear witness to them that this is my Son. Believe also him when he bears testimony of himself and says: “If I bear witness of myself, my testimony is true, because I know whence I come and whither I go” (John 8). Believe also the Holy Spirit, concerning whom the Son himself says to his disciples: “When the Paraclete shall come, whom I will send you from the Father, the Spirit of truth, he shall bear witness concerning me” (John 15), so that in our Trinity nothing diverse or separate may be thought to exist; rather, what the distinctive property of each person accomplishes is to be understood as the common operation of the whole Trinity. Because of all these things, know that this is my Son.

And if perhaps you hear some contradicting this truth, do not be scandalized, do not be shaken, do not be carried about by every wind of false doctrine. They are raised up that you may be tested; they are kindled that you may be purified. But when you are purified, they are extinguished; when you shine, they are darkened; when you are given life, they die; when you are crowned, they are punished forever. Therefore do not believe them; do not assent to falsehood; but believe my unchangeable truth, and know without doubt that this is my Son. Let the unbeliever deny and say, “He is not the Son of God.” I, God his Father, say: “This is my Son.”

Rightly, therefore, rejecting falsehood and confessing truth, you will hear and believe that this is my Son. And he added, “beloved.” He is beloved to me because I begot one who is beloved; for I could not beget except one beloved, nor could I love anything as I love what I have begotten. For as our nature is unique, so the love belonging to that same nature is unique. As my Son’s generation from me is unique, so my love toward him is unique. Therefore, although in its own manner I love what I have created, nevertheless I love above all things him whom I have begotten.

Hence “this is my beloved Son” is still specially beloved for this reason: through him my wrath toward wretched mortals is restrained, my indignation calmed, and my sentence condemning them changed. Thus their love toward us, which had grown cold, is rekindled; affection is stirred and desire aroused, so that they may be ashamed of their former life, turn from the path of error, and by the way—my Son made man—come to life, that is, to God himself, my Son. And because he thus draws hostile human beings after him from love of the world to love of me—without which my Son never is, nor can my servant ever be—therefore he is my beloved Son. Thus is fulfilled what he himself, praying to me the Father, said: “That the love wherewith thou hast loved me may be in them, and I in them” (John 17).

Indeed the love by which I loved the Son was in human beings, because I loved him for this purpose: that he might call others; that he might justify those called; that he might glorify those justified. And because through him others are likewise saved by this love, he, who loved them first, is also loved by them. “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.” What I now say of this one, I could say of no other, because in none besides him was I well pleased.

Not in Adam, the father of all, whom I created excellent; because I was not well pleased in him, I expelled him from paradise (Gen. 3). Not in those who inherited from him both nature and vice: because I was not well pleased in them, I said, “It repenteth me that I made man. I will destroy man whom I created from the face of the earth” (Gen. 6). Certainly I was pleased in none of them, and therefore I destroyed all of them in the flood. Nor was I pleased in any of their successors, because I cast down to the lower regions all who resisted my good pleasure.

If any one among them acknowledged me by faith and worshipped me by works, I was indeed pleased in him, but not so well pleased as in this one. For just as there was in every righteous person in whom I was pleased something in which I was not pleased, so—even if he observed the way of righteousness to the extent of his ability—he nevertheless departed from it in some respect. Although my grace lived mightily in him, something from corrupted nature nevertheless crept in. But in this one, who kept all the commandments, who departed from righteousness in no respect, who, as he himself said, always does what is pleasing to me, I was not merely pleased but well pleased.

In those who always performed things contrary to righteousness, I was never pleased in any respect. In those who observed righteousness for the most part but nevertheless transgressed its limit in some point, I was not well pleased because of their negligence, yet I was pleased in them because of the righteousness they preserved. But in this one I was both pleased and well pleased because of innocence wholly preserved and righteousness supremely maintained. This is he of whom I said beforehand through the prophet: “Behold my servant whom I have chosen, my elect; my soul is pleased in him” (Isa. 42). Therefore, although God’s good pleasure is upon those who fear him, this is he in whom my soul is pleased above all those who fear God.

Know therefore that this is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased: hear him. For this is my Son—not adopted, but proper; not temporal, but eternal; not inferior, but equal; not from elsewhere, but consubstantial. He is beloved eternally; uniquely beloved to me; universally beloved because he gathers many sons to me; he is the one in whom I am well pleased in innocence, well pleased in righteousness, well pleased in superabounding grace. Therefore, O human beings, whom until now I despised because of your evils, whom I held hateful because of your immense crimes, whom I had not until now deemed worthy of such conversation with me as now: hear him, believe him, and assent to him in all that he tells you.

Thanks be to thee, highest Trinity; thanks be to thee, true unity; thanks be to thee, sole goodness; thanks be to thee, gracious divinity. Humble man, thy creature and thy exalted image, gives thee thanks: because thou dost not allow him to perish; because thou dost rescue him from the mass of perdition; because thou dost abundantly pour out upon him the bowels of thy mercy. According to his ability he offers thee a sacrifice of praise, offers incense of devotion, and pours out whole burnt offerings of rejoicing. Thou, Father, sendest the Son; thou, Son, comest into the world in the flesh; and thou too, Holy Spirit, art present in the conceiving Virgin, present through the dove in the Jordan, present in the cloud on the mountain. Thou workest together, whole Trinity, indivisible God, for human salvation, that humanity may acknowledge itself saved through divine power.

Therefore man, saved and liberated from thee through the Son, confesses thee, O highest Father. He confesses that thou justly allowest him to perish whom thou hadst made the seal of thy likeness, and that, merciful, thou hast compassion upon him as he perishes. For thou seest him fall like lightning from heaven with his companions, and dost not care; thou seest man expelled from paradise, and dost call him back. They say to thy Son, “Art thou come hither before the time to torment us?” (Matt. 8); the same Son says concerning man, “The Son of Man came to seek and to save that which was lost” (Luke 19). The heavenly angels are tormented and thou art silent; lest human beings be tormented with them, thou criest from heaven: “This is my Son, in whom I am well pleased; hear him.”

Again and again, thanks be to thee, because thou hast sent thy beloved Son to us and hast given him to us as teacher. Today, I say, thou hast perfected him for us; today thou hast crowned him with glory and honor; today thou hast set him over the works of thy hands; today thou hast placed all things beneath his feet (Ps. 8). For through sheep, oxen, and beasts of the field, the earth and what is in it; through fish of the sea, the sea and what is in it, thou hast shown all bodily and incorporeal things subject to him. Or by beasts thou hast signified earthly people longing for earthly things; by fish, those now seeking the heights, now falling into the depths; by birds, those whose manner of life is in heavenly things.

Rejoice, precious portion of the creation of heaven; be glad, because you have not become vile in God’s sight, since the Son of God has been given to you as teacher. No longer follow the path of error, from which the teacher’s command calls you back. Be a teachable hearer, because a perfect instructor has been given to you. Do not despise so great a teacher, lest you experience him as avenger of contempt shown to him. Submit to him as he teaches on earth, that you may be able to reign with him as he sits in heaven. For you cannot obtain there the glory of the exalted King unless here you hear the teaching of the Master. He who shall appear there as the high King first appeared here as the gracious Master. He appeared as Master, as that heavenly Master himself said to his disciples: “Be not called masters, for one is your master, Christ” (Matt. 23).

On this present day the Father gave him to you as Master when he cried from heaven: “Hear him.” Hear him, he says, as my Son; hear him as truly God; hear him as the supreme teacher; hear him as the giver of life. You once heard the serpent and lost paradise; hear the Savior now and possess heaven. You heard the enemy and incurred death; hear life and return to life. For this my Son is true life, because he, as I am, is true God. Then you believed one promising a false divinity; believe now this one who gives true blessedness. You heard the crafty deceiver; hear the gracious instructor. You heard the most wicked betrayer; hear the most merciful Redeemer. You heard the evil destroyer; hear the eternal Savior. Then you stopped your ear against truth and opened it to falsehood; you shut it against supreme kindness and opened it to impious malice.

You are still given a place for repentance; a way of obedience is still set before you, so that through it the entrance to returning to life may stand open. In paradise the tree of the knowledge of good and evil was forbidden you, but you did not submit, and from good you became evil. You certainly wished to learn by experience what evil was. Behold, you have learned by experience how great an evil it is not to obey. It would, I say, have been better to know good alone, so that there might be no evil to fear. But since you have learned by unhappy experience what evil is, recognize at least by that unhappy experience how great an evil disobedience is, and how justly so great a misery follows it: the misery of incorruption lost, immortality lost, eternity lost.

If you wish to avoid this misery and recover such great goods, take care to obey him whom I appoint today as your Master. Submit to him without contradiction; hear him in all things as my beloved Son. Hear him, because “whosoever shall not hear him,” as Moses says, “shall be cut off from his people” (Deut. 18). But whoever, as David says, “hears by the hearing of the ear” and obeys him, “shall be in everlasting remembrance” and “shall not fear evil tidings” (Ps. 111), when it is said to others, “Depart from me, ye cursed, into everlasting fire” (Matt. 25). Rather, joyfully as a saint he shall hear: “Come, ye blessed of my Father, receive the kingdom” (ibid.), in which, joined to his Lord forever, he shall exult and glory through all ages of ages. Amen.

## Admonition concerning the following three sermons

(Martène, *Anecdota*, vol. V, col. 1417.)

[Col. 0971]

André Duchesne discusses Peter Maurice, the ninth abbot of Cluny, commonly called the Venerable, and his many writings in the *Bibliotheca Cluniacensis*, in which he took care to publish in print every work of Peter’s that he could find. As he compiles a catalogue of Peter’s works and, among other items, enumerates his sermons, he writes:

> The same Peter also wrote four very useful and most elegant sermons. The first is on the Transfiguration of the Lord; the second sermon is *In Praise of the Lord’s Sepulchre*; the third sermon is on St. Marcellus, pope and martyr; the fourth is entitled, *On the Veneration of Any Relics Whatever*.

Of these four sermons, you have only the one *On the Transfiguration of the Lord* in the Cluniac library; the others were sought in vain by André Duchesne. We found the remaining three, by no means unworthy of public light, among Mabillon’s papers; the third and fourth, moreover, in an old Cluniac manuscript written in the author’s lifetime, containing readings to be recited at the nocturnal vigils. From this we infer that these sermons were once chanted at Cluny in the divine offices.

## Sermon II. In Praise of the Lord’s Sepulchre

[Col. 0973A]

“Who can hold back a conceived discourse?” says divine Scripture. For no small time, dearest brothers, has passed since the mind began striving to pour itself out in praise of the divine sepulchre and longing, according to its ability, to exalt with devout proclamations that saving place in which the Savior’s flesh rested. Because the duty of the office entrusted to us has hitherto prevented this, with the help of him whose cause is at issue, let it at last gird itself, as it is able, to discharge the debt of this long-cherished desire.

Let others raise the tombs of their ancestors with lofty pyramids, glittering marble, and laboriously worked stones, striving to adorn the ashes of their dead. Let us honor with faithful service, raising it from the earth to the summits of heaven, the cavern of incorruption and the cave from whose enclosure hell was conquered. Let them display their feelings toward their dead by carved stones and painted walls; let us show what love we bear toward our dead one in the depths of our soul, by pouring out that soul itself in praises and tears. Let them scatter upon tombs, dreadful in their corruption, flowers of many kinds; let us sprinkle the sepulchre from which incorruption sprang forth into life with lilies of chastity, violets of humility, roses of sufferings, spices of devotion, and the aromas of prayers.

That blessed place deserves this from us—and more than we can offer—because, having been worthy above all places on earth to receive the grain of wheat falling into the ground and dying, it provided us, when he rose from it, with the bread of everlasting life.

The earth, cursed by God in the beginning of the world when man sinned, knew—indeed, after the sentence of death had been pronounced, when it was said to man, “You are earth, and into earth you shall go” (Gen. III)—that it received human beings unto death and corruption. It knew that it received the substance of man—created from itself for immortality and incorruption and returning to its own origin by the deserved penalty of its own fault—and reduced it from its former state to nothing. It opened its bosom to those born from it and returning to it through death, in order to corrupt them, never to preserve them. It opened its bosom so that earthly man might see himself returned to kindred earth, and that nothing at all of the form of the limbs created by God might remain in him, even in the least degree. [Col. 0973D] It opened, I say, its bosom to all flesh, not, as has been said, to preserve it, but to rot it: to dissolve the softness of the flesh, the hardness of the bones, the balance of the humors, and finally the whole structure of the human body, and to compel it to return to the shapeless matter from which it had been taken.

But now, for the first time among the sons of Adam, it received one alone, dead among all the dead, in whom it marvelled that the right of universal corruption had perished and the law imposed upon all the dead had vanished. The earth marvelled, certainly, that the body of this one man remained unharmed by the misery of corruption; hell marvelled that a spirit free among the spirits of the dead not only feared nothing, but freely did all things among and concerning those very spirits. For “God, the Lord of avengings, God hath acted freely” (Ps. XCIII). This, then—this is the chief reason, O man, why you ought to rejoice in Christ your Saviour; why you ought to cultivate with especial devotion the tomb in which he himself, dead for your life, rested; why you ought to venerate it with singular reverence above all places in the whole world. For the gracious Saviour, descending from the heights to the depths in search of you, who had perished away from him, sought not only for you wandering upon earth, but also for you hidden in graves beneath the earth, even in hell itself, paying the penalties due to contempt of God. He sought, I say, and found you; and, shaking the graves of all the dead by this his grave, he restored the bodies of the dead through his own body to the immortal life from which they had fallen; and [Col. 0974B] through his blessed soul and the power of supreme majesty he recalled the souls of his own from places of darkness to free light. Thus, raising you in himself from the grave, renewing you from ashes, restoring you from corruption, and by the bestowal of so great a benefit, he demonstrated that the grave in which he lay buried, beside the cross, and the resting-place of so great a benefactor, is worthy of heavenly honour.

We honour, indeed, as is right, the manger in which the Mother of God and Virgin laid down the infant God newly born; but with more excellent glory we venerate the tomb in which, after enduring many great labours, after the cross and death, he rested. A mother’s affection wrapped her Son, who was also the Son of God, in swaddling-clothes when she laid him in the manger; the devotion of the saints Joseph and Nicodemus wrapped that same one in clean linen with spices [Col. 0974C] when they took him down from the cross and buried him in a tomb hewn from the rock. Great honour is certainly due to that place which received the heavenly King descending from on high to do battle with the enemy; but greater glory should be bestowed upon that which received him already triumphant over his enemies. Great honour is due to the place that opened its bosom to the Saviour about to save the world; but greater praise is due to that which opened its bosom for his rest when the world had already been saved by him.

I know, indeed, that insensible things do not deserve praise in themselves, since only a rational creature, freely obeying the Creator’s will, merits the glory of praise. Hence holy angels alone, or holy human beings, merit praise from created beings and grace from the Creator, because they have turned to God’s service, under his inspiration, the free choice of their will by which they could have turned away from God. But in this way—that is, on its own merits—we do not praise the Lord’s tomb; rather, we praise it because, chosen to receive the Lord’s body, it was sanctified by the body of the Lord which it received. For we call holy not only angels or persons pleasing to God, but also places sanctified by God. Thus the temple of the Lord was holy; thus the holier portion of the temple was called the Holy of Holies. Thus it is said of the city Jerusalem itself: “Then the devil took him”—that is, Christ—“into the holy city” (Matt. IV, 15). Thus elsewhere in the holy Gospel it is written: “Many bodies of the saints who had fallen asleep [Col. 0975A] rose and came into the holy city” (Matt. XXVII). Thus the vessels in which the ancient Fathers ministered to God and offered sacrifices of different kinds were called holy. Thus the Levitical and priestly vestments, and above all the pontifical vestments, were called holy, the Lord speaking to Moses: “You shall make a holy garment for Aaron and his sons, that they may minister to me” (Exod. XXVIII). Thus, above all these things, God’s altar and his ark were shown to be holy: so that Uzziah, approaching the altar to offer sacrifice to God, indeed, but unlawfully, was immediately made leprous; and Uzzah, wishing even in the course of his duty to support the ark, was at once slain by God in the sight of all.

Therefore, in this present time, O Christian, not to the one temple of God, which alone existed in the world, [Col. 0975B] but to innumerable temples of God spread throughout the whole world, and likewise to sacred vessels and vestments, the same reverence is due and rendered. For the same God who had chosen and sanctified that one temple—and what it contained—as sufficient for that one people, and so forth, himself both chooses and sanctifies many thousands of temples necessary for many thousands of peoples, together with what they contain. And he does this not through any merit of the places themselves, but for the sake of the peoples who believe in him and obey him. Hence he consecrated among the Jews in their time, and does not cease to consecrate in our time until the end of the age, not only those who worship divine things, but also the places where divine things are more familiarly worshipped and the sacraments necessary to human salvation are administered. Thus, just as the Lord’s cross [Col. 0975C] is called holy not through any merit of its own, but because it was consecrated in his body, so the Lord’s tomb is called holy not through any merit of its own, but because it was consecrated by that same body of Christ which rested in it.

If the temple of God, constructed for prayers to be poured out to God, is called holy, is not the tomb which contained within itself the temple of God—that is, Christ, “in whom God was reconciling the world to himself,” who says of himself, “Destroy this temple, and in three days I will raise it up” (John II)—much more holy? If God’s altar, receiving the carcasses of animals offered to God, is holy, is not the Lord’s tomb, in which the body of the Lamb of God, who takes away the sins of the world, rested as an offering to God, [Col. 0975D] much more holy? If God’s ark, in which were the law of God, Aaron’s rod, and manna from heaven, was called holy, is not the Lord’s tomb, containing within itself the Lord’s body, in which lay hidden the Word of God, the rod of righteousness, and the bread of eternal life, much more holy? Since, then, this tomb of the Lord is holy not only as other holy places are, but even more than they, it deserves greater praise than all of them from everyone, so that not merely the place itself, but God, the sanctifier of all holy places, who then sanctified it, may be glorified by us and by all. Therefore this is the reason for praising the Lord’s tomb: that whatever is said about it should be referred solely to the honour of the buried Lord. Hence the Lord’s tomb is preferred not only to the temple, not only to the ark, not only to the Lord’s manger, [Col. 0976A] but indeed, without any exception, to all sacred places.

But why, in distinguishing the honour that places of salvation have deserved because of the Saviour’s glory, do I prefer the Lord’s tomb to the Lord’s manger? We must undertake something higher, so that, according to a certain likeness to the Lord’s mother, the Lord’s tomb may appear in loftier glory. That virginal womb was prepared by God’s Spirit to receive the coming of the Son of God who was to be born. By the providence of that same Holy Spirit the saving cave was prepared to receive the body, torn by suffering, of the Son of God who was to rise again. Of that Virgin, the heavenly mother, and of her righteous spouse Joseph, it is written: “Before they came together, [Col. 0976B] she was found to be with child by the Holy Spirit” (Matt. I), because no presumptuous person had approached that palace of divinity, nor would anyone ever approach it. Of this saving lodging of the Saviour it is written: “In which no one had yet been laid” (Luke XXIII), because the corruption of no dead body had defiled it. From that Virgin, while still clothed in mortal death for mortal life, the Saviour came forth like a bridegroom from a bridal chamber, preserving uninjured the virginal seals of the eastern gate; from this tomb, with corruption now transformed into incorruption and death swallowed up in victory, he brought forth his body while the tomb remained closed and sealed.

For these reasons, the great glory of the Lord’s manger, the greater glory of the Lord’s tomb, is shown to stand next to the very glory of the Lord’s mother; and this is further demonstrated [Col. 0976C] by Gospel testimonies and miracles. For it was fitting that not only the royal chamber of the virginal womb—which first prepared a fitting dwelling for God coming to humankind, and pleased him through heavenly grace and singular merit—should be illuminated by heavenly miracles, but also that places devoid of reason and perception, prepared to receive the Son of God clothed in human flesh, should be shown sacred by sublime miracles. For I see the angel Gabriel sent by God from heaven speaking with that blessed Virgin, greeting her with a form of veneration previously unheard of, announcing by heavenly proclamation the coming of the Holy Spirit and the conception of the Son of God, and indicating how great an honour was due to that bridal chamber of the heavenly King. Then I see a joyful and terrifying angel descending with a mighty whirlwind, sitting upon the stone rolled back from the Lord’s tomb, striking down the guards of the impious by the terror of his arrival alone, and announcing to the holy women—who wished to minister to the Lord even after his burial—that he had risen from the dead, as he had foretold. I perceive, to increase the astonishing miracle, two angels seated not outside but within the enclosure of the venerable tomb, where Jesus’ body had been laid. I behold Mary Magdalene, sighing in impatient love for Christ, looking in a second time, and hearing from those same angels: “Woman, why are you weeping?” (John XX). Again I hear angels speaking to shepherds, not only for the glory of the Lord newly born, but also for the honour of the Lord buried: “This shall be a sign to you: you shall find the infant wrapped in swaddling-clothes and laid in a manger” (Luke II). In like manner I hear, not only for praise of the buried Lord, but also for the honour of the Lord’s tomb, an angel saying to the blessed women: “You seek Jesus of Nazareth, who was crucified; he has risen; he is not here” (Mark XVI). And immediately: “Behold the place where they laid him” (ibid.). You see, brethren, that the Virgin, the dwelling of the Lord who was to be born; the manger, the lodging of the Lord born; and the tomb, the resting-place of the Lord buried, are distinguished by angelic proclamations and heavenly honours; and that, by the honour of the guest, angelic ministries indicate how greatly these lodgings themselves should be honoured above human dwellings. Great indeed and surpassing among created things is the honour of the Mother of the Lord; yet, although it cannot be compared with it, the honour of the Lord’s tomb is nevertheless joined most closely to it. But, as was said above, although the honour of the Lord’s manger ought to be great, the glory of the Lord’s tomb, as reason and miracles show, is far more excellent.

Since angels bear witness to this glory, as has been said, let the Lord of angels himself also come and bring forward, for the glory of his tomb, the testimonies and examples of his prophets. For when the Jews tested him and in malicious curiosity sought signs, you have heard what he answered: “An evil and adulterous generation seeks a sign, and no sign shall be given to it except the sign of Jonah the prophet. For as Jonah was in the belly of the whale three days and three nights, so the Son of Man shall be in the heart of the earth three days and three nights” (Matt. XII). “No sign,” he says, “shall be given them except the sign of Jonah” (ibid.). What sign? It was not a sign that the creature which swallowed him could not consume him; it was not a sign that the prey it had swallowed descended into its belly. But it was a sign that heavenly power preserved from corruption the one enclosed in the innards of the enormous beast. It was not a sign that the prophet, with his lesser body, was swallowed by the fish’s vast body; but it was a sign that, though swallowed, he did not die, and, though buried, he did not decay. Therefore this sign of Jonah was given to the Jews when Christ, wickedly killed by them, was placed in the tomb by devout persons who obeyed him in devout goodwill.

This was then given and granted to the wicked Jews: that, to fill up the measure of their fathers, their iniquity demanding it, after the prophets whom those fathers had killed, these Jews should kill Christ; after the servants whom those fathers had slain, these should kill the Lord; after the holy men whom those fathers had destroyed, these should kill the Holy of Holies—indeed, the Lord himself appearing in human flesh—and, because he was dead and seemed to need burial, should bury him not by rendering service but by persecuting him. This sign had to be given from the earth to those seeking signs from heaven, because earthly people, thinking earthly thoughts, were to be convicted for their impieties by earthly miracles, whereas heavenly people are adorned with heavenly signs. They were, I say, to be convicted by the most sublime miracle performed from the earth: so that, either confessing Christ—whom they had killed as a man and shut in the tomb as powerless—as the Lord rising again and as the Almighty coming forth from the tomb while it was closed and sealed, [Col. 0978A] they might be saved; or, denying him, they might be punished.

For, as was said of Jonah, it was not a sign that Christ died, but that in his death the death of all was extinguished. It was not a sign that he was buried, but that he was held within the enclosure of the tomb for only three days. It was not a sign that he entered the tomb dead in flesh, but that from the tomb he restored his own flesh to immortal life. It was not a sign that, according to the common condition of all mortals, he allowed himself to die and be buried; but that, against the common condition of all, restoring his body, as has been said, to eternal life, he brought forth in himself from their own graves all his people, even those who were yet to come, and restored them to the blessed life they had lost. Thus, by his life-giving tomb he made the graves of all the dead alive, and willed them to be not so much storehouses of corruption as seedbeds of incorruption. For, according to the Apostle, “the natural body is sown; the spiritual body shall rise; it is sown in corruption; it shall rise in incorruption; it is sown in weakness; it shall rise in power” (I Cor. XV).

“So shall the Son of Man be,” says Christ, “in the heart of the earth”; “he shall be,” he says, “in the heart of the earth.” Turn your minds to understanding the heart of the earth, all you who have hearts to understand; turn, I say, your hearts toward this heart, and behold the sublime mystery hidden in this heart of the earth. Behold the eternal Wisdom of God disposing all things not only mightily but sweetly: choosing not only the persons who served the human incarnation, not only the manner appropriate to that restoration, but also providing before the ages places most suited to the salvation of humankind. The omnipotent author of this salvation could indeed have chosen for the accomplishment of this work the remotest retreats, the furthest borders of Gaul, the scorching south, the frozen north, or any other places in the wide world. But because the fruit of this salvation concerned all equally, and because he intended to save not a part of the world but the whole world at once, he preferred to perform the work of redemption not in a corner of the world, but in the middle of the world; not in one part of the lands, but in the middle of the lands, as though equally adjoining all regions. A work common to all required a common place, [Col. 0978D] lest, if it took place in some remote part of the earth, one farther removed might reach his salvation more slowly, and that salvation itself might spread to those far away more slowly; nor would its sound go out into all the earth so readily. Therefore a central and common place in the world was chosen, that salvation might be spread commonly and swiftly through the world, and that no one might claim as his own what, without any exception, belonged generally to all.

This, plainly, is that central place of the world which the Saviour calls the heart of the earth, and in which he declares that he will rest for three days after the likeness of the prophet Jonah. Certainly that tomb of the Redeemer is properly called the heart of the earth—that is, the central place of the world—although the city of Jerusalem itself, indeed the whole land called the land of promise, may fittingly be understood by this designation, “heart.” For just as the human heart, or that of any animal, is in the middle of the body [lacuna], it appears to be situated in the middle place of the world surrounded about it, in that land where the ancient Fathers of the Christian faith lived. Hence the whole land of the holy Fathers is universally designated by the name “heart of the earth”; the city of Jerusalem itself, where the Holy of Holies is found, is designated more particularly; and the Lord’s tomb, in which the Holy of Holies rested, most particularly. Since the Gospel of the kingdom of heaven was to be spread from the city of Jerusalem itself to all nations, he was present who said: “From Zion shall go forth the law, and the word of the Lord from Jerusalem” (Isa. II); and after his resurrection the King of Heaven himself declares in the Gospel: “For thus it is written, and thus it was necessary for Christ to suffer and to rise from the dead on the third day, and for repentance and remission of sins to be preached in his name to all nations, beginning from Jerusalem” (Luke XXIV).

But from where is it proved that Jerusalem holds the middle position in the whole world? What is called philosophical reasoning might indeed support us in this matter, but an assertion strengthened by divine authority has no need to be propped up by human reasoning. Therefore, that it may be known without a cloud of doubt, let the clear testimony of the prophet Ezekiel come forward, by which the Spirit of God, speaking of the Jerusalem just mentioned, confirms the truth of what we say: “This is Jerusalem,” he says, “I have set her in the midst of the nations, and lands round about her” (Ezek. V). Concerning this middle place—and especially in David’s prophecies, wishing in his accustomed manner to leave none of the saving mysteries unexpressed—God “is our king before the ages; he has worked salvation in the midst of the earth” (Ps. LXXIII). He says not in a corner of the world, not in any one part of the lands, but “in the midst of the earth” our God and King has worked salvation.

Indeed, our God and King of the ages works salvations in every region, near and remote alike, because in every place and at every time, according to the decrees of his eternal counsel, he saves people and beasts. But at the time ordained before the ages for this purpose, he worked in this middle of the earth of which we speak—not a partial but a universal salvation—he who “commands the salvations of Jacob.” For he says truly concerning Jacob, not through the philosophy of Balaam, who wished to deceive: “He who is to be condemned shall be.” [Materially uncertain/OCR-corrupt wording.]

See, therefore, beloved people—see, I say, you students of sacred things, you who give yourselves to divine meditation, you who devote unceasing effort to the word of God, whose food and sustenance is not so much earthly bread as that of which the prophetic Scripture says, “Man ate the bread of angels” (Ps. LXXV), and of which the Saviour himself says, “I am the living bread who came down from heaven” (John VI).

See and search the Scriptures, in which you recognize yourselves to have eternal life—not as malicious Jews suppose, but as gracious Christians certainly know. See how nearly all the righteous persons to whom the sacred pages bear witness of righteousness inhabited this land of which we speak, situated, as has been said, in the middle of all lands—this very land, I say, and no other. For it was fitting that, during the five thousand years while the world lay in evil and was occupied by the prince of darkness, that land in which the Son of God was to be born for the salvation of the age should be inhabited not by the impious, who despised the Lord, but by pious worshippers; and thus, sanctified by divine worship and separated from the deeds of the unjust through works of righteousness, it should be cleansed from the filth of the unclean and made fit for the coming of its Creator and Restorer. Therefore, as has been said, nearly all the righteous inhabited it from the beginning until Christ; and by their continuous dwelling there they indicated that the ruler of the ages would at some time do something great, singular, and unprecedented from or within that land.

Thus, concerning Adam himself, the first parent of all, expelled from paradise, Scripture does not tell in what place he lived through the many years of his life; yet it does not pass over in silence where he was buried when dead. Scripture, speaking of the city Hebron, which was formerly called Arbe but is now called by another name, says: “There Adam, greatest among the Anakim, was laid” (Josh. XIV). Perhaps you blush?

Therefore, if you wish to render something in return to the buried Lord, because for you he lay dead in the tomb, become yourself his tomb, so that his memory may remain and flourish in you not merely for three days but forever. Let Jesus Christ lie hidden within you in firm faith and perfect love: although, as when he lay in the tomb, he is not visible to human sight, let him nevertheless be manifest, as he remains in you, to divine sight. Let your life, according to the Apostle, be hidden with Christ himself in God, so that, when he who is your life appears, you too may appear with him in glory (Col. III). Let your soul assume the part, character, and love of that beautiful bride who, in the song of wounded love, uttering words of charity, says: “My beloved is mine, and I am his, who feeds among the lilies” (Song II). “My beloved,” she says, “is for me and for others,” because the Son of God became man not for heaven and earth, not for sun and moon, not for the angels themselves nor for any creature, but for me; he suffered for me, died for me, was buried for me, rose for me, ascended for me; for me he prepared in this age suffering in imitation, and in the other life in resurrection, ascent to heaven in his own ascension, and a kingdom in his kingdom. But I am his: that is, hoping in him alone and not in another; loving not another or anything else; obeying him in all his commands; spending in his service the whole substance of myself which he created; and dying for him too, if occasion or time should present itself.

“He feeds among the lilies,” because my beloved, to whom every good thing is pleasing, takes singular delight, among all things that please him, in chastity; he delights in a purified conscience; he delights in a life set apart from the filth of unclean deeds. For he is the Son of a Virgin and the spotless Lamb, and therefore cannot dwell in a body subjected to sins, since, as is written concerning his Spirit, “it flees deceit and withdraws from thoughts that are without understanding, and is rebuked by iniquity when it comes” (Wis. I). Speak also with the same bride in the same Song: “My beloved is a bundle of myrrh to me” (Song I). For although my beloved is sweet and surpasses every sweetness, although he hides a great abundance of his sweetness for those who fear him (Ps. XXX), nevertheless, lest I delight in the world, lest I be drawn away by the pleasure of this life, lest perhaps, adding sins to sins, I rot in them and diffuse the stench of an evil reputation, through multiplied evils, to those near or far, my beloved will be for me myrrh of bitterness. Thus, by remembrance of his fear and love, he may keep me incorrupt from the rot of evils, remove harmful pleasure by his power, and preserve my flesh undefiled from every disordered love and my soul from every superfluous affection.

And because, according to the divine sentence, human wickedness is not small but great (Gen. VI), and, according to the apostolic word, “where iniquity abounds, charity shall grow cold” (Rom. V), my beloved has become for me not a small quantity of myrrh but a bundle of myrrh (Song I): because much of his grace is necessary to me against much wickedness, much bitterness of his fear against the great intemperance of flesh and blood, much of his power against such great vices. He “shall abide between my breasts” (ibid.), because he shall never at any time be separated from the memory of my breast or heart, which claims for itself a central place between the breasts even in my body. In this too I shall imitate his tomb, which, as situated in the middle of the earth, contained his body, by holding in my heart—located, as it were, in the middle between my breasts—his perpetual remembrance. Thus, spiritually and firmly always retained by me and, as it were, buried in a tomb, he shall abide between my breasts; he shall always be with me, and, as I have said, shall never at any time be separated from me. Truly he shall never be separated at any time, because, after all other things have been despised and cast aside, Jesus shall be my life, Jesus my sustenance, Jesus my rest, Jesus my joy, Jesus my homeland, Jesus my glory, Jesus my all—as far as I can here through spirit and love, until I may be able there, where it is promised, to contemplate him face to face. In this way, if you receive him into yourself, if in your death you prepare for him such rest, you will become not his mortal tomb but his life-giving tomb—that is, a tomb containing life.

Applying this example of the Lord’s tomb to yourself with sound understanding, you will prepare a happier resting-place for Christ than did that stone, and you will also obtain a happier departure for the Christ you have received. For that stone in which the Saviour rested bodily will never receive any reward. But if you bury Christ within yourself in the manner I have described, paradise will receive you. That stone cannot obtain grace because it has no merit; you, by grace and merit, can obtain the kingdom of heaven. The substance of that stone will at some time be reduced to nothing; but the substance of your body, though it may appear for a time to be reduced to nothing, will nevertheless be restored whole at the time of the general resurrection. For the Creator of all and Saviour of his people did not purpose to rest in an insensible rock through the flesh for any benefit to it, but wished to rest there for a time for your eternal salvation. This was the sole and entire purpose of that rest: that, just as he himself, after countless sufferings and the death of the cross, now suffers no longer, now dies no longer, and neither suffering nor death shall ever thereafter rule over him, so you too, after becoming his life-giving tomb and containing him while you live in the manner described, may, when this miserable life is ended, suffer no longer and die no longer; and may not be reduced in that stone tomb to fragments or nothingness, but, restored from decay, ashes, or nothingness, be renewed in eternal resurrection, now immortal and blessed with Christ.

But while we admire the mysteries of the saving cave and draw from Gospel, apostolic, and even prophetic books testimonies to its glory, why do you, Isaiah, greatest of the prophets, remain silent so long? Speak; be silent no longer. As you serve the Saviour’s glory in all things, so make known the glory of his sacred tomb as his Spirit taught you. For as you instructed us concerning the rod and the flower, the Virgin and her childbirth, Christ and his passion, the rejection of the Jews and the calling of the Gentiles—as, I say, you taught us concerning these and all the mysteries of our faith—so indicate what we should think concerning the magnificence of the Lord’s tomb. “In that day,” says Isaiah, “the root of Jesse, who stands as a sign for the peoples—the nations shall entreat him—and his tomb shall be glorious” (Isa. II).

Hear, all peoples; hear, nations scattered through the world; attend, diverse tongues and nations, who think yourselves disregarded, whom you have considered worthy of contempt until now. Attend and rejoice that your Creator has not forgotten you; that, no longer willing to restrain his mercies in his wrath, he now mercifully wills to save not merely those Jews, few in number, but also the countless multitude of you. Hear the divine prophet—indeed, the foremost among prophets—turning his prophetic eye toward you many ages beforehand. See the Spirit of God, who “breathes where he wills” (John III), inspiring him and foretelling long beforehand, as I have said, that your salvation would be accomplished through the Saviour: “In that day,” he says, “the root of Jesse, who stands as a sign for the peoples”; and truly, the root of Jesse.

Before this prophecy was uttered there were David, Solomon, Rehoboam, Abijah, and the rest. After it was uttered there were Josiah, Jehoiakim, Zerubbabel, Shealtiel, and very many others down to Christ; yet none of them was set up as a sign for the peoples, until he arose from that same root of Jesse who was set up as a sign for all peoples. For, as he himself says, “God the Father has sealed him” (John VI); he sealed him, certainly, that he might be a sign. But for what sign did he seal him? Namely, that, raised on the most lofty sign of the cross after the manner of the bronze serpent, exalted in the midst of the camp not merely of the Jewish people but of the whole world, [Col. 0983A] he might turn all eyes toward himself, draw all hearts toward himself, exhort all to place their whole hope in his death which he endured on the cross, and, by healing all their infirmities, forgiving all their sins, and opening to all the kingdoms of heaven long shut, demonstrate, according to the prophecy of the great patriarch Jacob, that he was the one who was to be sent, he was the one called the expectation of the nations. For he himself lifted up this sign among the nations, that he might gather the fugitives of Israel and collect the scattered of Judah from the four winds.

“The nations shall entreat him” (Isa. XI). What could be clearer than this word? What more luminous than this statement? What more manifest than this prophecy? Why do you wait, O nations, for it to be expounded as obscure, when it cannot fail to be seen even by the blind wherever they are situated throughout the world? Do not you yourselves, who have been called “nations” by all the prophets of the Old Testament, continually entreat Jesus Christ, the root of Jesse, set before you as a lofty sign? Although the small number of Jews chosen by God has been rejected because of excessive impieties and rendered hateful; although a certain part of you, because they rejected the grace of God which they had received, has been permitted to be led astray and rejected by the wicked Muhammad; nevertheless, you—whether in freedom or under the bodily servitude of unbelievers, which does no harm to your eternal salvation—scattered throughout the world, behold your Redeemer raised everywhere as the sign of salvation, entreat him, and rejoice that in you the prophecy of the great prophet Isaiah has been fulfilled. Rejoice, I say, that in you the prophecy of so blessed a proclamation has been fulfilled.

Exult also that the great king and prophet David confirms him by his testimony and speaks in the Spirit of God: “All nations whatsoever thou hast made shall come and worship before thee, O Lord” (Ps. LXXXV)—“whatsoever thou hast made.” But why did he say, “whatsoever thou hast made”? Did not he make all the peoples or nations of the earth? Does not holy Scripture say elsewhere: “For thou hast made heaven and earth, and whatever is contained in the compass of heaven” (Isa. XXXVII)? Just as there is no other Creator of all nations, so there can be no other Saviour of all nations. Therefore you are included among all the nations whom he made. For this reason you entreat him; for this reason you bend the knee in his name; for this reason you not only pray to him but worship him as God, as the author of your nature and restorer of your salvation. And in doing these things you show, both in name and in reality, that he is Jesus—that is, the Saviour of yourselves and of all.

And his tomb shall be glorious. The tomb of him who is called the root of Jesse; of him who is set up as a sign to the peoples; of him whom the nations are written as being to beseech. “His tomb,” he says, “shall be glorious.” Hear, lovers of worldly glory; hear, you who are accustomed to glory in fleeting shadows, fading flowers, and empty winds. Hear, you who are accustomed to place your glory in fragile power, unstable wealth, and perishing pride [Col. 0984A]. See all this glory of yours transferred to the tomb of a dead man, and that tomb preferred above every human desire or boast. For thus Christ the Lord corrected the perversity of the world by the rule of justice: what men themselves held great, he showed to be cheap and contemptible by despising it; and what they trampled as worthless and fled as dreadful, he judged, by enduring them, to be borne and preferred to all those things. Therefore he despised pride, riches, and all else that is loved in the world. Therefore he disregarded even bodily life itself, for preserving which all toil as far as they can. Therefore he preferred his death to it; therefore he voluntarily rested in the tomb, which all flee as far as they can.
