Thus, by performing glorious works concerning it both in heaven and in hell, he showed that it ought to be glorious [Col. 0984B]: glorious through it by despoiling hell; glorious through it by opening heaven; glorious through it by destroying death; glorious through it by rising immortally; glorious through it by restoring mortal human beings, through his resurrection, to immortal life; and, further, glorious by calling the peoples of the world to his own tomb, receiving those called, justifying those received, saving those justified, and proving himself Lord of death and life in the salvation of those whom he frees from the death of sins and from hell, and whom he raises to the life of justice and eternal blessedness.

For what else, O nations, do you hope for when you come to his tomb? What else do you wish to carry away from his tomb [Col. 0984C]? What other reward for your labour? What other recompense for the dangers of the various deaths which you continually suffer on the way to it? What other prize do you expect for your course than this? What indeed gathers you from the unknown regions of the East, from the remote parts of the West, from the furthest retreats of South and North, to the tomb of one once dead; and unites such great peoples of such diverse lands and languages in the narrow enclosure of a single stone cave? What else, O peoples of Gaul and Germany; what else, you Dacians and Noricans, fierce in barbarism and valour—some of whom, by land and others by sea, rescued the holy place from the yoke of Persians and Arabs through the toils of war and shed blood, but with splendid victory [Col. 0984D]—what other recompense did you endure for such great labours? You sought the tomb, but you did not seek in it, as the good women or the apostles once did, the one who had been buried. You knew that he who had once rested there as dead was seated in heaven; you knew that he now ruled angels and human beings not from that tomb, but from the throne of divine majesty. You knew him no longer dead but living; no longer subject to Jews or Romans, but subjecting all things to himself by the power of his divinity. You knew that he was no longer held by tomb or hell, but ruled the whole earth—and hell itself—from the heavenly places. For it could not be hidden from you that at the name of Jesus every knee must bend, of those in heaven, on earth, and under the earth; and that every tongue must confess that [Col. 0985A] the Lord Jesus Christ is in the glory of God the Father (Phil. 2); nor that there is no other name given under heaven to human beings in which they must be saved (Acts 4). Knowing all this, you came to the tomb of God and of your Lord, Creator, and Redeemer, not as enemies, but as creatures, servants, and redeemed persons. With pious swords you cleansed the place and dwelling of heavenly purity from the filth of the impious, and ensured that wicked servants could no longer bar beloved sons from access to the Father’s tomb. In doing this, O saved nations, by giving your souls to the tomb of our Saviour—by offering up your bodies—you certainly rendered nothing worthy in return for such great benefits bestowed upon you by him. Yet you showed that, if the means had been granted, you wished [Col. 0985B] to make recompense. By these deeds you showed fulfilled in yourselves the solemn prophecy of the prophet Isaiah, through whom God, solicitous long ages beforehand concerning you and foreknowing your salvation, which he himself had hidden with himself from eternity, said:

> “I will set a sign among them, and from among those who have been saved I will send to the nations: to the sea, to Africa, to Lydia, those who draw the bow; to Italy and Greece; to the distant islands; to those who have not heard of me and have not seen my glory. And they shall proclaim my glory among the nations, and they shall bring all my brethren from all nations as a gift to the Lord, on horses and in chariots, in litters, on mules, and in carts, to my holy mountain Jerusalem, says the Lord” (Isa. 66).

Although this was fulfilled when you and your fathers received the Christian faith through the apostolic ministry [Col. 0985C], it was fulfilled far more fully when, through you, the glorious tomb of Christ, your Lord and God, was liberated from the dominion of the faithless. In the fruitful zeal of your devotion, you preferred the Lord’s tomb to your life; exposed yourselves to every misfortune for it; feared no dangers for it; most steadfastly despised dreadful torments and death itself for it; and subjected all your own glory, and the world’s glory, to his glory. In all these things, indeed, according to the tenor of the preceding prophecy, which said, “His tomb”—that is, Christ’s—“shall be glorious” (Isa. 11), you declared that tomb to be glorious [Col. 0985D] above all places of earthly habitation.

But why do I set forward, as though it were human glory alone, to glorify the place of the Lord’s tomb, when, as the Saviour says of himself, “I have testimony greater than John,” we may have concerning the glory of the Lord’s tomb a testimony greater than that of any human being? Testimony greater than any human being indeed is that which [Col. 0986A] comes not from earth but from heaven; greater than any human being is that which comes not from a human being but from God alone; greater than any human being is that which has not arisen from low places but has come forth from the heights. Come here, all peoples of the earth, to whom I speak, and behold, for the glory of the Lord’s tomb, a miracle unique and unheard of and unseen since the beginning of the world; marvel that it takes place in the world. You have heard of the miracles of the prophets; you have heard of the miracles of the apostles; you have heard of the miracles of the Saviour himself while he still lived among human beings; you have heard of the countless and wondrous works of innumerable disciples of his, by which both the knowledge of God was more effectually poured into mortals and the divine goodness at times made manifest the merits of good human beings. But now [Col. 0986B] I shall not say, “Hear,” but, “Attend, see, come, and consider”: he who, in this time, has offered this wonderful sign to the glory of his tomb not to your ears but set it before your eyes—set before, indeed continues to set before, your eyes heavenly fire.

> **Note:** [Col. 0985D] He here denotes the remarkable miracle which formerly occurred every year at the Lord’s tomb, where, on the vigil of Easter, divine fire descending from heaven, in the sight of all, lit the lamps of the church. Witnesses of this miracle include Bernard the monk, who travelled to Jerusalem in the year 870 and reports in his *Itinerary* that he saw it; an old Pontifical of the Church of Poitiers, written by hand eight hundred years ago [Col. 0986D]; Rodulfus Glaber, *History*, book IV, chapter 6; Leo of Ostia, *Chronicle of Monte Cassino*, book III, chapter 3; Hugh of Flavigny, in the *Chronicle of Verdun*; the author of the *History of the Holy War*, vol. I; Mabillon’s *Italian Museum*, no. 102; William of Malmesbury, *On the Kings of the English*, book IV; the Chronicle of Andres, *Spicilegium*, vol. IX; and the Chronicle of Fontenelle, ibid., vol. X.

By it he honours his own tomb not once, but yearly. He intimates—indeed, openly proclaims—how great the honour with which people ought to venerate it, when they see heaven itself render such splendid service. From the Father of lights a light is sent from heaven to earth; driving bodily darkness from the Lord’s tomb, it demonstrates more clearly than any light, and confirms more strongly than any argument, that the light which enlightens every human being once lay hidden there and once rose from there. It banishes from [Col. 0986C] the darkness of human beings—all whom grace, the guide of all unto life, nevertheless illumines—all the darkness of doubt; and it does not permit the faith which is in Christ to waver even slightly, since so unprecedented a sign is seen to be possible only from God, and truth, which is God, is known to be able to bear witness only to truth. This illustrious miracle fully takes the place of the ancient miracles; and one who attentively considers it will judge that, after it, those miracles are not necessary to him for strengthening the grace of faith.

For what if you, who require signs for the strengthening of your faith from prophets preaching Christ, from apostles preaching Christ, and also from innumerable other disciples of his—signs in which the blind are given sight, the deaf restored hearing, the mute made to speak, lepers healed, demons cast out, every disease removed, [Col. 0986D] the dead raised, mountains moved, and other signs of diverse kinds beyond all number—have not seen these things? Have you not seen with your own eyes, rather than another’s, this wonderful sign, almost to be preferred above them all, performed at his tomb by the same author of signs? Or, if perhaps you did not see it because you were not present, have you not heard it reported by innumerable thousands of people who saw it [Col. 0987A]? For although the miracles already mentioned do not now occur so frequently in our days, because they are no longer necessary as in the first times, now that the world is filled with the knowledge of the Lord, and because those who have cast away the faith held by their fathers are not worthy of them; although, I say, miracles so frequent as before do not occur, yet this miracle has been granted to our age, which, as was said, can fully take the place of all the others.

For, to speak of the worthier miracle among miracles, is it not greater—or at least equal—to bring fire down from heaven and to call back a soul from hell? Does it not seem equally impossible and astonishing to mortals both that a spirit should return from the depths and [Col. 0987B] that fire should come from the heights? Are not both the spirits of the dead and the bodily, fiery power of heaven alike contained within the grasp of divine power? This miracle is not, like the prodigies of magicians, empty or illusory; it is true, bodily, and substantial, because bodily fire, sent by God from heaven for the glory of the Lord’s tomb, joins itself to physical material of papyrus or tow, and feeds upon the substance of oil and wax. It appears in visible brightness to human beings; by its heat it makes known to human touch that it is bodily fire. Fulfilling the duties of annual service laid upon it, it renders bodily and public service in honour of the Lord’s body, once placed in that bodily tomb.

Why then do you seek to see a dead person rising [Col. 0987C] from the earth, when you see fire shining from heaven upon the earth? This sign has plainly been given you from heaven, just as a sign from earth had been given to the Jews. To them, as unbelieving and earthly persons, a sign was given from earth; to you, as believing and heavenly persons, a sign was given from heaven. To them Christ was given as a sign from earth, buried in the heart of the earth—that is, in this age—so that by the death which they themselves had inflicted they might either be condemned if they turned away, or saved if they turned back. To you a sign was given from heaven: first Christ rising and ascending into heaven; then fire sent by him from heaven, so that you may be illuminated more spiritually by heavenly light, inflamed more spiritually by its heat, and thus, illuminated by divine knowledge and kindled by heavenly brightness, may in due time be borne up to heavenly things. [Col. 0987D] Therefore, as has been said, heavenly fire comes from heaven, so that people, enlightened and kindled by it, may be encouraged to love heavenly things, and may be raised by Jesus Christ their Lord, the author of so great a miracle, to those things: before the tomb in their souls, after the tomb in their bodies.

This also must be noted for the increase of the miracle: that this heavenly light does not illuminate Nazareth, where Christ was conceived; Bethlehem, where he was born; Capernaum, where he was reared; or any other places of Judaea or Galilee where he was brought up, stayed, and lived as an infant, child, adolescent, and young man. Rather, it illuminates only the Lord’s tomb and honours it by shining upon it in reverence. This also must be added in commending the greatness of the remarkable sign: it is not on [Col. 0988A] the day of the Lord’s Conception, Nativity, Manifestation, or Presentation, but on the day of the Passion—on the one day of the Lord’s burial—that this heavenly fire appears on earth. Of the three days and nights during which the Saviour lay in the tomb, it customarily chooses no day but Saturday, that is, the day of rest, for its manifestation. Although the memorial of the Lord’s passion or burial is not fixed on the same calendar day in each yearly recurrence, but is celebrated earlier or later according to the rules of the Fathers, the certainty of the recurring miracle does not fail. Rather, heavenly kindness, following the devotion of its Church, joins the heights of heaven to earthly lowliness on the day when Christ, resting in the flesh in the tomb, is remembered and adored; and adorns the festivals of its Christians [Col. 0988B] with so noble and delightful a miracle.

It would indeed have been great and wonderful if this sign had appeared to mortals only once, whether in the times of the Fathers or in ours. But who does not see that it is now far greater and more wonderful, when, across the span of many years, heavenly mercy, attentive to human faith and salvation, has exempted no year in either the Fathers’ days or ours from this miracle? Such a succession of ages has now been continued by this miracle that not even among the most aged old men can anyone be found who admits that he has ever heard from any predecessor when this very great sign began. Thus the almighty Dispenser, who provides and apportions times to each, willed this miracle to succeed in place of the earlier miracles as they became rarer, after it had already endured for a long time [Col. 0988C]; and decreed it to be so great that it might both fill the role of the preceding signs and show that he cannot fail the world and the Christian faith not only by grace, but also by wondrous works where they are necessary.

Why is this? Why, I say, are the places or days of conception, birth, manifestation, presentation, even resurrection and ascension, placed below the place or day of burial by heavenly judgment, as heavenly distinctions indicate? The reason is clear—clear, and to be embraced with all the arms of affection. For by Christ’s conception, birth, manifestation, presentation, and similar things, the work of our salvation was begun; but by his death alone it was perfected. Hence, on the cross on which he suffered death, to show that this was so, he said, “It is finished” (John 19) [Col. 0988D]. Therefore, as in all useful works, the completion of this divine work is worthier than its beginning; consummation than commencement; the end than the beginning. Christ’s being born, circumcised, baptized or baptizing, preaching, or performing divine and wondrous works would have profited us nothing unless his death had been offered to the justice of God for the life of dead human beings. But after the justice of God had been satisfied by the death of his body, and his mercy had followed, the dead human being was restored to life. Thus the death undertaken for the life of all human beings was the completion of all his works. Therefore, because he himself died for the dead by this grace, he preferred this place of the tomb, in which he chose to rest, above all holy places [Col. 0989A] by this choice. For just as his death is preferred above all his works, so the place of his death is deservedly preferred above all the places of his wondrous works.

In placing the day of resurrection, and also the day and place of ascension, below the day or place of the Lord’s burial or death, I indicated not a hierarchy of dignity, but a distinction of cause and effect. For just as human sin was the cause of death, so that same death of Christ was the cause of resurrection and ascension. Christ would not have died unless the sin for which he died had first existed, nor would he have risen from the dead unless he had first died. And just as Christ’s death was the effect of the cause called sin, so resurrection and ascension [Col. 0989B] were the effect of the cause called Christ’s death. Because sin came first, resurrection and ascension followed. I do not therefore, as I said, prefer the Lord’s death to resurrection or ascension in respect of dignity; rather, I show the source from which they arise. Christ’s death is the cause of resurrection and ascension; his resurrection and ascension are effects of that cause. Christ’s death is the victory of battle; resurrection and ascension are the triumph of victory. Christ’s death is the price; resurrection and ascension are the reward. Therefore, just as in human transactions the reward of purchase cannot follow unless the price of sale comes first, and the reward of recompense cannot follow unless the price of service comes first, so in this divine transaction the reward of resurrection could not follow unless the price of redemption had first come. Therefore, because through redemption one comes to recompense, the day of redemption is preferred to the day of resurrection; and by the same principle the day and place of redemption are placed above the day and place of ascension [Col. 0989C]. Thus it is clear by this reasoning that in this place the price is not incongruously put before the reward, because, as has been said, there would be no way to the reward unless the price came first. For this reason the day of resurrection, together with the day and place of ascension, is placed after the day and place of the Lord’s burial. And although it belongs to weakness to die, to strength to rise; to disgrace to descend, to glory to ascend; yet, because strength is reached through weakness and glory through disgrace, weakness is here preferred to strength, and disgrace to glory.

[Col. 0989D] Lest any mortal should doubt these matters or think them invented rather than true, you, almighty Father, came to meet the dark coverings of the human mind; by sending heavenly light to the tomb of your Son, you drove away every darkness of this obscurity. You certainly drove away human darkness by heavenly light, and showed that the tomb in which the light born from your light lay hidden, as though darkened by the death of assumed flesh, ought to be preferred above all earthly places. In the glory of his tomb you commended to be embraced magnificently his sublime humility, because humility could not have been lower than when your same Son bowed himself from the highest seat of your majesty not merely living down to earth, but dead even down to the tomb. For natural majesty was not to be commended by you as greatly as assumed mortality; innate power not as greatly as borrowed weakness; proper exaltation not as greatly as alien abasement, yet assumed in you [Col. 0990A]. Therefore, you who make your ministers a burning fire honour his tomb more than the other places of his humanity by sending fire from heaven, so that what might seem lower because of the abasement of such great humility may be plainly more glorious through such exalted miracles. You indicate that both the humility of your Christ and the devotion of your Christians are pleasing to you in this, since by the sign through which you showed that the devotion of the saints of old pleased you, you likewise show that these services please you.

Formerly you distinguished between the offerings of Abel and Cain by this sign [Col. 0990B], that is, by heavenly fire; and through your Scripture, which says, “The Lord kindled fire upon Abel’s offerings, but upon Cain’s offerings he did not kindle fire,” you taught us what in the one was acceptable and what in the other was displeasing to you. You gave the same sign through the great prophet Elijah to Jews who had turned away from you; and by the same sign of fire you showed how great was the difference between the worship of Creator and creature. Your aforesaid servant Elijah said to the people: “How long will you limp between two sides? If the Lord is God, follow him; but if Baal, follow him” (3 Kings 18). And again, concerning the priests of idols: “Let two bulls be given to you, and let them choose one bull, cut it in pieces, and place it upon the wood, but put no fire beneath it. I shall prepare the other [Col. 0990C] bull and lay it on the wood, and I too shall put no fire beneath it. Call upon the names of your gods, and I shall call upon the name of the Lord; and the God who answers by fire, he shall be God” (ibid.). Thus your servant Elijah cried out, and, by sending fire from heaven to consume his burnt offering, you taught that you alone are God of all.

So indeed, O Lord, so, almighty Creator, you do now between us and the Jews or pagans. Thus you reject their vows, prayers, and offerings, and show them to be hateful to you. Thus, after rejecting them, you approve ours; thus you declare the sacrifices, prayers, and vows of your Christians pleasing to you, when you send down from above the same fire to the tomb of your Son, which they alone honour, so that it may be revealed; when you kindle their hearts in love for you by that same [Col. 0990D] fire; when you enlighten them by its brightness here and forever. And because the faithless enemies of your Christ despise his death more than any other work of his humiliation, you show, by adorning the place of his death with the miracle of so great a light, how great are the darknesses of folly in which they are held. They especially despise him as dead; you especially honour the tomb of the dead one. What they consider most shameful, you declare by so wondrous a sign to be more glorious. You reject the Jews as envious Cain; you reject the Gentiles as worshippers of Baal, and kindle fire upon their sacrifices. You choose the offerings of the Christian people as Abel’s gifts; you approve their sacrifice as Elijah’s burnt offering, while you illuminate with fire sent from above the tomb in which your Son, made an offering for us, rested.

Formerly your same Son lay hidden in little Bethlehem, a small place, small according to the flesh; you wonderfully disclosed him to people ignorant of him by the guiding star. But now you illuminate the place of his tomb more wonderfully with heavenly light, and show that he does not lie hidden in the tomb as a dead human being, but rules living and dead as Lord from the heavenly places [Col. 0991A]. Drawn by that miracle, but especially by your grace, all nations run to your tomb, Jesus Christ, Son of the Most High, and confess you not only as their God and Lord, but also as mediator, redeemer, and saviour. They offer themselves to you, who offered yourself as a sacrifice for them; nor do they fear any dangers of land or sea in order that they may approach you at your tomb. They know indeed that you no longer lie in that tomb as dead, but reign in heaven as the living God; nevertheless, by venerating the stone on which you lay—indeed, by venerating you yourself through the stone—they show the affection they have for you. Penitent sinners kiss your stone with devout hearts; and, because like that sinful but penitent Mary they cannot kiss your feet, set above the summit of angels, they show their wounds there with tears, lest your bowels, ever dripping mercy upon the wretched, should be able to restrain themselves from pitying them. They know that, since the time of your passion, death, and burial, you are moved toward them by greater mercy than before, because you do not readily allow them to die [Col. 0991B]. They know that you cannot endure calmly that the price of so great a price which you gave for the life of mortals should be rendered futile, nor bear patiently that, after your death, those for whom you died should die. For you caused the kingdom of life to succeed the kingdom of death, which had extended as far as you; and you exchanged so dreadful and long a slavery for so great and everlasting a grace of freedom.

By the very day on which you died, and the very place in which you were buried, you showed for whom and why you willed to die and be buried; and you taught ignorant people this better by deeds than by words. Did you not create man on the sixth day because at the sixth hour, by atoning for what he had sinned through the wood, you recalled man to paradise? Walking in paradise toward the evening breeze, you rebuked the sinner, saying: “Adam, where are you?” (Gen. 3). In the afternoon, at the ninth hour, giving up your spirit, you led the sinner back to paradise [Col. 0991D], saying to him: “Today you shall be with me in paradise” (Luke 23). In order to show that through your death and burial access to that paradise was opened to all after the thief, you willed to suffer in paradise—that is, in a garden—to be crucified in paradise, die in paradise, be buried in paradise, and also rise from paradise. For thus your beloved disciple, your apostle, your evangelist speaks. Thus indeed he says concerning the place where you were seized and began to suffer: “Jesus went out with his disciples across the torrent of Cedron, where there was a garden” (John 18). Thus Peter also testifies concerning the place of your death and burial: “There was,” he says, “in the place where he was crucified a garden, and in the garden a new tomb” (John 19). What else therefore, O Lord, O invincible Power of the eternal Father, O highest Wisdom, who disposes all things not [Col. 0992A] only powerfully but beautifully and sweetly (Wis. 8)—what else, I say, did you signify by being seized in a garden, crucified in a garden, dead in a garden, buried in a garden, and raised from a garden, except humanity’s return through all these things to the garden, that is, to paradise? In the garden you atoned for what had been committed in the garden; and, in order to wash away the guilt committed in the garden, you underwent in the garden the punishment that blotted out that guilt. The sin of the garden brought eternal death upon humankind; the punishment in the garden restored eternal life to humankind. Thus, mercifully and elegantly renewing your work, O Saviour, restoring what had perished, by your death you destroyed the death of your human creature; by the rest of your tomb you provided rest for the souls of your own; by the resurrection [Col. 0992B] of your flesh from the tomb you prepared for human flesh the glory of resurrection.

Therefore give a gracious hearing to the prayers of those who come to your tomb; incline it also to the devotion of those who, far away, venerate you at your tomb. For that kindness and common compassion cannot be unavailing to those whom good will also joins together. For the peace which, when born, you announced to people of good will through the holy host of the heavenly army, you yourself bestowed upon those same people of good will when, rising from the tomb, you said, “Peace be with you.” Therefore, because you are eternal, by naming peace you indicated not a transitory but eternal peace. Those near to your tomb, and those far from it even in body, implore this peace from you. Receive, therefore, you who lay dead [Col. 0992C] in the tomb and rose from the dead out of the tomb, the prayers, tears, and devotion of your people: those called Christians from your name; marked with the sign of your cross; distinguished by that sign, after the manner of the Israelites, from the Egyptians—that is, from the whole number of unbelievers; washed from all sins by your baptism; refreshed unto eternal life by your body and blood; spiritually dead and buried. Raise up with yourself all these, you who, having risen from the dead, die no more (Rom. 6); empty their tombs by your tomb; destroy their death by your death; renew their life by your life; prepare their ascension by your ascension; and, to bring to its due end all that you have done for them, give them the kingdom of heaven—you who are King and Lord of the kingdom of heaven [Col. 0992D]. Grant that, hindered neither by the devil, sins, nor the world, they may not be disappointed in their expectation; but through you, who are called “the expectation of the nations” (Gen. 49), may their blessed hope at your coming be changed into glory and eternal blessedness. Then the glory of your tomb will appear far greater, when those who have attended you, buried in humility, with devout services, are exalted not only in their souls but also in their bodies by the everlasting resurrection from the tomb and by the glory of immortality. For you who, in this pilgrimage, became the way through the humility of assumed flesh for them as they journey toward their homeland, will appear to them, through the majesty of divine power, as truth and everlasting life—you who live and reign as God through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON III. ON SAINT MARCELLUS, POPE AND MARTYR

[Col. 0993A]

Brothers, today you have undertaken to celebrate with honour and joy the feast-day of the glorious martyr and supreme pontiff of God, Marcellus. And rightly with honour and joy, so that you may signify that by this his feast-day he attained the highest honour and everlasting joy. And how do we prove this? How, I say, do we prove it? How do we show that the day of his death is his birthday, and that by this birthday he attained the highest honour and everlasting joy? Beloved, in the divine Scriptures the day is called a birthday, or day of generation, on which one comes, as from a womb, so from death, to life. Thus the Lord, spiritually teaching that every human being must be born again to life, said to Nicodemus [Col. 0993B]: “Unless one is born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God” (John 3). Again, calling “generation” the resurrection of bodies which is to occur at the consummation of the age, he said to the disciples: “In the regeneration, when the Son of Man sits on the throne of his majesty, you too shall sit upon twelve thrones” (Matt. 19). Therefore, just as human beings renewed through water and Spirit from the death of sin to the life of righteousness are said to be born again, and just as bodies rising from tombs to immortal life are declared to be regenerated, so the saints of God, freed by the grace of God from this body of death and transferred to the life given them after death, are rightly said to be born. Hence the day on which they pass from misery to blessedness, darkness to light, and death to life, is celebrated not as a day of funeral mourning, but as a birthday with rejoicing. For this birth of the saints is far truer than that of the flesh, in which they do not emerge from their mothers’ wombs into a wretched life soon to end, but ascend from the narrow darkness of the world to free light and eternal life, concerning which the Lord says: “I am the resurrection and the life; whoever believes in me, even if he has died, shall live” (John 11) [Col. 0993C].

In this manner, therefore, the day of blessed Marcellus’s happy passage from earth to heaven is called his birthday. Let us hear from the Lord how by this birthday he attained the highest honour and everlasting joy: “If anyone serves me,” he says, “my Father who is in heaven will honour him” (John 12). We must consider how blessed Marcellus served Christ and how, serving well, he deserved to be honoured by the Father. He served Christ in every ministry of the clergy; he served in the office of pontiff; he served in manifold martyrdom. For he was not permitted to serve in peace, but necessity was laid upon him to fight as well. Nor was he commanded merely to provide for material resources as a wise and faithful steward, but as a proven soldier and skilled commander in war he became a member of the heavenly army amid the great dangers of battle. This is proved by the persecutors’ cruelty, more savage than usual, which arose in his time. It is proved by the martyrs’ blood, flowing abundantly everywhere. It is proved by the whole world fighting against Christ with all its strength [Col. 0993D].

Indeed, Satan had previously devised many assaults against God’s Church, beginning from the time of Nero and stirring up many storms. But, recognizing that he was making no progress, in the days of this blessed man he poured out the whole force of his fury. Vomiting from his swollen womb the entire fullness of the poisonous plague, he set all kingdoms in motion against it and fiercely incited the Roman rulers, who ruled almost all peoples, to uproot it if possible. For, leaving aside the many kinds of death and passing over the innumerable companies of Christians slain by those persecutors, thirty days alone added seventeen thousand persons, made purple by their own blood in confession of Christ, to the flowers of the heavenly fields [Col. 0994A].

Then blessed Marcellinus, bishop of the supreme apostolic see and chief shepherd of Christ’s sheep, was joined by the crown of martyrdom to those same sheep entrusted to him. At that time blessed Marcellus, whose passion makes this present day illustrious, was distinguished by the honour of the priesthood; and, after Marcellinus and together with him, he bore the principal care of the Church of God, allowing nothing to be relaxed. Rather, the greater the danger he saw approaching, the greater courage he prepared for enduring everything.

Meanwhile the pontiff Marcellinus is led away to the sacrifice; the presbyter Marcellus follows toward the crown. The disciple desires to suffer with his master, but is kept back to fight longer. He is not permitted to accompany him to rest, because he is reserved for greater labour [Col. 0994B]. He goes with him as though about to die together with him, but, by God’s providence, does not die, being destined to succeed the bishop. Christ prepares a suitable ruler for his Church. He provides for his ship, hard pressed by the great force of waves, a most learned pilot. He preserves in a fiercer contest a most courageous combatant. He hides in the quiver the arrow with which he will later pierce the hard enemy.

Accordingly, before he suffered, the blessed pope adjured the priest not to consent in any respect to the impious commands of the emperors. Perhaps the holy martyr, warned by the Spirit, had learned that he was to be set over Christ’s Church in his stead, and therefore thought fit to admonish him so earnestly at the very moment when he was almost shedding his own blood. By these words he foretold that the Lord’s flock was to be scourged with a severe blow, and he urged its shepherd so intently not to fail. Thus Christ also, the supreme Shepherd, when his Passion was at hand and He was concerned for the flock He seemed about to leave, said to Peter: “Simon, behold, Satan has demanded you, that he might sift you like wheat. But I have prayed for you, that your faith may not fail; and when you have turned again, strengthen your brethren” (Luke XXI). So blessed Marcellinus, holding Peter’s place and leaving it to blessed Marcellus, warned him not to fail and encouraged him to endure with equanimity the evils that were to follow. Nor should anyone suppose that he feared so greatly for this blessed man, already tested in many trials, as rather that, in him, he represented those others for whom there was cause to fear and instructed them by such words. For although there was no reason to fear for a strong man, a martyr of Christ, there were nevertheless weak persons for whom fear was certainly warranted; and, solicitous with paternal care for them, he commended them with particular earnestness to the shepherd who was to succeed him.

Thus the holy pontiff consummated his course in glorious martyrdom, and Marcellus remained in greater danger than before. He was obliged to consider the flock which he saw bereft of its own shepherd. See, brethren, how great before God was our martyr, whose feast you solemnly celebrate today. See, I say, what judgment heaven rendered concerning him, and thus you will see how great he was. Seek the emperor’s verdict concerning the courage of the soldier. A violent pressure of persecution rose against Christ’s soldiery. The world conspires in arms; the nations rage and the peoples devise vain things; the kings of the earth take their stand and the princes gather together [Col. 0995B] as one against the Lord and against His Christ. They draw their swords, overthrow the army, kill its very commander, and scatter in flight the rest wherever they can. But our soldier recalls those who have fled, gathers those recalled, restores the battle line, exhorts them to war, attacks the enemies, fights fiercely, gains the victory, and exults as victor. Thus, thus blessed Marcellus, acting in the spiritual conflict, shone forth as eminent in courage in Christ’s soldiery. For the sword raged on every side and the persecutor pressed everywhere. While Diocletian and Maximian were violently driving on the persecution and so many thousands of saints were slain, he, as we have said, was uniquely preserved for a time, so that he might defend by his merits, fortify by counsel, and sustain by labour [Col. 0995C] the Church, bereft of its shepherd and trembling for a long time.

Attend, brethren, and consider how great a fire of tribulation tested the Church of God by consuming it at that time, when for seven [Note: [Col. 0995D] Peter the Venerable took this from the book *On the Roman Pontiffs* attributed to Damasus; but it certainly cannot stand. For, since Marcellinus was crowned with martyrdom in the year 304, near the end of the reign of the emperor Diocletian, whereas Marcellus, after occupying the see for five years and several months, died at least in the year 310, the see could not have been vacant for seven years, but only for some months.] years, six months, and twenty-five days—a thing never recorded to have happened either before or after—the Roman see could have no bishop, nor could the universal Church have an apostolic pontiff set above the rest. The storm of persecution prevented it: the clergy and people who remained had neither the possibility of assembling nor the freedom to elect. Throughout this whole period, blessed Marcellus, before bearing pastoral responsibility, performed the pastoral office: instructing the ignorant, strengthening the fearful, administering Christ’s sacraments, [Col. 0995D] and ceaselessly providing for everything amid such terror of death. He carefully sought out, collected, and buried those who had died for confession of the faith, whose heaps were made almost daily. Thus he came by night with priests and deacons, removed the bodies of blessed Pope Marcellinus and of the holy martyrs Claudius and Sirinus, which had lain in the street for thirty-six days by Diocletian’s command to terrify Christians, and buried them with God’s praises in the famous crypt on the Salarian Way.

[Col. 0996A] Then, when the heat of persecution had somewhat subsided, he was raised to the supreme pontificate. The Church rejoiced that at last it had so great a shepherd: a defender tried against every conflict and most valiant. That these two qualities especially shone in him—namely, that he provided diligently for those entrusted to him and resisted his enemies courageously—was proved even more fully by the office he undertook. For that he was attentive and ever vigilant in governing and ordering the Church is shown by the many sound measures which he arranged and established, as the circumstances of the time allowed. For among other things it is written of him in the *Acts*: “He made a cemetery on the Salarian Way, and twenty-five titular churches in the city of Rome. He also established dioceses because of the baptism and penance of many who [Col. 0996B] were converted from the pagans, and because of the tombs of the martyrs. He ordained twenty-five priests in the city of Rome, and two deacons in the month of December.”” Truly a great organizer; truly a provident steward of Christ’s household. He did not think of the naked swords poised over the necks of his enemies, nor heed the danger hanging over him; but, as though enjoying tranquil peace, he never ceased providing for all things, and he risked his own death in place of everyone else’s.

Therefore the blessed martyr was again seized by the tyrant; the church was turned into a stable, public animals were gathered in it, and the pope was compelled under strict guard to be a stableman. For a long time he toiled in an office so laborious and so degrading, serving the animals with great patience, [Col. 0996C] naked and clothed in haircloth. He was not slain by the sword, not consumed by fire, not drowned in waters, not dashed down from a precipice, lest, brought swiftly to an end, he might exchange labour for rest and pains for joys. Instead, he was assigned to such service that its disgrace burned him more than flames could have done and excessive exhaustion wore down his body. Nor, even after a long interval, was it brought to an end: the sight recoiled from filth, the smell could not endure the stench, harsh and unremitting work consumed his flesh, hunger pressed sharply from one side, nakedness multiplied miseries from the other; and amid the manifold kinds of distress, not dying, he continually failed in a condition more miserable than death. Thus the eminent martyr, serving not so much animals as Christ, [Col. 0996D] attained to that honour of servants of which we spoke at the beginning of this sermon, concerning which the Lord Christ Himself says: “Where I am, there also shall my servant be” (John XII). By serving well, then, the blessed man advanced to so great an honour that he ascended to the place where the Son of God is.

And what joy he obtained for so many distresses the Lord Himself indicates when He speaks to the disciples: “And you therefore now indeed have sorrow; but I will see you again, and your heart shall rejoice, and no one shall take your joy from you” [Col. 0997A] (John XVI). The saints truly have sorrow now, not because they undergo the evils of the world unwillingly, but because, fleeing things naturally troublesome to the senses, they are disturbed by them. The Lord Himself deigned to take this disturbance or sorrow upon Himself, saying in the Gospel: “Now is my soul troubled” (John XII), and again: “My soul is sorrowful even unto death” (Matthew XXVI). Holy men suffer this sorrow, as stated, from their bodily senses, as we read in the Psalm: “They went forth and wept, casting their seed” (Psalm CXXV). The apostle Peter suffered it, to whom it was said: “You shall stretch forth your hands, and another shall gird you and lead you where you do not wish” (John XXI). Peter certainly wished to suffer for Christ; for if he had not wished it, he would not have suffered. He wished, I say, to suffer for Christ, [Col. 0997B] but the weakness of the flesh resisted the will of the spirit, concerning which the Lord says: “The spirit indeed is willing, but the flesh is weak” (Matthew XXVI). Blessed Marcellus, successor of blessed Apostle Peter, shared such sorrow with him and with Christ’s other disciples, and therefore deserved to rejoice when joy succeeded it.

“I will see you,” He says, “and your heart shall rejoice” (John XVI): I shall see you with the kindly eyes of My mercy; I shall see you, no longer turning My face away from you; I shall see you, recognizing you as members of My household; I shall see you, rewarding your former labours and cherishing you in My bosom as My own children. Your heart shall rejoice, retaining no sorrow within itself; your heart shall rejoice, not in part but wholly; your [Col. 0997C] heart shall rejoice—that is, your entire inner person; your heart, which alone can rejoice, shall rejoice; your heart shall rejoice, stripped of every misery and filled with every blessedness. “And no one shall take your joy from you” (ibid.): with your heart rejoicing with Me, which had grieved with Me, no one shall take your joy from you. Do not fear that the joy with which your heart will be filled may ever be taken from you. Do not fear that the great joy I shall give may at some time be suspected of having an end. It will not begin in such a way as ever to end; it will not be commenced in such a way as to be finished even after many ages. What is given by Him who is without time will not depart with time. The joy that has neither [Col. 0997D] beginning nor end in itself cannot be finished. I Myself am your joy, I who in Myself am always what I am. Once you have attained this joy, no one shall take it from you, because no one can separate Me from you.

To this joy, after the sorrow of his sufferings, blessed Marcellus is brought today; and, after many palms of victory, the warrior is presented in the sight of the eternal King. For the martyr and God’s pontiff dies in an eminent confession, passes from the stable to the kingdom of God, and in his death imitates the birth of the Son of God.

Rightly, brethren, the heavenly birthday of blessed Marcellus is near [Col. 0998A] to Christ’s Nativity: near in time because it is not remote in resemblance. For the place of his heavenly birth is not unlike the place of this Passion. Marcellus died in such a place as Christ was born. There Christ received a temporal beginning; there Marcellus received the beginning of a life without end. His eternal birthday was therefore there, where Christ’s temporal rising was; a manger received the infant at His birth, a stable receives the martyr in his suffering. Supreme Majesty endured a lowly resting-place; the supreme pontiff endured a filthy dwelling. Divine infancy was wrapped in poor cloths; condemned innocence was covered in very rough haircloth. Christ, born, was a spectacle for the animals that perhaps were present; Marcellus, serving animals, was made an object of mockery. [Col. 0998B] At the birth of God the child in a manger, the angelic choir sang glory in the highest; the martyr, dying in a stable, today attains the glory of the angels. He attains glory, joined to the citizens above; but he too leaves behind him that peace for humankind which the angels then proclaimed. For in him the fury of the enemies, as though wearied out, came to rest, and the heat of the furnace cooled once the Church had been purified. Among the apostolic pontiffs, he alone was the last who deserved to be crowned with martyrial confession in the persecutions of pagan rulers. Peter was the first among them to enter the contest of martyrdom; Marcellus, fighting bravely, was the last among them to finish it, and through this end he came to the Beginning without end, our Lord Jesus Christ, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives [Col. 0998C] and reigns as God through all ages of ages. Amen.

## SERMON IV. ON THE VENERATION OF ANY RELICS

[Note: [Col. 0997] In the copy sent to us from Cluny, this sermon is marked as delivered at the reception of the relics of St Marcellus the martyr.]

Rejoice, dearest brethren, with solemn and singular gladness on this day, because through it a singular occasion for rejoicing is given you. The commemoration of all saints is indeed common to the veneration of all the faithful; but the Church here present rightly offers special devotion to those whose sacred pledges enrich it. Great, I say, and to be magnificently proclaimed, is the gift of heavenly generosity by which He has willed to adorn this temple with the body of a great and illustrious martyr—more splendid than all silver, brighter than all gold, more precious than every pearl [Col. 0998D]. Rightly, when this blessed body was once received, the Church here present rejoiced; for it is certain that, when its blessed soul was received, the Jerusalem above exulted. Rightly also do we congratulate him today on earth, with whom the entire heavenly company rejoices eternally in heaven.

Already, according to the Saviour’s promise, the spirit of that righteous man shines like the sun in the kingdom of his Father (Matthew XIII), though this bodily fabric contains his blessed limbs. Divine condescension divided its martyr, as it were, in equal shares: it retained his soul for itself among the ranks of blessed spirits [Col. 0999A] and, in wondrous generosity, bestowed the venerable relics of his sacred body upon the faithful still living in the flesh. But someone may ask: “What benefit is there in honouring lifeless bodies? What does it avail to celebrate bones that lack sensation with hymns and praises?” Far, far from the hearts of the faithful, brethren, be thoughts of this kind; let them depart from the holy meditations of God’s servants; let them be far from minds seeking to draw near to God. There were once impious people who entertained such thoughts, and they were, as useless limbs, cut off from Christ’s body—that is, His Church—by the just desert of their impiety. Therefore, so that your assembly, united in the Holy Spirit in this present solemnity, may know how worthily and salutarily saints’ bodies and relics are honoured by the faithful, let the authority of Holy Scripture be brought forward.

For God, the Creator of spiritual and bodily things, after creating by His almighty hand angelic spirits and this bodily mass of the world, created the human creature in order to display the glory of His ineffable craftsmanship. By an excellent work He united it from rational spirit and flesh. In this, His wisdom was displayed all the more wonderfully because the one person of a human being is joined more powerfully from diverse substances. Magnifying the unity of this marvellous union with a blessedness proper and fitting to each nature, He granted both righteousness to the soul and incorruption to the body. He decreed that the latter should depend upon the former: while free choice remained in force, so long as righteousness was preserved by the spirit, [Col. 0999C] no corruption would oppress the flesh. But when the spirit abandoned righteousness, the flesh immediately became subject to the laws of corruption. Then wretched humanity cast aside this law of righteousness imposed upon it, and at once was subjected to the harsh misery of corruption which you know; and the one whom the gracious Creator had made for everlasting glory fell into the deserved punishment of impiety.

At last, at the time ordained before the ages and fitting for humanity’s restoration, the Son of God came. Neither abandoning though abandoned, nor scorning though scorned, He re-created humanity by the goodness through which He had created it, and restored righteousness to the soul and incorruption to the body. But because the order established at first was that righteousness of spirit should go before and that incorruption of flesh, justified through the spirit, should follow, He decreed that the justification of the whole human being should come first in this life, while the incorruption or immortality of the flesh should be delayed until the life to come. He also willed this to preserve the merit of faith; for there would then be no faith if Christ bestowed in the present what He promised us for the future. Nor should we now hope in things above for the promise of the heavenly kingdom, if we believed it already granted to us in the low regions of the earth. Therefore, in the eternal life which we await through faith, and which He who is faithful in His words has promised, we know that the spirits of the righteous live blessedly in the meantime; and in their bodies we await resurrection with immortality and complete incorruption. Hence [Col. 1000A] we do not cast away the bodies of those who cultivated righteousness in this life as lifeless, do not despise them as insensible, and do not trample them like the carcasses of brute animals. Rather, we venerate them as temples of the Lord, cherish them as palaces of the Godhead, store them as pearls to be set in the eternal King’s crown, and preserve them with all the devotion we can as vessels of resurrection to be reunited to blessed souls—not because God needs our help to restore them, but because, in His habitual manner of kindness, He is more eager to delight in our service toward His saints for the sake of our salvation.

There is a twofold reason for offering such honour to holy bodies. The limbs of God’s servants, having formerly served God through righteousness in this life, are judged worthy of service; and the faithful do not in the least doubt that they will rise again to eternal blessedness. In this hope the saints of old regarded neither their own bodies nor those of their kin as deserving contempt. With this confidence the great patriarchs Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob chose the double cave. With this thought Joseph’s descendants, carrying his bones from Egypt by command, buried them in the land of promise. For although nothing prevented persons unequal in merits from being buried together, they nevertheless chose to be separated in body also from those divided from them in faith and separated in conduct. By this distinction of bodies they taught that various differences of souls, according to their merits, must be understood. God Himself showed that the bodies of His servants are of great price in His sight when He did not allow Moses, the lawgiver of the Old [Col. 1000C] Testament, to be laid in a tomb by human hands in the customary manner, but deigned to bury him Himself: “Moses, the servant of the Lord,” Scripture says, “died, and the Lord buried him” (Deuteronomy XXXIV). Though, as some think, by this act He removed an occasion of idolatry from a people prone to evil, He nevertheless showed that the corpse of a righteous dead man was by no means vile in His sight.

The Saviour Himself, who for this reason had to be buried through human services—that when people saw Him truly dead and buried with their own eyes, they might not doubt that He was truly raised from the dead—taught by His own example what He said near His Passion in Bethany and what He thought about the service of reverence to be bestowed upon holy bodies. A woman came with precious nard. She anointed feet set above the heads of angels; then, lifting herself to the sacred head, she broke the alabaster vessel containing it and poured the whole quantity of that most costly liquid upon Christ’s body. When it had been poured out, the house was filled with the fragrance of the ointment, and the still-hidden impiety of the traitor was openly revealed: “Why,” he said, “this waste?” (Mark XIV). And according to John: “Why was this ointment not sold for three hundred denarii and given to the poor?” (John XII). The Lord replied: “Let her alone, that she may keep it for the day of my burial” (ibid.). And in Matthew, speaking under the plural designation of the disciples: “Why do you trouble this woman? She has done a good work to me; for you always have the poor with you, but you do not always have me. For in pouring this ointment upon my body, she did it for my burial” [Col. 1001A] (Matthew XXVI).

Behold, brethren, you have heard the blessed woman anointing the holy Lord with devoutness, the avaricious traitor disparaging her good work, and the gracious Saviour magnificently praising that good work: “She has done,” He says, “a good work to me.” Who, then, would dare any longer to think it not a good work to honour the bodies of the blessed dead, when he hears the Lord commend with magnificent praises the honour of anointing His own body—not dead, but soon to die? “She did it for my burial,” He says. She poured the ointment upon my body, not while it was living but while it was about to die, and bestowed it for burial. Before the tomb, [Col. 1001B] she rendered the honour of burial; and what, amid the disturbances then prevailing, she could not later do—for piety, knowing no delay, anticipated it. She feared that my persecutors might take away the opportunity to anoint my body and, with the same spite by which they would kill me alive, might deprive me when dead also of the humanity and reverence due to me. Therefore what she feared would not be permitted to her at that time, she has now done as she could, in devotion worthy to be praised throughout the world. Hence it follows: “Amen I say to you, wherever this Gospel is preached in the whole world, what she has done shall also be told in memory of her” (ibid.). The whole world, He says, hearing of this good work by this woman, shall praise it together; and because she did it in memory and honour of Me, it too shall preserve the perpetual memory of so blessed a work for its own edification.” In saying this, the Saviour shut the mouths of the foolish, removed harmful thoughts even for times far in the future, and showed by the example of His own body that reverence must be offered to sacred bodies, when He praised those who rendered such reverence so highly.

Why, indeed, should it be surprising if flesh joined to spirit, completing the one human person by its unity, and serving the Creator along with the spirit, is said to deserve honour even after the soul’s departure, when even the coverings of the flesh itself are deservedly believed worthy of veneration? For just as we venerate the body, subject to God through the spirit, for the sake of that same blessed subjection—not only while living but also when dead—so we receive with due honour whatever adheres externally to that body and is, as it were, sanctified by its very contact with a saint. [Col. 1001D] The Church also customarily does this with devout affection; and when it cannot possess relics of saints’ bodies, it exercises its devotion through however small a portion of sacred garments. It consoles its longing by such a remedy, so that, while it yearns with all the fervour of its mind for the eternal fellowship of the saints, it may meanwhile feed its hunger upon their garments or gifts (*xenia*). All this is referred to God’s glory: His Church, agreeing with His judgment in all things, studies in many ways to honour on earth those whom it believes He glorifies ineffably in heaven. And, that all this may be confirmed by the strength of a heavenly oracle, listen, beloved, to Holy Scripture, which deceives no one in these matters; consider also divine power. You will undoubtedly recognize that not only the limbs but also [Col. 1002A] the coverings of sacred limbs are to be venerated, so that you may know how precious in the Lord’s sight are the bodies of the righteous even after death, when divine power itself declares that their garments are worthy of honour.

The Lord’s own garment bears witness to these statements. By touching its fringe a woman was healed from an issue of blood, and through it the hidden power of the divine body was openly shown to all; of this power the Lord Himself said: “I perceived power going out from me” (Luke VIII). Let the apostle Paul also be brought forward to establish this point: from his body handkerchiefs or aprons were carried to the sick, and, as Scripture says, illnesses departed from them and evil spirits went out (Acts IX). If we take something also from the Old Scripture, you will see Elisha take up Elijah’s cloak, which had fallen from him as he was being carried up on high. Carrying it with him, he struck the Jordan three times with that garment and said: “Where is now the God of Elijah?” (IV Kings II). When the Jordan was divided by that stroke, a dry path opened for the prophet amid the waters, and divine power declared the outstanding merit of that saint by the noble miracle performed through his garment. Therefore garments and any similar things belonging to saints are venerable, not for their own sake but for the honour of the saints themselves, just as the saints themselves became illustrious in heaven and on earth not from themselves but from the gift of Him whom they obeyed.

Accordingly, as Scripture says, the righteous person living in hope in the present life, raising himself to attain heavenly things and already holding in charity in part what he believes and hopes, does what can be done here. He beholds in His saints Him whom he cannot yet contemplate in Himself; and those whom he could not keep long while living, he honours as living even after death through whatever smallest relics of them he may possess. [Col. 1002C] I say, he bestows the honour of the living upon those whom he knows live eternally with God, as the Saviour says in the Gospel: “God is not the God of the dead but of the living, for all live to Him” (Luke XX). Evil persons indeed live by their own essence, which they never lose; but good persons live for God in a special sense through the blessed life which they can never lack in Him. They do not attain this while they live in the flesh; their spirits, already glorified by God, are stored in the bosom of the heavenly courts until, in the common resurrection of the flesh, each receives his own body for glory. Let us hear from the Lord Himself what kind, or how great, that glory of bodies will be. For when He treated of the resurrection of the righteous, He said among other things: “In the resurrection they neither marry nor are given in marriage, but are as the angels of God in heaven” (Matthew XXII); and again: “They are equal to the angels of God” (Luke XX), “and are sons of God, being sons of the resurrection.”

Those whose bodies, brethren, you venerate; whose ashes make you rejoice; for whose blessed bones you prepare golden tombs: they are sons of God, equal to angels, sons of the resurrection. Therefore you receive them reverently as sons of God and exalt them with equal praises as equals of angels; you hope that, as sons of the resurrection, they will rise again in their own flesh. Made more certain by this hope than by any human reality, you do not despise the bones of the martyr before you as though dry, but honour them as though already flourishing with the future incorruption; and you hear him exulting in the prophet’s voice: “My flesh has flowered again” (Psalm XXVII), and the same prophet saying elsewhere: “Your youth shall be renewed like the eagle’s” [Col. 1003A] (Psalm CII). Although you do not yet see in your martyr flesh flourishing instead of dry, or youth restored instead of old age, you do not in any way despair of their future fulfilment on the authority of these sacred words. Thus, as said, though you still walk by faith and not yet by sight, and the life of saints’ bodies is by no means open to your bodily eyes, the harmonious authority of both Testaments shows it more clearly than light. This authority ordinarily has such force with faithful minds that they do not need to see with the eyes of the flesh what they hear it affirm.

Therefore, beloved, since you have Jesus Christ, the author of the old Law and of new grace, first promising through the ancient saints and later showing in His own body the resurrection of the flesh and the glorification of the whole human substance to His servants, let us honour with due reverence the body of this blessed martyr: though we possess it as dead, yet as destined to rise and to be clothed in immortal glory. Let us believe that he lives to God, whose life and death he willed to serve. I say that the bodies of saints live to God: even the body of the dead prophet Elisha proves this, for although it was lifeless, by contact with a corpse laid in the tomb it restored the life that corpse had lost. The countless miracles everywhere experienced by those who have approached their venerable tombs with devout minds prove that such bodies live to God. The Apostle too teaches that they live to God, forbidding the faithful to grieve over those who sleep. He calls sleeping, not dead, those whom he affirms will awaken as from sleep, saying: [Col. 1003C] “This we say to you in the word of the Lord: that we who are alive, who are left, shall be caught up together with them to meet Christ in the air; and so shall we always be with the Lord” (I Thessalonians IV). And elsewhere: “This corruptible shall put on incorruption, and this mortal shall put on immortality” (I Corinthians XV). And Isaiah: “Your bones shall spring up like grass” (Isaiah LXVI).

Therefore, because the bones of the martyr before us, rising to eternal life, shall spring up like grass; because this corruptible shall put on incorruption and this mortal immortality; because this righteous body, caught up to meet Christ, shall remain always with Him—who would not with all affection judge worthy of honour in this life what he believes will be exalted to the glory of so great an honour in the life to come? For the Saviour has not forgotten His words: “Where I am, there also shall my servant be” (John XII); nor was it said to the Father without purpose: “I will that where I am, they also may be with me, that they may see my glory” (John XVII). For the vision of that glory, as has been said, He created humankind in the beginning; for the vision of it He restored our martyr [Col. 1004A] through the mediation of assumed flesh and through works of righteousness. Until this takes place when Christ comes to judge, hear joyfully this precious member of the body taking to itself the voice of the Head once its own and saying: “In peace the martyr sleeps and rests together” (Psalm IV)—in the peace which his spirit now possesses and which he awaits in the flesh; “together,” from whom Christ does not separate him even in death. He sleeps, to awaken when the sleep of mortality is complete; he rests, to pass from present labours into eternal rest. Hence it follows: “For thou, O Lord, hast singularly established me in hope” (ibid.), because strangers shall no longer pass through Jerusalem, nor shall anything defiled or working abomination enter it. This is the hope of resurrection which, according to the Apostle, the God who does not lie has promised, and of which He also says in the Gospel: “The hour is coming in which all who are in the tombs shall hear His voice. And those who have done good shall come forth to the resurrection of life; but those who have done evil, to the resurrection of judgment” [Col. 1004B] (John V). Established singularly in this hope, the martyr will be glorified in the flesh in his own time; he has taught us to think this concerning his body and shown what you should hope concerning your own bodies. To nourish you in that hope through patient faith, the apostle James also exhorts you, saying: “Be patient until the coming of the Lord” (James V). And he adds a comparison: “Behold, the farmer awaits the precious fruit in its season, patiently enduring until he receives the early and the latter rain” (ibid.). Explaining what he had said, he adds: “Be patient also, and strengthen your hearts, because the coming of the Lord draws near” (ibid.).

You too will await securely this coming of the Lord, when you yourselves are to be glorified in your bodies, if, strengthening your hearts with the affection of heavenly desire, you keep not only the martyr’s body but also his example. Then he will delight in your service when he sees that you do not stray from his path. Christ was his path; walking steadfastly by Him, he came to Him. To Him, I say, he passed: through humility to His exaltation, through labours to rest, through ignominy to glory, through death to life. By following your martyr, you too will come through Christ to this life; and now you have in him a great refuge and singular protection [Col. 1004D] with Christ. Filled with the charity in which he now rejoices in God, he embraces your service of love; its due reward cannot fail, unless perhaps—far be it!—love itself should fail.

Recall the untiring love of the holy women toward the body of the buried Lord. Because they diligently ministered to Him when dead, they deserved to be the first to see His glory when He had risen. Jewish ferocity did not frighten them, nor the governor’s power, nor the savagery of the guards; but through the dreadful cruelty of persecutors they fearlessly reached the Lord’s tomb. To them the angelic vision was shown in the magnificence of the Lord’s resurrection, so that they might rejoice that they had received no less than the perfect reward of blessedness, since with all their heart’s affection they had rendered perfect service. For this is the perfect recompense of saints: when the fellowship of holy angels is given to the pure in heart and the Lord Himself is bestowed in the full presence of eternal fellowship. You, beloved, can deserve this after the example of the holy women if, devoutly serving the holy bodies committed to you by God, you strive to bring the perseverance of your blessed service to its due end [Col. 1005A]. The recompense for your service will not be inferior if the devotion of those rendering comparable service is not unequal. Blessed service to the blessed body will grant fellowship with angels and lead those who serve to the eternal vision of the King of heaven, who with the Father and the Holy Spirit lives and reigns as God through all ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 1005]

## THE NINTH: RHYTHMS, PROSES, VERSES, AND HYMNS OF PETER THE VENERABLE, ABBOT OF CLUNY

A defence of the poems of his Peter of Poitiers against their detractors, the argument of which is:

[Col. 1005B]

The eminent leader himself pleads for his poet;  
with these weapons he pierces rabid envy.

I hear, devouring Envy, that you gnaw at sacred song  
and cavil at words written with a divine pen.

Though your will is wicked and base,  
and you regard the misfortunes of all as your own gain,

yet scarcely can anyone persuade me to believe this of you,  
nor do I believe that anyone could think a crime so great:

that you would attempt to muddy with your own filth  
a glass-clear stream flowing from a pure spring.

But what shall be? I am compelled to believe a truthful report,  
which proves its words by certain indications.

Ah, crime! A mind fit to be submerged in the Stygian deep,  
[Col. 1005C] which vomits dreadful poisons from its own cave.

Spirits of Tartarus, restrain such a tongue,  
which in madness could utter unspeakable words.

Cut into pieces the tongue drawn from the abyss of its mouth,  
so that ravenous flame may presently make it ash.

Close up the passages of the throat that gives such wicked speech,  
and let the throat swell, lest it sound what is unlawful.

Fear to be heard, O voice unworthy even to sound;  
I advise you: fail, and suppress yourself in silence.

Let no such noise pollute human ears;  
let the very breath deny it its ordinary use.

But can I be the avenger of so great a crime,
Can the matter require the stricter judgment of a judge?

Or shall I try with a frail reed to expiate a crime  
which even the hoof of iron could scarcely scrape away?

[Col. 1005D] Nor does this injury harm me alone;  
rather, it concerns men of outstanding distinction.

You, O foremost cultivators of philosophy,  
whom that same lady rears in her own household,

You, I say, nourished and made drunk at her breast,  
whom she has imbued from her own mouth with sacred studies—

Ovid, Horace, Vergil, Statius, Lucan, Boethius,  
and whoever else has adorned her work with verse—

The sword of this envy threatens to strike you;  
[Col. 1006B] it also devises your destruction.

For he injures you who does not fear to injure him  
whom Calliope gave to you as a companion.

Among the rest she placed him with equal lot,  
unwilling that he should be inferior to anyone.

That sacred choir willingly granted him a lofty chair,  
giving him a seat in their midst.

Do not wonder that I rank those who come later with the first:  
time can rightly take nothing from merit.

Nor are old men displeased to be compared with the young;  
for a wise son is his father’s glory.

Therefore we compare this young man with his elders,  
this man whom the Muse makes equal to the fathers.

For the ancient tongue of the Fathers possesses no greater  
splendour, weight, or reason than his.

[Col. 1006C] Light gleams in his words; his meaning is weighty in substance;  
neither elegance nor gravity stands apart from the other.

He exalts what ought to be exalted, and presses down what should be pressed down;  
speaking nothing that ought to be silent, silent about nothing that should be recited.

He weeps when weeping is fitting; he rejoices when prosperity requires it,  
rendering to each thing what accords with its office.

He has learned to write so that he seems to paint everything:  
no art, no colour, is absent from him.

The words indeed resound, but the things themselves seem more present,  
as a beautiful image fashions a living man.

The eyes seize these things through the ears; what is heard is seen,  
and no one can read without marvelling.

A many-coloured brush, blending diverse colours,  
soon makes the pictured sea gleam;

[Col. 1006D] everything accords with the subject undertaken,  
nor could anyone have spoken the words better.

Happy subject, exalted by so great an honour,  
which the heavenly Muse deigned to address.

You were cheap, slight, languishing, wholly prostrate;  
but whatever praise you possess, a golden tongue has given.

Let no one’s lyre try to set itself before yours:  
none has ever sung a sweeter melody.

And because nothing better can be seen in any poem,  
he who does not accept this destroys everything together.

[Col. 1007A] What safety will remain for you poets in the world,  
if he is driven from so well-defended a place?

Nor do I wish to flatter: the fortune of the two is equal,  
whether one approves the good or reproves the evil.

If you have spoken well, each has spoken well alike;  
if badly, the same fault binds both accused men.

Can one suppose that such great poets erred,  
whom the world’s abundant reverent love follows?

But these men are not to be thought to have erred;  
whoever thinks it is exceedingly foolish.

But if it is not lawful to suppose that such men erred,  
who can say that one equal to them errs?

Yet I see the poison which you still keep beneath your breast,  
which has long oppressed your heart with envy.

Therefore beware of silently enduring that dreadful burden,  
[Col. 1007B] lest your skin burst under its swelling plague.

Speak, I beg you; speak, and quickly vomit out the pestilence that oppresses you,  
thus relieving the secrets of your heart.

Speak, speak: why are you silent? Are you perhaps held by shame,  
and afraid to utter wicked words again?

If you are afraid, rightly so: everyone favours this fear.  
Yet he asks from your mouth whether it is true.

You report a marvel: our young man composed poems  
deservedly worthy of immeasurable applause,

which could be rivalled by none in brilliance,  
unless the stain of shameful flattery darkened them.

But nothing faulty pleases me in the order of things;  
therefore no faulty poems please me.

Take back this filth which you have vomited from your filth;  
and lest it flow, close your throat with a strong lock.

[Col. 1007C] Otherwise you will either drive everyone away by excessive stench,  
or compel each person to close his nostrils.

But lest you perhaps complain that you are pressed by words,  
receive peacefully what I wish to say.

Explain more clearly, I pray, what fault you mean,  
by which the Muse cannot please you because it is faulty.

If because it has praised—O how many does that charge hold guilty!  
How many and how great men does this chain bind?

With these men may I deserve to be bound in this happy lot,  
than which no day could be more welcome to me.

If I mention the sages or poets of the world  
who composed books full of praises,

perhaps you will object to me their condemned religion,  
by which alone learned men were foolish.

Yet I condemn the impiety by which they displeased;  
I approve no less the fact that they were wise.

[Col. 1007D] For a skilled hand knows how to pluck a grape  
so as cautiously to avoid the thorn at the same time.

But passing over these, so that every murmur may be silent,  
let us choose to enumerate Christians alone:

those whom merit made great, fame made illustrious throughout the world,  
and blessed life bore up to heaven.

Here, impious madness, you will find nothing to censure,  
nothing that you can gnaw with your biting tooth.

Their virtue compels you either freely to yield,  
or, if you refuse, you will then be more thoroughly defeated.

Now then let the twin columns come forward,  
supported by which the hall of God fears no fall.

These are the blessed Jerome and Augustine,  
[Col. 1008A] whom the law of the Church commands us to follow as authorities.

How greatly the former raises his Paula to the stars  
with praises shines clearly in his outstanding eloquence.

His eloquent tongue so extols her virtues  
that its words allow none of her merits to perish.

Nor after her dreadful tomb was it enough for him to sing her praises  
and happily discharge his dutiful vows.

While she was still safe and sound, he often revived her by letters sent,  
not hesitating to make her known through praise of her.

The daughter followed her mother in holy pursuits,  
drawing like dispositions from her parent.

Nor did he permit her either to lie hidden beneath a dark cloud,  
but took care to make her illustrious by his writings:

I mean Eustochium, who gave Christ  
the virginal lodging of an inviolate body.

[Col. 1008B] It now delights the Church to recite Paula frequently,  
and reading no less often sounds Eustochium’s name.

He swears that he cannot keep their praises silent,  
nor fears that he has displeased envy by my song;

because he wrote encomia for each while she lived,  
envy judges him guilty together with me.

But surely such an accusation is a great honour to me,  
because I am reckoned guilty with such a companion.

Now, if it pleased me to name the praised men individually,  
not two but an innumerable multitude would gather.

Whoever wishes to know them should not run to my poems,  
but drink abundant streams from the sacred fountain.

Let the studious lover consult those book-cases  
whose bosom is known to be heavy with books;

and when Jerome has then been read through many volumes,  
[Col. 1008C] every page read will be my witness.

After him let that indomitable warrior come,  
whose hand alone wears down many thousands;

one who has never been accustomed to be conquered, but always to conquer,  
and forces the weapons of opponents into the ground.

This is Augustine, whom Africa sent us,  
the third part of the world, greater in extent and thus more eminent.

That land is smaller in territory than the other two parts;  
yet by her Augustine she conquers them both.

Nothing more abundant has grown amid Libyan ears of grain,  
by whose fruit you may drive away hunger of soul.

The heavens, brighter henceforth, make us serene with their twin suns;  
but this new sun shines more brightly than the old.

For he banishes dark shadows from minds,  
[Col. 1008D] while the other merely illumines bodily darkness.

While he lived, he dedicated praises to Ambrose,  
which he strove to publish for peoples by voice and pen.

His letter flatters Jerome with many words;  
each writes to the other as to a father.

He took nothing away from the titles of his praise, and left nothing  
that could be glory and praise for that excellent man.

What if now his pen records his equal spouses,  
holy Paulinus and his Therasia?

Will it not strike your stony wall with a tempest, O rival,  
so that all your ramparts soon fall—

from which, secure, you watch the enemy from afar
