and laugh cheerfully at the threats he casts?

He shows that they abandoned their native soil for Christ,  
that they preferred heaven to earth.

[Col. 1009A] He praises them for putting behind them wealth, noble rank,  
and the bonds of marriage for God.

He relates that, coming from the western quarter of the sun,  
they took paths hitherto unknown

and won pious dwellings in the nearby East,  
so that their passage into rest might be nearer.

He entrusted their praises to their own ears,  
fearing nothing on that account either for himself or for them.

If now my pen should attempt to record the rest  
whom he excessively exalted in his own books,

days would fail together with thought, words together with time,  
and talent, crushed by the heavy mass, would collapse.

Now let Ambrose come, to be numbered among the foremost,  
loftier than the Italian Alps.

The nearby Eridanus does not inundate the lands more deeply  
[Col. 1009B] when its proud flood, swollen with rain, rages,

than the river of Father Ambrose’s eloquence,  
increased by heavenly showers, waters parched hearts.

Whoever wishes to write fitting praise of him  
must undertake a work rightly demanding much labour.

But it will suffice me, leaving the burden of praise aside,  
to possess with me the man who is the whole of praise.

It is clear that he sent praises to two emperors,  
drawing royal minds toward God,

that he might better teach their rigid minds by persuasion  
to submit their hard necks to Christ’s gentle yoke.

Nature is said to have given noble minds this disposition:  
that, once eager for praise which they have deserved,

they always add praiseworthy deeds to deeds already praised,  
so that lasting honour may be won for themselves.

[Col. 1009C] Cicero knew this and left it written for us,  
to whom the Latin tongue owes great credit.

He enriches its poverty with such a rich tongue  
that no speech is now richer.

“The commonwealth,” he says, “stands while its own ruler stands;  
in his fall it too falls together.

Accordingly, the causes of ruin must be removed,  
and constant strength added to the ruler who stands,

so that, the appetite of his mind refreshed by lavish praise,  
glory may avert the ruler’s hunger.

Thus the commonwealth fears no disaster,  
while it continually renews the ruler’s strength.”

Therefore the holy man nourished kings with pious praises,  
that by praise he might banish their hunger,

[Col. 1009D] so that, filled by this food and renewed in strength of mind,  
they might govern more vigorously the law of the great empire.

Now, Cyprian, deign to follow your own followers,  
whom you precede in time or merit.

These lilies illuminate the heavenly fields,  
but yours are joined to purple roses.

You are joined to them in word; you surpass them by sacred blood,  
by which the Punic land is more richly red than usual.

How much blood of many did your tongue make red,  
men whom it taught to lose life by a pious death!

Under your leadership warlike Carthage again grows proud,  
and again shakes her arms against the soil of Latium.

Nor does she fear being conquered as in Hannibal’s time,  
but remains secure, trusting in her leader:

with him, overthrowing Roman battalions without bloodshed,  
[Col. 1010A] she triumphed when slain, and Rome yielded.

She subdues enemies far better by dying,  
living as she dies and dying as she kills.

Blessed Pope Cornelius, you did not hesitate to ennoble him with your writings.

He strove by writing to make many men illustrious,  
whom the glory of martyrdom made famous.

Now come to us, holy Sidonius, called the glory of Auvergne,  
whom you adorn with so many virtues;

and, recounting the praises which you bestowed on saints,  
strike faithless hearts in your customary manner—

hearts which dare to grunt that praises should be denied to us  
when virtue’s merit demands them.

Therefore now sing of Mamertus of Vienne,  
and how, by his teaching, the pious wolf preserves the flock.

[Col. 1010B] You recount how much merit belonged to the bishop  
who patiently ruled watery Lyons.

Nor is Faustus absent—abbot, hermit, priest—  
whom your tongue by no means allows to lie concealed.

Nor should I pass you by, Fortunatus, worthy to be ranked with the foremost poets,  
as your genius proves.

The land of Italy sent you to the peoples of Gaul  
to sing as a new poet the deeds of men of old.

After the ancients you also wished to sing of the moderns,  
of whose merits you yourself were a witness.

You praise Gregory, illustrious by Auvergnat birth,  
to whom Martin’s lofty chair gives place.

You also celebrate the character and churches of Panthonian Leontius,  
both of which he built adorned with equal splendour.

[Col. 1010C] There is no leisure to enumerate all those whom your page presents;  
for time forbids and the material presses.

It is enough for you who read this poem to know these men:  
for anyone may most fittingly praise the good.

For if they are worthy, they will not lack praise even while alive—  
not to say that praise is the work of death alone.

Therefore do not at all fear to praise the lives of the good:  
he who is good will become better through your praise.

The reward of this fault, not punishment, will follow you,  
and a worthy crown will adorn your head.

Now you who rule star-bearing Olympus by your nod,  
whom the venerating mass of the world worships,

O Peter, greatest of the great after Christ,  
my Muse now calls upon you, if you deign.

That you did not keep silent about Paul’s praises while he lived,  
[Col. 1010D] innumerable witnesses and your writings prove.

Let Paul come last, yet crush the enemy more strongly than all  
by apostolic authority.

No one is better than he; not even that greatest John,  
whom Peter rejoices to have as his equal in merits.

He alone declares war upon the whole world,  
and one man battles against nations.

Neither fear of enemies, nor force, nor a thousand wounds,  
nor blood poured out, can overcome him.

But, conquering the world with his own victorious leader,  
he proves himself to be the commander of an unconquered king.

By this power he puts my enemies to flight, and the darts  
cast by his hand pierce their very hearts.

For as often as his letter sends out praises,  
so often it strikes their hard hearts.

[Col. 1011A] Romans, Galatians, together with Ephesus and Corinth,  
obtained the honour of apostolic praise.

But my verses, too long already, forbid my recalling  
the other peoples whom he exalted with praises.

Let my rival hear attentively what I say,  
and not think that I pour out so many words in vain.

If my poet is guilty because he praised,  
the equal fault binds everyone who praises.

Since no one can deny this by any argument,  
it is clear that the saints named above are therefore guilty.

But if this charge ensnares so many saints,  
I think no one fails to see how great an abyss lies open.

For if anyone attempts to mingle the just in the multitude of the accused,  
he himself will become the greatest guilty man.

If you wish, O our critic, to avoid this chaos,  
[Col. 1011B] you will allow what you customarily forbid.

Nor will you now judge that praise must be kept silent,  
when you see that such great men were not silent.

But perhaps you will say: “He wished to please by praising;  
at least on that account he is guilty and must be condemned.”

O crime, truly an exceedingly damnable offence!  
May it please me, I pray, to join myself to such wickedness.

If I am held under a just judge for such a fault,  
when the case is known, it will give rewards, not punishments.

For who would condemn me for following the precepts of the great,  
which, if I did not follow, I deserved prison?

Paul says that he pleases all men in all things,  
and teaches everyone to strive to please.

But now I am compelled to contend by the opposite road,  
[Col. 1011C] and am condemned unless I follow every deviation.

Yet it is not lawful for me, abandoning the ancient path,  
to follow sects of errors and every novelty.

Therefore the commands of ancient Paul must be followed,  
and novelties must likewise be condemned along with the novel.

Once these concessions, which cannot rightly be denied, have been granted,  
it is clear that wishing to please good men is good.

Is there anything still that you can say against this,  
sluggish envy? Speak, if you have anything.

“I have nothing,” I confess, “once you have untied those two knots  
which strove to trouble my mind.

Many complain that your poem has sung false things,  
while it wishes too greatly to celebrate your praises:

thus music becomes discordant when its measures are not observed,  
while it strives truly to touch the lofty heavens with its voice.”

[Col. 1011D] Therefore, I pray, show me the usefulness of poetry,  
without which no poem has any value.

For what does a tree beautiful with leaves and flowers avail,  
unless its fruitful trunk bears me apples?

I have heard the winds which move a strong tower,  
and I see how much force they shake.

O, O, how firmly the oak clings by its roots!  
And how firmly that house remains built,

which Boreas does not uproot and Eurus does not destroy!  
Yet a single flying fly can overturn it.

You say that you doubt whether my poems were true:  
listen, and after this doubt no further.

Yet much uncertainty turns over in my mind  
how I may now make clear to you what you ask.

For you are pressed by so much darkness, by such a mist,  
[Col. 1012A] that bright stars are hidden from your sight.

That you may see these fully once the cloud has been removed,  
let the veil which covers them be taken away.

Worldly custom holds that the end of all disputes  
is that which the chance of judgment has given;

therefore let us both hasten together to a just tribunal,  
for no one is ashamed to submit his neck to law.

There no one’s case can fail,  
but the judicial decision will give each man his due.

And if I am compelled to prove my words by judgment,  
as is customary by unquestionable witnesses,

you will presently see me produce thousands of witnesses  
who, in rivalry, prove these things to have been true.

But if the judges prefer us to contend more effectively  
[Col. 1012B] in a fierce duel, reason gives sufficient answer:

you will immediately see savage Mars boiling over on the plain,  
with the very ground now trembling beneath his feet.

From this side dreadful warriors will rise to battle,  
or the field here will produce hard champions.

Both battle-lines will soon mingle their weapons,  
so that one may drink the death of the other’s darts.

Thus may our soldier send his companion down to Avernus,  
or your champion yield his surrendered club.

This is commonly the final settlement of cases;  
thus may your quarrels obtain their end.

Suppose that some things in the poem were false:  
the man writing these poems will nevertheless not be false.

For he could have been mistaken, thinking true what he wrote,  
as the human mind, ignorant of truth, is mistaken.

## Rhythm on the Praise of the Saviour

[Col. 1012C]

Sent from the Father, born upon earth: God from a Virgin.  
He suffers as man, teaches, and willingly dies for man.

Through the forbidden tree our mortality received destruction;  
by the gibbet of the tree lost dignity is restored to the world.

The fruit is eaten by which life is lost, from the tree of death;  
the blood is poured out, received by faith, from Christ’s body.

The dragon is slain; the world is redeemed at the price of blood.  
This draught brought death upon him, but gave life to us.

[Col. 1012D] Cast out from his own homeland, he dwelt in the world—  
he who, swelling with impious pride against God, refused to be subject.

God, merciful from the ages, had compassion on his perils,  
and for his sake willed that the Son undergo the punishment of death.

But He, sent from His own throne, soon clothed Himself with flesh;  
and while that flesh is struck and crucified, it diminishes God in nothing.

Nor did He delay long, but immediately bestowed life from death:  
a marvellous work, to which nothing is like in divine bounty!

Adam is cast out; the thief is brought back: wondrous exchange!  
Then first became clear what the Creator’s Passion had benefited the world.

Mortality assumed is taken down from the cross and laid in the tomb.  
[Col. 1013A] Strong and splendid divinity subdues the burning realm of hell.

Shining, He irradiates eternal darkness and blind hiding places.  
The chorus of holy men, recognizing the Lord, dances for joy.

Hell bellows again; Cerberus, author of wickedness, trembles,  
stupidly seeing the sun of justice shine in black abodes.

He powerfully shatters cruel barriers, bolts, and bars;  
with immense glory and highest victory He tramples down the proud one.

Then the dragon felt the iron sting which flesh had concealed.  
Then for the first time he grieved, for the first time groaned, because he had devoured.

At last he learned that nothing is stronger, nothing wiser, than God,  
when he perceived forces overcome by forces, and arts by arts.

[Col. 1013B] Here madness swiftly falls while it proceeds headlong.  
Thus divinity permitted the blind man to run, and the runner to fall.

Him, fallen, it thrust back into the fiery cage into which he had plunged himself;  
without delay it freed countless wretches whom he had captured.

With a mighty right hand He broke open the entrails of the ancient prison.  
Those which had seized the mass of the human race had greatly feared.

The king’s victory searches every hiding place of death;  
strong power dissolves the strong bonds of the accused.

These spoils Christ, victor after battle, bore away from hell;  
[Col. 1013C] these He brought above to the joyful citizens of heaven.

When three days had been completed, restoring life in His dead body,  
He rises at once, no longer to suffer at any time again.

A sea-monster had swallowed Jonah but had not consumed him;  
having carried him through, it cast him out and remained empty.

Thus Christ, emerging from the waves, proclaims salvation to the nations.  
Then the world feared; fearing, it repented and renounced its sins.

He then appeared to those who were afraid and despairing,  
and offered Himself to them visible and able to be touched.

But as they wondered and, for joy, did not believe,  
[Col. 1013D] He shows at a meal that He truly lives and bears flesh.

They immediately recognize that He is the Lord who rose;  
nor are they slow to believe Him whom they see alive, as He foretold.

After the Creator of man had poured enough light upon the earth,  
He prepares to ascend and carry with Him what He had taken from it.

But, arranging to do this before faithful witnesses,  
He takes His household and leads them to Bethany to disclose these things to them,

so that through the disciples the power of so great a miracle  
might truly become clear among peoples and subject the world’s pride to Him.

Ascending, therefore, He is lifted up on high before their eyes;  
a cloud receives Him, and He is seen no longer by those standing by.

[Col. 1014A] He is borne to the heavens, transcends the stars,  
and advances our humanity above the angelic and all heavenly order.

Then a heavier mass was made lighter, when earthly flesh,  
formerly lower, is now made higher by fiery power.

Rejoice, mortality: eternity returns, by which you shall be restored.  
Whatever you are accustomed to fear in death, fear it no more.

Life restored through the God-man gives assurance—  
the life which He bore in Himself and bestowed on you when death was put off.

O new dignity! Divinity gives a place to human dust.  
No work will set itself before or compare itself with so great a work.

Clay fit to be trodden underfoot, now fit to be adored above the heavens,  
rules all things while the highest powers tremble.

[Col. 1014B] What Adam perversely wished by evil counsel in the beginning,  
he has now obtained through justice, not through pride.

While he feared God, he could not become what he had desired;  
made humble, he becomes like God and rules the heavens.

He whom a place horrible with shadows, horrible with flames, possessed,  
has deserved through God’s Son to hold the Father’s throne.

I urge you, man, not to mourn but to rejoice for him whom He has brought into heaven,  
whom He has more wonderfully and more sublimely raised into God.

Let the groans of old cease entirely: there is now no place at all  
for misery, for the time of grace has come from heaven.

[Col. 1014C] And you, O heavenly beings, mourn no longer the losses to your number;  
rather, when the impious have been expelled, learn to rejoice in new companions.

God then showed you a great miracle, a great inspiration,  
when hidden beneath the covering of flesh He appeared for man.

Worthily marvel at this new order—man set above the highest spirits—  
and do not disdain it in your kindly minds.

Yet you sing to him and bend the knee to him in the heavens,  
who bears earthly flesh, as a royal robe, from earthly things.

[Col. 1014D] Hence, to those asking why He came from Bozrah in dyed garments,  
the ever-truthful prophetic word recounts what He said:

while the grape is pressed, wine is poured out;  
while flesh suffers under the weight of the press, blood is poured out beneath the cross.

The garment of the treader is dyed when it is stained with the redness of wine.  
The body in which God is covered is stained with blood poured out.

This redness of the garments signifies the suffering which He endured willingly,  
yet from which, conquering, He brought back glory and victory.

Why say more? Christ now sits at the Father’s right hand,  
[Col. 1015A] whence, as God, He rules heavenly and earthly beings.

What of the disciples? They stand with eyes searching the heights,  
and marvel with minds held suspended at the unfamiliar sight.

Him lifted from their sight and received by clouds,  
they follow with spiritual affections, their bodies themselves almost following.

Then splendid men, clad in white and sent from heaven,  
began to speak to those who were contemplating and wondering:

“O why do you gaze upward? This man whom you see transcending heaven  
will descend again to discern the causes of everyone’s deeds,

[Col. 1015B] just as His ascent will become a return, when the judgment  
of mortals occurs and all the powers of heaven are shaken.

When He comes, a cloud will receive Him as it received Him  
when He ascended before you who saw and were astonished.

That judgment will then be fulfilled through God’s Son,  
when the Judge is seen by believers and unbelievers.

Here He first appeared to you humble and contemptible,  
when He lay hidden under the covering of flesh assumed from the Virgin.

But then all things that tremble will show, at the Judge’s and Avenger’s nod,  
what omnipotence He had and what lay concealed.

Then utmost terror and greatest horror will shake the world.  
Then whatever is firmer and more stable will flee away.

Heaven will be folded; the sea will dry up; earth will fail.  
[Col. 1015C] It will produce no more seed or grass.

Like shifting water, long-lasting solidity will waver, unstable.  
As wax melts, the solidity of earth will dissolve in fire.

Then springs will wholly deny their water, rivers their courses;  
then passage will be forbidden to ships and flight to birds.

Then the beauty of groves, the fruit of trees, and every green thing,  
their lovely blossoms burned up, will wither, dry.

Water will not serve fish, nor air birds.  
Nor will the earth deign to be trodden by mortal feet.

The heavens will blaze; the stars will grow black when their light is driven away.  
Then perpetual night, night devoid of light, with dreadful darkness,

[Col. 1015D] with winds and mighty tempest, will cover the ordered world.  
Then that gaping sulphurous pit will open its mouth,

and pouring seas of flame from its flaming womb,  
will burn the lowest regions with the highest, the highest with the infernal.

That fire, like the flood, will fill all things.  
The world will be condemned; Noah will be saved with his whole family.

Then the heavenly trumpet, the voice of the archangel sounding from above,  
will thunder terribly with dreadful cries and crashes,

and will cry to the peoples who are in the tombs: “Rise, all of you!  
Joined again with your spirits, resume life in your bodies.

Stand together, just and impious, before Christ’s throne,  
[Col. 1016A] and now receive whatever each of you did while living.”

When the voice of the Most High on the last day has sounded,  
the earth will no longer be able to keep anything down beneath any mound.

What was formerly hidden will at last be revealed,  
when the earth’s entrails, which long covered and concealed them, give back the corpses.

What dog gnawed, wild beast crushed, worm consumed,  
fire took, water washed away, air scattered,

returns through the Lord to its former condition; for as He knew  
how to create by grace, so by power He knows how to restore.

Do you ask, when it perishes, whence the substance of flesh will afterward return?  
The whole answer is the heavenly command, that is, power.

[Col. 1016B] Consider what existed before He made heaven and earthly things,  
whence the bodily mass stood or proceeded,

when, though nothing existed from which He might make anything, He created all things,  
with no material giving counsel or assistance.

As at the beginning He could do this as soon as He willed,  
so, as soon as He wills, He will immediately be able to do this at judgment.

Then flesh will be put upon bones and skin upon flesh.  
Then the body will be clothed with quantities and qualities.

And He commands the bodies which He had made long ago  
to rise more swiftly than speech, than which nothing is swifter.

The resurrection of the human body occurs in a moment of time.  
[Col. 1016C] The display of the new miracle happens in the twinkling of an eye.

Then souls, leaving the heavenly seats nearest to God,  
where they shine more sublimely and brightly than the stars,

will be joined to this incorruptible vessel of flesh, no longer frail.  
Then Satan, crushed, sends forth from dark caverns

those whom he had formerly captured and bound in fiery chains,  
not remitting the punishment of the wretched, but sending them forth so that they may expiate their wicked deeds

with bodies and spirits alike, doubly.

Thus, when heavenly and infernal dwellings are emptied,  
the earth alone will marvel when it is filled with human beings;

for of the countless whom it had gradually poured from mothers’ wombs,  
[Col. 1016D] it regenerates all at once by an unfamiliar and sudden birth.

O how terrible and fearsome that day will break in!  
Alas, alas, how ghastly! Alas, alas, how troubled a face it will assume!

It will strike kings with grief, nations with dreadful lament,  
when each person fails through sorrows and anguishes of mind.

With heavens burning and earth trembling, the Judge will come,  
whom the world will behold as wondrous and terrible.

Then, with the cross going before Him, He will bring from heaven  
the signs of death and set them before earthly beings, willing and unwilling.

The people will see, and every eye will behold Him;  
both he who believed and he who mocked will contemplate Him.

[Col. 1017A] Jew, look: behold Jesus, whom you once despised.  
Behold the man known to you, once subjected, whom you saw;

behold, He governs all things; behold, He commands the heavens—He whom you blasphemed.  
He whom you crucified now sits as judge of all alike.

Consider Jesus, king of heavenly and earthly beings,  
whose rule and judgment make the heavens tremble.

Do you still believe Him God, when you are now to be handed over by Him to hell,  
when you are already shut in the fiery cage with the wretched?

[Col. 1017B] Christ my God, guilty as I am, I cry to You, whom I hope for as Judge:  
that then I may feel mercy, not wrath, from the avenger of evils.

When You sit upon the throne prepared for so great a judgment,  
and place the sheep at Your right, the goats on the other side,

then do not deny a place to the last sheep, O best Shepherd;  
nor, I pray, separate me from those blessed flocks.

Remember the sheep of Cluny amid so great a tempest,  
and lead them, gracious Lord, to everlasting pastures.

Your final voice plunges Satan with the lost,  
given as food to sulphurous fire, into the depths of the flaming pit.

[Col. 1017C] After this, returning to the Father’s throne, You will put on splendour  
and restore to heaven Christ’s followers, inhabitants of the earth.

Then what You promised and long concealed will be revealed,  
when God, highest above man, is seen without end. Amen.

## Rhythm on the Resurrection of the Lord

Strong, He brought force against the gates of death;  
He struck down its leader by the cross.

Bright light shone in the dwelling places of darkness,  
when He willed to save and restore what He had created.

Hence the Creator dies lest the sinner die;  
by His death, life arises for us in a new lot.

[Col. 1017D] Satan, defeated, groans from that by which the Victor redeemed us.  
That which is lethal to him becomes life-giving to man.

While he seeks to seize, he is seized; while he kills, he dies—  
he who, having captured men in hell’s prison, was accustomed to spare no one.

Thus fittingly, thus mightily, the King conquering hell,  
leaving the depths, returned on the first day to the heights.

He rose again, and God carried man back with Him,  
restoring the origin which He had given by creating.

Through the Creator’s Passion the first colonist now returns  
to the lost land; therefore this joyful sound is made here.

## Prose in Honour of the Mother of the Lord

With a voice of joy, alleluia: Truth sprang from the earth  
when Christ was born from flesh.

Let there be new glory in heaven, new joys upon earth.

[Col. 1018A] The Creator of things, pitying His creature destined to perish, came;  
and to those captured by the enemy He offered the right hand of freedom.

Heaven pours dew upon earth; earth brings forth the Saviour.  
The choir of angels sings, since their king is an infant.

That virginal womb, God’s special chamber, is made fruitful by the Spirit;  
and as a rod bears a flower, so the Virgin bears the Redeemer, veiled in fleshly garb.

The boy God is nourished with the sacred milk of His untouched mother:  
a thing wondrous throughout the ages.

He lives on another’s food, through whom all things remain full:  
no miracles are equal to this.

[Col. 1018B] He who grants life to flesh is fed by the nourishment of flesh.  
He whom the Father’s throne possesses has His mother’s lap.

The Virgin comforts the Son she has borne, and venerates Him as God:  
Emmanuel with us, salvation of Israel.

Mind, voice, and eyes of the Christian people  
receive You, O Mother; through You they thirst

to have the One born of You propitious,  
and a safe refuge.

Therefore, Lady of the world, mercifully bend your eyes, dissolving sins.  
Let wickedness be driven away; let justice return by the grace of Jesus Christ.

## Another Prose

Heaven, rejoice; earth, applaud; let no one be mute in praise.

[Col. 1018C] Through the Virgin man returns to his ancient origin.  
The Virgin has borne God; hence the old strife perishes.

The ancient discord perishes; peace and glory succeed.  
Then the guilty man rises from dung when God lies in hay.

Then a lowly stable conceals the sustenance of heavenly food.  
The Virgin nourishes the Creator, the Redeemer made from herself.

Divine wisdom lies hidden in childhood.  
The mother’s breasts drip milk; the child’s bowels pour out milk,

while through assumed humanity He gives the sweetness of grace.  
Therefore let us sound forth, O Mary, with sweet melody,

with devout voices and loud affections.  
Hail, blessed Virgin, who drove away curses.

Hail, Mother of the Most High, bride of the gentlest Lamb.

[Col. 1018D] You conquered the serpent, whose head you crushed,  
when God born from you became his destruction.

You are empress of heaven, restorer of the earth;  
men sigh toward you, wicked demons tremble before you.

You are window, gate, fleece, hall, house, temple, earth;  
lily of virginity and rose through martyrdom;

enclosed garden, fountain of gardens, washing away the filth of sinners,  
purifying the defiled and giving life to the dead;

mistress of angels, hope of the ages after God,  
the King’s resting-place and throne of Deity.

Shining star of the East, driving away the shadows of the West,

[Col. 1019A] dawn preceding the sun, and day knowing no night;  
parent of our Parent, and mother of Him who begets us.

In confidence in a merciful Mother, reconcile your children to the Father.  
Pray, Mother, to God your Son, that He may loose our guilt,

and, after forgiveness granted, give grace and glory.  
Amen.

## Hymn in Honour of Saint Mary Magdalene

The great and celebrated day shines by the merits of Mary Magdalene.  
On this day let the angelic and human choir praise the Lord of Mary.

Freed from the prison of the body, in splendid starlike light  
she leaves the darkness of exile and enters heavenly dwellings.

Christ joins her to Himself and places her in the citadel of the Father,  
[Col. 1019B] granting hope of pardon to the wretched when, in mercy, He gives Mary pardon.

For weeping greatly, she had washed the Lord’s feet with tears;  
washing away all her sins with them and expiating vain joys by weeping,

she deserved to wipe them with her hair, and was no less worthy to anoint them.  
She gives kisses to the Lord’s feet, and the Lord gives pardon to her.

Therefore, Mary, pray to God, bearing our prayers to Him,
By which, relieving those weighed down by the burden of their sins, he may raise them to heaven;

[Col. 1019C] May he also grant the people’s prayers, himself mindful of your service;

Granting joys with those above, and bestowing the good that remains without end.

Glory to you, gracious Christ, and to the Spirit and to God the Father,

Who, raising Mary above the stars, make her a companion of the heavenly host.

Hymn for holy Father Benedict.

Among the eternal crowns of those above,

Which they retain, won by sacred struggle,

You shine, resplendent with lofty merits,

O Benedict.

Holy old age adorned you even as a boy;

No pleasure carried anything of you away for itself:

[Col. 1019D] The flower of the world withered for you, your mind

Raised on high.

Thus, having fled in flight, you forsake homeland and parents,

A fervent inhabitant of the wilderness;

You chastise the flesh and subject it to Christ,

A harsh tormentor [of yourself].

Lest you should long remain safely hidden in seclusion,

The signs of your pious deeds reveal you.

Your blessed fame is scattered swiftly

In its flight through the world.

By most mighty prayer you restore what was broken;

With the cross you shatter the draught of death set before you;

An unknowing monk runs over the waves,

At his father’s command.

You strike a brother; the savage enemy flees.

[Col. 1020A] At your command iron returns from the depths to the hand;

The rock pours forth streams

Watering the fields.

A wild bird fulfils the command laid upon it;

In pity you release the bonds of one seen bound;

You behold the world in a single ray,

Caught up to the stars.

By prayer you call a dead man back to life;

As a prophet, you penetrate the hearts of many;

You see souls borne up to heaven,

Glorified.

May the creating Godhead, exulting, praise you;

May the unending jubilation of our choirs praise you:

We all beseech you, join us

To the heavenly choirs of the sky. Amen.

Another hymn for the translation and likewise the deposition of the same Father.

[Col. 1020B]

Join in jubilation, Gaul, with bright songs;

Rejoice in the bones of Father Benedict:

Happy you are, who in your own bosom,

Keep his illustrious limbs laid away.

He had shone in Italy through wondrous deeds;

Dead in body, he sheds his light upon Gaul:

More frequently he shines with signs at his tomb,

Illuminating his new homeland.

Thus he revives the deeds of ancient seers.

Though dead, he commands death as it pleased him.

By his own bones he raises up one who had died.

O what wondrous power!

[Col. 1020C] A ship swims down the river without a helmsman;

With wondrous force it cuts through the ice,

Bearing the saint’s limbs against the current,

And drives the waters back.

When the dry land perceived him brought forth from the river,

Disregarding the coldness of the wintry season,

It at once clothes all things with new flowers,

The soil’s appearance transformed.

Now dwelling in heaven, O most excellent Father,

Instruct your servants in divine rules;

Grant them to ascend by the narrow way,

And bestow the everlasting kingdoms.

All-ruling omnipotence,

You who behold all things from the throne of heaven:

Graciously receive the songs

[Col. 1020D] Of those who sing, pleading in vows and voice. Amen.

Rhythmical poem on Saint Hugh, Abbot of Cluny.

Hugh, pious Father, illustrious in lineage,

Is shown yet more illustrious by the grace of his virtues.

While he still lies hidden, enclosed in his mother’s womb,

A sacred victim is offered for the boy:

In the chalice is seen the image of the little one himself,

A sign of the great miracle.

If anyone asks what I think of this,

The victim foreshadows the victim yet to come.

Then the boy is born, and, once born, is nourished;

In the course of age he acquires strength.

With strength of body sufficient for youth,

He applies himself to virtue with burning zeal.

[Col. 1021A] He despises the world and its joys,

Knowing that all of them swiftly pass away.

He renounces the world and joins himself to God.

Thus fleeing earth, he draws near to heaven.

Thereafter inspired by the divine Spirit,

His heart transformed, his habit too is changed:

Within the Lord’s sheepfolds he remains,

A distinguished sheep among Christ’s sheep.

Diligently he obeys the pastor’s commands;

He neglects none of those things which the Rule commands.

With vigorous effort he tramples pride,

Conquering malice by wisdom.

He endures the holy hunger for righteousness;

He follows Christ’s blessed poverty.

As time proceeds, growing in virtues,

[Col. 1021B] He appeared wondrous even to the elders themselves.

Now dead to the world, he shows by holy deeds

To mortals that he lives for Christ.

Then the shepherd dies, and the sheep is set over them.

Vigorously he performs the shepherd’s duties.

He instructs those subject to him by words and deeds,

Offering himself as an example of good to all.

Severe toward crimes, mercifully

Tempering both, he becomes an equitable judge.

Like a prudent physician, he anoints what is sick;

What health rejects, he cuts away as rotten.

High office did not exalt him,

Who remained in mind lower than all.

Teacher of the gentle, father of the humble,

[Col. 1021C] He places this humble man in the place of the exalted.

From the Spirit’s gift holiness increases;

The perfection of the Law is present; charity is not lacking.

The poor are nourished by a most ready mind;

God gives what is to be given through a most generous hand.

Christ’s nakedness—or that of the poor—is clothed;

The store of good works increases.

This man enriches the venerable monastery

Of the Cluniacs more than its ancient Fathers did.

Through his zeal religious observance grew,

And the number of brothers in the community grew.

The Lord enriches this house with possessions:

Thus he shows how greatly he loves Hugh;

Blessed servitude yields so many revenues:

While he serves, the man subject to God rules.

[Col. 1021D] Not content only with active endeavor,

He applies himself to the leisure of the contemplative life:

Anxious with Martha, he fulfils the duty;

With Mary, he hears Christ’s discourse.

With Leah he multiplies children for God,

Whom in devotion he applies to God’s worship.

With Rachel, barren yet beautiful in face,

He searches with subtle heavenly vision.

Reading is joined to continual silence,

Nor is fervent prayer lacking tears.

Frequent sacrifices consecrate him;

While he offers sacrifice, he himself becomes the victim.

What more shall I add concerning his works,

Since these shine more brightly than all the stars?

[Col. 1022A] For his works are like stars,

Which remain innumerable because of their number.

Verses for the epitaph of Count Eustace.

This present soil is ennobled by the remains

Of Prince Eustace, by whom Gaul once flourished.

The Persian kingdoms trembled before this man’s arms,

And Babylon feared him, Babylon that was the terror of the world.

Ethiopia’s blackness reddened with its own blood,

Which the duke’s holy right hand shed for Christ.

The East still pales, stunned by the slaughter of its people,

While it fears once again to be crushed by an enemy from the West.

Royal Jerusalem, venerable through Christ’s trophies,

Under this leader raises its captive head to heaven.

Cluny, this man entrusted to you the hope of his salvation,

[Col. 1022B] That through you he might make God favorable to himself.

Coming as a pilgrim from far-off shores in this hope,

Here he lies and, behold, pleads with you for himself.

The golden cross, the twin cella, and the sea-fish

Proclaim that you can rightly refuse him nothing.

As you have provided your enclosure for his limbs,

So by your prayer provide the heavenly kingdoms for his spirit.

You who also cover these bones with a blessed tomb,

After this lodging restore them to their homeland.

Verses for the epitaph of Prior Bernard.

An eminent elder, to whom nothing youthful clung,

Prior Bernard rests buried in the earth.

Entering the heavenly camp after his warfare here,

He grew old, contending long in this struggle.

[Col. 1022C] For you, Cluny, this man never spared himself;

Therefore no day was without labor for him.

Thus, nobly bearing the burden of the whole day,

He rejoicingly carries home, late, the earned coin.

Brothers, remember this man when buried,

And let not the ground that covers his bones fall from your mind.

Verses for the epitaph of Rainald, Archbishop of Lyons.

Here lies Rainald, glory of bishops,

A great man laid in a small lodging.

First Abbot of Vézelay, afterwards patriarch,

He shone at Lyons, made honor’s very honor.

Estates, treasures, lofty dignities proclaim

With what zeal he governed his first office.

The summit of Lyons would have joined its horns to heaven,

[Col. 1022D] Had swift death not stolen him away.

He who was your monk, and was born near your breast,

Now rests in your bosom, O Cluny:

Commit him, entrusted to you, to the number of the devout,

And by your prayers make him penetrate heaven.

Verses for the epitaph of Peter Abelard.

The Socrates of the Gauls, the greatest Plato of the West,

Our Aristotle—equal or superior to all who were masters of logic;

Known to the world as prince of studies, manifold in genius,

Subtle and keen, surpassing all things by the power of reason

And by the art of speech—such was Abelard. But then he conquered all things still more,

When, professing the monastic habit and observance of Cluny,

[Col. 1023A] He passed over to Christ’s true philosophy,

In which, worthily completing the end of a long life,

[Col. 1024A] He gave hope that he would one day be numbered among good philosophers,

When May renewed its eleventh day before the Kalends.

[Col. 1025]

THE STATUTES OF PETER THE VENERABLE, NINTH ABBOT OF CLUNY, FOR THE CLUNIAC CONGREGATION.

(Lucas Holstenius, *Codex Regularum*, edited by Rev. Fr. Marianus Brockie, Augsburg, 1759, folio.)

CRITICAL OBSERVATION.

Among the branches of the sacred Benedictine order, the Cluniac congregation holds first place. It began indeed to become renowned throughout the whole world after Saint Berno, about the year 910, had laid the foundations of the monastery of Cluny, while William, duke of Aquitaine and of Gothia or Septimania, generously supplied lands and revenues for the support of the monks. This monastery was situated in the district of Mâcon and ordered according to the Rule of Saint Benedict. Saint Berno there observed that Rule most strictly and gave a beginning to the reformation of the monastic state, which in that iron age had collapsed and which he most devoutly restored.

But the complete reformation of monastic discipline seems to have been reserved for Saint Odo, formerly Saint Berno’s disciple and afterwards his successor in the abbacy. Like another Ezra, he became the principal support and ornament of the restored monastic law: he led not only the monks entrusted to him to a stricter observance of Benedict’s Rule, but also drew many religious men from neighboring monasteries to embrace the discipline newly restored. So great, indeed, was Saint Odo’s reputation for holiness, and so great the integrity of life of the Cluniac monks, that already in the year 937 more than seventeen monasteries were serving under the discipline of the Cluniac congregation. Mabillon counts that many by this year in his *Annales Benedictini*, vol. II, book XLIII, p. 436, asserting that kings, bishops, and magnates competed with one another to establish new monasteries or reform old ones according to the custom of the Cluniac monks.

In this way the sacred Cluniac order increased so greatly that by the twelfth century nearly two thousand monasteries in Europe served under its discipline, besides many others established among Eastern peoples, as Calmet relates in his catalogue of religious orders at the end of his commentary on the Rule of Saint Benedict. Meanwhile neither Saint Berno nor Saint Odo prescribed a particular monastic rule for their monks; rather, they set before all the Rule of Saint Benedict as the primary norm of life to be observed. Thus the Cluniacs were true Benedictine monks.

Nor did the statutes issued by the Cluniacs depart from Benedictine discipline. They were wholly directed toward ensuring that this sacred Rule should be observed most strictly by all. Hence Blessed William, abbot of Hirsau, when undertaking the reform of Benedictine monasteries throughout Germany about the year 1112, requested from the Cluniacs themselves a copy of these Statutes, which he received through the notable assistance of Saint Ulrich, a noble Bavarian but a Benedictine monk at Cluny. This is how he is described by Acheri in his *Spicilegium*, vol. I of the new edition, who calls these Statutes the older customs of the monastery of Cluny. We forgo reproducing them here because of their length. Those customs, with regard to more minor prescriptions, were subject to changes according to varying circumstances of place and time, as Peter the Venerable, abbot, wished to note in the preface to his renewed Cluniac statutes. We therefore present these statutes here, taken from the *Bibliotheca Magna SS. Patrum*, Lyons edition, vol. XXI.

Peter Maurice was born of noble stock among the Arverni. In his early years he followed military service, but at last renounced the world, assumed the monastic habit at Cluny, and, surpassing the others in piety and learning, was elected in 1123 as the ninth abbot of that most celebrated congregation. He governed it with such holiness of life and dignity of conduct that while still among mortals he deserved to be called the Venerable Abbot; after his translation to the heavenly company he was entered in the calendars of the saints and is therefore called Saint Maurice. In framing these statutes, the Venerable Abbot employed the counsel of the entire chapter of Cluny and wished to preface an apologetic introduction concerning certain older customs changed in his own time; indeed, he appended to every statute the cause and rationale for its enactment. All these things show the prudence, piety, and humility of this most holy abbot, and the statutes which follow deserve the reading of devout persons.

APOLOGETIC, THAT IS, EXCULPATORY PREFACE OF LORD PETER, ABBOT OF CLUNY, CONCERNING CERTAIN CUSTOMS CHANGED IN HIS TIME.

[Col. 1025]

[Col. 1025A] Since it is always useful to commit deeds, and especially religious deeds, to memory, it seemed good to me to transmit in writing for the knowledge of those now living and of posterity those things which, during the twenty-four years—that is, since I unworthily undertook the pastoral office—have been changed, added, or removed in the institutions of Cluny. I resolved to do this in such a way that I should state not only those matters which, as has been said, have been changed, added, or removed, but should also append the reason why they were altered. Of these two things, one will serve knowledge of the facts; the other may perhaps suffice to prevent scandal among those who, ignorant of the reason for the changes, either have been disturbed or might be disturbed. For no wise person should regard as new, unusual, or strange a necessary and frequent alteration of ecclesiastical usages, [Col. 1025B] because one thing is what the Lord commands to be kept immovably by eternal law, and another what human beings prescribe for a time, not forever, for some purpose of utility. The first must not be changed because, if it is not observed, eternal salvation cannot be preserved in any way. The second, however, is sometimes changed because what was useful at one time is proved harmful at another.

To put it more clearly: things belonging to true virtue must never be changed; but the aids to virtues must beneficially be administered according to the appropriateness of circumstances, persons, and times. For the commandment of faith, hope, or charity, and the commands contained under charity itself—chastity, humility, truth, and sincerity—cannot be changed by any administrator or by any dispensation. [Col. 1025C] Fasts, however, vigils, manual work, bodily exercise—which, according to the Apostle, is useful indeed, but only a little (1 Tim. 4)—and similar things, too numerous to list, ought, for a certain necessity or for charity’s sake, to be reduced at one time, increased at another, and sometimes entirely withdrawn by the authority of superiors. The apostles themselves followed this rule; so did their successors, the apostolic pontiffs; so did the holy Fathers of monks and hermits; and so did the great and distinguished founders who preceded us in the Cluniac order. If necessity required that I name them individually, I would show that from the first Saint Odo to the last Father Hugh, marked with the title of holiness, all changed many established customs in their own times, when necessity pressed, but always for a useful reason. For predecessors usefully established many things which their successors usefully changed when a fitting cause intervened.

Following them, therefore, I have altered certain former usages when a certain useful cause advised it. And for that reason I did not, as some formerly whispered in corners, withdrawing into secluded places in order to gnaw at their brothers’ flesh, set myself above them by doing these things. Rather, by this alteration of the holy Fathers I have not departed from their path. [Col. 1026A] Yet I did this not by my judgment alone, but, according to the Rule’s command, by the counsel of certain God-fearing and wise brothers. Finally, I did it with the assent of the general chapter. And since what had to be said beforehand has been said briefly, let my pen now approach the matters for whose sake these words have preceded. But because the Rule commands that nothing be preferred to the work of God, neither will I prefer anything to it in writing; rather, I shall take my beginning from the divine work itself, that is, the ecclesiastical office.

[Col. 1026B] I. It has been enacted that all verses of the canonical Hours, except hymns, shall be chanted under one moderate pause, so that all voices together may finish the verse which is to end, and, after the moderate pause I have mentioned, together begin another. I call it moderate to distinguish it from the pause some customarily make, in the interval of which I myself formerly completed the Lord’s Prayer, often twice and sometimes three times. Therefore it must be long enough that it may always be fully taken by all, and that the pause itself may relieve the labor of the singers. The convent of Cluny alone is excepted from this ordinance, where this cannot be observed, because neither the daytime nor the nighttime Hours seem sufficient for it.

[Col. 1026C] The reason for this enactment was that the confused lack of unity among the singers—some beginning and ending earlier, others later—might be brought into unity; that the understanding itself might be restored, as it were, by all pausing in a common silence; and that the time formerly expended in superfluous and less useful matters of the daytime or nighttime Hours might be expended upon the divine work, so useful and heavenly.

II. It has been enacted that the Sunday office shall not be interrupted on account of any feast of twelve lessons, except those feasts which are customarily celebrated in copes or in albs and which possess the proper form of the nocturnal chant, namely complete responsories; and except the octaves of the apostles Peter and Paul and of the Assumption of Saint Mary. Apart from these exceptions, [Col. 1026D] if a feast of twelve lessons falls on Sunday, Sunday shall retain the first eight lessons with their responsories. The commemoration of that saint shall claim for itself only the remaining four, together with Matins, Lauds, and the Mass of the morning.

[Col. 1027A] The reason for this enactment was that frequent new solemnities, added to ancient feasts for various reasons, almost continually interrupted the immeasurable glory of the Sunday Resurrection and our blessed hope, through it, of the future resurrection—two things which every Sunday commends—and at times removed the lessons and chants proper to Sunday for four or five years together. Therefore, in order that reverence for the most holy Sunday might be restored as far as reasonably possible, and that the ears of our Church might not be deprived of the Gospel, apostolic, and Old Testament readings assigned to Sunday, this was commanded.

III. It has been enacted that no solemnity whatsoever falling [Col. 1027B] on Sunday may prevent the commemoration of Sunday at Matins and at Vespers.

The reason for this enactment is that stated above: reverence for Sunday.

IV. It has been enacted that on Sunday no one shall bend the knees in prayer, except in those genuflections made by the priest before and after Mass; and except that which, by long-established use, is observed by almost the whole Church, when in the profession of faith at Mass there is sung, “And he was made man”; and that which communicants customarily observe before receiving the Lord’s Body. There is also the genuflection customarily made by those who meet the bearer of the Eucharist in any place, and those *metanoeiae* which occur in chapter by daily custom and are commonly called “pardons.”

[Col. 1027C] The reason for this enactment was the reverence for Sunday already mentioned and the observance decreed by the universal Church in the canons.

V. It has been enacted that in all monasteries and churches belonging to Cluny, the Transfiguration of the Lord shall be celebrated, except for the procession, in the same manner as the Purification of Saint Mary, with lessons, responsories, and offices proper to the day.

The reason for this enactment was the dignity of Christ’s Transfiguration itself—admirable and inferior to no other solemnity after his Nativity or Resurrection—and the ancient and modern practice of many churches throughout the world, which commemorate the Transfiguration with no less honor than the Epiphany and Ascension of the Lord.

[Col. 1027D] VI. It has been enacted that while the principal Mass is sung in convent, no one anywhere in the whole monastery shall sing Mass, because on account of those Masses the greater and principal Mass was neglected to such an extent that scarcely a fourth part [of the community] was present when it was celebrated.

The reason for this enactment was that already stated: lest, on account of private Masses, that Mass be neglected in which the solemn sacrifice was instituted by the Fathers to be offered to almighty God not only by the priest but also by the whole congregation present, except those who could in no way attend.

VII. It has been enacted that shortly before the Mass just mentioned begins, two bells shall be rung somewhat longer on ordinary days, in order to invite those who at that hour are dispersed outside the church in various places.

[Col. 1028A] The reason for this enactment was that, as I have said, the brothers dispersed in obediences and various tasks during the Hours preceding Mass did not know when Mass was being sung, and often thought it had not yet begun when it had already ended. Therefore, lest they themselves lose through this ignorance so profitable an hour for the soul, and lest laypeople remaining outside or pilgrims assembling from whatever place fail to know the time of that solemn Mass, it was decreed that by such a signal all alike, diligent and negligent, should be reminded to assemble.

VIII. It has been enacted that the anniversary day of all deceased Cluniac monks shall be observed by all the brothers of our congregation, on the vigil of Saint Michael the Archangel, in the manner of solemn anniversaries; and that on the vigil of the Conversion of Saint Paul another anniversary shall be observed in the same manner for all parents, of both sexes, of all the brothers of our congregation.

[Col. 1028B] The reason for this enactment was that, although whatever is done by the Church of God still placed on earth for the departed faithful benefits all departed faithful without exception who need this assistance, nevertheless it seemed just that something beyond the customary observances should be added for those more closely connected with us, so that it might aid them in particular and, as has been said, all who need this care in general.

IX. It has been enacted that on the first Sunday of the Lord’s Advent the beginning of the Gospel according to [Col. 1028C] Mark shall be read, which begins: “The beginning of the Gospel of Jesus Christ, Son of God, as it is written in Isaiah the prophet,” and the rest.

The reason for this enactment was that the Gospel formerly read—by whose institution and from what time being unknown—had little or nothing to do with the day of the Lord’s Advent, on which he first appeared to the world by his birth, and was more appropriate to the prelude of his Passion than to his Incarnation or Nativity, namely: “When he had drawn near to Jerusalem and had come to Bethphage, to the mountain” (Matt. 21).

X. It has been enacted that all Cluniac brothers shall abstain from fat every Friday, except the Nativity of the Lord if it falls on that day.

The reason for this enactment was the no small impropriety [Col. 1028D] that not only clerics and laypeople, but even children and sick persons throughout the whole Latin Church, abstained on that day, out of reverence for the Lord’s Passion, from every eating of meat—whether solid, minced, or liquefied—according to ancient custom, while the monks just mentioned alone poured fat into their vegetables and took various dishes fried in it. Moreover, this seemed so absurd to everyone other than monks that even the poor would not eat leftovers of such foods given to them, but either saved them for the following day or angrily threw them away at once. Therefore, in order that so disgraceful a reproach might be removed from our order, and that the public reverence of abstinence in honor of the Lord’s Passion might not be violated by those who seem more to take up the Lord’s cross [Col. 1029A] than to follow him, this was commanded.

XI. It has been enacted that all brothers of the Cluniac order shall abstain from every preparation of honey and spices with wine, commonly called *pigmentum*, except only on the Lord’s Supper, on which day antiquity permitted honey mixed with wine without spices.

The reason for this enactment was some, though small, increase of abstinence. Not only this, but also the true saying of the great Father Benedict, speaking, as is known, of the measure of monks’ drink: “Although,” he says, “we read that wine is by no means for monks,” and the rest. If, according to these words, wine is by no means for monks, yet because later monks were weaker than the first monks it was scarcely permitted. By what authority or reason, then, was a spice from overseas or the East, sought with great labor and bought at great price, afterwards mixed into the wine of poor and abstinent monks? And since the Apostle, as though from a great condescension to a weak disciple, commands, saying: “Use a little wine for your stomach’s sake and your frequent infirmities” (1 Tim. 5), what will monks say who are not sick but sound, not infirm but robust, using not a little but much wine; not merely much but honeyed wine; not merely honeyed but wine prepared with royal spices? And since the Apostle just mentioned commands both them and laypeople: “Do not become drunk with wine, in which is debauchery” (Eph. 5), what will become of monks who do not merely fail to avoid drunkenness, but, in order to provoke it the more, excite the palate with foreign flavors?

XII. It has been enacted that, except for the sick and utterly infirm, no one shall eat meat.

The reason for this enactment was the authority of the Rule itself, in which this same thing is commanded and a sound monk, possessing full strength, is forbidden to eat flesh. Moreover, no reasonable cause could be found for altering this chapter, as one was found by the Fathers in the case of certain other chapters of the same Rule altered long ago.

XIII. It has been enacted that if the vigils of feasts which have public fasts fall on Sunday, the fast shall be observed on the preceding Saturday.

[Col. 1029D] The reason for this enactment was first reverence and love for the saints, but secondarily the unsuitable and unseemly divergence of our custom from the practice of other churches; for both the Roman Church and the whole body of other churches, ours alone excepted, observed the fasts of vigils in the manner written above.

XIV. It has been enacted that our regular fasts from the Ides of September to the beginning of Lent shall be observed by eating once a day, except on the feast of Saint Michael, the Dedication of the Church, and the feasts of the Apostles falling outside Advent and Septuagesima; the feasts of the abbots of Cluny; the eight days of the Nativity of the Lord; only the first day of Epiphany; the feast day of Saint Marcellus Pope and Saint Vincent [Col. 1030A] Martyr; and the Purification of Saint Mary. On the Conversion of Saint Paul the fast shall not be relaxed, because at other times of the year the Church celebrates other feasts of the same apostle. On the Chair of Saint Peter the fast likewise shall be relaxed, also because that feast always falls within Septuagesima. Then, immediately after the principal Mass, Sext shall be sung, and after an interval None shall follow.

The reason for this enactment was the multiplicity of newly invented feasts, increased perhaps more by the desire for certain advantages—which I do not wish to mention—than by love for the saints, and likewise by the acclamation of something like an untaught populace. These occupied the greater part of the time just mentioned and, through the frequency of good meals, had now almost wholly excluded the fasts imposed by the Rule. Therefore, maintaining moderation in both respects, the matter was decided thus: the honor of saints established in feasts of twelve lessons should not be diminished, and the fast commanded by the Rule should be observed insofar as it could reasonably be done.

XV. It has been enacted that on every day of the Lord’s Advent, except the first Sunday, all shall abstain from the fat customarily used on feasts of twelve lessons; nor shall they eat twice either on those feasts, as ancient custom likewise allowed, or on the feast itself of Saint Thomas the Apostle.

The reason for this enactment was the greater abstinence customarily observed by almost the whole Church during those days in preparation for the Lord’s Nativity, so that our monks might at least dedicate those sacred days to moderate fasts, while many others dedicate them to more severe ones.

XVI. It has been enacted that none of our brothers shall be clothed in fabrics called *galabruni* or *isembruni*, nor in those called *scalfarii* or Frisian cloths, except English monks or monks neighboring England; nor in those called *agnelini*, except German monks and those adjoining them—on this condition, however, that they cannot find in their regions garments of black color more fitting for religious life.

The reason for this enactment was, beyond what I wish to say—as I myself saw—the notably unseemly and disgraceful extravagance of such garments. Formerly many of ours adorned themselves, no differently from secular people, with various sorts of silk [Col. 1030D] or grey garments; and, although black was chosen as the humblest of all colors to signify the inward humility of the heart, they strove with the utmost zeal, nature itself protesting, to adorn themselves as though bridegrooms coming forth from the bridal chamber. The matter had now become habitual, and, blinded by very long custom, they did not realize that they were sinning in these things.

XVII. It has been enacted that none of the Cluniac brothers shall wear cat skins or other foreign furs which they had customarily used; indeed, they shall wear no skins whatever, except sheep, lamb, and goat skins, and, solely for making coverlets, skins of *putosiores* and, in another language, *vesones* [bison], as may be more agreeable.

The reason for this enactment was the considerable, notable, and blameworthy extravagance of cat skins and other furs, as was said above concerning fabrics. [Col. 1031A] It had gone so far, as I myself knew, that Gallic cat skins were despised and the curiosity of religious men migrated to Iberian or Italian cats. A not inconsiderable multitude of devout persons and of those attached to them thought themselves to possess nothing unless their beds were at once fortified and adorned with a costly coverlet woven of the hairy, dense skins of the cats of Numantia—that is, in modern terms, Amorensian cats. This evil gradually growing had now reached the point that coverlets purchased for nearly one hundred solidi, together with the considerable price of garments as well, heavily burdened richer houses with accumulated debt and almost utterly ruined poorer ones.

XVIII. It has been enacted that no one shall possess scarlet cloths, *barracani*, or costly *burelli* made at Regensburg—that is, at Rainesbors—or straw mats decorated in any fashion, but only haircloth with merely two overlaid cloths of moderate price, white and black and of a color mixed from both; and these are to be simple, not double, quadruple, or multiple, as some customarily make them, and are to be laid beneath the brothers.

The reason for this enactment was that the extravagance condemned in other kinds of clothing might also be removed from monks’ beds, especially since before the time of Saint Hugh no one used anything but haircloth with only one plain cloth laid over it.

[Col. 1031C] XIX. It has been enacted that in the infirmary of Cluny, which is distinguished by five dwellings divided under one roof, silence shall be observed with this distinction: in that part where the brothers die, which is in the middle, and in the part above it on the south side, silence and conversation shall be observed according to ancient custom; but in the other three, the silence of the regular cloister shall be maintained. Likewise, in the novices’ cell and the adjoining cloister or workshops, except that the novices and their master may speak where and when they customarily speak; and except that visiting bishops and abbots, the major prior, and the subpriors, guardians of the order, may themselves speak in the areas of that novices’ cell, and others only in their presence. In all workshops, however, continual silence shall be kept, [Col. 1031D] except only by one master in each workshop-house, and except by the workmen of the new church and their workshops. Moreover, cloister silence shall be maintained in the cemetery and the cemetery cloister, in all sacristies, and on the way leading to the upper houses which are beside the greater church, and in adjoining places, except for the above-mentioned abbots and priors, who may speak in those places in the manner stated above.

The reason for this enactment was the most necessary usefulness of silence in every religious life, without which, unless observed in fitting ways, religious life can neither be called nor be such. Its praise in Holy Scripture is so great that, among its innumerable commendations, the great prophet [Col. 1032A] Isaiah says of it: “The service of righteousness is silence” (Isa. 32). Because at Cluny it had for some time been greatly corrupted on account of the frequency of business and the multitude of visitors, it seemed necessary that this manner of silence, distinguished as stated above, should be established.

XX. It has been enacted that during Lent, with three days added to silence—Tuesday, Thursday, and Saturday, on which, according to ancient custom, conversation had been permitted in the cloisters—continuous silence shall be maintained throughout the whole of Lent.

The reason for this enactment was reverence for such holy days: it did not seem wholly religious that, on days of the highest abstinence and of every virtue, the virtue of silence should be publicly interrupted by conversations that were far from necessary. [Col. 1032B]

**XXI.** It was enacted that, of the two customary periods of conversation in the cloister, the second should be removed at every season of the whole year.

The reason for this enactment was its absolutely no usefulness and no necessity—whereas for religious persons to spend even an hour of the day in such a way is not merely idle but harmful. For useless, indeed harmful, talk occupies that interval of time which beneficial silence now devotes to reading and divine chant.

**XXII.** It was enacted that silence at table should be observed everywhere and by everyone, as in the regular refectory. But if anyone should arrive while a monk is eating outside the refectory, he shall rise; and, when he invites him, he shall speak; he shall speak while standing for as long as necessary; after sitting down again, he shall remain silent as before. [Col. 1032C]

The reason for this enactment was that the Apostle commanded even laypeople: “Let each eat his own bread in silence.” Saint Benedict likewise commands monks, saying: “Let the greatest silence be kept at table”; and religious persons both ancient and modern relax nowhere the strictness of silence wherever they eat. Nor is it fitting that Cluniacs should appear less religious, through whom religion, long withered in Gaul, Germany, England, Spain, Italy, and almost all Europe, flowered again, and through whom the inveterate lukewarmness of many grew warm again, divine grace leading and accompanying it.

**XXIII.** It was enacted that no cleric or layperson should enter the cloister or the other regular houses, except either for the sake of some work, or to view the buildings, as respectable guests customarily do, or to treat the sick lying in the infirmary. [Col. 1032D]

The reason for this enactment was the excessively frequent coming and going through the cloister, for all sorts of reasons, of clerics and laypeople—and especially servants—so that the cloister seemed almost to have been turned into a public street, and in their comings and goings they appeared by now scarcely to differ at all from monks.

**XXIV.** It was enacted that no lay servants should attend the sick themselves, or any persons eating in the infirmary, as used to happen; rather, only monks or bearded converts should do so.

[Col. 1033A] The reason for this enactment was that the companionship of converts was more fitting for monks than that of secular servants; and that converts serving the brothers might not have material for stealing what remained from the table of those eating in the infirmary. The former servants customarily carried off to their wives, children, and whatever little household they had established in the town whatever they could openly or secretly steal from the brothers. Besides this, another reason was that, continually residing in the regular workshops, they either saw or heard the secrets of monastic order and regular observances, which, in the manner of secular people, they disclosed by spreading them among secular people.

**XXV.** It was enacted that, instead of servants who used disgracefully to call the brothers lying in the infirmary to Mass by shouting in the morning, a bell suspended in a high place in the infirmary should be rung for this purpose.

The reason for this enactment was that it seemed more suitable and decent for brothers sleeping in the infirmary to be awakened by the sound of a signal used everywhere than to be startled, as often happened, by an inappropriate spoken word during the time of deepest silence. [Col. 1033B]

**XXVI.** It was enacted that the brief and pretended midday rests on fast-days, which are customarily made in summer after Sext, should be abandoned; and that, during the time thus uselessly spent, the brothers should sit in the cloister and read, chant Masses, or perform some necessary work.

The reason for this enactment was, as has been said, this same useless use of time. For by ancient custom, on fast-days falling in summer, before Mass and the meal, the brothers had to undress and take off their shoes—not in order to sleep or rest, but to pretend to sleep and rest—arranging themselves in their beds as though for a long sleep and preparing themselves with good coverings. Indeed, the ancient monastic custom was to make up, by suitable sleep before the meal on fast-days, for the loss of customary sleep. Hence Jerome says: “One must often sleep on an empty stomach.” But because later monks, more fastidious than the ancients and followers of medicine, judged sleeping on an empty stomach to be harmful to the body, they reduced the midday sleeps of fast-days to such brevity that they retained no reality of midday rest, [Col. 1033C] but only an image of its reality. To this pretence they added—though I say it with due respect—a superstition even more laughable: as though they had slept heavily, they were awakened by a longer sounding of the bell; and, as though rough and unkempt from a long tossing in bed, they washed their hands, combed their heads, and performed every ceremony of the longest midday rest. It was therefore judged that the time spent in labour so useless to the body should be given to reading, chant, divine sacrifices, or any useful exercises. [Col. 1033D]

**XXVII.** It was enacted that, at the time when the brothers customarily go to drink after None, each should drink from his own cup, not from those wine-vessels called “justices” (*iustitiae*), from which they had formerly been compelled to drink.

[Col. 1034A] The reason for this enactment was that this manner of drinking was itself absurd and displeasing to everyone: the brothers were forced, after setting aside their own cups, to drink from the “justices,” and even in the season of flies could not discern what was hidden inside.

**XXVIII.** It was enacted that they should not wash their shoes with their straps on Saturday, since this was uselessly laborious.

The reason for this enactment was that formerly, whenever necessity arose, monks working outdoors on rainy and muddy days, compelled by the needs of their work, would generally return to the cloister with shoes soiled with mud and wash them. From this arose a superstition: although the former did this out of necessity, those who for a year or two never went anywhere outside the cloister were not compelled to wash their own very clean, new footwear—for it was not necessary—but were commanded merely to pour two or three drops of water upon the outermost tips of two fingers. [Col. 1034B]

**XXIX.** It was enacted that brothers travelling on horseback should not be compelled to wear both a *froccus* and a cappa, but should make the journey clad, if they wished, either in the *froccus* alone or in the cappa alone.

The reason for this enactment was to preserve the cleanliness of those garments, lest, as used to happen, the *frocci* and tunics of brothers entering the cloister should appear offensive and filthy from mud accumulated on rainy or muddy days; also, that the labour of travelling might be lightened and the ancient, usefully established practice in this matter restored.

[Col. 1034C] **XXX.** It was enacted that they should not be compelled, if they wished to maintain the old custom by which one was forbidden to ride more than a league without leg-wrappings, to do so.

The reason for this enactment was that no reason appeared why they should be obliged, without necessity, to wrap their legs in any coverings and to wear without any necessity what had been permitted only because of necessity.

**XXXI.** It was enacted that the psalms beginning “O God, our ears have heard,” customarily sung after the prayer made before Vespers, should be omitted on every feast of twelve lessons.

The reason for this enactment was the gradually augmented multiplicity, for many reasons, of the laborious—indeed, to many, burdensome—customary psalms. Since this burdened many, it was altered in this respect at the request of many and of almost the entire convent. [Col. 1034D]

**XXXII.** It was enacted that, for our deceased brothers—that is, all the professed—fifty prebends should be given on the anniversary day when, as is customary, their names are recited by the reader in chapter; on this condition: whether the number is greater or less than fifty, the prebends shall neither be increased nor diminished beyond the number stated.

The reason for this enactment was a remarkable exercise of discretion, because it seemed difficult, indeed intolerable, that if the number of deceased persons should extend to eighty, a hundred, or perhaps an unlimited number as brothers continually died, the number of prebends should increase in the same manner. No monastery’s resources could long suffice for this if the custom established by predecessors were maintained. Yet even now the names of deceased brothers only rarely reach the number of fifty. [Col. 1035A]

**XXXIII.** It was enacted that whatever remains from the brothers’ daily table should be received by the common alms.

The reason for this enactment was that, contrary to the custom of nearly all religious and secular persons, if so much bread remained for any brother that it could remain on the table according to the custom concerning bread without mishap, it was returned not to the alms but to the keeper of the refectory, to be kept for the next day. Whatever wine remained—except on certain fast-days and on the day on which a deceased brother was buried—the keeper of the wine likewise reserved for the next day. Since this appeared improper, and so that it might moreover be added to the alms, all leftovers, without any exception, from the tables of the refectory and infirmary were given to the alms. [Col. 1035B]

**XXXIV.** It was enacted that the days of shaving should be altered in part from what had been customary, as follows. The first shaving should take place on the day before the vigil of the Nativity of the Lord. The second, because of the continual variation in the beginning of Lent, should take place, at the abbot’s or prior’s discretion, on the middle or another suitable day between the aforesaid Nativity shaving and the first Sunday of Lent. This second shaving now falls earlier, now later, but at times more than five weeks, at times fewer than three weeks, before that Sunday. The third should be on the Saturday preceding that first Sunday of Lent; the fourth on Tuesday of Palm Week; the fifth on the Saturday of Easter Sunday, on which “Make a joyful noise unto God” is sung; the sixth on the Friday before Pentecost and the feast of the Apostles Peter and Paul, when the length of the interval requires it; [the seventh is missing]; the eighth on the day before the vigil of the Apostles Peter and Paul; the ninth on the vigil of Saint James the Apostle; the tenth on the day before the vigil of the Assumption of Blessed Mary; [the eleventh is missing]; the twelfth on the vigil of Saint Michael; the thirteenth on the vigil of All Saints; and the fourteenth on the vigil of Saint Andrew the Apostle. [Col. 1035C]

The reason for this enactment was the troublesome and, especially in winter, burdensome frequency of these shavings for the brothers. [Col. 1035D]

**XXXV.** It was enacted that no one should be received as a Cluniac monk without the command and permission of the abbot of Cluny, as is customary, except for aid at the point of death; save for persons of great importance and usefulness, who, if delayed, might perhaps draw back through weakness of resolve and fail to persist in their begun purpose of conversion.

The reason for this enactment—or rather, for this renewed enactment—was the very frequent and indiscriminate reception of useless persons in almost all Cluniac places. Through that indiscriminate reception, now peasants, now children, now old men, now fools, and persons useful for no task whatever, had been admitted, until matters had reached the point that such persons were already nearly the greater number. Their frequency and the unspeakable evils committed by them—unseemly even to recount—I pass over in silence, though they were heard of almost continually from different regions of the earth. [Col. 1036A]

**XXXVI.** It was enacted that no prospective monk, even by special permission, should be clothed in regular garments before reaching twenty years of age.

The reason for this enactment was the premature and excessively hasty reception of children, who, before they could possess any rational understanding, were clothed in the garments of sacred religion. Mingled with other childish foolishness, they disturbed everyone; and, to omit certain matters and gather much into brief compass, they did almost no good for themselves and considerably—indeed sometimes very greatly—impeded the religious purpose of others. [Col. 1036B]

**XXXVII.** It was enacted that, in place of the annual and regular probation, a probation of at least one month should be observed for novices before they are bound by the vow of promised obedience.

The reason for this enactment was that the annual probation commanded by the Rule, moderated by the discretion of later Fathers, had come to this: I do not say that a year, or half a year, but not even a month, a week, or sometimes even a full day was kept for testing novices. Since this was wholly contrary both to reason and to the Rule’s decree—which commands that spirits be tested to see whether they are from God (1 John [Col. 1036C] 4)—it seemed reasonable that novices should at least undergo a probation of one month.
