They are to be clothed only in the *froccus* and, like the others, regularly shaven and tonsured; without any verbal or written profession, they are to remain according to custom with the others, both in the novices’ cell and in the cloister. If, once the month is finished, he confirms his stability verbally before the prior and brothers and in writing before the lord abbot, and professes obedience, he shall be joined to the body of the monastery in accordance with the words of the Rule. But if he wishes to leave within that stated month, he shall be granted full freedom to do so.

**XXXVIII.** It was enacted that novices received outside Cluny, in the manner previously described, should be brought to Cluny for blessing by their first, second, or at latest third year; and that meanwhile they should neither advance, as Cluniac usage requires, to ecclesiastical orders, nor sing Mass before they are ordained, nor administer outside the cloister the care of any obedience. [Col. 1036D]

The reason for this enactment was the excessively delayed arrival at Cluny of novices received outside Cluny. Accordingly this law was issued: because priors, sparing expense, postponed bringing and sending novices to Cluny for ten, fifteen, or even sometimes thirty years, they should be compelled at least by the prescribed law to bring or send them to Cluny either for blessing, or, if they have been blessed outside, again for obedience before the brothers.

**XXXIX.** It was enacted that the ancient and holy work of the hands should be restored at least in some measure, either in the cloisters themselves or wherever it can be performed suitably out of the sight of secular people; so that at every time, except on feast-days when work is forbidden, the brothers should always occupy themselves in some useful work.

The reason for this enactment was that idleness, which Father Benedict calls the enemy of the soul, had taken possession of so great a part of our people, especially of those called converts, that in the cloisters or outside them, apart from a few who read and rare persons who wrote, they either dozed against the cloister walls or—from sunrise itself, so to speak, until sunset, indeed almost until midnight—those permitted to do so with impunity spent nearly the entire day in empty, idle, and, what is worse, often slanderous words. [Col. 1037A–B]

**XL.** It was enacted that no prior or other person travelling should take with him more than three mounts; or, if he is a prior of the order, four, or at most five. This is required both for propriety and as a witness to companionship, and so that the offices of the church may be sung more diligently.

The reason for this enactment was that pride or ostentation might not be observed in officials or travellers, and that the burden placed on monasteries or any hosts might, as far as possible, be avoided.

**XLI.** It was enacted that, wherever the resources of the place permit, twelve brothers, excluding deans and with a third prior added, should ordinarily maintain the order. [Col. 1037C]

The reason for this enactment need not be written, because it is evident to all.

**XLII.** It was enacted that, where twelve brothers cannot be present, perfect silence should nevertheless always be kept at least in the refectory and dormitory, and in the cloister from the evening hour until the third hour of the following day. For it is certain that this ought always and everywhere to be kept universally in all churches.

The reason for this enactment was that, if brothers in such places could not or would not maintain the full order, they should at least retain some shadow, trace, or fragment of order, lest, spending the whole day on frivolous words or matters, they should appear in no respect to differ from secular people. [Col. 1037D]

**XLIII.** It was enacted that none of our members should be advanced to the priesthood before thirty, or at least twenty-five, years of age.

The reason for this enactment was that, in accordance with the decrees of the sacred canons, neither adolescents nor unlearned persons nor those still unable to understand how great, how divine, and how excellent the priestly office is should approach those heavenly sacred things as rash presumers rather than worthy administrators.

**XLIV.** It was enacted that no one should dare, without the command or counsel of the lord abbot, to give away, sell, exchange, deposit as a pledge anywhere or with anyone, or pawn lands or treasures of churches. Whoever does so should know himself excluded from communion with his brothers and with the whole Church. [Col. 1038A]

The reason for this enactment was the reported and known recklessness of certain priors who have been proved sometimes to have acted thus.

**XLV.** It was enacted that men or servants of clerics or laypeople not belonging to us should by no means be made stewards, cellarers, or provosts of Cluniac houses.

The reason for this enactment was the frequent experience of losses inflicted upon many Cluniac monasteries by such persons or on their account.

**XLVI.** It was enacted—or rather renewed—that no prior transferred from one priory to another should bring from his former place a servant to live with him. [Col. 1038B]

The reason for this enactment was suspicion—indeed, rather proof—of certain improper matters, not fit to be spoken of, which had formerly arisen in such transfers of servants from place to place. This decree provided, as far as possible, that they should not arise henceforth.

**XLVII.** It was enacted that religious women or converted women should in no way be permitted to dwell near monastic houses within at least two leagues.

The reason for this enactment was that, in matters requiring the greatest caution, no place should be given to the devil contrary to the Apostle’s command, but that, together with the fuel of wrongdoing, every suspicion of it should be removed. The recklessness of certain persons prompted this enactment even more: for the sake of money from lands, they had already begun to provide dwellings close to monastic houses for women professing religious life or conversion. [Col. 1038C]

**XLVIII.** It was enacted that those called *familiares*—that is, neither monks nor converts, and the worst destroyers of certain monasteries—should not be received anywhere, even for the greatest profit.

The reason for this enactment was the well-known perversity of these *familiares*: serving neither God nor manual work, and providing nothing useful for the houses, they were fed and clothed in certain monasteries in order to chatter, slander, and waste whatever they could.

[Col. 1038D] **XLIX.** It was enacted that none of our brothers should sleep at night without a light, at least in his own quarters. If anyone is so poor that he cannot provide a lamp for his own dormitory, he should take the lamp that is in the church and carry it to the dormitory.

The reason for this enactment was that sons of light should always walk in physical light as well, because, as the Apostle says when speaking of spiritual light: “You are all children of light and children of the day; we are not of the night nor of darkness” (1 Thess. 5). Although, as I have said, he speaks of that spiritual light, the Lord says the same thing concerning both physical and spiritual light: “Everyone who does evil hates the light and does not come to the light, lest his deeds be exposed; but whoever does the truth comes [Col. 1039A] to the light, that his deeds may be made manifest, because they have been done in God” (John 3).

**L.** It was enacted that, on the six days within the octave of the Assumption of the holy Virgin, Mother of the Lord, and likewise within the octave of the Apostles Peter and Paul, twelve lessons from the Gospel and twelve others from the prophets or prophetic books, or from the Acts of the Apostles or their Epistles—as selected by me—should be read at the principal Mass. Within the octave of Saint Mary, namely, there shall be six from the Gospel and again six from the prophets, as stated, or from prophetic books. Within the octave of the Apostles, likewise, six shall be from the Gospel and six from the Acts of the Apostles or their Epistles.

The reason for this enactment was the special affection of love which, after our Savior, we ought to have for his holy Mother and for the holy Apostles Peter and Paul; and because lessons heard almost throughout the whole year did not kindle most hearers so strongly toward their veneration and love as lessons heard less frequently did. [Col. 1039B]

**LI.** It was enacted—though this was ancient but neglected—that no brother rising from the common table of the refectory should leave the church choir, which all must enter according to custom, before all alike have given thanks, until the final *Benedicamus*, to the kind giver of all good things for the benefits received; except the reader at table, or its keeper, if that same reader has been assigned the duty of keeper.

The reason for this enactment was that most, indeed many, brothers entering the church with the convent after the meal would immediately withdraw from the choir for some slight reason and would not give the thanks owed to God together with their brothers. [Col. 1039C]

**LII.** It was enacted that lighted candles should not be placed upon the great crown, most elegantly made of bronze, gold, and silver, which hangs suspended in the middle of the choir by a strong chain, except on the five principal feasts, the feast of the Dedication of the church, and All Saints. On other feasts, when that iron structure commonly called *crza* [reading uncertain] used to be lighted, glass lamps should illuminate it instead.

[Col. 1039D] The reason for this enactment was the superfluous expense—seeming, as it were, to proceed from abundance though it could arise only from scarcity—and the excessively frequent lighting of those candles upon the crown, which cheapened the dignity of the solemnities. For, according to the sayings of ancient sages, nothing is so dear and precious that it is not made cheap by continual use.

**LIII.** It was enacted that the part of the new monastery situated to the left beyond the left choir should not be opened to clerics or laypeople, nor should anyone except monks have access to it at any time, as formerly happened; except on Sundays and solemn feasts of the Church, and then only from the beginning of the third hour until the end of the principal Mass. The night of the Nativity of the Lord, the night of the Apostles Peter and Paul, and the night called that of Saint Peter ad Vincula are excepted. Also excepted are all pilgrims wishing to approach the high altar or the morning altar for prayer or offering. [Col. 1040A]

The reason for this enactment was that, apart from the old church of Saint Peter, the brothers had no place where they could perform certain sacred and more secret observances belonging to religious persons. Therefore they claimed for themselves, by day and night, that aforesaid part of the new church, where they might continually offer to God the holy and secret incense of prayers; implore their pious Creator with frequent *metanoeiai*—that is, prostrations—or genuflections; and often wear down their bodies with three scourges, either in penance or to increase merit. In these and similar sacred exercises, as though in a desert and removed from human eyes, they unceasingly commended themselves and their own to the Lord. [Col. 1040B]

**LIV.** It was enacted that at the altar of the morning Mass, which is consecrated in honour of Blessed Mary, a Mass of the same Mother of the Lord should be sung daily in private.

The reason for this enactment was that the Mother of the Lord also might be specially honoured by daily offering to the Lord, and that by such services she might be encouraged, after the Lord, to help her special servants.

**LV.** It was enacted that, when the lord abbot enters chapter, the convent—which by ancient custom used not only to rise for him but to descend through all the lower steps down to the ground—should indeed rise reverently, but should not go below the footstool-bench. [Col. 1040C]

The reason for this enactment was that, although it had been decreed by ancient and good men from the great and longstanding love and reverence Cluniac brothers show to their Fathers, it nevertheless seemed right to spare the very great multitude this exertion on account of the old and weak. For at that time their number was greater among three hundred or four hundred brothers than it had been formerly among sixty, or at most eighty, brothers.

**LVI.** It was enacted that young schoolboys should not be compelled to stand while eating in the refectory, according to the ancient custom, when prayers are said for the intercession of the saints.

The reason for this enactment was that a necessity should not be imposed upon a weaker age which is not required of a stronger one. For the compassionate Father Benedict says concerning such persons: “Although human nature itself is moved to mercy toward those ages, namely the old and children, nevertheless the authority of the Rule itself should provide for them.” [Col. 1040D]

**LVII.** It was enacted that on the feasts of the twelve Apostles the *Credo in unum Deum* (“I believe in one God”) should be said at the principal Mass and at any other Masses sung apart from the convent.

The reason for this enactment was the reasonable custom of other churches, and nearly all of them, which they retain as established by the ancient Fathers: that on the Apostles’ feasts they sing the profession of the Christian faith, upon whom and through whom, chiefly after Christ, the faith of the Church was founded. The great Apostle Paul writes the same thing to the Ephesians when he says: “Built upon the foundation of the apostles and prophets” (Eph. 2), and what follows. [Col. 1041A]

**LVIII.** It was enacted that, on the solemn night of the Nativity of the Lord, the prose whose opening is *Coeleste organum* (“The heavenly instrument”) should be sung at the Mass of the dawn.

The reason for this enactment was that the textual sequence of the one beginning *Nostra tuba* (“Our trumpet”) was disordered, contained almost nothing concerning the Savior’s Nativity, and—with a melody still much more unpolished—was displeasing to all who noticed this.

**LIX.** It was enacted that during the first four weeks of Lent the antiphons customarily said on Thursday at the *Benedictus* and *Magnificat* should be changed and others sung instead.

On Thursday of the first week, at the *Benedictus*: *Si manseritis in sermone meo* (“If you remain in my word”); at the *Magnificat*: *Cognoscite veritatem* (“Know the truth”).

On Thursday of the second week, at the *Benedictus*: *Non possum a meipso* (“I can do nothing of myself”); at the *Magnificat*: *Non quaero voluntatem meam* (“I do not seek my own will”).

On Thursday of the third week, at the *Benedictus*: *Operamini non cibum qui perit* (“Work not for the food that perishes”); at the *Magnificat*: *Hoc est opus Dei* (“This is the work of God”).

On Thursday of the fourth week, at the *Benedictus*: *Non potest Filius a se facere quidquam* (“The Son cannot do anything of himself”); at the *Magnificat*: *Pater diligit Filium* (“The Father loves the Son”). [Col. 1041B]

The reason for this enactment was that the formerly used antiphons belonged to other seasons and, when sung in those other seasons, were sung again in Lent as though borrowed: *Pater Abraham* (“Father Abraham”); *Fili, recordare* (“Son, remember”); *Exibant autem daemonia a multis* (“Demons also went out from many”); *Cum sol autem occidisset* (“When the sun had set”); *Propheta magnus surrexit in nobis* (“A great prophet has arisen among us”); *Accepit omnes timor* (“Fear seized them all”). Still more absurdly, on Thursday of the first week the antiphons *Missus sum ad oves* (“I was sent to the sheep”) and *O mulier, magna est fides tua* (“O woman, great is your faith”) were said. These antiphons were sung again immediately on the following second Sunday from the Gospel of that Sunday itself. As I learned from certain priors, this occurred because those Thursdays formerly had no proper Gospels from which antiphons could be taken for singing. Such Gospels were later selected from the Gospel of John by later Fathers zealous for the divine offices. Therefore, once those Thursdays began to have proper Gospels, new antiphons were also made from those Gospels. [Col. 1041C–D]

**LX.** It was enacted that, just as the other Hours of the holy Virgin, Mother of the Lord, are customarily sung every day in the church of the sick, which is consecrated in her honour, Compline of the same Virgin should also be sung there; and that at every Hour, before the psalms, the verse should be prefixed: *Memento, salutis auctor*, with its *Gloria*—“Remember, author of salvation.”

The reason for this enactment was the honour due in a singular manner to the Mother of the Lord above every creature; and that, because her Hours could not be sung in the public convent owing to the multitude of brothers, the multiplicity of offices, and lack of time, they might at least be sung there in their entirety by a smaller number in her chapel. [Col. 1042A]

**LXI.** It was enacted that on non-festal days, from All Saints’ Day until Easter, regular Prime and the Prime of Saint Mary—formerly sung in the infirmary chapel in the deep night, after the preceding Matins and after the other psalmody had ended, before the arrival of the convent—should be deferred until dawn and until the sound of the bell customarily rung in the infirmary in the morning.

The reason for this enactment was that the psalmody was often not yet completed by the sick because of its length when the convent arrived, and the arriving convent drove out the sick themselves—indeed, everyone it found in that church. Further, they often sang at almost midnight, while the sun was still hidden most deeply beneath the earth: *Jam lucis orto sidere* (“Now that the star of light has risen”). Therefore, lest so great a falsehood should any longer be uttered before God by the children of truth, and lest the words of those praying to and praising the Lord should be at variance, this was enacted. If anyone objects, “Why has this not also been corrected in other cases where a similar mark of falsehood is found?”—when, still far into the night, they sing *Aurora lucis rutilat* (“The dawn of light gleams”), *Aurora jam spargit polum* (“Dawn now spreads across the sky”), *Lux intrat* (“Light enters”), *Albescit polus* (“The sky grows white”), and many things of this kind—I answer that I indeed greatly wish that all such things could be corrected among us and everywhere, if it could be done peacefully. But since, as I judge, this cannot be done, I shall use the words of Pope Gregory the Great: “If I cannot bring back many sheaves from the Lord’s field, at least I shall bring back a few; at least two; at least one.” [Col. 1042B–C]

**LXII.** It was enacted that, when sick brothers are anointed with holy oil in accordance with ecclesiastical custom, they should not be offered a golden or silver cross for veneration, but a wooden cross bearing a painted image of the crucified Lord, fitted with a fragment of the wood of the Lord’s own cross, mounted in gold and inserted into that cross beneath the feet of the painted crucified figure.

The reason for this enactment was that it seemed more reasonable and devout that the sick person should be presented with a cross made not from any other metal or other thing but from the same material of wood upon which the Savior was crucified, and that there should be no, or only a slight, note of falsehood in the words customarily sung while it is venerated. For they do not say, “Behold the gold of the cross” or “Behold the silver of the cross,” but: “Behold the wood of the cross, on which the salvation of the world hung; come, let us adore.” This is certainly true, because Christ was crucified not on gold or silver but on wood. Yet in saying this I do not condemn or criticize crosses made of gold or silver for the honour of the Lord’s cross—something that should especially be approved and praised by Catholic lips. But the preciousness of metal, which moves simple minds to greater veneration of the sacred cross, is one thing; the usefulness of wood, which moves spiritual minds to more ardent devotion toward the cross and the Crucified One, is another. Therefore, so that the devout mind might be more inflamed with love for the Savior’s Passion, a fragment of the wood of that very first cross, as I have said, has been set beneath the feet of the painted Crucified One. Immediately after the kiss of the feet, it presents itself to the eyes, mind, and mouth of the sick person venerating and kissing the cross. [Col. 1042D–1043A]

Yet it was decreed that this wooden cross, which I had fitted in the manner described for the purpose stated, should be brought for veneration not to the dead but to the dying. As I have done this at Cluny, so, wherever it may be done among our houses, although I hesitate to command it, I nevertheless desire that it be done.

**LXIII.** It was enacted that the *staminiae*, which by ancient custom used to be torn for brothers to be more severely scourged for grave offences and forcibly pulled down to the waist, should no longer be torn. Rather, while the *staminia* remains intact, the brother to be beaten should take it off completely.

The reason for this enactment was both to prevent the frequent loss caused by torn *staminiae* and to allow the more fully stripped brother to be beaten more readily. [Col. 1043B]

**LXIV.** It was enacted that, after the reading in the refectory has ended, baskets should no longer be carried through the refectory, as under the ancient custom, to receive the leftover bread.

The reason for this enactment was that baskets were formerly carried around to receive the portions of remaining bread so that they might be returned to the grain-keeper, rather than the almoner, for later distribution. But since now none of the refectory’s bread is returned to the grain-keeper and all is returned to the almoner, it seemed unnecessary for the same baskets to be carried any longer through the refectory. [Col. 1043C]

**LXV.** It was enacted that, at the morning and principal Mass, after the singing of the offertory has ended and until the Preface, the convent should not be compelled to stand, as formerly occurred. Rather, once the chant has ceased, those wishing to sit may sit. Nevertheless, when the priest, turned toward the choir, says, “Pray, brothers,” they should on non-festal days modestly raise the footstools attached to those seats and recline upon them according to custom; but on festal days they should bow before the benches.

The reason for this enactment was that the great and continual labour of the Cluniac convent might be relieved by this very small relaxation. [Col. 1043D]

**LXVI.** It was enacted that young schoolboys, if they are good, should not in the course of time lose anything of others’ rank.

The reason for this enactment was that, from I know not what origin, though so report had it, there was said to be a custom that none of the boys among the scholars should ever, at any time, obtain either the office of weekly minister of the principal Mass, or that of prior, or keeper of order, or any other privilege of monastic dignity, whatever might be involved. Even slight reflection shows how contrary this is to common justice and reason. For when the prince of the apostles says: “In every nation, whoever fears God and works righteousness is acceptable to him” (Acts 10), if, I say, in every nation, then surely also in every order? And if in every order, then surely in every rank, every condition, every age? Since a clear matter needs no lengthy proof, I state briefly that every monastic or ecclesiastical dignity has publicly been restored by us to the scholars, if they are good and worthy; for he whose faith, learning, and life are approved is most unjustly excluded from any ecclesiastical dignity.

LXVII. It was enacted that the *pneuma*—the chant sung at the end of antiphons—should no longer be sung where several antiphons follow one another, as at Vespers and Matins, except on the five chief feasts: the Nativity of the Lord, Easter, Pentecost, the feast of the Apostles Peter and Paul, and the Assumption of the Blessed Virgin. Likewise it was decreed that, at the suffrages of the saints, except for the prayer of the Holy Cross, of Saint Mary, of the Apostles Peter and Paul, and the final prayer, the phrase “through our Lord,” with what follows through “Amen,” namely “through Christ our Lord,” should not be said.

The reason for this enactment was weariness caused by the prolixity of the many additions which at different times had been added by different persons to the ecclesiastical offices. This was established both to give some relief from that weariness and because it was observed in no Cluniac monastery other than Cluny.

LXVIII. It was enacted that the proper hymns for Saint Stephen the first martyr, Saint John the Evangelist, the Holy Innocents, Saint Lawrence, and Saint Vincent, taken from the Hymnal of Saint Ambrose or from the hymnal of Prudentius, a learned and religious man, should henceforth be sung everywhere on the solemnities of those saints by our brethren who are able to obtain them.

The reason for this enactment was love and reverence for those saints. Since John, the beloved of Christ, is, after Peter and Paul, among the foremost apostles, and since the martyrs just named are among the highest and most eminent martyrs, it seemed incongruous that they should be celebrated with the common hymns of other apostles or martyrs—especially because, apart from the hymns, they possess all their other proper chants, both nocturnal and diurnal.

LXIX. It was enacted that two mature and diligent brothers should always guard the dormitory, by day and night: either together when they can be, or in turns when they cannot. When they cannot both be there because of the meal, as they may agree between themselves, one shall take refreshment and the other shall keep watch. The same shall be done when another reason intervenes.

The reason for this enactment was that frequent complaints arose because of the absence of guards and the multitude of persons gathering there: people often lost their clothes or other articles of regular clothing and could not easily recover what had been lost. This was therefore decreed both to prevent this and to guard against every other possible adverse occurrence.

LXX. It was enacted that neither the abbot of Cluny, nor the prior, nor any of the priors or brethren of Cluny, whether living at Cluny or elsewhere, should buy or give to his servants skins of any kind except sheepskins. It was further added that, putting aside red, green, and every other colour of clothing, they should clothe servants riding with them and assigned to their personal service either in moderately priced coarse woollens (*burelli*) or in black cloth—that is, in lambskin garments, or garments of equal or lesser value.

The reason for this enactment was, first and chiefly, the increase of religious observance, and the manifest impropriety, known to all, that attendants serving monks dressed according to the Rule should themselves wear secular clothing. For, according to the word of the Lord, those who wear soft garments are accustomed to be or dwell not in the houses of monks but in the houses of kings. Secondly, it was intended that the many heavy expenses which were being wastefully and badly consumed on those superfluous and harmful garments should be spent properly and reasonably on necessary and useful things.

LXXI. It was enacted that no Cluniac should say or sing, in responsories or antiphons concerning the baptism of the Lord, “Listen to him” (*Ipsum audite*). For example, it used formerly to be added to the responsory which begins: “In the form of a dove the Holy Spirit was seen; the paternal voice was heard: ‘This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased’”: “Listen to him.” Likewise, in the antiphon: “A voice sounded from heaven, and the voice of the Father was heard: ‘This is my Son, in whom I am well pleased,’” and in any similar antiphons or responsories, it was forbidden that anyone should add: “Listen to him.”

The reason for this enactment was the evident and plain falsehood uttered unthinkingly by those who sang or read when they added “Listen to him” to those sacred words. The witnesses are not insignificant persons, but the most holy and truthful Evangelists themselves—Matthew, Mark, and Luke. Writing with one accord that the Spirit of God appeared over Christ at his baptism in the form of a dove, and that the Father’s voice came from heaven saying either, “This is my Son, in whom I am well pleased,” or, “You are my Son; in you I am well pleased,” they nowhere add, “Listen to him.” These words were added not at Christ’s baptism but at his Transfiguration. At that Transfiguration, I say, “Listen to him” was joined to similar words; and reason itself plainly demonstrates this. For since at Christ’s baptism only the Baptist, after Christ, heard that voice of the almighty Father, one would not say to one person, “Listen to him,” but “Listen to him” in the singular. It is therefore evident that this was not said at the baptism to the one man who was present, but was commanded at the Lord’s Transfiguration to the three apostles—Peter, James, and John—and in them and through them to the universal Church which they prefigured: not in the singular but in the plural, “Listen to him.”

LXXII. It was enacted that on the Nativity of the Lord no brother should either celebrate or hear Mass anywhere before the end of that Mass which is called “of the Light” and is customarily sung in the convent. Excepted from this regulation are the sick who eat in the infirmary; ancient custom ordained that, just as three Masses are sung in the convent on that holy day, so three Masses should likewise be celebrated for them at the same time in the chapel of Saint Mary assigned to their services.

The reason for this enactment was that priests, not by custom indeed, but through a certain thoughtless haste, used immediately after the Gospel of that Mass to leave the convent with certain others who either assisted them or wished to communicate at their Masses, each to celebrate for himself the Mass of the day whose introit is “A child is born to us.” Thus it happened that not only did the choir remain almost empty, but they did not even hear what remained of that Mass after the Gospel. This had by then become so habitual that they thought it to be a custom, and almost half the Cluniac convent, perhaps even more, on the day of the Lord’s Nativity neither heard what remained after the Gospel in the Mass of the Light nor heard that Mass itself. They did not hear it because they lost its greatest and best part, namely the celebration of the divine sacrifice, from whose dignity the Mass takes its name most especially. This regulation was made to prevent this from happening thereafter.

LXXIII. It was enacted that from every wine vessel in the cellar intended for the use of brethren, guests, or poor—that is, from each one—the brother customarily responsible for providing wine for Masses should take, on the vigil of the Nativity of the Lord, only as much as may suffice for celebrating all the Masses of that sacred night and day.

The reason for this enactment was a matter attested, as I have heard, by many persons and often reported to me: namely, that the wine in a vessel from which however small a portion has been taken for celebrating the sacraments of the Nativity just mentioned can never turn sour or acquire an unnatural and corrupt taste.

LXXIV. It was enacted that the *Kyrie* whose chant has prose verses beginning, “Merciful eternal Ruler, boundless Father, have mercy” (*Clemens Rector aeterne, Pater immense eleison*), which by ancient usage was sung in many monasteries belonging to Cluny, should also be sung at Cluny on the five chief feasts. It was further added that on those same solemnities, and on any greater feasts as desired, at Vespers or Lauds, “Let us bless the Lord” (*Benedicamus Domino*) should be sung according to the melody of that verse, new indeed but good and already public, which many sing on the Nativity of the Blessed Mother of God:

> “The Virgin, bearer of God, is the rod; her son is the flower.”

The melody, however, was taken not from the entire verse but from its end: “Her son is the flower” (*Flos filius ejus*).

The reason for this enactment was that a more solemn chant might be more fitting for more solemn days, and that variation in the chants themselves might produce greater devotion in those singing.

LXXV. It was enacted that on the feasts of the Finding of the Holy Cross and its Exaltation, at morning Lauds, verses should be sung taken from the hymn beginning:

> “Sing, O tongue, of the glorious conflict of the contest”  
> (*Pange, lingua, gloriosi praelium certaminis*),

of which the first is “Faithful Cross” (*Crux fidelis*), the second “Bend your branches” (*Flecte ramos*), and the third “You alone were worthy” (*Sola digna tu fuisti*), with the following *Gloria*, namely, “Glory and honour to God” (*Gloria et honor Deo*).

The reason for this enactment was that, on the aforesaid solemnities of the saving Cross, it seemed more devout and elegant pleasantly to vary the hymns containing its praises than tediously to repeat the same ones. Previously the hymn beginning “The royal banners advance” (*Vexilla Regis prodeunt*) was sung at both Vespers offices of each feast and then repeated at morning Lauds.

[Col. 1048A] LXXVI. It was enacted that the antiphon composed concerning the sacred Mother of the Lord, beginning “Hail, Queen, Mother of mercy” (*Salve, Regina, mater misericordiae*), should be sung by the convent during the procession on her feast of the Assumption; and further, in processions customarily made from the principal church of the Apostles to the church of that Virgin Mother, except on the feasts of those saints on which ancient custom requires chants pertaining to the same saints.

The reason for this enactment was no other than the highest and greatest love which every rational creature ought, in every way reasonably possible, to show, after the author of all things, to the mother of the author of the universe.

[Col. 1047]

## Arrangement of the Temporal Affairs of Cluny, Made by Lord Peter, Ninth Abbot of Cluny

(Year 1150.)

[Baluze, *Miscellanea*, Luc. edition, folio, vol. III, p. 72.]

[Col. 1047B] Since human memory is very unstable, and men, who are continually dying, cannot always leave their descendants a true report of deeds done, the aid of writing was invented by the first wise men. For what is written does not admit variation and, unless corrupted by accident or design, passes down the truth of events to successors impartially in one and the same form. I have therefore done this in certain matters concerning spiritual things alone. I now do it in certain matters pertaining at once to bodily and spiritual advantage.

I, brother Peter, humble abbot of Cluny, therefore make known to all who read this that, when I was raised to this office twenty-six years ago, I found a great Church, religious and famous, but most poor: burdened by great expenditures and, when its revenues were compared with its expenses, almost without revenues at all. There were three hundred brothers or more, and that house could not maintain even a hundred from its own resources. There was always a crowd of guests and an infinite number of poor persons. Grain gathered from all the deaneries scarcely lasted four months, sometimes not even three; wine collected from every source never lasted two months, sometimes not even one. The bread was small, black, and full of bran. The wine was greatly diluted, tasteless, and truly vile. Besides other expenses and loans received at heavy interest, the chamberlain of Cluny spent more than twenty thousand shillings solely on buying grain and wine.

Seeing these hardships, and having taken counsel with the wise brethren then living, I established monthly provisions (*mesatica*) through the deaneries, as seemed reasonable to them and to me. I ordained that certain deans should provide for the Cluniac convent with bread, beans, and their fat—some for one month, some for two months, some for three weeks, some for fifteen days, some for eight days—that is, for the entire year. And so that this arrangement should always be observed annually, I ordered and confirmed it in writing in chapter with the assent and will of all the brethren.

This was observed as decreed for many subsequent years. Later, it seemed good both to me and to the brethren that certain parts of the earlier arrangement should be changed and that some deaneries which made monthly provisions should, as reason required, be assigned to other uses of the monastery. Accordingly, the deanery called Masiliis, because it is more productive of oats than wheat, was assigned to provide fodder for all guests’ horses. Certain other provisions for the brethren were imposed upon Galiniac. Juliacus was excused from the monthly provision imposed on it because of its enclosed fields, which we turned into vineyards, and because of an annual provision for the convent on behalf of Lord Hugh, bishop of Auxerre. The deanery of Saint Hippolytus was likewise exempted from the monthly provision for a definite reason.

It was therefore enacted that, because the first arrangement which provided for the convent throughout the year from the things written above had thus been altered or changed, a new arrangement should be made which would likewise provide throughout the whole year for all the brethren with bread, beans, and their fat, as stated. It is as follows: the dean of Cavariac shall provide for all September; the dean of Cluny for all October and half of November; the dean of Perrona for the remaining days of November; the dean of Scutiolae for the first sixteen days of December; the dean of Caviniae for the remaining days of December together with all January; the dean of Lordon for all February together with March; the granary officer for all April, all May, and all June with half of July. The chamberlain, however, must pay this granary officer beans for one month and a half. The dean of Laisiaco shall provide for what remains of July; the dean of Bersoniac for all August except the last eight days; and the dean of Saint Gengulf for those last eight days of August.

These monthly provisions were established so that the aforesaid officers should give the granary officer not merely three or four *sextarii* of wheat, or more or less, for each day’s service, but as much as shall be necessary. The granary officer, however, as a faithful steward who gives the measure of wheat in due season, shall faithfully preserve what the officers give him, lest, by defrauding the monastery’s goods, he suffer in his soul the death of Ananias and Sapphira, according to the teaching of blessed Benedict. If general meals, whether obligatory or gratuitous, should intervene and excuse them from supplying bread or beans, they shall be excused. But if gratuitous meals do not occur, or obligatory ones fail for any reason, they shall nevertheless make up those days. They shall afterward demand the grain or beans expended from those who ought to have made those provisions as an obligation, except for those meals which the chamberlain provides without annual revenues. For those meals for which he receives sufficient money yearly, they shall require from the same chamberlain the bread and beans expended.

This second arrangement again remained in force for a long time. But because, as it is written, “where there are many counsels, there is great safety,” and however good any plan may be, it must without doubt be changed when a better one supervenes, just as the better second arrangement succeeded the first, so a best third arrangement succeeded the better second. It is as follows.

It was established that the dean of Lordon, both he of Lordon and that of Saint Hippolytus, with the assistance of eight days from Saint Gengulf, should always provide the entire Cluniac convent, both healthy and sick, with good bread, according to the larger weight which I myself established at the beginning of the monthly provisions. He shall provide not only for the convent—that is, for those who eat in the refectory or infirmary—but also for all those whom the deans making the monthly provisions had been accustomed to supply from those provisions; and he shall do whatever they had been accustomed to do. The deans, however, shall give the chamberlain as much wheat and of the same quality as they had customarily given the granary officer while making the monthly provisions. They shall likewise give him the fat for the beans. But the beans they shall give to the aforesaid dean of Lordon, since he has also become granary officer together with his deaneries. As was said above concerning the deans, if general meals, obligatory or gratuitous, do not occur, or obligatory meals fail for any reason, he shall according to custom provide both bread and beans on those days. The chamberlain shall do likewise in the matter stated. They shall afterward demand payment from those who ought to have made the provisions. If those persons can repay it, they shall receive it from them; if they cannot, those named above shall make up the customary amount.

Nor should the following matter, which pertains to the present subject, be left unmentioned. It was an ancient custom that on every day when the names of deceased brethren of our congregation—that is, professed brethren—are pronounced from the book in which the Rule is written, on the day of their death, bread, wine, and a general dish should be given for them. But in exchange for the general dish, our holy father Hugh made this compensation: the almoner of Cluny should hold certain ovens of the town of Cluny and their revenues, which had formerly belonged to the chamber.

First, I myself granted to the almoner whatever bread and wine remained to those eating in the refectory or infirmary, which the granary officer or keeper of the wine had originally claimed for himself by custom. Concerning bread, it was established that fifty pounds by weight should be given to the aforesaid almoner—not according to the weight now given to the brethren, but according to that formerly given to them before our time. To make these weights known to those unfamiliar with them, they should know that there were three different ones: a lesser weight, called that of the guests; another, greater than that, used for the convent throughout the year except in Lent; and the Lenten weight, which was greater still.

When, as written above, monthly provisions were first established, we changed the second weight into the third, greater weight: that is, the convent was to receive throughout the year bread of the same weight as had formerly been given only in Lent.

Concerning the fifty pounds just mentioned, which we decided should be given on the anniversary day when deceased brethren are named, it was established that they should be given not according to the weight formerly called Lenten, and now used by the brethren, but according to the lesser weight which they had customarily had before this arrangement of ours.

Lest anyone wonder that this infinite number of the dead is fixed at the definite number of fifty, he should know that this was done with the following purpose: lest, as time passed, the ever-increasing dead should drive out the living, since the small revenues of the Church could not maintain at least three hundred living persons and perhaps at some time a thousand dead. For, as one has said, in words now become proverbial:

> “There is a measure in things; there are, in short, fixed limits.”  
> (Horace, *Satires* I.1.106.)

And, as another says:

> “Consider long what burdens they refuse,  
> what burdens the shoulders can bear.”  
> (Horace, *Ars Poetica* 39; variant: “turn over,” *versate*, for “consider,” *pensate*.)

For it is foolish to impose upon a person’s strength, weight, and shoulders a burden which he cannot bear—indeed, under which he must unwillingly and by compulsion collapse. On this consideration, therefore, the number and weight of these fifty pounds were thus decreed. If, however, a provision is made for the brethren as an obligation, then the deceased persons in question shall receive bread according to the same weight as is given to the convent. The three poor persons to whom bread and wine are customarily given every evening as alms shall receive daily neither less bread nor bread of another kind, but bread of the same sort and amount as the convent receives.

And because, as I have said, the granary, together with its deaneries, has been entrusted to the dean of Lordon to provide for guests and household, the chamberlain shall give him, so far as bread is concerned, five hundred and sixty *sextarii* of wheat and five hundred of rye, as he customarily gave to other granary officers.

So that later generations may know the rationale of these arrangements, those reading this should know that at first the chamberlain gave the granary officer only five hundred *sextarii* of wheat. But afterward sixty were added to those five hundred so that he might feed certain young noble clerics then being educated in the town of Cluny and increase, at the cooks’ discretion, the bread to be crumbled into certain dishes of the principal table. In this new and final arrangement, thirty *sextarii* of wheat or beans for the monthly provision from Masiliis were added to the five hundred and sixty; moreover, thirteen for the beans of eighteen prebendaries.

Thus, when all these *sextarii* are counted together, the total of wheat and beans is six hundred and three *sextarii*. Of these six hundred and three, the granary officer will receive three hundred less six—that is, two hundred and ninety-four—from the granary’s monthly provisions. The remaining amount he shall receive from the wheat customarily paid apart from the monthly provisions: two hundred from Caviniae, one hundred from Lasiacum, and one hundred from Perrona. If the chamberlain cannot pay them from these sources, he shall see that they are paid from his own resources. Of the five hundred *sextarii* of rye, he shall receive three hundred at Mont Bertald and two hundred at Ronias. If for any reason he cannot obtain these there, he shall require the entire amount from the chamberlain, who may not refuse it.

Concerning the prebendaries mentioned above, the following must be added. Before our time they were given bread such as is customarily given to the inferior household, namely the bread of the *vassalli* (“vassals”; the printed reading is OCR-damaged); afterward it was decreed that their bread should be like that of the convent or guests, but according to the weight which, as stated above, ancient custom prescribed for the convent throughout the year except Lent. There are eighteen pounds for those prebendaries, of which the granary officer was ordered to provide nine and the almoner the other nine.

Since I have begun to speak of arrangements of this kind, I shall add other similar matters. These, then, were the provisions established concerning the bread and legumes of the convent and the bread of guests and household. Concerning wine, because it could not be managed otherwise and the revenues of Cluniac lands did not allow another arrangement, I turned my attention, with the brethren’s counsel, to newly planting and cultivating vineyards. In order that those already planted might be appropriately cultivated in their seasons, I decreed that certain known English revenues should be paid annually to the brother charged with cultivating and guarding them. Unless excessive barrenness of the land should occur, or the cultivators should through fault neglect the work of cultivation, this arrangement will be able to supply wine abundantly for three hundred, indeed almost four hundred, monks, and will suffice in large part not only for the monks but also for guests.

In consequence of these measures, the general dish of the brethren, customarily given to them after the legumes and often the subject of many complaints, was arranged as follows. The chamberlain of Cluny shall receive in the town of Cluny one hundred pounds and five hundred Cluniac shillings of the local currency; adding the Poitevin rent and the twenty thousand herrings given by Count Eustace of Boulogne, together with cheeses either owed or produced from the livestock raising customarily carried on at Cluny or at Metz, he shall provide it completely and without any complaint whatever. This has now been done in this way for many years.

Those who read this must also know that afterward it was established that the dean of Masiliis should provide abundantly in oats for the horses of all guests and, should they have pledged their sureties for oats not superfluous but necessary, should redeem them.

Before this arrangement he gave the chamberlain only twelve hundred *sextarii* of oats each year under the first arrangement I made; these were spent indiscriminately on the horses of guests and of the abbot, prior, cellarer, and chamberlains. But because each of these persons took from that sum of oats whatever he could for himself, frequent complaints and neglect regarding guests’ horses were heard. I therefore decided that, all others being set aside, he should provide for guests alone, however much they needed and however long they stayed, and should redeem their pledges as stated. This applies chiefly to external guests.

For domestic persons—that is, brethren of the congregation—he shall provide for their horses only on the first night, except for the priors who reside in Spain, those who live in England, and the priors of Paredo, Bourbon, and Silviniac. The chamberlain had customarily provided for the horses of these persons, as for those of guests, for as long as they remained at Cluny. All these shall be equal to travelling guests with respect to provision for their horses.

Concerning the prior of Cluny, it was established that he should receive three hundred *sextarii* of oats from the dean of Scutiolae for supplying his horses.

Concerning the chamberlain of Cluny and all his companions, it was decreed that, receiving one hundred *sextarii* of oats owed by the dean of Saint Victor and another hundred from the obedience of Bellimont, together with the oats customarily exacted from oat-sellers in the town of Cluny, he shall demand nothing further with respect to oats.

After these matters, what was arranged concerning the brethren’s clothing must be added, lest it perish through forgetfulness in the passage of time. For I know not by what mischance, when I was summoned to this pastoral office, I found nothing ordered concerning these matters, just as concerning almost all other external affairs. The chamberlain, upon whom all external matters had been imposed, was hindered both by the poverty of the estate and by manifold occupations to which he was unequal; he provided clothing for the brethren with difficulty, confusion, and insufficiency, and did not distribute it according to the apostolic rule and the Rule of Saint Benedict, according to each person’s need.

Accordingly, this duty was imposed in large part upon the prior of Cluny: he should sufficiently provide for all brothers living at Cluny tunics, commonly called *froccos*, cowls, fur garments, lambskin hoods or caps, woollen shirts, breeches, and *flumae*, that is, pillow coverings. To enable him fully to perform these imposed duties, twenty marks of silver from the Italian rent, twenty from the Spanish rent, twenty from an English manor called Opifortis, and fifteen marks from an English manor given by Count Eustace were decreed for him. Subject to the preservation of this Cluniac rent, Count Eustace wished the latter manor to belong to the monastery of Rumeliacum, which he had also given to the Church of Cluny. In addition, the whole rent of Provence, formerly belonging to the Cluniac chamber, was given him: from the priory of Terniacum, which lies on the Rhône, and from that of Talviacum as far as the Alps of Provence and the sea, together with the rents of those priories. These duties were imposed upon the prior of Cluny.

I initially assigned the brethren’s *trabuci* and stockings to the keeper of the works of the new church. But because the revenues he had in England were failing through newly arising wars, I imposed on the chamberlain the duty which that officer had customarily performed: namely, to provide *trabuci* and stockings for the brethren from three hundred shillings of the *gatgeria* of Humbert the Hungarian. When he was going to Jerusalem, Humbert gave us this *gatgeria* in pledge for four thousand shillings which he received from us. I granted that *gatgeria* to the dean of Lordon on condition that he should receive all its fruits and revenues and from them pay the said shillings to the chamberlain for the purposes named above. But if that *gatgeria* should be redeemed and the keeper of the works of the greater church can obtain at least sixty marks from the hundred marks of the manor of Ledecumba which King Stephen of England gave to the Church of Cluny in my time, then, as he formerly did, he shall provide *trabuci* and stockings for all the brethren.

[Col. 1053]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son in Christ, PETER, abbot of Cluny, and to his successors canonically appointed in perpetuity.

[Col. 1055]

## Diplomas and Charters of Supreme Pontiffs, Kings, Archbishops, Bishops, Dukes, and Others, Concerning Certain Abbeys, Priories, Churches, etc., Granted or Confirmed to the Cluniac Monastery in the Time of Peter the Venerable, Ninth Abbot of Cluny

(*Bibliotheca Cluniacensis*, p. 1387.)

I. Charter of Lord Adalbero, bishop of Liège, concerning Bertrées. (Year 1124.)

In the name of the holy and indivisible Trinity. I, ADALBERO, by the grace of God bishop of Liège, make known to our faithful, present and future, that Walter of Trudignei, a free man, has granted to St. Peter and the brothers of the monastery of Cluny the church of Bertrées, with all its usages, tithes, and other appurtenances, in Hanua, Puceis, Trudeneis, and Eurenais, for the salvation of his soul and of the souls of [Col. 1056C] his father and mother, upon this condition: that the brothers whom the abbot of Cluny shall send there to serve God may hold it, and whatever belongs to it, as freely as Walter himself held it; and that these brothers shall pay each year, at Easter, only one gold penny of the coinage of Liège at the altar of St. Peter’s church at Cluny.

Moreover, the men enfeoffed with land belonging to that church, who rendered Walter fidelity on that account, shall seek that land from the hand of the prior of the church and render to that prior of the same church their fidelity and service. The jurisdiction of the village shall likewise belong to the church, [Col. 1057A] so that Godescalc, Walter’s brother, who is advocate of the same allod, shall hold from the Church one half of that jurisdiction; and thereby he shall defend that Church and all that belongs to it against every injustice. Walter likewise granted the restoration-due to St. Peter and to those brothers, so that the Church shall hold one half of that due and the advocate the other half. He also granted them one half of Chorveda, which was Walter’s; for the other half belongs to the Church and abbot of St. Lawrence.

He gave to those brothers the mill of Bavigneis, with all its rights of use, and the entire half of the wood of Trudineis, as he had held it for his own uses and in lordship. He granted the advocacy to his brother Godescalc and to Godescalc’s descendants, upon this condition: [Col. 1057B] that he hold that advocacy from the Church of Cluny and from the hand of the prior whom the abbot of Cluny shall send there; that no advocate or sub-advocate be there other than themselves; and that they inviolably preserve the freedom of that allod and defend it from evil men.

Thus the allod shall be free, and the Church itself, with all its appurtenances, shall retain the right of its freedom, so that, apart from what has been established for the advocate to hold from that Church—namely, one half of the village jurisdiction and one half of the restoration-due—he shall exercise no right, power, lordship, or violence over that allod or over the men belonging to that Church. In every injustice committed within [Col. 1057C] that allod, concerning which the prior of that Church must plead with his brothers and men, nothing shall belong to the advocate, unless he is summoned to perform or maintain a justice which they cannot settle by themselves. Then, from the justice which he performs, the brothers shall have two pence and he the third penny.

Likewise, if anyone commits an injustice concerning the half of the wood which Walter gave to those brothers, the brothers shall have two pence for the exaction of justice; the advocate of that wood shall always receive the third penny. But with respect to whoever belongs to the altar of the church and pays rent there, nothing shall belong to the advocate. The advocate shall have no right or power over them; he shall not implead them, nor inflict violence upon the Church because of them, nor sit with the prior for the purpose of exacting justice from them. Then, as stated, he shall have the third penny from the aforesaid justice.

It was further established that the prior of that Church, together with his brothers, shall belong to no one else and shall be attached to no other cell, but only to the abbot and prior of the monastery of Cluny. Should the abbot of Cluny wish to act otherwise—namely, to place this church under the oversight or power of some cell or another prior—the bishop of Liège and the advocate shall prohibit this from being done; and it shall lie within their protection and judgment to retain and defend this privilege and constitution forever. The goods bestowed upon that Church, or which shall at any time be confirmed to it by the faithful, shall serve the needs of the brothers serving God there, and shall never [Col. 1058A] be transferred to other uses or brought under another’s power.

Walter therefore gave and confirmed this alms to St. Peter, so that the brothers serving God there may remember him publicly and privately in their daily prayers and grant him daily absolution. They shall devoutly commemorate both his anniversary and the anniversaries of his father and mother in vigils, masses, and their other suffrages.

In order that this establishment or grant may remain ratified and unshaken, we have committed it to the present writing for the remembrance of posterity, without [further] confirmation; and, in a general synod, with the consent of the holy Church of Liège, we have confirmed it by episcopal authority and strengthened it with our seal. The suitable witnesses who were called and recorded in this charter are: Andrew, [Col. 1058B] provost and archdeacon; Alexander; Henry, archdeacon; Almannus, archdeacon; Stepo, archdeacon; Arnulf, canon of St. Lambert; William; Henry; Stepo, scholasticus; among the noble and illustrious men, Geoffrey, count of Namur; Gislibert, count of Duras; Lambert, count of Mont-Acut; free men; Godescalc, advocate of the same allod; Adelo of Namur; and many others.

Done at Liège, in the year of the Incarnation 1124, indiction II, in the reign of Henry IV, in the twenty-fifth year of his empire, under Adalbero, bishop of Liège.

## II. Charter of Rainald, Archbishop of Rheims, concerning the relinquishment of the altar of Tour-sur-Marne. (1125.)

[Col. 1058C]

In the name of the holy and indivisible Trinity. Let the diligence of present and future generations know that I, Rainald, by God’s grace humble and unworthy archbishop of Rheims, laboured long and greatly to recover from the same usurpers the altar of Tour-sur-Marne, which had long been occupied by lay hands through unlawful usurpation. Certain powerful men of Plaiotro had so appropriated shares of the offerings, tithes, and revenues accruing to that altar for their townsmen that—more disgracefully still—they bestowed them in marriage upon their wives and daughters. At last, with the help of the Holy Spirit, who breathes where He wills, I recovered it from those invaders on the following condition.

For when I had very often admonished the aforesaid lords of Plaiotro and had used every means to persuade them [Col. 1058D] to withdraw from possession of God’s sanctuary, which they had long held unjustly, lest by unjustly and violently usurping the patrimony of the Crucified One they incur eternal condemnation, at length, moved by our repeated admonition and persuasion and yielding to our counsel, they surrendered the aforesaid altar on these terms: namely, that I should freely bestow it upon the holy Church of Cluny, which is as it were a great luminary of the whole world, together with its offerings, tithes, and other appurtenances, and grant it to be held personally by the venerable brothers of that monastery.

Readily and devoutly assenting to their just and religious request, so that I might deserve to be made a participant in all the good works present in so great a congregation, I delivered the said [Col. 1059A] altar to them to possess personally in perpetual right, with all that belongs to it. Only this agreement was added, at the humble request of the aforesaid lords of Plaiotro: that the priest of that place, who at that time held the persona and parish through them, should possess them freely and quietly for as long as he lives, unless perhaps he should lose them through faults of his own requiring it.

When he has entered upon the way of all flesh, or has been removed for any reasonable cause, the Church of Cluny shall receive what is its own—namely, the altar and the persona with its appurtenances—to possess by perpetual right, thereafter having free power to appoint to that church whatever suitable priest it chooses. Once presented to us or to our successors in the course of time, as is customary, and after he has undertaken the care of souls, that priest shall render them fidelity and show due reverence, saving its right in those matters known to belong to the fief of the priesthood. And that these provisions may remain ratified and unshaken, we have caused them to be strengthened by the authority of our seal.

Sign of the venerable Archbishop Rainald. Sign of Joyrannus, abbot of St. Nicholas. Sign of Ursus, abbot of St. Denis. Sign of Hugh, archdeacon. Sign of Leo, cantor. Sign of Alberic, master [Ambrose, master]. Sign of John of Pi. [Col. 1059C] Sign of John of Germany. Sign of Libert, dean. Sign of Odo, dean of the city.

Done at Rheims in the year of the incarnate Word 1125, indiction III, in the eighteenth year of the reign of Louis, king of the French, and in the first year of the archiepiscopate of Lord Rainald.

Fulcrad, chancellor, wrote and subscribed.

## III. Concerning the priesthood of Tour-sur-Marne [Materne]. (1125.)

In the name of the holy and indivisible Trinity. Let the diligence of present and future generations know that the long dispute between the priest of the Church of Tour and the monks of Cluny, to whom the parish of that [Col. 1059D] village belongs, was settled by Lord Rainald, the venerable archbishop of Rheims, in this way: the aforesaid priest renounced all the matters concerning which he was making complaint—namely, the revenue of the tithe, straw, hay, and the small tithe.

Accordingly, for the sake of peace and concord, it was granted to the aforesaid priest that every Sunday, from the common offering at the celebration of Mass, he should have bread, wine, and the offering-gift, together with half of the offerings of parishioners belonging to the benefice of the priesthood; all the rest shall belong to the monks. On Monday, from all that comes into his hand in the celebration of masses, [Col. 1060A] he shall receive half. On the remaining days, if the offering is worth no more than three pence, he shall retain it; whatever exceeds that amount he shall divide with the monks.

With regard to alms and bequests made by the dying, he shall proceed in this manner: after summoning lawful witnesses, he shall urge the parishioner first to leave something to those monks for the remedy of his soul, since they are established at the head of the sanctuary. All these provisions, as specified above, while preserving the right of the privilege of the aforesaid Church of Tour, were decreed by the said venerable Archbishop Rainald for the sake of re-establishment and perpetual peace, and were confirmed by the drafting of this chirograph, the impression of the episcopal seal, and the attestation of trustworthy witnesses and authentic persons.

Sign of the same venerable Archbishop R. Sign of Loyrannus [Joyrannus], abbot of St. Nicholas. Sign of Ursus, abbot of St. Denis. Sign of Hugh, archdeacon. Sign of Leo, cantor. Sign of Ambrose, master. Sign of John of Pi. Sign of John of Germany. Sign of Odo, dean of the city. Sign of Libert, dean.

Done at Rheims, in the year of the incarnate Word 1125, indiction III, in the nineteenth year of the reign of Louis, king of the French, and in the first year of the archiepiscopate of Lord Rainald [Col. 1060C].

Fulcrad, chancellor, wrote and subscribed.

## IV. Charter of King Louis concerning St. Peter of Poitiers. (1130.)

In the name of the holy and indivisible Trinity. I, LOUIS, by the grace of God king of the French, wish it to be known to all, present and future, that a certain knight named Gilbert, surnamed Strangulatus, for the remedy of his soul, gave to the church of St. Peter of Poitiers—[Note: [Col. 1059] immediately dependent on the monastery of Cluny.]—and to the monks serving God there, where he had come for conversion, a certain estate, namely his allods of Verinis, to hold in perpetuity.

Afterward it pleased the same monks, providing for the advantage of their church, [Col. 1060D] to admit us as a participant in the cultivation and settlement of that land, on this condition: that we should receive half of all revenues of that land, and of every exaction and tallage and all other customary dues. Moreover, if any addition may hereafter be acquired for that land by purchase, we shall give half of the money, and the monks shall pay the other half.

Concerning the mayors and servants, we have likewise decreed that no mayor or provost shall in any way be appointed in the said land without the monks’ permission and consent, and that each of them shall render his fidelity to those monks. It was also established and granted that none of the settlers or men of the said land shall, for any offence, be summoned to justice or drawn into litigation anywhere other than in that land or in the monks’ court. In order that this might not be erased by forgetfulness in succeeding times or weakened by posterity, with the consent of Philip our son, already crowned king, we have committed it to writing and confirmed it by the authority of our seal and the character of our name, in the presence in our palace of those whose names and signs are subscribed.

Sign of Philip the younger king. Sign of Louis, butler. [Col. 1061B] Sign of Hugh, constable. Sign of Manasses, chamberlain.

Done in the year of the incarnate Word 1130, the twenty-second of our reign.

Given by the hand of Simon, chancellor.

## V. Charter of King Louis concerning the toll at Montreuil and the exactions which he granted to the Church of Cluny. (1130.)

In the name of the holy and indivisible Trinity. I, LOUIS, by the grace of God king of the French, wish it to be known to all, future as well as present, that, with the consent of Philip our son, already crowned king, and Queen Adelaide, for the remedy of our soul and of the souls of [Col. 1061C] our predecessors, we have given and granted in perpetuity to the holy Church of Cluny that none of the brothers of Cluny shall henceforth pay any pediale toll at Montreuil, nor any custom belonging to royal administration. We have also commanded that none of the royal officials shall henceforth demand this in any manner from any of the aforesaid brothers. If anyone should presume to do so, let him know that he has made himself not only guilty before the divine majesty, but also a transgressor of our decree.

That this may stand firm, we have committed it to writing and confirmed it by the authority of our seal and the character of our name, in the presence in our palace of those whose names and signs are subscribed.

Sign of Philip the younger king. [Col. 1061D] Sign of Louis, butler. Sign of Hugh, constable. Sign of Manasses, chamberlain. No seneschal being present.

Done in the year of the incarnate Word 1130, the twenty-second of our reign.

Given by the hand of Simon, chancellor.

## VI. Concerning one hundred marks in England. (1131.)

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son PETER, abbot of Cluny, and his successors regularly appointed in perpetuity.

“Gifts and benefices,” etc. See under Innocent II, at the year 1143.

## VII. Charter of Ambronay. (1132.)

[Col. 1062A]

The truth of things done, if it is solemnly committed to writing for the sake of remembrance and thereby preserved, is an authority of no slight worth. Therefore, availing ourselves of this, we have taken care to make known to our successors in writing that I, called Hisinio, abbot of Ambronay, and Lord Peter, abbot of Cluny, in the presence of Lord Pope Innocent, agreed and ratified the agreement in his hand: namely, that the dispute which had existed between us concerning the place of Prins should be settled by the judgment and counsel of Lord Ilio, abbot of St. Just.

After counsel had been taken, it pleased Lord Ilio and the others who were present with him that our dispute should be resolved by the following agreement: the Church of Cluny should possess that place of Prins by right of ownership; but the Church of Ambronay should retain, by parochial right, the burials, tithes, and offerings of the aforesaid estate insofar as it belongs to its parish, except the burial of its own household and the tithes of its own house. Concerning these it was decided that the brothers of that place should pay the Church of Ambronay seven ass-loads of rye each year for all their proper tithes; and that they should have free burial for their own household, unless perhaps one of their hired servants is from our parishioners and chooses to be buried in his own parish: no one shall oppose that person’s last will.

Nor shall the men of Ambronay have any authority to bury [Col. 1062C] parishioners without the guidance or consent of the priest whose parishioner the person is. The customary freedom of knights, however, is reserved, as is that of their wives, sons, and daughters, who may be buried wherever they choose. If anyone from another parish should choose to be buried in that place, or if any parishioner of the Church of Ambronay should wish, for the salvation of his soul, to offer the brothers of that place something movable or immovable—excepting our lands—they shall hold it by right of grant under our agreement.

Witnesses to this matter are: Lord Ilio, by whose hand it was done; Matthew, bishop of Albano; Stephen of Condiac; William of Marciac; and many others.

Done at Lyons in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation [Col. 1062D] 1132, in the second year of the pontificate of Lord Pope Innocent II.

## VIII. Diploma of Pope Innocent II concerning the obedience of Limanz. (1132.)

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son in Christ PETER, abbot of Cluny, and his successors regularly appointed in perpetuity.

“Matters relating to the peace of the Church,” etc. See under Innocent II, at the year 1143.

## IX. Confirmation of Saints Facundus and Primitian [Primitivus] in Spain. (1133.)

[Col. 1063A]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son PETER, abbot of Cluny, and his successors regularly appointed in perpetuity.

“The Lord came to bring fire,” etc. See above.

## X. Charter concerning Ledecombe [otherwise Labdecombe] in England and one hundred marks of silver. (1136.)

STEPHEN, king of the English, to the archbishops, bishops, abbots, counts, barons, and all his faithful established throughout England, greeting.

[Col. 1063B] Know that King Henry, my uncle and predecessor, of venerable memory, for the soul of his father, my grandfather, and for the souls of our fathers and predecessors, gave in alms every year to God and to the church of Blessed Peter at Cluny one hundred marks of silver from his own treasury. I, moreover, being by obligation both successor and devoted imitator of his good deeds, and a diligent executor through the grace of heavenly mercy, assign in perpetuity to that church, in the fixed revenues of the land specified below, what my aforesaid uncle bestowed upon it in money from his treasury. I give and grant forever to that church, in place of those hundred marks of silver, my manor of Ledecombe, which is of my own demesne.

[Col. 1063C] For I will and firmly command that Cluny hold that manor, with all its customs and appurtenances in lands and demesne, [lacuna] with all the exemptions, liberties, and property belonging to that manor, as freely as that manor had them when it was in my hand and in that of my predecessors. And that this my grant may endure forever, ratified and unshaken, for that church, I confirm and strengthen it by the attestation of my present seal and the subscription of those named below.

At Winchester, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1136, the first of my reign.

Sign of King Stephen. Sign of Queen Matilda. [Col. 1063D] Sign of Eustace, the king’s son. Sign of Henry of Soilly. Sign of Henry, bishop of Winchester. Sign of Roger, bishop of Salisbury. Sign of Alexander, bishop of Lincoln. Sign of Nigel, bishop of Ely. Sign of Alan, count of Richmond. Sign of Roger, count of Warwick. Sign of Alberic de Vere. Sign of Robert de Vere. Sign of Albert de Lacy.

## XI. Confirmation concerning Labdecombe.

HENRY, by the grace of God king of the English, lord of Ireland, duke of Normandy and Aquitaine, count of Anjou, [Col. 1064A] to archbishops, bishops, abbots, priors, counts, barons, justices, vicars, provosts, officials, and all his bailiffs and faithful, greeting.

We have inspected the confirmation of H., king, our grandfather, in the following words:

“HENRY, by the grace of God king of the English, duke of Normandy and Aquitaine, and count of Anjou, to archbishops, bishops, abbots, counts, barons, justices, vicars, and all his faithful, French and English throughout all England, greeting. Know that I grant and confirm to God and the Church of St. Peter of Cluny, and to the monks serving God there, the manor of Ledecombe in perpetual alms, for the salvation of King H., my grandfather, and all my predecessors, and for my own salvation. King Stephen gave and assigned that manor to them in return for the hundred marks which the aforesaid King Henry used to give every year to the same Church of Cluny.

“Therefore I will and firmly command that the aforesaid Church and monks hold that manor well, peacefully, freely, quietly, and honourably in perpetuity, with all its appurtenances in woodland and open land, meadows, pastures, waters, mills, ponds, men and their tenures, and with all its liberties, as fully, freely, and advantageously as King Henry ever held it in my hand.” Witnesses:

R., bishop of Winchester; G., bishop of Ely; John, bishop of Norwich; H., bishop of Durham; William, count of Arundel; the count of Mandeville; [Col. 1064C] Richard de Lucy; Richard de Camville; Ranulf de Glanville; Hugh de Cressy; Thomas de Bardum; Bertram de Verdun; William son of Ralph; Ralph Briter. At Northampton.

We therefore hold this grant ratified and accepted, and grant and confirm it for ourselves and our heirs to the abbot of Cluny and the monks serving God there. Witnesses: the venerable fathers W., bishop of Carlisle, and W., bishop of Worcester; John, count of Lincoln and constable of Chester; Simon de Montfort; William de Ralegh; Peter de Malolacu; John son of Geoffrey; Amaury of St. Amand; Geoffrey, dispenser; William Gernum; and others.

Given by the hand of the venerable Father R., [Col. 1064D] bishop of Chichester, our chancellor, at Westminster, on 22 January, in the twenty-second year of our reign.

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son PETER, abbot of Cluny, and his brothers, present and future, regularly appointed in perpetuity.

“For this purpose in the government of the Apostolic See,” etc. See Innocent II, *Patrologia*, vol. CLXXIX.

[Col. 1065A]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son in Christ PETER, abbot of Cluny, and his successors regularly appointed in perpetuity.

“The good and diligent householder,” etc. See above.

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son in Christ PETER, abbot of Cluny, and his successors regularly appointed in perpetuity.

[Col. 1065B] “The good and diligent householder,” etc. See above.

## XV. Concerning the grant of two altars in the diocese of Amiens. (1138.)

In the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Amen. GUARINUS, by the grace of God humble bishop of Amiens, to the sons of holy Church, present and future: may you happily press toward the prize of the heavenly calling.

Let your charity and affection know that Bernard de Balliol, a distinguished knight, yielding wisely to divine counsels, our exhortations, and those of religious men, and making provision for the souls of his predecessors, his own salvation, and that of his successors, granted to the monastery of Cluny certain altars belonging to himself and his predecessors by hereditary right. Although a layman, he had long held them unjustly, to the peril of his soul; but, moved by divine inspiration, he granted them to Cluny.

His brothers, his wife Matilda, his sons Ingelrannus, Wido, Eustace, and Bernard, and his daughter Hatuildis attended this grant; and, for the remedy of their souls, willingly gave their consent. Delivering the same altars into our hands, they freely and quietly relinquished them of their own accord. Considering the religious life of the monastery of Cluny, in the presence of our archdeacons Ralph [Col. 1065D] and Baldwin, our priests Achard and Walter, and many others, clergy and laity alike, religious persons and many of Bernard’s men, we gave these same altars and confirm them in perpetuity by episcopal authority, saving the customary payments anciently rendered by the altars to the Church of Amiens, to ourselves, our successors, and our officers.

That is: the monks who serve God in the church of Lord Peter shall pay one mark of silver each year to the chapter of Cluny, and shall thus freely and quietly retain, for the uses and expenses of their church, all revenues of these altars: namely, the church of Lord Peter; the altar of Balliol; the altar of Turs; the altar of [Col. 1066A] Ardicuria; the altar of Ramburellis; and the altar of Alenai.
