Done happily in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1138, indiction II. Amen.

## XVI. Confirmation of the house of Montpellier, and of St. Gervasius and St. Renobert. (1138.)

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son PETER, abbot of Cluny, and his successors regularly appointed in perpetuity.

“Those whom the almighty Lord,” etc. See Innocent II, *Patrologia*, vol. CLXXIX.

## XVII. Agreement between Cluny and St. Benedict-on-the-Po. (1140.)

[Col. 1066B]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the abbot and convent of Cluny, greeting and apostolic blessing.

“To those coming to the Apostolic See,” etc. See above.

## XVIII. Grant of the churches of Barbona, Lintis, and Lintellis, and of one prebend in the church of St. Peter of Troyes, by Lord Hato, bishop.

In the name of the holy and indivisible Trinity. HATO, by the grace of God humble minister of the Church of Troyes, to all the faithful in perpetuity.

The supreme power of God, wisely governing all things and mercifully coming to instruct human life, has wisely foreseen and justly and piously ordained that those devoted to ecclesiastical services should rightly receive ecclesiastical benefices. Whatever, therefore, we strive to accomplish for the benefit of God’s servants, we trust will profit us toward the attainment of eternal blessedness.

Accordingly, we wish it to be known to the faithful, present and future, that our most beloved brothers of Cluny humbly approached us and asked us, for the love of God, to deem worthy of granting some benefice to that most holy house of Cluny. Since divine mercy does not permit one to close one’s ears to just petitioners, we considered their request pious and gladly assented to it. We have given and granted the church of Barbona, [Col. 1066D] and the churches of Lintis and Lintellis, to possess by perpetual right, on the following terms: the priest Iterius, for as long as he lives, shall pay five solidi every year to the Church of Cluny from the church of Barbona; and my nephew Wiricus, ten solidi during his lifetime.

After their deaths, the three aforesaid churches shall come into the monks’ own possession, so that they may freely choose suitable priests for those churches. Upon presentation to the bishop of Troyes, those priests shall receive from his hand the care of souls. The monks, moreover, shall make measured provision for those priests from ecclesiastical benefices.

With the approval and consent of our clergy, and at the request and insistence of Pope Innocent, we have also given to the Church of Cluny one prebend in the church of Blessed Peter at Troyes, to hold in perpetuity. Lest this should be altered or weakened through any antiquity of time or change of persons, we have ordered this charter to be strengthened by the authority of our seal and to bear below it the names of suitable persons who were present.

Sign of Odo, archdeacon. Sign of Manasses, archdeacon. Sign of Fulk, archdeacon. Sign of Teger, canon. Sign of Wiricus, the bishop’s nephew.

## XIX. Confirmation of St. Remigius of Plaore [Plaiotro], of Barbona, of Lintis, of Lintellis, and of St. Silvester in the diocese of Troyes.

[Col. 1067B]

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons PETER, abbot, and the monks of Cluny, greeting and apostolic blessing.

“Those matters granted to you and your brothers,” etc. See Innocent II, *Patrologia*, vol. CLXXIX.

## XX. Confirmation concerning Prins, with its appurtenances.

INNOCENT, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons in Christ PETER, abbot, and the monks of Cluny, in perpetuity.

“From the administration of the Apostolic See,” etc. See above.

## XXI. Diploma of Pope Lucius concerning St. Saba with its appurtenances. (1144.)

[Col. 1067C]

LUCIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son PETER, abbot of Cluny, and his successors regularly appointed in perpetuity.

“Although the care of all churches,” etc. See Lucius II, at the year 1145.

## XXII. Diploma of Pope Eugenius III concerning Calderia of Ledone.

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons PETER, abbot of Cluny, and his brothers, present and future, professing the regular life, in perpetuity.

“Those things which are done by the faithful of God’s Church,” etc. See Eugenius III, at the year 1153.

## XXIII. Charter of Count William concerning the agreement between himself and Lord Peter, abbot of Cluny, respecting the monasteries of Mauziac and Celsiniac.

[Col. 1067D]

The prudent custom has been to commit to writing deeds performed for salvation, lest they fall from human memory through the passage of time. Let it therefore be known that I, William, Count of Auvergne, in restoring peace with Lord Peter, Abbot of Cluny, and his brethren, for the wrongs which I unjustly inflicted upon the monasteries of Mozac and Sauxillanges, freely give to the aforesaid monastery of Mozac and its inhabitants, and grant them to possess for ever, one half of all the tolls which shall at any time be collected in the town of Riom. But if anyone should raise a dispute against the aforesaid inhabitants concerning this half of the tolls, I, the same WILLIAM, by satisfying the claimant, shall cause the monks of Mozac to retain it in peace.

[Col. 1068A] Concerning the market called that of Charnac, I willingly restore and grant to be held for ever to the prior of Sauxillanges and his monks one half of all provisions, such as salt; and also the annual rent which can be collected from the land on which the market is held—only from that land which belongs by right to Saint Peter—according to the arrangement established, or to be established, for each person. If at any time (which God forbid) I, or anyone subject to my power, should commit any wrong against the monks or their men at the aforesaid markets, or if anyone should do so, and the abbot of Mozac, the prior of Sauxillanges, or someone acting in their name should warn me to make amends, I swear to satisfy them with my own hand within forty days after the warning.

Moreover, I renounce the evil customs concerning tolls which I, or my men through me, introduced within the town called Charnac, and the other injuries which I unjustly inflicted upon the people of the town or upon the prior of that place. Likewise, with regard to Vareris, Brenac, and the other lands belonging to the right of Sauxillanges which I invaded by occupation or devastation of the woods, I shall compel satisfaction to be made to the aforesaid prior and to the inhabitants of the church.

For the restoration of this peace it was also necessary that I and Eustace, abbot of Mozac, should order those whom we knew to be the worthier men of that town to be bound by oath, so that they might state unanimously what customs my father had peacefully maintained in the town of Mozac and with which I should be content.

[Col. 1068B] This was accordingly done. In return for these customs, I shall faithfully protect the town and its inhabitants, as well as strangers coming and going and their goods deposited in the town. I shall faithfully protect the market of Mozac and the market of Sauxillanges, as I do the market of Riom and that of Charnac. I shall also allow free men who have gone from the abbot’s town into my own to return freely. If any should perhaps refuse to return, the abbot may arrange and dispose as he wishes, and to whom he wishes, of the lands belonging to the right of Mozac which they had held. Those subject to customary obligations, however, shall return to their own places, except one who shall remain, as has been decreed.

[Col. 1068C] Moreover, if I or my men have occupied any lands belonging by right to Saint Austremonius, I renounce them and shall cause my men to renounce them. If anyone should refuse to render justice concerning any of our people, I shall not fail the abbot in enforcing his right.

I, Count William, made this settlement of the dispute and this peace in the chapter-house at Cluny with Peter, abbot of that monastery; Eustace, abbot of Mozac; and Peter, prior of Sauxillanges; in the presence of the community of the same monastery, Ademarus, Stephen of the Castle, Stephen of Ermonens, Bertrand Rigaldellus, and many others. I order this charter, containing the terms of this peace and to remain valid for ever, to be secured by my own seal; and I ask and desire that the bishop and chapter of Clermont, and also the lord pope, do the same.

## XXIV. Charter of Alfonso, Emperor of Spain, concerning Saint Vincent of Salamanca. (Year 1153.)

[Col. 1069A]

Since Scripture exhorts us to do good to all churches and churchmen, the true worshippers of God, alms ought especially to be bestowed upon them, according to that saying of the Apostle: “While we have time, let us do good to all, but especially to those of the household of faith” (Gal. 6). Therefore I, Alfonso, Emperor of Spain, together with my wife Berengaria, with grateful heart and of my free will, for the salvation of myself and my parents, and for the remission of our sins, give in hereditary right to the Church of Cluny, founded in honour of Saint Peter, and to Lord Peter, abbot of that church, and to all the monks serving God there and their successors for ever, the church of Saint Vincent of Salamanca, with all its inheritances given to it either by me or by others. At the request and with the consent of Lord Aliuco, prior of that church, and Lord Berengarius, bishop of the same city, I grant it to them to possess hereditarily for ever.

[Col. 1069B] That is, I give the aforesaid church of Saint Vincent to the aforesaid Church of Cluny and to the aforesaid Lord Peter, its abbot, so that he may change the canonical habit now worn there into the monastic habit, and may always govern and provide for that church and its possessions as father and lord.

If any ecclesiastical or secular person should hereafter oppose this my gift and violate it, may he be cursed by almighty God and condemned in hell with Judas the traitor, unless he repents; moreover, for his rash presumption, after restoring twice the inheritance taken from the Church of Cluny, he shall pay one thousand marks of silver to the royal authority.

[Col. 1069C] The charter was made at Nájera, on the fourth day before the Kalends of November [29 October], in the era 1181, while the aforesaid Emperor Alfonso ruled at Toledo, León, Saragossa, Nájera, Castile, and Galicia.

I, Alfonso, Emperor, make this gift to the Church of Cluny concerning the aforesaid church of Saint Vincent into the hand of Lord Guy, cardinal and legate of the Roman Church; I give it, confirm it by my authority, and grant that it shall remain firm and stable for all time.

[Col. 1069D] I, Empress Berengaria, confirm it. I, Sancho, the emperor’s elder son. I, Raymond, Archbishop of Toledo. I, Peter, Archbishop of Compostela.

## XXV. Confirmation of Saint Vincent of Salamanca in Spain

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons PETER, Abbot of Cluny, and his brethren: greeting and apostolic blessing.

“Since, by the duty laid upon us,” etc. See under Celestine II, *Patrologia*, vol. CLXXIX.

## XXVI. Charter of Lord Frederick, Emperor, concerning the monastery of Baume. (Year 1153.)

[Col. 1070A]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Frederick, by the favouring mercy of God, august king of the Romans.

If we graciously receive the vows and petitions of religious persons, and bestow gracious favour upon them for the cultivation of divine religion, we do not doubt that, by a happy exchange, we acquire for ourselves the rewards both of temporal and eternal blessedness. Therefore let the diligent industry of all, present and future, know how, at the reverence and request of our beloved Peter the Venerable, Abbot of Cluny, we too strengthen and confirm by royal authority the decree of donation bestowed upon the Church of Cluny concerning the abbey of Baume and all its possessions by our reverend father Pope Eugenius III, by Humbert, Archbishop of Besançon, and by William, illustrious Count of Burgundy. By the privilege of this present charter, to remain valid for ever, we transfer them from our own lordship and that of the kingdom into the lordship of the monastery of Cluny and of its abbots, saving nevertheless the right by which the said church of Baume is known to be subject to the kingdom.

[Col. 1070B] We likewise command by royal authority that the same church shall have no advocate except one whom the abbot of Cluny may choose; and that it shall retain in firm and undisturbed peace everything which it possessed in the time of Abbot Alberic, or which it possessed at the time when the abbot of Cluny undertook its governance. We also order that all who formerly performed homage to the abbot of Baume by right shall now likewise do so to the abbot of Cluny without any objection.

For the salvation of our soul and of all our parents, we have taken under our protection the church of Baume itself and all things belonging to it. By royal authority we forbid any person, great or small, to exact from the men of that church any *districtus* [seigneurial jurisdictional levy] or other exaction, or to presume to impede the monks of Baume from pursuing their rights in their own possessions. We have judged it necessary to specify some of these by name:

[Col. 1070C] namely, the monastery of Saint Mary of Grandfontaine with all its appurtenances; the monastery of Saint Peter of Gade with all its appurtenances; the monastery of Saint Mary within the city of Besançon, called Vison, with all its appurtenances; the monastery of Saint Eugendus of Étique; the monastery of Saint Lawrence; the monastery of Saint Desiderius of Lons, with all their appurtenances; Musnet, Créancet, Noviacum, Buvliacu, Sabomacum, Lafrautem, Saint Maurice, Saint Robert; the monastery of Saint Stephen of the Bridge; the monastery of Saint Agnes, Sisinciacum, the chapel of Beneventum; the monastery of Sciense; the monastery of Dole; and the monastery of Strabon.

[Col. 1070D] All these, together with the remaining acquisitions made or to be made, we confirm by royal authority to the church of Baume and, through it, to Cluny, and grant them to be possessed for ever, adding that no one may presume to violate the settlement of this our transfer. If anyone should rashly attempt to act contrary to it in any respect, he shall be subject to the royal ban and shall pay one thousand pounds of gold to our treasury.

And that all these things may remain eternally valid and unshaken, we have ordered this present charter to be marked with the impression of our seal. The following witnesses were present, whose names appear subscribed: Arnold, Archbishop of Cologne; Gunther, Bishop of Speyer; Conrad, Bishop of Worms; Anselm, Bishop of Havelberg; Conrad, Bishop of Augsburg; Wibald, Abbot of Corvey and Abbot of Stavelot; Henry, Duke of Saxony; Henry, Duke of Bavaria; Berthold, Duke of Carinthia; Theodore, Count of Holland; Herman, Count Palatine; Hugh, Count of Tagesburch.

[Col. 1071A] The sign of the lord Frederick, first and most unconquered king of the Romans.

I, Arnold, chancellor, have authenticated it.

Given at Worms, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1153, indiction 1, on the third day before the Ides of June [11 June], in the second year of the reign of the glorious lord Frederick, king of the Romans, happily in Christ. Amen.

## XXVII. Diploma of Pope Adrian IV concerning the abbey of Baume, with its appurtenances, in the archdiocese of Besançon. (Year 1155.)

[Note: [Col. 1071D] Pope Urban III also confirmed this abbey to the monastery of Cluny in the year of the Incarnation 1185, the first of his pontificate, charter LXXIX; Clement III in 1187, the first year of his pontificate, charter XVIII; and Celestine III in 1191, the first year of his pontificate, charter LV.]

ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son in Christ PETER, Abbot of Cluny, and his successors canonically appointed for ever.

[Col. 1071C] “Glorious and wonderful,” etc. See under Adrian IV, for the year 1159.

## XXVIII. Charter of Richard, Bishop of Coutances, concerning the church of Morsalines

I, RICHARD, by God’s grace Bishop of Coutances, having been petitioned by Lord Peter the Venerable, Abbot of Cluny, confirm, by the charter and seal of my authority, the agreement made between the abbot and monks of Montebourg and the church and monks of Saint Cosmas of the Church of Morsalines: namely, that the monks of Montebourg shall have and hold two thirds of the tithe of crops from all the land which the monks of Saint Cosmas possess at Morsalines, and shall annually pay ten Angevin or Rouen shillings to the prior and monks of Saint Cosmas in acknowledgement thereof.

[Col. 1071D] The church itself, the appointment of the priest, and those things belonging to the altar and cemetery shall remain freely and peacefully with the prior and monks of Saint Cosmas. In order that this agreement between the aforesaid churches may remain valid and unshaken for ever, I confirm the same agreement, through the testimony of this present charter and by the authority of my seal, together with the letters of Lord Peter, Abbot of Cluny.

Witnesses: William, archdeacon; Peter, chaplain; Robert de Milleto; Humphrey, dean; William Malaterra; William de Vernon; Richard de Waravilla.

## XXIX. Another charter concerning the same church

To all Christ’s faithful to whom this present writing shall come, Master RICHARD, bishop, and PHILIP, Archdeacon of Coutances, greeting in the Lord.

We wish it to be known to you all that the case, which was pending before us by commission of the Apostolic See, between the abbot and monks of Montebourg on the one hand and the prior and monks of Saint Cosmas on the other, concerning the church of Morsalines, was stated in these words:

[Col. 1072A] ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons Master Richard, bishop, and Philip, archdeacon. The complaint of our beloved sons the abbot and monks of Montebourg has reached our hearing: William, prior, and the monks of Saint Cosmas, in the diocese of Coutances, unjustly retain their right in the church of Morsalines and refuse to restore it. Therefore, by apostolic letters, we command your discretion that, when the parties have appeared before you, you hear what they may put forward on either side and, setting appeal aside, bring their case to a canonical conclusion; and that, by ecclesiastical censure, you cause what you have determined to be firmly observed, etc. Given at the Lateran, on the tenth day before the Kalends of May [22 April], in the fourth year of our pontificate.

[Col. 1072B] By authority of this mandate, therefore, we summoned the parties before us; and, having heard what was advanced on both sides, we brought the disagreement between them concerning the aforementioned church of Morsalines to peace and concord in the following manner. The monks of Montebourg shall freely and peacefully possess for ever two thirds of the tithe of crops from all the land which the monks of Saint Cosmas have in the parish of Morsalines, and shall annually render ten Angevin or Rouen shillings to the prior and monks of Saint Cosmas in acknowledgement thereof.

[Col. 1072C] But the church of the same town, the appointment of its cleric, the things belonging to the altar and cemetery, together with one third of the tithe of crops, shall remain freely and peacefully for ever with the prior and monks of Saint Cosmas. This agreement was made with the assent and consent of Peter, abbot, and the brethren of Cluny, and was confirmed by the parties on either side in our presence through the taking of an oath.

And lest a complaint concerning this matter should arise anew hereafter, and what has been canonically done suffer repetition, we have strengthened this agreement by the authority of this present writing and the affixing of our seals.

[Col. 1072D] Witnesses: Alfred, cantor; Robert de Pererio, canon of Coutances; Peter, chaplain; William de Vernon; Richard de Wallivilla; Robert of Saint-Germain, then viscount; Robert the hunter; Richard de Saucerio; William de Han; Ralph Gaam; and many others.

# IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1157: ROBERT OF KETTON

[Col. 1073]

## NOTICE

(FABRICIUS, *Bibliotheca mediae et infimae Latinitatis*, vol. VI, p. 107.)

Robertus Retenensis—rather than Ketenensis, as certain manuscript codices cited by Montfaucon have it—an Englishman, travelled through France, Italy, Dalmatia, Greece, and Syria, and finally settled in Spain. He died as archdeacon of Pamplona. He translated into Latin the *Alcoran*, reduced to a compendium; it was published at Nuremberg in 1543 in volume I of Bibliander’s *Mahometica*, and at Basel in 1543–1550. His preface to the *Alcoran*, addressed to Peter the Venerable, Abbot of Cluny, is found in the *Bibliotheca Cluniacensis*. Huet does not judge this translation very favourably in *De claris interpretibus*, p. 141. A Vatican manuscript, in Montfaucon’s catalogue of manuscripts, p. 74, attributes to him the *Deeds concerning Jerusalem*; learned men may judge of this. The *Chronicles of the Saracens* are ascribed to him in the Library of the King of France.

[Col. 1073]

## ANOTHER NOTICE

(ANTONIO, *Bibliotheca Hispana vetus*, vol. II, p. 25.)

A certain Peter, Master of Toledo, lived at about the same time (1157). The record survives of his work in the translation of the *Alcoran* from Arabic into Latin, made by order of Peter the Venerable, Abbot of Cluny, then staying in Spain, in a certain manuscript codex which belonged to Marsilio Ficino as a gift from the two full brothers Antonio and Michele Miniati, and was written in 1459. Martin Sireula, formerly one of our few friends while he lived, a portionary canon of our metropolitan church at Seville, a man remarkable for integrity and learning, assured us that he had seen it himself, or at least had obtained from it the notes which we now reproduce. The book contained a Latin translation of the *Alcoran*, and at its end this note:

“By command of the illustrious Peter, Abbot of Cluny, his Englishman Robert of Ketton translated this book in the year of Christ 1143, the year of Alexander 1043, the year of the Hijra 536, and the year of the Persians 511.”

Yet this second note followed it:

“This book was caused to be translated from Arabic into Latin by Lord Peter, Abbot of Cluny, through Peter, Master of Toledo, while the abbot himself was residing in Spain with the glorious Alfonso, in the year when the glorious emperor made the city of Coria …”

[Note: [Col. 1073] You may read substantially the same words in Royal Library of Turin manuscript 156, vol. I, p. 46, col. I; likewise in another manuscript of John Selden’s in the Bodleian, class VII, codex 3419; and finally in the Dresden Zaluski Library catalogue of Johann Daniel Andreas Janocki, 1752, codex 258, p. 77. We have thought it desirable to transcribe them in full, and in the same order of writing, so that at a single glance the reader may observe the variant readings and decide for himself, and form a judgement, concerning the true author of this translation.]

[Note: [Col. 1073] The following three columns—REGIUS TAURINENSIS, ODLEIANUS, and ZALUSCIANUS—appear in parallel in Migne.]

### ROYAL TURIN MANUSCRIPT

“At the command of the illustrious Peter, Abbot of Cluny, his Englishman Robert of Kertnensis translated this book in the year of Christ 1143; in the year of Alexander 1403; in the year of the Hijra 537; and in the year of the Persians 511.

“Lord Peter, Abbot of Cluny, caused this book to be translated from Arabic into Latin by Peter, Master of Toledo, while he himself, the abbot, was residing in Spain with the glorious Alfonso, in the year when the emperor took the city of Coria.”

### BODLEIAN MANUSCRIPT

“At the command of the most illustrious and glorious Peter, Abbot of Cluny, his Englishman Robertus Retinensis translated this book in A.D. 1143, in the year of Alexander 1403, in the year of the Hijra 537, and in the year of the Persians 511.

“Lord Peter, Abbot of Cluny, caused this book to be translated from Arabic into Latin by Peter, Master of Toledo, with the assistance of Peter the monk-scribe, while the same lord and venerable abbot was residing in Spain with the glorious Emperor Alfonso, in the year when that emperor took the city of Coria and drove the Saracens out of it.”

### ZALUSKI MANUSCRIPT

**Title of the book.**

“At the command of the illustrious and most glorious Peter, Abbot of Cluny, his Englishman Robertus Retenensis translated this book in the year of Christ’s birth 1143, in the year of Alexander 1403, in the year of the Hijra 537, and in the year of the Persians 511.”

**Thus far the title of the book. At its end, however, one reads:**

“Lord Peter, Abbot of Cluny, caused this book to be translated from Arabic into Latin by Peter, Master of Toledo, with the assistance of Peter, monk-scribe, while that same lord and venerable abbot was residing in Spain with the glorious Emperor Alfonso, in the year when that same glorious emperor took the city of Coria and drove the Saracens out of it.”

[Note: [Col. 1073] Thomas Tanner, bishop of St Asaph, in his *Bibliotheca Britannico-Hibernica*, p. 454, under Ketton (Robert), or Retinensis, has nearly the same account, borrowed from the Bodleian manuscript. Of these three codices, however, the Turin manuscript is recent, written in the sixteenth century; the Bodleian has no date, nor does the Zaluski manuscript, which is nevertheless called very ancient by the founder of that library. The other manuscript, seen by Martin Sireula according to our authority, was said to have been written in 1459. All agree in asserting that Peter, Master of Toledo, translated the book of the *Alcoran* from Arabic into Latin.]

[Col. 1075A]

It is certainly said that Peter of Cluny engaged Robert of Ketton, interpreter of the *Alcoran*, who lived in this century and, returning from the East, remained in Spain after obtaining the archdeaconry of the sacred church at Pamplona, for substantial payment to complete this work. This was acknowledged by Nicholas of Cusa in his *Cribratio* of the same *Alcoran*; by John Pits in *On the Illustrious Writers of England*, under the year 1143; by Aubertus Miraeus in the supplement to *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, chapter 373; and, after others, by the Saxon August Pfeiffer in his *Collection of Philological Dissertations*, dissertation 4. Yet, on Erpenius’s authority, Pfeiffer associates with this Ketton a certain Hermann of Dalmatia as his companion in that translation.

Our aforementioned Sireula, prompted by this, conjectured that some other work, likewise translated from Arabic into Latin by Peter of Toledo at the order of the same Peter of Cluny, had formerly been bound together with the *Alcoran* translation in that same codex, and that this later note ought to be referred to it. But the abbot of Cluny could very well have employed two translators on a work which he wished to have translated as well as possible, since Ketton’s translation is today criticized by many as not very accurate and as only rather rarely expressing faithfully, outside plainly historical material, the true meaning of the Arabic idiom—to use Erpenius’s own words.

[Note: [Col. 1075] In his preface to the old translation, appended to his edition of Sura 12 of the *Alcoran*.]

Or else it is “wholly inept and miserably perverts the meanings; moreover, it is at times harsh and thin, yet immediately swells to excessive bulk, so that no one can promise himself an understanding of the *Alcoran* from it,” as Peter Daniel Huet says in Book II of *On Interpretation*. John Albert Widmanstetter, German jurist, furthermore warns in the preface to his *Theology of Muhammad and Epitome of the Alcoran*—which Alphonsus Ciaconius saw published at Nuremberg in 1343, as he records in his notes—that Ketton’s translation is only an epitome of the *Alcoran*. Moreover, Peter of Toledo is somewhere praised by Joseph Scaliger as an interpreter of the *Alcoran*, although the recently mentioned Pfeiffer, who collected those who devoted themselves to translating that work into Latin and into the languages of other peoples, says nothing of this Peter.

[Note: [Col. 1075] We have seen the conjectures of Martin Sireula and of our author concerning the true interpreter of the book of the *Alcoran*. Of these, the one which pleases me more is that derived from John Albert Widmanstetter’s preface: namely, that Ketton’s translation is only an epitome of the *Alcoran*; or, what comes to the same thing, that Ketton first reduced the book of the *Alcoran* to an epitome and then translated his Arabic epitome into Latin. Gesner agrees in this, saying: “He translated into Latin four books of the *Alcoran*, reduced to an epitome”; and Tanner, in the cited place, says that Ketton reduced Muhammad’s *Alcoran* to an epitome and translated it from Arabic into Latin.

But four manuscripts of the same tenor leave no room to doubt that Peter of Toledo was the interpreter of the more faithful—that is, complete—text of the *Alcoran*, for in them one reads that, at the prompting or command of Peter of Cluny, the book of the *Alcoran* was translated from Arabic into Latin by him. If you compare this with what the aforementioned codices say almost unanimously of Ketton at the very beginning of the book’s title or dedication—namely, “Robert of Ketton translated this book [of the Alcoran]”—you will find that these latter words are much more general than those written in the same codices concerning Peter of Toledo, and can apply no less to the copyist or transcriber of the codex than to its translator. Add that Peter of Toledo is somewhere praised by Joseph Scaliger as an interpreter of the *Alcoran*, as our author indicates in this same entry.

The four mentioned codices designate as 1143 after Christ’s birth the year in which the city of Coria was taken from the Saracens; but the learned Flórez argues vigorously that it was 1142, or era 1180, vol. XXI, p. 314, no. 20.]

[Col. 1075]

## PREFACE OF ROBERTUS RETENENSIS TO PETER THE VENERABLE, ON THE BOOK OF THE LAW OF THE SARACENS WHICH THEY CALL THE ALCORAN, TRANSLATED BY HIM

(It appears above, col. 657, prefixed to Peter the Venerable’s book *Against the Saracens*.)

# IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1158: WIBALD, ABBOT OF STAVELOT AND CORVEY

[Col. 1075]

## HISTORICAL NOTICE

(FABRICIUS, *Bibliotheca mediae et infimae Latinitatis*, vol. VI, p. 319.)

Wibald—called also Guibald, Wibold, and Cuicbold—was born of distinguished family near Liège, namely from the noble house of Prats. From infancy he was educated in the monastery of Stavelot; afterwards he went to the schools at Liège, where he was still studying in 1115. In 1117 he entered the monastery of Waulsort. There he directed the schools until he was made abbot of Stavelot in 1130, of Monte Cassino in 1136, and finally of Corvey in 1137; he died there in 1158.

He possessed great influence with Emperor Lothair, who calls him archchancellor of the Roman Empire in a letter drawn by Mabillon from the archives of Monte Cassino. This letter appears in our author’s *Life*, p. 165. He also took a large part in civil and military affairs. For his life, consult Peter the Deacon, *Chronicle of Monte Cassino*, IV.124 ff., and Schaten in the *Annals of Paderborn*. Above all, Edmond Martène and Ursin Durand surpassed everyone in diligence: in volume II of their *Very Large Collection*, pp. 153–183, they worked up Wibald’s life at considerable length. The same two men published 441 of his letters from a Stavelot manuscript, pp. 183 ff.; until then only one had been published, in vol. II of D’Achery’s *Spicilegium*, p. 708 of the new edition, and in vol. III of the *Acts of the Saints* for April, p. 807, addressed to Theodoric, abbot of Waulsort. In this collection it stands sixth.

[Col. 1077]

## LITERARY NOTICE

(*Literary History of France*, by Benedictine religious, vol. XII, p. 555.)

What we possess of Wibald’s literary work consists only of letters. Yet these letters, which are very numerous, prove that he was capable of producing formal works even on the most elevated subjects, and that he lacked only leisure to do so. Dom Martène collected them in the second volume of his great Collection, together with those addressed to the author or written on his occasion, making a compilation of 441 letters. An analysis of all these documents would certainly shed much light upon history; but since this would carry us too far, we must confine ourselves to what is most striking and most likely to awaken the readers’ curiosity.

The first two were written from Monte Cassino to Emperor Lothair, to implore his protection for that monastery, whose government he had obliged Wibald to assume. Nothing is more moving than their depiction of the desolation to which the troops of the king of Sicily had reduced not only Monte Cassino but the whole surrounding country.

“You had obtained, lord, before your departure,” says the author, “an oath from the Lombards and Normans that they would remain faithful to you. But alas, how much better they would have done not to swear than to commit perjury! For all who inhabit those regions have apostatized in order to turn toward Satan [lacuna]. Since your departure, finding the country peaceful, they spread everywhere with the Saracens, devastate everything, and count arson and murder as nothing [lacuna]. How many bishops, priests, deacons, monks, nobles, and commoners, of both sexes and every age, now perish beneath the swords of these barbarians! How many do they torture for money belonging either to themselves or to the Church! When torture forces these wretches to surrender what they possess, far from being set free, they are tortured still more cruelly, because it is imagined that they have yielded only part of their treasure and not all of it; so that the more they give, the more they are thought to be concealing [lacuna]. As for great buildings—churches, castles, cities—when they cannot destroy them by fire, they raze them and leave not even traces to recall their former beauty. If one is unwilling to take my word for this, I shall cite as witnesses for what I assert the towns of Pozzuoli, Alife, and Telese, where only ruins remain to prove that they once existed. A great number of other cities, once flourishing, are either entirely deserted or contain very few inhabitants [lacuna]. This is especially so with Capua, formerly the second city after Rome, the capital and glory of Campania [lacuna]. For, not content with having driven out almost all its inhabitants, they set it on fire and reduced its nobles to slavery.”

Speaking next of the damage they had done at Monte Cassino, Wibald says that in the time of Abbot Seniorectus, his predecessor, Roger, after imposing a levy upon the abbey, sent his chancellor to turn it into a fortress, remove the monks, and transport them to Sicily with the body—supposedly—of Saint Benedict, the church treasury, and all the household furnishings. The monks opposed this and would inevitably have succumbed without a reinforcement of two thousand men sent them by the emperor.

Wibald had as the master of his studies at Stavelot Reinhard, a professed monk of Helwardishusen,

[Note: [Col. 1077] Leibniz, *Scriptores Brunsvicenses*, vol. II, Introduction, article 43.]

afterwards abbot of Reinhausen in Saxony, whose origins he wrote. Gratitude on one side and affection on the other, combined with mutual esteem, formed between them an intimate and lasting correspondence, evidenced by the mutual letters they wrote one another (Ep. 12, 34, 35, 36, 36, 119).

Before leaving for Asia, Emperor Conrad had his son Henry elected King of the Romans.

[Note: [Col. 1077] Henry died in 1150.]

But because of the prince’s very tender age, he needed a guide to govern the empire during his father’s absence. The Archbishop of Mainz and Abbot Wibald were therefore appointed his regents. The prelate, satisfied with the honour of the commission, left its burden to his colleague. The letters that Wibald wrote to the prince, and the replies he received from him (Ep. 73, 87, 88, 89, 93), show the zeal with which he fulfilled his duties toward his illustrious ward and the latter’s deference to his counsel. This appears especially from the following letter of Henry to our abbot, which we shall transcribe (Ep. 89):

“Henry, by the grace of God King of the Romans, to the venerable Wibald, Abbot of Corvey, whose friendship he desires to possess in its full measure. We cannot thank you enough because, persisting since the departure of our lord and father in the attachment and fidelity which you were accustomed to show him, you make us ourselves experience their effects through the care you take to uphold and increase the honour of our rank, both among the princes of Germany and at the papal court. We are therefore disposed in all things to follow your wishes.

“Nevertheless, having appointed, by the counsel of the lords, a diet at Frankfurt for the Nativity of the Virgin, we ask you to attend, so that we may take your advice there concerning the reform of abuses and the preservation of the empire’s tranquillity. And since it is our intention that all our public and private affairs be governed by your wisdom and care, we command you to come to join us at Nuremberg on the first of September, so that, having been informed about everything concerning us, you may be able to defend our person and interests at that diet.”

There are many reciprocal letters between Wibald and his religious at Stavelot and Corvey (Ep. 14, 25, 37, 38, 40, 41, 70, 74, 76, 77, 78, 81, 82, 83, 84, 85, 86, 103, 104, 105, 106). They constitute an exchange of filial love and paternal tenderness, in which the children set before their father the difficulties to which his frequent, though unavoidable, absences exposed them; while he, on the other side, employed the soundest counsels and most effective means to console them.

We have two of his letters to his sister Hawide, a religious woman and, as stated, afterwards abbess of Gerresheim (Ep. 79, 220). In the first, he excuses the infrequency of his writing by the extent of the cares occupying him during Emperor Conrad’s absence. In the second, he congratulates her upon her advancement to the abbatial dignity and gives her excellent instructions for faithfully fulfilling its duties.

The chapter of the cathedral of Liège placed particular confidence in the wisdom of our abbot. Having a dispute with the provostships of the other churches in the city, which refused to obey it, it wrote to Wibald, who was still only abbot of Stavelot, asking him to attend a deliberation that was to be held on the matter (Epp. 90–91). In his reply, our abbot expresses surprise that, although the chapter had founded all the provostships of the city in order to enhance its own dignity, increase the number of its members, and extend its jurisdiction; although it had endowed them and until then governed them with full authority; their members should be so ill advised, ungrateful, and proud as to rise against superiors on whom they depended in several respects. It appears that the principal issue concerned appointments to these provostships, or collegiate churches: the canons maintained that the right belonged to them, while the clergy of those churches contested it.

Our author says that the canons have settled what concerns the elections of archbishops and bishops, and that the Rule of St Benedict has determined what concerns the election of an abbot; but for subordinate offices, custom alone decides. He says that he would speak more fully if he could attend the deliberation to which he was invited, but his occupations did not permit him to go.

In like manner, the canons of the Church of Paderborn addressed our abbot in 1148 (Epp. 97–98), asking him to restrain the vexations of a certain Folcuin, who continually harassed their dependants. Wibald replied that he had spoken for them to their bishop, and offered them every assistance in his power to put an end to these oppressions.

Among these canons was a capable scholasticus named Manegold (Ep. 146), another and later man than the person of the same name already mentioned. We possess a letter from him to our author (vol. IX, pp. 280–286), in which he extols Wibald’s literary learning in emphatic terms.

Wibald made a very modest reply. After thanking him for the tokens of affection contained in these praises, he says that, occupied throughout the day, he had taken a few hours from his sleep in order to answer him (Ep. 147). He addresses him in the singular, “which,” he says, “is contrary to my custom; for among our monks we are accustomed to speak in the plural”: *Contra morem meum facio, ut singulari numero loquar, qui cum monachis pluraliter dicere consuevimus*—“I act contrary to my custom in speaking in the singular, since we who live with monks are accustomed to speak in the plural.” “But,” he adds, “I am speaking to a scholastic, to a man engaged in the course of philosophy, who has drawn from the treasury of his studies the praises with which he has overwhelmed me.”

While protesting that he does not deserve such praise, Wibald nevertheless admits that he had acquired a sound acquaintance with all the branches of learning esteemed in his day. “I have learned,” he says, “under good masters the liberal arts, and matters relating to medicine and agriculture. Very orthodox and learned teachers instructed me in theology. I have read many good treatises and commentaries on sacred, ecclesiastical, and secular books; but indiscriminate and excessively varied reading yields as little profit as it gives pleasure.” The author develops this reflection for the benefit of his correspondent. He further shows him that learning is dangerous through the pride it causes when it lacks charity. “This is not, however,” he adds, “because I wish thereby to turn you away from the love you have for reading, composition, and declamation. These are exercises with which I myself occupy my time, especially striving to retain well what I have read. When I am in bed, it is my custom, while awaiting sleep, to review in my mind some difficult question that I have seen treated in a book: the arguments offered to clarify it, the method by which they are arranged, and the conclusions drawn from them.”

Manegold had particularly praised our author’s talent for speaking. On this subject Wibald tells him:

> When you credit me with any eloquence, it is your affection, not your judgment, that has dictated the praise. For much time, great study, and long practice are required to attain a knowledge of the different dispositions of minds and the way of handling them: to know how to stir the sluggishness of some, moderate the impetuosity of others, and guide them at will by the force of speech, as by powerful reins. Indeed, although nature is capable of receiving every impression one wishes to give it, and although a skilled teacher carefully teaches us the rules of eloquence, yet if practice in speaking is lacking—as it ordinarily is in cloisters—the result is that darkness obscures the light and ashes smother the fire instead of feeding it. An orator must himself be disciplined by practice in order to be able to discipline others. This strength and efficacy of eloquence has been banished from our age, since it can find no place either in secular courts or in ecclesiastical tribunals. For at the bar it is unlettered laymen who plead—men indeed sometimes endowed with good natural intelligence; but in Germany the practice is not to declaim. One is content to state the case without any ornament. The other branch of jurisprudence, namely canon law, is, I admit, exercised by very learned persons [lacuna]. But they have learned from the supreme Lawgiver: “Let your speech be: this is so, or this is not so; what is beyond this comes from evil” (Matt. 5:37). Thus, when neither suspicion nor conjecture nor any other pretext requires an extended presentation of proofs, nothing remains but simply to establish the point in dispute. “Have you done it?” “Yes, I have done it”; or, “No, I have not done it.” The masters among the Gentiles themselves established that one manner of speech belongs to the rhetorician and another to the censor.

Manegold had also lavishly praised the abbey of Corbie. Wibald admits that it was in good condition, both spiritually and temporally; but he wished that everything there were still better regulated. “For,” he says, “nowadays disobedience is so great and minds are so little receptive to discipline that no household remains willing, I do not say to receive correction, but even to endure anything approaching it.”

He then speaks of the buildings of the abbatial residence: “Before our time,” he says, “they were ruinous and too narrow; through our care they have been rebuilt on a scale suited to receive the multitude of guests who come to us every day [lacuna]. My name,” he adds, “is inscribed above the southern gate, together with a number indicating what place I hold in the catalogue of abbots.”

Manegold had objected that our abbot used three separately written vowels at the beginning of his name, which he wrote *Uuibaud*, a practice that he regarded as contrary to correct orthography. “You think,” our author replies, “that this cannot be done regularly, and you would have the first *U*, being separate, possess the force of a vowel, or be joined to the following letter so as to stand for a consonant. But, Mr Scholasticus, if in a proper or common noun two consonants may be placed before a vowel, as in *gnato*, *gnevis*, and so forth, why may not two vowels be placed in succession in order to make one consonant? Besides, to free myself from this question, I shall add that barbarian names are expressed only with difficulty by Latin letters. We are Germans, not inhabitants of Long-haired Gaul (*Gallia Comata*), where it is customary to put a *G* at the beginning of such names in place of a *U*.”

Wibald had occasion to write several letters to Pope Eugenius (Epp. 44, 112, 120, 122, 218), and received highly satisfactory answers, in which one may observe signs of the high esteem in which that pontiff held him.

When Albero, archbishop of Bremen, died in 1148, the chapter’s first wishes for his replacement favored our abbot (Ep. 148). Yet, for reasons unknown to us, Harwich prevailed over him at the moment of election. Though victorious, this rival found it difficult to forgive the chapter’s original inclination toward Wibald, as if Wibald had secured it by intrigue. Informed of the prelate’s ill disposition, Wibald wrote to disabuse him. He tells him that, far from having intrigued to obtain his office, he had known only four persons in the chapter of Bremen: Hatwich himself, another man of the same name, the provost Erfon, and the canon Albert. He had entered the city only once, in the evening, and had left the next morning. At the time of the election he was in his monastery of Stavelot, seven days’ journey from Bremen, unaware of what was taking place there; and finally, he had made no solicitation and had sent no one there to act in his name. It appears that Harwich abandoned his prejudices, for several letters of Wibald to this prelate survive, recommending to him Wibald’s affairs and those of his friends.

In 1149 the German Benedictines held their first general chapter in Saxony (Ep. 150). Although invited, Wibald could not attend because imperial business called him into Lorraine. This he writes to the abbot of St Godehard, offering prayers for the successful outcome of the assembly and promising to devote every effort to securing execution of its decrees.

On returning from Asia, Emperor Conrad wrote from Regensburg to our abbot, announcing his arrival and thanking him for the care he had taken of the King of the Romans and of the empire’s affairs during his absence (Ep. 162).

In his reply Wibald expresses great joy at seeing him restored to his dominions (Ep. 163). “This feeling,” he says, “is shared by all who have remained faithful to you. But those who have failed in what they owe you are affected very differently by your return. They rightly dread the presence of him who has been appointed to avenge the plunder and exactions of every kind which they have committed.” Wibald then excuses himself for not having come to meet him, because the daily brigandage in Lorraine did not permit him to leave it. “Since, by divine goodness,” he adds, “you have returned safe and sound, stretch out a helping hand to the oppressed; relieve orphans; defend widows; protect the Church. This is all the easier for you to accomplish because Heaven, amid the greatest dangers and most incredible labors, has granted you the most wonderful and unexpected triumphs. Do not doubt it: your courage and ability have made you terribly formidable to your enemies. Therefore hasten to act while all are afraid; seize the moment to bend what is beginning to yield and to crush terrified rebels before they have leisure to recover from their consternation.” The author ends by complaining of the bishop of Minden, who refused to put Corbie Abbey in possession of a monastery which the emperor had united to it.

Conrad wrote a second letter to our abbot, pressing him to attend the diet he had appointed at Frankfurt for the feast of the Assumption (Ep. 169). Soon afterward Henry, this prince’s secretary, sent Wibald another letter (Ep. 170), saying that he had explained word for word to his master the letter Wibald had sent him to deliver—proof that Emperor Conrad did not understand Latin. But circumstances had not permitted Henry to press the reasons Wibald had alleged for excusing himself from coming. The prince needed his counsel both on an embassy which he proposed to send to the pope and the Romans, and on the expedition he contemplated in Italy, as well as on his plan to restore his sister, the duchess of Poland.

Wibald complied with the emperor’s wish; and while he was at court, news suddenly arrived that on 8 February 1150 the young King of the Romans had won a battle against Welfon [Note: [Col. 1081] Welfon claimed the duchy of Bavaria, of which the emperor had deprived his brother Henry the Proud in order to give it to the margrave of Austria.], uncle of Henry the Lion, duke of Saxony, and had captured him together with Gondebold, his general. This is how the news is recounted in two letters which our abbot wrote immediately (Epp. 184–218). But the report of Welfon’s capture proved false: for Emperor Conrad and the King of the Romans, writing separately to the emperor and empress of Constantinople (Epp. 187–190), both say that Welfon escaped under cover of night: *Noctis beneficio adjutus vix evasit*—“aided by the favor of night, he barely escaped” (Ep. 188).

In a letter to Herman, bishop of Constance (Ep. 186), our abbot complains that this victory—overlooked by modern German historians—was not used to secure all the advantage that might have been hoped from it. At the diet of Fulda, held immediately afterward, a treacherous counsellor, whom he does not name and whom he calls a new Ahithophel, argued, he says, that rather than press Welfon to the end by arms, the sanctity of the approaching Lent required that he instead be summoned to a regular judicial hearing and that mercy be shown to the prisoners taken from him.

> The peaceful office with which we are invested did not allow us to say plainly what we thought; but, to speak openly to a bishop and father, we were convinced that it was expedient for not merely one man but several to die, lest the whole nation perish. The speech of that cunning old man was a popular speech, well suited to the negligence, indolence, and carelessness of men in our day. Yet we refuted it sufficiently by maintaining that success in war depends on the reputation of one’s arms; that great enterprises require swiftness; that delays have always harmed those prepared to act; and that the voice of those much-vaunted judicial proceedings was heard only in a small number of towns and villages, whereas the fame of a military exploit of any brilliance resounded through the greater part of the world. But I was not heard. The unarmed man was obliged to yield to the arguments of an armed man, who nevertheless, with his arms, had prevented the prince whom he sought to persuade from setting the final seal upon his victories. Thus it has happened that, by ceasing to wage war and without exercising judicial power, we waste time feeding upon vain hopes. [Col. 1083]

What Wibald had predicted came to pass. But Welfon having remained inactive for a time, Conrad, secure concerning the state of Germany, occupied himself only with carrying war into Italy. His chief purpose was to conquer Apulia, both to avenge himself on King Roger, who was fostering Welfon’s revolt, and to create a diversion in favor of his brother-in-law, the emperor of Constantinople, whom that prince was devastating through frequent incursions and conquests in the Greek Empire (Ep. 188). Secondary designs were joined to this principal purpose: to be crowned by the pope and to restore imperial authority in the cities of Italy, most of which, especially those of Lombardy, had almost entirely cast off the yoke.

While he was preparing this expedition, he received a letter from the Roman senate and people (Ep. 211), inviting him to come and resume in this capital of the world the sovereignty which the Constantines and Justinians had exercised there. “We have seized,” they told him, “the towers and castles of all those who had conspired with the pope and the Sicilian to resist you; we have demolished some of these strongholds and hold the others in your name. But as the reward for all that we do in your service, the pope, the Frangipani, the family of Peter of León, the men and friends of the Sicilian—with the exception of Jordan, the leader of your faithful men, Tolomeo likewise, and several others—harass us on every side in order to prevent us from placing the imperial crown upon your head. Yet we vigorously repel their attacks and have already driven out several of them as dangerous enemies—as indeed they are—of the empire.”

They then announce that they had rebuilt the Milvian Bridge, which the popes had destroyed in order to close Rome’s entrance to the emperors, and that, by means of a high wall built upon it, his army could cross there without fearing attacks from Castel Sant’Angelo, occupied by the men of Peter of León.

“We have learned,” they add, “that the pope has made the following agreement with the Sicilian. The pope gave him the staff, ring, dalmatic, mitre, and sandals, promising not to send a legate into his lands unless he requested one. On his side, the Sicilian gave the pope a large sum of money to use against you and the Roman Empire.”

[Note: [Col. 1083] At the end of this letter are the following verses, expressing the Romans’ wishes:

> May the king prosper; may he obtain whatever he desires over his enemies;  
> May he hold the Empire, sit in Rome, and rule the world,  
> Prince of the lands, as Justinian did;  
> [Col. 1084] Let Caesar receive from the priest what is Caesar’s own,  
> As Christ commanded when Peter paid the tribute.]

The deputies entrusted with this letter were the senator Guy, James son of Sixtus the procurator, and Nicholas, counsellor of the Roman court—that is, of the senate.

Informed of this action, the pope had Cardinal Guy, chancellor of the Roman court, write to our abbot, asking him to dissuade the emperor from undertaking anything against the rights of the Holy See (Ep. 214). Guy died shortly after this letter.

Wibald addressed his response to the pope himself, assuring him that the emperor had no evil intention either against him or against the Holy See (Ep. 218).

Welfon, meanwhile, at the instigation of the king of Sicily, had crossed into Italy (Ep. 239). The Frangipani secretly introduced him into Rome, but the senators expelled him. Some of his men were captured and found carrying letters from the king of Sicily to Frederick, duke of Swabia; Henry the Lion, duke of Saxony; and Conrad, duke of Cebering, urging them to declare war on the emperor. Thereupon John, secretary of the city, wrote to two German lords attached to the emperor in order to warn them of the conspiracy.

As war with Welfon was about to begin again, he obtained from the emperor a conference at Cranaha in order to consider whether some means of settlement might be found. As the emperor was preparing to go, he hesitated for fear of a surprise attack. Our abbot wrote to dispel his suspicions and make him see the bad impression which his absence would produce on the minds of the lords, leading them to think that he suspected their fidelity (Ep. 240). “Go,” he tells him, “to this conference with the equipment befitting a master and an emperor; and if anyone’s good faith appears to waver there, you will certainly gain this point: your enemies will no longer wish to trust one who has not acted sincerely with you. Besides, let neither the insinuations, flatteries, nor threats of anyone make you abandon the courageous resolution you have taken to wage war on that proud man and reduce him beneath your feet.”

History does not tell us the outcome of this conference. But even if circumstances compelled Welfon to renounce his claims upon Bavaria, subsequent events showed that this renunciation was no more sincere than that which had been extracted a few years earlier from his nephew Henry the Lion.

From time immemorial, the monastery of Hastière [Note: [Col. 1084] Then in the diocese of Liège; today in that of Namur.] had had no abbot other than the abbot of Waulsort. Under the government of Thierry II, successor of Widric, the monks of Hastière attempted in 1151 to escape this dependence by giving themselves a particular abbot. Wibald, a professed monk of Waulsort, did not forget the interests of his house on this occasion. He wrote to the religious of Hastière to point out the rashness of their undertaking (Ep. 270). Seeing that they would not listen, he addressed a letter to Thierry, bishop of Metz, asking him to restrain this revolt by his authority (Ep. 271). The prelate sent Wibald, in a gracious reply, all his powers for reducing the factionalists. The bishop of Liège, following a second letter from Wibald (Ep. 272), also came to the assistance of the abbot of Waulsort; and in a synod he [Col. 1085] suspended the monks of Hastière from clerical functions until they returned to obedience and subordination. To make these measures more effective, Wibald obtained from the emperor a diploma dated 1151 which, after examination of the title-deeds, confirmed Waulsort Abbey’s jurisdiction over the house of Hastière (Ep. 276).

In the same year, a diet was held at Würzburg on 11 June. After the Italian expedition had been decided upon, the abbot of Corbie was appointed, along with Arnoul, provost of the Church of Cologne and vice-chancellor of the empire, to go and notify those concerned of this decision. The commission pleased neither man, because it was to be executed at their own expense. They wrote to the emperor asking to be released from it (Epp. 260–264); but when the prince insisted, Wibald himself urged Arnoul to comply with his will (Ep. 263). Conrad nevertheless soon changed his mind regarding these two ambassadors and substituted the bishops of Basel and Constance (Ep. 279).

While the two prelates were on their way, Arnoul was promoted to the archbishopric of Cologne (Ep. 315). Since he was obliged to go to Rome for consecration, the opportunity was used to send a new embassy to Italy, whose duties Wibald and Secretary Henry shared with him. They carried three letters from Conrad: one to the Roman people, thanking them for their attachment and fidelity and exhorting them to concert their measures with the ambassadors sent to them (Ep. 322); a second to the pope, assuring him that the Italian expedition aimed only at the advantage of the Church and the Holy See (Ep. 323); and a third to the Pisans, urging them to have ready the troops and ships needed for a landing on the coast of Naples (Ep. 324).

Arnoul and his two colleagues had scarcely returned when, with Conrad’s death [Note: [Col. 1085] Conrad died, as already stated, on 15 February 1152 at Bamberg.], they saw his great designs for Italy expire. In announcing his death to the religious of Corbie, Wibald orders them to celebrate, solemnly and royally, the obsequies of a prince to whom they were under such great obligations (Ep. 340). In this letter he gives moving expression to the grief caused him by this loss.

Frederick, surnamed Barbarossa, nephew of the deceased emperor, succeeded him ten days after his death. Wibald informed Pope Eugenius of this double event (Ep. 344). “What we feared, venerable Father,” he tells him, “has therefore occurred”—he speaks of Conrad’s death—“and this is why, as though I had been a prophet, when I was with you I urged and pressed you to accept the reasonable and sound terms of peace that the Romans might offer you.” After recounting the new emperor’s election, he says that on the day after his coronation the prelates present urged him to follow his predecessor’s plan of avenging the injuries done to the Holy See. “But,” he adds, “the lay lords, perhaps through simplicity, turned him from it, arguing that it was unsuitable for the prince, at the beginning of a reign, to contract an undertaking of such importance, lest the discontented take the occasion of so sudden a departure to proceed to the utmost extremities.”

Stephen, bishop of Bamberg, having been appointed ambassador to Rome, our abbot composed for this prelate a lengthy instruction which he sent him with a letter (Ep. 346), asking him to excuse the liberty he took on behalf of their old friendship. “In our youth,” he says, “when we entered the court about thirty years ago, we found in certain grave persons remnants of the imperial majesty which they retained from the ceremonial of the court of old Henry. They knew by heart the formulas of the speeches addressed to the pope and to the city; and in these formulas, whose words were, as it were, weighed in scales and measured by compasses, they did not allow us to make any change or alteration in our embassies, lest the emperor’s majesty thereby be diminished and the discipline of the palace impaired.”

Shortly after his election, Emperor Frederick wrote to Manuel, emperor of Constantinople, asking for his daughter in marriage (Ep. 387). Wibald appended to Frederick’s letter one of his own, in which he thanked the Greek emperor for a piece of silk cloth sent to him and asked him to grant his master’s wishes (Ep. 388).

Manuel replied to our abbot that he desired nothing more ardently than to strengthen peace and union between the Eastern and Western Empires; that he would omit nothing to accomplish it; and that his apocrisiaries were conveying to Frederick his intentions concerning the proposed marriage (Ep. 407). This alliance did not take place.

In a new letter to this prince, Wibald promises to contribute, as far as he can, toward removing everything that might impair harmony between the two empires (Ep. 408). He assures Manuel that he and his community offer sincere prayers for the prosperity of Manuel’s dominions, person, and arms.

Let us conclude this article with the translation of a letter from Frederick to our abbot (Ep. 413):

> What fame proclaims, your conduct proves: that among the various virtues with which your soul is adorned, fidelity holds first place, and so remarkably that it would be as difficult for you to depart from it as for the sun to lose its light. Therefore the complete confidence which we have in your wisdom and integrity leads us to regulate the most important affairs of the empire by your counsels; and, as you are the most distinguished among our faithful men for uprightness, zeal, and ability, we also desire you to be foremost and most assiduous in our counsels. If we have allowed some time to pass without summoning you to us, it is because, after the incredible labors which you endured in the Italian expedition and in your embassy to Greece, we believed that we ought to allow you some rest. Another reason is that we had not come sufficiently near your region to call you to our court without inconveniencing you. But now that we are directing our route toward the Low Countries, and wish to conduct all the affairs of that province by your prudent counsels, we ask you to join us at Nijmegen on the third Sunday after Easter. Moreover, we inform you that, having recently learned that the Greeks have been entirely driven from Apulia, we have judged it fitting to exempt the princes from the expedition against that country which we had decided upon at Würzburg. We are persuaded that our attention should be directed principally toward the matters in which the glory of the empire is involved and toward injuries which we can no longer dissemble without compromising our honor. We mean the insolence and rashness of the Milanese, which, as you know, is most ruinous to the churches and cities of Lombardy, which they have destroyed and continue daily to destroy, in contempt and disgrace of our empire. Certainly, unless we use our power and act swiftly to forestall their designs, the empire is threatened with the greatest disasters. Therefore, at the diets of Fulda and Ulm, with the advice of the princes, we determined upon an expedition against Milan, which is to begin on the eve of Pentecost next year. We notify you of this decision and commend its success to your prudence. Furthermore, since you had our seal elegantly engraved according to your own design, we ask you likewise to have the empress’s seal engraved and bring it to us at Aachen in good condition. [Col. 1087]

This letter is from the year 1157.

We leave this fine collection with regret. In respect of history, we regard it as a precious and abundant mine, scarcely yet worked. Wibald’s letters have, over all the other letters contained in it, this advantage: historical anecdotes, although highly interesting, form only their least merit. They bear, moreover, in strongly impressed characters, the stamp of a soul strong, vigorous, and elevated; no less firm in adversity than moderate in prosperity; of a noble and religious heart; of sound judgment and exquisite discernment; of a broad genius, fertile in resources and capable of applying them; and of a mind endowed with great natural facility and cultivated by sound studies. Although most were written in haste, they have neither the dryness nor the negligence characteristic of ordinary dispatches. Their diction is correct, pleasing, and ornate, interspersed with maxims sometimes drawn from the author’s own thought, sometimes borrowed from sacred books or from ecclesiastical and secular works of antiquity, and always employed with taste.

# LETTERS OF WIBALD, ABBOT OF STAVELOT AND CORBIE, A MAN MOST DISTINGUISHED BOTH BY THE SPLENDOR OF HIS LINEAGE AND BY HIS PIETY AND ACHIEVEMENTS

(Martène, *Amplissima Collectio*, II, 153, from a contemporary manuscript codex of the imperial monastery of Stavelot: *συγχρόνω*.)

[Col. 1087]

# PRELIMINARY OBSERVATIONS

In which his Life is described from the ancient records of both monasteries and from other reliable authors.

[Col. 1087A] Since we prefixed the ancient documents of the monastery of Stavelot to Wibald’s letters [Note: [Col. 1087B] “The letters follow among us.” —Ed.], we had equally in view the learned and the ascetics of that imperial foundation itself, to whom it seemed likely to be pleasing to review their entire literary treasure thus assembled and heaped together. For, to omit for the sake of brevity that those documents contain many matters concerning Wibald—matters highly worthy of notice—which time had erased, their agreement with his letters is so great that the documents may be elucidated by the letters, and the letters in turn by the documents [Note: [Col. 1087B] See below, in the Appendix to Wibald’s letters, no. 13, the charter of Albero, issued in 1139, indiction III.]. If this must be confirmed by one or two examples, we may cite Letter 40, in which Wibald complains to Henry, bishop of Liège, concerning the nobleman Eustace: “Your Eustace, your parishioner, has invaded the village of Tornines.” Whoever wishes, therefore, to identify that Eustace will discover, upon more careful examination of the documents, that he was brother of Albero, bishop of Liège, kinsman of Godfrey, count of Namur [Col. 1087B], and finally advocate [Col. 1088A] of Liège. During the time of Innocent II, having been struck by the aforesaid bishop with ecclesiastical censure, he was compelled to restore the same village of Turnines, which he had occupied with equal violence [Note: [Col. 1087B] See there the charter of Wibald concerning the failure of the cattle-herds, no. 17 below, dated 1140; and the letter of Pope Celestine [Col. 1088B] II to the archbishop, clergy, and people of Liège, which immediately follows Wibald’s charter.].

Thus also the name of Erhebert, Wibald’s brother, of whom honourable mention is made in Letter 79, becomes known only from two documents to which he is recorded as having subscribed. Nor, we think, will it be found anywhere else that, as Letter 346 indicates, Wibald frequented the emperor’s court in the very flower of his age and thus served four emperors. Yet weighty evidence for this fact is supplied by that exceptional diploma which, though not yet abbot, he was able to obtain in his own name in 1128 at the full synod of Liège [Note: [Col. 1088D] See in the Appendix, no. 1, the diploma of Frederick, archbishop of Cologne, concerning the subjection of the monastery of Malmedy to the monks of Stavelot.], and by the two ensuing instruments of privilege of Emperor Lothair and King Conrad, in which his fidelity and vigour in administering the kingdom are expressly praised, as though he then sat at the helm of the realm.

[Col. 1088B] Now, since each of these monuments shows [Col. 1089A] that Wibald was pre-eminent in his age and almost second to none—whether one considers his virtue and keenness of intellect or the glory of his achievements—and that he deserved exceedingly well of Church and Empire in the most difficult times, we cannot sufficiently wonder that the memory, indeed almost the name, of this man has been buried in silence. For what have German writers, ancient or modern, handed down concerning him—especially those on whom this duty chiefly rested: Otto of Freising, Rahewin, and other contemporaries? What have Saxon chroniclers recorded?

Indeed, ten years ago there appeared, through the labours of the most distinguished D. Leibniz, a brief chronicle of New Corvey [Note: [Col. 1089D] *Scriptores Brunsvicenses*, vol. II, p. 296.], which continuously enough recounts the man’s principal deeds. But that wretched work is so polluted with shameful errors that we suspect it to be the offspring of some mediocre and very recent writer who scarcely knew Corvey at all. How, indeed, could he have extended Wibald’s life to the year 1174, contrary to the testimony of every monument of that celebrated monastery?

[Col. 1089B] That error alone, to omit many others, gave Meibom—if this writer of whatever sort came into his hands—an occasion to distinguish Wibald of Stavelot, whom he knew from elsewhere, a learned man who died in Greece in 1158, from Wibald of Corvey, and thus to fabricate two abbots out of one. “Otto of Freising,” he says, “writes that Wibold”—whom he himself calls Wibald—“was sent by the emperor’s command into Greece, to Constantinople; Wibald of Stavelot, a prudent man, was his colleague on this embassy.” And, a few words later: “Guibald of Stavelot, colleague of Wickbold in the overseas embassy, died, not without suspicion that poison had been administered to him.” Such are his words.

Nor do the compilers of the *Annals of the Church of Liège* appear to have been more diligent, though Wibald was the light and pillar of that Church for more than thirty years. One of them, after examining with the greatest care all archives, both civic and ecclesiastical, as well as the other monuments of the province, wrote these few words concerning him not long ago, as though hesitantly [Note: [Col. 1089D] Bulen., book X of *Sacred Liège*, under the year 1145.]:

“Wibold began to be renowned for learning, practice, and truth in sacred matters, and to illuminate the entire diocese. A monk of Valciodorus”—thus the archives of the monastery have it—“and abbot of Stavelot, he spread his fame everywhere, so that the monks of German Corvey requested that he be placed over them as abbot. At what time? I have nothing except what he himself wrote to Bernard, bishop of Hildesheim, to this effect: ‘I was in the monastery of Stavelot, scarcely restored to health after a fever which had detained me at Viterbo for five weeks, when, on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of December, men came to me to announce that I had then been designated abbot of Corvey, while Bishop Henry held an assembly of the sacred order at Liège.’”

These are his words, which are certainly stated with insufficient certainty and are not particularly exact.

Peter the Deacon, monk of Monte Cassino [Col. 1089D] and Wibald’s contemporary, celebrated Wibald in his writings somewhat more fully and accurately; so too did Nicolaus Schaten, the learned Jesuit of our age and author of the *Annals of Paderborn* [Note: [Col. 1089D] *Chronicle of Monte Cassino*, book IV, ch. 124, etc.]. But how slight is this material! The latter touches only upon what the ancient documents of Corvey report; the former recounts only what occurred at Monte Cassino when, by Lothair’s command, Wibald was carried off to the abbacy of Cassino. Thus neither author says anything of his origin, his childhood, or his studies—matters commonly noted in outstanding men as sure foretastes of their future.

From this one may see how difficult it is to restore to its due light a man worthy of immortal memory, enveloped in such darkness. Nevertheless, in order in some measure to fulfil our earlier undertaking—namely, to elucidate the deeds of those more eminent men whose letters are published in this work—we have attempted a sketch, however slight, of his life [Col. 1090A], using both the cited authors and the ancient monuments of Corvey and Stavelot, most kindly shared with us. In return, we most affectionately offer this small effort to the dearly beloved ascetics and brethren of both houses.

At Liège in the eleventh century and the following centuries flourished the noble lords of Prato, distinguished by many great titles of dignity. John of Stavelot, monk of Saint Lawrence, inserted in his commentaries, while treating Wibald’s brother Erlebold, that Wibald derived his origin from that family. The poet of the *Ligurinus* lends some support to this author when he sings that Wibald was “born of an illustrious stock” (book IV). The monuments of Stavelot agree, sufficiently indicating that he was from Liège. Wibald himself more than once calls the province of Liège his homeland. “Moreover, dearest brethren,” he says in Letter 305, “not only the disturbance of the Church of Stavelot but also that of all [Col. 1090B] Lotharingia prevents us from hastening our return to you. This is indeed our homeland, which bore us, reared us, and advanced us.” Add to this his brother Erebert, sole heir to the paternal wealth, who possessed a house or castle not far from the monastery of Stavelot.

The siblings were two brothers and one sister: Erebert, Erlebold, and Havidis, all surely equally deserving of praise. The first, having taken the cross, followed King Conrad, whose chancellor he was, to Palestine in 1148. He was the perpetual defender of the monks of Stavelot; on their account he suffered many losses and was at one time despoiled of his very castle, as is sufficiently evident from the letter of Celestine to Albero, bishop of Liège, published by us [Note: [Col. 1090D] See among the letters of Pope Celestine II, *Patrologia*, vol. CLXXIX, no. 20.].

Erlebold, however, first a monk of Saint Lawrence at Liège and then of Stavelot, after displaying many examples of virtue under his brother Wibald’s abbacy, was appointed his successor in 1158. He acted vigorously in many embassies to supreme pontiffs and emperors [Col. 1090C] [Note: [Col. 1090D] Short manuscript history of the abbots of Stavelot.]. Finally, after a happy and glorious administration, he resigned his dignity in 1192 in order to devote himself solely to God; not long afterward he happily fell asleep. Havidis, the third, became Christ’s bride in the monastery of Gerigesheim [perhaps Gerisheim], and deserved to be set over the sisters about the year 1150. For in that year Wibald congratulates her, sending a ring, in Letter 220.

Wibald appears to have been the eldest of these three. Snatched away from the world from his earliest infancy, he was entrusted to the monks of Stavelot to be instructed in the rudiments of religion. “The Church of Stavelot,” says Letter 78, “[lacuna] nourished us with the milk of piety; and, not remembering the sins of our youth and our ignorances, it advanced us—if any dignity is thought to belong to us in prelation—to the highest rank of its governance.” Elsewhere he calls that same Church his mother, nurse, and educator (Letter 41).

As the years of tender age gradually passed, he was devoted to grammar [Col. 1090D] and rhetoric under the instruction of the venerable Reinard, who then governed the schools of Stavelot with remarkable wisdom. Reinard so loved the young Wibald because of his extraordinary natural virtue and intellect that, after some years, when he had become the first abbot of Reinehusen and later had grown old, he regarded him as a son until the end of his life. Exercising the privilege of age in a fatherly way, he frequently warned him, when he was being raised to the highest ranks of dignity, not to allow himself to be ensnared by the allurements of a deceitfully flattering world. This can be seen in certain of his letters, which indeed breathe no ordinary piety.

Under this master Wibald made great progress. Soon ready for higher studies, he was immediately summoned to the greater schools of Liège. There the outstanding felicity of his intellect and force of judgement shone forth, so that in the span of a few [Col. 1091A] years he was instructed in dialectic, rhetoric, arithmetic, geometry, and astronomy. He indicates in a letter to Pope Eugenius written about 1152 that he was still attending those schools in 1115 (Letter 37): “Almost thirty-seven years ago, when we were boys under scholastic discipline in the aforesaid city,” namely Liège. But, already weary of the world, he contemplated retirement, wavering only over the place.

The ancient merits of the monks of Stavelot invited him to turn toward them; but he sought a solitude more remote from human society, and perhaps feared the proximity of relatives, whose company everyone who dedicates himself to God avoids. Having duly weighed all this with Richer, his companion in studies and purpose, he chose in 1117 the vast solitude of Valciodorus.
