At that time the reputation of Valciodorus under Abbot Widric drew wise and learned men from every quarter. “From all sides they gathered,” says an ancient [Col. 1091B] author [Note: [Col. 1091D] *Chronicle of Valciodorus*, *Spicilegium*, vol. VII.], “to submit their necks to the light yoke of obedience, to restrain the fever of fleshly life by drinking in heavenly sweetness, and to say with the prophet: ‘My soul thirsted for you; how greatly my flesh longs for you!’ (Psalm XLI).” Having tasted the sweetness of this delight, the same author continues, Master Wibald and Master Richer, without any delay of deliberation, approached the aforesaid abbot. Confessing to him their ardours, at his advice they exchanged their former dress for a religious habit in hope and professed the religious life under him.

Yet Wibald, whom the most good God called rather to the labours of an active life than to the leisure of contemplation, did not find at Valciodorus the peace he had hoped for. Once Widric had learned both the depth of his scholarship and the maturity of his character, he almost set him over the schools before Wibald had pronounced the solemn vows of religion. The monks of Stavelot, meanwhile, urged him to return to them, bitterly complaining that he had been taken from them; [Col. 1091C] finally they drew him away, retained him among themselves, and, after seven or eight years had passed, made him their abbot.

That departure was doubtless grievous alike to Wibald and to the monks of Valciodorus: to them, because they lost a master both learned and devout; to him, because he was dragged from tranquillity onto a rock. He knew that Stavelot was frequented by crowds of nobles and that, because both of the place’s renown and the supreme veneration of Saint Remaclus, emperors sometimes held, as they say, their courts there. On the other hand, the monks of Stavelot rejoiced that this man had been restored to them, by whose authority and prudence they could be restored to their former dignity.

For after the death of the venerable Abbot Folmar, which occurred about 1106, the affairs of the monastery had been declining. His successor Poppo of Bellemont had alienated many estates by granting them out in fief, as the expression is; hence he was called “the despoiler” [Note: [Col. 1091D] See below, in the Appendix to Wibald’s letters, no. 2: a survey of the possessions of the monastery of Stavelot.]. After Poppo’s death, a certain Werner, having usurped the abbatial dignity, ruled as an intruder for five years and, after being deposed, exercised the office of provost. How much [Col. 1091D] such evils damage discipline is wholly clear to everyone. Wibald therefore seemed eminently fitted to remedy them.

But the precise year of his arrival at Stavelot has nowhere been found. Yet since it is otherwise certain that he was made abbot in the year of salvation 1130, one must conclude that he had lived there before Emperor Henry V’s death; for, as we have already said, he was not immediately made abbot. Here Peter the Deacon, continuator of the Chronicle of Monte Cassino, agrees with us in some measure, although he is less exact [Note: [Col. 1091D] *Chronicle of Monte Cassino*, book IV, ch. 124.]. Speaking of Wibald, he says: “A Lotharingian by birth, made a monk from childhood in the monastery of Stavelot, [Col. 1092A] fully educated in grammar, dialectic, and so forth, he received from Emperor Henry V the duty of governing the abbey of the same monastery of Stavelot.”

Cuno, Poppo’s legitimate successor, finding in Wibald an excellent assistant, entrusted to him not only the schools, as the already cited Chronicle of Valciodorus relates, but also the monastery gate—the principal office at Stavelot, because of the frequent visits, as we have said, of princes and the emperor. Indeed, he consulted him in every major matter and most willingly used his counsels. While Wibald managed affairs in this way, those grave disputes, long since arisen over the allod of Bras between Evrard d’Isiere and the men subject to the monastery, were settled in 1124 on fixed conditions. The property at Calco, which the negligence of administrators had reduced almost to nothing, was improved. In 1127 a pact and alliance were made with the vicar of Sprimont, with whom much required ordering [Note: [Col. 1092D] Manuscript history of the abbots of Stavelot.].

[Col. 1092B] But nothing was closer to his heart than to bring the monks of Malmedy into order. As we showed in the preliminary observation on the documents of Stavelot, they could never endure except with the greatest reluctance being in some fashion subject to the monks of Stavelot. They had often attempted to cast off that yoke imposed upon them by Saint Remaclus himself, asserting their antiquity with more levity than truth. From that source discord had flowed into both monasteries from that time onward; but it then raged more fiercely, perhaps because the monks of Malmedy believed an opportune time had come when the affairs of Stavelot were in disorder through the bad administration of Poppo and Werner. Wibald pursued this matter so vigorously that in 1128 he brought it to a happy conclusion, obtaining a distinguished diploma from the archbishop of Cologne. It decreed that Malmedy should obey the Church of Stavelot by the same right of subjection by which all cells or provostries are seen to be subject to their monasteries [Note: [Col. 1092D] See the diploma of Frederick of Cologne concerning the subjection of the monastery of Malmedy to the monks of Stavelot, below in the Appendix, no. 1.].

[Col. 1092C] At that time he also won, both in Italy and Germany, so many noble and necessary friends for himself and the monastery that one may readily suppose the foremost princes of Germany and Emperor Henry V himself made frequent use of his services. Certainly, he then formed a friendship with Cardinal Gerard, who later attained the supreme pontificate and was called Lucius II. Wibald himself declares this in writing about 1148 to Cardinal John, Gerard’s nephew through either his brother or sister:

“Why do we trouble ourselves,” he says (Letter 50), “when we have a favourable judge, whom indeed we do not fear, because by the office of his see he holds the guardianship of the Catholic Church and jurisdiction in canonical litigation? But we love him because he is the nephew of the former supreme pontiff Pope Lucius, who loved us singularly before he reached the highest rank of advancement, and, once established at the summit of the apostolate, bestowed the greatest honour upon our Church and ourselves.”

And a little below: “May the nephew protect him whom the uncle loved; may he defend one ordained by that uncle whom he advanced; may the cardinal-priest uphold the judgement of the supreme pontiff, so that he permits no one to harass with exactions the man whom that pontiff thought worthy of honour. O what confidence of true affection was there at the very beginning of our entering into familiarity—indeed, of our acquaintance! Thus we speak to you safely and freely, just as we used to converse with him, that uncle of yours, with whose intimate and pleasing friendship we enjoyed—or, to use a less usual but truer expression, of which we partook—for twenty years and more without offence.”

I would be prolix if I wished here to enumerate all the bishops and cardinals whom, while still a private man, he thus bound to himself. He was producing these proofs of his worth [Col. 1093A] when Lord Cuno died. The monks of Stavelot record his death, not without great celebration of his virtues, on the fourth day before the Ides of December, 1128 [Note: [Col. 1093D] Manuscript history of the abbots of Stavelot.]. We think no one more worthy than Wibald could have been found to succeed this abbot. Yet, whether he was absent, occupied in affairs of state, or whether this exceptionally modest man declined the dignity—which we shall show that he did more than once—John Rulland was substituted: a pious and industrious man, indeed, but otherwise wholly unknown. He presided for two years, and then, having died, left the abbey to Wibald on the third day before the Kalends of November, 1130. Wibald was elected on the fourth day after John’s death.

Nor was it without the counsel of the most good God that he was elected in precisely the year when Pope Innocent II, Peter Leo having prevailed, was driven from his see. Germany would surely never have aided the legitimate pope had it lacked Wibald’s counsel. Hardly a few years had passed since nearly the whole world had blazed with a most sorrowful schism [Col. 1093B]. The remnants of that conflagration still smouldered in various places and could be rekindled by the slightest breath.

The princes and ministers of the Empire repeatedly urged Lothair that the Romans, out of excessive greed to extend their rights beyond their established bounds, had seized the investitures. They added that the recently arisen schism offered an opportunity to recover them, since the supreme pontiff could in no way be restored to his see without the emperor’s support. For several months already France, which is accustomed to be a refuge for supreme pontiffs, had kept Innocent most eagerly. Yet, indulgently paternal toward the Germans—who were too envious of their nation’s prosperity—he intended to move to the outermost borders of Belgium, and it was announced that he would shortly come to Liège.

On hearing this, Lothair crossed the Rhine from Saxony at the beginning of 1131. Having been informed of the pope’s arrival, he himself went out to meet him with many princes of the Empire and received him with honour at Liège on the eleventh day before the Kalends of October. Again, in an assembly of thirty bishops and fifty-three abbots, the pope placed the crown upon the king and his consort Richiza. Peter Leo having been condemned in these proceedings, Lothair promised Innocent every assistance against the false pope. But when mention was made of investitures, it caused him no slight anxiety, which was nevertheless removed in an instant when Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, advised that the old question, settled with such great labour, should not again be agitated.

What part Wibald then played, the monuments of Stavelot are entirely silent about; nor do we read anywhere whether he was personally present at so great a gathering. His new dignity, which gave him a place among the princes of the Empire, suggests that he was present; the proximity of his monastery admitted no excuse. When the assembly at Liège had ended, however, Lothair and Richiza, travelling toward Trier to celebrate the holy day of Easter, arrived at Stavelot on the day before the Ides of April with Matthew, legate of Albano, and a great train of nobles. It was Palm Sunday, the day on which the mysteries of Christ’s death are first opened [Col. 1093D]. On the following day the king and queen entered the basilica and lay prostrate for a long time, venerating the sacred remains of Saint Remaclus.

Then Lothair approved Wibald’s election there and, having confirmed the monastery’s privileges by the distinguished diploma which we print below, continued on to Trier. The bishop of Liège followed the king among the princes, but soon returned to Stavelot and, after Easter Day had passed, inaugurated Wibald. More than three months had now elapsed since his election, and he had scarcely had any time in that period to gather himself. Once he had obtained a little rest, he deeply felt the immense burden laid upon him: on one side, he saw the greater part of the monastery’s goods dispersed or neglected; on the other, discipline declining day after day.

Since these two things are repaired with difficulty in any place [Col. 1094A], they could scarcely be repaired at Stavelot, because affairs of the Empire continually called the abbot away. As a prince, he was obliged to attend regularly the solemn assemblies of the realm, to follow the emperor on campaigns, to provide troops, and to enter into dangers themselves. Wibald appeared likely to be more subject to all these obligations than others, both because of his remarkable sagacity in counsel and because of his incredible speed in execution. When Lothair first recognized these two qualities as outstanding in him, he admitted him, as it were, as his associate in administering the Empire.

The opening of the document which the same emperor granted him at Würzburg in 1136 confirms this [Note: [Col. 1093D] See below in the Appendix, no. 8.]: “Let the diligence of all our faithful, both present and future, know that we, considering, venerable Abbot Wibald, the constancy of your fidelity and the labours which you endure with us in administering our Empire, have decreed to defend your Church in every respect and to fortify it with privileges.”

[Col. 1094B] Yet, recognizing that the abbot of Stavelot fulfilled not only the role of a prince but also that of a pastor, and that the care entrusted to him was no less that of the monastery than of the Empire, he applied himself equally to both, allowing no time to pass free of labour.

With regard to the monastery, he first applied himself to the reform of regular discipline. So that, with everyone pursuing the same goal, he might attain the happy outcome of his purpose, he assigned a distinct office to each person whom he knew to be more worthy. Among these he appointed Warner, and, upon Warner’s death, Robert—his companion in study under Reginard—as prior or dean, the rank at Stavelot immediately below the abbot. Robert excelled in prudence and virtue, and especially in eloquence. “I pass over,” says the aforesaid Reginard, writing to Wibald, “the Ciceronian eloquence of Brother Robert, dean of Stavelot, who once nevertheless heard us for some time, and which I have admired in the same studies; [Col. 1094C] in my judgement, certainly, the style of few ancient writers—not to speak of modern ones—seems superior to his style.”

He placed over the schools the monk Henry, truly devout and learned, whose labours and merits he celebrated more than once in his letters [Note: [Col. 1093D] See Wibald’s charter concerning the failure of the cattle-herds, [Col. 1094D] dated 1140, no. 17; and the subscriptions to the diploma concerning the tithe of the church of Comblenz, etc., in the Appendix, no. 27.].

Finally, he summoned his full brother Erlebald, who had professed religious vows at Liège among the monks of Saint Lawrence. He first made him his chaplain, then his keeper; this is the title given to the person entrusted with the archive of documents. This appointment should not, however, be ascribed to blood relationship, since the young man already seemed most worthy of the foremost offices.

With these three helpers especially, it could not but happen that lax observance soon grew warm again. Certain letters from the monks of Stavelot to Wibald, and Wibald’s in turn to them, offer some traces of that new fervour—above all the one in which he mourns the death of four brethren. “The hand of God,” he says [Col. 1094D] (Letter 136), “is stretched out over our monastery, calling our brethren to himself and taking them from us—men most useful and necessary indeed for divine things. We grieve, brethren, and mourn that those have been taken from us who prayed for the people and for our city, whose heart and voice were continually intent upon the love and praise of their Creator, who humbly pursued obedience, and who sincerely loved our person. But Christ rejoices in heaven with the angels that, by the gift of his grace, they have become citizens of his glorious city.”

Those four brethren are identified only by initial letters. Since these do not correspond at all to the aforesaid three—Robert, Henry, and Erlebald—it is evident that at that time not a few men of great piety flourished at Stavelot.

[Col. 1095A] But what piety, however great, can long flourish in a monastery where affairs are wholly disordered and disturbed? None whatever. Wibald recognized this. Having undertaken the administration of the affairs and goods, he carefully investigated what the monastery’s revenues produced, what had been taken from them, dispersed, or usurped, and whether and how they could be restored without injustice. This inquiry was surely too great an undertaking for him to make alone, for he found everything so confused—indeed, so desperate.

We said above that Poppo II had leased out many of the monastery’s estates for exceedingly small annual payments. Such grants were called *beneficia*; those to whom they were made, *beneficiarii* or *ministeriales*; and finally those annual payments were called *census*. But the very smallness of the payments, to use his own words, reduced the once wealthy monastery to such poverty that it could scarcely provide even a few brethren with the necessities of worship and sustenance. Yet [Col. 1095B] the beneficiaries were not content with such great profit: some did not pay the rents; others denied that they were due; certain men usurped estates adjoining those leased to them. Thus countless lawsuits and the flames of war were stirred up daily.

The monastery’s patrons, called advocates, forgetful of their title, took advantage of these disturbances and repeatedly ravaged the very subjects of that monastery, stripping them of their goods, plundering their houses, and finally burning them. But let us hear Wibald himself describe these evils in his usual manner, addressing his intimate friend Henry (Letter 294):

“Great is the ruin of our order, and in such manifold lack of necessities we do not trust that we can support ourselves. Moreover, there is among you such scarcity of resources and daily want of provisions that, even if the whole kingdom enjoyed the firmest peace, the Church of Stavelot could scarcely maintain itself. Your advocates, through sins at work, are not defenders of the poor but most cruel ravagers and most hostile plotters against your liberty. Your ministerials, who ought especially to support the Church, have become a crooked bow: they neither obey commands nor assist in the cultivation of the land where they themselves are stewards. Rather—and this is worse—they obstruct and devastate. Hardly any possession of your Church is free from these losses, and especially those estates are empty and neglected from which the principal supplies and additions to the daily provision used to be obtained.”

The steadfast man, more provoked than cast down by those unjust vexations, did not lose heart. Instead, arranging everything prudently and acting tirelessly, he gradually restrained them, sometimes by agreement, sometimes by force.

First he attacked the ministerials and decreed [Note: [Col. 1095D] See Wibald’s charter concerning matters performed and corrected by him at the estate of Andernach, dated 1132, in the Appendix, no. 4.] that alienations would be invalid unless confirmed by the consent of the brethren, the lawful grant of the abbot, and the advocate’s assent, in a testamentary instrument. [Col. 1095D] This decree readily opened for the monks of Stavelot a way to recover whatever had been alienated without such conditions. Many such properties were found, but especially at the estate of Andernach, and they were recovered in 1132. Then, pressing these same persons more insistently, he brought it about through “manifold and, to use his own words, almost inextricable dangers” that half the benefices Poppo had granted were surrendered to him, both by the free men of the monastery and by the ministerials.

Wishing also to repel by force the advocates and the monastery’s other adversaries—or rather, plunderers—he undertook the complete construction of fortifications and the transfer of a large village or town, namely Longia. Certainly no prince in those most difficult [Col. 1096A] times would have undertaken this unless he possessed great wealth; and he completed all of it, if not in the very year he had intended, then certainly in the seventh year. A document drawn up by him in 1138 may be seen on this matter; there he describes vividly, in his own fashion, the location and condition of the old village, the reasons for its transfer, the privileges granted to the new inhabitants, and other highly noteworthy matters.

Meanwhile, he applied himself more readily to affairs that concerned in a special way the glory of God or the cult of some saint. His two predecessors, Cuno and John, had long ago granted two churches in feudal right to Heribrand of Longia: one in the aforesaid village of Longia and another on Mount Saint Rainier. They had further conceded that, whenever priests died and those churches fell vacant, that layman himself might provide new priests by employing a person to confer investiture of the altar [Note: [Col. 1095D] See Wibald’s charter that investiture of the churches of Longia [Col. 1096D] and Mount Rainier ought not to be received from laymen, in the Appendix after the letters, no. 5.]. This man, by no means ignorant of the holy canons, would not endure churches being granted by a layman; and he corrected that abuse, whether Heribrand wished it or not, in 1133.

[Col. 1096B] He sought to restore the village of Bovinias, situated on the furthest boundary of Namur, which had offered refuge to the sacred relics of Saint Remaclus during the raging violence of the Northmen and therefore enjoyed great veneration among the people of Liège. He requested that its usufruct be granted him during his lifetime, for it had been assigned to the brethren’s wardrobe fund [Note: [Col. 1096D] See there the charter of the monks of Stavelot, dated 1136, no. 5.]. Having recovered it—utterly ruined and deprived of inhabitants and tenants—he restored it to its former dignity.

Wibald did very many other things vigorously, set out more fully in the documents of Stavelot published by us. But these few matters sufficiently show how diligently he fulfilled every duty of an abbot.

We shall more willingly recount what labour he bestowed on affairs of the Empire, since it is chiefly in that part of his life that he should be considered.

We saw above that, when the assembly at Liège had ended, Lothair, having raised and then suppressed the question of investitures, had at last promised aid to Innocent and arrived at Stavelot with the other princes of the Empire [Col. 1096C]. Who would not immediately perceive the principal reason for this journey?

We think that the king wished to confer more privately with Wibald about giving that aid. Hence we infer that the first counsels concerning the Italian expedition were discussed at Stavelot—the expedition whose outcome was so prosperous and won immortal glory for Lothair. What followed the conference supports this conclusion. Not only did the troublesome question of investitures collapse, but the king, immediately gathering an army, marched toward Italy at the end of the following year.

Then what great labors Wibald endured! The king had not yet moved a foot from the city of Augsburg of the Vindelici when, behold, a messenger arrived: Conrad, duke of Swabia, who had seized the Italian kingdom, had broken into Germany and was throwing everything into confusion, since very many were inclining to his party. Alarmed by the report of the expedition, he had fled from Italy by out-of-the-way routes with his army, intending to create disturbances. Thus it fell to Wibald, as also to the other princes of the empire, to restrain the attempts of the rebels, to strengthen others in loyalty to Caesar, to provide the army at once with necessities, and finally to take every precaution lest that unforeseen evil spread more widely.

[Col. 1096D] Ancient writers do not weigh each of these matters, any more than many others; but it is certain that on this occasion Wibald gave remarkable proofs alike of loyalty and courage, and of outstanding skill in conducting affairs. These surely induced Lothair, once the expedition was completed, henceforth to consult that man more frequently concerning the empire’s principal affairs. Before long we shall see him in Italy placed in command of a great fleet, exposing himself to dangers and devising plans against the schismatics.

Caesar returned from Italy in 1133, as the [Col. 1097A] author of the Hildesheim Chronicle writes, in agreement with the records of New Corbie; thus scarcely one year was spent on the expedition. In that interval, evidently, he subdued all Italy with a modest army and restored Innocent to his own see after overthrowing the treacherous schismatics.

Contemporary authors add that Conrad, who had rebelled, was immediately restored to favor, chiefly through the intervention of St Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux. Yet minds of princes alienated from one another are not so easily reconciled; and it is quite probable that they were gradually brought to this point by Wibald’s counsels and entreaties—Conrad, to seek pardon from Caesar once the expedition had ended, and Caesar, to grant Conrad pardon. This was the source and origin of that long-standing intimacy subsequently existing between this prince and Wibald—so close that, after Conrad had been raised to the royal throne some years later, he repeatedly preferred Wibald to his own brothers, although they occupied the very highest rank of princely power (Epistle 340).

[Col. 1097B] Caesar, illustrious through many victories, was beginning to taste the sweetness of this peace when he was again warned by frequent letters from Innocent that the rebellious schismatics, whom he had defeated shortly before, had now recovered new strength; that they were attacking on every side; and, finally, that the time was drawing near when he must defend the crown of the Roman Empire from the yoke of its enemies and free the divided Church for peace, concord, and unity. . . .

> [Note: Col. 1097D, *Chronicle of Monte Cassino*, Book IV, chapter 97.]

Moved by these reports, and judging that war had to be waged against a stubborn enemy, Caesar held several general assemblies in different places, where a new Italian expedition was discussed. Setting aside all delay, he arranged for forces to be gathered from every side. Over them he placed his son-in-law Henry the Proud, duke of Bavaria, associating with him Conrad, duke of Swabia, of whom we have spoken above, and Abbot Wibald.

At length, having entered Italy through the Tridentine Alps at the beginning of September 1136, he went into winter quarters at Ravenna with a fully equipped [Col. 1097C] army, having stormed, destroyed, or received into surrender every fortress and town encountered. At Ravenna they deliberated upon carrying the war into Apulia and lower Italy, and upon invading Sicily itself, so that no refuge might thereafter be left to the enemy and that this whole plague might completely collapse.

Wibald was appointed over this naval expedition, which required great dexterity in its commander, but on the condition that he should not leave the emperor until the fleet then being equipped had at last put to sea. Hence Wibald was almost everywhere at Caesar’s side, lending counsel no less than courage. When winter had passed, the emperor led out his army and divided it into two parts. Sending his son-in-law Henry with one division into Campania, he himself, with the other division and with Wibald associated to him, brought the provinces of Umbria, Emilia, Flaminia, and Picenum under Roman rule.

“Then,” says Peter the Deacon,

> [Note: Col. 1097D, *Chronicle of Monte Cassino*, Book IV, chapter 106.]

“moving his camp above Bari, the capital of all Apulia, he pitched his tents; and, received by the citizens of the city, he began by every means to assault the fortress which Roger had splendidly built, and at last, with great labor, razed it to the ground.”

Meanwhile Henry, the emperor’s son-in-law, having reduced the principality of Capua with scarcely anyone resisting, received Benevento into surrender—into which Roger the tyrant had brought twenty thousand soldiers—and restored it to Pope Innocent. He immediately returned with it to the emperor.

> [Note: Col. 1097D, ibid., chapter 105.]

Thus, their forces having been employed, all the cities of Apulia were shortly subjected to Roman rule, and Roger, prince of Capua, was expelled and fled to Sicily.

Then Lothair, having called an assembly at Melfi, sent Wibald, commander of the naval expedition, to Naples

[Col. 1098A]

to equip the fleet with soldiers and arms.

> [Note: Col. 1097D, ibid., chapter 105.]

He himself advanced with the army toward Salerno, intending, after capturing that city, to cross into Sicily, whither the enemy had withdrawn. But Wibald, not forgetful of his profession, first wished to visit the sacred thresholds of holy Father Benedict, which were not so far away. He would surely lament his own circumstances: his whole life, as he thought, was being turned into one wholly alien to Benedict’s institutions.

Turning these and similar thoughts over in his mind, this devout man—who disdained military glory—ascended the holy mountain, treading reverently those same paths which almost countless saints, traveling toward the heavenly homeland, had once followed. Received by the brethren with the honor that befitted him, he grieved deeply that they were at variance among themselves and that the treacherous schismatics prevailed more strongly each day in that holy place.

One author of the dissension and evil was identified: Raynald the Tuscan, who occupied the abbacy. For in the preceding year, after the death of Abbot Seniorectus, when he had been elected by a few and had as his competitor Raynald of Colmenta,

[Col. 1098B]

a devout and prudent man, in whose favor the votes of the sounder party had united, some turbulent and more audacious monks, supporters of that Tuscan, feared that he would be wholly rejected. This was partly because he had received only the sacred order of subdeacon, and partly because he had been ordained by Anacletus, whom the emperor did not recognize; moreover, he could be convicted of simony. Therefore, tumultuously and seditiously—as Peter the Deacon puts it—

> [Note: Col. 1098D, *Chronicle of Monte Cassino*, Book IV, chapter 104.]

“all the other brethren resisting,” they seized him and, placing him in the chair of holy Father Benedict, established him as their abbot.

From that time this intruder had held the abbey, although the Cassinese had repeatedly complained of him to the emperor while he wintered at Ravenna. But he was most recently summoned to the assembly at Melfi to answer for all the matters mentioned; and no one knew how the affair would turn out, since he had won many friends for himself by money and gifts.

Deeply distressed by these matters and by many other consequences which such tumults commonly bring,

[Col. 1098C]

Wibald summoned all the brethren to chapter and gently admonished them:

> [Note: Col. 1098D, Peter the Deacon, *Chronicle of Monte Cassino*, Book IV, chapter 124.]

They ought to remember how from that place streams of preaching and the first principles of monastic life had flowed through almost the whole world; how great and what mighty deeds Father Benedict, relying upon divine power, had wrought there; and how, by his bodily resting-place and by the writing of his Rule, he had established the Cassinese monastery, the head of all monasteries, for all time. Finally, since through the son of Peter Leo they had been severed and separated from the Church, they must endeavor to be reformed, so that the streams flowing from so great a place might return to their former state of splendor and that they might turn to Pope Innocent, whom the whole world followed.

Having delivered this speech, he commended himself to Father Benedict and to the brethren, and departed for Naples.

Meanwhile, at the assembly of Melfi Raynald had sworn an oath of loyalty to Pope Innocent and Caesar. Through the intervention of friends he obtained permission to return

[Col. 1098D]

to Cassino, on the condition that he induce his followers to take the same oath. On his return he carried out what had been commanded. But the wicked man did not long remain faithful to his promise. He immediately summoned Gregory Adenulf of St John, so that he might fortify Cassino against the emperor, as he had done shortly before when Henry, duke of Bavaria, invaded Campania.

> [Note: Col. 1098D, *Chronicle of Monte Cassino*, Book IV, chapter 118.]

Perhaps he hoped that the emperor, whom rumor said was about to cross into Sicily, would never return because of his advanced age. But his hope deceived him. For the emperor, after besieging and taking the city of Salerno, felt his strength failing day by day. Changing his plan, he withdrew to Capua, intending to depart for Germany before winter.

There, after hearing from the Cassinese that

[Col. 1099A]

Raynald had, contrary to his pledged faith, defected to the schismatics, he became very angry. He sent Bruno the *campidoctor*—the field commander—with a force of soldiers to the monastery to keep guard over the perjurer. Not long afterward he himself came to the city of St Germanus, intending to exact punishment for Raynald’s disloyalty. He ordered him kept in the sacristy of the basilica of the Lord Savior and, finally, as Peter the Deacon says,

> [Note: Col. 1099D, *Chronicle of Monte Cassino*, Book IV, chapter 118.]

“after a few days he was sent back under no small guard to the monastery, where he was to be examined; and he was lawfully deprived of office,” Pope Innocent and the emperor jointly concurring in this, since the Cassinese had entrusted his case to their judgment.

On the day when sentence was to be pronounced, there were present with the emperor many cardinals, archbishops, bishops, abbots, and an innumerable multitude of nobles. Outstanding among them were Aimeric, cardinal and chancellor of the Holy Roman Church; Gerard, cardinal of Holy Cross; Peregrine, patriarch of Aquileia; and Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux. Speaking in his customary manner,

[Col. 1099B]

Bernard greatly inclined the minds of all to expel this schismatic and intruder from the holy place. Since all had jointly decided this, the assembly was dissolved and they went to the church of Blessed Benedict.

Then the cardinals named above, together with the patriarch, summoned Raynald and pronounced sentence before the altar. “And so, by their command,” Peter the Deacon continues, “in the presence of the emperor and all the magnates of the empire, he laid down the staff and ring, and likewise the Rule, upon the body of most holy Benedict”—he indicates the place where Benedict’s sacred remains had formerly been venerated.

When these matters had been completed and all had returned to the chapter-house to deliberate on appointing a new abbot, a serious dispute arose immediately between the cardinals and the Cassinese monks and consumed the entire day. Gerard, cardinal of Holy Cross, wanted twelve brethren to be chosen from the monastery, who, acting solely in the pope’s stead, should nominate an abbot together with him. He further argued that they were being treated very generously, since the pope could exercise his full right. Because they had submitted themselves to his judgment in Raynald’s case, the entire election for this occasion had, he said, devolved upon him.

But the Cassinese, fearing for many reasons—which it would take too long to set out here—that an abbot might be imposed on them from outside their own body, as they say, opposed their privileges to the cardinal and strove to prevent their violation with all their strength.

[Col. 1099C]

The dispute flared so strongly that the cardinal, inflamed with anger, in the Church’s name forbade any election. But the pope, entreated by the emperor, revoked the cardinal’s interdict on the following day, granting the monks permission to choose an abbot while preserving the integrity of their privileges, provided that the Church of Cassino should not be made subject to any outsider. For it had given to the Roman see Stephen VIII, Victor III, and the second Gelasius as popes.

The Cassinese privileges nevertheless stated that Henry the Pious had granted to the seventh [eighth] Pope Benedict [Col. 1099D] the consecration of Theobald, abbot of Cassino, whom the emperor himself had appointed, together with one meal going to and returning from Benevento; all else he had reserved to the Roman Empire. Conrad and his son Henry had confirmed the same. From this it was evident that several outsiders had been appointed abbots of the monastery of Cassino, and that some had also been designated by the emperors themselves. By a certain special right, and with the brethren’s consent, they were presented to the pope after taking possession, in order to be inaugurated.

That right, commonly called the right of investitures, emperors formerly exercised everywhere, but without any foundation. Yet in the Church of Cassino, which was an imperial chamber and belonged to the empire by right of patronage, it was still believed to be owed to them.

Then the emperor ordered Wibald to be summoned. Foreknowing what would occur, says Peter the Deacon, an eyewitness,

[Col. 1100A]

he had withdrawn from the place and, alleging the emperor’s orders at Naples, was waiting idly—contrary to his custom—for a Cassinese abbot to be created, hoping that, while he was absent, no one would think of him. For nothing did that great man, born for the highest things, fear more than having this burden imposed upon him.

When, therefore, he came at the emperor’s summons and was told why he had been called, he absolutely refused, steadfastly declaring that he would never undertake so grave and immense a burden. But because the emperor knew that the man’s mind was altogether averse to dignities, he had gathered in his chamber several archbishops, bishops, abbots, and other magnates of the empire, together with the patriarch of Aquileia, so that Wibald, surrounded on all sides and, as it were, overcome by everyone’s entreaties, might cease resisting.

First the emperor began to exhort him, then to urge him, and afterward by many arguments to demonstrate how important it was to Church and empire that he accept the abbey offered to him [Col. 1100B].

Then the most serene empress Richiza pressed her entreaties; on the other side the monks, prostrate at his feet, repeatedly cried that he should pity their lot. At last everyone in his own way pressed him more vigorously. But he remained unmoved and unconquered, repeating the same words: he would never undertake so grave and immense a burden.

Seeing, therefore, that entreaties made no progress, the emperor ordered him to be handed over to the monks and taken to the chapter-house, where he was immediately proclaimed abbot of Cassino by the unanimous voice of all. Without delay the emperor put him in possession of the Church and territory of Cassino by handing him his sceptre, saying, as Peter the Deacon, who was present, writes:

“We did not receive from you an oath of loyalty concerning the abbey of Cassino because long ago you gave us loyalty concerning the monastery of Stavelot. I do not wish your successors to cite you as a precedent and say that they will not render loyalty to my successors concerning the monastery of Cassino because the majesty of our empire did not require it from you.

[Col. 1100C]

But let them render the customary loyalty which, from the times of Charles onward, abbots have rendered concerning the abbey of Cassino.”

When this had been done, the emperor descended to St Germanus to commend the new abbot, who had been presented to the pope, in many words. He then turned aside toward ancient Aquino and pitched his tents near the city. Otto, dean of Cassino, Raynald of Colmenta, Peter the Deacon, Bertulf, and other leading monks of the Cassinese community immediately came there with Abbot Wibald. They were to thank the emperor in the community’s name for his singular goodwill, which, they said, all had experienced during the full eight days he had spent at Cassino; to wish him a prosperous return to Germany; and finally to seek his assistance against Pandulf, son of Landulf, count of Aquino. Pandulf had without any right built a fortress in the wood of Trilla, which belonged to Cassino’s domain, so that he might sally out from it and plunder with impunity the monastery’s surrounding estates.

The emperor received those admitted to his presence kindly, as was his custom, returning thanks for their good will. Greatly moved by Pandulf’s unjust oppression of innocent men, he immediately summoned Bruno the *campidoctor* and sent him with a cohort to set fire to the stripped fortress. Then he ordered Raginulf, duke of Apulia, Robert, prince of Capua, indeed all the counts of the principality of Capua, the counts of Aquino, and the Normans dwelling throughout the region, to acknowledge the service due to Wibald. And, in order that no one might thereafter dare in any way to molest Wibald or his dependents, he had two notable diplomas drawn up, confirming all the privileges of the monasteries of Cassino and Stavelot.

We cannot speak of the diploma intended for the Cassinese, because it is only briefly mentioned in the *Chronicle of Monte Cassino* and is not otherwise known to us. But the other,

[Col. 1101A]

wholly written in gold letters, has already been published by us among other documents of Stavelot. We shall therefore note here only what pertains to this subject:

“We judge the person of the lord and venerable Abbot Wibald, who canonically presides over that monastery, worthy of our special love and friendship. His loyalty and devotion toward the stability and honor of our empire shone sufficiently in this Italian expedition. After many labors and dangers, which he faithfully endured for us and with us in the administration of our empire in Apulia, when we were returning, he was seized in the monastery of Cassino by the brethren of that place and by all the people, through an altogether violent and astonishing election, and made abbot. Remaining for the honor and security of our empire, he petitioned our highness to deign to protect and confirm the monastery of Stavelot, whose care he had not laid down, and the properties belonging to it,” etc.

The subscribers were Albero, archbishop of Trier; Conrad, archbishop of Magdeburg;

[Col. 1101B]

Meingold, bishop of Merseburg; Albero, bishop of Basel; Albero, bishop of Liège; Andrew, bishop of Utrecht; Anselm, bishop of Havelberg; Henry, bishop of Toul; Conrad, abbot of Fulda; Henry, duke of Bavaria and margrave of Tuscany; and many other magnates—altogether distinguished witnesses. All of them followed the emperor, saw Wibald daily, and spoke with him.

On the same day on which the commemoration of St Maurice was more solemnly observed, the pope celebrated the sacred rites in the basilica of St Peter. When these were completed, the emperor invited Wibald and the Cassinese, together with the others just named, to dinner. The bishops mentioned above were present, as anyone can easily judge, together with other magnates. “For Lothair,” says Peter the Deacon, “was never separated from the company of bishops.”

But turning to Wibald—with a kindness surely remarkable in the supreme emperor, at whose nod almost the whole world was moved—he said: “I think, unless I am mistaken, that this will be my last day of eating and drinking with you.”

The devout prince sensed that the final day of his life was near. He then looked intently at the other Cassinese monks, and among them silently intended to take Peter the Deacon with him to Germany, judging him especially worthy to occupy Wibald’s place. He had often heard Peter, when summoned with the pseudo-abbot Raynald to the assembly at Melfi, defending the rights of his monastery most vigorously. At that same assembly he had appointed him *logothete*, secretary (*exceptorem*), auditor, keeper of charters, and chaplain.

When dinner had ended, the emperor took him aside and instructed him to make ready at once for the journey, to perform imperial services always.

When Wibald heard this, he humbly explained to Lothair that, as a kind of exile and stranger in a most remote place, utterly deprived of all help from his own people, he could in no way do without the assistance of Peter the Deacon, in whom he placed the greatest trust. Lothair should instead permit him, after resigning the abbey of Cassino,

[Col. 1101D]

to return to his own monks at Stavelot.

The emperor replied: “Since you say that you are unwilling to remain without him, I commend him to your loyalty with the utmost zeal and affection of mind, on this condition: if there remain in your heart any traces of my love or affection, show them in this man; and for love of us regard him in the place of a most dear and only son.”

Then, addressing the bishops and other magnates, he said: “The majesty of our empire, which God preserve, has made this disciple whom you see the disciple of Henry, bishop of Regensburg and chancellor; it has rewarded him with the office of *logothete*, secretary, and auditor, and granted him a seat at the right foot. He alone has been found among the Roman people who would oppose himself to the men of Constantinople on behalf of the empire and the Roman pontiff.”

Thus the emperor left Peter the Deacon with Wibald. Having granted both of them, as also the other brethren, leave to depart, he set out the next day, the ninth day before the Kalends of October [23 September], traveling with Pope Innocent toward Rome. A few days [Col. 1102A] later, leaving the city pacified, he turned aside to Tivoli.

There, troubled beyond his custom—whether by failing health, which old age daily weakened, or because Wibald’s absence itself distressed him greatly—he again arranged to take Peter the Deacon with him into Germany, as though the things which he had promised not long before, before all, to the abbot of Cassino had already slipped from his mind. Nevertheless all the courtiers, so prone are such men to flattery, complied with the emperor’s will, indeed applauding it, and advised that Peter be summoned from Cassino as soon as possible. The following letter was written for that purpose:

> Lothair, by the grace of God august emperor of the Romans, to his beloved faithful man Guibald, hierarch of Cassino, archchancellor of the Roman Empire, master of the chapel, and prince of peace: his favor and goodwill.
>
> By imperial letters we command your loyalty to endeavor to send to our majesty, which God preserve, Peter, deacon of Cassino, whom our imperial serenity has appointed *logothete*, Italian secretary, keeper of charters,
>
> [Col. 1102B]
>
> and chaplain of the empire. He will receive the reward of fitting recompense for the service of his loyalty. For you should know without doubt that our majesty and the colleagues of the empire do not wish to be deprived of his presence, on account of his knowledge of antiquities and his accounts of deeds done. Send also through him all the charters of our predecessors which we formerly gave him at Aquaspendente to keep.
>
> Given at the suburban district of Tivoli, the day before the Kalends of December [30 November].

It should be noted in passing that many titles of dignity are attributed to Wibald in this letter which are found nowhere else, and that our Mabillon copied the letter from the archives of Monte Cassino.

But the bearer of the letter found him in the utmost extremity of distress, vigorously preparing war against Raynald the Tuscan, who was besieging the holy mountain on every side. That treacherous man was attacking in this manner a friend who had deserved well of him. For, after he had been removed and deprived of the abbey at the pope’s and emperor’s direction, as we explained above, he feared that he would be transported as an exile to Germany. With Wibald’s help, which he had sought, he obtained the provostship of St Magnus, situated near the city of Fondi, so that there he might be safe from Caesar’s anger.

But whoever does good to the wicked often makes them worse. Although he ought to have gone there [Col. 1102C], he had entered the fortress called Castrum Coeli, which his relatives held, already intent upon recovering the abbey. After the emperor’s departure was announced, he acted more openly and, gathering forces from every side, spread devastation everywhere.

Meanwhile King Roger, bursting rapidly into Apulia like a torrent, was swiftly recovering the cities and provinces which he had lost during the interval of a few months. It was now reported that he had crossed the Strait [the *Pharus*] and was about to recover the principality of Capua in the same way.

Nevertheless, encouraged by the emperor’s letter, the abbot of Cassino hoped that, once the news of the rebellion had spread, aid would soon come to him from the emperor. On the fourth day he wrote a longer reply,

[Col. 1102D]

setting out more bitterly the attacks which the schismatics had already made since the emperor had departed, the threats uttered, and the dangers hanging over him:

> “How great and what sufferings I and the Church of Cassino endure, through the most impious peoples of the Lombards, Normans, and Saracens, for loyalty to the Roman Empire and the Apostolic See, no pen suffices to write. . . . They have left the Church of Cassino nothing but unutterable tribulation. And behold, alas! while Roger, king of the Normans, exults with his army, the sole assembly of the faithful is consumed with great sorrow; Christian blood is shed; monks are bound in the chains of prison; the people devoted to God are laid waste by continual slaughter,” etc.

And below:

> “Therefore, most excellent of Caesars, . . . unless you aid us with the hand of your protection, once Christians’ hope of life has been removed, either we shall be subjected to the pagans themselves, or . . . defeated by their multitude, we shall perish to [Col. 1103A] the utter ruin of Christianity.”

In order to satisfy the emperor’s request for Peter the Deacon, he added:

> “But because a few words suffice for so great an emperor, . . . you shall learn from the words of our son Peter” (Epistle 1), “the composer of this letter, faithful in every respect to the Roman Empire, whom we have decided to send into Alemannia, Saxony, Denmark, Swabia, and Lotharingia.”

The emperor replied without offering any hope of aid. He said that all the forces of Roger and Raynald could be restrained solely by the efforts of the counts of Aquino and other princes, who had voluntarily pledged him loyalty only a few days earlier. But all of them, to a man, had defected; and even the citizens of St Germanus, the Cassinese watchmen, so to speak, were wavering greatly. Some time afterward they finally surrendered themselves to the enemy, who was to storm Mount Cassino with them.

Here it is worth briefly considering the astonishing instability of human affairs. He whom we had lately beheld as victor, intimate and friend of the unconquered emperor, commander of a [Col. 1103B] fleet, and indeed almost arbiter of Italy and the empire, was now held captive; a few days had brought so great a reversal of fortune. He describes these things mournfully in his reply to Lothair’s second letter, Epistle 2, which is addressed to the most serene Empress Richiza as well as to Lothair.

Unable to endure the treason of the citizens of St Germanus, he gathered such forces as he had, which were very slight, and sent the brave Landulf of St John into the city.

> [Note: Col. 1103D, *Chronicle of Monte Cassino*, Book IV, chapter 127.]

Landulf alone among many had persisted against Roger. For many days he had worn down the pseudo-abbot Raynald by frequent raids, and would utterly have defeated him if the emperor had brought even a little aid. On this occasion, certainly, he burst forth with such force that, after scattering Raynald’s numerous army, he either captured or killed the traitors of the city after setting the city on fire.

But hardly had the battle ended when this success was gravely darkened by the widespread and constant report that Roger, having recovered Capua,

[Col. 1103C]

had occupied the surrounding country and would shortly arrive with Raynald and a huge army. Cassino’s affairs had been reduced to such straits that, with every hope of aid excluded, they must either surrender themselves and all that they possessed to the victor’s power or suffer themselves to be buried beneath Cassino’s ruins. Both alternatives seemed to Wibald equally wretched and desperate.

Yet, lest he be thought to have omitted anything in so great a danger, he summoned all the monks to chapter and reminded them that Roger was both a man and a prince. He could, as human nature requires, be softened by submission; and a prince’s disposition was apt to mercy. Roger loved and revered the Church of Cassino, which, shortly before Lothair’s arrival, he had adorned with gifts and privileges. If they humbly entreated for peace, perhaps they would recover their former friendship as well.

Accordingly, several brethren were sent to Capua—perhaps Peter the Deacon among them, since he was accustomed to carry out such missions, both because of the renown of his name and because of his remarkable eloquence. As they proceeded into the midst of the enemy, they were astonished at the devastation being inflicted everywhere; not even sacred buildings were spared, and they feared that they had truly come into danger of their lives.

This was the outcome of the embassy. Roger, raging against Wibald, whom he knew had from the beginning of the war labored for his destruction and was wholly devoted both to Innocent and to the emperor, first addressed the envoys harshly, then spurned them and dismissed them unheard, threatening Wibald with an evil cross.

> [Note: Col. 1103D, *Chronicle of Monte Cassino*, Book IV, chapter 127.]

When these things were reported to Wibald, he encouraged the dismayed brethren with a calm and steadfast mind. They should hope well: he alone was being sought; war was being declared against him alone from private hatred, not against the Cassinese. If necessary, he would willingly lose his life for religion and for them; otherwise he would be able to look after his own safety.

Meanwhile, having received fifteen marks from Otto the dean,

[Col. 1104A]

he seriously deliberated how he might finally escape to a safe place. Only Landulf of St John was admitted to share the plan, since Wibald particularly needed his help. Entrusting Cassino’s defense to Landulf, he escaped at night with his assistance, unknown to all, on the fourth day before the Nones of November [2 November], leaving Roger greatly to regret his escape.

> [Note: Col. 1104D, ibid.]

As soon as he was safe from Roger’s cruelty, he informed the Cassinese by letter of his purpose in fleeing, declaring that he had taken thought more for them, who were oppressed on his account, than for himself. Yet he would not return any longer, because he had hitherto been an unprofitable tree in God’s field and should therefore be cut down. Accordingly, he wrote (Epistle 3):

> “I command you, by virtue of holy obedience, setting aside party spirit, removing all ambition and venality, without favor or hatred or respect of any person, according to the Rule of St Benedict, to elect without delay as your [Col. 1104B] abbot a Catholic and regular person from the body of your congregation. . . . For we have determined that, if you observe this form in electing your abbot, then, upon restoring to you the insignia of your Church, we shall jointly absolve you all from obedience and subjection to us and make you free from us for the advancement of the future abbot.”

These insignia which he had taken with him were the seal and ring handed to the abbot of Cassino at his inauguration. Having received those commands, the Cassinese obeyed, fully certain that Wibald would adhere firmly to his purpose and that Raynald the Tuscan, whose election had been forbidden, might be restored by Prince Roger. Thus, on the twelfth day after Wibald’s departure, Raynald of Colmenta was lawfully elected. He was a man, in Peter the Deacon’s words, “most honorable in bearing, gait, and conduct, and distinguished in divine and human learning.” This is the man whom, after Seniorectus’s death, we said above had contended with Raynald the Tuscan.

Wibald rejoiced at this news and sent the insignia, together with his promised resignation,

[Col. 1104C]

to the man elected, congratulating him in words which wonderfully express his modesty (Epistle 4):

> “Hearing that you have been elected by the common assent of the brethren and canonically ordained in the Church of Cassino, we rejoiced with joy. . . . Therefore, in the name of the Lord, by these present writings we absolve you from the obedience which you promised us. And we, who once unworthily presided over you, are not ashamed to be and to be called your subjects and servants.”

Then, commending to the elected abbot his beloved Otto the dean and the other brethren, together with the men of St Peter who had remained faithful, he added:

> “We return to you one ring and our former seal, by which we make a complete renunciation of the abbey of Cassino; yet we shall never withdraw our counsel and assistance from that Church.”

Writing to Otto in nearly the same manner, he also gave an account of certain movable goods which had been disposed of during his tenure (Epistle 5).

Perhaps we have related at greater length than was proper the events at Cassino under Wibald. Yet scarcely anywhere, except perhaps at Corbie, as will become clear below, did all his virtues shine so brightly: above all his modesty, his exceptional aversion to dignities, constancy in adversity, and singular devotion to the sheep entrusted to him.

If anyone should object that he abandoned them at the very time when they most needed his aid, we answer that no author hitherto has branded him with this mark of disgrace—not Peter the Deacon, certainly an honest writer, nor the other Cassinese writers. They would never have spared an outsider, but would at least have damaged his memory in their writings.

He presided over the Cassinese for forty-four days, as the anonymous Cassinese writer expressly states:

> “In the year 1137, in the fifteenth indiction, . . . Abbot Seniorectus died. Raynald the Tuscan becomes abbot. Raynald, elected for this place,
>
> [Col. 1105A]
>
> is deposed. Guibald is ordained; he withdraws after forty-four days.”

It is probable that, after laying down the burden of his office at Cassino, he went to the emperor, who, being at the point of death, a few days later died, according to Otto of Freising, in a most wretched hut, on 3 December, in the thirteenth year of his reign and the fifth of his empire. He was received by the most serene empress as a prince of peace, capable by his counsels of preventing the dissensions then foreseen. For the question was that of creating a new king, and there were two candidates, both most powerful and conspicuous for glory in affairs: Henry, duke of Bavaria and Saxony, son-in-law of Lothair; and Conrad, duke of Swabia, brother-in-law of Henry V. The former excelled in wealth and power, but was excessive in pride and arrogance, whence he was given the name “the Proud”; he was less acceptable both to the nobles and to the common people. The latter, however, had won over almost everyone by gentleness and clemency, qualities especially looked for in a king.

It is not our purpose here to set out the course of the election [Col. 1105B] and the subsequent movements of war, although we do not doubt that Wibald’s prudence and equity shone everywhere. We shall bring forward only what is recorded in writing concerning him. Conrad was preferred to Henry at an assembly held about mid-Lent in the town of Koblenz, chiefly through the efforts of Albero, archbishop of Trier, and Abbot Wibald, Theodwin, bishop and cardinal-legate of the holy Roman Church, being present. Conrad soon came to Aachen and was anointed king by the aforesaid cardinal, with the cooperation of the archbishops of Cologne and Trier and the other bishops, as Otto of Freising writes. Accordingly, the author of the Paderborn Annals must be corrected, since, through a lapse of memory, he wrote that Conrad was anointed at Koblenz.

At that time Wibald visited his Stavelot brethren, who had long awaited him, hoping to enjoy with them the desired retirement and to pass the few remaining [Col. 1105C] years of his life more quietly. This was the one thing he desired the king, toward whom he had rendered great service, to grant him. Yet he first had to conclude the monastery’s affairs that he had begun before the expedition and, what seemed very difficult, restrain the continual vexations of the ministeriales.

Therefore, after celebrating holy Easter with the brethren and discussing there the matters of greatest urgency, he set out for Cologne, where Conrad was holding a solemn court. There, in a notable assembly of nobles, he first complained that the estate of Turnines, a principal property of the Church of Stavelot, was unjustly held by the count of Namur. He then requested confirmation for himself of the laws which he had enacted for the aforesaid castle and village of Longia, of the fairs recently established there, of the goods acquired, and of the other possessions of the monastery of Stavelot. Conrad granted the requests by a distinguished diploma, first adjudicating, in accordance with the decision of the council, the aforesaid estate of Turnines.

> [Note: [Col. 1105D] See below, in the Appendix to Wibald’s letters, no. 11, for the year 1138; compare Wibald’s charter of the same year, about the middle.]

Nevertheless, because Eustace, advocate of Liège, opposed it, [Col. 1105D] the estate could not be recovered before the following year. Yet Conrad himself, having taken up Wibald’s cause, at an assembly held at Liège at nearly the same time, strongly ordered Bishop Albero not to delay in restraining that vexation by his brother—for Eustace was Albero’s full brother.

> [Note: [Col. 1105D] See the diploma of Albero, bishop of Liège, “On the possession of Turnines, restored to the monastery of Stavelot by pontifical and royal authority,” in the Appendix, no. 13 [Col. 1106D].]

Since, so far as we know, this assembly is mentioned nowhere, we shall add that Wibald there pronounced judgment against the estate-managers of the monastery of Stavelot, who strove to possess as a benefice the estate-administrations entrusted to them and the judicial offices, and to hold them as if by hereditary right, whereas previously they had customarily been exercised only at the abbot’s pleasure [Col. 1106A]. Conrad confirmed this judgment by a new diploma at another assembly held at Worms in 1140.

> [Note: [Col. 1106D] See the Appendix, no. 14.]

In the same year, two instruments were obtained at a full synod at Cologne, chiefly through Wibald’s efforts. By one, the supreme authority of the abbot of Stavelot over the monks of Malmedy was declared; by the other, tithes of newly cleared lands were granted in the village of Bullinge, which belonged to the jurisdiction of the monastery of Malmedy.

> [Note: [Col. 1106D] See ibid., nos. 15, 16.]

Nor did the excellent abbot’s supreme concern for his children stop here. Whoever examines the documents we have prefaced will find, on the one hand, letters of the supreme pontiffs obtained by him, expressly confirming all properties and privileges; on the other, various instruments relating to acquisitions. How great were the cares and anxieties he devoted to these affairs, and how many journeys he undertook—not to mention his other exertions. At one time he had to visit King Conrad, at another the bishop of Cologne, at another the bishop of Liège. At almost every [Col. 1106B] imperial diet and episcopal synod, some new matter concerning the monastery of Stavelot was being dealt with. The misconduct of the ministeriales alone—although it ought to have been entirely suppressed after the judgments at Liège, Worms, and many other places—continually broke out again and imposed endless cares upon him.

One should read that splendid letter which he wrote to the bishop of Hildesheim about the year 1149. “The estate-managers,” he says (Letter 131), “wished to possess the sanctuary of God hereditarily; taking the very offices of estate-administration by paternal and ancestral succession, they lorded it over the properties, annulled our ordinances and those of the provosts, oppressed the tenants with unlawful and continual exactions, and did not render the monastery its due payments. Thus, often and exceedingly embittered by the wretched and incessant outcry of the people, whose land was now almost laid waste and deserted, as well as by the hunger of the monks and the ruin of the order through lack of provisions, we began, at an unfavourable time, to resist tyrants, knowing, so far as could be known about what lay ahead, that [Col. 1106C] we would either endanger our salvation or be unable to bring so necessary a cause to a salutary conclusion. For—what we say with grief and groaning—all rights have perished, the laws have fallen, moral discipline has been extinguished, ancient custom has been abolished, and the strength and authority of king and princes have vanished: everyone may do whatever he wishes, and whatever he decrees has the force of law.”

At last, as he writes in the same place, he was compelled to go to the apostolic see itself, to implore its assistance. Indeed, in the year in which Innocent II died, he was at Rome and obtained from his successor, along with letters of privilege, other letters to Albero, bishop of Liège. In these the supreme pontiff exhorts him, in taking the part of the Stavelot community, to punish, if necessary, their estate-managers and ministeriales with the spiritual sword.

> [Note: [Col. 1106D] See among the letters of Pope Celestine II, no. 20, *Patrologia*, vol. CLXXIX.]

He further adds—an important point—that Albero should compel Henry of the Rock, a knight who had destroyed the house of Erhebert, Wibald’s brother, at a time when the exercise of hostilities was wholly forbidden, to restore what he had taken from the abbey’s goods. This establishes what we said at the beginning: Erhebert’s house or castle was near Stavelot [Col. 1106D]. The letter has been published among the documents, p. 119.

On returning from Italy with Celestine’s letters, Wibald saw the long-hoped-for peace, as it were, approaching from afar. The affairs of the Stavelot community having improved somewhat, he spent one or two years fairly peacefully.

Yet his great reputation made him known, and neighbouring churches repeatedly sought him with prayers as their shepherd, asking that they might not be denied [Col. 1107A] what had for some time been granted to the monks of Cassino, foreigners wholly unknown to them. But he gave them that prophetic answer: “I am not a physician; there is no garment in my house; do not appoint me ruler of the people.” And he said: “Thus, free from habits of avarice, content with what was at hand, we served the monastery to which we had been assigned—if not by an example of good living, at least by the zeal of faithful administration” (Letter 131). Seeing him immovable, they pressed him no further.

Meanwhile, near the end of August 1144, a solemn court was held at the very celebrated monastery of Corvey, situated on the bank of the Weser at the furthest borders of Westphalia. Wibald, together with other abbots, was summoned there for judgment to be rendered concerning Henry, abbot of that place. This Henry was accused of many things, more fully pursued by the Corveyans in their letter to Bernard of Hildesheim, but especially of violent intrusion into the abbatial [Col. 1107B] office, disobedience, simony, and very bad administration. Present with him were all his accusers, not a few brethren whom he had enlisted, some by payment and some by threats, certain nobles, and especially the monastery’s ministeriales. For noble Corvey was most pitiably divided into almost two factions, which tore one another to pieces.

Wibald, having regard for the honour of the place, obtained—after humbly entreating the king—that the accusers’ action and the judicial process should not proceed after the charge had been formally entered against the defendant (Letter 131). Thus he spared the unfortunate man great shame, and stopped the mouths of slanderers who, mocking monks, as commonly happens, might have reproached the Corveyans that one of their rulers had once been solemnly condemned in a court and expelled. Henry proved utterly unmindful of this benefit, and Wibald never experienced any enemy more hostile.

But at this first encounter the Corveyans came to love the abbot of Stavelot. They were wonderfully captivated by his humanity and singular [Col. 1107C] modesty, and envied the Stavelot brethren that precious pearl, to use their own words. They observed that these men, though their revenues were not very large, flourished; daily they undertook great works and were distinguished by piety and learning. They themselves, though much richer, were deprived of everything and made a mockery to all: benumbed in idleness and cursing one another. They recalled the former years of Corvey—what it had been like in the time of Adalard and Paschasius—and even fifty years earlier, when, as they themselves wrote to Pope Eugenius (Letter 15), the monastery’s resources and dignity, both inwardly and outwardly, were diminished beyond belief.

Another assembly of princes was held at Corvey toward the end of the following year, where Wibald could become still better known. Present with him were Theodwin, bishop of Santa Rufina, and Thomas, priest-cardinal, legates of the holy Roman Church and apostolic see; Bernard, bishop of Paderborn; [Col. 1107D] Rudolf of Halberstadt; Bernard of Hildesheim; Philip of Osnabrück; Henry of Minden; Frederick of Magdeburg; Thietmar of Verden; Anselm of Havelberg; Henry of Olomouc; and the other leading men of the empire. There the Corveyans’ fishing right at Houcwar was restored, but, so far as we know, nothing was done concerning Abbot Henry. Not long afterward, however, Thomas, priest-cardinal, summoned the brethren in chapter, convicted Henry on examination of simony committed in the sale of the church of Linwert, and finally deposed him at Paderborn, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, in the presence of many abbots of Westphalia and Saxony, in 1146.

> [Note: [Col. 1107D] *Paderborn Annals*, book VIII, under the year 1143.]

Then Wibald, having received commands from the king at a solemn court at Aachen, set out for Rome on the ninth day before the Kalends of April, to carry out an embassy. Having begun his journey, he learned that Pope Lucius, whom he had long loved most dearly, [Col. 1108A] had died. Although the same message brought word that Bernard, abbot of the monastery of Saint Anastasius and equally Wibald’s friend, had succeeded him, we think that grief at this news, together with the hardship of the journey, scarcely after the end of winter, brought him into extreme danger of death. He lay ill for five weeks at Viterbo with Roman fever, as he writes to the bishop of Hildesheim (Letter 131), and, his skin and all his hair having been lost through the force of the illness, barely escaped the jaws of death.

Returning on the sixth day before the Nones of August, with his health scarcely recovered, he gladly learned that at last a new abbot had been appointed for the Corveyans: Henry, provost of the monastery. But how brief was that joy, and how quickly it was turned into deepest grief. Henry, excessively harassed by those brethren who supported his predecessor’s party, wasting away from sorrow, as the manuscript Annals of Corvey plainly suggest, died in that same year [Col. 1108B] on the eighth day before the Ides of October. Here one wonders that Nicholas Schaten, author of the Paderborn Annals, who had all the Corvey records in his possession, omitted this abbot.

> [Note: [Col. 1108D] *Paderborn Annals*, book VIII, under the year 1146, p. 767.]

The Church of Corvey, deprived of its shepherd, was worn down by new disasters. Henry, eager to be restored, fostered dissensions among the brethren through his agents on the one hand, and on the other raged cruelly, as in hostile territory, invading the monastery’s estates in arms with his brother Count Siffrid. When all had assembled in chapter on the day fixed for the election, no person could be found capable of binding up those wounds and gathering into one the children of God and of the Church who had been scattered abroad (Letter 15).

Compelled by these necessities, on the eleventh day before the Kalends of November, after invoking the grace of the Holy Spirit and taking the advice of religious and wise men, by the common desire of all, without the opposition of any person great or small—indeed, with the favourable consent of all—and with the venerable Bernard, bishop of Paderborn, present [Col. 1108C] and advising them, they chose as father and shepherd of their souls, that is, as their abbot and lord, the lord Wibald, abbot of Stavelot, by whose religious devotion and prudence the monastery of Corvey might be restored to its former state of dignity.

Lest he perhaps allow himself only with difficulty to be drawn away from his own brethren, they invoked the emperor’s authority. They immediately sent brethren to Würzburg, as we suppose—for Conrad seems to have gone there at the same time—who obtained letters addressed to the elect from both king and princes, inviting him courteously and humbly to undertake the government of so great a matter (Letter 131). They then hastened to Stavelot, bringing also the written record of the election. On the day of their arrival, Wibald, returning from the winter synod of the sacred order of Liège, had gone aside to Malmedy to celebrate solemnly the feast of All Saints on the following day. But when the delegates’ arrival was announced, he hastened to them at once.

Thus the unanimous consent of the Corveyans regarding his election was communicated to him on the day before the Kalends of November [Col. 1108D], not on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of December, as Fisen writes in his *Sanctalegia* under the year of Christ 1145. Learning from the delegates the most ardent desire of all, including the king himself, he postponed his answer until the next day, uncertain what to do: whether to comply, or, as was his custom, to resist more stubbornly. On the one hand, he feared that in declining the burden offered, out of a desire for a quieter life, he might be consulting his own interests more than the will of God Most High, which was made sufficiently evident by that universal agreement. On the other, remembering the troubles at Cassino, he pleaded his own weakness and lack of strength.

While he gradually reflected upon these and other matters, part of the night passed; the appointed hour for the night office came, and, having awakened the brethren, he went into the church. What that great man experienced then, and how at last, wholly poured out before God, he reached a decision, he explains at greater length in the already cited letter [Col. 1109A] to Bernard of Hildesheim. Since it bears the piety of the Church’s earliest times and the sincerity of a soul fearing even the least fault, we have thought it should be inserted here.

“In this anticipatory meditation, in which the fire of desire to choose what was better had already blazed up, we went to church, uttering something from the Psalms with our tongue, although our mind had wandered far from their saving meaning. When we came before that altar where we received episcopal blessing in the name and office of abbot, a certain familiar and intimate love which we bear for the most holy Remaclus, patron and founder of that monastery, suddenly stirred us; and the depths of our soul were shaken by a certain affectionate fear, namely because we turned over in our mind whether we should continue to leave his monastery thus.

“Our soul therefore cried to God, and to him with a vehement cry, in an inward word, a word [Col. 1109B] of hope not doubting, without sound of the bodily mouth: ‘LET YOUR WILL BE DONE, LORD. HENCEFORTH WE HAVE DETERMINED TO FOLLOW NEITHER THE COUNSEL OF OUR FRIENDS, BUT DESIRE IN THIS PRESENT MATTER TO FOLLOW YOUR WILL AND YOU, WHO ARE THE WAY, THE TRUTH, AND THE LIFE.’

“But how shall we know your will—you who are present in majesty, while we, feeding swine in a distant country of unlikeness, have departed from you? It would be rash for us to presume to seek a certain declaration of your will in this matter, such as you might deign to indicate to us by an angel, by some creature subject to you, by a vision, or by an oracle. Yet it is neither impious nor presumptuous to search out the secret of your will through those in whom you dwell. Therefore, bound to you by such a vow, we judge that the decision of our brethren and sons must be followed: whatever they say must be held fast, since you entrusted their souls to us for safekeeping, while we ourselves are poor guardians of our own soul” (Letter 131).

Having formed these thoughts [Col. 1109C], and after matins had been completed, he summoned the brethren to chapter at the customary hour and ordered the letters brought, together with the written election, to be read. When they had been read, he burst forth in these words:

“Since it has pleased divine providence, which disposes all things sweetly, through the ministry of your unanimous consent, to raise us—last of all men in merit of life and in learning of wisdom—to the government of this Church, our power over mind and body has ceased to be our own, and all that has been bestowed upon us by God in the substance of both the inward and outward person has passed and been made over to your rule and power as by a kind of proprietary right. We are yours and do not wish to abandon either you or your monastery. Therefore, asking your counsel as though it were a divine answer, we await it.

“Let no fear, no suspicion deter you from speaking, under God’s inspiration, whatever seems expedient. For we have entered into such a covenant of vow and promise with our God that we cannot in any way depart from the word of your counsel. For if the offer of this dignity [Col. 1109D] were pleasing to us, if we desired, according to their election, to preside over the Church of Corvey, we would not deliberate under the uncertainty of the consensus of a multitude, following the purpose of our own desire. But now, with God’s help, we have so established the intention of our heart that whatever portion of counsel shall be communicated to us by your brotherhood through the gift of the Holy Spirit will be most welcome to us.

“We do not hesitate, however, to admonish your prudence of this alone: insofar as it is permitted to your discretion, through the providence of God who moves human hearts and works in them, bending their wills wherever he chooses, to foresee, advise, and recommend this: that which you judge most useful and safe for our souls and bodies and for your monastery” (Letter 131).

The brethren, amazed and troubled by the novelty of the matter, admitted the delegates after Wibald had departed and pressed them to explain the course of the election again.
