As the delegates praised beyond measure the dignity, wealth, and other [Col. 1110A] advantages of Corvey, the children’s love for their father was so moved that, wholly forgetting their own interest, they advised almost with one voice that he should not, for their sake, deprive himself of such great and unexpected benefits—especially since they hoped that, with them, there would be no end of labours and troubles.

But some of them feared that the delegates might be imposing upon them, for what they reported seemed incredible. They wisely took precautions that a more careful inquiry into everything should first be made. For that purpose Master Henry, dean, a man of outstanding talent and prudence and endowed with singular firmness, was sent to Corvey. The Corveyans, however, resenting that this very slight delay had been inserted between them and their wishes, brought new commands from the king, informing Wibald that he should finally appear at Frankfurt on the eighth day before the Ides of December. “To receive,” he says (Letter 7), “from my hand those things which pertain to the gift of royal dignity, so that you may henceforth provide, as a spiritual father and prudent steward, for the Church of Corvey, which suffers grievous loss through your absence.”

Therefore, compelled to obey, at the beginning of December, with his health scarcely recovered, he committed himself to the journey. Arriving at Frankfurt on the fifth day before the Ides of that month—the day on which Conrad had gone aside to Lorsch—he encountered not a few monks of Corvey together with ministeriales, displaying great signs of joy, as if he had already willingly accepted the government of their monastery. But, as is commonly the case, imprudent joy is excessively effusive: they could not long conceal what was being plotted at Corvey. He learned that same day that he would have many disputes with Henry, that Henry had been restored at Rome and was returning in triumph. Such, at any rate, was the report, wholly contrary to what the delegates had said.

When he learned this, and saw himself and his men so deceived, he was first seized with deep grief and resolved to return to Stavelot. On the following day, considering himself released from the brethren’s vows and from every religious obligation, he greeted no one and went to the king, who was holding court at the estate of Vincheim [Col. 1110C], to entreat him and the princes that no force be used against him.

“In the royal household,” he says in the already cited letter (Letter 131), “we sought intercessors—we who had previously often interceded even for many condemned persons—and, as though doubting the loyalty of our friends, we appealed urgently to Anselm, the venerable bishop of Havelberg, and Arnold, provost of the greater church of Cologne and chancellor of the royal court. From our youth we had embraced them with the greatest affection and revered them with diligent devotion and daily increase of love; with great urgency of prayer we begged them to stand by us and turn the prince’s mind away from this intention.”

But, as the saying goes, he sang to the deaf, especially because the monks of Corvey pressed the matter and had captured the king’s mind. Accordingly, after the election had been confirmed in a crowded court amid the unbelievable applause of all, he was invested with royal insignia on the day before the Ides of December.

Then, what we can scarcely sufficiently wonder at, Wibald [Col. 1110D], in so great a conspiracy, devoutly and piously revered the will and decree of God Most High. He accepted with such cheerfulness the burden which he had so persistently refused that at once he resolved to face every danger against Henry and to pursue all his rebellious supporters. Not the slightest trace of disturbance or sadness appeared on his countenance. Armed with this resolve, he was dismissed, the king adding to the monastery of Corvey the two nunneries of Kemnade and Wisbech. For a long time their inhabitants had lived most disgracefully; by no means had they been capable of reform, nor did they offer any happier hope for the future.

He entered Corvey on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of January, while the brethren rejoiced with gladness, for they had most ardently desired his arrival. Hastening without delay to recover what Henry had wickedly alienated, he went to Goslar at the beginning of January and, travelling about the country in every direction [Col. 1111A], recovered almost everything within a few days, beyond expectation and without anyone resisting: at Cropenstedt, twenty holdings; in Northland, one entire estate at Loningen; one entire estate at Buochuru; at the estate of Wisbick, two holdings; at the estate of Loten, one holding; and many other things too numerous to list. Even Henry’s associates, terrified by the first report of the man, voluntarily entrusted themselves to his clemency.

Meanwhile Conrad, moved by the example of Louis, king of the French, and urged by the frequent exhortations of Saint Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, received the life-giving sign of the cross at Speyer in February.

> [Note: [Col. 1111D] Otto of Freising, book I, chapter 40.]

He then held a more celebrated assembly at Frankfurt. After the preparations for the holy war had been arranged, another war, demanded by the Saxon nobles—among whom we now count Wibald—was proclaimed against the Lutici and Obotrites, a cruel people of the Slavs devoted to the worship of idols, who most grievously harassed the Christians of the transalpine region and of Denmark. Provision was next made for the commonwealth, lest it be disturbed during the king’s absence. Finally, by unanimous consent, his son Henry, still a boy, was admitted to the royal throne, with Henry, archbishop of Mainz, appointed as his guardian; by the ancient privilege of his see, the custody and administration of the kingdom during the prince’s absence belonged to him.

Present at this assembly, among many leaders of the Church, were Albero, archbishop of Trier; Burchard of Worms; Anselm of Havelberg; Henry, bishop of Liège; Sifrid, elect of Würzburg; Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux; and our Wibald. The latter brought back two notable instruments.

> [Note: [Col. 1111D] See below, in the Appendix to Wibald’s letters.]

By one of these, the two aforesaid monasteries of Kemnade and Wisbech were confirmed to Corvey; by the other, the privileges of that monastery were renewed, especially its right of patronage and administration over the nuns of Herford. There was an innumerable company of dukes, counts, margraves, and nobles, a great part of whom had taken the name of Christ’s soldiery.

After the assembly was dissolved, Wibald was sent, together with Burchard of Worms and Anselm of Havelberg, to meet Pope Eugenius, who [Col. 1111C] was then passing from Italy into Gaul. They carried the king’s letters, in which he first reported what had been determined at the assembly. He then excused himself for having taken the token of the cross without consulting the pope. The king’s words deserve notice:

“As for those complaints,” he says (Letter 20), “that you allege we undertook so great a matter—namely, the sign of the life-giving cross and the plan of so great and long an expedition—without your knowledge: it proceeded from a great affection of true love. But the Holy Spirit, who breathes where he wills and is accustomed to come suddenly, permitted us no delay in seeking your counsel or anyone else’s. As soon as he touched our heart with his wondrous finger, he impelled the whole intention of our mind to follow him without any intervening interval of delay.”

In the same letters the king then urgently requested the supreme pontiff to turn aside a little toward the bank of the Rhine and come to Strasbourg on the Friday after Easter [Col. 1111D], for a conference concerning the peace of the Churches. Finally, he commends the delegates themselves by name: “men,” he says, “indeed prudent and discerning, lovers of the holy Roman Church and of the kingdom, and most dear to us.”

These three most distinguished men travelled by long stages and met Eugenius at Dijon on the third day before the Kalends of April. When Wibald’s arrival was announced, Eugenius was greatly delighted and immediately received them graciously. Yet when he read the king’s letter and noticed that Wibald was styled abbot of Corvey, he was astonished that a man until then most devoted to the Roman pontiff had accepted this dignity without consulting him. For he considered that, if an abbot or any ruler of one church undertook the administration of another church as well, this belonged to the reins of his own governance (Letter 131). [Col. 1112A] Somewhat disturbed, he demanded the production of reliable testimony from the Corveyans (Letter 14), by which it might appear that Wibald’s election had been entirely free. He could not be induced to confirm it in the manner previously proposed; indeed, when Wibald requested other letters for Corvey (Letter 131), both against Henry and for confirmation of the abbeys of Kemnade and Wisbech, he refused altogether.

Thus that holy pontiff, the emulator of his father Bernard of Clairvaux, when Christ’s patrimony was at stake, spared no consideration—not of friends, not of princes, nor even of the emperor himself—though he certainly knew well enough that they had promoted this affair. Nevertheless, after hearing what we have just said (Letter 131) about the Slavic war and that the Saxons with the bishops of the province were preparing themselves for it, he commanded Wibald, by the authority granted him by God, to devote every effort to this undertaking. He reminded him that it was his own cause that was being pursued, since the faith was to be spread in those regions where it had once been planted by the first monks of his own Corvey [Col. 1112B]. The war was undertaken for this end: that the barbarians might be subdued more by the power of evangelical truth than by the edge of the sword. He himself imposed a distinctive emblem on the expedition.

“The cross,” says Otto of Freising,

> [Note: [Col. 1111D] Book I, chapter 40.]

“was not simply sewn onto the garments, such as was worn by the soldiers of the eastern expedition, but extended upward from a wheel placed beneath it.”

Wibald accepted the pontiff’s commands all the more willingly because he ardently desired to rescue the wretched people from the filth of idolatry. Moreover, Corvey’s own cause pressed upon him (Letter 131). The island of Rügen, granted to Corvey by Emperor Lothair in 846,

> [Note: [Col. 1112D] See the *Paderborn Annals*, book II, under this year.]

after a notable victory won through the merits of Blessed Vitus over the Obotrites, in which their king Gestimulus was killed, had long been seized by these most impious barbarians, the Christian name being utterly erased. There was hope that, if the expedition succeeded, it might be completely recovered or at least restored to its former faith. But one consideration held back the prudent man: the equipment for this war, so far as it concerned him, could be furnished only at very great expense; perhaps it was less permissible that these expenses should be demanded from him before he was confirmed as abbot of Corvey [Col. 1112C].

Nevertheless, since no time for deliberation was allowed and April was imminent—the month in which the army generally had to be set in motion—he departed together with Guy, cardinal and chancellor, whom the supreme pontiff was sending as legate to the king. He had first warned the brethren of Corvey (Letter 14) to communicate as soon as possible to Eugenius and his legate the requested evidence of the assembly. Travelling rapidly, they first reached Würzburg during Easter week, then Bamberg, where Conrad had celebrated holy Easter. Conrad received and dismissed Guy, then in many words commended his son Henry, the boy king, to Wibald’s loyalty. This was Conrad’s final pledge of goodwill to his dearly loved abbot before they parted.

From this we may state with complete certainty that the archbishop of Mainz, by the right of his Church, had indeed the title and dignity of guardian, but Wibald undertook the burden of the guardianship. Anyone who reads Letters 30, 31, 89, and many others scattered throughout must acknowledge this, if he is a fair judge of matters [Col. 1112D].

Then, as the king proceeded to Frankfurt, thence to Nuremberg, and afterward to Regensburg, as the ancient writers relate, Wibald withdrew to Corvey to await confirmation in his see at Corvey. For the monks of Corvey had appointed two of their number: Walter, prior of the monastery, and Reinher, provost of Cresburch, men of approved testimony and honourable conduct. They met Eugenius near Paris at the monastery of Saint-Denis, but found him so overwhelmed with business that they could scarcely be heard at Meaux ten days later.

Henry, a monk of Stavelot, who had been added to them as a third at Wibald’s command on account of his remarkable eloquence, candidly sets out the course of this embassy [Col. 1113A] in a letter to Wibald himself:

“On the Tuesday of Pentecost,” he says (Letter 25), “we reached the lord pope at Saint-Denis, where, because of the very great tumult surrounding the lord pope at the departure of the lord king, we presented ourselves only to the lord chancellor. On the following day, before the lord pope, who intended to proceed to Meaux, departed, we were presented to the lord pope through the chancellor and gave him the letters which we had brought. From there we reached Meaux on Thursday. But on Friday we alone were summoned into the presence of the lord pope, the bishops, and the cardinals.

“Yet the lord Florentine had instructed us beforehand what we were to say and who was to speak—namely, one of the Corveyans, whose cause was being conducted. But since one of them was less fluent in speech, as you know better, and the other was seriously ill, I, who [Col. 1113B] was present among the Corveyans at your command, came with them before the lord pope as though I were a Corveyan. Since the matter had to be conducted before all those present on your behalf, I, acknowledging that I was a Corveyan only from the necessity already described, set out before the lord pope, as was fitting, the entire course of the election, which I knew well.

“Accordingly, after the pope had heard all the necessities for which they had elected you and had also learned the benefits—which we had not kept silent—that followed the election, he said that he would consult with his brethren and answer us according to their counsel. We were held in this suspense for ten days.”

After a few intervening words, he adds:

“What finally happened? On the tenth day after your election case had been heard, we were summoned, and after much praise of your person, your wisdom, and your eloquence, in the presence of the bishops and all the cardinals, he adjudged and granted that the election made in your favour should stand and be valid. This was done more by the dispensation [Col. 1113C] of the Roman Church, as he himself testified, than by any authority.”

While those worthy brethren were thus long detained at the pontiff’s court, the time fixed for the expedition gradually slipped away, and Corbie could scarcely supply anything for its costs and equipment, since the resources of that wealthy monastery had been utterly exhausted by the repeated attacks of Henry, the former abbot. What then did Wibald do? He undertook an action truly noble and wholly consonant with the ancient usages of the Church; and he proved in very deed that, when reduced to such straits, he could bear an unshaken spirit alike amid adversity and prosperity. For a long time the monks of Corbie had been accumulating in the sacred building a certain sum of money from the daily offerings of the faithful, piously earmarked both for repairing the church itself and for the monastery’s pressing needs. He devoted this treasure—and indeed the very vessels of the altar—to the restoration of living temples for the worship of the true God and to the overthrow of idols. Having summoned the brethren and set before them, as we have related, the circumstances of the expedition and the fact that Eugene had laid the cross upon him, he took from the altars of Saint Stephen and Saint Vitus thirty marks of gold, together with a gold chalice of six marks, while nevertheless providing, by a most solemn decree, and even binding all by oath, that this treasure should be restored as quickly as possible. We here print that decree from a manuscript history of Corbie, which, by the command of the most serene prince, was most graciously shared with us, to serve posterity as a notable example.

The brethren of Corbie, great and small, assembled in the same monastery in the Lord, to all whom these presents shall reach: peace and charity.

We wish all the faithful of our Church, both present and future, to know that, by the common counsel of our chapter and of our lay ministerials—that is, of the Church of Corbie—with the consent of our lord and reverend father Wicbold, abbot of Corbie, we have taken certain things from the treasures for certain public and common advantages of our monastery, upon which we have spent those same treasures. These are the things that we have taken: from the altar of Saint Stephen, twenty-four marks of gold; from the altar of Saint Vitus, six marks of gold; a gold chalice weighing six marks of gold; and half of an excellent *plenarium* [a complete service-book], which has been pledged to the duke of Saxony for sixty marks of silver.

And since these treasures had been deposited in our church by our forebears—men surely pious and religious—both for the adornment of God’s house and for relieving the necessities of the church whenever need arose; and since we found in our time that our church had been enriched and adorned with these treasures through the labour of our Fathers and the alms of the pious: desiring to imitate the examples of our predecessors, by the common counsel of our chapter and with the consent of our reverend lord and father, the aforesaid abbot, we have ordained and established with our said lord abbot that each year we shall take from our prebend, whether it be from wine, furs, or charitable distributions, twelve marks of silver from all sources, and contribute them to restoring the treasures which we have taken from the church.

[Col. 1114B] The lord abbot likewise promised that, for the same work, until the whole has been restored, he will annually give all the revenues of his estate at Huldessen, and in addition as much as is needed to make up twelve marks. Our lay ministerials also, who were present at the deliberation that treasures should be taken from the church in order to restore those same treasures, vowed to give their goods annually until the work should be completed: one half a talent, another five shillings, each according to his means and as God may inspire him, so that they may render what they have vowed to God and His saints.

But we, together with the lord abbot, have bound ourselves by these vows to our most sacred patrons Stephen and Vitus, around whose holy and venerable relics we have expended the gold: namely, that we shall devoutly pay annually the same amount of silver which we have promised. And if perchance barrenness of the land or some other such necessity should arise, so that in one year or in two the aforesaid money cannot be paid by the lord abbot and by us, then in the next following year, when we are able to pay, the entire deficiency shall be made good with goodwill both by the lord abbot and by us; and this shall be faithfully and piously paid every year until the restoration of the treasures which we have taken from the church.

Therefore, wishing to leave to our successors as an example this pious and faithful undertaking of ours, just as we received it from our Fathers, we have committed this very pledge of ours to writing. And, that it may possess inviolable force, we have sealed it with the seal of Saint Vitus, our most sacred patron, and moreover with the seal of our lord abbot.

Done in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1148 (read: 1147), in the tenth indiction, in the 324th year from the foundation of New Corbie, in the second year of Lord Wicbold’s abbacy in the Church of Corbie.

These are the laymen who promised their assistance annually until the work should be completed: Conrad of Fralin …, half a talent annually; Herebold of … and his son Conrad, five shillings; Thiederic Grossus and his son Erenfrid, five shillings; Count Thiederic of Huxere, five shillings; Helmewig of Godolumen, three shillings; Reiner of Porta, five shillings; Adelbert of Bodelevessen, half a talent; Elverin of …, five shillings; his brother Tiederic, five shillings; Charles of New Church, three shillings; Raban, five shillings; Bruno, five shillings; Goswin of Weten, five shillings; Reinmar, three shillings.

Thus increased by the sacred treasure, Wibald set out with the other magnates of Saxony toward the end of May, having waited for some time for the supreme pontiff’s confirmation—a confirmation which, it seems, was delayed too long for the dignity of the man concerned. So great was the army of Christians that, once the Elbe had been crossed, the whole land trembled before them. With no hope at the very outset shining upon the commanders of subduing Slavonic savagery, King Niclot, so to speak, having turned to frenzy, they ravaged everything for almost three months, as the ancient author writes; they set cities and towns alight, and burned down, together with the city itself, even the temple with its idols that stood before the city of Malchow.

But after much slaughter on both sides, when the decisive point of the war lay in taking the strongly fortified castles of Demmin and Dubin, and the army, now divided in two, was pressing both fortresses, surrounded and besieged at the same time, with greater vigour [Note: [Col. 1115D] Helmold, book I, ch. 66; Otto of Freising, book I, ch. 44.], a disagreement arising among the commanders brought that great expedition to an end with little gain.

Wibald was present at the siege of the castle of Demmin toward the end of June, as he writes to Bernard of Hildesheim; but neither he himself, in his customary extreme modesty, nor Helmold nor any other writer has recorded what he did there. In truth, this war seems to have stirred up against him all the monsters of hell. For it is scarcely credible that men, however cruel and unjust, could have devised all that was wickedly and outrageously attempted against this innocent man from the time he crossed the Elbe. Nothing whatsoever in either Corbie or Stavelot remained secure from the violence of the unjust: estates were plundered, the richer villages occupied, and the brethren and dependants of both monasteries were at last cruelly abused in shameful ways.

Here Count Godfrey of Namur, having broken the truce which in the preceding year he had made with the monastery’s advocate until the Kalends of October of this year, devastated everything with fire and sword in the region of Liège, in Hesbaye, and in Condroz; and, with his consent, the village of Turnines was again occupied by Eustace, advocate of Liège. There, under the leadership of Duke Henry, a wicked band attacked the noble monastery, trying the constancy of the brethren now with threats, now enticing them with blandishments, that, rejecting Wibald, they might receive this distinguished duke—a man surely utterly unworthy, in perfidy and iniquity, of the name of monk, indeed of priest and abbot. At that time the faithfulness of the Corbie brethren stood unshaken; all without exception fortified the monastery with defensive works and arms, intending, by the law of nations, to repel force with force (Letter 131).

Yet if we choose to glance even briefly at the following years, we shall see other brethren and dependants of that same place, with the same Henry as instigator of the disturbance, stirring up open rebellion in the monastery, openly taking his side, and others—more daring men—laying snares for the abbot. But, what is worse, the man’s integrity, held in the highest regard by all down to that day, was torn by false accusations and exposed even to the suspicion of good men.

Before he had even set foot to undertake the expedition, a rumour was already being spread everywhere that the abbot of Corbie, by laying impious hands upon sacred furnishings, had rashly distributed to the king riches dedicated to divine worship. That rumour had indeed been somewhat checked at the Roman court by the two brethren whom we said above had been sent to the supreme pontiff, as Henry, monk of Stavelot, testifies in the letter there cited [Col. 1115D] (Letter 25). But after their departure, like a flame bursting from ashes, it flared up again to such a degree that the supreme pontiff, to the consternation of Wibald’s friends and especially the monks of Stavelot, caused a legate to be sent to Corbie in December of that same year to investigate the matter more carefully.

The following year the brethren of Corbie wrote them a letter of consolation, from which the man’s innocence is sufficiently evident. Although, to conceal nothing, we wonder that neither here nor in the decree printed above is any mention made of the expedition against the Obotrites, on whose occasion this storm had arisen.

“We have heard,” they say, “that your unanimity has been disturbed by a report which Master G. communicated to us last year concerning treasures removed from our church … He therefore came to us … last year about the feast of Saint Thomas … At that time the chief provost of our church was at home … He asked him why our sanctuary had been despoiled of its treasures. ‘Our sanctuary,’ said the provost, ‘has not been despoiled, because whatever has been taken from it has been spent for the advantage of our church.’”

And, after some intervening matter:

“For the common necessity of the church, we have taken a certain part of the treasures in the church with the common consent of our chapter, and with them have acquired certain very useful possessions for our church. Everything else has been preserved intact in the church. What we have now received on account of necessity, we have resolved, God granting, to repair and restore as soon as we can.” Thus they wrote.

From this we may infer that money was taken from the sacred building more than once in that year; nor was all that taken on the occasion of the expedition spent merely on the expenses of that expedition, as the manuscript history of Corbie suggests. Rather, some part of it was perhaps intended for the king hastening against the unbelievers [Col. 1116B], and for the monastery’s more urgent affairs; this equally clears Wibald of every charge of wrongdoing.

But let us proceed no further. Returning from the Slavonic expedition at the beginning of September, he relieved the monastery from siege; and, having with remarkable humanity and clemency calmed the turbulent disturbances which, as we have said, had been raised to his dishonour and injury, he went to Stavelot scarcely a month later, to bring aid to a flock oppressed by the continual wars of Count Godfrey of Namur, Waleran of Limburg, Eustace the advocate of Liège, and other nobles of Lotharingia. While he himself was being torn by the bites of the envious, he had assumed the nature of a lamb; but then, more anxious over the losses of his own people, he assumed the spirit of a lion, raging even against the dead in order to strike fear into the living. This will become especially clear from the document printed below [Note: [Col. 1116D] See Appendix, no. 27.].

Nor was he so occupied with settling the affairs of Stavelot that, in Conrad’s absence, he neglected the business of the empire itself. At the council of Trier at the beginning of 1148, he was present in the name of Henry, the younger king; then at Reims, where he proposed many matters which we have elsewhere discussed. From there he was summoned to the assembly held at Weinsberg on the Kalends of September, and then to Frankfurt, to assist the king with counsel and aid in establishing the condition of the kingdom and confirming peace (Letter 89). Meanwhile, tirelessly attending to his native Moselle Lotharingia, which was entirely aflame with warfare, he restrained some by negotiated truces and brought others into friendship and alliance itself.

He writes this expressly to the brethren of Corbie, who felt his absence rather grievously. “That your brotherhood may know,” he says (Letter 84), “that no idle time has passed for us: between the count of Namur, the count of Los, and the count of Dasburg, whose discord was tearing the whole land apart, with God as author we made peace lasting until the feast of Saint Remigius; and between the count of the Rock, who is our advocate, and the count of Montaigu, who, at the prompting of many, were waging the greatest wars against one another, we restored a final concord beneficial to the whole land.”

While Wibald was occupied with these concerns and again residing at Stavelot, Conrad returned from Palestine in 1149 (Letter 169) and ordered him to be summoned to the assembly convened at Frankfurt for the feast of the Assumption, intending separately to discuss with the high princes of the empire those matters which were to be publicly expounded in the assembly. The king was undertaking two affairs of greater importance (Letter 149): an Italian expedition and the restoration of Ladislaus, the exiled duke of Poland. After losing his flourishing army in the East, he was no more able to accomplish these two matters, equally difficult though they were, than he had been before; although during nearly the three years which remained to him they were repeatedly discussed in various assemblies, and envoys were more than once sent both to the supreme pontiff and to the Poles. Wibald was invited by the king and present at nearly all these assemblies.

First, at Frankfurt in 1149 [Col. 1117A] (Letter 261), then at Bamberg (Letters 217, 261), where he was maintained at royal expense for nine weeks and more, shortly to have been sent to Rome with Arnold, provost of Cologne and chancellor of the realm, had most weighty affairs of state not intervened. Then he was at Speyer early in February, and at Fulda on the third day before the Nones of April (Letters 217, 184); indeed, he remained at the king’s side for fully five months. At about this time he continually opposed the Roman rebels, who were seeking the king’s favour against Pope Eugene through frequent letters, vigorously undertaking the Church’s cause (Letters 211, 212).

“We came,” he writes to that same pontiff from Bamberg (Letter 228), “to the court of your glorious son Conrad, king of the Romans, on the vigil of the Nativity of the Lord, and remained there continuously until the Thursday of Easter week, in the expectation that he would send both us and his chancellor to the presence of Your Sublimity, as he had long since agreed and had also made known to Your Greatness. During this period we laboured zealously by day and night to inflame his mind strongly toward love and reverence for your person, toward the defence of our most holy mother, the Roman Church, and of all Churches … But, because certain great affairs of the realm intervened, he was unwilling to be without either our person or his chancellor.”

Nevertheless, when the Italian expedition was decreed the following year, both at Regensburg and at Würzburg, both men were sent as envoys to the supreme pontiff and to the Romans, that they might advance it in Italy by their counsel and prudence (Letters 320, 323, 324). But the embassy was scarcely completed when Conrad died, and Frederick, his successor, postponed the same expedition to another time.

Now Wibald’s very great authority and favour with the king did not at all disappear, as commonly happens. After Conrad’s death he became still dearer to Frederick, who, like everyone else, held his grey-haired wisdom and loyalty in the highest reverence. He became the arbiter of all Frederick’s counsels and, so to speak, alone sustained by his prudence the entire burden of the empire during the first years of Frederick’s kingship and empire. Anyone who carefully reads the letters which Frederick either wrote or received from the time when he was taken as partner in the kingdom must recognize this. Happy and fortunate would he have been, had fortune preserved such a minister for him long!

Wibald survived Conrad by only five years, but, if examined more carefully, these years seem to equal his earlier life in the glory of deeds accomplished. First among them was Frederick’s elevation to the throne; Frederick himself testified in a charter written in golden letters at the general assembly held at Merseburg in 1153 that Wibald had laboured not a little for this.

This year of Christ 1153 was especially glorious for Wibald because of the exchange of letters with Emperor Manuel, concerning the marriage of King Frederick to that emperor’s daughter. Wibald himself, who pursued that marriage so actively, had urged Frederick, the future emperor, to join himself to the emperor by affinity. Letter 90 testifies to this in these words addressed to Manuel: “I have not ceased earnestly striving that my illustrious and victorious lord, Emperor Frederick, might enter into a treaty of friendship with your most steadfast empire and take a wife from your blood; and your wisdom will undoubtedly hasten to bring this to completion.”

What shall we bring forward about the following years? Brevity obliges us to choose. At Wibald’s prompting Frederick set out on the Italian expedition toward the end of 1154; and in the following year, after notable triumphs, he was crowned king of the Lombards. Advancing further, with Wibald as his companion, he entered Rome and on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of June was crowned emperor by Pope Adrian [IV]. The supreme pontiff, anxious about the king’s arrival and uncertain whether he approached as enemy or friend, had sent envoys to meet him. But with Wibald present, what was there for the pontiff to fear? Adrian later gratefully acknowledged this most fully [Note: [Col. 1117D] See below, Appendix, no. 33.]; and, grateful to our abbot for his outstanding service in this peaceful meeting with the emperor, he renewed by new charters the rights and privileges of the monasteries of Stavelot and Corbie.

The most joyful year had not yet ended when Wibald was sent to the emperor of Constantinople, who had dispatched to the emperor the most noble of the Greeks, Palaeologus, a magnate of royal blood, as Otto of Freising writes (book II, ch. 12), and the distinguished Marodocus, bearing considerable gifts. When this embassy had been completed in 1156 and a few months had intervened, Frederick, then moving against the Poles to restore the exiled Duke Ladislaus, invited him to undertake in the following year an expedition against the Milanese (Letter 423).

But alas! God most good, by whose will all things are governed, had provided otherwise. For when Frederick returned victorious from Poland (Letter 434), and arranged a second embassy to Manuel, Wibald was sent again. At last, returning in the following year, he died at Butella in Paphlagonia, poisoned, as was suspected, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of August [Note: [Col. 1117D] Manuscript history of the abbots of Stavelot.]. Hence, as the learned Nicholas Schaten, author of the Paderborn Annals, writes from Radewicus [Note: [Col. 1118D] *Annales Paderbornenses*, book VIII, under the year 1157.], the envoys of the Greek emperor, who were present with Frederick in 1159, shrank from entering the assembly of princes unless they were first assured by the public pledge of the princes that they would be safe, since they were held either suspected or hated on account of the great man’s hastened death by poison [Note: [Col. 1118D] Radewicus, book II, ch. 22.].

Such was the end of Abbot Wibald: a man, if his character be considered, most worthy of the earliest ages of the Church; if his natural gifts, prudence, and other qualities of mind be considered, inferior scarcely to anyone of his age—an age indeed fertile in outstanding men.

With regard to character, the virtues that shone most conspicuously in Wibald were those farthest removed from princely courts: proven integrity; candour wholly free from guile; charity truly Christian toward all, which no injuries could ever extinguish; and great contempt for himself.

We have often wondered that, among so many letters and documents printed here, not a single word should have escaped him about his household, parents, or paternal property—unless perhaps in Letter 79, where he writes that his brother was the king’s chancellor, and on one occasion mentions his sister. He was also accustomed to speak of himself so humbly and lowly that he seems more than once to have disclaimed every nobility of birth. Thus in Letter 148, replying with great modesty to Harwic, archbishop-elect of Bremen, who complained that Wibald had aspired to the see of Bremen after Adalbero’s death—for the greater part of the clergy’s votes had turned toward Wibald—he says:

“You are displeased with us because, when the election of an archbishop of Bremen was being considered while the see was then vacant, the votes of almost all seemed to incline toward our person. We do not willingly enter upon such a hazardous dispute, in which questions of birth and character are debated with the utmost subtlety and error is very frequent; and, being well aware of our weakness and humility, we would by no means presume to approach the undertaking and timely management of so great and venerable a matter.”

And in Letter 86: “Had the Church of Stavelot not reared us; had she not raised us needy from the dust and lifted us poor from the dungheap, that we might sit with princes …”

We have already seen how wholly averse his mind was to every dignity. He was forcibly taken to the see of Monte Cassino; not long afterward he relinquished it most willingly; and, having declined many other offices [Col. 1119A] which he did not name, he came to the Corbie brethren only under compulsion (Letter 131). The mitre of Bremen, in a manner offered to him, and later that of Cologne (Letters 148, 210), he avoided—not openly, since that can scarcely be done without ostentation, but indirectly and as though pursuing another matter—judging himself unworthy of every honour.

If any adversity befell his monks, he imputed it to himself (Letters 41, 86); if he himself acted vigorously and beneficially, he attributed everything to God, who used a worthless and insignificant instrument (Letter 41). Thus he confessed himself unworthy even of the remembrance of the most insignificant persons. “Our conscience,” he says to Frederick, first abbot of Saint Godehard (Letter 117), who had praised him somewhat, “grievously attacks and accuses us, and judges us worthy, I do not say of your commendation, but not even of the commendation of any lowliest man.”

He experienced enemies everywhere and always most hostile; and nothing occurs more frequently in his letters than the complaints of the men of Stavelot or Corbie against such persons, who exercised their hatred now by plundering estates, now by arson. What did he not suffer at Monte Cassino from Rainald the Tuscan? What at Corbie from that disgraceful Abbot Henry, who, though deprived of office by apostolic authority, could never be induced to obey the decree of the supreme pontiff? What from Harwic, archbishop of Bremen; from Henry of Minden; from the bishop of Osnabrück and other magnates of the empire; from Judith, abbess of Kamen; and, finally, from his sons [i.e. monks/dependants]?

“We have often been tossed,” he says (Letter 315), “by dreadful dangers, and especially by dangers among false brethren.” Though he could have crushed them all by a nod alone, he sought to win them by benefits. He provided Rainald the Tuscan with a safe escape from Caesar’s anger; Henry of Corbie, Henry’s kinsmen, and others equally faithless, he enriched with benefits such as friends themselves would not have hoped for (Letter 131). He regarded all these persons in some sense as sacred instruments of divine justice. “Those who persecuted us,” he said (Letter 35), “were servants of divine justice; and although by their evil intention they deserved eternal woe, nevertheless they were the rod of our most just God and the staff of His wrath, though they themselves did not know it.”

Accordingly, when Frederick, abbot of Saint Godehard, earnestly begged him to receive the penitent Henry back into favour, he replied in words that deserve to be engraved in letters of gold (Letter 117):

“Regarding his desire to be reconciled with us, we are greatly concerned what meaning or judgment may be contained in the word ‘reconciliation.’ For our conscience bears witness that we have committed no offence against him. But if he has sinned against us, we forgive him everything from a perfect heart for the sake of divine love, and we desire true good to come to him both in soul and body. Nor do we begrudge him, provided our peace is preserved and the monastery safeguarded, if some more fruitful repose may be granted to him; for we too are human beings, have been scourged with human beings, and do not regard anything human as alien from ourselves.”

[Col. 1119D] If we descend now to those virtues more naturally implanted in him, he surely must have been endowed with consummate prudence, having endured for more than thirty years, amid so many adversaries, no changes of fortune at court. For in 1122, not yet an abbot and perhaps not even a monk of Stavelot, indeed scarcely of the age accounted legally qualified for public offices, he was known at Rome and was intimate with the chief cardinals of the sacred college (Letters 50, 393, etc.). A few years later he was made head of Stavelot, then archchancellor of Lothair, commander of a very great fleet in the Italian expedition, and finally abbot of Monte Cassino, that he might reform the monastery and restrain all Campania and the schismatic rebels.

After Lothair’s death, he possessed such favour and authority with Conrad that he always experienced in him more than paternal affection (Letter 340). He was beloved by Frederick. Under these emperors nothing of greater importance was done without consulting him. He was continually engaged in the greatest affairs of the empire and in the most weighty embassies, and everywhere employed such skill that he seemed to have bent the minds and wills of the princes with whom he dealt exactly where he most wished. Let this, if one pleases, be ascribed to his eloquence, which Reinhard, abbot of Reinhausen, called Ciceronian (Letter 34).

But the fact that, while he lived, the empire had no dispute with the Roman See should, we think, be attributed rather to his experience and practical knowledge. For from what has been said it is quite clear that Wibald alone managed Roman affairs in addition to the empire’s other administration. If to these concerns we add the troubles of Stavelot and Corbie and the private affairs of his friends—for he served everyone, insofar as he could—no one will doubt that he possessed a mind of immense capacity, since he alone could meet so many, such great, varied, and continuous demands. Yet he was not so occupied that he did not from time to time give himself to leisure studies (Letter 147).

[Col. 1120B] He cultivated literature continually and every day, at fixed hours and times, learned something new. We admit that he seems to have devoted more than enough attention to poets, both Greek and Latin, to ancient philosophers and orators, and especially to Cicero, whose works he caused to be sought out everywhere and copied—unless perhaps that man ought to be excused for restoring a mind wearied by more serious cares through the most delightful charms of such writers rather than by any other, less useful relaxation.

He also said quite aptly (ibid.) that he crossed over into a foreign camp not as a deserter or runaway, but as a scout and one eager for spoils, in the hope that he might seize a Midianite woman and, after her hair had been shaved and her nails pared, be lawfully able to join her to himself in marriage. But as he grew older, he devoted himself wholly to the study of sacred letters. The very weighty judgment which he gave in Letter 147 on the foremost Fathers of the Church—Cyprian, Lactantius, Hilary of Poitiers, Ambrose, Jerome, Augustine, and Leo the Great—shows that these writers were very familiar and well known to him. In the same letter he also testifies that he had read Bede, Haimo, Ambrose Autpert, Rabanus Maurus, John Scotus, and many other pious writers of the Middle Ages.

He acquired such expertise in sacred law that he was sometimes consulted (Letter 356). Letter 357 should be read, in which he answers Arnold, archbishop of Cologne, who had asked him whether nuns might take the veil at Pentecost. Therefore, when the provost of Hildesheim—from whom he had requested Cicero’s *Philippics* and letters together with that author’s speeches *On the Agrarian Law* (Letter 205)—perhaps rather sharply reminded him to remember that he was a Christian, not a Ciceronian, he wrote in his customary gentle manner (Letter 206):

“You rightly remind us, brother, that although we possess Cicero’s books, we should nevertheless remember that we are Christians … We no longer have Cicero’s dishes either among the principal courses or at the first table; but, if after we have been satisfied with better food we sometimes desire something, we partake of them as sweetmeats are customarily served at the second course,” etc.

Whether he published any treatises is unknown; but he often urged friends, brethren, or sons to write: Anselm, bishop of Havelberg, in Letter 142; Henry, monk of Stavelot, in Letter 106; and Theodoric, abbot of Waulsort, in the sixth letter. The ancient rites of the Church of Corbie, which are still preserved in its library, likewise seem, from the work’s loftiness and the ancient script of the codex, to have been restored and arranged at his command. They are precious remnants of the vast store of books which he had assembled through immense labour.

Thus this man—the glory of our Gaul, the light of the empire, and, in the Church of Rome’s most difficult times, a pillar in Germany—was carried off at Butella in Paphlagonia by Greek treachery, as the shorter Annals of Stavelot relate, on the fourteenth day before the Kalends of August, in 1158. His bones, deposited in the basilica of that city, were most honourably transferred to Stavelot in the following year through the agency of Brother Erlebold, his successor; and, with Henry, bishop of Liège, celebrating the funeral rites, they were laid in the middle of the choir on the seventh day before the Kalends of August.

We append here [Col. 1122A] the epitaph which the Annals of Corbie derive from the Chronicle of Höxter, although the opinion at Stavelot is that nothing was inscribed on his monument beyond Wibald’s name and the day of his death.

WICBALD, FOR GOD AND THE CHURCH.

[Col. 1121]

He who, while he lived, was the happiest of all abbots among mortals,  
Most dear to the supreme [Note: [Col. 1121] Indeed, to at least five popes and four emperors.] pontiff, the emperor, and princes,  
Here laid down the remains of his body,  
To be most highly and forever commended to all posterity  
For piety, diligence, and singular zeal.  
You who shall sit after him, do likewise, and you shall live.

[Col. 1121B] Thus far we have set out Wibald the abbot’s deeds at some length, grieving that the memory of so great a man might be wholly obliterated. It is now pleasant to add a few remarks on his letters. All, except only eleven, come from an ancient codex of Stavelot; these eleven, by right of antiquity, will occupy the first place here. That codex contains very many autograph annotations, which we do not wish to examine, lest we detain readers further. But it is incomplete: fourteen leaves have been torn out at the very beginning, and these undoubtedly contained writings concerning Wibald’s election as abbot of Corbie, together with several letters of Emperor Conrad and of princes inviting him to undertake the governance of so great a matter. For all that follows was written only from that period onward. We infer that Wibald’s letters were divided into at least two volumes, of which the earlier has been lost. How great a loss this is to the republic of letters will be judged from the later portion.

Here the principal acts of Emperor Conrad, his son Henry, and Frederick are set forth severally. The history of the churches of Cologne, Mainz, Bremen, Minden, and other noble churches of Germany is remarkably illuminated. Some proceedings of the councils of Trier and Reims in 1148, hitherto lost, are restored. Finally, ecclesiastical as well as monastic discipline is elucidated in many places, as we have already discussed in the general preface.

We owe this treasure to the most reverend father, the lord chief prior of the imperial Church of Stavelot, who not only shared the manuscript codex but also supplied a transcription together with the monastery’s documents. The most reverend Lord Anscharius de Grass, canon and prior of the free and imperial Church of Corbie, general vicar in spiritual matters and archdeacon of the most exalted and most reverend prince and abbot of the Holy Roman Empire, also sent us five letters (Letters 7, 8, 9, 10, and 11). Finally, the most illustrious lord abbot of Waulsort gave us one letter together with the principal records of his monastery. We have prefixed these six letters, along with five others excerpted by us partly from Mabillonian papers and partly from the Chronicle of Monte Cassino.

And lest anything concerning Wibald that lay within our power should be lacking, we have added at the end, in the manner of an appendix, those documents and letters of privilege which he himself, as abbot and prince of Corbie, either made or obtained, although they have already been published in part, along with other monuments of Corbie, in the Paderborn Annals.

[Col. 1121]

# THE LETTERS OF WIBALD

## LETTER ONE. WIBALD, ABBOT OF MONTE CASSINO, TO EMPEROR LOTHAIR,

composed by Peter the Deacon. He sets before him the calamities of the monastery of Monte Cassino and implores his aid and protection.

*(In the year 1137.—Mabillon extracted it from a manuscript of Monte Cassino.)*

[Col. 1121D]

LOTHAIR, by the grace of God most invincible Caesar of the Romans, Augustus Emperor, and perpetual conqueror: Wibald, by the grace of God minister of the monastery of Monte Cassino, unworthy, offers the service of due fidelity.

After the innumerable cares by which the imperial eminence of Rome is necessarily burdened, we recognize, most Christian Emperor and invincible conqueror, the praiseworthy purpose of your clemency: namely, that, after removing every seed of discord and complaint which the enemy of humankind [Col. 1122D] had sown in the Lord’s field, you wished, with the most devout affection of your mind, to provide for the holy Catholic Church of Monte Cassino. In this purpose and desire of your heart, the concern of your clemency, inspired by the Spirit of God, shows how greatly divine providence deigns to favour human affairs. Being, after the manner of Roman emperors, beneficent toward all, it may therefore, as though God looked on, always happily rule and govern the people of the Lord committed to it; nor may it any longer permit them to be dashed by any storms of this age or shaken by malicious disturbances, so that, after the sovereignty of this present life, you may attain the heavenly kingdom and hold it eternally with the Lord.

Accordingly, because of so great a devotion and sincerity of heart as you have shown not only in words but also in shining deeds toward the Church of Monte Cassino [Col. 1123A] and our own insignificance, we earnestly ask that you may not disdain, by your powerful assistance, to aid and defend in every respect, in this dangerous time, the holy Church of Monte Cassino—the special and singular chamber of the Roman Empire. Thus may your imperial glory, through the interceding merits of our most blessed father Benedict, increase ever more each day throughout all parts of the Roman world, and receive worthy recompense from the almighty Lord.

But what and how great are the sufferings borne by me and the Church of Monte Cassino, because of our fidelity to the Roman Empire and the Apostolic See, at the hands of the most impious peoples, the Lombards, the Normans [Note: [Col. 1123] Here he calls “Normans” those who, coming from Neustria under Duke Guiscard, conquered Apulia, Calabria, and finally Sicily by arms.], and the Saracens—no pen is sufficient to write them. Even if all the trees of the forests, grasses of the fields, waves of the sea, and [Col. 1123B] sands of the shores were turned into tongues, they could not recount them. For they have left the Church of Monte Cassino nothing but unspeakable tribulation. And behold—alas!—while Roger, king of the Normans, rejoices with his army, the sole company of the faithful is consumed by great sorrow; Christian blood is poured out; monks are bound in the chains of prison; and the people devoted to God are laid waste by continual slaughter. Whoever escapes fire or sword becomes plunder, is dragged away captive, sold, and made an exile forever.

Behold: cities, strongholds, churches, and monasteries, emptied of inhabitants, have perished; provosts and monks, scattered here and there, have been left only the thresholds of Blessed Benedict as a refuge. Their monasteries have been reduced to lairs of wild beasts; and they themselves, found wandering and roofless, are no longer permitted to preach the Lord’s name, but must beg. Behold, invincible Emperor, the sword has reached even the soul. Behold the day in which we cry: “Blessed are the barren who did not bear, and the breasts which did not nurse” (Luke 23). Behold those perilous times foretold by the voice of Paul (2 Tim. 3). Therefore one is moved to cry with Jeremiah: “Who will give my head water and my eyes a fountain of tears?” (Jer. 9), that I may mourn such and so great misery, such and so great a destruction of our country.

The Church of Monte Cassino sits in sorrow—or rather, in ruin: the head of all monasteries, mother of all religious houses, consolation of the sorrowful, harbour of those in peril.

[Col. 1123D] Behold, I say, truly a day of tribulation and distress, a day of calamity and misery, a day of darkness and gloom, a day of cloud and tempest, a day of trumpet and alarm. For in the past year the men of Blessed Benedict sowed, but because of the military campaigns of your invincible Empire they did not reap; in this year, however, they do not sow, nor is there any hope of reaping. What, indeed, shall I say of the army of Sicily, when the counts of Aquino, the men of the land of Blessed Benedict, and all who dwell round about—contrary to the oath which they made to you, to the Roman Empire, and to the Church of Monte Cassino—do nothing better?

[Col. 1124A] For “the caterpillar has consumed what the locust left,” as the prophet says (Joel 1). For what do the Normans do that the counts of Aquino do not do worse? The former occupy the land; the latter leave nothing from either towns or countryside. The former kill with the sword; the latter, after taking all things away, murder by hunger. The former lead people into captivity; the latter reduce them to slavery for themselves. When inquiry is made as to who will fight against the enemies, none are found, since all are held fast by their oppression and are found utterly unable to come at our command.

Yet although we cry out, pressed in on every side, there is none to hear, none to answer, none to help, none to save, none to protect. And what can I say or speak, when the sword has reached even the [Col. 1124B] soul, and the blood of all who have been slain cries from the earth to God? For all people, of every sex and age, stand gathered within the walls of the monastery of Monte Cassino; and, with everything outside laid waste and reduced to wilderness, nothing remains except—the Lord avert it—the destruction of the Church of Monte Cassino itself.

Moreover, what we seem to possess, we possess in name alone, so that we never find anyone’s assistance either for the monastery’s defence or for any benefit of that Church. Above all, to me, whom your majesty appointed there, they offer not merely no aid but also relentlessly take away whatever remains from the enemy, and trample under their violence all our administration in the land of Blessed Benedict. [Col. 1124C] Thus there remain among all our goods neither provisions nor any beasts of burden, nor does our eye behold anyone who might pity us or grieve for our sobbing and groaning.

But since a few words suffice for so great an Emperor and so great an Augustus, from what has now been said, invincible conqueror—and from the words of our son Peter, the composer of this letter and in every respect faithful to the Roman Empire, whom we have determined to send into Alemannia, Saxony, Denmark, Swabia, and Lotharingia—you will learn what we cannot utter because of the groaning and affliction of our heart. Know also that he has not yet completed the history of the western emperors which you commanded him to dictate. Pressed by various tribulations and distresses, he was more inclined to weep than to write.

[Col. 1124D] Therefore, most eminent of Caesars, now, now come to the aid of our calamity; relieve the miseries of the monastery of Monte Cassino; now stretch forth the hand of your power. Do not allow that Church—which always has been and is the special and singular chamber of the Roman Empire—to perish, lest the Roman Empire itself be diminished and its loss become known throughout the whole Roman world. For, since we stand beside a precipice, unless you help us with the hand of your protection, with hope of living among Christians removed, we shall either be subjected to the pagans themselves, or—may divine power avert it!—overcome by their multitude, perish in cruel slaughter, to the total detriment of Christendom. Thus Christ’s name will be blasphemed among the nations, and the past achievements of your reputation will be consigned to oblivion.

Therefore, cast wholly to the ground, we entreat your August clemency; and we adjure you by the coming judgement and by all divine and human mysteries that are in heaven and on earth. Together with the whole Church of Monte Cassino, over which divine condescension willed to set me, we earnestly petition your Empire, divinely protected, with all our strength and pour forth many prayers with suppliant vows: grant, without every pretext and without all delay, every possible assistance in defence and due protection to the holy Church of Monte Cassino, crushed, ravaged, desolated, and deprived of every human aid. Thus may we, who [Col. 1125B] are shaken and distressed by countless tribulations and tortured by miseries for the monks entrusted to us, rejoice when restored by your consolations; and, peace having been gained through you, deserve to attain the desired liberty, as is fitting, through so benign and holy an Emperor.

For you, who strive in the contest so as to reach the prize of the heavenly calling and to receive the incorruptible crown, must abstain from all other things and contend lawfully for the Church of Monte Cassino, which is the singular chamber of the Roman Empire. What could be more lawful than that, above all and before all else, you should care for your own chamber, which is the head and mother of all monasteries, and which in your time succumbs without ceasing to such great and dreadful perils?

Finally, if the Church of Monte Cassino, head of all monasteries, flourishes, the other religious houses, which are its members, though weak, do not lose hope of recovery. They plainly lack all strength if it should happen that their head alone is weakened; how much more if it should be extinguished—may almighty God avert this through the merits of the most holy Father Benedict! Then Benedict and Maurus too are submerged with the sheep entrusted to them.

Raise them, therefore, from the waves, invincible Emperor, so that Father Benedict may raise you from the floods of your transgressions and, by the prayers of his intercessions, open to you the courts of the heavenly kingdom; that he may grant you, among angels and archangels without end, the pasture of eternal life—what eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has entered into the human heart (1 Cor. 2). May Christ the Lord happily preserve, guard, and defend the magnificence of your Empire through the years. Fare well.

## LETTER II. WIBALD TO EMPEROR LOTHAIR AND HIS WIFE RICHENZA

He recounts the plundering inflicted upon the monastery of Monte Cassino by Saracens, Normans, and Lombards.

(Year 1137.—Mabillon extracted it from a manuscript of Monte Cassino.)

To the most devout and serene lord, the August Emperor Lothair, Caesar and perpetual conqueror, and to his wife Richenza, God-protected Empress of the Romans: victories in conflicts, the prize of everlasting life, the subjection of nations, and, with enemies laid low, the good of peace everywhere. Guibald, unworthy minister of the holy monastery of Monte Cassino.

Placed amid varied, many, and diverse tribulations, I hoped that your aid would come day by day; but, as I see, my hope has deceived me. For from the reports of those coming to us at Monte Cassino from your most devout serenity, we learned that you had already drawn near to Aquileia. Even the hearing of this excessively grieved and cast down our spirit, and fixed so great a dart of sorrow in our heart that no speech of human tongue suffices to express it. For the sorrow now arising in us because of your departure from [Col. 1126B] Italy affects us more deeply than the grief which formerly afflicted us when, by your imperial command, I undertook to bear the burdens of the monastery of Monte Cassino.

As for your venerable words which you sent us through your messengers concerning the oaths of the Normans and Lombards—would that they were not charged against them! For it would have been better for them not to swear than to swear and commit perjury. For all who dwell in these regions, apostatizing, have turned to Satan; and they say and do nothing except what the devil’s finger writes upon their hearts. Whatever wickedness, malice, perversity, or crookedness can be spoken or conceived, we see in their deeds.

Through my most beloved son Peter I had intended to inform you of the calamities, tribulations, and persecutions which I suffer from them; but because the length and conclusion of the journey prevented this, I shall disclose a little. After your departure, the Saracens, Normans, and Lombards, finding the land at peace, go wherever they please, laying it waste and depopulating it, annihilating everything by fire and murder. They spare not even fruit-bearing trees, lest those previously concealed by mountains, steep places, or any secluded locations should be nourished by their produce. Repeatedly raging in such cruelty, they have left none untouched by their contagion, none glad, and no place exempt from their attack—especially among the possessions of the most sacred monastery [Col. 1126D] of Monte Cassino. They rage still more criminally also against other churches, basilicas of saints, and monasteries, burning houses of prayer with greater conflagrations than cities and all towns.

There is now fulfilled in the churches what the holy man cries to the Lord, saying: “Where our fathers praised you has become a burning [Vulgate: ‘into a burning’] of fire” (Isa. 64). Now the hour has come when all who plunder, burn, and ravage our land, and bind peasants and monks in fetters, burden them with shackles and handcuffs, kill, sell, torture, and persecute them, think that they render service to God. Where they find the gates of venerable halls closed, they vie in opening the entrances with the meshes of nets cast by their right hands, so that it may rightly be said: “As in a forest of trees, with axes they cut down its doors all together; with axe and hatchet they brought them down; they burned your sanctuary with fire; they defiled on the ground the dwelling-place of your name” (Ps. 73).

[Col. 1127A] How many bishops, priests, deacons, monks, nobles and commoners, of different sex and age, are now killed by them! How many are tortured so that they may surrender whatever gold or silver, private or ecclesiastical, they possess! When, under pressing punishments, they more readily give what they have, the tormentors again press them with cruel tortures, imagining that only some part, not all, has been handed over; and the more they give, the more the aggressors believe that they possess. Neither the weaker sex, nor regard for nobility, nor reverence for priestly rank or monastic habit softens their most cruel minds. On the contrary, the rage of their fury is intensified where they see the honour of rank.

The maturity of old age and venerable grey hair, whitening the hair of the head like white wool, claim no mercy from the enemies. Barbarian rage even snatches little children from their mothers’ breasts and dashes innocent infancy upon the ground. What the Jews once sang is now fulfilled: “The enemy says, ‘I shall burn my borders and dash my little children to the ground.’” In the buildings of great churches, houses, and cities, where their ingenuity cannot bring about destruction by fire, they level the walls with the ground, so that not even what the former beauty of the buildings was can now be seen at all.

If anyone should deny credence to these words, the cities of Pozzuoli, Alife, and Telese bear witness, for they show nothing except that they once existed. Moreover, very many other towns are inhabited by few or by no inhabitants. For even today, those that remain are continually desolated, as they did to the city of Capua, which once, after Rome itself, was both the head and glory of all Campania. After they had emptied it of people and despoiled it of gold and silver, lest the place should yield to impiety even for an hour, they consumed it with fire. They reduced its ancient, free, and noble liberty to slavery, led its leading people into captivity, and carried away the gold, silver, gems, garments, and whatever they found precious or dear.

[Col. 1127D] Since some courtiers of your triumphant Empire do not know these things, and what we describe appears incredible to them, let them hasten here, if they please, and they will find true what we have written. But who can recount what and how great injuries they and their duke inflicted upon the monastery of Monte Cassino, both after and before your arrival? Yet lest we seem to leave this matter unattempted, I shall describe certain things concerning it, so that your invincible imperial clemency may clearly know how fiercely they now attack the Church of Monte Cassino out of hatred for the Roman Empire, since they have persecuted it so monstrously, impiously, and severely.

After the capture of the city of Capua, Seniorectus, who before us held the administration of your chamber, was summoned by him and bound by oath, contrary to the decrees of the canons and to the commands of our Lord Jesus Christ, of all the apostles, and of Father Benedict. But when even this did not yet suffice for that king’s mind, he took from the monastery golden [lacuna]. After he had fulfilled all these things according to his will, he sent his chancellor [lacuna], to seize the monastery so that a fortress might then be made there, expel the monks, and send to himself in Sicily the whole monastery treasure and all its furnishings together with the body of Blessed Benedict.

When the monks learned of this, they resolved to resist and to die rather than surrender the holy place. But when he heard that your triumphant clemency had decided to send two thousand Germans [Col. 1128B] with Anno, abbot of the monastery of Lüneburg, to defend the monastery, he deceived the abbot and brethren and bound both groups by oath to his own allegiance: the abbot upon the Gospels, the monks according to their order.

When the abbot had died, while his bier was still in the church, agents were sent by Carolinus, who at that time acted for Roger in these regions, ordering that no one, in his absence, should presume to discuss the election of an abbot. The matter was therefore deferred, and, despite the monks’ objections and grief, prolonged until his own arrival. When he had arrived there, and they showed him Father Benedict’s command concerning the election of an abbot, together with the provisions of privileges and precepts, he replied that such a showing was of no force for the present, but that the election must be deferred until the knowledge of my lord; otherwise, “Hand over the fortress of Bantra [Note: [Col. 1127] It is now called Rocca Vantra, in view of Monte Cassino.] and elect whom you wish, provided that he first makes fealty to my lord.”

When the brethren said that they would not comply, he gathered an army and withdrew all the monastery’s strongholds from its jurisdiction. Behold the benefits which they conferred upon the Church of Monte Cassino before your arrival—and still worse things they do every day. Therefore, invincible Emperor, we ask you to aid your afflicted, destitute, and desolated chamber, lest the Saracens, Normans, and Lombards say, “Where is their emperor?” Raise up, therefore, raise up your invincible arms, guarded by God, and deliver the Church of Monte Cassino, [Col. 1128D] mother of all monasteries, from the hands of the impious.

For just as among all the stars the sun indisputably holds primacy in the heavens, so the Roman Empire undoubtedly surpasses all worldly powers. Although it is magnificent in itself, it is evident nevertheless that it shines more augustly when ruled by a good and illustrious man. Therefore may your goodness come to the aid of the Church of Monte Cassino, lest the radiant jewel of heaven—that is, the Church of Monte Cassino—be removed from the head of all monasteries, dashed to the earth, and trampled under the feet of Saracens who do not know God.

Our son Peter, moreover, faithful to you in all things, earnestly commends himself to your most sacred [Col. 1129A] Empire. May the God of all grace so deign to order your times that, through the happiness of this present life, you may be co-heirs of the eternal kingdom.

## LETTER III. WIBALD, ABBOT, TO THE MONKS OF MONTE CASSINO

He grants them freedom to elect another abbot; if the election is canonical, he promises to release them from the obedience promised to him. (Year 1137.)

Wibald, by the grace of God unworthy minister of the holy monastery of Monte Cassino, to his beloved sons and brothers in Christ, serving God in the same Church: may you abound in the spirit of counsel and fortitude.

Until now, in the field of the Lord’s cultivation—that is, in the prelateship of [Col. 1129B] your brotherhood—I have occupied the ground as a tree producing shade rather than fruit, not without fearfully hearing the Lord’s voice saying: “Cut it down, for it does not itself bear fruit and prevents the ground beneath it from being fruitful.” Since, therefore, the axe has been laid to the root so that every tree not bearing fruit may be cut down, we could not longer disregard the prophetic counsel. But because through me a dangerous and desperate storm has arisen, while the sailors stood idle, I did not shrink from casting myself into the sea.

Therefore, because I have thus departed from you, as God is witness, not through fear of death, but because my death could bring you no benefit and indeed much danger, so that I have determined not to return to you further, I command you, by the power of holy obedience: putting aside party interests, removing every ambition and venality, without favour, hatred, or regard for any person, and invoking the grace of the Holy Spirit, elect without delay, according to the Rule of St Benedict, a Catholic and regular person from the body of your congregation as abbot for yourselves and shepherd of your souls, preserving the liberty of the monastery of Monte Cassino.

For we have determined that, if you observe this procedure in electing your abbot, then, after restoring to you the insignia of your Church [Note: [Col. 1129D] Namely, the ring and seal, and perhaps certain other jewels.], we shall release all of you alike from obedience and subjection to us and make you free from us for the advancement of the future abbot. But if—God forbid—those diabolical and contentious conspiracies and combinations among you should presume to attempt and subvert this matter, and if anyone should permit himself to be thrust in by such faction, know that we shall retain no full authority or care over you; and against such a person, as an intruder, invader, and usurper, we shall always proceed in every council and court, both by spoken word and in writing.

Concerning the monastery’s goods, we tell you this lest anyone among us, or because of us, take occasion for evil: our lord dean and our brethren provided us only fifteen marks of silver for the expenses of so great a journey. All the rest they themselves received from the treasury and spent themselves amid so many and great necessities. Preserve our—that is, your and my—reputation in rewarding the people who served us. Preserve for me my Walter, who remained sick among you. Of Rainald [Note: [Col. 1129D] At that time there were two men named Rainald in the monastery of Monte Cassino: one from Colementa, the other Etruscan. The latter favoured Roger, king of Sicily, and, after the order was disturbed, was elected abbot by certain brethren while others objected; Pope Innocent declared his election void.], the invading and perjured monk, let there never be any mention among you. May the God of peace and love always be with all of you. Farewell.

## LETTER IV. WIBALD, ABBOT, TO R., ABBOT OF THE MONASTERY OF MONTE CASSINO

He congratulates him on his election, releases him from the obedience promised to himself, and returns his ring and seal as a sign of resignation from the abbacy. (Year 1137.)

[Col. 1130B]

To the reverend Father R. [Note: [Col. 1130D] Rainald of Colementa, whom the sounder party among the brethren proposed to elect after Seniorectus’s death.], venerable abbot of the holy monastery of Monte Cassino: Brother Wibald, by the grace of God servant of the Church of Stavelot, wishes blessing and life for ever.

Hearing that you have been elected by the common agreement of the brethren and regularly ordained in the Church of Monte Cassino, we rejoiced with joy. For although we have ceased to administer that Church in office, we retain an unchanged mind in affection and concern. Therefore, in the Lord’s name, by this present writing we wholly release you from the obedience which you promised us; and we who once unworthily presided over you are not ashamed both to be and to be called your subjects and servants.

We commend to your charity our most beloved lord Dean O. and our remaining brethren and the men of St Peter, who faithfully persevered with us in our tribulation. We return to you one ring and a seal, formerly ours, by which we make a complete renunciation of the abbacy of Monte Cassino. Yet we shall never withhold our counsel and aid from that Church. Farewell; receive kindly, for love of us, our messenger passing through your territory; and, if he returns by way of you, inform us by letter of the state of your affairs.

## LETTER V. WIBALD, ABBOT, TO ODO, DEAN OF MONTE CASSINO

He releases him and the other brethren of Monte Cassino from obedience promised to himself, and explains certain items taken from the monastery. (Year 1137.)

[Col. 1130D]

Brother Wibald, by the grace of God servant of the Church of Stavelot, to his most dear brother and friend O., dean of Monte Cassino: greeting and blessing.

God, the searcher of hearts, knows how deeply I am moved by your calamities and how deeply I sympathize with your vexations. Although I can neither be personally present with you nor preside over you, nevertheless we love, and shall always love, the Church of Monte Cassino with no less concern. Yet because divine preordination has thus arranged matters, and the character of the time, corresponding to our deserts, requires it, lest you be made liable to everlasting punishments by the violated obligation of your promise, and we by neglected administration of the government undertaken, we fully release you and all the brethren of the Church of Monte Cassino from the obedience which you promised us. Likewise, we grant that the laymen who swore to us may be free from their oaths.

But lest anyone’s judgement, by detracting from us, may incur sin: as is known to you and to most of the brethren, when we departed from you, the following listed things had been alienated. Landulf held as security for eighty-five pounds one gold chalice, two gold crosses with stones, and two silver candlesticks. At St Germanus there were one silver candlestick for three pounds and one censer for thirty solidi; all these were received and disbursed through the hands of Brother Rainald Theod. and Brother Bertold. Moreover, our servants who went ahead of us lost one small gold cross, one ring, and an image of the wood of the Lord. We have kept the cope and shirt which you gave us, awaiting, according to your promise, your completion for us of the rest that belongs to the chapel. [Col. 1131C] We have returned the seal and ring to the lord abbot. Farewell.

## LETTER VI. WIBALD TO THEODERIC, ABBOT OF WAULSORT

He approves the miracles of St Forannan, committed to writing by the monk Robert. (About 1140.—Communicated by the most reverend abbot of Waulsort.)

Brother Wibald, by the grace of God servant of the Church of Stavelot, to Lord Theoderic, venerable abbot of the Church of Waulsort, and to the reverend community of brethren: may you always watch over divine pursuits and advance in gifts.

[Col. 1131D] We give thanks, beloved brothers, to the inestimable grace of the Creator of all things. He, the same ever-new and ever-perfect craftsman, does not cease, at appointed times and in wonderful order, to adorn the beauty of his universal Church through great authors, so that each Church throughout the world, though it sometimes endures the waves of the sea, may at times rejoice in the firmness of the shore, while the disciples in the boat awaken the sleeping Christ and Christ commands the waves.

Certainly, brothers, following the apostolic example, you too awaken Christ in your boat when you render honour and devotion to the patrons by whom your Church is governed, and when you desire to bring to the knowledge and edification of many persons the miracles which he himself works in them.
