Through our brother and your son Robert [Note: [Col. 1131D] Unless my conjecture deceives me, this is Robert, who was abbot of Waulsort after Theoderic.], you wrote to us concerning the Life and Miracles of Blessed Forannan, confessor, bishop, and abbot [Note: [Col. 1131D] St Forannan, a Scot by nation, was bishop and first abbot of the monastery of Waulsort; buried there, he is still preserved in that place with the highest veneration.], composed with no slight care. As he himself told us, your purpose was that our insignificance might polish or remove anything seeming less well composed or superfluous, and that our collaboration might strengthen the entire small body of the work. If I judged the task necessary, I would by no means refuse to undertake what he enjoined and you enjoin.

But because the work is proved praiseworthy in every respect, I desire henceforth to obey your commands if our labours for the Church and the affairs of the kingdom by which we are bound should have favourable outcomes and, with some cares set aside, at length allow us leisure. Meanwhile, continue with the zeal you have begun to cherish the miracles of the Blessed Confessor and take care to commit them to writing. For if your devotion persists, your zeal does not slacken, and your religious observance grows, those whose bodily eyes have been granted to see such manifest miracles will deserve to behold the glorification of the sacred body.

Would that our presence might deserve to share in the happiness of that time, our insignificance to serve it; and may the glorification of the sacred ashes be a confirmation of our faith in the hope of resurrection, consolation amid our present tribulations, and a passage from exile to our homeland, from death to life.

## LETTER VII. KING CONRAD TO ABBOT WIBALD

He orders him to come to Frankfurt to receive from his hand the regalian rights of the abbey of Corvey.

(Year 1146.—From a manuscript of Corvey.)

[Col. 1132C]

Conrad, by the grace of God king of the Romans, to Wibald, abbot of Stavelot: his favour with affection.

After the Church of Corvey was deprived of its abbot, it immediately, prompted by divine inspiration, chose you by canonical election as its lord and spiritual father. Thereafter, disturbed and ruined in both temporal and spiritual matters because of your absence, it suffered grave loss. Therefore, in commanding, I request your affection to come into our presence at Frankfurt on the feast of St Nicholas. There, receiving from our hand those things that pertain to the gift of royal dignity, you shall henceforth provide for the Church of Corvey as its spiritual father and prudent steward. Farewell.

These were written and issued at Würzburg, and were presented to the abbot in the church of Stavelot on the third day before the Kalends of December.

## LETTER VIII. ABBOT WIBALD TO KING CONRAD

He replies to the preceding letter: the election of him by the people of Corvey must be examined; he excuses himself for not having come to the king’s court.

(Year 1146.—From a manuscript of Corvey.)

[Col. 1133A]

To his illustrious conqueror and most serene lord Conrad, by the grace of God august Emperor of the Romans: Brother Wibald, by divine majesty servant of the Church of Stavelot, greeting in him who gives salvation to kings.

We have received the letter of your piety, which your magnificence deigned to transmit to us through Provost Bruno. It brought us very great joy and exultation because, by sure indications of experience, we learned that we had found exceptional favour in the sight of your majesty; yet it brought much concern and anxiety to our insignificance because of the matter which it contained.

For your greatness was pleased to tell us that the Church of Corvey, bereft of its shepherd, had elected us, with equal desire and unanimous consent, as its father and shepherd of souls. Your kindness urges us to undertake this burden and follow the command of the divine calling, hastened by the authority of a royal command. But because none of the monks had come to us—although the matter chiefly belongs to them both in its beginning and its completion—we believed that the whole affair should be deferred for the counsel of religious persons, until the Church of Corvey should meet in the presence of your majesty and the princes and explain, as is canonical and fitting, what it has done, and in what order.

Further, may your gentleness not be disturbed because we did not come to the present court in accordance with your command’s good pleasure. For, God guiding, we shall come on the feast of Blessed Nicholas, when the Church of Corvey intends to attend your court. If our small but faithful devotion has any value with your excellency, deign to assign us a place near Würzburg at the feast of Blessed Nicholas, so that we may conveniently meet you there with those who are to come.

## LETTER IX. KING CONRAD TO THE BRETHREN OF STAVELOT

He exhorts them to bear their abbot’s absence with equanimity and to place very great confidence in his favour.

[Col. 1133D]

Conrad, by the grace of God king of the Romans, to Rupert, dean of Stavelot, and the other brethren, also to the ministerials and the whole household of the same Church: his favour and every good.

As divine providence ordained, in accordance with the counsel of our faithful men and at the request of the Church of Corbie, we have placed our faithful servant Wibald, your abbot, over the monastery of Corbie, while retaining for you the supervision and care which he previously exercised. And because from this, as we hope and intend, the greatest benefit may accrue to the Church, we earnestly exhort and request your whole community by these present letters that you bear patiently his absence, necessary indeed for the realm and not without benefit to us; and that, if any more serious difficulties arise in the needs of your Church, you zealously devote the service of pious concern to them. If in any matter our aid should be necessary to you, then, as hitherto we have always been favourably disposed toward you, so now above all you shall always find us gracious.

## LETTER X. FROM THE MEN OF CORBIE TO THE MEN OF STAVELOT

They give thanks that the latter have not begrudged them Wibald as abbot, and exhort them to endure his absence with equanimity.

*(Year 1146.—From a Corbie manuscript.)*

The men of Corbie—to the dean and provost of Stavelot, and to the other most beloved lords and brethren of the holy Church of Stavelot—Walter, prior, Adelbert, provost, and the whole convent of the Church of Corbie: the dutiful offering of brotherly affection, and whatever further service and devotion may avail.

Since God, not forgetful of His benefits, which endure from everlasting, has assigned to our Church a lord and father—formerly yours indeed, but now both yours and ours—so that, as sons of one father, we are now beginning, through God’s mediation, to be joined together in no insignificant bond of genuine charity: first of all our Church renders to your affection the greatest and most devout thanksgiving, because your fraternity has not begrudged to our need so great a man and one of such authority, whose ability is renowned at the king’s court and is not unknown in the Roman Church. Because, I say, you have not begrudged us this man, necessary to our need [Col. 1134C], we rejoice not merely for the present; rather, again and again, the more welcome to us what has been done is, the more devoutly shall we rejoice in your goodwill.

We also no less earnestly beg that you bear with equanimity the absence of so great a father, and rejoice with us as he provides for the needs of our Church, as the occasion requires. For we do not despair that the advancement of both Churches—ours, that is, and yours—will be equally desired by each; and because there is one shepherd of these two flocks, that through his mediation they may be joined into one, and thus there may be one fold and one shepherd. Farewell.

## LETTER XI. FROM THE MEN OF STAVELOT TO THE MEN OF CORBIE

They congratulate them on Wibald’s election and commend him to them.

*(Year 1146.—From a Corbie manuscript.)*

[Col. 1134D]

To their most reverend fathers and lords in Christ, Walter, venerable prior of Corbie, Adelbert, provost, and the entire holy convent of that Church: Brother R., dean of the Church of Stavelot, Simon, provost, and the humble flock serving Christ in the same place, the most ready offering of every devotion and of prayers.

Having received and read the letter which your kindness sent to our littleness through our brethren, we rejoiced exceedingly with spiritual joy—especially because that pearl, most excellent by a heavenly gift, which until now had scarcely been displayed to any merchant from among the treasures of our Church [Col. 1135A], has at last appeared to you most precious in the rays of its splendour. Its brightness—whose sight is most health-giving and delightful—has worthily become known and pleasing to your eyes. Since, by God’s ordering, she who was our own has become common property, now yours and ours, your learning knows better how zealously she ought to be cherished and how carefully kept and held.

And although we have no small confidence in the gentleness of your kindness and the sweetness of your graciousness, nevertheless, because we owe much to him whom we love sincerely and purely, we implore you by God, than whom nothing is higher, and by brotherly charity, than which nothing in this world is loftier, that you hold in fitting honour him who has for your sake been withdrawn for a time from our interests and committed to your fidelity. Thus he may labour the more gladly in the care of the government he has undertaken, the more freely you lend your shoulders to support Moses’ hands [Col. 1135B]. By this means the enemies of both Churches—yours, namely, and ours—will readily be overcome with Amalek.

## LETTER XII. FROM MASTER REINARD [REINARDUS], ABBOT, TO THE SAME WIBALD

[Note: [Col. 1135D] Reinard, the first abbot of Reinhausen, wrote a small work on the beginnings of his Church, published in volume II of the *Scriptores Rerum Brunsvicensium*, p. 703. Gottfried Leibniz, a most distinguished man, noted from Heinrich Hofmann that he had been a monk at Helwardshausen, in the introduction to that volume, art. 43. Yet he seems to have directed the school of the monastery of Stavelot at the beginning of the twelfth century [Col. 1136D], when Wibald and Henry—who became dean of that same place—were entrusted to the monks for instruction. See below, Letter 34, and in the Appendix the charter of Conrad for the monastery of Reinhausen.]

He congratulates him on his election, mingling joy with fear concerning his elevation.

*(Year 1146.)*

… *tationis* [*meditationis*, “meditation”] and reading, and no less by earnest labour, he continually exercised his perseverance [Col. 1135C]. Yet because excessively frequent storms repeatedly tossed the little vessel of my mind amid billowing and tempestuous troubles—

[Note: [Col. 1136D] He described those troubles more fully in the aforesaid small work on the beginnings of his monastery.]

—and severely disturbed the tranquillity I desired in the woods, I followed counsel which seemed to me not useless: I relinquished to my brethren all the revenues of the monastery, so that they themselves might receive everything through their officials and might not look to my hands for … such matters. For my own work, however, I reserved only ten solidi from these revenues, together with a few fields in a certain solitude, which I myself caused to be cultivated. For I prefer to have less power, or what seems advantageous, in order that I may possess more tranquillity.

But let us now return to you, considering the wonders of the Lord which He has wrought in manifold ways concerning you. Indeed, whenever I often ponder them silently within myself, I rejoice in amazement and am amazed in rejoicing; yet even in that very joy I am not without fear. Certainly I rejoice, as friendship requires, at the so manifold and, to confess the truth, at times wholly unexpected exaltation of your person; for now I speak not to an abbot but to my own Wibald. Yet I fear—as is human—that your mind may be somewhat raised up in pride.

But you, my friend, taught by the Prophet: “What shall you render to the Lord for all that He has rendered to you?” [Col. 1136A] Take the cup of salvation and call upon the name of the Lord; and, the greater you are, so far as circumstances permit, humble yourself in all things. Call, I say, upon the Lord’s name, asking and imploring that you may not be numbered among those of whom it is terribly written: “You cast them down when they were lifted up.” You must fear, most beloved friend, lest—God forbid!—you receive your good things in your lifetime. Therefore always heed God, terrible in His counsels over the children of men; and, that His counsel may become saving for you, continually strive by every means in your power to win His grace.

But what are we doing, my soul? To whom are we speaking—to one taught or untaught? We speak indeed to one whom we once taught; but, to our great delight, we have found that in some things he has surpassed us, though we once had him as a pupil [Col. 1136B]. Yet the force of affection has made us somewhat foolish, since we have uttered such admonitions as though to one less wise, as though we surpassed him in wisdom. Let no one think that I mean to teach one more learned as though he were less learned; but I cannot conceal my heart’s affection.

For the present, however, let this suffice, until we see how far these things themselves advance. Since almighty God, by His judgment which He Himself knows, has granted me your neighbourhood, I shall not be reluctant to visit you more often, now by letters and now in bodily presence itself, if it please you; indeed, I shall rejoice in your companionship, of which I have now been deprived for very long. Farewell.

## LETTER XIII. FROM EMPEROR CONRAD TO POPE EUGENIUS III

He asks that the election of Wibald, absent and unwilling, as abbot of Corbie, and the union of Keminade and Visbik with the monastery of Corbie, be confirmed.

*(Year 1146.)*

[Col. 1136C]

To his most beloved father in Christ, Eugenius, supreme pontiff of the holy Roman Church: Conrad, by God’s grace king of the Romans and ever august, filial affection in all things and due reverence in the Lord.

We wish Your Holiness to know that, after the deposition of Henry, formerly abbot of Corbie, who had been most unserviceable to that Church, the brethren of the said monastery chose as their abbot a certain Henry, provost of that same Church [Col. 1136D]. Not long afterward he died; and the whole Church of Corbie, bereft of its spiritual father, by equal vote and unanimous consent chose for itself as father and shepherd of souls Wibald, abbot of Stavelot, so that through his ability and our assistance that noble Church, which through the negligence of its preceding abbots had fallen far from its former greatness, might, through God’s preceding mercy, be in some measure restored [Col. 1137A].

And since this our aforesaid faithful man, abbot of Stavelot, was not only absent when these things occurred concerning him, but was also far away, we summoned him by royal authority, though he long resisted and protested; and, at the request of the whole Church of Corbie, we compelled him, entirely against his will, to undertake the burden to which he had been called. Thus in the monastery of Corbie both the religious observance of divine worship might be reformed through him and the service due from the realm for the defence of God’s holy Church might thenceforth be rendered more readily and more abundantly.

Nearby were two small convents of women which supplied neither the realm nor us with any assistance, whether in military service or in another service. They were so disordered and undisciplined that it is better to be silent than to speak of the life and morals of their inhabitants [Col. 1137B]. Therefore, after being long admonished by you in many exhortations concerning the correction of such places, we granted those two places to the Church of Corbie by right of ownership, namely Keminade and Visbike, so that religious observance might be reformed there and the abbey of Corbie might in this abbot’s time be increased by us in honour and wealth.

[Note: [Col. 1137D] We published, from an autograph found by us in the archives of the monastery of Corbie, in volume I, the foundation charter of the convent of Keminade on the river Weser by Countess Imma and Count Gero. Visbik—called in the Saxon Chronicle, which we are to publish, the convent of girls at Wisbik [Col. 1138D]—owes its origin to Empress Adelaide and her daughter Matilda, abbess, by whom it was built about 992.]

Concerning this matter, we earnestly exhort and request your integrity, in which we have the greatest confidence, that you do not refuse to strengthen by the written instrument of your privilege what we have confirmed by a lawful grant in a charter to the same abbot and to the monastery of Corbie concerning the two aforesaid cells; and that you incline a gracious ear of hearing to the abbot in his needs. For it is fitting that those whom we have received into our favour in a more gracious bond [Col. 1137C] you should embrace with the arms of kindly goodwill; and that those whom you, conversely, purpose to cherish and protect, we should strive to defend against every attack and duly honour.

## LETTER XIV. FROM ABBOT WIBALD TO THE MEN OF CORBIE

That they should give testimony to the supreme pontiff concerning his election as abbot of Corbie.

*(Year 1146.)*

Brother Wibald, by God’s grace servant of the Church of Corbie, to W., venerable prior, and A., provost, and to the other dearest sons and brethren, monks of the same monastery: blessing and life unto age upon age.

[Col. 1137D]

When we came to our lord the pope, we were received kindly and honourably, both out of reverence for our lord the king and because of the familiarity of our long-standing acquaintance, through which he has hitherto deigned to show us favour. And when, in the letter of our lord the king, where the names of the envoys were inscribed—

[Note: [Col. 1138D] Namely Buko, bishop of Worms; Anselm, bishop of Havelberg; and Wibald, abbot of Corbie; see Letter 20.]

—he had read our name under the title of the Church of Corbie, he asked us to present to him your testimony concerning our election among you. Therefore we instruct your whole community to make known truthfully to the lord pope how your election concerning our person proceeded. And have as many as you can of our senior brethren, in this sudden turn of events, make themselves ready and come to us at Würzburg in the octave of the coming Easter; for you will find us there then, along with the chancellor of the lord pope, a venerable man named Guido. Send him also a separate and particular letter concerning what you have done in our regard. Farewell; and may the God of peace always be with you all.

Had these matters not been awaited, our privileges concerning Keminade and Visbike would have been confirmed.

## LETTER XV. FROM W., PRIOR, AND THE BRETHREN OF THE MONASTERY OF CORBIE TO POPE EUGENIUS III

They ask that the election of Abbot Wibald and the union with Corbie of two convents of girls be confirmed.

*(Year 1146.)*

[Col. 1138B]

To their most reverend father and lord in Christ, Eugenius, by divine grace supreme and universal pontiff: W., though unworthy prior of the Church of Corbie, and all the other brethren who serve God in the monastery of Corbie, devoted obedience and humble prayers in the Lord.

We inform Your Holiness that, after the deposition of Henry, formerly our abbot, who was canonically removed by your venerable legate, Master Thomas, for his manifest faults, for the salvation of our whole monastery, which he was ravaging in many ways [Col. 1138C], we united in choosing one of our brethren, Henry, who administered the office of provost, and elected him, although some of our brethren did not assent and many of the lay order protested, stubbornly favouring the party of that deposed man. After his promotion he lived only a few months, then died, leaving us full of grief and anxiety, and not without some discord.

Since through the negligence of our abbots for almost fifty years the resources and dignity of our monastery, both within and without, had been diminished beyond belief, and since we were by no means wholly united [Col. 1138D], at that time no person could be found in our Church who was capable of binding up our wounds, so that the children of God and of our Church who were scattered might be gathered into one. Compelled by these necessities, having invoked the grace of the Holy Spirit and taken the counsel of religious and wise men, by the common desire of all, without the objection of any person, great or small—indeed, with the favourable assent of all—and with the presence and counsel for this purpose of your venerable son B., bishop of Paderborn [Col. 1139A], we chose in our chapter as father and shepherd of the souls of Corbie, that is, as abbot and lord, the lord Wibald, abbot of Stavelot, by whose religious devotion and prudence the monastery of Corbie might be restored to its former state of dignity.

[Note: [Col. 1139D] Bernard, who was elected in 1128 and administered the bishopric of Paderborn with great distinction for thirty-two years.]

Although for many days he had refused to do this or to consent to our election, and though our envoys could by no means draw him from his monastery to take counsel for us, at last he was summoned to court by royal authority. Compelled by our lord Conrad, emperor and king of the Romans, he was forced to follow our brethren and laymen, who had assembled there in large numbers, and to come to us [Col. 1139B].

And we give thanks to almighty God that we have not been disappointed of our desire and of the hope which we had conceived regarding this our father. For by remarkable ability he has recalled all our dissensions to peace and concord, and with great prudence and effectiveness has recovered for the use of the monastery no small possessions which that deposed man had alienated. Moreover, in our neighbourhood are two convents of women—

[Note: [Col. 1140D] Namely Keminade and Visbik, or Walbik, mentioned above.]

—which by the obstinacy of their scandalous conduct have very often offended the eyes and ears of ours and of all religious persons. Some of our abbots had begun to labour for the removal of this abuse, so that the possession might be bestowed on our Church and religious observance reformed there; but they were unable to obtain this [Col. 1139C]. But our lord Abbot Wibald, having won the prince’s favour by his many services, obtained from our lord the king that these same places, with all their appurtenances, should be granted to our monastery and that the lawful transfer should be confirmed by the privilege of royal authority.

Therefore, with knees of the heart bent before you, we humbly implore your mercy, dear to us, that since our aforesaid father has diligently doubled the five talents he received, you, imitating Christ the true and good householder, may set him over ten cities, according to the saying: “To everyone who has, more shall be given.” Strengthened by your apostolic blessing, may he be sent back to us with joy, so that he may both preside over us and benefit us [Col. 1139D]; and may you deign to confirm by the page of your privilege the donation which our lord the king made to our monastery of the aforesaid two cells.

## LETTER XVI. FROM THE MONKS OF CORBIE TO CARDINAL GUIDO

Concerning the election of Abbot Wibald and the union with Corbie of two convents of girls.

*(Year 1146.)*

To Lord and venerable Guido, chancellor of the supreme apostolic see [Col. 1140A], all the brethren of the Church of Corbie: humble prayers in the Lord.

Since we have learned from the testimony of many religious and holy men that you show wonderful and immeasurable compassion toward the afflicted and those oppressed by the various miseries of calamity, we have endeavoured to appeal by the letter of our humility to the ears of your kindness concerning the manifold disturbance of our Church. Since we have sent our envoys to the lord pope to transact the affairs of the Church, may we more easily obtain a settlement through your assistance.

We therefore lay before your magnanimity that Lord Henry, who had been abbot of this Church, when accused before Lord Thomas, legate of the apostolic see, who was in our place, on certain charges, was unable to defend himself when witnesses had been produced; and, moreover, was openly proved guilty by his own confession. He was therefore punished by the deserved sentence of deposition [Col. 1140B], and Lord Henry the provost was installed in his place. Since a serious protest was made against his election by some of our brethren and also by our laymen, and the Church was disturbed by grave discord, God, in His habitual mercy for the salvation of all, removed him from their midst. For he presided scarcely four months.

After he was removed, Lord Wibald, abbot of Stavelot, was elected with great devotion by the unanimous consent of monks and laymen and with the great agreement of all, in the presence of B., bishop of Paderborn, and Count Herman, advocate of our Church [Col. 1140C], who applauded and acclaimed his election. Since he could not be drawn from his monastery for the honour of this prelacy, he was summoned by the king’s command to court. There, although at first he resisted greatly, at last, overcome by the royal favour and the prayers of all, and being unable to resist, he consented, though unwillingly.

When he came to us, we found in him, by God’s favour, nothing lacking in uprightness of conduct, distinction in learning, and prudent counsel and management of divine and human affairs—nothing, that is, except what we had always wished to find in a spiritual father. The revenues of our Church, which the deposed Lord Henry, being more devoted to military concerns than attentive to monastic discipline, had granted to laymen in benefice [Col. 1140D], he recovered for the most part by the counsel of his most sagacious intelligence. Moreover, by royal donation he acquired for our place two cells of consecrated women, which by the enormity of their crime had caused every canonical institution in Saxony to stink and become contemptible in the ears of the populace; and there he restored from our monastery the service of divine worship.

For this purpose he approached the apostolic lord, seeking to obtain that, made firm by the privilege of his authority, these arrangements might remain ratified and unshaken. Therefore we ask you mercifully to support these matters, and whatever others we have to transact with the lord pope, since they are many [Col. 1141A], relying on the sole consolation of our monks’ prayers—that is, on the recommendation of those prayers—so that, having at last cast off the anguish of our many disturbances, we may be restored to the unity of desired peace.

## LETTER XVII. FROM COUNT HERMAN TO POPE EUGENIUS III

He gives testimony concerning Wibald’s election as abbot of Corbie.

*(Year 1146.)*

To his lord and father Eugenius, by God’s grace pontiff of the universal Church: Count H., obedience in devoted service.

[Note: [Col. 1141D] Count Herman, advocate of the monastery of Corbie, mentioned in the preceding letter.]

[Col. 1141B]

A report from the brethren of Corbie has reached us, announcing that you had sought testimony concerning the election of my lord Wibald as abbot of Corbie. Therefore we testify that the bishop of Paderborn and I were both present at his election, and that no one protested against the unanimity of his election. He was enthroned in the see by a proper election, as we ourselves then saw and as other faithful witnesses who were present can testify, so that in no respect did canonical order suffer injury in its observance.

[The bishop was Bernard.]

Moreover, we have heard from the religious monks of that Church that, after he arrived there, he has made himself so incomparable both in his conduct and in his diligent administration of the Church’s affairs that all declare him to have been sent to them from heaven by God [Col. 1141C]. Therefore we desire that thanks be rendered to him also by you and that he be further honoured with your blessing.

## LETTER XVIII. FROM EMPEROR CONRAD TO H., DUKE OF SAXONY

He commends Wibald, abbot of Corbie, to him.

Conrad, by God’s grace king of the Romans, to H., duke of Saxony: his favour and every good.

As divine providence ordained, in accordance with the counsel of our faithful men, at the request of the Church of Corbie we have placed our faithful servant Wibald, abbot of Stavelot, over the monastery of Corbie. We therefore earnestly exhort and request your diligence that you protect his person honourably in every way [Col. 1141D], and provide him counsel and assistance in recovering and administering the possessions of the Church of Corbie. You should in no way doubt that this will be most pleasing to us.

Concerning his property which your man Poppo of Blankenburg and his sons violently took from the same abbot at Gröningen, we command your prudence and, under the protection of our favour, order that you have everything restored to him in full.

## LETTER XIX. FROM THE CHURCH OF BREMEN AND THE CONGREGATION OF BÜCKEN TO WIBALD, ABBOT OF CORBIE

They choose him, together with the bishop of Verden, as arbiter of their cause.

*(Year 1147.)*

[Col. 1142A]

To the venerable lord Wibald, abbot of the holy Church of Corbie: all the brethren of the greater and lesser Church of Bremen, and also the congregation of the church of Bücken, their offerings of prayers together with the voluntary service of obedience.

How greatly we rejoice that we have wholly entrusted the examination and determination of our entire cause to the counsel or judgment of your holiness: first, because our enemies might believe that we were in every respect resisting both the works of justice and those of peace; secondly, because we trust that this stain of reproach will be erased by the testimony both of your authority and of the lord of Verden, who has likewise entered upon the examination of our cause by commission of the lord pope.

May it therefore please the excellence of your fatherhood, in return for the humble service of our littleness, to grant us a written statement of your authority, no less than a visible and truthful testimony from the lord of Verden [Col. 1142B], and to regard with merciful protection the straits of our cause, as we trust from so great a father.

## LETTER XX. FROM EMPEROR CONRAD TO POPE EUGENIUS III

He informs him that his son Henry has been elected king of the Romans by the common acclamation of the princes, and that he is preparing, having taken up the cross, for an expedition to Jerusalem.

*(Year 1147.)*

[Col. 1142C]

To his most beloved father in Christ, Eugenius, supreme pontiff of the holy Roman Church: Conrad, by God’s grace king of the Romans and ever august, filial affection in all things and due reverence in the Lord.

We received with the greatest gratitude the letters of Your Holiness, sent through your legate, a man indeed to be named among us with every affection and honour, T., bishop of Santa Rufina.

[Note: [Col. 1141D] Theodewin, a German cardinal created by Innocent II and sent by him as legate into Germany. According to Otto of Freising, he placed the imperial diadem upon Conrad himself at Aachen, the archbishop of Cologne—whose right it was to perform that office—having recently been elected and not yet granted the pallium [Col. 1142D].]

What those letters contained we have put into effect with filial and deepest affection. For concerning the ordering of the realm granted us by God, regarding which you took care to admonish and exhort us with fatherly concern, we dealt diligently and effectively, by God’s aid, with great attentiveness and care in a large assembly of princes at Frankfurt, where we held a general court. Having established and secured a firm peace throughout all parts of our realm by common agreement, we have resolved, through God’s preceding mercy, to crown our son Henry—elected king and successor to our sceptre by the unanimous agreement of the princes and the joyful acclamation of the whole realm—at the palace of Aachen during the present Lent [Col. 1142D].

[Note: [Col. 1142D] The monk of Gembloux, in Miraeus, writes that this took place in 1147, so that after the emperor’s departure the realm might not remain without a prince.]

Certainly, what you say—that we undertook so great a matter, namely the reception of the sign of the life-giving cross and the purpose of so great and lengthy an expedition, without your knowledge—proceeded from the great affection of true love. But the Holy Spirit, who blows where He wills and is accustomed to come suddenly, permitted us to make no delay in seeking your counsel or anyone else’s. Rather, as soon as He touched our heart with a wondrous finger, He impelled the whole intention of our mind to follow Him without any intervening delay.

And since we have learned, both from your letters and through your legate, that you are coming into the regions of Gaul, we invite your venerable fatherhood with the highest affection and earnest exhortation to come to the Rhine, so that, being together [Col. 1143B], we may by God’s mercy jointly consider and arrange those matters through which the peace of the Churches and the order of the Christian religion may be increased by fitting progress, and the state of the realm granted us by God may be secured by appropriate decrees with an increase of our honour.

Since at the point of our departure no length of time is available to us, we desire to see your longed-for face at Strasbourg on the Friday occurring in Easter week. We commend to your integrity our envoys—men truly prudent and discerning, devoted to the holy Roman Church and the realm, and most dear to us—namely Buko, bishop of Worms; Anselm, bishop of Havelberg; and Wibald, abbot of Corbie [Col. 1143C]. Hear what they tell you as though from our own mouth, and do not refuse formally to deliberate and arrange with them matters concerning the holy Roman Church and the realm.

## LETTER XXI. FROM ANNO TO ABBOT WIBALD

Concerning a certain Ebroin, to whom, at Wibald’s urging, he had shown favour.

*(Year 1147.)*

To his lord and friend Wibald, abbot of Stavelot: Anno—

[Note: [Col. 1143D] This Anno was abbot of the monastery of Inda, situated two leagues from Aachen, as appears from the following letter [Col. 1144D].]

—by the same grace what he is, greeting and blessing.

Let your affection know first that we especially rejoice in your successes, as those of our lord and friend, and cheerfully render thanks to God for them [Col. 1143D]. We also submit to your discretion that Lord Ebroin frequently presses us concerning the favour formerly shown him by us. Although we gave him this favour by your counsel and out of love for preserving the peace and tranquillity of the Church, certain persons nevertheless condemn the action under the sinister name of simony. Yet we have withdrawn it from him temporarily, not for that reason, but because of the troubles he has caused us and you.

It is also said that, through the lord of Prüm, he has recently made peace with you. Therefore we earnestly ask you, if it is your will and may be done without sinister intrigue, that the agreed favour be rendered to him in future. Furthermore [Col. 1144A], we wish to inquire about the affairs of the lord pope, of which we believe you have some knowledge: namely, whether he is intending to come to us or to hold a council in our regions. Farewell.

## LETTER XXII. FROM ABBOT WIBALD TO ANNO, ABBOT OF INDA

That nothing be given to Ebroin, expelled from the monasteries of Inda and Stavelot.

*(Year 1147.)*

To his reverend father Anno, abbot of the Church of Inda: Brother Wibald, abbot of Stavelot, greeting and blessing.

We do not doubt that your integrity rejoices in spirit at our prosperity, if there is any; and rightly indeed, for we are borne toward you by an equal affection of love [Col. 1144B]. It is not our counsel that you should give anything to that Ebroin, whom Pope Eugenius, by a written sentence, has banished forever from both your monastery and ours. That would be to procure poison for poisoners, furnish weapons to rebels, and offer a club to madmen.

While he seemed to be a brother in your monastery, you could, under the guise and title of a prebend, purchase peace at the cost of your resources by stopping the mouths of those who spoke wickedness. But now, after he has ceased to be a brother and to hold a prebend, having been condemned by the lord pope, to give him that by which he may harm you is not merely shameful simony but manifest insanity. We could not hear the lord pope himself concerning making peace with him, much less the man of Prüm.

## LETTER XXIII. FROM EMPEROR CONRAD TO H., DUKE OF SAXONY

Concerning the right of advocacy in Kaminade and Visbik, which he had united to the monastery of Corbie.

*(Year 1147.)*

[Col. 1144C]

Conrad, by God’s grace king of the Romans, to H. [Henry], duke of Saxony: his favour and every good.

Your affection knows that we have placed our most faithful and beloved Wibald, abbot of Stavelot, over the same monastery, because of the unanimous election and request of the Church of Corbie. On account of his distinguished merit, earned by faithful service for the realm, in accordance with the request of his predecessor and the entreaty of the Church of Corbie, we granted to him and to the Church of Corbie by right of ownership in perpetual possession two convents of women [Col. 1144D] in which monastic observance had already failed—namely Kaminade and Visbik—for the restoration in them of the religious worship of God, by judgment of the princes, while preserving your right of advocacy which you hold in those places.

We further will and command your affection that, if you and he come to an agreement, you resign to him, in our stead, the right of advocacy over those places, as you were bound to us; and likewise receive the advocacy from him and from the Church of Corbie.

[Note: [Col. 1144D] This Henry the Lion performed at Brunswick in 1147, in the tenth indiction, the tenth year of Conrad, second king of the Romans. “We do not refuse,” he says, “to do this from our benefice at the humble request of our lord the king, especially because the aforesaid venerable abbot Wibald, most dear to us, served our most glorious grandfather, Emperor Lothair, long, earnestly, and faithfully, and adhered to him with singular constancy in the administration of the Roman Empire until his death. It is fitting that, as heirs of possessions we succeeded that emperor, so we should prove ourselves successors not unworthy in gratitude toward his friends and faithful servants” [Col. 1146D]. See the complete diploma below in the Appendix.]

But if you do not come to an agreement on this matter, then you are hereby commanded under the protection of our favour, by this present charter, to strive faithfully and vigorously to protect against every molestation the donation which we have made to the Church, and to administer, in confirmation of our donation, the advocacy which you hold from us over these same places [Col. 1145A].

## LETTER XXIV. FROM CONRAD TO J., ABBESS OF HEREVORD

That he had charged Abbot Wibald, after an inquiry into the monastery of Herevord, to correct its failings.

*(Year 1148.)*
CONRAD, by the grace of God King of the Romans, to I. [Note: Judith, to whom Pope Adrian granted a privilege in 1154.], venerable abbess of Herford [Note: The celebrated convent of virgins at Herford or Herivord, in the diocese of Paderborn, was founded in 825 by Count Walger of Herford, who summoned there nuns from St Mary’s at Phartenone near Soissons. In the course of time they took for themselves the name of canonesses.], his favour and every good.

As it pleased the divine ordinance, and as the unanimous and concordant election of the Church of Corvey required, we have set over the monastery of Corvey the venerable man Wibald, abbot of Stavelot—dear to us and to our kingdom on account of his fidelity—although he was unwilling and long resisted. Since we have learned both from the abbot himself and from the privileges of the Church of Corvey that a special affection has existed between your two houses and their prelates, and that whatever you are unable to correct belongs to the abbot’s care, we have therefore charged our beloved and faithful servant, that same abbot, diligently to inquire of you and yours into the deficiencies of your monastery, both within and without, and, relying on our assistance, faithfully to extend to you the hand of counsel and aid in all your needs. Whatever, moreover, he shall tell you on our behalf, you are to believe without hesitation and, as we trust of you, endeavour to carry into effect.

## LETTER XXV. HENRY THE MONK TO ABBOT WIBALD

He gives an account of what he had done with the pope for confirmation of Wibald’s election as abbot of Corvey. (1147.)

To his most reverend father and lord, WIBALD, abbot of Stavelot, HENRY, the least of all his servants, whatever a devoted son owes his father.

Dearest Father, I have sent letters to your sincerity, so that I might report to you more fully what was heard or done by us before the lord pope; not because I understood matters different from or more profound than those who are returning to you and are wholly yours, nor because I laboured more than they did, but so that, while they stand before you in their own cause, the affection of our devotion toward you might not be lacking.

On the Tuesday of Pentecost we arrived at Saint-Denis before the lord pope. There we presented ourselves only to the lord chancellor, because of the great tumult surrounding the lord pope at the departure of the lord king. On the following day, before the lord pope—who intended to cross to Meaux—set out, we were presented to him through the chancellor and gave him the letters which we had brought. We reached Meaux on Thursday. On Friday we alone were summoned into the presence of the lord pope, the bishops, and the cardinals; yet Lord Florentinus had beforehand instructed us what we should say and who should speak—namely, one of the men of Corvey, whose cause was being handled.

But since one of them, as you know better, was rather impeded in speech, while the other was quite ill, I, who was present with the Corvey men by your command, approached the lord pope with them as though I myself were a Corvey man. There, when your election was to be discussed in the presence of all those assembled, I—who, for the necessity already mentioned, admitted that I was then a Corvey man—recounted to the lord pope, as was fitting, the whole order of the election, which I knew well.

The pope, having heard all the grounds on which they had elected you, and having also learned the advantages which we had not left unmentioned and which had followed upon the election, said that he would take counsel with the brethren and would reply to us according to their counsel. In this suspense we were kept for ten days: sometimes we watched half the day at the lord pope’s door, for he rarely went out; sometimes we continually attended before the chancellor’s gate; and sometimes, worn out by excessive tedium, we slept almost until night along with many others.

Meanwhile we also dealt with every cardinal individually in his own house, since otherwise they would neither receive nor answer us, in order that we might receive a favourable response both in this matter and concerning the privilege for Kemnade and Visbek. All of them, apart from a few, comforted us with gracious conversation and said that all would turn out prosperously for us, though matters were proceeding more slowly than we wished. [lacuna] Meanwhile, by true and certain arguments, we also refuted the lies which, a few days before our arrival, I do not know who—or by whom they had been sent—had spread abroad: namely, that you had given the entire treasure of the church to the lord king. Blessed in all things be God, because, just as it was evident that they proclaimed falsehoods, so it became clear that they disappeared at once upon our arrival and left no one believing their inventions.

What more need be said? On the tenth day after your electoral cause had been heard, we were summoned; and, after much commendation of your person, wisdom, and eloquence, in the presence of the bishops and all the cardinals, he adjudged and granted that the election made in your favour was valid. This, as he himself declared, was rather by dispensation of the Roman Church than by any authority. He commanded the prior and us who were then present—and through us all those belonging to the Church of Corvey—that thereafter we should obey you; and that, as we had been eager to have you as our father, so we should be diligent in reverencing your person, and should not then for the first time begin to take offense when you wished to undertake the reform of the order.

Concerning the privilege, however, we received the answer that the matter was disputed, and that for no reason could or would he allow, at that time, what had been done to be confirmed by apostolic authority—especially since the written complaint of the nuns was kept in his possession. When we wished to press the matter further, all with one voice urged us to seek nothing more at that time. They said that this should suffice us, and that it was a great favour of the lord pope that he did not forbid us the places themselves: just as he did not confirm what had been done, so neither did he invalidate it. Since at last we could not obtain what we wanted, we had to want what we could obtain. We then came to the petitions, of which we obtained only two; copies of them have been sent to you. You will be able to learn from those travelling to you whatever else may be lacking. May God preserve your fatherhood unharmed for the honour of His Church.

## LETTER XXVI. CARDINAL GUIDO TO ABBOT WIBALD

That he may transfer from the abbacy of Stavelot to that of Corvey. (1147.)

GUIDO, cardinal-deacon and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, to his dearest brother and special friend WIBALD, abbot of Corvey, greeting.

It is certain that true love cannot be idle. At the appointed time we received your messengers with your letters; and, so that they might obtain an effective result in the matters for which they had come, they laboured earnestly and faithfully with us, and we with them. As for Stavelot, therefore, I shall not call it ours; we do not know [why], although it is yours [the wording is uncertain]. Toward Corvey you may now, for the first time—thanks be to God—go forth openly, with banners displayed and with an unrestrained countenance.

If anything has been insufficiently accomplished, whether in confirming those two churches by an apostolic privilege or in any other matter, you should know that this has happened neither through the negligence of your messengers, who laboured to the extent of their powers, nor through any lukewarmness of our own inactivity. If, when an opportunity arises, we can again be of service for your benefit, we shall by no means neglect it, the Lord being our author.

## LETTER XXVII. ABBOT WIBALD TO CARDINAL GUIDO

Concerning his visit to the cardinal and the captives of the Roman Church whom he had redeemed. (1147.)

To his beloved father and friend GUIDO, cardinal-deacon of the holy Roman Church and chancellor of the apostolic see, WIBALD, by the grace of God the least thing that is, gives himself and all that is his.

Your learning has written to us, and it is true that true love cannot be idle. It is equally certain that this same true love is neither mistrustful nor suspicious, neither accepting persons nor despising them. Hence it is that, exceeding the measure of our littleness, we have become accustomed to speak and write to your loftiness with a certain confidence, plainly and almost as an equal: considering not to whom we write, but how greatly we love.

You will arrange our coming to you in a way worthy of your excellence and suited to our weakness. We have sent you an antidote against winter cold. Let this be *diacalamus* [term uncertain], which, although it brings a small price, is nevertheless equally potent, as poor Arduenna asserts, with *diamargariton* [“pearl-like remedy”]. You will carefully commend and elegantly embellish the service which we have rendered to the lord pope and the holy Roman Church in freeing captives; you will understand it more fully from the letters which we have sent to the lord pope and from the report of our envoys.

## LETTER XXVIII. POPE EUGENIUS III TO THE BISHOP OF HAVELBERG

That he should ensure the restoration of Corvey property usurped by his subjects. (1147.)

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother A., bishop of Havelberg, greeting and apostolic blessing.

Our beloved son Wibald, abbot, and the monks of Corvey have complained to us that Poppo of Blankenburg, his son C., and your canon R. have violently taken from them and unjustly retain all the revenues which they possessed at Kroppenstedt and Gröningen. Therefore, since by the obligation of our office we neither wish nor ought to fail them in their justice, we command and enjoin you by these apostolic letters: if their complaint rests upon truth, strictly admonish those invaders to restore in full what they have taken. Otherwise, within two months after receiving this document, administer canonical justice against them.

## LETTER XXIX. POPE EUGENIUS III TO REINHERIUS, CANON OF HAVELBERG

That he should restore twenty *mansi* which he had taken from the monastery of Corvey. (1147.)

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to REINHERIUS, canon of Havelberg, greeting and apostolic blessing.

We have received the complaint of our beloved sons Wibald and the monks of Corvey that, in the village of Kroppenstedt, you have unjustly and violently taken from them twenty *mansi* [landholdings]. Therefore, since we do not believe you are ignorant with what severity invaders of ecclesiastical property ought to be compelled, we command and enjoin you by apostolic letters to restore in full both the aforesaid *mansi* which you have seized and all other things taken thence. If you prove contemptuous, we want you to know that we shall not let the matter pass without grave punishment if a renewed cry concerning the aforesaid injury reaches us.

## LETTER XXX. HENRY, KING OF THE ROMANS, TO ABBOT WIBALD

He praises and seeks Wibald’s counsel in administering the kingdom and establishing peace. (1147.)

HENRY, by the grace of God King of the Romans, to WIBALD, abbot of Corvey, the fullness of his favour.

We are certain that you embrace both us and our father with the same affection of sincerity, and that with great steadfastness of faith you strive to preserve and advance the honour of each. Therefore we receive with all eagerness of heart the counsel of your discernment concerning the administration of the kingdom, the establishment of peace, and the reception and honouring of princes; and, in these matters as in others, we desire to follow the familiar teaching of your prudence. We shall keep the riding-horse sent us by your generosity as a memorial and token of your affection at our saddle.

## LETTER XXXI. EMPEROR CONRAD TO ABBOT WIBALD

He commends himself to Wibald’s prayers and asks him not to cease guiding his son. (1147.)

CONRAD, by the grace of God King of the Romans, to WIBALD, venerable abbot of Corvey, his favour and every good.

That the progress of our journey may tend toward the prosperity of the whole Church and the honour of our kingdom, we hope for and request very much the aid of your prayers. We therefore report to your affection concerning the state of our health, in which we have thus far remained. Thanks be to God, we are sound and whole. Descending through Hungary, we have reached Greece, where the king of the Greeks gives us honourable service. Moreover, we earnestly commend our beloved son to your fidelity, asking that your prudence not cease to guide and govern his childhood.

## LETTER XXXII. A., ABBOT OF FULDA, TO WIBALD

He requests Wibald’s intercession with the supreme pontiff. (1147.)

To WIBALD, venerable abbot of Corvey in Christ [Note: Ascholf, who is said to have been deposed by Pope Eugenius III because of his harsh government of the monks. See below the letter of Abbot Wibald to Pope Eugenius, col. 1150D, in which he informs him, in 1149, of the condition of the monastery of Fulda.], A., humble overseer of the abbey of Fulda, the obligation of brotherly love and prayer.

How kindly you have condescended to our grief is shown by your conduct. For when you first took up our cause, you wished to comfort us by your letters; and these were a remedy all the greater because they could be sent by so great a man. Your favour, therefore, giving birth in us to great confidence, affords a singular ground for seeking counsel and assistance from you, as a lover of religion and teacher of regular discipline.

You already understand what evils are growing up for us through our subjects, and you know how damaging they are to our whole purpose. To alleviate this matter, be a comfort to us by sending your testimony to the apostolic lord, if you cannot come by the time of our summons. Whatever may be the state of affairs, let your affection know that we are to depart on the day after the feast of All Saints; and our faithful community there earnestly wishes that you be present with us.

## LETTER XXXIII. ABBOT WIBALD TO CARDINAL GUIDO

He commends to him the cause of the abbot of Fulda and also of Abbot Reinard, formerly his own teacher. (1147.)

To his reverend father and lord GUIDO, cardinal and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, WIBALD, by the grace of God that which he is, gives himself with all his possessions in the Catholic Church.

Many of our brethren have heard that we have found favour in your sight; and they therefore ask that we should earnestly commend them to your clemency. Although we do this with hesitation, fearing to burden your mind, which is filled with concern for the whole world, yet any occasion which gives us an opportunity to visit and greet your sweetness is most welcome to us.

We therefore commend to your goodness our brother, the abbot of Fulda, that for the sake of our request you may deign to protect his cause. For, as we have learned concerning him, he is a mature and weighty man, constant and useful in recovering possessions and building up his monastery. Concerning his adversaries it is certain that they act contrary to their profession: abandoning the observance of their religious profession, which by written pledge and spoken word they promised to observe, they occupy themselves with lawsuits contrary to the holy Rule because of ambition, and possess private property from which they divide the expenses of their journeys.

The bearer of this letter, the venerable Abbot Rheinard, teacher and instructor of our youth and trainer in divine service, seeks confirmation of the privileges of the church over which he presides as first superior. He is poor in possessions but rich in merits; he meditates on the law of God by day and night, and his delight lies in searching it out and writing it. He is indeed a man of great abstinence and an enemy to his flesh. For God’s love and at our recommendation, receive him graciously.

## LETTER XXXIV. A FRIEND TO WIBALD

He congratulates him on overcoming his adversaries and praises Robert, dean of Stavelot. (1147.)

To the beloved, from one who loves: whatever the affection of devotion seeks.

[Note: This was undoubtedly Reinard, abbot of Reinhausen, formerly Wibald’s teacher, as is clear from the following letter, in which Wibald replies to this one. This abbot died in 1150, not without a great reputation for holiness. See his epitaph in vol. II of *Scriptores rerum Brunsvicensium*, in the introduction by the most distinguished Gottfried Leibniz.]

Having read and reread, my Wibald, dearest of men, the letters written and sent by you, to you, and for you, I confess that I have been affected in many ways and made tearful by these emotions. For when I consider to what miseries, calamities, pressures, labours, and distresses the man long dearest to me has been subjected; how much he has suffered at the hands of those least suited to inflict it—I could not but be moved, through the compassion due to past evils as though they were present, by these troubles and afflictions; nor could I fail to be stung by zeal for justice against such great wrongs and presumptions.

Again, on the other hand, when I contemplate how kindly, seasonably, powerfully, and mercifully divine pity has protected and strengthened him, and how gloriously it has granted him to triumph over those warring against him, I can scarcely find an end to my joy. Moreover, because I read such praises of your integrity, shrewdness, virtue, and diligence in letters sent on your behalf by our brethren of Stavelot to eminent persons in Church and kingdom; because bishops, abbots, communities, and convents bear testimony to the same effect; and because those very greatest persons favour you, write on your behalf, and support you—because, I say, I read such things in these letters, I am utterly unable to express in writing or speech how greatly my heart dances and applauds itself, since I seemed to have laid, in such a man, some foundation upon which so lofty an excellence of praiseworthy integrity has risen and grown.

I pass over the Ciceronian eloquence alike of yourself and of Brother Robert, dean of Stavelot, who also heard us for a while some time ago, which I have admired in these same letters. In my judgment, certainly, the style of few—even of the ancients, to say nothing of moderns—seems to surpass his pen. All these things, I say, and many others which I refrain from writing at greater length, lest someone perhaps ascribe them more to the excessive affection which I have for my dearest friend than to truth—all these make me rejoice with you and make me bear my anxieties, poverty, and labours more lightly, while I see him divinely rescued from such great evils among his own people and, as I hope, set beside me by the mercy of divine providence for my special consolation.

But in all things, good Jesus, Saviour and lover of humankind, stretch over us the right hand of your propitiation, and defend us by your protection against the manifold snares of the adversary. May prosperity not exalt us; may adversity not cast us down; may Martha’s portion not take Mary’s portion away from us; and, to conclude briefly, may we so pass through temporal goods that we do not lose eternal ones.

## LETTER XXXV. ABBOT WIBALD TO REINARD, ABBOT OF REINHAUSEN

He replies to the preceding letter. (1147.)

To his reverend father and teacher REINARD, abbot of Reinhausen, his pupil WIBALD: whatever it is, in the Catholic Church, through attained purity of heart, to see the God of gods in Zion.

With what zeal of charity you have read the letters concerning our affairs—some troublesome indeed, yet all laborious—the tenor of your letter makes clear. In it, having briefly included the principal points of all matters, you grieved over our adversities with a father’s compassion and, while others defended us, added also the title of your own praise in commendation of our person.

But, to confess the truth plainly to your sincerity: by God’s ordering of human affairs, those who persecuted us were instruments of divine justice. Although, because of their evil intention, they deserved everlasting woe, they were nevertheless the rod of our most just God and the staff of His wrath. But they did not know it, and war was made against us in a marvellously perverse fashion. For, since our adversaries were deficient in their case and deprived of every support of truth, the one refuge of their conceived malice was to tear us with insults and reproaches—[Note: Here he perhaps alludes to the calumnies by which he was accused before the supreme pontiff of having given the treasure of his church to the king; see below the letter of Henry the monk to Abbot Wibald.]—because they could not overcome us by reason. By defiling our reputation with malignant words, they embittered the minds of their hearers against us before the truth of the facts could prevail in their hearts.

But Christ extended His most merciful right hand to one labouring for Him and, with the temptation, gave the means of escape, so that we might endure. Those, however, who protected us, delighted by the justice of our cause, were mistaken in their estimate of our way of life and character, believing that so necessary and arduous a business could not have been undertaken by a person of humble and austere life.

But rejoice with us in dovelike simplicity that our labours in the Catholic Church have been doubled and increased beyond the capacity of our strength, and that we have come to a nation which we did not know, where we need the protection of your prayers as much as our anxiety of care is greater and the character of the time and manners more dangerous. Since a whole day is insufficient for explaining our occupations, we have written this brief night-work in our own hand for your sincerity after the morning vigils, earnestly begging that, as we trust in your affection, you may deign to pray for us. Farewell.

## LETTER XXXVI. REINARD TO ABBOT WIBALD

Concerning their mutual affection. (1147.)

To Lord WIBALD, REINARD, however insignificant, yet most faithful: whatever is sweetest.

Dearest of men, in return for your many and great benefits I have taken care to send you letters, if indeed they are in return; and I would wish to render some sort of thanks proportionate to those benefits, were I not aware that your freely bestowed goodness requires them in no way. Yet the travail of my heart does not permit that nothing should burst forth from its inward conception.

What, then, can I say, except that you—being, as someone says, another self to me—do what you ought to do? For when the truth of that saying is considered, you abundantly cherish me in your own inmost being; and whatever you seem to bestow upon me, you are undoubtedly found to confer proportionally upon yourself. You read and understand well that command of the divine law: “Whatever you wish people to do for you, do also yourselves.” That is, if the condition of your life were so arranged that you, placed in need, had a friend superior to you in wealth and resources, then, although you would not demand it, if his voluntary kindness received you, perhaps you would not refuse n[?] [lacuna]; nor has that saying from Cicero’s dialogue *On Friendship* escaped my memory, which runs as follows: [lacuna] “To love is nothing else than to cherish the very person whom you love, with no need and no advantage sought”; yet that advantage itself blossoms from friendship, even though you have pursued it less.

For I too loved you, as you yourself know, when neither was I constrained by any need—for I had enough of what was supplied—nor did your condition in that kind of circumstance allow my mind to conceive or seek anything of the sort from you. But now, burdened with concern for others and, as it has pleased the Lord, somewhat troubled by a shortage of necessities, I unhesitatingly ascribe this very thing to divine consolation: that God Himself may touch someone’s heart. For, apart from you, hardly anyone at this time is so disposed toward me as to open his eyes over me and, out of the abundance which he has received by the gift of our Creator, supply with brotherly compassion my want, which I endure for others’ sake.

For small means, or even very small ones, would easily suffice for myself alone, because, insofar as circumstances allow, I do not greatly seek superfluities. But why should I longer occupy your busy eyes or ears by recounting such matters? Though it is pleasant and delightful to me to converse often and long with my dearest friend. Let there therefore now be some measure in my speech, since there is no measure in affection. Farewell.

## LETTER XXXVII. THE MONKS OF STAVELOT TO ABBOT WIBALD

They congratulate him on his return, complain of Count Godfrey, who had broken the truce agreed with him, and of the seizure of the village of Tornines. (1147.)

To their most reverend father and lord in Christ, WIBALD, venerable abbot of Stavelot, the humble community of the same church: filial affection and due obedience.

How much joy, dearest Father, has been bestowed on us by the safe return of you and yours [Note: This return of which the Stavelot monks speak is undoubtedly the return from the Slavic expedition, mentioned in Letters 41 and 131, as is clear to an attentive reader.], your learning will readily perceive, since it has always known both our sincerity toward you and the purity of our heart concerning your successes. Blessed therefore in all things be God, who, as we have learned, has deigned in your safety to show His faithful that “the Lord is near to all who call upon Him.”

Meeting your fatherhood unanimously in these letters, we receive you as returned—or rather, still returning; in receiving, we greet; in greeting, we embrace you. We entreat you not to refuse to come to us by the term appointed in your promise, so that we may enjoy your presence face to face and rejoice in it, and be more fully refreshed by your conversation, whose counsel has often and many times strengthened us.

Let our dearest Father, so necessary at this time, therefore come to us—that is, to his beloved sons—not only for us who are shut within, but also for those without. For the truce or armistice which our advocate, Count Godfrey, and his men had pledged on their faith to observe and maintain until the feast of Remigius was violated immediately after your departure; and nearly all that belongs to us, on both sides, has been laid waste by plunder, robbery, and fire. Thus the entire weight of all malice has fallen solely upon us and ours, and so it comes about that:

> “Whatever madness kings commit, the Achaeans pay the penalty.”  
> —Horace, *Epistles* I.2.14.

To crown our miseries, Eustace, with the consent of the count of Namur, has again violently occupied our village of Tornines. How much we have laboured in this matter, how insistently we have urged the bishop of Liège to execute canonical justice upon the invader, and what alone remains to be done, your prudence will more fully judge from the copies of letters sent to you.

Meanwhile, in order to humble our souls before God, we have laid upon the ground the relics or bodies of all the saints which are kept among us, together with the image of our Saviour [Note: Monks who once suffered harsh persecution used to lay holy relics, crosses, and images upon the ground and cover altars with haircloth and thorns. On this matter see, if desired, what we wrote in book III, chapter 3, *On the Ancient Rites of the Church.*]. As earnestly as we can, we beseech the mercy of the supreme Divinity to cast down by the right hand of His power those who trust in their own ferocity, and to deliver us from their oppression—for He alone regards the labour and pain of the humble.

## LETTER XXXVIII. ROBERT, DEAN OF STAVELOT, TO ABBOT WIBALD

He congratulates him on his return. (1148.)

To his most reverend lord and father in Christ, WIBALD, abbot of Stavelot, Brother ROBERT: unceasing devotion of prayers and submission, obedience and affection.

We bless the Lord of heaven for the return and safety of you and yours; we give thanks to the Father of mercies for the restoration to us, through you, of the fullness of gladness and joy. Yet we cannot help being distressed by your delay, since we desire to be refreshed by the consolation of your presence. We are shaken by many things, not so much cares as pressures, and therefore desire your presence more than written replies. You will learn the condition of our land both from the written reports and from the spoken account of this bearer.

## LETTER XXXIX. PROVOST BOVO TO ABBOT WIBALD

Concerning damage inflicted upon the provostship by the count of Namur and others. (1148.)

To his lord WIBALD, venerable abbot of Stavelot, Brother Bovo: whatever a son owes his father.

Placed in great distress and suffering unbearable loss after your departure, we longingly await your arrival; for we are afflicted not only by outsiders, but are also mercilessly oppressed inwardly and outwardly by our own people. In the affairs belonging to you which are around us, I labour as faithfully as I can. But in the provostship, in which I act in your stead, know that I can obtain no profit, because we are ravaged by plunder and fire not only by Rad and Macharius in Condroz, but also by the count of Namur and his adversaries in Hesbaye.

## LETTER XL. ABBOT WIBALD TO HENRY, BISHOP OF LIÈGE

That he should restrain Eustace, his parishioner, who had seized the village of Tornines. (1148.)

To his reverend father and lord HENRY, venerable bishop of the holy Church of Liège, Brother WIBALD, by the grace of God servant of the Church of Stavelot: devoted prayers and devoted service.

Our brethren and sons, the monks of Stavelot, servants of your holiness, have brought us a grave complaint because Eustace, your man and parishioner, has seized the village of Tornines, which belongs to the brethren’s daily allowance, and has violently taken away the revenues of that village, which provide daily fare for the brethren.

We do not doubt that you know how we recovered that same village by judgment and by the dictates of justice; how for a long time now we have held it in free possession and peacefully administered it; and how we have assigned all its revenues to the needs of our brethren as the necessities of the monastery required. We also recovered, with great labour, the tithe and other things which had been scattered here and there. We were in possession at the time when the lord pope laid upon us the sign of the holy cross, so that we should undertake an expedition against the pagans beyond the Elbe, and received our person and all our property under the protection of blessed Peter and his own. During that period the said Eustace seized the village, not without sacrilege.

Therefore, prostrate in spirit at the feet of your greatness, we earnestly beg your discretion to restrain the said Eustace from this rashness, since he is your particular man, as it were one of your household and intimate retainers. Allow us to owe this favour rather to you than to the lord pope, who is shortly to come into the regions of Lotharingia. There are many evils in your bishopric—such as have not generally been heard there since ancient days—but you can easily suppress this evil. Do not permit right and wrong to be confounded in the time of your priesthood.

Remember that we ought to appear and be numbered among the foremost of our mother Church of Liège, both by the time and place of our establishment and by our age; and that we have humbly and faithfully served the same our mother in every need, and are prepared and desire to do this until the end. Remember also that Pope Honorius wrote to Bishop Alexander concerning the doing of justice in Tornines; that Pope Innocent commanded Lord Albero orally once at Olivento near the city of Melfi, a second time at Rome in council, and a third time by his letters, which we presented to him in a full synod at Liège. Nor could Albero spare flesh and blood, though for his negligence he received such great punishment from God that thereafter he never lived in peace and quiet in his bishopric and honour.

## LETTER XLI. ABBOT WIBALD TO HIS MONKS OF STAVELOT

He laments the calamities which they suffered during his absence. (1148.)

Brother WIBALD, by the grace of God servant of the Church of Stavelot, to Robert the dean and the other brethren of Stavelot: may you abound in the spirit of counsel and fortitude.

We received your letter of sincerity, which at its beginning [Col. 1156D] was full of grace, charity, filial affection, singular longing, joy, sweetness, and good hope; and which, in one and the same instant, filled both our heart with richer gladness and our eyes with abundant tears called forth by your kindness. Believe us: it was sweet and delightful to our soul to live; sweet and delightful, amid so many dangers which we endured day and night on the expedition against the pagans beyond the Elbe in the Hercynian Forest, to have preserved life and safety, so that we might cheerfully enjoy such great benefits as we received from your greeting and visitation.

But when, with our mind intent upon better things and having enjoyed the participation of so great a good, we ran through your letter, our spirit suddenly shuddered, our face grew pale, [Col. 1157A] and our choir was turned into mourning when we came upon those pitiable complaints of yours. They could pierce heaven, if, as our sins deserve, it had not been made brazen so that prayer might not pass through; they could, I say, move the earth, if the elements did not rebel against us because their Creator has been offended.

Entering therefore into the inner chambers of our heart and the secret recesses of our soul, and lamenting long and bitterly, we argued with our conscience, investigating and judging whether it ought rightly to be imputed to us or to all of you that, through our long absence, the monastery of Stavelot is being torn apart in such lamentable ways. Are you at fault, who, having in every respect authority over us, sent us—or at least allowed us to go—to govern the Church of Corbie? Or are we [Col. 1157B] guilty, who at your wish—let us not say command—have involved ourselves in such anxieties and hostilities, leaving, indeed, or, as we fear, deserting our mother, our educator and nourisher, the Church of Stavelot?

Although, through your exhortation and by God’s working, we are great according to the name of the great who are on earth, you may nevertheless know that the higher we are seen to have ascended, the more we must fear the varied chance of a fall; and the more the gifts of honors increase, the more the accounts required for those gifts are augmented. Certainly, to pass over our other disadvantages, we are not permitted to grow old—or rather, we grow old every day—but the rest prepared for old men and veterans is denied us at Corbie. New labors, new exertion, new eloquence, new gifts, [Col. 1157C] new magnificence are demanded of us daily, although, long wearied already, we had looked forward to some end of our labors and hoped for some rest from our fatigue. Either one must fail in one’s duty to the commonwealth, or endure men’s hostilities.

Moreover, in our age all shame has departed, all reverence has been extinguished, faith has perished, and uprightness is dead. Why, then, did it please you to double our labors? How much fruit we can produce in reforming and maintaining religious life, your own shortcomings and your own labors—which daily increase because of the wickedness of evil men—can teach you very easily. Furthermore, what use are riches in the absence of peace? You therefore conclude that neither in spiritual matters nor in . . . . [Col. 1157D] can we possess solid joy.

But God, our hope, our honor, our lineage, our exaltation, our rejoicing, in administering His commonwealth uses our smallness as His instrument, though cheap and slight; and through whatever advances in rank He wills, He graciously draws us, as it were by certain little gifts, toward love of His name. He deigns to restrain the excesses of our frailty by daily—indeed, continual—labors, like certain scourges and bitter medicines, lest we depart from Him.

We grieve over Tornines as greatly as we cannot express in words, as you may see in the copy of the letter which we sent you. If the lord pope, as is reported, is to come to Trier, wait for us ourselves to carry through this case; [Col. 1158A] but if not, as rumor has it, send promptly to the lord pope our beloved son Brother Henry and Brother Erlebald, taking with them all the documents concerning Tornines which you safely hold on our behalf, and especially the sealed letters of Pope Innocent which he sent to Alberon, bishop of Liège, concerning this same matter. As for coming to you soon, we are making ready by every means, and are already, as it were, gathering our baggage. Pray for us.

## LETTER XLII. HENRY, BISHOP OF LIÈGE, TO ABBOT WIBALD

He desires the benefit of his presence for the correction of moral defects. (Year 1148.)

[Col. 1158B] HENRY, by the grace of God bishop of the people of Liège, to the venerable abbot of Stavelot, WIBALD: greeting in the highest Savior.

I have learned by experience, even more than you, the intolerable character of the evils weighing upon our bishopric, since experience is superior to report. And since, as our sins demand, evils multiply from day to day, your discerning judgment cannot doubt that we need the aid of your counsel and assistance all the more, because a grace more choice and ardent than that granted to others has been divinely bestowed upon you in both respects.

Yet, measuring your occupations by our own, we patiently endure your absence, though it is very burdensome both to us and to those especially dependent upon you; [Col. 1158C] and we earnestly and confidently urge your affection to make haste, with more zealous effort, to come to relieve our burdens. For it is necessary that, through the united endeavor of us both, the offences and insolences of your men may be corrected in your presence, and that the malice on our side may, with God’s favor, be somewhat mitigated.

## LETTER XLIII. WIBALD TO THE BISHOP OF LIÈGE

He desires the benefit of his presence. (Year 1148.)

A subject to his lord, a son to his father: greetings to his beloved.

Troubled by grievous cares, frequent expenses, and continual [Col. 1158D] pressures, we are indeed at a loss, but not abandoned, while awaiting your arrival, necessary alike for us and for the land. We judge that then, if not complete peace of heart, we shall at least have rest for the body. Therefore we pray you not to delay coming to those who love you.

We received, after the synod, the letter which you sent us concerning the synod, although both at the synod and from the Kalends of August onward we had spoken before the Church of Liège concerning Tornines. We write nothing about the evils of our land: abundance has made us poor.

## LETTER XLIV. ABBOT WIBALD TO POPE EUGENIUS III

That he allowed envoys of the men of Erveta, captured by a ministerial of Stavelot, to depart free. (Year 1148.)

[Col. 1159A]

To his most reverend father and lord EUGENIUS, sole and universal pontiff, Brother WIBALD, by God’s and your grace what he is: in the Catholic Church, the devotion of a son and obedience of a servant.
