On hearing of your arrival in the regions of Lotharingia, we hastened to arrange the affairs of the Church of Corbie and to meet your holiness more swiftly, so that, both in our own person and in the matters entrusted to us by God and by your goodness, we might render to your holiness service as devout as it is due. And, by the working of divine mercy, a more prompt effect followed our pious and faithful intention.

For we found envoys of the men [Col. 1159B] of Erveta, who were traveling to your exalted presence on certain ecclesiastical causes, captured in a castle belonging to a ministerial of the Church of Stavelot. At the very moment of our arrival, before tasting bread, we besieged that same stronghold for the honor of your person and the defense of ecclesiastical justice. Through labor, expense, and grave enmities, we brought them out of the prison in which they were held and sent them free to the knees of your holiness, although they had already made an agreement that they should pay nearly fifty marks of pure silver for their ransom.

We could not recover their goods which they had lost, because they were not held by those by whom they had been captured. But for your honor [Col. 1159C] we bestowed upon them two mounts and provisions for the journey.

## LETTER XLV. THE MONKS OF CORBIE TO THE MEN OF STAVELOT

They give thanks because they granted them Wibald as abbot; they recount how excellently he has conducted himself among them in spiritual and temporal matters, and concerning mutual association. (Year 1148.)

To their beloved and ever-to-be-beloved lords and brothers, sons of the holy Church of Stavelot, the brothers of Corbie: the intimate affection of true brotherhood and the most devoted offering of continual prayer.

In this, reverend fathers and lords, we have recognized that the charity of God has been poured into your hearts through the Holy Spirit given to you: because [Col. 1159D] you loved your brothers and neighbors—namely us—so greatly, and sympathized so deeply with our labors and tribulations, that you shared with us what you had among yourselves that was dearest and best. You sent to us, who awaited his arrival with great longing, the man who knew among you how to heal the broken in heart and bind up their wounds in the time of your tribulation, so that he might also come to the aid of our calamities.

For this reason we render boundless thanks to your goodness. We gladly and gratefully recount to you that this same most beloved father and lord of ours is laboring strenuously for our Church and has already overcome by his energy many of its troubles, like the strong man armed who guards his courtyard; and that, if he lives, he will overcome still more. [Col. 1160A] Indeed, our community, which for many past years had suffered from no slight dissension and had been dispersed in many places through that same discord, he recalled, like a pious shepherd, to fraternal peace and to the cloister. What had fallen into decay in our order he reformed by attentive effort, so that we now see its ancient splendor and the firm observance of our religious life flowering again, and recognize our Corbie in its true image.

Moreover, he wholly recovered and restored to the monastery’s uses the possessions alienated by that Henry whom the venerable legate of the Apostolic See, Lord Thomas the cardinal, canonically deposed by the judgment of the Holy Spirit—possessions amounting to more than nearly one hundred mansi of good and fertile land. [Col. 1160B]

For benefits such as these, and for other like or greater benefits which we still hope for from him, we give thanks to God and to you, the givers of so great a father. At the time of his election we loved him because of our good hope; now, because of the reality and the benefits bestowed on us, we love him unanimously and with inward affection as a man worthy of every love.

We have heard from our beloved brother Henry, bearer of this letter, and from Lord W., then our prior, and from Brother R., the provost, that when they stayed for several days among you, you treated them kindly and honorably, and, among other acts of kindness, granted them brotherhood and association among you, as you would to one of your own. For this also we give thanks to your kindness. [Col. 1160C]

As for the matter concerning which both we wrote to you and they themselves discussed with you—the matter, that is, of this same brotherhood and association—we are unanimously agreed that your Church and ours should be one in Christ; and we earnestly ask that this same thing may please your unanimity. We desire this union of the two Churches to be effected through our beloved lord and father.

Through him we promise you the obligations of brotherhood according to our custom, provided that we in turn receive from you the obligations of brotherhood according to your custom. And if any brother of either Church should be expelled because of his faults, he shall, until his reconciliation, be cherished and maintained with a mother’s care by the other Church.

## LETTER XLVI. THE MONKS OF CORBIE TO THE MEN OF STAVELOT

How they conducted themselves with the pope’s legate when he asked them what they had done with the Church’s treasures. (Year 1148.)

[Col. 1160D]

To their most reverend and most beloved brothers in Christ, ROBERT, venerable dean, and the other brothers of holy Stavelot: F. W., prior of the Church of Corbie, and the other brothers of the same monastery, ever to be at leisure and see how sweet the Lord is.

We have heard that your unanimity has been disturbed by a certain matter which Master G. discussed with us last year concerning the treasures removed [Col. 1161A] from our church. Since we think this did not reach you by a truthful report and consequently produced scandal among you, we have judged it fitting to disclose to you the whole sequence of events.

The same Master G., then legate of the Apostolic See, came to us last year around the feast of St Thomas, while the lord abbot was staying in your region. He was received as a guest among us, treated humanely, and observed by us with every diligence and devotion, as befitted the legate of the lord pope; he was honorably provided for from the resources of our monastery.

At that time the provost of the greater church of our house was at home. While he busied himself diligently with the legate’s service and sometimes sat with him in order to converse, he asked the legate, among other things said, why our sanctuary had been stripped of its treasures, or what benefit our church had gained from them. “Our sanctuary,” said the provost, “has not been stripped, because whatever was taken from it was spent for the benefit of our church, [Col. 1161B] which has been enlarged in its possessions every year by no fewer than one hundred mansi.”

When, however, the same legate of the lord pope was to leave early the following morning, he ordered the provost to assemble the entire community that same evening, so that he might address us by mandate of the lord pope. But the day had already advanced to a late hour, and our community was not, by rule, supposed to meet for a conference. When our provost had explained this impossibility to the legate, the conference was deferred until the following day.

As soon as dawn broke, he again summoned the provost and once more ordered that a chapter meeting be held, in which he might speak with the brothers. “It is not,” said the provost, “the custom of our order to assemble for chapter at such an early hour.” But since the legate was hurrying to depart and could not wait for the hour of chapter, at last this same legate of the Apostolic See was brought before the community before the third hour, while we were customarily engaged in reading. Sitting among us, he inquired carefully, among the other matters which he brought to our attention, why the treasury of our church had been dissipated. To him we replied through our prior and provost in the following manner: [Col. 1161D]

“Because of the common need of the church, with the common consent of our chapter we took a certain part of the treasures in the church, and with them acquired certain very useful possessions for our church. All the rest has been preserved intact in the church. What we have now taken because of necessity, we have resolved, with God’s permission, to replace and restore as quickly as we can.”

Having heard this, he was satisfied and asked nothing further on the matter. Farewell.

## LETTER XLVII. CARDINAL GUIDO TO ABBOT WIBALD

That he showed Wibald’s letter to the pope, and that Wibald should present himself to the pontiff. (Year 1148.)

[Col. 1162A]

GUIDO, cardinal-deacon and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, to his dearest friend, the abbot of Corbie: greetings.

The sincerity of affection which we have begun to have toward you is not diminished but increased. We showed the lord pope the letter which you sent us through your German.

[Note: [Col. 1161] Erlebald, undoubtedly a monk of Liège, who, after Wibald’s death, became abbot of Stavelot.]

But, to speak briefly, we prefer to promise our friends little and to do more. Enough has been said to the wise. It seems good to us that you should have presented yourself to the lord pope because of the vexations caused by those who disparage you. [Col. 1162B]

## LETTER XLVIII. WIBALD TO CARDINAL GUIDO

He commends to him his men of Stavelot. (Year 1148.)

To his reverend father and lord GUIDO, cardinal-deacon of the holy Roman Church and chancellor of the Apostolic See, Brother WIBALD, by the grace of God, the little that he is: himself.

As you indicated to us—and this was not said lightly, for we receive more from your nod than we hear in words—we were so concerned about the service of providing for the lord pope that we were foremost in devotion and in no way found among the grumblers. The Church of Stavelot, whose abbot you are, has the greatest need of the protection of its abbot—that is, of you—and you will promptly and mercifully assist it as befits a father. Its complaint will be more fully made known to your exaltedness by our brother—ours, I say, not by the customary manner of monastic speech, but properly and specially yours and ours. [Col. 1162C]

## LETTER XLIX. ABBOT WIBALD TO CARDINAL JORDAN

What he did for providing for the pope at Liège. (Year 1148.)

To his reverend lord JORDAN, cardinal-priest of the holy Roman Church, Brother WIBALD, by the grace of God, the little that he is: himself.

[Col. 1162D] We have done what you commanded. Concerning the service of providing for the lord pope, arranged in the bishopric of Liège, we were not only concerned but zealous, so that we might furnish more than the share estimated to fall to the monastery of Stavelot, and might in no way increase the number of those who murmured.

We earnestly request, by attentive entreaty, that your paternity, dear to us, commend our devotion with a gracious word and faithfully lay up within the bosom of apostolic mercy the complaint of the monastery of Stavelot, which will be made known to your kindness through our brothers.

## LETTER L. ABBOT WIBALD TO CARDINAL JOHN

He requests his protection. (Year 1148.)

[Col. 1163A]

To his reverend father and lord JOHN, cardinal-priest of the holy Roman Church, Brother WIBALD, by the grace of God, what he is: himself and his possessions.

You have before you a defendant who confesses. Grant pardon, I ask—not pardon for error, not for negligence, which are foreign to wisdom, though we do not possess it, yet love it—but grant pardon for ignorance, which, in this mortal life, cannot be far even from the most purified souls. This indeed is the readier path to the mercy of absolution.

But why do we labor, when we have a favorable judge? We do not indeed fear him because, by the office of his see, he has the guardianship of the Catholic Church and authority to decide canonical litigation; rather, we love him because he is the nephew of the late supreme pontiff, Pope Lucius, who uniquely loved us before attaining the highest degree of advancement, and, once established at the summit of the apostolate, honored our Church and us magnificently. While living, he earned from us—if we are human—that we should love not only his flesh and blood and whoever he loved, but should embrace, perhaps, even some relics or memorials of his with most ardent affection. [Col. 1163B]

You are therefore ours by a certain proper and special right of possession. Receive under your protection, by hereditary right, your dependent, a servant of your household; advance his person and defend the causes which arise, God’s grace protecting us, not from crimes but from the advancement of our Church. Let the nephew protect him whom the uncle loved; let the man ordained by that uncle defend him whom he advanced; let the cardinal-priest preserve the judgment of the supreme pontiff, so that he does not permit him whom that pontiff judged worthy of honor to be worn down by any exactions. [Col. 1163C]

O how great is the confidence of true affection at the very beginning of a familiarity—or rather acquaintance—to be formed! We speak with you so securely and freely as we were accustomed to converse with that uncle of yours—I mean that uncle—with whose intimate friendship we enjoyed, or, to speak less customarily but more truly, benefited, for twenty years and more without offence.

But in conclusion we say to you: We do not love you because you are so great, but because you come from one so great.

## LETTER LI. CARDINAL JOHN TO ABBOT WIBALD

He promises that he will take the greatest care of Wibald’s causes. (Year 1148.)

To the most reverend father in Christ, WIBALD, by God’s grace venerable abbot of Corbie and Stavelot, JOHN, by the same grace cardinal-deacon of Saint Mary the New: greeting with sincere affection.

From your letter we learned that you earnestly request pardon because you did not come more diligently and promptly into closer contact with the knowledge of our humility—a person [lacuna] [Col. 1164A] whom my lord Pope Lucius loved with such affection and cherished for so long, and to whom, as we ourselves saw and as you write, he failed in nothing until the end of his life.

To this is added that Lord Guido of Florence, upon his departure from us, out of the singular and special affection which he bears toward both us and you with inward love, especially commended you and your causes to us. Hence it was that, though neither asked nor urged by you, we have until now protected, defended, and sustained your causes as our own; and where no prayers were offered, we offered them ourselves.

Finally, even if there were no other reason, there is nevertheless, God granting it, such prudence in you that you ought to be held closely and embraced tightly because you have always stood wisely and effectively by the Roman Church. [Col. 1164B] Therefore, granting the pardon which you request, we embrace with both arms your favor and the special affection which you offer; and we promise you our presence in every way for your own, even though we can do more, and as you especially claim it.

## LETTER LII. POPE EUGENIUS III TO THE MONKS OF CORBIE

He urges them to render humble reverence to Abbot Wibald. (Year 1148.)

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons the monks of Corbie: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We remember that by other letters we commanded you [Col. 1164C] to obey our beloved son Wibald with the humility due to an abbot. When he recently came to us, we received him with paternal kindness and earnestly instructed him concerning the restoration and preservation of religious life in your monastery.

We therefore send him back to you with the favor of the Apostolic See and the support of our letters, and command, admonish, and exhort all of you in the Lord to love and honor him as good and humble sons; to render him the reverence due to your shepherd; and to stand by him manfully and faithfully in recovering and retaining the possessions and goods of the monastery of Corbie. For we love this same abbot with paternal affection, [Col. 1164D] and are willing to grant what we can to him according to God.

## LETTER LIII. POPE EUGENIUS III TO HENRY, BISHOP OF LIÈGE

That he restrain those who despoil the goods of the monastery of Stavelot. (Year 1148.)

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother HENRY, bishop of Liège: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Those who seize ecclesiastical goods, etc. See under Eugenius III, at the year 1153.

## LETTER LIV. HENRY, KING OF THE ROMANS, TO POPE EUGENIUS III

He requests the pope’s patronage. (Year 1148.)

[Col. 1165A]

To his reverend father and lord in Christ, EUGENIUS, supreme and universal pontiff, HENRY, by God’s grace king of the Romans: the sincerity of due affection and obedience.

Blessed be God, who has deigned to raise the discernment of your sincerity to the office and administration of the supreme pontificate, etc. See among the letters of various persons to Eugenius III.

## LETTER LV. POPE EUGENIUS III TO HENRY THE YOUNGER, KING OF THE ROMANS

He praises his zeal for the Church and wishes him every prosperity. (Year 1148.)

[Col. 1165B]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son in Christ HENRY, younger king of the Romans, son of the illustrious King Conrad: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Considering your father’s devotion toward blessed Peter and the holy Roman Church, etc. See under Eugenius III.

## LETTER LVI. HENRY, KING OF THE ROMANS, TO POPE EUGENIUS III

That he receive kindly Henry, archbishop of Mainz, and others going to the pope; absolve the duchess of Poland from excommunication; and hold Abbot Wibald commended to him. (Year 1148.)

[Col. 1165C]

To his most beloved father in Christ, EUGENIUS, supreme and universal pontiff, HENRY, by God’s grace king of the Romans: filial affection in all things and due reverence in the Lord.

We render many thanks to your sincerity with all the strength of our soul because you received our envoys and letters with paternal affection, etc. See under Eugenius III, after his Register.

## LETTER LVII. B., BISHOP OF HILDESHEIM, TO POPE EUGENIUS III

He praises the merits of Abbot Wibald and asks the pontiff to ratify the union of Kaminata with the monastery of Corbie. (Year 1148.)

[Col. 1165D]

To his reverend father and lord, EUGENIUS, supreme pontiff of the holy Roman Church, B., by God’s grace humble minister of the Church of Hildesheim: devotion and obedience to a father, as due as they are devoted.

[Note: [Col. 1165D] Bernard, count of Rottenburg on the Tubara, who erected at Hildesheim the magnificent church and monastery of St Gotthard of the Order of St Benedict, [Col. 1166D] and obtained that he should be entered among the saints, renowned for miracles.]

We commend to your serenity our beloved brother Wibald, abbot of the Church of Corbie, a man of good reputation among us and well known in the Catholic Church. We rejoice greatly that he has come to our region, since we place the greatest confidence in his prudence and industry.

We therefore beseech [Col. 1166A] your fatherhood mercifully to hear him in his petitions, especially concerning the Church of Kaminata. In that church, where there had been much neglect of the observance of religious life, he, as a religious and prudent man, reformed its worship. Likewise, as a vigorous man, he nearly wholly recovered and restored to the monastery’s benefit the revenues and possessions which the abbess of that monastery—whose reputation among us was not good—had, after her deposition, squandered with vain and superfluous persons and granted to knights as benefices.

Therefore stand by this man, who has zeal for God, as a pious and merciful father; and strengthen by your authority the labors which he has undertaken in the Church of God. Know without doubt that the change made in the aforesaid [Col. 1166B] monastery pleases all the religious people of our land, but displeases those who had been there on account of irreligion.

## LETTER LVIII. HENRY, DUKE OF SAXONY, TO POPE EUGENIUS III

On the same matter. (Year 1148.)

To EUGENIUS, supreme pontiff of the most holy Roman Church, HENRY, duke of Saxony: the devotion of ready and dutiful service.

We commend to your fatherhood my beloved lord Wibald, venerable abbot of the Church of Corbie, etc. See under Pope Eugenius III, among the letters of various persons to him.

## LETTER LIX. COUNT HERIMANN OF WINCENBURG TO POPE EUGENIUS III

On the same matter. (Year 1148.)

[Col. 1166C]

To his most holy father and lord EUGENIUS, supreme pontiff of the holy Roman Church, HERIMANN, count of Wincenburch and advocate of the Church of Corbie: the inward devotion of his service.

Venerable Father, we commend to your fellowship my most beloved lord Wibald, venerable abbot of Corbie, a man certainly religious and distinguished among us by every integrity and prudence. We commend to you the labors which he has faithfully [Col. 1166D] and tirelessly borne in the Church of Corbie from the day of his promotion: both in reforming religious life in that monastery and recovering its possessions, and in the pious and praiseworthy effort by which he has worked diligently in two monasteries, namely Kaminata and Visbike, received from my lord the king, to restore religious life within them.

For we had great need in our land of this laborer, especially in these two monasteries where religious life had greatly declined, and which this man is laboring prudently and honorably to reform. We therefore ask your excellency, in accordance with the request of my lord the king, to confirm this grant of his by your [Col. 1167A] authority; to aid my lord the abbot in restoring divine service; and to furnish us an example in helping churches.

## LETTER LX. H., ABBOT OF BLESSED MARY AT FLECHTORP, TO POPE EUGENIUS III

On the same matter. (Year 1148.)

To his most holy father and lord EUGENIUS, supreme pontiff, H., by God’s grace humble minister of the church of Blessed Mary at Flechtorp: devoted prayers and due obedience.

[Note: [Col. 1167D] The monastery of Flechtorp was founded in the year of Christ 1101 by the nobleman Erpo, count of Padberg, in the diocese of Paderborn, in honor of the Virgin St Mary, and was distinguished by the relics of St Landelin. That monastery endured until the time of heresy, when its last abbot, Balthasar, having taken a wife and laid aside his habit, embraced heresy. See more in the Annals of Paderborn, book VII, under the year 1101, and concerning the relics of St Landelin.]

We have learned, venerable Father, that our most beloved father and lord Wibald, abbot of the Church of Corbie, has come to your excellency. [Col. 1167B] We love him greatly, and at his arrival we conceived much hope for our land; we ask that he be commended to your fatherhood.

For he has labored in our region like a warrior arousing zeal for the restoration of divine religion, both in his own monastery and in the monasteries which he received by the gift of the lord king—namely Kaminata and Visbike. There, not divine services, but rather the shameful sports of a brothel were practiced, to such an extent that the abbess of Kaminata, a woman young both in conduct and in age, after her deposition granted to her lovers more than one hundred mansi from the revenues of that church as benefices. Before her deposition, by her most depraved conduct and her irreligious advancement—by which she had been promoted to various abbeys and removed because of her offences—she had provoked against herself all the religious men of our land. [Col. 1167C]

We therefore beseech your fatherhood kindly to hear the aforesaid abbot, who has begun to remove such shameful practices, when he comes to you; to confirm by your authority both the royal generosity and the labors which he expends in restoring divine religion; and by your goodwill to increase his zeal for the worship of the Church.

## LETTER LXI. W., ABBOT OF ST BLAISE, TO POPE EUGENIUS III

On the same matter. (Year 1148.)

To his most reverend father and lord EUGENIUS, supreme [Col. 1167D] and universal pontiff, W., by God’s grace, what he is, humble minister of the church [Note: [Col. 1168D] The abbey of St Blaise, formerly situated on Mount Wederonis, was transferred to Minden in the year 1104 by Bishop Riaward because of the unhealthiness of the air.] of Blessed Blaise: whatever strength is possessed by due obedience and the most devoted constancy of prayer.

We greatly rejoice that you are accustomed to receive kindly our beloved father Wibald, abbot of the Church of Corbie, when he comes to your fatherhood, and to hear his petitions mercifully. We earnestly ask your excellency to continue doing the same. For this man has shone forth in our land like the radiance of a heavenly star. You will give him thanks for the watchful zeal with which he labors in the Church of God, and by your exhortation will give him confidence to persevere diligently and faithfully in the same labor. [Col. 1168A]

For after receiving from the hand of the lord king the two monasteries of women, namely Kaminata and Visbixe, he has striven greatly, as a faithful and prudent servant, to restore and reform the service of religious life which had utterly perished there. This year he also labored greatly in recovering the possessions which the abbess of Kaminata, a woman altogether blameworthy, had dispersed among her lovers; and, with God’s help, he recovered almost wholly everything that she had alienated and restored it to the use of those serving [Col. 1168B] God.

We commend to your holiness the labors and exertions of this man, of whom the Church in our regions had great need, as do also our other fellow brothers and all the religious of our land. We humbly entreat you to deign to strengthen them by your authority for the advancement of the Church of God.

## LETTER LXII. C., ABBOT OF BLESSED MARY AT GREVENKERKEN, TO POPE EUGENIUS III

On the same matter. (Year 1148.)

To EUGENIUS, supreme pontiff of the universal Church, C., humble minister of the church of Saint Mary at Grevenkarken, [Col. 1168C] due obedience to a father.

We rejoice in the Lord because we have learned that our most beloved father and lord Wibald, the venerable abbot of the Church of Corvey, has found favour in your sight—a man by whose arrival our land has been greatly enlightened, and through whose diligence we see the Church of God in our regions has already made considerable progress and will henceforth make still greater progress. For he is a man as devout in his own manner of life as he is zealous that divine religion should be enlarged in others. This has appeared clearly both elsewhere and especially in the two nunneries, namely Kemnade and Fischbeck, which the lord king gave to the Church of Corvey. In these, almost no trace of divine religion had remained; [Col. 1168D] but now, by God’s grace, God is worshipped there where, a little before, shameful impurities were worshipped.

We know that the aforesaid man acted thus, impelled by zeal for justice, love of God, and the cry of the Church. We bear before your fatherhood witness to his honourable conduct, approved life, and praiseworthy diligence concerning the churches named above; and we beseech you to deign to grant the petition which he makes and which we believe to be according to God.

## LETTER LXIII. FROM ST MARY’S AT HAMELUNGESBURNEN TO POPE EUGENIUS III.

On the same subject. (Year 1148.)

[Col. 1169A]

To the reverend father and lord, EUGENIUS, supreme pontiff of the holy Roman Church: the abbot, by God’s grace, of the church of the Mother of God at Hamelungesburnen, [Note: [Col. 1169D] Perhaps the same as the monastery of Amelungsborn on the Weser, founded in 1133, concerning which see Bruschius, *Centuria* 1.] due and devoted obedience to a beloved father.

We commend to your fatherhood our beloved lord and father Wibald, abbot of the Church of Corvey: a man of good repute among us and a lover of the Roman Church. We rejoice unreservedly that he has come into our regions, since we place the greatest confidence in his wisdom and industry. [Col. 1169B] We therefore beseech your fatherhood graciously to hear him in his petitions, and especially concerning the Church of Kemnade. There, as a wise and devout man, he restored the observance of divine religion, which had been greatly neglected in that church; and, as an energetic and diligent man, he has recovered almost in their entirety the revenues and possessions which the abbess of that monastery—a woman of ill repute among us—had dissipated after her deposition with vain and superfluous persons, and had granted in benefice to her knights and lovers. He has restored them to the uses of the monastery.

Therefore support this man, who has zeal for God, as a merciful and compassionate father; and strengthen by your authority the labours which he has undertaken in the Church of God. Know this clearly: [Col. 1169C] the change made in the aforesaid monastery pleases all the religious persons of our land and those who fear God; but it displeases those who had been there because of irreligion.

## LETTER LXIV. POPE EUGENIUS III TO HENRY, THE YOUNGER KING.

He promises to provide for the king’s aunt. (Year 1148.)

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son in Christ HENRY, younger king of the Romans, illustrious son of the emperor Conrad: greeting and apostolic blessing.

We have received your letters and messengers with due kindness and have carefully considered their petitions. Indeed, we love your person with true charity in the Lord, etc. See Eugenius, under the year 1153.

## LETTER LXV. POPE EUGENIUS III TO THE GERMAN PRELATES.

That they should support the younger king Henry and assist him with their counsel and efforts. (Year 1148.)

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brothers the archbishops and bishops, and his beloved sons the abbots established throughout the German kingdom: greeting and apostolic blessing.

As your prudence plainly recognizes, our dearest son Conrad, king of the Romans, stirred by the ardours of divine love and having taken up the sign of the life-giving Cross, etc. [Col. 1170A] See above.

## LETTER LXVI. POPE EUGENIUS III TO A., ARCHBISHOP OF BREMEN, H., BISHOP OF MINDEN, AND T., BISHOP OF VERDEN.

That they should ensure the restoration of estates of Kemnade monastery usurped by various persons. (Year 1148.)

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brothers A., [Note: [Col. 1170D] Adalbero.] archbishop of Bremen; He., [Note: [Col. 1170D] Henry.] bishop of Minden; and T., [Note: [Col. 1170D] Thietmar.] bishop of Verden: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The possessions of churches are known to be the patrimonies of the poor and the price of sinners; and therefore, if [Col. 1170B] anyone presumes to retain them against justice, etc. See above.

## LETTER LXVII. POPE EUGENIUS III TO THE MONKS OF CORVEY.

He confirms the deposition of Abbot Henry. (Year 1148.)

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons the monks, free men, and ministerials of Corvey: greeting and apostolic blessing.

How necessary it is to provide for the peace of monasteries, etc. See Eugenius III under the year 1153.

## LETTER LXVIII. POPE EUGENIUS III TO THE PEOPLE OF FULDA.

He declares invalid their election, made contrary to his command, and orders them to elect an abbot from another monastery in the presence of certain abbots whom he names. (Year 1148.)

[Col. 1170C]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons, the monks, free men, and ministerials of Fulda monastery: greeting and apostolic blessing.

If the attention of the head’s discernment has not been directed to governing its members reasonably, etc. See above.

## LETTER LXIX. POPE EUGENIUS III TO THE ABBOTS OF EBRACH, EBERBACH, HERSFELD, AND CORVEY.

That, upon going to Fulda, they should arrange for an abbot to be elected from another monastery. (Year 1148.)

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved [Col. 1170D] sons, the abbots of Ebrach, Eberbach, Hersfeld, and Corvey: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Placed by God’s ordinance upon the watchtower of the Apostolic See, etc. See Eugenius.

## LETTER LXX. FROM A., PROVOST OF CORVEY, TO ABBOT WIBALD.

The chamberlain of Fulda desires his presence at the election of an abbot, as do the people of Corvey for the restoration of their affairs. (Year 1148.)

To his most beloved father and lord WIBALD, venerable [Col. 1171A] abbot of the Church of Corvey: from the provost, whatever a son owes his father and a servant his lord.

A few days ago we had with us the chamberlain of Fulda, namely Hermann, and another of the brothers. They had come to invite you to Fulda at the time of the election, and they returned very sorrowful because they had not found you. Through them we sent the people of Fulda letters in your name, a copy of which we have now also transmitted to you. We likewise sent you the lord pope’s letters, which they had brought to us from Fulda sealed with his seal. We are also certain that this same Hermann will come to you shortly; at his request, we have written you a letter of recommendation for him.

Their elect, if you have not yet heard, has disappeared from their midst. Furthermore, [Col. 1171B] all your friends await your return to us with great longing, both for other necessary reasons and especially because all your people are alarmed lest Count Hermann seize and fortify Mount Brunesberch. This has been reported to us as certain and beyond doubt; therefore we did not wish to conceal it from you, just as we would conceal no matter which, if kept silent, might harm your honour.

## LETTER LXXI. FROM ABBOT WIBALD TO THE PEOPLE OF FULDA.

He excuses himself because he cannot come to them; he seeks to console them and urges them to proceed quickly to an election. (Year 1148.)

[Col. 1171C]

To the dean, provost, and other brethren beloved in Christ, free men, and ministerials of the Church of Fulda: WIBALD, by God’s grace servant of the Church of Corvey, blessing and life for ever.

How much grief, how much fear, how much anxiety we bear because of the long exhaustion and repeated loss suffered by your church—so distinguished, so renowned, and once so honourable—we would rather, if the moment allowed, lament in your presence than declare from afar by writing. But because from of old we have always greatly loved the honour of you all, in the tribulation which we perceive now weighs upon you, we devotedly offer to your affection by this letter such consolation as is possible, together with the admonition which [Col. 1171D] we cannot give in person.

The sum of our admonition is this: if, as we have understood, while you are still gathered before the lord pope, you cannot retain your elect, return as quickly as possible to concord and unanimity. As you love your honour and the peace of your Church, return united, knowing that he did not lie who said: “Every kingdom divided against itself shall be laid waste.” And if you have among yourselves someone whom you can elect, do not delay; but if he must come from elsewhere, hasten that too. For under delay certain [Col. 1172A] troubles may arise. We shall not fail you in our counsel.

## LETTER LXXII. FROM COUNT HENRY OF NAMUR TO POPE EUGENIUS III.

He declares himself ready to observe what had been arranged at Trier in the papal court concerning the suit between himself and the archdeacon of Verdun. (Year 1148.)

To his reverend father and lord EUGENIUS, supreme pontiff of the holy Roman Church: HENRY, count of Namur and Luxembourg, a son’s devotion together with faithful service.

As it was arranged between me and Richard, archdeacon of Verdun, in your court at Trier, through the mediation of the abbot of Clairvaux [Note: [Col. 1171D] St Bernard, who was then at Trier with Eugenius.], and confirmed in the presence of your [Col. 1172B] company, so on the appointed day I afterwards wished in every way to observe and fulfil it, under the testimony of the bishop of Verdun [Note: [Col. 1172D] Namely Albero, bishop, and Abbot Wibald.] and the abbot of Corvey, etc. See Pope Eugenius III, after his *Regesta*.

## LETTER LXXIII. FROM ABBOT WIBALD TO HENRY, KING OF THE ROMANS.

Concerning the elect of Fulda, obedience to the pope’s decrees, etc. (Year 1148.)

To his glorious and most serene lord HENRY, king of the Romans, crowned by God, son of Conrad, august victor and illustrious emperor of the Romans: WIBALD, by God’s grace abbot of Corvey, greeting in Him who grants salvation to kings.

[Col. 1172C]

With what zealous devotion we were present at the council of Rheims for the stability of the kingdom bestowed upon you by God and for the increase of your honour, we believe has been sufficiently made known to your excellency by those who were present. Certainly, your sublimity must in no way doubt our loyalty and zeal for the advancement of your person and kingdom.

The reason for this letter to your highness, after the many matters which we recently discussed with Master Henry, notary of your court, concerning your health and safety and the provision, ordering, and governance of your kingdom, is that the elect of Fulda refuses to be blessed under the title of abbot and is moreover declared unfit by many persons. If, therefore, he is removed—as indeed we did not doubt when we left Rheims—then your good judgment will have a great burden: namely, to prevent any disturbance of innovation from arising in Fulda monastery. Rather, just as lately, through God’s inspiration, you wisely and energetically completed all things there in honour of our holy mother the Roman Church and of your own dignity, so now also, in your presence, cause all things to be carried out magnificently, with great peace and discipline, for the increase of your honour.

For, dearest lord—our lord in rank and office, but our son in affection—we most earnestly lay before and urge upon your understanding that you love with all your heart your father Pope Eugenius, [Col. 1173A] who has most graciously honoured you; and that, at anyone’s prompting, you do not oppose his decrees or the enactments of your most holy mother, the Roman Church. If intercession must be made for princes or your other faithful men, make it with such moderation of discernment that the concern of your clemency for your own may earn praise, while importunity incurs no offence.

For we fear that, through another’s persuasion, you may strike against the Roman Church; and this might be for you a stone of offence and a rock of stumbling. We have thought it necessary also to add this admonition: do not go either into Swabia, Saxony, or Lotharingia unless summoned by the princes for some important and publicly known matter capable of being settled in a short time. For your father, lord and parent of the kingdom, is still expected; [Col. 1173B] and you might easily fall into blame, particularly from those accustomed to render the services owed to the kingdom unwillingly and as though compelled.

And a good name is better than great riches.

[Note: [Col. 1173D] The *Auctarium Affligemiense* in Miraeus places his departure in the year 1149, where it says: “Emperor Conrad and Louis, king of France, break up the expedition without any result and return from the journey to Jerusalem—such misfortune for so great an army had never been heard of.” [Col. 1174D]]

## LETTER LXXIV. FROM THE PRIOR OF CORVEY TO ABBOT S.

Through the mediation of Abbot Wibald, he forgives him whatever he had committed against the men of Corvey. (Year 1148.)

To the reverend abbot S., beloved brother in Christ: Brother E., prior, and the other brethren of Corvey, fraternal love.

We have received with due reverence the petition which, through our most beloved father and lord Abbot Wibald, you offered to our lowliness; and whatever offence you have committed against us knowingly or unknowingly, we have forgiven without pretence. We desire and grant that you be loved and honoured as one more closely incorporated into our fellowship, and that you share in our humble prayers.

For at the arrival among us of our aforesaid father, every seed of enmity was utterly extinguished. Among those whom the storm of dissension had scattered, he placed himself in the middle, like a good cornerstone, with the bond of true charity and discreet humility; and he gathered into one body of intimate affection the children of God who had been so far removed and estranged in the distant land of discord. In return, as he labours with tireless zeal for the welfare and reform of our [Col. 1173D] monastery, assist his work, for the sake of our love and request, with singular steadfastness and love of duty, as becomes your prudence.

## LETTER LXXV. FROM ABBOT WIBALD TO MASTER BALDRIC.

That he should exercise his talent. (Year 1148.)

Brother WIBALD, by God’s grace what he is in the catholic Church, to his beloved brother and friend Master Baldric: blessing and life for ever.

[Col. 1174A]

At last released from the great occupations which, as you yourself know, long held us entangled hither and thither, we have begun at times to be able to greet our friends and, all anxiety driven away, to show some gentler affection. Therefore, greeting your industry with paternal and intimate affection, we ask and exhort you in the Lord: do not permit that noble and most acute talent of yours, implanted in you by nature through God’s gift and excellently cultivated by the finest arts in your youth, to grow sluggish through idleness. Otherwise the honour bestowed on you as a kind of reward for labour, because of the brilliance of your learning, may be able to bring a certain tarnish of obscurity upon your excellent studies.

Certainly, by humility, as by a kind of brilliance of gems, you will adorn both keenness of intellect and glory of eloquence, as well as the dignities you have attained. Remember that honours must be preserved by the same arts through which you attained them. For, to speak in worldly terms, rising may have been fortunate; but to govern yourself in high position is indeed a matter of skill.

Let your very presence be discipline for your hearers; for if you are continually present, there will rarely be need for correction. Your position entails more than the office of teaching; for you must also display the severity appropriate to a censor, since you know that you have been appointed to correct conduct. This discipline and exercise is subtler than all others and more fruitful than any. Let a few words suffice for one who knows—not that we should teach a teacher, but lest we neglect our duty.

## LETTER LXXVI. FROM THE MONKS OF CORVEY TO ABBOT WIBALD.

That he should not cease to labour while absent for his Church, and that he should confirm by his privilege the union of two monasteries. (Year 1148.)

[Col. 1174C]

To their beloved father and lord WIBALD, by God’s grace venerable abbot of Corvey: E., prior, and the whole congregation of his sons, serving God in the same monastery under his rule, whatever diligent prayer can accomplish, and the love due from those who love so beloved a father.

We endure your prolonged absence with great pain, except that we know that in this absence you are labouring for the advancement of our Church. We exhort and admonish you, so far as we presume to do so, to bear that labour manfully; [Col. 1174D] and we continually beseech God’s mercy that it may end well.

Furthermore, we give thanks to your fatherhood because, between two walls, you sat in the middle as a prudent imitator of that true Cornerstone, in order to join them in one fellowship; and you have brought to completion the communion of our most beloved brethren, long desired by us, and the union desirable in Christ. [Note: [Col. 1174D] This concerns the association between Stavelot and Corvey.]

Therefore put the finishing touch to the completed work: namely, confirm by your privilege, for the perpetual remembrance of our successors, whatever has been written or done on either side by your permission in this memorable union of the two Churches; and order that this testimony be carefully preserved in each church as a matter worthy of remembrance. We likewise ask that, since we requested this union to be made for the praise of God and the remedy of our souls, you establish that fitting honours be bestowed reciprocally upon the holy patrons of the two Churches. Thus, as in each Church we pray for one another that we may be saved, we may be aided in attaining the salvation we seek through the united patronage of both sides.

May it therefore please you to establish some sign and memorial from the possessions of each Church on the feast of each patron [Note: [Col. 1175D] This he did at Corvey in 1151, assigning Mount St Michael and the church with all its appurtenances for the solemn annual observance of the commemoration of St Remaclus. See the document in the Appendix.], and by this work of piety make both your own memory and that of the patrons perpetual among your dependants. [Col. 1175B]

## LETTER LXXVII. FROM THE MONKS OF CORVEY TO ABBOT WIBALD.

They set forth how much they suffer from his absence and urge him to return quickly. (Year 1148.)

To their dearest father and lord, the venerable abbot of Corvey WIBALD: E., prior; A., provost; and the other brethren and ministerials of the Church of Corvey, whatever sons owe their beloved father and faithful servants their lord.

How painfully, heavily, and intolerably we endure your prolonged absence, we can neither fully express nor venture to tell you, lest perhaps our excessiveness and importunity disturb your equanimity. Yet know that our Church, which you undertook to protect and govern in the time of its tribulation, which through God’s mercy you raised from many hardships, and which by your many labours you have striven unceasingly to advance with honourable increase from the day of your promotion, now suffers greatly in your absence.

For Lord Folcuin, in whom you had placed much of your hope for defending and protecting your affairs among us, has violently despoiled, beyond all others, your men of Höxter of their goods to the amount of not less than one hundred and fifty marks. His men attacked your reeve of Immenkusen and would have killed him [Col. 1175D] had he not barely escaped from their hands, over a certain benefice which he had granted them from the brethren’s grain-rent; for he is accustomed to grant benefices to his men from the brothers’ provision. Moreover, many others both dissipate the brothers’ provision and harass your men. You will hear more than enough about them as soon as, God willing, you return to us.

For these and many similar reasons, which we both endure and fear that we shall endure, we brothers, ministerials, and the entire body of men and faithful dependants of your Church have sent you earnest letters of petition. With all the devotion within our power we beseech you [Col. 1176A] to hasten your return to us as quickly as possible and, while you are still able, to make haste to relieve both our present pressures and those which we fear are to come. Count Hermann also desires your return in every way; and men assert that it will greatly harm both you and your Church if you do not return soon.

## LETTER LXXVIII. FROM ABBOT WIBALD TO HIS MEN OF CORVEY.

His presence had been especially necessary to the people of Stavelot; his affairs having been settled, he will hasten to Corvey as soon as possible. (Year 1148.)

Brother WIBALD, by God’s grace servant of the Church of Corvey, to his beloved sons and brethren in Christ—E., [Col. 1176B] venerable prior; A., provost; the other brethren; and also the ministerials of the monastery of Corvey—abundance of the spirit of counsel and strength.

That the Church of Corvey, which by God’s guidance we have undertaken to govern, should be wearied in our absence by any anxieties or hardships grieves us as much as, before God’s eyes and in the fear of God, we love that Church entrusted to our lowliness. You, indeed, having tasted the bitterness of a few events, are anxiously afraid of the future.

But the Church of Stavelot, which nourished us with the milk of compassion and, not remembering the sins and ignorances of our youth, raised us—if there is thought to be any dignity in prelacy—to the highest rank of its governance, has meanwhile, while we minister to you, been torn apart in manifold and pitiable ways: by plunder, fires, daily robbery, and slaughter. Since we departed from the lord pope, we have, by God’s favour, laboured not unprofitably to heal these disasters, at the prayers of our brethren who look to us for help. With the shield of divine grace surrounding us, we have seen the enemies of the Church—made drunk by their prosperity and enriched from the goods of our poor—humbled under the yoke of ecclesiastical discipline and seeking reconciliation with the Church which they had offended.

But because the case is difficult, and in this disturbance many persons have been grievously harmed both in themselves and in their property, the work of full reconciliation could not readily proceed. Yet we hope, with such confidence in God’s grace, that its end is near, that, when matters are settled and pacified, we may return to you free and released, without a longer delay. For to come to you now would not be to provide for you, but shamefully to abandon the Church of Stavelot with the stigma of a fugitive.

Nor do we delay in order to provide ourselves rest and recovery after the many labours and anxieties in which we have now long been engaged; for since the beginning of our promotion we have never endured such continual exhaustion of mind and body. Let your prudence take care that the rumour being spread concerning your Mount Brunesberch [Col. 1177A] is not fed and enlarged by those who desire to involve us, not without great labour and expense, in building upon that same mountain.

Concerning the loss suffered by our citizens and ministerials of Höxter, [Note: [Col. 1177D] Louis the Pious gave the royal estate of Höxter—now Höxter—to the people of Corvey in the tenth year of his reign. The charter of donation is published in Book II of the *Annals of Paderborn*.] we have, with great grief, quickly sent a complaint to the lord pope. We ask him, according to the form of the decree recently issued by him at the council of Rheims, diligently to admonish our lord, the bishop of Paderborn, to induce—or, under penalty of excommunication, compel—Folcuin, violator of the peace established in the lord’s sacred possession, to restore everything and make satisfaction.

## LETTER LXXIX. FROM ABBOT WIBALD TO HIS SISTER HADWID.

He excuses himself for not having visited her for a long time and recounts what he has done for the kingdom, his own people, and his friends. (Year 1148.)

[Col. 1177B]

Brother WIBALD, by God’s grace what he is in the catholic Church, to his beloved sister HADWID, [Note: [Col. 1178D] In the nunnery of Gerigesheim, perhaps Gerishem, to which she was appointed as head in 1150. See below, Letter 220.] blessing and life for ever.

Perhaps your affection rebukes and accuses us because, as though forgetful of our former affection, sincere love, and fraternal love by which we have loved to be bound to one another, we have delayed to visit and console you at this time, when your brother by blood—the chancellor of the royal court, the flower and ornament of his lineage, the pillar and protection of his friends—is absent. He is indeed travelling, bearing his cross and following his Christ, as he seeks Jerusalem in the company and service of our and his most beloved lord, Conrad, king of the Romans.

Your thought will therefore say: “That most beloved man, received and enrolled among the number of our brothers by blood, while our exalted and gracious brother was present, cultivated our household and visited us with constant conversation; now he sends us no message. Therefore, either he was not a true friend then, or he is now negligent or forgetful. But true love admits neither negligence nor forgetfulness; it follows that he was feigned and no friend.”

Yet, dearest sister, if you consider carefully the circumstances of this time and the affairs in which we are engaged, this accusation of yours, so subtle and plausible, readily comes to rest. For since Lord Pope Eugenius came into the regions of Lotharingia, great care and concern have pressed upon us: that we might suitably advance the affairs of the monasteries of Stavelot and Corvey, entrusted to us by God’s foreordaining mercy and constantly in need of apostolic protection; that we might serve with due loyalty the lords of these affairs—our kings, both father and son; and also that we might assist our friends and dependants with zeal and effort in their needs. In this undertaking of difficult matters, [Col. 1178A] divine compassion’s grace has deigned to accompany us, so that we have returned empty-handed from none of the business we undertook.

Indeed, our Churches have been increased by no small advances and strengthened by apostolic privileges. Further, divine majesty has granted us success in affairs of the kingdom. For certain persons of no slight influence were urging our younger lord king to conduct himself so as to offend the lord pope in some matters and to oppose the canonical decrees. By God’s most generous goodness and our diligence, this was prevented, and all things were changed for the better.

For the king, the son, honoured the lord pope and his decrees with watchful diligence; and conversely, the lord pope both addressed him as “king of the Romans” and wrote to him—something which rarely happens outside Rome—and wrote to all the princes, exhorting them with all goodwill and paternal affection to show loyalty to this special son of his and of blessed Peter, and to offer him counsel and assistance in administering the kingdom bestowed upon him by God through succession from his father.

As for the degree to which we have advanced the causes of our friends, we prefer that it be learned from them rather than from us. Moreover, before our arrival there was great disturbance in the Church of Stavelot; and for calming and settling it, no day or night was free from labour for us. Through the working of divine compassion’s grace, we have better hope that within a short time we shall bring all things to a saving and desired end.

These and many other occupations, then, have held our attention entangled in grave cares [Col. 1178C] and have until now delayed us from the duty of greeting you. Therefore, now greeting your excellency in the Lord, we ask and exhort you that, if any difficulty arises in protecting and caring for the affairs of our absent brother, you make use of our assistance whenever appropriate, and trust in us as in a true and steadfast friend.

## LETTER LXXX. FROM EMPEROR CONRAD TO ABBOT WIBALD.

He relates what happened to him on the holy expedition. (Year 1148.)

CONRAD, by God’s grace king of the Romans, to the venerable WIBALD, abbot of Corvey and Stavelot: his favour and every good thing.

Because we have often learned by many proofs that your loyalty has been tested toward us and our kingdom, we do not doubt that, when you hear of the prosperity of our condition, you will rejoice greatly. We therefore inform your loyalty that, when we had reached Nicaea with our army intact and in good order, wishing to finish the expedition swiftly, we began to proceed by a shorter route towards Leonium, guides acquainted with the roads showing us the way. We carried thither necessities as far as we were able. [Col. 1179A]

And behold: when ten days’ journey had already been completed and an equal distance still remained, provisions had failed almost everyone, especially the mounted troops; meanwhile the Turks did not cease to attack and kill the foot-soldiers, who could not keep up with the army. Grieving for the plight of the exhausted people, who were perishing both by death itself and by the arrows of the enemy, at the request of all the princes and barons we led the army back from that desolate country to the sea so that it might recover. We preferred to preserve it intact for greater things rather than win so bloody a victory over archers.

When we came to the sea and had pitched camp, the king of the French, in a violent storm and without waiting for clear weather, came upon our tents without our knowledge, to our great joy. He was grieved indeed that our army had been worn down by hunger and toil, but he took no small joy in our companionship. He and all his princes faithfully and devotedly offered us their service; moreover, they placed at our disposal their money and whatever they possessed.

Accordingly, joined with our forces and with the princes—some of whom had remained with us, while others, being ill and unable to follow because of lack of money, withdrew from the army—we reached St John’s, where his tomb and a spring of manna are said to be seen, without any difficulty, intending to celebrate there the Nativity of the Lord. [Col. 1179B] We arrived there, rested for several days, and wished to proceed once health was restored, since illness had seized both us and many of our people; but as the sickness worsened, we were wholly unable to go.

The king therefore departed sorrowfully with the army and waited for us as long as he could, but prolonged illness held us back. When our brother, the emperor of the Greeks, heard this, he was deeply grieved. With our most beloved daughter, the empress—namely, his wife—he hastened down to us, generously providing us and our princes with his own resources and necessities for our journey. So that we might be cured more quickly by his physicians, he brought us, almost by force, to Constantinople and his palace, showing us there as much honour as we have ever heard to have been shown to any of our predecessors.

From there, God guiding us, we have resolved to depart for Jerusalem on Reminiscere Sunday, intending to gather a new army there at Easter and to proceed to Rohas. [Col. 1179C] We ask that you pray yourself, cause your brethren to pray, commend us to all the faithful, and hold our son entrusted to your loyalty, so that God may deign to make that journey of ours prosperous.

## LETTER LXXXI. FROM THE MONKS OF CORVEY TO ABBOT WIBALD.

They congratulate him on his successful actions and desire his prompt return to them. Year 1148.

To their beloved father and lord in Christ WIBALD, venerable abbot of Corvey: the brethren of the Church of Corvey, due obedience to their father and devoted persistence in prayer.

We congratulate your fatherhood on the favourable outcome you have had in reconciling those who were in conflict among your people: for your own sake, for that of our brethren of Stavelot, and also for our own, since we await your presence with great longing. Because we love you as a father, we would always wish to have you present. But because your providential care extends to the administration of many people and for that reason cannot be directed to us alone, we beseech your fatherhood, after the many days in which we have painfully lacked your presence, not to refuse to return to us.

Know beyond doubt that we now need your presence no less than our brethren of Stavelot do. We do not begrudge them your presence; rather, we grieve deeply over your absence from us. Since, therefore, we hear that you have been somewhat released from the labours undertaken, [Col. 1180B] we ask once more that, as soon as you have received this message of yours, you make arrangements for your return to us and no longer allow your sons to be afflicted by your absence. Almost everyone in our region predicts that you will return no more.

## LETTER LXXXII. FROM A., PROVOST OF CORVEY, TO ABBOT WIBALD.

He desires his prompt return to the people of Corvey. (Year 1148.)

To his venerable lord, the Abbot of Corbie, brother A., provost of Corbie, his obedience, as devoted as it is due, to his Father.

Let it not seem harsh to you if we call you back more urgently than usual. For our fear for your honour and our apprehension of injury to [Col. 1180C] your Church arise from the love with which we love you, out of the fidelity which we owe to the Church. Many things are happening among us for which we have very great need of your presence; when present, you yourself will see them more fully than we can convey to one absent by writing—besides those things which we fear will yet occur because of your absence if you delay longer. For all who love you speak with one voice and one judgement: it is expedient that you return without delay and, lest any disturbances arise among us which would afterwards have to be suppressed with difficulty, that you take precautions.

Although we do not fail to realize that, if you return at present, you will have to purchase all the grain supply at a price, nevertheless we do not think it safe for you to remain away longer on that account. Rather, immediately upon receiving this letter, make arrangements for your return to us; for it is surely more praiseworthy, and dearer to us, that you should lose your silver than your honour. We also know that, when you come, you will obtain through your own efforts many things which neither your chamberlain nor we can obtain, because by God’s mercy we know you to be such a man as can be a comfort both to yourselves and to us.

Do not be troubled because you have no house in which to dwell among us. Near the holy martyr we have provided for you a very convenient and private lodging until your house is finished, where we ourselves shall gladly serve you with devotion—if only we may have you present. We can now extract the brothers’ grain allowance from our stewards only with difficulty, [Col. 1181A] if at all. The people of Fulda likewise await your presence with great longing, because their Church, being without a shepherd, is everywhere battered, plundered, and scattered. Therefore the abbot of Hersfeld sent us the letters of the lord pope which he had addressed to you and the other abbots; and he himself has long desired that you return, because of the business entrusted to him and to you.

## LETTER LXXXIII. FROM WALTER, CHAMBERLAIN OF CORBIE, TO ABBOT WIBALD

He gives an account of the buildings under construction and desires him to return to Corbie as soon as possible. (1148.)

[Col. 1181B]

To his reverend Father and lord WIBALD, venerable abbot of Corbie, brother WALTER, his chamberlain, his due obedience to his Father.

We have applied every effort to completing your buildings, which will certainly require no small expenditure before they are completed. We do not, however, wish you to be unaware that for many days now we have borrowed all the money expended upon this work, and that in borrowing we have already reached fifteen marks, apart from what we shall still need for the remainder of the work.

We await your presence with great longing, for many reasons which daily we see and hear among ourselves, indoors and out, and for which your presence would be very necessary to us and to the Church. All who love you and your honour greatly fear that, if you delay longer, you may find among us some new developments capable of seriously disturbing your peace; you may indeed hear something about these from your servant Louis. Were it not for this fear, we should prefer that you postpone your return until the new harvest, because if you return earlier you will find none of your grain supply from which to eat or drink even for one day, unless you buy it. Yet we think it more tolerable that you should buy grain among us for some time than that you should permit disturbances to arise here which will burden you unexpectedly. Therefore we earnestly wish you to break off every delay and, on receiving [Col. 1181D] this present message from your servants, hasten to return to us. It is from our fidelity and devotion that we urge your return so insistently.

## LETTER LXXXIV. FROM ABBOT WIBALD TO HIS BRETHREN AT CORBIE

Being now shortly to return to them, he relates how many good things he has accomplished while at Stavelot. (1148.)

WIBALD, by God’s grace abbot of Corbie, to his beloved sons and brothers in Christ, E., venerable prior, and the other sons of the Church of Corbie: blessing and life for ever.

The reason for our plan and purpose required that we should make a longer stay at Stavelot—not only in order to remove the disturbances which were harassing the Church of Stavelot [Col. 1182A] and the whole land of Lotharingia, but also because a certain order of affairs and a necessity perceived by few seemed to demand that we remain absent from you until the beginning of winter. Yet we, who are accustomed even in a matter foreseen and especially arranged by ourselves to follow the common judgement of many, no longer dare not come after having so often been summoned by you. We prefer, if need be, to err by your judgement rather than to remain fixed in the purpose of our own deliberation, however right and logical it may seem.

That your brotherhood may know that the time has not passed idly for us: between the count of Namur, the count of Loon, and the count of Dagsburg, whose discord was tearing apart the entire country, by God’s authorship we made peace until the feast of St Remigius [Col. 1182B]; and between the count of Roche, who is our advocate, and the count of Montaigu, who, incited by many persons, were waging the greatest wars against one another, we restored a final concord beneficial to the whole land. We subdued, by divine power, our adversaries who had plundered the goods of our Church, so that they restore what is ours to us with ample satisfaction. As for quieting the discord between them and our ministerials, although we have laboured long and hard, we have taken a little time in which, with the help of God’s mercy, we may bring everything to completion; and on the vigil of the Assumption of St Mary we shall arrive among you with the joy of charity.

## LETTER LXXXV. FROM THE MONKS OF CORBIE TO ABBOT WIBALD

They urgently press him to return to Corbie. (1148.)

[Col. 1182C]

To their dearest lord and Father WIBALD, venerable abbot of Corbie, E., prior, A., provost, and W., chamberlain: their due obedience.

So far as it is lawful, we reproach your prudence because, although through your messenger and our letters we have made known to your fatherhood our anxieties, you have not yet given us any certain information concerning your return. This is especially so since in every letter in which on this occasion we asked that your return be hastened, we added, as the chief point and with all diligence, that immediately on receiving the letters you should make arrangements, without [Col. 1182D] any delay whatsoever, to return to us. And now for nearly three weeks we have waited in suspense for your messenger; beneath this expectation we are tormented by great longing, and we receive from you no consolation whatever.

What, then, are we to do at last? For it was not without cause that we demanded so urgently that your return be hastened. Battles without, troubles within—to say nothing of everything else—we are almost “being put to death all day long” by the rumour, indeed the contention, of people who maintain that you will return to Corbie no more. Now that our messenger has not returned by the day hoped for, they assail us with reproaches, affirming that we are wasting our hope in vain. Finally, had we not known very well how firm and unshakable your constancy is, we ought to have been bent to despair by so many rumours and so many outcries of people. Count Hermann likewise strongly complains of your prolonged absence. Therefore, with every devotion and every effort, we beg your fatherhood that at least on this occasion you will in no way defer returning immediately after receiving our letters, knowing beyond doubt that if you delay any longer now, you will bring your friends to no small despair.

## LETTER LXXXVI. FROM ABBOT WIBALD TO HIS BRETHREN AT CORBIE

He reproves them for pressing his return on so many repeated occasions. (1148.)

Brother WIBALD, by God’s grace abbot of Corbie, to his beloved brothers in Christ E., prior, A., provost, [Col. 1183B] and W., chamberlain: health and blessing.

The sacred Law commands that salt be offered in sacrifice. And the Apostle says: “Let your speech be seasoned with salt.” Whatever is not seasoned with salt is tasteless and wholly unfit to benefit human refreshment. There is no virtue which remains sound when discretion abandons it; discretion is the salt and seasoning of things counted among good things. Virtues are placed in the middle between excess and deficiency. This is the royal road, upon which the proud hide snares for us, and upon which we must walk so as neither to turn to the right through the unconsidered ardour of over-eager zeal, nor to stray to the left through the lethargy of loose indulgence.

Why say this? Because in calling us back so frequently and insistently, [Col. 1183C] you seem to exceed the measure which accompanies discretion. Since our holy and venerable mother, the Church of Stavelot, had been worn down by many pressures, after wicked people seized the opportunity created by our following the divine calling and your unanimous election and coming over to you, it would have been impious—and crueler than any raging beast—to abandon her amid straits and impending ruin. We entered that Church through the door: we do not presume to say this of our life and character, but we do not fear plainly to affirm it of all our administration and achievements.

We saw not one wolf approaching—unless perhaps we understand the whole phalanx of demons as one wolf—but countless armies of many wolves, which with savage fury were gaping to devour the Church of Stavelot and a great part of Lotharingia. But God sent the Holy Spirit from heaven and shut the lions’ mouths; and, at the command of Jesus, who had been sleeping because of our sins, there came a calm in the winds and the sea—a calm, indeed, suspicious and full of plots and snares, such as our age is accustomed to produce, but still some measure of calm.

Your affection in recalling us is therefore praiseworthy and most welcome to us; but the time and cause of the recall deserve no title of praise. The time, indeed, because it is unsuitable. The cause, moreover, is so childish—not to say foolish—that it was not worthy of such exertions. For this is the chief reason for your hasty summons: that, to use your own words, you are almost [Col. 1184A] “being put to death all day long” by the rumour, indeed the contention, of people who maintain that we shall return to Corbie no more. And lest we think you absurd in voicing such great frivolity, your convent wrote to us—contrary to the gravity of so great a body and to its own severity, which ought to have been more restrained—using these words: “Almost everyone in our region prophesies that you will return no more.”

O prudent men! O strong men! Intent upon old women’s tales, they both agitate themselves and never cease to weary us, who are occupied with serious matters. The little women who have besieged the walls of your courtyard, and who are accustomed to devour the substance of our house, measure with their fingers; and, after an abominable and ridiculous divination, sneeze and swear, “By all Christian souls, it is true: he will not return.” The prophet says: “Woe to those who prophesy from their own hearts”; “the spirit has gone out from before the wrath of the Lord”; and “a lying spirit has come into the mouth of all the prophets.”

These are the straits, these the wars, these the fires, these the killings, these the robberies which have surrounded the Church of Corbie. But may divine protection keep all these other evils far from her. Yet tell us about your prophets, who have seen foolish and false things for you. You have not attended to the true Prophet, who says: “Blessed is the man whose hope is the name of the Lord, and who has not looked to vanities and false madness.” What they prophesy, they either prophesy truly or utter false predictions. If they prophesy truly, why do you summon us so often and so earnestly, since it is evident that a true prediction cannot fail or be shaken? [Col. 1184C] But if they speak falsely from a spirit of lying, why do you disturb yourselves and trouble yourselves over so empty and foolish a report?

We shall certainly return to you, if God permits and we live. For we have not conducted ourselves among you in such a way as to blush to see you; nor have you shown yourselves towards us such that we should fear to behold you. We shall certainly come on the time and day fixed in our letters, which we sent to you through our servant Louis—although, for certain, imminent, and dangerous reasons, the Church of Stavelot reluctantly endures our absence.

If the Church of Stavelot had not brought us up, if she had not raised us from the flocks of sheep, if she had not taken us from tending the nursing ewes to feed Jacob and Joseph, God’s inheritance; if she had not raised us needy from the dust and lifted the poor from the dung-heap, that we might sit with princes—yet brotherly charity required that, if there were a physician in the Church of Corbie, in whose house there was clothing, you should not deny your sister, the Church of Stavelot, some share in your consolation. But we let these matters pass. You, however, see to it that when we come we have a dwelling in our new lodging.

## LETTER LXXXVII. FROM ABBOT WIBALD TO HENRY, KING OF THE ROMANS

Concerning the case of Everard and Cuono. (1148.)

To his glorious lord H[enry], illustrious king of the Romans, [Col. 1185A] son of the august and victorious Conrad, emperor of the Romans, W., by God’s grace what he is in the Catholic Church, health in Him who gives health to kings.

Since leaving the synod of Reims, we have remained at the monastery of Stavelot because of the many and varied disputes and pressures existing in the land. With the Lord cooperating and strengthening our efforts, in nearly all the neighbouring places we have established such small measure of peace as we could, intending shortly to travel towards Corbie. Now we earnestly ask your Majesty to deign to hear us concerning the case about which we sent to your clemency.

Women inherit fiefs of the monastery of Stavelot where no males survive. A certain Widric, our ministerial, had an only daughter and died; Cuono, the son of his sister, occupied his possessions. Subsequently a certain Everard married the aforesaid daughter of Widric, and, according to the custom of the land, received from us the whole fief which belonged to the girl from her father. But the aforementioned Cuono expelled Everard from possession. Therefore, lawfully summoned by us and brought to court concerning this matter, when Everard charged him with having violently despoiled him of his fief, Cuono replied that the aforesaid vill was his own allod and belonged to him by proprietary right; that his uncle—the father of the girl whom Everard had married—had held the said Nova Villa not as a fief but as his own allod, and had given Cuono one half of it as an inheritance in dowry for Cuono’s mother.

Conversely, Everard maintained that the oft-mentioned Nova Villa had been granted by his wife’s grandfather to the Church of Stavelot in proprietary right for an annual rent of four denarii, and had been received as a fief from the abbot’s hand both by that grandfather and by all his successors. We acknowledged this to be true and were ready to prove it through legal instruments according to principles of unquestioned law. Both Cuono and Everard offered adequate proof for their respective allegations and requested that a judicial sentence be pronounced. When our ministerials were questioned under the proper oath, they adjudged the burden of proof to Everard, who had opposed to his litigant the title of a lawful fief, [Col. 1185D] thus, to be sure, combining equity with law and truth with judgement. Franco, the bearer of this letter, was first in declaring the sentence of judgement, all the others concurring in the same decision.

Cuono, on the other hand, replied that Franco had lied and that both he and the others had delivered a false judgement. They numbered twenty-one. On this point he appealed to the presence of your Majesty. When we heard the Emperor’s name and the appellant’s declaration, considering that no injury had been done to us, we ceased further proceedings in the action. We have full confidence in the height of royal Majesty: if both parties come to your court, each will receive, according to the standard of legal institutions, the acquittal or condemnation due to him. But if the appellant neglects to come, your authority will not leave him unpunished, nor will he gain a postponement of penalty through his futile appeal, so that all your subjects may fear you when they see God’s wisdom in you for executing judgement. Whatever your court judges in this matter, deign to make known to us by your letters, and to Lord H., bishop of Liège, H., count of Namur, and H., count of Roche, advocate of Stavelot.

## LETTER LXXXVIII. FROM HENRY, KING OF THE ROMANS, TO ABBOT WIBALD OF STAVELOT

He confirms the judgement pronounced by Franco in Everard’s favour. (1148.)

HENRY, by God’s grace king of the Romans, to the venerable abbot of Corbie and Stavelot: his favour and [Col. 1186B] every good thing.

We have carefully examined and investigated the case which your diligence transmitted to us in writing. By both the counsel and judgement of our court, and especially of our ministerials, we have deemed valid the judicial sentence pronounced by Franco; and by royal authority we have confirmed that Franco himself and those who followed him judged rightly. Therefore we condemn for you Cuono, your ministerial, to ten pounds of denarii of approved currency, and each of his peers and fellow-ministerials to three pounds under the royal ban—not only for his futile appeal, but also for the excessively insolent abuse with which he assailed their opinion.

Therefore, trusting in our favour and protection, uphold justice; do not delay in bringing into effect the judgement confirmed by us; and strive by every means to ensure that Everard may possess peacefully.

## LETTER LXXXIX. FROM HENRY, KING OF THE ROMANS, TO ABBOT WIBALD

He thanks Wibald for the service rendered to him and to his father, desiring his presence in other affairs. (1148.)

HENRY, by God’s grace king of the Romans, to WIBALD, venerable abbot of Corbie: the fullness of his favour and affection.

We offer thanks to your discretion, since you have most devotedly shown to us, for the increase of our honour both among the princes of the realm and with the lord pope, the steadfast fidelity and affection which you were accustomed to render to our lord and Father. After his departure, mindful of the closeness of affection by which you had been united to him, you have done this; consequently, we shall henceforth be ready to comply with your wishes.

Nevertheless, because after consulting the princes we have decided to hold a court at Frankfurt on the Nativity of St Mary, we ask your affection not to refuse attendance at that court, but to assist us with counsel and aid in ordering the condition of the realm and establishing peace.
