And because we desire all our business, private as well as public, to be arranged through you, and wish you to support us and [Col. 1187A] our affairs at that court, we command you to meet us at Nuremberg on the Kalends of September. The messenger will report the rest; concerning the condition of our lord and Father, we take care to write to you as he instructed us in his letters.

## LETTER XC. FROM THE CHAPTER OF LIÈGE TO ABBOT WIBALD

In difficult affairs they seek his counsel. (1148.)

To lord WIBALD, by God’s grace most beloved and most reverend abbot of Stavelot, the humble community of St Mary and St Lambert: greeting and the compassion due to its sweetest mother.

We shall speak briefly in this letter to your prudence and discretion—briefly in quantity of words, [Col. 1187B] but abundantly and gravely in significance. Something new—indeed, viper-like—long conceived among us from the fatness of wickedness and the root of pride, now strives to emerge, believing that a favourable time has come. It will indeed be favourable if there is no one to resist, no one to help—may that be far from us! On this matter the mother Church of Liège, pious and always made all things to all persons for good, requires your special counsel not merely by common right but, as it were, by a special obligation of affection, confidence, and familiarity. Therefore we unanimously ask you to deign to attend our chapter at Liège on the Tuesday of the coming week. Farewell.

## LETTER XCI. FROM ABBOT WIBALD TO THE CHAPTER OF LIÈGE

He excuses himself for being unable to attend their chapter and sets forth in writing the counsel he would have given had he been able to be present. (1148.)

[Col. 1187C]

To the most reverend fathers and lords in Christ, and to the venerable provost of the greater church, as well as to the archdeacons, H., dean, and all the canons of the Church of St Mary and St Lambert: brother Wibald, by God’s grace servant of the Church of Stavelot, wishes abundance of the spirit of counsel and fortitude.

A weighty occupation has prevented us from coming to your assembly in accordance with your summons: namely, the restoration of peace among the people of our land, whose discord, as you well know, has long shaken our Church with many and very great injuries. Yet although absent in body, we are present in spirit and in mind as devoted and obedient sons of our mother, the Church of Liège, praying Almighty God that He may crush Satan beneath your feet and deliver you from troublesome and wicked people, who strive by needless and empty innovations to tear apart and overthrow the primacy and glory of their mother.

These are a brood of vipers, which extinguish their mother while she brings them forth to life, who return evil for good—the people, I mean, grown fat and kicking, who through excessive ingratitude have forgotten their benefactor. For the cathedral church, in which you are priors and canons, has established and enlarged the other provostships in [Col. 1188A] the city as beautiful lights for the increase of its dignity and the adornment of its greatness. From the bishopric’s own resources it laid their first foundations, and thereafter it provided for canonical stipends and ecclesiastical worship, so that the clergy serving God might increase in their communities both in merit and in number. And the same persons were governors who were founders, until our unhappy times, in which there has now come “the falling away, that the son of perdition may be revealed, who exalts himself above all that is called God or is worshipped.”

For every person has separated from every other, so that scarcely two agree about anything; indeed God the Father does not hear us when we pray. Man, I say, has separated from man because he has separated from charity, obedience, modesty, and reverence; and people have become lovers of themselves, heaping up teachers with itching ears. Yet do not fear, little flock, for it has pleased your Father to give you the kingdom. Go up against the enemy; set a wall in defence of the house of Israel.

Let your learning recall how great was the branded disgrace of Esau, because he sold his birthright for the greed of his belly and a dish of lentils. The Lord says through the prophet: “I will not give my glory to another.” “If I am Lord,” He says, “where is my fear? If Father, where is my honour?” If the most holy and weighty name of election is set before you—an institution established indeed by the authority of the sacred canons to preserve the peace and unanimity of the Church—nevertheless, from this good beginning many evils have followed through human abuse, so that the licence of election has been extended even to the appointment of cellarers, kitchen keys, and stewardship offices. The sacred authority of the decrees sets forth elections of the Roman pontiff, archbishops, and bishops. Monks are instructed by the text of the holy Rule how and what sort of abbot they should elect. But by what judgement of authentic Scripture the election of stewards and of those who undertake no care of souls in governance is prescribed, we have not yet been able to discover.

When blessed Benedict gave instruction about appointing deans and provosts, he said: “Finally, let the abbot see to whom he may safely divide his burdens, assigning the chief share of counsel to him upon whom rests the danger of having to render an account.” These matters, and others of the kind, are set forth according to our understanding and ability. Had it been permitted us to be present in your venerable assembly, we would have spoken more fully and urgently, begging our brothers to consider attentively with an open gaze of mind that there is scarcely a house in which someone has not died; and to devote greater effort to restoring religious life than to raising material for contention. Without transgressing the boundaries laid down for them by their fathers, they should appoint to offices of provision such persons as would be aided by the greater support both of the merit of their life and of the eminence of their position. May the God of peace and love henceforth always be with you all.

## LETTER XCII. FROM ABBOT WIBALD TO HENRY, BISHOP OF LIÈGE

Concerning violence inflicted by Theodoric of Salcey-sur-Vive upon the people of the monastery of Stavelot. (1148.)

[Col. 1189A]

To his reverend Father and lord H., venerable bishop of the holy Church of Liège, brother WIBALD, by God’s grace servant of the Church of Stavelot: his humble prayers and devoted service.

Theodoric of Salcey-sur-Vive, your ministerial from Bouillon, came into the territory of the Church of Stavelot, to the vill called Daverdeus, and there carried off not a few animals as plunder. When an outcry arose in the district, our men, from Wellin as well as from other places, pursued them in order to recover what had been taken from us, [Col. 1189B] and followed the plunderers farther. The latter, having assembled a large crowd from your castle and from the greater territory, attacked our men; they captured seven men, killed twelve men of our Church, and most cruelly wounded many others.

We have heard that you intend to place our church at Wellin under interdict because those who were killed were buried in that church’s cemetery. We could not possibly believe this. For your discretion knows that even by the law of nations it is permitted to repel force by force, and that people are to be excommunicated on earth, as Scripture says: “Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven.” Thus, just as according to the authority of Leo and Gelasius we cannot communicate with those with whom we did not communicate while they lived, so conversely [Col. 1189C] the Church ought not to cast out in death those whom it did not avoid while they lived. Let your prudence therefore take care that, in addition to the grave wrong and loss which we have suffered through injury, we do not endure some further burden through the accusation of our enemies. As for Theodoric of the Tower, we have made a complaint so frequent, so importunate, and so prolonged without result that even our Church is ashamed, while we are weary.

## LETTER XCIII. FROM HENRY, KING OF THE ROMANS, TO ABBOT WIBALD

That he should meet him at Weinsberg. (1148.)

HENRY, by God’s grace king of the Romans, to WIBALD, abbot of Corbie and Stavelot: the fullness of his most intimate affection.

The discord recently arising in Swabia compels us partially to depart from our plan. Although we had intended to remain at Nuremberg, we are compelled to turn aside in order to settle the disturbances of the Swabians. Therefore we most earnestly ask your affection not to find it burdensome to meet us at Weinsberg on the same date which we had fixed for you at Nuremberg. But if this cannot be done, then, setting aside every excuse, hold the proclaimed court at Frankfurt with us. The messenger will report the rest.

## LETTER XCIV. FROM THE MONKS OF FULDA TO ABBOT WIBALD

They promise to meet him at the appointed time. (1148.)

[Col. 1190A]

To WIBALD, venerable abbot of the Church of Corbie, the congregation of Fulda: the devoted gift of prayer and affection.

Although at this critical time we are battered by a thousand pressures and hardships, we have nevertheless been greatly comforted by the visitation of your letter, for which we thank you with our whole heart’s affection. At the time designated for us in your letter, we are ready to meet you gladly; do not disdain to aid us with counsel and help from the prudence bestowed on you by God. For we [Col. 1190B] hope for every fatherly act from your sincerity.

## LETTER XCV. FROM BERNARD, BISHOP OF PADERBORN, TO ABBOT WIBALD

He asks that, while returning to Corbie, Wibald turn aside to visit him for a conversation. (1148.)

The humble overseer of the people of Paderborn by divine providence, to his beloved brother in Christ WIBALD, abbot of Corbie: in prayer and service, whatever may be more devoted, whatever may be more faithful.

We receive your return to us with joyful heart, since we have endured your long absence with considerable distress because of our many common affairs. Therefore we ask—and ask again—that, without any intervening hindrance, you turn aside to us for hospitality; and that you use all things in our house, not merely for necessity but even according to your wish, as though they were your own. Let us also have the freedom to discuss each matter in person, for while absent we can neither remember nor speak of many things. If you reject this request, you will compel us to doubt your friendship.

## LETTER XCVI. FROM WIBALD TO CARDINAL GUY

He commends to him the abbot of Brauweiler. (1148.)

To his reverend Father and lord GUY, venerable cardinal-deacon of the holy Roman Church and chancellor of the Apostolic See, brother WIBALD, by God’s grace what he is [Col. 1190D] in the Catholic Church: his devoted prayers and himself.

This which your clemency unceasingly shows toward us bears the likeness of divine generosity. For, though no merits of ours exist, the liberality of your benefits abounds toward us so greatly that, not without reason, we are compelled to declare with great admiration: “What shall I render to the Lord for all that He has rendered to me?” Therefore, under such confidence in your unwearying kindness, the confidence of our lowliness grows, so that we presume even to intercede for our friends, although it might suffice us and be thought a difficult attainment merely to taste in some measure the sweetness of your affection.

We therefore commend to you the venerable abbot of Brauweiler, who, as is certain, was prevented by bodily illness from coming to the synod of Reims and who, as you will hear more fully from him, was entirely innocent in the matter charged against him by his enemies. Therefore, out of regard for our request, be both father and patron to him.

> **Note:** [Col. 1191D] The monastery of Brauweiler, of the Order of St Benedict, is very celebrated, two leagues distant from Cologne; elsewhere we have reported the confirmation of its foundation and other acts not to be disregarded, vol. I.

## LETTER XCVII. FROM THE CHAPTER OF ST LIBORIUS TO ABBOT WIBALD

They complain of Folquin’s vexations and ask Wibald, on meeting the bishop, to urge him to assist them. (1148.)

To lord WIBALD, abbot of the holy Church of Corbie, most worthy of every reverence, W., provost, [Col. 1191B] A., dean, and the rest of the little flock of Saint Liborius: the faithful offering of their prayers and service.

Because after our lord bishop divine ordinance has promoted you to first place in our bishopric, we especially flee to you in our distress, hoping that your prudence will apply remedy and counsel to our evils. Lord Folquin, a grievous guest, repeatedly oppresses our poor tenants, continually extorting money from them, and now doing so more insolently; he has so reduced them that they are unable not only to pay their dues, but would rather beg anywhere among the nations than henceforth be subjected to such pressures.

I also, W., provost, although I have been sufficiently endowed with benefices besides my provostship, have spent from my own resources more than three months making up the annual deficiency in the prebend. Thus I am so depleted in means that I can neither henceforth serve the brothers nor provide for my own necessities. Therefore, as soon as I see the face of my lord bishop, I desire to be without and stripped of the office and title of provost. For, to the extent that I make concessions in sparing the poverty of the poor, to that same extent the aforesaid lord Folquin presses upon them with various exactions and wears them down.

Therefore, with one heart and a strong cry, holy Father, we beg your mercy that you meet our lord bishop and, as you know how to do and as we trust of you, remind him to help his Church in its extreme distress, lest we be necessarily deprived of the assistance without which we cannot serve as soldiers, [Col. 1191D] and the house of God, its ministers failing or scattered, lack divine service.

> **Note:** [Col. 1192D] That is, the cathedral church of Paderborn, which recognizes Saint Liborius, bishop of Le Mans, as its patron.

## LETTER XCVIII. FROM ABBOT WIBALD TO THE CANONS OF PADERBORN

Reply to the preceding letter. (1148.)

To his reverend fathers and lords in Christ, W., venerable chief provost of the Church of Paderborn, and the other canons of the same church, [Col. 1192A] brother WIBALD, by God’s grace what he is in the Catholic Church: the angel of great counsel.

We have received the letter of your whole community, full of anxious grief, full of troubled sadness, full of serious complaint: namely, because, as you wrote, the household of your church is oppressed by unjust exactions and compelled to cry out both to God and to you, that you may provide them with a helper and protector. It is indeed a great calamity, an intolerable misery, to be deprived of the necessary and appointed provision for divine service, and silently to endure the oppression of the household of the Church. Yet your steadfastness will, by careful consideration, guard against your falling into that saying of prophetic reproach: “Dumb dogs, unable to bark.” Likewise: “You do not go up against the enemy, nor have you set up a wall for the house of Israel, nor stood in battle on the day of the Lord” [Col. 1192B].

For our part, sympathizing in filial and brotherly affection with your distress, we have laid all your hardship before our lord and father, the bishop, beseeching and exhorting him that, since divine generosity has bestowed upon him many precious gifts which may serve for the defence and adornment of God’s house, he should rise with his whole heart to repel this injury and protect his Church; and the counsel and assistance of our small estate shall not fail him. We also faithfully and devotedly offer to you and to our whole holy mother, the Church of Paderborn, such resources of ability and possessions as we have, however slight, to share with you in this tribulation and in every one that may attempt to harass you [Col. 1192C]. Moreover, our father and lord the bishop answered our representation kindly and mercifully, deeply grieving in his heart over your misfortunes. He promised to devote himself wholly, and, if need be, his resources, for your deliverance and that of your poor, and to conduct the entire matter chiefly according to your counsel.

## LETTER XCIX. HENRY, KING OF THE ROMANS, TO POPE EUGENIUS III

He excuses the Archbishop of Mainz for not having attended the Council of Rheims, and commends him as he sets out for the pope. (A.D. 1148.)

[Col. 1192D]

To his most beloved father in Christ, EUGENIUS, supreme pontiff of the holy Roman Church: HENRY, by the grace of God junior King of the Romans, son of the great Conrad, illustrious conqueror, King of the Romans and ever Augustus, filial love in all things and due reverence in the Lord.

“Our most dear father, a worshipper of the Catholic faith, departing from us and from his kingdom,” etc. See under Pope Eugenius III, at the year 1153, after his *Regesta*.

## LETTER C. ABBOT WIBALD TO G., A GOLDSMITH

He urges him to apply himself diligently to the work entrusted to him. (A.D. 1148.)

[Col. 1193A]

Brother WIBALD, by the grace of God what he is in the Catholic Church, to his beloved son G., goldsmith: greeting and blessing.

Men of your craft are often accustomed not to keep their promises, because they undertake more work than they can complete. “The root of all evils is greed.” But your noble talent, your eager and distinguished hands, will escape every reproach of false promise. Let faith commend your craft; let truth accompany your work; let your undertaking obtain its result; let your promise answer to its appointed time [Col. 1193B]. We thought it proper to remind you of this obligation arising from your promise, since in the abode of so refined a talent there is no suspicion of deceit or falsehood. What is the purpose of this? Namely, that you may apply yourself zealously to the works which we have ordered you to make for us, and meanwhile undertake none that might hinder the completion of ours. You know that our desire runs swiftly and is quick: what we want, we want immediately. Seneca, *On Benefits*: “He gives twice who gives quickly.” Hereafter we intend to write to you at greater length concerning the care and management of your household, the government and ordering of your household staff, and the observance and discipline of your wife. Farewell.

## LETTER CI. G., THE GOLDSMITH, TO ABBOT WIBALD

He replies to the preceding letter. (A.D. 1148.)

[Col. 1193C]

To Lord WIBALD, by God’s grace abbot of Stavelot and Corvey, from his G.: greeting and due service.

I have received, both gladly and submissively, your counsels drawn from goodwill and the treasury of wisdom; indeed, both the useful gravity of their subject and the authority of their sender made them welcome. I have therefore committed to memory, and as it were locked away, the injunction to commend my craft by faithfulness, pursue my work in truth, and bring my undertakings to completion. Yet it is not always in the power of one who promises to fulfil what is promised: often the fault lies with the person to whom the promise is made, when through him the promise is nullified or delayed [Col. 1193D].

Therefore, if, as you say, your desire runs swiftly and you want what you want immediately, hasten so that I may run in your work. For I run and will run, unless necessity causes delay. Our purses have been exhausted; none of those whom I served has provided anything. Even the man concerning whom you promised that he would give lamps to my wife has almost brought darkness upon us, since, by holding out the hope of a benefit, he has suspended the benefit itself. Therefore, since human need rejoices in replenishment after exhaustion, provide for necessity, apply a remedy; give quickly, that you may give twice, and you will find me faithful, steadfast, and finally devoted to your work. Farewell. Consider with yourself how much time there is from the beginning of May to the feast of Saint Margaret [Col. 1194A], and then from that time until the feast of Saint Lambert. Enough has been said to a wise man.

## LETTER CII. ABBOT WIBALD TO THE MONKS OF FULDA

He excuses himself for being unable to travel to Fulda, meanwhile giving them salutary advice concerning the future election of an abbot. (A.D. 1148.)

Brother WIBALD, by God’s grace what he is in the Catholic Church, to his reverend fathers and brothers in Christ, B., venerable dean, T., provost, and the other superiors and sons of the Church of Fulda: the Angel of Great Counsel.

Your brother Othwin came to us at Corvey, bringing us no written communication from your community, but earnestly requesting an audience on behalf of you all [Col. 1194B], so that we might come to you at Fulda on the twelfth day before the Kalends of November [21 October], to take part in your assembly, where, under God’s guidance, you had appointed to deliberate concerning the election of a future abbot.

Therefore, dearest brothers, although we were most ready in spirit to carry out what would accord with your commands and the common good, nevertheless, detained by great and manifold business of our monastery, we could by no means come to you. But, offering prayers for you to divine mercy, we have sent the provost of our monastery to your assembly for visitation and consolation. What our small estate could have suggested in person to your excellence in this affair, we briefly declare in our absence: namely, that, putting aside party spirit [Col. 1194C], you may all return in unanimous concord through the Holy Spirit; that you may all be of one mind in Christ; and that you may all obey the commands of the lord pope with every obedience, not merely from necessity but also willingly.

“It is hard to kick against the goad”; “there is none who can hide himself from his heat.” He is the supreme pontiff, and moreover your particular one. The monastery of Fulda is the special possession of blessed Peter and of our holy mother, the Roman Church. Examples from your own house can sufficiently teach you that small things grow through concord, while great things collapse through discord. While peace and religion flourished in your monastery, with God’s favour governing human affairs, your dignity and possessions increased beyond measure. But what disgrace, poverty, and ruin then accomplish, your understanding may truly gather by comparison with better times [Col. 1194D].

Put aside hatred now; reject contentions; keep God before your eyes. For “cursed is the man who trusts in man and makes flesh his arm.” Be sons of peace and men of counsel, mindful of the words of Pope Saint Leo: “It is difficult,” he says, “for things begun under an evil principle to be brought to a good end.” Farewell; and in this most difficult affair may the grace of the Holy Spirit be with you.

## LETTER CIII. THE MONKS OF STAVELOT TO ABBOT WIBALD

They seek advice concerning certain temporal affairs. (A.D. 1148.)

To the reverend father and lord in Christ WIBALD, venerable abbot of the Church of Stavelot [Col. 1195A], the humble community of the same Church: faithful love and utter submission due in all things.

Mindful, most loving Father, of your gracious kindness, in which we continually rejoice, and daily keeping before our eyes the sure fruits and enduring memorials of your paternal care, we do all that we can: receiving the cup of salvation and calling upon the name of the Lord, we continually beseech God’s mercy in prayer for your safety and success. Hence we continually desire the presence of your fatherhood; hence we always love and revere you when absent, fear and embrace you.

Thus, unanimously greeting even now the abundance of your sweetness, we flee to the sole refuge of your protection [Col. 1195B], informing you that the beloved wife of the late Anselm the reeve, being at the point of death, after arranging her other affairs, placed in the hands of the Church, for the remedy of her soul and the salvation of Anselm the reeve of pious memory, the *Fornagia* which she held in our village of Stavelot by your grant. The arrangement was that, if, supported by your protection, we could enjoy her gift, it should certainly be held valid; but if not, we should retain her pledge, established for ten pounds of denarii.

Therefore, while this same lady is still alive, we devoutly invoke your customary mercy of counsel in this matter; and, falling humbly at your knees, we earnestly beg that the Church may not, through lack of your aid and protection [Col. 1195C], be deprived of that which it had desired for so long. For Margaret, sister of the same Odilia, and her husband Anselm, together with the reeve of Malmedy, seek by many threats to frighten us into rejecting the donation received in your name: at one time promising that they will give the same benefice to the son of Walter of Rulant; at another threatening that they will take ten pounds of denarii from your lord Lambert, reeve of Baldou, for that benefice itself.

We therefore seek, in a reply from your graciousness, the timely benefit of your counsel on all these matters. If we obtain it, we despise the threats of those who oppose us. Moreover, if until now we have been subject to certain deficiencies, henceforth we hope for better things through God’s mercy. May God keep your fatherhood always useful to us [Col. 1195D] and safe.

## LETTER CIV. ABBOT WIBALD TO HIS MONKS OF STAVELOT

He replies to the preceding letter. (A.D. 1148.)

Brother WIBALD, by the grace of God what he is in the Catholic Church, to ROBERT, venerable dean, and to the other beloved sons and brothers in Christ who belong to the community of Stavelot: blessing and life for ever.

Very welcome and pleasing to us is any suitable occasion that supplies us with the opportunity to write to your whole community—or rather, as though conversing with persons present, to express our affection. And the subject is all the more brilliant and agreeable to us [Col. 1196A] because, after the distress of our mind has been wiped away, it pours more abundantly into our thoughts something serene and tranquil. This happens, indeed, with richer grace as often as we learn that your condition, both in persons and in property, is advancing without the serious loss or damage of anyone.

From the tenor of your letter we have received the customary sincerity of your hearts toward us and the goodwill that surpasses itself by daily increase. Although we judge ourselves unworthy of such great encomiums of praise, and do not presume in any way to recognize our own merits toward the growth and benefit of your Church, nevertheless we do not cease, with all the affection of our heart and service of our voice, to render thanks to divine grace—to which we ascribe all that we are—because it has kindled more abundantly the desire of your minds for love toward our person, though lowly and insignificant [Col. 1196B]. Neither weariness from long duration, nor contempt from continual familiarity, nor any novelty arising from occasion has entered your community; rather, with a more earnest bond of charity, you honour one another, and honour all of us, each and every one, by loving us, and love us by honouring us. Bound more firmly in the cement of this most holy unity, you endure courageously the adversities of this world, which shake you and your possessions with frequent and most violent blows; and, though continually troubled by the troublesome lack of resources, you do not cease to increase and advance the adornment of God’s house.

But if any blemish of discord appeared among you, or if some ambitious stain of novelty defiled you, you could not merely grow [Col. 1196C], but could not even stand. Moreover, as to your awaiting our counsel and command concerning the common advantage, we do not think that this comes from distrust of obtaining it, but rather from eagerness to obey. For our disposition has long been very well known to you: with willing and ready purpose, whatever we could wrest from laymen, keeping the regard of divine judgment before our eyes, we have assigned to your use and that of the poor.

Trusting, therefore, in divine protection and in the assistance of our small estate, reclaim for the use of the monastery that possession of *Fornagiae* from the woman Odilia, whether deceased or still living, especially for the support of the poor, in whom Christ is received and nourished in person. For thereby a greater reward and abundant recompense will be bestowed on your behalf with God [Col. 1196D]; and among men you will obtain easier justification, more devoted support, and stronger defence. We are able to serve what lies close to your heart insofar as we recognize that you yourselves are able; and we would wish to be with you at all times, if that could fittingly be done. The threats of men are winds. By the law of nations it is permissible to repel force by force. It lies within your minds and your hands. We have sent you, on a larger sheet, certain questions which recently arose among us at Corvey.

## LETTER CV. ABBOT WIBALD TO HIS MONKS OF STAVELOT

He recounts certain disturbances that occurred in the monastery of Corvey and forbids them to receive rebels among themselves. (A.D. 1148.)

[Col. 1197A]

Brother WIBALD, by the grace of God what he is in the Catholic Church, to ROBERT, venerable dean, and the other beloved sons and brothers in Christ, monks of the monastery of Stavelot: blessing and life for ever.

Although it is altogether right that, because of the filial affection by which you are bound to our small estate with a closer bond, all our affairs should be naked and open to your knowledge, nevertheless we are somewhat ashamed to reveal to you the weaker condition of the monastery of Corvey—except that knowledge of all our affairs concerns you, and that we are anxious to defend and preserve our reputation against the slanders of detractors [Col. 1197B]. For, according to Saint Augustine, “He who neglects his reputation is cruel.” And that most learned pagan, Cicero, says that reputation is “no insignificant weapon for conducting affairs.”

For this reason also we judged that these things should not be withheld from your knowledge: certain brothers of Corvey have gone out from us, but they were not of us; and, on account of the established form of fraternity between the monks of Stavelot and the monastery of Corvey, they think that they can obtain either lawful and secure residence with you, or a return to their brothers through the favour of your intercession. We therefore set before you the long course of events in a brief account.

When at Corvey we were celebrating in Christian fashion the anniversary of our predecessor Abbot Henry [Col. 1197C], three of our younger brothers deliberately and by prior agreement withdrew themselves from our community and from the funeral rites which we were paying to the deceased abbot. When we asked why they had done this, they replied that they could not safely pray for an excommunicated man whose corpse had, contrary to canonical justice, been buried within the church. We asked the remaining brothers—for all were present, old men together with younger—whether they consented to this statement. All denied that such an unheard-of assertion had proceeded with their connivance, especially since that same Abbot Henry, whom those three rashly asserted had never been abbot, had never, while alive [Col. 1197D], been convicted or confessed guilty of any crime, nor had he even been formally charged in judicial procedure.

Those three were harmful men in the community: discordant, arrogant, and boldly most ready to bring about every ruin of order and destruction of cloistered discipline. For a long time already, despite the objection of many counsellors, we had borne with them patiently for the sake of peace. Yet, again turning to patience and assuming a fatherly disposition, we began openly and urgently to warn them not to “walk in things great and wonderful above themselves”; to lay aside their inveterate hatreds, which drag on toward eternal ruin; to cease persecuting the ashes of a dead man; and to stop giving scandal to us and to their brothers.

“We,” I said, “were found here as men elected and called, and ordered to come in obedience [Col. 1198A], administering this church without anyone’s objection and celebrating the divine offices. For the two years since he departed this life, we have received no letters or commands from our prelates containing any declaration of excommunication against that person or an order for the removal of his body. The Lord says in the Gospel to Saint Peter: ‘Whatever you bind on earth shall be bound in heaven, and whatever you loose on earth shall be loosed in heaven.’ He says ‘on earth,’ not ‘under the earth,’ because the living, not the dead, ought to be excommunicated or absolved. Solomon also says: ‘If a tree falls to the south or to the north, in whatever place the tree falls, there it shall lie.’ The prophet Ezekiel explains this in many words and judgments, as you will find in his book, maintaining that in all persons the end of life [Col. 1198B] should be judged rather than its beginnings.

“The judgment of Pope Saint Leo and Pope Saint Gelasius is: ‘Those with whom we did not communicate while they lived, we cannot communicate with when they are dead.’ Therefore it seems consequent to our small estate that those whom we have not separated from Christian communion while living should not be excommunicated after death. There is much chaff on the threshing-floor to which the winnowing-fan has not yet come.”

But at these and similar exhortations those three, like the deaf asp that stops its ears, did not hear the voice of the charmer. Instead, they begged most earnestly that we should not use force against them, asserting that the man ought not to be called abbot or reckoned among the number of abbots because he had deposed his lord and had sat in his seat contrary to the canons [Col. 1198C].

For, dearest brothers, though we speak unwillingly, among those same brethren—as in many cloisters subject to royal authority and appointment—there is no discussion of the Rule, no mention of the custom of Cassino, Cluny, or the ancient monasteries. Instead, they continually speak of canons, decrees, appeals, councils, rights, laws, condemnations, retaliations, arguments, proofs, and accusations; every day they desire new abbots and new priors. No provost, no cellarer, can please them. Bread, beer, and pottage are always at fault; the estates arrange the benefices of princes and ministerials. These are the first topics introduced for discussion in chapter; on these they spend the day. But of morals [Col. 1198D], religion, patience and humility, obedience and charity, there is never a word; all memory of moderate clothing, tonsure, and manner of walking has entirely vanished. And while they overthrow everything day and night, they are the first to criticize everything like censors and men of the strictest morality, lest, being themselves blameworthy, they should be blamed.

After we had spent long labour fruitlessly in admonishing them, at last, lest the authority of the chapter be held in derision, we said: “Because you receive no remedy, but rather, having turned to madness, rage openly among us, it now follows from your course of action that you prove your brothers polluted by alien communion. We shall be innocent, because we have only now first learned of this vice in the community; but you will appear not merely disobedient [Col. 1199A] and rebellious, but also profane and sacrilegious, because you persecute the dead with wicked hatred, although Solomon teaches that we ought not even rejoice at the death of enemies. What, then, did that Abbot Henry commit, or in what respect did he depart from the purpose of Christian profession or the path of canonical institution, so as to incur the snare of excommunication?”

To this they testified that the lord Cardinal Thomas of blessed memory, legate of the apostolic see, had undertaken to judge that Henry who had once presided over the monastery of Corvey after being deposed by him. Once the accusation had been formulated and the case joined before him, while he was sitting as judge, Henry excommunicated before all men, under his stole, anyone who would give or receive money in that cause, in order to defend his innocence. Yet the same Henry in question later publicly confessed that, in the same affair, he had given six marks of silver to the aforesaid lord cardinal [Col. 1199B].

“Therefore,” I said, “your blasphemy is greater and horrible: your tongue ranges not only over the earth in order to disinter the ashes of a priest who died in the peace of the Church, but you have set your mouth against heaven by charging our holy mother, the Roman Church, with heresy.”

Having then sought the advice of our brethren, we ordered them to withdraw to the infirmary, so that through a longer period of deliberation we might decide what should be done. When they refused, we forbade the brethren, under virtue of obedience [Col. 1199C], to celebrate the divine offices in their presence. Thus compelled by the brothers, they entered with high heads the dwelling assigned to them. Since in that house they did not observe obedience but gave themselves to laughter and mockery, wandering idly here and there, by sentence of the priors we judged that it was not good to take the children’s bread and cast it to dogs. And so, not without grief and tears, we expelled these men—unrepentant, indeed openly rebellious—from the community and cloister.

Moreover, so that your discernment may know what reputation and what holiness belonged to these grave and severe men who thought themselves polluted by the merits of the dead: the first of them, named Evernard, discordant from his youth and effeminate in bearing and gait, in the time of the younger Henry [Col. 1199D], who then held the monastery of Corvey, secretly stole a book and committed sacrilege. Condemned to punishment for this, he was allowed to flee from under the hand of the provost, no one interceding for him, though many were ashamed on account of the disgrace to the order. Since he promised, with all insistence, every amendment, we received him into the cloister out of supreme mercy, lest he perish.

The second of the three, named Adelbert, on another occasion raised his heel against the decrees and work of our most holy mother, the Roman Church, by adhering to that Henry whom Lord Cardinal Thomas, then legate of the apostolic see, had deposed as convicted and confessed of simony, and whom he had, by judgment of the Holy Spirit, excommunicated as one refusing to obey the sentence—indeed, as a rebel and usurper of ecclesiastical property [Col. 1200A]. For this, the same Adelbert afterwards publicly repented; and, released from the excommunication by which he had been stained by our predecessor—whom he was now attempting to disinter—he was scarcely received into the communion of the brothers and the community after a long show of humility.

The third, Godescalc, had been made cellarer of the monastery by his contemporaries, contrary to the counsel of the elders and quite unreasonably, before we undertook the government of that monastery. He consumed its substance in evil living; it is more honourable to be silent than to speak concerning his life and morals. Should these three perhaps come to you, judge them unworthy of your hospitality. Nor does the ordinance of your fellowship with the monks of Corvey extend so far that you should consent in any way to shelter such men or reconcile them to us and to their former monastery [Col. 1200B].

## LETTER CVI. ABBOT WIBALD TO H., A MONK

He praises his virtues and asks him to write to him. (A.D. 1148.)

Brother WIBALD, by God’s grace what he is, to his most dear son H. in Christ: blessing.

We write to you for the second time: we stir up your zeal, seek a reply, and demand a return in kind. But because you now use neither pen nor ink in answer, the explanation of your silence is thought to teach us that by action and the thing itself you strive to speak to us more than by articulate and vocal instruments, in accordance with that saying of the Apostle John [Col. 1200C]: “Let us not love in word or tongue, but in deed and truth.” If we have begun to build anything in the house of the Lord for the salvation of souls and for the refreshment and health of bodies, you complete it: you bring unfinished things to completion, adorn neglected things, repair ruined things, gather scattered things, and preserve what has been gathered. Blessed are you, my son, by the Lord: you honour your father, love your teacher, cherish your instructor, and embrace your provider. You have fulfilled the law, increased your monastery, and adorned the Church of God.

Nevertheless, write to us with the pen of a man, together with the pen of your works. Lords have delicate ears; the rich are caught by flattery. But as flattery is absent and wholly foreign to your holy morals, so we do not embrace it [Col. 1200D]. Rather, the visits of our friends and the sweet converse of letters are homeland to us, consolation to us, and defence to us. Write, therefore, that you may obtain pardon for your former silence; that your praise may never fail from our mouth; and that we may reply, if not eloquently, yet affectionately. Let our example provoke you, imitation urge you on, and concern kindle you. Distracted by such great and bitter occupations, we gather our mind and write with our own hand, while you, young and unencumbered, are silent. Yet in the work which we ordered you both to write and to dictate, we wish you to give earnest attention, so that we may receive an enduring fruit from your talent, just as we rejoice not a little in the work of your hands.

## LETTER CVII. THE MONKS OF FULDA TO ABBOT WIBALD

They ask that he will attend the future election of the abbot of Fulda. (A.D. 1148.)

[Col. 1201A]

To WIBALD, religious abbot of the holy Church of Corvey: the humble community of Fulda, G. the advocate, and the entire household of Saint Boniface, the services of most devoted obedience and prayer.

Because in the overwhelming tribulations and distresses which have found us in these days we have experienced your fatherly affection through diverse benefits, we cannot doubt the abundance of your mercy. Therefore, show the love of a kind father through the customary favour you have shown us, and do not delay to come to our aid by coming to us on the day before the Nones of November [4 November], when we are troubled by the desert of our iniquity [Col. 1201B]. For we are prepared to obey the commands of the lord pope in electing an abbot. Accordingly, we have judged it fitting to summon by our letters you and the other religious abbots appointed by the lord pope for the same election. But because, after God, we place our chief confidence in you, we humbly implore your fatherhood again and again not to be unwilling to come to us at the aforesaid time, and not to disdain to assist us with your counsel and help.

## LETTER CVIII. THE MONKS OF FULDA TO THE MONKS OF CORVEY

That Abbot Wibald may be willing to attend the election of the abbot of Fulda. (A.D. 1148.)

[Col. 1201C]

To the venerable lords and our fellow-brothers of the holy Church of Corvey: the community of Fulda, sincerity of brotherly love in Christ.

We cannot render worthy thanks for your brotherly consolations, which have fully gladdened our souls, because, made drunk with misery and affliction, we have now learned by experience that salvation is far from sinners. Yet if the Father of mercies and God of all consolation should at some time deign to comfort us through the riches of his glory, your remembrance among us will be more fully and perfectly held in blessing, because of your exceeding faith and devotion toward us. We therefore ask your blessedness to take care to urge your lord abbot to come to us at the time appointed for him by us [Col. 1201D], without any excuse, so that through his counsel and help the heart of the contrite may be revived and the spirit of those who mourn may be relieved. For we hope every brotherly and friendly thing from you.

## LETTER CIX. THE MONK STEPHEN TO ABBOT WIBALD

He greatly desires to return to the monastery of Stavelot and writes that he has been unable to impose the estate-management office upon Godin. (A.D. 1148.)

To his most dear lord and father WIBALD, venerable abbot of Stavelot and Corvey [Col. 1202A], Brother STEPHEN, by God’s mercy and his own what he is: submission, devoted affection, participation in prayers, and, to say it briefly, himself with all that is his.

The letter recently sent to my humility by your greatness has given me such strength and confidence that I walk more securely and know beyond doubt that from that time my affairs will proceed more prosperously. Giving thanks to your highness for this, I ask Almighty God only and humbly that he may deign to make me such a man as may deserve long to enjoy your companionship and your so sweet exhortation. But with what ardour I seek your presence and desire your coming, I do not think your knowledge is unaware, since I am supported by your help and delighted by your counsel [Col. 1202B].

As to what you ordered me to do—namely, to impose Godin of Barsiez upon the office of estate-manager at Lemgo—I announced your command to the peasants, but I could not at all obtain their acceptance of the same Godin until your presence should investigate the matter. When I persisted in demanding that your order be carried out, they approached the advocate; and thus everything was deferred, though not without great loss to our possessions, and left contentious until your presence. Whatever you command me, however, by writing or by word, I am ready to fulfil according to my ability and knowledge.

Furthermore, concerning the *pasnages* about which you wrote to me, that I should exact and collect them: they are few [Col. 1202C], but I shall exact them not only devotedly and diligently, but also gather them faithfully. May God deign to preserve your fatherhood safe for many years, useful to us and to our Church. Amen.

## LETTER CX. O., ABBOT OF SAINT REMIGIUS, TO ABBOT WIBALD

He informs him of the death of Stephen, monk of Stavelot. (A.D. 1148.)

To the reverend father and friend WIBALD, by God’s grace venerable abbot of Saint Remaclus, and to the prior and entire convent of the same Church: Brother O. [Note: [Col. 1201D] Odo, formerly a monk of Morigny near Étampes, became abbot of Saint Crispin at Soissons and afterwards of Saint Remigius at Rheims. At the expense of his monastery he established the Charterhouse of Mont-Dieu; he commended his soul to God in the year 1151.] [Col. 1202D], by the same grace humble servant of blessed Remigius: may you multiply like the cedar of Lebanon in the house of the Lord.

Although it is most unusual for us to intimate or report anything untoward to our brothers and friends, nevertheless, since it belongs to no one to set bounds to God’s bounds, we report that our brother Stephen, your monk, has departed, so that you, like us, may render him the due service, and may henceforth provide for your house, which now lacks a steward. We send you the statement he left, written above his breast at his dictation, folded within your letter. Farewell.

## LETTER CXI. THE MONK HENRY TO ABBOT WIBALD

He gives thanks for his goodwill and promises always to serve him with what is his own, etc. (A.D. 1148.)

[Col. 1203A]

To his most reverend lord WIBALD, venerable abbot of the Church of Stavelot, from the lowly HENRY: whatever a humble monk and devoted son owes to so great and beloved a father.

Having read, most loving Father, the counsels of your sincerity, by which you have deigned to instruct my ignorance, rebuke my idleness, and reprove my folly, I have been filled with great joy. For I confess that I am nothing except insofar as I deserve to be loved, cherished, and sustained by your greatness. Since, therefore, I shall never be able to repay even small—indeed, no—returns for your many benefits [Col. 1203B], you shall at least experience my goodwill toward your highness in this: so long as I survive, I shall serve you with the service of my craft, if perhaps not very quickly, nevertheless devotedly and tirelessly. For I know of nothing else in my person that may please your highness.

Moreover, in accordance with the care of your admonition, I have driven away the vice of idleness; I no longer take part in tales, whenever I have leisure; I have renounced wandering about. On the contrary, I apply myself to Scripture, attend choir regularly, and, at the request of the brothers, serve in the school under my master Henry, who recently completed the buildings of the infirmary wonderfully. Finally, one thing alone remains: I lack your presence. If I had it, I should think that nothing was lacking to me; and I pray Almighty God that I may soon enjoy it [Col. 1203C]. I love Melota greatly, both for your affection and for her own benefit. May your fatherhood prosper in the Lord.

## LETTER CXII. ABBOT WIBALD TO POPE EUGENIUS III

Concerning the election of the abbot of Fulda. (A.D. 1148.)

To his most reverend father and lord EUGENIUS, one and universal pontiff, Brother WIBALD, by the grace of God and yours what he is in the Catholic Church: love as to a father, obedience and service as to a lord.

We are not unmindful of the abundance of mercy which you deigned to show to our insignificance at the Synod of Rheims [Col. 1203D], and especially in the affair of the men of Fulda, which, because of the great humility with which your sacred heart is endowed by divine inspiration, you were pleased to discuss with us in counsel. And we indeed, as we had agreed with Your Highness, took care that no disturbance should arise on account of your command—so much so that, although your order concerning the holding of an election at Fulda was issued at Rheims on 8 April, our lord the younger king received the letters in the castle of Nuremberg in Bavaria on 15 April. How carefully and urgently we fortified and forewarned him in them, you will be able to observe from the copy of the letters sent to him, which we have transmitted to your discretion [Col. 1204A].

Most sweet Father, we do not wish to accuse anyone before your judgment, nor provoke your gentleness to anger; but we state to your piety, as truthfully as briefly, that those by whom the boy king ought to have been guided opposed this affair, working with all their might that something might be done in the Church of Fulda which would in some measure offend your authority. We, however, were far away; and even when present we could not resist persons more numerous and more powerful than ourselves. Kindly lend your ear to our petitions appended below, so that, living more safely under the shadow of your wings, we may serve your greatness more devotedly and more abundantly. We give thanks to God for the recovery of your health [Col. 1204B], praying that He may deign long to preserve Your Holiness unharmed for the government of the Catholic Church.

## LETTER CXIII. OF ABBOT WIBALD TO CARDINAL GUIDO.

He commends to him the elect of Bremen and Provost Hartwig. (A.D. 1148.)

To his reverend father and lord GUIDO, cardinal-deacon of the holy Roman Church and chancellor of the Apostolic See, brother WIBALD, by the grace of God, that which he is in the Catholic Church—himself.

Not without reason do we offer this possession to your exalted rank, which you hold so mindfully and affectionately that, although the care of the whole world concerns you and the affairs of the Catholic Church occupy you [Col. 1204C], you are nevertheless not unmindful of our insignificance. This was sufficiently shown by the two letters which you sent to Bishop Anselm [Note: [Col. 1203] Apparently of Havelberg, whose three books of *Dialogues* are found in volume XIII of the *Spicilegium*.], in which, with kindly remembrance, you added the subscribed greeting to our person.

We received your letters, which you transmitted to us through our young man Louis, and rejoiced greatly in them because the lord pope and you wished to lay upon us, as upon your faithful servant, some task in which our zeal and devotion in service to the Roman Church might appear. We humbly commend to your clemency the cause of the elect of Bremen, whom we do not doubt can be of very great benefit to that Church. The bearer of this letter, Provost Hartwig [Col. 1204D], is a prudent and learned man, of high birth in his own country, long known and dear to our insignificance. We believe him worthy that you should show him your favor with goodwill and mercifully hear him in his petitions.

## LETTER CXIV. OF ABBOT WIBALD TO POPE EUGENIUS III.

Concerning proceedings in the election of the abbot of Fulda. (A.D. 1148.)

Since we must render an account of the stewardship which Your Highness entrusted to our insignificance, we need brevity, lest a lengthy report detain too long your mind, which is occupied by care for all the Churches of the world [Col. 1205A].

After your discretion, by the just judgment of the Holy Spirit, removed Roger [Note: [Col. 1205D] The Sammarthani write that this Roger, or Ruggerus, attended the Council of Rheims and withdrew to Monte Vergine in order to devote himself to divine matters. Yet the context of several letters of Wibald establishes that Pope Eugenius III reduced him to the ranks on account of his own faults, annulled his election, and that the zeal of the Fulda brethren was not then so great, among whom regular discipline had so declined that they were ordered to seek an abbot in another cloister.]—the elect of the monastery of Fulda—from the government of that Church because of a canonical blemish, you directed the brethren of the said monastery, by letters of your gracious condescension, not to elect a person from their own community, but to summon to themselves, for the visitation of their church, the reverend abbots of Eberac, Everbac, and Hersfeld, and ourselves, the least of all; and, through their counsel, to endeavor, with God as author, to elect from another cloister such a person as might, with the Lord’s aid, support the ruined monastery of Fulda both in religious observance and in possessions.

You also sent letters of your command to the aforesaid four persons [Col. 1205B], requiring them to come to the monastery of Fulda by your authority and, in accordance with the tenor of your order, offer counsel in making the election. We first received these letters on the third day after the feast of the Nativity of the Blessed Mary. For the brethren of Fulda had appealed to your clemency to obtain their elect, whom you had censured by two decrees supported by canonical reasoning; but, with Peter, they found the rock.

Their envoys therefore returned without your commands or letters and approached our insignificance, asking us to attend their election, which they intended to hold on 21 October. But, considering that the state of the case had changed [Col. 1205C], and that no new command had come to us from the exalted holiness of Your Holiness, we hesitated to come, because a widespread report declared that your legate would come and arrange the monastery of Fulda in person. Nevertheless, we sent them our letters through two brethren; a copy of these we have taken care to send with this letter for your judgment.

But shortly afterwards the chamberlain of Fulda came to us with another brother, bringing letters from his convent both to us and to our convent, asking that, out of reverence for your name, we come to Fulda without delay. The three abbots named above were to be there, and an election was to be held at your command, unless it was prevented by our absence [Col. 1205D]. They further alleged their monastery’s lack of the necessities of life, since all was being plundered by those who stray from the way.

Long and greatly hesitating, we feared that either by acting or by refraining we might offend your fatherhood. Yet finally, hoping for the counsel of the religious men whom we had heard would come, we reached Fulda with the abbot of Hersfeld on 9 November. But since the abbots of Eberac and Everbac had not come [Col. 1206A]—the latter because, as he confessed through a messenger, he had not received your command on this matter; the former because, as we later learned from his letter, he had excused himself before your clemency for not coming—we were troubled in heart and lacking counsel, greatly afraid lest our imprudence should incur your displeasure.

Accordingly, this conclusion of our counsel with the abbot of Hersfeld was proposed and confirmed: since those two were absent, who were far wiser and better than we, we would give no assent in the business of the election, but would leave everything suspended and uncertain, awaiting anew your command and the authority of your legate. At last, called by the brethren into their chapter-house, we both entered; and, being ordered to give them a word of exhortation [Col. 1206B], we spoke, as the Holy Spirit gave us at the moment, concerning charity, obedience, and humility.

When this was ended, the provost of the greater monastery rose and wished to go out to Count Lothair, the regional count, and to certain other laymen. But we detained him, strongly urging and requesting that he be reconciled with his brethren who, in the time of discord, had departed or been expelled from the monastery; so that, if the election were to be undertaken, he whom all ought to obey might be elected by all together. For we concealed our wish to defer the affair until, in their words or conduct, we might find something suitable and convenient whereby we could withdraw, the business remaining unfinished, without incurring envy and hatred [Col. 1206C].

Thus, when we two and the brethren who had come with us had withdrawn, they prolonged the matter by lengthy consultation. Then, recalling us to the book-room [Note: [Col. 1206D] In all ancient monasteries, a book-room was ordinarily located near the chapter-house, so that brethren devoted to reading in the cloister might have books readily available.] and admitting only a few of their brethren, they replied that they could not be reconciled with those brethren on whose behalf we wished to intercede unless an abbot were first appointed, who could admonish and compel them by right of authority.

“And what,” I said, “did the laymen discuss with you concerning the business now at hand?” “They urge,” they said, “that we should assume no person already bound and ordained in another monastery.” “Rightly,” I said, “and canonically, and in accordance with the judgment of the holy Rule, do they admonish you. Since both the possessions and the sacred character of this monastery belong equally to our lord the Roman pontiff [Col. 1206D], you must elect one upon whom, according to the ancient dignity of your monastery, he may lay hands. For if you elect an ordained abbot, it will be something for you to desire rather than to obtain; for you will not be able to deal with him by the canonical and direct right of election. Rather, it will be necessary, with much labor and entreaty, to explain what necessity compelled you to depart from the path of the holy rules.

“Moreover, many have convinced the lord pope, whom you have already troubled for a long time [Col. 1207A], that, laying aside the fear of God, you all seek what is your own, not what belongs to Jesus Christ. Nor is it safe for you henceforth to act rashly without fearing to provoke him to anger.” The lord of Hersfeld supported our words with the greatest approval, enlarging and embellishing their meaning in the mother tongue.

While this was taking place, Count Godfrey, advocate of the same Church, was admitted to us. In his own name and with the unanimous voice of the laymen, he begged us not to wish to enact anything contrary to the freedom of canonical election, for which their forefathers had shed their blood in many battles. Nothing, he said, should be done by which the power of kings might be taken away through the force of election; the liberty of election had been asserted for churches by the bow and sword of laymen [Col. 1207B]. If the pope wished to arrange churches at his own discretion and promote persons in them, it would have been better to endure royal force than pontifical force. By every means they wished and advised that some brother from the very community of Fulda should be taken up for the government of all, unless perhaps—which could not happen—no one in it could be found worthy to preside.

Desiring to soften all this with gentle and mild speech and to find an opportunity to withdraw from their proceeding under some honorable pretext, we asked them to leave us for a while, until, after all opinions had been exchanged, we could answer with one equal and harmonious voice [Col. 1207C]. They withdrew indeed, but after a very short interval returned in greater numbers, urgently asking that the privileges of the Church of Fulda concerning elections of abbots be disclosed to them. They declared it a crime that these should be violated, and asserted themselves ready to stand for the dignity of the monastery unto death. If the privileges contained a provision that no one should be elected from the monastery, that must be followed and maintained; but if the contrary were true, it would be ruin and the destruction of all if there were any departure from them.

We earnestly urged the brethren not to invoke the authority of any privilege against your new command, made under pressing necessity and at utility’s demand; not to sow material for dissension among persons to whom those privileges in no way belonged [Col. 1207D]; but, in accordance with the tenor of your order, unanimously to adapt themselves to a salutary provision for their Church, knowing that, if they presumed otherwise, “the hands of Moses are heavy.”

Further, judging that we ought no longer to conceal matters under the pretext of propriety, we answered those defenders of liberty that nothing violent, nothing unprecedented, nothing contrary to the justice and liberty of the universal Church, nothing contrary to the privileges and dignity of the monastery of Fulda, had been done by Your Sublimity in this case. For, I said, the prohibition laid down by the lord pope—that in the present crisis no person should be taken from the community of Fulda for governance—flowed from the sacred fountain of the Rule of Saint Benedict, which commands that, if a community united in evils [Col. 1208A] wishes to elect a person consenting to its vices, the bishop to whose diocese the place seems to belong must not allow the agreement of the wicked to prevail.

What your election was like, which was recently annulled by apostolic authority, did not escape our lord the pope, who is your special lord and bishop, while the whole region cried out and the elect himself proclaimed it. And what sort of man your elect would be in the future he plainly taught in his beginnings, which were very harmful: he employed the counsel of the advocate and laymen for scattering, not for gathering together. And the sacred canons say that he deserves to lose a privilege who abuses the liberty of privilege. Your liberty, therefore, has not been overthrown but corrected; for no honor can be lawful [Col. 1208B] if it has been conferred through transgression.

This prohibition was granted temporarily as medicine against a violent disease; it was not to remain in force longer than necessity endured. It was always lawful, and always will be lawful, for the Roman pontiff, according to the nature of circumstances and the variation of times, to tighten or relax the rigor of the canons and apply new remedies to new diseases. Moreover, that visitors were sent from the Apostolic See to secure the integrity of your election is shown to be canonical by the venerable authority of the sacred canons in very many written passages. Nor ought you to have rejected or despised those two abbots, religious and wise men indeed, to whom the duty of visitation and the principal authority of counsel were assigned. Without their presence and direction [Col. 1208C], we two can offer neither counsel nor consent.

As for your opposing with such weight the most holy and sweet title of liberty, let it be said with everyone’s leave: it is rather a covering for malice than a defense of justice. One man builds a castle in the jaws of the monastery; another usurps the rents customarily paid to the monastery; another devastates by fires; another harasses it with plundering and robbery. The brethren in the cloister suffer hunger, thirst, and nakedness, so that they cannot even extend the offices of hospitality and humanity to us, their brethren and servants of the lord pope.

Set the Church’s peace in order; pay the brethren the necessary and owed allowances; summon again, for another day, not only the abbots of Eberac and Everbac but also many other prudent and God-fearing men [Col. 1208D], by whose counsel and effort, with the Holy Spirit granting it, such a man may be elected abbot that through his conduct and zeal they may be able to receive the effect of correction in both spiritual and temporal affairs.”

The laymen were by no means angered by these words, truth defending itself and compelling them to recognize and admit that what had been said was not without the force of reason. They therefore began to consult among themselves and confer in pairs, threes, or fours. Since no one spoke with us, and the day had already advanced to the eighth hour, we went out and entered the dormitory. Then, after a short interval, we returned and met certain priors with some brethren, who threw themselves at our feet [Col. 1209A] and earnestly, with tears, begged that we give them help in their necessity: that the lord abbot of Hersfeld might undertake the burden of that prelation. One of them added: “For,” he said, “he was our monk and brother before he was promoted to be an abbot.”

To this we replied: “Dearest brethren, we have openly and plainly declared what we believed pleasing to our lord the pope concerning the election of any abbot, salutary for your Church, and safe for your persons; nor can we betray our judgment. Moreover, we do not believe that an abbot possessed of canonical discernment would accept this burden of government without the lord pope’s command—an undertaking requiring long time [Col. 1209B], great expense, infinite labor, and of uncertain outcome. If the lord of Hersfeld trusts in his own powers, or hopes for the favor and consent of the lord pope, let him rely upon his own deliberation rather than our counsel.”

After hearing this, the brethren nevertheless asked us to keep back the abbot, whom we had left with them for a little while, and to remove him from awareness of this proposal until they had entered the chapter-house together and requested the assent of all concerning his election. They entered; we remained outside. Taking the abbot aside, we told him what the brethren of Fulda had done with us. When he hesitated and asked our counsel, we referred him to his own heart and conscience. And when he declared that he would by no means consent [Col. 1209C], we suggested that, as we ourselves were withdrawing from them, so he too should withdraw, lest the undertaking which they were carrying out in our absence and despite our dissuasion should appear to have our consent.

He departed, and we sat down at table to restore our bodies with food. After supper, we took leave of the abbot and also of the brethren of Fulda, indicating that we wished to leave at dawn. The brethren begged us to remain, since they had elected an abbot, but the laymen had postponed their consent until the following day. We in no way yielded to their request and departed at first light.

These, dearest Father, are the things we learned by being present at Fulda. What was done after our departure you will be able to learn from letters which a certain brother of Fulda sent us, written not on parchment but on a tablet; we have had copies of them sent to the feet of Your Holiness [Col. 1209D]. For with you are manna; with you is the rod; with you is the dispensation of the canons; with you is the interpretation of decrees; with you is the moderation of the Rule; with you are wine and oil; your right hand knows how

> To spare the conquered and to subdue the proud.  
> (Virgil, *Aeneid* VI.853)

We have endeavored to set everything before your discretion in order, so that your pious and clear-sighted spirit, to which discernment of spirits has been granted by God, may understand more by reading [Col. 1210A] than we did by seeing and acting. If anywhere, armed with zeal for piety, we have unwisely defended your decrees and commands and, as it were, attempted to support heaven on our shoulders, then, although the result deserves no praise, our devotion will nevertheless obtain pardon from your clemency.

## LETTER CXV. OF H., APPARENTLY A MONK OF FULDA, TO ABBOT WIBALD.

He writes that the elect gave his assent to his election. (A.D. 1148.)

To his most reverend lord, H., his own man—himself.

Since, dearest Father, I embrace and fear you as my lord, I do not hesitate in all things to follow your commands [Col. 1210B]. I therefore notify Your Holiness that after your departure our brethren met with certain laymen concerning the election. But many of them, on hearing of your departure, disdained to attend. Those who assembled asked the elect himself to undertake the burden of government; but he resisted, as one unwilling to prevail. At length, therefore, he consented.

Certain laymen and monks also charged you with wishing your provost to be elected, and asserted that I had given assent to this. After the elect’s departure, however, we agreed that we ought to summon you and the other two abbots by the feast of Saint Nicholas. Your legate did not find the porter with us. May Your Holiness prosper.

## LETTER CXVI. OF ABBOT WIBALD, OR DIPLOMA.

Concerning the leasing of a certain property. (A.D. 1148.)

[Col. 1210C]

In the name of the Lord: WIBALD, by the grace of God abbot of Corvey. Let all know that, in the possession of our monastery which is at Meretha, we have granted a lease to Conrad of Orio under an agreement for four marks of tested silver. Every year, on the feast-day of Saint James the Apostle, he shall pay these at Koiforde, in the house now held by a certain woman named Sigardis, to the monastery’s chamberlain or to his appointed messenger. If he neglects to pay, he shall thereafter forfeit both the possession and the agreement [Col. 1210D]. If his son wishes to inherit, he shall give the abbot four marks at investiture as an acknowledgment fee. Nothing from that whole possession has been alienated by sale or exchange by us or by our predecessors.

Done at Anlon in the year of the Lord 1148, in the presence of Lord Haribert, bishop of Utrecht, and many others.

## LETTER CXVII. OF F., ABBOT OF SAINT GODEHARD, TO ABBOT WIBALD.

He urges him to be willing to be reconciled with the deposed Abbot Henry. (A.D. 1148.)

To his venerable lord, WIBALD, abbot of Corvey [Col. 1211A], F. [Note: [Col. 1211D] Frederick, the first abbot appointed by Saint Bernard. Some call him abbot of Corvey, others of Fulda; the latter appears more certain from the *Chronicle of Saint Godehard*, vol. II of the *Scriptores Brunsvicenses*, p. 407.], an unworthy little servant of blessed Godehard [Note: [Col. 1212D] Saint Godehard: a notable abbey of the Benedictine order in the city of Hildesheim, founded by Bishop Bernard, who secured Saint Godehard’s enrollment among the saints.], that which hope that does not disappoint promises to those who love God.

Since I recently came to know you, though only during a brief interval, I have become so attached to you from my heart that, if it were possible, I would wish to cling to your side as an inseparable servant. But since I do not see that this can be done, I shall visit you more frequently by letters and also in bodily presence when opportunity arises.

Moreover, concerning Lord Henry, the former abbot, whom you complained in your community was, to the extent of his ability, a source of scandal to you: know that, after I returned from you, I immediately rebuked and admonished him concerning this affair through the provost of Richenberg, with whom he was then staying. He, not recalling himself altogether innocent in this matter, as it seems to me [Col. 1211B], replied only this: if in anything, even the least matter, he had offended against you in words, he had done so under the pain of his humiliation; henceforth he desired to be reconciled to your favor in such a way that no fault of his should ever again estrange him from you.

For this settlement, he and the provost appealed to me once and a second time by letters, then often in person, after you had visited the new king, asking me to act as mediator. They adjured me by Him who is true peace, Christ, and in view of the reward which He promised in the Gospel to the blessed peacemakers. Therefore, falling on my knees before your fatherhood with him and for him, I beg you to be reconciled with him, and to assist him, in what is easy for you, in the matter which I communicated to you more privately through the bearer of this letter [Col. 1211C].

I await your reply concerning this, and, if it so pleases you, letters to Margrave Adalbert, the reply to which I may see. For I trust that in this matter you may do what you wish. You know what we have done concerning the assembly of abbots; but some of ours say that the abbot of Heinsberg must be awaited, who, we hope, will soon return from the lord pope. I hear that you have been at Fulda. If you please, tell us what is being done or ought to be done there concerning the abbot of that place. May Your Holy Fatherhood, most dear to me, prosper in the Lord.

## LETTER CXVIII. OF ABBOT WIBALD TO FREDERICK (F.), ABBOT OF SAINT GODEHARD.

Rejecting the praises offered him, he replies that he remits from his heart every injury committed by the deposed Henry, abbot of Corvey; but that only the pope can remit the censures imposed upon him by the Apostolic See. (A.D. 1148.)

[Col. 1211D]

To the reverend father in Christ F., venerable abbot of the Church of blessed Godehard, brother WIBALD, by the grace of God that which he is in the Catholic Church: prayer with true affection.

We received your letter full of welcome consolation and grace, and were gladdened by it as by a certain heavenly gift and a gift of divine mercy. For your praise filled us with good hope, since the charity of God, poured into your heart through the Holy Spirit who dwells in you, could not wholly be deceived in judging that good things, whether present or certainly future, were to be proclaimed in us [Col. 1212A]. Yet our conscience grievously assails and accuses us, and judges us worthy, I will not say of your commendation, but not even of that of the lowliest person. Nevertheless, since you have seen fit to think thus of our insignificance, we shall endeavor to be what you affirm; we shall strive to be conformed to the grace which you proclaim.

But concerning that Lord Henry, who once presided over the monastery of Corvey, which we now serve under God’s guidance, we answer your kindness as follows. When he was accused on many counts, both of his violent intrusion [Col. 1212B] and of certain other charges, we were not merely absent but ignorant of all these affairs, and far away at the court of the lord pope. After nearly six months, repeatedly summoned and ordered to come, and compelled in no small degree, we undertook the government of the Church of Corvey with care, anxiety, and great fear; and between his deposition and our appointment another man had been advanced by the unanimous and concordant election of the brethren.

He himself has sorely tried our innocence—we who had previously zealously supported him while he was assailed by frequent accusations—and, disobedient to the Roman Church and in no way obeying its decrees, with his mouth set against heaven he sowed scandals among our brethren and, so far as lay in his power [Col. 1212C], gave every possible occasion for regular discipline and monastic order not to proceed in our monastery along their due and canonical course.

He has indeed been reconciled with those who, while he presided, were flattering to his face and biting in his absence; who compelled him, as though by salutary counsel, to do the very things which they soon afterwards censured and accused; and who, though authors of the evils, brought him to judgment as though guilty. But he is hostile to us, though we never knowingly showed hostility to him even in word; and, if it could be done without compromising our religious profession and honor, we would rather be absent than preside in a time of such disturbance.

As to his wish, recorded in your letter, to be reconciled to us [Col. 1212D], we are deeply concerned to know what meaning or judgment is contained in the word “reconciliation.” For our conscience bears witness that we have committed no wrong against him. If he has sinned against us, we forgive him all things from a perfect heart out of regard for divine love; we desire that true good may come to him in both soul and body; nor do we begrudge him, provided our peace is preserved and our monastery safeguarded, if some more fruitful repose is granted him. For we too are human beings, scourged with human beings, and we do not consider anything human foreign to ourselves [Col. 1213A].

But regarding letters to be sent to Margrave Adalbert concerning his affair, the way to a ready decision was not open to us, because the same margrave, certainly a prudent man and a model of all uprightness and discipline, did not consult us on the matter, though he is bound to us by intimate trust and friendship. Now the Roman Church obtained on earth from God, before all mortals, this privilege: that it alone may say with Him, “I kill and I make alive; I wound and I heal.” What strength or power, then, have we, that we should be able to raise up one whom the most almighty hand has struck down?

Lord Henry himself, after being excommunicated by the legate of the Apostolic See and deposed from every dignity of abbacy and ecclesiastical office [Col. 1213B], obtained no letters of reconciliation from the clemency of the Roman Church—perhaps because, according to the custom and institutions of the Apostolic See, he refused to swear upon the most holy Gospels that henceforth he would not harass the Church of Corvey either personally or through a subordinate agent.

Then, at the Synod of Rheims recently held, the lord pope confirmed both orally and in writing the sentence of his legate, Master Thomas, which he had pronounced against the aforesaid Henry. The pope, as stated, both deposed him from rank and ecclesiastical order and struck him with a sentence of anathema as disobedient—indeed, openly rebellious. How great a sin it is to receive what the Roman Church rejects, the pages of the sacred canons have plainly taught your learning [Col. 1213C].
