Terrified by these and other difficulties, we could not easily discover, given our mental weakness, what we ought to reply to your wisdom or how we might provide for the Church entrusted to us and for our own peace. But your discernment will consider, observe, and choose what our holy mother the Roman Church wishes to permit in this matter; what suits the peace of the Church of Corvey; what benefits our peace; and finally, what the church of Adesleve and our friend the margrave may safely undertake in this affair.

For the matter of Adesleve, which you communicated to us through your messenger, not in writing, as something secret, was already widely known among us. That same good man, with his habitual fickleness, had divulged these same matters not to friends but to those who had deposed him; not to intimates, but had made them public after his deposition [Col. 1213D]. He had asked them to come on the day on which he and we were to meet, although we were wholly ignorant of this meeting; indeed, the conference concerning reconciliation was suspected by us before it was known to us.

## LETTER CXIX. OF ABBOT R. TO ABBOT WIBALD.

He asks him to have mercy upon Henry, formerly abbot of Corvey. (A.D. 1148.)

To Lord WIBALD, venerable abbot of Corvey [Col. 1214A], brother R. [Note: [Col. 1213D] Perhaps Reinard, abbot of Reinhausen.], least in the number of abbots: whatever a most devoted and faithful heart can offer.

Most dear of men, I had intended to present myself bodily before your beloved presence, but lack of the means of riding [perhaps *equitaturae*] prevented it—a want caused me by the fraud and deceit of a certain vain and faithless man. I therefore come by letter and spirit, greeting your beloved person with that affection which, I do not doubt, you have long proved.

The matter which made me wish to come at this time, besides my desire to visit you, I commit to your most approved discretion and likewise to your piety, so that my written words may have no less force with you in its behalf than words spoken in person, and so that those who wished me to take part in this case may know that my friendship with you has some influence [Col. 1214B]. It concerns Lord H., formerly called abbot of Corvey, upon whom you ought to cast the eyes of paternal mercy, so that the very effect of that mercy may demonstrate, by laudable truth, that he has not vainly hoped for some consolation.

May that good Samaritan who gathered up the wounded man deign to provide for and preserve the welfare of both your men, most dear of abbots.

## LETTER CXX. OF POPE EUGENIUS III TO ABBOT WIBALD AND THE BRETHREN OF CORVEY.

That the deposed Henry should find no place among them. (A.D. 1148.)

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son WIBALD, abbot, and the chapter of Corvey: greeting and apostolic blessing [Col. 1214C].

How necessary it is to provide for the peace of religious monks, etc. See under Eugenius III, A.D. 1153.

## LETTER CXXI. OF HENRY, ARCHBISHOP OF MAINZ, TO WIBALD.

He gives an account of what he had done at the Council of Erfurt. (A.D. 1149.)

H., by the grace of God humble minister of the see of Mainz, to his special friend WIBALD, venerable abbot of the Church of Corvey: the devoted and ready offering of love and kindness in all things.

[Col. 1214D] For your faithful admonition and pious devotion, which you showed us on our journey to the lord pope, we not only return thanks, but are also prepared, at the proper place and time, to answer with a fitting performance in deed. In accordance with the request of your envoy, we take care to make known to you the handling of certain affairs which, by command of the lord pope, we discussed and settled at Erfurt in the presence of our suffragans.

The first case concerned a certain abbot of Burgelin, of the Order of Saint Benedict, whose monastery was united to the Bursfeld Congregation in the year 1510. He had a complaint against Count Sizo, alleging that the count had violently taken certain goods of his church and stubbornly retained them. This case, entrusted to us by the lord pope, we settled, with the counsel and assistance of our brethren, after peace and concord had been made between both parties.

The second concerned Count H., who had dismissed his wife and taken another. The proceedings in this affair were as follows. The lord bishop of Hildesheim asserted that, on account of kinship, a canonical separation had been made between him and the former woman whom he had held as wife; but he did not affirm that the count had undertaken or completed penance for the incest which he had committed with his niece. Therefore, our brethren decreeing that before his penance had been completed he neither could nor ought to contract a marriage, we summoned him to Mainz, to our synod on the Monday after the Ascension of the Lord, in order to make satisfaction.

Moreover, because the abbot of Herford, having accepted the abbey of Fulda without consulting our church and without our authorization, had withdrawn himself from our obedience, we summoned him at the direction of our brethren. After this there were many other matters, which it would take long to enumerate individually; but we judged that you especially wished to know these.

## LETTER CXXII. OF ABBOT WIBALD TO POPE EUGENIUS III

He writes on behalf of the abbot of Saint Medard against Baldwin, a canon of Liège. (Year 1149.)

To his reverend Father and lord EUGENIUS, the one and universal pontiff, brother WIBALD, by the grace of God what he is in the Catholic Church, the affection of a son and the devotion of a servant.

Our venerable brother J., abbot of the church of Saint Medard—Ingrannus, made abbot of Marchiennes from being a monk of Corbie, succeeded Walter, abbot of Saint Medard at Soissons, upon Walter’s death in 1148, according to the short Chronicle of Saint Medard, *Spicilegium*, vol. II; he resigned in 1177 and was succeeded by Geoffrey—whose church especially belongs to your devotion and protection, asked our lowliness to report to your highness the case which he brought before us against Master Baldwin, canon of the Church of Liège. So far as we can remember, it stands as follows.

The monastery of Saint Medard possesses, in the diocese of Liège, an estate called Hanzines. Not far from it lies another estate, called Hanzineles, belonging to the canons of the church of Blessed Lambert. The administrator and provost of this estate on behalf of his fellow canons is the aforesaid Master Baldwin. At Hanzineles there is a chapel which, by synodal and canonical right, is subject to the mother church at Hanzines, together with the entire tithe paid by the tenants of the aforesaid estate.

Master Baldwin wished to obtain from the abbot of Saint Medard a silver chalice for the aforesaid chapel and all the implements both of the altar and of the Mass. Yet, without having summoned either the abbot or his monks through regular judicial procedure concerning this demand, he denied the whole tithe of Hanzineles to the monks of Saint Medard and, with the consent and command of the canons of Liège, detained it.

The brethren of Saint Medard complained before the synod of the bishop of Liège that this had been done to them without any canonical proceeding or judicial sentence having preceded it. They requested that what had been taken from them should be restored, declaring that they would afterwards answer according to the rule of law. The bishop denied, and the archdeacon denied, that to their knowledge or with their consent the aforesaid tithe had been detained by Master Baldwin or the canons. Accordingly, by due process of law, the same Master Baldwin was compelled to make full restitution.

Because it seemed disgraceful to the cathedral church that it should openly be accused of robbery, and because the church of Saint Medard was being supported by our efforts and those of many others out of reverence for your lordship, Master Baldwin, with the consent of the canons, requested that the case be deferred until the conclusion of the assembly, which had then convened in large numbers, and thereafter be placed under the authority and counsel of the abbot of Lobbes and other religious men. This was straightforwardly granted.

Lambert, who died in 1149, according to the short Chronicle, vol. III of the *Anecdota*.

After the large gathering of clerics had dispersed, the lord abbot of Lobbes, having associated with himself religious and prudent men, advised Master Baldwin and the canons to restore what they had taken and to cease demanding the chalice and the other objects. No chapel, he said, is customarily entitled by law to demand these from its mother church, since those who built chapels promised to provide, out of their own contributions, for every need of the chapel, so as to spare themselves the labor of travelling a long distance to the mother church.

When Master Baldwin would not accept this judgment, and the monks of Saint Medard saw that delay had frustrated them and that they could recover what was theirs neither by law nor by agreement, they appealed to the presence of Your Highness. They summoned Master Baldwin to appear before your tribunal on the octave of Saint Martin, in the hearing of ourselves and many others.

## LETTER CXXXIII. OF ABBOT WIBALD TO ALL THE FAITHFUL OF THE PARISH OF LIENWART

Concerning the negligence of four priests. (Year 1149.)

WIBALD, by the grace of God abbot of Corbie, to all faithful Christians in the parish of Lienward: greeting and blessing.

We make known to you that none of those four persons who hold prebends in your church has yet come to us or received from us possession of our church, although we have now held the abbey of Corbie for two years. Moreover, through their negligence we have suffered labor and loss, because they did not receive the altar-gift; for this reason our whole church was adjudged into the right and power of the bishop. But, through the mercy of God and the favor of that bishop, we have now received the church back entire, as we possessed it before.

We appoint a day for those four who hold the church: on the coming feast of the Purification of Saint Mary they are to appear before us at Corbie and show us what right they have in our possession. If they do not come then, let them know for certain that we shall pursue our right to the utmost and shall remit to them nothing of what is ours by right.

## LETTER CXXIV. OF THIEBOLD TO ABBOT WIBALD

Concerning the abbess of Geseke. (Year 1149.)

To the venerable brother and friend WIBALD, abbot of Corbie, THIEBOLD, by the grace of God, if he is anything at all, with service, his most intimate affection.

We have not lost the remembrance of the affection you have shown us; and although we have by no means returned thanks as we ought, we have not been ungrateful, nor ever shall be. Your affection knows, my lord, that it would be exceedingly improper for us if, after the abbess of Geseke had placed her affair in our counsel, she should lose through us both her case and the settlement.

Geseke, a convent of virgins, was founded in Westphalia in 946 by Ahold, count of Anholt, under the invocation of Blessed Mary and Saint Cyriacus; Emperor Otto confirmed its foundation in 952.

Therefore we earnestly remind your affection that you should make your own the word which you gave me concerning this matter, permit the said settlement to take effect, and write back to us shortly concerning the state of this affair.

## LETTER CXXV. OF ABBOT WIBALD TO PROVOST THIEBOLD

Concerning the abbess of Geseke. (Year 1149.)

Brother WIBALD, by God’s mercy what he is in the Catholic Church, to his beloved brother and friend THIEBOLD, venerable provost: affection and blessing.

It is very pleasing to us that your memory firmly retains with what sincere affection we have loved you from long ago, with what zeal of loyalty we have rejoiced in the increase of your honor, and that, on the strength of your definite promise, we expect fitting recompense for these things.

Your prudence should remember that last year, when the lord pope was to come to Trier, and we learned by report that you intended to bring the abbess of Geseke before the lord pope and plead her case against us, we warned you, as a discerning man and an intimate friend, not to direct your efforts against an innocent person and a friend in a cause of little honor and weak foundation.

For that abbess had been deposed almost nine months before we came to the governance of the Church of Corbie. She had been removed from the abbey of Kamen by Lord Thomas, cardinal-priest; and, when she attempted to retain it by force contrary to the canons, she was expelled with no little humiliation by the advocate of that church. After her removal, two were elected amid contention, and a third candidate was disputed.

Since everything, both spiritual and temporal, was collapsing into a worse state, our lord the king, to whose authority the place belonged, at the counsel and admonition of the lord pope entrusted the ordering of the aforesaid abbey to the Church of Corbie and to us. In these circumstances, as stated above, we considered it proper to suggest to your discernment that you should not appear to support that woman against the decrees of the Roman pontiff and against the commands of the lord king.

You wrote back to us, if we remember correctly, that you could not fail a member of the Church of Cologne. Nevertheless, she came to Trier before the lord pope without you and did all she could against us, concealing the truth and speaking falsehood. But the lord pope, having learned the truth from our letters, appointed a day of hearing for us and for her at the Council of Reims. We came; she did not come. The snare was broken, and we were delivered. The lord pope confirmed her deposition by decree and, under threat of anathema, restored to the monastery the possessions which she had alienated.

Dearest brother, we do not remember what we may have promised you concerning her, whether orally or by letter, after she departed from Trier, since we are capable of keeping our promises in memory.

## LETTER CXXVI. OF ABBOT WIBALD TO ARNOLD, ARCHBISHOP OF COLOGNE

Concerning certain ministerials who had conspired against him. (Year 1149.)

To his reverend Father and lord ARNOLD, venerable archbishop of the holy Church of Cologne, brother WIBALD, what he is in the Catholic Church: humble prayers and devoted service.

Because after God and the lord king you are the head of all the princes in this land, and because the preservation of the peace of the land especially concerns you, we complain to you as to Father and Lord that certain ministerials of the monastery of Corbie, who were continually in our household, one night while we were dining left our table, broke open our stable, stole our horses, and killed with swords some horses which they could not lead away.

When the cry “To arms!” was raised, as is the custom of the land, other ministerials of the church assembled in greater number. To preserve their own pledged faith and the honor of all their peers, they challenged to duel certain persons by whose counsel so great a crime had been committed, intending to fight them on the octave of Epiphany. For their plan and contrivance had been that those very robbers should kill us or mutilate us, as we afterwards learned truly; and since they could not carry this out, they attacked our horses in their nocturnal theft.

Therefore, prostrate in spirit at the feet of Your Highness and of all the princes, nobles, and others in your court, we humbly implore your aid: for the sake of divine mercy, reverence for the lord king and all princes, and the maintenance both of divine and human law, set the shield of your protection against such audacity. Provide, as befits your greatness, that those evildoers find no refuge in your land, and send us some of your men as aid for the aforesaid day. Farewell.

## LETTER CXXVII. OF EMPEROR CONRAD TO ABBOT WIBALD

What happened to him while he was besieging Damascus. (Year 1149.)

CONRAD, by the grace of God august king of the Romans, to the venerable WIBALD, abbot of Corbie: his favor and every good.

Because we have learned that above all you desire news from us concerning the prosperity of our condition, we have considered it appropriate to inform you of this first. By God’s mercy we are well. Having completed all that either God willed or the peoples of that land allowed in those regions, we boarded ships to return on the feast of Blessed Mary in September.

We speak of men because, when by common counsel we came to Damascus and pitched camp before the gate of the city at great peril to our men, and when the city was even on the point of being taken beyond doubt, betrayal was committed by persons of whom we had been least wary. They asserted that the city was impregnable at that location and deliberately led us to another side, where neither was water available for the army nor was any approach open to anyone. All were thereby turned alike to indignation and grief, and returned with the undertaking unfinished.

Yet they unanimously promised that they would then move on an expedition against Ascalon and fixed a place and day. When we came there according to agreement, we found scarcely anyone. Having waited there in vain for the whole body for eight days, deceived by them a second time, we set out for home.

In short, God willing, we shall shortly come to you. We return the thanks due to you because you supported our son and showed us every loyalty; and we ask you not to be reluctant to do so hereafter, promising to reward all your goodwill worthily.

## LETTER CXXVIII. OF HENRY, BISHOP OF MINDEN, TO ABBOT WIBALD

He desires to employ the counsel of the bishops of Paderborn and Münster concerning the dispute between them. (Year 1149.)

To the venerable lord WIBALD, abbot of the holy Church of Corbie, HENRY—made bishop of Minden after having been a monk of Bursfelde and abbot of Saint Maurice—by God’s mercy what he is in the Church of Minden: the devoted offering, insofar as he is permitted, of prayers and faithful service.

We have often heard your envoys and letters, offering us brotherly satisfaction for every injury and grievance by which we consider ourselves harmed on your side. But the fact that we have delayed until now to reply to you has not arisen from contempt for your person or any pride of heart. Rather, we have waited in hope that the venerable lords, namely the bishops of Paderborn and Münster, would assist in the affair by their presence and, by their prudence and counsel, bring to a brotherly settlement the matters at issue between us.

But although those aforesaid lords and friends of ours, contrary to their promise—as you heard at Reims—are delaying, and, occupied by their own impediments, do not come to the assistance of our cause, we nevertheless cast our care upon God and have resolved still to await their consolation and counsel. By the judgment of their consciences together with mine, it shall be determined that I have not complained of you without cause.

## LETTER CXXIX. OF BERNARD, BISHOP OF HILDESHEIM, TO ABBOT WIBALD

He intercedes for Henry, formerly abbot of Corbie, that he may be received in the cloister of his profession. (Year 1149.)

BERNARD, by the grace of God humble minister of the Church of Hildesheim, to his venerable brother WIBALD, abbot of Corbie: the affection of sincere brotherhood and love in the Lord.

The sorrowful and shifting course of human calamities warns us to suffer with the afflicted and, considering our own grief or labor in the distress of others, to support those broken in heart, so far as we can, by counsel and aid.

Accordingly, Brother Henry, formerly abbot of Corbie but now humbled by the hand of the Lord, has fled to us and begs that through our intervention he may find mercy with you: namely, that you kindly receive him into the cloister of his profession and, by paternal consolation, foster and relieve his contrition.

And if perhaps you suspect that this may cause some controversy for your piety among any of your people, whether inward or outward, you shall receive from him whatever assurance you judge fitting in this matter, as well as enduring submission in obedience. I therefore ask that he may obtain through the goodwill of your affection what he trusts he can obtain through us. Farewell.

## LETTER CXXX. OF BERNARD, BISHOP OF HILDESHEIM, TO THE MEN OF CORBIE

On the same subject. (Year 1149.)

BERNARD, by the grace of God humble steward of Hildesheim, to his beloved brethren at Corbie: may you go from strength to strength until you see the God of gods in Zion.

As grave sorrow arises in the minds of religious persons at the loss of the holy flock, so joy and thanksgiving arise when the scattered are gathered again. Therefore Brother Henry, formerly abbot of this place but now brought low by the Lord’s judgment, desiring to return to you, asks that through our intercession he be commended to you: that you receive him in brotherly compassion for love of us, and that you reconcile to him the merciful affection of the lord abbot.

If he has perhaps grieved any one of you by his fault in any respect, he himself will make satisfaction to the extent of his ability; and your charity, compassionating the calamity which he has suffered, will mercifully forgive him. May the prayers of mercy and justice, therefore, prevail with the affection of your brotherhood, so that he may obtain with the desired effect that which he seeks through us. May the God of peace sanctify you in all things.

## LETTER CXXXI. OF WIBALD TO BERNARD, BISHOP OF HILDESHEIM

He relates at length the entire course of his election as abbot of Corbie and what followed it. (Year 1149.)

To his reverend Father and lord BERNARD, venerable bishop of the holy Church of Hildesheim, brother WIBALD, by the grace of God what he is in the Catholic Church: humble prayers and faithful service.

We delayed replying to the letters of your wisdom, which your graciousness sent us through our venerable fellow-brother, the abbot of the church of Saint Godehard, not from forgetfulness or negligence, but because afterwards we were occupied in business and travelling with such great cares and labors that no opportunity for writing back could come to us.

Now, therefore, offering to Your Highness the devoted service of greeting, we should wish, if it were possible, to reply briefly to your request, which bears with us the weight of a command. Yet the sequence of events is so extensive that knowledge of the truth would be excluded by a brief narrative.

First, we wish your discernment to know that, in the case of that Brother Henry whom Your Highness seeks to reconcile with the Church of Corbie, we gave neither counsel nor aid to those who deposed him. On the contrary, at the court held at Corbie in 1144, on the feast of the Apostle Saint Bartholomew, by Lord King Conrad, while the aforesaid brother then governed that same monastery, we stood for him not only steadfastly but effectively. By persistent entreaty, we obtained from the clemency of the lord king that the action of his accusers and the judicial procedure should not proceed against him once the suit had been formally instituted.

But when, before and under the jurisdiction of Lord Thomas of blessed memory, cardinal-priest and legate of the Apostolic See, he was convicted and confessed in the chapter at Corbie of simony committed in the sale of the church of Linwert, we were wholly unaware of those matters, being at the monastery of Stavelot, six days’ journey from Corbie.

And when, on the twelfth day before the Kalends of April, he was deposed by the aforesaid judge at the city of Paderborn, whither he had excused himself from coming, in a solemn assembly of religious persons, we were at Stavelot, prepared and equipped to depart for Rome on a royal embassy. This we did, leaving there immediately on the ninth day before the Kalends of April.

Thus, having been deposed there both from priestly office and from the dignity of the abbacy, and moreover excommunicated if in any way he harassed or disturbed persons or property of the monastery, he did not acknowledge the hand of the Lord upon himself or submit to the sentence of the judge. Instead, turning to rebellion and open violence, he plundered the goods of the abbey with extreme excess wherever he could; and at the following Easter, in the monastery of Hasungen, he went about adorned with the insignia of an abbacy and publicly celebrated the divine office.

Hasungen was a splendid Benedictine monastery, begun by Aribo, archbishop of Mainz, in honor of the holy Apostles Peter and Paul and Saint Heimerad the Confessor, and completed by Archbishop Sigefrid.

He granted whole estates of the abbey in fief and alienated many holdings, both by pledging them and by grants. When these things had been done, he presented himself before the royal presence at the court held at Kuina on the eighteenth day before the Kalends of May, believing that royal equity could be bent so that he might obtain by violence the abbey which he had lost by judicial process. But because the king’s honor loves judgment, not even money offered could twist the rod of rectitude of that illustrious ruler, so as to prevent the emperor from confirming what had proceeded from Peter.

Meanwhile, while he thus harassed and attacked the monastery with threats, gifts, and promises, our reverend Father Bernard, bishop of Paderborn, being summoned to the Church of Corbie, pronounced from the pulpit in a general assembly that the same Henry was excommunicated by apostolic authority, together with all his supporters and helpers. Consequently, a great many people, terrified by fear of God, withdrew from his party.

Meanwhile, the apostolic command pressed the Church of Corbie by many decrees to elect, through the Holy Spirit, as abbot a person able to repair the ruins of the Church of Corbie both in spiritual and temporal matters. But, because the factions were still too ardently devoted to their own interests, a canonical and unanimous election could not take place until the Nones of May, on which day we were at Sutri, a city of Tuscany, at the court of Pope Eugenius III.

Then, at last and only with difficulty, they chose a single man of unblemished reputation and praiseworthy conduct: Henry, provost of that same monastery. He was installed by the lord king on the sixth day before the Nones of August. At that time we were at the monastery of Stavelot, our health scarcely, and not fully, restored, because we had lain ill at Viterbo for five weeks with Roman fever; stripped by the violence of unnatural heat of skin and every hair, we had scarcely escaped the jaws of death.

The appointed predecessor therefore held office until the eighth day before the Ides of October and entered upon the way of all flesh. The Church of Corbie, again bereft of its shepherd, unanimously and willingly adopted and elected us—absent and far away—as father and shepherd of their souls, in the chapter at Corbie on the eleventh day before the Kalends of November.

They came to Stavelot and courteously and earnestly invited our weakness to the governance of so great a matter, both by their own letters and by the letter of the lord king, the lord bishop of Paderborn, and certain other princes, as well as by the personal address of envoys.

We were then at the synod of the Church of Liège, which our venerable Father Henry II, bishop of Liège, was holding according to custom. On our return we had turned aside to the monastery of Malmedy to celebrate the feast of All Saints. When we were already ready to enter the evening synaxis, a messenger from Stavelot came and informed us that envoys of the royal court were awaiting our arrival at Stavelot. They would not leave the place or communicate the words of their embassy elsewhere, except in the church of Stavelot, before the assembled brethren of that monastery.

Out of reverence for our lord the king, we immediately mounted horses and hastened to cross to the monastery of Stavelot. There, when it was already late, we received the commands of our lord the king and the princes, and also the request of the Church of Corbie, both in writing and through the words of the envoys.

Having examined and heard everything, we postponed the whole matter until the next day, in order to prepare our reply.

Now, venerable Father, in narrating we have reached a point at which we dare neither remain silent—because the consciences of our brethren redeemed by Christ’s blood must be healed and strengthened—nor speak safely, because of the mockery of those puffed up by pride and inflamed by ambition, and because of the good of our secret, which we fear may be made void. But let people take it as they will and judge it as they will: since we entered upon this in innocence, we shall report the truth, God being witness.

When we had been awakened for the morning synaxis by the canonical sound, this thought arose in us: after the completion of the morning office, we ought to summon our faithful people, both brethren and laymen, so that, after deliberating slowly and carefully upon the word we had received, we might answer with counsel.

Our uncertainty whether to take either course, and our failure to reject with the proper strength of humility—or, perhaps, fear—the position of honor offered to us, was urged by a memory of certain past events. For even before this, some churches had called us to a place of governance, deceived by the public acclaim of popular judgment. But conscious of our own weakness and ignorance, we answered them in full and true freedom with the prophetic words: “I am not a physician; there is no clothing in my house; do not appoint me ruler of the people.” Thus, our habits having been formed without avarice and content with present circumstances, we served the monastery to which we were enrolled, even if not with a model worthy to be seen or a zeal sufficient for faithful administration.

Meanwhile, through the instigation of the enemy of all good, a grave and protracted dispute arose between us and certain bailiffs of the monastery of Stavelot—men powerful in lineage, following, and wealth. These bailiffs wished to possess the sanctuary of God hereditarily; receiving the offices of bailiff by paternal and ancestral succession, they lorded it over the property. They stubbornly nullified the ordinances made by us and our provosts, oppressed the tenants with unlawful and incessant exactions, and paid the monastery none of the just dues.

Thus, often and severely distressed by the miserable and importunate outcry of the people, whose land was now almost wasted and desolate, as well as by the monks’ hunger and the collapse of discipline through lack of food, we began, at an unfavorable time, to resist the tyrants. We were certain, as far as one could be certain concerning the future, either that our safety would be endangered or that we could not bring so necessary a cause to a salutary conclusion.

For, to say it with pain and groaning, all rights had perished, laws had fallen, the discipline of morals had been extinguished, the custom of antiquity had been abolished, and the authority and power of king and princes had become obsolete. Everyone was free to do whatever pleased him, and whatever anyone ordained possessed the force of law.

Therefore, while amid that turmoil we endured boundless labors and expenses, both at the Roman Church in the city—by whose clemency and protection we were greatly defended—and at the court of our most serene and illustrious lord Conrad II, king of the Romans, by whose favor and generosity above all we marvellously sailed through those wondrous swelling waves of the sea, through the wonderful Lord on high, amid the hardships of travel and something like exile, amid the fatigue of journeying and conducting affairs, amid the stings of dangers, thoughts of our own weakness murmured against us and bitterly pricked the ear of our heart, saying:

“You suffer these things deservedly, because your God—refuge, strength, and helper in tribulations which have found you exceedingly—has already more than once offered you refuge in himself and through himself, whereby you could either have avoided these miseries altogether or endured them more safely.”

And although, venerable Father, we had by then entered some harbor of repose from the aforesaid storms, nevertheless, uncertain of the future and fearing similar or harsher things, we remained undecided, as stated, whether we ought to accept or refuse the favor offered to us. For we had formerly resolved never to preside over two abbeys at once, nor under any circumstances to endure being transferred to another, whether greater or wealthier.

In this twofold meditation, while the fire of desire to choose what was better had already been kindled, we proceeded to church, uttering some words of the psalms with our lips, though our mind wandered far away from their saving meaning. When we came before that altar at which we had received the episcopal blessing into the name and office of abbot, a certain familiar and intimate love which we bear toward the patron of that place—namely the most holy confessor and bishop of Christ, Remaclus, founder of that monastery—suddenly moved us. The inmost parts of our soul were shaken by an affectionate fear as we considered whether we would proceed to leave his monastery in this way.

Therefore our soul cried to God and to him with a vehement inward cry, in a word of hope that did not doubt, without bodily sound of the mouth: “Lord, let your will be done. Henceforth we have resolved to follow neither our own deliberation nor the counsel of our friends, but we desire in this present affair to follow your will and you, who are the way, the truth, and the life.

“But how shall we know your will? You are present in majesty, but we have departed far from you into a land of unlikeness, feeding swine. It is rash for us to presume to demand that you deign to make known to us your certain will concerning this matter, whether through an angel, through some creature subject to you, through a vision, or through an oracle. Yet it is neither impious nor presumptuous to search out the secret of your will through those in whom you dwell. Therefore, bound to you by this vow, we judge that we must follow the decision of our brethren and sons: whatever they say must be maintained, since you have entrusted their souls to our care, while we ourselves are poor guardians of our own soul.”

Thus, all doubt removed and all concern for reasoning and judgment laid aside, with peaceful mind and thoughts calmed and ordered, we completed the morning praises with the brethren. At the appointed hour, when the brethren entered the chapter-house, we entered with them. After a word of exhortation and after cloister discipline, we ordered the letters bearing the seals of the lord king, the princes, and the Church of Corbie to be brought in.

Having read the letters, the brethren, astonished at this unexpected turn of events, waited attentively for the expression of our will and our reply. “To this, my brothers, I say: since it has pleased divine Providence, which disposes all things sweetly, to advance us—who are the least of all in merit of life and in learning of wisdom—to the governance of this Church through the ministry of your unanimous consent, the control of both my soul and my body has ceased to be mine; and all that has been bestowed upon us by God in the substance of both the inward and outward person has passed over and been assigned to your lordship and authority, as if by a certain right of ownership. [Col. 1225D] We are yours, and we do not wish to abandon either you or your monastery. Therefore, seeking your counsel as an answer from God, we await it. Let no fear, no suspicion, deter you from speaking, under God’s inspiration, what seems expedient; for we have entered into such a covenant of vow and promise with our God that we cannot in any way depart from the word of your counsel. For if the offer of this dignity pleased us, if we desired to preside over the Church of Corbie in accordance with its election, we would not be handling this matter under the uncertainty of a multitude’s consent, evidently following the design of our own desire. But now, with God’s help, we have so firmly settled the intention of our heart that that part of your counsel will be most welcome to us which, by the gift of the Holy Spirit, is communicated to us by your brotherhood. We do not hesitate only to admonish your prudence that, insofar as it is lawful for your discernment—through God’s providence, which moves human hearts and works within them so as to incline their wills wherever He wishes—you should provide, counsel, and urge that which you judge to be most useful and safe for our souls and bodies and for your monastery.”

At first the brethren were dismayed by the weight thus laid upon them. They earnestly requested permission to await the presence of their absent brethren and of the Church’s ministerials, so that, after sharing counsel with them, they might together decide what seemed best to do. We, on the contrary, urged the pressing need of the envoys, who already wished to depart, [Col. 1226B] and especially the bond of our vow and promise, by which we were so bound that at that very hour those who were present had to release us in one direction or the other. Thus, after we had been sent out of the chapter-house, the brethren, exceedingly anxious and distressed, carefully considered both sides of the matter; and after long and extensive hesitation between the two, they at last admitted the envoys, wishing to learn more fully the entire course of the affair.

Bruno, provost of the New Church, who was the more distinguished among the envoys, spoke great things: namely, that the Church of Corbie possessed the free right of election, which it had now exercised unanimously and without dissension even over the slightest word; that it would sooner spend three thousand marks of silver than desist from securing [Col. 1226C] its chosen man; that Corbie had very great and peaceful wealth; that the brethren maintained religious life and desired and sought to increase it; that the ministerials were very wealthy, and that no dispute or litigation had arisen among them concerning the lawful possession of estates. Every fief or benefice would become free and unencumbered wherever male heirs did not succeed their fathers. Service due to the king, both in military expeditions, attendance at court, and provision of lodging, was abundant. That brother Henry, concerning whom the present question was raised, bore patiently the judgment of God and the sentence of his deposition; that he himself eagerly awaited the arrival of the man elected, rejoicing that none of those who had opposed him would succeed him; and that the deficiency of the monastery of Stavelot could be removed from the abundance of Corbie.

It seemed indeed an object of envy that a father and provider should wish to be defrauded of such great and unexpected advantages, when in the resources of the Church of Stavelot there was nothing but labor and sorrow. Yet these things seemed incredible. Therefore, when we had been summoned back to speak with them, they granted us the burden of undertaking the counsel involved in this prelacy, on the condition that the state of affairs at Corbie should be found to be as they had represented it.

Although the envoys strongly resisted, we sent to Corbie one of the monks of Stavelot, namely Brother Henry, a man of outstanding ability and prudence and endowed with singular steadfastness, together with letters attesting our position, [Col. 1227A] so that by careful inquiry he might investigate diligently the whole procedure of the election and the entire condition of the affairs of the monastery of Corbie. On arriving at Corbie, he was received dutifully and joyfully by all; yet they were grieved that our arrival was in some manner delayed. When he had been admitted to the common assembly of the brethren, he found no discord in the entire conduct of the election. Rather, once the fault of rash and presumptuous word or deed had been excluded, the wishes of all agreed together.

With the greatest caution it was ensured that he should not discover that Lord Henry had already set out for Rome to restore his case and reclaim the abbey; for they had already learned with certainty from the envoys that we would not willingly move even to secure circumstances, nor would we wish to undergo a contest in order to obtain any [Col. 1227B] prelacy. Our aforesaid brother was sent back to us with letters from the Church containing fuller testimony of the desire and concurrence of all concerning our person, and inviting us with favorable affection to assume their governance.

But our lord king repeatedly summoned us to his court by frequent commands, severely angered because the Church of Corbie—a by no means small member of his realm—was collapsing through what he regarded as our negligence or delay. We therefore came to the town of Frankenevort on the fifth Ides of December [9 December], believing that the lord king was there, as he himself had informed us through messengers and letters. There we found not a few monks, clerics, and laymen of Corbie, who had come by mandate [Col. 1227C] and testimony of all the rest in order to secure their election.

Then, by a circumstance which the Corbieans did not wish us to know, we learned that Lord Henry had approached the presence of the pope for his restoration. How greatly fear and sorrow affected us cannot be expressed in words. We were held by the obligation of the divine command which we had received through the mouth of the brethren of Stavelot: namely, that we should continue the journey once begun in response to the summons of the Corbieans. Yet our own reasoning resisted us, and the not implausible supposition terrified us that we might offend against the Roman Church and be grievously crushed beneath a mighty hand if the pope should insist upon reopening the case of the Corbieans. We grieved and wept, and it went ill with us.

[Col. 1227D] Therefore, at the first crowing of the cocks, while the Corbieans slept, we withdrew—not secretly—hoping that we might find our lord king at the monastery of Lorsch, as we had received word from him through a messenger, and might somehow prevail with him, if perhaps it were God’s will that we should not reach Corbie.

[Note: [Col. 1227D] Lorsch, afterward called Aldenmunster, was a distinguished Benedictine monastery on an island in the diocese of Mainz. It was founded about the year 764 by Cancor, the illustrious count of the Rhenish district, and his religious mother Williswinda, under the patronage of Saints Peter and Paul; Saint Nazarius was added not long afterward as patron, because the relics of that saint were translated there.]

When morning came, the Corbieans followed us indignantly; and, by God’s ordering, before they reached us they encountered the lord king on the road. With all the power of their ingenuity they pleaded with his clemency not to leave them—who trusted in him—bereft of their hope and [Col. 1228A] election and placed in perilous uncertainty. He kindly comforted them and made them full of good promise; he had them lodge with him in the village called Winheim.

On the following day we came not merely summoned, but also adjured by faith and oath—more compelled by the urgency of God’s ordinance, which had sounded through the mouth of His servants, than driven by fear of royal majesty and displeasure. That day was spent in the pleadings of each side. In the royal household we sought intercessors—we who had often previously interceded even for many condemned persons—and we importuned our friends, as though doubting their loyalty: namely, the venerable Anselm, bishop of Havelberg, and Arnold, provost of the greater church at Cologne [Col. 1228B] and chancellor of the royal court. From our youth we had embraced them with the greatest affection and venerated them with earnest devotion, our charity increasing daily. With great urgency of prayers we begged them to stand by us and turn the prince’s mind away from this purpose.

For what gave us courage to dispute and resist beyond the firmness of our vow and the answer received was that our brethren had given their counsel subject to a stipulated condition: that we should follow that course only if no fault or deception lay concealed in the action or report. Why prolong the matter? All that was said could not be comprehended either by the brevity of time or of a letter. Therefore, troubled and deprived of all counsel, amid the greatest interruption of tears [Col. 1228C] and sobs, we relinquished the defense of our cause, committing the outcome and decision of the affair to the judgment of the lord king. Yet we had considered this prudent course: royal clemency would then be compelled to withdraw from its purpose when we had entrusted ourselves, our honor, and our reputation to his good faith.

But he persisted in the firmness of his promise and, as though triumphing in the successful progress of his will, summoned the Corbieans; and while we were silent, he publicly invested us, according to solemn custom, with the abbey of Corbie. There we assumed a certain more resolute constancy of mind, deciding first to expose our person and all our possessions to loss rather than to strip the Church of Corbie of our counsel and aid [Col. 1228D] against the attacks of the aforesaid Henry. Dismissed from the royal court, we reached Corbie on the fifteenth day before the Kalends of January [18 December], where we were received with marvelous favor from all.

At Goslar, on the Nones of January [5 January], we were informed that this same Henry had returned from Rome, his business completed. Nevertheless, strengthened by the Holy Spirit, we proceeded to secure the Church’s affairs; and, contrary to the expectation of human judgment, we recovered without the obstacle of any great difficulty both the persons who had adhered more faithfully to him and the possessions which he had alienated.

[Col. 1229A] These are the possessions which, after his deposition, he had bestowed with a liberal hand: twenty *mansi* at Cropenstedem; in Nortlandia, the entire estate of Loningen and the entire estate of Buochoru; two *mansi* in the estate of Visbich; one *mansus* in the estate of Loten; one *mansus* in the estate of Werletem; one *mansus* in the estate of Mettesdorp; and certain other things—all of which, by God’s favor, we recovered.

But the report which we had received of his restoration was false. For he accomplished so little that he returned from the Apostolic See without a formal letter, bringing neither letters of recommendation nor evidence that he had recovered the priestly office and been absolved from the bond of excommunication. What the sacred authority of the canons decrees concerning letters to be received from the lord pope—especially from those who come before [Col. 1229B] him with a case—your learning knows better.

Accordingly, once all dissensions of the Church of Corbie, both within and without, had been calmed by God’s mercy and all difficulties leveled, we were sent by the lord king, together with the bishops of Worms and Havelberg, to meet Lord Pope Eugenius as he entered Gallia Comata (Long-haired Gaul). We met him in the town of Dijon on the third day before the Kalends of April [30 March] in the year of the Lord 1147. When it had been represented to him that the Church of Corbie had elected us abbot, guided by apostolic discretion and singular foresight, he did not wish to send any letters to the Church of Corbie, whether privileges or epistles, under our name, until he had learned more fully [Col. 1229C] the entire course and integrity of the election. He also judged that the transfer of persons from church to church, or the situation in which one person holds the office of pastor in one Church and that of visitor in another, belonged to the governance of his own authority.

Nevertheless, he treated us generously and honorably, not only out of reverence for the royal majesty whose embassy we bore, but also from private affection, since he had deigned piously to embrace us as one already long known to him. He then also enjoined upon us, by virtue of obedience and for the remission of our sins, that we should make war beyond the Elbe against the pagans, enemies of the Christian name and devastators of God’s Church. Yet he knew that this could in no way be done by us except at the expense and with the military resources of the Church of Corbie.

[Col. 1229D] Therefore, by common counsel and with our assent, the Church of Corbie sent two of its brethren: Walter, prior of the monastery, and Reinher, provost of Cresburch—men indeed of proven character and honorable conduct, but neither of profound speech nor discernment; armed not with skill but with truth, not with eloquence but with innocence. They had never previously entered the Roman court. They came to the lord pope at Saint-Denis in the territory of Paris. Ten days later they were absolved in the city of Meaux, after our election and appointment in the Church of Corbie had first been confirmed in a celebrated assembly, dated the tenth day before the Kalends of July [22 June].

[Col. 1230A] For that reverend and pious Father deigned to commend our insignificance by public praise and to recommend us in the most ample terms to those who did not know us. He commanded the envoys, and through them all persons, to love and honor us as their father and lord; and, since we had pleased them so greatly after being sought with such effort and labor, they should not begin then to find us displeasing when we attempted to reform religious life and recover possessions. Rather, both for the restoration of discipline and for the recovery of estates, they were to support us with common counsel and aid.

For the man of subtle intelligence had understood that we labored under no taint of ambition either in obtaining or preserving the dignity of this prelacy, [Col. 1230B] but had stood for our innocence and reputation, and for certain undertakings of ours which we had begun at no small cost for the advancement of the monastery of Corbie.

Before the envoys had returned, we had crossed the Elbe with an armed force and the army of Christian princes into the land of the Lutici. We were besieging the fortress of Dunin [read: Dimin], under the banner of the Crucified One, when the oft-mentioned Henry came to Corbie with a small number of armed men but with a spirit much armed. Sending his envoys, he reminded the Church of its faith and oath and demanded that they receive him as their rightful lord. But they, mindful of true faith and their oath, fortified the monastery with arms [Col. 1230C] and defensive works, which still stand today, and undertook by the law of nations to repel force by force.

He had previously done something similar at the monastery of Aldesleve. There, after his return from Rome, he had been received as a guest by Hillin, abbot of that monastery, who had been taken there from the congregation of Corbie and was considered by many to be a discerning and learned man. With that abbot’s permission, Henry appeared in festal processions marked with a pastoral staff. The transgressor himself repaid the presumptuous adviser for this betrayal: when the abbot was absent, he seized his seat and abbey in the chapter-house; but soon afterward, surrounded by Fritheric, advocate of that place, he escaped punishment by flight on foot.

[Col. 1230D] That aforesaid abbot, indeed a despiser of the canons and of the Apostolic See, abandoned the care of his monastery and brethren and set out for Jerusalem with the armed host; there he was drowned at sea. When his death was announced, the aforesaid Henry wished to obtain the abbey without canonical election and attempted to secure through us his installation by Margrave Adelbert.

There survives a letter—

[Note: [Col. 1229D] Letter 117, to F., abbot of Saint Godehard.]

—in which we replied to his persuasion and to that of certain men of no obscure name. Having returned from the Slavonic expedition on the Nativity of the Blessed Mary [8 September]—an expedition which, though we did not carry it out effectively because of our sins, we nevertheless completed obediently—we found the Church disturbed by the attack of the aforesaid man. Both concern for Christian [Col. 1231A] salvation and a special interest of our monastery had drawn us to that expedition: namely, the recovery of a certain region called *Ruiana* by the Germans and *Rana* by the Slavs, which Emperor Lothair had granted to the monastery of Corbie by imperial donation. We grieved and feared more because of the treachery and obstinacy of those who had supplied him counsel and assistance than because of his own rashness.

Last year we were at Trier, at the court of the lord pope. Returning thence with grace and the strengthening of the apostolic blessing, we received letters to the Church of Corbie full of favor and good hope. They directed the Corbieans to love and honor us as good and humble sons; to offer us, their pastor, due reverence and obedience; and to stand manfully by us in recovering and retaining the possessions and goods of the Church of Corbie.

[Col. 1231B] His so frequent deposition, our so repeated confirmation, and the so persistent command of apostolic authority were of no avail. The land is sown with lies, sown with scandals; and, as is the custom of the people, they first suffocate a man with false accusation before he realizes that he himself is being attacked. We came to the Synod of Reims, held in the middle of Lent. Wishing to provide for the peace and tranquility of the Church of Corbie, the lord pope confirmed by word and writing the sentence which our venerable father of blessed memory, Thomas, cardinal priest and legate of the Apostolic See, had pronounced verbally against Henry, formerly abbot of that monastery.

[Col. 1231C] The sentence of the aforesaid cardinal and legate—which we possess in writing and sealed with his image—was as follows:

> “We,” he says, “having taken counsel with the bishop of Paderborn and others who were present, deposed him from abbey and priesthood because of the unfitness of his person, his confession of simony, disobedience, and other grounds; releasing the monks from obedience and all who had sworn him fidelity from the obligation of their oath. If, upon seeing or hearing these letters, he should stubbornly wish to remain in the abbey, and should attempt, either personally or through any subordinate person, to harm the Church in its persons or property, we excommunicate him from the next Palm Sunday.”

[Col. 1231D] Let him consider his absolution; let him consider the restoration of his priestly office. These things were pronounced against him in judgment and written under seal. But see how, though admonished so often and so sharply, he has come to his senses.

In June he came to Geseke, to the house of his sister, an abbess who had neither received the sacred veil of a virgin through episcopal consecration nor received from a bishop the blessing for governing an abbey. Yet previously she had violently seized two abbeys, namely Eskenewage and Kaminata, besides the one which she now holds. There he consulted with four of our ministerials, the only laymen among them all who had exerted themselves most vigorously for his deposition.

He was reconciled to them with the kiss of peace—would that it had been for the sake of Him who is charity. But deceit was found in their mouths. One of them, in hope of some temporal bargain, both summoned him and he came there; the account of this matter ought neither to burden your most holy ears nor to contaminate our profession or style. From the fruits we clearly recognized the root of their meeting and the tree of their counsel.

[Col. 1232A] Departing from that conference, they began gradually and secretly, through persons of the lowest condition and fortune, to spread among the populace that we would by no means return, that the lord to whom they had been reconciled would recover the abbey, whether by right or wrong; meanwhile they disseminated among the people cursed and incredible insults concerning our person and manner of life. Their audacity advanced. They began to assail their equals and, casting aside reverence for our name and authority, attacked them with plundering and robbery. Moreover, within the walls of our monastery precinct they brought a class of desperate men: robbers, thieves, and certain outlaws, concerning whom public complaint cried out that they beset roads and routes and filled all places with brigandage.

By secret counsels they stirred the hearts of certain brethren who had become lax in their religious order. This evil prevailed to such an extent that, after our return—which this necessity had caused us to hasten before the appointed and suitable time—three younger brethren, although repeatedly urged to pray with us for our predecessor Abbot [Col. 1232C] Henry on the anniversary of his death, refused, because, they said, he had deposed their lord and had sat in his seat against the canons. For this rebellion and contempt, they were expelled from the monastery as disobedient and rash by the common judgment of all. The whole affair has been written out in separate letters.

[Note: [Col. 1231] Above, in the letter of this same Wibald to his brethren of Stavelot.]

There is no doubt that this poison flowed from the furnace of the aforesaid cabal. The hostility grew daily and, augmented by fresh developments, advanced so far that the very men of whom we have spoken attempted, through hired assassins, to murder us on the fourth day before the Kalends of January [29 December]. Frustrated in this wicked attempt, they broke open our stable, drove away four horses, and stabbed three with swords. This deed is on everyone’s lips [Col. 1232D] with a curse, and has filled us with anxiety and concern.

Let the reverend Father now weigh and let your prudence judge concerning your request that this brother be received into our cloister: he is a man of such changeable and unstable mind, accustomed to yield to the counsels of the wicked rather than the prudent. This is to hide fire in one’s bosom. You have now heard what evils he has done us; understand now what benefits we have conferred upon him.

A certain young man, Conrad by name, son of his brother, had been in his service; he returned to us before the sweat of his Roman journey had yet dried. We treated him [Col. 1233A] not merely mercifully but familiarly, providing food, drink, and sleep as though he were the guardian of our body. We also raised him through honor, property, and an honorable marriage. He had left at Corbie a boy, his sister’s son, born in that manner concerning which the laws and ordinances of the Fathers decree that those so conceived should be confined in the prison-houses of monasteries. He himself had been unable to place the boy in a monastery; but we, in view of divine recompense, had him tonsured, clothed in the garments of the Rule, and joined to the community of brethren.

One of those with whom he was recently reconciled, to whom he frequently sends envoys, had branded him with the searing iron of grave disgrace: he had destroyed certain buildings near the monastery and prevented their inhabitants from entering [Col. 1233B] the monastery. Prompted by shame at such inhumanity, we hastened to erase that stigma. We approach this subject with shame and hesitation because of the Apostle’s words: “Considering yourself, lest you too be tempted”; and: “Let him who stands take heed lest he fall.” We think it best to pass over one true matter, which, although it was a gift, we do not reckon as a benefit from us: namely, that we clothed him with all his double garments on the very day when we almost lost our lives, together with the horses, at the hands of hired robbers.

Therefore ambition is detestable: it blinds the eye of the mind, darkens the sight of religion, and annihilates fear of God and reverence for human beings. O height of divine counsel! O most righteous depth of providence! O unsearchable [Col. 1233C] ways of God! While, conscious of our frailty, we reject honor, we are caught by divine counsel; when in body and soul we strive toward long-desired rest, by the judgment of eternal providence we fall into inextricable and anxious labors. On this way of the Lord, when we love, we receive hatred; when we show mercy, we are afflicted. Certain accusers, witnesses, and collaborators in the deposition of that man rally around the man they had crushed, kindle hatreds, arm wrath, and strengthen presumption—not because they love him, but because they themselves are restless.

What your learning wrote—that we should kindly receive the oft-named brother into the cloister of his profession and foster his contrition by raising it with paternal consolation—seems to advance a certain legal argument. But to our weakness it appears in no way just, lawful, or regular that he should return for protection to that guardianship from which he was once emancipated. By emancipation we understand an abbot’s promotion, because one diminished in civil status cannot lawfully become a guardian. Therefore, just as one deposed from the prelacy of a dignity cannot by law be compelled to live unwillingly where he formerly presided, so it seems to us that a Church cannot be compelled to receive into the innermost place of its dwelling, with fear of future scandal, one whom it has deposed—not to say nourish him—unless perhaps he bears patiently the sentence of his deposition and, having returned to concord with his adversaries, grants in assent to the election the man whom thereafter he may have as father and guardian without obstacle of contradiction.

[Col. 1234A] That man neither attended nor accepted the two elections which, after his deposition, were celebrated according to the order of canonical institution. Rather, he opposed them, and to this day does not cease to cry that he was deceived and oppressed by force, although his own confession, the testimony of his accusers, and the irrefutable evidence of this deed plainly show that he was justly condemned. It is neither safe, honorable, nor peaceful for him to live in one house among persons who, by God’s judicial action, deposed him through their accusation and testimony—unless worldly ambition has been completely purged from his mind, firmly grounded in humility.

Moreover, we do not wish your Excellency to be unaware that, in the letters in which Lord Pope Eugenius confirmed his deposition, he is known to have decreed that if this same Henry should presume to disturb the peace of the monastery of Corbie and, having been admonished twice and a third time, should not come to his senses, he should not merely have no further office of prelacy there, but should also be forbidden thereafter to remain there among the subjects.

[Col. 1234B] When he was returning from that assembly of evil men held at Geseke, as mentioned above, he lodged outside the gates of the monastery in the house of a certain layman formerly familiar to him. There he was visited by some young men eager for novelty, summoned to church in the hours before dawn, and greeted. On leaving in the morning, he found workmen on the wall of the new buildings which we had begun to erect. He urged them to diligence in their work and promised that they—and likewise our chamberlain, upon whom we had imposed this responsibility—would receive due reward from him personally.

These were the words of a foolish man. But, as you know, the people began to magnify them and filled everything with suspicion and fear, so that even men who ought to have shown greater judgment were led into offense. For this reason we admonished him through our venerable fathers and fellow abbots: namely, through the abbot of Reinehusen, the abbot of Northeim, the abbot of Saint Godehard, the abbot of Gravenkirch, the abbot of Flietorp, and the provost of Richenberch. Thus we believe the sentence of the lord pope to be confirmed: that the same lord should henceforth be neither resident nor lord of the monastery of Corbie.

[Col. 1234D] Dearest Father, we judged it fitting to write these things to you—perhaps at greater length than suits your occupations or health—but we have done so in order that the whole sequence of events might become more fully known to you, and that our insignificance might find a calm excuse before your discernment for the fact that such necessity does not permit us to grant your request.

That we write in the plural does not arise from pride of heart or pomp of language, nor to make speech more bloated by swollen diction or more numerous by extended expression. Rather, we do this from our custom—that is, the custom of monks—who possess nothing singular or private except: “Through my fault, I have sinned.” Perhaps we take on an unnecessary but nevertheless dutiful task: teaching Minerva the arts, carrying wood into the forest, sending waters into rivers, helping the sunlight with lighted torches.

[Col. 1235A] Do not grieve, dearest Father, that you do not have what bedbugs and little worms have—

[Note: [Col. 1235D] That is, eyes, of which Bernard had been deprived for nine years before he departed this life. Therefore he took as coadjutor Bruno, dean of the supreme chapter, according to the Chronicle of the Bishops of Hildesheim, published in vol. II of *Scriptores Brunsvicenses*, p. 292.]

—for you have what many people do not have. Do not, I say, be sad that you lack that by which no one has ever seen God, because you possess that by which blessed are those who will see God. God’s judgments are a great abyss; and: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God! How incomprehensible are His judgments and unsearchable His ways!” He grants security and abundance of every possession to tyrants and destroyers of churches, but takes away the sight of the eyes from devout and learned bishops, lest they see their flock with eyes of flesh and be able to fulfill the office of the altar.

[Col. 1235B] The Apostle too endures something he does not wish, on account of which he entreats the Lord three times. But he is told: “My grace is sufficient for you.” To humble the pride arising from revelations, a certain reminder of human weakness is added, in likeness of triumphant men, to whose chariot a companion clung behind, saying at every acclamation of the citizens: “Remember that you are a human being.” Farewell.

## LETTER CXXXII. THE MONKS OF CORBIE TO BERNARD, BISHOP OF HILDESHEIM

They set forth three reasons which deter them from receiving Henry, their former deposed abbot. (Year 1149.)

[Col. 1235C] To the most holy lord and father BERNARD, venerable bishop of the holy Church of Hildesheim: the community of the Church of Corbie offers the earnestness of devout prayer and the due constancy of charity.

The venerable abbot of Saint Godehard came to us—

[Note: [Col. 1236D] Undoubtedly Frederick, mentioned above: long beloved and familiar to the Corbieans, and therefore called by some “of Corbie”; although the popular chronicles more firmly establish that he was of Fulda.]

—a man long beloved and familiar in our monastery. He brought to our insignificance letters from your Holiness requesting that we be reconciled with Lord Henry, formerly abbot of our Church, and not reject him if he wished to live among us. The reason why we delayed at that time to answer your fatherhood in person was that we were held in great anxiety concerning this matter. In so difficult a question, which could cause scandal to our Church, we judged it inappropriate to determine anything without consulting all, most of whom were then absent.

[Col. 1235D] What we have now found in counsel we make known to your Highness through this letter expressing our unanimity, asking at the outset that our lord not be angry with us because we cannot comply with your request. The man for whom you intercede has inflicted great affliction upon our Church: first, when he was violently thrust into the dignity of the abbey by his brother Count Sifrid; next, when, having been placed in authority, he proved useless and harmful to the Church; and afterward, when, deposed by God’s judgment, he persecuted our Church with many and great wrongs insofar as he could.

To ensure that we may be excusable before your Excellency, we shall set forth in a few words his violent intrusion into the abbey, in which we shall speak as truthfully as we grieve over things seen and experienced. When our lord Abbot Adelbero, of pious memory, had entered upon the way of all flesh, Lord Henry was still among us in the years of adolescence, recently released from the yoke of cloistered discipline. He aspired to the dignity of the abbey and obtained it through the assistance of his brother Sifrid.

[Col. 1236A] For at the very moment when the elder abbot had died, that count sent secret messengers to the archbishop of Mainz. While we remained unaware of this, he craftily arranged for us to postpone by three days the election which, according to the custom of the monastery, we ought to have held on that same day. After the three days had passed, envoys of the lord of Mainz arrived with letters sent to us by him. The letters contained the archbishop’s request and recommendation that the count’s brother be chosen abbot, and finally even a certain threat if we did not give assent to his request for that person.

“If,” he said, “you do not elect him, and something untoward should result, it will be neither my wrongdoing nor my sin.”

The envoys of the same man moreover spoke certain monstrous threats, [Col. 1236C] declaring that, if another were chosen, their lord the archbishop would forbid his consecration and would finally oppose us before the lord pope. The day therefore came when, after the solemn invocation of the Holy Spirit according to the custom of the Church, we sat in chapter to choose a father and shepherd of our souls. But the aforesaid count was anxious to secure the promotion of his brother. Accordingly, by personally approaching, one by one, all who might advance his desire, and through secret messengers, he solicited one by persuasion, another by flattery, another by threats, to support the election. Indeed, through confidential messengers, he promised our provost under a strict threat [Col. 1236D] that, if he impeded his brother’s election in any respect, he would utterly strip him of every honour in our Church.

When therefore the count’s will had been publicly stated, and certain brothers, filled with the Spirit of God, resisted and gave many fitting reasons for their objection—whether because the said Henry, whom they were being compelled to elect, was under age; or because, being almost unlettered, he was in no way capable of discharging the office of so great a dignity by word and teaching; or because, lacking counsel and every kind of [Col. 1237A] prudence, he could neither govern himself nor direct or rule so great a concern; or because the liberty and regular order of election seemed annulled by one who was to be appointed more from fear of his brother than from regard for God and the common good—when, I say, such grounds of excuse were set out, the count, who sat with us in chapter attended by armed men, raged with great fury and anger against those who spoke thus. It later became quite clear to them what he was then plotting against them.

Finally, when agreement in the election could in no way be achieved, this grave pronouncement was laid before us: unless we elected this named person, we would soon see the body of our venerable father, Abbot Adelbero—a blessed old man indeed, whose memory [Col. 1237B] is in peace among us—cast out of the church to our disgrace. The same count nevertheless promised that, if his brother were elected, he would give the Church much assistance and would serve faithfully and devotedly both in his own person and through his resources. How he fulfilled this promise was demonstrated by the outcome of events: once his brother had been made abbot, he continually descended upon him and the Church with his wife and a great multitude, and did not leave him until he had consumed the provisions on which he was to live for the entire year so completely that he left not even bread for his table.

Thus we elected his brother, not so much induced by these promises, which we suspected to be empty and false, as overcome by the terrors and threats of one whom alone we regarded as prince and lord over [Col. 1237C] us—especially lest an outrage be committed against the Church in the person of our dead father. We did not dare refuse what we clearly perceived to be his will. Yet the election was not unanimous, for the aforesaid brothers persisted in their objection; and when he returned from Fulda, having received investiture from the lord king, though the king was greatly unwilling and compelled by his brother’s prayers, they withdrew from his reception because they would not consent to an election not made according to God. Therefore the count and the new abbot, without consulting us, exiled these same men, four in number. Some of them were quite learned and had lived honourably among us; they were much loved by us and were removed from [Col. 1237D] our community not without great grief.

One of them, who had appealed to the presence of the lord pope, was afterwards seized by the same Lord Henry, thrown into chains, intolerably afflicted by hunger and thirst, cold and nakedness, and consigned to prison for three months. Such was his entry into the abbacy. How useless he was in the Church during his prelacy, and how foolishly he conducted everything, may sufficiently be shown by a single example.

When his brother’s benefice had reverted freely to the Church—a benefice from which our resources might have been greatly increased—he let it slip from his hands without benefit either to himself or to us. He utterly neglected this honourable opportunity to do good, which God had offered him as though he were asleep; and, through the entanglement of various arrangements, he ensured that none of his successors [Col. 1238A] could derive benefit from it. We refrain here, lest we weary the reader by prolixity, from setting out how he was finally deposed by Lord Thomas, cardinal-priest and legate of the Apostolic See, having been accused and convicted of simony, violent intrusion, personal incapacity, and disobedience; for we do not believe this to be unknown to your discernment.

Since, therefore, through God’s mercy our Church has been freed from his person, we give thanks to God and have firmly established by a pledge to remain valid for ever that henceforth he shall be neither lord nor resident of our place. Nor did we consent to his deposition in order that we might set him over us again. For we know that, unless he were aspiring to [Col. 1238B] restoration to his dignity, he would by no means so earnestly seek to remain subject where he had once ruled—especially since at first he rebelled against the Apostolic See, and, after the heads of so many of his attempts had been cut off, he has daily ventured to rise again in threefold assaults. Therefore we do not wish him to be among us, since, should an opportunity arise, he might again desire to lord it over us.

We have also received this present year letters of the lord pope confirming his deposition. In them he commanded that, if Henry should presume to harass the Church of Corbie and, after being admonished once, twice, and a third time, should not come to his senses, he should not only lack the dignity of prelacy from which he was deposed in the monastery of Corbie, but should thereafter not even dwell among its subjects. Our lord abbot, therefore, with the common counsel of our chapter, has already admonished him more than three times, through venerable and religious persons, while he was harassing our Church; yet even after admonition he did not cease from harassing us. Bound, then, by the lord pope’s command, [Col. 1238C] we do not presume to receive him into our fellowship, lest through our disobedience we fall into the hands of the lord pope and prove ourselves likewise disobedient.

We therefore beseech your fatherhood not to take harshly our inability to comply with your request for his reception. We have set forth to your discernment, as briefly as we could, the reasons for our impossibility; considering these with the prudence innate in you, hold us excused in your favour. Excepting this request, which we grant to no mortal, you will find us ready and devoted servants for all that lies within our power. Farewell in the Lord.

These letters were read in the common assembly of the brothers and approved by the testimony of all. The following brothers were present: Prior Walther; Erminold; Ingram; Engelger; Theoderic; Herman; Provost Adelbert; Adolf; Conrad; Elving; Metfrid; Ysico; Thegenhard; Henry; Bruno; Abraham; Marquard; Bruning; Eico; Luidolf; Lampert; Erkebard; Henry; Adelbert; Werncher; Othelric; Arnold; Reimar; Frederick; Unarch; Wernher; Ruopert; Hartmann; Saxo; Adelbert; Reinher.

## LETTER CXXXIII. LETTER OF ABBOT WIBALD

Concerning the agreement between Provost Reinher and Count Elvir. (Year 1149.)

[Col. 1239A]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. WIBALD, by the grace of God abbot of the Church of Corbie, to all present and future, for ever.

The office of our prelacy seems to require that we keep vigilant watch with prudent foresight over ecclesiastical property and persons which, by God’s ordering, we have undertaken to govern and administer, lest the Church entrusted to us suffer loss in its possessions, or our subjects be disturbed on account of the Church’s property by some occasion of schism, as commonly happens. For surely, just as one who sows discord among brothers deserves God’s wrath, so we hope to receive grace from God when we sow concord among brothers.

Let the whole body of our faithful know, therefore, how we recalled our beloved son Reinher, provost of Eresburg, and our ministerial Elvir, count of Horhusen, to peace and concord concerning the agreement for the tithes of Nien and Heflike, which belong to the custody of the Church of Corbie. Although the custodian of Corbie had always freely held these tithes in his own hand, selling or assigning them to whom he wished, Elveric obtained, in the time of our predecessor the elder Lord Henry, the right to redeem half of those tithes for one year only. After this had been granted, in the following year he again obtained, through many entreaties directed to us and to the custodian, the redemption of the same tithes, without yet raising any claim concerning an agreement. Nevertheless, in the third year he asserted that he had received them from our predecessor Lord Henry under an agreement of redemption. When we contradicted him and denied that there had been any agreement, he wished, despite our objection, to establish his asserted agreement concerning those tithes by judicial process and according to the law of his peers. But because we prevented this, he was long and greatly troublesome to us, as though we were depriving him of his right.
