Finally, since we could find no way to settle this case so that peace and concord might be maintained between him and the provost of Eresburg, we ended the dispute by the following counsel. With the advice of our faithful men, we divided the redemption of the same tithes between them: the provost of Eresburg shall redeem one half, and Elveric the other half each year, but only until the end of Elveric’s life, on condition that, on the vigil of St James, each of them shall send to the custodian of Corbie thirty solidi for the tithes through his own messengers. After Elveric’s death, his half of the tithes shall freely revert to the hand of the custodian of Corbie. And so that this settlement may remain firm and inviolable for Elveric, the provost of Eresburg, and the custodian of Corbie, we have ordered this charter to be drawn up as testimony to the transaction and sealed with the seal of St Vitus.

## LETTER CXXXIV. ABBOT WIBALD TO PROVOST B.

The difference between lying and stating a falsehood. (Year 1149.)

[Col. 1240A]

Brother WIBALD, by the grace of God what he is in the Catholic Church, to his beloved brother and friend Provost B., greeting and blessing.

These are the words of a certain wise man: “There is a difference between stating a falsehood and lying. He who lies is not himself deceived; he attempts to deceive another. He who states a falsehood is himself deceived.” He added likewise: “He who lies,” he says, “deceives, so far as lies within him; but he who states a falsehood does not deceive, so far as lies within him.” He also says this on the same matter: “A good man [Col. 1240B] ought to take care that he does not lie; a prudent man, that he does not state a falsehood.” And we, dearest brother, have by no means lied; but it was not imprudence, but necessity, that compelled us to state a falsehood. Accordingly, we ask for a further extension of the truce, so that we may be proved neither to have lied nor to have stated a falsehood.

## LETTER CXXXV. THEOTUIN AND GUIDO, CARDINALS, TO HENRY, BISHOP OF MINDEN

They reproach him for having prohibited the celebration of divine offices in the church of Kaminat. (Year 1149.)

T., bishop of Santa Rufina, and G., cardinal-deacon and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, to their venerable brother HENRY, bishop of Minden: greeting.

The brothers of the monastery of Corbie have complained to us that, when they had gone to the lord pope and remained with him for some time, you prohibited the celebration of the divine offices in the church of Kaminat, where they themselves had begun to restore religious observance. Since it is by no means compatible with your office that you should unjustly harass servants of God persevering in a good purpose, we command your affection to reach such an agreement with the aforesaid brothers that they may have no grounds upon which they can justly complain before the Apostolic See.

## LETTER CXXXVI. ABBOT WIBALD TO HIS BROTHERS OF STAVELOT

He mourns the death of his brothers, while rejoicing in their blessed end; but he especially grieves over the passing of E., in whom were found more faults of avaricious holding than was expedient. (Year 1149.)

[Col. 1240D]

Brother WIBALD, by the grace of God what he is in the Catholic Church, to the venerable dean Robert and the other beloved brothers in Christ, sons of the Church of Stavelot: blessing and life for evermore.

For a long time now we have received mournful letters from your side—not through any fault of yours, for you have always been accustomed both to wish and to report favourable things to us, and to conceal whatever might be more bitter until the final moment of necessity—but because God’s hand is stretched out over our monastery, calling our brothers to himself and taking from us brothers most useful and necessary, indeed, for divine matters. We are sorrowful, brothers, and mourn that those have been taken away from us who prayed for our people and our community, ever intent in heart and voice upon the love and praise of their Creator, humbly pursuing every obedience, and truly loving our person. But Christ rejoices in heaven with the angels that, by the gift of his grace, they have become citizens of his glorious city.

Lord Jesus, forgive us because we weep for those whom you receive: we do not begrudge you what you possess, but grieve that the bravest warriors have been withdrawn from our battle-line. Yet they now assist us more intimately with you, secure concerning themselves but concerned for us. You too, Lord, wept for Lazarus, perhaps because you were about to restore him to endure again the miseries of this life, though death had given him rest. Yet you shed tears from whatever human and friendly affection; and we shed tears not from despair but love, not from hatred but longing—not because they have passed to you, but because they have departed from us.

But just as those four brothers G., S., A., and W., dying a holy and Catholic death, full of hope and confidence, summoned us to follow them, so this last brother, E.—a man indeed of disciplined life, wholly occupied day and night with the law of his God—disturbed us by his unexpected death in one respect, not without the scruple of a serious offence. For, as you know, we had entrusted to him a certain part of the administration, from which he ought to have met the monastery’s obligations. In this he was led astray by the fault of avaricious retention, so as to leave behind more than was expedient for his salvation. Concerning all these things, commanding you collectively, we order that none of you presume to claim them as private or common property, or as though assigned by testament; but let all be preserved safe and intact at the dean’s disposal until, by divine grace’s help, we are restored to you and carefully determine together with you what is to be done with them.

Let your learning remember the spoil of Jericho devoted to the curse and to fire, and the danger of Achan, who secretly removed something from that same accursed thing—not because an inanimate and insensible creature, made for human use, deserves reward or punishment, but because by its destruction human disobedience is to be punished and avarice restrained.

The report recently received concerning us, which disturbed you with anxiety [Col. 1241D] for our safety, is partly false and partly true. For we have suffered some loss and a great injury; but God graciously dispenses the vicissitudes of human affairs and, by the moderation of an interposed bitterness, checks the swelling pride that might arise from the wonderful bestowal of his gifts, so that we may truly say with the Song of Songs: “My beloved is to me a bundle of myrrh.” Yet what has been committed by a few desperate robbers is being expiated with such zeal for vengeance by all the others who desire to preserve their fidelity and devotion that we greatly fear divine displeasure, while meanwhile suffering no danger to our honour or safety. God, however, is able mercifully to deliver us from all these things [Col. 1242A] and restore us to you at the acceptable time.

## LETTER CXXXVII. ABBOT WIBALD TO BERNARD, BISHOP OF PADERBORN

He leaves a certain case of his to be settled by Bernard’s judgment. (Year 1149.)

To his reverend father and lord BERNARD, venerable bishop of the holy church of Paderborn, Brother WIBALD, by the grace of God what he is in the Catholic Church: a son’s affection and a servant’s obedience.

We owe many thanks, and render many thanks, to your holiness because from long ago you have deigned to love and honour us with paternal affection. We have especially experienced this now, when the bitterness of such manifest calumny as we have endured has struck us more severely. For you bore both labour and expense not merely patiently, but even gladly; and you exercised such moderation in giving counsel that the cautious and circumspect standard of your discernment can be imitated by few. Therefore, having become from a friend one most dear to us, we have judged that the conclusion of our affair should be entrusted to your judgment, so that, without the distress of doubt, we may consider ourselves bound to follow that counsel which the prudence of your compassion and fidelity proposes to us.

Theoderic, count of Huxara, wishes, to use his own words, to “place himself in our mercy,” and to approach our satisfaction and reconciliation in whatever manner his peers—namely, the ministerials of the Church of Corbie chosen by our own selection and designated by name—shall prescribe. Since we are troubled and shaken like a drunken man, and whatever wisdom there was in us has been swallowed up, while the necessity of circumstances compels us to overlook some things and endure others, lest the vessel be broken while we seek to scrape away its rust, nevertheless we have determined to follow no course unless we perceive it to have met with your approval. For this reason, we have postponed dealing with and answering this case until next Monday, so that, fortified by the counsel of your discernment, we may more safely and better carry out what must be done. Nor do we wish the bearer of our letter to understand a word of what he carries or receives, since he is one of those involved [Col. 1242D]; rather, we wish to be fully informed of everything through your letter.

## LETTER CXXXVIII. BERNARD, BISHOP OF PADERBORN, TO ABBOT WIBALD

Reply to the preceding letter. (Year 1149.)

BERNARD, by God’s mercy the humble servant of the people of Paderborn, to his beloved brother WIBALD, venerable abbot of the holy Church of Corbie: prayers in the Lord, with every service of charity.

We strive to preserve inviolate the affection of love which we began to have for you from the time we came to know you, so that we spare neither our person nor our resources in preserving your honour and advancing your purpose. We desire to help you in all things, thoughtfully providing, insofar as God grants, whatever may benefit you. Therefore, in arranging the present case, we faithfully urge your discernment to do nothing without the counsel of your faithful men, both friends and retainers, so that, should anything of this kind arise hereafter—which God forbid—you may find them ready to support you.

We confess that necessity compels one to endure or overlook many things. Yet just as, in order to avoid a graver wound, it is sometimes the part of a wise man not to cut decayed flesh away to the quick, so, at times, unless healing of a wound arises from its very depth, a more grievous torment follows. And, as has been said, in order to fortify your prudent care, we exhort you not to admit any settlement without the confirmation of weighty testimony. For we think it safer to have open enemies than hidden ones who, with cheerful countenance, feign peace. “A new vessel long retains the scent with which it was first imbued.”

## LETTER CXXXIX. GUIDO, CARDINAL, TO ANSELM, BISHOP OF HAVELBERG

He communicates his wishes to him through the legate sent to Poland. (Year 1149.)

To his dearest brother and friend ANSELM, venerable bishop of Havelberg, GUIDO, cardinal-deacon and chancellor of the holy Roman Church: greeting.

Since we cannot often enjoy your presence, [Col. 1243C] we receive your letters with glad heart as standing in the place of your person. Through our brother Cardinal G., who is being sent to the regions of Poland, we have sent you letters containing our wishes on his behalf and concerning him. In brief, we embrace all matters concerning you: we keep you in memory and desire that every good thing may succeed for you. Greet in our name our common friend, the abbot of Corbie.

## LETTER CXL. THE SAME TO THE SAME

He desires to be informed of Anselm’s circumstances. (Year 1149.)

To his dearest brother and special friend ANSELM, bishop of Havelberg, GUIDO, cardinal of the holy Roman Church and chancellor: greeting.

Reflecting on the sweetness of your heart, which we have often tasted, we renew our friendship through this letter, desiring that you should make known to us as soon as possible your condition, which we wish to be prosperous. Through you we greet in the Lord our common friend, the abbot of Corbie.

## LETTER CXLI. ANSELM, BISHOP OF HAVELBERG, TO ABBOT WIBALD

He complains that his friend does not write to him and announces his imminent journey to the pope. (Year 1149.)

To his dearest brother and special friend, Abbot WIBALD, ANSELM, the poor man of Christ, sends himself.

[Col. 1244A] A certain wise man said that one ought to keep short accounts with friends; but for a long time now you have kept with me neither long accounts nor short ones, and you have not greeted me even with a single letter—especially since you, not I, have a supply of envoys. What is this? Where are you? Where have you got to? What is there between you and me? Why have you left me?

Weser, run backward; yet let the Havel run straight. Still, I always hold your absence present, whether you wish it or not. If you wish it, your will is with me; if you do not wish it, then it follows truly that, in the absence of your absence, you yourself are present, and likewise your will is with me. I am shortly going to the lord pope; if you wish to send any instruction, you can act through me as through yourself. I shall set out on the Sunday *Esto mihi*. The chancellor loves you greatly. That you may know this more certainly, I am sending you the letter which he recently sent me; when you have read it, send it back to me.

## LETTER CXLII. ABBOT WIBALD TO ANSELM, BISHOP OF HAVELBERG

He commends certain business to Anselm on his journey to Rome, especially in favour of the abbot of Hersfeld. (Year 1149.)

To his reverend father ANSELM, venerable bishop of Havelsberg, of a poor city and a small clergy, Brother WIBALD, by the grace of God what he is in the Catholic Church, sends himself.

You reproached what you consider our negligence in words drawn from the innermost sanctuary of love, because through so great an interval of time we have neither seen nor greeted you, especially since we do not lack a supply of envoys. But far be from us, dearest Father, that Lethean forgetfulness, that negligence not childish but utterly foolish, which might tear the memory of you and our deep love from our heart. It is written: “Where your treasure is, there also is your heart.” You, indeed, and the very few among the number of the perfect whom the goodness of divine generosity has given us as friends, without any prerogative of merits or affinity of likeness, are our treasure. From it we often draw, yet it is not diminished; thieves cannot take anything from it; moth and rust cannot corrupt it. Believe me, bishop: if we possessed the whole world but did not have you and those like you—who can be very few—as friends, we would be poor.

Mindful of you, therefore, and increasingly more ardently kindled in love, we waited for a favourable time when we might enjoy your long-desired presence and in prolonged conversation pour out the waves of our soul, by which we are daily troubled and shaken like a drunken man. For, most loving Father, we formerly had a wife who was bleary-eyed, barren, and moreover thin; but this latter wife, to whom we are joined in marriage, is indeed fatter, but no less bleary-eyed and barren, and moreover more obstinate, seeking novelties and grieving at her own peace. Would that you, good Jesus, granted me that transporting power of the prophet Habakkuk, [Col. 1245A] so that, when Bishop Anselm comes to Rome to that chancellor of ours who remembers us so kindly, we might lay bare the secrets of our soul to both of them and be strengthened by their counsel and consolation. For, divided between the two, we hold the wolf by the ears.

We had sent to Rome to notify the lord pope of the election at Fulda, at which we had been present by his command. On 30 December our messenger left the lord pope safe and well at Viterbo, and our chancellor Guido full of joy and good hope. In a rather long letter he showed us the affection he has conceived for our lowliness and so often expresses in his letters with longing. We love him as much as we can and understand—not because he helps us, but because he loves us; not because he is powerful, but because he is good. The lord pope also, by his kindness and clemency, has truly made us his own, so that love has cast fear outside. Greet him most warmly in our name, returning immense thanks for every benefit bestowed upon our lowliness.

Tell our common friend the chancellor that, even if we should never again see the Roman Church and City, even if we lived in the remotest wilderness, we should nevertheless belong to him in a singular manner, and that we shall diligently observe to the end what he directed us in his letters. We have sent to the feet of your compassion the abbot of Hersfeld, who, because he suffers violence—[Note: [Col. 1245D] See above the letter of the archbishop of Mainz to Pope Eugenius III.]—answer for him, since he does not know what to say to his enemies; so great are men’s rashness and madness. The substance of our petition on this abbot’s behalf is this: recover for him his office from the lord pope; and then, if you are willing and able, obtain from the lord of Bremen—which is easy for you—that he restore him to his abbey and determine his case by canonical law. Whatever you do for him, you will do for me.

See how unmindful of you we are! It is not said “we have been,” which concerns past and future, but “we are,” which concerns the present—that is, eternity. We had reflected upon a not ignoble question about the creation of angels, which we had resolved to write to your learning in order to stir your zeal by the necessity of answering. Likewise, we wished repeatedly to request from you your investigation—or reasonings [Col. 1245D] and arguments—concerning that “positive justice” of yours, so that we too might be alert by contributing, objecting, or agreeing. Would that we might be allowed, on your return from the City, to embrace and kiss you in the arms of true love, and to confer with you more privately and at greater length about the state of our most holy mother, the Roman Church, as well as the condition of the whole kingdom and the state of the whole world! For you are almost alone, or one among very few, who know how to enter and follow any path of reflection on these matters.

## LETTER CXLIII. ABBOT WIBALD TO POPE EUGENIUS III

He informs him concerning the condition of the monastery of Fulda. (Year 1149.)

[Col. 1246A]

To his most reverend father and lord Eugenius, sole and universal pontiff, Brother WIBALD, by the grace of God and yours what he is in the Catholic Church: affection as to a father, obedience and service as to a lord.

After A., formerly abbot of Fulda—[Note: [Col. 1246D] Ascholf, concerning whom see above the letter to Abbot Wibald.]—was deposed at Trier by the judgment of your equity, the Church of Fulda never returned to general concord. For those who had stood with the abbot and for the abbot were almost all expelled from the monastery, especially those who had appeared to hold offices of administration from long before. [Col. 1246B] This evil of dissension increased to such an extent that Brother Dudo, the bearer of this letter, as soon as he had delivered the letters of your command concerning the holding of an election, was seized at the gate of the monastery.

We too, commanded by your highness to come to Fulda, earnestly attempted to call them back to peace and to have them receive their brothers into the community, but because of sin we achieved nothing. Since it belongs to your moderation, therefore, after the likeness of the divine power which heals the broken in heart and binds up their wounds, to have care of all with mercy, provide that the wandering sheep may not be torn by wolves’ bites, and that the Church of Fulda—most extensive both in its territories and in your special lordship, and reformed by you in peace and religious observance—may hold the primacy of all honour.

## LETTER CXLIV. ABBOT WIBALD TO HENRY, ABBOT OF FULDA AND HERSFELD

That he may be willing graciously to receive his scattered sons. (Year 1149.)

To his most reverend father and friend H., venerable abbot of Fulda and Hersfeld, and to all sons of the Church of Fulda, both monks and laymen, Brother WIBALD, by the grace of God what he is in the Catholic Church: humble prayers and devoted service.

Your sons and brothers Lampert and Dudo, and certain others, have very often approached our lowliness, either personally or through their messengers, earnestly asking that, by the intercession of our request, we might open the way to your peace and reconciliation and to their return to their monastery, from which they complain they have been unjustly driven. Undertaking this at last, though reluctantly, out of regard for charity, we cast ourselves in spirit at the feet of each and every one of you and humbly beseech you to have mercy on your brothers. Since they neither left nor were expelled from the Church through fault in their own conduct, but a certain common discord—which ought firmly to be laid to rest—drove them from your fellowship, receive them with good grace into the community [Col. 1247A] and cherish them with kindly love as your sons and brothers. The judgment and petition of all our brothers present with us is the same, for they fear that some graver scandal may perhaps arise from this.

## LETTER CXLV. NOTICE OF A DUEL COMMUTED INTO AN OATH

(Year 1149.)

In the year of the Lord 1149, and the third year of the prelacy of Lord Wibald, abbot in the Church of Corvey, Count Theoderic of the town of Höxter was challenged to a judicial duel by Reinher of Porta. Reinher charged him with having caused, on his advice, the horses of his lord the abbot to be carried off and killed, and proposed to prove this against him by single combat. Since, therefore, on suspicion of such treachery, [Col. 1247B] Theoderic was held accursed and hateful both by the lord abbot and by almost all his fellow-ministerials, he declared himself ready and willing to clear himself of the imputed treachery by a duel against Reinher. But their wiser fellow-household members, considering that such a combat between two men of equal rank might take place only to the common disgrace of their peers, earnestly begged the lord abbot to accept Theoderic’s satisfaction, since he was prepared to return to his favour and make satisfaction for the crime alleged against him, whether through justice or mercy.

The lord abbot did not refuse this request. He chose eight of his ministerials—namely, old Charles, [Col. 1247C] Count Elveric, Henry of Riteh, Henry of Liutem, Godescalc of Godenlevesse, Bruno, Udo, and Reinmar—and appointed them counsellors for this reconciliation, promising that he would follow whatever they might decide in counsel, consistently with his own honour and that of the Church. Having therefore explained to them the reasons why Theoderic was not in his favour, he left it to them, after deliberating together, to arrange the reconciliation in a manner consistent with his honour and that of the Church, after first stipulating that they should not exclude Reinher from the reconciliation.

After long deliberation, the aforesaid eight at last agreed that the lord abbot should, by his authority and command, remove the duel between Reinher and Theoderic [Col. 1247D]; between Reinher and Theoderic; that Theoderic should swear upon the sacred relics of St Vitus that he was innocent of those acts which Reinher had charged against him and for which he had summoned him to combat; and that this oath should be taken without Reinher’s objection. Thus they were to be reconciled in the present matter by the lord abbot, both concerning this affair and concerning any other matters that might exist between them.

Theoderic was then to swear on the same relics that the lord abbot had lost his horses without either his will or his knowledge. Afterwards he was to swear that, after Lord Henry’s deposition, he had made no reconciliation with him. Further, he was to give the lord abbot twelve hostages from among his kinsmen, as security that henceforth he would knowingly do nothing against [Col. 1248A] the lord abbot either by deed or counsel. If he should ever violate this undertaking, he was to regard these twelve hostages as enemies and adversaries no less than the lord abbot himself.

The lord abbot accordingly acted as he had promised. Theoderic fulfilled the first oath, the one concerning Reinher. The second and third oaths, which concerned the lord abbot, the abbot of his own accord, even without being asked, remitted to him out of mercy. He forbade combat between the two men and then reconciled them with one another.

Thereupon Theoderic gave twelve hostages from among his kinsmen as pledges of his faith: namely Frither, the dapifer; Buno; Godescalc of Godenlevesse; Reinmar; Conrad Damet; Liuddag and Henry [Col. 1248B], brothers; Bertold; Count Elveric; Godefrid of Munekhusen; and two who were not present, whom he promised shortly to bring—Wernon of Jesikhe and Helmwig of Codolumen. The ten who were present, having pledged their faith and each individually placed his own hand in the abbot’s hand, promised in one and the same form that, if Theoderic violated his faith toward him, they would hold themselves continually as his enemies and adversaries unless he regained the abbot’s favour without their intervention.

When these sureties had been received upon this condition, the lord abbot restored his favour to Theoderic and received him with the kiss of peace. These things were done at Corvey on the sixth day before the Ides of February [8 February], in the presence of our senior brethren and of the noble young men, retainers of the Church: Count Adelbert [Col. 1248C] of Evelstein, Widikind of Sualemberch. Florentinus, son of Count Sifrid of Erteneburch, was also present, as were many of the Church’s ministerials.

## LETTER CXLVI. MANEGOLD TO ABBOT WIBALD

He praises Wibald for his knowledge of the liberal arts.  
(Year 1149.)

To Lord Wibald, venerable abbot of the Corveyans: Manegold, his man in all business, ready to use either hand as his right.

Whenever I consider the marriage of Mercury and Philology, sought with such concern by Virtue and Apollo and approved by the whole assembly of the gods; when, among other matters, I reflect on the coming of the seven Nymphs and attend to the distinctive properties of each [Col. 1248D], I ascribe to you the embraces of that most desirable marriage, offered not with fleshly arms. For with you I find the flower of all philosophy, knowledge both of divinity and of the seven liberal arts and of all their handmaids, and a library most excellently fitted for study. Besides this special industry, there is praised in you an inseparable accident and a proper attribute: namely, outstanding nobility of character.

Since natural philosophers maintain that people differ according to the qualities of their constitutions, it may easily be proved that you are tempered by the best constitution. Therefore you, who are not whitewashed on the wall but dark upon the surface of the body, shine in your breast with a marvellous brightness of virtues, knowledge, and character. [Col. 1249A] If I were to set out proofs of all these things to the degree that I know them, I should fear, by smoothing your ears with a favourable breeze, to be charged with the fault of flattery and hyperbole; and I should exceed the bounds of an epistolary compendium.

If, therefore, nature had polished anything perfect among human attainments, full perfection would surely not be lacking in you. Yet I have found nothing deserving correction, either in you, in your house, or in your household; nothing at all, whether in what is contained or in that which contains it, which now, under your skilful ordering, needs correction—except something contrary to orthography upon the lintel of the southern door. This was done neither through ignorance nor negligence, but through some design known to you.

For all these reasons, beyond what can be said or believed, the presence of your delightful company [Col. 1249B] is desired by me: not merely because you recently fed my body with many kinds of dishes, but because you refreshed my mind with more pleasing seasonings—namely gentleness and cheerfulness.

> Many, in rounded speech, have taught about the world:  
> For what purpose it was made, at what time it was touched, and whence it came.  
> From the writings of authors it is made clear to us from what source  
> And by what numerical reckonings  
> Those who say that all things had their earliest beginnings  
> In spring's favourable tempering.  
> It is evident that such beginnings assigned them aptness for things.  
> The king of spring is such;  
> Such is the constitution of spring.  
> Since earth, bound by frost, cannot bear fruit while dry,  
> It is ordinarily made alive by warmth, yet also by moisture.  
> Thus the world becomes fruitful  
> With renewed growth.
>
> Abbot, this marvellous constitution is seen in you;  
> [Col. 1249C] its reign in you is proved by its effects.  
> It has ploughed your heart to yield such beautiful fruits;  
> This has caused virtue to bear fruit in your heart,  
> Which commends fair character  
> And increases honours.  
> Therefore who could wonder at your prosperity,  
> When virtue favours you amid such integrity?

## LETTER CXLVII. ABBOT WIBALD TO MANEGOLD, MASTER OF THE SCHOOL

He replies to the preceding letter.  
(Year 1149.)

Wibald, by God’s grace steward of the Church of Corvey, to his beloved brother and friend Manegold, canon of the greater church at Paderborn and master of the school: may he understand the law in order that he may be wise; be wise in order that he may be provident; be provident [Col. 1249D] in order that he may live.

Brother, I was delighted by your letter—not because you praise me, but because I perceive that you are devoted to study; not because you exalt me with encomiums, but because you love me. No praise can be offered without love. For irony and whatever is spoken crookedly or obliquely are not praise. Praise derives its origin from the fountain of love; hence it is that we often even delight in the faults of friends. Pupils defend the opinions of their teachers not because they are true, but because they love their authors. School rages against school through hatred or love of their masters, and men defend with shouting what they cannot defend by reason.

Blessed Augustine says: “Those who love us seek the good things which they may praise in us; those who do not love us seek the bad things which they may say about us.” Thus [Col. 1250A] it is true that the proof of love is the performance of an act; for praise is a kind of act. Therefore I have attempted to reply to your natural talent not because I have been praised by you, especially in a false matter—for I neither feel nor recognize in myself the titles of praise which you ascribe to me—but in order to inflame your love more strongly and kindle in you the pursuits of learning. I have stolen from public business the night-hours in which I might answer you.

Contrary to my custom, I speak in the singular, although with our monks we are accustomed to speak in the plural. But I am writing to a scholar, one entering the paths of philosophy, who has drawn the ornaments of my praise from the very inner chambers of his studies. But what shall I say, or what shall I urge, when nothing can be said that has not already been said? Cicero denies that, even if [Col. 1250B] his lifetime were doubled, he would have time to read the lyric poets—much less, in the same time, the dialecticians. Perhaps you think he said this because, being a grave and serious man devoted to explaining the disciplines of philosophy, he cast aside such things as trivial and foolish? Yet his books are filled not only with their ideas but with their very words.

Before him, tragic, comic, lyric, dialectical, and sophistical poets had written so much that I say nothing of philosophy and of the teachers of the liberal arts. Even rustic matters—agriculture and architecture—had already been published in books by no few writers in his time. How many philosophers and poets lived in his age and after him! Read Tranquillus; read Cornelius Nepos and certain other pagans on illustrious men; you will understand that writings exist so numerous that scarcely even the most diligent student [Col. 1250C] can read them all.

I shall turn to our philosophers of the Christian law. Examine Eusebius’s *Ecclesiastical History* and the other ecclesiastical history called the *Tripartite History*. Turn over the books of Jerome the presbyter, Isidore the presbyter, and Gennadius the abbot, *On Illustrious Men*, and you will see what leaders the Church had after the apostles. You will understand that everything which can be said was preoccupied by those supreme philosophers, so that nothing new can now be said: not even a new place for error has been left.

Many have erred, and better men have rebuked and refuted their errors. Those very persons who strive to become heretics for disgraceful glory do not discover novelties, but repeat old things. They introduce into controversy superfluous [Col. 1250D] novelties of expression, which the Apostle commands us to avoid and which have been rendered obsolete by the correction of many, as though they had been discovered by their own reasoning.

What shall I say of the other most learned men who, after those already named, left splendid memorials of their intellect in the Church of God through writing and disputation? I mean Bede, Ambrose, Haimo, Autpert, Rabanus, John Scotus, and many others whose works we read; and likewise those whom we ourselves have seen—Anselm of Laon, William of Paris, Alberic of Rheims, Hugh of Paris, and very many others—whose teaching and writings have filled the world. Yet we, devoted to sloth and avarice, allow them to lie hidden beneath the blind night of forgetfulness, illuminating neither them nor their works [Col. 1251A] by any utterance.

Can I then forge new things when writing to you? By no means. Yet there will be something new, because, if things are plucked from the orchards of the ancients, they will seem new when planted elsewhere; and they will be new in that they are written to you, to whom they were not written before.

Now, therefore, in replying to the lines of your letter, I first accept gratefully and commend the fact that you took the beginning of my praise from your own art, according to Flaccus:

> Physicians promise what belongs to physicians;  
> Craftsmen handle craftsmen’s work.  
> —Horace, *Epistles* II.1.116.

But take care lest your judgement has erred in proclaiming in me knowledge and eloquence which are fashioned in that manifold [Col. 1251B] and enigmatic epithalamium of Martianus Capella. I have received from excellent teachers the arts called liberal and the other matters written about medicine or agriculture. I have listened, less diligently than was fitting, to the exposition of sacred writings by Catholic and most learned men. I have read many treatises and commentaries in both sacred and secular literature. But varied and manifold reading takes away as much usefulness as it brings pleasure. I speak as a natural philosopher.

Many and diverse dishes are bad for the stomach and burden health rather than restore it. Those who have begun to be ill from foreign and varied foods are returned to customary and simple fare. The prodigal son desired to fill his belly with the husks which [Col. 1251C] the swine ate, because, in the Psalmist’s words, he had forgotten to eat his bread. Extensive reading, tasted merely with the lips, charms the mind but does not nourish it; it delights but does not instruct. There is a certain avarice in knowledge, and the first parents were tempted by it: “You shall be like gods, knowing good and evil.” Many things are learned not from zeal for learning but from curiosity; not that we may become better, but that we may become prouder. “Knowledge puffs up, but love builds up.” We must therefore use lawfully that knowledge which, according to the Apostle, shall be destroyed, so that we may hold fast to that which never fails.

I do not say this to frighten you away from the study of reading, meditation, writing, and declamation. I myself am now chiefly occupied in that course, ardently desiring to attain this: that I may commit what I read [Col. 1251D] to a more tenacious memory. I am accustomed to practise this by, after reading a volume on some difficult question, rehearsing from memory, with the book put aside, its passages and arguments, the methods of disputation, and the snares of its conclusions.

Examples of industry and study are set before us for imitation: Cato, who, at the age of eighty-six, pleaded his own case when accused by enemies of a capital crime, and no one noticed that his memory had grown slower, his bodily strength was shaken in any respect, or his speech hindered by hesitation; he learned Greek literature in old age. Terence Varro, Publius Crassus, Marcus Cicero, and Julius Caesar held the first rank among students of Latin. Among the Greeks were Demosthenes, greatest of orators; Pythagoras, philosopher; Plato, whose lot gave him [Col. 1252A] Athens as homeland and Socrates as teacher—place and man most fertile for learning; Democritus, the natural philosopher; Carneades, a laborious and long-serving soldier of wisdom, who before disputing with Chrysippus purified himself with hellebore; Anaxagoras, who, when he returned to his homeland after a lengthy absence devoted to study and saw his estates abandoned, said, “I should not be safe, if these had not perished”; Socrates, whom I mentioned above, who in advanced age began to devote himself to playing the lyre; and the poets Sophocles and Simonides.

Among industrious commanders were Themistocles, who retained in memory the names of all his fellow citizens; Cyrus, who knew the names of all his soldiers; and Mithridates, who learned the languages of the twenty-two peoples under his rule—Cyrus [Col. 1252B] so that he might greet his army without prompting, and Mithridates so that he might address those under his command without an interpreter. It would be a long task to record memorable facts about each individual and weave a catalogue of the deeds of illustrious men.

But lest you perhaps begin to rebuke and accuse me—a monk and one already beginning to turn grey—for reading or contemplating such things, know that I enter these camps not as a deserter and fugitive, but as a scout eager for spoils, in case I may seize a Midianite woman and, after her hair has been shaved and her nails cut, lawfully join her to myself in marriage.

But I shall turn to our own men, whose talents and studies we can admire and praise, though we cannot equal or imitate them. Cyprian, martyr and bishop; Lactantius; [Col. 1252C] Hilary of Poitiers; Ambrose of Milan; Jerome of Ephrata; Augustine of Hippo; Leo the Great, bishop of the city of Rome; and very many other eminent and illustrious men possessed an easy, abundant, graceful talent, and that which is the greatest virtue of speech, clarity. One could not distinguish whether they were more ornate in speaking, more successful in exposition, or more powerful in persuasion.

Yet, although they were formed within one and the same rule of the Catholic faith, they wrote things not merely different but even contradictory. Thus Lactantius, following a Jewish novelty, introduced the tale of a thousand years, during which, he says, after the resurrection the Lord will reign bodily with the saints. Cyprian held the contrary view concerning the rebaptizing of those baptized by heretics, but [Col. 1252D] expiated his error with his blood. Ambrose and Jerome speak oppositely concerning the second marriage of a priest, and each defends his own opinion with the strongest and seemingly unanswerable authority of Scripture. Augustine and Jerome disagreed in a long controversy, in varied and discordant writings, concerning Paul’s resistance to Peter “to his face.”

It is therefore no wonder if the philosophers of the nations—marvellous in learning, seekers of truth through thought and disputation, yet by no means attaining its discovery—disagreed among themselves and against one another; if natural philosophers fought against logicians and logicians against ethicists. In physical and logical disputes and contradictions, however, pardon could be granted, because, whether they said something, they [Col. 1253A] benefited no one; whether they raved, they harmed no one. But in moral matters there is no place for dissension or error: all must think alike, and philosophy itself must speak as though with one voice, because, if anything is mistaken, the whole of life is overthrown.

In the former area, as there is less danger, so there is more difficulty, because the obscure nature of things compels diverse and various thoughts. In the latter, as there is greater danger, so there is less difficulty, because the very use of things and daily experience can teach what is better and truer. Thus schools cry out against schools: Epicurus against the Stoic; the Stoic against the Peripatetic; the Peripatetic against the Academic. The whole throng of pupils contends for the acuity and discoveries of their teachers; each defends and multiplies the opinions and deeds [Col. 1253B] of his masters by his own fortifications.

Observe how greatly they disagreed on the one matter which is supreme and principal, the pivot on which all wisdom turns. Epicurus judges the highest good to be pleasure of the mind; Aristippus, pleasure of the body. Callipho and Inomachus, Cyrenaics, joined honourableness with pleasure. Diodorus placed the highest good in freedom from pain; Hieronymus, in not suffering pain. The Peripatetics confess that the highest good lies in the goods of mind, body, and fortune. For the Hebilli, the highest good is knowledge; for Zeno, living in accordance with nature; for certain Stoics, following virtue. These are nearly all the opinions of all men. Amid such diversity, whom should we follow? Whom should we believe, [Col. 1253C] when all possessed equal authority—unless he had come who said, “I am the way, the truth, and the life,” and, “You believe in God; believe also in me”?

All this has been said at such length so that you may know that writing correctly, reading distinctly, pronouncing clearly, knowing the categories and the seats of argument, persuading by diction, understanding the force and nature of numbers, discerning harmony and intervals, excelling with the abacus, gnomon, and astrolabe, and judging constitutions and the connections of degrees, are of little or no value if God is not known and loved. If we know him, follow him in love, and by following reach him, then, together with him who knows all things, we shall know all things. There the rustic and unlettered man will discover keenly, judge subtly, and [Col. 1253D] discourse abundantly. And this is the true path of learning, which leads to presence, since every living being fears not-being.

Therefore I advise and exhort you: read, and do not neglect; read books, and do not neglect character. “Good understanding [belongs] to all who practise it.” “The servant who knows his lord’s will and does not do it shall be beaten with many blows.” “The mighty shall suffer mighty torments.” You should neither practise arrogantly nor wholly despise the quibbles and sophistical little conclusions called *gualidicae*, after a certain Gualo. Such are these:

> What you have not lost, you have;  
> but you have not lost horns;  
> therefore you have horns.

Likewise:

> “Mus” is a syllable;  
> but a syllable does not gnaw cheese;  
> therefore a mouse does not gnaw cheese.

Our lord King Conrad marvelled at things [Col. 1254A] subtly said by the learned, and said that it could not be proved that a man was an ass. We were enjoying ourselves at table, and most of those with us were not unlettered. I told him that this could not occur in the nature of things, but that a false conclusion, arising from an undetermined concession, could bind falsehood upon truth. When he did not understand, I attacked him with a ridiculous sophism. “Do you have one eye?” I asked. When he granted it, I asked, “Do you have two eyes?” When he unconditionally assented, I said: “One and two make three; therefore you have three eyes.” Caught by this verbal trick, he swore that he had only two. Yet, having been taught to resolve many such problems, he said that learned men led a pleasant life.

But even if we cannot solve these matters, what danger or inconvenience threatens us? [Col. 1254B] Neglecting discussion of justice, piety, frugality, and both forms of chastity—one consisting in abstinence from another’s body, the other in care for one’s own—brings loss, not through forfeiting the public breath of praise for disputation, but rather through injury to life and character.

Moreover, in attributing to me some share of eloquence, your judgement has been enticed and deceived by love. It is no matter of little time, slight study, or moderate exercise to know the power and nature of minds, stir up the sluggish, restrain those who are running, and, as with powerful reins, turn them about. For though nature is adaptable, soft, and tractable in receiving every form, and although a teacher may expound diligently and abundantly, still, if the activity of frequent [Col. 1254C] practice is lacking—a practice far removed from monastic cloisters—the light is choked by darkness; the fire is not nourished by ashes but extinguished.

An orator must both be conquered and conquer, so that he may know how to protect both himself and his own people with a shield and strike with a sword. Read Quintilian on the education of the orator: he begins shaping an infant from the mother’s womb and forming him into the substance of the perfect orator. This power and capacity has retreated far from our age, because every jurisdiction is either ecclesiastical or secular.

In the secular court unlettered laymen pronounce the law: they are sometimes endowed with an excellent natural ability, but among the German people the custom of declaiming is rare. Usage has made them signify briefly and, as it were, by certain points, rather than [Col. 1254D] explain. The other division of law, called canon law, is administered by men most learned in letters, in whose mouth is the law of God. From it they hear: “Do not judge, lest you be judged”; through it they learn that among Christians the miserable man is not he who suffers wrong, but he who commits it. In the decree of that supreme lawgiver they read: “Let your speech be: Yes, yes; No, no; but whatever is beyond these is from evil.” And one orator of that excellent court says: “Remove the reproach which I have suspected.” Therefore, if nothing is admitted for proving or disproving a point by suspicion, conjecture, or opportunity, only the simple statement of the case remains: “Did you do it?” “I did,” or “I did not.”

Even the eloquent pagans established in their definitions that a censor ought to speak differently from a rhetorician. A rhetorician [Col. 1255A] is permitted to use false, bold, crafty, and deceptive propositions, provided only that they are plausible and can, by whatever trick, insinuate themselves into the healing of men’s minds. Moreover, they think it disgraceful for an orator to leave anything in a bad case undefended or unattacked. It is therefore not fitting for a holy man endowed with faith and gravity to say before Christian ears something that appears untrue to himself and to all others. A person who speaks eloquently in a canonical case is thought to serve his own glory rather than the usefulness of the matter itself. The Areopagites, the most scrupulous judges of Greece and Athens, permitted no one to use either prologues or epilogues, but required a plain and entirely uncoloured narration. Thus nearly all the foundations of rhetoric were shaken.

[Col. 1255B] Yet in the Church there is sometimes an occasion in which the art of speaking is exercised blamelessly, especially in the office of preaching. In the first rank of this grace, in my judgement, stands Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, a man very illustrious in our times. I should not wrongly call him an orator, whom rhetoricians define as “a good man skilled in speaking.” For that good man, worn down by the long austerity of the wilderness, by fasts and pallor, and reduced to a kind of thinness of spiritual form, persuades by his appearance before he persuades by his hearing.

He has been granted by God an excellent natural ability, the highest learning, incomparable diligence, enormous practice, clear delivery, and bodily gestures suited to every manner of speech. It is therefore no wonder that by the mighty force of such great [Col. 1255C] endowments he rouses sleepers—indeed, to say more, the dead—and, with the Lord working together with him and confirming his word, transforms men and draws to God’s yoke captives who had been in Pharaoh’s chariots.

You would truly call him eloquent: he does not destroy by deed what he preaches by word; he is not Nero within and Cato without. If you see him, you are taught; if you hear him, you are instructed; if you follow him, you are perfected. And if you are touched by the glory of speaking, choose one man to follow, whose eloquence may delight your mind. It is the agreed opinion of the greatest orators that one can speak more ornately and abundantly by imitating eloquent speakers than by following the precepts of an art. But enough on these matters, so that you may know what I do not know.

You praised my character [Col. 1255D], led not by the testimony of truth but by goodwill. But if you had been introduced into the chambers of my heart—which is small and inscrutable—and heard, in the court of my mind, when reason sits as judge, the most grievous clamours and bitter examinations of thoughts accusing one another, where neither tonsure, habit, pallor, nor thinness can cast a vote, you would see a creature horrible and more deformed than every monster. There the accuser prosecutes with an argument as strong as it is true; there the defender is either absent or confesses.

But take care not to say that upright character proceeds from nature, because “every best gift and every perfect gift is from above, coming down from the Father of lights.” [Col. 1256A] Although I was conceived in summer and born in spring—seasons which, according to your natural philosophers, are most favourable for a good constitution—yet by God’s grace I am what I am, and every day, with his help, I strive to become better. Therefore it is not my birth-star nor the descent of my parents that determines how I shall live, but divine grace, which goes before and helps; and I ought not, like an ungrateful man, kick against or resist it when it calls—indeed, draws me. I certainly have brothers born of the same womb in whom God has not deigned to exercise so great a power of his goodness.

You exalt our house with praises. It is indeed far better than I deserve, but more disorderly than I would wish. For such is the contumacy of this age, such the overthrow of discipline, that no household wishes either to receive correction or even to feel it. And the maxim [Col. 1256B] so long praised often proves false: “As is the master of the household, so is his house.” Yet our household is no narrower than that of the first parent Adam, in which brother drenched the earth with his brother’s blood through parricide; nor more confined than Noah’s household in the ark, in which there was a son who, having mocked his father’s nakedness, subjected his descendants in their very stock to a curse; nor more numerous than Solomon’s household, in which there was Adath the Idumaean, persecutor of his lord.

Was there not, in the house of him from whom all wisdom comes, one Judas the traitor among the twelve apostles? We, however, sometimes err as human beings; sometimes we are negligent; or, overcome by necessity, we keep silent. The dwellings of the abbot of Corvey were narrow and ruinous. We erected new and strong ones, able to contain their [Col. 1256C] number, keeping before our doors and our eyes that saying of Tully: “The master is not honoured by the house, but the house by the master.”

My name is written upon the lintel of the southern door, with the number indicating my place in the catalogue of abbots. I did this not to make void the hope laid up in my bosom, but to teach posterity not to be greedy, prodigal, or idle. There is written there in Greek letters that saying from Apollo’s temple: “Know yourself.” You object that at the beginning of my name three vowels are joined contrary to the rule of correct writing; two of them, when inserted, stand for consonants and make the name trisyllabic. You think this cannot be done according to rule, and you demand that the first letter of my name, U, either stand separately [Col. 1256D] with the force of a vowel or, joined to the following identical letter, have the force of a consonant, so that the name becomes tetrasyllabic.

But, in scholastic fashion: if in a proper or common noun two consonants can be joined before a vowel, as in *gnato*, *gnavis*, *spiro*, *flores*, and *fructus*, why cannot two vowels, standing in place of consonants, be glued and fused together? But to free myself from your question, and so that you may depart from me either angry or appeased: barbarian names cannot be confined by Latin letters; and we are Germans, not long-haired Gauls, who in such names [Note: [Col. 1255D] Not only the Gauls but also Italians use the letter G in names of this sort. Hence, in the letters which he issued as abbot of Cassino, he styles himself Guibaldus, not Wibaldus.] put G in place of the initial U.

These things, dearest brother, have been written to you more cheerfully, for the sake of your friendship and to kindle your studies more strongly, contrary to the strictness of [Col. 1257A] our rule. I do not fear critics, because love is kind, patient, believes all things, and endures all things.

While writing this, I remembered something found in the books of those who recorded memorable deeds or sayings. Whenever the Emperor Augustus came forth from the palace, a certain little Greek used importunately to meet him, offering him some epigrams in praise of Augustus. Irritated by the man’s frequent and untimely flattery, the emperor—being a lover of literature and knowing Greek—once anticipated him and handed the Greek to read an epigram which he himself had composed in the Greek’s praise. After reading through it, the Greek exclaimed, “My lord’s genius rises to the level of his praises,” and, putting his hand into his purse, drew out [Col. 1257B] the only as which he possessed: “Take it, Emperor,” he said, “not according to your fortune, but according to mine.” The prince, delighted by this agility of wit, enriched him with a more generous gift.

Following this example, in return for the two sheets of your praises I send you a full letter, poured forth amid cares and manifold labours in the little night-work of two nights.

## LETTER CXLVIII. ABBOT WIBALD TO HARTWIC, ARCHBISHOP OF BREMEN

He attempts to reconcile to himself Archbishop Hartwic, who was angry with him because, in the election of a bishop of Bremen, the votes of the electors appeared to have united in favour of Wibald.  
(Year 1149.)

To the reverend lord H., venerable archbishop of the Church of Bremen [Col. 1257C], Brother Wibald, by God’s grace that which he is in the Catholic Church, offers humble prayers and devoted service.

Our clerk Henry of Kaminata, whom we sent to convey certain petitions of ours to your highness, reported on his return that you were gravely angered against us; that before many persons you had made serious complaint concerning us; and that, moreover, you had uttered threats against us and ours. We could by no means believe this, since our conscience truthfully bears witness that we have knowingly done nothing, either in word or deed, against your person or dignity. And since our law judges no one unless he has first been heard, your discretion ought therefore to have provided that, [Col. 1257D] because we were bound by no slight bond of friendship, you should first inquire and afterward judge.

For, as your prudence well remembers, two agreements were contracted between us, one divine and the other human. The human one may indeed, according to human laws and institutions, be dissolved and altered: namely, that you who hitherto were our man and, as it were, our knight by homage, should now begin to be our lord and father. But the compact of the divine agreement remains valid for ever, because of Him who commanded in His law that we should not take His name in vain, and because of Him who swore and will not repent. Hence David also says: “I have sworn,” he says, [Col. 1258A] “and have resolved to keep [it].”

Remember that, before you ascended to the height of the archbishopric, we sent letters to your prudence, in which, with deep affection, we endeavoured to forewarn and fortify you concerning certain matters. Had it pleased you to heed our counsel in these, today both the Church of Bremen and you would enjoy a better peace. Yet, it is said, you are angered with us because, when the election of the Archbishop of Bremen was under discussion, while the see was then vacant, the votes of almost everyone seemed to incline toward our person.

[Note: [Col. 1257] How unjust this accusation is is clear from Wibald’s letter above to Guy, the cardinal, in which he commends to him the elected Archbishop of Bremen.]

We know no one in the Church of Bremen except your person, your namesake Hartwig the provost, Erfo the provost, and Albert the canon. Apart from these, we know neither names nor faces. We have entered the city itself only once: we arrived late, when the day was already declining, [Col. 1258B] and departed when morning came. When your predecessor, Archbishop Albero of blessed memory, died and you succeeded him, we were in the monastery of Stavelot, which lies seven days’ journey from Bremen, wholly ignorant of all that was being done there. No person was solicited or sent by us.

We do not readily enter into such a hazardous contest, where people dispute most subtly about birth as well as character, and err very frequently. Indeed, being well aware of our own weakness and humility, we would never presume to undertake so great and so venerable an office fittingly, especially since that same Church—formerly mistress of nations and princess of provinces—has become like a widow under tribute. To heal its ruins, [Col. 1258C] if your learning, prudence, nobility, and strength are not sufficient, it must rather despair than place confidence in the assistance of any man.

Therefore, casting from the sincerity of your breast all bitterness of suspicion and driving away every deception of slanderers, love again us who truly love you. For we speak to you in Him who is Truth: we have directed against you neither letters nor any spoken word at the Roman Church. On the contrary, we are prepared in every way to assist the advancement of your dignity. We earnestly ask your discretion, however, that, as the lord pope wrote to your predecessor, you render us justice concerning your parishioners and ministerials who have seized the goods of the Church of Kaminata, [Col. 1258D] to whom we have given or granted absolutely nothing, nor do we acknowledge that anything was given. We commend to your mercy the bearer of this letter.

## LETTER CXLIX. Wibald, Abbot, to H., Bishop of Minden

He asks him to appoint a time and place at which they may meet and amicably settle their affairs. (1149.)

To his reverend father and lord H., venerable bishop of the Church of Minden, Brother Wibald, by God’s grace what he is in the Catholic Church: humble prayers and devoted service.

We give thanks to your highness because you have visited our lowliness through our beloved father Master C. and through the letters of your affection. Since we were concerned about the matter between us, and preferred that sincere affection should exist between us rather than any stain of discord, we recently, as your fatherhood remembers, sent through our brother C. letters to your sincerity, in which we offered this to your excellence: since your lords, the bishops of Paderborn and Münster, perhaps hindered by weightier affairs, had postponed coming to settle our case, we would meet you without them at such place and time as might please your graciousness.

We persist in this request, and urgently ask that you appoint for us a day and place at which we may conveniently and safely meet you. [Col. 1259B] For we are prepared, as we have been accustomed to say from the beginning of your admonition, to show you our innocence in this matter; wherever we are less able to demonstrate it, we wish to make full satisfaction, both to you and to your Church, in every matter of justice. We leave to your direction the day and place at which we may suitably and safely come. For your envoy has sufficiently understood, by direct observation, the necessity, the straits we endure, and part of our dangers.

## LETTER CL. Wibald, Abbot, to the Abbot of St. Godehard

He excuses himself for being unable to attend the assembly of the abbots of Saxony, and urges that the case of the Abbot of Hersfeld be discussed there. (1149.)

[Col. 1259C]

To his reverend father F. [Frederick], venerable abbot of the Church of Blessed Godehard, Brother Wibald, by God’s grace what he is in the Catholic Church: humble prayers and devoted service.

We rejoiced at the things said to us: that our dearest fathers and lords, the abbots of Saxony, are arranging to meet together

[Note: [Col. 1259D] Here occurs the first mention of congregations or general chapters of the abbots of the Order of St. Benedict in Saxony. In the same century, in the time of Pope Innocent II, they had begun to celebrate them in Gaul; on these, see, if desired, our preface to vol. IV of the *Anecdota*.]

and to deal more closely and diligently with, and make regulations concerning, those matters known to pertain to the reform of our life and the discipline of our monasteries. We, the least servants of all, would gladly desire to attend that holy assembly and enjoy the long-desired sight and conversation of them, were we not now called away toward the regions of Lotharingia by certain pressing concerns. [Col. 1259D]

The Holy Spirit will be present with you; and, while standing with you in spirit, we shall strive to bring to effect whatever you ordain, with Him as mediator and author, for the adornment of God’s house. Among other things, stronger action must be taken against that evil: the monks of Hersfeld have expelled our brother, their abbot, from his cloister and abbacy; and, with no judicial procedure carried out against him, he is compelled to live in exile and beg [Col. 1260A] before learning his offence or crime.

And because we know you to be merciful, we ask your kindness with the greater confidence that, on behalf of him, of ourselves, and of all our fellow brethren, you present him to the lord Archbishop of Bremen, so that he may either show him mercy or conduct a judicial proceeding according to the course of the canons. Pray for us, and earnestly commend us to your brethren.

## LETTER CLI. Wibald, Abbot, to B., Abbot of St. Michael

He congratulates him and his church upon his election. (1149.)

To the reverend father B. [Burchard], venerable abbot of the Church of St. Michael,

[Note: [Col. 1260D] The church of Hildesheim, of the Order of St. Benedict, founded by St. Godehard, bishop, about the year 1026. Besides this, there is another abbey of the same order at Hildesheim, distinguished by the name of St. Godehard, as we observed above.]

Brother Wibald, by God’s grace [Col. 1260B] what he is in the Catholic Church: humble prayers and devoted service.

We offer abundant congratulations both to your Church and to your person: to the Church, because God has deigned to provide it with the saving assistance of His care; to your person, because predestination has raised it through fitting promotions of honour. For an unsuitable person is dishonoured by the exaltation of an office, and a Church is not burdened by the lowliness of a person. But where the person adorns the Church and the Church honours the person, there is a sweet harmony and indeed a salutary concord. We desire to cleave more closely to your friendship and diligently to accomplish whatever your goodness may wish of us.

## LETTER CLII. Wibald, Abbot, to H., Archbishop-elect of Bremen

He writes on behalf of the Abbot of Hersfeld, whom his monks had expelled. (1149.)

[Col. 1260C]

To his most reverend father and lord H. [Hartwig], venerable archbishop-elect of the holy Church of Bremen, Brother Wibald, by God’s grace what he is in the Catholic Church: to be joined to the ointment that descends from the head upon the beard, Aaron’s beard.

Our venerable brother A., Abbot of Hersfeld, came to us and tearfully complained before many of our brethren and fellow abbots who had assembled at Corvey that he had suffered many injuries at the hands of his monks and had finally been violently expelled from his monastery by them. That monastery is now governed, contrary to the authority of the sacred Rule, by a layman and illiterate man who contrived this hostility against his abbot.

Although he has already often brought this complaint to the feet of your highness, he has not only received no help in his need; his adversaries have even been encouraged to such a spirit of presumption that, contemptuous of the Rule, they write and circulate certain insults and reproaches against him among neighbouring churches. [Col. 1261A] Yet the Rule commands monks to honour abbots even if the abbots themselves—God forbid!—act otherwise; and it commands them neither to send nor receive letters without their abbots’ consent and will. They are ignorant also of the canons, which prohibit writings of this sort under severe penalty and impose upon their authors punishments of the gravest censure.

They have leisure and therefore cry out: they see the speck in their abbot’s eye but do not consider the beam in their own. They reproach the abbot because he checked the insolence and rash talkativeness of one of his monks with a single slap. We too do not regard this as praiseworthy, since such presumption could have been punished more vigorously, at a proper time and by regular discipline, for the correction of many. Yet these men, forgetful of patience, humility, [Col. 1261B] and obedience, magnify the abbot’s lack of restraint with so heavy an accusation; and in the very matter in which they censure him, they condemn themselves.

They do not recall that Benedict, the father and leader of all monks, struck a disorderly monk with a rod. Nor do they follow the example of the monk Libertinus, of whom it is read in Book I of the *Dialogues* of Blessed Gregory: when, in a grave outburst of anger, he had been struck by his abbot with a footstool and his face became swollen and bruised, he not only bore it patiently, but, when asked how it had happened to him, answered with such moderation of speech that he neither disclosed his father’s fault nor incurred the sin of falsehood.

Accordingly, we—and through us almost all the abbots of Saxony—humbly implore your clemency: because this scandal has presumed to sprout and break forth at the beginning of your elevation [Col. 1261C] to ecclesiastical rule, correct it with such zeal of discernment that the Church of God may rejoice that in your learning, nobility, and power it has found consolation; that in the days of your priesthood all presumption may be trampled down; and that justice and truth may receive increase.

I speak the law to one who knows it. Those expelled or despoiled of their goods cannot be summoned to trial or judged, because there is no privilege by which persons already stripped may be further despoiled. All things taken from them must by law be restored to their power; and afterward they must not be summoned to state their case within a restricted period, but, while they have full control of all their affairs, must be allowed as much time as they appear to have been despoiled or expelled. [Col. 1261D]

As for the assertion that he was removed for the good of peace, lest the monks perhaps rage against him more violently: may God avert this peace and this good from His Church—that prelates should flee for this reason, lest subjects go mad! Rather, those men ought to be cast out and banished far beyond the boundaries, who, abandoning the Rule of their own profession and the ordinances of the sacred canons, take up arms against their fathers and, while complaining of one offence of his, do not fear to fill the world with scandals.

Send to Corvey those very brave men who proceed against their abbots first with clubs rather than arguments, with fists rather than words, [Col. 1262A] and only begin to defame them in writing when they have expelled them from the whole congregation and abbacy—so that they may know that there is a prophet in Israel.

Therefore your discernment, your mercy, will do through compassion what it is to do through the canons; and, once the abbot has been restored in the full integrity of his goods and possessions, it will call everything back to peace, if possible, or at least weigh the whole matter under judicial examination. Blessed be God, who has given you in those regions the power to accomplish whatever He inspires you to will; and therefore it is good that you aid the oppressed, lest, abandoned by mercy and justice, he be compelled to appeal to the clemency of the supreme Judge.

As for the affairs of the Church of Kaminata, we ask your kindness again and again not to disdain to proceed against your parishioners, who are also your ministerials and men, in the manner enjoined upon your predecessor, Archbishop Albero of blessed [Col. 1262B] memory, by the lord pope both orally and in writing. At the request of your provost Hartwig, we wrote to the lord chancellor on your behalf; in that letter the affection of our devotion toward you was sufficiently apparent.

## LETTER CLIII. The Monks of Corvey to Abbot Wibald

Concerning a boy who died accidentally at Kaminata. (1149.)

To their dearest lord and father Wibald, Abbot of Corvey, [Col. 1262C] the brethren of Corvey: due obedience and steadfastness in devoted prayers.

We are deeply grieved that we must trouble your fatherhood with the accident of this sad event. But since it is fitting that everything be bare and open to your knowledge, we make known to your prudence, not without great groaning of heart, what recently happened at Kaminata, by God’s permission and because of our sins.

On the twelfth day before the Kalends of May, one of our schoolboys, Herimannus, a kinsman of our senior brother H., had climbed with another little boy onto the roof of the church of Kaminata, which is being newly roofed, without the knowledge of our brethren. By accident he fell from the very summit [Col. 1262D] of the roof through the ceiling onto the pavement, immediately expired there, and was carried out dead. The place of the fall was in the north apse, beside the altar of St. Dionysius. Although careful inquiry was made, it could not be found that the church had been polluted by his blood. The body of the deceased was buried at Novale, at St. Mary’s. Thereafter the brethren of Kaminata did not celebrate the divine office in the church. We await your command in this matter.

Nor should this escape your discretion: in the tower of the church at Kaminata there is a separate dedication,

[Note: [Col. 1261D] Formerly our fathers used to erect an altar in towers and dedicate it to St. Michael as protector of the monastery, as may be shown by many examples.]

where, if it is permissible to celebrate divine services, let your prudence decide.

## LETTER CLIV. [Wibald, Abbot, to His Corvey Brethren]

He consoles them concerning the death of the brother who died at Kaminata. (1149.)

[Col. 1263A]

Wibald, by God’s grace Abbot of Corvey, to his beloved brethren and sons in Christ, the men of Corvey: blessing and life for ever.

Your letters sent to us have disclosed that you are sorrowful and distressed in spirit over the death of your boy and Brother H. But if you remember that the prince of envy, the devil, sought by pernicious persuasion to cast down from the pinnacle of the Temple our very Head, our very Creator and Redeemer, the Lord Himself of the whole world and of all things; if you recall what is written, that all who desire to live godly lives in Christ suffer persecution; if you keep in mind that, when the unclean spirit has been expelled from its dwelling, it returns, taking with it seven others more wicked than itself—you will readily despise the empty judgments of the barking crowd, [Col. 1263B] and, with hope most firmly established in God, will devote yourselves more zealously to the cleansing and restoration of the Church of Kaminata.

What is read concerning our most holy father Benedict should have come to the aid of your grief and wiped away the vexations of your spirit: when he had shattered the idol of Apollo in the fortress of Monte Cassino, overturned its altar, and cut down its sacred groves, he built oratories of the blessed John and Martin. Then the demon, inhabitant of that place, began to roar against the holy man with dreadful cries, to mock his brethren with many harassments—now by the weight of a stone, now by the phantom of a kitchen on fire—and also, by the crushing of a boy monk and the tormenting of a certain elder into whom it had entered, to deter them, by the detestable sport of its art, from cleansing the place and from holy life there.

Let old wives’ tales, then, not deter you. Rather, confident in God’s mercy and His protection, establish religion in the Church of Kaminata, where it had wholly perished before our arrival; cleanse both the place and the souls from the companionship of demons; and carefully observe their wiles. Once you have received our letters which we have sent [Col. 1263D] to you, approach the presence of the lord and our father, the Bishop of Minden, and, concerning the reconciliation of that church—which he judges polluted by the accident and death of our brother—implore his mercy. We appoint Provost A. and Chamberlain R. to carry out this mission. If, however, the tower of the church of Kaminata was separately dedicated on a different day of the Kalends from the rest of the body of the church, our brethren may safely celebrate the divine mysteries in it.

## LETTER CLV. [Wibald, Abbot, to the Bishop of Minden]

That he may deign to reconcile the church of Kaminata. (1149.)

To his reverend father and lord H., venerable [Col. 1264A] Bishop of the Church of Minden, Wibald, by God’s grace what he is in the Catholic Church: humble prayers and devoted service.

While our brethren were labouring, by command of the lord pope and the lord king, at the restoration of the church of Kaminata, they were tempted and afflicted by the enemy of all salvation. A boy monk fell from the summit of the church roof, on which they were then engaged in re-roofing work, was dashed upon the pavement of the church, and died, though no blood was shed. Therefore, cast down in spirit at the feet of your sincerity, we ask that, for reverence toward the lord pope and for the honour of the lord king and kingdom, you provide, according to the discretion granted you by God, that that place not be deprived of divine offices on this account. We grieve greatly [Col. 1264B] that we could not enjoy the meeting with you which we have so long desired and so often sought, since we are ready truly to serve and honour you.

## LETTER CLVI. [Wibald, Abbot, to His Brethren of Malmedy]

Concerning a disorderly brother who, having cast off the monastic habit, departed. (1149.)

Brother Wibald, by God’s grace servant of the Church of Stavelot, to his beloved brethren and sons in Christ, the monks of Malmedy: blessing and life for ever.

We received kindly, as far as we could, our brother, formerly called Liebertus, when he came to us. When, in the presence of the brethren and of those whom he had frequently offended—both ourselves and the Church—we had sufficiently reproved him in a fatherly manner, as occasion and circumstance required, we imposed upon him as a penalty, if indeed it can be called a penalty, that he remain with us in brotherly fashion at Stavelot until, after examining his humility, we might see, with God’s aid, what should be done.

Not only did he refuse to comply; but, turning to fury and to the madness attributed to the possessed, he began to seek knives and weapons by which to kill both himself and us; to utter words of despair with a sacrilegious mouth; to disparage the Creed—that is, “I believe in God”; and, raging and tearing himself, to say that he would never again call upon God. Our brethren could not endure the madness of this desperate man, who even before the altar of Blessed Remaclus attempted to kill himself, in violation of the church, [Col. 1264D] and threatened to burn the monastery. They therefore came to us—we who, after pronouncing sentence, had left the assembly—asking with grief and tears for our counsel concerning so detestable a man.

After taking counsel with our priors, we entered the chapter house at the sound of the tablet, since the principal Mass had already been sung. We asked him whether, after the injury caused by his rebellion had been accepted, he was willing to be obedient to us and to the holy Rule. When he persisted in saying that in every way he wished to separate his person from us, we also offered him the choice either to obey us according to the ordinances of monks or, after laying aside the habit of religion, to depart from us and from his monastery, never to return. [Col. 1265A]

We did this because of the hardness of his heart, fearing lest perhaps he should be plunged into the abyss of despair and into a desire for his own death. We preferred that he should live in any fashion whatsoever rather than end his life with an unrepentant mind. He, however, without any hesitation and almost rejoicing—for an evil spirit had already taken possession of his mind—cast off the monastic habit and departed cheerful and laughing, leaving us in the greatest fear for the destruction of his soul.

As for us, greatly fearing the wrath of God because of our sins and judging nothing in this world rashly, we nevertheless believe that we understand in a pious and Catholic sense that he has fallen into this blindness of mind and snare of obstinacy because of the blasphemy which he always directed against God; because of the envy, curses, and insults with which [Col. 1265B] he attacked the most serene confessor of Christ and bishop, Remaclus; and because of fraternal hatred and the seeds of scandal which he never ceased to sow between the two places, Stavelot and Malmedy, bound together by a singular bond of charity—as we read of Judas the traitor, who, after selling the Lord, went away and hanged himself with a noose.
