Concerning him we direct and, by the power of the Holy Spirit, command you through the word of holy obedience: neither in conversation, counsel, nor assistance, indoors or out, are you to support him. Rather, as one excluded from Christian communion and a subverter of all obedience and religious life, you must strive to avoid and oppose him with all truth and diligence.

## LETTER CLVII. Wibald, Abbot, to Walter, a Monk

He charges the wicked monk Walter with many crimes. (1149.)

Wibald, by God’s grace Abbot of Corvey, to Brother Walter: conceive the spirit of the fear of the Lord; bring humility to birth; give birth to obedience.

Many grave reports about your conduct are repeatedly brought to us, both by the brethren with whom you live and by honourable laymen. They grieve that through you God’s name is blasphemed among secular people, our person injured, the monastery of Corvey [Col. 1265D] defamed, and the whole monastic order made contemptible. Although we have frequently admonished you concerning this with fatherly affection, you have wholly refused to amend. Returning evil for good, you repay the barrenness of our soul with curses and imprecations against your correctors.

For we have heard a matter concerning you that is joined to madness—indeed, is filled with sacrilege and abomination: namely, that, inflamed daily by the frenzy of despair, you celebrate without interruption a Mass of the Holy Trinity, under the purpose of your blinded mind that by this means both our person and your provost may be more grievously harmed, both in temporal prosperity and in the health of our bodies. O man to be bewailed with every shower of tears, who makes perfidy out of faith, sacrilege out of piety, and idolatry out of religion!

That supreme, glorious, and ineffable Trinity is worthily and laudably invoked by those who invoke it in order to attain and possess it, so that those who call upon its name may enjoy its vision and may be governed by it amid the adversities and prosperities of this world; for they acknowledge themselves created by it and delivered from eternal death through Jesus Christ. Let that name be invoked over us which neither destroys the innocent nor saves the guilty. Let it be invoked, I say, not by the address of a hardened heart and faithless mouth, but by the service of innocence and purity.

Furthermore, you are charged with having fallen into an error of impiety no less similar: that is, with having anathematized a certain merchant, your associate and friend in secular trading, dealings forbidden to you. [Col. 1266B] For, having recently handled the life-giving sacraments, you are accustomed to leave the church and go out into the brethren’s cemetery, so that from there you may look down upon the town of Horenhusen, which lies in the valley; and, gazing at your companion’s house, excommunicate him, his wife, and his children.

Who made you a ruler of the people? When you ascended to the rank of priesthood, you received the power to consecrate the body and blood of God, not the power to bind and loose. The Catholic Church received this power with Blessed Peter, but it was not spread among all who exercise the priestly office: it was bestowed only upon those chosen for the administration of spiritual care.

Do you not remember the prophet Balaam when you do such things? He went up a mountain to curse the people of God, and, blinded by the darkness of avarice and repeatedly forbidden, while stubbornly desiring to curse, bestowed the gift of abundant blessing together with the grace of prophecy. Thus you bless when you think that you curse; the curse turns back upon you, and the blessing passes to your neighbour.

We have seen fulfilled in some persons the Psalmist’s words: “Before I was humbled, I transgressed.” Those whom the slippery wantonness of the flesh had overthrown became more submissive and readier for every practice of service and patience; by modest service and by bearing with the conduct of others, they made recompense for whatever loss they had incurred through the fall of the flesh. But you do not heed David when he says: “Do not become like horse and mule.” Rather, you proclaim your sin like Sodom and do not hide it; and, what is worst, by lying, swearing, and uttering imprecations, you offend the brethren. [Col. 1266D]

It is also said that you possess certain characters and write them down for certain magical displays, diabolical incantations, and wicked practices—things to which no learned and honourable pagan even wished to give credence. When, to investigate these and certain other matters concerning which the whole province cries out against both you and us, we sent Brother Isico of Ersborch, formerly prior of our monastery, all the brethren, both unlearned and learned, the women consecrated to God, and the rest of the household of the cell gave unanimous testimony against you. But you, with the shamelessness in which you surpass all men, resisted everyone, not by speaking truth but by heaping insults upon all.

And now, because the outcry against you rises daily, we command you through the word of holy obedience to abstain from the office of altar and Mass; not to set one foot outside the four walls of the cloister; and not to hold conversation with laymen and secular persons, either personally or through an agent, until, having learned your obedience and humility, we may provide, with God’s aid, what must be done. [Col. 1267A] If you prove a contemner and transgressor of this our command, imposed by the common judgment of the brethren, know with certainty that all residence in that cell and all return to us or to the dwellings of our monastery is entirely forbidden you.

## LETTER CLVIII. Wibald, Abbot, to His Brethren of Corvey

Concerning H. and A., ministerials of the monastery of Corvey, received into his favour. (1449.)

[Col. 1267B]

Brother Wibald, by God’s grace Abbot of Corvey, to his beloved brethren and sons in Christ, the monks of Corvey: blessing and life for ever.

The ministerials of the Church of Corvey, H. and A., came to us at Stavelot. As you know, they had stolen our horses at Corvey. In the custom of their people, they surrendered themselves to our mercy in a great assembly of the people, with swords drawn. Moved to pity for them by this humility, the unusual spectacle of the swords, and the exertion of their long journey, our men of Stavelot—both the brethren, all of whom were present [Col. 1267C] in the church, and the ministerials of our Church, most of whom had assembled before us that day for another reason—by great urgency of entreaties induced us, though reluctant and resisting, to receive them into favour and to determine their guilt, punishment, and satisfaction by the counsel and judgment of you and of the ministerials of the Church of Corvey.

We have therefore written to our lord of Paderborn that he may absolve them from the bond of excommunication by which they were bound, subject to the firmness of the aforementioned condition, and allow them to have peace in the land until our return to you.

## LETTER CLIX. G., Abbot of Solignac, to Abbot Wibald

That the men of Solignac may give thanks to St. Remaclus, who delivered them from tribulations. (1149.)

[Col. 1267D]

To our dearest and most reverently named lord, Guibald,

[Note: [Col. 1267D] Wibald had observed above that the French begin his name with the letter G, whereas the Germans, conversely, begin it with V.]

Abbot of St. Remaclus of the Ardennes, G.,

[Note: [Col. 1267D] Gerald of Terrazo, who attended the funeral of Eustorgius, Bishop of Limoges, in 1137, and lived until the time of Pope Anastasius IV, from whom he obtained a privilege.]

his abbot of St. Peter of Solignac,

[Note: [Col. 1268D] The once renowned monastery of Solignac, founded by St. Eligius, lies two leagues below Limoges. Its first abbot was St. Remaclus, who afterward laid the foundations of the monasteries of Stavelot and Malmedy.]

may go from strength to strength and see the God of gods in Zion.

Above all, dearest ones, we ask that you may deign, as domestic sons, to give thanks to our common father, St. Remaclus, and together to pour forth prayers for us, [Col. 1268A] your brethren. Thanks, indeed, because our merciful father, with God’s help, has rescued us from great tribulations and at present established us in great peace; and likewise prayers, that, as he has hitherto graciously been accustomed to do, he may never cease to protect us for ever.

We also wish to know about your needs: how our merciful father and patron acts and assists on your behalf. Farewell, brethren and lords.

## LETTER CLX. Wibald, Abbot, to the Men of Solignac

Reply to the preceding letter.

To his reverend father and lord G., venerable abbot of the holy Church of Solignac, and to the brethren there serving God, [Col. 1268B] Brother Guibald, by God’s grace servant of the Church of Blessed Remaclus at Stavelot: greeting in Him who commands deliverances for Jacob.

Your letters, conveyed to us by boys, were witnesses to your prosperity and well-being. They filled us with joy all the more eager because through them we were more assured that your faith—which works through love—holds most firmly and in no way doubts that every good gift and every perfect present is from above and descends from the Father of lights.

You have indeed lifted your eyes to the mountains, whence help comes to you, when, religiously considering the merits of our common father and patron, the most holy confessor of Christ Remaclus, through his patronage you obtained what common sins seemed to hinder. And although your learning and devotion abundantly understand that prosperity must be preserved by the same practices through which you attained it, nevertheless your concern does not judge it pointless if we too admonish you with filial and inward affection and assist you in this same end with suppliant prayers.

For your prosperity is ours, and all things are so far common to us with you that we judge nothing foreign or separate, except insofar as we are divided by the longer distance of places—a distance which we greatly resent. Since your pious anxiety of mind is concerned about the condition of our affairs, let your sincerity know that we are in the labour of men and are scourged with men, because, as administrators of concerns so numerous and so far-flung, we can never, or only rarely, let time pass without vexation. [Col. 1268D]

Yet, with God propitious and through the merits and intercession of our venerable shepherd and patron Remaclus, the whole of our affairs is secure, although it suffers some loss in particular regions. We ourselves are healthy and unharmed in person, and truly your friends.

At the beginning of autumn, send back to us the blind bearer of this letter; provide him also with a guide for the road, and send us by him four rabbits, namely two males and two females. [Col. 1269A]

## LETTER CLXI. Wibald, Abbot, to H., Bishop of Utrecht

Concerning providing a pastor for the Church of Lienward. (1149.)

To his reverend Father and lord H., [Note: [Col. 1269] Heribert, or Ardebert, called of Beren from his place of origin in Frisia, who succeeded Andrew of Cuijk as bishop of Utrecht-on-the-Rhine.] venerable bishop of the holy Church of Utrecht, brother Wibald, by the grace of God what he is in the Catholic Church, offers his humble prayers and devoted service.

As we have already informed your Highness, we caused both prebend and benefice to be adjudged away from the clerics who held the church of Lienward, on account of three charges, each of which could have been decisive. First, because they neglected to receive from you the gift of the altar and the cure of souls, [Col. 1269B] whence that church—which is a possession of the Church of Corvey—was adjudged to you as your proprietary right, but through your grace and mercy was restored to us and to our monastery with all its integrity. Second, because they neglected for two years to pay the rent due by ancient right. Third, because, although nearly three years of our prelacy at Corvey have now elapsed, they neither came to us nor rendered the reverence and honour due.

Since this is so, we have sent to the feet of your Holiness the chamberlain of the Church of Corvey, under this instruction of prudent moderation: since you commanded that a person be presented to you who might undertake the cure of that same church, if your favour inclines toward any person, he is to present that person to you on our behalf, our right and the church’s rent being reserved. Although that person alone receives the cure, he shall nevertheless be appointed by you to a fourth part of the prebend. And if, concerning the three remaining prebends, it pleases your discretion that some person agreeable to you be invested, we shall gladly comply with your will in this also. But if you have no wish to appoint any of your friends, he shall present to you the person whom we have designated to him by name. Moreover, to add to the benefaction which you have generously bestowed upon us, and to earn a fuller increase of our service, bring what you have begun with a good beginning to an excellent conclusion, and make us—your friend—most friendly to you. [Col. 1269D]

## LETTER CLXII. CONRAD, EMPEROR, TO WIBALD.  
He praises his loyalty and reports that he arrived at Regensburg on the octave of Pentecost. (1149.)

Conrad, by the grace of God Augustus, king of the Romans, to W., his beloved, venerable abbot of the Church of Corvey: his favour and every good thing.

Because among all the princes of our realm no one has been found who, after our departure, has stood by us or our son more faithfully according to his ability, we intend especially to render thanks to your loyalty both in deeds and in words. We therefore wish you to know that we arrived safe and well at Regensburg on the octave of Pentecost, since we learned that this was what you chiefly desired to know. [Col. 1270A]

## LETTER CLXIII. WIBALD TO CONRAD, EMPEROR.  
He congratulates him on his return from the holy expedition, urges him to assist those unjustly oppressed, and complains about the bishop of Minden. (1149.)

To his serene lord Conrad, Augustus, emperor of the Romans, illustrious conqueror crowned and exalted by God, brother Wibald, by the grace of God and yours what he is in the Catholic Church, wishes salvation in him who gives salvation to kings.

[Col. 1270B] Just as the minds of the unbelievers have been greatly dismayed by your unexpected arrival, so the hearts of your faithful have been exceedingly gladdened by the benefit of so great a heavenly gift. Our smallness, not without reason included in their number, rejoices with such joy that we can say with the prophet Jacob: “It is enough for me; I will go and see my lord.”

Although we have always been with you in spirit, prayer, and faith, we should already have come to meet you in bodily presence at the very beginning of your entry into the empire, had not plundering and fires, with their daily assaults, afflicted Lotharingia and especially wretched Ardennes. In this struggle of miseries bitter necessity compels us to stand girded as though in battle-line. And since divine mercy has restored you safe and sound to the fatherland which longs for you and is now almost collapsing, [Col. 1270C] stretch out your saving right hand to the oppressed; lift up orphans; defend widows; aid the Catholic Church. You can now accomplish this with so much greater power and effectiveness as heavenly majesty, by its merciful protection, has advanced your Excellence through wonderful and unexpected triumphs, incredible labours, and extreme dangers.

Your valour and industry have, through God’s power, made you exceedingly terrible to your enemies. Therefore delay must be cast aside; while all things are afraid, the opportunity of the moment must be used; what has already begun to bend must be bent further; and the hearts of rebels must be struck before they begin to recover from fear.

We complain to your Serenity, however, [Col. 1270D] that the bishop of Minden grievously oppresses us and has hitherto hindered us concerning the properties which you bestowed upon the Church of Corvey—namely Kaminata and Visbick. At Kaminata, where by your command we established our brethren, he has forbidden the celebration of the divine office; and we have lost almost half the possession there. At Visbick we have never entered, nor have we yet obtained a foot’s breadth of the entire property belonging there, because the bishop of Minden and Count Adolf of Schowenburg prevent it. There likewise the bishop of Minden arranged the monastery’s affairs through the brethren of Cappenberg. For this reason the men of Corvey, who had sworn to pay you money, [Col. 1271A] could not pay it, the whole church protesting. What adversities and expenses we have endured for these same places we shall more fully relate in due time, prostrate at the knees of your Clemency. And now, insofar as your Majesty deigns and our modest estate is able to bear it, do not refuse to inform us, your faithful servants, concerning your condition and that of the realm. May almighty God preserve you victorious and unharmed.

## LETTER CLXIV. POPE EUGENIUS III TO CONRAD, EMPEROR.  
He consoles him concerning the unhappy outcome of the Jerusalem expedition, sends envoys to him, and desires to be informed of his condition. (1149.)

[Col. 1271B] Eugenius, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son in Christ Conrad, illustrious king of the Romans: greeting and the apostolic blessing.

“Since in this world the order of mutability corrupts all things,” etc. See Pope Eugenius III, under the year 1153.

## LETTER CLXV. CARDINAL G. TO ABBOT WIBALD.  
He orders him to come to him, intending to use his counsel. (1149.)

G. [Note: [Col. 1271] Perhaps Gregory, cardinal deacon created by Eugenius III and sent by him as legate into Germany.] by the grace of God cardinal deacon of the holy Roman Church and legate of the Apostolic See, to his venerable brother Wibald, abbot of Stavelot: greeting and affection.

We have decided to notify your Fraternity by this letter [Col. 1271C] that, after completing the lord pope’s legation in Poland, we came into Saxony; and there, for the completion of that same lord’s legation concerning the establishment of bishops in Luticia, and also concerning the affair of Duke Lothair, which is not unknown to you, we are necessarily delayed. Since in both affairs we have the greatest need of your help and counsel, we earnestly ask your Fraternity and, on behalf of the lord pope and the lord chancellor, command you that, upon receiving this letter and setting aside every excuse and delay, you come to us, so that in the aforesaid affairs you may render such assistance as is fitting and as the lord pope trusts.

## LETTER CLXVI. ABBOT WIBALD TO CARDINAL G.  
Reply to the preceding letter. (1149.)

[Col. 1271D]

To his reverend Father and lord G., venerable cardinal deacon of the holy Roman Church and legate of the Apostolic See, brother Wibald, by the grace of God what he is in the Catholic Church, offers his humble prayers and devoted service.

After we learned by trustworthy report of your passage into Poland, we remained for a long time at Corvey, anxious and in suspense, hoping that on your return we might suitably meet you and render, with all faithfulness and sincerity, service both devoted and due—in person [Col. 1272A] and in resources—for reverence toward the lord pope and the lord chancellor, and for the honour of your person. But because the frequent evils which afflict Lotharingia and especially our Ardennes with continual raids, plunderings, and fires have compelled us to cross there and hold us entangled, fighting as it were in battle-line under daily pressures, we grieve deeply that, being so far away, we cannot come in response to your command.

This is particularly grievous because Bishop Anselm, who might greatly support your discretion by his prudence and faithful counsel, is lacking as a fellow-worker in your anxieties. Moreover, when our lord Conrad, king of the Romans, arrived at Regensburg on the octave of Pentecost, he sent us envoys with letters commanding us to appear before him, without any impediment of delay, on the feast of the martyrdom of the apostles Peter and Paul. We have sent to the feet of your Excellence [Col. 1272B] our agents, whom you may confidently direct to assist your needs from our resources according to your pleasure. Your goodness, as we trust concerning you and the whole Roman Church, will not refuse them necessary protection.

## LETTER CLXVII. CONRAD, EMPEROR, TO H., BISHOP OF MINDEN.  
He reproves him for harassing the brethren of Corvey. (1149.)

[Col. 1272C] Conrad, by the grace of God king of the Romans, to H., venerable bishop of Minden: his favour and every good thing.

The complaint of our faithful abbot of Corvey has been brought to us: that concerning two monasteries situated in your bishopric, namely Kaminata and Visbich, which we bestowed upon the monastery of Corvey both by the counsel and judgment of the princes, you have created a great impediment; and that, although often and urgently requested, you neglected to reconcile the church which is said to have been polluted by the fall of a boy monk. In this matter your discretion ought carefully to consider what the concern of priestly office should have supplied in such a case. Your discretion ought indeed to have understood that, just as your church has been exalted and endowed from our royal possessions, [Col. 1272D] so we could also honour the Church of Corvey from the property of the realm.

Accordingly, by this present letter we command your discretion that henceforth you wholly abstain, if you love us, from harassing the aforesaid abbot of Corvey and the property of his monastery; and that you do not delay to reconcile the aforesaid church. For, with a view to divine religion and at the exhortation and request of our reverend Father Pope Eugenius, we have endeavoured to devote the aforesaid places to divine service. Not only that province but our realm also was offended by their shameful and utterly infamous manner of life. It greatly befits your moderation to cooperate in this holy work of reforming the order. [Col. 1273A]

## LETTER CLXVIII. ABBOT WIBALD TO H., BISHOP OF MINDEN.  
He complains that the church of Kaminata has not been reconciled. (1149.)

To his reverend Father and lord H., venerable bishop of the holy Church of Minden, brother Wibald, by the grace of God what he is in the Catholic Church, offers his humble prayers and devoted service.

We have frequently asked your Excellence through letters and envoys to perform for the church of Kaminata the office of reconciliation which it is said to require; [Col. 1273B] but, because of our sins, we have not merely been unable to obtain what we requested, but have also, as we hear, been troubled with harsher answers. Now, for support of our petition, we have added even the intercession of our lord King Conrad, although we would rather rely upon our own merits than upon greater patronage before your Highness.

We do not wish your Sincerity to be unaware that, through privileges of the Roman pontiffs, the Church of Corvey has obtained this prerogative of dignity: if its diocesan bishop refuses to perform what belongs to his office, it may obtain this from another Catholic bishop and freely make use of it. We have shown you the reverence due to you and are prepared to serve you henceforth.

## LETTER CLXIX. CONRAD, EMPEROR, TO ABBOT WIBALD.  
On his return from the holy pilgrimage, he summons him to court. (1149.)

[Col. 1273C]

Conrad, by the grace of God king of the Romans, to Wibald, abbot of Corvey and Stavelot: his favour and every good thing.

We are certain that, as one foremost among our faithful, you receive our unexpected return with the highest gladness of heart and, as a special friend of both our realm and ourselves, greatly rejoice in our prosperity. We desire that, at our arrival, the Church and realm may advance in reform through the prayers [Col. 1273D] of the holy Church and through both the counsel and assistance of the faithful of the realm. We therefore entrust and command your diligence that, setting aside every excuse, you do not delay to come to the court which we shall celebrate at Frankenevort on the Assumption of Saint Mary. There we intend to confer familiarly with you concerning both our private and public affairs.

What we have bestowed upon the Church of Corvey, out of affection for you, in the abbeys of Kaminata and Visebach, we shall preserve for its use, God willing, being certain that the men of Corvey will without doubt pay us the money which they promised under oath.

## LETTER CLXX. H. TO ABBOT WIBALD.  
That his king needs his counsel. (1149.)

[Col. 1274A]

To his lord Wibald, abbot of Corvey and Stavelot, H. [Note: [Col. 1273] The H. designated here appears to us to be none other than Henry, the emperor’s notary.], his servant’s service.

As your Kindness commanded me, I faithfully interpreted for the lord king, word for word, your letters sent to him. Although I might have obtained leave from the lord king to remain at Stavelot, I did not wish even to attempt it, because, considering the multiplicity of affairs, I perceived that it would be harmful both to the king and to you; what I say is confidential.

The lord king intends, with the counsel of his faithful men, to arrange an embassy both to the Romans and to the lord pope. [Col. 1274B] In this counsel your discretion will be necessary to the lord king. The king must also have your advice regarding the projected expedition into Italy and the restoration of his sister, the duchess of Poland. He is earnestly and effectively labouring to restore and confirm peace. Let every man pay his due in such a manner that none at all of his debt remains outstanding.

## LETTER CLXXI. ABBOT WIBALD TO PETER, ABBOT OF CLUNY.  
Concerning the dispute between the church of Nameka and the church of Marcha. (1149.)

To his reverend Father and lord Peter, venerable abbot of the holy [Col. 1274C] Church of Cluny, brother Wibald, by the grace of God what he is in the Catholic Church, wishes salvation in him who commands salvation for Jacob.

Recognising in every respect that we are your sons and servants, we have customarily assisted both the persons and the property of your monastery in every affair, and, as one of the persons of Cluny, defended the concerns of Cluny according to our means, with truth and justice. But we have learned that the dispute between the church of Nameka and the church of Marcha has been reported to you otherwise than the truth of the matter stands. We therefore believe that the true sequence should briefly be made known to you by us, lest the splendour of your religious order suffer some cloud through the defence of an unknown and insufficiently sound cause.

The provost of the canons [Col. 1274D] of the church of the blessed apostle Bartholomew complained in the synod of Liège that a certain free man named Berenger had intruded upon a possession belonging to his right—namely, a certain portion of the tithes of the church of Marcha. The man replied that he had done nothing by force, but that, because he was advocate of the church of Namecha and that tithe belonged within the boundary of that church, he had taken the tithe by right of defence.

On the other hand, the provost maintained that the aforesaid tithe lay within the boundaries possessed by the church of Marcha, which had possessed it peacefully until the aforesaid man had introduced an interruption without any legal procedure; he therefore requested complete restoration to himself. After the pleadings on both sides had been heard, the bishop, following the custom of his church, asked the assessors for their judicial decision. They debated long among themselves whether restoration ought to be made. But we, giving the greatest consideration to equity together with law and loving truth together with judgment, urged that, leaving aside the claim of restoration, explicit inquiry be made peacefully among the neighbouring inhabitants concerning the boundaries and possessors. The proposed decision, which wholly excluded procedural cavilling, was approved by all.

Accordingly, the elder neighbouring inhabitants came from both sides and, having sworn oaths to tell the truth, began to distinguish the respective possessions by definite boundary-marks. The estate of the manor of Namecha extends nearly to the village of Marcha. Therefore the advocate of the church [Col. 1275B] of Namecha maintained that the tithe belonged by ancient right to the aforesaid land and church; but he asserted that in ancient times a certain priest of Namecha had transferred it to a man of Marcha so that he might have charge of certain of his parishioners who lived nearer to him.

Conversely, the men of Marcha asserted that they had possessed that same tithe peacefully, without dispute, and in good faith—not by a right of loan or of borrowing, but as their own property continuously for more than thirty-one years—which they promised to prove by suitable witnesses. The controversy was reported to the synod; and, without objection from any person, it was unanimously judged that, if the provost of Saint Bartholomew, whom both sides recognised as possessor, although one side called him a possessor in bad faith, could prove by lawful witnesses—able by age and understanding to give a certain judgment concerning prescription of time—that he had possessed it peacefully and canonically, the burden of proof should rest more upon him than upon one who was unquestionably known to have recently intruded into the same possession. The judgment pleased the men of Namecha more than those of Marcha. [Col. 1275C] These are the things which we both saw and heard concerning this case, and therefore we cannot but speak them.

## LETTER CLXXII. CONRAD, EMPEROR, TO H., BISHOP OF MINDEN.  
He reproves him because he did not reconcile the church of Kaminata and did not take care to fulfil his commands. (1149.)

[Col. 1275D]

Conrad, by the grace of God king of the Romans, to H., bishop of Minden: his favour and every good thing.

We remember that in earlier letters we admonished your episcopal care not to delay reconciling and purifying the church of Kaminata, which you judged polluted because of the accident and death of a boy monk working to repair the roof. We are astonished that you fulfil neither our commands nor your own office. For a sufficiently long time you have supported the misconduct of the women who lived there, and you have opposed too strongly the establishment there by us and ours of religious divine worship.

Let your prudence likewise understand and judge whether you ought to have transferred the abbey of Visbicke [Col. 1276A] and assigned it to certain persons without our command. Therefore, for these matters and others in which you did not hesitate at all to offend us, we command you by this present letter and order you, under pain of forfeiting our favour, to present yourself before us at Aachen at the forthcoming Nativity of the Lord, there to answer us before the judgment of the princes concerning the matters in which you appear to have neglected us and our commands. Moreover, if you attempt any longer to delay the reconciliation of the church of which we have spoken above, since he who abuses granted authority deserves to lose his privilege, we shall by no means be able any further to overlook its purification.

## LETTER CLXXIII. LETTER OF CARDINAL G., LEGATE, TO HENRY, BISHOP OF MINDEN.  
He orders him to reconcile the church of Kaminata. (1149.)

[Col. 1276B]

G., cardinal deacon of the holy Roman Church and legate of the Apostolic See, to Henry, bishop of Minden: greeting and affection.

Our venerable and beloved brother, the abbot of Corvey, has informed us that the church of Kaminata is polluted because a certain boy monk fell from the roof onto the pavement and died, and that, although he has repeatedly petitioned you, you have delayed its reconciliation until now. Therefore, since the upright character of this same brother compels us to stand by him in his petitions as though for ourselves, we earnestly request and command your Fraternity [Col. 1276C] that you by no means further delay the purification or reconciliation of the aforesaid church.

## LETTER CLXXIV. B., BISHOP OF PADERBORN, AND ABBOT WIBALD TO EUGENIUS III.  
Concerning the dispute between Provost Z. and the bishop of Speyer. (1149.)

To their reverend Father and lord Eugenius, supreme and universal pontiff of the holy universal Church, Bernard, by the grace of God humble minister of the Church of Paderborn, and brother Wibald, by the same grace and yours what he is in the Catholic Church, offer enduring service with all devotion and obedience.

[Col. 1276D] When we came to the town of Frankenevort on the Assumption of Blessed Mary, to the court of your son, Conrad, serene king of the Romans and illustrious conqueror, your son Z., provost of Speyer, laid out his complaint in the presence of the churches of Mainz and Worms, with us also hearing it. He had testimony from all that, after returning from your Holiness, before he had wiped away the sweat of his journey, and before he had conveyed your commands to the bishop of Worms and the abbot of York—whom you had charged to hear and determine the dispute brought against him—he was summoned to judgment by the bishop of Speyer and his canons. By the word of holy obedience he was ordered [Col. 1277A] to restore to the brethren, within fifteen days, whatever had been lacking to them from their prebend while he was travelling as a pilgrim toward Rome.

When that prescribed period had expired during the execution of your commands, only on the fifteenth day did the bishop begin to accuse the aforesaid Provost Z. of disobedience, and on this ground to seek from the clerics a sentence almost canonical. But when the aforesaid provost perceived that he was being heavily burdened by the canons’ unjust hatred and that all ecclesiastical benefices were being adjudged away from him contrary to custom and order, he appealed to the metropolitan archbishop of Mainz. Thus, before the sentence which his adversary Gevehardus was first to pronounce had been given, commending himself and all his possessions to your protection, he departed from them.

Summoned by his metropolitan, the bishop of Speyer came with his clerics to Mainz. There, since the repeatedly mentioned Provost Z. could find neither mercy nor judgment, he appealed to your presence. [Col. 1277B] These, dearest Father, are the things which we truthfully heard and which, because of the oppression of our brother, we have taken care to report to your Piety, knowing beyond doubt that in your sight mercy exalts itself over judgment, and that you will not permit the decrees of the sacred canons to be violated in any respect.

## LETTER CLXXV. CONRAD, EMPEROR, TO POPE EUGENIUS III.  
That he may deign to confer the provostship of Xanten upon his chaplain Thiebald, canonically elected. (1149.)

[Col. 1277C] “We have decided to reply more fully, in another letter and through other envoys, to the letters of your Fatherhood, full of most kindly affection, joy, and congratulations,” etc. See, under the year 1153, among the letters of various persons to Pope Eugenius III.

## LETTER CLXXVI. ABBOT WIBALD TO GUIDO, CARDINAL AND CHANCELLOR.  
That the provostship of Xanten be conferred upon the chaplain Thiebald. (1149.)

To his reverend Father and lord Guido, cardinal deacon of the holy Roman Church and chancellor of the Apostolic See, brother Wibald, by the grace of God what he is [Col. 1277D] in the Catholic Church, offers himself and all that is his.

Our present word to you is brief, and this is the sum of our urgent purpose: that the petition of the lord king for granting the provostship of Xanten to Lord Thiebald be granted. Thus the prince will be satisfied, and the sin of the disobedient man punished by princely penalty. David struck the Philistine in the forehead. He likewise says in the psalm: “Fill their faces with disgrace, and they will seek your name, O Lord.” No disturbance will arise from this; rather fear and trembling will come upon us. We believe that we shall see your face before the Purification of Saint Mary.

## LETTER CLXXVII. POPE EUGENIUS III TO KING CONRAD.  
He confirms the provostship of Xanten for his chaplain Thiebald, provided that he resign the other provostship which he formerly held. (1149.)

[Col. 1278A]

Eugenius, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son in Christ Conrad, illustrious king of the Romans: greeting and the apostolic blessing.

“We have received with due kindness the letters of your Excellence, in which we have fully learned the devotion and affection which you bear toward your mother, the holy Roman Church, and ourselves,” etc. See Eugenius III.

Given at Tusculum, 5 October.

## LETTER CLXXVIII. A. TO ABBOT WIBALD.  
He gives thanks for Thiebald’s obtaining the provostship of Xanten, and asks for Wibald’s and the emperor’s intervention with the pope on his behalf against the archbishop of Cologne. (1149.)

[Col. 1278B]

To his most beloved lord Wibald, A. [Note: [Col. 1277D] The author of this letter is known only from the first letter of his name; we think that he was Arnold, provost of the Church of Cologne, [Col. 1278D] to whom several letters of Abbot Wibald survive.], devoted servant of his sincerity, offers himself wholly.

Your inward and faithful lord, Thiebald of Xanten, gives thanks to God, to my lord, and to your Excellence; your discerning achievement has made him a creation of your industry. And I, according to my small measure, prostrate myself at your feet on his behalf with manifold thanksgiving. But after watering and growth you must provide further care, lest your planting be uprooted if it is not helped with the necessary supports.

For the lord of Cologne, soon setting out for Rome with Brother F. of Bonn, intends to burden him. If he can win the lord pope’s favour with his money—since he lacks other sources of patronage—he plans to remove Lord Thiebald from the provostship of Xanten and invest Lord F. with it. We therefore desire your love, which has never abandoned us, to be entreated so that your and our petition may obtain from my lord the king confirmation for him, lest he fall again. If the archbishop obtains what he seeks, let Thiebald be commended to his protection by the authority of the lord pope, so that, if the election of another church calls him to be its provost, such a promotion shall not be denied him by the lord pope through my lord’s intervention.

I humbly ask that, since there is no more learned scribe, your discretion may not disdain to dictate this letter; and that you send the gold seal together with the letter by the bearer of this present communication with haste. [Col. 1278D] Henceforth we do not dare send headless letters, though we did so before not without reason.

## LETTER CLXXIX. THIEBALD, PROVOST OF XANTEN, TO ABBOT WIBALD.  
On the same subject. (1149.)

To his beloved lord Wibald, venerable abbot of the Church of Corvey, Thiebald, by the grace of God what he is, provost and archdeacon of the Church of Xanten, offers with prayer and service his heartfelt and intimate affection.

First, we wish you to know beyond every doubt that we are and shall remain, in every respect, devoted to your service with friendship and fidelity. For we have experienced by certain proofs what you have done for us and what affection you have borne toward us. Therefore we shall always acknowledge ourselves wholly your debtors.

Furthermore, we do not wish you to be unaware that our lord the archbishop intends to go to Rome, and that some of those who go with him will be our adversaries in every way they can. We therefore humbly and most earnestly request that you cause the royal Majesty to write [Col. 1279B] promptly on our behalf. To this end also, if the lord pope has raised us in one respect at the request of our lord king, may he grant likewise that, if canonical and just election jointly calls us to other offices, this be permitted. Farewell.

## LETTER CLXXX. P., BISHOP OF ASCOLI, TO ABBOT WIBALD.  
That he may deign to intercede for him with the emperor. (1149.)

To Wibald, most religious and wise abbot of the monastery of Stavelot, P., by the grace of God bishop of Ascoli, though unworthy, offers fellowship in the same purpose.

God’s wisdom, which orders all things when and how it wills, chose you, an honourable, religious, and wise man, to sit with princes and hold the throne [Col. 1279C] of glory; through you they may either settle everyone’s causes by judicial decision or conclude them by friendly agreement. It has bestowed upon you the favour of so great a prince in richer measure, so that you may make glad those saddened by him and by some marvellous ingenuity restore the despairing to the hope of life.

I therefore earnestly beseech you, dearest lord, to whom God has bestowed this grace, that, for the love of God and of our service, your sincerity may deign to intercede for me with the king and my lord. For it was not under compulsion but, if I dare say so, at his invitation that I came to him nine months ago, believing that, once he knew the tribulation which I suffer from the Sicilian for his loyalty, he ought to have released me sooner.

## LETTER CLXXXI. CONRAD, EMPEROR, TO POPE EUGENIUS III.  
He writes in favour of Provost Thiebald of Xanten and the cleric Otto. (1149.)

[Col. 1279D]

To his dearest Father in Christ Eugenius, supreme pontiff of the holy Roman Church, Conrad, by the grace of God king of the Romans and ever Augustus, offers filial love in every respect and due reverence in the Lord.

“It is most welcome to us, and we remember with grateful goodwill in the secret place of our heart, that you have promoted our beloved chaplain Thiebald to the provostship of Xanten out of regard for our affection and intercession,” etc. See Pope Eugenius III under the year 1153, among the letters of various persons to him.

## LETTER CLXXXII. ABBOT WIBALD TO HIS SUCCESSORS.  
Concerning certain acts undertaken during his administration. (1149.)

[Col. 1280A]

Wibald, by the grace of God abbot of Corvey, to his successors in perpetuity.

Just as it is our office to arrange and administer with all diligence and fear of God the matters entrusted to us, so it likewise belongs to this same care to transmit in writing for the memory of posterity whatever is done by us during the time of our administration, lest some error arise through forgetfulness or ignorance. Therefore we wish it to be known to the prudence of all the faithful of Christ and of our church that our beloved son Henry, [Col. 1280B] provost of our monastery at Groningen, reported to us with complaint, among the burdens which the shared wickedness of the world imposes upon him and his church, that one of our ministerials, named Hezo, had without any legal right occupied a portion of the field situated beside the river Bode, which down to our own time had customarily been common pasture.

Upon diligent inquiry into the truth among our wise men and elders, we learned concerning this matter that this same field belongs, without any doubt whatever, to the brethren’s prebend and to the provost’s jurisdiction. Likewise, concerning the mill which Wunnerus rebuilt near the village of Helmerikesdorp, we learned by trustworthy report that a certain man named Hoierus [had occupied it] without any legal basis; the source omits the verb. We likewise learned beyond doubt concerning one manor which had belonged to Henry Rufus of Groningen. [Col. 1280C] Since we have understood that all these things truly belong to the prebend of the community and to the provost’s hand, we confirm them to them immovably by this present document, entreating our successors never to grant or acknowledge them to any layman under the name of a benefice.

Given at Corvey in the year of the Lord 1149, in the thirteenth indiction, in the reign of our lord Conrad, second king of the Romans, in the fourth year of our installation at Corvey.

## LETTER CLXXXIII. POPE EUGENIUS III TO CONRAD, EMPEROR.  
At his request he again confirms the election of the provost of Xanten and postpones the deposition of the archbishop of Cologne. (1149.)

[Col. 1280D]

Eugenius, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son in Christ Conrad, illustrious king of the Romans: greeting and the apostolic blessing.

“We believe that your Clemency has recognised from very many proofs how great an affection we bear toward your person and the realm entrusted to you by God. Remaining inflexible in this, we admit the petitions of your Excellence as far as we can with God,” etc. See Eugenius III under the year 1153.

## LETTER CLXXXIV. ABBOT WIBALD TO THE PROVOST OF COLOGNE.  
Concerning the younger king’s victory over Welf, the forthcoming conference at Fulda, to which he invites him, and the Roman embassy. (1150.)

[Col. 1281A] To his beloved lord and friend A., venerable chief provost of the holy Church of Cologne and chancellor of the royal court, brother Wibald, by the grace of God what he is in the Catholic Church, offers himself and all that is his.

We have grown accustomed to receiving unsigned letters from you; those who write them are like people who dine with unwashed hands. Having been corrected once, amend this henceforth. To your next-to-last letter we reply among our first communications to you that, when we meet, we shall have more to report to your affection—matters which it was neither brief nor safe to commit to a letter. Moreover, much has been entrusted to us, namely this: by God’s mercy raining down from heaven, Welf, with almost all his men, has been defeated and captured in battle by the young king. It is indeed probable, and quite consonant with a true inference, that had divine clemency not granted this benefit, great disturbances would have arisen in the kingdom—disturbances which we now trust can easily be restrained and stifled. You will be able to learn this more fully from your clerk E.

So far as our capacity can understand and judge, our lord the king is directing all his effort and counsel toward ordering and governing public affairs; he does not merely gain time, nor evade cases by a perfunctory hearing. Thus, having seriously and reasonably arranged [Col. 1281C] his affairs—which are, in a sense, linked together in a necessary sequence—he wishes to hold a conference with the Saxons at Fulda on the Sunday upon which *Judge me, O God* is sung; and he commands and directs you by every means to be present there. For he intends to send an embassy to Rome with great dignity, befitting both his kingdom and his own person; in these matters he relies very heavily upon your counsel, and he keeps us, as it were captives, until your arrival.

It is plainly fixed and settled in his mind that, if he can restore his sister to Poland without arms, he will at once organize an Italian expedition with splendid equipment. We no longer dare to doubt this, especially since propitious Divinity has added to the plan he had conceived this marvelous and unexpected opportunity [Col. 1281D]. The rest, God granting, we shall discuss when you arrive. What we learned as boys, we now experience as old men: those who hurry across the sea change their sky, not their soul. You may have washed away your sins in the water of the Jordan, but you could not wash away your habits. Indeed, you brought back from there not only your habits but also your moroseness.

## LETTER CLXXXV. H., BISHOP OF CONSTANCE, TO ABBOT WIBALD

That he should procure, by the emperor’s authority, the release of his kinsman Henry, held by Welf. (1150.)

To WIBALD, by God’s grace venerable abbot of Corvey, H. [Note: [Col. 1281] Hermann of Arbon, bishop of Constance on the Rhine, confirmed by Innocent II about 1140; he held office until 1156.] by the same grace humble minister of the Church of Constance: devout prayers in the Lord, together with faithful service.

We have rejoiced greatly that you are presently attending, as is fitting, the court of our lord the king. For although we have experienced your discretion in many matters, we ask in particular that, amid the present prosperity, our most beloved lord may use your counsel in such a way that joy may be increased among the faithful of the kingdom—and especially among us, who above many others cherish the honor of the kingdom—while terror may be struck into lost sons and sons of perdition.

Furthermore, we humbly entreat your brotherhood, in whom we certainly place confidence, to suggest to our most beloved lord that he should first demand from Lord Welf and his ministeriales the release of a certain kinsman [Col. 1282B] of mine, named Henry, a faithful man also of the lord king, who has been imprisoned without cause; and, as we trust in him, command that he be released, both for our sake and for God’s.

## LETTER CLXXXVI. ABBOT WIBALD TO HERMANN, BISHOP OF CONSTANCE

He writes that he advised the emperor, after winning the victory, to continue pressing his enemies, but that the contrary view prevailed. (1150.)

To his reverend father and lord H., venerable bishop of the holy Church of Constance, Brother WIBALD, by God’s grace that which he is in the Catholic Church: greeting in him who commands Jacob’s deliverances.

Because of the moderation with which your sweet soul is endowed, it pleased your kindness to congratulate the royal court because we now offer it our constant presence. But, venerable Father, we do not know the turning-points of affairs, nor can we contribute any benefit to public business; and, as our own opinion has it, we are among those who exist merely to consume the fruits.

For after the unexpected victory—almost wholly beyond every human design and action, and bestowed from heaven—we desired, and advised as far as was fitting in a military matter, that our lord the king, whom propitious Divinity preserves and advances by marvelous and merciful favors, should not cease to press his successes and attack his enemies, already afflicted by incomparable loss [Col. 1282D] and struck down by fear and anguish of mind; and that, taking advantage of so marvelous an opportunity, he should at last bestir himself to execute judgment and justice and to aid his mother, the Church.

That inveterate Ahithophel objected, scarcely able to conceal his immense grief. Assuming the guise of a friendship ratified by agreement, he argued from the season and the weather; he proclaimed and maintained the religious obligation of the most holy fast. He declared that a man whom the righteous Lord, who loves righteous deeds, had already judged ought to be summoned to court by lawful judgments and citations; and that it was pious and fitting for no injury to be inflicted upon prisoners. As for these matters, we had formed no judgment, considering the innocence required by our office. Yet, to confess to a father and bishop, it was in our mind that not merely one man but many should die for the people, lest the whole nation perish.

The old man’s speech was popular, and suited to men’s negligence, sluggishness, and indolence. Yet we resisted and maintained that wars depend upon reputation, that great undertakings are helped by speed, that delay has always harmed those who are ready; that the voice of legal proceedings, raised with so much weight against us, can be heard within only a very few districts, whereas a military operation conducted with some splendor is spread through the greater part of the world. The argument of the armed man defeated the unarmed man—although that armed man’s weapons had caused the person whom he was persuading not to have won completely. Thus it has come about that we neither wage wars nor administer justice, but feed our minds upon hope of empty things [Col. 1283B].

Concerning your prisoner, you have been fully answered favorably. We shall take persistent care that deeds follow words. Farewell.

## LETTER CLXXXVII. EMPEROR CONRAD TO E., EMPEROR OF CONSTANTINOPLE

He excuses himself for having been prevented by illness from fulfilling his promises. (1150.)

CONRAD, by God’s grace Augustus, emperor of the Romans, to his dearest brother and only friend E., by the same grace Augustus, emperor of the Greeks, exalted, PORPHYROGENNETOS, fortunate: brotherly love and every good.

[Col. 1283C] No forgetfulness of things can ever tear from the tenacious memory of our soul how earnestly you received us, with what charity and devotion, with what zeal of faith and humility, in the holy seats of your glorious empire; nor with what grace of humanity and generosity you ministered to us in the bed of our illness, not only through your representatives and resources but also in your own person and with your own hands. This was when the hand of almighty God had struck us not only through the loss of our army, but also through the scourge of bodily sickness.

With equal and like constancy of remembrance, we hold fixed in our minds the nature of the mutual compact between us: what we promised Your Highness, and what we undertook to accomplish. But after we had bodily departed from the realm of Your Sublimity—in which we feel ourselves to dwell through faith and goodwill—we found that the empire granted to us by the supreme Majesty had, in certain regions, been disturbed because of our long absence. While we were applying our whole heart to suppressing those disturbances and restoring peace, that merciful Father, because “he scourges every son whom he receives,” stretched out his hand in requital and held us, utterly weakened and nearly useless through a severe quartan fever, for six months.

Therefore, although our purpose has for a time been delayed by God’s hindrance, it has not been wholly nullified; the fulfillment of our promise has been postponed rather than frustrated. Accordingly, to excuse the necessity of our delay and to greet the noble well-being of Your Serenity, we have taken care to send with this letter a swift and efficient messenger, who may make you certain and glad of our good health and may in turn gladden us with news of the well-being of yourself, of our daughter—your most beloved wife and partner in the empire—and of the prosperity of your affairs [Col. 1284A].

Moreover, after the court which, God being its author, we have decreed to hold at Merseburg on the Kalends of May with the princes of Saxony, Poland, Bohemia, and Lusatia, we shall send our envoys, men certainly eminent and distinguished, to your presence together with your prudent and honorable legate, namely Michael Bardales. They will not allow Your Magnificence to doubt our pledges and promises.

Our beloved son Henry, the young king of the Romans, greets Your Greatness, and our dearest daughter, who is certainly his maternal aunt. The bearer of this letter will declare orally what great glory God granted him in the earliest auspices of his military command.

## LETTER CLXXXVIII. EMPEROR CONRAD TO THE EMPRESS OF THE GREEKS

He excuses himself for being unable, when seized by fever, to fulfill the promises of the emperor of Constantinople; reports his victory over Welf; and requests a niece of her husband as wife for his son Henry. (1150.)

CONRAD, by God’s grace Augustus, emperor of the Romans, to his most dearly beloved daughter E., by God crowned [Col. 1284C] and exalted empress of the Greeks: paternal affection and sure, faithful aid in every need.

Previously we loved your distinguished character greatly, both by reason of the bond of kinship and because of the affection of adoption. But your faith, piety, devotion, and generosity, which you dutifully displayed toward us when the Lord’s hand had deeply afflicted and humbled us both by bodily illness and by reverses in our affairs, increased in our heart such ardor of holy charity toward you that no difficulty, danger, or change of circumstances can extinguish it.

We have therefore resolved in our mind and firmly established in our heart, with all doubt removed, that even if no obligation of treaty or closer friendship had ever stood between us and your husband—our glorious and most beloved brother, the magnificent and exalted emperor of the Greeks—we should nevertheless be ready and intent upon loving all that is his as our own, and upon resisting his enemies as ours.

Now, in the treaty concluded between us and him and confirmed with every goodwill, a necessary condition was imposed: namely, that we should fulfill the matters already named and set down, unless one or both of us were prevented from accomplishing them by death, severe sickness, or danger of losing the empire; and that, once that serious and by no means negligible necessity had passed, we should again apply ourselves to discharging and fulfilling the agreement [Col. 1285A].

Therefore we now disclose familiarly and briefly to you, as to our dearest daughter and kinswoman of our empire, the reasons why, after leaving you, we were unable to remain in Lombardy and fulfill our promises; and why the sequence of events and a report reaching us of the outcry of our empire persuaded us, not without weighty counsel, to hasten by every means to the regions of Germany.

For, as your wisdom knows perfectly, that Lord Welf, a man of great nobility and power in our kingdom, was moved neither by the fidelity with which we assisted him in his extreme need nor by the benefices through which we suitably advanced him. He returned from Jerusalem through the tyrant of Sicily, accepted no small sum of that infamous man’s money, and confirmed to him by oaths and hostages that he would labor by every means to disturb and harass us, ours, and our empire. After returning home, he immediately began to do this, having joined to himself certain faithless persons of no small standing and name among us: he attacked our sons—your most beloved nephews, full of good promise—and built hostile castles in their land, which belongs to them by hereditary right.

When we received news of so atrocious a deed, and rumor, as is customary in such matters, multiplied everything for the worse, we hastened to forestall and suppress the whole affair, and came suddenly and unexpectedly into the regions of Germany. While we were diligently occupied in arranging and pacifying all things, such bodily sickness assailed us at the end of August that until the Lord’s Easter we could scarcely be useful for weightier matters [Col. 1285C].

During this time, while we were in the city of Speyer to administer the justice of the kingdom and hold public courts, the aforesaid Welf fought in pitched battle near our castle of Flocperch against our most sweet nephew—your nephew, a youth now of fine character, whom, God being the author, we and our princes had crowned to the height of the Roman Empire. There, divine mercy protecting us, Welf barely escaped under cover of night, having lost many of his men both by slaughter and capture.

Having received this gift of heavenly mercy, while we were striving to free and prepare ourselves against the rash insolence of our common enemy, namely the Sicilian tyrant, word was brought to us that the entire people of the Franks, with their king, had conspired against the empire of our most eminent brother—namely your most glorious husband—and, at the prompting and instigation of the Sicilian tyrant, were preparing to take up arms with all the strength of their power. We judged that this matter should not lightly be despised or neglected, but resolved to await the outcome, either to suppress the disturbance or to place ourselves and our empire in defense of our brother and his interests.

We believe ourselves sufficiently excused, since the truth is steadfast, both by the invasion of the borders of our kingdom and by bodily illness. We have full confidence in divine aid that shortly we shall faithfully fulfill our promises—not only because we pledged them, but also because we most earnestly desire to avenge ourselves upon the invader of our empire [Col. 1286A].

And so that your exalted husband may have greater certainty of our friendship and of the fulfillment of the agreements, we now intend to establish a firmer affinity between us, just as was discussed and settled when we were present together. That is: our glorious son, designated and crowned as successor and heir of our empire, shall at this time take as wife one of the two nieces of your exalted husband, the emperor of the Greeks. Which one is to be sent to us shall be determined by the wisdom of your heart: namely, the one whom you, who raised them, know to surpass the other in character and beauty.

We have entrusted to Count Alexander of Gravina the remaining matters that seem necessary for duly completing the same marriage agreement. While we were with you, he customarily served both empires with manifest and perpetual fidelity, and, by command of each side, acted as mediator and negotiator in this affair. We summoned him from Venice to us while he was faithfully laboring, as always, in matters concerning your empire, so that through his diligence this secret undertaking may, as in other matters, be brought to an excellent conclusion. We earnestly urge your kindly understanding to secure his swift return, since your exalted nephew is now grown up and provision must be made without delay, both for his person and for our empire, by contracting the marriage [Col. 1286C]. Let our enemies, who seek to disturb and divide us by spreading lies, know that the bond of our friendship remains indissoluble.

## LETTER CLXXXIX. KING HENRY THE YOUNGER TO EMMANUEL, EMPEROR OF CONSTANTINOPLE

He reports to him the victory he had won over Welf. (1150.)

To his illustrious, triumphant, magnificent, and exalted uncle E., PORPHYROGENNETOS, emperor of the Greeks, HENRY, son of the glorious and most serene Conrad, Augustus, emperor of the Romans, and himself by God’s grace king of the Romans: the indissoluble favor of filial affection [Col. 1286D] and the firmest bond of perpetual friendship.

As propitious Divinity and my father’s love have made me successor and heir to my father’s empire and possessions, so my judgment considers it right that I should honor and love my father’s allied friends, and pursue and crush his enemies and the enemies of his house. Therefore, sharing in paternal affection for you and your empire, and embracing you with whole and filial love as our dearest uncle and most gracious father, I judged it right to notify Your Highness of the favorable events which, by God’s merciful gift, have occurred around us.

On the eighth day of February that proud and faithless Welf, forgetful of so many benefits from my father, invaded our land with hostile intent. My father was far away, occupied with public affairs, while I had been left with part of the army in one of our castles. The castle which he approached is called Flocperch; we were in another castle, Horbruc, a distance of a rope and a half from it [Note: [Col. 1287D] A *resta* or *restis*, according to Juan de Mariana, *On Weights and Measures*, is an agricultural measure of thirty-three palms, so that eighty *restes* make a league. But in this place the *restis* seems much longer.].

Upon receiving news of so great an outrage, I hastened to pursue the enemy. After we had advanced five long miles behind him, we sent ahead the swiftest horsemen to press upon his rear and delay his flight, while we pursued him with two united battle-lines. When we had begun to strike down the rear of his column, he was forced to turn and face us. But with God fighting for us from heaven, we gained so great a victory that, had they not concealed themselves in the darkness of night, not a single one could have escaped [Col. 1287B]. Three hundred knights were captured, and no small number of horses were killed, some pierced by lances and others cut down by swords. My father has now proclaimed a general expedition against this same Welf and is undertaking to exterminate him utterly, so that thereafter he may be free to pursue and destroy the common enemy of your empire.

## LETTER CXC. KING HENRY THE YOUNGER TO THE EMPRESS

He reports to her the victory he had won over Welf. (1150.)

To his dearest mother and maternal aunt E., by divine providence most gracious empress of the Greeks, HENRY, son of the glorious and most serene Conrad [Col. 1287C], Augustus, emperor of the Romans, and himself by God’s grace king of the Romans: the indissoluble favor of filial affection.

It is certain, and no prudent person has doubted, that things which have their origin and development in nature are more firmly enduring than those put together and joined by human skill. Since, then, by the degree of consanguinity and closeness through my natural mother you are related to us, no necessity can divide or estrange us so that we are not joined forever in enduring charity and goodwill.

Because I know that you greatly rejoice and glory in my successes, I judged it right to notify Your Highness of the favorable events which, by God’s merciful gift, have occurred around us. On the eighth day of February that proud and faithless Welf, forgetful of so many benefits from my father, invaded our land with hostile intent. My father was far away, occupied with public affairs, while I had been left with part of the army in one of our castles. The castle which he approached is called Flocperch; we were in another castle, Horburc, a distance of a rope and a half from it.

Upon receiving prompt news of so great an outrage, I hastened to pursue the enemy. After we had advanced five long miles behind him, we sent ahead the swiftest horsemen to press upon his rear and delay his flight, while we pursued him as he went away with two united battle-lines [Col. 1288A]. When we had begun to strike down the rear of his column, he was forced to turn and face us. But with God fighting from heaven, we gained so great a victory that, had they not concealed themselves in the darkness of night, not a single one could have escaped. Three hundred knights were captured, and no small number of horses were killed, some pierced by lances and others cut down by swords.

My father has now proclaimed a general expedition and is undertaking to exterminate him utterly, so that thereafter he may be unencumbered and free to pursue and destroy the common enemy of your empire. And just as it is not fitting that my character should depart from my father’s provision, so it is most pleasing to my judgment that the whole substance of the plan has been entrusted to your exalted prudence [Col. 1288B].

## LETTER CXCI. ABBOT WIBALD TO ARNOLD, CHIEF PROVOST OF THE CHURCH OF COLOGNE

That he should come to Fulda for the emperor’s court; and that it is not fitting for the king to request from the pope two provostships for Theobald. (1150.)

To his dearest lord and friend ARNOLD, venerable chief provost of the holy Church of Cologne and chancellor of the royal court, Brother WIBALD, that which he is in the Catholic Church: himself and all that is his.

[Col. 1288C] Our lord the king has no doubt, nor should you doubt, that you will come to the court which is to be held at Fulda on the Sunday [Note: [Col. 1288D] That is, Passion Sunday, on which the introit of the Mass begins with the words, “Judge me, O God.”] *Judge me, O God*, lest whatever is omitted through difficulty or negligence in conducting public business be imputed to your absence.

Regarding the case of our common friend Theobald, provost of Xanten, in which and for which we are greatly pleased that you have achieved the result and, as it were, gained the palm of victory, we have labored no less that it may remain secure than if our own person were at issue. For, because we truly love your person and honor, we do not at all doubt that everything dear to your heart pertains to us.

But concerning the clause of your letter [Col. 1288D] in which you wrote that, should the election of another church summon this same friend of ours to become its provost, such promotion ought not be denied him by the lord pope through the intervention of our lord the king: we did not think it right to write a direct petition in the person of our lord the king, because it does not become princely eminence to request things which may lawfully be denied it. For our holy mother, the Roman Church, founded upon the rock, by no means destroys laws which she herself has enacted, nor sanctions contradictions in any fashion, although she customarily dispenses and moderates her decrees according to the variety of times, the suitability of places, and the character of circumstances and persons, and thus, as it were, suffers loss.

Therefore she will neither command nor confirm that one person be advanced to two dignities; but, when this has occurred without complaint, she will overlook it in paternal discretion. You may believe us in this, not because of knowledge of the canons, but because of the sense and force of experience. We have used rhetorical art in the letters of our lord the king, because we affirmed by denying and asked without asking. We have therefore sent them to you not yet sealed, so that, if you wish, you may alter, add, or remove something from our contrivance. Live and fare well. Bring the little brother Erlebald with you to court.

## LETTER CXCII. ABBOT WIBALD TO POPE EUGENIUS III

He writes on behalf of the canons of the collegiate church of St Bartholomew in the city of Liège. (1150.)

[Col. 1289B]

To his reverend father and lord EUGENIUS, sole and universal pope, Brother WIBALD, by God’s and your grace that which he is in the Catholic Church: a son’s devotion and a servant’s obedience.

While we were in the house of your illustrious and most victorious son Conrad, king of the Romans, at his castle of Nuremberg, the canons of the church of St Bartholomew, situated in the suburb of the city of Liège, requested of our lowliness that we lay before Your Holiness a certain case of their church. The case, concerning the Church at Marcha and the Church at Nameka, was heard in our presence at the synod of Liège and adjudicated to its due conclusion.

Since it had recently been handled, we sent it to our reverend father, the abbot of Cluny, to whom the same matter seemed to belong. We have now taken care to send Your Discretion a transcription found written in our papers. In them we have taken care to remind your discretion—not in presumptuous boldness, but in the spirit of devotion—to observe that, in this action, the judge was not challenged before the joinder of issue; that there was no appeal from the judgment; indeed, that the men of Nameka were more satisfied than the provost of St Bartholomew; and whether appeal should be made from the judgment, not from its execution [Col. 1289D].

We would both write much to Your Highness and communicate much orally through envoys, were it not that we daily expect the envoys of your elder son, our most beloved lord, the unconquered king of the Romans, to depart for your presence; then we may lay before you all matters worthy of your knowledge.

## LETTER CXCIII. ABBOT WIBALD TO STEPHEN, PRIOR OF ST JAMES AT LIÈGE

He urges him to undertake the burden of pastoral care, to which he had been canonically elected and which he declined out of humility. (1150.)

[Col. 1290A] Brother WIBALD, by God’s grace servant of the Church of Stavelot, to his beloved brother and friend STEPHEN [Note: [Col. 1289D] I find that Stephen was abbot of St James at Liège, successor to Olbert, who died in 1135; another Stephen was appointed in 1150, when Elbert, deprived of sight, resigned. This letter appears to have been written to the latter.], elected prior of the church of St James at Liège: be strengthened in the Lord.

“I rejoiced at the things said to me: We shall go into the house of the Lord.” We have heard, brother, and rejoiced, that your brethren, deprived of their spiritual father, have chosen you together, by a concordant and unanimous vote, as ruler and shepherd of their souls. But you, conscious of holy humility, decline to bear the burden imposed upon you. Indeed, it is a devout intention full of Christian religion that you have chosen rather to be lowly in the house of your God [Col. 1290B] than to dwell in the tents of sinners. It is beneficial for you, brother, but not necessary for others; and just as, by the justice dictated by equity, one who desires office should be rejected, so, by the course of canonical reason, one who refuses must be compelled.

Act, then, brother: give thanks to the divine dispensation, which has supplied you with a spirit of humility and self-restraint and has mercifully called you to share in its authority and name. For we have received the spirit of adoption as sons, in which we cry, “Abba, Father God”; *abba*, father in human terms, canonically and according to rule elected to the prelacy of a monastery.

Now follow, brother, the Rule as your guide, under which you have professed that you will live. Though humility makes you despair of your own strength, yet, conscious of God’s grace, accept the command of him who orders you and set your shoulder to bear the burden. “The hinges of the earth are the Lord’s”: he humbles one and exalts another; he makes poor and makes rich; he raises the needy from the dust, that he may sit with princes and hold the throne of glory.

You fear the savagery of the times, shrink from the savagery of tyrants, and dread the harshness of subjects; but hope in the Lord and do good. Would that the Lord might open your spiritual eyes, so that you may see that those with us are far more numerous than those with them; and remember him who made Paul out of Saul. Give your heart, therefore, to wisdom; hold fast the grace that calls you; and, effectively yielding to our prayers, admonition, and counsel, nourish your mother who nursed you; govern the mother who brought you up; bear the care of your servants. Christ says to Peter: “Do you love me? Feed [Col. 1290D] my sheep.” If you love, feed them; if you do not feed them, you do not love. Let no one deceive you with empty words: truth does not lie; the proof of love is the performance of a deed. We both promise and offer to your sincerity our humble prayer, devoted assistance, and faithful service, for the comfort of the Church that calls you.

## LETTER CXCIV. ABBOT WIBALD TO THEOBALD, PROVOST OF XANTEN

He rejoices that his favor has benefited him. (1150.)

To his beloved brother and friend in Christ THEOBALD, [Col. 1291A] venerable archdeacon of the holy Church of Cologne and provost of Xanten, Brother WIBALD, by God’s grace that which he is in the Catholic Church: blessing and life for ever.

If the effort of our lowliness, if the effect of our diligent work, has advanced in any degree the increase of your honor, we rejoice exceedingly. For from long ago we have loved your person and reputation with true charity, and have in return been loved by you. But we do not wish your prudence to be unaware that in this affair we did not serve your friendship alone. Rather, we gladly exerted ourselves in support of that man whose work for advancing his friends we do not wish to be broken, overcome, or defeated. From his goodwill we acknowledge that we have the ability [Col. 1291B] sometimes to say and write at the court of the Roman emperor things that serve the Catholic Church, that imperial eminence does not reject, that benefit good people, and that harm evil people.

That man—yes, that man who, in the performance of a deed, has proved the force of his love—planted your advancement and enabled both others and ourselves to water it; and blessed in all things is God, who gave the increase. After divine mercy you owe everything that you are to that true and steadfast friend, who is not accustomed to flatter his friends but to help them; who does not know how to cajole but how to give generously; who cannot embellish with the enticements of words, but knows how to honor through the effectiveness of deeds.

May God require it at your hand, and may the days of your honor be short [Col. 1291C], if you should ever fail in his honor or attach yourself in any degree against him to those who wished to defraud you and exclude you from so great a dignity. We have taken care to make the reason why we wished to write to the lord pope in this manner in the person of the lord king more fully known to the chancellor of whom we speak. We believe it additionally necessary to urge Your Nobility to reward generously the labors of your clerk Manno.

## LETTER CXCV. EMPEROR CONRAD TO POPE EUGENIUS III

That he should graciously receive Arnold, archbishop of Cologne, and send him back restored to his see. (1150.)

To his dearest father in Christ EUGENIUS, supreme pontiff of the holy Roman [Col. 1291D] Church, CONRAD, by God’s grace king of the Romans and ever Augustus: filial affection in all things and due reverence in the Lord.

How welcome to your holy mind are the condition of our honor, the preservation of our person, and the peace and tranquility of the kingdom granted to us by the supreme Majesty, was clearly shown by the words of Your Greatness which we first received after our return from the Jerusalem expedition, etc. See under Eugenius III, at the year 1153, among the letters of various persons to him.

## LETTER CXCVI. ABBOT WIBALD TO CARDINAL GUIDO

He writes that the king has entrusted him with an embassy to the pope. (1150.)

[Col. 1292A]

To his reverend father and lord GUIDO, cardinal-deacon of the holy Roman Church and chancellor of the Apostolic See, Brother WIBALD, by God’s grace that which he is in the Catholic Church: himself.

We would have filled your hand with a longer memorandum, containing fuller information about the entire state of the kingdom and matters pertaining to you, had the lord king not directed us to carry his embassy to the lord pope with certain others. We shall therefore discuss these matters more safely and pleasantly in person—before the fire, if it is cold; in the shade, if it is harvest-time [Col. 1292B].

But lest we now remain wholly silent, we have found our prince changed: stern in severity, a lover of justice, and vigorous in administering judgment. The bearer of this letter is not unworthy that you should receive him honorably for our request and assist him kindly in his own cases and petitions. Farewell in the Lord.

## LETTER CXCVII. EMPEROR CONRAD TO THE NUNS OF QUEDLINBURG

He sees no reason why they should refrain from divine offices. (1150.)

CONRAD, by God’s grace king of the Romans, to the venerable [Col. 1292C] community of the church of Quedlinburg [Note: [Col. 1291D] Quedlinburg, the celebrated monastery of virgins in the diocese of Halberstadt, was founded about the year 936 by Queen Matilda; she lies buried there with her husband, King Henry the Fowler.], and to the barons and ministers of the same church: his favor and every good.

It seems improper to us that divine offices should cease in your church and that you should be barred from the burial of Christians, especially since you live under the rule of ecclesiastical and canonical discipline and are content with a common refectory and dormitory. We therefore do not wish you henceforth to be afflicted by the penalty of those who live unjustly and irregularly.
