Accordingly, we command that the divine offices in the church of Quedlinburg be celebrated canonically, devoutly, and solemnly, together with all that is due to you.

## LETTER CXCVIII. JOHN, ABBOT OF FRITHSELS, TO WIBALD, ABBOT.  
He writes that he is going to the king. (1150.)

[Col. 1292D]

To Lord WIBALD, venerable abbot of the holy church of Corvey, brother JOHN, with the whole community of the monastery of Frithsel, whatever may be of greater worth from a devoted mind and heart.

Just as your prolonged absence produced sorrow, so your return in peace has produced joy for us all. Now let your excellence know that I am going to the king; and, if it should please you perhaps to entrust any matter to me, let me learn it as swiftly as possible through some faithful messenger of yours sent to me. May almighty God keep your holiness safe.

## LETTER CXCIX. WIBALD, ABBOT, TO JOHN OF FRITHSEL.  
As John goes to the king, he commends to him the affairs of his monastery of Corvey, especially concerning the union of the convent of virgins at Wibeke. (1150.)

Brother WIBALD, by God’s grace what he is in the Catholic Church, to his beloved brother and friend JOHN and the whole convent of the church of Frithsel: humble prayers and devoted service.

Your affection ought to remember how, when we strongly resisted and wept most bitterly, you compelled us by your most urgent persuasion to undertake the government of the church of Corvey; and how, after undertaking it, before we had tasted bread with the Corvey brethren, you led us by your most earnest counsel to take upon ourselves the labour and expense of obtaining the churches of Kaminata, Wibeke, and Hildwardehusen. You also then presented to us letters from our friend Count Hermann, who earnestly urged us to do this very thing.

Therefore, with you as the chief author and guide of all counsels, both at the court of the lord king and at home, and with the Corvey brethren striving alongside us with the greatest zeal, we yielded to your judgment against the judgment of our own mind. For we feared to undertake a matter so arduous, so difficult, and so presumptuous, not being ignorant or inexperienced of how many obstacles and changes might arise in such affairs. We believe that you had zeal for God and that you were ready and forceful in promoting this work, not only for removing the enormity of the women who lived there, but also for the advancement of the church of Corvey.

Yet into how many miseries, into how many vexations of mind and body, into what losses of our possessions we have fallen through this counsel, not only your understanding, which is close to the events, but the whole realm of Germany has learned through the loudest public outcry against us. And now, since you intend to go to the court of our lord king and transact our affairs, we commend to your fidelity and goodness with earnest devotion that you act as becomes a religious and honourable man, so that, by God’s grant, you may remove all things harmful to us and apply diligence to all things advantageous.

We trust without any scruple of doubt in the grace and mercy of the lord king. At his court at Frankfurt we were received with great honour and dismissed with great cheerfulness; and we were ordered to come to the court which is to be held at Aachen at the approaching Nativity of the Lord, in order that there we might receive his command concerning the acquisition of the church of Wibeke.

But, dearest brother, we do not at all wish to undertake that labour, because both the treasures of our church have been exhausted and the bishop of Minden as well as all the clerics bitterly oppose us in this matter. We also wish this to be made known and entrusted to your kindness, as we trust in you: when, God prospering, you return to us, disclose nothing whatsoever to any mortal concerning our cause except to us. We thought it necessary to warn your prudence of this because that most shameless woman of Gisecke has spread among the people the rumour that what she did was done by the authority and command of the lord king—something no honourable person ought to believe.

Take with you the bearer of this letter, that he may carry our letters from the court to our household associates and faithfully report to us whatever you discover.

## LETTER CC. WIBALD, ABBOT, TO CONRAD, EMPEROR.  
Concerning the rebellion of the abbess of Kaminata, against whom he implores the emperor’s protection. (1150.)

[Col. 1294B]

To the illustrious triumpher, crowned and exalted by God, his most serene lord CONRAD, Augustus, emperor of the Romans, brother WIBALD, by God’s grace what he is in the Catholic Church: greeting in him who gives salvation to kings.

After we received from your highness the command that, having arranged our affairs, we should be so free and prepared as to carry your embassy with your chancellor to the lord pope in the city of Rome within a short time, we hastened toward the church of Stavelot, which is grievously harassed by continual plundering and robberies committed by wicked men, so that, after establishing whatever peace we could, we might travel more safely to the church of Corvey.

In this interval of time, namely on the vigil of the Nativity of Saint Mary, that abbess of Gisecke entered the church of Kaminata with an armed force. Having violently expelled the brethren of Corvey whom, by your command, we had established there to serve God, she ordered the provost of the monastery to be thrown into the river, and fortified the church tower as a castle by placing armed men and provisions in it.

In response, the freemen and ministerials of Corvey, being without our presence and unable to use our counsel, fell upon these same evildoers; repelling force by force, they expelled them from the church and place with disgrace, and brought some captives away with them. When we learned this while still staying at the monastery of Stavelot, we were deeply grieved in spirit, especially because the aforesaid woman and her supporters had proclaimed throughout the land that what had been done was performed by your will—a thing which neither we nor any honourable men could possibly believe.

For, most merciful Caesar, by your command and by the judgment of your princes—indeed great and numerous men—we entered the church of Kaminata through the grant of your privilege, through letters of your authority sent by your own envoy; and according to the tenor of your command we began, though hindered by many, to restore divine religious observance there.

But that woman, who neither can nor ought to be called an abbess, because she was neither veiled nor consecrated as a nun or as an abbess by any bishop, changes and casts off the habit of her profession for black and white clothing. Nearly a full year before we entered the aforesaid place, she had been deposed by the envoy of the lord pope and disgracefully cast out of the place by the advocate and ministerials of Kaminata because she refused obedience.

Therefore, with our spirits cast at the knees of your majesty, we humbly implore your clemency: remembering our small service and our no small fidelity, which we have shown to you and to your realm with unwearied zeal, may you deign to defend and protect us from these injuries. For we shall come to you at Aachen at the Nativity of the Lord; and if anything has been neglected by the Corvey brethren, the whole matter shall remain subject to your favour.

## LETTER CCI. WIBALD, ABBOT, TO H., NOTARY OF THE ROYAL COURT.  
He commends to him before the emperor the cause of the Corvey brethren concerning Kaminata and Wibeke. (1150.)

[Col. 1295B]

Brother WIBALD, by God’s grace what he is in the Catholic Church, to his beloved brother and friend H., notary of the royal court: blessing and life unto eternity.

We have several times entrusted to your learning the task of explaining word for word to our lord king the letters which we sent him. Until now we have done this for pleasure; but now necessity compels us to ask it. For the letters that we have written to the lord king will plainly show your affection how great are the insults we suffer both in our person and in our possessions.

Indeed, this especially burns our heart and kindles our thoughts to grief: our enemies assert that the evils which have befallen us occurred by the nod and will of our lord king; and our faithful supporters draw this inference because, while our lord king was absent and the realm was thought somehow to be faltering, no such deed was ventured.

But your experience ought to remember, and bring to the recollection of our lord king, how, in response to our first letters—when in them our devotion went forth to meet him on his return, and we presented him with a suppliant complaint concerning the hindrances that had befallen us at Kaminata and Wibeke—he deigned to reply in words of this kind:

> “Those things which we have bestowed upon the church of Corvey for love of you—namely, Kaminata and Wibeke—we shall, God consenting, preserve for its use, being certain that the Corvey brethren will unquestionably pay us the money which they promised under the assurance of an oath.”

In the same letters we were commanded to come to court at Frankfurt on the Assumption of Saint Mary, where the royal highness would deign to confer with our lowliness in familiar counsel concerning both private and public affairs of the realm.

Within that period a court was held at Würzburg, where the princes of Saxony met our lord king. To that court came a certain priest hired by the abbess of Gisecke for half a mark, who had no concern at all in the affair of Kaminata. As we have only now first heard, he lodged many complaints against us. Having obtained, by what intervention we do not know, letters of our lord king—whose contents we have not yet been able to learn—he spread throughout all Saxony the claim that he had received in those letters an order that whatever had been done by us at Kaminata ought to be annulled and changed by the lord king.

When you were conversing familiarly with us at Frankfurt, however, you told us that, once the money which we had given was received, we should leave the aforesaid places free. This report was also heard in Saxony and brought us and our people under grave suspicion. Moreover, it has reached our ears in part by what promoters and upon what pledges it is promised that the money can be assembled.

We therefore beseech your diligence by the divine judgment: since you have influence with our lord king both in authority and counsel, provide by every means for his welfare, lest through the counsel of some layman who neither fears God nor respects man he give assent to the loss and destruction of churches. We indeed place great confidence in his truth, judgment, and steadfastness; but the reproaches of those who reproach us fall upon us, as they say among themselves. I have seen what happened to one who was a deservedly favoured intimate and household member, always admitted to secret counsels.

But, to bring our words to an end, we have never sought the patronage of any layman at court, but have been accustomed to arrange all our affairs through clerics. Since your fidelity and discretion are especially well known in the Church and in the realm, we earnestly commend our cause to your diligence, so that, with the Lord favouring and the clemency of our lord king granting it, you may defend it in such a way that we are compelled not only to abandon Corvey, but even to leave and forsake the entire realm of our lord king. On this matter we desire to be informed through the present messengers by letters both from you and from our lord king.

## LETTER CCII. HENRY, NOTARY OF THE ROYAL COURT, TO WIBALD, ABBOT.  
A reply to the preceding letter. (1150.)

[Col. 1296D]

To his lord WIBALD, abbot of Corvey, HENRY, his own.

Brother John clearly laid before the lord king your dangers, losses, and hardships. I, moreover, explained your letters to him word by word and ventured, according to my small ability, to say some things for the advantage of your cause. I have learned, and am certain, that the lord king is greatly distressed by the injury inflicted upon you; and he has sent a messenger with his letters to you to pursue the advantage of your cause. What he has bestowed upon the church of Corvey for love of you, he considers ratified and intends in every way to confirm.

## LETTER CCIII. WIBALD, ABBOT, TO CONRAD, EMPEROR.  
He laments that he has received no reply from him concerning the affair of the church of Kaminata. (1150.)

[Col. 1297A]

To the illustrious triumpher crowned by God, his most serene lord CONRAD, glorious Augustus, emperor of the Romans, brother WIBALD, by God’s grace what he is in the Catholic Church: greeting in him who commands salvations for Jacob.

In accordance with the command of your good pleasure, we awaited your messenger and your letters. When the appointed time had passed and we received neither, we were affected by heavy sorrow and great confusion of mind. But brother John, returning to us from your court, greatly wiped away our grief and much cheered our spirit, namely by reporting that you had recovered well from your illness.

Nevertheless, he brought back nothing certain, nothing favourable, concerning our affair. And now the church of Corvey sharply reproaches us because, after being induced by good hope from your gentleness to choose our lowliness, according to your good pleasure, for its government, it has obtained not only no favour or mercy but has also ruinously lost its labour and its treasures.

Since we have learned that you wish to have a conference with the princes of Saxony at Bamberg fifteen days before the Nativity of the Lord, and since we are uncertain what we ought to do, we have taken care to send to your highness, that, out of regard for divine mercy and for the increase of our perpetual service, you may free us from the evils under which we are oppressed.

For you cannot have a lesser claim upon the Corvey brethren for money before you extend to us the right hand of aid and protection than you have now, when all the goods of the church of Kaminata, as though they were vacant lordless property, have been seized by the advocates. It would be our desire that you reserve our labour and expenses for the affairs which you have decided to conduct in the regions of Saxony; nevertheless, whatever may please your majesty, our lowliness will strive to fulfil even beyond its means.

## LETTER CCIV. WIBALD, ABBOT, TO HENRY, NOTARY OF THE ROYAL COURT.  
He commends to him the affairs of the monastery of Corvey. (1150.)

[Col. 1297D]

Brother WIBALD, by God’s grace what he is in the Catholic Church, to his beloved brother and friend H., notary of the royal court: greeting and blessing.

We give thanks for your concern, because you watch with diligent care for the increase of our honour and the enlargement of our advantages, although at this time, through the working of our sins, we derive little benefit from these things. For a remarkable reversal of circumstances is taking place: those whose fidelity was doubted by many—or rather, to speak more truthfully, whose perfidy became known to nearly everyone—are raised to honours and riches, while we, whose fidelity has been approved by the acclaim of the whole realm, have now become almost strangers.

For, dearest brother, it has happened contrary to the custom of the realm that, although we recently sent both letters and a messenger to the court, we have been able to obtain no reply. This especially tends to happen to those whose punishment is already being decreed under the Julian law concerning persons accused of treason. We may say with the poet:

> “I hoped for better, because I thought I had deserved it.”

We therefore ask your experience that, through your industry, replies helpful to our cause may now be sent back to us. Above all, your prudence must take care that our lord king does not discuss our affair with any of the princes of Saxony at the conference he is to have with them at Bamberg. For they would count it as a triumph if they should now assist us in that court in which we have often sustained their causes, since we could not secure their help without payment, either of some estate or of money.

Our lord king commands that our Corvey brethren observe their obligation to pay him money, although we not only do not receive what he granted us, but even lose it after it has been seized. Therefore, having been carefully advised by your discretion, let him, I pray, send us letters suited to our necessities addressed to the duke of Saxony, the bishop of Minden, and Count Hermann; and you will take care to send us copies of them. You may know that, God being propitious, you will usefully employ all your labour on behalf of us and the church of Corvey.

We also wish the most gracious Augustus to understand through your representation that, unless his protection establishes the church of Kaminata in our hands, no community and no observance of divine religion can henceforth be restored there. Farewell.

## LETTER CCV. R. TO WIBALD, ABBOT.  
He asks him for certain books and promises him others. (1150.)

To his venerable lord, the abbot of Corvey, R.: good health and happiness.

Although you desire to possess books of Tully, I know nevertheless that you are a Christian, not a Ciceronian. For you cross even into foreign camps, not as a deserter but as a scout. We would therefore have sent you the books of Tully that are with us—*On Agrarian Affairs*, the *Philippics*, and his *Letters*—but it is not our custom for books to be granted by anyone to anyone without good pledges.

Send us, therefore, Aulus Gellius’s *Attic Nights* and Origen on the *Song of Songs*. And if any of our books, which we have now brought from France, please you, we shall send them to you.

## LETTER CCVI. WIBALD, ABBOT, TO R., PROVOST OF HILDESHEIM.  
Concerning his own interest in humane letters. (1150.)

Brother WIBALD, by God’s grace what he is in the Catholic Church, to his beloved brother and friend R., venerable provost of Hildesheim: blessing and life unto eternity.

You rightly remember, brother, that although we possess Cicero’s books, we nevertheless remember that we are Christians. As you wrote, and as your Seneca says of himself, we sometimes cross into foreign camps, not as deserters and fugitives but as scouts and desirous of spoils, in case perhaps we may seize a Midianite woman and, after her hair has been shaved and her nails pared, may lawfully unite her to ourselves in marriage.

And although we ought not to travel as pilgrims in a far country but rather to live in exile, we nevertheless prefer to be satisfied with the living bread which came down from heaven rather than to fill our belly with the husks which swine eat. We no longer place Cicero’s dishes either among the chief courses or on the first table; but if, when we have been satisfied with better food, we sometimes desire something further, we take them as sweetmeats are customarily served with the second course.

There is also for us a certain pleasure in not being idle. Nor, to omit other considerations, can we endure that that noble genius, those brilliant discoveries, and those great ornaments of things and words should perish through forgetfulness and neglect. Rather, we wish all his works, however many can be found, to be made into one volume. We have nothing in common with those who, the richer they are, the more needy they become; who, neglecting liberal studies, are anxious about transient things; who gather in order to scatter, and scatter in order to gather.

They imitate above all a ball-game, in which the players both take eagerly and throw back quickly; thus they have no moderation either in receiving or in returning. If you love us, you will avoid their teaching—as poison and the death of the soul—even though it is praised by wicked men of the world.

As pledges for your books we have sent you Origen on the *Song of Songs*; and in exchange for Aulus Gellius’s *Attic Nights*, which book we have not at present been able to obtain, [we have sent] the book which they call in Greek *Stratēgēmatōn* (“of stratagems”), which is military in character.

## LETTER CCVII. ANONYMOUS TO WIBALD, ABBOT.  
He declares his gratitude for benefits received from him and laments that certain persons seek to turn Wibald away from him. (1150.)

[Col. 1299D]

To his most beloved lord WIBALD, his own [servant]: whatever can be said, believed, or be happier.

That servant of yours greets you from the inmost affection of his heart, whom you raised needy from the dust. Having often experienced your goodwill in time of necessity, he wishes neither to be forgetful nor ungrateful for your benefits. They are, as it were, engraved with an iron stylus across the breadth of his heart, so that they may never be erased by any age, by the varied succession of events, or by the changeability of times.

For he knows—he whom no one can deceive—how greatly I hold you in the inward parts of Jesus Christ, how singularly I love you, how singularly I desire all things that pertain to your honour. Henceforth neither the length of time nor the distance of places will be able to blot out your memory.

My mind remembers, lord; it frequently turns over in the cave of my heart that, had not the sons of Belial, the sons of iniquity, sons whom the soul detests—who have often been drunk with my blood and satisfied with my flesh—stood in the way, had they not turned you from unhappy me more enviously than justly, I should have found more enduring mercy in the sight of your favour.

But I entrust all these things to the hand of the living God, who will repay each person according to the finding out of his ways. I earnestly beg you not to take grievously what I say, for my soul is greatly troubled; but the compassion of your mercy has now given me no small measure of rest. Therefore I offer to God the calves of my lips, and I shall not cease to offer them for your prosperity: that you may live happily and flourish, and that all you undertake may be prosperously directed by God in your hands.

## LETTER CCVIII. WIBALD, ABBOT, TO ANSELM, BISHOP.  
Concerning the king’s displeasure with him. (1150.)

To his reverend father and lord ANSELM, bishop of the poor city, brother WIBALD, by God’s grace what he is in the Catholic Church: himself and all that is his.

Your prudence is still displeased with us because we send you no letters, or few letters; in this fault we too recognize that you labour, and we grieve and reproach you for it. Greeting, therefore, your paternity beloved by us in the Lord, we profess without doubt—so far as we can speak of future matters—that we intend to remain in that grace of charity which God long ago bound together between us, unless perhaps some increase toward perfection may be added.

We have read the letters which, in excuse of yourself concerning the displeasure of our lord king, you sent to our mutual friend. But, on the report of someone not wholly ignorant of the secrets of the court, we have learned that some more hidden poison from the slander of certain persons was the cause. We expect neither longer nor greater favour. For your fault, if indeed it is a fault, is also common to us with you and with certain bishops; we did not judge it at all safe to indicate it to you in writing.

A court is to be held at Bamberg, though not a large one, to which we have been ordered to come on familiar terms, while grave necessity draws us there on account of the affairs of the church of Kaminata. In those affairs we bear much labour but have hitherto received little support from the quarter where we hoped for it.

## LETTER CCIX. R., PROVOST, TO WIBALD, ABBOT.  
A rumour is being spread that he is shortly to be chosen archbishop of Cologne. (1150.)

To his lord WIBALD, abbot at Corvey, praiseworthy in every respect, R., humble provost: service with prayers.

[Col. 1301A]

My messenger, recently returned from Cologne, has stated with the greatest confidence that the lord archbishop will withdraw without opposition from episcopal care and dignity.

[Note: [Col. 1301D] Above we saw that Arnold, archbishop of Cologne, had been suspended from his dignity at the Council of Rheims and had gone to Rome in an attempt to recover it. But when he could obtain nothing from the supreme pontiff, firmly attached to what was right, the leading men of the church of Cologne advised him to resign voluntarily.]

He further adds that my household associates have heard and ascertained that you are being marked out as successor, which I deemed worthy of being disclosed to you. Whatever, therefore, your discretion may choose concerning this matter, let it be communicated in a reply to me, your most faithful servant; and my devotion will strive most carefully to satisfy your will and good pleasure.

For I intend to go there during this feast of the Nativity of the Lord; and if you think of entrusting anything, whether in writing or in plain words, to any of your faithful associates, I shall carry it out most devotedly. May your fatherhood flourish in the Lord.

## LETTER CCX. WIBALD, ABBOT, TO R., PROVOST.  
Reply to the preceding letter. (1150.)

[Col. 1301B]

To his reverend brother and friend R., venerable provost, brother WIBALD, by God’s grace what he is in the Catholic Church: blessing and life unto eternity.

Having read your sincere letter, we rejoiced greatly because you love our advancement with such constancy of fidelity and congratulate us with so benevolent a spirit over a matter that does not yet exist. But we earnestly beg your sincerity not to do that which, even if our strength were able to bear it, is untimely to do and, although it can profit nothing, can harm greatly. For it can furnish fuel for suspicion, envy, and hatred.

We had indeed heard that our lord and father, the archbishop of Cologne, was being diligently advised by the lords and fathers who are the leading men of the church of Cologne that, since he appeared to neglect both the dignity of his church and the duties of his office, and, already failing in mind as well as body, could insufficiently support the declining church, he should provide for his own welfare and begin voluntarily to do what he is believed likely to do under the pressure of necessity. It is thought that neither he nor his associates will readily accept this counsel.

As for that other rumour which concerns our person: since we neither desired it nor hope for it, since it is wholly premature, and since we have heard nothing of it and do not suppose that it has even been raised, it will be for your goodwill and discretion to take care, just as you have customarily retained a pleasant and favourable memory of us in every conversation, that in this conversation you say nothing which might in any way detract from our integrity and reputation. Farewell, and continue, as you do, to love us.

## LETTER CCXI. THE SENATE AND PEOPLE OF ROME TO CONRAD, EMPEROR.  
They urge the emperor to come to Rome, offering themselves and all they possess to him against the pope and the Sicilian. (1150.)

[Col. 1302A]

To the most excellent and illustrious lord of the City and of the whole world, CONRAD, by God’s grace king of the Romans, ever Augustus, the senate and people of Rome: greeting, and the happy and illustrious government of the Roman Empire.

In many previous letters we have carefully set forth to your royal excellence our actions and affairs: how we remain in your fidelity, and how daily we contend for the exaltation and complete enlargement of your imperial crown. Since royal diligence has not deigned to answer these letters as we requested, we openly marvel enough, as sons and faithful subjects, at our lord and Father.

For whatever we do, we do for your fidelity and honour. Desiring to exalt and enlarge the Roman kingdom and empire entrusted by the Lord to your government, and to restore it to the state in which it stood in the time of Constantine and Justinian—who held the whole world in their hands through the power of the Roman senate and people—we have zealously and unanimously laboured to this end. The senate has, by God’s grace, been restored for all these purposes; and those who had always rebelled against your empire and had usurped so great an honour from the Roman Empire have in large part been crushed, so that you may possess fully and in all things whatever belongs to Caesar and the emperor. Out of zeal for this matter we have laid a good beginning and foundation.

For we preserve peace and justice for all who desire them. We have captured the strongholds—that is, the towers and houses—of the powerful men of the City who were preparing to resist your empire together with the Sicilian and the pope. Some of these we hold in your fidelity; others we have destroyed and levelled to the ground.

But for all these things which we do in faithful service to your love, the pope, the Frangipani, and the sons of Peter Leo, men and friends of the Sicilian—except Jordan, who is a standard-bearer and helper in your fidelity—together with Ptolemy and many others, attack us on every side, so that we may not freely, as is fitting, be able to place the Roman imperial crown upon the royal head.

[Note: [Col. 1302D] This Jordan, according to Otto of Freising, book VII, chapter 31, was excommunicated by Eugenius.]

But because no labour is burdensome to one who loves, although we sustain very many losses thereby, we bear them gladly for your love and honour. For we know that we shall therefore receive our reward from you as from a Father, and that you will inflict vengeance on them as enemies of the empire.

Since, therefore, our fidelity toward you is so great and we endure so much for you, we pray that this hope may not fail us; that royal dignity may not despise us, your faithful subjects and sons; and that, if an unfavourable breeze concerning the senate and ourselves should blow into royal ears, it may not heed or regard it. For those who suggest evil things about us to your highness wish—God forbid!—to rejoice in discord between you and us, and seek craftily, as they are accustomed, to oppress both parties.

Let royal prudence, as is fitting, be solicitous and provident that these things do not happen. Let your sagacity remember what and how great evils the papal court and those former citizens of ours have inflicted upon the emperors who were before you, and how they now attempted worse things together with the Sicilian. But by Christ’s grace we resist them manfully in your fidelity and have driven out many of them as the worst enemies of the empire that they are.

Let the power of royal highness therefore draw near to us, because you will be able to obtain whatever you desire in the City. To speak briefly and succinctly: in the City, which is the head of the world, you will be able to dwell powerfully as we desire, and to rule all Italy and the German realm more freely and better than almost all your predecessors, every obstacle from clerics having been removed.

Come therefore without delay, we pray; and meanwhile deign to gladden us by royal letters or messengers concerning your condition, which we always desire to be sound and prosperous, and concerning all these matters. For in every respect we are always ready to obey your will.

Know furthermore that we are restoring with great effort the Milvian Bridge, not far outside the City, which for a long time had been destroyed because it was hostile to the emperors. This is so that your army may pass over it and so that Peter Leo’s men, from the castle of Sant’Angelo, may not harm you as they had planned with the pope and the Sicilian. With God’s help, it will be completed in a short time with a very strong wall and stonework.

We have learned that the agreement between the Sicilian and the pope is as follows. The pope has granted the Sicilian the staff and ring, dalmatic, mitre, and sandals; and [has agreed] not to send any legate into his land except one whom the Sicilian requests. And the Sicilian has given a great deal of money for the harm of you and of the Roman Empire, which by God’s grace is yours. May your prudence, most excellent king, take note of all these things.

> May the king flourish, obtain whatever he desires over his enemies,  
> Hold the empire, sit in Rome, and rule the world,  
> Prince of lands, as Justinian did;  
> Let Caesar receive the things that are Caesar’s, and the prelate what is his,  
> As Christ commanded, when Peter paid tribute.

We further ask you kindly to receive our envoys and to believe what they tell you, because we could not commit it to writing. They are noble men: Guido, senator; James, son of Sixtus the procurator; and Nicholas, their companion.

## LETTER CCXII. SIXTUS, NICHOLAS, AND GUIDO, COUNSELLORS OF THE ROMAN COURT, TO CONRAD, EMPEROR.  
On the same subject. (1150.)

To the most excellent and magnificent lord of the City and the world, CONRAD, by God’s grace king of the Romans, ever Augustus, SIXTUS, NICHOLAS, and GUIDO, counsellors of the court, procurators of the sacred senate and of the public welfare of the commonwealth: faithful services to the full extent of our power in all things, and the restoration of the Roman Empire.

As has now been communicated to royal majesty in many letters, seeing that the Roman Empire had greatly declined from its strength through the rash usurpation of clerics, whereby the Roman people had been greatly dishonoured, we have, with Christ’s aid and with the utmost zeal, raised up the senate in order to bring the world beneath your feet. The senate, preserving peace in the City and administering justice, by exalting the good and destroying the wicked, suitably prepares the way for your dignity as you come to the City to obtain the imperial crown, all clerical hindrance having been removed.

By Christ’s grace both the senate and we have already done this manfully. For we have expelled from the City Cencius Frangipani and the sons of Peter Leo, whom we learned had conspired with the pope and the Sicilian for the diminution of your empire; and we have laid waste many of their possessions, so that they are in no way able to resist you.

Nothing else therefore remains, if it pleases you, except that you quickly draw near and bring aid to your people. For whatever the imperial heart desires in the City, it will undoubtedly be able to obtain there. We further commend to you these our messengers, your faithful subjects. For we have sent them to you in fidelity to your love; and we pray that you may deign to gladden and honour us also with your letters.

### Letter CCXIII. From a Certain Senator to Emperor Conrad  
*On the same subject. (A.D. 1150.)*

[Col. 1304C]

To the most illustrious and magnificent lord of the world, CONRAD, by the grace of God King of the Romans, ever-triumphant Augustus—than whom none is better, and to whom none in the world is second—from a certain faithful servant of the senate, most faithful among the servants of the king: whatever so small a servant may offer to so great a lord.

Let it be certain and firmly established for Your Royal Majesty that I have, in the senate and wherever I could, given continual effort toward the exaltation of your empire; and therefore I write to you, though boldly, yet confidently:

> Do not, lord, despise the useful counsel of your servant.

If, therefore, a servant may offer counsel to his lord, I advise your royal prudence [Col. 1304D] to come to Rome without delay; and, placing yourself between the people and the pope, to receive the senate and people under your protection. For you will be able to take the Castle of Saint Angelo with the Romans, and thus ensure that henceforth no apostolic pontiff is ever appointed in the City without your command and direction.

For so it was in the time of blessed Gregory, who could not become pope without the consent of Emperor Maurice; and this continued until the time of Gregory VII. For this reason I affirm that it is useful, lest wars or killings be brought about in the world by priests. For it is not lawful for them to bear both sword and chalice, but rather to preach, and to confirm their preaching by good works—not at all to engage in wars and disputes in the world.

### Letter CCXIV. From Cardinal Guy to Abbot Wibald  
*That he should turn Emperor Conrad away from undertaking anything harmful against the Roman Church. (A.D. 1150.)*

[Col. 1305A]

To his dearest and special friend WIBALD, Abbot of Corvey: GUY, deacon-cardinal and chancellor of the holy Roman Church, greetings and blessing.

Both your messenger and the letter sent to us through him have removed the uncertainty concerning your condition which had occupied our mind. For we pray in the Lord that all things may always be healthful and prosperous for you, and that heavenly mercy may protect you in your undertakings by the aid of its celestial compassion, so that you may accomplish [Col. 1305B] those matters for which, on this occasion, you asked the lord pope. Finding him well-disposed toward you, we have willingly exerted ourselves, as will appear from his letter to you.

Moreover, we speak to you as to a cautious and prudent man, proven in affection. It is certain that after the departure of the lord Conrad, King of the Romans, war would have been stirred up against his son, the younger king, and no small disturbance would have arisen, unless the lord pope had given a particular and strict prohibition. But now, as has been reported to the lord pope and to us—and as rumours too have increased—his father, King Conrad, is attempting, God avert it, to repay evil for good; and, together with the Emperor of Constantinople, he intends, if he can, gravely to afflict and [Col. 1305C] harass the holy Roman Church, mother of all Catholics.

Therefore, as that same mother of ours and we, her foster-children, trust in your faithful service and devoted fidelity toward her, so, on behalf of the lord pope and ourselves, we admonish your beloved self; by admonishing, we ask; and we earnestly exhort you to strive, by every means in your power, as a true athlete of Christ, founded in the faith of the prince of the apostles, to prevent such waves from rising against the apostolic Roman Church. Or, should they perhaps begin to arise through the perversity of some persons, restrain them, together with the other faithful of the Church of God, according to the strength and prudence granted you by God.

We write this not because the lord pope or we ought to doubt the steadfastness of the aforesaid king, but [Col. 1305D] because it is our desire that the disposition which, during the conference we held with him, he showed in words toward the apostolic see, he may demonstrate even more abundantly by the performance of deeds.

### Letter CCXV. From Emperor Conrad to Pope Eugenius III  
*He commends to him the Bishop of Regensburg, who is travelling to Jerusalem. (A.D. 1150.)*

To his dearest father in Christ, EUGENIUS, supreme pontiff of the holy Roman Church: CONRAD, by the grace of God King of the Romans and ever Augustus, filial love and due reverence in Christ.

“Our faithful man, the son of your holiness, the Bishop of Regensburg,” etc. See under Pope Eugenius III, after his *Regesta*.

### Letter CCXVI. From Conrad to Manuel, Emperor of Constantinople  
*He commends to him the Bishop of Regensburg, setting out for Jerusalem. (A.D. 1150.)*

CONRAD, by the grace of God Emperor of the Romans and ever Augustus, to his dearest brother in Christ, EMMANUEL, most mighty Emperor of the Greeks: an indissoluble affection of fraternal love.

[Col. 1306B]

Our faithful Bishop of Regensburg, closely related to your nobility, although he would have been very useful and advantageous to us in the affairs of our empire, could nevertheless not be detained from journeying to Jerusalem under the sign of the Crucified, out of ardour for the faith and desire to fulfil his vow. When he comes into the presence of your Highness, receive him, at the intercession of our affection, with your customary kindness; and, having assisted him in whatever his need requires, both by the protection of your hand and by the support of your princes, send him forth gladly to accomplish his purpose.

### Letter CCXVII. From Abbot Wibald to Pope Eugenius III  
*Concerning the restoration, through the assistance of Abbot Eilulf—whose election he asks to have confirmed—of discipline wholly collapsed in the monastery of Murbach. (A.D. 1150.)*

[Col. 1306C]

To his reverend father and lord EUGENIUS, sole and universal pontiff: Brother WIBALD, by the grace of God and of yourself, that which he is in the Catholic Church—his son’s love and servant’s obedience.

After the death of our fellow-brother Berthold, Abbot of Murbach—[Note: [Col. 1305D] Murbach monastery, an ancient and distinguished house of the Order of Saint Benedict in the diocese of Basel, situated amid the Vosges Mountains [Col. 1306D], was founded by Count Eberhard about the year 727.]—the brethren and household of that monastery partly united around their cellarer and brought him to the court of your glorious son, our lord Conrad, King of the Romans, which he celebrated at Bamberg during the most recent past Christmas season, his health having now been restored.

But another party, both monks and laymen, opposed those electors, saying that it was not an election but rather an underhanded seizure, and that the man was less suitable to bear such a burden and to heal the wounds of that monastery. Also present at that court was your venerable son Orthlieb, Bishop of Basel. Asked by the lord king, amid the disputes of the litigants, about the condition of the aforesaid monastery, situated in his diocese, he replied that those brethren lived very disorderly lives, contrary both to their profession and to monastic propriety. They had refused to make profession; they possessed individual houses and separate property; [Col. 1307A] and they had neither a common refectory nor a common dormitory.

He further asserted, supported by the testimony of his cleric and of many religious abbots and monks, that the aforesaid abbot, before departing this life, had complained to him that his monks were disobedient and utterly rebellious, and refused to accept discipline or correction of any kind. The same abbot had communicated this to our lord king before many hearers.

We too, dearest Father, saw with our own eyes, when present in that monastery, that they possessed private houses and received prebends in the manner of secular clergy. Likewise, when they appeared before the royal court amid so great a dispute, they displayed neither the tonsure nor the habit of monks, but showed themselves as quasi-laymen, fit to be mocked. Religious men further alleged that they had deliberately elected a man accommodating their vices.

Accordingly, when the substance of these objections had been assembled, it was adjudged that non-monks could not elect an abbot—especially one who had never been a monk. Both the monks and the beneficed clergy and ministerials of the Church were then ordered to attend the court held at Speyer on the Purification of the Blessed Virgin Mary. There, after much obstinacy by the monks, they finally requested, by equal vote and unanimous consent, that there be given them as father and shepherd of their souls a man of renowned religious life, a son of your holiness: namely Eilulf, Abbot of Erlach.

Our lord king, after taking counsel [Col. 1307C] with the Bishop of Basel and other religious persons, granted the monastery of Murbach to the aforesaid man, upon the hope and condition that he would reform that church in divine worship and monastic observance. Therefore, prostrate in humility at the feet of your Highness, we devoutly implore your clemency: that you may bring to completion by your blessing and confirmation, for the honour of God, what has been so well begun and by the support of such worthy persons; and that you may not deign to incline your ear of compassion to certain pseudo-monks wishing to oppose proceedings so rightly conducted.

### Letter CCXVIII. From Abbot Wibald to Pope Eugenius III  
*That the emperor is undertaking nothing against him; and concerning the victory won by the younger king over Welf and Godebald. (A.D. 1150.)*

[Col. 1307D]

To his reverend father and lord EUGENIUS, sole and universal pontiff: Brother WIBALD, by the grace of God and of yourself, that which he is in the Catholic Church—himself and all that is his.

The Apostle John says: “Let us not love in word or tongue, but in deed and truth.” Therefore, imitating the devotion of those accustomed to say little and do much, we rarely proclaim to your Highness our zeal and devotion toward you and toward our most holy mother, the Roman Church. Yet by daily and unceasing endeavour we do not cease diligently to render faithful service to blessed Peter and to yourself—a fact which, by the Lord’s favour, we do not doubt will be made known to your Blessedness by other eminent persons.

If anything concerning matters that pertain to you had been finally decided by your illustrious son, our lord the King of the Romans, we would have carefully informed you without any lengthy delay, either in person or by letter; and, when this occurs, [Col. 1308B] we shall hasten to do so.

Let your Blessedness also be certain that, so far as our modest capacity allows, and so far as divine clemency has granted us influence and opportunity with the most serene prince, we never cease to soften and incline his mind, his speech, and all his action toward love and reverence for your person and toward the honour of his holy mother, the Roman Church, whose defender he has been appointed by God.

While we were writing these things at Speyer, at the court of the lord king, news suddenly came to us that Welf had been captured, Godebald and many of Welf’s knights had fallen in battle, and your illustrious son, the younger king—the son of our lord king—had fought against him. By this we trust that every obstacle which seemed to hinder [Col. 1308C] the lord king’s entry into Italy has been levelled.

### Letter CCXIX. From Emperor Conrad to Pope Eugenius III  
*He sends envoys to him, asks that Eilulf be confirmed as abbot of Murbach monastery, and that the cleric Otto be absolved. (A.D. 1150.)*

To his dearest father in Christ, EUGENIUS, supreme pontiff of the holy Roman Church: CONRAD, by the grace of God King of the Romans and ever Augustus, filial love in all things and due reverence in the Lord.

“After we returned, God propitiously governing our frailty, from the Jerusalem expedition,” etc. See under Pope Eugenius III, in the year 1153, [Col. 1308D] among the letters of various persons addressed to him.

### Letter CCXX. From Abbot Wibald to H., His Sister  
*He congratulates her upon her election as abbess of the nunnery at Gerresheim. (A.D. 1150.)*

Brother WIBALD, abbot by the grace of God, to his beloved sister H., Abbess of Gerresheim—[Note: [Col. 1307D] Gerresheim, a noble nunnery of the Order of Saint Benedict in the diocese of Cologne, about two miles from Düsseldorf; its nuns later declined into the status of secular canonesses. Concerning this nunnery Werner Rolevinck, the Carthusian, in Book III, chapter 8, of *On the Situation and Customs of the Ancient Saxons*, relates the following: “The blessed man and duke Gericus rests in the convent of nuns at Gerresheim, which he himself caused to be built.”]—blessing and life for ever.

[Col. 1309A]

We offer immeasurable thanksgivings to divine goodness because it has deigned to call you to govern its Church and to confer upon you a share in its own name, in which we cry, “Abba, Father,” so that the lamp of your care, hitherto hidden beneath the bushel of private life, may be set upon the lampstand and shine for the salvation of many.

Until now you were our sister; henceforth you shall be to us both sister and bride, and all the more familiarly so because, by your title, you have come nearer to our burden. We have sent you a ring of betrothal, that you may admit no lover besides Christ.

### Letter CCXXI. From Emperor Conrad to Pope Eugenius III  
*He commends to him Archbishop Peter of Capua, through whose help he had recovered his health. (A.D. 1150.)*

[Note: [Col. 1309D] Concerning this archbishop’s pontificate there is profound silence in *Italia Sacra*, where he should have a place between [Col. 1310D] Geoffrey, who seems to have died in 1130, and Alphanus, said to have held office from 1163 to 1183.]

[Col. 1309B]

To his dearest father in Christ, EUGENIUS, supreme pontiff of the holy Roman Church: CONRAD, by the grace of God King of the Romans and ever Augustus, filial love in all things and due reverence in the Lord.

“God propitiously governing our affairs,” etc. See under Eugenius.

### Letter CCXXII. Of Pope Eugenius III to the Prelates of Poland  
*He rebukes them because they do not observe the sentence of interdict pronounced by the messenger G.; and, that they may repent, confirms that same sentence. (A.D. 1150.)*

[Col. 1309C]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brethren the archbishops, bishops, and other prelates of churches established throughout Poland: greeting and apostolic blessing.

“That we greet you with words of blessing,” etc. See under Eugenius.

### Letter CCXXIII. From G., Deacon-Cardinal, to Emperor Conrad  
*Since he has laboured greatly in his legation on behalf of the Duke of Poland, he asks that the emperor provide aid to him. (A.D. 1150.)*

To CONRAD, by the grace of God glorious Augustus, King of the Romans: G., deacon-cardinal of the holy Roman Church, his devoted service and perseverance in prayer.

[Col. 1309D]

It was not unknown to you that, at the command of the lord pope, we laboured sufficiently in the cause of the noble and illustrious Duke of Poland and his wife, your sister. But because their opponents persisted in their hardness, we did not hesitate to execute justice upon them, as had been enjoined upon us by the lord pope and as the counsels of your exhortation suggested.

Since that affair now seems in some measure to concern you, we earnestly ask Your Majesty’s Highness to strive to extend to that duke the hand of your aid and the arm of your strength, so that you may vigorously [Col. 1310A] uphold the force of ecclesiastical office in this matter and may obtain praise from God and men for the peace granted to the duke and your sister.

The lord pope and the Roman Church have ratified the sentence which we pronounced against the opponents of Duke W. and your sister, and they will by no means relax that sentence until those opponents repent and return to peace.

### Letter CCXXIV. From Abbot Wibald to E., Emperor of Constantinople  
*He prays that God may make him victorious over the tyrant of Sicily, and that he may renew and confirm the treaty formerly concluded with Emperor Conrad. (A.D. 1150.)*

To the glorious, exalted, and supreme conqueror, magnificent [Col. 1310B] and most mighty E., PORPHYROGENITUS, most excellent Emperor of the Greeks: WIBALD, by the grace of God Abbot of Corvey and Stavelot, continual prayers and devoted service.

That I dare to write to your glorious Majesty and to your holy and dread empire, though unknown to you both in person and in service, has been persuaded to me by your most sacred faithfulness, charity, and kindness, which you showed to my dearest lord Conrad, most serene Augustus, Emperor of the Romans, in the territory of your empire and great power, at such a crisis of time and affairs as is customarily the proving-ground of a true friend.

And because I have understood truly that my said lord loves you and your empire and intends to fulfil all that he has confirmed with you by treaty and agreement, I too, in my small degree, love and honour your Highness greatly. I humbly and devoutly beseech God that you may win a splendid victory and exact a severe vengeance from the common enemy of your empire.

Indeed, that tyrant of Sicily expelled me from the monastery of Saint Benedict on Monte Cassino and wished to kill me, although I had been appointed abbot there by the common vote and acclamation of all—or rather, had been unwillingly drawn into it in the time of Emperor Lothair of happy memory. I rejoice that I have such helpers—indeed, leaders and princes—against that aforesaid enemy of God.

For that malignant man and many others are devising and daily contriving many evils against your magnificent [Col. 1310D] and powerful empire. But I trust in the omnipotence of God and in his most merciful justice: that so great and such an empire—one in which divine worship flourishes, in which there is an order of laws and the system of civil law, in which there are military courage and discipline, in which there is an inexhaustible abundance of riches—cannot in any way be overthrown and defeated by wicked, perverse, and godless men.

Concerning the enlargement and firmer improvement of the treaty between your holy empire and the exalted Majesty of my lord, I urge your Magnificence not to delay fulfilling the intention which he now makes known to your wisdom. If your Highness deigns to count my lowliness among those known to you, and to greet me by your glorious letters, you will make me, from faithful, most faithful.

### Letter CCXXV. From Abbot Wibald to Cardinal G.  
*Concerning Emperor Conrad’s treaty with the Emperor of Constantinople against the King of Sicily, which greatly troubled the pope. (A.D. 1150.)*

To his reverend father and lord G., deacon-cardinal of the holy Roman Church: Brother WIBALD, by the grace of God, that which he is in the Catholic Church—humble prayers and devoted service.

If constancy had begotten familiarity, and familiarity had won for us with your excellency the favour of affectionate regard and service, [Col. 1311B] we would dare to write certain things more safely to your Highness and perhaps receive from you certain information that would not be useless in the present condition of affairs. Such confidence was produced in us toward Guy, chancellor of blessed memory—[Note: [Col. 1311D] This Guy, a Pisan of the Counts of Caprona, was created deacon-cardinal by Innocent II in 1130. Since he had been Wibald’s intimate friend for twenty years, he must be said to have survived to 1150 but no later, as is evident from this letter, which calls him “the chancellor of blessed memory.” Accordingly Ciaconius, who records his death in 1153, must be corrected.]—by acquaintance of twenty years and a charity that grew daily between us, so that we could safely say or write to him whatever came to our lips.

Now, when that blessed man recently wrote to us, he deigned familiarly to inform our lowliness that a certain rumour had disturbed both the lord pope and his court: namely, that our most serene lord Conrad, King of the Romans, was said to have made a treaty with the Emperor of the Greeks, intending, if he could, grievously to afflict and trouble the holy Roman Church, mother [Col. 1311C] of all Catholics.

He also instructed our lowliness on behalf of the lord pope and himself, and earnestly exhorted us, to endeavour by every means in our power that such waves should not rise against the apostolic see; or, if they perhaps had begun to rise through the perversity of some persons, that we should restrain them with the other faithful of the Church of God according to our strength.

We did as he commanded. By prolonged association and continual conversation, we instilled the good of humility and obedience into a man corrupted not by a concluded treaty, but somewhat by the arrogance and disobedience of the Greeks; and we sometimes sternly repressed, with the boldness of intimacy, the words of certain persons.

Moreover, at the beginning of Lent the Abbot of Clairvaux sent letters to the lord king through the Bishop of Freising, [Col. 1311D] in which he praised that lord of Sicily because he had been useful and necessary to the Catholic Church in many matters, and would be still more useful if he were not prevented by the strength and power of our prince. He promised that he would gladly work for their peace and concord, if he knew that it would not be unwelcome to our lord.

[Note: [Col. 1311D] We have two letters of Saint Bernard to Conrad, namely nos. 183 and 244, in which he exhorts him to show reverence to the apostolic see. Yet in them there is not even the slightest word concerning the King of Sicily, whom, however, in certain other letters—nos. 207, 208, and 209—he praises, extolling remarkably his magnificence and almsgiving. In letters which he had earlier written to Innocent II in the name of Adalbero, Archbishop of Trier, he calls him “the Sicilian tyrant,” letters 176 and 177. It is evident, moreover, that the letter praised here by Wibald has been lost.]

The lord T., Bishop of Santa Rufina, seemed to intimate the same in his own letter, written to our lord after he had returned from Jerusalem and had passed through Sicily.

[Note: [Col. 1312D] Theodewin, a German, was created cardinal by Innocent II.]

In response to these words we were entirely unwilling to incline either our own mind or our lord’s counsel, insofar as lay in us, until we had learned more certainly what was pleasing to the lord pope in this matter. Yet we did not presume to write to him concerning these matters, lest we appear to seek things too lofty for ourselves and, by rash and importunate insistence, to intrude into his hidden counsels. But if we have made ourselves foolish before you, the faith which we have toward the holy Roman Church, [Col. 1312B] and your humble and gracious kindness, have compelled us.

If your silence and favourable reply assist our effort, we shall henceforth be readier in services of this kind. Your senators wrote to our lord grave and harsh letters against the lord pope, [Note: [Col. 1312D] These letters appear above, nos. 21, 212, and 213.] which were brought to him in January. We would have brought you copies of them if we had come to the City, as had been arranged.

Trusting greatly in your diligence, we earnestly urge and ask you to ensure that the petitions which we have written to the lord pope are brought to effect. When we wrote these things, we were at the monastery of Fulda and had withdrawn from the court at Würzburg, affairs having been so arranged [Col. 1312C] that Master Henry, notary of the royal court, was to proceed at once to the lord pope.

### Letter CCXXVI. From Emperor Conrad to Pope Eugenius III  
*He sends to him as envoy Master Henry, notary of his court. (A.D. 1150.)*

To his dearest father in Christ, EUGENIUS, supreme pontiff of the holy Roman Church: CONRAD, by the grace of God King of the Romans and ever Augustus, filial love in all things and due reverence in the Lord.

“Since propitious divinity,” etc. See under Eugenius III, after his *Regesta*.

### Letter CCXXVII. From Abbot Wibald to Pope Eugenius III  
*He reports to him and requests confirmation from him of the election of Marquard as Abbot of Fulda. (A.D. 1150.)*

[Col. 1312D]

To his reverend father and lord EUGENIUS, [Col. 1313A] sole and universal pontiff: Brother WIBALD, by the grace of God and of yourself, that which he is in the Catholic Church—honour as to a father, fear as to a lord.

After your glorious son, our most serene lord, the King of the Romans, had returned from the Jerusalem expedition, our beloved brother H., Abbot of Hersfeld, resigned the administration of Fulda Abbey which he had undertaken. Therefore our lord king delayed settling the monastery, both because of the innumerable troubles with which the Church of Fulda was daily harassed within and without, and because of party interests not easily reconciled. Although he could be powerful and effective in recovering possessions which had been disorderly dispersed, he could not keep watch and give attention to the care of souls, which is the most precious possession of churches.

Often reminded of the matter by our lowliness, by the Abbot of Ebrach, and by other religious men, he finally yielded to this recommendation and came to Fulda on 3 April, the third day before the Nones. At that court there were present your venerable sons: the Archbishop of Bremen and the Bishops of Würzburg and Halberstadt, together with many princes and nobles of the lay order. Amid the other affairs of the realm, the king asked them how he might, by God’s help, so arrange Fulda monastery that there “the things of God” might be rendered to God, and “the things of Caesar” to Caesar.

There was long hesitation, as commonly happens in affairs of this kind, particularly because of the many changes of abbots in a short period [Col. 1313C] and because of the party interests and dissensions still known to be fervent in that monastery. All discussion being therefore suspended, the lord king said that religious men had pointed out to him a certain person of good testimony and unblemished reputation, who had increased a small establishment in religious observance, possessions, and buildings; and concerning whose piety, fidelity, and steadfastness they did not doubt that he could both preside over and benefit the Church of Fulda. If all votes agreed upon the election of this man, the Church of Fulda would soon recover, through his more gracious and more favourable protection, the honour of its former dignity.

All present were pleased by the king’s devout purpose and religious judgment. His proposal was conveyed to the electors by the above-named bishops, by the Abbots of Ebrach [Col. 1313D] and Hattelsburg, by ourselves, and by other princes; all received this speech, as though sent by God, with one accord and unanimous vote, and demanded that the name of the man supported by such praise and royal favour should be disclosed to them.

Thus, by the public assent of all, they chose as abbot, ruler of their souls, and lord of the Church of Fulda, Lord Marquard, Abbot of the monastery of Tholekingen. He had been nourished and educated from childhood in the monastery of Saint Michael on the Mount in the city of Bamberg, and had lived without reproach. He had governed his aforesaid monastery for eight years, possessed good testimony even from outsiders, and had advanced it in both divine and temporal matters.

Because he is greatly praised by those who know him intimately, was elected not only in absence but without his knowledge, and was compelled, very unwilling and strongly resisting, to undertake this burden—after our lord king earnestly exhorted him, promised him benefits, and in a sense forced him—our lowliness also presumes, in the boldness of holy charity, earnestly to request your Highness to heal the broken people of Fulda and bind up their wounds. By the hand of your blessing, which alone can supply a remedy for their infirmities, may you confirm the work begun concerning this man.

We have also wished to tell your Highness that, on that day at Fulda, all the brethren of Fulda, in regular order and humility, promised submission and obedience to their elected abbot. May almighty God keep you safe and sound, and preserve you for the governance of the Catholic Church.

### Letter CCXXVIII. From Abbot Wibald to Pope Eugenius III  
*Prevented from fulfilling the legation entrusted to him to the pope, he sends through a substitute envoy several requests for Corvey monastery. (A.D. 1150.)*

To his dearest father and lord EUGENIUS, sole and universal pope: Brother WIBALD, by the grace of God and of yourself, that which he is in the Catholic Church—himself and all that is his.

We came to the court of your glorious son Conrad, King of the Romans, [Col. 1314C] on the vigil of the Nativity of the Lord, and remained there continuously until Thursday of Easter week, expecting that he would send both ourselves and his chancellor to the presence of your Highness, as he had long since agreed and had also reported to your Magnitude.

During that time, day and night, we earnestly endeavoured to kindle his mind strongly toward love and reverence for your person, toward the defence of our most holy mother the Roman Church and of all churches. In this exercise of zeal, we possess testimony not only from our own conscience, but also from your faithful servants and certain others, who are accustomed, gladly blaming the times, to disparage good men and sow discord.

But because certain great affairs of the realm intervened, he was unwilling to be without either our person or his chancellor, though he only reluctantly permitted us to return to our monastery until the coming mildness of autumn. Meanwhile he sent Master Henry, notary of his court, a wise and upright man, and wholly faithful to you. We believe it superfluous to remind your prudence and kindness that you should receive him honourably and dispatch him efficiently and quickly.

We would eagerly have come to you not only for the honour and advantage of God and the Roman Empire, but also that we might deserve to behold your face, which we regard as the countenance of an angel, and humbly to lay before your Excellency certain matters which we do not dare entrust [Col. 1315A] to writing—both because events are varied and uncertain, and lest we be judged rashly and importunately to have thrust ourselves into arduous and secret affairs, into the depths of your confidence.

We humbly beseech that the requests contained in writing may be humbly heard by your clemency. Unless you stretch out to our weakness the blessed hand of your aid for enduring the burdens of the Church of Corvey, we must take flight and find rest from faintness of spirit and the storm.

May God in his mercy deign to preserve your Holiness for the governance of the Catholic Church for a long time.

Abbot Wibald of Corvey asks that the lord pope write to H., Bishop of Minden, requiring him without delay to reconcile the church of Kemnade. He had judged it polluted because a boy, a monk, while assisting builders repairing the roof of the church, fell from the ridge to the church floor and thus died without any shedding of blood; nevertheless, for nearly a year he had refused to reconcile it. He further asks that the bishop administer justice concerning Dietrich of Recklinghausen, Reinbert, and Dietrich his sons, parishioners who seized estates of Kemnade church: if, within thirty days after receiving the letters, they have not surrendered the possessions and fully restored what they took, he is to subject them to excommunication.

Likewise, he asks that the lord A., Archbishop of Bremen, be written to, requiring him to help the abbot retain the estates of Kemnade church situated within his territory, [Col. 1315C] especially those possessions which Abbess Judith alienated after her deposition; and to excommunicate the invaders unless they repent within thirty days after receiving the letters. Likewise, he asks that H., Bishop of Verden, be written to in the same terms. Likewise, he asks that the Duke of Saxony be written to with the same ruling.

Likewise, he asks that both the Archbishop of Cologne and the Church of Cologne be written to strictly and severely concerning Judith, Abbess of Geseke, an abbey situated in the estate and parish of Cologne. She has not only not been confined and corrected, but also roams throughout the whole land with her corrupters; and [there is the matter of] the goods of Kemnade church, from which she was deposed by Thomas, cardinal of blessed memory and legate of the apostolic see, [Col. 1315D] and whose sentence of deposition was confirmed by the lord pope at the synod of Reims. Unless she is deposed or excommunicated, she will by no means desist.

### Letter CCXXIX. From H. of the Moravians to Abbot Wibald  
*He dissuades him from his desired journey to the pope. (A.D. 1150.)*

To WIBALD, his most serene lord and venerable father, Abbot of the holy Church of Corvey: H., by the patience of God that which he is called among the Moravians, the participation of servitude with devotion and mutual prayer.

We received your letter with the reverence due to your kindness. From it, since we learned, as we had desired, that you are well, we render thanks to the divine mercy; for we desire your safety and prosperity no less than our own, and we ask Him who can grant these things, by prayers though unworthy, to increase and preserve them. Although your kindness greatly desires to see us in person, we give thanks; yet we ask you not at all to grieve because it has not been able to see us, since neither distance of places nor the continual torments of illness can remove your presence from the memory of our heart. Moreover, since the excellence of your high estate does not disdain so greatly to humble itself for us as to promise that it will convey the little words of our insignificance to our lord the pope, we humbly bow before it, and with every good wish pray that the angel of God may accompany your journey. And since at present we have nothing else to send to the aforesaid our lord, we ask that our continual little prayers be commended to him, and that our illness also be made known through your gracious report.

## LETTER CCXXX. D., BISHOP OF PRAGUE, TO ABBOT WIBALD

He sends a gift to Wibald, who is setting out for the pope, and asks him to remember him before the pontiff. (Year 1150.)

To Wibald, his most reverend lord and father, abbot of the churches of Corvey and Stavelot: D., by the grace of God, though unworthy, bishop of the people of Prague, with sincerity of service, his humble prayers.

[Col. 1316C] We rejoice that you are occupied in royal affairs and seated at the royal side. For your favour has long secured this for our lowliness through many benefits: that we may rejoice in your advancement. Yet because you have deigned to send your letters, full of every sweetness and honeyed delight, we offer as many thanksgivings to your sincere fatherhood as we are presently able; and although the diversity of places separates us in body, nevertheless your presence, daily held before the eyes of our spirit, has now been renewed through your writings. Moreover, since the Lord has bestowed such favour upon our humility in your eyes that you are willing to remember us also at the Roman court, we thank you for this and earnestly ask that you not refuse to make whatever small remembrance you may deem fitting of our undeserving person before the apostolic lord. Furthermore, we have sent your sincerity a small token of affection, begging and entreating you in the Lord to receive it favourably, and at least to permit a horse belonging to your attendant to be shod from it. Deign to greet your honourable, God-devoted, and beloved household on behalf of our lowliness, and also our friend the lord chancellor. May the Lord God bring and lead back your sincerity, so necessary to us and praying for us, sound and safe in peace and prosperity, and preserve you for a long life.

## LETTER CCXXXI. THE MONK EMELERI TO ABBOT WIBALD

He commends to him A., bearer of the present letter. (Year 1150.)

[Col. 1317A]

To his lord, W., abbot of Corvey, truly holy and worthy of every reverence: brother Emeleri, that humble and whatever sort of vessel in the house of the great Householder he may be, with the service of fraternal affection, whatever the affection of our mind can offer.

If you live and are well and . . . stir the inward parts . . . I gladly wish, and well . . . to love the person of your holiness, best of men, because, as I was able to learn from your own lips, you judged my lowliness worthy of your affection even while absent and still unknown to you in bodily appearance, on account of certain good things that my friends said to you about me; and afterwards, when present and more familiarly known, you honoured me beyond my powers and merits wherever the two of us could meet. Therefore I wish your most beloved fraternity to know without doubt of my fidelity that, wherever I can, I shall gladly defend your cause and increase the renown of your good name; this I have done and do daily, because I expect the like from you. I earnestly commend to your mercy the lord A., bearer of this letter, a man sufficiently afflicted and in need of the consolations of good people, so that, as you have mercifully begun to deal with him, you may persevere until the end in dealing with him according to the circumstances of his case. For the end of every good beginning and right work [Col. 1317C] is to be desired. Moreover, I pray that the Lord may be with you and that your spirit may be with us.

## LETTER CCXXXII. H., BISHOP OF HAMBURG, TO ABBOT WIBALD

Concerning the abbot of Reesveld, whom his monks had expelled. (Year 1150.)

H., by the mercy of God alone whatever he is, of the holy church of Hamburg, to his beloved and venerable brother Wibald, reverend abbot of the people of Corvey: steadfast love in Christ, with greeting.

Having recently examined more closely the letter of your fraternity, full of ornament of language and weight of thought, we learned that it had been reported to you that the abbot of Reesveld had been deprived and expelled from his place and dignity, without reason and without judgment, by those subject to him—namely, the provost and the other brethren of that place. You accordingly suggested, with sufficient prudence, that he ought to be reinstated in his dignity and possessions. But the chapters of law which you cited are indeed true, though not applicable in this matter. For the venerable bishop Anselm of the church of Havelberg, together with the entire chapter of our church, was present at your delegation; the abbots of Minden and Sancinen were present as well, with several other abbots and provosts. In their presence it was most plainly established, by the testimony of many religious persons, that the said abbot had suffered no violence of expulsion. Thus the law which says that those expelled or despoiled of their goods cannot be summoned to trial or judged was not appropriately introduced, since there is no privilege by which persons already stripped can be despoiled, and so forth—arguments which you advanced after hearing only one side. But rhetorical art in pleadings calls a defective opening one which the opposing party can claim for itself: for when one side says, “Assist me, who have a just cause,” the opposing party says the same. Finally, through your intervention we entrusted ourselves to the decision of those who had been sent to us by you and by our lords and brethren in this matter; and thus, satisfying your request and theirs, we fixed a day on which this affair, in the presence of the brethren of that place, may at last be concluded in the Lord with the end of peace, either by the rigour of justice or by the tranquillity of mercy.

## LETTER CCXXXIII. EMPEROR CONRAD TO ABBOT WIBALD

Concerning H., duke of Saxony, who had not come to court but had attempted to seize the duchy of Bavaria. (Year 1150.)

Conrad, by the grace of God king of the Romans, to Wibald, abbot of Corvey: his favour and every good thing.

Let it be known to your holiness that, by the counsel and request of the princes, we summoned Duke H. of Saxony to a court at Ulm on the octave of Epiphany, to press his claim for feudal justice. Yet he not only neglected to come to that court, but even attempted by armed force [Col. 1318C] to occupy the duchy of Bavaria. Therefore, attending rather to the duty of royal authority than to his actions, we appointed him another court at Regensburg, by judgment of the princes, on the feast of the apostle Barnabas, intending, God helping us, to satisfy his complaint. The messenger will report the rest.

## LETTER CCXXXIV. THE MONKS OF STAVELOT TO ABBOT WIBALD

They ask him to forgive J., a monk of Corvey, his past offences. (Year 1151.)

To their reverend father and lord in Christ, Wibald, venerable abbot of the churches of Stavelot and Corvey: brother Robert, dean of the church of Stavelot, [Col. 1318D] and the humble congregation of the same place, filial love and due submission.

Since the infrequency of your messengers leaves us uncertain of the state of your health, dearest Father, nothing in our affairs can bring us either comfort or joy. Therefore, being at times mindful of ourselves, we offer to God a propitiatory offering and sacrifices of prayers for our afflictions; and there we always remember you, where angels descend and present each person’s vows and gifts to almighty God the Father. For by this, we believe, rough places become level and mountains and hills are brought low. But, Father, we refrain from writing anything to you concerning the condition of our affairs or the state of your church, since your return to us is expected shortly—namely, about the Purification of blessed Mary and the arrival of the lord king in Lotharingia. Meanwhile we humbly make known to the gentleness of your kindness that, because of the unity of love and the favour we bear toward the church of Corvey, we received with due compassion your brother J., a son of the church of Corvey, when he came to us, and kept him with us for some time. Although we perhaps bestowed less upon him than his need required, we nevertheless gave him fraternally what the scantiness of our resources could bear. And since, having fulfilled a vow of prayer, he has decided to return to the place of his profession, to the church which nourished and raised him, we earnestly beseech the mercy of your holiness that, through the intervention of our petition and the humble satisfaction of us all on his behalf, you so forgive every fault of the past period that you mercifully restore him to the fellowship of his brethren without sentence of a graver punishment. For him, dearest Father, the harshness of a severe winter and the considerable difficulty of a long journey suffice as pardon for all his transgressions. Therefore again and again we beseech you that the intercession of our petition may avail for his mercy and repose.

## LETTER CCXXXV. ANSELM, BISHOP OF HAVELBERG, TO ABBOT WIBALD

He declares that henceforth he wishes to remain in his church with his brethren, whom he praises. (Year 1151.)

[Col. 1319C]

To Wibald, venerable abbot and most dear to him: Anselm, a poor man of Christ, daily prayers and service ever ready.

Dearest friend, you wrote to me familiarly and briefly; but few things do not suffice for one who wishes to know much about you and me. Would that we might sit together for even three days, and that our chancellor might sit among us, so that through mutual conversation what each kept shut within himself might become known to us all! For my part, I have now returned again into the channel of my heart; nor do I intend henceforth voluntarily to overflow so far as, like a torrent, to gather mud in which I may be entangled and again suffer the muddy turmoil which I have often endured. What have I to do among those who grind, even though one is sometimes taken, where the circuit is continuous and endless? What have I to do in the field, where, although one may be taken, the burning sun and smiting heat, or some other inclemency of temptation, scarcely ever fail? Rather, let me rest in my little bed, where, although one is sometimes left, the other, taken up, is by no means more frequently exposed to so many temptations. In my manger at Havelberg I remain, a poor man of Christ, with my brethren, poor men of Christ.
