> [Note: [Col. 1319D] From what he here relates concerning his brethren or canons of the church of Havelberg, there is no slight ground for conjecturing [Col. 1320D] that they were regular canons, and indeed, as I conjecture, of the Order of St Augustine.]

There some build a tower of strength against the face of the enemy; others keep watch to defend against the assaults of pagans; others, devoted to the divine offices, daily await martyrdom; others purify their souls, to be rendered to God, by fasts and prayers; others, applying themselves to reading and holy meditation, and imitating the life and examples of the saints, train themselves. But all of us, naked and poor, follow as far as we can the naked and poor Christ.

We have played enough; henceforth let serious business be done. Christ in the manger, Christ in the judgment hall: otherwise there, otherwise here. There—that is, over Christ lying in the manger—the praising angels sang together; here—that is, over Christ standing before rulers in the judgment hall—the Jews cried out: “Let him be crucified, let him be crucified.” O seal of divine Scripture, who will open you for me? Who, I say, unless it be the Lamb slain from the foundation of the world? Believe me, dearest brother: it is better and safer [Col. 1320B] to lie with Christ in the manger and to cry out the miseries of the human condition, while the new star shines above, the angels sing glory, and kings offer varied gifts, than to stand in the judgment hall amid soldiers mocking, scourging, spitting, striking with verbal slaps, and plaiting a crown of thorns—truly thorny, truly dry, truly lacking the sap of eternal life, truly thorny and pricking, bearing the barbs of detraction after praise—while the sun of divine contemplation is darkened, the earth of the body trembles, the rock of faith is split, and the veil of the temple is divided. Believe me, dearest brother: it is safer in the manger than in the judgment hall. There are consolations; here, terrors. Enough. For while I write and wish to make a longer letter, a messenger of the archbishop of Mainz arrived; after delivering letters and an oral message, he prepared to depart that same hour and forced me to cut this letter short, because I had to send my messenger at once with him. While you are near him, guard diligently my lord and yours, the most humble Augustus; and because God has made you faithful and wise, do what you can and know, so far as you are permitted. Greet our chancellor from Anselm, yours and his.

## LETTER CCXXXVI. R., A MONK, TO ABBOT WIBALD

He gives an account of what he has done for the monastery’s benefit, and asks him for a prebend for his nine-year-old kinsman. (Year 1151.)

[Col. 1320D]

To his lord and father, Wibald, venerable abbot of Stavelot: brother R., with devotion in prayers, the good of obedience.

Since I know myself to be the servant of your holiness, the son of your fatherhood, and the friend of your affection, I make continual remembrance of you in my prayers, that the true God of all, the almighty God of mercies, may always govern and protect you and shine upon you with the dew of his grace. And because the proof of love is the performance of a work, I rejoice with you in your works, in will and in deed. Thus I labour at clearing the new cemetery and rebuilding the watercourse; I do not neglect the chapel of Blessed Nicholas, the upper steps of the dormitory, the entrance to the common latrines, or the walls of the new orchard, following the example of the woman who cast all that she had into the treasury, though it was little. Yet the flask of oil and the jar of meal, and likewise love and obedience, are not diminished. Now, since you have rebuilt the walls of Stavelot on no small scale, the utmost care must be taken that the walls of Jerusalem be built. Because of the length of this letter, I have left matters concerning the condition of your place, worthy of report to you, to be communicated according to the opportunity of time by your brother and ours, the bearer of this letter. Commending his concern for his brother’s son, I ask you to fulfil his wish in this matter, because thereby he orders charity in one by whose ordering day endures; and while there is time, good must be done [Col. 1321B] to all, especially to those of the household, so that they may become members both of the faith and of the order and portion of Jesus Christ. Therefore, giving you many thanks for your innumerable benefits, since not one blessing . . . [lacuna] grant also to my nearer kinsman, nine years old, a prebend and a place among us. For even if I cannot repay you, God will do so, if you become for him the way and gate by which he may come to share, through patience, in Christ’s sufferings in the monastery under the monastic habit. Your brother will act for me in this matter; it is yours to look upon one who hopes in you and to extend the hand of mercy to a supplicant with confidence. Farewell.

## LETTER CCXXXVII. THE MONKS OF STAVELOT TO ABBOT WIBALD

They ask that, if possible, he return to them and press before the king their complaint concerning Hengebach. (Year 1151.)

[Col. 1321C]

To their reverend father and lord in Christ, Wibald, venerable abbot of Stavelot: the humble flock serving Christ under him in the same place, reverence of due submission and love.

Although at this time our whole community has written to you less frequently than usual, Father, we are not therefore enkindled with any less ardour of love for you, since we consider you present with us as often as we perceive the care of your kindness for us and our place. Therefore we always wish for your health and prosperity; in wishing, we long; in longing, we pray. Greeting your fatherhood, we most devoutly ask that, if it can be obtained without offence to the favour of our lord the king, you not refuse to return to us, since your presence would be necessary and useful both for the care and ordering of internal affairs and for the provision of external affairs of your church and children. Meanwhile we beseech you to advance our complaint, which we have sent to the lord king, against those of Hengebach; for unless they are sternly restrained concerning what they have now perpetrated a second time against you and our church, they will not fear to commit still graver acts. Moreover, lest a longer note or more prolix letter burden your mind, perhaps occupied with greater matters, we have entrusted the remaining matters to be reported to your brother, namely the keeper of the church. From him you will be able, if expedient, to hear more fully of the state of our affairs, both of what is within and of what is done without. May almighty God preserve your fatherhood safe for the honour of his church. If an opportunity occurs, we ask you to mention Vilippes before the king.

## LETTER CCXXXVIII. THE MONKS OF STAVELOT TO EMPEROR CONRAD

They complain concerning Goswin of Hengebach and his brother Everard. (Year 1151.)

[Col. 1322B]

To their most glorious and unconquered lord, Conrad Augustus, emperor of the Romans: the humble congregation of the church of Stavelot, whatever so small a community owes and can offer to royal majesty.

If our smallness could in any way render thanks to your excellence, most serene lord, we would labour to do so all the more diligently because you have more willingly deigned to show mercy in restoring our father to the church in which we are established. Therefore, by continual celebrations of Masses and vigils, by unceasing prayers and alms, we devoutly pray God for the condition of your realm, for your welfare and that of your people, asking that He in whose hand are all powers and the rights of kingdoms may powerfully restrain through you those who trust in their own ferocity, so that thereafter your clemency may more freely provide for the peace and welfare of the churches of God. Moreover, gentlest lord, since your majesty is in a special manner bound to protect those churches which have been exalted by your illustrious predecessors, emperors or kings, with more honourable observance and more ample magnificence, we dare to approach you with special confidence. Prostrate at the knees of your clemency, we humbly complain concerning Goswin of Hengebach and his brother Everard, who, contrary to all justice, on a day of peace—namely the feast of the apostles Simon and Jude—violently took from us six cartloads of wine together with the animals, and, having captured our poor men who followed the wagons, afflicted them with the harshest punishments. When we were ready to seek your justice concerning this, at last, on account of the lord chancellor, who compassionately accommodated himself to our loss, they returned our men nearly naked and restored to us some portion of the wine and animals taken, promising that within a short time they would restore everything before the lord chancellor. Having accepted this pledge, we waited until now, deceived by a vain hope; at last, after a long delay and heavy expenses, certain that we would receive nothing from them unless your royal authority compelled them through an effective messenger to do so, the whole community of your church humbly asks you, for God’s sake, to deign to act.

## LETTER CCXXXIX. JOHN THE NOTARY TO PRINCE R. AND COUNT RIC.

Concerning Welf’s alliance with the Sicilian king. (Year 1151.)

[Col. 1323A]

To his dearest lords, Prince R. and Count RIC.: John, their most faithful notary, greeting and the services of a servant.

Being faithful to you in all things, I report to you what I know and render service wherever I can. Know, therefore, that Welf, traitor to the lord King Conrad, is allied with the Sicilian, has received a great sum of money from him, and secretly passed to Rome under the guidance of Cencius Frangipani and Gataguefus. Yet his men, with four Saracens and an equal number of destriers, were captured and released at Rome by the senators. They were carrying letters on behalf of the Sicilian to Frederick, duke of Swabia; Henry, duke of Saxony; Berthold, son of Duke Conrad; and Conrad, duke of Cebring, concerning damage to and war against the lord King Conrad. In these letters they were warned and asked by the Sicilian to do whatever Welf might tell them for their own advantage. Therefore make every effort to report these things to the king’s son, and also to the lord King Conrad and his faithful men, so that they may be on their guard; and let those men be captured, if possible. Furthermore, know that Cencius Frangipani strives as much as he can to harm you, and that the pope acts by his counsel. This is so true that the cardinals boasted before C. Frangipani and said that they had shut you in—and the Greeks at Venice—as dogs and mastiffs, so that you could do the Sicilian no harm from that quarter. The pope himself has sent envoys to the Sicilian to your detriment, if he can accomplish with him what he wishes, and he still has a truce with him for four years. Therefore do not trust him, nor surrender yourselves or the Greeks to him from your resources, because you would lose all of it; it would have been better had you given sandals to the poor or to your own men. Make an agreement, therefore, with the Roman senate and people, because with their help, God assisting, you will be able to prevail. Let the Greeks distribute their resources generously, because, as Solomon says, “All things obey money.” The Sicilian relies upon the Greeks’ avarice; therefore at a fitting time he spends his own resources. Let them do likewise, if they wish to conquer.

## LETTER CCXL. ABBOT WIBALD TO EMPEROR CONRAD

He advises that Conrad has nothing to fear, that the conference at Cranaha should not be omitted, and that the enemy must be pursued. (Year 1151.)

[Col. 1323D]

To his illustrious conqueror and magnificent lord, Conrad Augustus, emperor of the Romans by the grace of God: brother Wibald, by the same grace what he is in the Catholic Church, greeting in Him who gives salvation to kings.

Although we are situated rather far beyond the borders of the Saxons and cannot attend their frequent conferences, nevertheless with every zeal and urgency we make careful inquiry lest anything whatever be undertaken against your peace. Although your chaplain Herebert, who lately travelled through the entire land and investigated everything closely, can more fully inform your prudence about all this, we briefly suggest to your highness that we have been able to discover absolutely nothing that ought to move your magnanimity. Yet there will not be lacking some who, under the appearance of firmer loyalty and the pretext of more devoted affection, lay before your wisdom certain frightful and great matters in order to obtain from you, under the title of pious concern and warning, some advantage for themselves. But that great prudence, more abundantly bestowed upon you by the giver of all good things, will test all things and hold fast what is good. Let your majesty, however, give no assent to anyone who urges you not to come to the conference at Cranaha, since the spirits of your princes would grow weary and they would find material for a shrewd suspicion—that you regarded as suspect those whom you did not wish to see, though summoned so often. Rather, come as becomes a lord and emperor, especially since the conference will be brief; and if anyone’s loyalty seems to falter, you will so restore it that, if he does not act with you in truth, he will nevertheless not afterwards easily be trusted by your enemies. Let no person’s counsel, no person’s flattery, nor even any person’s threats turn your strength from its purpose: namely, that you invade and trample under your feet as an enemy the man who fills your whole empire with lies and foolishly boasts that he is thought willing or able to act otherwise against you. Through Brother John carefully and firmly admonish Count Herimann to act more effectively with us, lest we be compelled against our will to seek other protectors.

## LETTER CCXLI. ABBOT WIBALD TO H., ARCHBISHOP OF BREMEN

He thanks him for visiting his monastery, urges him to stay longer with his brethren and inspect the books of the book-room, and discusses the impending conference of bishops at Minden. (Year 1151.)

To his reverend father and lord H., venerable archbishop of the holy church of Bremen: brother Wibald, by the grace of God what he is in the Catholic Church, humble prayers and devoted services.

We find it very pleasing and sweet that your highness has deigned to enter our monastery, visit and console our brethren, enter our dwellings—which we hold dearer for this very reason—and commend our endeavour. But what is most pleasing and wholly dear to us is that you promised to come to these same buildings, stay there longer, and turn over and examine not only the volumes but even the loose sheets of our book-room.

> [Note: [Col. 1323D] In monasteries, the armarium was the place in the cloister, near the chapter house, where books were kept, so that [Col. 1324D] brethren who customarily applied themselves to reading in the cloister might have them readily at hand.]

Would that we may live, would that we may see it, [Col. 1325A] would that we may be able to enjoy peace, quiet, and leisure, and in these studies mutually exercise and sharpen one another, and either be taught or teach! That life would be happier in proportion as it was nearer to beholding and earning salvation, and farther from this world’s muddy abyss. Come, therefore, and feed your soul; honour the priesthood; instruct the clergy; strengthen the order; spread the sacrament. But enough of this. We are uncertain whether the conference of bishops which you had resolved to hold at Minden—and at which, relying on your kindness, we had decided to be present also because of private matters—will take place, because we have learned for certain that the bishops of Paderborn and Münster will not come there. We have indeed heard in part the reasons for and purpose of the meeting, and we rejoice greatly in Christ that the fire which Jesus sent upon earth, and wished to burn, has been vehemently kindled in your breast. Yet we fear, and in fearing grieve, that present times cannot bear your energy and fervour of spirit, because the Apostle says: “All seek what is their own, not what is Jesus Christ’s.” If the fire which burns in your heart begins to flash and send forth brightness and sparks, we fear that you may more truly than Elijah be able to say: “I alone am left.” Therefore, by the present messenger and by your letters, we desire to be informed of your entire intention in this matter. We wish to learn your pleasure concerning the abbot of Hersfeld, who is with us, because we do not wish either to have and retain, or even to love, anyone who troubles you or yours by any kind of harm. Carefully and familiarly admonish your friend Count H.

> [Note: Hermann, advocate of Corvey.]

to devote himself more effectively to repelling our injuries, as he has received orders from the lord king to do; for our captives are still held in chains, and our wrongdoers remain in his castle.

## LETTER CCXLII. ABBOT WIBALD TO HENRY, BISHOP OF MINDEN

He complains that Henry refused to accept and grant the peace offered and requested. (Year 1151.)

[Col. 1325D]

To Henry, bishop of Minden: Wibald, abbot of Corvey, abundance in the spirit of knowledge and piety.

After returning from your conference to our monastery and informing both our brethren and the other faithful of the church of Corvey about what was done at Hameln, they greatly wondered and grieved that the church of Corvey, which for some time both raised and educated you, should be so much despised and so indiscreetly treated by you in our person. You had first sent word to us through the provost of our church, then a second time through the priest Henry, that you would summon us to a peaceful conference and bring our case—which has now been pursued between you and us for nearly four years, not without great exhaustion—to a favourable conclusion. When we came to you, you acknowledged this very thing before the whole assembly, as befitted your dignity; but the outcome showed that you did not perform in deed what you had expressed in speech. For although we had proved our innocence as truthfully as humbly, and offered you satisfaction for whatever offence of yours had been provoked, whether justly or unjustly, you not only refused to accept it but placed your whole counsel and word in the mouths of laymen, although a canonical case was being treated: namely, those who subjected our person to grave insults and violently and sacrilegiously plundered the goods of our church. You did not avoid their communion—indeed, their familiar companionship, conversation, and counsel—as ecclesiastical discipline teaches. We, who had written to you that we would come for peace, holding in our hearts what we had on our lips, offered you peace in deed and truth. But because our offer of peace found no response from you, we could lawfully have appealed on account of our many grievances, fearing nothing that might happen to us such as befell your abbot of the island in his appeal. For your laymen are accustomed to judge appeals made to the lord pope with drawn swords—those who were now the leaders of your counsel—so that in us might be fulfilled what was said through Moses: “Our enemies are our judges.” Those same men of yours, your parishioners, wished to harm us both in person and property while we were making a peaceful approach to you and relying on the safe-conduct firmly promised us in your confidence. Therefore it is not the counsel of our church that we come to your council as had been agreed, especially lest you have an excuse before the lord king for failing to come to his court, to which you have now been summoned for the third time by the judgment of your peers on account of our case. But concerning the injuries and damages inflicted upon us by your men at your command, may God see and judge. We, who have been silent and patient until now, both out of reverence for your person and for the honour of your church, will speak as women in labour and will take care to report at the Roman church what we have suffered, seen, and heard. For no evasion could be found in our word, since we were willing to submit to the judgment of chosen judges from whom appeal is not permitted: namely, our dearest lord and father, the bishop of Paderborn, the reverend bishop of Münster, and our most beloved bishop of Osnabrück.

## LETTER CCXLIII. ABBOT WIBALD TO H., ARCHBISHOP OF MAINZ

He asks him to absolve Folcuin of Sualenberg, who had complained against the archbishop and the bishop of Paderborn but had at last submitted. (Year 1151.)

[Col. 1327A] To his most reverend father and lord in Christ, H.

> [Note: Henry, surnamed “the Faithful,” a pious man, to whom Saint Bernard’s Letter 323 is addressed.]

venerable archbishop of the holy church of Mainz: brother Wibald, by the grace of God what he is in the Catholic Church, humble prayers and devoted service.

We render manifold thanks to your graciousness, because you did not refuse both to receive us generously as guests and to honor us most humanely through your people. We too, according to our means, have been neither unmindful nor ungrateful, but with every zeal and diligence have risen and labored toward fulfilling your will and advancing your friends. [Col. 1327B] We especially rejoice that you have now obtained the fruit of this labor in the benefit and promotion of your own people.

We inform your Excellency that Folcuin of Swalmenberg holds many and extensive possessions from the Church of Corvey, and that both he and his late father Widekind were accustomed to serve our predecessors and ourselves faithfully and intimately, both because of their proximity and because of their capability. Accordingly, after our return from court, this same Folcuin came to us and lodged a grave complaint, not only before us but before all the bishops of Saxony and other princes, against our lord and father, the venerable B., bishop of Paderborn. He complained that, although the lord [Col. 1327C] bishop is his bishop and the shepherd of his soul, he had separated him from his flock and fold and exposed him to an alien tribunal, contrary to the canons, contrary to the laws, and contrary to custom. For he maintains that he was born and reborn, and is synodically subject, in the Church of Paderborn; and that his wife ought rather, through marriage, to have passed into his jurisdiction than he to have migrated under a woman's laws; and that, even if she were not his wife, he ought to have been proceeded against in the defendant's forum rather than the plaintiff's.

Furthermore, he made many complaints about your Highness: that, although you had been judge in his case, he had suffered many and grievous burdens in many respects; and that, while he was ready to submit himself for the execution of justice, he was attacked by armed men and incurred danger to both life and honor. We therefore, having taken the counsel of prudent and religious [Col. 1327D] men, endeavored to soothe and settle the swelling of his anger, so that he might adopt Christian humility and obey more devoutly the divine laws and the commands of yourself and his bishop. By God’s favor this has proceeded so far that, in accordance with our counsel, he rendered obedient and humble satisfaction to our lord the bishop of Paderborn for every complaint and for a certain quasi-rebellion which he had maintained against him; and he hastens to obtain absolution and to receive, in the Christian manner, his lawful wife.

Therefore, earnestly requesting, we urge your venerable Highness: since our aforesaid [Col. 1328A] venerable bishop of Paderborn has not spared his own flesh and blood, and has deferentially yielded to you as to his father, so that justice might proceed in its proper order, kindly receive his prayers; graciously receive the aforesaid Folcuin; and, when you begin to draw near to our region, bring his wife with you and restore her to him, and restore him paternally to holy communion.

## LETTER CCXLIV. HENRY, BISHOP OF MINDEN, TO ABBOT WIBALD

He clears himself of the accusations made against him above by Wibald. (1151.)

HENRY, by the grace of God bishop of Minden, to WIBALD, abbot of Corvey: may you be filled with the spirit both of piety and learning.

[Col. 1328B] We reply to your brotherhood under the compulsion of charity, which endures all things, not under terror of the threats which you make more harshly than is fitting. For we trust that in the Roman Church or at the king’s court no prejudice will be done to an innocent person, but that judicial sentence will punish the aggressor rather than the sufferer.

We are said by you, though injured, to have caused injury, whereas God is my witness that I have never, either myself or through any of my people, by my will, counsel, or assistance, harmed you; I have merely sought brotherly satisfaction for injuries done to us. The Church of Corvey, which both brought me up and educated me, I have neither utterly despised nor treated indiscreetly, but I honor and shall honor it; I seek, as I have sought, satisfaction only for our injuries. What I conveyed to you orally through Provost Adalbert and through the priest Henry, I would have fulfilled in deed also, if you had offered satisfaction which seemed full to our faithful men—and indeed to certain of yours as well.

[Col. 1328C] We did not place our counsel and our word concerning the canonical case in the mouths of laymen; but, for the sake of making peace, we used the counsel of faithful clerics and laymen, just as you did. I neither associated nor associate with violent and sacrilegious persons who plunder the property of the Church; if I recognize them as manifest offenders, I avoid them as enemies of God.

We are sons of peace. We offered you peace with our lips; we kept it in our hearts. We sought peace; we seek peace. We have burdened you with no grievance. Thus you had no need of an appeal; yet, if you had needed one, you could have appealed without fear, protected as you were by so great a mass of armed men that you would not easily have yielded even to a very powerful opponent. Indeed, you did not need armed protection even for the defense of an appeal, because—though you say this—our people are not accustomed to adjudicate with drawn swords appeals made to the lord pope. Laymen are not, and have not been, the guides of our word; nor have your enemies acted as judges, especially since no judgment was delivered there, but only counsel was held concerning the making of peace.

[Col. 1328D] If our men, our parishioners, wished to injure your person or your goods as you were making your way toward us, God is my witness that I knew absolutely nothing of it. I sent you our safe-conduct as you requested; and because the case could not be concluded that day, I dismissed you in peace, under our safe-conduct, together with all who wished to return home but whom the late hour had delayed. A day was fixed, according to the pleasure of both parties, on which we should again meet to make peace.

We neither wished nor ordered injuries and losses to be inflicted upon you: let God see and judge. We have experienced none at all of the patience which you professed; rather, you added new injuries to old ones, which anyone may read and hear in the text of your letter. Because you threaten to speak as a woman in labor, may God spare you and stop the mouths of those who speak iniquity. Certainly know that I fear neither the hearing of any majesty nor the presence of any rank, [Col. 1329B] because I have as my witness that I walk straightforwardly.

## LETTER CCXLV. ABBOT WIBALD TO HENRY, BISHOP OF MINDEN

Reply to the preceding letter. (1151.)

To Lord H., venerable bishop of Minden, WIBALD, by the grace of God abbot of Corvey: the Angel of Great Counsel.

From the tenor of your letter we have learned that your Highness was offended by the letter which we recently sent you, and that it seemed harsher and more severe to your understanding than it became our modest station to write [Col. 1329C] and your Highness to receive. Let your learning know that it was done with this intention: since we had many times written to you humbly and peacefully about this same affair and had received neither peaceful speech nor the effect of peace, your prudence might at last be certain that extreme necessity compelled us to approach a judge.

Far be it from the purpose of our humility that we should presume, by any rash or contumacious speech, to assail episcopal excellence—especially in the person of one belonging to monastic religion. Yet because that same letter of yours contained nothing certain, nothing final, concerning our case, we likewise could write nothing determinate, and therefore nothing new, to your greatness. For we had frequently and urgently offered, both personally and through honorable, great, and very numerous mediators, to you and your Church whatever humility could recommend for satisfaction and justice could prescribe for correction. If it had pleased you to choose any article from all these matters and indicate it to us, we should have been as ready to perform as we were devoted in offering.

[Col. 1329D] Your learning could undoubtedly perceive this as well: there was absolutely no evasion in our word and promise, since we were willing to submit to the judgment of chosen judges, from whom no appeal is permitted—namely, our lord and father, the bishop of Paderborn; the reverend bishop of Münster; and the bishop of Osnabrück, most dear to us. We cannot at all observe the appointed day for the conference, because, having departed from you without mercy, we arranged to pursue our case before certain great persons at the time fixed for the conference. This was knowingly arranged by our mediators, not so that we should observe it, but so that we might not depart from you indecorously and as if hostile.

## LETTER CCXLVI. HENRY, BISHOP OF MINDEN, TO BERNARD, BISHOP OF PADERBORN

Concerning the case between himself and the abbot of Corvey. (1151.)

To the venerable lord BERNARD, bishop of the holy Church of Paderborn, [Col. 1330B] HENRY, by the mercy of God what he is in the Church of Minden: the devotion of faithful service and unceasing prayers in Christ.

A city set upon a mountain cannot be hidden; so too the virtue, kindness, and steadfastness of your faith shown toward us, when the case of the lord abbot of Corvey and ourselves was being dealt with, could not be hidden or obscured. Therefore we offer your Highness due and fitting thanks, and we stand ready to devote the zeal of our service more earnestly to your honor.

From the beginning of this dispute we have followed your counsel; and when the appointed time and the truce established by you arrived, your counsel was to be accepted and observed by us. We conceived and undertook nothing else in heart or deed concerning the aforesaid affair except that every controversy ought, through the disposition of your counsel, to be brought to an honorable end and praiseworthy conclusion.

[Col. 1330C] But while, on the advice of my faithful men, I was preparing myself for what concerned peace and charity, the lord abbot of Corvey, your friend, attacked us with harsh writings and bitter invective. If you feel with us, then the dignity and reverence of your name has likewise been injured and wounded by this, because within the term granted and established by you he ought not to have disturbed us by any vexation or severity of threats. Therefore, as you yourself know, take thought for your honor in these matters, and through the present messenger and your letters advise us, as we trust in your charity, concerning what will be most salutary for us and most conducive to honor.

## LETTER CCXLVII. BERNARD, BISHOP OF PADERBORN, TO HENRY, BISHOP OF MINDEN

He declares himself ready to resume the negotiations for peace between Henry and the abbot of Corvey. (1151.)

To the venerable lord HENRY, bishop of the holy Church of Minden, B., of the Church of Paderborn, what he is: the faithful offering of his brotherly service and prayer.

Because we are commanded to pursue the things that make for peace, and eternal blessedness is promised to the peaceful, [Col. 1331A] we have devoted our labor, together with our brethren, to the cause of peace and good settlement, in order to still the evil of discord which has truly arisen between you and the abbot of Corvey, our friend, and has increased with time. Although the hoped-for result has by no means followed, yet because your dignity acknowledges this on our part, we greatly rejoice and are made readier to resume the effort, if it should be expedient.

We cannot now discover counsel sounder than that which we conveyed to you at Hameln, our brethren the provosts of Hildesheim agreeing with us in this very matter; in it we believed sufficient provision had been made for the honor of us all. We therefore leave it to the sagacity of your discerning judgment [Col. 1331B] to deliberate, and to inform us by friendly letters whether you would deign to accept either the reconciliation then proposed or another suitable way of reconciliation. If we learn this from you without ambiguity—so that our labor may not prove fruitless if we undertake it again—we shall not cease, so far as we can, faithfully to labor that the lord abbot may meet you at a place to which he can safely come, and that the present dissension may receive an honorable end.

## LETTER CCXLVIII. ABBOT WIBALD TO HIS MONKS OF STAVELOT

He displays paternal affection for them and excuses himself for not returning to them sooner. (1151.)

[Col. 1331C]

Brother WIBALD, by the grace of God servant of the Church of Stavelot, to the venerable dean ROBERT and the other beloved sons of the Church of Stavelot: blessing and life for ever.

Your love remembers with what watchfulness and affection we have always been intent upon sustaining and advancing the interests of our beloved mother, the Church of Stavelot; and, so far as God deigns to assist our labors, we shall henceforth do the same with no less diligence. As for our delay in coming to you at once, after we had been released from the service of the lord king and from court, in order to relieve your needs: it was prevented by the many cares and very grave labors which we undertook in the Church of Corvey, [Col. 1331D] to which, by your counsel and leave, we came according to divine ordinance. From our first entrance there we have been in the labors of men and have been scourged with men.

The heavier labors which we endure in that Church concern the Church of Kemnade; your brotherhood has heard something of them. We entered upon them in our innocence by the common judgment of the brethren and faithful men of the Church. Yet we have suffered harsh tribulations on behalf of that chapter, while we faithfully and devotedly assist in accomplishing what we began and in retaining those same goods of the Church. At present we cannot in any way withdraw from it without loss of honor unless we wish to abandon it amid the greatest disturbances—a thing which we believe neither your [Col. 1332A] brotherhood desires nor our own honor permits.

We therefore ask our brotherhood, most dear to us, to bear our delay and absence with equanimity, as beloved sons, as you have often been accustomed to do; to endure our shortcomings patiently in the charity with which you love us; and, especially during these feast days, when there is customarily a greater gathering and greater concourse of people among you, to take more diligent care that your poverty may not become apparent to anyone.

Moreover, before our departure from you we carefully admonished your provost and cellarer orally, and afterward through our letters, to take every care that you should suffer no negligence concerning your provision. If they have observed this admonition well, they have gained no small favor with us; but if they have neglected it, they have grievously offended our good will. We have also commanded the dean that, if they neglect their duty, he himself must nevertheless not neglect it, and that, by common counsel, whether from the goods of the Church or from whatever source he can, if necessary, [Col. 1332B] he should supply your deficiencies until our return.

Above all, earnestly admonishing your unanimity, we ask that you take care to bear, with the same good will by which you have often supported us, both your own shortcomings and our delay; so that when we return, you may find us the readier and more cheerful to relieve your need, the more kindly you have meanwhile shown yourselves to us in your patience. We also beseech all of you to strive more attentively to invoke the mercy of the Almighty upon us, upon yourselves, and upon the Church of Corvey: that the merciful Father, who visits our iniquities with a rod and our sins with scourges, may nevertheless not scatter his mercy from us and from his Churches.

## LETTER CCXLIX. EMPEROR CONRAD TO HENRY, DUKE OF SAXONY

That he should ensure that the monks of Corvey enjoy the Church of Kemnade. (1151.)

CONRAD, by the grace of God king of the Romans, to H., duke of Saxony: his favor and every good.

Your nobility remembers that, often after [Col. 1332D] our return from the Jerusalem expedition, we admonished and asked your diligence to help the Church of Corvey and its faithful abbot in defending and preserving the goods of the Church of Kemnade. We also wish your diligence to remember that you received from the hand of the abbot of Corvey, at your own request, the advocacy of Kemnade which you had held from us; accordingly, you became more bound to him to protect those places.

Therefore we again earnestly admonish and ask your nobility to restrain Theoderic of Recklinghausen and his sons from the injury and outrage which they inflict upon the aforesaid abbot in those same possessions; and mercifully to restore to the same monastery the brother monks whom they have now expelled for the second time, [Col. 1333A] and cause them to serve God there.

Let your prudence also know this: that lady of Jesika, who has dissipated the goods of the Church of Kemnade and does not cease to dissipate them still, did not enter upon them with our permission. Indeed, we are greatly astonished at the prudence of yourself and the other princes: why do you permit such a woman, along with worthless men, to squander and scatter possessions given to the Church for the service of God? If the abbot’s men have done anything against her perversity and invasion, by which she invaded the Church, they do not appear to have acted contrary to law, because, where no law forbids it, they repelled force by force. We therefore judge that vengeance falls rather upon the wrongdoers than upon those who exact vengeance.

In every way, then, we ask your diligence to assist the aforesaid abbot vigorously in preserving those same possessions. You may certainly know that, if for our request you are gracious to him, you will find us gracious in your own causes and petitions and those of your friends.

## LETTER CCL. EMPEROR CONRAD TO ABBOT WIBALD

That he should remain near Corvey until the feast of Saint James. (1151.)

CONRAD, by the grace of God king of the Romans, to WIBALD, abbot of Corvey: his favor and every good.

Since we require the counsel of your discretion in conducting certain of our affairs, we ask you to remain near Corvey until the feast of Saint James, and to send your representative to our presence at Rothenburg on the Ides of July [Col. 1333C]; through him we shall communicate to your belovedness a definite statement of our will and purpose.

## LETTER CCLI. POPE EUGENIUS III TO ABBOT WIBALD

That he should excommunicate Godebold, canon of Minden, unless he restores to Everard the Church of Homeringen which he had seized. (1151.)

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son WIBALD, abbot of Corvey: greeting and apostolic blessing.

Everard, the bearer of the present letter, has now come five times into our presence, etc. See under Pope Eugenius III, at the year 1153.

## LETTER CCLII. ABBOT WIBALD TO GODEBALD, CANON OF MINDEN

That he should restore to Everard the Church of Hemeringen which he had seized; otherwise he announces that he is excommunicated and can be absolved by the pope alone. (1151.)

[Col. 1333D]

WIBALD, by the grace of God abbot of Corvey, to GODEBALD, canon of Minden: the Angel of Great Counsel.

Our reverend father and lord Pope Eugenius has commanded our insignificance in his letters to admonish you that, within twenty days after receiving this our warning, you restore in its entirety to Everard, bearer of this letter, the church of Saint Peter at Hemeringen and other things taken from him by you or persons acting under your direction, [Col. 1334A] and henceforth permit him to possess them in peace. If you disdain to do so, from that moment we publicly declare you excommunicated; nor can you be absolved from the bond of excommunication until, for so great a rebellion, you come to the presence of the lord pope to answer.

As we were commanded, we give you this warning in person. Moreover, we have sent you, for your consideration, a copy of the lord pope’s letter which he wrote us in this case. We exhort your brotherhood in the Lord not to neglect, in concern for your reputation and peace, to make satisfaction and be reconciled with the aforesaid Everard. Seize the opportunity, and make a virtue of necessity. Let your belovedness know that we did not seek these measures, but we cannot possibly disobey; and it is as hard for us as for you to kick against the goad.

## LETTER CCLIII. POPE EUGENIUS III TO ABBOT WIBALD

He praises Wibald’s zeal for the Roman Church, and, at Wibald’s request, writes to the bishop of Minden and the archbishop of Bremen. (1151.)

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son WIBALD, abbot of Corvey: greeting and apostolic blessing.

The letter of your belovedness, etc. See under Eugenius.

## LETTER CCLIV. POPE EUGENIUS III TO HENRY, BISHOP OF MINDEN

That the Church of Kemnade, because of an unforeseen incident and the death of a certain monk, does not need reconciliation; and that he should cause what has been taken from that Church to be restored. (1151.)

[Col. 1334C]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother H., bishop of Minden: greeting and apostolic blessing.

It has come to our ears, etc. See under Eugenius.

## LETTER CCLV. POPE EUGENIUS III TO H., ARCHBISHOP OF BREMEN

He commends Abbot Wibald to him and directs him to cause the estates taken from the Church of Kemnade to be restored. (1151.)

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother H., [Col. 1334D] archbishop of Bremen: greeting and apostolic blessing.

It is the duty of the episcopal office, etc. See under Eugenius.

## LETTER CCLVI. EMPEROR CONRAD TO ABBOT WIBALD

That he should prepare himself for the Roman embassy. (1151.)

CONRAD, by the grace of God king of the Romans, to WIBALD, abbot of Corvey: his favor and every good.

After you departed from us, our faithful men from the Roman court repeatedly admonished us, both by letters and in private conversations, to send our envoys to the lord pope and to the City for the ordering of the affairs of the realm. The lord pope also asserts in letters most recently sent to us [Col. 1335A] that he awaits principal envoys, as we have already promised a second time in our letters, who may effectively advance by counsel the promotion of the Church and the realm between ourselves and him.

Since your ability has shone forth in affairs of Church and realm, and since we are certain of the affection of your devotion toward us, the utility of the realm requires, and our will has ordained, that, at the request of our affection, you undertake together with our chancellor the labor of this embassy. We therefore earnestly ask that you come to Nuremberg at the Nativity of the Blessed Mary so prepared that you may proceed in carrying out that embassy. What we have done concerning the injury inflicted upon you by the bishop of Minden and Theoderic, our chaplain Heribert will report to you more fully.

## LETTER CCLVII. POPE EUGENIUS III TO EMPEROR CONRAD

He welcomes Conrad’s embassy, by which the affairs of Church and realm may be strengthened; he has entrusted the affair of Morbach Abbey to the bishop of Lausanne; and he writes concerning Otto, who had cut off a cleric’s nose. (1151.)

[Col. 1335B]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son in Christ CONRAD, illustrious and glorious king of the Romans: greeting and apostolic blessing.

That through distinguished envoys, etc. See under Eugenius.

## LETTER CCLVIII. H., NOTARY, TO ABBOT WIBALD

Why he is accustomed to write him briefly. (1151.)

[Col. 1335C]

To his lord WIBALD, abbot of Corvey, H., notary of the royal court: the service of a servant.

Your prudence reproves me because I am accustomed to write to you briefly. Therefore let your fatherhood not wonder: whether I begin to speak to you in person or in your absence, I become slower and more impeded of tongue, and almost mute. For whom would not the unceasing torrent of your eloquence daunt? There is another reason compelling me to speak to you concisely: I understand many things, but because they are poised either way—that is, toward being or not being—and I can make you certain of nothing, I fear to disturb the serenity of your mind with the surface of mere words.

Trusting in the favor which [Col. 1335D] you promised me concerning my brother, I send him to the regard of your favor and lordship. Theoderic of Recklinghausen, having been severely charged in the presence of the lord king concerning the injury he inflicted upon you, and much rebuked by the king, promised that he wishes henceforth to serve you in order to recover the regard of your favor.

## LETTER CCLIX. G., CARDINAL, TO ABBOT WIBALD

He praises Wibald’s zeal for the Roman Church, etc. (1151.)

G., by the grace of God cardinal-deacon of the holy Roman Church, to his beloved and venerable brother WIBALD, abbot of Stavelot: greeting and affection.

Having acquired [Col. 1336A] knowledge of your belovedness in a brief conversation, and having established by many proofs through experience the worth and ability of your character, we have become so gracious and kindly disposed toward your brotherhood that I am one with whom you may speak as securely as with yourselves about everything. Or if anything seems to be lacking to the friendship established between us, whether through brevity of time or because a pledge of words has not hitherto been exchanged, believe without doubt that it is supplied by the ardor of affection and the indissoluble bond of charity.

The sequence of your letters plainly declares to us the earnest concern which you have hitherto had, and continue constantly to have, toward your mother, the holy Roman Church. We praise it with the favor due to such kindness, and in true charity in the Lord ask your filial devotion to render to your mother, the holy Roman Church, the assisting services customarily owed [Col. 1336B] by the office of piety.

Know that the matter which, as you indicated, had been proposed to the most serene lord King Conrad by certain religious persons proceeded in no way from the will or knowledge of the lord pope. Especially since we know that the man whom you mentioned would show no honor to the royal majesty unless he perceived, with absolute certainty, that the king’s arrival in Tuscany or Romagna was imminent; nor would it be advantageous to the Roman Church that, with it excluded, such persons should meet concerning so great a matter.

But if divine providence draws the royal majesty into Italian regions, then the holy Roman Church can fittingly and honorably intervene, [Col. 1336C] and by urging prayers and almost force upon our lord King Conrad, and by addressing the other man with threats and terrors, it will without doubt be able to settle whatever is pious, holy, and most worthy of royal magnificence.

## LETTER CCLX. ABBOT WIBALD TO EMPEROR CONRAD

He excuses himself from undertaking the Roman embassy at his own expense. (1151.)

To his lord, the renowned conqueror CONRAD, by the grace of God glorious emperor Augustus of the Romans, brother WIBALD, by that same grace what he is in the [Col. 1336D] Catholic Church: greeting in Him who gives salvation to kings.

Your chaplain Heribert came to us at Corvey with letters from your graciousness, containing the instruction that, at the Nativity of Saint Mary, we should come to the presence of your Highness at Nuremberg so equipped and prepared that, with your chancellor, we might carry your embassy to the lord pope and to the City. Although we endured many injuries and grave losses not only throughout the preceding year but even at present, to the insult of the realm and of ourselves, we nevertheless sought to obey your commands both from duty and from devotion. On the vigil of Saint Lawrence we departed from Corvey Abbey and traveled by long stages toward the Church of Stavelot, [Col. 1337A] which had been shattered and worn down by many robberies, burnings, and other vexations because of the dispute between the bishop of Liège and the advocate of our church, the count of Montaigu.

Coming to Cologne to your venerable chancellor, we discussed at length and carefully the practicability of our journey and the benefit of our embassy. It did not seem to us, given our limited understanding, that this embassy ought at present to be undertaken considering the character of the times and the state of your affairs, especially since it is uncertain what Count Alexander of Gravina will report from the emperor of the Greeks. In that serious discussion, as we tried to choose what was best in every respect, we heard from your chancellor that it was your will that we should serve in this journey at our own expense.

[Col. 1337B] Yet, most merciful emperor, your most serene Majesty well knows that from the beginning of your reign we have never failed in your public labors. In person and in resources, we have always served with you and for you; frequently, without you, we have campaigned at no small expense. We should wish to do so now as well, if the slenderness of our resources permitted it in any way. But since in Saxony we have incurred great expenses for almost a whole year because of the dissension of our people and the depredations of Theoderic of Recklinghausen, we have no possible means of undertaking this duty [Col. 1337C] in a manner proportionate to the excellence of your name and the weight of this embassy.

Therefore let not your goodness be angry with your humble servants, always and everywhere ready for your service, if we do not in this manner fulfill what we are wholly unable to fulfill. Rather, since either the chancellor alone, or with him the bishop of Constance, Lausanne, or Basel, can suitably carry out this embassy, permit us, with your gracious leave, to rest and repair the losses we have sustained. For at Corvey we learned nothing, either from your letters or through your messenger, about the matter of travel expenses to be borne by ourselves in this embassy. We humbly entreat you concerning the bishop of Minden, that you grant him your favor.

## LETTER CCLXI. ABBOT WIBALD TO ARNOLD, PROVOST OF COLOGNE

He sets out how great the expenses already incurred by him for the emperor and his empire have been. (1151.)

[Col. 1337D]

To his dearest lord and friend A., venerable provost of the venerable holy Church of Cologne and chancellor of the royal court, brother WIBALD, by the grace of God what he is in the Catholic Church: himself and all that is his.

As we have partly lamented before your Highness, we wonder with considerable grief whether it arises from the heart of the most serene Augustus or from the suggestion of those who hold the first place in counsel with him, [Col. 1338A] that our wealth should seem to him so great and abundant. First, after his return, he sent Roger of Ariano to us, that, out of reverence for his affection, we might provide him clothing and arms. We did this diligently and incurred an expense of no less than twenty marks.

Then, summoned, we came to the court at Frankfurt, at no small expense both to ourselves and to you. Afterwards, when commanded, we came to Bamberg with a large retinue and remained at court for nearly ten weeks. Although we were generously and most honorably maintained by the most merciful prince, nevertheless believe us that throughout that whole period in which we were absent from Corvey, we spent forty marks of silver from our own resources.

But it is said that he remitted to us the three hundred marks which we owed him. Yet according to our agreements [Col. 1338B] and covenants, we neither owed him those three hundred marks nor paid them; rather, we paid more than two hundred because, as provided in our terms, we did not receive from him the justice due and promised to us.

Moreover, dearest friend, it has not escaped us that other brethren and fellow abbots of ours serve in the realm, and are not merely our equals but even our superiors, although we have borne the burden and heat of the day and the sword has often pierced our soul. But let us put these matters aside. It would not be honorable for our lord, his empire, or our own lowliness if we appeared meanly equipped in so great an embassy.

But because we fear that, if this command is not fulfilled by us, some occasion for indignation may be sought, we would rather make the journey somehow on an ass [Col. 1338C] than lose, through failure to carry out this command, so much time spent in most devoted service. And happy are our labors, which earn offense for what is impossible, although our Church has received no great advantage from them.

## LETTER CCLXII. EMPEROR CONRAD TO ABBOT WIBALD

That an embassy to the pope cannot be conducted through anyone other than himself and the emperor’s chancellor. (1151.)

CONRAD, by the grace of God king of the Romans, to WIBALD, abbot of Corvey: his favor and every good.

The business which we must conduct with the lord pope cannot be handled through any persons other than your discretion and that of our chancellor. [Col. 1338D] Moreover, in the course of the embassy matters arise, on the one hand from our brother the Emperor of Constantinople, and on the other from ROGER [Note: [Col. 1337] King of Sicily, who was strongly opposed to Conrad.], in the handling of which we neither wish nor are able to admit any persons besides yourselves. We have learned in full from your chaplain H. of the many wrongs and grave losses which you have endured, not only throughout the whole past year but even now, to the dishonour of the kingdom and of ourselves; and at a suitable time we shall, as is our duty, support you in setting these matters right. We therefore ask, and wish to be assured, that you undertake with the chancellor the labour of our embassy to the lord pope, and that at the feast of St Michael you come with him to Regensburg and [Col. 1339A] attend our presence. The travelling expenses which you cannot obtain through yourself, secure by pledging your sureties; with God’s favour, we are ready to redeem them as soon as an opportunity presents itself.

## LETTER CCLXIII. WIBALD, ABBOT, TO ARNOLD, PROVOST OF COLOGNE

He writes that the Roman embassy must necessarily be undertaken, and asks him to specify the day on which he may meet him. (A.D. 1151.)

To his dearest lord and friend A., chief provost of the holy Church of Cologne and chancellor of the royal court, Brother WIBALD, by God’s grace what he is in the Catholic Church, himself and all that is his.

You have plainly understood the tenor of the letters of our lord the king, both from [Col. 1339B] our messenger and from the chaplain of that same lord of ours, as we have learned. Although in this matter and in Saxony we are constrained by the greatest and gravest cares, although we leave our brethren in deficiencies that are almost unbearable, nevertheless, lest it be imputed to us that the honour, dignity, and advancement of the Roman Empire are hindered or delayed by us, we are prepared to satisfy the will of our lord—not according to the excellence of royal dignity, indeed, but according to the ready and abundant goodwill of our limited means. For at this time we judge it safer and more salutary for us to put aside the interests of our brethren and leave our churches in perilous danger, than, by failing to obey [Col. 1339C] our dearest lord, to incur anger which we have not deserved and suddenly lose all the devoted services which we have often and almost continually rendered in royal courts.

We shall go, therefore, we shall go—not as befits royal majesty, but as men in some fashion driven from our house and exiled, content with small expenses and few companions. Let your kindness therefore deign to inform us of the day on which we are to come to you, so prepared that we may proceed with you to the court appointed for us. For on this journey and in this embassy, as always, we wish to be devoted to you in all things. Through the present messenger, therefore, take care to give us certainty on this matter by your written reply. Yet we believe that, since our lord has decided to send us so urgently and attentively, [Col. 1339D] some great benefits to the kingdom must result from our embassy.

## LETTER CCLXIV. THE CHANCELLOR TO ABBOT WIBALD

He again excuses himself from undertaking the Roman embassy. (A.D. 1151.)

The chancellor to the lord abbot.

I have heard my lord’s will both from his messengers and from his letters, but I alone know my own impossibility. Therefore, not to make a long delay in writing, nor begin to range through each individual matter that hinders me, I shall briefly disclose the conclusion of the matter to your affection. If I were to go with you to Rome at this time, I should have to renounce everything that I possess and then set out alone and naked. [Col. 1340A] For there is no day on which I can or dare be absent from the brethren and the cloister, since neither their estates nor their stewards pay them provisions or any services; rather, they live from my own earnings. Wine, as you yourselves know, has failed throughout the whole land; yet they, not heeding the plague and hand of God, demand it from me.

I therefore wish you to be informed and entreated to hold me faithfully excused before my lord, whose command I have never failed to obey; for you alone are sufficient for this embassy, nor would I do anything with you except appear as a messenger—doing nothing and saying nothing in your presence; and if I spoke, I should reveal my inexperience, and, as it were, perish like a mouse through my own testimony. But if you were willing to wait for me fifteen days after the feast of blessed Remigius [Col. 1340B], and if in the meantime I could free and prepare myself, I would come with you to my lord, and whatever I should do would be done with his favour preserved. Farewell.

## LETTER CCLXV. WIBALD, ABBOT, TO A., THE CHANCELLOR

He urges him, difficulties overcome, to undertake the Roman embassy. (A.D. 1151.)

To his dearest lord and friend A., venerable chancellor, Brother WIBALD, by God’s grace what he is, himself and all that is his.

The words which you wrote us concerning the difficulty of your departure and preparation for the Roman journey are undoubtedly our own words also; and you consider, in the case of your brethren, what our condition is [Col. 1340C] in our churches, or what possibility there is at this time of leaving our brethren, when we see already before our eyes impending over them—not, I would say, the dearness of provisions, but the harsh want caused by the greatest barrenness. Although, therefore, it seems impious to us to leave our brethren under the danger of hunger and want, yet on the other side we see it as grievous to incur the anger of the prince and, by passing over his command on a single occasion, suddenly lose all the service by which we have ever served him and the kingdom. Distresses indeed surround us on every side; but it is better for us at this time to leave our affairs exposed to danger than, by failing to satisfy [Col. 1340D] the will of our lord the king, to incur his offence, lose through some negligence the favour for which we have laboured through many years, and in some degree delay matters advantageous to the Empire or to the honour of its ruler and profitable to the holy Church.

As to what you wrote us—that we alone would suffice for this embassy and that you regarded yourself as appointed in the embassy in the place of a count—this shall not be so. Rather, in this embassy you are greater and more worthy, because you are either of Cologne or of Mainz, because you hold the keys of the kingdom and ought to direct the highest counsel in the kingdom. Accordingly, you shall have us as counts and faithful servants in your service. Since, therefore, the king’s command presses us, though we are poorly able, we shall nevertheless go in order to satisfy his will, and we expose our person [Col. 1341A] to labours and dangers according to his will.

But because we must still summon from Saxony the young men whom we shall have on this journey, we ask you to appoint a fixed day on which we may come to you as far as Rintorp, so prepared and equipped that together with you we may proceed to the lord king. We wish no one except your note to know the day to be appointed. As for the fifteen days after the feast of Remigius for which you ask us to wait, we accept them gladly; and, should you wait a little longer at your convenience, we shall gladly wait. Yet take care not to prolong the time of departure into the severe winter. Besides, it now rests upon your efforts that, just as we have already done through our messenger, so you too, through your messenger, take care diligently to excuse both us and yourselves before our lord the king for not coming to court on the day fixed. [Col. 1341B]

## LETTER CCLXVI. WIBALD, ABBOT, TO HENRY, BISHOP OF MINDEN

Concerning their mutual reconciliation. (A.D. 1151.)

To the reverend father and lord in Christ H., venerable bishop of the holy Church of Minden, Brother WIBALD, by God’s grace abbot of Corvey: humble prayers and devoted service.

Your beloved sons, our venerable brethren D. Warner, provost of your greater church, [Col. 1341C] and Master Conrad, came to us and announced to us a good word from your fatherhood, a word of consolation: namely, that your anger against us had been turned into mercy, and that the Lord, who commands the sea and the winds, had calmed the storm of the greatest disturbance into a gentle breeze. We therefore rejoiced in what was said to us, since for a long time past we have desired that our innocence, and our devotion and reverence toward you and toward the holy Church of Minden, might be proved to your highness.

Indeed, your aforesaid provost Warner, before our brethren and fellow priests, joined hand in hand from your person and your Church into our hand and pledged us certainty and faith upon your soul and his own: that you would love our brethren who are now at Kaminata, or who may hereafter be there, as your subjects and spiritual sons; that you would no longer impute to us or to them their entrance without your permission; but that you would wish to foster, protect, and maintain, by due and canonical justice, both them and the goods of the Church of Kaminata situated within your bishopric. [Col. 1341D] Concerning the injury and offence by which we are accused of having harmed you and the Church of Minden, you would make no further complaint, but would place our reconciliation in the counsel of our lords, namely the bishops of Paderborn, Münster, and Osnabrück. If one of them, or certainly two, could not be present, you would leave the whole matter to the will and decision of our lord the bishop of Paderborn.

We likewise shall hereafter be ready to serve your fatherhood and the Church of Minden devotedly; and by our good offices we shall endeavour, through God’s mercy, to soften every disturbance which you were said to have had against us, so that where discord has abounded, love and grace may abound still more. For since you grieve that you have already incurred the offence of our lord the king because of us, we shall diligently labour wholly to mitigate and calm for you all his indignation against you on that account, and shall henceforth endeavour, if you do not disdain to communicate them to us, to advance all your causes and bring them to effect with no less zeal than our own.

Finally, if you send your messenger and letters of excuse to our lord the king at the court at Nuremberg, to which he summoned you on the Nativity of the Blessed Mary, [Col. 1342B] we shall work with him so that he replies to you mercifully and graciously remits to you, both by his letters and through your messenger, the anger and indignation which he had against you because of us. Since we are also now setting out on our lord the king’s embassy to the lord pope, we further assure your excellency that we shall negotiate nothing with the lord pope against your honour or that of your Church. But if the lord pope writes to you concerning our complaint, we shall cause such things to be written to you as will compel you to render justice concerning the invaders of [Col. 1342C] our property, while not disturbing your tranquillity and the peace of the Church of Minden.

This too was included in the agreement: if God should call us from this world within the period of this delay, the Church of Corvey and our successor, whom God may appoint there after us, shall remain with you and with the holy Church of Minden, with faith inviolate, in the same peace and concord which has been set forth above. The same things which Provost Warner, at Corvey, pledged and confirmed to us before our brethren, on his faith given into our hand, Master Conrad, at Paderborn, confirmed for you upon his own soul to Lord Bishop Bernard before his church, on his faith given into that bishop’s hand. And both of them confirmed to us, by the kiss of peace which they gave us—Provost [Col. 1342D] Werner at Corvey, and Master Conrad at Paderborn—your reconciliation and friendship restored to us.

## LETTER CCLXVII. CONRAD, EMPEROR, TO HENRY, BISHOP OF MINDEN

He is pleased that he has returned to peace with the abbot of Corvey, and remits every offence which he had incurred. (A.D. 1151.)

CONRAD, by God’s grace king of the Romans, to H., venerable bishop of Minden: his favour and every good.

Our faithful servant, the abbot of Corvey, has thanked our clemency, both by letters and through his messengers, [Col. 1343A] because, in reverence for our affection and command, you have remitted every disturbance which you had had against him and his Church; because you have received into favour and peace, as a pious father and good shepherd, his monks whom he had established in the Church of Kaminata; and because you have firmly promised that hereafter you will foster them and defend them by canonical justice. Although you have done this more slowly and later than had been entrusted to your diligence, we nevertheless find it very pleasing; and we strictly enjoin upon your prudence that you honour and love that same abbot, and at every occasion lend him counsel and aid concerning both the Church of Kaminata and his other affairs—especially against Thideric of Rikelinga, who, setting aside fear of God and reverence for us and the kingdom, disturbs the aforesaid abbot and his Church and presumes to harass them. [Col. 1343B] Therefore we mercifully remit to you all our indignation and offence which you had justly incurred, and absolve you from the summonses and judgments promulgated against you concerning this matter.

## LETTER CCLXVIII. HENRY, BISHOP OF MINDEN, TO ABBOT WIBALD

He defends the innocence of Godebold, whom Everard, priest of Hemerin, was accusing. (A.D. 1151.)

To the lord WIBALD, reverend abbot of the holy Church of Corvey, HENRY, by God’s mercy bishop of the Church of Minden: continual prayers in Christ [Col. 1343C] and the devotion of faithful service.

From experience of the truth we can testify to the ears of your discretion concerning the innocence of life of Master Godebold, our beloved brother, and the uprightness of his whole conduct. Regarding the troublesome complaint which Everard, priest of Hemerin, has unjustly brought against him, we would much more gladly and fully discuss the matter with you orally than in writing, if place and time suitable for an exchange of words had been available. For whenever the aforesaid priest Everard brought us letters from the lord pope, we were ready to render him justice; and Master Godebold, before us and the whole Church of Minden, canonically offered his purgation, namely, that neither he himself nor persons sent by him had ever plundered Everard’s goods. [Col. 1343D] You may hold it certain from our testimony that he would long ago have offered the same purgation before the lord pope, if the weakness of continual illness had not prevented him.

But recently, having heard the letters of the lord pope which that same Everard brought, and with an added admonition from your Serenity that peace and an end of toil might come to the aforesaid persons, we wished, for the love and tranquillity of our brother Godebold, to pay the priest Everard three [an uncertain or incomplete amount] in this manner; and concerning the other persons from whom he complains that his goods were taken away, we promised that we would administer ecclesiastical justice. Of these proposals he was unwilling to accept any part for our counsel, but, renewing his complaint, declared that he would seek justice from the Apostolic See. But because you are a lover of peace and merciful toward fraternal weakness, we entrust to your prudence, with supplication, the task of endeavouring to settle, through yourself and with our humble mediation, the whole tempest of the controversy. That is, order the said Everard, sternly admonished by your words, to return to us, so that, laying aside litigation, he may receive the fruit of the aforesaid agreement and thereafter, if he is a good man, possess his own in peace. If this cannot be done, let the Church of Minden feel in this matter the affection of your charity, so that [Col. 1344B] you endeavour to excuse before the lord pope our beloved son Master Godebold and to make peace for him amid the frequently renewed complaints of his adversary.

## LETTER CCLXIX. H., DUKE OF BAVARIA AND SAXONY, TO ABBOT WIBALD

He receives the goods of the Church of Corvey under his protection. (A.D. 1151.)

To WIBALD, venerable abbot of the Church of Corvey, H., by God’s grace duke of Bavaria and Saxony: faithful service.

At your request I receive the goods of your Church under the protection of my guardianship, and in these matters [Col. 1344C] and in all others which concern the advancement of your honour or benefit, I show myself ready and faithful. I therefore trust securely in your reciprocal goodwill: may remembrance of me be in blessing among you, both before the lord pope and before the king.

## LETTER CCLXX. WIBALD, ABBOT, TO THE PRIOR AND BRETHREN OF HASTERIA

That, content with the ancient custom of the place, they may return to concord with their brethren of Waulsort. (A.D. 1151.)

Brother WIBALD, by God’s grace what he is in the Catholic Church, to I., venerable prior of the Church of Hasteria, and to the rest who in that place serve God and peace: [Col. 1344D] blessing and life for ever.

There is no need to repeat to your learning with what affection of love we have loved the Church and yourselves; for our deeds have until now been able to bear witness to our love for you. Yet we have heard what we could by no means have expected to hear from your brotherhood: namely, that, attempting to overstep the boundaries set for you by your fathers, you have begun by new and needless disturbances to harass your mother Church of Waulsort [Note: [Col. 1343D] An ancient monastery of the Order of St Benedict situated on the Meuse. Its history may be found in volume VII of Acheri’s *Spicilegium*, where the following, suitably relevant to this and the following letters, is read: “Lord Wibald, summoned from the mastership of the school in the Church of Stavelot to the same office in this monastery, became at one and the same time abbot not only of it but also of Monte Cassino and Corvey. He renewed the ancient privilege of Emperor Otto I in the courts of Emperors Lothar and Frederick and of King Conrad, obtaining new and clearer privileges; he ordained that their confirmation should be preserved in perpetuity in the Church of St Stephen at Metz, which is both the mother and lady of this monastery. He also renewed the privilege of Pope Benedict VII, as may still be seen, and those of Popes Adrian and Eugenius III, by which it is clearly shown that the place of Hasteria ought, as a cell or provostship—or by whatever name it is called in the documents preserved in the treasury of our monastery—to adhere to Waulsort as a member to its head and obey it in all things.”], and Lord [Col. 1345A] Abbot T., who through that Church also regularly presides over your place [Note: [Col. 1346D] Theodoric II, thirteenth abbot of Waulsort, successor of Widricus.], contrary to the privileges of that Church and the purpose of your religious profession.

For it is most certainly established that the Church of Waulsort, from the beginning of its foundation, has been endowed with the Church of Hasteria, its village, and all its appurtenances by privileges of emperors and kings, and especially by the decree of Pope Benedict VII; and that the monastic order was established there by the abbot of Waulsort. No one doubts that your Church is subject to that Church and ought to be content with the abbot of that place. We therefore, who are among the sons of the Church of Waulsort, recognizing that we too are your brethren, send this counsel to your whole community: hasten as quickly as you can to return to peace and concord with your abbot and brethren, content with the custom and arrangements established for you by your fathers; for you are not better than your fathers.

But if you had first received the counsel and letters of our discretion, your cause would by no means, we believe, have gone so far, nor would the fragrance of your good reputation have turned into a stench. If, accepting our counsels, you strive toward the unity of peace and concord, you will receive our goodwill more closely and will hold with us the place and name of good sons and brethren. But if, persisting in your obstinacy, you do not obey our salutary admonitions, [Col. 1345C] from that point we appeal against you to the hearing of the lord pope and appoint for you a day at the Circumcision of the Lord, prepared to answer us concerning the charges upon which we have summoned you.

## LETTER CCLXXI. WIBALD, ABBOT, TO STEPHEN, BISHOP OF METZ

That he may deign to protect the privileges of the monastery of Waulsort and restrain the audacity of the Hasterian monks. (A.D. 1151.)

To his reverend father and lord STEPHEN, venerable bishop of the holy Church of Metz, Brother WIBALD, by God’s grace what he is in the Catholic Church: [Col. 1345D] humble prayers and devoted service.

Your prudence knows, reverend Father, that from the beginning of the affection which you have deigned familiarly to offer us, we have loved you and all that is yours with sincere affection of charity; and wherever we have been, we have supported, according to our capacity, the honour of your person and Church. With the same confidence we dare to petition your fatherhood and ask that you grant our request: that you order the Church of Waulsort, which clothed us with the monastic habit when we fled the shipwreck of this world, [Col. 1346A] to remain in its justice and honour, as you may see in the privileges of emperors and kings.

For the ears of your holiness ought not to be lent to the false monks of Hasteria, who, given over to idleness, study fables, meditate vain and superfluous things, and disturb the peace of the Church. For the Church of Waulsort, from the beginning of its foundation, has been endowed with the Church of Hasteria, its village, and all its appurtenances by privileges of kings and emperors, and especially by the decree of Pope Benedict VII; and the monastic order was established there by the abbot of Waulsort. Since this is so, and since many still remember that even deceased brethren of Hasteria were formerly buried in the cemetery of Waulsort, [Col. 1346B] we ask your holiness to restrain with the rod of your authority the rashness of the mad Hasterian monks and compel them to return to the peace and concord of their brethren; or, if they refuse, to have them expelled from the monastery as rebels and disobedient to apostolic decrees. We humbly and earnestly await your timely reply. For we intend shortly to set out for Rome on the embassy of our lord the king and the kingdom, where we shall also endeavour by every means to advance the cause of the abbot of Waulsort.

## LETTER CCLXXII. STEPHEN, BISHOP OF METZ, TO ABBOT WIBALD

That he compel the monks of Hasteria to obey the Church of Waulsort. (A.D. 1151.)

[Col. 1346C]

STEPHEN, by God’s grace, though unworthy bishop of Metz, to WIBALD, venerable abbot of Stavelot: greeting and affection.

As you say that you rely upon my affection and friendship, know certainly that you may rely upon them very greatly. As for what you wrote to me concerning the monks of Hasteria—that they resist being subject to the Church of Waulsort with something like the fierceness of a bull-necked stubbornness—I entrust it to your sagacity to compel them, by my command and will, to remain now also in the same condition and manner in which you have learned and know that they were formerly. [Col. 1346D] For if they wish to remain in the peace of that body whose head is Christ, they must, as members of the body submit to the head, so humbly submit to their own mother Church of Waulsort, if matters are as you assert. Know indeed for certain that I do not wish lightly to alter in my time those things which have been well and lawfully established of old by the authority of pontiffs, the generosity of princes, and the assent of other Catholic faithful.

## LETTER CCLXXIII. WIBALD, ABBOT, TO THEODORIC, ABBOT OF WAULSORT

He promises him his protection, orders him to investigate the intentions of the Hasterians, and send him the privileges of kings and popes. (A.D. 1151.)

[Col. 1347A]

To his reverend father T., abbot of Waulsort, Brother WIBALD, by God’s grace what he is in the Catholic Church.

The Lord commands in the Law: “Honour your father and your mother, that you may be long-lived upon the earth.” Mindful also of this command, if any benefit accrues by our effort and labour to your person and Church—our own mother—we rejoice in every way; and we shall faithfully labour, according to the means granted us by God, that it may be increased more abundantly both in growth of honour and in increase of advantage.
