But because we are already proceeding upon our embassy, we order you, after carefully investigating the intention of the Hasterians—whether it be one of dissension, which God forbid, or reconciliation, which may God grant—to ensure that we are fully informed by you of everything up to the feast of Luke the Evangelist. [Col. 1347B] Send us also carefully corrected copies of the privileges of both emperors and Roman pontiffs, so that, if necessary, carrying them to the City, we may uphold the justice and honour of your Church by the liberation of truth, which is Christ, and by their testimony.

## LETTER CCLXXIV. STEPHEN, BISHOP OF METZ, TO THEODORIC, ABBOT OF WAULSORT

Accused of squandering property, he summons him to the synod of Metz. (A.D. 1151.)

[Col. 1347C]

STEPHEN, by God’s grace bishop of Metz, to T. [Note: [Col. 1347D] Wibald complains in the following letter about this superscription, since Hasteria is a cell, not an abbey.], abbot of Hasteria: greeting and affection.

Certain brethren of the monastery of Hasteria have appeared before us and complained greatly that their Church is diminished by you in many ways and that its goods are improperly alienated through your negligence [Note: [Col. 1347D] Certainly, in his time the Church of Hasteria was stripped of precious gems and splendid ornaments of gold, as the chronicler of Waulsort testifies, p. 572; yet this was not Theodoric’s fault, but that of the Hasterian monks, as is clear from the following letter.]. Since, therefore, the care of that Church pertains to our honour, and its defence lies especially upon us, we command you [Col. 1347D] by injunction to come, with those monks and with every excuse set aside, before our presence at the next synod of Metz, held in the week following the Mass of All Saints, so that, after the complaint and defence of both sides have been heard, our discretion may judge between you with equity observed on either side. We further command that, both on their journey there and on their return, your provision shall not refuse to furnish the complaining monks with the necessary expenses.

## LETTER CCLXXV. WIBALD, ABBOT, TO STEPHEN, BISHOP OF METZ

He complains concerning the rebellion of the Hasterian monks and matters contained in the preceding letter. (A.D. 1151.)

[Col. 1348A]

To his reverend father and lord STEPHEN, venerable bishop of the holy Church of Metz, Brother WIBALD.

Your discretion recalls that a few days ago we wrote to your sincerity concerning the affair of our beloved father T., abbot of Waulsort, namely concerning the rebellion of the monks of Hastière. Forgetful of monastic order and regular discipline, they proved not merely disobedient but openly rebellious against their abbot, until the outcry over their contumacy reached the ears of the lord bishop of Liège; and by the judgment of the archdeacons, abbots, and the whole clergy, they were suspended from the divine offices until they should repent of their obstinacy and make fitting and regular satisfaction both to that bishop and to their own abbot, whom they had despised.

Indeed, in the monastery of Hastière there were two wandering monks, Julian and M., whom the abbot, finding them vagrant, foreign, and in want of bread, had received out of the highest mercy, intending during their period of hospitality to test whether they were worthy in conduct to be joined to the community of brethren by a special bond of fraternity. But they not only lived outrageously, but also deliberately sowed scandals and dissensions among the monks of Waulsort and Hastière and against the abbot himself. Thus, sometimes casting aside their sacred and regular habit, they girded themselves with weapons, invaded the possessions of Waulsort, and ravaged their boundaries without any assertion of legal right. Although the abbot had long delayed correcting this and had postponed cutting down the evils as they sprang up with the sickle of justice, at length, admonished by our counsel and that of his fellow abbots, he entered the chapter-house of the monks of Hastière and, relying upon the authority of the most holy Rule of our blessed father Benedict, courteously commanded the newcomers and sowers of disputes to depart.

When they refused to do this and shamelessly hurled insults at the abbot, he ordered the others not to retain them in their fellowship and decreed that, so long as those two lived within the monastery’s precincts, all should wholly abstain from the divine offices. But they became “a crooked bow” and scorned obedience in both respects: both by retaining those who had been ordered to leave, and by rashly conducting the divine offices in their presence and together with them. This violent presumption, not without contempt for the divine name, as we have said above, was reported to the Church of Liège and was punished by canonical judgment with due severity.

When we had set this case before your Excellency by letter and messenger, and had poured out humble prayers to your greatness for the welfare of our mother Church of Waulsort, it pleased your Highness to write back to our lowliness that, by your will and in your stead, we should compel the monks of Hastière to render due reverence to the abbey of Waulsort and its abbot. But we, being prepared and equipped to depart upon the embassy of our lord king, could by no means become involved in such troublesome affairs.

Yet those same men of Hastière came to you and brought back to their abbot letters issued in your name and sealed with your seal. We could by no means believe that they had been written and issued by your learning, because of their disagreement in many respects with reason, authority, and usage. For the very opening of the document is contrary to authority and usage, since those letters are addressed to the “abbot of Hastière”—a title which neither authority supports nor usage confirms.

For from the beginning of its foundation, that is, for one hundred and eighty-one years, the abbey of Waulsort has possessed the name and authority of an abbey. This was established by the most noble count E., founder of that place, and by Theoderic, most holy bishop of the Church of Metz; and it was likewise confirmed and asserted by a charter of privilege by Otto, first emperor of that name. They decreed that Waulsort should be an abbey and granted Hastière, with all its appurtenances, thereunto for the increase of the provision of those serving God. The venerable Albero, bishop of Metz, predecessor indeed of the aforesaid Theoderic, had granted Hastière from the right of his own inheritance to the Church of Metz and to St Stephen the proto-martyr. This is more fully attested by the privileges granted to the abbey of Waulsort by kings, emperors, and Roman pontiffs, and by the book of life of Saint D.

[Note: Eilbert, son of Count Ebroin and Bertha, daughter of Count Wederic; brother of Count Udo of Roix, Count Heribert of Saint-Quentin, Count Gerard of Oudenarde, Counts Boso and Witers, and Bishop Marquard, as the chronicler of Waulsort testifies.]

Usage itself has preserved this arrangement down to our time without interruption, and no one has been found who called the abbot “abbot of Hastière,” since Hastière is a cell and provostship of the Church of Waulsort. Reason likewise does not permit our prelacy to be styled by as many titles as there happen to be villages subject to us. It would be inappropriate, indeed, if someone called you not bishop of Metz from your city and see, but rather bishop of Gorze or of Vic from some monastery, town, or village.

Nor do the canons receive, nor do the laws permit, that a man despoiled of his property should be summoned to judgment, since there is no privilege by which one already stripped bare can be stripped further. We say this because the same abbot has been ordered to come before you at your next synod, again to answer the monks of Hastière concerning a dispute already settled.

Moreover, since in this same year you summoned both the abbot and the monks to court upon the monks’ accusation, carefully examined the entire controversy on both sides, and by the judgment and counsel of your Church absolved the abbot from the monks’ accusation—an especially false one—it is not credible that you should wish, contrary to the principles of canon law, to reopen a suit that has been decided. The civil laws also say that judgments already rendered must stand.

And since you hold the summit of apostolic dignity both in order and profession, you are not, according to the Apostle, given to fickleness, so that with you there should be “yes and no”: that is, that you should again call before your tribunal for judgment a case thoroughly heard and prejudged by you, and entrusted to us for settlement.

For the aforesaid monks complain that the goods of the Church of Hastière are being alienated unlawfully through the abbot’s negligence. To speak before a gracious judge, they have said almost the truth: for they are said, without the abbot’s knowledge, to have spent from the treasures of that Church, both on their journey to you and on their return to the lord bishop of Liège, a chalice of six marks and a silver cross, besides many other things by which, through their disorderliness and superfluous lawsuits, they have impoverished the Church. Nor will they cease unless their high-handedness is restrained by the yoke of firmer discipline.

Therefore, falling at the knees of your holiness, we earnestly beseech you: have pity on an abbot now failing amid these disputes; spare an old man, spare a poor man, who can scarcely endure the burden amid the tyranny of advocates and the want of every necessity. We have sent to your discretion one who is our brother by blood, obedience, and charity, whom you will honor and hear in all things as though he were ourselves.

## LETTER CCLXXVI. DECREE OF EMPEROR CONRAD II FOR THE MONASTERY OF WAULSORT

At the intervention of Abbot Wibald, he confirms the privileges of the monastery of Waulsort. (1151.)

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. CONRAD, by the favor of divine clemency, second king of the Romans. It belongs to munificence to repay rewards to those who have deserved well of the commonwealth, and to set them before others rising to the service of the Empire as an example or a token of good hope.

[Note: This decree of Emperor Conrad survives in the archives of the monastery of Waulsort. The most reverend abbot of that monastery had granted us a copy before we came to Stavelot.]

Therefore let the diligence of our faithful subjects, both present and future, know that, at the intervention of our beloved and faithful Abbot Wibald—who now, under God, presides over the monasteries of Stavelot and Corvey—we ordered the privileges of the monastery of Waulsort, in which the aforesaid abbot received the sacred habit of religion and made his profession according to the Rule of blessed Benedict and the institutions of the holy Fathers, to be read and explained. These contained in writing that a certain illustrious man, Count Elbert, built a monastery according to the rule and order of monks on land belonging to his own inheritance in the district of Lomme, and transferred and conveyed it from his own right and property into royal right and lordship.

Emperor Otto I, to whom it had been given by the aforesaid count, certainly his kinsman, granted that monastery with all its appurtenances to the Church of Metz through the hand of Theoderic, venerable bishop of Metz, subject to the following arrangement: that this bishop should attach, by way of assistance, to the aforesaid abbey a certain place called Hastière, formerly granted from the right of his own inheritance by his most holy predecessor Bishop Adelbero to St Stephen the proto-martyr in the Church of Metz; and that, because they are joined by close proximity, the aforesaid places—Waulsort and Hastière—should be bound together by an indissoluble bond under the lordship and administration of one abbot.

This settlement, confirmed both by a charter of venerable sanction from the aforesaid Augustus of blessed memory and by apostolic decrees of the most holy Pope Benedict, has remained unshaken and inviolate down to our times, although the monks of the other place—that is, Hastière—have always endeavored to oppose the prerogative of the abbey of Waulsort and to resist the ordinances of its abbots with rash presumption. Their insolence dared to grow to such foolish lengths that they attempted to sever themselves from the connection and subjection of the abbey of Waulsort and of Theoderic, venerable abbot of that place, until they were checked by the judgment of our court, supported by laws and reason, and recalled to unity and obedience.

Therefore, by authority to endure forever, we decree that the place of Hastière, entrusted and joined to the monastery of Waulsort, shall always be subject to that abbey, just as a cell, provostship, or whatever else it may be called of an inferior should belong to its superior. Upon the death of Theoderic, the abbot who now, by God’s grant, regularly presides there, and of his successors to be regularly appointed forever, the monks of Hastière shall come to Waulsort both to celebrate devoutly the obsequies of the deceased abbot and to conduct in disciplined concord the election of the future shepherd; on this condition, namely, that the first assent, first voice, and first nomination shall rest with the judgment of the monks of Waulsort, and that a person from their community, if a suitable one is found, shall be elected without objection from the monks of Hastière. But if one cannot perhaps be found there, and a suitable person is found in the Church of Hastière, then a superior shall be chosen from them rather than from another monastery.

And so that this settlement may remain ratified and unshaken throughout all future ages, we have ordered this present decree to be written and, our seal-image having been impressed, have ordered the witnesses who took part in the act and judgment to be named below:

Arnold, elected of the Church of Cologne, chancellor of our court; Henry, bishop of Liège; Otto, our brother, bishop of Freising; Warner, bishop of Münster; Philip, bishop of Osnabrück; Albert, bishop of Meissen; Hermann, elected of Utrecht; Wibald, abbot of Stavelot and Corvey; Lambert, abbot of Werden; Count Adolf of Monts; Count Henry of Guelders; Godfrey and Hermann, brothers of Cuijk; Marquard of Grünbach; Albert of Grüningen.

The sign of the most invincible lord Conrad II, king of the Romans.

Done in the palace of Nijmegen, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1151, in the thirteenth indiction, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of June [17 May], in the fourteenth year of the reign in Christ of the lord Conrad, second king of the Romans. Amen.

I, Arnold, chancellor in place of Henry, archbishop and archchancellor of Mainz, have authenticated this.

## LETTER CCLXXVII. EMPEROR CONRAD TO H., BISHOP OF LIÈGE

He promises vengeance upon the enemies of the Church of Liège and orders him also to refrain from troubling the Church of Stavelot. (1151.)

CONRAD, by the grace of God king of the Romans, to H., venerable bishop of Liège: his favor and every good.

[Note: Henry of Limburg, of whom Alberic writes under the year 1164 that, after the death of Victor the antipope, he refused the papacy offered him by the emperor and consecrated Paschal, Victor’s successor.]

The cry of the Church of Stavelot has reached us, grieving and complaining that your Church is wickedly harassed by certain tyrants and that your person is troubled by new and unheard-of methods at the hands of men who had sworn you fealty. Yet we trust in the protection of God, who keeps us safe and sound and grants us victory over our enemies, that, by the counsel and judgment of the princes, we shall shortly punish this affront with due severity.

Furthermore, it has been reported to us that, because of your hatred for Henry of La Roche, advocate of the Church of Stavelot, both you and your men have planned to commit arson and robbery upon the goods of that Church. Those goods are so free from the advocate’s service that he receives from them no share, either of lawful rents or of legal compositions. Since to injure that Church is contrary not only to royal majesty but also to the holiness of your order and to every equity of divine and human law, we command your diligence and, under the protection of our favor, order you to restrain yourself and your men from injury and oppression of the aforesaid Church. Know that, if anything otherwise be presumed, it shall not escape the just vengeance of our indignation.

## LETTER CCLXXVIII. EMPEROR CONRAD TO ABBOT WIBALD

He excuses him from the Roman embassy. (1151.)

CONRAD, by the grace of God king of the Romans, to WIBALD, abbot of Corvey: his favor and every good.

We have learned by experience and are certain that you tirelessly support the advancement of our honor and interests with the utmost constancy of fidelity. Therefore, had the exigency of affairs required it, you would have undertaken, as we expected, the office of our embassy to the lord pope. But because we have learned that you are impeded by great difficulties of affairs, while giving thanks for your good will and not doubting that your sincere service will be most ready for our other concerns, we have entrusted the labor of our embassy to the lord pope to other princes, namely the bishop of Basel and the bishop of Constance.

## LETTER CCLXXIX. HENRY, BISHOP OF LIÈGE, TO ABBOT WIBALD

He complains of Count Henry of La Roche and of the count of Namur. (1151.)

HENRY, by the grace of God humble minister of the Church of Liège, to Lord WIBALD, by the same grace venerable abbot of Stavelot: greeting and brotherly love in Christ.

Because great necessities have unexpectedly arisen, we can by no means attend to lesser matters. Your prudence is not unaware that the fomenters of this evil, hitherto shielded by a show of envious flattery, have trampled underfoot the reverence due royal majesty and broken through every avenue of pretence.

For Henry, count of La Roche, has shamelessly violated by arson and robbery against us and our Church the truces which, through the hand of the count of Namur and his other men, he had firmly established in stable peace in the hands of our princes—though we made no objection. He thinks that to the excommunicated it has been said: “Let him who is filthy be filthy still.”

The count of Namur, prompted, we know not by what rumor of royal weakness, rages against us and our churches through the venomous plotting of other princes. After first sending messengers of affection and loyalty, he immediately thereafter, in the same hour, sent a messenger bearing a renunciation of our lordship; while this very embassy was still in progress, he utterly burned our demesne village of Ciney.

Since I am accustomed to speak with you of my secrets as with myself, I lay this cause of disturbance in the bosom of your counsel and consolation, so that you and I, who are faithful members of the same household at the same court, may be found, when need arises, partners one for the other in truth and fidelity. May your belovedness fare well. The bearer of this letter will explain the rest.

## LETTER CCLXXX. ABBOT WIBALD TO POPE EUGENIUS III

He writes that he had been ready to undertake the Roman embassy and commends the bearer of this letter. (1151.)

To his reverend father and lord in Christ, EUGENIUS, one and universal pope, Brother WIBALD, by the grace of God and of Your Holiness what he is in the Catholic Church: filial love and due submission in all things.

The prudence of your Highness, dearest Father, is not unaware that, since the glorious and illustrious Conrad, king of the Romans and son of your holiness, returned from the Jerusalem expedition, he had planned to send effective and industrious ambassadors from his side to the excellence of your greatness. Since even the person of our lowliness had been named and called for the vigorous execution of this task, matters had advanced so far that we had already gone out of Lorraine, ready and equipped to set forth.

If the weakness of our little talent had been able in any way to perceive that the labor of this embassy would in any degree serve the Catholic Church, your dignity, or the advancement of the Roman Empire, we would in no wise have spared our affairs or our person.

The bearer of this letter is known to belong to the Church of Stavelot by hereditary right. When he brought us a complaint that a certain Godfrey, dean of the church of Blessed Mary in the town of Maastricht, was violently taking from him a house which belongs to him by paternal and ancestral hereditary right, we wrote on his behalf to the son of your holiness, Henry, venerable bishop of Liège, asking him to restrain his dean by due authority from so great and unusual a violence. But when that cleric refused to desist from his unjust design, saying that the man acting against him was excommunicated, the same layman was compelled to appeal to your protection and come into your presence.

Therefore, most merciful Father, deign in your customary clemency to hear him, lest he grieve that he has undertaken so many labors and dangers uselessly and in vain, and that other oppressed persons may learn from this example to hope in your mercy.

## LETTER CCLXXXI. ABBOT WIBALD TO EMPEROR CONRAD

He complains of the bishop of Liège and the counts of Namur, La Roche, and Montaigu. (1151.)

To his illustrious conqueror and magnificent lord, CONRAD, emperor august of the Romans by the grace of God, Brother WIBALD, by the same grace what he is in the Catholic Church: salvation in Him who gives salvation to kings.

The humility of our lowliness wrote formerly to your Majesty that we had armed ourselves for carrying out your embassy to Rome, not without serious loss to our own affairs, and that, if the lord chancellor could have set out, we would have labored according to our ability for the increase of your honor and kingdom. Returning from this, we found our land shaken by excessive robberies and arsons.

For the lord bishop of Liège, the count of Namur, the count of La Roche, and Count G. of Montaigu, being at odds, had driven the good of peace from our borders. Although neither our people nor we injured anyone, and we inclined toward neither side, after the lord bishop had already pronounced a sentence of anathema against the count of Namur and his supporters, Count G. of Montaigu, with his own troops and those of the lord bishop, ravaged and burned our village of Okeriis, which for nearly three months supplied the monastery with necessities.

He also intends to ravage and burn the other possessions belonging to the same monastery unless he is diverted from this design by very heavy ransoms and exactions. Since our possessions are violently laid waste and plundered, and this is done with the assistance of the lord bishop—without whom Count G. himself would not dare to undertake it—it becomes your royal Majesty to defend us, who are yours, and to extend the hand of mercy to the innocently afflicted.

Accordingly, we humbly beseech the greatness of your dignity, which we have always found gracious: if the lord bishop should come into the presence of your Majesty, confront him, as is your duty, concerning the unjust oppression of us by his people and of our people; and, having received his pledge, cause what still remains of ours, though not untouched by his men, and which the same G. hastens to destroy with his help, to be preserved as it stands. But if he does not come, let your gentleness command him more sternly by writing on this matter; and order him, by your letters and by his own authority, to restrain that Count G. from ravaging our possessions.

For the men of Corvey have added to our danger by recalling us. What troubles and ambushes we endure among them, what was plotted against us during the time when we were equipped in the service of the kingdom and of yourself, and what was done, we shall report more fully to your Majesty when we come to you. We have resolved, if we can by any means withdraw ourselves from these cares and labors, to come to you at the Purification of Saint Mary [2 February], wherever we learn that you are.

## LETTER CCLXXXII. R. OF STAVELOT TO ABBOT WIBALD

Concerning proceedings at Liège against the incendiaries of the estates of Stavelot. (1151.)

To his lord and father WIBALD, venerable abbot of Stavelot, Brother R.: the most devoted offering of obedience, submission, and prayers.

On the Saturday after your departure we set out for Liège and arrived on Sunday. There we found the abbot of Floreffe making complaint concerning the violent plunder of his goods.

[Note: Floreffe is a notable and wealthy abbey of the Premonstratensian order, founded by Godfrey, count of Namur, two leagues distant from Namur; there the founder himself received the habit and profession of the conversi.]

The archdeacons and abbots answered him on that same day, and us on the next, that the bishop would come on the following Saturday; that we ought to return that day in order to make our complaint publicly; and that they would assist us in every respect in obtaining our justice.

We went and returned; and on the appointed day, before a great assembly of archdeacons, abbots, and clergy, we presented your letters to the lord bishop. When Brother Henry had publicly read them out distinctly, the bishop replied that he doubted whether you could excommunicate free men who were his parishioners, but that he would act in all things according to the judgment and counsel of the archdeacons.

Both our case and that of Floreffe were postponed until the next day. When, in the presence of a more numerous assembly, the bishop was questioned, he said that our case rested upon the answers of the archdeacons; nevertheless, the archdeacons declared that they would not overthrow, either by their counsel or judgment, the privileges and rights of our Church.

Then the bishop said: “When I have seen your abbot and his privileges and charters, I shall, with the counsel of my men, do what is just.” But we, forewarned by this answer, met his evasions as follows: “In the time of your predecessor, Lord Albero, who was unwilling to hold valid the excommunication of our Church, the archdeacons who are still alive and present judged valid the excommunication pronounced by us against Walter of Warnant and Baldwin of Hozémont. Let your prudence consider whether it can oppose the judgment and testimony of the archdeacons and senior members of your Church.

“Nevertheless, since the lord abbot is absent, in whose custody and power are the privileges of our Church—he will produce them for reading when necessity requires, at a time, place, and before a person suitable to the occasion—we shall leave aside this point concerning our Church and, by the authority of Pope Eugenius, confirm his sentence against incendiaries, requesting that it be observed with regard to our men as it is with regard to yours.”

Having produced the written sheet and read the chapter concerning incendiaries, we urged him, by the authority of the lord pope, to hold valid and observe the pope’s sentence concerning our incendiaries.

[Note: The decree of Pope Eugenius against incendiaries survives from the Council of Rheims held in 1148, chapter 15.]

At last, moved either by our insistence or lest he incur the lord pope’s displeasure, he said that he did not wish to oppose the privileges and that he willingly wished to obey the commands of the lord pope. He immediately ordered the archdeacons, by the authority of the lord pope, to observe the excommunication pronounced against our incendiaries.

When they demanded their names from his own hand, and he himself was unwilling to give them, the day dragged into night. At length he received the schedule of names himself, though he would never observe the sentence against our incendiaries unless compelled. Thus we left him still little certain what he had done in this matter.

It was reported and established that the lord bishop had sent his messengers to Rome and intended to go to the present court of the lord king at Worms, having given a thousand marks to induce the lord king to bring ruin and devastation upon the count of Namur. The count, however, earnestly asked us through the abbot of Floreffe that you should support his cause before the lord king and bring it, if possible, to a good conclusion.

The bishop and the count are by no means willing to desist from war, but intend again after Christmas to ravage everything. Count Godfrey, it is said, is entering our territory at Harzé, intending to ravage at Condroz and in the Ardennes unless he ceases after receiving a ransom. Count Henry has not yet recovered. The count of Looz will ravage our territory of Tournines and holds the brothers Boso and Goswin captive. Bishop Wellin says that after Christmas he will lay waste by fire; we warned him by the authority of the lord pope not to do so, since we were going to approach him. You too should endeavor to forbid this, by the authority both of the lord pope and of the lord king.

The condition of your affairs, both within and without, is the same as it was at your departure. Therefore, if you intend to command or arrange anything, write us your pleasure. For we need the foresight of your counsel and direction. Farewell in the Lord; again I say, farewell and rejoice.

## LETTER CCLXXXIII. ABBOT WIBALD TO THE BISHOP OF MINDEN

Concerning the case of Master Godebold and the priest Everard. (1151.)

To his reverend father and lord in Christ, H., venerable bishop of the holy Church of Minden, WIBALD, by the grace of God abbot of the Church of Corvey: humble prayers and devoted service.

We received on the seventeenth day before the Kalends of October [15 September], at a certain estate of the Church of Stavelot, your letters written to us concerning the case of Master Godebold and the priest Everard of Hemeringen. But because we were then far from your regions, and because afterward, as time advanced, several matters befell us, both public affairs of the kingdom and private occupations, we could not meet the aforesaid priest Everard in accordance with your request.

When we returned to these parts, we summoned him when he came to us and tried to persuade him to comply with your request and gladly accept whatever should be offered him by your gentleness for the good of peace and concord. He, however, complains that he has again suffered fresh plundering from the same men who had previously inflicted injuries upon him and taken away his property; and that, since the time he brought us the mandate of the lord pope, they have taken from his pigs what is worth fifteen shillings and, moreover, have appropriated for themselves all the produce which he ought to have had from his pannage this year, which he reckoned at a large sum.

When, therefore, we set before him many considerations on both sides and urged him, for the ending of a discord of so long duration, to accept what had been offered, he finally yielded to our admonition through the intervention of better counsel. He promised that he would accept the three talents which you offer him for Godebold’s peace and goodwill, provided that, concerning the other persons from whom he complains that his goods have been alienated, you render him ecclesiastical justice as you promised.

Whether, therefore, this controversy between him and Master Godebold is settled on these terms or in any other way, and whether justice is rendered him for his goods that have been taken away, we earnestly admonish and ask your discretion to bring all this to completion within fifteen days; for we do not presume to keep longer in silence the sentence of the lord pope which he ordered us to announce, if this is not accomplished.

The same priest Everard further complains that the cleric of Jacheim, wherever he can, whether personally or through agents, takes away his goods and has as his household retainers the same laymen who do not cease to despoil him of his property—to his injury. Let your discretion consider how absurd this is and how unsuitable to his order.

## LETTER CCLXXXIV. THE PROVOST, DEAN, AND CANONS OF MINDEN TO ABBOT WIBALD

They entrust to him for settlement the peace unsuccessfully attempted between Godebold and Everard. (1151.)

To their lord, WIBALD, reverend abbot of the holy Church of Corvey, W., by the mercy of God provost of Minden, R., dean, together with all their brethren: continual prayers in Christ and the faithful service of submission.

Our lord bishop received and heard at a certain castle of the Church called Wilippa the letters of your holiness which you wrote concerning the case of Master Godebold and Brother Everard, and afterward forwarded them to us. We received them with due reverence and sought in many ways to persuade Brother Everard to lay aside every complaint and contention, to be a good man in the future, and, by the service of submission and the entrance into peace, to appease the innocent and excellent Master Godebold, whom he had harassed with many injuries. But that brother showed himself intractable to our counsels, and therefore we could find no opening for a settlement with him.

Accordingly, through our faithful brethren, who are most devoted to your holiness, we refer to the ears of your piety the whole handling and counsel of this matter, to be settled by your discretion and direction together with our brethren. We do this both so that they may show you our brother’s innocence and so that we may have you as a witness concerning the matters established and confirmed in your presence; and so that, if the aforesaid Brother Everard should presume to disturb our peace and violate the settlement of peace, you may be our helper, because, as a son of truth and a protector of many, you will free us from an attack of this kind.

## LETTER CCLXXXV. ABBOT WIBALD TO GODEBOLD

He communicates to him the terms of the peace made with the priest Everard. (1151.)

Brother WIBALD, by the grace of God what he is in the Catholic Church, to his beloved brother and friend Godebold: blessing and life for ever and ever.

Your belovedness remembers that we received letters from the lord pope, directing us earnestly to admonish you to restore completely to the priest Everard, within twenty days after you had been admonished by us, the church of Hemeringen and everything taken from him by you and others, and thereafter to allow him to possess it peaceably. We therefore did what had been commanded us; and we rejoice that both the lord pope’s command and our admonition prevailed so far that, by the counsel of religious and wise men, you returned to concord with the aforesaid Everard. The terms of the concord and reconciliation, to remain effective in future, are these. On your behalf we gave the same Everard three talents of denarii, on condition that he should release and discharge you from every complaint of his, both concerning injuries and concerning losses previously inflicted upon him, while he himself should henceforth hold his aforesaid church in peace. Accordingly, under suitable testimony of monks, clerics, and laymen, he placed in our hand every complaint which he had held against you up to the present day; he returned with you to favour and true peace; of his own accord he released us from execution of the lord pope’s mandate; he gave thanks to the lord pope for the justice he had obtained; and he devoutly bestowed his blessing on us for the diligence of our concern. Therefore, both by this letter and by other means as occasion requires, we bear witness to your brotherhood that, in devout obedience to the commands of the lord pope and to our admonition, you have avoided religiously and prudently the sentence which had been threatened against you in punishment of disobedience. But concerning those who plundered the property of the aforesaid Everard, he will seek justice from the lord bishop, as the lord pope has enjoined upon that same our lord bishop; and the bishop has promised us in his letters that he will do so faithfully. You, however, must henceforth remember no offence against the same Everard, but in good faith maintain with him true peace and concord concerning every past dispute.

## LETTER CCLXXXVI. Wibald, Abbot, to Henry, Bishop of Minden

After peace had been made between Godebald and Everard, he directs him to render justice to the same Everard concerning what others had taken away. (1151.)

[Col. 1359D]

To his reverend Father and lord H., venerable bishop of the holy Church of Minden, Brother Wibald, by God’s grace servant of the Church of Corvey: humble prayers and devoted service.

Your fatherhood remembers that we received letters from the lord pope directing us earnestly to admonish your canon, Master Godebald, to restore completely to the priest Ever[ard], within twenty days after receipt of our admonition, the church of Hemeringen and everything taken from him by himself and by others, and thereafter to allow him to possess it peaceably. We therefore did what had been commanded us. But your exaltedness graciously and carefully instructed our lowliness to labour to be mediators of reconciliation and concord, namely on the condition that the same Ever[ard] should receive three talents of money, while you should administer ecclesiastical justice to him against the other persons from whom he complains that his goods have been alienated. Although the same Ever[ard] hesitated considerably to accept that condition, nevertheless, through our efforts being more devoutly directed toward peace for the Church of Minden, it was accomplished as you had wished. For, after receiving three talents of money from our hand, he voluntarily withdrew every complaint and action which he had hitherto had against Master Godebald, and without pretence or deceit returned with him to true peace and favour. We therefore ask your highness, whom we love exceedingly in true charity in the Lord, to provide canonical justice, without the obstacle of further delay, to the aforesaid priest Everard—who has long wearied the ears of apostolic clemency with repeated cries—against those who violently seized his goods. Do so both out of reverence for the lord pope, who imposed this upon your discretion both orally and by letter, and at the intervention of our petition: for in true and humble faith we urge this upon you, and, as a debt, claim it from the promise you made in your letters.

## LETTER CCLXXXVII. Wibald, Abbot, to H., Archbishop of Mainz

Concerning the dissolution of the marriage of Folcuin of Sualemberg, because of his wife’s concealed illness. (1151.)

[Col. 1360C]

To his reverend Father and lord H., venerable archbishop of the holy Church of Mainz, Wibald, by God’s grace servant of the Church of Corvey: humble prayers and devoted service.

We have learned from the report of Lord Folcuin of Sualemberg that, in accordance with the dignity of your priestly office, you strictly uphold justice toward him and his wife, and, setting aside the affection of flesh and blood, follow the spirit which is the author and promoter of freedom. We too greatly rejoice with your glory in the Lord, since in this matter we love nothing but truth; and if we offend anyone, we offend them for truth’s sake. The aforesaid Folcuin indeed testifies that, before he betrothed this same wife, he had learned for certain from some persons that she suffered from the falling sickness [epilepsy]; and he asserts that he can prove by the testimony of many religious men that he would not have wished to be joined to her had she truly been afflicted by such an illness, and that he openly informed the girl’s parents of this. Your learning knows, moreover, that although fraud and deceit must be absent from every contract, especially in contracting a marriage, where faith and sacrament are involved, no admixture of deceit ought to be introduced. If this is so, he can be bound by no rule to follow that which he neither intended when he acted nor willed when he became aware of it. We speak of the law to one who knows it, not to one ignorant of the danger into which this layman and young man has now fallen for a long time. If you come into our region, we are prepared to come before your highness concerning this same cause.

## LETTER CCLXXXVI. Wibald, Abbot, to Henry, Bishop of Minden

He writes on behalf of the canon Regenbern, whom the abbess of St Mary on the Mount was harassing. (1151.)

To his reverend Father and lord H., venerable bishop of the holy Church of Minden, and to his beloved brothers and lords, the canons of that same church: Brother Wibald, by God’s grace servant of the Church of Corvey, humble prayers and devoted service.

[Col. 1361B] Brother Regenbern, a canon of the church of Blessed Mary on the Mount, came to us and related in order how, on the occasion of a certain matter, the abbess of the said church had, as it seems to us, oppressed him improperly and forbidden him his prebend. Therefore, because in your Church we have begun to be lovers of peace and co-workers for concord, we earnestly ask your fatherhood, through the brotherly charity in which we have great confidence among you, and, as far as we may, exhort you in the Lord, not to allow any dissension to arise and grow in your Church. For it often happens that the greatest conflagrations arise from the smallest sparks. Indeed, it has sufficiently been suggested to your learning in a few words that certain secular rights cannot be confused or mingled with ecclesiastical rights. We say this because the aforesaid cleric could neither obtain his canonry through homage nor lose it by refusing homage.

## LETTER CCLXXXIX. Wibald, Abbot, to W., Major Provost of the Church of Minden

He writes on behalf of the canon Regenbern. (1151.)

Brother Wibald, by God’s grace what he is in the Catholic Church, to his beloved brother and friend W., venerable major provost of the holy Church of Minden: blessing and life for ever.

[Col. 1361D] We earnestly ask your belovedness, in whom we have great confidence, that, just as in your recent letter you took care to advise and exhort us to labour for the peace and concord of the Church of Minden in the case of Master Godebald, so now you may graciously endeavour, in Regenbern’s case, that nothing contrary to right and equity be done against him or his property. For ecclesiastical possessions are by no means to be assessed according to secular law; and just as a cleric’s canonry is not regularly acquired by lay law, so it is lost only through canonical procedure. Enough has been said to the wise: from small fomentations of hatred, the greatest enmities and endless troubles sometimes grow.

## LETTER CCXC. H., Duke of Saxony and Bavaria, to Abbot Wibald

He asks him to be present with him before the king at the court at Regensburg. (1151.)

[Col. 1362A]

To Lord Wibald, venerable abbot of the Church of Corvey: H., by God’s grace duke of Bavaria and Saxony—may you ascend the mountain of the Lord and stand in His holy place.

Because we have known many proofs of your excellence, we have great confidence in your goodwill. With this great confidence before us, therefore, because the Lord has bestowed upon you, beyond many others, both boldness to speak the truth and the knowledge to express it with discernment, we earnestly approach your goodwill, beseeching you to stand by us at the court which the king has appointed to be held at Regensburg on the second Ides of June [12 June], and to hear what judgment he gives against us. For he has promised that he will answer us according to justice or the counsel of the princes who assemble at court. Farewell, and be assured of the affection of our most wholehearted love. We commend Lord Theoderic of Rikelingen and his sons to your affection, and earnestly ask that you show them kindness.

## LETTER CCXCI. Wibald, Abbot, to Pope Eugenius III

He writes on behalf of the canon Regenbern. (1151.)

[Col. 1362C]

To his most reverend Father and lord Eugenius, sole and universal pope of the holy Catholic Church, Brother Wibald, by the grace of God and of yourself what he is in the Catholic Church: the love of a son and the service of a servant.

The bearer of this letter has been deprived by violence, as he complains, of his canonry in a certain church of the diocese of Minden. Before his appeal, we attempted to give him the assistance of reconciliation; but as he made no progress in this, he finally appealed to the presence of your highness and summoned his adversaries thither, for a fixed day, by your authority. Therefore, prostrating ourselves in devoted spirit at the feet of your exaltedness, we humbly implore your clemency, so far as is granted to our lowliness, to deign mercifully to hear his case and to extend the hand of most gracious protection to relieve his oppressions. May almighty God long preserve your fatherhood.

## LETTER CCXCII. Wibald, Abbot, to A., Provost of Cologne, etc.

He gives thanks for benefits bestowed. (1151.)

To his dearest lord and friend A., venerable major provost of the holy Church of Cologne and chancellor of the royal court, Brother Wibald, by God’s grace what he is in the Catholic Church: greeting and blessing.

Send us by this our servant the white silk cloth which you intended to send: when we asked, you did not give it; when we did not ask, you offered it. The estate of the Church of Stavelot has experienced your generosity and zeal; our pantry has experienced it, our table has experienced it, our purse has experienced it, our stable has experienced it. But that our poor and modest chapel might experience your bounty, munificence, and generosity, neither Gaul nor Germany nor all Greece nor the East could have helped. Yet we are grateful and mindful; wholly removed, in deed and spirit, from every kind of ingratitude, we acknowledge that we have received very much and returned either nothing or little. If anything has been newly decided in the counsel of our lord after our departure, do not consider it burdensome to inform us.

## LETTER CCXCIII. Wibald, Abbot, to His Monks of Stavelot

Uncertain whether he ought to govern two abbeys so far apart, he asks their advice about what he ought to do amid so great a danger. (1151.)

[Col. 1363B]

Brother Wibald, by God’s grace what he is in the Catholic Church, to Robert the dean and the other brothers of the Church of Stavelot: may you abound in the spirit of counsel and fortitude.

We are compelled to deliberate upon, and put into effect, what your brotherhood remembers that we have often discussed in your assembly: namely, that we are by no means equal to presiding over two monasteries so far distant from one another, of such extensive possessions and households, although we are graciously allowed this by the masters of the Churches and by our most serene lord king. For how great has been the increase of wickedness in these times—when we are aided neither by ecclesiastical nor secular justice—your grievous oppression, which by daily plunderings and raids wastes and afflicts your monastery, has taught your experience through cruel proofs. Yet, just as we did not turn aside to the government of the monastery of Corvey through headlong ambition, but after a divine calling through the title of canonical election, and in all things made use of your authority, counsel, and direction, so now, carefully weighing the difficulties and dangers of circumstances and utterly succumbing under so great a burden, we have recourse to the customary oracle of your counsel. We in no way doubt that whatever, in a matter so uncertain and so far beyond the capacity of our own choice, may be enjoined upon us by the unanimity of your brotherhood has been procured by divine mercy and providence. Far be it, however, from the piety of your hearts to believe that we have suddenly fallen into these thoughts through anger impelling us, emotion forcing us, or the desire to escape some labour persuading us. We dread the judgments of God in these matters with great contrition of mind, and we somewhat fear human judgments and outcries. Even if delight in the rank of a double dignity should tempt us, nevertheless let it be plain to all who judge rightly that, in administering affairs so remote and so great, we daily suffer irreparable losses both of discipline and of possessions. Our departure from you, which seemed to some disturbed and sudden, had long been foreseen and was necessary because of certain clamours from the monastery of Corvey which harassed us. For our soul was greatly troubled over your affairs—not because of agitation over any word, but because of the continual devastation of the whole land by killings, burnings, and plunder. Our departure had to be secret because of the complaints and importunate detentions of an afflicted people, and because of the ambushes of many great robbers occupying almost every road. Farewell; and in this cause of your mother may the grace of the Holy Spirit be with you.

## LETTER CCXCIV. Wibald, Abbot, to H., a Monk of Stavelot

He sets out the reasons which deterred him from retaining the abbacy of Stavelot. (1151.)

[Col. 1364B]

Brother Wibald, called abbot, to his beloved son H.: blessing.

You will be able to learn more certainly from the common letter about the state—indeed, the wavering—of our mind. Nevertheless, though you cannot be ignorant of what deters us from governing the monastery of Stavelot, we shall briefly note it for your vigilance. First, there is the great ruin of our order, which, amid so manifold a lack of necessary resources, we do not trust ourselves able to repair. Further, among you there is such scarcity of resources and such a daily failure of prebends that, even if the whole kingdom enjoyed the firmest peace, the Church of Stavelot could scarcely sustain itself. Your advocates, through sins, are not defenders of the poor but most cruel despoilers and most hostile plotters against your liberty. Your ministeriales, who ought above all to support the Church, have become a crooked bow; they neither obey commands nor help to carry on agriculture where they themselves are stewards, but—what is worse—obstruct and lay it waste. Almost no possession of your Church is free from these losses; and those great estate-centres are empty and neglected, from which the chief supplements for the prebends were customarily drawn. Amid these daily scourges, moreover, we receive no help either from ecclesiastical or secular power. It is therefore no wonder if all these things, carefully considered, cause our soul to waste away like a spider, and make us think more anxiously about salvation and those entrusted to us. You know better, since you were present while we were absent, how our appointment in the Church of Corvey was confirmed by Pope Eugenius in the city of Meaux.

## LETTER CCXCV. The Monks of Stavelot to Abbot Wibald

They dissuade him from resigning the abbacy of Stavelot. (1151.)

To their lord and Father, the venerable abbot of Stavelot Wibald, Brother R. with all the monks of Stavelot: act manfully and be strengthened in the Lord.

[Col. 1365A] Having received, most loving Father, the letters of your sincerity, which disclosed the purpose of a mind not agitated but guarding against the future, not wavering but considering times, customs, and the weight of affairs, and thereby showed the paths of your deliberation, sorrow upon sorrow was laid upon us. For we are so placed that, when one “woe” has not passed among us, another and another comes upon us; one of Job’s messengers speaks, and another comes without delay; God has set a cloud before Himself so that prayer cannot pass through. Then we grieved most deeply when we understood that we, who in our oppressions have often been accustomed to be relieved by your consolations, must now at last, while placed in need, be deprived for whatever reason of the sweetness of your fatherhood. Yet no writ of divorce was ever given to Leah or Rachel; a good shepherd never abandoned the shepherd’s office when he saw the wolf; indeed, the blood of one who perishes is required from the hand of a negligent watchman. A father’s affection ought not to disown his own children. Moreover, if the retention of the abbacy of Corvey is at issue, the first calling and the first bride ought rather to be regarded and retained. For your prudence also remembers that, when you were summoned to the Church of Corvey’s government by letters and petition of the lord king and princes, as well as by that Church itself, you were lent to us rather than given away, so that no one might understand this as an emancipation from, or renunciation of, the Church of Stavelot. Since at that time we sufficiently made this known to everyone, both orally and in writing, you, having recognized the sincerity of our assembly and chapter in this matter and having justly weighed the truth of the case, must never tear the Church of Stavelot—your mother, your nurse, your bride—from your heart; never abandon the care of your brothers and sons, who are not merely sons by adoption but by the womb. It is not right that we, who expected to be assisted from the riches of the Church of Corvey in accordance with the promise, should now, on that Church’s account, be deprived of your fatherhood’s care. Therefore, casting aside every tribulation of heart, return as quickly as possible to those who love you, and be personally present with the helping hand of your counsel for us, who are in great need and await you with God’s help.

## LETTER CCXCVI. Henry, Monk of Stavelot, to Abbot Wibald

On the same matter. (1151.)

[Col. 1365D]

To his most reverend Father and lord Wibald, venerable abbot of the Church of Stavelot, Henry: whatever a devoted son owes to his dearest Father.

Having carefully read your graciousness’s letter, most dear Father, the slowness of my little intellect could find in it nothing that might worthily deter your prudence and kindness from us or disturb the disposition of your mind from governing the Church of Stavelot. For whenever your diligence directs its attention to the growth of the order and the restoration of the prebend, that charity will provide these things for you which, in repairing the ruins of our Church, has always supplied every resource for your goodwill without grave peril. The negligence of our ministeriales and the insolence of the advocates—which your occasional absence from us has sufficiently fostered—will be greatly checked by our daily outcry and by the more prolonged constancy of your presence: for “the drop hollows out the stone, not by force but by falling often.” What was done at Meaux concerning the appointment of the Church of Corvey in my presence, I do not know; for, “if I am wise, I do not know what I know.” Those things which, under the appearance of piety, return to poverty are usually more lightly endured than those which, under the name of prosperity, aim to exchange slender means for the highest riches. But, most loving Father, to answer briefly what you wrote to the brothers collectively: in no way do we wish, or can we bear, to lack the governance of your fatherhood or the direction of your rule. We have agreed and firmly hold that we would rather lack even that small treasure which is among us than lose the governance of your person under the title of another Church. Therefore, Father, with the special confidence with which you have always been accustomed to call me your son, I earnestly beg your kindness not to intend any longer to trouble us over this matter, lest you soon behold with bodily eyes—the thought is horrifying—the ruin and desolation of the place which you built.

## LETTER CCXCVII. Wibald, Abbot, to His Monks of Stavelot

He writes that they were too hasty in giving advice; the monks of Malmedy and other neighbours should also have been consulted, and prayers to God should above all have been employed. (1151.)

[Col. 1366C]

To his reverend brothers and lords in Christ, Robert the venerable dean and the other sons of the Church of Stavelot, Brother Wibald, by God’s grace what he is in the Catholic Church: may the Angel of Great Counsel be with you.

We recognized in the letter which your unanimity recently sent us that incorruptible and unconquerable affection toward us with which you have persevered from the beginning in embracing and cherishing us, so that we may truly call you friends, who have remained with me in my temptations. Yet, dearest brothers, we grieve that you were too hasty in a matter so difficult, so arduous, so necessary, concerning which we sought the counsel of your whole community as though it were a divine response. Neither prayers were first offered, nor the brethren of Malmedy called, nor the faithful laymen and sons of the Church invited. We fear—let it be said with peace to all—that you may be prophesying from your own hearts and giving too little provident counsel to us, for whom the matter concerns our soul. For if we return to you, to say nothing of our lord king, we greatly fear the displeasure of the lord pope. If they are disregarded and stirred against us, we could be of little use to you or anyone. Prayers, therefore, must be poured out to God with every humility and devotion; the counsel and support must be sought not only of your whole Church but also of the neighbouring churches, so that divine mercy may deign to grant you such a shepherd as may, by His gift, heal the broken-hearted and bind up your wounds. As for what you wrote, that a good shepherd has never abandoned the pastoral office on seeing a wolf, your prudence ought to recall how many, how great, how fierce wolves we have endured in governing the Church of Stavelot during these twenty years in which we have served it—not without danger of death, grave scandals, and reproaches. We would not even now refuse to bear them if we were assigned to that Church alone. But since wolves are not lacking in the Church of Corvey, and the pastor’s prudence and vigilance are necessary there as well, we have chosen to serve one—or, if that is expedient, neither—rather than, by attending to both, benefit neither. And, to answer the words of the old history, do not in any way believe that we have preferred the love of the later wife to the first; she does not calmly allow us even, for Reuben’s mandrakes, to go in to the former to propagate offspring. Rather, in all things we seek the purpose of divine goodness through the support of your prayers and counsel. May the grace of the Holy Spirit deign to enlighten your hearts. Amen. The greater the pressures suffered by your Church, the more it needs common counsel; for we wish to do nothing rashly or precipitately in this affair, but with such mature deliberation that our action may please our Creator and offend no sound human judgment.

## LETTER CCXCVIII. Wibald, Abbot, to Henry, Monk of Stavelot

He persists in his intention to resign the abbatial dignity of Stavelot and wishes thereby to know God’s good pleasure. (1151.)

Brother Wibald, called abbot, to his beloved son Henry: greeting and blessing.

A headache and weakness of the eyes advise us to write to your learning more briefly than either time or subject requires, especially because what we write is so confidential that we dare not use the assistance of another’s hand. We shall now pass over the good hope with which your kindly charity exhorts us to endure and repair difficult—indeed almost impossible—matters, and strives through zeal of affection to advance us, lest we also see with bodily eyes the collapse of those things which, by much labour and expense, we have built in the monastery of Stavelot for the worship of divine religion—things which would better have been expended on the cultivation of souls than on the splendour of walls. We shall answer what you wrote: that you do not know what was done at Meaux regarding our appointment in the Church of Corvey. For you say, “If I am wise, I do not know what I know.” You add what seems to you easier and more plausible, rather than what the order requires, the rule teaches, or obedience demands. That proverb, however, is not taken from the Law, the Gospel, the Apostle, or ecclesiastical teaching: it is pagan, secular, comic; it belongs to a frivolous person who advises one to avoid beatings or some inconvenience. It does not concern the salvation of souls, love of God and neighbour, fear of Gehenna, or desire for the heavenly homeland. We, while young, taught you these things when you were a boy, when we were cultivating your capacity by playing at these studies, so that you might clearly understand and correctly pronounce Latin—not that you might speak falsely or keep silence about truth against God. Now our school professes and teaches this: “If you are wise, you know what you know; and what you do not know, you inquire into and learn,” at least in those matters which concern religion, the worship of God, and the salvation of souls. Therefore, dearest son, disobedience must be avoided by you as by us, lest in governing another Church we be admitted otherwise than through the door, or the flock hear the voice of a stranger, and the shepherd be a thief and invader, while the flock is deceived and transgresses. So far as we are wise, we know what we know: namely, that the lord pope has dealt with us concerning this same matter both orally and in writing. We desire to learn what, in so arduous a affair, may please our God, accord with our salvation, benefit both Churches—which we are now insufficient to serve—and not conflict with sound human judgments. But you think that we covet riches and shun poverty. Believe me, son in the Lord: this is not true. Rather, we strive to find God by the way of obedience, and thus to leave one Church so that we may benefit the other. If this cannot be done, it is better to leave both than to make progress in neither. This is a great matter and must be sought from God.

## LETTER CCXCIX. The Monks of Stavelot to Abbot Wibald

They state that the wishes of the monks of Malmedy agree with their own in retaining him. (1151.)

To their lord and Father, the venerable abbot of Stavelot Wibald, Brother Robert and the whole congregation of the Church of Stavelot: due submission.

Having received the statement of your concern, our brothers of Malmedy differ from us in no respect. For we all think the same, and there are no schisms among us. We signify this all the more earnestly to the sincerity of your fatherhood because we never wish to be separated from your fatherhood or depart from the guidance of your rule. The fact that this matter was not made known to the laymen through us was required by the circumstances of the time: lest they rashly cast themselves into our hands with more confidence than usual; lest they be able in any way to detract from our fidelity and constancy; and lest they boast that your going or return depended upon them. We unceasingly pour out prayers to God because of our great and continual afflictions, asking that He grant us peace of mind and body together with the spirit of counsel and fortitude; for our condition depends on your peace. Therefore again and again the face of our whole community entreats you: remembering your brothers, sons, and friends, come to the aid of the Church of Stavelot, now already collapsing, and of the poor entrusted to you amid their manifold tribulations; and do not withdraw the hand of counsel and aid from those now almost at the final extremity of necessity.

## LETTER CCC. Henry, Monk of Stavelot, to Abbot Wibald

That the best father should not abandon obedient sons. (1151.)

To his most reverend Father and lord Wibald, venerable abbot of Stavelot, Henry: whatever a son owes his Father.

Although, most loving Father, the manifold complaints and daily vexations of our poor have so filled my heart and soul with bitterness that I can scarcely hold in mind any words but “woe, woe,” nevertheless I have taken care to write a few words to the sincerity of your affection—not because I intend to instruct your learning or your mind, always provident and always wise in high matters, but in order, in my customary simplicity, always to show filial devotion to my dearest Father. Passing over, therefore, all the propositions of questions and conclusions of arguments concerning the matters touched upon by “I know” and “I do not know,” so far as the slowness of my capacity can understand: neither order requires, nor rule teaches, nor obedience commands, nor right or law shows, that a father should disown obedient children, that a mother should withdraw her breasts from her children in time of need, or that a good shepherd should leave gathered sheep to be wickedly scattered by strangers. Nor is it contrary to the salvation of souls, to love of God and neighbour, or alien from the desire for the heavenly homeland, to preside over and provide for children, to love and govern the Church which you know has been entrusted to you. Although it is now scourged because sins demand it, God is able to free it—He who chose before the ages the place in which it stands for His service. Therefore, dearest Father, be content with the poverty of our Church, which nourished, fed, and advanced you almost from your earliest age; do not abandon it. For this would be far from paternal affection according to men’s just estimation and sound judgments, and, according to God, the Apostle, and Christian doctrine, alien from all the piety of religion. Moreover, you will understand more fully from the assembly’s letter why laymen were not admitted to the brothers’ counsel. We do not wish in any way to share the secrets of our counsel with those who are always against us, who always violently plunder what is ours and yours. Therefore let your fatherhood’s prudence understand that what has been done by counsel in your Church has been done sincerely.

## LETTER CCCI. Henry, Monk of Stavelot, to Abbot Wibald

Again he beseeches him not to cast aside the abbatial dignity of the monastery of Stavelot. (1151.)

[Col. 1370A]

To his dearest lord Wibald, venerable abbot of Stavelot, humble Henry: obedience, submission, and devotion.

I had resolved, dearest Father, to put my finger to my mouth, so that I who do not know how to speak might at least begin to learn how to be silent. But before my eyes I have how much you have bestowed upon our church in gold, silver, gems, and various ornaments; with what honorable and useful buildings you have advanced it; and how you have not merely safeguarded its estates and lands intact, [Col. 1370B] but have also recovered and increased those which your predecessors had wrongly alienated. When I further remember how much dignity, discipline, solicitude, and exemplary conduct I have observed in you; and finally—what touches my heart most deeply—how piously you took me in from childhood, how mercifully you treated me, and how gently you brought me up, I take courage, compelled by affection—indeed driven by great necessity—and no longer blush, though humble and unlearned, to address a lofty prince and most eloquent speaker.

[Note: [Col. 1369] Thus already in Wibald’s lifetime the abbots of Stavelot were princes of the Holy Roman Empire.]

Why, most merciful lord, does your gentleness abandon us? Why does your prudent pastoral care leave a flock exposed, behold, to so many wolves? What in us has displeased your fatherhood, that first through me in bare words, and now [Col. 1370C] once and again by letters and effective messengers, you have troubled—indeed disturbed—your church, seeking counsel about resigning the other abbacy and, as we understand it, forcibly demanding release from ours, as though the other possessed more religion and order? Does your wisdom not know that you, chosen from among us by us, invested among us, consecrated among us, having lived among and over us for sixteen years without enduring fruit, were rather lent than given as our abbot and shepherd to the calling of the Corveyans and the petition of the king and princes, as though only recently? Why, in so grievous a matter concerning us, do you resolve to seek counsel concerning us from others, from strangers and outsiders, when we have firmly resolved not to let you go? Who has impressed this upon your magnanimity: that, desiring to abandon the church which reared you from youth, received you, and enlarged you, you should pour out our blessing upon the church to which you were lent, and not without supplanting us? Let the purpose of this concern of yours cease, I beg, lord; let your paternal affection cease from wishing so cruelly to cast off its own sons, who, to put it briefly, have resolved to die wandering and exiled rather than, while you live, to have no father and lord. Faith compelled me, father, to write this; love persuaded me. Yet if perhaps I have exceeded due measure by speaking words rashly and uncouthly to so great a [Col. 1371A] prince, may your learning forgive me and receive them simply and faithfully, as they have been spoken in truth. Henceforth may almighty God protect you and direct for you a plan of swift return to us.

## LETTER CCCII. THE MONKS OF CORVEY TO ABBOT WIBALD

They ask him not for the present to resign the abbacy of the Stavelotians. (Year 1151.)

To their dearest lord and Father WIBALD, venerable abbot of the church of Corvey, the community of the same church offers due obedience.

We have sent to your sincerity our prior and chamberlain, and have charged them to lay before your [Col. 1371B] fatherhood certain words resulting from the common deliberation of our chapter. We should indeed have put these before you while you were still among us, but through the customary error of human nature we neglected to do so. Therefore may your loving-kindness not disdain still to consider them mercifully and receive them with your accustomed generosity.

While you were still present with us, we spoke with your holiness about relinquishing the abbey of Stavelot, desiring by every means that you might continually be with us and, freed from other occupations, might provide more quietly and peacefully for our needs. But, considering the iniquity of these present times and hearing also of the distress and hardship of our brothers at Stavelot, [Col. 1371C] we have plainly recognized that our request was not suited to the condition of the present time, nor could that church be left by you at this time without its gravest loss. Therefore we place in your discretion our request that you leave that church, and leave to your judgment and will the time for leaving it and the opportunity of transferring to us.

If we have improperly put before your gentleness any other matters, we make satisfaction to your fatherhood, as we ought to do in person, prostrate at your feet; and we humbly entreat you mercifully to put them out of your heart. On the Sunday just past, the provost announced in chapter that from that date he would supply bread and drink to the community for four weeks, but afterward would neither have them nor provide them. Since therefore we have no other provider besides you when the provost does not give us necessities, we cast all our care concerning this announcement upon you, and ask your fatherhood to care for us as persons deprived of every consolation.

## LETTER CCCIII. ABBOT WIBALD TO H., A MONK OF CORVEY

He appoints him prior of the monastery of Corvey. (Year 1151.)

Brother WIBALD, by God’s grace what he is in the Catholic Church, to his beloved son H., greeting and blessing.

Brother, we appointed you prior in an evil time, [Col. 1372A] and for a long time deferred removing your predecessor, because it was plain that no one else could be appointed to whom the assent of our affection would extend. Now you remain alone in the midst, destined later to bear a heavier burden when we must depart. For either one must yield to the ambition of the multitude, to the great injury of justice and the Church, or one must resist with scant support and at the greatest peril.

You will be able to learn more fully what has been done concerning our cause at court, both from our lord king’s letters sent to the community and from the oral report of our envoys. The lord king will hold court at Speyer at Easter, and we have been ordered to meet him at Boppard on the octave, to travel down with him as far as Utrecht; nor do we hope to be able to leave him before the octave of Pentecost, even if we can obtain permission not to proceed with him as far as Regensburg.

Therefore let your diligence report to us with the greatest speed whether the provost intends to administer to his brothers, or to resign the office of provost. For it is not our intention to suffer loss in that from which he himself has drawn profit; and when he ceases to administer, let him also cease to manage the estate, since we plainly see the common resources being destroyed by private and excessive expenditures. Yet, however he may conduct himself, if he fails, let your prudence diligently provide the brothers with necessities, taking pledges from the Church treasury. Write carefully to us about everything: also what Count Herman has subsequently [Col. 1372C] undertaken concerning the church of Corvey, and what reply he presently makes to the lord king’s letter.

## LETTER CCCIV. H., PRIOR, AND THE COMMUNITY OF THE MONASTERY OF CORVEY TO ABBOT WIBALD

They complain of the monastery’s provost, who denied them the necessities of life. (Year 1151.)

To the reverend Father and lord in Christ WIBALD, abbot of Corvey: Brother H., prior, and the community of the church of Corvey offer devoted prayers and due obedience.

As you had commanded our whole community in your letter to meet with our provost, so that [Col. 1372D] he might supply us with necessities without failure, we endeavored to do so. But we could accomplish nothing, for he alleged his own lack while we insisted that he supply us with necessities. Finally, after many announcements by which he had declared that bread and drink would fail us, the matter between him and us proceeded so far that during Rogation Days and on the very holy day of the Lord’s Ascension he left us without drink, and on the next following Saturday without bread and drink alike—something which, we believe, had never happened at Corvey.

Accordingly, as we sat at table that day in accordance with our rule and custom, awaiting the usual food, and received nothing from him, we rose fasting and, proceeding to church according to our rule, [Col. 1373A] blessed God with a psalm. We then immediately assembled together and took common counsel about what had to be done. We agreed among ourselves that this necessity should quickly be made known to your fatherhood. Meanwhile we imposed this charge upon Brother A., our chamberlain, though unwilling and strongly resisting: until our messenger should return from you, he was to provide us, wherever possible, with bread and drink borrowed on credit. He took as a pledge the silver which we had assigned this year for the sarcophagus. Since therefore you see the need pressing upon us, we beseech your beloved fatherhood to hasten your return to us as quickly as possible, so that you may rescue us and the Church from imminent danger, from which we cannot escape without your presence.

## LETTER CCCV. ABBOT WIBALD TO HIS CORVEYANS

He commends their patience in enduring the lack of necessities and excuses himself because he cannot return to them so soon. (Year 1151.)

Brother WIBALD, by God’s grace abbot of Corvey, to H., prior of the church of Corvey, and to his brothers and sons: blessing and life for ever.

We grieve from our hearts, God bearing witness, that such great and unheard-of deficiencies should have occurred at this time in the church of Corvey. Yet, caught in a great storm of affairs, we are unable to demonstrate the effect of our good will by deeds. But divine mercy has provided us one consolation amid the great evils of our misery: that you bear patiently and with equanimity these hardships, so disorderly and so unheard of, which we believe never before befell the church of Corvey; nor do you assail us over our absence, which is thought to harm your interests, with a bitter word of reproach. [Col. 1373C] By this you bind our solicitude to you in the closest affection, so that henceforth there is no labor and no injury which, for love of you and for the common justice, we shall refuse to undergo and bear according to our strength.

Moreover, dearest brothers, not only the upheaval and ruin of the church of Stavelot, but also of all Lotharingia, prevents us from hastening our return to you. This is indeed our native land: it bore us, reared us, and advanced us. Our lord king and many princes of the realm forbid us to leave it and to transfer ourselves to you in mind as well as body. Yet it would be the utmost impiety to recoil from and flee our parent placed amid such sufferings. For nearly six weeks, while we were with our lord king, we exerted ourselves ardently beyond the measure of our capacity to restore its peace; but, because sins bring all things to ruin, we could accomplish nothing. Nevertheless, if within these next ten days no final peace or truce intervenes, all hope for the safety of the whole land must be abandoned.

Yet we shall endeavor by whatever means we can that, not long after [Col. 1374A] the feast of the apostle Barnabas, either we ourselves may come to you, or we may send such messengers as can certainly provide for your needs by prudent counsel. Your learning does not fail to know how difficult it is at this time to provide both for our household, which is expensive beyond the cloistered measure, and for the whole monastery. Meanwhile we direct your charity that, through the diligence of your prior and Brother A., your chamberlain, all things be arranged for the present so that the brothers do not lack food and the divine offices among you do not cease.

## LETTER CCCVI. EMPEROR CONRAD TO POPE EUGENIUS

That he confirm the election of Herman, bishop of Utrecht, and absolve the count of Are from excommunication. (Year 1151.)

[Col. 1374B]

To his most beloved Father EUGENIUS, supreme pontiff of the holy Roman Church: CONRAD, by God’s grace king of the Romans and ever august, filial love in all things and due reverence in the Lord.

After the see of Utrecht became vacant on the death of Bishop Haribert of pious memory, etc. See under Eugenius III, for the year 1153, after his *Regesta*.

## LETTER CCCVII. ABBOT WIBALD TO B., ARCHDEACON OF LIÈGE

He excuses himself from the conference at Huy. (Year 1151.)

[Col. 1374C] To his beloved brother and friend B., venerable archdeacon of the holy church of Liège: Brother WIBALD, by God’s grace what he is in the Catholic Church, blessing and affection.

Our brother, whom we had sent to you to ascertain the intention of our lord bishop and to learn your whole community’s will concerning peace, returned to us later than the order of events and the circumstances required. Since, because of his prolonged delay, we had despaired of the conference to be held at Huy, we turned to bodily care and had blood drawn shortly before that same brother returned. Let your discretion therefore regard our health as excused, and by no means entertain in your heart the thought that, because of private enmities and hatreds, we wish the peace of the land and the public order to be disturbed or overthrown.
