For your philosophy—that teacher and mistress of yours, instructress and educator in things divine and human—has not so formed and shaped our character that we should abandon common goods on account of a private claim. Divine philosophy says: “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called children of God,” and, “Blessed are the feet that bring peace.” Human philosophy did not disdain, for the preservation of the republic, to admit even mortal enemies into participation in magistracies. Since we have learned that the tyrants are now driven into madness, let your diligence take care, with every humility and calmness of mind, that the hope of peace is not broken off and that there is no headlong rush to arms. For after these three days, when our strength has returned, [Col. 1375A] we have resolved to spare neither persons nor property, so that peace and tranquillity may be secured for the Christian people through us sinners, if this pleases the Godhead. Other matters properly concerning us and our church we shall pursue with no less zeal.

## LETTER CCCVIII. ABBOT WIBALD TO THE BROTHERS OF GLADBACH

He offers them his counsel and assistance, and speaks of injuries inflicted upon them by ministerials. (Year 1151.)

To the reverend brothers in Christ, the monks of the church of Gladbach: Brother WIBALD, by God’s grace what he is in the Catholic Church, blessing and life for ever.

[Note: [Col. 1375D] Gladbach, a notable monastery of the Order of Saint Benedict, in the principality of Cleves and the diocese of Cologne; its foundation history is found in volume XII of the *Spicilegium*.]

[Col. 1375B] A twofold reason moves us to affection for your love and charity: namely, that we share the habit of one order and the name of one religious profession, and that we glory in the intercession of one and the same patron, namely the blessed martyr Vitus. Although unworthy, we are nevertheless, by God’s ordering, regarded as his vicars; and we most confidently hope both to be aided by his patronage and to follow the faith with fitting devotion.

Therefore, dearest brothers, we offer all the charity of our affection to your brotherhood, and readily offer you our counsel and assistance, so that you may trust in them in every way, knowing that in all matters in which we can serve according to God, we shall stand by you as circumstances require and according to our ability. Concerning the matter about which you have appealed to us, as to all sons of the Catholic Church, we answer grieving and in supplication: “The sons of my mother have fought against me.” It may be strange and astonishing to the whole world to whom, or to which persons, your ministerials ought to answer. If they do not answer to you, to whom they ought to minister, serve, and obey, although all that they are or can be is yours, and although authority over both their persons and their property has been assigned by laws and canons to you and your monastery—then to whom will they answer?

If the matter concerned a chapter lawsuit and a peremptory summons, or title to possession, you would of course need secular advocates, as in a secular cause. But when the case concerns injury and damage inflicted, not only those who belong by proprietary right to [Col. 1375D] your monastery, but every kind of person, in the judgment of our own insignificance, could not refuse to answer and make satisfaction to you according to the course of the laws. In this presumption of your ministerials, the vigilance of our beloved fellow-brother and co-abbot is blameworthy—if we may say so with his leave—for he does not “go up against the enemy” or “set up a wall for the house of Israel,” but allows, as the saying goes, footstools to climb onto benches. They have leisure, and therefore cry out; they wish to trample their mother and lady underfoot in the mud; and, fed from the Church’s goods, grown fat, thickened, and enlarged, they kick against her. Henceforth you ought to place the fullest confidence in our prayers and our intimate service, both in this cause and in every other.

## LETTER CCCIX. HENRY, BISHOP OF LIÈGE, TO POPE EUGENIUS III

He asks that the election of Arnold, archbishop of Cologne, be confirmed. (Year 1151.)

To his reverend Father and lord EUGENIUS, supreme and universal pontiff of the holy Roman Church: H., by God’s grace humble minister of the church of Liège, offers obedience both devoted and due in complete submission, and ready and faithful service in all things.

After the death of A., archbishop of Cologne, of blessed memory, see among the letters of various persons to Eugenius [Col. 1376B].

## LETTER CCCX. THE CHURCH OF COLOGNE TO POPE EUGENIUS III

Concerning the election of Arnold, provost of the greater church of Saint Peter, as archbishop of Cologne. (Year 1151.)

To their most reverend Father and lord EUGENIUS, supreme pontiff of the holy Roman Church: W., dean; the archdeacons, abbots, provosts, clergy, dignitaries, and whole people of the church of Cologne offer obedience both devoted and due in complete love and submission.

We do not believe that it has escaped your Excellency’s notice that our mother, the church of Cologne, etc. [Col. 1376C] See above.

## LETTER CCCXI. ABBOT WIBALD TO ARNOLD, ELECT OF COLOGNE

He wishes him every prosperity. (Year 1151.)

To his most reverend Father and lord A., venerable bishop-elect of the holy church of Cologne: Brother WIBALD, by God’s grace what he is in the Church, offers humble prayers and devoted service.

We are not of Pythagoras’s school, so as to compel our hearers to swear by our words. You may therefore diminish, remove, and add to our writing without provoking the bitter offence of our mind. For each person abounds in his own understanding. We and our brothers—certainly your servants because of your benefits to us—humbly pray God, whom neither distances of place nor intervals of time separate from those whom he protects, that, with his grace going before, he may direct your way and with his grace following may deign to accompany it, so that you may rejoice in your conduct and welfare through the safeguards of his mercy. [Col. 1376D]

## LETTER CCCXII. EMPEROR CONRAD TO HENRY, ARCHBISHOP OF MAINZ

He rebukes him because he deprived the elect of Cologne, who had not yet assented to his election, of the provostship of Lempurch. (Year 1151.)

CONRAD, by God’s grace king of the Romans, to H., venerable [Col. 1377A] archbishop of Mainz: his favor and every good.

More than three times we requested your prudence by our letters and commands that you should dispose, in accordance with our wish and request, and in hope of faithful recompense, what is recognized as being within your right concerning the provostship of Lempurch—at a suitable time, namely, when the sacred laws did not forbid it. But you have not merely failed to grant our request: you have even stripped the elect of the church of Cologne of his possession, although he had not yet consented to that calling, contrary to canonical ordinances.

For since he still refuses to accept a burden too heavy to bear and has deferred the whole matter until the presence and authority of the lord pope, he ought not to have been removed from a lower rank when he feared to ascend to a higher one. And since examination precedes consecration, some persons may be removed from the office of the high priesthood who can nevertheless rightly administer other ecclesiastical stewardships. We therefore earnestly request and admonish your prudence to correct by a swift and judicious change your action, which transgresses the rule of canonical teaching; and, when that same provostship has lawfully become vacant, not to refuse our request. For we shall preserve intact for him until his consecration all things that he holds from us.

## LETTER CCCXIII. EMPEROR CONRAD TO POPE EUGENIUS III

Concerning the election of Arnold as archbishop of Cologne, which he requests be confirmed. (Year 1151.)

[Note: [Col. 1377D] From this letter of Emperor Conrad to Pope Eugenius, and from the preceding and following letters, *Gallia Christiana* must be corrected, since it dates Arnold II’s election to 1155, whereas Conrad died in February 1151; and in the above-mentioned instrument of the year 1151 concerning Walciodorus, Arnold is called elect of Cologne.]

[Col. 1377C]

To his most beloved Father in Christ EUGENIUS, supreme pontiff of the holy Roman Church: CONRAD, by God’s grace king of the Romans and ever august, filial love in all things and due reverence in the Lord.

The church of Cologne, which by its size and splendor excelled nearly all the churches of Germany and Gaul, had fallen into such calamity through the negligence of its shepherds [Note: [Col. 1378D] Especially Arnold, whom Eugenius III suspended from office for simony.] etc. See among the letters of various persons to Eugenius.

## LETTER CCCXIV. ARNOLD TO ABBOT WIBALD

He postpones the journey of his clergy, dignitaries, and ministerials to the pope until peace is fully secured. (Year 1151.)

[Col. 1377D]

To lord WIBALD, by God’s grace venerable abbot of Stavelot: ARNOLD, by the same grace whatever he is, greeting and ready and faithful service in all things.

We give due thanks to your eminence because we perceive that the experience of your prudence is in every way favorable to our honor. What the power of the Most High, without whom nothing has strength, has accomplished while we were present [Col. 1378A] in Westphalia and on the borders of Saxony, the outcome itself and common report will sufficiently make known to you. Moreover, the clergy, dignitaries, and ministerials, fearing that peace still tender and newly established might easily be disturbed by our absence, have persuaded us with urgent entreaties for the present to defer our journey to the lord pope, until peace is fully consolidated and no storm of evils may disturb it even after our departure. Let us know where and when you wish to see us and discuss our affairs with us.

## LETTER CCCXV. ABBOT WIBALD TO ARNOLD, ELECT OF COLOGNE

He rejoices at Arnold’s prosperous affairs; concerning peace to be made with the bishop of Liège. He urges him not to defer his journey to Rome, and to receive honorably the envoys of the Apostolic See passing through Cologne. (Year 1151.)

[Col. 1378B]

To his most reverend Father and lord ARNOLD, venerable elect of the holy church of Cologne: Brother WIBALD, by God’s grace what he is in the Catholic Church, humble prayers and devoted service.

That your affairs are advancing with prosperous results, God increasing them, and that peace long desired by us is being restored through your diligence, with the audacity of robbers suppressed, gives us a twofold cause for joy: first, that these things occur in our times, when we have almost despaired of good things; and second, that they occur through your proven ability, which from long ago we have sought to love [Col. 1378C] and adorn with praises. Yet, set in our old woodland solitude, we hear less frequently of such welcome causes of joy.

On the same day that Brother Hillinus arrived with us on his return from you, several religious abbots from the diocese of Liège came to us near our monastery, urgently asking that, for the time being setting aside the serious injury which we have often received in deed and word both from the lord bishop of Liège and from the count of Namur, we should negotiate a settlement of peace between them. Since the lord bishop was nearby, we promised our assistance to such honorable men and met with him concerning the same matter. Accordingly, with his approval, a day has been set for the next Saturday, when religious and wise men from the whole bishopric may assemble and, if it so pleases the supreme Divinity, apply every effort and diligence to the peace of the land.

Since we are presently occupied with public affairs, we cannot at once give you a definite reply, as you ordered, concerning our coming into your presence. Concerning the matter of which your eminence has deigned to notify us—that at the counsel of your whole church you have deferred at this time your journey to the lord pope [Col. 1379A]—we do not presume to strive against or oppose it, since the result of affairs concerns the interests of those who are authors of the decision. Yet, because each person abounds in his own judgment, it seems to us, who have often been tossed by dreadful perils, especially dangers from false brothers, that when the acquisition of the highest dignity is at stake nothing can be done too quickly. For when one aims at difficult things, not only withdrawal but even delay is rightly feared.

The rule of the Fathers and the decisions laid down by the most holy councils forbid a metropolitan see to remain widowed for more than three months, as your learning fully knows. Moreover, the envoys of the Roman Church are coming to these regions to settle the cause of the Utrecht election.

[Note: [Col. 1379D] The contenders were Herman, provost of St. Gereon’s at Cologne, elected by the provost, dean, clergy, and nobles of the country; and Frederick of Cologne, likewise provost of St. George’s, elected while below the requisite age and orders by certain members of the clergy, as appears from Emperor Conrad’s letter to Pope Eugenius related above.]

Let your church, whose counsel it is fitting for you to follow, see how, in the present condition of affairs, these same envoys are to be received in your city and treated, in deciding that same dispute, as becomes the Roman and Cologne churches and the dignity of your person. Around the feast of the blessed apostle Bartholomew we expect to be traveling toward Saxony; wherever it then pleases your discretion, we shall be ready to speak with you and serve you.

## LETTER CCCXVI. EMPEROR CONRAD TO ABBOT WIBALD

He orders him to attend a conference of princes at Würzburg on the appointed date. (Year 1151.)

[Col. 1379C]

CONRAD, by God’s grace king of the Romans, to WIBALD, abbot of Corvey: his favor and every good.

We wish your discretion to know that, on the eighth day after the Nativity of Saint Mary, certain princes will appear before us at Würzburg to discuss with us the affairs of Church and kingdom and our expedition. We need your presence among them, since we intend to discuss each matter more privately and fully with you. Therefore by these present letters we command your diligence, putting aside every delay and excuse, to present yourself before us on the date mentioned above, content with a small retinue.

## LETTER CCCXVII. CHAPLAIN HERIBERT TO HENRY, PRIOR OF CORVEY

That he send Wibald the king’s letter without delay. (Year 1151.)

[Col. 1379D]

To lord HENRY, venerable prior of the church of Corvey: HERIBERT, chaplain, offers his service.

I presume to lay this command more urgently upon your diligence: send the lord king’s letter to the lord abbot without delay, because he is summoned to court on important and private affairs as well.

## LETTER CCCXVIII. KING SWEYN OF DENMARK TO EMPEROR CONRAD

He gives thanks for benefits and asks that Conrad continue to protect him. (Year 1151.)

[Col. 1380A]

To CONRAD, by God’s grace glorious emperor of the Romans and ever august: SWEYN, by the same disposition king of the Danes, offers filial love and due submission.

Not unmindful of your generous benefit, we continually give thanks to the mercy of your fatherhood and unceasingly pray God, the rewarder of all, that where recompense from our insignificance fails, he may deign in his supreme mercy to repay you. May the proven kindness of your serenity receive this: from the flower of earliest youth we have fixed the anchor of our support in your majesty, and after God always desire it to remain immovably fixed; and, with life as our companion, we desire fittingly [lacuna] continually. [Col. 1380B] It is therefore proper for your fatherhood to provide for the honor of a son and, if any arise for our destruction, to restrain their rashness.

Desiring to see the splendor of the court and the welcome face of your eminence, we earnestly ask that you appoint both a place convenient for coming and a suitable time for preparations, and secure safe-conduct for us. We have entrusted our embassy to these faithful friends of ours, namely the lord archbishop of Bremen and Margrave O., so that we might avoid the duke’s ambushes. Farewell; stir up your princes to the subjugation of the Slavs, and write back concerning those matters which appear fitting. [Col. 1380C]

## LETTER CCCXIX. KING KNUT OF DENMARK TO EMPEROR CONRAD

Deprived of his kingdom, he flees to Conrad. (Year 1151.)

To CONRAD, by God’s grace august emperor of the Romans: KNUT, king of the Danes, greeting.

Since the King of kings has appointed you for this and chosen you from among many, adorning you with the glory of his name, so that you might become a father of justice and a son of peace, you ought rightly in all things to strengthen justice and provide consolation to those unjustly oppressed. Therefore, deprived not only of [Col. 1380D] our kingdom but even of our patrimony, we make complaint to Christ and to you, that, justice so requiring, you may condescend to and have compassion on us exiles. For, driven out, we flee to the Roman Empire because we hoped to find counsel and assistance there. We humbly beseech your royal power to help us; to act toward us in a fatherly way for the sake of your honor; and to enable us, through the severity of your sword, to recover what we have unjustly lost. We, for our part, shall steadfastly follow all your commands as sons.

## LETTER CCCXX. ABBOT WIBALD TO MANUEL, EMPEROR OF CONSTANTINOPLE

Conrad the emperor prepares an expedition against the Sicilian. (Year 1151.)

[Col. 1381A]

To the illustrious conqueror and most serene ruler, glorious and most sacred emperor of the Greeks and of Romania, MANUEL—exalted, sublime, Porphyrogenitus—WIBALD, by God’s grace abbot of two noble monasteries, namely Stavelot and Corvey, offers devoted and perpetual service in the Lord and continual prayers to God.

We render infinite thanksgiving to God, the giver of all good things, who has deigned to inspire your gentleness to write to our insignificance and to signify the intention of your will. We therefore do what you commanded, and with humble and continual prayers, together with the brothers entrusted to us, endeavor to beseech the mercy of almighty God that he may deign to grant to both your eminence and to my lord, your brother Conrad, august emperor of the Romans, health, safety, and victory over enemies; and to extend and magnify your empires over all kingdoms of the earth, as the histories of the ancients show them to have been in former times.

We also urge and continually exhort that our most exalted and glorious emperor preserve faithfully and firmly your friendship and alliance [Col. 1381C] and fulfill without any diminution all that has been promised to your majesty. Persevering with great steadfastness of mind in this purpose, that most fortunate prince is vigorously arranging his expedition into the regions of Sicily and Apulia against the common enemy of both empires.

Accordingly, in the middle of this past September he summoned certain princes of his empire to the city of Würzburg. There assembled also the archbishop of Cologne, the archbishop of Bremen, the bishop of Halberstadt, the bishop of Liège, the bishop of Bamberg, the bishop of Merseburg, the bishop of Würzburg, the bishop of Strasbourg, the bishop of Worms, and the bishop of Prague; likewise envoys of various bishops and princes. Among the lay princes there assembled the margrave of Wettin, the margrave of Brandenburg, the count palatine of Bavaria, the count of Winzenburg in Saxony, the prefect of the city of Mainz, the prefect of the city of Würzburg, the prefect of the city of Bamberg, and many other counts, dignitaries, and nobles. All of them, with great cheerfulness of will, having pledged faith and sworn an oath, promised that they would come to and join this expedition with all the strength and power of their military forces.

We too, serving our lord with our own forces in the same expedition, shall deserve, God granting it, to behold your most sacred countenance and the splendor of your very great empire. We give thanks to your imperial generosity [Col. 1382A] because you have sent us your blessing while we were still unknown to you.

### Letter CCCXXI. The Emperor of Constantinople to Abbot Wibald

He offers Emperor Conrad his forces against the Sicilian. (1151.)

An imperial letter to the most precious abbot of the monastery of Stavelot.

Most precious abbot of the monastery of Stavelot: when my Empire learned from many persons of the virtue flourishing in you, and how you strive for the honour of the most noble king of Rome, the most beloved brother and kinsman of my Empire, and for the advantage of Christians, it has conceived great devotion and affection toward your precious person and continually invokes your prayers. My Empire therefore wishes that your preciousness should again labour for the honour of the most noble king. For he will never find a better helper for service against the Sicilian and for his other enterprises. My Empire also wishes to be informed, through your letters, of his welfare. For my Empire has great affection for your preciousness, since it certainly learned of the virtue flourishing in you.

At Abadon, the great city having been preserved, in March, indiction XIV: “a white *exametum megalo [lacuna] gmon diplarion* was sent to you” [materially uncertain Greek-derived ceremonial description].

### Letter CCCXXII. Conrad to the Romans

He announces his imminent arrival in Italy, and meanwhile sends them legates. (1151.)

[Col. 1382C]

CONRAD, by the grace of God king of the Romans and ever Augustus, to the Prefect of the City, the consuls, captains, and all the Roman people, both lesser and greater: his favour and goodwill.

After our return from the Jerusalem expedition, we frequently received letters from your community, which reported with what zeal of faith and devotion you contend, with untiring spirits, to advance the dignity of our person and restore the condition of the Roman Empire. Although the [lacuna] of the letters seemed unequal to the great matters which they conveyed, we nevertheless received them most gratefully, and have resolved to honour your goodwill, proceeding in its begun course, with an imperial recompense.

Accordingly, being duly and honourably invited by your prudence, we have effectively arranged an Italian expedition and our arrival at the City, with the great support of our princes and the eagerness of all our soldiery: first at the celebrated court at Regensburg, secondly in the city of Würzburg. We have thereafter strengthened our purpose, so that, moving more swiftly to the remaining parts of our realm, peace having everywhere been established through God’s mercy, we may proceed to pacify and secure the territories and cities of Italy in such a manner as, with God’s help, to recompense both the faithful and the rebellious with punishment. [Col. 1383A]

For this reason we send to your experienced community our legates, men indeed distinguished and moderate: Arnold, chancellor of our court and elected archbishop of Cologne; Wibald, abbot of Corvey; and Henry, notary—men most faithful and intimate to our Empire—so that through them you may learn the certainty of our will and counsel. Therefore, by earnest command we entrust to your diligence that, for reverence toward us and for the order of the City, you receive these our legates honourably; receive from them, as from our own mouth, what must be done in the present state of affairs; and conduct them honourably and conveniently as the requirements of the journey demand.

### Letter CCCXXIII. Conrad, Emperor, to Pope Eugenius III

He states that he is preparing the Italian expedition for the benefit of the Church, and commends the archbishop of Bremen and Abbot Wibald. (1151.)

[Col. 1383B]

To his dearest father in Christ, EUGENIUS, supreme pontiff of the holy Roman Church, CONRAD, by the grace of God king of the Romans and ever Augustus, filial love in all things and due reverence in the Lord.

“As we have often experienced, both formerly and now, the goodwill of your fatherhood in all our own affairs and those of our people,” etc. See under Eugenius, among the letters of various persons.

### Letter CCCXXIV. Conrad, Emperor, to the Pisans

Concerning his expedition into Italy against the Sicilian. (1151.)

[Col. 1383C]

CONRAD, by the grace of God king of the Romans and ever Augustus, to the consuls, captains, and entire people of Pisa, both lesser and greater: his favour and goodwill.

After our return from the Jerusalem expedition, we had turned the whole intention of our mind toward entering, without the intervention of a longer delay, upon the ordering and pacification of Italian affairs. Hence we sent the legates of our most excellent brother, the emperor of the Greeks, to your community, having very great confidence in your faith and constancy, so that by their diligence and your powerful strength the enemy of both Empires might be continually shaken by martial attacks until our arrival. [Col. 1383D]

It is fitting for the ruler of his country to return thanks and goodwill to those who were not unequal in spirit and deed to accomplishing so outstanding a work; whereas a harsher punishment is deservedly due to those who attempted to destroy such great advances of the commonwealth. But the most ardent purpose of our will was for some time restrained by the hand of God—whom no mortal can escape—through an illness sent from heaven. Having recovered health through that same most merciful God, however, after the feast of holy Pentecost had passed, we held a general court at Regensburg and, in royal fashion, proclaimed our expedition toward Italy, with the great support of the princes and the eagerness of all the soldiery. [Col. 1384A]

Likewise this was done at Würzburg in the middle of September. Thus, our purpose firmly established, we shall move more swiftly to all parts of the realm granted us by God; peace having everywhere been established through God’s grace, we may reach the City and yourselves in such a way that we ought to repay rewards to those who deserve well and punishment to rebels.

To make the knowledge and certainty of this matter evident, we have sent these present legates—men distinguished and among our princes most intimate to us—namely Arnold, venerable archbishop of the Church of Cologne; Wibald, abbot of Stavelot and Corvey; and Henry, notary of our court, to our reverend father Pope Eugenius, to the city of Rome, and also to the other cities of Italy. When they come to your city, which from the beginning has always been accustomed to be the dwelling-place of the Roman Empire in peace and in war, by land and sea, receive them honourably, as your worth is accustomed to do. Inform us through them of the number both of soldiers and of ships which you will furnish for the Sicilian expedition, in return for the everlasting reward of a happy recompense. [Col. 1384B]

Moreover, concerning the request which you made to us through our legates—the bishops of Constance and Basel and the marquis of Montferrat—for the perpetual humbling of your enemies, know that your prayers have been heard. Whatever our aforesaid envoys confirm to you in this respect, do not doubt that we shall observe; know that we are enemies to your enemies, and will afflict those who hate you. [Col. 1384C]

### Letter CCCXXV. Arnold, Archbishop of Cologne, to Abbot Wibald

He asks him to wait, so that they may return together to the emperor. (1151.)

To Lord WIBALD, by the grace of God venerable abbot of Corvey, A., by God’s patience whatever he may be: greeting and service.

We have been greatly troubled that you wish so unexpectedly to leave us and, with the king’s business in some manner unfinished, neither return with us nor defer the conclusion of your legation until you are with him. Since this is unfitting both for us and for you, and altogether useless and improper toward our lord the king, who awaits your return, we advise and earnestly entreat that ancient affection of yours—which we never wish to be severed—that, as you have ever loved us, you may be willing, for the sake of service to us, of your own honour, and of reverence for the king, to await our arrival tomorrow and return with us, without delay or the loss entailed by a detour, to the place from which we set out and to our lord the king, in joy and affection.

For we were ready, and were already putting on our spurs to visit you, because the Lucchese, as you had foretold, had fed us only with words. But behold, the messenger arrived with your letters; immediately we made ready to mount our horses, but the consuls detained us with urgent and abundant entreaties. We therefore ask, and ask again, that, mindful of our lord the king, you await us tomorrow during the day. [Col. 1385A]

### Letter CCCXXVI. Pope Eugenius III to the People of Cologne

He sends back to them Archbishop Arnold, consecrated with his own hand and adorned with the pallium, commanding them to obey him, etc. (1151.)

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons GU., provost; F., dean; the archdeacons, priors, and all the clergy and people of the Church of Cologne: greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 1385B] “When he came to the clemency of the apostolic see,” etc. See under Eugenius.

### Letter CCCXXVII. Pope Eugenius to Emperor Conrad

He states that he honourably received Conrad’s legates and in every respect complied with his wishes. (1152.)

Lord Pope EUGENIUS to CONRAD, king of the Romans.

“The more often concerning the condition of your welfare and good will,” etc. See under Eugenius.

### Letter CCCXXVIII. Pope Eugenius III to the Bishop of Liège

He commands him to compel the counts of Looz and Montaigu to restore property taken from the monastery of Stavelot. (1152.)

[Col. 1385C]

Lord Pope EUGENIUS to HENRY, bishop of Liège.

“For the aid of those persons,” etc. See under Eugenius.

### Letter CCCXXIX. Cardinals Gregory and Jacob to Henry, Bishop of Liège

They ask him to ensure that injuries inflicted on the monastery of Stavelot are repaired by the count of Namur. (1152.)

To HENRY, bishop of Liège: GREGORY, cardinal deacon of Saint Angelo, and JACOB, cardinal deacon of Saint Mary, greeting.

Where apostolic command and authority lead the way, we can and especially ought to write more safely to a friend and insert friendly requests. Accordingly, in writing to your beloved person, we carefully command and amicably entreat that, since our most beloved Wibald, abbot of Stavelot, lost much—indeed, countless things—through your soldiery in that outcome of armed conflict between you and the man of Namur, and since his Church suffered great and in many respects irrecoverable loss, your prudence and discretion should conduct and deal with him by a fitting recompense in such a way that one with the other may remain inseparably one and the same as it was and ought to be; and that afterward no report of this matter may return to us without its redress. [Col. 1386A]

### Letter CCCXXX. Pope Eugenius to M., Archbishop of Bremen

He orders him to ensure the restoration of estates taken from the monastery of Kammin by his parishioners. (1152.)

Lord Pope EUGENIUS to H., archbishop of Bremen.

“From the complaint of our beloved son Wibald, abbot of Corvey, we have learned,” etc. See under Eugenius.

### Letter CCCXXXI. The Same to Henry, Archbishop of Mainz

He orders him to arrange for the restoration of property taken from the monastery of Corvey by his parishioners. (1152.)

[Col. 1386B]

The same to HENRY, archbishop of Mainz.

“That everyone should remain content with his own possessions,” etc. See in the same place.

### Letter CCCXXXII. Pope Eugenius III to Bernard, Bishop of Paderborn

He commands, under the severity of anathema, that property taken from the monastery of Corvey by Wittekind be restored. (1152.)

Lord Pope EUGENIUS to BERNARD, bishop of Paderborn.

“Coming into our presence,” etc. See in the same place.

### Letter CCCXXXIII. The Same to Herman, Bishop of Utrecht

He orders him to preserve the estates of the monastery of Corvey situated in his diocese. (1152.)

[Col. 1386C]

The same pope to HERMAN, bishop of Utrecht.

“The authority of our office warns and exhorts us,” etc. See in the same place.

### Letter CCCXXXIV. Pope Eugenius III to Ulric, Bishop of Halberstadt

He orders him to restrain his parishioners from molesting the brothers of Corvey. (1152.)

Pope EUGENIUS to ULRIC, bishop of Halberstadt.

“The authority of the government entrusted to us exhorts us,” etc. See in the same place.

### Letter CCCXXXV. Pope Eugenius III to Henry, Duke of Saxony

He commends to him Wibald, abbot of Corvey. (1152.)

[Col. 1386D]

Pope EUGENIUS to HENRY, illustrious duke of the Saxons.

“Among the principal deeds of powerful men,” etc. See in the same place.

### Letter CCCXXXVI. Pope Eugenius III to the Bishop of Verden

He complains that the bishop’s brother and other parishioners are seizing the goods of the monastery of Kammin. (1152.)

The same pope to the bishop of Verden.

[Note: [Col. 1385D] Herman, who was held in great reputation and fidelity by Emperor Frederick I and by the whole court, as [Col. 1386D] is recorded in the *Chronicle of the Bishops of Verden*, vol. II of the *Writers of Brunswick*.]

[Col. 1387A] “If the care of the universal Church,” etc. See in the same place.

### Letter CCCXXXVII. Pope Eugenius III to the Bishop of Minden

He asks him to continue showing favour to the monastery of Corvey. (1152.)

The same pope to the bishop of Minden.

[Note: [Col. 1387D] Henry, formerly abbot of Saint Maurice on the Island, of the Order of Saint Benedict.]

“It is pleasing and welcome to us,” etc. See under Eugenius.

### Letter CCCXXXVIII. Pope Eugenius III to the Abbot of Lüneburg

That Henry, abbot of Corvey, having been deposed, had not been restored to his office. (1152.)

The same pope to the abbot of Lüneburg.

“We wish your beloved person to know,” etc. See in the same place.

### Letter CCCXXXIX. Pope Eugenius III to Prelates, Counts, and Barons

He calls upon them to support Emperor Conrad in the Italian expedition. (1152.)

[Col. 1387B]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brethren the archbishops and bishops, and to his beloved sons the counts and barons established throughout Germany: greeting and apostolic blessing.

“As from God the ruler,” etc. See in the same place.

### Letter CCCXL. Abbot Wibald to His Monks of Corvey

He announces his return from the Roman legation and the emperor’s death, ordering solemn funeral rites to be celebrated for him. (1152.)

[Col. 1387C]

Brother WIBALD, by the grace of God what he is in the Catholic Church, to his beloved sons and brethren in Christ, H., venerable prior, and the other sons of the Church of Corvey: blessing and life for ever.

With the grace of almighty God accompanying our paths and your prayers attending our journey, we have returned safe and sound as far as Cologne from the lord pope and the City, on account of the royal legation which we had undertaken. In every matter entrusted to us, we have brought back complete success, with favour and goodwill. For, as the course of events itself will show, we were graciously heard in every request, both in private and public affairs; thus we suffered no difficulty either in obtaining privileges or in securing letters suited to our needs. [Col. 1387D]

But the death of our most serene lord, the illustrious king of the Romans, has embittered all this joy gained according to our desire. Though his passing has deservedly stirred the minds of your whole community, it ought not to trouble them by a more grievous shock, since God is able to preserve the Church of Corvey in the condition of its dignity and not utterly to abandon the lowliness of our person. We earnestly enjoin upon the charity of all of you that you celebrate the funeral rites of this most merciful lord of ours with solemnity and royal ceremony. [Col. 1388A]

But why do we call him lord, when we always experienced in him feelings of more than paternal affection? He did not rank us behind his sons in any degree of honour; he frequently placed us before his brothers, although they occupied the highest summit of princely power. Every office and name of holy affection flowed toward us from his most sacred heart.

Now, amid the grief of losing so excellent and friendly a prince, and amid concern for the future settlement of his realm, this care especially occupies us: that your fraternity be administered without complaint by your officials. We have turned aside briefly to the Church of Stavelot, so that, after consoling it, we may return to you after a short interval, freer and intending to remain longer. We further wish your whole community to know that Lord Henry, who formerly presided over your monastery, did not receive from the lord pope the priestly order from which he had been deposed. In confirmation of this matter we have received letters from the same lord pope. [Col. 1388B]

### Letter CCCXLI. Abbot Wibald to Stephen, Bishop of Metz

He asks him to defer proceedings concerning the election of the abbot of Waulsort until a new king of the Romans is elected. (1152.)

[Col. 1388C]

To his reverend father in Christ, STEPHEN, venerable bishop of the holy Church of Metz, Brother WIBALD, by the grace of God what he is in the Catholic Church: humble prayers and devoted service.

We believe that your eminence has heard that our lord of happy memory, the late illustrious king of the Romans, Conrad, sent us to the lord pope and the city of Rome to transact affairs of the realm. Before our return, however, our lord, Theoderic, abbot of Waulsort, entered upon the way of all flesh; and disagreement arose between the monks of Waulsort and those of Hastière concerning the election of the future abbot. For the settlement of this dispute, we understand that you have appointed a place and day for these monks.

[Note: [Col. 1388D] Theoderic, thirteenth abbot of Waulsort; see the chronographer.]

Since we still have in our hands the commands of the lord pope, prostrate in spirit at the feet of your discretion, we earnestly ask your kindness, for reverence toward the same lord pope, to postpone action with them until, through the mercy of almighty God, a new king has been appointed. The princes of the realm are already holding frequent conferences among themselves concerning his election, and they do not permit us to be absent because of our recent Italian legation. Then we may be able to take part in that cause. For we neither ought nor wish to neglect the labours of our mother, the Church of Waulsort, but are ready to serve it in every necessity, with reverence for your dignity and honour for the holy Church of Metz preserved. [Col. 1389A]

### Letter CCCXLII. Abbot Wibald to the Monks of Waulsort

He grieves with them over the death of their abbot, and sends them the privilege which he obtained for them from Pope Eugenius, together with copies of his letters to the bishop of Metz and to the monks of Hastière. (1152.)

Brother WIBALD, by the grace of God what he is in the Catholic Church, to all his beloved brethren in Christ, the sons of the Church of Waulsort: blessing and life for ever.

When we heard by report of the death of our reverend father, we grieved deeply with you in spirit, especially because we fear the many troubles facing your Church amid this change of circumstances. We grieved particularly when we learned of the proposal of your election, which can bring no benefit whatever to your whole community and will somewhat diminish the standing of our person.

[Note: [Col. 1389D] For, as the chronographer testifies, they had elected Wibald himself as shepherd of their souls. His words are these: “But the prior of this monastery, seeing their—that is, the men of Hastière’s—arrogance, and fearing that, if the election were delayed, an uproar might arise, confirmed the decision of their election in favour of the often-mentioned Wibald, abbot of Stavelot, with the consent of the entire convent. After returning from the emperor’s court—for he had stayed there for some months—and hearing this, he came to Waulsort and, lying prostrate on the ground, humbly excused himself from this burden,” etc.]

We wish your beloved persons to know that, being presently occupied with affairs of the realm, we have been unable to come as far as Stavelot. But once a new king has been appointed for us by the grace of almighty God, and we are somewhat freer from public occupations, we shall be ready to assist in your need—not indeed on account of the proposal of election, but from the duty of brotherhood.

Meanwhile, for your consolation, we have sent you the privilege which we obtained for your Church from our lord and father Pope Eugenius. We have also sent you our letters, which we are sending to the lord bishop of Metz concerning the same matter, advising your diligence to ensure that they are conveyed to him with all speed. We have taken care to send you for inspection a copy of these letters together with a copy of those which we sent to the men of Hastière; we wish them to be shown to your friends and religious men, and especially to our fellow abbots. [Col. 1389C]

### Letter CCCXLIII. Abbot Wibald to the Monks of Hastière

He asks them to defer proceedings concerning the dispute between themselves and the monks of Waulsort until, after the emperor’s election, he comes to them. (1152.)

[Col. 1389D]

Brother WIBALD, by the grace of God what he is in the Catholic Church, to his beloved fathers in Christ, J., venerable prior, and the other sons of the Church of Hastière: blessing and life for ever. [Col. 1390A]

When we heard by report of the death of our reverend father, we grieved deeply with you in spirit, especially because we fear the many troubles facing your Church amid this change of circumstances. We grieved particularly when we learned of the proposal of your dissension, which will greatly harm your whole community and create scandal for our person.

Since we still have in our hands the commands of the lord pope, to whom we were sent, and since the princes of our realm have summoned us by letters to their conference, where the settlement concerning the future king will be conducted, we prostrate ourselves in spirit at the feet of your whole community and earnestly beseech your fraternity, for reverence toward the lord pope, in whose legation we are, and in order to secure our perpetual service, to defer proceeding in this controversy. When, God guiding us, we come to you, we may speak and act, with the counsel of the abbots of Gembloux, Florennes, Lobbes, Floreffe, and Malonne, concerning those matters which pertain to peace between you and our brethren of Waulsort. [Col. 1390B]

[Note: [Col. 1389D] Gembloux, once a distinguished monastery founded by Count Saint Guibert, still flourishes under the Rule of Saint Benedict; its abbot takes precedence over all the nobles of Brabant in the count’s general assemblies.]

[Note: [Col. 1390D] The monastery of Saint John at Florennes, founded at the beginning of the tenth century by Gerard, bishop of Cambrai, still flourishes under the Rule of Saint Benedict.]

[Note: [Col. 1390D] Lobbes, a most ancient and noble Benedictine monastery in the diocese of Liège, a nursery of men illustrious for holiness and learning; Saint Ursmar was its founding abbot.]

[Note: [Col. 1390D] Floreffe, of the Premonstratensian Order, mentioned above.]

[Note: [Col. 1390D] Malonne is perhaps the same as the monastery of Mala, mentioned by Ansegisus in his testament. Today it belongs to regular canons.]

For your discretion should not suppose that we seek in this cause anything which is our own. Rather, we seek the things of Jesus Christ; and we neither ought nor can permit our mother, the Church of Waulsort, to be violated and diminished, even if we had to expend for this cause all the property which we are seen to possess.

### Letter CCCXLIV. Abbot Wibald to Pope Eugenius III

Concerning Emperor Conrad’s death, Frederick’s election, and matters relating to the Italian expedition which followed it. (1152.)

[Col. 1390C]

To his reverend father and lord EUGENIUS, by divine grace the one and universal pope, this brother of yours, by the grace of God and of yourself what he is in the Catholic Church: himself, in faith and truth.

Behold, venerable Father, what I feared has happened. On this account, when I was with you, as if moved by a divine and foreknowing spirit, I neither concealed nor kept silence, but urged and testified that you should receive without delay the peace of the Roman people, if it could be honourable and secure. Although we did not at all foresee this event, over which we deservedly grieve, we were nevertheless troubled by a certain presentiment of future things: lest perhaps your hope, which you had conceived regarding the [Col. 1391A] forthcoming expedition, should waver through some turn of events. [Col. 1390D]

For many things which we have read, heard, and seen done and said between the reverend pontiffs of the City and emperors filled us with not unwarranted anxiety. Although your discerning learning is at present more fully informed concerning every condition of the German realm, both by the letters of your glorious son and our lord Frederick, most invincible king of the Romans, and by the writings of certain of your devoted sons, namely bishops, our devotion toward you and our most holy mother, the Roman Church, ought not to have grown weak to the point that we failed, at least in some degree, to forewarn your eminence about matters most particularly concerning you. For each person abounds in his own judgment.

When we reached Speyer on our return from you, there met us a report more horrible than any sound, more terrible than any fury: namely, that three days earlier your sweetest and most devoted son, Conrad, the most serene former king of the Romans, had departed this life. You need not doubt or ask how great was the sorrow which overwhelmed our minds at the loss of so gracious and merciful a prince toward us, and at our fear of the future change in the Empire. [Col. 1391B]

We sailed with the utmost speed to Cologne, so that the archbishop of Cologne might be more cautious and freer in providing for the commonwealth, insofar as he would be safer among his own people from every assault of a turbulent assembly. The highest princes then began, through envoys and letters, to seek a conference among themselves for the ordering of the realm. Thus it happened that, although very few were thought likely to come, a very great multitude of nobles assembled at the town of Frankfurt on the seventeenth day after the death of the aforesaid magnificent prince. [Col. 1391C]

Accordingly, as the wishes of all converged—or rather, to speak more truly, as the desires of each vied to run ahead—Frederick, formerly duke of Swabia and now ruler of affairs, was elected with the highest assent of all. With equal eagerness and admiration, on the fifth day afterward, he was raised at Aachen by sacred anointing to the royal throne, according to the custom of the ancestors.

Certainly, with all reverence preserved for divine omnipotence, which was working in human hearts to incline their wills wherever it pleased, in this incredible and rapid unanimity each person was drawn by his own inclination. Many voices, at the very placing of the crown, called for him to confirm and complete the Italian expedition which his uncle had vigorously arranged. On the following day, moreover, the counsel and exhortation both of the archbishop of Cologne and of the bishops present there was that, having received military oaths for the same expedition, he should advance the Italian expedition to repel the injuries done to the apostolic see. [Col. 1391D]

But the lay princes, perhaps with straightforward intent, earnestly proposed that the ruler should not be bound by so grave a pledge amid this new state of affairs, lest the insolence of rebels, assured of his swift departure, burst forth into the utmost audacity of madness. They further held that it was fitting for him to come when called by you rather than of his own accord. Thus the undertaking was easily turned into rest.

Indeed, the heart of the king is in God’s hand, and God turns it where He pleases according to the merits of subjects. We say this because our prince, not yet, we believe, thirty years old, has hitherto been keen in intellect, ready in counsel, successful in war, eager for difficult undertakings and glory, wholly intolerant of injury, affable and generous, and splendidly eloquent according to the idiom of his own language. May God increase in him the growth of every virtue, so that he may administer judgment and justice on earth and may be with you an angel of great counsel, so that you may declare him king and defender of the Roman Church and enjoin upon him and his princes those acts which advance the honour of the Catholic Church and the salvation of the Christian people. [Col. 1392A–B]

### Letter CCCXLV. Emperor Frederick to Pope Eugenius III

Through his legates he informs Eugenius of his election and promises sincere protection of the Roman Church. (1152.)

To his most beloved father in Christ, EUGENIUS, supreme pontiff of the holy Roman Church, FREDERICK, by the grace of God king of the Romans and ever Augustus: filial love in all things and due reverence in the Lord.

“It befits the father of his country vigilantly to observe the venerable institutions of ancient kings,” etc. See under Eugenius for the year 1153, among the letters of various persons to him.

### Letter CCCXLVI. Abbot Wibald to E., Bishop of Bamberg

He gives him certain counsels to be observed in his legation. (1152.)

[Col. 1392C]

To his most reverend father and lord E., venerable bishop of the holy Church of Bamberg, Brother WIBALD, by the grace of God what he is in the Catholic Church: humble prayers and devoted service.

We are not of Pythagoras’s school, to compel our hearers to swear by our words. It will therefore be permissible for you, without a harsh reproach to our intelligence, to alter, remove, or add to our composition. For each person abounds in his own judgment. Yet, since no art is mastered to complete certainty without a teacher, although your kindly mind is not lacking in learning and eloquence, the outlines of our words, which we have laid beneath the picture of your eloquence, must not be entirely obliterated by any ornament of rhetoric. [Col. 1392D]

For when, still young, we entered the court some thirty years ago, more or less, we found among certain more serious men remnants of the imperial majesty, derived from the companionship and training of the elder Emperor Henry. They retained by memory, as though weighed and measured, the words directed to the lord pope and to the City; nor did they permit us to alter them in legations or allow them to be changed by inexperienced envoys, lest the majesty of the Empire and the order of discipline fall into disuse.

Compared with other kings—namely the emperor of Constantinople and the kings of the Hungarians, Danes, Norwegians, and other peoples, both barbarian and Latin—the words of our ruler are humble. With a subtle balancing of words, we must take care not to distort in any manner of speech or action the rectitude of our sincerity between two powers, sometimes even discordant, to both of whom we are bound by a bond of fidelity. [Col. 1393A]

When, God guiding you, you have had a successful return, do not decline to repay our effort by informing us of the successful outcome of your mission; for although you surpass us in office and piety, you will not disdain to regard us as an equal in friendship. If it should please you to write to the Roman people—as indeed in this juncture it seems especially necessary for us to do—your learning may employ, in your letters to them, the same or similar words and expressions as in those written to the lord pope, with very few alterations made for the differing persons. [Col. 1393B]

### Letter CCCXLVII. Henry, Notary, to Abbot Wibald

He asks him to send the seal and golden bulls to the bishop of Bamberg. (1152.)

To his beloved lord WIBALD, abbot of Corvey, II., notary of the royal court: service.

It is the mark of a wise man to undertake, through counsel and deliberation, the business proposed to him for advancement, and, once undertaken, to commit it to fulfilment with due regard for the fitting balance of circumstances and time. The bishop of Bamberg, a prudent and steadfast man, is awaiting the seal and golden bulls, as you promised, equipped long ago on your behalf for the journey in order to carry out the legation of the lord king entrusted to him. Yet you have sent bare letters to the court for the king’s business. Certainly, if we had as great an abundance of golden bulls as of words, our lord’s legation would long ago have proceeded, advanced and completed in every respect.

Know concerning the lord king’s condition and progress that he is well. Having duly accomplished everything at Utrecht, he is proceeding through Deventer toward the regions of Saxony. [Col. 1393C–D]

### Letter CCCXLVIII. Abbot Wibald to Henry, Notary of the Royal Court

He replies to the preceding letter. (1152.)

Brother WIBALD, by the grace of God what he is in the Catholic Church, to his beloved companion and friend in Christ, II., master and notary of the royal court: the ability to judge rightly between the children of men.

You were pleased, in the manner of a censor, to rebuke us for rashness and inconsistency, even adducing a philosophical maxim, because, as you assert, we sent you bare letters and delayed the lord bishop of Bamberg, a prudent and steadfast man [Col. 1394A] already equipped to carry out the embassy of our lord the king. Among us there is a common proverb which, though inelegantly, we shall take pains to render literally for you: “Hearing ill causes one to understand ill; and understanding ill causes one to err.” For our lord the king, in the presence and with the assent of the lord bishop of Bamberg, so arranged the instruments necessary for the embassy that, once they had been carefully completed by us, they were to be sent to Anselm, steward at Aachen, to be conveyed by him as far as the bishop of Bamberg. This we endeavoured to accomplish with the greatest and most urgent diligence. Indeed, on the fifth day after your departure from us, at Aachen we gave our boy Godin a completed silver seal to convey, lest the affairs of the kingdom should any longer be entrusted [Col. 1394B] to that new and impermanent person.

As for the bare letters which we sent with the same seal, let readers and hearers judge whether they are altogether bare in the splendour of their sentiments and the ornament of their language. Yet, by royal command and at the bishops’ request, we were compelled to lay them down—not for your instruction, but as certain outlines for your portrait, because the subject was new—and we sent them to you to keep, for preservation of knowledge of these affairs. On the tenth day thereafter, that is, on Maundy Thursday, the implements for stamping gold seals were completed; we sent them to you swiftly through the provost of Marsna. On that same day we sent to the steward at Aachen a tin seal carefully impressed after the form [Col. 1394C] of the silver one, and two completed gold bullae, with all the letters and greetings appropriate for the lord bishop of Bamberg. We further added our own letter of admonition, which he could without doubt have received on the Wednesday of Easter week, if it was not neglected by the messengers.

Your prudence, therefore, ought not to have disturbed the prince’s ears as though his work and command had been omitted by us, since from our youth we have learned, under three illustrious emperors, to obey the princely command watchfully. But from the time when certain persons entered the royal court—persons who had grasped neither through knowledge nor experience the majesty and dignity of empire—our services, and those of certain other princes, [Col. 1394D] either wholly ceased or were regarded as superfluous. We do not say this because, impatient of our quiet life, we desire to roam about and concern ourselves with other people’s affairs, or because we wish to pass judgment upon everyone and pronounce sentence upon all things.

Moreover, we greatly rejoice that you have boasted of an abundance of words in preparing royal answers, an abundance which has long and sufficiently been desired not by us alone but by many faithful men of the realm. We give thanks, however, to almighty God for the safety of our lord the king. But when we asked your diligence about his condition, our attention was directed not to his bodily health—though that too concerns us—but to the first beginnings of the new ruler: whether he loves justice, he who judges the earth; whether he remained ardent or sluggish in the same purpose, [Col. 1395A] effective or idle. We have sent our boy to our lord himself and to your present experience, so that you may reply to us without delay whether our lord is to pass through Corvey.

## LETTER CCCXLIX. THE MONKS OF WALCIODOR TO ABBOT WIBALD

They beg him to undertake the governance of the monastery, to which they had elected him. (Year 1152.)

To the distinguished lord Wibald, pre-eminent among abbots in the teaching of every kind of prudence: the community of Walciodor, hungering for the prudence that may console it, wishes him to acquire, through the moderation of sacred administration, the joy of both lives [Col. 1395B].

Venerable father and lord, our flock has been deprived of the comfort of a pious shepherd; his sheepfold lies exposed to the bites of many dogs barking together on every side. Greatly shaken by fear of this assault, we recognize without doubt from such indications that the setting of his death will bring about the event of our desolation, unless the present haven of your prudent consolation comes to us in our danger. Therefore, terrified by this crisis of disturbance, after God and His mother—namely, the most blessed Mary—we have placed the anchor of our hope in the bosom of your consolation. We flee beneath the protection of your wings; trusting in your magnificent piety, we have elected you, with everyone’s assent, as abbot for the governance of our souls and the safeguarding against impending adversities, so that both we and our possessions may be delivered from imminent danger by your direction [Col. 1395C].

With heartfelt prayers, therefore, we ask that the counsel of your supporting aid may be at hand for us, so that, strengthened by your consolation, we may obtain tranquillity of body and soul under the rule of your administration. And, lest your gracious courtesy be able to defer that governance under the weight of any excuse, prostrate at your knees we humbly beg you to accept it. May the Holy Spirit, guardian of all good things, deign to guide and preserve you for the common benefit of the kingdom, the Church, and ourselves.

## LETTER CCCL. HENRY, BISHOP OF LIÈGE, TO STEPHEN OF METZ

Against the monks of Hastière, who wanted two abbots at Walciodor. (Year 1152.)

[Col. 1395D]

To his reverend brother and friend Stephen, venerable bishop of the Church of Metz: Henry, by God’s grace humble minister of the holy Church of Liège, brotherly prayers and the affection due in the Lord.

The concern of our pastoral office warns us to exercise watchful care over the sheep entrusted to us, [Col. 1396A] so that, after the manner of the supreme Shepherd, we may restore wanderers to the fold, and lead those who are obedient and unstained by any blemish of discord to the pastures of life, calling them by name. Accordingly, we inform your discretion that the monks of Hastière, wandering and erring, intent upon innovations, are utterly ruining the goods of that monastery. By both payment and promises they entice certain supporters of their perversity, desiring to gain this advantage from their obstinacy: that in one abbey, namely that of Walciodor, two abbots should be appointed contrary to the ordinances of the sacred canons and the authority of an apostolic privilege.

We therefore admonish your prudence, beloved by us in Christ, not to allow so grave a scandal to be fostered and grow among you. Deal with measured discretion concerning the proprietary right which the Church of Metz is known to possess in the abbey of Walciodor, so that you do not encroach upon the bounds of the Church of Liège, [Col. 1396B] whose office it is to examine the election and consecrate the person elected. For we, fearing divine vengeance, cannot any longer dissemble without compelling them, by canonical severity and in discharge of our office, to conform to the order of a regular election; especially since, though paternally admonished and even after five religious abbots were delegated to visit them, they have hitherto scorned obedience.

## LETTER CCCLI. HENRY, BISHOP OF LIÈGE, TO THE MEN OF WALCIODOR AND HASTIÈRE

That they should elect such an abbot as may restore a discipline nearly dead. (Year 1152.)

[Col. 1396C]

Henry, by God’s grace bishop of Liège, to the brothers at Walciodor and Hastière: may you abound in the spirit of counsel and piety.

Since your abbot has entered upon the way of all flesh, and since, in accordance with the charge committed to us, concern for your churches too has been laid upon us, we pour forth prayers to God that He may appoint for His flock such a minister that, through his assistance and diligence, the blessed religious life of monks may gain strength and increase. Because this religious life has for some time grown lukewarm among you and has disturbed the fragrance of its good repute more than was necessary, by the authority granted us from God we command you [Col. 1396D] to assemble the religious abbots of the surrounding area—of Florennes, Brogne, Gembloux, and Floreffe—and elect for yourselves such a shepherd as may revive in you a religious observance now almost dead. Farewell.

[Note: Brogne [Col. 1395D] is an abbey of the Order of St Benedict in the diocese of Namur, founded by St Gerard, abbot; its abbatial revenues are today united to the bishopric of Namur.]

### Names of the Abbots of Walciodor and Hastière

These are the names of the abbots who presided over the monastery of Walciodor and held the Church of Hastière, with all its dependencies, under the name of a single abbey: Lord Forannanus, bishop and abbot; Lord Kadroc; Lord Machalanus; Lord Immo; Lord Theoderic; Lord [Col. 1397A] Frembertus; Lord Rodolfus; Lord Lambertus; Lord Godescalcus; Lord Wulricus; Lord Theoderic.

## LETTER CCCLII. STEPHEN, BISHOP OF METZ, TO ABBOT WIBALD

He appoints a day on which he may meet him. (Year 1152.)

Stephen, by God’s grace bishop of Metz, to Wibald, by the same grace abbot of Stavelot, his beloved: greeting and every good thing.

We gladly received the letter of your affection, from which we learned of your intended arrival with us concerning the dispute between the men of Walciodor and Hastière. But since we cannot keep the day requested by you, we appoint another for you: namely, [Col. 1397B] the Monday immediately following the sixth [day] named by you; and this at Metz. Farewell.

## LETTER CCCLIII. AGREEMENT BETWEEN KING FREDERICK AND DUKE BERTHOLD

(Year 1152.)

This is the agreement between Lord King Frederick and Duke Berthold.

The lord king shall give the same duke the land of Burgundy and Provence, and shall enter the aforesaid lands with the duke and help him, in good faith and with the counsel of the princes who will be on that expedition, to subdue those lands. Concerning the land now held by Count William of Mâcon through his niece, [Col. 1397C] he shall render justice to the duke; or, by the counsel or judgment of the princes themselves, the lord king shall have lordship and administration of both lands as long as he remains in those lands. After the king’s departure, the duke shall retain both lands under his own power and administration, except for archbishoprics and bishoprics, which pertain specially to the hand of the lord king. If Count William or other princes of that land have invested any bishops, the duke shall invest those same bishops.

That this agreement shall be kept on the lord king’s part was guaranteed by pledged faith by Henry, duke of Saxony; Lord Welf; Arnold the chancellor; Count Odelric of Lenzburg; Count Egeno; Count Odelric of Hornung; Marcq. of Gronbach; Arnold of Biberbach; Otto, [Col. 1397D] count palatine of Wittelsbach; Walter the seneschal; Hildebrand the cupbearer; Conrad Colbo; and his brother Sigefrid.

Duke Berthold shall have one thousand armoured knights with the lord king as long as the lord king remains in those lands. For the Italian expedition he shall lead with the lord king, for as long as he remains on that expedition, five hundred armoured knights and fifty crossbowmen. And, as security that the duke shall observe all these things without deceit or fraud, he shall give the lord king his allodial possession, namely Teck Castle with all ministerials and estates belonging there; Hetligen, Williggen, and Erstem, with all their appurtenances. And that the duke shall observe all these things, his men Burchard and [Col. 1398A] Werhner swore. The lord king, moreover, shall set the expedition in motion for the aforesaid lands from the next Kalends of June, which fall within the year of the fifteenth indiction.

## LETTER CCCLIV. OTTO, BISHOP OF FREISING, TO ABBOT WIBALD

He explains a verse of a psalm. (Year 1152.)

To his venerable brother in Christ and intimate friend Wibald, abbot of Corvey: O., minister of the Church of Freising, that which he is—greeting, with devoted service.

That the business for which you sent [someone] to the court did not receive its due progress was not owing to us. [Col. 1398B] As to the question which you raised with us at Aachen—namely, how what is read in the psalm may be referred to the Ascension of the Lord: “Lift up your gates, O princes; and be lifted up, eternal gates”; and, “Who is this King of Glory?”—we answer briefly that three senses are found in the same authority, of which this is one.

Read the glosses on the Psalter and you will find, concerning “Lift up the gates,” that the ministering powers cried out to the other heavenly powers to open the way. Astonished by the new mystery of one clothed in flesh, they ask, “Who is this?” You will also be able to find there the interpretation which you mentioned, concerning the princes of darkness and the gates of death, whence comes that utterance, “I am made King of Glory.” Yet the eternal gates are not infernal [Col. 1398C] but likewise heavenly. Hence again that Gloss: “Lift up,” that is, “remove,” “the gates of death which were set by the prince, the devil; and be lifted up, eternal gates, against the gates of death.” That is, every grace which was given at Christ’s coming. And elsewhere: “The angels going before to hell say: ‘Remove your power.’”

And at the Ascension, according to you, they say to the princes of darkness, in the descent to hell: “Lift up,” that is, “remove, O princes, your gates”; according to us, in the ascent to heaven they say to their own princes: “Lift up,” in the sense of “open,” so that “Lift up the gates” has the same meaning as “Be lifted up, eternal gates.” The third sense of the same reading is mortal.

We have written this to your affection, not because we presume that your wisdom should be taught by our folly, but because we desire that our ignorance may be excused before your discernment. Since the sense of Scripture is known to be manifold, do not charge us [Col. 1398D] with having introduced this authority concerning the Ascension of the Lord, while speaking of the ascent to the people, from our own heart rather than from that of the holy Fathers. For in the first sense those in the psalm say, “Who is this King of Glory?” who in the prophet say, “Who is this who comes from Edom?” Do not be angry at the style, since we wrote in haste. We love your person in true charity toward God; and we grieve greatly over everything that can harm you, especially over what has been inflicted upon your brotherhood by the Saxons, the ancient enemies of the realm.

## LETTER CCCLV. ABBOT WIBALD TO CARDINAL JORDAN

He gives thanks for benefits shown to him and asks that he entrust the case of the provost of Xanten to the archbishop of Cologne for settlement. (Year 1152.)

[Col. 1399A]

To his reverend father and lord Jor., venerable presbyter-cardinal of the holy Roman Church and legate of the Apostolic See: Brother Wibald, by God’s grace that which he is in the Catholic Church, [sends] humble prayers and devoted service.

[Note: St Bernard sharply attacks this cardinal, legate of the Apostolic See, in Letter 290 to the cardinal of Ostia, where he describes his wickedness and avarice.]

We offer your dignity manifold thanksgivings, because, while you were in Lotharingia, you remembered our smallness with great goodwill and blessing, and readily supported our people and our interests [Col. 1399B] with your defence as circumstances allowed, as we learned from letters of our faithful men who were far away. For these services of such fatherly mercy, we have resolved henceforth to love your person more devotedly and to venerate the Roman curia more attentively, so that neither death nor life can tear us from its charity.

When, returning from Rome, we reached Cologne with the lord archbishop, we found Lord Theobald, provost of Xanten, so weakened by a grave and prolonged illness that, with skin clinging to his bones, he could scarcely draw a feeble breath. We heard the priors of the Church of Cologne confess in a great assembly of clergy that the aforesaid provost had repeatedly presented himself in the Church of Cologne for every judicial proceeding [Col. 1399C] concerning the complaint which his canons had against him, whereas those same canons, although often summoned for this matter by the senior provost and the priors, had refrained from coming.

Accordingly, we, your sons, in the boldness of the true charity by which we love you in the Lord, suggest to your clear-sighted discretion that you remit this same case to the lord archbishop of Cologne to be heard and settled; and do not allow anyone to persuade you of an injury done by the aforesaid provost.

## LETTER CCCLVI. ARNOLD, ARCHBISHOP OF COLOGNE, TO ABBOT WIBALD

He asks him whether he may veil nuns at Pentecost. (Year 1152.)

[Col. 1399D]

Arnold, by God’s grace, if he is anything, humble minister of the holy Church of Cologne, to Lord Wibald, by the same grace venerable abbot of Corvey: greeting and service.

On the octave of Pentecost we intend to veil a nun, but certain persons have told us that this is not permitted except on the Epiphany of the Lord, the feasts of the Apostles’ births, and the Monday of Easter. Therefore, not fully remembering what we were taught on this matter by the lord pope, we consult your prudence, which knows the provisions of sacred law [Col. 1400A] more fully, and ask that your learning may deign to certify us in writing whether a nun may be veiled only on the aforesaid solemnities, [Note: We have discussed the consecration of virgins in Book II of *On the Ancient Rites of the Church*, chapter 6, where we considered the day of consecration, no. 5.] or only on Sundays, as we seem to recall having received from the lord pope.

## LETTER CCCLVII. ABBOT WIBALD TO ARNOLD, ARCHBISHOP OF COLOGNE

He replies to the preceding letter and treats certain other matters. (Year 1152.)

To his reverend father and lord in Christ Arnold, venerable archbishop of the holy Church of Cologne: Brother Wibald, by God’s grace that which he is in the Catholic Church, humble prayers and devoted [Col. 1400B] service.

The humility of the most eminent Teacher, who commanded His followers, “But you are not to be called Rabbi,” and the charity which “is not puffed up,” have taught you to deign to seek from our smallness the ordinances of the sacred canons, whose knowledge is very familiar to your learning. Indeed, concerning the time when the consecration of virgins should take place, we have in chapter 11 of the decrees of Pope Gelasius the following words:

> “The sacred veil is not to be imposed upon devoted virgins except either at Epiphany, or during the Easter Albs, or on the feasts of the Apostles’ births; and not before the age of twenty-five, unless perhaps, as was said concerning baptism, they are seized by grave illness, lest they depart from this world without this gift; in that case it is not to be refused to those who ask for it.”

If, then, you recall that something has been done by any bishop contrary to the form of this sacred rule, what has been presumed out of necessity or neglected through ignorance by one person or a few cannot become an observance of all. Yet as to your not clearly remembering what you were taught by the lord pope concerning the veiling of nuns: so far as our memory can recall, it concerned not the veiling of nuns but the consecration of bishops. On this point he asserted that canonical authority exists to the effect that it should be done on the feasts of the Apostles’ births and other solemnities, and only on Sundays. This authority is as follows, from Leo’s letter to Dioscorus:

> “That ordinations of priests are celebrated on Sunday we know to derive not only [Col. 1400D] from custom but also from apostolic teaching. Scripture makes this clear: when the apostles, at the Holy Spirit’s command, sent Paul and Barnabas to preach the Gospel to the nations, fasting and praying they laid their hands upon them, so that we may understand with what devotion both those giving and those receiving must take care that the sacrament of so great a blessing may not seem to have been performed negligently. Indeed, you will act piously and laudably in conformity with apostolic ordinances if you yourself preserve this form for the ordination of priests throughout the churches over which the Lord has willed you to preside: so that the blessing is never conferred upon those to be consecrated [Col. 1401A] except on the day of the Lord’s Resurrection, whose beginning is known to be reckoned from the evening of Saturday. This day is consecrated by such great mysteries of the divine dispensations that whatever the Lord has established most remarkably has been accomplished in the dignity of this day. On it the world received its beginning; on it, through Christ’s resurrection, death received its beginning and life its increase.”

Our prince offers a well-founded assurance of hope to those who deserve well of him. With great goodwill and delight he remembers the service which you rendered him freely and more than freely in his advancement to the summit of empire; and afterwards, in his first beginnings, you stood by the commonwealth and his interests with singular loyalty and steadfastness without failing. Hence Lotharingia is your kingdom, and he intends to order all things through your provision and action. The chancellor and notary are faithful informants concerning this matter, and indeed appropriate ones in view of the barking attacks of certain laymen.

Concerning the castle which you lately and gloriously captured, you may, without offence to the royal mind, arrange whatever is most advantageous. Spare the abbot of Prüm, [Note: Prüm is an imperial monastery in the diocese of Trier, newly built by Pippin, king of the Franks, and his wife Bertha on the River Prüm; it is made most famous by the retirement of Emperor Lothar, who lies buried in the middle of its choir.] lest the serene emperor sin against God with even a slight detriment to his reputation.

We shall come to you on the feast of the martyrdom of Peter and Paul; yet, though urgently requested by the bishop of Minden because of his own case, we shall be with you and at your side. The monks of St Remigius [Note: This was a cell dependent on the chief monastery of St Remigius at Reims, situated first one stone’s throw from Maastricht on the Meuse, formerly in the diocese of Liège and now in that of Roermond. Queen Gerberga founded it on the advice of Gerard, bishop of Toul; see Marlot, Book III of the *History of Reims*.] at Marsna are much harassed by the cunning of Goswin; unless your piety [Col. 1401C] protects them, they will be utterly deceived.

## LETTER CCCLVIII. ARNOLD, ARCHBISHOP OF COLOGNE, TO HENRY, BISHOP OF MINDEN

He complains that Vortlevius was mutilated by his followers at Henry’s instigation, summons Henry to Cologne, and summons all accomplices in this crime to answer there. (Year 1152.)

Arnold, by God’s grace, if he is anything, humble minister of the holy Church of Cologne, to Henry, by the same grace venerable bishop of Minden: greeting and prayers in the Lord.

A mournful and altogether pitiable complaint concerning a new and most unspeakable crime, brought to us and [Col. 1401D] to our holy mother, the Church of Cologne, disturbed all minds with the sharpest grief, terrified them with horror, and moved them to compassion. Brother Vortlevius returned from the city of Minden to the city of Cologne, where he was born—a man who, while he lived among us, was certainly of blameless life. In the house of blessed Peter, in the presence of the entire Church of Cologne and many princes [Col. 1402A] who had come for the solemn royal reception, he suddenly threw himself at our feet. Miserably displaying the dreadful scars of wounds and the cavities of his eyes, deprived of the eyes themselves, he made a grave complaint against your person—would that it were foreign to your serenity!—affirming that, after a complaint against him had been made to your followers at your prompting and direction, they mutilated his limbs and, what is most miserable in life, made him blind.

Since, though unworthy, we sit in the chair of blessed Peter under the force of an apostolic command, we adhere to the lines of justice. Having assembled the abbots and all the priors of Cologne, and having had before them the complaint made against you repeated, we command your brotherhood, by apostolic authority and our own, to present yourself to us at Cologne for the judgment of the Church forty days after receiving this letter of ours, [Col. 1402B] as the reckoning of time establishes the canonical interval. And because one who neglects his reputation is cruel—may God avert this from your serenity—we likewise command you strictly to warn those whom the aforesaid Vortlevius names as perpetrators of so great a sacrilege, and whom he says returned to you after committing the crime and lived familiarly with you in your household, to come to Cologne on that same day to answer for themselves, for the reputation of your glory. Your learning knows what the apostolic decrees have ordained concerning offenders of this kind.

Furthermore, we ask you by every means to present with yourself those whom Vortlevius calls as witnesses that, in their presence, your threats against him and your complaint [Col. 1402C] to those who blinded him were uttered; and also the two brothers whom he denounced for betrayal.
