Thus may the truth of deeds and words be made clear, and justice be rendered to each person with the end that his spirit may be saved. We have written the names of the aforesaid below.

Perpetrators: Elgerus, Wluerus, Bernardus, Poppo, Fridericus, Wikerus, Arnoldus, Eiluardus, Robertus.

Witnesses called: the abbot of Insula; Wernerus, provost; Anno, provost; Robertus, dean; Godeboldus, master of the school; Nithardus, abbot of Bursfelde.

[Note: Bursvelde or Bursfelde is a monastery of the Order of St Benedict in Saxony, in the diocese of Mainz, founded in honour of the holy Apostle Thomas and St Nicholas the Confessor by Count Henry of Northeim and his wife Gertrude. It gave its name to the most celebrated congregation in Germany and has today become prey to the Lutherans.]

Those denounced for betrayal: Eppo, Reimarus.

## LETTER CCCLIX. ABBOT WIBALD TO EMPEROR FREDERICK

He seeks redress for the outrage inflicted upon his people by Folcuin and Widikind. (Year 1152.)

[Col. 1402D]

To his illustrious conqueror and most serene lord Frederick, by God’s grace glorious emperor of the Romans, Augustus: Brother Wibald, by God’s grace that which he is [Col. 1403A] in the Catholic Church, greeting in Him who gives salvation to kings.

Unable to explain in our own words the injury inflicted upon the Church of Corvey and upon ourselves, we groan with the prophet, saying: “We looked for peace, and it did not come; for a time of healing, and behold, trouble.” For we had hoped that in the time, and especially at the beginning, of your reign—when God by His marvellous and swift power, with the highest and welcome concurrence of all princes, raised you to the throne of the realm—the hands of robbers would be restrained, theft punished, and treachery eliminated. Since no wickedness can withstand your power, our own men, who had sworn fidelity to us and have received great benefits from us, attacked us while we were secure in this confidence and fearing nothing at all. With armed force they entered our town of Höxter. Having first sent their soldiery gradually and in troops, at last Folcuin and Widikind, brothers, armed and with banners unfurled, fell upon the unsuspecting people and occupied the whole place with hostile devastation [Col. 1403B].

They remained there for three days, utterly devastating the whole surrounding district which belongs especially to the brethren’s maintenance. Everywhere they committed most heinous crimes against men and women. After the public and common plunder, estimated at nine hundred pounds of denarii, they extorted two hundred and fifty-three pounds of coin from the better captives, whom they had separated from the poorer crowd. Moreover, though they were advocates of that place, they destroyed the rampart and fortifications which had been built by royal authority and especially by the privilege of your uncle and predecessor of blessed memory [Col. 1403C].

There was no hostility between us and them. Quite recently we had parted from them with the kiss of peace; they had never brought any complaint, either to us or to anyone else, concerning the aforesaid townsmen; nor was any suspicion of evil entertained between them and our people. Because of this atrocious wrong, while we were absent our brethren laid the bodies of Saints Vitus and Justin, which rest among us, upon the ground; and, having lowered the images of our crucified Saviour, they have since abstained from every solemn divine office and from the ringing of bells.

Prostrate at the knees of your majesty, therefore, we, our brethren, and the entire household of Corvey humbly beseech your clemency not to delay, as befits princely excellence, in avenging this notable outrage, which in no small degree obscures your dignity [Col. 1403D]. Otherwise, not only shall we no longer be able to serve you and the realm, as we hold it our special duty to do, but we shall not even be able to live honourably in the land of Saxony.

## LETTER CCCLX. ABBOT WIBALD TO BERNARD, BISHOP OF PADERBORN

That he should take vengeance upon Folcuin and Widikind, who had attacked and violated the Church of Corvey. (Year 1152.)

To his reverend father and lord in Christ Bernard, venerable bishop of the holy Church of Paderborn: Brother Wibald, by God’s grace that which he is in the Catholic Church, humble prayers and devoted service.

We trust in God’s mercy and your kindness that it adheres more firmly to your memory how greatly we have loved your fatherhood for a long time, and that we have never sought to disturb your peace. We also recall gratefully and gladly that in equal return we have continually been loved by you. Your discretion knows, however, how violently and dishonourably your kinsmen and men—both yours and ours—Folcuin and Widikind attacked us and the Church of Corvey, and with how great disgrace they treated our town and townspeople [Col. 1404B], and with what rashness they violated the church and consecrated places. They dragged our men, fleeing to the church as to a singular refuge, from the sacred buildings by armed force; and besides the common plunder of household goods, which can scarcely be reckoned, they compelled the wretched men, under peril of captivity and death, to pay two hundred and fifty-three marks for their own safety.

Since we cannot any longer overlook these manifold and grievous injuries, among other matters we bring before you that which concerns episcopal redress—namely, the violation of the holy church. We urgently appeal to you, both for God’s charity and out of reverence for the lord pope, to render us justice, as for a notorious crime, against those named and against the other violators of churches in your diocese whose names we have sent you [Col. 1404C]. We shall at a suitable time offer you the two letters of the lord pope concerning the same case which we have in our possession.

We also wish your discretion to know that concerning the rebuilding of our town’s fortifications, at the recent court held at Würzburg, we received the judgment of the realm before the lord king and all the princes. Since the marshal of the lord king is present with us for this work, we earnestly admonish and ask your affection to restrain your ministerials from harassing us, should those lords perhaps wish to molest us again. We beseech you to take care to inform us by your letter and by the present messenger what you intend to do concerning our petition [Col. 1404D].

We seek swift vengeance for a notorious crime because it is manifest to all and cannot be denied that they violated the church and sacred cemetery, and violently dragged men from there in order to extort the sum of money stated above.

## LETTER CCCLXI. ARNOLD, ARCHBISHOP OF COLOGNE, TO ABBOT WIBALD

He sympathizes with his adversities and informs him of the siege of Seyne Castle. (Year 1152.)

To Wibald, his beloved brother and venerable abbot of the holy Church of Corvey: Arnold, by God’s grace, if he is anything, humble minister of the people of Cologne, greeting with heartfelt affection and service.

Although the course of our friendship, happily begun and thereafter happily maintained, cannot be expressed in words, it is nevertheless so sweet to speak a little of it and to enjoy its remembrance that it can indeed be understood by the mind but finds no adequate expression in speech. Since I sympathize, as duty requires, with all your adversities, I grieve especially, and more rightly, that when you came to our synod you suffered an attack by wicked men. Whatever you deem fitting for your honour in these matters, I shall gladly pursue until fitting satisfaction is made.

Now, lest you be unaware of our situation, know that we are engaged in the siege of Seyne Castle, its outcome still unknown, and we regard the mind of the lord of Trier as though it hung in the balance [Col. 1405B]. Yet many reports, both fearful and hopeful, reach our ears; but charity casts out fear, and hope does not disappoint. May God, the searcher of all things, know that I pursue violators of peace not from private hatred but for justice and the duty of pastoral care. For because the land has long been shaken and troubled, its breaches must be healed. And now, since all enemies of peace have become my enemies, I beg that prayers for my sins be offered by your Church, so that, by His aid—without whom nothing is strong—we may stand firm. Farewell. If anything else happens to us, you will not be left unaware.

### Letter 362. Arnold, Archbishop of Cologne, to Pope Eugenius III

He refers to him the case of the bishop of Minden concerning the blinding of the cleric Wortliev, having meanwhile pronounced a sentence of excommunication against the authors and supporters of this crime. (1152.)

[Col. 1405C]

To the reverend Father and supreme pontiff EUGENIUS, ARNOLD, humble servant of the holy Church of Cologne; W., provost of the greater church; A., dean; T., provost of Xanten; G., provost of Bonn; and the entire convent of the aforesaid church: due obedience with every submission.

Concerning the dispute which was argued before us between the bishop of Minden and a poor cleric named Vortliev [Col. 1405D], we have been admonished and requested by both parties to bear witness regarding the things which we saw and heard, and which were handled before us; we therefore bear witness. We make known to Your Excellency's Majesty that the aforesaid poor man, coming into our presence, laid before us a pitiable and tearful complaint: that, by the consent and command of the bishop, he had been blinded by the bishop's ministerials.

Having therefore taken counsel with our brethren concerning this matter, it seemed good to us that the bishop should be summoned to our hearing and heard upon this charge. When he appeared before us to answer the accusation and had been charged with this abominable deed, he confessed that eleven ministerials [Col. 1406A] had gone out from his household and returned to it after committing, without his knowledge, this utterly detestable crime. He added that, after pronouncing Your sentence of excommunication upon all those who had both consented and acted, he had been compelled, by a popular disturbance, to absolve certain persons who had been in the company, because they denied laying hands upon the cleric.

After this confession, when he offered us a purgation of his innocence, the whole Church almost cried out against it. We did not dare to hear it, both because it seemed dangerous to us in view of such a confession, and because you have reserved to yourself alone the punishment of offences of this kind. But upon all the evildoers, both those consenting and those acting, we proclaimed Your sentence, together with all our suffragans [Col. 1406B], except the bishop of Utrecht, who happened to be absent at the time, so that they may be firmly held in our bonds until they present themselves before Your presence and submit themselves, according to Your command, to fitting satisfaction. It therefore belongs to Your fatherhood, under such testimony concerning words and deeds, to judge this affair according to the good pleasure of Your discernment and prudence.

### Letter 363. The Nuns of Ostermere to Abbot Wibald

They complain of his ministerials, who were seizing the tithe he had granted them. (1152.)

To their distinguished Father and most worthy lord, Lord WIBALD, abbot of Corvey: his special daughters in [Col. 1406C] the place called Ostermere, progressing from Leah's bleary-eyed condition to Rachel's beauty, greeting.

If we attempted to set forth in writing what magnificence of praise befits the greatness of your exalted rank, our limited understanding would fail us. Yet the ever-burning fire of our prayers shall continually offer upon the altar of incense the memory of you, most sweet to us; and may the overflowing Rewarder repay your fatherly graciousness, which, though we are unworthy, you have hitherto piously shown us in all our affairs; and may Christ grant the hearing of your serenity to the complaints of His poor women.

Therefore, most holy Father, our prayer, knowingly aflame, hastens to you as to a fountain of mercy, that you may thoroughly investigate and resolve the cause [Col. 1406D] of our business as the Holy Spirit shall dictate to your heart. We therefore make known to your nobility—indeed, we complain tearfully to your honey-sweet fatherhood—that your ministerials grievously harass us over the tithe which, divine mercy permitting, your providence granted us. They wish to violate and nullify what has been established by your authority and counsel, and they endeavour in every way to take it away unless they are admonished by your dignity.

Most reverend lord, we cannot escape through our own efforts this injury of such unspeakable grief and this affront to your person—for you yourself were party to the case—unless we are sustained by your compassion. Therefore, O pious consolation of our souls, O our hope after [Col. 1407A] the Lord: though absent in body, yet present in spirit, we cast ourselves down humbly, with every affection of heart and mind, at the bosom of your fatherly mercy. Beseeching your clemency with supplication and a contrite spirit, we ask that, for the sake of God and of the lord archbishop, who most earnestly commended us to your mercy, you send your letters to the bishop of Paderborn and ask him to confirm by his authority that we may no longer be harassed and that the possessions which we lawfully hold may remain inviolate.

Farewell. We earnestly commend our dearest father to Your Holiness, and urgently ask that you show him consideration in all his troubles.

### Letter 364. Abbot Wibald to Pope Eugenius III

On behalf of Abbot Sifrid of Ullesheim, whom the bishop of Verden expelled from his monastery though he had neither been accused nor convicted. (1152.)

[Col. 1407B]

To his reverend Father in Christ and lord EUGENIUS, supreme pontiff of the holy Roman Church, brother WIBALD, by the grace of God that which he is in the Catholic Church: humble prayers and devoted service.

The bearer of this letter, a son of the Church of Corvey, our colleague and brother in the Lord, Sifrid, was taken from the monastery of Corvey to the office of abbot of Ullesheim [Note: [Col. 1407] Commonly called Ulsen, founded in 990 for women; Bishop Ditmar of Verden, about 1140, replaced them with monks taken from Corvey.]. He has administered it for more than twelve years [Col. 1407C], with discipline and growth in his order and increase in temporal goods, so that he enjoyed a good testimony even from those outside.

The lord H., bishop of Verden, in whose diocese that monastery lies, expelled him from his abbey without summons, without hearing, neither convicted nor confessing; and for more than a year now he has stripped him of all the monastery's goods. Although he has often and earnestly been admonished concerning this by us and also by our reverend fellow-brethren, the abbots of nearly all Saxony, he has refused either to restore our fellow-brother or to deal with him according to canonical procedure.

Moreover, to crown this intolerable affront, he gathered again into that church of evildoers, as into a sewer, certain pseudo-monks whom the aforesaid abbot had expelled from the monastery because of the enormity [Col. 1407D] of their way of life. Whatever these wicked and angry men, eager to avenge themselves, could fabricate against the abbot's reputation, he wrote down and circulated.

Therefore, in spirit we cast ourselves at the feet of Your Exaltedness, together with all our brethren, and pour forth humble prayers: receive with the gentleness of your goodness the aforesaid abbot when he comes to your clemency—a man indeed honourable and learned—and, having heard him in his necessity, restore him by letters and commands of your authority, through some faithful legate of yours, to the full possession of his dignity.

### Letter 365. Abbot Wibald to Arnold, Archbishop of Cologne

He congratulates him on his victory and intercedes with him for the bishop of Minden. (1152.)

[Col. 1408A]

To his reverend Father in Christ and lord ARNOLD, venerable archbishop of the holy Church of Cologne, brother WIBALD, by the grace of God that which he is in the Catholic Church: humble prayers and devoted service.

We rejoiced at the things said to us, and went rejoicing and giving thanks into the house of the Lord, because you have won a glorious triumph over tyrants and robbers. Everywhere, through the working of sin, they have now grown so numerous [Col. 1408B] that no church and no place, sacred or secular, can at all be defended from their attacks. May divine power grant this victory to Your Blessedness for many years.

We wish Your Exaltedness to know that, at the most recent feast of the blessed apostle James, we went down to Minden at the bishop's request and the clergy's petition, in order to settle and compose certain dissensions by which the harmony of bishop and clergy had been disturbed. These causes were neither criminal nor decisive, but concerned rather estates: namely, mills, marshes, common pastures, inheritances, and patrimonies. Over these the bishop's estate-managers disputed against the canons' estate-managers, and certain clerics against certain laymen.

This disturbance had become somewhat more inflamed against the bishop because, at the Council of Cologne, he had undergone an accusation and a severe rejection. Yet, so far as we could investigate, no one had proceeded so far as to be willing in any way to support or testify for the statement and accusation of that blinded man, or even for Walder's complaint. Indeed, at the celebration of that same feast, the aforesaid bishop publicly announced from the church pulpit that those who had blinded the cleric, or had contributed counsel or assistance to this crime, were excommunicated; and he pronounced a sentence of anathema against them.

When, therefore, by God's favour all had been restored to concord, we also tried to dissuade that Walder from his obstinacy [Col. 1408D] in harassing the bishop. But he himself, in the hearing of many, asserted that you had forbidden him, under a pledged faith, to make peace with the bishop.

We, who have long known your nobility and greatness of mind, could by no means believe that you would wish to inflict this affront upon your suffragan, who has always served the metropolitan see devotedly and has loved and honoured your person above all others: namely, that you would not allow his cause—one which you had been unable to conclude judicially because of the importunate insolence of the accusers—to be brought to an end by agreement.

For your learning knows by whose counsel and under what discipline those same opponents of the bishop presumed to reject your judgment, which had been supported by the testimony and assent of your suffragans and your Church; and in what manner, and under what truces granted, they appealed. Your discernment will be able to consider this from copies of their documents, while we retain copies of them here.

And although, as stated above, we clearly know that the greatness of your mind could not possibly have descended to such base and contemptible devices as entering into such outrageous terms with the aforesaid Walder, nevertheless, because of the familiar and intimate affection with which we have long loved Your Holiness, we have not hesitated to admonish your crown not to disdain to free your glory, in the eyes of the lord of Minden and his Church, from this suspicion.

The tenor of your letters [Col. 1409B] written to the lord pope, which seemed to do nothing for the bishop's innocence, heightened his fear. We wholly denied that they had been written or even read by you, precisely because your understanding well recognizes that it is the office of an inferior judge, when an appeal has been made from him to a superior, to take care in recounting the course of the action that, fairness being preserved, he may seem to have inclined favour toward neither side. You will recognize that this was by no means done in these letters.

> “I, Walder, by the grace of God deacon and however unworthy a canon of the holy Church of Minden, appeal to the pope, committing myself and my goods to his protection. I summon you, Henry, bishop of Minden, before him to answer on the Nones of September concerning the violent usurpation of my deanship and concerning other matters which I have against you.
>
> “I, Vortliev, subdeacon, summon you, H., bishop of Minden, before the presence of the lord pope concerning sacrilege, because by your counsel and command I have been blinded and beaten. I appoint the day as the Kalends of October.”

Such appeals—or rather confusions—were thrown upon the pavement after the bishop's doors had been broken open, not without bloodshed. They were neither presented to the bishop nor seen by him; we received them on that same day from the hand of the dean of the church of Saint Martin at Minden.

### Letter 366. Emperor Frederick to Abbot Wibald

He promises to avenge the injuries done to him. (1152.)

[Col. 1409D]

FREDERICK, by the grace of God king of the Romans, to WIBALD, abbot of Corvey: his favour and every good.

Beyond the common law of charity by which we are bound to honour all the princes of the realm, we embrace your person with special affection, and willingly desire in every way to advance those things known to concern your honour. Therefore, sharing with due affection your grief over the injuries inflicted upon the Church of Corvey, we counsel and commend to your discretion that you bear the present adversities with equanimity and do not begrudge to await our vengeance with a calmed [Col. 1410A] mind.

For shortly, when an opportunity of time presents itself to us, with the Lord's favour, we shall inflict such vengeance for you that others will tremble to commit similar acts. Moreover, we do not wish you to be unaware that, on the third Ides of October, with life spared to us and by counsel of the princes, we shall hold a general court at Würzburg. There we desire you to appear before us.

### Letter 367. Emperor Frederick to the Monks of Corvey

On the same subject. (1152.)

FREDERICK, by the grace of God king of the Romans, to the entire convent of the Church of Corvey: his favour and every good.

[Col. 1410B]

We share with due affection the sorrows of your community and deeply grieve at your distresses. When opportunity presents itself to us, with the Lord's favour, we intend so to avenge your injuries that your grief must be entirely relieved and all who experience the vengeance will not presume to commit similar acts.

But because, as we hear, owing to these same injuries the divine offices have ceased in your church, crosses are laid down, and saints' relics are removed, we most earnestly advise and command your discretion that, after restoring the crosses and holy relics to their former state, you celebrate the ecclesiastical offices and apply yourselves to divine worship as usual, firmly hoping that, if life remains to us, we shall obtain full vengeance for you.

### Letter 368. Emperor Frederick to the Citizens of Höxter

On the same subject. (1152.)

[Col. 1410C]

FREDERICK, by the grace of God king of the Romans, to all the burgesses of Höxter: his favour and every good.

We have heard sufficiently of the injuries inflicted upon you by F. and W. [Note: [Col. 1409D] Folcuin and Widikind.]. If life remains to us, we shall inflict such vengeance upon them that others will not presume to commit similar acts. But since, as we hear, you have promised to pay money to these evildoers, by this present writing we firmly command you to pay them no money. We also command you to endeavour, to the best of your ability, to rebuild under our protection the rampart and your other fortifications which are known to have been recently destroyed [Col. 1410D].

### Letter 369. Abbot Wibald to A., Abbot of Mont

He gives thanks because the latter charitably received the dispossessed Abbot Sifrid. (1152.)

To his reverend Father in Christ and lord A., venerable abbot of Mont, brother WIBALD, by the grace of God that which he is in the Catholic Church: greeting in the Lord and the indissoluble bond of fraternal charity.

We owe manifold thanksgivings to your beloved fraternity in Christ [Col. 1411A], because you kindly received our dear brother and colleague in the Lord, Sifrid, venerable abbot of Hullesheim, when he came to you in his tribulations and distresses. So far as was in your power, you showed him the affection of a compassionate comforter and grieved, with due sympathy, for the affront inflicted in his person upon our order.

We too deeply grieve for the justice despised in him: both because of the general degradation of the whole monastic order and because of the particular disgrace of the Church of Corvey, of which he is a son. We proclaim with mournful and heartfelt complaint this violence done to his person in the hearing of Your Holiness and all venerable brethren—namely our fellow abbots—and of all who live in holy religion: that he has been deprived of the dignity and goods of his abbey without summons, without judgment, without hearing, and without confession from his own mouth. Neither through our petition, nor through the intercession of the Church of Corvey, nor that of any order or dignity, could he obtain after this deed that he be summoned to judgment and his cause handled according to canonical procedure.

We therefore bear witness before the lord pope and the holy Roman Church to the injustice inflicted upon him; and, insofar as lies in us, we shall not fail in the duty of our office to support his complaint wherever he may need it. We urgently ask this of your fatherhood: as you have done thus far, graciously bestow your consolation upon him [Col. 1411C]. Make his cause known to the holy Fathers in the region around you, and earnestly stir them up by your admonitions and exhortations to sympathize with his affliction and to raise his spirits, both through letters bearing their testimony and through other aids of humanity.

In particular, we commend this poor man, cast down and humiliated, to our dearest elder and brother in Christ, Etbert, venerable abbot of Huisbruc, whose holiness of life we embrace with true charity in the Lord. With all devotion we beseech him to grieve in Christ's stead for this man's cause, and, as far as he can, to comfort his abasement.

### Letter 370. Henry the Notary to Abbot Wibald

The emperor has summoned Folcuin and Widikind concerning injuries inflicted upon the brethren of Corvey; the bishop of Bamberg has been granted the abbey of Altaha; etc. (1152.)

[Col. 1411D]

To his lord WIBALD, venerable abbot of Corvey, HENRY, notary of the royal court: the service of a servant.

As you instructed me, I diligently set forth to the lord king your embassies and complaint [Col. 1412A]. Greatly troubled by your injury and grievance, he summons the evildoers, namely Folcuin and Widikind, to appear before him at Worms on the feast of the apostle Bartholomew, in order that he may demand, by strict judgment, satisfaction for the injury inflicted upon you and the Church of Corvey. He also earnestly requests the duke of Saxony to administer full justice upon the aforesaid evildoers. He writes and sends commands, as you informed me, to the Church of Corvey and to the burgesses of Höxter.

Concerning the state of the court, know that the bishop of Bamberg returned from the lord pope bearing favourable news, but sought a rather great reward for his labour: the abbey of Alta [Note: [Col. 1411D] Altaha is a double monastery, Upper and Lower, both most celebrated houses of the Benedictine order in Lower Bavaria beside the Danube, founded by Duke Odilo in the eighth century and still flourishing.] has been assigned by the lord king to the Church of Bamberg. The people of Alta, however, oppose this decision with great indignation.

The lord king will undertake no expedition this year either against the Hungarians or toward Arles. We await a cardinal sent to us as legate from the side of the lord pope. After the court held at Ulm, the lord king will proceed to Speyer. There he will hand over his niece, betrothed to the king of Spain and splendidly endowed, to be conducted in a great retinue.

### Letter 371. Abbot Wibald to Pope Eugenius III

On the controversy publicly litigated between the abbot of Saint Lawrence at Liège and the abbot of Saint Giles at Mont. (1152.)

To his most reverend Father, Lord EUGENIUS, supreme pontiff of the holy Roman Church, brother WIBALD [Col. 1412C], by the grace of God that which he is in the Catholic Church: the fullness of all devotion, affection, and obedience, as much due as heartfelt.

Concerning the controversy between the abbot of the monastery of Saint Lawrence in the suburb of the city of Liège and the abbot of Mont Public, we shall endeavour to lay before Your Exaltedness in this letter those things that we truly learned nearly thirty-seven years ago, when as boys we were living under scholastic discipline in the aforesaid city. This is not because we had been admitted to counsel or action in such matters, or asked to inspect such agreements or compacts as witnesses; but because the report, widely circulated among clergy and students, concerning the terms contracted between the aforesaid abbots could not have been wholly unknown to us.

Berenger [Note: [Col. 1412D] Berenger, formerly prior of the monastery of Saint Hubert at Andage, was first made prior and then abbot of Saint Lawrence at Liège about 1075. A man of great merit, he governed with great praise until 1113.], abbot of the monastery of Saint Lawrence, gave the church of Saint Giles, situated at Mont Public in the aforesaid city, to a regular canon named Geric and certain brethren of the same profession, for inhabitation and enlargement according to the rule of Saint Augustine. The condition was that, if the aforesaid place should prosper and grow by divine bounty to such an extent that the brethren ought regularly to elect a pastor for themselves, the person elected should receive corporal investiture from the aforesaid abbot and should also be presented by him to receive episcopal blessing. This constitution was to remain valid through all successors.

In those regions, the practice had not yet developed whereby canons called regular should create abbots, being content in the office of prelacy with the title of provost [Note: [Col. 1413D] Most are still content with the title of provost in Belgium, and all are so in the Congregation of Windesheim, which still flourishes in Germany.]. We have learned from the authority of the holy Rule [Note: [Col. 1413D] Rule of Saint Benedict, chapter 65.] of the blessed Benedict that abbots can and customarily do ordain abbots, where it says: “Through the appointment of a provost scandals frequently arise, especially in those places where the provost is appointed by the same priest or by those abbots who appoint the abbot himself.”

One of the earliest inhabitants of that place still survives, and he was himself its first abbot: a religious man fearing God, now advanced in a good old age [Col. 1413B] and as it were on the brink of the grave. Before the whole Church of Liège he acknowledges the conditions described above.

Nevertheless, certain regulars from the aforesaid place obtained a privilege from Pope Innocent of blessed memory, in which the prerogative of the abbot of Saint Lawrence is passed over in silence. Perhaps they employed the same simplicity that they employed against us in the same privilege concerning the Church of Stavelot: they caused our holding at Heran [Note: [Col. 1413D] The instrument of this lease was issued in 1136 under Adalbero, bishop of Liège.], which they held by a leasehold right from the jurisdiction of the Church of Stavelot under a fixed annual rent, to be entered among the Church's own estates.

For sixteen years ago, pitying the poverty of the aforesaid church and of brethren whom we loved in the Lord, we granted to the present abbot the aforesaid church of Heran [Col. 1413C], together with the tithe belonging to the brethren of Stavelot, and invested him with our grant, on condition that he pay annually to the Church of Stavelot three marks and one ferton. This has also been diligently observed until now.

But because in that privilege, of which we have only now first learned, they defrauded the Church of Stavelot as described above, the agreement that had been made has, owing to the bad faith that intervened, been dissolved on the part of the Church of Stavelot; and the privilege which they obtained must be invalidated and abolished by your authority.

Moreover, we believe that Your Discretion need not doubt the innocence of the abbot of the monastery of Saint Lawrence. In the same monastery over which, by God's authorship, he now presides, he has been most excellently educated from childhood not only in regular discipline but also in the liberal arts. He was also present at the aforesaid agreements, and now meditates day and night upon the law of his God and awaits the hour of his calling with lamp alight. We devoutly beseech you to deem him worthy of your love and honour.

### Letter 372. A Certain Regular Canon to Abbot Wibald

He presents certain difficulties for him to resolve. (1152.)

[Col. 1414A]

To Lord GWIBALD, one who is his own: the grace of God and the keeping of himself.

“In apostolic fashion, you are a debtor both to the wise and to the unwise.” Therefore, deign to answer me, an unwise man, as your debtor. Some say that our order ought not to have an abbot, because Augustine did not establish this; and that we are converts and, indeed, ought to be called neither clerics nor monks.

Those who say this do not sufficiently distinguish themselves, nor do they consider that blessed Benedict, who instituted a simple penitence for monks, did not prescribe for them either the pastoral staff or ecclesiastical ranks [Note: [Col. 1414D] On the contrary, the Rule of Saint Benedict, chapter 62, “On the priests of the monastery,” is extant.]. Why, then, if they accept certain things from the Church, are they unwilling for us to accept certain things from that same Church?

In calling us “converts,” whether they wish it or not, they associate us with the apostles, who were converted to the Lord; and in this likewise they join us to monks, who are similarly converted to the Lord. Those who disparage our order for its novelty [Note: [Col. 1414D] Here the author of this letter clearly acknowledges that the institution of regular canons is new.] and commend theirs for its antiquity plainly err, because time is shown to contribute nothing in this matter; and Horace mocks such people:

> “They admit nothing except what the bier has consecrated.”  
> —Horace, *Epistles* II.1.49

But clerics, who ought principally to be subject to bishops, lower their dignity beneath an abbot by just as much as an abbot is inferior to the pontiff of all men. Determine for us what is more certainly to be maintained. Farewell.

Inform us what the abbot of Saint Lawrence ought to give the abbot of Saint Giles by means of the pastoral staff. He cannot give the care of souls, which belongs to the bishop. He will not give estates, because the staff contradicts this, since it signifies spiritual things. But abuse is the contradiction of law.

### Letter 373. Abbot Wibald to an Anonymous Correspondent

He replies to the preceding letter. (1152.)

Brother WIBALD, by the grace of God that which he is in the Catholic Church, to a certain one of his own and to all friends: a conscience clear to himself and a good reputation toward his neighbour.

[Col. 1414D] Having received the letter of your learning, in which, suppressing your name, you propose many questions to us, we recalled the Gospel parable of the mustard seed: although it is the least of all seeds, if it falls into good ground, it grows so great that the birds of heaven can nest as in a tree. So your letter is short in extent but broad in meaning [Col. 1415A]. If handled by a learned respondent, it can both grow high and yield fragrance, though not without some taste of sharpness.

But we, long exercised amid numerous labours and anxious, frequent dangers, impaired in the health of head and eyes, and now preparing to follow the court of our emperor—even if skill in such matters had ever been available to us, which we neither feel nor say of ourselves—could not, having so long abandoned study and reading, suffice to answer, especially since you have asked with the mind of one putting us to the test.

But let this for the present be your answer: what authority and reason have taught, and long-standing antiquity has observed. Moses, dwelling in the wilderness while fleeing the king of Egypt, had a staff and was the first leader and forerunner of monks. The Lord said to him: “What do you hold in your hand?” He answered, “A staff.” With the Lord's assistance, when he cast it upon the ground, it was changed into a serpent by a wondrous and mystical transformation, and then changed back into itself.

Aaron, chief of the priests, had a staff, which blossomed and bore fruit as testimony to the priesthood bestowed upon him by God's command. From these authorities of Holy Scripture, the holy Church, full of the Spirit of God, reasonably established that the successors of Aaron and Moses—of whom it is written, “Moses and Aaron among His priests,” namely bishops and abbots of monks—should receive and carry mystical staffs for the governance of their own people. From the times of the apostles to the present, for more than a thousand years, she has carefully and reverently observed this.

[Col. 1415C] If, then, as you write, clerics ought principally to be subject to bishops, it follows that the prince of clerics alone should carry a staff among clerics, as a shepherd among his own sheep. Sheep ought not to threaten the shepherd; rather, the shepherd sometimes goes before the sheep and sometimes follows them. Sometimes he draws them back, sometimes drives them away, with the staff he carries in his hand, so that they may hear his voice.

Besides, this question—or rather these questions of yours, fertile like a hydra for their own destruction and multiplying into many when one head is cut off—cannot, as stated, at this time be thoroughly examined and discussed by us in every aspect of the objections which arise. But lest your word return empty to you, we have taken care to indicate to you these few points out of many.

[Col. 1415D] This too should briefly be added: Noah's ark, which, while the Flood raged, saved eight souls under the governance of divine providence, was broad below and finished above in one cubit. By this the Holy Spirit signifies that those who abandon the broad way leading to death and direct their hearts and works upward through the narrow and confined way are higher in the Church of God—if not in office, then in merit.

Your ingenuity further asks us what the abbot of Saint Lawrence ought to give the abbot of Saint Giles by means of the pastoral staff. We in turn ask your ingenuity: if the possessor of your estate, who pays you the due rent for your field under a hereditary agreement—for example, one who holds a *mansus* from you—and, at death, leaves lawful heirs, that is, natural sons, what, I ask, do those heirs receive from you by bodily investiture, although they do not doubt that they succeed by right to their father's goods?

And to approach the matter more closely: do you suppose, brother, that everyone who receives a pastoral staff immediately becomes a bishop or abbot? Do you believe that everyone to whom a pastoral staff is handed is thereby consecrated bishop or abbot? Therefore, my brother—if indeed you are not a false brother—if you maintain a measured distinction of discernment between the signs of things and the things themselves; if, putting envy and error far away, you reject innovations that avail for nothing except the destruction of charity and human society; and if you observe with humble and obedient reverence the ancient institutions and customs of the holy Fathers [Col. 1416B], then you will clearly see how childish and frivolous are these matters with which you thought our occupations should be troubled by questioning.

Nevertheless, if after our return from the imminent court divine favour grants us health and leisure, we may answer your inquiry more fully; although, if you consider carefully, your objection ought to have been answered in these few points.

### Letter 374. Waltar, Abbot of Saint Lawrence at Liège, to Abbot Wibald

He gives thanks because Wibald undertook his defence at the synod of Liège. (1152.)

[Col. 1416C]

To the reverend Father WIBALD, by the grace of God abbot of Corvey and Stavelot, brother WALTARIUS—himself also, by God's grace, whatever he is—of the church of Saint Lawrence at Liège: sincere affection and devoted service in the Lord.

Beloved Father in Christ, I give devout thanks for your great goodwill because, at Liège in the general synod, even in my absence, you did not fail openly to uphold and defend with true and steadfast assertion the just cause of Saint Lawrence regarding the right which he has in the church of Mont Public [Note: [Col. 1415D] Namely Saint Giles, concerning which Wibald wrote above to the supreme pontiff in Letter 371.]. Thus, by your authority, the mouths of those speaking vain things have been completely stopped.

For this, we and the little flock of Saint Lawrence pray both especially and devoutly for your safety and welfare. I ask that you hear the bearer of this letter, our brother, with your customary kindness and goodness, and guide him in the cause which he presents by your counsel and protection. I hope soon to see the welcome presence of your reverence, so that I may duly seek and obtain your counsel and assistance concerning necessary matters. May heavenly mercy preserve you with everlasting protection.

### Letter 375. Abbot Wibald to Pope Eugenius III

Concerning the letter he wrote to him after the king's election. (1152.)

To his most beloved Father in Christ and lord EUGENIUS [Col. 1417A], sole and universal pope, brother WIBALD, by the grace of God and yours that which he is in the Catholic Church: himself and all that is his.

The letters which we wrote to Your Highness after the ordination of our lord, the new king, were delivered in reverse order. For those which had been written first and entrusted to Brother Franco for delivery, when we believed that he would soon return to Your Blessedness, were presented later. Master Balderic of Trier had brought first the second letters which we wrote to Your Greatness. And now we write with some anxiety and uncertainty because of your legate, whom we have heard is coming but have not yet received upon his arrival, [Col. 1417B] so that, after hearing from him your good pleasure, we—your willing servants, obedient to every nod of your will and ready to carry out your commands—might communicate more definite particulars to Your Excellency.

Indeed, if our kingdom could at last cease from its internal and most destructive disturbances, Your Charity need have no doubt that our most holy mother, the Roman Church, might recover the splendor of her former dignity through the strength of our prince. And would that, good Jesus, you who truly said, “I have prayed for you, Peter, that your faith may not fail,” might also deign, together with the Father whom you entreat, to grant that it need not depend upon human protection, but only upon your help, and may be withdrawn from harmful things and directed toward salutary ones. For it is hard [Col. 1417C] that those whom you have deigned to place upon the highest summit of imperial power should be servants. But enough of this. For your wisdom, enlightened by God, has been accustomed both to understand us and prudently to arrange very many matters. We shall write more openly and at greater length when we have heard from your legate what needs to be done.

Concerning the case of the bearer of this letter, we kiss the feet of Your Holiness, asking that you may strengthen him against the presumption of laymen, lest they boast that they possess God’s sanctuary as an inheritance, which they are even hastening to profane by succession—namely, by appointing in the Church the sons of their predecessors.

## LETTER 376. ABBOT WIBALD TO HERMANN, CANON OF BONN.

He entrusts him and his niece with the stewardship of Castiniac. (1152.)

[Col. 1417D]

WIBALD, by the grace of God abbot of Corvey, to his beloved brother and friend HERMANN, canon of the Church of Bonn: blessing and life unto everlasting.

We entrust to your fidelity our stewardship of Castiniac, with all its appurtenances, as Louis the nephew held it: that is, according to the agreements and conditions which our predecessor of happy memory, Lord Erchembert, ordained and established concerning that estate and stewardship. Namely, you are to rebuild what has been destroyed and restore what has fallen into disrepair, [Col. 1418A] both in the demesne house and in the cellar, wine-press house, cattle-shed, and in the other buildings and enclosures.

After your death we also grant the same stewardship, in the manner stated above, to your niece, the daughter of the aforesaid Louis, upon this condition: that the same girl be transferred to the Church of Corvey into the legal status of ministeriales from her present lords, to whom she now belongs; and that this be accomplished without labor or expense to us, within the year beginning from the present feast of St. Michael the Archangel, which falls in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1152, indiction 1. Further, when the said girl reaches marriageable age, she is not to marry except with the permission of us or of whoever shall canonically succeed us in the abbacy of Corvey.

[Col. 1418B] If any of the prescribed conditions is omitted or violated by you or by the same girl, you shall thereafter forfeit the aforesaid stewardship with all its benefice, without hope of recovery. But if you are negligent in paying wine, grain, money, vessels, or other rents on the appointed days, you shall answer for such an offense either before the court of the household at Castiniac or before the court of our ministeriales in our hall at Corvey, whichever of these we prefer; and in settlement you shall pay twelve solidi in money.

Whatever your nephew Louis has pledged or alienated, whether as a pledge or as a benefice, from the property of the already named manor of Castiniac—whether fields, vineyards, rents, or woodland—has been annulled by judgment [Col. 1418C] of our court, or adjudged incapable of remaining in force after the steward’s death. We entrust these things to you to recover, on the condition that if you do not do so within this year, you shall lose the stewardship and the whole agreement.

The reason why we have granted the stewardship after your departure to the daughter of the late Louis is not that we acknowledge for her any hereditary succession, either in the stewardship or in her father’s benefice; for this has been universally disallowed by our ministeriales. Rather, we have been inclined to do it because of your service and that of your friends.

## LETTER 377. ABBOT WIBALD TO HILLIN, ARCHBISHOP OF TRIER.

He congratulates him on his new dignity, offers him his services, and commends to him his brethren living in his diocese. (1152.)

[Col. 1418D]

To his reverend father and lord H., venerable archbishop of the holy Church of Trier, Brother WIBALD, by the grace of God what he is in the Catholic Church: humble prayers and devoted service.

We trust in the cultivation of your kindness that the familiar affection which hitherto has grown between us through reciprocal services ought not to be diminished because of the advancement of Your Highness. For, if we hold to the rule taught us earlier by experience—while we have lived amid the labors of men [Col. 1419A] and been scourged with men under the burden of prelacy—then men of faith and constancy, who love you rather than what is yours, will be dearer to your diligence in proportion as they are rarer to find among the whole multitude of humankind.

Among that small number, we, who ought neither to deceive nor wish to be deceived, count ourselves with undiminished devotion of good will; and we greatly rejoice in the Lord at this glorious promotion of your person. [Note: [Col. 1419D] Alberic records his elevation in the year 1152, when, upon the death of Archbishop Albero, he succeeded him.] By the favor of divine providence you have been granted the ability both to benefit and to preside over that most ancient and most noble city, which is recognized as the head and metropolis of the whole of Belgic Gaul.

Accordingly, with ready devotion we offer to the support of your dignity whatever it is that God has allowed us to be, to be called, or to be able to do in his Church; and we desire that, without detriment to your prosperity, an occasion may be afforded you in which you may receive clear proof of our affection and fidelity. When we are next able to return from Saxony toward Lotharingia, we also desire to visit and greet Your Blessedness in person. Meanwhile, we commend to your kindness our brethren of Corvey who are at Liège, and all our possessions—both those of the monastery of Corvey and those of Stavelot—situated in your diocese, asking that, for the sake of your affection for us, you may deign to take them under the defense of your protection.

## LETTER 378. POPE EUGENIUS III TO EMPEROR FREDERICK.

He congratulates him on his election, hoping that he will complete what Conrad began for the exaltation of the Church. (1152.)

[Col. 1419C]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his dearest son in Christ, FREDERICK, illustrious king of the Romans: greeting and apostolic blessing.

“To the messengers of your distinguished nobility,” etc. See under Eugenius III, for the year 1153.

## LETTER 379. BISHOP BERNARD OF PADERBORN TO ABBOT WIBALD.

That he may deign to release his prior Henry, who has been chosen abbot of the monastery of St. Mary. (1152.)

[Col. 1419D]

To his beloved friend in Christ, Lord WIBALD, reverend abbot of the holy Church of Corvey, B., humble minister of Paderborn: the faithful rendering of his prayers and service.

The brethren of the monastery [Note: [Col. 1419D] This monastery is called the monastery of Sualenberg in a bull of Pope Innocent, because it was built on its own land by Count Widikind of Sualenberg and his wife, principally through the promotion of Bernard, bishop of Paderborn. He calls it in this letter “his new plantation” because it was founded in his time, namely in 1128. It is commonly called Marienmünster; it is situated in the diocese of Paderborn, between Paderborn and Corvey, and it still flourishes under the Bursfeld Congregation.] of St. Mary, bereft of their abbot—who, despite our many admonitions and prayers that he should not abandon the flock committed to him, nevertheless undertook the labors of the eremitical life, as he then declared was his intention—unanimously elected as their abbot the venerable brother [Col. 1420A] Lord Henry, prior of your monastery.

We therefore earnestly ask your fatherhood, and with all the desire of our heart hope that our request has been granted: may you kindly release him to them, compassionately considering the pressing need of our new foundation, which is known to you. If, with your permission and by his own kindness, he is willing to submit himself to the care of the burden offered him, we shall strive in every way to comfort, support, and faithfully assist him.

## LETTER 380. ABBOT WIBALD TO BISHOP BERNARD OF PADERBORN.

He excuses himself from releasing his prior. (1152.)

[Col. 1420B]

To his reverend father and lord in Christ, B., venerable bishop of the holy Church of Paderborn, Brother WIBALD, by the grace of God abbot of the Church of Corvey: the heartfelt devotion of prayers and service.

Certain brethren of the monastery of St. Mary came to us with letters from Your Holiness, earnestly requesting that we grant to them as abbot our beloved brother Henry, prior of our church, whom the same brethren had elected. In reply to this request, by the counsel of our chapter, we say to your discretion first that we do not see adequate reasons why our beloved brother Conrad, who had presided over that monastery, abandoned the care of the flock entrusted to him. On account of the eremitical life, he ought not to have deserted his brethren, whom he had undertaken to guard, [Col. 1420C] among whom there were some to whom he could have been of benefit. This is plainly shown by blessed Pope Gregory in the books of the *Dialogues* (Book II, chapter 3): “There, he says, the wicked are to be borne patiently when they are gathered together, where some good persons are found who may be helped.”

There is another reason why we cannot assent to the election of the aforesaid brethren. The rule of our monastery—and indeed all monasteries of our order observe this practice—is that, if any one of our brethren is to be chosen abbot of another monastery, he is first to be chosen by us and our brethren rather than by outsiders. No person is to be designated to us from among our brethren as abbot by another monastery or by any human being; rather, the selection of any one of our brethren is to be left to our judgment and to the election of his brethren. [Col. 1420D] This is especially so because the countenance of our flock is better known to us and to themselves than to outsiders, and because it is more fitting that the worthy man be chosen by us and his own household. This rule and this observance concerning promotion, since it has always been kept in our monastery with great care and reason, can in no way be altered in our time.

## LETTER 381. POPE EUGENIUS III TO THE CHAPTER OF MAGDEBURG.

That they should not support the bishop of Zeitz, an invader of the Church of Magdeburg. (1152.)

[Col. 1421A]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the entire chapter of the Church of Magdeburg: greeting and apostolic blessing.

“It has come to our ears,” etc. See under Eugenius.

## LETTER 382. POPE EUGENIUS TO E., ARCHBISHOP OF SALZBURG, AND OTHER BISHOPS.

He rebukes them for courting the favor of princes more than is right, and refuses the translation of C., bishop of Zeitz, to the see of Magdeburg. (1152.)

[Col. 1421B]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brethren E. [Note: [Col. 1421D] Eberhard, count of Hiltpolstein, abbot of Biburg, called the father of the poor.] of Salzburg; A. [Note: [Col. 1421D] Adalbero.] of Bremen; and H. [Note: [Col. 1421D] Hillin.] of Trier, archbishops; E. [Note: [Col. 1421D] Eberhard.] of Bamberg; H. [Note: [Col. 1421D] Hermann.] of Constance; H. [Note: [Col. 1421D] Henry.] of Regensburg; O. [Note: [Col. 1421D] Otto, formerly abbot of Morimond of the Cistercian order, [Col. 1422D] bishop of Freising, a holy man and distinguished writer.] of Freising; C. [Note: [Col. 1422D] Conrad, son of Leopold the Pious, margrave of Austria, later archbishop of Salzburg.] of Passau; D. [Note: [Col. 1422D] Daniel.] of Prague; A. [Note: [Col. 1422D] Anselm.] of Havelberg; and B. [Note: [Col. 1422D] Burchard.] of Eichstätt, bishops: greeting and apostolic blessing.

“The letters which your prudence sent to us concerning the affair of the Church of Magdeburg,” etc. See under Eugenius.

## LETTER 383. POPE EUGENIUS III TO ABBOT WIBALD.

He commends to him the cause of A., bishop of Chur, and asks him to defend ecclesiastical immunities against laymen. (1152.)

[Col. 1421C]

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son, the abbot of Corvey: greeting and apostolic blessing.

“Of whose pure devotion we have no doubt,” etc. See under Eugenius.

## LETTER 384. WETZEL TO EMPEROR FREDERICK.

He urges him, having shaken off the yoke of the supreme pontiff, to receive the Empire from the Roman senate and people. (1152.)

To his dearest F., by God’s grace, WETZEL wishes progress on every side toward the highest joys of soul [Col. 1421D] and body.

I am moved by immense joy that your people have elected you their king. Yet I deeply regret that, at the counsel of clerics and monks—whose teaching confounds divine and human things—you have not consulted, as you should, the most holy City, mistress of the world, creator and mother of all emperors, in this matter; and that you have neither sought its confirmation, by which all emperors have ruled, [Col. 1422A] and without which no prince ever ruled, nor written to it as to a mother, if indeed you have proposed to be its son and minister.

For who can advance in a stable order unless he is loved and promoted by Rebecca? Although Father Isaac wished and strove to give precedence in the blessing to Esau, Jacob—summoned by his mother, and himself fearing her advice as though it were foolish—obtained the blessing and dominion because Esau delayed in hunting, while the other [altero] grieved. To come to the matter and explain it more fully, attend carefully to what I say.

The election of your predecessors of old, and yours also even now, was made by the blind—that is, by Julianist heretics and apostate clerics and false monks, who violate their own order; who exercise dominion contrary to evangelical, apostolic, and canonical ordinances; who resist both divine and human laws; and who disturb the Church of God and secular affairs. [Col. 1422B] That such men are of this kind is shown by blessed Peter, whose vicars they falsely claim to be, when he says: “Having escaped the corruption that is in the world through desire, supply in faith virtue; in virtue, knowledge; in knowledge, self-control; in self-control, patience; in patience, godliness; in godliness, brotherly love; in brotherly love, charity.” “These things [are] for you above . . .” [Materially uncertain or defective quotation.] “For the one to whom these things are present is blind and groping with his hand.”

Again the same apostle says of them: “There will be false teachers, who in avarice will make merchandise of you; abounding in pleasures, luxuriating with you in their banquets; having eyes full of adultery; through whom the way of truth will be blasphemed. These are springs without water.” How can such men say with Peter: “Behold, we have left everything and followed you”? Or again: “Silver and gold I have none”? How do they hear from the Lord: “You are the light of the world; you are the salt of the earth”? What follows surely suits them: “But if salt has lost its savor, with what shall it be salted? It is no longer good for anything except to be trampled underfoot by men or pigs.”

Hence John says: “He who says that he believes in Christ ought himself also to walk as he walked.” Likewise: “He who says that he knows God and does not keep his commandments is a liar, and the truth is not in him.” To Peter and Peter’s vicars the Lord says: “As the Father sent me, so I send you.” [Col. 1422D] But he explains how he himself was sent by the Father when he says: “If I do not do the works of my Father, do not believe me.” If Christ, who committed no sin, was not to be believed without works, how are these men to be believed when they not only act badly, but publicly do evil things? Hence it is said: “How can you speak good things when you are evil?” Not only indeed can they not speak good things, but neither can they believe, as the Lord himself says: [Col. 1423A] “How can you believe, who seek glory from one another?” For faith without works is dead.

How can these men, who covet every kind of riches—men who, by luxuriously living according to their false teaching, have destroyed the riches that were salutary for the whole world, through the use of which such great and such peace existed throughout the world that the Son of God came down from the bosom of the Father into the bosom of his mother—hear that first command of the precepts of evangelical teaching: “Blessed are the poor in spirit,” when they are poor neither in fact nor in desire? Hence blessed Jerome: “Flee a trading cleric, one who becomes rich from poverty, or glorious from obscurity, as you would a plague.”

How do these men, occupied with secular business, fulfill, as deaf hearers, the first of all the decrees of the Roman pontiffs, introduced by blessed Clement in [Col. 1423B] his first letter but promulgated by blessed Peter the apostle? Among other things, when Peter ordained Clement and laid this charge upon him, he said:

“You must live blamelessly and strive with the greatest zeal to cast off all occupations of this life: do not become a guarantor; do not become an advocate in lawsuits; and do not allow yourself to be entangled at all in any occupation of worldly business. For Christ has not commanded that you be ordained today as a judge or a hearer of secular cases, lest, choked by present human cares, you should be unable to devote yourself to the word of God. Let laypeople render to one another those services which we have said are less fitting for you, and let no one occupy you by making you undertake secular concerns. It is thus a sin for every layperson not to lend faithful assistance to one another even in matters that concern [Col. 1423C] the common use of life; but let all labor together to free you from matters which you ought not to pursue. If perhaps laypeople do not understand this of themselves, they must be instructed through the deacons, and the concerns of the Church alone must be left to you. For if you are occupied with worldly cares, you deceive both yourself and those who hear you. You will not be able fully to distinguish matters pertaining to salvation; and the result is that you are deposed, while your disciples perish through ignorance. Therefore you were called for this one purpose: to teach the word of God without interruption.”

That lie and heretical fable, in which it is reported that Constantine granted imperial prerogatives in the City to Sylvester by simony, has been so exposed that even mercenaries and little women can confound any of the most learned men on this point, and the so-called apostolic lord, with his cardinals, does not dare to appear in public in the city for shame. For St. Miltiades, predecessor of St. Sylvester, says in his decrees that Constantine was baptized: [Col. 1423D] “When the Church increased amid the upheavals of the world, it reached such a point that Roman rulers flocked to the faith of Christ and the sacraments of baptism; among them the most religious man Constantine was the first to attain the faith of truth.” The *Tripartite History* likewise testifies that he was a Christian before the emperor ever entered the City.

Attend to what I say. Esau, not remaining at home, ignorant of his mother’s rudiments and counsels, seeking Sylvester and summoned by a blind man, has until now lacked the promises. But Jacob, obedient to his mother, covering his bare neck and hands with the domestic garment of disciplines, [Col. 1424A] by divine will seized what the blind man promised to Sylvester.

The emperor ought not to be uncultivated (*silvester*), but skilled in laws, as Emperor Julian testifies in the first pronouncement of all laws, saying: “Imperial majesty ought to be adorned not only with arms but also armed with laws, so that it may rightly govern both the time of war and that of peace.” A little later he likewise shows from whom the Roman prince has authority to rule and enact laws: “What pleases the prince has the force of law,” and he adds the reason: “because the people have granted to him and vested in him all their authority and power.”

But since the Empire and every dignity of the commonwealth belong to the Romans, and since the emperor belongs to the Romans rather than the Romans to the emperor, whoever considers what follows must ask: what law, what reason prevents the senate and people from creating an emperor? Do not hesitate to send Count Rudolf of Ramesberg, Count Udalric of Lenzburg, and other suitable men—namely Eberhard of Bodman—together with legal experts who know and dare to argue the law of the Empire, to Rome as quickly as possible; and take care to forestall anything new that may arise there against you.

Born of one father and one mother:

[Col. 1424C]

**Frederick**

He begot Frederick of Büren. Frederick of Büren begot Duke Frederick, who founded Staufen. Duke Frederick of Staufen begot Duke Frederick by a daughter of King Henry. Duke Frederick begot Frederick the king.

**Bertha**

She begot Bezelin of Villingen. Bezelin of Villingen begot Berthold with the Beard. Berthold with the Beard begot Lutgard. Lutgard begot Margrave Theobald. Margrave Theobald begot Adela.

## LETTER 385. AGREEMENT BETWEEN POPE EUGENIUS AND EMPEROR FREDERICK.

(1152.)

[Col. 1424D]

In the name of the Lord, amen. This is the form of agreement and convention between Lord Pope Eugenius, etc. See under Pope Eugenius III.

## LETTER 386. POPE EUGENIUS III TO ABBOT WIBALD.

He commends to him his legates to Emperor Frederick. (1153.)

EUGENIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved [Col. 1425A] son WIBALD, abbot of Stavelot: greeting and apostolic blessing.

“Of whose devotion and sincere charity we have the fullest confidence,” etc. See under Pope Eugenius III.

## LETTER 387. EMPEROR FREDERICK TO EMPEROR MANUEL OF CONSTANTINOPLE.

He desires to have a wife from Manuel’s bloodline, and meanwhile prepares an expedition into Sicily. (1153.)

FREDERICK, by the grace of God august emperor of the Romans, great and peaceable, crowned by God, to his beloved brother and friend MANUEL PORPHYROGENITUS, [Col. 1425B] exalted and glorious emperor of Constantinople: brotherly affection and victory over enemies.

We recently received with goodwill and joy the letters of Your Greatness sent to our presence through your messenger. Having examined and carefully understood them, we rejoiced both at the well-being of Your Highness and the prosperity of your empire, and at your affection toward union with our brotherhood. For our predecessor and uncle of blessed and holy memory, the illustrious conqueror, the most serene Emperor Conrad, when dying and declaring us the successor of his empire, urgently exhorted us, among the chief counsels of his pious and fatherly admonition, [Col. 1425C] faithfully to embrace your friendship and bind the bond of brotherhood between us with an indissoluble tie, so that our empires might become one through mutual affection and each might have the same friend and the same enemy.

Therefore, hastening to fulfill his admonition in deed, and responding with brotherly goodwill also to your intention, which we have perceived from your letters, in order to confirm friendship between us, we desire, God willing, for the strengthening of a firmer concord and the increase of both empires, that a marriage chamber be prepared for us from the court of your empire and that we take a wife from your bloodline. Accordingly, we have taken care to send swift and ready messengers to Your Highness, so that, once they have been sent back to us with all speed, [Col. 1425D] we may quickly learn your will in this matter.

Since all provinces throughout the breadth of our empire enjoy tranquil peace through the grant of almighty God, we have arranged an expedition toward Apulia and Sicily, confirmed in the customary way by the oaths of all, with the great support of our princes and of the whole army. Moreover, when summer comes—the season in which kings usually proceed to war—we have resolved to cross the Alps with the great strength of our empire. Let unquestioning credence be given to the matters which, concerning the urgent business, we have directed our present legates to state orally.

## LETTER 388. ABBOT WIBALD TO EMPEROR MANUEL OF CONSTANTINOPLE.

He urges him toward sincere concord with Emperor Frederick, whom he persuaded to take a wife from Manuel’s bloodline. (1153.)

[Col. 1426A]

To the glorious, exalted, and most high magnificent conqueror, the most mighty MANUEL PORPHYROGENITUS, most excellent emperor of Constantinople, WIBALD, by the grace of God abbot of two noble monasteries, namely Corvey and Stavelot: continual prayers and devoted service.

Imperial majesty ought to be endowed not only with generosity but also with gracious memory, so that it forgets no service or fidelity; for the kindly remembrance and gratitude of a prince more readily stir the affection of subjects. Therefore I have not hesitated to make known to your most sacred empire that I confidently trust Your August Majesty remembers how, by letters from my lowliness, I greeted Your Highness and deserved to receive your most blessed words. [Col. 1426B] Accordingly, from a devoted servant I became a most devoted servant, and I have not ceased to labor and strive for the advancement and glory of your most sacred empire, until the most clement Emperor Conrad of most blessed memory sent messengers to Your Magnificence so that, for the increase of greater concord between you and him, he might take a wife from your bloodline.

But when in the meantime he was taken from this mortality into the land of the living, the grief which had occupied my mind at his passing received no small consolation because his nephew, who now holds power—the magnificent Emperor Frederick—not only obtained the summit of empire, but also honored my lowliness with equal and similar goodwill and trust. Therefore I have not ceased earnestly to persuade my illustrious and victorious lord Emperor Frederick to enter into a treaty of friendship with your most steadfast empire and to take a wife from your bloodline. Your wisdom too will undoubtedly hasten to fulfill this. We and our brethren give immense thanks for the white *exsamitum* [Note: [Col. 1425] *Exsamitum* is wholly silken cloth.] sent to us, and we do not cease to pour out devout prayers to God [Col. 1426D] for the safety of your empire.

## LETTER 389. CARDINALS BERNARD AND GREGORY TO O., BISHOP OF HALBERSTADT.

That he restrain Liudolf and Count Palatine Frederick, who are harassing the monastery of Corvey. (1153.)

BERNARD, priest, and GREGORY, deacon, by the grace of God cardinals and legates of the holy Roman Church, to their venerable brother O. [Note: [Col. 1425] Odalric or Udalric, who succeeded Bishop Rudolf, who died in 1149.] bishop of Halberstadt: greeting.

Our venerable brother, the abbot of Corvey, made complaint to us concerning certain of your parishioners, namely Liudolf and Count Palatine Frederick: they have taken from him grain, provisions, and certain other goods, and are harassing his men. Yet your prudence ought most certainly to see to it that so great a man, so acceptable to the lord pope and to the entire kingdom, is not offended in your diocese. Accordingly, since we can neither be absent from nor ought to fail his cause of justice, by this present letter we command you to admonish the aforesaid men strictly to restore what they have taken and thereafter to leave the monastery’s goods quiet and unharmed. Otherwise, if within thirty days after receiving this admonition they have not made satisfaction to the aforesaid abbot, restrain them by ecclesiastical censure; and make the sentence which you impose upon them be firmly observed [Col. 1427B] until satisfaction is rendered.

## LETTER 390. CARDINALS BERNARD AND GREGORY TO POPE EUGENIUS.

They commend to him the bearer of this letter. (1153.)

To their reverend father and lord, EUGENIUS, by the grace of God supreme pontiff, B., priest, and G., deacon, cardinals of the holy Roman Church: service due in every respect.

“The bearer of this letter is a nobleman,” etc. See under Eugenius, among various persons’ letters to him.

## LETTER 391. CARDINAL GREGORY TO ABBOT WIBALD.

Recalled after the pope’s death, he summons certain bishops to Worms and desires Wibald’s presence before the emperor. (1153.)

[Col. 1427C]

GREGORY, by the grace of God cardinal and legate of the holy Roman Church, to his reverend brother WIBALD, his like-minded friend, abbot of Corvey: greeting.

Although the report of the death of the lord pope has troubled us, [Note: [Col. 1427D] Pope Eugenius III died on 8 July 1153, not without a reputation for holiness. His successor was Conrad, cardinal-bishop of Sabina, who, after changing his name, was called Anastasius IV.] nevertheless, having heard who has been appointed lord vicar, we rejoiced, knowing that he is an old master of the Church and loves and honors us in every way as himself.

But because we are urgently recalled by our friends, on the feast of Michael we have summoned to Worms the bishops of Bremen, Hildesheim, and Minden, intending to give them certain instructions. [Col. 1427D] Therefore we would gladly have you present again before the lord king, so that your prudence might assist us in the matters we must conduct with him and in obtaining leave to depart, and that your integrity might commend us to the lord king.

## LETTER 392. CARDINALS BERNARD AND GREGORY TO ABBOT WIBALD.

As they are to have a conference before the king, they ask him to come to Würzburg. (1153.)

BERNARD, priest, and GREGORY, deacon, [Col. 1428A] by the grace of God cardinals and legates of the holy Roman Church, to their beloved brother WIBALD, abbot of Corvey: greeting.

As we remember having sent word to your brotherhood in other letters, so again by this present letter we command you to come to us at Würzburg on the coming Wednesday, where at the same time we are to have a conference with the king. Since we love the Church of Stavelot with true charity in the Lord and willingly attend to its advantage, we also command you to come to us so prepared that, after our conference, you may honorably proceed to that same church.

## LETTER 393. ABBOT WIBALD TO POPE ANASTASIUS.

He congratulates him on his election and asks for his favor. (1153.)

[Col. 1428B]

To his reverend father and lord ANASTASIUS, sole and universal pope of the holy Catholic and Apostolic Church, Brother WIBALD, by the grace of God and yours what he is in the Catholic Church: humble prayers and devoted service.

Ever since divine providence, through your most devout solicitude, has disposed that you should govern our most holy mother, the Roman Church, we have especially desired to present ourselves before you in person, so that by some surer token you might more fully understand the filial affection which we bear toward you, and so that we might more confidently set forth in familiar conversation before your exaltedness certain matters which it would be lengthy, and perhaps useless, to commit to the trust of paper and ink. But since the Italian expedition now imminent, for which we are urgently preparing in spirit and resources, prevents us from doing this, we offer our devotion to your highness through these present tokens and a brief message. With humble prayer we beseech the mercy of almighty God that He may deign to deliver you from troublesome and evil men, and may not refuse to raise up, amid the waves by which it is constantly shaken, the little ship of blessed Peter, whose helm you hold, lest it be submerged. “The floods of the sea are wondrous; but wondrous is the Lord on high.”

The Apostle Paul, writing to his disciple Timothy, says: “Let no one despise your youth.” We, disciples and servants, in the boldness of charity suggest to our master and lord: let no one despise your old age, since your past life has been so innocent that you need neither be ashamed to live nor in any way reluctant to die. For during the past twenty-five years we have known Your Blessedness through a sufficiently intimate and familiar acquaintance, and by your favour and gentle patronage we have deserved to enjoy, with every kindness and effectiveness, your help in every matter—private or public—which we have pursued before the Roman Church.

Hence the intolerable grief that had wounded our soul with rightful sorrow at the passing of our reverend father—your predecessor, indeed—was alleviated by no small consolation when God, the disposer of times, caused Your Holiness to sit in his chair by blessed succession, so that your illustrious life might enlighten all the Churches and that you might grant us the gracious effect of your customary mercy. For by a certain right of affection we request again from Your Highness the familiar favour which we have long obtained from your predecessors: namely, that we may, without the charge of presumption, communicate certain matters concerning the care of the Churches and the condition of the realm. We shall begin to do this confidently when we have been instructed to do so by your most sacred letters. The petitions which we submit to your clemency on account of our necessities are appended below; we pray that they may be granted, for the increase of our perpetual service.

## LETTER CCCXCIV. Wibald, Abbot, to Cardinal Bernard

He congratulates him on his safe return to the City, and asks his protection for the monastery of Corbie, and that of his colleague Gregory for the monastery of Stavelot. (1153.)

To his reverend father and lord in Christ, BERNARD, venerable cardinal-priest of the holy Roman Church, brother WIBALD, by God’s grace that which he is in the Catholic Church, scant prayers and devoted service.

If you have been able to reach the City with your health unharmed and your affairs wholly preserved, we rejoice exceedingly in the Lord, because our desire concerning your welfare has been fulfilled. We therefore ask your clemency—which has deigned to grant us great boldness of familiarity and patronage—that you may kindly commend our lowliness to the lord pope and to the lord cardinals, and may not refuse to ensure that our petitions obtain their effect, so that henceforth you may have in us a devoted servant from one who is devoted.

For we have thus divided our needs: since you did not disdain to reside for a time in the monastery of Corbie, may you undertake the advancement of the causes of that Church and gladden your sons, who serve God in that monastery, by the protection of your kindness. But may your colleague, namely our lord Cardinal Gregory, since he deigned to visit the Church of Stavelot and saw its miseries by direct observation, not refuse to undertake the promotion of the affairs of that monastery, as we have great confidence in his goodness.

## LETTER CCCXCV. Wibald, Abbot, to Cardinal Gregory

On the same subject. (1153.)

To his dearest father and lord, GREGORY, venerable cardinal-deacon of the holy Roman Church, brother WIBALD, by God’s grace that which he is in the Catholic Church, scant prayers and devoted service.

If you have returned in health and prosperity to the City and to your own territories, nothing could more abundantly fulfil the joy of our desire. Although we have come to know, not slightly, the steadfast diligence of your spirit and the alertness of your mind, which is keen and subtle in avoiding dangers, nevertheless, since the condition of human fortune is fragile, we were always under grave anxiety lest anything unwelcome should happen to Your Excellency.

Therefore, with earnest prayer, we beseech Your Greatness not to refuse to commend us and our affairs to the lord pope—who has known us and deigned to love us from long ago—and likewise to the lord cardinals; and to help our petitions attain their desired effect. For if the will is present to you, you will find the ability to accomplish it.
