For we have thus divided our needs: since you did not disdain to visit the monastery of Stavelot, may you undertake the advancement of the causes of that Church and gladden your sons, who serve God in that monastery, by the protection of your kindness. You will be able to bring this about all the more effectively because you saw the miseries of that place by direct observation. But may your colleague, namely our lord Cardinal Bernard, who was willing to reside for a time in the monastery of Corbie, not refuse to undertake the promotion of the business of that abbey—provided, however, that just as you were indivisibly one in carrying out your legation, so you may remain one in assisting our need.

## LETTER CCCXCVI. H. de Baux to Wibald, Abbot

That he may inform the emperor how much he suffers for the emperor’s service from the Count of Barcelona. (1153.)

To WIBALD, by God’s grace abbot of Stavelot, his most excellent lord, H. de BAUX and his brothers, greetings.

Your Serenity knows, from his own presence and from the letters which he often sent to you, what affection our father bore toward the Empire from long ago. Nor are we forgetful of the benefit which you strove to confer upon our brother G. and, through him, upon us in the emperor’s court. For this favour we again and again offer supplication and promise you without hesitation every service, should opportunity of place and time present itself to us.

We therefore earnestly pray that you may deign to hear, through the bearer of this letter, what great evils the Count of Barcelona has inflicted upon us and is preparing to inflict, because we wish to remain faithful to this king. Admit our prayers before the emperor; protect us before him by your support; and inform us what we ought to hope concerning his arrival. May both your mind and the king’s will be made known to us in your letter.

## LETTER CCCXCVII. A. to Wibald, Abbot

That he may secure his enjoyment of the gift granted him by the emperor. (1153.)

To his dearest lord WIBALD, by God’s grace abbot of Stavelot, A., his own man because he is yours, greetings with faithful service.

I render Your Greatness all the thanks that I can, because the kindness which you received from the Father of lights, though you extend it to all according to your custom, you nevertheless extend by special and continual favour, beneficially and graciously, even to my lowliness. Therefore, prompted by your benefits and ready, whenever it may please you, faithfully to render heart for heart, I ask that you obtain for me—even by compulsion, if need be—from Count Emisch of Liniges that gift of the lord king which was conferred upon me through your efforts, but which has not yet been received or paid out.

For it is disgraceful to me and gives my detractors cause for laughter if I must repeatedly request in vain what I should have received when the time had elapsed. Further, if all matters are proceeding rightly and prosperously with you, then it is as I wish. Write to us, if you please, concerning your condition; for just as it is no burden for you to write to me, so it is neither useless nor an empty courtesy for me to receive your letters with pleasure.

Count Ach, count of the sacred largesses and of pleasant companions, greets you. Hugh, clerk and our companion, greets you.

## LETTER CCCXCVIII. Stephen, Bishop of Metz, to Wibald, Abbot

He seeks some consolation from him and asks that, through the emperor, the disgrace inflicted on himself and his Church be redressed. (1153.)

To his most beloved Wibald, by God’s grace that which he is in the royal court, STEPHEN, by the same grace bishop of Metz, gives himself wholly in affection and service.

Had a sudden illness of our body not grievously overtaken us, our person, not a letter, would have come to visit the presence of the lord king and of yourself, whom we greatly desire to see—especially in order that we might receive from you some consolation concerning the misfortune of our adversity. For, to confess the truth, what appears to have been arranged by the lord of Clairvaux for the good of peace and safety did not merely bring no remedy to our grief, but even wounded our mind with a more grievous sore. For the authors of so great a crime, raising their horns because of the success of their malice, not only escaped unpunished, but even received a reward for it. We therefore ask your brotherhood to procure through the lord king redress for the disgrace inflicted upon us—or rather upon the whole Church—which for the present we must endure.

> **Note:** This was Saint Bernard’s final work: when the reconciliation took place, he unexpectedly settled the utterly deplorable war of Metz and recalled the peace that had been banished. Though confined to his sickbed, he was somewhat restored and compelled to undertake this work of charity; the weaker he appeared, the stronger he proved—as Geoffrey says in Book V, chapter 1, of the *Life of Saint Bernard*.

## LETTER CCCXCIX. Frederick, Emperor, to Wibald, Abbot

He says that he has ordered the injuries done to him by the Count of Sommerschenburg to be redressed, and desires his presence at Cologne. (1153.)

FREDERICK, by God’s grace king of the Romans, to WIBALD, abbot of Corbie: his favour and every good.

If the Count Palatine of Sommerschenburg had come to court, he would not have escaped censure and judicial sentence for the injury which he has inflicted upon your beloved person. Nevertheless, by command under the assurance of our favour, we have ordered him to restore to you the estate of Hienstede, to return to your men the benefice from which he expelled them, and, if he values our favour, to desist altogether from harassing you and yours.

Concerning our progress, know that we shall come to Cologne on the feast of All Saints, where we desire you to present yourself before us. After we have there learned, by familiar report, of your injuries and burdens, we shall plainly show you and the men of your land that, on account of the devoted and long-standing service which you have hitherto graciously rendered to us and to the realm, you have obtained our favourable support in all things. Whoever disturbs your serenity in any respect shall without doubt know that he has incurred the displeasure of our favour.

## LETTER CCCC. The Monks of Stavelot to Wibald, Abbot

Having suffered much from their adversaries and fearing that the church will be burned, they ask him to come and settle everything peacefully. (1153.)

To their most reverend father and lord in Christ, WIBALD, venerable abbot of the Church of Stavelot, the entire community of the same Church gives whatever devoted sons owe to a pious father.

It belongs to your messenger, the bearer of this letter, to say in what necessities he found us constrained and by what disturbances we were made anxious. But it belongs to your true sons, when their own strength fails, to call upon their pious father and humbly implore the kindly protection of his presence.

Thus far, dearest Father, though we had suffered loss and damage to our possessions, we had remained silent, in some fashion always hoping for better things. But now that the enemies whom you have never offended threaten to burn your church—the church, I say, which you have adorned with such great labours and expense, as we learned from the mouth of the lord bishop of Liège—we cry to you in tears. Kindly come at the fitting time to prevent and avert so great a crime.

For we hope in the Lord and hold it certain that at your arrival whatever human adversities devise against us will be brought to nothing [read: “reduced”], and that, with God directing your steps, everything taken from us in your absence will be restored to you entirely according to your will. For those who are most opposed to us, namely the men of Salm, desire your coming no less than we do, and wish that whatever has been committed by either side may be settled and repaired through you.

Therefore, dearest Father, turn aside a little to your sons; and, once peace has been established among those who assail us on every side, you will be able to return without disturbance to those who enjoy your presence more for delight than necessity. May almighty God bring you to us sound and safe.

## LETTER CCCCI. Wibald, Abbot, to Henry, Count of Salm

He recounts all the damages inflicted on the monastery of Stavelot by the count’s men and asks that they be redressed. (1153.)

To the distinguished and illustrious Count of Salm, HENRY, brother WIBALD, by God’s grace abbot of Stavelot, wishes an abundance of the spirit of knowledge and piety.

Having returned to Stavelot by command of the lord king and order of the lord cardinals, we found that same Church vexed and disturbed by the numerous seizures and plunderings which your ministerials and servants had committed and carried into your castle. Indeed, besides other very great evils which it would be lengthy to recount, your men took from us in our village of Paletenmet one hundred animals, one hundred and twenty sheep, eight pigs, and three goats; in Beringerivalle, sixteen animals; at Erkenbert’s holding, twenty-eight oxen; and in another village near your castle, twenty-four excellent oxen. They did this on the pretext that our reeve’s brother from Lernau had taken only twenty calves from your men.

May the discernment of your prudence consider how foreign to all nobility and justice it was to afflict a noble Church with such evils merely because our reeve of Lernau attempted, justice requiring it, to deprive of his eyes one of your men, caught after he had stolen away the wife of one of our men together with her other goods. Your own men had granted him this right: to pursue the author of the crime and, if possible, to repay him according to his deed.

When we had frequently approached you amicably and humbly concerning this matter—especially since your men had already violently seized bread prepared for our reeve’s wedding and the six oxen carrying that bread—we achieved not only nothing; rather, as subsequent events show, you appear to have encouraged all your men to oppress us. For no one thinks that they could have undertaken and completed such great acts without your command.

Let the honour of your free birth therefore consider whether you ought so greatly to oppress us and our brothers, who embrace and love your person above all the princes of our land, for the sake of men who, although they are ours, nevertheless—as you yourself have seen and heard—cannot in any way be restrained by us. Some, being wanderers and fugitives, evade our attacks through the uncertainty of their dwellings; others have so bound the minds of princes to themselves by their services that they are constantly protected by them to our injury and the oppression of our Church.

Yet, mindful in all this of our ancient friendship, we have taken care to inform the kindness of your nobility by letter of the substance of our complaints, so that, for love of God and of the blessed apostles Peter and Paul and of our holy father Remaclus, and in regard for our prayers, we may receive redress for our losses through you rather than through any other authority. But if not, we shall complain of the violence inflicted upon us to God, to the lord king, to all the princes of the realm, and to our men and the faithful of the Church of Stavelot.

## LETTER CCCCII. Henry, Count of Salm, to Wibald, Abbot

He leaves all their controversies to be settled by Wibald’s judgment. (1153.)

To WIBALD, by God’s grace abbot of Stavelot, H., Count of Salm, whatever one friend owes another.

Let Your Belovedness know that I rejoice exceedingly at your arrival, both because of the hope of your wise counsel and because of the restoration of the customary peace between my men and yours. Although your men—or rather your adversaries—are endeavouring to break the bond of our affection, thanks be to God it has remained unbroken.

It would be lengthy to recount what injuries and how great they appear to be on either side. I therefore leave to your diligent and prudent administration the settlement of the injuries committed on both sides, by virtue of the prerogative of your dignity and the familiarity of our association. For you know that my castle of Salm and all that I possess, in peace and in war, shall always be ready to serve you as they are to serve me.

Be pleased to preserve and, by preserving, protect your honour and mine, both in my absence and in my presence. That you have communicated to me in writing the complaint concerning your injuries, I affirm to have proceeded from the bosom of your affection. I would have communicated mine to you earlier, had your return been known to me. I shall come to you as soon as I can, to speak with you and, while preserving the honour of both parties, to comply with your prudent counsels.

## LETTER CCCCIII. Letters of Wibald, Abbot, to His Successors

Concerning the reform of an abuse introduced by Abbot Poppo II. (1153.)

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. WIBALD, by God’s mercy abbot of Stavelot, to his successors and to all Christ’s faithful for ever.

The burden of our prelacy and the character of our office constantly admonish us that we ought not only to preserve what has been gathered together and direct it according to the discipline of right living, but also to gather what has been scattered, recall it to the rule of justice, and commit more diligently to memory through the benefit of written records both what we ourselves do rightly and what was wrongly done by the ancients and is corrected.

Therefore let the diligence of all the children of holy Church know that Abbot Poppo the Second, indeed our predecessor, among many acts not merely useless but harmful to all our posterity, which he wickedly committed against the Church entrusted to him and against his own soul, after he had grossly dissipated much of the monastery’s substance, also exposed persons belonging to the Church to everlasting reproach. He gave to a certain Everard of Richen as a benefice—or rather, to speak more truly, as a malefice—the claims and revenues from men and women, apart from the rent alone which they paid to the Church, who lived from the forest nearest the monastery, called Sanias, as far as the river called Wisera.

He cloaked this work of wickedness under the name of law and called those thus enfeoffed “church wardens” (*aeditui*), a name customarily applied to religious monks of God’s temple and guardians of sacred things. This evil in our time spread with such destructive growth that these wardens—or rather agents of iniquity—not only between Sanias and the Wisera but everywhere they could range, harassed the Church’s servants with cruel exactions: by claiming lodging, demanding contributions, and afflicting them by dividing their property if any man had not married a wife from the Church’s household.

They cried to the Lord in their tribulation; and after many long cries to the Church and to us, He delivered them from their necessities at the time when our illustrious lord King Frederick was staying at Aachen. Moved by our outcry and that of the men—some two hundred of whom had gathered at his court—the king sought a legal judgment from a certain nobleman, Marquard of Grumbach: whether any abbot could grant to any layman as a benefice the rent or other revenues of men who belonged to the altar by proprietary right, from whose payments the lights and roofs of the church are maintained.

With the consent of Lord Arnold II, archbishop of Cologne; Lord Henry II, bishop of Liège; Lord Anselm, bishop of Havelberg; and all those present, it was judged according to legal principle that this could not be done and ought to be revoked as void. The most pious king did so at our request, although he was then suffering from a quartan fever, and decreed that such wardens should be abolished for ever.

Thereafter, when we had returned to our house in that same town, the whole multitude gathered in our chapel, and at our command all swore, touching the most sacred relics, fidelity to the Church and to us. Immediately after this they were adjured and questioned, and said that it was their law that they neither owed nor paid lodging or contribution to anyone; but that every kin-group or family should have its own rent-collector, appointed by election of his kinsmen through the hand of the church warden—that is, one of our brethren—and set over his own kindred in this manner: he was to collect the annual rent and pay it to the church warden; if any offence contrary to the decrees of the law should be committed by one of his people, whether in shedding blood, killing a man, or violating women, he was to exact redress both personally and through the advocate, and from the compositions he was to render two parts to the church warden and the third to the advocate—namely Arnold, then advocate, and his lawfully appointed successors.

No one may take a wife from another household except by permission of his own rent-collector. If he lacks such permission and marries a wife who is not from the Church’s household, the compensation and penalty for this offence shall be at the discretion of the rent-collector. But he who, with permission as stated, marries a woman from another household, upon his death shall have his wife or children give the rent-collector his best garment—that is, a cloak or mantle—and thereby his property shall not be divided, as had formerly been done.

Twelve of their elders swore that this had been the law of their fathers and ancestors, and their relationship to the Church. Their names, written below, are: Peter, Werric, Herman, Godfrey, John, Willebert, Herward, Ruzekin, Gislebert, Everlin, Jordan, and John. There are likewise the names of thirteen men who testified that their oaths were true: Eimund, Walter, Azelin, Gislebert, Theoderic, Godfrey, Wenric, Everwin, Herman, Baldwin, Godfrey, Waldo, and Rumbert.

Both then in the present place and afterwards at the monastery of Stavelot, in a solemn assembly, we, having taken stole and pastoral staff and with the consent of all our brothers, forbade under sentence of excommunication any person, small or great, to presume to harass the aforesaid men and their descendants or in any way dare to infringe, against their will, the law that has been written. And so that these provisions may remain ratified and unshaken through all succeeding times, we have ordered this charter to be marked and secured with our seal and that of the Church, and the witnesses who were present to be noted below.

I, Wibald, abbot of Stavelot, have subscribed.

## LETTER CCCCIV. Pope Anastasius IV to Wibald, Abbot

He grants him the use of a ring for his lifetime only. (1154.)

ANASTASIUS, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son, the abbot of Corbie: greetings and apostolic blessing.

“The Apostolic See has always,” etc. See under Pope Anastasius IV, for the year 1154.

## LETTER CCCCV. Cardinal Gregory to Wibald, Abbot

Concerning the ring granted him by the Apostolic See and to be conveyed by Cardinal Gerhard. (1154.)

GREGORY, by God’s grace cardinal-deacon, to his reverend brother and wholehearted friend WIBALD, abbot of Stavelot: greetings and charity, than which nothing is dearer.

Because among the other abbots of the realm we have joined your person to ourselves with a particular prerogative of affection, we have, divine grace accompanying us, effectively laboured for the glory and exaltation of your honour. Indeed, in accordance with our desire and prayers, your mother, the holy Roman Church, has gladdened your person with the oil of rejoicing, granting you episcopal insignia, so that Stavelot may truly shine with the twofold adornment of the dignities of abbot and bishop, having deserved a greater share of its mother’s affection than its companions.

“Our father Isaac has grown old, but Rebecca nevertheless serves him.” Therefore act so that the mother may recognize in the son that by which the son will be recognized by many. Gerhard, cardinal-deacon and legate of the Apostolic See, will bring you the ring; he will invest you with so great a favour and strengthen you with apostolic protection. As for us, understand that we are as solicitous in your needs as the power of friendship cannot be idle in a friend’s cause. Regarding your other petitions, the legate will do you justice; the regions of the Germans have been entrusted to his discretion.

## LETTER CCCCVI. O. to the Dean, Archdeacons, etc., of Halberstadt

He declares Frederick, Count Palatine, excommunicated. (1154.)

O., by God’s grace the little that he is, to his beloved son E., dean, to the other archdeacons, and to the whole holy Church of Halberstadt: greetings and blessing.

Your discretion knows clearly that the lord cardinal-deans, legates of the Apostolic See, instructed us by their letters to warn Count Palatine F. strictly to restore the goods taken from the Church of Corbie and to cease harassing the men of that Church; and that, if after our warning he did not fulfil this within thirty days, we should restrain him by canonical justice.

> **Note:** Frederick, mentioned above.

Having therefore been diligently warned by our letter on this matter, as your brotherhood knows, he not only scorned to listen to us but even did not fear to incur the crime of sacrilege by laying hands upon a priest. Therefore, by apostolic authority and our own, we excommunicate the aforesaid Count Palatine F. as sacrilegious and disobedient. Announcing him to you as excommunicated, we command you in true obedience entirely to withdraw yourselves from his communion and to ensure that all your clergy and laity likewise observe this firmly.

Whoever neglects to maintain and announce to others this command of the holy Roman Church and ours shall without doubt incur the loss of his office and benefice; we shall report him to the lord pope as disobedient.

## LETTER CCCCVII. Manuel, Emperor of Constantinople, to Wibald, Abbot

Concerning the marriage of Emperor Frederick. (1154.)

MANUEL, faithful king in Christ God, Porphyrogenitus, sublime, mighty, exalted Augustus and emperor of the Romans, Comnenus, to the most honourable and most holy abbot of the monastery of Stavelot: his favour and good will.

The letter of your reverence has been delivered to my empire. It declared that you always pray for my empire; that my empire, hearing from every tongue of the exceptional quality of your virtue, always calls upon your prayers; and that it desires Your Holiness to remember it in your prayers to God and to pray to Him for the prosperity of our empire.

Concerning the matter of the marriage, about which the most noble king of Rome and beloved brother of my empire made known his wishes to our empire, my empire has more fully conveyed its intention to him through these present envoys of my empire. For my empire desires ever more greatly the union of both realms.

In November, second indiction. Sent from the castle of Pelagonia, 22 November, second indiction.

Imperial letter to the most venerable abbot of the monastery of Stavelot.

## LETTER CCCCVIII. Wibald, Abbot, to Emperor Manuel

He will, to the extent of his power, strengthen the friendship between the two empires. (1154.)

To his illustrious conqueror and glorious lord MANUEL, faithful king in Christ, Porphyrogenitus, sublime, mighty, exalted Augustus and emperor of the Romans, Comnenus, WIBALD, by God’s grace abbot of the venerable monasteries of Corbie and Stavelot, offers faithful prayers and devoted service.

We have received the words of Your Most Sacred Empire, which Your Highness deigned to send us through your most prudent envoys, as a kind of heavenly gift. Together with the brethren gathered with us in Christ, we do not cease to pour out humble prayers to God’s mercy both for the safety of your glorious person and for the prosperous condition and strength of your entire most sacred empire.

Moreover, we are devoting careful effort, to the extent of our ability, to establishing friendship and trust between my lord, the most noble Frederick, Augustus and emperor of the Romans, and your sacred empire. We greatly desire that, according to the wisdom granted by God, you may give your assent to the wish of your most beloved brother, which he communicates to Your Majesty through his envoys. May the King of kings and Lord of lords deign, for His own honour and glory, to preserve your life and peace from enemies for a long time.

## LETTER CCCCIX. Wibald, Abbot, to Pope Anastasius

He gives thanks and commends to him Heribert, the king’s chaplain. (1154.)

To his reverend father and lord in Christ, ANASTASIUS, one and universal pope, brother WIBALD, by God’s grace that which he is in the Catholic Church, devoted service and due obedience in the Lord.

We render humble and devoted thanks to Your Highness because you have always graciously attended to our advancement and necessities from the time when we first deserved to become known to Your Dignity; and especially recently, when we sent to Your Holiness our petitions concerning our needs and difficulties. You both mercifully received them and kindly caused them to be fulfilled.

We now earnestly commend to Your Excellency Heribert, chaplain of the lord king, that you may receive him piously when he comes before Your Blessedness, treat him kindly, and mercifully hear him in his petitions.

## LETTER CCCCX. C., Abbot of Paderborn, to Wibald, Abbot

He congratulates him on his return and regrets that he did not receive him when he passed through Paderborn. (1155.)

To the abbot, C., called the humble abbot of Paderborn, gives himself wholly with every devotion.

> **Note:** Conrad is said to have governed the monastery of Saint Peter at Paderborn, commonly called Abdinghof, after Hamuko, from 1154 until 1180.

At your return that Virgilian passage came to mind and fixed itself firmly in my heart, as though it had been spoken especially concerning you:

> O light of Dardania, O most steadfast hope of the Teucrians,  
> What long delays have held you back? From what shores,  
> long-awaited Hector, do you come?  
> (*Virgil, Aeneid* II.282–284.)

Therefore thanks be to almighty God, who has restored you safe and sound and in this has heard the prayers of His suppliants. Yet I grieve, and, angry with myself, offer myself to deserved punishment, because recently, when you passed through our region, I did not meet you and was not permitted to see your long-desired face—a sight without which my soul refuses consolation until I see it. Yet welcome indeed; and may you fare most excellently in the Lord.

## LETTER CCCCXI. W., Bishop of Minden, to Wibald, Abbot

A man commended to him by Wibald was badly treated by Count Otto. (1156.)

To the reverend lord WIBALD, abbot of the holy Church of Corbie, W., by God’s mercy that which he is in the Church of Minden, offers constant prayers in the Lord together with faithful service of devotion.

[Col. 1440A] Desiring to render to Your Holiness every reverence and the service of devotion, we rejoice exceedingly at your return and safe preservation, and shall be ready to serve in all matters which your fatherhood may command us. When you departed this land in the service of the realm, you chose to entrust to our protection the bearer of this letter together with his property. We guarded him, with all that was his, unharmed and untouched within and beyond our borders, for love and remembrance of you. But while he was at a certain market on his own affairs, Count Otto seized this poor man as though he had fled from his advocacy, and detained him until he paid him ten marks. To pay this sum, he pledged the house which he possessed in our city; and, because the interest has continued to mount, he has not been able to redeem it to this day. [Col. 1440B] Deeply troubled by the losses and injuries of your man, and unable to console him in this matter, we devoutly entreat your fatherhood that, receiving consolation from you, he may return to us with joy; for out of reverence for you we shall not cease to protect and support him.

### LETTER CCCCXII. Wibald, Abbot, to Emperor Frederick

He complains of the bishops of Osnabrück, who had taken certain tithes; of the count of Schwalenberg, who had killed the count of Huxaria; and of the count of Tecklenburg, who had occupied certain property of the brethren of Corvey. (Year 1156.)

[Col. 1440C] To his illustrious conqueror and glorious lord, FREDERICK, by God’s grace Roman Emperor Augustus, crowned by God, great and peace-giving: Brother WIBALD, by God’s grace that which he is in the Catholic Church—may he rule and reign in Him who gives salvation to kings.

Although we have not deserved to learn the condition of your affairs and the glory of your victories through your most sacred communications, nevertheless, since by report of fame—which sometimes commonly spreads uncertain matters as truth—we have received good and consoling news concerning your safety and prosperity, we render devout and continual thanks to the Giver of all good things. Together with the company of our brethren, we beseech God’s mercy in humble prayer, that He may grant you [Col. 1440D] long days, ever order them happily in His peace, and swiftly crush all your enemies beneath your feet.

We further inform your Serenity that the bishops of Osnabrück have for a long time taken from the Church of Corvey certain tithes in Northland, of no small value. Relying on divine and your favour in protesting this injury, we have proceeded so far that the lord pope has entrusted his authority in this case to the lord archbishop of Magdeburg. He has summoned both us and the lord bishop of Osnabrück to appear before him at the city of Merseburg on the twenty-first day of January. [Col. 1441A] Therefore we urgently entreat your clemency, in which we have no small confidence, that you may deem it worthy to send imperial letters to that lord archbishop, so that, out of reverence for your command, he may receive our cause favourably and determine it without delay. Let him not in any way oppose the Church of Corvey, which received these same tithes from its founders by the gift and privileges of your predecessors, held them in quiet and peace for long periods, and lost them through manifest violence without any legal process.

Moreover, prostrate at the feet of your Majesty in mind and body, we bring again to the ears of your Highness our complaint concerning the killing of Count Thider of Huxaria. [Col. 1441B] He served you strenuously and faithfully in your Italian expedition; yet Lord Widekind of Schwalenberg, with his own hands and those of his retainers, killed him while he sat within the jurisdiction which he had lawfully held from us as a hereditary right, upon the consecrated wall of a church.

Furthermore, both we and all our brethren lamentably complain to your power that the count of Tecklenburg has violently seized the goods belonging to us, our brethren, and the poor who live from the hospital. By plundering and robbing us, he wishes to force us to surrender, without legal justification, a certain estate which the Church of Corvey peacefully possessed in the time of four of our predecessor abbots. Yet we are ready—and have often offered him—to stand concerning that estate before your court, [Col. 1441C] or before that of a duke or count; and, if we lose it by law, to withdraw from possession without obstruction.

### LETTER CCCCXIII. Pope Adrian IV to Archbishop Wichmann

He entrusts to his judgment the determination of the dispute concerning tithes between the bishop of Osnabrück and Abbot Wibald. (Year 1156.)

ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother WICHMANN, archbishop of Magdeburg: greeting and apostolic blessing.

“We have learned from the report of our beloved son WIBALD, abbot of Corvey,” etc. See among the letters of [Col. 1441D] Pope Adrian IV, under the year 1159.

### LETTER CCCCXIV. Archbishop Wichmann of Magdeburg to Philip, Bishop of Osnabrück

He summons him to answer the charges made by Abbot Wibald. (Year 1156.)

WICHMANN, by God’s grace minister—would that he were not unworthy—of the Church of Magdeburg, to PHILIP, bishop of Osnabrück: greeting and brotherly love.

Lord Wibald, abbot of Corvey, has asked for and obtained from the lord pope the appointment of myself as his judge in a claim for the recovery of certain tithes, which he complains have been unjustly taken from him and are held by you. Therefore, bound by the lord pope’s command and, as [Col. 1442A] you may learn from the tenor of his letters, exercising his office in this cause by his authority, since it is necessary and right that we obey, we command your fraternity: present yourself before us at Merseburg on the tenth day before the Kalends of February [23 January]. There we shall hear the aforesaid complaint of the lord abbot and your reply; and, after carefully examining the arguments on both sides, shall determine what is equitable in judgment.

### LETTER CCCCXV. Archbishop Wichmann of Magdeburg to Abbot Wibald

He writes that he has summoned Philip, bishop of Osnabrück, before himself. (Year 1156.)

[Col. 1442B]

WICHMANN, by God’s grace archbishop of Magdeburg, to his beloved brother in Christ WIBALD, venerable abbot of Corvey: brotherly service with prayers.

Concerning your case, we have written to the lord bishop of Osnabrück what the lord pope has laid upon us, and by apostolic authority have directed him to appear before us at Merseburg on the tenth day before the Kalends of February [23 January]. We wish your fraternity to know this, lest you hasten to come before the day named.

### LETTER CCCCXVI. Archbishop Wichmann of Magdeburg to Abbot Wibald

He communicates to him the reply of the bishop of Osnabrück. (Year 1156.)

[Col. 1442C]

WICHMANN, by God’s grace that which he is in the Church of Magdeburg, to his beloved brother in Christ WIBALD, venerable abbot of Corvey: the affectionate rendering of prayer and service.

Concerning your affair, we have informed the lord of Osnabrück what the lord pope has enjoined upon us. We designated for him Merseburg as the place and the tenth day before the Kalends of February [23 January] as the day. We have received no other reply from him thus far, except that, as our messenger testified, he said that he would rather resign his bishopric than lose, during his episcopate, those tithes which his church had peacefully possessed for sixty years and more. [Col. 1442D] Yet through the same messenger, by word and not in writing, he sent us word that he was willing gladly to render us all fitting reverence; but concerning this matter he wished to obtain the counsel of his entire church, clergy and people alike, and to make that counsel known to us through reputable and leading persons of that church by Epiphany.

Therefore, passing over all other matters, we make this one reply to your fraternity: if our life is preserved, we shall be at the appointed place on the tenth day before the Kalends of February, for so we have resolved by counsel; and whether the lord of Osnabrück comes or does not come, according to the counsel of our brethren and fellow bishops we shall, so far as lies in us, not disappoint your desire for due justice. We have sent the copy of the letter [Col. 1443A] which you requested; we have received no other.

## On the Emperors Descended from Charlemagne

Emperor Charles [Note: What is here said concerning Charles is found in the Chronicle of Halberstadt, published in vol. II of the *Scriptores rerum Brunsvicensium*, part III; although a few things are sometimes interpolated.] defined the diocese of Halberstadt on every side by fixed boundaries, and confirmed it by his imperial authority and inviolable privilege, on the Ides of May, 804, in the tenth indiction, the thirty-fourth year of his reign, the third of his empire, and the twenty-second of Bishop Hildegrin’s ordination, in the palace called Sarh [elsewhere, Saltz]. [Note: This royal palace was unknown to the learned Mabillon.]

At the same time, at an assembly held in that same palace, the emperor granted all Saxons their ancient liberty. For preserving the Catholic faith, he released them from every tribute, except that he commanded all of them, rich and poor alike, faithfully to render to Christ and His priests the tithes of all their agriculture and livestock. [Col. 1443B]

Charlemagne was succeeded by his son Louis the Pious. After him succeeded Louis, son of the aforesaid Louis. On his death he was succeeded by his third son, Louis. He too was succeeded by his son, King Charles. In the eighth year of his reign he was deposed from the kingdom, and Arnulf was crowned king. Arnulf died in the thirteenth year of his reign and was succeeded by Louis, surnamed the Child, who reigned thirteen years. Since he had no son, the princes of the realm wished by common counsel to elect as king the illustrious Otto, duke of Saxony. But on Otto’s advice Conrad, duke of the Franks, who was related to the fourth Louis, was crowned; he lived nine years. Thus far the descendants of Charles held the summit of royal power. [Col. 1443C] Thereafter Saxon emperors succeeded. The first of them was Henry, duke of the Saxons, son of the aforesaid Duke Otto and father of Emperor Otto I.

### LETTER CCCCXVII. Emperor Frederick to Archbishop Wichmann of Magdeburg

He commends to him the cause of the monastery of Corvey against the bishop of Osnabrück. (Year 1156.)

FREDERICK, by God’s grace Roman Emperor Augustus, to his beloved WICHMANN, archbishop of Magdeburg: his favour and every good thing.

Our most serene predecessors, the emperors, [Col. 1443D] taught by the divine Spirit, decreed that matters pertaining to the rights of the most blessed Church should be guarded by all with reverence, as belonging to the holy and religious Church itself, inviolate; and especially that things bestowed by the imperial house upon any religious community should not be alienated by force, fraud, or under any pretext of a rash transaction. To follow these reasonable footsteps of theirs is the charge laid upon our piety; and it is the purpose of our benevolence to preserve the rights and possessions of all God’s churches, especially those known to be subject in a special manner to imperial jurisdiction.

Accordingly, since we have learned that the pontiff of our nurturing city of Rome has appointed you judge in the matter being pursued between our venerable princes, the abbot of Corvey and the bishop of Osnabrück, concerning certain tithes bestowed upon the Church of Corvey by Emperor Augustus Louis of blessed memory but later transferred, under I know not what title of alienation, to the bishopric of Osnabrück, [Col. 1444A] we desire you to understand that we entreat your prudence diligently to consider the tenor of the privileges of the Church of Corvey and bring this cause to its due and desired conclusion.

### LETTER CCCCXVIII. Emperor Frederick to Abbot Wibald

He reports how prosperously all things are proceeding with him. (Year 1156.)

[Col. 1444B]

FREDERICK, by God’s grace Roman Emperor Augustus, to his beloved WIBALD, abbot of Corvey: favour and every good thing.

Not doubting that, as one especially close to us, you rejoice in the state of our prosperity, we wish your learning to know that, after magnificently arranging our affairs in Burgundy, by the favour of Him who gives salvation to kings, we have returned by a prosperous journey to the regions of the Rhine and gloriously celebrated the Nativity of the Lord at Speyer. We shall also hold a court at Ulm on the Purification of Saint Mary, in order to confirm the good of peace. When it is concluded and the affairs of that land have been settled, we have resolved to proceed to the lower regions of the Rhine, in order to cut off, by the arm of our strength, the horns of the pride of those [Col. 1444C] who have dared to raise their hands against our most serene empire. Thus their sons and grandsons, corrected by their fathers’ example, may learn not to oppose the empire but to submit to its commands with due honour and reverence.

To accomplish this swiftly, we invite you as one close to our heart. We have ordered what you requested from our Serenity in your letters to be done for the advantage of your cause; and, God being our author, we desire to avenge your injury at the proper place and time with due severity.

### LETTER CCCCXIX. Werner, Bishop of Minden, to the Archbishop of Magdeburg

The bishop of Osnabrück, on his way to him, remained ill at Hildesheim. (Year 1156.)

[Col. 1444D]

To the reverend lord, archbishop of the holy Church of Magdeburg: W., by God’s mercy that which he is in the Church of Minden, continual prayers in the Lord, with the faithful service of devotion.

Desiring to render every reverence to the Apostolic See and every service of devotion to your fatherhood, we give thanks to divine mercy that the lord pope has so approved your discernment as to entrust the lofty and exalted affairs of churches to the diligence of your discretion. Indeed, our venerable [Col. 1445A] brother Philip, bishop of Osnabrück, intending under the lord pope’s command to approach your presence, was received as a guest by us at Minden; but in the very course of his journey an exceedingly severe illness seized him. First, because of the seriousness of his sickness, he endured many sufferings; then, through the exertion of travel, the same illness grew until his body failed.

Accordingly, when this venerable brother of ours went down to the city of Hildesheim, we accompanied him on his way, wishing to bring him as far as your presence. But his illness became so evident to us that he could not possibly have gone further, since this excessive sickness had seized him both before and during the journey. Therefore, with all diligence, we ask the benevolence which we have hitherto experienced from you in every good matter, that you may mercifully excuse the absence, caused by this necessity, of the aforesaid Lord Bishop Philip, in consideration of our devotion and service; and mercifully dismiss the honourable persons who present this letter and bear his embassy to your prudence; and fatherly admonish the beloved lord of Corvey to desist from this proceeding.

### LETTER CCCCXX. Frederick, Bishop of Münster, to Archbishop Wichmann

He commends to him the bishop of Osnabrück. (Year 1156.)

[Col. 1445C] To the reverend Lord WICHMANN, archbishop: FRIEDRICH, [Note: This Frederick was ordained bishop at Aachen in 1152 by the same prelates who anointed Emperor Frederick; he was omitted from Bucelinus’s catalogue of the bishops of Münster in his *Germania Sacra*.] humble minister of the Church of Münster, his most heartfelt devotion in service and prayer.

The bishop of Osnabrück has brought before us the matter of his grievance, and we have sympathized: both because he is ill and unable to endure labour, and because the abbot of Corvey seems to be inflicting an injury upon him. Therefore we wish and earnestly ask that your Excellence be admonished to support him as your senior and fellow bishop, and to permit no injury whatsoever to be done to him. For it is evident that if—God forbid—one should be oppressed, so great an impropriety would spread to many bishops and archbishops alike. Farewell.

### LETTER CCCCXXI. B., Bishop of Hildesheim, to Archbishop Wichmann of Magdeburg

He asks that the bishop of Osnabrück, detained by illness and unable to come to him, be excused. (Year 1156.)

[Col. 1445D]

To the reverend lord WICHMANN, archbishop of the holy Church of Magdeburg: B., [Note: Bruno, who succeeded Bernard, who died in 1153, until 1160.] by God’s grace humble minister of Hildesheim, devout prayers in the Lord and service.

Our venerable brother Philip, bishop of Osnabrück, intending under the lord pope’s command [Col. 1446A] to approach your presence concerning the affair of the lord abbot of Corvey, was seized in the very course of his journey by an exceedingly serious illness. Because of the severity of his illness he first endured many and grave sufferings; but through the exertion of the journey he had undertaken, his sickness was greatly intensified. When this aforesaid venerable brother of ours was making this journey and came down to our city, his illness became so evident to us that he could not possibly have proceeded, unless he wished altogether to set aside the preservation of his own life.

Therefore, with all diligence, we ask the benevolence you have hitherto shown us: patiently excuse, in consideration of our petition and service, the absence necessitated by the condition of the aforesaid Lord Bishop Philip; and mercifully and affectionately dismiss the honourable persons who present this letter and carry his embassy to your prudence. For he himself, rescued by divine grace from imminent danger, will, wherever your Highness directs, present himself before you without evasion in the matter stated above. May God’s grace be with you.

### LETTER CCCCXXII. Archbishop Wichmann of Magdeburg to Pope Adrian

He gives an account of the cause committed to him between the bishop of Osnabrück and the abbot of Corvey. (Year 1157.)

[Col. 1446C]

To ADRIAN, by God’s grace supreme and most worthily reverend pontiff of the holy Roman Church: WICHMANN, humble overseer of Magdeburg, voluntary as well as due obedience, with prayers and faithful service.

Your fatherhood enjoined upon us, concerning the complaint which the venerable Lord Wibald, abbot of Corvey, brings against Lord Philip, bishop of the Church of Osnabrück, for certain tithes of the Church of Corvey taken by the men of Osnabrück unjustly, as the lord abbot asserts, that we should summon both parties before us and, having heard the allegations [Col. 1446D] of each side and carefully examined the arguments from both directions, bring this great controversy to its due conclusion. For this purpose we sent letters to both sides and assigned them a fixed place and day; moreover, we summoned the suffragan bishops of our church to assist us in examining so important a matter.

The day arrived; we came with our brethren and fellow bishops to the appointed place. The lord abbot too, with his Church of Corvey, obediently appeared before us. Alone of all those summoned, the lord bishop of Osnabrück was absent, though he sent in his place as messengers two canons of his church, Thid. and Theth. The case was called; the complaint of the men of Corvey was read through in order. It was not a matter newly arising from nothing, as was being suggested, but one long debated before our lords and fathers, the Roman pontiffs.

When they had heard the sequence of the complaint, the aforementioned envoys rose and asserted that their lord bishop, out of reverence for and obedience to your command, had indeed set out after us and had travelled no small distance from his home; but on the very journey by which he was coming he had been so burdened by bodily illness [Col. 1447A] that he could go no further, and that this necessity had forced him, not without great hardship, to return to the place whence he had come. They added that, once his health was restored, he would gladly come before us at another place and another time.

To make their assertions more readily believed, they held in their hands letters of the lords bishops of Hildesheim and Minden, each of whom had received the same bishop into his house; these letters had the same content as the messengers’ words. Since they were still not wholly believed, they said that they wished to establish by oath that their lord had not failed to come because he was unwilling, but because he was unable.

The lord abbot replied: “Such an oath will not readily establish for us belief in so great a weakness in the lord of Osnabrück; for he who was able to return to his own place, if his will had not failed him, was also able to proceed onward.” He further added that the lords bishops whose letters had been read there had testified rather incautiously about a matter insufficiently certain. As they disputed in this manner on both sides, he unexpectedly made an appeal in these words:

[Col. 1447C] “I, Wibald, by God’s grace abbot of Corvey, appeal to Lord Pope Adrian and summon Lord Philip, bishop of Osnabrück, to appear before him, to answer the lord pope and us on the octave of Saint Martin the bishop, concerning the tithes of the baptismal churches in Nortl[and], Wrederen, Meppie, Aschentorp, Loninge, and Visbike, with their ancient boundaries—tithes which he unjustly takes from the Church of Corvey. I also summon Provost Thid. [Col. 1447D] and Master Thethd., who wish to swear about an uncertain matter to the detriment of our case, to answer on the prescribed day in the presence of the lord pope.”

Having heard the appeal, we presumed to proceed no further in the case, but leave it for examination by your judgment, venerable Father.

### LETTER CCCCXXIII. Emperor Frederick to Abbot Wibald

Having praised his fidelity, he summons him to Nijmegen and speaks of an expedition against the Milanese. (Year 1157.)

FREDERICK, by God’s grace Roman Emperor ever Augustus, to his beloved WIBALD, abbot of Corvey [Col. 1448A] and Stavelot: his favour and every good thing.

What fame proclaims is demonstrated by the assessment of deeds: your person, adorned with many virtues, shines forth in admirable steadfastness and purity of faith, and departs from fidelity to the empire less readily than the sun from its brightness. Therefore, wholly confident in your integrity, we declare that the weightier affairs of the empire are to be managed by your counsel; and, as you are outstanding in faith and uprightness, so we desire you to be first and constant in our affairs.

The reason why we have not for a long time ordered you to come to us was that, having recently returned from the immense labours of the Italian expedition and the Greek embassy, we thought that you ought to be granted a period of daily rest. Another reason was that we had never come so near your regions that we could summon you to us without difficulty to yourself. But now, because immediately after Easter we are directing our journey toward the lower regions, wishing to manage all the affairs of that province by the counsel of your wisdom, we ask you to meet us at Nijmegen on the third Sunday after Easter.

Furthermore, we wish you to know that the expedition which we proclaimed at Würzburg for Apulia, having learned that the Greek people have been driven out of Apulia, we have thought proper to release the princes from it, devoting ourselves more particularly to those urgent concerns by which the honour of the empire is more seriously pressed and which we can neither can nor ought longer to overlook without injury to our honour: namely, the pride and recklessness of the people of Milan. By this, the churches and cities of Lombardy have, as our own men know best, been devastated in many ways and are daily devastated in contempt of the empire. [Col. 1448C] Unless our power forestalls their designs with swift action, a more grievous danger will arise for the empire.

Therefore, on Palm Sunday at Fulda, upon the counsel of the princes, we proclaimed an expedition against Milan, to begin on the coming vigil of Pentecost and to proceed for a year from Ulm. We impose this expedition upon your prudence under the expectation of our favour. We ask that, just as you arranged our seal according to a suitable design at your own discretion, [Col. 1448D] so you should also endeavour without delay to design the seal of your lady, and bring it to us at Aachen, engraved and well polished.

### LETTER CCCCXXIV. Emperor Frederick to King Henry of England

He commends to him Gerald, abbot of Solignac. (Year 1157.)

FREDERICK, by God’s grace Roman Emperor Augustus, great and peace-giving, crowned by God, to his most beloved brother and intimate and special friend HENRY, illustrious king of the English, duke of the Normans and Aquitanians: the firmest bond of brotherly love and indissoluble friendship.

[Col. 1449A] Imperial dignity properly extends the healing hand of clemency to the holy churches and religious monasteries in their needs, so that they may devote themselves more freely to divine worship and may more earnestly entreat God’s mercy for the salvation of ourselves and our people. Accordingly, we have kindly received and honourably treated the venerable man Gerald, abbot of the monastery of Solignac, who came to us from Aquitaine. He was most earnestly commended to us by our most faithful and beloved Wibald, abbot of the holy monasteries of our empire, Stavelot and Corvey, and we have mercifully heard him in his just petitions.

Among these, his chief request was that, since the monastery of Solignac is known to lie within your principality, we should provide him with imperial letters to your Magnificence, for his recommendation and the protection of the monastery entrusted to him. He had particular confidence in our mutual and most firm friendship, of which he had learned by fame’s report, that for the sake of our intercession you would accomplish a just and honourable matter with a kindly and more ready mind. [Col. 1449B] Therefore we earnestly admonish your nobility that, as befits royal clemency, you hold the person of the aforesaid abbot and the aforesaid monastery, commended to you, under your protection, and defend them from the assaults of wicked men by the power divinely granted to you.

Given in the palace at Aachen, on the second day before the Nones of May [6 May], in the fifth indiction.

### LETTER CDXXV. Henry, Duke of Bavaria and Saxony, to Emperor Frederick

Concerning the favour granted to Widikind of Schwalenberg and the penance imposed on him. (Year 1157.)

[Col. 1449C]

I inform Your Serenity that we have forgiven Widikind of Schwalenberg his misdeeds under this penance, on the counsel and petition of the lord bishop of Paderborn and his brother Folkwin, as well as of his other friends. At the assembly which I held at Corvey during Rogationtide, he forswore all German land which the Rhine separates from us, being to cross over by the feast of Saint James and never to return except at my summons. First, however, [Col. 1449D] he shall make satisfaction and peace, according to my counsel and command, with the lord abbot of Corvey and with the widow and orphans of Count Theoderic, whom he killed. I have recovered my castle of Dasemberg without any condition or provision of favour; and thus he who previously lost his benefices from me under the law of benefices has surrendered this also.

### LETTER CDXXVI. Abbot Wibald to Pope Adrian

He writes on behalf of Gerard, canon of Aiuncurt. (Year 1157.)

To his reverend father and lord in Christ, ADRIAN, the one and universal pope: Brother WIBALD, by God’s grace [Col. 1450A] that which he is in the Catholic Church, filial love in Christ and ready service of devotion in all things.

When we were at the synod of the lord bishop of Liège, a certain Gerard, a scholar, complained that one Gilbert of Aiuncurt [Note: This collegiate church of Aiuncurt, founded by Berengar, abbot of Saint Lawrence, was transferred three hundred years ago to Louvain, to the church of Saint James.] was taking from him a prebend which Lord Walter, abbot of the monastery of Saint Lawrence, who now governs that monastery according to the rule, had given him in the presence of many witnesses: namely, a vacant prebend which had belonged to the late clerk Rumbert, recently deceased. He complained further that the aforesaid abbot, by letters and trustworthy messengers, had ordered him to receive the revenues of the named prebend, but that the aforesaid Gilbert had forcibly prevented him, even threatening death.

Gilbert, however, replied that the same prebend belonged to him by right, because the predecessor of the aforesaid Abbot Walter had given him the first prebend that should fall vacant in that church. After hearing the allegations of both parties, the lord bishop, according to the custom of that church, asked his archdeacons and the whole clergy for their judicial decision. All declared with one harmonious voice that the prebend belonged by right to Gerard, who had lawfully received it upon the recent death of the clerk Rumbert, rather than to Gilbert, who had sought to ensnare a promise by watching for someone’s death.

This decision, pronounced by one of the archdeacons, was approved by all who were present in the synod. When the bishop, relying on the authority of all, ordered the aforesaid scholar Gerard to be fully restored to his prebend, his opponent Gilbert appealed—not from the judgment, but from its execution—to the name of your Highness. [Col. 1450C] Since it belongs to your authority to judge the validity of appeals, we earnestly beseech your Blessedness with devoted concern that you may regulate the remedy of appeal with such discernment that what was instituted by divine inspiration, not only by our most holy and venerable fathers, the pontiffs of our holy mother the Roman Church, to reveal the causes of the oppressed, but also by the most prudent emperors of the secular realm with remarkable foresight, may not, through the frivolous and superfluous licence of appellants, become the destruction of the innocent instead of the salvation provided for the oppressed.

Nor should your Highness delay to cut out this evil at its root, lest in the bishopric of Liège, which has always been free from this vice, some ambitious person buy, seek, desire, or contrive another’s death. Rather, ecclesiastical benefices should be granted when, upon the death of the person holding them, they have lawfully become vacant.

### LETTER CDXXVII. Pope Adrian IV to Abbot Wibald

He commends to him the Camaldolese of Betardingen and of Saint Peter of Rota. (Year 1157.)

[Col. 1451A]

ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son, the abbot of Stavelot: greeting and apostolic blessing.

“Although the care and solicitude of all churches rests upon us,” etc. See Adrian IV under the year 1159.

### LETTER CDXXVIII. Pope Adrian IV to the Archbishop of Cologne, the Bishop of Constance, and the Abbot of Stavelot

He commends to them the monastery of Saint Antimo. (Year 1157.)

[Col. 1451B]

ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brothers the archbishop of Cologne and the bishop of Constance, and to his beloved son the abbot of Stavelot: greeting and apostolic blessing.

“The order both of reason and of equity,” etc. See the passages cited above.

### LETTER CDXXIX. Pope Adrian IV to the Abbot of Corvey

He commends to him, before the emperor, the affairs of the Roman Church and his legates who are to negotiate with him. (Year 1157.)

ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son, the abbot of Corvey: greeting and apostolic blessing.

[Col. 1451C] “Your devotion and reverence,” etc. See Pope Adrian IV under the year 1159.

### LETTER CDXXX. Pope Adrian IV to Abbot Wibald

He commends to him his legates to the emperor. (Year 1157.)

ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son, the abbot of Stavelot: greeting and apostolic blessing.

“Proved now in many matters,” etc. See Adrian.

### LETTER CDXXXI. Pope Adrian IV to the Archbishop …, the Bishop of Bamberg, and Abbot Wibald

He commends to them, before the emperor, the abbot and convent of Farfa. (Year 1157.)

[Col. 1451D]

ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to the venerable archbishop … and bishop of Bamberg, and to his beloved son WIBALD, abbot of Corvey: greeting and apostolic blessing.

“Because the monastery of Farfa,” etc. See Adrian.

### LETTER CDXXXII. Emperor Frederick to Abbot Wibald

Concerning the Polish legates. (Year 1157.)

FREDERICK, by God’s grace Roman Emperor and ever Augustus, to his beloved WIBALD, abbot of Corvey and Stavelot: his favour and every good thing.

[Col. 1452A] We render due thanks to your affection, because after the court at Bamberg you were so near at hand and ready to assist us that, if summoned by our majesty, you would perhaps without hesitation or delay come devotedly to carry out all our commands. We wish, therefore, that your prudence should know that the principal envoys of the Poles came to us at Halle; but they brought us no such proposal as would give us an occasion to remain, having been encouraged in this hope by certain of their supporters—that we could in no way carry out the impending expedition. Therefore, placing all our confidence in the mercy of God, in whose hand is the heart of the king, we set out on campaign on the second day before the Nones of August [4 August], earnestly asking your affection to obtain for us, by unwearied prayers before the divine mercy, prosperous [Col. 1452B] success and a happy return. If, however, the Greeks arrive in the meantime, we have directed them to await our return at Worms. You too, summoned thither by our letters after our return, are to come without fail, since we propose to conduct no negotiations with the Greeks without consulting you.

### LETTER CDXXXIII. OF MONK R. TO ABBOT WIBALD

He gives thanks because, through Wibald’s intercession, he was honourably received by the bishop of Metz. (A.D. 1157.)

To his lord and reverend father WIBALD, abbot of Stavelot and Corvey, Brother R., humble by the grace of God: his scanty prayer and devoted service.

[Col. 1452C] The favour of your kindness accompanied me on my journey to Metz; it was with me and laboured with me, so that at this time I might find acceptance with my lord the bishop. For I was received, entertained, and dismissed by him and his household honourably and familiarly, so that I might plainly recognize, according to the common saying, that “my chin is supported by your hand while I swim.” Relying, therefore, most greatly upon your prudence in these and similar matters, I give thanks to the supreme Provider, earnestly beseeching that He may preserve you, sound and safe without end, for us and for our people, and that He Himself may repay what I cannot.

### LETTER CDXXXIV. OF EMPEROR FREDERICK TO ABBOT WIBALD

Concerning the victory gained over the Poles. (A.D. 1157.)

[Col. 1452D]

FREDERICK, by the grace of God Emperor of the Romans and ever August, to his beloved WIBALD, abbot of Corvey and Stavelot: his favour and every good.

How great a favour divine mercy bestowed upon us in the Polish expedition [Note: [Col. 1451] Radewicus assigns this expedition against the Poles to the year 1157, chapter 1; consult him if you wish.] which we recently accomplished gloriously, and with how great glory and honour it exalted the Roman Empire, the Poles themselves, reduced beneath the yoke of our dominion, attest; and we have thought it right to make this known to your affection as fully as we can. Although Poland was exceedingly well fortified by art and nature, so that our predecessors, kings and emperors, [Col. 1453A] had scarcely reached the River Oder except with great difficulty, yet we, by the power of God, who visibly went before us, penetrated their barricades—which they had made in narrow places by dense masses of felled trees and had blocked with a great contrivance of engineering—and on the octave of the Assumption of Saint Mary [22 August] crossed with our whole army, contrary to the Poles’ expectation, the River Oder, which encloses that whole land as though with a wall and by its depth shuts everyone out.

So great, indeed, was everyone’s eagerness to cross that some plunged into deep whirlpools, while others swam across. At this sight the Poles, utterly terrified and now expecting nothing but the ruin and devastation of their land, burned the very strongly fortified camps of Głogów and Bytom, and many others which had previously not been taken by an enemy; [Col. 1453B] and they themselves fled before us, although they had assembled a very great army with the assistance of neighbouring peoples—the Ruthenians, Parthians, Prussians, and Pomeranians. We pursued them in their flight; passing through the bishopric of Wrocław and the bishopric of Poznań, we devastated almost the entire land with fire and sword.

Therefore, when the duke of Poland saw that the whole land and people were endangered before the might of our hand, he approached our princes, both through his envoys and in person, and by many prayers and many tears scarcely at last obtained the favour of being allowed to return beneath the yokes of our dominion and recover our grace. Accordingly, in the aforesaid bishopric of Poznań, in the territory of Erisgowe, the aforesaid Duke Bolesław, [Col. 1453C] throwing himself at the feet of our majesty, was received into our favour through the intervention of the princes on the following terms.

First, he swore for himself and for all the Poles that his brother, an exile, had not been expelled to the dishonour of the Roman Empire. Next, he promised to give two thousand marks to us, one thousand to the princes, twenty marks of gold to our wife, and two hundred marks of silver to our court, for his negligence in not coming to our court and in not rendering to us the loyalty due from his land. He also swore to undertake the Italian expedition. Then he swore that he must come to our court to be held at Magdeburg at the Nativity of the Lord, there to give a full answer concerning the complaint of his expelled brother. Thus, after fealty had been sworn to us and hostages received for the faithful performance of all the foregoing—Casimir, the duke’s brother, and other nobles—we return gloriously, with God as our guide. Moreover, because in the embassy from the Greeks we desire your prudence to be present with us, we request by this command that your affection hasten to meet us at Würzburg on the vigil of Saint Michael.

### LETTER CDXXXV. OF HENRY, DUKE OF BAVARIA AND SAXONY, TO ABBOT WIBALD

He rejoices in Wibald’s prosperity, promises that he will take charge of the estate of Pappenheim, and that Widikin will pay him what is owed. (A.D. 1158.)

[Col. 1454A]

To WIBALD, venerable abbot of the holy Church of Corvey, his most beloved lord, HENRY, by the grace of God Duke of Bavaria and Saxony: devoted service with all sincere affection.

With all our heart we love and desire that everything relating to the increase of your honour may proceed in good order. Henceforth, concerning your estate at Pappenheim, as you have informed us, we shall most willingly make provision, and shall carefully impose this responsibility upon our castellans of Daseberg. Moreover, what Lord Widikin promised before us and did not pay after our return from the expedition, he shall pay; and if not freely, at least in accordance with your and our good pleasure. [Col. 1454B]

### LETTER CDXXXVI. OF EMPEROR FREDERICK TO H. OF LIMBURG

That he should honour Abbot Wibald and undertake nothing against the property of the monastery of Stavelot. (A.D. 1158.)

FREDERICK, by the grace of God Emperor of the Romans and ever August, to H. of Limburg: his favour and every good.

It is right, and highly becoming to imperial magnificence, that persons who serve our empire with more ready devotion should both be loved more closely by us and be preserved with due reverence by all who cherish the honour of our empire. Therefore, we earnestly request and admonish your diligence to strive to honour and love our faithful servant Wibald, abbot of Stavelot, who has now laboured much and long in our service and for the interests of the empire; and not to cease to protect and preserve the Church of Stavelot over which he presides. [Col. 1454C] We further forbid you, and command you under pain of forfeiting our favour, to inflict any violence upon the possessions granted to that Church by your predecessors, or in any manner to attempt to harass it. Know without doubt that this same Church, with all that belongs to it, has been placed under the protection and defence of our empire; therefore, whoever injures it will offend us.

### LETTER CDXXXVII. OF POPE ADRIAN IV TO BERNARD, BISHOP OF PADERBORN, AND GI., ABBOT OF LIESBORN

He entrusts a certain case to them for settlement. (A.D. 1158.)

[Col. 1454D]

ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother B., bishop of Paderborn, and his beloved son Gi., [Note: [Col. 1453D] Liesborn is an ancient Benedictine monastery in the diocese of Münster, founded, it is said, by Charlemagne in favour of his sister Roswindis; in the twelfth century it passed to monks and continues to flourish under the Bursfeld Congregation.] abbot of Liesborn: greeting and apostolic blessing.

“The bearer of the present letter,” etc. (See under Adrian at A.D. 1159.)

### LETTER CDXXXVIII. OF A., ARCHBISHOP OF MAINZ, TO ABBOT WIBALD

He complains about the Count Palatine of the Rhine and requests the emperor’s assistance against him. (A.D. 1158.)

[Col. 1455A]

A. [Note: [Col. 1455] Arnold of Selenhofen, formerly chancellor and subsequently made archbishop, is said to have been killed by the citizens in 1160.], by the grace of God humble minister of the see of Mainz, to WIBALD, reverend abbot of the Church of Corvey: greeting and heartfelt affection.

We render no small measure of thanks to your kindness because you took care to visit us in your letters so fraternally and affectionately, and, by assuring us that the condition of the lord king and of yourself was, by God’s grace, prosperous, to remove from our heart the wound of anxiety. Having, therefore, good confidence in you as in a brother and friend, we inform you with complaint [Col. 1455B] that the Count Palatine of the Rhine—God is witness—having no cause against us, contrary to the faith and oath by which he was bound to us, suddenly and unexpectedly laid violent hands upon the Church of Mainz and upon us, together with certain accomplices in his wickedness. He destroyed our castles, took our men captive, devastated our estates not only by plunder but also subjected them to his dominion; he despoiled holy cemeteries and churches, stripped the altars themselves and the venerable relics of their ornaments, burst into monasteries of monks, broke open their treasuries, and did not fear to commit sacrilegious plunder.

The authors of this wickedness also assert and spread abroad everywhere that they inflict this injury upon the churches of God and upon us by command of the lord king; but we know that, as sons of falsehood, they have falsely invented this. [Col. 1455C] Therefore, we most earnestly entreat your fraternity, which we have always found favourable toward us in good things, that, sharing sorrow for these pressures and tribulations of ours, you may suggest to the lord king that he deign to aid His Church and us with the assistance due, and that, by letters directed into our regions, he may wish to rebuke and refute those false informers for the rash falsehood by which they presumed to accuse and stain the most sincere good faith of his majesty.

### LETTER CDXXXIX. OF POPE ADRIAN IV TO ABBOT WIBALD

That he should urge the emperor to remain in reverence for the Apostolic See. (A.D. 1158.)

[Col. 1455D]

ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son WIBALD, abbot of Stavelot: greeting and apostolic blessing.

“Your devotion,” etc. See under Adrian.

### LETTER CDXL. OF EMPEROR FREDERICK TO FREDERICK, BISHOP OF MÜNSTER

He entrusts to him for settlement a case between Maurinus, a ministerial of Corvey, and Folker, his own dependent. (A.D. 1158.)

FREDERICK, by the grace of God Emperor of the Romans, August, [Col. 1456A] to F., bishop of Münster: his favour and every good.

We have received the complaint of our beloved and faithful Abbot of Corvey and of his ministerials concerning a certain man named Maurinus, whom a free man named Folker, from your territory, holds captive. The men of Corvey assert that he is a ministerial of their Church. Since we especially exalt the dignity of our empire when we render judgment and justice to those who flee to us, we earnestly charge your diligence that, upon receipt of this our letter, you appoint a day for each party; and, after hearing the allegations of both parties and carefully investigating the truth, if the men of Corvey can prove through kinsmen that he is a ministerial servant of the Church [Col. 1456B] of Corvey, you are to restore him to freedom; but if they cannot establish this, you are to return him to the aforesaid man.

### LETTER CDXLI. OF EMPEROR FREDERICK TO THE CHAPTER OF OSNABRÜCK

That they should settle amicably the dispute between themselves and the men of Corvey concerning tithes. (A.D. 1158.)

FREDERICK, by the grace of God Emperor of the Romans, August, to the provost, dean, and all the clergy of the Church of Osnabrück: his favour and every good.

Mindful of your petition, which you unanimously poured forth in our presence when we were among you, asking us to attempt to quiet and settle the complaint of our beloved and familiar servant Wibald, [Col. 1456C] abbot of Corvey, and of his brethren concerning tithes in the bishopric of Osnabrück, we discussed this matter with that same faithful servant of ours at the court which we held at Bamberg on the octave of Saint John the Baptist. But after learning from him the whole case more plainly and fully—namely, that the Church of Corvey had lawfully possessed these tithes from the beginning of the foundation of that monastery, having received them from its founder, Emperor Louis, and having had them confirmed by privileges of all his successor emperors and kings, until the time of our great-grandfather Emperor Henry IV, who, during that conflict which existed between himself and the Roman pope, granted the tithes out of a certain resentment to a bishop of Osnabrück—[Col. 1456D] after hearing, I say, the whole course of this case, we urged the aforesaid faithful abbot of ours to desist for the present from his complaint, though it was just, and, out of love for us, to withdraw from the appeal by which he had summoned your bishop, Provost Theoderic, and Master Thethard before the Apostolic See. Although he strongly resisted, we at last obtained this from him only with difficulty.

We do not wish you to take this postponement of the complaint as an occasion for increased arrogance. Rather, we command you, after this warning, to make efforts again to settle that same complaint with the aforesaid abbot and the Church of Corvey. For when we have an opportunity, if it has not first been settled, we ourselves shall investigate the same complaint and, both for the Church of Corvey, which belongs to the right of our empire, [Col. 1458A] and for the person who presides there, who has served the empire long and greatly, shall determine the case either by judicial procedure or by another suitable settlement.

[Col. 1457]

## APPENDIX TO THE LETTERS OF WIBALD

So that learned men may find nothing lacking in us for illustrating the memory of the distinguished man Wibald, abbot of Stavelot and Corvey, it has seemed good to append to his letters, by way of an Appendix, certain records or diplomas which either he himself obtained or which concern him, and which may contribute not a little to his commendation. These have been collected by us either from the manuscripts of the distinguished monastery of Corvey or from elsewhere.

### I. Diploma of Frederick, Archbishop of Cologne, concerning the subjection of the monastery of Malmedy and the superiority of Stavelot over it. (A.D. 1128.)

[Col. 1457B]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. FREDERICK, by the grace of God archbishop of the holy Church of Cologne, to the brethren dwelling together in the monastery of Stavelot: eternal salvation in the Lord.

Mindful of Scripture, which says, “Blessed are the feet that bring peace,” just as we strive to preserve the good of peace and concord in our churches, so we strive to cut off in them and from them occasions of scandals and dissension; and just as we wish our own affairs to remain in their proper state, so we dread overturning things justly possessed by others. [Col. 1457C] Therefore, wishing to cut away the source of dissension and division which has until now troubled the Churches of Stavelot and Malmedy by a long-standing feud, and being assisted by Brother Wibald, [Note: [Col. 1457D] Not long afterward he became abbot of Stavelot, then of Celles, and subsequently of Corvey; he was in favour with four emperors, [Col. 1458D] Henry IV, Lothair II, Conrad II, and Frederick I.] master and porter of the Church of Stavelot, we carefully reread the foundation records of the aforesaid places and the privileges of the Church of Stavelot.

In them it was found that Saint Remaclus, founder of both places, after first constructing Malmedy himself, chose Stavelot as the principal place for the dwelling and burial of himself and his successors; and that, because this place lies in the diocese of Liège, all abbots of both places in succession ought to be consecrated by the bishop of Liège. [Col. 1457D] There is also the fact that all privileges—both those concerning the ban-league and the election of abbots, and those treating the right of the advocate—which have been bestowed many times upon these same places by emperors and kings, and confirmed by apostolic authority by Popes Gregory V and Leo IX, and by which each Church maintains its right, are kept at Stavelot. Among these appears the pre-eminent dignity of the Church of Stavelot: without prejudice to the men of Malmedy, the men of Stavelot hold the first part in electing an abbot, and may choose from among themselves a suitable person without objection from the men of Malmedy.

Such being the facts, it is clear that the Church of Stavelot holds primacy and that Malmedy owes it subjection and obedience. The men of Malmedy have until now attempted to weaken this so far as to wish, during the dissension in the time of Otto II of blessed memory, to have an abbot of their own. This was annulled by the judgment of twenty bishops at Ingelheim, as may be read in the privilege of the aforesaid emperor concerning the same matter. Likewise, in the time of Lord Emperor Henry IV, when separation was again effected through Lord Archbishop Anno, an abbot of Malmedy was indeed appointed; but when Saint Remaclus shone forth through incomparable miracles at the royal court, all those of the opposing party who were present being refuted, Malmedy was restored to the men of Stavelot. [Col. 1458C]

We, then, as has been said, desiring to remove from the aforesaid places every source of dissension and scandal in accordance with the tenor of truth and reason, establish and permanently confirm by this present privilege that one abbot, elected in accordance with the aforesaid privileges, shall always preside over both places; and that Malmedy shall obey the Church of Stavelot with that right of subjection by which all cells or provostships are seen to be subject to their monasteries. Except in the necessity of death, they are to make and render monastic blessing and the written instruments of their profession in the Church of Stavelot, and not, as they did this year, elsewhere. Nor can it or ought it to assist them as a precedent that, after the aforesaid dissension had already arisen, Abbot Theoderic blessed and caused certain men of Malmedy to make profession at Malmedy, intending thereby to make them more faithful and subject to himself—an intention which the outcome showed he did not achieve. [Col. 1458D]
