Nor shall any of our successors, namely the archbishops of Cologne, ever burden the abbot of Stavelot with requiring him to become subject to himself and to assume responsibility for the place of Malmedy, as was attempted in our time; rather, at his consecration he shall assume the care of both Churches. Further, because ordinations and consecrations for the place of Malmedy belong to our diocese, if the abbot wishes to send ordained brethren to Malmedy, we do not deny this to him, since it is done everywhere among monks in places of this kind; or, if under the title of that place he wishes to present candidates to us for ordination, we shall lay hands upon them as well.

Moreover, in order to forestall every perversion of scandal, we also establish that if any serious cause or offence should arise at Malmedy, it may by no means be settled or amended without the deliberation and consent of the men of Stavelot. The abbot shall have free power, as seems good to him, to transfer, support, and receive [Col. 1459B] his brethren. That all these things may remain stable and unshaken, we decree them under the sanction of an anathema, and have caused the witnesses present at the granting of this privilege to be subscribed below: Arnold, provost of Saint Peter; Hugh, dean; Bruno, provost of Saint Gereon; Arnold, provost of Saint Mary ad Gradus; Robert, abbot of Deutz; Gerard, abbot of Saint Pantaleon; Count Adolf of Saffenberg; likewise Adolf of Berg, Theoderic of Gladbach, and many other most approved persons of both orders.

Done at Cologne in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1128, in the sixth indiction, in the reign of Lord King Lothair III.

### II. Concerning the possessions of the monastery of Stavelot under Abbot Saint Poppo. (A.D. 1130.)

[Col. 1459C]

From the first foundation of the monastery, the abbot never assigned any private estates to his own service or that of the realm, but held the churches of the abbey serving his own needs and those of the realm, except certain ones belonging to the use of the brethren. And as Abbot Poppo, restorer of our monastery, who died eighty-two years ago [Note: [Col. 1459] Saint Poppo died in 1048; consequently this instrument was issued about the year 1130.], himself held them and left them to be held by his successors, so we shall record the churches and possessions belonging to the service of the abbot and the realm. Then we shall list what Abbot Poppo, despoiler of our place, gave away or sold.

[Col. 1459D] The church of Oyeis paid six pounds into the abbot’s hand; the church of Graisde, four pounds; Olfait, two pounds; Osisines, three pounds; Fineval, two pounds; Spontin, seven pounds; Haletin, five pounds; Jupille, two pounds; Izers, three pounds; Longia, two pounds; Hoseumont, ten pounds; Rochelevenges, ten pounds; Awogne, five pounds; Lovigneis, two pounds; Verviers, two pounds; Keren, five pounds; Buiteback, forty shillings; Bolenges, thirty shillings; at the estate of Wellin, sixteen pounds; at the estate of Neuville, nine pounds; at the estate of Walendor, nine pounds; at the estate of Bacinga, ten pounds; at Leignon, three pounds; at Comblenz, three pounds; at Seignaces, two pounds; from the censuses at Oseis, three pounds; from the census at Aiflois, two pounds; at Okeriis, two pounds; at Bra, [Col. 1460A] three pounds: total, 133 pounds.

At Lernau, one cartload of wine; at Baldau, one; at Rahieres, one; at Chevrons, one; at Sanctovito, two; at Tumbis, four; at Waimis, one; at Amblavia, two; at Lorenceis, one; at Novavilla, two; the mill of Malmedy, one cartload of wine. At Wellin, forty rams; at Lengun, twenty; at Olzieres, thirty-eight; at Generez, twenty-two; at Lovengeis, thirty; at Lernau, thirty. The holding of Chenruus contains twenty-five *bonuaria* of land; the holding of Rahieres contains twenty-four *bonuaria*.

### III. Diploma of Emperor Lothair II granted to Abbot Wibald

He confirms the possessions and immunities of the monastery, the election of its abbot, its sole advocate, etc. (A.D. 1131.)

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. LOTHAIR [Col. 1460B] III, by the grace of God King of the Romans, to WIBALD, abbot of Stavelot, and his successors.

Although the care of royal providence ought not to be lacking to all the Churches of Jesus Christ, nevertheless, in accordance with the apostolic teaching by which good ought especially to be bestowed upon those of the household of faith, we ought to show more earnest support of our aid to those Churches which stand under the protection of our care and do not cease to pray with special devotion for our welfare and that of the whole empire. For indeed it is no lesser grace to restore what has been destroyed than to build something new.

Therefore let the diligence of all our faithful, both present and future, know that we, together with our wife Richenza, devoutly visited the place of Saint Remaclus at Stavelot, [Col. 1460C] where we carefully heard and reread from the brethren of that Church the rights and privileges of the place. Accordingly, at the petition and out of reverence for Abbot Wibald, we confirm and ratify the privileges granted to that Church by Kings Sigebert, Hilderic, Clovis, and Dagobert, who were founders of the aforesaid place; likewise those granted by Emperors Charles, Louis, and the three Ottos, also Conrad and the five Henrys, and by the other faithful persons who bestowed any goods upon that Church.

Let the monks of that place therefore have free authority to elect an abbot according to the Rule of Saint Benedict and the form of the canons, so that both monasteries—namely Stavelot and Malmedy—shall always remain under the rule of one abbot. Because Saint Remaclus chose a place of burial in their principal house, namely Stavelot, election shall always take place at Stavelot; and the following consideration shall prevail: that a suitable person from the community of the Church of Stavelot, if one is found, shall first be chosen. [Col. 1460D] If, however—which we do not believe—no one can be promoted from that place, then a suitable person shall first be sought from Malmedy or from another place.

Whatever they have until now possessed peacefully and without disturbance, and whatever they have exchanged by *concambia* [exchanges], we decree that they shall henceforth possess inviolate. We also establish that they shall have only one advocate. If he wishes to appoint a second in his stead, that second must receive the ban from us. The advocates must have neither residences nor lodgings on the estates of that Church, and at none of the abbot’s pleas may they be present or demand any right. They are not to impose forced exactions, take palfreys, demand fines, provisions, or redemption-payments, or make any exaction whatever. But if they are summoned by the abbot for a necessary cause, they shall receive one third only in those cases which they have remedied for the abbot; nor shall they ever acquire in the possessions which that Church may yet obtain any right other than that set forth above. [Col. 1461A]

We have also caused this to be adjudged in that place and, by the present privilege, have inviolably enacted that stewards or judges shall not hold office by hereditary right, but that both offices—that of steward and of *juvveria*—shall remain in the abbot’s power and favour, and that the abbot shall determine their term and conditions by the right and law of offices, not by the law of benefices. We condemn under perpetual law all benefices granted by the second Abbot Poppo, and decree them void, according to the judgment of our predecessor Emperor Henry.

We confirm in perpetual right to the brethren the village of Turnines, belonging to the brethren’s table, which Count Godfrey of Namur unjustly took from them and renounced by judgment of the court into the hand of Emperor Henry; and we restore with eternal validity to the brethren the village of Vilippa, according to the privilege of the same emperor, which Warner of Kerpen had unjustly invaded. We confirm the boundaries of the ban-league according to the decrees of all our predecessors, namely kings and emperors, [Col. 1461C] and secure them by the imposition of our ban. And that all may remain ratified and undisturbed, we have confirmed these matters by the present privilege and caused them to be sealed with the impression of our seal.

The sign of Lord Lothair III, by the grace of God most unconquered King of the Romans.

I, Thietmar, acting for Adalbert, archchancellor, have authenticated this.

Given at Stavelot on the Ides of April [13 April], in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1131, the ninth indiction, in the sixth year of the reign of Lord Lothair III, most serene King of the Romans. Happily. Amen.

### IV. Charter of Wibald, Abbot of Stavelot, concerning matters transacted and corrected by him at the estate of Andernach. (A.D. 1132.)

[Col. 1461D]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. WIBALD, by the grace of God abbot of Stavelot, to his successors.

Since we ought, as we have promised, to gather together what has been scattered and preserve what has been gathered, we have resolved, in reliance on God’s mercy, to devote every care to restoring the excessively neglected and decayed affairs of our Church. Therefore we wish it to be known to posterity and to the present generation that at our estate of Andernach our possessions were greatly diminished by unfaithful officials, partly mortgaged by them and partly exchanged for things of lesser value.

We therefore came there with the faithful men [Col. 1462A] of the Church; having reviewed the possessions and counted the rents of the people, we found very many things alienated contrary to the interest of our Church, without our consent and without confirmation by our predecessors. We reasonably decreed all these unjust arrangements void, judgment having been publicly pronounced, in conformity with canonical form, by both our men and the *scabini* [assessors] of the same estate: that no exchange or alienation of ecclesiastical property should be valid unless confirmed by the consent of the brethren and the lawful gift of the abbot, with the advocate’s assent, in a formal instrument.

Accordingly, after recovering certain things and taking counsel with our faithful men, we allowed and confirmed the exchange of an estate—commonly called a *mansio* or a *census*—belonging to our demesne. It had been exchanged with a certain Adelbert for his estate and vineyard, which can yield four *amae* of wine. Retaining the vineyard wholly for ourselves, we granted that a certain member of the household, named Nicheiz, should peacefully possess the estate received in exchange, which he had built upon, and should pay annually twenty denarii as rent for it. [Col. 1462B] Another of our estates, at Lodenesdorp, had been exchanged with a certain Henry for his estate at Andernach and for a vineyard capable of producing three *amae* of wine. Retaining the vineyard, we granted the estate itself to the same Nichoz for twenty denarii of rent, which our estate had likewise paid previously.

Done at our estate and house at Andernach, [Col. 1462C] in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1132, in the tenth indiction, in the reign of Lord Lothair III, King of the Romans, and of Lord Albero, archbishop of Trier.

Witnesses to this matter are Hillinus, provost; Ebroinus, provost; Albricus; Warnerus, monks; and, among laymen, Widericus Albus, Hillinus of Alriniunt, Arnulfus of Osnes, Godfrey of Cittene; among the *scabini*, Folbertus, Siboldus, Borchardus, Bezelinus, and many others.

### V. Ordinance of Abbot Wibald: concerning the investiture of the churches of Longia and Mount Saint Rainier not to be received from a lay hand. (A.D. 1133.)

[Col. 1462D]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. WIBALD, by divine mercy abbot of Stavelot, to HERIBRAND of Longia and his successors.

The course of events is usefully and prudently transmitted in writing to the knowledge of those to come, lest through ignorance the law [lacuna] be altered. Therefore let all our posterity know that you had held, for yourself and your successors, by feudal right from our predecessors—namely Lord Abbot Cuno and Lord Abbot John—the church in the village of Longia and that on Mount Saint Rainier, as an addition to the benefice which you hold on condition that you should always and continually reside in our castle of Longia. That is, whenever the aforesaid [Col. 1463A] churches became vacant through the death of their priests, you were to grant those churches by your own hand and yourself bring the person for investiture with the altar.

But in our time, after the death of Brother Robert the priest, who had held those same churches, we could by no prayers or counsel [lacuna] be induced to allow possession of churches to be granted by a layman. Yet because we love you greatly as a good and faithful man, and wished to preserve both you and your heirs in the residence of our castle, we took care, with the counsel of our brethren and men of the Church, to make another provision suited to the Church’s interest and to your honour.

For we grant to you, and permanently establish by this present writing, that whenever the aforesaid churches are vacant, it shall be yours to present to us or to our successors a suitable and canonical person for investiture. Nor shall it ever be lawful for us or for any abbot to burden or delay, by any condition or exaction, the person presented by you or your heirs; rather, without any compact, they shall grant the aforesaid churches from their own hand to that person, and, after receiving an oath of fidelity, shall bring him to the gift of the altar by their letters and witnesses. [Col. 1463B] But if anyone should at any time attempt to weaken or violate our ordinance and, against your will, intrude any person into the aforesaid churches, may he incur the wrath of God, of the blessed Apostles Peter and Paul, and of Saint Remaclus on the dreadful Day of Judgment.

Done at Stavelot in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1133, in the reign of Lord Lothair III, King of the Romans, [Col. 1463C] with Alexander as bishop at Liège.

The witnesses among the brethren are Warnerus, dean; Rodulfus, custodian; Heribrand, cellarer; Hozelo, cantor. Among the laymen: Nicholas of Longia; Adelard, his brother; Widericus of Villa; Widericus Albus; Widericus Niger; Anselm, steward; and many others.

### VI. Charter of the Monks of Stavelot

They grant to Abbot Wibald for restoration the village of Bovianicum, reduced to nothing, in which the body of Saint Remaclus had lain hidden during the persecution of the Danes. (A.D. 1136.)

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. The brethren [Col. 1463D] of the monastery of Stavelot, to both future and present generations.

As it belongs to the discernment of prelates diligently and vigorously to serve the needs of their subjects, so likewise it is fitting that subjects promptly give assent to the honorable and useful will of their prelates. Therefore, Father Abbot Wibald, we grant your religious petition concerning our village of Boviniacum, which belongs to our wardrobe. Since during the persecution of the Danes the holy and venerable body of Saint Remaclus, our father and patron, lay safely hidden in that village—which has now been reduced to wilderness and left [Col. 1464A] without an inhabitant—and since you foster and embrace with singular desire and honor all things pertaining to the commemoration of our holy father, you propose, in honor of that same holy father, to restore and rebuild the said village.

We therefore grant you the aforesaid village with all its appurtenances, acquired or to be acquired, so that throughout your lifetime, wherever you may be placed, whether among us or elsewhere, in whatever estate or rank, in peace or adversity, you may freely administer and dispose of it for your own benefit, and use its revenues as you wish. This condition is imposed: you may not pledge the village, nor alienate it by fief or by any exchange without our common consent. After your death, however, the village [Col. 1464B], with all its increase and improvement and with every present and future revenue, shall return to our wardrobe, as it was before, without any opposition from the abbots.

And so that this agreement may remain firm, unshaken, and stable, with the consent of all in our common chapter, by the book of the Rule of blessed Benedict and by the hand of Lord Warner, dean, we gave you the village; we confirm it by this present writing; and at the dreadful judgment of God we condemn with a terrible anathema those who violate these conditions.

These things were enacted at Stavelot, in chapter, in the year of the Lord 1136, in the fourteenth indiction.

## VII. Charter of Wibald, Abbot of Stavelot, for Azo, Abbot of Mont Public

He grants him the church of Heran subject to an annual payment. (1136.)

[Col. 1464C]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Wibald, by the mercy of God abbot of the church of Stavelot, to his beloved brother and religious fellow abbot Azo of Mont Public at Liège, and to his successors in perpetuity.

[Note: [Col. 1463D] Azo was abbot of the monastery of Saint Urgidius at Mont Public outside the city of Liège, of the order of the regular canons of Saint Augustine. Its principal founder was Beringer, abbot of Saint Lawrence, as is evident from the letters of Abbot Wibald to be published below.]

If that steward in the Gospel was praised by the Lord’s own mouth for his use of unrighteous mammon, though he seemed to have committed fraud, then all the more must we, to whom God has entrusted the administration of His Church and who can exercise works of mercy from the offerings of the faithful, strive for the name and reward of true praise. [Col. 1464D] Therefore, instructed by these and similar examples, if from the property of our church we can provide something to needy churches without loss or diminution of our possessions, we wish to do so with ready will and cheerful hand.

Accordingly, venerable brother, we grant to you, and through you to your successors in perpetuity, the church of Heran for sixty-five solidi of Liège denarii, payable each year to our church. You shall pay one half of this sum within the octave of the Nativity of Saint John the Baptist, and the other within the octave of the feast of Saint Lambert. This is on the condition that, just as you have now [Col. 1465A], according to the custom of other persons to be invested, received from our hand in our—that is, the chapter of Stavelot—the grant and investiture of that church, and have sworn an oath of fidelity to us or to our church, so the successive overseers of the place shall do the same to us or to our successors and receive the church according to the right and custom of our church.

It has also been established with the common consent of the entire chapter that, from this day forward, your successors, upon their entry, after the privilege of this present charter has been read before the brethren, shall receive the grant of the aforesaid church under the prescribed condition and agreement, with no exaction, price, or gift imposed. They shall thereby discharge toward us or our successors every customary obligation of other investees, both in holding judgments concerning their peers and in attending provincial synods with us.

We have also granted you that you may devote the income of that church, as usefully as you can, to the needs and benefit of your brethren, while preserving episcopal right in all matters. You and your successors shall also discharge, without assistance from us, whatever belongs to episcopal or synodal justice, service, or the uses of the church.

Moreover, if anything in the aforesaid conditions is disturbed, altered, or made void by you or yours, or if you neglect to pay the aforesaid money on the appointed days, then, after you have been admonished up to a third time by us through our invested clerics [Col. 1465C], unless you wish according to law and justice to correct the neglect and make legal satisfaction, you shall lose the church and all its benefice without any possibility of recovery. But however circumstances may change in future times, since we have granted this church to you as stated above, two portions of the tithe shall belong to the wardrobe of our brethren, and the third to the prebend of the priest of that church.

This was enacted in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1136, in the fourteenth indiction, in the presence of Lord Abbot Wibald, in the sixth year of his ordination; while Lord Lothair III, Emperor Augustus of the Romans, was reigning, and Albero was elect at Liège.

The witnesses from among the brethren are Warner, prior; Arnulf, provost; Ellebold, cellarer; Cono, chamberlain; [Col. 1465D] and the entire congregation of the same place. From among the laity: Anselm, steward, and his brother Adelard; Albric and his brother Condric; Ebroin; Erchempert; Franco of Francorchamps; and many other sons of the church.

## VIII. Diploma of Emperor Lothair Granted to Abbot Wibald

He receives the monastery under his protection and confirms all its privileges. (1136.)

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Lothair, by God’s grace Emperor Augustus of the Romans, to Wibald, abbot of Stavelot, and his successors.

Although the care of imperial [Col. 1466A] providence ought not to be lacking to any of the churches of Jesus Christ, nevertheless, according to the apostolic command by which we are especially ordered to do good to those of the household of faith (Galatians 6), we ought to extend the support of our aid more earnestly to those churches which stand under the protection of our guardianship and do not cease to pray with special devotion for the welfare of us and of the whole empire. Nor is it a lesser grace to restore what has been built than to construct what is new.

Therefore let the diligence of all our faithful, both future and present, know that we, venerable Abbot Wibald, considering the constancy of your fidelity and the labors which you bear with us in the administration of our empire, have decreed to defend your church in all respects and fortify it with imperial privileges. Whatever, therefore [Col. 1466B], has been granted to your church—that is, to Stavelot—by Kings Sigibert, Hilderic, Clovis, Dagobert, or the others who were founders of the aforesaid place, or by Emperors Charles, Louis, and the three Ottos, also Conrad and the five Henries, and by other faithful persons who bestowed any goods upon the same church, we confirm and strengthen.

Let the monks of the same place therefore have free power to elect an abbot according to the Rule of Saint Benedict and the form of the canons, so that the two monasteries, namely Stavelot and Malmedy, may always remain under the rule of one abbot. And because blessed Remaclus chose Stavelot, their chief monastery, as his burial-place, election shall always be held at Stavelot [Col. 1466C], with this overriding consideration: a suitable person from the community of the church of Stavelot, if one is found, shall be chosen first. If no one can be promoted from that place—which we do not believe—then a suitable person shall first be sought from Malmedy or from another place.

Whatever they have hitherto possessed peacefully and undisturbed, and whatever they have exchanged by mutual exchanges, we decree that they shall possess immovably. We also establish that they shall have only one advocate, who, if he wishes to appoint a subordinate advocate, must receive the ban from us. Such advocates must have neither residences nor lodgings in the courts of the same church; they must not attend any pleas of the abbot, demand any right there, impose forced loans, take relay-horses, demand freda, provisions, or redemptions, or make any exaction whatsoever. But if they are invited by the abbot for a necessary cause, they shall receive a third part only in those cases which they settle for the abbot; nor shall they ever obtain, in properties which the church may hereafter acquire, any right other than that stated above.

We also confirm, according to the ancient constitution, that the abbots shall never furnish to us or to our envoys any military expedition, army, arms, ransom on their behalf, or provisions. Rather, the advocate, who holds a benefice from us and from the abbot precisely for this purpose, shall carefully discharge these obligations without support from the abbot or any of his people. We have also caused it to be adjudged in that place, and by the present privilege we inviolably decree [Col. 1467A], that stewards or judges shall not hold office by hereditary right, but that both offices—the stewardship and the *juweria*—shall remain within the power and favor of the abbot; and that abbots shall assign them their term and law according to the right and law of offices, not according to the right of benefices.

We condemn in perpetuity and decree void all benefices which Abbot Poppo II granted, in accordance with the judgment of our predecessor Emperor Henry. We confirm to the brethren as their own right the village of Turnines, which belongs to the brethren’s table, which Count Godfrey of Namur unjustly took from them and which he renounced into the hand of Emperor Henry by judgment of the court. We restore to the brethren with perpetual security the village of Vilippa, in accordance with the privilege of that same emperor, which Warner of Kerpen had unjustly seized.

We confirm the bounds of the league-ban according to the decrees of all our predecessors, namely kings and emperors, and strengthen them by the imposition of our ban. Whatever the same church has acquired or may justly acquire—namely villages, castles, estates, holdings, serfs, tolls, bridge-tolls, dues of entry or return, and every kind of public and royal tax—we decree by imperial authority that, as it has held them hitherto, so it shall henceforth possess them firmly without any opposition or disturbance. And in order that all these things may remain ratified and unshaken, we have confirmed them by this present privilege and caused it to be marked with our seal.

The sign of Lord Lothair III, most invincible Emperor of the Romans.

[Col. 1467C] I, Ebenurdus, acting for Uderip of Urulo, have verified this.

Given in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1136, on the sixteenth day before the Kalends of September, in the fourteenth indiction, in the second year of Lothair’s reign as king and the third of his empire.

Enacted at Würzburg, happily in Christ’s name. Amen.

## IX. Diploma of Lothair II, Written in Gold Letters and Marked with a Golden Bull

In favor of Abbot Wibald, whose fidelity and services it praises, it confirms all immunities and possessions of the monastery of Stavelot, and establishes the election of an abbot from the monastery of Stavelot in preference to Malmedy, if a worthy man is found, the rights and duties of advocates, and other matters. (1137.)

[Col. 1467D]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Lothair, by God’s grace Emperor Augustus of the Romans, to Wibald, abbot of Stavelot, and his successors in perpetuity.

Since our imperial solicitude and power ought to provide for the peace, tranquility, and interests of all God’s churches, we believe that the zeal of our goodwill and care ought especially to watch over those churches which belong to our empire and, so to speak, adhere to our empire; for they aid us and our empire through the continual and constant support of their prayers, and faithfully bear our labors and expenses in the temporal administration of the empire.

Accordingly, because we cherish more closely as our own the monastery of Stavelot [Col. 1468A], nobly founded by our predecessors, kings and emperors, enlarged by great possessions, magnificently honored with many privileges, and endowed with singular liberty, and because we wish to assist it justly in every respect, we consider especially worthy of our particular affection and favor the person of Lord and venerable Abbot Wibald, who rightly presides over that monastery. His faithfulness and devotion toward the stability and honor of our empire shone sufficiently and plainly in this Italian expedition. After many labors and dangers which he faithfully endured for us and with us in the administration of our empire in Apulia, when we were returning, he was forcibly and most remarkably drawn by the brethren of Monte Cassino and all the people of that place into election as abbot [Col. 1468B]. Remaining there for the honor and stability of our empire, he petitioned our majesty that we might deign to fortify and confirm by our imperial privilege the monastery of Stavelot, whose care he had not relinquished, and the things belonging to it.

Granting ready assent to his pious and reasonable petition, we have received into our protection the said monastery of Stavelot together with Malmedy and all its appurtenances, according to the enactments and commands of Kings Sigibert, Dagobert, Theoderic, Childeric, and others, and also of Emperors Charles, Louis, and the three Ottos, Conrad as well, and the five Henries. That is to say, it shall never be lawful for any king or emperor to sever this abbey, with its full integrity and the advocacy of all its possessions, from the kingdom by any form of alienation; to impose another lord upon it; or to grant it to anyone in benefice or exchange. [Col. 1468C] Rather, it shall always remain with unshaken stability under the hand and service of us and our successors, and shall peacefully enjoy the liberty granted to it. Neither the monks nor their people shall pay, anywhere in our realm, any toll, bridge-toll, transit- or exit-dues, or any public impost or payment by land or water. It shall possess immovably through succeeding times the bounds of the league-ban [Col. 1468D], as they are named and entered in the older privileges, together with all their immunity and jurisdiction, just as the same church has possessed them hitherto.

We also decree, following the custom of our predecessors, that Malmedy, with all its appurtenances, shall never be torn or separated from the monastery of Stavelot. This has already been attempted three times, but has been lawfully quashed by judgment of princes and finally settled by imperial privileges. Therefore, when the abbot dies, the monks of both places shall come together harmoniously to the chapter-house at Stavelot and have the fullest freedom, according to the Rule of Saint Benedict, to elect an abbot. Yet this consideration shall prevail: because blessed Remaclus, founder and first abbot of both churches, chose to rest at Stavelot and to prefer that place to Malmedy [Col. 1469A] by his burial and by the ordination of abbots, the monks of Stavelot shall have the first voice in the election and shall elect an abbot from the community of Stavelot, if a worthy person is found. If no suitable person is found there—which we do not believe can happen—an abbot shall rather be chosen from the community of Malmedy than from outsiders. But if they find among themselves no person suitable for this office, they may freely elect an abbot from any other regular house without anyone’s objection. He shall receive investiture from us or our successor according to the custom of the realm, and consecration and the ordination of his monks from the bishop of Liège, to whom he owes no service, lodging, or meal, without payment or any exaction.

[Col. 1469B] He shall receive an advocate from our hand, who shall render to us the army-service and expedition, and all things belonging thereto, in return for the value and obligation of his benefice, while the abbot and all his people remain free of this burden and furnish neither ransom nor supplement for it to us or to the advocate. If the advocate wishes to appoint a subordinate advocate, that second advocate must receive the ban from our hand. We prohibit perpetually, by our imperial ban, the establishment of more advocates in the courts of the same abbey. The advocate shall have in the courts and villages no lodging, plea, or exaction whatsoever; he shall not exact *freda* or redemption-payments, make forced levies or assessments, or take riding-horses. Rather, the whole power and administration, [Col. 1469C] justice and profit, of all things and offenses shall freely reside with the abbot, the monks, and those whom they appoint. Where the abbot and his men cannot suffice to administer justice, if the advocate comes at the abbot’s request—for he must never come otherwise—he shall have a third share of that alone which accrues from such justice.

We decree that the castle of Longia, with the whole mass of the mountain, both valleys, and its jurisdiction, shall always belong and pertain to the abbot’s demesne hand, power, and administration, together with all benefices and dependent holdings which belong to the guard of that castle. We do not permit the advocate to have any residence or authority in that castle [Col. 1469D] or in possessions belonging to it.

Whatever the same church has obtained through the generosity of kings or emperors, or through the grants of devout Christians—whether lands, churches, chapels, tithes, or all their appurtenances and revenues—as it has possessed them hitherto; and whatever, great or small, it may hereafter obtain by just means wherever they may be situated, we immovably confirm to it under the power of our protection. We confirm especially its possession at Aachen: namely, its demesne and free chapel, thirty houses—twenty-five on one side [Col. 1470A], situated continuously and in order from the house which belonged to the bishop of Cambrai to the ditch on the side leading toward Harduin’s bridge—and five houses on the other side of the road before the aforesaid chapel of Saint Aldegundis; also six *bonuaria* of land lying all around there, seven *bonuaria* in the village called Vals, and one holding on Mount Hillini. We establish that all these things, with their uses, services, and rent, belong freely to the church of Stavelot. No marshal or prince of ours may, against the will of the abbot of Stavelot, have lodging or any service in the aforesaid houses.

Because there was disagreement between our ministerials and those of the church of Stavelot concerning the service which the church of Stavelot [Col. 1470B] owes each year—the former asserting that the church owed some kind of service from each crop, while the latter asserted on the contrary that it owed full royal service in the seventh year—we, in consideration of the merits of the aforesaid Abbot Wibald and at his petition, which we cannot refuse, grant and confirm in perpetuity that he and his successors shall pay to us or our successors, if we come to Aachen, twenty marks or service worth twenty marks each year. If it happens that we or our successors come either to Stavelot or to villages belonging to that monastery, he shall pay thirty marks or service worth thirty marks. But nowhere except in the houses of the monastery itself [Col. 1470C] or at Aachen shall he furnish to us or our successors the aforesaid service or redemption of the service.

Whenever he renders service to us, he shall receive from each of his clerics who hold mother churches five solidi, from each of his stewards five solidi, and twelve denarii from every holding of the church; no holdings being exempt from this payment on account of any benefice, agreement, pledge, or service. And in order that this may remain ratified and unshaken for all time, we have signed this precept with our own hand and caused it to be marked with a golden bull.

We have also ordered the witnesses present to be recorded below: Albero, archbishop of Trier; Conrad, archbishop of Magdeburg; Meingold [Col. 1470D], bishop of Merseburg; Albero, bishop of Basel; Albero, bishop of Liège; Andrew, bishop of Utrecht; Anselm, bishop of Havelberg; Henry, bishop of Toul; Conrad, abbot of Fulda; Henry, duke of Bavaria and margrave of Tuscany; Conrad, margrave of Wettin; Meinfrid, margrave; Frederick, margrave of Ancona, and his brother Warner; Count Landulf; Bucca Vitelli; Count Poppo; Count Adulph; and many other barons of the Roman Empire.

The sign of Lord Lothair III [Note: [Col. 1469D] Although Lothair was properly the second emperor of that name, he nevertheless styles himself the third, because he was the third of the German kings bearing the name Lothair to be raised to the empire. We find this observed in many other charters, although the second Lothair was king only and never emperor.] most invincible Emperor of the Romans.

[Col. 1471A] I, Ethardus, acting for Henry, bishop of Regensburg and archchancellor, have verified this.

I, the monk Engelbertus, acting for the notary Bertulf, wrote this.

Given in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1137, in the first indiction, on the tenth day before the Kalends of October; in the thirteenth year of Lothair’s reign as king and the fifth of his empire.

Enacted at Aquino in Campania, happily in Christ’s name. Amen.

## X. Charter of Wibald, Abbot of Stavelot

He grants the tithes of Femala to the church of Saint Martin at Liège. (1138.)

[Col. 1471B]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Wibald, by God’s grace abbot of Stavelot, to his successors.

Let all, future as well as present, know that in the eighth year of our ordination a certain Walter restored into our hands the share of property and tithe which he held in the church of Female. With the common counsel of our brethren and laity, we granted it to the brethren of the church of Blessed Martin at Liège to possess by hereditary right, on the agreement that they should pay two denarii each year in acknowledgment of that possession.

[Col. 1471C] This was enacted in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1138, in the first indiction, while Lord Conrad II, king of the Romans, was reigning, and Albero II was bishop at Liège.

The witnesses from among the brethren are Warner, dean; Ebroin; Robert; Cono; together with the entire community of the same church. From among the laity: Anselm, steward of Stavelot; Ebroin; Gundric; Henry of the Valley; Franco of Francorchamps; Godfrey of Beves; and many other sons of the church.

## XI. Diploma of Emperor Conrad

In favor of Abbot Wibald, it confirms all the monastery’s privileges, but especially Lothair’s golden bull. (1138.)

[Col. 1471D]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Conrad, by the favor of divine clemency king of the Romans.

Since our royal solicitude and power ought to provide for the peace, tranquility, and interests of all God’s churches, we believe that the zeal of our goodwill and care ought especially to watch over those churches which belong to our kingdom and, so to speak, adhere to our kingdom; for they also aid us and our kingdom with the continual and constant support of their prayers, and faithfully bear our labors and expenses in the temporal administration of the kingdom.

Accordingly, because we cherish more closely as our own the monastery of Stavelot, nobly founded by our predecessors, kings and emperors, enlarged by great possessions [Col. 1472A], magnificently honored with many privileges, and endowed with singular liberty, and because we wish to assist it justly in every respect, we consider particularly worthy of our special affection and favor the person of Lord and venerable Abbot Wibald, who rightly presides over that monastery. His fidelity and devotion toward the stability and honor of our kingdom shone sufficiently both in the Italian expedition under our predecessor Emperor Lothair and in our own elevation to royal dignity.

Therefore, at the petition of that abbot, to whom we wish to deny nothing just, we receive into our protection the said monastery of Stavelot with all its appurtenances, according to the enactments of Kings Sigibert, Dagobert, Clovis, and others, as also of Emperors [Col. 1472B] Charles, Louis, and the three Ottos; of Conrad, our great-grandfather, the emperor of blessed memory; and of the three Henries. That is to say, it shall never be lawful for any king or emperor to sever this abbey, with its full integrity and the advocacy of all its possessions, from the kingdom by any form of alienation, to impose another lord upon it, or grant it to anyone in benefice or exchange. Rather, it shall always remain, with unshaken stability, under the hand and service of us and our successors and shall peacefully enjoy the liberty granted it.

Neither the monks nor their people shall pay anywhere in our kingdom any toll, bridge-toll, transit- or exit-dues, or any public impost or payment by land or water [Col. 1472C]. It shall possess immovably through succeeding times the bounds of the league-ban, as they are named and entered in the older privileges, together with all their immunity and jurisdiction, just as the same church has possessed them hitherto.

We also decree, after the fashion of our predecessors, that Malmedy with all its appurtenances shall never be torn or separated from the monastery of Stavelot. This has already been attempted three times, but has been lawfully quashed by judgment of princes and finally settled by imperial privileges. Therefore, when the abbot dies, the monks of both places shall come harmoniously to the chapter-house at Stavelot and shall have the fullest freedom, according to the [Col. 1472D] Rule of Saint Benedict, to elect an abbot. Yet this consideration shall prevail: because blessed Remaclus, founder and first abbot of both churches, chose to rest at Stavelot and to prefer that place to Malmedy for his burial, the monks of Stavelot shall have the first voice in the election and shall elect an abbot from the community of Stavelot, if a worthy person is found. If no person is found there—which we do not believe can happen—an abbot shall rather be chosen from the community of Malmedy than from outsiders.

But if they find among themselves no person suitable for this office, they may freely elect an abbot from any other regular house, without anyone’s objection. Once invested by us or our successor according to the custom of the kingdom, he shall receive consecration and the ordination of his monks from the bishop of Liège, to whom he owes no kind of service [Col. 1473A]. He shall receive an advocate from our hand, who shall perform for us the expedition and the matters belonging to it, in return for the amount and obligation of his benefice, while the abbot and all his people remain free of this burden and render neither ransom nor supplement for it to us or to the advocate.

If the advocate wishes to appoint a subordinate advocate, he must receive the ban from our hand. We permanently prohibit by our royal ban the establishment of more advocates in the courts of the same abbey. The advocate shall have in the courts and villages no lodging, plea, or exaction whatsoever; he shall not exact *freda* or redemption-payments, make forced levies or assessments, or take riding-horses. Rather, the whole power and administration, [Col. 1473B] justice and profit, of all things and offenses shall freely rest with the abbot, the monks, and those whom they appoint. Where the abbot and his men cannot suffice to administer justice, if the advocate comes at the abbot’s request—for he must never come otherwise—he shall receive a third share only of what accrues from that justice.

We decree that the castle of Longia, with the whole mass of the mountain and both valleys, shall always belong and pertain to the abbot’s demesne hand, power, and administration, with all benefices and dependent holdings belonging to the guard of that castle. In its valley, we establish a market and public fairs by royal authority, having given our market-gloves for selling.

Whatever the same church has obtained through the generosity of kings or emperors, or through the grants of devout Christians, whether lands, churches, and all their appurtenances and revenues, as it has possessed them hitherto, and whatever it may hereafter obtain by just means, great or small, wherever situated, we immovably confirm to it under the power of our protection. We confirm especially the village of Tornines [Col. 1473C], restored to the aforesaid church by Emperor Otto of blessed memory. Count Godfrey of Namur had seized it; but, summoned on this matter by the aforesaid abbot before our court at Cologne, he restored and renounced it into our hands by the judgment of our princes, especially the Salian princes. By the text of this present privilege, we have assigned it into the abbot’s hand [Col. 1473D] for the use of the brethren.

We also restore to the aforesaid monastery the village of Vilippa, unjustly taken away in the time of our uncle, Emperor Henry of pious memory. We confirm in perpetuity the village of Sprimont, with its church, tithes, and lands belonging to that church, just as Duke Frederick granted it to the church for the sake of his soul. Whatever our predecessor Emperor Lothair granted by golden bull to the aforesaid faithful servant of his and ours, the abbot who remained at Monte Cassino for the honor of the kingdom, we too grant and confirm to him firmly.

And so that this may remain ratified and unshaken for all time, we have marked this precept with the impression of our seal and with our own hand. We have also ordered the witnesses present to be recorded below [Col. 1474A], whose names are: Thedewin, cardinal bishop of Santa Rufina and legate of the Apostolic See; Arnold, archbishop of Cologne; Albero, archbishop of Trier; Albero, bishop of Liège; Andrew, bishop of Utrecht; Embrico, bishop of Würzburg; Warner, bishop of Münster; Udo, bishop of Osenburg; Nicholas, bishop of Cambrai; Duke Waleran; his son Henry; William, Count Palatine; Godfrey of Ascha, who rendered judgment concerning Tornines +; Godfrey of La Roche; his brother Henry; and Theoderic, judge of Aachen.

The sign of Conrad II, most invincible king of the Romans.

I, Arnold, chancellor, acting for the archchancellor of Mainz [Col. 1474B], wrote and subscribed this.

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1138, in the first indiction.

Given at Cologne, on the third day before the Ides of April.

## XII. Charter of Abbot Wibald

Concerning the restoration of the castle and the transfer of the village of Longia. (1138.)

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. Wibald, unworthy abbot of Stavelot by God’s mercy, to his successors and to all faithful of the monastery of Stavelot, both future and present.

Mindful of the mercies and compassions of God which are from everlasting, and magnifying God in all His benefits for the grace bestowed upon us, we praise and proclaim Him wonderful, who advanced us, humble and unworthy though we are, to the governance of the monastery of Stavelot, and within the house of that monastery raised us to the preeminence of the abbacy by royal investiture through the lord Lothair III, emperor of the Romans of blessed memory, and by priestly blessing through the lord Alexander, bishop of Liège. Therefore, recalling the benefits divinely conferred upon us through these persons and through all those bestowed in the same church, we have diligently watched over, according to our capacity and means, the honor and advantage of the place, both future and present. But, hindered by the malignity of the times and continually occupied and wearied by frequent royal services, labors, and expenses, we have by no means been able to bring into effect as much of the work as we desired.

The castle of Logne, which our predecessors—men indeed prudent and religious—built for the protection of all our land, and carefully organized with necessary guards and watches and with many great estates bestowed upon it, was almost wholly collapsed, inhabited only sparsely, and, as evils upon the land and men’s faithlessness increased, gave cause to fear treachery. Therefore, by the common counsel of our brethren and men, although unequal in resources, we nevertheless undertook to build up the whole mass of the mountain, restoring some parts anew and repairing others. Accordingly, on that part of the mountain which faces north, we built a new tower at our own expense. Having granted an annual benefice of one hundred solidi, we gave it to be guarded by our ministerial Nicholas as our own property, bound by no fief whatsoever. From him we received sufficient security by oath and hostages that, at our will and command, he would restore that same tower to us without deceit or fraud, and would never retain it against the will of us and of our successors canonically appointed.

It was likewise established upon the same conditions that his heir or successor, who succeeded him in the same benefice and custody, should belong to the church’s own household; and that no man or woman of another condition should obtain any hereditary right to guard that house. But because there was a certain wilderness around the castle and its buildings, these provisions did not suffice for the necessary furnishing, fortification, and supply of victuals. And because the village called Logne, scattered far apart along the course of a stream and remote from the castle, lay exposed to every injury, it seemed good to us to establish that village beneath the castle, in the valley toward the east, and thus, by instituting fairs and a market, to assist the castle with dignity, fortification, guard, and necessary provisions.

Moreover, the whole village belonged to our men either by inheritance or allodial tenure, while only the county jurisdiction and ban-right belonged to us. Yet they claimed that part of the mountain and the whole valley now built upon were theirs by hereditary possession. Therefore, with no small labor and some expense, all obstacles having been removed, we recovered into the hand of ourselves and our successors the valley, with the whole mass of the mountain, free and released from every lordship and claim. Thus, after measuring out the market street—nearly three hundred feet long and more than sixty broad—and setting four boundary markers, we suitably distributed the remainder of mountain and valley for habitation, having obtained permission for settlers to move there with the consent of their lords.

We caused all this to be confirmed at Cologne, in the court of our lord Conrad II, the illustrious and most victorious king of the Romans, by his privilege; and, having obtained a royal ban for establishing fairs in the market, for the sale of their gloves (*chirotecae*). And in order that the same place might always be inhabited by a greater multitude, we granted to its inhabitants in perpetual ownership all the land which they occupied by houses and other buildings, gardens, or any manner of cultivation, so that they should pay from it no rent, service, or judicial due whatsoever to any man. Rather, they are to possess, use, enjoy, sell, and exchange it freely, no one opposing or demanding anything on that account.

Whoever of our men dwells there, whether belonging to the principal altar, to other altars of our churches, or to our estates not yet bound by fief and belonging to us in whatever way, shall be free: that is, he shall pay neither rent nor redemption, nor any due for a deceased hand; and, if he has a wife belonging to another church, he shall pay no sum on that account. He shall give neither pannage, toll, passage-payment, extraordinary levy, nor provision to us, to any advocate, viscount, or royal envoy, but shall enjoy every liberty. Nevertheless, if the serf of another wishes to dwell in that place, he shall render to his lord all his customary dues and judicial obligations, and shall provide him without objection whatever possessions . . . except only the aforesaid holdings, all . . .

But to us and our successors . . . canonically appointed, they shall render only these services: they shall provide lodging for us and ours; houses in which no guests are staying . . . they shall furnish to us; and those who sell meat, bread, or ale shall extend us credit for twelve denarii, while the wine-seller shall extend five solidi, beyond which they shall not be obliged by law to give us credit. They shall be subject to no . . . except for matters belonging to the county jurisdiction, for a public brawl . . . for manifest deceit, fraud, or falsification in measures and weights . . . for an injustice inflicted upon one who complains, or for money denied to one who demands it. The composition for all these offences shall be seventy solidi, except for two . . . No one of our successors may grant the same village as a fief, pledge it, exchange it, alienate it in any manner, or impose other customs without the consent of our brethren, our ministerials, and the inhabitants themselves. [Col. 1476C] If anyone, of whatever rank or dignity, presumes to do so, let him be anathema.

Done publicly in the monastery of Stavelot on the Nones of June, the day of the dedication of the church; and confirmed under the anathema pronounced by us, all our brethren, and many priests who had assembled for the same feast, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1138, the first year of the reign of the lord Conrad H, most victorious king of the Romans, in the first indiction. Waleran being duke of Lotharingia, that is, of the Moselle region; Godfrey of the Rock advocate of Stavelot; and Frederick of Asca subadvocate, who themselves also confirmed it; in the eighth year of our ordination. And so that this may be believed more truly and remain firm and unshaken through succeeding times, we caused this charter to be marked with our own seal and the common seal of the Church, and wrote below the names of our brethren.

Sign of the lord Abbot Wibald. Sign of Warner, dean. Sign of Ebroin. Sign of Robert. Sign of Cuno. Sign of Engo. Sign of Emmo. Sign of Anselm. Sign of Warner. Sign of Gislebert.

Witnesses from the household of the Church are Nicholas of Logne and Adelard his brother; Reiner and Heribrand of Logne, castellans; Adelard and Wideric of Ville; Wideric the White and Wideric the Black of Rona; Baldwin of Loregeis; Arnulf and Nicholas of Holdrichamp; Anselm, steward of Stavelot; Ebroin, Gundric, Erchenbert, Erlebold, and many other sons of the Church.

### XIII. Diploma of Albero, Bishop of Liège.—Concerning the possession of Turnines, restored to the monastery of Stavelot by pontifical and royal authority. (1139.)

[Col. 1477A]

In the name of the holy and indivisible Trinity. ALBERO, by the foreordaining clemency of God bishop of the Church of Liège, though unworthy, to his beloved brother WIBALD, venerable abbot of the Church of Stavelot, and to his successors for ever.

The solicitude of our office requires that, speaking truth with our neighbor, we should not deal deceitfully with our tongue, but should testify without respect of persons to what we have seen and heard. Therefore, deeply sympathizing with paternal affection in the calamity and labors which the Church of Stavelot has undergone concerning its possession of Turnines, while we were present and working to the extent of our ability, we have taken care to transmit the matter in this writing to the remembrance of our successors.

Accordingly, although the Church of Stavelot possessed, by a privilege of Emperor Otto I of divine memory, the provision that the village of Turnines, belonging to that monastery by ancient right, might not be granted in benefice by the authority of any person whatsoever, but should serve perpetually for the sustenance and daily expenses of the brethren of Stavelot, that village had nevertheless, despite the protest of the convent of brethren and contrary to the ordinances of the sacred canons, been taken from the brethren’s allowance by the grant of certain abbots. The lord Wibald, abbot of Stavelot, consequently brought a claim in the court of our lord Conrad II, most serene king of the Romans, against our uncle Godfrey, count of Namur, who held the village unjustly; and by judgment of the court recovered the aforesaid village.

Somewhat later, however, our brother Eustace, advocate of Liège, seized the oft-mentioned village of Turnines by force, alleging this reason: that Wiger of Woronna, whose daughter he had married, had received that same village in benefice from our aforesaid uncle, the count of Namur. Nevertheless, moved by the consideration of manifest justice, both through the admonition of our most reverend father Pope Innocent and by the command of our most pious king Conrad II, while the lord Arnold, metropolitan and archbishop of the holy Church of Cologne, and Albero, archbishop of Trier and legate of the Apostolic See, were diligently exerting themselves for the Church of Stavelot, we spared neither flesh nor blood. By ecclesiastical authority we compelled our brother so far that he restored the village of Turnines, with everything taken from it, to the monastery of Stavelot, and moreover made before us a promise that he would henceforth inflict no violence concerning that property. We ratified this by our episcopal ban and, at the request of our brethren the canons of the greater church, committed it to a more lasting remembrance by this present document.

Present at this matter were the prelates and canons of the greater church: Frederick, provost and archdeacon; Elbert, archdeacon and provost of the church of Saint Martin; Dodo, archdeacon and provost of Saint Bartholomew; Reiner, archdeacon and provost of Saint Paul; Alexander, archdeacon and keeper; John, archdeacon and provost at Eche; Reinzo, dean and abbot of the city; Elbert, abbot of Saint James; Wazelin, abbot of Saint Lawrence; Gislebert, abbot of Saint Hubert; Theoderic, abbot of Walciod; Walter, abbot of Flône. Also present were our fellow-brother Albero, bishop of Verdun, and Odo, abbot of Saint Remigius at Reims; [Col. 1478B] noble and free men: Count Lambert, Henry of the Rock, Ebald of Floreffe, William of Chimay, Stephen of Meanz, Gozuin of Falconis-monte, and many others.

This was done publicly at Liège in the chapter house of Saint Mary and Saint Lambert, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1139, in the third indiction, in the reign of the lord Conrad II, the second year of his reign and of our ordination.

> [Note: [Col. 1477D] Frederick, provost of the Church of Liège, [Col. 1478D] Reinzo the dean, and the whole chapter issued a similar charter containing the same matters; we therefore consider it superfluous to publish it.]

### XIV. Diploma of Conrad II, emperor, granted to Abbot Wibald.—Confirms various privileges of the monastery of Stavelot. (1140.)

[Col. 1478C]

In the name of the holy and indivisible Trinity. CONRAD II, by God’s favoring clemency king of the Romans.

If we graciously hear the just and honorable petitions of our faithful subjects, we gain the grace of God Almighty, who makes poor and enriches, humbles and exalts; and we more vigorously kindle in our faithful subjects goodwill and devotion toward us. Therefore we make known to all the faithful of Christ and ours, future as well as present, how our faithful and most dear Wibald, venerable abbot of the Church of Stavelot—whose zeal and labor have long shone forth faithfully in our service and that of the realm—came tearfully before us, complaining, among the other troubles that he suffered in rebuilding his church, which had for a long time greatly fallen into ruin, that this did him especial harm: his ministerials wished to hold the offices of his estates, namely the judicial offices and stewardships, by fief and hereditary right. Thus the administration of the abbot and provosts became ineffective, and the tenants of the church were reduced to poverty.

Accordingly, by the common counsel of our princes and of our general court held at Liège, at the request also of the same venerable Abbot Wibald, we caused judgment to be rendered that no judge—commonly called a *scultetus*—and no steward—commonly called a *major*—may have or retain his office longer than he is able to serve with the abbot’s favor. Whenever ordered to surrender it, he shall surrender it without objection; nor shall a son after the father’s death reclaim it by hereditary right.

Further, as it has often been granted by us and by our predecessors, we concede and confirm to the Church of Stavelot with perpetual stability that at no time may the same abbey be granted as a benefice or exchange to any person whatsoever. It shall always remain under the protection, government, and *mundiburgium* of kings or emperors, enjoying its own ancient liberty and never rendering service or subjection to any mortal save ourselves and our successors—that is, kings or emperors.

Let the monks have free power to elect whatever abbot they wish according to the Rule of Saint Benedict, provided that when the monks of Malmedy assemble at Stavelot in chapter, the men of Stavelot hold the first voice and authority in counsel and election, and that they elect principally from the convent of Stavelot, if a worthy person is found, without opposition from the men of Malmedy. We also immovably ordain that Malmedy shall never be separated from Stavelot, but, as was established from the beginning, Malmedy, subject as to its superior, shall be governed inseparably by one abbot.

And because the violent rapacity of advocates can scarcely be restrained by the many documents and privileges already issued, we grant and command with firm stability to the Church of Stavelot that the advocate shall have in the estates of that church, among its ministerials, or in its entire household, no jurisdiction, court, lodging-right, levy, exaction, or service whatsoever. Rather, all jurisdiction, all lawsuits, and every profit arising from cases and courts shall belong to the abbot and to whomever he chooses. But if the abbot cannot correct something himself or through his own men, the advocate shall come at the abbot’s summons without delay or objection, and receive one third of whatever accrues solely from that jurisdiction.

The advocate shall provide military expedition and arms, in payment and discharge of his benefice, for us and our successors; the abbot, ministerials, entire household, and all possessions of that church being free in this respect and rendering no supplement either to us or to the advocate. We also immovably ordain what our predecessor Emperor Lothair III settled concerning the service of the Church of Stavelot and confirmed by a golden bull: it shall render service nowhere except at Aachen, where, after each harvest, if we come there, it shall owe twenty marks of silver or service worth twenty marks. Moreover, in the ministerial offices or villages belonging to the monastery it shall render thirty marks or service worth thirty marks.

When the abbot performs service, every mother church within his jurisdiction and administration shall pay five solidi, and every *mansus* twelve denarii in the currency current in the county where the possessions lie. No churches or holdings are exempt from this payment by any agreement, benefice, or pledge; for the service of the realm cannot and must not be bound or delayed by any form of alienation.

We decree that the castle of Logne, together with the town which the same venerable Abbot Wibald built beneath the mountain, shall belong for ever to the hand and authority of the abbot. The advocate shall have there no jurisdiction, power, or right of lodging, and no abbot may grant anything from it to any mortal as a benefice, exchange, precarious grant, or pledge. We confirm in secure possession the boundaries of the league-ban, as contained in the ancient privileges, so that no duke, margrave, count, viscount, or secular or ecclesiastical person, great or small, may exercise therein any authority, jurisdiction, or judgment. No person dwelling there shall have any lord but the abbot, nor shall he answer to anyone but the abbot for an unequal marriage, bloodshed, or a deceased hand. We confirm to the aforesaid Church of Stavelot all possessions which it has peacefully held during the previous ten years, with their entire integrity and use. And so that this may remain ratified and unshaken through all time, we ordered this decree to be written and marked with our seal, and strengthened it with our own hand, as appears below.

We also employed suitable witnesses for this confirmation of ours, whose names are these: Adelbert, archbishop of Mainz; Albero, archbishop of Trier, legate of the Apostolic See; Albero, bishop of Liège; Stephen, bishop of Metz; Sigefrid, bishop of Speyer; Bucco, bishop of Worms; Embrico, bishop of Würzburg; Udo, bishop of Chur; Bernard, bishop of Paderborn; Udo, bishop of Osnabrück; Frederick, duke of the Swabians and of Alsace; Adelbert, duke of Saxony; Godfrey, duke of Louvain; William, count palatine; Hermann, margrave; Thibald, margrave of Vohburg; Gebehard, count of Sulzbach; Henry, count of Namur.

Sign of the lord Conrad II, most victorious king of the Romans.

[Col. 1480D] I, Arnold, chancellor in place of Adelbert, in place of Adelbert, archbishop of Mainz and archchancellor, have recognized this.

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1140, third indiction, Conrad reigning as second king of the Romans, in the second year of his reign.

Given at Worms, on the fifth day before the Ides of February. Happily in Christ. Amen.

### XV. Diploma of Arnold, Archbishop of Cologne, granted to Abbot Wibald.—At a general synod he grants to Wibald and his successors the tithes of newly cleared land in the village of Bullinga. (1140.)

In the name of the holy and indivisible Trinity. ARNOLD, by God’s mercy archbishop of the holy Church of Cologne, to WIBALD, abbot of Stavelot, and to his successors to be canonically appointed for ever.

As, by God’s calling and mercy, we are seen to hold a superior position in the Church of God, so we ought more earnestly to bear care for our brethren and the poor, so that things justly ordered may be preserved in their state, while those which have been weakened in some degree may, with God as author, be restored to the strength of their ancient dignity. Therefore let the diligence of all God’s faithful, future as well as present, know that our venerable son Wibald, abbot of Stavelot, coming to the general synod which, God granting, we held at Cologne, complained to us that in the village called Bullinga, whose church belongs to him, the tenants had long since begun, after abandoning the fields, to clear the forest and derive abundant produce from it. Although the tithe of the profit collected from pasturing pigs in that forest belongs to the abbot without anyone’s objection, the tithe of grain belongs to the church of Bullinga and the abbot; hence the tithe of those newly cleared lands, however great it may be, belongs by right to the aforesaid church and abbot.

So that this may be observed by all for all time, we grant to you, venerable Abbot Wibald, and through you to your successors for ever, by just judgment, the tithe of all produce from the newly cleared land of the aforesaid forest. You are to apply it wholly to the uses of yourself and your monks and possess it lawfully, provided that you or your successors never bind it to any person by any mode of alienation, but that it serve continually the needs of God’s servants. We also confirm to your church, to you and your successors, by the authority of this present document, the tithes granted and confirmed to your church by our predecessor, Archbishop Heribert of happy memory.

If anyone knowingly presumes to act contrary to this our constitution and, after admonition, does not quickly correct his error, let him incur the terrible indignation of the holy apostles Peter and Paul and the excommunication, with curse, of ourselves and our successors.

Witnesses present were Arnold, provost of the greater church; Walter, dean; Gerard, [Col. 1481D] provost and archdeacon of Bonn; Hermann, provost and archdeacon of St. Cassius; Bruno, provost of Saint Gereon; Thiebald, provost of Saint Severin; William, provost of Saint Mary ad Gradus and dean of the same deanery; Berno, provost of Saint Cunibert; Theoderic, provost of the Holy Apostles; Beringer, provost of Saint Andrew; Frederick, provost of Saint George; Gerard, abbot

> [Note: [Col. 1481D] Of the Order of Saint Benedict, in the city of Cologne itself.]

of Saint Pantaleon; Rodulf, abbot

> [Note: [Col. 1481D] Likewise of the Order of Saint Benedict, outside the city on the opposite bank of the Rhine.]

of Deutz; Amelius, abbot

> [Note: [Col. 1482D] Of the Order of Saint Benedict; that monastery is two hours distant from Cologne.]

of Brauweiler; Theoderic, abbot of

> [Note: [Col. 1482D] Of the Cistercian Order and father of several monasteries in Germany.]

[Col. 1482A] Camp; Fulcold, dean of Saint Cunibert; Robert, dean of Saint Gereon; Fulcuin, dean of Saint Mary ad Gradus; Obert, master of the schools of the church of Saint Peter; John, second master in the same church; Godin, scholasticus of Saint Gereon; Beringer, scholasticus of Saint Mary ad Gradus.

Done publicly at Cologne in the greater church, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1140, third indiction, Conrad II reigning as king of the Romans, in the third year of his reign.

### XVI. Diploma of Arnold, Archbishop of Cologne, granted to Abbot Wibald.—Concerning the authority and power of the abbot of Stavelot over the monks of Malmedy. (1140.)

[Col. 1482B]

In the name of the holy and indivisible Trinity. ARNOLD, by the foreordaining clemency of God archbishop of the holy Church of Cologne, to his beloved son and brother WIBALD, venerable abbot of the Church of Stavelot, and to your successors for ever.

As the Church ought not to lose its own property, so it ought not, under the ardor of greed, to seize what belongs to others. And since it is written, “Blessed are the peacemakers, for they shall be called sons of God” (Matthew 5), the solicitude of pastoral care exhorts us to restore and preserve peace among the churches. Therefore, dearest brother Abbot Wibald, according to the document of our predecessor Archbishop Frederick of happy memory, granted to your predecessor Abbot Cuno, desiring utterly to cut away that ancient cause of discord which long and greatly troubled both your monastery, namely Stavelot, over which by God’s will you canonically preside, and the monastery of Malmedy, joined to it from its first foundation, we establish and confirm by sacred pontifical authority that Malmedy, although situated in our diocese, shall never be separated from the monastery of Stavelot. It shall always be governed by one abbot without objection from any person, and shall always be and be called one abbey.

When the abbot dies in succession and is buried where he ordered while living, the monks of both places shall meet at Stavelot in chapter. Though all have free power of election, with the prior assent and concurrence of all, the supreme authority in the election and the first voice shall belong to the men of Stavelot; and a suitable person from that same church, if one is found, shall be chosen. For the privileges of the Apostolic See and the many decrees of emperors and kings granted to the Church of Stavelot declare this.

The bishop of Liège, to whom this belongs without objection from us or our successors, shall bless the abbot thus elected and shall, according to custom, entrust him with the care of souls. The abbot so appointed shall have full authority to organize, maintain, and transfer the monks of Malmedy. None of our successors shall demand obedience or subjection from the abbot. Rather, at Malmedy and in other places of our diocese belonging to him, he may freely celebrate Masses; nor may he be compelled to come to our synod unless perhaps someone has brought a complaint against him. He shall freely possess, for his own uses and those of his brethren, the tithes of the churches of Malmedy, Amblève, Aldendorf, and Bullinga, and of others which he has lawfully acquired.

No archdeacon, dean, archpriest, or any officer of ours shall exercise any authority or jurisdiction in the monastery of Malmedy itself or in the buildings of its cloister. Rather, authority, correction, and administration over all the brethren and property shall rest in the free power of the abbot. If anyone knowingly attempts to violate this written document and, when admonished, does not quickly repent, let him incur the wrath of God, the holy apostles Peter and Paul, and all the saints, and be bound for ever by the curse of anathema. But upon those who preserve these terms may the blessing of Almighty God descend.

Witnesses present were Arnold, provost of the greater church; Walter, dean; Gerard, provost and archdeacon of Bonn; Hermann, provost and archdeacon of St. Cassius; Bruno, provost of Saint Gereon; Thiebald, provost of the church of Saint Severin; William, provost of Saint Mary ad Gradus and dean of the same deanery; Berno, provost of Saint Cunibert; Theoderic, [Col. 1483C] provost of the Holy Apostles; Beringer, provost of Saint Andrew; Frederick, provost of Saint George; Gerard, abbot of Saint Pantaleon; Rodulf, abbot of Deutz; Amelius, abbot of Brauweiler; Theoderic, abbot of Camp; Fulcold, dean of Saint Cunibert; Robert, dean of Saint Gereon; Beringer, scholasticus of Saint Mary ad Gradus.

Done publicly at Cologne in the greater church, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1140, third indiction, Conrad II reigning as king of the Romans, in the third year of his reign.

### XVII. Charter of Abbot Wibald concerning the shortage of cowherds at the estate of Lernou. (1140.)

[Col. 1483D]

In the name of the holy and indivisible Trinity. WIBALD, by God’s favoring clemency humble servant of the Church of Stavelot, to his successors for ever.

We make known to your discernment that, when we came to our estate of Lernou, made inquiry concerning the fidelity owed from that estate, and especially complained about the lack of cowherds—namely, whether persons might by right be compelled afresh from that estate to tend the cows and their produce—the assessors reported that there was there a certain lineage obliged by hereditary right to render this service to us and our successors.

Hearing this, those who appeared to be nearest of that lineage—namely the brothers Ruezelin, John, and Adelard, and their two sisters Ansbera and Elenburgis—came before us, begging that, since at other times too they had unjustly been named and pressed to perform this service, our authority should allow them to prove, through the testimony of many persons confirmed by oath, that their fathers—neither their great-grandfather, grandfather, nor father, whether personally or through their men—had ever been obliged to tend the cowherd service.

Investigating the matter ourselves and through our men, and attending to the truth, we allowed them, having been summoned, to establish it by oath. The aforesaid men accordingly swore what we have set forth: namely, that neither their parents, nor themselves, nor their descendants were subject to that law requiring them to perform service for our cowherd establishment unless they wished to do so voluntarily. Confirming this by the judgment of our men and assessors, both of that estate and of Stavelot, we caused it to be committed to this present document, marked with our seal, and subscribed by the witnesses who were present, so that none may ever dare in succeeding times by rash presumption to violate them in this their legal status.

Done publicly in our house at Stavelot in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1140, third indiction, in the reign of the lord Conrad II, most victorious king of the Romans, Albero II being bishop at Liège, and in the ninth year of our ordination.

The names of those present are these: Arnulf, cantor; Gislebert, custodian; Erlebold, our brother and chaplain. Of the laity: Anselm, steward; Adelard his brother; Erchenbert,

> [Note: [Col. 1483D] I conjecture that this brother of Wibald was the chancellor of King Conrad, who set out with him on the expedition to the Holy Land, as we have seen in Wibald’s letters.]

our brother; Adelard, steward of Lernou. Of the assessors: Gislen, Hartwin, Robert, and Lyetbert. Happily, Amen.

### XVIII. Letter of Pope Celestine II to the archbishop, clergy, and people of Liège.—Confirms the sentence of excommunication pronounced by them against those molesting the monastery of Stavelot, and urges them to see that the alienations of property made by Poppone II are restored, etc. (1143.)

[Col. 1484D]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his venerable brother

> [Note: [Col. 1484D] Adalbero II of that name, son of the count of Guelders, who was elected bishop of Liège in 1136 from the office of primicerius at Metz and held that see until 1146.]

AD., bishop, and to his beloved sons, the clergy and people of Liège: greeting and apostolic blessing.

“It is pleasing to us,” etc. See under Celestine II, *Patrology*, vol. CLXXIX, no. 20.

### XIX. Privilege of Pope Celestine II granted to Abbot Wibald.—Receives the monastery of Stavelot under the protection of the Apostolic See and confirms its various privileges and immunities. (1143.)

[Col. 1485A]

CELESTINE, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved sons WIBALD, abbot of Stavelot, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life, for ever.

“The clemency of apostolic governance,” etc. See above, no. 21.

### XX. Privilege of Pope Lucius III for the monastery of Stavelot. (1144.)

LUCIUS, bishop, etc.

[Col. 1485B] “Apostolic governance,” etc. See under Lucius, *Patrology*, vol. CLXXIX, no. 67.

### XXI. Decree of Conrad II, king of the Romans, obtained by Wibald, abbot of Stavelot, for the monastery of Reinhausen. (1144.)

> [Note: [Col. 1485D] Reinhard mentions this instrument in his little work on the foundation of his monastery of Reinhausen, published by Leibniz in vol. I of *Scriptores rerum Brunsvicensium*, p. 703. “The lord Conrad II, king of the Romans,” he says, “granted my monastery the striking of coinage, the use of tolls, the establishment of fairs, and immunity. Yet in these matters I have received more loss than gain.” From this we infer that the little work was written after 1144. If it is supposed to have been written in 1146 or the following year, he was made abbot of Reinhausen in 1126 or 1127, for he wrote in the twentieth year of his government, as he himself indicates there in these words: “My most beloved brethren of Hildesheim also, wishing to revoke the donation made by Abbess Elika, spare me, decrepit and poor as I am, as they say. I receive this most willingly with every expression of thanks, and endeavor to deserve it by my service. But they now first attempt this in vain, because the Church of Reinhausen possessed it peacefully, by just title and in good faith, for twenty years before my entrance and for just as many thereafter without interruption.” But if he was decrepit in 1146, he must certainly already have been advanced in age in 1126; and he himself confirms this in the same little work: “For from the first time of my stewardship,” he says, “I have been deprived of strength by old age and of assistance.” He may therefore, at the beginning of this century, have been summoned from the monastery of Helmwardeshausen, where he had professed religion—if Hofmann is to be trusted—to direct the schools of Stavelot, as we have said elsewhere. See above, Reinhard’s own letter, col. 1135.]

In the name . . . CONRAD, by divine clemency second king of the Romans . . .
