We wish it to be known, Reverend Abbot Reinhard of the monastery of Reinhausen, that, at the intervention and request of our dearest and most faithful Wibald, venerable abbot of Stavelot, whose instructor and master you were, we confirm by the privilege of royal majesty the liberty and immunity of your aforesaid place [Col. 1485C] [lacuna] and all the possessions which have been bestowed upon it both by Count Conrad and by his brother Udo, formerly bishop of Hildesheim, who were the first founders of that venerable monastery, and also by Herman of illustrious memory, count of the region, and likewise by Abbess Eilika, Countess Beatrice, or other faithful Christians [lacuna] have been bestowed. We therefore decree that the aforementioned venerable place of Reinhausen, with all its appurtenances, shall be free and exempt from every public impost and from the revenues due to the realm [lacuna]. We have also granted you authority to hold a market in that place, establish public fairs, regulate the striking of coin, and collect tolls, on this condition: that [Col. 1485D] whatever profit or composition may accrue from the aforesaid matters shall in every way go to the use of the brethren serving God, [Col. 1486A] and of the poor and pilgrims. And, so that these provisions may remain valid for all time, we have ordered this document of the present command to be authenticated with the impression of our seal.

We have caused to be recorded below the witnesses who were present, whose names are these: Henry, Archbishop of Mainz; Buco, Bishop of Worms; Wiger, Bishop of Brandenburg; Wibald, Abbot of Stavelot; Henry, Abbot of Hersfeld; Conrad, Abbot of Helmwardishusen; Adalbert, Margrave of Brandenburg; Count Herman of Winzenburg and his brother Henry; Louis, Landgrave of Thuringia.

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1144, indiction VII, in the seventh year of the reign of Lord Conrad, second King of the Romans [Col. 1486B]. Given at Hersfeld, the seventeenth day before the Kalends of November [16 October], happily in Christ. Amen.

The sign of Lord Conrad, most invincible second King of the Romans.

I, Arnold, chancellor in the place of Henry, Archbishop of Mainz and archchancellor, have certified it.

Below hangs the seal of Conrad seated upon the royal throne, bearing this inscription: CONRAD, SECOND KING OF THE ROMANS.

## XXII. Privilege of Pope Eugenius III for the monastery of Stavelot. (A.D. 1146.)

[Col. 1486C] EUGENIUS, etc.

“Of apostolic governance,” etc. See under Eugenius III, at the year 1153.

## XXIII. Letter of the monks of the monastery of Stavelot to Abbot Wibald.—They grant him for life the estates of Bouvignies and Germigny, even should he cease to be their abbot. (A.D. 1146.)

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. To their reverend father and lord WIBALD, venerable abbot of the Church of Stavelot, the whole community of the same monastery, in perpetuity.

Just as it is necessary that grants made by the more powerful be strengthened by the firm records of privileges, [Col. 1486D] so it is no less clearly most useful that what is granted by subjects to their prelates or superiors [Col. 1487A] be confirmed by certain attestations of seals—not because religious men would ever wish, or ought, to alter what they have granted, but lest the forgetfulness or ignorance of posterity should at some time presume to alter the institutions of their predecessors. Therefore we wish our brethren of this Church, both present and future, to know that we have granted to you, Reverend Father Wibald, by unanimous consent and harmonious goodwill, in perpetuity, our two estates, namely Bouvignies and Germigny. For a long time past these estates had not merely been useless to us, but had also caused loss through very heavy expenses. The grant is made on this condition: throughout your whole lifetime, in whatever position you may be—whether you are promoted to another see, or released from our government (which God forbid), and, to state it absolutely, [Col. 1487B] whether you are called abbot or not—you shall thereafter freely use and enjoy these estates with all their appurtenances and produce, owing us no payment from them and making up no deficiency; rather, everything shall be assigned to you as to their proper possessor and lord.

Although we have never entertained any doubt of your faith and your pious concern for us and for what is ours, nevertheless, for the fuller security of the arrangement proposed, we wish above all things, and strictly forbid, that you should ever be permitted to sell, alienate, mortgage, or impair these possessions or estates; nor may you at any time establish there persons of another profession or order, or grant the place for habitation. But upon your death they shall freely return, with their whole [Col. 1487C] integrity and all acquisitions, into the right and administration of ourselves or our successors—that is, the brethren of this Church: Bouvignies, namely, into the hands of the Vestiarian, to whom it formerly belonged; Germigny, however, to the use and lordship of all the brethren. And so that confirmation of this our grant may remain unimpaired throughout your lifetime, we have caused this document to be marked with the impression of the seal of our Church, and have caused the names of all of us who made this grant to be written below.

Done publicly in the chapter-house at Stavelot, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1146, indiction IX, in the ninth year of the reign of Lord Conrad, second King of the Romans, [Col. 1487D] and the fifteenth year of the rule of Lord Abbot WIBALD, happily in Christ. Amen.

I, Robert, prior, have subscribed.

The sign of Warner. The sign of Robert, Radulf, Emmo, Anselm, Henry, Gislebert, Hillin.

## XXIV. Charter of Abbot Wibald concerning the tithe of the Church of Comblain, granted for life to Radulf of Comblain. (A.D. 1146.)

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. WIBALD, by God’s grace abbot of Stavelot, to his successors in perpetuity.

It is very useful and prudent to commit to writing the acts which we perform concerning the possessions of our monastery, [Col. 1488A] so that revenues and possessions may be paid at their appointed time without diminution, and so that our successors may know, in each matter, what was done at the demand of advantage or under compulsion of necessity. Therefore let all faithful persons of our Church and of ourselves know that the tithe of the Church of Comblain, which belongs to the wardrobe of our brethren at Malmedy, had been leased by our predecessors for six pounds of Liège currency, to be paid each year. Thus Macharius of Semaces held it after his father Warner until the end of his life. When he died, we wished to administer this tithe ourselves for the benefit of the brethren, since it had been disadvantageously leased. [Col. 1488B] But, because of the evil of the times, which has increased excessively in our days, and because of the agreement confirmed by our predecessors, we were unable to bring this about. We were therefore prepared to restore the aforesaid tithe, at the stated rent, to Nicholas, son of the aforementioned Macharius.

But Nicholas, having received no small sum of money from Radulf of Comblain, willingly and of his own accord relinquished into our hand, by the formal ceremony of handing over a twig, what had belonged to him hereditarily through his father under the agreement concerning that tithe. We therefore, having received from the same Radulf six pounds in denarii—which, according to the established law of all agreements among us, were given to us in acknowledgment of our proprietary right and for investiture in his holding under the lease—granted and gave to the same Radulf [Col. 1488C] and to his wife Ida the entire tithe of the Church of Comblain, as Warner and Macharius had held it, under an annual agreement. That is: on the Sunday immediately preceding the holy day of Pentecost, they shall pay six pounds in denarii of Liège currency; and, so long as both are alive and pay the aforesaid rent every year to the reeve of Comblain on the fixed day, they shall possess it without anyone’s disturbance.

After both have died, no one shall hold that possession unless he has a wife from among the ministerials of the Church and pays six pounds for investiture from the abbot. If they neglect to pay the whole rent on the appointed day, then, having been summoned for three consecutive days by the reeve of Comblain, whoever he may be at the time, and formally cited before the court of that estate, [Col. 1488D] they shall thereafter lose the possession and the right of inheritance without hope of recovery. If the reeve neglects to demand and cite them, the possessor, when summoned by the abbot himself, shall be judged by the ministerials, with the shortest possible delay allowed for each summons, namely because clothing must be bought for the brethren and because of the terms of this agreement. Whenever any possessor dies, investiture shall be given in the chapter-house at Malmedy; for it the abbot shall receive six pounds in denarii, and the brethren one *ama* of wine.

Done publicly in the monastery of Malmedy, on the fifth day before the Ides of October [11 October], on the feast of the martyrdom of Nigasias, Quirinus, and Scuviculus, in the year from the Incarnation of the Lord 1146, indiction X, in the ninth year of the reign of Lord CONRAD the king [Col. 1489A], in the presence of Lord Abbot WIBALD.

The witnesses of this matter are Albert, dean; Anselm, provost; Erlebold, custos of Stavelot; Bovo, porter; and the other brethren. Of the clerics: Poppo of Semaces. Of the laity: Francho, reeve of Malmedy; Hillin of Alrimont; Philip; John; Alard of Lernou; Warner of Cresonia; Lietbert of Wallaria; and many others.

## XXV. Diploma of Conrad, King of the Romans, for the monastery of Corbie.—He assigns to Corbie the monasteries of Kemnade and Wibeke. (A.D. 1147.)

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. CONRAD, [Col. 1489B] by divine favour and clemency second King of the Romans.

It befits the munificence of princely dignity to repay rewards to those who have deserved well of the commonwealth, and to set before others as an example and as a sign of good hope those advanced through suitable degrees of honour. Thus they may receive the lasting fruits of their labours, while others may understand that they too will not be denied the favour of a similar reward. Therefore let the diligence of all our faithful subjects, both future and present, know that, in our gracious favour, considering the faithfulness, labours, and constancy of our most faithful and dearest Wibald, abbot of Corbie, we have granted in perpetuity to the monastery of Corbie, to the abbot Wibald who now presides over it by divine calling [Col. 1489C] and by the common and unanimous election of the brethren, and also to all his successors, by authority effective for ever, the two monasteries of women, namely Kemnade and Wibeke. We have transferred and confirmed them out of our own right and that of the realm, through the hand of Herman, Count Palatine of the Rhine, whom we had appointed advocate for carrying out this act properly, upon the relics of the body of St Vitus the martyr, by the golden ring of our donation, into the power and lordship of the monastery of Corbie. This was done into the hand of the aforesaid Abbot Wibald and of Adalbert, Margrave of Brandenburg, who, in the place of Herman, Count of Winzenburg, advocate of the monastery of Corbie, received this our donation [Col. 1489D] or transfer.

That is, the monastery of Corbie shall have, possess, administer, use, and preserve the two aforementioned monasteries, Kemnade and Wibeke, with all estates, woods, and waters belonging to those places, both outside and within, just as it holds under its governance, by proprietary right, the three small abbeys which Louis the Pious, son of Charlemagne, founder of the same New Corbie, granted to Corbie: namely Eresburg, once a noble Saxon fortress, Meppen, and Wibeke. [Note: [Col. 1489] Louis the Pious gave Eresburg to Corbie in 826; Meppen in 834, according to the *Annals of Paderborn*, book II.] Certainly neither military service nor any other service was owed to us or to the realm from the two aforesaid places. And since dignity has been conferred upon the monastery of Corbie both in military service [Col. 1490A] and in other service for the honour of the realm and defence of holy Church, we decree, by judgment of the princes, that this arrangement shall remain as prescribed for the augmentation of our crown.

The first judgment was pronounced by Burchard, Bishop of Strasbourg; he was followed by Albero, Archbishop of Trier; Anselm, Bishop of Havelberg; Henry, Bishop of Liège; Sifrid, bishop-elect of Würzburg; Frederick, Duke of Swabia and Alsace; Herman, Count Palatine of the Rhine; Conrad, Duke of Zähringen; Conrad, Margrave of Wettin; Adalbert, Margrave of Brandenburg; Otto, his son and likewise margrave; Herman, son of the same Margrave Adalbert; Louis, count of the land of Thuringia; Herman, Margrave [Col. 1490B] of Baden; Werner, Count of Baden; Ulrich, Count of Lenzburg; Ulrich, Count of Orlamünde; Henry, Count of Katzenelnbogen; Marquard; Sibodo; Theoderic, Count of Montbéliard; and many others who were then present.

We also wish it to be known that our venerable father Eugenius, supreme pontiff of the holy Roman Church, repeatedly exhorted us, through both his and our legates, that we should deign to regulate and reform the women’s monasteries which belong especially to our dominion and administration in our realm, and in which religious observance had wholly decayed. Since the often-named monasteries of Kemnade and Wibeke, not so much monasteries as places open in sin to all passers-by, [Col. 1490C] could not be reformed despite many efforts, and since they are near the monastery of Corbie, we delivered them there both for correction and as property, no one objecting unless he should prove an enemy of the holy Rule and a foe of chastity. By our royal authority we grant to the aforesaid two cells of Kemnade and Wibeke, and confirm by a decree to remain valid for ever, the same liberty possessed by the monastery of Corbie: namely, the prefecture of the district, commonly called *Burgban*, on this privileged condition, that no duke, margrave, count, or advocate shall have authority to exercise judicial power in the court of the aforesaid churches. Rather, whatever offence against right and equity may be committed by the *muli* (servants), who serve both abbot and community [Col. 1490D] daily, shall be corrected by the abbot, or by the person to whom he entrusts this task. And, that all these provisions may remain valid and unshaken for ever, we have ordered this command to be written and marked with the impression of our image.

The sign of Lord Conrad, second King of the Romans.

I, Arnold, chancellor in the place of Henry, Archbishop of Mainz and archchancellor, have certified it.

Done in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1147, indiction X, in the ninth year of the reign of Lord Conrad, most invincible second king.

Given at Frankfurt, happily in Christ. Amen.

## XXVI. Diploma of Conrad II, King of the Romans, for the monastery of Corbie.—In consideration of Abbot Wibald’s outstanding fidelity and the merits of the men of Corbie and Herford, he renews their privileges. (A.D. 1147.)

[Col. 1491A]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. CONRAD, by divine favouring clemency, second King of the Romans.

It belongs to the munificence of royal dignity to bestow the rewards of virtues upon those who have deserved well of the commonwealth, so that they may receive the fruits of their labour for the constancy of their faith, and that others, full of good hope and eager, may be encouraged to perform the duties of the empire. Therefore let the diligence of all our faithful subjects, both future [Col. 1491B] and present, know that our faithful and dearest Wibald, venerable abbot of the monastery called New Corbie, approached our clemency, asking that we should deign to renew and confirm the privileges of the Church of Corbie over which that venerable abbot is now known to preside. Inclining the ear of our favour to his religious request, because of his outstanding fidelity toward us and toward the realm granted us by God, through the tenor of this present document we receive under the protection of royal majesty that place, namely New Corbie, with all that belongs to it both within and without. Endowing it with perpetual liberty, we establish it by our own authority and that of all the princes, by a law to remain for ever, [Col. 1491C] so that the aforesaid monastery, New Corbie, shall not pass into the power, dominion, or subjection of any person or of any ecclesiastical or secular dignity by any gift or exchange. Rather, it shall always remain under the administration and protection of kings or emperors, and shall for ever enjoy the liberty which it has hitherto possessed.

And since two monasteries were founded by Emperor Louis and enriched with honour and wealth by our predecessors—one, namely, of monks, called New Corbie, patterned after Old Corbie; the other at Herford, of nuns, modelled upon the monastery of Soissons—and since they decreed that the abbot of Corbie, whoever he might be at the time, should undertake the oversight of the Church of Herford, so that, according to the custom by which communities of the handmaids of God are customarily provided for, he should, as a provost of ecclesiastical order, be their overseer and patron both in discipline and in all affairs which Christ’s handmaids could not perform on account of their sex and profession, [Col. 1491D] we too, following in the footsteps of our predecessors, confirm and establish by a decree to remain for ever that all abbots of the monastery of Corbie in succession shall exercise the aforesaid oversight and patronage without anyone’s opposition, and, preserving the dignity of the abbess, shall assist the [Col. 1492A] community of Herford in matters where this is expedient.

We also confirm what our predecessor Emperor Louis granted to the aforesaid monasteries as alms for his family: namely, the cell called Meppen, with tithes and possessions belonging to it on every side, and the church of Eresburg and, around it, for two Saxon *rastas*, to New Corbie. [Note: [Col. 1491] A Saxon *rasta* denotes a fixed measure of distance on roads. Two leagues, or three miles, make one *rasta*, as Bede states in *On the Division of Numbers*.] To the monastery of Herford, moreover: in the diocese of Osnabrück, the Church of Buinidi with the churches subject to it; and, in the parish of Minden, the Church of Reni with the churches belonging to it. All the proceeds of tithes and other revenues are to accrue to the aforesaid monasteries, and the subject peoples are in return to be served by them in baptism, the Eucharist, burials, and the hearing of confession [Col. 1492B] of sins. The priests who held the principal churches were to perform the office of archpriests, carrying out all things customarily performed by archpriests of bishops. When bishops were required to conduct their visitations there, provision for their lodging was to be made, as is prescribed in the capitularies of our predecessors: namely, enough was to be given them, and the bishops were neither to demand more nor come with more persons than could be adequately provided for.

Moreover, lest more than was necessary should be demanded in the total of service owed to bishops, the bishops of the aforesaid churches, with synodal consent before our predecessor Emperor Otto, Archbishop Raban and the others conducting the synod with him, established that at each church there should be supplied: four pigs, each worth twelve denarii, or eight rams of the same value; four piglets; four geese; eight hens; twenty buckets of mead; twenty of honeyed ale; sixty of unhoneyed ale; 120 loaves; 100 measures of oats; and 600 sheaves. It was to be within the bishops’ power whether they wished to receive these provisions from each church for one lodging-stay or for two. [Col. 1492C]

We also establish and grant, in accordance with the decrees of our predecessors, that each place shall always have free authority in future times to elect from its own community a suitable person to govern it. No public judge shall have licence to exercise any judicial authority over the people belonging to the aforesaid monastery; all their affairs shall be decided before [Col. 1492D] their advocate. No one shall presume to usurp in the same place the jurisdiction called *Burchban*, except one to whom authority has been granted by the abbot of that monastery. Free persons shall have licence to confer their estates upon the same monastery; nor shall any judge or royal authority thereafter extort from them the customary due or public tax. They may commit themselves into the ownership of that Church, with the legal status of ministerials; and the abbot shall have authority to make ministerials from the lowest rank, namely from *liti* or rent-payers.

The sign of Lord Conrad, second King of the Romans.

[Col. 1493A] I, Arnold, chancellor in the place of Henry, archchancellor of Mainz, have certified it. In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1147, indiction X, in the tenth year of the reign of Conrad, second King of the Romans.

Given at Frankfurt, happily. Amen.

## XXVII. Concerning Winand of Limburg, excommunicated for injuries inflicted upon the monastery of Stavelot. (A.D. 1148.)

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1548 [an obvious error for 1148], Winand of Limburg, who was called “of the Tower,” had harassed the Church of Stavelot with many robberies and depredations together with his accomplices. For this, after a canonical summons to make satisfaction, he had been bound by Lord Abbot Wibald in the bond [Col. 1493B] of anathema. Meanwhile, by the ordering of divine mercy, which had compassion on the manifold misfortunes of the Church of Stavelot, Winand suddenly died. Nowhere in the whole diocese of Liège, through fear of the same lord abbot and of the excommunication, could he be buried in the Christian manner. Rather, to terrify all surviving unbelievers, and for the perpetual protection and honour of the lord abbot, by whose exertion this was accomplished, and of the Church, he was buried outside the cemetery walls at Baille, which is near Limburg.

Yet because this same Winand was kinsman of Lord Henry, then bishop of Liège, and because he was a great man, his people did not grieve only slightly at his having died in this manner. With insistent humility, taking with them their two noble lords, [Col. 1493C] Henry of La Roche and Henry of Limburg—one of whom, that is, the man of La Roche, was advocate of our Church, while the other was the son of the aunt of the other Henry—they came to the lord abbot and the Church, humbly begging that, upon receiving compensation for the damages, they would not deprive their dead man of Christian burial. After many entreaties, the value of the goods taken was reckoned at one hundred marks. The two aforesaid nobles promised the lord abbot, together with their men whom we shall name later, that they would pay or render service for this amount.

Furthermore, the two aforementioned nobles swore that neither in person nor through a subordinate would they ever thereafter harass or disturb the Church of Stavelot in its lands, possessions, or liberties. Certain members of the households of both likewise swore, and moreover did homage to Lord Abbot Wibald and swore fealty to the lord abbot and the Church: that henceforth they would preserve the lands, possessions, and household of that Church, wherever situated, free and untouched by every unjust and undue oppression. [Col. 1493D] If any of them rashly violated this undertaking, the aforementioned two nobles, Henry of Limburg and Henry of La Roche, swore to expel and drive him from their castles and possessions until he restored in full what had been taken and made suitable satisfaction to the lord abbot and the Church for the injury.

## XXVIII. Charter of Abbot Wibald concerning what he granted as a benefice to Reiner of La Roche at Neuville. (A.D. 1148.)

[Col. 1494A]

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. WIBALD, by divine favouring clemency abbot of Stavelot, to his successors in perpetuity. When, in matters entrusted to us by God, we arrange or establish something according either to considerations of utility or to the necessity of administration, it is fitting that we diligently transmit it in writing to the memory of posterity. Therefore we wish all to know that, after we had laboured through manifold and almost inextricable dangers and expenses to have half of those benefices which Abbot Poppo II had granted, and which were called new benefices, surrendered into our hands by both our [Col. 1494B] free men and ministerials, our faithful Reiner of La Roche, who held from us the *juaria* at Neuville and Saint Vitus, came to us. Of the thirty-nine solidi which he held from the new benefice at Neuville, he renounced twenty solidi into our hands for the use of the brethren of the Church of Malmedy.

When we nevertheless demanded from him half of the thirty solidi which he received yearly in the same village, he proved by sufficient testimony of both laymen and our brethren of Malmedy that his father, formerly E., had surrendered to the Church of Malmedy in exchange for these thirty solidi the forty solidi which he held from the very ancient benefice at Wellines. Again, when we wished to take half of the lands—namely, the two *mansi*—which he was said to hold at [Col. 1494C] the aforesaid Neuville, and half of the seven peasants which he was also said to hold from the new benefice within the ban of Malmedy, our mind was moved by the intervention of the illustrious and eminent Duke Waleran, whose fidelity and assistance both we and our predecessors have often employed in our Church; by his most noble wife Judith and his son Henry, who likewise loved and honoured both us and the goods of our Church with deep affection; especially by the entreaty and urging of our brethren of Malmedy; and, further, by regard for the service of the same Reiner, who had always faithfully stood by us in all our needs, both personally and with his resources. We abandoned our intended severity, judging it more useful to endure the small loss of a few things than not to heed our brethren or not to accede to the requests of so many of our noblemen and faithful men.

For all urged that it ought to suffice us to have received twenty solidi from our faithful man, while he retained his entire benefice as he had held it under four of our predecessors—Lord Poppo II, Lord Warner, Lord Cuno, and Lord John—down to our own time; that a man who devoted himself wholly to us should not receive evil for good; and that it was fitting for him to enjoy the gentleness of our mildness and our goodness, so that, by the example of this pious zeal and praiseworthy purpose, others might be stirred to our service [Col. 1495A] and thereby the zealous might become more zealous, and the devoted more devoted. Although we approved sufficiently the words of both our nobles and faithful men, and although we felt considerable affection for the person of our faithful Reiner, whose case was at issue, we persisted until the brethren of Malmedy came to us, earnestly and attentively urging us to yield to the requests of so many nobles. They said that the goodwill of so many princes could bring greater advantage to the Church than the loss arising from the surrender of a few peasants and one *mansus*, which, if it perhaps returned to the Church’s use, would quickly become wholly useless without a cultivator; or, if it began to be productive, would again be taken away from the Church through someone’s violence.

Therefore, when with many persuasions of this sort they persistently pressed us before the men then present, so that we should not seem ungrateful for the benefits and services of our faithful Reiner, by the common consent and request of our brethren of Malmedy and through the intervention of the aforesaid persons, we granted to the same Reiner, and through him to his heirs, as a perpetual benefice at Neuville the two *mansi* in dispute and the seven peasants who lived beyond the ban of Malmedy, namely at Dulfum, Kefosse, and Richolfiville. [Col. 1495B] He was to hold them by the same right by which he held those possessions which were his by right from the most ancient succession of the benefice; that is, he and his heirs might thereafter apply those two *mansi* and the seven peasants living in the aforesaid [Col. 1495C] places to every advantage of themselves and their heirs in whatever way they wished.

So that all these things might afterward remain valid and unshaken, we wish to insert in this record of our grant all that Reiner ought to possess from the hand of the abbot of Stavelot, whether from the new or the old benefice. We had granted this document to Reiner with the consent of all our brethren in the chapter-house at Malmedy, at the request of the aforesaid Duchess Judith and her son Henry—for Duke Waleran of glorious memory had already died—and with the testimony and approval of our ministerials. This we do so that neither Reiner nor his heirs might ever usurp anything beyond what we granted them, nor—God forbid—might any of our successors afterward attempt to diminish anything of the same benefice for Reiner or his heirs. [Col. 1495D]

Reiner has from us and our successors, abbots of Stavelot, at Neuville: fourteen solidi from the new benefice on the feast of Saint Lambert; likewise, there on the feast of Saint Martin, the thirty solidi for which his father formerly gave in exchange to the brethren of the Church of Malmedy, before our appointment, forty solidi from the old benefice at Wellines. Of those thirty solidi he surrendered six solidi to us and the brethren. Likewise, at Neuville on the Epiphany of the Lord, he held eight solidi from the new benefice, which he returned in full to us and the brethren. Again, there in mid-May, seventeen solidi, of which he renounced five solidi into our hands for the use of the brethren. The same Reiner also held at Neuville from the old benefice one *juaria*-mansus; likewise, there from the old benefice, half a *mansus* and half a mill in the village called Brunefa. Likewise, at Neuville from the new benefice, two *mansi*; and, within the ban of the town of Malmedy, namely at Dulfum, Chefosse, and Richolfiville, seven peasants, who belong to the new benefice. From the old benefice, however, he held half a *mansus* at La Roche, half a mill at Warcham, and land at Lonfait on which a certain Godescalch lived.

Thus the total of this Reiner’s new benefice was thirty-nine solidi, of which twenty solidi were restored by him to us and the brethren; two *mansi* at Neuville; [Col. 1496B] and seven peasants around Malmedy. Of these, we granted to Reiner and his heirs as a benefice the half which belonged to us, as stated above, at the request of our brethren and illustrious men. Everything else is known with complete certainty to have belonged to the old benefice. Reiner and his heirs must observe that, on no pretext, shall anything ever be diminished from the twenty-two solidi to be paid each year to the brethren. For we have so established and granted to both parties that every shortfall in the entire aforesaid rent shall fall not upon the brethren but upon Reiner or his heirs, so that, as we have said, the brethren shall receive twenty solidi each year without [Col. 1496C] deficiency.

Since we have written these things neither from fickleness nor from any rash impulse, and in order that they may be preserved inviolate for ever, we have ordered this document to be marked with the impression of both our seal and the seal of our Church. We have caused the witnesses who were present to be recorded below, beseeching our successors, by the grace which is in Christ, never to apply their effort or hand toward invalidating what has been done by the common counsel of our brethren and faithful men and by a prudent administration; but instead to devote diligence to preserving what we found preserved with the greatest labour, or to restoring what we found dispersed, for the use of the brethren, the poor, and guests.

## XXIX. Diploma of King Conrad for Abbot Wibald.—He permits free mining of silver and metals in Mount Eresburg. (A.D. 1150.)

[Col. 1496D]

CONRAD, by God’s grace second King of the Romans, to WIBALD, abbot of Corbie, and his canonically appointed successors, in perpetuity.

The veins of metal—namely gold, silver, copper, lead, and tin—and all money, whether uncoined or coined, which lies hidden within Mount Eresburg, known to belong by proprietary right to the Church of Corbie, we grant and give to you and, through you, to the Church of Corbie, and confirm by this present document. You and your successors may, without the opposition of any person, mine in that mountain, [Col. 1497A] extract and smelt every metal found, and freely apply it to your own use and that of your brethren, so that the Church of Corbie may better serve both the things of God and those of the realm.

This charter of record was given at Würzburg in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1150, indiction XIII, on account of the faithful service of the above-written abbot.

## XXX. (A.D. 1150.) Diploma of Conrad II, King of the Romans, for the monastery of Corbie.—Moved by the prayers of his beloved and faithful Abbot Wibald, he protects the monastery of Corbie against the insolence of its ministerials.

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. CONRAD, by divine favouring clemency second King of the Romans.

[Col. 1497B] If, with devout and benevolent care, we provide for the peace and tranquillity of the Churches of God, we hope to receive this recompense from our pious Creator: that we may be able in this present age to hold the reins of the kingdom entrusted to us by God in peace and tranquillity, and that after the kingdom of this age we may find rest, with God the just Judge, in the kingdom of eternal blessedness. Therefore we wish all the faithful of our realm, both men of the present age and of ages to come, to know how our beloved and faithful Wibald, abbot of the monastery of Corvey, constrained by the manifold necessities of that monastery, laid before the ears of our clemency the inconveniences and injuries which certain of his predecessors had endured from their stewards and cupbearers, and which he himself had suffered in the same monastery from the day of his appointment as superior. For the stewards and cupbearers, and the others who hold a ministerial office in the household of the abbot of Corvey—a dignity which in common speech they call *officia*—have usurped certain abuses in those offices: namely, that they should keep under their own custody all provisions and the entire substance of their lord’s household; that, without consulting their lord, they should entrust those goods to whomever pleased them for safekeeping and widespread distribution; and that they should claim such authority in these offices as openly, and as though by their own right, to forbid their lords from entrusting the keys and custody of their property to anyone. For they are accustomed to support their own [Col. 1497C] households from their lords’ goods and to feed their own knights, so that in their own houses they frequently spend as much as, or even more than, their lords spend from those resources which they ought to have preserved; and in dissipating those goods they observe no measure whatsoever.

When, therefore, the aforesaid our faithful and beloved Wibald, abbot of Corvey, had attempted to remove from that household such superfluous and damaging dissipations of its property and to order his house according to the honour of God and its own advantage, one of his ministerials, Rabano, who was then performing the office of steward, together with his brother Liudolf and a few of his kinsmen, strongly opposed his arrangements. With many threats he asserted that he would never, while he lived, surrender the authority of his office which he had hitherto exercised in that house: so that all his lord’s provisions should remain under his control, and he should have power to give them to whomever he wished, without rendering to his lord any account of what had been given or received, and that no one might keep the keys of the property unless he himself had appointed him. [Col. 1497D]

This dispute was accordingly argued before the ministerials of the Church of Corvey by the aforesaid abbot, their lord; and by their judgment all authority to entrust the keys and to keep their lord’s property was adjudged away from Rabano himself and from all who usurped for themselves such lordship over their lord’s goods. By the unanimously pronounced sentence of judgment, they adjudged this authority to the abbot of Corvey: that he might entrust the keys and custody of his property, without the counsel of the steward and cupbearer, to whomsoever he wished. But they devised the following judgment concerning the steward and cupbearer: that they should have absolutely no authority to give anything from their lord’s provisions without his will; but, when they had served at table with their lord according to the duty of their office, they should receive this honour from their office, namely, that after their lord had dined, they should dine at his table with the other servants from their lord’s goods, and that beyond this they should exercise no other authority over his property. [Col. 1498A]

When that same Rabano refused to acquiesce in the judgment of his peers, our aforesaid faithful abbot of Corvey obtained from our clemency that, in our full court which we held at Speyer, we should seek a judgment on the same question from the ministerials of the realm. In the presence of ourselves and the princes of the realm, they likewise affirmed by equal consent the same judgment which the men of Corvey had rendered. [Col. 1498B]

The same Rabano further presumed to inflict another grievance upon the brethren serving God in the monastery of Corvey: he claimed for himself, within the walls and enclosure of the cemetery of that church, a hereditary dwelling-place. Although he had been sufficiently admonished concerning that dwelling, both by his lord, by the monk brethren, and by his peers, to desist from it, he refused to obey their salutary admonitions. Therefore, when the ministerials of the Church of Corvey were asked for a sentence of judgment, they adjudged away from him, and from all laymen, any benefice in the court of the Church, and likewise adjudged that no abbot could grant such a benefice. When he nevertheless continued to resist, our aforesaid faithful abbot of Corvey appealed to us; and, when we had asked our ministerials about the same judgment, in our presence and that of the princes they adjudged away from him every hereditary dwelling within the church court, and from all abbots and monks the grant of such a benefice. [Col. 1498C]

Yet another act of presumption arose from the same Rabano: within the walls of the monastery of Corvey he claimed for himself by hereditary right a certain semblance of authority, which they call the prefecture, and he caused himself to be called *Burckgrave* [burghgrave]. This was despite the fact that all abbots of the same monastery had always held this authority under themselves: whatever offence was committed within the walls by their people, the abbot himself either corrected it or entrusted its correction to his chamberlain, steward, or someone else of his household, without any authority remaining permanently in that person. But the aforesaid Rabano abused this authority so greatly that he called it in the common tongue *Burgban*, and, after the fashion of some great jurisdiction, frequently held pleas within the walls; these pleas he called *Burdinck*. To these pleas the servants of the monk brethren—from the kitchen, bakery, or any other of their services—were compelled to come. Even if, because they were occupied with the brethren’s service, they could not attend, Rabano’s servants violently or insultingly dragged them away, forcing them to leave the brethren’s bread and food unfinished. [Col. 1499A]

We therefore utterly prohibit, by the judgment of the princes of the realm, such presumption concerning this prefecture in relation to the monastery of Corvey, and decree that this authority shall remain in the abbot’s hand, as it was of old. For the ancient enactments of kings and emperors provide that no duke, no count, and no secular power has jurisdiction to exercise authority within the walls of that church; rather, whatever is committed by the servants of the monastery contrary to law and equity must be judged through the abbot and the persons temporarily appointed by him. And if the princes themselves may not act contrary to an imperial privilege, it is evident that ministerials may do so still less. We therefore permit no one whatsoever to usurp or claim by hereditary right in the aforesaid monastery this prefecture, the aforesaid lay dwelling-place within the walls, or the authority of steward and cupbearer to entrust keys. Instead, by a decree valid in perpetuity, we prohibit all laymen from these three aforesaid usurpations, in accordance with the judgments of our ministerials and the sentence of the princes of the realm, and confer all authority over them upon the abbot. [Col. 1499B]

Conrad, our ministerial of Haga, rendered the judgment concerning the keys. He gave judgment concerning the dwelling-place within the walls and concerning the prefecture. Likewise our ministerial Conrad of Wallehuson, our chamberlain in charge of the treasury.

The following princes were present with their ministerials: Ortlew, bishop of Basel, and his ministerials; Heremann, bishop of Constance, and his ministerials; Gunther, bishop of Speyer, and his ministerials; Eilulf, abbot of Murbach, and his ministerials; Walther, abbot of Selz, and his ministerials; the abbot of Kempten and his ministerials; the abbot of Wissembourg and his ministerials; the clergy and people of the Church of Worms, which was then vacant; the clergy and people of the monastery of Fulda, which was then vacant; the clergy and people of the monastery of Lorsch, which was then vacant; Frederick, duke of Swabia and Alsace, and his ministerials; [Col. 1499C] Otto, Count Palatine of Wittelsbach, and his ministerials; Herimann, margrave of Baden, and his ministerials; Wernher, count of Haveklesperch; Othelric, count of Lensemburg; William, count of Glizperch; Count William of Jülich; Count Imikho of Leiningen; Count Wulfram of Wertheim; Marquard of Grunbach; Arnold the steward of Rotenburg; Henry the marshal; Reinger the cupbearer; and Thiepert of Winsperch, chamberlain.

The sign of the most invincible lord Conrad, second king of the Romans.

Given in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1150, in the thirteenth indiction; in the twelfth year of the most invincible lord Conrad, second king; and in the third year of Wibald, abbot of Corvey. [Col. 1499D]

Done at Speyer, happily in Christ.

### XXXI. Charter of Abbot Wibald, by which he assigns Mount St Michael for the celebration of the feast of St Remaclus and of the anniversary of his own appointment.  
*(Year 1151.—From the archives of New Corvey.)*

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. WIBALD, by God’s grace abbot of Corvey, to his successors regularly appointed in perpetuity.

Because with the highest desire we wish our memory to remain continually in blessing among our brethren, we devote devout care to providing good things for them not only in spiritual but also in bodily matters. Therefore we wish all the faithful of our Church, present and future, to know how we have assigned the mount called St Michael—namely, the church with all its appurtenances—for the feast of St Remaclus and for our anniversary. For that same mount, which had belonged to the brethren’s prebend, our predecessor of pious memory, Abbot Erckenbert, once intending to go to Jerusalem, had, overcome by many prayers, restored to the brethren. But after he had departed, induced by one of his ministerials, Gerbert of Luttemarssen, he granted that same mount to him as a benefice. After Gerbert’s death, when his son Henry had occupied it, it was recovered from him through Lord Abbot Volcmar, upon the promise that, as soon as a benefice became vacant among the ministerials, he should receive one talent from the abbot as a benefice. In the meantime, however, he began to withhold the service owed by one abbot at Luttemarssen, of whose manor he was reeve, and said that he would retain it until he obtained the promised benefice. [Col. 1500A]

Since, in the days of our prelacy, we could not calmly endure that such a great deficiency should be inflicted every year upon the abbot’s table through injustice, we summoned the same Henry. Though with much labour, we nevertheless so defeated him by the judgments and sentences of his peers, convicting him by just grounds, that he surrendered that service to us and to the table of the abbot of Corvey, on the condition that, as soon as one talent should become vacant to us or to our successors, he should receive it as a benefice. Therefore, when we had the aforesaid mount free in our own hand—although the brethren had long demanded it, they had by no means received it from our predecessors or enjoyed any revenue from it—and considering at the same time that the mount was always liable to laymen’s rivalry and claims, we have assigned that same mount, for the commemoration and veneration of blessed Remaclus, our lord and patron, and for the remedy of our soul, with all its appurtenances, namely the church with its endowed holding and the estate with its holdings and fields belonging to it, and the newly cleared lands which our brother Godamin had cleared and cultivated upon that mount, for the refreshment of the brethren of Corvey on the feast of our aforesaid patron and on the anniversary of our appointment—that is, on the vigil of the Eleven Thousand Virgins. [Col. 1500B]

The arrangement is that our clerk Hildeward, who now holds the mount, or whoever holds it after him, shall pay to the cellarer of the brethren fifteen shillings for the feast, on the Beheading of St John the Baptist, and likewise fifteen shillings for the anniversary day of our election on the feast of St Dionysius, so long as we live. But after God has called us from this life, on the anniversary of our death the brethren shall receive those same fifteen shillings in perpetuity in memory of us.

Moreover, we wish all to know that we have entrusted this mount to our clerk Hildeward, with the church, estate, and all its appurtenances, as written above, on this condition: so long as he pays the brethren thirty shillings at the times indicated above, he shall not be deprived of the same benefice. But as soon as he refuses to pay this sum, he shall cease to hold the benefice both of the church and of the manor. At no time may the church and its appurtenances be separated from the manor and its appurtenances; rather, joined together, they shall pay thirty shillings annually. The brethren, of their own free will and by common agreement, have ordained that the feast of Blessed Remaclus be celebrated solemnly in copes and with five candles. On that feast day they shall celebrate the first Mass of St Remaclus in the greater church, and the principal Mass of the Dedication in the chapel adjoining our house and consecrated under his title. [Col. 1500C]

Therefore, lest any of our successors presume at any time to take away, diminish, or in any manner alienate this charity established by us for the brethren without the consent of the chapter of Corvey, we ordain and establish, under attestation of the divine name and by a decree to remain in force for ever, the aforesaid Mount St Michael for the brethren of Corvey, for the feast of Blessed Remaclus and for our anniversary, according to the foregoing arrangement. And, in order that this enactment may remain valid and inviolate through all times, we strengthen and confirm this charter of our enactment with the impression of our seal. [Col. 1500D]

These are the names of the brethren in whose presence and testimony this enactment was made: Henry, prior; Engelger; Thiederic; Walter; Adelbert, provost; Thiederic; Adulph; Conrad, cellarer; Elumig; Mechtfrid; Isiko; Heremann; Tegenhard; Bruno; Conrad; Reinard, provost of Eresburg; Heis; Henry, provost of Groningen; Reinard, provost of Kemnade; Conrad, porter; Adelbert, chamberlain; Bruning; Abraham; Fiko; Lambert; Othelric; Heremann; Tiederic; Cono; Berenwig; Ludolph; Arnold; Reinmar; Giselbert; Mus; Frederick. The boys: Rocholf, Unarg, Werner, Robert, Hartmann, Reiner, Dadfo, Burchard, Markward, Wizzelm, Anthony, Heitholf, Heremann. [Col. 1501A]

Done at Corvey in chapter, in the year of the Lord 1151, in the fifteenth indiction, on the feast day of St Remaclus, confessor of Christ and bishop, and in the sixth year of the prelacy of Lord Wibald, abbot of Corvey. [Col. 1501B]

### XXXII. Diploma of Frederick, king of the Romans, written in golden letters and granted to Abbot Wibald in the celebrated assembly at Merseburg.—It restores the rights and privileges of New Corvey.  
*(Year 1152.)*

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. FREDERICK, by favour of divine clemency king of the Romans.

It belongs to the munificence of royal dignity to bestow the rewards of virtue upon those who have deserved well of the commonwealth, so that they themselves may receive the fruits of their labour for the steadfastness of their fidelity, and that others, full of good hope, may become eager to carry out the duties of the empire. Therefore let the diligence of all our faithful, present and future, know that our faithful and most beloved Wibald, abbot of the monastery called New Corvey, appealed to our clemency, requesting that we might deign to renew and confirm the privileges of the Church of Corvey, over which that venerable abbot is now known to preside. Inclining the ear of our mercy to his religious petition on account of his distinguished fidelity toward our lord and uncle, our predecessor of blessed memory, the illustrious King Conrad, and likewise toward our own elevation to the kingship, whose governance, by God’s authorship, we assumed after Conrad’s death, we receive, through the tenor of this present charter, that place—namely New Corvey—with all its appurtenances both within and without, under the protection of royal majesty. Granting it perpetual liberty, as we know that our predecessor of pious memory and his ancestors, kings and emperors before him, had done, we establish this by our own authority and that of all the princes, under a law valid in perpetuity. [Col. 1501C]

The aforesaid monastery, New Corvey, shall not pass by any donation or exchange into the power, dominion, or subjection of any person or of any ecclesiastical or secular dignity, but shall always remain under the ordering and protection of kings or emperors and shall enjoy for ever the liberty which it has hitherto possessed.

And because two monasteries were founded by Emperor Louis and increased by our predecessors in honour and wealth—the monastery of monks called New Corvey, patterned on Old Corbie, and Herford, a house of nuns, modeled on the monastery of Soissons—they decreed that whichever abbot of Corvey should hold office should exercise the administration of the Church of Herford. That is, according to the custom by which communities of God’s handmaidens are administered by provosts of ecclesiastical rank, he should be their overseer and patron both in discipline and in all matters which Christ’s female servants could not perform because of their sex and profession. [Col. 1501D]

Following therefore in the footsteps of our predecessors, we confirm and establish by a decree of perpetual validity that all abbots in succession of the monastery of Corvey shall exercise the aforesaid administration and patronage without anyone’s contradiction, and, while preserving the dignity of the abbess, shall assist the congregation of Herford where it is expedient. We also confirm, by authority valid for ever, to the abbot Wibald who now, by divine calling and the common, unanimous election of the brethren, presides over the monastery of Corvey, and to all his successors, a certain monastery called Kemnade. Our most pious predecessor and uncle, King Conrad of blessed memory, gave it, on the relics of the body of St Vitus the martyr, by the golden ring of his donation, into the power, right, and lordship of the monastery of Corvey, because of the fidelity and at the request of our aforesaid faithful and most beloved Abbot Wibald. [Col. 1502A]

Thus the aforesaid monastery of Corvey shall have, possess, administer, use, and preserve the aforesaid monastery of Kemnade with all its estates, woods, and waters, belonging to that place both within and without, just as it is known to have been confirmed to the same monastery of Corvey by a privilege under the authority of our reverend father Pope Eugenius; and it shall hold it by proprietary right, under its own governance, just as it holds the three small abbeys which Louis the Pious, son of Charlemagne, founder of that same New Corvey, bestowed upon Corvey: namely Eresburg, once a noble Saxon stronghold, with the tithes lying round about it for two Saxon *rastae*; and likewise Meppen and Wibike, with the tithes and possessions belonging to them on every side. [Col. 1502B]

To the monastery of Herford, moreover, in the diocese of Osnabrück, belong the church of Buinidi, with the churches subject to it in the parish of Mimiernivord; the church of Rhen with the churches belonging to it; and, in addition, whatever has been established from the beginning of those same monasteries—namely Corvey and Herford—by our predecessors.

We likewise wish it to be firmly observed that wherever the monasteries themselves or their cells possess houses or estates from property which they acquire there by their own labour, they shall give tithes at the gate of the monastery and shall not be compelled to give them elsewhere, so that from them provision may be made for passing pilgrims and guests, to our own everlasting reward and that of all mankind. This is as has been allowed by a royal capitulary and synodal decree: that hostels and other hospitals of the faithful and poor be built, and as it has always been customary to grant to sacred monasteries. [Col. 1502C]

We further decree that bishops or their archpriests shall not prohibit their priests from celebrating Mass in their churches; but if they consider that something of their own right is being denied them in this matter, they shall bring it before our presence and the judgment of synodal examination. We also decree that they shall keep and possess their tithes or tithe churches—indeed, all their possessions—in whatever bishoprics, especially in Bremen, Osnabrück, and Paderborn, where they possess very many estates and tithes, as fully intact as they have hitherto held and possessed them from our predecessors, namely kings and emperors.

We also grant, according to the decrees of our predecessors, to each place the free power of choosing, from its own community, a suitable person to govern it. And we establish that no public judge shall exercise any judicial authority over persons belonging to the monastery of Corvey or to its aforesaid cells; rather, all their affairs shall be decided before their advocate. No one shall presume to usurp for himself the jurisdiction called *Burchban*, except the person to whom authority has been granted by the abbot of that monastery. Free persons shall have permission to give both themselves and their estates to that monastery; nor shall any judge or royal authority hereafter extort from them the customary due or public tax. [Col. 1502D]

Certainly, what we know our most pious predecessor, the illustrious and glorious prince, our lord and uncle King Conrad of happy memory, established in full court by the judgment of the princes and ministerials of the realm, we too, following in his footsteps, confirm and establish by a decree of perpetual validity: no layman shall ever dare to usurp by hereditary right a dwelling-place within the walls of the aforesaid monastery of Corvey, but the cemetery, as is proper, shall at all times remain free and open for the dwellings of religious persons. We likewise strengthen by our command, with equal firmness, the provision that the stewards and cupbearers of the abbot of Corvey shall have no authority whatsoever to entrust the keys of their lord’s goods; but the abbot shall possess freely and in perpetuity the authority to give the keys and order the affairs of his household, as we know was determined by a sentence of judgment under our predecessor. And in order that all these things may be held valid and inviolate for ever, we have ordered this charter to be drawn up and marked with the impression of our seal. [Col. 1503A]

The following witnesses were present: Sweyn, king of the Danes, who there received the kingdom from the hand of the lord king; Knut, the other Dane, who there surrendered the kingdom into the hand of the lord king; Hartwig, archbishop of Bremen; Othelric, bishop of Halberstadt; Burchard, bishop of Strasbourg; Wicmann, bishop of Citice; Daniel, bishop of Prague; Bernard, bishop of Paderborn; Henry, bishop of Minden; Heremann of Verden; Anselm of Havelberg; Emehard of Mecklenburg; Wikker of Brandenburg; Marquard, abbot of Guld; Henry, abbot of Hersfeld; Arnold, abbot of Nienburg; Henry, duke of Saxony; Lord Welf, his maternal uncle; Conrad, margrave of Meissen, and his sons; Margrave Adelbert and his sons.

The sign of the most invincible lord Frederick, king of the Romans.

I, Arnold, chancellor in place of Henry, archchancellor of Mainz, have recognized this document.

Given at the court at Merseburg, in the year of the Lord’s Incarnation [Col. 1503B] 1152, in the fifteenth indiction, in the first year of Lord Frederick, king of the Romans. Done happily in Christ. Amen.

### XXXIII. Privilege of Pope Adrian IV for the monastery of Stavelot.  
*(Year 1154.)*

ADRIAN, etc.

“Whenever that,” etc. See under Adrian, at the year 1159.

### XXXIV. Privilege of Pope Adrian IV granted to Abbot Wibald.—It confirms the use of sandals and the dalmatic, together with other privileges of the monastery of Corvey.  
*(Year 1155.)*

ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved [Col. 1503C] sons GUICBALD, abbot of Corvey, and his brethren, present and future, professing the regular life, in perpetuity.

“The authority of our office admonishes and invites us,” etc. See Pope Adrian IV, at the year 1159.

### XXXV. Diploma of Pope Adrian IV granted to Abbot Wibald.—It unites the monastery of Werben, severely impaired in temporal and spiritual matters, to Corvey.

ADRIAN, bishop, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son WIBALD, abbot of Corvey, greeting and apostolic blessing.

“The most holy Roman Church,” etc. See under Adrian.

### XXXVI. Letter of Pope Adrian IV to the bishop of Mainz.—That he should sternly admonish and bring into order Bobbo, advocate of the abbey of Werben, who had made many threats against Abbot Wibald.  
*(About 1155.—From the manuscript History of Corvey.)*

[Col. 1503D]

ADRIAN, servant of the servants of God, to his beloved son in Christ, the bishop of Mainz, greeting and apostolic blessing.

“Imitating the footsteps of our predecessors,” etc. See under Adrian.

### XXXVII. Letter of Abbot Wibald to his successors.—He grants a portion of woodland to the hospital at Groningen.  
*(Year 1156.—From the archive of New Corvey.)*

In the name of the holy and undivided Trinity. WIBALD, by God’s grace abbot of the Church of Corvey, to all his successors in perpetuity.

[Col. 1504A] If we take care to supply the needs of the poor from our abundance, we establish for ourselves great confidence before the most high God by almsgiving, and leave an example to our posterity. Therefore let the diligence of all the faithful of the Church of Corvey, present and future, know that we, in view of divine recompense, were urgently asked by certain laymen to grant them in benefice a certain part of the wood which we possessed near Groningen. For the remedy of our soul and for the salvation of all our successors as abbots of the monastery of Corvey, we have granted to the obedience of the hospital at Groningen the wood which we possessed in the forest called Hachel, at the request of our brethren of Corvey, and especially at the urging of Brother Ruchard, who was then in charge of that obedience, that we should complete this almsgiving. [Col. 1504B]

When this land had thus been granted to the hospital at Groningen, we adjure all our successors, by the dreadful future examination of God’s judgment, never at any time to take this same almsgiving away from that hospital or to diminish it, but to strive continually to preserve it there in return for eternal life. And so that this grant of ours may remain valid and inviolate for the hospital of Groningen through all future times, we have made known to our successors by this letter the grant which we made. For testimony and confirmation of our donation, we have ordered it to be marked with our seal. [Col. 1504C]

The following ministerials were present as witnesses: Conrad of Amelungessen; Reiner of Porta; Godescalc, cupbearer; Heis; Henry; Luther; Alwin, his son; Volckwin; and Werner, his brother.

In the year of the Lord’s Incarnation 1156, in the tenth year of the prelacy of Lord Wibald in the Church of Corvey, on the fourth Ides of February, between chapter and the sixth hour. Happily in Christ. Amen.

### XXXVIII. Letter of Theoderic, abbot of New Corvey.—Concerning the writing of chronicles of the monasteries.  
*(Year 1337.—From a manuscript of New Corvey.)*

THEODERIC, abbot of the monastery of the holy martyrs Stephen and Vitus at Corvey, to all who shall read this, everlasting grace and greeting in the Lord. Most beloved brethren, it is indeed of great importance that the antiquities, foundations, endowments, rights, privileges, and praiseworthy usages and customs of our Church and of the others subject to it, together with other notable matters, should be collected and written down for the remembrance of future posterity and for our instruction and pleasure. Since, therefore, our pious predecessors Marquard and Wigbold, whose memory be blessed, commanded their brethren and beloved sons—especially the senior men, those distinguished by experience of affairs, and those appointed to a provostship or another office—that each should compose a chronicle of the Church or monastery over which he presided at the time, or continue one perhaps begun by another; and since various brethren, obeying these admonitions, have admirably demonstrated their diligence, we, following in their illustrious footsteps, renew and restore the same command by the tenor of this document. We will that each person carefully preserve whatever chronicle previously written he possesses concerning his monastery or Church, and faithfully continue it in chronological order down to his own times. [Col. 1504D]

But if none yet exists, let him himself compile one, or arrange for it to be written by another suitable and trustworthy man. We shall willingly provide from the archive and library whatever may be necessary; moreover, as did our predecessors, we shall especially honour each person’s diligence. Farewell in the Lord.

Given in our imperial abbey in the year of grace 1337, on the very day of Blessed Veronica.

IN THE YEAR OF THE LORD 1156: ERNALD, ABBOT OF BONNEVAL IN THE DIOCESE OF CHARTRES.

[Col. 1507]

## HISTORICAL-LITERARY NOTICE

OUDIN, *Script. eccles.*, vol. II, p. 1288.

Arnald, or Ernald, abbot of Bonneval in the valley of Chartres, though a man of obscure birth, was nevertheless not of obscure reputation. He was a contemporary of St Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, and most intimate and familiar with him, as also with Peter of Celle. He professed the rule of St Benedict at Bonneval in the diocese of Chartres, as is probable, where he wholly devoted himself to those studies by which Christian and religious piety is customarily nourished and fostered. Thus instructed in divine and human letters, he was in the course of time, by merit of observance, placed over this monastery as abbot, to the great honour and benefit of the monastery, which was founded in the territory of Chartres scarcely six miles from the city itself. In that same city Peter of Celle exercised the episcopal office shortly after Ernald’s death.

This is the Ernald whom St Bernard, abbot of Clairvaux, loved greatly, as is attested by Bernard’s Letter 310, written to him in Bernard’s own hand near the end of his life. This is the Ernald also praised by Arnulf, bishop of Lisieux, to whom Arnulf wrote, when Ernald was ill, in these words:

> There began to come back to me the pleasant things which had arisen from your friendship. There came back to me, indeed, that holy and sweet conversation by which you excel in instructing the minds of your hearers through skill in matters, and in delighting their ears by the sweetness of agreeable speech. I remembered how great a grace for writing divine goodness had bestowed on you; in it I do not know whether I ought more to admire the fruitfulness of your thoughts or your mastery of expression. For these correspond to one another in you with such equality that neither does the majesty of the matters seem constrained by the narrowness of the words, nor the dignity of the discourse weighed down by any loftiness of the thoughts.

There are also other letters of the same writer to the same recipient, in which Ernald is always so named, as likewise by Henry of Ghent.

Although our Ernald possessed such great learning and piety, some of his writings have hitherto remained hidden, others have been ascribed to other authors or have disappeared, with only a few reserved to their true author. “Ernald,” says Henry of Ghent, “abbot of Bonneval, composed a Life of Saint Bernard in four books, besides the one written by William, abbot of Saint-Thierry; touching here and there upon many matters that seemed to him relevant to the subject he was writing. He also commented upon the five or six last words of the Lord on the cross, discussing them in various and subtle ways.” Henry, however, erred in assigning the four books of the Life of Saint Bernard to Ernald; Trithemius more correctly assigns him one book and certain letters. For, among the five books of Bernard’s Life commonly encountered, the first is Ernald’s offspring; the second belongs to William, abbot of Saint-Thierry and later a monk of Signy of the Cistercian Order. The remaining three belong to Geoffrey, once Bernard’s secretary or amanuensis and later the fourth abbot of Clairvaux. Moreover, Henry is mistaken when, in his book *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, he calls Ernald a Cistercian; it is certain that he belonged to the Benedictine institution. Besides these, other little works bear Ernald’s name in various libraries; others have remained hidden until now or have wholly perished.

From all these works of Ernald, the following appeared in the latest edition of the Works of the divine Cyprian, published at Oxford in England in 1682, from the Sheldonian Theatre, and corrected from many earlier editions: *On the Seven Words of the Lord on the Cross*; *On the Principal Works of Christ*, a little work hitherto wrongly attributed to Saint Cyprian, bishop of Carthage; *On the Works of the Six Days*; *On the Praises of the Blessed Virgin Mary*; and various *Meditations*. Likewise, among the Works of the divine Bernard, there has often appeared the first book of the *Life of Saint Bernard*, attributed by most people to another Bernard, said to have been abbot of Bonneval among the Viennese. It will not be unsuitable, for the reader’s instruction, to seek here an occasion to say a little more about each of these works.

The little work *On the Seven Words of the Lord on the Cross* is ascribed by everyone to Arnold, abbot of Bonneval, although some both err and lead others into error by interpreting him as abbot of Bonneval among the Besançonnais. But the inscription attached to a Cistercian copy decisively settles the question: “Arnaud, abbot of Bonneval [Col. 1509] in France, on the Words of the Lord.” Under the name “France,” Bonneval in the territory of Chartres is sufficiently distinguished from other monasteries of the same name, whether situated in the dioceses of Vienne, Poitiers, or Rodez; all who understand French affairs know this easily. This little work was first printed by the learned Jean Gagneius, first counsellor and almoner to Francis I, king of France, under the title: “Ernald, abbot of Bonneval in the diocese of Chartres, on the Words of the Lord on the Cross.”

The book *On the Principal Works of Christ*, published hitherto among the works of Saint Cyprian, is also ascribed to our Arnold in both the Cistercian and Clairvaux copies and in the Oxford copy of All Souls College, although in that last copy the abbot’s name is mistakenly read as *Bonavillanensis* instead of *Bonavallensis*. For the inscription in the Clairvaux exemplar reads: “Book of Lord Ernald, abbot of Bonneval, on the Principal Works of Christ”; and another adds: “which he wrote to Pope Adrian,” namely Adrian IV, who was promoted to the Roman See in 1154.

A good many had already assigned this book to that Arnold: Robertus Locus in his *Censure*; Philippe Labbe in the Dissertation appended to Bellarmine’s *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, vol. I, under “Cyprian”; François Combefis in the apparatus to the *Library of Preachers*, under “Arnold”; and Jean Mabillon in the notes to Letter 210 of Saint Bernard, abbot, in the Paris edition of 1667. That the true author’s name remained unknown so long resulted from the writer’s modesty; for near the end of the prologue he asks that his name be suppressed in these words: “Therefore, I have sent to your fatherhood, with my name suppressed, the little book which I wrote on the principal works of our Christ.” Behold Arnold’s modesty, the enemy of the itch to write.

It is astonishing that this little work should have been attributed to Saint Cyprian, when reading it alone proves the contrary. One example will suffice. Speaking of Christ’s baptism, the writer says that baptism is the same by whomever it is performed; that this does not depend on merits but upon grace; and that God’s omnipotence properly reserves its effect to itself. Saint Cyprian could scarcely have said this, since he rejected every baptism conferred by heretics.

2. What of the fact that the biblical quotations correspond to the Vulgate version, which is immensely distant from Cyprian’s time?

3. Speaking of the anointing with chrism, the author writes: “Today prisons stand open, and the condemned are granted freedom; today judges, laying aside severity, become gentle.” This must be understood of Christian kings and judges; and no one fails to see how foreign this is to Cyprian’s time, when nearly all judges were pagans.

4. Finally, in the same sermon he still affirms that the honor of anointing remained not only among kings and priests, but that the fullness of this grace was poured out upon the whole Catholic people, whereas the use of anointing among both kings and priests came long after Cyprian’s time.

Yet even if we set aside the various parchment codices that vindicate this work for Ernald, this would be apparent from the similarity of style and from comparison with his other works. For example, in the book *On the Principal Works of Christ*, when speaking of the Nativity, the author says: “The mother is a midwife, and devotion renders to the beloved child the service of a client.” Again in the same place: “Nor should the preceding delight demand any interest in punishments.” Both passages occur in this form in Ernald’s little book *On the Praises of the Blessed Virgin Mary*: “There the virgin, both midwife and mother, rendered service to herself in that celebration.” And below: “There she voluntarily demanded no interest of punishments for pleasure.”

A further striking proof is that the author of this book attributed to Cyprian, when treating the Passion, holds the same opinion about Christ’s entrusting Mary to John as Arnold does in Sermon 3 *On the Words of the Lord on the Cross*. There Arnold says:

> Behold, John, you receive the testament of a loving inheritance; you are chosen and in this are set before all others. Joseph, who had served until then, yields when you are substituted for him, and does not assert marital rights, so that the mouth of those who thereafter speak wickedly may be stopped, since that marriage had served the divine dispensation, not carnal union. Therefore Joseph does not complain, when John receives her as his mother, of the dissolution of a marriage which he had entered into for the sake of the dispensation, without any commerce of carnal union.

But that other author says as follows:

> Reason now required that the appearance of marriage be removed, and that he who had hitherto held the place of father and husband should no longer be regarded as Christ’s father. In this disposition of Christ, Joseph would have had reasonable ground for objection when Mary was entrusted to another, had he known himself to be her carnal husband, etc.

In both places the author judges that Joseph survived the Passion, and says that Mary was entrusted to John, with her spouse passed over, in order that the impression of carnal union might be removed. If we add the testimony of the manuscript codices that attribute that book to our Ernald, it will be beyond all question that this work is a genuine offspring of our Ernald. What most commends the author is that this labor of his was deemed worthy of being attributed to Cyprian, the most eloquent of almost all the Latin Fathers.

The treatise *On the Works of the Six Days*, also entitled *On Paradise* in manuscript codices of the library formerly of Foulques of Mont and now of the Colbert Library in Paris, was first published under the name of Arnold or Arnald through the efforts of Dionysius Peronnet, cleric of the city of Auxerre. It bears its author’s name in many manuscript codices, from which Lord Bertrand Tissier, prior of Bonnefont in Thiérache, of the Cistercian Order in the archbishopric of Reims, once copied it and sent it to Lord Luc d’Achery. It was also often printed under the same name in the *Library of the Ancient Fathers*. The same must be said of the little book entitled *On the Praises of the Blessed Virgin Mary*. The book of *Meditations*, however, was published only in 1682 at the end of the Works of Saint Cyprian by the bishop of Exeter.

As for the second book of the *Life of Saint Bernard, Abbot*, it is astonishing with what heat—and with how much zeal and error combined—Charles de Visch, prior of Blessed Mary of the Dunes in Flanders, enrolled this Arnold, abbot of Benedictine Bonneval in the territory of Chartres, among his Cistercians in the *Library of Writers of the Cistercian Order*, p. 25. To establish his assertion, he cites a great company of writers who affirm the same thing, whom he calls weighty authorities: Sixtus of Siena in the *Sacred Library*; John Trithemius and Bellarmine in *On Ecclesiastical Writers*; Possevino in the *Sacred Apparatus*; William Eisengrein in *Orthodox Writers*; Conrad Gesner in the *Universal Library*; Philippe Seguin in the manuscript *Cistercian Library*; likewise Henry of Ghent, *On Illustrious Men*, chap. 11; Aubert Miraeus in his scholia on Henry of Ghent mentioned above; Hippolytus Maracci in the *Marian Library*, pp. 144–145; and finally Jongelinus, both in the *Notice of the Abbeys of the Cistercian Order* and in the *Origins and Progress of the Same Order*.

Yet notwithstanding this number of authorities who say so, the most learned Jean Mabillon demonstrates in his final edition of the Works of the divine Bernard—issued in two folio volumes at Paris in 1667, by Frédéric Léonard, Rue Saint-Jacques, under the sign of the Venetian Shield—that this Arnold, author of the second book of the *Life of Saint Bernard*, was not a Cistercian abbot of Viennese Bonneval but the unique abbot of Benedictine Bonneval in the territory of Chartres. Thus, at the end of the first volume of Bernard’s Works, in his notes on Letter 310, p. 39, he writes:

> “Later writers—namely Horstius, Charles de Visch, and the author of the French Life of Saint Bernard—contrary to the opinion of Trithemius, Bellarmine, and others, wish this Arnold to be distinct from the author of the second book of the *Life of Saint Bernard*. That author they call Bernard, and make him abbot of Bonneval, not in Poitou or Rouergue, [Col. 1511] but in Vienne, of the Cistercian Order. They call the other Arnold abbot of Bonneval in the territory of Chartres, a house of Benedictine monks, to whom this letter was written. But, with due respect to such great men, I would say that they are one and the same.
>
> “For as regards the difference of name, the author of the second book of the *Life of Saint Bernard* is called Ernald in a very ancient manuscript codex of Corbie; and by this name our Arnold, abbot in the territory of Chartres, is designated by Arnulf, bishop of Lisieux, in the letters which he wrote to him. But, leaving aside the controversy over the name, it is certain that Book II of the *Life of Saint Bernard* was written while Geoffrey was still bishop of Langres; for in chapter 5, no. 29, one reads: ‘Geoffrey, prior of the same place, his kinsman in flesh and spirit, who afterwards became bishop in the Church of Langres, and to this day perseveres commendably in going in and going out.’
>
> “It was therefore written before 1161, when Geoffrey, having resigned the bishopric, returned to Clairvaux to the embrace of his Rachel, as the Clairvaux Chronicle writes; there it is recorded that he died in 1164, on the sixth day before the Ides of November. But from the foundation of Cistercian Bonneval in Vienne in 1117 until 1180, no abbot there bore the name Arnold or Bernard. Saint John was first in charge, from 1118 to 1138, when he was made bishop of Valence and yielded his place to Gozevin, the second abbot, who was appointed abbot of Cîteaux in succession to Raynald in 1151. Peter succeeded as third at Bonneval; in 1171 Saint Hugh, formerly abbot of Léoncel, succeeded him, and presided over Viennese Bonneval until 1180, when he is reported in the Cistercian Menology to have died. Where, then, is the Arnold or Bernard, abbot of Viennese Bonneval, who could have written the second book of the *Life of Saint Bernard* before 1164, the year of Geoffrey of Langres’s death? All this is established by the evidence of Manriquez’s *Annals*.
>
> “Therefore the author of the aforesaid book and that friend of Saint Bernard, to whom Bernard, near death, wrote this letter, are one and the same: namely our Arnold or Ernald, abbot of Bonneval in the territory of Chartres. Concerning him the most learned Father Bertrand Tissier made these observations.
