Possessing our Arnold’s works and knowing that they could not be assigned to the Cistercian *Library of the Fathers*, he sent them most generously to our d’Achery, to be printed someday, God willing, with that candor and judgment in which he excels. These observations, I say, he made concerning our Arnold.”

From these words of Mabillon it is clear that Jean Merlon Horstius wrongly entitled this second book of the *Life of Saint Bernard*, which he placed in his Prolegomena to Bernard’s Works, as though composed by Abbot Bernard. It certainly belongs to Arnold, abbot of Benedictine Bonneval in the territory of Chartres, who was a particular friend of the divine Bernard during his lifetime and wished to honor the memory of his friend by his own writing.

A commentary on Psalm CXXXII, “Behold, how good and how pleasant,” etc., occurs under Arnold’s name, together with his other undoubted works, in a manuscript codex of excellent authority, contemporary with the author, in the library of Longpont, of the Cistercian Order in the diocese of Soissons. I discovered it in 1676, while examining various ancient libraries of the Gallican realm; later I arranged for it to be copied for me by a monk of that house. In the same year he also sent another copy of this work to Jean Mabillon, a Benedictine monk, who was then considering collecting and publishing all Ernald’s works together. It was published in octavo at Leiden in 1692 by Pieter van der Meerche, with other works by other authors. It possesses Ernald’s genius and a sweetness of expression not inferior to that which breathes everywhere in his writings; I think no one, after reading it, will fail to reach the same opinion as ours. Although in Homilies 4 and 5, abandoning the text, this author seems to have taken up an argument different from the proposed subject, he nevertheless very much resembles Ernald in piety even where he strays from the text and the argument of the work.

A little work on the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit survives in manuscript under the same Ernald’s name in the library of the mother-house of Cîteaux. In 1655 Jacques de Launoy, a monk of that monastery, a man born to assist scholars, sent Luc d’Achery an accurate copy which he had made himself. The codex is of excellent authority; and by reason of the doctrine it contains, this little work is most worthy of Abbot Ernald, whose name it bears and whose piety it reflects. Yet we cannot deny that its style does not always attain the elegance and ornament which Ernald displays in his other treatises. I add that citations from Scripture are more frequent in it than in Ernald’s other little works, although it is a work of great diligence in its own kind and does not depart from the solidity of our abbot. The distinctive doctrine found in chapter 8, *On the Washing of Feet*, agrees entirely with Ernald’s doctrine in *On the Principal Works of Christ*, as will be apparent to anyone who compares the two little works. The ancients did not always proceed in their works with the same adornment, but sometimes more loosely and sometimes more intensely, according to the occasion or subject. This work was printed with the preceding little work at Leiden in 1692 through my efforts.

Finally, François Titelmann, who revised Arnold’s little work *On the Seven Words of the Lord on the Cross* and arranged for its publication after Jean Gagneius, also ascribes to him a book *On the Body and Blood of the Lord* in the prologue prefixed to his edition. He writes:

> “The same author is reported, besides these two treatises—namely *On the Words of the Lord on the Cross* and *On the Praises of the Blessed Virgin Mary*—to have written other little works as well, *On the Works of the Six Days* and *On the Body and Blood of the Lord*, which have not hitherto been seen by us.”

But perhaps that book *On the Body and Blood of the Lord* belongs to William, abbot of Saint-Thierry, who belonged to the same institution and lived in the same period. He wrote a book on that subject which we have often seen joined and collected in manuscript codices with the little works of Abbot Ernald; perhaps for this reason some people judged it to belong to Ernald. Or that book *On the Body and Blood of the Lord* may be no other work than the treatise *On the Principal Works of Christ*, in which he also treats the Eucharist with distinction.

So much at length concerning the writings of Ernald, whom Charles de Visch, prior of Blessed Mary of the Dunes in Flanders, mentions extensively in the *Library of Writers of the Cistercian Order*, p. 25, although he argues much but vainly that this Ernald belonged to the Cistercian Order; Caesar Egassius Bulaeus in Book IV of the *History of the University of Paris*, in the catalogue of the illustrious academics of that century; the aforesaid Jean Mabillon in the notes to Letter 510 of the divine Bernard in the cited edition, p. 39; I myself in the Supplement to Bellarmine’s *On Ecclesiastical Writers*, both under Cyprian at the year 250 and under Ernald at the year 1160—see those entries; Philippe Labbe, in the same place; William Cave in the *History of the Writers of the Church*, century IV, under the year 1162, p. 680; along with many others.

[Col. 1513]

# TREATISE OF ABBOT ERNALD ON THE WORKS OF THE SIX DAYS

Published by Dionysius Perronnet of Melun, cleric of Auxerre.

(*Library of the Fathers of Lyons*, vol. XXII, p. 1284.)

## Dedicatory Epistle

To the Most Reverend and Most Illustrious Cardinal, Lord DU PERRON, Archbishop of Sens and Grand Almoner of France.

It has always been the custom of learned and good men, most illustrious cardinal and most highly accomplished in every kind of learning, not only to devote their labors and vigils to public usefulness, but also to encourage others by their example to deserve well of all people. Among them was Jean Gagneius, formerly first counsellor and almoner to Francis I, the invincible king of France: a man of no common learning, and also a diligent and discerning investigator of ancient records. By drawing them, as it were, out of darkness and bringing them into the light, he sought to make the Catholic Church better instructed by their excellent teachings, so that students of truth, guided as it were by a torch into the path of truth, might persevere in it more steadfastly and cling more firmly to the orthodox faith.

He published many books. In one of them, entitled *Arnald, Abbot of Bonneval in the Diocese of Chartres, On the Seven Words of the Lord on the Cross*, he observes near the end that this Arnald also wrote another treatise *On the Works of the Six Days*. He asks all into whose hands this book may fall to commit it to the press, as a book of better quality and one contributing to God’s glory and the edification of the Church.

I was so persuaded by the words of so great a man that, as soon as I read them, I resolved to follow in his footsteps and to leave nothing untried in finding such a book wherever in the world it might lie concealed. To that end I visited such famous and well-stocked libraries as I could, both of cathedral churches and of celebrated religious houses, especially those of the Cistercian Order, of which that learned man was a member.

Indeed, thirty-five years ago, when the most illustrious Cardinal de Gondi, then bishop of the Church of Langres, sent me to Langres, the canons of that church received me kindly and introduced me to their library. Having examined many things there, at last the treasure I sought came forth, as it were, from the deepest darkness into the light. I asked Lord Comestor, bishop of Négrepont and ecclesiastic of Langres, to take it from the library to his house and keep it as a precious deposit until a suitable occasion should arise to send it to me at Paris. He very willingly promised this. But death overtook him, and thus he could neither fulfill his promise nor could I, disappointed of hope, obtain what I desired. A long time then passed before I heard anything—indeed, not even a word—about this little book.

But when the most learned Jacques Amyot, bishop of Auxerre, who preceded you in the office of the king’s grand almoner—a man whose praises and merits can never be adequately celebrated—brought me into these regions; and when, a little later, while visiting his diocese, he turned aside to Vermanton and stayed there briefly, I meanwhile went to the monastery of Saint Mary of Régny, of the same order as the author of this book, not far from that place. As I made inquiries there, the prey sought for so long happened to fall into my nets. When I recognized it, I asked the monks of that house to provide me with a copy of its original; and they obediently did so.

But finding this splendid jewel would not have been enough unless it came before everyone’s eyes, so that all good people might enjoy so great a benefit. Yet, whenever I considered bringing it to light, obstacles so adverse intervened in my undertakings that I was not permitted to fulfill my desire until this day. But now that supreme Goodness has been pleased to quiet civil disturbances, grant us peace, and restore to its former splendor this kingdom torn by arms and fires, it has seemed to me also—now enjoying more freedom for leisure—that the fitting time has come to satisfy both the desire of the learned and my own, and to make public what had been a private gift entrusted to me.

One thing alone remained: under the protection of which distinguished man should I chiefly commend this excellent work? Many most learned men came to mind, but none is more learned than you and none worthier. Add that you preside over the archiepiscopal Church of Sens, within whose bounds I was both born and educated; and that your illustrious house lies near the place where that pious and learned Abbot Arnald wrote this book. Therefore I earnestly ask you, most distinguished man, in accordance with your singular kindness, to receive this small gift as graciously as I offer it to you with goodwill. Farewell unto Nestor’s years.

At Auxerre, on the Ides of May, in the year of the Lord 1609.

Your most devoted,

Dionysius PERRONNET of Melun, cleric of Auxerre.

# HERE BEGINS THE TREATISE ON THE WORKS OF THE SIX DAYS

[Col. 1515]

[Col. 1515A] God, the one principle of all things that are, move, and live, decreed and established their origin in wisdom coeternal with himself. And, distinguishing the natures of things as though they were members of a great body, he assigned them their proper places and names, fitting measures and functions. Nothing in that beginning was confused before God, nothing formless, because the matter of things, when it was made, was immediately formed into species suited to it.

Whatever philosophers have thought concerning the eternity of the world, concerning *hyle*—matter—ideas, or that soul of the world which they call *nous* (“mind”), thereby introducing several principles, the first chapter of Genesis abolishes and confounds. It establishes one principle of every creature: namely God, in whom providence or wisdom, reason or order, life, form, and matter are not something other than himself. [Col. 1515B] In his Word, which is the manifestation of the eternal secret, what he says he makes, and what he illumines he forms.

Do not imagine solitude or poverty in him before the constitution of the world; nor suppose that anything accrued to his sovereignty or glory through the subjection or service of created things. The Trinity is never alone; divinity is never needy. The One who is present cannot be absent; the Wise One cannot be ignorant; the Omnipotent cannot become weak. Eternity does not grow old; truth does not change; charity never fails; what is solid is not broken; what is one is not divided; nothing is lacking to perfection; the whole does not increase; the universe does not diminish. As he was and will be, so he is—although “was” and “will be” are said of him improperly, because only the present belongs to him, to whom nothing either comes or passes away.

Therefore goodness, not necessity, is the sole cause of all things that are. Participation in glory has been granted to rational creation in such a way that, although it draws from that fullness, it is nevertheless not a part of the One to whom, being conformed, it participates after some manner as “father-like” (*patrissans*).

It is wholly unfitting and exceedingly absurd to believe that the unformed globe of the world and its maker existed eternally together, and that that mass, set apart, served no use—as if God either could not or would not distinguish and form it. For in God willing, being able, and doing are altogether the same. Indeed, will, power, and effect accompanied one another indivisibly in that construction of things, “for he spoke, and they were made; he commanded, and they were created” (Psalm 148). [Col. 1515D]

In his wisdom there was indeed an eternal plan for so magnificent a work; but its temporal beginning did not lie hidden, wrapped in that confusion called chaos. Nor was it fitting that the omnipotence, wisdom, or goodness of the Creator should oppress the matter once made through inertia, or should neglect through ages-long delays foundations of such excellence. For delay in a body once begun would have contributed nothing either to God or to creation. The Creator would have had no glory in the imperfection of his work; nor would the creature itself, being senseless and inanimate, have had either loss or gain in this matter, since that formlessness or uselessness would have been without harm to it.

Hence it is evident that the first principles of things were fitted together by the word of God, as the Apostle says, “so that visible things should come to be from invisible things” (Hebrews 11); and that the interwoven whole, under the distinctions and forms of the universe, pleased him, bound from eternity in indissoluble connection within that divine mind. The gate was opened, and from that ancient ark of the covenant there came forth an innumerable multitude of visible and invisible, spiritual and bodily things. Now place and time began to exist, because [Col. 1516B] in their own manner all things are subject to spatial limitation, except that one nature alone which precedes and surpasses all things and encloses the universe within itself.

Man thinks vainly of places or times in relation to that ineffable and immeasurable greatness. The universe is altogether less than its maker, and eternity encloses within itself everything temporal as though it were a point. It embraces all things: making them firm within, protecting them without, cherishing them above, sustaining them below; by discernible art joining diverse things together; by marvelous proportion binding them into peace and joining opposites into one; pressing down light things lest they escape; supporting heavy things lest they fall.

In one and the same body you may see fire and water come together; air spread about the earth; and that immovable mass rest on firm roots upon a light and subtle foundation. You may see unstable waters borne above it and not consumed by fires, so that, as we consider with deeper wonder the wisdom and omnipotence of the maker in this, he may draw us to reverence for himself, since we see that nothing is impossible to him. [Col. 1516C]

By his governance, diverse and opposite things come together in the unity of peace; both motionless things and wandering things are recalled to a fixed order. The greatest do not swell, nor are the least consumed. Nor does that entire fabric of the world, without any fear of collapse, fail to endure in its law and order: though composed of such unlike parts it is uniform; though of such diverse things it is one; though of such opposites it is tranquil, solid, and harmonious. All things subject to one Lord have nowhere to turn aside; nor is any escape from the ruler open except to the judge, and from the judge to the avenger.

“All things are from him and through him and in him” (Colossians 1), “in whom we live and move and are” (Acts 17). Whatever our number, we have a fixed measure and weight. From him we are by nature and origin; through him we are by teaching and governance; and in him we are by the unity of love and the fellowship of glory. [Col. 1516D] In his book all that we do is numbered and written down; and whatever transgression writes there, confession erases. Or rather, nothing is erased from the book of life, because that book belongs to eternity, in which nothing is corrected or changed.

The talents of gifts are weighed out; the distribution of graces is measured, so that a person may neglect nothing, withhold nothing, and presume nothing. And indeed, before this visible world—that is, before the creation of heaven and earth—the service of angelic brightness was not lacking to the Creator, and that spiritual nature preceded the bodily in origin. Thus Ambrose says in the *Hexameron*: “Angels, dominions, and powers also began at some time; they already existed when this world was made.” And Basil: “After those invisible and intelligible things, Scripture recounts the beginning of the generation of those things which are seen and apprehended by sense.” [Col. 1517B] Jerome, on the Epistle to Titus: “The six thousand years of our time have not yet been completed; and how many ages before, how many periods, how many beginnings of centuries must we suppose to have existed, in which angels, thrones, and dominions served God and, by God’s will, subsisted without the revolutions and measures of times.”

There are some who understand it thus: that not only the Creator, but the very creature of heaven and earth also, existed before times; because day and night are defined by the distinction between them—by the rising and setting of the greater and lesser heavenly bodies, which run their courses according to beginnings, ends, and recurring alternations—and are bounded by measured intervals, their number being fixed by definite hours; and time is distinguished by fixed aggregations of days. They say, moreover, that the works of the six days were established from nothing, having no matter either from themselves or from elsewhere, but brought forth solely by the will of the Craftsman, by whose word the cause, rationale, and origin of all things that exist were ordained.

They likewise think that the order of the spiritual—that is, angelic—nature was established in such fullness that no necessity requires seed to be mutually transmitted within that kind in order to restore or increase its succession; for whatever may perhaps be lacking from their number is supplied from humankind, whose multiplication restores and completes what was sought or lacking. And they say that the interval between work and work was as great as the spaces comprised by six days—that is, as great as the delay measured by one day and one night. Thus they understand that the individual things were made, some preceding and some following others, just as in a building the foundation is first laid in order, and the wall and roof are fitted upon it; and just as the mind and workmanship of the builder gradually arrange these into a house, so God set in order the mass and forms of his construction and, as it were, wove the world step by step.

Yet it is rash to determine the interval during which, before the alternations of time, the wisdom of God invisibly disposed the first works, especially since the canonical Scriptures have handed down nothing certain on this matter. Still, if the fall of the devil—who is read to have existed from the beginning—occurred before the creation of heaven and earth, I do not understand either whom he envied or of whom he was a murderer, when humankind did not yet exist. Hence that Scripture, “He who lives for ever created all things together” (Ecclus. 1), seems to affirm that the whole creation—angelic, human, and each of the remaining kinds—arose together through the word of God, although that distinction is most difficult; and yet there is a distinction by which the intellectual preceded the bodily.

In things, the rationale of their being is first investigated; then the order of their nature; lastly, the use and necessity of their cause. And since the same cause both unites, divides, and gathers again, it is the work of inquiry to understand something as first and something as last in the same matter. This we suffer because of the narrowness of our understanding when, in considering things, we are dull and blear-eyed from bodily grossness before the brightness of pure light. But the wisdom of God, “reaching from end to end” (Wis. 3) with the most subtle swiftness, beholds predestined and created things as coexisting; and what he comprehends all at once, we gather in parts and unite after collecting them through certain delays.

God therefore created heaven and earth, dwellings of rational creatures, so that the divinity filling heaven and earth might have in each a settler and a praiser. The higher ranks, joined more closely to God and, as intellectual or spiritual beings, participating more abundantly in the creative nature, remain fixed in their stability. But humankind—both earthly and heavenly, flesh and spirit, compounded from heaven and earth—sometimes remains soberly within itself, sometimes in mind exceeds itself toward God; and according to either nature is now below, now carried upward.

Certainly Moses said nothing concerning the angels, whose ranks, offices, and dignities the authority of the Fathers distinguishes in many places. But since elsewhere in this same book of Genesis he introduces their persons and offices, there is no doubt that he understands their creation under the name of heaven. Therefore heaven was not called empty and void even when the reprobate part had fallen: for the whole angelic company was not infected by the fall of some; nor does the sin of some overflow except upon fellow transgressors. For spirit is not born from spirit as flesh is from flesh, nor does that nature descend at all by propagation. Although all share one nature, nevertheless none has anything from another, because divine omnipotence is the special, individual—as one might say—birth and origin of each.

But the earth, whose inhabitant is humankind, was called empty and void because, although man was created in innocence, the strength of the flesh was not yet completely firm; and even before sin human understanding was altogether less pure and penetrating than angelic understanding. The body of our lowliness had not yet been re-formed and conformed to the body of divine glory (Phil. 3), nor was the human condition then in that state which the resurrection undoubtedly promises. Still empty of that fullness of blessedness which it was to receive, it learned, by approaching the light, how much it lacked for its complete perfection; surrounded by that light, and better recognizing its own imperfection, it turns to him who can fill and perfect human insufficiency, and without hesitation awaits its conformation and reformation. The earth was empty, having no possessor; void, having no beauty; for that is formless which God does not illuminate, and empty and needy which he does not fill.

“And God said, Let there be light; and there was light” (Gen. 1). It is written that “God is light” (1 John 1), and that he “dwells in inaccessible light” (1 Tim. 6). He himself is the light that was made: primordial light illuminating all things—that is, making manifest the efficacy of the causal principles which he had hidden within himself, making visible what was nevertheless intelligible to himself. This is the first light, driving away darkness and establishing day, banishing ignorance and purifying the understanding by wisdom. For through it the condition of all things was arranged, and knowledge of those very arrangements is called day.

Thus the first day is the understanding of wisdom itself; the second, the bodily ordering of creation; the third, when darkness has been separated from light, the certain knowledge of the usefulness of things, by which, when they are considered in their wonderful order and beauty, the invisible things of the Creator are drawn into admiration—contemplating through the things made—so that through this his everlasting power and divinity become known to us (Rom. 1). The fourth day is ecclesiastical teaching and holy Scripture divinely inspired, in which we find certain rules of faith, so that no one may be established by private judgment, but by the authority of eternal truth. The fifth day is reason’s struggle with concupiscences, as with innumerable creeping things: human weakness resists them, being bound in some of its members to the actions of this age, but in others taking flight and choosing for itself a heavenly manner of life and rest.

The sixth day, then, is, when concupiscences have been overcome and the triumph over the victory of this world celebrated, the knowledge and contemplation of God with a pure heart and peaceful spirit. Through it, laying aside the image of the earthly man and putting off the old man, we are re-formed and pass into the likeness and image of God: expressing the image by the seal of charity, but the likeness by steadfastness and peace. For considering or contemplating these things, the first light—that is, knowledge of truth—directs the human intellect like its investigator, revealing to it the several kinds of things; that is, distinguishing days and nights, illuminating its departure from ignorance so as to know the order of things, that under the name of heaven and earth it may understand all heavenly and earthly things. Scripture distinguishes and separates these through certain intervals, as through days and nights; and, lest anything be lacking or weakness find grounds for complaint, the Spirit of God moves over them, cherishing and forming rational desires, helping weakness, making barrenness fruitful, stirring devotion, covering excesses, and restoring what is scattered.

This is the Spirit, manifold, one, steadfast, moving, human, kindly, who breathes where he wills, teaches, fills, and suggests all things. From his inexhaustible fullness and pure outpouring, the hearts of believers, filled and built together in the Church as a dwelling for God, being of one disposition in a house, have uttered a good word, with invincible eloquence and unconquerable inconstancy against opponents who were brought low. Thus, when suddenly a sound came from heaven, unlettered and ordinary men became defenders of the faith, and fishermen became disputants (Acts 2). Without borrowed aid from elsewhere, he anoints those whom he pierces with compunction; he perfects those whom he calls; he accomplishes what he commands. Therefore, in the statement that he “moves over” them, observe the dignity of a teacher, the affection of a nourisher, the protection of a life-giver, the imprint of charity, kinship of nature, and benevolence of grace.

First, then, light; next, day; afterwards, the firmament; and in the fourth place those great luminaries are said to have been made. For that first angelic nature, strong in the good of nature and grace, while it stood in truth through humility, was separated from night by the one eternal light; it deserved to be made firm and confirmed, and now, secure in its glory and without danger of falling, has no further access to evil. For it is so adjacent to the higher light and shines with such splendor from it that no vapor of darkness can intervene between it and the light which it itself is.

Therefore, God is light illuminating; the angel, light illuminated; the firmament, the rational affection rooted in God. The first day, then, is the establishment of intellectual or spiritual nature; the second, the creation of bodily and visible things; the third, the distinction of things from one another and their fruitfulness according to their kinds; the fourth, the illumination of the mind through the word of God on the testimony of the Scriptures; the fifth, reason’s discrimination between the desires of flesh and spirit; the sixth, in understanding and action, as in a certain male and female sex, the expression of the divine image and likeness, from whose union the Church is filled with spiritual offspring.

There remains, then, only rest on the seventh day. From this Sabbath, whoever, renewed in the spirit of his mind, has approved the better things and emerged from the darkness of this world, will pass to the sabbatism of the eighth, dividing in all things between light and darkness and bearing fruit like a good tree according to the grace given him. For a person must first understand that God is; then what God is, which he gradually approaches through consideration of creation; then, once the light of truth has been kindled, with the firmament of reason fixed between carnal and spiritual things, as between the upper and lower waters, and the briny blast of temptations expelled, he must bring forth grasses and shrubs—that is, propagate the shoots of flourishing graces.

He must also diligently attend to the spiritual understandings born from the Scriptures: how truth itself, like the sun, illumines the soul; while the soul, like the moon, sheds light upon the night—that is, upon bodily senses—multiplying actions like stars, which are not overcome by the darkness of this world. He must also exercise such discernment between creeping things and birds that, because he sees some persons living a more excellent life, he does not despise the weak; for in all there is a living soul, and “we surround the less honorable members with more abundant honor.” By these exercises man advances toward the image of God, whose rest is the heavenly inheritance, whose glory is blessed eternity, and whose felicity is the happiness of the peace above that surpasses every understanding in the knowledge of God.

Justice and judgment were immediately evident in the first event, and without any delay each party of consenting and dissenting spirits received the recompense deserved by its members. Their fellowships were at once divided, and the holy and impious companies separated, those who had wished to exist without God being driven out and irreversibly cast down into the lower parts of the world, or into hell—whatever that may be. Torn forever from the beatific vision of God, without hope of mercy, they are indeed immortal, yet passible; and they envy the impassibility of the surviving holy angels. Though they cannot infect them, since those angels have a nature made firm and invulnerable, they persist in malicious envy and implacable hatred. This very torment of envy, the continual rust of malice, unceasing wrath, endless sorrow, hope of pardon cut off, lick about their bitter hearts on every side like avenging flames; and there is, as it were, a furnace of Gehenna always kindled by the desire to harm.

Evil will is like perpetual blindness—that is, a capacity cut off from the divine vision. But the holy angels, cleaving to God, always stand before his countenance and contemplate his face without any veil. They drink from the fountain of life itself and eat to satiety their supersubstantial bread, in which they have been confirmed. They reign without pride, serve without a yoke, rejoice without fear, obey but not slavishly; they see the end of every perfection, but not as an ending. They contemplate the height of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God; they rest in that peace which surpasses all human understanding. And if there is some higher and more secret peace which God alone inhabits, their blessedness consists precisely in having sufficiency in their own good and not presuming to be made equal to their superior.

For this was the sin of that evil one: that the marvelous greatness of his own excellence did not suffice him, but he wished to be like the Most High, either altogether as God or at least without God’s dominion. Therefore, though he had been light in the Lord, he became darkness in himself; and by the most just judgment, he who wished to be highest became lowest; he who was above light was assigned to night; he who was above a king was handed over to prison; from free he became a slave, from angel a devil, from conspicuous obscure, from noble and glorious contemptible and dreadful. Truly light was divided from darkness, and good and evil cannot exist in the same fellowship. “There is no fellowship of Christ with Belial; there is no participation of righteousness with iniquity” (2 Cor. 6). “The bed is narrow,” says Isaiah, “so that one falls off, and the short covering cannot cover both” (Isa. 28).

Moreover, a great chasm has been fixed between good and evil angels, and it has been irrevocably decreed that a good angel can never again become a devil, nor Satan pass into a good angel. For on both sides a firm and immovable sentence has been pronounced: those who fell can no longer stand; those who stand need not fear the danger of any fall. As sin no longer falls upon the elect, so righteousness does not return to the reprobate; for as the corruption of the guilty experienced no remedy, so the glory of the saints admits no corruption.

Origen is mistaken. Introducing a Platonic doctrine into the Church, he asserts in the books *Peri Archon* that Satan will return to his former state after many ages through a certain revolution of demons into bodies, as though, after an unworthy manner of life under the oppression of this gross bodily condition had been purified, he would again be cleansed through such revolutions. He also adds some sort of passible divinity, suffering invisibly again in the air for the redemption of the guilty. While laboring to draw blood from the authorities of certain Scriptures, and proclaiming God merciful and compassionate, he proves him a liar and unjust. He is a liar if the impious person does not go with the devil and his angels into eternal fire; unjust, if he gives the same recompense to the unjust and the just. But these monsters of words and prodigies of reasoning are not Christian doctrines.

Origen passed over the letter and did not understand Isaiah, who spoke mystically in the oracle concerning Tyre—words which that man of letters attempted to force into a literal sense. “And it shall be,” says the prophet, “in that day: God will visit the wickedness of heaven on high, and the kings of the earth who are upon the earth; and they shall be gathered in the gathering of one bundle into the pit, and shall be shut there in prison, and after many days they shall be visited” (Isa. 42). This visitation is not one of pardon but of severity and justice, just as those in prisons are often visited by guards, not in order to be released, but in order that, being guarded, they may be tortured longer and more harshly.

There are other scriptural authorities which he seized, as it were, from valleys and immediately ran to with shouting. He also held and wrote that human souls had been angels and would again return into angels; that in the restoration angels and demons and all human beings—Christians, Gentiles, Catholics, and heretics alike—would be equal; that souls would again return to new bodies; that from another beginning there would again be another world; and that thus, in alternating cycles unto infinity, all things would pass away and succeed one another. He held and wrote many other impious and abominable things which it is itself a crime even to repeat.

Therefore, lest the malignant spirits cast down into these lower regions should have free and widespread intercourse with humankind, and the continual conflict of demons should become for humanity a perpetual and obstinate scandal, leaving no form of peace where tireless hostility pressed on, the reprobate party was compelled, by God’s command, to make its importunate assaults—like most bitter waves—break against itself within prescribed limits. And it was said to it: “Thus far you shall come, and here you shall break your swelling waves” (Job 28). He who had said, “I will sit on the mountain of the covenant; I will be like the Most High” (Isa. 14), now does not dare even to enter a herd of swine unless permitted (Mark 5). But, with neck bridled, he foams and rages this way and that as far as the chain’s length reaches, lapping up again what he vomited; and that malice has no strength, that madness no effect, except insofar as divine justice permits it either to test or to punish the just or the unjust.

They too, under the prince of demons, have laws of office and allotted ministries; and, insofar as the higher power—that is, the power of the holy angels—allows, they serve under their rulers, go forth, range about, stir up storms, conceal snares, set traps, and by ingenious arts attempt now violence, now deception. As deceitful counselors, they persuade and suggest whatever is impious and whatever is shameful. Yet they do nothing by power over souls, for it lies rather in those souls’ own power and will to resist them in the sign of the cross and the blood of the Lamb, and to drive the confounded and conquered foe back to Gehenna. By the very delusions through which he provokes and attacks the servants of God, he himself is struck back and dashed to pieces; and he becomes the occasion of the crown and glory of those for whom he wished to be the snare and ruin of transgression.

And even if one of the predestined has at some time wasted away, infected by his blast, armed with the weapons of repentance he rose stronger and more secure; having experienced the shamefulness of his offense, he recoiled with remarkable indignation from the enemy who suggested it and from himself who consented, and returned to the conflict more cautious and more fortified. Thus defeated and repelled, they turn back upon themselves and are tortured in the brine of their own sea—that is, by their own envy—and waste away in the pain of ineffectual malice. This is “the great and wide sea, wherein are creeping things without number,” in which that ancient dragon ranges like an enormous sea-monster, mocked there by God’s ordinance (Ps. 103).

But through the assaults made by evil angels, the divine work in man is not destroyed but tested. When temptations recede and all spiritual wickedness is gathered, as it were, within its own sea, and when the marshes of pleasures have been dried up, the fruitful earth brings forth green grass and fruit-bearing trees with such increase that, once the filth of sin has been wiped from the hearts of the elect, they advance from the verdure of faith to the height of hope and to charity’s very summit, rooted like good trees in Christ and bearing fruit according to the measure of his gift, each according to its kind.

By the name of green herbs the simple and humble may be understood; while the height of trees expresses the dignity of loftier wisdom. The tree of wisdom, the tree of knowledge, and the tree of life, which are found in this Scripture, urge us to understand these things spiritually, although we must not tear away the foundation of the letter.

The establishment of bodily or spiritual creation, visible and invisible, which is like the first day of this world, was known by intelligible reasoning when the Word of God enlightened the mind. But it was necessary that a more abundant light of understanding should kindle that same light through the more vivid teachings of truth itself, and that truth should itself declare more acute and subtle doctrines than the capacity of human talent or reason could discover on its own. Wisdom therefore made two great luminaries and placed them in the firmament; and what it had intimated in part through the Spirit, it wished to speak through itself, so that divine authority might remain for posterity, and the impiety of heretics might have no room for error, ignorance, or perversion of the truth.

The decrees of nature and law indeed agree in one; but there is greater weight where God is the teacher than where the mind is the investigator. On Mount Sinai Moses received tablets of stone written by the finger of God (Exod. 20); the holy apostles received the Word which was in the beginning with God, and was God, and that same Word became flesh and dwelt among us (John 1). The Son of the Father spoke, and preached the Gospel not on stone tablets but in a living voice, writing inwardly in hearts and crying outwardly in ears: “I am the way, the truth, and the life” (John 1).

In these two Testaments God spoke in many ways to the fathers through the prophets, but to us through himself in the Gospels (Heb. 1). Having overturned the bushel-measure of veils and set the lighted lamp of truth upon a lampstand (Matt. 6; Luke 6), he presented, as it were, the day of the united fellowship of divine and human nature in the same person. For from Adam to Moses, the natural law, free from the servitude of ceremonies, taught and governed the primitive people under a familiar command. But, as we have said, because this teaching was not fortified by an authoritative definition, it could decline or be corrupted through succession. Therefore the written law was added as the lesser luminary, in riddles and figures, requiring the worship and veneration of the one God, yet concealing the truth of things under a manifold veil of words for the training of immature minds.

Moses made the tabernacle, the table of the presentation, the ark of the covenant, the veil before the Holy of Holies, and the cherubim of glory overshadowing the mercy-seat (Exod. 25). He wrote many commands concerning the rite of circumcision, the cleansing of leprosy, the law of jealousy, the offices of priests and Levites, the anointing of the high priest, cities of refuge, violators of Sabbaths, kinds of burnt offerings, and other ordinances of the law (Lev. 24). But, as the Apostle says, that luminary of the law brought no one to perfection (Heb. 7). Like a pedagogue it instructed under fear the tender infancy of the Church in its ignorance, and forcibly restrained the wantonness of its first age, until at the time appointed by the Father the people of God, advanced in spiritual understanding, should enter within the veil (Heb. 6), into the very Holy of Holies, where no one had presumed to enter except the high priest alone (Heb. 9).

But when grace—the greater luminary—lightened the intolerable burden of the law, and Jesus expired upon the cross, those veils were torn. That privilege no longer remained only with Aaron and his sons; free entrance was granted to the whole body of believers, both to the tree of life and to the Holy of Holies. The first to enter was the high priest of future good things, not with another’s blood; and when that great price of blood had been given, the gold of the law became worthless, and the Holy of Holies came and abolished the sacrifices of the Jews.

The lesser luminary shone according to its measure when God was known only in Judaea (Ps. 75), when even only a few elect persons of that time could scarcely grasp those shadows and riddles of the commandments. When the luminary of the Gospel’s gracious light shone forth, none could hide from its heat. Those coverings of figures and wrappings of words were torn apart, and all things became clean to the clean, accessible and intelligible to all. The multitude of examples was set aside; one remained for all, containing and surpassing all things, whose fullness all that beginning had prefigured: the holy and rational burnt offering, one order, one distinction, naked truth, pure charity.

No longer is only the Levitical tribe separated for sacred mysteries, nor is the royal person chosen from the tribe of Judah alone. The one tribe of the Christian people is a holy nation, a people for possession (1 Pet. 2); and Christ, our king and priest of the royal priesthood, grants dignity to the poor. Purity of life is no longer signified but displayed. The Lamb of God is pointed out with the finger; the Messiah is no longer awaited. Emmanuel now lives among us; the Sun of righteousness shines in the Church; the King is seen in his beauty. The eternal way of the saints, found through eternal redemption, has been revealed (Heb. 9).

There is nothing necessary for human perfection that these two Testaments do not teach: evangelical simplicity explains all the mysteries of the law, and the Apostle expounds the depth of prophecy. Clearly, moreover, the great mystery of godliness was made known in this light: “He was manifested in flesh, justified in spirit, appeared to angels, preached among the nations, believed on in the world, taken up in glory” (1 Tim. 3). The stars likewise set in the firmament give their light. Explaining this, Daniel says: “Those who are learned shall shine like the brightness of the firmament; and those who instruct many unto righteousness, like stars for everlasting ages” (Dan. 12). The learned and teachers are called stars: some make progress by example, and some by word and example alike.

This Scripture divides between day and night, separating the contaminations of heretics from the purity of Catholic teaching and rooting out from the conduct of the saints whatever is unfitting to uprightness. This light separates truth from falsehood, serious matters from trifles, discord from peace, idols from Christ, and whatever is impious and obscene from purity of religion. This light leads a heart made clean and divided from love of sin, first to chastity, then to peace, and onward to the mystery of divine contemplation.

The depiction of Jerusalem upon a brick, the siege set in order through Ezekiel against the city, the iron pan raised as a wall, and the other things; the Lord’s girdle, hidden beside the Euphrates and decayed; the eyes of the living creatures; and the wings, some of which fly while others cover the head and feet of him seated upon the throne—all were set forth by Isaiah as signs of a great matter. Through the Apostle, the mystery is signified in Christ and the Church when that same Apostle disputed concerning marriage and the marriage bond. Hagar and Sarah signify two Testaments; Isaac and Ishmael, two peoples. Holy Scripture is accustomed to set many such things as signs of some reality.

The revolution and passage of times and years from one to another distinguish the changeableness of mutable things from the stability of eternity. For the desire of reason, in its fervent circuit, hastens back to its own beginning, where there are neither years nor times nor any changeable alternations, but one holy day: the consummation and fullness of the saints, a light that does not wander, God all in all, the perpetual illumination of all.

Circumcision is a sign of stripping off the flesh of sin; baptism, of burial; the work of the altar, of crucifying the flesh; visible anointing signifies a dwelling sanctified for the Holy Spirit. The temple and the days are fitting understandings of the mind, and of these and similar things. Times are the collection and concord of the new and old, just as morning intervals converge upon fixed marks and boundaries. Although present, past, and future are properly reckoned under the name of time, nevertheless summer, winter, and similar things are also called times. Adapted to the changeability of understandings, they express the varieties of things and the end and unity of diverse matters, when causes are brought back to their own beginning and parts are joined.

The same is understood more extensively through years, which include days and times; and just as years themselves extend into ages, so the Word of God, the eternal light, declares and comprehends all things through holy Scripture. Moses speaks, the Holy Spirit revealing to him, about the establishment of the world, at which he was not present temporally or bodily. Paul preaches a Gospel which he did not learn from a human being, but through the revelation of Jesus Christ (Gal. 1). He ascends into paradise and hears certain mysteries which it is not permitted for a human being to speak (2 Cor. 12). John the Apostle ascends and reaches to the eternity of the Word, and to the consubstantiality and unity of Father and Son. Isaiah and Daniel speak much concerning the end of the world and God’s judgment. By these, as by certain rungs of a ladder, every diligent student ascends and descends, possessing Scripture and time as years, advancing into certain infinite ages; for when all these things have passed away, as it is written: “Heaven and earth shall pass away, but my words shall not pass away” (Matt. 24).

We said above that the Holy Spirit was borne over the waters, so that his inspiration might give life and fertility to the origin of the creature subject to him—not resting upon it, as though for its protection, according to Mani, against some nation of darkness or other, but enclosing it beneath himself, because nothing of itself either lives well or understands soundly unless that same Spirit cherishes it. By “waters” understand the generations of human beings, who, as they flow from spring to brook and from brook to river, so men hasten and run with restless current from conception to birth and from infancy to old age. The one and same Spirit works, as he wills, diverse things from the same material for various ministries: “To one is given the word of knowledge, to another the grace of healings, to another discernment of spirits” [Col. 1527A] (1 Cor. 12).

In the field of the human mind he sows the seed of righteousness, and predestines some crops to fill the barns of the active life, others the cellars of eternity; yet in such a way that he brings the incorruptible fruits of the active life, after the necessary uses of this present life, into the heavenly storehouses. From the same clump spring wheat and barley; and in the same bosom of earth gold and silver are mined. Some things are more excellent than others, yet each is useful and necessary in its own kind. From the human race, as from the nature of waters, both creeping things and birds proceed: for some creep amid these earthly things, while others, neglecting them, dwell in heaven.

He creeps and walks with slow step whom the bondage of marriage, the rank of authority, or the anxiety of office weighs down. By occasion of an office they often render to that office [Col. 1527B] more than they ought. Yet, though they pile up wood, hay, and stubble (1 Cor. 3), they do not depart from the stability of the foundation. They use this world as though they did not use it (1 Cor. 7); they plant and build, yet do not cling to these things in their heart. Rather, with deep affections they sigh for the city of God, “of which glorious things are spoken” (Ps. 86).

Nor does the king of that city exclude from his household the simple creeping things of this world. He cleansed Rahab, like a venomous reptile, and made her harmless; and he gathered Tyre, the people of Ethiopia, and foreigners, like many creeping things, and placed them there. He himself was born in the city founded by the Most High; and he willed that the children of adoption, made co-heirs with him, should rejoice and dwell together in the same city.

But contemplative men, [Col. 1527C] leaving the nest of human intercourse, strive and press toward the heights. By narrow ways, sparing not the body, they seek where the Beloved is; they hasten through thorns and briars, with flesh made bloody; they leap over hedges and burst into the golden resting-place, where the King, reclining at table, delights in the fragrance of nard (Song 1). They are admitted to the kiss; they suck at breasts better than wine; they are drawn by the fragrance; after the ointments they run together.

Boundless activity groans and sighs in its waves; contemplation rejoices and already tastes the first-fruits of angelic peace. Man, exposed amid vipers, is bitten by temptations as by serpents, and his bare side is pierced by the spears of desires; oppressed, he cries: “Wretched man that I am! Who shall deliver me from the body of this death?” [Col. 1527D] (Rom. 7). Contemplation feels nothing of this kind. Yet exceedingly rare indeed is the mind—if any such exists—which in this world so transcends in mind that it does not at some time look back, whether those things are abolished or suppressed, toward the illusions of the flesh and the itch of its ticklings. The Apostle says that even spiritual persons can be overtaken in a fault (Gal. 6). “You, whoever are spiritual, consider yourself, lest you too be tempted” (ibid.).

Within, in the thickness of the marrow, in the heat of the heart, an unceasing fire and persistent flame burns; it is extinguished by no waters, and wherever you flee, it follows. Human weakness creeps and is unequal to a long course; and even if it flees, it does not escape. Patience alone reduces all this fire to ashes: he who resists conquers; he who endures overcomes. Weakness feels, but reason does not consent; and sensation [Col. 1528A] is not sin, but consent is. Here discernment labours; here reason keeps watch; here is mire, here the mud of dregs, this is the region of storms, in which creeping things dwell. But, as we have said, with the Holy Spirit poured around it, whoever is subject to him profits however great the storms that surround him: by exercise he advances, by motion he is cleansed, by temptation he is tested, by testing he is strengthened.

Between these two kinds of life, one of which creeps and the other flies, both the weakness and the soundness of the creature perceive—in the former what it can do by itself, in the latter what it can do through God—so that no one may glory in himself, because it is “not of him that wills nor of him that runs, but of God who shows mercy” (Rom. 9).

Having enumerated and distinguished the things born from earth and those born from waters, man follows as though the charioteer of all lower things; leading before him cattle and beasts of burden, [Col. 1528B] indicating that beastly impulses are subject to him, he is established as lord of the world. In himself, as though displaying the structure of another world, he possesses the substance of all the elements and, in some respect, the nature of all creatures. By the dignity of spirit and the understanding of a rational soul he is another angel upon earth; by fellowship of flesh and life, motion and being, he participates so fully with human beings that—not only according to what we have defined morally or allegorically, but even by the property of nature—he has a multiple kinship and affinity with the whole universe.

We may behold in man, as it were, another world: a whole in miniature, compounded of heaven and earth, having visible creation beneath him and invisible creation above him, and embracing within the narrow space of one mind the seeds of the universe [Col. 1528C]. The mind in him, like a certain badge of divinity, orders and dispenses the affections subject to it. From the heavenly nature it possesses wisdom and understanding, counsel and knowledge, steadfastness and piety, and chaste fear; under this guide it humbly glories in him from whom it is.

Whatever is spiritual in us is from there. There is the pattern to whose form a man sharpens his understanding, fashions his conduct, adapts holiness, and orders charity. According to that nature—made a little lower than the angels because of passible flesh—he knows that he will sometime be released from the diversity of his conjunction and joined again more gloriously; no longer subject to dissolution, he will be made equal to angels even in body [Col. 1528D], and will attain the summit of that glory for which he now waits through patience.

The body indeed is from the earth; and in it, if you consider carefully, you will find in the smallest parts of the body all the members of this great world. These heavy elements, earth and water, are moved while the light elements, fire and air, surround them; and the weighty material, separated one from another by the interposition and mingling of subtler things, is not oppressed. Rather, with each thing distinguished and its contributions ordered, all serve one another. Thus the discord of things brought into such great peace is altogether astonishing: fire and water dwell together in the same vessel without any dissension, so that earth is not dissolved by waters and the subtlety of air is not excluded by so great a mass.

Indeed, they embrace one another peacefully, so that here too you may marvel at the Maker [Col. 1529A], and, in the harmony of the universe and the joining of all things, perceive how praiseworthy and commendable is the good of peace. And since natures contrary and discordant among themselves agree, how great and how indissoluble a covenant ought there to be among rational creatures, whose origin is one, whose function is one, whose final arrival is one.

Consider in the human head, in the substance of the brain, certain chambers established beneath a kind of vault of heaven, the upper skull; and certain membranes, called meninges, enveloping the brain, so that, like clouds, they moisten the upper heat with vapoury waters, lest that vital motion dry up through excessive dryness. Then, as though in the firmament, the two eyes shine as great luminaries, always kindled by an inward fire. In the passages of the nostrils, the entrance and exit [Col. 1529B] of air are plainly visible. The courses of waters are carried about in the channels of the veins as through their riverbeds, in a perpetual flow; and in the stomach and bladder you see the bilge and the sea of all refuse.

The fiery heart, unless cooled by the fan of the lungs, dries up the moisture of the body. Flesh, which is like earth in man, is quickened and made fertile by the heat of the heart. The liver and spleen, the arms and muscles, the kidneys and the remaining ministering members are, as it were, metallic things in the workshop of the body; by their offices this bodily and material substance is nourished, cleansed, increased, and diminished, as the order of nature requires.

In childhood man is green like grass; in youth he blossoms like a tree; and in old age he bears fruit. In decrepit age he creeps; when he is taught, he feeds like cattle; [Col. 1529C] like a beast of burden he serves when he obeys; he flies when he returns to his origin. Thus you will find the greater world in the lesser, and there is nothing in that immense mass which is not fittingly adapted to this small one.

But when we refer many things not to matter but to morals, and, enumerating the affections of the inward man, linger longer over that part which is superior, we do not in any way abolish the history which is the foundation of Scripture, nor do we force the letter by twisting its proper meaning into another sense. From the same vine-shoot come both cluster and wine; from the same ear come both bread and grain. We do the letter no injury and no violence if we unfold the hidden mystical meanings within it. Rather, we honour the foundation when, upon it, [Col. 1529D] we build for the Lord a temple from subtle and invisible material by spiritual labour.

Certainly, without any doubt, we believe that in the beginning heaven and earth were created together, in which, as we said above, lay the elemental cause of all things that were made or are made afterward.

But as to the statement that light was made afterward, while the sun did not yet exist: if this is thought to have occurred in intervals of hours, that light can scarcely be understood literally, unless perhaps that elemental fire shone by itself in its purity. But how, once elements have been mingled in matter, their separation should again take place, human reason scarcely comprehends, since their momentary separation is the destruction of that mixture. That fire, mingled with water, earth, and air, is said to have shone before the sun [Col. 1530A] is something rational sense has not learned from experience of things; for today, without those two great luminaries, nothing but darkness can be understood among bodily things, and the absence of the sun itself is night, while its presence, conversely, is day.

Therefore, if that first light was bodily, with sun and moon removed, I should wish to be shown a like light among visible things—unless perhaps the effect was set before its cause by anticipation, and Scripture first mentions the light and then the sun, whose light it is. But if that light existed by itself and separated day from night, the distinction between darkness and light was very slight, because the light itself was slight and wholly adjacent to confusion.

I say this because the ordinary use of things and the familiar course of nature suggest that one material light was sufficient for distinguishing day and night. And, to return to the spiritual sense, the first light was that of reason and mind: knowledge of the divine will appeared in visible things, and man understood in his mind the divine counsel concerning the constitution of the world, which he afterward beheld as subject to himself through bodily light. Is it unfitting that the spirit should first be illuminated and the body afterward? Indeed, just as reason precedes and foresees every natural action, so much more fittingly, in the order of things, the inward man ought to be illuminated before the outward [Col. 1530B], so that, obliged to the Creator for both consolations, since the causes of things were open to him, he might not doubt the outcome of the eternal disposition.

There is no doubt, so far as human understanding is concerned, that spiritual, intellectual, and bodily things had a beginning. The primal establishment itself was not light to itself; but knowledge of the creature was light to the one who understood, whereas to one who did not understand it was a dark abyss. Nor is it contrary to reason or opposed to authority if we believe that the rational creature was made first and then illuminated: illumination was one thing, creation another.

The same consideration applies to the rest: to day and night, morning and evening. “Morning and evening” are used in many places as though they meant “earlier and later.” “And evening and morning were one day,” when a full knowledge of earlier and later things shines forth. Morning is the opinion or conjecture of inquiry, not yet arriving at truth, yet in the inquiry itself perceiving in part what it seeks. For if it perceived nothing, it would seek nothing. But when the account of a thing is gathered fully, and clearly [Col. 1530C] and distinctly reaches from end to end, there comes one day, the attainment of that cause in whose examination many endeavours of meditation were spent like noonday hours.

In the first, second, and third days there is diligent examination and certain knowledge of the individual things created for the use of the inward or outward man. What that first man Adam—who imposed names upon all things—understood by the Spirit’s revelation concerning herbs and trees, creeping things and birds, beasts of burden and cattle, and whereby he recognized the cause and use of all things: according to the sequence and addition of revelations, that which was first opened to him was, as it were, the first day, and that which came later the second. Again, within the revelation itself, morning was the beginning of instruction, [Col. 1531A] while evening and morning were the fullness of knowledge. He could not know names, causes, or effects of things unless divine Wisdom taught him: Wisdom both set itself before him uniquely and distinguished, delivered, and subjected to him whatever it had created bodily.

Although the visible essence of the world was made simultaneously, it could not be spoken simultaneously. The universe of things could be expressed only through human words formed in temporal intervals; and what was simple and one with God, in whom there is neither time nor space, was seen, understood, and spoken by Moses in parts, distributed according to places, species, and offices.

Indeed, that same Moses, who distinguishes the first, second, third, and remaining days with so subtle a balance, immediately after enumerating the distinctions of the days adds that there was one day on which heaven and earth and every shrub and herb were created, so that you may understand the same in the other cases: “These are the generations of heaven and earth, in the day when God made heaven and earth, and every shrub of the field and every herb of the region” (Gen. 2). See how plainly Moses says that the creation of all things was accomplished in one day, though he describes the works of six days with remarkable subtlety.

The angelic nature, which we have understood under the name of heaven, has never lacked the vision of divine truth; nor has human nature, expressed through earth, lacked rational understanding, like light dividing day from night. The firmament dividing waters from waters is the discipline, enduring from eternity, between saints and wicked persons. The gathering of waters within one shore, and the fruitfulness of earth and trees [Col. 1531C], is the obedience of creation in its own kind. The two luminaries in heaven indicate that whatever is read in either Testament is from above. The light of the firmament is understanding of the Testament. Creeping things and birds brought forth from waters signify that active and contemplative persons arise from the same mass. These things cannot at all be said simultaneously; that they exist simultaneously no one doubts.

“And God said, Let us make man in our image and likeness” (Gen. 1). Of nothing else made by God do we read anything like this. But concerning all sensible and insensible things, and all things that exist and live, it was said that they should be, and they were. The sun and moon, luminaries of great and incomparable brilliance, hold a servile place among the remaining creatures [Col. 1531D]. Man alone, made in God’s image, is honoured by this singular privilege.

And indeed we read nothing that angels were made according to this likeness. For just as Scripture left their creation to our understanding, because they are intellectual natures, so it passes over their dignity or excellence. Nevertheless, it must be believed that this image is marked in them all the more expressly inasmuch as their nature is purer and nearer to the divine majesty. All other things do not belong to the image of eternity, because, subject to vanity, they obscure their changing conditions in the restless circuit of things. Nor do they attain stability of being through these courses and motions; and they will altogether cease to be what they now are, in no way to return, after dissolution, to their bodies or to any state whatever [Col. 1532A].

Even the sun itself will rest from this labour in the renewal of the world. There will be no need for distinctions of day and night, when there will be one eternal day and the one immovable sun will be God. With every creature at rest, there will be one stability of all nature, one firmness, one health, one peace, one equality. But whether the elements will then exist—that is, heaven itself and earth—or anything besides spiritual things, belongs to the vision of a pure heart.

Yet I do not know whether the saying, “Heaven and earth shall pass away” (Matt. 24), can be referred to this judgment. The Apostle Peter, in the second Epistle called Canonical, either expounding or following the evangelical word, says (ch. 3): “The day of the Lord will come as a thief, in which the heavens shall pass away with a great rush; the elements shall be dissolved by heat; and the earth and the things in it shall be burned.” And below (ibid.): “The heavens, being on fire, shall be dissolved, and the elements shall melt with the burning heat of fire. But we await new heavens and a new earth, according to his promises, in which righteousness dwells.”

No question remains concerning the abolition of the old world, so plainly has it been foretold by the prince of the Church. But what kind of thing that new heaven and new earth will be, or whether heavenly or earthly regions are again to be filled with new creatures, has been altogether passed over. But because righteousness is said to dwell in that renewal, it may be understood that in that restoration everything will be of another and far purer nature [Col. 1532C], and whatever is now either corruptible or corrupted will be purified in that regeneration; henceforth the whole will be a pure dwelling-place of pure holiness.

How much more will man, conformed to the body of God’s glory, possess no burden and no necessity in the body—which will indeed be spiritual, yet still a body. So too the dwelling of rational creatures will be paradise, certainly, yet a habitation. For whether those glorified bodies are in that new heaven or in that new earth, although they are moved according to angelic nature and glory, they will not be deprived of the reality of a body. Rather, as it is written: “The saints shall possess double things in their land” (Isa. 61).

Paradise—that is, that pleasantness, rest, peace, tranquillity, and all the other goods which eye has not yet seen nor have ascended into the heart of man [Col. 1532D] (Isa. 64; 1 Cor. 2)—will be the understanding and vision of God. For man will see and hear, and whatever God is will ascend into the heart of man. There will no longer be any concern or question about bodily places, smells, or tastes, because, as we have said, even if there is then some local delight, it will certainly be spiritual, not carnal.

Man, created in God’s image and then having nothing similar or common with unreasoning beasts, will understand his honour; in the image in which he was created he will behold himself, marvel, and have his heart enlarged. Clinging to that blessedness and fixed in divine visions, he will delight so greatly [Col. 1533A] in the abundance of its sweetness and glory in that fullness that he will neither desire nor seek the waters of springs, the shade of trees, or the fruits in their reality which that ancient and bodily paradise possessed. For God will be for him an unfailing spring, refreshing shade, tree of life, perpetual fruit, and infinite fullness.

In the present life, the outward senses wandering through visible things gather themselves less into unity, and the dignity of that image is less understood, because reason, poured outward through many channels and occupied, is distracted. Image is one thing; that of which it is the image another; likeness another. Likeness may be referred to some part, while image represents the integrity of substance. The Son is called the image of the Father, “the brightness of his glory and the figure of his substance” (Heb. 1), and his form, because there is no diversity and no distance between Father and Son, save that the Father is not the Son and the Son is not the Father.

Therefore in the Word, which is also the Wisdom of the Father, exists all the fullness of Divinity. The Son himself is called the image or figure of the substance because eternal Divinity has been revealed to us through the Word or Wisdom, just as the property of any thing is represented and made known to us through an image when it has been properly portrayed. When I look at myself in a mirror or in a most pure spring, I do not see myself; rather, my image displays to me all my bearing and gesture and, so far as the face can indicate it, the very affection of the mind. There you may see [Col. 1533C] whether I am pale or coloured, and clearly understand whether I appear troubled or calm.

The Son is therefore called the image because in him we understand the Father, and through him we have access to God. For the Word and eternal Wisdom, illuminating us, opens in the understanding of itself the understanding of its Father also, because “he who sees the Son sees the Father,” since Father and Son are one. Thus man was made in the image of God—that is, according to understanding and knowledge of the Son, through whom is understood and known that fatherhood which is named in heaven and on earth. With the fullness of that light expressed in the human mind, with conformity to that Wisdom, with communion in that glory, man shares in God’s righteousness; he is a participant in goodness [Col. 1533D], heir of eternity, companion of reason. In the desire for peace, the understanding of truth, and the love of charity, he represents that image—not aspiring to the likeness for which he who said, “I will be like the Most High” (Isa. 14), panted, but to that likeness of which it is written: “We are sons of God, but it has not yet appeared what we shall be; when he appears, we shall be like him” (1 John 3).

We bear the image of the heavenly one when Christ is formed in us, when in our conduct and life the nobility of that race becomes known. For just as the outward countenance presents evidence of paternal nobility, and the beauty or deformity of the parent is transmitted there, so that even from the face you may know whether a son is legitimate or adulterine, so in conduct it is most evident, if features of truth and righteousness, imitating the divine pattern at the sight of which every beauty and excellence is portrayed, have expressed that heavenly form: such a person is God’s Son and heir, whom you may judge not degenerate from paternal goodness [Col. 1534A].

This image is in the soul, not in the flesh; this honour belongs not to the body but to the spirit. The heresy of the Anthropomorphites is rejected: it falsely asserts that God has a body, measures divine likeness by bodily shape, and calls the image of God visible limbs subject to spatial limitation. The defenders of this madness did not understand that God is spirit, and that flesh and blood avail nothing for understanding the divine essence.

Insofar as man is male, he was made in the image of God; insofar as he is woman, in the likeness: “Male and female,” he says, “he made them” (Gen. 1). According to a more intense fullness of spirit, man; according to a more relaxed desire for contemplation, woman; according to perfection, neither male nor female, but, in newness of life, a creature whole and perfect.

Thus dominion over all things in earth and waters was given to man. Everything subject to him reveres in him a heavenly origin and, according to its purpose, obeys the Creator, paying him reverence not on account of a community of nature but on account of the prerogative of grace. We often see rebellious animals, tame and untamed, rise against man. But nothing causes this insolence of audacity and dissension except that man himself does not obey the Creator in his own order. He received, not by merit but by grace, that irrational creation should be moved at his will and governed by his command [Col. 1534C].

It is altogether just that one who dissents should be pressed on every side by every kind of hardship, and that against one who preferred his own will to the Creator’s will rebellion should grow from every quarter among all his kindred things; that outside him every creature’s persecution should blaze against him; that flesh should contend against spirit and spirit against flesh; and that to one unwilling to be subject to his superior, no subjection should be rendered by inferiors.

Great is the dignity of man: God his maker, an angel his companion, the world his servant, paradise his realm! There, amid dense, shady trees and darkening groves, among fragrant herbs [Col. 1534D] and aromatic grasses, in green meadows and the living outflows of that cardinal spring, he is placed among fruits delightful both to see and to use. In his very nakedness he shows that, just as no duplicity enshrouds innocence and simplicity, so confusion always covers what is feigned in the mind and malice surrounds it.

Before the transgression of sin no shame sought a covering; the flesh suggested nothing shameful; there was nothing to be hidden. Nakedness was not foul in the Lord’s eyes, nor was anything shameful where no impurity existed. Though everything else was laid open to him, he is commanded to refrain from one tree. With the law of obedience imposed and left to his own choice, he is tested in a small matter, though, if he stood firm in the command, he would immediately receive greater things.

But because we have resolved to write what we think about the works of the six days, and have in some measure done this with God as author, it will be the work of another labour to write what, according to the measure of the gift we have received, seems to our smallness concerning paradise, that spring, the tree of knowledge of good and evil and the tree of life, the serpent, the transgression, and the sentence pronounced upon serpent, man, and woman [Col. 1535A].

Man was made outside paradise and then brought into paradise, lest any grace should seem lacking; there it is later recalled that woman was made from his side. For the pleasantness of that place befitted man made in God’s image. Although no calamity could oppress the innocent man wherever he might be, still, in accordance with the outward senses, a collection of every delight was provided and crowded together in one place, lest, if anything were lacking there, his desire should be wearied by seeking or awaiting something distant. Rather, he should rejoice in the presence and use of all things.

If he stood firm, he would possess in the Creator the fullness of truth and peace for rational understanding, and the vision of that one goodness would fill his entire mind. In the same manner the outward man would have subject to his senses whatever sweet and pleasant things could delight human nature, so that God would be for man the sum of all spiritual joys and paradise the sufficiency of all temporal consolations. Hence that place was also called Eden, that is, “delight,” and a garden of pleasures because of the richness of its soil and its fruitful groves.

From the middle flowed a glassy spring, watering and moistening every blade of grass from its root; yet it did not overflow excessively, but by underground escape soaked the entire surface of that garden [Col. 1535C]. Broad foliage on tall trees shaded the grass below, while lower moisture and upper mildness sustained perpetual green in the turf. A breeze came at the midday hours, if there happened to be any heat to drive away and repel. The place was wholly ignorant of snow and hail, delightful in the unvarying temperateness of perpetual spring.

There was an aromatic sprinkling from the fruits and shrubs themselves, and perfumed oils burst forth from the very trunks. Storax dripped, and balsam liquid, as its bark burst, abundantly soaked the ground beyond its hard crust. Spicy nard ointments flowed through the meadows, and, with gums dripping without the violence of any blow, that whole region was everywhere suffused with innumerable fragrances [Col. 1535D]. Nothing there was sad, nothing corrupt, that could impede the rest, because all the plants of that garden exhaled the power of their planter and proclaimed the grace of heavenly glory.

The trees sweated richness; the charity of the saints was to emit purity; and in the fragrance of that sweetness were made known both the excellence of preaching and the intoxication of eternal blessedness. That fragrance, soothing the bodily senses, was like a kind of ecstasy; yet it did not put them to sleep or call man back from his due offices, but sharpened and purified the mind for whatever work and study.

Stacte and myrrh, amomum and spikenard, and medicinal seeds, falling of themselves, enriched the fertile clods [Col. 1536A].
