Though nature had no need, it was nevertheless aided by more abundant grace. There was no fever, yet there was already an antidote; no failure of nature as yet, yet remedies for sickness were already springing up.

Man worked, not building something new by laborious exertion, but by delightful cultivation either clearing something, or providing shade, or adapting certain enclosures and shelters for animals, lest, wandering everywhere, they should trample with heedless steps especially those places to which the dignity of perfumes demanded reverence. These and other such things a diligent cultivator could do without weariness or inconvenience; and, cooperating greatly in his gladness, they delighted him with their refined labour.

He guarded the garden inwardly, not fearing that anything would be stolen from him, but preserving with provident care, for the posterity to come, things entrusted and subjected to him by God, rejoicing in the obedience of all things. He also guarded it for himself, lest he admit anything through which he might deserve to be expelled from it. Would that he had watched over the plants of his own soul and the grasses of virtue with the diligence he ought, doing what was useful and preserving what had been given, learning from the obedience of lower things how great a subjection he owed to the Creator! Had he persevered in that command and kept what had been commanded, what was still uncertain would soon have been made firm, and from the delightful beauty of this bodily paradise he would have been carried into that spiritual tranquillity whose peace surpasses all understanding [Col. 1536B] (Phil. 4).

Concerning the blessedness of that paradise, according to the narrowness of our understanding and the measure of the gift, comparing spiritual things with spiritual, we shall briefly treat certain matters in what follows. But now, comparing sensible things with sensible, and proceeding outside the limit of the teachers, we have undertaken to speak of the bodily paradise. Something has indeed been said concerning the fragrances of that garden; other matters pertaining to the remaining senses still await treatment.

There were there fruit-bearing trees that ministered to taste and sight: beautiful to behold, pleasant to smell, delightful in every respect. Each, according to its kind, was assigned its proper powers—not merely to satisfy the appetite of the flesh, but also to preserve the human nature in its unimpaired state. [Col. 1536D] Desire could seek nothing outside or beyond what lay before the eyes and hands. Everything which not necessity, I say, but pleasure required, was at hand. Nor was any pleasure inflamed by a passion of longing, nor was there the heat of wanton licence; rather, amid overflowing abundance there was a temperate sufficiency and a most tranquil satiety. The glory of the trees was one thing, that of their fruits another; and there was nothing useless, nothing superfluous there, where trunk supplied richness, foliage shade, and fruit nourishment. Gum relieved weakness, shade heat, food want.

Those delights indeed belonged to the outward realm, not beyond our experience; yet we measure the unfamiliar from what is familiar. I myself have seen trees whose leaves or fruits winter does not [Col. 1537A] scorch, and fruits on a citron or pine-tree which remain unwithered for five or six years. Why then, in that place where neither winter’s severity nor any unseasonableness enters, but the fixed newness of continual spring remains—where, in harmony with the season itself, all things are in growth, and whatever lives brings forth from the nature and principle of fruitful matter—should we not speak of incorruptible trees, unfailing fruits, and the most efficacious effects of those tastes and scents, satisfying to fullness every appetite of taste, smell, and sight? What was lacking from that table, that singular banquet, where the eye was filled with beauty, taste with sweetness, and smell with fragrant breath?

There was also, to complete those delights, that spring, possessing amid the neighbouring and inward-growing grasses an agreeable power of refreshing and moistening the inner heat. [Col. 1537B] It tempered and cleansed the bodily veins, through which it flowed down as though through certain mounds, irrigating, as it were, another paradise and making fruitful, each in its own kind, the individual members assigned their proper functions. Hyacinth-blue and emerald-green flowers encircled the lips of the spring, while purple crusts formed suitable seats upon swelling clods, lest an unsupported position burden the necks or shoulders of those reclining. Beds fragrant with dill and saffron were spread upon the ground like carpets; nor did the biting gnat settle upon bare limbs. If that species existed there, it was harmless, and did not disturb the delights of that repose with its piercing darts.

Indeed, in these smallest and most contemptible winged creatures, after sin there is a marvellous and exceedingly sharp importunity of power: with an almost invisible and altogether frail sting they penetrate even the thickest hides of cattle and, as though a sponge were applied to a wound, drink up and drain whatever moisture or blood is within. Before sin, however, because there was no fault, neither could any troublesome affliction be a punishment inflicted by lower creatures, where the humble obedience of human reason rendered pure service to its superior. [Col. 1537C] I might seem excessive if I did not describe pleasure; yet whatever can be said falls short of those delights. For senses delirious and foolish, infected by the stain of sin, cannot at all be matched with those unspoiled and virginal senses which pure nature employed; and the abundant fullness of that most pure delight surpasses every experience of this corruption.

And lest melody be lacking to caress the hearing, on high among the branches of cedars or other trees the long-lived phoenix sang psalms, as did the parrot; and from the manifold sound of birds singing together there arose one harmony. Their joyous whole praised its Creator in its own measure, rejoicing with shouts before the Creator, delighting humanity and stirring its natural organs—and the instruments of original music established by God—to soothe it. The groaning of the turtledove and dove prefigured the sighs of this present age. Each of the other birds sang beforehand, like an oracle, of the condition of the present or future Church, expressing joy or some other affection according to the manner and nature of its kind.

Yet nothing sad, nothing mournful [Col. 1538A] was there, where the diversity of singing creatures did not produce discord. Whether their jubilant modulations were sent forth through narrow or broad pipes of throats, the rise and fall of their voices, through differences harmoniously converging, returned to the harmony of a single note. Pipe, sambuca, and the other instruments imitating nature, which delight the hearers of this age greatly, differ from the living and clear voices of that monochord as much as anything copied from another source differs from its exemplar. There is altogether less grace in hoarse bellows, joined reeds, or hollow lyres devised by human ingenuity than in those living instruments prescribed by nature, the artist.

Such flute-players kept watch at the table of the first-formed man; such cithara-players belonged to that original antiquity. Yet this was bodily consolation, not predestined blessedness. In paradise there was neither mime nor actor. Everything sported simply with everything else; no pretence of persons enacted comic scenes by deceitful illusions. Injured sensuality did not soften unrestrained souls into wantonness, nor did an extraordinary itch of carnal desire overstep its lawful bounds, but kept itself within the commandment. Voluntary motion restrained within fixed bounds and definite rules the form of all things delineated by the Creator; it rested, and, abundant in rational sufficiency, did not waste away in the fever of boundless intemperance.

For every intemperate use is a foul and shameful misuse; and whatever is not fulfilled, and does not employ fixed weights, measures, and numbers—as far as experience of things allows—makes one miserable. [Col. 1538C] Therefore, in a mind unbridled and dissolute, the appetite and use of pleasures rush into torment, because the violence and gluttony of intemperance are not soothed by fuel laid beneath them, but inflamed. Before transgression, man did not use those bodily delights so as, wandering aimlessly, to plunge himself into the dregs of the abyss. Rather, considering all things with decent and modest approach, he honoured the dignity of rational governance and ruled his affections with discriminating moderation, not tyrannical repression.

In those matters which we have touched upon summarily and in part, sight, hearing, smell, taste, and touch, persevering in the integrity of their virginity, had lamps alight without any dregs of curiosity; and with pure service the wakeful companies of all the senses went out with their lights to meet the Bridegroom who was coming. [Col. 1538D] Concerning those trees which God had planted in that garden, besides what we have said, much remains to be understood spiritually. For, through a certain proximity, bodily and spiritual goods were joined so closely that they almost became one; nevertheless, they must be assigned separately and properly according to their distinctions: visible things to the body, invisible things to the mind.

Yet of all the trees of paradise, the book of Genesis mentions two: the tree of life and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. Although there is no doubt that many others stood in that densest forest—for we read also of a tree of wisdom [Col. 1539A]—we do not in the least doubt that other trees too bore names of virtues according to their respective powers. We do not presume to uproot the material planting of that bodily paradise; rather, in the visible colony we gather spiritual fruit, taking from the olives both fruit and oil. We have experienced that gems which roll among the pebbles of that cardinal spring and reach us borne along by the flow of rivers possess very great power. Thus also, in trees whose scent and taste exceed the accustomed experience of our senses, who could doubt that there was inherent a singular grace or remedies for diverse conditions? Thus the tree of life might restrain the disease of old age, the tree of temperance extinguish the burning of gluttony, and likewise the tree of chastity was beyond doubt there: its power could so moderate nature that the generative members of the body were no more moved toward intercourse than the other members, each of which performs its appointed functions by ordered movements without any itching stimulus.

Even now camphor works this quite effectively in such weakness, when the powers of causes are already aging and drying up; often smelt or taken in, it dries up the receptacles of semen and contracts, as if frozen, the instruments of that activity. Many seeds and roots, now almost spent, do this. How much more, when the world was flourishing and in paradise, when all things glowed with the newness and purity of their primitive sap, would there have been available—not merely one particular herb—but seed or fruit, in service of the human being for whose sake these things were made, [Col. 1539C] so that, some according to this and others according to another cause, they might offer their lord and cultivator a draught of health and incorruptibility?

And if Solomon discoursed from the hyssop growing on the wall to the cedar of Lebanon, and if so many investigators of nature have been able, by conjecture or experience, to attain instruction in a matter so profound, could Adam, who belonged to God, have been ignorant of this? By God’s image and likeness he had this grace: that he understood the principle of every creature subjected to him. Certainly that firstborn of all bodily beings knew their temporal changes, their causes, motions, essences, and effects—of all things which elemental origin produced sensibly and visibly, and material substance nourished.

But since knowledge of good and evil is an affection of the mind, and knowing good or evil belongs not to the body but uniquely and properly to the soul, the thing itself seems to concern the property of its nature and essence; but the name of the thing—that is, “knowledge of good and evil”—belongs to spiritual sense and mystical understanding. [Col. 1539D] Far be it from Catholic faith that the eternal power and Godhead should be the creator of any evil! Let the madness of the Manichaeans be utterly rejected, which introduces a nation of darkness rebellious against God and I know not what diverse first principles. Let the Paterniani be far removed, who assert that the secret and shameful parts of the body were made by the devil rather than by God. Let the impiety of Menander and the heresy of Patricius be excluded from Christian understanding: Menander, a disciple of Simon Magus, declares that the world was made by angels and not by God; [Col. 1540A] Patricius lies in saying that the entire substance of human flesh is the devil’s creation.

Neither Mambres nor Jamnes created the serpents which Moses’ serpent swallowed before Pharaoh. Rather, through devilish magical arts, their rods—which were certainly God’s creatures—were turned into dragons, just as decaying flesh turns into worms or, when burned, into ashes. Who would deny that bodily substances are mutable, when you see maggots spring from your own flesh, moths from a garment, and flies or fleas emerge from sweat or any sort of decay? The rapid result obtained by the magicians, and the sudden conversion of rods into serpents, are to some an object of astonishment and amazement. Yet there is nothing strange in any thing that can happen, whether it happens slowly or quickly, since even the abilities of some people accomplish with all speed what the more unskilled and slower scarcely accomplish in a long time. [Col. 1540B] How much more can that devilish subtlety, which has known from ancient times the effects and causes of things, bring into public view nature’s hidden power whenever something must be brought about from a hidden thing, whereby it may deceive dull human senses and turn them from the truth, so that they serve the creature rather than the Creator, who is blessed for ever?

A creature can indeed be established only by God alone, who created nothing evil but each thing good, and all things very good (Gen. I). Moses’ serpent was a real serpent: when it pleased the Creator, he both fashioned it from a rod into a snake and commanded it again to return into a rod [Col. 1540C] (Exod. IV). Moses was neither author nor creator, but he was the minister of that miracle. Likewise, the dove which appeared over the Lord when he was baptized was a real dove; and, once the dispensation for which it had been brought forth to serve that purpose was completed, it immediately returned to the natural form from which it had been assumed (Matt. III; Luke III). Likewise, the three angels whose feet Abraham washed, whom we also read to have eaten of the loaves prepared by Sarah and of the calf cooked by Abraham himself (Gen. XVIII), appeared not in phantom but in real bodies. When their task was done, their assumption of those bodies did not vanish but returned into itself.

This manner of understanding must be observed whenever God spoke by words or visible signs, whether to Adam in paradise or to the prophets: you should know that wherever there is a voice, there is also a body. Yet whenever God spoke through the ministry of a bodily creature, do not suppose that the Word was incarnate. Rather, as we have said, that bodily and personal assumption was for a dispensation and a passing function, not an essential union of natures. [Col. 1540D]

We have wandered far afield on the occasion of heretics who make God the maker of some evil, or establish some other creator of evil, in order to squeeze from the authority of the holy Scriptures another principle, another artificer or creator. The tree of the knowledge of good and evil was not evil in its nature, nor was its fruit harmful either before the prohibition or afterwards. It was so named because in that prohibition there was set a test of obedience, [Col. 1541A] whose observance was good and whose transgression was evil.

Before sin, man did not possess knowledge of evil—that is, he did not know how great an evil it was not to obey God—but his own shame and the punishment of sin taught him what sin was. For if punishment did not follow transgression, and the reward of justice and injustice were the same, there would be no reason for God to be feared or loved. There would be no cause whatever for fear if disobedience were not punished; no ground for love unless fuller grace were rendered to those who love. Adam knew that God’s command must not be violated, but, having not experienced anger or judgment, he imagined indulgence easy, because he had not yet known severity or punishment.

It was altogether necessary that the strictness of discipline should begin there at once in the first parents, [Col. 1541B] lest easy pardon raise Adam’s children—the human race—to contempt for God, and lest a transgressing creature which dishonoured God become not a glory but an insult to its Creator. From the devil’s sin, whose casting down he did not fail to know, man could have considered the strictness of the Judge and, from that irrevocable sentence which excluded the evil one from hope of mercy, have feared a like judgment. It is the mark of a mad brain and a delirious mind to promise yourself pardon where you provoke wrath, to hope for mercy at the very moment when grace is despised and justice trampled underfoot. Whatever bond or compact of human association may exist, everything bound by custom or nature must be broken rather than God be offended. This is not Christian devotion which, once the authority of divine obedience has been despised, inclines us toward carnal affections.

For the grace and embraces of marriage, a man leaves father and mother, and the two are one flesh; yet God too must not be abandoned. By a spiritual marriage he makes the entire body of the Church, compacted in the unity of faith and charity, one body and spirit out of marriage, continence, and celibacy; he ordains for himself nuptials now in hope, but in his kingdom in truth itself. [Col. 1541C]

Adam’s own eye scandalized him—that is, his wife’s persuasion. It would have been more beneficial for him to pluck it out and cast it from himself than, yielding weakly to feminine blandishments, to accept those deadly counsels. Nor had he forgotten the command or the penalty with which God had threatened him should he transgress; but, presuming upon God’s mercy in some unknown hope, he weighed the smallness, not the gravity, of the command. He did not altogether fear a death which he had not encountered; perhaps he did not think he would be deprived of other goods, because the judgment of that prohibition and threat did not set out the sequence of calamity that would follow.

He ate the forbidden fruit, and that tree became an occasion of knowing good and evil—whence the tree itself received its name even before man touched it—not because knowledge of good or evil was in the tree’s nature, but because, in transgressing the command concerning the tree, experience of both would ensue. Immediately man felt what he had not felt before: he felt the evil of concupiscence [Col. 1542A] and the itch of rebellious members; shameful, involuntary appetites and motions of the flesh. He learned how great the difference was between the liberty and peace of flesh and spirit in which he had been, and their conflict and tantalizing stings, under whose piercing and pressing the dying, fermenting limbs made the languishing soul sweat.

Because of his own folly he was far from health; miserable and bent low, he bewailed the rotten and corrupt scars—the deceptive impulses of his loins—and ran to the leaves, himself now like a leaf carried by the wind, and made girdles of woven leaves. He hid the enormous flesh and covered, both he and the woman, the foul workshops of defilement, terrible to behold, while the coals of lust burned within. Though they were the same members as before, they were not shameful, [Col. 1542B] because there was nothing dishonourable in the body. All members had, in their proper order, fitting dignity, venerable appearance, rational use, and appropriate modesty. Everything was within measure; nothing was against the will; there was no conflicting law. Everything, peaceful and at rest, honoured both the Creator himself and created nature itself.

Truly, as the serpent foretold, their eyes were opened so that they might know the misery of their own shame—not so that they might attain the glory of that presumption by which they desired to be gods. They saw themselves and blushed; judging themselves unworthy of divine sight, they hid themselves fearfully in certain recesses—not as though they could hide from or escape the Judge, but as defendants already assigned to the millstone in the prison-house of their own conscience. [Col. 1542C] This alone was true in all that devilish persuasion: their eyes were opened, not to what he promised, but rather to perceive what the lying tempter intended, who begrudged them, as it were, a successor, with parricidal hatred.

Here the saying of that philosopher is aptly applied: “He harms most treacherously,” he says, “to whom thanks are offered for an injury.” In every other respect and in all that he promised, he was a liar and most deserving of detestation. At that word by which he asserted that they would by no means die but would become like gods, he ought immediately to have been recognized and rejected by reason’s indignation. But that promise found easy entry into the woman’s heart, since she was already seeking her own power, having shaken from her neck the dominion of the Creator. [Col. 1542D] If proud presumption had already entered her mind, she is convicted first as guilty of pride rather than disobedience.

Some interpreters have thought this; but, according to my own limited capacity, I understand this passage in such a way that I comprise pride and disobedience in the same instant, and I do not prejudge that Eve languished in the evil of exaltation before tasting the fruit. Truly, whoever offends in one point is guilty of all; and where charity, the mother of virtues, is wounded, the whole body of good things withers as though its root were cut away. The seven evil spirits dwell together, and it is not easy to tear one away from another; perhaps it is one and the same spirit which, according to many, is called by different names according to the effects of wickedness.

The Holy Spirit too is called sevenfold, though he is only one: where chaste fear is, there is piety; piety cannot lack knowledge; where knowledge is, counsel is not lacking; and constancy and fortitude accompany counsel. Thus the wisdom of God, which is the Word of the Father, is understood and loved where humility produces gentleness, gentleness compunction, compunction fervour, fervour kindness, kindness purity, and purity peace. [Col. 1543A] You see in the Prophet all impieties and injustices at once forgiven to those who repent; but from those who are negligent and return to their vomit, even what has been forgiven is demanded again. Every proud person is consequently envious, because whoever seeks his own excellence is always a detractor from another’s happiness. Thus prudence, which is good, does not exist without temperance; and whoever is intemperate can boast neither of fortitude nor of justice.

The virtues are one body, which neither schism nor heresy should divide; and the whole array of graces springs from the root of charity. Pride is the foundation and origin of all wickedness; and although it gives birth to the whole crowd of vices, its offspring are so united and coessential within it that it accomplishes absolutely nothing without its progeny and can never be found alone. The woman grew proud, and in that same moment was disobedient. This sequence of disobedience is not to be evaluated temporally, since the connection and origin of both are one and indivisible.

Bastard shoots sometimes rise together in interwoven bunches from a luxuriant root, so that you can distinguish the twigs by number but cannot perceive the principle of their growth. [Col. 1543C] The vine and its branch have one flavour; flesh and body one colour; wood and bark one scent. All human members, though their action is highly varied and manifold, nevertheless have one origin and an undivided creation. One poison produces different afflictions; the same diffusion which produces frenzy produces apoplexy. You may see some suddenly struck down and die from the same corruption, while others languish for a long time.

Two things were promised the woman: immortality and divinity. Neither resulted; instead, the condition of beasts and that of humans were pronounced under the comparison and condemnation of a single likeness. Behold Adam, into whose face God had breathed: God thereby purified and made fruitful, as it were, all the senses whose seat and domestic throne are there. Yet with bestial irrationality Adam repressed eyes, ears, and the other senses to lower things; turning the divine understanding away from spiritual things, he obeyed as a debased servant the lower members, the animal of the belly. Flesh, stripped of virtues, felt heat and cold; the emptied spirit felt corruptions and stenches; empty glory felt miseries and pains. [Col. 1543D]

Thus that same serpent dared in another paradise—not of delights, but of abstinence—to attack the Saviour, persuading him to make bread from stones, to cast himself down from the pinnacle of the temple, and, with senseless madness, to fall down and worship the devil (Matt. IV). But Christ, who did not regard equality with God as a thing to be grasped (Phil. II), while he was in the form of a servant until the time fixed by the Father and, though God of all, did not exceed the bounds of servitude, taught that the life of the soul must be preferred to the life of the body, and that neither the glory nor the power of this world is to be sought. [Col. 1544A] By his own example, the most gentle teacher showed how easily Satan can be repelled if patience is put forward.

At the first hiss the first man languished. Of him, after his sin and wholly just condemnation, God speaks as if mocking and reproaching: “Behold, Adam has become like one of us, knowing good and evil” (Gen. III). This figure in the Holy Scriptures is called irony, when figurative speech assumes the voice either of one reproaching or one indignant. Thus the Apostle, viewing as though already present what would come to pass after bodies had been made firm in the resurrection and the stings of flesh stilled, cried in reproach against death: “Where is your victory? Where, O death, is your sting?” (1 Cor. XV). [Col. 1544B] The Apostle mocked death, which gloried as though victorious because the Saviour had been killed and laid in the tomb. Since death itself will be destroyed in the general resurrection, he rejoiced in that victory and insulted the overthrow of death.

Likewise, through this figure, the holy city Jerusalem, once it had conspired in the Lord’s death, is invectively called through Isaiah “the valley of vision” (Isa. XXII). Holy Scripture employs this manner of speech in many places. Thus the Lord says of Adam: “Behold, Adam has become like one of us, knowing good and evil.” The honour of eternity and omnipotence is referred to the Father; the glory of wisdom and inheritance to the Son; the distinction of goodness to the Holy Spirit. According to these distinctions, the uncorrupted state of human nature expressed the likeness of the Trinity. [Col. 1544C]

But now, knowing evil by action—which he could have avoided by reason—he was deprived of eternity and power, inheritance and wisdom, goodness and justice. He was cast far from the tree of life, until by worthy satisfaction he expiated what he had committed and purged, by the repentance of true humility, the crime of disobedience and the evil of pride. It is as though God said: “Adam wished to be like God; let him learn from punishment and misery what such great presumption deserves. Let him experience exclusion from the pleasantness of this place, and learn how great is the distance between good and evil.”

I cannot sufficiently marvel that the human mind was so quickly bent toward the deceit of that temptation and the words of falsehood. [Col. 1544D] Man knew that among animals and creeping things none shared reason with him. He knew the natures of all, since he had assigned them their proper names. For God had brought before Adam every kind of living thing, thereby showing him that every irrational creature was subject to him and was presented as his domestic possession, so that he, the higher and more worthy being, might see the multitude of that kind beneath him harmoniously obeying him at God’s command, and might call them, as his own servants, by name, knowing the use of all.

For to know and call by name means to understand the proper offices and dispositions of each. They bellowed, roared, or neighed according to their kind and, according to the properties of their nature, gave signs, sounds, or motions by which their dispositions could be understood; speech belonged to the human being alone. [Col. 1545A] If God at any time spoke with a human voice, it was not man’s concern to investigate curiously how he spoke, since he did not doubt that the speaker was God and that he could speak as he pleased. He who gave speech to man could, whenever he wished, take and form what was his own in any body.

But now the serpent, speaking contrary to nature and blaspheming God, was certainly not from God; rather, as an enemy of God and an inventor of idolatry, he was already teaching that there would be many gods and sowing the error by which the one true divinity would be unknown amid a multitude of false deities. Did the woman recognize Satan’s presence? Perhaps she thought him truthful because she heard what she wished to hear. For we are accustomed to believe quickly when counsel is given us which accords with our desire.

But if Adam or Eve knew that it was the devil personally present in their ears, and, despising God, surrendered themselves in agreement to his most ruinous counsels, I understand here not only the crime of disobedience but also, with faith renounced, idolatry. For idolatry occurs when someone makes either himself a god, or anyone else, in place of the one God. As for the serpent, there could be no doubt that it was not uttering those words by its own nature. Among all God’s creatures there was none endowed with reason and possessing knowledge or power to persuade, advise, or reason, apart from angels and human beings alone.

It is therefore certain that the woman was not ignorant that the devil was truly speaking to her in the serpent. [Col. 1545C] But, overcome by the desire of independent power, because she wished to exist without God’s rule, she gladly listened to him who spoke against God and according to his own will. The names of man and woman are sometimes used indiscriminately because of the unity of the body and the likeness of the sin. Adam nevertheless heard those words not from the devil but from the woman, and neither resisted nor contradicted them. Even if perhaps he did not believe what the devil or woman advised, he nevertheless joined himself, by impious daring, to that action.

Some have thought that the serpent conveyed that transgression to the human being not by speech but by some sign; but this opinion requires an interpretation different from the event itself. Others deny that the devil was in paradise except in the manner in which he sends fires into the wandering and unstable motions of temptations. He is therefore said to kindle or agitate them because, since all reprobate persons are his body and he himself their head, their action cannot differ when their will is the same. This work is nothing other than agreement and unity in wickedness: through this communion, what we do badly is said to be done by him, and what he does we accomplish through assent. Thus, in Christ’s death, what the devil, Judas, the Jews, and Pilate did was done reciprocally and simultaneously by all. Before the Gospel relates that the devil entered Judas’s heart, it is written that Judas was a thief and kept the money-box (John XII). [Col. 1545D]

Accordingly, concerning this union of the evil person and the demon, it is written: “When the ungodly person curses the devil, he curses his own soul” (Ecclus. XXI). There is no incongruity, however, if the devil entered paradise with God’s permission, since in Job he is read to have stood among the sons of God (Job I); and in the Book of Kings, while the army of holy angels stood around, a lying spirit offered his service to deceive Ahab sitting upon the throne of his seduction (3 Kings II). Some also, according to allegorical rules, understand by the serpent pleasure, by the woman sensation, and by the man the mind: when pleasure has moved sensation and the mind, yielding to carnal sensation, has received the taste of pleasure, a human being is driven out from the glory of paradise—that is, from every quiet and peace of a good conscience. Nor is return to the tree of life thereafter open to him unless, through the mercy of God, [Col. 1546B] the cherub, which is the fullness of knowledge, bring the foolish sinner back to wisdom, setting his heart aflame to repentance, through which the sentence of punishment is customarily reversed and changed, and those appointed to death can return to the tree of life.

Something should now be said concerning the sentence of expulsion and curse; but first a few points must be touched upon concerning the spring and the rivers that proceed from it, lest we seem to have evaded a matter of so great a mystery. This does not mean that we have undertaken to expound every event concerning Adam down to Abel and Cain; rather, the arguments so closely adhere around the topics we have proposed that the very matters we wish to discuss invite, like kinsmen among a multitude of guests, related interpretations to the table of our discourse and compel them to enter.

[Col. 1546C] Man was not expelled from the place of delight immediately after his transgression; but, conscious of his crime, the pleasures of Paradise gave him no comfort. For all our glory lies not in a place but in the mind, since it is not a place that makes one happy, but one’s life. Whatever had previously delighted the soul subject to God was turned into torment for the transgressor: both because he knew that he would soon lose it, and that what he had possessed while standing could not remain with him when he had fallen; and because whatever abundance of temporal things may come without God does not fill its possessor, but always leaves him empty and void, however great the mass of vapours may be, like a wine-skin. Here man learned how far he was from the divinity he had desired, since now, naked in hiding, he begged for a covering for his misery and shame. [Col. 1546D]

Certainly no purple robe, no garment of royal dignity, could imitate the glory of that dignity which existed before sin. For decency did not need a double garment; just as today shamefulness is not made decent, but concealed, however costly the covering thrown over it. With God absent, the poor wretch truly feared and was troubled in his own heart; and he wasted away not so much in the bitterness of repentance as in stupefaction of mind and an ecstasy of reason.

The sentence was deferred a little. The final cry had not yet been raised, because even then the form of law had to be set down by divine example: before judgment, in human cases, the place for accusation and defence was not to be forestalled. Rather, after some respite had been given and the sentence meanwhile suspended, those upon whom the practical conduct of the case rests were to produce their safeguards in the midst of their proceedings. [Col. 1547A] According to the ancient order, it must be the one who has either confessed or been convicted who is punished. In this too divine mercy made provision for human errors, lest haste, impulse, or anger should suppress truth in matters not examined and condemn some innocent person through judgments darkened to the perception of reason.

Adam was withering from fear and expectation of wrath, and the impending disclosure of judgment afflicted his wretched soul. The mildness of the place no longer soothed him, nor the flowering meadows, shady groves, fruit-bearing trees, aromatic grasses, melody of voices, fragrance of scents, or life-giving freshness of that most healthful spring. Forgetful of all his dignity, emptied of all else, and burdened with disgrace, [Col. 1547B] he even feared the beasts.

There is no doubt that he gave names to the animals; but concerning the other names of primordial things one may ask whether they were invented by Adam or by Moses. I judge that Adam assigned fitting names to those rivers which flow out from that spring, divided into four branches: the first is Phison, the second Gehon, the third Tigris, the fourth Euphrates. Nor was the meaning of the names hidden from their inventor. While he was in honour, he understood the mystery of a profound reality; but now the corruptible body weighed down the soul, and the earthly habitation burdened the mind with its many thoughts (Wisdom 9). His wandering mind no longer gave itself to God, but ran through a sea of tumult. No longer did he, blinded, contemplate either the Creator in himself or the things that had been made; [Col. 1547C] rather, anxious amid the passions and goads by which he was pierced, he panted.

The very names of the rivers, of which he had been author and interpreter, could have pierced the wretch. Would that he had offered a contrite spirit and the humility of repentance as sacrifice, and that from his heart had burst forth a fountain of tears, watering the dryness of his whole body and flowing forth in streams of satisfaction! He would not have bent himself, proud and empty, toward words of wickedness or sought excuses for sins; but would have declared his own injustice against himself, and perhaps obtained forgiveness of sin. But now the serpent, as it were, ate the reprobate soul like dust. It was already creeping in the breast and belly of this earthly and animal man, who gave no heed to the things of God. If he himself, having swallowed the serpent—or deceived it by the remedy of confession—[Col. 1547D] had run to the fountain of mercy, he would have returned washed to righteousness, recovered strength, embraced temperance, and found prudence.

For these are the intellectual rivers flowing from the love of Christ, who is the living fountain. Thus Phison, the first of the rivers, signifies prudence, and it surrounds the whole land of Hevilath; there are the finest gold, the green gem, and the carbuncle. Phison is understood as “change of speech”; Hevilath as “bringing forth” or “sorrowing.”

First one must inquire what the intellectual Paradise is; then what that fountain is; and afterwards what the four rivers are. Thus, once the hinges of these realities are understood, and the order of the narrative flows on, as it were, through certain river-beds, each point may be fitted within its proper bounds, [Col. 1548A] lest perhaps the subject of delights and pleasure, if treated confusedly, become hateful through the incompetence of its expositor, though it is desirable by its own nature.

Anyone who diligently investigates the holy Scriptures understands from them that there is a bodily, a spiritual, and an intellectual Paradise: the bodily is in a place, the spiritual in the soul, and the intellectual in God, as reason and authority distinguish. In the bodily Paradise—which we call Eden—man was placed, woman was made, and blessing and curse were promulgated upon human nature in the same place according to the character of the respective causes. There the devil could both tempt and conquer man; yet later he found Job, swarming with worms and sitting on a dunghill (Job 2), far stronger than [Col. 1548B] Adam placed in the place of delight while both his substance and person remained whole. Nor did Job lack the goad of a woman’s tongue; but his firm mind mocked his wife’s foolishness, and with most restrained rebuke checked feminine presumption by manly dignity.

Indeed, Job was in the Paradise of an incorruptible mind amid the delights of virtues and the glory of a good conscience; no discharge from sores could defile him. Job did not blush or seek a hiding-place to conceal his wound. Seated in the citadel of virtues as upon a tribunal, he judged all who were falling; nor did he fear the face of God, before whom he gloried in innocence and, when questioned, answered with complete assurance. Adam was in Paradise in a very different condition. Where all things cooperated toward progress, he failed, though neither struck nor crushed, [Col. 1548C] so that his weakened posterity might learn through sickness and misery that without God there can be no happiness, no health, no peace, no wholeness.

The delight of that place was indeed good and pleasant, but it could not remain without the Creator, without whom neither angel above nor human being below could have stability in such a glory of excellence. If the root of sin had not sprouted in man, nor the spreading infection occupied the field of this offspring, that bodily place would of itself supply every advantage to its inhabitant, so that nothing whatever would be lacking outwardly, provided that the Holy Spirit remained inwardly in the heart, which is his proper dwelling. For the savour of all those delights and the whole grace of dwelling there consisted in heavenly sweetness; and that sweetness itself was the moderation and seasoning of all that pleasure. [Col. 1548D]

Some teachers relate that Elijah and Enoch were transferred there by God, and that they live and rest in that abundance untouched by miseries, until, in the last days, they come forth to die as witnesses to the truth before the lost man in whom all the fullness of diabolical power will dwell.

Something has been described above concerning the pleasantness of this place, so far as we—whose whole way of life is in bitterness—can perceive it; and, to speak truthfully, it has been touched upon, not defined. Now the promise urges us also to touch on the spiritual Paradise.

This garden of delights is within the soul. This peace and fruitfulness are within the spirit, where [Col. 1549A] the tree of life is love, and the tree of wisdom is the understanding of God; where the tree of knowledge of good and evil is the discernment of truth and falsehood; where the tree of righteousness is a rational and orderly distribution, rendering to each what is his own. All that growth bears the fruits of virtues and produces charisms. There are there, like branch-bearing supports for vine-shoots, certain props upon which the laden vine rests; these serve it, and those offspring of graces serve one another in turn. Abstinence serves chastity; devotion rests upon prayer; humility rests in fear, and purity of mind in love. Nothing is idle in the vineyard of holiness, where not even a leaf falls, and every tendril is some degree of righteousness; where even the rod is in the vine—that is, where the whole is in the Law. “The Law was given through Moses” (John 1).

The Gospel [Col. 1549B] expounded through the very Word of God extended incorruptible trees—the volumes it issued—into branches far and wide. The offshoots of the Scriptures filled the regions of the world, and the Church pours forth, full of the fruit of holy teaching. Heretics long laboured, with searching investigations, to cut down these trees; yet the heavenly planting did not fail under afflictions but grew. They stripped the branches, burned the leaves; yet, though the fruits were destroyed and even the trees themselves were razed to the ground, the root remained unharmed and, persisting with greater vitality, sprouted more abundantly. It was not diminished by cutting, but increased. Confession shone in peace, martyrdoms in tribulations; and the Lord’s field, often torn by the ploughshare of persecutions, yielded a more abundant harvest.

In contemplation of God the carnal [Col. 1549C] mind, cleansed of the body’s rust, refined and clarified, advanced; and spiritual cultivation produced rich fruit through religious exercise. In the Paradise of the soul, in the garden of a good conscience, in purity of heart, the peace of God gives birth to joy, and pure faith rests in truth. Righteousness arranges all things sweetly; temperance moderates harmoniously; wisdom teaches; courage strengthens; prayer cleanses; abstinence dries up every stain; hope gives strength; humility reigns; patience rules. This repose or glory of the soul in those beatitudes is that bosom of Abraham in which the rich man saw Lazarus’s soul (Luke 16), or that happiness which the Lord promised the thief from the cross (Luke 23).

Whatever the eye sees, the ear hears, or rises into the human heart is not that repose which God promises in eternal life to those who love [Col. 1549D] him. Yet we catch its scent—that peace which surpasses all understanding—and everything that can be reckoned or comprehended falls short of it. Whatever it is, it is neither place, sound, nor smell; it is neither touched nor seen. The bodily sense is bounded and enclosed by bodily dimensions, and moves and is known only within the density of its own nature. Even the keenness of spiritual nature, however subtle it may be, is struck back by the radiance of the higher light; and it can do absolutely nothing beyond that wisdom of God alone which reaches from end to end. Therefore no created thing can be the fulfillment of blessedness; and what lacks anything produces nothing complete. No bodily place, [Col. 1550A] no incorporeal spirit possesses full delights by its own nature, because fullness belongs to the whole, not to its parts; and every part, containing less, must return to its maker, fixing its end in him from whom it has its beginning.

At this point we encounter what the same Apostle says: that he was caught up as far as the third heaven and heard secret words which it is not lawful for a human being to utter. “Whether in the body or outside the body, I do not know; God knows” (2 Corinthians 12). He knows that he was caught up, but doubts the manner, about which he would not doubt at all if one alternative appeared possible and the other impossible. Now, since he could have been caught up with his body, a bodily Paradise may also be understood to be in heaven, although he has set heaven and Paradise forth as though distinct. If we say that he was caught up in the body, [Col. 1550B] we must understand that heaven as bodily. But if in spirit, then we understand not a place but an intelligible tranquillity of the divine vision.

Further, apart from the person of Christ alone, who rose as the firstfruits of those who sleep (1 Corinthians 15), the canonical Scriptures plainly report of no one among the dead that he already possesses double things in his own land (Isaiah 61), or that this corruptible body has put on incorruption before the general resurrection, or this mortal body immortality (1 Corinthians 15)—to say nothing for the moment of the Theotokos herself, or of those who rose with Christ, which is another and a most knotty question. Let us pursue, as far as we can, what we began concerning Paul.

Certainly, when he wrote these things he was in the flesh—indeed, in that flesh of which elsewhere [Col. 1550C] he wrote: “I perceive another law in my members, warring against the law of my mind” (Romans 7). And after other things: “Wretched man that I am, who will deliver me from this body of death?” (ibid.). He himself testifies that there was given to him a thorn in his flesh, an angel of Satan beating him with blows (2 Corinthians 12). How could he have been caught up bodily on high, unless perhaps in the manner in which Habakkuk was carried from Judea to Babylon (Daniel 14), or Philip from Azotus to meet the eunuch (Acts 8)? But if God does something of this sort contrary to nature, it is a matter of miracle and power; and human reason ought not presume to subtract anything from that eternal reason which is God’s will.

Yet that temporary—indeed momentary—assumption of Paul might have occurred in the way Christ was transfigured [Col. 1550D] in the presence of Peter, John, and James, when Moses and Elijah themselves also appeared with him in glory (Matthew 17). Christ was still capable of suffering, and before the resurrection he showed his disciples the glory of resurrection: not only his own, but also that of those who stood with him. Thus Paul too could, for an hour, be conformed to the glory he preached, and to the likeness of the spiritual bodies which the resurrection will refashion. His whole nature, sound and cleansed for a time and without awareness of any weakness, might be carried on high, so that he might see and hear something beyond his fellow servants—he who laboured more than all others amid dangers and varied toils in building the Church. And just as the sea was walkable for Peter while he was still mortal (Matthew 14), [Col. 1551A] so heaven could become penetrable to Paul in the body.

But if we say that Paul was caught up in spirit, there is no question at all. For truly transcending every bodily and spiritual creature in contemplation of God, fixed and resting in the Creator, the man full of the Holy Spirit neither dared to remain below nor to go beyond Majesty. He had ascended, as it were, two ladders—the rational creatures—and through the things that were made had reached the Creator as though the third heaven. For we believe that the intellectual Paradise is in him, to whose glory we shall rise again, meeting at the sound of the last trumpet “into a perfect man, into the measure of the age of the fullness of Christ” (Ephesians 4), and so we shall always be with the Lord (1 Thessalonians 4). The body of our humiliation will be conformed to that divine [Col. 1551B] glory (Philippians 3), and Christian faith will see the King in his beauty amid the splendours of the saints. Indeed, neither faith nor hope will languish there through the delay of expectation, when the kingdom of love alone has appeared.

There nothing will be seen through a mirror or in an enigma, but face to face; and we shall know as we are known (1 Corinthians 13). Christ will be seen, God understood, and the Holy Spirit will fill every heart. The Trinity, now incomprehensible, will be comprehended, and the mysteries of divinity will be opened to the whole Church. Angelic ministries will cease, nor will there be need for the movements of embassies; when the city of God is made perfect, the whole company of the elect gathered within, and God is all in all, then all things will truly have been brought to completion in one cubit. There will be one [Col. 1551C] language for all, unwearied jubilation, one affection, and eternal love. There will be one joy, security from stability, one peace, the tranquillity of eternal sufficiency. Truth will be manifest, love will fill all, and there will be complete health of body and soul. Glorified humanity will shine like the sun; the fellowship of spirit and flesh will be quiet and harmonious. Angels and human beings will share one fellowship, one bread for both, and one banquet. Love will not languish, affection will not dissolve; with every good present, there will be no affliction of delay. All the elect will be intoxicated by the abundance of the glory of that blessed Father and satisfied from the multitude of sweetness. This intoxication will not overthrow the mind, but will be forgetfulness of miseries and the everlasting continuance of holy joy. [Col. 1551D]

Nor will the immensity of that light be burdensome to sight. Rather, the whole sum of that highest blessedness will be this: that pure, unalloyed divinity is understood in its own being. God will be seen and known, understood and loved; and this vision or knowledge, understanding and love, will be the whole perfection of that happiness. For glorious things have been spoken of you, city of God; yet in your praises the proclamations of human tongues have failed. No pen, no affection, has expressed you. Great is whatever the bodily eye sees in you; greater what the spirit tastes; greater still what the keen intellect perceives and enjoys. The eye of flesh sees in you all material reality; the spirit sees, far otherwise, the principle and cause of matter; and the purified mind understands truth itself in an altogether different way.

For spiritual vision uses [Col. 1552A] enigmas and figures, and leads the soul onward through certain likenesses; but the mind, by a clear gaze, understands the thing itself as it is, without any images of phantasms. Belshazzar saw the fingers of a hand writing on the wall (Daniel 5); and, reconsidering in spirit what he had seen, he afterwards perceived it differently in thought. He knew and saw inwardly through the spirit that what had visibly been shown was a sign of a hidden reality, though he did not know what that reality was. Daniel was brought into the midst; in prophetic spirit he saw with his mind, and at once understood what the vision meant. Although everything in that kingdom is honour and glory, this understanding is nevertheless more glorious and worthy than all else; and this is the vision of God which fills and satisfies the human heart. It is the third heaven, the third [Col. 1552B] Paradise.

There is the end; there is unity; and the end is the same, because there is no diversity. In that peace there will be no diversity of languages, but a harmonious and friendly fellowship of dispositions and affections. In the torrent of that delight, fullness of health will desire nothing further; and forgetful of every sorrow, a joyous intoxication of mind will be absorbed in God alone. Though the saints’ glory differs according to their merits, there will not be a diversity that breeds envy in the lesser or pride in the greater; for in the distribution of crowns the distinction made by love will be so great that it both preserves order and grants to all the common dignity of glory. The blessed presence of divine majesty will be all things to all; in common there will be for all omnipotence, wisdom, righteousness, peace, [Col. 1552C] and understanding. Every wickedness will be excluded from that kingdom.

As though plucking a few leaves from the tree of life and sighing for a taste of its fruit, I have scarcely pressed out some juice from its bark. For what lies within has not yet ascended into the human heart, and no intellect has yet touched the marrow of that sweetness. Yet faith speaks, hope is not put to shame, and meanwhile love consoles us.

The fountain in the midst of Paradise is rightly understood as love, which flows with an ever-full stream when prophecies and tongues sometime dry up, and is never dried up itself. Nothing irrigates more fruitfully, nothing enriches the mind more effectively, than love itself, which is poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit. Nor is love a fountain belonging only to the saints, nor is anyone alien admitted to this draught. In tongues, faith, abstinence, signs, almsgiving, and martyrdoms, both the good and the false participate together; love alone separates itself from the assemblies of the impious. If this single pure affection is lacking, whatever religion may appear estimable is barren. [Col. 1552D]

For Christ is love: the most pure drink, the most unstained power, refreshment of souls, purification of minds. The sheer goodness of the Spirit does not enter polluted vessels, nor is anyone unclean anointed with that royal unction. For love is affection, and one who does not love cannot be loved. One who loves does not neglect, and love can never be idle. Without love every offering is confused and undiscerning; and you wholly sin [Col. 1553A] if you do not divide before you offer. God has no need, nor under the name of piety does he wish a bloody retainer: neither an oppressor of the poor nor a hired judge, as though he reclined amid those delights which execrable cruelty has built out of the sighs and blood of the wretched.

One who loves does not offend; and if perhaps he falls, mother-love puts out her hand and receives the falling person. Nor does it burst forth into streams of tears and, in the torrent of repentance, baptize and renew those who have fallen, immediately restoring and reforming those who have been shattered. It meets the compunct, receives the repentant—whom it itself both afflicts and pierces. It abhors and flees only those who persevere in wickedness. Even if you should prophesy or burn, even if you should fast or move mountains, even if you heap all that you possess into the bellies of the poor, [Col. 1553B] if you are a slave of sin, you labour in vain; for the duplicity of a false heart has no place in the depths of love.

This is the source of the four rivers whose names we set down above: from love prudence flows forth, righteousness flows, courage bursts forth, and temperance. From these cardinal goods, in alternating courses, streams and lesser-known fountains irrigate every dry place by hidden channels; and from the torrent of these virtues everything is born by which a human being advances and is cleansed. Every understanding of reason and discernment of mind serve under wisdom; every ordered action, measure and weight, and all equity incline toward righteousness. Moral integrity is born from temperance, patience from courage; and likewise from these innumerable subdivisions, a succession of graces [Col. 1553C] in manifold streams flows through the various chambers of the soul. This outpouring is not diminished by continuous floods, but increased.

Therefore Phison, which means “change of speech,” signifies wisdom or prudence, as we have said; it surrounds the whole land of Hevilath because the true work of prudence is to change and convert irrational and animal human beings to the knowledge and praise of God. For we are born animal, but enlightened through the teaching of wisdom, we become spiritual. Hence the Apostle: “Not first that which is spiritual, but that which is animal; afterwards that which is spiritual” (1 Corinthians 15).

Thus we change our speech; with lips purified by that prophetic coal, we do not blush but proclaim [Col. 1553D] the reproach of the cross. We do not mock, as empty philosophers do, that the Word became flesh; but we glory in the humility of almighty God, certain that, as we have been united to his person, so we shall be united also to his glory. We put off the old human being and put on the new; we change the skin of sin, and, girded with the belt of purity, run unencumbered (Ephesians 4). We change our speech, and we ourselves condemn what we have approved; becoming the strictest judges of ourselves, we outlaw and erase the customary practices of vanities and pleasures. We are angry and indignant that we were once such as we cannot remember without horror and torment. We change our speech when, having buried the monsters of vices, as though rising from the dead we renounce what we will, and plead the cause of truth before [Col. 1554A] human beings with reason, and before God with zeal and constancy.

Thus wisdom surrounds the land of Hevilath, which signifies mud or childbirth; for, while all creation groans and labours in childbirth until now (Romans 8), it is not the part of the wise to be cheerful in a place of terror or to seek a chamber of peace where there is a winepress of pain. “Prudence is not found in the land of those who live pleasantly,” as Job says; for Satan dwells in moist places, sleeping secretly beneath the shade of reeds (Job 4). Isaiah proclaims narrow bread and scant water (Isaiah 30), and David, by the word of God through the Holy Spirit, walks by hard ways. “In much wisdom is much indignation, and he who adds knowledge adds sorrow” (Ecclesiastes 1), because reason, always indignant against the embraces of vanities, [Col. 1554B] truly struggles, and holiness labours lest the integrity of the mind be corrupted by flattering enticement.

There is no such labour among the effeminate and soft, who willingly open themselves to every corruption. In the weakness of temptations, the strength of God’s servants is perfected and increased; and from the sorrow of compunction holy devotion conceives joy. The penitent makes a circuit, gathering together through the innermost recesses of the soul what has been scattered, and binding into bundles the acts he has committed. Circuit against circuit: for the twisting dragon coils its flexible body and, with tangled knotting, drives the wandering and unwary as far as the labyrinth, shutting those immersed in darkness within the abyss of despair. [Col. 1554C]

The mind pierced by divine fear examines and reconsiders everything. Exposed to temptations and miseries in the exile of pilgrimage, it mourns; it weeps because it does not know, and errs because it desires; it wastes away because it does not do the good it wishes, but performs the evil it hates. It weeps because, changeable and unstable, it is swept away by empty things, because it is weighed down by the burden of fragile and corruptible flesh. Wherever it turns, a cause for mourning presents itself. And as it is when funeral-bearers carry out the dead and the following throng resounds with a mournful cry, so the wise person, remembering his last things in all things before death, pronounces judgment on his own cause and, as though the corpse were already present, digs a grave.

A multitude of mourners both follows and goes before, because, examining himself, each person has much to mourn over from both the past and the present, [Col. 1554D] when one’s whole life cries out against sin; and, to add something more, even dreams themselves are not free from delusions. Amid such circuits of meditation, amid the tears poured out by the storm of a contrite spirit, devotion grows rich as if from morning dew, intention is cleansed, and fruitful prayer, fixed upon divine contemplation, bears fruit.

There is absolutely no comparison between the sorrows of the saints and the joys of the reprobate, because this carnal prosperity always presages punishments, while the mind gnawed by the stings of crimes fears the burning of avenging flames. There is no true peace, no tranquillity of true joy in the heart of transgressors: in their consciences Gehenna already prepares its fires before the time, while horrible worms and terrible shapes of demons sharpen hungry teeth to tear sinful flesh. For the present, this happiness [Col. 1555A] that is now pleasurable endures these goads and thorns, yet flatters itself and beguiles itself with uncertain hope, prolonging iniquity and extending wickedness, until suddenly the end of both life and guilt comes, and an endless exacting of punishments follows for crime.

But the saints, whose lives worldly madness regarded as an object of mockery and a likeness of reproach, and whose mourning and fasting seemed insanity, will pour a refreshing drop upon burning tongues and throats lately fattened; yet for both parties the sentence corresponding to their merits will remain immovable and fixed. Therefore their mourning, even in the present life, is not without heavenly joy, nor does it lack divine consolation.

[Col. 1555B] This consolation indeed declares peace and glory in the conscience, and still greater joy in its fruition; its very foretaste, though still held in hope, announces how great will be the fullness of that glory to come. For in the river itself, or in the land of Havilah through which it flows, are found the finest gold, the carbuncle, and the green stone. Certainly, in prudence—which is contemplation of truth itself—because no one can express it, and therefore one conceives it rather than brings it forth, there is gold: that is, the utterly purified discipline of right living, which shines as though refined from every earthly defilement. It also has the carbuncle, whose brilliance is not overcome by night, because truth is not darkened by any falsehood. It has also the green stone, that is, the contemplation of ever-flourishing eternity and the unfading state of perpetual life.

Thus Phison, which means “change of mouth,” is, for the reasons stated first, as it were the prudence necessary for understanding, discerning, standing firm, rising again, and abiding; in it are the discipline of uprightness, the truth of knowledge, and the way of attainment. In the second place Gehon proceeds from that source of Paradise. This is the Nile, which, in its very well-known course encircling Egypt, pours itself out in annual inundations, visiting at fixed times and in fixed measures as a generous benefactor of the whole region; and, as the beloved husband of its agriculture, by its desired union with that land’s bosom it fertilizes not only the soil but also the trees. This name signifies either “breast” or “opening.” According to the interpretation of the names, this river is understood as fortitude,

[Col. 1555D] because strength resides especially in the breast. By this river the children of Israel, settled in Egypt, first received the command concerning the eating of the lamb. The warning concerning girding the loins was also promulgated, because those devoted to divine service had to be ready, and it was not fitting that the solemn rites of burnt offerings should be performed by the impure. For fortitude was needed to bind up the loins, so that chastity, like a certain opening in the earth, might swallow all the passions of the body and bury within itself all the wantonness of the flesh. This virtue of chastity, in which the utmost fortitude and all one’s powers are required, flows through Ethiopia, which signifies baseness, because it extinguishes the fire of our utterly base flesh and, washing away the filth of shamefulness, restores what has been defiled to integrity through recovered strength.

[Col. 1556A] How black is the skin of sinners, scorched by the fires of passions! How base is the flesh which makes itself a slave of foulness and a sewer of every impurity! “How base you have become, repeating your ways”: we understand this as spoken through the prophet concerning sinners, who are certainly abominable and base because of the obscenity of prostitution to which they shamelessly offer themselves. Having driven away the Holy Spirit, they make the soul—which was God’s temple—into a shameful brothel of stench, indeed into Satan’s own whorehouse.

This is the fortitude of those who are set apart from the peoples to sacrifice the lamb, who are instructed in continence before receiving the law on Sinai (Exod. XIX). Before the priest grants David the loaves of presentation to eat, he carefully asks whether he has remained continent and is clean

[Col. 1556B] (I Kings XII). The torrent of fortitude had dried up when the dregs of the Israelite people had already become dry: then those burning incense to Baal-peor and initiating themselves into the embraces of Midianite women subjected captive souls, setting apostasy through transgression before them as the price of shamefulness. Nor was zeal’s fortitude lacking in Phinehas the priest, raging through the Spirit of God. As avenger of that shamelessness, he thrust through the adulterer and the prostitute together in their buttocks, driving in his dagger at one stroke through the mechanism of that foul intercourse (Num. XXV). Immediately the shaking ceased, and Gehon, having returned again to its channels, was not angered and did not renounce its benefaction because those men were—or rather had been—Ethiopians, that is, base; but it gathered again its scattered army, and, with the weak restored to health,

[Col. 1556C] celebrated victory once more in many ways.

The third river is the Tigris, which goes against the Assyrians and signifies temperance, resisting lust, which is greatly opposed to prudence’s counsels. For *Tigris* is interpreted “swift,” in which is understood the alacrity of temperance itself. The Assyrians, moreover, in Latin signify “those who direct.” See how swiftly the temperate person glides through the kingdoms of those who direct; how straight is the path of temperance, against which nothing meets to impede it. “All things are lawful for me,” says the Apostle, “but not all things are beneficial. All things are lawful for me; but I shall not be brought under the power of anything” (I Cor. VI). Temperance looks neither to unlawful nor to lawful things; rather, passing through even lawful things without turning to either side, it walks the royal road. It neither

[Col. 1556D] touches impurities nor approaches any dishonour; it recoils at the mention of pleasure and feels nausea at its smell. It does not seek dark little chambers for shameful beds, nor theatrical arches for committing disgraceful acts. It gathers itself within itself; victorious over itself and by lawful dominion it commands all its affections. It sees all things beneath itself and does not permit even what is allowed to pass beyond rational bounds.

In the fourth place is set Euphrates, interpreted “fertile” or “fruit-bearing.” It is the one which the Assyrian and Hebrew books call *Auxen*, because it cherishes and increases. It bears the fitting emblem of justice, because justice itself is especially fruitful in the human race. No virtue indeed produces more abundant fruits than justice and equity, which benefits others more than itself,

[Col. 1557A] disregarding its own advantages and preferring the common good. Nor is it said of this river, which is adapted to justice, against what it goes or what land it encircles. For justice concerns every part of the soul, because it is the soul’s own order and equity, by which those three are joined harmoniously to one another. The remaining virtues labour in their own courses, because wickedness stands opposed to prudence, incontinence to fortitude, and gluttony—and everything without measure—to temperance. Justice, however, since it is the welcome harmony of all virtues agreeing as one, is recognized not from the other virtues but from itself, because it is peace itself and the holiness of all unity: possessing within itself both the whole and the individual parts, though not being wholly present in each individual part.

[Col. 1557B] Having completed what we promised to say concerning Paradise, its source, and its rivers, our purpose compels us to return to Adam. As we said, after his sin he was ashamed of his own nakedness and, fearful of the shame of itching flesh, hid himself from God’s sight within some cleft of earth or rock. No longer did shame alone sting his stupefied mind; hunger, thirst, cold, and the mass of his other afflictions were now tormenting the wretch, especially because, with his conscience as his judge, he wasted away inwardly in every bitterness and anxiety.

When that voice reached him, “Adam, where are you?” (Gen. III), the sinful soul was thrown into consternation and utterly broken down, because, detected in crime, it had neither help nor any escape open to it. God was walking in the breeze after midday

[Col. 1557C] when he called Adam: in the calling he signified rebuke, and in the walking, departure. For as the heat of charity was cooling and the light of truth drew near to ignorance’s evening, God was leaving the human being and departing from his heart. By delaying his address with slow movement, perhaps he lingered and approached step by step so that, if the human being, pierced with compunction, should recognize his crime in however small an interval, judge himself, and repent, either the offence might be entirely forgiven or something milder might be decreed for one humbled.

As Ambrose says, the Lord did not call Adam from Paradise in a bodily voice, but through a power more excellent than bodily voice can be: namely, in that oracular manner by which he addressed the prophets, or by which Moses himself is read to have cried out when no sound of voice was heard, but only that of the mind. When asked the reason for his hiding and nakedness, he confesses it, although he ought to have been more ashamed of the sin itself than of the punishment of sin. He blushed, indeed, at the rebellion of his mind, the power of sin, and the moth of pleasure creeping in; but he ought to have felt more overwhelming shame because, stripped of the wedding garment, he had deserved to be cast from the glory of that banquet into outer darkness, bound hand and foot.

The virtues that had formerly adorned Adam, while he obeyed God, took away the coverings of his dignities; leaving the transgressor stripped, they subjected him to shame. The wretch was now weaving leaves of falsehood and beginning a web of excuse.

[Col. 1558A] He did not confess his error; rather, as though wrapping the weft around a reed and stretching it within the suspended sides of a loom, by his evasive answer he covertly transferred the cause and blame of his error to its author. “I hid myself,” he says, “because I was naked” (ibid.). Truly, no counsel is effective against the Lord, “who catches the wise in their craftiness” (I Cor. III), to whom every conscience speaks and before whom the secrets of the mind lie open; neither the chaos of hell obstructs his gaze nor the abyss obscures it. He himself saw the wretch, though the wretch did not see him but only heard him. God is seen by the pure in heart (Matt. V); the wicked person is removed from that blessed vision (Isa. XXV). The ability to hear and answer is not denied, because in examination of a case, when a matter is conducted according to the severity of justice,

[Col. 1558B] it is necessary for every accused person to be convicted from his own mouth before that judge, however much slippery ingenuity may abuse evasions.

“The woman whom you gave me gave me of the fruit, and I ate” (Gen. III). Willing or unwilling, he confesses the transgression; yet covertly he lays the burden of sin upon the Creator, who had provided the instrument of deception and had spread out a companion as a kind of snare into which he might fall. Abominable suspicion, stubborn thought directed against God’s goodness, malicious judgment, shameless answer—and by this fact alone, even if there were nothing else in the case, the human being was most deserving of death: that he could suppose the woman had been placed for him as an ambush, that he had been caught by a contrived inducement, and that, according to justice, he had not deserved a judge’s condemnation, because he had turned to consent in transgression not by his own desire but at the persuasion of the woman whom God had given him.

[Col. 1558C] Indeed, he seemed to complain that this nakedness had been wrongly inflicted upon him and that he had been prejudiced by an excessively hasty sentence. Nor did he reason with himself according to equity: he argued that he who had given the law ought to have removed both the stumbling-block and the reproach, and that blame ought to be redirected not upon him who had fallen but upon him who had provided the instrument of the fall. This is what Adam’s excuse seemed to contain: rebuking God and contending in seditious boldness against the tranquil and utterly true justice of God, which still awaited the guilty person’s repentance with much patience, while he himself, “by his hardness and unrepentant heart,” stored up wrath for himself “on the day of wrath” (Rom. II).

In the most just order, after the man God addresses the woman, who likewise excuses what she had done in obstinate pride, bringing forward the serpent who had advised her. Yet she says that she was deceived, grieving more that the devil’s promise lacked fulfillment than that she had consented to his suggestion. Therefore, since neither the man nor the woman devised the remedies of confession or repentance, but, adding transgression to the elaborate contrivances of empty arguments, laboured to convict God of injustice, the accumulated mass of sin was poured back upon proud and exasperating souls and crushed its supporters beneath the sudden collapse of its iniquitous weight.

[Col. 1558D] In the most orderly righteousness judgment began with the serpent, so that the one who had suggested sin might share also in torment; and that the one who had rejoiced at the fall of those consenting to him might, by the merit of his wickedness, have cause for grief. In the punishment of his rival the human being might recognize the judge’s charity, since the judge who had long awaited the fallen person’s repentance seemed almost unwilling and compelled to pronounce the sentence of banishment, while he punished the malice of the tempter with such indignation. Nothing is asked of the serpent; no questioning investigates the origin of its crime, because that inquiry is conducted in vain which bears no fruit and is accompanied by no correction.

But since he who “did not stand in the truth from the beginning” (John VIII) had already been judged, what does it mean that the establishment of a new decree is written into the ancient law, and that new statutes are added as though the enactments of that people had not contained the full measure of law owing to their lesser capacity?

[Col. 1559B] I think that the book of heavenly ordinances and the page of divine providence contain absolutely everything that the state and course of events disclose, and that both what antiquity has worn away and what eternity purposes are visible to the eye of Majesty in one instant. No chapter is abolished, changed, or added in the eternal law; but we, attending not to the causes of things but to their effects, suppose that things of which we formerly knew nothing are added, and that things of which we have no understanding are regretted or changed because we see them happen otherwise than our understanding had expected. But the purpose of the divine mind is fixed and unchangeable, ordering hearts as it moves times.

[Col. 1559C] For when the north wind blows in winter and the unrestrained violence of icy winds rages over the plain, it is necessary that all moisture, where the warmth that restrains excessive force is absent, should congeal into ice; yet it is not necessary that the winds’ rage should swell. Thus, while it is necessary that each cause be assigned its own efficacy, necessity itself does not compel. Justice punishes nothing except what it forbids; for it is alien to justice’s equity to avenge an action which it itself exacts as though by necessity. But prohibition comes first, lest a human being offend through ignorance or error; if he despises it, he accordingly falls under punishment by the necessity inherent in justice itself. Certainly, whatever can be avoided is plainly not necessary in any way. Therefore, whatever is set forth for avoidance by the choice of reason is neither forced by providence
