[Col. 1559D] nor violently drawn onward; and divine judgment punishes not necessity but will—unless perhaps that necessity is one which evil habit has made for itself, and the blinded malice of an obstinate mind. The Holy Spirit, even in its earliest infancy, while the world was still crying, was already convicting it concerning judgment, because it had handed itself over to the condemned prince in order to be condemned: not because he is judge of those who sin, but because he himself, and those who, having abandoned God, share with him in evil, are expelled by God the most just judge from the Paradise of delight—that is, from God’s glory—and dwell in darkness and burn together in flames.

In that casting down, when the wretch fell as soon as he was terrified, prophetic Scripture says nothing about his torment and only little about his degradation; but both Ezekiel and Isaiah touch briefly and obscurely on the ruin and on pride, hateful to God, as the cause of the ruin.

[Col. 1560A] Genesis reveals something more to its readers under the figure or name of the serpent, and from the world’s beginning it begins an unbroken connection of the curse’s sentence extending to the final judgment at the end of the age. There he will be neither tempter nor executioner, because he will attend only to himself—if it may be called attending to oneself when the wretch, enclosed and bound in the chasm of the hellish abyss, burns in eternal fire. Then he will be neither lord of the air, nor ruler of the world, nor prince, but the irrevocable inhabitant of infinite and unspeakable misery.

Meanwhile, cursed among all beasts of the earth and all living creatures, he is either permitted or commanded to go upon his breast and to eat earth all the days of his life. Hence Ambrose, in his book *On Paradise*, says: He did not say, “I make you walk upon your breast or belly and eat earth,” but, “You shall walk,” he says, “and eat” (Gen. III), so that he appears rather to have foretold what would happen in the future than to have known in advance what he would do. “Cursed among all beasts” (ibid.), that is, above all those who live beastly and animal-like, who can at some time become spiritual from carnal and heavenly from earthly, and who, though once darkness, may become light if they turn and return through God’s grace.

[Col. 1560B] But he, cut off from hope and wholly severed from grace because he hates and always persecutes charity, just as he persists in the obstinacy of hatred, so he claims for himself, above the curse, a special prerogative of mercilessness; he enacts and confirms forever against himself the decree of unforgivable wrath.

That he goes upon his breast and belly means this: in the breast there is said to be a certain recess of wisdom. Though he was able to enjoy its unique excellence in divine contemplation, he turned himself wholly away from the vision of peace toward earthly things; and the labor of his life is, as it were, an unwearied effort to persuade people to sin. He creeps among those “whose god is their belly,” whom the Apostle laments and declares enemies of Christ’s cross (Phil. III), breathing pride into them, inflaming them toward impurity, and devouring all whom he has subjected to himself like earth. Those who think earthly thoughts are the food of that serpent, the fodder of this viper. Upon those over whom he creeps or presses with his breast, he joins belly to belly,

[Col. 1560D] impregnating them with poisonous seed and producing from the corrupted soul offspring conformed to himself. His whole endeavor is to entwine himself with carnal affections and, having applied the coagulum of shamefulness to the human mind, to defile every path by which he wishes to go, so that something of that contagion’s mixture may cling both within and without, later breaking forth in the likeness of some monster.

“You shall eat earth all the days of your life,” he says, because until the day of judgment, when the death of his condemnation and eternal confinement comes, he continually licks up those whom he has stirred, burying and hiding foul, earthly souls in the dung-heap of his entrails. From such persons whom we have received through the belly—namely, those enslaved to gluttony and luxury,

[Col. 1561A] or those who pride themselves through a misuse of wisdom and, turned toward earthly things, obey the creature rather than the Creator—the shameless glutton gulps down the sewer of his voracity; and, with insatiable hunger, thrusts savoury morsels made from the flesh of the condemned into the hovel of his pestilence.

That enmities are appointed between the serpent and the woman, as though the man had no part in this conflict, has, I think, this reason: the devil’s temptations are not presumed to approach those who act manfully, but the importunate tempter intrudes upon feminine minds. Nor is the mind, which is as it were Adam, moved toward what is forbidden except when the fleshly sense has been enticed; but at the pleasure which the tempter kindles, carnal desire pants, and, weighed down by the mass of concupiscence, it subdues the resisting

[Col. 1561B] mind and opposing reason through the importunity of continual struggle.

Therefore future enmities between flesh and mind are foretold, because through the Word of God, “which became flesh and dwelt among us” (John I), it was to come about that the crucified flesh of penitents would at last bear fruit, that crops of virtues would grow from the seed of obedience, and that the continence of the flesh would triumph over hostile concupiscence. Hence the saying that “the kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it” (Matt. XI): because the woman—that is, the sense of the flesh—helped by the counsels of her husband, that is, reason, resists the serpent and its seed; she hates it as an enemy and drives away everything that opposes sound teaching and stains the honourableness of life. When the flesh has itself turned toward the husband, evil bodily habit is violently cut off by reason’s rule; and, as though the standard of another cross were planted, the flesh overcomes itself in the midst of continual conflict. Rather, the victorious spirit, with armed vigilance and at God’s command, afflicts and tames the flesh’s wantonness by a godly oppression.

[Col. 1561C] The kingdom of God does not disdain to suffer this violence. It does not reject the robber when he confesses, nor the chief of the apostles when, remembering the Lord’s word, he weeps bitterly; nor does it exclude the anointing and tears of that sinful woman, whose sight or touch Simon the leper recoiled from.

The devil’s seed is schism, heresy, avarice, slavery to idols, every kind of incontinence and impiety, and the abominable assemblage of every vice. The woman’s seed, as we have said—of the woman turned toward her husband

[Col. 1561D] and now subject to reason’s power—is whatever good chastity brings forth, whatever fasting’s labour, whatever martyrdom’s sweat, whatever most fruitful charity conceives from the embrace of diverse sufferings. Ancient enmities have emerged from ancient times between these families, and envy, the rival of virtue, has never been absent. Pride has always persecuted humility; wickedness and malice have set up opposing banners against wisdom and justice.

But while we are still established in the flesh, the serpent’s head is cast down for us by the victory on the cross of our Lord, and, shaken from breast and belly, it is now crushed beneath our feet, by his gift, while bound. The gall offered to the Crucified and refused made all the devil’s temptations contemptible; and the rejected draught of bitterness showed that the thirst of sin, which has a gall-like taste, can easily be restrained from his members—

[Col. 1562A] indeed, entirely extinguished by drinking the cup of that same blood. “What is weak in God is stronger” (I Cor. I)—I do not say stronger than human beings, but than demons. The weakness of this our bodily life triumphs over malignant spirits, spitting upon lusts and abhorring pleasures. The Apostle counts these as dung in order to gain Christ (Phil. III), and the saints’ patience, victorious over itself, tramples them down.

See: the tempter’s head is crushed by women and children, because every entrance of foulness is at once forbidden and the boldness of every impurity is immediately expelled from holy hearts. The adulterer is recognized and shamefully driven back to his brothels;

[Col. 1562B] no assembly of saints admits traces of any foulness. Pure justice shakes from its clean hands every gift, and does not offer itself for sale as a judge, since it received the office of judge not for a price but freely. Divine law forbids the price of a dog and the wages of a prostitute to be brought into the temple, because oppressors of the poor, barkers against the innocent, and those who corrupt and defile truth do not rightly sacrifice from the blood of that gain. Thinking gain to be godliness, they display the law; and truth and godliness cry out before God that they suffer insult through their ministry.

The first shepherd of the Church manfully crushed avarice’s head, casting Simon’s money—and Simon himself—into destruction. Paul cut off gluttony’s head,

[Col. 1562C] disciplining his body and reducing it to slavery (I Cor. IX). Likewise, he cut off the heads of almost all heresies, restraining pride and sedition among the Romans. In the First Epistle to the Corinthians he rebukes and reproves them because they could so quickly be drawn into and converted to the sect of the Jewish law, and because there were among them favoritism toward persons and schisms. There also, with vehement spirit, he crushes the head of fornication, handing over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh the man who publicly kept his father’s wife. He also sets forth and discusses much there concerning the rule of marriage and chastity, the authority of apostleship, and those in the wilderness who fell through fornication, murmuring, and idolatry; in these matters he shows the malignant one’s head both crushed and to be crushed.

In the Second Epistle to the same people, he most openly distinguishes and removes the evil one from the midst, declaring that Christ has no agreement with idols, justice no partnership with iniquity, and Christ and Belial cannot coexist.

[Col. 1562D] He rebukes and recalls the foolish Galatians, bewitched by false prophets and turned to the ceremonies of the law, and breaks the head of that seduction. He establishes the Ephesians in order: teaching women to be subject to their husbands, husbands to embrace their wives as their own body in honour, children to obey and honour their parents, fathers to be gentle with their children, servants to obey, masters not to be puffed up; and binding them in the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace, he uproots evil disobedience at its root. The whole body of the Epistles is thunder, and nearly every sentence is like a lightning-bolt scattering devastating coals. By their light or flames, the head of that ancient enemy is burned up by the power of Christian faith.

[Col. 1563A] Joseph comes forward; Susanna comes forward: he a boy, she a refined woman. The sacred histories do not pass over in silence how powerfully each crushed this monster’s dreadful head. It is impossible to enumerate individually how many victories the saints have celebrated over this wicked head, how often victorious hands have plunged into its brain, how many virgins and widows have, at its first approach, blown away the creeping intruder. Because it gains no advantage in open encounter and is immediately conquered wherever it is plainly recognized, it lays snares; and, if some numbness creeps into holiness and the rigor of justice grows weary or languid in any way, it waits attentively.

But if, by some negligence, rust clings to the weapons of virtues, or if, from some itching after justice, the scab of religiosity covers the skin,

[Col. 1563B] it immediately descends upon the moth-eaten crusts in which it recognizes something of its own, ready to lick and swallow the flowing pus. Truly, the desire for praise and human glory is the scab of virtue and the moth of holiness: the final evil which the often-defeated enemy frequently awaits at the end. For since our glory is the testimony of a good conscience, it often happens that, though victorious, we are conquered when we glory in the victory itself within us rather than in the Lord. And as security arises from virtue, so virtue is often dissolved through security; and when the heel is weakened, one neither walks rightly nor any longer crushes the hostile power with a languishing foot.

At first Satan attacks boldly; then, repulsed, he lays snares for the final stages, because all the glory of human warfare is commended by its last contests. Though many run in the stadium, only the one who does not grow weary in the race or fail receives the prize. Those who contend lawfully earn the crown; those who persevere to the end escape unharmed and uninjured from the tongue’s sting and the tail’s snare.

[Col. 1563C] Yet the cursed one eats earth all the days of his life before judgment, because he swallows and devours lovers of the world, puffed up and distended by the ruin of pleasures, with open jaws; and he fearlessly invades every house on whose doorposts the lamb’s blood does not shine, tirelessly killing every firstborn therein. The more manifest fulfillment of this curse still remains at the end, when, for this avidity to harm and continual effort, hell having opened its jaws, that wretch will be shut within that hellish chaos and plunged without end into that abyss of torments—in dark stenches and dreadful fires whose enormity surpasses every understanding.

[Col. 1563D] In the order of justice the woman who assented to the suggestion follows, and the due penalty is rendered to pleasure. She who had proudly desired liberty by shaking off the Creator’s dominion is placed under the husband’s servitude. Let no one think it without divine purpose that the name and class of slaves persist in the human race to this day, since original transgression deserved this and the rationale of this condition flowed from the first parents. Let the human being consider divine nobility,

[Col. 1564A] heavenly lineage, royal honour, the glory of power, eternal life, and the image of holiness; let him remember what he was, and let them blush at one another because of the yoke which they draw in turn, for guilt, not nature, deserved this shame of oppression. That people are slaves, degenerate, inglorious, and ignoble; that they are sinners and mortal—this was wrought by the mixture of that leaven, and that single infection took possession of everything derived from Adam.

Afflictions are multiplied, and the wretched mother gives birth in pain; the multiplication of conceptions emerging with distress nearly tears apart the womb of the woman giving birth. These things occur in flesh and in spirit. When the subject soul has received the seeds of reason or of the Scriptures, poured into it as by a husband through the application of teaching or understanding,

[Col. 1564B] it is made anxious in giving birth through many tribulations and pains, and scarcely succeeds in becoming accustomed to good work after evil habit has been overcome. “All who desire to live godly in Christ suffer persecution” (II Tim. III); inwardly they are tortured by the law of the members, while concupiscences press hard, until through long use the form of this world becomes empty, the phantasms of vanities disappear, and at last, the obstacles of allurements removed, Christ is formed in us.

On both sides there is misery; the groans accompanying childbirth belong to both natures, because flesh and spirit immediately pay tribute with interest to pleasures that take them captive, while concupiscence presses on, tearing away the shoots of wantonness with torment. Conceptions multiply under lust’s pressure; and because sin is not recognized in the disgrace of impurity,

[Col. 1564C] it is felt in its punishment. When the woman’s womb is convulsed, and the inner natural bonds are broken, the afterbirth flows out; with the infant crying, the business of true misery is enacted as the trembling hand of midwives comes to meet the child that clings within.

The hour of that distress sufficiently indicates what cause it is that breaks out into such effects, and that pleasure is wholly poisonous which pours forth so great a torrent of bitterness. The flesh, irritated by the vapours of certain itching persons, is attracted to lustful embraces; and when certain deceitful flatteries soothe its sense, it follows captive appetite. When it has immersed itself in the desired filth,

[Col. 1564D] only then does it understand, from the sweetness of that satiation, what flavor those pleasures have.

The first mother left this privilege of pain to the remaining mothers, and absolutely no one in the whole succession of this nature is excepted, save the Virgin alone, who alone conceived by the Holy Spirit and, being ignorant of marital intercourse, was utterly removed from the bond of this indictment. If Eve, in that Virgin’s likeness, had prepared a bridal chamber for the Holy Spirit in the temple of her heart by the discipline of humility and obedience, grace would not have been absent; and, under the overshadowing power of the Most High, no heat of concupiscence would have inflamed the soul dedicated to God. She would indeed have conceived by her husband in the manner in which earth, watered by rains, puts forth trees and shoots in most fertile produce; and, without any passion of desire,

[Col. 1565A] the husband would have made use of the marital bosom only for seminal principles.

To Adam also God said: “Because you listened to your wife’s voice and ate from the tree of which I commanded you not to eat, cursed is the earth in your work” (Gen. 3). For man’s sake the earth is cursed and condemned to barrenness. Though without any labour on the part of its master it was ready to offer every kind of delight, it is now foretold that, even when cultivated, it will bring forth thorns and thistles, so that the wretch might be pierced even by these punishments of his sufferings and, wearied by the rakes of repentance, with a contrite spirit make satisfaction to the most gracious Judge. For this very vengeance of his was instruction in how to invoke mercy, and the scourge an argument for it. “Because,” he says, “you broke the bond of obedience, you too shall be dissolved, [Col. 1565B] and shall go into the earth, because you are earth.” Understand the most merciful God even when he kills; and see that temporal afflictions serve correction, and that death itself is not so much an evil to man as the end of evils. In the dissolution of this corruption sin is cut off, and what is thought to be severity proves to be a remedy.

The charge of disobedience is set forth, and the wife’s persuasion is preferred to the divine command; and according to the order of justice, the recompense due to the cause is rendered according to its merit. Fruitless labour, the barrenness of farming, degenerate offspring, and, to crown all, death are announced. The reminder of his original material also carries the weight of reproach: the Judge’s care makes known to him, with such marked emphasis, that he was taken from earth, that he is earth, and that he will return to earth, that the audacity of his rashness, now confounded, might understand from the weakness of his own nature that, according to the condition of his origin, neither glory nor stability belonged to him, and that the honour of all excellence proceeds neither from merit nor from nature, but from grace alone.

From these words—or rather from the experience of the punishment itself—man learned to glory not in himself but in the Lord. The erect neck was humbled, upon which the bond of servitude was imposed as the rule of liberty. It had seemed a heavy burden to the woman to bear the weight of the command, and the authority imposed upon her like a crushing pressure. But once she had taken upon herself the yoke of sin and experienced the impious dominion of tyrannical power, perceiving the difference between a sweet yoke and a grievous one, [Col. 1565C] since she could not return to the state from which she had fallen, she swallowed the bitterness of most bitter spittle and inwardly gnawed the mass of rising disgrace.

The mixture of fermented nature swelled; the sincerity of the primordial unleavened bread was broken apart by the seething sharpness of corruption. The mocking ticklings, as it were, taunted the wretched soul, and importunate sensuality reproached it for its confidence in its own strength. No evasion remained when overwhelming shame had closed every avenue of reply; indeed, the vices themselves cried out against the sick person, attributing their infirmity not to nature but to pride, from whose root the shoots of all thoughts sprang. From that one womb came forth all vices, nursed together; and God’s judgment against them is so just and evident [Col. 1565D] that the very movements of lust detest their own character, and the consummation of shameful acts abominates and shudders at the passion of its own pleasure.

Finally, confusion and shame themselves, which always follow the camps of disgraceful acts, like the most cruel executioners of conscience, assail and reproach the sinner. They press upon him like certain Eumenides—driving Furies—fastening the goads of rebuke into his wounded heart. Wickedness condemns and punishes itself; truth employs contrary weapons in its own defence. The transgressor is expelled from delights and the wretch assigned to labours. Clothed in tunics of skins, and wrapped in the spoils of dead creatures instead of the garment of divinity, he understood, by wearing that covering, that his own skin resembled the skin of a beast—or, to express the matter itself, that he was in a misery still greater and more abject, since his weakness, unable to bear heat and cold, had to be warmed by another’s benefit. Indeed, with skins drawn over his naked body man appeared a beast; and what was inwardly present in his morals was altogether most suitably applied outwardly to his body.

Man played the part of an irrational creature, compared with senseless beasts, and expressed the ignorance of a brutish mind in that raw and shaggy equipment. Man, earthly from earth, now bent toward what is lowest, fixed his gaze upon the mud from which he had been taken. Oppressed by the burden of corruption, he offered his bent shoulders to sin as rider: a slave of the belly, a dependant of lust, a bondsman of vanity, and a household slave of vices. He had exposed his soul like an anvil to the blows of smiths; [Col. 1566C] and there lust, the craftsman of the workshops, fashioned images of every transgression. The fire of that workshop belched forth idols of anger, envy, and every blasphemy; monsters of temptations multiplied, sitting beside his thoughts, and reason, wearied by their multitude, was weighed down.

For God had abandoned the soul; and, turned back upon itself, it was troubled. This was man’s first death: when it lacked the guardianship of its Creator, who, angered at the ingratitude of the obstinate transgressor and detesting it, departed. At once he deprived man of glory and honour and extinguished in him life—that is, the light of his knowledge. The blinded soul, when it lost truth, breathed out at once both that beatific vision and all the remaining forms of blessedness. When [Col. 1566D] God departs, no good remains; and unless, upon his return, pardon and grace are given, the brightness of the extinguished illumination does not return to the abject and contemptible soul.

Yet the image or likeness of the Creator is not altogether erased even when the soul dies through sin. While God’s patience waits for offenders to repent, whatever has been darkened in that image through negligence can be washed by repentance. Thus one who rises from the dead is re-formed and restored; and the virtues return, through emancipation by pardon, to the works for which they were appointed. Then the soul lives again when it sees and hates and does whatever has been divinely commanded to it. For when it does none of these things, it is dead; because, since God is truly its life, no affection at all, in his absence, aspires [Col. 1567A] to any good.

This is the first death of the soul: when God abandons it and it remains, as though bound by the institutions of crimes, and buried. Yet the dry clod, in the cold of this winter, does not wholly uproot the remnants of hope, because God, rich in mercy, cries with a loud voice to one already four days dead and putrid: “Lazarus, come forth” (John 11). He groaned, cried out, and wept, showing rational souls how effective are the rain of tears, the trembling of repentance, and the cry of confession. This supplication is not rejected; indeed, it obtains pardon for crimes; and the one who rises, once loosed, immediately eats with others. No stench remains; no trace of decay remains in one whom God raises from the dungheap. Rather, he grants the risen person a seat with the princes of his people—that is, with the holy angels—and places him upon the throne [Col. 1567B] of glory (Ps. 112 [113]); he even admits him to his own banquet.

Let Novatian be indignant; let the Pharisee be angry. The supreme commendation of love, the perfected glory of omnipotence, are goodness and mercy; and nothing is more fitting for a saint than compassion. Nor is the Redeemer’s praise more honourable in any respect than when, through his mercy, human weakness recovers strength and is made firm. The rigour of divine justice is indeed dreadful; the Judge’s severity fearsome; the sternness and punitive judgment altogether to be revered. Yet mercy is lovable in its gentleness and praiseworthy in its grace. For where good is rendered for evil contrary to merits, the overflowing abundance of kindness is proclaimed; from its fullness our dryness [Col. 1567C] is watered.

It does not suffice for the Holy Spirit to be with saints: he also sanctifies the wicked. He does not reproach; he breathes, fills, teaches, anoints, and burns; he reforms and instructs tax collectors and prostitutes. The power which restores what has been crushed and repairs what has been broken is more wonderful than that which gathers and preserves intact vessels in fortified treasuries. Repentance indeed restores to life those dead in soul through fault; but the obstinacy of despair drags them into Gehenna. That death of despair utterly effaces and scrapes away the image, and no remedy meets such an injury; no drop of mercy pours itself into it.

Adam experienced that first death of the soul, deprived of divine consolation; he also experienced the departure of the rational soul from the body. But this latter death, [Col. 1567D] by which the bodily and spiritual substance was dissolved, broke apart the labours, sufferings, servitude he had deserved, and the bonds of his whole appointed calamity. Having received grace while alive and repentant, because the price earned by fault had been paid, he sang to the Lord of judgment and mercy. In the labours and reproaches of temporal life he stored up humility and patience; at the end, however hard and narrow, he gave thanks to his Lord for his own libation.

He is pierced by desires, labours and sweats and is tormented; expelled from the place of pleasure, he at last dies. In all these things, like a potter’s vessel baked in a furnace, with sin’s rust worn away by the many scrapings of its cracks, he returns to his natural brightness. Thus the Hebrew people was led about through the desert. Although they could, within a few days, if they travelled rightly, have reached the promised borders, they endured the loss of forty years, during which the insolence of that multitude was to be instructed by the straits of that pilgrimage. Thus, when it reached the promises long desired and awaited, it might not easily yearn with a relapsing heart either for Egypt or for kingdoms devoid of God’s worship. It had been torn from their bonds with such labour, and only at length, through long disuse, triumphed over the errors of the faithless nation, long imbibed through intimate association and evil habit.

For there they had seen idols, feasting and shameless beds associated with profane rites, to which souls prone to desire had subjected their captive affections; and they had clung to abominations which the teaching of their fathers Abraham, Isaac, [Col. 1568B] and Jacob had abhorred. Therefore came the law, therefore the plagues and blows; therefore, by delay in receiving the inheritance, the kingdom of such abundance and glory would not become cheap through easy acquisition. Rather, the possession acquired through such great exercises and severe constraints was to be preserved under the fear of God for most careful watchfulness.

What of the fact that our Redeemer cries out on the cross that he is forsaken? What of the fact that Life dies, the Judge is judged, the King mocked, the Prince suspended? Those injuries of the Saviour are mystical and sacramental; and that grain of wheat, falling into the earth and dying, loaded the wild ears with manifold increase. Thus Christ had altogether to suffer and enter into his glory. And what the title of the cross, inscribed incorruptibly in Hebrew, Greek, and Latin, contained was to be fulfilled in the salvation [Col. 1568C] of all nations, whom mother Charity was to raise, at Christ’s command and with the thief sent before, to the kingdom of the Crucified, united to obedience and humility.

Truly, for those predestined, all things work together for good: strength and weakness advance toward the crown; standing and falling together build up the labourer. For the one, from the other, both advances and is tempered: security in holiness descends when it considers weakness and is not puffed up, while dissolution, ashamed at the sight of purity, gains strength. Hence, in Book XIV of *The City of God*, Saint Augustine concludes thus: “I venture to say that it is useful for the proud to fall into some open and manifest sin, by which they may become displeased with themselves, since they fell already by being pleased with themselves.” Peter more beneficially displeased himself when he wept [Col. 1568C] than he pleased himself when he presumed.

We are often usefully abandoned; while we are corrected, we are amended; while we are scourged, we are loved. “For a time,” says Isaiah—or rather God through Isaiah—“I will forsake you, and with great mercies I will gather you” (Isa. 54). Adam is led out from the place of pleasure in order to do penance, because pleasure and mourning do not dwell well together, nor do delights and religion embrace each other. Yet he is stationed before Paradise to make satisfaction, so that often seeing whence he had come out, and considering what he had been and what he was, he might with humbled mind detest pride. After the reproaches of affliction, he might learn how great was the good of subjection and obedience, through which, even fallen and cast out, he would not despair of the outcome of his return and restoration. He saw—or rather understood—what was signified by that turning movement of the sword wielded by the cherubim. Since we have explained this above briefly, yet sufficiently for an intelligent reader, we judged it useless labour to repeat the same matter.

[Col. 1569]

## COMMENTARY OF ABBOT ERNALD ON PSALM 132: “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity,” etc.

[Note: [Col. 1569] From manuscript codices of the abbeys of Longpont and Cîteaux.]

(Galland, *Bibliotheca veterum Patrum*, vol. XIV, p. 487.)

## HOMILY I. On verse 1: “Behold, how good and how pleasant it is for brothers to dwell together in unity.”

[Col. 1569B]

### I. “Behold, how good,” etc.

“Behold” is the word of one looking and pointing out; “how” of one marveling and exclaiming. Four things are proposed, joined in this fitting order: observation, wonder, demonstration, and exclamation. Observation indicates purity of heart; wonder, the greatness of the thing observed; demonstration, the love of a sociable spirit; exclamation, the magnitude of that very love. See, then, with what praise he has extolled the matter which, in so abrupt an opening, he suddenly brought forth: by marveling, exclaiming, and inviting his friends, as it were with his very finger, to the spectacle.

### II.

“It is good,” he says, “and pleasant what I offer you; useful and delightful what I show.” Does not the poet say:

> He has carried every vote who has mingled the useful with the sweet.  
> (Horace, *Ars Poetica*, v. 343.)

Are there not many things good but not pleasant, such as fasts, which afflict the flesh; and many pleasant things not good at all, such as vices of the flesh, which offend God? He has mixed wine for us at wisdom’s table and set before us goodness together with pleasantness, usefulness with sweetness, in the cup of divine mercy. Let us approach and drink: for what is called good is not dishonourable, nor is what is described as pleasant burdensome.

And what, I ask, is this which affects the mind because of its pleasantness and draws affection because of its benefit? “For brothers to dwell together in unity”: [Col. 1569D] a brief description—and the briefer, the more obscure. In Scripture I find “brothers” named in four ways: by nature, as Jacob and Esau; by kinship, as Abraham and Lot; by nation, as the whole house of Jacob; and by faith, as all Christians. The first contend over an inheritance and are separated from one another (Gen. 28); the second are divided from each other on a much lighter occasion in Genesis (Gen. 13); the third “are divided by the anger of his countenance” (Ps. 54 [55]); and are called a foolish and senseless people [Col. 1570B] (Deut. 32). Even in the fourth degree many false brothers and many schismatics are found (Gal. 2; 1 Cor. 1).

Who, then, are these so blessed brothers, these brothers by blood so worthy of praise, whom neither anyone’s envy divides, as it divides the first; nor money separates, as it separates the second; nor folly cuts off from God, as it does the third; nor a multitude breaks apart into heresies and sects? “Many are called, but few are chosen” (Matt. 22). The many called make heresies; the few chosen remain as brothers. These few, these chosen ones, are Jesus’ brothers: they preserve unity of spirit against envy; voluntary poverty against money; love, strong as death, against folly; and brotherly charity against the malice of schismatics.

Therefore, apart from those few whom God chose to be made conformable to the image of his Son, so that they may be one as they themselves are one, you will scarcely—indeed, not at all—find throughout the whole world anyone able to dwell in unity. Observe, therefore, the very word “dwell,” which means to stand immovably in unity. Those who dwell with the dwellers of Kedar also dwell, but in flesh, not spirit; by necessity, not willingly; as strangers, not natives; as pilgrims, not members of the household; finally, as prisoners in chains, not as free persons. Therefore, at death, when they pass into the freedom of the glory of God’s children, they cry out and say: “The snare is broken, and we are delivered” (Ps. 122 [124]).

### III.

Perhaps what I have said—that the saints stand immovably in unity—will seem impossible to someone, since I understand that One, or that unity, to be none other than God himself. (That he alone is truly one—or rather, that he himself is unity itself—I shall demonstrate below.) And he will say: “Which mortal stands immovably in God, when it seems so rare and difficult even to go into him for a moment of time?” Notice that “into God” and “in God” are different expressions. “Into God” indicates motion; “in God” signifies stability.

When, therefore, we say “to dwell in unity,” or “to stand into God,” the Latin expression indeed jars, but the aptness of the meaning edifies. It is no great matter to commit an occasional error [Col. 1571A] against Priscian, if by such an error you can edify a Christian. Thus we say “to dwell into unity,” so that “to dwell” denotes stability and “into unity” signifies motion. We refer stability to the intention of one’s purpose, mobility to the progress of affection. Thus the saints dwell into God both stably and movably: movably, because the mind often falls back from God and again directs itself into him; stably, because the intention never changes.

In the same way philosophers regarded the sphere of heaven as movable and immovable: movable, because it revolves in perpetual motion around Galatia; immovable, because it is not transferred from its own place to another. So too the saints are mobile because they always hasten toward the prize, and immobile because they hold an unchangeable purpose. Therefore the saints dwell into God while they tend toward him steadfastly; angels dwell in God while they abide in him unchangeably: these into God, those in God. There will be a time, however, when all—saints and angels alike—will be at once in him, from him, through him, and with him. “In him” refers to righteousness; “from him,” to substance; “through him,” to grace; “with him,” to permanence. In righteousness is understood likeness; in substance, creation; in grace, reconciliation; in permanence, unchangeableness.

Nor should it trouble you that reconciliation is said to concern both human beings and angels alike. For just as human beings returned to God’s grace, so angels passed into peace with human beings, that there might be one flock, as also one shepherd. We now have all things in part; but when that which is perfect comes, that which is in part will be done away, and God will be all in all.

### IV.

“One” is said in many different ways. For it is said according to collection, as one flock, although gathered from many sheep; according to likeness, as the one voice of many singers, made one by likeness of harmony; according to composition, as one body composed of diverse parts; according to smallness, as one atom, which approaches unity the more because it admits no division; according to simplicity, as one soul, which, although it has diverse powers in itself, nevertheless has one simple substance.

An atom might also be called one according to simplicity; but more properly it is called one according to [Col. 1571D] smallness—as also a point is one, and an instant one—because, although they cannot themselves be divided, they can nevertheless be parts of things which can be divided. Thus several atoms constitute one divisible body; several points make one divisible line; several instants compose one discontinuous time. Perhaps the same might be said of the soul: that it is a constitutive part of one divisible thing, namely, the human being, and therefore is not properly called one according to simplicity. This is certainly true. Nothing is truly simple except God.

It is therefore necessary to confess that he alone is one, supreme, and one in the primary sense: he is neither composed of parts, nor assembled from diverse substances, nor made one from like or unlike things, nor reduced to indivisible smallness, nor dispersed into several powers, like soul, point, voice, flock, and body. Since God alone, then, is one, it is now plausible that unity is predicated of God alone.

### V.

Observe that this unity of which we speak here is far removed from the unity which is a part of number. This unity cannot be multiplied into number; nor can two, three, or any other number be constituted from it, as number is commonly said to be a collection of units. It derives its etymology from Greek and is called *unitas* as though *onitas*, that is, beingness or essentiality. Hence among the Greeks God is called ὢν (*ōn*), that is, “substantial,” namely, he who alone subsists in himself and through himself, immutably and always.

There is, however, a certain likeness between numerical unity and substantial unity. For just as unity is called the fountain and origin of all numbers, so God is in a certain sense the fountain and origin of all things: fountain, because of the majesty of his inexhaustible power; origin, because of the beginningless dignity of his creative substance.

### VI.

I should now like to explain each kind of unity in turn, so that one may arrive from the first to the highest unity. First, however, I wish briefly to gather the kinds of unity themselves, that I may succinctly describe what ought to be drawn from each. Unity, then, is called unity of collection, likeness, composition, smallness, and simplicity. Collection belongs to the monastic congregation, where the Good Shepherd gathered his sheep from East and West, that they may recline with Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob in the kingdom of heaven. Likeness concerns conformity of conduct: as we praise the Lord with one voice, so also with one heart and a harmonious likeness of conduct. Smallness suggests humility, which always opposes him who first abandoned unity through pride. Simplicity corresponds to purity of intention, which cleanses and prepares the eye for the vision of God, because “Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God” (Matt. 5).

That highest and blessed unity, the highest and blessed charity, one in itself, will then be all things in all, for ever and beyond, through all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY II. On verse 2: “Like ointment upon the head, which descends upon the beard, the beard of Aaron.”

[Col. 1572D]

### I. “Like ointment upon the head.”

Every word of this psalm has been weighed according to its proper weight; therefore not one iota or one stroke should be passed by untouched. “Like” is a mark of comparison. Comparison is especially familiar to theology for three reasons: ornament, usefulness, and sometimes necessity. Ornament belongs to the elegance of knowledge; usefulness, to ease of understanding; necessity, to the difficulty of the subject.

Comparison often adorns a thought, as in proverbs; it sometimes gives easier understanding in obscure and hidden matters, as when one says, “for example.” Whatever follows for this purpose is called a comparison with what precedes. Necessity also sometimes compels the use of a comparison, but only in matters which tend to exercise even men of keen intellect and render the sharpest minds perplexed: as when saints speak of the mystery of the Incarnation, the Virgin’s childbirth, or the properties of the Trinity. They employ comparisons by which they can somehow persuade us of what they think, because they are wholly unable to convey openly by rational explanation what they wish to say.

For this reason I said that this kind of comparison is especially serviceable to theology: nothing is so perplexing and, so to speak, entangled for human reason as treating matters which, although shown not to be contrary to reason, are nevertheless above reason. But to adorn thoughts and explain every obscurity by comparisons is shared by us with others. Consider, therefore, what comparison is given here and for what purpose; and all three—ornament, usefulness, and necessity—will occur together. For, in order more strongly to commend what he had called good and pleasant, he at once elegantly and gracefully adorned each term with its proper comparison, saying: good like you, pleasant like ointment. And because “to dwell in unity” might perhaps have been obscure to the unlearned, or even to the more capable, something similar had to be added to make understanding easier.

And because great—indeed, unspeakable—is the multitude of your sweetness, O Lord, which those feel whom you hide in the secret place of your countenance, this was the chief reason for saying, “like ointment upon the head”: so that at least by a likeness it might be understood what has not yet in any way been granted to me or to people like me to experience. You have hidden it from those who fear you; but, as those who have experienced it say, you have revealed it to those who love you. Therefore I too shall now at least begin to love, in case this love may perhaps be able to extend its bounds in my soul; for if friendship grows, surely that knowledge which is acquaintance with him will grow too. Let us now, then, approach the mystery of the comparison, since I rejoice that I have found grounds for the analogy.

### II. “Like ointment upon the head.”

By the ointment upon the head I understand the divinity in Christ the man, who was anointed with the oil of gladness, with the ointment of majesty and grace, so that that blessed soul was capable of that anointing [Col. 1573D] and glory. For that boundless anointing is sweet and delightful; yet the one into whom the whole fullness of divinity poured itself bodily received it without measure.

When I heard “bodily,” I breathed again, though I had been dead, with Elisha bending and shortening himself to raise the child. For when I was fleshly and could not savour the things of God, my soul clung after the Virgin’s Son; and I began to meditate—flesh upon flesh, man upon man—and found hidden honey in the comb, precious ointment in a most pure vessel. I have heard that this honey sometimes exhales its sweetness to those who seek it, and that ointment breathes out its fragrance. Blessed is the one to whom it is given to experience this.

One thing I know: it is exceedingly good and pleasant to dwell there in unity, so that, just as that comb always enjoys its honey and that blessed soul never lacks its blessedness, so too, though not equally, it may sometimes be tasted, even a little, by the little ones, “because he is sweet” (Ps. 33 [34]). For this is the bread that strengthens the human heart in this place of horror and our solitude, until the poor widow of Zarephath gathers all her vessels into one house and all are filled with Elisha’s oil to the brim; then the oil will stop.

But now it must not stop; it must flow and run down to the miserable man lying wounded by robbers on the road, who has great need of medicine. This ointment thus flows from the living fountain of the angelic region and waters the whole breadth of your earth, O Emmanuel. “Its going forth is from the height of heaven, and its course even to the valley of Jericho” [Col. 1574B] (Ps. 18 [19]), where it meets the wounded and sick, healing every sickness and every infirmity (Matt. 9). It now seems worthwhile to inquire who those blessed people are to whom that ointment, so powerful, effective, and sweet, deigns to descend.

### III. “Which descends upon the beard, the beard of Aaron.”

The beard is an impassible thing, preeminent over the whole body, adhering to flesh, receiving increase from flesh, but situated beneath the head. Such, then, I understand the supercelestial spirits to be: impassible by nature; surpassing the body of the whole Church by a certain privilege of dignity; adhering through perpetual love to the Word made flesh; awaiting from that same flesh their increase and restoration, so far as their number is concerned; yet worshipping above themselves that same God-man. For he alone has been granted that at his name every knee should bend (Phil. 2).

This is what he intended to confirm by repeating “beard”: he says it is not the beard of just anyone, but of Aaron alone—Aaron, who is called “mountain of strength,” namely, he who first was a small stone and grew into a great and lofty mountain: truly great, because he filled the whole earth; truly lofty, because he is above every virtue and principality. The beard belongs to him alone, then, because every angelic creature is subject to him alone. From him, therefore, as from the citadel of all things, the outpouring of graces descends to the angels nearest him.

“I lifted my eyes to those mountains of Israel,” to the powers of heaven, mountains very lofty and eminent, in case help might come to me from there. I went about the streets and lanes of the city, watching to see whether someone might grant me something from his fullness. But behold, each one holds what he has, lest another receive his crown, and there is none able to snatch anything from their hands. As I said, “Whence then shall help come to me?” I consulted the Prophet, and this answer was given me: “Because there is none who does good, not even one” (Ps. 13 [14]). Therefore I waited expectantly for that One, and he attended to me because he is merciful; and he who is mighty did great things for me.

Truly great things: for he opened the whole bosom of his mercy and gave humankind his flesh as food, his blood as drink, his soul as ransom, and his divinity [Col. 1575A] as ointment. He left nothing incommunicable; he made all that was his ours. Because the Lord of hosts himself ministered to us, all of them too—from the highest to the lowest, the whole court of angels—became ministers to us. “Are they not all ministering spirits, sent into service for those who shall receive the inheritance of salvation?” (Heb. 1).

### XV.

Note that it says “all”: none is excepted, not even those who stand before the ruler of the whole earth. And what is surprising in this? No invisible creature, virtue, or power can either wish or ought to regard service as beneath it, since the Lord of hosts himself deigned to minister in person and through himself—indeed, to give himself wholly—so much so that one of the saints says that he almost imperilled what was his own in order to save us.

Thus the abundance of ointment did not adorn the beard alone, but its rich sweetness descended even to the garment of our High Priest—indeed, even to the very hem of his garment. To describe the texture, shape, arrangement, or quality of his garment belongs to another undertaking and, I confess, exceeds my powers. I wish therefore to examine only the hem of his garment, which is its lower part, close to earth and far removed from the preeminent head. And surely, the more lowly and inferior it is, the nearer it is to me, who among the Gospel’s tax collectors and prostitutes may I at least obtain the lowest place! For although they seem far from the head, they are nevertheless counted in the Lord’s garment.

I see some around the Lord’s breast, who draw from and give drink from his inmost heart; others around his arms, who embrace and cherish the children of the one mother; others around his loins, who persevere in perpetual virginity; others around his calves, who support the members of the whole Church. The hem of the garment alone lies lower down, as lowly and unworthy; and yet, by some mercy of the Lord, it is never divided from the Lord’s garment.

This is the life of penitents, O excellent Psalmist of Israel, Prophet of the Lord, pipe of the Holy Spirit! How beautifully, how magnificently you have consoled penitents! My heart heard and trembled for joy; my inward parts were moved. For you make mention of the Bridegroom’s friends, of those who recline upon Jesus’ breast and are led apart onto the high mountain. It might be doubted only of sinners whether they too belonged to the royal priesthood. Therefore stoop down to the wretched, cherish the fallen, comfort those who mourn. “Which descends upon the hem of his garment”: the ointment which pours itself through the whole heavenly region, which cherishes and governs all the substances of the empyrean dwelling, which pours life-giving sap into every tree of Paradise—this same ointment descends to children of wrath, children of Gehenna.

A marvelous thing: it descends to wicked seed, to a brood of vipers. They existed, but not with him; they lived, but not for him; they understood, but not him: senseless, ungrateful, alien. Let the sinner’s spirit then come alive, and let it devote its whole being to the Creator, its life to the Redeemer, its understanding to the Inspirer, so that [Col. 1576A] it may attribute to no human being what it understands, lives, or subsists by; rather, let it attribute all wholly to all and wholly to each, because God is one ointment, one sweetness, one pleasantness, who lives and reigns through all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY III. On verse 3: “Which descends upon the hem of his garment, like the dew of Hermon, which descends upon Mount Zion.”

I. “Which descends upon the hem of his garment, as the dew of Hermon, which descends upon Mount Zion.” I think we should do what, according to Plato’s *Timaeus*, ought to be done in every treatise: at the outset consider what the subject under discussion is. The discourse does not arise from country houses and fields, nor from a subject ordinarily familiar to worldly and exalted minds. It concerns [Col. 1576B] that invisible anointing which enjoys a certain familiar fellowship with the meek and simple, and works wonderful and divine things in the contrite and humble heart: “The senseless man shall not know, nor shall the fool understand these things” (Ps. 91).

The senseless person is one who does not know himself; the fool, one who does not understand God’s goodness. Pride alone produces this twofold evil: it both steals from a person self-knowledge and snatches away from him understanding of God; and thus the number of its senseless people is now beyond counting. “He who is ignorant shall be ignored” (1 Cor. 14); therefore the senseless person shall not know. And, “The Holy Spirit will withdraw from himself thoughts that are without understanding” (Wis. 1); therefore the fool shall not understand.

What will he fail to know, and what will he fail to understand? “How magnified are thy works, O Lord” (Ps. 103): namely, the works by which you accomplish salvation in the midst of the earth, in the midst of the contrite and humbled heart, so that your Spirit may rest upon the humble, quiet person who trembles at your words. “I have hidden thy sayings in my heart”; fear and trembling came upon me; I felt your anointing, and rested from my perverse habit. I understood that without you I can do nothing, and I was humbled utterly. All this the fool fails to know, because he is haughty, turbulent, presumptuous. By presumption he offends God; by turbulence he harms his neighbor; by haughtiness he brings shame upon himself. Not without reason has it been said that the senseless and the fool shall perish.

O Lord, let not the foot of pride come upon me—the slippery foot, the accursed foot—on which all [Col. 1576D] humans and angels fell, evildoers working iniquity. For you resist the proud; therefore they were driven out and could not stand. But to the humble you give grace, which alone is powerful to free a person from the bond and fetter of sin, recall him to the way of righteousness, establish him in a good resolve, and bring him into the promised rest: first, lest he perish; second, lest he go astray; third, lest he fall again; fourth, lest he lack fruit. This is the fourth watch, in which it rescues those who labor.

Note the kinds of grace: there is liberating grace, justifying grace, strengthening grace, glorifying grace. This is that invisible, manifold, subtle, and efficacious anointing mentioned briefly above, which descends to the stones, that it may make sons of Abraham, raising the needy from the dust and lifting [Col. 1577A] the poor from the dung-heap. See what sort of person it finds, whence it brings him in, and to what it advances him, so that, restored at last to his former rank, he may sit with princes and be worthy to obtain the throne of glory.

It finds him sickly, swollen, and foul-smelling: from the sole of his foot to the crown of his head there was no health in him. Sickness pertains to incontinence, swelling to pride, stench to blasphemy. Blasphemy is completed in speech, pride in thought, incontinence in action. Therefore the most powerful physician sends an efficacious ointment to heal him; it immediately cures the sickness, suppresses the swelling, and drives away the stench. Since opposites are healed by opposites, he sets decency against incontinence, humility against pride, and the gravity of silence against blasphemy. He has done whatever he willed, and in one individual [Col. 1577B] raised those three dead persons of the Gospel—in the house, at the gate, and in the tomb: in heart, tongue, and hand. “A threefold cord is not quickly broken”; but all-powerful is the anointing which accomplishes these things.

II. He who has bestowed such gifts upon the stranger—see also how much he does at Israel’s departure from Egypt. He is present with the dying, present with the departing, present with the resting. For who could patiently endure the straits of death unless he had the consoling Spirit? Who would not be terrified at encounters with demons unless he had a helper? Who could pass into rest unless he had one going before him? Thus the anointing is everywhere, tenderly sustaining its sick person: that he may endure not merely patiently but sometimes even gladly; pass over steadfastly; rest happily.

O how great are the power, [Col. 1577C] grace, and glory of this ointment, which soothes such pains, puts horrors to flight, and breathes forth fragrances: in the anguish of departure, in the misery of passage, in Abraham’s bosom! There the poor person sits with the princes gathered with the God of Abraham; he has a place upon the throne that is high and lifted up—high above angels who never fall, lifted up among human beings who have risen. There the ointment descends even upon the hem of the garment—not in any ordinary or humble way, but as the dew of Hermon descends most abundantly upon Mount Zion.

Hermon means “exalted light.” It is Christ, who humbled himself even unto death. “Therefore God also exalted him” (Phil. 2), but not him alone. He alone was humbled, but he is not alone exalted: for he draws all things into himself, to himself, and through himself, as the way, the truth, and the life (John 14). He is the Way for those journeying here amid many errors and a vast exile; the Truth for those departing hence, when they leave behind vanity and falsehood; the Life for those arriving there at the land of the living. There Hermon distils upon them and into them his dew; there the true light flashes its splendor upon them; and it descends even upon the hem of the garment, as upon Mount Zion.

O Mount Zion, city of the true David, lofty tower set on high, with the guardianship of angels upon your walls! O holy city, whose king is Christ, whose senate is the multitude of saints, whose army is the choirs of angels, whose legions are the companies of martyrs who waged most victorious battles even to bloodshed! O beautiful city, wholly irradiated by the Sun of righteousness [Col. 1578A], wholly watered and made fruitful by Hermon’s dew! Wretched me, driven outside your camp like a leper! Would that I might pitch my tent in your courts, or at least in your suburbs! In your courts dwells one who is in ecstasy; in your suburbs, one who is making progress. Wretched I neither exceed nor advance; instead, through I know not what phantasms of thought, day by day I return to my vomit like an unclean dog.

I am not like the little dogs that eat of the crumbs falling there from that heavenly table, the table of God’s children, who recline at that supper upon Jesus’ breast. Only three things remain to me: to mourn, to restrain myself, to fear—because of evils past, present, and future. For I know that wherever these three are gathered in Jesus’ name, he is there in their midst; if not yet as Bridegroom, at least as Lord. He does not yet, as Bridegroom, imprint love; but, as Lord, he instills terror. Yet in both he is Jesus; in both, Savior, though in the latter he seems gentler and in the former harsher.

Yet I blush because I still remain under fear; indeed I blush, and can scarcely bear my weariness. But lest my soul be swallowed up by excessive sorrow, I am greatly consoled by what is written: “Blessed is the person who is always afraid” (Prov. 28). “Always”: I marked that word *always* and hid it in my heart. I fear when grace comes, when grace departs, when grace returns. Its coming makes me fear lest I offend it; its departure makes me tremble lest I immediately fall; its return instills fear lest I lose it once more. Given, it makes me glad; [Col. 1578C] taken away, it torments me; restored, it immediately summons me to greater diligence.

So let it be, Lord: may your fear always remain in me, because the longer it endures, the more chaste it becomes day by day, that it may endure for ever and ever. When it has been thoroughly purified and transformed into filial reverence, then I shall plainly read in the book of experience that your fear both justifies and humbles the sinner, so as to place him beneath the hem of your garment: the garment for healing, and the hem for humility. For I know that the saints and the humble in heart bless your name, and receive a share in your inheritance, in your kingdom of heaven, where the abundance of your anointing descends upon them, through all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY IV. On verse 4: “For there the Lord commanded the blessing, and life for ever.”

[Col. 1578D]

1. “For there the Lord commanded the blessing, and life for ever.” Most welcome is the beginning of this psalm, which laid its foundations in the goodness and pleasantness of the work that follows; but no less welcome is its conclusion, which ends the discourse in blessing and life. How wise a lyre-player is this noble youth, in whose harmony the final notes answer the first with such consonant movement!

In this short psalm it is pleasing to behold that four-horse chariot of Israel, that new cart of David, upon which the ark of the covenant was borne toward Jerusalem amid trumpet-blast and rejoicing and every musical instrument. It is no new interpretation that David figuratively represents Christ, and the ark of the covenant the Church, which, amid the trumpet-blast of confession and the rejoicing of devotion, in the harmony of every virtue, makes for that heavenly Jerusalem, our mother. She is set upon a cart, whose four wheels are found in this psalm: a pair fixed at the very beginning of the psalm, and an equal pair divinely arranged near its conclusion. The two front wheels are goodness and pleasantness; the two rear wheels, life and blessing. Pleasantness has its seat in love of God; goodness, in love of neighbor. Life consists in the incorruption of the body, blessing in the integrity of the soul. We possess the first two in actuality; we hold the last two in hope. By this four-horse chariot, as by Elijah’s fiery chariot, we are carried away from the midst of vanity.

I think the Prophet spoke of this fiery chariot when he said: “Its wheels are burning fire” (Dan. 7). Is not love openly called fire where it is said, “Many waters cannot quench charity” (Song 8)? The author of charity himself, when he divided it into two commandments, established it as the twin wheels of his chariot and ours. I shall show from the following comparison why we have called the two rear wheels, incorruption and integrity, fiery.

Dionysius the Athenian asserts, in his book *On the Sacred Hierarchy*, that the heaven in which angels were created is called empyrean, that is, fiery. Yet it is called fiery not because of heat but because of brightness; whereas, conversely, Gehenna is called fiery not because of brightness but because of burning. For infernal spirits burn but are not illumined, while heavenly spirits shine but are not tormented: among those below there is burning heat without brightness, among those above fiery brightness without heat. In this very manner, our bodily incorruption and spiritual integrity are believed to be fiery in the future, when bodily brightness shall adorn the soul itself.

And lest this perhaps seem, to anyone less trained, as inappropriate as it is unfamiliar—that I call the soul fiery, or the flesh fiery, and thus call the integrity of the soul and the incorruption of the body inflamed—let him know that in the definitions of philosophers the soul itself is called fire, though invisible. To prove this, they have said that fire has two active properties: one soothing, the other destructive. The latter either kills or consumes that to which it adheres; the former is soothing, by which it cherishes and governs the substance joined to it. In accordance with this, they have not inappropriately, I think, defined the soul as fire: it soothes and nourishes its own body with a certain moderated heat, draws light to itself through the windows of the eyes as something like itself, and rejoices in and loves it.

Having thus proved by reason as well as authority that the wheels of which we are speaking are deservedly called fiery, I shall now assign the very form, parts, and composition of each; then join together the whole cart, and so conclude the proposed discourse on the four wheels.

[Col. 1580A]

II. First, concerning form. The form of a wheel is denoted by its circle itself, being derived, that is, from roundness, which, according to Jerome’s testimony, is shown to be the most beautiful of all figures. Yet, unless I am mistaken, this figure is not so much beautiful to look at as profound to understand; and I shall show that it is more useful to minds than delightful to eyes.

The Apostle says: “The invisible things of God are clearly seen, being understood through the things that are made” (Rom. 1). Fixing the eye of contemplation upon the totality of visible things, I find no image more clearly or closely proclaiming the eternity of the Creator than the form of roundness with which they are adorned, because in them neither beginning nor end can in any way be indicated. Therefore it seems to me that whatever is more beautiful, more lofty, or brighter in the world—for example, the sun, moon, globes of the stars, and the very structure beneath whose circumference every body, as they say, is contained—is fashioned in that form so that rational creation may understand through these things the immensity of its Maker.

I pass over the golden crowns, circles, little spheres, rings, and many other objects of Jewish observance made in this fashion, without which neither temple could be completed, nor tabernacle erected, nor altar, table, or ark carried, nor poles put in place, nor lampstand completed, nor breastpiece joined to the ephod. All these breathe forth mysteries and the perfection of the Church: now in part, now as a whole; at one time in the members, at another in the head; sometimes concerning the present, sometimes the future; most often concerning the flesh, sometimes concerning the soul; frequently setting forth riddles and figures concerning the whole human person. I judged that to speak of them one by one would be burdensome to the reader and the business of another work.

I come to the mysteries of the New Testament, which I understand to be deeper precisely because they are more worthy; and among them, that fearful, divine, and unique mystery: Christ’s body. It is customarily consecrated by the Fathers in no form other than a round one [Note: [Col. 1579D] Thus in Ernald’s time.], so that you may understand that not only the flesh without sin but also the Word, who remains and subsists in his eternity, is always offered to the Father in his flesh. I consider this understanding in the priest’s soul greatly conducive to the growth [Col. 1580D] of that love which is accustomed to make blessed souls capable of devotion.

I see also another memorable point in the circle of the sacrament: since “Galilean” is interpreted “revolving,” the one who sits upon the cherubim is to be understood as being the same one at the altar-table, whose wheels in Ezekiel are called revolving because of the Galilean who presides. Since, therefore, as may be gathered from what has been said, roundness is the sign of perfection, I call those four wheels appropriate and rational: because in the first two, namely love of God and neighbor, the perfection of religion is indicated; while in the other two, bodily incorruption and integrity of soul, the consummation of human blessedness is possessed. For the poet too, when attempting to describe a perfect human being, added in summary:

> “… wholly smooth and round.”  
> (Horace, *Satires*, bk. II, sat. 7, v. 85.)

Now, after the description of the form, let the discourse proceed to the parts of the wheels.

III. The integral parts of wheels are rims, spokes, and hubs. I wish therefore to assign to each wheel its own rims, its own spokes, and its proper hub.

The first wheel is love of God. This wheel has knowledge of God as its inner hub, from which proceed the distinct and manifold spokes of meditations. Around them are joined and fixed the multiform and innumerable rims of devotions, in which perfection is especially indicated.

The second wheel is love of neighbor. Its inner [Col. 1581B] hub is the virtue of mercy, from which proceed the spokes of compassion and brotherly kindness. Upon these, as many rims project outwardly as there are works of piety performed to support one’s neighbor.

The third wheel is integrity of soul. It is put together from the hub of perfect righteousness, the spokes of full knowledge, and the rims of consummate joy. The parts of this wheel, when placed separately, are of little use, wholly useless, or even harmful by departing from rectitude; but set together opposite one another and, as it were, brought into the composition of a single wheel, they restore our soul—as far as my understanding can investigate—to complete and consummate happiness.

For there are six impediments that either disfigure or punish every good of the soul. Our joy is apt to be unclean because of the neighboring tinder of desire, or suspect because of the weakness of another conscience. Our righteousness often becomes burdensome because of the body that corrupts and weighs down the soul, and undiscerning because of the inborn ignorance in us that cannot be overcome. Our knowledge often puffs us up through the vanity of vainglory, or makes us sad when we recognize our own weakness.

But when God is all in all, pride or sadness will no longer oppose our knowledge; heaviness or ignorance will no longer hinder righteousness; suspicion or desire will no longer begrudge joy. Then conscience will be humble because of righteousness and cheerful because of joy; righteousness easy because of joy and discerning because of knowledge; joy pure because of righteousness and without complaint because of knowledge.

The fourth wheel follows, which was above assigned as incorruptible. It likewise, as do the others, has its hub: undisturbed and immortal vitality. From it rises, as it were, a fivefold arrangement of spokes—the perfect integrity of the five senses—subtle and in every respect conformable to the spirit. Its outer rims are arranged in proportion of shape, size, quality, and brightness. There nothing will be deformed, superfluous, unsuitable, or dark; rather, in every respect the body of our humility shall be refashioned in conformity with the body of divine glory, so that the promise may be fulfilled [Col. 1582A] in which it is said: “The righteous shall shine as the sun in the kingdom of their Father” (Matt. 13).

The composition of the wheels having been assigned as intended, we must now put together the joining of the cart itself. It must necessarily have at least three elements: two axles joining the four wheels, and the framework to which the two axles are attached at opposite ends.

IV. Thus in the front part, which is directed toward heaven, those two wheels—the integrity of the soul and the incorruption of the body—are joined by that peace of God which surpasses all understanding. I understand this peace itself to be none other than the power and wisdom of God, Christ Jesus. “He is our peace, who makes both one” (Eph. 2), so that the flesh no longer lusts against the spirit, nor the spirit against [Col. 1582B] the flesh; because “nation shall not lift sword against nation, neither shall they learn war any more.” Rather, there shall be Sabbath and everlasting rest in the city whose name is “The Lord Is There.”

We await the possession in reality of all these things—indeed, things far greater than human understanding can now grasp—which we already possess wholly in hope. For through hope we hold almost all things already, as the Apostle says: “We were saved in hope” (Rom. 8). We have already received the first-fruits of this peace, when no punishment inflicted by hostile power and no trouble from the corruption we bear can disturb us from the repose that is in Christ Jesus, while the Spirit helps our weakness.

V. In the rear of this cart, the twofold set of wheels—love of God and love of neighbor—is coupled by the axle of right intention, since this makes God loved chastely, that is, for his sake alone, and one’s neighbor loved purely, that is, for God’s sake. From the middle of this axle proceeds hope, which reaches all the way to Christ and thus continues and joins the entire cart.

Upon this sits the ark of the covenant, that is, the soul of any righteous person. It contains within itself the golden urn full of manna when it holds in memory Christ, the human being full of grace and truth; it contains the tablets of the covenant, in which the knowledge of God’s commandments is received; and Aaron’s rod that has flowered, namely the sweet recollection of blessed Mary joined with reverence.

And lest this ark easily fall from this cart, it must be supported by a fourfold wall: before it, longing for Christ’s presence; behind it, contempt for the world; on the left, fortitude against adversities; on the right, restraint amid prosperities. The oxen that draw this cart are all the ministering angels sent to serve on behalf of the ark of the covenant, so that it may receive the inheritance of salvation. These oxen, under the yoke of social concord joined to the pole of divine power, and firmly bound by the bonds of human charity, lead the ark of God to heavenly Zion, to the Jerusalem above, our mother.

What we read—that the oxen kicked, the ark tilted, and a priest seeking to raise it up perished through presumption (2 Sam. 6)—understand in this way: the soul must be exercised by temptations. As it goes about through the squares and streets of the city, perhaps seeking to find [Col. 1583A] the beloved, assaults are made upon it through good angels; the guards of the walls strike and wound it and take away its cloak, so that they may know whether it bears the naked beauty of virtue, whether it seeks its friend deceptively or in truth. Thus she sometimes, in the fervor of spirit, passes even beyond the guards, lest, overcome by difficulties, she discover by experience that “love is strong as death, jealousy hard as hell” (Song 8).

At other times, however, it is bent down like the ark of the covenant: humbled and cast down because it cannot bear the weight of glory, yet not crushed; bowed, yet not prostrate, because it is not received, as though weakened, upon the soft bed of a pure conscience. If anyone thinks that he belongs to the chosen race, the royal priesthood, let him not presume to place beneath this soul a support made of his own false virtue; let him not presume to rebuke one better than himself; let him in no way grieve a soul filled with God, lest indignation arise and presumption be confounded. For whoever touches such a soul is like one touching the pupil of God’s eye—God, who always hates presumption and pride and gives grace and glory to the meek, through all ages of ages. Amen.

## HOMILY V. On the definition of place and its many divisions; then on the place of penitence and solitude. Just as in the preceding homily he was carried away from the text into David’s cart, so here too, leaving the text aside, he wanders through various discussions.

I. I have heard very many mutually discordant and widely differing accounts concerning the description of place. If I wished [Col. 1583C] to compare and collect them all into one, I should seem to introduce material for disputation and contention rather than seek truth. Therefore, taking occasion from this passage, I shall attempt to explain what seems to me correct and whom I more nearly agree with, if indeed I can in any way make known what I think.

I judge “place” to be whatever it is in which something is in any manner; and when something is said to be in something, that in which it is is the place of what is in it. To make this clearer, this genus must be divided into its species, because every matter is better understood through division. One place is corporeal, another incorporeal; one simple, another composite. Composite place is either solid or mathematical. Incorporeal place is divided into imaginable, intelligible, affective, accidental, potential, natural, personal, and intellectible. Again, intellectible place is either imperfect or consummate. The consummate is either higher or lower; the imperfect is either dark, shadowy, bright, or luminous.

In all these I say nothing concerning the place which dialecticians call a “seat,” concerning which there is a long discussion and manifold division, entirely to be omitted here. Having therefore made this division of place through certain of its species, I now wish to run from the first to the last, so that I may make known what is this place of which we are speaking.

II. Simple corporeal place is the simple capacity of any body, as are drops that pass through the pores [Col. 1584A] of the human body, so small that, according to natural philosophers, bodily nature can possess nothing tinier. Corporeal simples are those that cannot be cut into parts, such as a unison, an atom, and similar things—all of which are properly and naturally called indivisibles.

I say “naturally” because “individual” is used in three ways: by solidity, as a diamond; by subjection to a species, as this hand; by smallness, as an *osonum* [reading uncertain]. Only that seems naturally and properly to be called indivisible which cannot be cut either by iron, like a hand; by art, like a diamond; or in any other way.

Some say that bodies of this kind do not possess quantity, nor division either, because, according to Aristotle, every quantity seems to be composite. [Col. 1584B] He divides quantity into continuous and discrete; and, defining both, he says that one has parts joined at a common boundary, while the other likewise has parts but not joined at a common boundary. Hence they infer that a simple body does not admit quantity; otherwise it could now be divided into parts and would thus be deprived of simplicity.

I do not agree that such a body is without quantity; rather, I think Aristotle gave his description not of simple quantity but only of composite quantity. Every body, then, admits quantity; therefore so does the place of a body, since judgment concerning place is made only in relation to body.

III. Composite and solid corporeal place is that empty space containing any such body to which height, breadth, and length can be assigned according to a definite measure, as with a chest and similar things. Mathematical place is any capacity within whose bounds is contained such a body as cannot be described at all in terms of height and breadth, or any other dimension: sound, voice, noise, whistle, and many similar things. These are called mathematical, that is, scientific.

IV.
