Incorporeal place is the manner in which any incorporeal thing is in something: imaginatively, as a chimera in thought; intelligibly, as genus in species; affectively, as love in the mind; accidentally, as righteousness in a person; potentially, [Col. 1584D] as an angel in a visible form; naturally, as surface in color; personally, as soul in its own flesh; or intellectibly, as a created spirit in the Creator Spirit.

The imaginable, according to the *Timaeus*, is what human thought perceives only with some phantasm. The intelligible is what reason beholds purely and without an image. The affective is whatever concerns desire, and is an inclination whose definition is: a vehement application to doing something with great will. The accidental, which may also be called adventitious, is that which, according to Augustine’s testimony, brings some change to the thing to which it happens, and may be present or absent without corruption of the subject. The potential is what, by a power innate to itself, can alter the usual course of nature. The natural is what, not exceeding the bounds of its customary and ancient course, endures from the beginning according to its institution. The personal is what represents in itself an individual of rational substance. The intellectible is that alone which is available for enjoyment to every good understanding and to it alone. Intellectibility is assigned to this alone; the other incorporeal substances are called intelligible.

V. Therefore intellectible place is the condition of any rational substance in relation to God. This condition, or place, is one thing in knowledge and another in love; and perfect knowledge of that Good can never exist without perfect love. Hence intellectible place is found either imperfect, as in human beings, or consummate, as in heavenly spirits.

Note that, just as corporeal place is judged according to body, so intellectible place is judged according to the measure of knowledge or love: that is, Michael the archangel is said to have one relation or place in God, and any being lower or higher in those orders another. Though all are perfect in knowledge without any deficiency, one is nevertheless more blessed than another and another lower in the same knowledge—not, I say, more imperfect, just as one circle is smaller than another but not more imperfect.

Since, then, they are perfect in knowledge, it follows that they are perfect in love also. For although some knowledge of that Good can exist without love, no love of it can exist without some knowledge of it; and in every devout understanding these two are joined in equal measure, where, according to Gregory’s testimony, love itself is knowledge. But because it will be easy to dispute about that abyss of love and knowledge only when, as promised, human substance has been translated to equality with the angels, I prefer to desire and hope for their perfection rather than define it. Therefore I am pleased to approach that intellectible place which is called imperfect, because it is easier to discuss and perhaps more useful to investigate.

VI. The imperfect, as assigned above, is divided into dark, shadowy, bright, and luminous. The dark has no love; the shadowy has much fear; the bright is somewhat mingled with love and fear; the luminous, all fear excluded, [Col. 1585D] is illumined by love alone. The first belongs to proud persons beyond correction; the second, to converts and beginners; the third, to those who have advanced and are advancing; it alone receives those who pass beyond.

The proud person is in darkness and walks in darkness, and does not know where he goes, because darkness has blinded his eyes. Yet insofar as he has even the slightest knowledge of God, he has an intellectible place, though one full of darkness. For “the light shines in darkness”; therefore it is an intellectible place. But “the darkness did not comprehend it”; therefore the place is darkened and terrible.

For every proud person who, like Pharaoh, has hardened his heart is convicted of impiety and commits wickedness against God. By a miserable likeness he becomes a member of him who first wickedly desired equality [Col. 1586A] with God and now opposes and exalts himself above everything called God or worshiped. Since the impious person, in imitation of him, is proud all the days of his life and his pride continually rises, while God resists the proud and humbles everyone arrogant, a great chasm has certainly been fixed between darkness and light. It is in no way permitted for anyone to pass from here to there, or from there to here.

For since God is light and there is no darkness in him, he has made darkness his hiding place for these people and dwells in inaccessible light; so that it is now rightly proclaimed in terrible terms: “Let the impious be taken away, lest he see the glory of God; for he shall not see light for ever” (Isa. 26).

VII. Alas for the blindness of the human heart, through which it has come about that there is now little or almost no difference between demons and human children of darkness! And—what is worse—they have not known nor understood that they walk in darkness; indeed, they turn away their faces lest they see to the end, stopping their ears like asps, lest perhaps they hear and understand and likewise reflect on that divine saying: “Return to your heart, you transgressors” (Isa. XLVI). But will they never hear, or never understand? They certainly will hear and understand, but fruitlessly, when, according to the prophet, “vexation alone shall give understanding to the hearing” (Isa. XXVIII). For they will not always, like madmen, mock these inward darknesses; rather, they shall be cast out into the outer darkness, where the Lord will crush them with a twofold breaking, because “they have provoked thee doubly, O Lord, by their vanities.” For they rejoice when they have done evil, and exult in the worst things—evil in deed, but most evil in thought. Although they gratify their own desire in many things, they can never fulfil what they desire; therefore, corrupted in flesh and corrupted also in soul, they must be clothed, as with a double garment, in their own shame.

To thee alone I give thanks, good Jesus, who didst bring me, thy guilty one, out of the darkness of that pride and swollen obstinacy—by a strong hand and an outstretched arm, through the waters of mighty temptation—into the wilderness of laborious repentance: a place of affliction, a place of fear. This is the place that was shortly before called gloomy and possessing much fear. I do not wish to pass over it so quickly or to confine my discourse within too narrow a compass, because in the book of experience I have read much concerning it, and for a long time I clung wholly to it with intense application.

In this place tribulation and anguish found me; the pains of eternal death surrounded me; and my roaring was like flooding waters, because the Lord, draining my spirit, enclosed me as an abyss and covered my head as a sea. Alas—an abyss of fear proceeding from three other abysses: namely, the abyss of sins, the abyss of judgments, and the abyss of infernal torments. In the abyss of sin the worm lies hidden, insatiably feeding always upon the conscience. In the abyss of God’s judgments an irrevocable sentence awaits. Woe to the wretch for whom the third abyss waits, where the fire is unquenchable! Thus the abyss of my sin called upon the abyss of God’s judgments, each abyss plunging the sinner into the abyss of everlasting destruction.

VIII. At this most dreadful consideration I was terrified, and all my bones were troubled; and I said: “I shall utterly not see, I shall not see the Lord God in the land of the living. But I shall descend to the gates of hell, and all that is mine shall descend into the deepest hell” (Job XVII). Thus day by day my soul dwelt in hell, and, like the ungodly man, at every moment I was cast away from before the eyes of God, so that the unhappy soul was often compelled to burst out in that cry: “I have despaired; I shall no longer live.”

All this, good Jesus, was wrought by the voice of thy cataracts: the voice of thy hidden, manifold, terrible inspirations. By this voice, O Lord, thou didst shake the earth and trouble it. This voice was like the sound of many waters, like the voice of God Most High; like a violent wind breaking the ships of Tarshish; like a great and strong wind—and truly great and strong, because it overturns the mountains of pride and breaks the rocks of obstinacy before the Lord. “The Lord was not in the wind; and after the wind, an earthquake” (III Kings XIX): for the earth was shaken and trembled, because the Lord looked upon the earth and made it tremble and move toward repentance. “The Lord was not in the earthquake; and after the earthquake, fire” (ibid.): fire, namely, the fire of the Lord’s zeal devouring all the earth; fire kindled in the wrath of the Lord and burning unto the lowest depths of hell, where the ungodly man shall lie badly lulled asleep amid darkness. The Lord was not in the fire.

Where then is the Lord? Is he in the noise of so great a crushing, shaking, and disturbance? No: “his place was made in peace” (Ps. LXXV). For after the great and strong wind, after the earthquake, after the fire, behold, “the whisper of a gentle breeze” (ibid.): that is, the subtle inspiration of divinity, known to few. Like a gentle breeze, sweet and beneficial, it blows through and makes fruitful the garden of the spiritual conscience, so that the fragrances of most pure meditation may flow forth and not flow away. This whisper is wholly unknown to those who are beginning repentance; nor is it much customary or familiar to those making moderate progress, because it is very closely related to those who are soaring on high.

[Col. 1587D] IX. Therefore I should rightly call the place of initial repentance cloudy, dark, or troubled, where the Lord is not seen and the light and glory of the people Israel do not appear. But what is there? Fire, sulphur, and the spirit of storms: the portion of the cup of those worthy of death—hell-fire, the sulphur of sin, and the spirit of storms of divine judgment. For in that unhappy conscience the day of the Lord, the day of judgment, is already being enacted as though present. The Judge appears already immoderately offended; the world is already burning; sentence is pronounced; Tartarus is opened. That day does not depart from thought; it cannot be torn from memory: the day of wrath, the day of tribulation and anguish, the day of calamity and misery, the day of cloud and whirlwind, the day of trumpet and blast.

Wrath proclaims and reveals God the offended Judge, whom no one can endure even when he is appeased; tribulation refers to the torment of the accusing conscience; anguish, to the fearful expectation of that terrible sentence; calamity, to the damnation prepared for evil spirits; misery, to the joining of human beings with those same demons. The withdrawal of the luminaries will produce darkness; the stormy agitation of the stirred-up air, gloom; the conflagration of the whole world will raise a cloud; and the confusion of all the elect, a whirlwind. The trumpet belongs to the ministry of angels; the blast, to the onslaught and overthrow of all the ungodly. When these have been taken away, the angels shall fear and, terrified, shall be purified. If therefore the angels shall fear, if the righteous man is scarcely saved, where shall I appear—ungodly toward God, unjust toward my neighbour, a murderer of myself? Whither shall I go from the spirit of my Judge, and whither shall I flee from his face? No one can evade him, no one resist him, no one deceive him, no one corrupt him; for he himself is everywhere, is almighty, and is supremely good.

Therefore I meditated in the night with my heart; I consulted reason; I addressed my conscience concerning what must be done. And while my spirit was distressed and my thoughts troubled me, the Spirit of counsel came near and whispered in my ears that our God is himself the God of salvation, “a fountain opened for the washing of sin and of the menstruous woman,” and “a rock, a refuge for hedgehogs”; that “he was wounded for our iniquities, bruised for our crimes, and by his bruise we have been healed.” Therefore everyone who believes in him shall not be put to shame; faith itself shall be reckoned to him for righteousness, because he in whom we believe bore our sins in his body upon the tree. I understood that this counsel was not the counsel of Ahithophel, David’s enemy, but the counsel of Hushai—whose name signifies “silence”—that is, of the Holy Spirit, who teaches a person knowledge without the noise of words.

X. On hearing the messenger’s voice, my spirit immediately revived; and, as though awakening from a heavy sleep, I began to leave that place of cloud and darkness. Then the Lord said, “Let there be light”; and there was light (Gen. I), because while I dwelt in the region of the shadow of death, light arose for me. “And there was evening and morning, the first day” (ibid.). Not morning and evening, but evening and morning: because “that which is spiritual” is not first, “but that which is natural; afterward that which is spiritual.” Before this day—the day of kindness, the day of consolation—I could not at all understand that God had created my heaven and earth, my soul and my body, “in the beginning,” precisely in order to work exceedingly good works in these two and to prove to me, not by arguments but by deeds, that he is the one “who alone does great wonders” (Ps. CXXXV).

For even before these wonders, my earth was “void and empty” (Gen. I): void, because it was wholly given over to vanity through temporal glory, rejoicing not in the living God but in vain and inflated discourses, arguments, sophistries, and such things; this was my portion in the days of my vanity. My earth was also empty, because everything in it had been emptied out even to its foundation; no good, no grace, remained in it, except only this: that God’s creature could not fail to exist. And darkness was upon the face of that inward abyss, upon the face of the sinful conscience, like the veil upon Moses’ face; for my foolish heart was darkened, my mind and conscience defiled, and I was unable to see. Yet “the Spirit of God moved upon the waters” (Gen. I), as one merciful and compassionate, governing the waters of my fluctuation and instability, lest I flow wholly away and perish.

XI. “And God saw the light, that it was good” (ibid.): the light of his visitation, the light of my illumination; and he divided it from the darkness, so that Christ may now have no participation with Belial, nor light any fellowship with darkness. He called this light day: the person who walks in it does not stumble. And he called that darkness night, because no one can work in it. Thus one day, the first day, was made: one, because that duality which first departed from unity has no part in this day; first, because in the order of penitential progress there are six days of divine operation through which one passes to the Sabbath of contemplation. This is the first of those days, having an evening of fear and a morning of consolation; and on this first day a person begins to enter that intelligible place which I called luminous.

Now, lest I expose my simplicity to the mockery of those who seem to be something, and who, when they hear something new, either deride and distort it according to the standing of the speaker, or spread it abroad with favourable report to the stars—not because it has been well or badly said, but because it has been produced by such-and-such a person—let such a one know that I called these places “intelligible” in relation to the grace of the Divinity toward which, and into which, one tends through them. Therefore they ought not to appear absurd or presumptuously stated, since among ecclesiastical teachers I find Christ the Lord called a certain blessed region, in which, according to the diversity of souls, a different character of dwelling-places may indeed be understood. Hence Augustine’s saying: “Beyond all controversy, God himself is a certain region of the soul’s blessedness.”

Therefore, now that Christ has mercifully allowed me to enter this place by the journey of one day, I desire to hasten onward; and the will lies ready for me to proceed in order through the remaining days, until the Sabbath, where alone and especially one is granted leisure, Sabbath-rest, and the sight that the Lord is sweet—he who lives and reigns through all ages of ages. Amen.

[Col. 1589]

# A Little Book of Abbot Ernald on the Gifts of the Holy Spirit

(Galland, *Bibliotheca Veterum Patrum*, vol. XIV, p. 496.)

## Prologue

[Col. 1589C]

Let no one, on seeing these chapters, expect to read a treatment of God’s wisdom according to what is written: “Thou hast made all things in wisdom” (Ps. CIII); and again: “She reaches mightily from end to end, and orders all things sweetly” (Wis. VIII). Nor [should he expect a treatment] of understanding according to what is written: “Thou hast understood my thoughts from afar” (Ps. CXXXVIII); or of counsel according to that saying: “The counsel of the Lord stands for ever” (Ps. XXXII), and “Who has known the mind of the Lord, or who has been his counsellor?” (Isa. XL); or even of knowledge, such as that in: “Behold, O Lord, thou hast known all things,” etc.; “Thy knowledge has become wonderful to me; it has been strengthened, and I shall not be able to attain unto it” (Ps. CXXXVIII).

For I, knowing my measure, yield a treatment of such matters to men endowed with prophetic and apostolic grace, being content to treat, though in slender language, of that measure of spiritual gifts which the Apostle commended when he said: “To one is given by the Spirit the word of wisdom; to another, the word of knowledge” (I Cor. XII). If anyone is offended when he reads that knowledge is referred to humility, let him remember that I am speaking of that Spirit of knowledge who rested upon Christ. For before Christ’s coming there existed in the world knowledge of letters, knowledge of the liberal arts, and other kinds of knowledge; only the knowledge of perfect humility was lacking. A man, deceived by the devil through the knowledge of good and evil, and puffed up by that very knowledge, did not know how to humble himself before man; nor did he know how before God. Therefore God, made man, humbled himself before man even to washing his feet, and humbled himself before God the Father even to obedience unto death; and God made man taught man to humble himself before God, and to humble himself before both man and God.

But man, because he did not humble himself before God, became wretched and mortal; if, however, he humbles himself, he will become blessed and immortal. Great, therefore, is the knowledge by which a person is taught to humble himself before God: for he is taught to escape misery and death; and unless he escapes these, no knowledge will profit him. It is not, therefore, absurd to refer Christ’s knowledge to humility. Though in him “all the treasures of wisdom and knowledge are hidden” (Col. II), he nevertheless wished that this should be learned from himself in a special way.

If anyone thinks that I have said nothing worthy of so great a subject, neither do I deny it. I shall at least have provided an occasion for someone to speak better, if the same Spirit gives it to him. But if anyone is pleased with what has been said, I ask him to pray for the one who has said it. It is pleasant to me, most devout and beloved brother, to comply with your pious desire and, though unlearned, to speak with you from the holy Scriptures. Hence I have presumed to promise you matters beyond my strength, since through love for you I delight to converse with you. For to treat of the gifts of the Holy Spirit belongs to a spiritual man, and one acquainted with divine things ought to speak of divine things. Yet because our hope is in God, he who makes the torrents of great rivers overflow can also let something trickle down into our little spring—something which your holy thirst may not draw as a great abundance, but should not deem wholly to be poured away.

# Chapter I. On Wisdom and Understanding

I. There are, then, four gifts of the Holy Spirit—namely wisdom and understanding, counsel and knowledge—so closely related to one another that they seem almost to be one thing. You wished these to be treated in such a manner that each might be made clear in what it differs from the others. It seemed good, in the common treatment, not to omit the other three gifts entirely, but to introduce each of them as the subject required, in its own place and order.

II. There have been men whom God’s wisdom deigned to honour so greatly that, although themselves mortal, through them it made immortality known to mortals of its own; it issued commandments, promised rewards, threatened punishments, and declared ordinances. Such was Moses, such Job, then Solomon, John the Baptist, Paul the Apostle, and any others like them. These, then, whom God’s wisdom valued so greatly as to introduce them without a human mediator into its inner sanctuary and make them its familiars, were enlightened and glorified by the spirit of wisdom.

There were likewise men of lesser, yet still great, grace, who, aided by the Holy Spirit, merited sublimely and divinely to understand those familiars of wisdom. Using them, as it were, as guides and mediators, they too entered wisdom’s chamber and attained its familiarity, though on a nearly equal level. Those, therefore, who merited to penetrate those first familiars of wisdom with an eye of understanding clearer than that of others were enriched by the spirit of understanding.

But because men of such wisdom now either do not exist at all, or at least are exceedingly rare—although no wise person would say that the spirit of wisdom has deserted the Church, especially when Scripture says, “A multitude of wise men is the health of the world” (Wis. VI)—it seems that wisdom should be discussed in a somewhat more human fashion, so to speak. Therefore, since Scripture says:

> **[Note: Col. 1591.]** He appears, it seems, to allude to Eccl. I.26: “The beginning of wisdom is the fear of the Lord.”

“Behold, *theosebia*—that is, the worship of God—is wisdom itself”: whoever worships God with right intention and devout diligence, I believe, is truly wise and is guided by the spirit of understanding. Yet how many there are who worship God piously and holily, while not perceiving God’s invisible things understood through the things that have been made, nor discerning his eternal power and divinity, cannot, I think, readily be estimated. The vast number of God’s simple servants proves it; the abundant fruitfulness of that Leah who prefigured for us the active life bears witness to it.

Therefore, just as it is evident that these persons excel in the spirit of wisdom precisely because they do not savour earthly things and run in thirst to the fountain of wisdom, so it is apparent that they do not excel in the spirit of understanding, either because they do not penetrate the obscurities of Scripture or because they do not understand the Creator from his creatures. But when the Lord reveals to any of them the things veiled in Scripture—for Rachel also, though she bore very few—then, with the spirit of understanding added to the spirit of wisdom, they increase and are enriched.

Yet it should be noted in this distinction that wisdom, although it may appear less exalted, is found more useful; and understanding, although judged more exalted, is proved inferior. For in the writings of the Fathers we find that heretics have wonderfully understood and expounded certain depths of Scripture; and the Apostle testifies that philosophers, through the things that have been made, have perceived God’s invisible things, understood them, and known God. Yet he himself rebukes them because afterward they erred shamefully and fell so far as to worship the creature.

The Psalmist does not simply say, “Blessed is he who understands” (Ps. XL), but adds, “the needy and poor” (ibid.), declaring that understanding profits only if it bends itself toward humility, if it does not conceal its inner poverty, and if it loves to sympathize with and serve Christ’s poor. And when he asked God for understanding for himself, saying, “Give me understanding” (Ps. CXVIII), he immediately added, “that I may learn thy commandments” (ibid.). Elsewhere also, speaking of understanding, he pronounced it good not simply in itself (Ps. CX), but “for all who practise it” (ibid.).

The wisdom of which we speak, however, is so good that it makes all its followers good, and no one becomes good except through it. It alone, without this understanding, suffices for salvation; whereas understanding itself, unless directed by wisdom, draws one farther from salvation. These things may perhaps seem contrary to what I said shortly before: that when those endowed with the spirit of wisdom receive the spirit of understanding, they increase and are enriched. Yet they are not contrary. If a great quantity of silver is given to one who possesses gold, his wealth is certainly augmented and increased. Nor, because we value wisdom more highly, do we deny that understanding is a great good. Would that every person understood, so as to act well!

# Chapter II. On Counsel, insofar as Scripture distinguishes it into Commandment and Counsel

Thus far concerning wisdom and understanding; let us now speak of counsel. Useful counsel is a precious thing: salutary to its giver, fitting for those set in authority, and necessary for those in tribulation. In Scripture some things are according to God’s commandment and others according to counsel: according to counsel, that we renounce earthly possessions; according to commandment, that, content with marriage, we do not commit adultery; according to counsel, that, touching no woman, we remain virgins; according to commandment, that we not be weighed down by drunken revelry nor intoxicated with wine; according to counsel, that we eat no flesh and drink no wine.

There are many among the laity who faithfully worship God by keeping his commandments, yet do not rise to counsel. These, therefore, possess the spirit of wisdom but do not receive the spirit of counsel. We see others advance so far in the spirit of understanding that they not only understand the depths of Scripture themselves, but also convey them for others to understand; and thus, because they teach divine things, they are now commonly called “divines.” Yet they shrink so much from the counsel to scatter their wealth and give to the poor that—alas, miserable men!—they violently twist the spiritual gift of understanding which they have received toward the acquisition of carnal riches. They read and expound: “If riches increase, do not set your heart upon them” (Ps. LXI). And by the very fact that they read and expound this, they set their heart upon having riches increase for themselves. These, therefore, have the spirit of understanding but lack the spirit of counsel.

There are others who, inspired by the spirit of wisdom and understanding, lift themselves also toward the spirit of counsel, yet are depressed by a certain fearfulness and sloth, or weakness of spirit. Hence the spirit of fortitude is rightly introduced after the spirit of counsel, because truly great fortitude is necessary for one to ascend the mountain of the Lord not merely to the slopes of the commandments, but even to the summit of counsel.

# Chapter III. Again on Counsel, namely insofar as the Spirit of Counsel Is Necessary for Those Who Must Give Counsel to Others

I. Thus far we have discussed the spirit of counsel insofar as counsel is received; and we have appended a very few words concerning the spirit of fortitude, as required by its place. Let us now consider counsel insofar as it is given. It must be understood that we need the counsel of the Holy Spirit not only in order to know what knowledge is, but also so that, from the things we know, those things necessary at the appropriate moment may occur to us.

Therefore, after we have received the spirit of knowledge in order sincerely to worship God, and after we have merited the spirit of understanding to penetrate the mysteries of Scripture, it remains for us, when counsel is sought from us, first prudently to know how to assess the character, condition, and calling of the person seeking it. Then, aided by the spirit of counsel, we must draw from the breadth of Scripture such counsel as may benefit the hearer and injure no one else. Next, we must support the judgment we have ventured to offer by examples from Scripture, by the strength of reason, or by the fitting of analogies, until the inquirer is satisfied.

We must also adapt our own feelings to the feeling of the other person: whether a cheerful person finds us sad, or a sad person cheerful, when he sees us rejoicing with the cheerful or suffering with the sad, he may believe our counsel to be faithful, and thus more readily yield and assent. Unless a suitable person is aided in this by the spirit of counsel, you may sometimes see a man endowed with the spirit of wisdom and understanding fall silent when counsel is requested of him, burdened by a certain heaviness of mind, and unable to offer the hearer anything welcome or acceptable. You may see that very same person at another time offer sound counsel, illuminate it with examples from Scripture, demonstrate it by an abundance of reasoning, and strengthen it with appropriately fitted analogies.

Whence comes this difference in one and the same person? Unless it is because the spirit of counsel, according to merits known to itself alone in speaker and hearer, and according to the counsels of its own height known to itself alone, now restrains and now sends forth its efficacy. I believe the spirit of counsel is also necessary for our expressing counsel itself so modestly and suitably that the very manner of presenting it may serve as a good seasoning for the counsel offered.

But if the matter on which counsel is sought is such that its counsel is not contained in divine Scripture, then by the spirit of counsel one must find such counsel as is not found contrary to divine Scripture. For it is not unbelievable that God’s wisdom wished, in the holy Scriptures, to provide counsel for so many and such great occurrences of human misery, in order thereby to reserve its own place for the spirit of counsel. For when one person gives counsel to another, peace and concord among people—and thereby salvation and benefit—increase.

Finally, since it is written, “Our Lord is great, and great is his power; and of his wisdom there is no number” (Ps. CXLVI), it seems to follow that all God’s wisdom cannot be contained in Scriptures of whatever size. Rather, it is credible that there always remains something of it that may be written, because it itself can be comprehended by no writing. If these things are so, God’s wisdom knew both how to abound abundantly in manifold counsels in the sacred Scriptures and yet to reserve its own place for the spirit of counsel. Hence we see even some who are ignorant of letters give good and sound counsel.

Solomon certainly had read the Law and excelled above the sons of men in the spirit of wisdom and understanding; yet, as we read, he did everything by the counsel of certain elders, doubtless exploring what answer the spirit of counsel would draw forth for him from its hidden place—that is, from the breasts of the elders. Let these things, then, benefit us in this: that no one, even if he worships God through religious living—which is the mark of the wise person—or penetrates the obscurities of Scripture—which is the mark of understanding—should presume to despise counsel as though he did not need it.

Certainly, those who give counsel from the divine Scriptures must know that not everything is said to everyone in those Scriptures, but that many of their statements are to be understood fittingly according to differences of persons or times. For example, when the Lord says, “When they persecute you in this city, flee into another” (Matt. X), whoever should wish this to be a universal command, one that no one may omit, would accuse Stephen, the first and chief martyr among all martyrs, of transgression because he did not flee, but by standing magnanimously was gloriously crowned. He would also accuse the apostles themselves, those outstanding rams of the Lord’s flock, who are reported, during the same persecution, not to have yielded by flight amid so great a storm, while the others were scattered throughout the regions of Judaea and Samaria, but to have stood firm by remaining. Yet who would fail to see what great rashness this would be?

We must therefore understand that this command to flee was given to the weak and to those unequal to the contest of martyrdom; or at least to the preachers of that time who, when the Jews rejected the word of the Lord and judged themselves unworthy of eternal life, turned to the Gentiles. Therefore, if in a time of persecution someone, driven by a spirit of recklessness or rashness, asks whether he should flee or undergo the contest, and you urge him to undertake it, while he proves insufficient and denies Christ, beware lest by your counsel you have destroyed one for whom Christ died. If some true athlete of Christ seeks counsel, but you discourage him and persuade him rather to flee, your counsel takes the crown from his head.

Likewise, if you rashly urge anyone to renounce the world, and he, looking back, either returns altogether to his vomit or at least makes his life and conduct a grief and persecution to good brothers, you must repent of your counsel, because the spirit of counsel did not govern it. Therefore the spirit of counsel is necessary even for those who, through the spirit of understanding, have merited to penetrate the holy Scriptures, so that they may know prudently how to distribute food from them to their fellow servants, to each according to his own strength.

I think that Naomi in the book of Ruth, not without the spirit of counsel, persuaded her daughters-in-law, when they wished to follow her, to return to their own people, lest, following her from shame rather than judgment, they soon repent of having followed. She was unwilling to promise them perpetual consolation, but preferred to urge their return to their own people—although the unfaithful and inconstant daughter-in-law lost herself. Thus, thus, aided by that spirit of counsel and trusting in the counsel, the daughter-in-law was wholly saved and rejoiced in the consolation of her own people. If many prelates of our time both knew and wished to preserve this discernment in receiving brothers, they would serve God with fewer indeed, but in peace. “One who fears God,” says Wisdom, “is better than a thousand ungodly children” (Ecclus. XVI).

II. The spirit of counsel is very properly placed after the spirit of wisdom and understanding, because whoever lacks either of these will be unfit to give counsel. For one who is truly wise by worshipping God, if he does not understand the dispensations of Scripture, may judge everything according to the fervour of his own devotion and be deceived in counselling. Likewise, one who understands the Scriptures, unless he is wise by loving and worshipping God, will find it difficult in giving counsel to persuade another to do what he himself does not love. It remains, therefore, that one who lacks the spirit of wisdom and understanding should not claim the spirit of counsel for himself.

But one who possesses the spirit of counsel must also be strengthened by the spirit of fortitude, so that, if he has given someone good counsel and adversity arises from it, he may not be broken, but, trusting in the Lord, may act courageously until the good counsel is brought to effect. If, however, he is not listened to in his counsel, he must no less be governed by the spirit of fortitude, lest, becoming faint-hearted like Ahithophel, he who gave counsel to others should perish by acting without counsel toward himself.

# Chapter IV. That the Spirit of Counsel Especially Befits Prelates

Certainly Scripture teaches that the spirit of counsel especially befits prelates, saying: “Ask thy father, and he will declare it to thee” (Deut. XXXII). Because they become known to many through the very marks of their good qualities, many seek counsel from them. In the Old Testament, indeed, God was consulted and answered in many ways and by many modes; but now, rather, counsel for so numerous a people of God rests with its prelates. Therefore the spirit of counsel must flourish especially in prelates.

Let one who is insufficient to give counsel to others at least possess the spirit of counsel in this: that he seek counsel from a wise person and trust it once sought. But if he disdains to do this, that evangelical saying remains: “If the blind lead the blind, both fall into the pit” (Matt. XVI); and this: “If the light that is in thee be darkness, how great shall that darkness be!” (Matt. VI). Yet because the Lord enlightens the blind, let him approach the Lord and say from all his heart: “My God, enlighten my darknesses!” (Ps. XVII).

# Chapter V. That the Work of Counsel Is Most Necessary for Those in Tribulation
In those who are in tribulation, counsel is most necessary, lest, overcome by the troubles of their very tribulations, they do something rash and thereby offend God, and so bring upon themselves still greater tribulations, not only in the present but also in the future. Yet there is one counsel for those in tribulation: “Call upon me in the day of tribulation, and I will deliver you, and you shall glorify me” (Ps. 49 [Vulgate]). But because he invokes God in vain with his voice who provokes him by living wickedly, then especially one must devote oneself to correcting one’s life, according to the saying: “Tribulation and distress have found me; your commandments are my meditation” (Ps. 118 [Vulgate]). It is difficult—indeed impossible—that one who is in tribulation, if he faithfully calls upon God and appeases his face by the sacrifice of righteousness, should fail to deserve divine consolation. Only let him not lose patience. “In the day,” he says, “of my tribulation I sought God; by night my hands were stretched out toward him, and I was not deceived” (Ps. 76 [Vulgate]).

But some fail unless they are quickly delivered, like those of whom it is written: “They acted quickly; they forgot his works; they did not await his counsel” (Ps. 105 [Vulgate]). They do not at all attend to the fact that blessed Jacob remained long in grievous mourning, and that holy David was tested by frequent tribulations succeeding one another. Tobias also, so just and pious—and, according to the interpretation of his name, “good of the Lord”—according to certain copies, endured blindness for fourteen years. It is also useful for those in tribulation to remember that tribulation does not fail the servants of God, established only in this present world, wherever they may be. Hence blessed Peter says: “Knowing that the same suffering is being accomplished in your brotherhood throughout the world” (1 Pet. 5).

For some, when placed in tribulations, think to heal themselves by changing their location; but such a remedy is unreliable and sometimes turns to the contrary. For we know places in which peace and religion had formerly flourished but which were afterward filled with scandals and sorrows, so that in them that saying of blessed Job was fulfilled: “The earth from which bread sprang up in its place was overturned by fire” (Job 28). And likewise Isaiah’s saying: “All our desirable things have been turned into ruins” (Isa. 64). We also know other places formerly marked by scandals, even infamous for scandals, which afterward, through God’s regard and the grace of peace, shone forth and breathed the fragrance of virtues. To these Isaiah’s saying may be applied: “In the haunts where dragons formerly dwelt, green growth of reed and rush shall spring up” (Isa. 35). Thus even now Lebanon is daily turned into Carmel, and Carmel is reckoned as a forest.

Therefore a change of places is not certain counsel for those in tribulation, since the places to which they flee may be deprived of God’s grace, while those from which they flee may be restored by God’s regard. But their most certain counsel is to hope in God, invoke God, please God through obedience, and await God’s goodness with long-suffering. If, however, human ingenuity can discover anything that is not unjust and is helpful to a person in tribulation, let him do it. For David, through the counsel of Hushai, frustrated Ahithophel; the Apostle escaped when the brethren lowered him in a basket; and by stirring dissension among his persecutors he eased his tribulation. But since we have heard that one tribulation is never so cut down that another does not grow up, the spirit of fortitude is always necessary, lest we fail in tribulations.

## CHAPTER VI. Again, a more subtle and elevated treatment of the spirit of counsel

Thus far the spirit of counsel has been treated according to a fourfold distinction. But because these counsels are common to good and evil alike, and because few persons—those excelling in wisdom and faith—are ordinarily admitted to counsel, there is, besides these, one secret counsel, of which only the good and elect are aware: the counsel of the Holy Spirit. That is, his inward inspiration, by which he counsels his own to avoid the snares of the devil and the traps of sin; to bear with equanimity the evils of this present exile; to sigh with twofold, ineffable longing for the goods of the heavenly homeland; to hasten tirelessly toward these rewards of pious works; to be anxious for the salvation of their fellow-citizens; and, at the remembrance of the face of their Lord, to weep with a sweet bitterness.

Hence a certain Wise Man, when recounting God’s benefits toward the righteous, says: “In secret places he will take counsel with him” (Ecclus. 39). Hence the Lord says through the Prophet: “Why are you consumed with grief? Is there no king in you, or has your counsellor perished?” (Mic. 4). As though he said: You ought by no means to consume yourself with hopeless sorrow, you who have Christ as king and are not deprived of the inward counsel of the Holy Spirit. Great indeed is the hope of the soul which has deserved to hear this counsel, just as immense is the fear of that soul which has become deaf to hearing it.

Hence the Psalmist says: “My God, do not be silent to me” (Ps. 27 [Vulgate]). And to show what danger threatened one to whom God was silent, he says: “Lest perhaps you be silent to me, and I be made like those who go down into the pit” (ibid.). For a man, when pride demands it, deprived of that inward counsel of God and abandoned to his own counsel, is made like those who go down into the pit, because he too becomes like those who have fallen into the abyss of sin, gradually growing cold and slipping. He is said to be made like those not *falling* but *going down* into the pit, because, so that he may not perceive his own fall, he slips little by little and bit by bit until he reaches the depths of sin.

Yet even then he must not despair, but must cry to the Lord from the depths and wait in hope until he draws him out of the pit of misery. Here also the spirit of fortitude is especially necessary, by whose help and strength the soul rises from the pit of misery—that is, from love and habit of sin. For it must both cry to the Lord and strive with all its might, because neither of these can help it without the other. But it is much easier and happier to take care not to fall than to struggle after a fall: “If my people had heard me, if Israel had walked in my ways, perhaps I would have humbled their enemies as nothing” (Ps. 88 [Vulgate]).

## CHAPTER VII. On knowledge: showing that the spirit of knowledge, which rested upon Christ, pertains especially to humility

[Col. 1598C]

I. Let us now consider the spirit of knowledge. The name “knowledge” is common, since it is applied both to great matters and to small. But here the discussion concerns that knowledge which is a principal gift of the Spirit of God; which in the Scriptures is called the knowledge of God; which “adds sorrow”; and of which it is said: “To depart from evil is knowledge” (Job 28). So great is the diversity of kinds of knowledge that knowledge may puff up, while knowledge may add sorrow. Yet puffing up is pride, while sorrow is not merely humility but profound humility.

Therefore, however much one may know and however much one may be puffed up, let him know that he is still far from the knowledge of God if he does not grieve either for his sins or for the prolongation of this exile; for “he who adds knowledge adds sorrow.” For he does not know the beauty of righteousness, nor the goods of the Lord in the land of the living, who remains as yet deprived of these things and does not grieve. And if someone grieves for his sins but does not depart from them, neither does he possess perfect knowledge; for “to depart from evil is knowledge.” Therefore he is shown to know the knowledge of God who both knows how to grieve for sins and has learned to depart from sins.

Moreover, this knowledge begins in humility and perseveres in humility. Therefore, when the knowledge of the Spirit of God is under discussion, I gladly understand it as the knowledge of humility, because that Lord of all knowledge, that one Teacher, especially commanded that he himself be learned from, saying: “Learn from me, because I am meek and humble of heart” (Matt. 11). He took care to show, not only by word but by deed together with word, how highly he valued the knowledge of humility.

For when God, humbling himself at human feet, came to blessed Peter, Peter—although with lofty humility, yet not having been fully taught the whole mystery of humility—refused such a service from such a minister, and he said: “What I do, you do not know now; but you will know afterward” (John 13). He calls him ignorant whom he knew had not yet fully learned the knowledge of humility; and, about to speak concerning humility, he introduces knowledge first. And lest it appear a small matter, he does not immediately pour it forth, but postpones it to the future, holding his hearers’ minds in suspense for its expectation.

But after he had washed their feet, when they were attending to nothing else but were intent only upon his speech, he first commends his authority, declaring that he is both called and truly is Master and Lord. For the knower of the human heart knew how highly proud man would value such a teaching if a teacher other than such a one delivered it. Nor without purpose did he first cause himself to be believed God through miracles and wonders, and then teach the knowledge of humility; for truly no one would believe one promising knowledge but teaching something else, unless he had first been believed to be God himself.

The sum of the teaching was this: that, as the Lord washed the feet of servants, so servants should wash the feet of fellow-servants. Then he added: “If you know these things, you will be blessed if you do them.” What, I ask, are “these things”? To wash feet—as if it were difficult to find anyone who did not know this. O knowledge hidden from the wise and prudent and revealed to little ones! O knowledge which all appear to know and very few deserve to attain! For “the foolishness of God is wiser than men” (1 Cor. 1). And what is the foolishness of God except that “he humbled himself, becoming obedient unto death, even death on a cross” (Phil. 2)?

Hence the same Apostle says: “We preach Christ crucified: to the Jews indeed a stumbling-block, and to the Gentiles foolishness” (1 Cor. 1). For if someone professed himself a teacher, and when the time came to fulfill his promise taught people to wash feet, who would not laugh at him? Who would not think him foolish? Therefore, if anyone, as the Apostle says, wishes to be wise, let him become foolish in order that he may be wise (1 Cor. 3): let him become humble, that he may be blessed. “If you know these things,” he says, “you will be blessed if you do them.”

II. The knowledge of the world lies in eloquent words; the knowledge of Christ, in deeds of humility. The knowledge of the world lies in one person confuting another with words; the knowledge of Christ, in a brother serving his brother through humility. Therefore, Lord, teach me this knowledge, because I have believed your commandments (Ps. 123 [Vulgate]): knowledge which you deigned to value so greatly that, in commending it, you, God, washed the feet of man.

It was a thing now to behold and marvel at: him who looks upon the earth and makes it tremble; beneath whom those who bear the world are bowed; at whose name every knee bends, in heaven, on earth, and under the earth—bending his own knees and bowing his whole body to wash human feet, though scarcely one man in the world could have been found worthy to wash his feet. Indeed, he than whom none greater has arisen among those born of women confesses himself unworthy to carry his sandals, much less to wash his feet.

Let others marvel at him commanding the winds, walking upon the sea, and restoring the dead to life. For it is altogether just, fitting, and appropriate that the Creator should rule and command his creature. But that the eternal God, the great Lord, he to whose nod all things are subject, should bow himself to serve mortal and frail man—this must be received by every creature with immense wonder and marvelous devotion; this must not be heard by any creature without a certain pious awe. Pious servants, too, ought to dissolve in tears as they reflect upon such great humility in their Lord. And all this was done for this one purpose: that man might be taught the knowledge of humility.

These considerations have led me to refer the spirit of knowledge which is in Christ to humility. This could have been shown more fully if it had seemed right to linger longer over these matters. Yet this should further be noted: it was by no means without reason that humility was expressed in the washing of feet, since it is clear that this cleanses the steps of our actions. Let each person consider whether he wishes to understand the knowledge of Christ as pertaining especially to humility. Certainly no one who believes Christ can deny that the humble possess a greater knowledge of God than others, as he himself testifies: “Because you have hidden these things from the wise and prudent and revealed them to little ones” (Matt. 11).

Again, when the Lord says: “Upon whom will my Spirit rest, except upon the humble?” (Isa. 66), it is certainly clear that the rest which is in the Holy Spirit is both experienced and known by the humble, while the proud remain ignorant of it. Of this it is rightly said to those whom knowledge puffs up: “But they have not known my ways, to whom I swore in my wrath: They shall not enter into my rest” (Ps. 94 [Vulgate]). Moreover, if it still seems difficult to some to assign the knowledge of Christ to humility, let them read how the ancient and holy Fathers expound that saying of the Lord to the Jews: “You have taken away the key of knowledge” (Luke 11); and perhaps they will then assent.

## CHAPTER VIII. On the spirit of piety

The two remaining gifts, piety and fear of God, also bear witness that they are nothing but the shadow of humility: the one directed toward human beings, the other toward God. For no one is properly called pious toward himself, but toward the one concerning whom he is moved by a pious affection, and upon whom, if needy, he devoutly bestows the things belonging to charity.

In Scripture piety is also used for all religion; but such piety is not so much one special gift as it consists of all seven gifts. According to this kind of piety, God too is called pious toward man, because he bent down in wonderful compassion to raise him from the dung-heap of his misery. I believe the mystery of this was prefigured in the bow set as the sign of a covenant between God and the earth, lest it should again be destroyed by a flood; for the Father says of Christ through the prophet: “I have given you as a covenant of the people” (Isa. 42).

Therefore, since Christ is given as the covenant of the people, while the bow is set as the sign of the covenant, it is surely evident that the bow signifies Christ. The bow is set as a sign of the covenant so that the flood may not again destroy the earth; Christ is given in the covenant itself so that the wrath of God may not destroy with the reprobate the Church of those who believe in him. For, while preserving the tradition that baptism is signified through the flood, and that the wrath of God is represented by it, the book of Ecclesiasticus testifies, saying: “As the flood drenched the dry land, so his wrath shall inherit the nations that did not seek him” (Ecclus. 39).

Concerning the bow it is said: “Look upon the bow, and bless him who made it; for it is exceedingly beautiful in its splendor” (Ecclus. 43). It commends beauty in the bow; and surely the Wisdom of God is more beautiful than the sun, Christ “beautiful in form above the sons of men.” Hence the bride says: “He is altogether desirable” (Song 5). And Peter says: “Into whom angels desire to look” (1 Pet. 1). The Father himself says: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 17); and the prophet says of his splendor: “His splendor shall be as the light” (Hab. 3).

Of this bow the same canticle says: “You will arouse, you will arouse your bow” (ibid.). And explaining who this bow is, it says: “The oaths to the tribes which you spoke” (ibid.). For the Lord swore by himself to Abraham that in your seed—that is, Christ—all nations of the earth would be blessed. And in the psalm: “All tribes of the earth shall be blessed in him” (Ps. 71 [Vulgate]). If anyone should think that the testimony cited does not concern Christ or the nations because it says, “the oaths to the tribes which you spoke” (for “tribes” are indeed more commonly said of Jews than of nations), let him remember that Davidic saying: “For there the tribes went up, the tribes of the Lord” (Ps. 121 [Vulgate]). No wise person will say that these tribes belong more to carnal than to spiritual Israel.

I also believe that what is read in the Apocalypse, “A rainbow was around the throne” (Rev. 4), is the same as what is read in the psalm: “The Lord is around his people” (Ps. 124 [Vulgate]). For he sits upon his throne in order to teach; he surrounds his throne in order to protect. But to state what properly pertains to the spirit of piety: that beautiful bow bends itself from heaven down to earth; and the Son of God, going forth from the highest heaven, in marvelous compassion humbles himself as far as the assumption of our mortality and death, and descends for us not merely to the earth but even to hell.

## CHAPTER IX. On the spirit of the fear of the Lord

Now the fear of God is nothing other than humility. Yet here is not meant the humility by which we outwardly humble ourselves before our neighbors for God’s sake, but that by which we inwardly humble ourselves before God in conscience. It is rightly placed seventh, and at the same time highest, because that humility is lofty when someone is perfect both by human judgment and by his own judgment, yet still fears before God’s judgment and is not yet secure.

Such was the apostle Paul. Since neither another person nor he himself could find anything in him to rebuke, he said confidently: “It is a very small thing to me that I should be judged by you or by a human day; but neither do I judge myself. For I am conscious of nothing against myself” (1 Cor. 4). Yet because he still feared under God’s judgment, he in no way claimed security for himself: “But,” he says, “I am not justified by this; for the one who judges me is the Lord” (ibid.).

There is also another fear that is not in charity, because perfect charity casts out fear. But it is one thing when a person who has grievously offended fears lest he perish; another when one who is pleasing fears lest, offending even in the slightest matter, he should please less. This fear, then, is proof of true knowledge of God, because he is shown truly to know God who is humbled unto his perfect fear. For one who loves so greatly that he greatly fears to offend even in a small thing—of such a person, in this present time, may rightly be understood what is written: “Blessed is the man who is always fearful” (Prov. 28). “Always” is added lest he should ever, while he lives, presumptuously rely on his righteousness and, because he neither fears nor takes care, fall.

Of this fear the Scripture in Ecclesiasticus says: “Great is he who finds wisdom and knowledge; but none is above him who fears God” (Ecclus. 25). It places the fear of God above all things. Blessed is he to whom it is granted to possess the fear of God!

## CHAPTER X. On knowledge and the remaining gifts

Therefore we do not deny that knowledge of letters and knowledge of the various arts are knowledge. But just as someone who knows how to provide necessities for himself and his household, to possess the favor of his lords and neighbors, and to conduct himself honorably among people according to this world, is called wise in this respect—yet, although all wisdom is from the Lord God, if he is not wise in providing for himself and his household in eternal things, he is not to be said to have received the spirit of wisdom—so too one who knows letters, arts, and even the divine writings themselves, so long as he does not know how to humble himself in order to do the good that he knows: if he trusts that he has received the spirit of knowledge, he has deceived himself.

For no such spirit of knowledge rested upon Christ, of whom it is written that “he began to do and to teach” (Acts 1). “He who says that he knows God and does not keep his commandments is a liar” (1 John 2). Solomon says: “What more has the wise man than the fool, and what has the poor man, except that he goes on to where life is?” (Ecclus. 6). By this alone he distinguishes the wise from the fool: that the wise man, humbly doing good—and therefore he calls him poor—proceeds toward life, whereas the fool either does not know how or disdains to go there.

Would that those who, when exhorted to conversion, prefer to go away to study would take heed of these things; and that those who, after conversion, wish to return to their vomit under the pretext of study would learn rather to learn by doing than, by learning, not to act. These things have been said concerning the seven gifts insofar as they rest in the members of Christ. But how they rested in Christ himself, our head, let us see—if he reveals it to us, or if he has revealed it to any others.

Yet wisdom and knowledge, which occur more frequently in the Scriptures, may easily be distinguished according to the way they rested in him. He had wisdom because he knew that the Father’s will must be obeyed in all things. He also had knowledge because nothing present, past, or future—whether in human, demonic, angelic, or divine matters—was hidden from him. Therefore let each person have the spirit of wisdom, that he may worship God; the spirit of understanding, that he may investigate the Scriptures; the spirit of counsel, that he may counsel others concerning them; the spirit of fortitude, that he may gird himself for the strong works of virtue; the spirit of knowledge, that he may know that whatever he does is nothing without humility; the spirit of piety, by which he may expend the works of humility upon his brethren; and the spirit of the fear of God, by which in all these things he may trust not in his own works but in God’s mercy.

## CHAPTER XI. A comparison of the first seven days with the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit; first, concerning the first day, compared with the spirit of wisdom

[Col. 1603B]

Let us now see whether the works of the first seven days correspond by some likeness to these seven inward and daily works of the Holy Spirit. On the first day light was made, and a certain Wise Man said of wisdom: “I proposed to possess her rather than light, because her light is unquenchable” (Wis. 7). Therefore, when someone is enlightened to worship God, new light is created in him. Hence the Apostle says to such people: “You were once darkness, but now you are light in the Lord” (Eph. 5).

This happened generally, at Christ’s coming, throughout the whole world, when God the Lord came and shone upon us. It happens daily and individually in everyone who, remembering and turning to the Lord, casts off the works of darkness and walks as a child of light, in all goodness, righteousness, and truth. For Genesis describes darkness as first made, and light afterward, by the Lord (Gen. 1).

## CHAPTER XII. A comparison of the second day with the spirit of understanding

On the second day the firmament was made, dividing waters from waters, and it was called heaven. This fits well with the gift of understanding. And the psalm says: “Who made the heavens in understanding” (Ps. 135 [Vulgate]). For by waters is signified the knowledge of Holy Scripture, as the prophet, foreseeing that the mysteries of the Scriptures would be opened at Christ’s coming, summoned people to understand them, saying: “All you who thirst, come to the waters” (Isa. 55).

But these waters have a division, because one part of them belongs to spiritual persons and another to carnal persons. When Scripture speaks of purity of heart, virginity of body, loving compunction, spiritual meditation, contemplation of eternity, and sets before us spiritual things to imitate, it sets the upper waters above the firmament. But when it commands one to love one’s wife, obey one’s parents, do no evil to one’s neighbor, lend no money at interest, or share in the necessities of the saints, it sets waters beneath the firmament for the weak. Such precepts should indeed be transcended by spiritual persons. For these spiritual persons, because their citizenship is in heaven, are rightly called heaven; and, founded upon the firm rock, they do not withdraw in the time of temptation.

Therefore, since it pertains to the spirit of understanding to divide waters from waters in this way—that is, to discern between spiritual and carnal precepts—the works of the second day are found to correspond with the works of the second gift. Sometimes one statement is divided between both waters in such a way that, through intellectual division, it ascends to the upper waters and descends to the lower waters. Hence Paul, citing a testimony from Genesis—“Therefore a man shall leave his father and mother and cleave to his wife, and the two shall be one flesh” (Eph. 5)—first suspends the statement among the upper waters according to its mystical meaning: “This,” he says, “is a great sacrament; but I speak concerning Christ and the Church” (ibid.).

For he shows that the Church, or any Christian soul, should cleave by the faith of love to that eternal Bridegroom who, by assuming weak and mortal flesh, deigned to unite himself to her. He also shows that, at the very beginning of the world, the prophet showed through this statement Christ’s incarnation and the betrothal of the Church. This, I say, he showed—but to those who understand. Therefore the water descends as far as the firmament through intellectual division, so that the weak also may drink. For that higher understanding, set as it were above the firmament, gives drink to the spiritual person. It follows, therefore: “Nevertheless, let each of you love his own wife as himself” (ibid.).

Thus in the Scriptures there are matters suited only to carnal persons; matters suited only to spiritual persons; and matters suited to both carnal and spiritual persons, if they are divided spiritually. Moreover, the spirit of understanding, when it touches one effectively, makes that person skilled in this division, so that he knows how to divide his waters in the streets.

## CHAPTER XIII. A comparison of the third day with the spirit of counsel

On the third day the earth brought forth green herbs and fruit-bearing trees, both bearing seed. This can be referred quite aptly to the spirit of counsel. For good counsel is surely good seed. Green herb and fruit-bearing tree bear seed with their fruit when those who do good, by the seed of good counsel, draw others also to do good.

And the fact that, when the waters had been gathered together into one place, dry land is said to have appeared, is not thought to have occurred without purpose. For first, one must see the refreshment of others who are already united to God, and one’s own dryness. Thus, in hope fixed upon him, one should look to him for the rain which God set apart for his inheritance, so that, once watered by his sprinkling, one may bear fruit in good works and provide for others the seed of good counsel.

One may now see David recognizing and bewailing his dryness: “My soul is before you like land without water” (Ps. 142 [Vulgate]); and elsewhere: “I have withered like grass” (Ps. 101 [Vulgate]). One may see the same man trusting in heavenly watering: “Your good Spirit will lead me into a level land” (Ps. 142 [Vulgate]); and elsewhere: “The Lord looked down from his holy height; the Lord looked from heaven upon earth” (Ps. 101 [Vulgate]). He also promises the seed of good counsel: “I will teach the wicked your ways, and the ungodly shall be converted to you” (Ps. 50 [Vulgate]).

Although these testimonies were fulfilled long ago in general in the fall and restoration of the human race, they do not cease daily to be fulfilled in each of the elect.

## CHAPTER XIV. A comparison of the fourth day with the spirit of fortitude

On the fourth day the stars were set in the firmament of heaven to illumine the earth. This pertains to the spirit of fortitude, because, in order to offer sinners the example of light, not merely beginners and the weak but the strong and robust must be established. Hence the Lord says: “You shall receive the power of the Holy Spirit in you, and you shall be witnesses to me” (Acts 1); and again: “Remain in the city until you are clothed with power from on high” (Luke 24).

Certainly they had already been enlightened by the spirit of wisdom for worship; he had already opened their understanding so that they might understand the Scriptures; they had already scattered seeds of preaching, indeed even of miracles, under his teaching. Yet they are not permitted to succeed Christ himself in the governance of the Church until they are clothed with the power of the Spirit from on high. And the fact that they are set in the firmament of heaven in some manner requires steadfastness of strength from them.

The Psalmist also agrees with this sense: “The moon and the stars which you have founded” (Ps. 8). For, as it seems to me, among all virtues, throughout all Scripture, fortitude is especially taken away from man and ascribed to God. Hence David says: “I will love you, O Lord, my strength” (Ps. 17 [Vulgate]); and again: “You have girded me with strength for battle” (ibid.); and again: “In his mighty acts is the salvation of his right hand” (Ps. 19 [Vulgate]); and again: “The Lord is the strength of his people” (Ps. 27 [Vulgate]). There are many testimonies to this; their abundance exceeds measure.

Therefore, since man is weak both by origin and by constitution—and since a very great part of his strength consists precisely in knowing his own weakness, as Paul testifies, “For when I am weak, then I am strong” (2 Cor. 12)—if he is ever able either to overcome his own vices or to endure those of others, he must in no way attribute it to himself, but reserve his strength for God, because without him we can do nothing.

Moreover, it is not said of the lights, as of the herbs above, that the earth should bring them forth; nor, as will be said below of creeping things, that the water should produce them. Rather, it is written that God alone made them, lest the human soul should dare to ascribe anything of its strength either to itself or to its own ingenuity, and so deserve to lose it. For Samson too, whose name sounds like the sun, and who long shone in strength beyond human measure, offended him through whom he was strong and was captured. Blessed Peter also, while glorying in his own powers, was compelled to experience his weakness.

The saying in the Gospel concerning both the city set upon a mountain (Matt. 5) and the lamp placed upon a lampstand (Luke 11) may also be understood most aptly in this way: that the whole Church in general is borne by Christ, the mountain of mountains; and that each of his preachers, like a lamp, is sustained by the same Christ as by a lampstand. For a mountain remains immovable, whereas a lampstand is accustomed to be moved. And the Lord, as an immovable mountain, never ceases to sustain the Church; but if a preacher offends, he immediately hears Christ say in the Apocalypse: “Repent, and do the first works; otherwise I will move your lampstand from its place” (Rev. 2). It is as though he said: I used to sustain you as I moved in you, so that you should not fall; but now, because you have offended, I will withdraw from you that same grace of sustaining you, unless by repentance and amendment you please me.

Just as the plural “mountains” may be understood as preachers without preventing the singular mountain from being understood as Christ, so the seven lampstands in the Apocalypse, signifying seven churches, do not prevent one lampstand from signifying Christ, who is the one true support of his lamps and the unique, sole strength of his teachers.

It also seems to me that the sun and moon—one made to rule the day, the other the night—could very fittingly prefigure priesthood and kingship: the former for enlightening spiritual people, as it were the day, by doctrine; the latter for restraining carnal people, as it were the night, from wickedness. If this is so, holy priests have demonstrated how much strength this work requires: laboring in the governance of holy Church, they fought for righteousness even unto death. Much more could be said to show increasingly clearly how fortitude corresponds to the works of the fourth day.

## CHAPTER XV. A comparison of the fifth day with the spirit of knowledge, in which knowledge, as above, is referred to humility

On the fifth day creeping things and birds were produced from the waters; and this looks especially to the gift of knowledge. For waters signify knowledge, as we have taught above. Thus the waters produce creeping things and birds, because some, puffed up from knowledge, remain like creeping things, while others, humbled, rise toward heavenly things like birds in flight.

But humility is the cause of true exaltation, as the Lord testifies: “Everyone who humbles himself shall be exalted” (Luke 14), and conversely. That knowledge causes some to conceive humility is taught both by daily experience and by the previously cited saying of Solomon: “He who adds knowledge adds sorrow” (Eccl. 1). You may see great sea-creatures, abounding in roaring amid the waters of the sea, never suspending themselves in the free air and never uttering any sweetness of song. You may likewise see birds themselves, easily flying through the heights of heaven because of their smallness, delighting in the purity of the air and in the light and warmth of the sun, chirping forth the praise of their Creator in sweet modulation.

Compare the former with those great teachers, formidable by the fame of their very learning, continually dwelling in their cold learning, ignorant of the love of heavenly things and of spiritual joy, mute in praise of their Creator. Compare the latter with the humble of Christ, who, through the merit of their own humility and the benefit of their Lord, often enjoy the peace of an intent mind; who now desire from the true sun, Jesus, the light of spiritual knowledge, now the ardor of sweet love; and who rejoice from the depths of their being in praises of their Creator.

## CHAPTER XVI. A comparison of the sixth day with the spirit of piety
On the sixth day the wild beasts, cattle, and creeping things—or, according to another translation, serpents—were created; and man also was created in the image and likeness of God. These may fittingly be referred to the spirit of piety. For, according to the inward man, this creation must be referred to the affections. Wild beasts, then, according to the divine Scriptures, are untamed animals, free from the yoke of man, everywhere indulging their pleasures as they please [Col. 1607B]. Thus it is written of the Lord fasting in the wilderness: “He was with the wild beasts” (Mark 1). Likewise in the Psalms: “You appointed darkness, and night came; in it all the beasts of the forest pass through” (Ps. 103 [104]). Serpents, moreover, are eager to do harm; while cattle assist human weakness by carrying both men and their burdens—whence they are called *jumenta* [beasts of burden]. By wild beasts, therefore, is figuratively expressed that weakness in man which is greedily drawn toward the abuse of fleshly pleasures; by serpents, that weakness which incites men maliciously to harm others. Consequently, because man is weak, he must be carried; he must necessarily be helped. Thus by cattle—that is, tamed and burden-bearing animals—is denoted that humane and pious affection by which one person comes to another’s aid, serves, and assists him: “We who are stronger,” says the Apostle, “ought to bear the infirmities of the weak” (Rom. 15).

It is indeed natural for a human being to feel kindly toward another human being, especially toward relatives. But no one is sufficient, unless inspired by the spirit of piety and animated by hope of eternal things, to render the debts of charity to every neighbour. We therefore need the spirit of piety, so that we may make ourselves beasts of burden for one another, carrying the loads of fraternal weakness. Hence we read that that Samaritan, upon whom the spirit of piety pre-eminently rested, placed the wounded man, half dead, upon his own beast. Nor is this inconsistent with the statement that man was made in the likeness of God; for “God is love” (1 John [Col. 1607D] 4). Having set forth the likeness concerning the Samaritan and the wounded man, he says: “Go, do likewise” (Luke 10). Again, after he had washed the disciples’ feet: “I have given you an example,” he says, “that as I have done to you, so you also should do” (John 13). The Apostle Paul likewise, wishing to instruct us how we may make ourselves beasts of burden for our own brethren, says: “Bear one another’s burdens” (Gal. 6). And the prophet says of the Lord: “He himself bore our infirmities and carried our pains” (Isa. 53); while John says: “We ought to lay down our lives for one another” (1 John 3). But he had first said: “As Christ laid down his life for us” (ibid.). Therefore, we are fashioned in the image of God insofar as, through the spirit of piety, we bear our brethren’s weakness.

## CHAPTER XVII. Comparison of the Seventh Day with the Spirit of the Fear of the Lord

[Col. 1608A]

On the seventh day God rested from his works. He himself explains the mystery of this day through the prophet, saying: “Upon whom shall my Spirit rest, if not upon the humble, the quiet, and the one who trembles at my words?” (Isa. 66). God therefore rested on the seventh day after completing his works in six days, because the Holy Spirit rests in the person who, perfected in good works, perseveres humbly in the fear of God; and in turn makes that person rest in him. This does not mean that any good work can be accomplished without his working; rather, it is one thing when he supplies help to one who struggles, and another when he refreshes a victor with a feast. “I will enter in to him,” he says, “and dine with him, and he with me” (Rev. 3).

[Col. 1608B] Nor is the statement that he sanctified and blessed the seventh day found to be unrelated to the seventh gift: “The Lord,” says the Psalmist, “has remembered us and blessed us” (Ps. 113 [115]); and shortly afterward: “He has blessed all who fear the Lord, the small together with the great” (ibid.).

## CONCLUSION OF THE LITTLE BOOK

Behold, beloved friend, you have one small book on the seven great gifts of the Holy Spirit, written concerning him whom you love above all things by one whom you devoutly love among all things. If what is offered does not please because it is undeserving, let at least the devotion of its offerer please you. If anything I have said gives rise to doubt, believe that I have simply set down, not what I rashly affirm, but what seemed to me to be so. For even in the expositions of the holy [Col. 1608C] Fathers one finds more than once, “I think,” “I judge,” and “I suppose”; and if this is so in men of such stature, how much more in me, who am smoke? Yet some matters would have been clearer had I not avoided burdensome length. For while I was treating knowledge, it occurred to me to ask what the Apostle means when he says, “Knowledge shall be destroyed” (1 Cor. 13), since it is certain, on his own affirmation, that in the future the perfect shall come—that is, that knowledge, brought to completion, shall attain its fulfilment. But for the reason mentioned, I left the matter aside.

I beg your love to write back whether my labour is welcome to you. Yet I am sufficiently confident that what I have written to you personally will be welcome, since you gladly look upon even those things which I have laboured over for others. As I reflect upon it, however, I am well pleased that I began this little work, without then thinking of it in this way, from one and the same pre-eminent gift among the seven gifts, namely the spirit of piety. Therefore I beg you—yes, I beg you, sweetest and devout friend—to be willing to implore on my behalf, with pious affection, that Spirit of whom we have written: that he may deign to water and make fruitful my inward dryness with his own good gifts, not only for writing about him but for enjoying him. For evils have multiplied, and daily multiply, upon the earth; and therefore to be deprived of his consolation is the height of misery. May he himself govern, console, sustain, and lead us onward. But let that sweet conversation with the Beloved at last come to an end—come to an end; yet may the sweetness of his love itself never end. Amen.

[Col. 1609]

# BOOK OF ERNALD, ABBOT, ON THE PRINCIPAL WORKS OF CHRIST, UP TO HIS ASCENSION TO THE FATHER, ADDRESSED TO ADRIAN IV, SUPREME PONTIFF

*(Works of St Cyprian, ed. Nicolas Rigault, p. 393.—Paris, 1648, folio.)*

## PROLOGUE

[Col. 1609A]

Mothers commonly give names to newly born infants at the very entrance of life, assigning them from some preceding or surrounding circumstance, from lineage, or from events, so that at the very beginnings of life certain reminders may be set before those entering it. Thus their name might not become a disgrace to them if the transmitted course of their original nature should deviate from its accustomed path, and an unworthy offspring, degenerating from the virtue of its fathers, should display the countenance of a monster rather than of a human being.
