Rather, they should look to their names or offices, whose consideration might instil in them the pattern and instruction of honourable conduct, so that they might honour natural causes and rational disciplines, and neither embitter elemental sweetness in any respect nor offend against primary dignities.

For formerly names were imposed upon things haphazardly or thoughtlessly; but from the time when each thing was brought to Adam so that he might call it and give it its proper name (Gen. 2), provision was made and established among the ancient people that names should have some rationale: names should interpret a life and express some distinctive property of a person, according to which that person either differed from others or shared something with them. Thus the names of the patriarchs Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob were signs of great matters and foretold things to come; nor was certainty lacking that the names given would have effects corresponding to their meanings.

[Col. 1609C] Among the Gentiles too, later, this practice was observed not in personal names but in surnames bestowed by illustrious men: the nobility of lineage or the glory of virtue would illuminate descendants, honouring succeeding offspring with the title of Augustus or Caesar and irradiating the heirs of imperial dignity with the splendours of their first origin. Thus also ancient philosophers and teachers prefixed titles to their treatises, giving a foretaste of the breadth of a great subject in a brief heading and protecting their own glory by placing their name before it. In this way both the integrity of the work and the author’s labour would preserve their authority for the future, in both style and person; and the subtlety of the writing would readily reveal whether some envious hand had sewn a coarse patch into the polished fabric of a refined treatise, or had inserted its own trifles by a furtive transplantation, as though what another had commendably dictated were its own.

[Col. 1610A] Thus each writer placed himself as author at the head of his book, so that style might serve the author and author the style, while their common glory might be secured by mutual authority. Such distinction was deserved by the splendid talents of illustrious men; through these means their vigorous fame and indelible glory endure. But we, who scarcely understand what they have said and are altogether unequal to them in thought and eloquence, judge anything we may sometimes write unworthy of a title, lest perhaps the noble subject to whose exposition we devote our study should consider itself disfigured rather than adorned by our presumption.

Yet because fathers sometimes smile at childish trifles and take pleasure in stammering tongues, humility deserves indulgence when, by whatever access it can, it offers itself to the hands of your sublimity to be handled—not begging glory but favour. I, indeed, seek a name neither from myself nor from another; for I do not think myself to be anything, since I am nothing. With the most earnest entreaty I asked you that I might not be what I am, and humbly begged that your clemency would free me from this flame in which I am tormented. I tried, if your hand sustained me, to descend honourably; but because I could not do so amid the pressing flames, I did not consider where I might leap, so long as the devouring fire did not burn me.

[Col. 1610C] Lofty subjects require interpreters of subtle intellect; nor does one who does not know the arts readily judge rightly concerning the arts. Those trained in the liberal disciplines, provided their natural ability and study correspond, can philosophize and safely undertake hidden matters. To their endeavours, difficulty, once penetrated, shows itself passable; and, when riddles are unravelled, the face of secret things is laid open, whose brightness had been veiled by an intervening cloud and a darkness spread over truth. Therefore, both in divine teaching and in the doctrines of philosophers, it is neither safe nor honourable for persons untrained and ignorant of the meanings relevant to those writings to rush into the examination of what they do not know and arrogate to themselves mastery over matters of which they are ignorant.

[Col. 1611A] The form of this truth is found in the seraphim, which veils the face and feet of God (Isa. 6). To those seeking what lies in the middle, the outspread wings, covering above and below the beginning and end of the divine majesty, forbid rash interpreters or writers access to themselves. Divinity does not allow itself to be seen clearly; faithful inquiry may in some manner scent or feel it, but neither sees nor comprehends its pure essence. For an affirmative statement concerning God’s essence cannot be readily possessed: Divinity cannot be defined. More truly and more accurately, negation indicates what God is not than assertion indicates what he is, since whatever lies under perception cannot be that which surpasses every intellect. Whatever can be heard, seen, or known is not fitting for majesty. Every keenness of the senses is dull in this consideration, and vision grows dim.

[Col. 1611B] Six wings on either side surround and conceal this invisible light and inaccessible nature by their position and flight (ibid.): by their position showing the immobility of eternity, but by their flight its height, raised so high above that, however far a person may ascend to a lofty heart, “God is exalted” (Ps. 63 [64]) and escapes the importunity of comprehension. Yet those wings which veil God’s substance do not flee our sight; rather, they make themselves visible to pure minds. The rationale of God’s works—whether of things which exist from nothing, or things which have been or are made from matter—sets itself forth as intelligible; and the sincerity of the heart can in some degree contemplate the things of the world that are about God and beneath God.

The first constitution of things, established in six days, acknowledges an artificer and declares the work’s author. No one could be the maker of himself, nor could anyone create new matter; nor could there be many and diverse first principles of things, because unless all things had reference to one, all would, troubled by discord and infinity, be rolled back into chaos. Conflicting materials would resist and collide with one another, unless the authority of their maker ruled over all and the monarchy of one power ordered the causes and efficacies of the universe.

[Col. 1611D] Man therefore received authority over lower things, knowing who had conferred this honour upon him. Yet he was not illuminated with such perfection of knowledge as to know the Creator in the manner in which the remaining creatures are subject to his knowledge. Rather, he was to experience the greatest distance between highest and lowest things, and by this very fact become inclined toward God and humble, because he could in no respect compare himself to his Maker. He could neither escape that Maker’s dominion, penetrate his counsel, nor avoid his judgment.

Thus the angelic spirits who are about him, though of invisible nature, nevertheless make themselves manifest to hearing and sight in their embassies; and we very often experience them as ministers of our salvation, their offices and names being found in Holy Scripture. Those higher ranks indeed proclaim God to us; they do not disclose him. They announce what they are commanded, carrying out the spiritual business entrusted to them, not expounding knowledge of the universe; for number, measure, and weight pertain to us. But God is not confined by any of these.

[Col. 1612A] Transcending all things and eternally preceding them, his power and strength have nothing coeval with them, nor does any creature, heavenly or earthly, measure the depth of his immensity. The things beneath him, however, fill the temple; and the present Church attains knowledge of those matters that belong to the worship of righteousness, the ordering of life, the stages of ascent, the fittingness of conduct, the honourableness of this manner of life, and the grace of contemplation. These are done and practised in the present temple; through them God is sought, though when sought he is not immediately found. We taste, sample, and smell him, and he is near; yet when you have approached, he departs farther away.

And just as lightning breaks apart the clouds and a sudden flash not so much illuminates as dazes the eye, so sometimes, in a manner I do not know, you are touched and perceive that you are touched; yet you do not behold him who touches you. Certain inward, secret words are spoken to you which you are unable to utter; so that you cannot doubt that he who stirs you is near you—indeed, within you—yet he does not grant that you see him as he is. Rachel desires Leah’s mandrakes for their scent, not for eating; you are joined to the bridegroom by faith, not embrace; you conceive by hope until Christ is formed in you and, the burden of this corpse laid aside, flesh and spirit are of the same purity and renewed nature gives birth to an immaculate offspring. For Rachel signifies “the beginning of vision.”

[Col. 1612C] What the Word, in the beginning, was with God in his own proper being (John 1), is not clear to me. Yet I invoke God by certain names and say: Justice, Truth, Sanctification, Love; and I seek certain kinds or forms through which I may in some manner express what I perceive. For that “the Word was made flesh” (ibid.) I see more readily if I incorporate it into my perception as though by food; but that Beginning I scarcely perceive, passing by as it were through the faintest and most distant scent.

Those intellectual realities, through visible creatures, so far as it is permitted the soul to see or foresee, we behold at a distance by the divine mind. In many matters we are carried around through a sea of opinions and conjectures; in many we cling to truth; in many we are overwhelmed by the greatness of things and cry out with the Apostle: “O the depth of the riches of the wisdom and knowledge of God!” (Rom. 11). God therefore offers himself to our heart and pours into it some light of his own, inviting and drawing it on. For unless he were perceived in some manner, there would be neither hope nor capacity for desiring or seeking him.

[Col. 1612D] But because he is perceived in part, that fragrance and taste—having no likeness to fleshly sweetness and differing from it in every respect by its delightfulness—becomes an object of wonder. It is desired more abundantly because it surpasses every other delight. Desire purifies those who seek; and purification, having excluded deformities, advances those who ascend toward the image of God. Thus, in its work, the image and likeness of God at last discloses to itself its own dignity through many laborious advances.

Had the teaching of the incarnate Word not been added to this inquiry into things so profoundly deep, human intellects would have failed; and I do not know whether anyone would even dare to rise to the attempt. But divinity joined to flesh willed that the assumed nature should, in some measure, share in its brightness; and with heaven opened above our Teacher and Lord, it introduced our sight to higher things. “We saw his glory, glory as of the Only-begotten from the Father” (John 1), and some portion from the fullness of grace and truth which is in him was instilled into us (ibid.).

[Col. 1613A] And with Philip we heard: “He who sees me sees the Father also” (John 14). Yet even in this vision there can be no full sufficiency until, “in the splendours of the saints, on the day of his power” (Ps. 109 [110]), there is known the relation of the begetting, the begotten, and the proceeding—what eye has not seen, ear has not heard, nor has yet ascended clearly into the heart of man (1 Cor. 2).

In all that has been said, the loftiness of the subject altogether surpasses our understanding, the sheer weight repels the pen, and the difficulty of the steep ascent overwhelms us. But, most excellent Father, the necessity of your command compelled me to try whether, by the importunity of study, I might perhaps pluck something from the furnishings of the sanctuary and, drawing the veil a little aside through a narrow and subtle entrance, behold the mercy-seat. Meditation presumed to look from afar, search out eternal years, and inquire what existed before the ages of time—if indeed an age or time can be said to exist before light, day, and sun; and how, before elemental causes and material origins, that infinity of eternity existed, if the omnipotence were solitary in itself, if ministering spirits were lacking to it, if eternal Divinity remained in itself without place, what realm wisdom could have when there was nothing to govern, and how that empty antiquity could lack both use and form.

[Col. 1613C] Repelled from all these questions, I was compelled to return to visible things of time. And would that I knew and understood myself! If I know neither the origin nor the extent of my soul, which holds authority over my body, nor can sufficiently behold its nature; if the reason is unknown to me why it takes pleasure in the body which persecutes it; if I do not know who engraved this law upon the members, that by such violent dominion the body oppresses the spirit and the better and worthier nature yields to the worse—then I ought patiently to endure my failure to understand the maker of the universe, when I confess my blindness even in the smallest particles of his works.

This question seems insoluble: why a rational human being strives after what is denied and forbidden, and always delights in unlawful things. It is altogether rare and difficult to become good; it is easy and inclined to become evil. We are imbued and taught in this doctrine, without teacher or example, from the very years of adolescence. Look at those who profess holiness: what religious observance closes its hand to gifts offered? What solitude shuts its ears against offered favours? What appetite is content with common flavours? Who would consider himself lowly if he saw a humble person? Who would think it disgraceful if he felt himself without glory? Who could enumerate the monsters rather than the forms of pleasures which, through fleshly desires, drag the unwilling soul secretly and openly from bedroom to marketplace, from brothel to theatre?

[Col. 1614A] First, shame having been wiped away and modesty torn out, crime does not hide itself; reason does not hesitate, nor does discernment resist the affections of the flesh. The captive spirit renders a compliant service.

The expression I have just used, “affections of the flesh,” is improper, because these vices belong properly to the soul, which perceives, moves, and lives. Sin is imputed to it, because to it have been given choice, judgment, knowledge, and power, by which it can reject evil and choose good. The soul uses the body as a craftsman uses hammer or anvil, upon which it fashions idols of every shamefulness and makes images of whatever pleasures it chooses. The flesh is not the author of sin, the inventor of malice, the maker of thoughts, or the planner of acts; it is the workshop of the spirit, which in it and through it performs and completes whatever it desires.

[Col. 1614B] That the flesh itself is without sensation is recognized when the spirit departs; after its departure, it remains a rotting mass and heap of mire, fit for no use. Whatever it feels is proved alien to the nature of the body. When it is said that “the flesh contends against the spirit and the spirit against the flesh” and that they resist each other (Gal. 5), I think this too is said improperly, because this conflict belongs to the soul alone, which quarrels with itself and disputes with its own choice. It is more certain, in questions of this kind, what is good and what is evil than, in investigations of other matters, what is true and what is false.

For in examining hidden causes and nature’s secrets, a person may err or be deceived, since human understanding does not in every respect reach from end to end. But in matters lying before the eyes and hands, no subtlety hinders judgment: foul things are readily distinguished from what is not foul, beautiful from ugly, bitter from sweet, hard from soft, and harmonious from discordant. Yet the mind, drunk with the poison of its desire, gives the body over to disgrace; and, joined in embraces, both slip away into deadly sweetness and fall asleep. When they awaken, shame brings repentance too late, and horror at their defilements confronts the polluted mind.

[Col. 1614D] In all other evils maliciously committed, such retribution pursues the sinner, and he, gorged with the filth of lusts, vomits himself out. But the ardour of avarice and gain alone neither satisfies the covetous person nor makes him regret accumulating what he wishes to increase, not diminish; and stubborn in disorder, he diligently heaps up what he may always sacrifice to his idol.

Whence comes this thirst for riches that sits upon miserable hearts, and the briny lust of ambition that takes possession of the thirsty soul, so that some force themselves into higher places by right and wrong, even from wilderness hiding places, and panting emerge from every rank where any entrance lies open? They run to judges, flatter intermediaries, hire helpers, and labour by every means to sit with princes, at such a profit that God may curse what they bless and bless what they curse. Why this law of sin, in these and similar cases, crushes the law of righteousness, and why weakened reason, though able to stand, falls so miserably, is difficult to comprehend—especially since this defect hangs upon the sentence of condemnation, and ancient transgression has received this unavoidable punishment as its lot.

[Col. 1615A] Therefore, if I do not know myself, if I am ignorant of the substance and nature of my own soul, if I do not understand the rationale of what is within me, with what audacity shall I raise my eyes above myself to behold the Beginning without beginning and attain the End without end? The excellence of majesty commands us to desist from such attempts, and impossibility itself repels every effort of our intellect.

Let us therefore touch what is lawful and granted. Around the Saviour’s cradle let us taste the first foods of his infancy; and, circumcised and washed, the devil conquered, let us recline at supper with the Lord in the affections of holiness. There, refreshed with the bread of angels, after the delights of that food let us rise for the passage, so that by the vehicle of the cross we may be carried from this world to heaven, the Holy Spirit filling us so that he may thereafter bear us onward and disclose whatever the burden of the body and the dimness of imperfection have rendered obscure during the pilgrimage of this exile.

[Col. 1615B] I have therefore sent to your fatherhood, suppressing my own name, the book which I wrote on the principal works of Christ our Lord. In it the source of the sacraments and the origin of the discipline in which we stand, setting before us the form and example of right living, rises step by step from his humble coming to his glorious return to the Father. I desire this book to be written rather in our minds than on a page; and would that, in the sight of your holiness, a suppliant affection may merit remembrance and recollection of us!

# I. ON THE NATIVITY OF CHRIST

The greatly desired and long-awaited Nativity of Christ is here; the renowned feast is here. In the presence of the Saviour, the holy Church throughout the world returns thanks and praise to her visitor. Joy is announced to us from heaven; gladness is commanded. This night, conscious of the sacred birth, is illuminated with new brightness. Those above glory in heaven; peace is established on earth for people of good will. Angels are present and speak with shepherds. They do not disdain to speak to humble persons, and though they themselves are exalted, they do not despise the lowly.

[Col. 1615D] The shepherds are not frightened either by the unfamiliar light or the angels’ presence. Men of sound and pure faith delight in hearing the harmonious heavenly voices of those who praise God, chanting proclamations of divine glory and grace. Nor was it enough to disclose above the hidden mysteries of heaven: peace restored to human beings is also announced, and the affection of good will is consecrated by the bounty of a new gift. It was fitting that, at his coming, the good Lord should assure and gladden the good wills of those awaiting him, and by multiplying witnesses give sure tokens of his presence, so that he might no longer be awaited as one who was to come, but be seen as one who had come. The angels became witnesses of the holy birth and place which the new infancy of Christ had consecrated for them.

[Col. 1616A] Gabriel alone announces to the Virgin the overshadowing power of the Most High; the rejoicing multitude of the heavenly host proclaims that the Saviour of the world has come and sings that earthly things have been reconciled to heavenly. The ancient counsel has come openly forth. It is no longer secret, but Christ’s kindness, revealed before the nations, has become publicly known; the Saviour’s humanity has been offered to the world, differing from us in nothing except that it was free of sin.

The Gospel begins with heavenly embassies, and angels were its first heralds. No longer are figures and riddles wrapped up in the hands of prophets; rather, the promises and their fulfilment alike stand firm and agree together in angelic jubilation, human writing, and the evident proof of events. The shadows having been removed, Law and Gospel are united. Witnesses are multiplied; the heavenly army cries aloud; the band of shepherds believes and rejoices. He who reveals himself to little ones does not seek testimony from the wise and prudent. Pride and ambition are condemned at once in the beginning of this teaching. No rhetorical colouring or persuasive devices are brought forward: reason and miracles encompass the order of these events.

[Col. 1616B] At the outset, signs were joined to faith; and the teachings had their greatest efficacy in this, that word and deed worked together, leaving no escape for the resistance of unbelievers. That night was brighter than every day; the words of angels, announcing peace to human beings and indicating Bethlehem, encourage the search for the child. Those shepherds, enlightened more in mind than by carnal eyes, hasten to behold Emmanuel. Taught inwardly by the invisible instruction of the Holy Spirit, they confess that the little one whom they see is immeasurable, and offer him the affection of their devout reverence.

The simplicity of humble persons is chosen, so that a rule might be laid down and an unbreakable pattern given: the humility of Christ lies open only to the poor in spirit, and Truth cannot admit the proud to the sight of itself. They come to Bethlehem; Emmanuel, whom Gabriel foretold, is found: a small city, a very poor house, scant furnishings. There is no domestic splendour—only a reclining-place in a stable, the mother on hay, the son in a manger.

[Col. 1616D] Such lodging did the maker of the world choose; such were the delights attending the sacred Virgin’s childbirth. Swaddling-clothes stand in place of purple; scraps of cloth are heaped up instead of fine linen for royal adornment. She is both mother and midwife, rendering devoted service to her beloved child: she touches him, embraces him, joins kisses to him, offers him her breast. The whole scene is full of joy; there is no pain and no injury to nature in the childbirth. Her household means did not permit maidservants; scant resources and a poor table excluded the service of slaves. The cramped dwelling concealed no separate room, and that little hut had no private recesses. The roof lacked panelling, and bare walls clothed it all around.

There was no place there for the baths usually prepared for women after childbirth, since no injury of nature had harmed the Lord’s mother: she gave birth without torment, having conceived without pleasure. Yet, following custom in order to satisfy the Law, she lay down on the appointed days, as though her situation in this matter were like that of other women. She acknowledged the fatigue of laying down her burden and submitted to the repose provided. During the days of separation, she abstained not from Joseph’s bed—he had never touched her—but from entering the temple and from the other things forbidden by the Law.

[Col. 1617A] The ripe fruit slipped of its own accord from the fruit-bearing tree: what came forth willingly did not need to be plucked. Retribution demanded nothing in this matter, nor did preceding pleasure exact any return of punishment. By the Holy Spirit’s overshadowing, original fire was extinguished. Therefore it was not fitting that the innocent woman should be afflicted, nor did justice permit that vessel of election should be wearied by common injuries; for although she differed greatly from others, she shared their nature, not their guilt.

Her special privilege, which no woman either before or afterward deserved to obtain, was that she was at once mother and virgin, distinguished by each title. Thus fullness of grace was due to her as mother, and fuller glory as virgin. Distinguished by integrity of flesh and mind, she enjoyed Christ’s presence inwardly and outwardly, spiritually and bodily. The ornaments that were lacking, even if they had been present, would have had no eyes to inspect them. For the presence of the little child so occupied the eyes of those present—Joseph, and perhaps anyone else who was there—so illuminated their minds and attracted their hearts, that in this highest good there seemed to be a united gathering of every good. There was no need to wander about or beg in separate parts for what omnipotent infancy offered to the faithful all at once in itself alone.

[Col. 1617C] Certainly, it must not be thought that angelic ministries were absent, nor had the Holy Spirit, who came at Gabriel’s word, withdrawn from the venerable breast of the mother. He possessed his own house and adorned the temple which he had consecrated for himself. He guarded his sanctuary and honoured the chamber of holiness. Consolations such as these gladdened that blessed soul; reverence for so great an indweller drove away the playthings of desires. The law of the flesh did not assail the law of the mind; no rebellion afflicted one whom the Spirit possessed.

The little child, nursing at her breast, received pure nourishment, and the fountain of that sacred breast poured undefiled food into his most pure mouth. Yet certain sweetnesses exceeding human understanding also filled the mother’s heart. Thus there was a wonderful joy on both sides, when the devout humility of the holy mother and the immeasurable kindness of the Holy of Holies were united and immersed in mutual affections.

Outwardly, the things that were seen were bare and poor; in that poverty nothing appeared divine, except to those to whom it had been revealed from above. The first of these were the shepherds mentioned above, whose innocence and simplicity were chosen, so that the praise of Christ might be perfected, and so that in later times fishermen and shepherds might confound orators, and the preaching of poverty might have its beginning from the poor and humble. The Egyptians customarily execrate this class of men, and sheep and cattle are abominable to them. Yet such an occupation possessed authority from the beginning: Abel the shepherd offered gifts from flocks of sheep, and in that they were seen to be consumed by heavenly fire it became known to all that they were pleasing to God. Shepherds were Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, men intimate with God; shepherds were the twelve patriarchs; Moses himself was a shepherd, who, in the solitude of the wilderness, while following his flocks, beholds God in the bush and, having received the power of signs, receives leadership of the people. Elisha is made a prophet from the plough; David is taken from following the ewes with young and placed upon the throne of the kingdom. The lamb which the Egyptian abominates God commands to be sacrificed to himself; and its blood, smeared upon the doorposts of the Israelites, repels and drives away the destroying angel. Nor is the danger of death feared where a sign of such great reverence is seen. At Peter's shadow the sick rise up; demons are subject to the apostles; the eloquence of the reprobate yields to the unlearned; as Paul preaches, peoples and kingdoms fold captive hands. The poor are chosen, the proud neglected; neither arrogance nor high rank has any place in discipleship to Christ. Christ, being poor, rejects rich disciples. A poor mother, a poor son, a lodging without means: these offer an effective lesson to those who serve in the Church according to the pattern of this school. Shepherds adored him in the cradle; and, confessing the little child, they knew as God—simply yet reasoningly, in spirit and truth—him whom they adored.

It had indeed been a miracle that, when the heavens were opened, the light of an unaccustomed radiance shone upon them by night; that angels were heard and seen; that the shepherds had been taught and instructed by them. Yet, although these things had preceded, no human reasoning supplied evidence of the divinity disclosed concerning the child's infancy; nor, amid the narrow confines of that manger, while the infant wailed among his wrappings, was there any indication of majesty. But faith, obedient to what it heard, believed that no word is impossible with God; and through the Holy Spirit it was introduced, by the most subtle approaches of understanding, into comprehension of this mystery. The same Spirit who long before had taught the prophets, now also poured himself into the minds of the humble, enlarged the narrowness of human understanding, and opened inward eyes, so that invisible things might be seen and those things understood which human sense cannot reach nor the intellect of reason penetrate.

Hence Isaiah had foretold: “A little child is born to us, and a son is given to us” (Isa. 9). This could be seen; faith asks no merit for this. But what follows—“His name shall be called Emmanuel” (Isa. 7), “Wonderful, Counsellor, Mighty God, Father of the age to come, Prince of Peace” (Isa. 9)—if the eyes of the mind are shut, I do not know what you gain by the outward eyes. He who does not yet speak: how shall he be counsellor? How is a little child believed to be almighty God? Altogether weak: in what will he appear mighty? Possessing absolutely nothing: by what ascents will he attain the summit and pinnacle of royal rule and dominion? But if you pursue the mystery of faith, in all these things you will find the most subtle and pure reasons, and you will clearly recognize why it was altogether necessary that the immeasurable One should become little, and that the Son of God should become the son of man.

[Col. 1619A] Your heart too will marvel and be enlarged when you understand the most profound mystery in this: that he who was made contemptible is Wonderful; that he who did not learn letters and was not instructed in the laws is a sufficient counsellor in things divine and human; how divinity and humanity came together in one person; how, where weakness was assessed, strength was found; and how the body of our humility, conformed to divine brightness (Phil. 3), may possess everlasting dominion—not in this world, but in heavenly glory. Christ comes to little ones, and is kept company with little ones; he instructs, creates, and makes the poor. He himself, in the synagogue of the Jews, after reading from the scroll of Isaiah on the Sabbath and rolling up the book, taught that this prophecy had been fulfilled in himself: that he had been anointed by the Holy Spirit and that the Father had sent him to bring good news to the poor (Luke 4). Likewise in the Gospel he rejoices, giving thanks and confessing to the Lord of heaven and earth that divine mysteries have been revealed to little ones (Luke 10), from whose understanding the loftiness of this world has been excluded—for it cannot be subject to God while, according to flesh and blood, it investigates his invisible reality by its own rules.

This is the first entrance into religion, just as it was Christ’s first entrance into the world: that whoever wishes to live devoutly may think humbly of himself and may not presume to walk above himself in wonders. Humility has always been the foundation of holiness; proud loftiness could not stand even in heaven. Our little one, entering the world, brought this first grace; and, wishing us to be conformed to himself from the cradle, he wished to be held in life as he displayed himself in person. Since we are children of God, he wished through participation in humanity to become our brother, so that we might be co-heirs with him of blessedness and so that the whole constitution of the human being might possess perfect and complete joy: when the spirit represents the divine image and our flesh the likeness of Christ’s body. We obtain the benefit of consummated fellowship when, sharing Christ’s name and inheritance, we partake of the divine nature through the spirit and of the human through the body. “The Lord has sworn and will not repent” (Ps. 109); and, not forgetful of his promises, as he had sworn that he would give himself to us, so he fulfilled it.

[Col. 1619D] “A son is given to us” (Isa. 9), who, though he was in the form of God (Phil. 2), the brightness of his glory and the image of his substance (Heb. 1), was not ashamed to empty himself into the form of a servant (Phil. 2), so that those who glory in being his brothers and wish to ascend may not be ashamed to descend. Rather, let them lean upon the same ladder with Jacob (Gen. 28), and, singing the Song of Ascents, climb from the lowest things to the higher. O Lord, how admirable is your name (Ps. 8); truly you are God who works wonders (Ps. 76). I marvel not merely at the structure of this world, nor at the stability of the earth while the revolving firmament encompasses it; not at individual days, nor at the moon’s waning and increase, nor at the sun always whole and its unceasing course, nor at the alternation of seasons, in which some things wither, some flourish, and those that now appear dead afterward live again. I marvel at God in a Virgin’s womb; I marvel at the Almighty in a cradle; I marvel how flesh adhered to the Word of God, how the incorporeal God put on the covering of our body. I marvel, in this dispensation, at so great an expenditure of time and such slow stages toward obedience to the Saviour. The work could have been accomplished quickly, and so great a labour shortened to Christ’s word alone, just as the world was made and all things ordered at his command. Yet the rational human being is worthier than the elemental world, since it is readily believed from the fact that all things were made for human service. In other matters some explanations suffice in one way or another; here wonder alone encompasses me.

[Col. 1620B] And with Habakkuk I sing: “I considered your works and was afraid” (Hab. 2). I marvel at the fast; I marvel at the temptations; I marvel at the Almighty lying in the tomb; I marvel at him slain and risen. These are the new wonders which Jeremiah foretold: “The Lord will make a new thing upon the earth: a woman shall encompass a man” (Jer. 31). “He will do his work, and his work is strange from him.” Jesus Christ, yesterday and today (Heb. 13), begotten before the morning star (Ps. 109), took the beginning of flesh from a Virgin: he whom the heaven of heavens cannot contain (3 Kings 8), who, while filling all things, is in all things, yet is neither contained nor held by them. It is new and unheard of that, in the narrowness of a mother’s womb, frail flesh enclosed within itself the power of the Most High and that the wisdom of God changed the order of things and the course of nature. Divinity, extended everywhere and pouring the fullness of itself into a tiny vessel, was thus enclosed by a woman’s womb, though it encompassed the universe, filled all things, surpassed all things, contained all things within itself, and embraced all things outside itself. Him whom we know as a little child the prophet calls a man, suggesting that strength was never lacking to him, but that the fortitude of mature manhood was always present, though infant weakness concealed it. Therefore he made his own work: saving what he had created, recalling to life what had perished, restoring to life what was dead. But it was a strange work in God that “the Word became flesh” (John 1), that he became visible and comprehensible, capable of suffering and mortal; and strange to majesty: a child nursing at the breast, wrapped in little cloths, enduring insults, the Son of God set upon the gibbet.

This little child is also called Counsellor, and elsewhere “Angel of Great Counsel,” because he publicly revealed the secrets of God that had been hidden from human beings. Since no one knew the Father except the Son himself, he opened the hidden things of God and unfolded the inquiry into the Trinity: speaking to the Father, receiving an answer from the Father, and pouring the Holy Spirit into the disciples; making known the grounds of generation and procession, subtly establishing the properties of the persons and the unity of the indivisible essence. He taught other counsels too, lower indeed but nevertheless necessary: that a person may understand benefits bestowed, give thanks for the state in which he stands, and, through God’s grace, rise again when he has fallen.

“Concerning virgins,” says the Apostle, “I have no commandment of the Lord; but I give counsel, as one who has obtained mercy” (1 Cor. 7). By the Lord’s command he wills and praises that women who have married should remain as they are; but that those who are virgins for God should offer to Christ wholeness of integrity through the abundance of chastity. In this way, whatever stands immovable by divine authority should remain so; but where freedom of choice may incline either way, let persons choose the former place. For although marriages are good and instituted by God, continence is better, and virginity more excellent: not compelled by necessity or commandment, but recommended by the counsel of perfection.

[Col. 1621B] But if temptations oppose divine counsels and call free minds back to fleshly desires, Mighty God is at hand. Let no one put hope in a human being or trust in the arm of his flesh (Jer. 17), because he who conquered the world (John 16) promises victory to his soldiers; and those who are conquerors of themselves do violence to heaven, since, as it is written, “The kingdom of heaven suffers violence, and the violent seize it” (Matt. 11). In the name of this little child we engage the ancient enemy; and the strong armed man is powerfully driven from the court which he had long possessed when one stronger comes upon him (Luke 11), and the boldness of his presumptuous attack is commanded to be silent. From Christ’s flesh strength is restored to the defect of our flesh, which had languished infected by the primitive dregs of original evil. The participation of the sacraments, through which we are united to the purity of his body, strengthens us so greatly that we gain victory over the world, the devil, and ourselves; and, cleaving by sacramental taste to life-giving mysteries, we become one flesh and one spirit, as the Apostle says: “He who cleaves to the Lord is one spirit” (1 Cor. 6). Thus those to whom the word is addressed are called gods and sons of the Most High: sharers in name, inheritance, and eternity; through the strength of fellowship with Christ they subdue temptations, and though they are human beings of baser material, they reduce demons to captivity, spit upon them, and bind them.

Indeed, in this present time the Christian soldiery trains itself in the arena of this life, beneath the leading banner of Christ, whom we have seen as a little child and known as God. Armed by the spirit of counsel and strength, we can neither be conquered nor deceived—made distinguished by instruction, divine knowledge, and power. Yet such discipline at present seems to be not of joy but of sorrow (Heb. 12), because contests are waged not without danger. But to those who fight the good fight (2 Tim. 4), the Prince of eternal peace (Heb. 12) will give in the future the most peaceable fruit to those trained in righteousness, sealing to himself in blessedness those whose nature he shared. To him be glory and dominion from now and for ever. Amen.

## II. ON THE MEANING OF CIRCUMCISION

Among all the sacraments of the Old Testament, ancient religion celebrated nothing more solemnly than circumcision; nor did this tradition take root only among the Hebrews, but also among Phoenicians and Arabs. Other nations ridicule both the command and the practice; nor do they at all maintain that it befits God for the Saviour’s benevolence to take delight in the wounds of infants and to consign the innocent, at life’s very beginning, to the danger of death. They judge it absurd and irrational to think this of the good Lord, who wills that no one should perish. Yet the other sacrifices are not all an object of horror to them; following natural law in many matters, they retain means of expiation, sacrifice victims, burn fat, and with perfumes and libations pour out vows and prayers before God. We read that Job, approved by God’s testimony, was occupied with continual sacrifices (Job 1); we do not read that he was circumcised. There may have been in those times, in various places, many distinguished men subject to God’s righteousness who lacked this sign, although the sons of Esau and Ishmael should be regarded as not unacquainted with this tradition.

But since both antiquity commends this practice and the authority of the one commanding it enjoins it, the reason for so great a mystery must be sought—a mystery commanded with such weight specifically to Abraham and his seed that whoever in that people lacked the distinction of this sign was reckoned a Gentile, not a Jew, and was erased and proscribed from the title of the children of Israel. Since it was commanded to be performed on the eighth day and for a name to be assigned to the circumcised person (Gen. 17), those deemed worthy of the fellowship of the saints were given to understand that their names should be written in heaven and that they should become heirs and sharers of eternal blessedness, which the eighth day follows after the week of this life, whoever had consecrated themselves to the Lord by innocence of life and the holiness of celibacy.

[Col. 1622C] Tender infancy, therefore, had to be imbued with such teaching; and before the desirous impulses which sin had earned, the severity of a pitiable punishment and unavoidable vengeance had to be applied even to little children. Before the cauldron of lusts boiled over, provision was made for a fan by which the wandering heat and all-surveying blaze of the ravaging flame might be cooled and extinguished. Thus pain was set against pleasure, and blood of torment against blood of delight, so that in their first elements little children might learn, always mindful of their own cutting, to cure opposites by opposites; and that, to restrain and curb shameful appetites, it is necessary to rub the itching of the flesh with corrosive salt and continually dry up the putrefactions that break out anew. For this purpose the Apostle mortified his body, not merely by circumcising that generative member, but by crucifying his whole self and setting a cautery against every irregular motion, reducing his body so completely into slavery (1 Cor. 9) that he could say: “Now it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” (Gal. 2).

We, imitators of this deed, are ashamed concerning the shameful parts; and when the covering of shame is uncovered and cut, although conscience, as a witness, always exposes to us the snares of sin springing up within, and although we cannot escape inward judgment, we must nevertheless stand bravely. The tickling sensations must be rebuked with the authority of reason, and we must watch most carefully lest consent follow. This shame cannot be wholly abolished within us, because not the whole member, but only its front portion, was commanded to be circumcised. It is indeed a great matter if the contagion of this corruption does not issue forth; if the raging beast of corrupt breath is bound with iron chains in the deepest recesses of the soul; and if, with its teeth broken, captive desire gnaws and corrodes itself within.

[Col. 1623A] Shame therefore remains because of sensation, so that one who strives in the contest, knowing the mystery of circumcision, may abstain from everything (1 Cor. 9) that can furnish fuel to this flame. Yet this death-dealing struggle of sensuality is not fatal to those who contend, but a test; rather, the contest between spirit and flesh has been instituted so that the human being, victor over sin and punishment, may after solemn triumphs be crowned in glory, thereafter free from assaults, free from sin and punishment. The soul, subjected to vanity against its will after transgression, has endured this shame; it bears force under the pressure of unrest, and, wearied by involuntary motions, laments the misery of its unhappiness, desiring to be delivered from this body of death (Rom. 7) and asking God for the freedom of a peaceful and tranquil condition. In daily conflict spirit and flesh wrestle, and reason complains against the domestic evil that exercises such dominion within it, as though vice were nature and the first creation had brought sin along with it. The first condition of creation certainly does not experience this; it is the punishment that followed the transgressor, and an inseparable penalty clung to sin. All who desire to see the King in his beauty with a pure heart (Matt. 5; Isa. 33) will be ashamed of it.

Who is not confounded amid such incessant delusions? Who does not blush amid such great indignities? For the tinder of this evil lurks within dark recesses and, when it sees the soul otherwise occupied and less careful in guarding itself, bursts forth in violent attacks, lays poisons beneath blandishments, and assaults the purity of chastity by unexpected onsets. Thus the shamefaced person covers his nakedness and, confused, hides his foulness. With these wounds continually renewed and always smeared with this discharge, throughout the whole week of this life an unceasing cutting away of putrefactions and continual circumcision of scars is necessary. In other respects all the members obey the command of reason and retain freedom of choice. But here, when Babylon’s furnace has blazed up and, as though sprinkled with pitch and naphtha (Dan. 3), the desires of lust have boiled over, inflamed flesh is deprived of the honour of freedom, so that rebellious members, whether one wishes it or not, boldly rise into wicked motions.

Formerly, coverings of things signified the abolition of sin and advanced in their beginning toward perfection. Christ did not wish to withdraw this sacrament from ancient custom; and although it was not necessary at that time, nevertheless, lest ancient religion should seem altogether rejected, he wished the seal of circumcision to be applied to himself. Certainly original sin, which flowed from the first fathers into the whole succession of this race, had to be expiated at every time by certain remedies, although these signs did not possess their full power until the reality itself arrived, hidden beneath the veil of figures. Though the mysteries of the sacraments were not open to all, their power and effect could not be unknown, because from Adam to Noah sacrifices are known to have been acceptable to God, sacrifices which up to that time the first human being performed through a divinely inspired institution, without the distinction of the law. Those sacrifices were performed either in the blood of animals or by burning other offerings—not because God delighted in smoke or in the deaths of cattle, but so that the unchangeable judgment and the sentence pronounced against sin from the beginning might be understood.

[Col. 1624B] An unchangeable decree had gone forth from eternal law: desire was to be afflicted and the sinner punished by death. No remedy through outward wounds could intervene so that the sting of the flesh would not, without any exception, strike the weak person and troublesome death pursue the captive until dissolution. Death of the flesh did indeed cut off the mockeries of desires, and that which had been predestined and given over to decay and dissolution could sin no more. But after the death of the flesh there remained the soul’s labour and the spirit’s affliction; nor could that condemnation be absolved in any way unless the Life of all came to the aid of the death of all, and God’s grace administered a singular antidote for the general disease. God revealed this ancient plan of our redemption to the holy fathers and willed that human beings should gradually become accustomed to the necessary Passion and death, should set the offering of a voluntary death against it, and should transform punishment into medicine and execution into remedy. The ancient sacrifices contained the teaching of this offering; their burnings and deaths prefigured the grace of this consummation.

For this reason, when the times of faith were now drawing near, circumcision was commanded, and that part of the body in which lies the seedbed of pleasures and the workshop of lust was commanded to be cut away in little children, so that they might offer the first fruits of their own blood to him who was about to offer all his blood, and that the common sacrifices of individual persons might precede the unique whole burnt offering. But when Christ the Lord came, of whom it had been written at the head of the book that in his death he would fulfil the Father’s will (Heb. 10), sacrifices ceased. The Gospel no longer commanded the cutting off of the foreskin, but circumcision of the heart (Col. 2); and, by an unchangeable decree, it commanded that every wantonness both of members and of affections be cut away by the sword of the Spirit (Eph. 6). That single offering of our Redeemer was of such dignity that it alone sufficed to take away the sins of the world. He entered the holy places in his own blood with such authority (Heb. 9) that thereafter no petition of suppliants required another’s blood (Heb. 7). Therefore, from the days of our visitation, the kingdom of heaven suffers violence (Matt. 11): circumcision is no longer performed in the stripping off of flesh, but by the power of the Holy Spirit the discharge of ancient oldness is cleansed away.

## III. ON THE STAR AND THE MAGI, AND THE DEATH OF THE INNOCENTS

[Col. 1625A]

When the Saviour was born in Bethlehem, the report of his presence on earth was heard in Ephrathah, and the fame of this new birth was extended even to the woods and fields of the Gentiles. In Judaea these joys were first celebrated by shepherds and angels; and not long afterward knowledge of the event penetrated the borders of the Arabs, while the heavenly divinity of a star of brilliant light announced it to the inhabitants of Sheba through new splendours. In those regions were men accustomed to observing the stars, who by mathematical art knew the power and course of the planets; for, measuring the divisions of time from the nature of the elements, they had learned from fixed experiments the functions assigned to stars by their own effects. Long ago these men had heard from Balaam’s prophecies that a star would rise in Jacob, and a man in Israel (Num. 24), whose strength would be like that of a rhinoceros; that ships with three banks of oars would come to him from Italy; that they would overcome the Assyrians and lay waste the Hebrews (ibid.); and that in those times there would be no idol in Jacob nor image in Israel (Num. 23). Those men had long awaited the fulfilment of this prophecy. When the fullness of time came (Gal. 4) and a new star suddenly arose, they returned to the ancient books; fortified both by the testimony and by the sign, they rode upon dromedaries into Judaea and arrived with the star as guide.

Nor could persons of so notable a name escape the notice of Palestine’s inhabitants. But when it was heard that they were following the star which indicated a little child born in Bethlehem, Herod was informed of the inquiry after a new king (Matt. 2). Therefore, having summoned the Magi, he investigates the order of this affair with every care. He hears that a little child has been born in Bethlehem, whom those who had come from Sheba, professing him King and God, hasten to adore and venerate. He is informed of what the Moabite prophet, though a Gentile, had foretold from ancient times; he compares the prophecies of holy prophets with the writings of the nations—prophecies whose writings were read every Sabbath, and concerning which no one among the Jewish people doubted that what they had declared concerning the past, or foretold concerning the future, was reliable. Concerning the strength of him who, like a unicorn, would pierce those opposing him; concerning the avenging Italian triremes which would come into Judaea’s borders for his service; and concerning an empire which would be extended to the end of the world—Herod, anxious, was frightened and afraid.

[Col. 1625D] He was also disturbed by the testimony written in Micah: “For from Bethlehem, which is Ephrathah, shall go forth a little child who shall be ruler in Israel, whose going forth is from the beginning, from days of eternity” (Mic. 5). When he understood that what the domestic books contained agreed with what foreigners said, attempting to resist divine counsels, he deceitfully feigned assent to religion. He promised the Magi that he too would immediately come with every devotion to adore the little child, once he had received certainty about the child through their return. Jerusalem is troubled with the malignant king; it does not rejoice. It is terrified and wastes away, yet is ashamed to deny what Scripture attests. The sacrilege of the scribes was no less dreadful than Herod’s impiety, because the Jews, abusing their own privilege and proving ungrateful for divine visitation, made their cause common with Herod. From both sides impiety and unbelief raged against the Lord and his Christ, and together they agreed in their hatred of him. Behold, foreigners come in supplication from the rivers of Ethiopia to the little Christ, and sons of those dispersed bring gifts. Those who were far draw near, while those who were near depart; in a humble place and amid mean furnishings, the King of kings and Lord of lords is found, recognized, and adored by others.

Since the ancient law teaches that no one may appear empty before God (Exod. 23), while transgressors of the law depart empty, the first fruits of the nations bring forth sacramental gifts from their treasuries and present gold and perfumes to the Lord, declaring by the meaning of the gifts what they believed and thought about him whom they adored. In the gold they confess him as king; in the frankincense, as priest; in the myrrh, as incorruptible though capable of suffering. This offering both expounds the mysteries of the incarnate Word and, by a brief and subtle indication, expresses the unity of both natures, human and divine, while distinguishing what belongs severally to each. For Christ, the high priest and pontiff, offered himself to God the Father, whose kingdom and dominion fills the world with its splendours, as an odour of sweetness. His flesh, burned by the coals of suffering, sent the fragrance of his offering to heaven; and that most sweet fragrance endures without failing to this day in the earthly and heavenly Church. That the passibility which, obedient to God, he voluntarily assumed was strengthened by incorruption, is shown by the effect of myrrh, which opposes decay; and the visible meaning of the gifts supplies manifest proof of firm immortality.

[Col. 1626C] Having adored the Lord, the Magi return joyfully by another route to their own country, because those who believe unto righteousness must also confess with the mouth unto salvation (Rom. 10), and must then choose narrower paths and bind themselves to stricter commands. For broad paths and steep descents lead to the lower regions, but narrow and difficult ways return to the heights. For the words of God’s lips every devout person enters hard paths (Ps. 16), and the slayer of pleasures securely attacks the enemy standing opposite. Chastity is a narrow way; humility a constricted path. To be afflicted by fasting and to reduce the flesh to slavery are rocky tracks; but armed soldiers return to their higher homeland only through difficult passages. A return to Herod is not safe, nor is it expedient to make compacts with those who hate God, or to enter into religious counsels with the malicious, whose intimacy zealously persecutes Christ’s infancy. Before Christ is formed in us, at the very beginning of devout conduct, such intimacy labours utterly to extinguish the spirit and suffocate the life of righteousness.

Herod complains that he has been deceived when he learns that the Magi have gone by another route, because it is most grievous to the prince of darkness when he knows that persons tempted by his devised snares have escaped. Inflamed with harsher rage, he raves in the slaughter of the Innocents. Thus the cruel tyrant is mocked by persecutions of the saints: while he thinks that he destroys those whom he kills, he procures for them the state of a better life. What he contrives for destruction, they use for a benefit; through these momentary losses they acquire the gains of eternal life by swift advantage. Behold these little children, whom Herod—the enemy of nature, foe of piety, monster of bestial ferocity and unheard-of cruelty—killed: they suddenly become martyrs. Torn from their mothers’ breasts and cut down in Christ’s place and for Christ, they render by suffering the testimony which they could not yet render by speech; the cause suffices for testimony, although it is not yet distinguished by utterance.

[Col. 1627B] At once the spirit leaves the vessel that contained the infant body; it is no longer held by the time of a tender body and newly begun age. Freed from those infant clots, the soul, having attained fullness of reason and understanding, hastens to meet Christ. Seeking from him the wages of its service, it is sent beforehand to the joys of eternal light and peace; it celebrates the festival of Epiphany in heaven, glorying not in the light of any star but in the very brightness of the divine presence. The feast of the Nativity is celebrated above by rejoicing angels; below, praise is perfected from the mouths of infants and nursing children, while the trumpets of victory sound even to heaven. The wailing of little children is turned into joy and mourning into jubilation, as the army of the Innocents follows not a star but the Lamb, bearing the solemn standard of a most glorious triumph. Nor could the world defile this infant army, newly entered into the contest. The feet which had not yet trodden mud were not allowed by their urgent and swift passage to be stained by any foulness. At life’s beginning that whole harmless phalanx was transferred, without any loss of integrity, to the glory of a more substantial life.

The discernment of reason that might have been expected after the passage of years suddenly found the goal of all perfection, no longer subject to the periods of that age, and escaped the changing contingencies of events. The senses, oppressed by the sleep of infancy, awoke; their eyelids burst open, they beheld the light, and in a moment attained the blessedness owed to the peaceable and pure in heart. Ascending through all the degrees of virtues without the exercise of human instruction, they found its full measure, so that among the order of saints they hold the first place as proto-martyrs. Knowing divine secrets, in closest intimacy they entreat the mercy of God for our labours—those whom murderous Herod persecutes even today and in whose blood and death the devil delights.

These, then, transferred from the cradle to heaven, became senators and judges of the heavenly capitol, obtaining pardon for some who are undeserving. They attend upon divine mercies and judgments, but use the Lamb’s gentleness more often than anger or fury—the Lamb whom they follow wherever he goes (Rev. 14). Recently washed in milky blood, they consecrated the first fruits of baptism by martyrdom, handing down to posterity the pattern that, where an urgent necessity excludes delay, blood is no less effective for the washing of the soul than waters sanctified by solemn words—especially since blood does not lack this element, but flows through the whole channel of the body by the movement of waters. The Holy Spirit is borne over both waters and blood; he cherishes and washes those subject to him. When he baptizes, killing accomplishes the same as immersion; each sacrament contains the extinguishing of the life of sin and of virtue that had died. For he himself baptizes, whether in this manner or another, whatever that manner may be; and what is done through Christ our Lord in pure faith is referred to the same end.

## IV. ON CHRIST’S BAPTISM AND THE MANIFESTATION OF THE TRINITY

[Col. 1628B]

It is not enough that angels spoke to the shepherds, that a star appeared to the Magi, that the prophecies—fitting the birth, the person, and the place—converged in one testimony to Christ through the report of the faithless nation. A loftier and more perfect testimony is divinely brought forth: the invisible Father himself is heard; the splendid voice of almighty God reaches human ears; and a form of faith unheard of through the ages is declared. Christ came for baptism, not needing the washing, since there was no sin in him, but so that enduring authority might be given to the sacrament and that no respect of persons might commend the power of so great a work. For remission of sins, whether granted through baptism or through other sacraments, belongs properly to the Holy Spirit alone; to him alone remains the prerogative of this efficacy. The solemnity of words, the invocation of the holy Name, and the signs assigned by apostolic ordinances to the ministries of priests celebrate the visible sacrament; but the Holy Spirit fashions and effects the reality itself. Invisibly the author of all goodness applies his hand to visible consecrations; the richness of the divine anointing pours the fullness of grace into official acts of sanctification; and he completes and perfects the sacramental reality.

If the grace of baptism were bestowed in Peter’s or Paul’s name, one person might seem higher than another; and this singular grace might be assessed according to the merits of ministers, so that the baptism of one thought holier would be better, while that received from one commended by no greater esteem would be inferior. This injury would extend to the other sacraments as well: there would be diversity rather than unity in them, if those administered by better persons were judged better, and those administered by unworthy persons were thought to have less usefulness and weight. Thus one Eucharist would be believed better than another, and baptism better or worse according to its minister. Far be such a leaven of corruption from Catholic faith; far from Christian religion! “One faith, one Lord, one baptism” (Eph. 4). If it should happen to have been consecrated by an unworthy person, the righteous person does not dare repeat or correct what has once been done, because, through whomever it is performed, it is the same. This privilege has not been given to merits but to grace, and almighty God properly reserves this effect to himself.

For Paul was not crucified for us, nor do we glory in Paul; rather, we glory in the cross of the Lord, whose power accomplishes all the sacraments. Without that sign nothing is holy, nor does any consecration attain its effect. From this arises the height and depth of all sanctifications, and the fullness of graces is spread far and wide. Lest any presumption should thereafter claim glory for itself from this gift, in this as in other matters the kindness of our Lord provided for his Church: he himself was baptized by a servant, so that fellow-servants might not disparage the ministry of fellow-servants, or one person be preferred to another in this work. For whether Judas or Paul baptizes, Christ washes, absolves, and destroys sin.

Thus Rachel and Leah give Bilhah and Zilpah to their husbands and receive children from the wombs of their maidservants. The scribes and Pharisees sitting in Moses’ seat, when they do what belongs to the seat, exercise the fullness of authority in every respect; and it is the office, not the life, that is honored by such effects. Demons obey exorcists: “Jesus we know, and Paul we recognize; and we go out, adjured in the name of Jesus whom Paul preaches; but you we wholly do not know” (Acts 19). Behold, mercenary exorcists accomplish nothing in their own name, nor do the demons themselves profess submission to them; rather, the name of Christ retains the power of its glory even through those who pursue profit. In such cases hired ministers are like merchant ships which carry traders across the sea, while their captains hunger more for the money of those whom they convey than for their safety. Yet the sea of this world needs such transporters; otherwise commerce would cease, nor would the abundance of overseas regions aid the scarcity of others, nor would the resources of regions meet one another if conveyances were removed from the trackless way and the impassable sea left so. For the ministries of evil persons often serve the good.

The Redeemer’s humility, therefore, places its holy neck beneath human hands; and though this baptism does not possess its full efficacy, Christ nevertheless receives John’s baptism. John prepared the way for the Lord by outwardly washing bodies, so that an outward washing might precede the baptism to follow, in which cleansing of souls and remission of sins would be bestowed. What was partial came first, so that completion might follow. Yet John trembles and does not permit Christ’s sacred head to bend down before him, because the ancient rules oppose the greater being blessed by the lesser, and he judged it a culpable usurpation of authority. The Baptist had proclaimed that all had received from Christ’s fullness, himself included among the rest; therefore he judged it rash that a human being should lay hands upon God, and superfluous to wash him in whom there was no sin. Having confessed himself unworthy to loosen the strap of Christ’s sandal, he feared to offer what was subordinate, if he himself should vainly attempt in his master what he recognized as necessary to receive from him. Therefore, trembling, he humbly declines assent to the ministry requested—not because he withholds obedience from one commanding, but because majesty ought not, in his judgment, to be subjected to a servant.

“You come to me,” he says, “and am I to be baptized by you?” (Matt. 3). To him the Lord replied: “Allow it now; for thus it is fitting for us to fulfill all righteousness” (ibid.). John’s humility is not rebuked, nor did Christ judge blameworthy this refusal arising from simplicity, prompted by reverence rather than obstinacy. He declares, therefore, that all righteousness is fulfilled in this: that example should precede teaching; that those who occupy the greater and lesser place should honor one another in advance; that the greater should become the lesser, and the leader as one who serves (Luke 22); that all should assemble together in the unity of the sacraments; and that they should not break the bonds of ecclesiastical peace.

Christ is baptized, and Jordan does not thereafter turn backward. Jewish anointings have dried up; ceremonies have decayed. The grace of baptism flows in a perpetual stream to posterity and is dried up by no age. The eternal Divinity deigned to be present at such great mysteries and to make its presence known. When the heavens were opened, the Holy Spirit, showing himself there in the form of a dove, willed both to be understood and to be seen; arriving in the gentlest descent, he rested and remained upon Christ. For John had received from that same Spirit a familiar answer concerning this: that he upon whom he saw the Holy Spirit in this form was the one with whom the authority of baptism remained—the one who would take away the sins of the world (John 1), who alone, sanctified by none and sanctifying all things, not so much merely was present at every sanctification and sacrament as performed them.

The Father’s voice too was heard from heaven: “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased” (Matt. 3); “hear him” (Matt. 17). Until now, holy Lord Father, we had not heard you speaking—you who formerly spoke to the fathers in many ways through the prophets, and through holy angels to whom missions from you were often assigned for diverse mysteries. Before this time we had not heard you yourself speaking in such a manner that the utterance you made might be personally assigned to you. No one can doubt that this voice came from your Fatherhood; none dares claim this word for himself; among the heavenly hosts there is none who dares call his Lord Jesus his son.

Certainly the Trinity is known to you alone; the Father alone knows the Son, and the Son knows the Father, nor has he been known by anyone except through the Father’s revelation. In this school of divine teaching, the Father teaches and instructs; the Son reveals and opens to us the mysteries of God; the Holy Spirit fills and imbues us. From the Father we receive power; from the Son, wisdom; from the Holy Spirit, innocence. The Father chooses, the Son loves, the Holy Spirit joins and unites. From the Father eternity is given to us; from the Son conformity to his image; and from the Holy Spirit wholeness and freedom. In the Father we are; in the Son we live; in the Holy Spirit we move and advance.

Eternal divinity and temporal humanity came together, and the unity of the two natures was made with such constancy that what has been joined cannot be separated from the other. Yet Word and flesh are one essence in such a way that their sincere union makes a perfect and complete unity. It is not an injury but God’s grace when what seems lesser is joined to what is worthier, since the inferior nature does not contract the insult and reproach of sin. Nor is it a diminution of majesty, but an advance of poverty; nor does a humility exercised in the economy of salvation dishonor God’s height in any respect.

This testimony was heard: he whom John holds in his hands is the Son of God—true man, true God, the Father’s only Son; invisible in his own nature, visible in ours—so that teaching may be supported by faith and experience, as one attains knowledge of the incarnate Word both by sight and understanding. Beloved by the Father, he loved us though undeserving; of his own accord he bestowed upon us the benefit of his visitation, of his own accord healed us, of his own accord cured us, of his own accord gave us freedom. This love pursues and recalls even the ungrateful; nor does he then hate when he corrects and scourges. Love led Christ even unto death; and, risen from the dead, he holds dear those to whom he displays the affection of so great a love.

Two welcome names, “Son” and “Beloved,” are impressed upon our minds by God himself speaking, so that the communion of names may associate us with the fellowship of gifts, and the names of such sweetness may soften our hearts and kindle the affection of devotion. In every respect the Father was well pleased in the Son; in him no traces of the serpent were found, nor did God repent of his priesthood. For the sacrifice which he offered on the cross remains so acceptable in God’s good pleasure and stands with such enduring power that today that offering is no less effective before the Father than on the day when blood and water came out from his wounded side (John 19); and the wounds preserved in his body forever demand the price of human salvation and claim the gift of obedience.

To this beloved Son of yours, Lord, you command us to be obedient. “Speak, Lord, for your servant hears” (1 Sam. 3). “You will give joy and gladness to my hearing” (Ps. 50). I embrace your teaching; your utterance is sweet to me—your word living and effective, more penetrating than a two-edged sword, reaching even to the division of my spirit and soul (Heb. 4). Within me it separates and sets apart fleshly from spiritual affections; distinguishing precious things from worthless, it drives from the inner temple of mine which you inhabit every traffic of trade, as though with a whip woven from cords. It does not allow the merchandise of doves in your courts, but excludes every sale from the sanctuary of your grace (Matt. 21).

I hear you when you are angry; I hear you when you show mercy. Whether you spare or scourge, I proclaim you just and good. In wrath I entreat you; in clemency I give thanks; nor do I oppose your holy words. Speak, good teacher: I gladly hear you; and even when you oppose me, amid wounds and pains I understand your discipline. Taught by you, I know that the cautery is useful for drying the rottenness of my corruptions, and that the salt of your discipline, poured in while your Gospel heals, cleanses old scars. You command me to apply hyssop to the diseased lung, so that, after drinking the sweetness of your Spirit, the swelling of all malice may subside.

Learning humility from you, good God, we bear you as rider with the quiet step of gentle animals, finding under this burden not weariness but rest, because your yoke is not heavy but light (Matt. 11). Your law, testimonies of righteousness, commandments, fear, and judgments contain mysteries of things delightful in themselves. Your law teaches us to avoid sin and reproves transgressors; so that, with washed and clean feet, they may walk in the blameless way, it shows beforehand every obstacle and points out the detours by which dangerous passages are avoided. It commands nothing impossible, nothing harsh.

In some matters the rewards promised through your law invite us; in many, proposed penalties, punishments, or losses withdraw frightened minds from the desire for crimes. Nor does your written law differ in any respect from the law of nature. Rejection of evil and choice of good are divinely implanted so deeply in the rational soul that no one rightly complains of this, because no one lacks either knowledge or power for pursuing these things: we know what must be done, and what we know we are able to do. If your commands were impossible, burdened with such great difficulties, or if your will were so hidden that it could not be understood what your majesty demanded of us, then—even though no one sins unwillingly—many might excuse their fault. But the moderation of the command, knowledge of the truth, and distinction of what must be done have, by cognizable authority, provided for us, and possibility and ease, knowledge and power, embrace one another together.

You command me, Lord God, to love you: this I both can and ought to do. You command that my whole self, inwardly as well, should be subject to you; and concerning my neighbor you command that I should embrace him according to my own measure. I give you thanks, most merciful God, because what you seek from me you first gave yourself. How you have loved me, even if I spoke with the tongues of men and angels, I cannot worthily express, nor can I encompass all that the abundance of your grace has bestowed on me.

It is right, Lord, that we should love you, because you yourself love us; and it is altogether unjust that your beloved should offend you in any respect. Truly this commandment encompasses the Law and the Prophets, and in this word the volumes of all the Scriptures are compressed. This is what nature declares, this reason, this, Lord, the authority of your word; we have heard this from your mouth. Here every religion finds its completion. This is the first commandment and the last; written in the book of life, it presents an unfailing lesson to humans and angels alike. Let Christian religion read this one word and meditate on this commandment; it will find that the rules of all teachings flow from this Scripture, that whatever ecclesiastical discipline contains is born from here and returns here, and that in all things whatever love does not confirm is void and frivolous.

Whoever does not love you does not belong to you, Lord, nor is he of yours; nor does he love you who knowingly offends you. Whoever crosses the boundaries set by you, transgresses and despises the decrees of your Gospel, detracts from love of you. He does not love you who loves money: no one serves both you and Mammon at once. Those who have a form of godliness while denying its power do not belong to you; nor do those entangled in the business affairs of this age fight in your service. Those who serve sin and are lovers of fleshly pleasures do not hear you; rather, like the asp, they stop their ears (Ps. 57), lest your word penetrate their hearts.

Your law, God, confirmed by the testimony of apostles and martyrs, bestowed wisdom upon your little ones, poor in spirit, to whom it pleased you to give your kingdom; and your righteous acts made glad their souls, in which they lived after being taught by that same law. This commandment of love so enlightened the minds of believers that, living in peace and holiness, they saw you with peaceful and pure hearts; and holy love and chaste fear together obeyed their persevering zeal for you. By such ascents they came so near to you that they became conscious of your judgments, and through them you exercised your judgments both then and afterward.

You commanded, Lord, that we should hear your beloved Son. We give you thanks because you committed us to his teaching. We, therefore, by your command entrust ourselves to be formed by his doctrine; and, clinging to him, we shall gladly hear him at all times, under the guidance of the Holy Spirit.

## V. ON CHRIST’S FASTING AND TEMPTATIONS

In the thirtieth year after he assumed flesh, when the Lord had been baptized in the Jordan and it had become known through the Father’s revelation that he was the Son of God, it was no longer fitting that he should be thought Joseph’s son or be subject to him. Yet he did not immediately employ his power for signs, miracles, and teaching. For the time being he restrained his authority, and before making himself known to the world he exposed himself to the devil’s temptation—not so that the wholeness of his divinity might be tested, but so that the presumptuousness of the tempter might be confounded. For through hunger and weariness after fasting the truth of his humanity was manifest, though, united with divinity, it was wholly without the sensation and consent of sin.
