This age reasonably indicated the time for teaching, and an example was given that it is wrong to take up the teaching office before such limits; for it is not fitting for immature years to sit in the chair, and the Law forbids plowing with firstborn oxen. But now that the proper age and time had arrived, and the command to obey Christ’s word had come from heaven, the Wisdom of God nevertheless chose first to train people by example and to set before them lessons against temptations, so that human reason might hear, see, and feel how unconquerable and victorious over sin it is when freedom of choice is directed by free self-control.

Therefore Christ enters the wilderness. There he dwells with his own guide and companion, that is, the Holy Spirit. A secluded place is chosen because fasts must be undertaken under God’s judgment alone, and these contests especially require God as their sole observer and helper; nor is there more dangerous warfare in any contests. Empty glory flatters no religious exercise more deceitfully, nor does favor so seductively court any virtue. Intrusive praise insinuates itself into the toils of fasting; penetrating the soul with most subtle stings, while it exalts, it weakens, and while it anoints, it pricks. It turns virtue into hypocrisy and perverts what began simply. Like a moth it gnaws at and occupies what was whole, uprooting and scattering the foundations of holiness. This most subtle evil strangles the hypocrite with his own noose and attacks holiness with its own weapons. Chastisement of the flesh inflates the spirit, and bodily emaciation makes the weakened person fat with arrogance. Contempt hunts for veneration; hunger and hardship are sated with praises. A mind steeped in this poison luxuriates in miseries, and, occupied by this itch, glories in sores. Religion becomes superstition, and contrived ambition succeeds it. When the spirit is extinguished, only the wrappings remain for a corpse four days dead: a lifeless appearance of virtue and an image of holiness.

So great is the madness of hypocrites that they use foul odors as fragrances, judge precious things cheap and harsh things sweet, regard the taste of favor as surpassing every seasoning of sweetness, and delight, in every delirious sensuality, in contraries. For this reason Christ, while fasting, chose solitude without spectators and a desert empty of the retinue of flatterers: that the struggle might be not with flesh and blood but with spiritual wickedness; that, once occasions for threats had been removed, a human being might wrestle with the devil; and that Christ and Antichrist, Spirit and anti-spirit, might be alone in the arena.

Nor should a person suppose that he has escaped dangers when he has come into the wilderness, for the more subtly the tempter attacks, the more difficult he is to repel. Sitting at the doors of thoughts, he endeavors to strangle every germ of virtue at its very birth. Desiring to erase Christ’s image, he overlays natural beauty with counterfeit colors and corrupts and clouds the brightness of the spirit. Yet the freed soul confronts the assailant more freely where the fetters of hindrances are absent and it knows no incitements of sight; the conflict is safer where individual things do not continually tug at the combatant and the enticements of pleasures do not intoxicate the mind.

We struggle more honorably with spirit than with flesh, because the embrace of the flesh, exhaling a foul vapour, contaminates in some degree anyone who clings to it; nor has anyone escaped the bites of lusts unharmed. That pestilential breath infects even those far away, and this kind of battle requires flight rather than attack. Since demons are usually subdued by prayer and fasting, the fortification of the desert, furnished with this kind of armor, receives Christians after the example of their Master. Even if a place cannot accommodate everyone, solitude of mind is wholly necessary: there, with the watchtower raised, the wakeful mind may keep watch over itself and, its rust wiped away and its arms shining, frighten off and repel the troublesome enemy.

By fasts the bilge-water of vices is dried up, insolence withers, desires languish, and fleeting pleasures depart. The fire of burning Etna is extinguished, and Vulcan’s flame-belching furnace, quenched within, no longer scorches the neighboring mountains. If fasting is governed by discretion, it subdues every rebellion of the flesh, despoils and disarms the tyranny of the throat. Fasting shuts and restrains extraordinary impulses in stocks, and tightens and binds wandering appetites. If adorned with humility, fasting makes God’s servants contemptuous of the world. Fasting strengthens cleansed unleavened flesh; it consumes and dries up the corruptions that arise from fat. Fasting feeds on the delights of Scripture, is refreshed by contemplation, strengthened by grace, and nourished by heavenly bread.

Through fasting Daniel receives the interpretation of dreams, and the three youths emerge unharmed from that Babylonian fire. Moses, remaining with the Lord on the mountain for forty days, merits through fasting both familiar conversation with God and the ministry of the Law. Elijah too, abstaining for the same number of days, lives in the wilderness. The usefulness of fasts appeared more clearly in Christian times; practiced by many, it spread itself abroad among multitudes. Of all the men of virtue whom we have seen, we do not read that any ascended without fasting; nor did they undertake anything great unless abstinence had first preceded it. Whenever they sought to obtain something from God, they devoted themselves to fasts and tears; keeping vigil in prayers, with haircloth clinging to their flesh, they humbly sought benefits. Nor was success absent where humility lay prostrate at God’s feet, offering the sacrifice of a contrite heart. God was near to those who called upon him; he stretched out his hand to the shipwrecked and helped the afflicted.

If the Church had Moses, Aaron, and Samuel today, they would be heard when they called; and, if Job, Noah, and Daniel prayed, the people would be spared. Rare today is Phinehas to pierce the shameless; rare is Moses to kill the sacrilegious; rare is Samuel to mourn the disobedient; rare is Job to offer sacrifice for the negligence of his children; rare is Aaron to announce divine threats before Pharaoh; rare is Noah to provide a pitch-coated ark for those threatened with drowning. Weeping with the Apostle, I speak of enemies of the cross, earthly-minded rulers whose god is their belly (Phil. 3), who shamelessly rejoice and glory in matters which it is wicked even to mention.

The dangerous times foretold by the Apostle have come, in which people are lovers of pleasures rather than of God, “having a form of godliness but denying its power” (2 Tim. 3). Countless leaders are found who do not lift a finger for fasts and prayers, whose hands contain iniquities and whose right hand is weighed down with gifts [bribes] (Ps. 25). Miracles are sought from them in vain and aid implored in vain: they are not fit intercessors, but despisers of the Lord. They neither approach him fittingly in order to appease him nor reconcile him whom they offend. Prayer is effective when fasting goes before it; and when holy practices precede, devout petition does not suffer rejection.

Solitude is chosen so that the soul, free for God alone, having sacrificed its pleasures within itself through self-restraint, may fly to heavenly things with its affections purified; seeing God, it may pray and adore, and may taste beforehand the sweetness of what is above. Therefore, the pattern of fasting having been set forth and the example fixed, after the Lord completed an abstinence of forty days, Satan approached when he saw him hungry. The preceding time had been held in quiet, and the Savior had carried out that outstanding work alone with the seal of silence; now, when an opportunity supplied by hunger was offered, the disturber came out from hiding and, with a deceptive profession of compassion, urged him to assist nature in its danger: “If you are the Son of God, command these stones to become loaves of bread” (Matt. 4).

The devil neither wishes to confess nor dares deny that Christ is the Son of God. Advising with ambiguity and calculation, he weaves snares into flattering words, so that he may make Christ, if obedient to him, subject to himself, and may make himself acceptable under an appearance of compassion. Flesh, weariness, and the other things of this kind testified to humanity; but the integrity of virtue and a life wholly free from sin ascribed to him a more perfect privilege, and his most powerful divinity could not be denied from its effects themselves.

Before Christ there had been distinguished men—prophets and priests—but they were conceived and born in sins; they were free from neither original nor personal fault. In all of them there was found either ignorance or insufficiency; in these respects the erring sinned and needed God’s mercy (Rom. 3). Taught and restored through that mercy, they gave thanks to God, confessed that they lacked much for fullness of righteousness, and, hoping in God, did not presume to assign any firmness to themselves. Not so Christ, in whom the nature of Word and flesh came together in such a way that no harm came to either from the other: divinity found no stain in the flesh joined to it, neither following nor preceding it. This union of natures blinded the devil, because it seemed impossible to him either that divinity could hunger or that bodily humility could possess such endurance and such power.

Therefore, with winding craftiness, he begins a twofold inquiry, so that Christ himself might answer whether he is the natural Son of God and thus give him certainty. If Christ confesses himself God, it will seem absurd that God should hunger; and whichever way the answer turns, the necessity of his conclusion confronts him: “If you are the Son of God, hunger does not befit you; but if you are hungry, it is evident that you are not the Son of God, whom the violence of necessity confines within the common needs of the indigent. Relieve necessity, if you can,” he says, “otherwise you will fail; change these present stones into the substance of bread. Thus you will escape danger, and if you can do this, prove yourself to be God.”

The malicious question did not deserve an answer. Yet the Lord was not ignorant of the devil’s tricks, but he answered the cavilling devil with a divine utterance, teaching by a most subtle doctrine that the life of body and soul requires support from their proper foods; that the food of the soul—that is, God’s word—must be preferred to bodily victuals; and that the mind must be provided for sooner and more attentively than the belly. There was no need to make himself known to the plotter by this act, since no sign could change the envy of one whose incorrigible wickedness despair had branded. It was therefore superfluous to work miracles there at his suggestion, which could be of no benefit, when it was enough for the attentive observer to see that the appetite for food did not overcome Christ though hungry, and that the stirring of desire was not weakness but strength.

No necessity compelled or ruled Christ in any respect. By the governance of his own will he ordered and paid what humanity demanded. As it was in his own will to consecrate fasting, so it was in his power to take food at the fitting time. This certainly was not to be arranged by the devil’s ministry or counsel, because both the judgment and the power regarding abstinence and refreshment belonged to Christ himself. Thus the deceiver extracted no certainty, but was dismissed doubtful and uncertain. He did not obtain that Christ should reveal himself by miracle, or should hasten intemperately toward food in obedience to the seducer’s counsel, as though only then, after instruction was given and a ruling received, he had learned what ought to be done.

Repelled by the authority of Scripture and the firmness of Christ’s resolve, he failed in his investigation; nevertheless he did not cease from attacking by another way. Adding other falsified arguments to the earlier ones, by which he might extract from Christ some answers agreeing with himself, he set him upon the pinnacle of the Temple. Him whom gluttony could not overcome, he endeavors to overthrow through vain glory.

Many question whether this was a bodily transportation—whether Christ permitted himself to be transferred from place to place in the manner in which Habakkuk was carried from Judaea to Chaldaea, and Philip from Azotus to meet the eunuch, who, returning from Jerusalem and not understanding Isaiah, was turning over the scroll. But it seems unfitting that the devil bodily carried him, that the Savior sat upon his shoulders and used as a vehicle one whom he knew to be a precipitant, or that he entrusted himself to be carried by one whose snares he recognized.

He should therefore be understood to have been led by his own Spirit both into the desert and upon the Temple; and in both places the devil took him up to tempt him. The first temptation occurred locally in the wilderness; but the tempter’s craftiness led him through the others in that manner, or the Savior’s patience allowed itself to be led, as Ezekiel, while sitting beside the river Chebar, was carried in spirit to Jerusalem, builds and measures the city, and restores its walls and Temple. In this way Christ was in spirit upon the summit of the Temple, knowing what the anti-spirit desired and preparing an opportunity for the enemy who would assault him through vain glory.

Taking occasion from the place, therefore, he urges and advises him that, in the holy city and before the crowds of people, like a new tightrope-walker hanging high in the air, he should fearlessly cast himself down to be a spectacle for the populace. He adds from Scripture’s testimony that angels would give assistance, receive him as he fell, and preserve him unhurt. O accursed malice of the devil! O foolish wickedness! O senseless cunning! O blinded presumption! The evil one thought that he whom gluttony had not conquered could be overcome by vain glory. For experience had taught him, and he had proved in many cases, that conquerors of vices are often corrupted by the trifles of praise; that flattery is an evil kindred and near to virtues; and that scarcely anyone can avoid gladly lending ears to the songs of flatterers and delighting in the melodies of those who praise him.

And just as one who bears evil things said of himself with equanimity is rare, or nonexistent, so one who does not wish to be thought well of is rare; and, if he lives rightly, rare is the person who does not wish himself to be judged steadfast in uprightness of life. If works of virtue have gone abroad, rare is the person who scorns human judgments and despises human praises. Satan thought to suggest this general evil of the human race to the Savior on the basis of the opportunity afforded by his preceding victory: that he might wish to be exalted by popular praises and make for himself a name beside the name of the great who are on earth, if, by a twofold miracle, the constancy of his fasting became known to the people and, supported without harm by angels who bore him, he proved himself the Son of God both by such powerful abstinence and by the obedience of angels.

[Col. 1638B] By counsels of this kind Satan had been accustomed to corrupt the children of men, and even into strong and manly minds he casts such thoughts. And if, by resistance of consent, he is shut out from the entrance to the mind, yet, so as to vomit forth there something of his own filth, he compels them to be nauseated by the horror of abominations. Thus, to introduce something poetic, the drunken Cyclops, desiring an unlawful union, though repelled by Pallas, nevertheless emits Erichthonius into her lap; and though Minerva remains incorrupt, the misshapen monster nevertheless survives, nor do wholly desired crimes die from the memory.

“You shall not tempt the Lord your God,” says he (Matt. IV). This is written in Deuteronomy (Deut. VI). Behold, law is set against law; and Satan, abusing the authority of Scripture, [Col. 1638C] as an evil interpreter of the law, urges the precipice as though it were demanded by reason. But his deceitful and false interpretation is confounded by unalloyed truth; and by a general ordinance it is shown to be forbidden that, because some escape lies open in every strait, God should be tempted by any presumption.

The malignant tempter tries to adduce other arguments; and, at the summit and climax of his wickedness, he attacks the self-controlled and humble man with an offered power. Showing him the height and glory of this world—as though it were unworthy that a teacher of so great authority and performer of distinguished works should be obscured beneath a lowly and contemptible appearance—he entices a mind worthy of honour with universal dominion and enjoyment, and promises to give him everything if, in return for so great a gift, he thanks him and, falling down, [Col. 1638D] worships the bestower of so exalted a rank.

Such illusions are accustomed to present themselves to men of virtue; and, when the testimony of conscience attests their religion and others judge them worthy of honours, they readily acquiesce. Bewitched alike by their own judgment and by that of others, they fall from uprightness; the throne of the mind is overturned, and they are dashed to the ground with their necks broken. Suddenly and at once what had been acquired by much toil is obliterated when ambition rushes in; and by the force of this whirlwind whatever the labour of ancient religion had gained is torn away.

This evil struck down and prostrated Adam in paradise when, scorning the subjection he owed to God, he sought dominion. And when he wished to be like God, he saw and recognized himself to be without God; and he recoiled from the ugliness of Eve’s flesh which, [Col. 1639A] although he covered it, remained there as an everlasting disgrace, standing fast and clinging to him. At the devil’s persuasion, ambition cast down the soul, made subject to vanity. His posterity could have learned from his destruction how miserable a change it was to migrate from delights to thorns and thistles, and to have avarice condemned to mattocks and hoes.

The Saviour resisted this evil and taught us to resist it: however far a person has advanced, let him be subject to God alone, so that in him—or rather, he himself—may be our substance. Let it be clear to us that, just as a height sought after is fatal, so an offered height is most dangerous. This is not because authority which comes from God is blameworthy, or because the divine ordering is an accomplice of sins; but because humility ought so to embrace excellence, of which the Holy Spirit is the author, that one called to a higher place [Col. 1639B] may not know himself to be exalted, and that in every respect the creature may acknowledge the Creator and grace its giver.

The disciples once gloried and took pleasure in miracles, rejoicing that even demons obeyed them; but their presumptuous simplicity was repressed by the Lord’s rebuke: “I was watching Satan fall like lightning from heaven” (Luke X). By these words he intimated to their minds that, before this temporal beginning, he himself, existing in the beginning—or rather, himself being the Beginning—with God, had seen, before the creation of man, the fall of the devil in his pride; and that ambition for an usurped dominion had been the cause of his overthrow. Nor should anyone rejoice merely because he had received the prerogative of eminence; rather, this is the sure and steadfast goal of true joy: that our calling [Col. 1639C] should be secured by justification, and that only then should the outcome of blessedness be firmly established if the record of this order were kept indelible in God’s sight.

Therefore, attending to this—that we are not sufficient in ourselves, as if from ourselves, but our sufficiency is from the Lord (II Cor. III)—and content with God alone, all must necessarily incline toward him to whom we owe everything: that we live, that we move, that we are (Acts XVII). From his fullness he meanwhile distributes gifts to us, according as each has need, until completed abundance reaches its fullness—so packed and heaped together a measure that nothing more may be added or taken away, but every desire both of soul and [Col. 1639D] body may attain a sure end and stable goal in the knowledge of God.

Therefore the devil vainly shows or promises the transient and mutable kingdoms of this world to the immutable and eternal King, when he himself says that his kingdom is not of this world (John XVIII). This is not because, rejecting his own creation, he has subjected it to the power of demons; but because the Godhead does not deign to make its dwelling in those who set love of the world before love of God, and because it is impossible for those who have handed themselves over to the devil to be ruled by God, since there is no fellowship of Christ with Belial, nor can there be any communion of righteousness with iniquity (II Cor. VI).

This kingdom belongs not to nature but to malice; it is persecution, not protection. The entire strength of this power works toward the death and condemnation of those who serve beneath this prince. [Col. 1640A] This kingdom is fortified by vices and surrounded by crimes; its towers are offences, its weapons are contrivances of every sort of shamefulness. The tax-collectors of this king are oppressors of the poor; his tribunes are deceivers; his prefects are perverters of judgments. His chamberlains are hookers of profit, merchants and shippers, priests of the treasury, teachers of money-changing, hired advocates, vendors of crafty speech or counsel, auxiliaries for sale, double-tongued lawyers, composers of lies, makers of sin, those clothed in soft garments and dressed in variegated robes.

In the house of this king are those who sweep floors in trailing military cloaks, transform themselves into women by wearing women’s hair, and disgrace manly dignity, not without injury to nature. In this kingdom are all who exchange the truth of God [Col. 1640B] for a lie; all who, like auctioneers in a tavern of vices, display souls for sale to be corrupted by utterly impure demons. Here the greedy join their avaricious hands over gifts; here, with bent knee, each worships the idol of his own desire and adores the image of his own lust.

This glory does not move you, Lord Jesus; you do not hold the empire of this world; you do not fall or are cast down through desire for these things. You do not worship wickedness; you are not subjected to sin—you who subject demons to your servants and destroy and confound all the boasting of this world.

Most insane Satan, with what face, with what tongue, did you dare tell the Saviour to fall before you—he who stands inflexible and immovable? That he who had condemned you should worship you, the condemned one? What audacity, [Col. 1640C] what shameless presumption was this? What did you hope for, desperate one? Did you think that the Son of God could become an apostate with you?

If you boast that you have dominion over the visible world—that is, heaven and earth and what takes place in it—you are neither the maker of heaven nor of earth. You neither move the sun nor give the stars their course, nor does the firmament revolve through you. You neither see nor understand God; you have no fellowship with the heavenly host and no access at all to the brightness of the higher world. Your portion of this lower world is its scab; yours are the sores of sickness: these you scratch, these you, unclean one, lick. Wherever there is vice, wherever corruption, you sit beside corpses; you handle rottenness, stir up dregs, turn over stenches. You are the evil spirit, [Col. 1640D] the unclean fermenter in the old leaven of this age, the corrupter of holiness and disturber of the simple, the incendiary of lusts and inventor of every shamefulness. You reign among those whom you defile, and rule those whom you pollute. Fornicators and adulterers have you as their instigator and will have you as their torturer; avenging fires will also burn you with them.

No access should be granted to a Christian heart for foolish and empty promises; rather, it should oppose the first ticklings of temptation, driving them away with the hand. Nor should the serpent be cherished until it becomes a dragon. The devil is a liar and promises to give much to those who obey him.

This evil ranges through the whole Church, and the common pestilence seizes countless persons, [Col. 1641A] so that those who were free sell themselves into slavery for the glory of this world, are assigned to servitudes through their vices, and, bound by a compact, draw up for the devil the written bond of their subjection. Pleasures are bought by every iniquity and abundant lusts are sought through every crime.

That traitor Judas, intending to sell his teacher, demanded the stipulated price from the chief priests: “What will you give me,” he says, “and I will hand him over to you?” (Matt. XXVI). Even to the Lord’s death, love of gain intrudes; desire for profit does not spare the Saviour’s life. Ambition even sleeps in the bosom of priests; there it lies beneath the shade, there it fraudulently hides itself in the secret chamber. Simon, in the time of the apostles, thinking the Holy Spirit saleable, approaches Peter with gifts [Col. 1641B] and tries to buy the power by which he might gain more.

This form of sacrilege runs through every office and rank, and ambition leaves nothing unattempted. Let no one doubt that these are the devil’s dealings, and that whoever carries on such commerce is his trader; nor that anything of this kind is granted by him except when apostasy has first preceded it. The tempter shamelessly approaches the ambitious and, after setting forth a ruinous condition, promises rewards beyond which desire itself cannot extend: namely, monarchy over all kingdoms and dominion over the universe, so that one person might have power over all worldly things as though he were God, all things might be subject to one man, and everything might pay a universal tribute to supreme excellence.

What more do you seek greedily? What further thing do you desire avariciously? Can your ambition be fulfilled even thus, or your hunger satisfied, when this world’s morsel is put between your teeth and the entire mass of things is forced down your throat? [Col. 1641C] You have the world; you do not have God. The world will pass away; with that which does not stand you will fall, pass away, and collapse. These are fatal counsels which promise you other things, in which you must perish either by vomiting or by burst entrails.

And the price demanded is that you should bow down and worship the devil, and make a god for yourself of one whom you do not doubt is a deceiver. If you consent and yield, you cannot excuse your fall as unwitting, since he himself declares beforehand your falling and ruin and demands the precipice—he who makes himself such a merchant [Col. 1641D] of lofty rank and promises you such heights of power.

Christ’s kingdom is not of this world. God promises you the kingdom of heaven: worship him alone; remember to serve him alone. Having repelled the tempter, he too will crown you with glory and honour after victory, if you stand in the uprightness of righteousness and do not, by obeying false promises, bend down in worship of the devil and become a participant in his condemnation.

## VI. ON THE LORD’S SUPPER AND THE FIRST INSTITUTION OF THE SACRAMENT THAT CONSUMMATES ALL SACRAMENTS

After Lazarus had been raised, the report had spread throughout Jerusalem, and so great a miracle had stirred the people to venerate Christ. Therefore, when he entered the city, they went out to meet him with palm branches; and, rejoicing amid resounding praises, they brought him into the city as he sat upon an ass, confessing him to be the King of Israel and acclaiming that the Son of David had come in the name of the Lord—he whose eternal empire the prophecies of old had proclaimed.

Yet it was not hidden from the Lord, who knew all things, that at the boundary of that journey he was to drink from the torrent of his Passion; and that, through the veneration bestowed upon him by the people, the envy of the rulers would be further inflamed, their embittered minds disturbed by fiercer madness, and the counsels of their malignant conspiracy would no longer be able to remain concealed, nor could what they had devised for his destruction be delayed further. But the merciful teacher wished, when the sentence [Col. 1642B] of his condemnation was already being pronounced and the time of his crucifixion was near, to give proofs of his power: so that he who had recalled Lazarus’s soul from the lower regions and restored life to one dead for four days might be recognized as having accomplished so great a work by divine, not human, power; that it might be impossible for his own soul to be held by hell when he had authoritatively drawn out another’s; that he was driven to death not by necessity but by obedience; and that the life he restored to others would immediately return to him also whenever he commanded.

Therefore, intending to put an end to the legal ceremonies, he wished the Passover to be prepared for himself, and according to the custom of the Law required what the solemnity demanded: a lamb, unleavened breads, and wild lettuces. The ministers of the New Testament ought not to be leaven-makers; the holy feast seeks minds pure and sincere. Let roasting on the spit of the cross, fragrant with goodness, bake away every rawness of carnal perceptions and harden and strengthen the mind’s dispositions; and let there be no stain in the sacrifice of the holy Church, but let pure simplicity and innocence of life be offered, in the one house of the Catholic Church, by believers leaving Egypt, passing through the Red Sea, and having their dispositions washed by Christ’s blood.

[Col. 1642C] Thus, when the supper had been arranged, ancient and new institutions met one another amid sacramental food. Once the lamb prescribed by ancient tradition had been consumed, the teacher set before the disciples food that cannot be consumed away. The people are no longer invited to banquets elaborately prepared with expense and art, but nourishment of immortality is given: differing from ordinary food, retaining the appearance of bodily substance, yet proving by the invisible efficacy of divine power that the divine presence is there.

The sacraments prefigured from the time of Melchizedek come forth; and for the sons of Abraham who do his works, the High Priest brings forth bread and wine: “This,” he says, “is my body” (Luke XXII). They had eaten and drunk from the same bread according to its visible form, but before those words that food was common, useful only for nourishing the body and supplying support for bodily life. But from the moment the Lord said, “Do this in remembrance of me” (ibid.), “this is my flesh,” and “this is my blood,” whenever this has been done with these words and this faith, this supersubstantial bread and the cup consecrated by solemn blessing avail for the life and salvation of the whole person—[Col. 1643A] both medicine and holocaust, for healing infirmities and cleansing iniquities.

The distinction between spiritual and bodily food was also made manifest: one thing was previously placed before them and consumed; another was given and distributed by the teacher. While those foods prepared for the feast were being taken by the apostles eating together, the memory of the old Passover was being observed. Judas, still belonging to the old life, was not yet compelled to depart, though the devil was invading and occupying his mind. But once the treacherous mind touched the sacred food and the sanctified bread entered the criminal mouth, the parricidal mind, unable to bear the force of so great a sacrament, was blown away like chaff from the threshing floor; and headlong it ran toward betrayal and its price, toward despair [Col. 1643B] and the noose.

As is read in the Gospel of John, a question once arose over the novelty of this saying, and the hearers were astonished at the teaching of this mystery when the Lord said: “Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you will not have life in yourselves” (John VI). Because some did not believe and could not understand this, they went back, since it seemed horrible and impious to them to eat human flesh. They thought it was said in such a way that they were being taught to eat his flesh boiled or roasted and cut limb by limb. Yet if the flesh of that person were divided into pieces, it could not suffice for the whole human race; once consumed, the religion would seem to have perished, since no victim would remain thereafter.

But in thoughts of this kind flesh and blood are of no benefit, because, as the teacher himself explained, these words are spirit and life; nor does carnal perception penetrate the understanding of so great a depth unless faith is added (ibid.). Bread is food; blood is life; flesh is substance; the body is the Church: body, because its members come together into one; bread, because it is suited to nourishment; blood, because it gives life; flesh, because of the property of assumed humanity. Christ sometimes calls this sacrament his body, sometimes flesh and blood, sometimes bread: a share in eternal life, of which, according to these visible things, he communicated to bodily nature.

[Col. 1643D] This ordinary bread, changed into flesh and blood, produces life and growth for bodies. Thus the weakness of our faith has been aided and taught through the familiar effect of things, by a perceptible argument, that the visible sacraments contain the effect of eternal life and that we are united to Christ not so much by bodily as by spiritual transition. For he himself has become bread, flesh, and blood—the same food, substance, and life—for his Church, which he calls his body, giving it participation in the Spirit.

And indeed, when we were flesh and blood, with the nature of body and soul corrupt and weak, we could not be reformed or return to the likeness of God unless a fitting poultice were applied to the inveterate disease; unless, in healing a desperate infirmity, opposites were removed by opposites and like things joined to like. This bread which the Lord [Col. 1644A] held out to the disciples, changed not in appearance but in nature, became flesh by the omnipotence of the Word. And just as in Christ’s person humanity was seen while divinity was hidden, so in the visible sacrament divine essence ineffably poured itself in, so that reverence might be given by religion to the sacraments and a more sincere access might be open to the truth of which body and blood are sacraments—up to participation in the Spirit. This unity does not extend to consubstantiality with Christ, but to the most genuine fellowship with him.

For the Son alone is consubstantial with the Father, and the substance of the Trinity is neither divisible nor partible. But the union between us and him neither mixes persons nor unites substances; rather, it associates dispositions and binds wills together. Thus the Church, made Christ’s body, obeys its head; and the higher light, poured into the lower, reaches in the fullness of its brightness from end to end (Wisdom VIII), remaining wholly in itself while wholly communicating itself to all, and the identity of that warmth cleaves so closely to the body that it does not depart from the head.

[Col. 1644B] Therefore this unleavened bread, true and sincere food, sanctifies us through its outward form and sacrament by contact, illumines us by faith, and conforms us to Christ by truth. As ordinary bread which we eat each day is the life of the body, so this supersubstantial bread is the life of the soul and health of the mind. We eat the bread of angels under a sacrament on earth; we shall eat the same bread more openly without a sacrament in heaven—not by bodily ministry, returning to it through frequently repeated acts, but when our priesthood has been consummated. It will be and remain a perpetual and stable sufficiency, filling and refreshing us; for the presence of the supreme Priest will show himself openly, visible to all without any coverings.

Sacraments, insofar as they are in themselves, cannot be without their own power; nor does the divine majesty in any way absent itself from the mysteries. Yet although the sacraments permit themselves to be received or touched by the unworthy, such persons cannot be participants in the Spirit when their unbelief or unworthiness opposes so great a holiness. Therefore for some these gifts are an odour of life unto life, for others an odour of death unto death, because it is altogether just that despisers of grace should be deprived of so great a benefit and that the purity of such grace should not make its dwelling in the unworthy.

[Col. 1644D] The teaching of this sacrament is new; the evangelical schools first set forth this instruction, and under Christ as teacher this doctrine first became known to the world: Christians were to drink blood, although the authority of the ancient Law most strictly forbids the eating of it. The Law forbids the eating of blood; the Gospel commands that it be drunk. In these commands Christian religion ought chiefly to distinguish this: that the blood of animals, differing in every respect from Christ’s blood, has an effect only of temporal animation; their life has an end and reaches its fixed limit without any restoration. Therefore that which, once buried, does not rise again, and whose roots death has entirely dried up with no hope remaining, cannot avail to attain eternity.

[Col. 1645A] Human life, although it has some affinity with blood, is not governed by blood alone. The soul gives blood the effect of warmth and nourishment, as it distributes its particular offices to the other things in the body, apportions movements, and as it were distributes talents. Nor ought the blood of cattle to be mingled with human blood, because the rational life of a human being ought not to be associated with bestial life. Rather, this carnal opinion must be entirely wiped away from believers’ souls as though it were impure blood: lest human life be thought transitory in the way that the life of cattle vanishes, or lest blood be thought consubstantial with the soul and both necessarily dissolved when suffocation comes upon them.

We are like animals in flesh, but unlike them in life. Therefore, what we have in common with them we may lawfully incorporate into ourselves; but what does not accord with our dignity and seems alien to eternity, we separate from ourselves by the most subtle discernment of the Law. We drink Christ’s blood at his own command, participating with him and through him in eternal life; we abhor the sins of animal life as impure blood, and confess that by tasting sin we were deprived of blessedness and condemned, unless Christ’s mercy had restored us by his blood to fellowship in eternal life.

[Col. 1645B] Therefore, for us—for whom Christ’s blood was offered on the cross and whom it reconciled to God—this unique sacrifice, surpassing every victim, Christ himself, acting as cupbearer, offered in this cup and taught us: so that we might not merely be smeared outwardly with this blood, but that the soul might also be fortified inwardly by the omnipotent sprinkling; and that the penetrating force of so great a medicine might drive out whatever hardness was within and renew and heal whatever corruption of the old life had attached the disease of sin to flesh or spirit.

The master of this ordinance had indeed said that unless we ate his flesh and drank his blood, we would not have life in ourselves. By this spiritual teaching he instructed us and opened our understanding to a reality so hidden that we might know that our dwelling in him is eating, and drinking is a kind of incorporation: obedience rendered, wills joined, affections united.

Therefore the eating of this flesh is a certain longing [Col. 1645D] and desire to remain in him, through which we so imprint and draw out within ourselves the sweetness of love that the infused savour of charity adheres to our palate and inward parts, penetrating and imbuing every recess of soul and body. Drinking also belongs to the same meaning: just as bodily substance is nourished, lives, and remains sound by food and drink, so the life of the spirit is nourished by this proper food. What food is to flesh, faith is to the soul; what nourishment is to the body, the Word is to the spirit—accomplishing eternally and with greater power what bodily foods accomplish temporally and finally.

When we celebrate the sacraments, we are reminded, like an animal that parts the hoof and chews the cud, to bring back to the mouth and chew in small pieces the example of the Lord’s institution, [Col. 1646A] so that the Passion may always remain in memory. Let the punishments of death not terrify the heirs of the Crucified, but let them feed upon and be refreshed by the joyful solemnities of the resurrection now brought to maturity.

How splendid is this cup, how religious the intoxication of this drink! Through it we go beyond ourselves toward God; forgetting what lies behind, we stretch toward what lies before. We do not have the mentality of this world, but despising the delights of the rich man clothed in purple, we cling to the cross, suck the blood, and fix our tongue within the very wounds of our Redeemer. Thus reddened inwardly and outwardly, we are judged mad by the wise of this age, who, abhorring the command of this religion, still go backward today and flee and withdraw from the divine secrets which contain within themselves the sum of all mysteries.

Whoever eats this bread shall hunger no more; whoever drinks shall thirst no more. For the grace of this mystery so satisfies and its understanding so refreshes that, once the fullness of so great a reality has become known to anyone, and the end of every consummation has been found, the bearer of Christ carries him in the breast and bears him in the mind. At every time, let words and deeds harmonious with rejoicing resound in praise of the one dwelling within, and let thanksgivings be sung.

[Col. 1646B] This intoxication does not kindle sin but extinguishes it. In this wine there is no sensual excess, nor is wantonness stirred to play after this drink. When forgetfulness has put all the flesh’s mockeries to sleep, he experiences marvellous things, sees great things, and speaks unheard-of things—the one in whom this Paschal Lamb dwells and whose soul the strength of this pure wine gladdens and delights with inexplicable joy.

The natural person is not admitted among the guests of the Lord’s table; whatever flesh and blood dictate is excluded from this company. Nothing that the subtlety of human perception contrives tastes of anything or profits anything. Whatever seems to depart from its own reasonings, the wise of this world ascribe to madness and deem alien to truth. But truth could not be comprehended by erring human beings; and when human presumption wished to fix its eyes upon the sun, unable to bear the power of the light, it was blinded rather than enlightened, and dimness clung to its sight.

The poor in spirit see these sacraments; content with this one dish, they despise all the delights of this world. Possessing Christ, they disdain to possess any household goods [Col. 1646D] of this world. When those who hunger and thirst for righteousness have been filled, observe what they do; understand what they say; consider how holy is the fragrance diffused by that fullness: a good word, disciplined conduct, chaste affections, peaceful thoughts—this inward sincerity spreads all these everywhere. After these sweet scents, the sharers in this grace run about, embrace one another in mutual affection, and, since they have one bread, they are one body; the heart of all is one and the soul one, clinging to the one Christ, rejecting all else as though leavened, and rejoicing in the sincerity of the one unleavened bread.

This sacrifice is perpetual, an ever-abiding holocaust. No multitude consumes this bread; no age makes it old. There is one house, the Church, [Col. 1647A] in which the Lamb is eaten; no one shares it who is not commended by the nobility of the Israelite name. The manna which rained in the wilderness was a figure of this bread; thus, when the true bread was reached in the land of promise, that food ceased.

Every Sabbath, the loaves of presentation, now cold and hard, used to be changed, and warm loaves of the same number placed upon the table. Now no change of bread takes place: there is one bread of continuous warmth and undiminished condition, which, once offered to God, remains in sweetest savour and purest whiteness. Nor does a Levitical prerogative admit priests alone to bread of such dignity: the whole Church is invited to these feasts; an equal portion is given to all. It is distributed whole and is not dismembered when distributed; it is incorporated, not injured; received, [Col. 1647B] not enclosed. Dwelling with the weak, it is not weakened; nor does it disdain the service of the poor. Pure faith and a sincere mind delight this indweller; the narrowness of our poor little house neither offends nor confines the greatness of the immense and omnipotent God.

This bread of angels, possessing every delight by wondrous power (Wisdom XVI), tastes according to the desire of all who receive it worthily and devoutly. It fills and satisfies the appetites of those who eat it more abundantly than the manna of the desert, surpassing every allurement of bodily flavours and every pleasure of sweetness.

See how, for those who commemorate Christ’s Passion within the sacred offices, torrents seem to flow through certain channels from interior springs, and the soul is delighted beyond all pleasures by nectar-like tears. Consider what sweetness the sighs of contemplation draw forth in a soul seeking where its God is. These are not rains poured down by a stormy tempest; they are morning dew dripping from heaven, like an anointing of the Spirit soothing the mind. Piety stirs those groans, and affection, looking backward and forward between day and night, divides itself by forgiving what has been given; it gives thanks to the giver of so abundant a benefit. Recognizing itself healed and sanctified, it washes itself with tears and baptizes itself with weeping.

[Col. 1647D] But those who are dry in heart and arid in mind, who attend the sacred rites or even partake of the gifts only in words, indeed lick the rock but draw neither honey nor oil from it. They are nourished neither by any sweetness of charity nor by the richness of the Holy Spirit; they neither judge themselves nor discern the sacraments. Rather, irreverently treating sacred gifts as ordinary food, they shamelessly thrust themselves upon the Lord’s table in a muddy garment. It would have been better for them to be plunged into the sea with a millstone hung around their neck (Matt. XVIII) than, with an unwashed conscience, to receive the morsel from the Lord’s hand—he who even today creates, sanctifies, blesses, and distributes this his most true and most holy body to those who receive it devoutly.

In his presence tears do not vainly beg forgiveness, nor does he ever allow the sacrifice of a contrite heart to be rejected. Whenever I see you sighing in the Lord’s sight, I do not doubt that the Holy Spirit is breathing upon you; when I behold you weeping, I perceive one who forgives.

If you violate the temple of the Holy Spirit, [Col. 1648A] if you overthrow and defile within yourself God’s sanctuary, if with Christ’s cup you partake also of the cup of demons, it is insult, not religion; injury, not devotion. It is service of idols and a horrible abomination to wish to serve Baal and Christ at once. Go back with your shrines, you who pant after profits and pursue rewards; you who, rich in Zion, carouse daily; who recline on ivory beds and indulge yourselves on inlaid couches; who are clothed in soft garments and live pleasantly in the land of the living; whose hands are full of blood; whose loins are girded, yet who run without the fastening of a belt. You have no part in this word (Acts VIII), because you take from God what belongs to God and consecrate the image of God to an idol.

But the Holy Spirit chooses and loves the poor in spirit for this mystery, [Col. 1648B] and detests the services of those who thrust themselves pompously and gloriously upon the sacred altars. Uzziah, though a king, was struck with leprosy because of presumption, repelled from entrance into the sanctuary, and his offering rejected as foul. The smell of incense from unclean hands was reckoned a stench; presumption earned wrath, not favour, because, usurping an unlawful thing contrary to right, it rashly ascended to holy things.

Because of the insolence of the wicked, God also rejects his altar and curses their consecrations; he hates Sabbaths, abhors solemn feasts, scents stink, and burnt offerings displease him. In all these things God says that he is wearied; with stern indignation he declares that his will is not in impure ministers.

But the devout hierarch, whom the Holy Spirit pierces, [Col. 1648C] awakens, indwells, and sanctifies, represents the mystery of the cross by raising his hands, and confidently prays for his own ignorance and that of the people. With the confession of a shamefaced and contrite heart, he recalls that at one time, when sin prevailed against him, he was forsaken, in accordance with what David says in weeping: “You turned your face away from me, and I was troubled” (Ps. XXVIII). And the Lord says through Isaiah: “For a short time, and in a little measure, I shall forsake you” (Isa. LIV). He is ashamed to confess, yet he confesses the sins of his youth. But the accusing conscience must answer before the judge; and there can be no escape where the very witness is the accuser, and nothing can be hidden from him who judges. But where one who is judged pleads with the judge, and himself takes the role of accuser, approving, [Col. 1648D] even in his own proscription, the sentence of the one condemning him, he experiences the mercy of the Savior and joyfully sings: “Lord, in your favor you bestowed strength upon my beauty” (Ps. XXIX). And again he hears through Isaiah: “With great mercies I shall gather you” (Isa. LIV).

Even at that very instant, when the soul is already hastening to depart and has emerged at the lips of the dying person, the kindness of the most merciful God does not reject repentance. What is true is not too late; what is voluntary is not beyond forgiveness. Whatever necessity compels repentance, neither the magnitude of the crime, nor the brevity of the time, nor the last extremity of the hour, nor the enormity of one’s life—provided that contrition is genuine and the turning away from pleasures pure—excludes one from pardon [Col. 1649A]. Rather, in the breadth of her bosom motherly charity receives prodigals returning; and, whether the heretic Novatus wishes it or not, God’s grace receives penitents at every time.

Our Lord himself, assuming on the cross the person of those who are forsaken, complains that he has been forsaken (Matt. XXVII). And lest even those at their last extremity should despair, he hastens immediately to help them; when the matter is urgent, he does not postpone his favor, but at once establishes an example and proof of swift forgiveness, saying to the thief: “Today you shall be with me in paradise” (Luke XXIII). Robbery had deserved condemnation and punishment, but a contrite heart changed the penalty into martyrdom and blood into baptism. In a moment impiety became religion; cruelty put on piety. Immediately, made perfect, he was sent beforehand into the kingdom as a citizen of the saints and a member of God’s household [Col. 1649B], carrying with him to the heavenly places the privilege of human reconciliation. Performing before God the Father the office of so great an embassy, containing in himself the realization of this Scripture, he entered by a free and secure access and presented it.

What more, Lord, did you grant to Stephen? What more did your beloved receive, who reclined upon your breast at supper? What more did Paul’s labors deserve? What did the labors of the saints deserve? What did the torments of so many years deserve? What did the wounds of the martyrs deserve? In a single hour this man received the reward to which they came through so many perils. Thus, Lord, you immediately make herdsmen prophets, shepherds kings, tax collectors apostles, fishermen teachers. Nor does sickness slowly leave those whom you heal [Col. 1649C]; rather, anyone whom you restore wholly immediately recovers strength, because what you do is complete, and what you bestow is perfect.

Recalling this grace of God, one who drinks from the sacred cup thirsts more greatly. Raising desire toward the living God, he is held by so singular a hunger and by that one longing that henceforth he recoils from the gall-like cups of sins, and every taste of carnal delights is to him like sour vinegar, rancid and sharply biting upon the palate. Thereupon, amid the sacred mysteries, he turns to thanksgiving; bowing his head, having attained purity of heart, and recognizing that he has been made complete, the sinner restored renders back to God his sanctified soul, as a deposit faithfully kept. Henceforth he glories and rejoices with Paul, saying: “I no longer live, but Christ lives in me” [Col. 1649D] (Gal. II).

These things are considered anew by the faithful in the commemoration of Christ. Their souls having been clarified, the food of his flesh is not an object of horror but of honor, and the spirit delights in the drink of holy and sanctifying blood. Whenever we perform these things, we do not sharpen our teeth to bite; rather, in sincere faith we break and distribute the holy bread, distinguishing and separating what is divine from what is human, and likewise joining together the things thus distinguished and separated, confessing one who is both God and man. Moreover, we ourselves, having become his body, are joined and united to our head by the sacrament and by the reality of the sacrament: each of us is a member of the other, rendering to one another the service of love. We share in charity; we participate in mutual concern; we eat the same food and drink the same drink which flows and streams from the spiritual rock [Col. 1650A]. That food and drink is our Lord Jesus Christ.

## VII. ON THE WASHING OF THE FEET

The Lord had now distributed the sacraments of his body to the apostles; Judas had now gone out. Then, suddenly rising from the table, he girded himself with a towel and, about to wash Peter’s feet, the Lord himself, kneeling at Peter’s knees, offered to his servant the service of consummate humility. And lest anything should be lacking to the perfection of his teaching, he established a distinction between fixed and immovable commands and those which may be repeated and renewed. Thus, while all else was established once for all without alteration, he commended to the faithful this final kind of washing, allotted to daily expiations. And just as the Law required particular sacrifices for [Col. 1650B] individual offenses, so there might be represented one remedy of Christian faith to which a person might run whenever he recognized that he had sinned.

This had not yet been revealed to Peter, since he had not yet heard the teaching of this tradition. He is therefore taught what is the permanence of baptism and of the other sacraments; how much humble devotion and devout humility avail for expiation; and how the washing of feet must be continuously practiced and repeated at all times. By this washing, rightly understood, the defilements clinging to the soul are cleansed by daily satisfaction. For ecclesiastical rules forbid baptism to be repeated; and after one has once been sanctified, no hand that consecrates may thereafter presume to approach again [Col. 1650C]. No one renews sacred orders once conferred; no one anoints or consecrates again what has been anointed with holy oil; no one disparages the laying on of hands or the ministry of priests. For it would be an insult to the Holy Spirit if what his sanctification had established could be rendered void, or what he had once decreed and confirmed could be altered.

The high priest himself is the founder and author of his sacraments; in the others, men had the Holy Spirit as their teacher. And as the divinity of the Holy Spirit and of Christ is equal, so in their institutions their authority and power are equal. What the apostles handed down at the prompting of the Holy Spirit is no less binding than what Christ himself handed down and commanded to be done in remembrance of him. Each thing retains its proper dignity, and the action of each stands uniform within its own kind [Col. 1650D]: nothing can be added, nothing removed, nothing corrected or changed.

The Church has been adorned and honored like paradise. At the center of its expanse it contains a fountain of singular grace, producing rivers that leap up into eternal life; it has a living source and an unfailing course. From it issue the four rivers of the Gospel, bearing throughout the whole world the washing of regeneration. From the hidden and most secret gift of the Holy Spirit the stream of this grace flows forth, washing those infected by ancestral stain so thoroughly that after that washing neither actual nor original stain leaves any trace behind. Once past sins have been washed away, life thereafter must be led by one’s own choice; yet, when actual sins at times revive [Col. 1651A], original sins are no longer imputed, nor is one whose original sins have once been forgiven in baptism liable to condemnation because of them.

For in original sins the corruption of nature deserved to be cast off and destroyed. But because the will had no part in that guilt, God provided a remedy for universal condemnation and tempered the sentence of his justice, removing the hereditary burden from the offspring and mercifully cleansing away, by washing and medicinal anointing, the ferment of original corruption. But upon those who, after the grace of this forgiveness, have wandered voluntarily through sins—who misuse their own freedom and are led by will rather than necessity—indignation and wrath justly return. No benefit from Christ’s death remains for them; rather, the benefits they have despised most justly condemn them.

Yet God does not immediately avenge this contempt [Col. 1651B]. The wrath of the judge does not pursue every offense individually. Nor has he closed the doors and manifold channels of the fountain of his mercy; rather, he meets those who flee and compels the despairing to return, showing them the way of repentance, than which none is broader. To those who return he grants that the sacraments they had injured may again profit them; without repentance they could in no way thereafter experience their effect.

For this reason, most gracious Lord, you wash your disciples’ feet: because after baptism, which reverence for itself does not permit to be repeated, you provided another washing which ought never to be interrupted. Yet you yourself do what you teach, so that we may learn from your kindness how great a gain this work is [Col. 1651C]. When your majesty bends down to our feet, human pride—which stands arrogantly against neighbors and raises itself against God—is confounded, and clay learns, through God’s humility, to think humbly of itself.

The disciples are awestruck and do not dare to speak against him. It is as though ecstasy held them, or as though their minds, otherwise carried away, wandered abroad. They neither resist their master nor ask what this is or why it is done. Peter alone, knowing that he had borne witness that Christ was the Son of the living God (Matt. XVI), and that he had the words of eternal life (John VI), judged it unworthy and unfitting that the Holy of holies should bend his knees at sinners’ feet. “You shall never wash my feet,” he says (John XIII). To endure the service of such humility is not for us [Col. 1651D], who ought to worship in the place where your feet stand (Ps. CXXXI); it is enough for us that, like little dogs, we eat from the remnants of your table (Matt. XV).

You once endured this from the sinful woman, and did not disdain, at a formal banquet where many were dining together, to receive the service of a notorious woman. Her devotion there used her hair as a towel, her eyes as a basin, and her tears as baptism: she touched, washed, and anointed with ointment (Luke 7). Her soul, sacrificed inwardly, brought its own blood into holy things. Each part rendered its own service: the contrite heart burst forth into tears; faith washed; charity anointed. Piling up before you these many burnt offerings, she drew from the fountain of her heart the tears she offered; from the casket of repentance, the ointments [Col. 1652A] she brought; and she spread her head as a footstool. With hair flowing around her, she wrapped and wiped your sacred feet. Retaining nothing of herself for herself, she devoted her whole self to you. And you, attending to her affection rather than her deed, anointed the one who anointed, washed the one who washed, and inwardly wiped clean the penitent.

Simon the leper, with a proud eye, could not behold this attentive mercy of yours; rather, he was offended that the Lord allowed himself to be touched by such a person. If he had considered you the cleanser of his own leprosy, he would not have disdained it: if others receive from the fullness of your grace; if you wash the unclean, justify the ungodly, and call back exiles and outcasts. Your honor, O God, loves judgment; it is fitting that all the earth should worship you and that every knee should bend in your name. Yet that you bend before your creature, that you wash servants’ feet [Col. 1652B], does not seem fitting to majesty.

Peter had zeal for God as his excuse, but not according to knowledge (Rom. X). What humility suggested might in some degree have seemed tolerable, had not obstinacy been striving to resist the teacher. “You shall never wash my feet,” he says (John XIII). “If I must die with you, I am ready” (Luke XXIII). This is what I owe; this is what I embrace. For you I gladly offer my neck to the executioner; but I cannot allow, I dare not endure, my God and my Lord cast down at my feet.

John likewise tried to resist the Lord when he came for baptism; but, rebuked more gently, he immediately obeyed [Col. 1652C] (Matt. III), and because he had also received an answer concerning this (John I), though frightened, he yielded. Peter, however, understanding the difference of this case, judged it tolerable to wash and minister to his master. But to be washed by him, and to endure so profound a self-abasement of his humility, seemed so unworthy that he could not at all be compelled unless an exceedingly grave warning constrained him.

The Lord said to him: “Unless I wash you, you shall have no part with me” (John XIII). Little by little the necessity of this mystery is made clear, which the stated condition renders unavoidable. If we cannot otherwise have a share with Christ unless he washes our feet, then, since consent is thus compelled, let him wash and wipe us and explain to us the power of this sacrament [Col. 1652D]. We said above that those once washed in baptism have no further need of that same washing; but this washing was instituted for daily transgressions. Its continual reconsideration, extending to one’s final end, must search out every deed and every individual thought, correct and cleanse desires roaming through vices and carrying the wandering, unstable soul into vanities. Nothing in life should be left unexamined which has not been expiated by groans and sighs.

When the Lord had loved his disciples unto the end, at the end he established and declared that no one can have perfect cleansing unless fortified by this care. Thus he combined command and example, so that, instructed by this example, they might not disdain to do for one another what had been done by their master; and so that the authority of the command might be confirmed for the religious practice of later generations [Col. 1653A]. Therefore he adds: “If I, the Lord and teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet” (John XIII). Let not the servant be ashamed if he is commanded to do what the Lord first did. Nor should it be difficult for us, if, as he forgave us, we too forgive one another; for by bearing one another’s burdens, we thus fulfill the law of Christ (Gal. VI).

Whenever we encourage the fainthearted, and persuade those who have served Pharaoh in mud and brick to leave Egypt; whenever we are weak with the weak and burn with those who suffer scandal; whenever we groan with the afflicted—then, with whatever care we can, we wash away the clinging mud of sins. Not that our washing by itself is sufficient, unless the devout master comes to wash us at every time. In this danger the struggling soul complains in the Song of Songs: “I have washed my feet; how shall I defile them?” (Cant. V). It fears to defile again what has been washed. But on a muddy road it scarcely finds any firm place upon which to set its foot, and it dreads the defilements of the marshes in which it has often fallen.

Most merciful Master, how often have I transgressed the rules of your teaching? How often have I despised your commands, holy Lord? When you said to me, “Return,” I did not return; when you threatened, I did not fear; when you were good and gentle, I provoked you. More than seventy times seven [Col. 1653C] I have sinned against heaven and before you (Matt. XVIII; Luke XV): who will wash away so much filth? Who will scrape off the accumulated dung? Whatever Peter may say, you yourself must wash us. For we cannot wash ourselves; in everything we do we need the washing of your forgiveness.

Judas the traitor was admitted to participation in your table, but, excluded from this saving washing, he could not be washed at the end, because by detestable greed he defiled the honor of his apostleship. But because with you is the fountain of life and an infinite depth of mercies that are from everlasting (Ps. XXIV), transfer those whom you have washed in baptism, whom you have washed in your blood, whom you continually wash by forgiving daily sins, from the marshes of this world and from the mud of the present life to the most pure kingdom of your glory. There is no scab or bleary eye there; no one suffers a discharge of blood [Col. 1653D], no one is unclean; there is no further need of any washing. Our body being conformed to the body of your glory (Phil. III), you must fulfill your promises and complete and establish through yourself, Christ our Lord, the good work which you began in us (Phil. I).

## VIII. ON THE ANOINTING WITH CHRISM AND THE OTHER SACRAMENTS

This day is honored by many mysteries. On this day the breaking of bread was first entrusted to us, and the table of the Church set before human beings the bread of angels to eat. Today Christ washed the apostles’ feet and instituted that this should be done at all times with solemn devotion. Today, in the Church, along with the other anointings, sacred chrism is prepared to sanctify the people acquired for God (1 Pet. [Col. 1654A] II), admitting them to participation in dignity and name. In it balsam is mixed with oil, expressing the unity of royal and priestly glory—the dignities for whose initiation anointing was divinely instituted.

Today sinners are reconciled to the Church; those cast out are brought back to their mother’s breasts; those excluded from the assembly of saints return to the communion of which they had been deprived. Today prisons are opened and the condemned are granted freedom. Today judges lay aside severity and become gentle; and on every side the united works of mercy bury, as though abortive offspring, ancient traditions and give birth to the newness of Christian religion. For Moses has died and the enigmas of the old letter have decayed. At the appearance of the new oil, the old anointings have dried up; the whole disordered fabric of the Old Testament has fallen apart [Col. 1654B]; the tabernacle has been demolished, the ark captured by the Philistines, and all the temple’s splendor carried off to the Assyrians.

For it was not fitting that Christian religion, occupied with visible ornaments, should take delight in things made by hands. Rather, the consumption of the tabernacle itself, the ruin of the temple, and the exposure of holy things to plunder were to signify the permanence of a more excellent glory; and the sacraments that endure forever were to train their worshippers to contemplate invisible things, so that our desire, withdrawn from bodily things, might seek and pursue the beauty of the heavenly temple. Its religion neither becomes obsolete nor grows old; in it an inextinguishable lamp shines without end. There animal blood is not brought into holy places; there are no hereditary successions of high priests, nor ministries assigned to the tribe of Levi alone [Col. 1654C]. Rather, from every tribe, nation, and language, divine election appoints as priests those whom it finds worthy and fit, according to merit of life rather than birth. To these it has entrusted for keeping and dispensing the cup of his blood, ever filled by the abundance of inexhaustible fullness, so that by its sprinkling and communion hearts and bodies may be cleansed within and without.

Today, as we have said, ointment is prepared for sanctification. Its fragrance delights young women and youthful souls approaching the faith; touched by the sweetness of its pouring out, they love and follow the giver of perfumes, are drawn by that breath even to the king’s couch, and, after that scent, run thirsting everywhere under the urgent pressure of holy desire [Col. 1654D].

This oil has nothing in common with fluids pressed from the fatness of certain fruits. Its power does not arise from a penetrating thickness which, according to certain natural principles, softens and moderates congealed humors that dryness commonly contracts within or corruption gathers into a mass. This anointing was not instituted to heal bodies. When the elements have been sanctified, their own nature no longer produces the effect; divine power works more mightily. Reality is present to the sign, and the Spirit to the sacrament, so that both the dignity of grace may be apparent in the very efficacies of things and it may become known what authority is given through these things to the inner person in godlike conduct and heavenly character.

In ancient times priests and kings were consecrated with this oil; even the stones of altars, when anointed, signified that a spiritual richness was present in the sacred mysteries [Col. 1655A]. And as oil floats and rises above every liquid, so the excellence of priestly and royal dignity, after the pattern of God and Christ, holding all things beneath itself, possesses the rule and defense both of active and contemplative life. From this moisture all distributions of graces are known to descend, which the Holy Spirit apportions and grants to each as he wills.

By the benefit of this anointing, wisdom and understanding are divinely given to us; counsel and strength descend from heaven; knowledge, piety, and fear are poured in by heavenly inspirations. Anointed with this oil, we wrestle against spiritual evils, and cannot be impregnated with counterfeit stinks when we are fragrant with the odor of spiritual balsam [Col. 1655B]. This oil freed under the prophet Elisha a poor woman from the usury of her creditors. In Elijah’s time it fed the woman of Zarephath, and the jar did not fail though it was poured out three times. With this oil Jacob anointed the stone that he had placed beneath his head. Instructed by a familiar command, and seeing God supported upon the lofty ladder amid the mysteries of ascents and descents and the journeys of angels, he understood what power this anointing possessed.

With this oil Moses anointed the tabernacle and sacred vessels, and poured it in such abundance upon Aaron’s head that it descended to his beard and ran down upon the hem of his garment (Ps. CXXXII). Samuel likewise does not approach the initiation of kings without oil. This tradition continued among that people until the failure and rejection of carnal ceremonies [Col. 1655C]. But when the Jewish vessels failed, grace failed and the oil ceased. When the prophetic vessels were filled and the holy kings gathered to their fathers, the unstable people, turned to apostasy and dissipation, retained in themselves no place which the Holy Spirit could inhabit. Vessels full of dregs did not receive the liquid; the lees remained at the top, hardened by long standing; and where there had been a dwelling of religion, a dungheap of sin rotted.

Yet, although these things which had grown customary under the ancient rite ceased—when circumcision now seemed condemnable among the Christian people and sacrifices were reckoned idolatry—Christian religion did not despise the mystery of anointing. With all the others condemned by the common agreement of the saints [Col. 1655D], not only did the honor of anointing remain among kings and priests, but the fullness of this grace was poured out upon the whole Catholic people. Thus, as Christ was called from chrism because God anointed him with oil of singular excellence, so all who share in him may share both in the anointing and in the name, and, being called Christians from Christ, may be rulers and leaders themselves under Christ their leader, offering God the daily sacrifice, priests of holiness ordained by God.

Nor without reason was the cause of so great a work assigned to this day, and from it these sacraments received their beginning. For today, in the sacrament of Christ’s cup, the unity of the Church; in the washing of feet, harmonious fellowship, reciprocal forgiving charity, and submissive humility; and in anointing, the dignity of the Christian name [Col. 1656A], the excellence of spiritual distinction properly bestowed, and perpetual authority and dignity confirmed upon the children of adoption, are established.

Accordingly, at the table where he shared his final meal with the apostles, our Lord gave bread and wine with his own hands; but on the cross he surrendered his body to soldiers’ hands to be wounded. Thus, in the apostles, the sincere truth secretly impressed, and true sincerity, might explain to the nations in what way wine and bread were flesh and blood, by what grounds the causes accorded with their effects, how different names or forms were reduced to one essence, and how things signifying and things signified were designated by the same names.

Sanctified by these privileges of heavenly grace, refreshed by eating the sacred bread, washed and anointed, they recover not the freedom they had lost but a greater and worthier freedom [Col. 1656B]. Cast naked out of paradise, today they return clothed to the tree of life, their robe restored and the ring brought forth; they are reconciled to mother Church, from whom the evil of disobedience had expelled them. The cherub has removed the flaming sword from the entrance to a peaceful state and harmless way of life.

Today, leaving behind in the cursed earth the hoes, the heavy weight of plowshares, and the goads drenched in the blood of exhausted oxen, and wiping away the sweat from faces scorched by heat, exiles are brought back to their father’s house. Going out to meet his returning son, the joyful father does not spoil mercy by reproach or stain forgiveness with insults; rather, he honors the magnificence of his goodness and magnifies his generosity with rejoicing. Musical instruments resound at the reception of this festival [Col. 1656C], and a common jubilation, in equal harmony, gives thanks to the Father of mercies. At his command hell disgorges its ancient prey, demons are bound, and those long shattered return free when iron bonds have been broken.

This day adjoins that night in which the Lord began the work of our absolution: the night when, led from the chief priests to the Roman governor, the judge of all endured judgment, the king suffered mockery, and life suffered death. Descending into hell, he led back the captivity held captive from ancient times (Eph. IV). By today’s rite he left his Church this example: that forgiveness of sins might take place in the Church; that the outcasts might be restored to their inheritance; and that penitents—who, according to their deserts, would have been condemned unless grace intervened—might be granted freedom by the benefits enumerated above [Col. 1656D]. It is altogether fitting that, at the time when Christ led captives out of hell, reconciled sinners should be returned to the Church; that when the barriers of the infernal prison were broken, judicial severity should grow gentle; and that when infernal torments ceased, human punishments should lay aside the horror of cruelty.

## IX. ON THE PASSION OF CHRIST

“Lord, I have heard your report and was afraid” (Hab. III). When the traitor Judas drew near and the hour of the Passion threatened, I was terrified by what you said to the Father: “Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass from me” (Matt. [Col. 1657A] XXVI). Before the apostles, overwhelmed by excessive anguish and drenched in bloody sweat, you declared yourself sorrowful unto death. Hearing these things, I was terrified. For who would not fear if he fears whom all things fear? If he trembles before whom every knee bends (Phil. II)? If he who is death to death and the sting of hell (Hos. XIII) is terrified at approaching death?

Had you not come for this very purpose, and had you not foretold that it would happen? Had not signs, oracles, and the prophecies of prophets proclaimed this from the beginning of the world? If you willingly obeyed the Father, and necessity did not compel you to suffer, why do you complain? Why do you protest? Had you not taught and instructed your faithful not to fear those who kill the body, because tyrannical violence does not reach as far as the soul? (Matt. X).

But that fear expressed the common feeling of human weakness [Col. 1657B]: that all living in the flesh are oppressed by this pain; that the dissolution of bodily and spiritual nature cannot lack this distress; and that this punishment has been imposed without exception upon Adam’s entire succession, so that the difficulty of the final passage might be feared. This distress rightly falls upon those who come to give account before God’s judgment: those who, convicted by their accusing conscience of having abused the benefit of life and reason and the abundance of other gifts, fear that examination from which there is no evasion. The very tearing away of the spirit ruptures and wounds the tenderness of the flesh. No one has escaped this anguish; no one, when the soul departs, has passed out without bitterness [Col. 1657C].
