But you, Lord, who are judge of all, who lay down your life by your own power and take it up by your own power, whom punishment does not pursue by necessity, and for whom the Father’s presence cannot be fearful—why are you anxious? Why do you run trembling to prayer? While the apostles sleep, you keep watch for the traitor, yet you do not hide yourself. Rather, you go out to meet those who come to bind you and drag you to Pilate’s tribunal, led by Judas as their standard-bearer in practiced malice.

“Lord, I have heard your report and was terrified,” when you ask those who seek you what they seek, though you know that they seek you, and tell them that you are Jesus of Nazareth. Immediately your fear seized those whom you had feared; they fell lifeless to the ground. The voice of one man terrified an armed cohort [Col. 1657D], and omnipotence hidden in humanity showed you fearful to your disciples and terrible before your persecutors (John XIX). But, that the Father’s will might be done and the sacrifice of the flesh might begin in fear and sorrow, the burning coals of desolation were beneath the victim (Ps. CXIX), and the fat melted by obedience extinguished them. When you were dragged bound before the governor, you did not entreat the officers; rather, you restrained Peter’s zeal. You did not allow the aid of swords to be employed; indeed, you despised the pomp of both Herod and Pilate. The highness of authorities could not force an answer from you when you were questioned.

Now fear set aside, as though employing a more powerful authority, amid spitting, blows, and the rest of the mockery, you disturb the deranged minds of persecutors by patience and gentleness [Col. 1658A]. Jewish malice feels itself despised in its insults and revilings, and is therefore more violently enraged; yet Christ’s sweetness and loving-kindness triumph over impiety and malice.

In vain, judge, do you wash your fatal hands in the praetorium, professing yourself innocent of the Lord’s blood. You yourself, after diligently investigating the charge of death, confess that you found none in him. Your own wife had instructed you to have nothing to do with this just man; certainly, through her mouth the demons testified that judgment threatened them in that sentence. You do not excuse yourself but accuse yourself; you make your cause common with that of the Jews. They condemn themselves by betrayal, you by parricide. They kill with the tongue, you with the sword: the crime of unheard-of cruelty envelops you as much as them.

Your soul will come into the hands of the judge whom you condemn [Col. 1658B]. When your tribunals have been shattered, you will be judged and plunged into the depths of hell. For you and for wicked Judas there will be, in darkness and the flames of Gehenna, irremediable punishments, unconsumed fires, perpetual pains, and eternal torments.

Indeed, the Son of Man, as it is written of him, goes (Matt. 26): he is condemned in order to free the condemned; he suffers in order to heal the sick; he fears in order to make others secure; he endures reproaches so that the insults of detractors may not move the elect. Counted among the ungodly—of whom one was received and the other rejected—he was made an enduring example and pattern for later generations: neither in the last extremity does God’s mercy exclude the penitent, nor is any hour late for one whom earnest contrition meets [Col. 1658C]. Nor are those who have become true judges of their own lives, at whatever point in time, judged again; for when the sinner, sparing neither himself, assumes the roles of judge and executioner, persecuting himself, while honoring confession through shame, the burning of this holocaust obtains pardon before God. For God does not judge twice for the same thing (Nah. 1:9, according to the LXX); rather, he judges and condemns the impenitent. But those who repent, because he receives them as judged by themselves, he absolves; nor does heavenly justice add anything to the judgment pronounced by the severity of human repentance.

The Egyptians were judged when the returning waves of the sea overwhelmed them; the Sodomites were judged when, their cities overthrown, they were burned by sulphurous flames. Yet, if in those same destructions they had groaned in repentance [Col. 1658D], eternal punishment would not have followed temporal punishment; rather, suffering would have been their remedy and torment their absolution; nor would eternal judgment have crushed and weighed down those contrite in heart. Thus the thief confessing upon the cross deserved not merely forgiveness, but, made Christ’s intimate companion, was sent beforehand into Paradise and made a participant in the kingdom—by confession made a fellow-sharer in martyrdom. But no mercy could assist the blasphemer, because he despaired of the Lord’s power; nor could fellowship in the cross benefit one whose wickedness was not cleansed by the washing of repentance.

You ascended the palm tree, Lord, because that wood of your cross foreshadowed triumph over the devil, or victory over principalities, powers, and spiritual wickednesses [Col. 1659A]. In your hands were two horns, in which your strength was concealed; and your dominion was upon your shoulder. You yourself, bearer of your own gallows, clung to the wood that you had carried, enduring the anguishes and labors of ascent and suffering.

“I considered your works and was afraid.” Though nails pierced your sacred feet and your hands were pierced through, you do not speak of the anguish of your wounds. Though thorns pricked your sacred head, you do not complain; rather, you labor to make known to posterity why you seemed forsaken by God, exposed to insults and the mockery of the Jews. Pilate himself had declared that no cause of death was in you; and Caiaphas, being high priest that year, had prophesied that your death would make satisfaction for the hostile people. You do not speak about death [Col. 1659B]; you do not contend concerning insults. But you will have it understood what is the cause of death, what its gain: so that, once both matters are known, sin and grace may appear; and so that the effect of each may demonstrate how weighty they are. For original death could have no remedy except in Christ’s death; nor could any offering reconcile to God the exiles and condemned, except this unique sacrifice of blood.

And God could, without this holocaust, have forgiven so great a sin; but the ease of pardon would loosen the reins for unbridled sins—sins which even Christ’s sufferings scarcely restrain, which scarcely tear criminal minds away from the dregs of pleasures. Certainly, for so rotten a wound and the stench of ancient scars, no fitting medicine could be found unless the old wound were anointed with the ointment of this blood, and the poisons which that ancient deceiving serpent had poured into the heel of the first man and all his posterity were dried by the poultice of flesh stretched upon the cross [Col. 1659C]. This single remedy consumed those scars which had grown beyond measure; corruption lost the force of its desires; and, with the record of condemnation erased, freedom was assigned and restored by new letters—the charter of pardon being confirmed by the seal of the wound in his side.

I consider your works, and I marvel at you fastened to the cross among the condemned: now neither sad nor fearful, but, with uplifted hands, triumphantly conquering Amalek, the victor over punishments; as though from on high sanctifying the people, raised up aloft and, as it were, near heaven, presenting to those above the standard of your completed contest, and raising for those below a ladder to meet the Father [Col. 1659D]. There, forgetful of pains and insults, you investigate with subtlety and yourself explain why you were forsaken, showing that the words of that anxious complaint were the words of the sins whose person and cause you had assumed—so fully that through Moses and through the Apostle you endured being called “sin” and “curse,” because of likeness in punishment (Deut. 21; Gal. 3), not in guilt. You wished this to be understood on behalf of those who deserved to be forsaken by God on account of their sins, whose reconciliation you were undertaking.

In this case, a subtle advocate for servants, you do not disdain to assume a servant’s person; and you so suffer with the weak that you neither blush nor fear to be crucified, nor to die, provided that they may live and, through your advocacy, not perish. Leaving your height, you empty for a time the majesty of your glory, so that the scattered may return and the forsaken may breathe again [Col. 1660A].

This is why you were forsaken: that by your self-emptying you might gather and recall those who had been forsaken; and that those who had been without God while sin ruled over them, restored to righteousness and conformed to Christ, might become Christ’s and gods. Hence it is written: “I said: You are gods” (Ps. 81).

I consider you, Lord, on that gallows where you seemed without help, and see how, by imperial power, you send the thief before you into the kingdom. In his reception it is already clearly shown how much you have accomplished among the forsaken: this man, the first of them, is crowned with glory and honor, made on that very day a citizen of Paradise and a member of the heavenly court [Col. 1660B]. For it was impossible that your holy soul should be held by hell, concerning which you yourself say to the Father: “You will not leave my soul in hell” (Ps. 15), nor that my flesh should decay in the tomb (ibid.). For when, in his presence, hell was broken open and captivity taken captive, the victorious soul was presented before the Father and returned without delay to its body. Those who were far from salvation drew near to salvation; and, free among the dead (Ps. 87), he granted perpetual freedom to those subject to death.

I consider you on the cross concerned for your mother (John 19). In earlier days, when she wished to speak with you while you were preaching, you had denied her an interview and preferred to your mother those who heard the word, the poor in spirit, saying that those who obey the Father’s will were mother and brothers to you (Luke 8).

Now you are moved by maternal affection, and you entrust the bridal chamber of your humanity to your beloved chamberlain; you diligently provide for her who is blessed among women the apostolic protection, and commit the service of the Virgin to the virgin disciple. Thus Joseph no longer bears the charge of so great a mystery, but John does, because reason now required that the supposition of marriage be removed, and that he who until then had held the place of father and husband should no longer be regarded as Christ’s father [Col. 1660C]. Joseph would have had reasonable grounds for objection in this arrangement of Christ, when Mary was entrusted to another, if he had known himself to be her carnal husband [Col. 1660D]. But because the mystery of that union had been enacted in the Spirit, Joseph bore with equanimity the appointment above him in this service of one whom he judged worthier than himself—especially because his master’s choice so arranged the matter.

Moreover, bringing forward in their midst the privilege of priestly authority, as mediator between us and the Father you pray for those who added insults to the pain of your wounds. You obtain pardon for enemies; you plead and entreat that this iniquity may be forgiven them, and that they may be held guiltless of your death—the very persons who pray that your blood may remain upon themselves and their children (Matt. 27). They are so blinded that they neither understand their crime nor does the very death of the Crucified extinguish their hatred of Christ. But meanwhile your love suspends judgment [Col. 1661A], and your patience provides a place and time for repentance to guilty and ungrateful people; it delays punishment for those deserving destruction, praying that their eyes may be opened and that they may recognize the power of the cross, the efficacy of the blood, and the magnitude of the offense and the gift, of grace and sin.

So dense was the veil, so thick the teaching in which they had been schooled by the writings of Moses. Their senses were so dull and their minds so dark that in the words of the Law they tasted nothing divine. They saw nothing but the coverings of an outward shadow, nor did they penetrate by any searching inquiry of the understanding into the secrets of the mysteries. Indeed, if anyone wished to lead them into holy things and introduce them to the hidden and profound mysteries, they considered it impious and foolish “to suck honey from the rock and press oil from the hardest stone” [Col. 1661B].

Therefore, as Christ prayed, sin was forgiven; and blindness was in large part enlightened; at last the faithlessness of the malicious believed and understood. From the winepress of the cross it pressed out, received, and drank must; and in the cup which Moses had offered it separated pure wine from the lees. Behold: the gift had more power than the offense, and grace than sin. Those liable by the debt of condemnation were freely absolved, without any merit of their own, by the gracious benefit of mercy; at Christ’s command judgment gave place to mercy, and justice, under the Lord’s ordering, gently accepted the moderation of its strictness.

Now the Hebrew sees—and everyone who longs to pass from Egyptian slavery to the liberty of the promised homeland—that Christ’s blood drives away hostile powers more effectively than the blood of the lamb which Israel sacrificed in Egypt. Its authority and power today are so great that it not only guards Israelite thresholds, but even among those who do not live in an Israelite manner, the sign of the sacrament alone repels demons; wherever it is seen, the power of the sacred name and the mark of the blood are terrible to them [Col. 1661C]. Finally, whoever the ministers of the sacraments may be, whatever the hands which either immerse those coming to baptism or anoint them, whatever the breast from which the sacred words proceed: the power of operation in the figure of the cross gives effect to all sacraments; and the name which is above every name (Phil. 2), invoked by the deputies of the sacraments, accomplishes all things.

And although those who receive them are unworthy, the reverence due to the sacraments nevertheless prepares a nearer approach to God; and when they return to their heart (Isa. 46), the gift of washing remains valid and the disposition appropriate to the gifts returns. There is no need to seek or repeat the saving sacrament elsewhere. Now your blood, Lord, does not demand vengeance; your blood washes crimes and forgives sins. Abel’s blood cries out; the sins of the Sodomites cry out; parricide and lust deserve vengeance. You were once the God of vengeances (Ps. 93); now you have mercy and spare those who have offended. You heal the contrite in heart and bind up the wounded; you do not reproach the prodigal son returning for his dissipation; you do not throw prostitution in the face of the adulterous woman; you do not refuse the service of the public sinner; you forgive the monetary debt of one who owes it [Col. 1662A]. To the faithless Jews also you gave grace, and remitted the crime of crimes and the sin of sins.

From your side flows a fountain springing up into eternal life (John 4); and from the same, consubstantial source, though issuing through distinct channels, water and blood flow forth (John 19), sacraments enduring forever for the completion and perfection of all righteousness. The abundance of that fountain, by its perpetual flow, waters and makes fruitful the whole Church. From this fountain we draw not only the waters of the first washing by which those who come to Christ are initiated, but also perennial streams of contrition and tears flow from it; the sweetness of mercies and the effect of all piety proceed from it.

You, holy Lord and priest, who “in the time of wrath became reconciliation” (Ecclus. 44), left the enduring fullness of this holy blood and handed down forever the benefit of this sacred liquid. You established for us an inexhaustible life-giving drink, the sign of the cross, and the example of mortification [Col. 1662B]. When all things are completed, go to the Father and draw us after you. Grant us in this present life to be bearers of your cross without compulsion, and with all the saints to comprehend what the breadth, length, height, and depth of this wood signify (Eph. 3). When it is seen, may the serpent of the wilderness neither harm nor bite us (Eccl. 10); but may we follow you unharmed through all things. May we be little children with you; be circumcised with you; be baptized with you [Col. 1662C]; fast with you; with washed feet eat with you the bread of angels; crucified to the world with you, live with you; and, filled with the Holy Spirit, abide with you in body and spirit forever—you who live and no longer die, unto ages of ages.

## X. ON THE RESURRECTION OF CHRIST

Having procured spices to anoint the Lord Jesus laid in the tomb, the holy women assembled after taking counsel together. Finding there the grave-cloths without the body, they thought that he whom they did not find had been taken away. For the rolled-away stone and the empty tomb suggested such conjectures to simple minds: a body bound in linen cloths could not have been moved from its place unless it had been carried away, nor could a stone of great weight have been rolled away in any manner except by human force. Therefore, when they came in the morning, they anxiously asked how the stone could be rolled from the entrance of the tomb [Col. 1662D].

But the Lord who had inspired them to come had gone before those coming. Having departed from the tomb, he left the place empty; and, with its entrance opened, he gave free access to those wishing to enter, as though warning them to seek him elsewhere, since he could not be hidden by that narrow enclosure. Thus the holy women wept, believing that they had lost him whom they wished to serve; grief had numbed them because their devotion was deprived of its desired result. They had regarded him as a prophet, no less believing than those disciples who said that Jesus of Nazareth had been “a man, a prophet, mighty in deed and word” (Luke 24).

Although, as a provident teacher, he had instructed both the apostles and the other disciples—among whose company these women had deserved to be—concerning his resurrection, the punishment of the cross and the horror of death had nevertheless struck doubt and fear into all. Yet the love by which they had clung to him could not be torn from their hearts: nor could their remembrance of the signs they had seen, their admiration for the teaching they had heard, or the wonderful holiness of the pious manner of life by which they had been formed. They did not yet walk with firm step; the foot of those who doubted wavered. Yet they sought him whom they loved and did not despair maliciously; and so the perseverance of love deserved the reward of finding [Col. 1663A].

Those who loved more ardently and sought more devoutly were therefore the first to see and recognize him. Having spoken with Christ and been assured that he himself had risen from the dead, they announce to Peter and the others (Mark 16) that Christ, rising from the dead, now dies no more (Rom. 6). They proclaimed as good news the one who lives, though he had been thought dead. No longer do they serve his burial with bodily perfumes; rather, with the spices of firm faith, certain hope, and sincere love, they minister to the reigning Lord. They offer the fragrance of virtues not to one under judgment, but to the Judge.

The apostles rejoice. The world had terrified them as though it were splitting apart and, as though shaken by the dissolution of the elements, threatened to cast down all things in a headlong ruin with horrible menace. But once heavenly and earthly things were established and joined together, eternal redemption having been found, they gladly worship him whom they had abandoned; they believe and hesitate in nothing; so far as they can, they stand by him from whom they had fled [Col. 1663B].

Who would not have been terrified by that crash of the world, when the earth shook, the sun grew pale, and the darkened sun hid the rays of its light? The tombs themselves cast away the stones laid upon them; the upper and lower regions, indignant at darkness, tremors, and rents, showed the feeling of their compassion and violent anguish. The world could not bear to look upon the crime of Jewish faithlessness. The senseless elements seemed to possess fuller perception than human beings, who had reason by nature; and those humans, abusing understanding, proved more cruel than wild beasts. They thirsted so greatly for Christ’s blood that they condemned themselves by an eternal curse and fixed the remnants of that anathema upon their little children with immovable permanence [Col. 1663D].

But lest we linger too long over the crime of those who were rejected and destroyed to the end, whose parricidal prayers earned them servitude and extermination, and who, with Dathan and Abiram—whom the opening earth swallowed alive for the disgrace of dissension—are certainly sealed in the darkness of hell: lest the memory of such abominations cloud the Paschal serenity, let us attend with devoted and eager minds to the joys of this illustrious feast. For it is not right that any sad matters should be recited by us during these days. Rather, just as it was granted to the sons of Korah always to sing and prophesy joyful things, and all psalms bearing their names proclaim joys and threaten no adversities, so let us, who belong to Christ—whose blood, according to ancient tradition, sprinkled Adam’s skull, for he is said to have been buried beneath the place where the Lord’s cross was fixed [Col. 1664A]—rejoice and delight in the Lord, sanctified by the outflow of that same blood.

Let the death of the teacher no longer be a horror to lovers of the cross; let punishment no longer bring grief nor suffering shame, since all these are instruments of our life. For his death was a sacrifice for our sins; the punishment of the cross met the punishment due to transgressions; his labor set down our burdens; his pain healed us; and his undeserved condemnation absolved us from eternal condemnation. If his holy humility seemed at that time to suffer anything shameful, the effect of events today makes manifest what the Apostle says: that this sort of foolishness is wiser than human beings, and weakness stronger than all strength; through it the wisdom of this world was rejected (1 Cor. 1), and the poor in spirit triumphed most powerfully over the wise and mighty in the name of the Crucified.

“Let us sing to the Lord, for he has been gloriously honored” (Exod. 15). The people go free from Egypt with Moses as their leader; the sea becomes passable; a fiery pillar flashing by night goes before the Israelite army; the sea stands suspended to right and left; with the mud of the deep dried out, the abyss affords an unharmed crossing. Once God’s people have gone out, the sea closes over Pharaoh and his people, rushing down upon them in sudden mass [Col. 1664B].

The lamb which Israel had sacrificed in Egypt had already gone before them. Because the thresholds were reddened by its blood, the destroying angel dared not touch them; and the people did not fear the exterminator’s sword. That spotless sacrifice, the divided sea, and all Egypt’s strength extinguished prepared victory for them even over spiritual wickednesses. That first ancient Passover shone with these miracles; and, after leaven was excluded, it was commanded that the feast of those days be kept with unleavened bread. The joys of this feast were not to be darkened by servile works, nor was any malice at all to defile the glory of so great a purity.

The Law gave a precise distinction: what the Paschal offering was to be, and its time, place, and manner—when, where, and how the sacred victim ought to be sacrificed. The victim was a lamb; the place, one house for each family; the flesh was not boiled but roasted; the time was evening. When these things were done then in figure, they spoke typologically of what we perform in truth [Col. 1664C]. And when the veil of the Temple was torn apart in Christ’s death [Col. 1664D], the true Lamb—Christ alone, without blemish among the children of men—is, in the final age, when the state of the world is growing toward evening, roasted upon the cross by the one household of the Christian people in the unity of the Church. The leavens of heretics are cast out; the sound fabric of sincere faith is made firm; and he is eaten, believed, and held inexhaustibly.

Under this name the new and old have come together. Israel departs from Egyptian slavery; God’s people depart from the devil’s kingdom. The Hebrews are baptized in the cloud and the sea; and now God’s people are cleansed from sins by the Holy Spirit and Christ’s blood. From diverse families one house comes into being; one tribe comes into being; there is one food: signifying things and things signified, realities and signs, invisible power and visible sacraments [Col. 1665A], which thus make one body, just as flesh and spirit do; and what is seen is reckoned Christ’s body both by name and by power.

In this correspondence of realities Christ has been gloriously honored, and today the rejoicing Church sings the triumphs of glorious praise. In the cornerstone it joins walls once separated, which the marvelous builder cemented into one by poured-out blood. As the foundation of faith, long rejected by the malicious, he joined the divided walls by the bonds of his love; he brought parts into a whole and many things into one; the united walls became one house and a stable foundation. Christ has been gloriously honored, rising from the dead, conqueror of death, despoiling hell and sending captives ahead to the realms above.

Having ascended thus far through the steps of humility, now crowned with glory and honor [Col. 1665B], retaining nothing mortal or passible, he has bestowed upon us the glory of impassibility and immortality and established us, raised again, in everlasting blessedness. Some indeed rose before Christ, but in his name and faith: one under Elijah while he lived in the body; and two who had died through Elisha, living and dead. Yet they returned again to the death which they had tasted. Lazarus also rose, and some others at Christ’s command; having enjoyed the benefit of life for a time, they again returned to the funeral rites. It was indeed an honorable deed and a powerful dominion to recall the spirit to a lifeless body; but incomparable is the dignity of that resurrection whose firstfruits are in Christ—a resurrection followed neither by corruption, dissolved by no antiquity, nor shaken by any change [Col. 1665C].

We marveled at the transfiguration made upon the mountain in the presence of the apostles Peter, James, and John, when the Savior’s face shone like the sun, and his garments, surpassing every brightness, dulled the sight of the apostles. But that momentary splendor wonderfully displayed an image, not the reality; a likeness, not the substance; a part, not the fullness, of transformation. Nor did it show the same glory as before; rather, they saw what they had been accustomed to see. The fullness of that brightness which he promised us was deferred: perfect in him, yet awaiting perfection in us, brighter and purer than anyone can estimate, or than even that brightness could intimate, of which we received the firstfruits in Christ transfigured [Col. 1665D].

The angelic spirits themselves celebrate these Paschal joys in heaven; they marvel at the glory of the risen Lord, rejoice, and delight because the form of a servant has returned to the form of God, and the self-emptying of humility has returned to the majesty of its relinquished height. Their joys are multiplied also in this: that he deigns to make the benefit of so great an excellence common to those for whom he humbled himself, and has willed to share with us the abundance of his brightness. Thus after the resurrection the body will not weigh down the soul, but flesh will be without bulk and weight: agile and mobile, shut in by no obstacles, penetrating and reaching all things through sight and hearing, moving wherever it wills without hindrance.

The bodies of those raised will possess freedom subject to no vanity [Col. 1666A]: incapable of being compelled to anything, suffering in nothing, brought now from hope into fruition, enjoying the reality itself, suspended by no expectation, confirmed in most tranquil peace, and wholly free from fear. That unceasing abiding will blossom again amid spiritual delights.

How wonderful is your knowledge, O God: it is strengthened above us, and we cannot attain to it (Ps. 138). This is the height of your wisdom: by the command of your word alone you created the world not from pre-existing matter; but to bodily creatures you gave their beginning from the substance of the world, adorning the several elements with their inhabitants. You made man from the world and set him over all creatures living on land, in water, and in air, so that each might serve its governor according to its kind [Col. 1666B]. To some you provided temporal life, to others perpetual life. In a wonderful order you change and renew some things; for all irrational creatures you established a fixed term and appointed to created nature a boundary of dissolution which it cannot pass.

Because man is composed of heavenly and earthly material, clothed externally with skin and flesh, he received a time at which, by your command, he would return to earth what he had taken from earth, while the spirit would return to its immaterial origin, whose nature admits no injury of dissolution. A body destined to be consumed by decay and flesh by worms could not, according to the principle of its nature, enjoy the privilege of eternity; nor could it demand from its Creator what did not belong to it by right. Nor did any inquiry of theirs deserve an answer concerning this [Col. 1666C].

But you, best Lord, willingly desiring to grant grace to the spirit, mercifully decreed that the flesh might receive some benefit from the companionship and service which it had rendered to the soul. Having been its vehicle and partner in endeavors, in recompense for its service it might return, again joined to its beloved inhabitant, chaste and peaceful, bringing with it no insults by which it might thereafter disturb the purity of inward repose. You also added this to the fullness of your gift: that thereafter there might be no division between the law of the flesh and the Spirit, nor, after the covenant was made, any rebellion again break out between them; but that reconciliation ordered by your hand might remain firm forever.

At your command, therefore, earth becomes flesh; and, driven from the house, she is again joined to her husband, no longer a slave but free [Col. 1666D]. They dwell in the house with one disposition, their murmurings silenced, which conflicting desires once stirred up as they fought each other. Who, Lord God, is sufficient to contemplate these works of yours? Who can thicken clay into flesh? Who can form it into a human being? Who can infuse a soul? Who can restore life? Who can give eternity? Who can add blessedness?

Toward this end human creation labored; this was always the expectation of the faithful. This was the desire of that humble king who knew himself imperfect: that you might add to your creation what it lacked, perfect and establish your work [Col. 1667A], which corruption and mortality continually used to afflict with many reproaches and assail with various insults. You command death, and, swallowed up, it is crushed. Corruption is emptied when the sick person is healed by the healer. You tasted death for the children of men, so that those who had died with you might live with you and, sharing in tribulations, might also rejoice in consolation.

The resurrection is indeed universal, and the just and the ungodly must stand in the body before Christ’s tribunal. God’s justice so ordains, so that piety and impiety may receive in their practitioners their due rewards; those who despised to set an end to evils may be enclosed in endless punishment for endless vengeance, while those who gloried in the cross, reigning with the Crucified, may become participants in blessed eternity. Those whom ambition condemns do not share in this joy; one who keeps stolen purses cannot take part in the Paschal solemnities [Col. 1667B]. The betrayer and seller of the master, the profane maker of leaven, has nothing in common with unleavened bread. Everyone unclean in soul is forbidden to approach the eating of this lamb.

No faithlessness is admitted to this joy; every malice is excluded. Let everyone who is pure and sincere, a true person without deceit—feet shod in readiness to proclaim the Gospel, loins girded and devoted to holiness, staff in hand, hastening to leave Egypt’s idols, following Moses, and not fearing life’s perils—come and eat. Secure that he will rise again, let him choose death in order to reach eternal joys, in which our life remains above and draws us toward heavenly goods. He lives, etc.

## XI. ON THE ASCENSION OF CHRIST

After the solemn victory upon the cross had been celebrated, and after the Lord had restored the temple of his body which Jewish persecution had demolished, he did not wish immediately to ascend to the Father and bring the presence of his glorified body into heaven. Instead, in a necessary dispensation, providing for the weakness of the disciples, he usefully delayed. For forty days he remained on earth, was often seen, spoke with the apostles, ate and drank. He displayed, for their sight and touch, the wounds which he had retained in his body to remove their doubt; and by the manifest reality of events he taught them that the things foretold in the Scriptures had been fulfilled in himself [Col. 1667D].

This delay was necessary so that, appearing with many proofs, he might restore those whom fear had driven into flight and whom the punishment of the cross had terrified, strengthening minds that had wavered through distrust. Thus he might prove, both by eating with them and by being handled, that the body which had risen was not phantom-like but real. The glory of the Ascension was delayed also so that, during this interval of days, earlier teaching might be strengthened in their affections—or rather, so that the disciples’ desires might come to seek his bodily departure. For the fullness of spiritual presence could not arrive while he was present to sight in the flesh. Gradually they were led to be willing, though accustomed to intimate association, to be deprived of it, when the indwelling Holy Spirit, possessing their souls by an invisible coming, would infuse purer affections in them and open their inward eyes to behold with pure understanding the Father of lights (Isa. 1). The substance of things hoped for (Heb. 11), once set before them, would bury appearances; and no scruple of uncertainty would remain when the Lord and teacher, whom they had proved to be truly human, ascended to heaven before their eyes. They would then confidently believe that they too would follow, and that it was not impossible for them also to be carried to the realms above in flesh and spirit [Col. 1668A].

Therefore, when all had gathered for so delightful a sight, he said: “I ascend to my Father and your Father, my God and your God” (John 20). Once the Holy Spirit had disclosed the force of these words to them, their authority could exclude all distrust. Their minds rejoiced, illumined by the honor of divine fatherhood and honored by fellowship in Christ’s brotherhood, when they heard and believed that they were children of God and brothers of Christ, in whom dwelt the fullness and sufficiency of every excellence.

They no longer applauded this saying carnally, like ignorant and dull persons. Rather, with the greatest subtlety they saw that the generation and dignity of the creature had their beginning from the will and ordinance of the Creator, and that God’s image and likeness were in the inward person. They recognized—by understanding rather than sight—the kinship of father and son, and that adoptive sons, made conformable to the substantial and natural Son, possess much from nature from their first origin, and much from grace [Col. 1668B].

Indeed, this participation in nobility, by which together with Christ we are children of God, sets forth and reveals the nobility of our existence. If we remain in that honor and do not degenerate, it is altogether certain that the Father cannot be at variance with his children. For those made godlike, access to fatherhood is secure; nor can those appointed to possess the inheritance suffer rejection in divine petitions. Whenever a son addresses his begetter filially, the goodness of the giver must justly fulfill the petitioner’s will—especially since the Father himself, who gives these things, suggests that we ask for what he does not delay graciously to bestow [Col. 1668C].

And paternal love delights especially in good children and heirs. This also adds to the glory of Christ, the beloved only-begotten: he does not allow the greatness of his blessedness to remain solitary, but adds brothers—not brothers who diminish his excellence as though it were divided among many, but participants and companions who adorn the height of his riches. Since it is certain that he who is Father is himself God [Col. 1668D], and since the Son attests that he is our God as well as his own, then, in that we are children, he possesses us; and in that he is our God, we ourselves properly possess him to whom we belong.

I say therefore to my Lord, “You are my God,” and my Lord says to me, “I am the Lord your God.” What more does the person whose God is God seek? If you suffice for God, let God suffice for you. God has no need of your goods: you can neither give Him anything nor take anything away. If He were hungry, He would not tell you. His is the world [Col. 1669A] and its fullness; even the heaven of heavens cannot contain His greatness. He does not grow weak; He needs neither clothing nor food. He knows all things, can do all things, contains all things: in Him we all live, move, and are (Acts 17). What can you offer Him as though He were needy? He desires you alone through goodness, not necessity. It is written—indeed, at His own command engraved upon tablets of stone—that you should love Him with all your heart, with all your soul, and with all your mind (Matt. 22). Love, and you shall be loved; your reward is near, the prize is held out in His hands. Be God’s, and your God will be yours. Unequal indeed is this exchange, an unequal price; yet He who for our sake was valued at thirty pieces of silver (Matt. 27) wished it to be understood how great was the disparity in value between what was paid for Him and what He Himself gave for the [Col. 1669B] world: He was bought and sold for a little silver, yet redeemed those condemned at so great a price. Thus there can be no doubt that the greatness of the price surpassed the transaction; nor could the loss—which just condemnation had wholly deserved—be equated with Christ’s obedience, which advanced in its weight even to death and freely paid what it did not owe.

Understanding these things, the apostles, like the sons of the prophets of old, knew that the true Elijah would ascend, and joyfully awaited that hour. No longer did they suffer anxiety as though in travail; rather, with joy arisen, they stood ready to accompany Him as He departed, not in the least doubting that they too, after a little while in this present life, after drinking from the torrent of suffering on this way (Ps. 109), would follow their Lord to heavenly things, with head uplifted and raised.

Therefore, raising His hands [Col. 1669C] and leaving them an hereditary blessing (Luke 24), Christ was not borne up by a vehicle made with hands, nor lifted by the aid of chariots; rather, using the power proper to the divine nature, He carried His flesh into heaven and presented His glorified body before the Father’s sight. He had no need of angelic bearers to remove obstacles from His path and carry Him in their hands. Instead, those preceding and following applauded the victor; joining in exultation, they sang the new song, and the harmony of that consonance filled heaven. Thrones and dominions obeyed the Son seated beside the Father; cherubim and seraphim surrounded His feet of peace; and divine brightnesses shone everywhere, with [Col. 1669D] supercelestial splendors which neither enduring fire consumes, nor the blast of any tempest extinguishes, nor the intrusion of any darkness conceals.

The heavenly host rejoices in the magnificence of so great a triumph. Those who, before the shepherds of Bethlehem, had sung lofty praises at His descent now rendered more solemn service, with fuller efforts and more ardent rejoicing, to Him returning to the Father. With festive devotion they venerated the man exalted above themselves, whom the Father had crowned with glory and honor (Ps. 8), placed at His right hand, and granted the singular privilege that at His name every knee should bend, and that His name should be honored as more excellent than every name (Phil. 2). No one can adequately recount how great was heaven’s joy at His reception [Col. 1670A]; the magnificence of this event surpasses all understanding. Though someone speak with the tongues of men or angels (1 Cor. 13), or exert all the sharpness of any intellect in wishing to define the Father’s gladness at the Son’s return; or if perhaps that everlasting joy then admitted some increase, if the immovable greatness of eternal stability could somehow change itself: that searcher into majesty will be overwhelmed by glory (Prov. 25). And one must beware lest, in straining to express words more forcefully than is fitting, he milk blood instead of milk.

Nevertheless, it is manifest that the invisible God received the visible Son at His right hand, and that the humility of our flesh, honored on the judicial throne, pleased the Father’s majesty: that henceforth two kinds of peoples should be assigned to the heavenly city, of which glorious things have been spoken (Ps. 86) [Col. 1670B], and should stand above the resident humans and angels, and that the glory of that blessedness should forever be thronged by these two orders. This is the reward of Christ’s obedience; these are the wages of the cross and death; this labor of suffering earned that the body of our lowliness should be made conformable to the body of Christ’s glory (Phil. 3), that this mortal should put on immortality and this corruptible incorruption (1 Cor. 15), and that human beings should become judges with Christ in heaven—those who had borne with Him the judgments of the wicked and had been companions in tribulations even unto death.

On this day this unheard-of novelty was first brought into heaven; and the Father rejoiced at His enlarged inheritance, His multiplied offspring, and the promises [Col. 1670C] which He had spoken through the prophets rendered and fulfilled. Of all that has been foretold, judgment alone remains; the ancient oracles still reserve a place for the final examination. For after Christ’s removal, after the times of mercy that hasten toward their end, judgment and distress remain, so that judgment may accompany justice, each may receive what he deserves, the worthy may be honored with honor, and the despiser may be put to shame without glory.

This also the two angels testified when Christ ascended: He who departed from those being judged would return as a terrible Judge. Then the whole human race will see gathered into one the hands that it pierced, the side that it bored through, the face upon which it spat; and, when the inflexible sentence has been pronounced publicly, while the elect go to meet the Savior [Col. 1670D], the wicked will remain assigned to endless torments. How great will be the lamentations following that decree; how dreadful the blast of that final trumpet! The flow of those tears will be unceasing and superfluous; unquenchable flames will drive that gnashing of teeth. The wretched will live immortal; fires and inextinguishable flames will lap at their naked bodies. The purple-clad rich man will burn, and there will be none to pour a drop of water upon his burning tongue. Lusts fried in their own fat will boil; wretched bodies will be burned amid flaming pans; and despair will afflict the condemned more cruelly than every torment. God will no longer have pity, nor then hear those who repent; that confession will be too late. When the door has been shut, those lacking oil will cry out in vain, excluded.

[Col. 1671A] There will be no refreshment there, no remedy. Christ descended to hell once; He will descend no further. Those sealed in darkness will no longer see God; that sentence will be irreversible, the judgment unchangeable, and the fixed decree of this condemnation will stand immovable. But the saints shall exult in glory (Ps. 149): they shall see God and rejoice; they shall delight and take pleasure and enjoy glory, and in eternal blessedness they shall be glad. There they shall not merely taste how sweet God is, but shall be filled and satisfied with wondrous sweetness. Nothing will be lacking to them, nothing will harm them; Christ, present, will fulfill their every desire. They will no longer grow old, waste away, or decay: perpetual health and the happy eternity of blessedness will assure their sufficiency.

There will be no lust [Col. 1671B] in their members, no rebellion of the flesh will arise again; but the whole state of the human being—chaste and peaceful, nature wholly restored to health—will thereafter remain without every spot or wrinkle. Finally, God will be all in all (1 Cor. 15), and His presence will fulfill every desire of soul and body. When all things have been completed, the ministries of angelic powers will henceforth cease; and when the City of God has been wholly filled and ordered, the state of fixed and consummated blessedness will neither be renewed nor changed again.

Therefore, to Him before whose tribunal we shall stand (Rom. 14), who now appears before the face of God for us (Heb. 9), and who cared so greatly for us that He was willing to be born and die for us, we pray in the present time that He may take care to heal [Col. 1671C] us and grant us authority and power to judge and correct ourselves, so that, called and gathered among the elect in that terrible judgment of His, freed from slavery and captivity, we may be joined to the citizens of heaven and enjoy the good things which He Himself promised beforehand to those who love Him—things which neither eye has seen nor ear heard (1 Cor. 2).

## XII. ON THE HOLY SPIRIT

Be present, Holy Spirit; descend from heaven upon those awaiting your consolation. Sanctify the temple of our body and consecrate your dwelling-place. Gladden the souls that desire you by your presence; make ready a house worthy of you as its inhabitant. Adorn your bridal chamber and surround the couch of your rest [Col. 1671D] with the variegated virtues; strew its floors with spices. Let your dwelling shine with fiery carbuncles and the brilliance of gems; let the fragrances of every charism breathe within it. May an abundance of balsam’s liquid steep your chamber in its fragrance; and, driving away from it whatever is decayed and whatever is a seedbed of corruption, make this our joy steadfast and everlasting, and establish forever the renewal of your creation in unfading beauty.

We have attended the sacred infancy of the Word and accompanied the Virgin in childbirth; with the heavenly host we have sung glory to the little child, and confessed as almighty Him whom we saw crying in the cradle. We have celebrated the mysteries of circumcision, and, with the foreskin of pleasures cut away, have learned to be enslaved to holiness. [Col. 1672A] We attended the Savior’s baptism; hearing the Father’s voice from heaven, we were handed over to obedience to Christ and instructed from heaven how love joins and unites Father and Son. Thus even in the names themselves the distinction of persons is indicated, while the unity of nature is made altogether evident.

Moreover, amid those mysteries we saw the Holy Spirit in the form of a dove. From that form we understood that sighs of repentance and desires for divine contemplation proceed continually from simplicity of heart and innocence of unblemished life; and that no one, unless such sighs go before and divine inspiration gives warning, can aspire to heavenly things—so that sighing, inspiration, and aspiration have from the Holy Spirit alike their cause, their effect, their material, and their outcome. We also followed the Lord fasting into the wilderness and saw the devil’s temptations powerfully repelled.

[Col. 1672B] We attended the supper and drank from the Lord’s cup; we washed feet; we died with Christ, and behold, we live. We follow Him as He ascends and await the Holy Spirit promised to us, whose anointing may teach us concerning all things (1 John 2); who may teach us through invisible instruction and train us in heavenly disciplines; who may dull carnal senses and crush appetites. This Holy Spirit is read to have been borne over the waters from the very beginning of the world (Gen. 1)—not over material waters as though needing them for a vehicle, but rather waters which He Himself bore. He gave the waters encompassing the firmament their fitting motion and their appointed limit.

Although ancient philosophers, investigators of the world, could not properly discover in its own nature His eternal power and divinity, nevertheless by most subtle conjectures they discerned that, amid the composition of the world and the combined and differentiated dispositions of the elements, a soul was present in all things, supplying life and motion according to the kind and order of each, fixing inviolable bounds, and assigning stability and use. [Col. 1672C] Philosophers called this life, this motion, this essence of things “the soul of the world,” thinking that heavenly bodies—the sun, moon, stars, and the firmament itself—were moved and governed by the power of this soul, and that water, earth, and air were impregnated by its seed. If they had believed it to be the Spirit, Lord, Creator, giver of life, and nourisher of all things beneath Him, they would have had a fitting approach to faith. But the majesty of so great a reality was hidden from the wise and prudent. The arrogance of human intellect could not share in heavenly secrets or penetrate to the height of the superessential nature. And though they understood that a divinity truly existed which creates and governs things, they could in no way distinguish what the Trinity of the Godhead was, or its unity, or the proper characteristics of the persons.

The sanctifying Spirit was indeed borne over the purifying element, already then declaring the power of baptism. Already then were prefigured those times when Noah’s ark, borne upon the waters of the flood, kept the family of the righteous man unharmed, after the adulterous generation had been destroyed—those who, unrestrained in beastly wantonness toward the daughters of men, had foolishly mingled with them, fearing neither divine nor human eyes in their public crimes. [Col. 1673A] The Holy Spirit then governed, and still governs, that ark which bore the type of the Church. Whoever strays outside it in faithlessness, entangled in the waves, sinks into the deep. It is impossible for one to live over whom the Spirit of life is not borne; His life-giving heat animates, cherishes, advances, and makes all things fruitful.

This Holy Spirit is the soul of all living things. So abundantly does He pour Himself out upon all through His generosity that all rational and irrational creatures have from Him, according to their kind, both their existence and their activity in the fitting order of their nature. Not that He is the substantial soul of each individual thing; rather, remaining singularly in Himself [Col. 1673B], as a magnificent distributor from His fullness, He apportions and bestows His proper operations upon each. Like the sun warming all things beneath it, He nourishes all things and, without any diminution of Himself, lends and imparts from His inexhaustible abundance, whole and undiminished, what is enough and sufficient for all.

This Spirit dried up the waters of the Red Sea. Holding back the mighty waves on either side, He led the people unharmed from the fleshpots and Egyptian dishes into the spiritual freedom of the wilderness. He fed them with heavenly provisions, pouring manna like morning dew upon the grass, which they were commanded to gather by measure. The full measure was present throughout the week, while the Sabbath day was exempt; and the preceding sixth day, doubling the usual quantity of food, [Col. 1673C] prefigured the eighth-day rest, in which the elect will feast in delights without labor or anxiety and be satisfied, possessing a double portion in their land: enriched by the blessed perpetuity of body and soul and by perpetual happiness.

This is the Holy Spirit whom the magicians in Egypt, convicted by the appearance of the third sign, called “the finger of God” when they confessed that their enchantments had failed; and they indicated to the ancient philosophers that His presence had been lacking to them. Although the Platonists had perceived some things concerning the Father and the Son, their proud spirit, craving human approval, could not merit the sanctification of the divine intellect. When they came to the depth of the mysteries, all their subtlety grew dark, and unbelief could not draw near to holiness.

[Col. 1673D] This finger of God, judge and avenger of worldly unbelief, powerfully expels demons in the time of the New Testament. He does not labor in acting, but accomplishes all things by a mere nod: what He says, He does; what He commands, He fulfills. He discloses secrets, lays open what is hidden, reveals what is unknown, dulls the keen, and refutes the perceptive. By this finger the Law was first written upon tablets of stone and entrusted to Moses on Mount Sinai on the fiftieth day after Israel’s departure from Egypt. But the wicked people and stiff-necked nation, from whose minds had departed the terror which blazing death, fiery yokes, the trumpet’s blast, flashing torches, and dreadful thunders had lately instilled, turned to apostasy. Despairing of Moses’ return, they were judged unworthy of the Law sent by God, because before their eyes Moses shattered the tablets, destroying and effacing both words and their instruments.

[Col. 1674A] Indeed, after the vengeance for their crime had been exacted, he returned to the mountain to the Lord. Fasting and conversing for forty days, he finally obtained permission himself to cut from stone other tablets like the former, upon which he might engrave and form the same writing that had been on the first. By the wonderful dispensation of the heavenly judgment it came about that the Law written by the Holy Spirit was erased, while that restored by a human hand was afterward retained. This may be understood as having been done because the former people, walking and living according to the flesh, were shown unworthy of divine discourse and spiritual commands; faithless minds could neither receive holy things [Col. 1674B] nor understand mysteries veiled by the covering of figures.

But the truth of the New Testament, disclosed when Christ preached the Gospel, remained indissoluble after being uttered by Christ’s word, and was thereafter supported by the firm authority of perpetual stability. For the humble received the grace offered to them, and the Son found among the poor in spirit a house in which to lay His head. Rightly, then, visible tablets point out the rejected as despisers of the invisible God, and identify believers who hear the incarnate Word and worship Him devoutly as deserving greater honor.

Thus the Law is given on the fiftieth day after the sacrifice of the paschal lamb; and the solemnity of so great a matter received its name, Pentecost, from the Law, gathering up in the very number of days the meaning of a great mystery. For the number seven, turned seven times, makes fifty when one unit is added. This one is the boundary of the present age and the beginning of the future, containing eternity under the name of the eighth; it thus ends present things while introducing us to everlasting things.

[Col. 1674C] This sacred number seven has possessed authority from the creation of the world, since God’s first works were completed in six days and the seventh was consecrated to rest, honored as though by a holy and sanctifying festival of cessation, and assigned to the sanctifying Spirit. Hence the people, ceasing from servile works, are commanded to sanctify the Sabbath day and attribute to the Spirit of uprightness, holiness, and strength whatever proceeds straightly, honorably, and courageously. For it is wholly through His guidance that the wayward are set straight, the ungodly converted, and the weak strengthened.

The upright Spirit, the Holy Spirit, the princely Spirit rules, orders, completes, and perfects the minds He inhabits and the hearts He possesses. He does not permit those whom He has taught, possessed, and girded with the sword of most mighty power to go astray, be corrupted, or be conquered. This number seven, composed of four and three, while held honorable in itself for the reasons stated above, possesses the highest excellence from its parts, since it seems to express and distinguish the primary substances of maker and matter: three proclaims the Creator because of the Trinity, and four contains within the brevity of this number the creature because of the four elements, which are the causes and seeds of all things.

The Holy Spirit proceeding from the Father, from the Father and [Col. 1675A] the Son, is borne over the number four; and the gracious Creator embraces His work and loves what He fashioned. The Holy One Himself sanctifies His creature, associates it with Himself, and establishes and squares it by the bond of love. By these and other more hidden reasons, which the subtler minds of illustrious men have investigated, the number seven in Holy Scripture often encompasses sacramental meanings; both singly and multiplied, it gives rise to understandings necessary for comprehending divine works.

Among the Hebrews, in weeks the seventh day is called Sabbath, that is, “rest.” This number is observed not only in weeks but also in years. Once a week of years is complete, the seventh year is a year of rest; a Sabbath is commanded even for the land, and no one may lawfully sow or reap anything in that year. Rather, what grows of itself in the ground, vineyards, or trees is assigned for the food of the poor. The weeks of years among the Hebrews also make the fiftieth year, which they call the Jubilee. By the decree of the Law, as stated above, in it there is release for the land, freedom for slaves, restoration of possessions alienated by sale up to that time, and other such things freely return to their hereditary order.

[Col. 1675B] Much having been said about the number seven, more remains which is especially commended in the Law and the Gospel. The fiftieth year therefore completes the Jubilee, and the fiftieth day from Passover makes Pentecost. On that day, when the Holy Spirit was truly poured out upon the apostles, those who had been sold under sin and exiled from their heavenly inheritance—whom poverty and want had subjected to the devil as master—return to it. With seven priests sounding trumpets, Jericho fell; by seven petitions the Son taught that the Father should be prayed to. Forgiveness of sins is commanded to Peter at twice seven times seven. A leper is judged by the priest’s inspection on the seventh day; the consecration of the high priest is completed in seven days. The Lord Jesus Christ feeds five thousand persons with seven loaves; and every righteous person speaks praises to God seven times a day. The Lord Jesus Himself is found, according to the generations recorded by Luke (Luke 3), to be the seventy-seventh from Adam, so that by His coming [Col. 1675C] He might bring to an end the vengeance proclaimed against Lamech seventy-sevenfold (Gen. 4). Unleavened bread is eaten for seven days at Passover; for seven days in the seventh month the feast of tabernacles is celebrated. Solomon’s temple is built in seven years; the lampstand is adorned with seven branches and as many lights. Both we and the Jews celebrate the fiftieth day, but they do so in type, while we do so in truth: we do not so much signify it as perform it.

Therefore, celebrating Pentecost, we commemorate what was done of old under Moses in the Old Testament and what was done under Christ. After His Ascension into heaven, the Holy Spirit visibly appeared over the apostles in tongues of fire (Acts 2), and, after the pattern of the former age, He wished the whole body of believers to be of one speech (Gen. 11), so that those whose heart [Col. 1676A] and soul were one might also have one language. No diversity of words could then obstruct believers’ understanding; rather, when evangelical teaching was delivered in each person’s own language, it attained the same effect upon all hearers, so that for Greeks, barbarians, and every people the word of the Gospel was intelligible as though the idioms of the language in which they were born sounded in their own ears.

Medes, Elamites, Mesopotamians, and Arabs were present. Although the apostles preached in the Hebrew language, and their Jewish speech unfolded the elements of its utterance in its customary course, no interpreter explained it. Instead, through the Holy Spirit power and grace were present in their word, so that those dwelling in Pontus and Asia said that the language they heard was their own—as though the freedom of the original language, having returned to the source of antiquity, had escaped the disgrace of confusion.

Nor was this grace bestowed only on the apostles: the same Spirit was poured out on the multitude of believers, who burned within and spoke outwardly. Love and the word embraced each other, and speech, kindled by the Spirit’s heat, burned ardently. [Col. 1676B] With all fear now excluded, they publicly professed that they must obey God rather than men (Acts 5), and they counted it glory to suffer injury for Christ.

In this manner Moses was once commanded to share of his spirit with seventy men whom he himself judged to be elders, so that they might bear a share of the responsibility for affairs. When Moses laid his hands upon them, the Holy Spirit rested on them. This Spirit was not taken from Moses as though Moses himself remained without Spirit, nor was the same Spirit cut into parts. Rather, according to the measure of the divine gift, the grace which in Moses had been singular became manifold and common, and many received authority in the matter formerly directed by Moses’ authority alone.

So Elisha received Elijah’s spirit twofold—not because the one Spirit was divided into two substances or because the holy prophet had two Spirits, but because the Christian people, of whom Elisha bore the type, upon receiving the Holy Spirit were given power in deed and word. Having followed Elijah—that is, Christ—as he ascended, with devout desire, this people shone in faith and understanding, in life, signs, miracles, and examples.

[Col. 1676C] This Spirit distributes the sacred orders: He makes kings and princes, consecrates bishops, and chooses priests. He endows Solomon with wisdom, Daniel with understanding, Joseph with counsel, Samson with strength, Moses with knowledge, David with piety, and Job with fear. He makes the souls of the saints fruitful in every kind of virtue, advancing peaceful dispositions so greatly that our citizenship is already in heaven (Phil. 3), because love has been poured into us through the Holy Spirit who has been given to us (Rom. 5).

He establishes His dwelling in chaste minds. He has humble celibates as members of His household; He abominates coiners and detests falsifiers. He condemns the hireling Gehazi to leprosy and places Jeroboam, who sells priesthoods, among apostates. He disinherits Simon, the trafficker in God’s grace, from the fellowship of the saints; avenging ruin confounds and shatters his detestable ventures.

[Col. 1677A] He imposes silence upon Balaam, hired to curse; rebuked through the she-ass, with his foot crushed against the wall (Num. 20), empty of money, burdened with disgrace, and limping, He sent him back in confusion to his own home. He is present in all the Church’s sacraments, which He Himself effects and brings to completion. He washes away sins; He justifies the ungodly and calls the dead back to life. He makes the discordant peaceful, binds and fastens them in the bond of love. [Col. 1678A] He carries us into heaven and, tearing us away from the vanities of this world, makes us heirs of the heavenly kingdom. Its highest happiness is that this body will dwell among the angels in a spiritual state; there will no longer be any appetite of flesh and blood, but God, who can be known, and the indwelling Holy Spirit will be the full sufficiency of all.

[Col. 1677]

# TREATISE OF ERNALD, ABBOT, ON THE SEVEN WORDS OF THE LORD ON THE CROSS, WITH SCHOLIA AND THE CORRECTION OF FRANCIS TITELMANN OF HASSELT

*(Bibliotheca Veterum Patrum, Lyons edition, vol. XXII, p. 1260.) (G)*

First word: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” Second: “Amen, I say to you: today you shall be with me in paradise.” Third, to the mother: “Woman, behold your son”; and to the disciple: “Behold your mother.” Fourth: “I thirst.” Fifth: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing.” Sixth: “It is finished.” Seventh: “Father, into your hands I commend my spirit.”

Yet according to the more common opinion, Christ is not said to have spoken these words in this order. For the word placed here in the first position is made fourth. There is agreement concerning the second and third. The fifth is usually given fourth place; the first, fifth place. There is no disagreement concerning the sixth and seventh. Those who examine the Scriptures carefully and compare each passage diligently with the others will also find that this latter order is more probable and more consonant with the Evangelists’ narrative. Perhaps the author followed this ordering of the words not because he thought they were spoken in that sequence, but because he wished it to serve the impulse of his devotion. But there is no need at present to dispute anxiously about the order of the sayings themselves or the rationale of their order. Rather, let us hear attentively, with ears pricked and our whole heart intent, the matters to be spoken.

# ERNALD’S PREFACE

[Col. 1677B] The last words of Christ, which, fixed to the cross, He set before the heirs of the New Testament to be expounded, seem indeed to have been explained here and there by some writers in commentaries on the Gospels. Yet reverence for these holy words moved me to search their inner meanings more deeply, and to consider that, in that [Col. 1678B] hour in which what had been prophesied concerning Him seemed to be fulfilled—

> **Note: [Col. 1677B]** The author here indicates two reasons why those final words of Christ spoken on the cross deserve deeper consideration. The first is that Christ uttered them at the time when it seemed least to be a time for speaking and teaching: namely, when He was wholly oppressed by the torments of suffering. Since He could not be prevented from uttering these words even by such grievous afflictions of torment, we understand that those words must be exceptionally weighty and contain very great usefulness and necessity. Thus, when we see a grave man speak at a time least suited to speech, we understand that such speech is of great necessity or usefulness. Likewise, the matters which fathers of households speak, at the very final moment of departure when they are going away from home on a journey, to those whom they leave at home are usually most serious and most concerned with the welfare of the household. For the very circumstances then require matters of greatest seriousness to be addressed. Thus, because our Lord, about to depart from us on a journey, spoke these last words at the very moment of His departure, there is no doubt that they are words of great weight in themselves and of the utmost benefit to us.
>
> The second reason is that, in wonderful brevity, they contain a very great benefit of holy instruction. When considered more deeply, these few words seem to contain in marvellous compendium Christ’s entire teaching, formerly preached diffusely and at length. For this reason he calls this brief collection of a few words a small seed, saying that an abundant harvest arises from it—an especially fitting comparison. For just as a seed is very small in quantity and bulk, yet encloses and hides within itself an admirable power by which it can produce from itself a tree of great size once it has been hidden and died in good soil, so too these words, few in number of syllables, contain in themselves the greatest power of sacred instruction. This power will finally bring itself forth when the words have been hidden and thoroughly died within good soil—that is, a gentle and humble heart. There a great harvest will be seen to rise from a small seed. In this way also one should understand his statement that in these words there lies hidden a highly fruitful causal and seminal principle.

—were uttered when the matter at hand was no longer teaching but suffering; and that in them Christ recapitulates all His doctrines and compresses into brief chapters what He had previously preached at such length. Thus [Col. 1679A] in that compendium of words the rationale of Christian faith shines forth, and from a small seed there rises an immense harvest destined to benefit the whole body of believers. For the more briefly these things were spoken, and the more they were spoken at that moment when the circumstances demanded the treatment of serious and necessary matters, the more diligently they must be investigated; and the more deeply contemplated, because within them lies hidden a more fruitful causal and seminal principle.

Once the causes have been unfolded, you bring forth into public view, as though from certain hidden recesses and from a golden reclining couch, the venerable majesty of inward meanings; and truth, which you previously did not know because of intervening veils, will emerge openly in its beauty, capable of being known. When you draw nearer and it pours itself into you, illuminating your understanding with the rays of divine truth, you will understand [Col. 1679B] and see a conflagration in a spark; in a drop you will discover an ocean; and in a flask of oil, wherewith you may repay the creditor, while enough remains in abundance for you as inexhaustible food. [Note: [Col. 1679D] He alludes to that miracle of Elisha the prophet which we read in the fourth book of Kings, chapter four: at the request of a poor woman oppressed by debts, he wonderfully multiplied the small amount of oil that alone remained in her house, so that not a few vessels were filled from it. When this had been done, Elisha said: “Go, sell the oil and pay your creditor; and you and your sons, live on what remains.”]

Before beginning, however, let us consider who this is that cries himself abandoned. Is it not he who promises and grants Paradise to the thief? In each case understand the power of the Word. Hear what this final school of subtle teaching instructs. This same one who complains that he has been abandoned does not ask the Father on the thief’s behalf; rather, by his own authority, remitting sins undeservedly, he suddenly sanctifies a criminal, brings him into the heavenly dwelling-places, and sets him with himself in glory. It is evident with every kind of proof that this is the foundation of faith, this the probable and necessary argument: that Christ’s kingdom was fully effective even upon the cross. Nor is the dignity of his dominion diminished by the lowliness of the flesh; indeed, it pertains to the Crucified One’s glory that, amid the disgrace of the cross, the venerable mystery of the incarnate Word—which was judged foolish and weak—conquers and surpasses the wisdom and strength of this world [Col. 1679C] (1 Cor. 1).

For the Son’s complaint in the person of those abandoned is not an indication of inability. Rather, it signifies that this lowering of the higher excellence supplies an increase to the lowliness of the body; and, conversely, that lowliness and sublimity share between themselves the work by certain reciprocal movements: the form of God emptying itself, and the form of a servant receiving the name that is above every name (Phil. 2). He is not abandoned in every respect; rather, the respective character of the individual natures is expressed by an ordered dispensation, because abandonment, suffering, and death are certain narrow and difficult passages [Note: [Col. 1679D] It is said of the serpent that, when it feels itself weighed down by old age and its old skin, as it were, covered with scurf or decay, it chooses for its healing some narrow passage and tight [Col. 1680C] opening. Forcing its whole body through it with great violence, it casts off its old skin together with its scurf, and so, freed from its old skin, is renewed, as it were, in its whole body. They say likewise of the eagle that it is rejuvenated by rubbing its curved beak against a rock. Some ancient writers believe and interpret this to be what the Lord means in the Gospel when he admonishes his disciples to be prudent as serpents (Matt. 10). This is the point of the statement here that being abandoned, suffering, and dying are certain narrow passages through which a human being must pass to the appointed state of renewal and immortality, after first casting off the skin of sin and scraping away every scurf.] through which the renewed human being reaches a firm and unshaken state, as though after laying aside the skin of sin and cleansing away every scurf of vices.

Thus it would be thankless and dull to leave without examination the fact that the fountain of life thirsts on the cross; that, while Christ intercedes, even those crucifying him have room for pardon; that amid insults and torments he is moved by filial devotion toward his mother; and that, when all is completed, he departs as victor to the Father. Each of these themes requires its own ordered treatment, [Note: [Col. 1680C] “Its own syntagma,” that is, its own order or arrangement. For the Greek συντάσσω means “I arrange,” “I compose,” or “I order”; whence σύνταγμα means “an ordering” or “an arrangement.”] and here students of God’s law may find the seeds of the whole religious life, from which a mind trained in divine meanings may reap abundant fruits.

Though I judge myself unequal to investigating these matters, and do not dare to gaze with impure eyes upon the pure light, nevertheless, withdrawing for the present beneath the shadow of divine secrets, abstaining from what is forbidden and inaccessible, I have presumed to stretch out my hands toward the other trees of Paradise [Note: [Col. 1680D] In Paradise the first parent Adam was permitted to take, taste, and eat from certain trees; but the tree of the knowledge of good and evil was forbidden to him (Gen. 2). Yet he presumed to stretch out his hands not only toward what was permitted but also toward the forbidden trees. So in divine matters, some investigation is forbidden: namely, that which through curiosity seeks things greater than the human understanding can grasp. Of such investigation the Wise Man says: “The searcher into majesty shall be overwhelmed by glory” (Prov. 25). But some investigation is permitted: namely, that which does not exceed human capacity and builds up the mind in true piety. Therefore, one who presumes to search out what is forbidden in divine matters is rightly said to stretch out his hand toward the forbidden tree; but one who humbly considers what has been granted is said to stretch out his hands toward the other, non-forbidden trees.] and to discover by taste what savor the abundant sweetness set forth [Col. 1680C] within contains.

## FIRST TREATISE

On that saying: “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” (Mark 15)

[Col. 1681]

[Col. 1681A] After the rules of faith had been proclaimed in evangelical doctrine, after signs and miracles and proofs of righteousness, because “the way is long through precepts” (Seneca, *Epistle* 6), there came also a shorter and more effective way through examples. And lest anything be lacking in the teaching, its pattern followed. This was deferred until the end so that the surviving children might embrace all the more devotedly, as a testament of a pious inheritance, their privileges when they saw them inscribed with Christ’s blood and saw the image of his obedience displayed by an imperishable seal.

Accordingly, from that chair of the cross a kind of Deuteronomy was dictated, [Note: [Col. 1681B] He very aptly calls this compendium of the seven final sayings a kind of Deuteronomy. In Greek it is, as it were, δεύτερος νόμος, that is, “second law” or “repeated law.” We call the fifth book of Moses by this name because in it Moses briefly recapitulates nearly everything that he had described at greater and fuller length in the earlier books, whether concerning deeds done or doctrine delivered. Likewise, because this compendium of seven sayings briefly embraces Christ’s entire teaching, previously preached by him at length, it may rightly be called a Deuteronomy: as it were, a second law or a repeated law.] where, in brief recapitulation, things formerly spread abroad at great length are gathered together. At once the good Master hastens to do and to teach (Acts 1), and to complete his teaching by example; to be not so much an instructor in truth [Col. 1681B] as a witness.

Now he speaks of his own accord, though a little before he had been silent under the examinations of Herod and Pilate (Luke 23). Despising the curiosity and arrogance of fearful men [perhaps: “the curiosity of men swollen with pride”], he instructs the poor in spirit from the gallows. There he establishes anew the school of religion, setting forth a few headings in which he both discloses the affection of charity and commends imitation of holy zeal. Torments cannot impede teaching; iron is treated as though blunt and contemptible. Watchful compassion provides that the disciples’ conduct may correspond to the rule of faith, and that, when the foundation has been squared, the building may stand firmly and securely upon it.

Thus he displays himself now as human, now as God; now as omnipotent, now as weak, so that sublimity and humility may divide between themselves the functions appropriate to the matter. Now he entreats; now he commands. Now he says that he is abandoned; now he promises Paradise to the thief. In accordance with each nature, he does what the situation demands.
