In one he is despised; in the other he bestows glory and a kingdom.

Before the cross mocking cries resounded, and the bloodthirsty crowd added insults to the pain of his wounds. [Note: [Col. 1681C] He seems to allude to the Psalm: “They added [insults, or something of this sort] to the pain of my wounds” (Ps. 68). In what immediately follows—“it gnashed,” etc.—he describes the characteristic of dogs, which in anger snarl by contracting their noses. Scripture calls Christ’s persecutors dogs, as when Psalm 21 speaks in Christ’s person: “Many dogs surrounded me” (Ps. 21).] It snarled and fixed fierce looks upon the face it had spat upon, and with one unanimous shout cried: “Ha! You who destroy the temple of God and rebuild it in three days!” (Matt. 27; Mark 15).

See how much evil the error and faithlessness of the leaders had smeared upon the people; how much of their own rust the authority of the priests had rubbed upon [Col. 1682B] the unthinking multitude; how powerful had become the conspiracy against Christ when they killed him and blotted his name out from among them. They did not fear to be marked forever by the title of murderers. [Note: [Col. 1681D] This occurred when the Jews cried out against Christ: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. 27). Then they took upon themselves the title of murderers, confessing themselves authors of his death. Then they heaped upon themselves and their little children the remnants of so great a crime—that is, the vengeance owed for such a crime. For the remnant of sin is the punishment and penalty owed for wrongdoing. Then they also subscribed the bond of their own condemnation, since [Col. 1682B] by their own voices they confessed [Col. 1682C] themselves murderers.] In a single act they heaped upon themselves and their children the consequences of so great a crime, and willingly subscribed the bond of their own condemnation.

Christ had not yet breathed his last; but with hands and feet pierced, and with his head torn by thorns, he lived upon the cross. Seeing the desires of parricidal minds, he was pierced not so much by the sharpness of the nails as by their crime. Therefore he turns to the Father on their behalf. [Note: [Col. 1682C] At first sight, what is said here seems not to pertain to the saying proposed, “My God, my God, why have you forsaken me?” but rather to: “Father, forgive them, for they do not know what they are doing” (Luke 23). Yet when we attend more carefully, we find that everything is rightly understood of the earlier saying. According to the author’s view, by this saying Christ, in a noble, gentle, and humble complaint, demanded from the Father the reward of his passion: the salvation of human beings and the conversion of sinners. He acts, as it were, by an appeal to justice before the Father, indicating that he would be wronged if, being equal to the Father in divinity, he had voluntarily subjected himself in assumed human nature to such misery of abandonment, and the salvation requested for human beings—on whose behalf he had thus emptied himself—were not granted him. This is what the author shortly afterward means in saying, “He puts before God the Father the question whether sin can do more than righteousness.” Christ could demand human salvation under the claim of justice after having endured such contests for them. For it would have been unjust that the Son’s great labors should prove vain and fruitless before the Father. The author expresses this more clearly shortly afterward: “Otherwise Christ complains that the wages of his struggles have been withheld from him,” etc.; and still more clearly later, after many intervening matters: “But when the Son speaks of himself as abandoned, he seems to be demanding the reward of obedience.”]

Bringing the argument of charity into public view, this new orator adopts an unheard-of manner of pleading: he argues the case of his enemies and, though they are unwilling and heedless, supports the opposing side. He puts before God the Father the question whether sin can do more than righteousness. [Col. 1683A] He shows that it is unfitting for transgression to have greater force than grace, for wickedness to prevail over goodness, and destruction over salvation. For while he strives for their salvation, and the Jews strive for their condemnation, the charity of the Son ought to have greater power before God than the blindness of the people. And this has no slight weight: the advocate of this cause is not a stranger but the Son; nor is the public good diminished by this pardon but increased. Therefore a tempered judgment detracts neither from the laws nor from the judge; for, since courts serve the common good, an institution is not contrary to itself when it returns to its purpose by whatever path and restores what had fallen away from its state of integrity.

Otherwise Christ complains that the wages of his struggles have been withheld, declaring that the labors of so great a contest bring no gain if those on whom such labor has been spent are thus left behind; if this humility proves ineffective for their salvation; and if the Son’s blood is so cheapened in the Father’s sight that it obtains not all that it asks. He therefore cries: “Eloi, Eloi, why have you forsaken me?” (Matt. 27). He does not reproach the Father, nor does he call himself abandoned as though the disgrace of the cross seemed contrary to his purpose. For he voluntarily exposed both his arms to the gibbet and his palms to the iron. [Note: [Col. 1683D] “He was offered because he himself willed it” (Isa. 53).] Rather, by asking he suggests how great the foundation and summit of obedience are, showing himself both lesser and equal. Humility is abandoned; majesty is present. What the Jew and Greek judge foolish and weak in Christ is stronger and wiser than every human strength and understanding (1 Cor. 1).

In the form of a servant, he does not blush for the ministry of his embassy; nor does he deny the fleshly nature that is capable of suffering and death. In this form the attentive Mediator gently addresses the Father; he does not deny what is apparent, nor does he think it robbery if he speaks something from authority and at times addresses the Father as an equal.

He therefore calls him *his* God, lest anyone suppose that what properly belongs to one is alien when applied to the other, or presume to cut apart what appears common, as though divided. [Col. 1683D] The communion of divine nature between Father and Son admits no division; although there is personal distinction, the divinity and natural essence are one. He says “his” so that it may be manifest that he who is his can in no respect oppose him. He calls him his God so as to show us a judge whom we need not fear: one whom he can bend as his own, and to whom access is safe, since he calls him not alien but his own.

Nor does the closeness of this familial bond require slight confidence: before the Father it bears such concern for those abandoned that, even in what is admittedly voluntary and spontaneous, he does not hesitate to call himself abandoned. Certainly it is impossible that ingratitude should be found in the good Father, who is of good will, and that he should not rather take delight in the affection of his beloved Son, so graciously disposed toward him. But when the Son speaks of himself as abandoned, [Col. 1684B] he seems to demand the reward of obedience. He does not endure that the benefit should long be delayed, which he confidently declares is owed to him as he goes forth in obedience to meet death: “Why,” he says, “have you forsaken me?”

The world had not yet understood the meaning of this mystery; the effect of so great a sacrament had not yet openly appeared. It was necessary that both the work and power of this holocaust should become known, and that this pattern should be impressed upon the hearers of the Gospel, so that from the present rule they might learn that henceforth each person must enter into the holy places in his own blood, [Note: [Col. 1683D] This may be understood in two ways. First, of Christ’s own blood, in which and through which we have entrance into the holy places—that is, entry into the heavenly kingdom. Thus the Apostle says of Christ that “not through the blood of goats or calves, but through his own blood, he entered once into the holy places, having obtained eternal redemption” (Heb. 9). Secondly, the meaning may be taken of each person’s own blood: everyone who wishes to enter heaven with Christ must enter there through his own blood, not another’s—that is, by slaying and sacrificing himself, by crucifying the flesh with its vices and desires, according to the Apostle’s counsel (Gal. 5), and so conforming ourselves to Christ’s passion. This agrees well with what he adds shortly afterward concerning slaughtering goat-like or bull-like dispositions. Both meanings suit the subject. For in Christ’s hanging thus abandoned upon the cross and crying, “My God,” etc., we are first shown that he himself is the true victim, through whom remission of sin and inheritance of the heavenly kingdom are received, since he who spoke for us in this way was both Mediator and sacrifice. Then he also taught by his example that we must sacrifice ourselves to God as a living victim (Rom. 12), as he sacrificed himself there, so that, made companions of his sufferings and conformed to the likeness of his death (2 Cor. 1), we may also become companions of his consolations and sharers in his glory.] and that the end had come for those expiations previously made in another’s blood.

For the authority of religion would perish and be altogether diluted if it were again occupied with images and shadows of truth, rather than laying hold of truth itself, [Col. 1684C] slaying within itself bull-like and goat-like dispositions, and burning incense of fragrant devotion upon the inward altar, while directing its affection toward the piety and holiness signified by the turtledove and dove.

Christ is abandoned after the manner of the prophet Jonah: the belly of the beast receives him cast into the sea (Jonah 2). Yet near at hand was the morning reception, of which the Father had foretold, saying to the Son: “Arise, my glory” (Ps. 56); and the Son says to the Father: “I will arise at dawn” (ibid.). The ship was disarmed and the oarage shattered, [Note: [Col. 1684D] He speaks by comparison with the danger of shipwreck, [Col. 1685C] in which it sometimes seems to happen that, after all the arms and instruments by which a ship was steered have been lost, its oarage broken, and all hope abandoned, through someone’s skill the vessel is at last directed again toward its proper course and the harbor of rest. Thus the matter seemed desperate with respect to accomplishing our salvation when Christ had died and been laid in the tomb, as the disciples themselves said while speaking on the road: “We had hoped that he was the one to redeem Israel” (Luke 24), as though the matter had now become hopeless. Yet shortly afterward the great helmsman restored everything and brought it to a good conclusion.] but, gathering up the remnants, the great helmsman again equips the ship’s gear for its course. He whose case seemed beyond hope while he was enclosed in the tomb came forth victorious, conquering death, and commanded [Col. 1684D] the winds and the sea (Matt. 8).

And hell was astonished at the judge, whom, as though its own particular prey, it had according to its indiscriminate custom drawn in with claws [Col. 1685A] fixed in the flesh. Indeed, that Psalm whose title is “For the end, concerning the morning reception” [Note: [Col. 1685D] This Psalm is twenty-first in order, because, beginning with the misery of the Passion, it ends in the glory of resurrection and great joy. Therefore it is inscribed rather from its end, “concerning the morning reception,” which took place in the resurrection, than from its beginning, “concerning the evening abandonment,” which belonged to the time of the Passion. In the words that follow, “But these were words of sins,” some manuscripts had “of those abandoned,” others “of sins.” “Of sins” appears more suitable to the subject, for it seems to refer to the Psalm: “Far from my salvation are the words of my sins” (Ps. 21). In the following exposition the author shows why the Lord says “the words of my sins,” explaining how he calls sinners his own and therefore also their sins his own.] begins in Christ’s person: “My God, my God, look upon me; why have you forsaken me?” (Ps. 21). “But these were words of sins” (ibid.), that is, words uttered in the person of those to whom he had united himself and to whom he was like in every respect except sin (Heb. 2). He calls sinners his own because he had come for them and was their head; nor did he judge it fitting for his members to be cut off from himself. Otherwise, if you seek a body wholly without the mark and stain of sin, you establish a head without a body; and goodness has none to benefit if there is no weakness beneath it to be governed.

Thus the head pleads the cause of its body; and the physician, concerned for his weak ones, sympathizes so completely that he does not disdain to become weak in some respect, and—to say still more—becomes sin, he who was scraping away sin. In the respect in which he suffers, he is abandoned, because it cannot in any way befit the impassible nature to be injured or to suffer. Divinity withdraws itself from the Passion: this belongs to the flesh alone. In this alone the Son signifies that he is abandoned, so that the truth of sound faith may shine out on every side and it may be plain that, insofar as he is God, he does not die at all; while insofar as he is human, he is abandoned for a time, by an ordered dispensation, in order to die.

He is therefore abandoned with the abandoned and, for the nature he assumed, pays the tribute. Intending to carry his race with himself beyond this world’s sea, he offered to the rapacious pirates the fare of his flesh; and, their teeth being smeared with birdlime, [Col. 1685C] he deceived those devourers, [Note: [Col. 1686C] He calls the devils pirates, because before Christ they seized for hell all those sailing over the sea of this world—that is, passing out of the world. Christ also offered them his flesh as fare when, according to it, he willed by dispensation to die. When he says, “their teeth being smeared with birdlime,” etc., the author appears to speak from the custom of sailors at sea. When great fish encounter them and they fear the ship may be damaged or overturned, they throw something outside the vessel. While the ravenous creatures are occupied in tearing or devouring it, the ship passes unharmed. Sometimes they also coat what they throw out with birdlime or similar substance, so that, sticking to their mouths and throats, it hinders the devourers from pursuing ship and sailors. We read that Daniel dealt in this way with the dragon worshiped among the Babylonians (Dan. 14). He made cakes from pitch, fat, and hair, threw them into the dragon’s mouth, and killed it. This figure is not ill suited to the present passage.] withdrawing and raising up both himself and his prey. He offered himself as debtor for debtors and did not refuse voluntarily to owe what he did not owe from himself. Therefore the collector exacted the whole sum of the debt from him who gave himself for all.

He saw him abandoned for a time and supposed that he could be utterly extinguished. But that voluntary abandonment was not without omnipotence; and that cup of bitterness tore away from its depths the poisons of desire long since poured in, [Col. 1686A] and in sudden vomiting the whole lump of the old leaven was cast out. Therefore, stretching out his arms upon the cross, Christ embraced his entire body lying beneath him. Gathering our race beneath the wings of the cross, there he both protected and cherished it where he was thought able to do nothing; and in that in which he was considered defeated, he raised the banners of greatest victory. For neither did death prevail over him in every respect, nor could the Father in any way deny the Son the privilege of mercy which charity, prostrate at his feet, sought.

Thus the lowly bowing of the head obtained pardon for the body; and when the head was struck, the members were made whole. Let this recompense not be thought slight; and let the human being for whom Christ died always meditate upon and reread in this pattern what he owes Christ. Let this proof of charity be fixed before the eyes; let this living instruction and example of continual persuasion remain.

But for us also, who are abandoned as often as temptations buffet us, it is a question not to be neglected: to ask why we are abandoned and, after understanding the causes, to seek remedies. For a stain cannot creep long into a mind that has sought to fortify itself by prudent watchfulness. We are sometimes abandoned when we neglect this care, and rebuffs drive us back and warn us to be vigilant. Shame sometimes heals negligence; the very disgrace of temptations compels some, once ashamed of having gone astray, to seek the remedies of confession. Pride is often chastised by a fall, and presumption by ruin. Holiness is struck lest it be exalted, and is troubled that it may be exercised. [Col. 1686C] For a time it is abandoned in a small degree, and then gathered again in great mercies. It falls and is raised; it fails and is not sufficient of itself to return to the physician.

The question put forth by Christ upon the cross invites us to this kind of inquiry whenever the thorn of the flesh does not prick us, or the exaltation of the mind carries us away into wonders above us. Yet the itching of sin that flares up again is not to be judged fatal [Note: [Col. 1686D] Sin flares up anew in a person and arouses itching when desire again invites and entices us to a sin once committed. Yet this itching of revived sin is not unto death for the sufferer; the temptation to evil is not decisive or deadly, provided reason strives against it, not allowing the scurf of wickedness to spread more widely, but applying cautery and remedy. However great and violent the temptation may appear, if consent is absent and reason thus sets itself against it, no harm can occur. Rather, by God’s grace, according to the Apostle, all things shall work together for good to one who loves God (Rom. 8), and there shall be no condemnation. [Col. 1687D] The author then indicates this by a fine comparison drawn from a great fire extinguished by a single drop of grace.] when reason goes to meet it and applies cautery to the serpent-like [Col. 1687A] scurf.

For though fanned fires may send up smoke, and the ravenous flame may already be licking the tops of the roofs, one drop of grace and a sudden glance of mercy will reduce them to ashes with one breath. [Col. 1688A] When the storm is divinely calmed, what seemed a loss proves a consolation, and what was abandoned and forgotten is taken up and restored.

## SECOND TREATISE

On that saying: “Truly I tell you, today you will be with me in Paradise” (Luke 23)

[Col. 1687]

[Col. 1687A] “O Lord, our Lord, how wonderful is your name in all the earth” (Ps. 8), who perfects praise even from [Col. 1687B] the mouths of the ungodly. [Note: [Col. 1687D] The Psalmist sings to the Lord that he perfected praise for himself from the mouths of infants and nursing children (Ps. 8). Our author heightens this by saying that God perfected praise for himself even from the mouths of the ungodly, which he clearly demonstrates in the thief who received mercy. He says that in this work of divine compassion there were confounded the heretical enemy, the perverse betrayer-disciple, and the slanderous Jew, fittingly assigning one description to each. Of the last two he demonstrates this well, though in reverse order: first the slanderous Jew, then the heretic as avenger or defender. But he omits to pursue the betrayer-disciple, since this is left evident from other matters. For the one who despaired that he could obtain pardon for his sin was confounded when such numerous and great crimes were so readily forgiven to this thief.]

Behold, one of those abandoned is received. That thief crucified at your side, condemned for crimes—you appoint him the forerunner of your victory, and, made alive by grace, send him ahead into Paradise. In him the enemy was confounded, and the heretic as avenger, and the perverse betrayer-disciple, and the slanderous Jew.

The Pharisees charged Christ with wrongdoing because he associated at table, not only in word but in common meals, with sinners whom the law excluded, thereby injuring the law. For when the ritual and decree drove lepers and the unclean outside the camp, prescribed that the walls of houses in which they had lived should be scraped away, and likewise the very benches upon which they had sat, and ordered a special purification (Num. 5; Lev. 14), they accused Christ [Col. 1687C] because he avoided neither the table nor the house of such persons but received and healed them.

Superstition had grown deep, and, through the occasion of a law understood carnally, the ministers of the law pursued sin while they themselves were not free from sin. They subscribed their own condemnations, reserving no place [Col. 1688A] for mercy. [Note: [Col. 1688C] Undoubtedly because, according to blessed James’s judgment, judgment without mercy shall be given to those who have not shown mercy (Jas. 2); and, as Paul says, in judging another one condemns oneself (Rom. 2).] They thought it wicked that Christ healed on the Sabbath (Luke 13; John [Col. 1688B] 7), and that he taught mercy must be preferred to judgment.

So too certain heretics, among whom are the Novatians, who wish to appear defenders of the Church, [Note: [Col. 1688C] The author appears to wish to apply separately the words of the Psalm, “that you may destroy the enemy and the avenger or defender” (Ps. 8), one to the Jews and the other to heretics. He calls the Jew “enemy,” as an envious [Col. 1688D] slanderer and persecutor; but calls the heretic “avenger” or “defender,” because heretics commonly boast of themselves as though they were champions of truth and defenders of the Church. Concerning these Novatians, their leader Novatus, and their error, one may learn from the books of orthodox Fathers who fought against them in writing.] hold that those who have fallen into any sin after baptism are unworthy of repentance; that impiety dogmatizes that one whom human weakness has brought into any crime can by no means be restored. But Christ, by this present judgment, destroys and refutes both heretics who are false defenders of faith and Jews who are enemies of grace, changing law into grace, terror into gentleness, harshness into mildness, shadow into truth, and judgment into mercy.

A new king, a new law; a new leader, a new light. After the former tablets were broken and stone shattered against stone, [Note: [Col. 1688D] “Stone shattered against stone.” He alludes to the history in Exodus, where Moses, angry, cast from his hands at the foot of the mountain the stone tablets containing precepts inscribed by God’s finger, and broke them into pieces. New tablets then had to be cut and written anew (Exod. 32). This signified the change—or rather the renewal and completion—of the old law through the new evangelical law. He says that stone was shattered against stone because the tablets were of stone and were broken against the mountain, which was stony.] he affixes the title with new inscriptions; compassion dictates, [Col. 1688C] and charity distinguishes all things.

Christ’s kingship is written in three notable languages—Hebrew, Latin, and Greek—and his dominion, destined to extend among the nations, is engraved upon the cross. Pilate did not wish to alter what he had written; and although the faithlessness of the Jews clamored for so notable an inscription to be erased, it was in no way able [Col. 1689A] to obtain this (John 19).

Already the crucified thief belonged to this inscription, and those letters enclosed him within themselves. Hope had already entered the convert, because, with the world crucified to him, he longed for heavenly things. Expanded by charity, as though he had spat out and rejected the things below, he spoke with Christ about the kingdom, desired the things above; and when his soul, hastening to depart, was already upon his lips [Note: [Col. 1689C] It is proverbially said that a person’s soul is “upon his lips” when death is near, when the soul is close to departing from its dwelling.], and his final hour was at hand, he went with tranquil mind. The fear of punishments did not press upon a conscience that felt itself washed by Christ’s blood flowing past.

The Jews, blaspheming Christ, sharpened their venomous tongues; they shouted together and hurled insults, and as though victorious mocked him hanging there. The apostles had fled. Only the accursed populace, hardened in wicked speech, [Col. 1689B] celebrated the mockery, while the Roman soldiers yielded to the tumultuous disturbances, rendering service from official duty rather than consent. [Note: [Col. 1689C] He says this to show how much more cruel and insolent toward Christ the Jews were, although execution of the judicial sentence did not belong to them but to the gentile servants of the governor, whose task it was to execute their lord’s sentence. It is not likely that this insolence pleased Roman soldiers of free birth, since it was not customary to mock with such brazenness persons condemned and hanging in such extreme misery. Nor is there doubt that the gentile servants of the governor marveled at the Jews’ outrageous rage and insatiable abuse, which they did not cease to inflict upon a man so miserably condemned.]

But the other thief too, agreeing with the barking crowd, declared that Christ could save neither himself nor others. He mocked his fellow sufferer, who placed hope in one whom he saw under the same condemnation as himself; and it appeared utterly absurd to believe that one was king or God whom the same reproach and like torment had overwhelmed together with him.

There was therefore one mocker, the other a confessor; one a reviler, the other a worshipper; this man hoping, that one despairing; [Col. 1690A] this man loving, that one indifferent. The judge of that controversy was present, and, having pronounced sentence, sent the blasphemer ahead to Tartarus and the confessor ahead to the kingdom.

Indeed, this thief of whom we speak, mild of spirit, and—as became a witness of Christ—set forth arguments of faith before a public audience. By a new manner of philosophizing, forgetful of so great a punishment, he disputed with that blasphemer concerning the fear of God and justice. “Do you not fear God,” he says, “since you are under the same condemnation? And we indeed justly, for we receive what our deeds deserve; but this man has done nothing evil” (Luke 23). He believes and confesses; he testifies to Christ’s innocence; he rebukes the reviler and does not spare himself. Yet, accusing only himself, he prosecutes himself against himself, having pronounced the true sentence.

“The condemnation,” he says, “is indeed alike, but the cause [Col. 1690B] differs: he has been appointed to this through obedience, while we are here because of our crimes.” He condemns the cause, not the punishment; he abhors his own crime and does not reject the judgment. “Do you not fear God?” He is not ashamed to confess as God the one whom he knew to have been crucified through envy, not through desert. For, with neither flesh nor blood revealing it, but the very one to whom he bore witness, he was already able to understand that what was being done was voluntary, not necessary.

> [Note: [Col. 1689C] Christ’s Passion was simply voluntary and not simply necessary. Yet it might seem not wholly voluntary, because it had thus been determined [Col. 1689D] in the counsel of the Godhead that Christ should suffer. Since this counsel cannot fail of fulfillment, Christ’s Passion might seem not wholly voluntary but partly necessary. But the author removes this doubt when he immediately adds: “because it had been voluntarily determined that it should happen thus.” For Christ’s Passion was simply voluntary, because Father and Son voluntarily determined that the Son should suffer in the assumed human nature. Hence, although, once that determination had been posited, its fulfillment necessarily followed—because God’s counsel, established by his will, cannot be frustrated—that determination was nonetheless fulfilled voluntarily, just as it had been voluntarily determined.  
>   
> Some manuscripts, however, read this passage as an assertion of apparently contrary sense: “What was being done was voluntary and necessary.” To explain how it was necessary, the text adds: “because it had been voluntarily determined that it should happen thus.” Thus, [Col. 1690C] since what has been determined cannot fail to be fulfilled, it seems to follow that, given that determination, Christ’s suffering was necessary. Theologians call this necessity not necessity simply speaking, but conditional necessity, or necessity of consequence; they call the former necessity necessity simply speaking, or absolute necessity. Thus neither reading contains falsehood, but the former seems more fitting to the passage, and that is the reading we too have followed.]

For it had been voluntarily determined that it should happen thus. There, therefore, he philosophizes, preaches, and confesses, where not merely the apostles flee and tremble, but even the malignant spirits themselves, already feeling the bit imposed upon them, chew their mouthpieces.

> [Note: [Col. 1690C] He draws a most apt comparison from fierce horses to malignant spirits. We see that fierce horses, when bits have been placed upon them through their ears and mouthpieces have also been put or thrust into their mouths—those iron instruments which pass through the mouth and have little movable iron knots or balls—show great impatience. As though longing to break the bits, they continually bite, roll about, and, as it were, chew those mouthpieces by incessant biting and continual movement of the tongue, so that abundant saliva flows from their mouths. [Col. 1690D] Thus fierce horses show impatience even before a heavy rider mounts their backs or spurs them on.  
>   
> Applying this fact to the malignant spirits, he indicates that, even before Christ’s consummation through death, while he was still in his Passion, the demons began to feel Christ’s power. Therefore, struggling against it, they began to bite the bit imposed upon them and chew the mouthpieces—that is, they tried to hinder Christ’s Passion. They did this through the tongue of a woman, namely Pilate’s wife, whom the demons had troubled in dreams for this purpose: that through her they might prevent Christ’s death, as certain saints have interpreted that passage. He calls the feminine tongue the devil’s ancient instrument, because through it the serpent had seduced Adam from the beginning and destroyed the whole human race. Therefore, by the same means through which he had formerly brought us to destruction, the devil then wished to hinder our restoration.]

Through their ancient instrument, [Col. 1691A] the feminine tongue, they strove to dissolve those bonds of impiety, knowing that this strong man, armed with a two-edged sword, was about to cast them out of the long-possessed courtyard of this world.

Thus the illustrious preacher, having offered the fragrance of confession and faith, and having imposed silence upon the blaspheming thief, turns to Christ, demanding from the judge the palm and earnest of his victory, and says: “Remember me, Lord, when you come into your kingdom” (Luke 23).

It is necessary to consider what place, what manner, and what time this case had, how swift a hearing the confession deserved, what repentance can accomplish, and how the good Lord does not neglect his servant who cries to him with a troubled heart even at the final point of sin. It was the hour of death, and the confessor’s [Col. 1691B] soul was already clinging to his throat; distress was already binding his tongue. At that very instant salvation was almost despaired of even by the apostles. The manner of the Passion was the cross, the most shameful and terrible of all punishments.

Setting these matters aside, as though forgetful of wounds and blood, the thief becomes the spokesman of the Gospel. And—what was difficult to believe at that hour—he confesses Christ as God upon the cross. There he prays; there he worships; there he embraces many offices of devotion at once. He believes, fears, is pierced with compunction and repents; he confesses and preaches, loves, trusts, and prays. He is enlightened by faith, made subject by fear, stirred by compunction, shaken by repentance, cleansed by confession, made zealous by preaching, enlarged by love, [Col. 1691C] hopes by confidence, and obtains by prayer.

Do not be angry, Prince of the Apostles. I speak to you, Peter, to whom the keys of the kingdom of heaven were entrusted (Matt. 16). Christ had looked upon you in love when you wept, and had forgiven the guilt of your denial; for you had fallen away not deliberately but through weakness (Matt. 26). Yet I do not see you beside the cross. Terrified, you lie hidden; you do not even accompany Christ’s mother and the holy women, who stood motionless at that mournful spectacle. Nor do you exercise apostolic authority there, where Savior and sinner, fastened to neighboring crosses, exchange private words with one another. You were absent; and the keys of your ministry—if I may say it with your leave—you do not bring forth on this occasion.

The high priest supplies your place. The ancient bolts are opened, and the thief, the first-fruits of those abandoned, is brought in, [Col. 1691D] Christ opening the way, into the kingdom of heaven. The ever-watchful guard at the entrance of Paradise, established from the beginning, is removed, together with that threatening, turning sword which the cherub had not wielded from ancient times (Gen. 3). There the thief is placed, whence Lucifer fell. And he whom perhaps you would have been unwilling to forgive more than seven times—guilty more than seventy times seven, yet absolved by the good Jesus—now dwells with the angels [Col. 1692A].

Rise, and learn to forgive. Do not count sins or multiply occasions. Divine mercy is not confined by a number, enclosed by an end, or bounded by any limits whatever. Let there be one who calls upon it, and there will be one who hears; let there be one who repents, and one who grants pardon will not be lacking. This penitent is not assigned fasts of many years; he is not afflicted with barefoot observances or sackcloth. At the same moment he confesses, is justified, and is glorified. Look at the hour; note the person. The final hour, a sinful person, many and ancient sins: grace immediately wipes them away. Pardon does not, by a gradual process and delay of time, wear down and corrode the rust of guilt. Rather, when the Holy Spirit descends at the sudden heavenly sound, whatever had been soaked with the corruption of sin is dried; no trace of ugliness remains upon the wound [Col. 1692B] which the washing of mercy has cleansed.

Lazarus too, four days in the tomb, stank (John 11); when raised, he does not waste away in sickness, but rises, is unbound, and immediately eats with others. No rough broken edge of leprosy, no hollow remains upon Simon’s face.

> [Note: [Col. 1691D] *Crepido* derives from *crepo*, according to the sense in which it means “to break.” Thus *crepido* denotes a projecting break or a high fissure of some precipitous rock. *Sinus*, on the other hand, means a curve or indentation; thus shores are called *sinuous* when they have many turns or bends, enclosing the waters themselves in the manner of a bay. In the flesh of lepers, by analogy, we see, as it were, certain broken ledges [Col. 1692D] and hollows produced by the erosion of the flesh, which creates the appearance of such ledges and hollows. Hence, to indicate complete healing, the author says: “No rough broken edge of leprosy, no hollow remains upon Simon’s face; the host, whole, renders cheerful service to his healer,” etc.]

The host, restored to health, renders cheerful service to his healer; before those accompanying the Master, he displays no mark of horror, being at once guest and servant (Luke 7). Mary Magdalene weeps and prays at Christ’s feet, wipes them, and anoints them. Christ neither reproaches her infamous life and shamelessness, nor sets against her what he washes away, nor reproves what he forgives. Whatever he does in such cases, the Holy Spirit accomplishes by a swift nod; he does not beg assistance from elsewhere, for he does what he says and fashions what he enlightens [Col. 1692C], he who immediately makes fishermen teachers and unlearned men preachers.

In this grace expectation is not distressed by postponement, nor is there an interval between what is desired and what is given. David says, “I have sinned” (2 Sam. 12). And the prophet says, “Your sin has been taken away” (ibid.). Cain is told, “You have sinned; be at rest” (Gen. 4). To the woman caught in adultery: “Neither do I condemn you; sin no more” (John 8). Why should I mention the Ninevites, whose repentance suddenly turns the judge from his sentence? (Jonah 3.) Why Ahab and Manasseh, impious kings, whose contrition in distress divine mercy did not reject? (1 Kings 21; 2 Chron. 32.)

Among the other examples of mercy, our thief comes before us: a rule of repentance, a model of confession, a herald of pardon, an example [Col. 1692D] of hope. As he groans, he immediately finds what he seeks, receives what he asks, and at once hears: “Today you will be with me in Paradise” (Luke 23). The confessor is not sent to purgatorial places and the avenging flames of sinners; he is not led away to places of darkness and torments. No opposing party dares bring any accusation against the grace of God. One punishment of the cross abolishes all crimes [Col. 1693A]—indeed, not punishment but grace. Therefore this herald of our absolution is sent beforehand into Paradise, granted freedom as a witness to the first-fruits of our freedom; he was the first to bring it in to the citizens of Paradise, who awaited and longed for it.

## THIRD TREATISE. On the Lord’s words: “Woman, behold your son” (John 19)

[Col. 1693]

[Col. 1693A] “Where are your ancient mercies, O Lord?” (Ps. 88.) Why do you delay? The hour has now come: your mother is before you, and John whom you love. You speak to the thief, and do not speak to your mother? She, blessed among women, looks upon you; and, with eyes fixed upon you, [Col. 1693B] she contemplates your wounds with maternal tenderness. Though she does not fail to know what good your Passion brings to the world, still, with a parent’s affection, she dies with you, and her motherly breast is constricted by the enormity of grief.

She sighs inwardly and checks her tears as they burst forth; and her anguish swells all the more because it is restrained from coming out and dissolving itself in weeping and lamentation. Groans indeed sometimes arose, but, rebuked, they were repressed; they returned into the bosom of the mind from which they had come and dashed against one another within. In that soul there was a mighty storm.

> [Note: [Col. 1693C] He makes an almost poetic comparison of the swelling waves of the sea, dashing against and breaking one another, with those inward movements of grief that were in Mary’s soul as she stood beside the cross of her only-begotten Son.]

As though marrow were frying in a pan, bitterness boiled up; persistent anguish cooked and coagulated it. For fear commanded [Col. 1693C] grief to be silent, and the grim eyes of the Jews, gnashing their teeth at her, stifled those whirlwinds.

> [Note: [Col. 1693C] This must not be understood as though the Lord’s mother feared the Jews with a fleshly and vain fear—lest, namely, she suffer some harm from them if she showed outwardly her inward grief—but because dignity and constancy forbade her to display outward gestures before those wicked people, lest they should glory and rage still more against her Son if they saw the mother so afflicted by his torments; likewise, lest she give the spectators [Col. 1693D] occasion to suspect that the Son’s Passion was compulsory and not voluntary.]

But she drank down the brine of so many storms. And—what was most difficult—she was dying [Col. 1694A] and could not die. With the torment of so great a sorrow shut up within, she showed another countenance openly. From her face one could not discern that cross of the soul and gibbet of the spirit upon which she was a living sacrifice, pleasing to God, a holocaust full of marrow. As she herself [Col. 1694B] kindled it, she employed only the ministry of conscience; silently sacrificing herself upon the inward altar, she piled up wood, flames, and waters.

> [Note: [Col. 1693D] He describes the offering of an inward and spiritual holocaust by comparison with the offering of a bodily holocaust upon an outward altar, where wood, flame, and waters are needed—the waters being called *latices*, from *lateo*, “to lie hidden.” He adds water either because bodily sacrificial victims had first to be washed before they were offered or burned, or because he has in view Elijah’s sacrifice offered on Mount Carmel, where the holocaust was abundantly drenched with water before it was consumed by fire (1 Kings 18).]

Certainly, in that tabernacle you would see two altars.

> [Note: [Col. 1693D] In the ancient tabernacle there were two altars. One, assigned to the immolation of victims, was covered with bronze and had all the vessels of its ministry made of bronze; of it we read in Exodus 27. The other was the altar of perfume or incense, clothed with purest gold and placed before the mercy-seat. Upon it [Col. 1694C] the high priest Aaron was required, by the Lord’s command, to burn sweet-smelling incense morning and evening. Upon its horns also, once each year, the high priest had to make supplication and propitiate the Lord with the blood offered for sin, as we read in Exodus 30.  
>   
> In these two altars the author finds a figure of mother and Son. He compares the mother to the former altar, on which victims were offered, but neither the evening sacrifice nor the victim of that general expiation; for although the mother sacrificed herself in her heart, she could not herself offer the sacrifice of consummation and expiation for the sins of the world. He makes the Son the altar of perfume [Col. 1694D] or incense, because in him the evening sacrifice was offered in the fullness of time: the consummation of all preceding sacrifices. In him too the general expiation of the world’s sins was made, in blood offered for sin. The author indicates this comparison when he subsequently says: “She herself desired, namely the mother, to add the blood of her flesh to the blood of her soul”—that is, to be sacrificed in body as well as spirit—and “to celebrate with her Son the evening sacrifice,” etc. These words, considered more deeply, possess great sweetness of devotion.]

One altar was in Mary’s breast, the other in Christ’s body. Christ offered his flesh; Mary offered her soul. She herself wished to add the blood of her flesh to the blood of her soul, to raise her hands upon the cross and celebrate with her Son the evening sacrifice, and with the Lord Jesus, by bodily death, to complete the mystery of our redemption. But it was the privilege of the high priest alone to bring the gift of blood within the holy places. This dignity could not be shared with anyone; and in the restoration of [Col. 1694C] humankind, no angel and no human being had, or could have, authority in common with him.

Yet that maternal affection cooperated greatly, in its own manner, in propitiating God.

> [Note: [Col. 1694D] Here he seems to give the reason why he compared Mary the mother to the former altar of victims rather than the latter altar of incense. For just as God was worshipped at the former altar through the daily victims offered upon it, although the chief and greatest sacrifice of incense—the morning and evening sacrifice—or that blood [Col. 1695C] of general expiation was not offered there, nevertheless those victims in some manner worked to appease God, as it were through reference to and the power of that most acceptable sacrifice and general expiation accomplished on the other altar of incense. So he says that the mother’s affection cooperated greatly in its own manner [Col. 1695D] in propitiating God: Christ’s love, burning in her heart like sweetest incense, bore the mother’s prayers together with his own to the Father, just as the burning of incense, which was the chief sacrifice, in some manner rendered acceptable before God the offerings of the other victims.]

[Col. 1695A] Christ’s love bore both his own prayers and his mother’s to the Father: what the mother asked, the Son approved, and the Father granted. The Father loved the Son, and the Son the Father; but the mother burned in love after each of them. It was one thing toward which the distinct offices were directed: what the good Father, the devoted Son, and the holy mother intended; what love labored for in common. Devotion, love, and goodness mutually embraced one another: the mother supplicating, the Son interceding, the Father showing mercy.

The Son looked toward his mother’s breast and breasts; the Father toward the Son’s cross and wounds. What would not so great pledges move among them? What would that school of holiness teach if not devotion? What would it form if not mercy? Love, holiness, and goodness could entertain nothing opposed to themselves; it did not suit them to resist one another or oppose their concord. It was altogether fitting that supplication, sanctification, and answering should agree in a work of righteousness.

Jesus therefore, in order to commend every bond of devotion, observed the ancient decree which he had given concerning the honoring of parents. Wishing his mother still to remain alive for the consolation of the apostles, he preserved her, so that the apostolic council might be taught by what she herself had heard and seen from the beginning and had pondered in her heart, and the evangelical doctrine might be confirmed. He honors her also with the most intimate address. Though his speech was brief, the affection due to her was made known, and his singular love was expressed: “Woman, behold your son.” [Col. 1695C] John was present, to whom he also says: “Behold your mother” (John 19).

Christ did not permit Jewish rage to lay a profaning hand upon his sanctuary, or that temple of the Holy Spirit to be violated by any assault. A faithful guardian was appointed for the custody of so great a treasure. The disciple who at the Lord’s Supper had made the Master’s breast his pillow (John 13), behold, is honored again with another privilege. After that resting-place where he had seen, “In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with [Col. 1696A] God” (John 1), that workshop in which “the Word became flesh” (ibid.) is carefully entrusted to him by her Son. To the approved and beloved disciple are assigned the virginal modesty, the mother’s bridal chamber, and the integrity of holiness: that a virgin might be a fitting witness for a Virgin; a chamberlain of faith to the mother of his Lord; a devoted attendant out of reverence for his Master. The adoptive son takes the place of the natural Son, and filial affection is transferred to the servant. In both is formed and established a pleasing and harmonious embrace of one devotion, not from the propagation of nature but from the gift of grace.

Virginity therefore receives John and Mary into one household; one manner of life in one home, one purpose of integrity, one dwelling, and a shared way of life are granted them. Behold, John, you receive the testament of a pious inheritance; [Col. 1696B] you are chosen and in this are set above all others. Joseph, who had hitherto ministered, gives way when you are substituted in his place; he does not assert marital rights.

> [Note: [Col. 1695D] Most suppose that Joseph died before the time of Christ’s Passion. But in the present passage the author indicates that he held another opinion, which he also expresses more fully in the *Encomium of the Virgin* in these words: “Joseph was still alive, to whom until that time the chief duty of service had belonged, and to whom she had been betrothed for this very purpose; yet now, as though he were deemed unworthy of this ministry, John is chosen.”  
>   
> And there he pursues the same opinion in many further words. Nevertheless, nothing can be determined on this matter from the authority of Scripture, since no canonical Scripture records anything concerning Joseph’s [Col. 1696C] death or the time of his death.]

Thus the mouths of those who would later speak wickedness may be stopped, since that marriage had served divine dispensation, not bodily union. Therefore Joseph does not complain that the marriage is dissolved when John receives her as a mother, because it had been a dispensatory marriage, without any intercourse of bodily union. Christ gave this testimony to his mother’s integrity at the end, so that the holy Church might possess from the Gospel a stone to strike into the shameless brow of the heretics Bonosus and Helvidius.

> [Note: [Col. 1696C] He alludes to the story of David, who killed the blaspheming Goliath, uttering impious words against the camps of God, by striking him in the forehead with a very smooth stone taken from the stream, as Scripture relates (1 [Col. 1696D] Sam. 17). Every heretic in the Church is like Goliath: a giant proud in the strength of his own wisdom or knowledge and reproaching the true Israelites, the camps of the Lord—that is, the orthodox who remain in the unity of the Church, which is God’s house and camp. But every defender strong in the true faith is David: with stones from the clearest stream, that is, authorities drawn from the most lucid and pure Gospel, he strikes down Goliath—that is, refutes and confounds the heretic.]

They dared to utter impious and blasphemous nonsense against the unviolated virginity of the mother. You, therefore, holy John, are chosen for this: to minister and attend her, with the love of a Son, the obedience of a disciple, and the subjection of a minister and servant. The Church is entrusted to Peter (Matt. 16), Mary to you (John 19): to him, turbulent affairs; to you, peaceful and quiet ones; to him, the courts, vestibule, and altars of blood; to you are entrusted the altar of incense and the Holy of Holies.

> [Note: [Col. 1696D] The ancient tabernacle of the Israelites was divided into two parts. The first was simply called the Holy Place and contained lesser things; priests, even those who were not high priests, entered it daily to perform the duties of sacrifices, as Paul says (Heb. 9). The latter, by reason of its excellence, was called the Holy of Holies. In it were the golden censer, the ark of the covenant, the golden urn containing manna, and the tablets of the covenant. Wishing, therefore, to signify [Col. 1697C] that John was entrusted with what is most worthy in the Church’s tabernacle after God, he says that the altar of incense—which stood before the mercy-seat and was the chief altar, as stated above—and the Holy of Holies were entrusted to him. He makes John the high priest, to whom alone the care of the Holy of Holies was entrusted; but he compares Mary to the things contained in the holy places, calling her the golden urn containing manna, the mercy-seat or holy ark, and the casket of the divine law, or the tablets of the covenant. The reasons for all these comparisons may readily be recognized by anyone individually.]

No one is admitted with you to the summit of your ministry. You alone stand beside that mercy-seat; you alone, appointed high priest, guard that golden vessel [Col. 1697A] containing manna, that casket of the divine law. You have been placed in the Son’s stead and appointed to supply his place toward the mother. The holy mother does not refuse you as her representative: though far unequal and of lower rank, yet because this pleased the Son, she embraces his successor.

Certainly, you had been a fisherman, trained in that craft by your parents; no illustrious military exploit makes you noble.

> [Note: [Col. 1697C] The Greek word is στρατήγημα (*stratēgēma*), with two long *e*s, though Latin writers spell it with one, *stratagema*. It means a military deed, an outstanding and distinguished action in war, or a similar plan. The author shows here that John had no nobility, since he had neither drawn it from his parents by descent nor acquired it by industry or courage through any noble work—as some, born in the lowest station, obtain by virtue the nobility which they do not possess by birth through distinguished military actions.]

But he who chose the weak things of the world in order to confound the strong (1 Cor. 1) commended in choosing you the glory of poverty, humility, and chastity; and he honored with this singular title love firmly grounded and purity of an illustrious soul.

I therefore behold the four-horse chariot by which one must run to the Father.

> [Note: [Col. 1698C] He calls a connection of four things a “four-horse chariot,” because one proceeds in due order from one of them always to another. These are: John the disciple, Mary the mother, Jesus the Son, and God the Father. The author also applies to this chariot what we read in the Song of Solomon: “King Solomon made himself a litter from the woods of Lebanon; he made its pillars of silver, its reclining-place of gold, its ascent of purple; he paved its midst with love for the daughters of Jerusalem” (Song 3). He calls this fourfold chariot the litter by which the affection of believers is carried upward. In this litter he makes John the silver pillar, the mother the purple ascent, the Son the love in the midst, and, finally, the golden reclining-place the vision of the Father. The reasons for these things a devout mind can readily discern for itself.]

It must be distinguished thus: through you the affection of the penitent may reach the mother; through the mother, the Son; and through the Son [Col. 1697B] the Father. In this litter which lifts us from this age, you are the silver pillar; the mother the purple ascent; the Son the love in the midst; and the golden reclining-place the vision of the Father in his beauty and the joyful tranquillity of eternal peace.

Meanwhile virginity properly merits this glory. Through it the disciple is raised to this rank; through it the mother herself, both mother and Virgin, pleased God; and, when the power of the Most High overshadowed her (Luke 1), the Word became flesh in that blessed womb (John 1). Through it the archangel Gabriel was Mary’s familiar attendant—indeed, the whole multitude of the heavenly host and the glory of angelic nature, marvelling that it had found her so wholly intact on earth, offered reverence to related celibacy surrounding it on every side.

> [Note: [Col. 1698C] As blessed Ambrose says on Luke, virginity is always akin to angels, [Col. 1698D] because those who live celibate are in this respect like angels; those who are utterly ignorant of generation and the act of generation lead an angelic life on earth.]

And it rendered service to a divine indwelling. Yet Gabriel and John in particular, assigned to this office, ministered through their common pursuits; together, in heaven and on earth alike, they procured divine and human consolation: John providing assistance according to what circumstances required, and the archangel bearing pious prayers to the Son.

Thus it came to pass as the Lord had commanded: virginity and humility, love and purity, subjection and charity dwelt together in a good and joyful fellowship. There was a sharing of one mind and purpose between mistress and servant, as the Master’s authority had ordained.

Therefore the good Lord, bringing the mystery of devotion to its good end, justifies the ungodly upon the cross and renders the affection due to his mother. He also gives and hands down an example [Col. 1698B] that holiness should be chosen to preserve holy things; that the hidden mysteries of the sacraments ought not to be exposed to impure sight; and that no one can worthily minister sacred mysteries unless he has learned in the school of continence how to live. For it is fitting that one who performs an office for those being cleansed or already clean should shine with every kind of holiness, because it is wholly contrary to this pattern that one who is corrupt should handle incorrupt things, or an impure person lay hands upon purifying offices.

We do not say this because, in those already washed and sanctified, however great the shipwrecks from which they have escaped, some mark remains after pardon.

> [Note: [Col. 1698D] Take care not to understand this as saying that after sins have been forgiven no liability can remain in a person, as though remission of guilt immediately entailed the removal of every punishment. That would contradict Catholic doctrine and the determination of the orthodox Fathers. The author means only that, because of sins committed earlier and now removed through repentance, no one should be regarded as unclean or barred from sacred things. This is the point of the concluding statement: “Unless one returns to former contagions, a previous life prejudices no one.”]

For unless one returns to former contagions, a previous life prejudices no one.

## FOURTH TREATISE. On Christ’s word from the cross: “I thirst” (John 19)

[Col. 1697]

[Col. 1697C] Behold, once again mysteries and divine sacraments meet one another. An answer had been given from the cross to the thief [Col. 1698C] and to the mother; and, as a confirmation of hope and an example of loving-kindness, the thief is sent beforehand into the kingdom, while the mother [Col. 1699A] is meanwhile reserved because of the mystery of events. When these matters had been piously and providently arranged, Christ thirsts amid His sufferings. His sacred breast had been drained by the bloody sweat; the wood to which He was fastened had been borne upon His holy shoulders; and, as sleep commonly steals upon some through sorrow, so that thirst might have been kindled. Perhaps it was so. But I understand this thirst sacramentally: in it not so much drink is desired as the salvation of humankind. For no benefit could be expected from His mockers and murderers, all of whom, inclined toward impiety, were readier to increase their injuries than to show mercy or compassion. They still persisted; neither scourges, nor spittle, nor blows could satisfy them. Hence it does not seem likely that, when they heard of thirst, their heart was softened—those for whom it was too little that He hung upon the cross [Col. 1699B] and to whose malice even death itself did not appear sufficient.

Yet Christ, as He had foretold through David [Col. 1700A], when all rushed upon Him [Note: [Col. 1699B] The author refers to Psalm LXI, where we read: “How long do you rush upon a man? Do you all murder, like a leaning wall and a tottering fence? Yet they devised to cast away my price; I ran in thirst.” Expounding this passage as spoken in the person of Christ, holy Father Augustine says: “They repaid [Col. 1699C] evil for good (Ps. XXXIV). They were killing, they were casting away, and I was thirsting for them. They devised to cast away my honour; I thirsted to bring them into my body. For what do we do by drinking, except send into our limbs and draw into our body the moisture that stands outside?” After adding some intervening remarks, he continues: “Christ thirsts even to the end; He runs and thirsts. For He drinks many, yet He will never be without thirst. Hence: ‘I thirst; woman, give me to drink’ (John IV). That Samaritan woman at the well perceived the thirsty Lord, and was filled by Him who thirsted. She first perceived Him thirsting, so that He might drink her believing. And, set upon the cross, He said, ‘I thirst’ (John XIX), although they did not give Him what He thirsted for. For He thirsted for them; but they gave Him vinegar—not the new wine with which new wineskins are filled, but old wine, and badly old.” Thus far Augustine’s words. We have quoted them at such length because they seemed very fitting to the subject proposed.], “as upon a leaning wall and a tottering fence” (Ps. LXI), runs and thirsts. He thirsts for conversion; He runs toward forgiveness; He repays what He did not seize. And although they planned to reject that great price, having now swallowed the serpent He hastens to the washing-bath of His enemies [Note: [Col. 1699D] Blessed Augustine, commenting on the verse of Psalm XLI, “As the stag longs for streams of water,” recounts several characteristics of stags. Among the rest, he observes that they fight serpents and kill them, and that after killing them they burn with a greater thirst; for this reason, once they have killed the serpents, they run back more keenly and swiftly to the springs. The author has this characteristic of stags in view and compares Christ to a stag: because on the cross He fought with the serpent, the devil, and had now swallowed and conquered him, being near the completion of His victory He hastens to the washing-bath when He cries, “I thirst.” Christ thirsts for the washing-bath of His enemies because unbelievers and sinners, Christ’s enemies, were themselves Christ’s washing-bath, in which He sought refreshment after His labours: they were the spring and water from which He sought to drink after the serpent had been defeated.], dies for the ungodly, adopts rebels, and bestows upon the ungrateful the gift of so great a benefit.

This is also contained in the title of Psalm XXXIII, where David, in the person of Christ, is said to have feigned madness [Note: [Col. 1699D] This passage seems to contain much obscurity, especially if we consider the words of our text. For in the title of Psalm XXXIII we read nothing about David’s feigned madness or drumming, nor that he was carried in his own hands. For the title runs: “A Psalm of David, when he changed his countenance before Abimelech, and he dismissed him, and departed.” Likewise, in the history in the Book of Kings, where the account of this event is given more fully, according to the tenor of our Latin text translated from Hebrew by Jerome, nothing is said about feigning madness or being carried in his own hands. Thus we read in I Kings XXI: “David changed his expression before Achish, and staggered between their hands, and struck against the doors of the gate, while his saliva ran down upon his beard.” It should therefore be known that everything said here [Col. 1700C] is treated and applied according to the ancient edition, which, having altered certain matters, reads the already cited passage from the Book of Kings thus: “David was afraid and changed his countenance, and feigned madness and drummed at the gates of the city, and was carried in his own hands, and fell down at the doors of the gate, and his saliva ran down upon his beard.” Blessed Augustine expressly recounts the aforementioned history in these words in his exposition of the title in his treatise on Psalm XXXIII, where he discusses at length every point mentioned here and explains it most fully. To that passage, good reader, I refer you, so that you may yourself hear mellifluous Augustine preaching most sweetly upon these matters. Our author seems to have drawn all this from his honeyed mouth, and, if you wish, you may obtain a full understanding of it. But if you are unwilling or lack leisure to read the lengthy exposition of the title, at least read carefully the summary which he prefaces immediately before the exposition of the psalm, as though recapitulating it [Col. 1700D]. In it you will find, briefly, everything pertaining to this comparison. A diligent reader may also find some things to the same purpose in blessed Eucherius of Lyons, in his commentaries on I Kings, chapter XXIV, and likewise in Rupert, abbot of Deutz, book II of the *Commentaries on the Books of Kings*, chapter VIII.], when he is reported to have changed his countenance before Abimelech [Note: [Col. 1700D] Abimelech means “king of my father” or “kingdom of my father,” which is aptly applied to the Jews, who were the kingdom of God the Father and had been specially chosen for the kingdom through the promises made to the fathers. Augustine interprets Achish as “how is it?” But one who asks thus in a matter of faith is ignorant and mistaken; for this is how one who doubts, errs, and does not know asks. Hence it is subsequently said: “This Achish, that is, the ignorant one, is in part that people who neither believe nor understand.” The author applies both names to the Jews, calling them Abimelech and Achish.]. “David feigned madness and drummed at the gates of the city, and was carried in his own hands, and saliva flowed down upon his beard” (I Kings XXI).

For when Christ feigned madness and thirsted for this—that the provoking house might become gentle [Col. 1700B], that the stiff-necked people might be softened, and, after the antidote of repentance had been drained, might vomit out the bitter and clammy dregs of sin [Col. 1701A]—the words of this teaching appeared to them wholly irrational. They ascribed to madness His invitation to eat His flesh. They recoiled from drinking blood and judged it impious and wicked to set human flesh, as an unfamiliar food, before their tables (John VI). Such a saying was hard, because, oppressed by the mind of the flesh, they despised the spirit and life in His true words. The saliva flowing over David’s beard indicated this: that the Jews regarded these words as childish and frivolous; that the Lord’s sacraments were to be despised by the profane; and that the disciples of these doctrines and ministers of intellectual mysteries were to be thought possessed and frenzied.

But Christ, teaching the limits of patience, neither grows angry nor takes vengeance. Rather, He endures and waits; He feigns madness, that the people’s blindness may be enlightened; that its tyrannical and unbridled obstinacy, suffocated beneath the weight of unbelief, may recover strength and rise; and that at last truth may be revealed and impiety, converted, may return from error.

Therefore He drums at shut gates, at stopped-up ears, and thunders into unbelieving hearts. With the skin of His body stretched out upon the cross, He strikes the harmony of the Old and New Testament upon the ten-stringed psaltery; and, as though serpents had been charmed by an unfamiliar harmony, He renders them tame, makes detractors into singers, and the impious into musicians. Christ’s countenance is wholly changed in the appearance of the sacraments before Abimelech—that is, before the Jews, who seemed to belong to the kingdom of Christ’s God through the promises made to the fathers. [Col. 1701C] This Achish, that is, “the ignorant one,” is in part that people which neither believes nor understands.

Indeed, with His own hands He offers the Eucharist to His disciples—rather, to the whole Church—as though bearing Himself; whoever receives it worthily lives, and whoever despises it is deservedly cast out. To some, the mystery of so great a thing is “an aroma from life unto life”; to others, “an aroma from death unto death” (II Cor. II). Thus Achish dismisses David: because some of the Jews rejected this word and judged themselves unworthy of eternal life, Christ turned this teaching to the Gentiles (Acts XIII). Abimelech and Achish are not names of one person [Note: [Col. 1701D] In the annotations drawn from Hebrew on the title of Psalm XXXIII, we have said something on this subject in the commentaries on the Book of Psalms: namely, that Achish was the personal name of the king, whereas Abimelech was a common name for the kings of Palestine, just as the kings of Egypt were commonly called Pharaohs. This explains the statement that Abimelech and Achish are not names of one person: not both are peculiar to one individual; rather, one is, as it were, common, and the other particular and personal.]. But because they contain the meaning of one mystery, they are not inappropriately applied to one person under different aspects.

In part, Achish—that is, ignorance and [Col. 1701D] error—still persists in that same people. Those who seemed sons of the kingdom, despising Christ’s loving intention and the drum of the cross, dismiss David from themselves, as it were, that He may go, when they say to Christ: “Depart from us; we do not desire knowledge of Your ways” (Job XXI). The Jews still curse Christ and mock the baldness of the true Elisha [Note: [Col. 1701D] The history is clear in IV Kings, chapter II, where we read that boys mocked Elisha as he passed by, saying: “Go up, bald man; go up, bald man.” For this they were devoured by bears coming out of the forest. In this figure Elisha represents Christ, whom the Jews would mock and whose baldness they would mock, because on Mount Calvary they would afflict and kill Him. The boys said to Elisha, “Go up, bald man; go up, bald man,” when the Jews said to Christ hanging on the wood on Mount Calvary: “If you are the Son of God, come down from the cross,” and other such things. They will be given to bears, though vengeance is for the present delayed, because at last they will be food for demons.] (IV Kings I). Yet He does not at once hand these mockers over to bears, that is, demons; rather, in great patience He awaits repentance, delays, and does not inflict anger according to their deserts.

But the perverse and alienated mind of carnal people, not understanding the sacrament of this thirst, applies bitterness on a reed to the holy mouth and offers poisons to the fountain of mercy. Christ does not touch your cup, Jew; He does not taste your vinegar, from the outskirts of Gomorrah and the vineyard of Sodom (Deut. XXXII). That fountain from which living waters [Col. 1702B] flow, whose streams leap up into eternity (John IV), has not dried up, nor does it thirst to be filled by you. Rather, that abundant fountain thirsts that you may draw from it in fullest measure and be filled with its sweetness; that pure streams may refresh you and extinguish the coals of burning desires within you. It thirsts that green charity may endure within you; that, like a palm tree, you may lift the foliage of hope on high; and that, like the incorruptible cedar of Lebanon, you may live [Note: [Col. 1702D] He alludes to the psalm: “The righteous shall flourish like the palm tree; he shall multiply like the cedar of Lebanon” (Ps. XCI). It is as though he said: Christ thirsts to make you, by His moisture and greenness, such as the Psalmist describes when he says, “The righteous,” etc.] (Ps. XCI). This thirst distinguishes poisonous cupbearers and recoils from and rejects dispensers of bitterness. No heat of suffering dries up this fountain; no pressures exhaust charity. Even where you strike and mock, where you offer gall, sweetness is not changed into bitterness, nor does charity demand vengeance. Blood and water come forth from the wounded side [Col. 1702C] (John XIX): water for washing, and blood as an example of death.

The Trinity in heaven bears witness (I John V) to Christ’s charity, which hungers and thirsts for our righteousness (Matt. V): the Son who justifies, the Spirit who sanctifies, the Father who glorifies. For our righteousness, holiness, and glory are from above; and God’s testimony—which is greater than human testimony—commends, forms, and confirms these gifts of His in us. No less, on earth, through visible and bodily sacraments, what is invisibly wrought within is outwardly commended; and spirit, water, and blood bear witness to the Christian faith (ibid.). These three are one and remain indivisible; none of them is separated from its connection with the others. For the Catholic [Col. 1702D] Church lives and grows by this faith: that humanity is no longer believed without [Col. 1703A] true divinity, nor divinity without true humanity.

Nor could the testimony from heaven, which the Trinity bears concerning itself, suffice us for understanding the truth unless the truth of faith were also made known to us by certain signs and arguments. These three, then, are the Spirit of sanctification, the blood of redemption, and the water of purification. Blood redeems only those whom grace calls and raises; nor does the Spirit sanctify except those who have been washed and have died to sin. Redemption, washing, and sanctification are shared together. One cannot exist without the other; and what is done is one, not manifold. For the Holy Spirit hovers over the mysteries and is present in the sacraments, whose meaning is signified by the cleansing water. Water contains the sign of that reality whose effect [Col. 1703B] is supplied by the blood of Christ and the Spirit of God [Note: [Col. 1793C] Water signifies purification and cleansing from every stain. Yet water does not effect this by its own power, but only signifies it by the property of its nature. The Spirit of God and Christ’s blood effect that purification efficaciously. What the author subsequently adds, saying, “In water we are cleansed; in blood we are conformed,” means, as regards the latter part, that we must die and be crucified with Christ, and as it were shed our own blood, just as He shed His blood for us and willed to die. Thus we are said to be conformed in Christ’s Passion and death: namely, so as to die and suffer with Him; in His burial, to be buried with Him; and in His resurrection, to rise with Him, as the Apostle says (Rom. VI). The same point is stated more clearly in the following treatise in these words: “That blood purified us, Christ having sprinkled the people, brought once into the holy place; and we retain the pattern of a like entrance in our own blood, with our members crucified and our pleasures renounced.”].

In water we are cleansed; in blood we are conformed. Wonderful to say! Terrible to relate! While living waters flowed from the sacred side, and abundant streams issued from the rich fountain, Christ declared that He thirsted; and while Himself watering and making the world fruitful, He complains of dryness. Surely that thirst indicates that at that time there were few who believed, when the Apostles themselves were hiding and doubting in that hour. Blood and water had not yet penetrated deeply into the hearts of the disciples; nor had they been moistened by the drunkenness of the Spirit, they whose souls fear and uncertainty had dried up.

[Col. 1704A] Christ thirsts for you, Peter. Return and say boldly: “We must obey God rather than men” (Acts V). Return and trust; and when your brother is overtaken in some offence, you who are spiritual, judge in a spirit of gentleness (Gal. VI). You too were once tempted and fell away from your purpose at the word of one maidservant (Matt. XXVI). But your Master’s blood sprinkled away this guilt. The same grace remains for you; you are not deprived of the apostolate; your keys remain yours, and the same dignity of your pre-eminence endures. Rise and drink from the fountain of mercy. And when you have once turned, strengthen your brothers (Luke XXII); in the same measure in which it was poured out to you, measure it back to them (Matt. VII). Let him who stands, according to your example, take heed lest he fall (I Cor. X); and let him who has fallen add what is needed [Col. 1704B] to rise again (Ps. XL).

Christ’s charity thirsts even for you, murderous Jew. Change your intention; repeat your prayer. You said: “His blood be upon us and upon our children” (Matt. XXVII). What you say is good, if you intend it rightly. Let His blood be upon you, and be buried with Him through baptism into death (Rom. VI). Desire to be saved, not condemned; drink with us also from the cup of His Passion. This is not a cup of horror but of mercy. Anoint the lintel of your forehead with this blood; the destroying angel will pass by you and will not touch your firstborn. Egypt being crushed, you shall escape unharmed (Exod. XII).

## TREATISE V. On that word of the Lord upon the cross: “Father, forgive them, for they know not what they do” (Luke XXIII).

[Col. 1703]

[Col. 1703C] The Law commands that an eye be torn out for an eye and a tooth for a tooth (Exod. XXI; Matt. V). Moses spares no one, pursues and avenges every wrong done to him; and, without any compassion, the despiser of his decrees is killed. In the age of grace the ordinances are moderated, and evangelical gentleness excludes anger, insult, and contempt from the people of God’s possession [Note: [Col. 1704C] The Christian people is called “a people of possession” by the Apostle Peter, who says: “But you are an elect race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people of possession,” etc. (I Pet. II). The Christian people is called a people of possession because Christ acquired it for Himself and purchased it at a great price, namely His own blood. In adding, “It excludes anger, insult, and contempt,” the author explains by these three terms the Lord’s sentence forbidding anger, the calling of one’s brother *raca*, and the calling of him “fool.” In the first, he says that simple anger is forbidden; in the second, insult; and in the third, contempt.]. The discipline of our Master does not permit one to say *raca* (Matt. V) or “fool” (ibid.) to a brother, or even to be angry.

[Col. 1704C] He Himself, who is judge of all, to whom vengeance belongs (Rom. XII; Deut. XXXII), does not grow angry every day (Ps. VII). Commanding that the sword be returned to its sheath, He declares that those who strike with the sword will perish by the sword (Matt. XXVI). His back torn by lashes, His cheeks plucked, His face smeared with spittle, His head pierced with thorns, His side wounded, His palms bored through, His feet pierced—like a lamb at play with its slaughterer—He laid open His flesh without resistance [Col. 1705A] and patiently offered His naked body, like an anvil, to the blows of hammerers. He could indeed have summoned many thousands of angels to act for Him (Matt. XXVI) and have been delivered from such mockery. Yet He who had commanded the right cheek to be offered to one who strikes the left, and both tunic and cloak to one who takes away the cloak (Matt. V), confined Himself within His own rules. He willed that the pattern of patience should proceed from the head into the members, and that the imitation of the children should be proved in this: whether they would show themselves not degenerate.

Thus He reveals what He first thirsted for, and again, turning to the Father, prays that this ignorance may be forgiven the people. “Father,” He says, “forgive them, for they know not what they do” (Luke XXIII). What is this, Lord, that You say? You do not accuse; You do not seek vengeance. Rather, You excuse them, [Col. 1705B] mitigate the density [Note: [Col. 1705C] *Spissamentum*: “density,” from *spissum*, “dense.”] of that conspiracy, and, transferring the inherited burden from the ungodly, do not allege the crime of malice. You judge it to be forgiven because You Yourself testify that it was committed in ignorance.
