Where is what You had said earlier: “If I had not come and spoken to them, they would not have had sin; but now they have both seen and hated both Me and My Father” (John XV)? They saw, indeed, and hated. They proclaimed every Sabbath what Moses had written of You and what the ancient books had cried aloud. You entered the synagogue and, though it was plain that You had not been taught from a book, unfolded the book of Isaiah and read in the hearing of all: “The Spirit of the Lord is upon me, because He has anointed me; He has sent me to preach the Gospel to the poor” [Col. 1705C] (Luke IV; Isa. LXI). In public ministry You declared that this prophecy of Scripture had been fulfilled in You.

What place was there for ignorance, when, as they themselves asked how You knew letters that You had not learned, that very fact was proof of divine wisdom: they found You learned in the Law though they had never seen You studying elementary lessons in their schools. Certainly this could not be hidden; indeed, in this the whole multitude marvelled at You. You are wise from Yourself; You understand from Yourself; You publicly dispute concerning the Law with the scribes, and from the Law You convict the brutish and dull teachers. What place can there be for doubt, what ground for ignorance, where the blind see, [Col. 1706A] the lame walk, lepers are cleansed, the dead rise, and the poor receive the Gospel? (Matt. XI; Luke VII).

But because their minds were obstinate and unwilling to understand so as to act rightly (Ps. XXXV), the signs themselves were not persuasive to them, nor the mighty works effectual. Hatred of Christ had hardened so greatly in their hearts that even the good things which they could not deny they said were done not by God’s power but by demonic tricks. They attributed Christ’s works to Beelzebub (Matt. IX, XII), and the anointing of the Holy Spirit to demons [Note: [Col. 1705C] He says that the Jews attributed the Holy Spirit’s anointing to demons because the works Christ performed by the Holy Spirit, with whom He was anointed, they said were done by a demon.]. Yet Christ affirms that they do not know what they are doing, and therefore earnestly pleads with the Father for their error and blindness.

But even this petition had its order: in barren, marshy soil that produces weeds instead of crops [Note: [Col. 1705D] *Purgamenta*, that is, thorns, thistles, and many other weeds, from which the earth must be laboriously cleared in order to produce good fruit. *Purgamenta* are refuse or other superfluous things which are gathered and cast away in cleansing. In what follows—“and erroneous thoughts must first be removed from the deep *adyta*”—the word should be read with a *y*: *adytis*. An *adytum* is a more secret part of a temple, to which only priests were admitted, as Virgil says:

> “. . . . . And he carries back these sad words from the inner sanctuary.”  
> (*Aeneid* II, 115.)

The Greeks use ἄδυτον (*adyton*, “inner sanctuary”) in the neuter gender. The author therefore means that erroneous judgment had first to be removed from the more hidden places of the Jewish heart. Some manuscripts read *abditis* (“hidden places”) for *adytis*.], the foundations of faith had to be planted to the very depths, and erroneous thoughts first removed from the deep inner sanctuaries [Col. 1706B], so that truth might prepare and illuminate for itself a firm and stable house, and hope of glory might adorn the temple founded upon faith.

Yet, although the authority of the Mediator might wear away the weight of so great a crime, the obstinacy of that unbelief was not thereby excusable. The mind, deprived of reason and dim-sighted in beholding truths, had nothing to allege in its defence. The most straight appearance of truth was understood otherwise than it was—like an oar lowered into water, which presents the likeness of something bent and broken [Note: [Col. 1705D] He compares an erring sense with an erring understanding. The sense of sight is deceived by an oar lowered into water: though it is straight and sound, it appears bent and broken to the beholder’s eye. So understanding sometimes judges differently about a thing and its truth than the thing is in itself. Since the defect is not in the object, blame is to be ascribed to our eyes and our understanding. Squinting eyes, which do not look straight but sideways, are themselves the cause of their deception. So a mind looking and judging wrongly from itself deceives itself in its judgment; it is not deceived by truth. The author subsequently explains this well of the Jews, saying: “Therefore neither reason nor teaching was at fault,” etc.]. Though the thing itself stood before their eyes and no obstacle intervened, their gaze, looking obliquely from itself, was distorted. Therefore neither reason nor teaching [Col. 1706C] was at fault, for they certainly were not lacking.

But while superfluous things are sought with a great expenditure of time, an ingrained evil seated in their very inward parts did not admit the healing hand. Since they did not know themselves to be sick, they despised the remedies of health. Nothing was more hostile to their malignant eyes than light itself; lowering their eyelids and forcing them tightly shut, they violently imposed blindness upon themselves [Note: [Col. 1706D] Thus, when something is presented to our sight which we wholly do not wish to see, we are accustomed to lower our eyelids and force them shut, closing our eyes and preventing the sight of what is present. The Jews acted thus when they “were unwilling to understand so as to act rightly” (Ps. XXXV); for they lacked nothing except willingness. The evidence of the signs and the efficacy of the teaching were present. When the author goes on to say, “so voluntary in this evil that will made habit, and habit made necessity,” do not understand “necessity” simply, but as a kind of necessity: nothing other than a great hardening or obstinacy in some matter. Thus we say of someone habituated to a vice that it is impossible for him to do this or not do that; for example, of a person hardened in hatred, that he cannot love but must necessarily hate. Habit is, as they say, a second nature, and thus seems to bring a kind of necessity, so that it cannot be otherwise except with great difficulty.]. They were so voluntary in this evil that will made habit, habit made necessity, and necessity broke out into that madness in which they did not know what they were doing.

This was [Col. 1707A] the dullness of mind which Isaiah reproaches in the Jewish people, through which they had come to such stupor that, seeing, they did not see and, hearing, they did not hear (Isa. VI). For those who made their minds bitter deserved to be confounded in their own perceptions; and those who abused the teachings of righteousness and abhorred the rays of truth, being cast away from the light of nature and grace, should waste away in their blindness and have within themselves smoky exhalations that darkened all the brightness of understanding and sense. The saliva of the Law which they had long imbibed clung so stickily in their throats, and the taste of the old ceremonies so infected the palate of their faithlessness, that anyone who taught departure from Moses and drew from the West the life-giving Spirit rather than the letter was, to them, a Satan.

[Col. 1707B] Therefore, preferring Moses to Christ, they zealously armed their tongues as against a blasphemer: they preferred the servant to the Lord and the disciple to the Master (John VII, VIII). Nor could they deny the miracles; but their hatred was of such weight and their envy of such savagery that Christ’s good deeds and words had no savour for them. No access at all to truth stood open to their frenzied minds. What was evident and could not be hidden by any evasion they perversely interpreted as best they could. In defending the Law they now employed not so much arguments as insults. For they were convicted from the Law itself and shut in by their own doctrines. No escape remained for the transgressors except to malign and persecute [Col. 1707C] truth by violence; and the one common purpose of them all had conspired to stifle glory by insult and to blot out together both His name and His fame by the reproach of death.

All their counsel revolved around this, and every argument of their faithlessness converged upon this decision: to remove from their midst the Holy and Righteous One, because He was contrary to their works (Wis. II), and thus prove that He had no fellowship with the divine nature, since He seemed mortal and capable of suffering like other human beings. This was the blindness, this the ignorance of the erring people, which Christ’s charity asks to be forgiven, bestowing a benefit upon the ungrateful. This was in part fulfilled then and will be perfectly fulfilled at the end, when the whole mass of the Israelite people [Col. 1707D] shall gather within the embrace of this forgiveness, once the fullness of the Gentiles has entered (Rom. XI).

Jesus knew that the Father had given all things into His hands (John XIII). Though He could give what He asked and possessed this power by His own authority, for the time being He nevertheless assumed the role of one who petitions. Thus charity might be made known by His affection, humility by His subjection, and truth by the outcome: namely, that in absolving so great a crime [Col. 1708A] there was no conflict of wills between Advocate and Judge, but that both had one concordant plea in this matter. For there could be no place at all for severity where wounded Christ demanded the reward of His own blood.

Therefore He is heard because of His reverence (Heb. II); yet He does not receive it without cost, but pays out an immense price. Thus those for whom a matter of such weight is transacted may recognize how desperate the cause of humankind was: it could not otherwise be settled unless, for its peace, there were paid a price of such magnitude as Christ’s humility and assumed humanity uniquely possessed.

Justice and peace therefore met, and a kiss was given (Ps. 84); and the Deliverer set himself as a faithful surety for his captive. So great was the authority by which the privilege of this pardon was confirmed that, on the very parchment of Christ crucified, the letters of that absolution were written in his own blood; and the seal remains fixed to this day—the wound in his side—which the presence of the Saviour continually displays before the eyes of the Father. Our Testator therefore transmitted to posterity the perpetual inheritance of this grace; and, though sin breaks out afresh in many after the root of original evil has been cut off, its universality has nevertheless been so wiped away that, for the expiation of daily offenses, Christ need not be crucified again. Rather, one washing of confession suffices for every crime, and one victim of repentance for every outrage.

Thus the sacrifice of the cross became for us both healing and an example: for that blood itself properly cleansed us, when Christ, having entered once into the holy places, sprinkled the people (Heb. 9); and we retain the pattern of a like entrance in our own blood, when our members are crucified and pleasures renounced.

[Note: We have given the interpretation of this passage above in the scholia on the first chapter.]

Nor should we pass wholly untouched by the mysteries of the breadth, height, length, and depth of the cross (Eph. 3). By its depth this standard penetrates to our inmost parts, and with its very sharp point probes the interior; reaching even to the division of soul and spirit (Heb. 4), it is fixed in the affections themselves, restrains hidden and concealed impulses, and pierces every appetite of wantonness. This is what the hidden cross does in the depth of the heart. Within, it wounds the soul with compunction; and, when the poisonous serpent Leviathan has been pierced beneath by this stake, it makes our inward parts peaceful, fortifies the conscience, and sanctifies meditations. And as the wood shown by the Lord to Moses, when plunged into the waters of Marah, changed all their bitterness into sweetness (Exod. 15), so the power of the holy cross, stored within the mind, sweetens every briny bitterness of temptations by its immersion and touch.

Now the length, which rises from the feet to the joining of the crossbeam,

[Note: *Crusta*, feminine in gender, means a fragment or layer of stone, wood, or something similar. From *crusta* comes the verb *crusto*, and from it *incrusto*, meaning “to lay on a layer” or “to apply a covering.” Hence come *crustatio* or *incrustatio*, when a covering is applied to something. *Incrustatura* has the same meaning. “To the joining of the beam,” therefore, means to that place above where the crossbeam is attached and joined to the upright beam. Thus he distinguishes the length of the cross from its height: he takes its length from the lowest point at the feet to the junction of the crossbeam; but its height from what remains above that junction. This appears to be how the author imagines the form of the cross, approximately as painters usually depict it, although some think that no further part extended upward above the junction. See J. Lipsius, *De cruce*.]

is an indication of continual Christian mortification, and an effective lesson that thoughts and deeds alike must be crucified. For, however long the stretches of this age may be, throughout the whole of life an untiring person must always press toward the things that lie ahead, always raise himself by steadfast patience and persevering long-suffering.

But the breadth embraces all things in the wide reach of zealous charity: it becomes weak with the weak, and burns with those for whom there is scandal (2 Cor. 11). It extends and spreads itself over the afflicted, nourishing them by its affection; spreading its wings, it gathers unfledged chicks, cherishes them, protects them, and, exposing itself for the protection of little ones, disregards itself. In defending others it does not fear its own losses. Even with those who hate peace it is so peaceful (Ps. 119) that, when injured, it seeks no vengeance, and, when provoked, returns no insult. If it corrects, it acts with complete solicitude, so that goodwill accomplishes more than severity, exhortation more than agitation, humility more than power.

It embraces righteous and wicked alike: the one, that he may stand; the other, that he may rise again. Goodness is not foreign to it, nor does it borrow mercy from elsewhere. It is not driven by goads, laws, or straps to bear others’ burdens; of its own accord it bends its shoulders with lowered knee, does not consider it burdensome to bear those who cannot bear themselves, but makes another’s misery an occasion for beneficence and an adornment of generosity. If among the weak there are shameful things, it surrounds them with more abundant honor (2 Cor. 12); it does not reproach or defame. It heals rather than wounds; tends rather than tears; relieves rather than burdens. It covers sins rather than publicizing them.

Christ commended the mysteries of this breadth even amid his sufferings: in displaying himself in the midst between the thieves, with hands stretched out and left and right arms raised, he wished it to be understood that this benefit was common, that what was being done profited not the good alone but also the wicked, that he had offered these remedies to the sick rather than the healthy, and that this grace had freely bestowed the same gift both on those born of the free woman and on those born of the slave woman (Gal. 4).

There remains the height, indicated by the portion extending to the summit. This is the confidence of good hope, which carries those crucified to the world into heavenly things, and, through the testimony of a good conscience, joins them secure and certain to that glory. Already it reaches out a hand toward those good things; already it tastes, already opens its mouth, already samples, already lives with the angels, already follows those companies, already recognizes, already melts, already loves, already rejoices aloud, already is glad and delighted, becomes cheerful and rests, understands and loves. Yet, however greatly anyone may in perfection relish the things above, there remains a very great difference between faith and sight.

[Note: Some manuscripts read, “between faith and hope.” But that does nothing for the argument. It is therefore clear that *sight*, not *hope*, must be read. For now, as the Apostle says, “we walk by faith, not by sight” (2 Cor. 5). But in the heavenly homeland they see God by sight, without enigma, as he is (1 John 3).]

Nor is an enlargement into fullness without the cross for the elect. No temptation indeed shakes those already tried and brought to perfection; but, as we have said, this alone is lacking for the completion of peace: contemplation of the truth does not yet present itself wholly and entirely.

## SIXTH AND SEVENTH TREATISES

On the sixth and seventh final words of the Lord on the cross: “It is finished”; and, “Father, into your hands I commend my spirit” (Luke 23).

[Col. 1709]

After the myrrhed cup and the other mockeries of the cross,

[Note: The author treats the final two words—the sixth, “It is finished,” and the seventh, “Father, into your hands I commend my spirit”—in a single treatise. Of the latter he says very little, at the beginning itself; but of the former he speaks at greater length, showing in many ways how the legal shadows and ceremonies were fulfilled through Christ. To this purpose belong all that he expounds concerning the paschal lamb and the manner of eating it, and likewise concerning priestly garments and ornaments.]

what Matthew, Mark, and Luke had omitted, John did not pass over in silence: namely, that, when all things had been fittingly arranged, and the ordinances of the testament of grace and of sure hope had been assigned at the end, Christ, to declare that nothing at all was lacking for the teaching and pattern of righteousness, said, “It is finished”; and then, having commended his spirit into the Father’s hands, he bowed his head, as though giving thanks, and by his own authority gave up his life—thus bringing to completion the whole meaning of the legal sacrifices and setting the final hand upon the ancient enigmas.

[Note: That is, as Christ himself said, no one could take his life from him; rather, he laid it down of himself, for he had authority to lay down his life and authority to take it up again (John 10). In giving up his life thus, he is said to have completed the *ratio*, that is, the signification, of all legal victims. For all legal victims were nothing other than figures of the one most acceptable Victim. The final hand was also laid upon the ancient enigmas: that is, the shadows of the law attained their final perfection. For it is proverbially said that the “last hand” or “final hand” is applied to something when it receives its ultimate completion. It is evident, moreover, that all those ancient shadows and figures were perfected, completed, and fulfilled by the coming of Truth himself. Hence he himself said in the Gospel, “I have not come to abolish the law, but to fulfill it” (Matt. 5). And the Apostle Paul says, “We do not destroy the law, but perfect the law” (Rom. 3).]

He offered his whole self to the Father, and the fullness of that whole burnt offering was completed. Flesh and spirit alike were expended in that ministry, because the matter concerned both the flesh and the spirit of man; and the whole human being had Christ entire as healer. His flesh was offered upon the wood as medicine for flesh; and, to obtain the sanctification of the soul, that spirit descended to the lower regions and ascended to the heights, there breaking iron bars (Ps. 106), here opening everlasting gates (Ps. 23).

Although Christ’s soul withdrew from his body during those three days, it did not abandon his divinity as it abandoned the flesh. God was indivisibly present in it, reconciling the world to himself (2 Cor. 5), taking away from us the fear of death through the timely resurrection, cleansing by that bitterness whatever poisons of pleasures had infected, and displaying the glory of his victory to heaven and hell. Having taken away those who had long languished in that expectation, he also fulfilled the desire of the angels, to whom this restoration of humanity was welcome. Nor was there any delay between offering and obtaining: passion and absolution embraced one another with every swiftness. Thus the one followed from the other, so that at the same hour he both filled the upper regions and took the lower regions captive.

Yet those joys in heaven were carried on for a longer interval; Christ’s soul did not immediately return to his body, but meanwhile displayed to those whom he had delivered from such ancient darkness the exultant presence of divine splendor. To those who were in the world he delayed for a little while the dispensation of consolation, so that delay might increase longing and the sudden joy of the resurrection might fill their affection.

Therefore, because it had been written at the head of the book that the Son should do this will of the Father (Ps. 39), and because the long-awaited reality, prefigured in many ways, had brought its face, hidden from the age, into the light, Christ did not allow a people relieved of sins to be burdened any longer by superfluous observances. Henceforth it would be not religion but superstition if the dregs of ancient ceremonies were mixed with pure wine in the evangelical cup. He wished it to be understood that not only his sufferings but also those observances had reached their end: once Truth had come, figures must cease, and believers must no longer be needlessly harassed by thorny wanderings,

[Note: Some copies read *sinosis*; others, *spinosis*. Both readings yield a good sense. Those shadows of the law were *spinosae*, “thorny”: dry, afflictive, and pricking like thorns. They were also *sinosae*, “winding”: leading a person round by bends and detours, and not bringing one to Truth itself by a straight or short road. In the following words, “And he who was speaking would speak openly: Behold, I am here,” the author alludes to the oracle of the prophet Isaiah, who, speaking of Christ’s coming, says in Christ’s person: “Therefore my people shall know my name on that day, because I am he who was speaking: behold, I am here” (Isa. 52). “I,” he says, “who formerly spoke in many and various ways through the prophets” (Heb. 1), “am now present in assumed flesh, in order to fulfill all things.”]

while they strayed through byways, when Truth itself was showing them the way and was speaking openly: “I, who was speaking—behold, I am here” (Isa. 52).

Christ was anointed with the oil of gladness above all participants in human nature (Ps. 44); he also inherited a name more excellent than the angels (Heb. 1), and the Jewish anointing had now dried up before this oil.

[Note: In one phrase he enfolds a double prophecy, one from Isaiah and the other from Daniel. In Isaiah we read: “It shall come to pass in that day that his burden”—namely, Midian’s—“shall be removed from your shoulder, and his yoke from your neck; and the yoke shall decay before the oil” (Isa. 10). This oil is that with which Christ was anointed (Ps. 44); before that oil Midian’s yoke decayed—that is, the power of the devil and the captivity by which he held us under himself were removed. But in Daniel it is said concerning the Jewish anointing: “When the Holy of Holies comes, your anointing will cease” (Dan. 9). What is this but that, when the anointing of this oil comes, by which the Holy of Holies shall be anointed, then your bodily anointing shall cease? Before the oil of Christ, therefore, both the devil’s yoke had to decay and Jewish anointing had to cease; and both have now been perfectly fulfilled to the great joy of all the faithful.]

It was necessary that the ephod should be folded up and that the *teraphim* should not appear,

[Note: The ephod was a priestly garment under the old law. Concerning the *teraphim*, blessed Jerome says in his Commentary on Hosea, on the words, “The children of Israel shall sit without king and without prince, without sacrifice and altar, without ephod and without teraphim” (Hos. 3): “*Teraphim* are properly called μορφώματα [formed figures], that is, figures and images; in the present passage we may understand them only as cherubim and seraphim, or other things commanded to be made as ornaments of the temple.”]

and that whatever Bezalel had either woven or concealed should give place to living and rational teachings. Shadows, images, and typical coverings should disappear where Truth itself displays to those who behold it its naked form and pure appearance (Exod. 38).

Thus, at the end of Christ’s sufferings, it was shown that the end of the law had arrived. Whatever the law of old had variously decreed for the expiation of sins through the blood of goats and calves, or through any perfumes or libations whatever, grace reduced to brevity. Shortening the course of so great a labor, it set forth one blood, one burning, and one whole burnt offering containing all things; and it arranged this with such moderation that, however destitute a person might be, he possessed a sufficient price to procure it, and neither status nor place kept anyone from access to so great a condescension.

The Church, therefore, has one lamb; it is not necessary to seek another whenever Passover returns. Since the Christian people are one tribe and family, one victim suffices for one people, and one table is set in one house. The whole fellowship of faith has one bread and cup; one food is placed before the multitude of believers, and it is taken by all, yet not consumed. When it has filled everyone, it remains and abounds.

The loaves of presentation were changed every Sabbath: when warm ones were placed, cold ones were taken away,

[Note: The Apostle Paul, arguing in Hebrews about the ancient offerings in order to prefer Christ’s sacrifice, proves their imperfection from their repetition every year. For he says: “The law, having a shadow of good things to come, not the very image of the things, can never make perfect those who approach by the same sacrifices which they offer continually every year; otherwise they would have ceased to be offered, because the worshipers, once cleansed, would no longer have any consciousness of sins. But in them there is a remembrance of sins every year” (Heb. 10). In the present passage our author similarly infers from the changing of the loaves on every Sabbath that those offerings were not perfect and complete; otherwise they would not have been changed in this manner. He further observes a special mystery in the removal of cold loaves and the setting out of warm ones.]

because the very changing of the loaves declared that the old offerings, as cold and lacking the warmth of the Spirit, were to be rejected in the time of grace. Our Lamb is the same, and different lambs are not sacrificed for different families. Just as the unity of the Church cannot be split or divided, so it is necessary that all perform one act and that common devotion render a uniform service; the very singularity of the sacrifice commends the agreement of the whole community.

As for the eating of the lamb, if anything should remain, the neighbor joined to the house in which there was a remainder is commanded to be called (Exod. 12). This expresses the admission of the Gentiles into fellowship in the Church’s sacraments. Called by the Gospel, they were enticed by the savor of this banquet, and the gracious mother received, to these things which the Jewish people could not eat, those who had hitherto been hungry.

It is altogether wonderful to say, and the matter itself requires spiritual understanding, that, since the lamb could be sacrificed only by one family, what family could be so small, so lacking children, grandchildren, and other relatives, that it could not eat one small lamb by itself? This is especially so because the fruitfulness of that nation was so abundant, and many marriages multiplied their offspring. But, as we have said, the calling of the Gentiles was prophetically indicated. They were admitted through faith to participation in the sacraments, while the Jews clung to the carnal sense of the letter and could not attain the fullness of spiritual understanding.

Our Lamb, therefore, has been roasted upon the spit of the cross, with the coals of torments burning beneath. We now taste in him nothing raw or carnal, nothing boiled or soft; rather, the roasting of that sweet savor has so hardened in the flame of the gibbet, has been so made firm, that nothing further remains in him capable of suffering or death. The funeral pyre of death, kindled long ago, has been extinguished by the sprinkling of that blood. Therefore the incorruptible integrity of Christ stands secure both for himself and for us: what is altogether firm cannot decay, and what is eternal cannot diminish.

We eat his head with his feet and do not shrink from his inward parts, because our faith lives and advances in this, confesses this, and believes that the Word which was in the beginning with God became flesh (John 1) at the end of the ages; that divine majesty descended even to the inward parts of our weakness and did not shrink from the workshop of our frailty. He who was our beginning came also to our end, establishing in himself for us a goal and limit; through a temporal end he recalls us to the infinite end, and, joining the glory of body and head, bound them into one by an indivisible union.

Thus we eat the head, the feet, and the inward parts when we proclaim Christ’s height in such a manner that we are not ashamed of his humility; his weakness in such a manner that we do not deny his strength; his foolishness in such a manner that we wonder at his wisdom. For what is still more astonishing in that work of our redemption is that the sublimity of divinity allowed itself to be so emptied, than that immutable power and incomprehensible greatness remains in itself, immovably persevering in everlasting blessedness.

And so in Ezekiel the cherubim cover the face and feet of God as the first and last things, but leave only the middle parts exposed to sight (Ezek. 1), because what was with him before the foundation of the world, and what condition of things will be after the final judgment, is food for faith and hope. Meanwhile, while devout gentleness endeavors to understand the things done according to the flesh and to search out the affections of his humanity, as it were from the inward parts of his charity, it is nourished.

We eat the flesh in this manner, but burn the bones with fire,

[Note: I do not find it expressly said in the text of Exodus that the lamb’s bones were to be burned with fire. Yet this is stated by inference, since it is commanded that no bone be broken and that, if anything of the lamb remained, it should be burned with fire. Thus it was commanded: “You shall not break a bone of it” (Exod. 12) and again, “If anything remains, it shall be burned with fire” (Num. 9).]

because we visibly receive and take the sacraments—which are, as it were, the flesh of divine power and coverings of truth—according to their outward form. But the substance itself, firm and wholly solid in its unintelligible and invisible state, we neither break nor diminish; rather, we commit it to flames, that is, to spiritual understandings. For in the divine mysteries there are spirit and life, and it is not lawful for human understanding to break apart knowledge of so great a reality. Meanwhile the Holy Spirit gathers it within himself, until that which is partial is done away (1 Cor. 13), the perfect comes openly forth, and, knowing as we are known, we act no longer by this sacrament but by sight (ibid.).

Therefore we are commanded to kill the lamb at night, because the reason for this work, of which faith is the minister, does not yet shine forth clearly. Truth will reveal it amid the splendors of the saints, when new wine is drunk in the kingdom of God (Matt. 26), virgin souls with lamps kindled are admitted to the eternal marriage-feast (Matt. 25), and the inextinguishable lamp is set upon the lampstand. Then, for all who are in the house, both the truth of the sacraments and the very mystery of the Trinity will shine.

Meanwhile a matter of immeasurable gain is at stake:

[Note: Namely, because we now walk by faith rather than sight, we obtain for ourselves the inheritance of the heavenly kingdom and eternal life, which is the greatest gain of all.]

the visible effect declares the invisible power; bestowed benefits confirm the certainty of faith; and from the comparison of present things arises a firm and settled expectation of future things. This Lamb is given to us for food, and his blood is given for drink. We are commanded to place that blood itself outwardly upon the thresholds and doorposts of our houses as a sign (Exod. 12), so that what is open and what is hidden may be fortified, and flesh and spirit may have secure protections. The divine food and drink inwardly nourish and strengthen the soul; outwardly, the sign of the cross and the mark of blood drive away hostile powers.

There is no doubt that demons altogether dread the form of the Passion, and that the mere sight of this character strikes terror into them. Holy sacraments and signs of faith protect even those who, it is evident, do not conform themselves to Christian doctrine and chaste morals as fully as they ought. Yet, because of the regard paid to the foundation to which they cling in some manner, demons do not immediately rush upon all carnal persons merely on account of the wood and hay that they see carelessly built upon it (1 Cor. 3). They revere the foundation, flee from the life-giving sign, and do not rashly approach a house consecrated with the balm of blood.

Otherwise, if the power of the sacraments wholly withdrew its force at every individual transgression, the sign of the cross would be marked vainly upon the foreheads of the erring and no hope would remain for those who fall. Although the Holy Spirit may depart from such persons at the moment of their lapse, the sacraments nevertheless remain even in the guilty and are not empty. When the offender is moved to compunction, that same Spirit returns to them. So great is the dignity of the sacraments that, even in the Spirit’s absence, the hostile power does not dare enter,

[Note: This must be understood of entry for full and tranquil indwelling. For the devil enters a person in some sense whenever that person is defiled by a sin that drives out the Spirit—that is, mortal sin. Since one who sins in this manner becomes a child and servant of the devil, the devil has entry into that person in some manner. Yet it is not so full and free an entry that the person cannot easily expel him whenever he wishes to repent.

The author significantly adds: “Unless, through despair and habit and deliberate consent, the mind, conquered and made captive, has erased the holy sign with the scalpel of apostasy.” It should be observed here that many sin mortally and are deprived for a time of God’s Spirit, yet do not wholly alienate themselves from God by deliberate consent; nor are they abandoned by God as such. David, for example, fell into sin because he was overcome more by weakness or temptation than by malice or habit, and therefore was not abandoned by God. But those who, through despair, habit, or deliberate consent, subject themselves to sins from malice and purpose, erase, as it were with a scalpel, the sign of their sanctification; they in effect degrade themselves, so to speak, so that they are no longer reckoned among the household and house of God. Consequently demons claim unrestricted power over them, as though they had never been marked with such a sign. But these matters perhaps require a longer treatment.]

unless, through despair and habit and deliberate consent, the conquered and captive mind has erased the holy sign with the scalpel of apostasy. Hence, when the destroying angel struck every firstborn of the Egyptians, he saw this sign at the thresholds smeared with blood and, as though rebuked, restrained himself. When the Egyptians had been slain, those whose sides and foreheads had been reddened by the sprinkling of this blood remained unharmed and safe (Exod. 12).

Thus Rahab, although she was a prostitute, was saved when a scarlet cord was hung at her window; she alone escaped freely from Jericho, and her house was not exposed to devastation and plunder, protected as it was by reverence for so notable a sign (Josh. 6).

[Note: In each case there is a sign and figure of the salvation that was to be bestowed upon the world through Christ’s blood. As the blood of the lamb by which the Jewish doorposts were preserved signified Christ’s blood, and escape from the angel’s slaughter signified believers’ deliverance through Christ’s blood, so the scarlet cord, being red in color, prefigured the red blood of Christ, in which salvation has been given, just as salvation was granted through the scarlet cord. The former may be referred to the deliverance of the Jews and the latter to the deliverance of the Gentiles, so that in these two figures, both signifying the same thing, the liberation of each people is indicated.]

We are also commanded to celebrate this feast eagerly and in haste, with garments fit for travel, holding an unspecified object in their hands, and with loins girded, eating unleavened bread with wild lettuces (Exod. 12). For ministers of so great a work ought to be neither idle nor soft; nor, for those receiving provisions and about to leave Egypt, should lodging-places of pleasure be sought. Rather, in going out from a barbarous people (Ps. 113), bitterness of repentance and sincerity of life must be ordered together.

These things once profited in a carnal manner, as did the other enigmas of the law, while faith and piety were converging upon that which Truth had promised. But when the fullness of time came (Gal. 4), and Christ, the end of the law (Rom. 10), became, in the appropriate senses, whatever was commanded concerning lamb, kid, or red heifer, bringing all things together in himself according to their proper meanings, many observances ceased where the One established sufficiency. Signs were no longer to be employed once that which they signified had arrived.

Sacrifices made on a griddle or in a pan (Lev. 2) foretold the zeal and fervor of the saints; burnings of aromatic substances, the burnings of prayers and the pious vows and affections of the saints; burning fat, pleasures put to death. The garments of the priests contained the ornament of manifold graces.

The linen drawers, first prescribed for covering shameful parts (Exod. 28), teach that modesty in continence ought to be so great that it leaves no room even for suspicion, and that whatever bears the mark of indecency must be so hidden that no zealot’s gaze can by any chance be permitted to look upon it. Priestly conduct should present itself as though sexless and should wholly abhor such stain; indeed, it should be ashamed and blush even at the common members, cover nature itself that is conscious of itself, detest what it is able to do rather than what it does, and bury and hide those parts as though dead and fetid.

[Note: Everything from this point to the end concerns the garments and ornaments of priests, explained aptly and clearly in a moral sense. Because these matters do not directly pertain to the proposed subject of the Lord’s seven words, and because the author speaks clearly enough, I have not thought they should be either elucidated or burdened with many or lengthy scholia. For the garments and ornaments themselves in their literal sense, if you seek them, see Exodus 28 throughout the chapter; likewise chapter 39 of the same book, and Ecclesiasticus 45.]

The second garment, called the *poderis*, that is, the ankle-length garment, was of linen. It indicated perseverance in cleanliness and the brightness of an unstained life. It was close-fitting and clung to the body, because this vocation loves singleness, and those who minister at holy altars must be unencumbered, presenting flesh, clothing, and their entire conduct as solitary.

In third place was the belt, fastening the linen tunic between navel and breast, so that mind and action might agree under the bond of the same purpose and submit to the same law; so that both should act with a kind of mutual obligation; and so that carnal and spiritual affection might, by equal resolve, bind themselves to this rule and continually agree in the same thing with common zeal.

The fourth ornament was the tiara or *cidaris*. This adornment of the head—because there is the inner chamber of the senses and the proper house of wisdom—indicates the aim of philosophical contemplation and how great is the wisdom involved in choosing celibacy.

[Note: Some codices read “prophetic” in place of “philosophical”; others, “physical.” All these readings convey an equally true sense, because prophetic, philosophical, and physical or natural contemplation tend toward the same end: upward to God. This is signified by the tiara or *cidaris*, the mitre that rises upward. The same mitre indicates how great is the wisdom of choosing celibacy, because the head of the priest who chooses it is adorned with such a white ornament.]

All these things were commanded to be made from linen, from which fine linen (*byssus*) is prepared, so that it might not escape those devoted to this study and purpose that many washings are necessary if anyone, trained by discipline, is to attain this whiteness.

[Note: Before one can get from flax to *byssus*, or white linen cloth, much labor must be expended and many washings are needed. Each thread must be diligently twisted with the fingers in order to acquire solidity and firmness; for before the threads are twisted, they immediately break. In the same way, everyone who wishes to attain the whiteness of purity and gain stability in it must acquire it by much labor and continual exercise.]

Carnal affections must long be twisted and strengthened by habitual practice, lest they be easily broken by the weight of temptations. And indeed, to our Head, which is Christ, all the glory of our purity must be referred, as this *cidaris* signifies; only then can perseverance be secure, if hope is fixed in him and confidence rooted there.

These four garments were common, by law and ordinance, to the lesser priests and to the high priests. The remaining four belonged properly to the high priest. First, after the garments already mentioned, the high priest put on a hyacinth-blue robe; and from its lower edge there hung all around seventy-two bells, with one pomegranate between every two bells [Col. 1718B] (Exod. 28; Ecclus. 45). All were of the purest gold, so that he might enter the sanctuary wholly resonant; otherwise he would immediately die. This blue robe signifies that a soul nourished in holiness has attained such advancement that it lives by the Spirit, walks by the Spirit, is judged by no one, and judges all things (1 Cor. 2). For this is the supreme priesthood: to reach this summit of holiness, so that the righteous man may show himself wholly heavenly, display heavenly manners and the divine form, and, with his mind fixed upon the Creator alone, adhere to him in an undivided way of life. The robe of hyacinth colour expresses all this.

The bells, however, were golden, while the pomegranates were made of blue, purple, scarlet, and fine linen, formed in the shape of a little sphere. By this the Holy Spirit signifies [Col. 1718C] that contemplative men, whose citizenship is in heaven (Phil. 3), and who set their minds on things above, not on things upon the earth (Col. 3), ought to proclaim to the people the teaching of the Christian faith and, especially, the terrible last judgment. Their whole conduct and speech ought to ring with divine mysteries; nor should they suppress or choke in silence the divine grace given them. For it is not enough to have laid away the received talent in a napkin unless the servant returns from trading with a profit (Matt. 25; Luke 19). Nor does the blue robe avail; the badges of chastity and continence do not suffice the teacher; nor is his entrance to the holy altars peaceable, if he neglects to announce to the wicked man his way [Col. 1718D] and the wages of sin. For that man, lacking [Col. 1719A] a corrector, perishes in his sin; nor does the teacher’s own righteousness benefit him when the Judge requires the blood of the erring person from the watchman’s hand (Ezek. 3). Nor is it a great thing merely to live for oneself, unless one also strives to make others live with oneself. For, as Seneca says, one who flees things and people, who cannot bear to see others, but has hidden himself away through fear like a timid and sluggish animal, should not be said even to live for himself, but for sleep and the belly.

Therefore, when entering the Holy of Holies, the high priest ought to show himself wholly resonant, and to draw hearers by the power of the word as by fragrant flowers: so that preaching, like a bell of the purest gold, may signify the purity and perfection of singular understanding, and his speech may thunder on every side with the brightness of divine light. The colours of the flowers themselves show, in the blue, as has been said, heavenly desire; in the purple, royal greatness of spirit against sin; in the twice-dyed scarlet, the ardent affection of a devout mind in love for God and neighbour [Col. 1719B]. Priestly conduct must indeed always shine with the gold of wisdom, be raised upward by the blue of hope, be surrounded by the purple of kingship as a conqueror of sin and one reducing the monsters of demons to captivity, blaze with twice-dyed scarlet—that is, twofold love—and be ever diligent in the mortification and chastening of the flesh through twisted fine linen.

In the pomegranates, which contain many seeds beneath one rind, is expressed the manifold operation of virtues, enclosed on every side by the single covering of charity. And rightly [Col. 1719C] are pomegranates mingled with bells, when preaching and action cohere together and the teacher himself does what he says.

The sixth garment is then added, called the shoulder-piece; among the Hebrews it is also called the ephod. Samuel, while still a boy, is read to have had this (1 Sam. 2), and David wore it before the Ark (2 Sam. 6). But the ephod—that is, the shoulder-piece—which belonged to high priests, was woven of blue, purple, scarlet, and fine linen. The other ephod, which is also understood as a linen tunic, was plain and linen. In this shoulder-piece were set two onyx stones enclosed in gold, one at one edge and one at the other; and the names of the sons of Israel were engraved upon them, six on one stone and six on the other. Thus, in the high priest’s shoulder-piece, this must be understood: how he ought to conduct himself in bearing the burdens of his brothers, and how great, by reason of his office of governance, must be the concern laid upon him, so that upon his own shoulders he may bring the lost sheep back to the fold [Col. 1719D]. Here are signified endurance in good works and perseverance in labours.

The meaning of the colours of the shoulder-piece has been stated above. That it bears the names of the patriarchs upon the shoulders is certainly for their remembrance: so that, seeing the names of the Fathers written [Col. 1720A] upon the high priest’s garment, the people may imitate their righteousness, and may call to mind Abraham’s faith, Isaac’s gentleness, Israel’s patience, Joseph’s chastity, Moses’ discipline, Phinehas’ zeal, Joshua’s victory, Samuel’s sincerity, David’s humility, and the righteous deeds or sayings of the rulers or priests descended from those twelve patriarchs—those who through faith conquered kingdoms, worked righteousness, and obtained the promises (Heb. 11).

There is also a twofold reason why the high priest bears these names on his shoulders: that he may both set before his hearers the examples of the Fathers which they should follow, and himself bear in a spirit of gentleness those whom he instructs by word and example if they are overtaken in any fault (Gal. 6), striving more to relieve than to burden the weak. For by the law [Col. 1720B] of his office he must himself bear their burdens, and, according to the varied requirements of different diseases, both become weak with those who are ignorant or erring (Heb. 5), and burn with them (2 Cor. 11). The fact that six names were on the left and six on the right, engraved on onyx stones, means that those belonging to the registration of the heavenly inheritance include not only those who seem approved and perfect, but also those held in lesser esteem. For divine perfection does not reject our imperfection; it does not break the bruised reed or quench the smoking flax (Isa. 42). His right hand indeed embraces those worthy to be advanced to kisses; but his left also supports the heads of those (Song 2) whom the dizziness of weakness bends down [Col. 1720C]. He does not permit those who have fallen to be utterly crushed, but catches them as they fall and places his compassionate hand beneath those who are bowed down.

> **Note [Col. 1719D].** In Greek, *onyx* (ὄνυξ) means “fingernail”; and because of its resemblance to a human fingernail, that stone is called *onyx*, or an onyx stone. Christ is said to have presented himself to us as a fingernail, because, just as a fingernail covers and protects the tenderness of the flesh, so Christ covers the weakness of our flesh—that is, he removes sins—and clothes and fortifies soft flesh with his own hardness; that is, he strengthens our flesh’s weakness by his own firmness and preserves it from harm [Col. 1720D].

The onyx stone resembles a fingernail and sends forth little fires amid encircling white bands. Therefore, through this stone, upon which the names of the twelve sons of Israel are commanded to be engraved on the right and on the left, we rightly understand this Scripture to refer to Christ. In the assumed flesh he offered himself to us as a fingernail; he covered a multitude of sins with white bands—that is, by the teachings of continence he encircled the elect—and, by sparks of miracles, kindled them to faith. He burned within and shone without. He is that stone upon which the law is divinely written, and upon which are written the names [Col. 1720D] of all who do not take his name in vain. Once they have been engraved, no tribulation or adversity can erase or blot them out. Therefore they are placed on the right and on the left, because those founded or inscribed on the rock are shaken neither by height nor by depth, but proceed unconquered through the weapons of righteousness (2 Cor. 6), alike in prosperity and adversity.

The seventh garment follows, called in Hebrew *nosen*, in Greek λογικόν (*logikon*, “rational [breastpiece]”), and in Latin *rationale*. It is commanded to be made from the same materials and colours as [Col. 1721A] the shoulder-piece, and for the same reasons.

It was made double because of the weight of the stones, lest perhaps it should tear. It was also square, measuring a palm in both width and length. In its fourfold form understand the continual remembrance of evangelical teaching; in the measure of a palm, the full measure of law, so far as human action can attain it. For one who measures anything by the palm stretches out the hand with spread fingers in order to reach the place toward which he extends it. Thus the same measure should belong to devout intention in the length of good work and in the breadth of charity.

Twelve stones were also woven into it, arranged in four rows: three and three on one side, and three and three on the other. Upon each was engraved [Col. 1721B] one of the names of the sons of Israel, distinguished according to the tribes and their ages. At the four corners of the breastpiece were four golden rings, with four corresponding rings in the shoulder-piece, so that ring meeting ring, with golden chains inserted for this purpose on both sides, might join and mutually fasten shoulder-piece and breastpiece. Hooks were also fixed into the shoulder-piece, in which the chains were inserted; these bound together the rings meeting one another on either side. There were rings also on the sides and upper part of breastpiece and shoulder-piece: two at the top and two at the sides, with chains passing through each, below and above, so that fastenings might be present at the four corners and on both sides, and bindings might securely hold the two garments together at the shoulders, the extremities, [Col. 1721C] and the middle.

This garment, moreover, is called by the Lord not only the breastpiece, but also the breastpiece of judgment. Doctrine and truth are commanded to be placed in it, and with it the breast of the high priest is adorned when he enters the Holy of Holies. First, one must carefully observe that he who is clothed in this garment, in which doctrine and truth are inscribed in letters, should understand his breast to be consecrated to doctrine and truth. He ought not to be occupied with worldly business, activities, and gains, but should display the doctrine of faith by example and conduct. For it is altogether disgraceful to misuse reason, corrupt doctrine, and oppress truth by deceptions or contrivances [Col. 1721D].

For governing reason must so order all that it does, and assign mercy and judgment to their proper places, that when it judges, severity does not exclude clemency, and when it has mercy, compassion does not abandon justice. Whether it strikes or spares, it must not depart from the path of truth. Considering places, times, and modes of actions, as well as ages and ranks, priestly discernment should fit each thing to its proper rationale in number, weight, and measure. In the priest’s breast must be knowledge of these things; and his life itself must necessarily be doctrine. No place [Col. 1722A] in that soul should be given to falsehood, for whatever it teaches, does, ordains, or corrects ought to conform to the rule of divine judgment.

The shoulder-piece and breastpiece are also joined by their rings and mutually bound by the embrace of chains, so that pure thoughts may be joined in a holy mind with rational actions, all things may cohere in the bond of peace, and the embrace of charity may bind together the high priest’s entire ordering. Besides these fastenings, which correspond to heavenly desires and devout affections, and besides the ephod, which joined the *logion* at back and front, there was a belt binding above both the blue robe and the shoulder-piece and breastpiece themselves, with such firmness that the three garments seemed to form one appearance and all [Col. 1722B] clung closely together. This teaches how diligently holiness must be guarded: even after the glory of such great excellence, the gifts of virtues, and innumerable contests, struggles, and victories, dangers of the flesh often remain to the very end. Such watchfulness must always keep vigil within and without, so that unstained glory may endure in one’s actions and meditations to the end.

Even the highest mountains are struck by lightning.

> **Note [Col. 1721D].** From the poet Horace, Book II, Ode 10. The author applies this saying to his purpose, wishing by it to indicate that even those who seem most complete and perfect in every respect are not without danger from temptations while they live in this world—just as mountains, however high, are not free from a lightning-stroke on account of their height [Col. 1722D].

Unless, by this belt, reason and works are bound together in an unceasing union, even when all things have up to that point been well ordered, what appeared firm and suitably arranged when no storm drove against it may be separated and burst apart by the motions and assaults of diverse temptations. This belt was of purple and twisted fine linen [Col. 1722C], blue and twice-dyed scarlet, woven in a round pattern resembling a serpent’s skin.

Thus adorned, the high priest bears the names of the sons of Israel upon breast and shoulders for different reasons. On the shoulders, at right and left, for the reasons already stated. Or perhaps in only two rows because our High Priest, whose dominion is upon his shoulder (Isa. 9), both left the writing of the cross to the Gentiles and made known that their names were inscribed for redemption—their languages being contained in the title of the cross. In the breastpiece, however, as stated, the four rows of stones are separately placed at its four extremities, three above and three below. In the names of the patriarchs [Col. 1722D] resting against the high priest’s breast, it is signified that those in authority should always feel concern for those entrusted to their care and should, as far as possible, remember them by name and offer the aid of prayer. Nothing other than zeal for souls ought to occupy that breast, since it belongs to this office to call back the wandering, reconcile those in error, strengthen those progressing in righteousness, and encourage those who fail, lest they despair of pardon.

He must also conform himself to the examples of the preceding Fathers whose names he bears, so that, as he remembers their glory, he may imitate their life and not show himself alien to the faith and deeds of those whose acts and titles he carries about and approves [Col. 1723A]. The fact that the number twelve, divided into four rows, yields three in each part may suitably be understood to mean that the fourfold form of the Gospel sets forth the Trinity above all Scriptures. And this is apostolic doctrine, which fulfills the ten commandments of the Law in two (Matt. 22; Mark 12), and abbreviates and compresses the whole burden of ancient ordinances (Lev. 19) into love of God and neighbour.

The eighth adornment of the high priest follows: namely, the tiara, which some also call a cap or *cidaris*. Lesser priests too used this [Col. 1723B]. It was of fine linen, encircled with a golden band and made with woven work, just as the *phrygium* is commonly sewn today onto our bishops’ mitres.

> **Note [Col. 1723D].** Phrygian, or Phrygian-style, work was fashioned with remarkable variety of colours and great skill. Therefore, in Psalm 44, where our common reading has “clothed about with varieties,” others translate from the Hebrew, “clad in Phrygian garments,” or “garments of various figures.” We see such Phrygian or Phrygian-style work customarily sewn [Col. 1724D] onto our bishops’ mitres.

It was extended somewhat in the form of a helmet, rising above the crown of the head, and was bound to the head with a blue band, lest it slip by some accident while the priest was offering sacrifice. But the high priest’s tiara was more splendid and, besides these things, had a golden plate—called the *petalum*—set into the forehead, on which was written the name of God said among the Hebrews to be ineffable.

This tiara, which covers and adorns the high priest’s head and crowns and protects all his beauty, signifies, as said above, that all the faculties of the head are consecrated to God and that all [Col. 1723C] the glory of the body ought to be referred to the head. For all brightness of a good mind, splendor of wisdom, grace of preaching, glory of purity, kindness of charity, and whatever marks of holiness there are come from that universal head, from which the whole body, through joints and supports, grows and advances (Col. 2), is strengthened and perfected. Therefore, to signify complete brightness, the composed state of an ordered mind, and the harmony of all the faculties, a linen *cidaris* is placed upon the high priest’s head.

In the blue band binding the *cidaris* to the head is understood that love and desire for the heavenly kingdom crown this summit of perfection, and that regard unites and joins together all the connections of graces. The golden plate upon which [Col. 1723D] was inscribed that name of God which cannot be defined by humankind indicates that every creature is subject and subordinate to the divine essence. This name is placed above, so that whatever exists anywhere, however great it may be, may know itself to be lower and confess itself less worthy; and, if it has anything bright or distinguished, may refer it to the Name from which it received it and devoutly ascribe it to that excellence.

This name was the Tetragrammaton—that is, of four letters [Col. 1724A]: namely, *ioth, eh, vau, heth*—whose meaning in the Hebrew language is “ineffable,” not because it cannot be spoken, but because, as stated above, it can neither be grasped by human understanding nor defined as it is. The high priest bears this name on his forehead because it is above every name, at which every knee bends (Phil. 2). John’s Apocalypse likewise says that one hundred and forty-four thousand stood with the Lamb on Mount Zion, having his name and the name of his Father written on their foreheads (Rev. 14). For there is the seat of modesty, and it signifies the confidence of our profession, through which we glory not only in the name of God’s glory or omnipotence, but also in Christ’s cross. Thus the four letters themselves signify the four arms of the cross, concerning which Habakkuk says: “Horns were in his hands; there his strength was hidden” (Hab. 3).

Thus adorned, the high priest bore in his sacred garments a figure of all creatures; in their colours he displayed the likeness of the whole world. Fine linen is assigned to the earth, from which it grows; purple to the sea, because it is dyed from its shellfish; blue to the air, whose appearance it has; scarlet, because of its redness, to fire or ether [Col. 1724B]. For it was fitting that the high priest should pray to the Creator not only for Israel but also for the whole world, which consists of these four elements; that he should show all things to need God’s mercy; and that, when he sacrificed, the universal condition might be expiated. He should pray by voice and habit not only for children and parents, but for every creature.

[Col. 1724C] These things which have been said concerning the visible high priest direct us to the invisible ornaments of righteousness, of which it is said: “Let your priests be clothed with righteousness” (Ps. XIII). And elsewhere: “Righteousness shall be the belt of his loins, and faith the girdle of his reins” (Isa. 11).

> **Note [Col. 1724D].** Here he now applies the previously mentioned adornments of the legal high priest to Christ, and brings what has been said thus far to bear on the saying, “It is finished,” in order to show how all things were happily fulfilled in Christ, who lives and reigns gloriously with the Father and the Holy Spirit for all ages. Amen.

Our High Priest, clothed with majesty and strength (Ps. 93), fulfilled all these things in spirit and truth. Entering with a more sacred worship than Aaron’s, he wished us to fulfil in our conduct the reality itself of the virtues signified, rather than merely their vestments. By commanding that the loins be girded with a spiritual belt (Luke 12), he taught us in that girding that no one can attain the light of his understanding and divine knowledge without purity of flesh and mind.

Finally, he himself, clothed in the seamless robe as in a priestly *podere*, taught us to preserve the integrity [Col. 1724D] of charity and the unity of the Spirit in the bond of peace. About to offer sacrifice for the people, he laid the cross upon his shoulders as a shoulder-piece. His wound and blood, in place of the breastpiece, enclosed not only within himself the names of the twelve sons of Israel but also embraced the nature of the whole human race in that work, just as the title fixed above his head contained it, written in Greek, Hebrew, and Latin (John 19).

In comparison with Christ’s blood, the twice-dyed scarlet of the Law is nothing: our dye surpasses it more than seventy times sevenfold. Everything that the Law coloured typologically is pale; compared with truth, all that was woven in figures is withered. There is no comparison between blue and Christ’s flesh, because, when the Word became flesh (John 1), he was wholly heavenly, untouched by any stain of sin; nor had the prince of this world fastened anything of his own upon him. Neither fine linen nor purple can in any respect be fitted to his purity or glory. His power and holiness surpass all things; the holiness of his nature and the sovereignty of his righteousness are of a glory greater than any threads painstakingly worked by twisting fingers or steeped in the blood of shellfish.

A crown was placed upon Christ’s head in place of the *cidaris* [Col. 1725B], and thorns were woven into that wreath in place of the golden ornaments. In place of the golden plate on which God’s name was engraved, there was wood rising above his neck, on which Pilate, in place of Bezalel, wrote the name than which nothing in heaven or on earth is holier, more powerful, or more wonderful: “Jesus of Nazareth, King of the Jews.” This was written by a Gentile, not knowing that he himself was King also of the Gentiles. He wrote it, moreover—certainly without understanding—because the people of the Gentiles were someday to come to and be joined to this title [Col. 1726A].

The blood, more precious than balsam, anointed the hands of our priest—indeed, his head, feet, and side—which the piercings of thorns, nails, and spear drew out and poured forth externally. That liquid was more celebrated than every oil, not signifying but accomplishing our sanctification and cleansing. These things, and many others which the Law had hidden under the veil placed over Moses’ face, were revealed to a few disciples when Christ was transfigured on the mountain, and were made manifest to all when he was fulfilled upon the cross. For the veil of carnal coverings was torn; the lampstand, the bread of the Presence, the altar of incense, the cherubim, the mercy-seat, and the Holy of Holies were revealed.

The rocks too [Col. 1726B] were split and the tombs opened, because this fulfillment opens spiritual understanding even to stony hearts and restores the life-giving Spirit to those dead in sin, so that those who had been desperate and bound by the fetters of evil habit now appear living in the city of our God—that is, the holy Church; those who had long been ashes become teachers, and those who were buried become masters.

[Col. 1725]

## Short Treatise of Ernaldus, Abbot, on the Praises of the Blessed Virgin Mary

*(Bibliotheca veterum Patrum, Lyons, vol. XXII, p. 1281.)*

[Col. 1725C] “Though I speak with the tongues of human beings and of angels,” I shall be unable to say anything worthy or fitting concerning the glory of Mary, holy and perpetual Virgin, mother of Christ. For truly, in giving voice to her praises, no instrument adequate to the task can be found, and the intellect of any subtlety is dull. Since the fullness of due veneration looks to Christ, from whose fullness that which is proclaimed of Mary—“full of grace”—has been rained down from above (Luke 1), it is manifest that the glory of mother and Son is inseparable and their praise common, a mystery whose definition surpasses every understanding.

Even if that ancient counsel concerning the Word incarnate in the holy Virgin—the Word who was God with God (John 1)—has been made known openly to the world, nevertheless human understanding fears to approach the manner of so unprecedented an act, because it is miraculous and does not follow nature’s order [Col. 1725D]. It hesitates in divided feeling: the greatness of the work produces awe, yet it would be ungrateful to pass over the praises of its Author in silence. A marvellous and unheard-of reality: a virgin mother, the Word made flesh, God made man. Who could be silent amid so renowned a miracle? And who, on the other hand, could adequately proclaim these things? We know indeed that this undertaking is above us; but she in whose most sacred womb the Word was made flesh grants speech concerning the Word to those who speak of the Word. Nor is it right that the Church’s joys should be mute, when, filled by the Word, we have in our minds what the mother had in her womb.

She herself conceived the Father’s Only-Begotten first in her mind and then in her flesh. Greeted by the angel, she believed that her purpose of virginity would remain and that the Holy of Holies would be born from her, since she had also received this heavenly assurance: “With God no word shall be impossible” (Luke 1). In this exchange of blessedness, human things are joined to divine, earthly to heavenly. Humanity now has secure access to God, where it has the Son, the mediator of its cause, before the Father, and before the Son, the Mother. Christ, with his side laid bare, shows the Father his side and wounds [Col. 1726D]; Mary shows Christ her breast and her breasts. Rejection can in no way occur where these memorials of mercy and marks of charity, more eloquent than every tongue, meet and plead.

Before the Father, mother and Son divide between themselves the offices of compassion; by marvellous pleadings they sustain the cause of human redemption and establish between themselves the inviolable covenant of our reconciliation. [Col. 1727A] Mary offers herself in spirit to Christ and beseeches him for the salvation of the world; the Son obtains, the Father grants. Great indeed is the pardon granted to the thief; yet it is also astonishing that, when the dispensation of the Incarnation had been fulfilled, Jesus, about to die, honoured his mother with such affection. Victorious over sufferings and, as though forgetful of himself, he turned from the cross toward his mother and spoke to her, showing how great her merit and favour were with him: she alone was the one upon whom he looked at that moment, though his head was wounded, his hands and feet pierced, and he was at the point of death.

For love for his mother moved him; and then the will of Christ and Mary was wholly one, and together they both offered one holocaust to God: she in the blood of her heart, he in the blood of his flesh.

> **Note [Col. 1727D].** He says this because Mary, standing by the Lord as he hung upon the cross, was prepared in spirit and desired to be offered and to die together with her Son. The sword of sorrow passed through her soul, according to Simeon’s prophecy (Luke 1); but that sword did not reach her flesh, because, for the Church’s benefit, it was good that she should remain in the flesh for a time. He expresses this same thought more clearly and fully in the earlier Treatise on the Seven Words of the Lord. On the words, “Woman, behold your son” (John 19), he says: “Christ offered his flesh; Mary offered her soul.” She herself indeed wished to add the blood of her own body to the blood of her soul, and, with hands raised upon the cross, to celebrate with her Son the evening sacrifice, and together with the Lord Jesus, by a bodily death, to bring the mystery of our redemption to completion. We too have said something on this matter in our scholia on that passage [Col. 1728D].

[Col. 1727B] But the beginning of this work must be traced further back. We must briefly gather by what beginning and progress the holy Virgin came to this fullness of blessedness, so that she might have an effect shared with Christ in the salvation of the world and, reigning at his right hand in heaven, might stand in a gilded garment, clothed about with varieties (Ps. XLI).

The angel found the Virgin in Nazareth, alone and apart from the crowds, undoubtedly occupied in holy meditations. I believe that she was considering how, without offence to the Law, she might remain in her purpose of chastity; for she had chosen it, vowed it, and consecrated to the Lord the integrity of her flesh and spirit. The Law stood in opposition. Moses pressed her toward marriage, threatening a curse against the barren and demanding seed and offspring from the children of Israel [Col. 1727C]. No command concerning virgins had been given by the Lord, nor was there yet an Apostle to offer counsel (1 Cor. 7). Yet she had received from God through the Holy Spirit this very private command—not through an angelic response, but through secret inspiration—which had disclosed to her the inclination to virginity and bound her pure desire by the necessity of a vow.

Nevertheless, the eventual outcome had not yet been divinely disclosed to her. By such gradual advances the Holy Spirit was preparing in her a most pure workshop. For this reason I judge that she chose secluded solitude: so that by day and night, amid the constraints of this controversy, she might fortify herself with suitable arguments, by which her desired virginity could stand firm [Col. 1727D] without, nevertheless, treating the authority of the Law as though it were beneath contempt. For, as we have said, the Law required marriage indiscriminately of all for the propagation of God’s people, and did not allow even high priests exemption. A son had necessarily to replace his deceased father immediately; nor could anyone else be admitted to the high-priestly order [Col. 1728A].

Therefore, because a successor was needed, they had to have intercourse with wives, so that sons might be ready immediately when their father died, after consecration had been accomplished, to approach the incense of succession and to offer it daily, morning and evening, within the sanctuary according to the rite of the Law. Thus the necessity of the matter was such that, since no one contaminated or defiled by sexual intercourse with persons of any office from other tribes could have access to the sanctuary, the Law did not exclude the high priest alone from ministry because of this impossibility. Some, however, understand the matter to mean that they did not touch their wives at night because of the morning incense; and that if they had done so, they remained unclean from that hour until evening, at which time, once purified and without violation of the Law, they ministered in their appointed order [Col. 1728B].

Beset by these difficulties, since no course of human counsel occurred to her by which decree and vow might be reconciled together, Mary entrusted her cause to the Lord; devoting herself to meditation and holy prayers, she awaited counsel from heaven, where she prepared for herself a manner of life in spirit and mind, where her unmarried soul clung from its inmost depths. Nor was consolation lacking. The archangel Gabriel descends from above; alone he addresses her who is alone: “Hail,” he says, “Mary, full of grace, the Lord is with thee” (Luke 1).

Rarely in the Old Testament will you find anyone honored by an angelic greeting. Abraham is not greeted when he is exalted with the title of faith, when, without hesitation, he believes that a son will be born to him in his old age by a barren old woman [Col. 1728C] (Gen. 15); nor when he is commanded to sacrifice that same son, concerning whom and to whom the promises had been made, and does not hesitate (Gen. 22). He is not greeted when, after the five kings have been slain and Lot rescued, he returns victorious; and although he is worthy to be blessed by Melchizedek after tithes have been taken, he nevertheless does not deserve a heavenly greeting (Gen. 14). Under the oak of Mamre he speaks with God and follows with devout supplications Him who goes forth to avenge Sodom; and although he was found worthy of a banquet and hospitality, and would have obtained pardon for the rest if ten innocent persons had been found in those five wicked cities, he nevertheless did not attain the familiarity of a greeting (Gen. 18). Moses is not greeted when God speaks to him from the bush (Exod. 3), nor when he is honored on Mount Sinai with the tablets of the covenant [Col. 1728D] (Exod. 19).

With the announcement of Christ, greetings begin; and now, with Jesus, who is the Savior, close at hand, with the salvation of the world not far off, the word of holy hope, the word of our preservation and restoration, is brought down from heaven to earth. This word, formerly altogether rare, now begins to be frequent. The angel greets Mary; and not long afterward Elizabeth meets her, herself greeting and prophesying [Col. 1729A] (Luke 1). After the resurrection angels greet the holy women; Christ himself greets the disciples (John 20). Finally, the Church too, saved through Christ, rejoicing and ever mindful of her joys, maintains this custom of greeting. Everlasting joy has been found in Christ, and in him the remedies of eternal salvation have been set before us in the balms of repentance.

In the Syrian tongue Mary is called “lady”; Christ is Lord, Mary lady. And though she professes herself Christ’s handmaid, she understands that this kind of servitude is loftier than every kingdom. For she has been set over every creature; and whoever bends the knee to Jesus also bows down and prays before his mother. To the proud and to those beneath the earth, the Virgin who gives birth is a marvel; demons are astonished; [Col. 1729B] human beings rejoice; in heaven principalities and powers sing “Glory to God” (Luke 2). Jealousy does not arise among the angels, nor does that bright host waste away with the pallor of envy, nor are they offended at the order of flesh set over them; for although Christ was at one time made a little lower than the angels because he was capable of suffering, now, crowned with glory and honor, he holds all things subjected beneath his feet (Ps. 8; Heb. 2). Nor can the mother be separated from the dominion or power of her Son. One is the flesh of Mary and Christ, one the spirit, one the love; and from the moment it was said to her, “The Lord is with thee,” the promise and gift have remained inseparable. Unity does not admit division and is not cut into parts; and even if one thing has been made out of two, that thing [Col. 1729C] can no longer be divided. I judge the Son’s glory with his mother to be not so much shared as identical.

Behold the tabernacle of God, containing within itself the Holy of Holies, the rod of signs, the tablets of the covenant, the altar of incense, the two cherubim looking toward one another, manna, and the mercy-seat openly displayed without shadow. These things the sanctuary of the Virgin contained within itself, deposited not as figures but in their very reality, [Col. 1730A] presenting to the world law and discipline, the burning of zeal, the fragrance of chastity, the harmony of the covenants, the bread of life as imperishable food, holiness, humility, and the burnt offering of obedience—a safe harbor of repentance for all shipwrecked persons.

[Note: [Col. 1729C] When shortly afterward it is said, “These things the sanctuary of the Virgin contained within itself, deposited not as figures but in their very reality, presenting to the world law and discipline,” etc., observe carefully how each of these corresponds to and expresses each of the foregoing things. He compares Mary to the tabernacle with respect to the chief things contained in the tabernacle, saying that the significations of each are found in Mary.
