In the tabernacle [Col. 1729D] are the Holy of Holies and the rod of signs; and in Mary is Christ, who is the Holy of Holies and the rod of signs—namely, the rod of the Father’s power, as it is said in the Psalm: “The Lord shall send forth the rod of his power out of Zion” (Ps. 109).

Moreover, the tabernacle contains the tablets of the covenant; Mary presents to the world law and discipline. The tabernacle has an altar of incense, upon which incense of sweet fragrance is burned; Mary has the ardor of zeal and the fragrance of chastity. The tabernacle has two cherubim looking toward each other; Mary has within herself the two Testaments and their harmony. For the two cherubim signify the two Testaments, and their mutual gaze denotes the harmony of the two Testaments. The tabernacle moreover contains bodily manna; Mary contains the bread of life, imperishable food. The tabernacle has the altar of burnt offering and the offerings of burnt sacrifices; Mary has the burnt offerings of virtues—namely holiness, humility, obedience, and such things—which she continually sacrifices to God upon the altar of her heart.

[Col. 1730C] Finally, the ancient tabernacle had a mercy-seat, but one overshadowed by the two cherubim covering it and hidden by the intervening veil. Mary also contains within herself a mercy-seat, but one displayed to all without shadow and without covering. For she grants propitiation and remission to all penitents, receives all, and denies to none the propitiation of repentance.]

No injury is done to angelic dignity if the Virgin, exalted like the cedar in Lebanon, overshadows the summit of its excellence. The cedar is a lofty and incorruptible tree. Mary’s virginity likewise, because it is stained by no decay of carnal desire, appears in this respect loftier and higher than angelic virginity: for hers is a virtue, theirs a nature; hers is voluntary, theirs necessary. And to perform in the flesh what does not belong to flesh is a thing of incomparable merit and singular glory.

It is not our purpose to pursue the prophetic oracles written concerning Mary [Col. 1730B]; for our pen does not claim for itself a matter of such exalted height. How indeed could I describe that divine childbirth, celebrated by angels in Bethlehem, where the Virgin, lodging in a narrow hut and having no inn, laid the infant Jesus wrapped in swaddling-clothes in her lap (Luke 2); where virgin, midwife, and mother, she rendered service to herself in that celebration? For there was no pain there, no cry there; no repayment of punishments exacted interest for pleasure there.

[Note: [Col. 1730D] He aptly speaks of “interest on punishments.” For in those women who conceive and give birth according to the common law, a very great and prolonged pain follows in childbirth for the brief and slight pleasure found in intercourse and the marital act. Therefore vengeance is rightly said to exact repayment for pleasure: not simply punishments, but interest on punishments, because the measure of the subsequent punishments far exceeds the quantity of the preceding pleasures.]

For Christ, whose alone it is to overcome sin, was not conceived in sin. Hence, when he himself came forth, demanding no tribute of torment, nature of its own accord opened its doors. Cherubim and seraphim were present, [Col. 1730C] and the heavenly host joyfully sang, “Glory to God in the highest” (ibid.); the harmony of angelic concord resounded even to the ears of the shepherds keeping watch. The kings of Arabia and Sheba, setting out from the East and following a star of unusual light, bent their knees and, with purple flowing upon the ground, adored our Jesus in his poor wrappings and honored him with sacramental gifts (Matt. 2).

[Note: [Col. 1730D] He calls Christ *pannosus*, “clad in wrappings,” not as though wrapped in filthy rags, but in cloths which were cheap and of little value, though clean. For just as, because of poverty and need, his poor and foreign mother could not wrap him in cloths of great price, so, because of the reverence she had for her Son, it is altogether likely that she wrapped him in the cleanest cloths possible. He calls the Magi’s gifts sacramental because they were suited to signify divine mysteries.]

Thirty years had passed from the Savior’s birth [Col. 1731A] to his baptism (Luke 3), and during all that time his mother was not separated from her Son: she always stood inseparably by him, knowing the divine mystery, reverencing him with humble devotion as God and embracing him as Son. The time came for miracles, and immediately Jewish unbelief stirred up accusations; with a heart full of gall it persecuted evangelical teaching, and, snarling against Christ, foamed forth insults, saying that he cast out demons through Beelzebub (Matt. 9), and that he was not from God because he violated the Sabbath (John 9). A concise pen, hastening toward its end, passes over much. How should I pursue every detail?

Not even when Christ was dead did envy rest; nor was the malice of the bloodthirsty people satisfied, while nails clung to his feet and hands, a lance to his side, gall to his mouth, thorns to his head, and his whole body to the cross. [Col. 1731B] Soldiers watched the Crucified One; Jews mocked him; yet they did not force a reply from him. While the apostles fled, his mother had set herself before the face of her Son; with the sword of sorrow piercing her soul, she was wounded in spirit and crucified together with him in affection. What nails and lance did to Christ’s flesh, natural compassion and the anguish of maternal love did to her mind. She stood before the cross (John 19), not less than [perhaps, “I do not wonder, because”] befitted the mother of Christ. Perhaps, moreover, because in her Son’s death she understood the redemption of the world, and already supposed that by her own death she would add something to the public service.

[Note: [Col. 1731D] This must be understood piously: not as though Mary attributed so little to her Son that she thought his death insufficient, without her own, to accomplish the world’s redemption; nor as though she thought so highly of herself as to suppose that she could cooperate in so great a work with her Son as if he were insufficient in himself. Rather, only this is to be understood: Mary desired to expend herself also upon the same work upon which her Son expended himself. Seeing her Son die for the sins of the world, she herself would gladly have died with her Son for the world’s salvation—not because she judged him insufficient, but because she desired to be like and conformed to her Son.]

But Jesus did not need another’s assistance, he who said: “I have become like a man without help, free among the dead” (Ps. [Col. 1731C] 87). He accepted a parent’s affection, but did not seek assistance; indeed, he embraced her, among the rest for whom he offered to the Father the sacrifice of his blood, within that general benefit. Behold, good Jesus, your mother is before you. Why do you not now say: “Who is my mother, and who are my brethren?” (Matt. 12). Now you do not reject or fail to recognize your mother; instead, you entrust her to the disciple’s care and impose a vicarious solicitude upon him whom you especially love, who reclined upon your breast at the Supper (John 13). “Woman,” he says, “behold thy son” (John 19); and to the disciple, “Behold thy mother” (ibid.).

Joseph remained, to whom until that time the principal obligation of service had belonged, and to whom she had been betrothed for this very purpose; yet now, as though he were judged unworthy of this ministry, [Col. 1731D] John is chosen. This interpretation seems required by the context of the discourse.

[Note: [Col. 1731D] We have called attention to this in the scholia on the preceding work, in the treatise on the words, “Behold thy mother,” [Col. 1732D] where the same view is set forth.]

But by a more secret rationale virginity is entrusted to virginity, so that by this testimony [Col. 1732A] Bonosus the heretic and the profane Helvidius may be struck down—men who, with foul mouths, dared babble that another child besides Christ came forth from the virgin womb, and that after the Savior’s birth Joseph touched her with marital license. Christ himself, from the cross, is both judge and defender of his mother’s virginity. “The mouth of them that speak iniquity is stopped” (Ps. 62). John received her into his own home (John 19), Joseph neither objecting nor bringing any accusation; he received her into his own, not as a husband, but in a son’s place: as attendant and guardian, witness and confidant. Both indeed were in Mary’s service, Joseph yielding for a time and for a particular reason, John being placed over it.

Christ, exhausted by insults and torments and with the hour now drawing near, seemed to suffer more in his mother than in himself; [Col. 1732B] and, not concealing that he was pierced by human affection, in these last moments he expressed how great a reverence he wished the world to show his mother. In his final acts he left her such a proof of loving concern, declaring at the very point of death both that his mother’s virginity was inviolate and that an eternal inheritance of singular grace remained hers. Therefore the disciple received what had been entrusted to him, and Christ said, “It is finished” (ibid.). He said this and, with the good end of piety, completed the whole mystery.

The order of the subject required that we write something also concerning the other sayings which Christ uttered upon the cross, but we know ourselves unequal to laying hands upon mysteries of such depth.

[Note: [Col. 1732D] Arnold afterward gave a commentary: *On the Words of the Lord on the Cross*.]

For who could adequately discuss how he cries out upon the cross, as one weak, that he has been forsaken (Matt. 27), and [Col. 1732C] sends the thief beforehand into paradise, as God (Luke 23); how he prays for those who curse him and obtains pardon for his crucifiers (John 19); how at the same moment in which he pleads before the Father the cause of the entire world, he declares how properly and singularly he reveres his mother; how he speaks of thirst and not of his wounded body; how only then does he proclaim that all things are finished (ibid.), and thus, having commended his spirit into the Father’s hands and bowed his head, dies? These things seem to us more worthy of honor through silence than of rash handling by the presumptuous venture of unworthy speech.

[Note: [Col. 1732D] From this passage it appears sufficiently that this encomium of Mary was written by the author before the preceding work on the Seven Words of the Lord. Here he trembles before that work, so that he does not dare to touch what he afterward undertook when he had gathered holy confidence. Hence it is also inferred that the work had long been in the author’s mind and conception before he completed it, as good craftsmen commonly do: whenever they conceive some notable work, they long carry it in their minds and fashion it inwardly long before proceeding to outward execution.]

But, to continue briefly what we began concerning Mary: we have received this handed down to us from the Acts of the Apostles, that after Christ’s passion she lived unanimously with the apostles [Col. 1732D] in prayers and fasts until Pentecost (Acts 1). Thereafter, while John continued in service to her, her calling was not long delayed: [Col. 1733A] she departed to her Son, and, as angels met and bore away that glorious soul, she was assumed into heaven. Whether in the body or apart from the body, the authority of no canonical Scripture has determined; but however it may be, there is no doubt that she is with Christ. Nor is it lawful for a human being to speak of what glory that is, what fullness of blessedness she enjoys; for, as it is written, “That peace surpasses all understanding [sense]” (Phil. 4), and “eye has not seen, nor ear heard, nor has it entered into the heart of man” (1 Cor. 2; Isa. 64).

This is certain: that she is there where both she and her Son stand before the face of God, asking mercy for us, not [Col. 1734A] judgment (Heb. 9), and obtaining remission of sins for every penitent. Indeed, all judgment has been given by the Father to the Son (John 5), and it belongs to him to moderate and administer the decree of strict severity, for he does not readily condemn those whose advocate he is. And since he is both advocate and judge, he by no means judges cruelly, for he always intercedes mercifully. The reward of his death is the salvation of human beings. Nor does he readily allow that to perish for which so great a price of blood was paid; and so great was his concern for human reconciliation that he did not regard his own losses while winning back the one gone astray.

[Col. 1733]

# MEDITATIONS OF ABBOT ERNALD

[*Works of St. Cyprian*, edited by John Fell, Bishop of Oxford; Oxford and Paris, 1700, folio.]

[Col. 1733B] [Note: [Col. 1733C] “Fear not, daughter.” We judged that this work, found in an old Laudian manuscript which appears to be contemporary with the author himself, should be added to his other writings, although no mention of a treatise of this kind occurs in the published catalogues.]

“Fear not, daughter of Zion: behold, thy King comes to thee, gentle, and seated upon a colt, the foal of a beast under the yoke.” Come, Lord Jesus; come, desire of all nations, for my soul has slept from weariness at your delay, and my eyes have grown faint from lack of your light. Arise, beloved sun, that a human being may go forth to his work and to his labor until evening, and may work not for food that perishes, but for that which endures unto eternity.

Fear not, daughter of Zion: fear belongs to the small-minded. Therefore, daughter, because you still fear, you are not yet Jerusalem but daughter of Zion—that is, “watchtower”; therefore learn to keep watch. Fear not, because fear troubles the eye; a cheerful pupil watches clearly. Faith is the pupil of your eye. Just as the pupil of the eye is exceedingly delicate and, unless it is diligently and carefully guarded by [Col. 1733C] the eyelids, is clouded by the slightest touch of the finest dust, so the keenness of faith, unless it always has watchful guardianship, is disturbed by nothing more swiftly. But fear not, daughter of Zion: behold, your King comes to you; the sun rises for you, both to guard and enlighten you and to bring you where there is no dust. He comes to you gentle; such as he is, such he wishes you to be.

Be gentle in bearing his yoke, so that he too may sit upon you, his she-ass, and upon the colt, the offspring of the beast under the yoke. And what is this she-ass? That which is called flesh, and woman and *virago*, because she was taken from man. And who is her colt? The male human being. And how is he her colt? [Col. 1734B] Because “not that which is spiritual comes first, but that which is natural; afterward that which is spiritual.” First the flesh is tamed, that it may be fit beneath the yoke; then the colt is born and strengthened, so that it may be able to bear its rider. And why is he the offspring of a beast under the yoke? Because woman is under man, and man is the head of woman; yet he is the offspring of the beast under the yoke because man comes through woman, but she will give birth in pain. Let the gentle King sit upon both, making peace, lest they oppose one another. Let him sit, I say, so that spirit may rule flesh, and flesh obey spirit; and so that spirit and flesh may obey their Creator.

He comes gentle, he comes to you; and do you not go to meet him? Go forth from the land of your flesh, from the kindred of your mind, and from your father’s house: from the remembrance of [Col. 1734C] your father. Your father is an Amorite and your mother a Hittite; forget this father, and then the King will desire your beauty. It is great beauty if you hear and see and incline your ear. You hear through obedience, see through understanding, and incline your ear through humility: this is beauty, this is the whole glory within, in golden fringes; this beauty of yours the gentle King will desire.

Go forth from the city, because, he says, “I have seen iniquity and contradiction in the city.” Go forth with the Hebrew children, who pass simply onward to meet the Lord. Spread branches of olive in the way, that you may furnish works of mercy for his feet [Col. 1735A] to tread. Take palm fronds, that you may triumph over the princes of darkness. Let nothing remain in you which does not come forth to meet Jesus, because not one hoof is to be left in Egypt for Pharaoh. Let hand and heart sing *hosanna in the highest* in harmony with the tongue.

You have surely seen, O Lord God, the affliction of your people, who are in Egypt; and you have inclined your heavens and descended to deliver us. To me too, Lord, a little rest has been granted from the harshest works of darkness, by which the importunate taskmaster Pharaoh grievously afflicted my mind; and the preparation for your Sabbath has already gladdened my soul. Yet I have not yet reached the mirror, in which I may more fully discern the pustules and blemishes that stain [Col. 1735B] my face and are very displeasing in your eyes; for even if I wash myself with nitre and multiply for myself the herb Borith, I am stained by my iniquity.

And then, Lord, the days of your passion ought to press upon us more urgently than Pharaoh’s overseers; since in your works are righteousness, peace, and joy in the Holy Spirit. But we sleep while you, Lord, pray for us, because our eyes are heavy in our own time. Raise us up, that we may watch and pray, lest we enter into temptation; for tribulation is very near to us. How quickly the eye is closed lest it see you! Our foot slips in this great and spacious sea, where there are creeping things without number, which mock the attentive soul with the phantasms of its dreams and [Col. 1735C] draw it into the heart of the sea, from which return to higher things is not easy—unless you send forth your hand from on high and deliver us from many waters.

Raise us up, Lord, that we may watch and pray with you even one hour. But who is there who watches with you for one hour? For you have been torn away from us as far as a stone’s throw, and you agonize at greater length, so that a drop of your blood runs down to the earth. Far, far have you been torn away from us, because the stone was cut from the mountain without hands, and the stone was hurled and struck Goliath upon the forehead and the statue upon the feet. This is your being cast far from us, because you have even entered as forerunner for us into the inner place behind the veil, where you always intercede with the Father. But would that the drop of blood sweating from [Col. 1735D] your agony might run down even to our earth; that the earth might open its mouth and drink it, and cry out to you and with you to the Father, better than Abel’s blood.

But who is there, Lord, who watches with you for one hour? There was silence only for about half an hour. How much less shall we watch with you for one hour! How often and how often, Lord, do you come to us and find us sleeping, yet kindly raise us, and go away again a second and a third time, saying the same words. But as soon as you have departed, sleep again takes hold of us, and we cannot watch except while you are with us and raise us. You come in the second and third watch, but blessed is that servant whom you then find watching. No mention is now made of the first and fourth watches, because neither earliest [Col. 1736A] age receives the capacity for watching nor final age the hope of prolonged prayer.

And what is this, Lord, that when you return the third time you make provision for sleep: “Sleep now and rest”? Do you permit one kind of sleep in which there is rest, and prohibit another in which the eyes are heavy? It is so. Whoever watches in you sleeps sweetly and is silent, and rests in his sleep. But whoever sleeps apart from you, like one drunken at night, is grievously tossed about without knowing why.

“My soul,” he says, “is sorrowful unto death.” For who knows whether he will be to the right or to the left? Who knows how he will answer one who rebukes him, when the Judge shall speak like a woman in labor? Therefore let my sorrowful soul become like the pelican of the wilderness, which hates the city and their gatherings of bloodshed, and grows pale with the leanness of solitude; like the night-owl [Col. 1736B] that seeks food for itself all night among the ruins of Scripture; and let it fly forth into the sparrow upon the housetop, watching and guarding against the thief’s coming.

Or do you not see Judas: how he does not sleep, how watchful are the eyes of avarice, how he goes around the whole earth? His hand does not cease, his foot does not cease; and he stores up wrath for himself on the day of wrath. Yet Simon sleeps, James and John sleep. Why? Because they do not heed what will shortly happen. The greatness of danger drives sleep away. Did Peter sleep in the courtyard? Did those who fled after leaving him sleep? Did the young man sleep when they seized him, and he, leaving the linen cloth, fled naked? And it was cold then, for Peter stood and warmed himself. The greatness of danger makes one forget sleep, cold, and [Col. 1736C] hunger.

Awake, wretched soul, if not through love, at least through fear. Consider at least the torment you are already about to suffer in death. Certainly no cross is harsher than death; death itself, I say, is the most grievous cross prepared for you, toward which you hasten daily and do not attend. See how death crucifies you: the body stiffens, the legs are stretched out, the hands and arms fall limp, the breast gasps, the neck weakens, the lips foam, the eyes grow fixed, the face sweats, the countenance wastes away and becomes horrible, and grows pale like a potsherd. Thus the cross awaits you. I do not know whether one dies more gently in a soft bed or upon a rigid cross, except that the cross cuts short the pain more swiftly. The things which we see and feel are light compared with what the mind already tastes beforehand, [Col. 1736D] for sensation quickly departs from the body; death always accompanies its soul.

“When the living creatures went, the wheels went beside them.” If our life made progress, the wheel of Holy Scripture would go beside us. But because we go on foot through marshes and rocks and stumble, the wheels can scarcely follow us. The Lord’s passion is celebrated, and we devote ourselves to pleasure. From the cross he cries out to us: “O all you who pass by the way, attend and see whether there is sorrow like my sorrow!” And there is no one to hear, no one to console, no one to answer. “I thirst,” he says. Lord, what thirst? Does thirst then torment you more than the cross? You are silent about the cross and cry out concerning thirst? “I thirst”—for what? For your faith, your salvation, your joy; the concern for [Col. 1737A] your souls holds me more than the torment of my body.

“O all you who pass by the way, attend and see whether there is sorrow like my sorrow.” Attend to my sorrow, so that in my sorrow you may see your own sorrow; my sorrow is the image of your sorrow. What do you attend to in my body? Attend and see whether there is not a similar sorrow in your heart. You pass from yourselves to me; pass back from me into yourselves, and see whether there is not a sorrow in you like my sorrow. “Do not weep over me, but weep over yourselves, daughters of Jerusalem.” That sorrow of yours, which you pass by and do not heed, deserves weeping more than my sorrow; for I was struck because of your crime. These things you cry out to us from the cross, O gracious Jesus—even if not in words, yet in the thing itself.

What shall I answer you? What shall I say? What shall I render in return? You have therefore made your body for me a mirror of my soul. I did not know the insults and terrors and Satan’s unceasing buffeting of me, unless I saw your art of healing curing like by like and perceived in the balance, on this side your calamity, on that my iniquity. You gave your body to those striking you and your cheeks to those plucking them; you did not turn your face from those spitting upon you, so that your blows might remove my blows, your scourges might expiate scourges, and the reproaches of those reproaching you which fell upon you might take away from me everlasting reproach.

These are the purest linen cloths of your flesh, [Col. 1737C] with which you bound up my wounds, O merciful Samaritan, so that you might place upon your beast the man stripped by robbers and beaten with scourges and bring him to the inn; since you truly bore our infirmities and carried our sorrows, by whose wound we have been healed.

Therefore Christ is struck with fists in the high priest’s house with his face veiled, because the Christian is struck with fists in the house of conscience, with his mind blinded. For what Christ suffers openly, I suffer secretly; and what he suffers outside from Caiaphas’s servants, I suffer within from Satan’s wickednesses. For sinners have built upon my back, veiled my face, fixed my face upon the ground, and made my back their anvil. Sinners have built upon my back, [Col. 1737D] but I am still confined within the house, where the girl both dies and is raised; for Peter too denied there. I am no man: I attend to man, not God; I fear man, not God, whose truth I deny. Peter, do you not seem in these words to have had a veiled face? Hence he was struck with fists a third time, because he denied a third time. And Paul asked the Lord three times to remove from him the angel of Satan who buffeted him.

Thus both apostles were buffeted; both suffered shipwreck three times, he within, the other without. Satan indeed would have wished, had it been allowed him, to sift Peter by buffeting him like wheat until he had shaken from him all the marrow of faith. “But I,” he says, “Peter, have prayed for thee, that thy faith might not fail.” Therefore Christ looked upon [Col. 1738A] him, and, going outside, he wept bitterly.

Peter had his face veiled until Christ looked upon him. But did Christ not look upon him even earlier when he denied him? Indeed he did. But Peter did not look upon Christ looking at him, because he had a veiled face. Thus another Evangelist rightly says: “And Peter remembered.” Peter’s remembrance was Christ’s look. Therefore, when you remember your sin with weeping, you are seen by Christ; indeed, the veil having been removed, you see Christ. And he denied him because he wished to remain inside; yet when he denied him, he went outside. Outside from where? From the house of Christ, from the house of the faithful? But when he went outside from Caiaphas’s house, he was brought into Christ’s house.

[Col. 1738B] How many today say, “We are of Christ’s house; we are of the Church’s house,” and yet are of Caiaphas’s house—that is, hypocrisy! What Peter did by denying, they do by affirming. But unless they go outside by confession and weep bitterly, they do not enter Christ’s Church. The bitterness of tears washes the veil from the eyes. Therefore Christ was struck with fists in Caiaphas’s house because Peter was struck with fists in Caiaphas’s house; and what Peter suffered within from Satan, Christ endured outside from Satan’s servants. Attend then and see whether your sorrow is like my sorrow. Which endured the heavier reproaches: Christ outwardly in his body, or Peter inwardly in his heart?

[Col. 1738C] But now let us go to Pilate. When morning came, he was brought bound to Pilate. So long as guilt lies hidden, it is night; but when it begins to become known, morning comes. Then he is bound by the chief priests and handed over to Pilate—that is, to the prince of darkness. As the Apostle also says, such a person is to be handed over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh. The young man is brought from the house to the gate of the city, where Pilate sits on the judgment seat; for judgment was customarily held at the gate. Pilate then scourged the prisoner. Often, while guilt is uncovered, the sinner is unrestrained through shamelessness. Crimes increase, blows are multiplied; for many sins, many scourges.

With these scourges Pharaoh beat the children of Israel. After this he is handed over to the soldiers for mockery: this is the very army [Col. 1738D] of spiritual wickedness. See the origin of misery in the chief priests: he is handed over to the princes of darkness, who, having made him their slave by their scourges, expose him to their soldiers for deeper mockery, and afterward finally for crucifixion. After the cross no punishment remains, because sin ends with death; but, with death now near, the sinner is tossed about in a greater mockery by demons.

For they strip him of the garment of all Christian beauty and, as though in place of royal splendor, put around him a scarlet cloak—that is, a garment mingled with blood—when, because of the cruel bloodiness of his life, he is honored and surrounded by many. Hence, too, they plait a crown of thorns and place it upon his head, when, heaping up for him thorny riches from the plunder of the poor, they raise his head [Col. 1739A] to kingship. For money claims for itself what Wisdom says: “By me kings reign, and makers of laws discern what is just.” Where money is, there is law; there is a multitude of dependents. Hence they place a reed in his right hand; for the power and kingdom of the wicked is a reed shaken by the wind. But Christ’s kingdom is an iron rod. And the reed is rightly placed in his right hand, because their right hand is a right hand of iniquity. What follows is now clearer than light: because, bending the knee, they mock such a man rather than serve him.

“Hail, King of the Jews,” spitting upon him with superfluous praises. For the sinner is praised in the desires of his soul, and the wicked person is blessed. They took the reed and struck his head. For from such rulers their soldiers receive the power to harm and devour the poor; yet all of this redounds upon the head [Col. 1739B] whose authority they invoke for protection. This is the third death, when he sits stinking in the seat of pestilence. By these deaths the unhappy soul is fastened before the final cross of death; and, what is more pitiable, it delights in such reproaches as though they were great honors. Such a soul is daily led to the cross, itself carrying the instrument of its own condemnation.

But why, after the mockery, is he stripped of the cloak and clothed again in his own garments? Is it not because proud Adam often, when through the pain of the flesh he enters the borders of death, lays aside his arrogance and returns to the consideration of his own corruption? There, indeed, either by divine mercy he finds the fruit of repentance, or [Col. 1739C] through dreadful judgment he is crushed with a double crushing. Thus Herod, when, resplendent in royal apparel, he was acclaimed by the people beyond what was fitting, was immediately struck by an angel; stripped of his cloak, he put on his own garment again, and, consumed by worms, breathed his last.

Was he not rightly mocked? “Hail, King of the Jews.” Why are you proud, earth and ashes? Why do you glory in shining clothing? “The moth shall be spread beneath you, and the worm shall be your covering”: this is your garment. Those mocked you who clothed you in a scarlet cloak. Thus Antiochus, and Herod the enemy of the Lord’s nativity, having laid aside their borrowed garments, expired amid their own worms. Return at last to your heart; return, old Adam. [Col. 1739D] See where and how the new Adam sought and found you: in his own body he displayed to you the disgraces of your soul. It was not enough that, through blows and scourges and new kinds of mockery, crying out after you as you fled and pitying you, he ran after you; he pursued you even to the final punishment of the cross, found you as you were already drawing your last breath, and seized you.

For who was that thief except Adam? From the time when he first committed the murder of himself in Paradise, he fled from Christ as a guilty man and hid himself, until, at the moment of the cross, finally exhausted and apprehended, he could flee and hide no longer. There, at last apprehended by you, good Jesus, he was converted; he confessed his fault; he willingly embraced his punishment. For you admonished him not to shrink from suffering, [Col. 1740A] because he saw that you also suffered with him. Thus he alone, the one man from the whole world, clung to you; and therefore he alone from this whole world entered Paradise with you, where he has been joined so firmly—not now as guardian of Paradise, but as a citizen and member of God’s household—that he can fall from it no more. O most blessed thief—indeed, no thief, but martyr and confessor! For he turned necessity into willingness, punishment into glory, and the cross into triumph. In you, most blessed confessor and martyr, Christ gathered the remnant of faith from the barrenness of the entire world. While the disciples fled and Peter denied him, you rejoiced to become the companion and fellow-traveller of his Passion. You were Peter on the cross, while Peter in the house of Caiaphas was a thief. For Peter was a thief so long as, [Col. 1740B] hiding within, he denied Christ without; and therefore you went before Peter into Paradise. For he who embraced you on the cross, your leader and ruler, on the very day on which he himself entered, brought you with him as a faithful and glorious soldier.

“I am needy and poor, O Lord, and lame from my mother’s womb”; and behold, I sit at the gate of your temple called Beautiful, neither able nor willing to enter. Rather, in want of your good things, I beg outside for sustenance for my flesh—for airy and false images of men—where I may heap up for myself a talent of iniquity, burdensome bundles. And behold, it is the ninth hour of prayer. Your apostles Peter and John go up to pray in your holy temple. But I cling to earth and mire, savoring earthly and [Col. 1740C] vain things; while others enter, I remain outside, not seeking with them the things that are your Father’s, but those things which my first parents, who placed me out here, wickedly desired each day. And behold, now it is the ninth hour of prayer: the day has declined; night is near. When I rise early in the morning, of those things for which I now beg I shall find nothing in my hands. I say, it is the ninth hour of prayer; for at this hour, hanging on the cross, you prayed; you prayed with bowed head, cried with a loud voice, and expired. You prayed with bowed head in the spirit of humility, crying with a great voice—with the highest and most hidden affection of paternal and our own love. In that, Lord, strong cry you expired, and you carried with you the same [Col. 1740D] disposition of compassion which you had for us. And I believe, Lord, that you still preserve it with you, for your love does not know how to grow cold. Now it was the ninth hour of prayer. Why was this the ninth hour of prayer? Because about the ninth hour darkness came to be. The horror of darkness, which had covered the whole earth, had to be driven away; the gloom of the peoples had to be dispelled, which had begun to abound from the time when you began to walk in the evening breeze. From then on you did not cease crying, “Where are you, Adam?”—following behind the fleeing and hiding man, insofar as it lay in him to flee and hide. And he was sent forth from the Paradise of delight and came at last to the fitting torment for his iniquity. “And we,” he says, “receive the due reward of our deeds; but what has this man done?”

Adam, how late you broke forth into these words! Only now [Col. 1741A] he found you. “Amen, I say to you: today you shall be with me in Paradise.” Therefore it is the ninth hour of prayer: at the ninth he prayed, for at the tenth he entered Paradise. Moreover, the lame man did not enter the temple, because he had not yet come as far as the tenth generation; but Peter said to him, “In the name of Jesus Christ, arise and walk.” Truly you are the mountains to which I lifted up my soul, from whence help shall come to me. But my help is from the Lord, because you say, “In the name of Jesus Christ, arise and walk.” At Christ’s word you let down the net; at Christ’s word you raise the lame man; at Christ’s word his ankles and soles are made firm. What are his ankles? Faith and fear. And what are his soles? Hope and love.

Therefore Peter and John rightly went up together, [Col. 1741B] one bearing the emblem of faith, the other that of love. They went up to your temple, Lord, to pray together with you, so that they too might enter with you into the Paradise of your sanctuary, because at your death the veil that was over Moses’ face was rent. But do not fear to enter alone, for neither, Lord, did you enter Paradise alone. You bring in the thief; they bring in the lame man. But now there is neither a thief in Paradise nor a lame man in the temple. For how is he lame who stands and walks, leaps, and praises God? Or how is he a thief, if he is with Christ in Paradise? For “the evil one shall not dwell beside you.” He had been a thief when he hid himself before confession; but after prayer, he was righteous. For what did he pray? “Remember me, Lord, [Col. 1741C] when you come into your kingdom.” O great faith! O great hope! O great love! He prays for things future, not present; he does not wish to be taken down from the cross, but to be placed in Christ’s kingdom. What else is this than to say, “I desire to depart and to be with Christ”? Paul did not know what he could have desired more than this thief did. “Remember me,” O contrite and humbled heart! What could he have prayed that was less or more humble than that he should at least be remembered? “Remember me”: which me? Me, I say, so unworthy, so sinful. “I acknowledge my iniquity, and my sin is ever before me. I am ashamed to lift my eyes to you; against you alone have I sinned.” You alone can cleanse me from my sin. I did evil before you when I wished to hide myself from you. I am the thief of my own soul; the murder I committed I wished [Col. 1741D] to conceal; but I did evil before you. Remember me; have mercy on me. I have deservedly come into this misery, for I abandoned your blessedness. I was rich, and behold how wretched I have become. I could eat and delight in every tree of Paradise; and behold, I am tormented and die upon this tree. Remember me: I had forgotten you; but you, when you are angry, will remember mercy. “Have mercy on me, O God, according to your great mercy.” I see in you a great mercy, and one that is yours—that is, mercy fitting to you—which caused you to stoop down to misery like mine for my sake. And I, I say, receive the due reward of my deeds; but what have you done? I see you like me in punishment, whom I see so unlike me in action.

You could not follow me farther. Whence did you come? From [Col. 1742A] the highest heaven you came forth; from the Virgin’s womb you proceeded, beautiful in form; and you hang with me on the tree? Who brought you here? Mercy alone. According to this your great mercy, have mercy on me, O God. You are God, not merely man; you are God; I am man, your creature, I whom you made in your image and likeness. Have mercy, O God, on your image. But by what shall I know that you have mercy? By this: I see my image in you, like mine, suffering the same misery with me. What then remains but that I should hope? Who could ever despair in the face of such mercy? Therefore, remember me when you come into your kingdom. You go to your kingdom; you have accomplished your business. For this you came, that you might bring me back with you. I desire to go with you, and for this I do not tremble at, nor am ashamed of, the bitterest [Col. 1742B] death.

For how should I tremble, when I see you with me? “Though I walk in the midst of the shadow of death, I shall fear no evil, because you are with me.” Or how should I be ashamed, when I see myself carrying you, Lord of heaven? “Whoever is ashamed of me and of my words, of him you shall be ashamed when you come in your majesty, and that of the Father, and of the holy angels.” “Whoever does not bear his cross and follow me is not worthy of me.” This is your saying: whoever is ashamed of this saying, of him you shall be ashamed. For whoever is ashamed of your cross is ashamed of your glory: “far be it from me to glory except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ.” The cross is your glory; the cross is your sovereignty. [Col. 1742C] “Behold, your sovereignty is upon your shoulder.” You carry your cross; you carry that which carries you. Whoever carries your cross carries your glory; whoever carries your glory carries you. Yet you carry upon your shoulder the one who carries you, because your sovereignty is upon your shoulder. Therefore those who carry you are your sovereignty, for in them you reign, O greatest emperor. But how and whither do you carry your sovereignty upon your shoulder? Your shoulder is high; your shoulder is strong; your shoulder reaches to the Father’s session, above every principality and power and might. There you lead back the hundredth sheep; there you lead back Joseph’s sheep. Joseph’s sheep is led to the Father’s right hand. Go now in safety, Joseph’s sheep: Christ carries you on his shoulder. [Col. 1742D] His shoulder is strong—do not fear; it is high—do not look down to the depths, because “no one who puts his hand to the plough and looks back is fit for the kingdom of God.”

“A heavy yoke is upon the children of Adam from the day of their birth until the day of their return to the mother of all.” So long as I am a son of old Adam, I bear a heavy yoke; if I were a son of the new Adam, I should bear a light yoke. What is the heavy burden? A talent of lead. And what is the light burden? Christ’s cross. The former, as it is written, is submerged in mighty waters; the latter swims upon the waters. A marvelous thing: nothing is more fearful to a human being than to suffer the cross. But why do people fear the cross? Because they are thieves. If they were not thieves, they would not fear the cross; therefore whoever [Col. 1743A] fears it is a thief. “How,” you ask, “is he a thief?” Hear Christ: “You have made it”—that is, my house—“a den of thieves.” “The temple of God is holy, which temple you are.” Therefore human beings make themselves a den of thieves: they slaughter human beings and drag them into their den. For what murder is greater than for a human being to kill himself? Or what murder is graver: to kill the body or the spirit?

O how often a human being kills himself! How many murders he commits within himself! Whenever he deliberately and purposefully commits sin, what else does he do but slaughter himself? For “all who take the sword shall perish by the sword.” Sin is the sword of the soul; sin is the death of the soul. Whoever takes this sword in the hand of his own deliberate choice—that is, counts it acceptable and pleasing—first lays his hand upon himself and first kills himself. “Let their sword enter into their own hearts.” [Col. 1743B] Nor is it enough to kill once and rest; rather, thousands upon thousands of times they cruelly turn their hands against themselves, and “their feet are swift to shed their own blood.”

“Men of blood and deceit”: how deceitful? Because they heap the corpses of the dead in their den and cover them with a mound of earth, lest either they themselves see them or others see them. They do not wish to see them, lest the stench of the dead pour horror or foulness into their faces; they do not wish to be seen, lest perhaps, detected as thieves and murderers, they be dragged away to dreadful punishments. [Col. 1743C] But what is so dreadful among all punishments as the cross? Therefore thieves fear the cross, because the cross is the avenger of crimes, the cross the punishment of the wicked. With an equal balance the cross judges and rewards—on one side the innocent, on the other the guilty. Therefore the cross is terrifying to the wicked, but to the godly it is more gracious than all the trees of Paradise. Did Christ fear the cross? Did Peter? Did Andrew? Indeed, he desired it. “He rejoiced as a giant to run his course”; and, “With desire I have desired to eat this Passover with you before I suffer.” He ate this Passover with his disciples; he ate the Passover and endured the Passion when he passed from this world to the Father. “I have food to eat which you do not know; my food is to do the will [Col. 1743D] of my Father.” The Father’s will is that I drink his cup.

Therefore on the cross he ate and drank, became intoxicated, and slept. Accursed Ham laughed at his shame; but his reverent sons covered with a garment the mystery of that deepest sleep. For the Lord cast sleep upon Adam and took one of his ribs, forming it into a woman and bringing her to Adam. It is plain that Christ slept and was overcome by sleep, and that from his side the Church is daily built, fed, and nourished; and she is brought from the ends of the earth, that the queen may stand at his right hand in golden raiment, adorned with variety. Therefore on the cross he ate the Passover, because he ascended the palm tree and gathered its fruit. “When I am lifted up from the earth,” he says, “I shall draw all things to myself.” What things? Heaven and earth [Col. 1744A] and the underworld. He drew the Father to himself, because his cry entered into his ears; the earth shook, the rocks were rent, and the tombs opened, because they heard the voice of the Son of God. Thus the mediator of God and humankind, standing between heaven and earth, ate the Passover and gathered on every side the fruit of the tree, drawing it into his body; for all things flowed together to the tree of life which was in the midst of Paradise, since the flaming sword that had blocked the way was quenched. Who then should any longer fear the cross? Truly, whoever fears the cross bears witness against himself that he is still a thief. For every fruit of life hangs upon the cross: it is itself the tree of life in the midst of Paradise; it is height and breadth, sublimity and depth; it gathers and rewards the good, scatters and condemns the evil; [Col. 1744B] it is consolation for the sorrowful, refreshment for the hungry, and glorying for the perfect.

I can range, Lord, through heaven and earth, sea and dry land, and nowhere find you except on the cross alone: there you sleep, there you feed, there you lie down at noon. For your cross is faith, whose breadth is love; whose length is long-suffering; whose height is hope; whose depth is fear. Whoever finds you finds you upon this cross. Upon this cross the soul is suspended from the earth and plucks sweet fruits from the tree of life. Cleaving to its Lord on this cross, it sings sweetly: “You are my protector, my glory, and the lifter of my head.” Therefore no one seeks you, no one finds you, except as one crucified. O glorious Cross, take root in me, that I may ascend into you.

[Col. 1744C] But where did they crucify him? At the place of Calvary. Blessed indeed is the place where the cross is fixed; blessed baldness clothed with such foliage. Elisha went up to this baldness; see whether our Elisha was not bald: “The Son of Man has nowhere to lay his head.” See how bald he is, who has nowhere to lay his head. He is bald because his kingdom is not of this world; our Elisha is bald because all his disciples, leaving him, fled. For what are his disciples but the hairs of his head, all of which are numbered? Therefore the banner of the cross is raised at the place of Calvary. “Because the daughters of Zion walked with outstretched necks and wanton glances, the Lord shall make bald the crown of the daughters of Zion.” Let the Lord make bald the crown [Col. 1744D] of the hair that ranges abroad in its sins; let him make bald the daughters of Zion and make there a place of Calvary, so that there Christ’s glorious cross may be fixed where pride had set up its seat for itself. “Make your baldness broad as the eagle.” The bald eagle enjoys the clear sun; so too, the more widely the baldness of the soul extends, the more purely true light pours itself into it. But those who grow their hair acquire for themselves a condemnation of blindness and heaviness.

Therefore Absalom lost the blessed vision of this light, because his abundance of hair weighed him down. He was shorn only once a year, and his hair weighed two hundred shekels by the public standard; thus, suspended by that same hair from a tree, he perished.

[Col. 1745A] Absalom is “his father’s peace”; he is Judas, and everyone who in peace is the bitterest bitterness to Christ. “Hail, Rabbi.” By voice and kiss they offered peace to their father; with their mouth they blessed, but in their heart they cursed. “The man of my peace, in whom I trusted, who ate my bread, magnified his treachery against me.” He is one and they are many: behold Absalom; behold Judas; behold the body of Satan. But how did he grow his hair? “He was a thief, and he had the money-box.” For this abundance of hair weighed him down, and he was shorn once a year, when once he returned the thirty pieces of silver and threw them into the temple; they weighed two hundred shekels—a number belonging to the unclean—and this by the public standard, not the sanctuary standard. For, moved by repentance, he weighed his sin very heavily.

“I have sinned,” he said, “by betraying innocent blood.” Every [Col. 1745B] word is full of weight; but it is the public standard, not the sanctuary standard, because he was more ashamed of disgrace than of conscience; he weighed his own wickedness more heavily than God’s mercy. Hear the sanctuary standard: “I have sinned; I have done evil before you; blot out my iniquity. On the one hand I acknowledge my iniquity; on the other I attend to your great mercy: have mercy on me, O God.” Hear also the public standard: “My iniquity,” Cain says, “is greater than I deserve to be forgiven.” Therefore he returned the thirty pieces of silver and threw them into the temple. See how greatly he reckoned them to weigh. He did not throw them into the dung-heap, but into the temple: doubtless he had always devoted his temple to gods such as these. For “avarice is the service [Col. 1745C] of idols,” and avarice blinds the eyes of the wise. See the unhappy man, how he was blinded. He preferred to destroy himself rather than let the coins perish: he consigned the coins to the temple, himself to the noose. He loved his heirs, who would gather those same coins from there, and who even now keep them in their corban. He threw them into the temple and, departing, hanged himself by a noose. Indeed, he had long since departed from Christ and hanged himself by the noose of avarice; but what he had done in secret became publicly known to all. The character of the outward punishment revealed the manner of the penalty, because by the things through which a person sins, by those things he is also punished.

“Hanging, he burst asunder in the middle.” His belly was full, and his belly burst; he burst in the middle, where Satan had his seat. Therefore the vessel of dishonour burst, because it was not [Col. 1745D] among the potter’s vessels tested in the furnace. Accordingly, in the potter’s field he had no share in the burial of strangers; but, like a potsherd cracking in emptiness, he burst apart, and all his entrails were scattered. Money is the entrails of the avaricious man: these are scattered and lost; but the entrails of mercy are gathered together. Judas still hangs, like Absalom, by the hair of his head, and the mule upon which he rode passes on. “Do not become like horse and mule,” for the world passes away, and its desire. Absalom’s hair, by which he hangs, is the root of all evils: desire or avarice. Where this takes root, an abundance of every evil will grow as hair. The mule, moreover, is mixed from horse and ass: double is the mind which outwardly displays what it does not preserve within. Such was Judas; such was Absalom. Outwardly piety, [Col. 1746A] inwardly malice: double is their iniquity. The horse openly swells with pride; the ass walks simply; the wicked and deceitful mule casts down the unwary.

Open for us, Lord, open for us the door of your side, which is in your ark, so that you may bring us in with the clean animals, seven and seven. For you are the true Noah, whom God your Father alone found righteous before himself. “This is my beloved Son, in whom I am well pleased.” You know your sheep, and they know you, because they are clean animals, seven and seven: having obtained Sabbath from Sabbath through sevenfold grace and works of light, they are now worthy to be enrolled in the eighth, the number that alone was saved in the ark. Bring us in to yourself through the door of your side, which is the faith of the Church; and shut [Col. 1746B] the door from outside until iniquity passes over. When dawn has ceased, open again for us—not now the door of faith, but the door of hope, opposite the door shown to Ezekiel the prophet in the structure of the mountain. Yet meanwhile you have also a window in the ark, through which the Beloved puts in his hand and awakens his dove: “Arise, my beloved, my beautiful one, my dove, and come.” And when she flies out after you to seize you, you flee and ascend above the cherubim and fly upon the wings of the winds, so that the foot of your dove finds nowhere firm upon you where it may rest, unless she returns again to your ark and you take her in your hand and restore her to her little dwelling. For it is safer meanwhile to wait and rest in the harbour of faith than, in pursuing you too eagerly and vainly, to fall and be submerged in the impassable waters of the flood.

[Col. 1746C] For the waters flowing from the right side of the temple, when measured a thousand paces, reach to the ankles; after another thousand paces, to the knees; again, after another thousand paces, they rise to the loins; but after another thousand paces the river grows and swells so greatly that it cannot be forded, and one must rather return to the firm ground of the bank. Therefore the unclean animals went out and did not return; but the dove, when she found no place where her foot could rest, returned to the ark. But the raven, once sent out, does not know how to return, because, pursuing with no single eye, it is intercepted by the flood of vanity. And rightly so: [Col. 1746D] what has the dove to do with the raven? The white with the black? Judas with John? Christ with Belial? Yet Christ sits in the middle between Judas and John; he hangs in the middle between the chosen and rejected thief; and Noah is between the raven and dove. But the raven, once sent out, did not return, because Judas went out and was drowned in the air.

But what is this, O Lord, that one of the soldiers opened your side with a spear? Who is that one of the soldiers, unless perhaps he who received your seamless tunic? Assuredly this is the unity of the faithful, which serves you alone; with the spear of its preaching it opened your side to all believers. For the word of God is living and effective, and sharper than any two-edged sword. This is that spear which the prophet Habakkuk calls a flashing [Col. 1747A] weapon. David carried this spear, together with a vessel of water, away from the head of Saul his sleeping enemy, because the word of wisdom together with grace is withdrawn from the proud, envious, and negligent. But Abishai, son of Zeruiah, wished to pierce the sleeping man once, so that there would be no need for a second blow, unless David had kindly forbidden him; for unless the merciful and long-suffering patience of God upheld the sluggish and contemptuous sinner, Satan’s sword would kill him forever. For wicked Satan desires that the sleeper should not be enabled to rise again; but merciful David repeatedly cries out from a distant mountain summit: “Will you not answer, Abner?” For you render good for evil to sinners, most gentle David, and you admonish and wait longer, that he may answer [Col. 1747B] you once for a thousand times. But to them your voice seems troublesome, because you disturb their restless dream.

“Who are you,” he says, “who cry out and disturb the king?” At your rebuke those who mounted horses shall flee, and their driver does not wish them to awaken until the princes fall into the abyss. For the king of the wicked is pride: he sleeps in shade, in the secrecy of the chamber, in damp places, and the shadows cover his shadow. He is that Abner who guarded Saul: “Why do you disturb the king?” Yet even the proud heart is sometimes pierced by David’s voice, but not unto amendment. Proud Saul is bent by humble words when David says: “Whom do you pursue, king of Israel? Whom do you pursue? A dead dog [Col. 1747C] and a single flea, like a partridge in the mountains.” Not without reason does David compare himself either to a dead dog or to a single flea. A living dog is better than a dead lion: better is the dog who lives to God and is dead to the world than the proud and reprobate lion, dead to God and alive to the age. A little flea bites and leaps; so the humble righteous person confidently bites the vices of the flesh and leaps upon the mountains, where he has the safest refuge of virtues, so that he need not fear the adulterous partridge that persecuted Elijah and killed John the Baptist.

Grant me a portion, Lord, in the land of the living, in the burial-place of strangers, in the field of Haceldama, purchased at the great price of your blood. For there are buried all our fathers, who were strangers and sojourners upon [Col. 1747D] this earth. There Abraham buried his most beautiful wife, Sarah, in the double cave. But why did he refuse to receive the field itself freely, or to bury his dead in their chosen tombs? Because he did not believe that he could be saved through Christ without the price of Christ’s blood; nor did he think it good for himself to dwell in the stinking tombs of the world. “Bury your dead,” they say, “in our chosen tombs.” The world has chosen tombs: namely, those graves which the height of arrogance or the laboriousness of superstition makes conspicuous.

All Egypt is full of tombs, for there was no house in which a dead person did not lie. The children of Israel longed for those tombs in the wilderness: “[Col. 1748A] Were there no tombs for us in Egypt, that our corpses should lie naked and unburied in the wilderness?” The most holy patriarch did not wish to bury his dead in such tombs. But where? In the double cave, where hope of good works and contemplative love rest. For others also lie buried there; therefore Sarah and Leah lie hidden together in the double cave. The former, first barren but later already an old woman, bore only one son of joy; the latter ceased to bear after six sons, except that at the last she bore a daughter, the disgrace of a sacred lineage.

A marvelous thing: she who had six sons is said to have ceased bearing, whereas she who had only one is not said to have ceased bearing. But the active life has an end; the contemplative life always bears. The former gives birth in pain, the latter in [Col. 1748B] joy; yet both are buried in the same field. For Rachel was placed near Bethlehem beneath the oak of the cross. Assuredly she sits at Jesus’ feet, so that from the house of bread she may always give birth fruitfully. Therefore Sarah and Rachel will never cease bearing. But Leah, after six sons, either wholly ceases to bear or gives birth to a daughter. She is carnal pleasure, which sometimes steals into the active life under the appearance of discernment. Yet, if she is truly a widow, she shall be saved, not through the begetting of a daughter but through the begetting of sons.

The noble patriarchs were buried in the double cave with their wives. For they dwelt in tents as strangers and sojourners upon the earth; therefore both they and all their descendants possess by inheritance the burial-place of strangers. [Col. 1748C] But why is Jacob, advanced in age, buried there by his son Joseph with a greater splendour, sweetness, and glory than the others? In aged Jacob perfect love is expressed, in which the Father is buried with the Son—indeed, together with the Son—as Christ says: “If anyone loves me, he will keep my word; and my Father will love him, and we shall come to him and make our dwelling with him.” This is that glorious and sweet burial of the Ancient of Days, who buries with himself those who love him and hides them in the secret of his face from the disturbance of men. Thither also the bones of Joseph, the memorial of our saviour from Egypt, are daily brought back by the children of Israel. For Joseph’s bones are not in Egypt, because he detests foul-smelling [Col. 1748D] and whitewashed tombs. And God buried Moses, but his tomb is not found by any human being to this day.

Finally, who can go there, where he ascended through the midst of the cloud to the highest mountain, remained there forty days and forty nights, and saw and examined the pattern of the wonderful tabernacle which God pitched and not man? Therefore to this day, when Moses is read, his face remains veiled, because his tomb is not found by mortal man. In the same field of blood the glorious line of kings also received its lot: they were buried in the burial-place of their fathers in Jerusalem. There likewise the vision of the prophets and the martial valour of the Maccabees have been gloriously adorned.

[Col. 1749A] Let that tower of Babel—once glorious among kingdoms, illustrious in the pride of the Chaldeans—now, if you please, be compared with this burial-place of strangers. What is found like this burial-place of ours? There one language is torn into many; here five cities of Egypt speak no longer the Egyptian tongue but Canaanite, yet one is called the city of the sun. From that tower of Babel Jezebel, the prostitute, mother of fornications, worshipper of idols, and contriver of avarice, was cast down. When they wished to bury her, because she was a king’s daughter, they found nothing but the skull, the tips of the hands, and a wall sprinkled with blood. This indeed is the burial of the wicked; this is their fitting recompense. What remains of them but the fingertips—that is, scarcely the outermost traces of their works—and baldness, [Col. 1749B] the place of pride stripped of the grace of hair? “I saw the wicked highly exalted and lifted up like the cedars of Lebanon; and I passed by, and behold, he was not.” This is Jezebel’s skull, she who was arrayed in a harlot’s adornment and painted her eyes with antimony. The crown of pride has been made bald. There is no one worthy to look upon it except one who wishes to abhor her wickedness, wash his hands in the sinner’s blood, and, like a strong and swift horse, pierce the cast-down prostitute with his hoof, trample her, and pass on. For this reason the bloodstained wall was left behind, to frighten men of blood and deceit who, because of their avarice, stone humble Naboth. But the dogs, most shameless lovers of corpses, incorporate into themselves the flesh of the prostitute; consequently they also lap up her blood, [Col. 1749C] because they shall share alike in lust and in vengeance. But there are other dogs, made red by him from their enemies, who suffer hunger for righteousness, went round not the city of Babylon but of the Church, and consume and bury with themselves whatever they find there dead to vices. But woe to those whom birds—that is, demons flying through the empty air—devour when they are dead outside the city, such as Ahithophel and Absalom, Jezebel and Judas, who, having received their soul in vain, also breathed it out in vain.

But let us return to the field of Haceldama, that we may admire and emulate rather the dwelling and glory of blessed souls, since “the memory of the wicked shall perish with a sound,” but the memory of the righteous shall live for ever. Such were Joseph, who was a councillor, a just and good man; and Nicodemus, once a minister of the night but now of the day. To anoint the Lord’s body, he brought a mixture of myrrh and aloes, about a hundred pounds. Jesus loves such ministers of his burial, who boldly rescue his body from the power of darkness and claim it for themselves, so that each may know how to possess his vessel in honour and sanctification, binding it with the laws of chastity and the linen cloths of discipline, and preserving it from the corruption of worms by a mixture of myrrh and aloes. These spices are bitter indeed, but they remove corruption; for the chastening of the flesh is laborious, yet neither the mind nor the flesh itself is preserved incorruptible without it. [Col. 1750A] “About a hundred pounds.” O good measure, pressed down! A most exact balance must be maintained between body and soul, so that each may rejoice in possessing its own fullness, and peace and equality may arise between flesh and spirit, in order that measure may be kept and perfection not abandoned. These are, as it were, a hundred pounds which keep the body of Jesus always whole and fragrant in the tomb of the faithful.

Behold, forty mighty men surround Solomon’s bed, all holding swords and most skilled in war. Your bed, Jesus Christ, is more than Solomon’s: it is your burial, in which on the Sabbath you rested from all the work that you had accomplished. Your tomb is new and cut out in rock, because [Col. 1750B] your beloved, the faithful soul, is a garden enclosed; she is daily renewed in the knowledge of you and made firm in the rock of your love, burying herself with you in the inward person, in the secret of your chamber. There forty mighty men of the mightiest of Israel surround you, in whom the works of six days are very good and perfect works, so that in the six and the ten they may preserve your image and likeness of the law. These guard you better than the deceitful guard of the wicked, because they are most skilled in war, able to drive away not only the enticements of the flesh but also aerial powers and terrors of the night.

But those who, like men drunken by night, beset your tomb, trembled there with fear where there is no fear; [Col. 1750C] because the power of darkness, unable to endure the light, became like dead men at the announcement of life. It is not therefore the children of night who guard you, but the children of day: for your radiance strikes terror into the former, so that they flee from you; but brings joy to the latter, so that they draw near to you.

“While we were asleep, his disciples came and stole him away.” O liars! You spoke the truth, but iniquity lied to itself. For sleepers cannot guard Christ; rather, “those who keep watch for me in the morning,” he says, “shall find me.” And what appears to you while you sleep except dreams? Behold, you have that abundant money in your hands: if you can, guard it, lest thieves dig through and steal it. Christ’s disciples now diligently [Col. 1750D] guard their own treasure.

Everyone strives to preserve what he loves. Certainly Michal loved David more than her father Saul; therefore she let him down through the window and saved him. What does this mean? Michal, daughter of Saul, daughter of former pride, after marrying the beautiful David, begins to hate her father; and to her it is said in the Psalm: “Hear, daughter, and see; incline your ear, and forget your people and your father’s house.” Therefore she lets David down through the window; understand that window through which the Beloved puts forth his hand. Through this window he is let down by his beloved, to his beloved—that is, to himself—and is hidden in the inner person, where he may both live safely and confess the wicked. [Col. 1751A] For he hides himself and departs from the temple of unbelief; because, while he plays the harp before Saul in order to make the evil spirit of the Lord depart from him, that impious man tries to pin him to the wall with a spear. But when David evades him, what does it mean that the spear is fixed in the wall, except that, when Christ’s grace withdraws, the hardened mind is pierced by the weapon of its own malice?

What, moreover, does Saul, king of darkness, hate so bitterly today as David, his son-in-law? Therefore, while David is absent, he takes away his daughter and gives her to another, an ignoble husband. But when the mighty man returns and receives the kingdom, he claims her again for himself, because he had betrothed her to himself with two hundred Philistine foreskins—cutting away from her not only the impurities of the flesh but also those of the mind. Woe to sinners, Lord, [Col. 1751B] who beset your tomb; for you truly turn aside from them, and they do not find you upon their sweet and flower-strewn bed. Rather, they stumble against an image wrapped in the darkness of their heart, having at its head a goatskin stinking with the memory of their sins.

Blessed, however, is the one who watches at your tomb and guards you; who wrestles in the morning with the angel of the resurrection, and does not let him go until he hears something of his name, which is wonderful—so that Jacob’s name too may be changed into Israel, and, having crossed the river of sorrow, the sun of righteousness may immediately rise upon him.

“Who will roll away the stone for us from the entrance of the tomb?” The entrance of my mind is shut, Lord, and the stone of mortality weighs upon [Col. 1751C] my understanding, made heavy by the weight of my iniquity. Human strength cannot remove it at all, unless your almighty Word comes from the royal throne—the Angel of Counsel who destroys the wall of our enmities—and opens our understanding, so that we may understand the Scriptures and see the linen cloths set before us, the truest testimonies of your humanity and resurrection. Whoever, with your help, can search you out in these will taste beforehand something of the glory of the resurrection which you have prepared for those who love you. Its firstfruits you have already gathered into your bosom, offering them always before yourself and your Father, roasted by the fire of the Holy Spirit.

And that angel, the herald of so great a joy, who rolled away the stone and terrified impious minds, [Col. 1751D] but gently soothed devout ones and forbade them to fear—that Angel, I say, bore witness not only by word but also by face, dress, and action to the blessed resurrection. For he rolled away the stone and sat upon it: the stone, I say, which even now lies rolled against us and weighs down our face. There is no doubt that this occurs also in the first resurrection, that of the soul: the spirit, in a reversal, subjects beneath itself the burden of corruption which pressed upon it, and, like a judge and lord, assumes governance of its inferior part.

What is denoted by his raiment’s appearance, surpassing the whiteness of snow, except the cool and utterly pure chastity of our body? It both bears witness and renders [Col. 1752A] service to the angelic radiance presiding within it. Further, his inward countenance, upon which the light of your face, Lord, is sealed, is like lightning—both terrible and bright: terrible, to split the soul’s enemies asunder and terrify them; bright, so that it may always appear before you, the true light, together with righteousness. Such was Moses’ face through fellowship with your Word: bright and terrible, because it was horned to scatter enemies, and veiled because of the brightness which fleshly eyes could not bear.

And now, Lord, we know and rejoice that you have truly risen from the dead, and that you are still far removed from us mortals, because you have ascended upon your fiery horses and fiery chariot, manifold with ten thousands. Yet your mantle has fallen from you to us and [Col. 1752B] remains with us to this day: namely, the linen cloths of your body. By them may we experience the help of your power at the fitting time, so that your Spirit may become double within us, and we may love both God and neighbour in you. The pains of death have surrounded us, and torrents of iniquity have troubled us. The garment of our mortality has enclosed us, bubbling forth; worms, which continually consume us and do not sleep—pains that foretell that supreme pain which comes upon us like sand and strives to overwhelm us unawares. And indeed, who is so provident as to be able to endure its terror? Yet, whether we wish it or not, it must certainly be endured; it must certainly be passed through.

[Col. 1752C] But do not forget Elijah’s mantle; otherwise the torrent will not be divided for you without it. There are also other torrents of iniquity—the sea of my sins—which trouble me; and would that they troubled me in such a way that I might cry out in sorrow: “My father, my father, the chariot of Israel and its charioteer!” For the torrents of iniquity trouble me by taking away the light of my eyes, so that I cannot see most holy Elijah when he is taken from me. For if I saw, surely his spirit would become double in me, and I would cry, “My father, my father!” God has sent the Spirit of his Son into our hearts, crying, “Abba, Father.” The double Spirit cries doubly: “My father, my father—my father, Creator; my father, Restorer—my father, my father!”

O voice full of love: “the chariot of Israel and its charioteer”: [Col. 1752D] you bear and govern him. Whom? Israel—seeing you, believing in you, hoping in you, sighing for you. Behold, you have been taken up; your Elisha will see you no more. Yet your mantle remains with him in memory of you, so that the presence of your absence may continually both soothe his pain by increasing it, and increase it by soothing it. “Take this,” he says, “in remembrance of me.” This is the sacrament of your body, which we receive in remembrance of you, until you come. Your mantle is your flesh, with which clothed you came forth to us; and you hid yourself from the faithless, but showed yourself to your faithful ones, as you do to this day. Beneath this mantle your greatest strength is concealed.

O Samson, most strong: you did not conceal even your final secret from the beloved woman who did not love you, [Col. 1753A] in order to turn an enemy into a friend. You loved the woman who did not love you, but persecuted you, so greatly that, because of love, your wisdom became foolish and your strength weak. But what is foolish in God has become wiser than men, and what is weak in God stronger than men. For willingly offering yourself to suffering, and dying by your own power, you shook the princes of darkness and crushed their kingdom; and your cross became a stumbling-block to Jews, folly to Gentiles, but to those who believe, the power of God and the wisdom of God.

So long as we are in this body, we are away from you, Lord. You indeed walk with those who love you, speak with them, and grieve concerning you; yet your face is that of a stranger, and although you recognize them, you are not [Col. 1753B] recognized by them. Truly you are that Joseph who spoke more harshly to your brothers as though they were strangers, not in indignation but in compassion, when you drew near to those two walking sadly on the road, taught them, and reproved them: “O foolish ones and slow of heart to believe!”

Thus your brothers come to you as strangers, but you graciously draw near to them. They come to you with the asses of their own foolishness and slowness, and with empty sacks because of their poverty; but you not only fill them with grain, you even restore their money, tied in the mouth of the sack. “When one opened his sack,” it says, “to give fodder to his beast, he found the money in the mouth of the sack. ‘My money,’ he said, ‘has been restored; behold, it is in the sack.’” What is this that God has done to us? They come to you empty and foolish, [Col. 1753C] but you send them back laden and abounding in the grain of your wisdom. Moreover, you restore the money of eloquence, secured by the authority of Scripture, because you make the tongues of infants eloquent, so that they may give fodder to beasts that do not yet understand you, and a measure of wheat in its season.

Walk with us now, Lord, lest we be left desolate and sorrowful on this road which we travel. For you yourself once led the children of Israel by a pillar of cloud by day and a pillar of fire by night; and at your command they set down their tents and raised them again. What is the cloud that goes before the true Israelites except your most true and holy body, which we receive at the altar? In it [Col. 1753D] the height of day—the immensity of your majesty—is veiled from us, for mortal weakness could not endure either its heat or its radiance, unless the mediating cloud were interposed both to temper the heat from above and to show beneath itself the safe way beforehand.

All your host follows this cloud, Lord, King of Sabaoth. Whoever does not follow it is in darkness, walks in darkness, and does not know where he goes. For from this cloud shines forth the path leading to life: the path of humility and patience, the path of gentleness and mercy, and whatever you have deigned to reveal to humankind through the mystery of your incarnation. From it there shines for us the glory of the Law and the Prophets, when Moses and Elijah appeared with you on the mountain, but a bright cloud overshadowed them; [Col. 1754A] for they too, like us, could not have been saved without your protection. Yet to them, as friends and members of your household—indeed, as the foremost of your household and friends—the cloud of your sacrament was transparent; whereas to us, lying prostrate and cast away from before your eyes, it is very dim. But your eyes saw my imperfection, and all shall be written in your book; for beneath your cloud you nourish, perfect, and lead Joseph like a sheep. This is the pillar of cloud that went before Israel’s children by day; the pillar of fire, however, is the Holy Spirit, who appeared above the apostles in tongues of fire, illumines the darkness of our blindness, and raises us upward so that we may savour the things above, not things upon the earth. Thus, the cloud by day and the pillar of fire by night: because your flesh [Col. 1754B] tempers for us the heat of divinity, and the light of the Holy Spirit illumines the darkness of our mind. Therefore, while you spoke on the road to the two disciples travelling with you, and the cloud of a stranger concealed your face, they said: “Was not our heart burning within us concerning Jesus, while he spoke on the road and opened the Scriptures to us?” The pillar of fire burned within, because outwardly he spoke to them in the pillar of cloud.

But where at last did they recognize him? In the breaking of bread. The bread is your flesh. You broke your body with your hands, because you have power to lay down your life and to take it again. You broke the body which appeared outwardly and showed the marrow hidden within; for unless you suffered, you would not be recognized. “There,” it says, “his strength is hidden.” [Col. 1754C] And what is your strength except mercy, gentleness, humility, and patience? In the breaking of bread—that is, in your passion—you showed us these most strong and sweet virtues. By these virtues your flesh, which we are, is gradually nourished, grows, and advances.
