First, between the two millstones of hope and fear, it is ground like grain, so that it may become new dough. Then, after it has been formed into bread, it is baked in the oven of sufferings. Afterwards, when you have blessed it with every spiritual blessing and said, “It is finished,” you break also our body, which is in your hands and which we commend into your hands. There you are recognized, not in a stranger’s appearance but in your own face, so that [Col. 1754D] no longer may a spear open your side to us, but we may touch and see with the finger that you are, Lord, our God.

Father of orphans and judge of widows, do you not see this poor and desolate widow, my soul? She has neither brothers nor friends nor neighbours from whom she may borrow—not a few empty vessels, which my sons may bring me, and into which I may pour the little oil remaining to me from you—so that you may show the fullness of your blessing to all. For I understand, Lord, that the vessels are certain literal and historical senses of your Scriptures, which are not few, so that the whole world could not contain them. These vessels of your most holy temple the king of Babylon, [Col. 1755A] that is, the dominion of pride, carries off captive for himself; he compels them to serve his banquets, not for his glory but for his disgrace, arrogating to himself knowledge of your Law, drinking the wine of his prostitution from the vessels of the sanctuary, and defiling your gifts with a harlot’s ointments. Therefore, opposite the wall, a harsh yet just sentence against them is written: because every kingdom divided against itself shall be made desolate and handed over to the Medes and Persians, who neither seek silver nor desire gold, but kill their childish and foolish thoughts with poisoned and burning arrows.

But you, Lord, open and have mercy on the desolate widow, lest the most wicked and importunate creditor, who has lent me many talents of his iniquity at the interest of my destruction, [Col. 1755B] take away my two sons—the inward faculties of my soul—to serve himself. Your good and saving counsel is that I should borrow not a few vessels and, by the blessing of overflowing oil, redeem my sins, and thereafter live with my sons. But because I have neither neighbours nor children from whom I may borrow the exercise of my mind, as soon as I relax my hands that shameless creditor assails me and compels my two sons, that is, understanding and affection, to serve sloth and his empty illusions. Therefore, merciful defender of widows, since you are exceedingly rich and give abundantly to all, yourself, I say, lend me both vessels which you know to be useful for this purpose and oil, so that all things may be yours and [Col. 1755C] all may serve you. For I do not wish to carry my oil down into Egypt and thus sin against you. Only let me not eat the bread of idleness, but rather be occupied all day in your righteous ordinances and live. And behold, whatever the son of my memory offers me, as soon as it comes into my hands I shall seize it.

Elijah stood on the mountain summit, and the first captain of fifty was sent to him and consumed by fire; the second likewise; but the third was spared by the merit of humility and devotion. Behold a vessel, but empty, because, received in this way, it echoes cruelty rather than anything else. Let it be filled with oil, and its harsh sound will cease. For who is Elijah standing upon the mountain summit except you, Lord Jesus, who stand above beside the Father? The first captain of fifty comes to you, whom the world sends to you dry from excessive [Col. 1755D] aridity, and cries: “Man of God, come down from the mountain.” For the world knows that it cannot be saved without you. “Man of God,” and God-man: may the man whom you seek move you to condescend to man. Come down from the mountain: none can approach you unless you approach him; none can ascend to you unless you descend to him. Man of God, come down from the mountain. You are the mountain raised above the summit of mountains. Come down and have compassion upon us in the valley of tears. “If I am a man of God,” he says, “let fire come down from heaven and consume you”—for I came to cast fire upon the earth, and how I desire that it be kindled and devour you and your fifty! I beseech you, Lord, let that fire descend also upon me and devour in me the old man with his deeds. [Col. 1756A] This is the first captain of fifty, whom your fire devours so that it may cause him to rest from every servile work.

The second captain of fifty is the active life itself, which likewise has its end, sabbath after sabbath. Your fire also consumes this as a burnt offering. In the first fifty, indeed, a goat was burned; in the second, a ram is burned. But the third, which belongs to resurrection or contemplation, has no end, but lives forever with Elijah. Hence it is well read in the Gospel concerning the one hundred and fifty-three large fishes, all of which were brought together into one fish, which the seven disciples saw laid upon the coals; and they breakfasted with Jesus, who was the eighth. The number itself—that is, the one hundred [Col. 1756B] and fifty, which are three fifties, and the seven disciples—harmoniously signifies rest. And just as the individual fifties tend toward unity, so the seven disciples tend toward the eighth, that is, Christ; and all are perfected in the one.

But just as Christ and all the elect are one body, one bread, one man, or one fish, so the devil together with all the reprobate is one body and one enemy. For he is a great eagle with great wings: an eagle, because of the excessive penetration of his spiritual nature; great, because of the height of his pride; his great wings, the powers of evil spirits that cling to and exalt him; the long train of limbs, wicked human beings whose service he employs in waging war against the good [Col. 1756C]—and rightly long, because they still come daily and endure until the end of the age, following the leadership of pride; full of feathers, deceitful in wiles and variety, because he transforms the same arts in diverse ways for deception.

He came to Lebanon, that is, to the soul made white by the merit of faith and life. He took the pith of the cedar. The cedar is the height of hope, imperishable; its pith is charity, which the devil especially strives to overthrow. He plucks away the topmost foliage: that is, he tears the word of wisdom, which is most excellent, away from the love of God and carried it into the land of Shinar, that is, “of their stench,” which signifies vain glory.

“On that day the Lord will whistle for the fly that is at the far end of the rivers of the land of Egypt, and for the bee that is [Col. 1756D] in the land of Assyria.” Whistle, Lord, for this unclean fly, my sinful soul, so that your good Spirit may lead me in the right way and I may go to the high and mountainous land of promise, which is watered from above and awaits rain from on high—not like Egypt’s land, which a river bubbling from the earth covers entirely. For no mountain stands opposed, no obstacle exists for Egypt’s desires; rather, as they bubble from an earthly mind, they run without delay over the cast-down surface of the soul. The Egyptian river has seven mouths, which derive from one head, that is, pride. The farthest of them is understood as fleshly lust, from which flies are born, ever lovers of uncleanness. Yet the abundance of grace does not despise even this, but whistles [Col. 1757A] for it, calls it from the far end of the rivers, and joins it to the bee which was in Assyria, so that they may come and rest together in the torrents of the valleys, the caves of the rocks, all the thickets, and every hollow.

The bee is a virgin; but so long as it is in the land of Assyria, that is, of exaltation, it cannot make honey. The land of promise alone flows with milk and honey. But when grace whistles, fly and bee meet and rest together in the torrents of the valleys. In those torrents both the bee is cleansed of the filth of pride and the fly of the filth of lust. The torrents of the valleys are the disciplines of humility. Why torrents? Because any sadness or severity involved in correcting vices passes quickly; hence a woman has sorrow when she gives birth. [Col. 1757B] For labour turns into love, weariness into desire, and bitterness into sweetness; and so, from the torrents of the valleys, they advance to the caves of the rocks. The rocks are the Fathers, most steadfast and strong in faith; in their sufferings, as in models of their own, the fly and bee rest like doves making nests. Hence their hand does not cease, nor their foot; but they are continually exercised in every thicket of good works, and only then reach the hollows of contemplation. These, Lord Jesus, are the active works, for they are very good.

Thus you whistled to Mary Magdalene, from whom you cast out not one demon but seven, like the rivers of Egypt. See how she rested in the torrents of the valleys. She entered [Col. 1757C] among those reclining at table, ran to Jesus’ feet, and poured torrents of tears over them. To wash his footprints she brought no water but the stream of her own eyes; she used her hair in place of linen cloths. But when she burned more fiercely, and, like a coal sprinkled by a rain of tears, blazed more strongly, you saw the very frequent and insatiable kisses pressed by her upon those most sacred feet; you saw the whole house filled with the sweetness of the poured-out ointment. What then, if not that she rested in the torrents of the valleys, she from whom such numerous and great torrents of grace were poured forth? Hence her many sins were also forgiven her, because she had loved much.

Now, like a dove in mourning, she sat wholly at Jesus’ feet beside the fullest streams, while her sister Martha busied herself with much service. Why should I mention the duty she performed beforehand for his burial—ascending from the feet to anoint his head—when that stinking tomb of avarice, unable to endure the fragrance of compassion, raged against her? Such great love could not die to Christ even when he was dying. When the men—that is, the apostles—fled and hid themselves, the undaunted woman stood weeping at the tomb. She did not possess him alive, and she burned wholly over him dead. The body had been taken away; she could not leave the tomb. The more he was taken from her hands and eyes, the more ardently she pursued him in love. If it had been possible, to ransom the body she would have filled the tomb with tears. “She stood,” it says, “weeping”: that alone of herself [Col. 1758A] remained to her. The body had been taken away, but who could take weeping from her?

Yield, lady, yield with full rein, and strive to pour out tireless tears until you attain your Lord, who has been taken away—or rather, has risen. Again and again bend down; gaze repeatedly upon the empty place where he had lain. More and more that place itself provokes you to weep, by representing the absence of him whom you seek. “She saw,” it says, “two angels in white sitting, one at the head and one at the feet, where the body of Jesus had been laid.” “Woman,” they say, “why are you weeping? Whom do you seek?” Yet surely you knew well, O most compassionate angels, why she wept and whom she sought. Why did you, by reminding her, stir her again to tears? But the joy of unlooked-for consolation was near; let the entire force of grief and weeping now run its course. “Turning back, she saw Jesus standing, and did not know that it was Jesus.”

O pious and delightful spectacle of mercy! He who is sought and desired both conceals himself and reveals himself. He conceals himself so that he may be sought more ardently; when sought, found with joy; when found, held with anxious care; and when held, not released, until he introduces her to make her dwelling in the chamber of his love. By this art Wisdom plays in the world, and its delights are to be with the children of men. “Woman, why are you weeping? Whom do you seek?” You have the one whom you seek and do not know it. You have true and eternal joy, and [Col. 1758C] you weep? You have within you the one whom you seek without. Truly, you stand outside the tomb weeping: your mind is your tomb; there I rest, not dead but living forever. Your mind is my garden; you rightly supposed that I am the gardener. I am the second Adam; I cultivate and guard my paradise. Your weeping, your devotion, your longing are my work. You have me within you and do not know it; therefore you seek outside. Behold, I shall also appear outside, so that I may bring you back within and you may find within the one whom you seek without. “Mary, I know you by name; learn to know me by faith.”

“Rabboni”—that is, “Teacher”—what is it to learn? Teach me to seek you; teach me to touch and anoint you. “Do not touch me,” he says, as a man, nor as you formerly touched and anointed me, mortal. I have not yet ascended to [Col. 1758D] my Father, nor have you yet believed me equal, coeternal, and consubstantial with the Father. Believe this, then, and you have touched me. You see the man, and therefore do not believe; for what is seen is not believed. You do not see God; believe, and you will see. By believing you will touch me, just as that woman touched the fringe of my garment and was immediately healed. Why? Because she touched me by her faith. Touch me with this hand; seek me with these eyes; run swiftly to me with these feet. I am not far from you, for I am God who draws near; I am the word in your mouth and in your heart. What is nearer to a person than his own heart? There within I am found by all who find me. For the things visible without are indeed my works, but they are transitory, [Col. 1759A] perishable; whereas I, their maker, dwell in the most secret and purest hearts.

All power in heaven and on earth has been given to you, Lord Jesus, great king, king of powers, who became obedient to the Father unto death, even death on a cross. Behold, your magnificence has been exalted above the heavens, and all things have been subjected beneath your feet. David reigned first at Hebron seven years over Judah; afterwards he was anointed over Israel and reigned in Israel thirty-three years. When, most true David, you were anointed only over Judah at Hebron, Saul, king of pride, had already died in them; otherwise, while he lived and sin ruled them, they would not say to you, “We are your bone and your flesh.” For who can at once be a member of Christ and [Col. 1759B] of the harlot? Or what agreement has Christ with Belial? “Behold,” they say, “we are your bone and your flesh.” “But yesterday and the day before, when Saul was king over us, you were leading Israel out and bringing it back.” And truly it is so: while the prince of darkness still reigns over us, you endure with much patience vessels of wrath fitted for destruction; you go forth before us, calling us to battle against vices, and free and lead out the unworthy from the hand of sins. Therefore Judah, that is, confession, first anoints you king over itself at Hebron. For when Saul has died, it remembers your benefits and, confessing its error, makes a passage from sins to you, King of righteousness.

You reign, moreover, over Judah seven years at [Col. 1759C] Hebron, because you render to them sevenfold into their bosom and, having cleansed them from the seven vices over which proud Saul presided, reform them by your sevenfold power. Afterwards your kingdom passes to Jerusalem over all Israel, because through the business of confession the faculties now enlightened attain the vision of peace, in which your dwelling has been made. This also is the mountain which you appointed for the disciples to go to Galilee, to see and worship you there after your resurrection, because God, your God, has already anointed you with the oil of gladness above your companions, so that you might be the firstborn of the dead and ruler of the kings of the earth.

Moreover, you reign in Jerusalem thirty-three years; thirty-three contains three tens. In the ten is the Law, consisting of ten commandments; in the threefold number is understood the threefold progress of the soul, which keeps God’s Law by seeing, meditating, or loving it. Of the first it is said, “I will praise the Lord in my life”; of the second, “Your law is my meditation”; of the third, “How I have loved your law, O Lord!” The three beyond thirty signify certain most excellent contemplatives, who by devoutness of conscience, fullness of wisdom, and perfection of charity draw near to the supreme Trinity. This is also the number of the mightiest men in your army, O most powerful one; yet even their most eminent members do not attain to your wisdom and strength, for “who among the clouds shall be equal to the Lord, or who shall be like God among the sons of God?” [Col. 1760A] You are like the tenderest woodworm, who, born of a virgin, pierces every hardness by your humility and charity, slaying eight hundred military commanders by one onset of your Spirit.

Who is as strong as you, who as merciful? You wept over Jerusalem and made lamentation over the destruction of your enemies. And now, Lord, you grieve over Saul and his son Jonathan, who daily fall upon the mountains of Gilboa. For unless you grieved, you would not cry from heaven, “Saul, Saul, why do you persecute me?” And whom does Saul signify, except proud prelates in your Church, who see themselves as towering above all the people from the shoulder upward? And what does Jonathan signify except young people of teachable and refined intellect, who, corrupted by the habits and conversations of their elders, cannot cultivate friendship with David except secretly, as though wary of the snares of those who disparage and mock them?

Rightly, therefore, do you weep, O kindly David, over Saul and Jonathan his son. They would not be objects of lamentation if they had fallen well; but they fell upon the mountains of Gilboa, which slope down into the deep. No dew of grace nor rain of doctrine shall come upon you any more, because there the shield of the mighty was cast away—the shield of Saul. The shield of the mighty is hope in divine protection, by which the fiery darts of the devil are repelled; Saul was gravely wounded by archers with these darts, so greatly that he killed himself through despair. Saul’s shield, however, is confidence in one’s own strength, which cannot withstand the arrows of the uncircumcised.

[Col. 1760C] Woe, however, to those who have lost their support—that is, the shield of the mighty; and cursed is the one who trusts in man, which is Saul’s shield. For you, mountains of Gilboa, shall be like tamarisks in the desert, because neither dew nor rain shall come upon you. “How have the mighty fallen?” For if mighty, how have they fallen? And if they have fallen, how are they mighty? But let not the wise man glory in his wisdom, nor the strong man in his strength; rather, let the one who glories glory in the Lord, and let the one who stands take heed lest he fall.

For even if they are swifter than eagles, so as to fly over contemplatives by the speed of their understanding; and even if they are stronger than lions, so as to surpass true preachers in strength of work: nevertheless, if, presuming upon themselves, they cast away the shield [Col. 1760D] of salvation, they will fall before their enemies. But whoever trusts in the Lord, like Mount Zion, shall not be moved forever. Saul preferred, however, to lean upon his own spear rather than rely upon the Lord; therefore the reed-staff of Egypt pierced his hand. His own spear and his own charioteer, who drove the chariot of his insolence, killed him. “I knew,” he says, “that he could not live.” For arrogant obstinacy does not know how to humble itself so as to live. Command, most just King David, your servant—that is, the spirit of pure discernment—to kill in me this Amalekite, Saul’s armour-bearer, who has dared even now, daily, to lay his hand upon me.

[Col. 1761]
