grant of two altars in the diocese of Amiens. 1065 XVI.—Confirmation of the house at Montpellier, and of Saint Gervasius and Saint Renobert. 1066 XVII.—Agreement between Cluny and Saint Benedict on the Po. 1066 XVIII.—Donation, by Lord Hato the bishop, of the churches of Barbonne, Lintis, and Lintelles, and of one prebend in the church of Saint Peter of Troyes. 1066 XIX.—Confirmation of Saint Remigius of Plaore, Barbonne, Lintis, Lintelles, and Saint Sylvester in the diocese of Troyes. 1067 XX.—Confirmation of Prins, with its appurtenances. 1067 XXI.—Charter of Pope Lucius concerning Saint Sabas with its appurtenances. 1067 XXII.—Charter of Pope Eugenius III concerning Calderia of Lédon. 1067 XXIII.—Charter of Count William concerning an agreement between himself and Lord Peter, abbot of Cluny, regarding the monasteries of Manziac and Celsiniac. 1067 XXIV.—Charter of Alfonso, emperor of Spain, concerning Saint Vincent of Salamanca. 1069 XXV.—Confirmation of Saint Vincent of Salamanca in Spain. 1069 XXVI.—Charter of Lord Frederick, emperor, concerning the monastery of Baume. 1070 XXVII.—Charter of Pope Adrian IV concerning the abbey of Baume in the archbishopric of Besançon, with its appurtenances. 1071 XXVIII.—Charter of Richard, bishop of Coutances, concerning the Church of Morsalines. 1071 XXIX.—Another charter concerning the same church. 1072

## ROBERT OF KETTON

Notice. 1073 Second notice. 1073 Preface of Robert of Ketton to Peter the Venerable,

[Col. 1769] to the book of the law of the Saracens, called the Alcoran, translated by him. 1075

## WIBALD, ABBOT OF STAVELOT AND CORVEY
Historical Notice. 1075 Literary Notice. 1077 Preliminary Observations on Wibald’s Letters. 1087

# THE LETTERS OF WIBALD

**Letter I.**—From Wibald, abbot of Monte Cassino, to Emperor Lothair.—He sets before him the calamities of the monastery of Monte Cassino and implores his aid and protection. 1121

**Letter II.**—To Emperor Lothair and his wife Richiza.—He recounts the depredations inflicted upon the monastery of Monte Cassino by Saracens, Normans, and Lombards. 1125

**Letter III.**—To the monks of Monte Cassino.—He grants them freedom to elect another abbot; if that election is canonical, he promises to release them from the obedience they had promised him. 1129

**Letter IV.**—To R., abbot of the monastery of Monte Cassino.—He congratulates him upon his election, releases him from the obedience promised to himself, and sends him back his ring and seal as a sign of his resignation of the abbacy. 1130

**Letter V.**—To Odo, dean of Monte Cassino.—He releases him and the other brethren of Monte Cassino from their promised obedience, and gives an account of certain things removed from the monastery. 1130

**Letter VI.**—To Theoderic, abbot of Waulsort.—He approves the miracles of Saint Forannan, committed to writing by the monk Robert. 1131

**Letter VII.**—From King Conrad to Abbot Wibald.—He orders him to come to Frankfurt to receive from his hand the regalia of the abbey of Corvey. 1132

**Letter VIII.**—From Abbot Wibald to King Conrad.—He replies to the preceding letter: the Corvey monks’ election of him must be examined; he also excuses his failure to come to the king’s court. 1133

**Letter IX.**—From King Conrad to the brethren of Stavelot.—He urges them to bear their abbot’s absence with equanimity and to place the fullest confidence in his favour. 1133

**Letter X.**—From the monks of Corvey to those of Stavelot.—They give thanks that the Stavelot monks did not begrudge them Wibald as abbot and urge them to endure his absence patiently. 1134

**Letter XI.**—From the monks of Stavelot to those of Corvey.—They congratulate them on Wibald’s election and commend him to them. 1134

**Letter XII.**—From Abbot Reinard, his teacher, to Wibald himself.—He congratulates him on his election, mingling joy with fear at his elevation. 1135

**Letter XIII.**—From Emperor Conrad to Pope Eugenius III.—He requests confirmation of the election, despite Wibald’s absence and resistance, as abbot of Corvey, and of the union of Kemnade and Visbek with the monastery of Corvey. 1136

**Letter XIV.**—From Abbot Wibald to the Corvey monks.—That they should bear witness before the supreme pontiff concerning his election as abbot of Corvey. 1137

**Letter XV.**—From W., prior, and the brethren of the monastery of Corvey to Pope Eugenius III.—They request confirmation of Abbot Wibald’s election and of the union with Corvey of two convents of nuns. 1138

**Letter XVI.**—From the monks of Corvey to Cardinal Guy.—Concerning the election of Abbot Wibald and the union with Corvey of two convents of nuns. 1139

**Letter XVII.**—From Count Hermann to Pope Eugenius III.—He bears witness to Wibald’s election as abbot of Corvey. 1141

**Letter XVIII.**—From Emperor Conrad to H., duke of Saxony.—He commends Wibald, abbot of Corvey, to him. 1141

**Letter XIX.**—From the Church of Bremen and the community of Bücken to Wibald, abbot of Corvey.—They choose him, together with the bishop of Verden, as arbiter of their case. 1142

**Letter XX.**—From Emperor Conrad to Pope Eugenius III.—He informs him that his son Henry has been elected King of the Romans by the unanimous acclamation of the princes, and that he himself, having taken the cross, is preparing for the Jerusalem expedition. 1142

**Letter XXI.**—From Anno to Abbot Wibald.—Concerning a certain Ebroin, to whom, at Wibald’s urging, he had done a kindness. 1143

**Letter XXII.**—From Abbot Wibald to Anno, abbot of Inda.—That nothing should be given to Ebroin, who had been expelled from the monasteries of Inda and Stavelot. 1144

**Letter XXIII.**—From Emperor Conrad to H., duke of Saxony.—Concerning the right of advocacy in Kemnade and Visbek, which he had united to the monastery of Corvey. 1144

**Letter XXIV.**—From Conrad to J., abbess of Herford. [Col. 1770]—He states that he has enjoined Abbot Wibald, after making an inquiry into the monastery of Herford, to remedy its deficiencies. 1145

**Letter XXV.**—From the monk Henry to Abbot Wibald.—He gives an account of what he had done with the pope toward confirmation of Wibald’s election as abbot of Corvey. 1145

**Letter XXVI.**—From Cardinal Guy to Abbot Wibald.—That he may transfer from the abbey of Stavelot to that of Corvey. 1147

**Letter XXVII.**—From Abbot Wibald to Cardinal Guy.—Concerning his arrival before the cardinal and the captives of the Roman Church whom he had redeemed. 1147

**Letter XXVIII.**—From Pope Eugenius III to the bishop of Havelberg.—That he should see to the restoration of Corvey property usurped by his people. 1148

**Letter XXIX.**—From Pope Eugenius III to Reinher, canon of Havelberg.—That he should restore the twenty hides which he had taken from the monastery of Corvey. 1148

**Letter XXX.**—From Henry, King of the Romans, to Abbot Wibald.—He praises and seeks his counsel for the administration of the kingdom and the establishment of peace. 1149

**Letter XXXI.**—From Emperor Conrad to Abbot Wibald.—He commends himself to his prayers and asks him not to cease guiding his son. 1149

**Letter XXXII.**—From A., abbot of Fulda, to Wibald.—He begs for Wibald’s intercession with the supreme pontiff. 1149

**Letter XXXIII.**—From Abbot Wibald to Cardinal Guy.—He commends to him the cause of the abbot of Fulda and of Reinard, formerly his teacher. 1150

**Letter XXXIV.**—From Amicus to Wibald.—He congratulates him on overcoming his adversaries and praises Robert, dean of Stavelot. 1150

**Letter XXXV.**—From Abbot Wibald to Reinard, abbot of Reinhausen.—A reply to the preceding letter. 1152

**Letter XXXVI.**—From Rainard to Abbot Wibald.—Concerning their mutual affection. 1153

**Letter XXXVII.**—From the monks of Stavelot to Abbot Wibald.—They congratulate him on his return; complain of Count Godfrey, who had broken the snares laid by him; and of the invasion of the village of Tournay. 1154

**Letter XXXVIII.**—From Robert, dean of Stavelot, to Abbot Wibald.—He congratulates him on his return. 1155

**Letter XXXIX.**—From Bovo, provost, to Abbot Wibald.—Concerning damage inflicted on the provostship by the count of Namur and others. 1155

**Letter XL.**—From Abbot Wibald to Henry, bishop of Liège.—That he should restrain Eustace, his parishioner, who had invaded the village of Tournay. 1155

**Letter XLI.**—From Abbot Wibald to his monks of Stavelot.—He commiserates their calamities, which they suffered in his absence. 1156

**Letter XLII.**—From Henry, bishop of Liège, to Abbot Wibald.—He wishes to enjoy Wibald’s presence in order to correct defects of conduct. 1158

**Letter XLIII.**—From Wibald to the bishop of Liège.—He wishes to enjoy his presence. 1158

**Letter XLIV.**—From Abbot Wibald to Pope Eugenius III.—That he allowed envoys of the people of Erveta, captured by a certain ministerial of Stavelot, to depart free. 1159

**Letter XLV.**—From the monks of Corvey to those of Stavelot.—They thank them for yielding Wibald to them as abbot, relate how excellently he had conducted himself among them in spiritual and temporal matters, and speak of their mutual association. 1159

**Letter XLVI.**—From the monks of Corvey to those of Stavelot.—How they conducted themselves with the pope’s legate when he asked them what they had done with the treasures of the Church. 1160

**Letter XLVII.**—From Cardinal Guy to Abbot Wibald.—That he had shown Wibald’s writing to the pope, and that Wibald should present himself to the pontiff. 1162

**Letter XLVIII.**—From Wibald to Cardinal Guy.—He commends his monks of Stavelot to him. 1162

**Letter XLIX.**—From Abbot Wibald to Cardinal Jordan.—What he had done to arrange for the pope’s reception at Liège. 1162

**Letter L.**—From Abbot Wibald to Cardinal John.—He asks for his protection. 1163

**Letter LI.**—From Cardinal John to Abbot Wibald.—He promises that he will take the greatest care of Wibald’s affairs. 1163

**Letter LII.**—From Pope Eugenius III to the monks of Corvey.—He urges them to show humble reverence to Abbot Wibald. 1164

**Letter LIII.**—From Pope Eugenius III to Henry, bishop of Liège.—That he should restrain those plundering the goods of the monastery of Stavelot. 1164

[Col. 1771]

**Letter LIV.**—From Henry, King of the Romans, to Pope Eugenius III.—He begs for the pope’s protection. 1165

**Letter LV.**—From Pope Eugenius III to Henry the Younger, King of the Romans.—He praises his zeal for the Church and wishes him every prosperity. 1165

**Letter LVI.**—From Henry, King of the Romans, to Pope Eugenius III.—That he should receive kindly Henry, archbishop of Mainz, and others travelling to the pope; release the duchess of Poland from excommunication; and have Abbot Wibald commended to him. 1165

**Letter LVII.**—From B., bishop of Hildesheim, to Pope Eugenius III.—He extols Abbot Wibald’s merits and asks the pontiff to ratify the union of Kemnade with the monastery of Corvey. 1165

**Letter LVIII.**—From Henry, duke of Saxony, to Pope Eugenius III.—On the same subject. 1166

**Letter LIX.**—From Count Hermann of Winzenburg to Pope Eugenius III.—On the same subject. 1166

**Letter LX.**—From H., abbot of Saint Mary at Flechtorf, to Pope Eugenius III.—On the same subject. 1167

**Letter LXI.**—From W., abbot of Saint Blaise, to Pope Eugenius III.—On the same subject. 1167

**Letter LXII.**—From C., abbot of Blessed Mary at Grevenkerken, to Pope Eugenius III.—On the same subject. 1168

**Letter LXIII.**—From the abbot of Blessed Mary at Hamulungesburnen to Pope Eugenius III.—On the same subject. 1169

**Letter LXIV.**—From Pope Eugenius III to King Henry the Younger.—He promises that he will provide for his aunt. 1169

**Letter LXV.**—From Pope Eugenius III to the German prelates.—That they should support the younger King Henry and assist him with their counsels and deeds. 1169

**Letter LXVI.**—From Pope Eugenius III to A., bishop of Bremen, H., bishop of Minden, and T., bishop of Verden.—That they should ensure restoration of the lands of the monastery of Kemnade which various persons had usurped. 1170

**Letter LXVII.**—From Pope Eugenius III to the monks of Corvey.—He confirms the deposition of Abbot Henry. 1170

**Letter LXVIII.**—From Pope Eugenius III to the people of Fulda.—He declares void their election, made contrary to his command, and orders that, in the presence of certain abbots whom he names, they elect an abbot from another cloister. 1170

**Letter LXIX.**—From Pope Eugenius III to the abbots of Eberbach, Everbach, Hersfeld, and Corvey.—That, on going to Fulda, they should arrange for an abbot to be elected from another cloister. 1170

**Letter LXX.**—From A., provost of Corvey, to Abbot Wibald.—The chamberlain of Fulda desires his presence at the election of an abbot, as do the Corvey monks for restoration of their affairs. 1170

**Letter LXXI.**—From Abbot Wibald to the people of Fulda.—He excuses his inability to come to them, tries to console them, and urges them to proceed quickly to an election. 1171

**Letter LXXII.**—From Count Henry of Namur to Pope Eugenius III.—He declares himself prepared to observe what had been ordered at Trier in the pope’s court concerning the case between himself and the archdeacon of Verdun. 1172

**Letter LXXIII.**—From Abbot Wibald to Henry, King of the Romans.—Concerning the abbot-elect of Fulda, obedience to papal decrees, and so forth. 1172

**Letter LXXIV.**—From the prior of Corvey to Abbot S.—Through the mediation of Abbot Wibald, he forgives him whatever he had committed against the Corvey monks. 1173

**Letter LXXV.**—From Abbot Wibald to Master Baldrick.—That he should exercise his talent. 1173

**Letter LXXVI.**—From the monks of Corvey to Abbot Wibald.—That, though absent, he should not cease to labour for his Church, and that he should confirm by his privilege the union of the two monasteries. 1174

**Letter LXXVII.**—From the monks of Corvey to Abbot Wibald.—They set forth how much they suffer from his absence and urge him to return soon. 1175

**Letter LXXVIII.**—From Abbot Wibald to his monks of Corvey.—His presence had been especially necessary at Stavelot; once his business was concluded, he would hasten to Corvey as soon as possible. 1176

**Letter LXXIX.**—From Abbot Wibald to his sister Hadwig.—He excuses his long failure to visit her and relates how much he had done for the kingdom, his own people, and his friends. 1177

**Letter LXXX.**—From Emperor Conrad to Abbot Wibald.—He relates what befell him on the holy expedition. 1178

**Letter LXXXI.**—From the monks of Corvey to Abbot Wibald. [Col. 1772]—They congratulate him on his successful undertakings and desire his prompt return to them. 1179

**Letter LXXXII.**—From A., provost of Corvey, to Abbot Wibald.—He desires his prompt return to the Corvey monks. 1180

**Letter LXXXIII.**—From Walter, chamberlain of Corvey, to Abbot Wibald.—He accounts for buildings to be constructed and wishes him to return to Corvey as soon as possible. 1181

**Letter LXXXIV.**—From Abbot Wibald to his monks of Corvey.—Being now about to return to them, he relates the many good things he had accomplished among the monks of Stavelot. 1181

**Letter LXXXV.**—From the monks of Corvey to Abbot Wibald.—They press for his return to Corvey. 1182

**Letter LXXXVI.**—From Abbot Wibald to his monks of Corvey.—He rebukes them because they press for his return with such repeated requests. 1183

**Letter LXXXVII.**—From Abbot Wibald to Henry, King of the Romans.—Concerning the case of Everard and Cuono. 1184

**Letter LXXXVIII.**—From Henry, King of the Romans, to Wibald, abbot of Stavelot.—He confirms the judgment pronounced by Franco in Everard’s favour. 1186

**Letter LXXXIX.**—From Henry, King of the Romans, to Abbot Wibald.—He thanks Wibald for service rendered to himself and his father, desiring his presence for other business. 1186

**Letter XC.**—From the chapter of Liège to Abbot Wibald.—In difficult matters it seeks his counsel. 1187

**Letter XCI.**—From Abbot Wibald to the chapter of Liège.—He excuses his inability to attend their chapter and states in writing what advice he would have given had he been able to be present. 1188

**Letter XCII.**—From Abbot Wibald to Henry, bishop of Liège.—Concerning violence done to people of the monastery of Stavelot by Theoderic of Salcevivo. 1189

**Letter XCIII.**—From Henry, King of the Romans, to Abbot Wibald.—That he should meet him at Winzenburg. 1189

**Letter XCIV.**—From the monks of Fulda to Abbot Wibald.—They promise to meet him at the appointed time. 1190

**Letter XCV.**—From Bernard, bishop of Paderborn, to Abbot Wibald.—He asks that, while returning to Corvey, Wibald should turn aside to him for a meeting. 1190

**Letter XCVI.**—From Abbot Wibald to Cardinal Guy.—He commends to him the abbot of Brauweiler. 1190

**Letter XCVII.**—From the chapter of Saint Liborius to Abbot Wibald.—They complain of Folquin’s vexations and ask that, upon meeting the bishop, he urge the bishop to assist them. 1191

**Letter XCVIII.**—From Abbot Wibald to the canons of Paderborn.—A reply to the preceding letter. 1191

**Letter XCIX.**—From Henry, King of the Romans, to Pope Eugenius III.—He excuses the archbishop of Mainz for not having attended the Council of Rheims and commends him to the pontiff as he travels to him. 1192

**Letter C.**—From Abbot Wibald to G., goldsmith.—That he should diligently apply himself to the works Wibald had entrusted to him. 1193

**Letter CI.**—From G., goldsmith, to Abbot Wibald.—A reply to the preceding letter. 1193

**Letter CII.**—From Abbot Wibald to the monks of Fulda.—He excuses himself from travelling to Fulda and meanwhile gives them salutary counsel for the forthcoming election of an abbot. 1194

**Letter CIII.**—From the monks of Stavelot to Abbot Wibald.—They seek advice concerning certain temporal affairs. 1194

**Letter CIV.**—From Abbot Wibald to his monks of Stavelot.—A reply to the preceding letter. 1195

**Letter CV.**—From Abbot Wibald to his monks of Stavelot.—He relates certain disturbances which had occurred in the monastery of Corvey and forbids them to receive rebels among themselves. 1197

**Letter CVI.**—From Abbot Wibald to H., a monk.—He extols his virtues and asks him to write to him. 1200

**Letter CVII.**—From the monks of Fulda to Abbot Wibald.—They ask him to attend the forthcoming election of the abbot of Fulda. 1201

**Letter CVIII.**—From the monks of Fulda to the monks of Corvey.—That Abbot Wibald should attend the election of the abbot of Fulda. 1201

**Letter CIX.**—From the monk Stephen to Abbot Wibald.—He greatly desires to return to the monastery of Stavelot and writes that he had been unable to impose the management of an estate upon Godin. 1201

**Letter CX.**—From O., abbot of Saint Remigius, to Abbot Wibald.—He informs him of the death of Stephen, monk of Stavelot. 1202

**Letter CXI.**—From the monk Henry to Abbot Wibald. [Col. 1773]—He gives thanks for Wibald’s goodwill and promises that he will always be at his service. 1203

**Letter CXII.**—From Abbot Wibald to Pope Eugenius III.—Concerning the election of the abbot of Fulda. 1203

**Letter CXIII.**—From Abbot Wibald to Cardinal Guy.—He commends to him the Bremen elect and Provost Hartwig. 1204

**Letter CXIV.**—From Abbot Wibald to Pope Eugenius III.—Concerning the acts taken in the election of the abbot of Fulda. 1204

**Letter CXV.**—From H., apparently a monk of Fulda, to Abbot Wibald.—He writes that the abbot-elect had given assent to his election. 1210

**Letter CXVI.**—From Abbot Wibald, or a charter.—Concerning the lease of a certain possession. 1210

**Letter CXVII.**—From F., abbot of Saint Godehard, to Abbot Wibald.—He urges him to be willing to be reconciled with the deposed Abbot Henry. 1210

**Letter CXVIII.**—From Abbot Wibald to Frederick, abbot of Saint Godehard.—Rejecting the praises offered him, he replies that he forgives from his heart all injuries committed against him by the deposed Henry, abbot of Corvey; but that only the pope can remit the censures imposed upon Henry by the Apostolic See. 1211

**Letter CXIX.**—From Abbot R. to Abbot Wibald.—He asks him to have mercy on Henry, formerly abbot of Corvey. 1213

**Letter CXX.**—From Pope Eugenius III to Abbot Wibald and the brethren of Corvey.—That the deposed Henry should find no place among them. 1214

**Letter CXXI.**—From Henry, archbishop of Mainz, to Wibald.—He gives an account of what he had done at the Council of Erfurt. 1214

**Letter CXXII.**—From Abbot Wibald to Pope Eugenius III.—He writes on behalf of the abbot of Saint Medard against Baldwin, canon of Liège. 1215

**Letter CXXIII.**—From Abbot Wibald to all the faithful of the parish of Lienwart.—Concerning the negligence of four priests. 1216

**Letter CXXIV.**—From Thiebold to Wibald.—Concerning the abbess of Geseke. 1217

**Letter CXXV.**—From Abbot Wibald to Provost Thiebold.—Concerning the abbess of Geseke. 1217

**Letter CXXVI.**—From Abbot Wibald to Arnold, archbishop of Cologne.—Concerning certain ministerials who had conspired against him. 1218

**Letter CXXVII.**—From Emperor Conrad to Abbot Wibald.—What befell him while he was besieging Damascus. 1219

**Letter CXXVIII.**—From Henry, bishop of Minden, to Abbot Wibald.—He wishes to make use of the counsel of the bishops of Paderborn and Münster regarding the dispute between them. 1219

**Letter CXXIX.**—From Bernard, bishop of Hildesheim, to Abbot Wibald.—He intercedes for Henry, formerly abbot of Corvey, that he may be received into the cloister of his profession. 1220

**Letter CXXX.**—From the same Bernard to the monks of Corvey.—On the same subject. 1220

**Letter CXXXI.**—From Wibald to Bernard, bishop of Hildesheim.—He sets out at length the entire course of his election as abbot of Corvey and the events which followed it. 1221

**Letter CXXXII.**—From the monks of Corvey to Bernard, bishop of Hildesheim.—They set forth three reasons which deter them from receiving the deposed former Abbot Henry. 1235

**Letter CXXXIII.**—A letter of Abbot Wibald.—Concerning an agreement between Reinher, provost, and Count Elvir. 1239

**Letter CXXXIV.**—From Abbot Wibald to Provost B.—The distinction between lying and telling a lie. 1240

**Letter CXXXV.**—From Cardinals Theotwin and Guy to Henry, bishop of Minden.—They rebuke him because he had forbidden divine offices to be celebrated in the church of Kemnade. 1240

**Letter CXXXVI.**—From Abbot Wibald to his monks of Stavelot.—He mourns the death of his brethren, while rejoicing in their blessed departure; but he is especially grieved by the passing of E., in whom more defects of obstinacy were found than was expedient. 1240

**Letter CXXXVII.**—From Abbot Wibald to Bernard, bishop of Paderborn.—He leaves a certain case of his to be decided by Bernard’s judgment. 1242

**Letter CXXXVIII.**—From Bernard, bishop of Paderborn, to Wibald.—A reply to the preceding letter. 1242

**Letter CXXXIX.**—From Cardinal Guy to Anselm, bishop of Havelberg.—He communicates his will to him through the legate to Poland. 1243

**Letter CXL.**—From the same to the same.—He wishes to be informed of his condition. 1243

**Letter CXLI.**—From Anselm, bishop of Havelberg, to Abbot Wibald. [Col. 1774]—He complains that Wibald, his friend, does not write to him, and announces his forthcoming journey to the pope. 1243

**Letter CXLII.**—From Abbot Wibald to Anselm, bishop of Havelberg.—He commends certain affairs to him as he goes to Rome, especially on behalf of the abbot of Hersfeld. 1244

**Letter CXLIII.**—From Abbot Wibald to Pope Eugenius III.—He informs him of the state of the monastery of Fulda. 1246

**Letter CXLIV.**—From Abbot Wibald to Henry, abbot of Fulda and Hersfeld.—That he should kindly receive his scattered sons. 1246

**Letter CXLV.**—Notice concerning a duel commuted into an oath. 1247

**Letter CXLVI.**—From Manegold to Abbot Wibald.—He praises Wibald’s learning in the liberal arts. 1248

**Letter CXLVII.**—From Abbot Wibald to Manegold, schoolmaster.—A reply to the preceding letter. 1249

**Letter CXLVIII.**—From Abbot Wibald to Hartwig, archbishop of Bremen.—Hartwig the archbishop was angry with Wibald because, in the election of the bishop of Bremen, the votes of the electors seemed to converge upon Wibald; Wibald seeks reconciliation with him. 1257

**Letter CXLIX.**—From Abbot Wibald to H., bishop of Minden.—He asks him to appoint a time and place at which they may meet each other to settle their affairs amicably. 1258

**Letter CL.**—From Abbot Wibald to the abbot of Saint Godehard.—He excuses his inability to attend the assembly of the abbots of Saxony and urges that the cause of the abbot of Hersfeld be discussed there. 1259

**Letter CLI.**—From Abbot Wibald to B., abbot of Saint Michael.—He congratulates him and his church on his election. 1260

**Letter CLII.**—From Abbot Wibald to H., bishop-elect of Bremen.—He writes on behalf of the abbot of Hersfeld, whom his own monks had expelled. 1260

**Letter CLIII.**—From the monks of Corvey to Abbot Wibald.—Concerning a certain boy who died by accident at Kemnade. 1262

**Letter CLIV.**—From Abbot Wibald to his monks of Corvey.—He consoles them over the death of a brother who died at Kemnade. 1263

**Letter CLV.**—From Abbot Wibald to the bishop of Minden.—That he should deign to reconcile the church of Kemnade. 1263

**Letter CLVI.**—From Abbot Wibald to his monks of Malmedy.—Concerning a disorderly brother who had cast off the monastic habit and departed. 1264

**Letter CLVII.**—From Abbot Wibald to Walter, a monk.—He charges the wicked monk Walter with many crimes. 1265

**Letter CLVIII.**—From Abbot Wibald to his monks of Corvey.—Concerning H. and A., ministerials of the monastery of Corvey, received into his favour. 1267

**Letter CLIX.**—From G., abbot of Solemniac, to Abbot Wibald.—That they should give thanks to Saint Remaclus on behalf of the people of Solemniac, whom he had delivered from tribulations. 1267

**Letter CLX.**—From Abbot Wibald to the monks of Solemniac.—A reply to the preceding letter. 1268

**Letter CLXI.**—From Abbot Wibald to H., bishop of Utrecht.—Concerning the provision of a pastor for the church of Lienward. 1269

**Letter CLXII.**—From Emperor Conrad to Wibald.—He praises his fidelity and states that he arrived at Regensburg on the octave of Pentecost. 1269

**Letter CLXIII.**—From Wibald to Emperor Conrad.—He congratulates him on his return from the holy expedition, urges him to help those unjustly oppressed, and complains of the bishop of Minden. 1270

**Letter CLXIV.**—From Pope Eugenius III to Emperor Conrad.—He consoles him over the unhappy outcome of the Jerusalem expedition, sends envoys to him, and wishes to be informed of his condition. 1271

**Letter CLXV.**—From Cardinal G. to Abbot Wibald.—He orders him to come to him, intending to use his counsel. 1271

**Letter CLXVI.**—From Abbot Wibald to Cardinal G.—A reply to the preceding letter. 1271

**Letter CLXVII.**—From Emperor Conrad to H., bishop of Minden.—He rebukes him for harassing the brethren of Corvey. 1272

**Letter CLXVIII.**—From Abbot Wibald to H., bishop of Minden.—He complains that he has not reconciled the church of Kemnade. 1273

**Letter CLXIX.**—From Emperor Conrad to Abbot Wibald.—Having returned from the holy pilgrimage, he invites him to court. 1273

[Col. 1775]

**Letter CLXX.**—From H. to Abbot Wibald.—That the king needs his counsel. 1274

**Letter CLXXI.**—From Abbot Wibald to Peter, abbot of Cluny.—Concerning the dispute between the churches of Nameka and Marcha. 1274

**Letter CLXXII.**—From Emperor Conrad to H., bishop of Minden.—He rebukes him because he had neither reconciled the church of Kemnade nor taken care to fulfil the emperor’s commands. 1275

**Letter CLXXIII.**—From Cardinal Legate G. to Henry, bishop of Minden.—He commands him to reconcile the church of Kemnade. 1276

**Letter CLXXIV.**—From B., bishop of Paderborn, and Abbot Wibald to Pope Eugenius III.—Concerning the dispute between Z., provost, and the bishop of Speyer. 1276

**Letter CLXXV.**—From Emperor Conrad to Pope Eugenius III.—That he should deign to confer the provostship of Xanten upon his chaplain Thiebold, canonically elected. 1277

**Letter CLXXVI.**—From Abbot Wibald to Cardinal Guy and chancellor.—That the provostship of Xanten should be conferred upon Chaplain Thiebold. 1277

**Letter CLXXVII.**—From Pope Eugenius III to King Conrad.—He confirms the provostship of Xanten to his chaplain Thiebold, provided that he relinquish the other provostship which he had previously held. 1278

**Letter CLXXVIII.**—From A. to Abbot Wibald.—He gives thanks for Thiebold’s obtaining the provostship of Xanten and asks for Wibald’s and the emperor’s intercession with the pope on his behalf against the archbishop of Cologne. 1278

**Letter CLXXIX.**—From Thiebold, provost of Xanten, to Abbot Wibald.—On the same subject. 1278

**Letter CLXXX.**—From P., bishop of Ascoli, to Abbot Wibald.—That he should deign to intercede for him with the emperor. 1279

**Letter CLXXXI.**—From Emperor Conrad to Pope Eugenius III.—He writes on behalf of Thiebold, provost of Xanten, and Otto, a cleric. 1279

**Letter CLXXXII.**—From Abbot Wibald to his successors.—Concerning certain things accomplished during his administration. 1280

**Letter CLXXXIII.**—From Pope Eugenius III to Emperor Conrad.—At his request, he again confirms the election of the provost of Xanten and postpones the deposition of the archbishop of Cologne. 1280

**Letter CLXXXIV.**—From Abbot Wibald to the provost of Cologne.—Concerning the younger king’s victory over Welf, the forthcoming conference at Fulda to which he invites him, and the Roman legation. 1281

**Letter CLXXXV.**—From H., bishop of Constance, to Abbot Wibald.—That, by imperial authority, he should procure the release of his kinsman Henry, detained by Welf. 1281

**Letter CLXXXVI.**—From Abbot Wibald to Hermann, bishop of Constance.—He writes that he advised the emperor, after his victory, to continue pressing his enemies, but that the contrary opinion prevailed. 1282

**Letter CLXXXVII.**—From Emperor Conrad to E., emperor of Constantinople.—He excuses himself because illness prevented him from keeping his promises. 1283

**Letter CLXXXVIII.**—From Emperor Conrad to the empress of the Greeks.—He excuses himself because, seized with fever, he had been unable to fulfil the promises made to the emperor of Constantinople; he reports the victory over Welf and asks the emperor’s niece in marriage for his son Henry. 1284

**Letter CLXXXIX.**—From King Henry the Younger to Emmanuel, emperor of Constantinople.—He informs him of the victory he had gained over Welf. 1286

**Letter CXC.**—From King Henry the Younger to the empress.—He informs her of the victory he had gained over Welf. 1287

**Letter CXCI.**—From Abbot Wibald to Arnold, chief provost of the Church of Cologne.—That he should come to Fulda for the emperor’s court; it is not fitting that the king should request two provostships from the pope for Thiebold. 1288

**Letter CXCII.**—From Abbot Wibald to Pope Eugenius III.—He writes on behalf of the canons of the collegiate church of Saint Bartholomew in the city of Liège. 1289

**Letter CXCIII.**—From Abbot Wibald to Stephen, prior of Saint James at Liège.—He urges him to undertake the burden of pastoral care, to which he had been canonically elected but which he refused out of humility. 1290

**Letter CXCIV.**—From Abbot Wibald to Theobald, provost of Xanten.—He rejoices that his favour toward him has been effective. 1290

**Letter CXCV.**—From Emperor Conrad to Pope Eugenius III.—That he should kindly receive Arnold, archbishop of Cologne, and send him back restored to his see. 1291

[Col. 1776]

**Letter CXCVI.**—From Abbot Wibald to Cardinal Guy.—A legation to the pope has been imposed upon him by the king. 1292

**Letter CXCVII.**—From Emperor Conrad to the nuns of Quedlinburg.—No reason appears to him why they should refrain from divine offices. 1292

**Letter CXCVIII.**—From John, abbot of Fritheselle, to Abbot Wibald.—He writes that he will go to the king. 1292

**Letter CXCIX.**—From Abbot Wibald to John of Fritheselle.—As he goes to the king, Wibald commends to him the affairs of his monastery of Corvey, especially the union of the convent of Visbek. 1293

**Letter CC.**—From Abbot Wibald to Emperor Conrad.—Concerning the rebellion of the abbess of Kemnade, against whom he implores the emperor’s protection. 1294

**Letter CCI.**—From Abbot Wibald to H., notary of the royal court.—He commends to him before the emperor the Corvey monks’ cause concerning Kemnade and Visbek. 1295

**Letter CCII.**—From Henry, notary of the royal court, to Abbot Wibald.—A reply to the preceding letter. 1296

**Letter CCIII.**—From Abbot Wibald to Emperor Conrad.—He laments that he has received no answer from him concerning the affairs of the church of Kemnade. 1297

**Letter CCIV.**—From Abbot Wibald to Henry, notary of the royal court.—He commends to him the causes of the monastery of Corvey. 1297

**Letter CCV.**—From R. to Abbot Wibald.—He asks him for certain books and promises him others. 1298

**Letter CCVI.**—From Abbot Wibald to R., provost of Hildesheim.—Concerning his own devotion to humane letters. 1298

**Letter CCVII.**—From an anonymous writer to Abbot Wibald.—He testifies his gratitude for benefits received from him and laments that some people seek to turn Wibald away from him. 1299

**Letter CCVIII.**—From Abbot Wibald to Bishop Anselm.—Concerning the king’s displeasure with him. 1300

**Letter CCIX.**—From R., provost, to Abbot Wibald.—A rumour is being spread that he is shortly to be elected archbishop of Cologne. 1300

**Letter CCX.**—From Abbot Wibald to Provost R.—A reply to the preceding letter. 1301

**Letter CCXI.**—From the senate and people of Rome to Emperor Conrad.—They urge the emperor to come to Rome, offering themselves and all that they possess to him against the pope and the Sicilian. 1301

**Letter CCXII.**—From Sixtus, Nicholas, and Guy, counsellors of the Roman curia, to Emperor Conrad.—On the same subject. 1303

**Letter CCXIII.**—From a certain senator to Emperor Conrad.—On the same subject. 1304

**Letter CCXIV.**—From Cardinal Guy to Abbot Wibald.—That he should turn Emperor Conrad away from undertaking any evil against the Roman Church. 1305

**Letter CCXV.**—From Emperor Conrad to Pope Eugenius III.—He commends to him the bishop of Regensburg, travelling toward Jerusalem. 1305

**Letter CCXVI.**—From Conrad to Emmanuel, emperor of Constantinople.—He commends to him the bishop of Regensburg, travelling to Jerusalem. 1306

**Letter CCXVII.**—From Abbot Wibald to Pope Eugenius III.—Concerning restoring, through the assistance of Abbot Eilulf, discipline wholly collapsed in the monastery of Murbach; he requests confirmation of Eilulf’s election. 1306

**Letter CCXVIII.**—From Abbot Wibald to Pope Eugenius III.—That the emperor is undertaking nothing against him, and concerning the victory gained by the younger king over Welf and Godebald. 1307

**Letter CCXIX.**—From Emperor Conrad to Pope Eugenius III.—He sends envoys to him and asks that Eilulf be confirmed by him as abbot of the monastery of Murbach, and that the cleric Otto be absolved. 1308

**Letter CCXX.**—From Abbot Wibald to H., his sister.—He congratulates her upon her election as abbess of the convent of Gerresheim. 1308

**Letter CCXXI.**—From Emperor Conrad to Pope Eugenius III.—He commends to him Peter, archbishop of Capua, through whose assistance he had recovered his health. 1309

**Letter CCXXII.**—From Pope Eugenius III to the prelates of Poland.—He rebukes them because they do not observe the sentence handed down and, that they may amend their ways, confirms the same sentence. 1309

**Letter CCXXIII.**—From G., cardinal-deacon, to Emperor Conrad.—Since he had laboured greatly in his legation on behalf of the duke of Poland, he asks Conrad to provide him assistance. 1309

**Letter CCXXIV.**—From Abbot Wibald to E., emperor of Constantinople.—He wishes God to make him victorious over the tyrant of Sicily, and that he renew and strengthen the alliance formerly made with Emperor Conrad. 1310

[Col. 1777]

**Letter CCXXV.**—From Abbot Wibald to Cardinal G.—Concerning Emperor Conrad’s alliance with the emperor of Constantinople against the king of Sicily, which kept the pope especially anxious. 1311

**Letter CCXXVI.**—From Emperor Conrad to Pope Eugenius III.—He sends to him as envoy Master Henry, notary of his court. 1312

**Letter CCXXVII.**—From Abbot Wibald to Pope Eugenius III.—He informs him of, and requests confirmation of, the election of Marquard, abbot of Fulda. 1312

**Letter CCXXVIII.**—From Abbot Wibald to Pope Eugenius III.—Prevented from fulfilling the legation to the pope imposed upon him, he sends him through a substitute envoy certain petitions for the monastery of Corvey. 1314

**Letter CCXXIX.**—From H. of the Moravians to Abbot Wibald.—The desired journey to the pope for him.

He entreats [him]. 1315

EPISTLE CCXXX.—From D., bishop of Prague, to Abbot Wibald.—As Wibald is about to depart for the pope, he sends him a gift and asks him to remember him before the pontiff. 1316

EPISTLE CCXXXI.—From the monk Emelerus to Abbot Wibald.—He commends to him A., the bearer of this letter. 1317

EPISTLE CCXXXII.—From H., bishop of Hamenburg, to Abbot Wibald.—Concerning the abbot of Resveld, whom his own monks had expelled. 1317

EPISTLE CCXXXIII.—From Emperor Conrad to Abbot Wibald.—Concerning H., duke of Saxony, who had not come to court but had attempted to invade the duchy of Bavaria. 1318

EPISTLE CCXXXIV.—From the monks of Stavelot to Abbot Wibald.—They ask him to pardon J., a monk of Corvey, for his former offences. 1318

EPISTLE CCXXXV.—From Anselm, bishop of Havelberg, to Abbot Wibald.—He declares that henceforth he wishes to reside in his church with his brethren, whom he praises. 1319

EPISTLE CCXXXVI.—From R., a monk, to Abbot Wibald.—He gives an account of what he has done for the monastery’s benefit and asks him for a prebend for his nine-year-old kinsman. 1320

EPISTLE CCXXXVII.—From the monks of Stavelot to Abbot Wibald.—They ask him, if possible, to return to them, in order that he may press their complaint against Hengebach before the king. 1321

EPISTLE CCXXXVIII.—From the monks of Stavelot to Emperor Conrad.—They complain of Goswin of Hengebach and his brother Everard. 1322

EPISTLE CCXXXIX.—From John, notary, to Prince R. and Count Ric.—Concerning Welf’s alliance with the Sicilian king. 1323

EPISTLE CCXL.—From Abbot Wibald to Emperor Conrad.—He advises him that he has nothing to fear, that the conference at Cranaha must not be neglected, and, finally, that the enemy must be pursued. 1323

EPISTLE CCXLI.—From Abbot Wibald to H., archbishop of Bremen.—He gives thanks because he visited his monastery; urges him to remain longer among his brethren and to inspect the books of the library; and concerns the forthcoming conference of bishops at Minden. 1324

EPISTLE CCXLII.—From Abbot Wibald to Henry, bishop of Minden.—He complains that Henry refused either to accept or to grant the peace which had been offered and sought. 1325

EPISTLE CCXLIII.—From Abbot Wibald to H., archbishop of Mainz.—He asks him to absolve Folcuin of Sualemberg, who had complained concerning him and the bishop of Paderborn and had at last become obedient. 1327

EPISTLE CCXLIV.—From Henry, bishop of Minden, to Abbot Wibald.—He clears himself of the accusations previously made against him by Wibald. 1328

EPISTLE CCXLV.—From Abbot Wibald to Henry, bishop of Minden.—Reply to the preceding letter. 1329

EPISTLE CCXLVI.—From Henry, bishop of Minden, to Bernard, bishop of Paderborn.—Concerning the dispute between himself and the abbot of Corvey. 1330

EPISTLE CCXLVII.—From Bernard, bishop of Paderborn, to Henry, bishop of Minden.—He declares himself ready to resume peace negotiations between Henry and the abbot of Corvey. 1330

EPISTLE CCXLVIII.—From Abbot Wibald to his monks of Stavelot.—He manifests his paternal affection for them and excuses himself for not having returned to them sooner. 1331

EPISTLE CCXLIX.—From Emperor Conrad to Henry, duke of Saxony.—That he should ensure that the monks of Corvey enjoy the church of Kaminat. 1332

EPISTLE CCL.—From Emperor Conrad to Abbot Wibald.—That he should remain at Corvey until the feast of St James. 1333

EPISTLE CCLI.—From Pope Eugenius III to Abbot Wibald. [Col. 1778]—That he should excommunicate Godebald, canon of Minden, unless he restores to Everard the church of Hemeringen which he had taken away. 1333

EPISTLE CCLII.—From Abbot Wibald to Godebald, canon of Minden.—That he should restore to Everard the church of Hemeringen which he had taken away; otherwise Wibald announces that, once excommunicated, he can be absolved by the pope alone. 1333

EPISTLE CCLIII.—From Pope Eugenius III to Abbot Wibald.—He praises Wibald’s zeal for the Roman Church and, at his request, writes to the bishop of Minden and the archbishop of Bremen. 1334

EPISTLE CCLIV.—From Pope Eugenius III to Henry, bishop of Minden.—The church of Kaminat does not require reconciliation because of an unexpected occurrence and the death of a certain monk; he directs that what was taken from that church be restored. 1334

EPISTLE CCLV.—From Pope Eugenius III to H., archbishop of Bremen.—He commends Abbot Wibald to him and directs that the estates taken from the church of Kaminat be restored. 1334

EPISTLE CCLVI.—From Emperor Conrad to Abbot Wibald.—That he should prepare himself for the Roman embassy. 1334

EPISTLE CCLVII.—From Pope Eugenius III to Emperor Conrad.—He welcomes the embassy by which the affairs of Church and kingdom are to be strengthened. He has entrusted the affair of the monastery of Murbach to the bishop of Lausanne; and concerning Otto, who had cut off a cleric’s nose. 1335

EPISTLE CCLVIII.—From H., notary, to Abbot Wibald.—Why he is accustomed to write to him more briefly. 1335

EPISTLE CCLIX.—From G., cardinal, to Abbot Wibald.—He praises Wibald’s zeal for the Roman Church. 1335

EPISTLE CCLX.—From Abbot Wibald to Emperor Conrad.—He excuses himself from undertaking, at his own expense, the Roman embassy. 1336

EPISTLE CCLXI.—From Abbot Wibald to Arnold, provost of Cologne.—He sets forth how great the expenses were that he had already incurred for the emperor and his empire. 1337

EPISTLE CCLXII.—From Emperor Conrad to Abbot Wibald.—The embassy to the pope cannot be undertaken through anyone other than Wibald and his chancellor. 1338

EPISTLE CCLXIII.—From Abbot Wibald to Arnold, provost of Cologne.—He writes that the Roman embassy must necessarily be undertaken and asks him to name a day on which he may meet him. 1339

EPISTLE CCLXIV.—From the Chancellor to Abbot Wibald.—He excuses himself from undertaking the Roman embassy. 1339

EPISTLE CCLXV.—From Abbot Wibald to A., chancellor.—He urges him that, once the difficulties have been overcome, they should undertake the Roman embassy. 1340

EPISTLE CCLXVI.—From Abbot Wibald to Henry, bishop of Minden.—Concerning their mutual reconciliation. 1341

EPISTLE CCLXVII.—From Emperor Conrad to Henry, bishop of Minden.—He is pleased that Henry has returned to peace with the abbot of Corvey and remits every offence he had incurred. 1342

EPISTLE CCLXVIII.—From Henry, bishop of Minden, to Abbot Wibald.—He defends the innocence of Godebald, whom Everard, priest of Hemerim, was accusing. 1343

EPISTLE CCLXIX.—From H., duke of Bavaria and Saxony, to Abbot Wibald.—He receives the possessions of the church of Corvey under his protection. 1344

EPISTLE CCLXX.—From Abbot Wibald to the prior and brethren of Haster.—That, content with the ancient custom of the place, they should return to concord with their brethren of Walciodorus. 1344

EPISTLE CCLXXI.—From Abbot Wibald to Stephen, bishop of Metz.—That he may deign to protect the privileges of the monastery of Walciodorus and restrain the audacity of the men of Haster. 1345

EPISTLE CCLXXII.—From Stephen, bishop of Metz, to Abbot Wibald.—That he should compel the monks of Haster to obey the church of Walciodorus. 1346

EPISTLE CCLXXIII.—From Abbot Wibald to Theoderic, abbot of Walciodorus.—He promises his protection and directs him to investigate the intentions of the men of Haster and send him the privileges of kings and popes. 1347

EPISTLE CCLXXIV.—From Stephen, bishop of Metz, to Theoderic, abbot of Walciodorus.—He summons him, accused of squandering property, to the synod of Metz. 1347

EPISTLE CCLXXV.—From Abbot Wibald to Stephen, bishop of Metz.—He complains of the rebellion of the monks of Haster and of the contents of the preceding letter. 1348

EPISTLE CCLXXVI.—Ordinance of Emperor Conrad II for the monastery of Walciodorus.—Through the intervention of Abbot Wibald, he confirms the privileges of the monastery of Walciodorus. 1350

EPISTLE CCLXXVII.—From Emperor Conrad to H., bishop of Liège. [Col. 1779]—He promises vengeance upon the enemies of the church of Liège and directs him also to refrain from troubling the church of Stavelot. 1352

EPISTLE CCLXXVIII.—From Emperor Conrad to Abbot Wibald.—He excuses him from the Roman embassy. 1353

EPISTLE CCLXXIX.—From Henry, bishop of Liège, to Abbot Wibald.—He complains of Henry, count of La Roche, and of the count of Namur. 1353

EPISTLE CCLXXX.—From Abbot Wibald to Pope Eugenius III.—He writes that he had been prepared to undertake the Roman embassy and commends to him the bearer of the present letter. 1354

EPISTLE CCLXXXI.—From Abbot Wibald to Emperor Conrad.—He complains of the bishop of Liège and of the counts of Namur, La Roche, and Montaigu. 1354

EPISTLE CCLXXXII.—From R. of Stavelot to Abbot Wibald.—Concerning proceedings at Liège against the incendiaries of the estates of Stavelot. 1355

EPISTLE CCLXXXIII.—From Abbot Wibald to the bishop of Minden.—Concerning the case of Master Godebald and the priest Everard. 1357

EPISTLE CCLXXXIV.—From the provost, dean, and canons of Minden to Abbot Wibald.—They entrust to him for settlement the peace unsuccessfully attempted between Godebald and Everard. 1358

EPISTLE CCLXXXV.—From Abbot Wibald to Godebald.—He informs him of the terms of peace concluded with Everard the priest. 1358

EPISTLE CCLXXXVI.—From Abbot Wibald to Henry, bishop of Minden.—Peace having been made between Godebald and Everard, he directs him to secure justice for Everard regarding things taken from him by others. 1359

EPISTLE CCLXXXVII.—From Abbot Wibald to H., archbishop of Mainz.—Concerning the dissolution of Folcuin of Sualemberg’s marriage, on account of his wife’s concealed illness. 1360

EPISTLE CCLXXXVIII.—From Abbot Wibald to Henry, bishop of Minden.—He writes on behalf of Regenbern, a canon whom the abbess of Blessed Mary on the Mountain was harassing. 1361

EPISTLE CCLXXXIX.—From Abbot Wibald to W., senior provost of the church of Minden.—He writes on behalf of Regenbern the canon. 1361

EPISTLE CCXC.—From H., duke of Saxony and Bavaria, to Abbot Wibald.—He asks him to be present with him before the king at the court of Regensburg. 1362

EPISTLE CCXCI.—From Abbot Wibald to Pope Eugenius III.—He writes on behalf of Regenbern the canon. 1362

EPISTLE CCXCII.—From Abbot Wibald to A., provost of Cologne.—He gives thanks for the benefits bestowed. 1362

EPISTLE CCXCIII.—From Abbot Wibald to his monks of Stavelot.—Uncertain whether he ought to govern two abbeys distant from one another, he asks their advice concerning what ought to be done in so great a danger to himself. 1363

EPISTLE CCXCIV.—From Abbot Wibald to H., monk of Stavelot.—He explains the reasons that deter him from retaining the abbacy of Stavelot. 1364

EPISTLE CCXCV.—From the monks of Stavelot to Abbot Wibald.—They dissuade him from relinquishing the abbacy of Stavelot. 1364

EPISTLE CCXCVI.—From Henry, monk of Stavelot, to Abbot Wibald.—On the same subject. 1365

EPISTLE CCXCVII.—From Abbot Wibald to his monks of Stavelot.—He writes that they acted too hastily in giving advice; that the people of Malmedy and other neighbours should also have been consulted; and that prayers to God ought above all to have been made. 1366

EPISTLE CCXCVIII.—From Abbot Wibald to Henry, monk of Stavelot.—He persists in his intention to resign the abbatial dignity of Stavelot and desires to know God’s good pleasure in this matter. 1367

EPISTLE CCXCIX.—From the monks of Stavelot to Abbot Wibald.—They state that the wishes of the people of Malmedy agree with their own in urging him to remain. 1368

EPISTLE CCC.—From Henry, monk of Stavelot, to Abbot Wibald.—That the best of fathers should not abandon his obedient sons. 1369

EPISTLE CCCI.—From Henry, monk of Stavelot, to Abbot Wibald.—Again he entreats him not to cast aside the abbatial dignity of the monastery of Stavelot. 1370

EPISTLE CCCII.—From the monks of Corvey to Abbot Wibald.—That for the present he should not resign the abbacy of Stavelot. 1371

EPISTLE CCCIII.—From Abbot Wibald to H., monk of Corvey.—He appoints him prior of the monastery of Corvey. 1371

EPISTLE CCCIV.—From H., prior, and the convent of the monastery of Corvey to Abbot Wibald.—They complain of the monastery’s provost, who denied them the necessities of life. 1372

EPISTLE CCCV.—From Abbot Wibald to his monks of Corvey. [Col. 1780]—He praises their patience in enduring a lack of necessities and excuses himself for being unable to return to them so soon. 1373

EPISTLE CCCVI.—From Emperor Conrad to Pope Eugenius.—That he should confirm the election of Hermann, bishop of Utrecht, and absolve the count of Are from excommunication. 1374

EPISTLE CCCVII.—From Abbot Wibald to B., archdeacon of Liège.—He excuses himself from the conference at Huy. 1374

EPISTLE CCCVIII.—From Abbot Wibald to the brethren of Gladbach.—He offers them his counsel and assistance, and addresses the injuries inflicted upon them by ministeriales. 1375

EPISTLE CCCIX.—From Henry, bishop of Liège, to Pope Eugenius III.—He asks for confirmation of the election of Arnold, archbishop of Cologne. 1375

EPISTLE CCCX.—From the church of Cologne to Pope Eugenius III.—Concerning the election as archbishop of Cologne of Arnold, provost of the greater church of St Peter. 1376

EPISTLE CCCXI.—From Abbot Wibald to Arnold, archbishop-elect of Cologne.—He wishes him every prosperity. 1376

EPISTLE CCCXII.—From Emperor Conrad to Henry, archbishop of Mainz.—He reproves him because he deprived the archbishop-elect of Cologne, who had not yet assented to his own election, of the provostship of Lempurch. 1376

EPISTLE CCCXIII.—From Emperor Conrad to Pope Eugenius III.—Concerning the election of Arnold as archbishop of Cologne, which he asks to be confirmed. 1377

EPISTLE CCCXIV.—From Arnold to Abbot Wibald.—The clergy, nobles, and ministeriales delay his journey to the pope until peace is fully secured. 1377

EPISTLE CCCXV.—From Abbot Wibald to Arnold of Cologne.—He rejoices in Arnold’s prosperity; concerning making peace with the bishop of Liège. He urges him not to defer his Roman journey and to receive honourably the envoys of the Apostolic See passing through Cologne. 1378

EPISTLE CCCXVI.—From Emperor Conrad to Abbot Wibald.—He directs him to come to Würzburg by the appointed date for a conference of princes. 1379

EPISTLE CCCXVII.—From Heribert, chaplain, to Henry, prior of Corvey.—That he should send the king’s letters to Wibald without delay. 1379

EPISTLE CCCXVIII.—From Sweyn, king of Denmark, to Emperor Conrad.—He gives thanks for benefits and asks him to continue his protection. 1380

EPISTLE CCCXIX.—From Canute, king of Denmark, to Emperor Conrad.—Deprived of his kingdom, he flees to him. 1380

EPISTLE CCCXX.—From Abbot Wibald to Manuel, emperor of Constantinople.—Emperor Conrad is preparing an expedition against the Sicilian. 1381

EPISTLE CCCXXI.—From the emperor of Constantinople to Abbot Wibald.—He offers Emperor Conrad his forces against the Sicilian. 1382

EPISTLE CCCXXII.—From Conrad to the Romans.—He informs them of his impending arrival in Italy and meanwhile sends envoys to them. 1383

EPISTLE CCCXXIII.—From Emperor Conrad to Pope Eugenius III.—He declares that he is preparing an Italian expedition for the benefit of the Church and commends the archbishop of Bremen and Abbot Wibald. 1383

EPISTLE CCCXXIV.—From Emperor Conrad to the Pisans.—Concerning his expedition into Italy against the Sicilian. 1383

EPISTLE CCCXXV.—From Arnold, archbishop of Cologne, to Abbot Wibald.—He asks him to wait, since they are to return to the emperor together. 1384

EPISTLE CCCXXVI.—From Pope Eugenius to the people of Cologne.—He sends back to them Archbishop Arnold, consecrated by his own hand and invested with the pallium, commanding them to obey him. 1385

EPISTLE CCCXXVII.—From Pope Eugenius to Emperor Conrad.—He has honourably received Conrad’s envoys and has complied with his wishes in every respect. 1385

EPISTLE CCCXXVIII.—From Pope Eugenius III to the bishop of Liège.—That he should compel the counts of Loon and Montaigu to restore what they had taken from the monastery of Stavelot. 1385

EPISTLE CCCXXIX.—From Cardinals Gregory and James to Henry, bishop of Liège.—That he should see to the redress of injuries inflicted upon the monastery of Stavelot by the count of Namur. 1385

EPISTLE CCCXXX.—From Pope Eugenius to H., archbishop of Bremen.—That he should see to the restoration of estates taken by his parishioners from the monastery of Kaminat. 1386

EPISTLE CCCXXXI.—From the same to Henry, archbishop of Mainz.—That he should see to the restoration of what his parishioners had taken from the monastery of Corvey. 1386

EPISTLE CCCXXXII.—From the same to Bernard, bishop of Paderborn.—That, under the constraint of anathema, he should compel Witikind to restore what he had taken from the monastery of Corvey. [Col. 1781] 1386

EPISTLE CCCXXXIII.—From the same to Hermann, bishop of Utrecht.—That he should preserve the estates of the monastery of Corvey located in his diocese. 1386

EPISTLE CCCXXXIV.—From the same to Ulric, bishop of Halberstadt.—That he should restrain his parishioners who trouble the brethren of Corvey. 1386

EPISTLE CCCXXXV.—From the same to Henry, duke of Saxony.—He commends to him Wibald, abbot of Corvey. 1386

EPISTLE CCCXXXVI.—From the same to the bishop of Verden.—He complains that the bishop’s brother and other parishioners are seizing the property of the monastery of Kaminat. 1386

EPISTLE CCCXXXVII.—From the same to the bishop of Minden.—That he should continue to benefit the monastery of Corvey. 1387

EPISTLE CCCXXXVIII.—From the same to the abbot of Lüneburg.—That Henry, abbot of Corvey, after being deposed from office, has not been restored. 1387

EPISTLE CCCXXXIX.—From the same to prelates, counts, and barons.—That they should attend Emperor Conrad in the Italian expedition. 1387

EPISTLE CCCXL.—From Abbot Wibald to his monks of Corvey.—He announces his return from the Roman embassy and the emperor’s death, ordering solemn funeral rites to be celebrated for him. 1387

EPISTLE CCCXLI.—From Abbot Wibald to Stephen, bishop of Metz.—That he should postpone the matter of the election of the abbot of Walciodorus until a new king of the Romans is chosen. 1388

EPISTLE CCCXLII.—From Abbot Wibald to the men of Walciodorus.—He mourns with them over the abbot’s death and sends the privilege which he had obtained for them from Pope Eugenius, together with copies of his letters to the bishop of Metz and to the men of Haster. 1389

EPISTLE CCCXLIII.—From Abbot Wibald to the men of Haster.—That they should defer proceedings concerning the controversy between themselves and the men of Walciodorus until, after the emperor’s election, he comes to them. 1389

EPISTLE CCCXLIV.—From Abbot Wibald to Pope Eugenius III.—Concerning the death of Emperor Conrad, the election of Frederick, and what followed it concerning the Italian expedition. 1390

EPISTLE CCCXLV.—From Emperor Frederick to Pope Eugenius III.—Through his envoys he informs him certainly of his election and promises sincere protection to the Roman Church. 1392

EPISTLE CCCXLVI.—From Abbot Wibald to E., bishop of Bamberg.—He gives him certain instructions to be observed in his embassy. 1392

EPISTLE CCCXLVII.—From Henry, notary, to Abbot Wibald.—That he should send the seal and golden bulls to the bishop of Bamberg. 1393

EPISTLE CCCXLVIII.—From Abbot Wibald to Henry, notary of the royal court.—Reply to the preceding letter. 1393

EPISTLE CCCXLIX.—From the monks of Walciodorus to Abbot Wibald.—They ask him to accept the governance of the monastery to which they had elected him. 1395

EPISTLE CCCL.—From Henry, bishop of Liège, to Stephen, bishop of Metz.—Against the monks of Haster, who wanted two abbots at Walciodorus. 1395

EPISTLE CCCLI.—From Henry, bishop of Liège, to the men of Walciodorus and Haster.—That they should choose such an abbot as may revive the discipline that is almost dead. 1396

EPISTLE CCCLII.—From Stephen, bishop of Metz, to Abbot Wibald.—He appoints him a day on which he may meet him. 1397

EPISTLE CCCLIII.—Agreement between King Frederick and Duke Bertolf. 1397

EPISTLE CCCLIV.—From Otto, bishop of Freising, to Abbot Wibald.—He explains a verse of a psalm. 1398

EPISTLE CCCLV.—From Abbot Wibald to Cardinal Jordan.—He gives thanks for benefits bestowed upon him and asks him to entrust the case of the provost of Xanten to the archbishop of Cologne for settlement. 1399

EPISTLE CCCLVI.—From Arnold, archbishop of Cologne, to Abbot Wibald.—He asks whether he may veil nuns at Pentecost. 1399

EPISTLE CCCLVII.—From Abbot Wibald to Arnold, archbishop of Cologne.—He replies to the preceding letter and treats certain other matters. 1400

EPISTLE CCCLVIII.—From Arnold, archbishop of Cologne, to Henry, bishop of Minden.—He complains that Wortlevius was mutilated by his faithful men at Henry’s command; he summons Henry to Cologne, together with all accomplices in this crime, to answer before him. 1401

EPISTLE CCCLIX.—From Abbot Wibald to Emperor Frederick.—He seeks vengeance for the outrage inflicted upon his people by Folcuin and Widikind. [Col. 1782] 1402

EPISTLE CCCLX.—From Abbot Wibald to Bernard, bishop of Paderborn.—That he should take vengeance upon Folcuin and Widikind, who had invaded and violated the church of the Corvey brethren. 1403

EPISTLE CCCLXI.—From Arnold, archbishop of Cologne, to Abbot Wibald.—He sympathizes with his adversities and informs him of the siege of Seyne Castle. 1404

EPISTLE CCCLXII.—From Arnold, archbishop of Cologne, to Pope Eugenius III.—He refers to him the case of the bishop of Minden concerning the blinding of the cleric Wortlievius, meanwhile pronouncing a sentence of excommunication upon the instigators and supporters of this crime. 1405

EPISTLE CCCLXIII.—From the nuns of Ostermere to Abbot Wibald.—They complain of his ministeriales, who were seizing the tithe granted to them by him. 1406

EPISTLE CCCLXIV.—From Abbot Wibald to Pope Eugenius III.—On behalf of Sifrid, abbot of Ullesheim, whom the bishop of Verden had expelled from his monastery without accusation or conviction. 1407

EPISTLE CCCLXV.—From Abbot Wibald to Arnold, archbishop of Cologne.—He congratulates him on his victory and intercedes with him for the bishop of Minden. 1408

EPISTLE CCCLXVI.—From Emperor Frederick to Abbot Wibald.—He promises that he will avenge Wibald’s injuries. 1409

EPISTLE CCCLXVII.—From Emperor Frederick to the monks of Corvey.—On the same subject. 1410

EPISTLE CCCLXVIII.—From Emperor Frederick to the citizens of Höxter.—On the same subject. 1410

EPISTLE CCCLXIX.—From Abbot Wibald to A., abbot of Monte.—He gives thanks because he charitably received the dispossessed Abbot Sifrid. 1410

EPISTLE CCCLXX.—From Henry, notary, to Abbot Wibald.—Folcuin and Widikind had been summoned before the emperor concerning injuries inflicted upon the brethren of Corvey; the bishop of Bamberg had been granted the abbey of Altaha; and so forth. 1411

EPISTLE CCCLXXI.—From Abbot Wibald to Pope Eugenius III.—Concerning the controversy publicly conducted between the abbot of St Lawrence at Liège and the abbot of St Giles on the Mountain. 1412

EPISTLE CCCLXXII.—From a certain regular canon to Abbot Wibald.—He puts before him several difficulties to be resolved. 1414

EPISTLE CCCLXXIII.—From Abbot Wibald to an anonymous correspondent.—Reply to the preceding letter. 1414

EPISTLE CCCLXXIV.—From Walter, abbot of St Lawrence at Liège, to Abbot Wibald.—He gives thanks because Wibald undertook his defence at the synod of Liège. 1416

EPISTLE CCCLXXV.—From Abbot Wibald to Pope Eugenius III.—Concerning letters which he wrote to him after the king’s election. 1416

EPISTLE CCCLXXVI.—From Abbot Wibald to Hermann, canon of Bonn.—He entrusts to him and to his niece the management of Castiniacum. 1417

EPISTLE CCCLXXVII.—From Abbot Wibald to Hillin, archbishop of Trier.—He congratulates him on his new dignity, offers him his services, and commends to him his brethren residing in the archbishop’s diocese. 1418

EPISTLE CCCLXXVIII.—From Pope Eugenius III to Emperor Frederick.—He congratulates him on his election, hoping that he will complete what Conrad began for the exaltation of the Church. 1419

EPISTLE CCCLXXIX.—From Bernard, bishop of Paderborn, to Abbot Wibald.—That he may deign to release his prior Henry, nominated as abbot of the monastery of Mary. 1419

EPISTLE CCCLXXX.—From Abbot Wibald to Bernard, bishop of Paderborn.—He excuses himself from releasing his prior. 1420

EPISTLE CCCLXXXI.—From Pope Eugenius to the chapter of Magdeburg.—That they should not support the bishop of Cice, invader of the church of Magdeburg. 1421

EPISTLE CCCLXXXII.—From the same to E. of Salzburg and other bishops.—He reproves them because they are too eager for the favour of princes, and he refuses the translation of C., bishop of Cice, to the see of Magdeburg. 1421

EPISTLE CCCLXXXIII.—From the same to Abbot Wibald.—He commends to him the case of A., bishop of Chur, and directs him to protect ecclesiastical immunities against laymen. 1421

EPISTLE CCCLXXXIV.—From Wetzel to Emperor Frederick.—He urges him, having shaken off the yoke of the supreme pontiff, to receive the empire from the Roman senate and people. 1421

EPISTLE CCCLXXXV.—Peace agreement between Pope Eugenius and Emperor Frederick. 1424

EPISTLE CCCLXXXVI.—From Pope Eugenius III to Abbot Wibald.—He commends to him his envoys to Emperor Frederick. [Col. 1783] 1424

EPISTLE CCCLXXXVII.—From Emperor Frederick to Manuel, emperor of Constantinople.—He desires to take a wife from Manuel’s bloodline and meanwhile prepares an expedition into Sicily. 1425

EPISTLE CCCLXXXVIII.—From Abbot Wibald to Manuel, emperor of Constantinople.—He urges him toward sincere concord with Emperor Frederick, whom he has persuaded to take a wife from Manuel’s bloodline. 1426

EPISTLE CCCLXXXIX.—From Cardinals Bernard and Gregory to O., bishop of Halberstadt.—That he should restrain Liudelf and Frederick the Count Palatine, who were harassing the monastery of Corvey. 1426

EPISTLE CCCXC.—From Cardinals Bernard and Gregory to Pope Eugenius.—They commend to him the bearer of the present letter. 1427

EPISTLE CCCXCI.—From Cardinal Gregory to Abbot Wibald.—Having been recalled after the pope’s death, he summons certain bishops to Worms and wishes to enjoy Wibald’s presence before the emperor. 1427

EPISTLE CCCXCII.—From Cardinals Bernard and Gregory to Abbot Wibald.—Since they are to have a conference before the king, they ask him to come to Würzburg. 1427

EPISTLE CCCXCIII.—From Abbot Wibald to Pope Anastasius.—He congratulates him on his election and seeks his favour. 1428

EPISTLE CCCXCIV.—From Abbot Wibald to Cardinal Bernard.—He congratulates him on his happy return to the city and asks his protection for the monastery of Corvey, and the protection of Gregory, Bernard’s colleague, for the monastery of Stavelot. 1429

EPISTLE CCCXCV.—From Abbot Wibald to Cardinal Gregory.—On the same subject. 1429

EPISTLE CCCXCVI.—From Hu. de Baucio to Abbot Wibald.—That he should make known to the emperor how much he suffers from the count of Barcelona on account of the emperor’s service. 1430

EPISTLE CCCXCVII.—From A. to Abbot Wibald.—That he should enable him to enjoy the grant bestowed upon him by the emperor. 1431

EPISTLE CCCXCVIII.—From Stephen, bishop of Metz, to Abbot Wibald.—He seeks some consolation from him and asks him, through the emperor, to procure redress for the dishonour inflicted upon himself and the Church. 1431

EPISTLE CCCXCIX.—From Emperor Frederick to Abbot Wibald.—He has ordered the count of Sumereburc to make redress for injuries done to Wibald; he desires Wibald’s presence at Cologne. 1432

EPISTLE CD.—From the monks of Stavelot to Abbot Wibald.—Having suffered much from adversaries and fearing the burning of their church, they ask him to come to them to settle everything peaceably. 1432

EPISTLE CDI.—From Abbot Wibald to Henry, count of Salmes.—He recounts all the damages inflicted by Henry’s people upon the monastery of Stavelot and asks that they be made good. 1433

EPISTLE CDII.—From Henry, count of Salmes, to Abbot Wibald.—He leaves all their controversies to be settled by Wibald’s judgment. 1434

EPISTLE CDIII.—Letter of Abbot Wibald to his successors.—Concerning a certain abuse reformed by Abbot Poppo II. 1434

EPISTLE CDIV.—From Cardinal Gregory to Abbot Wibald.—Concerning a ring granted to him by the Apostolic See and to be conveyed through Cardinal Gerhard. 1436

EPISTLE CDV.—From Pope Anastasius IV to Abbot Wibald.—He grants him the use of the ring for his lifetime only. 1436

EPISTLE CDVI.—From O. to the dean, archdeacons, etc., of Halberstadt.—He declares Frederick, Count Palatine, excommunicated. 1437

EPISTLE CDVII.—From Manuel, emperor of Constantinople, to Abbot Wibald.—Concerning the marriage of Emperor Frederick. 1438

EPISTLE CDVIII.—From Abbot Wibald to Emperor Manuel.—He will, as far as his powers allow, strengthen friendship between the two empires. 1438

EPISTLE CDIX.—From Abbot Wibald to Pope Anastasius.—He thanks him and commends to him Heribert, the king’s chaplain. 1439

EPISTLE CDX.—From C., abbot of Paderborn, to Abbot Wibald.—He congratulates him on his return and regrets that he did not receive Wibald as Wibald passed through Paderborn. 1439

EPISTLE CDXI.—From W., bishop of Minden, to Abbot Wibald.—A man commended to him by Wibald was badly treated by Count Otto. 1439

EPISTLE CDXII.—From Abbot Wibald to Emperor Frederick.—He complains of the bishops of Osnabrück, who had taken certain tithes, and of certain other matters. 1440

EPISTLE CDXIII.—From Pope Adrian IV to Wichmann, bishop.—He entrusts to Wichmann’s judgment for settlement the case between the bishop of Osnabrück and Abbot Wibald concerning tithes. [Col. 1784] 1441

EPISTLE CDXIV.—From Wichmann, archbishop of Magdeburg, to Philip, bishop of Osnabrück.—He summons him to answer the accusations of Abbot Wibald. 1441

EPISTLE CDXV.—From the same Wichmann to Abbot Wibald.—He writes that he has summoned Philip, bishop of Osnabrück, before him. 1442

EPISTLE CDXVI.—From the same to the same.—He communicates to him the reply of the bishop of Osnabrück. 1442

EPISTLE CDXVII.—From Emperor Frederick to Wichmann, archbishop of Magdeburg.—He commends to him the case of the monastery of Corvey against the bishop of Osnabrück. 1443

EPISTLE CDXVIII.—From Emperor Frederick to Abbot Wibald.—He recounts how prosperously all matters are proceeding for him. 1444

EPISTLE CDXIX.—From Werner, bishop of Minden, to the archbishop of Magdeburg.—The bishop of Osnabrück, who was coming to him, had remained ill at Hildesheim. 1444

EPISTLE CDXX.—From Frederick, bishop of Münster, to Archbishop Wichmann.—He commends to him the bishop of Osnabrück. 1445

EPISTLE CDXXI.—From B., bishop of Hildesheim, to Wichmann, archbishop of Magdeburg.—He asks that the bishop of Osnabrück, prevented by illness from coming to him, be excused. 1445

EPISTLE CDXXII.—From Wichmann, archbishop of Magdeburg, to Pope Adrian.—He gives an account of the case entrusted to him between the bishop of Osnabrück and the abbot of Corvey. 1446

EPISTLE CDXXIII.—From Emperor Frederick to Abbot Wibald.—He summons him to Neumagen, praising his fidelity, and concerning an expedition against the Milanese. 1447

EPISTLE CDXXIV.—From Emperor Frederick to King Henry of England.—He commends to him Gerard, abbot of Solemniacum. 1448

EPISTLE CDXXV.—From Henry, duke of Bavaria and Saxony, to Emperor Frederick.—Concerning the favour granted to Witikind of Sualemberg and the penance imposed upon him. 1449

EPISTLE CDXXVI.—From Abbot Wibald to Pope Adrian.—He writes on behalf of Gerard, canon of Aiuncurt. 1449

EPISTLE CDXXVII.—From Pope Adrian IV to Abbot Wibald.—He commends to him the Camaldolese of Betarding and St Peter of Rota. 1451

EPISTLE CDXXVIII.—From the same to the archbishop of Cologne, the bishop of Constance, and the abbot of Stavelot.—He commends to them the monastery of St Antimo. 1451

EPISTLE CDXXIX.—From the same to the abbot of Corvey.—He commends to him, before the emperor, the affairs of the Roman Church and his envoys who are to negotiate with the emperor. 1451

EPISTLE CDXXX.—From the same to Abbot Wibald.—He commends to him his envoys to the emperor. 1451

EPISTLE CDXXXI.—From the same to the archbishop, the bishop of Bamberg, and Abbot Wibald.—He commends to them before the emperor the abbot and convent of Farfa. 1451

EPISTLE CDXXXII.—From Emperor Frederick to Abbot Wibald.—Concerning the envoys of the Poles. 1451

EPISTLE CDXXXIII.—From R., monk, to Abbot Wibald.—He gives thanks that, through Wibald’s intervention, he was honourably received by the bishop of Metz. 1452

EPISTLE CDXXXIV.—From Emperor Frederick to Abbot Wibald.—Concerning the victory won over the Poles. 1452

EPISTLE CDXXXV.—From Henry, duke of Bavaria and Saxony, to Abbot Wibald.—He rejoices in Wibald’s prosperity and promises to take charge of the manor of Papenheim, and that Widikin will pay him what he owes. 1453

EPISTLE CDXXXVI.—From Emperor Frederick to H. of Limburg.—That he should honour Abbot Wibald and undertake nothing against the property of the monastery of Stavelot. 1454

EPISTLE CDXXXVII.—From Pope Adrian IV to Bernard, bishop of Paderborn, and G., abbot of Liesborn.—He entrusts a certain case to them for settlement. 1454

EPISTLE CDXXXVIII.—From A., archbishop of Mainz, to Abbot Wibald.—He complains of the Count Palatine of the Rhine and seeks the emperor’s aid against him. 1455

EPISTLE CDXXXIX.—From Pope Adrian IV to Abbot Wibald.—That he should urge the emperor to remain in reverence for the Apostolic See. 1455

EPISTLE CDXL.—From Emperor Frederick to Frederick, bishop of Münster.—He entrusts to him for settlement the case between Morin, a ministerial of Corvey, and Folker, Frederick’s man. 1455

EPISTLE CDXLI.—From Emperor Frederick to the chapter of Osnabrück. [Col. 1785]—That they should amicably settle the controversy concerning tithes between themselves and the men of Corvey. 1456
## Appendix to the Letters of Wibald

I.—Charter of Frederick, Archbishop of Cologne, concerning the subjection of the monastery of Malmedy and the superiority of Stavelot over it. 1457  
II.—On the possessions of the monastery of Stavelot under Abbot St. Poppo. 1459  
III.—Charter of Emperor Lothair II granted to Abbot Wibald.—It confirms the monastery’s possessions and immunities, the election of the abbot, the sole advocate, etc. 1460  
IV.—Charter of Wibald, Abbot of Stavelot, concerning matters accomplished and corrected by him at the estate of Andernach. 1461  
V.—Constitution of Abbot Wibald: that investiture in the churches of Longia and Mount Rainher must not be received from a lay hand. 1462  
VI.—Charter of the monks of Stavelot.—They grant to Abbot Wibald for restoration the village of Bovineiacum, reduced to nothing, in which the body of St. Remaclus had lain hidden during the persecution of the Danes. 1463  
VII.—Charter of Wibald, Abbot of Stavelot, for Azo, Abbot of Monte Publico.—He grants him the church of Heran subject to an annual payment. 1464  
VIII.—Charter of Emperor Lothair granted to Abbot Wibald.—He receives the monastery under his protection and confirms all its privileges. 1465  
IX.—Charter of Emperor Lothair II, written in golden characters and distinguished by a golden seal.—In favor of Abbot Wibald, whose loyalty and services it praises, it confirms all the immunities and possessions of the monastery of Stavelot; it also determines the election of an abbot to be chosen from the monastery of Stavelot rather than Malmedy, if a worthy person is found, the rights and duties of advocates, and other matters. 1467  
X.—Charter of Wibald, Abbot of Stavelot.—He grants to the church of St. Martin of Liège the tithes of Femala. 1471  
XI.—Charter of Emperor Conrad.—In favor of Abbot Wibald, it confirms all the monastery’s privileges, especially Lothair’s golden bull. 1471  
XII.—Charter of Abbot Wibald.—On the restoration of Castellum and the transfer of the village of Longia. 1474  
XIII.—Charter of Albero, Bishop of Liège.—On the possession of Turnines, restored to the monastery of Stavelot by papal and royal authority. 1477  
XIV.—Charter of Emperor Conrad II granted to Abbot Wibald.—It confirms various privileges of the monastery of Stavelot. 1478  
XV.—Charter of Arnold, Archbishop of Cologne, granted to Abbot Wibald.—In a general synod, he grants to Wibald and his successors the tithes of newly cleared lands in the village of Bullinga. 1480  
XVI.—Charter of Arnold, Archbishop of Cologne, granted to Abbot Wibald.—On the authority and power of the Abbot of Stavelot over the monks of Malmedy. 1482  
XVII.—Charter of Abbot Wibald, concerning the shortage of cattle-herdsmen at the estate of Lernon. 1483  
XVIII.—Letter of Pope Celestine II to the archbishop, clergy, and people of Liège. 1484  
XIX.—Privilege of Pope Celestine II granted to Abbot Wibald.—He receives the monastery of Stavelot under the protection of the Apostolic See and confirms its various privileges and immunities. 1485  
XX.—Privilege of Pope Lucius III for the monastery of Stavelot. 1485  
XXI.—Writ of Conrad II, King of the Romans, obtained by Wibald, Abbot of Stavelot, for the monastery of Reinehusen. 1485  
XXII.—Privilege of Pope Eugenius III for the monastery of Stavelot. 1486  
XXIII.—Letters of the monks of the monastery of Stavelot to Abbot Wibald.—They grant him for life the villages of Boviniacum and Germiniacum, even should he cease to be their abbot. 1486  
XXIV.—Letter of Abbot Wibald concerning the tithe of the church of Comblentz, granted for life to Radulf of Comblentz. 1487  
XXV.—Charter of Conrad, King of the Romans, for the monastery of Corbie.—It secures the monasteries of Keminada and Wisbeka to Corbie. 1489  
XXVI.—Charter of Conrad II, King of the Romans, for the monastery of Corbie.—Because of the exceptional loyalty and merits of Abbot Wibald, it restores the privileges of the Corbieans and Herfordians. 1491  
XXVII.—On the excommunication of Winand of Limburg for injuries inflicted upon the monastery of Stavelot. 1494  
[Col. 1786]  
XXVIII.—Letter of Abbot Wibald concerning the things which he granted in benefice to Reiner of the Rock at New Village. 1494  
XXIX.—Charter of King Conrad for Abbot Wibald.—It permits the free working of silver and metal mines on Mount Eresburg. 1496  
XXX.—Charter of Conrad II, King of the Romans, for the monastery of Corbie.—Moved by the prayers of his beloved and faithful Abbot Wibald, he protects the monastery of Corbie against the insolence of its ministerials. 1497  
XXXI.—Letter of Abbot Wibald by which he assigns Mount St. Michael for the celebration of the feast of St. Remaclus and the anniversary of his own ordination. 1500  
XXXII.—Charter of Frederick, King of the Romans, written in golden letters and granted in the very celebrated assembly at Merseburg to Abbot Wibald.—It restores the rights and privileges of New Corbie. 1502  
XXXIII.—Privilege of Pope Adrian IV for the monastery of Stavelot. 1505  
XXXIV.—Privilege of the same pope granted to Abbot Wibald.—It confirms the use of sandals and the dalmatic, together with other privileges of the monastery of Corbie. 1505  
XXXV.—Charter of the same pope granted to Abbot Wibald.—It unites to Corbie the monastery of Werben, greatly impoverished in temporal and spiritual matters. 1505  
XXXVI.—Letter of Pope Adrian IV to the Bishop of Mainz.—That he should sternly admonish and bring into order Bobbo, advocate of the abbey of Werben, who had made many threats against Abbot Wibald. 1505  
XXXVII.—Letter of Abbot Wibald to his successors.—He grants a portion of woodland to the hospital of Groningen. 1505  
XXXVIII.—Letter of Theodoric, Abbot of New Corbie.—On writing the chronicles of monasteries. 1506  

## Ernald, Abbot of Bonneval

Historical and literary notice. 1507  
**On the Works of the Six Days.** Dedicatory epistle. 1513  
The treatise on the works of the six days begins. 1515

Homily I, on verse 1. 1569  
Homily II, on verse 2. 1572  
Homily III, on verse 3. 1576  
Homily IV, on verse 4. 1578  
Homily V.—On the definition of place and the many divisions of places; also on the place of repentance and solitude. 1583

Prologue. 1589  

Chapter I.—On wisdom and understanding. 1591  
Chapter II.—On counsel insofar as Scripture divides it into commandment and counsel. 1592  
Chapter III.—Likewise on counsel: namely, insofar as the spirit of counsel is necessary for those who ought to give counsel to others. 1593  
Chapter IV.—That the spirit of counsel is especially fitting for prelates. 1596  
Chapter V.—That the work of counsel is most necessary for those placed in tribulation. 1596  
Chapter VI.—Likewise, a more subtle and elevated discussion of the Spirit of counsel. 1597  
Chapter VII.—On knowledge, showing that the Spirit of knowledge, which rested upon Christ, pertains especially to humility. 1598  
Chapter VIII.—On the spirit of piety. 1600  
Chapter IX.—On the spirit of the fear of the Lord. 1601  
Chapter X.—On knowledge and the other gifts. 1602  
Chapter XI.—Comparison of the first seven days with the seven gifts of the Holy Spirit; first, of the first day compared with the spirit of wisdom. 1603  
Chapter XII.—Comparison of the second day with the spirit of understanding. 1603  
Chapter XIII.—Comparison of the third day with the spirit of counsel. 1604  
Chapter XIV.—Comparison of the fourth day with the spirit of fortitude. 1605
